text:
We show results based on a large suite of N-Body/SPH simulations of isolated,
flat dwarf galaxies, both rotating and non-rotating. The main goal is to
investigate possible mechanisms to explain the observed dichotomy in radial
stellar metallicity profiles of dwarf galaxies: dwarf irregulars (dIrr) and
flat, rotating dwarf ellipticals (dE) generally possess flat metallicity
profiles, while rounder and non-rotating dEs show strong negative metallicity
gradients. These simulations show that flattening by rotation is key to
reproducing the observed characteristics of flat dwarf galaxies, proving
particularly efficient in erasing metallicity gradients. We propose a
"centrifugal barrier mechanism" as an alternative to the previously suggested
"fountain mechanism" for explaining the flat metallicity profiles of dIrrs and
flat, rotating dEs. While only flattening the dark-matter halo has little
influence, the addition of angular momentum slows down the infall of gas, so
that star formation (SF) and the ensuing feedback are less centrally
concentrated, occurring galaxy-wide. Additionally, this leads to more
continuous SFHs by preventing large-scale oscillations in the SFR
("breathing"), and creates low density holes in the ISM, in agreement with
observations of dIrrs. Our general conclusion is that rotation has a
significant influence on the evolution and appearance of dwarf galaxies, and we
suggest angular momentum as a second parameter (after galaxy mass as the
dominant parameter) in dwarf galaxy evolution. Angular momentum differentiates
between SF modes, making our fast rotating models qualitatively resemble dIrrs,
which does not seem possible without rotation.
label: human

text: We investigated the relationship between racial candour and the WPA slave narratives, a collection of testimonies that provide a unique window into the experiences of enslaved individuals in the United States. Through a quantitative content analysis of 250 narratives, we found that African American writers employed various strategies to convey their experiences, including coded language, subtle hints, and implicit narratives, in an effort to avoid detection by white authorities and maintain their freedom. Our results indicate that these strategies were often successful, with only 12% of narratives explicitly stating the owner's name and 25% explicitly stating the location of the plantation. Furthermore, we discovered that the level of candour varied across different narrative types, with personal narratives exhibiting higher levels of explicitness compared to collective narratives. Our analysis also reveals that the use of coded language and implicit narratives was more prevalent among narratives written by women and older individuals. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complexities of racial candour in the WPA slave narratives and highlight the agency and resourcefulness of African American writers in navigating the oppressive social context of the time.
label: machine

We conduct a 350 micron dust continuum emission survey of 17 dust-obscured
galaxies (DOGs) at z = 0.05-0.08 with the Caltech Submillimeter Observatory
(CSO). We detect 14 DOGs with S_350 = 114-650 mJy and S/N > 3. By including two
additional DOGs with submillimeter data in the literature, we are able to study
dust contents for a sample of 16 local DOGs that consists of 12 bump and 4
power-law types. We determine their physical parameters with a two-component
modified blackbody function model. The derived dust temperatures are in the
range 57-122 K and 22-35 K for the warm and cold dust components, respectively.
The total dust mass and the mass fraction of warm dust component are
3-34$\times10^{7} M_\odot$ and 0.03-2.52%, respectively. We compare these
results with those of other submillimeter-detected infrared luminous galaxies.
The bump DOGs, the majority of the DOG sample, show similar distributions of
dust temperatures and total dust mass to the comparison sample. The power-law
DOGs show a hint of smaller dust masses than other samples, but need to be
tested with a larger sample. These findings support that the reason why DOGs
show heavy dust obscuration is not an overall amount of dust content, but
probably the spatial distribution of dust therein.

text: This study investigates the application of adjusted plus-minus statistics for National Hockey League (NHL) players, incorporating advanced metrics such as goals, shots, Fenwick, and Corsi. The objective of this research is to develop a more comprehensive and accurate measure of a player's on-ice performance, taking into account the complex interactions between various on-ice events.  The methodology employed in this study involves utilizing ridge regression analysis to adjust the traditional plus-minus statistic for the impact of goals, shots, Fenwick, and Corsi on a player's performance. The data used in this study consists of NHL player performance data from the 2015-2016 season, covering 1,032 games played by 335 players. The results of the ridge regression analysis reveal significant correlations between adjusted plus-minus and goals, shots, Fenwick, and Corsi, indicating that these metrics can provide valuable insights into a player's on-ice performance.  Key findings from this study include the identification of players with high adjusted plus-minus values who also possess high goals, shots, Fenwick, and Corsi metrics, suggesting that these players are highly effective in creating scoring opportunities. Conversely, players with low adjusted plus-minus values often have lower goals, shots, Fenwick, and Corsi metrics, indicating that they struggle to generate scoring chances. The study's results have important implications for NHL teams and analysts seeking to evaluate player performance and make informed decisions regarding roster construction and player evaluation.
label: machine

text: This study explores the HI emission and absorption characteristics in the nearby gas-rich galaxy NGC 5156, with a focus on the detection of intervening absorption features. Utilizing data from the Lane et al. survey and follow-up observations using the Green Bank Telescope and the Very Large Array, we aimed to better understand the interstellar medium dynamics and the structures of gas-rich galaxies. Our methodology involved a multiscale examination of HI profiles and the identification of absorption features across various line-of-sight measurements.   Our analysis revealed significant HI emission from NGC 5156, accompanied by distinct absorption signatures consistent with intervening gas clouds. We characterized the physical conditions of the absorbing gas, finding evidence for turbulence and complex kinematics within the galaxy’s interstellar medium. The detection of these absorption features not only supports the existence of ongoing star formation processes within the galaxy but also suggests interactions with its surrounding environment.  The key findings indicate that NGC 5156 presents a rich HI morphology, revealing layers of gas that may be influenced by gravitational interactions with nearby galaxies. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of gas dynamics in nearby galaxies and highlights the importance of studying HI emissions and absorptions to unravel the complexities of galactic evolution. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that observations of HI in both emission and absorption are crucial for advancing our knowledge of the interstellar medium in gas-rich galaxies.

Aims: The iron abundance gradient in the Galactic stellar disk provides
fundamental constraints on the chemical evolution of this important Galaxy
component. However the spread around the mean slope is, at fixed Galactocentric
distance, larger than estimated uncertainties. Methods: To provide quantitative
constraints on these trends we adopted iron abundances for 265 classical
Cepheids (more than 50% of the currently known sample) based either on
high-resolution spectra or on photometric metallicity indices. Homogeneous
distances were estimated using near-infrared Period-Luminosity relations. The
sample covers the four disk quadrants and their Galactocentric distances range
from ~5 to ~17 kpc. Results: A linear regression over the entire sample
provides an iron gradient of -0.051+/-0.004 dex/kpc. The above slope agrees
quite well, within the errors, with previous estimates based either on Cepheids
or on open clusters covering similar Galactocentric distances. However, once we
split the sample in inner (Rg < 8 kpc) and outer disk Cepheids we found that
the slope (-0.130+/-0.015 dex/kpc) in the former region is ~3 times steeper
than the slope in the latter one (-0.042+/-0.004 dex/kpc). We found that in the
outer disk the radial distribution of metal-poor (MP, [Fe/H]<-0.02 dex) and
metal-rich (MR) Cepheids across the four disk quadrants does not show a clear
trend when moving from the innermost to the external disk regions. We also
found that the relative fractions of MP and MR Cepheids in the 1st and in the
3rd quadrant differ at 8 sigma (MP) and 15 sigma (MR) level.
label: human

text: The analysis of Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) plays a crucial role in understanding the physics behind solar activities and their impacts on Earth. In this study, we focus on the fitting and reconstruction of thirteen simple CMEs observed between 1996 and 2006 using the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) on the Hinode spacecraft. Our primary objective is to improve the accuracy of CME characterization and enable better space weather prediction.  To obtain the best-fit CME models, we employed an iterative algorithm based on a two-step procedure (i) estimating the initial position, velocity, and width based on the CME morphology in SXT images, and (ii) refining the parameters by comparing model predictions to SXT data through a least-squares minimization technique. The obtained CME models served as the basis for further reconstruction, which included the calculation of the CME's magnetic field structure and mass distribution using the magnetic field estimation method and Hydrocode simulations, respectively.  The analysis of the thirteen CMEs revealed diverse morphologies, with some displaying a dense core surrounded by a cavity and others exhibiting an expanding fan structure. The fitted CME models accurately captured the morphological features, allowing us to assess their evolution and interaction with the ambient solar wind. Moreover, we were able to estimate the total masses, densities, and dynamic pressures for each CME, providing crucial information for space weather forecasting. Overall, our results demonstrate the significance of using accurate CME models for better understanding the solar atmosphere dynamics, predicting space weather impacts on Earth, and improving the performance of spacecraft and satellites.

text: This study presents a direct imaging of the water snow line at the time of planet formation using two ALMA continuum bands. The water snow line is a critical boundary in the formation of planetary systems, marking the transition from gas to solid particles in the disk surrounding a newly formed star. Understanding the location and characteristics of this boundary is essential for interpreting the formation and evolution of planetary systems.  The objective of this research is to directly image the water snow line at the time of planet formation using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) continuum bands. We utilized the ALMA 12 and 24 GHz continuum bands to map the distribution of water and solid particles in the disk of a protostellar system. By combining the two continuum bands, we were able to separate the water and solid particles, allowing for a more accurate determination of the water snow line.  The key findings of this study reveal that the water snow line is a complex and dynamic feature, with a location that varies depending on the specific conditions of the protostellar system. We observed a water snow line that is located at a distance of approximately 20 AU from the protostar, with a width of approximately 5 AU. The location and width of the water snow line are consistent with previous models of planetary system formation.  The results of this study provide new insights into the formation and evolution of planetary systems, highlighting the importance of the water snow line in determining the location and composition of planets. The direct imaging of the water snow line using ALMA continuum bands offers a new tool for understanding the early stages of planetary system formation and the formation of planets.

We clarify the confusion in a recent paper by Aurenche, Zakharov and Zaraket
(AZZ) \cite{azz} over the procedure and region of validity of the collinear
approximation in the twist expansion approach to induced gluon emission in
deeply inelastic scattering (DIS) off a nucleus target. We point out that, in
this approach to the semi-inclusive spectrum, the transverse momentum
$\vec\ell_\perp$ of the induced gluon must be fixed in the collinear expansion
in the transverse momentum $\vec k_\perp$ of the initial partons, therefore the
result is valid for $<k_\perp^2> \ll \ell_\perp^2 \ll Q^2$. In the twist-four
contribution, one can single out the double-hard term corresponding to
collinear quark-gluon Compton scattering which can be calculated independently
of the collinear expansion approach. We will discuss the connection between the
collinear approximation in the twist expansion approach and the small $k_T$
approximation of the results in the Light-Cone Path Integral (LCPI) and
Gyulassy-Levai-Vitev (GLV) opacity expansion approach. We point out the
misconstrued variable change by AZZ before the $k_T$ expansion in LCPI and
opacity expansion approach, without which one obtains the same result for the
induced gluon spectrum under collinear approximation as in the twist expansion
approach. We also show that corrections beyond the collinear approximation to
the transverse momentum integrated gluon spectrum within the static potential
model in the GLV approach give rise to a logarithmic factor difference from the
result of collinear approximation.

text: We investigate the dynamics of bubble behavior in microchannels, focusing on the interplay between inertial and capillary migration forces. Our study addresses the challenges associated with bubble transport in microfluidic systems, where precise control of fluid flow is essential for various applications, including chemical analysis and biomedical devices. We employed a combination of high-speed imaging and numerical simulations to analyze the migration patterns of bubbles in rectangular and circular microchannels under varying flow conditions.  Our results indicate that capillary forces dominate bubble behavior at low flow rates, leading to formation and stabilization of bubbles at specific locations within the channels. Conversely, as the flow rate increases, inertial forces become more significant, causing bubbles to experience distinct trajectories and behaviors, including oscillations and instability. We observe a critical transition point where the balance between these forces dictates the bubble's movement, suggesting the potential for enhancing or controlling bubble transport through tailored channel designs or flow adjustments.  We propose a theoretical framework that captures the dynamics of bubble migration by integrating force balance equations with empirical observations. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of multiphase flow dynamics in confined geometries and pave the way for innovative microfluidic applications. This research lays the groundwork for future studies aimed at manipulating bubble dynamics through strategic engineering, potentially leading to advancements in fields such as drug delivery, diagnostics, and microreactor design.

text:
In the near future, gravitational wave detection is set to become an
important observational tool for astrophysics. It will provide us with an
excellent means to distinguish different gravitational theories. In effective
form, many gravitational theories can be cast into an f(R) theory. In this
article, we study the dynamics and gravitational waveform of an equal-mass
binary black hole system in f(R) theory. We reduce the equations of motion in
f(R) theory to the Einstein-Klein-Gordon coupled equations. In this form, it is
straightforward to modify our existing numerical relativistic codes to simulate
binary black hole mergers in f(R) theory. We considered binary black holes
surrounded by a shell of scalar field. We solve the initial data numerically
using the Olliptic code. The evolution part is calculated using the extended
AMSSNCKU code. Both codes were updated and tested to solve the problem of
binary black holes in f(R) theory. Our results show that the binary black hole
dynamics in f(R) theory is more complex than in general relativity. In
particular, the trajectory and merger time are strongly affected. Via the
gravitational wave, it is possible to constrain the quadratic part parameter of
f(R) theory in the range |a_2|<10^{11} m^2 . In principle, a gravitational wave
detector can distinguish between a merger of binary black hole in f(R) theory
and the respective merger in general relativity. Moreover, it is possible to
use gravitational wave detection to distinguish between f(R) theory and a non
self-interacting scalar field model in general relativity.

text:
Stellar bars are a common feature in massive disc galaxies. On a theoretical
ground, the response of gas to a bar is generally thought to cause nuclear
starbursts and, possibly, AGN activity once the perturbed gas reaches the
central super-massive black hole. By means of high resolution numerical
simulations we detail the purely dynamical effects that a forming bar exerts on
the gas of an isolated disc galaxy. The galaxy is initially unstable to the
formation of non-axisymmetric structures, and within 1 Gyr it develops spiral
arms that eventually evolve into a central stellar bar on kpc scale. A first
major episode of gas inflow occurs during the formation of the spiral arms
while at later times, when the stellar bar is establishing, a low density
region is carved between the bar co-rotational and inner Lindblad resonance
radii. The development of such "dead zone" inhibits further massive gas
inflows. Indeed, the gas inflow reaches its maximum during the relatively fast
bar formation phase and not, as often assumed, when the bar is fully formed. We
conclude that the low efficiency of long-lived, evolved bars in driving gas
toward galactic nuclei is the reason why observational studies have failed to
establish an indisputable link between bars and AGNs. On the other hand, the
high efficiency in driving strong gas inflows of the intrinsically transient
process of bar formation suggests that the importance of bars as drivers of AGN
activity in disc galaxies has been overlooked so far. We finally prove that our
conclusions are robust against different numerical implementations of the
hydrodynamics routinely used in galaxy evolution studies.
label: human

text:
A graph $G$ covers a graph $H$ if there exists a locally bijective
homomorphism from $G$ to $H$. We deal with regular coverings in which this
homomorphism is prescribed by an action of a semiregular subgroup $\Gamma$ of
$\textrm{Aut}(G)$; so $H \cong G / \Gamma$. In this paper, we study the
behaviour of regular graph covering with respect to 1-cuts and 2-cuts in $G$.
  We describe reductions which produce a series of graphs $G = G_0,\dots,G_r$
such that $G_{i+1}$ is created from $G_i$ by replacing certain inclusion
minimal subgraphs with colored edges. The process ends with a primitive graph
$G_r$ which is either 3-connected, or a cycle, or $K_2$. This reduction can be
viewed as a non-trivial modification of reductions of Mac Lane (1937),
Trachtenbrot (1958), Tutte (1966), Hopcroft and Tarjan (1973), Cuningham and
Edmonds (1980), Walsh (1982), and others. A novel feature of our approach is
that in each step all essential information about symmetries of $G$ are
preserved.
  A regular covering projection $G_0\to H_0$ induces regular covering
projections $G_i \to H_i$ where $H_i$ is the $i$-th quotient reduction of
$H_0$. This property allows to construct all possible quotients $H_0$ of $G_0$
from the possible quotients $H_r$ of $G_r$. By applying this method to planar
graphs, we give a proof of Negami's Theorem (1988). Our structural results are
also used in subsequent papers for regular covering testing when $G$ is a
planar graph and for an inductive characterization of the automorphism groups
of planar graphs (see Babai (1973) as well).

text:
Recent observations of our neighbouring galaxy M31 have revealed that its
disk was shaped by widespread events. The evidence for this includes the high
dispersion ($V/\sigma$ $\le$ 3) of stars older than 2 Gyr, and a global star
formation episode, 2-4 Gyr ago. Using the modern hydrodynamical code, GIZMO, we
have performed 300 high-resolution simulations to explore the extent to which
these observed properties can be explained by a single merger. We find that the
observed M31 disk resembles models having experienced a 4:1 merger, in which
the nuclei coalesced 1.8-3 Gyr ago, and where the first passage took place 7 to
10 Gyr ago at a large pericentre distance (32 kpc). We also show that within a
family of orbital parameters, the Giant Stream (GS) can be formed with various
merger mass-ratios, from 2:1 to 300:1. A recent major merger may be the only
way to create the very unusual age-dispersion relation in the disk. It
reproduces and explains the long-lived 10 kpc ring, the widespread and recent
star formation event, the absence of a remnant of the GS progenitor, the
apparent complexity of the 3D spatial distribution of the GS, the NE and G
Clumps and their formation process, and the observed slope of the halo profile.
These modelling successes lead us to propose that the bulk of the substructure
in the M31 halo, as well as the complexity of the inner galaxy, may be
attributable to a single major interaction with a galaxy that has now fully
coalesced with Andromeda.
label: human

text:
We combine all available information about the spectral shape and morphology
of the radio halo of the Coma cluster with the gamma-ray upper limits obtained
by the Fermi-LAT and with the magnetic field strength derived from Faraday
rotation measures (RM). We explore the possibility that the radio halo is due
to synchrotron emission of secondary electrons generated via p-p collisions in
the intra-cluster-medium (ICM). First we investigate the case of pure secondary
models. We use the observed spatial distribution of the halo's radio brightness
to constrain the amount of cosmic rays (CRs) and their spatial distribution in
the cluster that are required by the model. Under the canonical assumption that
the spectrum of CRs is a power-law in momentum and that the spectrum of
secondaries is stationary, we find that the combination of the steep spectrum
of CRs necessary to explain the spectrum of the halo and their very broad
spatial distribution (and large energy density) result in a gamma-ray emission
in excess of present limits, unless the cluster magnetic field is sufficiently
large. However such a field appears inconsistent with constraints from RM.
Second we investigate more complex models based on secondary particles in which
CR protons and their secondaries are all reaccelerated by MHD turbulence. We
show that under these conditions it is possible to reproduce the radio data and
to predict gamma-rays in agreement with the Fermi-LAT limits without tension
with constraints on the cluster magnetic field. Reacceleration of secondaries
by MHD turbulence also requires a spatial distribution of CRs much flatter than
that of the ICM, if both the turbulent and magnetic field energy densities
scale with that of the ICM. However broader spatial distributions of turbulence
and field and/or the reacceleration of additional primary electrons in the ICM
greatly alleviate this requirement.
label: human

text: The behavior of thermodynamic Casimir forces (TCF) in isotropic systems during the crossover from low-temperature to high-temperature fluctuations is an intriguing phenomenon in the field of statistical mechanics. In this study, we investigate the TCF of simple isotropic systems, focusing on the Lennard-Jones (LJ) potential and the Ising model, using Monte Carlo simulation methods.  The background of this study includes the understanding of Casimir forces, which originate from the quantized fluctuations of the vacuum state. However, the extension of this phenomenon to thermodynamic systems is still a subject of ongoing research. In the context of isotropic systems, the interest lies in the fact that these systems exhibit two distinct temperature regimes the low-temperature regime, where the system is dominantly controlled by quantum fluctuations, and the high-temperature regime, where thermal fluctuations become the primary driver.  The objective of this study is to analyze the changes in the TCF behavior across this crossover temperature region. By employing Monte Carlo simulation techniques, we first determine the equilibrium properties of the LJ potential and the Ising model systems. Subsequently, we calculate the TCF for both systems at various temperatures, including the crossover region.  Our key findings reveal a sharp transition in the TCF behavior as we move from the low-temperature to the high-temperature regime. In the low-temperature region, the TCF exhibits an attractive character, while in the high-temperature region, it becomes repulsive. This transformation is attributed to the change in the nature of the dominant fluctuations. In the low-temperature regime, the attractive Casimir forces arise due to the quantum nature of the fluctuations, whereas in the high-temperature regime, the repulsive forces are predominantly thermal.  In conclusion, this study contributes to the growing body of research on the TCF behavior in isotropic systems by exploring the crossover from low-temperature to high-temperature fluctuations. The findings demonstrate that the TCF undergoes a significant transition from attractive to repulsive, highlighting the importance of understanding the interplay between quantum and thermal fluctuations in thermodynamic systems.
label: machine

text:
We investigate default-free bond markets where the standard relationship
between a possibly existing bank account process and the term structure of bond
prices is broken, i.e. the bank account process is not a valid num\'eraire. We
argue that this feature is not the exception but rather the rule in bond
markets when starting with, e.g., terminal bonds as num\'eraires.
  Our setting are general c\`adl\`ag processes as bond prices, where we employ
directly methods from large financial markets. Moreover, we do not restrict
price process to be semimartingales, which allows for example to consider
markets driven by fractional Brownian motion. In the core of the article we
relate the appropriate no arbitrage assumptions (NAFL), i.e. no asymptotic free
lunch, to the existence of an equivalent local martingale measure with respect
to the terminal bond as num\'eraire, and no arbitrage opportunities of the
first kind (NAA1) to the existence of a supermartingale deflator, respectively.
In all settings we obtain existence of a generalized bank account as a limit of
convex combinations of roll-over bonds.
  Additionally we provide an alternative definition of the concept of a
num\'eraire, leading to a possibly interesting connection to bubbles. If we can
construct a bank account process through roll-overs, we can relate the
impossibility of taking the bank account as num\'eraire to liquidity effects.
Here we enter endogenously the arena of multiple yield curves.
  The theory is illustrated by several examples.
label: human

text: This research paper explores the implementation of the Approximate Message Passing (AMP) algorithm enhanced with Universal Denoising and Gaussian Mixture Learning techniques for signal recovery in noisy environments. The objective of this study is to improve the accuracy and robustness of signal recovery by incorporating advanced denoising and learning methods within the traditional AMP framework.   The methodology involves integrating Universal Denoiser and Gaussian Mixture Learning modules into the iterative AMP algorithm to enhance its performance in reconstructing signals corrupted by noise. Universal Denoising aims to adaptively denoise the measurements during the recovery process, while Gaussian Mixture Learning assists in capturing complex signal distributions for more accurate estimation.  Key findings demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves superior signal recovery performance compared to conventional AMP methods, particularly in scenarios with high levels of noise and complex signal structures. The Universal Denoising and Gaussian Mixture Learning modules effectively enhance the algorithm's capability to recover signals accurately under challenging conditions.  In conclusion, the integration of Universal Denoising and Gaussian Mixture Learning techniques into the AMP algorithm presents a promising avenue for improving signal recovery in noisy environments. This research contributes to advancing the field of signal processing by offering a more robust and efficient method for recovering signals corrupted by noise.
label: machine

text: We investigated the problem of sharp support recovery from noisy random measurements by employing L1 minimization techniques. Our approach focuses on developing a robust method to accurately identify the support of a sparse signal from a set of noisy, randomly sampled measurements.   We formulated the support recovery problem as a L1-constrained optimization problem, where the objective function is the L1 norm of the difference between the observed measurements and the measurements generated by the true sparse signal. By minimizing this objective function, we can recover the support of the sparse signal, which corresponds to the non-zero coefficients of the signal.   Our method involves regularizing the L1 minimization problem with a prior knowledge of the sparsity of the signal, which is represented by a set of sparse constraints. This prior knowledge is incorporated into the optimization problem using a L1 penalty term, which encourages the model to produce a sparse solution.   We evaluated the performance of our method using a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, and compared it with other state-of-the-art methods for support recovery. The results show that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, particularly in the presence of noisy measurements. The key idea underlying our method is the use of L1 minimization to recover the support of a sparse signal from noisy, randomly sampled measurements, and the incorporation of prior knowledge of sparsity into the optimization problem using a L1 penalty term.
label: machine

text: The study investigates the tight subgiant branch (RGB) of the intermediate-age globular cluster NGC 411, focusing on its implications regarding the age of the stellar population within the cluster. Utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy, we analyzed the chemical abundances and kinematic properties of stars along the RGB to derive reliable ages. The results indicate that the observed RGB morphology and metallicity distribution suggest a single-age stellar population, consistent with previous studies of NGC 411. This finding supports theoretical models that predict the evolution of globular clusters over time and highlights the importance of RGB analysis in determining the true age and history of intermediate-age clusters.
label: machine

text: Helium detonations in astrophysical environments are crucial for understanding various stellar explosion phenomena, including supernovae and x-ray bursts. This abstract discusses the key conditions necessary for initiating and sustaining successful helium detonations in stellar interiors. Firstly, the background of helium ignition and the challenge of initiating a helium detonation is introduced. The objective of this study is to identify the minimum conditions required to trigger helium detonations. Numerical simulations are employed as the primary methodology, utilizing one-dimensional and three-dimensional models to investigate the impact of various parameters such as temperature, density, and velocity on the ignition and propagation of helium detonations. The results indicate that a minimum temperature of approximately 2.3×107 K and a density greater than 1010 kg/m3 are essential for initiating helium detonations. Furthermore, these detonations require an extensive helium fuel layer with a thickness greater than 150 m. The conclusions of this research demonstrate that successful helium detonations are dependent on the thermodynamic conditions of the stellar environment, specifically the temperature, density, and helium fuel layer thickness. This study contributes to our understanding of the mechanisms behind stellar explosions and highlights the importance of accurately modeling helium detonations in astrophysical simulations. Future work may explore the potential impact of magnetic fields and rotation on the initiation and propagation of helium detonations.
label: machine

text:
In this article, we study the 1 + 3 dimensional relativistic Euler equations
on a pre-specified conformally flat expanding spacetime background with spatial
slices that are diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^3.$ We assume that the fluid
verifies the equation of state $p = c_s^2 \rho,$ where $0 \leq c_s \leq
\sqrt{1/3}$ is the speed of sound. We also assume that the inverse of the scale
factor associated to the expanding spacetime metric verifies a $c_s-$dependent
time-integrability condition. Under these assumptions, we use the vectorfield
energy method to prove that an explicit family of physically motivated,
spatially homogeneous, and spatially isotropic fluid solutions is globally
future-stable under small perturbations of their initial conditions. The
explicit solutions corresponding to each scale factor are analogs of the
well-known spatially flat Friedmann-Lema\^{\i}tre-Robertson-Walker family. Our
nonlinear analysis, which exploits dissipative terms generated by the
expansion, shows that the perturbed solutions exist for all future times and
remain close to the explicit solutions. This work is an extension of previous
results, which showed that an analogous stability result holds when the
spacetime is exponentially expanding. In the case of the radiation equation of
state $p = (1/3)\rho,$ we also show that if the time-integrability condition
for the inverse of the scale factor fails to hold, then the explicit fluid
solutions are unstable. More precisely, we show that arbitrarily small smooth
perturbations of the explicit solutions' initial conditions can launch
perturbed solutions that form shocks in finite time. The shock formation proof
is based on the conformal invariance of the relativistic Euler equations when
$c_s^2 = 1/3,$ which allows for a reduction to a well-known result of
Christodoulou.
label: human

text:
We study the effects of Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI) on the cold
streams that feed high-redshift galaxies through their hot haloes, generalizing
our earlier analyses of a 2D slab to a 3D cylinder, but still limiting our
analysis to the adiabatic case with no gravity. We combine analytic modeling
and numerical simulations in the linear and non-linear regimes. For subsonic or
transonic streams with respect to the halo sound speed, the instability in 3D
is qualitatively similar to 2D, but progresses at a faster pace. For supersonic
streams, the instability grows much faster in 3D and can be qualitatively
different due to azimuthal modes, which introduce a strong dependence on the
initial width of the stream-background interface. Using analytic toy models and
approximations supported by high-resolution simulations, we apply our idealized
hydrodynamical analysis to the astrophysical scenario. The upper limit for the
radius of a stream that disintegrates prior to reaching the central galaxy is
~70% larger than the 2D estimate; it is in the range (0.5-5)% of the halo
virial radius, decreasing with increasing stream density and velocity. Stream
disruption generates a turbulent mixing zone around the stream with velocities
at the level of ~20% of the initial stream velocity. KHI can cause significant
stream deceleration and energy dissipation in 3d, contrary to 2D estimates. For
typical streams, up to (10-50)% of the gravitational energy gained by inflow
down the dark-matter halo potential can be dissipated, capable of powering
Lyman-alpha blobs if most of it is dissipated into radiation.
label: human

text: We investigate the self-wrapping phenomenon of an ouzo drop induced by evaporation on a superamphiphobic surface, a previously unexplored area of study in the realm of surface science. Through a combination of experiments and theoretical modeling, we demonstrate that the unique properties of the superamphiphobic surface, characterized by a high contact angle and low surface energy, facilitate the formation of a self-wrapping structure around the ouzo drop. This phenomenon arises from the interplay between the surface's hydrophobic and oleophobic properties, which enable the formation of a hydrophobic "skin" around the drop, while the oleophobic properties promote the formation of a oleophobic "skin" on the surface, effectively creating a self-wrapping structure.  Our results show that the self-wrapping process is highly dependent on the evaporation rate and the surface's surface energy, with higher evaporation rates and lower surface energies leading to more pronounced self-wrapping effects. We also observe that the self-wrapping structure exhibits a characteristic "hourglass" shape, with the ouzo drop forming a narrow neck at the top and a wider body at the bottom. Theoretical modeling reveals that this shape is a result of the balance between surface tension and surface energy, with the surface energy playing a dominant role in the formation of the self-wrapping structure.  Our study provides new insights into the behavior of liquids on superamphiphobic surfaces and has significant implications for the development of novel surface technologies, including self-cleaning and self-healing surfaces.
label: machine

For direct imaging of exoplanets, a stellar coronagraph helps to remove the
image of an observed bright star by attenuating the diffraction effects caused
by the telescope aperture of diameter D. The Dual Zone Phase Mask (DZPM)
coronagraph constitutes a promising concept since it theoretically offers a
small inner working angle (IWA \sim \lambda_0/D), good achromaticity and high
starlight rejection, typically reaching a 1e6 contrast at 5 \lambda_0/D from
the star over a spectral bandwidth \Delta\lambda/\lambda_0 of 25% (similar to
H-band). This last value proves to be encouraging for broadband imaging of
young and warm Jupiter-like planets. Contrast levels higher than 1e6 are
however required for the observation of older and/or less massive companions
over a finite spectral bandwidth. An achromatization improvement of the DZPM
coronagraph is therefore mandatory to reach such performance. In its design,
the DZPM coronagraph uses a grey (or achromatic) apodization. We propose to
replace it by a colored apodization to increase the performance of this
coronagraphic system over a large spectral range. This innovative concept,
called Colored Apodizer Phase Mask (CAPM) coronagraph, is defined with some
design parameters optimized to reach the best contrast in the exoplanet search
area. Once this done, we study the performance of the CAPM coronagraph in the
presence of different errors to evaluate the sensitivity of our concept. A 2.5
mag contrast gain is estimated from the performance provided by the CAPM
coronagraph with respect to that of the DZPM coronagraph. A 2.2e-8 intensity
level at 5 \lambda_0/D separation is then theoretically achieved with the CAPM
coronagraph in the presence of a clear circular aperture and a 25% bandwidth.
In addition, our studies show that our concept is less sensitive to low than
high-order aberrations for a given value of rms wavefront errors.
label: human

Cyber-physical systems (CPS) integrate sensing, computing, communication and
actuation capabilities to monitor and control operations in the physical
environment. A key requirement of such systems is the need to provide
predictable real-time performance: the timing correctness of the system should
be analyzable at design time with a quantitative metric and guaranteed at
runtime with high assurance. This requirement of predictability is particularly
important for safety-critical domains such as automobiles, aerospace, defense,
manufacturing and medical devices.
  The work in this dissertation focuses on the challenges arising from the use
of modern multi-core platforms in CPS. Even as of today, multi-core platforms
are rarely used in safety-critical applications primarily due to the temporal
interference caused by contention on various resources shared among processor
cores, such as caches, memory buses, and I/O devices. Such interference is hard
to predict and can significantly increase task execution time, e.g., up to 12x
on commodity quad-core platforms. To address the problem of ensuring timing
predictability on multi-core platforms, we develop novel analytical and systems
techniques in this dissertation. Our proposed techniques theoretically bound
temporal interference that tasks may suffer from when accessing shared
resources. Our techniques also involve software primitives and algorithms for
real-time operating systems and hypervisors, which significantly reduce the
degree of the temporal interference. Specifically, we tackle the issues of
cache and memory contention, locking and synchronization, interrupt handling,
and access control for computational accelerators such as GPGPUs, all of which
are crucial to achieving predictable real-time performance on a modern
multi-core platform.
label: human

Phospholipid monolayers at the air-water interface serve as model systems for
various biological interfaces, e.g. lung surfactant layers and outer leaflets
of cell membranes. Although the dynamical (viscoelastic) properties of these
interfaces may play a key role in stability, dynamics and function, the
relatively weak rheological properties of most such monolayers have rendered
their study difficult or impossible. A novel technique to measure the dynamical
properties of fluid-fluid interfaces have developed accordingly. We
microfabricate micron-scale ferromagnetic disks, place them on fluid-fluid
interfaces, and use external electromagnets to exert torques upon them. By
measuring the rotation that results from a known external torque, we compute
the rotational drag, from which we deduce the rheological properties of the
interface. Notably, our apparatus enable direct interfacial visualization while
the probes are torqued.
  In this fluid dynamics video, we directly visualize
dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine(DPPC) monolayers at the air-water interface
while shearing. At about 9 mN/m, DPPC exhibits a liquid condensed(LC) phase
where liquid crystalline domains are compressed each other, and separated by
grain boundaries. Under weak oscillatory torque, the grain boundaries slip past
each other while larger shear strain forms a yield surface by deforming and
fracturing the domains. Shear banding, which is a clear evidence of yield
stress, is visualized during steady rotation. Remarkably slow relaxation time
was also found due to slow unwinding of the stretched domains.
label: human

We consider the shortest path routing (SPR) of a network with stochastically
time varying link metrics under potential adversarial attacks. Due to potential
denial of service attacks, the distributions of link states could be stochastic
(benign) or adversarial at different temporal and spatial locations. Without
any \emph{a priori}, designing an adaptive SPR protocol to cope with all
possible situations in practice optimally is a very challenging issue. In this
paper, we present the first solution by formulating it as a multi-armed bandit
(MAB) problem. By introducing a novel control parameter into the exploration
phase for each link, a martingale inequality is applied in the our
combinatorial adversarial MAB framework. As such, our proposed algorithms could
automatically detect features of the environment within a unified framework and
find the optimal SPR strategies with almost optimal learning performance in all
possible cases over time. Moreover, we study important issues related to the
practical implementation, such as decoupling route selection with multi-path
route probing, cooperative learning among multiple sources, the "cold-start"
issue and delayed feedback of our algorithm. Nonetheless, the proposed SPR
algorithms can be implemented with low complexity and they are proved to scale
very well with the network size. Comparing to existing approaches in a typical
network scenario under jamming attacks, our algorithm has a 65.3\% improvement
of network delay given a learning period and a 81.5\% improvement of learning
duration under a specified network delay.
label: human

text: The abstract focuses on the investigation of the Infalling Cluster Lens (ICL) phenomenon within the context of Abell 2744, using the Chandra High Energy X-ray Survey Telescope (CHEFS). The study aims to disentangle the complex lensing effects caused by infalling galaxy clusters, providing insights into the dynamics and evolution of these systems.   Previous observations have highlighted the ICL as a distinctive feature in Abell 2744, which arises from the gravitational lensing of background galaxies by the cluster's mass distribution. However, the precise nature of this effect has been challenging to determine due to overlapping lensing signatures. This paper utilizes high-resolution X-ray data from CHEFS to isolate the ICL signal from other lensing phenomena.  The methodology involves detailed analysis of the X-ray images, employing sophisticated image processing techniques and statistical methods to identify and quantify the ICL. Additionally, simulations of the cluster's mass distribution are conducted to validate the observed features and to understand their implications for understanding the cluster's structure and the broader cosmological context.  Key findings reveal that the ICL in Abell 2744 extends beyond previously reported limits, indicating a more extensive distribution of dark matter within the cluster. This finding contributes to our understanding of how dark matter is distributed in the intracluster medium and aids in refining models of cluster formation and evolution.  In conclusion, this research provides a clearer picture of the ICL in Abell 2744, offering valuable insights into the complex dynamics of galaxy clusters and enhancing our comprehension of the interplay between visible and invisible matter in the universe.
label: machine

We show that it is possible to fit all of the HERA DIS (deep inelastic
scattering) data on $F_2^{\gamma p}$ at small values of Bjorken $x$, including
the data at {\em very low} $Q^2$, using a new model for $F_2^{\gamma p}$ which
both includes an asymptotic (high energy) part that satisfies a saturated
Froissart bound behavior, with a vector-dominance like mass factor in the
parameterization, and extends smoothly to $Q^2=0$. We require that the
corresponding part of the virtual $\gamma^* p$ cross section match the known
asymptotic part of the real $\gamma p$ cross section at $Q^2=0$, a cross
section which is determined by strong interactions and asymptotically satisfies
a saturated Froissart bound of the form $\alpha +\beta\ln s+\gamma\ln^2s$.
Using this model for the asymptotic part of $F_2^{\gamma p}$ plus a known
valence contribution, we fit the asymptotic high energy part of the HERA data
with $x\le 0.1$ and $W\ge 25$ GeV; the fit is excellent. We find that the mass
parameter in the fit lies in the region of the light vector mesons, somewhat
above the $\rho$ meson mass, and is compatible with vector dominance. We use
this fit to obtain accurate results for the high energy $ep$ and isoscalar $\nu
N$ total cross sections. Both cross sections obey an analytic expression of the
type $a +b \ln E +c \ln^2 E +d \ln^3 E$ at large energies $E$ of the incident
particle, reflecting the fact that the underlying strong interaction parts of
the $\gamma^*p$, $Z^*N$ and $W^*N$ cross sections satisfy the saturated
Froissart bound. Since approximately 50% of the $\nu N$ center of mass (cms)
energy is found in $W$---the cms energy of the strongly interacting
intermediate vector boson-nucleon system---a study of ultra-high-energy
neutrino-nucleon cross sections would allow us, for the first time, to explore
{\em strong interactions at incredibly high energies}.
label: human

We study the formation, evolution and physical properties of accretion disks
formed via wind capture in binary systems. Using the AMR code AstroBEAR, we
have carried out high resolution 3D simulations that follow a stellar mass
secondary in the co-rotating frame as it orbits a wind producing AGB primary.
We first derive a resolution criteria, based on considerations of Bondi-Hoyle
flows, that must be met in order to properly resolve the formation of accretion
disks around the secondary. We then compare simulations of binaries with three
different orbital radii (10, 15, 20 AU). Disks are formed in all three cases,
however the size of the disk and, most importantly, its accretion rate
decreases with orbital radii. In addition, the shape of the orbital motions of
material within the disk becomes increasingly elliptical with increasing binary
separation. The flow is mildly unsteady with "fluttering" around the bow shock
observed. The disks are generally well aligned with the orbital plane after a
few binary orbits. We do not observe the presence of any large scale, violent
instabilities (such as the flip-flop mode). For the first time, moreover, it is
observed that the wind component that is accreted towards the secondary has a
vortex tube-like structure, rather than a column-like one as it was previously
thought. In the context of AGB binary systems that might be precursors to
Pre-Planetary and Planetary Nebula, we find that the wind accretion rates at
the chosen orbital separations are generally too small to produce the most
powerful outflows observed in these systems if the companions are main sequence
stars but marginally capable if the companions are white dwarfs. It is likely
that many of the more powerful PPN and PN involve closer binaries than the ones
considered here. The results also demonstrate principles of broad relevance to
all wind-capture binary systems.
label: human

Among the solar proxies studied in the Sun in Time k Cet (HD 20630) stands
out as potentially having a mass very close to solar and a young age. On this
study, we monitored the magnetic field and the chromospheric activity from the
Ca II H & K lines of k Cet. We used the Least-Square-Deconvolution (LSD, Donati
et al. 1997) by simultaneously extracting the information contained in all
8,000 photospheric lines of the echelogram (K1 type star). To reconstruct a
reliable magnetic map and characterize the surface differential rotation of k
Cet we used 14 exposures spread over 2 months, in order to cover at least two
rotational cycles (Prot ~ 9.2 days). The LSD technique was applied to detect
the Zeeman signature of the magnetic field in each of our 14 observations and
to measure its longitudinal component. In order to reconstruct the magnetic
field geometry of k Cet, we applied the Zeeman Doppler Imaging (ZDI) inversion
method. ZDI revealed a structure in the radial magnetic field consisting of a
polar magnetic spot. On this study, we present the fisrt look results of a
high-resolution spectropolarimetric campaign to characterize the activity and
the magnetic fields of this young solar proxy.
label: human

text: The band gap problem in acceptor-doped barium zirconate has significant implications on its oxidation and hydration behavior. This research paper aims to investigate the relationship between the band gap issue and the oxidation and hydration processes in this material. The study employs a combination of experimental techniques, including X-ray diffraction, spectroscopic analysis, and electron microscopy, to characterize the oxidation and hydration behaviors of acceptor-doped barium zirconate. Key findings reveal that the band gap problem influences the material's susceptibility to oxidation and hydration, impacting its overall stability and performance. The results indicate that the band gap issue exacerbates the degradation of the material under oxidative and hydrated conditions. In conclusion, understanding the implications of the band gap problem on oxidation and hydration in acceptor-doped barium zirconate is crucial for the development of improved materials with enhanced stability and longevity in various applications.
label: machine

text: We present a comprehensive 2D semi-analytical kinetic model to investigate the dynamics of solar wind interactions around a comet. Our primary objective is to address the problem of understanding how solar wind particles interact with the cometary environment, influencing both the ionization and the overall structure of the comet's coma and tail. By employing a combination of fluid and kinetic approaches, we establish a self-consistent framework that captures the complex interactions between the solar wind and the cometary atmosphere.  Our results indicate a significant dependence of the solar wind dynamics on the comet's outgassing rate and solar wind parameters, such as velocity and density. We observe that increased outgassing significantly alters the density and velocity distribution of solar wind ions in the vicinity of the comet, leading to identifiable signatures that can be measured by in-situ observational instruments.   We also identify critical regions of enhanced particle acceleration and deflection, providing insights into the formation of bow shocks and pick-up ion populations. Our methodology involves solving the kinetic equations coupled with boundary conditions derived from cometary physics, yielding detailed profiles of solar wind parameters as functions of spatial coordinates and time.   These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of solar wind-comet interactions, with implications for future spacecraft missions aimed at studying comets and other small celestial bodies. Our model serves as a valuable tool for predicting solar wind behavior in heterogeneous environments and aids in the analysis of observational data collected from comets.
label: machine

text: We investigated the complex phenomenon of Saturn's aurorae using a novel multi-spectral approach, enabling simultaneous diagnosis of auroral activity across the planet's entire rotation period. Utilizing a combination of observations from the Cassini-Huygens mission and advanced data processing techniques, we developed a comprehensive diagnostic framework to analyze the dynamic interplay between Saturn's magnetic field, solar wind, and atmospheric conditions.  Through a series of data-driven experiments, we identified a set of key spectral signatures indicative of distinct auroral subtypes, including diffuse, discrete, and pulsating aurorae. Our results reveal that these subtypes exhibit unique temporal and spatial patterns, which are closely tied to Saturn's rotation period and the planet's complex magnetic field configuration. Notably, we discovered a previously unknown correlation between auroral activity and the planet's auroral oval, suggesting a previously underappreciated role for the solar wind in shaping Saturn's auroral morphology.  Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of Saturn's magnetosphere and the underlying physics governing auroral activity. By leveraging multi-spectral diagnostics, we have provided a more detailed and nuanced characterization of Saturn's aurorae, shedding light on the intricate relationships between the planet's magnetic field, solar wind, and atmospheric conditions. These results have far-reaching consequences for the study of auroral phenomena in planetary science and provide a foundation for future research into the complex dynamics of Saturn's magnetosphere.
label: machine

We present a novel interpretation of IceCube high energy neutrino events
(with energy larger than 60 TeV) in terms of an extraterrestrial flux due to
two different contributions: a flux originated by known astrophysical sources
and dominating IceCube observations up to few hundreds TeV, and a new flux
component where the most energetic neutrinos come from the leptophilic
three-body decays of dark matter particles with a mass of few PeV. Differently
from other approaches, we provide two examples of elementary particle models
that do not require extremely tiny coupling constants. We find the
compatibility of the theoretical predictions with the IceCube results when the
astrophysical flux has a cutoff of the order of 100 TeV (broken power law). In
this case the most energetic part of the spectrum (PeV neutrinos) is due to an
extra component such as the decay of a very massive dark matter component. Due
to the low statistics at our disposal we have considered for simplicity the
equivalence between deposited and neutrino energy, however such approximation
does not affect dramatically the qualitative results. Of course, a purely
astrophysical origin of the neutrino flux (no cutoff in energy below the PeV
scale - unbroken power law) is still allowed. If future data will confirm the
presence of a sharp cutoff above few PeV this would be in favor of a dark
matter interpretation.
label: human

Trees are a special sub-class of networks with unique properties, such as the
level distribution which has often been overlooked. We analyse a general tree
growth model proposed by Klemm {\em et. al.} (2005) to explain the growth of
user-generated directory structures in computers. The model has a single
parameter $q$ which interpolates between preferential attachment and random
growth. Our analysis results in three contributions: First, we propose a more
efficient estimation method for $q$ based on the degree distribution, which is
one specific representation of the model. Next, we introduce the concept of a
level distribution and analytically solve the model for this representation.
This allows for an alternative and independent measure of $q$. We argue that,
to capture real growth processes, the $q$ estimations from the degree and the
level distributions should coincide. Thus, we finally apply both
representations to validate the model with synthetically generated tree
structures, as well as with collected data of user directories. In the case of
real directory structures, we show that $q$ measured from the level
distribution are incompatible with $q$ measured from the degree distribution.
In contrast to this, we find perfect agreement in the case of simulated data.
Thus, we conclude that the model is an incomplete description of the growth of
real directory structures as it fails to reproduce the level distribution. This
insight can be generalised to point out the importance of the level
distribution for modeling tree growth.
label: human

The inelastic nature of 3-phonon processes is investigated within the
framework of perturbation theory and linearized Boltzmann Transport Equation.
By considering the energy conservation rule governing this type of interactions
in a statistical average sense, the impact of different forms of the
regularized energy-conserving Dirac delta function on 3-phonon scattering rates
was evaluated. Strikingly, adopting Lorentz distribution, in accordance with
the shape of eigenenergy broadening of phonon normal modes due to the leading
term of crystal anharmonicity, was found to play a critical role in activating
umklapp processes at low temperature, leading to intrinsic lattice thermal
conductivity peak at finite temperature for perfect crystal. This
characteristic behavior, unique to the Lorentzian, lays foundation for
developing adjustable-parameter-free computational models for reliable
prediction of the finite lattice conductivity at low temperature, even in the
absence of extrinsic scattering processes. An iterative solution scheme for
Boltzmann Transport Equation was used to compute the intrinsic thermal
conductivity of solid argon over the entire temperature range (2-80 K). For the
first time, the experimentally observed $T^2$ behavior in the low temperature,
$T$, limit and the peak temperature (~ 8 K) were successfully recovered, in
addition to the classical high temperature $T^{-1}$ behavior above 20 K by the
sole use of 3-phonon processes. The good agreement with experiment indicates
that phonon-phonon interactions dominate over the entire temperature range in
argon, contrary to previous hypotheses that phonon-defect scattering dominates
the sub-peak regime. Anisotropy in thermal conductivity of single crystal at
low temperature due to phonon focusing was observed. In addition, argon
conductivity is underestimated by an order of magnitude in Single Mode
Relaxation Time approximation.
label: human

Heterogeneous condensation of vapours mixed with a carrier gas in the
stagnation point boundary layer flow near a cold wall is considered in the
presence of solid particles much larger than the mean free path of vapour
particles. The supersaturated vapour condenses on the particles by diffusion
and particles and droplets are thermophoretically attracted to the wall.
Assuming that the heat of vaporization is much larger than the Boltzmann
constant times the temperature far from the wall, vapour condensation occurs in
a {\em condensation layer} (CL). The CL width and characteristics depend on the
parameters of the problem, and a parameter $R$ yielding the rate of vapour
scavenging by solid particles is particularly important. Assuming that the CL
is so narrow that temperature, particle density and velocity do not change
appreciably inside it, an asymptotic theory is found, the $\delta$-CL theory,
that approximates very well the vapour and droplet profiles, the dew point
shift and the deposition rates at the wall for wide ranges of the wall
temperature $\tilde{T}_{w}$ and the scavenging parameter $R$. This theory
breaks down for $\tilde{T}_{w}$ very close to the maximum temperature yielding
non-zero droplet deposition rate, $\tilde{T}_{w,M}$. For large $R$, we can
either assume that the width of the CL is zero (0-CL theory, then the vapour
density reaches local equilibrium with the condensate immediately after it
enters the dew surface), or use a nonlinear multiple scales theory. The 0-CL
theory corrects the $\delta$-CL theory for $\tilde{T}_w$ very close to
$\tilde{T}_{w,M}$ and any $R$, whereas the multiple scales theory is
appropriate for large and moderate $R$.
label: human

text: This study investigates the WASP-121 b, a hot Jupiter that orbits in a highly inclined polar configuration, nearly aligned with its host star's rotational axis. Our analysis leverages high-resolution spectroscopy and photometry data to explore the system's dynamics and physical properties. The results indicate that the planet experiences extreme tidal forces due to its proximity to the star and its orbital inclination. We propose that the planet is on the verge of tidal disruption, which would result from the cumulative effect of these forces over time. Key methodologies employed include numerical simulations to model the planet's evolution under various tidal scenarios and empirical analyses to constrain the mass and density of the planet. These findings contribute to our understanding of the evolutionary paths of hot Jupiters and the conditions under which they might be disrupted by their stars.
label: machine

text: We employed smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations to investigate the induced gravitational collapse scenario of long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) associated with supernovae. Our goal was to elucidate the underlying physical processes governing the collapse of a massive, compact object in the vicinity of a massive star undergoing a supernova explosion. We found that the collapse of the compact object was significantly influenced by the explosion's energy release, with the maximum collapse occurring when the explosion's energy was maximized. The simulations revealed a complex interplay between the explosion's energy, the compact object's initial mass, and the surrounding interstellar medium, leading to the formation of a massive, compact remnant. We observed that the collapse was accompanied by the emission of intense gamma-ray radiation, which was consistent with the observed properties of LGRBs. Our results suggest that the collapse of a compact object in the vicinity of a supernova explosion is a viable mechanism for the origin of LGRBs, and that the explosion's energy plays a crucial role in determining the final state of the compact object. The simulations also highlighted the importance of considering the effects of the surrounding interstellar medium on the collapse process.
label: machine

Based on the approach of flow distances, the international trade flow system
is studied from the perspective of multi-layer flow network. A model of
multi-layer flow network is proposed for modelling and analyzing multiple types
of flows in flow systems. Then, flow distances are introduced, and symmetric
minimum flow distance is presented. Subsequently, we discuss the establishment
of the multi-layer flow networks of international trade from two coupled
viewpoints, i.e., the viewpoint of commodity flow and that of money flow. Thus,
the multi-layer flow networks of international trade is explored. First,
trading "trophic levels" are adopted to depict positions that economies
occupied in the flow network. We find that the distributions of trading
"trophic levels" have the similar clustering pattern for different types of
commodity, and there are some regularities between money flow network and
commodity flow network. Second, we find that active and competitive countries
trade a wide spectrum of products, while inactive and underdeveloped countries
trade a limited variety of products. Besides, some abnormal countries import
many types of goods, which the vast majority of countries do not need to
import. It may indicate an abnormal economic status. Third, harmonic node
centrality is proposed and we find the phenomenon of centrality stratification.
It means that competitive countries tend to occupy the central positions in the
trading of a large variety of commodities, while underdeveloped countries
likely in the peripheral positions in the trading of their limited varieties of
products. Fourth, we find that manufactured products have significant larger
mean first-passage flow distances from the source to the sink than that of
primary products.
label: human

text:
The globular cluster $\omega$ Centauri (NGC 5139) is a puzzling stellar
system harboring several distinct stellar populations whose origin still
represents a unique astrophysical challenge. Current scenarios range from
primordial chemical inhomogeneities in the mother cloud to merging of different
sub-units and/or subsequent generations of enriched stars - with a variety of
different pollution sources- within the same potential well. In this paper we
study the chemical abundance pattern in the outskirts of Omega Centauri,
half-way to the tidal radius (covering the range of 20-30 arcmin from the
cluster center), and compare it with chemical trends in the inner cluster
regions, in an attempt to explore whether the same population mix and chemical
compositions trends routinely found in the more central regions is also present
in the cluster periphery.We extract abundances of many elements from
FLAMES/UVES spectra of 48 RGB stars using the equivalent width method and then
analyze the metallicity distribution function and abundance ratios of the
observed stars. We find, within the uncertainties of small number statistics
and slightly different evolutionary phases, that the population mix in the
outer regions cannot be distinguished from the more central regions, although
it is clear that more data are necessary to obtain a firmer description of the
situation. From the abundance analysis, we did not find obvious radial
gradients in any of the measured elements.
label: human

text: This study investigates the X-ray light curve of the massive colliding wind Wolf-Rayet (WR) star system WR21a, which consists of a WR star interacting with a massive O-type companion star. Through detailed analysis of Chandra X-ray Observatory data, we have obtained a high-resolution X-ray light curve that spans over two years, capturing the variability in X-ray emission. Our results reveal distinct X-ray flares and long-term variations in the X-ray flux, which are attributed to the dynamic interaction between the colliding stellar winds from both components. Key to our methodology is the application of spectral fitting techniques to differentiate between different plasma phases and to model the emission mechanisms. We find evidence of a strong correlation between the X-ray activity and the observed changes in the wind properties of the WR star. These findings contribute significantly to our understanding of the complex physical processes occurring within such systems, particularly regarding the interaction dynamics and energy release in the colliding winds.
label: machine

We process the Fermi LAT data on GRB130427A using the Fermi Science Tools,
and we summarize some of the key facts that render this observation truly
remarkable, especially concerning the quality of information on high-energy
emission by GRBs. We then exploit this richness for a search of spectral lags,
of the type that has been recently of interest for its relevance in
quantum-spacetime research. We do find some evidence of systematic soft
spectral lags: when confining the analysis to photons of energies greater than
5 GeV there is an early hard development of minibursts within this long burst.
The effect turns out to be well characterized quantitatively by a linear
dependence, within such a miniburst, of the detection time on energy. With the
guidance of our findings for GRB130427A we can then recognize that some support
for these features is noticeable also in earlier Fermi-LAT GRBs, particularly
for the presence of hard minibursts whose onset is marked by the highest-energy
photon observed for the GRB. A comparison of these features for GRBs at
different redshifts provides some encouragement for a redshift dependence of
the effects of the type expected for a quantum-spacetime interpretation, but
other aspects of the analysis appear to invite the interpretation as intrinsic
properties of GRBs.
label: human

text: This research investigates the general-relativistic monopole magnetosphere of neutron stars using a pseudo-spectral discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method. The study aims to simulate the complex electromagnetic fields surrounding neutron stars under extreme gravitational conditions, which are crucial for understanding their astrophysical implications. The objective is to develop a numerical framework capable of accurately capturing the nonlinear dynamics and boundary layers within these magnetospheres.  The methodology employed involves solving the Einstein-Maxwell equations in a coordinate system adapted to the geometry of the neutron star. A pseudo-spectral DG method is utilized to discretize the governing equations, enabling high-order accuracy and efficient handling of the intricate boundary conditions. This approach allows for precise computation of the electromagnetic field distributions and their evolution over time.  Key findings include the simulation of magnetospheric structures such as current sheets and magnetic null points, where significant energy conversion processes occur. The results demonstrate the presence of relativistic jets emanating from the poles of the neutron star, consistent with observations of gamma-ray bursts and other phenomena associated with neutron star magnetospheres. Additionally, the analysis reveals the importance of relativistic effects in shaping the morphology and dynamics of these systems.  In conclusion, the pseudo-spectral DG approach provides a robust tool for investigating the general-relativistic monopole magnetosphere of neutron stars, offering valuable insights into the physics governing these fascinating astrophysical objects. The findings contribute to our understanding of relativistic plasma physics and have implications for various astrophysical events observed in space.
label: machine

text: The formation of jets in the atmospheres of giant planets is a significant area of planetary research due to their potential role in shaping planetary environments and magnetic fields. In this study, we investigate the mechanisms responsible for jet formation on Jupiter and Saturn using a combination of observational data and theoretical modeling.  In the background section, we discuss the observed jets on Jupiter and Saturn and their similarities and differences. We then outline the proposed mechanisms for jet formation, including the magnetic shear instability (MSI) and the zonal flow instability (ZFI) theories.  The objective of our study is to provide a comprehensive understanding of the physical processes involved in jet formation on giant planets by examining the strengths and weaknesses of these theories using the available observational and theoretical data.  Our methodology involves a detailed analysis of high-resolution images and spectra of Jupiter and Saturn obtained from various observatories, such as the Hubble Space Telescope, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, and the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope. We also perform hydrodynamic and magnetohydrodynamic simulations to test the assumptions and predictions of the MSI and ZFI theories.  Our key findings suggest that both mechanisms may contribute to the observed jets on Jupiter and Saturn, but their relative importance depends on the specific planetary conditions. We also identify several areas where further research is required to fully understand the complex interplay between atmospheric flows, magnetic fields, and instabilities in the giant planet atmospheres.  In conclusion, this study provides valuable insights into the mechanisms of jet formation on giant planets, which has implications for our understanding of planetary evolution and the role of magnetic fields in shaping planetary environments. Our findings highlight the importance of continued observational and theoretical efforts to unravel the mysteries of these fascinating phenomena.

measurements might reveal these planet-planet interactions and yields a more
accurate view of such planetary systems. Like in the generic data modelling
problems, a fit to radial velocity data series has a set of unknown parameters
of which parametric derivatives have to be known by both the regression methods
and the estimations for the uncertainties. In this paper an algorithm is
described that aids the computation of such derivatives in case of when
planetary perturbations are not neglected. The application of the algorithm is
demonstrated on the planetary systems of HD 73526, HD 128311 and HD 155358. In
addition to the functions related to radial velocity analysis, the actual
implementation of the algorithm contains functions that computes spatial
coordinates, velocities and barycentric coordinates for each planet. These
functions aid the joint analysis of multiple transiting planetary systems,
transit timing and/or duration variations or systems where the proper motion of
the host star is also measured involving high precision astrometry. The
practical implementation related to the above mentioned problems features

text: We present the results of a comprehensive characterization of the K2-18 multi-planetary system using the High Accuracy Radial Velocity Planet Searcher (HARPS) spectrograph. Our analysis reveals that K2-18b, a previously discovered super-Earth, resides within the habitable zone of its host star, with surface temperatures potentially suitable for liquid water and life. Furthermore, we identify a second, warm super-Earth, K2-18c, on a non-coplanar orbit, which challenges our current understanding of planetary formation and migration. Utilizing HARPS data, we determine the masses and radii of both planets, as well as their orbital parameters, including eccentricities and inclinations. Our results indicate that K2-18c orbits its host star at a distance that could lead to atmospheric loss, while K2-18b's stable, coplanar orbit suggests a more conventional planetary formation scenario. The discovery of K2-18c highlights the complexities of planetary systems and underscores the need for further investigation into the dynamics of non-coplanar orbits. By combining HARPS data with computational simulations, we provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the K2-18 system and its implications for the search for life beyond Earth.

text: Bayesian inference has emerged as a pivotal tool in reconstructing evolutionary and epidemiological histories from genetic data. This study delves into the application of Bayesian inference for sampled ancestor trees, specifically within the realms of epidemiology and paleontology. The primary objective is to integrate static fossil records and dynamic epidemiological data to enhance the resolution of ancestral relationship reconstructions. We employed a novel Bayesian framework that simultaneously incorporates both fossil calibration and epidemiological sampling strategies, allowing for improved temporal estimation of diversification events. Our methodology leverages a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach, which facilitates robust sampling of the posterior distribution, coupled with tip dating techniques to accommodate the unique time-stamped challenges posed by fossil and pathogen data. Key findings indicate that our Bayesian model significantly outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, enabling the precise placement of sampled ancestors within the broader phylogenetic tree. Moreover, by incorporating disparate data types, the model provides enhanced estimates of evolutionary timelines and transmission dynamics. In conclusion, this integrative Bayesian approach offers a refined and more comprehensive framework for exploring the complexities of ancestral tree construction, bridging gaps between paleontological insights and epidemiological investigations. Our findings underscore the potential for such methodologies to inform public health strategies by elucidating pathogen evolution and informing fossil-based evolutionary studies.
