text: We investigate the electronic structure and crystal phase stability of palladium hydrides (PdHx) using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Our study aims to address the challenges associated with the variability in hydrogen content and the corresponding phase transformations in palladium hydrides, which play a crucial role in various applications, including hydrogen storage and catalysis. By systematically analyzing the electronic properties across different hydrogen concentrations, we elucidate the relationship between the electronic structure and the stability of various palladium hydride phases, including the face-centered cubic (FCC) and body-centered cubic (BCC) structures.  Our results reveal a distinct correlation between the hydrogen concentration and the electronic band structure, demonstrating an increase in the bandwidth with higher hydrogen content. We observe that the FCC phase exhibits greater thermodynamic stability in hydrogen-rich environments, while the BCC phase becomes favorable at lower hydrogen concentrations. Furthermore, we calculate the formation energies of different phases, confirming the prevalence of the FCC structure under typical storage conditions.  The insights gained from our comprehensive analysis provide a deeper understanding of the fundamental mechanisms governing the stability of palladium hydrides. Our findings contribute to the development of more efficient palladium-based materials for energy applications by delineating how the electronic structure influences phase behavior in response to varying hydrogen environments. Ultimately, this work establishes a framework for future investigations into transition metal hydrides and their applications in sustainable energy technologies.

Bohmian mechanics allows to visualize and understand the quantum-mechanical
behavior of massive particles in terms of trajectories. As shown by
Bialynicki-Birula, Electromagnetism also admits a hydrodynamical formulation
when the existence of a wave function for photons (properly defined) is
assumed. This formulation thus provides an alternative interpretation of
optical phenomena in terms of photon trajectories, whose flow yields a
pictorial view of the evolution of the electromagnetic energy density in
configuration space. This trajectory-based theoretical framework is considered
here to study and analyze the outcome from Young-type diffraction experiments
within the context of the Arago-Fresnel laws. More specifically, photon
trajectories in the region behind the two slits are obtained in the case where
the slits are illuminated by a polarized monochromatic plane wave. Expressions
to determine electromagnetic energy flow lines and photon trajectories within
this scenario are provided, as well as a procedure to compute them in the
particular case of gratings totally transparent inside the slits and completely
absorbing outside them. As is shown, the electromagnetic energy flow lines
obtained allow to monitor at each point of space the behavior of the
electromagnetic energy flow and, therefore, to evaluate the effects caused on
it by the presence (right behind each slit) of polarizers with the same or
different polarization axes. This leads to a trajectory-based picture of the
Arago-Fresnel laws for the interference of polarized light.

Privacy and data protection constitute core values of individuals and of
democratic societies. There have been decades of debate on how those values
-and legal obligations- can be embedded into systems, preferably from the very
beginning of the design process.
  One important element in this endeavour are technical mechanisms, known as
privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs). Their effectiveness has been
demonstrated by researchers and in pilot implementations. However, apart from a
few exceptions, e.g., encryption became widely used, PETs have not become a
standard and widely used component in system design. Furthermore, for unfolding
their full benefit for privacy and data protection, PETs need to be rooted in a
data governance strategy to be applied in practice.
  This report contributes to bridging the gap between the legal framework and
the available technological implementation measures by providing an inventory
of existing approaches, privacy design strategies, and technical building
blocks of various degrees of maturity from research and development. Starting
from the privacy principles of the legislation, important elements are
presented as a first step towards a design process for privacy-friendly systems
and services. The report sketches a method to map legal obligations to design
strategies, which allow the system designer to select appropriate techniques
for implementing the identified privacy requirements. Furthermore, the report
reflects limitations of the approach. It concludes with recommendations on how
to overcome and mitigate these limits.

text: In our study on the tidal evolution of planets orbiting brown dwarfs, we sought to elucidate the complex interactions and long-term orbital dynamics within such systems. The paucity of observational data has limited understanding of these celestial bodies' unique environments and evolutionary trajectories. By employing a computational model integrating tidal dissipation effects, orbital dynamics, and stellar evolution, we aimed to simulate the interactions between planets and their brown dwarf hosts over extended time scales.   Our results indicate that tidal forces significantly impact the orbital and spin parameters of planets within these systems, often leading to orbital decay or stabilization dependent on initial conditions such as orbital distance, planetary mass, and the brown dwarf's own evolutionary stage. Notably, we observed that planetary orbits within a critical range from the brown dwarf tend to experience more pronounced tidal effects, often causing them to migrate inward, potentially culminating in planetary engulfment or exacerbate thermal evolution of both bodies.  Moreover, our findings suggest that these tidal interactions can lead to energetically favorable configurations that may shorten the life span of planetary systems due to increased heat generated through tidal dissipation. This research narrows gaps in our understanding of planet-host interactions and sheds light on evolutionary outcomes for planets in orbit around substellar objects, providing a foundation for future observational endeavors and enhancing our grasp of planetary system lifecycles within such unique environments. We propose continued refinement of our model to better capture the vast parameter space and nuanced physics involved in these intriguing celestial systems.

text: We investigate the holographic R\'enyi entropy in the context of the AdS$_3$/LCFT$_2$ correspondence, a long-standing problem in the duality between gravitational theories and conformal field theories. Our approach involves calculating the R\'enyi entropies for the AdS$_3$ black hole, a boundary conformal field theory (CFT) constructed from a two-dimensional conformal field theory (CFT) on the boundary of the AdS$_3$ spacetime.   We derive the expressions for the R\'enyi entropies for the AdS$_3$ black hole using the dual CFT, and show that they satisfy the holographic R\'enyi entropy formula, which is a fundamental property of holographic systems. We also examine the behavior of the R\'enyi entropies as the temperature of the black hole approaches the Hawking temperature, and find that they exhibit the expected behavior.   Our results demonstrate the validity of the AdS$_3$/LCFT$_2$ correspondence in the context of holographic R\'enyi entropy, providing further evidence for the connection between gravitational theories and CFTs. We also discuss the implications of our findings for our understanding of the holographic principle and the holographic duality.

text: We investigate the bifurcation phenomena and the emergence of competing coherent structures in the context of the cubic-quintic Ginzburg-Landau equation, particularly focusing on the plane wave (CW) solutions. Our study reveals that the system undergoes a series of bifurcations as control parameters are varied, leading to the coexistence of multiple coherent structures. We employ both analytical and numerical techniques to elucidate the stability and dynamics of these plane wave solutions, identifying regions in the parameter space where transitions occur.   Through comprehensive bifurcation analysis, we pinpoint critical thresholds that delineate the onset of instability in the CW solutions, which in turn facilitates the nucleation of various localized structures, such as solitary waves and oscillons. We illustrate the role of nonlinear interactions that contribute to the coexistence and competition among these structures. Furthermore, we derive conditions under which the stability of the CW solutions is assured, helping to clarify the landscape of possible behaviors exhibited by the system.  The results underscore the intricate interplay between bifurcations and the formation of coherent structures, offering insights into the fundamental mechanisms underlying the dynamics of the cubic-quintic Ginzburg-Landau equation. Our findings not only enhance the theoretical understanding of nonlinear wave phenomena but also provide a framework for exploring similar behaviors in diverse physical systems characterized by higher-order nonlinearities.

address some problems that are of general interest when reconstructing the move

For a finite collection of graphs ${\cal F}$, the ${\cal F}$-M-DELETION
problem consists in, given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, deciding whether
there exists $S \subseteq V(G)$ with $|S| \leq k$ such that $G \setminus S$
does not contain any of the graphs in ${\cal F}$ as a minor. We are interested
in the parameterized complexity of ${\cal F}$-M-DELETION when the parameter is
the treewidth of $G$, denoted by $tw$. Our objective is to determine, for a
fixed ${\cal F}$, the smallest function $f_{{\cal F}}$ such that {${\cal
F}$-M-DELETION can be solved in time $f_{{\cal F}}(tw) \cdot n^{O(1)}$ on
$n$-vertex graphs. We prove that $f_{{\cal F}}(tw) = 2^{2^{O(tw \cdot\log
tw)}}$ for every collection ${\cal F}$, that $f_{{\cal F}}(tw) = 2^{O(tw
\cdot\log tw)}$ if ${\cal F}$ contains a planar graph, and that $f_{{\cal
F}}(tw) = 2^{O(tw)}$ if in addition the input graph $G$ is planar or embedded
in a surface. We also consider the version of the problem where the graphs in
${\cal F}$ are forbidden as topological minors, called ${\cal F}$-TM-DELETION.
We prove similar results for this problem, except that in the last two
algorithms, instead of requiring ${\cal F}$ to contain a planar graph, we need
it to contain a subcubic planar graph. This is the first of a series of
articles on this topic.

text: This research proposes a novel method to realize the $p$-wave superfluid state in a Fermi gas by introducing a synthetic spin-orbit interaction. The $p$-wave superfluid state, characterized by a topological order and non-trivial topology, is a fundamental concept in topological quantum field theory. However, its realization in cold atomic gases remains an open challenge. The conventional approach to achieving $p$-wave superfluidity relies on the presence of a strong spin-orbit interaction, which is difficult to implement in current experimental systems. In contrast, a synthetic spin-orbit interaction, generated through the interplay of magnetic fields and atomic interactions, offers a promising alternative. By exploiting this synthetic interaction, we demonstrate that a $s$-wave superfluid Fermi gas can be transformed into a $p$-wave superfluid state. Our approach involves the creation of a synthetic spin-orbit interaction by applying a controlled magnetic field to the Fermi gas, followed by the application of a phase modulation to the atomic interactions. The resulting $p$-wave superfluid state is characterized by a non-trivial topological order and exhibits the predicted properties of a topological quantum fluid. The proposed method offers a feasible route to the realization of the $p$-wave superfluid state, paving the way for the exploration of new quantum phases and phenomena in ultracold atomic gases.

We consider surface diffusion of a single particle, which performs
site-to-site under-barrier hopping, fulfils intrasite motion between the ground
and the first excited states within a quantum well, and interacts with surface
phonons. On the basis of quantum kinetic equations for one-particle
distribution functions obtained earlier we study the coherent and incoherent
motion of the adparticle. In the latter case we derive the generalized
diffusion coefficients and study various dynamic regimes of the adparticle. The
critical values of the coupling constant $G_{cr}(T,\Omega)$, which separate
domains with possible recrossing from those with the monotonic motion of the
adparticle, are calculated as functions of a temperature $T$ and a vibrational
frequency $\Omega$. These domains are found to coincide with the regions where
the experimentally observed diffusion coefficients change its behavior from
weakly dependent on $T$ to quite a sensitive function of the temperature. We
also evaluate the off-diagonal (relative to the site labels) distribution
functions both in the Markovian limit and when the memory effects become
important. The obtained results are discussed in the context of the "long
tails" problem of the generalized diffusion coefficients, the
recrossing/multiple crossing phenomena, and an eventual interrelation between
the adparticle dynamics at short times and the temperature dependence of the
diffusion coefficients measured experimentally.

text: The Bent-Tailed Radio Sources (BTS), a rare class of radio galaxies, are characterized by their peculiar bent and curved morphology. This abstract presents an analysis of BTSs in the Australia Telescope Large Area Survey (ATLAS) of the Chandra Deep Field-South (CDF-S). In the background section, we discuss the general properties and classification of BTSs, highlighting their unique morphology and the ongoing debates regarding their formation mechanisms. The objective of our study is to identify and characterize BTSs in the CDF-S using multi-wavelength data, including radio observations from ATLAS, X-ray data from Chandra, and optical data from the Deep Evolution Field survey. We employed a visual inspection methodology and used stringent selection criteria to ensure the reliability of our BTS candidates. Our key findings include the identification of 15 potential BTSs in the CDF-S, with sizes ranging from 12 to 112 kpc, and the confirmation of six previously known BTSs. We also examine the properties of these sources, including their radio spectral indices, X-ray luminosities, and environmental contexts. Our conclusions emphasize the importance of studying BTSs to better understand the role of AGNs in galaxy evolution and provide insights into the complex physical processes at work in the intergalactic medium. Further analyses of these BTSs, particularly regarding their jet formation mechanisms and their role in the evolution of cluster environments, are planned for future studies.

text: Brightest Cluster Galaxies (BCGs), particularly cD galaxies, exhibit unique morphological and structural features critical for understanding galaxy evolution in dense environments. Despite significant advancements, the automatic identification of cD galaxies remains a challenging task due to their complex structures and subtle distinguishing characteristics. This study aims to develop an efficient and accurate method for automatically identifying cD galaxies within clusters by leveraging advanced machine learning techniques on large-scale astronomical data. We employ convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on a comprehensive set of imaging data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). The dataset includes manually annotated images of BCGs to guide the learning process of distinguishing morphological attributes typical of cD galaxies, such as extended halos and central dominance. Key findings from our analysis indicate that the CNN model achieves a high accuracy rate, significantly outperforming traditional methods relying on photometric parameters alone. Furthermore, we explore the correlation between morphological features identified by the CNNs and structural properties statistically derived from data, gaining insights into the physical processes driving BCG formation and evolution. Our results demonstrate that automated identification can robustly capture the subtle differences between cD galaxies and other BCGs, offering a promising tool for expanding large-scale surveys. This methodological advancement not only enhances the classification of BCGs but also contributes to the broader understanding of galactic morphology and structure, facilitating further studies in galaxy evolution and the dynamics of galaxy clusters.

text: In this study, we present the results of Spitzer/MIPS 24-micron observations of the exoplanet HD 209458b, focusing on three eclipses, 2.5 transits, and a phase curve affected by instrumental sensitivity variations. Our work addresses the challenges posed by the instrumental noise in the data and explores methods to mitigate its effects on the observed phase curve of the exoplanet. By analyzing the temporal variations in the phase curve and comparing them to theoretical models, we aim to improve our understanding of the atmospheric dynamics of HD 209458b. We investigate different techniques to disentangle the true astrophysical signal from the instrumental artifacts, including detrending and statistical modeling approaches. Our findings suggest that the instrumental sensitivity variations significantly impact the phase curve of HD 209458b, underscoring the importance of careful data analysis in exoplanet studies. The methodology employed in this work combines advanced data processing techniques with theoretical modeling to extract meaningful information from the observations. The results shed light on the challenges of interpreting phase curves of exoplanets and provide valuable insights for future studies aiming to characterize the atmospheres of distant worlds.

text: This study identifies a very compact dense galaxy overdensity with a characteristic density ratio \(\delta \approx 130\) at \(z \approx 8\). The work seeks to address the formation mechanisms of early protoclusters and cluster cores during the epoch of reionization. Utilizing high-resolution spectroscopic data from the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based facilities, we have systematically analyzed the spatial distribution and clustering properties of these galaxies. Our analysis reveals that the overdensity exhibits a significant concentration of galaxies within a small volume, indicating the presence of a nascent cluster core. Key methodologies include photometric redshift estimation, spatial clustering analysis, and luminosity function modeling. The results suggest that the observed overdensity represents a critical phase in the evolution of massive structures, potentially marking the beginning of cluster formation. These findings contribute to our understanding of the hierarchical assembly of cosmic structures and the role of galaxy clustering in the early universe.

text: We develop a model structure on the category of small acyclic categories, providing a comprehensive framework for the study of these mathematical objects. Our approach is based on the notion of a model category, which is a category equipped with a model structure, a notion that generalizes the concept of a model category in homotopy theory. We establish that the category of small acyclic categories is a model category, and we provide a detailed description of its model structure, including the definition of the model functor and the fibrant objects.  Our work is motivated by the desire to provide a framework for the study of the relationships between homotopy theory and model category theory. We demonstrate that the model structure on the category of small acyclic categories is closely related to the notion of homotopy type theory, and we provide a new perspective on the connections between these two areas of mathematics.  We use a combination of categorical and homotopical techniques to establish the model structure, including the use of cofibrations, fibrations, and weak equivalences. Our approach is rigorous and systematic, and we provide a detailed analysis of the properties of the model structure, including its relation to the notion of a Quillen model category.  The model structure on the category of small acyclic categories provides a new tool for the study of homotopy theory and model category theory, and we expect it to have significant implications for our understanding of the relationships between these areas of mathematics.

text: We investigated the intersection of knot logic and topological quantum computing with Majorana fermions, with a focus on the theoretical framework and experimental feasibility of this emerging field. Our work aimed to elucidate the relationship between knot invariants and the topological properties of Majorana fermion systems, with the ultimate goal of developing a novel paradigm for quantum computing.  Through a combination of theoretical and numerical methods, we demonstrated the existence of topological phases of matter in Majorana fermion systems, which are characterized by non-trivial knot invariants. We showed that the knot polynomials of these systems exhibit non-trivial behavior, which is a hallmark of topological quantum computing. Our results suggest that the properties of Majorana fermions can be harnessed to create robust and fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.  We also explored the implications of knot logic on the design of quantum error correction codes for Majorana fermion systems. Our analysis revealed that certain knot invariants can be used to encode quantum information in a way that is resistant to decoherence and error. This has significant implications for the development of topological quantum computing architectures, which are essential for the creation of reliable and scalable quantum computing systems.  Our work provides a foundation for the development of a new paradigm for quantum computing, one that is based on the principles of knot logic and topological quantum computing. We believe that this approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of quantum computing and enable the creation of robust and fault-tolerant quantum computing systems.

Thin film transistors, with channels composed of In-X-Zn oxides, IXZO, with X
dopants: Ga, Sb, Be, Mg, Ag, Ca, Al, Ni, and Cu, were fabricated and their I-V
characteristics were taken at selected temperatures in the 77K<T<300K range.
The low field mobility, mu, and the interface defect density, Nst were
extracted from the characteristics for each of the studied IXZOs. At higher T
the mobility follows the Arrhenius law with an upward distortion, increasing as
T was lowered, gradually transforming into the exp [-(T0/T)1/4] variation. We
showed that mu(T, Nst) follows mu0exp[-Eaeff(T,Nst)/kT], with T-dependent
effective activation energy Eaeff(T, Nst) accounts for the data, revealing a
linear correlation between Eaeff and Nst at higher T. Temperature variation of
Eaeff(T, Nst) was evaluated using a model assuming a random distribution of
conduction mobility edge Ec values in the oxides, stemming from spatial
fluctuations induced by disorder in the interface traps distribution. For a
Gaussian distribution of Ec, the activation energy Eaeff(T, Nst) varies
linearly with 1/T, which accounts satisfactorily for the data obtained on all
the studied IXZOs. The model also shows that Eaeff(T, Nst) is a linear function
of Nst at a fixed T, which explains the exponential decrease of mu with NST.

Extended, steep-spectrum radio synchrotron sources are pre-dominantly found
in massive galaxy clusters as opposed to groups. LOFAR Two-Metre Sky Survey
images have revealed a diffuse, ultra-steep spectrum radio source in the
low-mass cluster Abell 1931. The source has a fairly irregular morphology with
a largest linear size of about 550 kpc. The source is only seen in LOFAR
observations at 143 MHz and GMRT observations at 325 MHz. The spectral index of
the total source between 143 MHz and 325 MHz is $\alpha_{143}^{325} = -2.86 \pm
0.36$. The source remains invisible in Very Large Array (1-2 GHz) observations
as expected given the spectral index. Chandra X-ray observations of the cluster
revealed a bolometric luminosity of $L_X = (1.65 \pm 0.39) \times 10^{43}$ erg
s$^{-1}$ and a temperature of $2.92_{-0.87}^{+1.89}$ keV which implies a mass
of around $\sim 10^{14} M_{\odot}$. We conclude that the source is a remnant
radio galaxy that has shut off around 200 Myr ago. The brightest cluster
galaxy, a radio-loud elliptical galaxy, could be the source for this extinct
source. Unlike remnant sources studied in the literature, our source has a
steep spectrum at low radio frequencies. Studying such remnant radio galaxies
at low radio frequencies is important for understanding the scarcity of such
sources and their role in feedback processes.

PEBPs (PhosphatidylEthanolamine Binding Proteins) form a protein family
widely present in the living world since they are encountered in
microorganisms, plants and animals. In all organisms PEBPs appear to regulate
important mechanisms that govern cell cycle, proliferation, differentiation and
motility. In humans, three PEBPs have been identified, namely PEBP1, PEBP2 and
PEBP4. PEBP1 and PEBP4 are the most studied as they are implicated in the
development of various cancers. PEBP2 is specific of testes in mammals and was
essentially studied in rats and mice where it is very abundant. A lot of
information has been gained on PEBP1 also named RKIP (Raf Kinase Inhibitory
protein) due to its role as a metastasis suppressor in cancer. PEBP1 was also
demonstrated to be implicated in Alzheimers disease, diabetes and
nephropathies. Furthermore, PEBP1 was described to be involved in many cellular
processes, among them are signal transduction, inflammation, cell cycle,
proliferation, adhesion, differentiation, apoptosis, autophagy, circadian
rhythm and mitotic spindle checkpoint. On the molecular level, PEBP1 was shown
to regulate several signaling pathways such as Raf/MEK/ERK, NFkB,
PI3K/Akt/mTOR, p38, Notch and Wnt. PEBP1 acts by inhibiting most of the kinases
of these signaling cascades. Moreover, PEBP1 is able to bind to a variety of
small ligands such as ATP, phospholipids, nucleotides, flavonoids or drugs.
Considering PEBP1 is a small cytoplasmic protein (21kDa), its involvement in so
many diseases and cellular mechanisms is amazing. The aim of this review is to
highlight the molecular systems that are common to all these cellular
mechanisms in order to decipher the specific role of PEBP1. Recent discoveries
enable us to propose that PEBP1 is a modulator of molecular interactions that
control signal transduction during membrane and cytoskeleton reorganization.

In WSN, each sensor is responsible for sensing environmental conditions and
sending them to the one or more base stations. Battery-operated sensors are
severely constrained by the amount of energy that can be spend for transmitting
these sensed data. However, aggregation of data (including removal of redundant
data) at intermediate sensors and forwarding of aggregate data reduce overall
energy consumptions in WSN. In general, data gathering refers to the process of
periodic collection of sensed data from various sensors to one or more base
stations (BS). Energy efficient data gathering scheduling is essential for
improving the lifetime of WSN. In this paper, we propose a distributed
algorithm to compute data-gathering schedule that aim to improve the lifetime
of WSN by suitably selecting energy-efficient data-flow paths from various
sensors to the base station. For a multihop WSN with $n$ sensors, the proposed
algorithm first computes a schedule in $O(n^2)$ time steps, and then this
schedule is periodically updated based the residual energy and the feedback
received from the BS. The system performs approximately $\log(\mathcal{L})$
schedule updates where $\mathcal{L}$ is the expected lifetime of the system in
number of data-gathering rounds. Moreover, each updation process uses the
existing active schedule (data-flow path) - thus consuming only a small
fraction of a single data gathering round activity. Such an algorithm thus
could precisely incorporate the energy consumptions due to updates and related
activities. Moreover, our algorithm does not assume any global knowledge of the
topology or the positions of various sensors. Through simulation study, we
found that our proposed algorithm achieves significantly higher network
lifetime compared to existing data-flow schedules based on the Minimum Spanning
Tree (MST), the Shortest Path Tree (SPT), the Weighted Rooted Tree (WRT).

Gas-rich galaxies in dense environments such as galaxy clusters and massive
groups are affected by a number of possible types of interactions with the
cluster environment, which make their evolution radically different than that
of field galaxies. The dIrr galaxy NGC 1427A, presently infalling towards the
core of the Fornax galaxy cluster, offers a unique opportunity to study those
processes in a level of detail not possible to achieve for galaxies at higher
redshifts. Using HST/ACS and auxiliary VLT/FORS ground-based observations, we
study the properties of the most recent episodes of star formation in this
gas-rich galaxy, the only one of its type near the core of the Fornax cluster.
We study the structural and photometric properties of young star cluster
complexes in NGC 1427A, identifying 12 bright such complexes with exceptionally
blue colors. The comparison of our broadband near-UV/optical photometry with
simple stellar population models yields ages below ~4x10^6 yr and stellar
masses from a few thousand up to ~3x10^4 Msun, slightly dependent on the
assumption of cluster metallicity and IMF. Their grouping is consistent with
hierarchical and fractal star cluster formation. We use deep Ha imaging data to
determine the current Star Formation Rate (SFR) in NGC 1427A and estimate the
ratio, Gamma, of star formation occurring in these star cluster complexes to
that in the entire galaxy. We find Gamma to be among the largest such values
available in the literature, consistent with starburst galaxies. Thus a large
fraction of the current star formation in NGC 1427A is occurring in star
clusters, with the peculiar spatial arrangement of such complexes strongly
hinting at the possibility that the starburst is being triggered by the passage
of the galaxy through the cluster environment.

The binary Bi-chalchogenides, Bi2Ch3, are widely regarded as model examples
of a recently discovered new form of quantum matter, the three-dimensional
topological insulator (TI) [1-4]. These compounds host a single spin-helical
surface state which is guaranteed to be metallic due to time reversal symmetry,
and should be ideal materials with which to realize spintronic and quantum
computing applications of TIs [5]. However, the vast majority of such compounds
synthesized to date are not insulators at all, but rather have detrimental
metallic bulk conductivity [2, 3]. This is generally accepted to result from
unintentional doping by defects, although the nature of the defects responsible
across different compounds, as well as strategies to minimize their detrimental
role, are surprisingly poorly understood. Here, we present a comprehensive
survey of the defect landscape of Bi-chalchogenide TIs from first-principles
calculations. We find that fundamental differences in the energetics of native
defect formation in Te- and Se-containing TIs enables precise control of the
conductivity across the ternary Bi-Te-Se alloy system. From a systematic
angle-resolved photoemission (ARPES) investigation of such ternary alloys,
combined with bulk transport measurements, we demonstrate that this method can
be utilized to achieve true topological insulators, with only a single Dirac
cone surface state intersecting the chemical potential. Our microscopic
calculations reveal the key role of anti-site defects for achieving this, and
predict optimal growth conditions to realize maximally-resistive ternary TIs.

Much attention has been recently devoted to the possibility that quantum
gravity effects could lead to departures from Special Relativity in the form of
a deformed Poincar\`e algebra. These proposals go generically under the name of
Doubly or Deformed Special Relativity (DSR). In this article we further explore
a recently proposed class of quantum field theories, involving noncanonically
commuting complex scalar fields, which have been shown to entail a DSR-like
symmetry. An open issue for such theories is whether the DSR-like symmetry has
to be taken as a physically relevant symmetry, or if in fact the "true"
symmetries of the theory are just rotations and translations while boost
invariance has to be considered broken. We analyze here this issue by extending
the known results to curved spacetime under both of the previous assumptions.
We show that if the symmetry of the free theory is taken to be a DSR-like
realization of the Poincar\'e symmetry, then it is not possible to render such
a symmetry a gauge symmetry of the curved physical spacetime. However, it is
possible to introduce an auxiliary spacetime which allows to describe the
theory as a standard quantum field theory in curved spacetime. Alternatively,
taking the point of view that the noncanonical commutation of the fields
actually implies a breakdown of boost invariance, the physical spacetime
manifold has to be foliated in surfaces of simultaneity and the field theory
can be coupled to gravity by making use of the ADM prescription.

We investigate line formation in gas that is outflowing and optically thick
to electron scattering, as may be expected following the tidal disruption of a
star by a super-massive black hole. Using radiative transfer calculations, we
show that the optical line profiles produced by expanding TDE outflows are most
likely primarily emission features, rather than the P-Cygni profiles seen in
most supernova spectra. This is a result of the high line excitation
temperatures in the highly irradiated TDE gas. The outflow kinematics cause the
emission peak to be blueshifted and to have an asymmetric red wing. Such
features have been observed in some TDE spectra, and we propose that these may
be signatures of outflows. We also show that non-coherent scattering off of hot
electrons can broaden the emission lines by $\sim 10000$~km~s$^{-1}$, such that
in some TDEs the line width may be set by the electron scattering optical depth
rather than the gas kinematics. The scattering broadened line profiles produce
distinct, wing-shaped profiles that are similar to those observed in some TDE
spectra. The narrowing of the emission lines over time in these observed events
may be related to a drop in density rather than a drop in line-of-sight
velocity.

text: In this study, we analyze and quantify the differential emission measure (DEM) and energetics of solar microflares by integrating observations from the Solar Dynamics Observatory's Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (SDO/AIA) and the Reuven Ramaty High Energy Solar Spectroscopic Imager (RHESSI). Our primary aim is to elucidate the temperature distribution and energy release mechanisms inherent in microflares, which, despite their smaller scale, contribute significantly to understanding solar atmospheric heating. We employ a DEM inversion method to derive temperature profiles and utilize RHESSI's X-ray spectroscopy to determine the non-thermal energy release. Through a comprehensive cross-analysis of the imaging and spectroscopic data, we identify distinct temperature components corresponding to both thermal and non-thermal processes. Our results reveal a complex multi-thermal structure with peak emission at temperatures between 5 and 10 MK. Additionally, we calculate energy contributions from both the thermal plasma and non-thermal electron acceleration, revealing that non-thermal processes dominate the energy budget of microflares. This methodology affords a robust mechanism for constraining the heating rate and temporal evolution during microflare events. Our integrated observational and analytical approach delineates the microflare phenomenology with unprecedented precision, providing new insights into their role in the larger context of solar magnetism and coronal heating. These findings suggest needful refinements in space weather prediction models and contribute to the broader quest of connecting microflare dynamics with solar atmospheric heating mechanisms. Our work highlights the synergistic potential of combining SDO/AIA and RHESSI data to deepen the understanding of micro-scaled solar eruptions.

text: The increasing demand for high-quality multimedia content over the Internet has highlighted the need for efficient image and video processing techniques. The use of Information Set Operations on multimedia (ISOM) has shown promise in enhancing the performance of multimedia applications.   This research aims to improve ISOM by incorporating filtering techniques to enhance the quality and efficiency of multimedia processing. The focus is on optimizing the processing of images and videos to reduce noise, enhance clarity, and improve overall visual experience.   A comprehensive study of different filtering algorithms such as median filtering, Gaussian filtering, and edge-preserving filters is conducted. These filters are integrated into the ISOM framework to enhance the processing of multimedia data. Experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed approach in terms of image quality, processing speed, and resource utilization.   The results demonstrate that integrating filtering techniques into ISOM significantly improves the quality of processed images and videos. The proposed approach shows a reduction in noise artifacts, improved image clarity, and enhanced visual appeal. Additionally, the processing speed is optimized, leading to better real-time performance of multimedia applications.   In conclusion, this research highlights the effectiveness of utilizing filtering techniques to enhance ISOM for multimedia processing. The integration of filters improves the overall quality and efficiency of multimedia applications, making them more suitable for a wide range of multimedia content delivery systems.

We investigate how star formation is spatially organized in the grand-design
spiral NGC 1566 from deep HST photometry with the Legacy ExtraGalactic UV
Survey (LEGUS). Our contour-based clustering analysis reveals 890 distinct
stellar conglomerations at various levels of significance. These star-forming
complexes are organized in a hierarchical fashion with the larger congregations
consisting of smaller structures, which themselves fragment into even smaller
and more compact stellar groupings. Their size distribution, covering a wide
range in length-scales, shows a power-law as expected from scale-free
processes. We explain this shape with a simple "fragmentation and enrichment"
model. The hierarchical morphology of the complexes is confirmed by their
mass--size relation which can be represented by a power-law with a fractional
exponent, analogous to that determined for fractal molecular clouds. The
surface stellar density distribution of the complexes shows a log-normal shape
similar to that for supersonic non-gravitating turbulent gas. Between 50 and 65
per cent of the recently-formed stars, as well as about 90 per cent of the
young star clusters, are found inside the stellar complexes, located along the
spiral arms. We find an age-difference between young stars inside the complexes
and those in their direct vicinity in the arms of at least 10 Myr. This
timescale may relate to the minimum time for stellar evaporation, although we
cannot exclude the in situ formation of stars. As expected, star formation
preferentially occurs in spiral arms. Our findings reveal turbulent-driven
hierarchical star formation along the arms of a grand-design galaxy.

A nearby super-luminous burst GRB 130427A was simultaneously detected by six
$\gamma$-ray space telescopes ({\it Swift}, Fermi-GBM/LAT, Konus-Wind,
SPI-ACS/INTEGRAL, AGILE and RHESSI) and by three RAPTOR full-sky persistent
monitors. The isotropic $\gamma-$ray energy release is of $\sim 10^{54}$ erg,
rendering it the most powerful explosion among the GRBs with a redshift $z\leq
0.5$. The emission above 100 MeV lasted about one day and four photons are at
energies greater than 40 GeV. We show that the count rate of 100 MeV-100 GeV
emission may be mainly accounted for by the forward shock synchrotron radiation
and the inverse Compton radiation likely dominates at GeV-TeV energies. In
particular, an inverse Compton radiation origin is established for the $\sim
(95.3,~47.3,~41.4,~38.5,~32)$ GeV photons arriving at $t\sim
(243,~256.3,~610.6,~3409.8,~34366.2)$ s after the trigger of Fermi-GBM.
Interestingly, the external-inverse-Compton-scattering of the prompt emission
(the second episode, i.e., $t\sim 120-260$ s) by the forward-shock-accelerated
electrons is expected to produce a few $\gamma-$rays at energies above 10 GeV,
while five were detected in the same time interval. A possible unified model
for the prompt soft $\gamma-$ray, optical and GeV emission of GRB 130427A, GRB
080319B and GRB 090902B is outlined. Implication of the null detection of $>1$
TeV neutrinos from GRB 130427A by IceCube is discussed.

In globular clusters, dynamical evolution produces luminous X-ray emitting
binaries at a rate about 200 times greater than in the field. If globular
clusters also produce SNe Ia at a high rate, it would account for much of the
SN Ia events in early type galaxies and provide insight into their formation.
Here we use archival HST images of nearby galaxies that have hosted SNe Ia to
examine the rate at which globular clusters produce these events. The location
of the SN Ia is registered on an HST image obtained before the event or after
the supernova faded. Of the 36 nearby galaxies examined, 21 had sufficiently
good data to search for globular cluster hosts. None of the 21 supernovae have
a definite globular cluster counterpart, although there are some ambiguous
cases. This places an upper limit to the enhancement rate of SN Ia production
in globular clusters of about 42 at the 95% confidence level, which is an order
of magnitude lower than the enhancement rate for luminous X-ray binaries. Even
if all of the ambiguous cases are considered as having a globular cluster
counterpart, the upper bound for the enhancement rate is 82 at the 95%
confidence level, excluding an enhancement rate of 200. Barring unforeseen
selection effects, we conclude that globular clusters are not responsible for
producing a significant fraction of the SN Ia events in early-type galaxies.

text: In this study, we investigate the dynamics of falling liquid films subjected to the influence of blowing and suction at the solid boundary, which are pivotal in many industrial applications involving enhanced heat and mass transfer. Our primary objective is to analytically and numerically explore how these boundary conditions affect the stability and flow characteristics of thin liquid films. Employing the long-wave approximation, we derive the governing nonlinear evolution equations that characterize the film's surface perturbations in response to both blowing and suction. Through linear stability analysis, we identify critical parameters influencing the onset of instabilities and delineate stability regimes. Furthermore, we perform direct numerical simulations to corroborate our theoretical predictions and provide a comprehensive understanding of the film’s behavior under varied blowing and suction intensities. Our results demonstrate that suction tends to stabilize the film, delaying the onset of wave instabilities, whereas blowing induces destabilizing effects, enhancing wave amplification. The intricate interplay between these boundary conditions results in a range of complex wave patterns, which we classify and analyze in detail. This study's key contribution lies in elucidating the mechanisms by which controlled blowing and suction can be employed to manage film stability, offering insights that can be directly applied to optimize processes such as coating technologies, heat exchangers, and chemical reactors where precise manipulation of liquid films is essential. Our findings pave the way for future research into the development of effective control strategies for thin film applications across various scientific and engineering disciplines.

Fix $R>0$ and let $B_R$ denote the ball of radius $R$ centered at the origin
in $R^d$, $d\ge2$. Let $D\subset B_R$ be an open set with smooth boundary and
such that $R^d-\bar D$ is connected, and let $$
L=\sum_{i,j=1}^da_{i,j}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_i\partial
x_j}-\sum_{i=1}^db_i\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} $$ be a second order elliptic
operator. Consider the following linear heat equation in the exterior domain
$R^d-\bar D$ with boundary flux: \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} &L u=0 \
\text{in}\ R^d-\bar D;\\ &a\nabla u\cdot \bar n=-h\ \text{on}\ \partial D;\\
&u>0 \ \text{is minimal}, \end{aligned} \end{equation*} where $h\gneq0$ is
continuous, and where $\bar n$ is the unit inward normal to the domain
$R^d-\bar D$. The operator $L$ must possess a Green's function in order that a
solution $u$ exist. An important feature of the equation is that there is no a
priori bound on the supremum $\sup_{x\in R^d-\bar D}u(x)$ of the solution
exclusively in terms of the boundary flux $h$, the hyper-surface measure of
$\partial D$ and the coefficients of $L$; rather the geometry of $D\subset B_R$
plays an essential role. However, we prove that in the case that $L$ is a \it
symmetric operator\rm\ with respect to some reference measure, then \it outside
of\rm\ $\bar B_R$, the solution to \eqref{LHE} is uniformly bounded,
independent of the particular choice of $D\subset B_R$. The proof uses a
combination of analytic and probabilistic techniques.

text: This study investigates the coupling between intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) and linear modes within solar microwave bursts. Utilizing advanced time-frequency analysis techniques, we identify and characterize these modes to understand their dynamics and interrelations during solar events. Our approach involves decomposing the burst data into IMFs using empirical mode decomposition (EMD), followed by spectral analysis to discern the linear modes. We find that certain IMF components predominantly contribute to specific linear modes, indicating a clear linkage between the two modes. This correlation is further supported by coherence analysis which reveals significant temporal and spectral alignment between IMF peaks and linear mode frequencies. The findings highlight the importance of considering both IMF and linear modes in the comprehensive understanding of solar microwave bursts, offering insights for improved solar flare forecasting and space weather modeling.

text: In complex network systems, assessing the reliability of $k$-terminal configurations is essential for ensuring operational integrity. However, evaluating failure frequencies in such systems can be computationally intensive and time-consuming. This study aims to present a fast and accurate method for approximating failure frequencies in $k$-terminal reliability systems, thus addressing the computational challenges associated with traditional approaches. We utilize a hybrid methodology that combines probabilistic modeling with advanced algorithmic techniques to enhance computational efficiency. The proposed approach leverages Monte Carlo simulations and analytical expressions to provide a balanced assessment of the failure probability without sacrificing precision. Key findings demonstrate a significant improvement in computational speed, achieving approximations that are within 5% accuracy of exact calculations while requiring substantially less processing time. Our results indicate that the new method can effectively handle larger networks and more complex configurations, suitable for real-time applications in critical infrastructure sectors. Conclusively, this research contributes a novel framework for reliability engineers and system designers, facilitating more efficient decision-making processes under uncertainty and aiding in the design of robust $k$-terminal systems. The efficacy of this approximation technique underscores its potential utility in both academic research and practical implementations in various engineering domains.

In this thesis, we perform investigations into the behaviour of
finite-temperature degenerate Bose gases using a classical-field formalism,
focussing in particular on the dynamics of quantum vortices in these systems.
We demonstrate that the coherence of the classical field can be characterised
by its temporal correlations, and discuss how the phase-symmetry-broken
averages familiar from mean-field theories emerge from the field trajectories.
We show that a finite-temperature condensate containing a precessing vortex in
a cylindrically symmetric trap can be realised as an ergodic equilibrium of the
classical-field theory, and demonstrate the identification of the rotationally
symmetry-broken condensate orbital and core-filling thermal component from the
field correlations. We then consider the nonequilibrium dynamics that result
when such a precessing-vortex configuration is subjected to a static trap
anisotropy which arrests its rotation, and observe novel coupled relaxation
dynamics of the condensed and noncondensed components of the field. Finally, we
consider the nucleation of vortices in an initially zero-temperature
quasi-two-dimensional condensate stirred by a rotating trap anisotropy. We
quantify the emergence of a rotating thermal component of the field, which
drives the nucleation of vortices from condensate-surface oscillations, and
study the relaxation and rotational equilibration of the initially turbulent
collection of vortices. We find that thermal fluctuations of the field prevent
the vortices from settling into a rigid crystalline lattice in this reduced
dimensionality, and that true condensation in the field is completely destroyed
by the disordered motion of vortices. We show, however, that the temporal
correlations of the field distinguish the quasi-coherent vortex-liquid phase in
the trap centre from the truly thermal material in its periphery.

text: The discovery of iron-based superconductors, particularly those containing layers of iron and arsenic, has sparked immense interest due to their high critical temperatures and unconventional superconducting mechanisms. Among these, Sr$_{2}$VO$_{3}$FeAs has emerged as a compound of notable interest. This study examines Sr$_{2}$VO$_{3}$FeAs in relation to other Fe-based superconductors, with the aim to elucidate its unique structural and electronic characteristics. Utilizing powder X-ray diffraction and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we conducted a comprehensive structural and electronic analysis. Our findings highlight that Sr$_{2}$VO$_{3}$FeAs possesses a tetragonal structure and features VO$_{3}$ layers that influence its electronic properties significantly. Notably, the V-doped layers introduce electron correlation effects, which differentiate its superconducting behavior from the more conventional FeAs-based superconductors like LaFeAsO and BaFe$_{2}$As$_{2}$. Furthermore, the electron pairing and notably high superfluid density observed in Sr$_{2}$VO$_{3}$FeAs suggest a different pairing mechanism might be at play, involving strong electron-electron interactions within the d orbitals of both vanadium and iron. Our comparative analysis reveals that the presence of VO$_{3}$ layers induces a potential novel electronic phase, which could offer explanations for the unique superconducting properties observed. The study concludes that Sr$_{2}$VO$_{3}$FeAs not only provides a fascinating insight into the interplay between structure and superconductivity in iron-based superconductors but also opens pathways for the development of new materials with enhanced superconducting capabilities.

text: This research focuses on the distribution-free detection of structured anomalies using permutation and rank-based scans. The objective is to develop a robust method for anomaly detection that does not rely on assumptions regarding the underlying data distribution. The methodology involves utilizing permutations and rank-based scans to identify anomalies in structured data without the need for distributional assumptions. Key findings of the study indicate that the permutation and rank-based approach effectively detects anomalies in structured data sets, outperforming traditional distribution-based methods in certain scenarios. The study concludes that the proposed method provides a reliable and versatile tool for anomaly detection in structured data, particularly in cases where distributional assumptions are not valid or difficult to ascertain.

text: The gravitational-wave confusion background, arising from unresolved cosmological compact binaries, presents a significant challenge for future terrestrial detectors aspiring to enhance sensitivity and accuracy. This paper explores the complex nature of this astrophysical background and its implications for next-generation gravitational-wave observatories. Our study aims to quantify the confusion noise contributed by binary neutron stars and black hole binaries distributed across the cosmos, particularly focusing on the frequencies relevant to terrestrial detectors like LIGO, Virgo, and future installations such as the Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope. Utilizing advanced population synthesis models and cosmological simulations, we predict the characteristic strain of this background and consider various evolutionary scenarios of binary systems. Our findings reveal that the confusion background could obscure weaker signals unless adequately mitigated, with its intensity contingent upon key parameters such as star formation rate, metallicity evolution, and the mass distribution of compact objects. We highlight that detectors with increased sensitivity and broader bandwidth may inadvertently accumulate higher confusion noise, necessitating more sophisticated data analysis techniques for signal separation. Importantly, our results underline the necessity for novel strategies in detector design, including optimizing detector networks and leveraging machine learning for enhanced source discrimination. The study concludes with a discussion on the potential of cross-correlating data between multiple observatories to better isolate genuine cosmological signals, thus maximizing the scientific yield from future gravitational-wave observations. This research sets the groundwork for developing robust methodologies to tackle the anticipated challenges posed by the confusion background in forthcoming gravitational-wave astronomy.

text: This study investigates the properties of Cherenkov photons emitted in extensive air showers of various primaries, incident at different zenith angles, and observed at a high-altitude level. Background Extensive air showers are complex astrophysical phenomena, involving the interaction of high-energy particles with the Earth's atmosphere, resulting in the production of a vast number of secondary particles. Cherenkov photons, produced by the rapid acceleration of these particles, play a crucial role in understanding the physics of these events.  The objective of this simulation study is to examine the effects of primary particle energy, zenith angle, and observation altitude on the properties of Cherenkov photons in extensive air showers. A detailed Monte Carlo simulation was performed, using a modified version of the Sibyll2.3 model, to generate extensive air showers of various primaries and zenith angles. The resulting Cherenkov photon spectra were analyzed to identify the dominant features and correlations with primary particle energy and zenith angle.  The results show that the Cherenkov photon spectra exhibit significant dependence on primary particle energy and zenith angle, with the most pronounced effects observed at higher energies and smaller zenith angles. The observation altitude also plays a crucial role in shaping the Cherenkov photon spectra, with a clear distinction between high-altitude and low-altitude observations. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the physics of Cherenkov photons in extensive air showers and have important implications for the development of next-generation air shower experiments.

The electronic properties of doped bilayer graphene in presence of bottom and
top gates have been studied and characterized by means of Density Functional
Theory calculations. Varying independently the bottom and top gates it is
possible to control separately the total doping charge on the sample, and the
average external electric field acting on the bilayer. We show that, at fixed
doping level, the band gap at the K point in the Brillouin zone depends
linearly on the average electric field, whereas the corresponding
proportionality coefficient has a non-monotonic dependence on doping. We find
that the DFT-calculated band gap at K, for small doping levels, is roughly half
of the band gap obtained with standard Tight Binding approach. We show that
this discrepancy arises from an underestimate, in the TB model, of the
screening of the system to the external electric field. In particular, on the
basis of our DFT results we observe that, when the bilayer graphene is in
presence of an external electric field, both an interlayer and an intralayer
screening occur. Only the interlayer screening is included in TB calculations,
while both screenings are fundamental for the description of the band gap
opening. We finally provide a general scheme to obtain the full band structure
of the gated bilayer graphene, for an arbitrary value of the external electric
field and of the doping.

Results of magnetic field and temperature dependent neutron diffraction and
magnetization measurements on oxy-arsenate Rb$_{2}$Fe$_{2}$O(AsO$_{4}$)$_{2}$
are reported. The crystal structure of this compound contains
pseudo-one-dimensional [Fe$_{2}$O$_{6}$]$^\infty$ sawtooth-like chains, formed
by corner sharing isosceles triangles of $Fe^{3+}$ ions occupying two
nonequivalent crystallographic sites. The chains extend infinitely along the
crystallographic $b$-axis and are structurally confined from one another via
diamagnetic (AsO$_{4}$)$^{3-}$ units along the $a$-axis, and Rb$^+$ cations
along the $c$-axis direction. Neutron diffraction measurements indicate the
onset of a long range antiferromagnetic order below approximately 25 K. The
magnetic structure consists of ferrimagnetic chains which are
antiferromagnetically coupled with each other. Within each chain, one of the
two Fe sites carries a moment which lies along the \emph{b}-axis, while the
second site bears a canted moment in the opposite direction. Externally applied
magnetic field induces a transition to a ferrimagnetic state, in which the
coupling between the sawtooth chains becomes ferromagnetic. Magnetization
measurements performed on optically-aligned single crystals reveal evidence for
an uncompensated magnetization at low magnetic fields that could emerge from to
a phase-segregated state with ferrimagnetic inclusions or from
antiferromagnetic domain walls. The observed magnetic states and the
competition between them is expected to arise from strongly frustrated
interactions within the sawtooth chains and relatively weak coupling between
them.

text: The field of object tracking has seen significant advancements in recent years, with the introduction of deep learning models that have surpassed the performance of traditional methods. One promising approach is semantic tracking, which uses the semantic meaning of object features to learn representations that enable robust tracking in the presence of various challenges. In this paper, we propose a novel method for semantic tracking using inter-supervised convolutional networks (IS-CNNs). The IS-CNN architecture consists of two branches a target branch and a context branch. The target branch is responsible for learning representations of the target object based on its semantic features, while the context branch learns representations of the surrounding context. We use a novel loss function to enforce alignment between the target and context branches during training. This loss function, called the inter-supervised loss, encourages the network to learn meaningful correspondences between the target and context representations. We evaluate our proposed method on two benchmark datasets the OTB-20 and OTB-100. Our results demonstrate that our method outperforms several state-of-the-art trackers, including the popular DeepSORT and CPM method. Moreover, our method is effective in handling various challenges, such as occlusions, deformations, and scale variations. Our work contributes to the advancement of semantic tracking by proposing a novel method based on inter-supervised learning, which enables the learning of meaningful correspondences between target and context representations. Furthermore, our method can be easily integrated into existing tracking pipelines, making it a valuable addition to the field of object tracking. Overall, our results show that semantic tracking with IS-CNNs represents a significant improvement over traditional tracking methods and offers promising avenues for future research. The target branch learns representations of the target object based on its semantic features, while the context branch learns representations of the surrounding context. text: This study presents the development of MAGNUS, a novel resistive magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) code that incorporates heat flow terms to simulate plasma dynamics more accurately. The code is designed to address the limitations of traditional resistive MHD codes by including thermal conduction and Joule heating effects, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for studying plasma behavior under various conditions. Problematically, existing codes often neglect these critical heat transfer processes, leading to inaccuracies in simulations. Our approach involves developing a robust numerical scheme that efficiently handles the coupled equations of motion, magnetic fields, and heat transport. Key methodologies include the implementation of high-resolution shock-capturing techniques and adaptive mesh refinement to manage complex flow structures. The results demonstrate improved accuracy in simulating plasma equilibria and stability, as well as enhanced predictions of heat flux distributions in tokamak configurations. These findings underscore the significance of incorporating heat flow terms in MHD modeling, paving the way for more precise simulations of fusion plasma environments.

text: This study presents a novel family of subgradient-based methods for solving convex optimization problems, formulated within a unifying framework. Our approach leverages the flexibility and universality of subgradient methods while maintaining the convergence properties and optimality guarantees of established algorithms, such as the gradient projection method and the proximity point method. The proposed family includes the Proximal Subgradient Method (PSM) and the Distributed Proximal Subgradient Method (DPSM). The PSM addresses the limitations of classical subgradient methods in dealing with non-differentiable or large-scale optimization problems, incorporating a proximal term that promotes faster convergence and preserves the original problem's structure. The DPSM builds upon the PSM by extending it to a distributed computing environment, offering an efficient alternative for solving large-scale problems by distributing the computation and storage across multiple machines.  The theoretical analysis of the proposed methods is provided, demonstrating their strong convergence properties and the relationships between various algorithms in the family. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the performance of the proposed methods compared to several state-of-the-art techniques. Results show that the proposed methods exhibit significant improvements in convergence rates and optimality guarantees for a wide range of convex optimization problems, highlighting their potential applications in various domains, including machine learning, control theory, and signal processing.  In summary, this study introduces a flexible and efficient family of subgradient-based methods for solving convex optimization problems, providing a unifying framework that covers both the Proximal Subgradient Method and Distributed Proximal Subgradient Method. The theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations demonstrate the strong convergence properties and superior performance of the proposed algorithms, offering valuable contributions to the field of convex optimization and its related applications.

text:
Sunspot numbers exhibit large short-timescale (daily-monthly) variation in
addition to longer timescale variation due to solar cycles.
  A formal statistical framework is presented for estimating and forecasting
randomness in sunspot numbers on top of deterministic (including chaotic)
models for solar cycles. The Fokker-Planck approach formulated assumes a
specified long-term or secular variation in sunspot number over an underlying
solar cycle via a driver function. The model then describes the observed
randomness in sunspot number on top of this driver function. We consider a
simple harmonic choice for the driver function, but the approach is general and
can easily be extended to include other drivers which account for underlying
physical processes and/or empirical features of the sunspot numbers. The
framework is consistent during both solar maximum and minimum, and requires no
parameter restrictions to ensure non-negative sunspot numbers. Model parameters
are estimated using statistically optimal techniques. The model agrees both
qualitatively and quantitatively with monthly sunspot data even with the
simplistic representation of the periodic solar cycle. This framework should be
particularly useful for solar cycle forecasters and is complementary to
existing modeling techniques. An analytic approximation for the Fokker-Planck
equation is presented, which is analogous to the Euler approximation, which
which allows for efficient maximum likelihood estimation of large data sets
and/or when using difficult to evaluate driver functions.

Detecting small objects is notoriously challenging due to their low
resolution and noisy representation. Existing object detection pipelines
usually detect small objects through learning representations of all the
objects at multiple scales. However, the performance gain of such ad hoc
architectures is usually limited to pay off the computational cost. In this
work, we address the small object detection problem by developing a single
architecture that internally lifts representations of small objects to
"super-resolved" ones, achieving similar characteristics as large objects and
thus more discriminative for detection. For this purpose, we propose a new
Perceptual Generative Adversarial Network (Perceptual GAN) model that improves
small object detection through narrowing representation difference of small
objects from the large ones. Specifically, its generator learns to transfer
perceived poor representations of the small objects to super-resolved ones that
are similar enough to real large objects to fool a competing discriminator.
Meanwhile its discriminator competes with the generator to identify the
generated representation and imposes an additional perceptual requirement -
generated representations of small objects must be beneficial for detection
purpose - on the generator. Extensive evaluations on the challenging
Tsinghua-Tencent 100K and the Caltech benchmark well demonstrate the
superiority of Perceptual GAN in detecting small objects, including traffic
signs and pedestrians, over well-established state-of-the-arts.

The galaxy power spectrum encodes a wealth of information about cosmology and
the matter fluctuations. Its unbiased and optimal estimation is therefore of
great importance. In this paper we generalise the framework of Feldman et al.
(1994) to take into account the fact that galaxies are not simply a Poisson
sampling of the underlying dark matter distribution. Besides finite
survey-volume effects and flux-limits, our optimal estimation scheme
incorporates several of the key tenets of galaxy formation: galaxies form and
reside exclusively in dark matter haloes; a given dark matter halo may host
several galaxies of various luminosities; galaxies inherit part of their
large-scale bias from their host halo. Under these broad assumptions, we prove
that the optimal weights "do not" explicitly depend on galaxy luminosity, other
than through defining the maximum survey volume and effective galaxy density at
a given position. Instead, they depend on the bias associated with the host
halo; the first and second factorial moments of the halo occupation
distribution; a selection function, which gives the fraction of galaxies that
can be observed in a halo of mass M at position r in the survey; and an
effective number density of galaxies. If one wishes to reconstruct the matter
power spectrum, then, provided the model is correct, this scheme provides the
only unbiased estimator. The practical challenges with implementing this
approach are also discussed.

text: In this study, we investigate the properties of extended Lyman-alpha haloes (LAHs) around high-redshift star-forming galaxies using the Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE) observations in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field (HUDF). Our analysis involves a comprehensive survey of LAHs associated with galaxies at redshifts ranging from 3 to 6. We employ a sophisticated modeling approach, incorporating both observational data and theoretical frameworks, to characterize the spatial extent and luminosity profiles of these LAHs. Our results reveal that the LAHs are considerably larger than the stellar components of their host galaxies, extending to several tens of kiloparsecs. The luminosity of these haloes exhibits a strong correlation with the star formation rates of the central galaxies, suggesting that intense radiation-driven processes potentially influence the properties of the circumgalactic medium. Furthermore, we identify a diversity in halo morphology, indicative of varying environmental interactions and intrinsic galactic properties influencing LAH structures. By comparing with lower redshift samples, we observe evolutionary trends in the LAH population, implying significant changes in feedback processes across cosmic time. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of galaxy formation and evolution, illustrating the significant role played by Lyman-alpha emission in tracing the growth of baryonic structures in the early universe. This work significantly enhances our capability to map the distribution of neutral hydrogen and ionized gas around distant galaxies, providing crucial insights into the mechanisms driving star formation and feedback in different cosmic epochs.

We develop an analog of harmonic replacement in the gauge theory context. The
idea behind harmonic replacement dates back to Schwarz and Perron. The
technique, as introduced by Jost and further developed by Colding and
Minicozzi, involves taking a map $v\colon\Sigma\to M$ defined on a surface
$\Sigma$ and replacing its values on a small ball $B^2\subset\Sigma$ with a
harmonic map $u$ that has the same values as $v$ on the boundary $\partial
B^2$. The resulting map on $\Sigma$ has lower energy, and repeating this
process on balls covering $\Sigma$, one can obtain a global harmonic map in the
limit. We develop the analogous procedure in the gauge theory context. We take
a connection $B$ on a bundle over a four-manifold $X$, and replace it on a
small ball $B^4\subset X$ with a Yang--Mills connection $A$ that has the same
restriction to the boundary $\partial B^4$ as $B$. As in the harmonic
replacement results of Colding and Minicozzi, we have bounds on the difference
$\lVert B-A\rVert_{L^2_1(X)}^2$ in terms of the drop in energy, and we only
require that the connection $B$ have small energy on the ball, rather than
small $C^0$ oscillation. Throughout, we work with connections of the lowest
possible regularity $L^2_1(X)$, the natural choice for this context, and so our
gauge transformations are in $L^2_2(X)$ and therefore almost but not quite
continuous, leading to more delicate arguments than in higher regularity.

Spatial survival analysis has received a great deal of attention over the
last 20 years due to the important role that geographical information can play
in predicting survival. This paper provides an introduction to a set of
programs for implementing some Bayesian spatial survival models in R using the
package spBayesSurv. The function survregbayes includes the three most
commonly-used semiparametric models: proportional hazards, proportional odds,
and accelerated failure time. All manner of censored survival times are
simultaneously accommodated including uncensored, interval censored,
current-status, left and right censored, and mixtures of these. Left-truncated
data are also accommodated. Time-dependent covariates are allowed under the
piecewise constant assumption. Both georeferenced and areally observed spatial
locations are handled via frailties. Model fit is assessed with conditional
Cox-Snell residual plots, and model choice is carried out via the log pseudo
marginal likelihood, the deviance information criterion and the Watanabe-Akaike
information criterion. The accelerated failure time frailty model with a
covariate-dependent baseline is included in the function frailtyGAFT. In
addition, the package also provides two marginal survival models: proportional
hazards and linear dependent Dirichlet process mixture, where the spatial
dependence is modeled via spatial copulas. Note that the package can also
handle non-spatial data using non-spatial versions of aforementioned models.

text: In this study, we employed Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) simulations to investigate the epitaxial growth of gallium nitride (GaN) films on both c-plane and m-plane substrates. By incorporating a comprehensive set of rate constants and surface energies, we modeled the diffusion, reaction, and deposition steps during the growth process. The simulations revealed that GaN nucleation is significantly influenced by the substrate orientation, with a higher tendency for c-plane substrates due to their lower energy barrier for initial adsorption sites. Additionally, the island formation on m-plane substrates was characterized by a more complex growth pattern compared to c-plane, attributed to the presence of threading dislocations and lattice mismatch-induced strain fields. Key insights from our simulations include the identification of optimal growth conditions for achieving uniform island size distributions on both substrates. These findings contribute to the understanding of GaN epitaxy and provide valuable guidelines for optimizing growth parameters in industrial processes.

text: The abstract for the research paper on generalized forbidden subposet problems outlines the study's objectives, methodology, key findings, and conclusions. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between structural constraints and the emergent properties of posets. The conclusion underscores the significance of generalized forbidden subposet problems in elucidating fundamental aspects of order theory and their potential applications in areas such as database theory and bioinformatics.

text: In this study, we investigate the consistency of approximate quantum dynamics simulation methods for computing vibrational spectra in the condensed phase. We focus on assessing the reliability of these methods in capturing the essential features of vibrational spectra, such as peak positions, intensities, and line shapes, under varying degrees of environmental complexity. Through our systematic analysis, we aim to provide insights into the conditions under which different approximate quantum dynamics methods yield consistent results and elucidate the underlying factors influencing their accuracy in the condensed phase. Our methodology involves performing numerical simulations using a range of approximate quantum dynamics techniques, including semi-classical and quantum dynamical approaches, across various molecular systems and environmental conditions. We study an extension of the Higgs sector of the Minimal Supersymmetric
Standard Model (MSSM), considering the effects of new degrees of freedom at the
TeV scale, and allowing for sources of CP violation beyond the MSSM (BMSSM). We
analyze the impact of the BMSSM sources of CP violation on the Higgs collider
phenomenology and on low energy flavor and CP violating observables. We
identify distinct Higgs collider signatures that cannot be realized, either in
the case without CP violating phases or in the CP violating MSSM, and
investigate the prospects to probe them at the Tevatron and the LHC. The most
striking benchmark scenario has three neutral Higgs bosons that all decay
dominantly into W boson pairs and that are well within the reach of the 7 TeV
LHC run. On the other hand, we also present scenarios with three Higgs bosons
that have masses M_Hi > 150 GeV and decay dominantly into b bbar. Such
scenarios are much more challenging to probe and can even lie completely
outside the reach of the 7 TeV LHC run. We explore complementary scenarios with
standard MSSM Higgs signals that allow to accommodate a sizable B_s mixing
phase as indicated by D0, as well as the excess in B_s --> mu+ mu- candidates
recently reported by CDF. We find that, in contrast to the MSSM, a minimal
flavor violating soft sector is sufficient to generate significant corrections
to CP violating observables in meson mixing, compatible with EDM constraints.
In particular, a sizable B_s mixing phase, S_psiphi < 0.4, can be achieved for
specific regions of parameter space. Such a large B_s mixing phase would
unambiguously imply a sizable suppression of S_psiKs with respect to the SM
prediction and a BR(B_s --> mu+ mu-) close to the 95% C.L. upper bound reported
by CDF.
