text: The S140 Perseus Dark Cloud (PDR) is a well-studied nearby star-forming region, where the interplay between ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the OB star HD 24770 and the molecular cloud leads to the formation of a complex photodissociation region (PDR). In this work, we investigate the origin of the [C II] 158µm emission, the dominant coolant in PDRs, using data from the HIFI instrument on board the Herschel Space Observatory. We focus on the southern part of the cloud, which shows a more evolved PDR structure than the northern part, allowing for a detailed analysis. Our analysis reveals that the [C II] emission originates from both the surface of the dense molecular cloud and the warm neutral gas in the PDR. The surface emission is attributed to the photodissociation of CO ice on grain surfaces and its subsequent recombination, while the PDR emission is produced by the collisionally excited neutral carbon atoms. We find that the PDR emission accounts for only a small fraction of the total [C II] emission in the southern part of S140. The results of this study provide new insights into the origin of the [C II] emission in PDRs and contribute to the understanding of the interplay between UV radiation and molecular clouds. Our analysis also highlights the importance of HIFI data in the study of complex astrochemical environments. Future work will focus on investigating the origin of the [C II] emission in other PDRs, as well as the effects of varying UV radiation intensities and PDR structures on the [C II] emission properties.

It is long debated if pre-biotic molecules are indeed present in the
interstellar medium. Despite substantial works pointing to their existence,
pre-biotic molecules are yet to be discovered with a complete confidence. In
this paper, our main aim is to study the chemical evolution of interstellar
adenine under various circumstances. We prepare a large gas-grain chemical
network by considering various pathways for the formation of adenine. Majumdar
et al. (2012) proposed that in the absence of adenine detection, one could try
to trace two precursors of adenine, namely, HCCN and NH_2CN. Recently Merz et
al. (2014), proposed another route for the formation of adenine in interstellar
condition. They proposed two more precursor molecules. But it was not verified
by any accurate gas-grain chemical model. Neither was it known if the
production rate would be high or low. Our paper fills this important gap. We
include this new pathways to find that the contribution through this pathways
for the formation of Adenine is the most dominant one in the context of
interstellar medium. We propose that observers may look for the two precursors
(C_3NH and HNCNH) in the interstellar media which are equally important for
predicting abundances of adenine. We perform quantum chemical calculations to
find out spectral properties of adenine and its two new precursor molecules in
infrared, ultraviolet and sub-millimeter region. Our present study would be
useful for predicting abundance of adenine.

text: Power allocation in multicell massive Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) systems is crucial in optimizing the system's performance by managing interference and enhancing capacity. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that dynamic power allocation schemes can significantly enhance the system's performance by efficiently allocating power among users to mitigate interference and improve overall spectral efficiency.   The results highlight the importance of adaptive power allocation strategies in optimizing the performance of multicell massive MIMO systems, showing potential improvements in spectral efficiency, capacity, and quality of service. These findings provide valuable insights for the design and implementation of next-generation wireless communication systems.

The broad success of optimally controlling quantum systems with external
fields has been attributed to the favorable topology of the underlying control
landscape, where the landscape is the physical observable as a function of the
controls. The control landscape can be shown to contain no suboptimal trapping
extrema upon satisfaction of reasonable physical assumptions, but this
topological analysis does not hold when significant constraints are placed on
the control resources. This work employs simulations to explore the topology
and features of the control landscape for pure-state population transfer with a
constrained class of control fields. The fields are parameterized in terms of a
set of uniformly spaced spectral frequencies, with the associated phases acting
as the controls. Optimization results reveal that the minimum number of phase
controls necessary to assure a high yield in the target state has a special
dependence on the number of accessible energy levels in the quantum system,
revealed from an analysis of the first- and second-order variation of the yield
with respect to the controls. When an insufficient number of controls and/or a
weak control fluence are employed, trapping extrema and saddle points are
observed on the landscape. When the control resources are sufficiently
flexible, solutions producing the globally maximal yield are found to form
connected `level sets' of continuously variable control fields that preserve
the yield. These optimal yield level sets are found to shrink to isolated
points on the top of the landscape as the control field fluence is decreased,
and further reduction of the fluence turns these points into suboptimal
trapping extrema on the landscape. Although constrained control fields can come
in many forms beyond the cases explored here, the behavior found in this paper
is illustrative of the impacts that constraints can introduce.

text: The Clusters AgeS Experiment (CASE) aims to enhance our understanding of stellar evolution by examining variable stars within globular clusters, focusing on M4, one of the closest clusters to Earth. The objective is to utilize these stellar populations to refine models of stellar dynamics and improve our knowledge of the early Milky Way formation. The methodology integrates multi-epoch photometric observations obtained via CCD imaging with comprehensive time-series analysis and period determination techniques to identify and characterize variable stars' properties. Advanced spectral analysis supplements this data, providing insights into their luminosities and surface compositions. The key findings reveal a diverse range of variable stars within M4, with newly identified eclipsing binaries contributing significantly to the refinement of the cluster's age estimation. Additionally, the improved period-luminosity relationship for RR Lyrae stars supports a more precise distance measurement to M4. These results lead to a revised age estimate for the globular cluster, suggesting older origins than previously thought. This research underscores the significance of variable stars as benchmarks for calibrating theoretical models of stellar evolution and tracing the astrophysical history of our galaxy. The findings enhance our understanding of globular clusters and their role in the broader context of galactic archaeology, offering a more nuanced view of the complexities involved in the early stages of the Milky Way's development.

If autonomous vehicles are to be widely accepted, we need to ensure their
safe operation. For this reason, verification and validation (V&V) approaches
must be developed that are suitable for this domain. Model checking is a formal
technique which allows us to exhaustively explore the paths of an abstract
model of a system. Using a probabilistic model checker such as PRISM, we may
determine properties such as the expected time for a mission, or the
probability that a specific mission failure occurs. However, model checking of
complex systems is difficult due to the loss of information during abstraction.
This is especially so when considering systems such as autonomous vehicles
which are subject to external influences. An alternative solution is the use of
Monte Carlo simulation to explore the results of a continuous-time model of the
system. The main disadvantage of this approach is that the approach is not
exhaustive as not all executions of the system are analysed. We are therefore
interested in developing a framework for formal verification of autonomous
vehicles, using Monte Carlo simulation to inform and validate our symbolic
models during the initial stages of development. In this paper, we present a
continuous-time model of a quadrotor unmanned aircraft undertaking an
autonomous mission. We employ this model in Monte Carlo simulation to obtain
specific mission properties which will inform the symbolic models employed in
formal verification.

The purpose of this paper is to show the unusual behavior of a number of
simple circuits under the effects of post-selection. A useful duality exists
between post-selected ensembles and a consistent picture of acausal physics
embodying the application of Novikov's consistency postulate to the
wave-function of a time machine. A competing view applies this postulate to
density matrices instead, but that lies outside the scope of this paper. To
find out the result of a measurement on a particular circuit, we consider a
weighted distribution of histories between some initial and final time, such
that each individually obeys ordinary quantum mechanics. The weight of a
particular history is given by a joint distribution over the values of a part
of the system dubbed the time machine, at two chosen times. In the dual
post-selection picture the weight is simply the probability for the 'periodic
bit' to satisfy the constraint, plus a small noise part, often assumed
constant, representing the error rate of the time machine's channel. The
emerging bit is one of a Bell pair, its partner kept in reserve to test that
the bit entering the time machine later matches the one which emerged. This is
done by interfering the incoming bit with the reserve member of the pair and
keeping the experimental runs that interfere constructively. Noise can be
effectively simulated by keeping a small proportion of runs that interfere
destructively, or by perturbing the reserve bit to decohere it by a similar
amount. Paradoxes remain but are tractable.

text: This research paper investigates the concept that the principle of no-signalling in quantum mechanics is equivalent to the free choice of measurements. The background of this study lies in the foundational principles of quantum mechanics, particularly the notion that measurements made on entangled particles can appear to affect each other instantaneously, even when separated by vast distances. The objective of this paper is to provide a thorough analysis of how the assumption of no-signalling leads to the implication that the choice of measurement settings on one particle is independent of any influence from the other, thereby preserving locality.   Methodologically, this research utilizes mathematical modeling and theoretical derivations to demonstrate the equivalence between the constraints of no-signalling and the freedom in selecting measurements. Key findings indicate that by assuming no-signalling, it logically follows that the outcomes of measurements are indeed due to the choices made locally at each measurement apparatus. This implies that any appearance of non-local effects in quantum systems can be reconciled through a proper understanding of the limitations imposed by no-signalling.  In conclusion, this study confirms that within the framework of no-signalling, the freedom to choose measurements independently is a valid and consistent interpretation in quantum mechanics. This contributes to a deeper understanding of the fundamental principles governing the behavior of entangled particles and sheds light on the nature of quantum correlations within a local and no-signalling framework.

The physical properties of metamagnetic Fe$_3$Ga$_4$ single crystals are
investigated to explore the sensitivity of the magnetic states to temperature,
magnetic field, and sample history. The data reveal a moderate anisotropy in
the magnetization and the metamagnetic critical field along with features in
the specific heat at the magnetic transitions $T_1=68$ K and $T_2=360$ K. Both
$T_1$ and $T_2$ are found to be sensitive to the annealing conditions of the
crystals suggesting that disorder affects the competition between the
ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM) states. Resistivity measurements
reveal metallic transport with a sharp anomaly associated with the transition
at $T_2$. The Hall effect is dominated by the anomalous contribution which
rivals that of magnetic semiconductors in magnitude ($-5 \mu \Omega$ cm at 2 T
and 350 K) and undergoes a change of sign upon cooling into the low temperature
FM state. The temperature and field dependence of the Hall effect indicate that
the magnetism is likely to be highly itinerant in character and that a
significant change in the electronic structure accompanies the magnetic
transitions. We observe a contribution from the topological Hall effect in the
AFM phase suggesting a non-coplanar contribution to the magnetism. Electronic
structure calculations predict an AFM ground state with a wavevector parallel
to the crystallographic $c$-axis preferred over the experimentally measured FM
state by $\approx$ 50 meV per unit cell. However, supercell calculations with a
small density of Fe-antisite defects introduced tend to stabilize the FM over
the AFM state indicating that antisite defects may be the cause of the
sensitivity to sample synthesis conditions.

As the total mass of stellar populations of fixed IMF, age and metallicity
tends to infinity, resulting intrinsic $M/L$ values quickly converge to fixed
numbers associated to the particulars of the stars in question. When going to
very small stellar populations, the stochastic sampling of the IMF will yield
an inherent spread for the $M/L$ values, which will become probabilistic
quantities. For the recently discovered ultra-faint dwarf spheroidal galaxies,
with total luminosities dropping below 10^3 L_V/L_o, it is important to asses
the amplitude of the probabilistic spread in inherent $M/L$ values. The total
baryonic masses of these systems are usually estimated from their luminosities,
assuming fixed, deterministic $M/L$ values, suitable for the infinite
population limit. These total baryonic masses are crucial for the testing of
structure formation scenarios, as the local ultra-faint dwarf spheroidals
represent the most extreme galactic scales known. Also subject to reliable
$M/L$ values, is the use of these systems as possible discriminants between
dark matter and modified gravity theories. By simulating large collections of
stellar populations, each consisting of a particular collection of individual
stars, we compute statistical distributions for the resulting $M/L$ values. For
total numbers of stars in the range of what is observed for the ultra-faint
dwarf spheroidals, inherent $M/L$ values of stellar populations can be expected
to vary by factors of upwards of 3, interestingly, systematically skewed
towards higher values than what corresponds to the infinite population limit.
This can explain part of the spread in reported baryonic masses for these
systems, which also appear as shifted systematically towards high dark to
baryonic mass ratios at fixed stellar velocity dispersions.

text: This research investigates the characteristics of axial and polar gravitational wave equations within the context of a de Sitter expanding universe, utilizing the Laplace transform as a methodological framework. As gravitational waves are fundamental to our understanding of the universe's dynamic behavior, it is crucial to explore their properties in cosmological models that reflect universal expansion, such as the de Sitter universe. The primary objective of the study is to analytically derive and analyze solutions to the axial and polar perturbation equations using the Laplace transform technique, which provides a robust framework for handling differential equations with boundary conditions at infinity. The methodology involves formulating the perturbation equations for a spherically symmetric spacetime embedded in a de Sitter background and applying the Laplace transform to obtain solutions in the frequency domain. These solutions are then analyzed and compared with those obtained through traditional methods to evaluate the efficacy of the Laplace transform approach. Key findings reveal that the Laplace transform significantly simplifies the problem, facilitating an in-depth understanding of the time evolution of gravitational waves in an expanding universe. The results demonstrate that axial and polar waves exhibit distinct propagation characteristics influenced by the de Sitter expansion. Conclusion drawn asserts that the Laplace transform is a powerful tool for exploring gravitational wave dynamics in cosmological models, providing insights that could be pivotal for interpreting observational data from gravitational wave detection experiments. Future work will focus on extending this framework to more complex spacetime geometries.

In many areas of research it is interesting how lattices can be filled with
particles that have no nearest neighbors, or they are in limited quantities.
Examples may be found in statistical physics, chemistry, materials science,
discrete mathematics, etc. Using Monte Carlo (MC) simulation we study the
kinetics of filling of square lattice (2D). Two complementary rules are used to
fill the lattice. We study their influence on the kinetics of the process as
well as on the properties of the obtained systems. According to the first rule
the occupied sites may not share edges (nearest neighbors occupations are not
permitted). Under this condition, the maximum possible concentration is 0.5,
forming a checkerboard type structure. However, we found that if the deposition
is done by random selection of sites the concentration of 0.5 is inaccessible
and the maximum concentration is Cmax(2D)=0.3638 (0.0003) for 2D lattice. If
the lattice is 3D we find that the maximal concentration is even lower
Cmax(3D)=0.326 (0.001). The second rule establishes permission to break the
first one with certain probability 0<=p<=1, thus the occupied sites can start
to share edges when p>0. In this case higher then 0.3638 concentrations are
accessible, even up to C=1. Therefore the percolation threshold Pc can be
reached. Its value depends on the value of the probability p. Our model
describes the kinetics of formation of thin films of particles attracted by the
substrate but repulsing each other.

text: This study investigates the optimality of multilevel preconditioners tailored for local mesh refinement in three-dimensional problems. The primary objective is to enhance computational efficiency by addressing the challenges posed by non-uniform grid structures that arise during adaptive refinement processes. We demonstrate through rigorous numerical experiments that our proposed multilevel framework significantly improves upon standard methods, achieving faster convergence rates for linear systems arising from finite element discretizations. Key methodologies include the construction of hierarchical basis functions and the design of smoother operators that are adapted to the local mesh characteristics. Our findings indicate that these techniques lead to preconditioners that are both robust and scalable, making them particularly suitable for large-scale three-dimensional simulations.

text: Protoplanetary disks, the birthplaces of planets, exhibit complex gas dynamics and chemistry. The presence of hot molecular hydrogen (H2) signatures is a crucial marker for understanding the thermal structure, gas surface densities, and ionization conditions of these disks. This study explores the non-thermal populations of H2 absorption lines observed in a sample of Class I and II disks using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). We analyzed the spectral data of 12 disks and identified the non-thermal H2 lines using spectral modeling and radiative transfer simulations. Our findings reveal that non-thermal H2 lines are prevalent in both Class I and II disks, with a detection rate of 75% and 83%, respectively. We attribute the presence of these lines to the presence of shocks or X-rays in the disks. We further find that the non-thermal H2 lines display a significant correlation with the disk's inner dust temperature. Our results suggest that non-thermal H2 lines provide crucial insight into the heating mechanisms and ionization conditions within protoplanetary disks. The investigation of non-thermal H2 populations in larger samples and at higher spatial resolutions will enable a more comprehensive understanding of the gas dynamics and chemistry in protoplanetary disks.

text: We present an updated analysis of radion-Higgs mixing phenomena, leveraging the latest data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This study aims to refine the theoretical understanding and experimental implications of the interplay between the radion and Higgs boson within the framework of extradimensional theories. The challenge addressed is the complex interaction between these scalar fields, whose mixing could result in modifications to the Higgs boson's properties, thereby impacting observed signal strengths at collider experiments. Employing a perturbative approach, we construct a modified potential accounting for radion stabilization mechanisms, integrating recent LHC measurements to constrain model parameters. Our methodology encompasses advanced fitting techniques, wherein we analyze signal strength modifiers and decay path signatures, facilitating accurate parameter estimation of the mixing angle and coupling strengths. Results indicate subtle yet significant deviations in the predicted branching ratios and production cross-sections when compared to a pure Higgs scenario. This evidence suggests that radion-Higgs mixing can produce measurable effects concurrent with LHC observations, without contradicting established data limits. Our findings underline the necessity for comprehensive model extensions in standard theoretical frameworks, addressing discrepancies observed in precision measurements. We further propose enhancements to experimental strategies, advocating for targeted searches that could isolate and identify characteristic signatures of radion dynamics. This work significantly contributes to the ongoing efforts in particle physics to elucidate the nature of scalar fields and their interactions, providing a robust foundation for subsequent experimental and theoretical investigations.

text: This paper presents a novel approach to instrumentation support for debuggers and other software tools. The background of the study highlights the challenges and limitations of existing instrumentation techniques, such as their inflexibility and inefficiency.  The objective of this research is to develop an instrumentation framework that overcomes these limitations and enables users to define custom instrumentation rules with ease. The methodology section details the design and implementation of Polyglot, which uses just-in-time (JIT) compilation, source transformation, and bytecode manipulation techniques to achieve instrumentation.  Key findings of the study include improved performance through dynamic JIT compilation and flexibility in defining custom instrumentation rules using source transformation and bytecode manipulation. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness and applicability of Polyglot by instrumenting popular open-source projects such as Apache OpenOffice, Google Chrome, and Mozilla Firefox.  In conclusion, this paper proposes Polyglot, a fast, flexible, and polyglot instrumentation framework that addresses the limitations of existing instrumentation techniques. By combining JIT compilation, source transformation, and bytecode manipulation, Polyglot offers an efficient and extensible solution for instrumenting various software tools, including debuggers, profilers, and monitors.

Coupled-wire constructions have proven to be useful tools to characterize
Abelian and non-Abelian topological states of matter in two spatial dimensions.
In many cases, their success has been complemented by the vast arsenal of other
theoretical tools available to study such systems. In three dimensions,
however, much less is known about topological phases. Since the theoretical
arsenal in this case is smaller, it stands to reason that wire constructions,
which are based on one-dimensional physics, could play a useful role in
developing a greater microscopic understanding of three-dimensional topological
phases. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive strategy, based on the
geometric arrangement of commuting projectors in the toric code, to generate
and characterize coupled-wire realizations of strongly-interacting
three-dimensional topological phases. We show how this method can be used to
construct pointlike and linelike excitations, and to determine the topological
degeneracy. We also point out how, with minor modifications, the machinery
already developed in two dimensions can be naturally applied to study the
surface states of these systems, a fact that has implications for the study of
surface topological order. Finally, we show that the strategy developed for the
construction of three-dimensional topological phases generalizes readily to
arbitrary dimensions, vastly expanding the existing landscape of coupled-wire
theories. Throughout the paper, we discuss $\mathbb{Z}^{\,}_m$ topological
order in three and four dimensions as a concrete example of this approach, but
the approach itself is not limited to this type of topological order.

text: This research explores the application of transfer learning techniques within recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for clinical time series analysis, aiming to enhance predictive accuracy and model efficiency.  Clinical time series data often exhibit complex temporal dependencies and require sophisticated models to capture these patterns accurately. Traditional machine learning approaches can struggle with the high dimensionality and variability of such data, leading to suboptimal performance.  The study aims to leverage pre-trained RNN models on large-scale non-clinical datasets to initialize weights and improve convergence speed during training on smaller, more specific clinical datasets.  The proposed approach involves fine-tuning existing pre-trained RNN models on a subset of clinical time series data, transferring knowledge from the pre-training phase to optimize the final model's performance on clinical tasks. Key findings The results indicate that transfer learning significantly improves prediction accuracy compared to baseline models, particularly in scenarios where training data is limited. Moreover, the approach demonstrates robustness across different clinical domains, achieving comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art models trained from scratch.  This research underscores the potential of transfer learning in enhancing clinical time series analysis through RNNs, suggesting it as a promising direction for improving diagnostic and prognostic capabilities in healthcare settings.

text: This study examines the relationship between coronal holes and the evolution of the solar global magnetic field from 1976 to 2012. The objective was to understand how coronal hole activity influenced the solar magnetic field dynamics over a significant period. Using a combination of solar observations from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) and data from the Wilcox Solar Observatory, we analyzed the correlation between coronal hole locations and changes in the solar global magnetic field strength and polarity.  The methodology involved detailed statistical analysis of HMI data to identify coronal holes and their positions relative to the sun's surface. We then correlated these observations with measurements of the total solar irradiance and the solar magnetic flux as recorded by the Wilcox Solar Observatory. Additionally, we employed numerical simulations to model the magnetic field evolution based on observed coronal hole patterns.  Key findings indicated that during periods of high coronal hole activity, there was a noticeable increase in the total solar magnetic flux, particularly in regions where coronal holes were present. This suggests a direct link between coronal hole formation and the expansion of the solar magnetic field. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the polarity of the solar magnetic field varied significantly across different coronal hole regions, indicating complex interactions within the solar atmosphere.  In conclusion, this research underscores the importance of coronal hole observation in understanding the long-term evolution of the solar global magnetic field. The findings highlight the need for continued monitoring of coronal holes to better predict solar activity cycles and their impacts on Earth's space environment.

Charge transport within Coulomb blockade regime in two-dimensional
nanoparticle arrays exhibits nonlinear I-V characteristics, where the level of
nonlinearity strongly associates with the array's architecture. Here, we use
different mathematical approaches to quantify collective behavior in the charge
transport inside the sample and its relationship to the structural
characteristics of the assembly and the presence of charge disorder. In
particular, we simulate single-electron tunneling conduction in several
assemblies with controlled variation of the structural components (branching,
extended linear segments) that influence the local communication among the
conducting paths between the electrodes. Furthermore, by applying the fractal
analysis of time series of the number of tunnelings and the technique of
algebraic topology, we unravel the temporal correlations and structure of the
phase-space manifolds corresponding to the cooperative fluctuations of charge.
By tracking the I-V curves in different assemblies together with the indicators
of collective dynamics and topology of manifolds in the state space, we show
that the increased I-V nonlinearity is fully consistent with the enhanced
aggregate fluctuations and topological complexity of the participating states.
The architecture that combines local branching and global topological disorder
enables the creation of large drainage basins of nano-rivers leading to
stronger cooperation effects. Also, by determining shifts in the topology and
collective transport features, we explore the impact of the size of electrodes
and local charge disorder. The results are relevant for designing the
nanoparticle devices with improved conduction; they also highlight the
significance of topological descriptions for a broader understanding of the
nature of fluctuations at the nanoscale.

text: This abstract outlines the research focused on identifying dense cores within galaxies extending up to redshift (z) = 2.5 across various large-scale surveys, including the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), UltraVISTA, and the 3D-HST/CANDELS fields. These dense cores, crucial for understanding star formation and galaxy evolution, were investigated through a comprehensive analysis of multi-wavelength data.  The primary objective was to map and characterize dense cores in galaxies at high redshifts, thereby contributing to our understanding of how star formation processes have evolved over cosmic time. To achieve this, we employed a combination of photometric and spectroscopic observations to identify and classify dense cores. We utilized wide-field imaging from SDSS and UltraVISTA, complemented by detailed multi-object spectroscopy from CANDELS and Hubble Space Telescope (HST).  Key findings included the identification of dense cores in galaxies with stellar masses ranging from a few times 10^9 to a few times 10^10 solar masses. Our analysis revealed that these dense cores exhibit higher gas fractions compared to less dense regions, indicating vigorous star formation activity. Additionally, we observed significant differences in the spatial distribution and morphological properties of dense cores between different redshift bins, suggesting variations in the physical conditions and environmental influences affecting star formation.  The study concluded with a discussion of the implications of these findings for our understanding of galaxy evolution and star formation histories. The results highlight the importance of studying dense cores in high-redshift galaxies to elucidate the role of feedback mechanisms and environmental effects on the cosmic star formation history. Future work will focus on refining our observational techniques and expanding the sample size to include even more distant galaxies.

text: Random sampling with removal, also known as sampling without replacement, is a statistical technique used to select a sample from a finite population while ensuring that every member of the population has a non-zero probability of being selected. This method contrasts with simple random sampling with replacement, where the same individual can be selected multiple times. The significance of random sampling with removal lies in its applicability to various fields, including quality control, market research, and statistical analysis.  The objective of this study is to investigate the impact of sample size and population size on the effectiveness of random sampling with removal. The methodology employed in this research includes generating random samples of varying sizes from finite populations using a random number generator. The effectiveness of the random sampling with removal method is evaluated by calculating the probability of selecting each member of the population in the sample and comparing it to the expected probability based on the sample size and population size.  Key findings indicate that as sample size increases, the probability of selecting any individual from the population approaches its expected value. Conversely, as population size increases, the difference between the actual and expected probabilities becomes more pronounced. Additionally, the study reveals that the use of random sampling with removal can lead to increased sampling efficiency, as the inclusion of duplicates, which can occur with simple random sampling with replacement, is eliminated.  In conclusion, this research illustrates that random sampling with removal is an effective statistical technique for selecting samples from finite populations, with the added benefit of increased sampling efficiency. The findings suggest that the choice of sampling method depends on the specific context of the research and the desirability of including duplicates in the sample. These results have implications for various fields, including quality control, market research, and statistical analysis, providing valuable insights for researchers and practitioners alike.

Decreasing transistor sizes and lower voltage swings cause two distinct
problems for communication in integrated circuits. First, decreasing inter-wire
spacing increases interline capacitive coupling, which adversely affects
transmission energy and delay. Second, lower voltage swings render the
transmission susceptible to various noise sources. Coding can be used to
address both these problems. So-called crosstalk-avoidance codes mitigate
capacitive coupling, and traditional error-correction codes introduce
resilience against channel errors.
  Unfortunately, crosstalk-avoidance and error-correction codes cannot be
combined in a straightforward manner. On the one hand, crosstalk-avoidance
encoding followed by error-correction encoding destroys the crosstalk-avoidance
property. On the other hand, error-correction encoding followed by
crosstalk-avoidance encoding causes the crosstalk-avoidance decoder to fail in
the presence of errors. Existing approaches circumvent this difficulty by using
additional bus wires to protect the parities generated from the output of the
error-correction encoder, and are therefore inefficient.
  In this work we propose a novel joint crosstalk-avoidance and
error-correction coding and decoding scheme that provides higher bus
transmission rates compared to existing approaches. Our joint approach
carefully embeds the parities such that the crosstalk-avoidance property is
preserved. We analyze the rate and minimum distance of the proposed scheme. We
also provide a density evolution analysis and predict iterative decoding
thresholds for reliable communication under random bus erasures. This density
evolution analysis is nonstandard, since the crosstalk-avoidance constraints
are inherently nonlinear.

text: This research paper presents an analytical treatment of the ultra-strong coupling regime in a Qubit-oscillator system. The Qubit-oscillator system is a paradigmatic model for studying the interplay between quantum mechanics and classical mechanics, and its ultra-strong coupling regime has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its potential applications in quantum information processing and quantum metrology. In this regime, the interaction between the qubit and the oscillator is so strong that the system exhibits quantum coherence and entanglement, leading to novel phenomena such as non-classical correlations and quantum squeezed states.  The objective of this study is to develop a rigorous analytical framework for understanding the behavior of the Qubit-oscillator system in the ultra-strong coupling regime. By combining techniques from quantum field theory and quantum optics, we derive a set of coupled differential equations that describe the dynamics of the system. We then apply these equations to a range of parameters, including the strength of the coupling, the frequency of the oscillator, and the initial conditions of the qubit.  Our key findings include the emergence of non-classical correlations and entanglement in the system, as well as the presence of quantum squeezed states. We also demonstrate the potential for the Qubit-oscillator system to be used as a quantum simulator for studying the behavior of ultracold atomic gases and other quantum systems. Our results have significant implications for our understanding of the behavior of quantum systems in the ultra-strong coupling regime, and provide a foundation for further research into the applications of Qubit-oscillator systems in quantum information processing and quantum metrology.

text: The dynamics of lipid vesicles interacting with surfactants have been of great interest in various fields, including pharmaceuticals and food industries. The solubilization kinetics of surfactants plays a crucial role in the pulsatory behavior of lipid vesicles. This study aims to investigate the influence of solubilization kinetics on the pulsatory dynamics of lipid vesicles using size and intensity correlation spectroscopy. Dextran sulfate liposomes with varying sizes were prepared and exposed to SDS surfactant at different concentrations. The size and intensity correlation functions were analyzed to determine the self-diffusion coefficients and average hydrodynamic radii of the vesicles. The pulsatory behavior of the vesicles was observed using dynamic light scattering, revealing that the pulsations became more frequent and smaller in amplitude with increasing surfactant concentration. The self-diffusion coefficients and average hydrodynamic radii decreased with the increasing surfactant concentration, indicating the formation of micelles and vesicle aggregates. These findings suggest that the pulsatory dynamics of lipid vesicles are determined by the solubilization kinetics of the surfactants, providing valuable insights for understanding the behavior of lipid-surfactant systems in various applications.

text: We investigate the paradoxical notion that greed can be beneficial in the context of deterministic scale-free networks. Through a comprehensive analysis of network topologies, we find that the introduction of greedy algorithms in the network formation process can lead to the emergence of robust and resilient scale-free networks. By exploiting the inherent structure of the network, greedy algorithms can optimize the distribution of nodes and edges, resulting in a more efficient and stable network. Our results demonstrate that the incorporation of greedy mechanisms in the network formation process can mitigate the effects of random fluctuations, leading to a more stable and reliable network. We also show that the greedy algorithms can adapt to changing network conditions, allowing the network to self-organize and respond to external perturbations. Our findings challenge the conventional wisdom that greed is inherently detrimental to network stability and highlight the importance of considering the role of greed in network formation. By developing a deeper understanding of the interplay between greed and network structure, we can design more effective and resilient network systems that can withstand a wide range of environmental challenges.

text: We investigate the Submodular Secretary Problem, a classical extension of the secretary problem that arises in various applications such as resource allocation and online decision-making. Our primary objective is to develop a linear-time algorithm that efficiently addresses the unique challenges posed by the submodular structures involved in the problem. Through a thorough analysis of the properties of submodular functions, we identify key characteristics that enable us to formulate a competitive algorithm with performance guarantees.   Our methodology involves constructing a novel selection strategy that leverages greedy principles while maintaining submodular constraints. We employ a randomized approach, which allows for adaptability in the face of uncertain inputs, and rigorously prove that our algorithm achieves a constant-factor approximation to the optimal solution in linear time complexity. We conduct extensive simulations and theoretical evaluations that demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed algorithm compared to existing ones.  The results reveal not only the viability of solving the Submodular Secretary Problem in linear time but also highlight the underlying structure of submodular functions that can be exploited for optimal decision-making. Our findings contribute significantly to the field by providing a scalable solution to a fundamental problem, thus enabling practical applications across various domains. Future work will focus on extending these results to other related problems and exploring additional constraints that may arise in real-world scenarios.

text: Title Maximum Induced Density of Almost All Graphs An Exact Analysis   The study of graph densities, specifically the induced density, has attracted much attention due to its applications in various fields, including computer science, social networks, and physics. However, finding the exact maximum induced density for a specific graph is often computationally infeasible. Thus, researchers have focused on understanding the behavior of maximum induced density for different graph classes.   This paper aims to provide an exact analysis of the maximum induced density of almost all graphs. We consider a random graph model, the Erdős-Rényi model (ER), with a given edge probability p to analyze the maximum induced density.   We employ a combination of analytical and probabilistic methods to determine the exact maximum induced density for the ER model. Specifically, we use the method of moments and Stirling's approximation to derive closed-form expressions for the expected size of maximum cliques and their probability distribution.   We establish that the maximum induced density in the ER model converges to a non-trivial limit as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Furthermore, we calculate the exact value of this limit for different edge probabilities, providing precise insights into the behavior of maximum induced density in random graphs.   Our findings contribute to the understanding of graph densities and their behavior in random graphs, providing valuable results for the theoretical analysis of complex networks and algorithms based on graph properties. We expect that our methods and techniques can be extended to study other graph properties, such as connectivity and vertex cover, in random graph models.

We consider a network where strategic agents, who are contesting for
allocation of resources, are divided into fixed groups. The network control
protocol is such that within each group agents get to share the resource and
across groups they contest for it. A prototypical example is the allocation of
data rate on a network with multicast/multirate architecture. Compared to the
unicast architecture (which is a special case), the multicast/multirate
architecture can result in substantial bandwidth savings. However, design of a
market mechanism in such a scenario requires dealing with both private and
public good problems as opposed to just private goods in unicast.
  The mechanism proposed in this work ensures that social welfare maximizing
allocation on such a network is realized at all Nash equilibria (NE) i.e., full
implementation in NE. In addition it is individually rational, i.e., agents
have an incentive to participate in the mechanism. The mechanism, which is
constructed in a quasi-systematic way starting from the dual of the centralized
problem, has a number of useful properties. Specifically, due to a novel
allocation scheme, namely "radial projection", the proposed mechanism results
in feasible allocation even off equilibrium. This is a practical necessity for
any realistic mechanism since agents have to "learn" the NE through a dynamic
process. Finally, it is shown how strong budget balance at equilibrium can be
achieved with a minimal increase in message space as an add-on to a weakly
budget balanced mechanism.

As a probe to explore the ability of invisibility cloaks to conceal objects
in the quantum mechanics domain, we study the spontaneous emission rate of an
excited two-level atom in the vicinity of an ideal invisibility cloaking. On
this base, first, a canonical quantization scheme is presented for the
electromagnetic field interacting with atomic systems in an anisotropic,
inhomogeneous and absorbing magnetodielectric medium which can suitably be used
for studying the influence of arbitrary invisibility cloak on the atomic
radiative properties. The time dependence of the atomic subsystem is obtained
in the Schrodinger picture. By introducing a modified set of the spherical wave
vector functions, the Green tensor of the system is calculated via the
continuous and discrete methods. In this formalism, the decay rate and as well
the emission pattern of the aforementioned atom are computed analytically for
both weak and strong coupling interaction, and then numerically calculations
are done to demonstrate the performances of cloaking in the quantum mechanics
domain. Special attention is paid to different possible orientations and
locations of atomic system near the spherical invisibility cloaking. Results in
the presence and the absence of the invisibility cloak are compared. We find
that the cloak works very well far from its resonance frequency to conceal a
macroscopic object, whereas at near the resonance frequency the object is more
visible than the situation that the object is not covered by the cloak.

The orientational dynamics of weakly inertial axisymmetric particles in a
steady flow is investigated. We derive an asymptotic equation of motion for the
unit axial vector along the particle symmetry axis, valid for small Stokes
number St, and for any axisymmetric particle in any steady linear viscous flow.
This reduced dynamics is analysed in two ways, both pertain to the case of a
simple shear flow. In this case inertia induces a coupling between precession
and nutation. This coupling affects the dynamics of the particle, breaks the
degeneracy of the Jeffery orbits, and creates two limiting periodic orbits. We
calculate the leading-order Floquet exponents of the limiting periodic orbits
and show analytically that prolate objects tend to a tumbling orbit, while
oblate objects tend to a log-rolling orbit, in agreement with previous
analytical and numerical results. Second, we analyse the role of the limiting
orbits when rotational noise is present. We formulate the Fokker-Planck
equation describing the orientational distribution of an axisymmetric particle,
valid for small St and general Peclet number Pe. Numerical solutions of the
Fokker-Planck equation, obtained by means of expansion in spherical harmonics,
show that stationary orientational distributions are close to the inertia-free
case when Pe St << 1, whereas they are determined by inertial effects, though
small, when Pe >> 1/St >> 1.

We consider the worst-case query complexity of some variants of certain
\cl{PPAD}-complete search problems. Suppose we are given a graph $G$ and a
vertex $s \in V(G)$. We denote the directed graph obtained from $G$ by
directing all edges in both directions by $G'$. $D$ is a directed subgraph of
$G'$ which is unknown to us, except that it consists of vertex-disjoint
directed paths and cycles and one of the paths originates in $s$. Our goal is
to find an endvertex of a path by using as few queries as possible. A query
specifies a vertex $v\in V(G)$, and the answer is the set of the edges of $D$
incident to $v$, together with their directions. We also show lower bounds for
the special case when $D$ consists of a single path. Our proofs use the theory
of graph separators. Finally, we consider the case when the graph $G$ is a grid
graph. In this case, using the connection with separators, we give
asymptotically tight bounds as a function of the size of the grid, if the
dimension of the grid is considered as fixed. In order to do this, we prove a
separator theorem about grid graphs, which is interesting on its own right.

We propose gradient adversarial training, an auxiliary deep learning
framework applicable to different machine learning problems. In gradient
adversarial training, we leverage a prior belief that in many contexts,
simultaneous gradient updates should be statistically indistinguishable from
each other. We enforce this consistency using an auxiliary network that
classifies the origin of the gradient tensor, and the main network serves as an
adversary to the auxiliary network in addition to performing standard
task-based training. We demonstrate gradient adversarial training for three
different scenarios: (1) as a defense to adversarial examples we classify
gradient tensors and tune them to be agnostic to the class of their
corresponding example, (2) for knowledge distillation, we do binary
classification of gradient tensors derived from the student or teacher network
and tune the student gradient tensor to mimic the teacher's gradient tensor;
and (3) for multi-task learning we classify the gradient tensors derived from
different task loss functions and tune them to be statistically
indistinguishable. For each of the three scenarios we show the potential of
gradient adversarial training procedure. Specifically, gradient adversarial
training increases the robustness of a network to adversarial attacks, is able
to better distill the knowledge from a teacher network to a student network
compared to soft targets, and boosts multi-task learning by aligning the
gradient tensors derived from the task specific loss functions. Overall, our
experiments demonstrate that gradient tensors contain latent information about
whatever tasks are being trained, and can support diverse machine learning
problems when intelligently guided through adversarialization using a auxiliary
network.

text: In our study on the magnetic topology of partially and fully convective stars, we investigated the complex interplay between stellar convection and magnetic fields. By employing observational data and theoretical models, we aimed to elucidate how the convective processes within stars influence their magnetic field configurations. Our results reveal that in partially convective stars, the interaction between the convective and radiative regions leads to the emergence of a diverse range of magnetic field topologies, including mixed poloidal-toroidal configurations. On the other hand, in fully convective stars, the dominance of convective motions results in the generation of predominantly toroidal magnetic fields. We also found that the presence of a convective envelope significantly impacts the orientation and strength of the stellar magnetic fields.  To address the complexities of the magnetic fields in convective stars, we employed numerical simulations and observational constraints to further understand the underlying physical processes. Our methodology involved analyzing magnetic field evolution models in conjunction with observational data of stellar magnetic activity. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of the connection between stellar convection and magnetic fields in partially and fully convective stars, shedding light on the intricate magnetic topology of these stellar bodies.

text: In this study, we investigated the relationship between computational capacity and energy consumption in complex resistive switch (RS) networks. Our experiments focused on a fully connected RS network consisting of 1024 nodes, where each node comprised a crosspoint RS memory cell. The network was programmed using binary weighted pulses to perform Boolean logic operations, enabling the computation of various digital circuits.      The computational capacity was evaluated using a set of well-known benchmark circuits, including AND, OR, XOR, NAND, and NOR gates. These circuits were designed to operate on fixed-size input sets and were implemented in the network using crosspoint RS memory cells. The resulting computational capacity was characterized in terms of the maximum number of digital circuits that could be computed per second, with an average throughput of 50 kHz.      The energy consumption was quantified using the total electrical energy consumed during the operation of the circuits. We used a commercially available power analyzer to measure the power consumption at the network input and output terminals. Our results indicated that the energy consumption increased proportionally with the size of the circuit, but the energy efficiency improved as the circuit complexity increased.      The key insights from our study revealed that complex RS networks could serve as high-performance and energy-efficient computing platforms. These networks offered a unique combination of computational power and energy efficiency that outperformed conventional computing architectures, particularly for low-power and battery-operated devices. We also proposed several potential improvements, including optimization algorithms for reducing energy consumption and the use of machine learning techniques for dynamic load balancing.      Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of complex RS networks in developing novel computing architectures that address the increasing demand for high-performance and energy-efficient systems. The findings may have significant implications for the design of future memory technologies, neural computing systems, and low-power sensing and communication networks.

Self-regulated feedback by active galactic nuclei (AGNs) appears to be
critical in balancing radiative cooling of the low-entropy gas at the centres
of galaxy clusters and in regulating star formation in central galaxies. In a
companion paper, we found steady-state solutions of the hydrodynamic equations
that are coupled to the CR energy equation for a large cluster sample. In those
solutions, radiative cooling in the central region is balanced by streaming CRs
through the generation and dissipation of resonantly generated Alfv{\'e}n waves
and by thermal conduction at large radii. Here we demonstrate that the
predicted non-thermal emission resulting from hadronic CR interactions in the
intra-cluster medium exceeds observational radio (and gamma-ray) data in a
subsample of clusters that host radio mini halos (RMHs). In contrast, the
predicted non-thermal emission is well below observational data in cooling
galaxy clusters without RMHs. These are characterised by exceptionally large
AGN radio fluxes, indicating high CR yields and associated CR heating rates. We
suggest a self-regulation cycle of AGN feedback in which non-RMH clusters are
heated by streaming CRs homogeneously throughout the central cooling region. We
predict {\em radio micro halos} surrounding the AGNs of these CR-heated
clusters in which the primary emission may predominate the hadronically
generated emission. Once the CR population has streamed sufficiently far and
lost enough energy, the cooling rate increases, which explains the increased
star formation rates in clusters hosting RMHs. Those could be powered
hadronically by CRs that have previously heated the cluster core.

For the past couple of decades, the Parkes radio telescope has been regularly
observing the millisecond pulsars in 47 Tucanae (47 Tuc). This long-term timing
program was designed to address a wide range of scientific issues related to
these pulsars and the globular cluster where they are located. In this paper,
the first of a series, we address one of these objectives: the characterization
of four previously known binary pulsars for which no precise orbital parameters
were known, namely 47 Tuc P, V, W and X (pulsars 47 Tuc R and Y are discussed
elsewhere). We determined the previously unknown orbital parameters of 47 Tuc V
and X and greatly improved those of 47 Tuc P and W. For pulsars W and X we
obtained, for the first time, full coherent timing solutions across the whole
data span, which allowed a much more detailed characterization of these
systems. 47 Tuc W, a well-known tight eclipsing binary pulsar, exhibits a large
orbital period variability, as expected for a system of its class. 47 Tuc X
turns out to be in a wide, extremely circular, 10.9-day long binary orbit and
its position is ~3.8 arcmin away from the cluster center, more than three times
the distance of any other pulsar in 47 Tuc. These characteristics make 47 Tuc X
a very different object with respect to the other pulsars of the cluster.

We present ATCA results of a 3 and 7 mm continuum survey of 20 T Tauri stars
in the Chamaeleon and Lupus star forming regions. This survey aims to identify
protoplanetary discs with signs of grain growth. We detected 90% of the sources
at 3 and 7 mm, and determined the spectral slopes, dust opacity indices and
dust disc masses. We also present temporal monitoring results of a small
sub-set of sources at 7, 15 mm and 3+6 cm to investigate grain growth to cm
sizes and constrain emission mechanisms in these sources. Additionally, we
investigated the potential correlation between grain growth signatures in the
infrared (10 \mu m silicate feature) and millimetre (1-3 mm spectral slope,
{\alpha}). Eleven sources at 3 and 7 mm have dominant thermal dust emission up
to 7 mm, with 7 of these having a 1-3 mm dust opacity index less than unity,
suggesting grain growth up to at least mm sizes. The Chamaeleon sources
observed at 15 mm and beyond show the presence of excess emission from an
ionised wind and/or chromo- spheric emission. Long-timescale monitoring at 7 mm
indicated that cm-sized pebbles are present in at least four sources.
Short-timescale monitoring at 15 mm suggests the excess emission is from
thermal free-free emission. Finally, a weak correlation was found between the
strength of the 10 \mum feature and {\alpha}, suggesting simultaneous dust
evolution of the inner and outer parts of the disc. This survey shows that
grain growth up to cm-sized pebbles and the presence of excess emission at 15
mm and beyond are common in these systems, and that temporal monitoring is
required to disentangle these emission mechanisms.
label: human

We present an analysis of MUSE observations obtained on the massive Frontier
Fields cluster Abell 2744. This new dataset covers the entire multiply-imaged
region around the cluster core. We measure spectroscopic redshifts for
HST-selected continuum sources together with line emitters blindly detected in
the datacube. The combined catalog consists of 514 spectroscopic redshifts
(with 414 new identifications), including 156 cluster members and 326 magnified
background sources. We use this redshift information to perform a
strong-lensing analysis of all multiple images previously found in the deep
Frontier Field images, and add three new MUSE-detected multiply-imaged systems
with no obvious HST counterpart. The combined strong lensing constraints
include a total of 60 systems producing 188 images altogether, out of which 29
systems and 83 images are spectroscopically confirmed, making Abell 2744 one of
the most well-constrained clusters to date. A parametric mass model including
two cluster-scale components in the core and several group-scale substructures
at larger radii accurately reproduces all the spectroscopic multiple systems,
reaching an rms of 0.67" in the image plane. Overall, the large number of
spectroscopic redshifts gives us a robust model and we estimate the systematics
on the mass density and magnification within the cluster core to be typically
~9%.
label: human

When modeling the distribution of a set of data by a mixture of Gaussians,
there are two possibilities: i) the classical one is using a set of parameters
which are the proportions, the means and the variances; ii) the second is to
consider the proportions as the probabilities of a discrete valued hidden
variable. In the first case a usual prior distribution for the proportions is
the Dirichlet which accounts for the fact that they have to sum up to one. In
the second case, to each data is associated a hidden variable for which we
consider two possibilities: a) assuming those variables to be i.i.d. We show
then that this scheme is equivalent to the classical mixture model with
Dirichlet prior; b) assuming a Markovian structure. Then we choose the simplest
markovian model which is the Potts distribution. As we will see this model is
more appropriate for the case where the data represents the pixels of an image
for which the hidden variables represent a segmentation of that image. The main
object of this paper is to give some details on these models and different
algorithms used for their simulation and the estimation of their parameters.
  Key Words: Mixture of Gaussians, Dirichlet, Potts, Classification,
Segmentation.
label: human

text: This study explores the application of a bole surface growth model to understand the transitional status of the -3/2 rule in tree growth patterns. The -3/2 rule, which posits a power-law relationship between tree height and basal stem diameter, is a fundamental concept in forest ecology and has been widely observed in tree growth dynamics. However, recent research has highlighted instances where this rule may not hold consistently throughout an individual tree's development. Our research aims to investigate this transitional status using a bole surface growth model, which incorporates both radial and height growth processes to provide a more comprehensive understanding of tree morphology.  Through the analysis of field data and model simulations, we observed deviations from the -3/2 rule during specific growth stages in tree development. These deviations suggest that the power-law relationship may not apply uniformly across all growth phases and highlight the importance of considering additional factors, such as competition, resource availability, and environmental conditions, in shaping tree growth patterns. Our findings provide valuable insights into the complexities of tree growth dynamics and emphasize the need for dynamic modeling approaches to capture the nuances of transitional growth patterns effectively. This research contributes to advancing our understanding of tree growth strategies and can inform forest management practices aimed at promoting healthy and sustainable ecosystems.
label: machine

text:
In a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) space-time background we study the
classical cosmological models in the context of recently proposed theory of
nonlinear minimal massive bigravity. We show that in the presence of perfect
fluid the classical field equations acquire contribution from the massive
graviton as a cosmological term which is positive or negative depending on the
dynamical competition between two scale factors of bigravity metrics. We obtain
the classical field equations for flat and open universes in the ordinary and
Schutz representation of perfect fluid. Focusing on the Schutz representation
for flat universe, we find classical solutions exhibiting singularities at
early universe with vacuum equation of state. Then, in the Schutz
representation, we study the quantum cosmology for flat universe and derive the
Schrodinger-Wheeler-DeWitt equation. We find its exact and wave packet
solutions and discuss on their properties to show that the initial singularity
in the classical solutions can be avoided by quantum cosmology. Similar to the
study of Hartle-Hawking no-boundary proposal in the quantum cosmology of de
Rham, Gabadadze and Tolley (dRGT) massive gravity, it turns out that the mass
of graviton predicted by quantum cosmology of the minimal massive bigravity is
large at early universe. This is in agreement with the fact that at early
universe the cosmological constant should be large.
label: human

text: The relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov (RHB) model is a powerful tool to describe the nuclear many-body problem, especially for studying the nuclear deformation. However, the calculation of axially deformed RHB systems with separable pairing interactions poses a significant challenge due to the complexity of the Bogoliubov equations. In this study, we propose a novel approach to tackle this issue, implementing a separable pairing force in the axially deformed RHB theory. This separable interaction is constructed based on a phenomenological Woods-Saxon potential. By introducing an angular-dependent form factor, the deformed pairing interaction becomes separable in the spherical and body-fixed frames. This separation allows us to perform a truncated configuration interaction calculation with a reduced Hilbert space.  The proposed methodology is applied to the axially deformed nuclei of 16O, 17O, and 16N, computing their ground-state properties. We find that, in contrast to the isoscalar case, the axially deformed neutron-neutron and proton-proton pairing interactions exhibit distinct behaviors. In particular, the neutron-neutron interactions have a stronger deformation dependence, while the proton-proton interactions show a more isotropic behavior. These results demonstrate the importance of a separable pairing force in axially deformed relativistic nuclear models.  In conclusion, this work presents a novel methodology for calculating axially deformed relativistic nuclear systems with separable pairing interactions. By implementing a separable pairing force, we overcome the computational challenges associated with deformed relativistic many-body theories. This new approach opens the door to a more systematic study of deformed nuclei using relativistic theories.
label: machine

In this paper we propose to use utterance-level Permutation Invariant
Training (uPIT) for speaker independent multi-talker speech separation and
denoising, simultaneously. Specifically, we train deep bi-directional Long
Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) using uPIT, for
single-channel speaker independent multi-talker speech separation in multiple
noisy conditions, including both synthetic and real-life noise signals. We
focus our experiments on generalizability and noise robustness of models that
rely on various types of a priori knowledge e.g. in terms of noise type and
number of simultaneous speakers. We show that deep bi-directional LSTM RNNs
trained using uPIT in noisy environments can improve the Signal-to-Distortion
Ratio (SDR) as well as the Extended Short-Time Objective Intelligibility
(ESTOI) measure, on the speaker independent multi-talker speech separation and
denoising task, for various noise types and Signal-to-Noise Ratios (SNRs).
Specifically, we first show that LSTM RNNs can achieve large SDR and ESTOI
improvements, when evaluated using known noise types, and that a single model
is capable of handling multiple noise types with only a slight decrease in
performance. Furthermore, we show that a single LSTM RNN can handle both
two-speaker and three-speaker noisy mixtures, without a priori knowledge about
the exact number of speakers. Finally, we show that LSTM RNNs trained using
uPIT generalize well to noise types not seen during training.
label: human

text: This study investigates the spectral signatures of quenched star formation activity in reionization-era galaxies by analyzing Lyman continuum (Lyα) emission leakage as observed through the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). Our primary objective is to discern whether the observed Lyα flux can be indicative of ongoing quenching processes within these distant galaxies. We employ detailed modeling techniques that incorporate the JWST's capabilities, including its high sensitivity and spectral resolution, to simulate and interpret the observed spectra. The analysis reveals distinct patterns in the Lyα emission that correlate with signs of recent quenching, such as reduced star formation rates and evidence of strong winds driven by feedback mechanisms. This research not only provides insights into the quenching mechanisms but also offers a new tool for identifying and characterizing galaxies at early cosmic times. Key methodologies include spectral fitting algorithms, radiative transfer simulations, and comparisons with theoretical models of galaxy evolution. Our findings suggest that the detection of Lyα leakage can serve as a robust proxy for quenching activities in reionization-era galaxies, offering valuable data for understanding the assembly of the first luminous structures in the universe.
label: machine

text:
We investigate the role of supernova (SN)-driven galactic winds in the
chemical enrichment of the intracluster medium (ICM). Such outflows on galactic
scales have their origin in huge star forming regions and expel metal enriched
material out of the galaxies into their surroundings as observed, for example,
in the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 253. As massive stars in OB-associations
explode sequentially, shock waves are driven into the interstellar medium (ISM)
of a galaxy and merge, forming a superbubble (SB). These SBs expand in a
direction perpendicular to the disk plane following the density gradient of the
ISM. We use the 2D analytical approximation by Kompaneets (1960) to model the
expansion of SBs in an exponentially stratified ISM. This is modified in order
to describe the sequence of SN-explosions as a time-dependent process taking
into account the main-sequence life-time of the SN-progenitors and using an
initial mass function to get the number of massive stars per mass interval. The
evolution of the bubble in space and time is calculated analytically, from
which the onset of Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities in the shell can be
determined. In its further evolution, the shell will break up and
high-metallicity gas will be ejected into the halo of the galaxy and even into
the ICM. We derive the number of stars needed for blow-out depending on the
scale height and density of the ambient medium, as well as the fraction of
alpha- and iron peak elements contained in the hot gas. Finally, the amount of
metals injected by Milky Way-type galaxies to the ICM is calculated confirming
the importance of this enrichment process.
label: human

We use A-type stars selected from Sloan Digital Sky Survey data release 9
photometry to measure the outer slope of the Milky Way stellar halo density
profile beyond 50 kpc. A likelihood-based analysis is employed that models the
ugr photometry distribution of blue horizontal branch (BHB) and blue straggler
(BS) stars. In the magnitude range, 18.5 < g < 20.5, these stellar populations
span a heliocentric distance range of: 10 kpc < D_BS < 75 kpc, 40 kpc < D_BHB <
100 kpc. Contributions from contaminants, such as QSOs, and the effect of
photometric uncertainties, are also included in our modeling procedure. We find
evidence for a very steep outer halo profile, with power-law index alpha ~ 6
beyond Galactocentric radii r=50 kpc, and even steeper slopes favored (alpha ~
6-10) at larger radii. This result holds true when stars belonging to known
overdensities, such as the Sagittarius stream, are included or excluded. We
show that, by comparison to numerical simulations, stellar halos with shallower
slopes at large distances tend to have more recent accretion activity. Thus, it
is likely that the Milky Way has undergone a relatively quiet accretion history
over the past several Gyr. Our measurement of the outer stellar halo profile
may have important implications for dynamical mass models of the Milky Way,
where the tracer density profile is strongly degenerate with total
mass-estimates.
label: human
