In this paper, we study the Multi-Round Influence Maximization (MRIM)
problem, where influence propagates in multiple rounds independently from
possibly different seed sets, and the goal is to select seeds for each round to
maximize the expected number of nodes that are activated in at least one round.
MRIM problem models the viral marketing scenarios in which advertisers conduct
multiple rounds of viral marketing to promote one product. We consider two
different settings: 1) the non-adaptive MRIM, where the advertiser needs to
determine the seed sets for all rounds at the very beginning, and 2) the
adaptive MRIM, where the advertiser can select seed sets adaptively based on
the propagation results in the previous rounds. For the non-adaptive setting,
we design two algorithms that exhibit an interesting tradeoff between
efficiency and effectiveness: a cross-round greedy algorithm that selects seeds
at a global level and achieves $1/2 - \varepsilon$ approximation ratio, and a
within-round greedy algorithm that selects seeds round by round and achieves
$1-e^{-(1-1/e)}-\varepsilon \approx 0.46 - \varepsilon$ approximation ratio but
saves running time by a factor related to the number of rounds. For the
adaptive setting, we design an adaptive algorithm that guarantees
$1-e^{-(1-1/e)}-\varepsilon$ approximation to the adaptive optimal solution. In
all cases, we further design scalable algorithms based on the reverse influence
sampling approach and achieve near-linear running time. We conduct experiments
on several real-world networks and demonstrate that our algorithms are
effective for the MRIM task.
label: human

text:
Objective: The study investigates the effect on cooperation in multiplayer
games, when the population from which all individuals are drawn is structured -
i.e. when a given individual is only competing with a small subset of the
entire population.
  Method: To optimize the focus on multiplayer effects, a class of games were
chosen for which the payoff depends nonlinearly on the number of cooperators -
this ensures that the game cannot be represented as a sum of pair-wise
interactions, and increases the likelihood of observing behaviour different
from that seen in two-player games. The chosen class of games are named
"threshold games", and are defined by a threshold, $M > 0$, which describes the
minimal number of cooperators in a given match required for all the
participants to receive a benefit. The model was studied primarily through
numerical simulations of large populations of individuals, each with
interaction neighbourhoods described by various classes of networks.
  Results: When comparing the level of cooperation in a structured population
to the mean-field model, we find that most types of structure lead to a
decrease in cooperation. This is both interesting and novel, simply due to the
generality and breadth of relevance of the model - it is likely that any model
with similar payoff structure exhibits related behaviour.
  More importantly, we find that the details of the behaviour depends to a
large extent on the size of the immediate neighbourhoods of the individuals, as
dictated by the network structure. In effect, the players behave as if they are
part of a much smaller, fully mixed, population, which we suggest an expression
for.
label: human

text: The study examines the convergence of simulations of self-gravitating accretion discs, focusing on the sensitivity of these simulations to different implementations of radiative cooling and artificial viscosity. Accretion discs are critical components in various astrophysical phenomena, with their behavior largely influenced by self-gravity and hydrodynamic processes. The objective of this research is to determine how variations in cooling algorithms and artificial viscosity affect the dynamical and thermodynamical evolution of self-gravitating discs. Using a suite of numerical simulations conducted with a smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) code, we explore a parameter space that includes various forms of radiative cooling prescriptions, such as optically thick and thin regimes, combined with differing treatments of artificial viscosity. Key findings reveal that the choice of cooling implementation significantly impacts the thermal equilibrium state and spiral structure formation within the disc. In contrast, variations in artificial viscosity primarily influence the angular momentum transport efficiency. Furthermore, simulations employing adaptive cooling show enhanced convergence with physical results, suggesting a crucial role of accurate radiative treatment. The study concludes that to achieve reliable self-gravitating accretion disc models, careful consideration must be given to both radiative cooling and artificial viscosity frameworks. These insights offer a pathway to enhancing simulation accuracy, which is essential for understanding the complex environments surrounding massive astrophysical objects. Future work could benefit from incorporating additional physical processes, such as magnetic fields, to further develop a comprehensive simulation model.
label: machine

text: The dynamics of epithelial jamming, a collective cellular transition critical to developmental biology and cancer metastasis, are governed by a complex interplay of forces and geometric constraints. This study aims to elucidate the universal geometric constraints that dictate the collective behavior of epithelial cells during jamming. We employed both computational simulations and in vitro experiments to investigate these constraints' roles in guiding cell movements and morphological changes. Utilizing a vertex model to simulate cellular monolayers, we analyzed how variations in cell shape, size, and packing affect jamming transitions. Additionally, we conducted experiments on cultured epithelial cells to validate simulation predictions, employing time-lapse microscopy and quantitative image analysis to measure cellular junction tensions and interfacial tensions. Our findings reveal that specific geometric parameters, particularly cell aspect ratios and junctional tension anisotropy, play critical roles in promoting or inhibiting jamming. Moreover, the study demonstrates that there exists a threshold in geometric alterations beyond which jamming is significantly altered, suggesting a precise architectural regulation of cell packing. These results offer a new perspective on how intrinsic cellular geometry can impact tissue function and development. In conclusion, understanding the universal geometric constraints inherent in epithelial jamming could lead to new insights into tissue engineering and the inhibition of pathological processes, such as cancer metastasis, by modulating these constraints to control cell collective behavior. This research contributes to the broader understanding of tissue morphogenesis and highlights the importance of geometric considerations in cellular dynamics.
label: machine

Measurements of $b$ hadron production ratios in proton-proton collisions at a
centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 3 pb$^{-1}$ are
presented. We study the ratios of strange $B$ meson to light $B$ meson
production $f_s/(f_u+f_d)$ and $\Lambda_b^0$ baryon to light $B$ meson
production $f_{\Lambda_b}/(f_u+f_d)$ as a function of the charmed hadron-muon
pair transverse momentum $p_T$ and the $b$ hadron pseudorapidity $\eta$, for
$p_T$ between 0 and 14 GeV and $\eta$ between 2 and 5. We find that
$f_s/(f_u+f_d)$ is consistent with being independent of $p_{\rm T}$ and $\eta$,
and we determine $f_s/(f_u+f_d)$ = 0.134$\pm$ 0.004 $^{+0.011}_{-0.010}$, where
the first error is statistical and the second systematic. The corresponding
ratio $f_{\Lambda_b}/(f_u+f_d)$ is found to be dependent upon the transverse
momentum of the charmed hadron-muon pair, $f_{\Lambda_b}/(f_u+f_d)=(0.404\pm
0.017 (stat) \pm 0.027 (syst) \pm 0.105 (Br))\times[1 -(0.031 \pm 0.004 (stat)
\pm 0.003 (syst))\times p_T(GeV)]$, where Br reflects an absolute scale
uncertainty due to the poorly known branching fraction Br(\Lambda_c^+ \to
pK^-\pi^+)$. We extract the ratio of strange $B$ meson to light neutral $B$
meson production $f_s/f_d$ by averaging the result reported here with two
previous measurements derived from the relative abundances of $\bar{B}_s \to
D_S^+ \pi ^-$ to $\bar{B}^0 \to D^+K^-$ and $\bar{B}^0 \to D^+\pi^-$. We obtain
$f_s/f_d=0.267^{+0.021}_{-0.020}$.

text:
Upcoming gravitational wave (GW) detectors might detect a stochastic
background of GWs potentially arising from many possible sources, including
bubble collisions from a strongly first-order electroweak phase transition. We
investigate whether it is possible to connect, via a semi-analytical
approximation to the tunneling rate of scalar fields with quartic potentials,
the GW signal through detonations with the parameters entering the potential
that drives the electroweak phase transition. To this end, we consider a finite
temperature effective potential similar in form to the Higgs potential in the
Standard Model (SM). In the context of a semi-analytic approximation to the
three dimensional Euclidean action, we derive a general approximate form for
the tunneling temperature and the relevant GW parameters. We explore the GW
signal across the parameter space describing the potential which drives the
phase transition. We comment on the potential detectability of a GW signal with
future experiments, and physical relevance of the associated potential
parameters in the context of theories which have effective potentials similar
in form to that of the SM. In particular we consider singlet, triplet, higher
dimensional operators, and top-flavor extensions to the Higgs sector of the SM.
We find that the addition of a temperature independent cubic term in the
potential, arising from a gauge singlet for instance, can greatly enhance the
GW power. The other parameters have milder, but potentially noticeable,
effects.
label: human

text: In the realm of consumer body scanning, the availability of portable depth cameras offers a promising solution for fast and affordable 3D body modeling. Im2Fit presents a novel approach to fast 3D body modeling using a single consumer depth camera and synthetic data. Our methodology combines model-based and data-driven techniques to accurately estimate 3D shape and anthropometric measurements from a single depth scan.  The core of our approach is a semi-automatic 3D shape fitting pipeline using a library of synthetic templates. Our pipeline consists of several stages, including initialization, shape registration, and refinement. The initialization stage locates the 3D model template on the depth map based on a set of predefined body landmarks. The registration and refinement stages iteratively optimize the model position and shape to minimize the error between the synthetic template and the depth data.  Anthropometric measurements are obtained from the refined 3D model using a template-based technique. We create a database of synthetic templates for all major body parts and calculate corresponding anthropometric measurements. We then use linear regression to learn the mapping between the 3D shape features and the anthropometric measurements.  We evaluate our approach using both real and synthetic data. The results show that our method achieves an average error of less than 2 cm for 17 anthropometric measurements. Our method also demonstrates real-time performance, fitting a 3D model in under 2 seconds. Compared to existing methods, Im2Fit offers a significant improvement in fitting accuracy and real-time performance using only a single depth camera. Our work represents a crucial step towards practical and affordable 3D body modeling solutions for consumers.
label: machine

text:
Distributed optimization has attracted lots of attention in the operation of
power systems in recent years, where a large area is decomposed into smaller
control regions each solving a local optimization problem with periodic
information exchange with neighboring regions. However, most distributed
optimization methods are iterative and require synchronization of all regions
at each iteration, which is hard to achieve without a centralized coordinator
and might lead to under-utilization of computation resources due to the
heterogeneity of the regions. To address such limitations of synchronous
schemes, this paper investigates the applicability of asynchronous distributed
optimization methods to power system optimization. Particularly, we focus on
solving the AC Optimal Power Flow problem and propose an algorithmic framework
based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) method that
allows the regions to perform local updates with information received from a
subset of but not all neighbors. Through experimental studies, we demonstrate
that the convergence performance of the proposed asynchronous scheme is
dependent on the communication delay of passing messages among the regions.
Under mild communication delays, the proposed scheme can achieve comparable or
even faster convergence compared with its synchronous counterpart, which can be
used as a good alternative to centralized or synchronous distributed
optimization approaches.
label: human

text: This research focuses on developing an efficient algorithm for finding the shortest paths in a weighted graph, leveraging the concept of radius stepping. The traditional Floyd-Warshall algorithm has a time complexity of O(n^3), making it impractical for large-scale graphs. In contrast, the radius stepping approach can significantly reduce the computational complexity to O(n^2), rendering it more suitable for real-time applications.  The objective of this study is to design and evaluate an optimized parallel shortest-path algorithm based on radius stepping, capable of handling large-scale graphs and multiple query patterns. The proposed algorithm, dubbed "Radius Stepping Parallel Shortest Paths" (RSPSP), combines the benefits of parallel processing and radius stepping to achieve improved performance.  The RSPSP algorithm is designed to be highly scalable, allowing it to efficiently handle large graphs and multiple query patterns. The methodology employed in this study involves the development of a parallelized implementation of the radius stepping algorithm, utilizing a combination of OpenMP and MPI for parallelization. The performance of the RSPSP algorithm is evaluated using a range of benchmarks, including synthetic graphs and real-world datasets.  Key findings indicate that the RSPSP algorithm exhibits significant improvements in terms of computational efficiency, scalability, and parallelization, outperforming traditional algorithms in terms of both time and space complexity. The results demonstrate that the RSPSP algorithm is capable of handling large-scale graphs and multiple query patterns, making it a suitable solution for real-time applications. The conclusions drawn from this study highlight the potential of radius stepping and parallel processing in solving shortest-path problems, paving the way for further research and development in this area.
label: machine

text:
The power of solar acoustic waves is reduced inside sunspots mainly due to
absorption, emissivity reduction, and local suppression. The coefficients of
these power-reduction mechanisms can be determined by comparing time-distance
cross-covariances obtained from sunspots and from the quiet Sun. By analyzing
47 active regions observed by SOHO/MDI without using signal filters, we have
determined the coefficients of surface absorption, deep absorption, emissivity
reduction, and local suppression. The dissipation in the quiet Sun is derived
as well. All of the cross-covariances are width corrected to offset the effect
of dispersion. We find that absorption is the dominant mechanism of the power
deficit in sunspots for short travel distances, but gradually drops to zero at
travel distances longer than about 6 degrees. The absorption in sunspot
interiors is also significant. The emissivity-reduction coefficient ranges from
about 0.44 to 1.00 within the umbra and 0.29 to 0.72 in the sunspot, and
accounts for only about 21.5% of the umbra's and 16.5% of the sunspot's total
power reduction. Local suppression is nearly constant as a function of travel
distance with values of 0.80 and 0.665 for umbrae and whole sunspots
respectively, and is the major cause of the power deficit at large travel
distances.
label: human

text: We investigated the properties of old star clusters in the FSR catalogue, a comprehensive collection of star clusters and stellar associations. Through a systematic analysis of the catalogue data, we aimed to identify the most ancient and pristine clusters, which would provide valuable insights into the early evolution of the Milky Way galaxy. Our approach involved a multi-step process, starting with the selection of clusters with high membership fractions and low contamination rates. We then applied a combination of photometric and spectroscopic techniques to determine the ages, metallicities, and kinematics of the selected clusters.  Our results indicate that a significant proportion of the FSR catalogue clusters are old, with ages ranging from 10 to 13 billion years. Notably, we discovered a subset of clusters with ages exceeding 14 billion years, which are likely to be among the oldest known star clusters in the Milky Way. By comparing the properties of these ancient clusters with those of younger counterparts, we gained insights into the evolution of the galaxy's chemical and dynamical structures. Our findings suggest that the FSR catalogue clusters provide a unique window into the early history of the Milky Way, and their study can inform our understanding of the galaxy's formation and evolution. By exploring the properties of old star clusters in the FSR catalogue, we shed new light on the complex and fascinating history of our galaxy.
label: machine

text: This research focuses on the selection of an optimal differential privacy level for accuracy-constrained exponential weighted mean (ERM) regression, a widely used machine learning algorithm. In the context of differential privacy, the goal is to balance the trade-off between data privacy and predictive accuracy. Background research indicates that existing methods often rely on heuristics or fixed levels of privacy, which may not always result in the optimal balance between accuracy and privacy.  The objective of this study is to develop a novel method for selecting the optimal differential privacy level for accuracy-constrained ERM. We propose a multi-objective optimization framework that considers both predictive accuracy and differential privacy. Our approach involves formulating a joint optimization problem that balances the two objectives, and then using a genetic algorithm to search for the optimal solution.  Our key findings indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and privacy. Specifically, we achieve state-of-the-art accuracy while maintaining a high level of differential privacy. The results also show that the proposed method can handle large datasets and varying levels of noise, making it a robust solution for real-world applications.  The conclusion of this study highlights the importance of accurately selecting the differential privacy level for accuracy-constrained ERM. Our results demonstrate that a data-driven approach can lead to significant improvements in both accuracy and privacy, and we propose a novel method for achieving this balance.
label: machine

text: We investigated the behavior of strongly coupled anisotropic plasmas, a regime where the interactions between particles are significantly enhanced due to the plasma's high density and the presence of anisotropic correlations. Our work aimed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the plasma's dynamics, with a particular focus on the interplay between particle-particle and particle-phonon interactions.  Through a combination of numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we found that the strongly coupled anisotropic plasma exhibits a rich phase diagram, characterized by the coexistence of various fluid-like and collective modes. We identified a critical point, beyond which the plasma undergoes a phase transition, giving rise to a novel, anisotropic fluid phase. This phase is characterized by a non-trivial, anisotropic structure, with particles arranged in a non-equilibrium configuration.  Our results suggest that the strongly coupled anisotropic plasma can be described by a novel, anisotropic hydrodynamic theory, which accounts for the plasma's non-equilibrium behavior and the interplay between particle-particle and particle-phonon interactions. We propose a new framework for understanding the dynamics of strongly coupled plasmas, with implications for the study of various astrophysical and laboratory systems. Our findings also highlight the importance of considering anisotropic correlations in the description of strongly coupled plasmas, and we provide a theoretical basis for future experimental and numerical investigations.
label: machine

text: In this work, we focus on the minimization of finite automata, a critical task in theoretical computer science that seeks to reduce the number of states in an automaton without altering its accepted language. We address the problem of achieving minimal representations of automata, which is essential for optimizing storage and improving the performance of automata in practical applications, such as lexical analysis and pattern matching.   We apply a combination of classical techniques, including partition refinement and equivalence checking, alongside contemporary approaches that leverage machine learning algorithms to enhance the minimization process. We employ the Hopcroft's algorithm as our baseline approach for state minimization and extend it by integrating heuristic optimizations to expedite convergence and reduce computational overhead.  Our experimental results demonstrate that our proposed methodology significantly outperforms traditional minimization algorithms, yielding up to a 30% reduction in state counts across a diverse set of benchmarks without sacrificing accuracy. Furthermore, we analyze the scalability of our approach in relation to automata size and complexity, providing insights into the potential for handling larger automata efficiently.  In conclusion, we present a novel framework for automata minimization that combines established theories with innovative techniques, yielding substantial improvements in both performance and efficiency. Our findings underscore the importance of continuous iteration on minimization strategies and pave the way for future research avenues in automata theory and applications in computational systems.

Distinguishing between the capacity of ecosystems to generate ecosystem
services (ES) and the actual use of these service (ES flow) in ES assessment
and mapping is important to develop an understanding of the sustainability of
ES use. This study assesses the spatial variation in ES capacity and flow in
the Mediterranean small island state of Malta. The services included in this
study were crop provisioning, beekeeping and honey production, fodder and
livestock production, crop pollination, air quality regulation, and aesthetic
ES. This assessment develops different spatial models, which make use of
available datasets, causal relationships between datasets, including a
generated land use land cover (LULC) map, and statistical models and indicators
based on direct measurements. Individual ES indicators were mapped to visualise
and compare their spatial patterns across the case study area. Subsequently, an
analysis of ES associations and bundles was carried out using Pearson
parametric correlation test, for both ES capacity and flow indicators generated
from this study, and through Principal Component Analysis. Results demonstrate
several significant synergistic interactions between ES capacity and flow in
rural landscapes characterised with agricultural and semi-natural LULC
categories, indicating high landscape multifunctionality. In contrast,
predominantly urban areas tend to be characterised with a low ecosystem
capacity and ES flow, suggesting that ES delivery in the landscapes of the
study area is determined by land use intensity. These findings support the
notion that multifunctional rural landscapes provide multiple ES, making an
important contribution to human well-being, and that land use planning that
develops green infrastructure in urban areas can significantly contribute to
support biodiversity and ES delivery.

We present mid-infrared photometry of the Orion Bar obtained with FORCAST
aboard SOFIA at 6.4, 6.6, 7.7, 19.7, 31.5 and 37.1 \um. By complementing this
observations with archival FORCAST and \emph{Herschel}/PACS images we are able
to construct a complete infrared spectral energy distribution of the Huygens
region in the Orion nebula By comparing the infrared images with gas tracers,
we find that PACS maps trace the molecular cloud, while the FORCAST data trace
the photodissociation region (PDR) and HII region. Analysis of the energetics
of the region reveal that the PDR extends for 0.28~pc along the line-of-sight
and that the Bar is inclined at an angle of $4\degr$. The infrared and
submillimeter images reveal that the Orion Bar represents a swept up shell with
a thickness of 0.1~pc. The mass of the shell implies a shock velocity of
$\simeq 3$ km/s and an age of $\simeq 10^5$ yr for the HII region. Our analysis
shows that the UV and infrared dust opacities in the HII region and the PDR are
a factor 5 to 10 lower than in the diffuse interstellar medium. In the ionized
gas, Ly$\alpha$ photons are a major source of dust heating at distances larger
than $\simeq0.06$~pc from \toc. Dust temperatures can be explained if the size
of the grains is between 0.1 to 1~\um. We derive the photo-electric heating
efficiency of the atomic gas in the Orion Bar. The results are in good
qualitative agreement with models and The quantitative differences indicate a
decreased PAH abundance in this region.

Spatial item recommendation has become an important means to help people
discover interesting locations, especially when people pay a visit to
unfamiliar regions. Some current researches are focusing on modelling
individual and collective geographical preferences for spatial item
recommendation based on users' check-in records, but they fail to explore the
phenomenon of user interest drift across geographical regions, i.e., users
would show different interests when they travel to different regions. Besides,
they ignore the influence of public comments for subsequent users' check-in
behaviors. Specifically, it is intuitive that users would refuse to check in to
a spatial item whose historical reviews seem negative overall, even though it
might fit their interests. Therefore, it is necessary to recommend the right
item to the right user at the right location. In this paper, we propose a
latent probabilistic generative model called LSARS to mimic the decision-making
process of users' check-in activities both in home-town and out-of-town
scenarios by adapting to user interest drift and crowd sentiments, which can
learn location-aware and sentiment-aware individual interests from the contents
of spatial items and user reviews. Due to the sparsity of user activities in
out-of-town regions, LSARS is further designed to incorporate the public
preferences learned from local users' check-in behaviors. Finally, we deploy
LSARS into two practical application scenes: spatial item recommendation and
target user discovery. Extensive experiments on two large-scale location-based
social networks (LBSNs) datasets show that LSARS achieves better performance
than existing state-of-the-art methods.

In Chapter 1 we give the basic background and notations. We also give a new
characterization of the Conrad property for orderings.
  In Chapter 2, we use the new characterization of the Conradian property to
give a classification of groups admitting (only) finitely many Conradian
orderings \S 2.1. Using this classification we deduce a structure theorem for
the space of Conradian orderings \S 2.2. In addition, we are able to give a
structure theorem for the space of left-orderings on a group by studying the
possibility of approximating a given ordering by its conjugates \S 2.3.
  In Chapter 3 we show that, for groups having finitely many Conradian
orderings, having an isolated left-ordering is equivalent to having only
finitely many left-orderings.
  In Chapter 4, we prove that the space of left-orderings of the free group on
$n\geq2$ generators have a dense orbit under the natural action of the free
group on it. This gives a new proof of the fact that the space of
left-orderings of the free group in at least two generators have no isolated
point.
  In Chapter 5, we describe the space of bi-orderings of the Thompson's group
$\efe$. We show that this space contains eight isolated points together with
four canonical copies of the Cantor set.

text: In the study of quantum spin systems, understanding the impact of dynamical paths on thermodynamic properties is crucial for advancing theoretical frameworks. This paper explores how variations in dynamical paths affect the energy gap and corrections to free energy in path integral formulations of mean-field quantum spin models. The objective is to delineate the relationships between path dynamics, energy quantization, and free energy corrections in such systems. Utilizing advanced path integral techniques, we analyze the mean-field Hamiltonian's response to different dynamical trajectories, applying numerical methods to simulate path integrals under varying conditions. Key findings reveal that the choice of dynamical paths significantly influences the calculated energy gap, leading to notable deviations in free energy estimates. Additionally, the results demonstrate that specific path configurations can enhance the robustness of the ground state energy, particularly under low-temperature conditions. These adjustments underscore the sensitivity of quantum spin systems to their dynamical history, with implications for theoretical modeling and experimental validation. The study concludes that incorporating the effects of dynamical paths into path integral analyses offers a refined understanding of energy landscape modifications in quantum mean-field systems, paving the way for more accurate predictions of thermodynamic behavior in quantum materials. This research contributes to the broader discourse on quantum thermodynamics, providing insights that may inform future studies in quantum computation and material science.

The symmetrized bidisc has been a rich field of holomorphic function theory
and operator theory. A certain well-known reproducing kernel Hilbert space of
holomorphic functions on the symmetrized bidisc resembles the Hardy space of
the unit disc in several aspects. This space is known as the Hardy space of the
symmetrized bidisc. We introduce the study of those operators on the Hardy
space of the symmetrized bidisc that are analogous to Toeplitz operators on the
Hardy space of the unit disc. More explicitly, we first study multiplication
operators on a bigger space (an $L^2$-space) and then study compressions of
these multiplication operators to the Hardy space of the symmetrized bidisc and
prove the following major results: (1) Theorem I analyzes the Hardy space of
the symmetrized bidisc, not just as a Hilbert space, but as a Hilbert module
over the polynomial ring and finds three isomorphic copies of it as $\mathbb
D^2$-contractive Hilbert modules. (2) Theorem II provides an algebraic, Brown
and Halmos type, characterization of Toeplitz operators. (3)Theorem III gives
several characterizations of an analytic Toeplitz operator. (4)Theorem IV
characterizes asymptotic Toeplitz operators. (5)Theorem V is a commutant
lifting theorem. (6)Theorem VI yields an algebraic characterization of dual
Toeplitz operators. Every section from Section 1 to Section 6 contains a
theorem each, the main result of that section.

text: In our study, we explore the shear viscosity of strongly interacting fermionic quantum fluids, a topic of significant interest due to its implications for understanding strongly correlated systems such as ultracold atomic gases and quark-gluon plasmas. We employ both theoretical and computational approaches to address the challenge of accurately determining the shear viscosity in the strongly interacting regime, where perturbative methods fail. Our methodology integrates the use of advanced quantum Monte Carlo simulations with analytical insights from the Kubo formula, facilitating robust calculations of transport coefficients directly from first principles.   Results indicate a pronounced minimum in the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio as the interaction strength is tuned, reaching values that adhere closely to the conjectured lower bound proposed by the AdS/CFT correspondence, suggesting universal behavior in these quantum fluids. This minimum is observed to occur near the unitary limit, where the scattering length diverges, reinforcing the hypothesis of universality at strong coupling. Additionally, the temperature dependence of the shear viscosity reveals important insights into the thermal behavior and quasiparticle dynamics in these fluids.  Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of non-perturbative phenomena in fermionic quantum fluids and extend the theoretical framework for describing transport properties in analogous systems. This work advances the fundamental knowledge necessary for experimental validation and offers a baseline for further exploration into exotic states of matter under extreme conditions.

text: We investigate the phenomenon of manipulating communication rules to exert influence over consensus formation in group decision-making processes. Our research reveals that individuals with the power to enforce and prevent consensus can significantly impact the outcome of discussions, often to their advantage. By carefully managing the rules of communication, such individuals can create an environment that favors their own interests, while hindering the ability of others to express their opinions and shape the consensus.  Through a mixed-methods approach combining experimental and survey-based studies, we examine the effects of communication rule manipulation on consensus formation in various contexts. Our findings indicate that the ability to enforce and prevent consensus is a valuable resource, one that can be leveraged to influence the direction of group discussions and shape the final consensus. We also identify specific strategies and tactics that individuals can use to manipulate communication rules and gain an advantage in group decision-making.  Our research highlights the importance of understanding the dynamics of communication in group decision-making and the role of power and influence in shaping consensus. We demonstrate that the ability to manipulate communication rules is a key factor in determining the outcome of group discussions, and that individuals who possess this power can often achieve their goals through subtle and often unnoticed means.

We consider two-player games played over finite state spaces for an infinite
number of rounds. At each state, the players simultaneously choose moves; the
moves determine a successor state. It is often advantageous for players to
choose probability distributions over moves, rather than single moves. Given a
goal, for example, reach a target state, the question of winning is thus a
probabilistic one: what is the maximal probability of winning from a given
state?
  On these game structures, two fundamental notions are those of equivalences
and metrics. Given a set of winning conditions, two states are equivalent if
the players can win the same games with the same probability from both states.
Metrics provide a bound on the difference in the probabilities of winning
across states, capturing a quantitative notion of state similarity.
  We introduce equivalences and metrics for two-player game structures, and we
show that they characterize the difference in probability of winning games
whose goals are expressed in the quantitative mu-calculus. The quantitative
mu-calculus can express a large set of goals, including reachability, safety,
and omega-regular properties. Thus, we claim that our relations and metrics
provide the canonical extensions to games, of the classical notion of
bisimulation for transition systems. We develop our results both for
equivalences and metrics, which generalize bisimulation, and for asymmetrical
versions, which generalize simulation.

We present a detailed analysis of high resolution near-infrared imaging and
spectroscopy of the potential star cluster IRS13E very close to the massive
black hole in the Galactic Center. We detect 19 objects in IRS13E from Ks-band
images, 15 of which are also detected reliably in H-band. We derive consistent
proper motions for these objects from the two bands. Most objects share a
similar westward proper motion. We characterize the objects using spectroscopy
(1.45 to 2.45 micrometer) and (narrow-band) imaging from H- (1.66 mircrometer)
to L'-band (3.80 micrometer). Nine of the objects detected in both Ks- and
H-band are very red, and we find that they are all consistent with being warm
dust clumps. The dust emission may be caused by the colliding winds of the two
Wolf-Rayet stars in the cluster. Three of the six detected stars do not share
the motion or spectral properties of the three bright stars. This leaves only
the three bright, early-type stars as potential cluster members. It is unlikely
that these stars are a chance configuration. Assuming the presence of an IMBH,
a mass of about 14000 solar masses follows from the velocities and positions of
these three stars. However, our acceleration limits make such an IMBH nearly as
unlikely as a chance occurrence of such a star association. Furthermore, there
is no variable X-ray source in IRS13E despite the high density of dust and gas.
Therefore, we conclude that is unlikely that IRS13E hosts a black hole massive
enough to bind the three stars.

text: In this work, we explore the integrability of Conformal Fishnet Theory, a novel framework within the realm of quantum field theory. Our study aims to address the problem of understanding the underlying integrable structures of this theory and its potential implications for theoretical physics. By investigating the integrability properties of Conformal Fishnet Theory, we seek to elucidate its behavior under various conditions and identify key features that may shed light on its applicability in describing physical phenomena.  Our results reveal that Conformal Fishnet Theory exhibits remarkable integrable properties, suggesting a rich mathematical structure underlying its formalism. Through a rigorous analysis utilizing advanced mathematical tools and techniques from integrable systems theory, we demonstrate intriguing connections between the conformal properties of the theory and its integrability, providing new insights into the nature of its solutions and dynamics.  The key ideas in our methodology involve leveraging the power of integrability concepts to probe the deep mathematical structures of Conformal Fishnet Theory. By employing techniques such as the analysis of integrable models and symmetries, we uncover the integrable nature of the theory and its implications for the broader theoretical physics landscape. Our findings offer a promising avenue for further exploration and potential applications of Conformal Fishnet Theory in diverse physical contexts.

Two main hypotheses for the origin of Galactic cosmic rays are the
"supernova" and "superbubble" origin hypotheses. We analyse the evidence for
the superbubble hypothesis provided by the measurements of the relativive
abundances of isotopes of cobalt and nickel in the cosmic ray flux. We compare
the measured upper limit on the abundance of 59Ni in the cosmic ray flux with
the 59Ni abundance predictions of the up-to-date stellar evolution models.
Non-detection of 59Ni in the cosmic ray flux has previously been attributed to
a large time delay of the order of 1e5 yr between the moment of supernova
explosion and the onset of particle acceleration process. This large time delay
was considered as an argument in favour of the "superbubble" scenario. We show
that the recent calculation of the 59Ni yield of massive stars, which takes
into account the initial mass range up to 120 solar masses and includes stellar
rotation, results in prediction of low 59Ni abundance relative to its decay
product 59Co. The predicted abundance is consistent with the upper bound on
59Ni abundance in the cosmic ray flux for the supernova parameters assumed.
This result removes the necessity of decay of 59Ni in the time interval between
the supernova explosion and the onset of acceleration process and restores the
consistency of measurements of 59Ni / 59Co abundances with the "supernova"
hypothesis of the CR origin.

text: The ARIEL space mission, scheduled for launch in 2029 by the European Space Agency, aims to provide a breakthrough in the study of planetary formation. This research paper investigates the contribution of the ARIEL mission to enhancing our understanding of planetary formation processes. Utilizing a spectroscopic approach, ARIEL will analyze the chemical composition and thermal structures of exoplanet atmospheres to unravel their evolutionary history. The methodology involves observing a wide range of exoplanets, from hot Jupiters to super-Earths, to gather crucial data on their atmospheres and composition. Key findings indicate that ARIEL's high-resolution spectrograph will enable the detection of key molecules and isotopes, providing insights into the formation mechanisms of different types of planets. By focusing on factors such as metallicity, mass, and orbital characteristics, ARIEL will offer a comprehensive analysis of planetary systems and their formation processes. In conclusion, the ARIEL space mission is poised to revolutionize our understanding of planetary formation by providing unprecedented data on exoplanet atmospheres, leading to significant advancements in the field of astrophysics.

Low mass dwarf spheroidal galaxies are key objects for our understanding of
the chemical evolution of the pristine Universe and the Local Group of
galaxies. Abundance ratios in stars of these objects can be used to better
understand their star formation and chemical evolution. We report on the
analysis of a sample of 11 stars belonging to 5 different ultra faint dwarf
spheroidal galaxies (UfDSph) based on X-Shooter spectra obtained at the VLT.
Medium resolution spectra have been used to determine the detailed chemical
composition of their atmosphere. We performed a standard 1D LTE analysis to
compute the abundances.
  Considering all the stars as representative of the same population of low
mass galaxies, we found that the [alpha/Fe] ratios vs [Fe/H] decreases as the
metallicity of the star increases in a way similar to what is found for the
population of stars belonging to dwarf spheroidal galaxies. The main difference
is that the solar [alpha/Fe] is reached at a much lower metallicity for the
UfDSph than the dwarf spheroidal galaxies.
  We report for the first time the abundance of strontium in CVnI. The star we
analyzed in this galaxy has a very high [Sr/Fe] and a very low upper limit of
barium which makes it a star with an exceptionally high [Sr/Ba] ratio.
  Our results seem to indicate that the galaxies which have produced the bulk
of their stars before the reionization (fossil galaxies) have lower [X/Fe]
ratios at a given metallicity than the galaxies that have experienced a
discontinuity in their star formation rate (quenching).

The Sequential Fully Implicit (SFI) method was proposed to simulate coupled
immiscible multiphase fluid flow in porous media. Later, it was extended to the
black-oil model, whereby the gas component is allowed to dissolve in the oil
phase. Most recently, the SFI approach was extended to fully compositional
isothermal displacements. SFI schemes solve the fully coupled system in two
steps: (1) Construct and solve the pressure equation (flow problem). (2) Solve
the coupled species transport equations for the phase saturations and phase
compositions. Experience indicates that complex interphase mass transfer
behaviors often lead to large numbers of SFI outer iterations compared with the
Fully Implicit (FI) method. Here, we demonstrate that the convergence
difficulties are directly related to the treatment of the coupling between the
flow and transport problems, and we propose a new SFI variant based on a
nonlinear overall-volume balance equation. The first step consists of forming
and solving a nonlinear pressure equation, which is a weighted sum of all the
component mass conservation equations. The second step of the new SFI scheme
entails introducing the overall-mass density as a degree-of-freedom, and
solving the full set of component conservation equations cast in the
natural-variables form. During the second step, the pressure and the
total-velocity fields are fixed. We analyze the `splitting errors' associated
with the compositional SFI scheme, and we show how to control these errors in
order to converge to the same solution as the Fully Implicit (FI) method. This
robust sequential-implicit solution scheme allows for designing numerical
methods and linear solvers that are optimized for the sub-problems of flow and
transport.

The purpose of this paper is to examine the Lagrangian stochastic modeling of
the fluid velocity seen by inertial particles in a nonhomogeneous turbulent
flow. A new Langevin-type model, compatible with the transport equation of the
drift velocity in the limits of low and high particle inertia, is derived. It
is also shown that some previously proposed stochastic models are not
compatible with this transport equation in the limit of high particle inertia.
The drift and diffusion parameters of these stochastic differential equations
are then estimated using direct numerical simulation (DNS) data. It is observed
that, contrary to the conventional modeling, they are highly space dependent
and anisotropic. To investigate the performance of the present stochastic
model, a comparison is made with DNS data as well as with two different
stochastic models. A good prediction of the first and second order statistical
moments of the particle and fluid seen velocities is obtained with the three
models considered. Even for some components of the triple particle velocity
correlations, an acceptable accordance is noticed. The performance of the three
different models mainly diverges for the particle concentration and the drift
velocity. The proposed model is seen to be the only one which succeeds in
predicting the good evolution of these latter statistical quantities for the
range of particle inertia studied.

text: We conducted a comprehensive mid-infrared imaging investigation of 25 local active galactic nuclei (AGN) utilizing the VLT-VISIR instrument, addressing the need for enhanced understanding of AGN environments and their interaction with host galaxies. Our primary objective was to explore the complex structures around AGN that are not readily observable in other wavelengths, due to dust obscuration. Through our observational campaign, we acquired high-resolution mid-infrared images, revealing distinct morphological features and temperature variations across the sample.   Our analysis indicated that a significant fraction of the AGN exhibit extended emission, suggesting the presence of heated dust and active star formation in their vicinity. We employed a combination of photometric analysis and spatial modeling to quantify the properties of these emissions, allowing us to classify the AGN based on their circumnuclear structures and thermal properties. Furthermore, we correlated our findings with existing optical and radio data, providing insights into the AGN evolutionary processes and feedback mechanisms.  The results underscore the role of mid-infrared observations in revealing the hidden complexities of AGN and their host galaxies, thereby enhancing our understanding of their life cycles and interactions. We conclude that the utilization of VLT-VISIR in the mid-infrared spectrum is invaluable for unraveling the intricacies of local AGN, paving the way for future studies aimed at deciphering the interplay between AGN activity and galaxy evolution. This work significantly contributes to the broader field of astrophysics, particularly in understanding the dynamics within the AGN-host interactions.

text:
Non-Abelian anyons promise to reveal spectacular features of quantum
mechanics that could ultimately provide the foundation for a decoherence-free
quantum computer. A key breakthrough in the pursuit of these exotic particles
originated from Read and Green's observation that the Moore-Read quantum Hall
state and a (relatively simple) two-dimensional p+ip superconductor both
support so-called Ising non-Abelian anyons. Here we establish a similar
correspondence between the Z_3 Read-Rezayi quantum Hall state and a novel
two-dimensional superconductor in which charge-2e Cooper pairs are built from
fractionalized quasiparticles. In particular, both phases harbor Fibonacci
anyons that---unlike Ising anyons---allow for universal topological quantum
computation solely through braiding. Using a variant of Teo and Kane's
construction of non-Abelian phases from weakly coupled chains, we provide a
blueprint for such a superconductor using Abelian quantum Hall states
interlaced with an array of superconducting islands. Fibonacci anyons appear as
neutral deconfined particles that lead to a two-fold ground-state degeneracy on
a torus. In contrast to a p+ip superconductor, vortices do not yield additional
particle types yet depending on non-universal energetics can serve as a trap
for Fibonacci anyons. These results imply that one can, in principle, combine
well-understood and widely available phases of matter to realize non-Abelian
anyons with universal braid statistics. Numerous future directions are
discussed, including speculations on alternative realizations with fewer
experimental requirements.
label: human

Motivated by the quasiparticle wavefunction in the composite fermion (CF)
theory for fractional quantum Hall filling factor $\nu = 1/m$, I consider a
suitable quasiparticle operator in differential form, as a modified form of
Laughlin's quasiparticle operator, that reproduces quasiparticle wave function
as predicted in the CF theory. I further consider the conjugate of this
operator as quasihole operator for obtaining a novel quasihole wave function
for $1/m$ state. Each of these wave functions is interpreted as expelled
electron into a different Hilbert subspace from the original Hilbert space of
Laughlin condensate while still maintaining its correlation (although changed)
with the electrons in the condensate such that the expelled electron behaves as
a CF with respect to the electrons in the condensate. With this interpretation,
I show that the ground state wavefunctions for general states at filling
fractions $\nu_{n,m}^{\pm} = n/[n(m\mp 1)\pm 1]$, respectively, can be
constructed as coherent superposition of $n$ coupled Laughlin condensates and
their conjugates, formed at different Hilbert subspaces. The corresponding wave
functions, specially surprising for $\nu_{n,m}^{-}$ sequence of states, are
identical with those proposed in the theory of noninteracting CFs. The states
which were considered as fractional quantum Hall effect of interacting CFs, can
also be treated in the same footing as for the prominent sequences of states
describing as the coupled condensates among which one is a non-Laughlin
condensate in a different Hilbert subspace. Further, I predict that the half
filling of the lowest Landau level is a quantum critical point for phase
transitions between two topologically distinct phases each corresponding to a
family of states.

text: We present a novel hybrid information retrieval model specifically designed for web images, which integrates the strengths of traditional image retrieval systems with the advantages of deep learning techniques. Our approach combines the robustness of feature extraction from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with the efficiency of traditional image features, such as SIFT and SURF, to improve the accuracy and efficiency of web image retrieval.  Through a comprehensive analysis of existing image retrieval systems, we identified the primary limitations of traditional models, including low accuracy and high computational requirements. To address these issues, we proposed a hybrid model that utilizes a CNN-based feature extractor to learn high-level semantic features, which are then combined with traditional image features to enhance the retrieval performance. Our experimental results demonstrate a significant improvement in precision, recall, and F1-score compared to state-of-the-art image retrieval systems.  Our model's efficiency is further enhanced through the use of a multi-stage ranking framework, which allows for the effective pruning of irrelevant features and the focus on the most relevant ones. We also employed a novel ranking metric, which takes into account the contextual relationships between images, to improve the retrieval performance. Our approach has been evaluated on several benchmark datasets, including ImageNet and COCO, and has achieved competitive results with the state-of-the-art models. Overall, our hybrid information retrieval model offers a promising solution for web image retrieval, providing a balance between accuracy, efficiency, and scalability.

text: This study examines the theoretical uncertainties in Effective Field Theory (EFT) power countings, which arise from residual cutoff dependence in the context of renormalization group (RG) flow. EFT power counting is a fundamental tool for determining the dimensionality of particles and fields in a theory, but it is known to be sensitive to non-perturbative effects, such as those arising from the residual cutoff dependence. The objective of this research is to assess the theoretical uncertainties in EFT power countings by investigating the impact of residual cutoff dependence on the RG flow and, consequently, on the power counting results.  The analysis is based on a numerical study of RG flows in a simplified model, where the residual cutoff dependence is simulated using a combination of numerical and analytical techniques. The power counting results are obtained by integrating the RG flow in the momentum space and are compared to the perturbative results. The key findings of this study are that the residual cutoff dependence leads to significant theoretical uncertainties in the power counting results, particularly at high energies. The numerical results show that the power counting results can differ by up to 20% due to the residual cutoff dependence. The study demonstrates the importance of taking into account the residual cutoff dependence in EFT power countings and highlights the need for more precise calculations to determine the theoretical uncertainties in this context.  The conclusions of this research have significant implications for our understanding of the theoretical framework of EFT power counting. The results suggest that the theoretical uncertainties in EFT power countings should be taken into account when making predictions about the properties of particles and fields in a theory. Furthermore, the study highlights the need for further research to develop more accurate methods for determining the theoretical uncertainties in EFT power countings.
label: machine

text: This research paper presents a multi-wavelength study of Supernova Remnants (SNRs) in six nearby galaxies, focusing on the detection of new X-ray selected SNRs using data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory. The objective is to identify and characterize previously unknown SNRs to enhance our understanding of the various stages of supernova evolution. The methodology employed involves the analysis of X-ray data obtained by Chandra, cross-referenced with data from other wavelengths such as optical and radio. Key findings reveal the discovery of a substantial number of new X-ray selected SNRs in the six targeted galaxies, with distinct characteristics and X-ray emission properties. Through the multi-wavelength analysis, correlations between X-ray emission and other wavebands are investigated, shedding light on the physical properties and environments of the SNRs. The results contribute valuable insights into the diversity of SNRs in different galactic environments and their role in the cosmic feedback processes. In conclusion, this study underscores the significance of multi-wavelength observations in advancing our knowledge of SNRs and their impact on the surrounding interstellar medium in a galactic context.

In this paper, we develop efficient decoders for non-binary low-density
parity-check (LDPC) codes using the alternating direction method of multipliers
(ADMM). We apply ADMM to two decoding problems. The first problem is linear
programming (LP) decoding. In order to develop an efficient algorithm, we focus
on non-binary codes in fields of characteristic two. This allows us to
transform each constraint in $\mathbb{F}_{2^m}$ to a set of constraints in
$\mathbb{F}_{2}$ that has a factor graph representation. Applying ADMM to the
LP decoding problem results in two types of non-trivial sub-routines. The first
type requires us to solve an unconstrained quadratic program. We solve this
problem efficiently by leveraging new results obtained from studying the above
factor graphs. The second type requires Euclidean projection onto polytopes
that are studied in the literature, a projection that can be solved efficiently
using off-the-shelf techniques, which scale linearly in the dimension of the
vector to project. ADMM LP decoding scales linearly with block length, linearly
with check degree, and quadratically with field size. The second problem we
consider is a penalized LP decoding problem. This problem is obtained by
incorporating a penalty term into the LP decoding objective. The purpose of the
penalty term is to make non-integer solutions (pseudocodewords) more expensive
and hence to improve decoding performance. The ADMM algorithm for the penalized
LP problem requires Euclidean projection onto a polytope formed by embedding
the constraints specified by the non-binary single parity-check code, which can
be solved by applying the ADMM technique to the resulting quadratic program.
Empirically, this decoder achieves a much reduced error rate than LP decoding
at low signal-to-noise ratios.

text:
Stagnation of a cold plasma streaming to the center or axis of symmetry via
an expanding accretion shock wave is ubiquitous in inertial confinement fusion
(ICF) and high-energy-density plasma physics, the examples ranging from plasma
flows in x-ray-generating Z pinches [Y. Maron et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 111,
035001 (2013)] to the experiments in support of the recently suggested concept
of impact ignition in ICF [H. Azechi et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 102, 235002
(2009); M. Murakami et al., Nucl. Fusion 54, 054007 (2014)]. Some experimental
evidence indicates that stagnation via an expanding shock wave is stable, but
its stability has never been studied theoretically. We present such analysis
for the stagnation that does not involve a rarefaction wave behind the
expanding shock front and is described by the classic ideal-gas Noh solution in
spherical and cylindrical geometry. In either case the stagnated flow has been
demonstrated to be stable, initial perturbations exhibiting a power-law,
oscillatory or monotonic, decay with time for all the eigenmodes. This
conclusion has been supported by our simulations done both on a Cartesian grid
and on a curvilinear grid in spherical coordinates. Dispersion equation
determining the eigenvalues of the problem and explicit formulas for the
eigenfunction profiles corresponding to these eigenvalues are presented, making
it possible to use the theory for hydro code verification in two and three
dimensions.

The overall characteristics of the solar and atmospheric neutrino oscillation
are approximately consistent with a tribimaximal form of the mixing matrix $U$
of the lepton sector. Exact tribimaximal mixing leads to $\theta_{13}=0$.
However, recent results from Daya Bay and RENO experiments have established a
nonzero value for $\theta_{13}$. Keeping the leading behavior of $U$ as
tribimaximal, we use a generalized Fridberg-Lee neutrino mass model along with
a complementary ansatz to incorporate a nonzero $\theta_{13}$ along with CP
violation. We generalize this model in two stages: In the first stage we assume
$\mu-\tau$ symmetry and add imaginary components which leads to nonzero phases.
In the second stage we add a perturbation with real components which breaks the
$\mu-\tau$ symmetry and this leads to a nonzero value for $\theta_{13}$. The
combination of these two generalizations leads to CP violation. Using only two
of the experimental data, we can fix all of the parameters of our model and
predict not only values for the other experimental data, which agree well with
the available data, but also the masses of neutrinos and the CP violating
phases and parameters. These predictions include the following: $\langle
m_{\nu_e} \rangle\approx(0.033-0.037)~eV$, $\langle m_{\nu_\mu}
\rangle\approx(0.043-0.048)~ eV$, $\langle m_{\nu_\tau}
\rangle\approx(0.046-0.051)~ eV$, and $59.21^{\circ}\lesssim \delta\lesssim
59.34^{\circ}$

We report here the first results of a multi-wavelength campaign focussing on
magnetospheric accretion processes of the classical TTauri star (cTTS)
V2129Oph. In this paper, we present spectropolarimetric observations collected
in 2009 July with ESPaDOnS at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT).
Circularly polarised Zeeman signatures are clearly detected, both in
photospheric absorption and accretion-powered emission lines, from time-series
of which we reconstruct new maps of the magnetic field, photospheric brightness
and accretion-powered emission at the surface of V2129Oph using our newest
tomographic imaging tool - to be compared with those derived from our old 2005
June data set, reanalyzed in the exact same way.
  We find that in 2009 July, V2129Oph hosts octupolar & dipolar field
components of about 2.1 & 0.9kG respectively, both tilted by about 20deg with
respect to the rotation axis; we conclude that the large-scale magnetic
topology changed significantly since 2005 June (when the octupole and dipole
components were about 1.5 and 3 times weaker respectively), demonstrating that
the field of V2129Oph is generated by a non-stationary dynamo. We also show
that V2129Oph features a dark photospheric spot and a localised area of
accretion-powered emission, both close to the main surface magnetic region
(hosting fields of up to about 4kG in 2009 July). We finally obtain that the
surface shear of V2129Oph is about half as strong as solar.
  From the fluxes of accretion-powered emission lines, we estimate that the
observed average logarithmic accretion rate (in Msun/yr) at the surface of
V2129Oph is -9.2+-0.3 at both epochs, peaking at -9.0 at magnetic maximum. It
implies in particular that the radius at which the magnetic field of V2129Oph
truncates the inner accretion disc is 0.93x and 0.50x the corotation radius in
2009 July and 2005 June respectively.

text: We present our findings from a Quantum Monte Carlo study investigating the magnetic-field-driven 2D superconductor-insulator transition. The problem we are addressing is the understanding of the behavior of a two-dimensional system as it undergoes this transition under the influence of a magnetic field. Our study explores the interplay between superconductivity and the insulating phase in the presence of varying magnetic fields, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms at play.  Through our simulations, we have successfully characterized the critical magnetic field strength at which the transition occurs, providing insights into the nature of the phase transition in the system. By analyzing the correlation functions and the behavior of the order parameter, we have identified key signatures associated with the superconducting and insulating phases, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of the system's evolution as the magnetic field is tuned.  Our methodology involves employing Quantum Monte Carlo simulations to capture the quantum mechanical effects in the system accurately. By simulating the 2D system with magnetic field variations, we have been able to track the evolution of the superconductor-insulator transition, providing valuable insights into the emerging phases and critical behavior. These results contribute to the deeper understanding of the interplay between superconductivity, magnetic fields, and quantum fluctuations in low-dimensional systems.

text: This research investigates the identification of potential hazardous events associated with the operation of unmanned protective vehicles (UPVs), which are increasingly utilized in hazardous environments to mitigate human risk. The objective of the study was to systematically identify, classify, and analyze potential hazards to enhance the safety protocols associated with these autonomous systems. The methodology consisted of a hybrid approach combining fault tree analysis (FTA) and hazard and operability study (HAZOP) techniques. This dual-method allowed for a comprehensive identification of failure modes and operational risks under diverse environmental conditions. A comprehensive database of past incidents involving similar autonomous systems provided a foundation for this analysis, while expert interviews supplemented the data. Key findings indicate that system malfunctions, environmental unpredictability, and cybersecurity threats constitute the primary categories of hazardous events. Additionally, human error during remote operations emerged as a critical risk factor, highlighting the importance of effective human-machine interfaces. The study's results underscore the necessity of integrating robust risk mitigation strategies, such as real-time monitoring systems and adaptive control algorithms, to enhance safety and reliability. The research concludes by recommending a proactive approach in hazard identification, emphasizing the need for iterative safety assessments in the developmental phases of UPV systems. These findings provide essential insights for designers and operators, facilitating informed decision-making in the advancement and deployment of UPVs in complex, hazardous environments.

Inferences about the spatial density or phase-space structure of stellar
populations in the Milky Way require a precise determination of the effective
survey volume. The volume observed by surveys such as Gaia or near-infrared
spectroscopic surveys, which have good coverage of the Galactic mid-plane
region, is highly complex because of the abundant small-scale structure in the
three-dimensional interstellar dust extinction. We introduce a novel framework
for analyzing the importance of small-scale structure in the extinction. This
formalism demonstrates that the spatially-complex effect of extinction on the
selection function of a pencil-beam or contiguous sky survey is equivalent to a
low-pass filtering of the extinction-affected selection function with the
smooth density field. We find that the angular resolution of current 3D
extinction maps is sufficient for analyzing Gaia sub-samples of millions of
stars. However, the current distance resolution is inadequate and needs to be
improved by an order of magnitude, especially in the inner Galaxy. We also
present a practical and efficient method for properly taking the effect of
extinction into account in analyses of Galactic structure through an effective
selection function. We illustrate its use with the selection function of
red-clump stars in APOGEE using and comparing a variety of current 3D
extinction maps.

text: This study investigates anomalous momentum states and non-specular reflections of phase-locked second harmonic pulses, focusing on their negative refraction properties. Building upon previous research on conventional light propagation, this investigation explores how second harmonic pulses can exhibit unique behaviors under specific conditions, deviating from classical optical principles. The primary objective was to elucidate the mechanisms behind these phenomena, particularly through the lens of momentum transfer and phase locking effects.  The methodology employed theoretical and computational simulations, leveraging the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) technique to model the interaction between second harmonic pulses and materials. By analyzing the dispersion relation and momentum distribution of the pulses within various material configurations, we aimed to identify critical parameters that influence the observed negative refraction and non-specular reflection patterns.  Key findings include the demonstration of momentum states where particles can absorb energy from a pulse while simultaneously gaining momentum, leading to unexpected changes in direction. These findings also revealed that phase-locking the second harmonic pulses enhances the negative refraction effect, enabling the redirection of the pulses through materials with refractive indices lower than those of the incident medium.  In conclusion, this research provides insights into the manipulation of light propagation using second harmonic pulses, offering potential applications in advanced optical devices and technologies. The results highlight the importance of considering momentum states and phase locking in the design and optimization of such systems, potentially paving the way for new optical phenomena and applications.

The study also reveals that Atlas exhibits highly irregular orbital motion, indicative of a complex dynamical environment influenced by nearby moonlets and ring material. We investigate the physical and chemical conditions in a typical star forming
region, including an unbiased search for new molecules in a spectral region
previously unobserved. Due to its proximity, the Orion KL region offers a
unique laboratory of molecular astrophysics in a chemically rich, massive star
forming region. Several ground-based spectral line surveys have been made, but
due to the absorption by water and oxygen, the terrestrial atmosphere is
completely opaque at frequencies around 487 and 557 GHz. To cover these
frequencies we used the Odin satellite to perform a spectral line survey in the
frequency ranges 486-492 GHz and 541-577 GHz, filling the gaps between previous
spectral scans. Odin's high main beam efficiency and observations performed
outside the atmosphere make our intensity scale very well determined. We
observed 280 spectral lines from 38 molecules including isotopologues, and, in
addition, 64 unidentified lines. The beam-averaged emission is dominated by CO,
H2O, SO2, SO, 13CO and CH3OH. Species with the largest number of lines are
CH3OH, (CH33)2O, SO2, 13CH3OH, CH3CN and NO. Six water lines are detected
including the ground state rotational transition o-H2O, its isotopologues
o-H218O and o-H217O, the Hot Core tracing p-H2O transition 6(2,4)-7(1,7), and
the 2(0, 2)-1(1,1) transition of HDO. Other lines of special interest are the
1_0-0_0 transition of NH3 and its isotopologue 15NH3. Isotopologue abundance
ratios of D/H, 12C/13C, 32S/34S, 34S/33S, and 18O/17O are estimated. The
temperatures, column densities and abundances in the various subregions are
estimated, and we find very high gas-phase abundances of H2O, NH3, SO2, SO, NO,
and CH3OH. A comparison with the ice inventory of ISO sheds new light on the
origin of the abundant gas-phase molecules.

text: We investigate the application of electron spin resonance (ESR) as a novel technique for the detection of long-range spin nematic order in low-dimensional quantum materials. The critical problem addressed in our work is the challenge of identifying and characterizing spin nematic states, which remain elusive in traditional magnetic resonance studies. By leveraging ESR, we aim to unveil the subtle signatures associated with spin nematic ordering, thereby providing insights into the underlying quantum phases of matter that are critical for the advancement of quantum computing and materials science.  Our methodology employs a combination of advanced ESR spectroscopy and theoretical modeling to probe the spin dynamics of various candidate materials. We systematically explore the temperature and magnetic field dependency of the ESR signals, seeking to distinguish between typical magnetic ordering and the unique characteristics of spin nematic phases. Our experimental findings reveal a notable enhancement in the spin relaxation rates, as well as a frequency shift in the ESR spectra correlating with the emergence of long-range spin nematic order.   These results corroborate theoretical predictions and establish ESR as a powerful tool for exploring exotic quantum states. We demonstrate that the detection of long-range spin nematic order via ESR not only deepens our understanding of quantum magnetism but also paves the way for future research into spintronic applications. Our work represents a significant advancement in the field, refining the techniques available for the exploration of complex quantum states and their practical implications.

text:
The modes of the electromagnetic field are solutions of Maxwell's equations
taking into account the material boundary conditions. The field modes of
classical optics - properly normalized - are also the mode functions of quantum
optics. Quantum physics adds that the excitation within each mode is quantized
in close analogy to the harmonic oscillator. A complete set of mode functions
forms a basis with which any new modes can be reconstructed. In full generality
each electromagnetic mode function in the four dimensional space-time is
mathematically equivalent to a harmonic oscillator. The quantization of the
electromagnetic field defines the excitation per mode and the correlation
between modes. In classical optics there can be oscillations and stochastic
fluctuations of amplitude, phase, polarization et cetera. In quantum optics
there are in addition uncertain quantum field components, quantum correlations
and quantized energies. Here, we present selected topics from classical to
quantum optics. We start in the second chapter with the classical optics
description of a light field and its spectral densities, their measurement and
their interpretation. In the third chapter the quantum properties of a single
light mode are reviewed as well as ways to measure these quantum properties.
Gaussian states of a light mode are emphasized, i. e. states for which the
Wigner function has a two dimensional Gaussian shape. The fourth chapter will
be concerned with more than one mode presenting a unifying approach to
quadratic Hamiltonians including phase conjugation which is related to time
reversal.
label: human

text:
In human crowds, interactions among individuals give rise to a variety of
self-organized collective motions that help the group to effectively solve the
problem of coordination. However, it is still not known exactly how humans
adjust their behavior locally, nor what are the direct consequences on the
emergent organization. One of the underlying mechanisms of adjusting individual
motions is the stepping dynamics. In this paper, we present first quantitative
analysis on the stepping behavior in a one-dimensional pedestrian flow studied
under controlled laboratory conditions. We find that the step length is
proportional to the velocity of the pedestrian, and is directly related to the
space available in front of him, while the variations of the step duration are
much smaller. This is in contrast with locomotion studies performed on isolated
pedestrians and shows that the local density has a direct influence on the
stepping characteristics. Furthermore, we study the phenomena of
synchronization -walking in lockstep- and show its dependence on flow
densities. We show that the synchronization of steps is particularly important
at high densities, which has direct impact on the studies of optimizing
pedestrians flow in congested situations. However, small synchronization and
antisynchronization effects are found also at very low densities, for which no
steric constraints exist between successive pedestrians, showing the natural
tendency to synchronize according to perceived visual signals.

text: The development of efficient numerical methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) is crucial for advancing various fields of science and engineering. The discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method, a high-order finite element technique, has gained popularity in recent years due to its ability to accurately capture complex geometries and nonlinear phenomena. However, the DG method can be computationally expensive, particularly for large-scale problems, which necessitates the development of efficient preconditioners to accelerate the solution process.  In this study, we investigate the application of matrix-free multigrid block-preconditioners to higher-order discontinuous Galerkin discretizations. The proposed preconditioner is designed to take advantage of the hierarchical structure of the DG mesh, allowing for efficient management of the computational cost. By combining the benefits of multigrid methods and block-preconditioning techniques, we aim to develop a robust and efficient preconditioner that can effectively reduce the solution time for a wide range of DG problems.  Our numerical results demonstrate that the proposed matrix-free multigrid block-preconditioner can achieve significant speedups compared to standard iterative solvers, particularly for problems with complex geometries and high-order DG elements. The preconditioner's performance is shown to be robust across various problem sizes and DG orders, making it a promising tool for large-scale DG simulations. The findings of this study contribute to the development of efficient numerical methods for solving high-order DG problems, with potential applications in fields such as fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, and quantum mechanics.
