text: In this study, we investigate the zeros and functional equation properties of the quadrilateral zeta function, a generalization derived from extending concepts within the classical zeta functions. To address long-standing challenges associated with the distribution of zeros in this function, we begin with an in-depth analysis of its analytic continuation and symmetry properties. Our methodology centers on establishing a rigorous framework to articulate the function's behavior in the complex plane. By leveraging techniques from analytic number theory, we construct a detailed functional equation that parallels those found in classical zeta functions. Through this framework, we successfully demonstrate the meromorphic continuation of the quadrilateral zeta function beyond its initial domain of convergence. Our results reveal that the functional equation posits a critical line analogous to the classical Riemann hypothesis implications. Numerical experiments verify the hypothesis that zeros lie symmetrically concerning this line. Furthermore, we apply sophisticated computational algorithms to explore potential zero-free regions, thereby enhancing the understanding of the function's arithmetic significance. Ultimately, this work not only provides substantial insights into the structural properties of the quadrilateral zeta function but also opens new avenues for tackling conjectures related to more general class of generalized zeta functions. The implications of our findings resonate broadly, offering potential applications in other areas of mathematical research, such as algebraic geometry and modular forms, further underscoring the integral role of zeta functions in contemporary mathematical inquiry.

Membrane proteins constitute a large portion of the human proteome and
perform a variety of important functions as membrane receptors, transport
proteins, enzymes, signaling proteins, and more. The computational studies of
membrane proteins are usually much more complicated than those of globular
proteins. Here we propose a new continuum model for Poisson-Boltzmann
calculations of membrane channel proteins. Major improvements over the existing
continuum slab model are as follows: 1) The location and thickness of the slab
model are fine-tuned based on explicit-solvent MD simulations. 2) The highly
different accessibility in the membrane and water regions are addressed with a
two-step, two-probe grid labeling procedure, and 3) The water pores/channels
are automatically identified. The new continuum membrane model is optimized (by
adjusting the membrane probe, as well as the slab thickness and center) to best
reproduce the distributions of buried water molecules in the membrane region as
sampled in explicit water simulations. Our optimization also shows that the
widely adopted water probe of 1.4 {\AA} for globular proteins is a very
reasonable default value for membrane protein simulations. It gives an overall
minimum number of inconsistencies between the continuum and explicit
representations of water distributions in membrane channel proteins, at least
in the water accessible pore/channel regions that we focus on. Finally, we
validate the new membrane model by carrying out binding affinity calculations
for a potassium channel, and we observe a good agreement with experiment
results.

Extended emission (EE) is a high-energy, early time rebrightening sometimes
seen in the light curves of short gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). We present the first
contiguous fits to the EE tail and the later X-ray plateau, unified within a
single model. Our central engine is a magnetar surrounded by a fall-back
accretion disc, formed by either the merger of two compact objects or the
accretion-induced collapse of a white dwarf. During the EE phase, material is
accelerated to super-Keplarian velocities and ejected from the system by the
rapidly rotating ($P \approx 1 - 10$ ms) and very strong ($10^{15}$ G) magnetic
field in a process known as magnetic propellering. The X-ray plateau is
modelled as magnetic dipole spin-down emission. We first explore the range of
GRB phenomena that the propeller could potentially reproduce, using a series of
template light curves to devise a classification scheme based on phenomology.
We then obtain fits to the light curves of 9 GRBs with EE, simultaneously
fitting both the propeller and the magnetic dipole spin-down and finding
typical disc masses of a few $10^{-3}$ $M_{\odot}$ to a few $10^{-2}$
$M_{\odot}$. This is done for ballistic, viscous disc and exponential accretion
rates. We find that the conversion efficiency from kinetic energy to EM
emission for propellered material needs to be $\gtrsim 10\%$ and that the best
fitting results come from an exponential accretion profile.

text: The abstract focuses on deformations of modules of maximal grade and their relationship to the Hilbert scheme of determinantal schemes. The study begins with an exploration of modules of maximal grade over a ring, emphasizing their significance in algebraic geometry. The objective is to investigate how these modules behave under deformations and how they relate to geometric objects known as determinantal schemes. The methodology employs advanced techniques from commutative algebra and algebraic geometry, including deformation theory and intersection theory. The analysis reveals that the Hilbert scheme provides a framework to understand the moduli space of modules of maximal grade, and it offers insights into the stability conditions and the deformation properties of these modules. The study concludes by highlighting the interplay between the geometric properties of determinantal schemes and the algebraic structure of modules of maximal grade, contributing to a deeper understanding of the Hilbert scheme's role in algebraic geometry.

The ultimate limits of performance for any classical optical system are set
by sub-wavelength fluctuations within the host material, that may be frozen-in
or even dynamically induced. The most common manifestation of such
sub-wavelength disorder is Rayleigh light scattering, which is observed in
nearly all wave-guiding technologies today and can lead to both irreversible
radiative losses as well as undesirable intermodal coupling. While it has been
shown that backscattering from disorder can be suppressed by breaking
time-reversal symmetry in magneto-optic and topological insulator materials,
common optical dielectrics possess neither of these properties. Here we
demonstrate an optomechanical approach for dynamically suppressing Rayleigh
backscattering within dielectric resonators. We achieve this by locally
breaking time-reversal symmetry in a silica resonator through a Brillouin
scattering interaction that is available in all materials. Near-complete
suppression of Rayleigh backscattering is experimentally confirmed through
three independent measurements -- the reduction of the back-reflections caused
by scatterers, the elimination of a commonly seen normal-mode splitting effect,
and by measurement of the reduction in intrinsic optical loss. More broadly,
our results provide new evidence that it is possible to dynamically suppress
Rayleigh backscattering within any optical dielectric medium, for achieving
robust light propagation in nanophotonic devices in spite of the presence of
scatterers or defects.

text: Massive stars play a crucial role in the synthesis of elements and the dynamics of galaxies. This study systematically investigates the effects of various wind mass loss algorithms on the evolutionary pathways of single massive stars. The objective is to determine how different mass loss prescriptions impact the stellar evolution process, particularly during key phases such as hydrogen burning and subsequent stages leading up to supernova events. To achieve this, a suite of stellar evolution models, with controlled variables including initial mass and metallicity, was created using a range of mass loss algorithms, including those based on empirical data and theoretical frameworks.  Key findings indicate significant discrepancies in evolutionary outcomes, including variations in lifespan, final mass, and nucleosynthesis products. Specifically, models utilizing higher mass loss rates resulted in earlier supernova events and a marked reduction in the formation of black holes versus neutron stars. Furthermore, the study highlights the sensitivity of critical endpoints, such as the Type II supernova luminosity and the retention of surrounding circumstellar material, to the chosen mass loss formalism.  In conclusion, this systematic survey emphasizes that the choice of wind mass loss algorithms can drastically alter the evolutionary trajectories of massive stars, with implications for our understanding of stellar populations, supernova rates, and the chemical enrichment of the universe. The findings advocate for improved observational constraints and suggest a need for calibration of mass loss rates to enhance the fidelity of stellar evolution models.

Collapse models including some external noise of unknown origin are routinely
used to describe phenomena on the quantum-classical border; in particular,
quantum measurement. Although containing nonlinear dynamics and thereby exposed
to the possibility of superluminal signaling in individual events, such models
are widely accepted on the basis of fully reproducing the non-signaling
statistical predictions of quantum mechanics. Here we present a deterministic
nonlinear model without any external noise, in which randomness - instead of
being universally present - emerges in the measurement process, from
deterministic irregular dynamics of the detectors. The treatment is based on a
minimally nonlinear von Neumann equation for a Stern-Gerlach or Bell-type
measuring setup, containing coordinate and momentum operators in a self-adjoint
skew-symmetric, split scalar product structure over the configuration space.
The microscopic states of the detectors act as a nonlocal set of hidden
parameters, controlling individual outcomes. The model is shown to display
pumping of weights between setup-defined basis states, with a single winner
randomly selected and the rest collapsing to zero. Environmental decoherence
has no role in the scenario. Through stochastic modelling, based on Pearle's
"gambler's ruin" scheme, outcome probabilities are shown to obey Born's rule
under a no-drift or "fair-game" condition. This fully reproduces quantum
statistical predictions, implying that the proposed non-linear deterministic
model satisfies the non-signaling requirement. Our treatment is still
vulnerable to hidden signaling in individual events, which remains to be
handled by future research.

We present the high-energy emission properties of GRB 160509A, from its
prompt mission to late afterglow phase. GRB 160509A contains two emission
episodes: 0-40s and 280-420s after the burst onset (t0). The relatively high
fluence of GRB 160509A allows us to establish an evolving spectrum above 100
MeV. During the first emission episode, the >100 MeV spectrum is soft with
\Gamma=>3.0, which can be smoothly connected to keV energies with a Band
function with a high-energy cutoff. The >100 MeV spectrum rapidly changes to a
hard spectrum with \Gamma<=1.5 after t0+40s. The existence of very energetic
photons, e.g., a 52 GeV that arrives t0+77 seconds, and a 29 GeV that arrives
t0+70 ks, is hard to reconcile by the synchrotron emission from forward-shock
electrons, but likely due to inverse Compton mechanism (e.g., synchrotron
self-Compton emission). A soft spectrum (\Gamma~2) between 300s and 1000s after
the burst onset is also found at a significance of about 2 standard deviations,
which suggests a different emission mechanism at work for this short period of
time. GRB 160509A represents the latest example where inverse Compton emission
has to be taken into account in explaining the afterglow GeV emission, which
had been suggested long before the launch of Fermi LAT.

text: We developed a comprehensive magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model to simulate the giant flares observed in magnetars, aiming to elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms driving these intense phenomena. The investigation addresses the complexities associated with the dynamic magnetosphere and its interplay with the strong magnetic fields intrinsic to magnetars. Our approach leverages a high-resolution MHD simulation framework that incorporates the effects of anisotropic magnetic tension and pressure, capturing both the global magnetospheric dynamics and localized perturbations responsible for the flares.  Our findings reveal that reconnection events, triggered by rapid magnetic field evolution due to crustal displacements, are pivotal in generating the substantial energy releases characteristic of giant flares. The simulation results indicate that the build-up of magnetic stress leads to a critical threshold, beyond which reconnection is initiated, producing a cascade of energy release mechanisms capable of explaining the observed luminosities and emission spectra.  Additionally, we identified key parameters influencing flare magnitude, including the initial magnetic field configuration and the velocity of crustal displacements. By comparing our model outputs with observational data from recent magnetar flare events, we achieved substantial agreement, thereby reinforcing the validity of our theoretical framework. This work establishes a foundation for future studies into magnetar flare dynamics and contributes to the broader understanding of extreme astrophysical phenomena, potentially guiding new observational strategies for high-energy astrophysics.

text: In this study, we present a novel spectrum-splitting approach for the Fermi-operator expansion, enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of all-electron Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Our methodology addresses the computational bottlenecks associated with electronic structure calculations, particularly the numerical challenges posed by spectral sharpness and the vast range of eigenvalues inherent in large-scale systems. By decomposing the Hamiltonian spectrum into distinct segments and applying tailored expansion techniques to each segment, we significantly reduce the overall computational cost while maintaining high precision levels. We employ polynomial expansions specifically adapted to the characteristics of each spectral region, leveraging the rapid convergence properties of Chebyshev polynomials for the low-energy spectrum and optimized exponential expansions for the high-energy spectrum. Our results demonstrate that this tailored approach not only accelerates convergence but also enhances stability compared to conventional methods. In benchmarking tests with a variety of atomic and molecular systems, we observe substantial reductions in computational time without sacrificing accuracy in eigenvalue estimations. This spectrum-splitting strategy facilitates scalable DFT calculations, making it a viable framework for addressing larger and more complex systems. The advancements provided by our approach promise to expand the scope of electronic structure analysis under the Kohn-Sham DFT framework, offering a potential tool for more extensive and detailed exploration of material properties. Our findings suggest that spectrum-splitting could serve as a foundational technique to optimize a broad range of quantum mechanical simulations in computational chemistry and materials science.

text: This research paper explores the development of a nanoaquarium for in situ electron microscopy in liquid media. The objective of this study is to provide a detailed methodology for constructing a nanoaquarium compatible with electron microscopy techniques, allowing observations in liquid environments. The methodology involved the design and fabrication of a specialized chamber capable of holding liquid samples for electron microscopy analysis. Key findings of this research demonstrate the successful implementation of the nanoaquarium for imaging biological samples in their native liquid environment at nanoscale resolution. The experiments conducted revealed the potential of this technique for studying dynamic processes in biological and material science applications. In conclusion, the nanoaquarium presents a promising tool for advancing the field of in situ electron microscopy, offering new opportunities for studying samples under conditions that closely mimic their natural state in liquid media without the need for extensive sample preparation.

text: We investigated the challenges associated with downlink heterogeneous cellular networks, where users are associated with different base stations based on their current location and quality of service requirements. Our primary objective was to develop a distributed pricing-based user association framework that optimizes network performance and user satisfaction.   We designed and implemented a novel, distributed algorithm that leverages game theory and machine learning techniques to determine the optimal user association strategy for each base station. This framework integrates real-time location information, traffic patterns, and pricing signals to make informed decisions about user association.   Our results show that the proposed framework significantly improves network utilization, reduces congestion, and enhances user satisfaction compared to traditional association methods. By analyzing the impact of pricing on user behavior, we identified key factors that influence user association decisions, including price elasticity and network congestion.   Key insights from our study highlight the importance of considering both user preferences and network constraints in designing effective user association strategies. Our findings also demonstrate the potential of distributed pricing-based frameworks to improve network performance in heterogeneous cellular networks.   Overall, our work provides a comprehensive framework for distributed pricing-based user association in downlink heterogeneous cellular networks, offering a promising approach for improving network efficiency and user experience.

The need to estimate a positive definite solution to an overdetermined linear
system of equations with multiple right hand side vectors arises in several
process control contexts. The coefficient and the right hand side matrices are
respectively named data and target matrices. A number of optimization methods
were proposed for solving such problems, in which the data matrix is
unrealistically assumed to be error free. Here, considering error in measured
data and target matrices, we present an approach to solve a positive definite
constrained linear system of equations based on the use of a newly defined
error function. To minimize the defined error function, we derive necessary and
sufficient optimality conditions and outline a direct algorithm to compute the
solution. We provide a comparison of our proposed approach and two existing
methods, the interior point method and a method based on quadratic programming.
Two important characteristics of our proposed method as compared to the
existing methods are computing the solution directly and considering error both
in data and target matrices. Moreover, numerical test results show that the new
approach leads to smaller standard deviations of error entries and smaller
effective rank as desired by control problems. Furthermore, in a comparative
study, using the Dolan-Mor\'{e} performance profiles, we show the approach to
be more efficient.

Observations show various jets in the solar atmosphere with significant
rotational motions, which may undergo instabilities leading to heat ambient
plasma. We study the Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) instability of twisted and rotating
jets caused by the velocity jumps near the jet surface. We derive a dispersion
equation with appropriate boundary condition for total pressure (including
centrifugal force of tube rotation), which governs the dynamics of
incompressible jets. Then, we obtain analytical instability criteria of
Kelvin-Helmholtz instability in various cases, which were verified by numerical
solutions to the dispersion equation. We find that twisted and rotating jets
are unstable to KH instability when the kinetic energy of rotation is more than
the magnetic energy of the twist. Our analysis shows that the azimuthal
magnetic field of 1-5 G can stabilize observed rotations in
spicule/macrospicules and X-ray/EUV jets. On the other hand, non-twisted jets
are always unstable to KH instability. In this case, the instability growth
time is several seconds for spicule/macrospicules and few minutes (or less) for
EUV/X-ray jets. We also find that standing kink and torsional Alfven waves are
always unstable near the antinodes due to the jump of azimuthal velocity at the
surface, while the propagating waves are generally stable. KH vortices may lead
to enhanced turbulence development and heating of surrounding plasma, therefore
rotating jets may provide energy for chromospheric and coronal heating.

Recent work has characterized the sum capacity of
time-varying/frequency-selective wireless interference networks and $X$
networks within $o(\log({SNR}))$, i.e., with an accuracy approaching 100% at
high SNR (signal to noise power ratio). In this paper, we seek similar capacity
characterizations for wireless networks with relays, feedback, full duplex
operation, and transmitter/receiver cooperation through noisy channels. First,
we consider a network with $S$ source nodes, $R$ relay nodes and $D$
destination nodes with random time-varying/frequency-selective channel
coefficients and global channel knowledge at all nodes. We allow full-duplex
operation at all nodes, as well as causal noise-free feedback of all received
signals to all source and relay nodes. The sum capacity of this network is
characterized as $\frac{SD}{S+D-1}\log({SNR})+o(\log({SNR}))$. The implication
of the result is that the capacity benefits of relays, causal feedback,
transmitter/receiver cooperation through physical channels and full duplex
operation become a negligible fraction of the network capacity at high SNR.
Some exceptions to this result are also pointed out in the paper. Second, we
consider a network with $K$ full duplex nodes with an independent message from
every node to every other node in the network. We find that the sum capacity of
this network is bounded below by $\frac{K(K-1)}{2K-2}+o(\log({SNR}))$ and
bounded above by $\frac{K(K-1)}{2K-3}+o(\log({SNR}))$.

In this work report unconventional sign change of field like spin orbit
torque in ultra-thin Chromium(1.5nm-5nm)/Nickel(8nm) bi-layer. We performed
standard spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) experiment in Cr/Ni
bi-layer by passing radio frequency current and measuring DC voltage. We
observe that when thickness of Cr layer is critically low (<6nm) spin orbit
torque by Cr on Ni significantly increases. Most importantly the sign of field
like torque is opposite to the Oersted field generated torque. To verify
interracial nature of this torque, 2 nm thin Cu is inserted between Cr and Ni
and field like torque behaves same as Oersted field induced torque. Hence
possible origin of such unconventional sign change of field like torque could
be inter-facial Rashba like spin orbit interaction which is present between Cr
and Ni but vanishes in Cr/Cu/Ni hetero-structure. From our experiment we can
estimate that approximately 35 Oe of effective Rashba like magnetic field is
created on 8 nm thicker Ni layer, when 1E12 A/m^2 current flows through Cr
layer. All experiments are done at room temperature. So Cr thin film is
expected to behave like paramagnet (Neel temperature of bulk Cr is 311K). Hence
Cr can be a good choice as a heavy metal to employ large spin orbit torque
combining bulk spin Hall effect and inter-facial Rashba interaction.

This paper presents a new method of constructing physical models in a
geophysical inverse problem, when there are only a few possible physical
property values in the model and they are reasonably known but the geometry of
the target is sought. The model consists of a fixed background and many small
"particles" as building blocks that float around in the background to resemble
the target by clustering. This approach contrasts the conventional geometric
inversions requiring the target to be regularly shaped bodies, since here the
geometry of the target can be arbitrary and does not need to be known
beforehand. Because of the lack of resolution in the data, the particles may
not necessarily cluster when recovering compact targets. A model norm, called
distribution norm, is introduced to quantify the spread of particles and
incorporated into the objective function to encourage further clustering of the
particles. As proof of concept, 1D magnetotelluric inversion is used as
example. My experiments reveal that the particles, starting from a fully
scattered distribution, are able to move towards the actual target location;
the quality of recovery depends on whether there is enough material (vertical
conductance in 1D) in the particles to build the target; and the use of
distribution norm can help produce tightened clustering. When the inversion
struggles to fit the data, it may indicate that the prior information about the
particles' conductivity and size are incorrect.

We combine the latest datasets obtained with different surveys to study the
frequency dependence of polarized emission coming from Extragalactic Radio
Sources (ERS). We consider data over a very wide frequency range starting from
$1.4$ GHz up to $217$ GHz. This range is particularly interesting since it
overlaps the frequencies of the current and forthcoming Cosmic Microwave
Background (\cmb) experiments. Current data suggest that at high radio
frequencies, ($ \nu \geq 20$ GHz) the fractional polarization of ERS does not
depend on the total flux density. Conversely, recent datasets indicate a
moderate increase of polarization fraction as a function of frequency,
physically motivated by the fact that Faraday depolarization is expected to be
less relevant at high radio-frequencies. We compute ERS number counts using
updated models based on recent data, and we forecast the contribution of
unresolved ERS in CMB polarization spectra. Given the expected sensitivities
and the observational patch sizes of forthcoming \cmb\ experiments about $\sim
200 $ ( up to $\sim 2000 $ ) polarized ERS are expected to be detected.
Finally, we assess that polarized ERS can contaminate the cosmological B-mode
polarization if the tensor-to-scalar ratio is $r< 0.05$ and they have to be
robustly controlled to de-lens \cmb\ B-modes at the arcminute angular scales.

This article describes a citizen-science project conducted by the Spanish
Virtual Observatory (SVO) to improve the orbits of near-Earth asteroids (NEAs)
using data from astronomical archives. The list of NEAs maintained at the Minor
Planet Center (MPC) is checked daily to identify new objects or changes in the
orbital parameters of already catalogued objects. Using NEODyS we compute the
position and magnitude of these objects at the observing epochs of the 938 046
images comprising the Eigth Data Release of the Sloan Digitised Sky Survey
(SDSS). If the object lies within the image boundaries and the magnitude is
brighter than the limiting magnitude, then the associated image is visually
inspected by the project's collaborators (the citizens) to confirm or discard
the presence of the NEA. If confirmed, accurate coordinates and, sometimes,
magnitudes are submitted to the MPC. Using this methodology, 3,226 registered
users have made during the first fifteen months of the project more than
167,000 measurements which have improved the orbital elements of 551 NEAs (6%
of the total number of this type of asteroids). Even more remarkable is the
fact that these results have been obtained at zero cost to telescope time as
NEAs were serendipitously observed while the survey was being carried out. This
demonstrates the enormous scientific potential hidden in astronomical archives.
  The great reception of the project as well as the results obtained makes it a
valuable and reliable tool for improving the orbital parameters of near-Earth
asteroids.

Although a seizure event represents a major deviation from a baseline
electroencephalographic signal, there are features of seizure morphology that
can be seen in non-epileptic portions of the record. A transient decrease in
frequency, referred to as slowing, is a generally abnormal but not necessarily
epileptic EEG variant. Seizure termination is often associated with a period of
slowing between the period of peak amplitude and frequency of the seizure and
the return to baseline. In annotation of seizure events in the TUH EEG Seizure
Corpus, independent slowing events were identified as a major source of false
alarm error. Preliminary results demonstrated the difficulty in automatic
differentiation between seizure events and independent slowing events. The TUH
EEG Slowing database, a subset of the TUH EEG Corpus, was created, and is
introduced here, to aid in the development of a seizure detection tool that can
differentiate between slowing at the end of a seizure and an independent
non-seizure slowing event. The corpus contains 100 10-second samples each of
background, slowing, and seizure events. Preliminary experiments show that 77%
sensitivity can be achieved in seizure detection using models trained on all
three sample types compared to 43% sensitivity with only seizure and background
samples.

text: This study investigates the majority vote model on complex networks when influenced by ancillary noise. We aimed to understand how random perturbations affect consensus formation in such systems. Through extensive simulations across various network topologies and varying levels of ancillary noise, we observed that the presence of noise can significantly alter the rate and stability of consensus formation. Our methodology involved modeling each node as a binary decision-maker influenced by both its neighbors' decisions and independent random fluctuations. Key insights include the identification of specific network structures that are more resilient to noise and the quantification of the impact of noise intensity on the system's dynamics. The results highlight the importance of considering noise in theoretical models of collective decision-making processes, providing valuable implications for applications ranging from social sciences to biological systems.

text: This study introduces a novel multivariate graphical stochastic volatility (MSV) model designed to capture the complex dynamic relationships among multiple financial assets. Building upon existing univariate MSV models, the proposed model incorporates graphical structures that reflect the conditional correlations between asset returns, thereby enhancing the model's ability to represent intricate market dynamics. The objective is to develop a robust framework that can accurately estimate volatility and correlation structures, even under high-dimensional settings. The methodology leverages advanced computational techniques such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms to efficiently sample from the posterior distribution of model parameters, addressing the computational challenges associated with large-scale MSV models. Key findings indicate that the proposed MSV model outperforms traditional factor models and contemporaneous univariate MSV models in terms of capturing the time-varying volatilities and correlations across different asset classes. The empirical analysis demonstrates significant improvements in forecasting accuracy and risk assessment compared to benchmarks. The study concludes by highlighting the practical implications of the model for portfolio management and risk control in financial markets.

We present a near-infrared study of the candidate star cluster Mercer 81,
located at the centre of the G338.4+0.1 HII region, and close to the TeV
gamma-ray source HESS 1640-465. Using HST/NICMOS imaging and VLT/ISAAC
spectroscopy we have detected a compact and highly extincted cluster of stars,
though the bright stars in the centre of the field are in fact foreground
objects. The cluster contains nine stars with strong Paschen-alpha emission,
one of which we identify as a Wolf-Rayet (WR) star, as well as an A-type
supergiant. The line-of-sight extinction is very large, $A_{V}\sim 45$,
illustrating the challenges of locating young star clusters in the Galactic
Plane. From a quantitative analysis of the WR star we argue for a cluster age
of 3.7$^{+0.4}_{-0.5}$\,Myr, and, assuming that all emission-line stars are
WRs, a cluster mass of $\ga 10^4$\msun. A kinematic analysis of the cluster's
surrounding HII-region shows that the cluster is located in the Galactic disk
at a distance of 11$\pm$2\,kpc. This places the cluster close to where the far
end of the Bar intersects the Norma spiral arm. This cluster, as well as the
nearby cluster [DBS2003]179, represent the first detections of active star
cluster formation at this side of the Bar, in contrast to the near side which
is well known to have recently undergone a $\sim 10^6$\msun\ starburst episode.

text: Topological orders represent a fascinating class of quantum phases with unique properties, enabling robust quantum states that are resilient to perturbations. However, the potential existence of global gauge anomalies poses significant challenges to our understanding of these phases. This study aims to explore the interplay between topological orders and global gauge anomalies, specifically focusing on their implications for the theoretical landscape of condensed matter physics. We employ a combination of mathematical frameworks and computational techniques, including category theory and gauge theory formulations, to systematically analyze various topological order parameters under the presence of global gauge anomalies. Our findings reveal that certain topological orders can indeed harbor global gauge anomalies, which necessitates a reevaluation of the conventional categorical descriptions of these phases. Notably, the presence of such anomalies leads to distinctive signatures in both edge states and bulk excitations, which could be experimentally observable in condensed matter systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these anomalies have implications for the classification of topological phases and for the realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation. In conclusion, this research highlights the critical relationship between topological orders and global gauge anomalies, paving the way for new insights into quantum matter and its applications in quantum technologies. Our results not only contribute to the theoretical foundations of topology in physics but also inspire future experimental investigations into engineered topological states with intrinsic anomalies.

While general object recognition is still far from being solved, this paper
proposes a way for a robot to recognize every object at an almost human-level
accuracy. Our key observation is that many robots will stay in a relatively
closed environment (e.g. a house or an office). By constraining a robot to stay
in a limited territory, we can ensure that the robot has seen most objects
before and the speed of introducing a new object is slow. Furthermore, we can
build a 3D map of the environment to reliably subtract the background to make
recognition easier. We propose extremely robust algorithms to obtain a 3D map
and enable humans to collectively annotate objects. During testing time, our
algorithm can recognize all objects very reliably, and query humans from crowd
sourcing platform if confidence is low or new objects are identified. This
paper explains design decisions in building such a system, and constructs a
benchmark for extensive evaluation. Experiments suggest that making robot
vision appear to be working from an end user's perspective is a reachable goal
today, as long as the robot stays in a closed environment. By formulating this
task, we hope to lay the foundation of a new direction in vision for robotics.
Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

text: In this study, we explore the efficacy of selection strategies applied to randomly partitioned genetic replicators within an evolutionary framework. Traditional models often overlook the stochastic nature of partitioning in genetic systems, leading to an underestimation of selection's impact on genetic variability. We aim to address this gap by examining how different selection mechanisms influence the evolutionary trajectory of these partitioned replicators. Using a series of computational simulations, we employed both deterministic and probabilistic selection strategies to evaluate their effects on replication success and genetic diversity. Our results demonstrate that probabilistic selection strategies significantly enhance the adaptive potential of the replicators, promoting greater genetic variability and resilience against environmental fluctuations. In contrast, deterministic selection was found to streamline adaptative success in stable environments but reduced diversity under variable conditions. These findings suggest a critical role of selection strategy choice in the maintenance and evolution of genetic diversity within partitioned populations. The methodology involved setting up a model system where replicators were initially distributed according to a random partition, followed by iterations of replication combined with a given selection strategy. Statistical analysis confirmed the consistency and significance of our results across multiple simulation runs. The present work not only enhances our understanding of genetic selection in partitioned systems but also provides valuable insights into designing more robust evolutionary algorithms and bio-inspired systems. Future research should consider extending this approach to more complex genetic structures and environments to further elucidate the interplay between selection strategy and genetic partitioning.

text: This research focuses on the effects of UV photoionization on the formation of the first supernova in a massive cloud. The study aims to investigate how feedback processes, specifically UV photoionization, influence the evolution of massive clouds and their potential to form supernovae. The methodology involves numerical simulations that incorporate hydrodynamics, radiative transfer, and chemical reactions to model the interactions between UV radiation and the cloud. The key findings reveal that UV photoionization plays a crucial role in regulating the physical and chemical properties of the cloud, affecting the conditions necessary for the onset of a supernova. The simulations demonstrate that the feedback from UV radiation significantly impacts the dynamics and evolution of the cloud, potentially influencing the timing and characteristics of the first supernova event. In conclusion, this research highlights the importance of feedback mechanisms, particularly UV photoionization, in shaping the environments where supernovae occur in massive clouds, providing valuable insights into the early stages of supernova formation and its connection to the surrounding interstellar medium.

text: We investigate the origin of the far-infrared continuum of the z ~ 6 quasar SDSS J1148+5251 through a comprehensive radiative transfer model. Our primary objective is to elucidate the contributions of various components to the far-infrared emission, thereby addressing the critical question of how early quasars influenced their environments. We employ a detailed radiative transfer methodology, incorporating both the intrinsic emission from the accreting supermassive black hole and the reprocessing effects of surrounding dust. Our results indicate that the far-infrared continuum is predominantly shaped by the interaction between the intense ultraviolet radiation emitted by the quasar and the dusty toroidal structure enveloping it. We demonstrate that the heating of dust grains, primarily located at distances ranging from 50 to 200 parsecs from the central engine, contributes significantly to the observed far-infrared emission. Furthermore, we observe that the model's predictions closely align with existing observational data from the submillimeter regimes, validating our approach. These findings suggest that the high far-infrared luminosities of z ~ 6 quasars can be significantly attributed to the dust processing of hard ultraviolet radiation from accreting black holes, illuminating the role of these quasars in the early universe. Our research not only provides a clearer understanding of the physical mechanisms underpinning the far-infrared continuum of early quasars but also lays the groundwork for future investigations into the interplay between quasar activity, star formation, and the surrounding interstellar medium in similar high-redshift environments.

In the literature on singular perturbation (Lavrentiev regularization) for
the stable approximate solution of operator equations with monotone operators
in the Hilbert space the phenomena of conditional stability and local
well-posedness and ill-posedness are rarely investigated. Our goal is to
present some studies which try to bridge this gap. So we discuss the impact of
conditional stability on error estimates and convergence rates for the
Lavrentiev regularization and distinguish for linear problems well-posedness
and ill-posedness in a specific manner motivated by a saturation result. The
role of the regularization error in the noise-free case, called bias, is a
crucial point in the paper for nonlinear and linear problems. In particular,
for linear operator equations general convergence rates, including logarithmic
rates, are derived by means of the method of approximate source conditions.
This allows us to extend well-known convergence rates results for the
Lavrentiev regularization that were based on general source conditions to the
case of non-selfadjoint linear monotone forward operators for which general
source conditions fail. Examples presenting the self-adjoint multiplication
operator as well as the non-selfadjoint fractional integral operator and
Ces\`aro operator illustrate the theoretical results. Extensions to the
nonlinear case under specific conditions on the nonlinearity structure complete
the paper.

In this manuscript, two novel multi-hop relay-assisted hybrid Free Space
Optical / Radio Frequency (FSO / RF) communication systems are presented and
compared. In these structures, RF and FSO links, at each hop, are parallel and
send data simultaneously. This is the first time that in a multihop hybrid FSO
/ RF structure, Detect and Forward protocol is used. In the first structure, at
each hop, received signals with higher Signal to Noise Ratio (SNR) is selected.
But in the second structure, at each hop, received FSO and RF signals are
separately detected and forwarded and selection is done only at the last hop.
Considering FSO link in Negative Exponential atmospheric turbulence and RF link
in Rayleigh fading, for the first time, closed-form expressions are derived for
Outage Probability (P_out) and Bit Error Rate (BER) of the proposed structures.
MATLAB simulations are provided to verify derived expressions. The main
motivation of this work is to answer this question that how much is the
difference of selection at each hop and selection at the last hop. Results
indicate that the structure with selection at each hop has better performance
than the structure with selection at the last hop. At different target Outage
Probability, selection at the last hop consumes about two times (~3dB) more
power than selection at each hop. Both structures are particularly suitable for
long-range communications. However, selection at each hop, in the cost of more
complexity, is recommended for applications which have problem with supplying
the required power for communication.

text: This study investigates the Arecibo Multi-Epoch HI Absorption Measurements Against Pulsars to probe the tiny-scale atomic structure of interstellar medium. The HI absorption lines, a signature of neutral hydrogen gas, are observed towards pulsars, which serve as natural probes for the interstellar medium. By analyzing the HI absorption spectra, we aim to determine the physical conditions, such as temperature, density, and magnetic field strength, of the interstellar medium at different distances from the Earth.  The data collected from the Arecibo Multi-Epoch HI Absorption Survey reveal a wealth of information on the tiny-scale atomic structure of the interstellar medium. Our analysis indicates that the HI absorption lines exhibit a complex pattern of absorption and emission features, which can be attributed to the presence of atomic and molecular species, such as HI, H2, and OH. The observed absorption spectra suggest that the interstellar medium exhibits a range of physical conditions, including temperatures ranging from 50 to 200 K and densities from 10^3 to 10^6 particles per cubic centimeter.  Our findings provide new insights into the tiny-scale atomic structure of the interstellar medium and have significant implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of stars and planets. The results also demonstrate the potential of HI absorption spectroscopy as a tool for probing the interstellar medium at small scales, which can be used to study the properties of dark molecular clouds and the formation of molecular species. Overall, this study contributes to the understanding of the complex interactions between the interstellar medium and the surrounding interstellar space.

The era of the universe's first (Population III) stars is essentially
unconstrained by observation. Ultra-luminous and massive stars from this time
altered the chemistry of the cosmos, provided the radiative scaffolding to
support the formation of the first protogalaxies, and facilitated the creation
and growth of now-supermassive black holes. Unfortunately, because these stars
lie literally at the edge of the observable universe, they will remain beyond
the reach of even the next generation of telescopes such as the James Webb
Space Telescope and the Thirty-Meter Telescope. In this paper, we provide a
primer to supernovae modeling and the first stars to make our discussion
accessible to those new to or outside our field. We review recent work of the
Los Alamos Supernova Light Curve Project and Brigham Young University to
explore the possibility of probing this era through observations of the
spectacular deaths of the first stars. We find that many such brilliant
supernova explosions will be observable as far back as $\sim 99$% of the
universe's current age, tracing primordial star formation rates and the
locations of their protogalaxies on the sky. The observation of Population III
supernovae will be among the most spectacular discoveries in observational
astronomy in the coming decade.

text: In this study, we investigate the impact of disorder on the far-infrared conductivity and microwave conductivity of two-band superconductors. Our research aims to address the challenge of understanding how disorder influences the electrical properties of such complex systems. We conducted detailed theoretical calculations and numerical simulations to explore the behavior of two-band superconductors under varying degrees of disorder. Our results demonstrate that disorder plays a crucial role in modifying the conductivity properties of these materials. We found that in the presence of disorder, both the far-infrared and microwave conductivities exhibit significant changes, with disorder-induced scattering processes affecting the transport of electrical signals in these systems. Our findings shed light on the intricate interplay between disorder and the conductivity of two-band superconductors, offering valuable insights into the mechanisms governing their electrical behavior. The methodology employed in this research involves theoretical modeling, numerical simulations, and analysis of the conductivity properties of two-band superconductors under different disorder scenarios. Overall, our study contributes to advancing the understanding of how disorder influences the electrical properties of complex superconducting materials, with implications for the development of future technological applications.

Apart from the well-known NNLO QCD and NLO electroweak corrections to W- and
Z-boson production at hadron colliders, the most important fixed-order
corrections are given by the mixed QCD-electroweak corrections of
$\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s\alpha)$. The knowledge of these corrections is of
particular importance to control the theoretical uncertainties in the upcoming
high-precision measurements of the W-boson mass and the effective weak mixing
angle at the LHC. Since these observables are dominated by the phase-space
regions of resonant W/Z bosons, we address the $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s\alpha)$
corrections in the framework of an expansion about the W/Z poles. Retaining
only the leading, resonant contribution in the so-called pole approximation,
the corrections can be classified into factorizable and non-factorizable
contributions. In this article we review our calculation of the numerically
dominant corrections which arise from factorizable corrections of
"initial-final" type, i.e. they combine the QCD corrections to the production
with the large electroweak corrections to the decay of the W/Z boson. Moreover,
we compare our results to simpler approximate combinations of electroweak and
QCD corrections based on naive products of NLO QCD and electroweak correction
factors and using leading-logarithmic approximations for QED final-state
radiation. Finally, we estimate the shift in the W-boson mass that results from
the $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s\alpha)$ corrections to the transverse-mass
distribution.

text: This work explores the application of SAT-based preprocessing techniques to enhance the efficiency of MaxSAT solvers. The study aims to identify and eliminate redundant clauses that do not contribute to the core of the problem, thereby reducing the search space and improving solving times. Problematically, existing approaches often struggle with large and complex instances, leading to inefficiencies. To address this, we introduce a novel preprocessing algorithm that utilizes conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) strategies commonly employed in SAT solvers. This approach is designed to identify and remove clauses that are unlikely to affect the final solution, thus streamlining the MaxSAT problem. Our methodology involves rigorous empirical evaluation on benchmark instances, demonstrating significant improvements in both solving time and success rate compared to state-of-the-art MaxSAT solvers without preprocessing. The key insights derived from our experiments include the effectiveness of CDCL-based techniques in identifying and pruning irrelevant clauses, which contributes to more efficient MaxSAT solving processes.

"Green fuzzies" or "extended green objects" were discovered in the recent
Spitzer GLIMPSE survey data. These extended sources have enhanced emission in
the 4.5um IRAC channel images (which are generally assigned to be green when
making 3-color RGB images from Spitzer data). Green fuzzies are frequently
found in the vicinities of massive young stellar objects, and it has been
established that they are in some cases associated with outflows. Nevertheless,
the spectral carrier(s) of this enhanced emission is still uncertain. Although
it has been suggested that Br Alpha, H2, [Fe II], and/or broad CO emission may
be contributing to and enhancing the 4.5um flux from these objects, to date
there have been no direct observations of the 4-5um spectra of these objects.
We report here on the first direct spectroscopic identification of the origin
of the green fuzzy emission. We obtained spatially resolved L and M band
spectra for two green fuzzy sources using NIRI on the Gemini North telescope.
In the case of one source, G19.88-0.53, we detect three individual knots of
green fuzzy emission around the source. The knots exhibit a pure molecular
hydrogen line emission spectrum, with the 4.695um v=0-0 S(9) line dominating
the emission in the 4-5um wavelength range, and no detected continuum
component. Our data for G19.88-0.53 prove that green fuzzy emission can be due
primarily to emission lines of molecular hydrogen within the bandpass of the
IRAC 4.5um channel. However, the other target observed, G49.27-0.34, does not
exhibit any line emission and appears to be an embedded massive young stellar
object with a cometary UC HII region. We suggest that the effects of extinction
in the 3-8um wavelength range and an exaggeration in the color stretch of the
4.5um filter in IRAC RGB images could lead to embedded sources such as this one
falsely appearing "green".

text: The evolution of X-ray outbursts and reflection features in accreting millisecond pulsars (AMPs) remains an open research question in the astrophysical community. In this work, we present an analysis of the X-ray light curve and reflection features of the AMP SAX J1808.4-3658, which experienced an exceptional X-ray outburst in 2002. By comparing the spectral properties before and during the outburst, we identify significant changes in the accretion disk geometry. Specifically, we find that the inner disk radius was truncated near co-rotation during the outburst, indicating the presence of a strong magnetic field that cleared the inner accretion disk. This result is consistent with the magnetospin alignment model for AMPs. Furthermore, we observe reflection features that can be attributed to the Compton-scattered emission from the innermost parts of the accretion disk. Our findings add valuable insights into the physics of AMPs and provide new constraints on their magnetic field strengths and accretion disk geometries. The results of this study can help improve our understanding of the emission mechanisms and variability properties of AMPs, with implications for their astrophysical relevance as cosmological probes.

We examine the conditions under which the disks of gas and dust orbiting
young gas giant planets are sufficiently conducting to experience turbulence
driven by the magneto-rotational instability. By modeling the ionization and
conductivity in the disk around proto-Jupiter, we find that turbulence is
possible if the X-rays emitted near the Sun reach the planet's vicinity and
either (1) the gas surface densities are in the range of the minimum-mass
models constructed by augmenting Jupiter's satellites to Solar composition,
while dust is depleted from the disk atmosphere, or (2) the surface densities
are much less, and in the range of gas-starved models fed with material from
the Solar nebula, but not so low that ambipolar diffusion decouples the neutral
gas from the plasma. The results lend support to both minimum-mass and
gas-starved models of the protojovian disk: (1) The dusty minimum-mass models
have internal conductivities low enough to prevent angular momentum transfer by
magnetic forces, as required for the material to remain in place while the
satellites form. (2) The gas-starved models have magnetically-active surface
layers and a decoupled interior "dead zone". Similar active layers in the Solar
nebula yield accretion stresses in the range assumed in constructing the
circumjovian gas-starved models. Our results also point to aspects of both
classes of models that can be further developed. Non-turbulent minimum-mass
models will lose dust from their atmospheres by settling, enabling gas to
accrete through a thin surface layer. For the gas-starved models it is crucial
to learn whether enough stellar X-ray and ultraviolet photons reach the
circumjovian disk. Additionally the stress-to-pressure ratio ought to increase
with distance from the planet, likely leading to episodic accretion outbursts.

We discuss quantum radiation of a massless scalar field from a spherically
symmetric nonsingular black hole with finite lifetime. Namely, we discuss a
sandwich black-hole model, where a black hole is originally created by a
collapse of a null shell of mass $M$, and later, after some time $\Delta V$, it
is disrupted by the collapse of the other shell with negative mass $-M$. We
assume that between the shells the metric is static and either coincides with
the Hayward metric or with a special generalization of it. We show that in both
cases for sufficiently large parameter $\Delta V$ the radiation after the
formation of the black hole practically coincides with the Hawking result. We
also calculated the radiation, emitted from the black hole interior. This
radiation contains peak at the moment when the second shell intersects the
inner horizon. In the standard sandwich metric (with the Hayward interior) this
outburst of the energy is exponentially large. In the modified metric, which
includes additional non-trivial redshift parameter, this exponent is
suppressed. This is a result of significant decrease of the surface gravity of
the inner horizon in the latter case. We discuss possible consequences of this
result in context of the self-consistency requirement for nonsingular models
with quantum radiation.

When data traffic in a wireless network is bursty, small amounts of data
sporadically become available for transmission, at times that are unknown at
the receivers, and an extra amount of energy must be spent at the transmitters
to overcome this lack of synchronization between the network nodes. In
practice, pre-defined header sequences are used with the purpose of
synchronizing the different network nodes. However, in networks where relays
must be used for communication, the overhead required for synchronizing the
entire network may be very significant.
  In this work, we study the fundamental limits of energy-efficient
communication in an asynchronous diamond network with two relays. We formalize
the notion of relay synchronization by saying that a relay is synchronized if
the conditional entropy of the arrival time of the source message given the
received signals at the relay is small. We show that the minimum energy-per-bit
for bursty traffic in diamond networks is achieved with a coding scheme where
each relay is either synchronized or not used at all. A consequence of this
result is the derivation of a lower bound to the minimum energy-per-bit for
bursty communication in diamond networks. This bound allows us to show that
schemes that perform the tasks of synchronization and communication separately
(i.e., with synchronization signals preceding the communication block) can
achieve the minimum energy-per-bit to within a constant fraction that ranges
from 2 in the synchronous case to 1 in the highly asynchronous regime.

text: In this study, we investigate the effective interactions between pairs of nanoparticles to elucidate their fundamental behavior in diverse applications, including drug delivery, catalysis, and material science. We adopt both theoretical and experimental methodologies to analyze the forces governing interaction mechanisms at play, focusing on van der Waals forces, electrostatics, and steric effects. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we systematically vary the size, shape, and surface functionalization of nanoparticles to assess how these parameters influence interparticle interactions. Our results reveal that nanoparticles exhibit a complex interplay of attractive and repulsive forces, depending significantly on their relative orientation and separation distance. Notably, we observe that surface modifications can enhance the stability of nanoparticle assemblies by mitigating agglomeration tendencies through tailored steric repulsion. Furthermore, we conduct experiments utilizing dynamic light scattering and electron microscopy to validate our theoretical predictions and propose a coherent model to achieve desired interaction outcomes. The findings indicate that optimizing nanoparticle characteristics can lead to enhanced performance in targeted applications, such as improved loading efficiency in drug delivery systems. This work addresses the critical challenge of controlling nanoparticle interactions, providing insights that will inform the design of next-generation nanomaterials with tailored functionalities. Ultimately, we present a comprehensive framework that integrates theoretical predictions and experimental validations, paving the way for innovative advancements in nanoparticle technology.

text: We present the results from the commissioning observations and pilot surveys of the LAMOST (Large Sky Area Multi-Object Spectrograph) Survey of Background Quasars in the Vicinity of the Andromeda and Triangulum Galaxies. Utilizing the LAMOST's high-efficiency spectrograph, we observed a total of 10,000 quasars across a 200° field of view, covering a significant portion of the Andromeda and Triangulum galaxy systems. Our initial survey revealed a diverse range of quasars, including a previously unknown population of ultra-faint quasars, with luminosities as low as 10^35.5 erg/s.  Through the commissioning observations, we successfully addressed the primary goal of the survey, which is to investigate the quasar population in the vicinity of the Andromeda and Triangulum galaxies. We employed a multi-wavelength approach, combining LAMOST spectroscopic data with archival observations from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Hubble Space Telescope. By combining these datasets, we were able to constrain the properties of the quasar population, including the redshift distribution, luminosity function, and host galaxy demographics.  Our results highlight the importance of LAMOST in understanding the quasar population in the vicinity of the Andromeda and Triangulum galaxies. The survey's unique capabilities, including its high-efficiency spectrograph and large field of view, enable us to probe the quasar population in unprecedented detail. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution, quasar activity, and the interplay between quasars and their host galaxies.

text: This research paper explores the application of Hierarchical Gaussian Descriptors (HGD) in the context of person re-identification. The background of the study involves the increasing need for effective person re-identification systems in various security and surveillance applications. The objective of the research is to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of person re-identification by employing HGD, a powerful feature extraction technique.   The methodology involves implementing a hierarchical framework for Gaussian descriptors, which captures both local and global information from person images. These descriptors are then used to match and identify individuals across different camera views in challenging real-world scenarios.   Key findings of the study indicate that the proposed HGD approach outperforms existing methods in terms of re-identification accuracy and robustness to variations in illumination, pose, and occlusion. The hierarchical structure of the descriptors enables better representation of distinctive features, leading to more reliable matching results.  In conclusion, the research demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating HGD in person re-identification systems, showing promising results for improving overall performance in complex surveillance environments.

text: Suspended graphene, a 2D material exhibiting exceptional mechanical and electrical properties, has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its potential applications in next-generation electronics and optoelectronics. However, the delicate nature of suspended graphene makes it susceptible to various environmental factors, including ballistic interferences. Ballistic interferences, which occur when electrons collide with impurities or defects, can significantly impact the material's performance, leading to degradation of its properties.  The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of ballistic interferences on suspended graphene, with a focus on the impact of temperature, humidity, and substrate material on electron transport. A custom-built experimental setup was designed to simulate various environmental conditions, and a combination of scanning tunneling microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy was employed to characterize the graphene samples.  The results showed that ballistic interferences significantly affected the electron transport properties of suspended graphene, leading to a decrease in conductivity and an increase in resistance. Furthermore, the study revealed that temperature and humidity had a more pronounced impact on electron transport than substrate material. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the effects of ballistic interferences on suspended graphene and highlight the importance of considering environmental factors in the design and fabrication of graphene-based devices.  The conclusions drawn from this study have significant implications for the development of high-performance graphene-based devices, and the results suggest that strategies to mitigate ballistic interferences, such as using substrates with reduced defect density or implementing environmental control systems, may be necessary to achieve optimal performance.

text: The background highlights the significance of ISM dynamics in galactic evolution and star formation. The objective is to understand the role of bubbles and superbubbles in shaping the ISM structure and the impact of non-equilibrium ionization processes. Key findings reveal the complex interplay between supernovae explosions, stellar winds, and magnetic fields in creating and dispersing bubbles in the ISM, along with the non-equilibrium ionization effects on the ionization balance. The research concludes that bubbles and superbubbles play a crucial role in redistributing matter and energy in the ISM, influencing star formation rates and galactic dynamics. Additionally, non-equilibrium ionization processes significantly affect the thermal and chemical properties of the ISM, highlighting the importance of considering these processes in modeling galactic evolution.

We extend the theory of neural fields which has been developed in a
deterministic framework by considering the influence spatio-temporal noise. The
outstanding problem that we here address is the development of a theory that
gives rigorous meaning to stochastic neural field equations, and conditions
ensuring that they are well-posed. Previous investigations in the field of
computational and mathematical neuroscience have been numerical for the most
part. Such questions have been considered for a long time in the theory of
stochastic partial differential equations, where at least two different
approaches have been developed, each having its advantages and disadvantages.
It turns out that both approaches have also been used in computational and
mathematical neuroscience, but with much less emphasis on the underlying
theory. We present a review of two existing theories and show how they can be
used to put the theory of stochastic neural fields on a rigorous footing. We
also provide general conditions on the parameters of the stochastic neural
field equations under which we guarantee that these equations are well-posed.
In so doing we relate each approach to previous work in computational and
mathematical neuroscience. We hope this will provide a reference that will pave
the way for future studies (both theoretical and applied) of these equations,
where basic questions of existence and uniqueness will no longer be a cause for
concern.

text:
The arrival of the Square Kilometer Array (SKA) will revitalise all aspects
of Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) astronomy at the lower frequencies.
In the last decade there have been huge strides towards routinely achieving
high precision VLBI astrometry at frequencies dominated by the tropospheric
contributions, most notably at 22GHz, using advanced phase referencing
techniques. Nevertheless to increase the capability for high precision
astrometric measurements at low radio frequencies (<8GHz) an effective
calibration strategy of the systematic ionospheric propagation effects that is
widely applicable is required. Observations at low frequencies are dominated by
distinct direction dependent ionospheric propagation errors, which place a very
tight limit on the angular separation of a suitable phase referencing
calibrator.
  The MultiView technique holds the key to the compensation of atmospheric
spatial-structure errors, by using observations of multiple calibrators and 2-D
interpolation. In this paper we present the first demonstration of the power of
MultiView using three calibrators, several degrees from the target, along with
a comparative study of the astrometric accuracy between MultiView and
phase-referencing techniques.
  MultiView calibration provides an order of magnitude improvement in
astrometry with respect to conventional phase referencing, achieving ca. 100
micro-arcseconds astrometry errors in a single epoch of observations,
effectively reaching the thermal noise limit.
  MultiView will achieve its full potential with the enhanced sensitivity and
multibeam capabilities of SKA and the pathfinders, which will enable
simultaneous observations of the target and calibrators. Our demonstration
indicates that the 10 micro-arcseconds goal of astrometry at ~1.6GHz using VLBI
with SKA is feasible using the MultiView technique.

text:
Negatively charged DNA can be compacted by positively charged dendrimers and
the degree of compaction is a delicate balance between the strength of the
electrostatic interaction and the elasticity of DNA. We report various elastic
properties of short double stranded DNA (dsDNA) and the effect of dendrimer
binding using fully atomistic molecular dynamics and numerical simulations. In
equilibrium at room temperature, the contour length distribution P(L) and
end-to-end distance distribution P(R) are nearly Gaussian, the former gives an
estimate of the stretch modulus {\gamma}_1 of dsDNA in quantitative agreement
with the literature value. The bend angle distribution P({\theta}) of the dsDNA
also has a Gaussian form and allows to extract a persistence length, L_p of 43
nm. When the dsDNA is compacted by positively charged dendrimer, the stretch
modulus stays invariant but the effective bending rigidity estimated from the
end-to-end distance distribution decreases dramatically due to backbone charge
neutralization of dsDNA by dendrimer. We support our observations with
numerical solutions of the worm-like-chain (WLC) model as well as using
non-equilibrium dsDNA stretching simulations. These results are helpful in
understanding the dsDNA elasticity at short length scales as well as how the
elasticity is modulated when dsDNA binds to a charged object such as a
dendrimer or protein.

text:
Most Type I superluminous supernovae (SLSNe-I) reported to date have been
identified by their high peak luminosities and spectra lacking obvious signs of
hydrogen. We demonstrate that these events can be distinguished from
normal-luminosity SNe (including Type Ic events) solely from their spectra over
a wide range of light-curve phases. We use this distinction to select 19
SLSNe-I and 4 possible SLSNe-I from the Palomar Transient Factory archive
(including 7 previously published objects). We present 127 new spectra of these
objects and combine these with 39 previously published spectra, and we use
these to discuss the average spectral properties of SLSNe-I at different
spectral phases. We find that Mn II most probably contributes to the
ultraviolet spectral features after maximum light, and we give a detailed study
of the O II features that often characterize the early-time optical spectra of
SLSNe-I. We discuss the velocity distribution of O II, finding that for some
SLSNe-I this can be confined to a narrow range compared to relatively large
systematic velocity shifts. Mg II and Fe II favor higher velocities than O II
and C II, and we briefly discuss how this may constrain power-source models. We
tentatively group objects by how well they match either SN 2011ke or PTF12dam
and discuss the possibility that physically distinct events may have been
previously grouped together under the SLSN-I label.

text: In recent years, the detection of gravitational waves (GWs) has opened a new window into the study of the universe. High-redshift GW sources offer a unique opportunity to probe the early universe, testing various theories and cosmological models. This abstract discusses the current state of knowledge on high-redshift GW source counts and investigates how models with extra dimensions might impact these counts.  Firstly, we provide an overview of the current understanding of high-redshift GW source counts based on observational data from ground-based and space-based detectors such as LIGO, Virgo, and LISA. The latest estimates suggest a sparse population of high-redshift sources, with a steep decline in source density towards higher redshifts.  Subsequently, we explore the potential influence of models with extra dimensions, such as those based on brane world scenarios or Kaluza-Klein theories. By considering modifications to the metric and matter content of these models, we evaluate their implications on the emitted GW spectrum and discuss their potential impact on high-redshift source counts.  Moreover, we investigate the interplay between high-redshift GW source counts and dark energy models. A substantial contribution from high-redshift sources could provide valuable insights into the nature and evolution of dark energy. We assess the potential for future observations by LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA and the planned space-based gravitational wave mission, LISA, to test these models and improve our understanding of the universe's structure and composition.  In conclusion, high-redshift GW source counts play a crucial role in our understanding of the early universe, and investigations into models with extra dimensions offer a promising avenue to make new discoveries. This abstract aims to provide a comprehensive review of the current state of knowledge on high-redshift GW source counts, discuss potential influences from models with extra dimensions, and highlight the importance of future observations in this field.

text:
Elements of a novel theory of quantum physics are developed, synthesising the
role of symbolism in describing quantum measurement and in the topological
representation of fractal invariant sets in nonlinear dynamical systems theory.
In this synthesis, the universe $U$ is treated as an isolated deterministic
dynamical system evolving precisely on a measure-zero fractal invariant subset
$I_U$ of its state space. A non-classical approach to the physics of $U$ is
developed by treating the geometry of $I_U$ as more primitive than dynamical
evolution equations on $I_U$. A specific symbolic representation of $I_U$ is
constructed which encodes quaternionic multiplication and from which the
statistical properties of complex Hilbert Space vectors are emergent. The
Hilbert Space itself arises as the singular limit of Invariant Set Theory as a
fractal parameter $N \rightarrow \infty$. Although the Hilbert Space of quantum
theory is counterfactually complete, the measure-zero set $I_U$ is
counterfactually incomplete, no matter how large is $N$. Such incompleteness
allows reinterpretations of familiar quantum phenomena, consistent with realism
and local causality. The non-computable nature of $I_U$ ensures that these
reinterpretations are neither conspiratorial nor retrocausal and, through a
homeomorphism with the ring of $2^N$-adic integers, are robust to noise and
hence not fine tuned. The non-commutativity of Hilbert Space observables
emerges from the symbolic representation of $I_U$ through the generic
number-theoretic incommensurateness of $\phi/\pi$ and $\cos \phi$. Invariant
Set Theory implies a much stronger synergy between cosmology and quantum
physics than exists in contemporary theory, suggesting a novel approach to
synthesising gravitational and quantum physics and providing new perspectives
on the dark universe and information loss in black holes.

text: This study investigates the intricate mechanisms of heating, gas uplift, and mixing within the core of the nearest galaxy cluster, providing essential insights into feedback processes. Building on previous research, our objective was to delve into the complex interplay between these factors within the cluster environment. Utilizing an extensive array of multi-wavelength observations complemented by high-resolution numerical simulations, we explored the physical processes governing the cluster's core dynamics. The methodology involved analyzing X-ray emissions, radio observations, and spectral line data to trace the influence of central active galactic nuclei (AGN) activities on the cluster environment. Key findings reveal that AGN feedback plays a pivotal role in regulating the thermal state of the cluster through shock heating and turbulence. The interplay of rising buoyant bubbles and the consequent uplift of lower entropy gas notably contributes to mixing processes that redistribute energy and metals within the core. Additionally, observational data underscore the significance of gas sloshing induced by gravitational instabilities and its impact on cluster core thermodynamics. The simulations corroborate these processes, suggesting a cyclical model of heating and cooling that maintains the cluster's structural integrity. In conclusion, our research illustrates the multifaceted nature of feedback mechanisms, emphasizing the importance of AGN activity in sustaining core temperature balance and preventing runaway cooling flows. The findings enrich our understanding of galaxy cluster evolution and the role of microphysical processes in shaping their dynamic equilibrium. Future studies are suggested to extend analyses to more distant clusters, allowing comparative evaluations and deeper insight into universal feedback mechanisms.
