Ponderomotive acceleration has been asserted to be a cause of the First
Ionization Potential (FIP) effect, the by now well known enhancement in
abundance by a factor of 3-4 over photospheric values of elements in the solar
corona with FIP less than about 10 eV. It is shown here by means of numerical
simulations that ponderomotive acceleration occurs in solar coronal loops, with
the appropriate magnitude and direction, as a "byproduct" of coronal heating.
The numerical simulations are performed with the HYPERION code, which solves
the fully compressible three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic equations
including nonlinear thermal conduction and optically thin radiation. Numerical
simulations of a coronal loops with an axial magnetic field from 0.005 Teslas
to 0.02 Teslas and lengths from 25000 km to 75000 km are presented. In the
simulations the footpoints of the axial loop magnetic field are convected by
random, large-scale motions. There is a continuous formation and dissipation of
field-aligned current sheets which act to heat the loop. As a consequence of
coronal magnetic reconnection, small scale, high speed jets form. The familiar
vortex quadrupoles form at reconnection sites. Between the magnetic footpoints
and the corona the reconnection flow merges with the boundary flow. It is in
this region that the ponderomotive acceleration occurs. Mirroring the character
of the coronal reconnection, the ponderomotive acceleration is also found to be
intermittent.

Users are rarely familiar with the content of a data source they are
querying, and therefore cannot avoid using keywords that do not exist in the
data source. Traditional systems may respond with an empty result, causing
dissatisfaction, while the data source in effect holds semantically related
content. In this paper we study this no-but-semantic-match problem on XML
keyword search and propose a solution which enables us to present the top-k
semantically related results to the user. Our solution involves two steps: (a)
extracting semantically related candidate queries from the original query and
(b) processing candidate queries and retrieving the top-k semantically related
results. Candidate queries are generated by replacement of non-mapped keywords
with candidate keywords obtained from an ontological knowledge base. Candidate
results are scored using their cohesiveness and their similarity to the
original query. Since the number of queries to process can be large, with each
result having to be analyzed, we propose pruning techniques to retrieve the
top-$k$ results efficiently. We develop two query processing algorithms based
on our pruning techniques. Further, we exploit a property of the candidate
queries to propose a technique for processing multiple queries in batch, which
improves the performance substantially. Extensive experiments on two real
datasets verify the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed approaches.

The methodology employed in this study combines advanced numerical modeling techniques with theoretical analyses, allowing us to gain a comprehensive insight into the intricate interplay between seismic waves and alluvial basin geometry. Our findings shed light on the mechanisms underlying in-depth motion and focusing effects in alluvial basins, offering valuable insights for seismic hazard mitigation strategies and enhancing our preparedness for potential seismic events.

text: The study revisits the Raspberry Model within the context of hydrodynamic interactions, particularly focusing on the effect of confinement on particle dynamics. The key findings demonstrate significant alterations in hydrodynamic correlations and mobility when particles are in proximity to boundaries compared to bulk conditions. Notably, confinement leads to enhanced particle ordering and anisotropic diffusion, which are attributed to the restricted flow fields and modified viscous drag. These observations are consistent with experimental studies in confined colloidal dispersions, thereby validating the model's applicability to real-world systems. The study also highlights previously unreported modes of force transmission and flow interaction, which become pronounced under confinement. We begin by identifying the limitations of traditional approaches in modeling the uncertainty inherent in wireless channel conditions. Our work attempts to solve these issues through the development of novel algorithms that leverage stochastic orderings to optimize transmission strategies. Specifically, we propose the use of stochastic dominance criteria to prioritize data packets for transmission based on their estimated importance and reliability. This approach allows for a more efficient allocation of resources, thereby improving overall system throughput and robustness.  Key methodologies include the application of order statistics, likelihood ratio ordering, and convex ordering principles to analyze and compare different wireless scenarios. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our proposed methods significantly enhance network performance metrics, particularly under varying channel conditions and load levels. The findings highlight the potential of stochastic ordering as a powerful tool for addressing challenges in wireless communications, paving the way for future research and practical implementations.

text: Scenario Submodular Cover (SSC) is a novel method for solving the subset selection problem in multi-instance learning, where each instance consists of a set of features and a set of outcomes, and the goal is to select a subset of features that best explains the outcomes of the entire dataset. In this paper, we present SSC, a scenario-based approach to the submodular cover problem. Unlike traditional methods that rely on global information, SSC utilizes scenario information to construct an approximate submodular function. The scenarios are derived from the instances using a clustering algorithm, and the submodularity is guaranteed by the Scenario Submodularity property. The method also includes a heuristic approach to efficiently find a near-optimal solution, which scales well to large datasets. We evaluate SSC on several benchmark datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art methods. The results show that SSC outperforms the traditional methods in terms of both computational efficiency and predictive performance. Our approach can be applied to various scenarios of multi-instance learning, including recommender systems, anomaly detection, and medical diagnosis, among others. The proposed method advances the state-of-the-art in solving the submodular cover problem in multi-instance learning scenarios and provides a valuable tool for data analysts and machine learning researchers.

The so-called 'raspberry' model refers to the hybrid lattice-Boltzmann (LB)
and Langevin molecular dynamics scheme for simulating the dynamics of
suspensions of colloidal particles, originally developed by [V. Lobaskin and B.
D\"unweg, New J. Phys. 6, 54 (2004)], wherein discrete surface points are used
to achieve fluid-particle coupling. In this paper, we present a follow up to
our study of the effectiveness of the raspberry model in reproducing
hydrodynamic interactions in the Stokes regime for spheres arranged in a
simple-cubic crystal [L. Fischer, et al., J. Chem. Phys. 143, 084108 (2015)].
Here, we consider the accuracy with which the raspberry model is able to
reproduce such interactions for particles confined between two parallel plates.
To this end, we compare our LB simulation results to established theoretical
expressions and finite-element calculations. We show that there is a
discrepancy between the translational and rotational mobility when only surface
coupling points are used, as also found in Part I of our joint publication. We
demonstrate that adding internal coupling points to the raspberry, can be used
to correct said discrepancy in confining geometries as well. Finally, we show
that the raspberry model accurately reproduces hydrodynamic interactions
between a spherical colloid and planar walls up to roughly one LB lattice
spacing.

We report follow-up observations of the Class I binary protostellar system
L1551 NE in the C18O (3--2) line with the SMA in its compact and subcompact
configurations. Our previous observations at a higher angular resolution in the
extended configuration revealed a circumbinary disk exhibiting Keplerian
motion. The combined data having more extensive spatial coverage (~140 - 2000
AU) verify the presence of a Keplerian circumbinary disk, and reveals for the
first time a distinct low-velocity (~< +-0.5 km s-1 from the systemic velocity)
component that displays a velocity gradient along the minor axis of the
circumbinary disk. Our simple model that reproduces the main features seen in
the Position-Velocity diagrams comprises a circumbinary disk exhibiting
Keplerian motion out to a radius of ~300 AU, beyond which the gas exhibits pure
infall at a constant velocity of ~0.6 km s-1. The latter is significantly
smaller than the expected free-fall velocity of ~2.2 km s-1 onto the L1551 NE
protostellar mass of ~0.8 Msun at ~300 AU, suggesting that the infalling gas is
decelerated as it moves into regions of high gas pressure in the circumbinary
disk. The discontinuity in angular momenta between the outer infalling gas and
inner Keplerian circumbinary disk implies an abrupt transition in the
effectiveness at which magnetic braking is able to transfer angular momentum
outwards, a result perhaps of the different plasma beta and ionization
fractions between the outer and inner regions of the circumbinary disk.

Thick disk evolution is studied using edge-on galaxies in two Hubble Space
Telescope Frontier Field Parallels. The galaxies were separated into 72 clumpy
types and 35 spiral types with bulges. Perpendicular light profiles in F435W,
F606W and F814W (B, V and I) passbands were measured at 1 pixel intervals along
the major axes and fitted to sech^2 functions convolved with the instrument
line spread function (LSF). The LSF was determined from the average point
spread function (PSF) of ~20 stars in each passband and field, convolved with a
line of uniform brightness to simulate disk blurring. A spread function for a
clumpy disk was also used for comparison. The resulting scale heights were
found to be proportional to galactic mass, with the average height for a
10^9.5-10^10.5 Msun galaxy at z=1.5-2.5 equal to 0.63+-0.24 kpc. This value is
probably the result of a blend between thin and thick disk components that
cannot be resolved. Evidence for such two-component structure is present in an
inverse correlation between height and midplane surface brightness. Models
suggest that the thick disk is observed best between the clumps, and there the
average scale height is 1.06+-0.43 kpc for the same mass and redshift. A
0.63+-0.68 mag V-I color differential with height is also evidence for a
mixture of thin and thick components.

In the Possible Winner problem in computational social choice theory, we are
given a set of partial preferences and the question is whether a distinguished
candidate could be made winner by extending the partial preferences to linear
preferences. Previous work has provided, for many common voting rules, fixed
parameter tractable algorithms for the Possible Winner problem, with number of
candidates as the parameter. However, the corresponding kernelization question
is still open and in fact, has been mentioned as a key research challenge. In
this paper, we settle this open question for many common voting rules.
  We show that the Possible Winner problem for maximin, Copeland, Bucklin,
ranked pairs, and a class of scoring rules that include the Borda voting rule
do not admit a polynomial kernel with the number of candidates as the
parameter. We show however that the Coalitional Manipulation problem which is
an important special case of the Possible Winner problem does admit a
polynomial kernel for maximin, Copeland, ranked pairs, and a class of scoring
rules that includes the Borda voting rule, when the number of manipulators is
polynomial in the number of candidates. A significant conclusion of our work is
that the Possible Winner problem is harder than the Coalitional Manipulation
problem since the Coalitional Manipulation problem admits a polynomial kernel
whereas the Possible Winner problem does not admit a polynomial kernel.

text: In this study, we investigate the concept of Wilf equivalence for consecutive patterns within permutations, aiming to enhance the understanding of structural properties that determine pattern enumeration. Our primary objective is to determine conditions under which two sets of consecutive patterns are Wilf equivalent, defined by equal counting sequences across all permutation lengths. Using a combination of generating functions, bijective proofs, and the permutation group theory, we have derived new results that not only confirm existing conjectures but also uncover novel equivalences. We introduce a framework for systematically analyzing consecutive patterns, leveraging symmetry properties and group actions to simplify complex enumeration problems. Our methodology emphasizes the extraction and transformation of generating functions to identify shared structures between ostensibly disparate patterns. Results demonstrate that several previously unexplored pattern pairs exhibit Wilf equivalence, suggesting deeper symmetries within permutation classes than traditionally recognized. Moreover, we establish a set of sufficient criteria that predict Wilf equivalence among generalized consecutive patterns, providing a modular approach to studying pattern-related phenomena. Our work contributes to the broader understanding of permutation patterns by expanding the catalog of known equivalences and offering refined analytic tools for future research. These findings open pathways for extending Wilf equivalence beyond the confines of specific pattern types, potentially impacting varied areas within discrete mathematics and combinatorial theory. Future research inspired by this study could explore the implications of these equivalences in algorithmic applications, such as sorting and compression techniques, where pattern efficiency remains a pivotal concern.

This paper presents a series of results on the interplay between quantum
estimation, cloning and finite de Finetti theorems. First, we consider the
measure-and-prepare channel that uses optimal estimation to convert M copies
into k approximate copies of an unknown pure state and we show that this
channel is equal to a random loss of all but s particles followed by cloning
from s to k copies. When the number k of output copies is large with respect to
the number M of input copies the measure-and-prepare channel converges in
diamond norm to the optimal universal cloning. In the opposite case, when M is
large compared to k, the estimation becomes almost perfect and the
measure-and-prepare channel converges in diamond norm to the partial trace over
all but k systems. This result is then used to derive de Finetti-type results
for quantum states and for symmetric broadcast channels, that is, channels that
distribute quantum information to many receivers in a permutationally invariant
fashion. Applications of the finite de Finetti theorem for symmetric broadcast
channels include the derivation of diamond-norm bounds on the asymptotic
convergence of quantum cloning to state estimation and the derivation of bounds
on the amount of quantum information that can be jointly decoded by a group of
k receivers at the output of a symmetric broadcast channel.
label: human

We have completed an optical spectroscopic survey of an unbiased,
extinction-limited sample of candidate young stars covering 1.3 square degrees
of the Rho Ophiuchi star forming region. While infrared, X-ray, and optical
surveys of the cloud have identified many young stellar objects (YSOs), these
surveys are biased towards particular stages of stellar evolution and are not
optimal for studies of the disk frequency and initial mass function.We have
obtained over 300 optical spectra to help identify 135 association members
based on the presence of H-alpha in emission, lithium absorption, X-ray
emission, a mid-infrared excess, a common proper motion, reflection nebulosity,
and/or extinction considerations. Spectral types along with R and I band
photometry were used to derive effective temperatures and bolometric
luminosities for association members to compare with theoretical tracks and
isochrones for pre-main-sequence stars. An average age of 3.1 Myr is derived
for this population which is intermediate between that of objects embedded in
the cloud core of Rho Ophiuchi and low mass stars in the Upper Scorpius
subgroup. Consistent with this age we find a circumstellar disk frequency of
27% plus or minus 5%. We also constructed an initial mass function for an
extinction-limited sample of 123 YSOs (A_v less than or equal to 8 mag), which
is consistent with the field star initial mass function for YSOs with masses >
0.2 M_sun. There may be a deficit of brown dwarfs but this result relies on
completeness corrections and requires confirmation.
label: human

We study the spin-down properties of PSR B0919+06 based on almost 30 years of
radio observations. We confirm that the time derivative of the rotational
frequency $\dot \nu$ is modulated quasi-periodically and show that it exhibits
a repeating double-peaked structure throughout the entire observation span. We
model the $\dot \nu$ variation of the pulsar assuming two spin-down rates with
sudden switches between them in time. Our results show that the double-peak
structure in $\dot \nu$ has a repetition time of about 630 days until MJD 52000
(April 2001) and 550 days since then. During this cycle, the pulsar spin varies
from the lower spin-down rate to the upper spin-down rate twice with different
amounts of time spent in each state, resulting in a further quasi-stable
secondary modulation of the two-state switching. This particular spin-down
state switching is broadly consistent with free precession of the pulsar,
however, a strong evidence linked with this mechanism is not clearly
established. We also confirm that the pulsar occasionally emits groups of
pulses which appear early in pulse phase, so-called "flares", and these events
significantly contribute to the pulse profile shape. We find the $\dot \nu$
modulation and the pulse shape variations are correlated throughout the
observations. However, the flare-state is not entirely responsible for this
correlation. In addition to the flare-state, we detect flare-like events from
the pulsar in single pulse observations. During these events, the shift in
pulse phase is small compared to that of the main flare-state and clearly
visible only in single pulse observations.
label: human

text:
We consider the problem of reliable epidemic dissemination of a rumor in a
fully connected network of~$n$ processes using push and pull operations. We
revisit the random phone call model and show that it is possible to disseminate
a rumor to all processes with high probability using $\Theta(\ln n)$ rounds of
communication and only $n+o(n)$ messages of size $b$, all of which are
asymptotically optimal and achievable with pull and push-then-pull algorithms.
This contradicts two highly-cited lower bounds of Karp et al. stating that any
algorithm in the random phone call model running in $\mathcal{O}(\ln n)$ rounds
with communication peers chosen uniformly at random requires at least
$\omega(n)$ messages to disseminate a rumor with high probability, and that any
address-oblivious algorithm needs $\Omega(n \ln \ln n)$ messages regardless of
the number of communication rounds. The reason for this contradiction is that
in the original work, processes do not have to share the rumor once the
communication is established. However, it is implicitly assumed that they
always do so in the proofs of their lower bounds, which, it turns out, is not
optimal. Our algorithms are strikingly simple, address-oblivious, and robust
against $\epsilon n$ adversarial failures and stochastic failures occurring
with probability $\delta$ for any $0 \leq \{\epsilon,\delta\} < 1$.
Furthermore, they can handle multiple rumors of size $b \in \omega(\ln n \ln
\ln n)$ with $nb + o(nb)$ bits of communication per rumor.
label: human

text:
Independently developed codebases typically contain many segments of code
that perform same or closely related operations (semantic clones). Finding
functionally equivalent segments enables applications like replacing a segment
by a more efficient or more secure alternative. Such related segments often
have different interfaces, so some glue code (an adapter) is needed to replace
one with the other. We present an algorithm that searches for replaceable code
segments at the function level by attempting to synthesize an adapter between
them from some family of adapters; it terminates if it finds no possible
adapter. We implement our technique using (1) concrete adapter enumeration
based on Intel's Pin framework (2) binary symbolic execution, and explore the
relation between size of adapter search space and total search time. We present
examples of applying adapter synthesis for improving security and efficiency of
binary functions, deobfuscating binary functions, and switching between binary
implementations of RC4. We present two large-scale evaluations, (1) we run
adapter synthesis on more than 13,000 function pairs from the Linux C library,
(2) using more than 61,000 fragments of binary code extracted from a ARM image
built for the iPod Nano 2g device and known functions from the VLC media
player, we evaluate our adapter synthesis implementation on more than a million
synthesis tasks . Our results confirm that several instances of adaptably
equivalent binary functions exist in real-world code, and suggest that adapter
synthesis can be applied for reverse engineering and for constructing cleaner,
less buggy, more efficient programs.
label: human

text: The top quark forward-backward asymmetry, observed at the Tevatron collider, has posed a significant challenge to the Standard Model predictions, prompting investigations into potential extensions that may account for this anomaly. Among the proposed solutions, the presence of a light axigluon, a hypothetical particle predicted by certain extensions of the color gauge group, offers a compelling explanation. This research aims to explore the parameter space wherein light axigluons could reconcile the observed asymmetry with theoretical models. Utilizing a combination of perturbative quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and non-standard model coupling dynamics, we systematically evaluate the parameter constraints imposed by current experimental data, including cross-section measurements and differential distributions in top quark pair production. Our study incorporates recent constraints from LHC data and employs advanced Monte Carlo simulations to ascertain the viability of axigluon masses ranging from 200 GeV to 400 GeV, with particular attention to their influence on asymmetry and associated kinematic distributions. The analysis reveals that specific parametric windows permit axiglusons to mediate top quark processes without conflicting with other stringent collider constraints, substantiating their potential role in explaining the asymmetry. Moreover, these findings propose new avenues for future experimental tests at the LHC, which could further illuminate the properties and existence of axigluons. Conclusively, this research underscores the necessity of continued experimental and theoretical scrutiny, advocating for a refined exploration of axigluons within broader particle physics contexts.
label: machine

text: We investigate the relativistic structure of one-meson and one-gluon exchange forces, which are pivotal in describing the lower excitation spectrum of the nucleon and the delta baryon. Our approach involves a combination of density functional theory and relativistic mean-field models to account for the complex interactions between the nucleons and the exchange forces. We find that the inclusion of relativistic corrections to the exchange forces leads to significant changes in the predicted excitation spectra, particularly in the case of the delta baryon.  Our results indicate that the one-meson exchange force, which is mediated by the pion, plays a crucial role in the formation of the nucleon and delta resonances. The relativistic treatment of the pion exchange force reveals a more complex and dynamic interaction between the nucleons and the pion field, which in turn affects the excitation spectra of the nucleon and delta. In contrast, the one-gluon exchange force, which is mediated by the gluon, is found to be less significant in the lower excitation spectrum of the nucleon and delta.  We also find that the inclusion of relativistic corrections to the exchange forces leads to a better agreement with experimental data, particularly in the case of the delta baryon. Our results suggest that a more comprehensive understanding of the relativistic structure of the one-meson and one-gluon exchange forces is necessary to accurately describe the lower excitation spectrum of the nucleon and delta.
label: machine

text: In this study, we address the vulnerability of distributed-storage systems against guessing attacks, where an adversary tries to guess file identifiers or storage locations. Our approach involves analyzing the entropy and redundancy levels within the system's metadata to quantify the security risk. We implement a series of simulations and experiments that demonstrate how different levels of redundancy affect the likelihood of successful guessing attacks. Key methodologies include statistical analysis of metadata entropy and probabilistic models of attack success rates. The results indicate that increasing redundancy significantly reduces the probability of guessing attacks, thereby improving overall system security. However, there is a trade-off between security and performance, which we also explore through our findings. This work provides a comprehensive framework for assessing and enhancing the resilience of distributed-storage systems against guessing attacks.
label: machine

We analyze the suppression of particle production at large transverse momenta
in ($0-5%$ most) central collisions of gold nuclei at $\sqrt{s_\textrm{NN}}=$
200 GeV and lead nuclei at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=$ 2.76 TeV. Full
next-to-leading order radiative corrections at ${\cal{O}}(\alpha_s^3)$, and
nuclear effects like shadowing and parton energy loss are included. The parton
energy loss is implemented in a simple multiple scattering model, where the
partons lose an energy $\epsilon=\lambda \times dE/dx$ per collision, where
$\lambda$ is their mean free path. We take $\epsilon=\kappa E$ for a treatment
which is suggestive of the Bethe Heitler (BH) mechanism of incoherent
scatterings, $\epsilon = \sqrt{\alpha E}$ for LPM mechanism, and $\epsilon=$
constant for a mechanism which suggests that the rate of energy loss ($dE/dx$)
of the partons is proportional to total path length ($L$) of the parton in the
plasma, as the formation time of the radiated gluon becomes much larger than
$L$.
  We find that while the BH mechanism describes the nuclear modification factor
$R_{\textrm{AA}}$ for $p_T \leq$ 5 GeV/$c$ (especially at RHIC energy), the LPM
and more so the constant $dE/dx$ mechanism provides a good description at
larger $p_T$. This confirms the earlier expectation that the energy loss
mechanism for partons changes from BH to LPM for $p_T \ge \lambda <k_T^2>$,
where $\lambda \approx$ 1 fm and $<k_T^2> \approx$ 1 GeV$^2$ is the average
transverse kick-squared received by the parton per collision. The energy loss
per collision at the $\sqrt{s_\textrm{NN}}$ =2.76 TeV is found to be about
twice of that at 0.2 TeV.
label: human

text:
PbSe is a low-gap semiconductor with excellent infrared photo-detection
properties. Here we report our high magnetic field and low temperature
electrical properties measurement performed on a moderately doped PbSe single
crystals with p-type bulk carrier density of around $1\times10^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$.
Longitudinal resistance (R$_{xx}$) and Hall resistance (R$_{xy}$) were
simultaneously measured between 0 T--18 T at several temperatures between 0.8
K--25 K. These transport measurements start showing oscillatory behavior around
and above 6 T of magnetic field. The quantum oscillation frequency is ~15 T,
giving an estimate for the carrier density of each L pocket in the BZ
participating in these oscillations. The effective mass of the free carriers is
estimated from the temperature dependence of oscillation amplitudes.
Measurements as the magnetic fields is rotated reveal the magneto-transport
properties of a 3D-like fermi surface. Free carrier scattering rate from the
transport data has been estimated which also gave an estimation of Dingle
temperature in PbSe. Room temperature optical measurements has been conducted
and other optical properties has been estimated. The Drude-Lorentz model fit
has been performed which show a low frequency phonon mode around 45 cm$^{-1}$
and bandgap of around 0.2 eV along with other interband electronic transitions.
Some of the optical and transport results has been compared against other
members of class IV-VI chalcogenides.
label: human

text:
We present results of a joint \textit{Chandra}/\textit{XMM-Newton} analysis
of the early-type galaxies NGC 4649 and NGC 5846 aimed at investigating
differences between mass profiles derived from X-ray data and those from
optical data, to probe the state of the hot ISM in these galaxies. If the hot
ISM is at a given radius in hydrostatic equilibrium (HE) the X-ray data can be
used to measure the total enclosed mass of the galaxy. Differences from
optically-derived mass distributions therefore yield information about
departures from HE in the hot halos. The X-ray mass profiles in different
angular sectors of NGC 4649 are generally smooth with no significant azimuthal
asymmetries within \(12\) kpc. Extrapolation of these profiles beyond this
scale yields results consistent with the optical estimate. However, in the
central region (\(r < 3\) kpc) the X-ray data underpredict the enclosed mass,
when compared with the optical mass profiles. Consistent with previous results
we estimate a non-thermal pressure component accounting for \(30\%\) of the gas
pressure, likely linked to nuclear activity. In NGC 5846 the X-ray mass
profiles show significant azimuthal asymmetries, especially in the NE
direction. Comparison with optical mass profiles in this direction suggests
significant departures from HE, consistent with bulk gas compression and
decompression due to sloshing on \(\sim 15\) kpc scales; this effect disappears
in the NW direction where the emission is smooth and extended. In this sector
we find consistent X-ray and optical mass profiles, suggesting that the hot
halo is not responding to strong non-gravitational forces.
label: human

Let $\mathfrak a$ be an algebraic Lie algebra. An adapted pair for $\mathfrak
a$ is pair $(h,\eta)$ consisting of an ad-semisimple element of $h \in
\mathfrak a$ and a regular element of $\eta \in \mathfrak a^*$ satisfying $(ad
\ h)\eta=-\eta$. An adapted pair $(h,\eta)$ is said to satisfy integrality if
$ad \ h$ has integer eigenvalues on $\mathfrak a$. Integrality is shown to hold
for any Frobenius Lie algebra which is a biparabolic subalgebra of a semisimple
Lie algebra; but may fail in general.
  Call $\mathfrak a$ regular if there are no proper semi-invariant polynomial
functions on $\mathfrak a^*$ and if the subalgebra of invariant functions is
polynomial. In this case there are no known counter-examples to integrality. It
is shown that if $\mathfrak a$ is the canonical truncation of a biparabolic
subalgebra of a simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ which is regular and admits an
adapted pair $(h,\eta)$, then the eigenvalues of $ad \ h$ on $\mathfrak a$ lie
in $\frac{1}{m}\mathbb Z$, where $m$ is a coefficient of a simple root in the
highest root of $\mathfrak g$.
  Let $\mathfrak a$ be a regular Lie algebra admitting an adapted pair
$(h,\eta)$. Let $\mathfrak a_\mathbb Z$ be the subalgebra spanned by the
eigensubspaces of $ad \ h$ with integer eigenvalue. It is shown that the
canonical truncation of $\mathfrak a_\mathbb Z$ is regular. Sufficient
knowledge of the relation between the generators for the invariant polynomial
functions on $\mathfrak a^*$ and on $\mathfrak a^*_\mathbb Z$ can then lead to
establishing the integrality of $(h,\eta)$. This method is used to show the
integrality of an adapted pair for a truncated parabolic subalgebra of a simple
Lie algebra of type $C$.
label: human

text: The increasing demand for efficient data transmission in Agile Software-Defined (Agile-SD) networks necessitates the optimization of underlying protocols, notably the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). This study aims to model and analyze the throughput of the Linux-based Agile-SD TCP, focusing on its performance under varying network conditions. Employing a combination of simulation and analytical modeling, we implemented enhancements to the existing TCP architecture suited for Agile-SD environments. Simulations were conducted using ns-3 network simulator, augmented to support Agile-SD functions and constraints. Key metrics such as packet loss rate, latency, and throughput efficiency were analyzed. The model incorporated components of delay modeling, congestion control algorithms, and adaptive window scaling to reflect the dynamic network topology typical of Agile-SD systems. Our findings reveal a significant increase in throughput efficiency—up to 30% improvement over traditional Linux TCP implementations—across diverse traffic loads and network configurations. Moreover, the model demonstrated robust performance against network volatility, maintaining stability and reducing latency peaks. This indicates that the proposed model effectively addresses bandwidth optimization issues and enhances overall TCP functionality within Agile-SD networks. In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive model that enhances the understanding of TCP performance in Agile-SD environments, paving the way for further optimization and practical deployment in real-world scenarios. Future work could explore AI-driven adaptation mechanisms to further leverage network dynamics, contributing to the growing field of smart networking solutions.
label: machine

We investigated the magnetic field dependence of the Hall and the bend
resistances in the ballistic regime for a single layer graphene Hall bar
structure containing a pn-junction. When both regions are n-type the Hall
resistance dominates and Hall type of plateaus are formed. These plateaus occur
as a consequence of the restriction on the angle imposed by Snell's law
allowing only electrons with a certain initial angles to transmit though the
potential step. The size of the plateau and its position is determined by the
position of the potential interface as well as the value of the applied
potential. When the second region is p-type the bend resistance dominates which
is asymmetric in field due to the presence of snake states. Changing the
position of the pn-interface in the Hall bar strongly affects these states and
therefore the bend resistance is also changed. Changing the applied potential
we observe that the bend resistance exhibits a peak around the
charge-neutrality point (CNP) which is independent of the position of the
pn-interface, while the Hall resistance shows a sign reversal when the CNP is
crossed, which is in very good agreement with a recent experiment [J. R.
Williams et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 107, 046602(2011)].
label: human

With the ever increasing influx of high resolution images of the solar
surface obtained at a multitude of wavelengths, various processes occurring at
small spatial scales have become a greater focus of our attention. Complex
small-scale magnetic fields have been reported that appear to have enough
stored to heat the chromosphere. While significant progress has been made in
understanding small-scale phenomena, many specifics remain elusive. We present
here a detailed study of a single event of disappearance of a magnetic dipole
and associated chromospheric activity. Based on New Solar Telescope H$\alpha$
data and {\it Hinode} photospheric line-of-sight magnetograms and Ca II H
images we report the following. 1) Our analysis indicates that even very small
dipoles (elements separated by about 0\arcsec.5 or less) may reach the
chromosphere and trigger non-negligible chromospheric activity. 2) Careful
consideration of the magnetic environment where the new flux is deposited may
shed light on the details of magnetic flux removal from the solar surface. We
argue that the apparent collision and disappearance of two opposite polarity
elements may not necessarily indicate their cancellation (i.e., reconnection,
emergence of a "U" tube or submergence of $ \Omega $ loops). In our case, the
magnetic dipole disappeared by reconnecting with overlying large-scale inclined
plage fields. 3) Bright points seen in off-band H$\alpha$ images are very
well-correlated with the Ca II H bright points, which in turn are co-spatial
with G-band bright points. We further speculate that, in general, H$\alpha$
bright points are expected be co-spatial with photospheric BPs, however, a
direct comparison is needed to refine their relationship.
label: human

text: This study aims to detect water vapor in the thermal spectrum of the non-transiting hot Jupiter upsilon Andromedae b, a challenging task due to its high temperature and lack of transits. We employed high-resolution spectroscopy to analyze the star’s light as the planet passes in front of it, which is not possible in the case of upsilon Andromedae b. Our methodology involved detailed modeling of the stellar spectrum and subtraction of known atmospheric features such as hydrogen lines. Through advanced data analysis techniques, we identified spectral lines characteristic of water vapor absorption. The presence of these lines confirms the detection of water vapor in the atmosphere of upsilon Andromedae b, thereby providing valuable insights into the composition and dynamics of exoplanetary atmospheres. This work advances our understanding of planetary atmospheres and contributes significantly to the field of exoplanet characterization.
label: machine

text: We investigate the contributions of penguin diagrams to the CP violation phases in \( B_{d,s} \) decays to charmonium, specifically focusing on the influence these loop processes exert on the determination of the angles in the Unitarity Triangle. We perform a comprehensive analysis that encompasses the characterization of both the tree-level and penguin contributions, employing the effective Hamiltonian formalism to facilitate our calculations. Utilizing recent experimental data from B-factories and LHCb, we extract relevant decay rates and CP-violating asymmetries, comparing them against the Standard Model predictions.   Our findings demonstrate that penguin contributions significantly impact the theoretical estimates of CP violation in \( B_{d,s} \to J/\psi K \) and \( B_{s} \to J/\psi \phi \) channels, with implications for the values of the CKM parameters \( \gamma \) and \( \phi_s \). Notably, we identify specific regions where the penguin effects enhance the CP violation observables, suggesting potential discrepancies with the naive expectations rooted in tree-level processes.   Moreover, we propose methodologies to disentangle the penguin effects from the tree-level contributions through angular analysis and branching ratios, thereby refining our understanding of the underlying processes. Our work not only clarifies the role of penguin contributions in the precise measurement of CP phases but also sets the stage for future investigations into new physics scenarios that may arise in \( B \)-meson decays.
label: machine

text:
Stars may be assembled in large growth spurts, however the evidence for this
hypothesis is circumstantial. Directly studying the accretion at the earliest
phases of stellar growth is challenging because young stars are deeply embedded
in optically thick envelopes, which have spectral energy distributions that
peak in the far-IR, where observations are difficult. In this paper, we
consider the feasibility of detecting accretion outbursts from these younger
stars by investigating the timescales for how the protostellar envelope
responds to changes in the emission properties of the central source. The
envelope heats up in response to an outburst, brightening at all wavelengths
and with the emission peak moving to shorter wavelengths. The timescale for
this change depends on the time for dust grains to heat and re-emit photons and
the time required for the energy to escape the inner, optically-thick portion
of the envelope. We find that the dust response time is much shorter than the
photon propagation time and thus the timescale over which the emission varies
is set by time delays imposed by geometry. These times are hours to days near
the peak of the spectral energy distribution and weeks to months in the sub-mm.
The ideal location to quickly detect continuum variability is therefore in the
mid- to far-IR, near the peak of the spectral energy distribution, where the
change in emission amplitude is largest. Searching for variability in sub-mm
continuum emission is also feasible, though with a longer time separation and a
weaker relationship between the amount of detected emission amplitude and
change in central source luminosity. Such observations would constrain
accretion histories of protostars and would help to trace the disk/envelope
instabilities that lead to stellar growth.
label: human

text: Cognitive Radio Networks (CRNs) represent a promising solution for enhancing spectral efficiency in wireless communications by allowing secondary users to access underutilized spectrum bands. The primary challenge in CRNs is the efficient allocation of channels to these users while minimizing interference with primary users and resolving access contention among secondary users themselves. This research addresses the dual problem of channel assignment and access contention resolution in CRNs. Our objective is to develop a robust method that ensures optimal channel allocation with minimized contention, thereby improving network performance.  We propose a novel hybrid algorithm that combines graph coloring techniques for effective channel assignment with a priority-based access contention resolution mechanism. The algorithm dynamically adjusts to real-time network conditions by leveraging spectral sensing data to identify available channels and implements a hierarchical access strategy to prioritize secondary users based on predefined criteria, such as transmission priority and time since the last successful access.  Through extensive simulations, our methodology demonstrates a significant reduction in contention-related delays and collision rates compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Key findings indicate that the proposed solution enhances overall network throughput and reduces channel access time for secondary users, thereby optimizing spectrum utilization.  In conclusion, this research contributes a comprehensive channel assignment framework tailored for CRNs, integrating real-time adaptability and efficient contention management. The results underscore the potential of the proposed method to significantly improve spectral efficiency and user experience in dynamic and heterogeneous wireless environments. This approach provides a foundation for further explorations into intelligent spectrum management solutions.
label: machine

text: The abstract focuses on exploring the relationship between the mu-vector, Morse inequalities, and a generalized lower bound theorem within the context of locally tame combinatorial manifolds. Starting with a background on the mu-vector, which is a topological invariant used in computational topology, the study delves into how it can be utilized to derive insights from Morse theory. Morse inequalities, fundamental in understanding the topology of smooth manifolds via critical points of functions, are extended to combinatorial settings. The research proposes a generalized lower bound theorem that leverages these concepts to establish bounds on the number of critical points of functions defined on locally tame combinatorial manifolds.  Methodologically, the study employs discrete Morse theory, a combinatorial tool that simplifies cell complexes while preserving topological information. This approach allows for the application of Morse inequalities in the discrete setting. Key findings include deriving new bounds on the mu-vector for various classes of locally tame combinatorial manifolds, which offer deeper insights into their topological structure compared to traditional methods. The results not only generalize existing lower bound theorems but also provide a framework for analyzing the complexity of combinatorial structures through the lens of Morse theory.  Concluding, the research demonstrates the utility of combining Morse theory with discrete Morse theory in the study of locally tame combinatorial manifolds. It highlights the potential for further exploration in understanding the interplay between topology, combinatorics, and algebraic structures, opening avenues for future research in computational topology and geometric combinatorics.
label: machine

In this article we address a problem of determination of light pressure upon
space structures of the complex geometric shape. For the surface element, we
wrote a condition that this element can interact with light only from the front
side, not from the back side. This condition To in the form of series of
Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind. Chebyshev expansion lets us move to
the series of tensors of increasing rank for the problem of determination of
force and moment. We obtained expressions for the fiber method for
determination of light pressure on space structures of complex geometry taking
into account self--shadowing and reflections within the structure. We also give
the expressions for tensor parametrization by the specularity coefficient in
case of specular-diffuse reflection. For these expressions we calculated the
principal moment and force upon two-sided flat solar sail, spherical and
cylindrical bodies, and approximated light pressure upon a perspective space
observatory Millimetron. The proposed expressions can be used in the ballistic
analysis of solar sails and other space objects, which are significantly
affected by the radiation pressure. Also, these results can be used to analyze
the dynamics of movement of large-scale space structures around the center of
gravity under the light pressure.
label: human

text: In this study, we investigate the dynamics of parallel adaptation through the examination of whether advantageous alleles propagate as single or multiple waves of advance. Our research aims to address the complex question of whether a single wave represents the most likely scenario in parallel adaptation or if multiple waves are more prevalent. Through the utilization of mathematical models and simulations, we explore the various conditions under which different wave patterns emerge in the spread of advantageous alleles. Our results reveal that the mode of advance of advantageous alleles is contingent on a combination of factors including selection strength, population size, and spatial structure. By comparing and contrasting the dynamics of single versus multiple waves of advance, we contribute novel insights into the mechanisms governing parallel adaptation in biological populations. Our methodology involves employing theoretical models combined with computational simulations to elucidate the intricate interplay of evolutionary forces shaping the spread of advantageous alleles. This research provides valuable implications for understanding the evolutionary processes underlying parallel adaptation and sheds light on the competing dynamics of single versus multiple waves of advance in allele propagation.
label: machine

text: In this study, we explore the role of Feshbach resonances and mesoscopic phase separation in understanding the behavior of multiband FeAs-based superconductors near a quantum critical point. Our investigation addresses the complex problem of elucidating the microscopic interactions that govern superconductivity and phase coherence in these compounds. We utilized advanced computational techniques to model the electron-electron interactions and the resultant emergent phenomena within a multiband framework. Our analysis reveals that Feshbach resonances play a significant role in enhancing superconducting pairing by coupling between bound and scattering states of electron pairs across the bands. Moreover, we observe that mesoscopic phase separation manifests in proximity to the quantum critical point, characterized by the coexistence of distinct electronic phases on a mesoscopic scale. This phase separation is intricately linked to the multiband nature of these superconductors and the competition between different magnetic and superconducting orders. Our results indicate that these phenomena contribute to the nontrivial temperature and doping dependence of superconducting properties observed in experiments. Methodologically, we employed a combination of renormalization group equations and numerical simulations to map the phase diagram and capture the intricate dynamics at play. Our findings provide novel insights into the interplay between electronic correlations and emergent order parameters, offering a theoretical framework that may guide the design of new superconducting materials. The study advances our understanding of quantum criticality in multiband superconductors, highlighting the pivotal role of Feshbach resonances and phase separation in shaping their physical properties.
label: machine

text:
Functional data are defined as realizations of random functions (mostly
smooth functions) varying over a continuum, which are usually collected with
measurement errors on discretized grids. In order to accurately smooth noisy
functional observations and deal with the issue of high-dimensional observation
grids, we propose a novel Bayesian method based on the Bayesian hierarchical
model with a Gaussian-Wishart process prior and basis function representations.
We first derive an induced model for the basis-function coefficients of the
functional data, and then use this model to conduct posterior inference through
Markov chain Monte Carlo. Compared to the standard Bayesian inference that
suffers serious computational burden and unstableness for analyzing
high-dimensional functional data, our method greatly improves the computational
scalability and stability, while inheriting the advantage of simultaneously
smoothing raw observations and estimating the mean-covariance functions in a
nonparametric way. In addition, our method can naturally handle functional data
observed on random or uncommon grids. Simulation and real studies demonstrate
that our method produces similar results as the standard Bayesian inference
with low-dimensional common grids, while efficiently smoothing and estimating
functional data with random and high-dimensional observation grids where the
standard Bayesian inference fails. In conclusion, our method can efficiently
smooth and estimate high-dimensional functional data, providing one way to
resolve the curse of dimensionality for Bayesian functional data analysis with
Gaussian-Wishart processes.
label: human

text: In this study, we address the challenge of high-precision trajectory tracking in dynamic environments, where external disturbances and variations can significantly impact performance. We propose an innovative framework that integrates $\mathcal{L}_1$ adaptive feedback control with iterative learning techniques. Our methodology commences with a robust disturbance estimation mechanism using $\mathcal{L}_1$ adaptive filters, effectively minimizing the influence of external perturbations on the system's trajectory. We then implement an iterative learning control strategy that leverages previously collected data to enhance future performance.   Through extensive simulations and real-world experimentation, we demonstrate that our approach successfully adapts to changing conditions while maintaining trajectory tracking accuracy. The results illustrate a significant reduction in tracking errors compared to traditional feedback control methods, with the system exhibiting resilience against both parameter uncertainties and varying environmental factors. We observe that the $\mathcal{L}_1$ adaptive component provides a swift response to alterations in environmental dynamics, while the iterative learning aspect reinforces the system's ability to improve over time through repeated exposure to similar trajectory tasks.  Quantitative analysis reveals that our proposed model consistently achieves high precision, characterized by minimal deviation from the desired trajectory. Overall, our work advances the field of trajectory tracking by providing a versatile and effective solution capable of adapting to unpredictable changes and enhancing system performance through intelligent learning mechanisms.

text: Rutile, a naturally occurring mineral composed primarily of titanium dioxide (TiO2), has been found to exhibit abnormal diffusion of transition metals, which significantly affects its optical, electrical, and magnetic properties. This phenomenon has sparked intense research interest in understanding the underlying mechanisms and exploring potential applications in various fields, including catalysis, energy storage, and biomedical devices.  The objective of this study was to investigate the origin of abnormal diffusion of transition metals in rutile, focusing on the role of defects, impurities, and structural factors. A comprehensive review of existing literature revealed that the diffusion of transition metals in rutile is influenced by the presence of defects, such as vacancies, interstitials, and grain boundaries, which provide pathways for metal ion migration. Additionally, the study highlighted the impact of impurities, such as water and oxygen, on the diffusion process.  The research employed a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches to investigate the diffusion of transition metals in rutile. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were used to characterize the surface and internal structure of rutile samples, respectively. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to simulate the diffusion process and evaluate the effects of defects and impurities on metal ion mobility.  The results of this study revealed that defects and impurities play a crucial role in facilitating the abnormal diffusion of transition metals in rutile. Specifically, the presence of vacancies and grain boundaries was found to increase the diffusion coefficient, while the incorporation of impurities, such as water and oxygen, reduced the diffusion rate. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the origin of abnormal diffusion in rutile and have significant implications for the design and optimization of rutile-based materials for various applications.
label: machine

text: In our recent study of Hickson Compact Group 57 (HCG 57), we investigate the galaxy group's interstellar medium dynamics and star formation properties, emphasizing the analysis of the strong far-infrared (Far-IR) cooling lines and peculiar CO kinematics. Our observations utilized the Herschel Space Observatory and the IRAM 30m telescope, enabling a comprehensive assessment of the physical conditions within these interacting galaxies. We report the detection of enhanced [C II] 158 μm and [O I] 63 μm emission lines, which indicate efficient cooling of the interstellar medium and possible heating mechanisms induced by galactic interactions. Notably, the CO(1-0) and CO(2-1) emission lines exhibit unique velocity profiles, suggesting disturbed molecular gas dynamics that deviate from typical rotational configurations. This kinematic peculiarity may correlate with disrupted star formation processes. Through this analysis, we address potential mechanisms for star formation suppression, highlighting tidal interactions and the role of feedback from existing stellar populations. Our results suggest that interactions within HCG 57 could be inhibiting new star formation, likely due to the chaotic redistribution and heating of the molecular gas, possibly exacerbated by shocks and enhanced turbulence. We propose that these mechanisms are critical in understanding the evolution of compact galaxy groups and their role as environments where stellar activity may be regulated. This study provides new insights into galaxy interaction dynamics, emphasizing the need for further high-resolution spectral observations to elucidate the essential processes governing star formation in similarly complex systems.

text: Red supergiants (RSGs) are massive, short-lived, and evolving stars with significant importance as cosmic abundance probes. This study investigates the abundance patterns of red supergiants in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC), two nearby irregular galaxies. We compiled a sample of 51 RSGs from the literature and analyzed their spectral features using spectroscopic data to derive the elemental abundances. Our analysis indicates that RSGs in both LMC and SMC exhibit a trend of increasing abundance ratios from oxygen to heavier elements, consistent with previous studies. However, we also found that RSGs in LMC generally show higher abundances compared to those in SMC, suggesting a higher star formation efficiency in LMC. Furthermore, we discovered that RSGs in LMC exhibit larger abundance scatter than those in SMC, indicating a more complex star formation history or a more diverse stellar population in LMC. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the chemical evolution in the Magellanic Clouds and the role of red supergiants as valuable probes of cosmic abundance.

text: This study examines the effects of resolution on accretion and drag force modeling for Supermassive Black Holes (SMBHs). Background research highlights the importance of accurately modeling the accretion and drag forces in SMBHs, as these processes significantly influence their growth and evolution. However, current numerical simulations often suffer from resolution limitations, which can lead to inaccurate results and a lack of understanding of the underlying physical mechanisms.  The objective of this research is to investigate the impact of resolution on accretion and drag force modeling for SMBHs, with a focus on improving the accuracy of numerical simulations. A comprehensive analysis of existing literature and a review of numerical methods used to model SMBH accretion and drag forces are conducted.  A custom-made numerical model is developed to simulate the accretion and drag forces in SMBHs, with varying resolution levels. The results show that increasing the resolution of the simulation significantly improves the accuracy of the accretion and drag force modeling. However, the optimal resolution level is found to be dependent on the specific SMBH model and the underlying physical mechanisms.  Key findings indicate that higher resolution simulations can capture more realistic accretion and drag force profiles, leading to improved predictions of SMBH growth and evolution. The study also highlights the importance of considering the effects of resolution on numerical simulations, and provides recommendations for future research in this area. Ultimately, this research contributes to a better understanding of the complex physical processes involved in SMBH accretion and drag forces, and has implications for the development of more accurate numerical models.

text: We investigate the role of Coulomb-gas electrostatics in governing the large fluctuations of the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation, which serves as a foundational model for non-equilibrium growth phenomena. Our research addresses the critical problem of understanding the influence of long-range interactions on the statistical properties of KPZ surfaces, particularly in the context of extreme fluctuation events, which have significant implications for various physical systems. Using a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, we employ a Coulomb gas representation to map the KPZ equation to a system of charged particles interacting through logarithmic potentials. This approach enables us to derive exact statistical distributions of the interface height and establish connections between the KPZ dynamics and electrostatic principles.   Our findings reveal that the inclusion of Coulombic interactions leads to a significant alteration in the fluctuation statistics, emerging as a pivotal mechanism controlling the universality classes of large deviations in the KPZ dynamics. We demonstrate that the electrostatic coupling enhances the correlation of fluctuations, allowing for the emergence of atypical growth patterns that deviate from the standard KPZ scaling. By systematically varying the interaction strength and analyzing the corresponding impacts on system behavior, we elucidate the complex interplay between local growth processes and long-range interactions. This work not only contributes to the theoretical understanding of KPZ universality but also offers novel insights into the broader implications of electrostatics in governing fluctuation phenomena across diverse fields, including biology, materials science, and statistical physics.

text: We investigated the possibility of generalizing the concept of torsion fields within braneworld scenarios, with a focus on their role in stabilizing the extra dimensions. Our analysis revealed that the inclusion of torsion fields in the effective action of a braneworld model can significantly impact the gravitational sector, leading to novel solutions for the stabilization of the compactified dimensions. By introducing a non-minimal coupling of the scalar field to the torsion field, we were able to generate a potential that dynamically breaks the symmetry of the extra dimensions, thereby providing a mechanism for their stabilization. Our results indicate that the inclusion of torsion fields can be used to generate a wide range of possible generalizations within braneworld scenarios, including the possibility of stabilizing the extra dimensions through the use of a non-minimal coupling. We also found that the presence of torsion fields can lead to the emergence of a new type of gravitational interaction, which we term the "torsion-mediated interaction." This interaction can potentially be used to explain a wide range of observational phenomena, including the observed anomalies in the large-scale structure of the universe. Our work provides a new framework for understanding the role of torsion fields in braneworld scenarios, and has significant implications for our understanding of the fundamental laws of physics.

The ability to quickly recognize and learn new visual concepts from limited
samples enables humans to swiftly adapt to new environments. This ability is
enabled by semantic associations of novel concepts with those that have already
been learned and stored in memory. Computers can start to ascertain similar
abilities by utilizing a semantic concept space. A concept space is a
high-dimensional semantic space in which similar abstract concepts appear close
and dissimilar ones far apart. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to
one-shot learning that builds on this idea. Our approach learns to map a novel
sample instance to a concept, relates that concept to the existing ones in the
concept space and generates new instances, by interpolating among the concepts,
to help learning. Instead of synthesizing new image instance, we propose to
directly synthesize instance features by leveraging semantics using a novel
auto-encoder network we call dual TriNet. The encoder part of the TriNet learns
to map multi-layer visual features of deep CNNs, that is, multi-level concepts,
to a semantic vector. In semantic space, we search for related concepts, which
are then projected back into the image feature spaces by the decoder portion of
the TriNet. Two strategies in the semantic space are explored. Notably, this
seemingly simple strategy results in complex augmented feature distributions in
the image feature space, leading to substantially better performance.

text:
We study the crossover from low- to high-temperature fluctuations including
critical fluctuations in confined isotropic O$(n)$-symmetric systems on the
basis of a finite-size renormalization-group approach at fixed dimension $d$
introduced previously [V. Dohm, Phys. Rev. Lett. {\bf 110}, 107207 (2013)]. Our
theory is formulated within the $\varphi^4$ lattice model in a $d$-dimensional
block geometry with periodic boundary conditions. We derive the finite-size
scaling functions $F^{\text ex}$ and $X$ of the excess free energy density and
of the thermodynamic Casimir force, respectively, for $1\leq n \leq \infty$,
$2<d<4$. Applications are given for $ L_\parallel^{d-1} \times L$ slab
geometries with a finite aspect ratio $\rho=L/L_\parallel$ as well as for the
film limit $\rho \to 0$ at fixed $L$. For $n=1$ and $\rho=0$ the
low-temperature limits of $F^{\text ex}$ and $X$ vanish whereas they are finite
for $n\geq 2$ and $\rho = 0$ due to the effect of the Goldstone modes. For
$n=1$ and $\rho>0$ we find a finite low-temperature limit of $F^{\text ex}$
which deviates from that of the the Ising model. We attribute this deviation to
the nonuniversal difference between the $\varphi^4$ model with continuous
variables $\varphi$ and the Ising model with discrete spin variables $s=\pm1$.
For $n\geq 2$ and $\rho>0$, a logarithmic divergence of $F^{\text ex}$ in the
low-temperature limit is predicted, in excellent agreement with Monte Carlo
(MC) data for the $d=3$ $XY$ model. For $2\leq n \leq \infty$ and $0\leq
\rho<\rho_0=0.8567$ the Goldstone modes generate a negative (attractive)
low-temperature Casimir force that vanishes for $\rho = \rho_0$ and becomes
positive (repulsive) for $\rho > \rho_0$. Our predictions are compared with MC
data for Ising, $XY$, and Heisenberg models in slab geometries with
$0.01\leq\rho\leq1$. Good overall agreement is found.

At present, the Boer-Mulders (BM) function for a given quark flavour is
extracted from data on semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering (SIDIS) using
the simplifying assumption that it is proportional to the Sivers function for
that flavour. In a recent paper we suggested that the consistency of this
assumption could be tested using information on so-called difference
asymmetries, i.e. the difference between the asymmetries in the production of
particles and their anti-particles.
  In this paper, using the SIDIS COMPASS deuteron data on the
$\langle\cos\phi_h\rangle$, $\langle\cos 2 \phi_h\rangle$ and Sivers difference
asymmetries, we carry out two independent consistency tests of the assumption
of proportionality, but here applied to the sum of the valence-quark
contributions. We find that such an assumption is compatible with the data. We
also show that the proportionality assumptions made in the existing
parametrizations of the BM functions are not compatible with our analysis,
which suggests that the published results for the Boer-Mulders functions for
individual flavours are unreliable.
  The $\langle\cos\phi_h\rangle$ and $\langle\cos 2 \phi_h\rangle$ asymmetries
receive contributions also from the, in principle, calculable Cahn effect. We
succeed in extracting the Cahn contributions from experiment (we believe for
the first time) and compare with their calculated values, with interesting
implications.

Action of solar wind on arbitrarily shaped interplanetary dust particle is
investigated. The final relativistically covariant equation of motion of the
particle contains both orbital evolution and change of particle's mass.
Non-radial solar wind velocity vector is also included. The covariant equation
of motion reduces to the Poynting-Robertson effect in the limiting case when
spherical particle is treated, the speed of the incident solar wind corpuscles
tends to the speed of light and the corpuscles spread radially from the Sun.
The results of quantum mechanics have to be incorporated into the physical
considerations, in order to obtain the limiting case. The condition for the
solar wind effect on motion of spherical interplanetary dust particle is
$\vec{p}'_{out}$ $=$ (1 $-$ $\sigma'_{pr} / \sigma'_{tot}$) $\vec{p}'_{in}$,
where $\vec{p}'_{in}$ and $\vec{p}'_{out}$ are incoming and outgoing radiation
momenta (per unit time) measured in the proper frame of reference of the
particle; $\sigma'_{pr}$ and $\sigma'_{tot}$ are solar wind pressure and total
scattering cross sections.
  Real flux density of solar wind energy produces shift of perihelion of
interplanetary dust particles. This result significantly differs from the
standard treatment of the action of the solar wind on dust particles, when
analogy with the Poynting-Robertson effect is stressed. Moreover, the evolution
of the shift of perihelion depends on orbital position of the parent body at
the time of ejection of the particle.

text: Circumgalactic medium (CGM) plays a crucial role in galaxy evolution by regulating gas inflow and outflow. Understanding the properties of CGM components, such as OVI, H I, low-ion absorption, line kinematics, and dust extinction, is essential to decipher the gas distribution around galaxies.   This study aims to investigate whether circumgalactic OVI can trace low-pressure gas located beyond the accretion shock. By analyzing the correlations between OVI, H I, low-ion absorption, line kinematics, and dust extinction, we aim to provide insights into the presence of low-pressure gas in the CGM.   We analyzed observational data of OVI, H I, low-ion absorption, line kinematics, and dust extinction around galaxies using spectroscopic techniques. By examining the relationships between these different components of the CGM, we aimed to determine if OVI can be used as a tracer for low-pressure gas beyond the accretion shock.   Our results indicate significant correlations between circumgalactic OVI, H I, low-ion absorption, line kinematics, and dust extinction. We found compelling evidence suggesting that OVI can indeed trace low-pressure gas beyond the accretion shock in the CGM.   This research provides valuable insights into the properties of the circumgalactic medium and its implications for galaxy evolution. The findings support the hypothesis that OVI can serve as a useful tracer for low-pressure gas in the outer regions of galaxies, shedding light on the complex dynamics of the CGM.

text:
Exoplanet orbital eccentricities offer valuable clues about the history of
planetary systems. Eccentric, Jupiter-sized planets are particularly
interesting: they may link the "cold" Jupiters beyond the ice line to close-in
hot Jupiters, which are unlikely to have formed in situ. To date,
eccentricities of individual transiting planets primarily come from radial
velocity measurements. Kepler has discovered hundreds of transiting Jupiters
spanning a range of periods, but the faintness of the host stars precludes
radial velocity follow-up of most. Here we demonstrate a Bayesian method of
measuring an individual planet's eccentricity solely from its transit light
curve using prior knowledge of its host star's density. We show that eccentric
Jupiters are readily identified by their short ingress/egress/total transit
durations -- part of the "photoeccentric" light curve signature of a planet's
eccentricity --- even with long-cadence Kepler photometry and
loosely-constrained stellar parameters. A Markov Chain Monte Carlo exploration
of parameter posteriors naturally marginalizes over the periapse angle and
automatically accounts for the transit probability. To demonstrate, we use
three published transit light curves of HD 17156 b to measure an eccentricity
of e = 0.71 +0.16/-0.09, in good agreement with the discovery value e =
0.67+/-0.08 based on 33 radial-velocity measurements. We present two additional
tests using actual Kepler data. In each case the technique proves to be a
viable method of measuring exoplanet eccentricities and their confidence
intervals. Finally, we argue that this method is the most efficient, effective
means of identifying the extremely eccentric, proto hot Jupiters predicted by
Socrates et al. (2012).

text: We present a microscopic nuclear collective rotation-vibration model that incorporates 2D submodeling to describe the complex dynamics of nuclear rotations and vibrations. This approach aims to bridge the gap between microscopic and macroscopic descriptions of nuclear collective phenomena, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics.   Utilizing density functional theory and quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we develop a 2D submodel that captures the essential features of nuclear rotations and vibrations, including the coupling of rotational and vibrational modes. The model is parameterized using experimental data from various nuclear reactions and spectroscopic studies, ensuring a high degree of accuracy and relevance.   Through extensive numerical simulations, we demonstrate the ability of the 2D submodel to reproduce a wide range of experimental observables, including rotational energies, vibrational frequencies, and collective excitations. Notably, the model successfully captures the complex interplay between rotational and vibrational modes, as well as the effects of shell effects and pairing on nuclear collective behavior.   Our results indicate that the 2D submodel provides a more nuanced and detailed understanding of nuclear collective dynamics, enabling the identification of novel correlations and relationships between different observables. The implications of this work are significant, as they suggest that the microscopic collective rotation-vibration model can be used to predict the behavior of complex nuclear systems, with potential applications in nuclear astrophysics, nuclear reactor physics, and nuclear spectroscopy.

text: We investigate the numerical evaluation of the bispectrum in the context of multiple field inflation, a theoretical framework that seeks to explain the origin and evolution of our universe. Our approach involves the use of advanced numerical methods to compute the bispectrum, a statistical measure that encodes information about the correlations between different fields in the early universe.   In multiple field inflation, multiple scalar fields interact and evolve in a complex manner, leading to a rich and dynamic landscape of possible outcomes. The bispectrum, a four-point correlation function of the fields, is a crucial quantity that can provide insights into the nature of this landscape. However, computing the bispectrum analytically is a challenging task due to the high dimensionality and non-linearity of the fields.  Our numerical strategy involves the use of a combination of numerical integration and machine learning techniques to efficiently evaluate the bispectrum. We employ a novel approach to discretize the fields, which allows for a more accurate and efficient computation of the bispectrum. Our results show that the numerical evaluation of the bispectrum can be performed accurately and efficiently, even in the presence of multiple fields and non-linear interactions.   The implications of our work are significant, as they provide a new tool for analyzing the predictions of multiple field inflation models. By computing the bispectrum numerically, we can gain insights into the properties of the universe, such as the distribution of matter and energy, and the formation of structure. Our results have the potential to shed new light on the fundamental laws of physics and the origins of our universe.
label: machine

We study the one-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain with competing
ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor J_1 and antiferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor
J_2 exchange couplings in the presence of magnetic field. We use both numerical
approaches (the density matrix renormalization group method and exact
diagonalization) and effective field-theory approach, and obtain the
ground-state phase diagram for wide parameter range of the coupling ratio
J_1/J_2. The phase diagram is rich and has a variety of phases, including the
vector chiral phase, the nematic phase, and other multipolar phases. In the
vector chiral phase, which appears in relatively weak magnetic field, the
ground state exhibits long-range order (LRO) of vector chirality which
spontaneously breaks a parity symmetry. The nematic phase shows a quasi-LRO of
antiferro-nematic spin correlation, and arises as a result of formation of
two-magnon bound states in high magnetic fields. Similarly, the higher
multipolar phases, such as triatic (p=3) and quartic (p=4) phases, are formed
through binding of p magnons near the saturation fields, showing quasi-LRO of
antiferro-multipolar spin correlations. The multipolar phases cross over to
spin density wave phases as the magnetic field is decreased, before
encountering a phase transition to the vector chiral phase at a lower field.
The implications of our results to quasi-one-dimensional frustrated magnets
(e.g., LiCuVO_4) are discussed.

We study the connection between the observed star formation rate-stellar mass
(SFR-$M_*$) relation and the evolution of the stellar mass function (SMF) by
means of a subhalo abundance matching technique coupled to merger trees
extracted from a N-body simulation. Our approach consist of forcing the model
to match the observed SMF at redshift $z \sim 2.3$, and let it evolve down to
$z \sim 0.3$ according to a $\tau$ model, an exponentially declining functional
form which describes the star formation rate decay of both satellite and
central galaxies. In this study, we use three different sets of SMFs: ZFOURGE
data from Tomczak et al.; UltraVISTA data from Ilbert et al. and COSMOS data
from Davidzon et al. We also build a mock survey combining UltraVISTA with
ZFOURGE. Our modelling of quenching timescales is consistent with the evolution
of the SMF down to $z \sim 0.3$, with different accuracy depending on the
particular survey used for calibration. We tested our model against the
observed SMFs at low redshift and it predicts residuals (observation versus
model) within $1\sigma$ observed scatter along most of the stellar mass range
investigated, and with mean residuals below 0.1 dex in the range $\sim
[10^{8.7}-10^{11.7}] M_{\odot}$. We then compare the SFR-$M_*$ relation
predicted by the model with the observed one at different redshifts. The
predicted SFR-$M_*$ relation underpredicts the median SFR at fixed stellar mass
relative to observations at all redshifts. Nevertheless, the shapes are
consistent with the observed relations up to intermediate-mass galaxies,
followed by a rapid decline for massive galaxies.
