text:
Many new physics models predict resonances with masses in the TeV range which
decay into a pair of top quarks. With its large cross section, t\bar t
production at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) offers an excellent opportunity
to search for such particles. The identification of very energetic top quarks
is crucial in such an analysis. We consider in detail the t\bar t\to\ell^\pm\nu
b\bar bq\bar q' (\ell=e, \mu) final state for high p_T top quarks. In this
phase space region, two or more of the final state quarks can merge into a
single jet due to the large Lorentz boost of the parent top quark. As a result,
a large fraction of t\bar t\to\ell^\pm\nu b\bar bq\bar q' events with an
invariant mass in the TeV region contains less than four observable jets.
Requiring one or two tagged b-quarks, we calculate the W+jets, Wb+jets, Wb\bar
b+jets, Wbt, and single top plus jets backgrounds for these final states, and
identify cuts which help to suppress them. In particular, we discuss whether a
cut on the jet invariant mass may be useful in reducing the background in the
\ell\nu+2 jets channel. We also investigate how next-to-leading order QCD
corrections affect high p_T top quark production at the LHC. We find that the
\ell\nu+2 jets and \ell\nu+3 jets final states with one or two $b$-tags will
significantly improve the chances for discovering new heavy particles in the
t\bar t channel at the LHC.
label: human

text:
In this paper we analyze the Hilbert boundary-value problem of the theory of
analytic functions for an $(N+1)$-connected circular domain. An exact
series-form solution has already been derived for the case of continuous
coefficients. Motivated by the study of the Hall effect in a multiply connected
plate we extend these results by examining the case of discontinuous
coefficients. The Hilbert problem maps into the Riemann-Hilbert problem for
symmetric piece-wise meromorphic functions invariant with respect to a
symmetric Schottky group. The solution to this problem is derived in terms of
two analogues of the Cauchy kernel, quasiautomorphic and quasimultiplicative
kernels. The former kernel is known for any symmetry Schottky group. We prove
the existence theorem for the second, quasimultiplicative, kernel for any
Schottky group (its series representation is known for the first class groups
only). We also show that the use of an automorphic kernel requires the solution
to the associated real analogue of the Jacobi inversion problem which can be
bypassed if we employ the quasiautomorphic and quasimultiplicative kernels. We
apply this theory to a model steady-state problem on the motion of charged
electrons in a plate with $N+1$ circular holes with electrodes and dielectrics
on the walls when the conductor is placed at right angle to the applied
magnetic field.
label: human

text:
The background noise between 1 and 1.8 microns in ground-based instruments is
dominated by atmospheric emission from hydroxyl molecules. We have built and
commissioned a new instrument, GNOSIS, which suppresses 103 OH doublets between
1.47 - 1.7 microns by a factor of ~1000 with a resolving power of ~10,000. We
present the first results from the commissioning of GNOSIS using the IRIS2
spectrograph at the AAT. The combined throughput of the GNOSIS fore-optics,
grating unit and relay optics is ~36 per cent, but this could be improved to
~46 per cent with a more optimal design. We measure strong suppression of the
OH lines, confirming that OH suppression with fibre Bragg gratings will be a
powerful technology for low resolution spectroscopy. The integrated OH
suppressed background between 1.5 and 1.7 microns is reduced by a factor of 9
compared to a control spectrum using the same system without suppression. The
potential of low resolution OH suppressed spectroscopy is illustrated with
example observations.
  The GNOSIS background is dominated by detector dark current below 1.67
microns and by thermal emission above 1.67 microns. After subtracting these we
detect an unidentified residual interline component of ~ 860 +/ 210
ph/s/m^2/micron/arcsec^2. This component is equally bright in the suppressed
and control spectra. We have investigated the possible source of the interline
component, but were unable to discriminate between a possible instrumental
artifact and intrinsic atmospheric emission. Resolving the source of this
emission is crucial for the design of fully optimised OH suppression
spectrographs. The next generation OH suppression spectrograph will be focussed
on resolving the source of the interline component, taking advantage of better
optimisation for a FBG feed. We quantify the necessary improvements for an
optimal OH suppressing fibre spectrograph design.
label: human

text: In the burgeoning field of gravitational lensing, the identification of new lensing phenomena has traditionally relied upon automated algorithms or small-scale expert analysis. This research explores an innovative approach by utilizing a citizen science initiative, Space Warps, which harnesses the collective efforts of the public to identify potential gravitational lenses. The primary objective is to assess the efficacy and accuracy of crowd-sourcing methods in detecting gravitational lenses compared to traditional techniques. Employing a distributed model, Space Warps engaged a global network of volunteers who analyzed wide-field survey images, providing annotations of potential lenses. This study rigorously evaluated the quality of these crowd-sourced identifications through cross-validation with known lenses and expert classifications. Our findings indicate that citizen scientists, aided by intuitive web-based tools and training interfaces, demonstrated a capability to identify genuine gravitational lens candidates with high precision and recall rates. Significantly, the initiative uncovered novel lens systems not previously recognized by algorithmic approaches. These discoveries underscore the potential advantages of integrating human pattern recognition abilities with computational methods. In conclusion, crowd-sourcing represents a viable, scalable strategy for expanding the catalog of known gravitational lenses. The success of Space Warps highlights the vast untapped potential of public participation in astrophysical research and suggests a paradigm shift in how large datasets may be processed in the future. This approach provides a robust framework for future studies and a blueprint for engaging non-experts in cutting-edge scientific discovery.
label: machine

text:
We use recent developments in local entropy theory to prove that chaos in
dynamical systems implies the existence of complicated structure in the
underlying space. Earlier Mouron proved that if $X$ is an arc-like continuum
which admits a homeomorphism $f$ with positive topological entropy, then $X$
contains an indecomposable subcontinuum. Barge and Diamond proved that if $G$
is a finite graph and $f:G \rightarrow G$ is any map with positive topological
entropy, then the inverse limit space $\varprojlim(G,f)$ contains an
indecomposable continuum. In this paper we show that if $X$ is a $G$-like
continuum for some finite graph $G$ and $f:X \rightarrow X$ is any map with
positive topological entropy, then $\varprojlim (X,f)$ contains an
indecomposable continuum. As a corollary, we obtain that in the case that $f$
is a homeomorphism, $X$ contains an indecomposable continuum. Moreover, if $f$
has uniformly positive upper entropy, then $X$ is an indecomposable continuum.
Our results answer some questions raised by Mouron and generalize the above
mentioned work of Mouron and also that of Barge and Diamond. We also introduce
a new concept called zigzag pair which attempts to capture the complexity of a
dynamical systems from the continuum theoretic perspective and facilitates the
proof of the main result.
label: human

text:
Inclusive energy distributions for light charged particles ($p, d, t$ and
$\alpha$) have been measured in the $^{20}$Ne (158, 170, 180, 200 MeV) +
$^{12}$C reactions in the angular range 10$^{o}$ -- 50$^{o}$. Exclusive light
charged particle energy distribution measurements were also done for the same
system at 158 MeV bombarding energy by in-plane light charged particle --
fragment coincidence. Pre-equilibrium components have been separated out from
proton energy spectra using moving source model considering two sources. The
data have been compared with the predictions of the statistical model code
CASCADE. It has been observed that significant deformation effects were needed
to be introduced in the compound nucleus in order to explain the shape of the
evaporated $d, t$ energy spectra. For protons, evaporated energy spectra were
rather insensitive to nuclear deformation, though angular distributions could
not be explained without deformation. Decay sequence of the hot $^{32}$S
nucleus has been investigated through exclusive light charged particle
measurements using the $^{20}$Ne (158 MeV) + $^{12}$C reaction. Information on
the sequential decay chain has been extracted through comparison of the
experimental data with the predictions of the statistical model. It is observed
from the present analysis that exclusive light charged particle data may be
used as a powerful tool to probe the decay sequence of hot light compound
systems.
label: human

text:
In this lecture I will explain the established pictures of the QCD vacuum
and, in particular, the underlying confinement mechanism. These are: the
magnetic monopole condensation (dual Mei\ss ner effect), the center vortex
picture and the Gribov--Zwanziger picture. I will start by giving a survey of
the common order and disorder parameters of confinement: the temporal and
spatial Wilson loop, the Polyakov loop and the 't Hooft loop. Next the dual
Mei\ss ner effect, which assumes a condensate of magnetic monopoles, will be
explained as a picture of confinement. I will also show how magnetic monopoles
arises in QCD after the so-called Abelian projection. The second lecture is
devoted to the center vortex picture of confinement. Center vortices will be
defined both on the lattice and in the continuum. Within the center vortex
picture the emergence of the area law for the Wilson loop as well as the
deconfinement phase transition at finite temperature will be explained.
Furthermore, lattice evidence for the center vortex picture will be provided.
Finally, I will discuss the topological properties of center vortices and their
relation to magnetic monopoles. I will provide evidence from lattice
calculations that center vortices are not only responsible for confinement but
also for the spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry. In the last lecture I
will present the Hamiltonian approach to QCD in Coulomb gauge, which is then
used to establish the Gribov--Zwanziger picture of confinement. Furthermore, I
will also relate this scenario to the dual Mei\ss ner effect and the center
vortex picture. Finally, I will study QCD at finite temperature within the
Hamiltonian approach in a novel way by compactifying one spatial dimension. The
Polyakov loop and the dual and chiral quark condensates will be evaluated as
function of the temperature.
label: human

text:
Shear thickening is a type of non-Newtonian behavior in which the stress
required to shear a fluid increases faster than linearly with shear rate. Many
concentrated suspensions of particles exhibit an especially dramatic version,
known as Discontinuous Shear Thickening (DST), in which the stress suddenly
jumps with increasing shear rate and produces solid-like behavior. The best
known example of such counter-intuitive response to applied stresses occurs in
mixtures of cornstarch in water. Over the last several years, this
shear-induced solid-like behavior together with a variety of other unusual
fluid phenomena has generated considerable interest in the physics of densely
packed suspensions. In this review, we discuss the common physical properties
of systems exhibiting shear thickening, and different mechanisms and models
proposed to describe it. We then suggest how these mechanisms may be related
and generalized, and propose a general phase diagram for shear thickening
systems. We also discuss how recent work has related the physics of shear
thickening to that of granular materials and jammed systems. Since DST is
described by models that require only simple generic interactions between
particles, we outline the broader context of other concentrated many-particle
systems such as foams and emulsions, and explain why DST is restricted to the
parameter regime of hard-particle suspensions. Finally, we discuss some of the
outstanding problems and emerging opportunities.
label: human

text:
The Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) on the Spitzer Space Telescope currently
offers the greatest potential for high-precision astrometry of faint mid-IR
sources across arcminute-scale fields, which would be especially valuable for
measuring parallaxes of cold brown dwarfs in the solar neighborhood and proper
motions of obscured members of nearby star-forming regions. To more fully
realize IRAC's astrometric capabilities, we have sought to minimize the largest
sources of uncertainty in astrometry with its 3.6 and 4.5 $\mu$m bands. By
comparing different routines that estimate stellar positions, we have found
that Point Response Function (PRF) fitting with the Spitzer Science Center's
Astronomical Point Source Extractor produces both the smallest systematic
errors from varying intra-pixel sensitivity and the greatest precision in
measurements of positions. In addition, self-calibration has been used to
derive new 7$^{\rm th}$ and 8$^{\rm th}$ order distortion corrections for the
3.6 and 4.5 $\mu$m arrays of IRAC, respectively. These corrections are suitable
for data throughout the mission of Spitzer when a time-dependent scale factor
is applied to the corrections. To illustrate the astrometric accuracy that can
be achieved by combining PRF fitting with our new distortion corrections, we
have applied them to archival data for a nearby star-forming region, arriving
at total astrometric errors of $\sim$20 and 70 mas at signal to noise ratios of
100 and 10, respectively.
label: human

text: This research paper explores the comparison of galaxy-galaxy lensing in the Evolution and Assembly of GaLaxies and their Environments (EAGLE) simulations with observational data from the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS) and Galaxy And Mass Assembly (GAMA) surveys spanning 180 square degrees. The objective is to investigate the agreement between the simulated effects of galaxy-galaxy lensing in the EAGLE simulations and the lensing signal observed in the KiDS and GAMA surveys.   The methodology involves analyzing the lensing signal produced by central and satellite galaxies in the EAGLE simulations and comparing it with the lensing signal measured from the KiDS and GAMA surveys over a wide area of the sky. Various statistical techniques are employed to quantify the degree of agreement between the simulated and observed lensing signals.  Key findings indicate a reasonable level of agreement between the simulated and observed galaxy-galaxy lensing signals in terms of amplitude and statistical properties over the surveyed area. However, slight discrepancies are identified, particularly in the lensing signal around satellite galaxies.  In conclusion, this study demonstrates that the EAGLE simulations successfully reproduce the galaxy-galaxy lensing signal observed in large-scale surveys like KiDS and GAMA, providing valuable insights into the gravitational lensing effects of galaxies in a cosmological context. Further refinement of the simulations could lead to a more precise understanding of galaxy formation and evolution.
label: machine

text:
We investigate numerically the zero-temperature physics of the
one-dimensional Bose-Hubbard model in an incommensurate cosine potential,
recently realized in experiments with cold bosons in optical superlattices L.
Fallani et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 98, 130404, (2007)]. An incommensurate cosine
potential has intermediate properties between a truly periodic and a fully
random potential, displaying a characteristic length scale (the quasi-period)
which is shown to set a finite lower bound to the excitation energy of the
system at special incommensurate fillings. This leads to the emergence of
gapped incommensurate band-insulator (IBI) phases along with gapless Bose-glass
(BG) phases for strong quasi-periodic potential, both for hardcore and softcore
bosons. Enriching the spatial features of the potential by the addition of a
second incommensurate component appears to remove the IBI regions, stabilizing
a continuous BG phase over an extended parameter range. Moreover we discuss the
validity of the local-density approximation in presence of a parabolic trap,
clarifying the notion of a local BG phase in a trapped system; we investigate
the behavior of first- and second-order coherence upon increasing the strength
of the quasi-periodic potential; and we discuss the ab-initio derivation of the
Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian with quasi-periodic potential starting from the
microscopic Hamiltonian of bosons in an incommensurate superlattice.
label: human

text: This research aims to develop 3GPP-like channel models specifically tailored for indoor office and shopping mall environments, aiming to enhance wireless communication performance under realistic indoor conditions. The study employs extensive measurements conducted in both settings to gather data on signal propagation characteristics, including multipath fading, shadowing, and environmental effects such as reflections and absorption. Utilizing statistical analysis and empirical modeling techniques, the models aim to capture the unique spatial variability and interference patterns observed within these environments. Key findings include improved accuracy in predicting signal strength and delay spread, which will be validated through simulations and practical implementation trials. The ultimate goal is to provide a robust framework for future indoor 5G deployments, ensuring reliable and efficient wireless services in challenging indoor scenarios.
label: machine

text: Magnetism in antiferromagnetic materials has profound implications for fundamental physics and potential technological applications. This study investigates the magnetic properties of a novel family of $S = 1$ square lattice antiferromagnets, specifically Ni$X_2$(pyz)$_2$ where $X$ represents Cl, Br, I, and NCS, with pyrazine (pyz) serving as the bridging ligand. The objective was to explore how varying the anion $X$ influences the magnetic interactions and overall behavior of the compounds. We employed a combination of neutron diffraction, magnetic susceptibility, and specific heat measurements to assess the magnetic ordering and phase transitions across the different compounds. Our findings reveal that the magnetic susceptibility and transition temperatures exhibit a strong dependency on the halide radius and electronegativity of the $X$ anion. Notably, NiCl$_2$(pyz)$_2$ demonstrates the highest Néel temperature, while NiI$_2$(pyz)$_2$ shows profound spin fluctuations indicative of reduced magnetic ordering. Furthermore, we observe distinct magnetostructural correlations that elucidate the role of geometrical frustrations in these square lattice systems. The results underscore the rich interplay between crystal chemistry and magnetism in this series of antiferromagnets, paving the way for further exploration of related materials and their potential applications in spintronic devices. This research contributes significant insights into the tailored design of magnetic materials with specific functionalities and enhances our understanding of the underlying magnetic mechanisms in low-dimensional systems.
label: machine

text: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are prominent sources of high-energy phenomena, including the emission of neutrinos and the interaction of cosmic rays. This study investigates these activities in two nearby galaxies, NGC 253 and NGC 1068, both harboring AGNs, to understand the underlying mechanisms connecting AGNs, neutrinos, and cosmic rays. Utilizing multi-wavelength data from observational facilities such as the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, IceCube Neutrino Observatory, and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, we analyze emission signatures and correlate observed neutrino events with cosmic ray energy spectra. The investigation employs statistical models to assess significance correlations between high-energy neutrino events and AGN activity. The key findings reveal distinct signatures in both galaxies NGC 1068 shows a pronounced correlation between high-energy gamma rays and detected neutrino events, suggesting an environment conducive to hadronic interactions within its AGN, while NGC 253 exhibits a moderate association with cosmic ray intensities potentially due to contribution from supernova remnants and starburst activities. These findings underscore the relevance of AGNs as potential accelerators of high-energy cosmic particles and highlight the role of environmental conditions in shaping their observable properties. The study concludes that, while AGNs like those in NGC 253 and NGC 1068 are prominent candidates for the origin of high-energy extragalactic neutrinos and cosmic rays, further comprehensive observational campaigns are necessary to unravel the complexities of multi-messenger astrophysics and confirm the universal applicability of these phenomena across diverse galactic environments.
label: machine

text: In this study, we present the third installment of our investigations into far-ultraviolet (FUV) extinction measurements using FUSE data. We explore the dependence of FUV extinction on the reddening parameter R(V) across 75 Galactic sightlines. Our methodology involves rigorous analysis of FUSE spectra, accounting for interstellar absorption and instrumental effects. We identify significant variations in FUV extinction values as a function of R(V), which correlate well with previously established trends in optical and infrared wavelengths. Additionally, we investigate discrete features within the FUV spectrum, delineating their influence on extinction estimates. By employing a robust statistical approach, we refine our understanding of these features, particularly their impact at the limits of detectability. Our findings contribute to a more comprehensive model of interstellar extinction in the far-ultraviolet regime, enhancing our knowledge of Galactic dust properties and star formation histories.
label: machine

text:
The production of invisible particles plays great importance in high energy
physics. Large part of interesting electroweak processes include production of
neutrinos, while many new physics scenarios predict the existence of similarly
weakly-interacting particles. In events with associated production of invisible
particles and hadronic jets, the measurement of the imbalance in transverse
momentum of the final state particles is the major leverage to reject the
otherwise dominant source of backgrounds in hadron colliders, i.e. the generic
production of many jets by QCD interactions. Here we discuss a novel technique
which utilizes the information derived from the spectrometer, eventually
coupled with the more straightforward calorimeter information, to infer the
passage of invisible particles. We check the validity of this technique in data
and Monte Carlo simulations in a broad range of topologies, starting from the
simplest, with two jets in the final state, to the ones with very large jet
multiplicities. We also suggest a new way, based on the same approach, to
measure the yields and model the kinematics of the QCD multijet background in
invisible particles plus jets signatures. The results are derived using data
collected with the CDF II detector; we argue that the application to LHC
experiments is straightforward.
label: human

text: This study explores the anomalous dimensions of operators in the context of rotating open strings within the framework of Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT) correspondence. We investigate the dynamics of these strings as they rotate, which allows us to probe the behavior of gauge theory operators in the dual CFT. Our approach involves numerical simulations of the string configurations and analytical calculations to extract the relevant couplings and boundary conditions that influence the anomalous dimensions. By analyzing the energy spectrum of the rotating strings, we derive expressions for the anomalous dimensions of the corresponding operators in the CFT. The key findings reveal a dependence on the rotation parameters and suggest a connection between the string's angular momentum and the operator's anomalous dimension. This work contributes to our understanding of how quantum field theories in flat spacetime can be holographically mapped onto gravitational theories in higher dimensions, providing insights into the structure of strongly coupled systems.

text: In this study, we investigate the implications of natural selection within variable environments where the returns on investment remain uncertain. Our work aims to elucidate how organisms optimize reproductive strategies and resource allocation in the face of environmental variability. To address this, we employ a mathematical model that elucidates the interactions between environmental fluctuations and fitness landscapes. Our approach synthesizes empirical data with stochastic modeling to simulate different environmental scenarios that species may encounter. We demonstrate that organisms with adaptive traits that accommodate environmental variability exhibit higher fitness compared to those with static allocation strategies. A key finding reveals a trade-off between investment in offspring number versus offspring quality under uncertain return conditions. Our results underscore the importance of plasticity in reproductive strategies, enabling species to maintain or enhance fitness across diverse ecological settings. Additionally, we identify critical parameters that influence the evolutionary stability of adaptive strategies, such as the mean and variance of environmental conditions, and the elasticity of resource allocation mechanisms. Through our study, we contribute to a deeper understanding of evolutionary dynamics in changing environments, addressing an overarching question of how natural selection drives the evolution of optimal strategies under uncertainty. These findings have potential applications in conservation biology and predicting responses to climate change, where managing genetic diversity and resilience become pivotal in preserving ecosystems. This research advances the field by integrating theoretical insights with practical implications, offering a rich framework for future exploration of evolution in complex ecological landscapes.

We derive an explicit formula, as well as an efficient procedure, for
constructing a generalized Jacobian for the projector of a given square matrix
onto the Birkhoff polytope, i.e., the set of doubly stochastic matrices. To
guarantee the high efficiency of our procedure, a semismooth Newton method for
solving the dual of the projection problem is proposed and efficiently
implemented. Extensive numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the
merits and effectiveness of our method by comparing its performance against
other powerful solvers such as the commercial software Gurobi and the academic
code PPROJ [{\sc Hager and Zhang}, SIAM Journal on Optimization, 26 (2016),
pp.~1773--1798]. In particular, our algorithm is able to solve the projection
problem with over one billion variables and nonnegative constraints to a very
high accuracy in less than 15 minutes on a modest desktop computer. More
importantly, based on our efficient computation of the projections and their
generalized Jacobians, we can design a highly efficient augmented Lagrangian
method (ALM) for solving a class of convex quadratic programming (QP) problems
constrained by the Birkhoff polytope. The resulted ALM is demonstrated to be
much more efficient than Gurobi in solving a collection of QP problems arising
from the relaxation of quadratic assignment problems.

Irregular galaxies are usually smaller and less massive than their spiral,
S0, and elliptical counterparts. Radio observations indicate that a magnetic
field is present in irregular galaxies whose value is similar to that in spiral
galaxies. However, the conditions in the interstellar medium of an irregular
galaxy are unfavorable for amplification of the magnetic field because of the
slow rotation and low shearing rate. We investigate the cosmic-ray driven
dynamo in the interstellar medium of an irregular galaxy. We study its
efficiency under the conditions of slow rotation and weak shear. The star
formation is also taken into account in our model and is parametrized by the
frequency of explosions and modulations of activity. The numerical model
includes a magnetohydrodynamical dynamo driven by cosmic rays that is injected
into the interstellar medium by randomly exploding supernovae. In the model, we
also include essential elements such as vertical gravity of the disk,
differential rotation approximated by the shearing box, and resistivity leading
to magnetic reconnection. We find that even slow galactic rotation with a low
shearing rate amplifies the magnetic field, and that rapid rotation with a low
value of the shear enhances the efficiency of the dynamo. Our simulations have
shown that a high amount of magnetic energy leaves the simulation box becoming
an efficient source of intergalactic magnetic fields.

text: X-ray spectroscopy of stars has emerged as a vital tool for understanding the internal dynamics and composition of celestial bodies. The universe is filled with various types of stars, ranging from O-type giants to M-type dwarfs, each with distinct characteristics that influence their X-ray emission. Despite the significance of X-ray spectroscopy in astrophysics, the existing literature lacks a comprehensive review of the current state of knowledge in this field.  This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of X-ray spectroscopy of stars, focusing on the latest advances in observational and theoretical techniques. The objective of this study is to synthesize the existing knowledge on X-ray emission from stars, highlighting the key factors that influence X-ray production and detection. A thorough examination of the current literature reveals that X-ray spectroscopy offers a unique window into the internal structure and composition of stars, allowing researchers to probe the magnetic fields, coronal heating, and mass loss processes that govern stellar evolution.  The methodology employed in this review involves a critical analysis of existing studies, which employed a range of X-ray spectroscopic techniques, including high-energy resolution spectroscopy and imaging. The key findings of this review highlight the importance of X-ray spectroscopy in understanding the complex interactions between stellar magnetic fields, coronal heating, and mass loss processes. The results of this study have significant implications for our understanding of stellar evolution, with potential applications in fields such as exoplanetary science and stellar astrophysics.

We study the problem of spectrum estimation from transmission data of a known
phantom. The goal is to reconstruct an x-ray spectrum that can accurately model
the x-ray transmission curves and reflects a realistic shape of the typical
energy spectra of the CT system. To this end, spectrum estimation is posed as
an optimization problem with x-ray spectrum as unknown variables, and a
Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence constraint is employed to incorporate prior
knowledge of the spectrum and enhance numerical stability of the estimation
process. The formulated constrained optimization problem is convex and can be
solved efficiently by use of the exponentiated-gradient (EG) algorithm. We
demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on the simulated and
experimental data. The comparison to the expectation-maximization (EM) method
is also discussed. In simulations, the proposed algorithm is seen to yield
x-ray spectra that closely match the ground truth and represent the attenuation
process of x-ray photons in materials, both included and not included in the
estimation process. In experiments, the calculated transmission curve is in
good agreement with the measured transmission curve, and the estimated spectra
exhibits physically realistic looking shapes. The results further show the
comparable performance between the proposed optimization-based approach and EM.
In conclusion, our formulation of a constrained optimization provides an
interpretable and flexible framework for spectrum estimation. Moreover, a
KL-divergence constraint can include a prior spectrum and appears to capture
important features of x-ray spectrum, allowing accurate and robust estimation
of x-ray spectrum in CT imaging.

We establish a biophysical model for the dynamics of lipid vesicles exposed
to surfactants. The solubilization of the lipid membrane due to the insertion
of surfactant molecules induces a reduction of membrane surface area at almost
constant vesicle volume. This results in a rate-dependent increase of membrane
tension and leads to the opening of a micron-sized pore. We show that
solubilization kinetics due to surfactants can determine the regimes of pore
dynamics: either the pores open and reseal within a second (short-lived pore),
or the pore stays open up to a few minutes (long-lived pore). First, we
validate our model with previously published experimental measurements of pore
dynamics. Then, we investigate how the solubilization kinetics and membrane
properties affect the dynamics of the pore and construct a phase diagram for
short and long-lived pores. Finally, we examine the dynamics of sequential pore
openings and show that cyclic short-lived pores occur at a period inversely
proportional to the solubilization rate. By deriving a theoretical expression
for the cycle period, we provide an analytic tool to measure the solubilization
rate of lipid vesicles by surfactants. Our findings shed light on some
fundamental biophysical mechanisms that allow simple cell-like structures to
sustain their integrity against environmental stresses, and have the potential
to aid the design of vesicle-based drug delivery systems.

The unique Higgs physics opportunities accessible at the CERN Future Circular
Collider (FCC) in electron-positron ($\sqrt{s}$ = 125, 240, 350 GeV) and
proton-proton ($\sqrt{s}$ = 100 TeV) collisions, are succinctly summarized.
Thanks to the large c.m. energies and enormous luminosities (plus clean
experimental conditions in the $e^+e^-$ case), many open fundamental aspects of
the Higgs sector of the Standard Model (SM) can be experimentally studied: (i)
Measurement of the Higgs Yukawa couplings to the lightest fermions: u,d,s
quarks (via rare exclusive $H\to(\rho,\omega,\phi)+\gamma$ decays); and e$^\pm$
(via resonant s-channel $e^+e^-\to H$ production); as well as neutrinos (within
low-scale seesaw mass generation scenarios); (ii) Measurement of the Higgs
potential (triple $\lambda_3$, and quartic $\lambda_4$ self-couplings), via
double and triple Higgs boson production in pp collisions at 100 TeV; (iii)
Searches for new physics coupled to the scalar SM sector at scales $\Lambda>$ 6
TeV, thanks to measurements of the Higgs boson couplings with subpercent
uncertainties in $e^+e^-\to H\,Z$; and (iv) Searches for dark matter in
Higgs-portal interactions, via high-precision measurements of on-shell and
off-shell Higgs boson invisible decays. All these measurements are beyond the
reach of pp collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. New higher-energy $e^+e^-$
and pp colliders such as FCC are thus required to complete our understanding of
the full set of SM Higgs parameters, as well as to search for new
scalar-coupled physics in the multi-TeV regime.

text: This study investigates the dynamics of inner dead-zone boundaries within protoplanetary disks, focusing on the conditions that influence their stability and evolution. The primary objective is to understand how variations in disk properties, such as temperature and viscosity, affect the location and width of these zones where inward radial migration of gas giant planet embryos is suppressed. Methodologically, we employ numerical simulations of disk-planet interactions using smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) techniques, incorporating detailed models of disk structure and planetesimal formation. Key findings indicate that the stability of the inner dead zone is significantly influenced by the disk's surface density profile and opacity. Additionally, the presence of planetesimals can perturb the disk and alter the boundary location, potentially leading to enhanced inward migration rates around these regions. The results suggest that the inner dead zones play a crucial role in controlling the early stages of planet formation and provide insights into the architecture of planetary systems.

text: This research explores the hypothesis that black holes could serve as a natural factory for generating wormholes, structures that connect distant regions of spacetime. Building upon previous theoretical work suggesting a connection between black hole evaporation and the creation of exotic matter, which in turn might facilitate the formation of wormholes, this study aims to investigate this phenomenon more deeply.  The primary objective of this research is to model the conditions under which black holes can potentially produce stable wormholes through processes such as Hawking radiation or direct matter/energy manipulation. To achieve this, we employ a combination of numerical simulations and analytical calculations based on general relativity and quantum field theory principles.  Key findings indicate that while black holes emit particles due to quantum effects (Hawking radiation), these emissions alone do not guarantee the creation of wormholes. However, the study suggests that under certain extreme conditions, particularly involving high-energy environments near the event horizon, the emitted particles could interact in ways that could lead to the formation of stable wormholes. Additionally, it was observed that manipulating specific types of matter or energy within or near a black hole might provide a pathway to creating wormholes, albeit with significant challenges related to maintaining stability over cosmic timescales.  The conclusion drawn from this research highlights the ongoing need for further investigation into the physical mechanisms behind black hole-wormhole interactions. While substantial progress has been made, the complex interplay between black hole dynamics and exotic matter remains poorly understood. This study underscores the potential for future research to explore these phenomena more thoroughly, offering new insights into the fundamental nature of spacetime and the possible existence of traversable wormholes.

text: In this study, we investigate the phenomenon of false vacuum decay catalyzed by black holes, aiming to elucidate the conditions under which such catalysis occurs and its implications on cosmology and particle physics. We employ a theoretical framework that integrates Hawking radiation from black holes with quantum field theory to model the dynamics of false vacuum decay. Our simulations reveal that the presence of a black hole can significantly accelerate the decay rate of the false vacuum state, leading to a substantial reduction in the energy barrier required for decay. Key insights include the critical mass and charge of black holes necessary to trigger significant catalysis, as well as the role of initial conditions in determining the efficiency of this process. The findings suggest that black holes may play a crucial role in the early universe's phase transitions and the formation of structures. This research not only advances our understanding of black hole physics but also provides new perspectives on the mechanisms governing vacuum decay processes in high-energy environments.

We study strange stars in the framework of $f\left(R,\mathcal{T}\right)$
theory of gravity where the strange quark matter distribution inside the
stellar system is governed by the phenomenological MIT Bag model equation of
state (EOS). Further, for a specific value of $B$ and observed values of mass
of the strange star candidates we obtain the exact solution of the modified
Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equation in the framework of
$f\left(R,\mathcal{T}\right)$ gravity and have studied in detail the dependence
of the different physical parameters due to the chosen different values of
$\chi$. To check the physical acceptability and stability of the stellar system
based on the obtained solutions we have performed different physical tests,
viz., the energy conditions, Herrera cracking concept, adiabatic index etc. In
this work, we also have explained the effects, those are arising due to the
interaction between the matter and the curvature terms in
$f\left(R,\mathcal{T}\right)$ gravity, on the anisotropic compact stellar
system. It is interesting to note that as the values of $\chi$ increase the
strange stars become more massive and their radius increase gradually so that
eventually they gradually turn into less dense compact objects. The present
study reveals that the modified $f\left(R,\mathcal{T}\right)$ gravity is a
suitable theory to explain massive stellar systems like recent magnetars,
massive pulsars and super-Chandrasekhar stars, which can not be explained in
the framework of GR. However, for $\chi=0$ the standard results of Einsteinian
gravity are retrieved.

We study the connection between the highly non-convex loss function of a
simple model of the fully-connected feed-forward neural network and the
Hamiltonian of the spherical spin-glass model under the assumptions of: i)
variable independence, ii) redundancy in network parametrization, and iii)
uniformity. These assumptions enable us to explain the complexity of the fully
decoupled neural network through the prism of the results from random matrix
theory. We show that for large-size decoupled networks the lowest critical
values of the random loss function form a layered structure and they are
located in a well-defined band lower-bounded by the global minimum. The number
of local minima outside that band diminishes exponentially with the size of the
network. We empirically verify that the mathematical model exhibits similar
behavior as the computer simulations, despite the presence of high dependencies
in real networks. We conjecture that both simulated annealing and SGD converge
to the band of low critical points, and that all critical points found there
are local minima of high quality measured by the test error. This emphasizes a
major difference between large- and small-size networks where for the latter
poor quality local minima have non-zero probability of being recovered.
Finally, we prove that recovering the global minimum becomes harder as the
network size increases and that it is in practice irrelevant as global minimum
often leads to overfitting.

As computational power has continued to increase, and sensors have become
more accurate, the corresponding advent of systems that are at once cognitive
and immersive has arrived. These \textit{cognitive and immersive systems}
(CAISs) fall squarely into the intersection of AI with HCI/HRI: such systems
interact with and assist the human agents that enter them, in no small part
because such systems are infused with AI able to understand and reason about
these humans and their knowledge, beliefs, goals, communications, plans, etc.
We herein explain our approach to engineering CAISs. We emphasize the capacity
of a CAIS to develop and reason over a `theory of the mind' of its human
partners. This capacity entails that the AI in question has a sophisticated
model of the beliefs, knowledge, goals, desires, emotions, etc.\ of these
humans. To accomplish this engineering, a formal framework of very high
expressivity is needed. In our case, this framework is a \textit{cognitive
event calculus}, a particular kind of quantified multi-operator modal logic,
and a matching high-expressivity automated reasoner and planner. To explain,
advance, and to a degree validate our approach, we show that a calculus of this
type satisfies a set of formal requirements, and can enable a CAIS to
understand a psychologically tricky scenario couched in what we call the
\textit{cognitive polysolid framework} (CPF). We also formally show that a room
that satisfies these requirements can have a useful property we term
\emph{expectation of usefulness}. CPF, a sub-class of \textit{cognitive
microworlds}, includes machinery able to represent and plan over not merely
blocks and actions (such as seen in the primitive `blocks worlds' of old), but
also over agents and their mental attitudes about both other agents and
inanimate objects.

text: Asteroseismic analysis of solar-mass subgiants KIC 6442183 and KIC 11137075 observed by Kepler   Solar-mass subgiants (SMSs) are essential objects for studying stellar interiors and evolution, providing insights into stellar structure and evolutionary stages. The Kepler spacecraft, with its precise photometric measurements, has enabled extensive asteroseismic investigations of SMSs.   In this study, we present the results of asteroseismic analyses of two solar-mass subgiants, KIC 6442183 and KIC 11137075, identified by the Kepler mission. The primary objectives of this work were to determine their stellar properties and to investigate their internal structures using asteroseismic methods.   We employed a combination of frequency analysis, eclipsing binary modeling, and asteroseismology inversion techniques. The periodicities identified from their light curves were used to determine the stellar pulsational modes and their associated frequencies.   Our analysis revealed multiple pulsational modes for both KIC 6442183 and KIC 11137075. For KIC 6442183, we identified twelve modes, five of which were high-order dipole modes, with the dominant mode being a p-mode of degree l=3 and order k=3. KIC 11137075 displayed six modes, three of which were low-order g-modes.  For KIC 6442183, we derived an estimated effective temperature of 5674 K, a surface gravity of 4.172 x 10^4 m/s^2, and a mass of 1.009 M_☉. For KIC 11137075, we determined an effective temperature of 5835 K, a surface gravity of 4.082 x 10^4 m/s^2, and a mass of 1.015 M_☉. text: The Dragonfly Nearby Galaxies Survey (DNGS) I explores significant variations in the diffuse stellar halos surrounding spiral galaxies. This study aims to investigate the structural diversity of these stellar systems through photometric measurements and morphological analysis. Utilizing the DNGS dataset, which comprises images of 43 nearby spiral galaxies, the methodology employed involves detailed visual inspection and automated classification techniques to quantify the extent and distribution of stellar halo features.  Key findings indicate substantial variability in stellar halo properties across different galaxies, including their size, shape, and luminosity profiles. Some galaxies exhibit extended, smooth stellar halos, while others show fragmented structures indicative of recent star formation events. Additionally, correlations between halo characteristics and galaxy properties such as mass, environment, and star formation history were observed.  The results highlight the importance of considering individual galaxy-specific halo structures when studying the larger scale of galaxy evolution and the intergalactic medium. This work contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of how spiral galaxies acquire and maintain their diffuse stellar components over cosmic time.

Context. Scattering and absorption processes in stellar atmosphere affect the
center-to-limb variations of the intensity (CLVI) and the linear polarization
(CLVP) of stellar radiation. Aims. There are several theoretical and
observational studies of CLVI using different stellar models, however, most
studies of CLVP have concentrated on the solar atmosphere and have not
considered the CLVP in cooler non-gray stellar atmospheres at all. In this
paper, we present a theoretical study of the CLV of the intensity and the
linear polarization in continuum spectra of different spectral type stars.
Methods. We solve the radiative transfer equations for polarized light
iteratively assuming no magnetic field and considering a plane-parallel model
atmospheres and various opacities. Results. We calculate the CLVI and the CLVP
for Phoenix stellar model atmospheres for the range of effective temperatures
(4500K - 6900K), gravities (log g = 3.0 - 5.0), and wavelengths (4000 - 7000
{\AA}), which are tabulated and available at the Strasbourg astronomical Data
Center (CDS). In addition, we present several tests of our code and compare our
results with measurements and calculations of CLVI and the CLVP for the Sun.
The resulting CLVI are fitted with polynomials and their coefficients are
presented in this paper. Conclusions. For the stellar model atmospheres with
lower gravity and effective temperature the CLVP is larger.

The spectra of fermionic excitations, pairing correlations and edge currents
confined near the boundary of a chiral p-wave superfluid are calculated to
leading order in $\hbar/p_f\xi$. Results for the energy- and momentum-resolved
spectral functions, including the spectral current density, of a chiral p-wave
superfluid near a confining boundary are reported. The spectral functions
reveal the subtle role of the chiral edge states in relation to the edge
current and the angular momentum of a chiral p-wave superfluid, including the
rapid suppression of $L_z(T)$ for $0 \lesssim T\ll T_c$ in the fully gapped 2D
chiral superfluid. The edge current and ground-state angular momentum are shown
to be sensitive to boundary conditions, and as a consequence the topology and
geometry of the confining boundaries. For perfect specular boundaries the edge
current accounts for the ground-state angular momentum, $L_z=(N/2)\hbar$, of a
cylindrical disk of chiral superfluid with $N/2$ fermion pairs. Non-specular
scattering can dramatically suppress the edge current. In the limit of perfect
retro-reflection the edge states form a flat band of zero modes that are
non-chiral and generate no edge current. For a chiral superfluid film confined
in a cylindrical toroidal geometry the ground-state angular momentum is, in
general, non-extensive, and can have a value ranging from $L_z > (N/2)\hbar$ to
$L_z < -(N/2)\hbar$ depending on the ratio of the inner and outer radii and the
degree of back scattering on the inner and outer surfaces. Non-extensive
scaling of $L_z$, and the reversal of the ground-state angular momentum for a
toroidal geometry, would provide a signature of broken time-reversal symmetry
of the ground state of superfluid \Hea, as well as direct observation of chiral
edge currents.

text: We present our investigation on the rotating starburst cores observed in massive galaxies at a redshift of z=2.5. Our study aims to unravel the mechanisms driving the intense star formation within these galaxies and understand their implications on galaxy evolution at high redshifts. By analyzing spatially resolved spectroscopic data from integral field spectroscopy, we have identified a sample of massive galaxies with rotating starburst cores. Our results indicate that these cores exhibit high levels of star formation activity and significant rotational motion, suggesting a connection between starburst activity and internal dynamics within these galaxies. Through in-depth kinematic analysis, we have found evidence of ordered rotation in the starburst cores, which may hint at the presence of disk-like structures or mergers triggering the bursts of star formation. This work addresses the pressing question of how massive galaxies at z=2.5 build up their stellar mass and morphological properties through intense star formation episodes. The methodology employed in this research involves detailed kinematic measurements using state-of-the-art spectroscopic techniques to probe the internal dynamics of these rotating starburst cores. Our findings contribute valuable insights into the processes shaping galaxy evolution in the high-redshift universe.

text: The exponential growth of high-throughput sequencing technologies has propelled the need for efficient algorithms capable of accurately mapping short reads to reference genomes. This paper explores the application of Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithms in the context of mapping short reads, focusing on their efficacy when applied to FAIRE (Formaldehyde-Assisted Isolation of Regulatory Elements) data, particularly in the TP53-WRAP53 gene region. The objective of this study is to enhance the precision and reliability of short read mapping by leveraging EM methodologies that iteratively refine the alignment of reads, thereby addressing common challenges associated with repetitive genomic areas and sequencing errors. We employed a comparative approach, analyzing the performance of EM algorithms against traditional mapping techniques through metrics such as mapping accuracy, computational speed, and robustness to noise. Our results indicate that EM algorithms significantly outperform conventional methods in terms of accuracy, particularly in complex genomic regions where reads may overlap or share similarities. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that incorporating prior knowledge about the genomic structure improves the mapping performance of EM algorithms. The findings demonstrate that the integration of EM algorithms offers a promising strategy for enhancing the analysis of FAIRE data, providing deeper insights into the regulatory landscapes surrounding the TP53-WRAP53 gene region. This work underscores the importance of advanced statistical methods in genomics and paves the way for future research focused on optimizing read mapping strategies in diverse applications of genomics and bioinformatics.

text: This study employs stochastic models to examine and forecast social dynamics on the web. Particularly, we consider the problem of user churn prediction in web communities. Using longitudinal data from a large-scale web community, we developed a Markov model to capture the stochastic nature of user behavior and account for the influence of different features on the likelihood of user churn. To validate our model, we compared its predictions with empirical data from the web community. Results demonstrate that the proposed Markov model provides reasonable predictions of user churn and outperforms several baseline models.    Further, we applied a discrete-time Markov chain model to model the dynamics of user engagement and investigate the effect of community size and content diversity on user engagement. The findings indicate that both community size and content diversity significantly influence user engagement, with larger communities and more diverse content leading to higher levels of engagement. Moreover, we discovered that the impact of content diversity on user engagement is nonlinear and saturates at a certain level.    Finally, we illustrate the applicability of our stochastic modeling approach to other domains, such as online advertising and recommendation systems. Our study contributes to the growing body of literature on stochastic models in social sciences and provides a theoretical foundation for analyzing and predicting web user dynamics.    In summary, this study leverages stochastic models to investigate user churn prediction and user engagement dynamics in web communities. The results demonstrate that our proposed Markov model outperforms baseline models and shed light on the significant impact of community size and content diversity on user engagement. Furthermore, we provide insights into the applicability of stochastic models to various web domains and pave the way for future research.

text: This study investigates the application of term graph representations in handling cyclic lambda-terms, a fundamental concept in mathematical logic and category theory. Lambda-terms are a way of representing functions and their compositions using the lambda calculus, a formal system for expressing computation. However, lambda-terms can become cyclic, leading to infinite reductions and rendering them unsolvable. The objective of this research is to develop and evaluate term graph representations for cyclic lambda-terms, with the aim of providing a more efficient and effective way of dealing with these structures.  The methodology employed in this study involves the construction of term graphs from cyclic lambda-terms and the development of algorithms for traversing and manipulating these graphs. A novel term graph representation is proposed, which utilizes a combination of graph theory and lambda calculus concepts. The proposed representation is evaluated using a set of test cases, including well-known cyclic lambda-terms and newly constructed examples. The key findings of this study indicate that the proposed term graph representation is able to efficiently handle cyclic lambda-terms, reducing the number of infinite reductions and improving the solvability of these structures.  The conclusion of this research highlights the potential of term graph representations for cyclic lambda-terms, offering a promising approach for solving problems in mathematical logic and category theory. The proposed representation and algorithms can be applied to a wide range of applications, including proof search, type inference, and model checking. Future research directions are discussed, including the extension of the proposed representation to more complex structures and its integration with existing formal systems.

text: Millimeter-wave observations are crucial for astronomical studies, yet they are significantly affected by atmospheric noise, especially at high altitudes. Mauna Kea, recognized for its dry, stable conditions, presents a unique opportunity to examine atmospheric characteristics impacting millimeter-wave astronomy. This study aims to characterize and quantify atmospheric noise above Mauna Kea to enhance observation precision and telescope operations. Utilizing data from radiometric instruments deployed around the Mauna Kea summit, we conducted a detailed analysis of atmospheric noise across multiple millimeter-wave bands. We adopted a methodology that integrates real-time radiometric observations with atmospheric modeling to assess noise fluctuations against various meteorological parameters. Key findings reveal that atmospheric noise levels are predominantly influenced by water vapor content, with fluctuations correlating significantly with diurnal and seasonal weather patterns. The analysis identified optimal observing windows during which atmospheric noise levels are minimized, thereby maximizing data quality. Furthermore, the study provides insights into the potential impacts of climate variability on future millimeter-wave observations. Our findings suggest that strategic scheduling of observational campaigns could significantly increase the efficiency and accuracy of millimeter-wave telescopic research. In conclusion, this research enhances understanding of atmospheric interference above Mauna Kea, informs telescope optimization strategies, and guides future site assessment methodologies for millimeter-wave astronomy.

text:
Living cells are continually exposed to environmental signals that vary in
time. These signals are detected and processed by biochemical networks, which
are often highly stochastic. To understand how cells cope with a fluctuating
environment, we therefore have to understand how reliably biochemical networks
can transmit time-varying signals. To this end, we must understand both the
noise characteristics and the amplification properties of networks. In this
manuscript, we use information theory to study how reliably signalling cascades
employing autoregulation and feedback can transmit time-varying signals. We
calculate the frequency-dependence of the gain-to-noise ratio, which reflects
how reliably a network transmits signals at different frequencies. We find that
the gain-to-noise ratio may differ qualitatively from the power spectrum of the
output, showing that the latter does not directly reflect signaling
performance. Moreover, we find that auto-activation and auto-repression
increase and decrease the gain-to-noise ratio for all of frequencies,
respectively. Positive feedback specifically enhances information transmission
at low frequencies, while negative feedback increases signal fidelity at high
frequencies. Our analysis not only elucidates the role of autoregulation and
feedback in naturally-occurring biological networks, but also reveals design
principles that can be used for the reliable transmission of time-varying
signals in synthetic gene circuits.

We consider the integrable multicomponent coherently coupled nonlinear
Schr\"odinger (CCNLS) equations describing simultaneous propagation of multiple
fields in Kerr type nonlinear media. The correct bilinear equations of
$m$-CCNLS equations are obtained by using a non-standard type of Hirota's
bilinearization method and the more general bright one solitons with single
hump and double hump profiles including special flat-top profiles are obtained.
The solitons are classified as coherently coupled solitons and incoherently
coupled solitons depending upon the presence and absence of coherent
nonlinearity arising due to the existence of the co-propagating
modes/components. Further, by obtaining the more general two-soliton solutions
using this non-standard bilinearization approach we demonstrate that the
collision among coherently coupled soliton and incoherently coupled soliton
displays a non-trivial collision behaviour in which the former always undergoes
energy switching accompanied by an amplitude dependent phase-shift and change
in the relative separation distance, leaving the latter unaltered. But the
collision between coherently coupled solitons alone is found to be standard
elastic collision. Our study also reveals the important fact that the collision
between incoherently coupled solitons arising in the $m$-CCNLS system with
$m=2$ is always elastic, whereas for $m>2$ the collision becomes intricate and
for this case the $m$-CCNLS system exhibits interesting energy sharing
collision of solitons characterized by intensity redistribution, amplitude
dependent phase-shift and change in relative separation distance which is
similar to that of the multicomponent Manakov soliton collisions. This suggests
that the $m$-CCNLS system can also be a suitable candidate for soliton
collision based optical computing in addition to the Manakov system.

The KAM theorem for analytic quasi-integrable anisochronous Hamiltonian
systems yields that the perturbation expansion (Lindstedt series) for
quasi-periodic solutions with Diophantine frequency vector converges. If one
studies the Lindstedt series, one finds that convergence is ultimately related
to the presence of cancellations between contributions of the same perturbation
order. In turn, this is due to symmetries in the problem. Such symmetries are
easily visualised in action-angle coordinates, where KAM theorem is usually
formulated, by exploiting the analogy between Lindstedt series and perturbation
expansions in quantum field theory and, in particular, the possibility of
expressing the solutions in terms of tree graphs, which are the analogue of
Feynman diagrams. If the unperturbed system is isochronous, Moser's modifying
terms theorem ensures that an analytic quasi-periodic solution with the same
Diophantine frequency vector as the unperturbed Hamiltonian exists for the
system obtained by adding a suitable constant (counterterm) to the vector
field. Also in this case, one can follow the alternative approach of studying
the perturbation expansion for both the solution and the counterterm, and again
convergence of the two series is obtained as a consequence of deep
cancellations between contributions of the same order. We revisit Moser's
theorem, by studying the perturbation expansion one obtains by working in
Cartesian coordinates. We investigate the symmetries giving rise to the
cancellations which makes possible the convergence of the series. We find that
the cancellation mechanism works in a completely different way in Cartesian
coordinates. The interpretation of the underlying symmetries in terms of tree
graphs is much more subtle than in the case of action-angle coordinates.

text: Through eight years of uninterrupted Fermi-Lat observations, we have delved into the elusive mysteries surrounding the gamma-ray flux variations of NGC 1275, the brightest and most variable active galactic nucleus (AGN) in the local universe. Our in-depth analysis reveals a complex emission scenario, with significant long-term flux modulations and short-term flaring episodes.  The long-term gamma-ray variability can be attributed to the periodic modulation of the accretion disk, which manifests in the form of brightness changes on timescales of years to decades. Furthermore, our observations indicate a strong correlation between the gamma-ray and X-ray emissions, suggesting a common origin for the high-energy emission components.  In addition, we identified several short-term flaring events, whose origins remain a subject of ongoing research. Some theories suggest that these flares could be the result of magnetic reconnection processes occurring in the vicinity of the supermassive black hole, while others propose the presence of intradisk shocks or the interaction between the AGN and its surrounding environment.  We employed advanced data analysis techniques, such as autoregressive moving average models and power spectral density analyses, to investigate the nature and causes of the observed variability. Our findings significantly contribute to the ongoing discussion surrounding the nature of AGN gamma-ray emission and provide essential insights into the complex processes taking place at the heart of active galaxies.  Moreover, the extended duration of the Fermi-LAT observations allows us to study the long-term variability of NGC 1275, revealing trends and patterns that were previously unobserved. This data offers a unique opportunity for future studies, allowing us to test and refine theoretical models of AGN variability and better understand the connection between the high-energy emission components and the underlying physics of active galactic nuclei.

text: This research paper examines the high-energy gamma-ray emission toward the Galactic Center using data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT). The methodology involves detailed analysis of the gamma-ray data collected over several years, with a focus on regions near Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), the supermassive black hole at the center of our galaxy. Key findings include the detection of extended gamma-ray emission structures that are consistent with previous radio observations but extend into higher energy ranges, indicating possible contributions from different astrophysical sources such as pulsars, supernova remnants, and dark matter annihilation. The analysis also reveals asymmetries in the gamma-ray emission that could be indicative of non-axisymmetric structures within the galactic disk. The conclusion highlights the importance of these observations for refining models of galactic dynamics and cosmic ray acceleration, as well as their implications for dark matter studies.

text: In this work, we explore the implications of Mensky's path integral formalism in the context of photon mass. The problem at hand is to reconcile the traditional massless nature of the photon with the implications arising from Mensky's path integral formulation. Our research investigates the theoretical framework proposed by Mensky, which extends the path integral formalism to include quantum systems with non-zero mass, and applies it to the case of photons.  Through our analysis, we have obtained results that suggest a potential reinterpretation of the concept of photon mass within the framework of Mensky's path integral. Our findings challenge the conventional understanding of the massless photon and open up new avenues for theoretical exploration in quantum electrodynamics.  The key idea behind this work is to leverage Mensky's formalism to address longstanding questions regarding the mass of the photon and its implications for quantum field theory. We employ a combination of mathematical derivations and theoretical considerations to elucidate the consequences of incorporating photon mass into the path integral description.  Overall, our study sheds light on the interplay between Mensky's path integral formalism and the notion of photon mass, offering a fresh perspective on the fundamental properties of photons in quantum mechanics.

text: We present in this technical report the development and implementation of a graph-structured sparse optimization algorithm for connected subgraph detection. Connected subgraphs are essential structures in graph theory and have wide applications in various fields, including bioinformatics, computer vision, and social network analysis. Our proposed methodology utilizes a graph-structured representation of a sparse optimization problem, enabling efficient computation and storage of large graphs. Our approach starts by defining a graph-structured objective function to measure the connectivity between nodes within a subgraph. We then formulate this problem as a sparse quadratic programming problem using a graph-sparse regularizer. By employing the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for optimization, we can obtain a scalable and efficient solution to the problem. Our methodology allows for both exact and approximate solutions and can be easily extended to more complex graph problems, including weighted graphs and directed graphs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methodology on several real-world datasets, including protein-protein interaction networks and social network graphs. The results show that our approach significantly outperforms traditional algorithms in terms of computational time and memory usage while maintaining a comparable level of accuracy. Furthermore, our methodology can identify connected subgraphs of various sizes and shapes, providing valuable insights for the application domains. In conclusion, we propose a novel graph-structured sparse optimization algorithm for connected subgraph detection, which offers significant advantages in terms of efficiency, scalability, and accuracy. The implementation and experimentation results showcase the potential of this methodology as a powerful tool for analyzing large and complex graphs in various fields. Our findings contribute to the ongoing research on graph theory and optimization, and we believe our approach can inspire further research in this area.

Color theme or color palette can deeply influence the quality and the feeling
of a photograph or a graphical design. Although color palettes may come from
different sources such as online crowd-sourcing, photographs and graphical
designs, in this paper, we consider color palettes extracted from fine art
collections, which we believe to be an abundant source of stylistic and unique
color themes. We aim to capture color styles embedded in these collections by
means of statistical models and to build practical applications upon these
models. As artists often use their personal color themes in their paintings,
making these palettes appear frequently in the dataset, we employed density
estimation to capture the characteristics of palette data. Via density
estimation, we carried out various predictions and interpolations on palettes,
which led to promising applications such as photo-style exploration, real-time
color suggestion, and enriched photo recolorization. It was, however,
challenging to apply density estimation to palette data as palettes often come
as unordered sets of colors, which make it difficult to use conventional
metrics on them. To this end, we developed a divide-and-conquer sorting
algorithm to rearrange the colors in the palettes in a coherent order, which
allows meaningful interpolation between color palettes. To confirm the
performance of our model, we also conducted quantitative experiments on
datasets of digitized paintings collected from the Internet and received
favorable results.

text: The study of exactly-solvable quantum problems has garnered significant interest due to their applicability in understanding complex systems, particularly in the context of hetero- and nano-structures exhibiting nontrivial topology. This paper aims to explore the mathematical frameworks that allow for the exact solvability of specific quantum models, such as the Dirac and Schrödinger equations, in the presence of topological features. Utilizing a combination of analytical techniques and numerical simulations, we investigate the manifestations of quantum phenomena like edge states, quantum Hall effects, and localization in systems with nontrivial topological configurations. Key findings suggest that certain solvable models can accurately predict critical behaviors and emergent properties of physical systems, including topological insulators and superconductors, and demonstrate robust quantum states that remain stable against perturbations. Additionally, our results indicate that exact solutions provide invaluable insights into the design and optimization of next-generation materials with desired electronic and optical properties. In conclusion, the study emphasizes the importance of exactly-solvable quantum problems as powerful tools in deciphering the fundamental principles governing topological phenomena in hetero- and nano-structures, paving the way for future research and technological advancements in materials science and condensed matter physics.

Aluminum, as a metallic material for plasmonics, is of great interest because
it extends the applications of surface plasmon resonance into the ultraviolet
(UV) region and excels noble metals in the natural abundance, cost and
compatibility with modern semiconductor fabrication process. Here, we present
UV to near-infrared (NIR) plasmonic resonance of single-crystalline aluminum
nanoslits and nanoholes. The high-definition nanostructures are fabricated with
focused ion-beam (FIB) milling into an ultrasmooth single-crystalline aluminum
film grown on a semiconducting GaAs substrate with molecular beam epitaxy (MBE)
method. The single-crystalline aluminum film shows improved reflectivity and
reduced two-photon photoluminescence (TPPL) due to the ultrasmooth surface.
Both linear scattering and non-linear TPPL are studied in detail. The nanoslit
arrays show clear Fano-like resonance and the nanoholes are found to support
both photonic modes and localized surface plasmonic resonance. We also found
that TPPL generation is more efficient when the excitation polarization is
parallel rather than perpendicular to the edge of the aluminum film. Such
counter-intuitive phenomenon is attributed to the high refractive index of the
GaAs substrate. We show that the polarization of TPPL from aluminum well
preserves the excitation polarization and is independent of the crystal
orientation of the film or substrate. Our study gains insight into the optical
property of aluminum nanostructures on high-index semiconducting GaAs substrate
and illustrates a practical route to implement plasmonic devices onto
semiconductors for future hybrid nanodevices.

text: This study presents an in-depth analysis of the abundances of secondary galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) detected by Voyager spacecraft beyond the heliopause, spanning the energy range of 10 to 200 MeV/nuc. The observations were obtained from the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft, which have been traveling through interstellar space for over three decades. By analyzing the data collected between 2012 and 2019, the researchers identified unexpected anomalies in the GCR abundances, which deviate significantly from the expected cosmic ray spectrum. These anomalies are particularly notable in the energy range of 5 to 28 GeV/nuc. To understand the underlying causes of these anomalies, the researchers employed a lattice Boltzmann model (LBM) for galactic propagation. The LBM simulation revealed that the anomalies are likely due to the interactions between the GCRs and the interstellar medium, specifically the density fluctuations within the local interstellar medium. The model also predicted the presence of a "galactic halo" around the Milky Way galaxy, which could be responsible for the observed anomalies. The findings of this study provide new insights into the propagation of GCRs beyond the heliopause and highlight the importance of considering the interstellar medium in models of galactic cosmic ray propagation. The results also have implications for our understanding of the structure and evolution of the Milky Way galaxy.

We introduce the concept of a hyperuniformity disorder length that controls
the variance of volume fraction fluctuations for randomly placed windows of
fixed size. In particular, fluctuations are determined by the average number of
particles within a distance $h$ from the boundary of the window. We first
compute special expectations and bounds in $d$ dimensions, and then illustrate
the range of behavior of $h$ versus window size $L$ by analyzing three
different types of simulated two-dimensional pixel pattern - where particle
positions are stored as a binary digital image in which pixels have value
zero/one if empty/contain a particle. The first are random binomial patterns,
where pixels are randomly flipped from zero to one with probability equal to
area fraction. These have long-ranged density fluctuations, and simulations
confirm the exact result $h=L/2$. Next we consider vacancy patterns, where a
fraction $f$ of particles on a lattice are randomly removed. These also display
long-range density fluctuations, but with $h=(L/2)(f/d)$ for small $f$. For a
hyperuniform system with no long-range density fluctuations, we consider
Einstein patterns where each particle is independently displaced from a lattice
site by a Gaussian-distributed amount. For these, at large $L$, $h$ approaches
a constant equal to about half the root-mean-square displacement in each
dimension. Then we turn to grayscale pixel patterns that represent simulated
arrangements of polydisperse particles, where the volume of a particle is
encoded in the value of its central pixel. And we discuss the continuum limit
of point patterns, where pixel size vanishes. In general, we thus propose to
quantify particle configurations not just by the scaling of the density
fluctuation spectrum but rather by the real-space spectrum of $h(L)$ versus
$L$. We call this approach Hyperuniformity Disorder Length Spectroscopy.
