Since the discovery of superconductivity\cite{1} at 26 K in oxy-pnictide
$LaFeAsO_{1-x}F_x$, enormous interests have been stimulated in the fields of
condensed matter physics and material sciences. Among the five different
structures in this broad type of superconductors\cite{2,3,4,5,6}, the ZrCuSiAs
structure has received special attention since the $T_c$ has been quickly
promoted to 55-56 K\cite{7,8,9,10,11} in fluorine doped oxy-pnictides REFeAsO
(RE = rare earth elements). The superconductivity can also be induced by
applying a high pressure to the undoped samples\cite{12,13}. The mechanism of
superconductivity in the FeAs-based system remains unclear yet, but it turns
out to be clear that any change to the structure or the building blocks will
lead to a change of the superconducting transition temperatures. In this
Letter, we report the fabrication of the new family of compounds, namely
fluorine-arsenides DvFeAsF (Dv = divalent metals) with the ZrCuSiAs structure
and with the new building block DvF instead of the REO (both the layers DvF and
REO have the combined cation state of "+1"). The undoped parent phase has a
Spin-Density-Wave like transition at about 173 K for SrFeAsF, 118 K for CaFeAsF
and 153 K for EuFeAsF. By doping electrons into the system the resistivity
anomaly associated with this SDW transition is suppressed and superconductivity
appears at 32 K in the fluorine-arsenide Sr$_{1-x}$La$_x$FeAsF (x = 0.4). Our
discovery here initiates a new method to obtain superconductors in the
FeAs-based system.

Binary black hole systems are among the most important sources for
gravitational wave detection. And also they are good objects for theoretical
research for general relativity. Gravitational waveform template is important
to data analysis. Effective-one-body-numerical-relativity (EOBNR) model has
played an essential role in the LIGO data analysis. For future space-based
gravitational wave detection, many binary systems will admit somewhat orbit
eccentricity. At the same time the eccentric binary is also an interesting
topic for theoretical study in general relativity. In this paper we construct
the first eccentric binary waveform model based on
effective-one-body-numerical-relativity framework. Our basic assumption in the
model construction is that the involved eccentricity is small. We have compared
our eccentric EOBNR model to the circular one used in LIGO data analysis. We
have also tested our eccentric EOBNR model against to another recently proposed
eccentric binary waveform model; against to numerical relativity simulation
results; and against to perturbation approximation results for extreme mass
ratio binary systems. Compared to numerical relativity simulations with
eccentricity as large as about 0.2, the overlap factor for our eccentric EOBNR
model is better than 0.98 for all tested cases including spinless binary and
spinning binary; equal mass binary and unequal mass binary. Hopefully our
eccentric model can be the start point to develop a faithful template for
future space-based gravitational wave detectors.

This paper can be considered as a sequel of [BS14] by Bernicot and Samoyeau,
where the authors have proposed a general way of deriving Strichartz estimates
for the Schr{\"o}dinger equation from a dispersive property of the wave
propagator. It goes through a reduction of H 1 -- BMO dispersive estimates for
the Schr{\"o}dinger propagator to L 2 -- L 2 microlocalized (in space and in
frequency) dispersion inequalities for the wave operator. This paper aims to
contribute in enlightening our comprehension of how dispersion for waves imply
dispersion for the Schr{\"o}dinger equation. More precisely, the hypothesis of
our main theorem encodes dispersion for the wave equation in an uniform way,
with respect to the light cone. In many situations the phenomena that arise
near the boundary of the light cone are the more complicated ones. The method
we present allows to forget those phenomena we do not understand very well yet.
The second main step shows the Strichartz estimates with loss of derivatives we
can obtain under those assumptions. The setting we work with is general enough
to recover a large variety of frameworks (infinite metric spaces, Riemannian
manifolds with rough metric, some groups, ...) where the lack of knowledge of
the wave propagator is a restraint to our understanding of the dispersion
phenomenon.
label: human

text: Inertial particle trapping in an open vortical flow is a complex phenomenon that has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its potential applications in various fields, including fluid dynamics, chemical engineering, and biotechnology. The open vortical flow, characterized by a rotating fluid core surrounded by a stationary outer layer, presents a unique environment for inertial particle trapping. This phenomenon occurs when particles, subjected to the vortical flow, experience a centrifugal force that causes them to be drawn towards the center of rotation.  The objective of this research is to investigate the effects of open vortical flow on the trapping of inertial particles, with a focus on the impact of flow parameters, such as velocity and angular velocity, on the trapping efficiency. A numerical simulation approach was employed to model the open vortical flow and simulate the behavior of inertial particles within this flow. The results show that the trapping efficiency increases significantly as the angular velocity of the vortical flow increases, while the velocity of the flow has a less pronounced effect.  The key findings of this study indicate that the open vortical flow can be effectively used to trap inertial particles, and that the trapping efficiency can be optimized by controlling the flow parameters. The findings of this research have significant implications for the development of novel particle trapping devices and systems, and highlight the potential of open vortical flows as a means of efficient particle separation.  Overall, this study contributes to the understanding of inertial particle trapping in open vortical flows and provides valuable insights into the optimization of particle trapping devices and systems. The results of this research demonstrate the potential of open vortical flows as a powerful tool for particle separation and manipulation, and have far-reaching implications for various fields of application.

The application of Effective Field Theory (EFT) methods to inflation has
taken a central role in our current understanding of the very early universe.
The EFT perspective has been particularly useful in analyzing the
self-interactions determining the evolution of co-moving curvature
perturbations (Goldstone boson modes) and their influence on low-energy
observables. However, the standard EFT formalism, to lowest order in spacetime
differential operators, does not provide the most general parametrization of a
theory that remains weakly coupled throughout the entire low-energy regime.
Here we study the EFT formulation by including spacetime differential operators
implying a scale dependence of the Goldstone boson self-interactions and its
dispersion relation. These operators are shown to arise naturally from the
low-energy interaction of the Goldstone boson with heavy fields that have been
integrated out. We find that the EFT then stays weakly coupled all the way up
to the cutoff scale at which ultraviolet degrees of freedom become operative.
This opens up a regime of new physics where the dispersion relation is
dominated by a quadratic dependence on the momentum \omega ~ p^2. In addition,
provided that modes crossed the horizon within this energy range, the
prediction of inflationary observables - including non-Gaussian signatures -
are significantly affected by the new scales characterizing it.
label: human

The recent net-proton fluctuation results of the STAR (Solenoidal Tracker At
RHIC) experiment from beam energy scan (BES) program at the BNL Relativistic
Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) have drawn much attention to exploring the QCD
critical point and the nature of deconfinement phase transition. There has been
much speculation that the non-monotonic behavior of $\kappa\sigma^{2}$ of the
produced protons around $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 19.6 GeV in the STAR results may
be due to the existence of QCD critical point. However, the experimentally
measured proton distributions contain protons from heavy resonance decays, from
baryon stopping and from direct production processes. These proton
distributions are used to estimate the net-proton number fluctuation. Because
it is difficult to disentangle the protons from the above-mentioned sources, it
is better to devise a method which will account for the directly produced
baryons (protons) to study the dynamical fluctuation at different
center-of-mass energies. This is because, it is assumed that any associated
criticality in the system could affect the particle production mechanism and
hence the dynamical fluctuation in various conserved numbers. In the present
work, we demonstrate a method to estimate the number of stopped protons at RHIC
BES energies for central $0-5\%$ \auau collisions within STAR acceptance and
discuss its implications on the net-proton fluctuation results.
label: human

text: We investigated the possibility of helium ignition in rotating magnetized CO white dwarfs, a scenario that could lead to the emission of fast and faint type Ia supernovae. Our analysis revealed that the rotation rate and magnetic field strength of the white dwarf play crucial roles in determining the outcome of helium ignition. We found that rapid rotation and strong magnetic fields can lead to a significant increase in the efficiency of helium ignition, resulting in the formation of a hot, compact core that can produce a fast and faint type Ia supernova.  Our simulations indicate that the ignition of helium in rotating magnetized CO white dwarfs is a complex process, involving the interplay between thermal and magnetic energy. We discovered that the rotation rate and magnetic field strength can influence the formation of a helium shell, which can either lead to efficient ignition or suppress it. Furthermore, we found that the resulting supernova can be characterized by a fast rise in brightness, a narrow light curve, and a faint maximum magnitude, all of which are distinct from the classical type Ia supernovae.  Our findings suggest that the ignition of helium in rotating magnetized CO white dwarfs is a viable mechanism for producing fast and faint type Ia supernovae. These objects may provide a new class of type Ia supernovae that can be used to constrain models of stellar evolution and cosmology.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the complex interplay between differential rotation and convection within the solar interior, aiming to enhance our understanding of solar dynamics. We employ a three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model to simulate the convective patterns and rotational profiles observed on the Sun. Our results reveal that differential rotation is significantly influenced by anisotropic convective motions, which manifest prominently in the solar convection zone. Through spectral analysis, we identify dominant flow structures, characterized by latitudinal gradients in angular velocity, which contribute to the maintenance of solar rotation profiles. We observe a consistent equator-ward drift of convective cells, supporting the development of the torsional oscillation pattern. Furthermore, helicity dynamics suggest intricate interactions between magnetic fields and velocity fields, which are crucial in shaping the differential rotation. The simulations demonstrate that the equatorial acceleration can be attributed to the non-linear Reynolds stresses emerging from convective turbulence. Our findings, corroborated by helioseismic data, elucidate the role of the meridional circulation in redistributing angular momentum, thereby sustaining the observed rotation gradients. These insights contribute to the broader understanding of solar magnetic activity and its cyclical nature. The methodologies employed, including the integration of realistic solar boundary conditions and refined numerical techniques, provide a robust framework for simulating solar interior dynamics. Future work will refine this model by incorporating solar magnetic feedback mechanisms, aiming to further resolve outstanding questions about the generation of the solar magnetic cycle and its relationship with differential rotation and convection.
label: machine

text:
Consider an $m$-bit query $q$ to a bitwise trie $T$. A wildcard $*$ is an
unspecified bit in $q$ for which the query asks the membership for both cases
$*=0$ and $*=1$. It is common that such partial-match queries with wildcards
are issued in tries. With uniformly random occurrences of $w$ wildcards in $q$
assumed, the obvious upper bound on the average number of traversal steps in
$T$ is $2^w m$. We show that the average does not exceed \[ \frac{m+1}{w+1}
\left( 2^{w+2} - 2 w - 4 \right) + m = O \left( \frac{2^w m}{w} \right), \] and
equals the value exactly when $T$ includes all the $m$-bit keys as the worst
case. Here the query $q$ performs with the naive backtracking algorithm in $T$.
It is similarly shown that the average is $O \left( \frac{k^w m}{w} \right)$ in
a general trie of maximum out-degree $k$. Our analysis for tries is extended to
a distributed hash table (DHT), which is among the most frequently used
decentralized data structures in networking. We show, under a natural
probabilistic assumption for the largest class of DHTs, that the average number
of hops required by an $m$-bit query $q$ to a DHT $D$ with random $w$ wildcards
meets the same asymptotic bound. As a result, $q$ is answered with average $O
\left( \frac{2^w m}{w} \right)$ hops rather than $\Theta \left( 2^w m \right)$
in the four major DHTs Chord, Pastry, Tapestry and Kademlia. In addition, with
a uniform key distribution for sufficiently many entries, we prove that a
lookup request to the DHT Chord is answered correctly with $O(m)$ hops and
probability $1 - 2^{-\Omega (m)}$. To the author's knowledge, the probability
$1 - 2^{-\Omega (m)}$ of correct lookup in Chord has not been identified so
far.

text: The increasing demand for transparency and accountability in global supply chains has led to a growing concern over the lack of traceability in complex systems. As a result, the ability to track the origin, movement, and ownership of goods has become a critical issue in various industries, including food, pharmaceuticals, and electronics. The Grand Challenges of Traceability pose significant obstacles to ensuring the safety, quality, and security of products, and the next decade will be crucial in addressing these challenges.  This research paper aims to investigate the current state of traceability in various industries and identify the key challenges that need to be addressed. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining both qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis methods. A survey of industry stakeholders and experts was conducted to gather information on the current state of traceability, while a review of existing literature and case studies was conducted to identify best practices and lessons learned.  The key findings of this study suggest that the lack of standardization, inadequate data management, and limited technological infrastructure are significant barriers to achieving effective traceability. Furthermore, the study highlights the need for a multidisciplinary approach that involves collaboration between industry stakeholders, regulatory bodies, and technology providers. The study also identifies the potential of blockchain technology and other emerging technologies to enhance traceability, but notes that their adoption is hindered by issues of scalability, cost, and interoperability. Ultimately, this research paper concludes that addressing the Grand Challenges of Traceability will require a coordinated effort from industry stakeholders, policymakers, and technology providers to develop and implement effective solutions that ensure the safety, quality, and security of products.

text: The investigation into wireless network modeling has seen a significant evolution, primarily through the development of Poisson Point Process (PPP) frameworks. While PPP provides simplicity and analytical tractability, it often falls short of capturing the spatial characteristics inherent in real-world cellular deployments. The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) presents a contrasting model by detailing realistic yet complex HetNet configurations, which are challenging to analyze mathematically. This research paper aims to bridge the gap between these distinct methodologies through the application of the Poisson Cluster Process (PCP). By amalgamating the analytical flexibility of PPP with the pragmatic structure of 3GPP models, the PCP framework presents a middle ground that can accurately emulate the spatial distribution of base stations while maintaining analytical solvability. Our methodology involves the deployment of PCP to model HetNets, comparing the key performance metrics, such as coverage probability and signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR), against traditional PPP and 3GPP models. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that PCP not only aligns closely with empirical data but also offers enhanced adaptability over standard models. The key findings indicate that PCP models exhibit higher degrees of accuracy in capturing the clustering behavior of small cells and user equipment, thus improving network planning and deployment strategies. In conclusion, the Poisson Cluster Process serves as an effective intermediary between simplistic and overly intricate models, offering a promising avenue for future research and application in cellular network design and optimization.

(Abridged) Cold fronts in cluster cool cores should be erased on short
timescales by thermal conduction, unless protected by magnetic fields that are
"draped" parallel to the front surfaces, suppressing conduction perpendicular
to the fronts. We present MHD simulations of cold front formation in the core
of a galaxy cluster with anisotropic thermal conduction, exploring a parameter
space of conduction strengths parallel and perpendicular to the field lines.
Including conduction has a strong effect on the temperature of the core and the
cold fronts. Though magnetic field lines are draping parallel to the front
surfaces, the temperature jumps across the fronts are nevertheless reduced. The
field geometry is such that the cold gas below the front surfaces can be
connected to hotter regions outside via field lines along directions
perpendicular to the plane of the sloshing motions and along sections of the
front which are not perfectly draped. This results in the heating of this gas
below the front on a timescale of a Gyr, but the sharpness of the density and
temperature jumps may still be preserved. By modifying the density distribution
below the front, conduction may indirectly aid in suppressing Kelvin-Helmholtz
instabilities. If conduction along the field lines is unsuppressed, we find
that the characteristic sharp jumps in X-ray emission seen in observations of
clusters do not form. This suggests that the presence of sharp cold fronts in
hot clusters could be used to place upper limits on conduction in the {\it
bulk} of the ICM. Finally, the combination of sloshing and anisotropic thermal
conduction can result in a larger flux of heat to the core than either process
in isolation. While still not sufficient to prevent a cooling catastrophe in
the very central ($r \sim$ 5 kpc) regions of the cool core, it reduces
significantly the mass of cool gas that accumulates outside those radii.

The index of refraction governs the flow of light through materials. At
visible and near infrared wavelengths the real part of the refractive index is
limited to less than 3 for naturally occurring transparent materials,
fundamentally restricting applications. Here, we carried out experiments to
study the upper limit of the effective refractive index of self-assembled
metasurfaces at visible and near-infrared wavelengths. The centimeter-scale
metasurfaces were made of a hexagonally close packed (hcp) monolayer of gold
nanospheres coated with tunable alkanethiol ligand shells, controlling the
interparticle gap from 2.8 to 0.45 nm. In contrast to isolated dimer studies,
the macro-scale areas allow for billions of gaps to be simultaneously probed
and the hcp symmetry leads to large wavelength shifts in the resonance mode,
enabling subnanometer length scale mechanisms to be reproducibly measured in
the far-field. We demonstrate for subnanometer gaps, that the optical response
of the metasurfaces agrees well with a classical (local) model, with minor
nonlocal effects and no clear evidence of ligand-mediated charge transfer at
optical frequencies. We determine the effective real part of the refractive
index for the metasurfaces has a minimum of 1.0 for green-yellow colors, then
quickly reaches a maximum of 5.0 in the reds and remains larger than 3.5 far
into the near infrared. We further show changing the terminal group and
conjugation of the ligands in the metasurfaces has little effect on the optical
properties. These results establish a pragmatic upper bound on the confinement
of visible and near infrared light, potentially leading to unique dispersion
engineered coatings

We study the relation between the metallicity of quasar broad line region
(BLR) and black hole (BH) mass ($10^{7.5}M_{\odot} \sim 10^{10}M_{\odot}$) and
quasar bolometric luminosity ($10^{44.6}erg/s \sim 10^{48} erg/s$) using a
sample of $\sim$130,000 quasars at $2.25\leq z\leq 5.25$ from Sloan Digital Sky
Survey (SDSS) Data Release 12 (DR12). We generate composite spectra by stacking
individual spectra in the same BH mass (bolometric luminosity) and redshift
bins and then estimate the metallicity of quasar BLR using
metallicity-sensitive broad emission-line flux ratios based on the
photoionization models. We find a significant correlation between quasar BLR
metallicity and BH mass (bolometric luminosity) but no correlation between
quasar BLR metallicity and redshift. We also compare the metallicity of quasar
BLR and that of host galaxies inferred from the mass-metallicity relation of
star-forming galaxy at $z\sim2.3$ and $z\sim3.5$. We find quasar BLR
metallicity is 0.3 $\sim$ 1.0 dex higher than their host galaxies. This
discrepancy cannot be interpreted by the uncertainty due to different
metallicity diagnostic methods, mass-metallicity relation of galaxy,
metallicity gradient in quasar host galaxies, BH mass estimation, the effect of
different spectral energy distribution (SED) models, and a few other potential
sources of uncertainties. We propose a possibility that the high metallicity in
quasar BLR might be caused by metal enrichment from massive star formation in
the nucleus region of quasars or even the accretion disk.

text: In this study, we investigate the structural shrinkage of nonparametric spectral estimators for multivariate time series, addressing the challenge of dimensionality that arises in high-dimensional datasets. Our primary goal is to enhance the accuracy and interpretability of spectral density matrix estimations in multivariate settings by imposing structural constraints. To achieve this, we incorporate shrinkage techniques into the estimation process, thereby overcoming the limitations posed by traditional nonparametric methods that are often sensitive to noise and require large sample sizes.  We develop a comprehensive framework that integrates shrinkage methodologies with multitaper spectral estimation to improve estimation precision while maintaining computational efficiency. Our approach leverages penalized likelihood functions adapted for spectral matrices, allowing for more reliable estimation under multicollinearity and other common multivariate series challenges. The proposed methodology enables us to effectively discover and exploit underlying sparsity and structural patterns within the data, ensuring robust spectral estimation.  We conduct extensive simulations to evaluate the performance of our proposed estimators against conventional approaches. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in mean-squared error and bias reduction, particularly in scenarios with limited sample sizes or when the true spectral structure is sparse. Additionally, we apply our framework to real-world multivariate time series data, showcasing superior performance in uncovering critical spectral features that are potentially obscured under standard estimation techniques.  This research offers a promising pathway for advanced spectral analysis of complex multivariate time series, enhancing the scope of applications in various scientific domains, including econometrics, neuroscience, and climatology.

We address the fundamental network design problem of constructing approximate
minimum spanners. Our contributions are for the distributed setting, providing
both algorithmic and hardness results.
  Our main hardness result shows that an $\alpha$-approximation for the minimum
directed $k$-spanner problem for $k \geq 5$ requires $\Omega(n
/\sqrt{\alpha}\log{n})$ rounds using deterministic algorithms or
$\Omega(\sqrt{n }/\sqrt{\alpha}\log{n})$ rounds using randomized ones, in the
CONGEST model of distributed computing. Combined with the constant-round
$O(n^{\epsilon})$-approximation algorithm in the LOCAL model of [Barenboim,
Elkin and Gavoille, 2016], as well as a polylog-round
$(1+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm in the LOCAL model that we show here,
our lower bounds for the CONGEST model imply a strict separation between the
LOCAL and CONGEST models. Notably, to the best of our knowledge, this is the
first separation between these models for a local approximation problem.
  Similarly, a separation between the directed and undirected cases is implied.
We also prove a nearly-linear lower bound for the minimum weighted $k$-spanner
problem for $k \geq 4$, and we show lower bounds for the weighted 2-spanner
problem.
  On the algorithmic side, apart from the aforementioned
$(1+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm for minimum $k$-spanners, our main
contribution is a new distributed construction of minimum 2-spanners that uses
only polynomial local computations. Our algorithm has a guaranteed
approximation ratio of $O(\log(m/n))$ for a graph with $n$ vertices and $m$
edges, which matches the best known ratio for polynomial time sequential
algorithms [Kortsarz and Peleg, 1994], and is tight if we restrict ourselves to
polynomial local computations. Our approach allows us to extend our algorithm
to work also for the directed, weighted, and client-server variants of the
problem.

text: This study investigates the mechanisms behind the formation and rupture of Ca$^{2+}$ induced pectin biopolymer gels. Our research aims to address the gap in understanding the structural transitions of pectin gels under the influence of calcium ions, crucial for various industrial applications in the food and pharmaceutical sectors. Through a combination of rheological measurements, microscopy techniques, and spectroscopic analysis, we characterized the gelation process and identified the key factors influencing gel strength and stability. Our findings reveal a multi-step gelation process, where pectin chains undergo conformational changes upon calcium ion binding, leading to the formation of a network structure. Furthermore, we elucidated the mechanisms responsible for gel rupture under mechanical stress, shedding light on the fragility of the gel network at different stages of its formation. The insights gained from this study provide valuable knowledge for optimizing gel properties and designing pectin-based formulations with tailored functionalities. By unraveling the complex interplay between pectin molecules and calcium ions, our research contributes to the fundamental understanding of biopolymer gelation processes and opens up avenues for innovative applications in the fields of food engineering and biomaterials science.

Vasiliev's type A higher spin theories in AdS4 have been conjectured to be
dual to the U(N) or O(N) singlet sectors in 3-d conformal field theories with
N-component scalar fields. We compare the O(N^0) correction to the 3-sphere
free energy F in the CFTs with corresponding calculations in the higher spin
theories. This requires evaluating a regularized sum over one loop vacuum
energies of an infinite set of massless higher spin gauge fields in Euclidean
AdS4. For the Vasiliev theory including fields of all integer spin and a scalar
with Delta=1 boundary condition, we show that the regularized sum vanishes.
This is in perfect agreement with the vanishing of subleading corrections to F
in the U(N) singlet sector of the theory of N free complex scalar fields. For
the minimal Vasiliev theory including fields of only even spin, the regularized
sum remarkably equals the value of F for one free real scalar field. This
result may agree with the O(N) singlet sector of the theory of N real scalar
fields, provided the coupling constant in the Vasiliev theory is identified as
G_N ~ 1/(N-1). Similarly, consideration of the USp(N) singlet sector for N
complex scalar fields, which we conjecture to be dual to the husp(2;0|4)
Vasiliev theory, requires G_N ~ 1/(N+1). We also test the higher spin AdS3/CFT2
conjectures by calculating the regularized sum over one loop vacuum energies of
higher spin fields in AdS3. We match the result with the O(N^0) term in the
central charge of the W_N minimal models; this requires a certain truncation of
the CFT operator spectrum so that the bulk theory contains two real scalar
fields with the same boundary conditions.

Security in passive resource-constrained Radio Frequency Identification
(RFID) tags is of much interest nowadays. Resistance against illegal tracking,
cloning, timing, and replay attacks are necessary for a secure RFID
authentication scheme. Reader authentication is also necessary to thwart any
illegal attempt to read the tags. With an objective to design a secure and
low-cost RFID authentication protocol, Gene Tsudik proposed a timestamp-based
protocol using symmetric keys, named YA-TRAP*. Although YA-TRAP* achieves its
target security properties, it is susceptible to timing attacks, where the
timestamp to be sent by the reader to the tag can be freely selected by an
adversary. Moreover, in YA-TRAP*, reader authentication is not provided, and a
tag can become inoperative after exceeding its pre-stored threshold timestamp
value. In this paper, we propose two mutual RFID authentication protocols that
aim to improve YA-TRAP* by preventing timing attack, and by providing reader
authentication. Also, a tag is allowed to refresh its pre-stored threshold
value in our protocols, so that it does not become inoperative after exceeding
the threshold. Our protocols also achieve other security properties like
forward security, resistance against cloning, replay, and tracking attacks.
Moreover, the computation and communication costs are kept as low as possible
for the tags. It is important to keep the communication cost as low as possible
when many tags are authenticated in batch-mode. By introducing aggregate
function for the reader-to-server communication, the communication cost is
reduced. We also discuss different possible applications of our protocols. Our
protocols thus capture more security properties and more efficiency than
YA-TRAP*. Finally, we show that our protocols can be implemented using the
current standard low-cost RFID infrastructures.

text: We investigated the pivotal role of multiple giant impacts in the formation of the Earth-Moon system, a paradigm that has garnered significant attention in the scientific community. Our research aimed to elucidate the dynamics underlying the Moon's origin, with a focus on the cumulative effects of successive impacts on the terrestrial planet.   We employed a combination of numerical simulations and theoretical modeling to simulate the Moon's formation through a series of giant impacts. Our results indicate that the Moon's size and composition can be effectively explained by the accumulation of debris from a series of high-velocity collisions with the early Earth.   The simulations revealed that the most massive impacts, occurring during the first few hundred million years of the solar system's existence, played a crucial role in shaping the Moon's size and orbital characteristics. Subsequent impacts, although less massive, contributed to the Moon's angular momentum and eccentricity.   Our findings suggest that the Moon's formation was a complex, multi-stage process, with multiple giant impacts playing a critical role in its evolution. The results of our simulations are consistent with the leading hypotheses for the Moon's origin and provide new insights into the early history of the Earth-Moon system.   Our study contributes to the ongoing debate regarding the Moon's origin and highlights the importance of considering the cumulative effects of multiple impacts in the formation of planetary systems.

text: In the context of beyond the Standard Model physics, the existence of dark matter and high-energy neutrinos have been extensively studied as potential signatures of new physics beyond the Standard Model. This research focuses on the possibility of multi-component fermionic dark matter and IceCube PeV scale neutrinos in the framework of a Left-Right Model with Gauge Unification. The Left-Right Model is a theoretical framework that attempts to unify the strong, weak, and electromagnetic forces, while the concept of Gauge Unification provides a mechanism to merge the Standard Model with a Grand Unified Theory.   The objective of this study is to explore the potential connections between multi-component fermionic dark matter and IceCube PeV scale neutrinos in the Left-Right Model with Gauge Unification. To achieve this, a set of Lagrangian terms are constructed, which describe the interactions between the fermionic dark matter components and the Standard Model particles. A numerical analysis is performed to determine the constraints on the model parameters and the implications for the observed dark matter and neutrino data.   Key findings of this research indicate that the multi-component fermionic dark matter and IceCube PeV scale neutrinos can be in good agreement with the observed data, suggesting that the Left-Right Model with Gauge Unification could be a viable framework for explaining the observed phenomena. The results also reveal that the model parameters are constrained to be within the allowed range of the observed data, indicating that the model is consistent with the current experimental constraints.   This study contributes to the ongoing research in the area of beyond the Standard Model physics, providing new insights into the possible connections between dark matter, neutrinos, and the Left-Right Model with Gauge Unification. The findings of this research suggest that further experimental searches and precise measurements of the model parameters could provide crucial evidence for or against the existence of multi-component fermionic dark matter and IceCube PeV scale neutrinos in the Left-Right Model with Gauge Unification.

text: This study investigates the implications of a 125 GeV Higgs boson discovery on the fundamental theory of particle physics, specifically the concept of naturalness. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts a Higgs boson with a mass of approximately 125 GeV, which was confirmed by the LHC experiments in 2012. However, the observed mass of the Higgs boson deviates from this prediction, raising questions about the validity of the Standard Model and the concept of naturalness.  Naturalness is a fundamental concept in particle physics, referring to the idea that the fundamental parameters of the theory are tuned to be close to the values predicted by the theory. The 125 GeV Higgs boson discovery presents a challenge to naturalness, as the observed mass of the Higgs boson is significantly different from the predicted value. This discrepancy has significant implications for our understanding of the early universe and the fundamental laws of physics.  To investigate the implications of the 125 GeV Higgs boson discovery on naturalness, this study employed a combination of theoretical and numerical methods. The study used a set of benchmark scenarios to explore the sensitivity of naturalness to the Higgs boson mass, as well as the impact of other fundamental parameters on the naturalness of the theory. The results of the study indicate that the observed mass of the 125 GeV Higgs boson presents a significant challenge to naturalness, and that the concept of naturalness may need to be revised in light of this discovery.  The study also found that the limits on naturalness imposed by the 125 GeV Higgs boson discovery are consistent with some alternative theories of physics, such as supersymmetry and extra dimensions. These findings suggest that the 125 GeV Higgs boson discovery may have implications for our understanding of the fundamental laws of physics, and that further research is needed to fully understand the implications of this discovery.

text: In this study, we investigate the dynamics and societal impacts of partisan content sharing on Facebook, a prevalent social media platform influencing political discourse. Our research aims to address the increasing polarization within online communities, stemming from the rapid dissemination of ideologically concordant information. By leveraging a dataset comprising public Facebook posts from diverse political affiliations, we apply a mixed-methods approach that combines quantitative analysis with qualitative content examination. This methodology enables us to identify patterns of partisan content sharing and assess its broader societal implications.  Our findings reveal that partisan sharing is often characterized by sensationalized narratives that reinforce existing ideological biases, thereby exacerbating echo chamber effects. We observe significant correlations between high-frequency sharing of partisan content and increased divisiveness among users, contributing to a fragmented public sphere. Moreover, the prevalence of false or misleading information in these shared posts raises concerns about the quality of political information consumed on the platform.  Importantly, our research highlights the role of Facebook's algorithmic design in amplifying polarized content, suggesting that platform policies significantly influence sharing behaviors. We propose actionable recommendations for social media platforms, including enhancing transparency in content curation algorithms and promoting diversity in user news feeds, to mitigate the adverse consequences of partisan sharing. Our study advances understanding of the nexus between social media use and political polarization, offering insights for policymakers and technology developers aiming to foster healthier online political engagement. Through this work, we contribute to the ongoing discourse on the responsibilities of social media platforms in sustaining democratic processes and societal cohesion.

Drug use by people is on the rise and is of great interest to public health
agencies and law enforcement agencies. As found by the National Survey on Drug
Use and Health, 20 million Americans aged 12 years or older consumed illicit
drugs in the past few 30 days. Given their ubiquity in everyday life, drug
abuse related studies have received much and constant attention. However, most
of the existing studies rely on surveys. Surveys present a fair number of
problems because of their nature. Surveys on sensitive topics such as illicit
drug use may not be answered truthfully by the people taking them. Selecting a
representative sample to survey is another major challenge. In this paper, we
explore the possibility of using big data from social media in order to
understand illicit drug use behaviors. Instagram posts are collected using drug
related terms by analyzing the hashtags supplied with each post. A large and
dynamic dictionary of frequent illicit drug related slang is used to find these
posts. These posts are studied to find common drug consumption behaviors with
regard to time of day and week. Furthermore, by studying the accounts followed
by the users of drug related posts, we hope to discover common interests shared

text: Cosmic reheating, a critical event in the early universe, refers to the process by which the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation was produced following inflation. This abstract provides an overview of the kinematics of cosmic reheating, focusing on the underlying physics and key findings.  In the context of inflationary models, cosmic reheating can be understood as the conversion of inflaton energy into radiation. The primary mechanism for this energy transfer is assumed to be through the decay of inflaton particles into radiation and matter particles.  Objectives of current research in this area primarily revolve around understanding the dynamics of cosmic reheating and determining its impact on the observed CMB anisotropies. One major open question concerns the identity of the inflaton particle itself, as well as the characteristics of its decay products. Recent advances in particle physics and cosmology have provided new insights into potential candidates for the inflaton particle and their decay channels.  Methodological approaches to studying cosmic reheating have been diverse, including the use of analytical models, numerical simulations, and experimental constraints from particle physics and cosmology. Collaborative efforts, such as the Planck satellite, have led to significant advancements in understanding the kinematics of cosmic reheating, particularly through precise measurements of the CMB anisotropies.  Key findings suggest that cosmic reheating occurred via a combination of inflaton decay and decay of its decay products. The decay of inflaton particles led to the generation of radiation and matter, while the decay of their decay products resulted in the production of large-scale structures observable today. The implications of these findings for the interpretation of cosmological observations, such as CMB anisotropies and large-scale structure formation, are significant.  In conclusion, the kinematics of cosmic reheating plays a crucial role in our understanding of the early universe and its subsequent evolution. Current research focuses on identifying the inflaton particle and its decay channels, as well as studying their implications for the observed structures in the universe. Ongoing advances in particle physics and cosmology are expected to provide further insights into this area.

text: In this study, we investigate the asymptotic structure of Poynting-dominated jets, which are prevalent in astrophysical phenomena such as active galactic nuclei and gamma-ray bursts. These jets, characterized by their electromagnetic field dominance, exhibit unique dynamics that challenge existing hydrodynamic models. Our primary objective is to elucidate the asymptotic properties of such jets by examining the balance between magnetic fields and kinetic energy as they propagate through the interstellar medium. We employ a combination of analytical techniques and numerical simulations to explore the evolution of jet parameters including, but not limited to, the Lorentz factor, magnetization, and energy flux distributions.  Our methodology focuses on reformulating the equations of motion to capture the influence of magnetic tension and pressure, which are critical in maintaining collimation at large distances. We analyze the self-similar solutions in both linear and non-linear regimes, revealing that the jets tend towards a quasi-steady asymptotic state with distinct scaling laws dictated by the initial magnetization levels. The results underscore the importance of magnetic helicity conservation and differential collimation effectiveness, which condition the acceleration and confinement profiles of these jets.  The insights gained from our study not only advance the theoretical understanding of Poynting-dominated jets but also provide observational signatures that could be verified by future high-resolution astrophysical surveys. Our findings bridge critical gaps in current jet models, facilitating a coherent theory that integrates electromagnetic dominance within classical jet dynamics, thus offering a robust framework for interpreting multi-wavelength jet observations in astrophysical settings.

We theoretically investigate the entangled states of an atomic ensemble that
can be obtained via cavity-feedback, varying the atom-light coupling from weak
to strong, and including a systematic treatment of decoherence. In the strong
coupling regime for small atomic ensembles, the system is driven by cavity
losses into a long-lived, highly-entangled many-body state that we characterize
analytically. In the weak coupling regime for large ensembles, we find
analytically the maximum spin squeezing that can be achieved by optimizing both
the coupling and the atom number. This squeezing is fundamentally limited by
spontaneous emission to a constant value, independent of the atom number.
Harnessing entanglement in many-body systems is of fundamental interest [1] and
is the key requirement for quantum enhanced technologies, in particular quantum
metrology [2]. In this respect, many efforts have been devoted to prepare
entangled states in atomic ensembles because of their high degree of coherence
and their potential for precision measurement. Spin squeezed states as well as
number states have been produced following methods based either on coherent
evolution in the presence of a non-linearity in the atomic field [3--5], or on
quantum non-demolition measurement [6--8]. Among methods of the first kind,
cavity feedback [5, 9] is one of the most promising: it has already allowed for
the creation of highly squeezed states [5] and the effective non-linearity
introduced by the atom-cavity coupling can be easily switched off, making it
very attractive for metrol-ogy applications. In this Letter, we analyze the
entangled states that can be produced by cavity feedback in different coupling
regimes from weak to strong, and derive the ultimate limits of the metrology
gain, extending the optimization of squeezing to unexplored domains of
parameters values. After optimization of both the coupling strength and the
atom number, we find a maximum squeezing limit that depends only on the atomic
structure.

A new sample of stars, representative of the solar neighbourhood luminosity
function, is constructed from the Hipparcos catalogue and the Fifth Catalogue
of Nearby Stars. We have cross-matched to sources in the 2MASS catalogue so
that for all stars individually determined Near Infrared photometry (NIR) is
available on a homogeneous system (typically K_s). The spatial completeness of
the sample has been carefully determined by statistical methods, and the NIR
luminosity function of the stars has been derived by direct star counts. We
find a local volume luminosity of 0.121 +/- 0.004 L_K_sun/(pc**3),
corresponding to a volumetric mass-to-light ratio of M/L_K = 0.31 +/- 0.02
M_sun/L_K_sun, where giants contribute 80 per cent to the light but less than 2
per cent to the stellar mass. We derive the surface brightness of the solar
cylinder with the help of a vertical disc model. We find a surface brightness
of 99 L_K_sun/(pc**2) with an uncertainty of approximately 10 %. This
corresponds to a mass-to-light ratio for the solar cylinder of M/L_K = 0.34
M_sun/L_K_sun. The mass-to-light ratio for the solar cylinder is only 10%
larger than the local value despite the fact that the local population has a
much larger contribution of young stars. It turns out that the effective scale
heights of the lower main sequence carrying most of the mass is similar to that
of the giants, which are dominating the NIR light. The corresponding colour for
the solar cylinder is V-K=2.89 mag compared to the local value of V-K = 2.46
mag. An extrapolation of the local surface brightness to the whole Milky Way
yields a total luminosity of M_K = -24.2 mag. The Milky Way falls in the range
of K band Tully-Fisher (TF) relations from the literature.

The Tensor-Vector-Scalar theory of gravity, which was designed as a
relativistic implementation to the modified dynamics paradigm, has fared quite
well as an alternative to dark matter, on both galactic and cosmological
scales. However, its performance in the solar system, as embodied in the
post-Newtonian formalism, has not yet been fully investigated. Tamaki has
recently attempted to calculate the preferred frame parameters for TeVeS, but
ignored the cosmological value of the scalar field, thus concluding that the
Newtonian potential must be static in order to be consistent with the vector
equation. We show that when the cosmological value of the scalar field is taken
into account, there is no constraint on the Newtonian potential; however, the
cosmological value of the scalar field is tightly linked to the vector field
coupling constant K, preventing the former from evolving as predicted by its
equation of motion. We then proceed to investigate the post-Newtonian limit of
a generalized version of TeVeS, with {\AE}ther type vector action, and show
that its \beta,\gamma and \xi parameters are as in GR, while solar system
constraints on the preferred frame parameters \alpha_1 and \alpha_2 can be
satisfied within a modest range of small values of the scalar and vector fields
coupling parameters, and for values of the cosmological scalar field consistent
with evolution within the framework of existing models.

text: Granger causality is a critical concept in time series analysis, often employed to determine whether one time series can predict another. However, its application in state space models remains underexplored. This study aims to bridge this gap by investigating the Granger causality in the context of state space models, offering a robust framework for understanding dynamic interactions in multivariate time series data. We employ a rigorous methodology that integrates the principles of state space representation with Granger causality testing. Specifically, we derive conditions under which Granger causality can be identified from state space models and propose an algorithmic approach to estimate model parameters while testing for causal relationships. Key findings reveal that traditional Granger causality tests may yield misleading results when applied directly to state space models without considering their dynamic structure. Instead, our framework emphasizes the necessity of model specification and includes simulation studies demonstrating improved accuracy in causality detection when the state space formulation is utilized. Ultimately, this research contributes to the statistical literature by establishing a comprehensive perspective on causality within state space systems, highlighting practical implications for econometrics and the social sciences. The proposed methodology can enhance empirical research by providing a more accurate interpretation of temporal relationships, thereby guiding decision-making in various fields where dynamic causality is critical.

Aims: We study the acceleration of the stellar winds of rapidly rotating low
mass stars and the transition between the slow magnetic rotator and fast
magnetic rotator regimes. We aim to understand the properties of stellar winds
in the fast magnetic rotator regime and the effects of magneto-centrifugal
forces on wind speeds and mass loss rates.
  Methods: We extend the solar wind model of Johnstone et al. (2015b) to 1D
magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of the winds of rotating stars. We test
two assumptions for how to scale the wind temperature to other stars and assume
the mass loss rate scales as Mdot ~ Rstar^2 OmegaStar^1.33 Mstar^-3.36, in the
unsaturated regime, as estimated by Johnstone et al. (2015a).
  Results: For 1.0 Msun stars, the winds can be accelerated to several thousand
km/s, and the effects of magneto-centrifugal forces are much weaker for lower
mass stars. We find that the different assumptions for how to scale the wind
temperature to other stars lead to significantly different mass loss rates for
the rapid rotators. If we assume a constant temperature, the mass loss rates of
solar mass stars do not saturate at rapid rotation, which we show to be
inconsistent with observed rotational evolution. If we assume the wind
temperatures scale positively with rotation, the mass loss rates are only
influenced significantly at rotation rates above 75 OmegaSun. We suggest that
models with increasing wind speed for more rapid rotators are preferable to
those that assume a constant wind speed. If this conclusion is confirmed by
more sophisticated wind modelling. it might provide an interesting
observational constraint on the properties of stellar winds.

text: Bayesian analysis has gained significant attention for modeling complex data structures, particularly with beta mixed models, which are well-suited for analyzing proportions and rates. This study focuses on applying Bayesian methodology to a specific class of beta mixed models to address challenges such as non-normality of response variables and hierarchical data structures. The objective is to enhance predictive accuracy and interpretation through a robust statistical framework. We employ Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques for parameter estimation, drawing from conjugate prior distributions to facilitate tractable posterior developments. Extensive simulations are conducted to evaluate the performance of our approach compared to traditional frequentist methods. Additionally, an empirical application using real-world data from a clinical study on treatment efficacy rates is presented to demonstrate practical applicability. Key findings indicate that Bayesian inference provides more accurate parameter estimates, captures uncertainty more effectively, and improves model fit, especially in the presence of small sample sizes and complex random effect structures. The hierarchical nature of the data is also better accommodated through the incorporation of random effects, enhancing model flexibility. Our results underscore the potential of Bayesian analysis in providing comprehensive insights and robust decision-making tools for practitioners dealing with beta-distributed outcomes. Conclusively, this work illustrates the advantages of adopting Bayesian approaches in beta mixed models, paving the way for their broader application in fields demanding nuanced data interpretation and prediction capabilities. Future research should explore more diverse prior settings and alternative MCMC algorithms to further optimize computational efficiency and model accuracy.

text: This research focuses on developing an automated approach for extracting valuable phrases from massive text corpora, a task that has significant implications for various natural language processing (NLP) applications. The extraction of phrases, also known as phrase mining, is a crucial step in text analysis, as it enables the identification of meaningful patterns, relationships, and trends in large volumes of text data.  The objective of this study is to design and evaluate an automated phrase mining system that can efficiently extract relevant phrases from massive text corpora, while minimizing human intervention. The proposed system utilizes a hybrid approach, combining machine learning algorithms and rule-based techniques to identify phrases with high precision and recall.  The methodology employed in this research involves the collection and preprocessing of a large-scale text corpus, followed by the application of the proposed phrase mining system. The system consists of two stages phrase extraction and phrase ranking. The phrase extraction stage uses a machine learning-based approach to identify potential phrases, while the phrase ranking stage employs a rule-based system to evaluate and rank the extracted phrases based on their relevance and importance.  The key findings of this study indicate that the proposed phrase mining system is effective in extracting relevant phrases from massive text corpora, with an average precision and recall of 0.85 and 0.90, respectively. The results also show that the system outperforms existing phrase mining approaches in terms of efficiency and scalability. The findings of this research have significant implications for various NLP applications, including information retrieval, text summarization, and sentiment analysis. Overall, the proposed phrase mining system offers a robust and efficient solution for extracting valuable phrases from massive text corpora, enabling the discovery of meaningful patterns and relationships in large volumes of text data.

We consider the problem of designing mechanisms that interact with strategic
agents through strategic intermediaries (or mediators), and investigate the
cost to society due to the mediators' strategic behavior. Selfish agents with
private information are each associated with exactly one strategic mediator,
and can interact with the mechanism exclusively through that mediator. Each
mediator aims to optimize the combined utility of his agents, while the
mechanism aims to optimize the combined utility of all agents. We focus on the
problem of facility location on a metric induced by a publicly known tree. With
non-strategic mediators, there is a dominant strategy mechanism that is
optimal. We show that when both agents and mediators act strategically, there
is no dominant strategy mechanism that achieves any approximation. We, thus,
slightly relax the incentive constraints, and define the notion of a two-sided
incentive compatible mechanism. We show that the $3$-competitive deterministic
mechanism suggested by Procaccia and Tennenholtz (2013) and Dekel et al. (2010)
for lines extends naturally to trees, and is still $3$-competitive as well as
two-sided incentive compatible. This is essentially the best possible. We then
show that by allowing randomization one can construct a $2$-competitive
randomized mechanism that is two-sided incentive compatible, and this is also
essentially tight. This result also closes a gap left in the work of Procaccia
and Tennenholtz (2013) and Lu et al. (2009) for the simpler problem of
designing strategy-proof mechanisms for weighted agents with no mediators on a
line, while extending to the more general model of trees. We also investigate a
further generalization of the above setting where there are multiple levels of
mediators.

The discovery of gravitational waves (GW) by Advanced LIGO has ushered us
into an era of observational GW astrophysics. Compact binaries remain the
primary target sources for LIGO, of which neutron star-black hole (NSBH)
binaries form an important subset. GWs from NSBH sources carry signatures of
(a) the tidal distortion of the neutron star by its companion black hole during
inspiral, and (b) its potential tidal disruption near merger. In this paper, we
present a Bayesian study of the measurability of neutron star tidal
deformability $\Lambda_\mathrm{NS}\propto (R/M)^{5}$ using observation(s) of
inspiral-merger GW signals from disruptive NSBH coalescences, taking into
account the crucial effect of black hole spins. First, we find that if
non-tidal templates are used to estimate source parameters for an NSBH signal,
the bias introduced in the estimation of non-tidal physical parameters will
only be significant for loud signals with signal-to-noise ratios $> 30$. For
similarly loud signals, we also find that we can begin to put interesting
constraints on $\Lambda_\mathrm{NS}$ (factor of 1-2) with individual
observations. Next, we study how a population of realistic NSBH detections will
improve our measurement of neutron star tidal deformability. For astrophysical
populations of $disruptive$ NSBH mergers, we find 20-35 events to be sufficient
to constrain $\Lambda_\mathrm{NS}$ within $\pm 25-50\%$, depending on the
chosen equation of state. In this we also assume that LIGO will detect black
holes with masses within the astrophysical $mass$-$gap$. If the mass-gap
remains preserved in NSBHs detected by LIGO, we estimate that $25\%$
$additional$ detections will furnish comparable tidal measurement accuracy. In
both cases, we find that the loudest 5-10 events to provide most of the tidal
information, thereby facilitating targeted follow-ups of NSBHs in the upcoming
LIGO-Virgo runs.

We study LHC signatures of Type III seesaw in which SU(2)_L triplet leptons
are introduced to supply the heavy seesaw masses. To detect the signals of
these heavy triplet leptons, one needs to understand their decays to standard
model particles which depend on how light and heavy leptons mix with each
other. We concentrate on the usual solutions with small light and heavy lepton
mixing of order the square root of the ratio of light and heavy masses,
(m_\nu/M_{\nu_R})^{1/2}. This class of solutions can lead to a visible
displaced vertex detectable at the LHC which can be used to distinguish small
mixing and large mixing between light and heavy leptons. We show that, in this
case, the couplings of light and heavy triplet leptons to gauge and Higgs
bosons, which determine the decay widths and branching ratios, can be expressed
in terms of light neutrino masses and their mixing. Using these relations, we
study heavy triplet lepton decay patterns and production cross section at the
LHC. If these heavy triplet leptons are below a TeV or so, they can be easily
produced at the LHC due to their gauge interactions from being non-trivial
representations of SU(2)_L. We consider two ideal production channels, 1)
E^+E^- \to \ell^+\ell^+ \ell^-\ell^- jj (\ell=e,\mu,\tau) and 2) E^\pm N \to
\ell^\pm \ell^\pm jjjj in detail. For case 1), we find that with one or two of
the light leptons being \tau it can also be effectively studied. With judicious
cuts at the LHC, the discovery of the heavy triplet leptons as high as a TeV
can be achieved with 100 fb^{-1} integrated luminosity.

In this work, we propose a new training method for finding minimum weight
norm solutions in over-parameterized neural networks (NNs). This method seeks
to improve training speed and generalization performance by framing NN training
as a constrained optimization problem wherein the sum of the norm of the
weights in each layer of the network is minimized, under the constraint of
exactly fitting training data. It draws inspiration from support vector
machines (SVMs), which are able to generalize well, despite often having an
infinite number of free parameters in their primal form, and from recent
theoretical generalization bounds on NNs which suggest that lower norm
solutions generalize better. To solve this constrained optimization problem,
our method employs Lagrange multipliers that act as integrators of error over
training and identify `support vector'-like examples. The method can be
implemented as a wrapper around gradient based methods and uses standard
back-propagation of gradients from the NN for both regression and
classification versions of the algorithm. We provide theoretical justifications
for the effectiveness of this algorithm in comparison to early stopping and
$L_2$-regularization using simple, analytically tractable settings. In
particular, we show faster convergence to the max-margin hyperplane in a
shallow network (compared to vanilla gradient descent); faster convergence to
the minimum-norm solution in a linear chain (compared to $L_2$-regularization);
and initialization-independent generalization performance in a deep linear
network. Finally, using the MNIST dataset, we demonstrate that this algorithm
can boost test accuracy and identify difficult examples in real-world datasets.

HI absorption studies yield information on both AGN feeding and feedback
processes. This AGN activity interacts with the neutral gas in compact radio
sources, which are believed to represent the young or recently re-triggered AGN
population. We present the results of a survey for HI absorption in a sample of
66 compact radio sources at 0.040 < z < 0.096 with the Australia Telescope
Compact Array. In total, we obtained seven detections, five of which are new,
with a large range of peak optical depths (3% to 87%). Of the detections, 71%
exhibit asymmetric, broad ($\Delta{v}_{\mathrm{FWHM}}$ > 100 km s$^{-1}$)
features, indicative of disturbed gas kinematics. Such broad, shallow and
offset features are also found within low-excitation radio galaxies which is
attributed to disturbed circumnuclear gas, consistent with early-type galaxies
typically devoid of a gas-rich disk. Comparing mid-infrared colours of our
galaxies with HI detections indicates that narrow and deep absorption features
are preferentially found in late-type and high-excitation radio galaxies in our
sample. These features are attributed to gas in galactic disks. By combining
XMM-Newton archival data with 21-cm data, we find support that absorbed X-ray
sources may be good tracers of HI content within the host galaxy. This sample
extends previous HI surveys in compact radio galaxies to lower radio
luminosities and provides a basis for future work exploring the higher redshift
universe.

text: This study explores the formation of different isotopomers of chloronium (HCl⁺) in the interstellar medium (ISM). The primary objective was to investigate how these isotopomers contribute to understanding the chemical processes occurring within the ISM, particularly focusing on their abundance and distribution. Employing theoretical models and computational chemistry techniques, the study aimed to simulate the conditions prevalent in the ISM, including temperature, density, and ionization levels. Key findings indicate that while HCl⁺ itself is abundant, its deuterated isotopomer (DCl⁺) is significantly less frequent, possibly due to more efficient deuteration reactions compared to protium. Additionally, the study revealed that the presence of water molecules plays a crucial role in the formation of DCl⁺, suggesting a potential role for water-mediated chemistry in the ISM. The conclusions emphasize the importance of further experimental studies to validate these findings and to explore the broader implications of these isotopomers for understanding interstellar chemistry.

This paper is aimed at deriving the universality of the largest eigenvalue of
a class of high-dimensional real or complex sample covariance matrices of the
form $\mathcal{W}_N=\Sigma^{1/2}XX^*\Sigma ^{1/2}$. Here, $X=(x_{ij})_{M,N}$ is
an $M\times N$ random matrix with independent entries $x_{ij},1\leq i\leq
M,1\leq j\leq N$ such that $\mathbb{E}x_{ij}=0$, $\mathbb{E}|x_{ij}|^2=1/N$. On
dimensionality, we assume that $M=M(N)$ and $N/M\rightarrow d\in(0,\infty)$ as
$N\rightarrow\infty$. For a class of general deterministic positive-definite
$M\times M$ matrices $\Sigma$, under some additional assumptions on the
distribution of $x_{ij}$'s, we show that the limiting behavior of the largest
eigenvalue of $\mathcal{W}_N$ is universal, via pursuing a Green function
comparison strategy raised in [Probab. Theory Related Fields 154 (2012)
341-407, Adv. Math. 229 (2012) 1435-1515] by Erd\H{o}s, Yau and Yin for Wigner
matrices and extended by Pillai and Yin [Ann. Appl. Probab. 24 (2014) 935-1001]
to sample covariance matrices in the null case ($\Sigma=I$). Consequently, in
the standard complex case ($\mathbb{E}x_{ij}^2=0$), combing this universality
property and the results known for Gaussian matrices obtained by El Karoui in
[Ann. Probab. 35 (2007) 663-714] (nonsingular case) and Onatski in [Ann. Appl.
Probab. 18 (2008) 470-490] (singular case), we show that after an appropriate
normalization the largest eigenvalue of $\mathcal{W}_N$ converges weakly to the
type 2 Tracy-Widom distribution $\mathrm{TW}_2$. Moreover, in the real case, we
show that when $\Sigma$ is spiked with a fixed number of subcritical spikes,
the type 1 Tracy-Widom limit $\mathrm{TW}_1$ holds for the normalized largest
eigenvalue of $\mathcal {W}_N$, which extends a result of F\'{e}ral and
P\'{e}ch\'{e} in [J. Math. Phys. 50 (2009) 073302] to the scenario of
nondiagonal $\Sigma$ and more generally distributed $X$.

text: The abstract for the research paper on the origin of the puzzling hard X-ray emission from γ Cassiopeiae is as follows  This study investigates the underlying mechanisms responsible for the anomalous hard X-ray emission observed from γ Cassiopeiae. The primary aim is to elucidate whether this emission originates from either the coronal region of the Wolf-Rayet star or the circumstellar material ejected during its mass loss phase. Utilizing high-resolution X-ray observations from multiple space missions, including Swift and NuSTAR, the analysis focuses on identifying spectral features indicative of different physical conditions. Key findings suggest that while the coronal region exhibits soft X-ray emission typical of a Wolf-Rayet star, the hard X-ray spectrum is better explained by the interaction between the stellar wind and the surrounding interstellar medium. This finding implies that the hard X-ray emission is predominantly due to the complex interplay between the stellar wind and the environment rather than directly from the stellar corona itself. The results provide new insights into the multi-wavelength properties of this binary system and highlight the importance of detailed observational data in understanding stellar wind interactions in extreme environments.

text: The abstract focuses on the study of neutralino dark matter within the context of collider experiments at energies of 14 TeV and 100 TeV. In recent years, high-energy particle accelerators have been pivotal in exploring the potential signatures of dark matter particles, particularly neutralinos, which are theoretical supersymmetric particles. This research aims to investigate the production and detection of neutralinos at these energy scales using state-of-the-art simulations and experimental data analysis techniques.  The study employs sophisticated models to predict the cross-sections of neutralino interactions at both accelerator energies, considering various parameters such as the mass of the neutralino and the properties of the Higgs boson. Experimental methodologies involve detailed analyses of collision events to identify any anomalous patterns that could indicate the presence of neutralinos.   Key findings include the identification of significant excesses in certain event types that align with theoretical expectations for neutralino interactions. These results suggest a possible correlation between the observed phenomena and neutralino dark matter. However, the interpretations are subject to stringent experimental validation and further theoretical scrutiny.  In conclusion, this research contributes to the ongoing quest to understand the nature of dark matter by providing robust evidence from collider experiments at high energies, thereby enhancing our comprehension of fundamental physics and cosmology.

text: This work presents our research on conducting multiscale simulations of polymer melt spinning utilizing the dumbbell model. The primary problem addressed in this study is the need for efficient and accurate simulations of the complex behavior of polymer melt spinning processes. We aim to analyze the flow-induced molecular orientation and stress distribution in polymer melts during the spinning process to enhance our understanding of the involved mechanisms.  Our results demonstrate the successful implementation of the dumbbell model in capturing the polymer chain dynamics and rheological properties at different length scales. By coupling the macroscopic flow with the microscopic behavior of polymer chains, we are able to investigate the structural changes and mechanical responses occurring during melt spinning. This approach offers insights into the relationship between processing conditions, polymer rheology, and the resulting fiber properties.  Key ideas underlying this study involve bridging the gap between molecular-level interactions and macroscopic flow phenomena in polymer processing. Our methodology involves integrating the dumbbell model into multiscale simulations to provide a detailed analysis of the melt spinning process. By considering chain connectivity and non-Newtonian flow behavior, we can predict the final fiber morphology and mechanical properties.  Overall, our work contributes to advancing the understanding of polymer melt spinning processes through comprehensive multiscale simulations using the dumbbell model, offering valuable insights for optimizing manufacturing processes and material design.

We present an approach to Intelligent Tutoring Systems which adaptively
personalizes sequences of learning activities to maximize skills acquired by
students, taking into account the limited time and motivational resources. At a
given point in time, the system proposes to the students the activity which
makes them progress faster. We introduce two algorithms that rely on the
empirical estimation of the learning progress, RiARiT that uses information
about the difficulty of each exercise and ZPDES that uses much less knowledge
about the problem.
  The system is based on the combination of three approaches. First, it
leverages recent models of intrinsically motivated learning by transposing them
to active teaching, relying on empirical estimation of learning progress
provided by specific activities to particular students. Second, it uses
state-of-the-art Multi-Arm Bandit (MAB) techniques to efficiently manage the
exploration/exploitation challenge of this optimization process. Third, it
leverages expert knowledge to constrain and bootstrap initial exploration of
the MAB, while requiring only coarse guidance information of the expert and
allowing the system to deal with didactic gaps in its knowledge. The system is
evaluated in a scenario where 7-8 year old schoolchildren learn how to
decompose numbers while manipulating money. Systematic experiments are
presented with simulated students, followed by results of a user study across a
population of 400 school children.

The formation of Pluto's small satellites - Styx, Nix, Keberos and Hydra -
remains a mystery. Their orbits are nearly circular and are near mean-motion
resonances and nearly coplanar with Charon's orbit. One scenario suggests that
they all formed close to their current locations from a disk of debris that was
ejected from the Charon-forming impact before the tidal evolution of Charon.
The validity of this scenario is tested by performing $N$-body simulations with
the small satellites treated as test particles and Pluto-Charon evolving
tidally from an initial orbit at a few Pluto radii with initial eccentricity
$e_{\rm C} = 0$ or 0.2. After tidal evolution, the free eccentricities $e_{\rm
free}$ of the test particles are extracted by applying fast Fourier
transformation to the distance between the test particles and the center of
mass of the system and compared with the current eccentricities of the four
small satellites. The only surviving test particles with $e_{\rm free}$
matching the eccentricities of the current satellites are those not affected by
mean-motion resonances during the tidal evolution in a model with Pluto's
effective tidal dissipation function $Q = 100$ and an initial $e_{\rm C}$ = 0.2
that is damped down rapidly. However, these test particles do not have any
preference to be in or near 4:1, 5:1 and 6:1 resonances with Charon. An
alternative scenario may be needed to explain the formation of Pluto's small
satellites.

text: This paper explores the application of dissociation and propagation techniques for approximate lifted inference within the framework of standard relational database management systems (RDBMSs). The background section introduces the concept of lifted inference and its challenges in RDBMSs, while highlighting the potential benefits of approximate inference. The objective of this research is to investigate the feasibility of using dissociation and propagation methods to efficiently perform approximate lifted inference within the confines of RDBMSs.  The methodology section outlines the proposed approach, which involves dissociating the complex relational joins required for lifted inference and applying approximation techniques to simplify the propagation process. We then describe the implementation of this approach using well-known RDBMSs, such as PostgreSQL and MySQL, and propose extensions to their systems for better support of approximate inference.  Key findings reveal that the proposed approach significantly reduces the computational cost and response time of approximate lifted inference in RDBMSs, making it a practical solution for handling large and complex query workloads. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the accuracy of the approximations remains satisfactory, even when dealing with noisy data or incomplete information.  In conclusion, this study demonstrates the viability of integrating dissociation and propagation methods into standard RDBMSs to enable efficient and accurate approximate lifted inference. The presented approach offers a powerful tool to handle the computational demands of complex relational queries and provides insights that can guide future research in this area.

text: In this study, we investigate the enhancement of the thermal stability of the toric code quantum error correction scheme by coupling it to a bosonic bath. Our approach involves constructing a hybrid system where the qubits of the toric code are coupled to a bosonic reservoir, thereby facilitating thermal dissipation processes that mitigate thermal fluctuations detrimental to the error correction capability. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that this coupling significantly reduces the critical temperature at which the toric code loses its topological order due to thermal noise. The key methodologies employed include quantum Monte Carlo techniques for simulating the dynamics of the hybrid system and perturbative calculations to estimate the thermal stability. Our results suggest that the incorporation of a bosonic bath not only stabilizes the toric code against thermal fluctuations but also potentially extends its operational range in practical quantum computing applications.
