We consider the problem of identifying a team of skilled individuals for
collaboration, in the presence of a social network. Each node in the social
network may be an expert in one or more skills. Edge weights specify affinity
or collaborative compatibility between respective nodes. Given a project that
requires a set of specified number of skilled individuals in each area of
expertise, the goal is to identify a team that maximizes the collaborative
compatibility. For example, the requirement may be to form a team that has at
least three databases experts and at least two theory experts. We explore team
formation where the collaborative compatibility objective is measured as the
density of the induced subgraph on selected nodes. The problem of maximizing
density is NP-hard even when the team requires individuals of only one skill.
We present a 3-approximation algorithm that improves upon a naive extension of
the previously known algorithm for densest at least $k$ subgraph problem. We
further show how the same approximation can be extended to a special case of
multiple skills. Our problem generalizes the formulation studied by Lappas et
al. [KDD '09] who measure team compatibility in terms of diameter or spanning
tree costs. Experiments are performed on a crawl of the DBLP graph where
individuals can be skilled in at most four areas - theory, databases, data
mining, and artificial intelligence. In addition to our main algorithm, we also
present heuristic extensions to trade off between the size of the solution and
its induced density. These density-based algorithms outperform the
diameter-based objective on several metrics for assessing the collaborative
compatibility of teams. The solutions suggested are also intuitively meaningful
and scale well with the increase in the number of skilled individuals required.

In this work we start by determining all irreducible spherical functions
$\Phi$ of any $K $-type associated to the pair $(G,K)=(\SO(4),\SO(3))$. The
functions $P=P(u)$ corresponding to the irreducible spherical functions of a
fixed $K$-type $\pi_\ell$ are appropriately packaged into a sequence of matrix
valued polynomials $(P_w)_{w\ge0}$ of size $(\ell+1)\times(\ell+1)$. Finally we
prove that $\widetilde P_w={P_0}^{-1}P_w$ is a sequence of matrix orthogonal
polynomials with respect to a weight matrix $W$. Moreover, we show that $W$
admits a second order symmetric hypergeometric operator $\widetilde D$ and a
first order symmetric differential operator $\widetilde E$.
  Later, we establish a direct relationship between the spherical functions of
the $n$-dimensional sphere $S^n\simeq\SO(n+1)/\SO(n)$ and the spherical
functions of the $n$-dimensional real projective space
$P^n(\mathbb{R})\simeq\SO(n+1)/\mathrm{O}(n)$. Concluding that to find all the
spherical functions of one of these pairs is equivalent to do the same it with
the other.
  Finally, we study the spherical functions of certain types of the
$n$-dimensional sphere $S^{n}\simeq \SO(n+1)/\SO(n)$, for any $n$. More
precisely, we give explicitly all the spherical functions whose associated
functions $H$ are scalar valued, including those of trivial type, and then we
study the irreducible spherical functions of fundamental type, describing them
in terms of matrix valued hypergeometric functions $_2!F_1$. Thereafter, for
every fundamental type we build a sequence of ortogonal matrix valued
polynomials with respect to a weight $W$, which are associated to the spherical
functions. We also prove that, for any $n$, $W$ admits a second order symmetric
differential operator.

text: This study investigates the phenomenon of three-dimensional chaotic advection by mixed layer baroclinic instabilities, a complex process that plays a crucial role in the dynamics of ocean currents. Background research suggests that baroclinic instabilities in the ocean's mixed layer can lead to chaotic advection, a phenomenon characterized by the irreversible mixing of fluids. However, the underlying mechanisms governing this process remain poorly understood, particularly in three-dimensional settings.  The objective of this research is to explore the effects of mixed layer baroclinic instabilities on three-dimensional chaotic advection in the ocean. A numerical model is developed to simulate the dynamics of the ocean's mixed layer, incorporating realistic representations of baroclinic instabilities and chaotic advection. The model is validated against observational data, demonstrating its ability to accurately capture the complex interactions between baroclinic instabilities and chaotic advection.  Key findings indicate that mixed layer baroclinic instabilities can significantly enhance three-dimensional chaotic advection in the ocean, leading to increased mixing and transport of heat and nutrients. The results also reveal that the strength and orientation of baroclinic instabilities play a crucial role in determining the extent of chaotic advection. Furthermore, the model suggests that the interaction between baroclinic instabilities and chaotic advection can have significant impacts on ocean circulation patterns and climate variability.  The conclusion of this study highlights the importance of considering the complex interactions between baroclinic instabilities and chaotic advection in understanding the dynamics of ocean currents. The findings of this research have significant implications for our understanding of ocean circulation patterns and climate variability, and suggest that mixed layer baroclinic instabilities may play a key role in shaping the Earth's climate system.

We conducted a deep narrow-band imaging survey with the Subaru Prime Focus
Camera on the Subaru Telescope and constructed a sample of Ly$\alpha$ emitters
(LAEs) at z=2.53 in the UDS-CANDELS field where a sample of H$\alpha$ emitters
(HAEs) at the same redshift is already obtained from our previous narrow-band
observation at NIR. The deep narrow-band and multi broadband data allow us to
find LAEs of stellar masses and star-formation rates (SFRs) down to
$\gtrsim$$10^8$ M$_\odot$ and $\gtrsim$0.2 M$_\odot$/yr, respectively. We show
that the LAEs are located along the same mass-SFR sequence traced by normal
star-forming galaxies such as HAEs, but towards a significantly lower mass
regime. Likewise, LAEs seem to share the same mass--size relation with typical
star-forming galaxies, except for the massive LAEs, which tend to show
significantly compact sizes. We identify a vigorous mass growth in the central
part of LAEs: the stellar mass density in the central region of LAEs increases
as their total galaxy mass grows. On the other hand, we see no Ly$\alpha$ line
in emission for most of the HAEs. Rather, we find that the Ly$\alpha$ feature
is either absent or in absorption (Ly$\alpha$ absorbers; LAAs), and its
absorption strength may increase with reddening of the UV continuum slope. We
demonstrate that a deep Ly$\alpha$ narrow-band imaging like this study is able
to search for not only LAEs but also LAAs in a certain redshift slice. This
work suggests that LAEs trace normal star-forming galaxies in the low-mass
regime, while they remain as a unique population because the majority of HAEs
are not LAEs.

Coupled backward and forward wave amplitudes of an electromagnetic field
propagating in a periodic and nonlinear medium at Bragg resonance are governed
by the nonlinear coupled mode equations (NLCME). This system of PDEs, similar
in structure to the Dirac equations, has gap soliton solutions that travel at
any speed between 0 and the speed of light. A recently considered strategy for
spatial trapping or capture of gap optical soliton light pulses is based on the
appropriate design of localized defects in the periodic structure. Localized
defects in the periodic structure give rise to defect modes, which persist as
{\it nonlinear defect modes} as the amplitude is increased. Soliton trapping is
the transfer of incoming soliton energy to {\it nonlinear} defect modes. To
serve as targets for such energy transfer, nonlinear defect modes must be
stable. We therefore investigate the stability of nonlinear defect modes.
Resonance among discrete localized modes and radiation modes plays a role in
the mechanism for stability and instability, in a manner analogous to the
nonlinear Schr\"odinger / Gross-Pitaevskii (NLS/GP) equation. However, the
nature of instabilities and how energy is exchanged among modes is considerably
more complicated than for NLS/GP due, in part, to a continuous spectrum of
radiation modes which is unbounded above and below. In this paper we (a)
establish the instability of branches of nonlinear defect states which, for
vanishing amplitude, have a linearization with eigenvalue embedded within the
continuous spectrum, (b) numerically compute, using Evans function, the
linearized spectrum of nonlinear defect states of an interesting multiparameter
family of defects, and (c) perform direct time-dependent numerical simulations
in which we observe the exchange of energy among discrete and continuum modes.

The multi-armed bandit problem forms the foundation for solving a wide range
of on-line stochastic optimization problems through a simple, yet effective
mechanism. One simply casts the problem as a gambler that repeatedly pulls one
out of N slot machine arms, eliciting random rewards. Learning of reward
probabilities is then combined with reward maximization, by carefully balancing
reward exploration against reward exploitation. In this paper, we address a
particularly intriguing variant of the multi-armed bandit problem, referred to
as the {\it Stochastic Point Location (SPL) Problem}. The gambler is here only
told whether the optimal arm (point) lies to the "left" or to the "right" of
the arm pulled, with the feedback being erroneous with probability $1-\pi$.
This formulation thus captures optimization in continuous action spaces with
both {\it informative} and {\it deceptive} feedback. To tackle this class of
problems, we formulate a compact and scalable Bayesian representation of the
solution space that simultaneously captures both the location of the optimal
arm as well as the probability of receiving correct feedback. We further
introduce the accompanying Thompson Sampling guided Stochastic Point Location
(TS-SPL) scheme for balancing exploration against exploitation. By learning
$\pi$, TS-SPL also supports {\it deceptive} environments that are lying about
the direction of the optimal arm. This, in turn, allows us to solve the
fundamental Stochastic Root Finding (SRF) Problem. Empirical results
demonstrate that our scheme deals with both deceptive and informative
environments, significantly outperforming competing algorithms both for SRF and
SPL.

Network coding is commonly used to improve the energy efficiency of
network-wide broadcasting in wireless multi-hop networks. In this work, we
focus on XOR-based broadcasting in mobile ad hoc networks with multiple
sources. We make the observation that the common approach, which is to benefit
from the synergy of XOR network coding with a CDS-based broadcast algorithm,
suffers performance breakdowns. After delving into the details of this synergy,
we attribute this behavior to an important mechanism of the underlying
broadcast algorithm, known as the "termination criterion". To tackle the
problem, we propose a termination criterion that is fully compatible with XOR
coding. In addition to that, we revisit the internals of XOR coding. We first
enhance the synergy of XOR coding with the underlying broadcast algorithm by
allowing each mechanism to benefit from information available by the other. In
this way, we manage to improve the pruning efficiency of the CDS-based
algorithm while at the same time we come up with a method for detecting coding
opportunities that has minimal storage and processing requirements compared to
current approaches. Then, for the first time, we use XOR coding as a mechanism
not only for enhancing energy efficiency but also for reducing the
end-to-end-delay. We validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm
through extensive simulations on a diverse set of scenarios.

text: We present a comprehensive analysis of the 2015 GK Persei dwarf nova event observed by the X-ray astronomy satellite Suzaku. Our investigation aimed to elucidate the underlying physics of this event, which was characterized by a sudden and transient increase in X-ray emission. Through a combination of Suzaku's high-resolution spectroscopy and imaging capabilities, we obtained detailed information on the spectral and temporal evolution of the nova.  Our analysis revealed a complex interplay between the nova's accretion disk and the surrounding interstellar medium, which led to the observed variability in X-ray emission. We detected a significant increase in the nova's X-ray luminosity, accompanied by a shift in its spectral index, indicative of a change in the disk's temperature and density. Furthermore, our data suggest that the nova's X-ray emission was modulated by the presence of a pre-existing circumstellar medium, which affected the disk's accretion rate and X-ray production.  Our results provide new insights into the physics of dwarf nova eruptions, highlighting the importance of considering the interplay between the accretion disk and the surrounding environment. The Suzaku observations of GK Persei 2015 offer a unique opportunity to study the complex processes involved in these events, and our findings have implications for our understanding of the underlying mechanisms that govern these transient astrophysical phenomena.

text: In this study, we investigate the problem of minimax estimation for a p-dimensional linear functional within the context of sparse Gaussian models, focusing particularly on achieving robust estimation of the mean. Sparse Gaussian models are prevalent in high-dimensional statistical analyses due to their capacity to capture the sparse structure inherent in many practical applications. We address the challenges posed by high-dimensionality and sparsity by constructing an estimator that optimally balances bias and variance in the presence of Gaussian noise, thereby achieving minimax optimal performance. Our methodology leverages novel techniques in convex optimization and penalization strategies to handle sparsity effectively. Furthermore, we incorporate robust statistical procedures to enhance the accuracy and reliability of mean estimation in potentially non-ideal conditions, such as outliers or heavy-tailed distributions. Our theoretical contributions include deriving sharp lower bounds for the minimax risk and providing tight characterizations of the estimator’s performance under various sparsity regimes. We demonstrate through extensive simulations and real-world datasets that our approach significantly surpasses existing methods in terms of mean squared error and robustness to model misspecification. The results suggest that our estimator not only attains robust performance in the classical Gaussian setting but also extends seamlessly to more generalized contexts. This work has significant implications for advancing estimation techniques in high-dimensional statistics, with potential applications in fields such as genomics, signal processing, and econometrics where high-dimensional data are commonly encountered. Our findings underscore the critical role of considering both sparse model structures and robustness in statistical inference.

text: The study focuses on the NLS1 (Narrow Line Seyfert 1) galaxies and their central black hole masses estimation using the X-ray excess variance method. NLS1 galaxies are known for their unusual X-ray properties, including a hard X-ray spectrum and a high degree of variability. In this research, we investigate the relationship between X-ray variability and black hole mass in NLS1 galaxies.  Our objective was to estimate central black hole masses of NLS1 galaxies by measuring their X-ray excess variance using the observed X-ray light curves. We analyzed archival XMM-Newton and Chandra data for a sample of 12 NLS1 galaxies. The X-ray excess variance was calculated using the standard method and corrected for the effects of Poisson noise.  Key findings indicated a strong correlation between the X-ray excess variance and the central black hole mass in NLS1 galaxies. Our results suggest that the X-ray excess variance method can be an effective tool for estimating central black hole masses in NLS1 galaxies. We also found that the X-ray excess variance values for NLS1 galaxies are systematically lower than those for typical Seyfert 1 galaxies, indicating that NLS1 galaxies have smaller black holes. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the physical properties of NLS1 galaxies and their central supermassive black holes.  In conclusion, this study demonstrated the use of the X-ray excess variance method for estimating central black hole masses in NLS1 galaxies. Our results showed a strong correlation between the X-ray excess variance and the central black hole mass and revealed that NLS1 galaxies have smaller black holes than typical Seyfert 1 galaxies. The findings of this study provide new insights into the X-ray properties of NLS1 galaxies and their central supermassive black holes.

We detect radio emission in an additional two epochs of the ultracool dwarf
binary LP 349- 25, finding that the observed emission is broadband and steady
on timescales between 10s and 10.7 hours, as well as on timescales of 0.6 and
1.6 years. This system is unusual for ultracool dwarfs with detectable radio
emission, in exhibiting a lack of any large scale variability, particularly the
bursting (periodic or aperiodic) behavior exhibited by the other objects with
detectable levels of radio emission. We explore the constraints that the lack
of variability on long and short timescales, and flat spectral index, imply
about the radio-emitting structures and mechanism. The temporal constraints
argue for a high latitude emitting region with a large inclination so that it
is always in view, and survives for at least 0.6 year. Temporal constraints
also limit the plasma conditions, implying that the electron density be n_e
<4x10^5 cm-3 and B < 130 G in order not to see time variations due to
collisional or radiative losses from high energy particles. The observations
and constraints provided by them are most compatible with a nonthermal radio
emission mechanism, likely gyrosynchrotron emission from a spatially
homogeneous or inhomogeneous source. This indicates that, similar to behaviors
noted for chromospheric, transition region, and coronal plasmas in ultracool
dwarfs, the magnetic activity patterns observed in active higher mass stars can
survive to the substellar boundary. We also present new epochs of
multi-frequency radio observations for the the ultracool dwarfs 2MASS
05233822-140322 and 2MASS14563831-2809473(=LHS 3003); each has been detected in
at least one previous epoch but are not detected in the epochs reported here.

Context:The HAGAR Telescope Array at Hanle, Ladakh has been regularly
monitoring the nearby blazar Mkn 421 for the past 7yrs.
  Aims: Blazars show flux variability in all timescales across the
electromagnetic spectrum. While there is abundant literature characterizing the
short term flares from different blazars, comparatively little work has been
done to study the long term variability. We aim to study the long term temporal
and spectral variability in the radiation from Mkn 421 during 2009-2015.
  Methods: We quantify the variability and lognormality from the radio to the
VHE bands, and compute the correlations between the various wavebands using the
z-transformed discrete correlation function. We construct the Spectral Energy
Distribution (SED) contemporaneous with HAGAR observation seasons and fit it
with a one zone synchrotron self Compton model to study the spectral
variability.
  Results: The flux is found to be highly variable across all time scales. The
variability is energy dependant, and is maximum in the X-ray and Very High
Energy (VHE) bands. A strong correlation is found between the Fermi-LAT (gamma)
and radio bands, and between Fermi-LAT and optical, but none between Fermi-LAT
and X-ray. Lognormality in the flux distribution is clearly detected. This is
the third blazar, following BL~Lac and PKS~2155$+$304 to show this behavior.
The SED can be well fit by a one zone SSC model, and variations in the flux
states can be attributed mainly due to changes in the particle distribution. A
strong correlation is seen between the break energy $\gamma_b$ of the particle
spectrum and the total bolometric luminosity.

text: This research paper presents a theoretical framework for the separable representation of energy-dependent optical potentials, a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics. The traditional approach to solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation often involves numerical methods, which can be computationally intensive and difficult to interpret. The objective of this study is to develop a novel analytical approach that allows for the separable representation of energy-dependent optical potentials, enabling a more efficient and insightful analysis of quantum systems.  The methodology employed in this research involves the use of a generalized Lagrange multiplier method, which is applied to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation to derive a set of coupled differential equations. These equations are then solved using a variational principle, resulting in a separable representation of the energy-dependent optical potential. The proposed approach is validated through numerical simulations of a range of quantum systems, including harmonic oscillators and atoms in electromagnetic fields.  The key findings of this study indicate that the separable representation of energy-dependent optical potentials can be used to simplify the analysis of quantum systems, enabling the identification of underlying symmetries and patterns that can inform our understanding of quantum behavior. The results also demonstrate the potential of this approach for the design of more efficient quantum algorithms and the simulation of complex quantum systems. Overall, the separable representation of energy-dependent optical potentials offers a promising new tool for the analysis and simulation of quantum systems, with implications for a wide range of fields, from quantum computing to condensed matter physics.

text: In this study, we explore the significant impact of anti-site defects on bulk conductivity within topological insulators, aiming to address the persistent challenge of enhancing their electronic properties for potential applications in quantum computing and spintronics. We focus on understanding how these intrinsic defects, which involve the swapping of elements within the crystal lattice, influence electronic behavior and charge carrier density. Employing a combination of first-principles calculations and experimental validation, we systematically investigate the formation energies and charge states of anti-site defects across various topological insulators. Our findings reveal that these defects play a crucial role in mediating bulk conductivity by either introducing localized states within the band gap or altering electron mobility, depending on their concentration and distribution. By manipulating the stoichiometry and growth conditions, we demonstrate a pathway to effectively control defect densities and, consequently, modulate the electrical characteristics of topological insulators. This research provides key insights into defect engineering and offers a pathway for the optimization of topological materials, thus opening new avenues for their integration into advanced technological applications. Our results underscore the necessity of controlling anti-site defects to leverage the full potential of topological insulators' surface states while minimizing the parasitic effects of bulk conductivity. This work contributes to the fundamental understanding of defect-driven phenomena within topological insulators and establishes a robust framework for tailoring their properties to enhance device performance.

text: In this work, we explore the use of weak memory techniques to accelerate the processing of complex programs with logical constraints. Specifically, we introduce a new method for generating laced caches, which we call "New Lace and Arsenic." The method involves incorporating logical constraints into cache line tags and using arsenic trioxide to dynamically alter tag values based on program logic.    Previous work in this area focused on utilizing weak memory for caching data structures or program control flow. Our approach, however, targets logical constraints, which are crucial for many applications, such as database systems, theorem provers, or electronic design automation. By incorporating logical constraints into cache line tags, we enable the processor to perform constant-time lookups and validations, reducing the overall execution time for programs with such constraints.    We evaluated the performance of New Lace and Arsenic through simulations and experiments on several benchmark programs with logical constraints. The results demonstrated an average improvement of 30% in execution time and a maximum improvement of 70%. Furthermore, we demonstrated that our method can effectively handle complex logical constraints, making it a promising solution for accelerating the processing of large, logically-constrained programs.    Our methodology involves extending the processor architecture with specialized hardware for managing weak memory and implementing a novel algorithm for generating and updating laced caches. The implementation was done using FPGA technology to enable rapid prototyping and further customization.    In conclusion, this work presents New Lace and Arsenic, a new method for using weak memory techniques to accelerate the processing of complex programs with logical constraints. The results showed significant performance improvements, making this a promising approach for improving the efficiency of many applications.

Online social networks play a major role in the spread of information at very
large scale and it becomes essential to provide means to analyse this
phenomenon. In this paper we address the issue of predicting the temporal
dynamics of the information diffusion process. We develop a graph-based
approach built on the assumption that the macroscopic dynamics of the spreading
process are explained by the topology of the network and the interactions that
occur through it, between pairs of users, on the basis of properties at the
microscopic level. We introduce a generic model, called T-BaSIC, and describe
how to estimate its parameters from users behaviours using machine learning
techniques. Contrary to classical approaches where the parameters are fixed in
advance, T-BaSIC's parameters are functions depending of time, which permit to
better approximate and adapt to the diffusion phenomenon observed in online
social networks. Our proposal has been validated on real Twitter datasets.
Experiments show that our approach is able to capture the particular patterns
of diffusion depending of the studied sub-networks of users and topics. The
results corroborate the "two-step" theory (1955) that states that information
flows from media to a few "opinion leaders" who then transfer it to the mass
population via social networks and show that it applies in the online context.
This work also highlights interesting recommendations for future
investigations.

text: Cloud destruction via turbulence is a complex process that influences various aspects of cloud evolution. The results suggest that higher Mach numbers lead to increased turbulence within clouds, resulting in higher mass-loss rates and the formation of distinct tails. These tails demonstrate a clear correlation with the Mach number, indicating a direct relationship between turbulence intensity and cloud destruction patterns. The findings highlight the importance of Mach number in understanding cloud evolution under turbulent conditions. In conclusion, this research enhances our understanding of the dynamics of cloud destruction and provides valuable insights into the role of turbulence in shaping cloud morphology and mass loss.

Proxima b is a planet with a minimum mass of 1.3 MEarth orbiting within the
habitable zone (HZ) of Proxima Centauri, a very low-mass, active star and the
Sun's closest neighbor. Here we investigate a number of factors related to the
potential habitability of Proxima b and its ability to maintain liquid water on
its surface. We set the stage by estimating the current high-energy irradiance
of the planet and show that the planet currently receives 30 times more EUV
radiation than Earth and 250 times more X-rays. We compute the time evolution
of the star's spectrum, which is essential for modeling the flux received over
Proxima b's lifetime. We also show that Proxima b's obliquity is likely null
and its spin is either synchronous or in a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance, depending
on the planet's eccentricity and level of triaxiality. Next we consider the
evolution of Proxima b's water inventory. We use our spectral energy
distribution to compute the hydrogen loss from the planet with an improved
energy-limited escape formalism. Despite the high level of stellar activity we
find that Proxima b is likely to have lost less than an Earth ocean's worth of
hydrogen before it reached the HZ 100-200 Myr after its formation. The largest
uncertainty in our work is the initial water budget, which is not constrained
by planet formation models. We conclude that Proxima b is a viable candidate
habitable planet.

In this paper we show how reliable measurements on porous ceramic films can
be made by appropriate nanoindentation experiments and analysis.
Room-temperature mechanical properties of the mixed-conducting perovskite
material LSCF6428 were investigated by nanoindentation of porous bulk samples
and porous films sintered at temperatures from 900-1200C. A spherical indenter
was used so that the contact area was much greater than the scale of the porous
microstructure. The elastic modulus of the bulk samples was found to increase
from 33.8-174.3 GPa and hardness from 0.64-5.32 GPa as the porosity decreased
from 45-5% after sintering at 900-1200C. Densification under the indenter was
found to have little influence on the measured elastic modulus. The residual
porosity in the dense sample was found to account for the discrepancy between
the elastic moduli measured by indentation and by impulse excitation.
Crack-free LSCF6428 films of acceptable surface roughness for indentation were
also prepared by sintering at 900-1200C. Reliable measurements of the true
properties of the films were obtained by data extrapolation provided that the
ratio of indentation depth to film thickness was in the range 0.1 to 0.2. The
elastic moduli of the films and bulk materials were approximately equal for a
given porosity. The 3D microstructures of films before and after indentation
were characterized using FIB-SEM tomography. Finite element modelling of the
elastic deformation of the actual microstructures showed excellent agreement
with the nanoindentation results.

text: The Cosmic Ray (CR) positron/electron ratio at energies above the TeV scale remains a subject of ongoing investigation due to its potential implications for astrophysical sources and dark matter models. In this work, we present measurements of the CR positron fraction using data recorded by the MAGIC telescopes during Moon shadow events, which provide an unprecedented level of shielding against background cosmic rays. Our analysis is based on a total exposure of 542 hours between 2009 and 2018, with energies ranging from 50 GeV to 100 TeV. We find that the positron fraction exhibits a significant excess over the expectation from primary proton interactions with the interstellar medium. This excess is most pronounced at energies around 100 GeV, where the positron fraction reaches a maximum of approximately 15% and subsequently decreases. The observed excess cannot be explained by currently known astrophysical sources, suggesting the possible presence of unidentified sources or new physical processes. Our results contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the origin of the CR positron excess and provide new constraints for dark matter models. Further investigations are required to confirm and extend these findings, as well as to understand the underlying mechanisms responsible for the observed anomaly.

text: Our research introduces a novel approach to heavy quark transport in hot and dense QCD matter through a linearized Boltzmann-Langevin model. By formulating a linearized Boltzmann-Langevin model, we seek to improve our understanding of how heavy quarks traverse and interact with the strongly interacting medium. Our results demonstrate that this model offers insights into the dynamics of heavy quarks by incorporating both collisional and fluctuating contributions. Through detailed numerical simulations using this model, we explore the evolution of heavy quark distributions, energy loss mechanisms, and their interactions with the surrounding medium. This work contributes to the ongoing efforts to comprehend the properties of quark-gluon plasma and the behavior of heavy quarks within it. The methodology involves deriving the linearized Boltzmann-Langevin equation, incorporating fluctuation-dissipation theorems, and utilizing numerical techniques to analyze the transport properties of heavy quarks. Overall, our study provides a valuable framework for studying heavy quark dynamics in hot and dense QCD matter, shedding light on the intricate interplay between heavy quarks and their surrounding medium in high-energy nuclear collisions.

text: We report the confirmation of HAT-P-57b, a short-period giant planet transiting a bright A8V star through Doppler tomography. This approach, which utilizes radial velocity data to reconstruct the internal structure of a planet's atmosphere, has previously been applied to large gaseous planets orbiting Sun-like stars. However, the application to a shorter-period planet and a rapidly rotating host star presented unique challenges.    Using the HARPS spectrograph at the European Southern Observatory, we obtained high-resolution, high-precision radial velocity measurements. We then applied a tomographic inversion technique to reconstruct the three-dimensional velocity maps of the star. By cross-correlating the reconstructed velocity maps with a model spectrum, we were able to isolate the planetary signal and determine its transit parameters.    Our results show that HAT-P-57b is a short-period Jupiter-mass planet with a semi-major axis of 0.037 AU and an orbital period of 4.2 days. Its transit depth is 0.014%, and we estimate its equilibrium temperature to be around 1500 K. Our Doppler tomography analysis also reveals the presence of strong tidal heating in the planet's atmospheric layers, with temperature anomalies reaching up to 200 K. The rapid rotation rate of the host star, with a projected rotational velocity of 150 km/s, introduces complexities in the velocity maps and requires additional modeling to accurately account for the planetary signal.    These findings highlight the potential of Doppler tomography as a powerful tool for studying short-period giant planets transiting bright, rapidly rotating stars. By providing detailed information about the atmospheric properties and tidal heating of these planets, this approach can help us better understand the formation and evolution of planets in various orbital configurations.

text: Topic modeling has been an essential tool for text mining and information retrieval in various domains. However, its application to short and imbalanced texts remains a challenge due to the sparsity and uneven distribution of words. In response to this problem, we propose a simple yet effective approach based on the Word Network Topic Model (WNTM). WNTM is a graph-based model that considers words as nodes and connects them based on their co-occurrence relationships. By introducing a label propagation algorithm into WNTM, we address the issue of topic representation in short texts and the problem of topic imbalance in long texts.  We evaluate the performance of WNTM on several benchmark datasets, including short and long texts with various imbalance ratios. The experimental results show that WNTM outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in terms of topic coherence, diversity, and stability. Moreover, WNTM can handle both short and long texts, and it requires less computational resources compared to other models.  In summary, this paper presents the Word Network Topic Model as a simple yet effective solution for text modeling in the presence of short and imbalanced texts. WNTM provides promising results in terms of topic representation and can be applied to various domains, such as social media, news articles, and scientific documents.

text: The study investigates the chromospheric signatures associated with small-scale magnetic flux emergence, utilizing data from the New Solar Telescope (NST) and the Hinode satellite. Small-scale flux emergence events play a critical role in the dynamic processes of the solar atmosphere, notably influencing chromospheric heating and solar magnetic field evolution. The objective of this research is to delineate the chromospheric manifestations linked to these flux emergence activities and assess their contribution to solar phenomena. High-resolution observations from the NST, specifically using the H-alpha spectral line, in conjunction with Hinode’s Solar Optical Telescope magnetograms, enabled a detailed examination of evolving structures and magnetic field interactions in the solar chromosphere. The methodology involved cross-referencing changes in the magnetic flux with chromospheric features, such as bright points and fibril dynamics, to establish correlated behaviors. Key findings indicate that small-scale flux emergence events are characterized by distinct brightening in the chromosphere, accompanied by increased fibril activity and transient changes in magnetic field topology. Additionally, these emergent flux regions often facilitate localized heating and contribute significantly to the structuring of the chromospheric network. The conclusion drawn from the analysis suggests that small-scale flux emergence ubiquitously influences chromospheric features and should be considered a vital factor in models addressing chromospheric behavior and solar atmospheric dynamics. Understanding these signatures enhances our comprehension of energy transfer mechanisms in the solar atmosphere and aids in predicting the implications of magnetic flux emergence on larger solar events.

In this thesis we consider the free surface flow due to a submerged source in
a channel of finite depth. This problem has been considered previously in the
literature, with some disagreement about whether or not a train of waves exist
on the free surface for Froude numbers less than unity. The physical
assumptions behind the accepted model are clearly stated and governing
equations and boundary conditions derived. Complex variable theory is then
employed to obtain a singular nonlinear integral equation, which describes the
flow field completely.
  The integral equation is evaluated numerically using a collocation method,
and implemented with mathematical software {\em Matlab}. The numerical
solutions suggest that indeed waves do exist on the free surface, but are
exponentially small in the limit that the Froude number approaches zero. An
asymptotic expression is also derived to solve the integral equation, valid for
small Froude numbers. This expansion is calculated to second order, which
improves on the leading order solution given previously in the literature. Such
a scheme is unable to predict waves on the free surface, since they are
exponentially small. It is discussed how exponential asymptotics could be used
to derive a more accurate analytic solution that describes waves on the free
surface.

NGC7538 is a complex massive star-forming region. The region is composed of
several radio continuum sources, one of which is IRS1, a high-mass protostar,
from which a 0.3 pc molecular bipolar outflow was detected. Several maser
species have been detected around IRS1. The CH3OH masers have been suggested to
trace a Keplerian-disk, while the H2O masers are almost aligned to the outflow.
More recent results suggested that the region hosts a torus and potentially a
disk, but with a different inclination than the Keplerian-disk that is supposed
to be traced by the CH3OH masers. Tracing the magnetic field close to
protostars is fundamental for determining the orientation of the disk/torus.
Recent studies showed that during the protostellar phase of high-mass star
formation the magnetic field is oriented along the outflows and around or on
the surfaces of the disk/torus. The observations of polarized maser emissions
at milliarcsecond resolution can make a crucial contribution to understanding
the orientation of the magnetic field and, consequently, the orientation of the
disk/torus in NGC7538-IRS1. The NRAO Very Long Baseline Array was used to
measure the linear polarization and the Zeeman-splitting of the 22GHz H2O
masers toward NGC7538-IRS1. The European VLBI Network and the MERLIN telescopes
were used to measure the linear polarization and the Zeeman-splitting of the
6.7GHz CH3OH masers toward the same region. We detected 17 H2O masers and 49
CH3OH masers at high angular resolution. We detected linear polarization
emission toward two H2O masers and toward twenty CH3OH masers. The CH3OH
masers, most of which only show a core structure, seem to trace rotating and
potentially infalling gas in the inner part of a torus. Significant
Zeeman-splitting was measured in three CH3OH masers. [...] We also propose a
new description of the structure of the NGC7538-IRS1 maser region.

text: We present a comprehensive analysis of interatomic methods to compute dispersion energy using the Adiabatic Connection Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem (ACFDT). Our primary objective is to address the limitations of traditional computational approaches in accurately predicting non-local correlation effects in molecular systems. Through a systematic implementation of the ACFDT, we derive robust expressions that connect the dispersion energy to fluctuations in electronic density, enabling more precise predictions in various physical contexts.   Utilizing density functional theory as a foundational tool, we explore several computational strategies that enhance the efficiency and accuracy of dispersion energy calculations. By reformulating the fluctuation-dissipation formula, we demonstrate that our approach effectively encapsulates the contributions of long-range correlation interactions, which are often inadequately modeled in standard methodologies.   Our empirical results indicate that the ACFDT-based interatomic methods outperform conventional techniques, significantly reducing errors in dispersion energy estimates across diverse molecular configurations. We validate our findings against established benchmarks, revealing a marked improvement in both qualitative and quantitative terms.   Key concepts in our methodology include the integration of many-body perturbation theory with electronic structure calculations, along with a nuanced treatment of density fluctuations. This work not only advances the theoretical framework surrounding dispersion forces but also provides practical tools for researchers in computational chemistry and materials science. We conclude that the ACFDT presents a viable alternative to traditional models, offering enhanced predictive capability for dispersion-driven interactions in complex systems.

text: We examine the breakdown of finite-time and finite-population scalings of the large deviation function in the large-size limit of a contact process. Our study targets the underlying mechanisms influencing the large deviation properties of stochastic systems characterized by contact interactions among particles. Through a combination of numerical simulations and analytical techniques, we explore the asymptotic behavior of the large deviation function as system size approaches infinity, revealing critical deviations from traditional scaling predictions.   We implement systematic perturbation analysis to investigate how the finite-time dynamics interact with population size effects, thereby unveiling a more intricate relationship than previously understood. By constructing a comprehensive framework that merges theoretical predictions with empirical observations, we elucidate the conditions under which the large deviation function exhibits non-standard scaling behavior.  Our results indicate that as system size grows, the large deviation function yields significant corrections that challenge the conventional wisdom surrounding scaling laws in critical phenomena. We identify specific thresholds in population density that catalyze transitions in the large deviation statistics, leading to a reevaluation of the applicability of classical scaling relations for large contact processes. Our findings advance the understanding of fluctuation behavior in interacting particle systems and can have implications for various fields, including statistical mechanics, biological modeling, and ecological dynamics. We assert that refining our comprehension of these scaling breakdowns is crucial for predicting the systemic behaviors of large populations in the presence of stochastic interactions.

In the dynamical systems approach to describing turbulent or otherwise
chaotic flows, an important quantity is the Lyapunov exponents and vectors that
characterize the strange attractor of the flow. In particular, knowledge of the
Lyapunov exponents and vectors will help identify perturbations that the system
is most sensitive to, and quantify the dimension of the attractor. However,
reliably computing these Lyapunov quantities requires robust nu- merical
algorithms. While several perturbation-based techniques are available in
literature, their application to commonly used turbulent flow solvers as well
the numerical convergence properties have not been studied in detail. The goal
of this work is two-fold: a) develop a robust algorithm for obtaining Lyapunov
exponents and vectors for low-Mach based sim- ulation of turbulent flows, b)
quantify the spatial and temporal convergence properties of this algorithm
using a series of progressively complex flow problems. In particular, a manu-
factured solutions approach is devised using the Orr-Sommerfeld (OS)
perturbation theory to extract Lyapunov exponents and vectors from OS eigen
solutions. While individual test cases show interesting results, overall the
spatial convergence rates of Lyapunov exponents follow the truncation order for
the discretization scheme. However, temporal convergence rates were found to be
only a weak function of time step used. Additionally, for some config-
urations, the convergence properties are found to depend on the Lyapunov
exponent itself. These results indicate that convergence properties do not
follow universal rates, and require careful analysis for specific
configurations considered.

text: We present a comprehensive analysis of precision ephemerides for the binary system Sco X-1, a compact object merger candidate that is a prime target for gravitational-wave searches. Our work builds upon previous attempts to model the orbital evolution of Sco X-1, which have been hampered by uncertainties in the mass of the compact object and the eccentricity of the orbit. To address these limitations, we employ a novel approach that integrates a Bayesian inference framework with a detailed numerical simulation of the binary's orbital dynamics. Our results indicate that the mass of the compact object is consistent with a black hole, and the eccentricity of the orbit is significantly lower than previously estimated. By refining the ephemeris of Sco X-1, we provide a more accurate representation of the binary's orbital parameters, which is essential for the detection of gravitational waves from this system. Our analysis also highlights the importance of accounting for the effects of general relativity on the binary's orbit, which can significantly impact the accuracy of predictions. The precision ephemeris we provide will be invaluable for future gravitational-wave searches, allowing for more precise tests of general relativity and the characterization of compact object mergers.

text: This research explores the application of Bayesian nonparametric hierarchical modeling to effectively handle multiple membership data within grouped attendance interventions. Traditional analytical approaches often face challenges due to the complexity and structural hierarchy inherent in such data, particularly when individuals participate in multiple groups with varying levels of attendance. Our objective is to provide a flexible and robust modeling framework that captures both group-specific and individual-level variations without relying on strict parametric assumptions. The study employs a Dirichlet Process Mixture Model (DPMM) as the foundational Bayesian nonparametric method, enabling efficient handling of the heterogeneous and potentially non-normally distributed data. We introduce a hierarchical structure that accounts for shared membership across groups, allowing for more accurate inference of intervention effects. The model was validated using simulated datasets reflecting realistic attendance scenarios and further applied to actual data from educational interventions aimed at improving student participation. Key findings highlight the model's superior performance in identifying nuanced patterns of attendance and intervention outcomes, compared to conventional fixed or random-effects models. Moreover, the Bayesian framework facilitates uncertainty quantification and accommodates the dynamic nature of group memberships across interventions. The results underscore the advantages of employing a nonparametric approach for such complex datasets, offering insights into maximizing the efficacy of intervention programs. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the utility of Bayesian nonparametric hierarchical models in addressing the challenges of multiple membership data, opening avenues for more tailored and effective intervention strategies in various fields.

text: The detection of information sources within the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) model is critical for effective network management and epidemiology. This study aims to develop a robust methodology for pinpointing the original source of information spread using a sample path-based approach within the context of the SIR model. By leveraging the stochastic nature of the SIR process, we model the propagation of information as it moves through a network, accounting for dynamic interactions between nodes. Our methodology integrates probabilistic reasoning with sample path analysis, a technique that allows for detailed tracking of the diffusion process over time. Through extensive simulations on synthetic and real-world networks, the approach was tested against traditional statistical models. Key findings demonstrate that our sample path-based technique significantly improves the accuracy of source detection, boasting higher specificity and sensitivity compared to current heuristic-based methods. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness in varied network structures and under incomplete path data conditions, which often constrain traditional models. Conclusively, these results highlight the potential of sample path analysis to enhance information source detection, providing a valuable tool for epidemiologists and network analysts. Our findings suggest that adopting this approach can lead to more targeted interventions and improved understanding of information diffusion dynamics, ultimately contributing to more effective management of network information flows and containment strategies in epidemic scenarios.

We investigate a model for fatigue crack growth in which damage accumulation
is assumed to follow a power law of the local stress amplitude, a form which
can be generically justified on the grounds of the approximately self-similar
aspect of microcrack distributions. Our aim is to determine the relation
between model ingredients and the Paris exponent governing subcritical
crack-growth dynamics at the macroscopic scale, starting from a single small
notch propagating along a fixed line. By a series of analytical and numerical
calculations, we show that, in the absence of disorder, there is a critical
damage-accumulation exponent $\gamma$, namely $\gamma_c=2$, separating two
distinct regimes of behavior for the Paris exponent $m$. For $\gamma>\gamma_c$,
the Paris exponent is shown to assume the value $m=\gamma$, a result which
proves robust against the separate introduction of various modifying
ingredients. Explicitly, we deal here with (i) the requirement of a minimum
stress for damage to occur; (ii) the presence of disorder in local damage
thresholds; (iii) the possibility of crack healing. On the other hand, in the
regime $\gamma<\gamma_c$ the Paris exponent is seen to be sensitive to the
different ingredients added to the model, with rapid healing or a high minimum
stress for damage leading to $m=2$ for all $\gamma<\gamma_c$, in contrast with
the linear dependence $m=6-2\gamma$ observed for very long characteristic
healing times in the absence of a minimum stress for damage. Upon the
introduction of disorder on the local fatigue thresholds, which leads to the
possible appearance of multiple cracks along the propagation line, the Paris
exponent tends to $m\approx 4$ for $\gamma\lesssim 2$, while retaining the
behavior $m=\gamma$ for $\gamma\gtrsim 4$.

Let $(A,\Delta)$ be a multiplier Hopf algebra. In general, the underlying
algebra $A$ need not have an identity and the coproduct $\Delta$ does not map
$A$ into $A\otimes A$ but rather into its multiplier algebra $M(A\otimes A)$.
In this paper, we study {\it some tools} that are frequently used when dealing
with such multiplier Hopf algebras and that are typical for working with
algebras without identity in this context.
  The {\it basic ingredient} is a unital left $A$-module $X$. And the basic
construction is that of extending the module by looking at linear maps
$\rho:A\to X$ satisfying $\rho(aa')=a\rho(a')$ where $a,a'\in A$. We write the
module action as multiplication. Of course, when $x\in X$, and when
$\rho(a)=ax$, we get such a linear map. And if $A$ has an identity, all linear
maps $\rho$ have this form for $x=\rho(1)$. However, the point is that in the
case of a non-unital algebra, the space of such maps is in general strictly
bigger than $X$ itself. We get an {\it extended module}, denoted by $\bar X$
(for reasons that will be explained in the paper).
  We study all sorts of more complicated situations where such extended modules
occur and we illustrate all of this with {\it several examples}, from very
simple ones to more complex ones where iterated extensions come into play. We
refer to cases that appear in the literature.
  We use this basic idea of extending modules to explain, in a more rigorous
way, the so-called {\it covering technique}, which is needed when using {\it
Sweedler notations} for coproducts and coactions. Again, we give many examples
and refer to the existing literature where this technique is applied.

Vacuum stability in the Standard Model is problematic as the Higgs quartic
self-coupling runs negative at a renormalization scale of about $10^{10}$ GeV.
We consider a non-supersymmetric SO(10) grand unification model for which gauge
coupling unification is made possible through an intermediate scale gauge
group, $G_{\text{int}}=\text{SU}(3)_C\otimes \text{SU}(2)_L\otimes
\text{SU}(2)_R \otimes \text{U}(1)_{B-L}$. $G_{\text{int}}$ is broken by the
vacuum expectation value of a 126 of SO(10) which not only provides for
neutrino masses through the seesaw mechanism but also preserves a discrete
$\mathbb{Z}_2$ that can account for the stability of a dark matter candidate,
here taken to be the Standard Model singlet component of a bosonic 16. We show
that in addition to these features the model insures the positivity of the
Higgs quartic coupling through its interactions to the dark matter multiplet
and 126. We also show that the Higgs mass squared runs negative triggering
electroweak symmetry breaking. Thus, the vacuum stability is achieved along
with radiative electroweak symmetry breaking and captures two more important
elements of supersymmetric models without low-energy supersymmetry. The
conditions for perturbativity of quartic couplings and for radiative
electroweak symmetry breaking lead to tight upper and lower limits on the dark
matter mass, respectively, and this dark matter mass region (1.35-2 TeV) can be
probed in future direct detection experiments.

text: This study investigates turbulent magnetic reconnection in both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) configurations to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of energy dissipation and particle acceleration. In the 2D simulations, we observe the formation of current sheets and the subsequent development of turbulence, which is characterized by intermittent bursts of energy release and enhanced particle fluxes across the reconnection region. In contrast, the 3D simulations reveal more complex structures, including filamentation of the current sheet and the emergence of vortical features, indicating that the spatial dimension significantly influences the reconnection process. Key methodologies include adaptive mesh refinement techniques to capture fine-scale phenomena accurately and sophisticated data analysis tools to quantify the energetic and particle properties of the reconnection event. The results suggest that the transition from 2D to 3D can lead to increased complexity and efficiency in the conversion of magnetic energy into kinetic energy, providing insights into solar flares and other astrophysical phenomena where turbulence plays a crucial role.

text: In the pursuit of enhancing the performance and sensitivity of the ATLAS Insertable B-Layer (IBL) upgrades, this study explores the development and characterization of new hybrid pixel module concepts. These novel modules are designed to combine the advantages of SiPM (Silicon Photomultiplier) and Sensors-on-Silicon (SoS) technologies. The proposed design features a monolithic integration of an SoS sensor with an SiPM array. The main objective is to minimize the radiation length and improve the electronics efficiency.  The fabrication and testing of prototype modules were carried out at the CERN Hightech Materials Laboratory (HTML). The results demonstrate that the hybrid module design reduces the overall active volume, leading to a significant decrease in the energy loss caused by ionizing radiation. Furthermore, the data obtained from test beam experiments and Monte Carlo simulations reveal that the integration of the SiPM array increases the charge collection efficiency and reduces the capacitance of the sensor.  The evaluation of various design alternatives, such as different SiPM arrays, was performed through comprehensive simulations to assess their potential impact on performance and cost. The findings indicate that the proposed hybrid module concept is a promising solution for the IBL upgrade, outperforming the conventional SiPM-only modules in terms of radiation tolerance and electrical efficiency.  This study highlights the importance of combining advanced sensor technologies in order to overcome the limitations of current modules and achieve better performance in the harsh radiation environment of the ATLAS experiment. Future work includes the optimization and characterization of fully integrated modules and their implementation in the ATLAS IBL upgrades.

We use the semi-analytical model of galaxy formation GALFORM to characterise
an indirect signature of AGN feedback in the environment of radio galaxies at
high redshifts. The predicted environment of radio galaxies is denser than that
of radio-quiet galaxies with the same stellar mass. This is consistent with
observational results from the CARLA survey. Our model shows that the
differences in environment are due to radio galaxies being hosted by dark
matter haloes that are ~1.5 dex more massive than those hosting radio-quiet
galaxies with the same stellar mass. By running a control-simulation in which
AGN feedback is switched-off, we identify AGN feedback as the primary mechanism
affecting the build-up of the stellar component of radio galaxies, thus
explaining the different environment in radio galaxies and their radio-quiet
counterparts. The difference in host halo mass between radio loud and radio
quiet galaxies translates into different galaxies populating each environment.
We predict a higher fraction of passive galaxies around radio loud galaxies
compared to their radio-quiet counterparts. Furthermore, such a high fraction
of passive galaxies shapes the predicted infrared luminosity function in the
environment of radio galaxies in a way that is consistent with observational
findings. Our results suggest that the impact of AGN feedback at high redshifts
and environmental mechanisms affecting galaxies in high halo masses can be
revealed by studying the environment of radio galaxies, thus providing new
constraints on galaxy formation physics at high redshifts.

Traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) typically use the same
activation function (usually ReLU) for all neurons with non-linear mapping
operations. For example, the deep convolutional architecture Inception-v4 uses
ReLU. To improve the classification performance of traditional CNNs, a new
"Multi-function Convolutional Neural Network" (MCNN) is created by using
different activation functions for different neurons. For $n$ neurons and $m$
different activation functions, there are a total of $m^n-m$ MCNNs and only $m$
traditional CNNs. Therefore, the best model is very likely to be chosen from
MCNNs because there are $m^n-2m$ more MCNNs than traditional CNNs. For
performance analysis, two different datasets for two applications (classifying
handwritten digits from the MNIST database and classifying brain MRI images
into one of the four stages of Alzheimer's disease (AD)) are used. For both
applications, an activation function is randomly selected for each layer of a
MCNN. For the AD diagnosis application, MCNNs using a newly created
multi-function Inception-v4 architecture are constructed. Overall, simulations
show that MCNNs can outperform traditional CNNs in terms of multi-class
classification accuracy for both applications. An important future research
work will be to efficiently select the best MCNN from $m^n-m$ candidate MCNNs.
Current CNN software only provides users with partial functionality of MCNNs
since different layers can use different activation functions but not
individual neurons in the same layer. Thus, modifying current CNN software
systems such as ResNets, DenseNets, and Dual Path Networks by using multiple
activation functions and developing more effective and faster MCNN software
systems and tools would be very useful to solve difficult practical image
classification problems.

In this paper we consider a network of agents monitoring a spatially
distributed arrival process. Each node measures the number of arrivals seen at
its monitoring point in a given time-interval with the objective of estimating
the unknown local arrival rate. We propose an asynchronous distributed approach
based on a Bayesian model with unknown hyperparameter, where each node computes
the minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimator of its local arrival rate in a
distributed way. As a result, the estimation at each node "optimally" fuses the
information from the whole network through a distributed optimization
algorithm. Moreover, we propose an ad-hoc distributed estimator, based on a
consensus algorithm for time-varying and directed graphs, which exhibits
reduced complexity and exponential convergence. We analyze the performance of
the proposed distributed estimators, showing that they: (i) are reliable even
in presence of limited local data, and (ii) improve the estimation accuracy
compared to the purely decentralized setup. Finally, we provide a statistical
characterization of the proposed estimators. In particular, for the ad-hoc
estimator, we show that as the number of nodes goes to infinity its mean square
error converges to the optimal one. Numerical Monte Carlo simulations confirm
the theoretical characterization and highlight the appealing performances of
the estimators.

text: This research proposes a robust time-domain beam alignment scheme specifically tailored for multi-user wideband millimeter wave (mmWave) systems. In the context of mmWave communications, which face significant challenges such as high channel dispersion and interference from multipath propagation, effective beam alignment is crucial for improving spectral efficiency and reducing interference among multiple users. The objective of this study is to develop a novel beam alignment technique that can adaptively adjust beamforming weights in real-time to optimize signal transmission across multiple users.  The proposed method utilizes a combination of channel state information feedback (CISF) and iterative algorithms to estimate channel responses accurately. It employs a time-domain approach to align beams by iteratively updating beamforming vectors based on received data symbols, ensuring that the alignment process is efficient and robust against channel variations. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly enhances the throughput and reliability of multi-user mmWave communication systems compared to existing methods, particularly in scenarios with high user density and complex channel conditions.  In conclusion, this research presents a robust and adaptive beam alignment scheme that addresses the unique challenges posed by mmWave systems. The proposed method offers improved performance in terms of data rate and interference mitigation, making it a valuable contribution to the field of mmWave communications.

Methylammonium lead iodide (CH3NH3PbI3) perovskite solar cell has produced a
remarkable breakthrough in the photovoltaic history of solar cell technology
because of its outstanding device based performance as a light-harvesting
semiconductor. Whereas the experimental and theoretical studies of this system
in the solid state have been numerously reported in the last 4 years, its
fundamental cluster physics is yet to be exploited. To this end, this study has
performed theoretical investigations using DFT-M06-2X/ADZP to examine the
principal geometrical, electronic, topological, and orbital properties of the
CH3NH3PbI3 nanocluster blocks. These clusters are found to be unusually
strongly bound, with binding energies lying between 93.53 and 125.11 kcal mol-1
(beyond the covalent limit, 40 kcal mol-1), enabling us to characterize the
underlying interactions as ultra-strong type. Based on this, together with the
unusually high charge transfers, strong hyperconjugative interactions,
sophisticated topologies of the charge density, and short intermolecular
distances uncovered, we have characterized the CH3NH3PbI3 as Mulliken inner
complexes. Additionally, the consequences of these, as well as of the
ultra-strong interactions, in designing novel functional nanomaterials are
briefly discussed. The various new results obtained in this study are not in
perfect agreement with those already reported experimentally (Nat. Commun.
2015, 6, 7124), and computationally (Chem. Commun., 2015, 51, 6434; Sci. Rep.
2016, doi:10.1038/srep21687; Chem. Mater. 2016, 28, 4259; J. Mat. Chem A 2016,
4, 4728; J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2016, 7, 1596).

text: We present in this study an approach to constructing multi-skill collaborative teams based on the densest subgraphs in social networks. The team formation problem is essential in organizations, and conventional methods of team selection, such as random selection or self-selection, do not consider the skills and connections between team members adequately. Our methodology seeks to maximize the number of skills represented in a team while minimizing the redundancy and ensuring effective communication. We first introduce the concept of the densest subgraph and describe its computational properties. We then present an algorithm to identify the densest subgraphs in a given social network. Next, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing the results of teams formed based on our method with those formed using conventional methods. Our findings suggest that teams formed based on our approach perform better in terms of overall skill diversity and communication efficiency. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our approach for organizations and propose directions for future research, including the integration of our approach with machine learning algorithms and its application to larger and more complex networks. Overall, our approach provides a valuable addition to the literature on team formation and network analysis, and we believe it can significantly improve the performance of organizations by enhancing the effectiveness of their collaborative teams. The team formation problem in organizations is crucial, and traditional methods, such as random and self-selection, do not optimally consider skills and connections among team members. This research proposes a methodology to construct multi-skill collaborative teams based on the densest subgraphs in social networks, maximizing skill representation and minimizing redundancy while ensuring effective communication. The densest subgraph concept, computational properties, and identification algorithm are introduced, and team performance comparisons with conventional methods show better skill diversity and communication efficiency. Future research includes machine learning integration and application to larger, complex networks. Our approach contributes significantly to team formation and network analysis literature.

Nowadays, huge amount of documents are increasingly transferred to the remote
servers due to the appealing features of cloud computing. On the other hand,
privacy and security of the sensitive information in untrusted cloud
environment is a big concern. To alleviate such concerns, encryption of
sensitive data before its transfer to the cloud has become an important risk
mitigation option. Encrypted storage provides protection at the expense of a
significant increase in the data management complexity. For effective
management, it is critical to provide efficient selective document retrieval
capability on the encrypted collection. In fact, considerable amount of
searchable symmetric encryption schemes have been designed in the literature to
achieve this task. However, with the emergence of big data everywhere,
available approaches are insufficient to address some crucial real-world
problems such as scalability.
  In this study, we focus on practical aspects of a secure keyword search
mechanism over encrypted data on a real cloud infrastructure. First, we propose
a provably secure distributed index along with a parallelizable retrieval
technique that can easily scale to big data. Second, we integrate authorization
into the search scheme to limit the information leakage in multi-user setting
where users are allowed to access only particular documents. Third, we offer
efficient updates on the distributed secure index. In addition, we conduct
extensive empirical analysis on a real dataset to illustrate the efficiency of
the proposed practical techniques.

The functions and elasticities of the cell are largely related to the
structures of the cytoskeletons underlying the lipid bi-layer. Among various
cell types, the Red Blood Cell (RBC) possesses a relatively simple cytoskeletal
structure. Underneath the membrane, the RBC cytoskeleton takes the form of a
two dimensional triangular network, consisting of nodes of actins (and other
proteins) and edges of spectrins. Recent experiments focusing on the malaria
infected RBCs (iRBCs) showed that there is a correlation between the elongation
of spectrins in the cytoskeletal network and the stiffening of the iRBCs. Here
we rationalize the correlation between these two observations by combining the
worm-like chain (WLC) model for single spectrins and the Effective Medium
Theory (EMT) for the network elasticity. We specifically focus on how the
disorders in the cytoskeletal network affect its macroscopic elasticity.
Analytical and numerical solutions from our model reveal that the stiffness of
the membrane increases with increasing end-to-end distances of spectrins, but
has a non-monotonic dependence on the variance of the end-to-end distance
distributions. These predictions are verified quantitively by our AFM and
micropipette aspiration measurements of iRBCs. The model may, from a molecular
level, provide guidelines for future identification of new treatment methods
for RBC related diseases, such as malaria infection.

text: Cette recherche explore l'identité professionnelle des enseignants universitaires en physique, en tant que levier potentiel pour initier des changements dans les pratiques pédagogiques. L'objectif principal est de comprendre comment l'identité des enseignants influence leurs méthodes d'enseignement et leur engagement dans l'innovation pédagogique. Pour ce faire, nous avons mené une étude qualitative à travers des entretiens semi-structurés avec des enseignants de différentes universités. Les données recueillies ont été analysées en utilisant une approche thématique, permettant de dégager des motifs récurrents et des perspectives variées sur l'identité professionnelle.   Les résultats montrent que l'identité des enseignants est profondément liée à leur parcours académique, à leurs valeurs et à leurs interactions avec les étudiants et les pairs. Il apparaît que les enseignants qui se perçoivent comme des agents de changement sont plus enclins à adopter des pratiques pédagogiques innovantes, alors que ceux qui se conforment à des modèles traditionnels ont tendance à maintenir des pratiques plus conventionnelles.   En conclusion, cette étude met en lumière l'importance de l'identité professionnelle dans la transformation des pratiques pédagogiques dans l'enseignement de la physique. Elle suggère que des initiatives de développement professionnel, axées sur la redéfinition de cette identité, pourraient favoriser une plus grande ouverture aux méthodes d'enseignement novatrices, contribuant ainsi à améliorer l'expérience d'apprentissage des étudiants.

We analyse the velocity dispersion properties of 472 z~0.9 star-forming
galaxies observed as part of the KMOS Redshift One Spectroscopic Survey
(KROSS). The majority of this sample is rotationally dominated (83 +/- 5% with
v_C/sigma_0 > 1) but also dynamically hot and highly turbulent. After
correcting for beam smearing effects, the median intrinsic velocity dispersion
for the final sample is sigma_0 = 43.2 +/- 0.8 km/s with a rotational velocity
to dispersion ratio of v_C/sigma_0 = 2.6 +/- 0.1. To explore the relationship
between velocity dispersion, stellar mass, star formation rate and redshift we
combine KROSS with data from the SAMI survey (z~0.05) and an intermediate
redshift MUSE sample (z~0.5). While there is, at most, a weak trend between
velocity dispersion and stellar mass, at fixed mass there is a strong increase
with redshift. At all redshifts, galaxies appear to follow the same weak trend
of increasing velocity dispersion with star formation rate. Our results are
consistent with an evolution of galaxy dynamics driven by disks that are more
gas rich, and increasingly gravitationally unstable, as a function of
increasing redshift. Finally, we test two analytic models that predict
turbulence is driven by either gravitational instabilities or stellar feedback.
Both provide an adequate description of the data, and further observations are
required to rule out either model.

text: Upon applying a magnetic field to a one-dimensional Mott insulator, we observed a sudden expansion of the insulator's charge and spin sectors. This phenomenon was accompanied by a transition from a gapped to a gapless state and the emergence of massless excitations. The expansion occurred for a specific range of magnetic fields and temperatures, highlighting the importance of tuning these parameters.  Our experimental data was analyzed using density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations, revealing the underlying microscopic mechanism responsible for the sudden expansion. We found that the application of a magnetic field resulted in a significant decrease in the exchange interaction between neighboring sites in the system, which in turn led to a destabilization of the Mott gap and the onset of charge and spin fluctuation.  Theoretical analyses using the strong coupling Hubbard model and the dynamic mean-field theory further supported our experimental findings. These analyses provided insights into the underlying physics of the system, including the role of collective excitations and quantum fluctuations in the sudden expansion.  Our work sheds light on the previously unexplored regime of Mott insulators in one dimension and offers a new perspective on the interplay between magnetism, charge transport, and quantum fluctuations in low-dimensional systems. The results have important implications for the design and optimization of materials with tunable conductivity and novel emergent properties, particularly in the context of spintronics and quantum computing applications.
