text: This research focuses on investigating the temporal evolution of the emission spectrum in a steeply rising submillimeter burst. Submillimeter bursts are important phenomena in astrophysics, often associated with energetic events such as solar flares and magnetar bursts. Understanding the evolution of emission spectra during these bursts can provide valuable insights into the underlying physical processes.   The main objective of this study is to analyze the changes in the emission spectrum over time during a steeply rising submillimeter burst. By doing so, we aim to unravel the mechanisms responsible for the observed emission and gain a better understanding of the burst dynamics.   To achieve our objective, we utilize observational data from submillimeter telescopes combined with data analysis techniques to track the evolution of the emission spectrum. We apply sophisticated modeling tools to interpret the observed spectral changes and relate them to the physical conditions in the burst environment.   Our analysis reveals significant variations in the emission spectrum during the steep rise of the submillimeter burst. We observe pronounced shifts in spectral features and intensities, indicating complex processes at play. The temporal evolution of the emission spectrum provides crucial clues about the energy release mechanisms and the properties of the emitting plasma.   In conclusion, this study sheds light on the temporal behavior of emission spectra in steeply rising submillimeter bursts. The findings enhance our knowledge of the physics underlying these energetic events and pave the way for further investigations into the nature of submillimeter bursts.

text:
Cyanogen (NCCN) is the simplest member of the series of dicyanopolyynes. It
has been hypothesized that this family of molecules can be important
constituents of interstellar and circumstellar media, although the lack of a
permanent electric dipole moment prevents its detection through
radioastronomical techniques. Here we present the first solid evidence of the
presence of cyanogen in interstellar clouds through the detection of its
protonated form toward the cold dark clouds TMC-1 and L483. Protonated cyanogen
(NCCNH+) has been identified through the J=5-4 and J=10-9 rotational
transitions using the 40m radiotelescope of Yebes and the IRAM 30m telescope.
We derive beam averaged column densities for NCCNH+ of (8.6+/-4.4)e10 cm-2 in
TMC-1 and (3.9+/-1.8)e10 cm-2 in L483, which translate to fairly low fractional
abundances relative to H2, in the range (1-10)e-12. The chemistry of protonated
molecules in dark clouds is discussed, and it is found that, in general terms,
the abundance ratio between the protonated and non protonated forms of a
molecule increases with increasing proton affinity. Our chemical model predicts
an abundance ratio NCCNH+/NCCN of 1e-4, which implies that the abundance of
cyanogen in dark clouds could be as high as (1-10)e-8 relative to H2, i.e.,
comparable to that of other abundant nitriles such as HCN, HNC, and HC3N.

text: The abstract focuses on a method designed to address mode mixing, a common issue encountered during the Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) process, which can degrade the quality and interpretability of decomposed components. Mode mixing occurs when multiple intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) are erroneously grouped together, complicating the analysis of complex signals. This study proposes a novel approach aimed at separating these mixed modes effectively. The methodology involves a two-step iterative procedure that first identifies candidate IMFs based on their frequency content, followed by a filtering step that uses a median filter to separate closely spaced IMFs. Key findings demonstrate significant improvements in signal clarity and accuracy of IMF separation compared to conventional EMD techniques. The proposed method enhances the reliability and utility of EMD in various applications such as biomedical signal processing, geophysical data analysis, and financial time series forecasting. The conclusion emphasizes the practical implications of this work, highlighting its potential to facilitate more accurate decomposition and interpretation of complex signals.
label: machine

text: We present a study on the unexpectedly low lattice thermal conductivity (LTC) of the simple layered compound BaNiS2, an unlikely candidate given its constituent small atoms. This discovery sheds light on the role of phonon scattering in materials with complex crystal structures.     In order to understand the LTC mechanism in BaNiS2, we employed a combination of density functional theory calculations and experimental measurements. Our calculations revealed the presence of strong phonon anomalies, particularly near the M point in the Brillouin zone. These anomalies were attributed to the interaction of Ba and Ni atoms with the sulfur vacancies, leading to a significant reduction in the phonon mean free path.     Our experimental measurements of LTC were performed using the time-domain thermoreflectance technique. The results showed excellent agreement with our theoretical predictions, providing strong evidence for the phonon scattering mechanism. Furthermore, the low LTC value was found to be consistent with the observed high electrical conductivity, suggesting a synergetic effect between charge carriers and phonons.     The study of BaNiS2 thus provides a valuable case study for understanding the role of small atoms in determining LTC in complex materials. Our findings offer insights into the design of new materials with tailored thermal properties and highlight the importance of considering unexpected candidates in materials research.     Future work will focus on investigating the effect of different atomic arrangements and doping on the LTC of BaNiS2 and related compounds. This research will contribute to the development of materials with superior thermal conductivity for various applications, such as thermoelectric energy conversion and cooling technologies.

text:
Supernovae are the most powerful cosmic sources of MeV neutrinos. These
elementary particles play a crucial role when the evolution of a massive star
is terminated by the collapse of its core to a neutron star or a black hole and
the star explodes as supernova. The release of electron neutrinos, which are
abundantly produced by electron captures, accelerates the catastrophic infall
and causes a gradual neutronization of the stellar plasma by converting protons
to neutrons as dominant constituents of neutron star matter. The emission of
neutrinos and antineutrinos of all flavors carries away the gravitational
binding energy of the compact remnant and drives its evolution from the hot
initial to the cold final state. The absorption of electron neutrinos and
antineutrinos in the surroundings of the newly formed neutron star can power
the supernova explosion and determines the conditions in the innermost
supernova ejecta, making them an interesting site for the nucleosynthesis of
iron-group elements and trans-iron nuclei. In this Chapter the basic neutrino
physics in supernova cores and nascent neutron stars will be discussed. This
includes the most relevant neutrino production, absorption, and scattering
processes, elementary aspects of neutrino transport in dense environments, the
characteristic neutrino emission phases with their typical signal features, and
the perspectives connected to a measurement of the neutrino signal from a
future galactic supernova.

We present optical integral field unit (IFU) observations of two gas pillars
surrounding the Galactic young massive star cluster NGC 3603. The high S/N and
spectral resolution of these data have allowed us to accurately quantify the
H-alpha, [NII] and [SII] emission line shapes, and we find a mixture of broad
(FWHM~70-100 km/s) and narrow (<50 km/s) components. The broad components are
found close to the edges of both pillars, suggesting that they originate in
turbulent mixing layers (TMLs) driven by the effect of the star cluster wind.
Both pillars exhibit surprisingly high ionized gas densities of >10000 cm-3. In
one pillar we found that these high densities are only found in the narrow
component, implying it must originate from deeper within the pillar than the
broad component. From this, together with our kinematical data, we conclude
that the narrow component traces a photoevaporation flow, and that the TML
forms at the interface with the hot wind. On the pillar surfaces we find a
consistent offset in radial velocity between the narrow (brighter) components
of H-alpha and [NII] of ~5-8 km/s, for which we were unable to find a
satisfactory explanation. We urge the theoretical community to simulate
mechanical and radiative cloud interactions in more detail to address the many
unanswered questions raised by this study.

text: In this study, we design and optimize a three-dimensional photonic band gap (PBG) cavity within a diamond-like inverse woodpile photonic crystal, aiming to enhance light confinement and control at the nanoscale. We address the problem of achieving strong localization of light in three-dimensional photonic structures, essential for applications in quantum computing and advanced photonic devices. Utilizing a systematic design methodology, we incorporate finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations to model and analyze the electromagnetic responses of the photonic crystal. Our results demonstrate that the optimization of structural parameters, including the geometry and refractive index contrast, leads to enhanced photonic band gaps and high-quality factors. We achieve a cavity design exhibiting a significant PBG centered around infrared wavelengths, with a calculated quality factor exceeding 10,000 and a mode volume approximating one cubic wavelength. A detailed parametric analysis reveals the impact of key parameters, such as rod positioning and filling fraction, on the band gap properties and mode confinement. The study further investigates the robustness of the PBG against structural perturbations, confirming the design’s resilience in practical implementations. Our findings advance the understanding of 3D photonic crystal cavities, offering a blueprint for harnessing diamond-like inverse woodpile structures to facilitate advancements in photonic integration, nonlinear optics, and on-chip photonic circuits. This research sets a foundational framework for future explorations into photonic crystal cavities with vast implications for both theoretical and practical innovations in optical science.

text: This study investigates the inelastic electron scattering and Raman scattering from collective excitations in quantum wires under zero magnetic field conditions. Quantum wires have garnered significant attention due to their unique one-dimensional properties and potential applications in nano-electronics and quantum computing. The primary objective of this research is to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the scattering processes and the resulting collective excitations. Utilizing a combination of theoretical models and numerical simulations, we analyze electron interactions and their influence on the energy levels of collective modes in the wire. Our findings reveal distinct signatures of inelastic scattering that correspond to various collective excitations, such as plasmons and phonons, providing a comprehensive view of their dynamical behavior. The simulations also demonstrate how the wire's geometrical parameters affect the scattering rates and the excitation spectrum. Notably, we identify the conditions under which collective excitations are enhanced due to electron scattering, contributing to a better understanding of electron correlations in low-dimensional systems. In conclusion, this research not only advances the theoretical framework for interpreting inelastic scattering phenomena in quantum wires but also paves the way for future experimental investigations aimed at probing the intricate relationships between electronic properties and collective excitations at zero magnetic field. Our results highlight the significance of tailoring quantum wire architectures to optimize scattering processes for potential applications in advanced materials and devices.

We investigate the alignment of haloes with the filaments of the cosmic web
using an unprecedently large sample of dark matter haloes taken from the
P-Millennium $\Lambda$CDM cosmological N-body simulation. We use the
state-of-the-art NEXUS morphological formalism which, due to its multiscale
nature, simultaneously identifies structures at all scales. We find strong and
highly significant alignments, with both the major axis of haloes and their
peculiar velocity tending to orient along the filament. However, the spin -
filament alignment displays a more complex trend changing from preferentially
parallel at low masses to preferentially perpendicular at high masses. This
"spin flip" occurs at an average mass of $5\times10^{11}~h^{-1}M_\odot$. This
mass increases with increasing filament diameter, varying by more than an order
of magnitude between the thinnest and thickest filament samples. We also find
that the inner parts of haloes have a spin flip mass that is several times
smaller than that of the halo as a whole. These results confirm that recent
accretion is responsible for the complex behaviour of the halo spin - filament
alignment. Low-mass haloes mainly accrete mass along directions perpendicular
to their host filament and thus their spins tend to be oriented along the
filaments. In contrast, high-mass haloes mainly accrete along their host
filaments and have their spins preferentially perpendicular to them.
Furthermore, haloes located in thinner filaments are more likely to accrete
along their host filaments than haloes of the same mass located in thicker
filaments.

text:
Physics is not just mathematics. This seems trivial, but poses difficult and
interesting questions. In this paper we analyse a particular discrepancy
between non-relativistic quantum mechanics (QM) and `classical' (Newtonian)
space and time (NST). We also suggest, but not discuss, the case of the
relativistic QM. In this work, we are more concerned with the notion of space
and its mathematical representation. The mathematics entails that any two
spatially separated objects are necessarily \ita{different}, which implies that
they are \ita{discernible} (in classical logic, identity is defined by means of
indiscernibility) --- we say that the space is $T_2$, or "Hausdorff". But when
enters QM, sometimes the systems need to be taken as \ita{completely
indistinguishable}, so that there is no way to tell which system is which, and
this holds even in the case of fermions. But in the NST setting, it seems that
we can always give an \ita{identity} to them by means of their individuation,
which seems to be contra the physical situation, where individuation
(isolation) does not entail identity (as we argue in this paper). Here we
discuss this topic by considering a case study (that of two potentially
infinite wells) and conclude that, taking into account the quantum case, that
is, when physics enter the discussion, even NST cannot be used to say that the
systems do have identity. This case study seems to be relevant for a more
detailed discussion on the interplay between physical theories (such as quantum
theory) and their underlying mathematics (and logic), in a simple way
apparently never realized before.
label: human

text: This study investigates the impact of viscoelasticity on droplet formation in microfluidic cross-junctions using the Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM). The research is motivated by the importance of understanding the behavior of non-Newtonian fluids in microfluidic systems, which have potential applications in various fields such as lab-on-a-chip devices and biotechnology.  The primary objective of this study is to explore the influence of viscoelasticity on droplet formation by comparing the results of simulations using Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids. To achieve this, we modeled a T-junction microfluidic device using the LBM, applying a pressure difference between the inlet and outlet channels.  The key findings of this study reveal that the addition of viscoelasticity significantly alters the droplet formation dynamics in the T-junction. Compared to Newtonian fluids, non-Newtonian fluids exhibit larger droplet size, longer formation time, and a more complex flow pattern. These observations can be attributed to the elastic component of the non-Newtonian fluid, which leads to a higher viscous stress and a delayed response to the applied pressure difference.  In conclusion, this research provides valuable insights into the influence of viscoelasticity on droplet formation in microfluidic cross-junctions using the Lattice Boltzmann Method. The results of this study have potential applications in the design and optimization of microfluidic systems involving non-Newtonian fluids. Further investigation is encouraged to explore the impact of various non-Newtonian flow models and other geometries on droplet formation dynamics.
label: machine

text: We present a novel theoretical framework and experimental protocol to demonstrate genuine multipartite entanglement and nonseparability in quantum systems absent of shared reference frames. Our work addresses the critical problem of reference frame-dependent limitations in the validation of multipartite quantum entanglement, a cornerstone in quantum information processing and quantum communications. By leveraging a robust approach built on invariants derived from permutation symmetry and local operations, we circumvent the need for a common reference frame, thereby expanding the operational applicability of quantum protocols in unconstrained environments. Our methodological development utilizes advanced entropic inequalities and graph theoretic constructs to identify and certify multipartite quantum states with genuine entanglement properties. Our results demonstrate, through both simulated and experimental data, that multipartite entangled states maintain their entanglement structure independent of any external reference alignments, thus providing a more flexible and reliable metric for entanglement validation. We further substantiate our findings through experimental implementation using photonic qubits undergoing rotations in Hilbert space, demonstrating persistent nonseparability despite arbitrary local operations. In dynamical systems with divided phase space, the vicinity of the boundary
between regular and chaotic regions is often "sticky," that is, trapping orbits
from the chaotic region for long times. Here, we investigate the stickiness in
the simplest mushroom billiard, which has a smooth such boundary, but
surprisingly subtle behaviour. As a measure of stickiness, we investigate P(t),
the probability of remaining in the mushroom cap for at least time t given
uniform initial conditions in the chaotic part of the cap. The stickiness is
sensitively dependent on the radius of the stem r via the Diophantine
properties of rho = (2/\pi) arccos r. Almost all rho give rise to families of
marginally unstable periodic orbits (MUPOs) where P(t) ~ C/t, dominating the
stickiness of the boundary. Here we consider the case where rho is MUPO-free
and has continued fraction expansion with bounded partial quotients. We show
that t^2 P(t) is bounded, varying infinitely often between values whose ratio
is at least 32/27. When rho has an eventually periodic continued fraction
expansion, that is, a quadratic irrational, t^2 P(t) converges to a
log-periodic function. In general, we expect less regular behaviour, with upper
and lower exponents lying between 1 and 2. The results may shed light on the
parameter dependence of boundary stickiness in annular billiards and generic
area preserving maps.

text: We present the results of Spitzer Space Telescope spectroscopic observations of the Kepler's Supernova Remnant (KSNR), a Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) that exploded in 1604. Our analysis focuses on the dust features identified in the infrared spectra and their implications for the progenitor system of SN Ia explosions.     We detected silicon and magnesium oxides, forsterite, and olivine in the spectra, indicating the presence of silicate grains. We also detected complex organic molecules such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and silicon carbide (SiC) grains. The detected dust features are consistent with those observed in other SN Ia remnants and suggest that a substantial dust component is present during the early phases of SN Ia explosions.     The presence of silicate grains indicates that the progenitor star had a wind-driven, mass-losing, carbon-oxygen white dwarf (CO WD) in its late stages. The detection of PAHs and SiC grains suggests the presence of a hydrogen-rich circumstellar medium (CSM) around the WD. The combined mass of the identified silicates, PAHs, and SiC grains is estimated to be ~0.02 solar masses (M☉).     Our results indicate that a substantial amount of dust is produced during the early phases of SN Ia explosions, challenging the traditional paradigm of SN Ia progenitors being dust-free. Furthermore, our findings provide important constraints on the properties of the progenitor system, including the CSM composition and the mass-loss rate in the years leading up to the explosion. The Spitzer observations of KSNR provide valuable insights into the dust and circumstellar environment of SN Ia progenitors, which is crucial for understanding the physics of these important astrophysical events.     In summary, our Spitzer spectroscopic observations of the Kepler's Supernova Remnant reveal the presence of a substantial dust component, including silicate grains, complex organic molecules, and silicon carbide, during the early phases of a SN Ia explosion. These findings challenge the traditional view of SN Ia progenitors being dust-free and provide important constraints on the progenitor system, including the CSM composition and mass-loss rate.

We assess the systematic uncertainties in stellar evolutionary calculations
for low- to intermediate-mass, main-sequence stars. We compare published
stellar tracks from several different evolution codes with our own tracks
computed using the stellar codes STARS and MESA. In particular, we focus on
tracks of 1 and 3 solar masses at solar metallicity. We find that the spread in
the available 1 solar mass tracks (computed before the recent solar composition
revision by Asplund et al.) can be covered by tracks between 0.97-1.01 solar
masses computed with the STARS code. We assess some possible causes of the
origin of this uncertainty, including how the choice of input physics and the
solar constraints used to perform the solar calibration affect the tracks. We
find that for a 1 solar mass track, uncertainties of around 10% in the initial
hydrogen abundance and initial metallicity produce around a 2% error in mass.
For the 3 solar mass tracks, there is very little difference between the tracks
from the various different stellar codes. The main difference comes in the
extent of the main sequence, which we believe results from the different
choices of the implementation of convective overshooting in the core.
Uncertainties in the initial abundances lead to a 1-2% error in the mass
determination. These uncertainties cover only part of the total error budget,
which should also include uncertainties in the input physics (e.g., reaction
rates, opacities, convective models) and any missing physics (e.g., radiative
levitation, rotation, magnetic fields). Uncertainties in stellar surface
properties such as luminosity and effective temperature will further reduce the
accuracy of any potential mass determinations.

(BHC) MAXI~J1543-564 using the RXTE data. We use Two-Component Advective Flow
(TCAF) solution to fit the data of the very initial rising phase of outburst
(from 2011 May 10 to 2011 May 15). $2.5-25$~keV spectra are fitted using the
TCAF solution {\it fits} file as a local additive table model in XSPEC. We
extract physical flow parameters such as the two component (Keplerian disk and
sub-Keplerian halo) accretion rates and size and the property of the Compton
cloud (post shock region close to a black hole). Similar to other classical
transient BHCs, monotonic evolution of low frequency quasi-periodic
oscillations (QPOs) are observed during the rising phase of the outburst, which

We present here our shape analysis method for a sample of 76 Galactic HII
regions from MAGPIS 1.4 GHz data. The main goal is to determine whether
physical properties and initial conditions of massive star cluster formation is
linked to the shape of the regions. We outline a systematic procedure for
extracting region shapes and perform hierarchical clustering on the shape data.
We identified six groups that categorise HII regions by common morphologies. We
confirmed the validity of these groupings by bootstrap re-sampling and the
ordinance technique multidimensional scaling. We then investigated associations
between physical parameters and the assigned groups. Location is mostly
independent of group, with a small preference for regions of similar longitudes
to share common morphologies. The shapes are homogeneously distributed across
Galactocentric distance and latitude. One group contains regions that are all
younger than 0.5 Myr and ionised by low- to intermediate-mass sources. Those in
another group are all driven by intermediate- to high-mass sources. One group
was distinctly separated from the other five and contained regions at the
surface brightness detection limit for the survey. We find that our
hierarchical procedure is most sensitive to the spatial sampling resolution
used, which is determined for each region from its distance. We discuss how
these errors can be further quantified and reduced in future work by utilising
synthetic observations from numerical simulations of HII regions. We also

We report here our latest search for molecular outflows from young brown
dwarfs and very low-mass stars in nearby star-forming regions. We have observed
three sources in Taurus with the Submillimeter Array and the Combined Array for
Research in Millimeter-wave Astronomy at 230 GHz frequency to search for CO
J=2-1 outflows. We obtain a tentative detection of a redshifted and extended
gas lobe at about 10 arcsec from the source GM Tau, a young brown dwarf in
Taurus with an estimated mass of 73 M_J, which is right below the
hydrogen-burning limit. No blueshifted emission around the brown dwarf position
is detected. The redshifted gas lobe that is elongated in the northeast
direction suggests a possible bipolar outflow from the source with a position
angle of about 36 degrees. Assuming that the redshifted emission is outflow
emission from GM Tau, we then estimate a molecular outflow mass in the range
from 1.9x10^-6 M_Sun to 2.9x10^-5 M_Sun and an outflow mass-loss rate from
2.7x10^-9 M_Sun yr^-1 to 4.1x10^-8 M_Sun yr^-1. These values are comparable to
those we have observed in the young brown dwarf ISO-Oph 102 of 60 M_J in rho
Ophiuchi and the very low-mass star MHO 5 of 90 M_J in Taurus. Our results
suggest that the outflow process in very low-mass objects is episodic with
duration of a few thousand years and the outflow rate of active episodes does
not significantly change for different stages of the formation process of very
low-mass objects. This may provide us with important implications that clarify
the formation process of brown dwarfs.

general circulation of the atmosphere or convective motions. Isentropic
analyses are commonly based on studies of different equivalent potential
temperatures, all of which are assumed to fully represent the entropy of moist
air. It is, however, possible to rely either on statistical physics or the
third law of thermodynamics when defining and computing the absolute entropy of
moist air and to study the corresponding third-law potential temperature, which
is different from the previous ones. The third law assumes that the entropy for
the most stable crystalline state of all substances is zero when approaching
absolute zero temperature.
  This paper shows that the way all these moist-air potential temperatures are
defined has a large impact on: (i) the plotting of the isentropes for a
simulation of the Hurricane DUMILE; (ii) the changes in moist-air entropy
computed for a steam cycle defined for this Hurricane; (iii) the analyses of
isentropic stream functions computed for this Hurricane; and (iv) the
computations of the heat input, the work function, and the efficiency defined
for this steam cycle.
  The moist-air entropy is a state function and the isentropic analyses must be
completely determined by the local moist-air conditions. The large differences
observed between the different formulations of moist-air entropy are
interpreted as proof that the isentropic analyses of moist-air atmospheric
motions must be achieved by using the third-law potential temperature defined

In time-reversal invariant electronic systems the scattering matrix is
anti-symmetric. This property enables an effect, designated here as "scattering
anomaly", such that the electron transport does not suffer from back
reflections, independent of the specific geometry of the propagation path or
the presence of time-reversal invariant defects. In contrast, for a generic
time-reversal invariant photonic system the scattering matrix is symmetric and
there is no similar anomaly. Here, it is theoretically proven that despite
these fundamental differences there is a wide class of photonic platforms - in
some cases formed only by time-reversal invariant media - in which a scattering
anomaly can occur. It is shown that an optical system invariant under the
action of the composition of the parity, time-reversal, and duality operators
(PTD) is characterized by an anti-symmetric scattering matrix. Specific
examples of photonic platforms wherein the scattering anomaly occurs are given,
and it is demonstrated with full wave numerical simulations that the proposed
systems enable bidirectional waveguiding immune to arbitrary deformations of
the propagation path. Importantly, our theory unveils a new class of fully
three dimensional structures wherein the transport of light is fully protected
against reflections and uncovers unsuspected links between the electrodynamics
of reciprocal and nonreciprocal materials.

We identify an invariant light-front coordinate $\zeta$ which allows the
separation of the dynamics of quark and gluon binding from the kinematics of
constituent spin and internal orbital angular momentum. The result is a
single-variable light-front Schrodinger equation for QCD which determines the
eigenspectrum and the light-front wavefunctions of hadrons for general spin and
orbital angular momentum. This frame-independent light-front wave equation is
equivalent to the equations of motion which describe the propagation of
spin-$J$ modes on anti-de Sitter (AdS) space. Light-front holography is a
remarkable feature of AdS/CFT: it allows hadronic amplitudes in the AdS fifth
dimension to be mapped to frame-independent light-front wavefunctions of
hadrons in physical space-time, thus providing a relativistic description of
hadrons at the amplitude level. In principle, the model can be systematically
improved by diagonalizing the full QCD light-front Hamiltonian on the AdS/QCD
basis. Quark and gluon hadronization can be computed at the amplitude level by
convoluting the off-shell $T$ matrix calculated from the QCD light-front
Hamiltonian with the hadronic light-front wavefunctions. We also note the
distinction between static observables such as the probability distributions
computed from the square of the light-front wavefunctions versus dynamical
observables such as the structure functions and the leading-twist single-spin
asymmetries measured in deep inelastic scattering which include the effects of
initial and final-state interactions.

relationships. Based on these considerations, we propose a novel attention

combining the HM-RNN and the attention mechanism and apply it to action
recognition. A newly proposed gradient estimation method for stochastic
neurons, namely Gumbel-softmax, is exploited to implement the temporal boundary
detectors and the stochastic hard attention mechanism. To amealiate the
negative effect of sensitive temperature of the Gumbel-softmax, an adaptive
temperature training method is applied to better the system performance. The
experimental results demonstrate the improved effect of HM-AN over LSTM with
attention on the vision task. Through visualization of what have been learnt by
the networks, it can be observed that both the attention regions of images and
the hierarchical temporal structure can be captured by HM-AN.

Recent results from direct and indirect searches for dark matter (DM) have
motivated the study of particle physics models that can provide weakly
interacting massive particles (WIMPs) in the mass range 1-50 GeV. Viable
candidates for light WIMP DM must fulfil stringent constraints. On the one
hand, the observation at the LHC of a Higgs boson with Standard Model
properties set an upper bound on the coupling of light DM particles to the
Higgs, thereby making it difficult to reproduce the correct relic abundance. On
the other hand, the recent results from direct searches in the CDMSlite,
SuperCDMS and LUX experiments have set upper constraints on the DM scattering
cross section. In this paper, we investigate the viability of light
right-handed sneutrino DM in the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Model (NMSSM)
in the light of these constraints. To this aim, we have carried out a scan in
the NMSSM parameter space, imposing experimental bounds on the Higgs sector and
low-energy observables, such as the muon anomalous magnetic moment and
branching ratios of rare decays. We demonstrate that the enlarged Higgs sector
of the NMSSM, together with the flexibility provided by the RH sneutrino
parameters, make it possible to obtain viable RH sneutrino DM with a mass as
light as 2 GeV. We have also considered the upper bounds on the annihilation
cross section from Fermi LAT data on dwarf spheroidal galaxies, and extracted
specific examples with mass in the range 8-50 GeV that could account for the
apparent low-energy excess in the gamma-ray emission at the Galactic Centre.
Then, we have computed the theoretical predictions for the elastic scattering
cross-section of RH sneutrinos. Finally, after imposing the recent bounds from
SuperCDMS and LUX, we have found a wide area of the parameter space that could
be probed by future low-threshold direct detection experiments.

text: In this work, we address the problem of asynchronous exclusive selection, which finds broad applications in distributed systems where simultaneous access to shared resources must be efficiently managed. Our study aims to develop a robust algorithm that enables a set of decentralized agents to individually and exclusively select a resource from a shared pool, without requiring global synchronization. We propose a novel, fault-tolerant algorithmic framework that operates effectively under the constraints of asynchronous communication and partial system knowledge.   Utilizing a combination of probabilistic analysis and local decision-making rules, our method ensures that the selection process remains free from conflicts, achieving high levels of fairness and liveness in resource allocation. Our key innovation lies in the development of an adaptive contention resolution mechanism which dynamically adjusts to the varying number of participating entities, thereby optimizing resource utilization efficiently. We rigorously prove the correctness and convergence properties of our algorithm, employing formal verification techniques.   Extensive simulations on a range of synthetic and real-world data sets demonstrate the robustness and scalability of our approach, with a marked improvement in average latency and throughput compared to existing asynchronous selection schemes. Our findings suggest that the proposed solution not only reduces the resource selection overhead but also enhances overall system resilience to node failures and dynamic network topologies. This work substantiates a significant advancement in distributed resource selection paradigms, paving the way for more seamless and efficient utilization in real-world distributed computing applications.

text: We present a comprehensive analysis of the infrared spectra of the peculiar post-Asymptotic Giant Branch (post-AGB) stars EPLyr and HD52961, aiming to resolve the uncertainties surrounding their elemental compositions and evolutionary stages. We collected high-resolution infrared spectra, employing spectroscopy techniques in the 2.5 to 30 µm range, to investigate the circumstellar environments and identify key spectral features linked to nucleosynthesis processes. Our results reveal distinctive emission lines associated with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), crystalline silicates, and metallic oxides, indicating varying degrees of dust formation and temperature gradients within the circumstellar shells.   Through comparative analysis, we establish a correlation between the identified spectral features and the physical parameters of the stars, including effective temperature and mass-loss rates. Moreover, the data suggest that EPLyr exhibits more prominent PAH features compared to HD52961, which we attribute to differences in the chemical composition of their circumstellar environments. We also discuss the implications of our findings in the context of stellar evolution, particularly in relation to thermal pulses and dredge-up events during the post-AGB phase.   Our study not only enhances the understanding of the complex interplay between stellar characteristics and their surrounding dust but also contributes to the broader discourse on the evolution of AGB stars into planetary nebulae. We propose that future investigations utilize multi-wavelength approaches to further unravel the intricacies of post-AGB stellar evolution.

For magnetically driven events, the magnetic energy of the system is the
prime energy reservoir that fuels the dynamical evolution. In the solar
context, the free energy is one of the main indicators used in space weather
forecasts to predict the eruptivity of active regions. A trustworthy estimation
of the magnetic energy is therefore needed in three-dimensional models of the
solar atmosphere, eg in coronal fields reconstructions or numerical
simulations. The expression of the energy of a system as the sum of its
potential energy and its free energy (Thomson's theorem) is strictly valid when
the magnetic field is exactly solenoidal. For numerical realizations on a
discrete grid, this property may be only approximately fulfilled. We show that
the imperfect solenoidality induces terms in the energy that can lead to
misinterpreting the amount of free energy present in a magnetic configuration.
We consider a decomposition of the energy in solenoidal and nonsolenoidal parts
which allows the unambiguous estimation of the nonsolenoidal contribution to
the energy. We apply this decomposition to six typical cases broadly used in
solar physics. We quantify to what extent the Thomson theorem is not satisfied
when approximately solenoidal fields are used. The quantified errors on energy
vary from negligible to significant errors, depending on the extent of the
nonsolenoidal component. We identify the main source of errors and analyze the
implications of adding a variable amount of divergence to various solenoidal
fields. Finally, we present pathological unphysical situations where the
estimated free energy would appear to be negative, as found in some previous
works, and we identify the source of this error to be the presence of a finite
divergence. We provide a method of quantifying the effect of a finite
divergence in numerical fields, together with detailed diagnostics of its
sources.

text: In this work, we investigate the efficacy of similarity function tracking through pairwise comparisons as a means to enhance machine learning model performance. We aim to address the prevalent challenges in optimizing similarity metrics, particularly in high-dimensional feature spaces where traditional methods often falter. Our methodology employs a systematic approach that incorporates pairwise comparison techniques to derive and refine similarity functions dynamically. We implement a novel algorithm that facilitates the comparison of item pairs, enabling the model to learn from both positive and negative instances effectively.   We conducted extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, assessing the algorithm's performance relative to conventional similarity tracking methods. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in classification accuracy and computational efficiency. Specifically, we observed that our pairwise approach yields a notable reduction in prediction error rates, achieving up to 15% improvement in some cases. Furthermore, our findings indicate that tracking similarity functions through pairwise comparisons enhances the model's adaptability to variations in data distributions, thereby maintaining robustness across diverse applications.  Our work contributes to the field by providing a scalable framework for similarity function tracking, highlighting the advantages of leveraging pairwise comparisons. We conclude that this methodology not only solves existing limitations in similarity metric optimization but also opens avenues for future research in adaptive learning systems, ultimately leading to more reliable and effective machine learning applications.

We study a problem of trust in a distributed system in which a common
resource is shared by multiple parties. In such naturally information-limited
settings, parties abide by a behavioral protocol that leads to fair sharing of
the resource. However, greedy players may defect from a cooperative protocol
and achieve a greater than fair share of resources, often without significant
adverse consequences to themselves. In this paper, we study the role of a few
vigilante players who also defect from a cooperative resource-sharing protocol
but only in response to perceived greedy behavior. For a simple model of
engagement, we demonstrate surprisingly complex dynamics among greedy and
vigilante players. We show that the best response function for the
greedy-player under our formulation has a jump discontinuity, which leads to
conditions under which there is no Nash equilibrium. To study this property, we
formulate an exact representation for the greedy player best response function
in the case when there is one greedy player, one vigilante player and $N-2$
cooperative players. We use this formulation to show conditions under which a
Nash equilibrium exists. We also illustrate that in the case when there is no
Nash equilibrium, then the discrete dynamic system generated from fictitious
play will not converge, but will oscillate indefinitely as a result of the jump
discontinuity. The case of multiple vigilante and greedy players is studied
numerically. Finally, we explore the relationship between fictitious play and
the better response dynamics (gradient descent) and illustrate that this
dynamical system can have a fixed point even when the discrete dynamical system
arising from fictitious play does not.

text: Bromotrifluoromethane (BrF3) is a bromine-containing halocarbon, widely used as a refrigerant, solvent, and in various industrial applications. Its unique chemical properties make it an interesting subject for rotational molecular dynamics studies. In this research, we employed laser manipulation techniques and X-ray absorption spectroscopy to investigate the rotational motion of BrF3. The study commenced with a thorough background analysis of BrF3, its vibrational and rotational states, and the previous research in this area. The objective was to gain insight into the rotational dynamics of BrF3 using laser manipulation and X-ray absorption techniques. The methodology involved using a laser to induce transitions in BrF3 molecules, followed by X-ray absorption spectroscopy to measure the rotational energy levels. The key findings reveal a complex rotational energy level structure, with several distinct rotational transitions observed. Furthermore, the data provide evidence for the presence of rotational Coriolis and centrifugal distortion effects. The conclusion emphasizes the significance of these findings, which contribute to a better understanding of the rotational dynamics of BrF3 and the potential implications for its industrial applications. The study also opens up possibilities for future research into the vibro-rotational dynamics of BrF3 and other halocarbons.

text: This study focuses on the Direction of Arrival (DoA) analysis within a two-layered heterogeneous wireless interference network, aiming to optimize resource allocation and signal processing techniques for improved performance. The primary objective is to analyze the impact of layering on DoA estimation accuracy and interference mitigation strategies. We present a comprehensive simulation framework that models both layers of the network, taking into account different propagation environments and interference sources. Key methodologies include employing machine learning algorithms to enhance the accuracy of DoA estimation under varying conditions. Results indicate significant improvements in DoA estimation accuracy when considering the interplay between layers, which are crucial for effective interference management. The study also highlights the necessity of adaptive algorithms to dynamically adjust parameters based on real-time channel conditions, thereby optimizing overall network performance.

text: The proliferation of social media has led to a significant increase in automated content generation, with autogenerated tweets becoming a common phenomenon. This study aims to develop an efficient methodology for the on-the-fly detection of such tweets, focusing on distinguishing between human-generated and machine-generated content in real-time. The methodology utilizes a hybrid approach combining natural language processing (NLP) techniques and machine learning algorithms. A dataset comprising both autogenerated and manually crafted tweets is employed for training and evaluation purposes. Key features such as lexical diversity, syntactic structure, and sentiment analysis are extracted and analyzed to build a predictive model using supervised learning techniques. The experimental results indicate a promising accuracy rate of over 90% for the classification of tweets, with ensemble methods outperforming individual classifiers. Furthermore, the system is designed to operate in real-time, enabling rapid identification and potential filtering of autogenerated content in users’ feeds. This study contributes to the ongoing conversation surrounding content authenticity in social media by providing a practical solution for recognizing automated tweets, which can help mitigate misinformation and enhance user engagement. The findings underscore the necessity for improved tools that can discern between human and machine-produced content, ensuring a more reliable social media environment. Future work will explore the integration of multilingual capabilities and the adaptability of the detection system across different social media platforms.

The DC and AC magnetic susceptibilities of Na0.85CoO2 single crystals were
measured for the different crystal orientations of H//(ab)- and H//(c)-axis.
The DC-magnetic susceptibility for H//(c)-direction exhibited the
antiferromagnetic transition at TN= 22 K. The thermal hysteresis between the
zero-field-cooled (ZFC) and the field-cooled (FC) magnetization below TN and
the large frustration parameter indicated the spin frustration along the
(c)-axis. For an applied magnetic field in H//(ab)-plane, the DC magnetic
susceptibility exhibited the logarithmic divergent behavior at low temperatures
(T < 6.8 K). This could be understood by the impurity spin effect, dressed by
the spin fluctuation. From the AC magnetic susceptibility measurements, the
real part of the AC-susceptibility for H//(ab) exhibited the spin glass-like
behavior at low temperatures (T < 4 K). Remarkably, for an applied AC magnetic
field with H//(c)-axis, the sign of the AC magnetic susceptibility changed from
a positive to a negative value with increasing AC magnetic field frequency (f >
3 kHz) at low temperatures (T > 7 K). We interpret the sign change of AC
magnetic susceptibility along the (c)-axis in terms of the sudden sign reversal
of the phase difference from in-phase to out-of-phase response with an applied
AC magnetic field in the AC-susceptibility phase space.

text: This research explores the numerical simulation of an unsteady two-dimensional incompressible flow involving heat and mass transfer under varying Reynolds numbers (low, moderate, and high). The primary objective was to investigate the influence of Reynolds number on fluid dynamics, heat transfer, and mass transfer characteristics. Utilizing computational fluid dynamics (CFD) techniques, specifically the finite volume method, simulations were conducted on a representative geometry with boundary conditions reflecting real-world scenarios.  The study employed a transient solver to account for the unsteady nature of the flow, and the governing equations were solved using the SIMPLE algorithm for pressure-velocity coupling. Various grid resolutions were tested to ensure accuracy and convergence. Key findings revealed that as the Reynolds number increased, so did the complexity of flow patterns, leading to enhanced heat and mass transfer rates. At lower Reynolds numbers, laminar flow dominated, resulting in smoother temperature and concentration profiles compared to turbulent regimes observed at higher Reynolds numbers.  The results underscored the necessity of considering Reynolds number effects for accurate predictions in engineering applications such as microscale devices and cooling systems. This research provides valuable insights into the behavior of fluids under different flow regimes, offering guidelines for optimizing design parameters to enhance efficiency and performance.

text: We investigated the magnetorotational collapse of supermassive stars, a critical process in the formation of black holes, and its implications for the emission of gravitational waves and the generation of jets. Our simulations revealed that the collapse of massive stars is driven by a complex interplay between angular momentum, magnetic fields, and gravitational forces, leading to the formation of a rotating black hole. We found that the spin of the black hole is closely tied to the strength of the magnetic fields present during the collapse, with higher magnetic field strengths resulting in more rapidly spinning black holes. Furthermore, our results indicate that the emission of gravitational waves is closely linked to the collapse of the star, with the most intense wave emission occurring during the final stages of collapse. We also observed the formation of jets, which are powered by the rapid spin-up of the black hole, and found that these jets are characterized by high-energy particle acceleration and relativistic outflows. Our findings provide new insights into the complex physics governing the formation of black holes and the emission of gravitational waves, and have significant implications for our understanding of the role of magnetorotational collapse in the formation of supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies.

To unbiasedly estimate a causal effect on an outcome unconfoundedness is
often assumed. If there is sufficient knowledge on the underlying causal
structure then existing confounder selection criteria can be used to select
subsets of the observed pretreatment covariates, $X$, sufficient for
unconfoundedness, if such subsets exist. Here, estimation of these target
subsets is considered when the underlying causal structure is unknown. The
proposed method is to model the causal structure by a probabilistic graphical
model, e.g., a Markov or Bayesian network, estimate this graph from observed
data and select the target subsets given the estimated graph. The approach is
evaluated by simulation both in a high-dimensional setting where
unconfoundedness holds given $X$ and in a setting where unconfoundedness only
holds given subsets of $X$. Several common target subsets are investigated and
the selected subsets are compared with respect to accuracy in estimating the
average causal effect. The proposed method is implemented with existing
software that can easily handle high-dimensional data, in terms of large
samples and large number of covariates. The results from the simulation study
show that, if unconfoundedness holds given $X$, this approach is very
successful in selecting the target subsets, outperforming alternative
approaches based on random forests and LASSO, and that the subset estimating
the target subset containing all causes of outcome yields smallest MSE in the
average causal effect estimation.

text: We present our recent advancements in model-independent exoplanet transit spectroscopy using a novel time-series analysis technique. Our methodology involves the use of artificial intelligence algorithms to identify transit signal signatures in the light curves of exoplanet host stars, allowing for the detection and characterization of exoplanets without the need for pre-defined atmospheric models. This approach not only increases the efficiency and speed of the detection process, but also enhances the capability to discover planets in various stages of atmospheric evolution.  Our analysis of data from the NASA Kepler mission demonstrated the ability to identify transit signals with high precision and accuracy, even in the presence of noise and instrumental artifacts. Moreover, our methodology can identify transit signals in multi-planet systems and can provide insights into the atmospheric properties of the detected exoplanets, such as their effective temperatures and compositions.  We also discuss the challenges and limitations of our methodology, including the need for large, high-quality data sets and the potential for false positives. Nonetheless, the potential benefits of this model-independent approach outweigh the challenges, as it enables the detection and characterization of exoplanets beyond the reach of current atmospheric models and opens new avenues for research in the field of exoplanetology.  Our ongoing research efforts focus on refining our methodology and expanding its applicability to various data sets and observational platforms, with the ultimate goal of increasing the number of detected and characterized exoplanets and advancing our understanding of their atmospheric properties and the formation and evolution of planetary systems.

We empirically analyze two versions of the well-known "randomized rumor
spreading" protocol to disseminate a piece of information in networks. In the
classical model, in each round each informed node informs a random neighbor. In
the recently proposed quasirandom variant, each node has a (cyclic) list of its
neighbors. Once informed, it starts at a random position of the list, but from
then on informs its neighbors in the order of the list. While for sparse random
graphs a better performance of the quasirandom model could be proven, all other
results show that, independent of the structure of the lists, the same
asymptotic performance guarantees hold as for the classical model. In this
work, we compare the two models experimentally. This not only shows that the
quasirandom model generally is faster, but also that the runtime is more
concentrated around the mean. This is surprising given that much fewer random
bits are used in the quasirandom process. These advantages are also observed in
a lossy communication model, where each transmission does not reach its target
with a certain probability, and in an asynchronous model, where nodes send at
random times drawn from an exponential distribution. We also show that
typically the particular structure of the lists has little influence on the
efficiency.

We propose a new method for opportunistic power control in multi-carrier
interference channels for delay-tolerant data services. In doing so, we utilize
a game theoretic framework with novel constraints, where each user tries to
maximize its utility in a distributed and opportunistic manner, while
satisfying the game's constraints by adapting its transmit power to its
channel. In this scheme, users transmit with more power on good sub-channels
and do the opposite on bad sub-channels. In this way, in addition to the
allocated power on each sub-channel, the total power of all users also depends
on channel conditions. Since each user's power level depends on power levels of
other users, the game belongs to the \emph{generalized} Nash equilibrium (GNE)
problems, which in general, is hard to analyze. We show that the proposed game
has a GNE, and derive the sufficient conditions for its uniqueness. Besides, we
propose a new pricing scheme for maximizing each user's throughput in an
opportunistic manner under its total power constraint; and provide the
sufficient conditions for the algorithm's convergence and its GNE's uniqueness.
Simulations confirm that our proposed scheme yields a higher throughput for
each user and/or has a significantly improved efficiency as compared to other
existing opportunistic methods.

text: This research paper investigates two-gluon correlations in heavy-light ion collisions, focusing on the effects of energy and geometry dependence, IR divergences, and $k_T$-factorization. The study aims to understand the intricate interplay between gluon dynamics and the characteristics of the collision system. The methodology involves a theoretical analysis of two-gluon correlations within the framework of quantum chromodynamics, taking into account the specifics of heavy-light ion interactions. Key findings reveal significant energy and geometry dependence in the two-gluon correlation patterns, highlighting the role of IR divergences and the applicability of $k_T$-factorization in describing the gluon dynamics. The results shed light on the underlying mechanisms governing gluon production and correlations in heavy-light ion collisions. In conclusion, the study provides valuable insights into the complexities of gluon interactions in high-energy nuclear collisions, offering a nuanced understanding of the energy and geometry effects on two-gluon correlations, while emphasizing the significance of $k_T$-factorization in this context.

text: In this study, we explore the interplay between black hole thermodynamics, conformal field couplings, and higher-order curvature corrections, specifically R^2 terms, in the context of quantum gravity theories. Our primary objective is to elucidate the modifications these elements introduce to black hole entropy and temperature, thereby addressing discrepancies within classical gravitational frameworks. We employ a conformal coupling approach to investigate their influence on the entropy-area relationship, incorporating fluctuations resulting from R^2 corrections. Utilizing a semi-classical analysis, we derive a modified entropy formula, highlighting significant deviations from the standard Bekenstein-Hawking paradigm in extreme curvature regimes. Furthermore, we examine the stability implications of these corrections on black hole solutions, revealing that R^2 terms can stabilize regions previously prone to singularities. Our results demonstrate that conformal couplings effectively regulate thermodynamic quantities and suggest potential pathways to resolve black hole information paradox challenges. We systematically incorporate variational methods within a conformal gravity framework, supported by analytical and numerical simulations, to derive the modified equations of motion. By comparing these results with existing thermodynamic laws, we identify a consistent extension to black hole thermodynamics, preserving the foundational principles while accommodating quantum corrections. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of quantum aspects of black holes, offering insights into the integration of higher-order gravitational theories and shedding light on their role in the ongoing quest for a unified theory of quantum gravity. Such insights pave the way for future explorations into the quantum corrections’ implications for Hawking radiation and black hole evolution.

text: We propose a novel approach to investigate the potential influence of future events on the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) operations, a groundbreaking experiment that has been instrumental in shaping our understanding of the universe. Our proposal seeks to validate the theoretical framework of quantum mechanics, specifically the concept of retrocausality, which suggests that the future can influence the past.  To test this hypothesis, we propose to implement a novel experimental design that incorporates a closed timelike curve (CTC) into the LHC's data acquisition system. This CTC would allow us to capture and analyze data from a hypothetical future event, which would then be used to inform the present-day LHC operations. Our approach involves the development of a sophisticated algorithm that can detect and interpret the subtle signatures of future influence on the LHC's data.  Through a series of simulations and theoretical calculations, we demonstrate that our proposed CTC-based approach can indeed detect and quantify the influence of future events on the LHC's data. Our results show that the algorithm can accurately predict the outcomes of future events with a high degree of precision, thereby validating the theoretical framework of retrocausality.  This proposal has significant implications for our understanding of the fundamental laws of physics and the nature of time itself. If our results are confirmed, it would provide strong evidence for the existence of retrocausality and challenge our current understanding of causality. Furthermore, our approach could have far-reaching applications in fields such as quantum computing, cryptography, and time travel.

We study several aspects of the realization of global symmetries in highly
entangled phases of quantum matter. Examples include gapped topological ordered
phases, gapless quantum spin liquids and non-fermi liquid phases. An insightful
window into such phases is provided by recent developments in the theory of
short ranged entangled Symmetry Protected Topological (SPT) phases . First they
generate useful no-go constraints on how global symmetry may be implemented in
a highly entangled phase. Possible symmetry implementation in gapped
topological phases and some proposed gapless spin/bose liquids are examined in
this light. We show that some previously proposed spin liquid states for 2d
quantum magnets do not in fact have consistent symmetry implementation unless
they occur as the surface of a 3d SPT phase. A second SPT-based insight into
highly entangled states is the development of a view point of such states as
SPT phases of one of the emergent excitations. We describe this in the specific
context of time reversal symmetric 3d U(1) quantum spin liquids with an
emergent photon. Different such spin liquids are shown to be equivalent to
different SPT insulating phases of the emergent monopole excitation of such
phases. The highly entangled states also in turn enrich our understanding of
SPT phases. We use the insights obtained from our results to provide an
explicit construction of bosonic SPT phases in 3d in a system of coupled
layers. This includes construction of a time reversal symmetric SPT state that
is not currently part of the cohomology classification of such states.

text:
D\'ungal's letter to Charlemagne on the double solar eclipse in the year 810
is extremely interesting both for its form and for its subject matter. Part I
of the present study deals with the epistula as a literary work (genre,
language, sources), dealing in turn with vocabulary, morphology and syntax,
rythmical prose and rhetorical figures, literary and Biblical references. If we
compare it with D\'ungal's other works, the letter is cast in the canonical
oratio structure similar to his later Responsa contra Claudium (ed. Zanna,
Firenze 2002) and it is likewise based on lengthy quotations drawns from
Macrobius' commentary In Somnium Scipionis. A possible echo of Vitruvius'
astronomical presentation in book IX of his De architectura is suggested.
Finally, we attempt to define how the author's persona as famulus et orator and
reclusus at St-Denis relates to Charlemagne and to abbot Waldo in his pursuit
of Chirstian wisdom based on the Bible rahter than of scholarship per se based
on academic research. Part II is a thorough technical discussion of the
astronomical issue presented to the Irish scholar by the Emperor, i.e. The
frequency of solar eclipses and their visibility in the two emispheres in the
year 810 (see maps provided). It assesses D\'ungal's case in terms of eclipse
theory and reviews previous comments on his letter to Charlemagne by astronomer
Ismael Bullialdus (1605-1694). It also introduces us to first-hand knowledge of
eclipses in history and nowadays, providing a glimpse into the complex problems
tackled by the Irishman and his sources in Late Antique and in the Early Middle
Ages. Ample footnotes to the Italian translation of D\'ungal's work are an
essential guiding tool for Latinists unfamiliar with astronomy.

text: Dans notre étude, nous avons abordé la problématique de la réduction de termes complexes dans les langues de spécialité, un défi majeur pour la compréhension et la communication au sein de domaines techniques. Notre objectif principal était d'identifier et de proposer des méthodes efficaces pour simplifier ces terminologies tout en préservant leur sens et leur précision.   Nous avons utilisé une approche méthodologique combinant l'analyse linguistique et la modélisation terminologique. D'une part, nous avons réalisé une étude comparative des termes complexes issus de plusieurs langues de spécialité, tels que la médecine, l'informatique et le droit. D'autre part, nous avons élaboré des stratégies de simplification en appliquant des techniques de normalisation et d’abstraction sémantique.   Nos résultats montrent que l'application de ces méthodes permet de réduire significativement la complexité des termes sans altérer leur intégrité conceptuelle. En effet, nous avons constaté une diminution de 30 % en moyenne du nombre de syllabes des termes simplifiés, tout en maintenant un haut niveau de reconnaissance et de compréhension par les interlocuteurs spécialisés.   Cette recherche souligne l'importance de la terminologie accessible dans les langues de spécialité pour favoriser l'interdisciplinarité et améliorer la communication entre les experts et le grand public. Ainsi, nous recommandons l'intégration de ces pratiques de simplification dans la formation des professionnels et la création de ressources linguistiques adaptées.

We report a NuSTAR observation of a solar microflare, SOL2015-09-01T04.
Although it was too faint to be observed by the GOES X-ray Sensor, we estimate
the event to be an A0.1 class flare in brightness. This microflare, with only 5
counts per second per detector observed by RHESSI, is fainter than any hard
X-ray (HXR) flare in the existing literature. The microflare occurred during a
solar pointing by the highly sensitive NuSTAR astrophysical observatory, which
used its direct focusing optics to produce detailed HXR microflare spectra and
images. The microflare exhibits HXR properties commonly observed in larger
flares, including a fast rise and more gradual decay, earlier peak time with
higher energy, spatial dimensions similar to the RHESSI microflares, and a
high-energy excess beyond an isothermal spectral component during the impulsive
phase. The microflare is small in emission measure, temperature, and energy,
though not in physical size; observations are consistent with an origin via the
interaction of at least two magnetic loops. We estimate the increase in thermal
energy at the time of the microflare to be 2.4x10^27 ergs. The observation
suggests that flares do indeed scale down to extremely small energies and
retain what we customarily think of as "flarelike" properties.

We modify the standard Abelian-Higgs model by introducing spatially-dependent
couplings for the scalar and vector fields. We investigate static,
non-cylindrically symmetric solutions of the resulting field equations and
propose a pinch solution which interpolates between degenerate vacua along the
string, labelled by $\pm |n|$. This configuration corresponds to a vortex which
shrinks to Planck scale before re-emerging as an anti-vortex, resulting in the
formation of a bead pair with one bead at either side of the intersection. The
solution is then topologically stable. A key assumption is that quantities such
as phase and winding number, along with those which depend on them like the
magnetic flux, become undefined at the Planck scale so that regions of opposite
winding may be joined via a Planck-sized segment of neutral string.
Similarities between this solution and the extra-dimensional windings of
strings in type IIB string theory are discussed and a correspondence between
field theory and string theory parameters is suggested. The spatial-dependence
of the field couplings is found to have a natural interpretation in the dual
string picture and results from the variation of the winding radius, giving
rise to a varying (effective) string coupling. An interesting result is an
estimate of the Higgs mass (at critical coupling) in terms of the parameters
which define the Klebanov-Strassler geometry and which, in principle, may be
constrained by cosmological observations.

Two complementary techniques for analyzing search spaces are proposed: (i) an
algorithm to detect search points with potential to be local optima; and (ii) a
slightly adjusted Wang-Landau sampling algorithm to explore larger search
spaces. The detection algorithm assumes that local optima are points which are
easier to reach and harder to leave by a slow adaptive walker. A slow adaptive
walker moves to a nearest fitter point. Thus, points with larger outgoing step
sizes relative to incoming step sizes are marked using the local optima score
formulae as potential local optima points (PLOPs). Defining local optima in
these more general terms allows their detection within the closure of a subset
of a search space, and the sampling of a search space unshackled by a
particular move set. Tests are done with NK and HIFF problems to confirm that
PLOPs detected in the manner proposed retain characteristics of local optima,
and that the adjusted Wang-Landau samples are more representative of the search
space than samples produced by choosing points uniformly at random. While our
approach shows promise, more needs to be done to reduce its computation cost
that it may pave a way toward analyzing larger search spaces of practical
meaning.

An interesting application of the gauge/gravity duality to condensed matter
physics is the description of a lattice via breaking translational invariance
on the gravity side. By making use of global symmetries, it is possible to do
so without scarifying homogeneity of the pertinent bulk solutions, which we
thus term as "homogeneous holographic lattices." Due to their technical
simplicity, these configurations have received a great deal of attention in the
last few years and have been shown to correctly describe momentum relaxation
and hence (finite) DC conductivities. However, it is not clear whether they are
able to capture other lattice effects which are of interest in condensed
matter. In this paper we investigate this question focusing our attention on
the phenomenon of commensurability, which arises when the lattice scale is
tuned to be equal to (an integer multiple of) another momentum scale in the
system. We do so by studying the formation of spatially modulated phases in
various models of homogeneous holographic lattices. Our results indicate that
the onset of the instability is controlled by the near horizon geometry, which
for insulating solutions does carry information about the lattice. However, we
observe no sharp connection between the characteristic momentum of the broken
phase and the lattice pitch, which calls into question the applicability of
these models to the physics of commensurability.

text: This research explores state transfer dynamics in quantum systems subjected to dissipative and dephasing environments. Key findings indicate that while pure dephasing leads to significant degradation of state transfer, dissipation can mitigate these losses when properly managed through tailored control protocols. Additionally, we identify optimal parameters for mitigating dephasing-induced errors, thereby enhancing the robustness of quantum state transfer. The results contribute to the understanding of practical challenges in implementing scalable quantum networks and offer insights into the design of fault-tolerant quantum communication schemes.

text: In modern communication networks, estimating arrival rates of packets in asynchronous networks is crucial for efficient resource allocation and improving overall network performance. However, due to the absence of a global clock and the decentralized nature of such networks, estimating arrival rates presents a significant challenge. In this paper, we propose a Bayesian approach for distributed estimation of arrival rates in asynchronous networks. We model the arrival process using a Poisson point process with an unknown rate parameter. Each node in the network maintains its local estimate of the arrival rate using a filtering algorithm. We exploit the Bayesian property of conditional independence and construct a novel distributed filter based on the Kalman filter. The proposed filter is shown to have desirable properties such as consistency, convergence, and low computational complexity. Furthermore, we analyze the performance of the proposed method under various network conditions and demonstrate its superiority over existing approaches through simulations. Overall, this work contributes to the development of efficient and distributed estimation methods for arrival rates in asynchronous networks, addressing a key challenge in modern communication systems.

The Partitioned Global Address Space (PGAS) programming model strikes a
balance between the locality-aware, but explicit, message-passing model and the
easy-to-use, but locality-agnostic, shared memory model. However, the PGAS rich
memory model comes at a performance cost which can hinder its potential for
scalability and performance. To contain this overhead and achieve full
performance, compiler optimizations may not be sufficient and manual
optimizations are typically added. This, however, can severely limit the
productivity advantage. Such optimizations are usually targeted at reducing
address translation overheads for shared data structures. This paper proposes a
hardware architectural support for PGAS, which allows the processor to
efficiently handle shared addresses. This eliminates the need for such
hand-tuning, while maintaining the performance and productivity of PGAS
languages. We propose to avail this hardware support to compilers by
introducing new instructions to efficiently access and traverse the PGAS memory
space. A prototype compiler is realized by extending the Berkeley Unified
Parallel C (UPC) compiler. It allows unmodified code to use the new
instructions without the user intervention, thereby creating a real productive
programming environment. Two implementations are realized: the first is
implemented using the full system simulator Gem5, which allows the evaluation
of the performance gain. The second is implemented using a softcore processor
Leon3 on an FPGA to verify the implementability and to parameterize the cost of
the new hardware and its instructions. The new instructions show promising
results for the NAS Parallel Benchmarks implemented in UPC. A speedup of up to
5.5x is demonstrated for unmodified and unoptimized codes. Unoptimized code
performance using this hardware was shown to also surpass the performance of
manually optimized code by up to 10%.

text: This paper presents a reconfigurable dual-mode IEEE 802.15.4 digital baseband receiver designed for diverse IoT applications. However, the limited bandwidth and modulation schemes hinder its flexibility in supporting various IoT applications. To address this limitation, we propose a reconfigurable digital baseband receiver that can operate in both single-carrier frequency-division multiple access (SC-FDMA) and orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA) modes. The receiver utilizes a novel digital signal processing (DSP) architecture, which enables reconfiguration of the receiver to adapt to different modulation schemes and bandwidths.  The proposed receiver is designed using a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) to facilitate reconfiguration and minimize power consumption. The FPGA-based implementation allows for rapid prototyping and verification of the receiver's performance. We evaluate the receiver's performance using various modulation schemes and bandwidths, including 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz frequencies. The results demonstrate that the reconfigurable receiver can achieve high sensitivity, linearity, and selectivity, making it suitable for diverse IoT applications.  The proposed reconfigurable dual-mode IEEE 802.15.4 digital baseband receiver offers several advantages, including flexibility, low power consumption, and ease of reconfiguration. The receiver's reconfigurable architecture enables it to support various IoT applications, such as smart home automation, industrial automation, and medical devices. The proposed design can be used as a building block for future IoT systems, enabling them to adapt to changing requirements and emerging applications.
