Flagellated bacteria on nutrient-rich substrates can differentiate into a
swarming state and move in dense swarms across surfaces. A recent experiment
measured the flow in the fluid around an Escherichia coli swarm (Wu, Hosu and
Berg, 2011 Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 108 4147). A systematic chiral flow was
observed in the clockwise direction (when viewed from above) ahead of the swarm
with flow speeds of about $10~\mu$m/s, about 3 times greater than the radial
velocity at the edge of the swarm. The working hypothesis is that this flow is
due to the action of cells stalled at the edge of a colony that extend their
flagellar filaments outwards, moving fluid over the virgin agar. In this work
we quantitatively test his hypothesis. We first build an analytical model of
the flow induced by a single flagellum in a thin film and then use the model,
and its extension to multiple flagella, to compare with experimental
measurements. The results we obtain are in agreement with the flagellar
hypothesis. The model provides further quantitative insight into the flagella
orientations and their spatial distributions as well as the tangential speed
profile. In particular, the model suggests that flagella are on average
pointing radially out of the swarm and are not wrapped tangentially.

text: We explore brain transcriptomic patterns through a topological analysis of spatial expression networks, addressing the critical challenge of understanding complex gene expression relationships in neural tissue. Our methodology involves the construction of spatial expression networks from high-throughput RNA sequencing data, facilitating the visualization of transcriptomic interactions within the spatial context of brain regions. We employ a combination of network analysis techniques, including clustering algorithms and centrality measures, to identify key transcriptional hubs and their spatial correlations.   Our results reveal distinct topological features of spatial expression networks that correlate with functional brain regions and their associated gene expression profiles. Notably, we observe that certain gene modules exhibit spatial segregation, suggesting region-specific transcriptional regulation mechanisms. Furthermore, we discover that highly interconnected genes correlate with significant biological processes, such as neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity, underscoring their importance in brain function and pathology.   Through our approach, we not only gain insights into the complex interplay of gene expression within the brain but also establish a framework for integrating spatial transcriptomics with network theory. This work lays the foundation for future research into the molecular underpinnings of neurological disorders and cognitive functions, as it highlights the potential of spatial expression networks as a powerful tool for elucidating the brain's transcriptomic landscape. Overall, we demonstrate that topological analysis provides a valuable perspective on the spatial organization of gene expression, thereby enhancing our understanding of brain biology.

We report on near-IR interferometric observations of the outburst of the
recurrent nova T Pyx. We obtained near-IR observations of T Pyx at dates
ranging from t=2.37d to t=48.2d after the outburst, with the CLASSIC
recombiner, located at the CHARA array, and with the PIONIER and AMBER
recombiners, located at the VLTI array. These data are supplemented with
near-IR photometry and spectra obtained at Mount Abu, India. Slow expansion
velocities were measured (<300km/s) before t=20d (assuming D=3.5kpc). From
t=28d on, the AMBER and PIONIER continuum visibilities (K and H band,
respectively) are best simulated with a two component model consisting of an
unresolved source plus an extended source whose expansion velocity onto the sky
plane is lower than 700km/s. The expansion of the Brgamma line forming region,
as inferred at t=28d and t=35d is slightly larger, implying velocities in the
range 500-800km/s, still strikingly lower than the velocities of 1300-1600km/s
inferred from the Doppler width of the line. Moreover, a remarkable pattern was
observed in the Brgamma differential phases. A semi-quantitative model using a
bipolar flow with a contrast of 2 between the pole and equator velocities, an
inclination of i=15^{\circ} and a position angle P.A.=110^{\circ} provides a
good match to the AMBER observables (spectra, differential visibilities and
phases). At t=48d, a PIONIER dataset confirms the two component nature of the H
band emission, consisting of an unresolved stellar source and an extended
region whose appearance is circular and symmetric within error bars.These
observations are most simply interpreted within the frame of a bipolar model,
oriented nearly face-on. This finding has profound implications for the
interpretation of past, current and future observations of the expanding
nebula.

text: This research investigates the presence of electron and hole pockets and the partial gap opening in the correlated semimetal Ca3Ru2O7. Through comprehensive analysis, we reveal the coexistence of both electron and hole pockets in the Fermi surface of Ca3Ru2O7, suggesting the presence of multiple charge carriers in the system. Furthermore, our results indicate the emergence of a partial gap within the electronic band structure, shedding light on the unusual properties of this correlated semimetal. These findings contribute to the fundamental understanding of Ca3Ru2O7 and pave the way for its potential applications in future electronic devices. In conclusion, this study provides valuable insights into the electronic properties of Ca3Ru2O7, highlighting its unique characteristics and setting the stage for further exploration in the field of condensed matter physics.

text: The study investigates C58 fullerenes' adsorption and behavior on Au(111) using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to gain insights into their electronic and structural properties. This research aims to elucidate the interaction mechanisms between C58 molecules and the gold surface, which is crucial for potential applications in nanotechnology and molecular electronics. We employed STM at room temperature to observe individual C58 molecules adsorbed on the Au(111) surface, allowing us to map their arrangement and bonding characteristics with high spatial resolution. Our study reveals that C58 molecules exhibit a preference for specific adsorption sites, influenced by the distinct herringbone reconstruction of the Au(111) surface. Detailed analysis of the STM images indicates that these fullerenes display asymmetrical electron density distributions, suggesting significant charge transfer between the C58 and the gold surface. Furthermore, we observed a variation in molecular orientation, which is attributed to local surface defects and variations in the gold substrate's electronic properties. This orientation variation contributes to differences in molecular interaction strength and suggests potential tunability of their electronic properties through surface engineering. Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the C58/Au(111) interface, highlighting the critical role of surface reconstruction and defects in determining the adsorption behavior. These insights can inform the design of fullerene-based devices, suggesting pathways to control molecular orientation and interaction strength through surface modification, ultimately enhancing the performance of molecular electronics.

text: Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) polarization features serve as a crucial observational tool for distinguishing between the imprints of cosmic inflation and the effects of reionization on the early universe. This study aims to delineate the contributions of inflationary physics from those due to reionization in the observed CMB polarization patterns. Utilizing a combination of analytical modeling and high-fidelity numerical simulations, we systematically analyze the B-mode and E-mode polarization signatures. Inflationary models predict distinct B-mode patterns due to primordial gravitational waves, while E-mode polarization is significantly influenced by both scalar perturbations during inflation and Thompson scattering during reionization. Our methodology involves comparing the results of varied inflationary potential models with scenarios including early and late reionization epochs. The simulations incorporate a robust dataset from the latest CMB observations, particularly data from the Planck satellite and ground-based telescopes. Key findings reveal that inflationary signals, notably the tensor-to-scalar ratio, are distinguishable with adequate precision when isolating the reionization-induced polarization at low multipoles. Furthermore, our results highlight the sensitivity of the polarization power spectrum's shape to the reionization optical depth, providing a constraint on the timing of reionization events. These insights suggest that current and future CMB polarization measurements can effectively discriminate between inflationary models, enhancing our understanding of the very early universe. The study concludes that disentangling the intertwined effects of inflation and reionization is not only feasible but vital for advancing cosmological models and constraining parameters that dictate the dynamics of the early universe.

text: In the era of advanced wireless communication, ensuring secure and efficient transmission remains a critical challenge. This research paper explores the innovative approach of Signal Space Alignment (SSA) in enhancing encryption messages within a Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) K-way relay channel framework. The primary objective is to assess the effectiveness of SSA in optimizing the decoding process of successive network codes while maintaining data security and integrity.   We employed a theoretical analysis complemented by simulations to evaluate the performance of the proposed SSA method under different channel conditions. Key parameters, including signal-to-noise ratio, computational efficiency, and error rates, were meticulously examined across various relay configurations.   The findings indicate that Signal Space Alignment significantly improves the resilience of encrypted messages against interception and decode errors in the MIMO K-way relay channel. Notably, the adoption of SSA leads to a marked reduction in decoding complexity, enabling superior performance compared to traditional encoding methods.   In conclusion, the integration of Signal Space Alignment in encryption message handling and successive decoding processes presents a robust solution for contemporary challenges in secure communications. Our results suggest that this approach not only enhances the reliability of data transmission but also contributes to the evolving landscape of network code design in multi-user environments. Future research will explore real-world applications and potential advancements in algorithm efficiency.

text: The advancement of computational methodologies in fluid dynamics has necessitated innovative approaches to tackle the intricacies associated with compressible flows. This study presents a novel polar coordinate lattice Boltzmann model designed to effectively simulate compressible flow phenomena in complex geometries. The primary objective of this research is to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of numerical simulations in polar coordinates, particularly at varying Mach numbers. We employed a second-order accurate lattice Boltzmann method adapted for compressible fluid dynamics, incorporating the ideal gas equation of state and employing boundary conditions suitable for polar domains. Key simulations were conducted to analyze common benchmark cases, including shock tube problems and flow around objects with various shapes. The results indicate that the proposed polar coordinate lattice Boltzmann model significantly outperforms traditional Cartesian approaches in terms of computational efficiency, especially in geometrically complex scenarios. The model demonstrates robust accuracy in capturing shock waves and flow separation phenomena, evidenced by a convergence rate that aligns with theoretical predictions. Additionally, the benefits of the polar coordinate system in handling radial symmetry were highlighted, providing computational savings and improved stability. In conclusion, this research establishes a compelling framework for future simulations of compressible flows in polar coordinates, significantly contributing to the field of computational fluid dynamics while opening avenues for further exploration into related applications such as aerodynamic design and atmospheric modeling.

Logs are widely used in modern software system management because they are
often the only data accessible that record system events at runtime. In recent
years, because of the ever-increasing log size, data mining techniques are
often utilized to help developers and operators conduct system reliability
management. A typical log-based system reliability management procedure is to
first parse log messages because of their unstructured format; and apply data
mining techniques on the parsed logs to obtain critical system behavior
information. Most of existing research studies focus on offline log parsing,
which need to parse logs in batch mode. However, software systems, especially
distributed systems, require online monitoring and maintenance. Thus, a log
parser that can parse log messages in a streaming manner is highly in demand.
To address this problem, we propose an online log parsing method, namely Drain,
based on directed acyclic graph, which encodes specially designed rules for
parsing. Drain can automatically generate a directed acyclic graph for a new
system and update the graph according to the incoming log messages. Besides,
Drain frees developers from the burden of parameter tuning by allowing them use
Drain with no pre-defined parameters. To evaluate the performance of Drain, we
collect 11 log datasets generated by real-world systems, ranging from
distributed systems, Web applications, supercomputers, operating systems, to
standalone software. The experimental results show that Drain has the highest
accuracy on all 11 datasets. Moreover, Drain obtains 37.15\%$\sim$ 97.14\%
improvement in the running time over the state-of-the-art online parsers. We
also conduct a case study on a log-based anomaly detection task using Drain in
the parsing step, which determines its effectiveness in system reliability
management.

text: In the evolving landscape of machine learning, the challenge of efficiently managing and utilizing large datasets has garnered significant attention, particularly in the context of bandit problems. This research explores scalable Generalized Linear Bandits (GLBs), focusing on online computation strategies and hashing techniques to enhance performance in high-dimensional settings. The primary objective is to develop a robust framework that optimizes the exploration-exploitation trade-off while maintaining computational feasibility. We employ a novel hashing mechanism that reduces the dimensionality of the feature space, enabling faster decision-making without substantial loss of information. Our methodology integrates online learning algorithms with hashing, facilitating real-time updates and adaptability to dynamically changing environments.   Key findings demonstrate that our proposed approach not only improves computational efficiency but also significantly enhances the regret bounds compared to traditional GLB methods. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets reflect a marked improvement in the performance of our scalable algorithm, achieving competitive results in lesser time frames. The results confirm that the integration of hashing techniques can effectively mitigate the computational burden associated with high-dimensional data in online learning scenarios. In conclusion, this study illustrates the viability of scalable GLBs through advanced online computation and hashing, presenting a promising direction for future research in optimization under uncertainty and real-time data analysis. Our findings lay the groundwork for further developments in scalable machine learning applications across diverse domains.

text: This study investigates the light curve of GD 358, a pulsating white dwarf, to uncover evidence of temperature change and oblique pulsation. GD 358 is a unique object, exhibiting a complex light curve that has been observed to vary in brightness over a period of several years. The light curve of GD 358 is characterized by a series of pulsations, with periods ranging from 2.45 to 3.45 hours, which are attributed to the white dwarf's rotational period.  By employing a non-linear least squares fitting method, we analyzed the light curve of GD 358 to determine the best-fit model that accounts for both temperature change and oblique pulsation. The results indicate that the pulsating white dwarf exhibits a significant temperature change, with a period of approximately 2.9 years, which is consistent with the observed pulsations. Furthermore, the analysis reveals evidence of oblique pulsation, where the pulsations are not confined to the rotational axis, but are instead projected onto the star's equator.  The findings of this study provide strong evidence for the presence of temperature change and oblique pulsation in GD 358, which has significant implications for our understanding of the pulsating white dwarf's internal dynamics and rotation. The results also highlight the importance of non-linear least squares fitting in the analysis of complex light curves, such as those observed in GD 358.

text: We investigate the structural transformation between long and short-chain forms of liquid sulfur using \textit{ab initio} molecular dynamics simulations. Our simulations reveal that sulfur exhibits a complex structural behavior, transitioning between a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure and a disordered, amorphous phase. We find that this transition is influenced by the chain length of the sulfur molecules, with shorter chains favoring the hcp structure and longer chains adopting the amorphous phase. This transition is accompanied by significant changes in the sulfur-sulfur bond length and angle, as well as a shift in the distribution of hydrogen bonding. Through a combination of structural analysis and dynamical properties, we identify a critical chain length above which the amorphous phase becomes thermodynamically stable. Our results demonstrate the importance of considering the chain length dependence of structural transformations in liquid sulfur. We also find that the \textit{ab initio} molecular dynamics simulations provide a more accurate representation of the structural behavior of sulfur than previous simulations based on empirical potentials. Our findings have implications for our understanding of the phase behavior of sulfur and the development of more accurate models for simulating liquid sulfur.

text: In this study, we investigate the spin reorientation transition and disordered rare earth magnetism in Ho₂FeCoO₆. This transition is further corroborated by neutron diffraction studies which reveal a structural transformation accompanying the spin transition. We also explore the effects of disorder within the system, noting that the presence of minor dopants disrupts the long-range order and alters the magnetic properties, consistent with previous theoretical predictions. Our methodology combines advanced magnetic measurement techniques with neutron scattering to elucidate the interplay between spin dynamics and structural changes in Ho₂FeCoO₆. These findings contribute significantly to our understanding of spin reorientation processes in multiferroic materials and offer insights into the role of rare earth elements in such phenomena.

text: In this study, we investigate the role of dimensionality reduction techniques in enhancing the performance of linear classification models. As high-dimensional data presents challenges such as increased computational complexity and the curse of dimensionality, we aim to identify effective methods to mitigate these issues while preserving essential feature information. We employ a combination of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) as our dimensionality reduction strategies to transform datasets from their original high-dimensional space into a lower-dimensional representation. Using benchmark datasets across various domains, we conduct a series of experiments to evaluate the impact of reduced dimensionality on the accuracy and efficiency of linear classifiers, including Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines. Our results demonstrate that dimensionality reduction not only accelerates training times but also improves classification accuracy by alleviating overfitting and noise in the data. Notably, we find that PCA outperforms t-SNE in terms of preserving global structure while maintaining essential class separability. Additionally, we analyze the trade-offs involved, emphasizing the importance of choosing appropriate dimensionality reduction techniques that align with specific dataset characteristics and classification goals. Through our comprehensive analysis, we highlight the critical role of dimensionality reduction in optimizing linear classification outcomes, thereby providing valuable insights for practitioners aiming to enhance model performance in high-dimensional settings. Our findings contribute to the ongoing discourse on efficient data handling and underscore the necessity of incorporating dimensionality reduction methodologies in the pipeline of machine learning applications.

text: We investigated the fundamental property of Ehrhart f*-coefficients in polytopal complexes, revealing a crucial connection to non-negative integer coefficients. Through a rigorous analysis of the Ehrhart f-polynomial, we demonstrated that the coefficients of this polynomial are inherently non-negative integers. This result has significant implications for the study of polytopal complexes, as it establishes a profound connection between the combinatorial and algebraic aspects of these geometric objects.  Our approach involved a detailed examination of the properties of Ehrhart f-polynomials, leveraging advanced techniques from algebraic geometry and combinatorics. By exploiting the relationships between the coefficients of the Ehrhart f-polynomial and the geometric structure of the polytopal complex, we were able to establish a clear and rigorous proof of the non-negativity of these coefficients. This proof relies on the interplay between the combinatorial properties of the complex and the algebraic structure of the Ehrhart f-polynomial.  Our findings have far-reaching consequences for the study of polytopal complexes, providing a fundamental insight into the nature of Ehrhart f-coefficients. The demonstration of their non-negativity opens up new avenues for research, enabling the development of more sophisticated models and algorithms for the analysis of polytopal complexes. Furthermore, the connections between the Ehrhart f-coefficients and non-negative integer coefficients have significant implications for the broader field of combinatorics, highlighting the deep interplay between geometric and algebraic structures.

Quantum teleportation is a process in which an unknown quantum state is
transferred between two spatially separated subspaces of a bipartite quantum
system which share an entangled state and communicate classically. In the case
of photonic states, this process is probabilistic due to the impossibility of
performing a two-particle complete Bell state analysis with linear optics. In
order to achieve a deterministic teleportation scheme, harnessing other degrees
of freedom of a single particle, rather than a third particle, has been
proposed. Indeed, this leads to a novel type of deterministic teleportation
scheme, the so-called hybrid teleportation. Here we report the first
realization of photonic hybrid quantum teleportation from spin-to-orbital
angular momentum degrees of freedom. In our scheme, the polarization state of
photon A is transferred to orbital angular momentum of photon B. The teleported
states are visualized in real-time by means of an intensified CCD camera. The
quality of teleported states is verified by performing quantum state
tomography, which confirms an average fidelity higher than 99.4%. We believe
this experiment paves the route towards a novel way of quantum communication in
which encryption and decryption are carried out in naturally different Hilbert
spaces, and therefore may provide means of enhancing security.
label: human

text: We investigate the fast magnetic rotator regime of stellar winds, a phenomenon characterized by the rapid rotation of magnetic field lines within the wind. Through a combination of numerical simulations and analytical modeling, we demonstrate that the fast magnetic rotator regime is a common feature of stellar winds with high angular velocities, particularly in the context of magnetized stellar atmospheres.   Our simulations reveal that the fast magnetic rotator regime is driven by the competition between the Coriolis force, which arises from the rotation of the star, and the magnetic pressure, which is generated by the interaction between the magnetic field and the stellar wind. We find that the fast magnetic rotator regime leads to the formation of complex magnetic field structures, including twisted and helical field lines, which can significantly impact the overall evolution of the stellar wind.  Our results also highlight the importance of the stellar rotation rate in determining the fast magnetic rotator regime. We find that stars with higher angular velocities are more likely to exhibit this regime, and that the fast magnetic rotator regime can lead to the formation of strong magnetic reconnection events, which can have significant implications for the overall energy budget of the stellar wind. Our study provides new insights into the complex interactions between the stellar rotation, magnetic field, and wind, and has significant implications for our understanding of the magnetized stellar atmospheres.
label: machine

text: This study investigates the impact of local randomization and device imperfections on the BB84 protocol, a widely used quantum key distribution (QKD) scheme. The BB84 protocol relies on the principles of quantum mechanics to encode and decode quantum keys between two parties, traditionally referred to as Alice and Bob. However, in practice, device imperfections and local randomization can compromise the security of the protocol, leading to reduced key rates and potential vulnerabilities.  The objective of this research is to analyze the effects of local randomization and device imperfections on the BB84 protocol's asymptotic key rate, with a focus on identifying the most critical factors that affect key rate degradation. The analysis is based on a theoretical framework, incorporating the principles of quantum mechanics and information theory.  The proposed method involves simulating various scenarios of local randomization and device imperfections, and evaluating their impact on the BB84 protocol's key rate. The results show that local randomization and device imperfections can significantly degrade the key rate, with the most severe effects occurring when both factors are combined. The study also identifies the optimal parameters for minimizing key rate degradation, providing valuable insights for the implementation of secure quantum communication systems.  The findings of this research have significant implications for the practical implementation of BB84 protocol, highlighting the need for careful consideration of device imperfections and local randomization when designing secure quantum communication systems. The results provide a foundation for further research into the optimization of BB84 protocol parameters and the development of more resilient quantum key distribution schemes.

Generalizing the definition of Cartier, we introduce $p^n$-typical formal
group laws over $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-algebras. An oriented cohomology theory in
the sense of Levin-Morel is called $p^n$-typical if its corresponding formal
group law is $p^n$-typical. The main result of the paper is the construction of
'Chern classes' from the algebraic $n$-th Morava K-theory to every
$p^n$-typical oriented cohomology theory.
  If the coefficient ring of a $p^n$-typical theory is a free
$\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-module we also prove that these Chern classes freely
generate all operations to it. Examples of such theories are algebraic $mn$-th
Morava K-theories $K(nm)^*$ for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and
$\mathrm{CH}^*\otimes\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ (operations to Chow groups were studied
in a previous paper). The universal $p^n$-typical oriented theory is
$BP\{n\}^*=BP^*/(v_j,j\nmid n)$ which coefficient ring is also a free
$\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-module.
  Chern classes from the $n$-th algebraic Morava K-theory $K(n)^*$ to itself
allow us to introduce the gamma filtration on $K(n)^*$. This is the best
approximation to the topological filtration obtained by values of operations
and it satisfies properties similar to that of the classical gamma filtration
on $K_0$. The major difference from the classical case is that Chern classes
from the graded factors $gr^i_\gamma K(n)^*$ to
$\mathrm{CH}^i\otimes\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ are surjective for $i\le p^n$. For some
projective homogeneous varieties this allows to estimate $p$-torsion in Chow
groups of codimension up to $p^n$.

We present observations of a chromospheric jet and growing "loop" system that
show new evidence of a fan-spine topology resulting from magnetic flux
emergence. This event, occurring in an equatorial coronal hole on 2007 February
9, was observed by the Hinode Solar Optical Telescope in the Ca II H line in
unprecedented detail. The predecessor of the jet is a bundle of fine material
threads that extend above the chromosphere and appear to rotate about the
bundle axis at ~50 km/s (period <200 s). These rotations or transverse
oscillations propagate upward at velocities up to 786 km/s. The bundle first
slowly and then rapidly swings up, with the transition occurring at the onset
of an A4.9 flare. A loop expands simultaneously in these two phases (velocity:
16-135 km/s). Near the peak of the flare, the loop appears to rupture;
simultaneous upward ejecta and mass downflows faster than free-fall appear in
one of the loop legs. The material bundle then swings back in a whiplike manner
and develops into a collimated jet, which is orientated along the inferred open
field lines with transverse oscillations continuing at slower rates. Some
material falls back along smooth streamlines, showing no more oscillations. At
low altitudes, the streamlines bifurcate at presumably a magnetic null point
and bypass an inferred dome, depicting an inverted-Y geometry. These
streamlines closely match in space the late Ca II H loop and X-ray flare loop.
These observations are consistent with the model that flux emergence in an
open-field region leads to magnetic reconnection, forming a jet and fan-spine
topology. We propose that the material bundle and collimated jet represent the
outer spine in quasi-static and eruptive stages, respectively, and the growing
loop is a 2D projection of the 3D fan surface.

Consider two data providers, each maintaining records of different feature
sets about common entities. They aim to learn a linear model over the whole set
of features. This problem of federated learning over vertically partitioned
data includes a crucial upstream issue: entity resolution, i.e. finding the
correspondence between the rows of the datasets. It is well known that entity
resolution, just like learning, is mistake-prone in the real world. Despite the
importance of the problem, there has been no formal assessment of how errors in
entity resolution impact learning.
  In this paper, we provide a thorough answer to this question, answering how
optimal classifiers, empirical losses, margins and generalisation abilities are
affected. While our answer spans a wide set of losses --- going beyond proper,
convex, or classification calibrated ---, it brings simple practical arguments
to upgrade entity resolution as a preprocessing step to learning. One of these
suggests that entity resolution should be aimed at controlling or minimizing
the number of matching errors between examples of distinct classes. In our
experiments, we modify a simple token-based entity resolution algorithm so that
it indeed aims at avoiding matching rows belonging to different classes, and
perform experiments in the setting where entity resolution relies on noisy
data, which is very relevant to real world domains. Notably, our approach
covers the case where one peer \textit{does not} have classes, or a noisy
record of classes. Experiments display that using the class information during
entity resolution can buy significant uplift for learning at little expense
from the complexity standpoint.
label: human

We present a systematic survey of multiple velocity-resolved H$_2$O spectra
using Herschel/HIFI towards nine nearby actively star forming galaxies. The
ground-state and low-excitation lines (E$_{\rm up}\,\le 130\,{\rm K}$) show
profiles with emission and absorption blended together, while absorption-free
medium-excitation lines ($130\,{\rm K}\, \le\, E_{\rm up}\,\le\,350\,{\rm K}$)
typically display line shapes similar to CO. We analyze the HIFI observation
together with archival SPIRE/PACS H$_2$O data using a state-of-the-art 3D
radiative transfer code which includes the interaction between continuum and
line emission. The water excitation models are combined with information on the
dust- and CO spectral line energy distribution to determine the physical
structure of the interstellar medium (ISM). We identify two ISM components that
are common to all galaxies: A warm ($T_{\rm dust}\,\sim\,40-70\,{\rm K}$),
dense ($n({\rm H})\,\sim\,10^5-10^6\,{\rm cm^{-3}}$) phase which dominates the
emission of medium-excitation H$_2$O lines. This gas phase also dominates the
FIR emission and the CO intensities for $J_{\rm up} > 8$. In addition a cold
($T_{\rm dust}\,\sim\,20-30\,{\rm K}$), dense ($n({\rm H})\sim\,10^4-
10^5\,{\rm cm^{-3}}$) more extended phase is present. It outputs the emission
in the low-excitation H$_2$O lines and typically also produces the prominent
line absorption features. For the two ULIRGs in our sample (Arp 220 and Mrk
231) an even hotter and more compact (R$_s\,\le\,100$ pc) region is present
which is possibly linked to AGN activity. We find that collisions dominate the
water excitation in the cold gas and for lines with $E_{\rm up}\le300\,{\rm K}$
and $E_{\rm up}\le800\,{\rm K}$ in the warm and hot component, respectively.
Higher energy levels are mainly excited by IR pumping.

text: We investigate the dynamics of Rayleigh-Taylor unstable flames, focusing on the speed at which these flames propagate under varying conditions of gravitational influence and density stratification. Our approach employs a series of numerical simulations and experimental setups that replicate the conditions necessary for observing Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities in reactive environments. Through systematic variation of parameters such as flame temperature, density differences, and gravitational acceleration, we delineate the thresholds at which flame propagation transitions from subsonic to supersonic behavior.  The results demonstrate a critical relationship between the instability growth rates and the speed of the flame front, revealing that under specific gravity-driven conditions, flames can achieve enhanced propagation speeds. Notably, we observe that increased density gradients lead to a significant acceleration of the flame front, a finding that contradicts traditional understandings of combustion dynamics in static mediums. By analyzing the interaction between buoyancy-driven flows and the combustion process, we provide insight into the underlying mechanisms governing flame dynamics in unstable environments.  Our methodology incorporates advanced computational fluid dynamics techniques alongside high-resolution imaging to capture transient phenomena in real time. We further validate our findings against established theoretical models and existing experimental data, solidifying our contribution to the field of combustion research. Through this work, we aim to elucidate the complex relationship between flame behavior and Rayleigh-Taylor instability, ultimately advancing our understanding of combustion in both natural and engineered systems.
label: machine

text: This study investigates the thermal boundary conductance across rough interfaces probed by molecular dynamics simulations. Thermal boundary conductance, a critical parameter in heat transfer, is often hindered by the presence of rough interfaces, leading to significant thermal resistance. The objective of this research is to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of thermal boundary conductance across rough interfaces and to develop a predictive model for thermal conductivity in such systems.  Molecular dynamics simulations were employed to model the thermal behavior of rough interfaces, with a focus on the role of surface roughness, interface roughness, and thermal boundary layer characteristics. The simulations were conducted on a range of interface geometries, including rough and smooth surfaces, and were characterized by varying levels of surface roughness and interface roughness. The results indicate that the thermal boundary conductance is significantly reduced in systems with rough interfaces, and that the degree of thermal resistance is directly correlated with the level of surface and interface roughness.  Key findings include the identification of a critical interface roughness threshold, beyond which the thermal boundary conductance is severely impaired. The results also reveal that the thermal boundary layer is significantly affected by the presence of rough interfaces, leading to increased thermal resistance and reduced thermal conductivity. These findings have important implications for the design and optimization of heat transfer systems, and provide a foundation for the development of predictive models for thermal conductivity in rough interface systems.
label: machine

text:
This article is about how the "SP theory of intelligence" and its realisation
in the "SP machine" may, with advantage, be applied to the management and
analysis of big data. The SP system -- introduced in the article and fully
described elsewhere -- may help to overcome the problem of variety in big data:
it has potential as "a universal framework for the representation and
processing of diverse kinds of knowledge" (UFK), helping to reduce the
diversity of formalisms and formats for knowledge and the different ways in
which they are processed. It has strengths in the unsupervised learning or
discovery of structure in data, in pattern recognition, in the parsing and
production of natural language, in several kinds of reasoning, and more. It
lends itself to the analysis of streaming data, helping to overcome the problem
of velocity in big data. Central in the workings of the system is lossless
compression of information: making big data smaller and reducing problems of
storage and management. There is potential for substantial economies in the
transmission of data, for big cuts in the use of energy in computing, for
faster processing, and for smaller and lighter computers. The system provides a
handle on the problem of veracity in big data, with potential to assist in the
management of errors and uncertainties in data. It lends itself to the
visualisation of knowledge structures and inferential processes. A
high-parallel, open-source version of the SP machine would provide a means for
researchers everywhere to explore what can be done with the system and to
create new versions of it.
label: human

text:
The galactic environment has been suspected to influence planetary
habitability in many ways. Very metal-poor regions of the Galaxy, or those
largely devoid of atoms more massive than H and He, are thought to be unable to
form habitable planets. Moreover, if such planets do form, the young system is
subjected to close stellar passages while it resides in its stellar birth
cluster. Various potential hazards remain after clusters disperse. For
instance, central galactic regions may present risks to habitability via nearby
supernovae, gamma ray bursts (GRBs), and frequent comet showers. In addition,
planets residing within very wide binary star systems are affected by the
Galaxy, as local gravitational perturbations from the Galaxy can increase the
binary's eccentricity until it destabilizes the planets it hosts. Here we
review the most recent work on the main galactic influences over planetary
habitability. Although there must be some metallicity limit below which rocky
planets cannot form, recent exoplanet surveys show that they form around stars
with a very large range of metallicities. Once formed, the probability of star
clusters destabilizing planetary systems only becomes high for rare, extremely
long-lived clusters. Regarding threats to habitability from supernovae, GRBs,
and comet showers, many recent studies suggest that their hazards are more
limited than originally thought. Finally, denser regions of the Galaxy enhance
the threat that very wide binary companions pose to planetary habitability, but
the probability that a very wide binary star disrupts habitability will always
be substantially below 100% for any environment. While some Milky Way regions
must be more hospitable to habitable planets than others, it is difficult to
state that habitable planets are confined to any well-defined region of the
Galaxy or that any other particular region of the Galaxy is uninhabitable.
label: human

We consider a class of optimization problems for sparse signal reconstruction
which arise in the field of Compressed Sensing (CS). A plethora of approaches
and solvers exist for such problems, for example GPSR, FPC AS, SPGL1, NestA,
$\ell_{1}_\ell_{s}$, PDCO to mention a few. Compressed Sensing applications
lead to very well conditioned optimization problems and therefore can be solved
easily by simple first-order methods. Interior point methods (IPMs) rely on the
Newton method hence they use the second-order information. They have numerous
advantageous features and one clear drawback: being the second-order approach
they need to solve linear equations and this operation has (in the general
dense case) an $O(n^3)$ computational complexity. Attempts have been made to
specialize IPMs to sparse reconstruction problems and they have led to
interesting developments implemented in $\ell_1\_\ell_s$ and PDCO softwares. We
go a few steps further. First, we use the matrix-free interior point method, an
approach which redesigns IPM to avoid the need to explicitly formulate (and
store) the Newton equation systems. Secondly, we exploit the special features
of the signal processing matrices within the matrix-free IPM. Two such features
are of particular interest: an excellent conditioning of these matrices and the
ability to perform inexpensive (low complexity) matrix-vector multiplications
with them. Computational experience with large scale one-dimensional signals
confirms that the new approach is efficient and offers an attractive
alternative to other state-of-the-art solvers.
label: human

text: We present an analysis of the mass function (IMF) of young stellar populations in the central regions of M87, the most massive galaxy in the local universe. By combining multi-band imaging from the Hubble Space Telescope with deep near-infrared spectroscopy obtained with the Gemini Observatory, we investigate the radial variations of M87's IMF. Our results reveal a flattening of the IMF towards the galaxy center, with a break mass of approximately 1.5 solar masses. This trend was not evident in previous studies based on Hα or optical imaging data alone, but is consistent with recent studies utilizing multi-wavelength data. We attribute this flattening of the IMF to the ongoing merger activity and the resulting quenching of star formation in the central regions of M87. Our findings suggest that the IMF in the central regions of massive galaxies may be shaped by environmental processes and that this effect is more prominent in the near-infrared wavelengths. The understanding of these processes is crucial for comprehending the formation and evolution of massive galaxies. Our methodology combines state-of-the-art observations with rigorous data analysis techniques, including the use of stellar population models and Bayesian inference to derive the IMF from our data. Our results contribute to the ongoing debate about the origin of the observed mass scale relation between massive galaxies and their central supermassive black holes.
label: machine

text:
Cygnus X is one of the most complex areas in the sky. This complicates
interpretation, but also creates the opportunity to investigate accretion into
molecular clouds and many subsequent stages of star formation, all within one
small field of view. Understanding large complexes like Cygnus X is the key to
understanding the dominant role that massive star complexes play in galaxies
across the Universe.
  The main goal of this study is to establish feasibility of a high-resolution
CO survey of the entire Cygnus X region by observing part of it as a
Pathfinder, and to evaluate the survey as a tool for investigating the
star-formation process.
  A 2x4 degree area of the Cygnus X region has been mapped in the 12CO(3-2)
line at an angular resolution of 15" and a velocity resolution of ~0.4km/s
using HARP-B and ACSIS on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope. The star formation
process is heavily connected to the life-cycle of the molecular material in the
interstellar medium. The high critical density of the 12CO(3-2) transition
reveals clouds in key stages of molecule formation, and shows processes that
turn a molecular cloud into a star.
  We observed ~15% of Cygnus X, and demonstrated that a full survey would be
feasible and rewarding. We detected three distinct layers of 12CO(3-2)
emission, related to the Cygnus Rift (500-800 pc), to W75N (1-1.8 kpc), and to
DR21 (1.5-2.5 kpc). Within the Cygnus Rift, HI self-absorption features are
tightly correlated with faint diffuse CO emission, while HISA features in the
DR21 layer are mostly unrelated to any CO emission. 47 molecular outflows were
detected in the Pathfinder, 27 of them previously unknown. Sequentially
triggered star formation is a widespread phenomenon.
label: human

text: This abstract discusses the revisit of the SDB (Subdwarf B) pulsating star V391 Peg and its potential giant planet companion using over a decade of time-series photometric data. Initially discovered through radial velocity measurements, V391 Peg has garnered attention due to its variability patterns and possible planetary influence. After analyzing 13 years of photometric observations, the study confirms the presence of a significant light variation that cannot be solely attributed to stellar pulsations. These variations suggest the existence of a companion orbiting within the star's radius, consistent with a giant planet hypothesis. The analysis employed Lomb-Scargle periodograms to identify periodicities indicative of planetary transit-like events, which were further confirmed by Bayesian statistical methods. Key findings include the establishment of a likely orbital period and the estimation of the mass and radius of the putative giant planet. The results contribute to our understanding of the complex dynamics within binary systems and provide new insights into the formation and evolution of planetary companions around subdwarf stars.
label: machine

In this paper we consider a massless scalar field, with a possible coupling
$\xi$ to the Ricci scalar in a $D$ dimensional FLRW spacetime with a constant
deceleration parameter $q=\epsilon-1$, $\epsilon=-{\dot{H}}/{H^2}$. Correlation
functions for the Bunch-Davies vacuum of such a theory have long been known to
be infrared divergent for a wide range of values of $\epsilon$. We resolve
these divergences by explicitly matching the spacetime under consideration to a
spacetime without infrared divergencies. Such a procedure ensures that all
correlation functions with respect to the vacuum in the spacetime of interest
are infrared finite. In this newly defined vacuum we construct the coincidence
limit of the propagator and as an example calculate the expectation value of
the stress energy tensor. We find that this approach gives both in the
ultraviolet and in the infrared satisfactory results. Moreover, we find that,
unless the effective mass due to the coupling to the Ricci scalar $\xi R$ is
negative, quantum contributions to the energy density always dilute away
faster, or just as fast, as the background energy density. Therefore, quantum
backreaction is insignificant at the one loop order, unless $\xi R$ is
negative. Finally we compare this approach with known results where the
infrared is regulated by placing the Universe in a finite box. In an
accelerating universe, the results are qualitatively the same, provided one
identifies the size of the Universe with the physical Hubble radius at the time
of the matching. In a decelerating universe however, the two schemes give
different late time behavior for the quantum stress energy tensor. This happens
because in this case the length scale at which one regulates the infrared
becomes sub-Hubble at late times.
label: human

Statistical studies of galaxy-galaxy interactions often utilise net change in
physical properties of progenitors as a function of the separation between
their nuclei to trace both the strength and the observable timescale of their
interaction. In this study, we use two-point auto, cross and mark correlation
functions to investigate the extent to which small-scale clustering properties
of star forming galaxies can be used to gain physical insight into
galaxy-galaxy interactions between galaxies of similar optical brightness and
stellar mass. The Halpha star formers, drawn from the highly spatially complete
Galaxy And Mass Assembly (GAMA) survey, show an increase in clustering on small
separations. Moreover, the clustering strength shows a strong dependence on
optical brightness and stellar mass, where (1) the clustering amplitude of
optically brighter galaxies at a given separation is larger than that of
optically fainter systems, (2) the small scale clustering properties (e.g. the
strength, the scale at which the signal relative to the fiducial power law
plateaus) of star forming galaxies appear to differ as a function of increasing
optical brightness of galaxies. According to cross and mark correlation
analyses, the former result is largely driven by the increased dust content in
optically bright star forming galaxies. The latter could be interpreted as
evidence of a correlation between interaction-scale and optical brightness of
galaxies, where physical evidence of interactions between optically bright star
formers, likely hosted within relatively massive halos, persist over larger
separations than those between optically faint star formers.

text: We present a novel approach to concurrent multi-domain simulations in linear structural dynamics using the Multiple Grid Multiple Time-Scale (MGMT) method. This method enables the efficient simulation of complex systems by dividing the computational domain into multiple grids and solving the equations of motion at different time scales simultaneously. By exploiting the hierarchical structure of the system, we can achieve significant reductions in computational time and memory requirements.  Our approach involves the decomposition of the system into multiple grids, each representing a distinct time scale or spatial region. The equations of motion are then solved on each grid using a combination of finite element methods and time-stepping schemes. The results from each grid are combined using a hierarchical interpolation scheme to produce a consistent and accurate solution across the entire domain.  Through a series of numerical experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the MGMT method in simulating complex linear structural dynamics systems. We show that the method can efficiently capture the dynamic behavior of systems with multiple time scales, including those with high-frequency oscillations and low-frequency modes. Our results also indicate that the MGMT method can achieve significant reductions in computational time and memory requirements compared to traditional simulation methods.  By developing a systematic and efficient approach to concurrent multi-domain simulations, we aim to enable the simulation of complex linear structural dynamics systems in a wide range of applications, including structural health monitoring, aerospace engineering, and civil engineering.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the diversity of electromagnetic transients associated with the birth of magnetars, focusing on their observational characteristics and underlying physical mechanisms. Our work aims to address the complexities in transient classification and the challenge of connecting observational signatures with theoretical models of magnetar birth. Through the application of advanced computational simulations, we model the dynamical processes involved in the magnetar formation, including the interplay between magnetic fields, rotational dynamics, and energy dissipation. We systematically analyze a comprehensive dataset of transient events, encompassing gamma-ray bursts, X-ray flashes, and fast radio bursts, utilizing multi-wavelength observational data. By synthesizing this empirical evidence with our simulations, we uncover distinct transient signatures that correlate with specific conditions during a magnetar's birth, such as varying initial magnetic field strengths and spin periods. These findings reveal a spectrum of transient behaviors, emphasizing the role of magnetic field configuration and rotational energy in shaping the observed phenomena. Furthermore, our results suggest a potential unification framework for seemingly disparate transient events, contributing to a more coherent understanding of magnetar-associated phenomena. The integration of observational data with theoretical modeling offers insights into the early magnetar evolution, providing a pathway for refining progenitor models. Our study serves as a pivotal step towards resolving ongoing debates within the astrophysical community regarding the nature of high-energy transient sources and enhances our capability to interpret forthcoming observations from advanced telescopes. This work not only advances our comprehension of magnetar birth but also enriches the broader field of transient astrophysics.
label: machine

The Kondo scale TK for impurity systems is expected to guarantee universal
scaling of physical quantities. However, in practice, not every definition of
TK necessarily supports this notion away from the strict scaling limit.
Specifically, this paper addresses the role of finite bandwidth D in the
strongly-correlated Kondo regime. For this, various theoretical definitions of
TK are analyzed based on the inverse magnetic impurity susceptibility at zero
temperature. While conventional definitions in that respect quickly fail to
ensure universal Kondo scaling for all D, this paper proposes an altered
definition of TK_{sc} that allows universal scaling of dynamical or thermal
quantities for a given fixed Hamiltonian. If the scaling is performed with
respect to an external parameter which directly enters the Hamiltonian, such as
magnetic field, the corresponding TK_{sc;B} for universal scaling differs, yet
becomes equivalent to TK_{sc} in the scaling limit. The only requirement for
universal scaling in the full Kondo parameter regime with a residual error of
less than 1% is a well-defined isolated Kondo feature with TK < 0.01D. By
varying D over a wide range relative to the bare energies of the impurity, for
example, this allows a smooth transition from the Anderson to the Kondo model.
label: human

Central finite difference schemes have long been avoided in the context of
two-phase flows for the advection of the phase indicator function due to
numerical overshoots and undershoots associated with their dispersion errors.
We will show however, for an incompressible flow, in the context of a specific
diffuse interface model, one can maintain the boundedness of the phase field
while also taking advantage of the low cost and ease of implementation of
central differences to construct a non-dissipative discretization scheme for
the advective terms. This is made possible by combining the advection and
reinitialization steps of a conservative level set scheme introduced by Olsson
and Kreiss [J. Comput. Phys., 210, 225 (2005)] to form a phase field equation
similar to that of Chiu and Lin [J. Comput. Phys., 230, 185 (2011)]. Instead of
resorting to specialized upwind methods as in these articles, we prove that the
boundedness of the phase field is guaranteed for certain choices of the free
parameters ($\epsilon$ and $\gamma$) for a specific central difference scheme
that we propose. The proposed discretely conservative and bounded phase field
equation, which is free of any reinitialization or mass redistribution,
possesses desirable properties that can be leveraged in the coupled finite
difference discretization of the two-phase momentum equation. Additionally, as
compared to the state-of-the-art conservative and bounded two-phase flow
methods, the proposed method boasts competitive accuracy-vs-cost trade-off,
small memory requirements, ease of implementation and excellent
parallelizability, providing a viable alternative for realistic two-phase flow
calculations.
label: human

Understanding single pion production reactions on free nucleons is the first
step towards a correct description of these processes in nuclei, which are
important for signal and background contributions in current and near future
accelerator neutrino oscillation experiments. In this work, we reanalyze our
previous studies of neutrino-induced one-pion production on nucleons for
outgoing $\pi N$ invariant masses below 1.4 GeV. Our motivation is to get a
better description of the $\nu_\mu n\to\mu^- n\pi^+$ cross section, for which
current theoretical models give values significantly below data. This channel
is very sensitive to the crossed $\Delta (1232)$ contribution and thus to spin
1/2 components in the Rarita-Schwinger $\Delta$ propagator. We show how these
spin 1/2 components are nonpropagating and give rise to contact interactions.
In this context, we point out that the discrepancy with experiment might be
corrected by the addition of appropriate extra contact terms and argue that
this procedure will provide a natural solution to the $\nu_\mu n\to\mu^-
n\pi^+$ puzzle. To keep our model simple, in this work we propose to change the
strength of the spin 1/2 components in the $\Delta$ propagator and use the
$\nu_\mu n\to\mu^- n\pi^+$ data to constraint its value. With this

Results from a new series of experiments on turbulent flows in a rotating
circular container are presented. Electromagnetic forcing is applied to induce
flow in a layer of fluid of constant depth. Continuously forced as well as
decaying flows are investigated. Optical altimetry is used to measure the
gradient of the surface elevation field and to obtain the velocity and
vorticity fields with high temporal and spatial resolution. Spectral analysis
of the flows demonstrates the formation of dual cascade with energy and
enstrophy intervals although the corresponding spectral fluxes of energy and
enstrophy are not uniform in these intervals. The energy interval is
characterized by the slope of approximately -5/3 in terms of wavenumber and is
limited in extent by the finite radius of deformation effect. In the enstrophy
range, the slope is steeper than -3 due to the presence of long-lived coherent
vortices. The spatial patterns of spectral fluxes in the flow indicate that
inverse energy transfer and direct enstrophy transfer occur mainly in elongated
vorticity patches. Cyclone/anticyclone asymmetry in favor of anticyclones is
observed in our flows. Dominance of anticyclones is most clear during the decay
phase of turbulence. The anticyclones remain circular while cyclonic vorticity
is stretched into elongated patches. Measurements show that skewness of
vorticity distribution increases with increasing Froude number of the flow.
Inertial and Kelvin waves are detected in our experiments; their
characteristics are analysed against the appropriate dispersion relations.

density of Omega_HI=(2.33+-0.07)*10^-4/h for the sample z=0.065. We discuss

Given a bimatrix game, the associated leadership or commitment games are
defined as the games at which one player, the leader, commits to a (possibly
mixed) strategy and the other player, the follower, chooses his strategy after
having observed the irrevocable commitment of the leader. Based on a result by
von Stengel and Zamir [2010], the notions of commitment value and commitment
optimal strategies for each player are discussed as a possible solution
concept. It is shown that in non-degenerate bimatrix games (a) pure commitment
optimal strategies together with the follower's best response constitute Nash
equilibria, and (b) strategies that participate in a completely mixed Nash
equilibrium are strictly worse than commitment optimal strategies, provided
they are not matrix game optimal. For various classes of bimatrix games that
generalize zero sum games, the relationship between the maximin value of the
leader's payoff matrix, the Nash equilibrium payoff and the commitment optimal
value is discussed. For the Traveler's Dilemma, the commitment optimal strategy
and commitment value for the leader are evaluated and seem more acceptable as a
solution than the unique Nash equilibrium. Finally, the relationship between
commitment optimal strategies and Nash equilibria in $2 \times 2$ bimatrix
games is thoroughly examined and in addition, necessary and sufficient
conditions for the follower to be worse off at the equilibrium of the
leadership game than at any Nash equilibrium of the simultaneous move game are
provided.

Vela X-1 is the prototype of the class of wind-fed accreting pulsars in high
mass X-ray binaries hosting a supergiant donor. We have analyzed in a
systematic way ten years of INTEGRAL data of Vela X-1 (22-50 keV) and we found
that when outside the X-ray eclipse, the source undergoes several luminosity
drops where the hard X-rays luminosity goes below 3x10^35 erg/s, becoming
undetected by INTEGRAL. These drops in the X-ray flux are usually referred to
as "off-states" in the literature. We have investigated the distribution of
these off-states along the Vela X-1 ~8.9 d orbit, finding that their orbital
occurrence displays an asymmetric distribution, with a higher probability to
observe an off-state near the pre-eclipse than during the post-eclipse. This
asymmetry can be explained by scattering of hard X-rays in a region of ionized
wind, able to reduce the source hard X-ray brightness preferentially near
eclipse ingress. We associate this ionized large-scale wind structure with the
photoionization wake produced by the interaction of the supergiant wind with
the X-ray emission from the neutron star. We emphasize that this observational
result could be obtained thanks to the accumulation of a decade of INTEGRAL
data, with observations covering the whole orbit several times, allowing us to
detect an asymmetric pattern in the orbital distribution of off-states in Vela
X-1.

Mechanism design is concerned with settings where a policymaker (or social
planner) faces the problem of aggregating the announced preferences of multiple
agents into a collective (or social), system-wide decision. One of the most
important ways for aggregating preference that has been used in multi-agent
systems is election. In an election, the aim is to select the candidate who
reflects the common will of society. Despite the importance of this subject, in
some situations, the result of the election does not respect the purpose of
those who execute it and the election leads to dissatisfaction of a large
amount of people and in some cases causes polarization in societies. To analyze
these situations, we introduce a new notion called social disappointment and we
show which voting rules can prevent it in elections. In addition, we propose
new protocols to prevent social disappointment in elections. A version of the
impossibility theorem is proved regarding social disappointment in elections,
showing that there is no voting rule for four or more candidates that
simultaneously satisfies avoiding social disappointment and Condorcet winner
criteria. We give conditions under which one of our new protocols always
selects the Condorcet winner under the assumption of single peakedness. We
empirically compare our protocols with seven well-known other voting protocols
and observe that our protocols are capable of preventing social disappointment
and are more robust against manipulations.

text: We investigate a novel scenario for inflationary magnetogenesis, one that avoids the need for strong coupling between the inflaton and magnetic fields. Our approach builds upon the notion that the magnetic field can be generated through the anisotropic diffusion of the inflaton, rather than through the interaction with a separate magnetic field. We demonstrate that this scenario can produce a robust and self-consistent magnetic field, with properties consistent with observations.   Our calculations reveal that the magnetic field can be generated through the anisotropic diffusion of the inflaton, resulting in a highly anisotropic and turbulent field structure. This structure is characterized by a large-scale magnetic field with a specific topology, which can be linked to the anisotropic diffusion process. We show that this scenario can produce a magnetic field that is consistent with the observed properties of the cosmic microwave background radiation and large-scale structure.  We also explore the implications of this scenario for the early universe, and find that it can provide a possible explanation for the observed magnetic field anisotropies. Our results suggest that the magnetic field can be generated through a process that is independent of strong coupling, providing a new perspective on the origins of the cosmic magnetic field. This work provides a novel framework for understanding the relationship between inflation and magnetogenesis, and opens up new avenues for research into the early universe.

In this survey we concern ourself with the question, wether there exists a
fix-free code for a given sequence of codeword lengths. For a given alphabet,
we obtain the {\em Kraftsum} of a code, if we divide for every length the
number of codewords of this length in the code by the total number of all
possible words of this length and then take summation over all codeword lengths
which appears in the code. The same way the Kraftsum of a lengths sequence
$(l_1,..., l_n) $ is given by $\sum_{i=1}^n q^{-l_i} $, where $q$ is the
numbers of letters in the alphabet. Kraft and McMillan have shown in
\cite{kraft} (1956), that there exists a prefix-free code with codeword lengths
of a certain lengths sequence, if the Kraftsum of the lengths sequence is
smaller than or equal to one. Furthermore they have shown, that the converse
also holds for all (uniquely decipherable) codes.\footnote{In this survey a
code means a set of words, such that any message which is encoded with these
words can be uniquely decoded. Therefore we omit in future the "uniquely
decipherable" and write only "code".} The question rises, if Kraft's and
McMillan's result can be generalized to other types of codes? Throughout, we
try to give an answer on this question for the class of fix-free codes. Since
any code has Kraftsum smaller than or equal to one, this answers the question
for the second implication of Kraft-McMillan's theorem. Therefore we pay
attention mainly to the first implication.

We introduce the notion of boundary representation for fractal Fourier
expansions, starting with a familiar notion of spectral pairs for affine
fractal measures. Specializing to one dimension, we establish boundary
representations for these fractals. We prove that as sets these fractals arise
as boundaries of functions in closed subspaces of the Hardy space $H^2$. By
this we mean that there are lacunary subsets $\Gamma$ of the non-negative
integers, and associated closed $\Gamma$-subspace in the Hardy space
$H^2(\bd)$, $\bd$ denoting the disk, such that for every function $f$ in in
$H^2(\Gamma)$, and for every point $z$ in $\bd$, $f(z)$ admits a boundary
integral represented by an associated measure $\mu$, with integration over
$\supp{\mu}$ placed as a Cantor subset on the circle $\bt := \{bd}(\bd)$.
  We study families of pairs: measures $\mu$ and sets $\Gamma$ of lacunary
form, admitting lacunary Fourier series in $L^2(\mu)$; i.e., configurations
$\Gamma$ arranged with a geometric progression of empty spacing, or missing
parts, gaps. Given $\Gamma$, we find corresponding generalized Szeg\" o kernels
$G_\Gamma$, and we compare them to the classical Szeg\" o kernel for $\bd$.
Rather than the more traditional approach of starting with $\mu$, and then
asking for possibilities for sets $\Gamma$, such that we get Fourier series
representations, we turn the problem upside down; now starting instead with a
countably infinite discrete subset $\Gamma$, and, within a new duality
framework, we study the possibilities for choices of measures $\mu$.

text: We present evidence that a compact jet plays a dominant role in shaping the broadband spectrum of the black hole accretor XTE J1550-564. Through a comprehensive analysis of archival X-ray and radio observations, as well as multi-wavelength spectral modeling, we demonstrate that the jet's emission is the primary contributor to the broad-band spectral features observed in the X-ray and radio spectra. Our results indicate that the jet's emission is strongly correlated with the accretion rate, with a significant increase in jet luminosity observed during the peak accretion phase. We also find that the jet's emission is not limited to the radio band, with evidence of jet emission detected in the X-ray band through the observation of a hard X-ray flare. Our spectral modeling reveals that the jet's emission is well described by a synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) model, which is consistent with the observed broad-band spectral energy distribution. The compact jet's dominance over the accretion disk is further supported by the observation of a strong jet-induced variability, which is not accounted for by the accretion disk alone. These findings provide new insights into the complex multi-wavelength behavior of black hole accretors and highlight the importance of compact jets in shaping the broadband spectral features of these systems.

We then performed simulations of a range of biomolecules, including proteins and nucleic acids, on both CPU and GPU architectures. Our results show that GPU-accelerated simulations exhibit significant performance gains, with speedups of up to 100x compared to CPU-based simulations. We also found that the accuracy of the simulations is preserved, with minimal impact on the simulation results. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the scalability of GPU-accelerated simulations is limited by the availability of GPU memory, but still offers substantial benefits over CPU-based simulations.  Overall, our study demonstrates the potential of GPUs to accelerate biomolecular simulations, offering a promising approach for large-scale simulations and simulations of complex biomolecular systems.

We also showed that the method can effectively handle time-dependent exposure patterns, recovering the true causal effects even in the presence of non-linear relationships and sparse effects.  Our findings have significant implications for the analysis of time-dependent exposures in high-dimensional settings, where traditional methods often fail to provide accurate estimates of causal effects. The study concludes that propagating low-frequency slow magnetoacoustic waves are prevalent in fan-like coronal loops, offering insights into the complex mechanisms of solar coronal heating. The observed characteristics further our understanding of wave dynamics in magnetically structured plasma, affirming the importance of wave-based energy transport in maintaining coronal temperatures. for the Langevin equation influences this blowup phenomenon. It is shown that
for a wide class of initial data and initial distributions of particles the
unbounded gradients are eliminated. The case of a linear initial velocity is
particular. We show that if the initial distribution of particles is uniform,
then the mean of the velocity for a given position coincides with the solution
of the Burgers equation and in particular does not depend on the constant
variance of the stochastic perturbation. Further, for a one space space
variable we get the following result: if the decay rate of the power-behaved
initial particles distribution at infinity is greater or equal $|x|^{-2},$ then
the blowup is suppressed, otherwise, the blowup takes place at the same moment
of time as in the case of the non-perturbed Burgers equation.

The recent discovery of the gravitational wave source GW150914 has revealed a
coalescing binary black hole (BBH) with masses of $\sim 30~M_\odot$. Previous
proposals for the origin of such a massive binary include Population III
(PopIII) stars. PopIII stars are efficient producers of BBHs and of a
gravitational wave background (GWB) in the $10-100$ Hz band, and also of
ionizing radiation in the early Universe. We quantify the relation between the
amplitude of the GWB ($\Omega_{\rm gw}$) and the electron scattering optical
depth ($\tau_{\rm e}$), produced by PopIII stars, assuming that $f_{\rm
esc}\approx 10\%$ of their ionizing radiation escapes into the intergalactic
medium. We find that PopIII stars would produce a GWB that is detectable by the
future O5 LIGO/Virgo if $\tau_{\rm e} \gtrsim 0.07$, consistent with the recent
Planck measurement of $\tau_e=0.055 \pm 0.09$. Moreover, the spectral index of
the background from PopIII BBHs becomes as small as ${\rm d}\ln \Omega_{\rm
gw}/{\rm d}\ln f\lesssim 0.3$ at $f \gtrsim 30$ Hz, which is significantly
flatter than the value $\sim 2/3$ generically produced by lower-redshift and
less-massive BBHs. A detection of the unique flattening at such low frequencies
by the O5 LIGO/Virgo will indicate the existence of a high-chirp mass,
high-redshift BBH population, which is consistent with the PopIII origin. A
precise characterization of the spectral shape near $30-50$ Hz by the Einstein
Telescope could also constrain the PopIII initial mass function and star
formation rate.

text: We present the results of our analysis of the Robo-AO Kepler Survey V, which investigated the impact of physically associated stellar companions on planetary systems. Through a comprehensive examination of 2,500 stellar systems, we identified a significant correlation between the presence of stellar companions and the frequency of planetary system architectures characterized by hot Jupiters and multiple planetary systems. Our findings suggest that the gravitational influence of stellar companions can trigger the migration of planets, leading to the formation of hot Jupiters and multiple planetary systems. Furthermore, we discovered that the type of stellar companion, whether a main-sequence companion or a red dwarf companion, influences the planetary system architecture, with main-sequence companions producing more hot Jupiters and red dwarf companions producing more multiple planetary systems. Our results are supported by simulations, which demonstrate that the gravitational influence of stellar companions can facilitate the migration of planets and the formation of complex planetary systems. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of planetary system formation and evolution, highlighting the importance of considering the role of stellar companions in shaping planetary system architectures.
label: machine

text: The abstract for the research paper on the environment of the gamma-ray emitting supernova remnant (SNR) G338.3-0.0 with a proposed hadronic interpretation for the gamma-ray emission from HESS J1640-465 is as follows  This study examines the environment surrounding the gamma-ray-emitting supernova remnant (SNR) G338.3-0.0, focusing on the potential for hadronic processes to explain the observed high-energy gamma-ray emission from the associated source, HESS J1640-465. Previous studies have suggested that the gamma-ray emission could be attributed to interactions between relativistic particles and cosmic rays with interstellar gas within the SNR.   The primary objective of this research is to investigate whether a hadronic model can satisfactorily account for the observed gamma-ray spectrum and spatial distribution. To achieve this, we employed multi-wavelength data analysis, including X-ray observations, radio continuum measurements, and gamma-ray fluxes from Fermi-LAT and H.E.S.S. instruments. Additionally, we utilized detailed simulations of particle interactions in the SNR environment.  Key findings indicate that the observed gamma-ray spectrum can be well-reproduced by a hadronic model where protons and pions are produced through interactions with the SNR's ambient medium. The spatial distribution of gamma-rays also aligns with predictions from this model, suggesting a significant contribution from hadronic processes. However, uncertainties remain regarding the exact nature of the particle acceleration mechanisms and the energy injection rates required to sustain the observed activity.  In conclusion, this research supports the hadronic interpretation for the gamma-ray emission from HESS J1640-465, providing valuable insights into the complex interactions within SNR environments. Further studies are needed to refine models and constraints on the physical conditions within G338.3-0.0.
