text: This study investigates the constraints on chromoelectric dipole moments (CEDMs) within the framework of supersymmetric (SUSY) models, focusing particularly on their implications for the fermion mass spectrum. The research employs a comprehensive analysis of existing theoretical models and experimental data to explore how CEDMs can be used as probes to constrain the parameters of SUSY theories. We identify the key problem of reconciling the predicted CEDMs with the absence of experimental detection, which is a significant challenge in natural SUSY models. Our methodology involves a detailed examination of various SUSY scenarios, including minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) variants, to assess the viability of these models under the constraints imposed by CEDM measurements. Results indicate that while certain SUSY models can accommodate viable CEDM values without conflict with current experimental bounds, others are constrained to specific parameter regions that are less favored by collider searches. Key findings suggest that further precision measurements of CEDMs could provide crucial insights into the nature of new physics beyond the Standard Model, particularly in the context of natural SUSY models.

text: This study focuses on the direct visualization of barrier crossing dynamics in a driven optical matter system, where an external driving force is applied to a system of interacting particles. The objective of this research is to elucidate the role of driving forces in modulating the transition rates and barrier heights in optical lattices, with a view to understanding the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of driven many-body systems.  To achieve this objective, we employed a combination of experimental and theoretical techniques, including real-time imaging of atomic motion and numerical simulations of the driven optical lattice. Our results reveal that the driving force significantly influences the barrier crossing dynamics, leading to an increase in the transition rates and a decrease in the barrier heights. Notably, we observed a strong correlation between the driving force and the emergence of coherent many-body states, which are characterized by enhanced quantum coherence and long-lived superposition states.  Our findings have important implications for our understanding of driven optical systems, where the interplay between driving forces and many-body interactions is crucial for the emergence of complex quantum phenomena. The direct visualization of barrier crossing dynamics in this system provides valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of driven optical matter systems, with potential applications in the development of novel quantum technologies.

text: Bottom mesons, heavy quark hadrons containing a b-quark, play a crucial role in understanding the quark dynamics and properties of the Standard Model. Their study is often carried out through semi-leptonic decays, which produce distinctive displaced vertices. In this study, we describe a method for reconstructing bottom mesons using displaced vertices from semi-leptonic decays. Initially, we select events with missing transverse momentum and isolated leptons. Subsequently, we search for displaced vertices with decay lengths longer than expected for hadronic jets, and reconstruct bottom meson candidates based on their decay topology.  We validate our method using simulated data and demonstrate its efficiency in identifying bottom meson candidates with high purity. We compare the performance of our technique with that of other reconstruction algorithms, such as the Jet Probability method and the Long Lived Particle (LLP) method. The results show significant improvements in bottom meson identification, especially for decays with small decay lengths.  Furthermore, we apply our method to collision data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), achieving a bottom meson identification efficiency of approximately 80%. Our results show that the proposed method for reconstructing bottom mesons using displaced vertices from semi-leptonic decays is effective and promising, opening new possibilities for quark physics studies.  In summary, this study presents a novel method for reconstructing bottom mesons using displaced vertices from semi-leptonic decays. The method is validated to be efficient and effective, improving the bottom meson identification efficiency and enabling new possibilities for quark physics research.

This paper is one of three companion papers presenting the results of our
in-depth analysis of the interstellar neutral helium (ISN He) observations
carried out using the IBEX-Lo during the first six Interstellar Boundary
Explorer (IBEX) observation seasons. We derive corrections for losses due to
the limited throughput of the interface buffer and determine the IBEX spin-axis
pointing. We develop an uncertainty system for the data, taking into account
the resulting correlations between the data points. This system includes
uncertainties due to Poisson statistics, background, spin-axis determination,
systematic deviation of the boresight from the prescribed position, correction
for the interface buffer losses, and the expected Warm Breeze (WB) signal.
Subsequently, we analyze the data from 2009 to examine the role of various
components of the uncertainty system. We show that the ISN He flow parameters
are in good agreement with the values obtained by the original analysis. We
identify the WB as the principal contributor to the global $\chi^2$ values in
previous analyses. Other uncertainties have a much milder role and their
contributions are comparable to each other. The application of this uncertainty
system reduced the minimum $\chi^2$ value 4-fold. The obtained $\chi^2$ value,
still exceeding the expected value, suggests that either the uncertainty system
may still be incomplete or the adopted physical model lacks a potentially
important element, which is likely an imperfect determination of the WB
parameters. The derived corrections and uncertainty system are used in the
accompanying paper by Bzowski et al. in an analysis of the data from six
seasons.

text: Open inflation, a theoretical concept in modern cosmology, proposes that the universe underwent a period of rapid expansion in the very early stages of its evolution, leading to the formation of structure and the distribution of matter as we observe it today. This phenomenon is thought to have occurred in the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang, when the universe was still extremely hot and dense. The open inflation model differs from the more widely accepted flat or closed inflation models, and its implications for our understanding of the universe's evolution and ultimate fate are significant.  The objective of this research is to investigate the potential consequences of open inflation on the large-scale structure of the universe, with a particular focus on the distribution of galaxies and galaxy clusters. Using a combination of theoretical models and numerical simulations, this study aims to shed light on the role of open inflation in shaping the cosmic landscape. By analyzing the effects of open inflation on the formation of structure and the distribution of matter, this research seeks to provide new insights into the fundamental laws of physics that govern the universe's evolution.  Numerical simulations of the open inflation model reveal that the rapid expansion of the universe in the early stages leads to a characteristic "bubble" structure, with regions of space that are separated by vast distances. This structure has significant implications for our understanding of the universe's large-scale structure, and is consistent with observations of the cosmic microwave background radiation. The findings of this research suggest that open inflation plays a crucial role in shaping the cosmic landscape, and highlights the need for further investigation into the fundamental laws of physics that govern the universe's evolution.

Reinforcement learning (RL) agents improve through trial-and-error, but when
reward is sparse and the agent cannot discover successful action sequences,
learning stagnates. This has been a notable problem in training deep RL agents
to perform web-based tasks, such as booking flights or replying to emails,
where a single mistake can ruin the entire sequence of actions. A common remedy
is to "warm-start" the agent by pre-training it to mimic expert demonstrations,
but this is prone to overfitting. Instead, we propose to constrain exploration
using demonstrations. From each demonstration, we induce high-level "workflows"
which constrain the allowable actions at each time step to be similar to those
in the demonstration (e.g., "Step 1: click on a textbox; Step 2: enter some
text"). Our exploration policy then learns to identify successful workflows and
samples actions that satisfy these workflows. Workflows prune out bad
exploration directions and accelerate the agent's ability to discover rewards.
We use our approach to train a novel neural policy designed to handle the
semi-structured nature of websites, and evaluate on a suite of web tasks,
including the recent World of Bits benchmark. We achieve new state-of-the-art
results, and show that workflow-guided exploration improves sample efficiency
over behavioral cloning by more than 100x.

We analyzed simultaneous archival XMM-Newton and RXTE observations of the
X-ray binary and black hole candidate Swift J1753.5-0127. In a previous
analysis of the same data a soft thermal component was found in the X-ray
spectrum, and the presence of an accretion disk extending close to the
innermost stable circular orbit was proposed. This is in contrast with the
standard picture in which the accretion disk is truncated at large radii in the
low/hard state. We tested a number of spectral models and we found that several
of them fit the observed spectra without the need of a soft disk-like
component. This result implies that the classical paradigm of a truncated
accretion disk in the low/hard state can not be ruled out by these data. We
further discovered a broad iron emission line between 6 and 7 keV in these
data. From fits to the line profile we found an inner disk radius that ranges
between ~6-16 gravitational radii, which can be in fact much larger, up to ~250
gravitational radii, depending on the model used to fit the continuum and the
line. We discuss the implications of these results in the context of a fully or
partially truncated accretion disk.

text: We investigate the emergence of gravitational dynamics in relativistic Bose-Einstein condensates, a long-standing problem in theoretical physics. Our work aims to bridge the gap between the macroscopic behavior of condensates and the underlying microscopic physics, with a focus on the role of gravity.   We employ a combination of analytical and numerical techniques to study the effects of general relativity on the macroscopic behavior of a relativistic BEC. Our approach involves solving the Gross-Pitaevskii equation coupled with the Einstein field equations, which describes the dynamics of the condensate and the spacetime curvature, respectively.   Our results reveal that the presence of gravity significantly alters the macroscopic behavior of the BEC, leading to the emergence of gravitational waves and a non-trivial interplay between the condensate and the spacetime geometry. We find that the condensate's density profile becomes increasingly anisotropic, with a pronounced peak in the direction of the gravitational field.   Our findings have important implications for our understanding of the interplay between quantum systems and gravity. We discuss the potential applications of our work, including the possibility of using relativistic BECs as probes of gravitational waves and the study of gravitational effects on quantum systems. Our results demonstrate the need for a deeper understanding of the interplay between gravity, quantum mechanics, and condensed matter physics, and highlight the importance of a multiscale approach to studying complex quantum systems.

text: In this study, we comment on the recent findings regarding superconductivity observed in electron-doped layered TiNCl materials with varying interlayer coupling. Our analysis focuses on the structural and electronic properties that influence the superconducting transition temperature (Tc). We highlight the importance of interlayer interactions in modulating the electronic structure, which can significantly affect the superconducting behavior. Key methodologies include density functional theory calculations to predict band structures and superconducting gaps, complemented by ab initio simulations to explore possible mechanisms underlying the observed superconductivity. The results indicate that while electron doping plays a crucial role, the precise nature and magnitude of interlayer coupling are essential factors in determining Tc. Our comments suggest further investigation into the interplay between these parameters and their impact on superconductivity in analogous materials.

We present measurements of the star formation rate (SFR) in the early-type
galaxies (ETGs) of the ATLAS3D sample, based on Wide-field Infrared Survey
Explorer (WISE) 22um and Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) far-ultraviolet
emission. We combine these with gas masses estimated from 12CO and HI data in
order to investigate the star formation efficiency (SFE) in a larger sample of
ETGs than previously available. We first recalibrate (based on WISE data) the
relation between old stellar populations (traced at Ks-band) and 22um
luminosity, allowing us to remove the contribution of 22um emission from
circumstellar dust. We then go on to investigate the position of ETGs on the
Kennicutt-Schmidt (KS) relation. Molecular gas-rich ETGs have comparable star
formation surface densities to normal spiral galaxy centres, but they lie
systematically offset from the KS relation, having lower star formation
efficiencies by a factor of ~2.5 (in agreement with other authors). This effect
is driven by galaxies where a substantial fraction of the molecular material is
in the rising part of the rotation curve, and shear is high. We show here for
the first time that although the number of stars formed per unit gas mass per
unit time is lower in ETGs, it seems that the amount of stars formed per
free-fall time is approximately constant. The scatter around this dynamical
relation still correlates with galaxy properties such as the shape of the
potential in the inner regions. This leads us to suggest that dynamical
properties (such as shear or the global stability of the gas) may be important
second parameters that regulate star formation and cause much of the scatter
around star-formation relations.

We found that integrating transcriptional and miRNA regulation resulted in a significant improvement in the stability of target gene concentrations, compared to either regulation alone. Furthermore, we identified specific transcriptional and miRNA regulators that interacted with each other to modulate gene expression. Our results suggest that the combination of transcriptional and miRNA regulation can be a powerful tool for improving gene expression in various cellular contexts, including gene therapy and cancer treatment. Overall, this study provides new insights into the complex interactions between transcriptional and miRNA regulation, and highlights the potential for combining these mechanisms to improve gene expression.

We present a detailed study of the six-dimensional phase space of the
electron beam produced by the Cornell Energy Recovery Linac Photoinjector, a
high-brightness, high repetition rate (1.3 GHz) DC photoemission source
designed to drive a hard x-ray energy recovery linac (ERL). A complete
simulation model of the injector has been constructed, verified by measurement,
and optimized. Both the horizontal and vertical 2D transverse phase spaces, as
well as the time-resolved (sliced) horizontal phase space, were simulated and
directly measured at the end of the injector for 19 pC and 77 pC bunches at
roughly 8 MeV. These bunch charges were chosen because they correspond to 25 mA
and 100 mA average current if operating at the full 1.3 GHz repetition rate.
The resulting 90% normalized transverse emittances for 19 (77) pC/bunch were
0.23 +/- 0.02 (0.51 +/- 0.04) microns in the horizontal plane, and 0.14 +/-
0.01 (0.29 +/- 0.02) microns in the vertical plane, respectively. These
emittances were measured with a corresponding bunch length of 2.1 +/- 0.1 (3.0
+/- 0.2) ps, respectively. In each case the rms momentum spread was determined
to be on the order of 1e-3. Excellent overall agreement between measurement and
simulation has been demonstrated. Using the emittances and bunch length
measured at 19 pC/bunch, we estimate the electron beam quality in a 1.3 GHz, 5
GeV hard x-ray ERL to be at least a factor of 20 times better than that of
existing storage rings when the rms energy spread of each device is considered.
These results represent a milestone for the field of high-brightness,
high-current photoinjectors.

We present results from high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations of isolated
SMC- and Milky Way-sized galaxies that include a model for feedback from
galactic cosmic rays (CRs). We find that CRs are naturally able to drive winds
with mass loading factors of up to ~10 in dwarf systems. The scaling of the
mass loading factor with circular velocity between the two simulated systems is
consistent with \propto v_c^{1-2} required to reproduce the faint end of the
galaxy luminosity function. In addition, simulations with CR feedback reproduce
both the normalization and the slope of the observed trend of wind velocity
with galaxy circular velocity. We find that winds in simulations with CR
feedback exhibit qualitatively different properties compared to SN driven
winds, where most of the acceleration happens violently in situ near star
forming sites. In contrast, the CR-driven winds are accelerated gently by the
large-scale pressure gradient established by CRs diffusing from the
star-forming galaxy disk out into the halo. The CR-driven winds also exhibit
much cooler temperatures and, in the SMC-sized system, warm (T~10^4 K) gas
dominates the outflow. The prevalence of warm gas in such outflows may provide
a clue as to the origin of ubiquitous warm gas in the gaseous halos of galaxies
detected via absorption lines in quasar spectra.

The results of our study have revealed significant correlations between the properties of black holes and the patterns of gravitational waves emitted during their mergers. These findings have far-reaching implications for our understanding of black-hole physics, including the role of spin and accretion in shaping the behavior of these cosmic objects. Our approach has also demonstrated the potential for gravitational-wave spectroscopy to provide new insights into the nature of black holes, and we envision a future where this technique becomes a powerful tool for the study of these enigmatic objects.

text: The interaction between light and matter has been extensively studied; however, the effects of strong rotating electric fields on non-linear Compton scattering remain relatively unexplored. This paper aims to investigate the dynamics of non-linear Compton scattering phenomena under the influence of a strong rotating electric field, specifically focusing on the resultant electron dynamics and photon emission characteristics. We employ a theoretical framework based on quantum electrodynamics (QED) principles, coupled with numerical simulations to model the behavior of charged particles in rotating electric fields. range of vibrational levels v' = 16-23. Extensive comparison is made with the
most recent experimental observations [Pio et al., J. Chem. Phys. 133, 014305
(2010)], molecular dynamics with quantum transitions (MDQT) simulations [Miguel
et al., Faraday Discuss. 118, 257 (2001)], and preliminary results from
24-dimensional Cartesian coupled coherent state (CCCS) calculations. A
sequential mechanism is found to accurately describe the theoretical dynamical
evolution of intermediate and final product populations, and both QCT and CCCS
provide very good estimates for the dissociation lifetimes. The capabilities of
QCT in the description of the fragmentation kinetics is analyzed in detail by
using reduced-dimensionality models of the complexes and concepts from
phase-space transport theory. The problem of fast decoupling of the different
coherent states in CCCS simulations, resulting from the high dimensionality of
phase space, is tackled using a re-expansion scheme. QCT ro-vibrational product
state distributions are reported. Due to the weakness of the vdW couplings and

text: In this study, we investigate the scaling behavior of Shor's algorithm when implemented using a banded quantum Fourier transform (BQFT). We derive analytical expressions that describe the reduced quantum circuit complexity for factoring integers, demonstrating that BQFT retains the asymptotic efficiency of standard quantum Fourier transforms while significantly decreasing the number of quantum gates required. The methodology involves modifying the canonical quantum Fourier transform circuit by introducing band limitations that reduce interactions between non-nearest qubits. Through comprehensive simulations and analyses, we quantify how this banded approach impacts both quantum depth and width, confirming a substantial reduction in the overall qubit connectivity needed. We find that this adjustment yields a scalable approach to Shor's algorithm without compromising the fidelity of the output, thus offering potential pathways to circumventing current hardware limitations. Our results suggest that employing a BQFT can enhance real-world factorization tasks via quantum computers by providing a more feasible and efficient framework suitable for implementation on near-term quantum architectures. Consequently, this work contributes to the ongoing discourse on augmenting quantum algorithmic processes by showcasing a viable modification that facilitates more accessible execution with reduced computational overhead. Our findings hold significance for optimizing quantum resource allocation in executing complex algorithms, advancing practical quantum computing capabilities.

We conducted extensive background estimation using both data-driven techniques and Monte Carlo simulations, effectively accounting for the dominant $t\bar{t}$ background as well as other irreducible processes. We implemented a series of statistical analyses to discriminate potential resonance signatures from the background noise, focusing on invariant mass distributions and applying multivariate techniques to enhance signal sensitivity.   Our results show no significant deviations from the standard model predictions within the explored mass range, leading us to set stringent limits on the production cross-sections of hypothetical heavy resonances, such as those predicted by several theoretical models. We summarize the implications of our findings for phenomenological studies and future search strategies, emphasizing the importance of continued exploration of $t\bar{t}$ resonances as a pathway to uncovering new physics phenomena.

text: We conducted a comprehensive survey of globular clusters in the nearby galaxy M81 using the Very Large Array (VLA) to search for the presence of intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs). Notably, our observations suggested that the central cluster of M81 may harbor an IMBH, with a mass of approximately 200-300 solar masses. Our results highlight the potential of the VLA for detecting IMBHs in nearby galaxies and underscore the importance of continued surveys of globular clusters in this context. Our results reveal that pedestrians tend to synchronize their stepping patterns, with a significant correlation between walking speed and the density of individuals in line. We observed that as density increased, individuals adapted by altering their stride lengths and frequencies, leading to a complex interplay between proximity and personal comfort zones. Furthermore, we implemented agent-based modeling to simulate pedestrian behavior, capturing the emergent patterns observed in our empirical data. The model accurately predicts pedestrian flow and demonstrates sensitivity to alterations in walking speed and density, contributing to our understanding of pedestrian dynamics. Ultimately, our findings offer insights into the design of pedestrian infrastructure and crowd management strategies, emphasizing the importance of accommodating natural stepping behaviors to enhance safety and efficiency in public spaces. Electrons that are confined to a single Landau level in a two dimensional
electron gas realize the effects of strong electron-electron repulsion in its
purest form. The kinetic energy of individual electrons is completely quenched
and all physical properties are dictated solely by many-body effects. A
remarkable consequence is the emergence of new quasiparticles with fractional
charge and exotic quantum statistics of which the most exciting ones are
non-Abelian quasiparticles. A non-integer quantized thermal Hall conductance
$\kappa_{xy}$ (in units of temperature times the universal constant $\pi^2
k_B^2 /3 h$; $h$ is the Planck constant and $k_B$ the Boltzmann constant)
necessitates the existence of such quasiparticles. It has been predicted, and
verified numerically, that such states are realized in the clean half-filled
first Landau level of electrons with Coulomb repulsion, with $\kappa_{xy}$
being either $3/2$ or $7/2$. Excitingly, a recent experiment has indeed
observed a half-integer value, which was measured, however, to be
$\kappa_{xy}=5/2$. We resolve this contradiction within a picture where smooth
disorder results in the formation of mesoscopic puddles with locally
$\kappa_{xy}=3/2$ or $7/2$. Interactions between these puddles generate a
coherent macroscopic state, which is reflected in an extended plateau with
quantized $\kappa_{xy}=5/2$. The topological properties of quasiparticles at
large distances are determined by the macroscopic phase, and not by the
microscopic puddle where they reside. In principle, the same mechanism might
also allow non-Abelian quasiparticles to emerge from a system comprised of
microscopic Abelian puddles.

text: In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of Per-Instance Differential Privacy (PIDP) as a refined approach to data privacy in machine learning models. Traditional differential privacy methods, while efficient, often lack the granularity needed to address individual data points in datasets that vary in sensitivity. Our work aims to tackle the challenge of ensuring privacy while maintaining utility across diverse instances within a dataset. We develop a PIDP framework that enables the application of differential privacy on a per-instance basis, thereby allowing variations in privacy guarantees based on the characteristics of specific data points.  Through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets, we apply our PIDP methodology across various machine learning algorithms, measuring both privacy preservation and model utility. We demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces the privacy loss for sensitive instances while still providing robust performance metrics across the dataset.   We find that by leveraging instance-specific noise addition tailored to data characteristics, we achieve enhanced utility compared to traditional approaches that offer a uniform privacy guarantee. Our results show that PIDP not only protects sensitive data effectively but also preserves the overall integrity and predictive power of the machine learning models.   Thus, we conclude that Per-Instance Differential Privacy presents a promising avenue for addressing privacy concerns in data analysis, offering a balanced approach that aligns individual data sensitivity with model performance, paving the way for future research in privacy-preserving machine learning frameworks.

We consider the effect on tipping from an additive periodic forcing in a
canonical model with a saddle node bifurcation and a slowly varying bifurcation
parameter. Here tipping refers to the dramatic change in dynamical behavior
characterized by a rapid transition away from a previously attracting state. In
the absence of the periodic forcing, it is well-known that a slowly varying
bifurcation parameter produces a delay in this transition, beyond the
bifurcation point for the static case. Using a multiple scales analysis, we
consider the effect of amplitude and frequency of the periodic forcing relative
to the drifting rate of the slowly varying bifurcation parameter.
  We show that a high frequency oscillation drives an earlier tipping when the
bifurcation parameter varies more slowly, with the advance of the tipping point
proportional to the square of the ratio of amplitude to frequency. In the low
frequency case the position of the tipping point is affected by the frequency,
amplitude and phase of the oscillation. The results are based on an analysis of
the local concavity of the trajectory, used for low frequencies both of the
same order as the drifting rate of the bifurcation parameter and for low
frequencies larger than the drifting rate. The tipping point location is
advanced with increased amplitude of the periodic forcing, with critical
amplitudes where there are jumps in the location, yielding significant advances
in the tipping point. We demonstrate the analysis for two applications with
saddle node-type bifurcations.

Purpose: Protoplasmic tubes of Physarum polycephalum, also know as Physarum
Wires (PW), have been previously suggested as novel bio- electronic components.
Until recently, practical examples of electronic circuits using PWs have been
limited. These PWs have been shown to be self repairing, offering significant
advantage over traditional electronic components. This article documents work
performed to produce practical circuits using PWs. Method: We have demonstrated
through manufacture and testing of hybrid circuits that PWs can be used to
produce a variety of practical electronic circuits. A purality of different
applications of PWs have been tested to show the universality of PWs in
analogue and digital electronics. Results: Voltage dividers can be produced
using a pair of PWs in series with an output voltage accurate to within 12%.
PWs can also transmit analogue and digital data with a frequency of up to 19
kHz, which with the addition of a buffer, can drive high current circuits. We
have demonstrated that PWs can last approximately two months, a 4 fold increase
on previous literature. Protoplasmic tubes can be modified with the addition of
conductive or magnetic nano-particles to provide changes in functionality.
Conclusion This work has documented novel macro-scale data transmission through
biological material; it has advanced the field of bio-electronics by providing
a cheap and easy to grow conducting bio-material which may be used in future
hybrid electronic technology.

text: Blue stragglers are peculiar stars found in young star clusters that appear bluer and more luminous than other stars of similar age. Understanding the formation and evolution of these stars is crucial for unraveling the mysteries of stellar populations. This study aims to model the behavior of blue stragglers in young clusters using advanced computational techniques.   The methodology involves simulating the dynamical interactions such as stellar collisions and mass transfer between binary systems within the cluster. By combining stellar evolution models with N-body simulations, we can account for the complex interplay of physical processes that lead to the creation of blue stragglers.  Key findings from our research indicate that the frequency of blue stragglers in young clusters is highly dependent on the initial conditions and the cluster's dynamical history. The simulations show that interactions between stars play a crucial role in the formation of blue stragglers, with binary interactions being a strong contributing factor.  In conclusion, our study provides valuable insights into the formation mechanisms of blue stragglers in young clusters. By incorporating both stellar evolution and dynamical interactions, we can better understand the origins of these enigmatic stars and their impact on the overall cluster evolution.

text: The Narrow-Line Seyfert 1 galaxy 1H 0323+342 has been extensively studied in various wavelengths, but its high-energy emission remains poorly understood. This study aims to investigate the gamma-ray emission and its connection to the broad-band spectral properties of this galaxy using Swift monitoring and Suzaku spectroscopy. A comprehensive analysis of the Swift data revealed a persistent and variable gamma-ray signal, which is likely associated with a Comptonized corona. The Suzaku spectroscopy provided detailed information on the coronal temperature and density, shedding light on the physical mechanisms driving the gamma-ray emission. The spectral analysis of the Suzaku data revealed a prominent iron line at 6.4 keV, which is indicative of a hot accretion disk. The Swift and Suzaku data were combined to constrain the physical parameters of the coronal emission, including the black hole mass, accretion rate, and coronal temperature. Our results indicate that the gamma-ray emission is driven by a Comptonized corona, with a temperature of approximately 20 keV and a density of 10^7 cm^-3. The black hole mass and accretion rate are estimated to be around 4.5 x 10^6 M and 0.03 M/s, respectively. These findings provide new insights into the physical mechanisms governing the gamma-ray emission in Narrow-Line Seyfert 1 galaxies, and highlight the importance of multi-wavelength observations in understanding the complex physics of these objects.

text: The collapse of domain walls in magnetic systems has been a subject of intensive study due to their role in various physical processes. In this work, we examine the time evolution of temperature and entropy of collapsing domain walls in three-dimensional Ising models with different boundary conditions. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we investigate the dynamics of domain wall collapse, and calculate the temperature and entropy profiles across the collapsing walls. Our results reveal that the collapse of domain walls is accompanied by a significant localized increase in temperature and entropy. We find that the temperature and entropy profiles exhibit distinct behaviors for different boundary conditions, which can be explained by the underlying symmetries of the system. Furthermore, we show that the localized heating and entropy generation during domain wall collapse are governed by the intrinsic dynamics of the system, which can be characterized by critical exponents. Our findings offer insights into the thermodynamic consequences of domain wall collapse, and provide a foundation for understanding the role of domain walls in various nonequilibrium phenomena.

Almost every star in our Galaxy is likely to harbor a terrestrial planet, but
accurate measurements of an exoplanet's mass and radius demands accurate
knowledge of the properties of its host star. The imminent TESS and CHEOPS
missions are slated to discover thousands of new exoplanets. Along with WFIRST,
which will directly image nearby planets, these surveys make urgent the need to
better characterize stars in the nearby solar neighborhood (< 30 pc). We have
compiled the CATalog of Stellar Unified Properties (CATSUP) for 951 stars,
including such data as: Gaia astrometry; multiplicity within stellar systems;
stellar elemental abundance measurements; standardized spectral types; Ca II H
and K stellar activity indices; GALEX NUV and FUV photometry; and X-ray fluxes
and luminosities from ROSAT, XMM, and Chandra. We use this data-rich catalog to
find correlations, especially between stellar emission indices, colors, and
galactic velocity. Additionally, we demonstrate that thick-disk stars in the
sample are generally older, have lower activity, and have higher velocities
normal to the galactic plane. We anticipate CATSUP will be useful in discerning
other trends among stars within the nearby solar neighborhood, for comparing
thin-disk vs. thick-disk stars, for comparing stars with and without planets,

text: This study presents a spectroscopic orbit for the late-type Be star β CMi using high-resolution spectra obtained over a period of several years. The primary objective was to accurately determine the orbital elements of β CMi, which is known for its variability and circumstellar material. We analyzed the light curves derived from these observations, accounting for the presence of the circumstellar disk, which affects both the continuum and line profiles. Our key findings include precise estimates of the semi-major axis, eccentricity, and orbital inclination, as well as the determination of the systemic velocity and projected rotational velocity. The analysis reveals that β CMi has a complex orbital configuration influenced by interactions between its stellar components and the circumstellar envelope. This work provides crucial insights into the dynamics of Be stars and their evolutionary processes.

text: In this work, we investigate the survival strategies necessary for sustaining propulsion innovations in rapidly evolving technological landscapes. Our aim is to address the persistent challenge of transitioning groundbreaking propulsion technologies from conceptual design to practical, market-ready solutions, while mitigating risks inherent in innovation sectors. Our methodology involves a comprehensive analysis of historical propulsion technologies that successfully transitioned to market, as well as those that failed, to identify key differentiators. We utilize this empirical foundation to construct a model that predicts potential pitfalls and opportunities within the lifecycle of propulsion innovations. Our model incorporates adaptive learning mechanisms and feedback loops, instrumental in refining technology readiness and aligning it with market demands and regulatory standards.  We present a case study to validate our framework, focusing on a recent propulsion technology concept. The results demonstrate that employing an integrated strategic approach significantly enhances the survivability and eventual success of propulsion innovations. Our findings underscore the importance of early-stage flexibility in design processes and a proactive approach to stakeholder engagement. We conclude that the convergence of technological foresight with strategic business planning is crucial in navigating the complexities of propulsion innovation landscapes, ultimately ensuring sustained growth and competitive advantage for stakeholders. Let $(X,\omega)$ be a compact connected K\"ahler manifold and denote by
$(\mathcal E^p,d_p)$ the metric completion of the space of K\"ahler potentials
$\mathcal H_\omega$ with respect to the $L^p$-type path length metric $d_p$.
First, we show that the natural analytic extension of the (twisted) Mabuchi
K-energy to $\mathcal E^p$ is a $d_p$-lsc functional that is convex along
finite energy geodesics. Second, following the program of J. Streets, we use
this to study the asymptotics of the weak (twisted) Calabi flow inside the
CAT(0) metric space $(\mathcal E^2,d_2)$. This flow exists for all times and
coincides with the usual smooth (twisted) Calabi flow whenever the latter
exists. We show that the weak (twisted) Calabi flow either diverges with
respect to the $d_2$-metric or it $d_1$-converges to some minimizer of the
K-energy inside $\mathcal E^2$. This gives the first concrete result about the
long time convergence of this flow on general K\"ahler manifolds, partially
confirming a conjecture of Donaldson. Finally, we investigate the possibility
of constructing destabilizing geodesic rays asymptotic to diverging weak
(twisted) Calabi trajectories, and give a result in the case when the twisting
form is K\"ahler. If the twisting form is only smooth, we reduce this problem
to a conjecture on the regularity of minimizers of the K-energy on $\mathcal
E^1$, known to hold in case of Fano manifolds.

text: With the increasing use of social media platforms, understanding the temporal dynamics of information diffusion has gained significant attention. Predicting when and how information spreads within social networks can provide valuable insights for various applications, such as disease outbreak response, marketing strategies, and crisis management.   This study aims to develop a novel machine learning model to predict the temporal dynamics of information diffusion in social networks. Specifically, we focus on the identification of the most influential nodes and the estimation of the diffusion curves for information propagation.   We employed a dataset of Twitter messages related to the 2011 Japanese earthquake and tsunami disaster. Using network analysis techniques and machine learning algorithms, we extracted features from the network and applied a random forest regression model to predict the diffusion curve for each message.   Our model accurately predicted the diffusion curve for 80% of the messages, outperforming existing methods based on linear models and naive estimation techniques. We identified key influential nodes in the network using a combination of centrality measures and machine learning algorithms. Our findings suggest that incorporating machine learning algorithms into network analysis can improve the accuracy of predicting the temporal dynamics of information diffusion.   This research contributes to the development of effective methods for predicting the temporal dynamics of information diffusion in social networks. The proposed model, based on a combination of network analysis and machine learning techniques, can be useful for various applications, including disease outbreak response, crisis management, and marketing strategies. Future research may focus on applying this model to other social media platforms and exploring different machine learning algorithms.

Recently the use of neural networks has been introduced in the context of the
signed particle formulation of quantum mechanics to rapidly and reliably
compute the Wigner kernel of any provided potential. This new technique has
introduced two important advantages over the more standard finite
difference/element methods: 1) it reduces the amount of memory required for the
simulation of a quantum system. As a matter of fact, it does not require
storing the kernel in a (expensive) multi-dimensional array, and 2) a
consistent speedup is obtained since now one can compute the kernel on the
cells of interest only, i.e. the cells occupied by signed particles. Although
this certainly represents a step forward into the direction of rapid
simulations of quantum systems, it comes at a price: the number of hidden
neurons is constrained by design to be equal to the number of cells of the
discretized real space. It is easy to see how this limitation can quickly
become an issue when very fine meshes are necessary. In this work, we continue
to ameliorate this previous approach by reducing the complexity of the neural
network and, consequently, by introducing an additional speedup. More
specifically, we propose a new network architecture which requires less neurons
than the previous approach in its hidden layer. For validation purposes, we
apply this novel technique to a well known simple, but very indicative,
one-dimensional quantum system consisting of a Gaussian wave packet interacting
with a potential barrier. In order to clearly show the validity of our
suggested approach, time-dependent comparisons with the previous technique are
presented. In spite of its simpler architecture, a good agreement is observed,
thus representing one step further towards fast and reliable simulations of
time-dependent quantum systems.

text: This research paper explores the concepts of uniform generalization, concentration bounds, and adaptive learning within machine learning frameworks. It begins with an overview of existing literature that highlights the importance of uniform generalization in ensuring that model performance is consistent across different data distributions. The objective of this study is to investigate how these principles can be leveraged to enhance the robustness and adaptability of machine learning models, particularly in scenarios where data distributions might vary significantly.  The methodology employed includes theoretical analysis of concentration inequalities, which provide probabilistic guarantees on the deviation of empirical risk from the true risk. Additionally, the study incorporates empirical studies using various adaptive learning algorithms to demonstrate their effectiveness in minimizing overfitting and improving generalization. The research also delves into the theoretical underpinnings of adaptive learning, examining how these techniques can be optimized to achieve better generalization in complex, high-dimensional datasets.  Key findings reveal that incorporating uniform generalization principles and employing adaptive learning strategies can lead to more reliable and accurate predictions across diverse datasets. The study finds that while traditional methods often struggle with varying distributions, adaptive learning algorithms exhibit superior performance due to their ability to adjust to new data patterns dynamically. Furthermore, the results highlight the significance of concentration bounds in quantifying the expected performance of these algorithms under uncertainty.  In conclusion, this research underscores the critical role of uniform generalization and adaptive learning in enhancing the reliability and adaptability of machine learning models. The findings suggest that integrating these concepts can significantly improve the robustness of predictive models in real-world applications where data distributions are not static. Future work will focus on developing more sophisticated adaptive learning algorithms and further validating these approaches through extensive empirical testing.

Autoignition delay experiments were performed for n-butanol in a heated rapid
compression machine. Experiments were performed at pressures of 15 and 30 bar,
in the temperature range 650-900 K, and for equivalence ratios of 0.5, 1.0, and
2.0. Additionally, the initial fuel mole fraction and initial oxygen mole
fraction were varied independently to determine the influence of each on
ignition delay. Over the conditions studied, it was found that the reactivity
of the mixture increased as equivalence ratio, initial fuel mole fraction or
initial oxygen mole fraction increased. A non-linear correlation to the
experimental data was performed and showed nearly second order dependence on
the initial oxygen mole fraction and nearly first order dependence on initial
fuel mole fraction and compressed pressure. This was the first study of the
ignition of n-butanol in this temperature and pressure range, and contributes
to a better understanding of the chemistry of this fuel under the conditions
relevant to practical devices. Experimentally measured ignition delays were
compared against the ignition delay computed from several reaction mechanisms
in the literature. The agreement between experiments and simulations was found
to be unsatisfactory. Sensitivity analysis was performed and indicated that the
uncertainties of the rate constants of parent fuel decomposition reactions play
a major role in causing the poor agreement. Further path analysis of the fuel
decomposition reactions supported this conclusion and highlighted the
particular importance of certain pathways. Based on these results, it was
concluded that further investigation of the fuel decomposition, including
speciation measurements, will be required.

We perform the baseline and energy optimization of the Neutrino Factory
including the latest simulation results on the magnetized iron detector (MIND).
We also consider the impact of tau decays, generated by nu_mu to nu_tau or nu_e
to nu_tau appearance, on the mass hierarchy, CP violation, and theta_{13}
discovery reaches, which we find to be negligible for the considered detector.
For the baseline-energy optimization for small theta_{13}, we qualitatively
recover the results with earlier simulations of the MIND detector. We find
optimal baselines of about 2500 km to 5000 km for the CP violation measurement,
where now values of E_mu as low as about 12 GeV may be possible. However, for
large theta_{13}, we demonstrate that the lower threshold and the backgrounds
reconstructed at lower energies allow in fact for muon energies as low as 5 GeV
at considerably shorter baselines, such as FNAL-Homestake. This implies that
with the latest MIND analysis, low- and high-energy versions of the Neutrino
Factory are just two different versions of the same experiment optimized for
different parts of the parameter space. Apart from a green-field study of the
updated detector performance, we discuss specific implementations for the
two-baseline Neutrino Factory, where the considered detector sites are taken to
be currently discussed underground laboratories. We find that reasonable setups
can be found for the Neutrino Factory source in Asia, Europe, and North
America, and that a triangular-shaped storage ring is possible in all cases
based on geometrical arguments only.

text: The Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) and associated shocks in the solar corona are fundamental phenomena for understanding space weather and its impacts on Earth. This study aims to explore the fundamental properties of CMEs and shock waves by merging multi-wavelength observations. We analyzed data from various spacecraft, such as the Solar Dynamics Observatory, Helioviewer, and Solar and Heliospheric Observatory, providing observations across the extreme ultraviolet, white light, and radio frequencies. By employing techniques such as co-temporal analysis, velocity mapping, and magnetic field extrapolation, we obtained insights into the relationship between CMEs, shock waves, and the ambient solar wind. Our results reveal that CMEs are often preceded by shock waves, and the shock's properties significantly influence the CME's evolution and structure. Moreover, we found that CME-associated shocks can lead to the formation of various structures such as surge, coronal rain, and interplanetary magnetic clouds. Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between CMEs and shocks in the solar corona, contributing to improved space weather forecasting and space environment modeling.

The extreme statistics of time signals is studied when the maximum is
measured from the initial value. In the case of independent, identically
distributed (iid) variables, we classify the limiting distribution of the
maximum according to the properties of the parent distribution from which the
variables are drawn. Then we turn to correlated periodic Gaussian signals with
a 1/f^alpha power spectrum and study the distribution of the maximum relative
height with respect to the initial height (MRH_I). The exact MRH_I distribution
is derived for alpha=0 (iid variables), alpha=2 (random walk), alpha=4 (random
acceleration), and alpha=infinity (single sinusoidal mode). For other,
intermediate values of alpha, the distribution is determined from simulations.
We find that the MRH_I distribution is markedly different from the previously
studied distribution of the maximum height relative to the average height for
all alpha. The two main distinguishing features of the MRH_I distribution are
the much larger weight for small relative heights and the divergence at zero
height for alpha>3. We also demonstrate that the boundary conditions affect the
shape of the distribution by presenting exact results for some non-periodic
boundary conditions. Finally, we show that, for signals arising from
time-translationally invariant distributions, the density of near extreme
states is the same as the MRH_I distribution. This is used in developing a
scaling theory for the threshold singularities of the two distributions.

Different models of social influence have explored the dynamics of social
contagion, imitation, and diffusion of different types of traits, opinions, and
conducts. However, few behavioral data indicating social influence dynamics
have been obtained from direct observation in `natural' social contexts. The
present research provides that kind of evidence in the case of the public
expression of political preferences in the city of Barcelona, where thousands
of citizens supporting the secession of Catalonia from Spain have placed a
Catalan flag in their balconies. We present two different studies. 1) In July
2013 we registered the number of flags in 26% of the the city. We find that
there is a large dispersion in the density of flags in districts with similar
density of pro-independence voters. However, we find that the density of flags
tends to be fostered in those electoral district where there is a clear
majority of pro-independence vote, while it is inhibited in the opposite cases.
2) During 17 days around Catalonia's 2013 National Holiday we observed the
position at balcony resolution of the flags displayed in the facades of 82
blocks. We compare the clustering of flags on the facades observed each day to
equivalent random distributions and find that successive hangings of flags are
not independent events but that a local influence mechanism is favoring their
clustering. We also find that except for the National Holiday day the density
of flags tends to be fostered in those facades where there is a clear majority
of pro-independence vote.

text:
In order to understand the origin of observed molecular cloud properties, it
is critical to understand how clouds interact with their environments during
their formation, growth, and collapse. It has been suggested that
accretion-driven turbulence can maintain clouds in a highly turbulent state,
preventing runaway collapse, and explaining the observed non-thermal velocity
dispersions. We present 3D, AMR, MHD simulations of a kiloparsec-scale,
stratified, supernova-driven, self-gravitating, interstellar medium, including
diffuse heating and radiative cooling. These simulations model the formation
and evolution of a molecular cloud population in the turbulent interstellar
medium. We use zoom-in techniques to focus on the dynamics of the mass
accretion and its history for individual molecular clouds. We find that mass
accretion onto molecular clouds proceeds as a combination of turbulent and near
free-fall accretion of a gravitationally bound envelope. Nearby supernova
explosions have a dual role, compressing the envelope, boosting accreted mass,
but also disrupting parts of the envelope and eroding mass from the cloud's
surface. It appears that the inflow rate of kinetic energy onto clouds from
supernova explosions is insufficient to explain the net rate of charge of the
cloud kinetic energy. In the absence of self-consistent star formation,
conversion of gravitational potential into kinetic energy during contraction
seems to be the main driver of non-thermal motions within clouds. We conclude
that although clouds interact strongly with their environments, bound clouds
are always in a state of gravitational contraction, close to runaway, and their
properties are a natural result of this collapse.
label: human

text: In this study, we investigate the carbon and nitrogen abundance ratio within the broad line region of tidal disruption events (TDEs), aiming to elucidate the compositional diversity and underlying processes contributing to the emission spectra of these astrophysical phenomena. TDEs occur when a star is disrupted by the gravitational forces of a black hole, resulting in the accretion of stellar material and the emission of broad spectral lines. Understanding the chemical composition, specifically the C/N ratio, offers insight into the stellar origin of the disrupted material and the conditions within the broad line region. We analyzed spectral data from multiple TDEs using advanced spectroscopic techniques and models to accurately estimate elemental abundances. Our results reveal a consistent enhancement in nitrogen relative to carbon, suggesting a possible link to the nucleosynthetic processes in the progenitor stars. This finding provides evidence for the preferential disruption of historically evolved stars, which supports existing theories regarding stellar composition influence on TDE spectra. Methodologically, we employed a combination of spectral line fitting and radiative transfer modeling to decipher the emission features with high precision. Our approach allowed us to account for broadening effects and potential contamination from host galaxy components. The implications of our results are significant for constraining the initial conditions of TDEs and for contributing to the broader understanding of stellar evolution and mass loss events preceding black hole interaction. Future work will focus on expanding our dataset to include more TDEs and refining models to further disentangle environmental effects from intrinsic compositional variations.
label: machine

text: This study investigates the enhancement of dark matter (DM) interactions through resonant scattering mechanisms, focusing on scenarios where DM experiences early kinetic decoupling and exhibits a velocity-dependent resonance width. Our approach involves theoretical models that incorporate these specific conditions within a framework of effective field theory. We demonstrate that under such conditions, the interaction cross-section can be significantly increased, leading to observable effects in current and future DM detection experiments. The methodology employed includes detailed calculations of DM-nucleon scattering amplitudes, taking into account both the initial state of the DM particles and their evolution over cosmological timescales. Results indicate substantial enhancement factors compared to standard assumptions, highlighting the importance of early kinetic decoupling and velocity dependence in enhancing DM-nucleon scattering rates. These findings underscore the potential of resonant interactions in explaining observed DM signals and suggest new avenues for experimental exploration.
label: machine

text:
The Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) has provided the most detailed view to
date of the emission towards the Galactic centre (GC) in high-energy
gamma-rays. This paper describes the analysis of data taken during the first 62
months of the mission in the energy range 1-100 GeV from a $15^\circ \times
15^\circ$ region about the direction of the GC, and implications for the
interstellar emissions produced by cosmic ray (CR) particles interacting with
the gas and radiation fields in the inner Galaxy and for the point sources
detected. Specialised interstellar emission models (IEMs) are constructed that
enable separation of the gamma-ray emission from the inner $\sim 1$ kpc about
the GC from the fore- and background emission from the Galaxy. Based on these
models, the interstellar emission from CR electrons interacting with the
interstellar radiation field via the inverse Compton (IC) process and CR nuclei
inelastically scattering off the gas producing gamma-rays via $\pi^0$ decays
from the inner $\sim 1$ kpc is determined. The IC contribution is found to be
dominant in the region and strongly enhanced compared to previous studies. A
catalog of point sources for the $15^\circ \times 15^\circ$ region is
self-consistently constructed using these IEMs: the First Fermi-LAT Inner
Galaxy point source Catalog (1FIG). After subtracting the interstellar emission
and point-source contributions from the data a residual is found that is a
sub-dominant fraction of the total flux. If spatial templates that peak toward
the GC are used to model the positive residual and included in the total model
for the $15^\circ \times 15^\circ$ region, the agreement with the data
improves, but none of the additional templates account for all of the residual
structure. The spectrum of the positive residual modelled with these templates
has a strong dependence on the choice of IEM. [Abridged]

text: This research focuses on enhancing the performance of mobile edge computing (MEC) systems by optimizing delay and energy consumption during task offloading. MEC involves transferring compute-intensive tasks from cloud servers to nearby edge devices to reduce latency and bandwidth usage. Traditional approaches often neglect the interplay between delay reduction and energy efficiency, leading to suboptimal resource allocation.  The study aims to develop an optimization framework that jointly considers these two critical factors to achieve better overall system performance. A novel algorithm is proposed, which employs machine learning techniques to predict optimal task offloading decisions based on historical data. This approach aims to minimize the total execution time while simultaneously reducing energy consumption.  Methodologically, the research utilizes simulation models to evaluate the performance of the proposed framework under various conditions. Key findings indicate that the joint optimization method significantly reduces average task execution times and energy consumption compared to existing strategies. Moreover, the proposed framework demonstrates robustness across different network scenarios and varying task loads.  In conclusion, the research successfully presents a comprehensive approach to delay-energy joint optimization for task offloading in MEC systems, offering substantial improvements in both system efficiency and resource utilization. Future work will focus on integrating real-world data and expanding the scope to multi-objective optimization problems.
label: machine

text:
We investigate spin polarized electron transport in ultra-thin
Si-Core/Ge-Shell and Ge-Core/Si-Shell nanowire system using semi-classical
Monte Carlo simulation method. Depolarization of electron's spin occurs in
nanowire mainly due to D'yakonov-Perel dephasing (DP-mechanism) and
Elliott-Yafet dephasing (EY-mechanism). We studied the dependence of spin
dephasing on ultra-thin silicon core diameter in Si-Core/Ge-Shell nanowire and
germanium core diameter in Ge-Core/Si-Shell nanowire. Variation in spin
dephasing length with varying core diameter ranging from 1 nm to 9 nm indicate
that spin dephasing length increases with increase in Si-core diameter in
Si-Core/Ge-Shell nanowire and spin dephasing length decreases with increase in
Ge-core diameter in Ge-Core/Si-Shell nanowire. We then studied the variation in
spin dephasing length with varying externally applied transverse electric field
ranging from 20 kV/cm to100 kV/cm. In the electric field dependence study we
found that spin dephasing length is weakly dependent upon applied electric
field. In the end, we studied the variation in spin dephasing length with
varying temperature in the range of 4 K to 377 K. In this simulational study we
found that for both Si-Core/Ge-Shell and Ge-Core/Si-Shell nanowire system spin
dephasing length shows a strong dependence on temperature and spin dephasing
length increases with decrease in temperature from room temperature range.
label: human

text:
We investigate the shape and mechanical properties of liquid interfaces down
to nanometer scale by atomic force microscopy (AFM) and scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) combined with in situ micromanipulation techniques. In both
cases, the interface is probed with a cylindrical nanofiber with radius R of
the order of 25-100 nm. The effective spring constant of the nanomeniscus
oscillated around its equilibrium position is determined by static and
frequency-modulation (FM) AFM modes. In the case of an unbounded meniscus, we
find that the effective spring constant k is proportional to the surface
tension {\gamma} of the liquid through k = (0.51 +- 0.06) {\gamma}, regardless
of the excitation frequency from quasistatic up to 450 kHz. A model based on
the equilibrium shape of the meniscus reproduces well the experimental data.
Electron microscopy allowed to visualize the meniscus profile around the fiber
with a lateral resolution of the order of 10 nm and confirmed its catenary
shape. The influence of a lateral confinement of the interface is also
investigated. We showed that the lateral extension L of the meniscus influences
the effective spring constant following a logarithmic evolution k ~
2{\pi}{\gamma}/ln(L/R) deduced from the model. This comprehensive study of
liquid interface properties over more than four orders of magnitude in meniscus
size, shows that advanced FM-AFM and SEM techniques are promising tools for the
investigation of mechanical properties of liquids down to nanometer scale.

text:
I consider neutron electric dipole moment contributions induced by flavor
changing Standard Model Higgs boson couplings to quarks. Such couplings might
stem from non-renormalizable $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ invariant Lagrange terms
of dimension six, containing a product of three Higgs doublets. Previously one
loop diagrams with such couplings were considered in order to constrain {\it
quadratric} expressions of Higgs flavor changing couplings to quarks. In the
present paper the analysis is extended to the two loop level, where there are
diagrams for electric dipole moments of quarks with a flavor changing Higgs
coupling to {\it first order only}. The divergent loops, due to
non-renormalisabillity, are parametrized in terms of an ultraviolet cut-off
$\Lambda$. I also consider QCD corrections, including the mixing with the color
electric dipole moment, while the contribution from the Weinberg operator is
found to be negligible. The effect of QCD corrections is to suppress the bare
result. Using the current experimental bound on the neutron electric dipole
moment, then for cut offs from one to seven TeV, I find a constraint of order
$10^{-3}$ for the imaginary part of the {\it product} of the Higgs flavor
changing coupling for $(d \rightarrow b)$-transition {\it and} the CKM element
$V_{td}$. Assuming that the previous bound of the {\it absolute value} of the
Higgs flavor changing coupling for $(d \rightarrow b)$-transition obtained from
$B_d - \bar{B_d}$-mixing is saturated, the experimental bound on the neutron
electric dipole moment would be reached for the {\it bare} result, {\it if} the
cut off were extended up to about ca 20 TeV. However, QCD corrections suppress
this result by a factor of order ten, and keep the nEDM below the experimental
bound.

text:
Frequencies of acoustic and mixed modes in red giant stars are now determined
with high precision thanks to the long continuous observations provided by the
NASA Kepler mission. Here we consider the eigenfrequencies of nineteen
low-luminosity red giant stars selected by Corsaro et al. (2015) for a detailed
peak-bagging analysis. Our objective is to obtain stellar parameters by using
individual mode frequencies and spectroscopic information. We use a forward
modelling technique based on a minimization procedure combining the frequencies
of the p modes, the period spacing of the dipolar modes, and the spectroscopic
data. Consistent results between the forward modelling technique and values
derived from the seismic scaling relations are found but the errors derived
using the former technique are lower. The average error for log g is 0.002 dex,
compared to 0.011 dex from the frequency of maximum power and 0.10 dex from the
spectroscopic analysis. Relative errors in the masses and radii are on average
2 and 0.5 per cent respectively, compared to 3 and 2 per cent derived from the
scaling relations. No reliable determination of the initial helium abundances
and the mixing length parameters could be made. Finally, for our grid of models
with a given input physics, we found that low-mass stars require higher values
of the overshooting parameter.
label: human

text: This research delves into the intricate interplay between particle composition, thermal cycling, and the formation of bicontinuous interfacially jammed emulsions (bijels). We explore how varying particle compositions, encompassing both hydrophilic and hydrophobic characteristics, influence the mechanism and stability of bijel formation under the influence of thermal cycling. Our study aims to address the challenge of achieving controlled bijel formation, a process crucial in numerous applications ranging from advanced materials synthesis to drug delivery systems. By subjecting mixtures of particles to precise thermal cycling protocols, we unravel the underlying principles governing bijel formation dynamics.  Through a series of experiments utilizing dynamic light scattering, confocal microscopy, and rheological characterization, we demonstrate the profound impact of particle composition and thermal history on the resulting bijel morphology and stability. Our results reveal the significance of tailored thermal cycling in promoting bijel formation and highlight the role of particle interactions in dictating the final bijel structure. We propose a methodology that combines systematic variation of particle types with controlled thermal treatments to optimize bijel formation, thereby offering insights into the fundamental parameters driving the assembly of these intricate structures. Consequently, this study contributes to advancing the understanding of bijel formation processes, aiding in the development of tailored strategies for designing bijels with desired properties.
label: machine

text: We report on the impact of uniaxial strain on the transport properties of the LaAlO3/SrTiO3 (LAO/STO) interface. Our study is based on the fabrication and characterization of LAO/STO heterostructures grown on piezoelectric substrates, allowing for controlled application and measurement of strain. We find that compressive strain applied along the [001] direction enhances the electrical conductivity and reduces the resistivity of the LAO layer by up to two orders of magnitude. In contrast, tensile strain reduces the conductivity and increases the resistivity. These observations cannot be explained solely by the strain-induced variation in the LaAlO3 bandgap but may result from a complex interplay between the strain-induced changes in the interface dipole and the LaAlO3 carrier concentration. Our findings demonstrate that uniaxial strain can be used to manipulate the transport properties of the LAO/STO interface, opening up possibilities for the development of new functional devices based on this system. This work highlights the importance of considering strain effects in the design and optimization of LAO/STO heterostructures for electronic applications.
label: machine

text:
We present early laboratory simulations and extensive on-sky tests validating
of the performance of a shaped pupil coronagraph (SPC) behind an extreme-AO
corrected beam of the Subaru Coronagraphic Extreme Adaptive Optics (SCExAO)
system. In tests with the SCExAO internal source/wavefront error simulator, the
normalized intensity profile for the SPC degrades more slowly than for the Lyot
coronagraph as low-order aberrations reduce the Strehl ratio from extremely
high values (S.R. $\sim$ 0.93--0.99) to those characteristic of current
ground-based extreme AO systems (S.R. $\sim$ 0.74--0.93) and then slightly
lower values down to S.R. $\sim$ 0.57. On-sky SCExAO data taken with the SPC
and other coronagraphs for brown dwarf/planet-hosting stars HD 1160 and HR 8799
provide further evidence for the SPC's robustness to low-order aberrations.
From H-band Strehl ratios of 80% to 70%, the Lyot coronagraph's performance vs.
that of the SPC may degrade even faster on sky than is seen in our internal
source simulations. The 5-$\sigma$ contrast also degrades faster (by a factor
of two) for the Lyot than the SPC. The SPC we use was designed as a technology
demonstrator only, with a contrast floor, throughput, and outer working angle
poorly matched for SCExAO's current AO performance and poorly tuned for imaging
the HR 8799 planets. Nevertheless, we detect HR 8799 cde with SCExAO/CHARIS
using the SPC in broadband mode, where the S/N for planet e is within 30% of
that obtained using the vortex coronagraph. The shaped-pupil coronagraph is a
promising design demonstrated to be robust in the presence of low-order
aberrations and may be well-suited for future ground and space-based direct
imaging observations, especially those focused on follow-up exoplanet
characterization and technology demonstration of deep contrast within
well-defined regions of the image plane.
