text:
Tuning of the electronic properties of heavy fermion compounds by chemical
substitutions provides excellent opportunities to further understand the
physics of hybridized ions in crystal lattices. Here we present an
investigation on the effects of Cd doping in flux-grown single crystals of the
complex intermetallic cage compound YbFe$_{2}$Zn$_{20}$, that has been
described as a heavy fermion with Sommerfeld coefficient of 535 mJ/mol.K$^{2}$.
Substitution of Cd for Zn disturbs the system by expanding the unit cell and,
in this case, the size of the Zn cages that surround Yb and Fe. With increasing
amount of Cd, the hybridization between Yb $4f$ electrons and the conduction
electrons is weakened, as evidenced by a decrease in the Sommerfeld
coefficient, which should be accompanied by a valence shift of the Yb$^{3+}$
due to the negative chemical pressure effect. This scenario is also supported
by the low temperature dc-magnetic susceptibility, that is gradually suppressed
and evidences an increment of the Kondo temperature, based on a shift to higher
temperatures of the characteristic broad susceptibility peak. Furthermore, the
DC resistivity decreases with the isoelectronic Cd substitution for Zn,
contrary to the expectation for an increasingly disordered system, and implying
that the valence shift is not related to charge carrier doping. The combined
results demonstrate excellent complementarity between positive physical
pressure and negative chemical pressure, and point to a rich playground for
exploring the physics and chemistry of strongly correlated electron systems in
the general family of Zn$_{20}$ compounds, despite their structural complexity.

text: The detection of very high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray sources in the Galactic Centre has been a topic of significant interest in astrophysics, yet precise localization remains a challenge. This study aims to enhance the understanding of VHE emission sources in this region by achieving milli-arcsecond accuracy in their localization. We employed a combination of very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) techniques and advanced multi-wavelength observations to refine the positioning of known and potential VHE sources. Utilizing data from contemporary gamma-ray telescopes and radio interferometers, we constructed a comprehensive dataset to facilitate cross-correlation of signals. Our methodology involved rigorous calibrations, atmospheric corrections, and the implementation of sophisticated imaging algorithms, allowing us to achieve unprecedented spatial resolution. Key findings reveal the precise coordinates of several VHE sources previously located with lower accuracy, including a closely associated emission region near Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the Galactic Centre. This enhanced localization corroborates theoretical models of relativistic jet emissions and opens new avenues for understanding cosmic phenomena such as particle acceleration and dark matter interactions in the Galactic environment. In conclusion, our results not only provide a clearer picture of the VHE landscape in the Galactic Centre but also lay the groundwork for future studies aimed at exploring the intricate dynamics of this enigmatic region, reinforcing the importance of high-precision astrometry in high-energy astrophysics.

text: The study of topological phases in ultracold atomic systems holds promise for unveiling novel quantum phenomena, particularly in the context of spin-orbit coupled Fermi gases. This research investigates the transition from three-dimensional to one-dimensional regimes in such systems, focusing on the emergence of uniform superfluid phases and Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov (FFLO) states. Our objective is to provide a comprehensive understanding of how dimensional crossover influences the topological properties and pairing mechanisms in these quantum gases. Utilizing both numerical simulations and analytical techniques, we explore the phase diagram by varying parameters such as the spin-orbit coupling strength and the interatomic interaction. Key findings reveal that the interplay between reduced dimensionality and spin-orbit coupling leads to the stabilization of exotic superfluid phases, characterized by spatial modulation of the order parameter indicative of FFLO states. Moreover, we identify a regime where topological uniform superfluidity is enhanced, with the presence of edge modes that could be harnessed for robust quantum information applications. The transition between these phases is marked by distinctive changes in the spin textures and quasiparticle excitation spectra. Our results underscore the rich interplay between topology, dimensionality, and spin-orbit effects, providing insights into the design of systems with tunable quantum states. This work paves the way for experimental observations of these phenomena in optical lattice setups, suggesting potential routes for engineering new quantum materials with tailored properties.

We use N-body/gasdynamical LambdaCDM cosmological simulations to examine the
effect of the assembly of a central galaxy on the shape and mass profile of its
dark halo. Two series of simulations are compared; one that follows only the
evolution of the dark matter component and a second one where a baryonic
component is added. These simulations include radiative cooling but neglect
star formation and feedback, leading most baryons to collect at the halo center
in a disk which is too small and too massive when compared with typical spiral.
This unrealistic model allows us, nevertheless, to gauge the maximum effect
that galaxies may have in transforming their dark halos. We find that the shape
of the halo becomes more axisymmetric: halos are transformed from triaxial into
essentially oblate systems, with well-aligned isopotential contours of roughly
constant flattening (c/a ~ 0.85). Halos always contract as a result of galaxy
assembly, but the effect is substantially less pronounced than predicted by the
"adiabatic contraction" hypothesis. The reduced contraction helps to reconcile
LambdaCDM halos with constraints on the dark matter content inside the solar
circle and should alleviate the long-standing difficulty of matching
simultaneously the scaling properties of galaxy disks and the luminosity
function. The halo contraction is also less pronounced than found in earlier
simulations, a disagreement that suggests that halo contraction is not solely a
function of the initial and final distribution of baryons. Not only how much
baryonic mass has been deposited at the center of a halo matters, but also the
mode of its deposition. It might prove impossible to predict the halo response
without a detailed understanding of a galaxy's assembly history. (Abriged)

text: Vulnerability scoring is crucial for assessing the security posture of cloud services. Existing scoring frameworks often lack accuracy and context awareness, which can lead to misprioritization of security measures and potential vulnerabilities going undetected.   This research proposes a novel non-intrusive vulnerability scoring framework for cloud services that integrates context-based information to enhance the accuracy and relevance of vulnerability assessments. The main goal is to improve the decision-making process regarding security measures and resource allocation in cloud environments.   The framework utilizes machine learning algorithms to analyze various contextual factors, such as service type, data sensitivity, and configuration settings, in combination with traditional vulnerability scanning results. By considering these contextual elements, the framework generates more precise vulnerability scores tailored to the specific environment.   The results of the study demonstrate that the context-based vulnerability scoring approach outperforms traditional scoring methods in terms of accuracy and relevance. The incorporation of contextual information leads to more actionable insights for improving security posture and prioritizing mitigation efforts effectively.   This research contributes a valuable framework for enhancing vulnerability scoring in cloud services, providing a more nuanced understanding of security risks and enabling organizations to bolster their defense mechanisms proactively. The findings emphasize the importance of context awareness in vulnerability assessment to ensure optimal protection of cloud resources.

text: This study explores the concept of Access Control Encryption (ACE) as a means of enforcing information flow in secure systems. The increasing demand for data protection and confidentiality has led to the development of various security protocols, including ACE. By integrating encryption techniques with access control mechanisms, ACE provides a robust solution for safeguarding sensitive information.  The objective of this research is to investigate the effectiveness of ACE in enforcing information flow, with a focus on its application in distributed systems. A comprehensive literature review reveals that existing solutions often suffer from limitations, such as scalability issues and performance degradation. Therefore, this study aims to fill this knowledge gap by proposing a novel ACE framework that addresses these challenges.  The proposed framework utilizes a hybrid approach, combining traditional encryption methods with machine learning-based access control algorithms. A case study is conducted on a distributed system, where ACE is integrated with a real-world application. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a significant reduction in unauthorized access attempts, while maintaining optimal system performance.  The key findings of this study indicate that ACE is a viable solution for enforcing information flow in secure systems. The proposed framework's scalability and performance are demonstrated to be superior to existing solutions. The study's contributions are twofold first, the development of a novel ACE framework that addresses scalability and performance issues, and second, the provision of empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness of ACE in enforcing information flow.  Overall, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the role of ACE in secure systems, highlighting its potential as a solution for enforcing information flow. The proposed framework's findings have significant implications for the development of secure distributed systems, and its contributions are expected to inform future research in the field of information security.

text:
Abrupt changes in the miner hash rate applied to a proof-of-work (PoW)
blockchain can adversely affect user experience and security. Because different
PoW blockchains often share hashing algorithms, miners face a complex choice in
deciding how to allocate their hash power among chains. We present an economic
model that leverages Modern Portfolio Theory to predict a miner's allocation
over time using price data and inferred risk tolerance. The model matches
actual allocations with mean absolute error within 20% for four out of the top
five miners active on both Bitcoin (BTC) and Bitcoin Cash (BCH) blockchains. A
model of aggregate allocation across those four miners shows excellent
agreement in magnitude with the actual aggregate as well a correlation
coefficient of 0.649. The accuracy of the aggregate allocation model is also
sufficient to explain major historical changes in inter-block time (IBT) for
BCH. Because estimates of miner risk are not time-dependent and our model is
otherwise price-driven, we are able to use it to anticipate the effect of a
major price shock on hash allocation and IBT in the BCH blockchain. Using a
Monte Carlo simulation, we show that, despite mitigation by the new difficulty
adjustment algorithm, a price drop of 50% could increase the IBT by 50% for at
least a day, with a peak delay of 100%.

text:
The background of this work is the problem of reducing the aerodynamic
turbulent friction drag, which is an important source of energy waste in
innumerable technological fields. We develop a theoretical framework aimed at
predicting the behaviour of existing drag reduction techniques when used at the
large values of Re which are typical of applications. We focus on one recently
proposed and very promising technique, which consists in creating at the wall
streamwise-travelling waves of spanwise velocity. A perturbation analysis of
the Navier-Stokes equations that govern the fluid motion is carried out, for
the simplest wall-bounded flow geometry, i.e. the plane channel flow. The
streamwise base flow is perturbed by the spanwise time-varying base flow
induced by the travelling waves. An asymptotic expansion is then carried out
with respect to the velocity amplitude of the travelling wave. The analysis,
although based on several assumptions, leads to predictions of drag reduction
that agree well with the measurements available in literature and mostly
computed through DNS of the full Navier-Stokes equations. New DNS data are
produced on purpose in this work to validate our method further. The method is
then applied to predict the drag-reducing performance of the
streamwise-travelling waves at increasing Re, where comparison data are not
available. The current belief, based on a Re-range of about one decade only
above the transitional value, that drag reduction obtained at low Re is deemed
to decrease as Re is increased is fully confirmed by our results. From a
quantitative standpoint, however, our outlook based on several decades of
increase in Re is much less pessimistic than other existing estimates, and
motivates further, more accurate studies on the present subject.

We theoretically consider the observed soft gap in the proximity-induced
superconducting state of semiconductor nanowires in the presence of spin-orbit
coupling, Zeeman splitting, and tunneling leads, but in the absence of any
extrinsic disorder. We critically consider the effects of three distinct
intrinsic physical mechanisms (tunnel barrier to normal leads, temperature, and
dissipation) on the phenomenology of the gap softness in the tunnel
spectroscopy of the normal-superconductor junction as a function of spin
splitting and chemical potential. We find that all three mechanisms
individually can produce a soft gap, leading to calculated conductance spectra
qualitatively mimicking experimental results. We also show that the
phenomenology of the soft gap is intrinsically tied to the broadening and the
height of the Majorana zero mode(MZM)-induced differential conductance peak
above the topological quantum phase transition point with both the soft gap and
the quality of the MZM being simultaneously affected by tunnel barrier,
temperature, and dissipation. We establish that the MZM splitting oscillations
can be suppressed by temperature or dissipation, but not by the tunnel barrier.
Since all three mechanisms are likely to be present in any realistic nanowires,
discerning the effects of various mechanisms is difficult, necessitating
detailed experimental data as a function of all the system parameters, some of
which (e.g., dissipation, chemical potential, tunnel barrier) may not be known
experimentally. While the tunneling-induced soft-gap behavior is benign with no
direct adverse effect on the Majorana topological properties with the zero-bias
peak remaining quantized at $2e^2/h$, the soft gap induced by finite
temperature and/or finite dissipation is detrimental to topological properties
and must be avoided as much as possible.

Magnetar magnetospheres are believed to be strongly twisted, due to shearing
of the stellar crust by internal magnetic stresses. We present time-dependent
axisymmetric simulations showing in detail the evolution of relativistic
force-free magnetospheres subjected to slow twisting through large angles. When
the twist amplitude is small, the magnetosphere moves quasi-statically through
a sequence of equilibria of increasing free energy. At some twist amplitude the
magnetosphere becomes tearing-mode unstable to forming a resistive current
sheet, initiating large-scale magnetic reconnection in which a significant
fraction of the magnetic free energy can be dissipated. This "critical" twist
angle is insensitive to the resistive length scale. Rapid shearing temporarily
stabilizes the magnetosphere beyond the critical angle, allowing the
magnetosphere of a rapidly differentially rotating star to store, and
dissipate, more free energy. In addition to these effects, shearing the surface
of a rotating star increases the spindown torque applied to the star. If
shearing is much slower than rotation, the resulting spikes in spindown rate
can occur on timescales anywhere from the long twisting timescale to the
stellar spin period or shorter, depending both on the stellar shear
distribution and the existing distribution of magnetospheric twists. A model in
which energy is stored in the magnetosphere, and released by a magnetospheric
instability, therefore predicts large changes in the measured spindown rate
before SGR giant flares.

text: In this study, we investigate the trigonometric parallaxes of massive star-forming regions to elucidate the structural parameters and dynamics of the Milky Way galaxy. By utilizing the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), we obtained high-precision parallax measurements for a substantial sample of masers associated with young stellar objects. Our primary objective is to refine the galactic distance scale and examine non-circular motions that deviate from ideal rotational dynamics. We applied a model of the Galactic rotation curve, accounting for the Sun's location and motion relative to the Galactic Center. Our results reveal significant insights into the spiral structure of the Milky Way, providing evidence for the existence and orientation of spiral arms more accurately than previous methods. Notably, we document peculiar velocities that suggest substantial non-circular movements, likely induced by spiral density waves and gravitational interactions within the Galactic disk. These findings contribute to a more nuanced view of Galactic kinematics and dynamics. We underscore the critical role of high-accuracy parallax data in amending models of Galactic structure and dynamics. Our methodology demonstrates a robust approach to resolving statistical uncertainties inherent in Galactic parameter estimation. The implications of our results hold considerable significance in understanding the mass distribution and formation history of the Milky Way and provide a foundational basis for future investigations into the larger framework of Galactic evolution.

We describe the first three-dimensional simulation of the gravitational
collapse of a massive, rotating molecular cloud that includes heating by both
non-ionizing and ionizing radiation. We find that as the first protostars gain
sufficient mass to ionize the accretion flow, their H II regions are initially
gravitationally trapped, but soon begin to rapidly fluctuate between trapped
and extended states, in agreement with observations. Over time, the same
ultracompact H II region can expand anisotropically, contract again, and take
on any of the observed morphological classes. In their extended phases,
expanding H II regions drive bipolar neutral outflows characteristic of
high-mass star formation. The total lifetime of H II regions is given by the
global accretion timescale, rather than their short internal sound-crossing
time. The pressure of the hot, ionized gas does not terminate accretion.
Instead the final stellar mass is set by fragmentation-induced starvation.
Local gravitational instabilities in the accretion flow lead to the build-up of
a small cluster of stars, all with relatively high masses due to heating from
accretion radiation. These companions subsequently compete with the initial
high-mass star for the same common gas reservoir and limit its mass growth. Our
findings show that the most significant differences between the formation of
low-mass and high-mass stars are all explained as the result of rapid accretion
within a dense, gravitationally unstable, ionized flow.

text: In this study, we present the results from an extensive analysis of the Crab Nebula spectrum utilizing the Major Atmospheric Gamma Imaging Cherenkov (MAGIC) telescopes, covering an unprecedented energy range extending over three decades from tens of GeV to tens of TeV. Our aim was to perform a precise measurement of the continuous spectrum of the Crab Nebula, a cornerstone source in astroparticle physics, to refine and constrain its theoretical emission models. We employed novel calibration techniques alongside enhanced analysis methods, which significantly improved the energy resolution and sensitivity of the MAGIC telescopes. Our observations reveal a consistent spectrum that is in concordance with existing datasets yet provides increased accuracy and detail across the broader energy range. By implementing advanced spectral fitting procedures, we discerned a spectral hardening at higher energies, potentially indicating additional energetic processes driving the emission. This outcome enhances our comprehension of particle acceleration mechanisms within the nebula and the interplay of synchrotron and inverse Compton scattering as dominant mechanisms of gamma-ray production. Furthermore, we compared our findings with multi-wavelength observations, supporting our interpretations of the observed spectral features. Our results hold substantial implications for the calibration of future gamma-ray instruments and enhance our understanding of the Crab Nebula as a standard reference source, thus providing a benchmark for astrophysical high-energy processes. This comprehensive evaluation not only reaffirms the Crab Nebula's role as a primary calibrator in observational gamma-ray astronomy but also opens new research pathways into the fundamental physics underlying extreme astrophysical phenomena.

text:
BosonSampling, which we proposed three years ago, is a scheme for using
linear-optical networks to solve sampling problems that appear to be
intractable for a classical computer. In arXiv:1306.3995, Gogolin et al.
claimed that even an ideal BosonSampling device's output would be
"operationally indistinguishable" from a uniform random outcome, at least
"without detailed a priori knowledge"; or at any rate, that telling the two
apart might itself be a hard problem. We first answer these claims---explaining
why the first is based on a definition of "a priori knowledge" so strange that,
were it adopted, almost no quantum algorithm could be distinguished from a pure
random-number source; while the second is neither new nor a practical obstacle
to interesting BosonSampling experiments. However, we then go further, and
address some interesting research questions inspired by Gogolin et al.'s
mistaken arguments. We prove that, with high probability over a Haar-random
matrix A, the BosonSampling distribution induced by A is far from the uniform
distribution in total variation distance. More surprisingly, and directly
counter to Gogolin et al., we give an efficient algorithm that distinguishes
these two distributions with constant bias. Finally, we offer three "bonus"
results about BosonSampling. First, we report an observation of Fernando
Brandao: that one can efficiently sample a distribution that has large entropy
and that's indistinguishable from a BosonSampling distribution by any circuit
of fixed polynomial size. Second, we show that BosonSampling distributions can
be efficiently distinguished from uniform even with photon losses and for
general initial states. Third, we offer the simplest known proof that
FermionSampling is solvable in classical polynomial time, and we reuse
techniques from our BosonSampling analysis to characterize random
FermionSampling distributions.

text: The BINGO (Basse Tonne d'Imagerie du Groupe d'Interprétation) telescope, inaugurated in 2017, represents a significant advancement in the field of 21-cm cosmology. This new instrument offers a unique capability to probe the neutral hydrogen (HI) gas in the early universe, which has been crucial for understanding the formation and evolution of galaxies and large-scale structures. Our research aims to utilize the BINGO telescope to explore the new 21-cm cosmological window, focusing on two primary objectives first, to map the distribution of HI in nearby galaxy clusters and filaments; second, to detect and characterize the HI emission from high-redshift sources, contributing to the cosmic reionization history.  Methodologically, we employed a multi-frequency imaging approach with BINGO, leveraging its wide-field capabilities and sensitivity to low-intensity signals. Data were analyzed using advanced image processing techniques to extract meaningful information about the HI gas distribution and kinematics. Key findings include the detailed mapping of HI structures in galaxy clusters, revealing complex filamentary distributions that align with theoretical predictions. Additionally, our observations have detected HI emission from high-redshift sources, providing insights into the timing and extent of cosmic reionization.  In conclusion, this study highlights the potential of the BINGO telescope as a powerful tool for advancing our understanding of the early universe through 21-cm cosmology. Our results not only corroborate existing models but also offer new perspectives on the dynamics of neutral hydrogen and the processes occurring during the epoch of reionization.

In this paper we investigate the statistical properties of the Baryonic
Tully-Fisher relation (BTFr) for a sample of 32 galaxies with accurate
distances based on Cepheids and/or TRGB stars. We make use of homogeneously
analysed photometry in 18 bands ranging from the FUV to 160 $\mu$m, allowing us
to investigate the effect of the inferred stellar mass-to-light ratio
$\Upsilon_{*}$ on the statistical properties of the BTFr. Stellar masses of our
sample galaxies are derived with four different methods based on full
SED-fitting, studies of stellar dynamics, near-infrared colours, and the
assumption of the same $\Upsilon_{*}^{[3.6]}$ for all galaxies. In addition, we
use high-quality, resolved HI kinematics to study the BTFr based on three
kinematic measures: $W_{50}^{i}$ from the global HI profile, and $V_{max}$ and
$V_{flat}$ from the rotation curve. We find the intrinsic perpendicular
scatter, or tightness, of our BTFr to be $\sigma_{\perp} = 0.026 \pm 0.013$
dex, consistent with the intrinsic tightness of the 3.6 $\mu$m luminosity-based
TFr. However, we find the slope of the BTFr to be $2.99 \pm 0.2$ instead of
$3.7 \pm 0.1$ for the luminosity-based TFr at 3.6 $\mu$m. We use our BTFr to
place important observational constraints on theoretical models of galaxy
formation and evolution by making comparisons with theoretical predictions
based on either the $\Lambda$CDM framework or modified Newtonian dynamics.

text: In this work, we explore the integrable heavenly type equations and their Lie-algebraic structure. We begin by presenting a comprehensive overview of these equations, highlighting their significance within the broader context of integrable systems. Our approach involves constructing novel Lie algebras that naturally accommodate the heavenly type equations, thereby elucidating their integrability properties. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, we demonstrate how these Lie algebras can be used to generate conservation laws and symmetries associated with the equations. Additionally, we investigate the bi-Hamiltonian structures inherent in these systems, which are crucial for understanding their integrability. Key methodologies include the application of representation theory and the construction of compatible Poisson brackets. The results obtained reveal a rich interplay between the algebraic and geometric structures of the equations, leading to new insights into the classification and solution methods for integrable heavenly type equations. Our findings contribute to the development of a deeper theoretical framework that can potentially extend to other nonlinear partial differential equations.

text: In this study, we introduce a general family of multi-peakon equations that extend the well-known Camassa-Holm equation by incorporating multiple peakons, which are solitary wave solutions with discontinuous first derivatives. We derive these equations through a Hamiltonian approach, ensuring that they maintain the integrability property characteristic of peakon equations. Our results include a detailed analysis of the dynamics of these multi-peakon solutions, including their interactions and stability under certain conditions. The methodology involves transforming the original partial differential equations into a system of ordinary differential equations for the peakon velocities, allowing for a straightforward computation of the peakon solutions. Additionally, we explore the conservation laws associated with our family of equations, demonstrating how these can be used to validate the numerical simulations of the peakon solutions. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of peakon behavior and offer new insights into the modeling of nonlinear wave phenomena.

text:
We study quantitative asymptotics of planar random walks that are spatially
non-homogeneous but whose mean drifts have some regularity. Specifically, we
study the first exit time $\tau_\alpha$ from a wedge with apex at the origin
and interior half-angle $\alpha$ by a non-homogeneous random walk on the square
lattice with mean drift at $x$ of magnitude $O(1/|x|)$ as $|x| \to \infty$.
This is the critical regime for the asymptotic behaviour: under mild
conditions, a previous result of the authors (see arXiv:0910.1772) stated that
$\tau_\alpha < \infty$ a.s. for any $\alpha$ (while for a stronger drift field
$\tau_\alpha$ is infinite with positive probability). Here we study the more
difficult problem of the existence and non-existence of moments
$E[\tau_\alpha^s]$, $s>0$. Assuming (in common with much of the literature) a
uniform bound on the walk's increments, we show that for $\alpha < \pi/2$ there
exists $s_0 \in (0,\infty)$ such that $E[\tau_\alpha^s]$ is finite for $s <
s_0$ but infinite for $s > s_0$; under specific assumptions on the drift field
we show that we can attain $E[\tau_\alpha^s] = \infty$ for any $s > 1/2$. We
show that for $\alpha \leq \pi$ there is a phase transition between drifts of
magnitude $O(1/|x|)$ (the critical regime) and $o(1/|x|)$ (the subcritical
regime). In the subcritical regime we obtain a non-homogeneous random walk
analogue of a theorem for Brownian motion due to Spitzer, under considerably
weaker conditions than those previously given (including work by Varopoulos)
that assumed zero drift.

text: The exploration of B+ → τ⁺ ντ decays provides valuable insights into the search for supersymmetry (SUSY) at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Recent data from particle physics experiments have highlighted the potential for these decays to offer unique signatures that could indicate the presence of SUSY particles. This study focuses on analyzing the latest experimental results, which include detailed measurements of decay rates and angular distributions, to assess their compatibility with theoretical predictions under various SUSY models.  The methodology employed involves rigorous statistical analysis of high-energy collision data collected by ATLAS and CMS collaborations at the LHC. These analyses are aimed at identifying patterns consistent with or inconsistent with SUSY expectations. Key findings include significant deviations from Standard Model predictions, particularly in the angular distribution of τ⁺ particles, which suggest the production of additional states not accounted for within the Standard Model framework.  The conclusion drawn from these analyses indicates strong evidence supporting the existence of new physics beyond the Standard Model, specifically pointing towards SUSY. However, the interpretation remains tentative due to the limited statistics and the need for further corroborative data from other channels. This preliminary result opens up avenues for more extensive investigations at future colliders, potentially leading to a definitive confirmation of SUSY contributions to the universe's fundamental interactions.

text: In this study, we investigate the processes of first-generation and second-generation planet formation in post-common-envelope binary (PCEB) planetary systems, aiming to discern their distinct characteristics and contributions to observed planetary populations. We use advanced numerical simulations to model the dynamic interactions that occur when a binary star system undergoes a common-envelope phase, focusing on the consequential alterations to the circumbinary disk, which may serve as a birthplace for planets. Our analysis leverages data from several PCEB systems to calibrate the simulations and validate the model outcomes.  We find that first-generation planets, formed during the pre-common-envelope phase, exhibit diverse evolutionary paths altered by the binary's interaction. Post-common-envelope dynamical instabilities can lead to significant orbital modifications or even ejections from the system. Meanwhile, second-generation planet formation, occurring after the ejection of the common envelope, often results in planetary bodies with distinct elemental compositions and orbital characteristics, heavily influenced by the altered disk structure.  Using our simulation framework, we identify key parameters that govern the likelihood of planet survivability and formation in PCEB systems, such as the remnant mass and envelope ejection efficiency. These parameters delineate specific evolutionary pathways and allow us to predict observable properties for both generations of planets.  Our work contributes to a deeper comprehension of planet formation processes in complex stellar environments and provides a foundation for interpreting observational data on PCEB systems, enhancing our understanding of their contribution to the galactic planetary census.

text:
We report X-ray constraints for 20 of 52 high-z ULIRGs identified in the
Spitzer xFLS to constrain their obscuration. Notably, decomposition of
Spitzer-IRS spectra for the 52 objects already indicates that most are weak-PAH
ULIRGs dominated by hot-dust continua, characteristic of AGN. Given their
redshifts, they have AGN bolometric luminosities of ~1e45-1e47 erg/s comparable
to powerful QSOs. This, coupled with their high IR-to-optical ratios and often
significant silicate absorption, strongly argues in favor of these mid-IR
objects being heavily obscured QSOs. At X-ray energies, we marginally detect
two ULIRGs, while the rest have only upper limits. Using the IRS-derived 5.8um
AGN continuum luminosity as a proxy for the expected X-ray luminosities, we
find that all of the observed sources must individually be highly obscured,
while X-ray stacking limits on the undetected sources suggest that the
majority, if not all, are likely to be at least mildly Compton-thick (NH>1e24
cm-2). With a space density of ~1.4e-7 Mpc-3 at z~2, such objects imply a lower
limit on the obscured AGN fraction (i.e., the ratio of AGN above and below
NH=1e22 cm-2) of >~1.7:1 even among luminous QSOs. Our findings, which are
based on extensive multi-wavelength constraints including Spitzer IRS spectra,
should aid in the interpretation of similar objects from larger or deeper
mid-IR surveys, where considerable uncertainty about the source properties
remains and comparable follow-up is not yet feasible.

text: In this study, we exploit the unprecedented capabilities of the Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT) to investigate the dust content and its implications in a high-redshift galaxy at z~9.6. Our objective is to elucidate the dust-to-gas ratio and its evolutionary consequences during the early stages of galaxy formation. Utilizing deep continuum observations afforded by the LMT, we detected faint emission indicative of substantial dust presence in this distant cosmic object. We performed meticulous analysis correlating the millimeter-wave emissions with spectroscopic data to refine constraints on the dust mass and temperature. Our findings suggest the presence of dust components at relatively higher temperatures, inferring active internal mechanisms such as star formation or potential interaction with active galactic nuclei that could contribute to dust heating. The deduced dust mass, when juxtaposed with theoretical models, implies an accelerated dust production mechanism operative even at such an early cosmic epoch, challenging existing paradigms of galaxy evolution. Our methodology integrated radiative transfer models with chemical evolution codes to generate predictions which align with the observed data, affirming the reliability of the inferred dust properties. This work not only reinforces the utility of the LMT in probing the high-redshift universe but also offers critical insights into the processes that govern dust accumulation and its potential impact on early galaxy dynamics. Consequently, our findings provide a pivotal step toward comprehending the intricacies of dust evolution and the role it plays in shaping the primordial universe.

text: In this study, we examine the impact of stochastic forces on the dynamical evolution of planetary systems, with a particular focus on Saturn's rings. Using advanced numerical simulations, we incorporate random perturbations to model the influence of stochastic forces such as interplanetary matter, solar irradiation, and planetary magnetic field variations. Our results indicate that stochastic forces play a significant role in altering the orbital parameters of celestial bodies over time. Specifically, we observe that variations in these forces contribute to the redistribution of angular momentum within Saturn's rings, leading to notable structural changes, including ring diffusion and potential ringlet formation. Our analytical approach employs perturbation theory and Monte Carlo simulations to quantify these effects, demarcating stochastic influence from deterministic forces. By developing a comprehensive stochastic model, we provide insight into the variance observed in the spatial distribution and density fluctuations within the ring system. This work attempts to bridge the gap in understanding the subtle yet consequential role stochastic forces play compared to the predominant gravitational interactions traditionally considered. The implications of our findings suggest that while stochastic forces do not alone redefine the macroscopic architecture of planetary systems, they are instrumental in driving nuanced dynamics such as ring shaping and the modulation of long-term orbital stability. Our methodology sets a precedent for future investigations into other planetary systems, where similar stochastic processes may offer common mechanisms underlying observed planetary phenomena.

text: This study presents the comprehensive DustPedia dataset comprising multiwavelength photometry and imagery of 875 nearby galaxies across 42 ultraviolet to microwave bands. The primary aim of this research is to create a robust database for studying dust properties in galaxies. Our results showcase the diversity of dust emissions and spectral energy distributions among different galaxy types. By utilizing data spanning a wide range of wavelengths, we can investigate the effects of dust on various physical processes in galaxies, such as star formation and extinction. The methodology involved in this work includes the collection of images and photometric data from multiple space-based and ground-based telescopes, enabling a detailed analysis of dust emission characteristics. The dataset produced by this study serves as a valuable resource for astronomers and astrophysicists interested in understanding the role of dust in galaxy evolution. Furthermore, the combination of UV to microwave observations provides a unique opportunity to explore the full wavelength range of dust emission, shedding light on the intricate interplay between dust, gas, and stars in galaxies.

text: This research paper explores the concept of Regularised Tripartite Continuous Variable EPR-type States with Wigner functions and CHSH violations. Background on the subject reveals that continuous variable EPR-type states have been extensively studied in the context of quantum mechanics, and their properties are crucial for understanding the foundations of quantum theory. The EPR paradox, proposed by Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen in 1935, is a thought-provoking example of the apparent non-locality of quantum mechanics.  The objective of this research is to investigate the properties of regularised tripartite continuous variable EPR-type states, focusing on their relationship with Wigner functions and CHSH violations. Wigner functions are a mathematical tool used to represent the quantum state of a continuous variable system, providing a more intuitive understanding of the quantum state than traditional wave functions. CHSH violations, on the other hand, are a measure of the non-locality of quantum mechanics, indicating the extent to which the system can exhibit non-local correlations.  The methodology employed in this research involves deriving the regularised tripartite continuous variable EPR-type states and calculating their Wigner functions and CHSH violations. The results show that the regularised states exhibit non-trivial Wigner functions, which are essential for understanding the quantum state of the system. Furthermore, the CHSH violations are found to be non-zero, indicating the presence of non-local correlations in the system. The findings of this research have significant implications for our understanding of the foundations of quantum mechanics and the nature of non-locality in quantum systems.
label: machine

text: We investigated the fate of initial state perturbations in heavy ion collisions, with a focus on their impact on the evolution of the quark-gluon plasma. Our analysis of the energy loss of leading protons and kaons in Au+Au collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) revealed that the initial state perturbations play a crucial role in determining the collective behavior of the system. We observed that the energy loss of leading particles is strongly influenced by the presence of initial state fluctuations, which lead to a significant enhancement of the jet-like structure in the azimuthal distribution of the particles.  Our simulation studies using the AMPT (A Multi-Phase Transport) model and the Quark-Gluon String Model (QGSM) demonstrated that the initial state perturbations lead to a significant increase in the energy loss of leading particles, resulting in a more pronounced jet-like structure. Furthermore, we found that the initial state perturbations also lead to a more rapid equilibration of the system, as evidenced by the rapid formation of a thermalized hadron spectrum.  The results of our study suggest that the initial state perturbations are a key factor in determining the collective behavior of the quark-gluon plasma in heavy ion collisions. Our findings have important implications for the understanding of the properties of the quark-gluon plasma and the development of new experimental strategies to probe its collective behavior.

text: We investigated the impact of episodic accretion on the phase transition of carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide (CO2) in low-mass star formation, shedding light on the complex interplay between accretion dynamics and chemical evolution in the early stages of stellar protostars. Through a combination of numerical simulations and laboratory experiments, we explored the effects of varying accretion rates on the phase transitions of CO and CO2, two crucial molecules in the chemistry of low-mass star-forming regions.  Our results show that episodic accretion leads to a significant increase in the abundance of CO and CO2, with CO2 exhibiting a more pronounced effect on the phase transition due to its stronger van der Waals interactions. We also found that the accretion rate plays a crucial role in determining the outcome of these phase transitions, with rapid accretion favoring the formation of CO2 and slow accretion promoting the formation of CO.  Our simulations suggest that the interplay between accretion and chemical evolution is a key factor in determining the final composition of low-mass star-forming regions. The findings of this study have important implications for our understanding of the formation of carbon-rich stars and the origins of complex organic molecules in the interstellar medium. By elucidating the effects of episodic accretion on the phase transition of CO and CO2, we have provided new insights into the complex and dynamic processes that govern the early stages of low-mass star formation.

We present high-resolution long-slit spectroscopy of a Balmer-dominated shock
in the northeastern limb of the Cygnus Loop with the Subaru high dispersion
spectrograph. By setting the slit angle along the shock normal, we investigate
variations of the flux and profile of the H-alpha line from preshock to
postshock regions with a spatial resolution of about 4 times 10^{15} cm. The
H-alpha line profile can be represented by a narrow (28.9+/-0.7 km/s) Gaussian
in a diffuse region ahead of the shock, i.e., a photoionization precursor, and
narrow (33.1+/-0.2 km/s) plus broad (130-230 km/s) Gaussians at the shock
itself. We find that the width of the narrow component abruptly increases up to
33.1+/-0.2 km/s, or 38.8+/-0.4 km/s if we eliminate projected emission
originating from the photoionization precursor, in an unresolved thin layer (<
4 times 10^{15} cm at a distance of 540 pc) at the shock. We show that the
sudden broadening can be best explained by heating via damping of Alfven waves
in a thin cosmic-ray precursor, although other possibilities are not fully
ruled out. The thickness of the cosmic-ray precursor in the Cygnus Loop (a soft
gamma-ray emitter) is an order of magnitude thinner than that in Tycho's Knot g
(a hard gamma-ray emitter), which may be caused by different energy
distribution of accelerated particles between the two sources. In this context,
systematic studies might reveal a positive correlation between the thickness of
the cosmic-ray precursor and the hardness of the cosmic-ray energy
distribution.

There has been significant progress in the implementation and manipulation of
singlet-triplet qubits in GaAs quantum dots. Given the considerably longer spin
coherence times measured in Si, considerable interest has been generated
recently in Si quantum dots. The physics of these systems is considerably more
complex than the physics of GaAs quantum dots owing to the presence of the
valley degree of freedom, which constitutes the focus of this work. In this
paper we investigate the physics of Si quantum dots and focus on the
feasibility of quantum coherent singlet-triplet qubit experiments analogous to
those performed in GaAs. This additional degree of freedom greatly increases
the complexity of the ground state and gives rise to highly nontrivial and
interesting physics in the processes of qubit initialization, coherent
manipulation and readout. We discuss the operational definition of a qubit in
Si-based quantum dots. We find that in the presence of valley degeneracy a
singlet-triplet qubit cannot be constructed, whereas for large valley splitting
(>>k_B*T) the experiment is similar to GaAs. We show that experiments on
singlet-triplet qubits analogous to those in GaAs would provide a method for
estimating the valley coupling in Si. A Zeeman field distinguishes between
different initialized states for any valley splitting and provides a tool to
determine the size of this splitting.

Most work in the area of statistical relational learning (SRL) is focussed on
discrete data, even though a few approaches for hybrid SRL models have been
proposed that combine numerical and discrete variables. In this paper we
distinguish numerical random variables for which a probability distribution is
defined by the model from numerical input variables that are only used for
conditioning the distribution of discrete response variables. We show how
numerical input relations can very easily be used in the Relational Bayesian
Network framework, and that existing inference and learning methods need only
minor adjustments to be applied in this generalized setting. The resulting
framework provides natural relational extensions of classical probabilistic
models for categorical data. We demonstrate the usefulness of RBN models with
numeric input relations by several examples.
  In particular, we use the augmented RBN framework to define probabilistic
models for multi-relational (social) networks in which the probability of a
link between two nodes depends on numeric latent feature vectors associated
with the nodes. A generic learning procedure can be used to obtain a
maximum-likelihood fit of model parameters and latent feature values for a
variety of models that can be expressed in the high-level RBN representation.
Specifically, we propose a model that allows us to interpret learned latent
feature values as community centrality degrees by which we can identify nodes
that are central for one community, that are hubs between communities, or that
are isolated nodes. In a multi-relational setting, the model also provides a
characterization of how different relations are associated with each community.

text: DeltaTree is a novel concurrent search tree designed to efficiently manage large-scale distributed databases with high concurrency and locality awareness. Existing concurrent search trees often suffer from scalability issues and poor locality due to their lock-based or non-blocking strategies. This paper introduces DeltaTree, which leverages a combination of lazy updates and speculative reads to minimize contention and maximize data locality. The objective of DeltaTree is to provide faster query responses and higher throughput compared to traditional locking-based approaches while maintaining consistency under concurrent access.  Methodologically, DeltaTree employs a hybrid approach where nodes are updated lazily and speculative reads are employed to predict future access patterns. This allows for efficient use of resources by reducing unnecessary locking and improving cache locality. The system ensures correctness through a combination of optimistic concurrency control and eventual consistency mechanisms. Extensive simulations and real-world benchmarking demonstrate that DeltaTree outperforms state-of-the-art concurrent search trees in terms of both query latency and throughput, even under high levels of concurrency.  Key findings indicate that DeltaTree achieves up to 30% improvement in query response times and up to 40% increase in concurrency over comparable systems. Furthermore, the system demonstrates superior performance in scenarios with spatial locality, such as spatial database queries, indicating its effectiveness in practical applications.  In conclusion, DeltaTree represents a significant advancement in the field of concurrent search trees, offering improved performance and better resource utilization. Its design prioritizes locality and concurrency, making it a viable solution for managing large, dynamic datasets in distributed environments.

text:
Axisymmetric magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) can be invoked for describing
astrophysical magnetized flows and formulated to model stellar magnetospheres
including main sequence stars (e.g. the Sun), compact stellar objects [e.g.
magnetic white dwarfs (MWDs), radio pulsars, anomalous X-ray pulsars (AXPs),
magnetars, isolated neutron stars etc.], and planets as a major step forward
towards a full three-dimensional model construction. Using powerful and
reliable numerical solvers based on two distinct finite-difference method (FDM)
and finite-element method (FEM) schemes of algorithm, we examine axisymmetric
steady-state or stationary MHD models in Throumoulopoulos & Tasso (2001),
finding that their separable semi-analytic nonlinear solutions are actually not
unique given their specific selection of several free functionals and chosen
boundary conditions. The multiplicity of nonlinear steady MHD solutions gives
rise to differences in the total energies contained in the magnetic fields and
flow velocity fields as well as in the asymptotic behaviours approaching
infinity, which may in turn explain why numerical solvers tend to converge to a
nonlinear solution with a lower energy than the corresponding separable
semi-analytic one. By properly adjusting model parameters, we invoke
semi-analytic and numerical solutions to describe different kind of scenarios,
including nearly parallel case and the situation in which the misalignment
between the fluid flow and magnetic field is considerable. We propose that
these MHD models are capable of describing the magnetospheres of MWDs as
examples of applications with moderate conditions (including magnetic field)
where the typical values of several important parameters are consistent with
observations. We discuss the challenges of developing numerical extrapolation
MHD codes in view of nonlinear degeneracy.

In this paper, phasor measurement unit (PMU) placement for power grid state
estimation under different degrees of observability is studied. Observability
degree is the depth of the buses' reachability by the placed PMUs and thus
constitutes an important characteristic for PMU placement. However, the sole
observability as addressed in many works still does not guarantee a good
estimate for the grid state. Some existing works also considered the PMU
placement for minimizing the mean squared error or maximizing the mutual
information between the measurement output and grid state. However, they ignore
the observability requirements for computational tractability and thus
potentially lead to artificial results such as acceptance of the estimate for
an unobserved state component as its unconditional mean. In this work, the PMU
placement optimization problem is considered by minimizing the mean squared
error or maximizing the mutual information between the measurement output and
grid state, under grid observability constraints. The provided solution is free
from the mentioned fundamental drawbacks in the existing PMU placement designs.
The problems are posed as binary nonlinear optimization problems, for which
this paper develops efficient algorithms for computational solutions. The
performance of the proposed algorithms is analyzed in detail through numerical
examples on large-scale IEEE power networks.

text: Understanding the variability of absorption lines in the spectra of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) is crucial for interpreting their physical environments and origins. This study focuses on GRB 080310, employing time-dependent excitation and ionization modeling of its absorption lines. Our objective was to explore the changes in ionization states within the surrounding medium and determine the physical conditions prompting these changes. Utilizing high-resolution spectroscopic data obtained over multiple epochs, we applied nonlinear time-dependent simulations of the photoionization processes induced by the GRB's intense radiation. These simulations accounted for varying incident radiation fields and the temporal response of different ions. Key findings revealed significant temporal changes in the column densities of Fe II and Mg II ions, correlated with the GRB’s light curve decay phases. Our results indicate that the variability in these absorption lines is driven primarily by the ionization response of the circum-burst medium to the evolving emission, rather than merely geometrical effects or external cloud structures. Additionally, the timescales of ionization processes observed imply a close proximity of these absorbers to the GRB, suggesting that the surrounding medium can significantly influence the afterglow spectrum. In conclusion, this approach enhances our understanding of the ionization dynamics in GRB environments and provides a framework for interpreting similar phenomena observed in other GRBs. Such insights can be instrumental in refining models of the circumstellar medium and the mechanisms of GRB afterglows, advancing our overall comprehension of these cataclysmic cosmic events.

text: This study presents the first 3D reconstructions of coronal loops using the Stereo A+B spacecraft, which provides unprecedented insights into the complex magnetic field structures of the solar corona. By analyzing high-resolution images of coronal loops captured by the Stereo A+B spacecraft, we aim to improve our understanding of the magnetic field topology and its impact on solar activity.  The objective of this research is to develop a robust method for reconstructing 3D coronal loop structures from Stereo A+B data, and to apply this method to a set of observations of coronal loops in active regions. Our approach involves a combination of image processing techniques, magnetic field modeling, and computational simulations to derive the 3D magnetic field structure of coronal loops.  The key findings of this study show that the Stereo A+B spacecraft provides high-resolution images of coronal loops with unprecedented detail, allowing for the reconstruction of complex 3D magnetic field structures. Our results indicate that the magnetic field of coronal loops is twisted and non-uniform, with a characteristic "twisted force-free" (TFF) field configuration. We also find that the TFF field configuration is a common feature of coronal loops in active regions, and that it plays a key role in the formation of solar flares and coronal mass ejections.  Overall, this study contributes to our understanding of the complex magnetic field structures of the solar corona, and highlights the potential of the Stereo A+B spacecraft for studying coronal loops and their impact on solar activity.

We study photometric properties, chemical abundances and sizes of star
formation regions in the two principal arms of the galaxy NGC 628 (M74). The
GALEX ultraviolet, optical UBVRI, and H-alpha? surface photometry data are
used, including those obtained with the 1.5-m telescope of the Maidanak
Observatory. The thirty brightest star formation regions in ultraviolet light
located in the spiral arms of NGC 628 are identified and studied. We find that
the star formation regions in one (longer) arm are systematically brighter and
larger than the regions in the other (shorter) arm. However, both luminosity
and size distribution functions have approximately the same slopes for the
samples of star formation regions in both arms. The star formation regions in
the longer arm have a higher star formation rate density than the regions in
the shorter arm. The regions in the shorter arm show higher N/O ratio at a
higher oxygen abundance, but they have lower ultraviolet and H-alpha?
luminosities. These findings can be explained if we assume that star formation
regions in the shorter arm had higher star formation rate in the past, but now
it is lower than for those in the opposite arm. Results of stellar evolutionary
synthesis show that the brightest regions in the longer arm are slightly
younger than the ones in the shorter arm (3.5+-2.2 Myr versus 6.0+-1.1 Myr).
Our results demonstrate that there is a difference in the inner structures and
parameters of the interstellar medium between the spiral arms of NGC 628, one
of which is long and hosts a regular chain of bright star formation complexes
and the other, shorter one does not.

text: The solar corona, the outer atmosphere of the Sun, is a complex and dynamic region where energy is deposited through various mechanisms, including unresolved flaring loops. These loops are magnetic structures that connect the Sun's surface to its corona, and their unresolved nature refers to the fact that they are not directly observable due to their small size and the limitations of current observational techniques. Despite their importance in understanding the solar corona and its role in space weather, the duration of energy deposition on these loops remains poorly understood.  This study aims to investigate the duration of energy deposition on unresolved flaring loops in the solar corona, with a focus on the relationship between energy deposition and loop evolution. To achieve this, we analyzed a large dataset of coronal observations from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) and the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS). Our analysis revealed that the duration of energy deposition on unresolved flaring loops is significantly longer than previously thought, with some loops experiencing prolonged energy deposition for up to several days.  Our results suggest that the duration of energy deposition on these loops is influenced by various factors, including loop size, magnetic field strength, and the presence of coronal mass ejections. The implications of these findings are significant, as they highlight the need for improved observational techniques and modeling approaches to better understand the dynamics of unresolved flaring loops and their role in shaping the solar corona.

text: We investigate the flow structure of compound droplets traversing through microchannels, focusing on their dynamics, deformation behavior, and interactions with the channel walls. Our study addresses the critical challenge of understanding how these droplets behave under varying flow conditions, which is essential for optimizing applications in microfluidics and pharmaceuticals. By employing a combination of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations and experimental techniques, we analyze the influences of droplet size, viscosity ratios, and flow rates on the motion and merging of compound droplets.  Our results reveal that the flow structure around compound droplets is significantly influenced by the droplet's internal composition and external hydrodynamic forces. We observe that changes in viscosity ratios lead to distinct deformation patterns, which subsequently affect the stability and movement of the droplets. Notably, we find that compound droplets exhibit a characteristic “squeezing” behavior upon approaching channel constrictions, which can enhance mixing efficiency within the droplet and influence reactions occurring in confined spaces.  Additionally, we demonstrate that the interaction between multiple droplets can result in complex flow patterns, including the formation of organized droplet trains. Our methodology integrates high-resolution imaging and advanced flow characterization techniques to map these interactions in real-time. Through these findings, we contribute to the understanding of droplet dynamics in microchannels, paving the way for improved design strategies in microfluidic systems that utilize compound droplets for targeted applications in diagnostics and drug delivery.

We will study a mathematical model of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
infection in the presence of combination therapy that includes within-host
infectious dynamics. The deterministic model requires us to analyze asymptotic
stability of two distinct steady states, disease-free and endemic equilibria.
Previous results have focused on investigating the global asymptotic stability
of the trivial steady state using an implicit finite-difference method which
generates a system of difference equations. We, instead, provide analytic
solutions and long term attractive behavior for the endemic steady state using
the theory of difference equations. The dynamics of estimated model is
appropriately determined by a certain quantity threshold maintaining the immune
response to a sufficient level. The result also indicates that a forward
bifurcation in the model happens when the disease-free equilibrium loses its
stability and a stable endemic equilibrium appears as the basic reproduction
number exceeds unity. In this scenario, the classical requirement of the
reproduction number being less than unity becomes a necessary and sufficient
condition for disease mitigation. When the associated reproduction number is in
excess of unity, a stable endemic equilibrium emerges with an unstable
disease-free equilibrium (leading to the persistence and existence of HIV
within the infected individuals). The attractivity of the model reveals that
the disease-free equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable under certain
assumptions. A comparison between the continuous and estimated discrete models
is also provided to have a clear perception in understanding the behavioral
dynamics of disease modelling. Finally, we show that the associated estimation
method is very robust in the sense of numerical stability since the equilibria
and the stability conditions are independent of the time step.

Since twenty years, a large population of close-in planets orbiting various
classes of low-mass stars (from M to A-type stars) has been discovered. In such
systems, the dissipation of the kinetic energy of tidal flows in the host star
may modify its rotational evolution and shape the orbital architecture of the
surrounding planetary system. In this context, recent works demonstrated that
the amplitude of this dissipation can vary over several orders of magnitude as
a function of stellar mass, age and rotation. In addition, the stellar rotation
evolution strongly impacts angular momentum exchanges within star-planet
systems. Therefore, it is now necessary to take into account the structural and
rotational evolution of stars when studying the orbital evolution of close-in
planets. The presence of planets may also modify the rotation of the host stars
and as a consequence their evolution, magnetic activity and mixing. In this
work, we present the first study of the dynamics of close-in planets of various
masses orbiting low-mass stars (from $0.6$ to $1.2~M_\star$) where we compute
the simultaneous evolution of the star's structure, rotation and tidal
dissipation in its external convective enveloppe. We find that tidal friction
due to the stellar dynamical tide, i.e. tidal inertial waves excited in the
convection zone, can be larger by several orders of magnitude than the one of
the equilibrium tide, especially during the PMS phase. Consequently, the
orbital migration of the planet is now more pronounced and depends more on the
stellar mass, rotation and age. This would very weakly affect the planets in
the habitable zone because they are located at orbital distances such that
stellar tide-induced migration happens on very long timescales. We also
demonstrate that the rotational evolution of host stars is only weakly affected
by the presence of planets except for massive companions.

We construct a new sample of ~1700 solar neighbourhood halo subdwarfs from
the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, selected using a reduced proper motion diagram.
Radial velocities come from the SDSS spectra and proper motions from the
light-motion curve catalogue of Bramich et al. (2008). Using a photometric
parallax relation to estimate distances gives us the full phase-space
coordinates. Typical velocity errors are in the range 30-50 km/s. This halo
sample is one of the largest constructed to-date and the disc contamination is
at a level of < 1 per cent. This enables us to calculate the halo velocity
dispersion to excellent accuracy. We find that the velocity dispersion tensor
is aligned in spherical polar coordinates and that (sigma_r, sigma_phi,
sigma_theta) = (143 \pm 2, 82 \pm 2, 77 \pm 2) km/s. The stellar halo exhibits
no net rotation, although the distribution of v_phi shows tentative evidence
for asymmetry. The kinematics are consistent with a mildly flattened stellar
density falling with distance like r^{-3.75}. Using the full phase-space
coordinates, we look for signs of kinematic substructure in the stellar halo.
We find evidence for four discrete overdensities localised in angular momentum
and suggest that they may be possible accretion remnants. The most prominent is
the solar neighbourhood stream previously identified by Helmi et al. (1999),
but the remaining three are new. One of these overdensities is potentially
associated with a group of four globular clusters (NGC5466, NGC6934, M2 and
M13) and raises the possibility that these could have been accreted as part of
a much larger progenitor.

text: Our work delves into the intriguing topic of the origin of structure in the universe by investigating the primordial bispectrum in the absence of non-Gaussianities. The core motivation behind our study is to unravel the underlying mechanisms that govern the formation of structures in the early universe without the influence of non-Gaussian perturbations. By exploring the primordial bispectrum devoid of non-Gaussianities, we aim to shed light on the fundamental processes that lead to the emergence of the large-scale structures observed in the cosmos today.  Through rigorous mathematical analyses and numerical simulations, we have uncovered remarkable results that challenge existing paradigms in cosmology. Our findings suggest that even in the absence of non-Gaussianities, the primordial bispectrum exhibits intricate patterns that are crucial for understanding the evolution of structures in the universe. We propose a novel methodology that combines theoretical modeling with computational techniques to investigate the origins of structure formation in a non-Gaussianity-free scenario.  Overall, our research contributes to advancing the field of cosmology by providing a fresh perspective on the origin of structure through the lens of the primordial bispectrum. By elucidating the intricate interplay of fundamental processes in the early universe, we aim to deepen our understanding of the cosmic evolution and the mechanisms responsible for shaping the vast cosmic structures we observe today.

text: This study investigates the application of Support Vector Machines (SVMs) to additive models, a class of statistical models that decompose complex relationships into a set of independent components. The primary objective is to establish the consistency and robustness of SVMs in fitting additive models, a crucial aspect for their adoption in real-world applications.    Additive models have gained popularity due to their flexibility in modeling complex relationships and interactions between variables. However, they often suffer from the curse of dimensionality, leading to model instability and overfitting. SVMs, on the other hand, have been widely used for regression and classification tasks, but their performance on additive models remains unexplored.    This study employs a simulation-based approach to evaluate the consistency and robustness of SVMs on additive models. A series of simulations are conducted using various datasets with different characteristics, including different numbers of variables, interaction terms, and noise levels. The performance of SVMs is evaluated using metrics such as mean squared error and cross-validation accuracy.   Key findings The results show that SVMs can be a competitive alternative to traditional methods for additive models, offering improved robustness and generalizability. The simulations reveal that SVMs can capture complex interactions and non-linear relationships, even in the presence of high-dimensional noise. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the choice of kernel and regularization parameters significantly affects the performance of SVMs on additive models.    This study provides evidence for the potential of SVMs in fitting additive models, highlighting their consistency and robustness in capturing complex relationships and interactions between variables. The findings have implications for the development of new statistical models and machine learning algorithms that can effectively handle high-dimensional data and non-linear relationships.

text: The study of liquid mixtures, primarily inhomogeneous in nature, necessitates a comprehensive understanding beyond local theoretical approaches. Traditional kinetic theories often fall short in accurately capturing the intricate behaviors of such mixtures due to their limited consideration of non-local interactions. This research aims to develop a non-local kinetic theory model that more effectively addresses the complexities present in inhomogeneous liquid mixtures. The methodology integrates statistical mechanics with extended thermodynamic principles, utilizing advanced computational simulations to assess the macroscopic properties that emerge from microscopic interactions. Our findings reveal that non-local interactions play a pivotal role in determining phase behavior, transport properties, and structural formations within these mixtures. The model accounts for long-range correlations and spatial heterogeneities, highlighting how non-local effects lead to deviations from predictions made by conventional local kinetic theories. Through extensive simulation data, we observed significant improvements in predicting properties such as viscosity, diffusivity, and thermal conductivity. The results underscore the necessity of incorporating non-local elements into the theoretical framework for a more accurate and comprehensive representation of inhomogeneous liquid mixtures. In conclusion, the research provides a robust foundation for further exploration into complex fluid systems, enhancing predictive modeling capabilities and offering valuable insights into the design and manipulation of liquid mixtures across various industrial applications. This non-local approach paves the way for more nuanced understanding and control of liquid mixture behaviors in practical applications, thereby pushing the boundaries of current kinetic theory methodologies.

text: ADQUEX is an innovative system designed to efficiently process federated queries over linked data, leveraging adaptive processing techniques and tuple routing strategies. The primary objective of this research is to enhance query performance and scalability by dynamically adapting to the varying characteristics of distributed data sources. Methodologically, ADQUEX employs a hybrid approach combining tuple routing with adaptive query optimization to manage the complexity and heterogeneity inherent in federated data environments. Key findings demonstrate that ADQUEX significantly improves query execution times and resource utilization compared to traditional federated query processing methods. The system effectively routes tuples across different data sources based on similarity metrics, minimizing communication overhead and optimizing data retrieval. Moreover, ADQUEX dynamically adjusts its processing strategies in response to query patterns and data source dynamics, leading to more efficient and flexible federated query processing. In conclusion, ADQUEX represents a robust solution for managing federated queries over linked data, offering substantial improvements in performance and adaptability.

In the framework of model-based clustering, a model allowing several latent
class variables is proposed. This model assumes that the distribution of the
observed data can be factorized into several independent blocks of variables.
Each block is assumed to follow a latent class model ({\it i.e.,} mixture with
conditional independence assumption). The proposed model includes variable
selection, as a special case, and is able to cope with the mixed-data setting.
The simplicity of the model allows to estimate the repartition of the variables
into blocks and the mixture parameters simultaneously, thus avoiding to run EM
algorithms for each possible repartition of variables into blocks. For the
proposed method, a model is defined by the number of blocks, the number of
clusters inside each block and the repartition of variables into block. Model
selection can be done with two information criteria, the BIC and the MICL, for
which an efficient optimization is proposed. The performances of the model are
investigated on simulated and real data. It is shown that the proposed method
gives a rich interpretation of the dataset at hand ({\it i.e.,} analysis of the
repartition of the variables into blocks and analysis of the clusters produced
by each block of variables).

Motivated by recent scanning tunneling and photoemission spectroscopy
measurements on self-organized gold chains on a germanium surface we
reinvestigate the local single-particle spectral properties of Luttinger
liquids. In the first part we use the bosonization approach to exactly compute
the local spectral function of a simplified field theoretical low-energy model
and take a closer look at scaling properties as a function of the ratio of
energy and temperature. Translational invariant Luttinger liquids as well as
those with an open boundary (cut chain geometry) are considered. We explicitly
show that the scaling functions of both setups have the same analytic form. The
scaling behavior suggests a variety of consistency checks which can be
performed on measured data to experimentally verify Luttinger liquid behavior.
In a second part we approximately compute the local spectral function of a
microscopic lattice model---the extended Hubbard model---close to an open
boundary using the functional renormalization group. We show that as a function
of energy and temperature it follows the field theoretical prediction in the
low-energy regime and point out the importance of nonuniversal energy scales
inherent to any microscopic model. The spatial dependence of this spectral
function is characterized by oscillatory behavior and an envelope function
which follows a power law both in accordance with the field theoretical
continuum model. Interestingly, for the lattice model we find a phase shift
which is proportional to the two-particle interaction and not accounted for in
the standard bosonization approach to Luttinger liquids with an open boundary.
We briefly comment on the effects of several one-dimensional branches cutting
the Fermi energy and Rashba spin-orbit interaction.
