text: Extragalactic Sources and Propagation of Ultra-High Energy Cosmic Rays (UHECRs) remain one of the most intriguing and complex phenomena in modern astrophysics. The observation of UHECRs, with energies exceeding 10^20 eV, has been a subject of extensive research and debate, with various theories attempting to explain their origin and propagation. This study aims to investigate the extragalactic sources and propagation mechanisms of UHECRs, with a focus on the interplay between astrophysical and cosmological processes.   UHECRs are believed to originate from a variety of sources, including active galactic nuclei (AGN), gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), and supernovae remnants. However, the exact mechanisms responsible for accelerating particles to such extreme energies remain poorly understood. The propagation of UHECRs through the universe is also shrouded in mystery, with several theories proposing different paths and interactions with the cosmic medium.   This study seeks to explore the possible extragalactic sources of UHECRs and their subsequent propagation, with a focus on the interplay between astrophysical and cosmological processes. The research aims to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the origin and evolution of UHECRs, and to shed light on the fundamental physics underlying these enigmatic particles.   This study employs a combination of theoretical and numerical simulations, using advanced computational models to investigate the behavior of UHECRs in various astrophysical and cosmological environments. The research also draws on existing observational data and theoretical frameworks, including the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array experiments.   The results of this study indicate that UHECRs may originate from a combination of AGN and GRB sources, with the latter providing a significant contribution to the observed flux. The propagation of UHECRs is found to be influenced by the intergalactic magnetic field, with the particles experiencing significant interactions with the cosmic medium. The study also reveals the importance of considering the role of dark matter in the propagation of UHECRs.   This study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the origin and propagation of UHECRs, highlighting the interplay between astrophysical and cosmological processes. The findings suggest that UHECRs may originate from a combination of AGN and GRB sources, with significant interactions with the intergalactic medium. The research underscores the need for continued observations and theoretical investigations to further elucidate the fundamental physics underlying these enigmatic particles.

text: We investigate the enumeration of independent sets within graphs characterized by small maximum degrees, specifically focusing on the upper bounds for the number of such sets. Our study addresses the problem of determining precise estimates for independent sets in sparse graphs, wherein traditional enumerative techniques face limitations due to density constraints. By employing probabilistic methods and exploiting the combinatorial structure inherent in low-degree graphs, we derive new upper bounds on the number of independent sets. Our key approach involves a detailed analysis of the graph's degree sequence, allowing an efficient recursive application of established combinatorial principles and advanced counting techniques to achieve tighter bounds than those previously known. The methodology integrates improvements on the Lovász local lemma and tailored use of entropy maximization frameworks, enabling the derivation of results that demonstrate the dependency of these bounds on the maximum degree. Through rigorous validation against known graph classes, including trees and subcubic graphs, we illustrate the effectiveness and general applicability of our bounds. Our research yields not only theoretical advancements in understanding the asymptotic behavior of independent sets in constrained-degree environments but also practical implications for algorithms in combinatorial optimization and network theory. These insights open avenues for further explorations into graph classes with other nuanced structural properties, fostering a deeper comprehension of independent set distributions across varied graph landscapes.

Spontaneous fluctuations of the BOLD (Blood Oxygen Level-Dependent) signal,
measured with fMRI (functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging), display a rich and
neurobiologically relevant functional connectivity structure. This structure is
usually revealed using time averaging methods, which prevent the detection of
functional connectivity changes over time. In this work we studied the
electrophysiological correlates of dynamical BOLD functional connectivity
fluctuations, by means of long (approx. 50 min) joint electroencephalographic
(EEG) and fMRI recordings. We identified widespread positive and negative
correlations between EEG spectral power and fMRI BOLD connectivity fluctuations
in a network of 90 cortical and subcortical regions. In particular, increased
alpha (8-12 Hz) and beta (15-30 Hz) power were related to decreased functional
connectivity, whereas gamma (30-60 Hz) power correlated positively with BOLD
connectivity between specific brain regions. Furthermore, these patterns were
altered for subjects undergoing vigilance changes, with an involvement of the
slow delta (0.4 - 4 Hz) band in localized positive correlations. Finally, graph
theoretical indices of network structure also exhibited sharp changes over
time, with average path length correlating positively with alpha power
extracted from central and frontal electrodes. Our results strongly suggest
that non-stationary BOLD functional connectivity has a neurophysiological
origin. Positive correlations of BOLD connectivity with gamma can be
interpreted as increased average binding over relatively long periods of time,
possibly due to spontaneous cognition occurring during rest. Negative
correlations with alpha suggest functional inhibition of local and long-range
connectivity, associated with an idling state of the brain.

We prove that the 3-D compressible Euler equations with surface tension along
the moving free-boundary are well-posed. Specifically, we consider isentropic
dynamics and consider an equation of state, modeling a liquid, given by Courant
and Friedrichs as $p(\rho) = \alpha \rho^ \gamma - \beta$ for consants $\gamma
>1$ and $ \alpha, \beta > 0$. The analysis is made difficult by two competing
nonlinearities associated with the potential energy: compression in the bulk,
and surface area dynamics on the free-boundary. Unlike the analysis of the
incompressible Euler equations, wherein boundary regularity controls regularity
in the interior, the compressible Euler equation require the additional
analysis of nonlinear wave equations generating sound waves. An existence
theory is developed by a specially chosen parabolic regularization together
with the vanishing viscosity method. The artificial parabolic term is chosen so
as to be asymptotically consistent with the Euler equations in the limit of
zero viscosity. Having solutions for the positive surface tension problem, we
proceed to obtain a priori estimates which are independent of the surface
tension parameter. This requires choosing initial data which satisfy the Taylor
sign condition. By passing to the limit of zero surface tension, we prove the
well-posedness of the compressible Euler system without surface on the
free-boundary, and without derivative loss.

The prominent blue shifts of Ne viii associated with the junctions of the
magnetic network in the quiet Sun are still not well understood. By comparing
the coronal magnetic-field structures as obtained by a potential-field
reconstruction with the conspicuous blue-shift patches on the dopplergram of Ne
viii as observed in an equatorial quiet-Sun region, we find that most of the
regions with significant upflow are associated with the funnel-like legs of
magnetic loops and co-spatial with increments of the line width. These
quasi-steady upflows can be regarded as the signatures of mass supply to
coronal loops. By using the square-root of the line intensity as a proxy for
the plasma density, the mass flux of the upflow in each funnel can be
estimated. We find that the mass flux is anti-correlated with the funnel's
expansion factor as determined from the extrapolated magnetic field. One of the
loop systems is associated with a coronal bright point, which was observed by
several instruments and exhibited various morphologies in different wavelengths
and viewing directions. A remarkable agreement between its magnetic structure
and the associated EUV emission pattern was found, suggesting an almost
potential-field nature of the coronal magnetic field. We also report the direct
detection of a small-scale siphon flow by both STEREO satellites. However, this
transient siphon flow occurred in a weak mixed-polarity-field region, which was
outside the adjacent magnetic funnel, and thus it is perhaps not related to
plasma upflow in the funnel. Based on these observations, we suggest that at
upper-TR temperatures the dominant flows in quiet-Sun coronal loops are
long-lasting upflows rather than siphon flows. We also discuss the implications
for coronal heating and unresolved magnetic structures.

text: This study presents the initial results from the MIDI+FSU (Mid-infrared Interferometric Dual Spectrometer Unit) experiment conducted at the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) using the K-band for fringe tracking. Our primary objective was to demonstrate the feasibility of high-resolution mid-infrared interferometry employing the K-band as a reference for fringe tracking. Key to our approach was the integration of a dual-spectral unit that allows simultaneous observation across the mid-infrared spectrum.   We achieved significant improvements in spectral resolution and stability through the application of K-band fringe tracking, which enabled us to maintain accurate phase control over the interferometric baseline lengths during the observation sequence. Results indicate a substantial enhancement in the achievable spectral resolution compared to previous studies using different bands, demonstrating the potential of the K-band for future interferometric observations in this spectral region.  Our methodology involved precise calibration of the K-band fringe tracker and detailed analysis of the resulting data to assess its impact on overall system performance. We employed advanced signal processing techniques to minimize noise and ensure consistent fringe tracking throughout the observation. The findings suggest that the K-band fringe-tracking technique offers a robust solution for high-precision interferometry in the mid-infrared regime, paving the way for future astronomical research utilizing the VLTI.

text: Supernovae Type Ia are a class of catastrophic stellar explosions that release enormous amounts of energy, leading to the ejection of elements into interstellar space. Among these ejected elements, silicon group elements, including silicon (Si), aluminum (Al), and magnesium (Mg), play a crucial role in the formation of planetary systems and the origins of life. However, the mechanisms that govern the nucleosynthesis of these elements during supernovae explosions are not yet fully understood.  The objective of this research is to investigate the nucleosynthetic pathways of silicon group elements during supernovae Type Ia explosions. Using a combination of theoretical models and computational simulations, we aim to determine the relative abundances of these elements and their isotopic compositions in the ejected material. Our approach involves a detailed analysis of the explosive nucleosynthesis of silicon group elements, taking into account the effects of various astrophysical parameters, such as the progenitor star's mass and the explosion's energy release.  Our results indicate that the nucleosynthesis of silicon group elements during supernovae Type Ia explosions is a complex process, involving multiple competing pathways and competing nuclear reactions. We find that the relative abundances of these elements vary significantly depending on the explosion's energy release and the progenitor star's mass. Our simulations also suggest that the isotopic compositions of these elements are influenced by the explosion's kinetic energy and the presence of heavy elements in the progenitor star. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the nucleosynthesis of silicon group elements in supernovae Type Ia explosions and their role in the formation of planetary systems and the origins of life.

Zero-delay transmission of a Gaussian source over an additive white Gaussian
noise (AWGN) channel is considered in the presence of an additive Gaussian
interference signal. The mean squared error (MSE) distortion is minimized under
an average power constraint assuming that the interference signal is known at
the transmitter. Optimality of simple linear transmission does not hold in this
setting due to the presence of the known interference signal. While the optimal
encoder-decoder pair remains an open problem, various non-linear transmission
schemes are proposed in this paper. In particular, interference concentration
(ICO) and one-dimensional lattice (1DL) strategies, using both uniform and
non-uniform quantization of the interference signal, are studied. It is shown
that, in contrast to typical scalar quantization of Gaussian sources, a
non-uniform quantizer, whose quantization intervals become smaller as we go
further from zero, improves the performance. Given that the optimal decoder is
the minimum MSE (MMSE) estimator, a necessary condition for the optimality of
the encoder is derived, and the numerically optimized encoder (NOE) satisfying
this condition is obtained. Based on the numerical results, it is shown that
1DL with non-uniform quantization performs closer (compared to the other
schemes) to the numerically optimized encoder while requiring significantly
lower complexity.

In the last decade, ground-based Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes
have discovered about 175 very-high-energy (VHE; $E >$ 100 GeV) gamma-ray
sources, with more to follow with the development of H.E.S.S. II and CTA.
Nearly 40 of these are confirmed pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe). We present results
from a leptonic emission code that models the spectral energy density of a PWN
by solving a Fokker-Planck-type transport equation and calculating inverse
Compton and synchrotron emissivities. Although models such as these have been
developed before, most of them model the geometry of a PWN as that of a single
sphere. We have created a time-dependent, multi-zone model to investigate
changes in the particle spectrum as the particles traverse through the PWN, by
considering a time and spatially-dependent magnetic field, spatially-dependent
bulk particle motion causing convection, diffusion, and energy losses (SR, IC
and adiabatic). Our code predicts the radiation spectrum at different positions
in the nebula, yielding novel results, e.g., the surface brightness versus the
radius and the PWN size as function of energy. We calibrated our new model
against more basic models using the observed spectrum of PWN G0.9+0.1,
incorporating data from H.E.S.S. as well as radio and X-ray experiments. We fit
our predicted radiation spectra to data from G21.5$-$0.9, G54.1+0.3, and HESS
J1356$-$645 and found that our model yields reasonable results for young PWNe.
We next performed a parameter study which gave significant insight into the
behaviour of the PWN for different scenarios. Our model is now ready to be
applied to a population of PWNe to probe possible trends such as the surface
brightness as a function of spin-down of the pulsar.

The fundamental description of nature, beyond the Standard Model (SM), may
include heavy neutrinos that mix and thus allow processes in which lepton
flavor is not preserved. We investigate the impact of charged currents that
couple heavy gauge bosons to heavy neutrinos and SM leptons on
lepton-flavor-violating decays of SM leptons into three charged leptons, with
no final-state neutrinos. We implement our expressions for the leading
contributions to ${\rm Br}(l_\alpha\to l_\beta\,l_\sigma\,l_\sigma)$, which
hold for either Dirac or Majorana neutrinos, to the trilepton decay $\mu\to3e$,
of the muon, and so determine sets of masses of heavy neutrinos and the heavy
gauge boson, within GeVs to few TeVs, that are consistent with the upper bounds
provided by the SINDRUM Collaboration. We find, however, that constraints
dictated by the upper bound on ${\rm Br}(\mu\to e\gamma)$, from the MEG
Collaboration, are more stringent. We utilize such parameters to find that the
contributions to tau decays are $\sim10^{-15}-10^{-13}$, well below bounds from
$B$ factories. The mixing of heavy and SM charged bosons is also investigated.
We find that current experimental data from MEG and SINDRUM would allow mixing
angles as large as $\sim10^{-2}$, for a relatively light new charged boson, but
the expected sensitivity of the Mu3e experiment would be capable of setting an
upper bound on this angle as small as $\sim10^{-4}$ if the mass of this boson
is within the range of few TeVs.

text: This work investigates the vulnerability of the Tor anonymity network to peer-to-peer (P2P) applications being utilized as a means to trace and profile users. By analyzing how P2P applications can be manipulated to reveal sensitive user information within the Tor network, we aim to highlight the broader security implications for users who rely on Tor for anonymity. Our findings reveal that P2P applications can be strategically deployed to carry out traffic correlation attacks, compromising the privacy of Tor users and potentially de-anonymizing them. Through a series of experiments and simulations, we demonstrate how an adversary can exploit the inherent characteristics of P2P traffic to unmask Tor users, exposing their online activities despite their use of anonymizing measures.  The key contribution of this work is the identification of a previously underexplored attack vector that poses a significant threat to the anonymity guarantees of Tor. By shedding light on this vulnerability, we pave the way for future research to develop robust defenses and mitigation strategies to safeguard user privacy within the Tor network. Our study underscores the importance of understanding the intricate interplay between different network protocols and the potential risks they pose to the privacy and security of users in an increasingly interconnected digital landscape.

Utilizing state-of-the-art experimental techniques and theoretical models, the study investigates how these perturbations influence current-voltage characteristics and carrier mobility. Key findings include the identification of distinct transport regimes and the development of predictive models that correlate with experimental observations. The conclusion highlights the implications of these findings for enhancing device performance in various technological applications, including high-speed electronics and energy conversion systems.

text: In this paper, we propose a novel O(|E|)-linear time complexity algorithm for solving the MaxCut problem in undirected graphs. The MaxCut problem is a fundamental problem in combinatorial optimization, where the goal is to partition a graph into two subsets such that the number of edges between them is maximized. Several efficient methods have been developed for solving the MaxCut problem, including the Hopfield network algorithm, the Kadanbey-Sinclair algorithm, and the Seidel algorithm. However, these methods require at least O(|V|^2) time complexity.  Our approach is based on a new data structure called the "cut-tree." The cut-tree is constructed in O(|E|) time complexity and maintains information about the minimum cut in each connected component. We show that by traversing the cut-tree and processing the information, we can compute the maximum cut in O(|E|) time complexity.  Furthermore, we prove that our algorithm works correctly for all connected undirected graphs, and our experimental results validate the efficiency of our proposed algorithm. Specifically, we show that our algorithm significantly outperforms the Seidel algorithm for dense graphs. Our results have important implications for applications in network optimization, image segmentation, and machine learning, where the MaxCut problem plays a crucial role.  In summary, we present an O(|E|)-linear algorithm for solving the MaxCut problem in undirected graphs, which significantly improves the time complexity of existing methods while maintaining accuracy. The proposed algorithm utilizes a novel data structure called the "cut-tree," which enables us to efficiently traverse and process the graph to compute the maximum cut. Our theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed algorithm.

text: This research paper presents a novel probabilistic model for visual segmentation, a fundamental task in computer vision that involves dividing an image into its constituent parts, such as objects, textures, and backgrounds. The background of the model is drawn from the existing literature on visual segmentation, where various methods have been proposed to tackle this problem. However, these methods often suffer from limitations, such as low accuracy, computational inefficiency, or failure to capture complex scene structures.   The objective of this research is to develop a probabilistic model that can effectively segment images in various scenarios, including those with complex scenes, occlusions, and varying lighting conditions. To achieve this, the proposed model combines the strengths of traditional graph-based models with the flexibility of deep learning techniques.   The proposed model is based on a conditional random field (CRF) framework, where the segmentation process is modeled as a probabilistic inference problem. The CRF is parameterized using a deep neural network that learns to predict the unary potentials of each pixel. The pairwise potentials are modeled using a set of hand-crafted features, which are learned to capture the structural relationships between pixels.   The key findings of this research show that the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness. The model is able to capture complex scene structures, handle occlusions, and adapt to varying lighting conditions. The results demonstrate the potential of the proposed model for real-world applications, such as image segmentation in medical imaging, surveillance, and autonomous driving.   In conclusion, this research contributes to the development of probabilistic models for visual segmentation, which have the potential to improve the accuracy and robustness of existing methods. The proposed model provides a new approach to visual segmentation that can be applied to a wide range of scenarios, and its potential for real-world applications makes it a promising area of research.

Various studies have implied the existence of a gaseous halo around the
Galaxy extending out to 100 kpc. Galactic cosmic rays (CRs) that propagate to
the halo, either by diffusion or by convection with the possibly existing
large-scale Galactic wind, can interact with the gas therein and produce
gamma-rays via proton-proton collision. We calculate the cosmic ray
distribution in the halo and the gamma-ray flux, and explore the dependence of
the result on model parameters such as diffusion coefficient, CR luminosity, CR
spectral index. We find that the current measurement of isotropic gamma-ray
background at $\lesssim$TeV with Fermi Large Area Telescope already approaches
a level that can provide interesting constraints on the properties of Galactic
cosmic ray (e.g., with CR luminosity $L_{CR}\leq 10^{41}$erg/s). We also
discuss the possibilities of the Fermi bubble and IceCube neutrinos originating
from the proton-proton collision between cosmic rays and gas in the halo, as
well as the implication of our results for the baryon budget of the hot
circumgalactic medium of our Galaxy. Given that the isotropic gamma-ray
background is likely to be dominated by unresolved extragalactic sources,
future telescopes may extract more individual sources from the IGRB, and hence
put even more stringent restriction on the relevant quantities (such as
Galactic cosmic ray luminosity and baryon budget in the halo) in the presence
of a turbulent halo that we consider.

text:
The magnetic fields observed in the Milky~Way and nearby galaxies appear to
be in equipartition with the turbulent, thermal, and cosmic ray energy
densities, and hence are expected to be dynamically important. However, the
origin of these strong magnetic fields is still unclear, and most previous
attempts to simulate galaxy formation from cosmological initial conditions have
ignored them altogether. Here, we analyse the magnetic fields predicted by the
simulations of the Auriga Project, a set of 30 high-resolution cosmological
zoom simulations of Milky~Way-like galaxies, carried out with a moving-mesh
magneto-hydrodynamics code and a detailed galaxy formation physics model. We
find that the magnetic fields grow exponentially at early times owing to a
small-scale dynamo with an e-folding time of roughly $100\,\rm{Myr}$ in the
center of halos until saturation occurs around $z=2-3$, when the magnetic
energy density reaches about $10\%$ of the turbulent energy density with a
typical strength of $10-50\,\rm{\mu G}$. In the galactic centers the ratio
between magnetic and turbulent energy remains nearly constant until $z=0$. At
larger radii, differential rotation in the disks leads to linear amplification
that typically saturates around $z=0.5$ to $z=0$. The final radial and vertical
variations of the magnetic field strength can be well described by two joint
exponential profiles, and are in good agreement with observational constraints.
Overall, the magnetic fields have only little effect on the global evolution of
the galaxies as it takes too long to reach equipartition. We also demonstrate
that our results are well converged with numerical resolution.

text: In the context of warped extra-dimensional models, the study of scalar particles produced in association with a Z boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the International Linear Collider (ILC) presents a compelling avenue for probing the mixed Higgs-radion system. Such models predict the existence of radions, scalar excitations accompanying the graviton in these higher-dimensional theories, which can mix with the conventional Higgs boson. The objective of this research is to analyze production cross-sections and potential signatures of these mixed states to improve the understanding of the underlying physics of warped geometries. Utilizing both analytical approaches and computational simulations, the research evaluates signal characteristics and backgrounds, leveraging leading-order perturbative Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and electroweak calculations. Our key findings indicate that the mixed scalar production in association with a Z boson provides identifiable signatures at high-energy collisions, particularly through the investigation of decay channels specific to the mixed scalar states. The analysis suggests enhanced production rates compared to standard model predictions, with distinct kinematic distributions that can be screened from the LHC's experimental data, as well as more precise measurements at the ILC. Conclusively, this mixed Higgs-radion system proposes a rich phenomenology, presenting an avenue to explore physics beyond the standard model, particularly in detecting potential deviations caused by extra-dimensional impacts. The insights from this research contribute significantly to the design of experimental strategies aiming at the discovery and differentiation of new scalar states in proposed collider environments.

text: We examine the influence of dynamical friction on the radial distribution of blue straggler stars (BSS) within star clusters by implementing both semi-analytical models and preliminary N-body simulations. Our research addresses the long-standing question of how dynamical processes affect the formation and spatial distribution of BSS, which are often thought to form via interactions in dense stellar environments. We developed a semi-analytical framework to describe the interaction between stellar mass loss, dynamical friction, and relaxation processes, allowing us to predict the expected BSS distribution in various cluster conditions. We further complemented our analytical results with N-body simulations that incorporate the effects of dynamical friction on stellar interactions. By conducting a series of simulations with varying initial mass functions and cluster densities, we analyzed how different configurations lead to varying BSS radial profiles. Our findings indicate a significant correlation between the strength of dynamical friction and the concentration of BSS towards the center of the cluster, reinforcing the notion that dynamical interactions play a pivotal role in BSS formation. Furthermore, we observed that environments with strong dynamical friction show a radial distribution skewed towards denser regions, while clusters with weaker friction exhibit a more uniform dispersion. These results offer a qualitative understanding of BSS formation mechanisms while laying the groundwork for more comprehensive studies that integrate stellar dynamics and evolutionary processes. Our work contributes to the broader understanding of stellar evolution in cluster environments, particularly highlighting the critical role of dynamical friction in shaping the observed spatial distributions of BSS.

text: In this work, we present a novel algorithm designed for simulating dusty gas dynamics using Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH). Our objective is to enhance the numerical treatment of dusty gas interactions, which are often prevalent in astrophysical environments such as protoplanetary disks and supernova remnants. We develop a comprehensive test suite to validate the efficacy of our SPH implementation, focusing on the unique challenges posed by the coupling of gas and dust phases.   Our methodology incorporates a multifaceted approach, including the dynamics of dust particles under varying gas densities and velocities, as well as the intricacies of momentum transfer between the gas and dust components. We employ a series of benchmarks to assess the accuracy and stability of our algorithm, comparing results against analytical solutions and established computational models. Key findings indicate that our SPH framework accurately captures the fundamental behaviors of dusty gas systems, including dust settling and drift phenomena.  Furthermore, we investigate the impact of dust-to-gas mass ratios on the overall dynamics, revealing critical insights into how these interactions influence the evolution of the medium. The results demonstrate our algorithm's versatility and reliability in simulating a range of scenarios, paving the way for future studies in astrophysical contexts. Overall, this work lays the foundation for further explorations into the role of dust in cosmic evolution, advancing both theoretical understanding and computational methodologies in planetary formation and other relevant fields.

A separable form of pairing interaction in the $^{1}S_{0}$ channel has been
introduced and successfully applied in the description of both static and
dynamic properties of superfluid nuclei. By adjusting the parameters to
reproduce the pairing properties of the Gogny force in nuclear matter, this
separable pairing force is successful in depicting the pairing properties of
ground states and vibrational excitations of spherical nuclei on almost the
same footing as the original Gogny force. In this article, we extend these
investigations for Relativistic Hartree Bogoliubov theory in deformed nuclei
with axial symmetry (RHBZ) using the same separable pairing interaction. In
order to preserve translational invariance we construct one- and
two-dimensional Talmi-Moshinsky brackets for the cylindrical harmonic
oscillator basis. We show that the matrix elements of this force can then be
expanded in a series of separable terms. The convergence of this expansion is
investigated for various deformations. We observe a relatively fast
convergence. This allows for a considerable reduction in computing time as
compared to RHBZ-calculations with the full Gogny force in the pairing channel.
As an example we solve the RHBZ equations with this separable pairing force for
the ground states of the chain of Sm-isotopes. Good agreement with the
experimental data as well as with other theoretical results is achieved.

text: We report on a comprehensive investigation of the orbital dynamics of the Mercury-Manganese binary system 41 Eridani A, shedding light on the complex interactions between the two distinct components. Through a combination of high-precision astrometric observations and advanced numerical modeling, we successfully recovered the orbital parameters of the system, including the semi-major axis, eccentricity, and orbital inclination.  Our results indicate that the binary system exhibits a highly eccentric orbit, with a semi-major axis of approximately 3.48 astronomical units and an eccentricity of 0.87. The orbital inclination was found to be 28.5 degrees relative to the plane of the ecliptic. Furthermore, our analysis revealed a significant orbital precession, with a nodal precession period of 45.6 years.  Our findings provide valuable insights into the evolution and stability of the 41 Eridani A system, highlighting the importance of considering both the gravitational interactions and the orbital precession in modeling the dynamics of complex binary systems. By integrating high-precision astrometry with advanced numerical simulations, we have improved our understanding of the orbital dynamics of 41 Eridani A, providing a more accurate representation of the system's behavior over time.

text: Aql X-1, a binary system consisting of a black hole and a companion star, is one of the most studied X-ray binary systems due to its unique characteristics. During its hard state, Aql X-1 exhibits a high-energy emission, which is attributed to the accretion of material onto the black hole. Despite numerous studies, the underlying mechanisms driving this hard state are still not well understood.  This research aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the hard state of Aql X-1, focusing on the thermal and dynamical properties of the system. We employ a multi-wavelength approach, combining X-ray, optical, and infrared observations to investigate the accretion process and the role of the companion star. Our analysis reveals that the hard state of Aql X-1 is characterized by a high accretion rate, strong magnetic field, and a large jet production, which is likely driven by the interaction between the accretion disk and the companion star.  Key findings from this study include the detection of a strong correlation between the X-ray flux and the optical variability of the companion star, indicating a direct link between the accretion process and the optical emission. We also find evidence of a large-scale jet production, which is consistent with the presence of a powerful magnetic field. Our results provide new insights into the complex interplay between the accretion disk, the companion star, and the jet production in Aql X-1 during its hard state. Overall, this study contributes to our understanding of the hard state of Aql X-1, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms that govern this unique X-ray binary system.

We investigate the long time behavior of a wavepacket initially localized at
a single site $n_0$ in translationally invariant harmonic and anharmonic chains
with random interactions. In the harmonic case, the energy profile $ \bar{<
e_n(t)>}$ averaged on time and disorder decays for large $|n-n_0|$ as a power
law $\bar{< e_n(t)>}\approx C|n-n_0|^{-\eta}$ where $\eta=5/2$ and 3/2 for
initial displacement and momentum excitations, respectively. The prefactor $C$
depends on the probability distribution of the harmonic coupling constants and
diverges in the limit of weak disorder. As a consequence, the moments $<
m_{\nu}(t)>$ of the energy distribution averaged with respect to disorder
diverge in time as $t^{\beta(\nu)}$ for $\nu \geq 2$, where $\beta=\nu+1-\eta$
for $\nu>\eta-1$. Molecular dynamics simulations yield good agreement with
these theoretical predictions. Therefore, in this system, the second moment of
the wavepacket diverges as a function of time despite the wavepacket is not
spreading. Thus, this only criteria often considered earlier as proving the
spreading of a wave packet, cannot be considered as sufficient in any model.
The anharmonic case is investigated numerically. It is found for intermediate
disorder, that the tail of the energy profile becomes very close to those of
the harmonic case. For weak and strong disorder, our results suggest that the
crossover to the harmonic behavior occurs at much larger $|n-n_0|$ and larger
time.

The present study is devoted to the possibility that tri-atomic molecules
were formed during or shortly after the Big Bang. For this purpose we consider
the ordinary $H_3^{+}$ and $H_3$ and the primitive tri-atomic molecular system,
$H_3^{++}$, which, as is shown, behaves differently. The study is carried out
by comparing the topological features of these systems as they are reflected
through their non-adiabatic coupling terms. Although the $H_3^{++}$ is not
known to exist as a molecule, we found that it behaves as such at intermediate
distances. However this illusion breaks down as its asymptotic region is
reached. Our study indicates that whereas $H_3^{+}$ and $H_3$ dissociate
smoothly, the $H_3^{++}$, does not seem to do so. Nevertheless, the fact that
$H_3^{++}$ is capable of living as a molecule on borrowed time enables it to
catch an electron and form a molecule via the reaction $H_3^{++} + e \to
H_3^{+}$ that may dissociate properly: $H_3^{+} \to H^{+} + H_2$ or $H +
H_2^+$. Thus, the two unique features acquired by $H_3^{++}$ namely, that it is
the most primitive system formed by three protons and one electron and
topologically, still remain for an instant a molecule, may make it the sole
candidate for becoming the \bold{cornerstone} for creating the molecules.

Following the induced gravitational collapse (IGC) paradigm of gamma-ray
bursts (GRBs) associated with type Ib/c supernovae, we present numerical
simulations of the explosion of a carbon-oxygen (CO) core in a binary system
with a neutron-star (NS) companion. The supernova ejecta trigger a
\emph{hypercritical} accretion process onto the NS thanks to a copious neutrino
emission and the trapping of photons within the accretion flow. We show that
temperatures 1--10~MeV develop near the NS surface, hence electron-positron
annihilation into neutrinos becomes the main cooling channel leading to
accretion rates $10^{-9}$--$10^{-1}~M_\odot$~s$^{-1}$ and neutrino luminosities
$10^{43}$--$10^{52}$~erg~s$^{-1}$ (the shorter the orbital period the higher
the accretion rate). We estimate the maximum orbital period, $P_{\rm max}$, as
a function of the NS initial mass, up to which the NS companion can reach by
hypercritical accretion the critical mass for gravitational collapse leading to
black-hole (BH) formation. We then estimate the effects of the accreting and
orbiting NS companion onto a novel geometry of the supernova ejecta density
profile. We present the results of a $1.4\times 10^7$~particle simulation which
show that the NS induces accentuated asymmetries in the ejecta density around
the orbital plane. We elaborate on the observables associated with the above
features of the IGC process. We apply this framework to specific GRBs: we find
that X-ray flashes (XRFs) and binary-driven hypernovae (BdHNe) are produced in
binaries with $P>P_{\rm max}$ and $P < P_{\rm max}$, respectively. We analyze
in detail the case of XRF 060218.

text: This research paper addresses the solutions of multi-component fractional symmetric systems, focusing on developing novel analytical and numerical methods to tackle these complex systems. The study aims to explore the behavior and properties of solutions within such systems, which often arise in various fields including physics, engineering, and applied mathematics.  To achieve the objectives, the methodology involves both theoretical analysis and computational simulations. Theoretical aspects include establishing existence and uniqueness criteria for solutions using fixed point theory and energy functionals. Numerical approaches leverage fractional calculus algorithms and iterative schemes to approximate solutions efficiently. Key findings reveal the existence of distinct solution patterns influenced by fractional orders and component interactions. The study also highlights the importance of initial conditions and boundary values in determining solution dynamics.  Conclusively, the research contributes to a deeper understanding of multi-component fractional symmetric systems, providing robust methodologies for their analysis and application in real-world scenarios. The findings underscore the potential of fractional calculus in modeling complex systems and offer valuable insights for future research endeavors.

The Density Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) is a
topometric algorithm used to cluster spatial data that are affected by
background noise. For the first time, we propose the use of this method for the
detection of sources in gamma-ray astrophysical images obtained from the
Fermi-LAT data, where each point corresponds to the arrival direction of a
photon. We investigate the detection performance of the gamma-ray DBSCAN in
terms of detection efficiency and rejection of spurious clusters, using a
parametric approach, and exploring a large volume of the gamma-ray DBSCAN
parameter space. By means of simulated data we statistically characterize the
gamma-ray DBSCAN, finding signatures that differentiate purely random fields,
from fields with sources. We define a significance level for the detected
clusters, and we successfully test this significance with our simulated data.
We apply the method to real data, and we find an excellent agreement with the
results obtained with simulated data. We find that the gamma-ray DBSCAN can be
successfully used in the detection of clusters in gamma-ray data. The
significance returned by our algorithm is strongly correlated with that
provided by the Maximum Likelihood analysis with standard Fermi-LAT software,
and can be used to safely remove spurious clusters. The positional accuracy of
the reconstructed cluster centroid compares to that returned by standard
Maximum Likelihood analysis, allowing to look for astrophysical counterparts in
narrow regions, minimizing the chance probability in the counterpart
association. We find that gamma-ray DBSCAN is a powerful tool in the detection
of clusters in gamma-ray data, this method can be used both to look for
point-like sources, and extended sources, and can be potentially applied to any
astrophysical field related with detection of clusters in data.

We explore the environmental dependence of star formation timescales in low
mass galaxies using the [$\alpha$/Fe] abundance ratio as an evolutionary clock.
We present integrated [$\alpha$/Fe] measurements for 11 low mass ($M_\star \sim
10^9~M_\odot$) early-type galaxies (ETGs) with a large range of cluster-centric
distance in the Virgo Cluster. We find a gradient in [$\alpha$/Fe], where the
galaxies closest to the cluster center (the cD galaxy, M87) have the highest
values. This trend is driven by galaxies within a projected radius of 0.4~Mpc
(0.26 times the virial radius of Virgo~A), all of which have super-solar
[$\alpha$/Fe]. Galaxies in this mass range exhibit a large scatter in the
[$\alpha$/Fe]--$\sigma$ diagram, and do not obviously lie on an extension of
the relation defined by massive ETGs. In addition, we find a correlation
between [$\alpha$/Fe] and globular cluster specific frequency ($S_N$),
suggesting that low-mass ETGs that formed their stars over a short period of
time, were also efficient at forming massive star clusters. The innermost
low-mass ETGs in our sample have [$\alpha$/Fe] values comparable to that of
M87, implying that environment is the controlling factor for star formation
timescales in dense regions. These low-mass galaxies could be the surviving
counterparts of the objects that have already been accreted into the halo of
M87, and may be the link between present-day low-mass galaxies and the old,
metal-poor, high-[$\alpha$/Fe], high-$S_N$ stellar populations seen in the
outer halos of massive ETGs.

text: The presence and characteristics of quiescent gas in galaxy clusters are fundamental to understanding the processes of star formation and galaxy evolution. This study focuses on the Spokes Cluster, a unique structure showing varying levels of star formation activity, to investigate the characteristics and distribution of quiescent gas. Our objective was to assess the role of quiescent gas in the dynamical evolution of galaxies within the cluster. We employed a multi-wavelength observational approach, utilizing data from optical, infrared, and X-ray surveys. Advanced computational modeling was applied to analyze the gas distribution and map its astrophysical properties. Key findings reveal a significant presence of quiescent gas associated with both cluster dynamics and galaxy morphology, suggesting that quiescent gas plays a vital role in inhibiting star formation in certain environments. Additionally, we identified a correlation between quiescent gas concentrations and environmental factors, such as tidal forces and ram pressure stripping. Our results indicate that the quiescent gas within the Spokes Cluster may serve as a reservoir influencing galaxy evolution over time. In conclusion, this research emphasizes the importance of quiescent gas as a critical component in the lifecycle of galaxies, reshaping our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution within the context of cluster environments. Future investigations should aim to explore the quiescent gas dynamics further, potentially revealing new insights into the universal processes governing galactic systems.

Few normal galaxies have been probed using near-infrared polarimetry, even
though it reveals magnetic fields in the cool interstellar medium better than
either optical or radio polarimetry. Deep H-band (1.6um) linear imaging
polarimetry toward Taurus serendipitously included the galaxy 2MASX
J04412715+2433110 with adequate sensitivity and resolution to map polarization
across nearly its full extent. The observations revealed the galaxy to be a
steeply inclined (~75 deg) disk type with a diameter, encompassing 90% of the
Petrosian flux, of 4.2 kpc at a distance of 53 Mpc. Because the sight line
passes through the Taurus Molecular Cloud complex, the foreground polarization
needed to be measured and removed. The foreground extinction Av of 2.00+/-0.10
mag and reddening E(H-K) of 0.125 +/- 0.009 mag were also assessed and removed,
based on analysis of 2MASS, UKIDSS, Spitzer, and WISE photometry using the
NICE, NICER, and RJCE methods. Corrected for the polarized foreground, the
galaxy polarization values range from zero to 3%. The polarizations are
dominated by a disk-parallel magnetic field geometry, especially to the
northeast, while either a vertical field or single scattering of bulge light
produces disk-normal polarizations to the southwest. The multi-kpc coherence of
the magnetic field revealed by the infrared polarimetry is in close agreement
with short wavelength radio synchrotron observations of edge-on galaxies,
indicating that both cool and warm interstellar media of disk galaxies may be
threaded by common magnetic fields.

text: Cylindrical quasi-optical cavity resonators with random-inhomogeneous side boundaries are of interest due to their applications in various fields such as quantum optics and microwave engineering. Understanding the spectral properties of such resonators is crucial for optimizing their performance.   This research aims to investigate the correlation between dephasing and dissipation in cylindrical quasi-optical cavity resonators with random-inhomogeneous side boundaries. By studying how these two factors interact within the resonator, new insights can be gained into the behavior of the system.   The spectral properties of the resonator are analyzed using a combination of theoretical modeling and numerical simulations. The effects of random inhomogeneities on the dephasing and dissipation processes are carefully examined to determine their relationship and impact on the resonator's performance.  Key findings The research reveals a clear correlation between dephasing and dissipation in cylindrical quasi-optical cavity resonators with random-inhomogeneous side boundaries. Specifically, it is found that the presence of random inhomogeneities can lead to enhanced dephasing, which in turn affects the dissipation characteristics of the resonator.   In conclusion, this study sheds light on the intricate relationship between dephasing and dissipation in cylindrical quasi-optical cavity resonators with random-inhomogeneous side boundaries. These findings not only contribute to the fundamental understanding of such resonators but also have implications for their practical applications in areas such as quantum information processing and sensing.

We used archival Hubble Space Telescope WFC3 images to obtain the Luminosity
Function of the remote globular cluster NGC2419 from two magnitudes above the
Horizontal Branch level down to \sim3.0 magnitudes below the Turn Off point (to
M_I\sim6.4), approximately covering the range of initial stellar masses 0.5
M_sun<= m <= 0.9 M_sun. The completeness-corrected Luminosity Function does not
display any change of shape over the radial range covered by the WFC3 data, out
to ~6 core radii (r_c), or, equivalently, to ~2 half-light radii. The
Luminosity Function in this radial range is also identical to that obtained
from ground based data at much larger distances from the cluster centre
(12r_c<= R<= 22r_c), in the magnitude range in which the two distributions
overlap (M_I<= 4.0). These results support the conclusion by Dalessandro et al.
that there is no significant mass segregation among cluster stars, hence the
stellar mass-to-light ratio remains constant with distance from the cluster
centre. We fitted the observed Luminosity Function with theoretical
counterparts with the proper age and metallicity from different sets of stellar
evolution models and we consistently derive a total V band mass-to-light ratio
1.2<= M/L_V<= 1.7, by extrapolating to the Hydrogen burning limit, with a

Key methodologies include the application of Fourier transforms to ultrasound signals, followed by beamforming operations tailored to minimize sidelobe effects and improve spatial resolution. The results indicate significant improvements in SNR and reduction of speckle noise, leading to clearer and more interpretable images. text: We present the results of a comprehensive Monte-Carlo simulation study of the performance of multi-object adaptive optics (AO) on the European Extremely Large Telescope (E-ELT). Our simulations aimed to investigate the impact of various parameters, such as object size, distance, and atmospheric conditions, on the AO system's ability to correct for aberrations and provide high-quality images. By utilizing a custom-built Monte-Carlo model, we simulated the performance of the E-ELT's multi-object AO system under diverse scenarios, including cases with and without atmospheric distortion, and with objects of varying sizes and distances.  Our results indicate that the multi-object AO system is capable of achieving high-quality images with minimal aberration correction errors, even in challenging atmospheric conditions. However, the performance of the system degrades significantly when objects are large and distant, or when atmospheric distortion is severe. We also found that the system's performance is highly dependent on the quality of the wavefront sensing and control systems, as well as the accuracy of the atmospheric model used in the simulation.  The key findings of our study have significant implications for the design and optimization of the E-ELT's multi-object AO system, and highlight the need for careful consideration of the system's performance in a variety of scenarios. Our results also underscore the importance of Monte-Carlo simulations in evaluating the performance of complex optical systems, and demonstrate the potential of this approach for optimizing the E-ELT's AO system for optimal performance.

text: The discovery of the Higgs boson has significant implications for particle physics, prompting a deeper exploration of its properties and interactions within various theoretical frameworks. The objective of this study is to elucidate the Higgs sector's predictions within this framework and to analyze its compatibility with current experimental results. We employ a combination of perturbative calculations and Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate Higgs production cross-sections and decay channels, focusing on both collider experiments and astroparticle observations. Our key findings reveal distinctive signatures of the Higgs boson that differentiate the Minimal $SU(3)_L \times U(1)_X$ model from the Standard Model, including enhanced decay rates to exotic channels and altered production mechanisms. We also assess the model's implications for electroweak precision observables. In conclusion, our analysis underscores the potential of the Minimal $SU(3)_L \times U(1)_X$ model to offer explanations for unexplained phenomena in particle physics, while providing a robust framework for future experimental investigations. The outlined Higgs phenomenology may serve as a benchmark for upcoming collider strategies, paving the way for deeper insights into fundamental forces and constituents of the universe.

text: In this study, we explore the mass spectrum and decay properties of the 1D strange-charm meson family using the Heavy Quark Effective Theory (HQET). Our approach is grounded in the HQET framework, which permits the separation of long-distance and short-distance physics, thereby allowing a more straightforward analysis of the data.  First, we calculate the leading-order mass corrections for the 1D strange-charm mesons employing non-relativistic QCD (NRQCD). These corrections arise from interactions between quarks and gluons in the long-distance theory, which contribute to the mass shifts of the meson states. Next, we investigate the mixing of the 1D strange-charm mesons through one-gluon exchange (OGE) and evaluate the decay constants using the QCD sum rules.  Our calculations reveal that the mass corrections contribute significantly to the mass splitting between the different members of the 1D strange-charm meson family. Furthermore, we observe that the decay constants exhibit noticeable variation among the various meson states.  The obtained results provide essential insight into the structure and dynamics of the 1D strange-charm meson family. This study demonstrates the efficacy of using HQET to analyze experimental data, offering valuable guidance for future investigations in this area. Our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on the quark-gluon interactions and the behavior of hadronic systems in the heavy quark limit.

text: Deep Inelastic Scattering (DIS) serves as a cornerstone for exploring the internal structure of nucleons. However, accurate interpretations of experimental data are significantly affected by radiative corrections, which account for the effects of virtual and real photon emissions. This paper aims to systematically quantify the radiative corrections to DIS processes, focusing on both electromagnetic and electroweak interactions. We employed a framework combining perturbative quantum electrodynamics and the renormalization group approach to compute these corrections in a structured manner.  Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, we analyzed data across various kinematic regions, examining the contributions from initial state radiation, final state interactions, and vertex corrections. Our findings reveal that the impact of radiative corrections can be substantial, especially at lower momentum transfers, where they alter the extracted structure functions significantly. We highlight that the corrections can lead to discrepancies in the extraction of fundamental parameters such as the Bjorken scaling variable and the nucleon structure functions.  Ultimately, this study demonstrates the necessity of incorporating comprehensive radiative correction calculations into DIS analyses to enhance the precision of parton distribution functions and to better understand the underlying physics of strong interactions. The insights from this research are expected to refine future experimental designs and theoretical models in high-energy physics, contributing to a more nuanced comprehension of the fundamental constituents of matter.

One of the main challenges of current tidal disruption events (TDEs) studies
is that emission arising from AGN activity may potentially mimic the expected
X-ray emission of a TDE. Here we compare the X-ray properties of TDEs and AGN
to determine a set of characteristics which would allow us to discriminate
between flares arising from these two objects. We find that at peak, TDEs are
brighter than AGN found at similar redshifts. However, compared to preflare
upperlimits, highly variable AGN can produce flares of a similar order of
magnitude as those seen from X-ray TDEs. Nevertheless, TDEs decay significantly
more monotonically, and their emission exhibits little variation in spectral
hardness as a function of time. We also find that X-ray TDEs are less absorbed,
and their emission is much softer than the emission detected from AGN found at
similar redshifts. We derive the X-ray luminosity function (LF) for X-ray TDEs
using the events from Auchettl et al. (2017). Interestingly, our X-ray LF
matches closely the theoretically derived LF by Milosavljevi\'c et al. (2006).
which assumes a higher TDE rate currently estimated from observations. Using
our results and the results of Stone & Metzger (2016), we estimate a TDE rate
of $(0.7-4.7)\times10^{-4}$ yr$^{-1}$ per galaxy, higher than current
observational estimates. We find that TDEs can contribute significantly to the
LF of AGN for $z\lesssim0.4$, while there is no evidence that TDEs influence
the growth of $10^{6-7}M_{\odot}$ BHs. However, BHs $<10^{6}M_{\odot}$ can grow
from TDEs arising from super-Eddington accretion without contributing
significantly to the observed AGN LF at $z=0$.

text: This study explores the application of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) for writer identification in music score documents, without the need for staff-line removal. Previous research on music score document identification mostly relies on staff-line removal techniques, which can be time-consuming and error-prone. In this paper, we propose an HMM-based method for writer identification, taking advantage of the temporal dependencies and recurring patterns in music scores.  Our methodology includes preprocessing techniques such as clef identification and key signature determination, followed by the application of HMMs on the note sequences. We use a dataset consisting of 125 music score documents from various composers, and we compare our approach with several state-of-the-art methods, including traditional methods based on staff-line removal and deep learning techniques. The results indicate that our proposed method achieves high accuracy levels without the need for staff-line removal, outperforming several existing methods.  In conclusion, this study offers a novel and efficient solution for writer identification in music score documents, making it a valuable contribution to the field of music information retrieval and musicology research. Furthermore, it also paves the way for future research on other music score document analysis tasks, such as tempo, melody, and harmony recognition, using HMM-based approaches.

The aim of this work is to shed some light on the problem of the formation of
carbon stars of R-type from a detailed study of their chemical composition. We
use high-resolution and high signal-to-noise optical spectra of 23 R-type stars
selected from the Hipparcos catalogue. The chemical analysis is made using
spectral synthesis in LTE and state-of-the-art carbon-rich spherical model
atmospheres. We derive their CNO content (including the carbon isotopic ratio),
average metallicity, lithium, and light (Sr, Y, Zr) and heavy (Ba, La, Nd, Sm)
s-element abundances. The observed properties of the stars (galactic
distribution, kinematics, binarity, photometry and luminosity) are also
discussed. Our analysis shows that late-R stars are carbon stars with identical
chemical and observational characteristics than the normal (N-type) AGB carbon
stars. We confirm the results of the sole previous abundance analysis of
early-R stars by Dominy (1984, ApJS, 55, 27), namely: they are carbon stars
with near solar metallicity showing enhanced nitrogen, low carbon isotopic
ratios and no s-element enhancements. In addition, we have found that early-R
stars have Li abundances larger than expected for post RGB tip giants. We also
find that a significant number (aprox. 40 %) of the early-R stars in our sample
are wrongly classified, being probably classical CH stars and normal K giants.
In consequence, we suggest that the number of true R stars is considerably
lower than previously believed. We briefly discuss the different scenarios
proposed for the formation of early-R stars. The mixing of carbon during an
anomalous He-flash is favoured, although no physical mechanism able to trigger
that mixing has been found yet. The origin of these stars still remains a
mystery.

Dispersion of a passive scalar from concentrated sources in fully developed
turbulent channel flow is studied with the probability density function (PDF)
method. The joint PDF of velocity, turbulent frequency and scalar concentration
is represented by a large number of Lagrangian particles. A stochastic
near-wall PDF model combines the generalized Langevin model of Haworth & Pope
with Durbin's method of elliptic relaxation to provide a mathematically exact
treatment of convective and viscous transport with a non-local representation
of the near-wall Reynolds stress anisotropy. The presence of walls is
incorporated through the imposition of no-slip and impermeability conditions on
particles without the use of damping or wall-functions. Information on the
turbulent timescale is supplied by the gamma-distribution model of van Slooten
et al. Two different micromixing models are compared that incorporate the
effect of small scale mixing on the transported scalar: the widely used
interaction by exchange with the mean (IEM) and the interaction by exchange
with the conditional mean (IECM) model. Single-point velocity and concentration
statistics are compared to direct numerical simulation and experimental data at
Re_\tau=1080 based on the friction velocity and the channel half width. The
joint model accurately reproduces a wide variety of conditional and
unconditional statistics in both physical and composition space.

text: This study examines the shape and dynamic behavior of seepage erosion within a horizontal granular bed, focusing on understanding the mechanisms that govern the formation and progression of erosional features. The primary objective is to investigate how water flow characteristics, such as velocity and pressure gradients, influence the spatial distribution and temporal evolution of erosion patterns. Key findings indicate that the morphology of eroded areas exhibits distinct patterns, including channels, pits, and ridges, which vary according to the hydraulic conditions. The analysis reveals that higher water velocities lead to more extensive and deeper erosion, while pressure gradients affect the lateral spread of erosion. Additionally, the interplay between flow dynamics and sediment properties significantly impacts the stability and persistence of erosion features. These results highlight the importance of considering both hydrodynamic factors and material properties in predicting seepage erosion behaviors.  The conclusion underscores the need for comprehensive models that integrate fluid mechanics with sediment transport principles to accurately forecast seepage erosion phenomena. This study contributes valuable insights into the complex interrelationships between hydraulic forces, sediment characteristics, and erosion dynamics in granular media.

text: Photo-induced SU(3) topological materials of spinless fermions are a burgeoning field of study in condensed matter physics. The objective of this research is to investigate the behavior of spinless fermions in the presence of light-induced SU(3) gauge fields and topological band structures. Our methodology involves theoretical calculations based on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model modified to include photo-induced gauge potentials. By examining the energy spectra, Chern numbers, and edge states of the system under various parameters of light irradiation, we uncover key findings revealing the emergence of novel topological phases and enhanced phenomena such as photo-induced topological phase transitions and light-induced edge state engineering. Additionally, we explore the possibilities of manipulating these photo-induced topological materials through external light sources to achieve desired topological properties. In conclusion, our research contributes to the understanding of light-matter interactions in topological materials and demonstrates the potential for designing optically controllable topological devices based on SU(3) symmetries in spinless fermion systems.

text: We present a novel generative approach to zero-shot and few-shot action recognition, where we leverage a multi-modal fusion framework to effectively adapt to unseen action classes. Our method, dubbed Action Adaptation via Generative Fusion (AAFG), combines a pre-trained action recognition model with a generative adversarial network (GAN) to generate new action features that bridge the knowledge gap between seen and unseen classes. We propose a novel attention mechanism, termed Action-Adaptive Attention (AAA), to selectively focus on informative features from the input video, thereby enhancing the robustness of the recognition model to varying action contexts. Through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, including UCF-101, HMDB-51, and Charades, we demonstrate the efficacy of AAFG in achieving state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot and few-shot action recognition tasks. Notably, our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin on the challenging few-shot action recognition task. The key contributions of our work include the development of a novel generative framework for action adaptation, an attention mechanism that adapts to action contexts, and a comprehensive evaluation protocol that assesses the robustness of our approach to unseen action classes. Our results show that AAFG can effectively generalize to new action classes, making it a valuable tool for real-world applications where action recognition is critical.

We have been monitoring 373 very bright (V < 6 mag) G and K giants with high
precision optical Doppler spectroscopy for more than a decade at Lick
Observatory. Our goal was to discover planetary companions around those stars
and to better understand planet formation and evolution around
intermediate-mass stars. However, in principle, long-term, g-mode nonradial
stellar pulsations or rotating stellar features, such as spots, could
effectively mimic a planetary signal in the radial velocity data. Our goal is
to compare optical and infrared radial velocities for those stars with periodic
radial velocity patterns and to test for consistency of their fitted radial
velocity semiamplitudes. Thereby, we distinguish processes intrinsic to the
star from orbiting companions as reason for the radial velocity periodicity
observed in the optical. Stellar spectra with high spectral resolution have
been taken in the H-band with the CRIRES near-infrared spectrograph at ESO's
VLT for 20 stars of our Lick survey. Radial velocities are derived using many
deep and stable telluric CO2 lines for precise wavelength calibration. We find
that the optical and near-infrared radial velocities of the giant stars in our
sample are consistent. We present detailed results for eight stars in our
sample previously reported to have planets or brown dwarf companions. All eight
stars passed the infrared test. We conclude that the planet hypothesis provides
the best explanation for the periodic radial velocity patterns observed for
these giant stars.

text: We have investigated the pre-main sequence (PMS) variables of the Orion Nebula Cluster (ONC), a rich source of young stellar objects. Our analysis revealed the discovery of novel PMS variables, which we have identified as a previously unrecognized population of stars undergoing significant mass loss and chromospheric activity. Through a combination of multiband photometry and spectroscopic observations, we have characterized the properties of these new variables, including their luminosity, temperature, and spectral types.  Our results indicate that these PMS variables exhibit a unique set of characteristics, including enhanced chromospheric emission, strong stellar winds, and a propensity for mass loss. We have also found that these variables are often associated with the formation of compact circumstellar disks, which may play a key role in regulating the mass loss and chromospheric activity of these stars.  Our study highlights the importance of considering the complex interplay between stellar evolution, circumstellar disk formation, and mass loss in the context of PMS variable formation. We have developed a new set of criteria for identifying and characterizing PMS variables, which will enable future studies to better understand the underlying mechanisms driving the evolution of young stars. By exploring the properties of these novel PMS variables, we have gained valuable insights into the complex processes that govern the formation and evolution of stars in the early stages of their lives.

A search for supersymmetry is presented based on proton-proton collision
events containing identified hadronically decaying top quarks, no leptons, and
an imbalance $p_\mathrm{T}^\text{miss}$ in transverse momentum. The data were
collected with the CMS detector at the CERN LHC at a center-of-mass energy of
13 TeV, and correspond to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. Search
regions are defined in terms of the multiplicity of bottom quark jet and top
quark candidates, the $p_\mathrm{T}^\text{miss}$, the scalar sum of jet
transverse momenta, and the $m_{\mathrm{T2}}$ mass variable. No statistically
significant excess of events is observed relative to the expectation from the
standard model. Lower limits on the masses of supersymmetric particles are
determined at 95% confidence level in the context of simplified models with top
quark production. For a model with direct top squark pair production followed
by the decay of each top squark to a top quark and a neutralino, top squark
masses up to 1020 GeV and neutralino masses up to 430 GeV are excluded. For a
model with pair production of gluinos followed by the decay of each gluino to a
top quark-antiquark pair and a neutralino, gluino masses up to 2040 GeV and
neutralino masses up to 1150 GeV are excluded. These limits extend previous
results.

This is complemented by screening methods like Morris’ method to identify the most influential parameters. The protocol was tested on a series of synthetic and real-world 2D hydraulic scenarios, demonstrating its robustness across different types of systems.  Results indicate that the tool effectively identifies critical parameters affecting hydraulic models, providing insights crucial for model calibration, uncertainty quantification, and decision-making in water resource management. The protocol not only aids in improving the reliability of 2D hydraulic simulations but also serves as a foundational framework for future studies involving more intricate and larger-scale applications.

We derive two main results: First, assume that $A$, $B$, $A_n$, $B_n$ are
self-adjoint operators in the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, and suppose that
$A_n$ converges to $A$ and $B_n$ to $B$ in strong resolvent sense as $n \to
\infty$. Fix $m \in \mathbb{N}$, $m$ odd, $p \in [1,\infty)$, and assume that
$T:= \big[( A + iI_{\mathcal{H}})^{-m} - ( B + iI_{\mathcal{H}})^{-m}\big] \in
\mathcal{B}_p(\mathcal{H})$, $T_n := \big[( A_n + iI_{\mathcal{H}})^{-m} - (

function $f$ in the class $\mathfrak F_{k}(\mathbb{R}) \supset
C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ (cf. (1.1)), $$ \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \big\|
[f(A_n) - f(B_n)] - [f(A)- f(B)]\big\|_{\mathcal{B}_p(\mathcal{H})}=0. $$
  Our second result concerns the continuity of spectral shift functions

self-adjoint in $\mathcal{H}$ we denote by $\Gamma_m(T)$, $m \in \mathbb{N}$
odd, the set of all self-adjoint operators $S$ in $\mathcal{H}$ satisfying
$\big[(S - z I_{\mathcal{H}})^{-m} - (T - z I_{\mathcal{H}})^{-m}\big] \in
\mathcal{B}_1(\mathcal{H})$, $z \in \mathbb{C}\backslash \mathbb{R}$. Employing
a suitable topology on $\Gamma_m(T)$ (cf. (1.9), we prove the following:
Suppose that $B_1\in \Gamma_m(B_0)$ and let $\{B_{\tau}\}_{\tau\in
[0,1]}\subset \Gamma_m(B_0)$ denote a path from $B_0$ to $B_1$ in
$\Gamma_m(B_0)$ depending continuously on $\tau\in [0,1]$ with respect to the
topology on $\Gamma_m(B_0)$. If $f \in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$, then $$
\lim_{\tau\to 0^+} \|\xi(\, \cdot \, ; B_{\tau}, A_0) f - \xi(\, \cdot \, ;

text: We investigate the waveforms generated in the context of massive gravity theories, focusing on their implications for the neutralization of gravitational wave signatures, specifically the ringing phenomena associated with giant black holes. Our work addresses the problem of understanding how massive gravity modifications affect the stability and resonant frequencies of black hole perturbations, which are critical for accurately interpreting astrophysical observations. We employ a systematic approach utilizing perturbative techniques to derive the equations governing wave propagation in the presence of a massive graviton, enabling us to identify the distinct features of the resulting waveforms compared to standard general relativity predictions.   Our results reveal that the presence of a non-zero graviton mass leads to significant alterations in the ringdown phase of black hole mergers, effectively damping and shifting the frequency spectrum of emitted gravitational waves. We demonstrate that these changes can enhance the detectability of certain modes, providing potential observational signatures that could be utilized to test massive gravity frameworks. Furthermore, we explore the implications of our findings for astrophysical black hole populations, proposing that certain waveforms could act as a tool for distinguishing between conventional black hole models and those featuring massive gravity alterations.  In conclusion, our comprehensive analysis establishes a foundational understanding of how massive gravity modifies black hole dynamics and highlights the unique signatures that emerge from these theoretical frameworks, paving the way for future observational campaigns aimed at unraveling the nature of gravity in strong-field regimes.

text:
The biological immune system is a robust, complex, adaptive system that
defends the body from foreign pathogens. It is able to categorize all cells (or
molecules) within the body as self-cells or non-self cells. It does this with
the help of a distributed task force that has the intelligence to take action
from a local and also a global perspective using its network of chemical
messengers for communication. There are two major branches of the immune
system. The innate immune system is an unchanging mechanism that detects and
destroys certain invading organisms, whilst the adaptive immune system responds
to previously unknown foreign cells and builds a response to them that can
remain in the body over a long period of time. This remarkable information
processing biological system has caught the attention of computer science in
recent years. A novel computational intelligence technique, inspired by
immunology, has emerged, called Artificial Immune Systems. Several concepts
from the immune have been extracted and applied for solution to real world
science and engineering problems. In this tutorial, we briefly describe the
immune system metaphors that are relevant to existing Artificial Immune Systems
methods. We will then show illustrative real-world problems suitable for
Artificial Immune Systems and give a step-by-step algorithm walkthrough for one
such problem. A comparison of the Artificial Immune Systems to other well-known
algorithms, areas for future work, tips & tricks and a list of resources will
round this tutorial off. It should be noted that as Artificial Immune Systems
is still a young and evolving field, there is not yet a fixed algorithm
template and hence actual implementations might differ somewhat from time to
time and from those examples given here.
