text: In this work, we investigate the interplay between mean curvature, threshold dynamics, and phase field theory on finite graphs. The main problem addressed is understanding how these concepts interact in the context of discrete structures. Through numerical simulations and mathematical analysis, we explore how mean curvature, a measure of surface smoothness, influences the evolution of phase boundaries on finite graphs. We also examine the role of threshold dynamics in governing the switching behavior of the phase field variables. The results reveal that mean curvature acts as a driving force for the evolution of the system, promoting the minimization of interfacial energy. Additionally, we observe that threshold dynamics introduce nonlinearity into the system, leading to complex patterns and dynamics. The key idea behind our methodology is the application of phase field theory to finite graphs, bridging the gap between continuous and discrete models. By incorporating mean curvature and threshold dynamics into the framework of phase field theory on finite graphs, we provide insights into the collective behavior of these fundamental concepts in a discrete setting. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how curvature, thresholds, and phase field theory interact on finite graphs, with implications for various fields such as materials science and mathematical biology.

The inner disk of the Galaxy has a number of young star clusters dominated by
red supergiants that are heavily obscured by dust extinction and observable
only at infrared wavelengths. These clusters are important tracers of the
recent star formation and chemical enrichment history in the inner Galaxy.
During the technical commissioning and as a first science verification of the
GIANO spectrograph at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo, we secured
high-resolution (R~50,000) near-infrared spectra of three red supergiants in
the young Scutum cluster RSGC2. Taking advantage of the full YJHK spectral
coverage of GIANO in a single exposure, we were able to identify several tens
of atomic and molecular lines suitable for chemical abundance determinations.
By means of spectral synthesis and line equivalent width measurements, we
obtained abundances of Fe and other iron-peak elements such as V, Cr, Ni, of
alpha (O, Mg, Si, Ca and Ti) and other light elements (C, N, Na, Al, K, Sc),
and of some s-process elements (Y, Sr). We found iron abundances between half
and one third solar and solar-scaled [X/Fe] abundance patterns of iron-peak,
alpha and most of the light elements, consistent with a thin-disk chemistry. We
found a depletion of [C/Fe] and enhancement of [N/Fe], consistent with CN
burning, and low 12C/13C abundance ratios (between 9 and 11), requiring
extra-mixing processes in the stellar interiors during the post-main sequence
evolution. Finally, we found a slight [Sr/Fe] enhancement and a slight [Y/Fe]
depletion (by a factor of <=2), with respect to solar.

text: We conducted a long-term observational study of the blazar Mkn 421 using the HAGAR Array of Telescopes, aiming to characterize its variability and spectral behavior across different time scales. Our analysis spanned over three years, during which we acquired a significant data set comprising multiple nights of observation in the TeV gamma-ray regime. The primary focus was to identify correlations between gamma-ray flares and lower-energy emissions, as well as to investigate potential periodicities in the observed light curves.   We employed a multi-wavelength approach, integrating our findings with X-ray data from satellite observatories and optical observations, allowing us to probe the underlying emission mechanisms driving variability in Mkn 421. Through the application of advanced statistical techniques such as Lomb-Scargle periodograms and discrete cross-correlation functions, we discerned patterns of variability that suggest a complex interplay between the relativistic jet dynamics and external photon fields.   Our results revealed significant flux variations, with prominent flaring events correlated with enhanced X-ray emissions, indicating a potential synchrotron self-Compton process at play. Moreover, we identified a possible periodicity of approximately 10 days, which may contribute to our understanding of the jet structure and the environment surrounding the supermassive black hole at the core of Mkn 421.  This comprehensive study emphasizes the necessity of long-term monitoring through ground-based observatories like HAGAR to unravel the intricacies of blazar behavior, thereby contributing valuable insights into high-energy astrophysics and the fundamental phenomena governing active galactic nuclei.

Although extensively investigated, the capacity of the two-hop half-duplex
(HD) relay channel is not fully understood. In particular, a capacity
expression which can be evaluated straightforwardly is not available and an
explicit coding scheme which achieves the capacity is not known either. In this
paper, we derive a new expression for the capacity of the two-hop HD relay
channel based on a simplified converse. Compared to previous results, this
capacity expression can be easily evaluated. Moreover, we propose an explicit
coding scheme which achieves the capacity. To achieve the capacity, the relay
does not only send information to the destination by transmitting
information-carrying symbols but also with the zero symbols resulting from the
relay's silence during reception. As examples, we compute the capacities of the
two-hop HD relay channel for the cases when the source-relay and
relay-destination links are both binary-symmetric channels (BSCs) and additive
white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels, respectively, and numerically compare the
capacities with the rates achieved by conventional relaying where the relay
receives and transmits in a codeword-by-codeword fashion and switches between
reception and transmission in a strictly alternating manner. Our numerical
results show that the capacities of the two-hop HD relay channel for BSC and
AWGN links are significantly larger than the rates achieved with conventional
relaying.

text:
During the transition from solar cycle 23 to 24 from 2006 to 2009, the Sun
was in an unusual solar minimum with very low activity over a long period.
These exceptional conditions included a very low interplanetary magnetic field
(IMF) strength and a high tilt angle, which both play an important role in the
modulation of galactic cosmic rays (GCR) in the heliosphere. Thus, the radial
and latitudinal gradients of GCRs are very much expected to depend not only on
the solar magnetic epoch, but also on the overall modulation level. We
determine the non-local radial and the latitudinal gradients of protons in the
rigidity range from ~0.45 to 2 GV. This was accomplished by using data from the
satellite-borne experiment Payload for Antimatter Matter Exploration and
Light-nuclei Astrophysics (PAMELA) at Earth and the Kiel Electron Telescope
(KET) onboard Ulysses on its highly inclined Keplerian orbit around the Sun
with the aphelion at Jupiter's orbit. In comparison to the previous A>0 solar
magnetic epoch, we find that the absolute value of the latitudinal gradient is
lower at higher and higher at lower rigidities. This energy dependence is
therefore a crucial test for models that describe the cosmic ray transport in
the inner heliosphere.

text:
Late-type stars interact with their close-in planets through their coronal
magnetic fields. We introduce a theory for the interaction between the stellar
and planetary fields focussing on the processes that release magnetic energy in
the stellar coronae. We consider the energy dissipated by the reconnection
between the stellar and planetary magnetic fields as well as that made
available by the modulation of the magnetic helicity of the coronal field
produced by the orbital motion of the planet. We estimate the powers released
by both processes in the case of axisymmetric and non-axisymmetric, linear and
non-linear force-free coronal fields finding that they scale as v_r (B_s)^(4/3)
(B_p)^(2/3) (R_p)^2, where v_r is the relative velocity between the stellar and
planetary fields, B_s the mean stellar surface field, B_p the planetary field
at the poles, and R_p the radius of the planet. A chromospheric hot spot or a
flaring activity phased to the orbital motion of the planet are found only when
the stellar field is axisymmetric. In the case of a non-axisymmetric field, the
time modulation of the energy release is multiperiodic and can be easily
confused with the intrinsic stellar variability. We apply our theory to the
systems with some reported evidence of star-planet magnetic interaction finding
a dissipated power at least one order of magnitude smaller than that emitted by
the chromospheric hot spots. The phase lags between the planets and the hot
spots are reproduced by our models in all the cases except for upsilon And. In
conclusion, the chromospheric hot spots rotating in phase with the planets
cannot be explained by the energy dissipation produced by the interaction
between stellar and planetary fields as considered by our models and require a
different mechanism.

text: This study investigates the phenomenon of resonance capture in multi-planet extrasolar systems, a process that can lead to catastrophic orbital instability and potentially catastrophic consequences for the habitability of the system. In our current understanding, planetary resonance occurs when the orbital periods of two or more planets in a system are in a harmonic relationship, resulting in a destabilizing transfer of angular momentum and potentially catastrophic orbital chaos.  The objective of this research is to explore the likelihood and mechanisms of resonance capture in multi-planet extrasolar systems, with a focus on the effects of system architecture, planet mass, and orbital eccentricity on the stability of the system. To achieve this, we employed a numerical simulation framework, utilizing a combination of N-body simulations and analytical models to investigate the dynamics of planetary systems with varying numbers of planets and system parameters.  Our key findings indicate that resonance capture is a relatively common occurrence in multi-planet extrasolar systems, with a significant proportion of systems exhibiting unstable orbital configurations. Notably, we found that systems with higher numbers of planets and more massive planets are more susceptible to resonance capture. Furthermore, our results suggest that the effects of orbital eccentricity on system stability are more complex than previously thought, and that the interplay between system architecture and orbital eccentricity plays a crucial role in determining the likelihood of resonance capture.  The implications of our findings are significant, as they highlight the importance of considering the potential for resonance capture in the search for habitable exoplanets. Our results also underscore the need for more detailed simulations and modeling of planetary systems to better understand the complex dynamics at play in these systems. Ultimately, this research contributes to our understanding of the complex and dynamic nature of multi-planet extrasolar systems, and has important implications for the search for life beyond our solar system.

Accurate determination of stellar atmospheric parameters and elemental
abundances is crucial for Galactic archeology via large-scale spectroscopic
surveys. In this paper, we estimate stellar atmospheric parameters -- effective
temperature T_{\rm eff}, surface gravity log g and metallicity [Fe/H], absolute
magnitudes M_V and M_{Ks}, {\alpha}-element to metal (and iron) abundance ratio
[{\alpha}/M] (and [{\alpha}/Fe]), as well as carbon and nitrogen abundances
[C/H] and [N/H] from the LAMOST spectra with amultivariate regressionmethod
based on kernel-based principal component analysis, using stars in common with
other surveys (Hipparcos, Kepler, APOGEE) as training data sets. Both internal
and external examinations indicate that given a spectral signal-to-noise ratio
(SNR) better than 50, our method is capable of delivering stellar parameters
with a precision of ~100K for Teff, ~0.1 dex for log g, 0.3 -- 0.4mag for M_V
and M_{Ks}, 0.1 dex for [Fe/H], [C/H] and [N/H], and better than 0.05 dex for
[{\alpha}/M] ([{\alpha}/Fe]). The results are satisfactory even for a spectral
SNR of 20. The work presents first determinations of [C/H] and [N/H] abundances
from a vast data set of LAMOST, and, to our knowledge, the first reported
implementation of absolute magnitude estimation directly based on the observed
spectra. The derived stellar parameters for millions of stars from the LAMOST
surveys will be publicly available in the form of value-added catalogues.

text: This research paper presents the development of a highly hydrogen-sensitive thermal desorption spectroscopy system for the quantitative analysis of low hydrogen concentration in thin-film samples. The background of the study highlights the importance of precise hydrogen quantification in various fields, including materials science, catalysis, and energy storage. However, conventional thermal desorption spectroscopy systems often struggle to detect low hydrogen concentrations due to their limited sensitivity.  The objective of this research is to design and develop a highly sensitive thermal desorption spectroscopy system capable of detecting hydrogen concentrations as low as ~1 x 10^16 atoms/cm3 in thin-film samples. To achieve this, the system incorporates a novel combination of high-temperature heating, optimized vacuum conditions, and advanced signal processing algorithms. The proposed system utilizes a high-resolution quadrupole mass spectrometer to detect hydrogen desorption species, allowing for the precise quantification of hydrogen concentration.  The methodology employed in this research involves the development and characterization of the thermal desorption spectroscopy system, followed by the analysis of thin-film samples with varying hydrogen concentrations. The key findings of this study reveal that the proposed system is capable of detecting hydrogen concentrations as low as ~1 x 10^16 atoms/cm3 with high accuracy and precision. The results demonstrate the potential of the developed system for the quantitative analysis of low hydrogen concentrations in thin-film samples, opening up new possibilities for the investigation of materials properties and behavior. The conclusions drawn from this research highlight the importance of highly sensitive thermal desorption spectroscopy systems in advancing our understanding of hydrogen-related phenomena in materials science and related fields.

We examine the properties of linear electrostatic waves in unmagnetized
quantum and classical plasmas consisting of one or two populations of electrons
with analytically tractable distribution functions in the presence of a
stationary neutralising ion background. Beginning with the kinetic quantum
plasma longitudinal susceptibility, we assess the effects due to increasing
complexity of the background distribution function. Firstly, we analyse
dispersion and Landau damping in one-component plasmas and consider
distribution functions with a variety of analytical properties: the Dirac delta
function, the Cauchy profile with two complex first-order poles, the squared
Cauchy profile with two second order poles, and the inverse-quartic profile
with four first-order poles; we also briefly discuss the non-meromorphic
totally- and arbitrarily-degenerate Fermi-Dirac distribution. In order to study
electrostatic instabilities, we then turn to plasmas with two populations of
electrons streaming relative to each other in two cases: a symmetric case of
two counter-streaming identical populations and a bump-on-tail case with a
primary population and a delta-function beam. We obtain the corresponding
linear kinetic dispersion relations and evaluate the properties of
instabilities when the electron distribution functions are of the delta
function, Cauchy, squared-Cauchy, or inverse-quartic types. In agreement with
other studies, we find that in general quantum effects reduce the range of
wavelengths for unstable modes at long wavelengths. We also find a second
window of instability at shorter wavelengths and elucidate its nature as being
due to quantum recoil. We note the possible implications for studies of
laboratory and astrophysical quantum plasmas.

We consider the problem of testing for a dose-related effect based on a
candidate set of (typically nonlinear) dose-response models using
likelihood-ratio tests. For the considered models this reduces to assessing
whether the slope parameter in these nonlinear regression models is zero or
not. A technical problem is that the null distribution (when the slope is zero)
depends on non-identifiable parameters, so that standard asymptotic results on
the distribution of the likelihood-ratio test no longer apply. Asymptotic
solutions for this problem have been extensively discussed in the literature.
The resulting approximations however are not of simple form and require
simulation to calculate the asymptotic distribution. In addition their
appropriateness might be doubtful for the case of a small sample size. Direct
simulation to approximate the null distribution is numerically unstable due to
the non identifiability of some parameters. In this article we derive a
numerical algorithm to approximate the exact distribution of the
likelihood-ratio test under multiple models for normally distributed data. The
algorithm uses methods from differential geometry and can be used to evaluate
the distribution under the null hypothesis, but also allows for power and
sample size calculations. We compare the proposed testing approach to the
MCP-Mod methodology and alternative methods for testing for a dose-related
trend in a dose-finding example data set and simulations.

Over the past decade, the Secret Lives of Cepheids (SLiC) program has been
carried out at Villanova University to study aspects and behaviors of classical
Cepheids that are still not well-understood. In this, the first of several
planned papers on program Cepheids, we report the current results for delta
Cep, the Cepheid prototype. Ongoing photometry has been obtained to search for
changes in the pulsation period, light curve morphology and amplitude.
Combining our photometry with the times of maximum light compilation by
Berdnikov 2000 returns a small period change of dP/dt ~ -0.1006 +/- 0.0002 sec
yr^-1. There is also evidence for a gradual light amplitude increase of
~0.011-mag (V-band) and ~0.012-mag (B-band) per decade over the last ~50 years.
In addition, HST-COS UV spectrophotometry and XMM-Newton X-ray data were
carried out to investigate the high-temperature plasmas present above the
Cepheid photospheres. In total, from the five visits (eight exposures) with
XMM-Newton, delta Cep is found to be a soft X-ray source (Lx [0.3--2 keV] ~
4.5-13x10^28 erg sec^-1) with peak flux at kT = 0.6-0.9 keV. The X-ray activity
is found to vary, possibly in phase with the stellar pulsations. From
2010-2013, nine observations of delta Cep were carried out with HST-COS. The UV
emissions are also variable, and well-phased with the stellar pulsations.
Maximum UV line emissions occur near, or slightly before, maximum optical
light, varying by as much as twenty times. This variability shows that
pulsation-induced shock-heating plays a significant role in Cepheid
atmospheres, possibly in addition to a quiescent, magnetic heating. The results
of this study show Cepheid atmospheres to be rather complex and dynamic.

text:
With the technology of the time, Kowalski's seminal 1974 paper {\em Predicate
Logic as a Programming Language} was a breakthrough for the use of logic in
computer science. It introduced two fundamental ideas: on the declarative side,
the use of the Horn clause logic fragment of classical logic, which was soon
extended with negation as failure, on the procedural side the procedural
interpretation which made it possible to write algorithms in the formalism.
  Since then, strong progress was made both on the declarative understanding of
the logic programming formalism and in automated reasoning technologies,
particularly in SAT solving, Constraint Programming and Answer Set Programming.
This has paved the way for the development of an extension of logic programming
that embodies a more pure view of logic as a modelling language and its role
for problem solving.
  In this paper, we present the \idp language and system. The language is
essentially classical logic extended with one of logic programmings most
important contributions to knowledge representation: the representation of
complex definitions as rule sets under well-founded semantics. The system is a
knowledge base system: a system in which complex declarative information is
stored in a knowledge base which can be used to solve different computational
problems by applying multiple forms of inference. In this view, theories are
declarative modellings, bags of information, descriptions of possible states of
affairs. They are neither procedures nor descriptions of computational
problems. As such, the \idp language and system preserve the fundamental idea
of a declarative reading of logic programs, while they break with the
fundamental idea of the procedural interpretation of logic programs.

text: This research paper investigates the detection of 63 microns [OI] emission in the debris disc of HD 172555. The study aims to analyze the unique properties of this emission line and its implications for understanding the composition and dynamics of the debris disc. Using high-resolution spectroscopic observations obtained from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the methodology involves analyzing the [OI] emission line to determine its intensity, line profile, and spatial distribution in the debris disc. The key findings reveal a significant presence of 63 microns [OI] emission in the disc, indicating the presence of atomic oxygen in the circumstellar environment of HD 172555. This detection provides valuable insights into the gas composition and physical processes occurring in the debris disc. In conclusion, the detection of the 63 microns [OI] emission line in HD 172555's debris disc sheds light on the chemical and dynamical properties of the system, contributing to our understanding of planetary system evolution and debris disc characteristics.

text: The advancement of natural language processing has significantly benefited from the integration of linguistic theories into computational tools. This research investigates the development of a FrameNet Resource Grammar Library for Grammatical Framework (GF), aiming to enhance multilingual computational linguistics applications. FrameNet provides a comprehensive database of semantic frames, which describe various scenarios with their associated roles, offering rich linguistic information. Our objective is to develop a library that uses GF's multilingual grammatical framework to encapsulate FrameNet's semantic data, thereby facilitating cross-linguistic understanding and translation tasks.  To achieve this, we leveraged GF's resource grammar library to incorporate the semantic frame structures from FrameNet, ensuring compatibility and flexibility across different languages. A modular design was employed, where semantic frames were linked with GF syntactic structures, allowing for the seamless generation and parsing of sentences within multiple grammatical frameworks. Key findings demonstrate that this integration not only preserves the semantic integrity of FrameNet but also improves the efficacy and accuracy of multilingual applications, such as machine translation and natural language understanding systems.  The performance evaluation indicates that our approach effectively captures and utilizes FrameNet's semantic insights within the GF environment, providing an efficient resource for developers and researchers engaged in linguistic and language processing tasks. This study concludes that a FrameNet Resource Grammar Library for GF is a valuable asset, offering substantial potential for future advancements in computational linguistics by bridging semantic and syntactic dimensions across languages.

In the framework of hierarchical structure formation AGN feedback shapes the
galaxy luminosity function. Low luminosity, galaxy-scale double radio sources
are ideal targets to investigate the interplay between AGN feedback and star
formation. We use VLA and BIMA observations to study the radio continuum
emission of NGC 3801 between 1.4 and 112.4 GHz. We find a prominent spectral
break at ~10 GHz, where the spectrum steepens as expected from cosmic-ray
electron (CRe) ageing. Using the equipartition magnetic field and fitting JP
models locally we create a spatially resolved map of the spectral age of the
CRe population. The spectral age of tau_int = 2.0 +/- 0.2 Myr agrees within a
factor of two with the dynamical age of the expanding X-ray emitting shells.
The spectral age varies only little across the lobes, requiring an effective
mixing process of the CRe such as a convective backflow of magnetized plasma.
The jet termination points have a slightly younger CRe spectral age, hinting at
in-situ CRe re-acceleration. Our findings support the scenario where the
supersonically expanding radio lobes heat the ISM of NGC 3801 via shock waves,
and, as their energy is comparable to the energy of the ISM, are clearly able
to influence the galaxy's further evolution.

text: In this work, we explore the mass transfer processes within eccentric binary systems using smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH). Our primary objective is to investigate how the eccentricity of these binaries influences the dynamics of mass transfer. We simulate a series of eccentric binary systems with varying eccentricities and angular velocities, focusing on the onset and evolution of mass accretion onto the donor star.  The simulations demonstrate that higher eccentricities lead to more complex and episodic mass transfer episodes, characterized by transient high-mass outflows from the donor star during pericenter passages. These outflows are crucial in preventing the system from reaching a stable Roche lobe overflow state. Additionally, we observe enhanced mass loss from the donor star due to tidal forces at periapsis, which significantly impacts the mass transfer rates and orbital decay.  Key methodologies employed include the implementation of SPH to model the hydrodynamic interactions between the stars and the circumstellar material. We have also developed algorithms to accurately track the position and velocity of particles representing the stellar envelopes, as well as the formation and evolution of jets and winds.  Our results highlight the importance of considering eccentricity in theoretical models of mass transfer in binary systems. The findings suggest that eccentric binaries can exhibit distinct mass transfer behaviors compared to circular binaries, offering new insights into the long-term evolution of such systems.

text: We present a novel approach in addressing the challenges associated with compositional simulation using natural variables through a Sequential Fully Implicit Formulation (SFIF). The primary issue this work tackles is the accurate representation of phase behavior and flow dynamics in multi-component systems with varying compositions. The SFIF method aims to enhance the predictive capabilities of numerical models by efficiently handling the complex interactions between different components in the reservoir fluids.   Our results demonstrate that the SFIF approach significantly improves the convergence rate and stability of compositional simulations compared to traditional methods. By sequentially solving the governing equations for each component while considering interactions with other components, our methodology effectively captures the intricate phase behavior and migration patterns within the reservoir. Additionally, our approach minimizes the computational burden by exploiting the sequential nature of the problem.  Key ideas revolve around the utilization of natural variables to directly describe phase properties and streamline the solution process. This abstract provides insights into the potential of the SFIF formulation to advance compositional simulation accuracy and efficiency in reservoir engineering. The blend of natural variables with fully implicit schemes offers a promising avenue for enhancing predictive capabilities in handling intricate compositional systems.

text: The integration of quantum memory with superconducting qubits presents a pivotal advancement in quantum information processing and storage. This study investigates the enhanced energy relaxation process in such a hybrid system, focusing on the interaction dynamics and their impact on quantum coherence. The primary objective is to improve the efficiency and reliability of quantum memory when coupled with superconducting qubits. We employed a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental validation to examine the energy relaxation mechanisms. The methodology involved fabricating superconducting qubits and integrating them with quantum memory systems under cryogenic conditions to meticulously monitor energy decay processes and coherence times. Key findings reveal that the coupling between quantum memory and superconducting qubits can significantly enhance energy relaxation rates, facilitating prolonged coherence times. This enhancement is attributed to optimized coupling strengths and tailored control techniques that mitigate decoherence pathways. The study demonstrates that by fine-tuning the qubit-memory coupling parameters, it is possible to suppress energy dissipation, thereby extending the operational lifespan of quantum states in these systems. The results show promise for scalable quantum computing architectures where long-lived quantum memory is essential. In conclusion, the enhanced energy relaxation process observed in this hybrid setup offers a viable pathway to improve quantum coherence and expand the practical applicability of quantum computing technologies. Future work will focus on exploring different material compositions and geometries to further refine the energy relaxation characteristics and capitalize on these findings for more robust quantum memory implementations.

text: Clumpy dust clouds and extended atmosphere play a crucial role in the understanding of the late stages of stellar evolution, particularly in Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars. This study focuses on investigating the characteristics of the AGB star W Hya through observations made with VLT/SPHERE-ZIMPOL and VLTI/AMBER II.   The main objective of this research is to analyze the time variations in the clumpy dust clouds and extended atmosphere of the AGB star W Hya between pre-maximum and minimum light phases. By studying these variations, insights into the dynamic processes occurring in the outer regions of AGB stars can be gained.   Observations of W Hya were conducted using VLT/SPHERE-ZIMPOL and VLTI/AMBER II instruments to capture high-resolution images and spectroscopic data. Data analysis techniques were employed to investigate the changes in the dust clouds and atmospheric structure of the star over different phases.   The study revealed significant time variations in the clumpy dust clouds and extended atmosphere of W Hya between the pre-maximum and minimum light phases. Analysis of these variations provides valuable information on the dynamics of the star's outer layers and the impact of evolving conditions on its surroundings.   The findings from this research enhance our understanding of the complex processes taking place in AGB stars, shedding light on the evolution of these stellar objects. The observed time variations highlight the dynamic nature of clumpy dust clouds and extended atmospheres in AGB stars like W Hya during different phases of their stellar lifecycle.

text: We investigate the mass modification of itinerant carriers in the context of Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) oscillations, specifically focusing on the implications of finite-range exchange interactions. Our work aims to elucidate the effects of localized magnetic impurities on the conduction electrons' effective mass and their subsequent impact on spin fluctuations within a metallic host. We implement a comprehensive theoretical framework, combining perturbative methods and numerical simulations, to analyze the strength and range of the exchange interactions and their influence on the electron mass renormalization. Our results reveal that finite-range interactions can significantly modulate the effective mass of itinerant carriers, leading to enhanced spin coherence lengths and altered oscillation periods in RKKY interactions. Notably, we observe that as the range of exchange interactions increases, a suppression of the effective mass occurs, which we attribute to enhanced screening effects and a more complex interplay between the itinerant carriers and localized spins. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the magneto-transport properties of metallic systems with localized magnetic moments and highlight the necessity to account for the spatial range of exchange interactions in theoretical models. Our study contributes to the broader discourse on spintronic applications, suggesting pathways for tuning electronic properties via interfacial interactions in future materials design. Ultimately, we provide compelling evidence that finite-range exchange interactions are critical in shaping the dynamics of itinerant carriers, thereby advancing our understanding of magnetism in complex metallic systems.

text:
The intra-cluster medium contains cosmic rays and magnetic fields that are
manifested through the large scale synchrotron sources, termed as radio halos,
relics and mini-halos. The Extended Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT)
Radio Halo Survey (EGRHS) is an extension of the GMRT Radio Halo Survey (GRHS)
designed to search for radio halos using GMRT 610/235 MHz observations. The
GRHS+EGRHS consists of 64 clusters in the redshift range 0.2 -- 0.4 that have
an X-ray luminosity larger than 5x10^44 erg/s in the 0.1 -- 2.4 keV band and
with declinations > -31 deg in the REFLEX and eBCS X-ray cluster catalogues. In
this second paper in the series, GMRT 610/235 MHz data on the last batch of 11
galaxy clusters and the statistical analysis of the full sample are presented.
A new mini-halo in RXJ2129.6+0005 and candidate diffuse sources in Z5247, A2552
and Z1953 are discovered. A unique feature of this survey are the upper limits
on the detections of 1 Mpc sized radio halos; 4 new are presented here making a
total of 31 in the survey. Of the sample, 58 clusters that have adequately
sensitive radio information were used to obtain the most accurate occurrence
fractions so far. The occurrence of radio halos in our X-ray selected sample is
~22%, that of mini-halos is 13% and that of relics is ~5%. The radio power -
X-ray luminosity diagrams for the radio halos and mini-halos with the
detections and upper limits are presented. The morphological estimators namely,
centroid shift (w), concentration parameter (c) and power ratios (P_3/P_0)
derived from the Chandra X-ray images are used as proxies for the dynamical
states of the GRHS+EGRHS clusters. The clusters with radio halos and mini-halos
occupy distinct quadrants in the c-w, c-P_3/P_0 and w - P_3/P_0 planes,
corresponding to the more and less morphological disturbance, respectively. The
non-detections span both the quadrants.

text: In this study, we present results of a comprehensive analysis of self-regulation cycles in cool core clusters using the X-ray surface brightness and entropy profiles. By utilizing the data from Chandra X-ray Observatory and ROSAT X-ray HIRES, we modeled the temperature, density, and gas entropy evolution, accounting for the cosmic ray heating effect. Our findings reveal a strong correlation between the gas entropy profile and the self-regulation cycle length. We further investigate non-thermal emission by incorporating the synchrotron emission model.    The results show that the non-thermal emission is significantly higher in cool core clusters with shorter self-regulation cycles, confirming the hypothesis that more frequent feedback events enhance the particle acceleration processes. The non-thermal emission efficiency is found to be a function of the cooling time, increasing towards the center of the cluster. We attribute this behavior to the complex interaction between cosmic rays, magnetic fields, and the intracluster medium.    Our findings advance the understanding of the self-regulation cycle in cool core clusters and provide new insights into the origin and properties of non-thermal emission. This work has significant implications for the overall evolution of galaxy clusters and the role of feedback mechanisms in shaping the cosmic web. Further investigations will be required to validate and expand upon these results, including additional data analysis, numerical simulations, and theoretical modeling.

For the first time, we present an extensive study of stars with individual
non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) abundances for 17 chemical elements
from Li to Eu in a sample of stars uniformly distributed over the $-2.62 \le$
[Fe/H] $\le +0.24$ metallicity range that is suitable for the Galactic chemical
evolution research. The star sample has been kinematically selected to trace
the Galactic thin and thick disks and halo. We find new and improve earlier
results as follows. (i) The element-to-iron ratios for Mg, Si, Ca, and Ti form
a MP plateau at a similar height of 0.3~dex, and the knee occurs at common
[Fe/H] $\simeq -0.8$. The knee at the same metallicity is observed for [O/Fe],
and the MP plateau is formed at [O/Fe] = 0.61. (ii) The upward trend of [C/O]
with decreasing metallicity exists at [Fe/H] $< -1.2$, supporting the earlier
finding of Akerman et al. (iii) An underabundance of Na relative to Mg in the
[Fe/H] $< -1$ stars is nearly constant, with the mean [Na/Mg] $\simeq -0.5$.
(iv) The K/Sc, Ca/Sc, and Ti/Sc ratios form well-defined trends, suggesting a
common site of the K-Ti production. (v) Sr follows the Fe abundance down to
[Fe/H] $\simeq -2.5$, while Zr is enhanced in MP stars. (vi) The comparisons of
our results with some widely used Galactic evolution models are given. The use
of the NLTE element abundances raises credit to the interpretation of the data
in the context of the chemical evolution of the Galaxy.

text: KELT-20b is a recently discovered exoplanet, characterized by its massive size and extremely short orbital period of approximately 3.5 days. Orbiting the early A-type star HD 185603, a relatively young and massive stellar object, this giant planet presents a unique opportunity to study the properties of hot Jupiters in close proximity to their host stars.   The objective of this study is to investigate the atmospheric properties of KELT-20b, with a focus on understanding the planet's thermal structure, atmospheric composition, and potential for habitability. To achieve this, we employed a combination of spectroscopic and transit analysis techniques, utilizing data from the KELT (Kilodegree Extremely Little Telescope) survey and the ESPaDOnS spectrograph.  Our key findings indicate that KELT-20b is a hot Jupiter with a highly eccentric orbit, resulting in significant temperature variations across the planet's surface. Spectroscopic analysis of the transit event reveals the presence of a thick atmosphere, primarily composed of hydrogen and helium, with possible absorption features indicative of metallic ions. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the planet's surface temperature may exceed 2000 K, making it one of the hottest known exoplanets.  The implications of these findings are significant, as they provide insights into the formation and evolution of giant planets in close proximity to their host stars. Our results also highlight the importance of continued study of KELT-20b, as further observations may reveal additional details about this fascinating exoplanet and its potential for hosting life.

Photometric and spectroscopic observations of a slowly declining, luminous
Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) SN 2011hr in the starburst galaxy NGC 2691 are
presented. SN 2011hr is found to peak at $M_{B}=-19.84 \pm 0.40\,\rm{mag}$,
with a post-maximum decline rate $\Delta$m$_{15}$(B) = 0.92 $\pm$
0.03\,$\rm{mag}$. From the maximum-light bolometric luminosity, $L=(2.30 \pm
0.90) \times 10^{43}\,\rm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, we estimate the mass of synthesized
\Nifs\ in SN 2011hr to be $M(\rm{^{56}Ni})=1.11 \pm 0.43\,M_{\sun}$. SN 2011hr
appears more luminous than SN 1991T at around maximum light, and the absorption
features from its intermediate-mass elements (IMEs) are noticeably weaker than
the latter at similar phases. Spectral modeling suggests that SN 2011hr has the
IMEs of $\sim$\,0.07 M$_{\sun}$ in the outer ejecta, which is much lower than
the typical value of normal SNe Ia (i.e., 0.3 -- 0.4 M$_{\sun}$) and is also
lower than the value of SN 1991T (i.e., $\sim$\,0.18 M$_{\sun}$). These results
indicate that SN 2011hr may arise from a Chandrasekhar-mass white dwarf
progenitor that experienced a more efficient burning process in the explosion.
Nevertheless, it is still possible that SN 2011hr may serve as a transitional
object connecting the SN 1991T-like SNe Ia with the superluminous subclass like
SN 2007if given that the latter also shows very weak IMEs at all phases.

This work studies two interrelated problems - online robust PCA (RPCA) and
online low-rank matrix completion (MC). In recent work by Cand\`{e}s et al.,
RPCA has been defined as a problem of separating a low-rank matrix (true data),
$L:=[\ell_1, \ell_2, \dots \ell_{t}, \dots , \ell_{t_{\max}}]$ and a sparse
matrix (outliers), $S:=[x_1, x_2, \dots x_{t}, \dots, x_{t_{\max}}]$ from their
sum, $M:=L+S$. Our work uses this definition of RPCA. An important application
where both these problems occur is in video analytics in trying to separate
sparse foregrounds (e.g., moving objects) and slowly changing backgrounds.
  While there has been a large amount of recent work on both developing and
analyzing batch RPCA and batch MC algorithms, the online problem is largely
open. In this work, we develop a practical modification of our recently
proposed algorithm to solve both the online RPCA and online MC problems. The
main contribution of this work is that we obtain correctness results for the
proposed algorithms under mild assumptions. The assumptions that we need are:
(a) a good estimate of the initial subspace is available (easy to obtain using
a short sequence of background-only frames in video surveillance); (b) the
$\ell_t$'s obey a `slow subspace change' assumption; (c) the basis vectors for
the subspace from which $\ell_t$ is generated are dense (non-sparse); (d) the
support of $x_t$ changes by at least a certain amount at least every so often;
and (e) algorithm parameters are appropriately set

text: We investigate the implications of Non-Relativistic Quantum Chromodynamics (NRQCD) in the context of quarkonia production within jets, addressing discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental observations. Our primary objective is to refine the understanding of quarkonium formation mechanisms in high-energy jet environments, thereby enhancing the predictive power of NRQCD. Utilizing a combination of perturbative and non-perturbative techniques, we conduct a series of simulations to model the behavior of quarkonium states as they emerge from the hadronization process of jets.   We implement an advanced Monte Carlo framework that incorporates recent advancements in NRQCD factorization, allowing us to systematically evaluate the contributions of various color-singlet and color-octet states to jet fragmentation. Our results illustrate significant enhancements in quarkonium production rates within jets, particularly for P-wave states, when aligned with experimental data from hadron colliders.   Furthermore, we analyze angular distributions and energy spectra of the resulting quarkonia, revealing distinctive patterns that are sensitive to the parameters of NRQCD. By contrasting our findings with existing experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider, we identify opportunities for improved calibration of NRQCD parameters. Our study highlights the critical role of jet dynamics in accessing the fundamental properties of quarkonia, providing a pathway for future investigations into heavy quark systems and their interaction with the QCD environment. We conclude that our methodology not only reinforces the validity of NRQCD but also sets the stage for a deeper understanding of quarkonium physics within the jet framework.

In this paper, new techniques are presented to either simplify or improve
most existing upper bounds on the maximum-likelihood (ML) decoding performance
of the binary linear codes over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels.
Firstly, the recently proposed union bound using truncated weight spectrums by
Ma {\em et al} is re-derived in a detailed way based on Gallager's first
bounding technique (GFBT), where the "good region" is specified by a
sub-optimal list decoding algorithm. The error probability caused by the bad
region can be upper-bounded by the tail-probability of a binomial distribution,
while the error probability caused by the good region can be upper-bounded by
most existing techniques. Secondly, we propose two techniques to tighten the
union bound on the error probability caused by the good region. The first
technique is based on pair-wise error probabilities, which can be further
tightened by employing the independence between the error events and certain
components of the received random vectors. The second technique is based on
triplet-wise error probabilities, which can be upper-bounded by proving that
any three bipolar vectors form a non-obtuse triangle. The proposed bounds
improve the conventional union bounds but have a similar complexity since they
involve only the $Q$-function. The proposed bounds can also be adapted to
bit-error probabilities.

text: We have developed a novel class of generalized semi-analytical models for predicting the light curves of type II supernovae, addressing the limitations of existing models by incorporating a more comprehensive and physically-motivated parametrization of the shock-heated material's optical properties. Our approach combines the strengths of both semi-analytical and full numerical methods, enabling us to efficiently capture the complex interplay between the shock-heated material's thermal and optical properties, as well as the effects of circumstellar interaction on the light curve.  Through a systematic exploration of the model's parameters and a comprehensive comparison with observational data, we have identified key correlations between the model's predictions and the observed light curves of type II supernovae. Notably, our results suggest that the shock-heated material's optical properties play a crucial role in determining the light curve's shape and duration, and that the circumstellar interaction can significantly impact the model's predictions.  Our models have been validated against a diverse set of observational data, including those from the Supernova Legacy Survey and the Palomar Transient Factory. The results indicate that our models can accurately reproduce the observed light curves of type II supernovae, with a high degree of precision and a low scatter. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the physics of type II supernovae and the development of more accurate models for predicting their light curves.

We study the quenching dynamics of a one-dimensional spin-1/2 $XY$ model in a
transverse field when the transverse field $h(=t/\tau)$ is quenched repeatedly
between $-\infty$ and $+\infty$. A single passage from $h \to - \infty$ to $h
\to +\infty$ or the other way around is referred to as a half-period of
quenching. For an even number of half-periods, the transverse field is brought
back to the initial value of $-\infty$; in the case of an odd number of
half-periods, the dynamics is stopped at $h \to +\infty$. The density of
defects produced due to the non-adiabatic transitions is calculated by mapping
the many-particle system to an equivalent Landau-Zener problem and is generally
found to vary as $1/\sqrt{\tau}$ for large $\tau$; however, the magnitude is
found to depend on the number of half-periods of quenching. For two successive
half-periods, the defect density is found to decrease in comparison to a single
half-period, suggesting the existence of a corrective mechanism in the reverse
path. A similar behavior of the density of defects and the local entropy is
observed for repeated quenching. The defect density decays as $1/{\sqrt\tau}$
for large $\tau$ for any number of half-periods, and shows a increase in kink
density for small $\tau$ for an even number; the entropy shows qualitatively
the same behavior for any number of half-periods. The probability of
non-adiabatic transitions and the local entropy saturate to 1/2 and $\ln 2$,
respectively, for a large number of repeated quenching.

text: In this study, we investigate the intricate relationship between the number of realizations for a given degree sequence of a graph and the concept of majorization. Our primary goal is to understand how the constraints imposed by degree sequences impact the number of possible graph realizations while exploring the degree of freedom afforded by majorization within this context. First, we employ a rigorous combinatorial approach to analyze degree sequences, defining necessary and sufficient conditions for their realizability. Utilizing methods from majorization theory, we develop novel algorithms to synthetically generate degree sequences and categorize their realizations systematically. Our results demonstrate that the degree of majorization within a sequence is profoundly indicative of the number of realizations; sequences with a higher degree of majorization tend to allow for a broader range of graph structures. This finding suggests potential optimization strategies in network design and graph enumeration tasks, where managing realizability is crucial. Moreover, our methodology provides a foundation for future research into more complex graph structures and their relevance in various scientific disciplines, including bioinformatics, social network analysis, and combinatorial optimization. By elucidating the interactions between degree sequences and majorization, we contribute an essential understanding of graph theoretical properties, advancing our ability to tackle practical problems involving complex network systems. Our findings highlight both the limitations and potential of majorization as a tool for controlling graph realizability, offering pathways for subsequent investigations in the field of discrete mathematics and its applications.

text: The message passing algorithm (MPA) on graphs is a popular method for solving problems on large-scale graph structures. In this study, we employ discrete geometric techniques to analyze the convergence and performance of MPA on various graph structures, including grids, small-world networks, and random graphs. We first introduce the fundamental concepts of discrete geometry and their relevance to MPA. We then present a detailed analysis of the convergence behavior of MPA on grids using discrete Chebyshev polynomials and discrete Fourier transforms. The analysis reveals that the convergence rate of MPA on grids can be significantly improved by utilizing the discrete cosine transform instead of the standard Fourier transform. Next, we extend our analysis to small-world networks and random graphs. By using discrete harmonic functions and the Laplacian matrix, we derive closed-form expressions for the steady-state distribution and convergence rate of MPA on these graph structures. Our results indicate that MPA exhibits faster convergence on small-world networks compared to random graphs. Furthermore, we propose a novel method to enhance the performance of MPA by incorporating discrete geometric insights. Specifically, we propose a discrete harmonic decomposition-based MPA that exploits the localized nature of discrete harmonic functions to improve message updating efficiency. We conduct extensive simulations to validate the performance gains of our proposed method and compare it to the standard MPA and other state-of-the-art algorithms. In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the convergence and performance analysis of MPA on graph structures using discrete geometric techniques. Our findings reveal significant improvements in convergence rate and efficiency, which can be valuable for applications in areas such as machine learning, social networks, and distributed computing.

text: This study investigates the distortion-rate function of sub-Nyquist sampled Gaussian sources, a fundamental concept in signal processing and communication systems. Gaussian sources are widely used in various applications, including telecommunications, data compression, and image processing, due to their optimal energy efficiency and spectral properties. However, the sub-Nyquist sampling of Gaussian sources introduces a trade-off between signal fidelity and sampling rate, leading to a degradation in signal quality.  The objective of this research is to derive a mathematical model that describes the distortion-rate function of sub-Nyquist sampled Gaussian sources. To achieve this, we employ a combination of signal processing and information theory techniques, including the Karhunen-Loève transform and the concept of mutual information. Our analysis reveals that the distortion-rate function exhibits a non-linear relationship between the sampling rate and the signal distortion, which can be characterized by a power-law dependence.  The proposed model is validated through numerical simulations and theoretical analysis, demonstrating its accuracy in predicting the distortion-rate function of sub-Nyquist sampled Gaussian sources. The results show that the distortion-rate function can be optimized by adjusting the sampling rate, allowing for a trade-off between signal fidelity and computational complexity. This research contributes to the understanding of sub-Nyquist sampling of Gaussian sources, providing valuable insights for the design of efficient signal processing systems and communication protocols.

text: This research paper addresses the challenge of estimating the False Discovery Proportion (FDP) when the dependence structure among test statistics is unknown. The objective of this study is to develop a methodology that can accurately estimate the FDP in the presence of unknown dependencies among statistical tests. To achieve this, a novel approach based on a resampling technique combined with a data-driven method for estimating the unknown dependence structure is proposed.   The methodology is applied to simulated data as well as real-world datasets to evaluate its performance in estimating the FDP under different scenarios of unknown dependence. The key findings suggest that the proposed methodology provides reliable and robust estimates of the FDP even when the underlying dependencies are complex and unknown. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in accurately estimating the FDP and controlling the false discovery rate in various settings.  In conclusion, the developed methodology offers a promising solution for estimating the FDP when the dependence structure is unknown, providing researchers with a valuable tool for conducting hypothesis testing and making informed decisions in the presence of complex dependencies among statistical tests.

text: This research presents the penultimate results from the Cygnus OB2 Radial Velocity Survey aimed at achieving a comprehensive understanding of massive binary stars within the Cygnus OB2 association. Focusing on high-mass stellar systems, the study employs advanced spectroscopic techniques to measure radial velocities with unprecedented precision, aiming to detect and characterize binary star systems. The methodology involves analyzing the radial velocity variations of stars observed through high-resolution spectroscopy, which are indicative of unseen companions orbiting these stars. Key findings include the identification of numerous previously undetected binary systems and the measurement of orbital parameters such as periods and eccentricities. This work contributes to the broader field of stellar astrophysics by providing insights into the dynamical interactions and evolutionary stages of massive stars in dense stellar environments. The ultimate goal is to complete a statistical overview of massive binary stars, thereby enhancing our comprehension of their formation, evolution, and impact on the surrounding interstellar medium.

A steeper fall of fusion excitation function, compared to the predictions of
coupled-channels models, at energies below the lowest barrier between the
reaction partners, is termed as deep sub-barrier fusion hindrance. This
phenomenon has been observed in many symmetric and nearly-symmetric systems.
Different physical origins of the hindrance have been proposed. This work aims
to study the probable effects of direct reactions on deep sub-barrier fusion
cross sections. Fusion (evaporation residue) cross sections have been measured
for the system $^{19}$F+$^{181}$Ta, from above the barrier down to the energies
where fusion hindrance is expected to come into play. Coupled-channels
calculation with standard Woods-Saxon potential gives a fair description of the
fusion excitation function down to energies $\simeq 14\%$ below the barrier for
the present system. This is in contrast with the observation of increasing
fusion hindrance in asymmetric reactions induced by increasingly heavier
projectiles, \textit{viz.} $^{6,7}$Li, $^{11}$B, $^{12}$C and $^{16}$O. The
asymmetric reactions, which have not shown any signature of fusion hindrance
within the measured energy range, are found to be induced by projectiles with
lower $\alpha$ break-up threshold, compared to the reactions which have shown
signatures of fusion hindrance. In addition, most of the $Q$-values for light
particles pick-up channels are negative for the reactions which have exhibited
strong signatures of fusion hindrance, \textit{viz.} $^{12}$C+$^{198}$Pt and
$^{16}$O+$^{204,208}$Pb. Thus, break-up of projectile and particle transfer
channels with positive $Q$-values seem to compensate for the hindrance in
fusion deep below the barrier. Inclusion of break-up and transfer channels
within the framework of coupled-channels calculation would be of interest.

text: This study investigates the physical processes occurring in collapsars that lead to the production of top-heavy jets and early-time plateaus in gamma-ray burst afterglows. By employing a combination of theoretical models and observational data analysis, we aim to elucidate the mechanisms responsible for the unique characteristics of these afterglows. Our methodology involves simulations of collapsar jets and their interactions with the surrounding medium, along with the analysis of observational data from various gamma-ray burst events. The key findings of this research include the natural formation of top-heavy jets in collapsars due to the influence of magnetic fields and rotation, leading to the emergence of early-time plateaus in gamma-ray burst afterglows. Through detailed numerical simulations and data comparisons, we provide insights into the underlying processes shaping the observed features of collapsar afterglows. In conclusion, our study contributes to a better understanding of the origins of top-heavy jets and early-time plateaus in gamma-ray burst afterglows, shedding light on the dynamics of collapsars and their implications for astrophysical phenomena.

text: In this study, we present our findings from conducting numerical relativity simulations on neutron star merger remnants using conservative mesh refinement. The primary goal of our work is to accurately model post-merger dynamics and gravitational wave emission in these systems.   Our simulations demonstrate that conservative mesh refinement techniques are effective in capturing small-scale features and resolving high gradients in the hydrodynamic fields within the merger remnants. By adapting the computational grid dynamically based on the evolving solution, we achieve enhanced resolution where it is most needed, leading to more accurate and reliable results.   Through the application of conservative mesh refinement, we address the challenge of capturing the complex dynamics of neutron star mergers, including the formation of a hypermassive neutron star or prompt collapse to a black hole. Our methodology involves solving the Einstein field equations coupled with relativistic hydrodynamics using high-order finite difference schemes on adaptively refined grids.   Our results show that conservative mesh refinement significantly improves the accuracy of our simulations and provides valuable insights into the post-merger phase of neutron star binaries. This work contributes to the advancement of numerical relativity studies of compact object mergers and enhances our understanding of the gravitational wave signatures associated with these events.

We study the general patterns of SUSY-breaking soft terms arising under the
assumption of Kahler moduli dominated SUSY-breaking in string theory models.
Insisting that all MSSM gauginos get masses at leading order and that the top
Yukawa coupling is of order the gauge coupling constant identifies the class of
viable models. These are models in which the SM fields live either in the bulk
or at the intersection of local sets of Type IIB D7-branes or their F-theory
relatives. General arguments allow us to compute the dependence of the Kahler
metrics of MSSM fields on the local Kahler modulus of the brane configuration
in the large moduli approximation. We illustrate this study in the case of
toroidal/orbifold orientifolds but discuss how the findings generalize to the
F-theory case which is more naturally compatible with coupling unification.
Only three types of 7-brane configurations are possible, leading each of them
to very constrained patterns of soft terms for the MSSM. We study their
consistency with radiative electroweak symmetry breaking and other
phenomenological constraints. We find that essentially only the configuration
corresponding to intersecting 7-branes is compatible with all present
experimental constraints and the desired abundance of neutralino dark matter.
The obtained MSSM spectrum is very characteristic and could be tested at LHC.
We also study the LHC reach for the discovery of this type of SUSY particle
spectra.

This paper proposes a non-phenomenological model of population growth that is
based on the interactions between the individuals that compose the system. It
is assumed that the individuals interact cooperatively and competitively. As a
consequence of this interaction, it is shown that some well-known
phenomenological population growth models (such as the Malthus, Verhulst,
Gompertz, Richards, Von Foerster, and power-law growth models) are special
cases of the model presented herein. Moreover, other ecological behaviors can
be seen as the emergent behavior of such interactions. For instance, the Allee
effect, which is the characteristic of some populations to increase the
population growth rate at a small population size, is observed. Whereas the
models presented in the literature explain the Allee effect with
phenomenological ideas, the model presented here explains this effect by the
interactions between the individuals. The model is tested with empirical data
to justify its formulation. Other interesting macroscopic emergent behavior
from the model proposed here is the observation of a regime of population
divergence at a finite time. It is interesting that this characteristic is
observed in humanity's global population growth. It is shown that in a regime
of cooperation, the model fits very well to the human population growth data
since 1000 A.D.

text: Galactic centers are known to host supermassive black holes, affecting the distribution of stars through a process known as binary disruption. This phenomenon leads to the creation of steep stellar cusps near the black hole.   This research aims to investigate the impact of binary disruption on the stellar distribution in galactic centers to understand how it shapes the density profiles, particularly focusing on the formation of steeper stellar cusps.   Using a combination of observational data and theoretical models, we analyze the stellar populations around supermassive black holes in galactic centers. We simulate the effects of binary disruption on the stellar orbits and study how the disruption process influences the central stellar densities.   Our study reveals that binary disruption leads to the development of steeper stellar cusps in the central regions of galaxies hosting supermassive black holes. The disrupted binaries contribute to the enhancement of stellar density close to the black hole, creating a signature cusp profile indicative of this interaction.   The presence of supermassive black holes in galactic centers significantly influences the stellar distribution through binary disruption, resulting in the formation of steeper cusps. This research sheds light on the dynamical processes operating in these environments and provides valuable insights into the evolution of galactic nuclei.

text: Human computation, a form of collaborative problem-solving, has gained significant attention in recent years as a means of engaging citizens in scientific research. Citizen science projects, in particular, rely heavily on human computation to analyze and process large datasets. However, understanding the factors that contribute to volunteers' engagement in these projects is crucial for their success. This study aimed to identify the engagement profiles of volunteers in human computation for citizen science projects, with a focus on the psychological, social, and environmental factors that influence their participation.  A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining both qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis methods. A survey of 150 volunteers participating in human computation tasks was conducted, supplemented by in-depth interviews with 30 participants. The data was analyzed using thematic analysis and statistical models to identify patterns and correlations between engagement factors and volunteer behavior.  The results revealed that volunteers' engagement profiles can be categorized into three distinct groups the 'Motivated', 'Curious', and 'Social'. The 'Motivated' group was characterized by a strong sense of purpose and intrinsic motivation, while the 'Curious' group was driven by a desire for knowledge and understanding. The 'Social' group, on the other hand, was influenced by social norms and peer pressure. Environmental factors, such as task complexity and feedback mechanisms, also played a significant role in shaping volunteers' engagement.  The findings of this study have implications for the design and implementation of citizen science projects, highlighting the importance of tailoring engagement strategies to the diverse needs and motivations of volunteers. By understanding the engagement profiles of volunteers, researchers and practitioners can develop more effective strategies for increasing participation, retention, and overall success in human computation for citizen science projects.

text: We developed a novel topological approach to classify proteins based on their spatial arrangements of secondary and tertiary structures. This method, dubbed "Protein Topological Atlas," integrates multiple structural data sources, including atomic coordinates, solvent-accessible surfaces, and secondary structure assignments, to generate a comprehensive topological map of each protein.  Through extensive testing and validation, our approach demonstrated superior performance in distinguishing between functionally related and unrelated proteins, achieving an accuracy of 97.4% in distinguishing between enzyme and non-enzyme proteins. Furthermore, we found that the topological features extracted by our method were robust against variations in protein sequences, folding rates, and solvent conditions.  Our approach relies on the application of graph theory and network analysis to represent the spatial relationships between protein structures. By mapping protein structures onto a high-dimensional topological space, we can identify patterns and motifs that are indicative of specific functional classes. We also developed a machine learning framework to train models that can predict protein function based on topological features.  Our results suggest that topological classification of proteins offers a promising alternative to existing methods, which often rely on sequence-based approaches that are limited by their inability to capture the complex spatial relationships between protein structures. We believe that our approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of protein classification and pave the way for a more comprehensive understanding of protein function and evolution.

For a clique cover $C$ in the undirected graph $G$, the {\it clique cover
graph} of $C$ is the graph obtained by contracting the vertices of each clique
in $C$ into a single vertex. The {\it clique cover width} of $G$, denoted by
$CCW(G)$, is the minimum value of the bandwidth of all clique cover graphs in
$G$. Any $G$ with $CCW(G)=1$ is known to be an incomparability graph, and hence
is called, a {\it unit incomparability graph}. We introduced the {\it unit
incomparability dimension of $G$}, denoted by$Udim(G)$, to be the smallest
integer $d$ so that there are unit incomparability graphs $H_i$ with
$V(H_i)=V(G), i=1,2,...,d$, so that $E(G)=\cap_{i=1}^d E(G_i)$. We prove a
decomposition theorem establishing the inequality $Udim(G)\le CCW(G)$.
Specifically, given any $G$, there are unit incomparability graphs
$H_1,H_2,...,H_{CC(W)}$ with $V(H_i)=V(G)$ so that and $E(G)=\cap_{i=1}^{CCW}
E(H_i)$. In addition, $H_i$ is co-bipartite, for $i=1,2,...,CCW(G)-1$.
Furthermore, we observe that $CCW(G)\ge s(G)/2-1$, where $s(G)$ is the number
of leaves in a largest induced star of $G$ , and use Ramsey Theory to give an
upper bound on $s(G)$, when $G$ is represented as an intersection graph using
our decomposition theorem. Finally, when $G$ is an incomparability graph we
prove that $CCW (G)\le s(G)-1$.

text:
Type IIP Supernovae (SNe) are expected to arise from Red Supergiant stars
(RSGs). These stars have observed mass-loss rates that span more than two
orders of magnitude, from $< 10^{-6}$ solar masses yr$^{-1}$ to almost $
10^{-4} $ solar masses yr$^{-1}$. Thermal bremsstrahlung X-ray emission from at
least some IIP's should reflect the larger end of the high mass-loss rates.
Strangely, no IIP SNe are seen where the X-ray luminosity is large enough to
suggest mass-loss rates greater than about $ 10^{-5} $ solar masses yr$^{-1}$.
We investigate if this could be due to absorption of the X-ray emission. After
carefully studying all the various aspects, we conclude that absorption would
not be large enough to prevent us from having detected X-ray emission from high
mass-loss rate IIP's. This leads us to the conclusion that there may be an
upper limit of $\sim 10^{-5} $ solar masses yr$^{-1}$ to the mass-loss rate of
Type IIP progenitors, and therefore to the luminosity of RSGs that explode to
form Type IIPs. This is turn suggests an upper limit of $\leq 19 $ solar masses
for the progenitor mass of a Type IIP SN. This limit is close to that obtained
by direct detection of IIP progenitors, as well as that suggested by recent
stellar evolution calculations. Although the statistics need to be improved,
many current indicators support the notion that RSGs above $\sim 19 $ solar
masses do not explode to form Type IIP SNe.

text: In this study, we investigate the performance and efficiency of bi-directional half-duplex protocols incorporating multiple relays in wireless communication networks. Our primary objective is to address the challenges associated with signal degradation and increased latency, commonly observed in traditional half-duplex systems. We propose a novel framework that optimizes relay selection and transmission scheduling to enhance throughput and reduce the overall communication delay.  We employ a systematic approach utilizing both theoretical analysis and simulation-based experiments to evaluate our proposed methodology. The key ideas include the implementation of adaptive relay selection algorithms based on channel state information, and a time-division multiplexing scheme that ensures fair access to the channel for all nodes involved. Our results indicate a significant improvement in end-to-end communication rates, demonstrating that our bi-directional half-duplex protocol outperforms existing models under varying network conditions, particularly in environments with high user density.  Furthermore, we assess the impact of relay positioning and diversity on system performance, revealing critical insights into optimal relay deployment strategies. The findings provide valuable guidance for the design of efficient communication protocols in future wireless systems, particularly in scenarios where bi-directional communication is crucial. We conclude that our proposed bi-directional half-duplex protocol with multiple relays effectively mitigates the limitations of prior protocols, offering a robust solution for contemporary wireless communication challenges.

text:
High-energy-density electron-positron pair plasma production and its dynamics
in a thin foil illuminated by two counter-propagating laser pulses are
investigated through multi-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations. We compare
the production of electron-positron pairs and gamma-photons via quantum
electrodynamics processes in the relativistic transparent and opaque regimes,
and find that the target transparency can significantly enhance the
electron-positron pair production due to the formation of stable standing wave
(SW). An optimum foil density of 200 - 280 n_c (n_c is the laser critical
density) is found for enhancing electron-positron pair production when laser
intensity reaches a few 10e23 W/cm2. At such foil density, laser energy
conversion to electron-positron pairs is approximately four times higher than
at foil density of 710n_c, whereas laser energy conversion to gamma-photons
keeps almost the same. Consequently, high dense electron-positron plasma with a
maximum intensity above 10e20 W/cm2 is produced. Modulation dynamics of created
pair plasmas is further observed when target foil becomes transparent. It is
shown that stable SWs formed directly by two counter-propagating lasers, not
only trap the created electron-positron pairs to their nodes, but also modulate
periodically average energy and phase-space and angular distributions of
trapped particles. However, similar trapping and modulation effects become
obscure in the opaque regime due to the absence of stable SW field.

text:
We demonstrate that blending fluorinated molecules in PEDOT:PSS hole
transport layers (HTL) induces charge transfers which impact on both charge
extraction and photogeneration within organic photovoltaic (OPV) devices. OPVs
fabricated with modified HTL and two photoactive polymer blends led
systematically to power conversion efficiencies (PCE) increases, with
PTB7:PC70BM blend exhibiting PCE of ~ 8.3 %, i.e. ~ 15 % increase compared to
pristine HTL devices. A reduced device-to-device characteristics variations was
also noticed when fluorinated additives were used to modify the PEDOT:PSS.
Shading lights onto the effect of HTL fluorination, we show that the morphology
of the polymer:PCBM blends remains surprisingly unaffected by the fluorinated
HTL surface energy but that, instead, the OPVs are impacted not only by the HTL
electronic properties (work function, dipole layer, open circuit voltage,
charge transfer dynamic) but also by alteration of the complex refractive
indices (photogeneration, short circuit current density, external quantum
efficiencies, electro-optic modelling). Both mechanisms find their origin in
fluorination induced charge transfers. This work points towards fluorination as
a promising strategy toward combining both external quantum efficiency
modulation and power conversion efficiency enhancement in OPVs. Charge
transfers could also be used more broadly to tune the optical constants and
electric field distribution, as well as to reduce interfacial charge
recombinations within OPVs.

text:
Advances in laser and Z-pinch technology, coupled with the development of
plasma diagnostics and the availability of high-performance computers, have
recently stimulated the growth of high-energy density laboratory astrophysics.
In particular a number of experiments have been designed to study radiative
shocks and jets with the aim of shedding new light on physical processes linked
to the ejection and accretion of mass by newly born stars.
  Although general scaling laws are a powerful tools to link laboratory
experiments with astrophysical plasmas, the phenomena modelled are often too
complicated for simple scaling to remain relevant. Nevertheless, the
experiments can still give important insights into the physics of astrophysical
systems and can be used to provide the basic experimental validation of
numerical simulations in regimes of interest to astrophysics.
  We will illustrate the possible links between laboratory experiments,
numerical simulations and astrophysics in the context of stellar jets. First we
will discuss the propagation of stellar jets in a cross-moving interstellar
medium and the scaling to Z-pinch produced jets. Our second example focuses on
slab-jets produced at the PALS (Prague Asterix Laser System) laser installation
and their practical applications to astrophysics. Finally, we illustrate the
limitations of scaling for radiative shocks, which are found at the head of the
most rapid stellar jets.
