text: In this study, we present observations of the fragmentation event of Comet 73P/Schwassmann-Wachmann 3B using data acquired with the Subaru Telescope's Suprime-Cam camera. The comet fragmented into multiple sub-comets in August 2006, and our analysis focused on the resulting debris stream visible as faint elongated structures in the sky. We employed photometric measurements to identify and track these features over time, providing insights into their spatial distribution and evolution. Our key findings include the identification of at least six distinct sub-comets within the debris stream, each with its own characteristic light curve and brightness variation. This work not only highlights the dynamic nature of cometary bodies but also demonstrates the effectiveness of wide-field imaging techniques in studying such events. The methodology involved detailed data reduction and analysis, including aperture photometry and light curve fitting, to accurately measure and characterize the observed features. These results contribute to our understanding of comet fragmentation processes and the mechanisms that govern the evolution of cometary nuclei under solar radiation and other environmental factors.

text:
The solar analogs of M67 let us glimpse the probable behavior of the Sun on
time scales surpassing the duration of human civilization. M67 can serve as a
solar proxy because its stars share a similar age and composition with the Sun.
Previous surveys of M67 observed that 15% of its Sun-like stars exhibited
chromospheric activity levels below solar minimum, which suggest that these
stars might be in activity-minimum states analogous to the Maunder Minimum. The
activity diagnostic used, the HK index (relative intensities of the Ca II H&K
lines integrated over 1 Ang. bandpasses), was measured from low-resolution
spectra ($R\approx 5000$), as is traditional and suitable for nearby, bright
stars. However, for stars beyond the Local Bubble, the interstellar medium
(ISM) imprints absorption lines in spectra at Ca II H&K, which negatively bias
activity measurements when these lines fall within the HK index bandpass. I
model the ISM clouds in the M67 foreground with high-resolution spectra of blue
stragglers and solar analogs. I demonstrate that ISM absorption varies across
the cluster and must be accounted for on a star-by-star basis. I then apply the
ISM model to a solar spectrum and broaden it to the lower spectral resolution
employed by prior surveys. Comparing HK indices measured from ISM-free and
ISM-contaminated spectra, I find that all stars observed below solar minimum
can be explained by this ISM bias. I conclude that there is no compelling
evidence for Maunder minimum candidates in M67 at this time.
label: human

text: The universe is home to numerous interacting double white dwarf binaries, which are characterized by the close proximity of two white dwarf stars in a binary system. These systems are thought to be the remnants of low-mass stars that have exhausted their fuel and shed their outer layers, leaving behind the hot, compact cores known as white dwarfs. The interaction between the two white dwarfs in these systems can lead to a variety of astrophysical phenomena, including mass transfer, orbital decay, and eventually, merger.  The objective of this research is to investigate the potential for merger in interacting double white dwarf binaries, with a focus on the role of mass transfer and orbital decay. By analyzing a sample of 20 interacting double white dwarf binaries, we have examined the relationship between the mass transfer rate and the orbital decay rate, as well as the effects of mass transfer on the binary's orbital evolution.  Our results indicate that the majority of interacting double white dwarf binaries are on a collision course, with the likelihood of merger increasing as the mass transfer rate increases. We have also found that the orbital decay rate is closely tied to the mass transfer rate, with more massive transfer rates leading to faster orbital decay. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that mass transfer can have a significant impact on the binary's orbital evolution, potentially leading to a more rapid merger than would be expected based solely on the orbital decay rate.  Overall, our research highlights the importance of considering the effects of mass transfer on the merger dynamics of interacting double white dwarf binaries. By better understanding the interplay between mass transfer and orbital decay, we can gain insight into the ultimate fate of these systems, which may ultimately lead to the formation of a single, more massive white dwarf.

text:
Combined ATLAS and CMS measurements of the Higgs boson production and decay
rates, as well as constraints on its couplings to vector bosons and fermions,
are presented. The combination is based on the analysis of five production
processes, namely gluon fusion, vector boson fusion, and associated production
with a $W$ or a $Z$ boson or a pair of top quarks, and of the six decay modes
$H \to ZZ, WW$, $\gamma\gamma, \tau\tau, bb$, and $\mu\mu$. All results are
reported assuming a value of 125.09 GeV for the Higgs boson mass, the result of
the combined measurement by the ATLAS and CMS experiments. The analysis uses
the CERN LHC proton--proton collision data recorded by the ATLAS and CMS
experiments in 2011 and 2012, corresponding to integrated luminosities per
experiment of approximately 5 fb$^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV and 20 fb$^{-1}$ at
$\sqrt{s} = 8$ TeV. The Higgs boson production and decay rates measured by the
two experiments are combined within the context of three generic
parameterisations: two based on cross sections and branching fractions, and one
on ratios of coupling modifiers. Several interpretations of the measurements
with more model-dependent parameterisations are also given. The combined signal
yield relative to the Standard Model prediction is measured to be 1.09 $\pm$
0.11. The combined measurements lead to observed significances for the vector
boson fusion production process and for the $H \to \tau\tau$ decay of $5.4$ and
$5.5$ standard deviations, respectively. The data are consistent with the
Standard Model predictions for all parameterisations considered.

text: We investigate the properties of trace maps on Mackey algebras, a class of algebras that generalize the notion of von Neumann algebras and exhibit rich geometric and analytic features. Our work focuses on the construction and analysis of trace maps on Mackey algebras, with a particular emphasis on their relationship with the algebraic and geometric structures of these algebras.  Through a combination of algebraic and analytical techniques, we establish the existence of trace maps on Mackey algebras and investigate their properties, including their behavior under conjugation and unitization. We also explore the connection between trace maps and the spectral theory of Mackey algebras, revealing a deep link between the geometric and analytic aspects of these algebras.  Our results include the derivation of a general formula for the trace map on Mackey algebras, which we use to establish a connection between the algebraic and geometric structures of these algebras. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of trace maps to the study of the geometric and analytic properties of Mackey algebras, including their representation theory and spectral theory.  Our approach is based on a rigorous and systematic treatment of the algebraic and analytical properties of Mackey algebras, combining techniques from algebra, analysis, and geometric analysis. By exploring the properties of trace maps on Mackey algebras, we shed new light on the underlying structures and properties of these algebras, and provide a new framework for the study of their geometric and analytic aspects.

text:
In this paper, a parametric simplex algorithm for solving linear vector
optimization problems (LVOPs) is presented. This algorithm can be seen as a
variant of the multi-objective simplex (Evans-Steuer) algorithm [12]. Different
from it, the proposed algorithm works in the parameter space and does not aim
to find the set of all efficient solutions. Instead, it finds a solution in the
sense of Loehne [16], that is, it finds a subset of efficient solutions that
allows to generate the whole frontier. In that sense, it can also be seen as a
generalization of the parametric self-dual simplex algorithm, which originally
is designed for solving single objective linear optimization problems, and is
modified to solve two objective bounded LVOPs with the positive orthant as the
ordering cone in Ruszczynski and Vanderbei [21]. The algorithm proposed here
works for any dimension, any solid pointed polyhedral ordering cone C and for
bounded as well as unbounded problems. Numerical results are provided to
compare the proposed algorithm with an objective space based LVOP algorithm
(Benson algorithm in [13]), that also provides a solution in the sense of [16],
and with Evans-Steuer algorithm [12]. The results show that for non-degenerate
problems the proposed algorithm outperforms Benson algorithm and is on par with
Evan-Steuer algorithm. For highly degenerate problems Benson's algorithm [13]
excels the simplex-type algorithms; however, the parametric simplex algorithm
is for these problems computationally much more efficient than Evans-Steuer
algorithm.
label: human

text:
After 33 years of extensive studies of SS 433, we have learnt much about this
unique system with moving emission lines in the spectrum. The orbital
inclination is known from spectroscopic observations of moving lines; the
distance is derived from radio interferometry of relativistic jets; the mass
ratio of its components is determined from X-ray observations of jets'
eclipses. In 2005, the accretion donor was detected as an A4 - A8 giant, and
its contribution to eclipse light was measured spectroscopically. In the
present paper, the A-type star was detected via multicolor photometry on the
basis of its Balmer jump. A method is proposed to estimate the interstellar
reddening, able to measure the individual law of interstellar absorption for SS
433 from spectrophotometry. The method is based on extracting the energy
distribution of the spectral component of a very hot source covered in eclipse
and on the comparison of its energy distribution to the Planck energy
distribution of a black body with the temperature exceeding 10^6 K. The
determination of general parameters of SS 433 leads to fairly accurate
estimates of luminosity, radius, and mass of the A star in the system, and
consequently leads to an accurate estimate of the mass of the compact
component, the source of jets. The latter mass is between 1.25 and 1.87 solar
masses. The reasons for overestimating this mass when using the dynamical
method are discussed. In our opinion, the presence of a black hole in this
system is excluded.
label: human

text: We investigate the role of magnetic impurities in spin-split superconductors and their impact on the superconducting order parameter and electronic states. Traditional theories suggest that magnetic impurities can induce localized spin moments, which may disrupt Cooper pairing and lead to enhanced pair-breaking effects. In our study, we employ a combination of mean-field theory and numerical simulations to analyze the superconducting gap structure and local density of states in the presence of magnetic impurities.   We systematically explore various concentration levels of magnetic impurities to characterize their effects on the superconducting properties. Our results reveal that at low impurity concentrations, the superconducting gap remains relatively robust, while at higher concentrations, we observe significant suppression of the gap, leading to a transition towards a mixed-state superconductivity characterized by non-trivial topological features. Moreover, we notice that the spin-splitting effect enhances the spatially inhomogeneous pairing interaction, resulting in complex vortex lattice structures that depend sensitively on the magnetic impurity distribution.  Through a detailed examination of both the thermodynamic and transport properties, we link the presence of magnetic impurities to observable changes in critical temperature and critical magnetic field. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between magnetic disorder and superconductivity in spin-split systems, offering insights that are crucial for the development of future spintronic devices. We conclude that managing magnetic impurities is essential for optimizing the performance of superconductors in practical applications.
label: machine

text: In this study, we present our work on implementing the ALICE High-Level Trigger Time Projection Chamber (HLT TPC) tracking algorithm for lead-lead (Pb-Pb) collision events on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). The primary objective of this research is to accelerate the track reconstruction process for heavy-ion collisions using parallel computing on GPUs, aiming to significantly reduce the processing time compared to traditional CPU implementations.  Our results demonstrate the successful parallelization of the ALICE HLT TPC tracking algorithm on GPUs, achieving notable speedup factors. By leveraging the massively parallel architecture of GPUs, we have significantly improved the computational performance of the track reconstruction task for Pb-Pb collision events. Our approach enables the processing of a large volume of data with complex track patterns in a more efficient manner, essential for online event selection in high-energy physics experiments.  The key ideas revolve around optimizing the track reconstruction algorithm for parallel execution on GPUs, utilizing their high computational power and memory bandwidth. We discuss the methodology of porting the ALICE HLT TPC tracking algorithm to GPUs, optimizing memory access patterns, and parallelizing the track finding and fitting procedures.  Overall, our work demonstrates the feasibility and benefits of GPU acceleration for the ALICE HLT TPC tracking algorithm, paving the way for improved real-time event processing capabilities in high-energy physics experiments.
label: machine

text: We investigate the peculiar spin frequency and radio profile evolution of PSR J1119$-$6127, a magnetar candidate, following a series of intense X-ray bursts. Through a comprehensive analysis of archival radio and X-ray data, we identify a unique pattern of spin frequency oscillations, characterized by a period of approximately 10 days, which is significantly shorter than the expected spin-down period of the magnetar. This unexpected behavior is accompanied by a notable evolution of the radio profile, with a pronounced increase in flux density at lower frequencies. Our results suggest that the X-ray bursts triggered a sudden reconnection of the magnetar's magnetic field, leading to a redistribution of energy and a change in the spin frequency oscillations. Furthermore, we propose that the radio profile evolution is a consequence of the magnetar's magnetic field configuration, which is being dynamically reconfigured by the reconnection process. Our findings provide new insights into the complex interplay between magnetic reconnection and spin frequency oscillations in magnetars, and have significant implications for our understanding of the underlying physics of these enigmatic objects.

text:
We present scattered light images of the TW Hya disk performed with SPHERE in
PDI mode at 0.63, 0.79, 1.24 and 1.62 micron. We also present H2/H3-band ADI
observations. Three distinct radial depressions in the polarized intensity
distribution are seen, around 85, 21, and 6~au. The overall intensity
distribution has a high degree of azimuthal symmetry; the disk is somewhat
brighter than average towards the South and darker towards the North-West. The
ADI observations yielded no signifiant detection of point sources in the disk.
  Our observations have a linear spatial resolution of 1 to 2au, similar to
that of recent ALMA dust continuum observations. The sub-micron sized dust
grains that dominate the light scattering in the disk surface are strongly
coupled to the gas. We created a radiative transfer disk model with
self-consistent temperature and vertical structure iteration and including
grain size-dependent dust settling. This method may provide independent
constraints on the gas distribution at higher spatial resolution than is
feasible with ALMA gas line observations.
  We find that the gas surface density in the "gaps" is reduced by 50% to 80%
relative to an unperturbed model. Should embedded planets be responsible for
carving the gaps then their masses are at most a few 10 Mearth. The observed
gaps are wider, with shallower flanks, than expected for planet-disk
interaction with such low-mass planets. If forming planetary bodies have
undergone collapse and are in the "detachted phase" then they may be directly
observable with future facilities such as METIS at the E-ELT.

text: Understanding the dynamics and characteristics of binary neutron star systems is crucial in the field of astrophysics. This research paper presents the discovery of a highly relativistic double neutron star binary system made by the PALFA survey. The objective of this study is to analyze the orbital parameters, mass distribution, and relativistic effects in this system using radio observations. The methodology involved data collection from radio telescopes and extensive computational modeling to determine the properties of the neutron stars and their binary orbit.   Key findings reveal that the double neutron star system exhibits significant relativistic effects, such as frame-dragging and gravitational wave emission, indicating the system's potential to contribute valuable insights into general relativity and gravitational wave astronomy. The masses of the neutron stars were found to be within the expected range for such systems, confirming the reliability of the observations. Moreover, the short orbital period and high eccentricity of the system provide unique opportunities to study strong gravitational interactions and test theories of gravity in extreme conditions.  In conclusion, the discovery of this highly relativistic double neutron star binary system by PALFA opens new avenues for studying relativistic astrophysics and gravitational wave physics. Further observations and analyses of this system could help refine our understanding of fundamental physics principles in the extreme environment of binary neutron stars.
label: machine

text:
HI kinematic asymmetries are common in late-type galaxies irrespective of
environment, although the amplitudes are strikingly low in isolated galaxies.
As part of our studies of the HI morphology and kinematics in isolated
late-type galaxies we have chosen several very isolated galaxies from the AMIGA
sample for HI mapping. Here we present GMRT 21-cm HI line mapping of CIG 340
which was selected because its integrated HI spectrum has a very symmetric
profile, Aflux = 1.03. Optical images of the galaxy hinted at a warped disk in
contrast to the symmetric integrated HI spectrum profile. Our aim is to
determine the extent to which the optical asymmetry is reflected in the
resolved HI morphology and kinematics. GMRT observations reveal significant HI
morphological asymmetries in CIG 340 despite it's overall symmetric optical
form and highly symmetric HI spectrum. The most notable HI features are: 1) a
warp in the HI disk (with an optical counterpart), 2) the HI north/south flux
ratio = 1.32 is much larger than expected from the integrated HI spectrum
profile and 3) a ~ 45" (12 kpc) HI extension, containing ~ 6% of the detected
HI mass on the northern side of the disk. We conclude that in isolated galaxies
a highly symmetric HI spectrum can mask significant HI morphological
asymmetries. The northern HI extension appears to be the result of a recent
perturbation (10^8 yr), possibly by a satellite which is now disrupted or
projected within the disk. This study provides an important step in our ongoing
program to determine the predominant source of HI asymmetries in isolated
galaxies. For CIG 340 the isolation from major companions, symmetric HI
spectrum, optical morphology and interaction timescales have allowed us to
narrow the possible causes the HI asymmetries and identify tests to further
constrain the source of the asymmetries.
label: human

text: We present AROMA, an innovative approach to generating radio maps for localization systems, enabling more accurate and efficient indoor navigation. By leveraging advanced machine learning techniques and real-time sensor data, AROMA automatically constructs radio maps that accurately reflect the wireless environment, reducing the need for manual mapping and increasing system reliability. Our system utilizes a combination of machine learning algorithms and sensor fusion to analyze radio signal strengths, signal-to-noise ratios, and other relevant factors, generating a comprehensive map of the indoor space. Through extensive experimentation and evaluation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of AROMA in various scenarios, showcasing its ability to achieve high accuracy rates and robustness in diverse environments. Key to AROMA's success is its ability to learn from real-time data, adapt to changing environments, and minimize the impact of interference and multipath effects. By providing a dynamic and adaptive radio map, AROMA enhances the performance of localization systems, enabling users to navigate complex indoor spaces with greater ease and precision. Our results show that AROMA outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, and adaptability, making it an attractive solution for a wide range of applications, including smart homes, public buildings, and industrial facilities.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the flagellar flows surrounding swarms of motile bacteria, focusing on the hydrodynamic interactions and collective dynamics observed at the micro-scale. Our research addresses the challenge of characterizing the complex flow patterns induced by the synchronized flagellar activity in densely populated bacterial systems, which are pivotal to understanding microbial locomotion and effective antibiotic targeting. We employ both experimental and computational approaches to capture high-resolution flow fields and elucidate the interactions between individual bacterial swimmers and their collective behavior. Using particle image velocimetry (PIV), we record and analyze velocity fields, mapping the intricate vortices characteristic of swarm motility. Computational simulations, employing both Stokesian and continuum hydrodynamic models, complement our experimental observations and provide insights into the underlying principles governing bacterial swarming. Our results reveal the formation of coherent structures at the swarm boundary, facilitating enhanced nutrient transport and efficient group dynamics. Importantly, we identify a critical bacterial density threshold at which hydrodynamic interactions dominate, leading to emergent coordinated movement patterns. This finding advances our understanding of microbial ecology and opens novel pathways for controlling bacterial proliferation through manipulation of their locomotive behavior. Our work underscores the significance of hydrodynamics in biological systems and offers a framework for further exploration of swarm-related phenomena, potentially informing the design of bio-inspired robotic systems and antimicrobial strategies.
label: machine

text: This research examines the impact of surface recombination on electroluminescence (EL) and photoconversion efficiency in amorphous silicon (a-SiH) thin-film solar cells integrated with crystalline silicon (c-Si) substrates. Surface recombination processes, such as interface recombination at the a-SiH/c-Si interface, significantly influence the overall performance of these heterojunction solar cells. The study employs both theoretical modeling and experimental characterization techniques to quantify the effects of surface recombination on EL intensity and photoconversion efficiency.  The methodology involves fabricating a-SiH/c-Si heterojunction solar cells with varying thicknesses of a-SiH layer and different c-Si substrate surfaces to control surface roughness and other physical properties. Photoluminescence spectroscopy, current-voltage measurements, and EL imaging were used to assess the EL characteristics. Additionally, transient photocurrent analysis was performed to evaluate the charge carrier dynamics and photoconversion efficiency.  Key findings indicate that increased surface recombination rates lead to reduced EL intensities and lower photoconversion efficiencies. This is attributed to higher recombination losses at the cell's surface, which impede the generation and extraction of photogenerated carriers. Furthermore, the results suggest that optimizing the a-SiH/c-Si interface through surface passivation treatments can mitigate these detrimental effects, thereby enhancing the overall performance of the heterojunction solar cells.  In conclusion, this research underscores the critical role of surface recombination in determining the performance of a-SiH/c-Si heterojunction solar cells. Future work will focus on developing more effective surface passivation strategies to further improve the efficiency of these devices.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the limits on commercial bank lending by analyzing the regulatory constraints, economic conditions, and market dynamics that influence loan issuance. We find that regulatory frameworks, particularly capital adequacy requirements and liquidity ratios, significantly impact lending activities. Economic downturns and low-interest-rate environments also limit banks' ability to extend loans due to reduced profitability and higher risk aversion. Additionally, market competition and technological advancements have altered traditional lending practices, necessitating more sophisticated underwriting processes. Our key methodology involves a comprehensive review of regulatory documents, econometric analysis of bank performance data, and case studies of notable lending practices across different regions. The results highlight the complex interplay between regulatory pressures and market forces, underscoring the need for flexible policy adjustments to support sustainable lending practices.
label: machine

text:
The axiom of choice ensures precisely that, in ZFC, every set is projective:
that is, a projective object in the category of sets. In constructive ZF (CZF)
the existence of enough projective sets has been discussed as an additional
axiom taken from the interpretation of CZF in Martin-Loef's intuitionistic type
theory. On the other hand, every non-empty set is injective in classical ZF,
which argument fails to work in CZF. The aim of this paper is to shed some
light on the problem whether there are (enough) injective sets in CZF.
  We show that no two element set is injective unless the law of excluded
middle is admitted for negated formulas, and that the axiom of power set is
required for proving that there are strongly enough injective sets. The latter
notion is abstracted from the singleton embedding into the power set, which
ensures enough injectives both in every topos and in IZF. We further show that
it is consistent with CZF to assume that the only injective sets are the
singletons. In particular, assuming the consistency of CZF one cannot prove in
CZF that there are enough injective sets. As a complement we revisit the
duality between injective and projective sets from the point of view of
intuitionistic type theory.

The observed population of the Milky Way satellite galaxies offer a unique
testing ground for galaxy formation theory on small-scales. Our novel approach
was to investigate the clustering of the known Milky Way satellite galaxies and
to quantify the amount of substructure within their distribution using a
two-point correlation function statistic in each of three spaces: configuration
space, line-of-sight velocity space, and four-dimensional phase-space. These
results were compared to those for three sets of subhaloes in the Via Lactea II
Cold Dark Matter simulation defined to represent the luminous dwarfs. We found
no evidence at a significance level above 2-sigma of substructure within the
distribution of the Milky Way satellite galaxies in any of the three spaces.
The "luminous" subhalo sets are more strongly clustered than are the Milky Way
satellites in all three spaces and over a broader range of scales in
four-dimensional phase-space. Each of the "luminous" subhalo sets are clustered
as a result of substructure within their line-of-sight velocity space
distributions at greater than 3-sigma significance, whereas the Milky Way
satellite galaxies are randomly distributed in line-of-sight velocity space.
While our comparison is with only one Cold Dark Matter simulation, the
inconsistencies between the Milky Way satellite galaxies and the Via Lactea II
subhalo sets for all clustering methods suggest a potential new 'small-scale'
tension between Cold Dark Matter theory and the observed Milky Way satellites.
Future work will obtain a more robust comparison between the observed Milky Way
satellites and Cold Dark Matter theory by studying additional simulations.

We present generalized supernova (SN) light curve (LC) models for a variety
of power inputs. We provide an expression for the power input that is produced
by self-similar forward and reverse shocks in SN ejecta - circumstellar matter
(CSM) interaction. We find that this ejecta-CSM interaction luminosity is in
agreement with results from multi-dimensional radiation hydrodynamics
simulations in the optically-thin case. We develop a model for the case of an
optically-thick CSM by invoking an approximation for the effects of radiative
diffusion. In the context of this model, we provide predictions for the time of
forward shock break-out from the optically-thick part of the CSM envelope. We
also introduce a hybrid LC model that incorporates ejecta-CSM interaction plus
Ni-56 and Co-56 radioactive decay input. We fit this hybrid model to the LC of
the Super-Luminous Supernova (SLSN) 2006gy. We find that this model provides a
better fit to the LC of this event than previously presented models. We also
address the relation between Type IIL and Type IIn SN with ejecta-CSM
interaction models. Forward and reverse shock power input due to CSM
interaction can produce the LCs of Type IIn SNe in terms of duration, shape and
decline rate. This model can also produce LCs that are symmetric in shape
around peak luminosity. We conclude that the observed LC variety of SNe Type
IIn and of the SLSNe is likely to be a byproduct of the large range of
conditions relevant to significant ejecta-CSM interaction as a power source.

In this paper we study coupled dynamical systems and investigate dimension
properties of the subspace spanned by solutions of each individual system.
Relevant problems on \textit{collinear dynamical systems} and their variations
are discussed recently by Montenbruck et. al. in \cite{collinear2017SCL}, while
in this paper we aim to provide a unified analysis to derive the
dimensional-invariance principles for networked coupled systems, and to
generalize the invariance principles for networked systems with more general
forms of coupling terms. To be specific, we consider two types of coupled
systems, one with scalar couplings and the other with matrix couplings. Via the
\textit{rank-preserving flow theory}, we show that any scalar-coupled dynamical
system (with constant, time-varying or state-dependent couplings) possesses the
dimensional-invariance principles, in that the dimension of the subspace
spanned by the individual systems' solutions remains invariant. For coupled
dynamical systems with matrix coefficients/couplings, necessary and sufficient
conditions (for constant, time-varying and state-dependent couplings) are given
to characterize dimensional-invariance principles. The proofs via a
rank-preserving matrix flow theory in this paper simplify the analysis in
\cite{collinear2017SCL}, and we also extend the invariance principles to the
cases of time-varying couplings and state-dependent couplings. Furthermore,
subspace-preserving property and signature-preserving flows are also developed
for coupled networked systems with particular coupling terms. These invariance
principles provide insightful characterizations to analyze transient behaviors
and solution evolutions for a large family of coupled systems, such as
multi-agent consensus dynamics, distributed coordination systems, formation
control systems, among others.

We present a detailed asymptotic analysis of the point indentation of an
unpressurized, spherical elastic shell. Previous analyses of this classic
problem have assumed that for sufficiently large indentation depths, such a
shell deforms by `mirror buckling' --- a portion of the shell inverts to become
a spherical cap with equal but opposite curvature to the undeformed shell. The
energy of deformation is then localized in a ridge in which the deformed and
undeformed portions of the shell join together, commonly referred to as
Pogorelov's ridge. Rather than using an energy formulation, we revisit this
problem from the point of view of the shallow shell equations and perform an
asymptotic analysis that exploits the largeness of the indentation depth. This
reveals first that the stress profile associated with mirror buckling is
singular as the indenter is approached. This consequence of point indentation
means that mirror buckling must be modified to incorporate the shell's bending
stiffness close to the indenter and gives rise to an intricate asymptotic
structure with seven different spatial regions. This is in contrast with the
three regions (mirror-buckled, ridge and undeformed) that are usually assumed
and yields new insight into the large compressive hoop stress that ultimately
causes the shell to buckle azimuthally.
label: human

text: In this study, we investigate the phenomenon of intermittent mass transfer in the nova-like cataclysmic variable star, BB Doradus, during its low accretion state. Our primary objective is to elucidate the process of mass accretion modulation in such systems, specifically focusing on the underlying mechanisms triggering the observed episodic mass flow. Utilizing comprehensive time-resolved spectroscopy and photometry data obtained from ground-based telescopes, we discover that BB Doradus exhibits sporadic enhancements in mass transfer rates while predominantly remaining in a low accretion regime. Our spectroscopic analysis reveals periodicities in emission line profiles that imply temporary accretion disk instabilities, potentially driven by magnetic field interactions or variations in the mass supply from the secondary star. Through the application of Doppler tomography, we ascertain the spatial distribution of accreting material and identify regions of enhanced activity correlating with these episodic mass transfer events. We propose a model involving magnetic reconnections as a plausible mechanism, which accounts for the observed variability in mass transfer. This investigation advances our understanding of episodic accretion phenomena and the associated dynamics in cataclysmic variable systems, contributing valuable insights into the evolutionary pathways of such binary systems. Future work directed towards high-cadence multi-wavelength observations will be instrumental in confirming the proposed mechanisms and further elucidating the complexities of accretion dynamics during low states in BB Doradus and similar systems. Our findings represent a significant step forward in understanding the intricate dynamics governing mass transfer variability in nova-like variables.

text: This research focuses on the development and application of ray mapping techniques to optimize double freeform surfaces for collimated beam shaping beyond the paraxial approximation. The study aims to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of optical designs by exploring non-paraxial geometrical optics principles. Utilizing ray tracing simulations, the research investigates how varying the curvature and topology of freeform surfaces affect the collimation and shaping of light beams. Key findings indicate that beyond the paraxial approximation, significant improvements in beam quality can be achieved with tailored freeform surfaces. The methodology involves rigorous computational modeling to map rays through designed surfaces, followed by quantitative analysis of beam parameters such as divergence, intensity distribution, and energy conservation. The results suggest that this approach offers a promising pathway for next-generation optical systems requiring precise control over light propagation, with potential applications in advanced laser technologies and high-resolution imaging systems.

text: In the quest for efficient drug discovery, there is a growing need to identify novel drug-target interactions. One promising approach is the use of gene-expression signatures to connect small-molecule drugs with their biological targets. Here, we present a simple and robust method for constructing gene-expression signatures and identifying drug-target relationships using gene-expression data and molecular interaction networks. Our approach involves selecting gene sets that exhibit significant correlation with drug response and constructing a gene-expression signature using a weighted sum of the gene set expression values. We then apply a network propagation algorithm to predict target genes based on the drug-gene interaction network. To evaluate our method, we analyzed gene-expression data from a large-scale drug screening campaign and compared the predicted targets with known targets and gene sets derived from external databases. Our results demonstrate that our method can accurately and robustly identify drug-target relationships, even in cases where the underlying biological mechanisms are not well understood. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be used to identify novel drug targets for known drugs and discover new drug-target interactions. Our findings have important implications for drug discovery and provide a valuable resource for the scientific community. Future work will focus on expanding the scope of our method to include additional data types and developing machine learning algorithms to further improve its performance.

We consider the problem of recovering linear image $Bx$ of a signal $x$ known
to belong to a given convex compact set ${\cal X}$ from indirect observation
$\omega=Ax+\xi$ of $x$ corrupted by random noise $\xi$ with finite covariance
matrix. It is shown that under some assumptions on ${\cal X}$ (satisfied, e.g.,
when ${\cal X}$ is the intersection of $K$ concentric ellipsoids/elliptic
cylinders, or the unit ball of the spectral norm in the space of matrices) and
on the norm $\|\cdot\|$ used to measure the recovery error (satisfied, e.g., by
$\|\cdot\|_p$-norms, $1\leq p\leq 2$, on ${\mathbf{R}}^m$ and by the nuclear
norm on the space of matrices), one can build, in a computationally efficient
manner, a "presumably good" linear in observations estimate, and that in the
case of zero mean Gaussian observation noise, this estimate is near-optimal
among all (linear and nonlinear) estimates in terms of its worst-case, over
$x\in {\cal X}$, expected $\|\cdot\|$-loss. These results form an essential
extension of those in our paper arXiv:1602.01355, where the assumptions on
${\cal X}$ were more restrictive, and the norm $\|\cdot\|$ was assumed to be
the Euclidean one. In addition, we develop near-optimal estimates for the case
of "uncertain-but-bounded" noise, where all we know about $\xi$ is that it is
bounded in a given norm by a given $\sigma$. Same as in arXiv:1602.01355, our
results impose no restrictions on $A$ and $B$.
  This arXiv paper slightly strengthens the journal publication Juditsky, A.,
Nemirovski, A. "Near-Optimality of Linear Recovery from Indirect Observations,"
Mathematical Statistics and Learning 1:2 (2018), 171-225.

text: The abstract focuses on investigating whether AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) encryption operations exhibit true randomness. Starting with a background on AES and its applications in cryptography, the study aims to explore if AES operates as a random number generator. Methodologically, the investigation employs statistical analysis and computational experiments to assess the randomness properties of AES output. Key findings indicate that while AES itself does not generate truly random numbers, it can be used effectively as a pseudo-random number generator under certain conditions. The results suggest that AES's security relies more on its key and algorithmic design rather than its ability to produce genuinely unpredictable sequences. The conclusion highlights the need for further research into hybrid methods that combine AES with additional sources of entropy to achieve true randomness in cryptographic applications.

Mobile device users can now easily capture and socially share video clips in
a timely manner by uploading them wirelessly to a server. When attending
crowded events, such as an exhibition or the Olympic Games, however, timely
sharing of videos becomes difficult due to choking bandwidth in the network
infrastructure, preventing like-minded attendees from easily sharing videos
with each other through a server. One solution to alleviate this problem is to
use direct device-to-device communication to share videos among nearby
attendees. Contact capacity between two devices, however, is limited, and thus
a recommendation algorithm, such as collaborative filtering, is needed to
select and transmit only videos of potential interest to an attendee. In this
paper, we address the question: which video clip should be transmitted to which
user. We proposed an video transmission scheduling algorithm, called CoFiGel,
that runs in a distributed manner and aims to improve both the prediction
coverage and precision of the collaborative filtering algorithm. At each
device, CoFiGel transmits the video that would increase the estimated number of
positive user-video ratings the most if this video is transferred to the
destination device. We evaluated CoFiGel using real-world traces and show that
substantial improvement can be achieved compared to baseline schemes that do
not consider rating or contact history.

We consider phase transitions on (eternal) de Sitter in an O(N) symmetric
scalar field theory. Making use of Starobinsky's stochastic inflation we prove
that deep infrared scalar modes cannot form a condensate -- and hence they see
an effective potential that allows no phase transition. We show that by proving
convexity of the effective potential that governs deep infrared field
fluctuations both at the origin as well as at arbitrary values of the field.
Next, we present numerical plots of the scalar field probability distribution
function (PDF) and the corresponding effective potential for several values of
the coupling constant at the asymptotic future timelike infinity of de Sitter.
For small field values the effective potential has an approximately quadratic
form, corresponding to a positive mass term, such that the corresponding PDF is
approximately Gaussian. However, the curvature of the effective potential shows
qualitatively different (typically much softer) behavior on the coupling
constant than that implied by the Starobinsky-Yokoyama procedure. For large
field values, the effective potential as expected reduces to the tree level
potential plus a positive correction that only weakly (logarithmically) depends
on the background field. Finally, we calculate the backreaction of fluctuations
on the background geometry and show that it is positive.
label: human

text: In this paper, we present an investigation into the Parallel Persistent Memory Model (PPMM) and its implications for data storage and retrieval in high-performance computing systems. The PPMM combines the benefits of parallel processing with the persistence of data in non-volatile memory, aiming to overcome the limitations of traditional storage technologies. Our research aims to address the challenge of efficiently managing data in large-scale parallel computing environments by leveraging persistent memory technologies.  Through a series of experiments and simulations, we demonstrate the advantages of the PPMM in terms of data access speed, fault tolerance, and scalability. Our results show that the PPMM outperforms traditional storage models in terms of both read and write operations, especially in scenarios with high concurrency and data-intensive workloads. Additionally, we propose a novel data allocation strategy for optimizing data placement in the PPMM to further improve performance.  Our research contributes to advancing the field of high-performance computing by introducing a new model for data management that combines the speed of parallel processing with the durability of persistent memory. The methodology employed in this study includes performance evaluations using benchmark applications and analysis of data access patterns in parallel computing environments. Overall, our findings suggest that the PPMM has the potential to revolutionize data storage in the context of parallel computing, paving the way for more efficient and reliable data processing in the future.
label: machine

text: Our work focuses on investigating the implications of reduced Large Hadron Collider (LHC) constraints for higgsino-like heavier electroweakinos. The problem we tackle is the potential relaxation of existing experimental limits on the masses and couplings of these particles in light of recent experimental data. Our goal is to provide insights into the consequences of these relaxed constraints on the parameter space of supersymmetric models featuring higgsino-like heavier electroweakinos.  Through a comprehensive analysis of the latest LHC data and theoretical considerations, we demonstrate that the reduced constraints open up previously unexplored regions of the parameter space. Our results show that the allowed mass ranges and couplings for higgsino-like heavier electroweakinos can be substantially broader than previously thought. This has significant implications for the search strategies and theoretical interpretations within the realm of supersymmetry.  Our methodology involves a combination of Monte Carlo simulations, statistical analysis, and comparison with experimental data. By leveraging these tools, we are able to quantitatively assess the impact of the reduced LHC constraints on the properties of higgsino-like heavier electroweakinos. Overall, our study sheds light on the evolving landscape of supersymmetric models in light of the latest experimental results, paving the way for future research directions in high-energy physics.

We model the normal state of ferromagnetic superconductors with two general
ellipsoidal Fermi surfaces (FSs), one for each spin projection
$\sigma=\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}$, each with its ferromagnetically split
chemical potential $\mu_{\sigma}$ and its three distinct single particle
effective masses, $\{m_{i\sigma}\}$, the geometric mean of which is
$m_{\sigma}$. We study this model in the presence of an arbitrarily oriented
magnetic induction, ${\bf B}=\mu_{0}{\bf H}+{\bf M_{0}}$, where ${\bf M_{0}}$
includes the Ising-like spontaneous ferromagnetic order, which for URhGe is in
the $c$-axis direction above the superconducting transition temperature $T_c$.
We assume the low-$T$ total particle density $\Sigma_{\sigma} n_{\sigma}({\bf
B})$ to be independent of ${\bf B}$, and obtain a self-consistent asymptotic
expansion for $\sum_{\sigma}\Pi^{3/2}_{\sigma}({\bf B})$ in even powers of
${\bf B}$, where $\Pi_{\sigma}({\bf B})=m_{\sigma}({\bf B})\mu_{\sigma}({\bf
B})$. We assume that the $\mu_{\sigma}({\bf B})$ are linear in ${\bf B}$ for
both spins due to the Zeeman interaction and that the remaining even ${\bf B}$
dependence in the $\Pi_{\sigma}({\bf B})$ arises only from $m_{\downarrow}({\bf
B})$. Our analogous expression for the Sommerfeld constant $\gamma({\bf B})$
leads to good fits to the $\gamma({\bf H})$ data of Aoki and Flouquet [J. Phys.
Soc. Jpn. \textbf{81}, 011003 (2012)] obtained for the ferromagnetic
superconductor URhGe in the ferromagnetic, non-superconducting phase, with the
applied magnetic field ${\bf H}$ along each of the three crystallographic
directions. We discuss this model in terms of the reentrant superconducting
properties of URhGe and UCoGe. This model can be generalized to an arbitrary
number of ellipsoidal FSs.

In this paper we propose and investigate a novel nonlinear unit, called $L_p$
unit, for deep neural networks. The proposed $L_p$ unit receives signals from
several projections of a subset of units in the layer below and computes a
normalized $L_p$ norm. We notice two interesting interpretations of the $L_p$
unit. First, the proposed unit can be understood as a generalization of a
number of conventional pooling operators such as average, root-mean-square and
max pooling widely used in, for instance, convolutional neural networks (CNN),
HMAX models and neocognitrons. Furthermore, the $L_p$ unit is, to a certain
degree, similar to the recently proposed maxout unit (Goodfellow et al., 2013)
which achieved the state-of-the-art object recognition results on a number of
benchmark datasets. Secondly, we provide a geometrical interpretation of the
activation function based on which we argue that the $L_p$ unit is more
efficient at representing complex, nonlinear separating boundaries. Each $L_p$
unit defines a superelliptic boundary, with its exact shape defined by the
order $p$. We claim that this makes it possible to model arbitrarily shaped,
curved boundaries more efficiently by combining a few $L_p$ units of different
orders. This insight justifies the need for learning different orders for each
unit in the model. We empirically evaluate the proposed $L_p$ units on a number
of datasets and show that multilayer perceptrons (MLP) consisting of the $L_p$
units achieve the state-of-the-art results on a number of benchmark datasets.
Furthermore, we evaluate the proposed $L_p$ unit on the recently proposed deep
recurrent neural networks (RNN).

text: In the realm of wireless communications, securing data transmission over frequency-selective fading channels presents a significant challenge. This research explores a novel approach to enhancing communication security using Vandermonde precoding, which can effectively address the issues posed by multipath propagation and channel variability. The primary objective is to develop a practical implementation of Vandermonde precoding techniques that ensure confidentiality and mitigate eavesdropping risks in real-world scenarios. We employed a combination of theoretical analysis and simulation studies to assess the performance of the proposed precoding scheme. Our methodology involved modeling the frequency-selective fading environment, applying Vandermonde matrices for signal encryption, and evaluating the robustness of the system against potential interception techniques. Key findings demonstrate that the proposed precoding approach substantially improves signal quality and resilience against fading while maintaining a low complexity compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the system exhibits an enhanced capacity for secure communication, with significant reductions in the probability of eavesdropping even in highly adverse channel conditions. In conclusion, the implementation of practical Vandermonde precoding represents a promising solution for secured communication over frequency-selective fading channels, providing both improved signal integrity and heightened data security. The findings encourage further exploration into advanced coding strategies that can be integrated with existing wireless standards to foster more secure communication infrastructures.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the impact of supernova feedback on the multi-phase interstellar medium (ISM) structure, addressing a crucial component of galaxy evolution models. Our work attempts to elucidate the mechanisms by which supernovae regulate the thermal, kinematic, and density properties of the ISM, ultimately affecting star formation rates and chemical enrichment processes. Employing high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations, we model a representative section of the galactic plane, incorporating advanced treatments of heating, cooling, and magnetic fields within a turbulent medium. Our key methodology involves the integration of a comprehensive supernova feedback algorithm, which accounts for both isolated and clustered supernova events, injecting momentum and energy into the ISM with varying temporal and spatial scales. The simulations reveal that supernovae are formidable drivers of ISM phase transitions, promoting the coexistence of hot, diffuse ionized gas with cold, dense molecular clouds. This results in a dynamic, self-regulated cycle where energy input from supernovae both disperses and compresses the ISM constituents. Our results underscore the pivotal role of supernova feedback in sustaining a complex, multi-phase ISM structure, which in turn mediates the efficiency of star formation. Furthermore, our findings indicate that feedback-driven turbulence is essential in maintaining pressure equilibrium across phases, preventing runaway cooling and star formation. This study provides critical insights into the self-regulation phenomena within galaxies and highlights the necessity of incorporating detailed supernova feedback models in simulations to achieve a realistic portrayal of ISM dynamics and its role in galactic evolution.
label: machine

We consider dust drift under the influence of stellar radiation pressure
during the pressure-driven expansion of an HII region using the chemo-dynamical
model MARION. Dust size distribution is represented by four dust types:
conventional polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), very small grains (VSGs),
big grains (BGs) and also intermediate-sized grains (ISGs), which are larger
than VSGs and smaller than BGs. The dust is assumed to move at terminal
velocity determined locally from the balance between the radiation pressure and
gas drag. As Coulomb drag is an important contribution to the overall gas drag,
we evaluate a grain charge evolution within the HII region for each dust type.
BGs are effectively swept out of the HII region. The spatial distribution of
ISGs within the HII region has a double peak structure, with a smaller inner
peak and a higher outer peak. PAHs and VSGs are mostly coupled to the gas. The
mean charge of PAHs is close to zero, so they can become neutral from time to
time because of charge fluctuations. These periods of neutrality occur often
enough to cause the removal of PAHs from the very interior of the HII region.
For VSGs, the effect of charge fluctuations is less pronounced but still
significant. We conclude that accounting for charge dispersion is necessary to
describe the dynamics of small grains.
label: human

text: In the rare-earth trichalcogenide YB$_6$, lattice instability is a crucial factor leading to the enhancement of superconductivity. At ambient pressure, YB$_6$ exhibits a tetragonal crystal structure, but under high pressure, it undergoes a phase transition to an orthorhombic structure. This structural transformation, driven by the displacement of the Y and B atoms from their ideal positions, is the source of lattice instability. The resulting distortion of the lattice enhances the superconducting transition temperature (T$_c$) and significantly increases its upper critical field (H$_{c2}$). The enhancement of T$_c$ and H$_{c2}$ is due to the increase in electronic density of states (DOS) at the Fermi level caused by the lattice instability. This increase in DOS at the Fermi level facilitates the pairing of electrons, thereby leading to an increase in superconducting critical temperature and magnetic field. Our studies have revealed that the lattice instability-induced enhancement of T$_c$ and H$_{c2}$ in YB$_6$ can be explained through the phonon-mediated mechanism, where the lattice distortion gives rise to the generation of phonon modes that strongly interact with the electrons, enhancing their pairing. Our results suggest that the manipulation of lattice instability through high pressure or other means could be an effective strategy for enhancing superconductivity in materials with similar crystal structures.
label: machine

text:
Starting from our recent chemical master equation derivation of the model of
an autocatalytic reaction-diffusion chemical system with reactions $U+2V
{\stackrel {\lambda_0}{\rightarrow}}~ 3 V;$ and $V {\stackrel
{\mu}{\rightarrow}}~P$, $U {\stackrel {\nu}{\rightarrow}}~ Q$, we determine the
effects of intrinsic noise on the momentum-space behavior of its kinetic
parameters and chemical concentrations. We demonstrate that the intrinsic noise
induces $n \rightarrow n$ molecular interaction processes with $n \geq 4$,
where $n$ is the number of molecules participating of type $U$ or $V$. The
momentum dependences of the reaction rates are driven by the fact that the
autocatalytic reaction (inelastic scattering) is renormalized through the
existence of an arbitrary number of intermediate elastic scatterings, which can
also be interpreted as the creation and subsequent decay of a three body
composite state $\sigma = \phi_u \phi_v^2$, where $\phi_i$ corresponds to the
fields representing the densities of $U$ and $V$. Finally, we discuss the
difference between representing $\sigma$ as a composite or an elementary
particle (molecule) with its own kinetic parameters. In one dimension we find
that while they show markedly different behavior in the short spatio-temporal
scale, high momentum (UV) limit, they are formally equivalent in the large
spatio-temporal scale, low momentum (IR) regime. On the other hand in two
dimensions and greater, due to the effects of fluctuations, there is no way to
experimentally distinguish between a fundamental and composite $\sigma$. Thus
in this regime $\sigma$ behave as an entity unto itself suggesting that it can
be effectively treated as an independent chemical species.

text:
As massive black holes (MBHs) grow from lower-mass seeds, it is natural to
expect that a leftover population of progenitor MBHs should also exist in the
present universe. Dwarf galaxies undergo a quiet merger history, and as a
result, we expect that dwarfs observed in the local Universe retain some
`memory' of the original seed mass distribution. Consequently, the properties
of MBHs in nearby dwarf galaxies may provide clean indicators of the efficiency
of MBH formation. In order to examine the properties of MBHs in dwarf galaxies,
we evolve different MBH populations within a Milky Way halo from high-redshift
to today. We consider two plausible MBH formation mechanisms: `massive seeds'
formed via gas-dynamical instabilities and a Population III remnant seed model.
`Massive seeds' have larger masses than PopIII remnants, but form in rarer
hosts. We dynamically evolve all halos merging with the central system, taking
into consideration how the interaction modifies the satellites, stripping their
outer mass layers. We compute different properties of the MBH population hosted
in these satellites. We find that for the most part MBHs retain the original
mass, thus providing a clear indication of what the properties of the seeds
were. We derive the black hole occupation fraction (BHOF) of the satellite
population at z=0. MBHs generated as `massive seeds' have large masses that
would favour their identification, but their typical BHOF is always below 40
per cent and decreases to less than per cent for observed dwarf galaxy sizes.
In contrast, Population III remnants have a higher BHOF, but their masses have
not grown much since formation, inhibiting their detection.

text: We investigated the thermalization of dipole oscillations in confined systems via rare collisions, a process previously underappreciated in the context of quantum dissipative dynamics. Our theoretical framework employed a hybrid approach, combining the principles of quantum field theory and classical molecular dynamics to model the interactions between a confined system and its environment. We found that the rare collision mechanism plays a crucial role in determining the rate of thermalization, with the frequency of collisions exhibiting a non-monotonic dependence on the system's confinement strength. This non-intuitive behavior arises due to the interplay between the system's quantum coherence and the environment's classical fluctuations. Through a series of numerical simulations, we demonstrated that the thermalization rate can be significantly enhanced by introducing a small amount of quantum coherence into the system, thereby mitigating the effects of rare collisions. Our results suggest that the thermalization of dipole oscillations in confined systems is a complex process, influenced by the interplay between quantum coherence and classical fluctuations. The findings of this study have important implications for our understanding of quantum dissipative dynamics in confined systems, and highlight the need for a more nuanced approach to modeling rare collision mechanisms.
label: machine

text: Heavy X-ray obscuration is a common phenomenon observed in Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) with significant accretion disk obscuration. The advent of all-sky surveys, such as the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE), has enabled the discovery of new AGN populations, including those with the highest luminosities. In this study, we explore the X-ray properties of the most-luminous galaxies detected by WISE, using the XMM-Newton archive. We find that 45% of these galaxies exhibit significant X-ray absorption, with column densities NH up to 10^25 cm^-2. We identify two distinct classes of these obscured systems those with high X-ray luminosity and those with low X-ray luminosity. The former group shows signatures of ultrahigh obscuration, with high-ionization Fe Kalpha lines absent or significantly suppressed. We attribute this phenomenon to the presence of a geometrically thick torus or a highly Compton-thick circumnuclear medium. The latter group, on the other hand, exhibits weaker X-ray absorption and is possibly characterized by a less dense torus or a lower circumnuclear column density. We also find evidence for a correlation between the infrared luminosity and the X-ray column density, suggesting that the AGN's mid-infrared emission can serve as a powerful indicator of X-ray obscuration. Overall, our results highlight the importance of considering X-ray observations in the study of high-luminosity AGN discovered by all-sky surveys, and provide valuable insights into the physical properties of these enigmatic objects.
label: machine

text: We conducted an in-depth analysis of ground level enhancement (GLE) events associated with solar eruptions throughout Solar Cycle 23 to elucidate their distinguishing properties and underlying mechanisms. Our study, encompassing a total of 16 GLEs recorded during this period, ventures to address the intricate dynamics and solar parameters influencing such phenomena. Utilizing a comprehensive approach, we analyzed data from multiple observational platforms, including neutron monitor networks and solar observatories, to capture the magnitude and temporal evolution of these enhancements.  Our findings indicate a significant correlation between the intensity of GLEs and the characteristics of their associated solar eruptions, including coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and solar flares. We observed that a substantial proportion of GLE events coincided with fast and wide CMEs coupled with intense X-class flares, suggesting a synergistic effect in particle acceleration processes at the Sun. Through statistical analysis, we derived key patterns in the temporal onset and peak flux of GLEs, which consistently reflected the CMEs' transit characteristics.  Furthermore, our analysis highlights a pivotal role of CME-driven shock fronts and their magnetic reconnection regions in the acceleration of solar energetic particles to relativistic speeds. The insights garnered from these observations enhance our understanding of the space weather impacts of solar eruptions and inform predictive models of GLE occurrences. This study underscores the importance of interdisciplinary methodologies in unraveling the complexities of heliophysical phenomena and augments the scientific framework for future solar cycle predictions.
label: machine

text: In our investigation of epidemic centrality, we scrutinize the often-overlooked influence of peripheral nodes within complex networks. We present evidence that these nodes, typically dismissed as less critical in transmission dynamics, can subtly but significantly alter the course of an epidemic. By employing a hybrid methodology combining network theory, simulations, and case studies of recent outbreaks, we facilitate a comprehensive analysis of infection spread across both central and peripheral network structures.   Our results indicate that peripheral nodes, under certain conditions, serve as reservoirs or amplifiers for pathogens, notably during the early stages of an epidemic when central nodes may be sparsely populated. We observe an exponential increase in infection rates when peripheral nodes are integrated into targeted intervention strategies, highlighting their potential role in sustaining or even exacerbating epidemic outbreaks.   Furthermore, we develop a metric for evaluating epidemic centrality that considers not just the degree of connectivity but also the role of peripheral nodes in maintaining network robustness and resilience. Our findings urge public health policymakers to re-evaluate existing frameworks for epidemic response, emphasizing the necessity of including peripheral nodes in surveillance and intervention strategies. The implications of our work extend beyond theoretical constructs, providing a pragmatic lens through which to enhance epidemic preparedness and response efforts. Through this exploration, we contribute to a nuanced understanding of network dynamics, advocating for a more inclusive perspective on epidemic centrality that recognizes the critical role of peripheral nodes in public health.
label: machine

text: The Old Open Cluster NGC 188 is a metal-rich, 15-kiloparsec-wide, and 12-Gyr-old star cluster located in the constellation Lyra, offering a unique opportunity to study the evolution of stellar populations. This study focuses on the direct N-body modeling of NGC 188's binary star and blue straggler populations, comparing theoretical and observed results.   The objective of this research is to investigate the formation and evolution of binary stars and blue straggler stars within the cluster, shedding light on the complex interactions between these stellar components and the cluster's overall dynamics. To achieve this, a detailed N-body simulation is conducted using a modified version of the N-Body Simulation Toolkit (NBST).   The simulation incorporates various physical parameters, such as stellar masses, radii, and orbital parameters, as well as a range of initial conditions, including binary star and blue straggler populations. The results are compared to observations of NGC 188's binary star and blue straggler populations, which are derived from a combination of spectroscopic and photometric data.   Key findings indicate that the N-body simulation reproduces the observed characteristics of the binary star and blue straggler populations, including their frequency, orbital properties, and spatial distributions. The simulation also reveals that the formation of blue straggler stars is closely linked to the cluster's dynamical evolution, with the latter playing a crucial role in shaping the distribution of these stars.   The study's conclusions highlight the importance of N-body modeling in understanding the complex interactions between stellar components and the cluster's overall dynamics, and demonstrate the potential of NGC 188 as a valuable testing ground for theoretical models of stellar evolution and cluster formation.
label: machine

text: This research paper delves into the exploration of continuous tensegrities, innovative structures that rely on the balance between tension and compression without the need for continuous support. The objective of this study is to investigate the unique characteristics and potential applications of continuous tensegrities in various engineering fields.   Methodology involves a comprehensive review of existing literature on tensegrity structures, focusing on the evolution from discrete to continuous designs. Additionally, computer simulations and mathematical modeling are employed to analyze the structural behavior and optimization of continuous tensegrities.  Key findings highlight the advantages of continuous tensegrities, such as their adaptability to dynamic environments, lightweight construction, and potential for scalable design implementations. The study also reveals the challenges in practical applications, including complexity in fabrication and limited understanding of their long-term durability. text: In this study, we explore infinite-duration Poorman-bidding games, a class of strategic interactions characterized by non-terminating bid sequences and a shared pool of resources among players. We address the fundamental problem of determining optimal bid strategies that maximize individual payoffs while ensuring fair access to the pooled resources. Our key methodology involves formulating the game as an infinite Markov decision process, allowing us to analyze the long-term behaviors of players under varying competitive conditions.   We establish conditions under which players can converge to stable bidding behaviors, employing tools from stochastic dynamic programming and game theory. Through rigorous simulations and theoretical proofs, we demonstrate that players can achieve equilibrium strategies that not only enhance their individual rewards but also maintain a sustainable resource distribution among all competitors. Our results reveal that the potential for cooperation increases as the value of the resource pool rises and the bidding costs decrease, significantly influencing players' decision-making processes.  Furthermore, we identify critical parameters that dictate the success of various bidding strategies, providing insights into how alterations in these parameters can shift equilibrium dynamics. We conclude that our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of infinite-duration bidding scenarios and offer practical implications for resource allocation problems in competitive environments. Our work opens avenues for future research on adaptive strategies in dynamic bidding contexts, where player interactions evolve perpetually.

text: This research paper investigates the design and analysis of comparator circuits over finite bounded posets, which are fundamental components in digital circuits and decision-making processes. A poset is a partially ordered set, and finite bounded posets are a subclass of posets that have a finite number of elements and satisfy certain properties. Comparator circuits are digital circuits that compare two or more input signals and produce an output signal based on the comparison result.  The objective of this research is to develop efficient and effective comparator circuits over finite bounded posets, with a focus on minimizing the number of transistors and power consumption while maintaining a high accuracy in comparison results. To achieve this, we propose a novel design methodology that takes into account the properties of finite bounded posets and optimizes the circuit's architecture and gate-level implementation.  Our approach involves modeling finite bounded posets as a graph, where each node represents an element and each edge represents the order relation between two elements. We then use graph-based algorithms to find the optimal comparator circuit structure, which is achieved by identifying the minimum spanning tree of the graph. We also develop a new gate-level implementation technique that reduces the number of transistors and power consumption while maintaining the accuracy of the comparator circuit.  Our key findings show that the proposed design methodology can achieve significant reductions in transistor count and power consumption compared to existing comparator circuits. The results also demonstrate that the proposed comparator circuits can accurately compare signals in a wide range of applications, including digital logic circuits and machine learning algorithms. Overall, this research contributes to the development of efficient and effective comparator circuits over finite bounded posets, which can be used in a variety of digital and analog applications.

In the past few years, the number of OLAP applications increased quickly.
These applications use two significantly different DB structures:
multidimensional (MD) and table-based. One can show that the traditional model
of relational databases cannot make difference between these two structures.
Another model is necessary to make the differences visible. One of these is the
speed of the system. It can be proven that the multidimensional DB organization
results in shorter response times. And it is crucial, since a manager may
become impatient, if he or she has to wait say more than 20 seconds for the
next screen. On the other hand, we have to pay for the speed with a bigger DB
size. Why does the size of MD databases grow so quickly? The reason is the
sparsity of data: The MD matrix contains many empty cells. Efficient handling
of sparse matrices is indispensable in an OLAP application. One way to handle
sparsity is to take the structure closer to the table-based one. Thus the DB
size decreases, while the application gets slower. Therefore, other methods are
needed. This paper deals with the comparison of the two DB structures and the
limits of their usage. The new results of the paper: (1) It gives a
constructive proof that all relations can be represented in MD arrays. (2) It
also shows when the MD array representation is quicker than the table-based
one. (3) The MD representation results in smaller DB size under some
conditions. One such sufficient condition is proved in the paper. (4) A
variation of the single count header compression scheme is described with an
algorithm, which creates the compressed array from the ordered table without
materializing the uncompressed array. (5) The speed of the two different
database organizations is tested with experiments, as well. The tests are done
on benchmark as well as real life data. The experiments support the theoretical
results.

The present paper is devoted to the construction of a catalog of isolated
galaxy pairs from the Uppsala Galaxy Catalog (UGC), using accurate radial
velocities. The UGC lists 12921 galaxies to declination larger than -2 deg 30
min and is complete to an apparent diameter of 1 arcmin. The criteria used to
define the isolated galaxy pairs are the following: 1) Velocity criterion:
radial velocity difference between the members lower than 500 km/s; 2)
Interdistance criterion: projected distance between the members smaller than 1
Mpc; 3) Reciprocity criterion: each member is the closest galaxy to the other
one, which excludes multiplets; 4) Isolation information: the catalog lists the
ratio between the projected distance to the closest UGC galaxy (having a
velocity difference smaller than 500 km/s) and the pair members interdistance,
thus allowing one to choose any isolation criterion (beyond the chosen limit
2.5). In addition, we have accounted for the small diameter bias by searching
for CGCG galaxies in the pair environment and used the same isolation
criterion. A peculiar investigation has allowed to gather very accurate radial
velocities for pair members, from high quality HI and optical measurements
(median uncertainty on velocity differences 10 km/s). Our final catalog
contains 1005 galaxy pairs. Then we give some global properties of the pair
catalog. We display the histograms of the radial velocity differences between
the pair members and of their projected interdistances (median 0.29 Mpc).
Finally, we provide an estimate of the contamination by cosmological false
"pairs", which is about 10 percent up to a velocity difference of 380 km/s,
beyond which all pairs are probably false.

The extreme luminosities of hot, massive stars drive strong stellar winds
through UV line-scattering. For OB stars with an orbiting circumstellar disk,
we explore the effect of such line-scattering in ablating disk material,
initially focusing on the marginally optically thin decretion disks of
classical Oe and Be stars. For this we apply a multi-dimensional
radiation-hydrodynamics code, assuming optically thin ray tracing for the
stellar continuum and a multi-ray Sobolev treatment of the line transfer. This
accounts for desaturation of line-absorption by Keplerian shear in the disk,
and associated driving by non-radial photons. Results show dense,
intermediate-speed surface ablation, consistent with the strong, blue-shifted
absorption seen in UV wind lines of Be shell stars. The asymptotic ablation
rate is typically an order-unity factor times the stellar wind mass loss rate,
leading to disk destruction times of order months to years for Be disks,
consistent with observations. The much stronger radiative forces of O stars
reduce this time to order days, making sustaining a disk difficult, and so
providing a natural explanation for the rarity of Galactic Oe stars.
Additionally, the weakened line-driving at lower metallicity implies both a
reduction in the winds that help spin-down stars from near-critical rotation,
and in the ablation of decretion disks, thus providing a natural explanation
for the higher fraction of Classical Be stars, and the presence of Oe stars, in
the Magellanic Clouds. We conclude with a discussion of future extensions to
study line-driven ablation of denser, optically thick, accretion disks around
pre-main-sequence massive stars.
