It is known that the Karhunen-Lo\`{e}ve transform (KLT) of Gaussian
first-order auto-regressive (AR(1)) processes results in sinusoidal basis
functions. The same sinusoidal bases come out of the independent-component
analysis (ICA) and actually correspond to processes with completely independent
samples. In this paper, we relax the Gaussian hypothesis and study how
orthogonal transforms decouple symmetric-alpha-stable (S$\alpha$S) AR(1)
processes. The Gaussian case is not sparse and corresponds to $\alpha=2$, while
$0<\alpha<2$ yields processes with sparse linear-prediction error. In the
presence of sparsity, we show that operator-like wavelet bases do outperform
the sinusoidal ones. Also, we observe that, for processes with very sparse
increments ($0<\alpha\leq 1$), the operator-like wavelet basis is
indistinguishable from the ICA solution obtained through numerical
optimization. We consider two criteria for independence. The first is the
Kullback-Leibler divergence between the joint probability density function
(pdf) of the original signal and the product of the marginals in the
transformed domain. The second is a divergence between the joint pdf of the
original signal and the product of the marginals in the transformed domain,
which is based on Stein's formula for the mean-square estimation error in
additive Gaussian noise. Our framework then offers a unified view that
encompasses the discrete cosine transform (known to be asymptotically optimal
for $\alpha=2$) and Haar-like wavelets (for which we achieve optimality for
$0<\alpha\leq1$).

text:
Massive stars, possibly red supergiants, which retain extended hydrogen
envelopes until core collapse, produce Type II Plateau (IIP) supernovae. The
ejecta from these explosions shock the circumstellar matter originating from
the mass loss of the progenitor during the final phases of its life. This
interaction accelerates particles to relativistic energies which then lose
energy via synchrotron radiation in the shock-amplified magnetic fields and
inverse Compton scattering against optical photons from the supernova. These
processes produce different signatures in the radio and X-ray part of the
electromagnetic spectrum. Observed together, they allow us to break the
degeneracy between shock acceleration and magnetic field amplification. In this
work we use X-rays observations from the Chandra and radio observations from
the ATCA to study the relative importance of processes which accelerate
particles and those which amplify magnetic fields in producing the non-thermal
radiation from SN 2011ja. We use radio observations to constrain the explosion
date. Multiple Chandra observations allow us to probe the history of variable
mass loss from the progenitor. The ejecta expands into a low density bubble
followed by interaction with a higher density wind from a red supergiant
consistent with ZAMS mass greater than 16 solar masses. Our results suggest
that a fraction of type IIP supernovae may interact with circumstellar media
set up by non-steady winds.

text: We investigate the fabrication and characterization of sputtered titanium nitride (TiN) films for application in superconducting coplanar waveguide resonators (CPWRs). Our primary objective is to address the challenges associated with achieving high-quality superconducting films that enhance the performance of quantum circuits. We employ a systematic approach, utilizing reactive magnetron sputtering to produce TiN films with varying thicknesses and deposition parameters. Comprehensive analyses of the resulting films reveal key insights into their surface morphology, crystalline structure, and superconducting properties.  Our results indicate that optimized sputtering conditions lead to TiN films with significantly improved critical temperatures (T_c) and reduced surface roughness, which are crucial for minimizing losses in CPWRs. Specifically, we achieved T_c values approaching 10 K alongside an enhanced quality factor (Q-factor) in resonators fabricated with these films. Moreover, we utilize techniques such as X-ray diffraction and atomic force microscopy to elucidate the relationship between film characteristics and superconducting performance.  This work underscores the potential of sputtered TiN films as a viable alternative to traditional materials in the development of high-performance superconducting resonators. Our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge surrounding material engineering for quantum applications and pave the way for further exploration of TiN's capabilities in next-generation superconducting circuits. We conclude that the strategic tuning of sputtering parameters is imperative to harnessing the promise of TiN in superconductivity and advancing quantum technologies.

text: The Gaia mission aims to provide precise astrometric data across a wide range of stellar populations. Calibration of such data necessitates the accurate determination of stellar parameters, particularly the surface gravity (log g). This paper explores a subset of stars observed by both the Kepler and CoRoT missions to enhance Gaia's calibration processes. The objective is to utilize large datasets acquired from Kepler's and CoRoT's photometric observations to derive precise log g values, which can be integrated into Gaia's extensive stellar database. Our methodology involves cross-matching stars from Gaia DR3 with Kepler and CoRoT catalogues, followed by the implementation of asteroseismic techniques to extract reliable log g measurements. Subsequent statistical analyses were employed to ensure the robustness and precision of these values. Key findings reveal that, by leveraging asteroseismic data, we can achieve log g measurements with enhanced precision compared to conventional methods. This precision facilitates a more refined calibration for Gaia, particularly in dense star fields where traditional methods face limitations. Moreover, our research underlines the compatibility of Kepler and CoRoT data in bolstering the reliability of Gaia’s astrometric outputs. In conclusion, this study significantly contributes to the development of a substantial and precise dataset of calibration stars for the Gaia mission. The results foster greater accuracy in Gaia's measurements, ultimately aiding in the advancement of stellar astrophysics through improved parameter determination. The approach outlined here can serve as a model for maximizing the utility of multispectral astronomical data across varied celestial surveys.

text: We present the discovery of large-scale diffuse radio emission in the low-mass galaxy cluster Abell 1931, a finding that enhances our understanding of the interplay between galaxy clusters and their surrounding environments. Our investigation addresses the critical issue of how diffuse radio emission occurs in low-mass systems, challenging the previous assumption that such phenomena are primarily confined to more massive clusters. Utilizing a combination of high-sensitivity radio interferometry and deep optical imaging, we systematically analyzed the radio properties of Abell 1931, revealing a significant extension of the radio emission beyond individual galaxy contributions.   Our results indicate that the radio emission is likely associated with a population of non-thermal electrons energised by cluster mergers or interactions, providing a compelling case for the presence of a diffuse radio halo within the cluster. We employed advanced spectral analysis techniques to further investigate the emission's morphology and polarization characteristics, establishing a clear correlation with X-ray observations from existing datasets.   We propose a novel framework to interpret these findings, suggesting that the evolution of low-mass clusters may play a crucial role in the generation and maintenance of diffuse radio structures. This work not only expands the catalog of known diffuse sources but also underscores the importance of investigating less massive clusters in understanding cosmic magnetism and the large-scale structure of the universe. Our findings highlight the rich astrophysical processes occurring in low-mass galaxy clusters, paving the way for future studies aimed at uncovering the mechanisms driving radio emissions in various cosmic environments.

Background. One important ingredient for many applications of nuclear physics
to astrophysics, nuclear energy, and stockpile stewardship are cross sections
for reactions of neutrons with rare isotopes. Since direct measurements are
often not feasible, indirect methods, e.g. (d,p) reactions, should be used.
Those (d,p) reactions may be viewed as three-body reactions and described with
Faddeev techniques. Purpose. Faddeev equations in momentum space have a long
tradition of utilizing separable interactions in order to arrive at sets of
coupled integral equations in one variable. Optical potentials representing the
effective interactions in the neutron (proton) nucleus subsystem are usually
non-Hermitian as well as energy-dependent. Potential matrix elements as well as
transition matrix elements calculated with them must fulfill the reciprocity
theorem. The purpose of this paper is to introduce a separable,
energy-dependent representation of complex, energy-dependent optical potentials
that fulfill reciprocity exactly. Results. Starting from a separable,
energy-independent representation of global optical potentials based on a
generalization of the Ernst-Shakin-Thaler (EST) scheme, a further
generalization is needed to take into account the energy dependence.
Applications to n$+^{48}$Ca, n$+^{208}$Pb, and p$+^{208}$Pb are investigated
for energies from 0 to 50~MeV with special emphasis on fulfilling reciprocity.
Conclusions. We find that the energy-dependent separable representation of
complex, energy-dependent phenomenological optical potentials fulfills
reciprocity exactly. In addition, taking into account the explicit energy
dependence slightly improves the description of the $S$ matrix elements.

text: The relationship between star formation rate (SFR) and gas surface density (Σ_g) is a fundamental aspect of galactic astrophysics, particularly within the context of the Milky Way. This study aims to elucidate this relationship and assess its implications for extragalactic research. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset encompassing observed SFRs and gas surface densities across various regions of the Milky Way, we employed statistical analyses to derive a local SFR-Σ_g relation. Our findings reveal a power-law correlation characterized by a slope consistent with previous studies, thereby reinforcing the validity of the Kennicutt-Schmidt law in a Milky Way framework. Additionally, we investigated the effects of environmental factors such as metallicity and density variations on the SFR-Σ_g relationship, highlighting the importance of these parameters. Notably, our results indicate a threshold gas surface density beyond which star formation becomes significantly more efficient, prompting further exploration into the physical mechanisms driving this transition. These insights have profound implications for extragalactic studies, suggesting that the findings from our galaxy can serve as a baseline for understanding star formation processes in distant galaxies. By comparing the SFR-Σ_g relationship in the Milky Way with that of various extragalactic systems, we propose a refined model that incorporates the influence of cosmic environment and evolutionary history. Overall, this research enhances our comprehension of star formation dynamics and offers a critical framework for interpreting stellar formation in a broader cosmic context.

text: This study aims to distinguish between interacting dark energy and the standard cold dark matter (wCDM) model by utilizing a combination of cosmological data. The standard wCDM model assumes that dark energy is a non-interacting component of the universe, while interacting dark energy proposes that dark energy interacts with normal matter and radiation. The interplay between these two components can significantly affect the large-scale structure of the universe, the distribution of galaxies, and the properties of the cosmic microwave background (CMB).  Our analysis focuses on a suite of cosmological data, including CMB temperature and polarization maps, weak lensing measurements, and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) surveys. We use a Bayesian approach to constrain the parameters of both the wCDM and interacting dark energy models. By comparing the predictions of these models to the observed data, we can determine the likelihood of each model and assess the statistical significance of the differences between them.  Our results indicate that interacting dark energy models are able to provide a better fit to the CMB data than the standard wCDM model, particularly in the low multipoles. However, the difference is not significant enough to rule out the standard wCDM model. The BAO data and weak lensing measurements also provide constraints on the model parameters, but the results are more nuanced, with the interacting dark energy models able to provide a better fit to the data when combined with the CMB constraints. Overall, our analysis suggests that the standard wCDM model remains the most favored model, but the interacting dark energy models should not be ruled out without further evidence.

text: Quantum information storage is a critical aspect of advancing quantum computing technologies, particularly in the integration of quantum systems with electronic devices. This study investigates the storage of quantum information in a nanoelectronic device for an unprecedented duration of 30 seconds, addressing a significant hurdle in long-term information retention. The objective is to enhance coherence times while maintaining the practicality of nanoelectronic interfaces. We engineered a nanoelectronic device utilizing superconducting qubits, coupled with advanced error correction protocols to stabilize and protect the quantum state. The methodology involved cryogenic temperatures to minimize thermal noise, combined with optimized electronic circuitry to preserve qubit fidelity. Experimental setups included precise measurement techniques for tracking quantum state evolution and decoherence rates. Key findings reveal an extended coherence time of 30 seconds, representing a substantial improvement over previous benchmarks. The results highlight the effectiveness of our integrated approach, particularly the role of error mitigation strategies and coherent control mechanisms in sustaining quantum information. This achievement not only demonstrates the feasibility of long-duration quantum information storage but also provides insights into future architectural improvements for quantum devices. In conclusion, the study marks a significant step forward in bridging quantum mechanics and nanoelectronics, paving the way toward more robust and reliable quantum processing units. Further research could explore scalability and integration with existing electronic infrastructures to facilitate ubiquitous quantum computing applications.

Fast liquid jets, called micro-jets, are produced within cavitation bubbles
experiencing an aspherical collapse. Here we review micro-jets of different
origins, scales and appearances, and propose a unified framework to describe
their dynamics by using an anisotropy parameter $\zeta$, representing a
dimensionless measure of the liquid momentum at the collapse point (Kelvin
impulse). This parameter is rigorously defined for various jet drivers,
including gravity and nearby boundaries. Combining theoretical considerations
with hundreds of high-speed visualisations of bubbles collapsing near a rigid
surface, near a free surface or in variable gravity, we classify the jets into
three distinct regimes: weak, intermediate and strong. Weak jets
($\zeta<10^{-3}$) hardly pierce the bubble, but remain within it throughout the
collapse and rebound. Intermediate jets ($10^{-3}<\zeta<0.1$) pierce the
opposite bubble wall close to the last collapse phase and clearly emerge during
the rebound. Strong jets ($\zeta>0.1$) pierce the bubble early during the
collapse. The dynamics of the jets is analysed through key observables, such as
the jet impact time, jet speed, bubble displacement, bubble volume at jet
impact and vapour-jet volume. We find that, upon normalising these observables
to dimensionless jet parameters, they all reduce to straightforward functions
of $\zeta$, which we can reproduce numerically using potential flow theory. An
interesting consequence of this result is that a measurement of a single
observable, such as the bubble displacement, suffices to estimate any other
parameter, such as the jet speed. Remarkably, the dimensionless parameters of
intermediate and weak jets only depend on $\zeta$, not on the jet driver. In
the same regime, the jet parameters are found to be well approximated by
power-laws of $\zeta$, which we explain through analytical arguments.

text: We present our findings on the combination of searches for the Higgs boson utilizing the complete CDF data set. The aim of this study is to improve the sensitivity of detecting the elusive Higgs boson particle by merging various search channels. The primary problem this work addresses is the enhancement of the statistical power to detect the Higgs boson by integrating multiple analysis strategies.   Our study incorporates data from different search channels, including various decay modes and production mechanisms of the Higgs boson. By combining these searches, we aim to boost our chances of both discovering and precisely measuring the properties of the Higgs boson. Our approach involves merging the results from various search channels using statistical techniques to increase the overall significance of the observed signals.  Key ideas in our methodology include optimizing the combination of different search strategies to maximize sensitivity and enhance the statistical robustness of our results. By exploiting the full potential of the CDF data set through this comprehensive combination of search channels, we provide a more robust analysis framework for the detection of the Higgs boson. Our results demonstrate an improved capability for Higgs boson discovery and characterization, contributing to the broader understanding of particle physics phenomena.

text: This research investigates the formation and evolution of young, low-mass stars embedded within halos that contain a high concentration of dark matter particles. The study aims to understand how these unique environments influence stellar development by considering the gravitational dynamics and potential effects on star formation rates and stellar properties. Employing numerical simulations, the methodology involves modeling the initial conditions of dark matter halos, including their mass distribution and density profiles, alongside gas dynamics to simulate the formation of molecular clouds. The simulations then track the subsequent collapse and fragmentation of these clouds into protostellar cores, followed by the birth and evolution of low-mass stars.  Key findings indicate that the high concentration of dark matter particles significantly alters the structure and stability of halos, leading to more frequent and intense star formation episodes compared to regions with lower dark matter content. Additionally, the simulations reveal that stars formed in these dense dark matter halos exhibit differences in metallicity and rotation rates when compared to stars in less dense environments. The conclusion suggests that the presence of high-density dark matter halos can act as a catalyst for rapid star formation, influencing the chemical enrichment and kinematic properties of young stellar populations.

text: This study investigates the impact of compressive ratio on the dynamics of molecular-cloud turbulence, focusing on the phenomenon of supernova driving. The compressive ratio, a measure of the relative compression of a turbulent region, plays a crucial role in determining the efficiency of supernova driving. By analyzing high-resolution simulations of molecular clouds, we examine the effects of varying compressive ratios on the turbulent velocity, density, and magnetic field.  Our simulations reveal that a higher compressive ratio leads to an increase in turbulent velocity, which in turn enhances the driving of supernovae. However, the relationship between compressive ratio and supernova driving is nonlinear, and the optimal compressive ratio for maximum driving efficiency is found to be dependent on the specific simulation parameters. Furthermore, our results indicate that the magnetic field plays a significant role in modulating the compressive ratio and, subsequently, the supernova driving process.  The key findings of this study demonstrate that the compressive ratio is a critical parameter in determining the dynamics of molecular-cloud turbulence and the efficiency of supernova driving. Our results have important implications for our understanding of the role of turbulence in star formation and the impact of supernovae on the interstellar medium. The study also highlights the need for further research into the nonlinear relationships between compressive ratio, turbulent velocity, and supernova driving, and the importance of considering the effects of magnetic fields on these processes.

text: The emergence of luminous TeV blazars has significant implications for our understanding of the cosmos, particularly regarding the intergalactic magnetic field (IGMF) and the extragalactic gamma-ray background (EGB). This study aims to investigate the influence of plasma instabilities associated with these high-energy sources on both the IGMF and the EGB. We employ a multi-faceted approach combining observational data from contemporary gamma-ray telescopes and theoretical modeling of plasma physics within astrophysical contexts. Key findings indicate that the emissions from luminous TeV blazars can enhance local magnetic field fluctuations, potentially contributing to a more robust IGMF than previously estimated. Furthermore, the interaction of gamma rays with the cosmic microwave background leads to cascade emissions that significantly alter the observed EGB, implicating that traditional models may underestimate variability caused by these blazars. Our results suggest that the interplay between plasma instabilities and gamma-ray emissions fosters complex astrophysical environments that should be considered in future cosmological models. In conclusion, this research not only elucidates the roles of luminous TeV blazars in shaping the magnetic fields and gamma-ray backgrounds of the universe but also propels further investigation into other high-energy phenomena that may influence intergalactic conditions, thereby enriching our comprehension of cosmic evolution.

text: In this study, we investigate the potential optical counterpart of the pulsar PSR J1357-6429, which remains enigmatic due to its location and characteristics. Our primary objective is to identify and characterize any optical emissions associated with this pulsar to enhance our understanding of its physical properties and surrounding environment. We employ multi-band imaging techniques using the latest photometric instruments and analyze archival data from various observatories to build a comprehensive spectral profile of the region surrounding PSR J1357-6429.  Our results indicate a candidate optical counterpart that exhibits varying brightness across different wavelengths, suggesting a complex interaction between the pulsar’s wind and its surrounding medium. We observe a significant flux variation consistent with pulsar activity, and further spectral analysis reveals features that align with predictions for an optical signature linked to pulsar wind nebulae. We also explore the implications of these findings in the context of neutron star evolution and the interaction between pulsars and their environments.  Furthermore, we employ statistical methodologies to assess the likelihood of our candidate's association with PSR J1357-6429, utilizing advanced astrophysical models to evaluate the data against potential background sources. Our study contributes to the broader field of high-energy astrophysics by providing insights into the environments of pulsars and their optical emissions, fostering future observations and theoretical modeling efforts aimed at elucidating the nature of neutron stars and their interactions.

text: The opacity broadening of $^{13}$CO lineweights is a significant phenomenon that affects the interpretation of spectroscopic observations in astrophysical environments. Background radiation, dust, and other molecular species can interact with $^{13}$CO, leading to the broadening of its spectral lines and altering the measured lineweights. This broadening can, in turn, impact the variance-sonic Mach number relation, a critical parameter in understanding the dynamics of astrophysical flows.  The objective of this research is to investigate the opacity broadening of $^{13}$CO lineweights and its effects on the variance-sonic Mach number relation. We employ a combination of theoretical modeling and numerical simulations to explore the impact of opacity broadening on the measured lineweights and the subsequent effects on the variance-sonic Mach number relation.  Our results indicate that opacity broadening can significantly alter the measured lineweights of $^{13}$CO, leading to a substantial change in the variance-sonic Mach number relation. We find that the broadening of lineweights results in a non-linear relationship between the variance and Mach number, which can be misinterpreted as a linear relationship if opacity broadening is not accounted for. Our findings highlight the importance of considering opacity broadening when analyzing spectroscopic observations in astrophysical environments.  The implications of our research are significant, as they have far-reaching consequences for our understanding of astrophysical flows and the interpretation of spectroscopic data. By accounting for opacity broadening, we can improve the accuracy of our measurements and gain a deeper understanding of the dynamics of astrophysical systems.

text:
A/B testing is ubiquitous within the machine learning and data science
operations of internet companies. Generically, the idea is to perform a
statistical test of the hypothesis that a new feature is better than the
existing platform---for example, it results in higher revenue. If the p value
for the test is below some pre-defined threshold---often, 0.05---the new
feature is implemented. The difficulty of choosing an appropriate threshold has
been noted before, particularly because dependent tests are often done
sequentially, leading some to propose control of the false discovery rate (FDR)
rather than use of a single, universal threshold. However, it is still
necessary to make an arbitrary choice of the level at which to control FDR.
Here we suggest a decision-theoretic approach to determining whether to adopt a
new feature, which enables automated selection of an appropriate threshold. Our
method has the basic ingredients of any decision-theory problem: a loss
function, action space, and a notion of optimality, for which we choose Bayes
risk. However, the loss function and the action space differ from the typical
choices made in the literature, which has focused on the theory of point
estimation. We give some basic results for Bayes-optimal thresholding rules for
the feature adoption decision, and give some examples using eBay data. The
results suggest that the 0.05 p-value threshold may be too conservative in some
settings, but that its widespread use may reflect an ad-hoc means of
controlling multiplicity in the common case of repeatedly testing variants of
an experiment when the threshold is not reached.

text: This study investigates the feasibility of determining open-cluster parameters, including age, distance, and metallicity, solely from BVRI photometry. Open clusters are crucial for understanding the formation and evolution of galaxies, and determining their parameters is essential for accurate stellar evolution models and cosmological studies. However, current methods often rely on spectroscopic data, which can be time-consuming and labor-intensive.  The objective of this research is to explore the potential of BVRI photometry as a substitute for spectroscopic data in determining open-cluster parameters. We employed a comprehensive analysis of 12 open clusters with well-established spectroscopic parameters, using a combination of Bayesian inference and machine learning algorithms to estimate age, distance, and metallicity from their BVRI light curves.  Our results show that BVRI photometry can provide accurate estimates of open-cluster parameters, with a median error of 10% for age, 15% for distance, and 5% for metallicity. The performance of our method is comparable to that of spectroscopic methods, and we demonstrate that it can be applied to a wide range of open clusters with varying properties.  This study has significant implications for the field of astrophysics, as it provides a novel and efficient approach to determining open-cluster parameters from photometric data. Our findings suggest that BVRI photometry can be a valuable tool for future studies, enabling researchers to explore the properties of open clusters in greater detail and with greater precision.

text:
The applications of machine learning techniques to chemistry and materials
science become more numerous by the day. The main challenge is to devise
representations of atomic systems that are at the same time complete and
concise, so as to reduce the number of reference calculations that are needed
to predict the properties of different types of materials reliably. This has
led to a proliferation of alternative ways to convert an atomic structure into
an input for a machine-learning model. We introduce an abstract definition of
chemical environments that is based on a smoothed atomic density, using a
bra-ket notation to emphasize basis set independence and to highlight the
connections with some popular choices of representations for describing atomic
systems. The correlations between the spatial distribution of atoms and their
chemical identities are computed as inner products between these feature kets,
which can be given an explicit representation in terms of the expansion of the
atom density on orthogonal basis functions, that is equivalent to the smooth
overlap of atomic positions (SOAP) power spectrum, but also in real space,
corresponding to $n$-body correlations of the atom density. This formalism lays
the foundations for a more systematic tuning of the behavior of the
representations, by introducing operators that represent the correlations
between structure, composition, and the target properties. It provides a
unifying picture of recent developments in the field and indicates a way
forward towards more effective and computationally affordable machine-learning
schemes for molecules and materials.

text:
Mochon's proof [Moc07] of existence of quantum weak coin flipping with
arbitrarily small bias is a fundamental result in quantum cryptography, but at
the same time one of the least understood. Though used several times as a black
box in important follow-up results [Gan09, CK09, AS10, CK11, KZ13] the result
has not been peer-reviewed, its novel techniques (and in particular Kitaev's
point game formalism) have not been applied anywhere else, and an explicit
protocol is missing. We believe that truly understanding the existence proof
and the novel techniques it relies on would constitute a major step in quantum
information theory, leading to deeper understanding of entanglement and of
quantum protocols in general. In this work, we make a first step in this
direction. We simplify parts of Mochon's construction considerably, making
about 20 pages of analysis in the original proof superfluous, clarifying some
other parts of the proof on the way, and presenting the proof in a way which is
conceptually easier to grasp. We believe the resulting proof of existence is
easier to understand, more readable, and certainly verifiable. Moreover, we
analyze the resources needed to achieve a bias $\epsilon$ and show that the
number of qubits is $O(\log 1/\epsilon)$, while the number of rounds is
$(1/\epsilon)^{O(1/\epsilon)}$. A true understanding of the proof, including
Kitaev's point game techniques and their applicability, as well as completing
the task of constructing an explicit (and also simpler and more efficient)
protocol, are left to future work.

text:
Variational approaches to data assimilation, and weakly constrained four
dimensional variation (WC-4DVar) in particular, are important in the
geosciences but also in other communities (often under different names). The
cost functions and the resulting optimal trajectories may have a probabilistic
interpretation, for instance by linking data assimilation with Maximum
Aposteriori (MAP) estimation. This is possible in particular if the unknown
trajectory is modelled as the solution of a stochastic differential equation
(SDE), as is increasingly the case in weather forecasting and climate
modelling. In this case, the MAP estimator (or "most probable path" of the SDE)
is obtained by minimising the Onsager--Machlup functional. Although this fact
is well known, there seems to be some confusion in the literature, with the
energy (or "least squares") functional sometimes been claimed to yield the most
probable path. The first aim of this paper is to address this confusion and
show that the energy functional does not, in general, provide the most probable
path. The second aim is to discuss the implications in practice. Although the
mentioned results pertain to stochastic models in continuous time, they do have
consequences in practice where SDE's are approximated by discrete time schemes.
It turns out that using an approximation to the SDE and calculating its most
probable path does not necessarily yield a good approximation to the most
probable path of the SDE proper. This suggest that even in discrete time, a
version of the Onsager--Machlup functional should be used, rather than the
energy functional, at least if the solution is to be interpreted as a MAP
estimator.

text:
Models of gravitational waveforms play a critical role in detecting and
characterizing the gravitational waves (GWs) from compact binary coalescences.
Waveforms from numerical relativity (NR), while highly accurate, are too
computationally expensive to produce to be directly used with Bayesian
parameter estimation tools like Markov-chain-Monte-Carlo and nested sampling.
We propose a Gaussian process regression (GPR) method to generate accurate
reduced-order-model waveforms based only on existing accurate (e.g. NR)
simulations. Using a training set of simulated waveforms, our GPR approach
produces interpolated waveforms along with uncertainties across the parameter
space. As a proof of concept, we use a training set of IMRPhenomD waveforms to
build a GPR model in the 2-d parameter space of mass ratio $q$ and
equal-and-aligned spin $\chi_1=\chi_2$. Using a regular, equally-spaced grid of
120 IMRPhenomD training waveforms in $q\in[1,3]$ and $\chi_1 \in [-0.5,0.5]$,
the GPR mean approximates IMRPhenomD in this space to mismatches below
$4.3\times 10^{-5}$. Our approach can alternatively use training waveforms
directly from numerical relativity. Beyond interpolation of waveforms, we also
present a greedy algorithm that utilizes the errors provided by our GPR model
to optimize the placement of future simulations. In a fiducial test case we
find that using the greedy algorithm to iteratively add simulations achieves
GPR errors that are $\sim 1$ order of magnitude lower than the errors from
using Latin-hypercube or square training grids.

text: In this study, we investigate the complex outflow structure observed in Barnard 5-IRS 1, focusing on the transition from a collimated jet to a wide-angle outflow. Through detailed analysis of infrared continuum images and polarized light maps, we have identified a distinctive "spider-like" feature emanating from the central source. This morphology suggests a significant change in the outflow's geometry, transitioning from a narrow jet to a broader outflow. Our findings indicate that the observed spider-like outflow is characterized by a series of radial extensions emanating from the central region, which may represent the expansion of a previously confined jet into a more diffuse medium. We propose that this transformation is driven by changes in the magnetic field configuration and the interaction between the jet and the surrounding interstellar medium. Our key methodology involves high-resolution imaging and modeling techniques to analyze the kinematics and dynamics of the outflow components. These results contribute to our understanding of the evolutionary stages in protostellar environments and the mechanisms governing the transition from collimated jets to wider outflows.

text: We present a novel continuum Poisson-Boltzmann model to simulate the behavior of membrane channel proteins, a class of proteins that play a crucial role in regulating ion and water transport across cellular membranes. Our model, which combines the strengths of continuum and discrete approaches, enables the simulation of complex membrane channel protein dynamics and interactions with surrounding solutes and membranes.  Through a series of numerical experiments, we demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of our model in capturing key features of membrane channel protein behavior, including ion selectivity, gating kinetics, and protein-ligand interactions. Our results show that the model is able to reproduce the experimentally observed behavior of a wide range of membrane channel proteins, including K+ and Na+ channels, and Ca2+ channels.  Our model is based on a combination of the Poisson-Boltzmann equation and a continuum description of membrane channel protein dynamics. We use a novel finite element method to discretize the membrane surface, allowing for the simulation of complex protein-ligand interactions and membrane channel protein dynamics. Our approach also incorporates a machine learning-based optimization scheme to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the model.  The key findings of our study highlight the potential of continuum Poisson-Boltzmann models for simulating membrane channel protein behavior, and demonstrate the importance of considering the interactions between membrane channel proteins and surrounding solutes and membranes in understanding their function.

text:
We study the propagation of finite bubbles in a Hele-Shaw channel, where a
centred occlusion (termed a rail) is introduced to provide a small
axially-uniform depth constriction. For bubbles wide enough to span the
channel, the system's behaviour is similar to that of semi-infinite fingers and
a symmetric static solution is stable. Here, we focus on smaller bubbles, in
which case the symmetric static solution is unstable and the static bubble is
displaced towards one of the deeper regions of the channel on either side of
the rail. Using a combination of experiments and numerical simulations of a
depth-averaged model, we show that a bubble propagating axially due to a small
imposed flow rate can be stabilised in a steady symmetric mode centred on the
rail through a subtle interaction between stabilising viscous forces and
destabilising surface tension forces. However, for sufficiently large capillary
numbers Ca, the ratio of viscous to surface tension forces, viscous forces in
turn become destabilising thus returning the bubble to an off-centred
propagation regime. With decreasing bubble size, the range of Ca for which
steady centred propagation is stable decreases, and eventually vanishes through
the coalescence of two supercritical pitchfork bifurcations. The depth-averaged
model is found to accurately predict all the steady modes of propagation
observed experimentally, and provides a comprehensive picture of the underlying
steady bifurcation structure. However, for sufficiently large imposed flow
rates, we find that initially centred bubbles do not converge onto a steady
mode of propagation. Instead they transiently explore weakly unstable steady
modes, an evolution which results in their break-up and eventual settling into
a steady propagating state of changed topology.

text:
In this paper, we show that all real zeros of the bilateral Hurwitz zeta
function $Z(s,a):=\zeta (s,a) + \zeta (s,1-a)$ with $1/4 \le a \le 1/2$ are on
only the non-positive even integers exactly same as in the case of $(2^s-1)
\zeta (s)$. We also prove that all real zeros of the bilateral periodic zeta
function $P(s,a):={\rm{Li}}_s (e^{2\pi ia}) + {\rm{Li}}_s (e^{2\pi i(1-a)})$
with $1/4 \le a \le 1/2$ are on only the negative even integers just like
$\zeta (s)$. Moreover, we show that all real zeros of the quadrilateral zeta
function $Q(s,a):=Z(s,a) + P(s,a)$ with $1/4 \le a \le 1/2$ are on only the
negative even integers. On the other hand, we prove that $Z(s,a)$, $P(s,a)$ and
$Q(s,a)$ have at least one real zero in $(0,1)$ when $0<a<1/2$ is sufficiently
small. The complex zeros of these zeta functions are also discussed when $1/4
\le a \le 1/2$ is rational or transcendental. As a corollary, we show that
$Q(s,a)$ with rational $1/4 < a < 1/3$ or $1/3 < a < 1/2$ does not satisfy the
analogue of the Riemann hypothesis even though $Q(s,a)$ satisfies the
functional equation that appeared in Hamburger's or Hecke's theorem and all
real zeros of $Q(s,a)$ are located at only the negative even integers again as
in the case of $\zeta (s)$.

We show that suprathermal particles, termed pick-up ions (PUIs), might reduce
the postshock temperature of the fast wind and jets in some planetary nebulae
(PNs) and in symbiotic systems. The goal is to explain the finding that the
temperature of the hot bubble formed by the post-shock gas in some PNs and
symbiotic nebulae is lower, sometimes by more than an order of magnitude, than
the value expected from simple hydrodynamical calculations. Although various
explanations have been proposed, there is as yet no prefered solution for this
low tempeature problem. PUIs have been invoked to explain the low temperature
behind the termination shock of the solar wind. While in the case of the solar
wind the neutral atoms that turn into PUIs penetrate the pre-shock solar wind
region from the interstellar medium (ISM), in PNs the PUI source is more likely
slowly moving clumps embedded in the fast wind or jets. These clumps are formed
by instabilities or from backflowing cold gas. Our estimates indicate that in
young PNs these PUIs will thermalize before leaving the system. Only in older
PNs whose sizes exceed ~5000 AU and for which the fast-wind mass loss rate is
below ~10^{-7} Mo/yr do we expect the PUIs to be an efficient carrier of energy
out of the postshock region (the hot bubble).

The popularity of touchscreen phones has been growing around the world since
the iPhones and Android phones were released. More and more mobile phones with
large touchscreen have been produced, however, the phones with small size
displays are still in the majority of touch phones. The foremost interface on
touch smartphones is the information input module using soft keyboards.
Traditional input methods on touch phones have either too small key buttons
(such as QWERTY) or too many functions (such as 3$\times$4 keyboard), which are
inconvenient to use. Moreover, the conventional soft keyboards only use tapping
to input texts while current touch smartphones allow various gestures on the
touchscreen, such as sliding. In this paper, a novel soft keyboard called QWERT
is proposed for touchscreen-based smartphones. The users can interact with
phones via finger gestures of tapping or sliding when input text by using the
QWERT. In doing so, the interactions between users and smartphones will be
faster and easier. An experiment carried out on inexperienced human subjects
shows that they can learn very fast due to their familiarities with QWERTY. A
simulation experiment based on a cognitive architecture, ACT-R, was also
conducted to predict the movement time (MT) of experienced human subjects. The
simulation results show that the MT using QWERT outperforms other default
keyboards. These outcomes imply that the novel QWERT is a viable option for
touch smartphone users. Based on the novel design, an application is released
on Android systems. This application is expected to give better user experience
for customers who use touch smartphones.

text: Functional data analysis has gained popularity in various fields due to its ability to model data as curves or functions. Quantile functional regression is a powerful tool that extends functional data analysis to study the relationship between functional predictors and scalar responses at specific quantiles. This research paper aims to explore the application of quantile functional regression using Quantlets, which are small functional algorithms in R.   The methodology involves fitting quantile functional regression models using Quantlets to analyze datasets with functional predictors and scalar responses. The key findings reveal the flexibility and effectiveness of quantile functional regression in capturing non-linear relationships and heteroscedasticity in the data. Moreover, the results demonstrate the utility of Quantlets in implementing sophisticated functional regression techniques efficiently.  In conclusion, this study highlights the significance of quantile functional regression for analyzing complex data structures where traditional regression methods may fall short. The integration of Quantlets in this framework provides a user-friendly approach for researchers and practitioners to utilize these advanced statistical tools. Overall, this research contributes to advancing the understanding and application of quantile functional regression in various fields of research.

text:
Adding noise to a sensory signal generally decreases human performance.
However noise can improve performance too, due to a process called stochastic
resonance (SR). This paradoxical effect may be exploited in psychophysical
experiments, to provide additional insights into how the sensory system deals
with noise. Here, I develop a model for stochastic resonance to study the
influence of noise on human perception, in which the biological parameter of
`lapse rate' was included. I show that the inclusion of lapse rate allows for
the occurrence of stochastic resonance in terms of the performance metric d'.
At the same time, I show that high levels of lapse rate cause stochastic
resonance to disappear. It is also shown that noise generated in the brain
(i.e., internal noise) may obscure any effect of stochastic resonance in
experimental settings. I further relate the model to a standard equivalent
noise model, the linear amplifier model, and show that the lapse rate can
function to scale the threshold versus noise (TvN) curve, similar to the
efficiency parameter in equivalent noise (EN) models. Therefore, lapse rate
provides a psychophysical explanation for reduced efficiency in EN paradigms.
Furthermore, I note that ignoring lapse rate may lead to an overestimation of
internal noise in equivalent noise paradigms. Overall, describing stochastic
resonance in terms of signal detection theory, with the inclusion of lapse
rate, may provide valuable new insights into how human performance depends on
internal and external noise.

text: This research paper proposes a novel approach to comparing street maps, focusing on path-based distance as a key metric. The widespread use of street maps in navigation systems, mapping applications, and urban planning has highlighted the need for efficient and accurate comparison methods. Current approaches often rely on pixel-based or vector-based distance metrics, which may not effectively capture the complexities of real-world streets.  The objective of this study is to develop a path-based distance metric that accounts for the topological and spatial relationships between streets, enabling more accurate and informative comparisons of street maps. A path-based distance metric is defined as the minimum distance between two paths, taking into account the order of nodes and the presence of obstacles. The proposed metric is evaluated using a large-scale dataset of street maps, which includes various types of roads, intersections, and land uses.  The methodology employed in this study involves the development of a graph-based representation of street networks, which is used to compute the path-based distance between two maps. The algorithm is designed to handle large-scale datasets and is optimized for performance. The results show that the proposed path-based distance metric outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and efficiency, particularly in cases where street maps exhibit complex topological relationships.  The key findings of this study have significant implications for the development of more accurate and informative street map comparison systems. The proposed path-based distance metric can be used to evaluate the similarity between street maps, identify differences in road networks, and support urban planning and transportation decision-making. Overall, this research contributes to the advancement of street map comparison techniques, enabling more effective use of street maps in a wide range of applications.

text: This study presents a suite of fast dynamic graph algorithms designed to efficiently solve parameterized problems on evolving graphs. The primary focus is on developing algorithms that can adapt quickly to changes in graph structure while maintaining optimal time complexity. We tackle the problem of finding minimum dominating sets and vertex covers, which are fundamental in graph theory and have applications in various fields such as network security and bioinformatics. Our approach involves integrating classic graph algorithms with data structures tailored for dynamic updates. Specifically, we introduce a novel dynamic data structure that supports edge insertions and deletions in nearly linear time relative to the current graph size. Through rigorous analysis, we demonstrate that our algorithms achieve significant improvements over static methods, especially in scenarios where the graph topology frequently changes. Key methodologies include amortized analysis to handle repeated updates and efficient update operations that minimize overhead. The results show substantial speedups compared to previous dynamic algorithms, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach in real-time processing environments.

text: We investigate the Higgs inflationary scenario within the framework of Gauss-Bonnet braneworld, a higher-dimensional theory that incorporates gravity and extra dimensions. By employing the conformal truncation method, we derive a consistent and consistent cosmological action for the Higgs inflationary model. Our approach enables us to study the dynamics of the Higgs field in the context of braneworld gravity, providing a novel understanding of the interplay between gravity and the Higgs sector.  We explore the implications of the Gauss-Bonnet term on the Higgs inflationary landscape, revealing potential constraints on the Higgs mass and the inflaton coupling. Our analysis demonstrates that the Gauss-Bonnet term can significantly impact the Higgs inflationary dynamics, potentially leading to a more robust and consistent model. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of the Gauss-Bonnet term on the reheating process, highlighting its potential impact on the cosmic microwave background radiation and the abundance of light elements.  Our results indicate that the Higgs inflationary scenario in the context of Gauss-Bonnet braneworld exhibits a rich phenomenological landscape, with potential implications for the early universe. We discuss the implications of our findings for the Higgs inflationary model, highlighting the need for further investigation into the interplay between gravity and the Higgs sector. Our work provides a foundation for future studies, enabling researchers to explore the intersection of braneworld gravity and Higgs inflation in greater detail.

text:
The recurring context in which objects appear holds valuable information that
can be employed to predict their existence. This intuitive observation indeed
led many researchers to endow appearance-based detectors with explicit
reasoning about context. The underlying thesis suggests that stronger
contextual relations would facilitate greater improvements in detection
capacity. In practice, however, the observed improvement in many cases is
modest at best, and often only marginal. In this work we seek to improve our
understanding of this phenomenon, in part by pursuing an opposite approach.
Instead of attempting to improve detection scores by employing context, we
treat the utility of context as an optimization problem: to what extent can
detection scores be improved by considering context or any other kind of
additional information? With this approach we explore the bounds on improvement
by using contextual relations between objects and provide a tool for
identifying the most helpful ones. We show that simple co-occurrence relations
can often provide large gains, while in other cases a significant improvement
is simply impossible or impractical with either co-occurrence or more precise
spatial relations. To better understand these results we then analyze the
ability of context to handle different types of false detections, revealing
that tested contextual information cannot ameliorate localization errors,
severely limiting its gains. These and additional insights further our
understanding on where and why utilization of context for object detection
succeeds and fails.

text:
The subject of this paper is an optimal consumption/optimal portfolio problem
with transaction costs and with multiple risky assets.
  In our model the transaction costs take a special form in that transaction
costs on purchases of one of the risky assets (the endowed asset) are infinite,
and transaction costs involving the other risky assets are zero. Effectively,
the endowed asset can only be sold. In general, multi-asset optional
consumption/optimal portfolio problems are very challenging, but the extra
structure we introduce allows us to make significant progress towards an
analytical solution.
  For an agent with CRRA utility we completely characterise the different types
of optimal behaviours. These include always selling the entire holdings of the
endowed asset immediately, selling the endowed asset whenever the ratio of the
value of the holdings of the endowed asset to other wealth gets above a
critical ratio, and selling the endowed asset only when other wealth is zero.
This characterisation is in terms of solutions of a boundary crossing problem
for a first order ODE. The technical contribution is to show that the problem
of solving the HJB equation, which is a second order, non-linear PDE subject to
smooth fit at an unknown free boundary, can be reduced to this much simpler
problem involving an explicit first order ODE. This technical contribution is
at the heart of our analytical and numerical results, and allows us to prove
monotonicity of the critical exercise threshold and the certainty equivalent
value in the model parameters.

text: In this two-part study, we develop and analyze a novel hybrid discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) method for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations (INSE) with relaxed H(div)-conformity. The proposed HDG formulation represents a significant advancement in the field of HDG methods for incompressible flows as it offers both stability and accuracy, even in the presence of large jumps in the fluid velocity across inter-element boundaries.  We begin with an overview of the traditional HDG approach for incompressible flows, identifying its limitations in terms of stabilizing the pressure degrees of freedom without compromising the discretization's overall accuracy. We then introduce our relaxed H(div)-conformity method, which retains the desired accuracy by incorporating a local L2 pressure correction term. This modification ensures the method is both stable and efficient, particularly when dealing with complex geometries and large jumps in the solution.  In Part I of this work, we establish the underlying mathematical framework for our method, including its weak and strong forms, and derive the stability conditions and error estimates. We also provide numerical examples that demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, demonstrating a significant reduction in pressure oscillations compared to the standard HDG method for INSE. Furthermore, we discuss some practical aspects of our method, such as its implementation on various parallel architectures and its sensitivity to time-step sizes. The results presented in Part I pave the way for a thorough comparison with existing methods in Part II and serve as a foundation for future studies in the field of HDG methods for incompressible flows.

text:
We perform a detailed theoretical-experimental study of the dynamical
decoupling (DD) of the nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond. We investigate
the DD sequences applied to suppress the dephasing of the electron spin of the
NV center induced by the coupling to a spin bath composed of the substitutional
nitrogen atoms. The decoupling efficiency of various DD schemes is studied,
including both periodic and periodic pulse sequences. For ideal control pulses,
we find that the DD protocols with the Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) timing
of the pulses provides best performance. We show that, as the number of control
pulses increases, the decoupling fidelity scaling differs qualitatively from
the predictions of the Magnus expansion, and explain the origin of this
difference. In particular, more advanced symmetrized or concatenated protocols
do not improve the DD performance. Next, we investigate the impact of the
systematic instrumental pulse errors in different periodic and aperiodic pulse
sequences. The DD protocols with the single-axis control do not preserve all
spin components in the presence of the pulse errors, and the two-axis control
is needed. We demonstrate that the two-axis control sequence with the CPMG
timing is very robust with respect to the pulse errors. The impact of the pulse
errors can be diminished further by symmetrizing this protocol. For all
protocols studied here, we present a detailed account of the pulse error
parameters which make strongest impact on the DD performance. In conclusion, we
give specific recommendations about choosing the decoupling protocol for the
system under investigation.

text:
In this paper we search for distant massive companions to known transiting
gas giant planets that may have influenced the dynamical evolution of these
systems. We present new radial velocity observations for a sample of 51 planets
obtained using the Keck HIRES instrument, and find statistically significant
accelerations in fifteen systems. Six of these systems have no previously
reported accelerations in the published literature: HAT-P-10, HAT-P-22,
HAT-P-29, HAT-P-32, WASP-10, and XO-2. We combine our radial velocity fits with
Keck NIRC2 adaptive optics (AO) imaging data to place constraints on the
allowed masses and orbital periods of the companions responsible for the
detected accelerations. The estimated masses of the companions range between
1-500 M_Jup, with orbital semi-major axes typically between 1-75 AU. A
significant majority of the companions detected by our survey are constrained
to have minimum masses comparable to or larger than those of the transiting
planets in these systems, making them candidates for influencing the orbital
evolution of the inner gas giant. We estimate a total occurrence rate of 51 +/-
10% for companions with masses between 1-13 M_Jup and orbital semi-major axes
between 1-20 AU in our sample. We find no statistically significant difference
between the frequency of companions to transiting planets with misaligned or
eccentric orbits and those with well-aligned, circular orbits. We combine our
expanded sample of radial velocity measurements with constraints from transit
and secondary eclipse observations to provide improved measurements of the
physical and orbital characteristics of all of the planets included in our
survey.

text: The infrared channel of the Spitzer Space Telescope's InfraRed Array Camera (IRAC) was utilized to explore the sparse phase curve of the exoplanet WASP-14b. This gas giant planet, located in the WASP-14 system, orbits its host star every 4.9 days, inducing substantial thermal emission variations. IRAC's long wavelength channels (3.6-8.0 μm) were employed to gather data at 69 unique phase angles. Our study aimed to investigate the thermal structure and radiation properties of WASP-14b by analyzing its sparse phase curve.  Data analysis commenced with removing instrumental noise and calibration errors, followed by correction for contamination from the host star. To model the planetary emission, the method of Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) was employed, accounting for both temporal and spatial correlations. Results revealed a pronounced peak in the 3.6 μm channel at the full phase, while 8.0 μm displayed a steady decrease in emissions as the planet traversed its orbit. We attributed this discrepancy to the presence of thermally emissive condensates and the varying temperature contrasts between the day and night hemispheres.  Our research contributes to the ongoing understanding of exoplanet thermal properties by examining the IRAC sparse phase curve of WASP-14b. These findings suggest intriguing implications for the atmospheric composition and dynamic processes of this gaseous world, offering a foundation for future investigations.
label: machine

text: We present the results of a comprehensive analysis of the spectral energy distributions and radio continuum spectra of northern extragalactic radio sources, as part of the Planck early results. Our investigation aimed to shed light on the physical properties of these distant objects, which are believed to be active galactic nuclei, quasars, or blazars. By analyzing the data from the Planck satellite, we have obtained a set of high-quality spectra for 1,300 extragalactic radio sources, spanning the frequency range from 30 GHz to 857 GHz. Our analysis reveals a clear separation between the radio-loud and radio-quiet objects, with the former exhibiting a more complex spectral energy distribution and a stronger radio continuum emission. We also observe a significant correlation between the radio luminosity and the X-ray luminosity of the sources, suggesting a common physical mechanism driving these phenomena. Furthermore, our results indicate that the radio continuum spectra of these objects can be accurately described by a power-law model, with a typical spectral index of -0.8. These findings provide valuable insights into the physical processes governing the emission of radio and X-ray radiation from distant active galactic nuclei, and have important implications for our understanding of the interplay between the central black hole and the surrounding accretion disk.

text: We report the results of a multi-wavelength analysis investigating the possibility of annihilating dark matter as the origin of the gamma-ray emission from the Andromeda galaxy, M31. Through a comprehensive examination of archival data from the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope, we observed a significant correlation between the gamma-ray emission and the distribution of dark matter within the galaxy. Our analysis revealed a distinctive signature of annihilating dark matter particles, characterized by a characteristic gamma-ray spectrum and a spatial distribution consistent with the predicted annihilation zone.  We attempted to replicate the results using various dark matter models and simulations, including the WIMP (Weakly Interacting Massive Particle) model and the Sterile Neutrino model. However, none of these models were able to reproduce the observed gamma-ray emission. Instead, we found that a novel dark matter model, which incorporates a new type of dark matter particle with a unique annihilation signature, provided a satisfactory fit to the data. This model, which we term "Annihilating Dark Matter with a Non-Standard Annihilation Process" (ADMN), predicts a characteristic gamma-ray spectrum and spatial distribution that is consistent with the observed emission from M31.  Our results provide strong evidence for the existence of annihilating dark matter as the origin of the gamma-ray emission from M31. The ADMN model offers a new perspective on the nature of dark matter and provides a promising lead for future research into the properties of dark matter particles.

text:
Using idealised N-body simulations of a Milky Way-sized disc galaxy, we
qualitatively study how the metallicity distributions of the thin disc star
particles are modified by the formation of the bar and spiral arm structures.
The thin disc in our numerical experiments initially has a tight negative
radial metallicity gradient and a constant vertical scale-height. We show that
the radial mixing of stars drives a positive vertical metallicity gradient in
the thin disc. On the other hand, if the initial thin disc is flared, with
vertical scale-height increasing with galactocentric radius, the metal poor
stars originally in the outer disc become dominant in regions above the disc
plane at every radii. This process can drive a negative vertical metallicity
gradient, which is consistent with the current observed trend. This model
mimics a scenario where the star-forming thin disc was flared in the outer
region at earlier epochs. Our numerical experiment with an initial flared disc
predicts that the negative vertical metallicity gradient of the mono-age
relatively young thin disc population should be steeper in the inner disc, and
the radial metallicity gradient of the mono-age population should be shallower
at greater heights above the disc plane. We also predict that the metallicity
distribution function of mono-age young thin disc populations above the disc
plane would be more positively skewed in the inner disc compared to the outer
disc.

text:
Molecular Dynamics simulations are reported for the structural and
thermodynamic properties of submonolayer xenon adsorbed on the $(111)$ surface
of platinum for temperatures up to the (apparently incipient) triple point and
beyond. While the motion of the atoms in the surface plane is treated with a
standard two-dimensional molecular dynamics simulation, the model takes into
consideration the thermal excitation of quantum states associated with
surface-normal dynamics in an attempt to describe the apparent smoothing of the
corrugation with increasing temperature. We examine the importance of this
thermal smoothing to the relative stability of several observed and proposed
low-temperature structures. Structure factor calculations are compared to
experimental results in an attempt to determine the low temperature structure
of this system. These calculations provide strong evidence that, at very low
temperatures, the domain wall structure of a xenon monolayer adsorbed on a
Pt$(111)$ substrate possesses a chaotic-like nature, exhibiting long-lived
meta-stable states with pinned domain walls, these walls having narrow widths
and irregular shapes. This result is contrary to the standard wisdom regarding
this system, namely that the very low temperature phase of this system is a
striped incommensurate phase. We present the case for further experimental
investigation of this and similar systems as possible examples of chaotic low
temperature phases in two dimensions.

text:
Dwarf galaxies are crucial to understand the formation and evolution of
galaxies, since they constitute the most abundant galaxy population. Abundance
ratios and their variations due to star formation are key constraints to
chemical evolution models. The determination of these abundances in the dwarf
galaxies of the Local Universe is thus of extreme importance. However, these
objects are intrinsically faint and observational constraints to their
evolution can be obtained only for very nearby galaxies. NGC 185 is one of the
four brightest dwarf companions of M31, but unlike than the other three, NGC
147, NGC 205, and NGC 221 (M32) it has an important content of gas and dust. We
obtained deep spectroscopic observations of the H$\alpha$ emitting population
of NGC 185 using GMOS-N at Gemini. As a result, in addition to the bright
planetary nebulae (PNe) previously found in the galaxy and reported in the
literature, we found other, much fainter, PNe. We then re-calculated the
electron temperatures and chemical abundances of the brightest ones, and
derived, for the first time, their electron densities. Our characterisation of
the PN population properties is interpreted in terms of the chemical evolution
of NGC 185, which suggests that it has suffered a significant chemical
enrichment within the last $\sim$8 Gyr. We also discovered the first symbiotic
star in the galaxy and enlightened the properties of a known supernova remnant
located close to the centre of NGC 185.

text: In this study, we present a model that investigates the Delta^{++}(1236)-resonance through a pion-field theoretical framework, eschewing the conventional reliance on quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Our work aims to elucidate the interaction dynamics and structure properties of this resonance, which plays a critical role in hadronic physics. To address the Delta resonance, we adopt an effective field theory approach, incorporating pion fields explicitly while neglecting the complexities of color charge present in QCD. We construct a Lagrangian that captures the key symmetries and interactions pertinent to the Delta(1236) and its coupling to pions. Through this model, we derive the general expressions for the scattering amplitudes and decay widths, providing insight into the energy spectrum and resonance behaviors. The results reveal that the pion-mediated interactions within our theoretical framework can accurately reproduce the expected resonance width and mass, albeit within the limitations of neglecting QCD effects. Additionally, our model offers a platform to analyze the role of chiral symmetry and its breaking in the mass generation of the Delta resonance. By employing this pion-centric methodology, we gain an alternative perspective on baryonic resonances that can complement QCD-based studies. Our findings underscore the viability of utilizing pion fields as core components in describing meson-baryon interactions, potentially contributing to a more nuanced understanding of resonance phenomena. This work sets the stage for further investigations into nucleon resonances using similar QCD-independent approaches, thereby broadening theoretical explorations in non-perturbative hadron dynamics.

text: The study of statistical properties of paired fixed fields plays a significant role in understanding algebraic structures and their applications in number theory and cryptography. This paper aims to explore the probabilistic behavior of paired fixed fields, particularly focusing on their distribution patterns, structural characteristics, and randomness properties. Utilizing a blend of theoretical analysis and computational methods, we examine the likelihood of occurrence of specific fixed field configurations within various Galois field extensions. Our approach involves the development of robust statistical models that characterize the pairing mechanism between these fields, with simulations conducted to validate theoretical predictions. Key findings demonstrate that paired fixed fields exhibit distinctive statistical invariants governing their formation, revealing non-trivial correlations between fixed fields and certain algebraic permutations. These patterns provide new insights into the inherent symmetry and unpredictability present in fixed field arrangements. Furthermore, we identify conditions under which these statistical properties hold consistently and explore their implications for constructing efficient algorithms in cryptographic systems. The results obtained highlight the potential for leveraging the statistical nature of paired fixed fields to enhance the security frameworks reliant on algebraic field theories. In conclusion, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the statistical dynamics of paired fixed fields and underscores their importance in both theoretical and applied mathematics, paving the way for future investigations into their role in complex algebraic systems and secure communications.

text: In this study, we present results from a triple chord stellar occultation combined with far-infrared photometry targeting the trans-Neptunian object (229762) 2007 UK126. The observations were conducted using multiple occultation paths through Earth's shadow to precisely determine the object's size and shape. We utilized the far-infrared data to investigate the thermal properties of the surface, providing insights into its albedo and composition. Our analysis reveals that 2007 UK126 has a highly elongated shape, elongated by approximately 1.4 times along its major axis. The far-infrared photometry indicates a relatively low albedo, suggesting a surface covered predominantly by icy materials rather than dark organic compounds. The methodology involved rigorous data reduction techniques to extract accurate parameters from the occultation data and detailed modeling of the light curves to infer the shape and reflectivity of the object. These findings contribute significantly to our understanding of the physical characteristics and potential compositions of distant solar system objects.

text: This study estimates the area coverage of active regions on the Sun using simultaneous measurements of He I lines at wavelengths 5876 Å and 10830 Å. We employed high-resolution spectroscopy data collected from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) instrument to calculate the areas covered by solar active regions. The methodology involved cross-correlation techniques to align spectra from both lines and then applying area-filling algorithms to estimate the total area covered by sunspots and plage regions. Our results indicate that the He I 5876 Å line is more sensitive to small-scale structures within active regions compared to the 10830 Å line, which is better suited for measuring large-scale magnetic fields. By comparing these two lines, we achieve a more comprehensive understanding of the active region's overall extent and structure. The findings contribute to our knowledge of solar activity patterns and their potential implications for space weather forecasting.

text: The abstract focuses on the Felzenszwalb-Baum-Welch (FBW) method, which is applied to event detection through changes in appearance. This technique integrates the Felzenszwalb algorithm for object segmentation with the Baum-Welch algorithm for probabilistic modeling, aiming to enhance the accuracy of detecting events based on visual appearance changes.  In this study, the primary objective was to improve event detection performance using the FBW framework. To achieve this, we first implemented the Felzenszwalb algorithm for efficient image segmentation, followed by applying the Baum-Welch algorithm to model the probabilistic transitions between different states representing the appearance of objects. The methodology involved training the model on a dataset of images annotated with event markers, where changes in object appearance were indicative of the occurrence of an event.  Key findings revealed that the FBW approach significantly improved the detection of events compared to traditional methods. The integration of the Felzenszwalb algorithm ensured robust segmentation of objects within images, while the Baum-Welch algorithm enabled more accurate probabilistic modeling of appearance changes. Consequently, the system demonstrated higher precision and recall rates in identifying events.  Concluding, the results underscore the effectiveness of the FBW method in enhancing event detection capabilities through the analysis of changing visual appearances. This approach offers a promising solution for applications requiring real-time or near-real-time event detection in dynamic environments.

text:
The mass distribution of prestellar cores is obtained for clouds with
arbitrary internal mass distributions using a selection criterion based on the
thermal and turbulent Jeans mass and applied hierarchically from small to large
scales. We have checked this methodology comparing our results for a lognormal
density PDF with the theoretical CMF derived by Hennebelle and Chabrier, namely
a power-law at large scales and a log-normal cutoff at low scales, but our
method can be applied to any mass distributions representing a star-forming
cloud. This methodology enables us to connect the parental cloud structure with
the mass distribution of the cores and their spatial distribution, providing an
efficient tool for investigating the physical properties of the molecular
clouds that give rise to the prestellar core distributions observed. Simulated
fBm clouds with the Hurst exponent close to the value H=1/3 give the best
agreement with the theoretical CMF derived by Hennebelle and Chabrier and
Chabrier's system IMF. Likewise, the spatial distribution of the cores derived
from our methodology show a surface density of companions compatible with those
observed in Trapezium and Ophiucus star-forming regions. This method also
allows us to analyze the properties of the mass distribution of cores for
different realizations. We found that the variations in the number of cores
formed in different realizations of fBm clouds (with the same Hurst exponent)
are much larger than the expected root N statistical fluctuations, increasing
with H.
