text: In this study, we propose two novel graph invariants, Rigidity Index (RI) and Redundancy Index (RI), for ensuring unique localizability in cooperative localization of wireless sensor networks (WSNs). The unique localizability problem refers to the challenge of determining the exact position of a target node in the presence of uncertain local measurements from multiple sensor nodes. Our approach leverages the graph theory and topology properties of WSNs to characterize the degree of connectivity and redundancy among the available measurements. We first introduce the concept of graph rigidity and define RI as a measure of the graph's rigidity in the context of WSN localization. The RI quantifies the minimum number of edges that need to be removed from the graph to disconnect it, thereby affecting the unique localizability of the target node. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RI through simulations and experimental results, which show that higher RI values correspond to more robust and accurate localization. Secondly, we propose RI as a measure of redundancy in WSN localization, which quantifies the degree of overlapping measurements among the neighboring nodes. RI is defined as the minimum number of redundant nodes required to ensure unique localizability, and we show that it is an essential complementary metric to RI. Simulation and experimental results validate our findings, indicating that the optimal RI and RI values depend on the network topology and the localization algorithm used. Overall, our work provides valuable insights into the role of graph invariants in ensuring unique localizability in cooperative localization of WSNs, and our proposed RI and RI metrics offer practical approaches to enhance the localization accuracy and robustness in various applications. Our findings contribute to the ongoing research in the field of WSN localization and provide a foundation for future developments.

Through analysis of Hα emission, near-infrared observations, and archival X-ray images, it was determined that the bubble exhibits a complex morphology with distinct edges and a central cavity filled with ionized gas. Velocity measurements reveal radial outflows with velocities up to several hundred kilometers per second, indicating a strong interaction between the bubble material and the surrounding interstellar medium. Key findings include the detection of temperature variations within the bubble, suggesting non-uniform heating processes. text: We investigated the performance of multi-layer transmission and hybrid relaying strategies for relay channels with multiple out-of-band relays, with the aim of improving the reliability and capacity of wireless communication networks. Furthermore, we demonstrated that hybrid relaying schemes, which combine the benefits of multiple relays and transmission techniques, can achieve even better performance.  We also explored the impact of relay placement and coordination on the network's performance, and found that optimal relay placement and coordination strategies can lead to significant improvements in network reliability and capacity. Our analysis highlighted the importance of considering the interplay between relay placement, transmission techniques, and hybrid relaying schemes in the design of wireless communication networks.  By providing a comprehensive analysis of multi-layer transmission and hybrid relaying strategies for relay channels with multiple out-of-band relays, our work aims to contribute to the development of more reliable and efficient wireless communication systems.

Many problems in Machine Learning can be modeled as submodular optimization
problems. Recent work has focused on stochastic or adaptive versions of these
problems. We consider the Scenario Submodular Cover problem, which is a
counterpart to the Stochastic Submodular Cover problem studied by Golovin and
Krause. In Scenario Submodular Cover, the goal is to produce a cover with
minimum expected cost, where the expectation is with respect to an empirical
joint distribution, given as input by a weighted sample of realizations. In
contrast, in Stochastic Submodular Cover, the variables of the input
distribution are assumed to be independent, and the distribution of each
variable is given as input. Building on algorithms developed by Cicalese et al.
and Golovin and Krause for related problems, we give two approximation
algorithms for Scenario Submodular Cover over discrete distributions. The first
achieves an approximation factor of O(log Qm), where m is the size of the
sample and Q is the goal utility. The second, simpler algorithm achieves an
approximation bound of O(log QW), where Q is the goal utility and W is the sum
of the integer weights. (Both bounds assume an integer-valued utility
function.) Our results yield approximation bounds for other problems involving
non-independent distributions that are explicitly specified by their support.

In this work we conduct a close-up investigation into the nature of
near-field heat transfer (NFHT) of two graphene sheets in parallel-plate
geometry. We develop a fully microscopic and quantum approach using
nonequilibrium Green's function method. A Caroli formula for heat flux is
proposed and numerically verified. We show our near-field-to-black-body heat
flux ratios generally exhibit $1/d^{\alpha}$ dependence, with an effective
exponent $\alpha \approx 2.2$, at long distances exceeding 100 nm and up to one
micron; in the opposite $d\rightarrow 0$ limit, the values converge to a range
within an order of magnitude. We justify this feature by noting it is owing to
the breakdown of local conductivity theory, which predicts a $1/d$ dependence.
Furthermore, from the numerical result, we find in addition to thermal
wavelength, $\lambda_{th}$, a shorter distance scale $\sim$ 10 - 100 nm,
comparable to the graphene thermal length ($\hbar v_{F}/k_{B} T$) or Fermi
wavelength ($k_{F}^{-1}$), marks the transition point between the short- and
long-distance transfer behaviors; within that point, relatively large variation
of heat flux in response to doping level becomes a typical characteristic. The
emergence of such large variation is tied to relative NFHT contributions from
the intra- and inter-band transitions. Beyond that point, scaling of thermal
flux $\propto 1/d^{\alpha}$ can be generally observed.

Several cosmic ray experiments have measured excesses in electrons and
positrons, relative to standard backgrounds, for energies from ~ 10 GeV - 1
TeV. These excesses could be due to new astrophysical sources, but an
explanation in which the electrons and positrons are dark matter annihilation
or decay products is also consistent. Fortunately, the Fermi-LAT diffuse gamma
ray measurements can further test these models, since the electrons and
positrons produce gamma rays in their interactions in the interstellar medium.
Although the dark matter gamma ray signal consistent with the local electron
and positron measurements should be quite large, as we review, there are
substantial uncertainties in the modeling of diffuse backgrounds and,
additionally, experimental uncertainties that make it difficult to claim a dark
matter discovery. In this paper, we introduce an alternative method for
understanding the diffuse gamma ray spectrum in which we take the intensity
ratio in each energy bin of two different regions of the sky, thereby canceling
common systematic uncertainties. For many spectra, this ratio fits well to a
power law with a single break in energy. The two measured exponent indices are
a robust discriminant between candidate models, and we demonstrate that dark
matter annihilation scenarios can predict index values that require "extreme"
parameters for background-only explanations.

text: We investigated the deformations of polyhedra and polygons under the action of the unitary group, a fundamental concept in differential geometry and topology. Our approach involved analyzing the symmetries and invariants of polyhedra and polygons, with a focus on the effects of unitary transformations on their geometric properties.  Through a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we demonstrated that the unitary group can induce significant deformations on polyhedra and polygons, leading to the emergence of new topological features and symmetries. Specifically, we found that unitary transformations can create new holes and cavities, distort the shape of faces and edges, and even lead to the formation of new vertices and faces.  Our results suggest that the unitary group plays a crucial role in shaping the geometric structure of polyhedra and polygons, and that these transformations can have profound implications for our understanding of their topological properties. Furthermore, we showed that the unitary group can be used to generate a wide range of novel polyhedra and polygons with unique geometric and topological characteristics.  Our study provides new insights into the interplay between symmetry and geometry in polyhedra and polygons, and has significant implications for fields such as materials science, computer graphics, and theoretical physics. The findings of this research open up new avenues for exploration and investigation, and highlight the importance of considering the effects of unitary transformations on the geometric structure of polyhedra and polygons.

text: In this work, we investigate the holographic confinement/deconfinement phase transitions of AdS/QCD in curved spaces. Utilizing the holographic principle, we construct an AdS Reissner-Nordström black hole background in curved space, and explore the transition from confining to deconfining phases by analyzing the renormalized energy-momentum tensor and the Wilson loop method. Our findings reveal a critical point at which the geometry transitions from a AdS Reissner-Nordström geometry to the AdS Schwarzschild one, accompanied by a zero-mass tensor mode, which is a signature of the critical point. Furthermore, we find that the transition is second order and the critical exponent is consistent with the theoretical prediction of mean field theory. The results obtained here indicate that the holographic principle provides a powerful tool for studying the confinement/deconfinement phase transitions in curved space, which is relevant to the understanding of strongly-coupled systems in various fields of physics. The analysis of holographic confinement/deconfinement phase transitions in curved spaces sheds light on the non-perturbative properties of the theory and offers insights into the possible applications of AdS/QCD in the study of black hole physics and cosmology.

In this paper, we study the problem of generating inputs to a higher-order
program causing it to error. We first study the problem in the setting of PCF,
a typed, core functional language and contribute the first relatively complete
method for constructing counterexamples for PCF programs. The method is
relatively complete in the sense of Hoare logic; completeness is reduced to the
completeness of a first-order solver over the base types of PCF. In practice,
this means an SMT solver can be used for the effective, automated generation of
higher-order counterexamples for a large class of programs.
  We achieve this result by employing a novel form of symbolic execution for
higher-order programs. The remarkable aspect of this symbolic execution is that
even though symbolic higher-order inputs and values are considered, the path
condition remains a first-order formula. Our handling of symbolic function
application enables the reconstruction of higher-order counterexamples from
this first-order formula.
  After establishing our main theoretical results, we sketch how to apply the
approach to untyped, higher-order, stateful languages with first-class
contracts and show how counterexample generation can be used to detect contract
violations in this setting. To validate our approach, we implement a tool
generating counterexamples for erroneous modules written in Racket.

Spontaneous symmetry breaking is well understood through the classical
"Mexican Hat" picture, which describes many quantum phases of matter. Recently,
several new classes of quantum phases of matter, such as topological orders and
symmetry protected topological (SPT) orders, were discovered. In an attempt to
address the transitions between all those phases of quantum matter under the
same framework, we introduced an analogous yet very simple picture for phase
transitions in the context of tensor-networks. Using a very simple iteration
process, we found that both symmetry breaking and some topological phase
transitions (for topological orders described by gauge theory and 1D SPT
orders) could be marked by a sudden change in the symmetry structure of the
so-called "environment matrix". In this process, the environment matrix serves
as an "order parameter" that captures patterns of entanglement in topological
phases. The symmetry change in the environment matrix is very much like the
symmetry breaking of conventional order parameters. We applied this method to
both the transverse Ising model (1D and 2D honeycomb), spin-1 model (1D), and
the Toric Code model in a magnetic field (2D honeycomb), and explored the
corresponding symmetry structure changes in their environment matrices in
details. With just a few variational parameters and a few minutes' run time on
a laptop, we could get the corresponding phase transition points within a few
percent error compared with the Quantum Monte Carlo results.

text: Quantum weak coin flipping is a pivotal protocol in the realms of cryptography and quantum computing, allowing two parties to agree on a binary outcome with minimized trust. Historically, achieving a protocol with an arbitrarily small bias has been a challenging problem. This paper presents a novel and simplified proof demonstrating the existence of quantum weak coin flipping protocols with bias approaching zero. The primary objective was to streamline the theoretical approach while maintaining rigorous veracity. Our methodology involved leveraging advanced quantum entanglement principles and harnessing unitary transformations to develop a more intuitive framework than previously established methods. We critically analyzed existing protocols, identified redundancies, and formalized a sequence of logical axioms conducive to achieving the minimal bias. Our key findings indicate that it is feasible to construct such protocols within a more accessible mathematical foundation, enhancing both understanding and implementation. Notably, this result is achieved without relying on complex constructions, which were often present in preceding approaches. This contribution is significant, as it simplifies the protocol's comprehension and potential application in practical scenarios. In conclusion, the simpler proof not only corroborates the theoretical underpinnings of quantum weak coin flipping with negligible bias but also opens avenues for more comprehensive research into scalable quantum communication systems. Such advancements could pave the way for robust quantum cryptographic frameworks and further innovations in secure quantum protocols.

text: In this work, we introduce WRS (Waiting Room Sampling), an innovative approach aimed at improving the accuracy of triangle counting in real graph streams. Traditional methods often suffer from high error rates due to limited memory and processing capabilities when dealing with large-scale data. Our method leverages a waiting room sampling technique that dynamically adjusts the sample size based on the current memory usage, ensuring more precise counts without compromising computational efficiency.  Problematically, existing sampling techniques can lead to significant errors in triangle counts, especially when dealing with skewed distributions and varying densities within graph streams. We address these issues by employing a combination of reservoir sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to maintain a representative sample while minimizing the impact of memory constraints.   The methodology involves initializing a waiting room with a small sample set, which then expands as needed to cover the entire stream. As new data arrives, samples are continuously added to the waiting room, and older samples are discarded to ensure freshness. This process is monitored using a dynamic threshold based on the current memory state, which allows us to balance between accuracy and resource utilization.  Experimental results demonstrate that WRS significantly reduces error rates compared to conventional sampling methods, achieving up to 95% accuracy in triangle count estimation across various synthetic and real-world graph datasets. These findings underscore the effectiveness of our proposed approach in handling real graph streams efficiently and accurately.

The object G2 was recently discovered descending into the gravitational
potential of the supermassive black hole (BH) Sgr A*. We test the photoionized
cloud scenario, determine the cloud properties, and estimate the emission
during the pericenter passage. The incident radiation is computed starting from
the individual stars at the locations of G2. The radiative transfer
calculations are conducted with CLOUDY code and $2011$ broadband and line
luminosities are fitted. The spherically symmetric, tidally distorted, and
magnetically arrested cloud shapes are tested with both the interstellar medium
dust and $10$~nm graphite dust. The best-fitting magnetically arrested model
has the initial density $n_{\rm init}=1.8\times10^5{\rm cm}^{-3}$, initial
radius $R_{\rm init}=2.2\times10^{15}{\rm cm}=17 {\rm mas}$, mass $m_{\rm
cloud}=4M_{\rm Earth}$, and dust relative abundance $A=0.072$. It provides a
good fit to $2011$ data, is consistent with the luminosities in $2004$ and
$2008$, and reaches an agreement with the observed size. We revise down the
predicted radio and X-ray bow shock luminosities to be below the quiescent
level of Sgr A*, which readily leads to non-detection in agreement to
observations. The magnetic energy dissipation in the cloud at the pericenter
coupled with more powerful irradiation may lead to an infrared source with an
apparent magnitude $m_{L'}\approx13.0$. No shock into the cloud and no X-rays
are expected from cloud squeezing by the ambient gas pressure. Larger than
previously estimated cloud mass $m_{\rm cloud}=(4-20)M_{\rm Earth}$ may produce
a higher accretion rate and a brighter state of Sgr A* as the debris descend
onto the BH.

text: This study explores the geometric properties of the Schramm-Loewner Evolution (SLE) light cone, SLE fan, and SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$ curves for $\kappa \in (0,4)$ and $\rho \in [\tfrac{\kappa}{2}-4,-2)$. The primary objective is to investigate how these curves behave under different parameter settings and their implications on the two-dimensional continuum random geometry.   The methodology involves computational simulations using complex analysis techniques to generate and analyze SLE paths with varying parameters. These simulations allow for the visualization and quantification of the light cones and fans, which are essential structures in understanding the boundaries of SLE processes.  Key findings include the observation that as $\rho$ decreases from $[\tfrac{\kappa}{2}-4,-2)$ towards negative infinity, the SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$ curve exhibits increasingly erratic behavior near the boundary, reflecting a more intricate structure. Additionally, the light cone's dimension was found to be dependent on $\rho$, with significant changes observed as $\rho$ crosses certain thresholds. Furthermore, the SLE fan, which is a collection of curves emanating from a point, shows distinct patterns depending on the value of $\rho$, revealing unique fractal dimensions and scaling exponents.  In conclusion, this research provides insights into the nuanced behaviors of SLE processes, particularly focusing on their geometrical properties and how they evolve with specific parameter settings. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of SLE and its applications in stochastic geometry and quantum gravity models.

We apply a new model for the spherically averaged correlation function at
large pair separations to the measurement of the clustering of luminous red
galaxies (LRGs) made from the SDSS by Cabre and Gaztanaga(2009). Our model
takes into account the form of the BAO peak and the large scale shape of the
correlation function. We perform a Monte Carlo Markov chain analysis for
different combinations of datasets and for different parameter sets. When used
in combination with a compilation of the latest CMB measurements, the LRG
clustering and the latest supernovae results give constraints on cosmological
parameters which are comparable and in remarkably good agreement, resolving the
tension reported in some studies. The best fitting model in the context of a
flat, Lambda-CDM cosmology is specified by Omega_m=0.261+-0.013,
Omega_b=0.044+-0.001, n_s=0.96+-0.01, H_0=71.6+-1.2 km/s/Mpc and
sigma_8=0.80+-0.02. If we allow the time-independent dark energy equation of
state parameter to vary, we find results consistent with a cosmological
constant at the 5% level using all data sets: w_DE=-0.97+-0.05. The large scale
structure measurements by themselves can constrain the dark energy equation of
state parameter to w_DE=-1.05+-0.15, independently of CMB or supernovae data.
We do not find convincing evidence for an evolving equation of state. We
provide a set of "extended distance priors" that contain the most relevant
information from the CMB power spectrum and the shape of the LRG correlation
function which can be used to constrain dark energy models and spatial
curvature. Our model should provide an accurate description of the clustering
even in much larger, forthcoming surveys, such as those planned with NASA's
JDEM or ESA's Euclid mission.

The detection of a stochastic background of gravitational waves could
significantly impact our understanding of the physical processes that shaped
the early Universe. The challenge lies in separating the cosmological signal
from other stochastic processes such as instrument noise and astrophysical
foregrounds. One approach is to build two or more detectors and cross correlate
their output, thereby enhancing the common gravitational wave signal relative
to the uncorrelated instrument noise. When only one detector is available, as
will likely be the case with the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA),
alternative analysis techniques must be developed. Here we show that models of
the noise and signal transfer functions can be used to tease apart the
gravitational and instrument noise contributions. We discuss the role of
gravitational wave insensitive "null channels" formed from particular
combinations of the time delay interferometry, and derive a new combination
that maintains this insensitivity for unequal arm length detectors. We show
that, in the absence of astrophysical foregrounds, LISA could detect signals
with energy densities as low as $\Omega_{\rm gw} = 6 \times 10^{-13}$ with just
one month of data. We describe an end-to-end Bayesian analysis pipeline that is
able to search for, characterize and assign confidence levels for the detection
of a stochastic gravitational wave background, and demonstrate the
effectiveness of this approach using simulated data from the third round of
Mock LISA Data Challenges.

Despite the abundance of bipartite networked systems, their organizing
principles are less studied, compared to unipartite networks. Bipartite
networks are often analyzed after projecting them onto one of the two sets of
nodes. As a result of the projection, nodes of the same set are linked together
if they have at least one neighbor in common in the bipartite network. Even
though these projections allow one to study bipartite networks using tools
developed for unipartite networks, one-mode projections lead to significant
loss of information and artificial inflation of the projected network with
fully connected subgraphs. Here we pursue a different approach for analyzing
bipartite systems that is based on the observation that such systems have a
latent metric structure: network nodes are points in a latent metric space,
while connections are more likely to form between nodes separated by shorter
distances. This approach has been developed for unipartite networks, and
relatively little is known about its applicability to bipartite systems. Here,
we fully analyze a simple latent-geometric model of bipartite networks, and
show that this model explains the peculiar structural properties of many real
bipartite systems, including the distributions of common neighbors and
bipartite clustering. We also analyze the geometric information loss in
one-mode projections in this model, and propose an efficient method to infer
the latent pairwise distances between nodes. Uncovering the latent geometry
underlying real bipartite networks can find applications in diverse domains,
ranging from constructing efficient recommender systems to understanding cell
metabolism.

Index coding models broadcast networks in which a sender sends different
messages to different receivers simultaneously, where each receiver may know
some of the messages a priori. The aim is to find the minimum (normalised)
index codelength that the sender sends. This paper considers unicast index
coding, where each receiver requests exactly one message, and each message is
requested by exactly one receiver. Each unicast index-coding instances can be
fully described by a directed graph and vice versa, where each vertex
corresponds to one receiver. For any directed graph representing a unicast
index-coding instance, we show that if a maximum acyclic induced subgraph
(MAIS) is obtained by removing two or fewer vertices from the graph, then the
minimum index codelength equals the number of vertices in the MAIS, and linear
codes are optimal for the corresponding index-coding instance. Using this
result, we solved all unicast index-coding instances with up to five receivers,
which correspond to all graphs with up to five vertices. For 9819
non-isomorphic graphs among all graphs up to five vertices, we obtained the
minimum index codelength for all message alphabet sizes; for the remaining 28
graphs, we obtained the minimum index codelength if the message alphabet size
is $k^2$ for any positive integer $k$. This work complements the result by
Arbabjolfaei et al. (ISIT 2013), who solved all unicast index-coding instances
with up to five receivers in the asymptotic regime, where the message alphabet
size tends to infinity.

text: In this work, we present two novel snap-stabilizing point-to-point communication protocols designed for message-switched networks. Our study addresses the challenge of ensuring reliable and efficient communication in dynamic network environments where nodes can exhibit transient failures. Through rigorous analysis and simulation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed protocols in achieving convergence to a correct state within a finite number of steps, regardless of the initial network configuration or transient faults.  The first protocol utilizes a distributed token-passing mechanism to coordinate message transmissions and ensure eventual message delivery. The second protocol adopts a leader election strategy, enabling nodes to establish a stable communication path by dynamically electing and following a leader node. Both protocols are shown to be snap-stabilizing, guaranteeing that the network can recover from any transient fault and achieve a correct communication state in a finite time.  Our contributions include formal proofs of correctness and convergence for both protocols, as well as comprehensive simulation results demonstrating their efficiency and fault tolerance. The novel approaches introduced in this work provide valuable insights into designing resilient communication protocols for message-switched networks, offering promising solutions for real-world applications where network topology and node failures are unpredictable.

text: The specific heat and muon spin rotation (μSR) studies were conducted on the noncentrosymmetric superconductor LaRhSi3 to elucidate its superconducting properties. Noncentrosymmetricity introduces unique magnetic interactions that can significantly influence superconductivity. In this work, specific heat measurements provided insights into the thermal behavior of LaRhSi3, revealing anomalies indicative of superconducting transitions. μSR experiments, sensitive to local magnetic fields and spin dynamics, were employed to probe these anomalies directly. The results indicated a sharp superconducting transition with a critical temperature \(T_c\) of approximately 1.8 K, consistent with previous reports. Furthermore, μSR data revealed a precession signal indicating the presence of a residual magnetic moment even below \(T_c\), which could be attributed to the localized moments associated with the noncentrosymmetric structure. This study underscores the importance of both thermodynamic and microscopic probes in understanding the complex interplay between symmetry breaking and superconductivity in LaRhSi3.

text: This study investigates the reverberation mapping technique applied to luminous quasars at high redshifts (z > 1). Utilizing multi-wavelength data from various telescopes, including X-ray, optical, and radio observations, the primary objective was to measure the size of the accretion disk around supermassive black holes. By analyzing the time delay between the emission from the broad line region and the continuum light, we aim to infer the size of the emitting regions. Key findings indicate that the observed sizes of these accretion disks are consistent with theoretical models, suggesting efficient accretion processes. However, significant discrepancies were noted in the variability timescales compared to predictions, indicating possible deviations from standard accretion disk dynamics. This research highlights the importance of reverberation mapping in understanding the physical conditions within quasar host galaxies and the role of feedback mechanisms in shaping their evolution.

The original 2017 version of this paper, published in Ann. Appl. Probab., 27,
1678--1801, contains a major gap in the proofs. In the subsequent publication
in Ann. Appl. Probab., 34, 3370--3374, 2024, we indicated how to fix this. For
convenience of the reader, we here update the original paper to incorporate the
suggested fix.
  Consider a Boolean model in $R^d$ with balls of random, bounded radii with
distribution $F_0$, centered at the points of a Poisson process of intensity
$t>0$. The capacity functional of the infinite cluster $Z_\infty$ is given by
$\theta_L(t) = P(Z_\infty\cap L \neq \emptyset)$, defined for each compact
$L\subset R^d$. We prove for any fixed $L$ and $F_0$ that $\theta_L(t)$ is
infinitely differentiable in $t$, except at the critical value $t_c$; we give a
Margulis-Russo type formula for the derivatives.
  More generally, allowing the distribution $F_0$ to vary and viewing
$\theta_L$ as a function of the measure $F:=tF_0$, we show that it is
infinitely differentiable in all directions with respect to the measure $F$ in
the supercritical region of the cone of positive measures on a bounded
interval.
  We also prove that $\theta_L(\cdot)$ grows at least linearly at the critical
value. This implies that the critical exponent known as $\beta$ is at most 1
(if it exists) for this model. Along the way, we extend a result of H.Tanemura
(1993), on regularity of the supercritical Boolean model in $d \geq 3$ with
fixed-radius balls, to the case with bounded random radii.

We study the corpuscular model of an evaporating black hole consisting of a
specific quantum state for a large number $N$ of self-confined bosons. The
single-particle spectrum contains a discrete ground state of energy $m$
(corresponding to toy gravitons forming the black hole), and a gapless
continuous spectrum (to accommodate for the Hawking radiation with energy
$\omega>m$). Each constituent is in a superposition of the ground state and a
Planckian distribution at the expected Hawking temperature in the continuum. We
first find that, assuming the Hawking radiation is the leading effect of the
internal scatterings, the corresponding $N$-particle state can be collectively
described by a single-particle wave-function given by a superposition of a
total ground state with energy $M=N\,m$ and a Planckian distribution for $E>M$
at the same Hawking temperature. From this collective state, we compute the
partition function and obtain an entropy which reproduces the usual area law
with a logarithmic correction precisely related with the Hawking component. By
means of the horizon wave-function for the system, we finally show the
backreaction of modes with $\omega>m$ reduces the Hawking flux. Both
corrections, to the entropy and to the Hawking flux, suggest the evaporation
properly stops for vanishing mass, if the black hole is in this particular
quantum state.

text: This research paper investigates the development of a novel approach to identifying sublatable binary code by synthesizing adapters. The increasing complexity and size of modern software systems necessitate the creation of adaptable, modular, and reusable code. However, the absence of a systematic method for identifying substitutable code blocks hinders the process of modularization and reuse.   The objective of this study is to present a framework for identifying sublatable binary code by synthesizing adapters. The proposed framework leverages the concept of adapters, which are designed to facilitate the integration of existing code components into new contexts. By synthesizing adapters, the proposed approach enables the creation of a library of pre-defined adapters that can be used to identify and substitute code blocks with similar characteristics.   The methodology employed in this study involves the development of a novel adapter synthesis algorithm, which is based on a combination of machine learning and graph theory techniques. The algorithm is trained on a dataset of existing software systems and their corresponding adapters, enabling it to learn patterns and relationships between code components.   The key findings of this study indicate that the proposed framework is effective in identifying sublatable binary code by synthesizing adapters. The results show that the adapter synthesis algorithm is able to identify a significant number of substitutable code blocks, with an average accuracy of 85%. The findings also demonstrate that the proposed framework can be used to improve the modularity and reusability of software systems.   The conclusion of this study highlights the potential of the proposed framework for improving the development and maintenance of software systems. The results suggest that the framework can be used to identify opportunities for modularization and reuse, leading to improved system maintainability and reduced development time.

text: This study investigates the contributions of star-forming galaxies to cosmic MeV and GeV gamma-ray emissions. We aimed to elucidate the physical processes that generate these high-energy photons within star-forming regions. Our analysis utilizes multi-wavelength data from the Fermi-LAT telescope and ground-based surveys such as the Hubble Space Telescope and Chandra X-ray Observatory. Key methodologies include spectral fitting techniques to isolate gamma-ray emission signatures from star-forming regions and comparison with galactic models of star formation and supernova activity. Results indicate significant contributions from young stellar clusters and supernova remnants, particularly in regions with high gas densities and ongoing star formation activity. This work advances our understanding of how star-forming environments can produce detectable gamma-ray radiation at both MeV and GeV energies, providing insights into the interplay between star formation and cosmic ray acceleration in galaxies.

text: In this work, we investigate the large-scale cosmic structure through the framework of quantum interference, positing the universe as a manifestation of coherent dark wave interactions. Our central aim is to address the enigmatic nature of dark matter and its elusive influence on cosmic architecture. By conceptualizing dark matter as a coherent wave phenomenon, we explore the interference patterns that arise from quantum superpositions of these dark wave states. Employing a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we derive novel equations governing wave interference in both linear and non-linear regimes, allowing for a more cohesive understanding of cosmological patterns observed in galactic structures.  We utilize advanced simulations, incorporating data from recent cosmic surveys, to validate our model against the empirical distribution of matter in the universe. Our findings demonstrate that the predicted interference patterns align closely with the observed filamentary web of galaxies, suggesting that the macroscopic arrangement of cosmic entities may be explained by the quantum mechanical principles that dictate dark matter behavior. Key outcomes include a refined model of matter clustering, characterized by coherence lengths that match the scale of known dark matter halos.  This research advances the theoretical discourse on dark matter by leveraging quantum wave mechanics to explain cosmological structures, offering a bridge between quantum physics and astrophysical observations. Our methodology serves as a promising paradigm for future inquiries into the cosmic role of dark energy and matter, enhancing our comprehension of the foundational principles underpinning the universe's grand design.

We develop an interferometric technique for making time-resolved measurements
of field-quadrature operators for nonequilibrium ultracold bosons in optical
lattices. The technique exploits the internal state structure of magnetic atoms
to create two subsystems of atoms in different spin states and lattice sites. A
Feshbach resonance turns off atom-atom interactions in one spin subsystem,
making it a well-characterized reference state, while atoms in the other
subsystem undergo nonequilibrium dynamics for a variable hold time. Interfering
the subsystems via a second beam-splitting operation, time-resolved quadrature
measurements on the interacting atoms are obtained by detecting relative spin
populations. The technique can provide quadrature measurements for a variety of
Hamiltonians and lattice geometries (e.g., cubic, honeycomb, superlattices),
including systems with tunneling, spin-orbit couplings using artificial gauge
fields, and higher-band effects. Analyzing the special case of a deep lattice
with negligible tunneling, we obtain the time evolution of both quadrature
observables and their fluctuations. As a second application, we show that the
interferometer can be used to measure atom-atom interaction strengths with
super-Heisenberg scaling n^(-3/2) in the mean number of atoms per lattice site
n, and standard quantum limit scaling M^(-1/2) in the number of lattice sites
M. In our analysis, we require M >> 1 and for realistic systems n is small, and
therefore the scaling in total atom number N = nM is below the Heisenberg
limit; nevertheless, measurements testing the scaling behaviors for
interaction-based quantum metrologies should be possible in this system.

text: The increasing complexity of computational tasks in engineering and applied sciences necessitates the development of robust statistical models for solving linear systems. This paper presents a novel error-in-variables (EIV) model aimed at enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of positive definite linear system solutions through the application of orthogonal matrix decompositions. The primary objective of this research is to mitigate the effects of measurement errors commonly encountered in linear models, thereby improving the reliability of the computed solutions. A comprehensive methodology is employed, integrating orthogonal transformations such as the QR decomposition and the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to effectively handle inherent data uncertainties. This study evaluates the performance of the proposed EIV model against traditional methods through extensive numerical simulations and real-world applications in structural engineering and systems control. Key findings reveal a significant reduction in estimation errors and computational times when using the proposed model, demonstrating its robustness in scenarios characterized by high noise levels and variable uncertainties. Furthermore, the analysis shows that the incorporation of orthogonal decompositions not only enhances system stability but also aids in achieving convergence in iterative solution methods. In conclusion, this new EIV model presents a substantial advancement in the resolution of positive definite linear systems, offering a powerful tool for practitioners aiming to improve accuracy in data-driven problem-solving environments.

text: We investigate the complicated variations of the early optical afterglow associated with the gamma-ray burst (GRB) 090726, aiming to elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms driving these phenomena. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset, we employ a multi-wavelength observational approach, integrating optical, near-infrared, and X-ray data to analyze the temporal and spectral characteristics of the afterglow. Our results reveal a complex light curve characterized by rapid fluctuations and notable brightness variations, suggesting interactions between the afterglow and surrounding media. By fitting these light curves with varying models, we identify significant contributions from both the underlying supernova component and the long-lasting emissions typical of afterglow mechanisms.   We also explore the implications of these variations for the expansive early universe conditions and potential contributions from the circumstellar environment, hypothesizing that the observed fluctuations may be due to inhomogeneities in the density profile surrounding the progenitor star. Our methodology includes statistical analysis and simulations designed to assess the significance of these fluctuations, leading us to conclude that the observed early optical afterglow behavior of GRB 090726 is influenced by a blend of internal shock activity and interaction with the surrounding medium. Consequently, we propose a revised model that better accounts for the observed complexity in the early afterglow light curves of GRBs. This work not only enhances our understanding of GRB 090726 specifically but also contributes to the broader field of high-energy astrophysics by providing insights into GRB afterglow behavior more generally.

text: We investigate the dynamic evolution of energy in fluid systems driven by rising bubbles, addressing the critical problem of energy transfer and dissipation within bubbly flows. Our study employs a combination of experimental observations and numerical simulations to analyze the energy distribution and its interaction with turbulent flow regimes. We observe that the presence of rising bubbles significantly alters the energy landscape of the fluid, enhancing energy dissipation rates and modifying turbulence characteristics compared to single-phase flows.  Through a series of controlled experiments, we quantify the energy extraction efficiency of the bubbles and the subsequent impact on the flow's kinetic and potential energy. We identify key parameters, such as bubble size, rise velocity, and fluid viscosity, that govern energy evolution in these systems. The results demonstrate a nonlinear relationship between bubble dynamics and energy transfer efficiency, revealing that smaller bubbles tend to enhance turbulence and energy dissipation more effectively than larger ones due to increased surface area and wake interactions.  Furthermore, we employ computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to develop a robust framework for predicting the energy dynamics in varied flow conditions, corroborating our experimental findings. Our methodology integrates multi-scale modeling techniques to capture the complex interplay between bubble behavior and turbulence across different scenarios. The insights gained from this work have significant implications for optimizing industrial applications involving bubbly flows, such as in chemical reactors and environmental systems, where efficient energy management is paramount.

We present ALMA observations of the CO(6-5) and [CII] emission lines and the
sub-millimeter continuum of the $z\sim6$ quasi-stellar object (QSO) SDSS
J231038.88+185519.7. Compared to previous studies, we have analyzed a synthetic
beam that is ten times smaller in angular size, we have achieved ten times
better sensitivity in the CO(6-5) line, and two and half times better
sensitivity in the [CII] line, enabling us to resolve the molecular gas
emission. We obtain a size of the dense molecular gas of $2.9\pm0.5$ kpc, and
of $1.4\pm0.2$ kpc for the 91.5 GHz dust continuum. By assuming that CO(6-5) is
thermalized, and by adopting a CO--to--$H_2$ conversion factor $\rm \alpha_{CO}
= 0.8~ M_{\odot}~K^{-1}~ (km/s)^{-1} ~pc^{2}$, we infer a molecular gas mass of
$\rm M(H_2)=(3.2 \pm0.2) \times 10^{10}\rm M_{\odot}$. Assuming that the
observed CO velocity gradient is due to an inclined rotating disk, we derive a
dynamical mass of $\rm M_{dyn}~sin^2(i) = (2.4\pm0.5) \times 10^{10}~
M_{\odot}$, which is a factor of approximately two smaller than the previously
reported estimate based on [CII]. Regarding the central black hole, we provide
a new estimate of the black hole mass based on the C~IV emission line detected
in the X-SHOOTER/VLT spectrum: $\rm M_{BH}=(1.8\pm 0.5) \times 10^{9}~
M_{\odot}$. We find a molecular gas fraction of $\rm \mu=M(H_2)/M^*\sim4.4$,
where $\rm M^*\approx M_{dyn} - M(H_2)-M(BH)$. We derive a ratio
$v_{rot}/\sigma \approx 1-2$ suggesting high gas turbulence, outflows/inflows
and/or complex kinematics due to a merger event. We estimate a global Toomre
parameter $Q\sim 0.2-0.5$, indicating likely cloud fragmentation. We compare,
at the same angular resolution, the CO(6-5) and [CII] distributions, finding
that dense molecular gas is more centrally concentrated with respect to [CII].
We find that the current BH growth rate is similar to that of its host galaxy.

The nanofabrication technology has taught us that an $m$-dimensional
confining potential imposed upon an $n$-dimensional electron gas paves the way
to a quasi-($n-m$)-dimensional electron gas, with $m \le n$ and $1\le n, m \le
3$. This is the road to the (semiconducting) quasi-$n$ dimensional electron gas
systems we have been happily traversing on now for almost three decades.
Achieving quasi-one dimensional electron gas (Q-1DEG) [or quantum wire(s) for
more practical purposes] led us to some mixed moments in this journey: while
the reduced phase space for the scattering led us believe in the route to the
faster electron devices, the proximity to the 1D systems left us in the dilemma
of describing it as a Fermi liquid or as a Luttinger liquid. No one had ever
suspected the potential of the former, but it took quite a while for some to
convince the others on the latter. A realistic Q-1DEG system at the low
temperatures is best describable as a Fermi liquid rather than as a Luttinger
liquid. In the language of condensed matter physics, a critical scrutiny of
Q-1DEG systems has provided us with a host of exotic (electronic, optical, and
transport) phenomena revealing their unparallel behavior characteristics unseen
in their higher or lower dimensional counterparts. Here, we embark on the
systematic investigation of the inelastic electron scattering (IES) and of
inelastic light scattering (ILS) from the elementary electronic excitations in
quantum wires in the absence of an applied magnetic field. To that end, we
begin with the Kubo's correlation functions to derive the generalized nonlocal,
dynamic dielectric function, the inverse dielectric function, and the Dyson
equation for the dynamic screened potential in the framework of Bohm-Pines'
full and famous random-phase approximation...

text:
Ice formation is ubiquitous in nature, with important consequences in a
variety of environments, including biological cells, soil, aircraft,
transportation infrastructure and atmospheric clouds. However, its intrinsic
kinetics and microscopic mechanism are difficult to discern with current
experiments. Molecular simulations of ice nucleation are also challenging, and
direct rate calculations have only been performed for coarse-grained models of
wate. For molecular models, only indirect estimates have been obtained, e.g. by
assuming the validity of classical nucleation theory. We use a path sampling
approach to perform the first direct rate calculation of homogeneous nucleation
of ice in a molecular model of water. We use TIP4P/Ice, the most accurate among
existing molecular models for studying ice polymorphs. By using a novel
topological approach to distinguish different polymorphs, we are able to
identify a freezing mechanism that involves a competition between cubic and
hexagonal ice in the early stages of nucleation. In this competition, the cubic
polymorph takes over since the addition of new topological structural motifs
consistent with cubic ice leads to the formation of more compact crystallites.
This is not true for topological hexagonal motifs, which give rise to elongated
crystallites that are not able to grow. This leads to transition states that
are rich in cubic ice, and not the thermodynamically stable hexagonal
polymorph. This mechanism provides a molecular explanation to the earlier
experimental and computational observations of the preference for cubic ice in
the literature.

text:
Alfv\'enic fluctuations in the solar wind display many properties reflecting
an ongoing nonlinear cascade, e.g. a well-defined spectrum in frequency,
together with some characteristics more commonly associated with the linear
propagation of waves from the Sun, such as the variation of fluctuation
amplitude with distance, dominated by solar wind expansion effects. Therefore
both nonlinearities and expansion must be included simultaneously in any
successful model of solar wind turbulence evolution. Because of the disparate
spatial scales involved, direct numerical simulations of turbulence in the
solar wind represent an arduous task, especially if one wants to go beyond the
incompressible approximation. Indeed, most simulations neglect solar wind
expansion effects entirely. Here we develop a numerical model to simulate
turbulent fluctuations from the outer corona to 1 AU and beyond, including the
sub-Alfv\'enic corona. The accelerating expanding box (AEB) extends the
validity of previous expanding box models by taking into account both the
acceleration of the solar wind and the inhomogeneity of background density and
magnetic field. Our method incorporates a background accelerating wind within a
magnetic field that naturally follows the Parker spiral evolution using a
two-scale analysis in which the macroscopic spatial effect coupling
fluctuations with background gradients becomes a time-dependent coupling term
in a homogeneous box. In this paper we describe the AEB model in detail and
discuss its main properties, illustrating its validity by studying Alfv\'en
wave propagation across the Alfv\'en critical point.

text: This study investigates why women are 1.5 times more likely to leave the STEM pipeline after taking calculus compared to men, identifying mathematical confidence as a potential factor. The research involved a survey of 300 university students, predominantly from STEM fields, where participants were asked about their experiences with calculus, perceived mathematical ability, and career aspirations. Results indicate that women reported significantly lower self-assessment of their mathematical abilities and greater anxiety towards math tasks, particularly those involving calculus. To address these issues, we propose interventions such as fostering a supportive learning environment, encouraging problem-solving skills, and providing additional resources to enhance mathematical confidence. Our findings highlight the importance of addressing these psychological barriers to promote gender equality in STEM education and careers.

E.Korobkina et al., PRB 70,035409) results of measurement of temperature
dependence of losses of ultracold neutrons (UCN) in a range from 4 K to 300 K
at UCN storage in a copper trap are presented. At interpretation of
experimental data it was artificially considered only the difference of losses
rate 1/tau(T)= 1/tau_exp(T)- 1/tau_exp(10K), (tau - UCN storage time in the
trap). It has been accepted for temperature dependence of losses which changes
from 0 to 3.3*10-4 per one collision of UCN with a trap surface. However, the
analysis of raw experimental data shows that in a trap at temperature 10 K
there is losses 1.0*10-3 per collision. They are considerably (in 3 times) more
than discussed temperature dependence and almost 10 times more than losses due
to capture cross section on copper. It is the most probable that these losses
are connected with leakage of UCN through a slit of trap shutter. Change of the
size of a slits on 25% at change of temperature from 300K to 10K can quite
explain discussed temperature dependence. Certainly, hydrogen is present on a

55, No. 2 25 Jan.1992) temperature dependence in 3 times lower, even on the
undegased surfaces than on the degassed and deuterated surface in work [1]. At
last, deuteration of a trap surface allows almost completely to suppress

The vertex-random graphs called proximity catch digraphs (PCDs) have been
introduced recently and have applications in pattern recognition and spatial
pattern analysis. A PCD is a random directed graph (i.e., digraph) which is
constructed from data using the relative positions of the points from various
classes. Different PCDs result from different definitions of the proximity
region associated with each data point. We consider the underlying and
reflexivity graphs based on a family of PCDs which is determined by a family of
parameterized proximity maps called proportional-edge (PE) proximity map. The
graph invariant we investigate is the relative edge density of the underlying
and reflexivity graphs. We demonstrate that, properly scaled, relative edge
density of these graphs is a $U$-statistic, and hence obtain the asymptotic
normality of the relative edge density for data from any distribution that
satisfies mild regulatory conditions. By detailed probabilistic and geometric
calculations, we compute the explicit form of the asymptotic normal
distribution for uniform data on a bounded region in the usual Euclidean plane.
We also compare the relative edge densities of the two types of the graphs and
the relative arc density of the PE-PCDs. The approach presented here is also
valid for data in higher dimensions.

text: In this study, we employ genetic algorithms (GAs) to optimize the configuration of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) dish antennas. The primary objective is to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio while minimizing the total cost associated with antenna placement and data transmission. Problematically, the complex nature of the SKA system introduces numerous variables and constraints that traditional optimization methods struggle to handle effectively. Our approach utilizes GAs, which are adept at navigating through large solution spaces and adhering to complex rules and objectives simultaneously. We iteratively evolve potential configurations, guided by fitness functions that evaluate both signal quality and cost efficiency. Through simulations, we demonstrate that our GA-based optimization significantly improves upon initial designs, achieving higher signal clarity with reduced financial expenditure. Key insights include the importance of considering not just individual dish performance but also the synergistic effects across the entire array. This research provides a robust framework for future SKA design iterations, ensuring optimal performance within budgetary constraints.

text: In our study, we explore the stability of content within groups of highly cited publications across varying citation window lengths. We aimed to address the inconsistencies and perceived volatility in citation metrics that researchers encounter, particularly when citation data is aggregated over differing time frames. Our methodology involved a comprehensive analysis of citation patterns by selecting a diverse range of highly cited articles from prominent academic fields. We employed statistical techniques to assess the correlation between the longevity of citations and the thematic content of the publications over short, medium, and long citation windows.   Our results reveal a striking degree of stability in both the content and citation rates of these publications, suggesting that significant works maintain their relevance regardless of the timeframe applied. Furthermore, we identified key thematic elements that consistently emerged across the analyzed papers, contributing to their sustained citation status. Through clustering techniques, we delineated distinct groups of publications that not only retained high citation counts but also exhibited thematic coherence over time, reinforcing the notion that impactful research addresses enduring questions in their respective domains.   In conclusion, our findings advocate for a reconsideration of citation window lengths when evaluating scholarly impact, highlighting the importance of content stability over time. This research contributes to the broader discourse on citation analysis and informs strategies for the assessment of academic influence, emphasizing that a stable thematic core can signal lasting significance in scholarly contributions.

text: In our work, we investigate the significant issues arising from mis-modelling in gravitational wave astronomy, specifically focusing on the inadequacies of waveform templates used in signal detection and parameter estimation. Gravitational wave signals, primarily from binary mergers, necessitate highly accurate templates for effective signal extraction. However, we identify that the current models often fail to account for various physical phenomena such as spin dynamics, eccentricity, and environmental noise. Through a series of simulations, we assess the impact of these mis-modelling factors on detection rates and parameter estimates. Our results reveal that inaccuracies in template matching can lead to false alarms and substantial biases in inferred source properties, particularly affecting the localization of sources and the characterization of their intrinsic parameters. We propose an enhanced methodology that incorporates machine learning techniques to refine template generation, allowing for real-time adjustments based on detected signals. By expanding template banks to accommodate a broader parameter space, we demonstrate improved robustness against waveform mismatches. Our findings underscore the necessity for ongoing refinement of gravitational wave models, emphasizing the potential for enhanced observational capabilities and better understanding of cosmological events. This work contributes to the foundational understanding of template mis-modelling, providing a pathway towards the development of next-generation gravitational wave analysis tools that ensure more accurate astrophysical interpretations.

We study the degrees of freedom (DoF) of cellular networks in which a full
duplex (FD) base station (BS) equipped with multiple transmit and receive
antennas communicates with multiple mobile users. We consider two different
scenarios. In the first scenario, we study the case when half duplex (HD)
users, partitioned to either the uplink (UL) set or the downlink (DL) set,
simultaneously communicate with the FD BS. In the second scenario, we study the
case when FD users simultaneously communicate UL and DL data with the FD BS.
Unlike conventional HD only systems, inter-user interference (within the cell)
may severely limit the DoF, and must be carefully taken into account. With the
goal of providing theoretical guidelines for designing such FD systems, we
completely characterize the sum DoF of each of the two different FD cellular
networks by developing an achievable scheme and obtaining a matching upper
bound. The key idea of the proposed scheme is to carefully allocate UL and DL
information streams using interference alignment and beamforming techniques. By
comparing the DoFs of the considered FD systems with those of the conventional
HD systems, we establish the DoF gain by enabling FD operation in various
configurations. As a consequence of the result, we show that the DoF can
approach the two-fold gain over the HD systems when the number of users becomes
large enough as compared to the number of antennas at the BS.

text: This work presents a microscopic approach to investigating high-temperature superconductors, specifically focusing on the pseudogap phase. The main problem addressed is the elusive nature of the pseudogap state and its relationship to superconductivity in these materials. By utilizing advanced theoretical models and experimental data, we aim to elucidate the key characteristics and mechanisms underlying the pseudogap phase. Our results reveal that the pseudogap phase arises from the formation of pre-formed pairs above the superconducting transition temperature, indicating its significance in the superconducting behavior of high-temperature superconductors. Additionally, we demonstrate that the pseudogap features a suppression of electronic density of states near the Fermi level, pointing towards its impact on the electronic structure of these materials. The methodology employed in this study involves a combination of theoretical calculations based on the Hubbard model and analysis of experimental data from various spectroscopic techniques such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Overall, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the pseudogap phase in high-temperature superconductors, shedding light on its role in the unconventional behavior of these materials.

We study the following elliptic system concerning the fractional Laplacian
operator $$(- \Delta)^ {s_i} u_i = H_i ( u_1,\cdots,u_m) \ \ \text{in}\ \
\mathbb{R}^n,$$ when $0<s_i<1$, $u_i: \mathbb R^n\to R$ and $H_i$ belongs to
$C^{1,\gamma}(\mathbb{R}^m)$ for $\gamma > \max(0,1-2\min \left \{s_i \right
\})$ for $1\le i \le m$. The above system is called symmetric when the matrix
$\mathcal H=(\partial_j H_i(u_1,\cdots,u_m))_{i,j=1}^m$ is symmetric. The
notion of symmetric systems seems crucial to study this system with a general
nonlinearity $H=(H_i)_{i=1}^m$. We establish De Giorgi type results for stable
and $H$-monotone solutions of symmetric systems in lower dimensions that is
either $n=2$ and $0<s_i<1$ or $n=3$ and $1/2 \le \min\{s_i\}<1$. The case that
$n=3$ and at least one of parameters $s_i$ belongs to $(0,1/2)$ remains open as
well as the case $n \ge 4$. Applying a geometric Poincar\'{e} inequality, we
conclude that gradients of components of solutions are parallel in lower
dimensions when the system is coupled. More precisely, we show that the angle
between vectors $\nabla u_i$ and $\nabla u_j$ is exactly
$\arccos\left({|\partial_j H_i(u)|}/{\partial_j H_i(u)}\right)$. In addition,
we provide Hamiltonian identities, monotonicity formulae and Liouville
theorems. Lastly, we apply some of our main results to a two-component
nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger system, that is a particular case of the above
system, and we prove Liouville theorems and monotonicity formulae.

text: We investigate the isotopic yields associated with cold binary fission of even-even isotopes of Californium ($^{244}$Cf to $^{258}$Cf). Our work addresses the gaps in understanding the fission fragmentation processes and the corresponding isotopic distributions of these heavy isotopes. We employed a combination of theoretical modeling and computational simulations, utilizing the liquid drop model and statistical decay processes to predict fission yield trends among the isotopes studied. Our results reveal a systematic variation in the isotopic yields that correlates with neutron number, demonstrating an evolution of fragment distributions influenced by nuclear shell effects and deformation properties. Specifically, we identified a strong preference for lighter fission fragments, with notable yield peaks suggesting the influence of favored fission pathways. The isotopic yield data indicate a pronounced dependence on excitation energy and the distribution of angular momentum, which we delineated through angular distribution analysis. Furthermore, we contrasted our findings with existing experimental data, highlighting the implications for the understanding of fission dynamics in heavy nuclei. Our work not only elucidates the complex interactions governing the fission process of Californium isotopes but also contributes to refining fission yield predictions for applications in nuclear physics and nuclear waste management. By providing a comprehensive analysis of isotopic yields in cold binary fission, we aim to enhance the theoretical framework and experimental validation for future studies in the field of nuclear fission.

text: In this work, we delve into the intricacies of the neutrino mixing matrix and its implications on leptogenesis and lepton flavor violation. We begin by exploring the See-Saw Mechanism, which offers a theoretical explanation for the observed neutrino masses through the existence of heavy right-handed neutrinos. This mechanism also paves the way for the occurrence of leptogenesis, a process believed to have contributed significantly to the generation of matter asymmetry in the early universe.  We proceed by examining the effects of neutrino mixing on leptogenesis, with a specific focus on the role of CP violation. We observe that neutrino mixing brings about complex phenomena, such as the presence of resonant leptogenesis and the potential for an enhanced leptogenesis signal. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of neutrino mixing on lepton flavor violation, which arises due to the non-diagonal terms in the neutrino mass matrix. These terms lead to the observed lepton flavor oscillations and may also impact lepton flavor violating processes.  In order to elucidate these phenomena, we employ a thorough analysis based on the Seesaw Type-I model and its extensions. This study provides new insights into the interplay between neutrino mixing, leptogenesis, and lepton flavor violation, shedding light on the potential implications for future experiments and cosmological observations. Our findings demonstrate the significance of the See-Saw Mechanism and its ability to address long-standing questions in particle physics and cosmology.  In conclusion, this study underscores the importance of understanding the complex interplay between neutrino mixing, leptogenesis, and lepton flavor violation in the context of the See-Saw Mechanism. By examining the effects of neutrino mixing on these processes, we provide valuable insights into the underlying physics and potential implications for future research in this field.

Magnetized plasma jets are generally modeled as magnetic flux tubes filled
with flowing plasma governed by magnetohydrodynamics (MHD). We outline here a
more fundamental approach based on flux tubes of canonical vorticity, where
canonical vorticity is defined as the circulation of the species canonical
momentum. This approach extends the concept of magnetic flux tube evolution to
include the effects of finite particle momentum and enables visualization of
the topology of plasma jets in regimes beyond MHD. A flared, current-carrying
magnetic flux tube in an ion-electron plasma with finite ion momentum is thus
equivalent to either a pair of electron and ion flow flux tubes, a pair of
electron and ion canonical momentum flux tubes, or a pair of electron and ion
canonical vorticity flux tubes. We examine the morphology of all these flux
tubes for increasing electrical currents, different radial current profiles,
different electron Mach numbers, and a fixed, flared, axisymmetric magnetic
geometry. Calculations of gauge-invariant relative canonical helicities track
the evolution of magnetic, cross, and kinetic helicities in the system, and
show that ion flow fields can unwind to compensate for an increasing magnetic
twist. The results demonstrate that including a species finite momentum can
result in a very long collimated canonical vorticity flux tube even if the
magnetic flux tube is flared. With finite momentum, particle density gradients
must be normal to canonical vorticities, not to magnetic fields, so
observations of collimated astrophysical jets could be images of canonical
vorticity flux tubes instead of magnetic flux tubes.

We examine e+e- --> Ds^-D_s^{*+} and Ds^{*-}Ds^{+} interactions at 4170 MeV
using the CLEO-c detector in order to measure the decay constant fDs with good
precision. Previously our measurements were substantially higher than the most
precise lattice based QCD calculation of (241 +/- 3) MeV. Here we use the D_s^+
--> ell^+ nu channel, where the ell^+ designates either a mu^+ or a tau^+, when
the tau^+ --> pi^+ anti-nu. Analyzing both modes independently, we determine
B(D_s^+ --> mu^+ nu)= 0.565 +/- 0.045 +/- 0.017)%, and B(D_s^+ --> mu^+ nu)=
(6.42 +/- 0.81 +/- 0.18)%. We also analyze them simultaneously to find an
effective value of B^{eff}(D_s^+ --> mu^+ nu)= (0.591 +/- 0.037 +/- 0.018)% and
fDs=(263.3 +/- 8.2 +/- 3.9) MeV. Combining with the CLEO-c value determined
independently using D_s^+ --> tau^+ nu, tau^+ --> e^+ nu anti-nu decays, we
extract fDs=(259.5 +/- 6.6 +/- 3.1) MeV. Combining with our previous
determination of B(D^+ --> mu^+ nu), we extract the ratio fDs/fD+=1.26 +/- 0.06
+/- 0.02. No evidence is found for a CP asymmetry between Gamma(D_s^+ -->
mu^+\nu) and \Gamma(D_s^- --> mu^- nu); specifically the fractional difference
in rates is measured to be (4.8 +/- 6.1)%. Finally, we find B(D_s^+ --> e^+ nu)
< 1.2x10^{-4} at 90% confidence level.

text: We present a comprehensive global analysis for the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), aimed at enhancing our understanding of gravitational wave sources and optimizing the observatory's detection capabilities. Our study addresses the pressing challenge of accurately modeling the complex signals emitted by a variety of astrophysical phenomena. By employing a multi-faceted methodological approach, we integrate state-of-the-art computational tools with advanced data processing techniques. We developed sophisticated simulations to model the gravitational waveforms from potential sources, encompassing both well-characterized sources such as merging black holes and less understood events like cosmic string interactions. Utilizing Bayesian inference, we construct a robust framework to distinguish and categorize these signals amidst substantial noise inherent in LISA's space-based environment. Our results demonstrate a significant improvement in the detection horizon and parameter estimation precision for key targets, including massive black hole binaries and galactic binaries. Specifically, our findings suggest an approximately 25% increase in the sensitivity range and a 40% reduction in error margins for key event parameter estimation. Additionally, our analysis reveals potential for novel detections across a broader spectrum of frequency bands than previously considered. This work not only augments our ability to unravel the gravitational wave sky but also contributes vital insights into the design and implementation strategies of LISA. Through this rigorous global analysis, we lay critical groundwork for exploiting the full potential of LISA as a pioneering tool in gravitational wave astronomy.

We consider the ADE-series of (2, 0) supersymmetric quantum theories on T^5
\times R, where the first factor is a flat spatial five-torus, and the second
factor denotes time. The quantum states of such a theory \Phi are characterized
by a discrete quantum number f \in H^3 (T^5, C), where the finite abelian group
C is the center subgroup of the corresponding simply connected simply laced Lie
group G. At energies that are low compared to the inverse size of the T^5, the
spectrum consists of a set of continua of states, each of which is
characterized by the value of f and some number 5r of additional continuous
parameters. By exploiting the interpretation of this theory as the ultraviolet
completion of maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory on T^4 \times S^1
\times R with gauge group G_{adj} = G/C and coupling constant g given by the
square root of the radius of the S^1 factor, one may compute the number N_f^r
(\Phi) of such continua. We perform these calculations in detail for the A- and
D-series. While the Yang-Mills theory formalism is manifestly invariant under
the \SL_4 (Z) mapping class group of T^4, the results are actually found to be
invariant under the \SL_5 (Z) mapping class group of T^5, which provides a
strong consistency check.

text: This research investigates the challenges of maintaining stable and consistent membership in distributed systems at scale, particularly in the context of rapidly changing network topologies and increasing user engagement. The proliferation of social media platforms, online marketplaces, and other complex systems has highlighted the need for robust membership management mechanisms that can adapt to evolving user behaviors and network dynamics.  The objective of this study is to develop a novel membership management framework that ensures stable and consistent membership at scale, even in the face of rapid changes. The proposed framework leverages advanced data analytics and machine learning techniques to identify and mitigate potential membership instability, while also providing real-time monitoring and feedback mechanisms to support proactive maintenance and optimization.  The proposed framework consists of three primary components (1) a dynamic membership model that incorporates real-time network topology changes and user behavior patterns, (2) a machine learning-based prediction module that identifies potential membership instability and provides early warning signals, and (3) a feedback loop that enables real-time monitoring and adjustment of membership parameters. The proposed framework was evaluated through a comprehensive simulation study, which demonstrated its ability to maintain stable and consistent membership even in the face of rapid changes.  The key findings of this study suggest that the proposed framework can effectively mitigate membership instability and maintain stable and consistent membership at scale, even in rapidly changing network environments. The results also highlight the importance of real-time monitoring and feedback mechanisms in supporting proactive maintenance and optimization of membership management systems. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the development of robust membership management frameworks that can support the growth and scalability of complex distributed systems.

Key findings include the identification of distinct wave modes and their dependence on plasma parameters such as temperature, density, and particle mass. The study also examines how these waves interact with plasma turbulence and their potential applications in plasma diagnostics and control. The modification of Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) method with Riemann
Solver is called Godunov SPH. We further extend the Godunov SPH to the
description of a medium with negative pressure. Under certain circumstances,
the SPH method shows an unphysical instability that results in particle
clustering. This instability is called the tensile instability. The tensile
instability occurs in positive pressure regions in a regular fluid if a very
large number of neighbor particles are used with certain shapes of kernel
functions, and it is significant in negative pressure regions that emerge in
stretched elastic bodies. We must suppress the tensile instability in SPH for
calculations of elastic bodies. In this study, we develop a new technique to
remove the tensile instability by extending the Godunov SPH method and
conducting a linear stability analysis of the equation of motion for the
extended method. We find that the tensile instability can be suppressed by
choosing an appropriate order of interpolation in the equation of motion of the
Godunov SPH method. We also derive an analytic solution for a Riemann solver
for a simple equation of state of an elastic body, and construct a Godunov SPH
method for the equation of state that allows negative pressure.

text:
The current generation of ground-based coronagraphic instruments uses
deformable mirrors to correct for phase errors and to improve contrast levels
at small angular separations. Improving these techniques, several space and
ground based instruments are currently developed using two deformable mirrors
to correct for both phase and amplitude errors. However, as wavefront control
techniques improve, more complex telescope pupil geometries will soon be a
limiting factor for these next generation coronagraphic instru- ments. The
technique presented in this proceeding, the Active Correction of Aperture
Discontinuities method, is taking advantage of the fact that most future
coronagraphic instruments will include two deformable mirrors, and is proposing
to find the shapes and actuator movements to correct for the effect introduced
by these complex pupil geometries. We here present the results of the
parametric analysis realized on the WFIRST pupil for which we obtained high
contrast levels with several deformable mirror setups (size, separation between
them), coronagraphs (Vortex charge 2, vortex charge 4, APLC) and spectral
bandwidths. However, because contrast levels and separation are not the only
metrics to maximize the scientific return of an instrument, we also included in
this study the influence of these deformable mirror shapes on the throughput of
the instrument and sensitivity to pointing jitters. Finally, we present results
obtained on another potential space based telescope segmented aperture. The
main result of this proceeding is that we now obtain comparable performance
than the coronagraphs previously designed for WFIRST. First result from the
parametric analysis strongly suggest that the 2 deformable mirror set up (size
and distance between them) has a important impact on the performance in
contrast and throughput of the final instrument.
