text: This research paper investigates the mutual duality property within planar graphs, exploring its implications and potential applications. Building upon foundational theories in graph theory, the study aims to identify conditions under which two planar graphs exhibit mutual duality. To achieve this, a series of theoretical proofs and algorithmic tests were conducted. Key findings indicate that mutual duality can be established between certain planar graphs through specific configurations of their vertices and edges. Moreover, the results suggest that mutual duality significantly impacts the structural properties and computational complexity associated with planar graphs. The study concludes by proposing new algorithms for detecting mutual duality in planar graphs, which could have implications for various fields including network design and computational geometry.

text: In the realm of astronomical research, the analysis of stellar systems' orbits and Schwarzschild modeling play a significant role in understanding their structural and dynamic properties. This study presents a new computational code for the orbit analysis and Schwarzschild modeling of triaxial stellar systems. The new code, named OrbitTriax, is designed to efficiently handle the complexity of triaxial systems and provides improved accuracy compared to existing methods.  The background of this research focuses on the limitations of current methods used for analyzing the orbits and modeling triaxial stellar systems. These methods often struggle with the computational demands and lack the precision required to fully capture the intricacies of triaxial systems. To address these challenges, we develop OrbitTriax, a custom-built code designed specifically for triaxial systems.  The objective of this research is threefold first, to create an efficient and reliable code for orbit analysis in triaxial stellar systems; second, to improve the accuracy of Schwarzschild modeling in these systems; and third, to demonstrate the capabilities of OrbitTriax through application to realistic stellar systems.  The methodology employed involves the development and implementation of OrbitTriax, which uses a hybrid symplectic integrator for orbit analysis and a generalized Schwarzschild method for modeling. To validate the new code, we perform a series of benchmark tests and compare its results with those of existing methods.  Our key findings reveal that OrbitTriax outperforms existing methods in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy. By employing a symplectic integrator for orbit analysis, we reduce the errors induced by time discretization, leading to a more accurate description of the orbits. Furthermore, our generalized Schwarzschild method significantly improves the modeling of triaxial stellar systems, particularly in capturing the shapes and structural properties of these complex systems.  In conclusion, this study presents a new and powerful computational tool, OrbitTriax, for analyzing the orbits and modeling triaxial stellar systems. With its enhanced accuracy and computational efficiency, OrbitTriax opens up new avenues for research into the intricacies of stellar systems, providing valuable insights for both theoretical and observational astronomers.
label: machine

text: In this study, we have investigated the photodissociation of C$_{60}$ molecules under various excitation conditions to elucidate their structural dynamics and fragmentation patterns. Our methodology involved employing ultraviolet laser pulses to induce dissociation and analyzing the resulting fragments using mass spectrometry techniques. The results obtained revealed distinct fragmentation pathways, primarily leading to the formation of linear carbon chains, as well as smaller molecular species such as C$_{28}$, C$_{14}$, and C$_6$. These findings suggest that C$_{60}$ undergoes complex fragmentation processes, influenced by the initial electronic state of the molecule and the energy of the incident photon. Key insights include the observation that higher-energy photons facilitate more extensive dissociation, leading to a greater variety of products. The methodology employed combines high-resolution spectroscopy with advanced data analysis tools to extract detailed information on the photodissociation dynamics. This research not only contributes to our understanding of the fundamental chemistry of fullerene molecules but also provides foundational knowledge for applications in materials science and nanotechnology.
label: machine

text: We investigated the possibility that planetary encounters with Near Earth Asteroids (NEAs) could reset their surfaces, potentially altering their orbital characteristics and impacting the long-term dynamics of the asteroid belt. Our research focused on the effects of gravitational interactions between NEAs and planets, particularly Mars and Jupiter, on the asteroid's surface morphology and composition.  We conducted a series of numerical simulations, utilizing a high-fidelity asteroid model and incorporating the effects of gravitational perturbations, atmospheric drag, and surface processes. Our results indicate that planetary encounters can indeed cause significant surface resurfacing on NEAs, resulting in the formation of craters, valleys, and other geological features. The extent of surface resetting depends on various factors, including the asteroid's size, shape, and composition, as well as the magnitude and duration of the gravitational interaction.  Our findings suggest that planetary encounters may be an important mechanism for shaping the surfaces of NEAs, potentially influencing their orbital evolution and interactions with other asteroids and planets. We also propose that surface resetting could be a key process in the formation and evolution of NEAs, with implications for our understanding of the asteroid belt's history and the delivery of water and organic materials to the inner solar system.

text:
Unveiling the structure of the Broad Line Region (BLR) of AGNs is critical to
understand the quasar phenomenon. Resolving a few BLRs by optical
interferometry will bring decisive information to confront, complement and
calibrate the reverberation mapping technique, basis of the mass-luminosity
relation in quasars. BLRs are much smaller than the angular resolution of the
VLT and Keck interferometers and they can be resolved only by differential
interferometry very accurate measurements of differential visibility and phase
as a function of wavelength. The latter yields the photocenter variation with
wavelength, and constrains the size, position and velocity law of various
regions of the BLR. AGNs are below the magnitude limit for spectrally resolved
interferometry set by currently available fringe trackers. A new "blind"
observation method and a data processing based on the accumulation of 2D
Fourier power and cross spectra permitted us to obtain the first spectrally
resolved interferometric observation of a BLR, on the K=10 quasar 3C273. A
careful bias analysis is still in progress, but we report strong evidence that,
as the baseline increases, the differential visibility decreases in the
Pa-alpha line. Combined with a differential phase smaller than 3 degree, this
yields an angular equivalent radius of the BLR larger than 0.4 milliarcseconds,
or 1000 light days at the distance of 3C273, much larger than the reverberation
mapping radius of 300 light days. Explaining the coexistence of these two
different sizes, and possibly structures and mechanisms, implies very new
insights into the BLR of 3C273
label: human

While it is widely believed that the gravitational collapse of a sufficiently
large mass will lead to a density singularity and an event horizon, we propose
that this never happens when quantum effects are taken into account. In
particular, we propose that when the conditions become ripe for a trapped
surface to form, a quantum critical surface sweeps over the collapsing body,
transforming the nucleons in the collapsing matter into a lepton/photon gas
together with a positive vacuum energy. This will happen regardless of the
matter density at the time a trapped surface starts to form, and as a result we
predict that at least in all cases of gravitational collapse involving ordinary
matter, a large fraction of the rest mass of the collapsing matter will be
converted into a burst of neutrinos, and {\gamma}-rays. We predict that the
peak luminosity of these bursts is only weakly dependent on the mass of the
collapsing object, and is on the order of ({\epsilon}_q/m_Pc^2)^1/4c^5/G, where
{\epsilon}_q is the mean energy of a nucleon parton and m_P is the Planck mass.
The duration of the bursts will depend the mass of the collapsing objects; in
the case of stellar core collapse we predict that the duration of both the
neutrino and {\gamma}-ray bursts will be on the order of 10 seconds.

Hybrid semiconductor-superconductor quantum dot devices are tunable physical
realizations of quantum impurity models for a magnetic impurity in a
superconducting host. The binding energy of the localized sub-gap Shiba states
is set by the gate voltages and external magnetic field. In this work we
discuss the effects of the Zeeman spin splitting which is generically present
both in the quantum dot and in the (thin-film) superconductor. The unequal
$g$-factors in semiconductor and superconductor materials result in respective
Zeeman splittings of different magnitude. We consider both classical and
quantum impurities. In the first case we analytically study the spectral
function and the sub-gap states. The energy of bound states depends on the
spin-splitting of the Bogoliubov quasiparticle bands as a simple rigid shift.
For the case of collinear magnetization of impurity and host, the Shiba
resonance of a given spin polarization remains unperturbed when it overlaps
with the branch of the quasiparticle excitations of the opposite spin
polarization. In the quantum case, we employ numerical renormalization group
calculations to study the effect of the Zeeman field for different values of
the $g$-factors of the impurity and of the superconductor. We find that in
general the critical magnetic field for the singlet-doublet transition changes
non-monotonically as a function of the superconducting gap, demonstrating the
existence of two different transition mechanisms: Zeeman splitting of Shiba
states or gap closure due to Zeeman splitting of Bogoliubov states. We also
study how in the presence of spin-orbit coupling, modeled as an additional
non-collinear component of the magnetic field at the impurity site, the Shiba
resonance overlapping with the quasiparticle continuum of the opposite spin
gradually broadens and then merges with the continuum.
label: human

We consider cosmological dynamics in the theory of gravity with the scalar
field possessing a nonminimal kinetic coupling to gravity, $\kappa
G_{\mu\nu}\phi^{\mu}\phi^{\nu}$, and the power-law potential
$V(\phi)=V_0\phi^N$. Using the dynamical system method, we analyze all possible
asymptotical regimes of the model under investigation and show that for sloping
potentials with $0<N<2$ there exists a quasi-de Sitter asymptotic
$H={1}/{\sqrt{9\kappa}}$ corresponding to an early inflationary Universe. In
contrast to the standard inflationary scenario, the kinetic coupling inflation
does not depend on a scalar field potential and is only determined by the
coupling parameter $\kappa$. We obtain that there exist two different late-time
asymptotical regimes. The first one leads to the usual power-like cosmological
evolution with $H=1/3t$, while the second one represents the late-time
inflationary Universe with $H=1/\sqrt{3\kappa}$. This secondary inflationary
phase depends only on $\kappa$ and is a specific feature of the model with
nonminimal kinetic coupling. Additionally, an asymptotical analysis shows that
for the quadric potential with N=2 the asymptotical regimes remain
qualitatively the same, while the kinetic coupling inflation is impossible for
steep potentials with N>2. Using a numerical analysis, we also construct exact
cosmological solutions and find initial conditions leading to the initial
kinetic coupling inflation followed either by a "graceful" oscillatory exit or
by the secondary inflation.
label: human

text: Excitons in mono- and bilayer MoS$_2$ exhibit unique valley depolarization dynamics and the Valley Hall effect. In this study, we employ time-resolved spectroscopy techniques to investigate the valley depolarization dynamics in mono- and bilayer MoS$_2$ under various experimental conditions. The results demonstrate that monolayer MoS$_2$ exhibits faster valley depolarization dynamics than bilayer MoS$_2$, which can be attributed to the coupling of exciton-phonon interactions and the confinement effect in the monolayer. The Valley Hall effect, which arises from the interaction between the spin and orbital degrees of freedom in the conduction band, is investigated using polarization-resolved spectroscopy. Our findings reveal that the Valley Hall effect in mono- and bilayer MoS$_2$ can be controlled by applying an electric field, providing insights into the design of valleytronic devices. Overall, this work elucidates the fundamental physics of exciton valley dynamics and the Valley Hall effect in mono- and bilayer MoS$_2$, and paves the way for the development of valleytronic applications.   Excitons in mono- and bilayer MoS$_2$ display distinctive valley depolarization dynamics and the Valley Hall effect. Through time-resolved spectroscopy, we examine the valley depolarization in mono- and bilayer MoS$_2$ under diverse experimental scenarios. Our findings unveil quicker valley depolarization in monolayer MoS$_2$ than bilayer MoS$_2$, caused by exciton-phonon interactions and confinement effects in the monolayer. Polarization-resolved spectroscopy is employed to probe the Valley Hall effect, which emerges from the spin-orbital coupling in the conduction band. Our results indicate that the Valley Hall effect in mono- and bilayer MoS$_2$ is controllable via electric fields, shedding light on the engineering of valleytronic devices. This study offers a deeper understanding of exciton valley dynamics and the Valley Hall effect in mono- and bilayer MoS$_2$, and lays the groundwork for the advancement of valleytronic applications.
label: machine

We present new and accurate radial velocity (RV) measurements of luminous
stars of all ages (old horizontal branch, intermediate--age red clump, and
young blue plume, as well as red giants of a range of ages; 20.6<V<22) in the
Carina dwarf spheroidal galaxy, based on low-resolution spectra collected with
the FORS2 multi-object slit spectrograph at the VLT. This data set was
complemented by RV measurements based on medium and high-resolution archive
spectra of brighter (V<20.6) Carina targets collected with the GIRAFFE
multi-object fiber spectrograph at the VLT. The combined sample includes more
than 21,340 individual spectra of ~2,000 stars covering the entire body of the
galaxy. To further improve the statistics, the accurate RV measurements
recently provided by Walker et al.(2007) were also added to the current data
set. We ended up with a sample of ~1,370 RV measurements of candidate Carina
stars that is ~75% larger than any previous Carina RV sample. The mean RV
across the body of the galaxy varies from ~220 km/s at a distance of 7arcmin
(~200 pc) from the center to ~223 km/s at 13arcmin, (~400 pc, 6sigma level) and
flattens out to a constant value of ~221 km/s at larger distances (600 pc,
4sigma level). Moreover and even more importantly, we found that in the Carina
regions where the mean RV is smaller the dispersion is also smaller, and the RV
distribution is more centrally peaked (i.e. the kurtosis attains larger
values). There is evidence of a secondary maximum in RV across the Carina
center (|D|<200 pc). The occurrence of a secondary feature across the Carina
center is also supported by the flat-topped radial distribution based on the
photometric catalog.

We consider the boundary value problem \begin{equation} - \Delta u = \lambda
c(x)u+ \mu(x) |\nabla u|^2 + h(x), \qquad u \in H^1_0(\Omega) \cap
L^{\infty}(\Omega), \leqno{(P_{\lambda})} \end{equation} where $\Omega \subset
\R^N, N \geq 3$ is a bounded domain with smooth boundary. It is assumed that
$c\gneqq 0$, $c,h$ belong to $L^p(\Omega)$ for some $p > N$. Also $\mu \in
L^{\infty}(\Omega)$ and $\mu \geq \mu_1 >0$ for some $\mu_1 \in \R$. It is
known that when $\lambda \leq 0$, problem $(P_{\lambda})$ has at most one
solution. In this paper we study, under various assumptions, the structure of
the set of solutions of $(P_{\lambda})$ assuming that $\lambda>0$. Our study
unveils the rich structure of this problem. We show, in particular, that what
happen for $\lambda=0$ influences the set of solutions in all the half-space
$]0,+\infty[\times(H^1_0(\Omega) \cap L^{\infty}(\Omega))$. Most of our results
are valid without assuming that $h$ has a sign. If we require $h$ to have a
sign, we observe that the set of solutions differs completely for $h\gneqq 0$
and $h\lneqq 0$. We also show when $h$ has a sign that solutions not having
this sign may exists. Some uniqueness results of signed solutions are also
derived. The paper ends with a list of open problems.
label: human

We study in detail the impact of dynamical quarks on the gluon mass
generation mechanism, in the Landau gauge, for the case of a small number of
quark families. As in earlier considerations, we assume that the main bulk of
the unquenching corrections to the gluon propagator originates from the fully
dressed quark-loop diagram. The nonperturbative evaluation of this diagram
provides the key relation that expresses the unquenched gluon propagator as a
deviation from its quenched counterpart. This relation is subsequently coupled
to the integral equation that controls the momentum evolution of the effective
gluon mass, which contains a single adjustable parameter; this constitutes a
major improvement compared to the analysis presented in Phys. Rev. D86 (2012)
014032, where the behaviour of the gluon propagator in the deep infrared was
estimated through numerical extrapolation. The resulting nonlinear system is
then treated numerically, yielding unique solutions for the modified gluon mass
and the quenched gluon propagator, which fully confirm the picture put forth
recently in several continuum and lattice studies. In particular, an infrared
finite gluon propagator emerges, whose saturation point is considerably
suppressed, due to a corresponding increase in the value of the gluon mass.
This characteristic feature becomes more pronounced as the number of active
quark families increases, and can be deduced from the infrared structure of the
kernel entering in the gluon mass equation.
label: human

text: In our work, we address the challenge of action recognition and detection by introducing Transition Forests, a novel approach that leverages discriminative temporal transitions. The core contribution of this research lies in the development of a framework that captures temporal dependencies between video frames, enabling the model to distinguish between subtle transitions within complex action sequences. We employ a data-driven strategy that constructs a forest of decision trees, each specifically tailored to model temporal transitions through hierarchically structured sequences. By integrating transition-based features as opposed to static ones, our model demonstrates significant improvements in capturing the dynamics of actions over time.  Using an extensive dataset of video sequences for model training and evaluation, we observed substantial advancements in both recognition accuracy and detection precision. Our experiments on benchmark datasets revealed a notable enhancement in distinguishing short-lived actions from similar context, which is a persistent challenge in existing methods. The precision, recall, and F1-score metrics significantly improved, validating our hypothesis that temporal transitions hold critical information for action understanding.  Through comprehensive analysis, we also demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in action recognition and detection, particularly in scenarios involving overlapping or rapidly switching actions. The adaptability of Transition Forests to various video contexts showcases its robustness and potential application in real-world scenarios. Our approach offers a promising direction for future research in leveraging temporal dynamics for improved performance in video data analysis.
label: machine

text:
(abridged) Observations of Faraday rotation for extragalactic sources probe
magnetic fields both inside and outside the Milky Way. Building on our earlier
estimate of the Galactic contribution, we set out to estimate the extragalactic
contributions. We discuss the problems involved; in particular, we point out
that taking the difference between the observed values and the Galactic
foreground reconstruction is not a good estimate for the extragalactic
contributions. We point out a degeneracy between the contributions to the
observed values due to extragalactic magnetic fields and observational noise
and comment on the dangers of over-interpreting an estimate without taking into
account its uncertainty information. To overcome these difficulties, we develop
an extended reconstruction algorithm based on the assumption that the
observational uncertainties are accurately described for a subset of the data,
which can overcome the degeneracy with the extragalactic contributions. We
present a probabilistic derivation of the algorithm and demonstrate its
performance using a simulation, yielding a high quality reconstruction of the
Galactic Faraday rotation foreground, a precise estimate of the typical
extragalactic contribution, and a well-defined probabilistic description of the
extragalactic contribution for each data point. We then apply this
reconstruction technique to a catalog of Faraday rotation observations. We vary
our assumptions about the data, showing that the dispersion of extragalactic
contributions to observed Faraday depths is most likely lower than 7 rad/m^2,
in agreement with earlier results, and that the extragalactic contribution to
an individual data point is poorly constrained by the data in most cases.
label: human
