We report the discovery by the CoRoT space mission of a new giant planet,
CoRoT-20b. The planet has a mass of 4.24 +/- 0.23 MJ and a radius of 0.84 +/-
0.04 RJ. With a mean density of 8.87 +/- 1.10 g/cm^3, it is among the most
compact planets known so far. Evolution models for the planet suggest a mass of
heavy elements of the order of 800 ME if embedded in a central core, requiring
a revision either of the planet formation models or of planet evolution and
structure models. We note however that smaller amounts of heavy elements are
expected from more realistic models in which they are mixed throughout the
envelope. The planet orbits a G-type star with an orbital period of 9.24 days
and an eccentricity of 0.56. The star's projected rotational velocity is vsini
= 4.5 +/- 1.0 km/s, corresponding to a spin period of 11.5 +/- 3.1 days if its
axis of rotation is perpendicular to the orbital plane. In the framework of
Darwinian theories and neglecting stellar magnetic breaking, we calculate the
tidal evolution of the system and show that CoRoT-20b is presently one of the
very few Darwin-stable planets that is evolving towards a triple synchronous
state with equality of the orbital, planetary and stellar spin periods.
label: human

text: This study investigates the high-resolution spectroscopy of a young, low-metallicity, optically-thin star-forming galaxy located in the early universe at a redshift of z=3.12, with a luminosity of L=0.02L*. The primary objective is to characterize the metallicity and ionization conditions prevalent in such distant galaxies and enhance our understanding of early galactic evolution. Utilizing spectral data from the Very Large Telescope (VLT) equipped with the X-shooter instrument, we conducted a detailed spectroscopic analysis to ascertain the chemical composition and physical conditions in this galaxy. Our methodology involved measuring key emission and absorption lines, allowing us to derive metallicity and analyze ionization parameters through photoionization modeling. The high signal-to-noise ratio enabled precise measurements of the low metallicity, which was found to be considerably lower than solar, corroborating the galaxy's nascent state. Additionally, the spectroscopy revealed dominant features of an optically-thin medium, characterized by prominent Lyman-alpha emission and weak continuum absorption. Key findings include the detection of chemical inhomogeneities and the presence of intense star-forming regions despite the low luminosity. The data suggest vigorous star formation activity, akin to what is observed in compact, young galaxies. Conclusively, this work provides insights into the elemental formation and the evolution of star-forming galaxies during the high-redshift epoch. It underscores the significance of high-resolution spectral observations in characterizing galaxies in the early universe, offering implications for cosmological models of galaxy formation and evolution.
label: machine

text: The study of the distributive properties of rational numbers forms a fundamental component of number theory and algebra. This research paper aims to explore the underlying principles and applications of distributive properties among rational numbers, specifically focusing on their arithmetic operations and implications within broader mathematical contexts. Utilizing a combination of theoretical analysis and practical examples, the methodology includes an examination of distributive laws, such as the distributive property of multiplication over addition and its applicability to both simple and complex rational expressions. Key findings reveal that the distributive property holds consistently across various operations involving rational numbers, reinforcing its significance in simplifying expressions and solving equations. Furthermore, through the exploration of rational number properties, this study also highlights the interplay between distribution and other mathematical concepts such as fractions, decimals, and percentages. The results indicate that a deep understanding of distributive properties not only enhances computational skills but also fosters a greater comprehension of higher-level mathematics. In conclusion, this research underscores the importance of distributive properties in the realm of rational numbers and advocates for their integration into educational curricula to promote mathematical literacy and logical reasoning. The implications of these findings extend to practical applications in fields such as finance, engineering, and computer science, thereby demonstrating the essential role of rational distributive properties in day-to-day problem-solving scenarios.
label: machine

text:
Visual patterns represent the discernible regularity in the visual world.
They capture the essential nature of visual objects or scenes. Understanding
and modeling visual patterns is a fundamental problem in visual recognition
that has wide ranging applications. In this paper, we study the problem of
visual pattern mining and propose a novel deep neural network architecture
called PatternNet for discovering these patterns that are both discriminative
and representative. The proposed PatternNet leverages the filters in the last
convolution layer of a convolutional neural network to find locally consistent
visual patches, and by combining these filters we can effectively discover
unique visual patterns. In addition, PatternNet can discover visual patterns
efficiently without performing expensive image patch sampling, and this
advantage provides an order of magnitude speedup compared to most other
approaches. We evaluate the proposed PatternNet subjectively by showing
randomly selected visual patterns which are discovered by our method and
quantitatively by performing image classification with the identified visual
patterns and comparing our performance with the current state-of-the-art. We
also directly evaluate the quality of the discovered visual patterns by
leveraging the identified patterns as proposed objects in an image and compare
with other relevant methods. Our proposed network and procedure, PatterNet, is
able to outperform competing methods for the tasks described.
label: human

text: This study investigates the generalisation of unit-refutation completeness and Strong Linear Unification Resolution (SLUR) via nested input resolution. Unit-refutation completeness is a fundamental property of resolution-based proof systems, ensuring that every refutation of a set of clauses can be transformed into a unit-refutation. SLUR is a variant of resolution that extends the linear unification of variables with constants. However, the existing literature on unit-refutation completeness and SLUR focuses primarily on the resolution systems with a single input, resulting in limited applicability to more complex scenarios.  To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework for nested input resolution, which enables the extension of unit-refutation completeness and SLUR to more intricate proof systems. Our approach involves integrating multiple input streams into a single resolution system, allowing for the exploration of a larger solution space. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework by providing a formal proof of unit-refutation completeness and SLUR via nested input resolution. The key findings of this study show that the proposed framework can generalise unit-refutation completeness and SLUR to a wider range of resolution systems, including those with multiple input streams. This work contributes to the advancement of resolution-based proof systems, enabling the development of more powerful and flexible proof assistants.
label: machine

text:
Interacting fermions on a lattice can develop strong quantum correlations,
which lie at the heart of the classical intractability of many exotic phases of
matter. Seminal efforts are underway in the control of artificial quantum
systems, that can be made to emulate the underlying Fermi-Hubbard models.
Electrostatically confined conduction band electrons define interacting quantum
coherent spin and charge degrees of freedom that allow all-electrical
pure-state initialisation and readily adhere to an engineerable Fermi-Hubbard
Hamiltonian. Until now, however, the substantial electrostatic disorder
inherent to solid state has made attempts at emulating Fermi-Hubbard physics on
solid-state platforms few and far between. Here, we show that for gate-defined
quantum dots, this disorder can be suppressed in a controlled manner. Novel
insights and a newly developed semi-automated and scalable toolbox allow us to
homogeneously and independently dial in the electron filling and
nearest-neighbour tunnel coupling. Bringing these ideas and tools to fruition,
we realize the first detailed characterization of the collective Coulomb
blockade transition, which is the finite-size analogue of the
interaction-driven Mott metal-to-insulator transition. As automation and device
fabrication of semiconductor quantum dots continue to improve, the ideas
presented here show how quantum dots can be used to investigate the physics of
ever more complex many-body states.
label: human

text: This study examines the interplay between theoretical models of massive star evolution and explosion mechanisms, and empirical evidence derived from remnant mass measurements. The evolution of massive stars (M > 8M) is a complex process involving intense nuclear burning, intense stellar winds, and ultimately, explosive mass loss. Despite significant advances in our understanding of these processes, there remains a discrepancy between theoretical models and observational data regarding the masses of compact remnants, such as neutron stars and black holes.  The objective of this research is to reconcile this discrepancy by investigating the role of remnant mass measurements in constraining theoretical models of massive star evolution and explosion mechanisms. A comprehensive review of existing literature on massive star evolution, explosion mechanisms, and remnant mass measurements is conducted, highlighting the current limitations and uncertainties in these fields.  A novel approach is employed to quantify the impact of remnant mass measurements on theoretical models, utilizing a combination of analytical and numerical techniques. The results indicate that remnant mass measurements provide a critical constraint on theoretical models, highlighting the importance of considering the effects of mass loss on the evolution of massive stars. The findings suggest that a more nuanced understanding of massive star evolution and explosion mechanisms is required to reconcile the discrepancy between theoretical models and observational data.  Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to a more accurate understanding of massive star evolution and explosion mechanisms, and to inform the development of more precise models that can be tested against empirical data.
label: machine

text: This research paper explores the feasibility of utilizing a Linear Sigma Model (LSM) to describe walking gauge theories at low energies. The objective of this study is to investigate whether the LSM, originally developed in the context of QCD (Quantum Chromodynamics), can accurately represent the unique features of walking gauge theories, specifically focusing on their behavior at low energy scales. To achieve this goal, an extensive computational methodology is employed, involving the analysis of the LSM parameters and their impact on the walking behavior of the gauge theories under consideration.   Key findings indicate that while the LSM exhibits promising capabilities in capturing certain aspects of walking gauge theories at low energies, discrepancies arise when attempting to model the full spectrum of their behavior accurately. The study highlights the importance of considering the specific characteristics of walking gauge theories when employing the LSM framework and emphasizes the need for further refinement and development to enhance its efficacy in this context.   In conclusion, this research contributes valuable insights into the potential application of the LSM in describing walking gauge theories at low energies, shedding light on both its strengths and limitations in capturing the intricate dynamics of these theories. Further research and refinement of the LSM framework are needed to fully elucidate the behavior of walking gauge theories at low energy scales.
label: machine

text: In this study, we introduce a novel approach named Glyph Sorting, designed to address the challenges of visualizing multi-dimensional datasets through interactive graphics. This methodology aims to enhance the interpretability and analytical efficiency of complex data by leveraging the glyph-based representation framework. By sorting and organizing data using visually distinct glyphs, our approach allows users to intuitively grasp intricate relationships and discern patterns across multiple dimensions. We employ a combination of multidimensional scaling algorithms and user-defined parameters, enabling dynamic interaction and real-time adjustments. Through comprehensive experimentation, we demonstrate that our Glyph Sorting technique significantly improves data comprehension compared to traditional visualization methods such as scatter plots and heatmaps. User evaluations with domain experts reveal that our interactive visualization system facilitates a more accessible exploration of data, ultimately leading to enhanced decision-making capabilities. Key results highlight a reduction in cognitive load and an increase in the accuracy of insights derived from complex datasets. We systematically validate our approach using synthetic and real-world datasets across various domains, confirming its adaptability and robustness. By integrating feedback mechanisms within the interface, we ensure that the visualization accommodates individual user preferences, thereby promoting a personalized analysis experience. Our findings underscore the potential of Glyph Sorting to revolutionize how data scientists and analysts interact with and interpret multi-dimensional data, paving the way for more informed and insightful data-driven conclusions. Future research will focus on further refining our algorithms and expanding the applicability of our tool across other fields and data types.
label: machine

text:
Context. Dome Fuji, the second highest region on the Antarctic plateau, is
expected to have some of the best astronomical seeing on Earth. However, site
testing at Dome Fuji is still in its very early stages.
  Aims. To investigate the astronomical seeing in the free atmosphere above
Dome Fuji, and to determine the height of the surface boundary layer.
  Methods. A Differential Image Motion Monitor was used to measure the seeing
in the visible (472 nm) at a height of 11 m above the snow surface at Dome Fuji
during the austral summer of 2012/2013.
  Results. Seeing below 0.2'' has been observed. The seeing often has a local
minimum of ~0.3'' near 18 h local time. Some periods of excellent seeing, 0.3''
or smaller, were also observed, sometimes extending for several hours at local
midnight. The median seeing is higher, at 0.52''---this large value is believed
to be caused by periods when the telescope was within the turbulent boundary
layer.
  Conclusions. The diurnal variation of the daytime seeing at Dome Fuji is
similar to that reported for Dome C, and the height of the surface boundary
layer is consistent with previous simulations for Dome Fuji. The free
atmosphere seeing is ~0.2'', and the height of the surface boundary layer can
be as low as ~11 m.
label: human

text: Differentially rotating stars exhibit low T/W dynamical instabilities characterized by the presence of unstable normal modes. Understanding these modes is crucial for comprehending the dynamic behavior of rotating stars.   This research aims to investigate the properties of unstable normal modes in differentially rotating stars and their implications on the stability of such systems. The focus is on identifying the conditions that lead to the emergence of these unstable modes and analyzing their behavior.   We employ numerical simulations to study the normal modes of low T/W dynamical instabilities in differentially rotating stars. By varying parameters such as rotation profiles and stellar structures, we explore the characteristics of these unstable modes and their dependence on the underlying physical properties.   Our analysis reveals the presence of various unstable normal modes in differentially rotating stars, each associated with specific rotation profiles and radial structures. We observe a correlation between the mode frequencies and the degree of differential rotation, shedding light on the mechanisms governing these instabilities.   In conclusion, this study enhances our understanding of the unstable normal modes present in low T/W dynamical instabilities of differentially rotating stars. The findings contribute to the broader knowledge of stellar dynamics and have implications for the stability and evolution of rotating stellar systems.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the characteristics of RR Lyrae variable stars and their relation to the horizontal branch in the globular cluster NGC 5904 (M5). Our research addresses the challenge of accurately characterizing the properties of RR Lyrae stars to enhance our understanding of stellar evolution within globular clusters. Utilizing photometric data obtained from advanced telescopes, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of RR Lyrae light curves, focusing on their periods, amplitudes, and pulsation modes. We employed Fourier decomposition techniques to refine period determinations and employed period-luminosity and period-amplitude relations to derive precise distance measurements to the cluster.  Our findings enhance the horizontal branch structure within M5, revealing a well-defined collection of RR Lyrae stars that demarcates the instability strip. We observe a bimodal period distribution, indicative of both fundamental mode (RRab) and first-overtone (RRc) pulsators, synchronized with recent theoretical models. The derived mean metallicity [Fe/H] aligns with prior spectroscopic studies, confirming the homogeneous chemical composition among the RR Lyrae population.  Our results demonstrate the critical link between RR Lyrae variability and horizontal branch morphology, supporting models of cluster age and helioseismic processes. Methodologically, our approach has led to precise calibration of RR Lyrae absolute magnitudes, improving the accuracy of M5’s distance estimate. This study contributes to the broader understanding of the evolutionary processes influencing horizontal branch stars and reinforces the value of photometric investigations in constraining the parameters of globular clusters.
label: machine

text: This paper investigates RF-based energy harvesting in decode-and-forward relaying systems with a focus on ergodic and outage capacities. The primary aim is to optimize energy efficiency in wireless communication networks by utilizing energy harvested from the radio frequency signals. Through theoretical analysis and simulations, we address the challenges of harvested energy integration and transmission for decode-and-forward relaying scenarios. Our results reveal the impact of energy-harvesting capabilities on the system's overall capacity, particularly in terms of ergodic and outage capacities. We propose novel strategies to enhance the performance of relaying systems by leveraging the harvested energy effectively. Our methodology involves deriving analytical expressions for ergodic and outage capacities while considering the energy harvesting process and transmission protocols. By exploring the trade-offs between energy consumption, transmission reliability, and system capacity, we offer insights into the interplay between energy harvesting and communication quality in relaying systems. This study contributes to the advancement of energy-aware communication networks, shedding light on the potential benefits and challenges associated with RF-based energy harvesting techniques in decode-and-forward relaying systems.
label: machine

text: This study investigates the system parameters, transit times, and secondary eclipses of exoplanets orbiting the stars HAT-P-4, TrES-2, TrES-3, and WASP-3 using data from the NASA EPOXI Mission of Opportunity. Our analysis reveals precise orbital periods and semi-major axes for each planet, enabling us to refine their masses and radii through transit timing variations (TTVs) and secondary eclipse depths. The methodology involves rigorous statistical analysis and modeling techniques to account for observational uncertainties and instrumental effects. Key findings indicate that the planets exhibit significant TTVs, which are crucial for understanding the gravitational interactions within these multi-planet systems. Secondary eclipse observations also provide valuable constraints on stellar limb darkening laws, enhancing our ability to model planetary atmospheres. Overall, this work contributes to the comprehensive characterization of these exoplanetary systems, providing insights into their dynamical properties and potential habitability.
label: machine

text:
Information about the neutron-star equation of state is encoded in the
waveform of a black hole-neutron star system through tidal interactions and the
possible tidal disruption of the neutron star. During the inspiral this
information depends on the tidal deformability Lambda of the neutron star, and
we find that Lambda is the best measured parameter during the merger and
ringdown as well. We performed 134 simulations where we systematically varied
the equation of state as well as the mass ratio, neutron star mass, and aligned
spin of the black hole. Using these simulations we have developed an analytic
representation of the full inspiral-merger-ringdown waveform calibrated to
these numerical waveforms, and we use this analytic waveform to estimate the
accuracy to which Lambda can be measured with gravitational-wave detectors. We
find that although the inspiral tidal signal is small, coherently combining
this signal with the merger-ringdown matter effect improves the measurability
of Lambda by a factor of ~3 over using just the merger-ringdown matter effect
alone. However, incorporating correlations between all the waveform parameters
then decreases the measurability of Lambda by a factor of ~3. The uncertainty
in Lambda increases with the mass ratio, but decreases as the black hole spin
increases. Overall, a single Advanced LIGO detector can measure Lambda for mass
ratios Q = 2--5, black hole spins J_BH/M_BH^2 = -0.5--0.75, neutron star masses
M_NS = 1.2M_sun--1.45M_sun, and an optimally oriented distance of 100Mpc to an
uncertainty of ~10%--100%. For the proposed Einstein Telescope, the uncertainty
in Lambda is an order of magnitude smaller.
label: human

text:
We use the CARMA millimeter interferometer to map the Antennae Galaxies
(NGC4038/39), tracing the bulk of the molecular gas via the 12CO(1-0) line and
denser molecular gas via the high density transitions HCN(1-0), HCO+(1-0),
CS(2-1), and HNC(1-0). We detect bright emission from all tracers in both the
two nuclei and three locales in the overlap region between the two nuclei.
These three overlap region peaks correspond to previously identified
"supergiant molecular clouds". We combine the CARMA data with Herschel infrared
(IR) data to compare observational indicators of the star formation efficiency
(SFR/H2~IR/CO), dense gas fraction (HCN/CO), and dense gas star formation
efficiency (IR/HCN). Regions within the Antennae show ratios consistent with
those seen for entire galaxies, but these ratios vary by up to a factor of 6
within the galaxy. The five detected regions vary strongly in both their
integrated intensities and these ratios. The northern nucleus is the brightest
region in mm-wave line emission, while the overlap region is the brightest part
of the system in the IR. We combine the CARMA and Herschel data with ALMA CO
data to report line ratio patterns for each bright point. CO shows a declining
spectral line energy distribution, consistent with previous studies. HCO+(1-0)
emission is stronger than HCN(1-0) emission, perhaps indicating either more gas
at moderate densities or higher optical depth than is commonly seen in more
advanced mergers.
label: human

text:
We report the experimental observation of spin reorientation in the double
perovskite Ho$_2$FeCoO$_6$. The magnetic phase transitions in this compound are
characterized and studied through magnetization and specific heat, and the
magnetic structures are elucidated by neutron powder diffraction. Two magnetic
phase transitions are observed in this compound - one at $T_\mathrm{N1}
\approx$ 250~K, from paramagnetic to antiferromagnetic, and the other at
$T_\mathrm{N2} \approx$ 45~K, from a phase with mixed magnetic structures to a
single phase through a spin reorientation process. The magnetic structure in
the temperature range 200~K - 45~K is a mixed phase of the irreducible
representations $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_3$, both of which are antiferromagnetic.
The phase with mixed magnetic structures that exists in Ho$_2$FeCoO$_6$ gives
rise to a large thermal hysteresis in magnetization that extends from 200~K
down to the spin reorientation temperature. At $T_\mathrm{N2}$, the magnetic
structure transforms to $\Gamma_1$. Though long-range magnetic order is
established in the transition metal lattice, it is seen that only short-range
magnetic order prevails in Ho$^{3+}$ - lattice. Our results should motivate
further detailed studies on single crystals in order to explore spin
reorientation process, spin switching and the possibility of anisotropic
magnetic interactions giving rise to electric polarization in Ho$_2$FeCoO$_6$.
label: human

text: This study investigates the velocity power spectrum in supersonic turbulence using hierarchical Bayesian analysis, a method that provides a robust framework for understanding complex statistical models. The objective of this research is to elucidate the underlying structures of supersonic turbulence and to quantify the impact of various parameters on the velocity power spectrum. Utilizing high-resolution observational data, we apply a hierarchical Bayesian modeling approach that accounts for the inherent uncertainties in the measurements and model assumptions. The methodology involves defining a hierarchical framework comprising priors and likelihood functions tailored to the turbulence characteristics, facilitating the estimation of parameters through Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling.  Key findings reveal that the velocity power spectrum exhibits strong dependency on the Mach number and intermittency of turbulence. Specifically, the results show a distinct scaling behavior that is consistent with theoretical predictions, highlighting the interplay between turbulence intensity and spectral energy distribution. Additionally, sensitivity analyses indicate that variations in the parameterization significantly alter the spectral indices, reinforcing the necessity for a comprehensive Bayesian approach in turbulence studies.  In conclusion, the application of hierarchical Bayesian analysis in this research provides deeper insights into the velocity power spectrum behavior in supersonic turbulence. It underscores the relevance of complex modeling techniques in astrophysical studies and enhances our understanding of turbulent flows in astrophysical environments, potentially informing future observational and theoretical explorations.
label: machine

text:
The polynomial chaos (PC) expansion has been widely used as a surrogate model
in the Bayesian inference to speed up the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)
calculations. However, the use of a PC surrogate introduces the modeling error,
that may severely distort the estimate of the posterior distribution. This
error can be corrected by increasing the order of the PC expansion, but the
cost for building the surrogate may increase dramatically. In this work, we
seek to address this challenge by proposing an adaptive procedure to construct
a multi-fidelity PC surrogate. This new strategy combines (a large number of)
low-fidelity surrogate model evaluations and (a small number of) high-fidelity
model evaluations, yielding an adaptive multi-fidelity approach. Here the
low-fidelity surrogate is chosen as the prior-based PC surrogate, while the
high-fidelity model refers to the true forward model. The key idea is to
construct and refine the multi-fidelity approach over a sequence of samples
adaptively determined form data, so that the approximation can eventually
concentrate to the posterior distribution. We illustrate the performance of the
proposed strategy through two nonlinear inverse problems. It is shown that the
proposed adaptive multi-fidelity approach can improve significantly the
accuracy, yet without a dramatic increase in the computational complexity. The
numerical results also indicate that our new algorithm can enhance the
efficiency by several orders of magnitude compared to a standard MCMC approach
using only the true forward model.
label: human

text: We investigated the gas content of normal galaxies, shedding light on the gas-rich early universe and the evolution of galaxy morphology. Through a comprehensive analysis of stellar and interstellar medium (ISM) properties, we found that normal galaxies possess a diverse range of gas content, from gas-poor dwarf galaxies to gas-rich spiral galaxies. Our results indicate that the gas content of normal galaxies is strongly correlated with their stellar mass, with more massive galaxies exhibiting higher gas fractions.  We developed a novel approach to quantify gas content, combining stellar mass loss rates, star formation rates, and ISM properties. This method allowed us to reconstruct the gas content of galaxies at different stages of their evolution, revealing a complex interplay between gas accretion, star formation, and galaxy mergers. Our simulations suggest that the gas content of normal galaxies is influenced by the interplay between gas accretion and galaxy mergers, with galaxies that experience more frequent mergers exhibiting higher gas fractions.  Our findings provide new insights into the two-phase galaxy formation paradigm, highlighting the importance of gas content in shaping galaxy morphology and evolution. We propose that the gas-rich early universe gave rise to the formation of normal galaxies, which subsequently evolved through a process of gas accretion and star formation. Our results have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution and the formation of structure in the universe, and will inform future studies of galaxy formation and evolution.
label: machine

text:
We study equal and unequal-mass neutron star mergers by means of new
numerical relativity simulations in which the general relativistic
hydrodynamics solver employs an algorithm that guarantees mass conservation
across the refinement levels of the computational mesh. We consider eight
binary configurations with total mass $M=2.7\,M_\odot$, mass-ratios $q=1$ and
$q=1.16$, and four different equation of states (EOSs), and one configuration
with a stiff EOS, $M=2.5M_\odot$ and $q=1.5$. We focus on the post-merger
dynamics and study the merger remnant, dynamical ejecta and the postmerger
gravitational wave spectrum. Although most of the merger remnants form a
hypermassive neutron star collapsing to a black hole+disk system on dynamical
timescales, stiff EOSs can eventually produce a stable massive neutron star.
Ejecta are mostly emitted around the orbital plane; favored by large mass
ratios and softer EOS. The postmerger wave spectrum is mainly characterized by
non-axisymmetric oscillations of the remnant. The stiff EOS configuration
consisting of a $1.5M_\odot$ and a $1.0M_\odot$ neutron star shows a rather
peculiar dynamics. During merger the companion star is very deformed;
about~$\sim0.03M_\odot$ of rest-mass becomes unbound from the tidal tail due
torque; and the merger remnant forms stable neutron star surrounded by a
massive accretion disk $\sim0.3M_\odot$. Similar configurations might be
particularly interesting for electromagnetic counterparts. Comparing results
obtained with and without the conservative mesh refinement algorithm, we find
that post-merger simulations can be affected by systematic errors if mass
conservation is not enforced in the mesh refinement strategy. However, mass
conservation also depends on grid details and on the artificial atmosphere
setup. [abridged]
label: human

text:
We study a Lagrangian decomposition algorithm recently proposed by Dan
Bienstock and Mark Zuckerberg for solving the LP relaxation of a class of open
pit mine project scheduling problems. In this study we show that the
Bienstock-Zuckerberg (BZ) algorithm can be used to solve LP relaxations
corresponding to a much broader class of scheduling problems, including the
well-known Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP), and
multi-modal variants of the RCPSP that consider batch processing of jobs. We
present a new, intuitive proof of correctness for the BZ algorithm that works
by casting the BZ algorithm as a column generation algorithm. This analysis
allows us to draw parallels with the well-known Dantzig-Wolfe (DW) algorithm.
We discuss practical computational techniques for speeding up the performance
of the BZ and DW algorithms on project scheduling problems. Finally, we present
computational experiments independently testing the effectiveness of the BZ and
DW algorithms on different sets of publicly available test instances. Our
computational experiments confirm that the BZ algorithm significantly
outperforms the DW algorithm for the problems considered. Our computational
experiments also show that the proposed speed-up techniques can have a
significant impact on solution time. We provide some insights on what might be
explaining this significant difference in performance.
label: human

text: Our research presents Machine-z, a novel machine learning approach designed to rapidly predict redshift values for Swift Gamma-ray Bursts (GRBs). The key motivation for this work is to address the challenge of obtaining redshift measurements for GRBs in a timely manner, which is crucial for understanding the properties of these high-energy astrophysical events. By utilizing a combination of supervised learning techniques, feature engineering, and optimization algorithms, we have trained Machine-z on a large dataset of GRBs with known redshift values. Our results demonstrate that Machine-z is capable of accurately predicting redshift values for new GRB observations with significantly reduced computational time compared to traditional methods. This advancement enables prompt insights into the distance, energetics, and cosmological implications of GRBs, ultimately contributing to our understanding of the universe's evolution. The methodology employed in this study involves feature selection based on physical properties of GRBs, training and validating the machine learning model with appropriate algorithms, and optimizing the model for efficient prediction capabilities. The successful implementation and validation of Machine-z showcase its potential as a valuable tool for real-time redshift estimation in the context of GRB research, offering a promising avenue for further exploration in the field of high-energy astrophysics.
label: machine

text: The study of multifluid magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) systems is crucial for understanding the complex behaviors within astrophysical and laboratory plasmas. This research investigates the decay of turbulence in multifluid MHD systems, focusing on how different components of a plasma interact over time to influence turbulence dissipation. The objective of this study is to analyze the interactions between charged and neutral fluids in plasma and the role these interactions play in turbulent decay processes. A multifluid MHD model is employed to simulate the decay of turbulence, incorporating the effects of ion-neutral collisions, magnetic field dynamics, and energy exchange between fluid components. High-resolution numerical simulations are conducted using a combination of spectral and finite-volume methods to ensure accuracy and stability in capturing the intricate dynamics of turbulent decay. The key findings reveal that the inclusion of multifluid interactions significantly alters the decay rates compared to single-fluid MHD models, resulting in a more complex, anisotropic decay pattern influenced by the relative densities and velocities of the components. Furthermore, ion-neutral collisions are observed to enhance the cascade of turbulent energy to smaller scales, thereby accelerating dissipation. These observations underscore the importance of considering multifluid effects in MHD turbulence studies and provide insights into the underlying mechanisms driving plasma ejections in space environments. Conclusively, this research highlights the necessity for multifluid approaches in accurately modeling plasma behavior, suggesting implications for better interpreting observations from astrophysical phenomena and improving magnetic confinement in fusion devices.
label: machine

text:
Extracting informative image features and learning effective approximate
hashing functions are two crucial steps in image retrieval . Conventional
methods often study these two steps separately, e.g., learning hash functions
from a predefined hand-crafted feature space. Meanwhile, the bit lengths of
output hashing codes are preset in most previous methods, neglecting the
significance level of different bits and restricting their practical
flexibility. To address these issues, we propose a supervised learning
framework to generate compact and bit-scalable hashing codes directly from raw
images. We pose hashing learning as a problem of regularized similarity
learning. Specifically, we organize the training images into a batch of triplet
samples, each sample containing two images with the same label and one with a
different label. With these triplet samples, we maximize the margin between
matched pairs and mismatched pairs in the Hamming space. In addition, a
regularization term is introduced to enforce the adjacency consistency, i.e.,
images of similar appearances should have similar codes. The deep convolutional
neural network is utilized to train the model in an end-to-end fashion, where
discriminative image features and hash functions are simultaneously optimized.
Furthermore, each bit of our hashing codes is unequally weighted so that we can
manipulate the code lengths by truncating the insignificant bits. Our framework
outperforms state-of-the-arts on public benchmarks of similar image search and
also achieves promising results in the application of person re-identification
in surveillance. It is also shown that the generated bit-scalable hashing codes
well preserve the discriminative powers with shorter code lengths.
label: human

text: The abstract focuses on the study of the footpoints of Giant Molecular Loops (GMLs) within the Galactic center region. GMLs are massive molecular structures observed at the Galactic center, providing insights into the star formation processes in dense environments. This research aims to investigate the spatial distribution and kinematics of these loops by analyzing their footpoints, which are the regions where the loops connect to the Galactic disk. Utilizing data from the Galactic Plane Survey and the Digitized Sky Survey, the study employed photometric and spectroscopic observations to determine the chemical abundances and kinematic properties of the footpoints. Key findings indicate that the footpoints exhibit distinct chemical signatures, suggesting different evolutionary stages or origins of the molecular material. Additionally, the analysis reveals variations in the kinematic structure of the footpoints across the Galactic plane, hinting at complex interactions between the Galactic disk and the central molecular zone. The research concludes with a discussion on the implications of these findings for understanding the star formation dynamics and the chemical enrichment history in the Galactic center.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the steady-state performance of a diffusion-based adaptive distributed detection algorithm in the slow adaptation regime. The primary objective is to analyze the cooperative decision-making process in sensor networks where local nodes share information to achieve a global consensus, thereby improving detection accuracy. To address this problem, we propose a diffusion strategy that allows nodes to adjust their detection thresholds adaptively, based on local data and information received from neighboring nodes. We employ a combination of local processing and information exchange, which significantly enhances the network's detection capabilities while maintaining a low communication overhead. Our methodological approach involves deriving analytical expressions for the steady-state detection performance and convergence properties in the slow adaptation regime, where the system parameters change incrementally to maintain stability. Through rigorous analysis, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves significantly improved detection performance, even under varying environmental conditions and sensor noise levels. Simulation results confirm our theoretical predictions, showing a marked improvement in detection probability and robustness compared to traditional non-cooperative methods. Additionally, the diffusion-based structure ensures that the network adapts efficiently to changes without extensive recalibration. Our findings contribute to the advancement of distributed detection in sensor networks, emphasizing the benefits of adaptive strategies in achieving reliable and efficient network operations. These insights extend the theoretical understanding and practical application of diffusion processes in adaptive distributed detection systems.
label: machine

text:
1. Based on observational data on evolution of quasars and galaxies of
different types along with the results of numerical simulations we make a
conclusion that on low redshifts ($z<0.5$) QSOI/II objects in massive
elliptical and spiral galaxies with classical bulges cannot be in late single
activity event (be "primordial"). Instead of it they have had events of
activity earlier in their evolution. It means that their presence on low
redshifts is connected with the recurrence phenomenon, sequential wet minor
mergings, because timescale of the activity does not exceed several units of
$10^7$ years.
  2. We define a new class - "AGN III" as active galactic nuclei in isolated
late-type spirals with low-mass rapidly rotating pseudobulges. We also state
that only such objects can be in the primordial phase of activity at low
redshifts. Black holes in such galaxies have masses $M_{BH}<10^7M_\odot$ and
also, probably very high spin. Such properties can explain their peculiar
emission spectra.
  A good representative of AGN III might be the galaxies with narrow (${\rm
FWHM}(H\beta)\leq1200$ km/s) broad permitted emission lines - NLS. It is
believed that their black hole masses are less than $M_{BH}<10^7M_\odot$ and
their host galaxies have pseudobulges instead of the classical ones. Because
host galaxies of NLS have pseudobulges and BLS (Broad-Line Seyfert galaxies)
have classical bulges these two types of objects cannot have evolutionary
connection. Presumably, the parent population of NLS are the quasars of
"population A".
label: human

text: In this study, we present our findings on imaging the heart of astrophysical objects using optical long-baseline interferometry. The problem addressed is the need for high-resolution imaging of these objects to better understand their inner structures and processes. Our work aims to resolve the inner regions of astrophysical objects with unprecedented detail by combining light from multiple telescopes using interferometric techniques.   Our results demonstrate the successful imaging of the central regions of various astrophysical objects, including active galactic nuclei and young stellar objects, revealing intricate structures such as accretion disks and jets. By achieving angular resolutions far beyond what individual telescopes can provide, we have been able to probe the physical mechanisms at work in these objects with remarkable clarity.  Key ideas in our methodology involve the coordination of multiple telescopes to simultaneously observe the same target, followed by the combination of the collected light to reconstruct high-resolution images using interferometric algorithms. By harnessing the power of optical long-baseline interferometry, we have pushed the boundaries of observational astrophysics, providing new insights into the inner workings of astrophysical objects.
label: machine

text:
The determination of the sample size required by a crossover trial typically
depends on the specification of one or more variance components. Uncertainty
about the value of these parameters at the design stage means that there is
often a risk a trial may be under- or over-powered. For many study designs,
this problem has been addressed by considering adaptive design methodology that
allows for the re-estimation of the required sample size during a trial. Here,
we propose and compare several approaches for this in multi-treatment crossover
trials. Specifically, regulators favour re-estimation procedures to maintain
the blinding of the treatment allocations. We therefore develop blinded
estimators for the within and between person variances, following simple or
block randomisation. We demonstrate that, provided an equal number of patients
are allocated to sequences that are balanced for period, the proposed
estimators following block randomisation are unbiased. We further provide a
formula for the bias of the estimators following simple randomisation. The
performance of these procedures, along with that of an unblinded approach, is
then examined utilising three motivating examples, including one based on a
recently completed four-treatment four-period crossover trial. Simulation
results show that the performance of the proposed blinded procedures is in many
cases similar to that of the unblinded approach, and thus they are an
attractive alternative.
label: human

text: We report on a study examining the relationship between the top quark mass and the Higgs boson mass in the context of the electroweak vacuum stability. Using current data from the Large Hadron Collider, we calculate the masses of the top quark and Higgs boson within the Standard Model, as well as in various extensions that address the hierarchy problem, such as the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model. We explore the effect of different masses on the potential energy of the Higgs field and the condition for vacuum stability.  Our findings suggest that, within the Standard Model, the measured top quark mass of approximately 172.5 GeV implies a Higgs boson mass below the currently observed value of around 130 GeV, which could challenge the validity of the electroweak vacuum. However, in extensions to the Standard Model, such as the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, higher top quark and Higgs boson masses are possible, providing a natural solution to the vacuum stability problem. We also investigate the impact of uncertainties in the input data and the choice of potential form on our results. Overall, our work contributes to a better understanding of the implications of top quark and Higgs boson masses on electroweak vacuum stability.  Our study employs numerical techniques and data analysis methods to analyze the relevant potential energy landscapes and investigate the conditions for vacuum stability. We utilize Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, as well as various optimization techniques, to explore the parameter space of the models and quantify uncertainties. Additionally, we perform sensitivity analyses to assess the impact of different assumptions on our results. By combining theoretical insights with empirical data analysis, we aim to advance the ongoing debate on the stability of the electroweak vacuum and the implications for new physics beyond the Standard Model.
label: machine

text: We investigate Type I planet migration in a magnetized disk, focusing on the impact of large-scale vertical and azimuthal magnetic field components. Our study aims to address the uncertainty surrounding the role of magnetic fields in influencing planet migration in protoplanetary disks. By conducting numerical simulations that include varying strengths of vertical and azimuthal magnetic fields, we explore how these components affect the migration behavior of forming planets. Our results show that strong vertical fields can alter migration rates significantly, leading to deviations from the classical Type I migration. Additionally, when considering azimuthal fields, we observe that they can either enhance or counteract the effects of vertical fields, depending on their relative strengths. These findings suggest that the combination of vertical and azimuthal magnetic field components plays a crucial role in shaping the migration paths of planets in magnetized disks. We propose that future studies should take into account the complex interplay between different magnetic field components to gain a comprehensive understanding of planet migration in protoplanetary environments. Our methodology provides insights into the mechanisms underlying Type I migration in the presence of magnetized disks, paving the way for further advancements in planetary formation theories.
label: machine

text: We investigate the probabilistic distributions of mass-to-light (M/L) values for ultra-faint dwarf spheroidal galaxies (UFDs) by employing a stochastic sampling methodology of the initial mass function (IMF). Our work addresses the problem of accurately estimating the M/L ratios for UFDs, which are critical for understanding their formation and evolution in relation to dark matter. We utilize a Monte Carlo simulation approach to account for the uncertainties inherent in both stellar populations and the IMF. Through this method, we sample various IMF parameters, including the upper mass limit and the slope, to model the resultant M/L ratios under different assumptions.   As a result, we provide robust probabilistic distributions of M/L values that reflect both the inherent uncertainties and the observed characteristics of UFDs. Our findings demonstrate a significant variation in M/L ratios depending on the specific IMF parameters employed, thereby highlighting the sensitivity of these galaxy systems to underlying stellar population assumptions. We report that typical M/L values cluster around a mean of 60, with a broad dispersion indicating the diverse stellar environments in these galaxies. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that higher M/L values correlate with steeper IMF slopes, suggesting a complex relationship between stellar formation processes and resulting mass distributions. This work not only enhances our understanding of UFDs but also underscores the necessity of including IMF variability in future stellar population studies, ultimately contributing to a more comprehensive picture of galaxy formation in the early universe.
label: machine

text:
I measure the physical properties of 38 transiting extrasolar planetary
systems, bringing the total number studied within the Homogeneous Studies
project to 82. Transit light curves are modelled using JKTEBOP, with careful
attention paid to limb darkening, eccentricity and third light. The physical
properties of each system are obtained from the photometric parameters,
published spectroscopic measurements and five sets of theoretical stellar model
predictions. Statistical errors are assessed using Monte Carlo and
residual-permutation algorithms and propagated via a perturbation algorithm.
Systematic errors are estimated from the interagreement between results
calculated using five theoretical stellar models. The headline result is a
major upward revision of the radius of the planet in the OGLE-TR-56 system,
from 1.23-1.38 Rjup to 1.734 +/- 0.051 +/- 0.029 Rjup (statistical and
systematic errors, respectively). Its density is three times lower than
previously thought. This change comes from the first complete analysis of
published high-quality photometry. Significantly larger planetary radii are
also found for Kepler-15, KOI-428, WASP-13, WASP-14 and WASP-21 compared to
previous work. I present the first results based on Kepler short-cadence data
for Kepler-14, Kepler-15 and KOI-135. More extensive long-cadence data s used
to improve the measured properties of KOI-196, KOI-204, KOI-254, KOI-423 and
KOI-428. Detailed analyses are given for HAT-P-3, HAT-P-6, HAT-P-9, HAT-P-14
and WASP-12, based on more extensive datasets than considered in previous
studies. I revisit the correlations between orbital period and surface gravity,
and orbital period and mass of the transiting planets, finding both to be
significant at the 4 sigma level. I conclude by discussing the opportunities
for follow-up observations, the sky positions and the discovery rate of the
known transiting planets.
label: human

text: This research paper focuses on Concurrent and Adaptive Extreme Scale Binding Free Energy Calculations. The objective of this study is to develop and evaluate a novel methodology that enables efficient and accurate calculation of binding free energies on an extreme scale.   The methodology involves concurrent sampling of multiple binding modes and adaptively allocating computational resources to regions of interest in the binding free energy landscape. This approach aims to enhance the exploration of conformational space and improve the convergence of free energy estimates.  Key findings reveal that the concurrent and adaptive strategy leads to significant acceleration in the calculation of binding free energies while maintaining high accuracy levels. The methodology demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional single-mode simulations, particularly for complex binding systems with multiple binding modes.  In conclusion, the Concurrent and Adaptive Extreme Scale Binding Free Energy Calculations approach represents a promising advancement in the field of binding free energy calculations, offering a scalable and efficient method for studying molecular interactions. This methodology has the potential to impact drug discovery efforts by providing faster and more accurate predictions of binding affinities.
label: machine

text: Our study focuses on utilizing amino-acid network clique analysis to evaluate the impact of protein mutations on lysozyme. We aim to uncover correlations between mutations and their effects on protein stability and function. By applying network theory to amino acid interactions within the protein structure, we identified key cliques representing clusters of highly interconnected amino acids. Through computational simulations and statistical analyses, we investigated how mutations disrupt these cliques and influence the protein's overall behavior.  Our findings reveal that certain mutations disrupt critical clique structures, leading to alterations in protein stability and function. Specifically, mutations affecting residues within essential cliques were found to have a more pronounced impact on lysozyme properties compared to mutations in less central regions. This demonstrates the importance of considering the network context of amino acids when assessing mutation effects on proteins.  By employing a combination of network analysis, computational modeling, and statistical approaches, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of how protein mutations influence structure-function relationships in lysozyme. This research contributes valuable insights into the intricate interplay between amino acid interactions and protein stability, offering a systematic framework for studying mutation effects in other proteins as well.
label: machine

text:
The stress-induced yielding scenario of colloidal gels is investigated under
rough boundary conditions by means of rheometry coupled to local velocity
measurements. Under an applied shear stress, the fluidization of gels made of
attractive carbon black particles suspended in a mineral oil is shown to
involve a previously unreported shear rate response $\dot \gamma (t)$
characterized by two well-defined and separated timescales $\tau_c$ and
$\tau_f$. First $\dot \gamma(t)$ decreases as a weak power law strongly
reminiscent of the primary creep observed in numerous crystalline and amorphous
solids, coined the "Andrade creep." We show that the bulk deformation remains
homogeneous at the micron scale, which demonstrates that if plastic events take
place or if any shear transformation zone exists, such phenomena occur at a
smaller scale. As a key result of this paper, the duration $\tau_c$ of this
creep regime decreases as a power law of the viscous stress, defined as the
difference between the applied stress and the yield stress with an exponent
ranging between 2 and 3 depending on the gel concentration. The end of this
first regime is marked by a jump of the shear rate by several orders of
magnitude, while the gel slowly slides as a solid block experiencing strong
wall slip at both walls, despite rough boundary conditions. Finally, a second
sudden increase of the shear rate is concomitant to the full fluidization of
the material which ends up being homogeneously sheared. The corresponding
fluidization time $\tau_f$ robustly follows an exponential decay with the
applied shear stress as already reported for smooth boundary conditions.
Finally, we highlight a few features that are common to attractive colloidal
gels and to solid materials by discussing our results in the framework of
theoretical approaches of solid rupture (kinetic, fiber bundle, and transient
network models).
label: human

text: In the context of cosmology, understanding the dynamics of symmetry breaking in de Sitter space is crucial for elucidating the early universe's evolution. This paper aims to explore symmetry breaking in de Sitter through a stochastic effective theory framework. We focus on capturing the stochastic dynamics arising from quantum fluctuations that play a significant role in symmetry breaking processes within this spacetime. Our approach involves formulating a stochastic differential equation derived from the long-wavelength modes of a scalar field on de Sitter background, using techniques from nonequilibrium quantum field theory. By treating the inflaton field dynamics nonperturbatively, our methodology accounts for the backreaction effects of quantum noise on classical fields. Key findings reveal that the stochastic effective theory provides a robust framework to describe the statistical properties of symmetry breaking, including the generation and distribution of domain structures. Interestingly, this approach highlights a nontrivial interplay between classical deterministic evolution and stochastic quantum fluctuation that influences the effective mass of fields. The emergence of a phase transition is delineated, characterized by fluctuation-dominated regimes preceding classical stability, which could have observable implications for cosmic microwave background anisotropies. Conclusively, our study demonstrates the efficacy of a stochastic effective theory in capturing complex dynamics of symmetry breaking in de Sitter space, offering a deeper insight into its implications for early universe cosmology. Further studies can extend this approach to multifield scenarios, potentially enriching our comprehension of inflationary processes and their observational consequences.
label: machine

text:
Early studies of nearby Seyfert galaxies have led to the picture that the
Narrow Line Region (NLR) is a cone-shaped region of gas ionized by radiation
from a nuclear source collimated by a dusty torus, where the gas is in outflow.
In this contribution, I discuss a 3D view of the NLR obtained via Integral
Field Spectroscopy, showing that: (1) although the region of highest emission
is elongated (and in some cases cone-shaped), there is also lower level
emission beyond the "ionization cone", indicating that the AGN radiation leaks
through the torus; (2) besides outflows, the gas kinematics include also
rotation in the galaxy plane and inflows; (3) in many cases the outflows are
compact and restricted to the inner few 100pc; we argue that these may be early
stages of an outflow that will evolve to an open-ended, cone-like one. Inflows
are observed in ionized gas in LINERs, and in warm molecular gas in more
luminous AGN, being usually found on hundred of pc scales. Mass outflow rates
in ionized gas are of the order of a few solar masses per year, while the mass
inflow rates are of the order of tenths of solar masses per year. Mass inflow
rates in warm molecular gas are ~4-5 orders of magnitude lower, but these
inflows seem to be only tracers of more massive inflows in cold molecular gas
that should be observable at mm wavelengths.
label: human

text:
We study the possibility that particle production during inflation could
source observable gravity waves on scales relevant for Cosmic Microwave
Background experiments. A crucial constraint on such scenarios arises because
particle production can also source inflaton perturbations, and might ruin the
usual predictions for a nearly scale invariant spectrum of nearly Gaussian
curvature fluctuations. To minimize this effect, we consider two models of
particle production in a sector that is only gravitationally coupled to the
inflaton. For a single instantaneous burst of massive particle production, we
find that localized features in the scalar spectrum and bispectrum might be
observable, but gravitational wave signatures are unlikely to be detectable
(due to the suppressed quadrupole moment of non-relativistic quanta) without
invoking some additional effects. We also consider a model with a rolling
pseudoscalar that leads to a continuous production of relativistic gauge field
fluctuations during inflation. Here we find that gravitational waves from
particle production can actually exceed the usual inflationary vacuum
fluctuations in a regime where non-Gaussianity is consistent with observational
limits. In this model observable B-mode polarization can be obtained for any
choice of inflaton potential, and the amplitude of the signal is not
necessarily correlated with the scale of inflation.
label: human

text: This research explores the multi-frequency properties of synthetic blazar radio light curves using the shock-in-jet (SIJ) model. The study aims to investigate how different radio frequencies reflect the underlying physical processes in blazar jets, particularly focusing on the interaction between shocks and magnetic fields. Utilizing numerical simulations, the objective is to generate realistic radio light curves that can be compared with observational data. Key findings include the identification of distinct frequency-dependent behavior indicative of shock heating and particle acceleration, as well as the emergence of spectral turnovers characteristic of synchrotron emission. The analysis reveals that higher frequencies show increased variability and more prominent spectral breaks, reflecting the dominance of non-thermal particles. This work provides insights into the multi-frequency dynamics of blazars and supports the SIJ model as a viable framework for understanding their radio emission mechanisms.
label: machine

text: This research investigates the spatial correlations, clustering behavior, and percolation-like transitions associated with homicide crimes within urban environments. The study aims to understand the underlying patterns and criticality in the spatial distribution of such crimes, which can inform strategic policing and urban planning efforts. Utilizing spatial analysis and statistical network modeling, we examined a decade-long dataset of reported homicides from several metropolitan areas. The methodology involved quantifying spatial correlations using Ripley's K-function and identifying clustering using the local Moran's I statistic. We further modeled the spatial crime network to explore percolation patterns, employing percolation theory to examine phase transitions occurring as connectivity within crime hotspots increases.   Key findings reveal significant spatial correlations and distinct clusters of homicide incidents that suggest non-random spatial patterns. In establishing thresholds for percolation, we discovered that certain urban areas experience abrupt transitions in their structural network, indicating critical points where isolated crime hotspots become interconnected, drastically altering the crime landscape. These patterns are indicative of potential vulnerabilities in urban environments that could facilitate increased crime rates if left unaddressed.  The study concludes that understanding the spatial dynamics of homicide crimes through the lens of spatial correlations and percolation theory can provide valuable insights into crime prevention strategies. Effective interventions could include targeted policing in identified critical areas and urban design adjustments aimed at disrupting potential pathways for crime escalation. Such insights underscore the importance of integrating spatial analysis with criminological frameworks to enhance urban safety and resource allocation.

text: Cluster-randomized experiments have become a widely used method to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions, particularly in developing countries. However, a crucial aspect of these experiments is often overlooked pair matching. Pair matching, the process of matching clusters to controls based on relevant characteristics, can significantly impact the validity of the experiment's findings. This study examines the essential role of pair matching in cluster-randomized experiments, using the Mexican Universal Health Insurance Evaluation as a case study.  The objective of this study is to investigate the impact of pair matching on the validity of cluster-randomized experiment results. A comprehensive review of existing literature on pair matching in cluster-randomized experiments is conducted, highlighting the benefits and challenges of this method. Additionally, a simulation study is conducted to evaluate the effect of pair matching on the precision of treatment effects. The results of the simulation study indicate that pair matching can significantly reduce the standard error of treatment effects, leading to more precise estimates of intervention effectiveness.  The Mexican Universal Health Insurance Evaluation provides a unique opportunity to test the impact of pair matching in practice. The evaluation, which randomly assigned clusters to treatment or control conditions, was conducted in 2009 to assess the effectiveness of Mexico's Universal Health Insurance Program. This study analyzes the data from the evaluation, using pair matching to compare the outcomes of treatment and control clusters. The results of this analysis indicate that pair matching can significantly improve the validity of the experiment's findings, providing a more accurate estimate of the intervention's effectiveness. Overall, this study highlights the essential role of pair matching in cluster-randomized experiments, emphasizing its importance in improving the validity and reliability of evaluation results.

text: This study investigates the diameter of Cayley graphs constructed from permutation groups that are generated by transposition trees. We explore how the structure and depth of these trees influence the connectivity within the permutation groups, thereby affecting the diameter of the Cayley graph. Our methodology involves systematically generating Cayley graphs for various permutations using different types of transposition trees and analyzing their diameters through computational algorithms. Results indicate that the diameter increases as the complexity and depth of the transposition trees increase. Key findings suggest that there is a direct correlation between the structure of the transposition trees and the computational complexity required to traverse the entire graph, which can be leveraged for applications such as error detection in data transmission protocols. The research contributes to the theoretical understanding of Cayley graphs and their practical implications in computational group theory and network analysis.

We present a technique for handling Dirichlet boundary conditions with the
Flux Coordinate Independent (FCI) parallel derivative operator with
arbitrary-shaped material geometry in general 3D magnetic fields. The FCI
method constructs a finite difference scheme for $\nabla_\Vert$ by following
field lines between planes and interpolating within planes. Doing so removes
the need for field-aligned coordinate systems that suffer from singularities in
the metric tensor at null points in the magnetic field (or equivalently, when
$q \to \infty$). One cost of this method is that as the field lines are not on
the mesh, they may leave the domain at any point between neighbouring planes,
complicating the application of boundary conditions.
  The Leg Value Fill (LVF) boundary condition scheme presented here involves an
extrapolation/interpolation of the boundary value onto the field line end
point. The usual finite difference scheme can then be used unmodified. We
implement the LVF scheme in BOUT++ and use the Method of Manufactured Solutions
to verify the implementation in a rectangular domain, and show that the error
scaling of the finite difference scheme isn't modified. The use of LVF for
arbitrary wall geometry is outlined.
  We also demonstrate the feasibility of using the FCI approach in
non-axisymmetric configurations for a simple diffusion model in a "straight
stellarator" magnetic field. A Gaussian blob diffuses along the field lines,
tracing out flux surfaces. Dirichlet boundary conditions impose a last closed
flux surface (LCFS) that confines the density. Including a poloidal limiter
moves the LCFS to a smaller radius.
  The expected scaling of the numerical perpendicular diffusion, which is a
consequence of the FCI method, in stellarator-like geometry is recovered. A
novel technique for increasing the parallel resolution during post-processing
is also described.

Understanding the patterns of human dynamics and social interaction, and the
way they lead to the formation of an organized and functional society are
important issues especially for techno-social development. Addressing these
issues of social networks has recently become possible through large scale data
analysis of e.g. mobile phone call records, which has revealed the existence of
modular or community structure with many links between nodes of the same
community and relatively few links between nodes of different communities. The
weights of links, e.g. the number of calls between two users, and the network
topology are found correlated such that intra-community links are stronger
compared to the weak inter-community links. This is known as Granovetter's "The
strength of weak ties" hypothesis. In addition to this inhomogeneous community
structure, the temporal patterns of human dynamics turn out to be inhomogeneous
or bursty, characterized by the heavy tailed distribution of inter-event time
between two consecutive events. In this paper, we study how the community
structure and the bursty dynamics emerge together in an evolving weighted
network model. The principal mechanisms behind these patterns are social
interaction by cyclic closure, i.e. links to friends of friends and the focal
closure, i.e. links to individuals sharing similar attributes or interests, and
human dynamics by task handling process. These three mechanisms have been
implemented as a network model with local attachment, global attachment, and
priority-based queuing processes. By comprehensive numerical simulations we
show that the interplay of these mechanisms leads to the emergence of heavy
tailed inter-event time distribution and the evolution of Granovetter-type
community structure. Moreover, the numerical results are found to be in
qualitative agreement with empirical results from mobile phone call dataset.

text: This study investigates the effects of single neutral substitutional 3d-transition metal substitution into GeTe and GeSb2Te4 on their electronic and thermoelectric properties using the screened exchange functional. Background research indicates that GeTe and GeSb2Te4 are promising thermoelectric materials due to their high Seebeck coefficients and low thermal conductivity. However, their performance can be further enhanced by optimizing their electronic structures.  The objective of this research is to systematically explore the influence of single neutral substitutional 3d-transition metal substitution on the electronic band structures, thermoelectric properties, and phonon dispersion of GeTe and GeSb2Te4. A combination of density functional theory (DFT) calculations and the screened exchange functional is employed to simulate the structural, electronic, and thermoelectric properties of these materials.  The results show that the substitution of Ge with 3d-transition metal atoms (e.g., Mn, Fe, Co) into GeTe and GeSb2Te4 can significantly modify their electronic band structures, leading to improved Seebeck coefficients and power factors. The optimized materials exhibit enhanced thermoelectric performance, with peak values of zT reaching up to 3.5 and 4.2 for GeMnTe and GeSb2MnTe4, respectively. The phonon dispersion analysis reveals that the substitution-induced changes in the material's crystal structure can lead to reduced phonon scattering, contributing to the improved thermoelectric performance. Overall, this research provides a theoretical framework for designing and optimizing thermoelectric materials with enhanced performance by incorporating single neutral substitutional 3d-transition metal substitution into GeTe and GeSb2Te4.

text: We investigated the X-ray emission from the binary central stars of three planetary nebulae, HFG 1, DS 1, and LoTr 5, with the aim of shedding light on the underlying mechanisms driving this phenomenon. Our study employed a multi-wavelength approach, combining archival Chandra X-ray observations with spectroscopic data from the Hubble Space Telescope and optical observations from the Kepler Space Telescope.  Our results reveal that the X-ray emission from the binary central stars is predominantly driven by coronal heating, with a significant contribution from magnetic reconnection processes. We observed a strong correlation between the X-ray flux and the luminosity of the central stars, suggesting that the X-ray emission is linked to the mass transfer rate between the two components. Furthermore, we detected a significant variability in the X-ray emission, with a peak frequency of 0.5 Hz, indicative of a binary pulsar-like behavior.  Our findings are consistent with a model of binary evolution, where the mass transfer from the secondary star to the primary star leads to a buildup of magnetic field strength and a subsequent increase in coronal heating. The observed variability in the X-ray emission is likely due to the changing mass transfer rate and magnetic field configuration. These results provide new insights into the complex interactions between the binary central stars and the surrounding planetary nebula, highlighting the importance of X-ray emission as a diagnostic tool for understanding the evolution of these systems.

We show that the fluctuations in the wounded-nucleon model of the initial
stage of relativistic heavy-ion collisions, together with the natural
assumption that the forward (backward) moving wounded nucleons emit particles
preferably in the forward (backward) direction, lead to an event-by-event
torqued fireball. The principal axes associated with the transverse shape are
rotated in the forward region in the opposite direction than in the backward
region. On the average, the standard deviation of the relative torque angle
between the forward and backward rapidity regions is about 20deg for the
central and 10deg for the mid-peripheral collisions. The hydrodynamic expansion
of a torqued fireball leads to a torqued collective flow, yielding, in turn,
torqued principal axes of the transverse-momentum distributions at different
rapidities. We propose experimental measures, based on cumulants involving
particles in different rapidity regions, which should allow for a quantitative
determination of the effect from the data. To estimate the non-flow
contributions from resonance decays we run Monte Carlo simulations with
THERMINATOR. If the event-by-event torque effect is found in the data, it will
support the assumptions concerning the fluctuations in the early stage of the
fireball formation, as well as the hypothesis of the asymmetric rapidity shape
of the emission functions of the moving sources in the nucleus-nucleus
collisions.

We initiate the study of Access Control Encryption (ACE), a novel
cryptographic primitive that allows fine-grained access control, by giving
different rights to different users not only in terms of which messages they
are allowed to receive, but also which messages they are allowed to send.
  Classical examples of security policies for information flow are the well
known Bell-Lapadula [BL73] or Biba [Bib75] model: in a nutshell, the
Bell-Lapadula model assigns roles to every user in the system (e.g., public,
secret and top-secret). A users' role specifies which messages the user is
allowed to receive (i.e., the no read-up rule, meaning that users with public
clearance should not be able to read messages marked as secret or top-secret)
but also which messages the user is allowed to send (i.e., the no write-down
rule, meaning that a user with top-secret clearance should not be able to write
messages marked as secret or public).
  To the best of our knowledge, no existing cryptographic primitive allows for
even this simple form of access control, since no existing cryptographic
primitive enforces any restriction on what kind of messages one should be able
to encrypt.
  Our contributions are: - Introducing and formally defining access control
encryption (ACE); - A construction of ACE with complexity linear in the number
of the roles based on classic number theoretic assumptions (DDH, Paillier); - A
construction of ACE with complexity polylogarithmic in the number of roles
based on recent results on cryptographic obfuscation;
