Seismic shaking is an attractive mechanism to explain the destabilisation of
regolith slopes and the regolith migration found on the surfaces of asteroids
(Richardson et al. 2004; Miyamoto et al. 2007). Here, we use a continuum
mechanics method to simulate the seismic wave propagation in an asteroid.
Assuming that asteroids can be described by a cohesive core surrounded by a
thin non-cohesive regolith layer, our numerical simulations of vibrations
induced by micro-meteoroids suggest that the surface peak ground accelerations
induced by micro-meteoroid impacts may have been previously under-estimated.
Our lower bound estimate of vertical accelerations induced by seismic waves is
about 50 times larger than previous estimates. It suggests that impact events
triggering seismic activity are more frequent than previously assumed for
asteroids in the kilometric and sub-kilometric size range. The regolith lofting
is also estimated by a first order ballistic approximation. Vertical
displacements are small, but lofting times are long compared to the duration of
the seismic signals. The regolith movement has a non-linear dependence on the
distance to the impact source which is induced by the type of seismic wave
generating the first movement. The implications of regolith concentration in
lows of surface acceleration potential are also discussed. We suggest that the
resulting surface thermal inertia variations of small fast rotators may induce
an increased sensitivity of these objects to the Yarkovsky effect.

text: In this study, we present a novel approach for the efficient dense labeling of human activity sequences captured from wearable sensors, employing Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs). Our primary objective is to address the challenges of accurately and promptly identifying and labeling a multitude of activities in continuous, real-time data streams generated by wearable devices. We developed a comprehensive FCN architecture, optimized for temporal feature extraction and classification, which enables high-resolution labeling of activity sequences.  By conducting experiments on a diverse set of real-world activity datasets, we demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms baseline methods in terms of labeling accuracy and computational efficiency. We implemented data augmentation techniques to enhance the model's robustness under varying conditions, such as differences in participants, activity types, and sensor noise. Additionally, we explored the use of dilated convolutions to capture long-range temporal dependencies inherent in human activity behaviors, which further improved classification performance.  The results indicate that our approach not only achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in dense labeling but also maintains low latency, making it suitable for real-time applications. Our findings underscore the potential of FCNs in wearable technology, opening avenues for advanced human-computer interaction, health monitoring, and personalized activity recognition. We conclude that the methodology established herein provides a strong foundation for future research in the field of human activity recognition, encouraging the integration of machine learning techniques in wearable systems.

text: This study introduces Dense Object Nets (DOns), a novel approach designed to learn dense visual object descriptors specifically tailored for robotic manipulation tasks. The primary objective is to enhance the ability of robots to understand and interact with objects by providing high-resolution feature maps that capture intricate details critical for grasping and manipulating items effectively. The methodology involves training DOns on large-scale datasets, focusing on the extraction of object-centric features that are robust to variations in viewpoint, scale, and occlusion. Problematically, existing approaches often struggle with ambiguity in object representations and the lack of comprehensive context, leading to suboptimal performance in manipulation scenarios. DOns addresses these challenges through a multi-scale convolutional network architecture that integrates both local and global information. Key innovations include the use of attention mechanisms to prioritize relevant features and the incorporation of task-specific priors during training to align learned descriptors with real-world manipulative goals. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in object recognition accuracy and grasp success rates compared to state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of DOns in enhancing robotic capabilities for manipulation tasks.

Cyber-physical systems increasingly rely on distributed computing platforms
where sensing, computing, actuation, and communication resources are shared by
a multitude of applications. Such `cyber-physical cloud computing platforms'
present novel challenges because the system is built from mobile embedded
devices, is inherently distributed, and typically suffers from highly
fluctuating connectivity among the modules. Architecting software for these
systems raises many challenges not present in traditional cloud computing.
Effective management of constrained resources and application isolation without
adversely affecting performance are necessary. Autonomous fault management and
real-time performance requirements must be met in a verifiable manner. It is
also both critical and challenging to support multiple end-users whose diverse
software applications have changing demands for computational and communication
resources, while operating on different levels and in separate domains of
security.
  The solution presented in this paper is based on a layered architecture
consisting of a novel operating system, a middleware layer, and
component-structured applications. The component model facilitates the
construction of software applications from modular and reusable components that
are deployed in the distributed system and interact only through well-defined
mechanisms. The complexity of creating applications and performing system
integration is mitigated through the use of a domain-specific model-driven
development process that relies on a domain-specific modeling language and its
accompanying graphical modeling tools, software generators for synthesizing
infrastructure code, and the extensive use of model-based analysis for
verification and validation.

text: The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has been a pivotal platform for particle physics research since its inception in 2008. One of the most intriguing discoveries made during this period was the detection of T-Quarks, a type of quark predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics. The LHC's unique capabilities allowed researchers to explore the properties of T-Quarks, shedding light on the fundamental forces governing the universe.  The objective of this research was to investigate the production and decay patterns of T-Quarks at the LHC, with a focus on the 2010-12 data sets. By analyzing the collision data, researchers aimed to verify the existence of T-Quarks and gain insights into their interactions with other particles. The study employed a combination of theoretical models and experimental data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC.  The key findings of this research revealed that T-Quarks were indeed produced and observed at the LHC, consistent with the predictions of the Standard Model. The analysis of decay patterns and kinematic properties provided valuable information on the interactions between T-Quarks and other particles, offering insights into the strong and electroweak forces. The results also highlighted the importance of precise measurements in particle physics, demonstrating the need for further experiments to refine our understanding of the fundamental forces.  The conclusion of this research emphasizes the significance of the LHC data in confirming the existence of T-Quarks and advancing our understanding of the Standard Model. The findings underscore the importance of continued research at the LHC, as well as the development of new experimental techniques to further probe the properties of subatomic particles.

text: Tidal disruptions (TD) occur when a star passes closely to a supermassive black hole (SMBH), leading to the disruption of its outer layers and the formation of an accretion disk. The composition of the fallback material, i.e., the material that survives the disruption and forms the accretion disk, carries crucial information about the mass and age of the disrupted star. This study explores the implications of the fallback material's composition for TDs of main sequence stars of varying mass and age.  We compile observational data from TD events and conduct Monte Carlo simulations to model the disruption process and the resulting accretion disk composition. Our findings suggest that the accretion disks of low-mass stars display higher heavy-element abundances than high-mass stars. This trend is consistent with the expectation that low-mass stars have less efficient stellar winds, resulting in a higher fraction of heavy elements being captured in the disk.  Moreover, our analysis indicates that TDs of younger stars result in accretion disks with higher heavy-element abundances than older stars. This observation may be explained by the fact that younger stars have not yet had time to expel a significant fraction of their heavy elements through stellar winds.  Our results have significant implications for the interpretation of TD data and the understanding of the environments around SMBHs. They contribute to the ongoing debate about the origin of heavy elements in the universe and offer new insights into the complex interplay between stellar evolution, black hole growth, and the chemical enrichment of the interstellar medium.

We consider a simple extension of the minimal left-right symmetric model
(LRSM) in order to explain the PeV neutrino events seen at the IceCube
experiment from a heavy decaying dark matter. The dark matter sector is
composed of two fermions: one at PeV scale and the other at TeV scale such that
the heavier one can decay into the lighter one and two neutrinos. The gauge
annihilation cross sections of PeV dark matter are not large enough to generate
its relic abundance within the observed limit. We include a pair of real scalar
triplets $\Omega_{L,R}$ which can bring the thermally overproduced PeV dark
matter abundance into the observed range through late time decay and consequent
entropy release thereby providing a consistent way to obtain the correct relic
abundance without violating the unitarity bound on dark matter mass. Another
scalar field, a bitriplet under left-right gauge group is added to assist the
heavier dark matter decay. The presence of an approximate global $U(1)_X$
symmetry can naturally explain the origin of tiny couplings required for
long-lived nature of these decaying particles. We also show, how such an
extended LRSM can be incorporated within a non-supersymmetric $SO(10)$ model
where the gauge coupling unification at a very high scale naturally accommodate
a PeV scale intermediate symmetry, required to explain the PeV events at
IceCube.

text: We have made significant progress in classifying spinor fields on 7-manifolds, a long-standing problem in theoretical physics. By developing novel mathematical tools and techniques, we have expanded the existing framework of spinor field classification to arbitrary dimensions. Our work involves a systematic analysis of the spinor field structure in 7-dimensional manifolds, incorporating both local and global aspects.  Through a combination of differential geometry, topology, and representation theory, we have identified new classes of spinor fields that are not captured by existing classification schemes. Specifically, we have discovered novel spinor field configurations on 7-manifolds with non-trivial topology, which have far-reaching implications for our understanding of supersymmetry and the structure of spacetime.  Our approach involves a detailed examination of the spinor field's Clifford algebra, which we have used to derive new constraints on the spinor field's behavior. By leveraging these constraints, we have developed a comprehensive classification framework that encompasses a wide range of spinor field configurations. Our results have been verified through a series of rigorous mathematical proofs and have been applied to various physical systems, including string theory and supersymmetric field theories.  The key insights from our work lie in the identification of new spinor field classes and the development of a systematic classification framework. Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of the structure of spacetime and the behavior of spinor fields in high-dimensional manifolds.

text: We investigated the development and implementation of a novel artificial immune system (AIS) designed to detect and eliminate malware in a dynamic network environment. Our approach employed a hybrid machine learning framework, integrating machine learning algorithms with evolutionary programming to mimic the human immune system's adaptive response. The proposed AIS was trained on a large dataset of labeled malware samples and normal network traffic, enabling it to learn patterns and relationships between different network components.  Through a series of simulations and experiments, we demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed AIS in detecting and mitigating malware attacks. Our results showed that the AIS was able to achieve a high detection accuracy of 95% and a false positive rate of less than 1%. Additionally, the AIS was able to adapt and evolve in response to new malware variants and network configurations, showcasing its ability to learn and improve over time.  We also explored the use of AIS in a real-world network environment, where it was integrated with existing security systems to detect and respond to malware attacks. Our results showed that the AIS was able to detect and eliminate malware threats in real-time, with minimal impact on network performance. Overall, our findings suggest that AIS has the potential to revolutionize the field of network security, providing a highly effective and adaptive solution for detecting and mitigating malware threats.

text: In this study, we investigate the global stability of the departure time user equilibrium (DTUE) within a network transportation model. The primary objective is to ensure that the system's traffic flow remains stable over time under varying conditions, ensuring efficient resource allocation without oscillations or divergence. We employ a Lyapunov function approach to establish the stability of the DTUE, which involves defining a scalar function that decreases along the trajectories of the system, indicating convergence towards a stable state.  Our methodology begins by formulating the network as a dynamical system where the decision variables are the departure times at each origin-destination pair. We then derive a Lyapunov function candidate that captures the essence of the system dynamics, including the influence of departure times on subsequent travel times. By analyzing the properties of this function, particularly its derivative along the trajectories, we prove that the system converges to a unique equilibrium point.  The problem of achieving global stability in DTUE has been approached using various methods, but our contribution lies in the rigorous application of Lyapunov theory, providing a theoretical foundation for understanding the long-term behavior of departure time strategies in complex transportation networks. Our results demonstrate that by optimizing departure times, it is possible to achieve a stable equilibrium state, thereby enhancing overall system efficiency and resilience against perturbations.

text: The accelerating expansion of the universe, described by the cosmological constant, has been a long-standing enigma in modern astrophysics. The Ricci dark energy, a general relativistic concept, has been proposed as a possible explanation for this phenomenon. In this context, the interacting holographic Ricci dark energy, a modified version of the holographic principle, has gained significant attention. The holographic principle, initially introduced in the context of black hole thermodynamics, suggests that the information contained in a region of spacetime is encoded on its surface.   This study aims to investigate the interaction between the holographic Ricci dark energy and the running vacuum, a concept that has been recently introduced in the context of modified gravity theories. The objective is to explore the potential implications of this interaction on the evolution of the universe and the properties of dark energy.   This study employs a combination of analytical and numerical methods to investigate the interaction between the holographic Ricci dark energy and the running vacuum. The modified Einstein field equations, which include the holographic Ricci dark energy and the running vacuum, are solved numerically to obtain the evolution of the universe. The results are then compared with observational data, such as the cosmic microwave background radiation and supernovae observations.   The numerical simulations reveal that the interaction between the holographic Ricci dark energy and the running vacuum leads to a significant modification of the universe's evolution. The results show that the interaction causes a reduction in the dark energy density, which in turn leads to a slowing down of the universe's expansion. The simulations also predict a significant change in the cosmological perturbations, which could have implications for the formation of structure in the universe.   This study provides evidence for the interaction between the holographic Ricci dark energy and the running vacuum, and demonstrates its potential impact on the evolution of the universe. The results suggest that this interaction could be a key mechanism for explaining the observed acceleration of the universe's expansion. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to explore the implications of this interaction for our understanding of the universe.

Several techniques for analysis and transformations are used in compilers.
Among them, the peeling of loops for hoisting quasi-invariants can be used to
optimize generated code, or simply ease developers' lives. In this paper, we
introduce a new concept of dependency analysis borrowed from the field of
Implicit Computational Complexity (ICC), allowing to work with composed
statements called Chunks to detect more quasi-invariants. Based on an
optimization idea given on a WHILE language, we provide a transformation method
- reusing ICC concepts and techniques - to compilers. This new analysis
computes an invariance degree for each statement or chunks of statements by
building a new kind of dependency graph, finds the maximum or worst dependency
graph for loops, and recognizes if an entire block is Quasi-Invariant or not.
This block could be an inner loop, and in that case the computational
complexity of the overall program can be decreased. We already implemented a
proof of concept on a toy C parser 1 analysing and transforming the AST
representation. In this paper, we introduce the theory around this concept and
present a prototype analysis pass implemented on LLVM. In a very near future,
we will implement the corresponding transformation and provide benchmarks
comparisons.

text: PEACE (Pulsar Evaluation Algorithm for Candidate Extraction) is a software tool designed to post-process data from large-scale pulsar surveys, facilitating the identification and verification of potential pulsar candidates. The primary goal of PEACE is to evaluate the statistical significance of candidate signals, which may have high false alarm rates, as well as to filter out spurious detections and known sources.  Our methodology comprises several key stages. Initially, PEACE ingests data from pulsar survey instruments, extracting potential candidate signals based on specified search parameters. Subsequently, the software performs a thorough investigation of the candidate environment, considering factors like the proximity to known sources, interference, and radio frequency interference (RFI). To assess the statistical significance of the candidate signals, PEACE employs a Bayesian statistical analysis technique called template matching, which calculates the probability of observing a given candidate signal based on a known pulsar template.  The application of PEACE has yielded impressive results in the field of pulsar astronomy. For example, using data from the North Celestial Cap Pulsar Survey, we were able to successfully identify and verify over 300 new pulsar candidates. Furthermore, PEACE enabled us to filter out approximately 80% of false positives, thereby increasing the efficiency of the pulsar search process. By automating various aspects of the pulsar search analysis, PEACE not only reduces the workload for astronomers but also facilitates more rapid discovery and validation of new pulsars.  In conclusion, PEACE represents a significant advancement in the realm of pulsar astronomy. Its unique features, such as RFI mitigation, Bayesian statistical analysis, and automated identification of candidate signals, make it an indispensable tool for large-scale pulsar surveys. As future surveys continue to expand our understanding of the universe, PEACE is poised to play a crucial role in processing and identifying potential pulsar signals, paving the way for new scientific discoveries.

Kepler-444 provides a unique opportunity to probe the atmospheric composition
and evolution of a compact system of exoplanets smaller than the Earth. Five
planets transit this bright K star at close orbital distances, but they are too
small for their putative lower atmosphere to be probed at optical/infrared
wavelengths. We used the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph instrument
onboard the Hubble Space Telescope to search for the signature of the planet's
upper atmospheres at six independent epochs in the Ly-$\alpha$ line. We detect
significant flux variations during the transits of both Kepler-444e and f
(~20%), and also at a time when none of the known planets was transiting
(~40%). Variability in the transition region and corona of the host star might
be the source of these variations. Yet, their amplitude over short time scales
(~2-3 hours) is surprisingly strong for this old (11.2+-1.0Gyr) and apparently
quiet main-sequence star. Alternatively, we show that the in-transits
variations could be explained by absorption from neutral hydrogen exospheres
trailing the two outer planets (Kepler-444e and f). They would have to contain
substantial amounts of water to replenish such hydrogen exospheres, which would
reveal them as the first confirmed ocean-planets. The out-of-transit
variations, however, would require the presence of a yet-undetected Kepler-444g
at larger orbital distance, casting doubt on the planetary origin scenario.
Using HARPS-N observations in the sodium doublet, we derived the properties of

Our results demonstrate that coherence is significantly influenced by noise levels and the number of measurements. Key methodologies include the use of covariance matrices to measure the spread of estimated parameters and statistical hypothesis testing to compare the reliability of different estimators. The findings suggest that coherent quantum estimators are more robust in environments characterized by high noise, providing a foundation for improving quantum sensing and metrology applications.

Cosmological magnetic fields pervade the entire universe, from small to large
scales. Since they apparently extend into the intergalactic medium, it is
tantalizing to believe that they have a primordial origin, possibly being
produced during inflation. However, finding consistent scenarios for
inflationary magnetogenesis is a challenging theoretical problem. The
requirements to avoid an excessive production of electromagnetic energy, and to
avoid entering a strong coupling regime characterized by large values for the
electromagnetic coupling constant, typically allow one to generate only a tiny
amplitude of magnetic field during inflation. We propose a scenario for
building gauge-invariant models of inflationary magnetogenesis potentially free
from these issues. The idea is to derivatively couple a dynamical scalar, not
necessarily the inflaton, to fermionic and electromagnetic fields during the
inflationary era. Such couplings give additional freedom to control the
time-dependence of the electromagnetic coupling constant during inflation. This
fact allows us to find conditions to avoid the strong coupling problems that
affect many of the existing models of magnetogenesis. We do not need to rely on
a particular inflationary set-up for developing our scenario, that might be
applied to different realizations of inflation. On the other hand, specific
requirements have to be imposed on the dynamics of the scalar derivatively
coupled to fermions and electromagnetism, that we are able to satisfy in an
explicit realization of our proposal.

One of the most promising strategies to treat cancer is attacking it with
viruses designed to exploit specific altered pathways. Here, the effects of
oncolytic virotherapy on tumors having compact, papillary and disconnected
morphologies are investigated through computer simulations of a multiscale
model coupling macroscopic reaction diffusion equations for the nutrients with
microscopic stochastic rules for the actions of individual cells and viruses.
The interaction among viruses and tumor cells involves cell infection,
intracellular virus replication and release of new viruses in the tissue after
cell lysis. The evolution in time of both viral load and cancer cell
population, as well as the probabilities for tumor eradication were evaluated
for a range of multiplicities of infection, viral entries and burst sizes. It
was found that in immunosuppressed hosts, the antitumor efficacy of a virus is
primarily determined by its entry efficiency, its replicative capacity within
the tumor, and its ability to spread over the tissue. However, the optimal
traits for oncolytic viruses depends critically on the tumor growth dynamics
and do not necessarily include rapid replication, cytolysis and spreading
currently assumed as necessary conditions to a successful therapeutic outcome.
Our findings have potential implications on the design of new vectors for the
viral therapy of cancer.

We present an alternative technique for measuring the precursor masses of
transient events in stars undergoing late stage stellar evolution. We use the
well-established techniques of stellar population modeling to age-date the
stars surrounding the site of the recent transient event in NGC 300 (NGC 300
OT2008-1). The surrounding stars must share a common turnoff mass with the
transient, since almost all stars form in stellar clusters that remain
physically associated for periods longer than the lifetime of the most massive
stars. We find that the precursor of NGC 300 OT2008-1 is surrounded by stars
that formed in a single burst between 8-13 Myr ago, with 70% confidence. The
transient was therefore likely to be due to a progenitor whose mass falls
between the main sequence turnoff mass (12 Msun) and the maximum stellar mass
(25 Msun) found for isochrones bounding this age range. We characterize the
general applicability of this technique in identifying precursor masses of
historic and future transients and supernovae (SNe), noting that it requires
neither precursor imaging nor sub-arcsecond accuracy in the position of the
transient. It is also based on the well-understood physics of the main
sequence, and thus may be a more reliable source of precursor masses than
fitting evolutionary tracks to precursor magnitudes. We speculate that if the
progenitor mass is close to 17 Msun, there may be a connection between optical
transients such as NGC 300 OT2008-1 and the missing type II-P SNe, known as the
"red supergiant problem."

text: Pulsar Wind Nebulae (PWNe) are complex astrophysical structures resulting from the interaction between the pulsar's relativistic wind and the surrounding medium. This study focuses on the spectral modeling of PWNe detected by the High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.), a leading ground-based gamma-ray observatory. The objective is to understand the mechanisms that govern the emission processes in these nebulae, particularly in the high-energy regime. To achieve this, we employed a multi-wavelength observational approach, integrating data from H.E.S.S., as well as radio, optical, and X-ray measurements. We developed a comprehensive spectral model that includes contributions from both the pulsar wind and the background emission. The analysis revealed significant variability in the spectral indices among different PWNe, correlated with their age and distance from the pulsar. Notably, the presence of inverse Compton scattering processes was confirmed as a dominant emission mechanism in several cases. Our findings indicate a need for further investigation into the composition and dynamics of the particle distribution within the nebulae, paving the way for improved models that may incorporate magnetic field contributions and particle acceleration mechanisms. In conclusion, this research enhances the understanding of PWNe and their role in the broader context of pulsar astrophysics, providing insights that could lead to more accurate predictions of their emission characteristics across different wavelengths.

The results have implications for our understanding of time, space, and the fundamental laws of physics. In conclusion, the study demonstrates the feasibility of testing time dilation under acceleration using M\"ossbauer spectroscopy, contributing to the body of evidence supporting Einstein's revolutionary theories of relativity.

text: Galactic disks are essential components of spiral and irregular galaxies, hosting a significant portion of their stellar populations and star formation activities. One key process influencing the structure and evolution of galactic disks is radial migration, the transfer of stars from the outer to inner regions. This study investigates the influence of radial migration on galactic disks, focusing on its origin, mechanisms, and impact on disk properties.  The background section discusses the observed evidence for radial migration in various galaxies and the theoretical arguments for its importance. The objective of the research is to provide a comprehensive understanding of radial migration and its effects on galactic disks, using both observational and theoretical approaches.  The methodology includes a thorough analysis of existing observational and simulation data, investigating the radial distribution of stellar populations, star formation rates, and dynamical features in different galactic environments. Additionally, we employ numerical simulations to model radial migration processes, such as secular bars, giant molecular clouds, and stellar encounters, and their resulting impacts on galactic disks.  Our key findings reveal that radial migration plays a crucial role in shaping galactic disks by replenishing the inner regions with stars from the outer parts, leading to continuous star formation and maintaining the disk's structural stability. Furthermore, we provide evidence suggesting that radial migration may influence the stellar initial mass function (IMF) in the inner regions of galactic disks and could be responsible for the observed radial variations in the IMF.  In conclusion, this research offers valuable insights into the origin, mechanisms, and significance of radial migration on galactic disks, shedding light on the ongoing evolution of these systems and the role of stellar migration in shaping the properties of galaxies as a whole.

text: This research explores the energy bands of atomic monolayers of various materials, with a focus on the possibility of energy gap engineering. The increasing interest in two-dimensional materials has led to a surge in studies on their electronic properties, particularly the band structure and energy gaps. Atomic monolayers of materials such as graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), and metal halides have been extensively studied, revealing unique electronic properties that make them suitable for various applications.  The objective of this research is to investigate the band structure and energy gaps of atomic monolayers of different materials, with a view to understanding the potential for energy gap engineering. Energy gap engineering is a technique that involves manipulating the energy gaps of materials to tailor their electronic properties for specific applications. This technique has the potential to revolutionize the field of electronics and optoelectronics.  The methodology employed in this research involves a comprehensive review of existing literature on the band structure and energy gaps of atomic monolayers of various materials. Theoretical calculations were also performed using density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the effects of strain and defects on the band structure and energy gaps of these materials. The results show that certain materials exhibit tunable energy gaps, which can be manipulated by applying external strain or introducing defects. These findings suggest that energy gap engineering is feasible in atomic monolayers of various materials, opening up new avenues for the development of novel electronic and optoelectronic devices.  The key findings of this research highlight the potential of atomic monolayers for energy gap engineering. The results demonstrate that certain materials can exhibit tunable energy gaps, which can be manipulated by applying external strain or introducing defects. These findings have significant implications for the development of novel electronic and optoelectronic devices, such as transistors, solar cells, and light-emitting diodes. The research concludes that energy gap engineering is a promising approach for tailoring the electronic properties of atomic monolayers, and further studies are needed to explore its potential applications.

text: We investigate the dynamical evolution of kicked stellar-mass black holes in star cluster environments, addressing the critical problem of understanding their long-term stability and spatial distribution. Employing N-body simulations, we model varying initial conditions, including black hole kick velocities and cluster densities, to explore their influence on black hole retention rates and trajectories. Our results reveal that low-velocity kicks allow a significant fraction of black holes to remain bound within their host clusters, where they contribute to the overall mass distribution and dynamical interactions. Conversely, high-velocity kicks typically eject black holes, reducing their contribution to the cluster dynamics but potentially populating intergalactic space. We determine that the retention efficiency is heavily contingent on both the initial velocity dispersion of the star cluster and the magnitude of the applied kick. Furthermore, our analysis highlights that the gravitational interactions within dense core regions play a pivotal role in governing the subsequent movements and potential mergers of retained black holes. A notable finding is the formation of black hole binaries, which can act as gravitational wave sources detectable by current observatories. We conclude that understanding the nuanced interplay of black hole kick velocities and star cluster parameters is essential for predicting the fate of these enigmatic objects. Our study contributes to the broader understanding of black hole populations in multiple environments and aids in refining models for gravitational wave event rates attributable to star cluster-origin black hole mergers.

One of the main lines of research in algorithmic randomness is that of
lowness notions. Given a randomness notion R, we ask for which sequences A does
relativization to A leave R unchanged (i.e., R^A = R)? Such sequences are call
low for R. This question extends to a pair of randomness notions R and S, where
S is weaker: for which A is S^A still weaker than R? In the last few years,
many results have characterized the sequences that are low for randomness by
their low computational strength. A few results have also given
measure-theoretic characterizations of low sequences. For example, Kjos-Hanssen
proved that A is low for Martin-L\"of randomness if and only if every A-c.e.
open set of measure less than 1 can be covered by a c.e. open set of measure
less than 1. In this paper, we give a series of results showing that a wide
variety of lowness notions can be expressed in a similar way, i.e., via the
ability to cover open sets of a certain type by open sets of some other type.
This provides a unified framework that clarifies the study of lowness for
randomness notions, and allows us to give simple proofs of a number of known
results. We also use this framework to prove new results, including showing
that the classes Low(MLR;SR) and Low(W2R;SR) coincide, answering a question of
Nies. Other applications include characterizations of highness notions, a
broadly applicable explanation for why low for randomness is the same as low
for tests, and a simple proof that Low(W2R;S)=Low(MLR;S), where S is the class
of Martin-L\"of, computable, or Schnorr random sequences. The final section
gives characterizations of lowness notions using summable functions and
convergent measure machines instead of open covers. We finish with a simple
proof of a result of Nies, that Low(MLR) = Low(MLR; CR).

text: In concentrated suspensions, shear thickening is a phenomenon characterized by an increase in viscosity with increasing shear rate, presenting notable implications for both fundamental science and industrial applications. This research aims to elucidate the phenomenological aspects and underlying mechanisms of shear thickening, and its relation to jamming in dense particle suspensions. We conducted a series of rheological experiments on model suspensions, characterized by varying particle sizes and concentrations, alongside advanced particle tracking techniques to observe microstructural dynamics under shear. Our findings reveal the critical role of hydrodynamic interactions and contact forces between particles, which transition from lubrication-dominated to contact-driven mechanics as the shear rate increases. At high concentrations, the system approaches a critical jamming threshold, marked by a drastic rise in viscosity and mechanical rigidity. This behavior is underpinned by the formation of dynamic particle clusters that restrict flow and contribute to the observed shear thickening. Additionally, we investigate the reversibility of this state by examining the cessation of shear, which indicates path-dependent dynamics akin to those observed in jamming transitions. Our results confirm that shear thickening and jamming share similar microstructural rearrangements, suggesting that the former could be a precursor to the latter under certain conditions. The research contributes to a comprehensive understanding of the conditions under which shear thickening leads to jamming, providing critical insights for tailoring suspension properties for various technological applications. Conclusively, our work affirms that controlling particle interactions and suspension microstructure is pivotal in modulating flow behaviors, offering pathways to mitigate adverse effects or harness the advantages of these phenomena in practical scenarios.

text: Compton scattering, a phenomenon that describes the interaction between a photon and a charged particle, is a fundamental process in quantum electrodynamics. The Klein-Nishina formula, derived from special relativity and quantum mechanics, provides an accurate description of Compton scattering. However, it does not account for the differential cross section, which is crucial for understanding the kinematic features of the scattering process. This study investigates the signatures of the differential Klein-Nishina electronic cross section in Compton scattering using a relativistic quantum theory. We employ the Dirac equation to derive the differential cross section for Compton scattering of an electron by a photon. By comparing our results with the differential Klein-Nishina formula, we identify the signatures of the differential cross section in the energy and angular distribution of the scattered electron. Our analysis reveals that the signatures of the differential cross section manifest as deviations from the Klein-Nishina formula, which become more pronounced at high energies and large scattering angles. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of Compton scattering and its role in various physical phenomena, such as X-ray production in astrophysical settings and the development of new technologies, like synchrotron radiation sources and particle detectors. The theoretical framework established in this study also serves as a basis for further research on the Compton scattering process and its applications.

Confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) is an advanced optical fluorescence
imaging technology that has the potential to increase intraoperative precision,
extend resection, and tailor surgery for malignant invasive brain tumors
because of its subcellular dimension resolution. Despite its promising
diagnostic potential, interpreting the gray tone fluorescence images can be
difficult for untrained users. In this review, we provide a detailed
description of bioinformatical analysis methodology of CLE images that begins
to assist the neurosurgeon and pathologist to rapidly connect on-the-fly
intraoperative imaging, pathology, and surgical observation into a
conclusionary system within the concept of theranostics. We present an overview
and discuss deep learning models for automatic detection of the diagnostic CLE
images and discuss various training regimes and ensemble modeling effect on the
power of deep learning predictive models. Two major approaches reviewed in this
paper include the models that can automatically classify CLE images into
diagnostic/nondiagnostic, glioma/nonglioma, tumor/injury/normal categories and
models that can localize histological features on the CLE images using weakly
supervised methods. We also briefly review advances in the deep learning
approaches used for CLE image analysis in other organs. Significant advances in
speed and precision of automated diagnostic frame selection would augment the
diagnostic potential of CLE, improve operative workflow and integration into
brain tumor surgery. Such technology and bioinformatics analytics lend
themselves to improved precision, personalization, and theranostics in brain
tumor treatment.

text: This study investigates extremal black holes within the framework of quantum gravity, focusing on their gravitational entropy and the dynamics of nonstationary metric fields. We employ advanced techniques from general relativity and quantum field theory to derive expressions for the entropy of extremal black holes. The analysis reveals that extremal black holes exhibit unique properties due to the equality between their mass and angular momentum, leading to a maximal entropy scenario. Problematically, the standard approach often encounters singularities when attempting to compute entropy directly from the metric. To address this, we introduce a novel method involving nonstationary metric fields, which allows us to circumvent these singularities. Through numerical simulations and theoretical derivations, we demonstrate that this approach successfully computes the entropy without encountering physical inconsistencies. Our findings suggest that nonstationary metric fields play a crucial role in understanding the thermodynamic behavior of extremal black holes, offering new insights into the interplay between geometry and quantum mechanics in extreme gravitational environments.

The space limitation and the channel acquisition prevent Massive MIMO from
being easily deployed in a practical setup. Motivated by current deployments of
LTE-Advanced, the use of multi-polarized antennas can be an efficient solution
to address the space constraint. Furthermore, the dual-structured precoding, in
which a preprocessing based on the spatial correlation and a subsequent linear
precoding based on the short-term channel state information at the transmitter
(CSIT) are concatenated, can reduce the feedback overhead efficiently. By
grouping and preprocessing spatially correlated mobile stations (MSs), the
dimension of the precoding signal space is reduced and the corresponding
short-term CSIT dimension is reduced. In this paper, to reduce the feedback
overhead further, we propose a dual-structured multi-user linear precoding, in
which the subgrouping method based on co-polarization is additionally applied
to the spatially grouped MSs in the preprocessing stage. Furthermore, under
imperfect CSIT, the proposed scheme is asymptotically analyzed based on random
matrix theory. By investigating the behavior of the asymptotic performance, we
also propose a new dual-structured precoding in which the precoding mode is
switched between two dual-structured precoding strategies with 1) the
preprocessing based only on the spatial correlation and 2) the preprocessing
based on both the spatial correlation and polarization. Finally, we extend it
to 3D dual-structured precoding.

I introduce $Profiler$, a new, user-friendly program written in $Python$ and
designed to analyse the radial surface brightness profiles of galaxies. With an
intuitive graphical user interface, $Profiler$ can accurately model a wide
range of galaxies and galaxy components, such as elliptical galaxies, the
bulges of spiral and lenticular galaxies, nuclear sources, discs, bars, rings,
spiral arms, etc., with a variety of parametric functions routinely employed in
the field (S\'ersic, core-S\'ersic, exponential, Gaussian, Moffat and Ferrers).
In addition to these, $Profiler$ can employ the broken exponential model
(relevant for disc truncations or antitruncations) and two special cases of the
edge-on disc model: namely along the major axis (in the disc plane) and along
the minor axis (perpendicular to the disc plane). $Profiler$ is optimised to
work with galaxy light profiles obtained from isophotal measurements which
capture radial gradients in the ellipticity, position angle and Fourier
harmonic profiles of the isophotes, and are thus often better at capturing the
total light than two-dimensional image-fitting programs. Additionally, the
one-dimensional approach is generally less computationally expensive and more
stable. In $Profiler$, the convolution of either circular or elliptical models
with the point spread function is performed in two-dimensions, and offers a
choice between Gaussian, Moffat or a user-provided data vector (a table of
intensity values as a function of radius) for the point spread function. I
demonstrate $Profiler$'s features and operation by decomposing three case-study
galaxies: the cored elliptical galaxy NGC 3348, the nucleated dwarf Seyfert I
galaxy Pox 52, and NGC 2549, a structurally complex, double-barred galaxy which
also displays a Type II truncated disc viewed edge-on. $Profiler$ is freely
available at: https://github.com/BogdanCiambur/PROFILER

text: Our research investigates the impact of heavy sterile neutrinos on the dynamics of stellar core-collapse events. We aim to understand how the presence of these heavy sterile neutrinos influences the evolution of massive stars during gravitational collapse and subsequent supernova explosions. By incorporating the effects of sterile neutrinos in our simulations, we seek to elucidate their role in altering the energy transport mechanisms and modifying the neutrino flux emitted during the core-collapse process. The key focus is on elucidating how the presence of heavy sterile neutrinos affects the stellar remnant's mass, composition, and the overall energetics of the explosion. Our methodology involves numerical simulations utilizing advanced computational models that incorporate the relevant nuclear physics, neutrino transport, and gravitational dynamics. The findings from our study shed light on the potential consequences of sterile neutrinos on the dynamics of core-collapse supernovae, offering insights into the astrophysical implications of these elusive particles within the context of stellar evolution and nucleosynthesis.

In this paper, we develop a quantile functional regression modeling framework
that models the distribution of a set of common repeated observations from a
subject through the quantile function, which is regressed on a set of
covariates to determine how these factors affect various aspects of the
underlying subject-specific distribution. To account for smoothness in the
quantile functions, we introduce custom basis functions we call
\textit{quantlets} that are sparse, regularized, near-lossless, and empirically
defined, adapting to the features of a given data set and containing a Gaussian
subspace so {non-Gaussianness} can be assessed. While these quantlets could be
used within various functional regression frameworks, we build a Bayesian
framework that uses nonlinear shrinkage of quantlet coefficients to regularize
the functional regression coefficients and allows fully Bayesian inferences
after fitting a Markov chain Monte Carlo. Specifically, we apply global tests
to assess which covariates have any effect on the distribution at all, followed
by local tests to identify at which specific quantiles the differences lie
while adjusting for multiple testing, and to assess whether the covariate
affects certain major aspects of the distribution, including location, scale,
skewness, Gaussianness, or tails. If the difference lies in these commonly-used
summaries, our approach can still detect them, but our systematic modeling
strategy can also detect effects on other aspects of the distribution that
might be missed if one restricted attention to pre-chosen summaries. We
demonstrate the benefit of the basis space modeling through simulation studies,
and illustrate the method using a biomedical imaging data set in which we
relate the distribution of pixel intensities from a tumor image to various
demographic, clinical, and genetic characteristics.

text: The phenomenon of recoiling supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in active galactic nuclei (AGN) has garnered significant interest due to its implications for galaxy evolution and SMBH dynamics. This study examines the changing-look AGN, Mrk 1018, which recently transitioned from a Type 1.9 to a Type 1 AGN, offering a unique opportunity to investigate the presence and effects of a recoiling SMBH. The objective is to analyze the potential connection between the AGN's optical variability and a recoiling SMBH. The variability patterns observed in Mrk 1018’s light curve align with theoretical predictions for SMBHs displaced from their central gravitational wells. Furthermore, the spectral changes over time corroborate models of a dynamic AGN structure adjusting to a recoiled SMBH. Our findings support the hypothesis that Mrk 1018 hosts a recoiling SMBH, highlighting its significant role in AGN variability and offering insights into galaxy merger aftermaths. These results underscore the importance of monitoring changing-look AGNs as potential candidates for detecting and further understanding black hole recoil phenomena.

text: In this study, we explore the detection probability of a low-mass planet in triple lens events within the framework of gravitational microlensing. We employ an extensive simulation approach, systematically varying the parameters that define binary lenses—such as mass ratio and separation—and introducing a third, low-mass planetary lens. Our methodology integrates inverse ray-shooting techniques and static magnification maps to analyze the parameter space relevant to triple lens configurations.   The results indicate a significant enhancement in the detection probability when binary superposition properties are optimized, suggesting a strong dependence of planet detectability on these characteristics. Specifically, we observe that the alignment of the planetary lens with the binary lenses' caustic structure critically affects magnification patterns, thus governing the success of detection. Additionally, our findings underscore the importance of resolving angular perturbations that arise due to the complex arrangement of multiple lenses, which often mimic or obscure the planetary signal.  These insights provide a more refined understanding of the conditions under which low-mass planets can be detected, highlighting the intricate interplay between gravitational lens components. Our study advances the current methodologies for identifying low-mass exoplanets, offering a framework adaptable to existing and future microlensing surveys dedicated to unveiling planetary systems in our galaxy. This work is pivotal in optimizing observational strategies and enhancing data interpretation in the dynamic field of exoplanetary discovery through microlensing.

The speed meter concept has been identified as a technique that can
potentially provide laser-interferometric measurements at a sensitivity level
which surpasses the Standard Quantum Limit (SQL) over a broad frequency range.
As with other sub-SQL measurement techniques, losses play a central role in
speed meter interferometers and they ultimately determine the quantum noise
limited sensitivity that can be achieved. So far in the literature, the quantum
noise limited sensitivity has only been derived for lossless or lossy cases
using certain approximations (for instance that the arm cavity round trip loss
is small compared to the arm cavity mirror transmission). In this article we
present a generalised, analytical treatment of losses in speed meters that
allows accurate calculation of the quantum noise limited sensitivity of Sagnac
speed meters with arm cavities. In addition, our analysis allows us to take
into account potential imperfections in the interferometer such as an
asymmetric beam splitter or differences of the reflectivities of the two arm
cavity input mirrors. Finally,we use the examples of the proof-of-concept
Sagnac speed meter currently under construction in Glasgow and a potential
implementation of a Sagnac speed meter in the Einstein Telescope (ET) to
illustrate how our findings affect Sagnac speed meters with meter- and
kilometre-long baselines.

The vision of the Internet of Things is to allow currently unconnected
physical objects to be connected to the internet. There will be an extremely
large number of internet connected devices that will be much more than the
number of human being in the world all producing data. These data will be
collected and delivered to the cloud for processing, especially with a view of
finding meaningful information to then take action. However, ideally the data
needs to be analysed locally to increase privacy, give quick responses to
people and to reduce use of network and storage resources. To tackle these
problems, distributed data analytics can be proposed to collect and analyse the
data either in the edge or fog devices. In this paper, we explore a hybrid
approach which means that both innetwork level and cloud level processing
should work together to build effective IoT data analytics in order to overcome
their respective weaknesses and use their specific strengths. Specifically, we
collected raw data locally and extracted features by applying data fusion
techniques on the data on resource constrained devices to reduce the data and
then send the extracted features to the cloud for processing. We evaluated the
accuracy and data consumption over network and thus show that it is feasible to
increase privacy and maintain accuracy while reducing data communication
demands.

For the first time, we have systematically explored the population of
discrete X-ray sources in the outskirts of early-type galaxies. Based on a
broad sample of 20 galaxies observed with Chandra we detected overdensity of
X-ray sources in their outskirts. The overdensity appears as halos of resolved
sources around the galaxies. These halos are broader than the stellar light,
extending out to at least ~ 10 Re (Re is the effective radius). These halos are
composed of sources fainter than ~5E38 erg/s, whereas the more luminous sources
appear to follow the distribution of the stellar light, suggesting that the
excess source population consists of neutron star binaries. Dividing the galaxy
sample into four groups according to their stellar mass and specific frequency
of globular clusters, we find that the extended halos are present in all groups
except for the low-mass galaxies with low globular cluster content. We propose
that the extended halos may be comprised of two independent components,
low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) located in globular clusters (GCs), which are
known to have a wider distribution than the stellar light, and neutron star
(NS) LMXBs kicked out of the main body of the parent galaxy by supernova
explosions. The available deep optical and X-ray data of NGC 4365 support this
conclusion. For this galaxy we identified 60.1+/-10.8 excess sources in the
4-10 Re region of which ~ 40% are located in GCs, whereas ~ 60% are field
LMXBs. We interpret the latter as kicked NS LMXBs. We discuss the implications

stars.

text: In this study, we present an extensive analysis of galaxy formation using adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) simulations, investigating the interplay between numerical and physical parameters. We aim to address the challenges posed by accurately resolving the complex processes of galaxy formation, particularly in the context of computational limitations. To this end, we employed a state-of-the-art AMR code that allows for dynamic refinement of the computational grid, thereby providing high-resolution insights into regions of interest while maintaining computational efficiency. Our methodology involved a comprehensive exploration of parameter space, including variations in star formation rates, feedback mechanisms, and cooling processes, to ascertain their impact on galaxy morphology and evolution. We systematically calibrated our simulations against a range of observational data, ensuring their validity and applicability. The results demonstrate that certain parameter combinations significantly influence the morphological features and star formation histories of simulated galaxies, offering new insights into the dominant processes driving galaxy evolution. Crucially, our findings highlight the sensitivity of simulation outcomes to the resolution and refinement criteria, underscoring the necessity for carefully tailored numerical setups. Through this work, we provide a framework for optimizing AMR simulations, thereby enhancing the predictive power of computational models of galaxy formation. This study contributes to the broader understanding of cosmic structure formation and offers a pathway for future investigations into the intricacies of galaxy evolution, paving the way for more accurate and efficient astrophysical simulations.

We consider the effects that accretion from the interstellar medium onto the
particles of an N-body system has on the rate of two-body relaxation. To this
end, we derive an accretion-modified relaxation time by adapting Spitzer's
two-component model to include the damping effects of accretion. We consider
several different mass-dependencies and efficiency factors for the accretion
rate, as well as different mass ratios for the two components of the model.
  The net effect of accretion is to accelerate mass segregation by increasing
the average mass $\bar{m}$, since the relaxation time is inversely proportional
to $\bar{m}$. Under the assumption that the accretion rate increases with the
accretor mass, there are two additional effects that accelerate mass
segregation. First, accretion acts to increase the range of any initial mass
spectrum, quickly driving the heaviest members to even higher masses. Second,
accretion acts to reduce the velocities of the accretors due to conservation of
momentum, and it is the heaviest members that are affected the most. Using our
two-component model, we quantify these effects as a function of the accretion
rate, the total cluster mass, and the component masses. We conclude by
discussing the implications of our results for the dynamical evolution of
primordial globular clusters, primarily in the context of black holes formed
from the most massive stellar progenitors.

text: In this study, we present the results of simulations of the winds of weak-lined T Tauri stars, focusing on the effects of a tilted magnetosphere and planetary interactions. Using the 3D magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model MHD-YORP, we investigated the interplay between a dipolar magnetic field and a tilting of the stellar rotation axis, as well as the influence of a planet located in the habitable zone. Our simulations show that a tilted magnetosphere can significantly affect the wind structure, particularly in the vicinity of the stellar equator. We find that the tilted magnetosphere modifies the magnetic fields in the stellar wind, leading to alterations in the wind morphology, such as asymmetric wind structures and enhanced magnetic field strengths. Furthermore, the presence of a planet leads to the formation of a planet-induced magnetospheric cavity, which can impact the planetary atmospheric escape and potentially influence the planet's climate. These findings offer new insights into the complex interplay between stellar magnetic fields, stellar rotation, and planetary interactions in weak-lined T Tauri stars. Our results contribute to a better understanding of the early evolution of planetary systems and the role of stellar winds in shaping planetary environments.

text: The investigation of the impacts of stellar evolution and dynamics on the habitable zone is critical for understanding planetary habitability. This study focuses on the roles of stellar rotation and magnetic activity, both of which significantly influence the evolution and characteristics of a star's habitable zone. By employing a combination of stellar evolution models and magnetohydrodynamic simulations, we examine how these factors affect the luminous output and magnetic emissions of stars over time. Our analysis considers a variety of stellar masses and rotational histories to determine the consequential changes in both the boundaries and the stability of the habitable zone. Key findings reveal that rapid stellar rotation typically leads to enhanced magnetic activity, which in turn directly affects stellar luminosity and wind, leading to alterations in the extent of the habitable zone. Furthermore, the decline in rotation rates over a star's lifespan generally diminishes magnetic activity, thereby stabilizing the habitable zone at later stages. Our results also emphasize that variance in magnetic activity induces fluctuations in atmospheric erosion rates, directly impacting the potential for sustained surface water on orbiting exoplanets. Consequently, stellar rotation and magnetic properties must be accounted for in assessments of exoplanetary environments. By integrating stellar dynamics into habitability models, this research provides a more comprehensive understanding of the factors that govern planetary habitability, underscoring the need for multidimensional approaches in the search for life beyond our solar system.

text: In this study, we investigate the concept of orderable groups, focusing on groups that have a total order compatible with the group operation. We explore the existence and characteristics of orderings on various classes of groups, including abelian groups, free groups, and certain classes of non-abelian groups. Our research aims to contribute to the understanding of how the algebraic structure of a group interacts with the ordering imposed on its elements.  Through our investigation, we identify conditions under which a group is orderable and characterize the orderability of specific groups. Additionally, we analyze the implications of the existence of orderings on group properties, such as the structure of subgroups and homomorphisms between orderable groups.  Our methodology involves a combination of algebraic techniques, particularly pertaining to group theory, order theory, and the interplay between these areas. By defining precise criteria for when a group can be ordered and exploring the consequences of orderability, we aim to deepen the mathematical community's comprehension of the intricate relationship between the algebraic structure of groups and the existence of compatible orderings. Ultimately, our findings shed light on the diverse manifestations of orderable groups and contribute to the broader field of algebraic structures.

text: This study focuses on the detection of topical communities within event-based social networks, where users interact and share content around specific events or topics. Background research indicates that social networks play a vital role in shaping public opinions and influencing behaviors, particularly during events. However, existing community detection methods often rely on static graph structures and fail to capture the dynamic nature of event-based social networks.  The objective of this research is to develop an effective algorithm for detecting topical communities in event-based social networks. To achieve this, we propose a hybrid approach that integrates graph-based methods with topic modeling techniques. Our methodology involves (1) constructing a graph representation of the social network, (2) applying a graph-based community detection algorithm to identify clusters, and (3) using topic modeling to refine the clusters and identify topical communities.  Our key findings indicate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score. The algorithm is able to detect meaningful topical communities, even in the presence of noise and heterogeneity in the social network. We also observe that the algorithm's performance is significantly improved when combined with topic modeling techniques.  The conclusion of this research highlights the potential of the proposed approach for real-world applications, such as event-based social network analysis, opinion mining, and public health surveillance. The findings also underscore the importance of considering the dynamic nature of social networks when developing community detection algorithms.

This paper studies the performance of hierarchical modulation-based
multimedia transmission in cognitive radio (CR) systems with imperfect channel
sensing results under constraints on both transmit and interference power
levels. Unequal error protection (UEP) of data transmission using hierarchical
quadrature amplitude modulation (HQAM) is considered in which high priority
(HP) data is protected more than low priority (LP) data. In this setting,
closed-form bit error rate (BER) expressions for HP data and LP data are
derived in Nakagami-$m$ fading channels in the presence of sensing errors.
Subsequently, the optimal power control that minimizes weighted sum of average
BERs of HP bits and LP bits or its upper bound subject to peak/average transmit
power and average interference power constraints is derived and a
low-complexity power control algorithm is proposed. Power levels are determined
in three different scenarios, depending on the availability of perfect channel
side information (CSI) of the transmission and interference links, statistical
CSI of both links, or perfect CSI of the transmission link and imperfect CSI of
the interference link. The impact of imperfect channel sensing decisions on the
error rate performance of cognitive transmissions is also evaluated. In
addition, tradeoffs between the number of retransmissions, the severity of
fading, and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) quality are analyzed numerically.
Moreover, performance comparisons of multimedia transmission with conventional
quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) and HQAM, and the proposed power control
strategies are carried out in terms of the received data quality and number of
retransmissions.

text:
The debate around the potential superiority of quantum annealers over their
classical counterparts has been ongoing since the inception of the field by
Kadowaki and Nishimori close to two decades ago. Recent technological
breakthroughs in the field, which have led to the manufacture of experimental
prototypes of quantum annealing optimizers with sizes approaching the practical
regime, have reignited this discussion. However, the demonstration of quantum
annealing speedups remains to this day an elusive albeit coveted goal. Here, we
examine the power of quantum annealers to provide a different type of quantum
enhancement of practical relevance, namely, their ability to serve as useful
samplers from the ground-state manifolds of combinatorial optimization
problems. We study, both numerically by simulating ideal stoquastic and
non-stoquastic quantum annealing processes, and experimentally, using a
commercially available quantum annealing processor, the ability of quantum
annealers to sample the ground-states of spin glasses differently than
classical thermal samplers. We demonstrate that i) quantum annealers in general
sample the ground-state manifolds of spin glasses very differently than thermal
optimizers, ii) the nature of the quantum fluctuations driving the annealing
process has a decisive effect on the final distribution over ground-states, and
iii) the experimental quantum annealer samples ground-state manifolds
significantly differently than thermal and ideal quantum annealers. We
illustrate how quantum annealers may serve as powerful tools when complementing
standard sampling algorithms.

text: The synthesis of Fe2O3/Co3O4 composite nanoparticles for ethanol sensing applications is investigated due to the increasing demand for efficient gas sensors. Ethanol, being a common volatile organic compound, poses challenges in terms of accurate and quick detection. This study aims to develop a sensitive and selective ethanol sensor utilizing Fe2O3/Co3O4 composite nanoparticles. The composites were synthesized via a hydrothermal method, followed by calcination, to achieve a nanoscale integration of Fe2O3 and Co3O4. The morphological and structural properties of these nanoparticles were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The gas sensing performance was evaluated by monitoring the resistance change in the presence of varying ethanol concentrations at different operating temperatures. Key findings indicate that the Fe2O3/Co3O4 composite exhibits superior sensing performance in terms of response, recovery time, and sensitivity at an optimal operating temperature of 200°C, compared to individual metal oxides. The unique synergistic interaction between Fe2O3 and Co3O4 enhances the electron transfer capability and surface activity, thereby improving the sensor's performance. Furthermore, the composite sensor showcased excellent selectivity towards ethanol over other gases such as acetone, methanol, and carbon monoxide. These results suggest that Fe2O3/Co3O4 composite nanoparticles are promising candidates for next-generation ethanol sensors. The study concludes that the strategic design of metal oxide composites significantly enhances gas sensing properties, paving the way for their development in practical applications.

With the advent of large-scale quantum annealing devices, several challenges
have emerged. For example, it has been shown that the performance of a device
can be significantly affected by several degrees of freedom when programming
the device; a common example being gauge selection. To date, no
experimentally-tested strategy exists to select the best programming
specifications. We developed a score function that can be calculated from a
number of readouts much smaller than the number of readouts required to find
the desired solution. We show how this performance estimator can be used to
guide, for example, the selection of the optimal gauges out of a pool of random
gauge candidates and how to select the values of parameters for which we have
no a priori knowledge of the optimal value. For the latter, we illustrate the
concept by applying the score function to set the strength of the parameter
intended to enforce the embedding of the logical graph into the hardware
architecture, a challenge frequently encountered in the implementation of
real-world problem instances. Since the harder the problem instances, the more
useful the strategies proposed in this work are, we expect the programming
strategies proposed to significantly reduce the time of future benchmark
studies and in help finding the solution of hard-to-solve real-world
applications implemented in the next generation of quantum annealing devices.

text:
We present a study of strong cool core, highly-luminous (most with L_x >
10^(45) erg/s), clusters of galaxies in which the mean jet power of the central
active galactic nucleus must be very high yet no central point X-ray source is
detected. Using the unique spatial resolution of Chandra, a sample of 13
clusters is analysed, including A1835, A2204, and one of the most massive cool
core clusters, RXCJ1504.1-0248. All of the central galaxies host a radio
source, indicating an active nucleus, and no obvious X-ray point source. For
all clusters in the sample, the nucleus has an X-ray bolometric luminosity
below 2 per cent of that of the entire cluster. Most have a nucleus 2 - 10 keV
X-ray luminosity less than about 10^(42) erg/s. We investigate how these
clusters can have such strong X-ray luminosities, short radiative cooling-times
of the inner intracluster gas requiring strong energy feedback to
counterbalance that cooling, and yet have such radiatively-inefficient cores.
If the central black holes have masses ~10^9M_sol then the power exceeds one
per cent of the Eddington luminosity, and they are expected to be
radiatively-efficient. Only if they are ultramassive (M_BH > 10^(10)M_sol),
would their behaviour resemble that of lower mass accreting black holes. Our
study focuses on deriving the nucleus X-ray properties of the clusters as
defined in the above question, while briefly addressing possible solutions.

text:
V391 Peg (alias HS2201+2610) is a subdwarf B (sdB) pulsating star that shows
both p- and g-modes. By studying the arrival times of the p-mode maxima and
minima through the O-C method, in a previous article the presence of a planet
was inferred with an orbital period of 3.2 yr and a minimum mass of 3.2 M_Jup.
Here we present an updated O-C analysis using a larger data set of 1066 hours
of photometric time series (~2.5x larger in terms of the number of data
points), which covers the period between 1999 and 2012 (compared with 1999-2006
of the previous analysis). Up to the end of 2008, the new O-C diagram of the
main pulsation frequency (f1) is compatible with (and improves) the previous
two-component solution representing the long-term variation of the pulsation
period (parabolic component) and the giant planet (sine wave component). Since
2009, the O-C trend of f1 changes, and the time derivative of the pulsation
period (p_dot) passes from positive to negative; the reason of this change of
regime is not clear and could be related to nonlinear interactions between
different pulsation modes. With the new data, the O-C diagram of the secondary
pulsation frequency (f2) continues to show two components (parabola and sine
wave), like in the previous analysis. Various solutions are proposed to fit the
O-C diagrams of f1 and f2, but in all of them, the sinusoidal components of f1
and f2 differ or at least agree less well than before. The nice agreement found
previously was a coincidence due to various small effects that are carefully
analysed. Now, with a larger dataset, the presence of a planet is more
uncertain and would require confirmation with an independent method. The new
data allow us to improve the measurement of p_dot for f1 and f2: using only the
data up to the end of 2008, we obtain p_dot_1=(1.34+-0.04)x10**-12 and
p_dot_2=(1.62+-0.22)x10**-12 ...

text: The study of electron spins in isotopically enriched silicon near clock transitions is crucial for advancing quantum information processing technologies. The coherence of electron spins is essential for the reliability and efficiency of quantum computing systems.   This research aims to investigate the decoherence mechanisms affecting electron spins in isotopically enriched silicon near clock transitions. Understanding these mechanisms will provide insights into how to prolong the coherence time of electron spins, which is vital for the practical implementation of quantum computing applications.   The research employs a combination of experimental techniques and theoretical models to study the decoherence of electron spins in isotopically enriched silicon near clock transitions. Electron spin resonance spectroscopy and pulse sequences are utilized to investigate the dynamics of spin coherence.  Key findings The study reveals that the dominant decoherence mechanisms affecting electron spins in isotopically enriched silicon near clock transitions are primarily due to magnetic field fluctuations, phonon interactions, and charge noise. These findings provide valuable information for developing strategies to mitigate the impact of decoherence and improve the coherence time of electron spins in quantum systems.   By elucidating the decoherence mechanisms of electron spins in isotopically enriched silicon near clock transitions, this research contributes to the ongoing efforts to enhance the performance of quantum computing technologies. The insights gained from this study have the potential to guide the development of future quantum computing devices with prolonged coherence times, ultimately advancing the field of quantum information processing.
