text:
Early deep inelastic scattering (DIS) experiments at SLAC discovered partons,
identified them as quarks and gluons, and restricted the set of the candidate
theories for strong interactions to those exhibiting the asymptotic freedom
property. The next generation DIS experiments at FNAL and CERN confirmed the
predictions of QCD for the size of the scaling violation effects in the nucleon
structure functions. The QCD fits to their data resulted in determining the
momentum distributions of the point-like constituents of nucleons.
Interpretation of data coming from all these experiments and, in the case of
the SLAC experiments, even an elaboration of the running strategies, would not
have been possible without a precise understanding of the electromagnetic
radiative corrections. In this note I recollect the important milestones,
achieved in the period preceding the HERA era, in the high precision
calculations of the radiative corrections to DIS, and in the development of the
methods of their experimental control. I present subsequently the measurement
strategies and discuss the advanced radiative correction tools for the HERA
experimental program, with an emphasis on their role in the first, model
independent, measurement of the partonic densities in the small-$x_{Bj}$
region. These notes are dedicated to Staszek Jadach as a contribution to the
celebration of his 60th-birthday.

text: In this study, we present MOVI, a model-free approach designed to optimize dynamic fleet management. Our primary objective is to address the complexities associated with real-time decision-making in managing transport fleets, particularly in environments characterized by uncertainty and high variability in demand and supply conditions. We employ reinforcement learning techniques to develop a decision-making framework that autonomously adapts to changing operational scenarios without relying on predefined models.   Our methodology involves a novel algorithm that integrates data-driven insights with a simulation-based approach, allowing MOVI to learn optimal dispatch and routing policies through direct interactions with the operational environment. We conduct extensive experiments using synthetic datasets and real-world case studies, demonstrating that our model significantly outperforms traditional fleet management strategies based on static heuristics. The results indicate that MOVI achieves substantial improvements in service levels, cost efficiencies, and responsiveness to dynamic demand fluctuations.  We also explore the implications of our findings for practitioners in the transportation and logistics sectors, emphasizing the adaptability of our approach to various fleet configurations and operational constraints. Overall, our work contributes to the growing body of research on intelligent transportation systems by providing a scalable, robust, and flexible solution to dynamic fleet management challenges, paving the way for broader applications across diverse operational contexts.

text:
We study the interaction of feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGN) and a
multi-phase interstellar medium (ISM), in simulations including explicit
stellar feedback, multi-phase cooling, accretion-disk winds, and Compton
heating. We examine radii ~0.1-100 pc around a black hole (BH), where the
accretion rate onto the BH is determined and where AGN-powered winds and
radiation couple to the ISM. We conclude: (1) The BH accretion rate is
determined by exchange of angular momentum between gas and stars in
gravitational instabilities. This produces accretion rates ~0.03-1 Msun/yr,
sufficient to power luminous AGN. (2) The gas disk in the galactic nucleus
undergoes an initial burst of star formation followed by several Myrs where
stellar feedback suppresses the star formation rate (SFR). (3) AGN winds
injected at small radii with momentum fluxes ~L/c couple efficiently to the ISM
and have dramatic effects on ISM properties within ~100 pc. AGN winds suppress
the nuclear SFR by factors ~10-30 and BH accretion rate by factors ~3-30. They
increase the outflow rate from the nucleus by factors ~10, consistent with
observational evidence for galaxy-scale AGN-driven outflows. (4) With AGN
feedback, the predicted column density distribution to the BH is consistent
with observations. Absent AGN feedback, the BH is isotropically obscured and
there are not enough optically-thin sightlines to explain Type-I AGN. A
'torus-like' geometry arises self-consistently as AGN feedback evacuates gas in
polar regions.

text:
The mechanism of non-Abelian color confinement is studied in SU(2) lattice
gauge theory in terms of the Abelian fields and monopoles extracted from
non-Abelian link variables without adopting gauge fixing.
  Firstly, the static quark-antiquark potential and force are computed with the
Abelian and monopole Polyakov loop correlators, and the resulting string
tensions are found to be identical to the non-Abelian string tension. These
potentials also show the scaling behavior with respect to the change of lattice
spacing.
  Secondly, the profile of the color-electric field between a quark and an
antiquark is investigated with the Abelian and monopole Wilson loops. The
color-electric field is squeezed into a flux tube due to monopole supercurrent
with the same Abelian color direction. The parameters corresponding to the
penetration and coherence lengths show the scaling behavior, and the ratio of
these lengths, i.e, the Ginzburg-Landau parameter, indicates that the vacuum
type is near the border of the type1 and type2 (dual) superconductor.
  These results are summarized that the Abelian fundamental charge defined in
an arbitrary color direction is confined inside a hadronic state by the dual
Meissner effect. As the color-neutral state in any Abelian color direction
corresponds to the physical color-singlet state, this effect explains
non-Abelian color confinement and supports the existence of a gauge-invariant
mechanism of color confinement due to the dual Meissner effect caused by
Abelian monopoles.

text: Deterministic sensing matrices play a crucial role in compressive sensing applications. Constructing sensing matrices with desirable properties is essential for efficient signal recovery in sparse signal reconstruction.   This research aims to construct a large class of deterministic sensing matrices that satisfy a statistical isometry property. The statistical isometry property ensures that the sensing matrices preserve the geometry of sparse signals, leading to improved signal reconstruction accuracy and stability.   We propose a novel construction method based on structured random matrices with carefully designed properties. By leveraging tools from random matrix theory and combinatorial design theory, we construct deterministic sensing matrices that satisfy the statistical isometry property for a wide range of signal sparsity levels.   Through extensive theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed construction method in generating deterministic sensing matrices with excellent statistical isometry properties. The constructed sensing matrices exhibit superior performance compared to existing methods, particularly in scenarios with high signal sparsity.   The successful construction of a large class of deterministic sensing matrices satisfying a statistical isometry property opens up new avenues for enhancing the performance of compressive sensing algorithms. These findings contribute to improving signal recovery accuracy and efficiency in various applications, such as medical imaging, communication systems, and signal processing.

text: Massive star clusters play a crucial role in the dynamics of star formation and the evolution of galaxies. However, their stability can be significantly affected by the expulsion of gas from their surroundings, a phenomenon that may lead to rapid disintegration or morphological changes. The objective of this study is to investigate the response of massive star clusters to gas expulsion and to explore how this reaction depends on the density of the clusters. We employed a series of high-resolution N-body simulations to model clusters with varying initial densities, simulating gas expulsion through sudden removal of the gas mass using a combination of hydrodynamic and direct N-body techniques. Key findings reveal that lower-density clusters experience a more pronounced expansion and subsequent disruption, whereas higher-density clusters exhibit greater resilience due to enhanced gravitational binding. We identified thresholds in cluster density that determine the degree of survival post-expulsion, with implications for star formation efficiency and the retention of stellar populations. These results underscore the complex interplay between cluster dynamics and environmental factors, suggesting that gas expulsion plays a pivotal role in shaping the evolutionary pathways of massive clusters. In conclusion, this study enhances our understanding of how cluster density mediates responses to gas loss, contributing to the broader knowledge of star cluster formation and stability within galaxies.

text:
We present a 70ks Chandra observation of the radio galaxy 3C293. This galaxy
belongs to the class of molecular hydrogen emission galaxies (MOHEGs) that have
very luminous emission from warm molecular hydrogen. In radio galaxies, the
molecular gas appears to be heated by jet-driven shocks, but exactly how this
mechanism works is still poorly understood. With Chandra, we observe X-ray
emission from the jets within the host galaxy and along the 100 kpc radio jets.
We model the X-ray spectra of the nucleus, the inner jets, and the X-ray
features along the extended radio jets. Both the nucleus and the inner jets
show evidence of 10^7 K shock-heated gas. The kinetic power of the jets is more
than sufficient to heat the X-ray emitting gas within the host galaxy. The
thermal X-ray and warm H2 luminosities of 3C293 are similar, indicating similar
masses of X-ray hot gas and warm molecular gas. This is consistent with a
picture where both derive from a multiphase, shocked interstellar medium (ISM).
We find that radio-loud MOHEGs that are not brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs),
like 3C293, typically have LH2/LX~1 and MH2/MX~1, whereas MOHEGs that are BCGs
have LH2/LX~0.01 and MH2/MX~0.01. The more massive, virialized, hot atmosphere
in BCGs overwhelms any direct X-ray emission from current jet-ISM interaction.
On the other hand, LH2/LX~1 in the Spiderweb BCG at z=2, which resides in an
unvirialized protocluster and hosts a powerful radio source. Over time, jet-ISM
interaction may contribute to the establishment of a hot atmosphere in BCGs and
other massive elliptical galaxies.

text: This research aims to develop a comprehensive theory that integrates curvature scaling with gravitational dynamics. It builds upon existing theories by examining how the scale of curvature affects gravitational interactions, focusing on the implications for large-scale structure formation and the behavior of black holes. Key findings indicate that curvature scaling modifies the effective gravitational force law at different scales, leading to novel insights into the cosmic microwave background radiation and the distribution of galaxies. The analysis also reveals that these modifications can explain observed phenomena such as the acceleration of cosmic expansion without invoking dark energy. The ultimate goal is to establish a robust theoretical framework that bridges quantum gravity and cosmology, offering new perspectives on the fundamental nature of spacetime and gravity.

text:
The mobile edge computing (MEC) has been introduced for providing computing
capabilities at the edge of networks to improve the latency performance of
wireless networks. In this paper, we provide the novel framework for
MEC-enabled heterogeneous networks (HetNets), composed of the multi-tier
networks with access points (APs) (i.e., MEC servers), which have different
transmission power and different computing capabilities. In this framework, we
also consider multiple-type mobile users with different sizes of computation
tasks, and they offload the tasks to a MEC server, and receive the computation
resulting data from the server. We derive the successful edge computing
probability (SECP), defined as the probability that a user offloads and
finishes its computation task at the MEC server within the target latency. We
provide a closed-form expression of the approximated SECP for general case, and
closed-form expressions of the exact SECP for special cases. This paper then
provides the design insights for the optimal configuration of MEC-enabled
HetNets by analyzing the effects of network parameters and bias factors, used
in MEC server association, on the SECP. Specifically, it shows how the optimal
bias factors in terms of SECP can be changed according to the numbers of user
types and tiers of MEC servers, and how they are different to the conventional
ones that did not consider the computing capabilities and task sizes.

text: This study investigates the potential synchrotron emission from dark matter within galactic subhalos, focusing on the Smith Cloud as a case study. We explore how the high-energy particles produced by dark matter annihilation or decay could generate detectable synchrotron radiation. Our analysis utilizes detailed simulations of dark matter distributions within the Smith Cloud's gravitational potential, assuming various models for dark matter interactions. Key findings indicate that under certain conditions—specifically when the density of dark matter particles is sufficiently high and the magnetic field strength is moderate—the synchrotron signal could be observable. Methodologically, we employ Monte Carlo simulations to model dark matter particle interactions and synchrotron radiation, incorporating observational constraints to assess the feasibility of detecting such emissions. This work highlights the importance of dark matter in shaping the dynamics of cosmic structures and underscores the potential of future observations to probe dark matter physics through its interaction with baryonic matter.

text:
A chain of metallic particles, of sufficiently small diameter and spacing,
allows linearly polarized plasmonic waves to propagate along the chain. In this
paper, we consider how these waves are altered by an anisotropic host (such as
a nematic liquid crystal) or an applied magnetic field. In a liquid crystalline
host, with principal axis (director) oriented either parallel or perpendicular
to the chain, we find that the dispersion relations of both the longitudinal
($L$) and transverse ($T$) modes are significantly altered relative to those of
an isotropic host. Furthermore, when the director is perpendicular to the
chain, the doubly degenerate $T$ branch is split by the anisotropy of the host
material. With an applied magnetic field ${\bf B}$ parallel to the chain, the
propagating transverse modes are circularly polarized, and the left and right
circularly polarized branches have slightly different dispersion relations. As
a result, if a linearly polarized transverse wave is launched along the chain,
it undergoes Faraday rotation. For parameters approximating that of a typical
metal and for a field of 2T, the Faraday rotation is of order 1$^o$ per ten
interparticle spacings, even taking into account single-particle damping. If
${\bf B}$ is perpendicular to the chain, one of the $T$ branches mixes with the
$L$ branch to form two elliptically polarized branches. Our calculations
include single-particle damping and can, in principle, be generalized to
include radiation damping. The present work suggests that the dispersion
relations of plasmonic waves on chain of nanoparticles can be controlled by
immersing the chain in a nematic liquid crystal and varying the director axis,
or by applying a magnetic field.

text: This study presents the results of a comprehensive reverberation measurement campaign to determine the inner radius of the dust torus in the active galaxy NGC 4151, conducted between 2008 and 2013. The galaxy NGC 4151 is a powerful Seyfert 2 galaxy known for its strong emission lines and complex dust structure, which can affect the measurement of its central black hole mass.  The objective of this research was to investigate the inner radius of the dust torus in NGC 4151 using high-resolution spectroscopic data and reverberation mapping techniques. A team of astronomers employed a combination of optical and ultraviolet spectroscopic observations to measure the light curves of several emission lines, including Hα and [O III], at different wavelengths.  The reverberation mapping technique was used to estimate the light travel time between the central black hole and the emitting regions. The flat bone develops through intramembranous ossification, in which the
mesenchymal cells are directly driven towards osteogenic lineage without the
formation of cartilage template. While long bone develops through endochondral
ossification, where cartilage template act as an intermediate stage between
mesenchymal and bone tissues. Although the avian sternum is a flat bone, some
studies describe formation of a cartilage template during its development. The
aim of the current study was to observe the mechanism of ossification in quail
sternum during embryonic development. Thirty quail embryos were collected for
the current study (5 embryos/ day) during the period between Day (D) 5 and D10
of embryonic development and processed for light microscopy. The
differentiation of mesenchymal condensation in to the chondrogenic cells was
observed at D5 whereas the secretion of extracellular matrix could be evident
at D6. The cartilage primordia were observed by D7 which were consisted of
chondrocytes, embedded in matrix and surrounded by perichondrium. Later these
primordia were developed in to cartilage template by D8 where the chondrocytes
were present in their lacuna. This template attained the shape of future
sternum by D9, which was more distinct at D10. These preliminary observations
suggested that the quail sternum grows through endochondral ossification. The
future study will further explore the histological changes of quail sternum
during post-hatching development.

text: In this study, we have developed a novel approach for achieving high-precision Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) astrometry at low radio frequencies by employing a multiview technique. The primary objective is to address the limitations in astrometric accuracy typically encountered at lower frequencies due to ionospheric distortions and instrumental instabilities. We implemented simultaneous observations of multiple calibrator sources strategically distributed around the target source, allowing for a more robust calibration of ionospheric perturbations and enhancing the fidelity of phase-referenced VLBI data. Our methodology also includes a sophisticated data reduction pipeline that integrates differential astrometry techniques and advanced ionospheric modeling. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in positional accuracy, achieving sub-milliarcsecond precision, which surpasses traditional single calibrator approaches. This advancement has broad implications for the study of astronomical objects that exhibit strong radio emissions at low frequencies, such as pulsars and active galactic nuclei, enhancing our ability to conduct precise parallax measurements and determine their spatial dynamics with higher precision. Our findings underscore the potential of multiview VLBI astrometry to overcome frequency-dependent limitations and pave the way for future astronomical observations that require pinpoint accuracy. These results contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the low-frequency radio universe and highlight the necessity of refining astrometric techniques to accommodate various atmospheric and instrumental challenges.

text: This study investigates the relationship between convex RP^2 structures and cubic differentials in the context of neck separation phenomena. The primary objective of our research is to analyze the behavior of cubic differentials when subjected to topological transformations, specifically during neck separation events in convex RP^2 surfaces. We employ a combination of analytic and geometric methods, examining the deformation spaces and moduli of convex projective structures while quantifying the variations in cubic differentials as necks emerge and disappear. Our key findings reveal that cubic differentials exhibit significant alterations in their geometric and topological configurations, resulting in a rich interplay of volume preservation and singularity formation. Notably, the study identifies threshold behaviors where the geometry transitions from finite to infinite volume, highlighting the critical nature of neck separation in the dynamics of these structures. In conclusion, the interplay between convex RP^2 structures and cubic differentials under neck separation provides insightful implications for understanding the stability and deformation of projective structures, suggesting broader applications in geometric topology and mathematical physics. This research contributes to the foundational knowledge in the area, opening potential avenues for future exploration surrounding the intricate behavior of differentials in geometric structures.

The first part of this thesis deals with certain properties of the quantum
symmetric and exterior algebras of Type 1 representations of $U_q(g)$ defined
by Berenstein and Zwicknagl. We define a notion of a commutative algebra object
in a coboundary category, and we prove that the quantum symmetric algebra of a
module is the universal commutative algebra generated by that module. That is,
the functor assigning to a module its quantum symmetric algebra is left adjoint
to a forgetful functor. We also prove a conjecture of Berenstein and Zwicknagl,
stating that the quantum symmetric and exterior cubes exhibit the same amount
of "collapsing" relative to their classical counterparts. We prove that those
quantum exterior algebras that are flat deformations of their classical
analogues are Frobenius algebras. We also develop a rigorous framework for
discussing continuity and limits of the structures involved as the deformation
parameter q varies along the positive real line.
  The second part deals with quantum analogues of Clifford algebras and their
application to the noncommutative geometry of certain quantum homogeneous
spaces. We introduce the quantum Clifford algebra through its spinor
representation via creation and annihilation operators on one of the flat
quantum exterior algebras discussed in the first part. The proof that the
spinor representation is irreducible relies on the Frobenius property discussed
previously. We use this quantum Clifford algebra to revisit Krahmer's
construction of a Dolbeault-Dirac-type operator on a quantized irreducible flag
manifold. This operator is of the form $d+d^*$, and we relate $d$ to the
boundary operator for the Koszul complex of a certain quantum symmetric
algebra, which shows that $d^2=0$. This is a first step toward a
Parthasarathy-type formula for the spectrum of the square of the Dirac
operator.

Context: Hard X-rays from solar flares are an important diagnostic of
particle acceleration and transport in the solar atmosphere. Any observed X-ray
flux from on-disc sources is composed of direct emission plus Compton
backscattered photons (albedo). This affects both the observed spectra and
images as well as the physical quantities derived from them such as the spatial
and spectral distributions of accelerated electrons or characteristics of the
solar atmosphere. Aims: We propose a new indirect method to measure albedo and
to infer the directivity of X-rays in imaging using RHESSI data. Methods:
Visibility forward fitting is used to determine the size of a disc event
observed by RHESSI as a function of energy. This is compared to the sizes of
simulated sources from a Monte Carlo simulation code of photon transport in the
chromosphere for different degrees of downward directivity and true source
sizes to find limits on the true source size and the directivity. Results: The
observed full width half maximum of the source varies in size between 7.4
arcsec and 9.1 arcsec with the maximum between 30 and 40 keV. Such behaviour is
expected in the presence of albedo and is found in the simulations. A source
size smaller than 6 arcsec is improbable for modest directivities and the true
source size is likely to be around 7 arcsec for small directivities.
Conclusions: While it is difficult to image the albedo patch directly, the
effect of backscattered photons on the observed source size can be estimated.
The increase in source size caused by albedo has to be accounted for when
computing physical quantities that include the size as a parameter such as
flare energetics. At the same time, the study of the albedo signature provides
vital information about the directivity of X-rays and related electrons.

text: Cognitive radio networks (CRNs) have emerged as a promising solution to alleviate the spectrum scarcity problem by dynamically exploiting idle spectrum. This research presents an order optimal policy for maximizing the utilization of available spectrum resources in CRNs while minimizing interference to primary users. The objective is to develop an efficient framework that can adaptively allocate idle spectrum to secondary users based on real-time availability and QoS requirements. We formulate the problem as a stochastic dynamic programming model, incorporating state transitions that consider user demands, channel conditions, and regulatory constraints. Through comprehensive simulations, we evaluate the performance of the proposed policy against conventional spectrum access strategies. Key findings indicate that the order optimal policy significantly improves spectrum utilization by up to 35% and reduces the average blocking probability of secondary users compared to baseline approaches. Additionally, the policy demonstrates robustness in varying network conditions, maintaining performance stability under different user traffic patterns. In conclusion, the proposed order optimal policy not only enhances the efficiency of spectrum usage in CRNs but also provides a scalable solution that can adapt to diverse real-world scenarios, paving the way for more intelligent and flexible spectrum management techniques in future wireless networks. This work contributes to the advancement of cognitive radio technology and its practical deployment, offering implications for both research and telecommunications industry standards.

text: We report the observation of room-temperature ferromagnetism in transparent conducting anatase Ti_{1-x}Ta_xO_2 thin films with x~0.05, a cationic vacancy concentration. Our results demonstrate that the incorporation of Ta ions into the TiO_2 lattice leads to the formation of a ferromagnetic phase, characterized by a saturation magnetization of 0.45 emu/cm^2 at room temperature. This phenomenon is attributed to the presence of cationic vacancies, which act as charge carriers and facilitate the exchange interaction between Ti and Ta ions. The ferromagnetic behavior is found to be highly sensitive to the Ta concentration, with a maximum ferromagnetic moment occurring at x=0.05. Our findings are supported by density functional theory calculations, which reveal that the cationic vacancies induce a spin-polarized electron density, leading to a ferromagnetic ordering. The observed ferromagnetism is also found to be stable over a wide temperature range, from 300 K to 400 K, indicating a potential application in next-generation transparent conductive devices, such as flexible electronics and optoelectronic devices.

text: This study explores the concept of trophic groups and modules in food webs, two distinct approaches to detecting groupings of organisms in ecosystems. Background research highlights the complexity of food webs, where individual species interact with each other in intricate networks, and the need for a hierarchical framework to analyze these interactions. The two main approaches, trophic groups and modules, differ in their definitions and applications. Trophic groups are defined as clusters of species that occupy similar trophic levels, whereas modules are defined as groups of species that interact with each other in a coordinated manner. The objective of this study is to compare the effectiveness of these two approaches in detecting groupings in food webs, with a focus on their implications for understanding ecosystem functioning and biodiversity.  The study employed a comprehensive analysis of 150 food webs from various ecosystems, using both trophic group and module detection methods. The results show that trophic groups are more easily detected in simple food webs, whereas modules are more prominent in complex food webs. Notably, the overlap between trophic groups and modules is significant, suggesting that these two approaches can be complementary rather than mutually exclusive. The key findings also reveal that the detection of trophic groups and modules can provide insights into ecosystem functioning, such as the distribution of nutrient fluxes and the stability of ecosystems. Overall, the study demonstrates the value of both trophic groups and modules in understanding the structure and function of food webs, and highlights the need for a more integrated approach to analyzing these complex ecosystems.

text: The abstract explores the capabilities of gravitational-wave (GW) observations in distinguishing between black holes (BHs) and neutron stars (NSs). Current GW detectors, such as LIGO and Virgo, have provided insights into binary systems through their detection of GW signals. However, the unique properties of BHs and NSs, including their masses, radii, and spin characteristics, offer distinct signatures in GW data that could potentially be exploited for classification purposes.   This study aims to identify the conditions under which GW observations can reliably differentiate between BHs and NSs, focusing on parameters such as chirp mass, mass ratio, and final orbital period. By analyzing simulated GW signals from various BH-NS merger scenarios, we evaluate the sensitivity of current GW detectors and propose future improvements to enhance the discrimination capability.   A comprehensive analysis was conducted using numerical relativity simulations to generate realistic GW signals. These signals were then processed through matched filtering techniques to extract characteristic features indicative of the source type. Statistical methods were employed to assess the performance of different detector configurations in separating BH and NS signals based on signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and false alarm rates.   Our results indicate that while both BHs and NSs can produce similar initial GW signals, there are observable differences in the higher harmonics of the signal spectrum. Specifically, the presence of significant quadrupole and octupole moments in the GW waveform is more pronounced for NSs compared to BHs. Furthermore, the final orbital period and the presence of glitches in the GW signal can also provide additional clues about the nature of the source.   Gravitational-wave observations present a promising avenue for distinguishing between BHs and NSs, especially when considering the detailed analysis of higher harmonics and post-merger dynamics. Future advancements in detector sensitivity and computational resources will further refine our ability to classify these sources, enhancing our understanding of compact object mergers and their astrophysical implications.

In the past six decades, lifespan inequality has varied greatly within and
among countries even while life expectancy has continued to increase. How and
why does mortality change generate this diversity? We derive a precise link
between changes in age-specific mortality and lifespan inequality, measured as
the variance of age at death. Key to this relationship is a young-old threshold
age, below and above which mortality decline respectively decreases and
increases lifespan inequality. First, we show that shifts in the threshold's
location modified the correlation between changes in life expectancy and
lifespan inequality over the last two centuries. Second, we analyze the post
Second World War trajectories of lifespan inequality in a set of developed
countries, Japan, Canada and the United States (US), where thresholds centered
on retirement age. Our method reveals how divergence in the age-pattern of
mortality change drives international divergence in lifespan inequality. Most
strikingly, early in the 1980s, mortality increases in young US males led
lifespan inequality to remain high in the US, while in Canada the decline of
inequality continued. In general, our wider international comparisons show that
mortality change varied most at young working ages after the Second World War,
particularly for males. We conclude that if mortality continues to stagnate at
young ages, yet declines steadily at old ages, increases in lifespan inequality
will become a common feature of future demographic change.

Various lines of evidence suggest that the cores of a large portion of
early-type galaxies (ETGs) are virtually evacuated of warm ionised gas. This
implies that the Lyman-continuum (LyC) radiation produced by an assumed active
galactic nucleus (AGN) can escape from the nuclei of these systems without
being locally reprocessed into nebular emission, which would prevent their
reliable spectroscopic classification as Seyfert galaxies with standard
diagnostic emission-line ratios. The spectral energy distribution (SED) of
these ETGs would then lack nebular emission and be essentially composed of an
old stellar component and the featureless power-law (PL) continuum from the
AGN. A question that arises in this context is whether the AGN component can be
detected with current spectral population synthesis in the optical,
specifically, whether these techniques effectively place an AGN detection
threshold in LyC-leaking galaxies. To quantitatively address this question, we
took a combined approach that involves spectral fitting with STARLIGHT of
synthetic SEDs composed of stellar emission that characterises a 10 Gyr old ETG
and an AGN power-law component that contributes a fraction $0\leq
x_{\mathrm{AGN}} < 1$ of the monochromatic luminosity at $\lambda_0=$ 4020 \AA.
In addition to a set of fits for PL distributions $F_{\nu} \propto
\nu^{-\alpha}$ with the canonical $\alpha=1.5$, we used a base of multiple PLs
with $0.5 \leq \alpha \leq 2$ for a grid of synthetic SEDs with a
signal-to-noise ratio of 5-$10^3$. Our analysis indicates an effective AGN
detection threshold at $x_{\mathrm{AGN}}\simeq 0.26$, which suggests that a
considerable fraction of ETGs hosting significant accretion-powered nuclear
activity may be missing in the AGN demographics.

text: The abstract for the research paper titled "Lexicographic Inquiry into Mary Astell's 'A Serious Proposal to the Ladies' An Analysis Using NooJ" begins with a brief introduction to Mary Astell, a prominent intellectual figure of the Enlightenment period who wrote 'A Serious Proposal to the Ladies' in 1700. This work was a pioneering attempt to address women's education and participation in public life, setting the stage for future feminist discourse.  The study focuses on a lexicographic analysis of selected passages from 'A Serious Proposal to the Ladies', employing the computational linguistic framework provided by NooJ. The objective of this research is to uncover the linguistic patterns, semantic nuances, and rhetorical strategies employed by Astell within her work. By using NooJ, a computational tool designed for natural language processing, the study aims to automate the extraction and analysis of lexical data, offering a quantitative approach to qualitative textual analysis.  Methodologically, the research involved segmenting the text into sentences and paragraphs, identifying key terms, and analyzing their frequency and distribution across different sections of the work. Additionally, the study examined the syntactic structure of Astell’s sentences and the cohesion between them, as well as the use of metaphor and analogy to convey her ideas.  Key findings indicate that Astell utilized sophisticated vocabulary and complex sentence structures, reflecting her ambition to engage with philosophical and theological concepts in a manner befitting a learned woman of her time. Her frequent recourse to metaphors and analogies served to make her arguments more accessible while also subtly reinforcing her argumentative stance. The analysis revealed a strong emphasis on the cultivation of virtue and the pursuit of knowledge as essential components of female empowerment.  In conclusion, this study not only provides a deeper understanding of Astell's linguistic choices but also highlights the importance of her work in the broader context of early modern feminist thought. The computational tools employed offer new avenues for scholarly research, enriching our comprehension of Astell's contributions to literature and philosophy.

In this paper, we explore the TGTG formula from the perspective of mode
summation approach. Both scalar fields and electromagnetic fields are
considered. In this approach, one has to first solve the equation of motion to
find a wave basis for each object. The two T's in the TGTG formula are
T-matrices representing the Lippmann-Schwinger T-operators, one for each of the
objects. The two G's in the TGTG formula are the translation matrices, relating
the wave basis of an object to the wave basis of the other object. After
discussing the general theory, we apply the prescription to derive the explicit
formulas for the Casimir energies for the sphere-sphere, sphere-plane,
cylinder-cylinder and cylinder-plane interactions. First the T-matrices for a
plane, a sphere and a cylinder are derived for the following cases: the object
is imposed with general Robin boundary conditions; the object is
semitransparent; and the object is magnetodielectric. Then the operator
approach is used to derive the translation matrices. From these, the explicit
TGTG formula for each of the scenarios can be written down. Besides summarizing
all the TGTG formulas that have been derived so far, we also provide the TGTG
formulas for some scenarios that have not been considered before.

We present results from sensitive, multi-epoch NuSTAR observations of the
late-type star-forming galaxy M83 (d=4.6 Mpc), which is the first investigation
to spatially resolve the hard (E>10 keV) X-ray emission of this galaxy. The
nuclear region and ~ 20 off-nuclear point sources, including a previously
discovered ultraluminous X-ray (ULX) source, are detected in our NuSTAR
observations. The X-ray hardnesses and luminosities of the majority of the
point sources are consistent with hard X-ray sources resolved in the starburst
galaxy NGC 253. We infer that the hard X-ray emission is most likely dominated
by intermediate accretion state black hole binaries and neutron star low-mass
X-ray binaries (Z-sources). We construct the X-ray binary luminosity function
(XLF) in the NuSTAR band for an extragalactic environment for the first time.
The M83 XLF has a steeper XLF than the X-ray binary XLF in NGC 253, consistent
with previous measurements by Chandra at softer X-ray energies. The NuSTAR
integrated galaxy spectrum of M83 drops quickly above 10 keV, which is also
seen in the starburst galaxies NGC253, NGC 3310 and NGC 3256. The NuSTAR
observations constrain any AGN to be either highly obscured or to have an
extremely low luminosity of $_{\sim}^<$10$^{38}$ erg/s (10-30 keV), implying it
is emitting at a very low Eddington ratio. An X-ray point source consistent
with the location of the nuclear star cluster with an X-ray luminosity of a few
times 10$^{38}$ erg/s may be a low-luminosity AGN but is more consistent with
being an X-ray binary.

text: The flyby anomaly, an unexpected variance in spacecraft speed relative to predictions, has intrigued physicists since its initial observation. This study investigates whether Juno, a spacecraft on its mission to Jupiter, experiences a similar anomaly and seeks to understand if deviations from expected velocity are explicable through known physical theories. The objective of this research is to analyze Juno's trajectory and velocity during its Earth flyby, exploring potential origins of any discrepancies observed. Utilizing Doppler tracking data and precise navigation models, we conducted a detailed assessment of Juno’s flyby to identify anomalous behavior. The research critically evaluates the gravitational and non-gravitational forces acting on the spacecraft, comparing observed speed changes against rigorous computational predictions. Initial findings reveal minor deviations during Juno’s flyby, with behavior not fully accounted for by standard gravitational interactions and atmospheric drag. These results echo the enigmatic flyby anomalies reported for previous missions. The analysis suggests potential contributing factors outside the scope of established physics, such as the interplay of relativistic effects or unmodeled geophysical phenomena. This paper also explores alternative hypotheses, such as instrumental or observational errors. In conclusion, while Juno's slight velocity discrepancies do not directly challenge standard physics, they invite further investigation into non-standard models and refined measurement techniques. Continued analysis across multiple flyby missions is crucial to enhance understanding of this anomaly, offering deeper insights into spacecraft navigation and gravitational theories.

The Mg II h&k lines are powerful diagnostics for studying the solar
chromosphere. They have become particularly popular with the launch of the IRIS
satellite, and a number of studies that include these lines have lead to great
progress in understanding chromospheric heating, in many cases thanks to the
support from 3D MHD simulations. In this study we utilize another approach to
analyze observations: non-LTE inversions of the Mg II h&k and UV triplet lines
including the effects of partial redistribution. Our inversion code attempts to
construct a model atmosphere that is compatible with the observed spectra. We
have assessed the capabilities and limitations of the inversions using the FALC
atmosphere and a snapshot from a 3D radiation-MHD simulation. We find that Mg
II h&k allow reconstructing a model atmosphere from the middle photosphere to
the transition region. We have also explored the capabilities of a
multi-line/multi-atom setup, including the Mg II h&k, the Ca II 854.2 nm and
the Fe I 630.25 lines to recover the full stratification of physical
parameters, including the magnetic field vector, from the photosphere to the
chromosphere. Finally, we present the first inversions of observed IRIS spectra
from quiet-Sun, plage and sunspot, with very promising results.

The study of the Higgs boson properties is one of the most important tasks to
be accomplished in the next years, at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and at
future colliders such as the Future Circular Collider in hadron-hadron mode
(FCC-hh), the potential 100 TeV follow-up of the LHC machine. In this view the
precise study of the Higgs couplings to weak gauge bosons is crucial and
requires as much information as possible. After the recent calculation of the
next-to-leading order QCD corrections to the production cross sections and
differential distributions of a Standard Model Higgs boson in association with
a pair of weak bosons, matched with parton shower in the POWHEG-BOX framework,
we present the gluon fusion correction $g g\to H W^+_{} W^-_{} ( H Z Z)$ to the
process $p p \to H W^+_{} W^-_{} (H Z Z)$. This correction can be sizeable and
amounts to $+3\,\%$ ($+10\,\%$) in the $H W^+_{} W^-_{}$ process and $+5\,\%$
($+18\,\%$) in the $H Z Z$ process at the LHC (FCC-hh). We also present the
first study of the impact of the bottom--quark initiated channels $b\bar{b}\to
H W^+_{} W^-_{} / H Z Z$ and find that they induce a significant $+18\,\%$
correction in the $H W^+_{} W^-_{}$ channel at the FCC-hh. We present results
on total cross sections and distributions at the LHC and at the FCC-hh.

Chemical and structural diversity present in hexagonal boron nitride ((h-BN)
and graphene hybrid nanostructures provide new avenues for tuning various
properties for their technological applications. In this paper we investigate
the variation of thermal conductivity ($\kappa$) of hybrid graphene/h-BN
nanostructures: stripe superlattices and BN (graphene) dots embedded in
graphene (BN) are investigated using equilibrium molecular dynamics. To
simulate these systems, we have parameterized a Tersoff type interaction
potential to reproduce the ab initio energetics of the B-C and N-C bonds for
studying the various interfaces that emerge in these hybrid nanostructures. We
demonstrate that both the details of the interface, including energetic
stability and shape, as well as the spacing of the interfaces in the material
exert strong control on the thermal conductivity of these systems. For stripe
superlattices, we find that zigzag configured interfaces produce a higher
$\kappa$ in the direction parallel to the interface than the armchair
configuration, while the perpendicular conductivity is less prone to the
details of the interface and is limited by the $\kappa$ of h-BN. Additionally,
the embedded dot structures, having mixed zigzag and armchair interfaces,
affects the thermal transport properties more strongly than superlattices.
Though dot radius appears to have little effect on the magnitude of reduction,
we find that dot concentration (50% yielding the greatest reduction) and
composition (embedded graphene dots showing larger reduction that h-BN dot)
have a significant effect.

This paper studies spatial capacity in a stochastic wireless ad hoc network,
where multi-stage probing and data transmission are sequentially performed. We
propose a novel signal-to-interference-ratio (SIR) threshold based scheduling
scheme, where by starting with the first probing, each transmitter iteratively
decides to further probe or stay idle, depending on whether the estimated SIR
in the proceeding probing is larger or smaller than a predefined threshold.
Although one can assume that the transmitters are initially deployed according
to a homogeneous Poisson point process (PPP), the SIR based scheduling makes
the PPP no longer applicable to model the locations of retained transmitters in
the subsequent probing and data transmission phases, due to the interference
induced coupling in their decisions. We first focus on single-stage probing and
find that when the SIR threshold is set sufficiently small to assure an
acceptable interference level in the network, the proposed scheme can greatly
outperform the non-scheduling reference scheme in terms of spatial capacity. We
clearly characterize the spatial capacity and obtain exact/approximate
closed-form expressions, by proposing a new approximate approach to deal with
the correlated SIR distributions over non-Poisson point processes. Then we
successfully extend to multi-stage probing by properly designing the multiple
SIR thresholds to assure gradual improvement of the spatial capacity.
Furthermore, we analyze the impact of multi-stage probing overhead and present
a probing-capacity tradeoff in scheduling design. Finally, extensive numerical
results are presented to demonstrate the performance of the proposed scheduling
as compared to existing schemes.

text: In our research, we explore the novel phenomenon of transporting spin-anisotropy without depending on conventional spin currents, which traditionally involve the movement of electrons and their associated spins. This study aims to address the limitations posed by resistive losses in spintronic devices by proposing a method to propagate spin information without physical spin transfer. Utilizing a theoretical framework based on the spin Hamiltonian and employing advanced numerical simulations, we establish that spin-anisotropy can be effectively transmitted through a medium via localized spin variations. Our methodology focuses on the manipulation of the spin exchange interactions and external magnetic fields within anisotropic spin systems, allowing for the adjustment of spin orientations in specific materials, thereby facilitating the travel of anisotropy signatures. The results demonstrate that certain spin-transport channels can be engineered to maintain information integrity over considerable distances without the need for spin currents. Key findings include the identification of conditions under which spin-anisotropy can travel solely through the modulation of internal degrees of freedom, offering a viable low-energy alternative for the storage and transmission of spin-based information. These insights offer a promising pathway for the development of next-generation, energy-efficient spintronic devices with enhanced performance characteristics. Further experimental validation and exploration of material-specific implementations could potentially broaden the scope of spintronic technologies by minimizing power consumption and mitigating Joule heating concerns. Our work thus contributes significantly to the fundamental understanding and practical advancement of spin transport mechanisms beyond traditional paradigms.

We study the dynamical effects of gravitational focusing by a binary
companion on winds from late-type stars. In particular, we investigate the mass
transfer and formation of accretion disks around the secondary in detached
systems consisting of an AGB mass-losing star and an accreting companion. The
presence of mass outflows is studied as a function of mass loss rate, wind
temperature and binary orbital parameters. A 2-dimensional hydrodynamical model
is used to study the stability of mass transfer in wind accreting symbiotic
binary systems. In our simulations we use an adiabatic equation of state and a
modified version of the isothermal approximation, where the temperature depends
on the distance from the mass losing star and its companion. We explore the
accretion flow between the components and formation of accretion disks for a
range of orbital separations and wind parameters. Our results show the
formation of stream flow between the stars and accretion disks of various sizes
for certain orbital configurations. For a typical slow and massive wind from an
AGB star the flow pattern is similar to a RLOF with accretion rates of 10% of
the mass loss from the primary. Stable disks with exponentially decreasing
density profiles and masses of the order $10^{-4}$ solar masses are formed when
wind acceleration occurs at several stellar radii. The formation of tidal
streams and accretion disks is found to be weakly dependent on the mass loss
from the AGB star. Our simulations of gravitationally focused wind accretion in
symbiotic binaries show the formation of stream flows and enhanced accretion
rates onto the compact component.

The asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star R Sculptoris (R Scl) is one of the
most extensively studied stars on the AGB. R Scl is a carbon star with a
massive circumstellar shell ($M_{shell}\sim 7.3\times10^{-3}~M_{\odot}$) which
is thought to have been produced during a thermal pulse event $\sim2200$ years
ago. To study the thermal dust emission associated with its circumstellar
material, observations were taken with the Faint Object InfraRed CAMera for the
SOFIA Telescope (FORCAST) at 19.7, 25.2, 31.5, 34.8, and 37.1 $\mu$m. Maps of
the infrared emission at these wavelengths were used to study the morphology
and temperature structure of the spatially extended dust emission. Using the
radiative transfer code DUSTY and fitting the spatial profile of the emission,
we find that a geometrically thin dust shell cannot reproduce the observed
spatially resolved emission. Instead, a second dust component in addition to
the shell is needed to reproduce the observed emission. This component, which
lies interior to the dust shell, traces the circumstellar envelope of R Scl. It
is best fit by a density profile with $n \propto r^{\alpha}$ where
$\alpha=0.75^{+0.45}_{-0.25}$ and dust mass of
$M_d=9.0^{+2.3}_{-4.1}\times10^{-6}~M_{\odot}$. The strong departure from an
$r^{-2}$ law indicates that the mass-loss rate of R Scl has not been constant.
This result is consistent with a slow decline in the post-pulse mass-loss which
has been inferred from observations of the molecular gas.

text: Dark matter, an enigmatic component of the universe, is believed to account for approximately 27% of its total mass. Although it remains undetectable through conventional means, recent theories suggest the possibility of dark matter interacting with ordinary matter. This study explores the potential implications of such collisions with the human body, specifically focusing on the consequences for human health.  The objective of this research is to examine the hypothetical interactions between dark matter particles and the atomic structure of human tissues. To accomplish this, a simulation model was developed, utilizing known physical properties of dark matter particles and human tissue. The model considers various collision scenarios, ranging from low-energy elastic collisions to high-energy inelastic collisions.  The results indicate that low-energy elastic collisions may lead to small ionization processes within tissues, potentially causing damage to biomolecules. Inelastic collisions, on the other hand, could result in more significant ionization and potentially lead to DNA damage. The magnitude and frequency of these collisions are dependent on the assumed dark matter particle properties, such as mass and charge.  In conclusion, this research suggests that dark matter collisions with the human body could have potential implications for human health. The findings indicate that both low-energy elastic collisions and inelastic collisions could lead to damaging effects on biomolecules. However, a more extensive investigation is required to determine the exact consequences and potential risks associated with these collisions. Further studies in this area will contribute to our understanding of the elusive nature of dark matter and its interactions with the known universe.

text: The local cosmic expansion, a phenomenon observed in the universe, has long been a subject of interest in cosmology. This expansion, driven by dark energy, has significant implications for our understanding of the universe's evolution and ultimate fate. Despite its importance, a comprehensive dynamical model of the local cosmic expansion remains lacking.   This study aims to address this knowledge gap by developing a novel dynamical model that incorporates the effects of dark energy and matter on the local cosmic expansion. Our model is based on a modified Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric, which allows for a more accurate representation of the universe's large-scale structure. We employ a combination of numerical simulations and analytical techniques to solve the equations of motion for the scale factor and density parameters.   Our results indicate that the local cosmic expansion is characterized by a complex interplay between dark energy and matter, leading to a non-linear evolution of the scale factor. We find that the expansion rate is sensitive to the values of the dark energy density parameter and the matter density parameter, with significant implications for our understanding of the universe's age and composition.   Our model provides a more nuanced understanding of the local cosmic expansion, highlighting the need for further investigation into the properties of dark energy and matter. The findings of this study have significant implications for cosmological models and the development of new observational and theoretical tools to study the universe's evolution.

We revisit the transport of spin-degrees of freedom across an electrically
and thermally biased tunnel junction between two ferromagnets with
non-collinear magnetizations. Besides the well-known charge and spin currents
we show that a non-zero spin-quadrupole current flows between the ferromagnets.
This tensor-valued current describes the non-equilibrium transport of
spin-anisotropy relating to both local and non-local multi-particle spin
correlations of the circuit. This quadratic spin-anisotropy, quantified in
terms of the spin-quadrupole moment, is fundamentally a two-electron quantity.
In spin-valves with an embedded quantum dot such currents have been shown to
result in a quadrupole accumulation that affects the measurable quantum dot
spin and charge dynamics. The spin-valve model studied here allows fundamental
questions about spin-quadrupole storage and transport to be worked out in
detail, while ignoring the detection by a quantum dot. This physical
understanding of this particular device is of importance for more complex
devices where spin-quadrupole transport can be detected. We demonstrate that,
as far as storage and transport are concerned, the spin anisotropy is only
partly determined by the spin polarization. In fact, for a thermally biased
spin-valve the charge- and spin-current may vanish, while a pure exchange
spin-quadrupole current remains, which appears as a fundamental consequence of
Pauli's principle. We extend the real-time diagrammatic approach to efficiently
calculate the average of multi-particle spin-observables, in particular the
spin-quadrupole current. Although the paper addresses only leading order and
spin-conserving tunneling we formulate the technique for arbitrary order in an
arbitrary, spin-dependent tunnel coupling in a way that lends itself to
extension to quantum-dot spin-valve structures.

There is general agreement that supernovae Ia correspond to the thermonuclear
runaway of a white dwarf that is part of a compact binary, but the details of
the progenitor systems are still unknown and much debated. One of the proposed
progenitor theories is the single-degenerate channel in which a white dwarf
accretes from a companion, grows in mass, reaches a critical mass limit, and is
then consumed after thermonuclear runaway sets in. However, there are major
disagreements about the theoretical delay time distribution and the
corresponding time-integrated supernova Ia rate from this channel. We
investigate whether the differences are due to the uncertainty in the common
envelope phase and the fraction of transferred mass that is retained by the
white dwarf. This so-called retention efficiency may have a strong influence on
the final amount and timing of supernovae Ia. Using the population synthesis
code SeBa, we simulated large numbers of binaries for various assumptions on
common envelopes and retention efficiencies. We compare the resulting supernova
Ia rates and delay time distributions with each other and with those from the
literature, including observational data. For the three assumed retention
efficiencies, the integrated rate varies by a factor 3-4 to even more than a
factor 100, so in extreme cases, the retention efficiency strongly suppresses
the single-degenerate channel. Our different assumptions for the common
envelope phase change the integrated rate by a factor 2-3. Although our results
do recover the trend in the theoretical predictions from different binary
population synthesis codes, they do not fully explain the large disagreement
among them.

text: This study presents PETALO (Positron Emission Time-of-Flight Apparatus based on Liquid Xenon), a novel design aimed at enhancing the efficiency and performance of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging systems. The primary objective is to overcome the limitations of existing TOF PET technologies by integrating liquid xenon as the detection medium, which offers superior timing resolution and reduced energy threshold compared to traditional scintillation crystals.   The initial phase involved rigorous simulations to optimize the geometry and layout of the PET detector, ensuring minimal dead time and maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio. Subsequently, experimental setups were constructed using prototypes, followed by detailed characterization tests to validate the theoretical predictions. Results from these tests confirmed that PETALO achieves a significantly higher timing resolution, essential for improving spatial resolution and reducing scatter and emission-related artifacts.  Key methodologies included the development of advanced readout electronics capable of processing high-speed signals generated by liquid xenon photodetectors. These components were integrated into the PETALO system to ensure real-time data acquisition and processing. Furthermore, the integration of machine learning algorithms was explored to enhance the reconstruction process, thereby minimizing image artifacts and increasing diagnostic accuracy.  In conclusion, PETALO represents a promising advancement in PET technology, offering enhanced performance through the use of liquid xenon as the detection medium. Future research will focus on further optimization and clinical validation to establish its potential impact on PET imaging capabilities.

text: The ultracompact X-ray binary 4U1820-303, located in the globular cluster M28, exhibits a complex X-ray light curve and negative orbital-period derivative (OPD). Previous studies suggested the presence of a third companion in the system. In this work, we propose an alternative explanation based on a circumbinary disk scenario. Using hydrodynamic simulations and three-body calculations, we investigate the formation and evolution of a gas disk around the binary system. We find that a gas disk with an inner radius of 0.04 au, an outer radius of 0.15 au, and a mass of 10E-5 M⊙ can survive in the system. The inner parts of the disk experience strong tidal forces from the binary components, leading to a complex X-ray emission. The outer regions of the disk, subjected to less tidal forces, exhibit a more stable X-ray flux. The OPD is attributed to the disk's precession induced by the gravitational interaction between the binary components and the inner parts of the disk. This model can explain the observed X-ray variability without requiring the presence of a third companion. Further observations and theoretical investigations are needed to confirm this hypothesis.

A generic feature of the known string inflationary models is that the same
physics that makes the inflaton lighter than the Hubble scale during inflation
often also makes other scalars this light. These scalars can acquire
isocurvature fluctuations during inflation, and given that their VEVs determine
the mass spectrum and the coupling constants of the effective low-energy field
theory, these fluctuations give rise to couplings and masses that are modulated
from one Hubble patch to another. These seem just what is required to obtain
primordial adiabatic fluctuations through conversion into density perturbations
through the `modulation mechanism', wherein reheating takes place with
different efficiency in different regions of our Universe. Fluctuations
generated in this way can generically produce non-gaussianity larger than
obtained in single-field slow-roll inflation; potentially observable in the
near future. We provide here the first explicit example of the modulation
mechanism at work in string cosmology, within the framework of LARGE Volume
Type-IIB string flux compactifications. The inflationary dynamics involves two
light Kaehler moduli: a fibre divisor plays the role of the inflaton whose
decay rate to visible sector degrees of freedom is modulated by the primordial
fluctuations of a blow-up mode (which is made light by the use of
poly-instanton corrections). We find the challenges of embedding the mechanism
into a concrete UV completion constrains the properties of the non-gaussianity
that is found, since for generic values of the underlying parameters, the model
predicts a local bi-spectrum with fNL of order `a few'. However, a moderate
tuning of the parameters gives also rise to explicit examples with fNL O(20)
potentially observable by the Planck satellite.

As video-streaming services have expanded and improved, cloud-based video has
evolved into a necessary feature of any successful business for reaching
internal and external audiences. In this paper, video streaming over
distributed storage is considered where the video segments are encoded using an
erasure code for better reliability. There are multiple parallel streams
between each server and the edge router. For each client request, we need to
determine the subset of servers to get the data, as well as one of the parallel
stream from each chosen server. In order to have this scheduling, this paper
proposes a two-stage probabilistic scheduling. The selection of video quality
is also chosen with a certain probability distribution. With these parameters,
the playback time of video segments is determined by characterizing the
download time of each coded chunk for each video segment. Using the playback
times, a bound on the moment generating function of the stall duration is used
to bound the mean stall duration. Based on this, we formulate an optimization
problem to jointly optimize the convex combination of mean stall duration and
average video quality for all requests, where the two-stage probabilistic
scheduling, probabilistic video quality selection, bandwidth split among
parallel streams, and auxiliary bound parameters can be chosen. This non-convex
problem is solved using an efficient iterative algorithm. Evaluation results
show significant improvement in QoE metrics for cloud-based video as compared
to the considered baselines.

Standard geostatistical models assume second order stationarity of the
underlying Random Function. In some instances, there is little reason to expect
the spatial dependence structure to be stationary over the whole region of
interest. In this paper, we introduce a new model for second order
non-stationary Random Functions as a convolution of an orthogonal random
measure with a spatially varying random weighting function. This new model is a
generalization of the common convolution model where a non-random weighting
function is used. The resulting class of non-stationary covariance functions is
very general, flexible and allows to retrieve classes of closed-form
non-stationary covariance functions known from the literature, for a suitable
choices of the random weighting functions family. Under the framework of a
single realization and local stationarity, we develop parameter inference
procedure of these explicit classes of non-stationary covariance functions.
From a local variogram non-parametric kernel estimator, a weighted local
least-squares approach in combination with kernel smoothing method is developed
to estimate the parameters. Performances are assessed on two real datasets:
soil and rainfall data. It is shown in particular that the proposed approach
outperforms the stationary one, according to several criteria. Beyond the
spatial predictions, we also show how conditional simulations can be carried
out in this non-stationary framework.

text: In this study, we investigate the computational complexity of computing critical points of polynomial systems using Gr\"obner basis methods. Specifically, we focus on two algorithms F5 and F4, and compare their performance on a series of benchmark problems. Our experiments reveal that while F5 generally outperforms F4 in terms of the number of arithmetic operations, F4 demonstrates superiority in terms of memory usage. These findings highlight the trade-off between computation time and memory requirements in Gr\"obner basis algorithms for critical point computation.  Our work extends the analysis of previous studies on Gr\"obner basis algorithms for polynomial systems by providing empirical evidence on their performance in finding critical points. We propose several possible explanations for the observed differences in performance between F5 and F4, including the nature of the input data and the underlying algorithmic structures.  To validate the generality of our findings, we consider a wide range of polynomial systems derived from various applications in science and engineering. Our results demonstrate that the choice of Gr\"obner basis algorithm depends on the specific problem instance and the available computational resources.  Furthermore, we propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of F5 and F4 to improve overall performance. This approach could be of significant value to practitioners in areas such as robotics, engineering design, and computational chemistry, where the accurate determination of critical points is essential.  In conclusion, this study contributes to the ongoing research on the application of Gr\"obner basis methods in polynomial systems and sheds new light on the computational complexity of critical point computation. Our findings provide valuable insights into the trade-offs between computation time and memory requirements and offer practical recommendations for the selection of Gr\"obner basis algorithms in different contexts.

text: The $q$-Queens Problem is a well-known generalization of the classical N-Queens Problem. In the classical version, N non-attacking queens are placed on an NxN chessboard. The $q$-Queens Problem, introduced by Marusic and Waterman in 1995, considers the placement of q queens on an NxN board such that no q queens threaten each other. This problem has applications in various fields such as coding theory, computer science, and graph theory.  The objective of this paper is to present the general theory of the $q$-Queens Problem. We begin by discussing the connection between the $q$-Queens Problem and the classical N-Queens Problem. We then present the necessary combinatorial and algebraic background required to understand the problem. Using this background, we derive the necessary conditions for the existence of a solution to the $q$-Queens Problem. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the $q$-Queens Problem and the Stern-Brocot tree, which provides a natural recursive construction for the solution of the problem. The paper concludes with a discussion of the complexity of solving the $q$-Queens Problem and some directions for future research.   We use a combination of combinatorial and algebraic techniques to analyze the $q$-Queens Problem. We begin by discussing the connection between the $q$-Queens Problem and the classical N-Queens Problem, and then present the necessary combinatorial and algebraic background required to understand the problem. Using this background, we derive the necessary conditions for the existence of a solution to the $q$-Queens Problem. We then explore the relationship between the $q$-Queens Problem and the Stern-Brocot tree, which provides a natural recursive construction for the solution of the problem.  Key findings We present the general theory of the $q$-Queens Problem, including the necessary conditions for the existence of a solution and the relationship between the problem and the Stern-Brocot tree.   The $q$-Queens Problem is a fascinating generalization of the classical N-Queens Problem, with applications in various fields. In this paper, we present the general theory of the problem, including the necessary conditions for the existence of a solution and the relationship between the problem and the Stern-Brocot tree. Our results provide a solid foundation for future research

text: In this work, we investigate the impact of disorder on the optoelectronic properties of GaN$_y$As$_{1-x-y}$Bi$_x$ alloys and heterostructures. Our study aims to address the challenges posed by disorder in these materials and its effect on their performance in optoelectronic devices. Through experimental measurements and theoretical modeling, we have characterized the changes in the electronic band structure, carrier mobility, and optical properties induced by disorder in GaN$_y$As$_{1-x-y}$Bi$_x$ alloys and heterostructures. Our results reveal a significant degradation in device performance with increasing disorder, highlighting the importance of understanding and mitigating these effects for the practical implementation of these materials in optoelectronic applications. We propose strategies to enhance the structural and compositional uniformity of these materials to minimize disorder-induced degradation, thereby improving their optoelectronic performance. The methodology employed in this study includes structural and optical characterization techniques, as well as theoretical modeling of electronic band structures and carrier dynamics. By elucidating the impact of disorder on the optoelectronic properties of GaN$_y$As$_{1-x-y}$Bi$_x$ alloys and heterostructures, this work contributes to the advancement of technology utilizing these materials for next-generation optoelectronic devices.

text: In this study, we propose a novel methodology for structured variable selection in Support Vector Machines (SVMs) based on a combination of mutual information maximization and regularized Least Angle Regression (LARS). The proposed approach, referred to as Structured-LARS-SVM, allows for the simultaneous selection of relevant features and the estimation of their corresponding coefficients in SVM models. The method is particularly useful in the context of high-dimensional data with a large number of correlated features, which is a common problem in many applications, including bioinformatics and image processing. To evaluate the effectiveness of Structured-LARS-SVM, we conducted extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, comparing it to several state-of-the-art methods for structured variable selection in SVMs, including the standard LARS-SVM, the LASSO-SVM, and the Elastic Net-SVM. The results demonstrate that Structured-LARS-SVM outperforms the comparison methods in terms of classification accuracy, computational efficiency, and the ability to handle structured data with both binary and continuous variables. The proposed approach also provides a more interpretable and biologically meaningful feature selection result compared to the other methods. In summary, this study presents a novel methodology, Structured-LARS-SVM, for structured variable selection in SVMs. The proposed methodology combines mutual information maximization and regularized Least Angle Regression, and it outperforms several state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability. The results of this study have important implications for the analysis of complex high-dimensional datasets with structured variables and correlated features, which are common in many domains, including bioinformatics and image processing.

text: In this study, we present our findings from an X-ray spectroscopic analysis of BaFeO$_{3}$ thin films, focusing on the characteristic features of Fe$^{4+}$ ions in the material. The investigation aims to unravel the electronic and magnetic properties of BaFeO$_{3}$ thin films, which are known to exhibit ferromagnetic behavior despite having Fe$^{4+}$ ions, typically associated with antiferromagnetic insulators. Our research seeks to elucidate the structural factors contributing to the observed ferromagnetism in BaFeO$_{3}$ thin films.  Through X-ray absorption spectroscopy and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism measurements, we have successfully identified the oxidation state and local magnetic moments of Fe$^{4+}$ ions in the thin films. The results reveal a significant deviation from the expected antiferromagnetic behavior, indicating a complex interplay of structural distortions and charge ordering effects that give rise to the observed ferromagnetic properties in BaFeO$_{3}$ thin films.  Our methodology involves the synthesis of BaFeO$_{3}$ thin films using pulsed laser deposition, followed by detailed X-ray spectroscopic measurements at a synchrotron facility. By combining experimental observations with theoretical calculations, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the Fe$^{4+}$ ferromagnetic insulator behavior in BaFeO$_{3}$ thin films, offering insights into the underlying mechanisms driving the unique magnetic properties of this material.

In this paper we consider a recent theoretical prediction (Bragg \emph{et
al.}, Phys. Fluids \textbf{28}, 013305 (2016)) that for inertial particles in
2D turbulence, the nature of the irreversibility of the particle-pair
dispersion inverts when the particle inertia exceeds a certain value. In
particular, when the particle Stokes number, ${\rm St}$, is below a certain
value, the forward-in-time (FIT) dispersion should be faster than the
backward-in-time (BIT) dispersion, but for ${\rm St}$ above this value, this
should invert so that BIT becomes faster than FIT dispersion. This non-trivial
behavior arises because of the competition between two physically distinct
irreversibility mechanisms that operate in different regimes of ${\rm St}$. In
3D turbulence, both mechanisms act to produce faster BIT than FIT dispersion,
but in 2D turbulence, the two mechanisms have opposite effects because of the
flux of energy from the small to the large scales. We supplement the
qualitative argument given by Bragg \emph{et al.} (Phys. Fluids \textbf{28},
013305 (2016)) by deriving quantitative predictions of this effect in the short
time limit. We confirm the theoretical predictions using results of inertial
particle dispersion in a direct numerical simulation of 2D turbulence. A more
general finding of this analysis is that in turbulent flows with an inverse
energy flux, inertial particles may yet exhibit a net downscale flux of kinetic
energy because of their non-local in-time dynamics.
