text: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic phenomena observed in the universe, characterized by intense emissions followed by an afterglow. This study investigates the dynamics and afterglow light curves of GRB blast waves, specifically examining scenarios involving a long-lived reverse shock. The objective is to understand how reverse shock interactions influence the overall light curve and emission properties. Utilizing a combination of semi-analytical models and numerical simulations, the paper explores the evolution of the forward and reverse shock components as they interact with the medium surrounding the GRB. The models account for varying environmental densities and the energy distribution between the forward and reverse shocks. Key findings indicate that the presence of a long-lived reverse shock contributes significantly to the early afterglow phase, manifesting as pronounced features in the light curve that are sensitive to the density profile of the ambient medium and the initial shock parameters. Specifically, the reverse shock's persistence is shown to enhance synchrotron radiation, leading to characteristic temporal signatures that differ notably from those predicted in models without such a shock. This study's insights suggest that observing these distinct afterglow characteristics can provide crucial information on the progenitor environment and the GRB's energy distribution mechanisms. The findings highlight the critical role of reverse shocks in GRB afterglow modeling and suggest avenues for future observational campaigns aiming to unravel the complex dynamics of GRB blast waves.

We report the discovery of 15 quasars and bright galaxies at 5.7 < z < 6.9.
This is the initial result from the Subaru High-z Exploration of Low-Luminosity
Quasars (SHELLQs) project, which exploits the exquisite multiband imaging data
produced by the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) Strategic Program survey. The
candidate selection is performed by combining several photometric approaches
including a Bayesian probabilistic algorithm to reject stars and dwarfs. The
spectroscopic identification was carried out with the Gran Telescopio Canarias
and the Subaru Telescope for the first 80 deg2 of the survey footprint. The
success rate of our photometric selection is quite high, approaching 100 % at
the brighter magnitudes (zAB < 23.5 mag). Our selection also recovered all the
known high-z quasars on the HSC images. Among the 15 discovered objects, six
are likely quasars, while the other six with interstellar absorption lines and
in some cases narrow emission lines are likely bright Lyman-break galaxies. The
remaining three objects have weak continua and very strong and narrow Ly alpha
lines, which may be excited by ultraviolet light from both young stars and
quasars. These results indicate that we are starting to see the steep rise of
the luminosity function of z > 6 galaxies, compared with that of quasars, at
magnitudes fainter than M1450 ~ -22 mag or zAB ~24 mag. Follow-up studies of
the discovered objects as well as further survey observations are ongoing.

text: This study investigates the potential for neutrino emission from dark matter annihilation and decay, with a focus on the implications for the observed cosmic positron and antiproton data. The background of the universe is characterized by a complex interplay of astrophysical and cosmological processes, including supernovae, active galactic nuclei, and the interstellar medium, which can produce high-energy particles that mimic the signature of dark matter annihilation.  The objective of this research is to explore the possibility of neutrino emission from dark matter annihilation and decay, and to assess the potential for this process to explain the observed excesses of cosmic positrons and antiprotons. To achieve this, we employ a combination of theoretical and observational approaches, utilizing numerical simulations of dark matter annihilation and decay, as well as an analysis of the latest cosmic positron and antiproton data from the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope.  Our results indicate that neutrino emission from dark matter annihilation and decay can potentially explain the observed excesses of cosmic positrons and antiprotons, although the implications of this process are still subject to significant uncertainties. The observed neutrino signal is found to be consistent with the predictions of certain dark matter models, but the data also reveal a number of features that are difficult to reconcile with these predictions. These findings highlight the need for further research into the properties of dark matter and the potential for neutrino emission from this process.

text: This study investigates the influence of classical anisotropy fields on the magnetic properties of Heisenberg antiferromagnets using unified molecular field theory. We explore how these fields affect the ordering temperature and the critical magnetic field, providing insights into the interplay between classical and quantum effects in antiferromagnetic systems. Problematically, existing theories often fail to account for the precise impact of classical anisotropy fields, which can significantly alter the phase diagrams and ordering behaviors. To address this, we develop a comprehensive theoretical framework that integrates classical and quantum contributions. The methodology involves solving the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation under the assumption of a uniaxial anisotropy field, allowing us to derive expressions for the energy landscape and the corresponding magnetization profiles. Our results reveal that the classical anisotropy fields can lead to significant deviations from predictions based solely on quantum fluctuations, particularly at low temperatures. These findings are validated through comparison with available experimental data and further support the necessity of incorporating classical anisotropy in theoretical models of Heisenberg antiferromagnets.

text: Weak measurements and weak values have provoked considerable debate in the interpretation of quantum mechanics. This paper aims to clarify the concept and significance of weak measurements and explore the implications of weak values, particularly in response to Kastner's recent critiques. We employ a theoretical framework grounded in quantum mechanics to revisit the mathematical underpinnings of weak measurement theory, comparing it against traditional measurement paradigms. Through a series of analytical derivations, we illustrate that weak values can provide meaningful information about a quantum system under certain conditions, specifically when they reflect properties of the system that are not accessible through strong measurements. Our findings reveal that weak values can yield surprising results, including values outside the eigenvalue spectrum of the observable, which challenges conventional interpretations of quantum measurements. We also engage with Kastner's arguments regarding the uncertainty and interpretative implications of weak values, affirming that while these values may defy intuitive understanding, they nonetheless enrich our comprehension of the quantum state and its interplay with measurement processes. Ultimately, this work contributes to the ongoing discourse on the philosophy of quantum mechanics by asserting that weak measurements and weak values do not merely serve as mathematical curiosities; rather, they open new avenues for investigating the foundations of quantum theory and the nature of reality itself.

text: In recent years, Ad-Hoc networks have gained significant attention due to their inherent flexibility, low cost, and ease of deployment. However, providing Quality of Service (QoS) guarantees in Ad-Hoc networks remains a significant challenge, especially in multicast scenarios. Mesh-based multicast routing protocols, which utilize a redundant network topology to ensure multicast group connectivity, have emerged as a promising solution for QoS provisioning in Ad-Hoc networks. This paper presents an overview of mesh-based multicast routing protocols in Ad-Hoc networks, their underlying concepts, and the challenges they face.  We discuss various mesh-based multicast routing protocols, including Core-Assisted Multicast Routing Protocol (CAMP), Multicast Ad hoc On-demand Distance Vector (MAODV), and Multicast Temporally-Ordered Reliable Multicast Protocol (MTRMP). The analysis of these protocols focuses on their multicast group management, routing efficiency, and QoS support. We investigate the challenges associated with implementing QoS-aware mesh-based multicast routing protocols, including resource constraints, mobility, and routing scalability. Furthermore, we propose some potential solutions to address these challenges, including the use of multiple classes of services, adaptive routing protocols, and traffic prioritization mechanisms.  Our study contributes to the ongoing research efforts in the area of QoS-aware mesh-based multicast routing protocols in Ad-Hoc networks. The findings of this paper can help network designers and researchers understand the concepts and challenges of mesh-based multicast routing protocols and provide valuable insights into designing and implementing QoS-aware multicast routing solutions in Ad-Hoc networks.

text: Group metric invariants are essential in the field of geometric group theory, providing valuable information about groups and their structures. Key findings reveal that any law of group metric invariant can be represented as an inf-convolution, highlighting a fundamental connection between these two concepts. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of group metric invariants and their underlying mathematical framework. In conclusion, the results emphasize the significance of inf-convolutions in characterizing group metric invariants, shedding light on the intricate nature of group theory and its applications.

The deposition of a high-$\kappa$ oxide overlayer is known to significantly
enhance the room-temperature electron mobility in single-layer MoS$_{2}$ (SLM)
but not in single-layer graphene (SLG). We give a quantitative account of how
this mobility enhancement is due to the non-degeneracy of the two-dimensional
electron gas system in SLM at accessible temperatures. Using our charged
impurity scattering model [Ong and Fischetti, Phys. Rev. B 86, 121409 (2012)]
and temperature-dependent polarizability, we calculate the charged
impurity-limited mobility ($\mu_{\textrm{imp}}$) in SLM with and without a
high-$\kappa$ (HfO$_{2}$) top gate oxide at different electron densities and
temperatures. We find that the mobility enhancement is larger at low electron
densities and high temperatures because of finite-temperature screening, thus
explaining the enhancement of the mobility observed at room temperature.
$\mu_{\textrm{imp}}$ is shown to decrease significantly with increasing
temperature, suggesting that the strong temperature dependence of measured
mobilities should not be interpreted as being solely due to inelastic
scattering with phonons. We also reproduce the recently seen experimental trend
in which the temperature scaling exponent ($\gamma$) of
$\mu_{\textrm{imp}}\propto T^{-\gamma}$ is smaller in top-gated SLM than in
bare SLM. Finally, we show that a $\sim37$ percent mobility enhancement can be
achieved by reducing the HfO$_{2}$ thickness from 20 to 2 nm.

We consider a parallel version of a classical Bayesian search problem. $k$
agents are looking for a treasure that is placed in one of the boxes indexed by
$\mathbb{N}^+$ according to a known distribution $p$. The aim is to minimize
the expected time until the first agent finds it. Searchers run in parallel
where at each time step each searcher can "peek" into a box. A basic family of
algorithms which are inherently robust is \emph{non-coordinating} algorithms.
Such algorithms act independently at each searcher, differing only by their
probabilistic choices. We are interested in the price incurred by employing
such algorithms when compared with the case of full coordination. We first show
that there exists a non-coordination algorithm, that knowing only the relative
likelihood of boxes according to $p$, has expected running time of at most
$10+4(1+\frac{1}{k})^2 T$, where $T$ is the expected running time of the best
fully coordinated algorithm. This result is obtained by applying a refined
version of the main algorithm suggested by Fraigniaud, Korman and Rodeh in
STOC'16, which was designed for the context of linear parallel search.We then
describe an optimal non-coordinating algorithm for the case where the
distribution $p$ is known. The running time of this algorithm is difficult to
analyse in general, but we calculate it for several examples. In the case where
$p$ is uniform over a finite set of boxes, then the algorithm just checks boxes
uniformly at random among all non-checked boxes and is essentially $2$ times
worse than the coordinating algorithm.We also show simple algorithms for Pareto
distributions over $M$ boxes. That is, in the case where $p(x) \sim 1/x^b$ for
$0< b < 1$, we suggest the following algorithm: at step $t$ choose uniformly
from the boxes unchecked in ${1, . . . ,min(M, \lfloor t/\sigma\rfloor)}$,
where $\sigma = b/(b + k - 1)$. It turns out this algorithm is asymptotically
optimal, and runs about $2+b$ times worse than the case of full coordination.

Using low-redshift (z<0.09) samples of AGNs, normal galaxies and groups of
galaxies selected from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), we study the
environments of type 1 and type 2 AGNs both on small and large scales.
Comparisons are made for galaxy samples matched in redshift, $r$-band
luminosity, [OIII] luminosity, and also the position in groups (central or
satellite). We find that type 2 AGNs and normal galaxies reside in similar
environments. Type 1 and type 2 AGNs have similar clustering properties on
large scales ($\gtrsim1$Mpc), but at scales smaller than 100 kpc, type 2s have
significant more neighbors than type 1s ($3.09\pm0.69$ times more for central
AGNs at $\lesssim30$kpc). These results suggest that type 1 and type 2 AGNs are
hosted by halos of similar masses, as is also seen directly from the mass
distributions of their host groups ($\sim10^{12}h^{-1} M_{\odot}$ for centrals
and $\sim10^{13}h^{-1} M_{\odot}$ for satellites). Type~2s have significantly
more satellites around them, and the distribution of their satellites is also
more centrally concentrated. The host galaxies of both types of AGNs have
similar optical properties, but their infrared colors are significantly
different. Our results suggest that the simple unified model based solely on
torus orientation is not sufficient, but that galaxy interactions in dark
matter halos must have played an important role in the formation of the dust
structure that obscures AGNs.

text: The study investigates the influence of Zinc (Zn) substitution on the electronic properties of La2-xSrxCuO4 (La214), with a focus on its impact on the superconducting transition temperature (Tc). Understanding the interplay between impurity-induced states and superconductivity provides insight into high-temperature superconductors' enigmatic mechanisms. This research primarily examines the emergence of Zn-induced in-gap electronic states and their correlation with the material's uniform magnetic susceptibility. Through systematic doping experiments and magnetic susceptibility measurements, we characterize the changes in the electronic structure brought about by Zn impurities. The methodology involves substituting Zn at Cu sites in La214 and evaluating the resultant modifications in both susceptibility and electronic gap states using tools such as SQUID magnetometry. Our findings reveal that Zn substitution leads to the creation of localized in-gap states, significantly enhancing magnetic correlations in the antiferromagnetic regime. These states are evidenced by distinct shifts in magnetic susceptibility and an observable suppression in Tc. A prominent feature of this study is the strong relationship between increased magnetic disorder and the reduction of superconducting coherence, suggesting that Zn-induced states adversely affect the superconducting pairing potential. The emergence of these in-gap states aligns with theories predicting enhanced local moment formation, thereby providing a plausible explanation for the Tc degradation. This research contributes to the broader understanding of impurity effects in cuprate superconductors, promoting further studies into the disruption of superconductivity by dopants. Consequently, these findings hold implications for improving superconducting materials through controlled impurity management.

text: In this work, we address the challenge of breaking the speed limit imposed by disk acquisition processes through the leveraging of data deduplication techniques. Data deduplication is a method commonly used to eliminate redundant data, thus reducing storage space requirements. Our study aims to explore how this technique can be extended to enhance the speed of disk acquisition processes, particularly in forensic investigations where acquiring data quickly and efficiently is crucial. The results of our research demonstrate that by integrating data deduplication into the disk acquisition workflow, significant improvements in speed can be achieved without compromising the integrity of the acquired data.  We propose a novel methodology that combines traditional disk acquisition methods with data deduplication algorithms to identify and eliminate redundant data blocks during the imaging process. This approach not only accelerates the acquisition speed but also optimizes storage utilization. By conducting experiments using various disk images and datasets, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed method in accelerating disk acquisition speed while maintaining forensic soundness.  Overall, this work contributes to enhancing the efficiency of disk acquisition processes in forensic investigations by leveraging data deduplication techniques. The successful integration of data deduplication into disk imaging workflows offers a promising solution to overcome the speed limitations associated with traditional acquisition methods.

We study in detail sub-GeV dark matter scattering off electrons in xenon,
including the expected electron recoil spectra and annual modulation spectra.
We derive improved constraints using low-energy XENON10 and XENON100
ionization-only data. For XENON10, in addition to including electron-recoil
data corresponding to about $1-3$ electrons, we include for the first time
events with $\gtrsim 4$ electrons. Assuming the scattering is momentum
independent, this strengthens a previous cross-section bound by almost an order
of magnitude for dark matter masses above 50 MeV. The available XENON100 data
corresponds to events with $\gtrsim 4$ electrons, and leads to a constraint
that is comparable to the XENON10 bound above 50 MeV. We demonstrate that a
search for an annual modulation signal in upcoming xenon experiments (XENON1T,
XENONnT, LZ) could substantially improve the above bounds even in the presence
of large backgrounds. We also emphasize that in simple benchmark models of
sub-GeV dark matter, the dark matter-electron scattering rate can be as high as
one event every ten (two) seconds in the XENON1T (XENONnT or LZ) experiments,
without being in conflict with any other known experimental bounds. While there
are several sources of backgrounds that can produce single- or few-electron
events, a large event rate can be consistent with a dark matter signal and
should not be simply written off as purely a detector curiosity. This fact
motivates a detailed analysis of the ionization-only ("S2-only") data, taking
into account the expected annual modulation spectrum of the signal rate, as
well as the DM-induced electron-recoil spectra, which are another powerful

text: We investigated the efficacy of module network learning algorithms by developing and validating a comprehensive simulation framework. Our approach employed a modular network architecture, comprising interconnected modules that interact and influence one another, to mimic real-world complex systems. To evaluate the performance of these algorithms, we generated a large dataset of simulated network dynamics, incorporating various types of module interactions, including causal and non-causal relationships.  Through extensive simulations, we explored the impact of algorithmic parameters, such as learning rates and regularization strengths, on the accuracy and robustness of module network predictions. Our results indicate that the optimal learning rates and regularization strengths significantly affect the algorithm's ability to capture the underlying module structure and dynamics. We also observed that the proposed algorithms outperform existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, particularly in cases with high-dimensional data and complex module interactions.  Key findings from our study highlight the importance of carefully tuning algorithmic parameters and incorporating regularization techniques to improve the performance of module network learning algorithms. Furthermore, our simulation framework provides a valuable tool for researchers to evaluate and compare different algorithms, accelerating the development of more accurate and reliable module network learning methods. By leveraging our validated simulation framework, future studies can focus on real-world applications, where the accuracy and robustness of module network learning algorithms can significantly impact decision-making processes.

(Abridged) Many of the observed CO line profiles exhibit broad linewidths
that greatly exceed the thermal broadening expected within molecular clouds.
These suprathermal CO linewidths are assumed to be originated from the presence
of unresolved supersonic motions inside clouds. Typically overlooked in the
literature, in this paper we aim to quantify the impact of the opacity
broadening effects on the current interpretation of the CO suprathermal line
profiles. Without any additional contributions to the gas velocity field, a
large fraction of the apparently supersonic (${\cal M}\sim$2-3) linewidths
measured in both $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO (J=1-0) lines can be explained by the
saturation of their corresponding sonic-like, optically-thin C$^{18}$O
counterparts assuming standard isotopic fractionation. Combined with the
presence of multiple components detected in our C$^{18}$O spectra, these
opacity effects seem to be also responsible of the highly supersonic linewidths
(${\cal M}>$8-10) detected in the broadest $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO spectra in
Taurus. Our results demonstrate that most of the suprathermal $^{12}$CO and
$^{13}$CO linewidths could be primarily created by a combination of opacity
broadening effects and multiple gas velocity components blended in these
saturated emission lines. Once corrected by their corresponding optical depth,
each of these gas components present transonic intrinsic linewidths
consistently traced by the three CO isotopologues within a factor of 2. Highly
correlated and velocity-coherent at large scales, the largest and highly
supersonic velocity differences inside clouds are generated by the relative
motions between individual gas components. This highly discretized structure of
the molecular gas traced in CO suggest that the gas dynamics inside molecular
clouds could be better described by the properties of a fully-resolved
macroscopic turbulence.

text: This research paper presents a novel approach to planning in conformant multi-agent systems, where agents adhere to pre-defined rules and norms. The objective is to develop an efficient method for planning in such systems, which is essential for ensuring the correctness and robustness of the overall system. Conformant planning is particularly challenging due to the need to consider the complex interactions between agents, their rules, and the environment.  The proposed approach utilizes symbolic model checking to analyze the planning problem and identify potential conflicts between agents. Model checking is a technique used to verify the correctness of a system by checking whether it satisfies a set of properties. In this context, the properties are defined by the rules and norms of the conformant planning problem. The approach involves representing the planning problem as a model, which is then checked against a set of properties to identify potential conflicts.  The proposed method has been evaluated using a range of benchmarks, including the well-known "banking" and "electricity" domains. The results show that the approach is able to efficiently identify potential conflicts and plan conformant actions, even in complex systems with multiple agents and rules. The proposed method has significant implications for the development of conformant planning systems, and is expected to improve the correctness and robustness of such systems. Overall, the approach presents a novel solution to the challenging problem of conformant planning, and has the potential to be applied in a wide range of domains, including multi-agent systems, robotics, and artificial intelligence.

The automation of posterior inference in Bayesian data analysis has enabled
experts and nonexperts alike to use more sophisticated models, engage in faster
exploratory modeling and analysis, and ensure experimental reproducibility.
However, standard automated posterior inference algorithms are not tractable at
the scale of massive modern datasets, and modifications to make them so are
typically model-specific, require expert tuning, and can break theoretical
guarantees on inferential quality. Building on the Bayesian coresets framework,
this work instead takes advantage of data redundancy to shrink the dataset
itself as a preprocessing step, providing fully-automated, scalable Bayesian
inference with theoretical guarantees. We begin with an intuitive reformulation
of Bayesian coreset construction as sparse vector sum approximation, and
demonstrate that its automation and performance-based shortcomings arise from
the use of the supremum norm. To address these shortcomings we develop Hilbert
coresets, i.e., Bayesian coresets constructed under a norm induced by an
inner-product on the log-likelihood function space. We propose two Hilbert
coreset construction algorithms---one based on importance sampling, and one
based on the Frank-Wolfe algorithm---along with theoretical guarantees on
approximation quality as a function of coreset size. Since the exact
computation of the proposed inner-products is model-specific, we automate the
construction with a random finite-dimensional projection of the log-likelihood
functions. The resulting automated coreset construction algorithm is simple to
implement, and experiments on a variety of models with real and synthetic
datasets show that it provides high-quality posterior approximations and a
significant reduction in the computational cost of inference.

In 1995, Erd\H{o}s and Gy\'arf\'as proved that in every $2$-colouring of the
edges of $K_n$, there is a vertex cover by $2\sqrt{n}$ monochromatic paths of
the same colour, which is optimal up to a constant factor. The main goal of
this paper is to study the natural multi-colour generalization of this problem:
given two positive integers $r,s$, what is the smallest number
$\text{pc}_{r,s}(K_n)$ such that in every colouring of the edges of $K_n$ with
$r$ colours, there exists a vertex cover of $K_n$ by $\text{pc}_{r,s}(K_n)$
monochromatic paths using altogether at most $s$ different colours? For fixed
integers $r>s$ and as $n\to\infty$, we prove that $\text{pc}_{r,s}(K_n) =
\Theta(n^{1/\chi})$, where $\chi=\max{\{1,2+2s-r\}}$ is the chromatic number of
the Kneser gr aph $\text{KG}(r,r-s)$. More generally, if one replaces $K_n$ by
an arbitrary $n$-vertex graph with fixed independence number $\alpha$, then we
have $\text{pc}_{r,s}(G) = O(n^{1/\chi})$, where this time around $\chi$ is the
chromatic number of the Kneser hypergraph $\text{KG}^{(\alpha+1)}(r,r-s)$. This
result is tight in the sense that there exist graphs with independence number
$\alpha$ for which $\text{pc}_{r,s}(G) = \Omega(n^{1/\chi})$. This is in sharp
contrast to the case $r=s$, where it follows from a result of S\'ark\"ozy
(2012) that $\text{pc}_{r,r}(G)$ depends only on $r$ and $\alpha$, but not on
the number of vertices. We obtain similar results for the situation where
instead of using paths, one wants to cover a graph with bounded independence
number by monochromatic cycles, or a complete graph by monochromatic
$d$-regular graphs.

text: The study of helical liquids, characterized by their distinct molecular arrangements, presents an intriguing avenue for exploring enhanced electrical conductivity. This research aims to investigate the conductivity mechanisms within a generic helical liquid, identifying the influence of molecular conformation and intermolecular interactions on electrical transport properties. Utilizing a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and theoretical modeling, we analyze the conductivity as a function of temperature and pressure, examining how variations in helical angle and chain length affect charge carrier mobility. Key findings indicate that helical liquid structures exhibit markedly higher conductivity compared to their linear counterparts, primarily due to favorable spatial arrangements that facilitate the alignment of dipoles and reduce resistance to charge flow. Additionally, a threshold temperature was identified beyond which conductivity significantly increases, attributed to enhanced molecular motion that promotes charge carrier delocalization. Our results suggest that the unique helical architecture may serve as an advantageous feature for the design of novel conductive materials. In conclusion, the insights gleaned from this investigation pave the way for future applications in organic electronics and advanced materials, elucidating the relationship between molecular structure and conductivity in helical liquids. Further studies are recommended to explore the implications of these findings in real-world applications, potentially leading to innovative solutions in the field of material science.

We address this challenge through the development of a sophisticated model that incorporates a comprehensive set of astrophysical priors derived from both theoretical predictions and empirical observations. Our methodology involves iteratively updating these priors using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques, which allows us to explore the parameter space efficiently and quantify uncertainties. Results indicate a significant reduction in posterior error bars compared to standard likelihood approaches, particularly for parameters related to dark energy and neutrino mass. This work not only enhances our understanding of the universe but also provides a robust framework for future cosmological analyses, enabling more reliable predictions and interpretations of cosmic phenomena.

The probability distribution of sequences with maximum entropy that satisfies
a given amino acid composition at each site and a given pairwise amino acid
frequency at each site pair is a Boltzmann distribution with $\exp(-\psi_N)$,
where the total interaction $\psi_N$ is represented as the sum of one body and
pairwise interactions. A protein folding theory based on the random energy
model (REM) indicates that the equilibrium ensemble of natural protein
sequences is a canonical ensemble characterized by $\exp(-\Delta G_{ND}/k_B
T_s)$ or by $\exp(- G_{N}/k_B T_s)$ if an amino acid composition is kept
constant, meaning $\psi_N = \Delta G_{ND}/k_B T_s +$ constant, where $\Delta
G_{ND} \equiv G_N - G_D$, $G_N$ and $G_D$ are the native and denatured free
energies, and $T_s$ is the effective temperature of natural selection. Here, we
examine interaction changes ($\Delta \psi_N$) due to single nucleotide
nonsynonymous mutations, and have found that the variance of their $\Delta
\psi_N$ over all sites hardly depends on the $\psi_N$ of each homologous
sequence, indicating that the variance of $\Delta G_N (= k_B T_s \Delta
\psi_N)$ is nearly constant irrespective of protein families. As a result,
$T_s$ is estimated from the ratio of the variance of $\Delta \psi_N$ to that of
a reference protein, which is determined by a direct comparison between
$\Delta\Delta \psi_{ND} (\simeq \Delta \psi_N)$ and experimental $\Delta\Delta
G_{ND}$. Based on the REM, glass transition temperature $T_g$ and $\Delta
G_{ND}$ are estimated from $T_s$ and experimental melting temperatures ($T_m$)
for 14 protein domains. The estimates of $\Delta G_{ND}$ agree well with their
experimental values for 5 proteins, and those of $T_s$ and $T_g$ are all within
a reasonable range. This method is coarse-grained but much simpler in
estimating $T_s$, $T_g$ and $\Delta\Delta G_{ND}$ than previous methods.

We analyze coding for energy efficiency in relay channels at a fixed source
rate. We first propose a half-duplex decode-forward coding scheme for the
Gaussian relay channel. We then derive three optimal sets of power allocation,
which respectively minimize the network, the relay and the source energy
consumption. These optimal power allocations are given in closed-form, which
have so far remained implicit for maximum-rate schemes. Moreover, analysis
shows that minimizing the network energy consumption at a given rate is not
equivalent to maximizing the rate given energy, since it only covers part of
all rates achievable by decode-forward. We thus combine the optimized schemes
for network and relay energy consumptions into a generalized one, which then
covers all achievable rates. This generalized scheme is not only energy-optimal
for the desired source rate but also rate-optimal for the consumed energy. The
results also give a detailed understanding of the power consumption regimes and
allow a comprehensive description of the optimal message coding and resource
allocation for each desired source rate and channel realization. Finally, we
simulate the proposed schemes in a realistic environment, considering path-loss
and shadowing as modelled in the 3GPP standard. Significant energy gain can be
obtained over both direct and two-hop transmissions, particularly when the
source is far from relay and destination.

The nature, size and orientation of the dominant structural components in the
Milky Way's inner ~4 kpc - specifically the bulge and bar - have been the
subject of conflicting interpretations in the literature. We present a
different approach to inferring the properties of the long bar which extends
beyond the inner bulge, via the information encoded in the Galaxy's X/peanut
(X/P)-shaped structure. We perform a quantitative analysis of the X/P feature
seen in WISE wide-field imaging at 3.4 $\mu$m and 4.6 $\mu$m. We measure the
deviations of the isophotes from pure ellipses, and quantify the X/P structure
via the radial profile of the Fourier n=6 harmonic (cosine term $B_6$). In
addition to the vertical height and integrated `strength' of the X/P
instability, we report an intrinsic radius of $R_{\Pi;{\rm int}} = 1.67\pm0.27$
kpc, and an orientation angle of $\alpha = {37^\circ}^{+7^\circ}_{-10^\circ}$
with respect to our line-of-sight to the Galactic Centre. Based on X/P
structures observed in other galaxies, we make three assumptions: (i) the
peanut is intrinsically symmetric, (ii) the peanut is aligned with the long
Galactic bar, and (iii) their sizes are correlated. Thus the implication for
the Galactic bar is that it is oriented at the same $37^\circ$ angle and has an
expected radius of ~4.2 kpc, but possibly as low as ~3.2 kpc. We further
investigate how the Milky Way's X/P structure compares with other analogues,
and find that the Galaxy is broadly consistent with our recently established
scaling relations, though with a moderately stronger peanut instability than
expected. We additionally perform a photometric decomposition of the Milky
Way's major axis surface brightness profile, accounting for spiral structure,
and determine an average disc scale length of $h = 2.54\pm0.16$ kpc in the WISE
bands, in good agreement with the literature.

text: Graphene's exceptional electronic properties and potential applications have spurred extensive research into its magnetic behavior. The study presents direct Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) evidence to elucidate the magnetic properties intrinsic to graphene, focusing on the origin and nature of magnetism in this two-dimensional material. Utilizing high-sensitivity ESR spectroscopy, we investigated exfoliated graphene samples to detect and characterize unpaired electron spins and their interactions, which are indicative of magnetic behavior. The experimental approach involved examining graphene at variable temperatures and different magnetic field strengths to observe changes in spin dynamics and resonance conditions. Our findings reveal distinct ESR signals attributed to localized magnetic moments, possibly arising from structural defects or edge states within the graphene lattice. These localized moments exhibit temperature-dependent behavior, demonstrating an antiferromagnetic coupling at lower temperatures and a transition to paramagnetism as temperature increases. The observed ESR line shapes and g-factor anisotropy further implicate graphene’s inherent structural features in contributing to its magnetic behavior. By providing a detailed analysis of the resonance data, we confirm the presence of intrinsic magnetic phenomena in pristine graphene, challenging the prevailing notion of intrinsic magnetism in carbon-based materials. Conclusively, this study establishes a foundational understanding of graphene's magnetic properties, potentially paving the way for the development of graphenic spintronic devices and opening new avenues for research in two-dimensional magnetic systems.

text: This study investigates the radial transport of large-scale magnetic fields in accretion disks, a crucial aspect of astrophysical magnetohydrodynamics. Accretion disks, the primary sites of energy release in compact objects, harbor strong magnetic fields that play a pivotal role in regulating the disk's evolution. The objective of this research is to explore the steady-state solutions of the radial transport equation and derive an upper limit on the vertical field strength in accretion disks.  To address this objective, we employ a combination of analytical and numerical techniques. We first derive a set of steady-state equations that govern the radial transport of magnetic fields in accretion disks. By solving these equations, we identify the critical parameters that control the magnetic field's behavior, including the disk's accretion rate, viscosity, and magnetic diffusivity. We then employ numerical simulations to explore the effects of these parameters on the radial transport of magnetic fields.  Our key findings indicate that the radial transport of magnetic fields in accretion disks is significantly influenced by the disk's accretion rate and viscosity. We also derive an upper limit on the vertical field strength, which is found to be inversely proportional to the disk's accretion rate and viscosity. This limit provides a fundamental constraint on the maximum magnetic field strength that can be sustained in accretion disks. Our results have significant implications for our understanding of the magnetohydrodynamic evolution of accretion disks, including the regulation of disk viscosity and the generation of magnetic reconnection events.

Our findings reveal that the stability of food webs is governed by complex interactions between trophic levels, and that certain structural properties, such as high connectivity or low redundancy, exacerbate the risk of catastrophic collapses. The notion of class is ubiquitous in computer science and is central in many
formalisms for the representation of structured knowledge used both in
knowledge representation and in databases. In this paper we study the basic
issues underlying such representation formalisms and single out both their
common characteristics and their distinguishing features. Such investigation
leads us to propose a unifying framework in which we are able to capture the
fundamental aspects of several representation languages used in different
contexts. The proposed formalism is expressed in the style of description
logics, which have been introduced in knowledge representation as a means to
provide a semantically well-founded basis for the structural aspects of
knowledge representation systems. The description logic considered in this
paper is a subset of first order logic with nice computational characteristics.
It is quite expressive and features a novel combination of constructs that has
not been studied before. The distinguishing constructs are number restrictions,
which generalize existence and functional dependencies, inverse roles, which
allow one to refer to the inverse of a relationship, and possibly cyclic
assertions, which are necessary for capturing real world domains. We are able
to show that it is precisely such combination of constructs that makes our
logic powerful enough to model the essential set of features for defining class
structures that are common to frame systems, object-oriented database
languages, and semantic data models. As a consequence of the established
correspondences, several significant extensions of each of the above formalisms
become available. The high expressiveness of the logic we propose and the need
for capturing the reasoning in different contexts forces us to distinguish
between unrestricted and finite model reasoning. A notable feature of our
proposal is that reasoning in both cases is decidable. We argue that, by virtue
of the high expressive power and of the associated reasoning capabilities on
both unrestricted and finite models, our logic provides a common core for
class-based representation formalisms.

We present a general overview and the first results of the SUMO project (a
SUrvey of Multiple pOpulations in Globular Clusters). The objective of this
survey is the study of multiple stellar populations in the largest sample of
globular clusters homogeneously analysed to date. To this aim we obtained high
signal-to-noise (S/N>50) photometry for main sequence stars with mass down to
~0.5 M_SUN in a large sample of clusters using both archival and proprietary U,
B, V, and I data from ground-based telescopes. In this paper, we focus on the
occurrence of multiple stellar populations in twenty three clusters. We have
defined a new photometric index cubi= (U-B)-(B-I), that turns out to be very
effective for identifying multiple sequences along the red giant branch (RGB).
We found that in the V-cubi diagram all clusters presented in this paper show
broadened or multimodal RGBs, with the presence of two or more components. We
found a direct connection with the chemical properties of different sequences,
that display different abundances of light elements (O, Na, C, N, and Al). The
cubi index is also a powerful tool to identify distinct sequences of stars
along the horizontal branch and, for the first time in the case of NGC104 (47
Tuc), along the asymptotic giant branch. Our results demonstrate that i) the
presence of more than two stellar populations is a common feature among
globular clusters, as already highlighted in previous work; ii) multiple
sequences with different chemical contents can be easily identified by using
standard Johnson photometry obtained with ground-based facilities; iii) in the
study of GC multiple stellar populations the cubi index is alternative to
spectroscopy, and has the advantage of larger statistics.

text: In the Standard Model of particle physics, the universe's large-scale structure is attributed to the presence of dark matter, a mysterious entity comprising approximately 27% of the cosmos. However, the existence of dark matter remains unconfirmed, and its nature remains one of the greatest mysteries in modern physics. Recent studies have explored alternative models, such as the Scale-Invariant Local $B-L$ models, which propose an alternative explanation for dark matter's existence. This research delves into the realm of accidental dark matter within these models, examining the possibility of dark matter arising as a byproduct of other physical processes.  The objective of this study is to investigate the potential for accidental dark matter in Scale-Invariant Local $B-L$ models, focusing on the interplay between the Higgs sector and the $B-L$ gauge boson. By analyzing the interplay between the Higgs and $B-L$ sectors, we aim to identify the conditions under which dark matter could emerge as an accidental consequence of other physical processes.  This research employs a combination of theoretical and numerical methods to explore the interplay between the Higgs and $B-L$ sectors. We utilize a suite of numerical tools to simulate the evolution of the universe, allowing us to probe the parameter space of the $B-L$ model. Our results indicate that, under certain conditions, the $B-L$ model can give rise to a dark matter candidate that is consistent with observed cosmological data.  The findings of this study have significant implications for our understanding of dark matter and the Standard Model of particle physics. By exploring the possibility of accidental dark matter in Scale-Invariant Local $B-L$ models, we shed light on the interplay between the Higgs and $B-L$ sectors, and demonstrate the potential for alternative explanations for dark matter's existence.

text: In this study, we utilize the integral field spectrograph MUSE to investigate the post-starburst host galaxy of the tidal disruption event (TDE) ASASSN-14li. Our main objective is to elucidate the dynamical history and recent merger activity that may have influenced the host galaxy's current state. Through detailed spectroscopic analysis, we identify clear signatures of a recent merger event characterized by disrupted stellar populations and kinematic disturbances within the galaxy. The spectroscopic data reveal a significant post-starburst stellar component, suggesting that the galaxy had experienced a substantial influx of new stars in the preceding 100 million years.   We employ a comprehensive methodology combining spectral synthesis modeling and kinematics to examine the stellar and gas components of the galaxy. Our findings indicate the presence of distinct stellar populations, where the kinematic signatures point to a recent minor merger or accretion event as the likely catalyst for the observed starburst. Additionally, we detect enhanced emission-line regions that align with the location of tidal features and the recently combined mass, further supporting the merger hypothesis.  Our study offers new insights into the complex interplay between galactic dynamics and star formation activities in the aftermath of galaxy mergers. This work not only contributes to the understanding of TDE host galaxy environments but also sheds light on the broader implications of galactic mergers in shaping the evolutionary pathways of post-starburst galaxies. Our findings underscore the importance of high-resolution spectroscopic tools such as MUSE in unveiling the nuanced histories of galaxies undergoing dynamic transformations.

text: This research paper explores the relationship between multiplicity and entropy within complex systems, aiming to derive the maximum entropy principle. Starting from the foundational concepts of statistical mechanics, particularly Boltzmann's entropy formula S = k ln W, where W represents the number of microstates corresponding to a macrostate (multiplicity), the study delves into how multiplicity influences entropy. By analyzing various thermodynamic scenarios and employing combinatorial methods to calculate multiplicity, the paper demonstrates how the system's multiplicity affects its entropy. The objective is to establish a mathematical framework that links multiplicity directly to entropy and then applies this framework to derive the maximum entropy principle, which states that a system will evolve towards a state of maximum entropy. Through rigorous derivations and case studies, the research concludes by validating the theoretical underpinnings and practical applicability of the maximum entropy principle in understanding complex systems, thereby providing a novel perspective on entropy determination in such systems.

text: We investigated the ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) properties of exchange-coupled multiferroic polycrystalline Pt/BiFeO$_3$/Ni$_{81}$Fe$_{19}$/Pt heterostructures to elucidate the interplay between magnetism and ferroelectricity in these complex materials. Our study aimed to address the challenges associated with the non-volatile magnetic behavior influenced by the ferroelectric order parameter of BiFeO$_3$. We synthesized the heterostructures using pulsed laser deposition and characterized the resulting films through X-ray diffraction and atomic force microscopy to confirm their structural integrity and surface morphology.  Applying FMR techniques, we demonstrated the presence of exchange coupling between the ferromagnetic Ni$_{81}$Fe$_{19}$ layer and the underlying BiFeO$_3$. Our results indicated that the resonance frequency and linewidth exhibited significant dependence on the external electric field applied to the BiFeO$_3$. Specifically, we observed an electric-field tunability of the magnetic resonance conditions, which we attribute to the modulation of effective magnetic anisotropy resulting from the ferroelectric polarization dynamics.   We employed micromagnetic simulations to analyze the FMR data further, revealing insights into the underlying mechanisms driving the tunable magnetic properties. The findings elucidate the coupling mechanisms between the multiferroic and ferromagnetic layers and provide a foundation for future studies aimed at harnessing the unique characteristics of multiferroic systems in spintronic applications. Through this work, we contribute to advancing the understanding of the complex interactions in heterostructures and their potential in next-generation magnetic devices.

text: M dwarf stars, the most abundant type of stars in the galaxy, host a higher frequency of starspot activity than their more massive solar-type counterparts. This increased starspot activity can present challenges for the detection of low-mass planets orbiting M dwarfs using radial velocity techniques. In this study, we explored the effect of M dwarf starspot activity on the detection of low-mass planets using radial velocity measurements. We modeled the radial velocity signals of simulated M dwarf stars with and without starspots, and compared their respective detection thresholds for low-mass planets using the Keck-HIRES radial velocity instrument.  Our results indicated that the presence of starspots led to significantly increased radial velocity variations for M dwarf stars compared to solar-type stars. These variations made the detection of low-mass planets more challenging, with threshold masses required for detection being approximately 1.5-2.0 times greater for M dwarf stars with moderate-to-strong starspot activity compared to those with weak activity.  To mitigate the impact of starspot activity on planet detection, we considered the use of starspot modeling in radial velocity data analysis. By modeling the effect of starspots on the radial velocity signal, we were able to improve the detection threshold for low-mass planets around M dwarf stars, making them more amenable to future detection efforts.  In conclusion, this study demonstrated that the presence of starspots on M dwarf stars significantly impacts the detection of low-mass planets using radial velocity techniques. By considering starspot activity and implementing starspot modeling in data analysis, we can improve the ability to detect and characterize low-mass planets orbiting M dwarf stars, contributing to a better understanding of planetary systems in our galaxy.

text: In this study, we explore the regular and chaotic dynamics of non-spherical bodies, focusing on the phenomenon known as "Zeldovich's pancakes." We investigate how the shape and orientation of these bodies influence their gravitational wave emission, particularly in the context of very long wavelength gravitational waves. Through numerical simulations, we observe that the irregular shapes of these bodies lead to more chaotic motion, which results in enhanced emission of gravitational waves. Key insights include the discovery that certain configurations of non-spherical bodies can produce significant power in the very long wavelength range, previously thought to be negligible. Our findings suggest that such objects could serve as natural sources of gravitational wave radiation, offering new avenues for detection methods beyond traditional spherical models. The methodologies employed include detailed modeling of body shapes, integration of equations of motion under various initial conditions, and analysis of gravitational wave signals using advanced waveform templates. These results contribute to our understanding of the broader implications of non-sphericity in astrophysical contexts and its role in gravitational wave astronomy.

text:
Migraine is a common disabling headache disorder characterized by recurrent
episodes sometimes preceded or accompanied by focal neurological symptoms
called aura. The relation between two subtypes, migraine without aura (MWoA)
and migraine with aura (MWA), is explored with the aim to identify targets for
neuromodulation techniques. To this end, a dynamically regulated control system
is schematically reduced to a network of the trigeminal nerve, which innervates
the cranial circulation, an associated descending modulatory network of
brainstem nuclei, and parasympathetic vasomotor efferents. This extends the
idea of a migraine generator region in the brainstem to a larger network and is
still simple and explicit enough to open up possibilities for mathematical
modeling in the future. In this study, it is suggested that the migraine
generator network (MGN) is driven and may therefore respond differently to
different spatio-temporal noxious input in the migraine subtypes MWA and MWoA.
The noxious input is caused by a cortical perturbation of homeostasis, known as
spreading depression (SD). The MGN might even trigger SD in the first place by
a failure in vasomotor control. As a consequence, migraine is considered as an
inherently dynamical disease to which a linear course from upstream to
downstream events would not do justice. Minimally invasive and noninvasive
neuromodulation techniques are briefly reviewed and their rational is discussed
in the context of the proposed mechanism.

We investigate the processes that lead to the formation, ejection and fall of
a confined plasma ejection that was observed in a numerical experiment of the
solar corona. By quantifying physical parameters such as mass, velocity, and
orientation of the plasma ejection relative to the magnetic field, we provide a
description of the nature of this particular phenomenon. The time-dependent
three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (3D MHD) equations are solved in a box
extending from the chromosphere to the lower corona. The plasma is heated by
currents that are induced through field line braiding as a consequence of
photospheric motions. Spectra of optically thin emission lines in the extreme
ultraviolet range are synthesized, and magnetic field lines are traced over
time. Following strong heating just above the chromosphere, the pressure
rapidly increases, leading to a hydrodynamic explosion above the upper
chromosphere in the low transition region. The explosion drives the plasma,
which needs to follow the magnetic field lines. The ejection is then moving
more or less ballistically along the loop-like field lines and eventually drops
down onto the surface of the Sun. The speed of the ejection is in the range of
the sound speed, well below the Alfven velocity. The plasma ejection is
basically a hydrodynamic phenomenon, whereas the rise of the heating rate is of
magnetic nature. The granular motions in the photosphere lead (by chance) to a
strong braiding of the magnetic field lines at the location of the explosion
that in turn is causing strong currents which are dissipated. Future studies
need to determine if this process is a ubiquitous phenomenon on the Sun on
small scales. Data from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly on the Solar Dynamics
Observatory (AIA/SDO) might provide the relevant information.

text: The search for magnetic monopoles and the Higgs particle, two fundamental particles predicted by grand unified theories (GUTs) and the Standard Model (SM), respectively, has been a major focus in modern physics. In recent years, several experiments have reported tantalizing evidence for the existence of magnetic monopoles, whereas the Higgs particle was discovered in 2012 by the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). However, the nature of these particles remains a subject of ongoing debate and investigation.  One intriguing possibility is that magnetic monopoles and the Higgs particle may coexist but have not yet been observed due to their distinct properties. Grand unified theories predict the existence of magnetic monopoles as topological defects arising from the symmetry breaking process during the early universe. On the other hand, the Higgs particle is a scalar boson that emerges from the Higgs field, responsible for giving mass to other fundamental particles.  Several experiments, such as the Monopole and Cosmic Ray Detector (Monaco) and the Quasar Absorption Line Search Experiment (QLSE), have searched for magnetic monopoles with no definitive evidence found. Moreover, the upper bounds on their masses have been improved, ruling out some theoretical predictions.  Regarding the Higgs particle, despite its discovery, several questions remain unanswered, such as its stability and the nature of the Higgs potential. Some models, such as the two-Higgs doublet model, propose the existence of multiple Higgs bosons. The search for these additional Higgs particles is ongoing, with the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) expected to provide new insights.  In conclusion, while significant progress has been made in the search for magnetic monopoles and the Higgs particle, their definitive discovery and understanding of their properties remain open questions. The ongoing experiments and the development of new technologies offer promising opportunities for resolving these mysteries and deepening our understanding of the fundamental nature of matter and the universe.  Keywords magnetic monopoles, Higgs particle, grand unified theories, fundamental particles, symmetry breaking, topological defects, scalar bosons, experimental search, Higgs potential, multi-Higgs particles.

We present a kinematical study of the optical ejecta of GK Per. It is based
on proper motions measurements of 282 knots from ~20 images spanning 25 years.
Doppler-shifts are also computed for 217 knots. The combination of proper
motions and radial velocities allows a unique 3-D view of the ejecta to be
obtained. The main results are: (1) the outflow is a thick shell in which knots
expand with a significant range of velocities, mostly between 600 and 1000
km/s; (2) kinematical ages indicate that knots have suffered only a modest
deceleration since their ejection a century ago; (3) no evidence for anisotropy
in the expansion rate is found; (4) velocity vectors are generally aligned
along the radial direction but a symmetric pattern of non-radial velocities is
also observed at specific directions; (5) the total Halpha+[NII] flux has been
linearly decreasing at a rate of 2.6 % per year in the last decade. The Eastern
nebular side is fading at a slower rate than the Western one. Some of the knots
displayed a rapid change of brightness during the 2004-2011 period. Over a
longer timescale, a progressive circularization and homogenization of the
nebula is taking place; (6) a kinematic distance of 400+-30 pc is determined.
These results raise some problems to the previous interpretations of the
evolution of GK Per. In particular, the idea of a strong interaction of the
outflow with the surrounding medium in the Southwest quadrant is not supported
by our data.

A gauge invariant action for the open bosonic string has been proposed in an
earlier paper. We work out the consequences of this proposal for the lowest
mode, viz. the tachyon. The action can be calculated for generic momenta,
perturbatively, order by order in the tachyon field. For on shell tachyons we
explicitly calculate the cubic action and show that it reproduces the correct
equations of motion and coincides wih the $\beta$ function to the required
order. The calculation is done in terms of bare fields with a finite cutoff,
which is the original prescription. We also show that it is possible in some
momentum regions to renormalize the theory and eliminate the cutoff dependence
so that the continuum limit can be taken. After renormalization, the parameter
$R\over a$ is replaced by $R\over L$ where $R$ is an IR cutoff, $a$ is the UV
cutoff and $L$ is some renormalization scale. There is also some arbitrariness
in the overall normalization due to the choice of regularization scheme - this
does not affect on-shell quantities. We also rederive within this scheme, the
action in the region of zero momentum, which gives the exact (tree level)
tachyon potential. The tachyon potential is consistent with Sen's conjecture
that the height of the potential is the same as the tension of the brane.

We present a concept study of a solar wind forecasting method for Earth,
based on persistence modeling from STEREO in-situ measurements combined with
multi-viewpoint EUV observational data. By comparing the fractional areas of
coronal holes (CHs) extracted from EUV data of STEREO and SoHO/SDO, we perform
an uncertainty assessment derived from changes in the CHs and apply those
changes to the predicted solar wind speed profile at 1AU. We evaluate the
method for the time period 2008-2012, and compare the results to a persistence
model based on ACE in-situ measurements and to the STEREO persistence model
without implementing the information on CH evolution. Compared to an ACE based
persistence model, the performance of the STEREO persistence model which takes
into account the evolution of CHs, is able to increase the number of correctly
predicted high-speed streams by about 12%, and to decrease the number of missed
streams by about 23%, and the number of false alarms by about 19%. However, the
added information on CH evolution is not able to deliver more accurate speed
values for the forecast than using the STEREO persistence model without CH
information which performs better than an ACE based persistence model.
Investigating the CH evolution between STEREO and Earth view for varying
separation angles over ~25-140{\deg} East of Earth, we derive some relation
between expanding CHs and increasing solar wind speed, but a less clear
relation for decaying CHs and decreasing solar wind speed. This fact most
likely prevents the method from making more precise forecasts. The obtained
results support a future L5 mission and show the importance and valuable
contribution using multi-viewpoint data.

Optical signal propagation through underwater channels is affected by three
main degrading phenomena, namely absorption, scattering, and fading. In this
paper, we experimentally study the statistical distribution of intensity
fluctuations in underwater wireless optical channels with random temperature
and salinity variations as well as the presence of air bubbles. In particular,
we define different scenarios to produce random fluctuations on the water
refractive index across the propagation path, and then examine the accuracy of
various statistical distributions in terms of their goodness of fit to the
experimental data. We also obtain the channel coherence time to address the
average period of fading temporal variations. The scenarios under consideration
cover a wide range of scintillation index from weak to strong turbulence.
Moreover, the effects of beam-collimator at the transmitter side and aperture
averaging lens at the receiver side are experimentally investigated. We show
that the use of a transmitter beam-collimator and/or a receiver aperture
averaging lens suits single-lobe distributions such that the generalized Gamma
and exponential Weibull distributions can excellently match the histograms of
the acquired data. Our experimental results further reveal that the channel
coherence time is on the order of $10^{-3}$ seconds and larger which implies to
the slow fading turbulent channels.

text: In this study, we investigate the age and binarity of Fomalhaut, employing multi-wavelength photometric data and theoretical models to refine our understanding of its stellar properties. Our analysis reveals that Fomalhaut is approximately 430 million years old, consistent with previous studies but with improved precision through the use of higher-resolution observations. We also conducted a comprehensive binary companion search using interferometric techniques, which indicated no significant secondary component within a projected separation of 1.5 arcseconds. This result supports the hypothesis that Fomalhaut is a single star, resolving a long-standing debate about its potential companions. The methodologies employed include high-cadence photometry across multiple wavelengths, adaptive optics imaging, and interferometric observations to achieve these findings. Our work contributes to the broader context of stellar evolution and the formation scenarios of stars in our solar neighborhood.

text: In this study, we present the discovery of two substellar binaries located at the T/Y transition, WISE J1536-1439 and WISE J1620-1617, based on the analysis of their near-infrared (NIR) colors and spectral features. The T/Y transition is a critical boundary in brown dwarf (BD) evolution where the object starts to exhibit T-type characteristics such as atmospheric methane and water vapor absorption features.  Our objective was to investigate the Y-band fluxes of the coolest BDs to understand the spectral evolution at the T/Y transition. For this purpose, we utilized the Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) data, which provides a rich database of mid-infrared (MIR) observations. By analyzing the WISE color-color diagrams, we identified two new BDs, WISE J1536-1439 and WISE J1620-1617, which exhibit Y-band fluxes consistent with the presence of methane and water vapor in their atmospheres.  We carried out additional spectroscopic observations using the SpeX instrument on the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility to confirm the atmospheric composition of these BDs. Our findings suggest that both WISE J1536-1439 and WISE J1620-1617 are in the late T-type or early Y-type regime, with temperatures around 800 K and spectral types around T8-T9.  Our key findings demonstrate that the Y-band fluxes provide valuable information on the spectral evolution of BDs at the T/Y transition. We propose that a comprehensive survey of this population using NIR and MIR data could significantly enhance our understanding of the atmospheric and evolutionary processes in substellar objects.

text: The search for third-generation scalar leptoquarks and heavy right-handed neutrinos is pivotal for uncovering physics beyond the Standard Model. This research investigates these phenomena through final states comprising two tau leptons and two jets, utilizing data from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of √s = 13 TeV, recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC. Our study sets out to explore possible signatures in these final states, prompted by theoretical predictions that suggest leptoquarks could mediate interactions between leptons and quarks, while right-handed neutrinos are potential components of the seesaw mechanism explaining neutrino masses. The methodology involves a selection of events characterized by two tau leptons and at least two jets, alongside advanced object reconstruction and identification techniques to optimize signal sensitivity while suppressing Standard Model backgrounds. A multivariate analysis framework is employed to enhance discrimination between signal hypotheses and background processes. Our findings report no significant excess above the expected background, leading to the establishment of upper limits on production cross-sections for various mass hypotheses. The results constrain the parameter space for third-generation scalar leptoquarks with masses up to several TeV and provide complementary limits on heavy right-handed neutrinos in this unique final state topology. This study contributes to the ongoing exploration of new physics at high-energy colliders, indicating the necessity for further scrutiny with larger data sets and refined theoretical models to unveil potential signals of new particles.

A debate has arisen concerning the fundamental nature of LBVs) and their role
in stellar evolution. While Smith and Tombleson proposed that their isolated
environments indicate that LBVs must be largely the product of binary
evolution, Humphreys et al. have recently expressed the view that the
traditional single-star view still holds if one appropriately selects a
subsample of LBVs. This paper finds the claim of Humphreys et al. to be
quantitatively unjustified. A statistical test of "candidate" as opposed to
"confirmed" LBVs shows no significant difference ($<$1$\sigma$) between their
environments. Even if the sample is further subdivided as proposed, the three
most luminous LBVs are spatially dispersed similar to late O-type dwarfs, which
have much longer lifetimes than expected for classical LBVs. Lower-luminosity
LBVs have a distribution associated with red supergiants (RSGs), but these RSGs
are dominated by stars of 10-15 M$_{\odot}$ initial mass, with much longer
lifetimes than expected for those lower-luminosity LBVs. If one's view is
restricted to the highest-luminosity LBVs, then the appropriate comparison is
with early O-type stars that are their presumed progenitors, when this is done,
it is clear that even the high-luminosity LBVs are more dispersed than
expected. Humphreys et al. also suggest that velocities of LBVs support the
single-star view, being inconsistent with runaways. A quantitative analysis of
the radial velocity distribution of LBVS in M31 and M33 contradicts this,
modest runway speeds expected from mass gainers in binary evolution are
consistent with the observed velocities, although the data lack the precision
to discriminate.

text: This work investigates the commissioning and operation of a newly developed energy system. The study aims to address the challenges encountered during the initial stages of system implementation and the subsequent operational phase. Through a series of experiments and analyses, our research highlights the importance of thorough commissioning procedures in ensuring the efficient and reliable functioning of the energy system. We identify key factors that influence the commissioning process, such as equipment readiness, system integration, and regulatory compliance.  Additionally, this study explores the operational phase of the energy system, focusing on performance optimization and maintenance strategies. By monitoring system parameters and performance metrics, we develop a comprehensive understanding of the operational dynamics and identify opportunities for enhancing system efficiency. Our findings emphasize the significance of regular maintenance activities and proactive troubleshooting to mitigate downtime and ensure continuous operation. Furthermore, we propose a systematic approach to operational decision-making, incorporating real-time data analysis and feedback mechanisms.  Overall, this research contributes to the existing body of knowledge on commissioning and operation practices in energy systems. The insights derived from this study can inform future projects in maximizing system performance, minimizing operational risks, and achieving sustainable energy production.

text: This research investigates the intricacies of knowledge-generating efficiency within innovation systems, focusing on the interplay between structural and temporal effects. The study recognizes that innovation systems are complex networks wherein knowledge creation is crucial for technological advancements and competitive advantage. Despite substantial research on innovation systems, the impact of structural configurations and temporal dynamics on knowledge efficiency remains underexplored. This study aims to address this gap by examining how these variables influence the efficiency of knowledge generation.  Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, we incorporate a quantitative analysis of patent data across different industries to identify patterns of knowledge dissemination and a qualitative assessment involving expert interviews to understand contextual factors. The quantitative component employs social network analysis to gauge the structural characteristics of innovation networks, such as centrality and density, while the temporal analysis examines knowledge flows over successive innovation cycles.  Key findings reveal that structurally cohesive networks exhibit higher knowledge-generating efficiency, facilitated by robust collaboration and resource sharing. However, temporal factors such as the speed of technological evolution and cycle length significantly modulate this efficiency. Rapidly evolving industries show diminished returns on structural cohesion over time, indicating a complex interplay between structural status and temporal influences.  In conclusion, our study underscores the necessity for innovation systems to balance structural cohesion with temporal adaptability to enhance knowledge-generating efficiency. These insights provide valuable direction for policymakers and industry leaders striving to foster sustainable innovation environments in an increasingly dynamic landscape.

text: In today's dynamic and competitive business environment, there is an increasing demand for efficient service systems that can handle a large number of requests while minimizing the number of servers required. In this study, we focus on a large-scale service system with packing constraints, where each server can only serve a fixed number of requests before needing to be taken offline for maintenance.  The objective of our research is to propose an efficient algorithm for minimizing the number of occupied servers in such a system. We formulate the problem as a variant of the well-known job shop scheduling problem and introduce a heuristic approach based on local search and dynamic programming techniques. Our algorithm seeks to pack as many requests as possible into each server while minimizing the number of servers needed to serve the entire request set.  We evaluate the performance of our algorithm using comprehensive simulation studies, testing it against various benchmark problems and real-world scenarios. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms other commonly used methods, such as the popular Minimal Processing Time (MPT) and Shortest Queue Length (SQL) algorithms.  Our research provides valuable insights into the design and optimization of large-scale service systems with packing constraints, which are prevalent in industries such as manufacturing, logistics, and telecommunications. The proposed algorithm can be incorporated into existing service systems to reduce the number of servers required, thereby improving efficiency and reducing costs.

text: In this study, we present a delay differential model aimed at understanding the variability of El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), focusing on parametric instability and the distribution of extreme events. Our model incorporates time lags to capture the feedback mechanisms between ocean and atmosphere dynamics, essential for accurately representing ENSO behavior. We employ numerical simulations to explore how varying parameters influence the onset and persistence of ENSO events. Results indicate that parametric instability plays a crucial role in triggering ENSO episodes and in determining their amplitude and duration. Furthermore, we analyze the distribution of extreme events using statistical methods to assess the frequency and magnitude of significant anomalies. Key methodologies include bifurcation analysis and sensitivity studies to identify critical parameter regimes. The findings contribute to our understanding of ENSO dynamics and provide insights into predicting extreme climate events.

To study the crucial range of Galactocentric distances between 12 and 16 kpc,
where little information is available, we have obtained VI CCD imaging of
Berkeley 20 and BVI CCD imaging of Berkeley 66 and Tombaugh 2, three distant,
old open clusters. Using the synthetic colour magnitude diagram (CMD) technique
with three types of evolutionary tracks of different metallicities, we have
determined age, distance, reddening and indicative metallicity of these
systems. The CMD of Be 20 is best reproduced by stellar models with a
metallicity about half of solar (Z=0.008 or 0.01), in perfect agreement with
high resolution spectroscopic estimates. Its age is between 5 and 6 Gyr from
stellar models with overshooting and between 4.3 and 4.5 Gyr from models
without it. The distance modulus from the best fitting models is always
(m-M)0=14.7 (corresponding to a Galactocentric radius of about 16 kpc), and the
reddening E(B-V) ranges between 0.13 and 0.16. A slightly lower metallicity (Z
~ 0.006) appears to be more appropriate for Be 66. This cluster is younger,
(age of 3 Gyr), and closer, (m-M)0=13.3 (i.e., at 12 kpc from the Galactic
centre), than Be 20, and suffers from high extinction, 1.2 < E(B-V) < 1.3,
variable at the 2-3 per cent level. Finally, the results for To 2 indicate that
it is an intermediate age cluster, with an age of about 1.4 Gyr or 1.6-1.8 Gyr
for models without and with overshooting, respectively. The metallicity is
about half of solar (Z=0.006 to 0.01), in agreement with spectroscopic
determinations. The distance modulus is (m-M)0=14.5, implying a distance of
about 14 kpc from the Galactic centre; the reddening E(B-V) is 0.31-0.4,
depending on the model and metallicity, with a preferred value around 0.34.
