text:
We study 14 large solar jets observed in polar coronal holes. In EUV movies
from SDO/AIA, each jet appears similar to most X-ray jets and EUV jets that
erupt in coronal holes, but each is exceptional in that it goes higher than
most, so high that it is observed in the outer corona beyond 2.2 RSun in images
from the SOHO/LASCO/C2 coronagraph. From AIA He II 304 {\AA} movies and
LASCO/C2 running-difference images of these high-reaching jets, we find: (1)
the front of the jet transits the corona below 2.2 RSun at a speed typically
several times the sound speed; (2) each jet displays an exceptionally large
amount of spin as it erupts; (3) in the outer corona, most of the jets display
measureable swaying and bending of a few degrees in amplitude; in three jets
the swaying is discernibly oscillatory with a period of order 1 hour. These
characteristics suggest that the driver in these jets is a magnetic-untwisting
wave that is basically a large-amplitude (i.e., non-linear) torsional Alfven
wave that is put into the reconnected open field in the jet by interchange
reconnection as the jet erupts. From the measured spinning and swaying we
estimate that the magnetic-untwisting wave loses most of its energy in the
inner corona below 2.2 RSun. We point out that the torsional waves observed in
Type-II spicules might dissipate in the corona in the same way as the
magnetic-untwisting waves in our big jets and thereby power much of the coronal
heating in coronal holes.
label: human

text: We investigated the Hilbert-Schmidt separability probability of real two-qubit systems, a fundamental problem in quantum information theory. Our approach involved a systematic analysis of the properties of entangled states and the development of a novel method to determine the separability of real two-qubit states. By leveraging the geometric properties of the Bloch sphere and the symmetries of the Hilbert space, we derived a set of conditions for the separability of real two-qubit states. Our results demonstrate that the Hilbert-Schmidt separability probability of real two-qubit systems can be significantly improved by exploiting these geometric and symmetrical properties.  Through a series of numerical experiments, we validated our analytical framework by comparing the separability probabilities obtained using our method with those obtained using existing algorithms. Our results show that our approach yields more accurate and efficient separability probabilities than existing methods, particularly for large-scale systems. Furthermore, we identified a set of minimal entangled states that are not separable using our method, providing new insights into the nature of entanglement in real two-qubit systems.  Our work provides a significant advance in the field of quantum information theory, enabling the more accurate and efficient determination of the Hilbert-Schmidt separability probability of real two-qubit systems. The developed method can be applied to a wide range of systems, including large-scale quantum systems and quantum simulation models, and has the potential to improve our understanding of entanglement and its properties in quantum systems.
label: machine

text:
Thermodynamics was developed in the XIXth century to provide a physical
description to engines and other macroscopic thermal machines. Since then,
progress in nanotechnologies urged to extend these formalism, initially
designed for classical systems, to the quantum world. During this thesis, I
have built a formalism to study the stochastic thermodynamics of quantum
systems, in which quantum measurement plays a central role : like the thermal
reservoir of standard stochastic thermodynamics, it is the primary source of
randomness in the system's dynamics. I first studied projective measurement as
a thermodynamic process. I evidenced that measurement is responsible for an
uncontroled variation of the system's energy that I called quantum heat, and
also a production of entropy. As a proof of concept, I studied an engine
extracting work from the measurementinduced quantum fluctuations. Then, I
extended this formalism to generalized measurements, which allowed to describe
open quantum systems (i.e. in contact with reservoirs). I defined work, heat
and entropy production for single realizations of thermodynamic protocols, and
retrieved that these quantities obey fluctuation theorems. I applied this
formalism to the canonical situation of quantum optics, i.e. a Qubit coupled to
a laser and a the vacuum. Finally, I studied a promising platform to test
Qubit's thermodynamics: a hybrid optomechanical system. The formalism developed
in this thesis is of interest for the quantum thermodynamics community as it
enables to characterize quantum heat engines and compare their performances to
their classical analogs. Furthermore, as it sets quantum measurement as a
thermodynamic process, it pave the ways to a new kind of thermodynamic
machines, exploiting the specificities of quantum realm in an unprecedented
way.
label: human

text: Turbulent density patterns represent a significant aspect of plasma behavior in nuclear fusion research. The Mean Motion of these patterns is a key parameter that impacts plasma stability and confinement. In this study, the BES system on MAST was utilized to detect and measure the Mean Motion of turbulent density patterns. The methodology involved data collection using the BES system and subsequent analysis to quantify the Mean Motion of the detected patterns. The key findings reveal the presence of distinct Mean Motion characteristics in different plasma conditions, shedding light on the underlying dynamics of turbulence in fusion plasmas. The interpreted physical significance of the measured Mean Motion provides insights into the behavior of turbulent density patterns and their implications for plasma performance. Overall, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of turbulence in fusion plasmas and highlights the importance of the Mean Motion parameter in characterizing turbulent density patterns detected by the BES system on MAST.
label: machine

text:
Let $F,E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be two self similar sets. First, assuming $F$
is generated by an IFS $\Phi$ with strong separation, we characterize the
affine maps $g:\mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$ such that $g(F)\subseteq
F$. Our analysis depends on the cardinality of the group $G_\Phi$ generated by
the orthogonal parts of the similarities in $\Phi$. When $|G_\Phi|=\infty$ we
show that any such self embedding must be a similarity, and so (by the results
of Elekes, Keleti and M\'ath\'{e}) some power of its orthogonal part lies in
$G_\Phi$. When $|G_\Phi| < \infty$ and $\Phi$ has a uniform contraction
$\lambda$, we show that the linear part of any such embedding is
diagonalizable, and the norm of each of its eigenvalues is a rational power of
$\lambda$.
  We also study the existence and properties of affine maps $g$ such that
$g(F)\subseteq E$, where $E$ is generated by an IFS $\Psi$. In this direction,
we provide more evidence for a Conjecture of Feng, Huang and Rao, that such an
embedding exists only if the contraction ratios of the maps in $\Phi$ are
algebraically dependent on the contraction ratios of the maps in $\Psi$.
Furthermore, we show that, under some conditions, if $|G_\Phi|=\infty$ then
$|G_\Psi|=\infty$ and if $|G_\Phi|<\infty$ then $|G_\Psi|<\infty$.
label: human

text: In this study, we address the challenge of achieving high spectral efficiency in massive Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) systems with a limited number of antennas. Traditional massive MIMO paradigms emphasize utilizing a very large antenna array to enhance data rates and system performance. However, such implementations can be impractical due to physical constraints and increased system complexity. Our research introduces an innovative approach that leverages advanced signal processing techniques to maximize spectral efficiency even with a comparatively smaller antenna array. We propose an optimized hybrid beamforming method, which combines analog and digital processing, to effectively exploit channel state information and enhance signal robustness. Furthermore, we employ machine learning algorithms for dynamic adaptation of the system parameters, thereby improving signal detection and interference management. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our approach achieves significant improvements in spectral efficiency, approaching the theoretical limits of massive MIMO systems that utilize a larger number of antennas. The results reveal that our methodology not only reduces implementation complexity but also enhances the energy efficiency of the system by minimizing power consumption. This work holds the potential to facilitate the deployment of massive MIMO technology in diverse practical scenarios where antenna scalability poses a challenge. Overall, our work contributes a viable solution for achieving the benefits of massive MIMO with fewer antennas, thus extending the applicability of this technology in the next generation of wireless communication networks.
label: machine

text: The phosphatase and tensin homolog associated protein kinase 1 (PEBP1) and the RSK3 (Ribosomal S6 Kinase 3) interacting protein (RKIP) are multifunctional proteins involved in various cellular processes, including cell growth, differentiation, and survival. PEBP1/RKIP has been implicated in the regulation of multiple signaling pathways, including the MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT pathways, whereas RKIP is known to modulate the activity of RSK3, a downstream effector of the MAPK/ERK pathway. Despite their distinct functions, recent studies have revealed a common role for PEBP1/RKIP in regulating cellular processes, including cell proliferation and apoptosis.  This review aims to summarize the current understanding of the multiple functions of PEBP1/RKIP and its potential role in common cellular processes. A comprehensive analysis of the literature reveals that PEBP1/RKIP interacts with various signaling proteins, including RSK3, and modulates their activity. The findings suggest that PEBP1/RKIP plays a critical role in regulating cell growth and survival by modulating the activity of key signaling proteins. Furthermore, the review highlights the potential therapeutic implications of targeting PEBP1/RKIP in the treatment of various diseases, including cancer and neurodegenerative disorders.  The study provides a comprehensive overview of the multiple functions of PEBP1/RKIP and its role in common cellular processes, highlighting the potential for therapeutic intervention in various diseases. The findings of this review contribute to our understanding of the complex interplay between signaling proteins and their regulatory mechanisms, providing new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular processes.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the impact of a galaxy's star formation history on the accuracy of measured star formation rates (SFRs). We analyze a comprehensive sample of galaxies across various cosmic epochs using multi-wavelength data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Hubble Space Telescope. Our findings reveal that galaxies with complex star formation histories exhibit significant variability in their SFR measurements, which can lead to systematic errors in assessing current star formation activities. To address this issue, we propose a novel method that incorporates a stellar population synthesis model to disentangle past and ongoing star formation contributions. This approach allows us to estimate more reliable current SFRs by separating the contributions from different epochs. The methodology employed involves spectral fitting techniques and machine learning algorithms to refine our models and improve the precision of our estimates. Our results indicate that accounting for the star formation history significantly enhances the reliability of SFR measurements, thereby providing a more accurate representation of star formation dynamics across cosmic time.
label: machine

text:
We present direct numerical simulations of Taylor-Couette flow with grooved
walls at a fixed radius ratio $\eta=r_i/r_o=0.714$ with inner cylinder Reynolds
number up to $Re_i=3.76\times10^4$, corresponding to Taylor number up to
$Ta=2.15\times10^9$. The grooves are axisymmetric V-shaped obstacles attached
to the wall with a tip angle of $90^\circ$. Results are compared to the smooth
wall case in order to investigate the effects of grooves on Taylor-Couette
flow. We focus on the effective scaling laws for the torque, flow structures,
and boundary layers. It is found that, when the groove height is smaller than
the boundary layer thickness, the torque is the same as that of the smooth wall
cases. With increasing $Ta$, the boundary layer thickness becomes smaller than
the groove height. Plumes are ejected from the tips of the grooves and
secondary circulations between the latter are formed. This is associated to a
sharp increase of the torque and thus the effective scaling law for the torque
vs. $Ta$ becomes much steeper. Further increasing $Ta$ does not result in an
additional slope increase. Instead, the effective scaling law saturates to the
"ultimate" regime effective exponents seen for smooth walls. It is found that
even though after saturation the slope is the same as for the smooth wall case,
the absolute value of torque is increased, and the more the larger size of the
grooves.
label: human

text:
An intriguing hypothesis, that there exists a decaying X-ray emission
component before the GRB trigger, has been suggested in order to explain the
shallow decay phase of the X-ray afterglow detected in many Swift GRBs. If this
"prior emission" is from an external shock, one would expect a corresponding
optical emission component during the GRB prompt emission phase. In this paper
we apply the available prompt optical emission data (both detections and upper
limits) to constrain such a scenario. We fit the shallow and normal decay
segments of the XRT light curves in our sample with a T_\Delta-shifted single
power law, and extrapolate the X-ray flux back to the time of the early optical
observations. We then use the synchrotron spectrum predicted by the standard
external shock model to extrapolate from the X-ray flux to the optical band,
and obtain the possible range of the predicted optical flux. Finally, we
compare the predictions with the observations. In the cases where later optical
data are available, we also compare the shapes of the optical light curves to
the predicted optical light curves from the external shock prior emission
model. We find that for a good fraction of GRBs (4 out of 8; up to December
2006), the available data already impose severe constraints on the hypothesis.
In particular, the expected optical flux from the prior external shock model is
higher than what the data allow. We conclude that if the shallow-decay X-ray
component were from a prior emission component, it would have to be of an
internal origin with optical flux suppressed.
label: human

text: Our study focuses on designing social network sensors for predicting flu epidemics, aiming to enhance early detection and response strategies. The key problem we tackle is the limitations of traditional surveillance methods in capturing real-time flu trends. By harnessing the vast amounts of data generated on social media platforms, we aimed to develop a proactive surveillance system that could provide timely and accurate forecasts of flu outbreaks.   Our results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of using social network sensors for flu forecasting. Through the analysis of users' interactions and content, we were able to detect early signals of flu activity, allowing for timely interventions to mitigate the spread of the virus. Leveraging machine learning algorithms and network analysis techniques, we developed a predictive model that outperformed traditional surveillance methods in terms of accuracy and timeliness.   Our methodology included collecting and analyzing data from various social media platforms, identifying relevant features for flu prediction, and training our forecasting model. The model was validated using historical flu data and compared against existing surveillance systems to assess its efficacy. Overall, our study showcases the potential of social network sensors as a valuable tool in enhancing epidemic forecasting and response efforts.
label: machine

text:
Modeling a sequence of design steps, or a sequence of parameter settings,
yields a sequence of dynamical systems. In many cases, such a sequence is
intended to approximate a certain limit case. However, formally defining that
limit turns out to be subject to ambiguity. Depending on the interpretation of
the sequence, i.e. depending on how the behaviors of the systems in the
sequence are related, it may vary what the limit should be. Topologies, and in
particular metrics, define limits uniquely, if they exist. Thus they select one
interpretation implicitly and leave no room for other interpretations. In this
paper, we define limits using category theory, and use the mentioned relations
between system behaviors explicitly. This resolves the problem of ambiguity in
a more controlled way. We introduce a category of prefix orders on executions
and partial history preserving maps between them to describe both discrete and
continuous branching time dynamics. We prove that in this category all
projective limits exist, and illustrate how ambiguity in the definition of
limits is resolved using an example. Moreover, we show how various problems
with known topological approaches are now resolved, and how the construction of
projective limits enables us to approximate continuous time dynamics as a
sequence of discrete time systems.
label: human

text: This study investigates the progenitor and supernova mechanism of the SN 2008ge event, which exhibits characteristics similar to those of SN 2002cx. The analysis employs multi-wavelength photometry and spectroscopy to determine the pre-supernova properties and the explosion dynamics. We propose that SN 2008ge originated from a low-mass asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star, consistent with its progenitor being a carbon-oxygen white dwarf in a binary system. Our model suggests that the progenitor underwent mass transfer and possibly accretion onto the white dwarf, leading to the explosive instability. Detailed modeling of the explosion process indicates that SN 2008ge likely resulted from a thermonuclear runaway on the surface of a white dwarf with a mass close to the Chandrasekhar limit. Key methodologies include spectral fitting, light curve fitting, and hydrodynamic simulations. The findings contribute to our understanding of the formation pathways of Type Ia supernovae and their diverse progenitors.
label: machine

text:
The approximate degree of a Boolean function $f \colon \{-1, 1\}^n
\rightarrow \{-1, 1\}$ is the least degree of a real polynomial that
approximates $f$ pointwise to error at most $1/3$. We introduce a generic
method for increasing the approximate degree of a given function, while
preserving its computability by constant-depth circuits.
  Specifically, we show how to transform any Boolean function $f$ with
approximate degree $d$ into a function $F$ on $O(n \cdot
\operatorname{polylog}(n))$ variables with approximate degree at least $D =
\Omega(n^{1/3} \cdot d^{2/3})$. In particular, if $d= n^{1-\Omega(1)}$, then
$D$ is polynomially larger than $d$. Moreover, if $f$ is computed by a
polynomial-size Boolean circuit of constant depth, then so is $F$.
  By recursively applying our transformation, for any constant $\delta > 0$ we
exhibit an AC$^0$ function of approximate degree $\Omega(n^{1-\delta})$. This
improves over the best previous lower bound of $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ due to
Aaronson and Shi (J. ACM 2004), and nearly matches the trivial upper bound of
$n$ that holds for any function. Our lower bounds also apply to
(quasipolynomial-size) DNFs of polylogarithmic width.
  We describe several applications of these results. We give:
  * For any constant $\delta > 0$, an $\Omega(n^{1-\delta})$ lower bound on the
quantum communication complexity of a function in AC$^0$.
  * A Boolean function $f$ with approximate degree at least $C(f)^{2-o(1)}$,
where $C(f)$ is the certificate complexity of $f$. This separation is optimal
up to the $o(1)$ term in the exponent.
  * Improved secret sharing schemes with reconstruction procedures in AC$^0$.
label: human

text:
The growing correlation length observed in supercooled liquids as their
temperature is lowered has been studied with the aid of a single occupancy cell
model. This model becomes more accurate as the density of the system is
increased. One of its advantages is that it permits a simple mapping to a spin
system and the effective spin Hamiltonian is easily obtained for smooth
interparticle potentials. For a binary liquid mixture the effective spin
Hamiltonian is in the universality class of the Ising spin glass in a field. No
phase transition at finite temperatures is therefore expected and the
correlation length will stay finite right down to zero temperature. For binary
mixtures of hard disks and spheres we were not able to obtain the effective
spin Hamiltonian analytically, but have done simulations to obtain its form. It
again is in the universality class of the Ising spin glass in a field. However,
in this case the effective field can be shown to go to zero at the density of
maximum packing in the model, (which is close to that of random close packing),
which means that the correlation length will diverge as the density approaches
its maximum. The exponent nu describing the divergence is related in d
dimensions to the Ising spin glass domain wall energy exponent theta.
label: human

text:
Our investigation concerns the estimation of predictive densities and a study
of efficiency as measured by the frequentist risk of such predictive densities
with integrated $L_2$ and $L_1$ losses. Our findings relate to a $p-$variate
spherically symmetric observable $X \sim p_X(\|x-\mu\|^2)$ and the objective of
estimating the density of $Y \sim q_Y(\|y-\mu\|^2)$ based on $X$. For $L_2$
loss, we describe Bayes estimation, minimum risk equivariant estimation (MRE),
and minimax estimation. We focus on the risk performance of the benchmark
minimum risk equivariant estimator, plug-in estimators, and plug-in type
estimators with expanded scale. For the multivariate normal case, we make use
of a duality result with a point estimation problem bringing into play
reflected normal loss. In three of more dimensions (i.e., $p \geq 3$), we show
that the MRE estimator is inadmissible under $L_2$ loss and provide dominating
estimators. This brings into play Stein-type results for estimating a
multivariate normal mean with a loss which is a concave and increasing function
of $\|\hat{\mu}-\mu\|^2$. We also study the phenomenon of improvement on the
plug-in density estimator of the form $q_Y(\|y-aX\|^2)\,, 0<a \leq 1\,,$ by a
subclass of scale expansions $\frac{1}{c^p} \, q_Y(\|(y -aX)/c \|^2)$ with
$c>1$, showing in some cases, inevitably for large enough $p$, that all choices
$c>1$ are dominating estimators. Extensions are obtained for scale mixture of
normals including a general inadmissibility result of the MRE estimator for $p
\geq 3$. Finally, we describe and expand on analogous plug-in dominance results
for spherically symmetric distributions with $p \geq 4$ under $L_1$ loss.
label: human

text:
We consider the role of quantum effects in the transfer of hyrogen-like
species in enzyme-catalysed reactions. This study is stimulated by claims that
the observed magnitude and temperature dependence of kinetic isotope effects
imply that quantum tunneling below the energy barrier associated with the
transition state significantly enhances the reaction rate in many enzymes. We
use a path integral approach which provides a general framework to understand
tunneling in a quantum system which interacts with an environment at non-zero
temperature. Here the quantum system is the active site of the enzyme and the
environment is the surrounding protein and water. Tunneling well below the
barrier only occurs for temperatures less than a temperature $T_0$ which is
determined by the curvature of potential energy surface near the top of the
barrier. We argue that for most enzymes this temperature is less than room
temperature. For physically reasonable parameters quantum transition state
theory gives a quantitative description of the temperature dependence and
magnitude of kinetic isotope effects for two classes of enzymes which have been
claimed to exhibit signatures of quantum tunneling. The only quantum effects
are those associated with the transition state, both reflection at the barrier
top and tunneling just below the barrier. We establish that the friction due to
the environment is weak and only slightly modifies the reaction rate.
Furthermore, at room temperature and for typical energy barriers environmental
degrees of freedom with frequencies much less than 1000 cm$^{-1}$ do not have a
significant effect on quantum corrections to the reaction rate.
label: human

text:
We report new CHARA/MIRC interferometric observations of the Cepheid
archetype $\delta$ Cep, which aimed at detecting the newly discovered
spectroscopic companion. We reached a maximum dynamic range $\Delta H $ = 6.4,
5.8, and 5.2 mag, respectively within the relative distance to the Cepheid $r <
25$ mas, $25 < r < 50$ mas and $50 < r < 100$ mas. Our observations did not
show strong evidence of a companion. We have a marginal detection at $3\sigma$
with a flux ratio of 0.21\%, but nothing convincing as we found other possible
probable locations. We ruled out the presence of companion with a spectral type
earlier than F0V, A1V and B9V, respectively for the previously cited ranges
$r$. From our estimated sensitivity limits and the Cepheid light curve, we
derived lower-limit magnitudes in the $H$ band for this possible companion to
be $H_\mathrm{comp} > 9.15, 8.31$ and 7.77 mag, respectively for $r < 25$ mas,
$25 < r < 50$ mas and $50 < r < 100$ mas. We also found that to be consistent
with the predicted orbital period, the companion has to be located at a
projected separation $< 24$ mas with a spectral type later than a F0V star.
label: human

text: This research paper explores the concept of cycling operations within braid groups, focusing on their algebraic properties and implications. Braid groups are fundamental in various mathematical fields including topology and geometric group theory. The primary objective is to investigate how cycling operations can be utilized to understand the structure and dynamics of braids more deeply.  Methodologically, the study employs theoretical analysis and computational methods. A series of experiments were conducted using software designed for group theory computations to explore the effects of cycling operations on different configurations of braids. Key findings include insights into the stability and variability of braid structures under cycling transformations, as well as the identification of invariant properties that remain consistent across various operations.  The results reveal that cycling operations can significantly alter the complexity of braid configurations but also maintain certain structural characteristics. These findings contribute to a better understanding of the underlying algebraic principles governing braid behavior and provide new tools for analyzing and classifying braids.  In conclusion, this research underscores the importance of cycling operations in the study of braid groups, offering valuable contributions to both theoretical and applied aspects of these mathematical structures.
label: machine

text: This study investigates the role of carbon dioxide in the cooling of terrestrial planet upper atmospheres, focusing specifically on the Earth's thermosphere. We present a comprehensive analysis of observational data and theoretical models to elucidate how CO₂ influences temperature profiles and dynamics in these regions. Our research identifies the significant contribution of CO₂ to radiative cooling, particularly in the mesopause region, where it acts as a strong infrared absorber. We employ detailed simulations to explore the thermospheric response under varying atmospheric compositions and solar activity conditions. Key findings indicate that changes in CO₂ levels can lead to substantial variations in thermospheric temperatures, which in turn affect atmospheric circulation patterns and the escape rate of neutral species from the atmosphere. The study also highlights the importance of considering greenhouse gases in long-term climate modeling of terrestrial planets, including Earth. Our approach integrates empirical observations with numerical modeling techniques, providing a robust framework for understanding the complex interplay between atmospheric chemistry and thermospheric dynamics.
label: machine

text: This study examines a select sample of strong cool core, highly-luminous galaxy clusters characterized by radiatively-inefficient nuclei. These clusters present unique opportunities to explore the interactions between central supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their surrounding intracluster medium (ICM). The objective of this research is to elucidate the influence of radiatively-inefficient accretion processes on the thermodynamic properties and X-ray emissions of these clusters. Utilizing observations from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA), we conducted a multi-wavelength analysis to assess the correlations between radio emissions associated with relativistic jets and the cooling rates in the core regions. The methodology involved detailed spatial and spectral analysis of X-ray data to derive temperature and density profiles, complemented by radio observations to evaluate the power and extent of radio jets. Key findings reveal a significant suppression of star formation within the strongest cool cores, likely due to feedback mechanisms from the SMBH that regulate cooling flows. Additionally, the power injected by the radio jets appears to offset radiative cooling in the core, maintaining a quasi-stable thermal balance. The results suggest that radiatively-inefficient accretion is a crucial factor in mediating the energy dynamics of these clusters. In conclusion, this investigation enhances our understanding of the complex interplay between SMBHs and their environments, providing insights into the role of AGN feedback in galaxy cluster evolution. Further studies are needed to explore these phenomena across a broader range of cluster environments.
label: machine

text:
The performances of the routing protocols are important since they compute
the primary path between source and destination. In addition, routing protocols
need to detect failure within a short period of time when nodes move to start
updating the routing table in order to find a new primary path to the
destination. Meantime, loss of packets and end-to- end delays will increase
thereby reducing throughput and degrading the performance of the network. This
paper proposes a new algorithm, DBRT (Driven Backup Routing Table), to improve
the existing proactive protocols such as DSDV (Destination Sequenced Distance
Vector) protocol by creating a backup routing table to provide multiple
alternative routes. The DBRT algorithm identifies adjacent nodes for each node
in the same range and then selects one of these as a backup next hop according
to the available path to the destination. The results show that loss of data
packets, throughput and end-to-end delay times between source and destination
are improved. The results show that the new protocol does not degrade the
network's performance despite sending extra messages to construct and update
the new backup routing table. Simulations (using an NS2 simulator) are
undertaken to demonstrate the difference between using a DSDV protocol with or
without the proposed schema.
label: human

text:
Given large amount of real photos for training, Convolutional neural network
shows excellent performance on object recognition tasks. However, the process
of collecting data is so tedious and the background are also limited which
makes it hard to establish a perfect database. In this paper, our generative
model trained with synthetic images rendered from 3D models reduces the
workload of data collection and limitation of conditions. Our structure is
composed of two sub-networks: semantic foreground object reconstruction network
based on Bayesian inference and classification network based on multi-triplet
cost function for avoiding over-fitting problem on monotone surface and fully
utilizing pose information by establishing sphere-like distribution of
descriptors in each category which is helpful for recognition on regular photos
according to poses, lighting condition, background and category information of
rendered images. Firstly, our conjugate structure called generative model with
metric learning utilizing additional foreground object channels generated from
Bayesian rendering as the joint of two sub-networks. Multi-triplet cost
function based on poses for object recognition are used for metric learning
which makes it possible training a category classifier purely based on
synthetic data. Secondly, we design a coordinate training strategy with the
help of adaptive noises acting as corruption on input images to help both
sub-networks benefit from each other and avoid inharmonious parameter tuning
due to different convergence speed of two sub-networks. Our structure achieves
the state of the art accuracy of over 50\% on ShapeNet database with data
migration obstacle from synthetic images to real photos. This pipeline makes it
applicable to do recognition on real images only based on 3D models.
label: human

text: The universe's reionization, a period of approximately 500 million years following the Big Bang, marked the transition from a neutral to an ionized intergalactic medium. During this epoch, the first galaxies began to emit ionizing radiation, shaping the cosmic landscape. CIV, a double-ionized carbon ion, is a key spectroscopic marker of this era. This study presents the spectroscopic detection of CIV in a galaxy at z=7.045, providing unprecedented insights into the ionizing spectra of reionization-era galaxies.  Our research focused on a galaxy located in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, observed using the Hubble Space Telescope and the Keck Observatory. We employed a combination of spectroscopic and photometric analyses to detect the faint CIV signal. Our findings confirm the presence of CIV in the galaxy, with a measured redshift of 7.045 ± 0.005. This detection has significant implications for our understanding of the ionizing spectra of reionization-era galaxies, as it suggests that these galaxies were capable of producing a substantial amount of ionizing radiation.  The implications of our results are twofold. Firstly, the detection of CIV in a galaxy at z=7.045 provides strong evidence for the reionization of the intergalactic medium by these galaxies. Secondly, our findings suggest that the ionizing spectra of reionization-era galaxies were more complex and varied than previously thought, with some galaxies capable of producing a significant amount of ionizing radiation. These results have far-reaching implications for our understanding of the early universe and the formation of the first galaxies.
label: machine

text:
Ion energy distributions have been determined at the rf-bias electrode in an
inductively-coupled acetylene-argon plasma for various substrate bias voltages
and frequencies under conditions suitable for film deposition. These are
compared with those obtained at the grounded wall of a capacitively coupled
plasma. In the former, for pressures up to 25 mTorr, the IEDs exhibit bimodal
structures with peak separation values that follow the expected dependence on
voltage and frequency. At higher pressures, 120 mTorr, the bimodal structure is
replaced by a single peak. For all conditions, the dominant ion is Ar+ or ArH+
despite a set C2H2:Ar flow ratio of 2:1, and this can be attributed to the high
electron dissociation of the parent molecule. Diamond-like carbon films
indicate a peak hardness at an ion energy of around 90 eV and a very sharp fall
in hardness is noted beyond this value. This is similar to the observed
bombardment energy relationship for sp3 bond formation in hydrogen-free
tetragonal amorphous carbon or bias-sputtered films. However, due to the lack
of carbon-based ions, an alternative film growth mechanism must be considered,
possibly based on argon knock-on implantation of surface adsorbed carbon
species. The results have shown that the use of high frequency bias or bias
harmonics may lead to much narrower ion energy distributions.
label: human

text:
Pyrochlore oxides show several fascinating phenomena, such as the formation
of heavy fermions and the thermal Hall effect. Although a key to understanding
some phenomena may be the Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya (DM) interaction, its
microscopic origin is unclear. To clarify the microscopic origin, we
constructed a $t_{2g}$-orbital model with the kinetic energy, the
trigonal-distortion potential, the multiorbital Hubbard interactions, and the
$LS$ coupling, and derived the low-energy effective Hamiltonian for a $d^{1}$
Mott insulator with the weak $LS$ coupling. We first show that lack of the
inversion center of each nearest-neighbor V-V bond causes the odd-mirror
interorbital hopping integrals. Those are qualitatively different from the
even-mirror hopping integrals, existing even with the inversion center. We next
show that the second-order perturbation using the kinetic terms leads to the
ferromagnetic and the antiferromagnetic super exchange interactions. Then, we
show the most important result: the third-order perturbation terms using the
combination of the even-mirror hopping integral, the odd-mirror hopping
integral, and the $LS$ coupling causes the DM interaction due to the
mirror-mixing effect, where those hopping integrals are necessary to obtain the
antisymmetric kinetic exchange and the $LS$ coupling is necessary to excite the
orbital angular momentum at one of two sites. We also show that the magnitude
and sign of the DM interaction can be controlled by changing the positions of
the O ions and the strength of the Hubbard interactions. We discuss the
advantages in comparison with the phenomenological theory and Moriya's
microscopic theory, applicability of our mechanism, and the similarities and
differences between our case and the strong-$LS$-coupling case.
label: human

text: We conducted a comprehensive analysis of tools used in online tutorials to evaluate their effectiveness in facilitating engaging and interactive learning experiences. Our investigation focused on comparing the performance of various capture devices, tutorial representations, and access devices in enhancing user engagement, understanding, and retention of complex information.   Through a mixed-methods approach, combining both quantitative and qualitative data, we examined the capabilities of 15 different capture devices, including webcams, microphones, and screen recording software, to capture high-quality video and audio content. Our results indicate that the use of 4K resolution, high frame rates, and noise-reduction algorithms significantly improves the overall quality of captured content.   Furthermore, we evaluated the efficacy of six different tutorial representations, including text-based, image-based, and interactive simulations, in conveying complex information to learners. Our findings suggest that interactive simulations and gamification elements can enhance learner engagement and motivation, while text-based tutorials remain effective for conveying straightforward information.   Additionally, we assessed the impact of three different access devices, including desktop computers, laptops, and mobile devices, on learner engagement and performance. Our results indicate that the use of mobile devices can facilitate more flexible and accessible learning, while desktop computers and laptops offer greater processing power and storage capacity.   Our study provides valuable insights into the design and implementation of effective online tutorials, highlighting the importance of selecting the right capture device, tutorial representation, and access device to suit the specific learning needs of the target audience.
label: machine

text: Classification algorithms are a pivotal aspect of machine learning, extensively utilized in diverse fields for predictive analysis and decision-making. This study explores the implementation of adaptive partitioning to enhance classification accuracy and efficiency. The objective is to evaluate the performance of adaptive partitioning compared to traditional static partitioning methods in classification tasks. We employ an experimental methodology, applying adaptive partitioning techniques within popular classification algorithms such as Decision Trees, Random Forests, and Support Vector Machines. Datasets from various domains, including healthcare, finance, and agriculture, are used to assess the reliability and generalizability of the proposed approach. Our key findings demonstrate that adaptive partitioning significantly improves classification accuracy by dynamically adjusting the decision boundaries according to the data distribution. The results indicate a marked reduction in computational cost and time, making it feasible for real-time applications. Furthermore, adaptive partitioning exhibits enhanced capability in handling imbalanced datasets, leading to a notable increase in sensitivity and specificity metrics. The study concludes that adaptive partitioning not only augments the performance of classification algorithms but also extends their applicability to complex, dynamic environments. This approach is particularly advantageous in scenarios requiring real-time analysis and those involving large-scale data. Future work could explore the integration of adaptive partitioning with ensemble learning techniques to further optimize predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. This research contributes to the advancement of machine learning by providing a more adaptive and responsive framework for classification tasks.
label: machine

text: In this study, we explore various dynamic coupling mechanisms within glassy colloidal mixtures, aiming to understand the underlying dynamics that govern their rheological behavior. We employ a combination of computer simulations and theoretical analysis to investigate how different types of interactions between particles affect the system's viscosity and relaxation times. Our results indicate that short-range repulsive forces significantly enhance the dynamic coupling among particles, leading to higher viscosities and slower relaxation processes compared to systems with longer-range attractive interactions. We also observe that the presence of a small fraction of hard-sphere particles introduces additional dynamical heterogeneity, affecting the overall flow properties. Key methodologies include molecular dynamics simulations and mean-field approximations to model collective particle motion and effective pair potentials. These findings contribute to our understanding of complex fluid dynamics in soft condensed matter systems and have implications for the design of materials with tailored rheological properties.
label: machine

text: We present the photonic band-gap (PBG) transmission characteristics of graphene embedded in a defective optical waveguide structure. By employing finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations, we investigate the effect of a deliberate air bubble defect on the optical properties of a 2D monolayer graphene sheet incorporated into a silicon photonic crystal (Si-PhC) waveguide. The obtained results demonstrate the appearance of PBGs within the near-infrared spectral range for the investigated structure, arising from the interplay between the graphene electronic properties and the crystalline lattice of the Si-PhC. We investigate the influence of Fermi energy, defect size, and position on the PBG bandwidth and transmission characteristics. The observed PBGs exhibit significant shifts and narrowing with increasing Fermi energy, suggesting a potential application in tunable optical devices. We also explore the sensitivity of the graphene PBG bandwidth to external electric fields, which could be useful in developing highly-sensitive optical biosensors or switches. The proposed defective Si-PhC waveguide system offers a promising platform for the study and manipulation of graphene's optical properties, providing insights into the design of efficient and tunable photonic devices based on graphene.
label: machine

text:
Photonic technologies offer numerous advantages for astronomical instruments
such as spectrographs and interferometers owing to their small footprints and
diverse range of functionalities. Operating at the diffraction-limit, it is
notoriously difficult to efficiently couple such devices directly with large
telescopes. We demonstrate that with careful control of both the non-ideal
pupil geometry of a telescope and residual wavefront errors, efficient coupling
with single-mode devices can indeed be realised. A fibre injection was built
within the Subaru Coronagraphic Extreme Adaptive Optics (SCExAO) instrument.
Light was coupled into a single-mode fibre operating in the near-IR (J-H bands)
which was downstream of the extreme adaptive optics system and the pupil
apodising optics. A coupling efficiency of 86% of the theoretical maximum limit
was achieved at 1550 nm for a diffraction-limited beam in the laboratory, and
was linearly correlated with Strehl ratio. The coupling efficiency was constant
to within <30% in the range 1250-1600 nm. Preliminary on-sky data with a Strehl
ratio of 60% in the H-band produced a coupling efficiency into a single-mode
fibre of ~50%, consistent with expectations. The coupling was >40% for 84% of
the time and >50% for 41% of the time. The laboratory results allow us to
forecast that extreme adaptive optics levels of correction (Strehl ratio >90%
in H-band) would allow coupling of >67% (of the order of coupling to multimode
fibres currently). For Strehl ratios <20%, few-port photonic lanterns become a
superior choice but the signal-to-noise must be considered. These results
illustrate a clear path to efficient on-sky coupling into a single-mode fibre,
which could be used to realise modal-noise-free radial velocity machines,
very-long-baseline optical/near-IR interferometers and/or simply exploit
photonic technologies in future instrument design.

text:
Identified as extinction features against the bright Galactic mid-infrared
background, infrared dark clouds (IRDCs) are thought to harbor the very
earliest stages of star and cluster formation. In order to better characterize
the properties of their embedded cores, we have obtained new 24um, 60-100um,
and sub-millimeter continuum data toward a sample of 38 IRDCs. The 24um Spitzer
images reveal that while the IRDCs remain dark, many of the cores are
associated with bright 24um emission sources, which suggests that they contain
one or more embedded protostars. Combining the 24um, 60-100um, and
sub-millimeter continuum data, we have constructed broadband spectral energy
distributions (SEDs) for 157 of the cores within these IRDCs and, using simple
gray-body fits to the SEDs, have estimated their dust temperatures,
emissivities, opacities, bolometric luminosities, masses and densities. Based
on their Spitzer/IRAC 3-8um colors and the presence of 24um point source
emission, we have separated cores that harbor active, high-mass star formation
from cores that are quiescent. The active `protostellar' cores typically have
warmer dust temperatures and higher bolometric luminosities than the more
quiescent, perhaps `pre-protostellar', cores. Because the mass distributions of
the populations are similar, however, we speculate that the active and
quiescent cores may represent different evolutionary stages of the same
underlying population of cores. Although we cannot rule out low-mass
star-formation in the quiescent cores, the most massive of them are excellent
candidates for the `high-mass starless core' phase, the very earliest in the
formation of a high-mass star.

text: This research explores the application of Generalized Approximate Message Passing (GAMP) for the estimation of signals from random linear mixing models. The study aims to improve the performance and robustness of signal recovery algorithms, particularly in scenarios where the mixing matrix is unknown or has a random structure.   The primary objective is to develop an efficient and accurate method for estimating signals that have been convoluted by a random linear transformation. To achieve this, the methodology involves formulating the problem within the GAMP framework, which allows for iterative updates to the posterior distribution of the signal under the assumption of Gaussian noise.  Key findings include the derivation of closed-form expressions for the GAMP updates under various signal and noise conditions, as well as empirical results demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional methods such as Expectation-Maximization (EM). The analysis shows that GAMP can effectively handle high-dimensional signals and sparse mixing matrices, achieving faster convergence rates and lower error rates.  In conclusion, the research underscores the potential of GAMP for enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of signal recovery in random linear mixing models. The proposed approach not only provides a theoretical foundation but also practical algorithms that can be applied to real-world problems involving compressed sensing and blind deconvolution.

text: This study investigates the various types of gaseous envelopes found around "Hot Jupiter" exoplanets in order to understand their characteristics and formation mechanisms. By analyzing a sample of Hot Jupiter exoplanets using data from telescopes such as Hubble and Spitzer, we have identified multiple categories of gaseous envelopes based on their composition and morphology. Our results reveal that these envelopes can range from dense and compact to extended and diffuse, with variations in temperature, density, and chemical composition.   The primary objective of this research is to elucidate the underlying factors contributing to the diversity in gaseous envelopes observed in Hot Jupiter exoplanets. By studying the connections between stellar irradiation, atmospheric escape processes, and planetary composition, we aim to provide insights into the formation and evolution of these envelopes.   Our methodology involves analyzing transmission spectra, emission spectra, and phase curves of Hot Jupiter exoplanets to characterize their gaseous envelopes. We employ spectral retrieval techniques and atmospheric modeling to constrain the properties of these envelopes and investigate their relationship to planetary parameters.   Overall, our findings contribute to a better understanding of the atmospheres of Hot Jupiter exoplanets and shed light on the complex interplay between planetary characteristics and gaseous envelope formation.

text: Our study delves into the intricate relationship between dark matter balls and the mechanism behind supernova explosions. By employing sophisticated simulations, we aimed to investigate the plausible role of dark matter balls in facilitating supernovae to explode. Our findings reveal that the presence of dark matter balls within the cores of massive stars can significantly impact the internal dynamics of these stars during their final stages of evolution. Through our simulations, we demonstrated that the gravitational interactions between dark matter balls and the stellar core can lead to enhanced energy transfer, potentially triggering a more efficient explosion process during a supernova event.  The primary problem addressed in this work is the longstanding mystery surrounding the exact trigger mechanisms that drive supernovae explosions. By considering the influence of dark matter balls, our research offers a novel perspective on this issue, shedding light on a previously overlooked aspect of stellar evolution and explosion dynamics.   Our methodology involved numerical simulations that integrated the effects of dark matter balls with the existing models of supernova mechanisms. This approach allowed us to observe how the presence of dark matter balls influenced the behavior of collapsing stars and the subsequent explosion dynamics. The results of our study provide valuable insights into the interconnected relationship between dark matter and stellar phenomena, offering a fresh understanding of the processes governing supernovae explosions.

text:
Water is perhaps the most simulated liquid. Recently three water models have
been developed following the adaptive force matching (AFM) method that provides
excellent predictions of water properties with only electronic structure
information as a reference. Compared to many other electronic structure based
force fields that rely on fairly sophisticated energy expressions, the AFM
water models use point-charge based energy expressions that are supported by
most popular molecular dynamics packages. An outstanding question regarding
simple force fields is whether such force fields provide reasonable
transferability outside of their conditions of parameterization. A survey of
three AFM water models, B3LYPD-4F, BLYPSP-4F, and WAIL are provided for
simulations under conditions ranging from the melting point up to the critical
point. By including ice-Ih configurations in the training set, the WAIL
potential predicts the melting temperate, TM, of ice-Ih correctly. Without
training for ice, BLYPSP-4F underestimates TM by about 15 K. Interestingly, the
B3LYPD-4F model gives a TM 14 K too high. The overestimation of TM by B3LYPD-4F
mostly likely reflects a deficiency of the B3LYP reference. The BLYPSP-4F model
gives the best estimate of the boiling temperature TB and is arguably the best
potential for simulating water in the temperature range from TM to TB. None of
the three AFM potentials provides a good description of the critical point.
Although the B3LYPD-4F model gives the correct critical temperature TC and
critical density, there are good reasons to believe the agreement is reached
fortuitously. Links to Gromacs input files for the three water models are
provided at the end of the paper.

text: Hyperbolic conservation laws on spacetimes represent a fundamental aspect of mathematical physics, particularly in the context of describing dynamic systems in relativity. This study aims to develop a robust finite volume scheme utilizing differential forms to effectively approximate solutions to hyperbolic conservation laws in curved spacetimes. The methodology leverages the geometric structure of spacetime, integrating concepts from differential geometry to ensure conserved quantities are computed accurately across arbitrary mesh partitions. We establish a framework that combines a stable discretization with a flexible cell-averaging process, allowing for the preservation of local conservation laws. Key findings reveal that our proposed scheme achieves optimal convergence rates, as demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments on test cases that include shock waves and rarefaction phenomena on curved geometries. We further investigate the scheme's performance in handling complex boundary conditions and its resilience against variations in grid topology. Our results indicate that utilizing differential forms not only enhances formulation elegance but also significantly improves computational efficiency compared to traditional methods. In conclusion, the finite volume scheme based on differential forms provides a powerful tool for solving hyperbolic conservation laws in spacetimes, contributing to both theoretical understanding and practical applications in computational fluid dynamics and general relativity. Future work will extend this approach to nonlinear problems and higher-dimensional spacetimes, further enriching the toolkit available for researchers in the field.

text:
Nanostructured semiconductors emit light from electronic states known as
excitons[1]. According to Hund's rules[2], the lowest energy exciton in organic
materials should be a poorly emitting triplet state. Analogously, the lowest
exciton level in all known inorganic semiconductors is believed to be optically
inactive. These 'dark' excitons (into which the system can relax) hinder
light-emitting devices based on semiconductor nanostructures. While strategies
to diminish their influence have been developed[3-5], no materials have been
identified in which the lowest exciton is bright. Here we show that the lowest
exciton in quasi-cubic lead halide perovskites is optically active. We first
use the effective-mass model and group theory to explore this possibility,
which can occur when the strong spin-orbit coupling in the perovskite
conduction band is combined with the Rashba effect [6-10]. We then apply our
model to CsPbX3 (X=Cl,Br,I) nanocrystals[11], for which we measure size- and
composition-dependent fluorescence at the single-nanocrystal level. The bright
character of the lowest exciton immediately explains the anomalous
photon-emission rates of these materials, which emit 20 and 1,000 times
faster[12] than any other semiconductor nanocrystal at room[13-16] and
cryogenic[17] temperatures, respectively. The bright exciton is further
confirmed by detailed analysis of the fine structure in low-temperature
fluorescence spectra. For semiconductor nanocrystals[18], which are already
used in lighting[19,20], lasers[21,22], and displays[23], these optically
active excitons can lead to materials with brighter emission and enhanced
absorption. More generally, our results provide criteria for identifying other
semiconductors exhibiting bright excitons with potentially broad implications
for optoelectronic devices.

text: The High Energy Stereoscopic System (HESS) J1702-420 is an unidentified very high energy (VHE) gamma-ray source located in the Galactic plane. This source exhibits a significant emission above 100 GeV with a total integrated flux of (1.6±0.2)×10^-12 cm^-2 s^-1. To better understand the nature of this source, we have analyzed its X-ray emission using data obtained from the Suzaku satellite. In this study, we focus on the X-ray spectral and temporal properties of HESS J1702-420, and we compare them with those of other known VHE gamma-ray sources.  Our analysis revealed that HESS J1702-420 exhibits a complex X-ray emission, which can be modeled by a power-law component with a photon index of Γ ≈ 2.2 and an absorbed blackbody component. The power-law component dominates the X-ray spectrum above 10 keV, and its flux varies on a timescale of hours. The blackbody component, on the other hand, is detected only below 3 keV and is likely to be associated with the non-thermal emission process.  We also compare the X-ray emission of HESS J1702-420 with that of other known VHE gamma-ray sources and find some similarities and differences. In particular, we note that the X-ray spectra of HESS J1702-420 and other sources show similar power-law components but differ in their blackbody components, suggesting that the emission mechanisms of these sources may vary.  In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the nature of HESS J1702-420 by analyzing its X-ray emission using Suzaku data. Our results reveal a complex emission scenario, with both power-law and blackbody components, and shed light on the possible emission mechanisms of this unidentified VHE gamma-ray source. Future studies will be required to confirm our findings and to identify the origin of the X-ray emission, which could be either the TeV emission region or a separate population of particles.

We present results from daily radio continuum observations of the Bootes
field as part of the Pi GHz Sky Survey (PiGSS). These results are part of a
systematic and unbiased campaign to characterize variable and transient sources
in the radio sky. The observations include 78 individual epochs distributed
over 5 months at a radio frequency of 3.1 GHz with a median RMS image noise in
each epoch of 2.8 mJy. We produce 5 monthly images with a median RMS of 0.6
mJy. No transient radio sources are detected in the daily or monthly images. At
15 mJy, we set an upper limit (2 sigma) to the surface density of 1-day radio
transients at 0.025 deg^-2. At 5 mJy, we set an upper limit (2\sigma) to the
surface density of 1-month radio transients at 0.18 deg^-2. We also produce
light curves for 425 sources and explore the variability properties of these
sources. Approximately 20% of the sources exhibit some variability on daily and
monthly time scales. The maximum RMS fractional modulations on the 1 day and 1
month time scales for sources brighter than 10 mJy are 2 and 0.5, respectively.
The probability of a daily fluctuation for all sources and all epochs by a
factor of 10 is less than 10^-4. We compare the radio to mid-infrared
variability for sources in the field and find no correlation. Finally, we apply
the statistics of transient and variable populations to constrain models for a
variety of source classes.

text: The Higgs boson, a fundamental particle in the Standard Model of particle physics, plays a significant role in the mechanism of mass generation for other elementary particles. However, the observed mass of the Higgs boson raises questions about the naturalness of the Standard Model. The Lee model, an extension of the Standard Model, provides an alternative explanation for the observed Higgs boson mass and spontaneous CP-violation.  In this paper, we explore the lightness of a Higgs boson and spontaneous CP-violation in the Lee model. We begin by providing a brief overview of the Standard Model and its challenges. We then introduce the Lee model, discussing its main features, including the existence of additional scalar particles and a novel mechanism for generating mass and CP-violation.  To examine the implications of the Lee model, we employ a simplified effective potential approach and analyze the mass spectrum and vacuum solutions. Our calculations reveal that a light Higgs boson with a mass around 115 GeV is a viable solution, while the heavier scalar particles remain hidden from current experiments.  Moreover, we demonstrate that the Lee model can accommodate spontaneous CP-violation, which is an essential ingredient for explaining the matter-antimatter asymmetry observed in the universe. We discuss the potential experimental consequences of this scenario, particularly the possibility of discovering the predicted heavy scalar particles at future collider experiments.  In conclusion, we propose the Lee model as an alternative to the Standard Model for understanding the observed lightness of the Higgs boson and the occurrence of spontaneous CP-violation. Our findings suggest that this model provides a promising framework for exploring new physics beyond the Standard Model and addressing the naturalness issue.

text:
"Portal" models that connect the Standard Model to a Dark Sector allow for a
wide variety of scenarios beyond the simplest WIMP models. Kinetic mixing of
gauge fields in particular has allowed a broad range of new ideas. However, the
models that evade CMB constraints are often non-generic, with new mass scales
and operators to split states and suppress indirect detection signals. Models
with a "portalino", a neutral fermion that marries a linear combination of a
standard model neutrino and dark sector fermion and carries a conserved quantum
number, can be simpler. This is especially interesting for interacting dark
sectors; then the unmarried linear combination which we identify as the
standard model neutrino inherits these interactions too, and provides a new,
effective interaction between the dark sector and the standard model. These
interactions can be simple $Z'$ type interactions or lepton-flavor changing.
Dark matter freezes out into neutrinos, thereby evading CMB constraints, and
conventional direct detection signals are largely absent. The model offers
different signals, however. The "portalino" mechanism itself predicts small
corrections to the standard model neutrino couplings as well as the possibility
of discovering the portalino particle in collider experiments. Possible
cosmological and astroparticle signatures include monochromatic neutrino
signals from annihilation, spectral features in high energy CR neutrinos as
well as conventional signals of additional light species and dark matter
interactions.
label: human

text:
Using the tight binding and Pariser-Parr-Pople (PPP) model Hamiltonians, we
study the electronic structure and optical response of multilayer armchair
graphene nanoribbons (AGNRs), both with and without a gate bias. In particular,
the influence of the number of layers ($n$), and the strength of the electric
field applied perpendicular to layers, for different types of edge alignments,
is explored on their electro-optical properties. As a function of increasing
$n$, the energy gap initially decreases, eventually saturating for large $n$.
The intensity of the linear optical absorption in these systems also increases
with increasing $n$, and depends crucially on the polarization direction of the
incident light, and the type of the edge alignment. This provides an efficient
way of determining the nature of the edge alignment, and $n$, in the
experiments. In the presence of a gate bias, the intensity of optical
absorption behaves in a nontrivial way. The absorption becomes more intense for
the large fields in narrow ribbons exhibiting a red shift of the band gap with
the increasing field strength, while in broad ribbons exhibiting a blue shift,
the absorption becomes weaker. However, for smaller electric fields, the
absorption intensity exhibits more complicated behavior with respect to the
field strength. Thus, the effect of the gate bias on optical absorption
intensity in multilayer AGNRs is in sharp contrast to the bilayer graphene,
which exhibits only enhancement of the absorption intensity with the increasing
electric field.

text:
We present the results of a very deep (500 ks) Chandra observation, along
with tailored numerical simulations, of the nearest, best resolved cluster cold
front in the sky, which lies 90 kpc (19 arcmin) to the north-west of M 87. The
northern part of the front appears the sharpest, with a width smaller than 2.5
kpc (1.5 Coulomb mean free paths; at 99 per cent confidence). Everywhere along
the front, the temperature discontinuity is narrower than 4-8 kpc and the
metallicity gradient is narrower than 6 kpc, indicating that diffusion,
conduction and mixing are suppressed across the interface. Such transport
processes can be naturally suppressed by magnetic fields aligned with the cold
front. Interestingly, comparison to magnetohydrodynamic simulations indicates
that in order to maintain the observed sharp density and temperature
discontinuities, conduction must also be suppressed along the magnetic field
lines. However, the northwestern part of the cold front is observed to have a
non-zero width. While other explanations are possible, the broadening is
consistent with the presence of Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities (KHI) on
length-scales of a few kpc. Based on comparison with simulations, the presence
of KHI would imply that the effective viscosity of the intracluster medium is
suppressed by more than an order of magnitude with respect to the isotropic
Spitzer-like temperature dependent viscosity. Underneath the cold front, we
observe quasi-linear features that are ~10 per cent brighter than the
surrounding gas and are separated by ~15 kpc from each other in projection.
Comparison to tailored numerical simulations suggests that the observed
phenomena may be due to the amplification of magnetic fields by gas sloshing in
wide layers below the cold front, where the magnetic pressure reaches ~5-10 per
cent of the thermal pressure, reducing the gas density between the bright
features.

text: In the realm of group theory, amenability is a critical property that signifies a group's resemblance to compact and locally compact groups. Several mathematical problems revolve around the comparison property of amenable groups. This property relates to the convergence of sequences of random variables indexed by elements of an amenable group.  Our work focuses on the comparison property of two distinct but closely related classes of amenable groups Bernoulli shifts and lattices. We begin by examining Bernoulli shifts, which are probability measure-preserving systems generated by the shifts on finite sequences of symbols. We prove that Bernoulli shifts satisfy the comparison property under weak assumptions on the underlying probability measures.  Subsequently, we turn our attention to lattices in Lie groups. These discrete subgroups of Lie groups possess various favorable mathematical properties. We prove that a wide range of lattices, including those in simple Lie groups, satisfy the comparison property. Our proof employs the well-known Kazdhan property and its connection to the Orlicz inequality.  By establishing the comparison property for these crucial classes of amenable groups, our research enriches the understanding of the underlying structures and their applications in various areas such as random processes, ergodic theory, and quantum mechanics. Moreover, our findings provide valuable insights for future work on the comparison property in broader classes of amenable groups, leading to potential advancements in geometric group theory and related fields.

text: The discovery and confirmation of globular clusters in the Milky Way present significant implications for understanding galactic formation and evolution. This study introduces FSR 1716, a newly confirmed globular cluster, using data from the Vista Variables in the Vía Láctea (VVV) survey. The primary objective was to verify the existence of FSR 1716 through the identification and analysis of RR Lyrae stars, renowned as reliable standard candles in the study of stellar populations. Utilizing photometric data from the VVV survey, we employed a comprehensive analysis to identify RR Lyrae candidates associated with FSR 1716. The spatial distribution and period-luminosity relation of these stars were scrutinized, affirming their membership within the cluster. Notably, the RR Lyrae stars revealed properties consistent with those typically observed in metal-poor and old globular clusters, which further confirmed FSR 1716's nature. Key findings include the precise determination of the cluster's distance modulus, reddening, and metallicity, adding substantial evidence to its status as a globular cluster. The study advances our understanding by highlighting the effectiveness of RR Lyrae stars in confirming new clusters and expanding the census of such clusters within the Milky Way. In conclusion, the identification of FSR 1716 not only contributes to the catalog of Milky Way's globular clusters but also enhances the methodology for detection and analysis using the VVV survey. This discovery underscores the potential for uncovering more hidden clusters, thereby providing a deeper insight into the structure and formation history of our galaxy.

The supertree problem asking for a tree displaying a set of consistent input
trees has been largely considered for the reconstruction of species trees.
Here, we rather explore this framework for the sake of reconstructing a gene
tree from a set of input gene trees on partial data. In this perspective, the
phylogenetic tree for the species containing the genes of interest can be used
to choose among the many possible compatible "supergenetrees", the most natural
criteria being to minimize a reconciliation cost. We develop a variety of
algorithmic solutions for the construction and correction of gene trees using
the supertree framework. A dynamic programming supertree algorithm for
constructing or correcting gene trees, exponential in the number of input
trees, is first developed for the less constrained version of the problem. It
is then adapted to gene trees with nodes labeled as duplication or speciation,
the additional constraint being to preserve the orthology and paralogy
relations between genes. Then, a quadratic time algorithm is developed for
efficiently correcting an initial gene tree while preserving a set of "trusted"
subtrees, as well as the relative phylogenetic distance between them, in both
cases of labeled or unlabeled input trees. By applying these algorithms to the
set of Ensembl gene trees, we show that this new correction framework is
particularly useful to correct weaklysupported duplication nodes. The C++
source code for the algorithms and simulations described in the paper are
available at https://github.com/UdeM-LBIT/SuGeT.

The existence of black holes of masses ~ 10^2-10^5 Msun has important
implications for the formation and evolution of star clusters and supermassive
black holes. One of the strongest candidates to date is the hyperluminous X-ray
source HLX1, possibly located in the S0-a galaxy ESO243-49, but the lack of an
identifiable optical counterpart had hampered its interpretation. Using the
Magellan telescope, we have discovered an unresolved optical source with R =
(23.80 +/- 0.25) mag and V = (24.5 +/- 0.3) mag within HLX1's positional error
circle. This implies an average X-ray/optical flux ratio ~ 500. Taking the same
distance as ESO243-49, we obtain an intrinsic brightness M_R = (-11.0 +/- 0.3)
mag, comparable to that of a massive globular cluster. Alternatively, the
optical source is consistent with a main-sequence M star in the Galactic halo
(for example an M4.4 star at ~ 2.5 kpc). We also examined the properties of
ESO243-49 by combining Swift/UVOT observations with stellar population
modelling. We found that the overall emission is dominated by a ~5 Gyr old
stellar population, but the UV emission at ~2000 Ang is mostly due to ongoing
star-formation at a rate of ~ 0.03 Msun/yr. The UV emission is more intense (at
least a 9-sigma enhancement above the mean) North East of the nucleus, in the
same quadrant as HLX1. With the combined optical and X-ray measurements, we put
constraints on the nature of HLX1. We rule out a foreground star and a
background AGN. Two alternative scenarios are still viable. HLX1 could be an
accreting intermediate-mass black hole in a star cluster, which may itself be
the stripped nucleus of a dwarf galaxy that passed through ESO243-49, an event
which might have caused the current episode of star formation. Or, it could be
a neutron star in the Galactic halo, accreting from an M4-M5 donor star.

text:
The three-dimensional (3D) coordinates of stereoscopically triangulated loops
provide strong constraints for magnetic field models of active regions in the
solar corona. Here we use STEREO/A and B data from some 500 stereoscopically
triangulated loops observed in four active regions (2007 Apr 30, May 9, May 19,
Dec 11), together with SOHO/MDI line-of-sight magnetograms. We measure the
average misalignment angle between the stereoscopic loops and theoretical
magnetic field models, finding a mismatch of $\mu=19^\circ-46^\circ$ for a
potential field model, which is reduced to $\mu=14^\circ-19^\circ$ for a
non-potential field model parameterized by twist parameters. The residual error
is commensurable with stereoscopic measurement errors ($\mu_{SE} \approx
8^\circ-12^\circ$). We developed a potential field code that deconvolves a
line-of-sight magnetogram into three magnetic field components $(B_x, B_y,
B_z)$, as well as a non-potential field forward-fitting code that determines
the full length of twisted loops ($L \approx 50-300$ Mm), the number of twist
turns (median $N_{twist}=0.06$), the nonlinear force-free $\alpha$-parameter
(median $\alpha \approx 4 \times 10^{-11}$ cm$^{-1}$), and the current density
(median $j_z \approx 1500$ Mx cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$). All twisted loops are found
to be far below the critical value for kink instability, and Joule dissipation
of their currents is found be be far below the coronal heating requirement. The
algorithm developed here, based on an analytical solution of nonlinear
force-free fields that is accurate to second order (in the force-free parameter
$\alpha$), represents the first code that enables fast forward-fitting to
photospheric magnetograms and stereoscopically triangulated loops in the solar
corona.

text:
We numerically examine the properties of a two-dimensional system of
particles which have competing long range repulsive and short range attractive
interactions as a function of density and temperature. For increasing density,
there are well defined transitions between a low density clump phase, an
intermediate stripe phase, an anticlump phase, and a high density uniform
phase. To characterize the transitions between these phases we propose several
measures which take into account the different length scales in the system. For
increasing temperature, we find an intermediate phase that is liquid-like on
the short length scale of interparticle spacing but solid-like on the larger
length scale of the clump, stripe, or anticlump pattern. This intermediate
phase persists over the widest temperature range in the stripe state when the
local particle lattice within an individual stripe melts well below the
temperature at which the entire stripe structure breaks down, and is
characterized by intra-stripe diffusion of particles without inter-stripe
diffusion. This is followed at higher temperatures by the onset of inter-stripe
diffusion in an anisotropic diffusion phase, and then by breakup of the stripe
structure. We identify the transitions between these regimes through diffusion,
specific heat, and energy fluctuation measurements, and find that within the
intra-stripe liquid regime, the excess entropy goes into disordering the
particle arrangements within the stripe rather than affecting the stripe
structure itself. The clump and anticlump phases also show multiple
temperature-induced diffusive regimes which are not as pronounced as those of
the stripe phase.
