The precession rate of this disk is notably low, allowing for sustained gas accretion onto the central region without significant disruptions. Our analysis reveals that the precession dynamics are influenced by gravitational interactions with neighboring structures, leading to variations in the accretion rate over time. Key methodologies include high-resolution imaging, spectral line analysis, and detailed modeling of the dynamical environment. The results indicate that the slow precession of the disk significantly contributes to the observed star formation activity in the M31 nucleus, providing insights into the complex processes governing galactic nuclei.

text: The prediction of outcomes using logarithmic distance metrics has garnered considerable attention in various fields, including machine learning, data analysis, and geographic information systems. Using regression analysis and machine learning algorithms, we evaluate the performance of models integrating logarithmic distance against traditional Euclidean metrics. Key findings reveal that models based on logarithmic distance significantly outperform those relying on conventional distance measures, particularly in scenarios involving non-linear relationships and distributions skewed by outliers. Additionally, our results indicate that logarithmic transformation mitigates the effects of noise and enhances the stability of predictions in variable-rich environments. The implications of these findings suggest that incorporating logarithmic distance into predictive modeling frameworks could provide researchers and practitioners with a more robust tool for analysis, potentially leading to more accurate and reliable forecasts. In conclusion, the study highlights the advantages of logarithmic distance in prediction and calls for further research to explore its applications across various domains, ultimately contributing to improved decision-making processes informed by enhanced predictive capabilities.

Hubble Space Telescope observations between 2001 and 2010 resolved the binary
components of the Cold Classical transneptunian object (79360) Sila-Nunam
(provisionally designated 1997 CS29). From these observations we have
determined the circular, retrograde mutual orbit of Nunam relative to Sila with
a period of 12.50995 \pm 0.00036 days and a semimajor axis of 2777 \pm 19 km. A
multi-year season of mutual events, in which the two near-equal brightness
bodies alternate in passing in front of one another as seen from Earth, is in
progress right now, and on 2011 Feb. 1 UT, one such event was observed from two
different telescopes. The mutual event season offers a rich opportunity to
learn much more about this barely-resolvable binary system, potentially
including component sizes, colors, shapes, and albedo patterns. The low
eccentricity of the orbit and a photometric lightcurve that appears to coincide
with the orbital period are consistent with a system that is tidally locked and
synchronized, like the Pluto-Charon system. The orbital period and semimajor
axis imply a system mass of (10.84 \pm 0.22) \times 10^18 kg, which can be
combined with a size estimate based on Spitzer and Herschel thermal infrared
observations to infer an average bulk density of 0.72 +0.37 -0.23 g cm^-3,
comparable to the very low bulk densities estimated for small transneptunian
binaries of other dynamical classes.

text: The Standard Model of particle physics predicts the existence of a single Higgs boson, responsible for endowing fundamental particles with mass. However, the discovery of a single Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has raised questions about the existence of additional Higgs bosons, potentially with different properties. This study aims to search for an additional, heavy Higgs boson in the $H\rightarrow ZZ$ decay channel at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}$ = 8 TeV, utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by the ATLAS detector.  The objective of this analysis is to constrain the existence of an additional Higgs boson, decaying into a pair of Z bosons, which would be a distinct signature from the observed single Higgs boson. The ATLAS detector's large sample of $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 8 TeV provides an ideal environment to search for such a signal. The analysis employs a multivariate technique, combining information from various kinematic and kinematic variables to distinguish between the $H\rightarrow ZZ$ and $H\rightarrow WW$ decay channels.  Key findings of this study indicate that there is no evidence for an additional, heavy Higgs boson in the $H\rightarrow ZZ$ decay channel. The observed signal is consistent with the Standard Model prediction, while the search for an additional Higgs boson is set at a 95% confidence level. These results contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the Higgs boson sector and provide further evidence for the validity of the Standard Model.

text: This paper revisits the Mass-Metallicity Relation (MZR) using the data from the Calar Alto Legacy Integral Field Area (CALIFA) survey. Key findings reveal a clear correlation between stellar mass and metallicity at global scales, consistent with previous studies. However, our spatially resolved analysis uncovers significant variations in metallicity within individual galaxies, indicating diverse chemical enrichment histories. Additionally, we find that the gradient of metallicity with stellar mass differs among galaxies, suggesting varying mechanisms involved in regulating metal enrichment processes.   In conclusion, this study provides a detailed examination of the Mass-Metallicity Relation using CALIFA data, emphasizing the importance of spatially resolved analyses in understanding the complex interplay between stellar mass and metallicity in galaxies. The results contribute to furthering our knowledge of galaxy evolution and the mechanisms governing the chemical enrichment of galaxies.

We consider stochastic semi-linear evolution equations which are driven by
additive, spatially correlated, Wiener noise, and in particular consider
problems of heat equation (analytic semigroup) and damped-driven wave equations
(bounded semigroup) type. We discretize these equations by means of a spectral
Galerkin projection, and we study the approximation of the probability
distribution of the trajectories: test functions are regular, but depend on the
values of the process on the interval $[0,T]$.
  We introduce a new approach in the context of quantative weak error analysis
for discretization of SPDEs. The weak error is formulated using a deterministic
function (It\^o map) of the stochastic convolution found when the nonlinear
term is dropped. The regularity properties of the It\^o map are exploited, and
in particular second-order Taylor expansions employed, to transfer the error
from spectral approximation of the stochastic convolution into the weak error
of interest.
  We prove that the weak rate of convergence is twice the strong rate of
convergence in two situations. First, we assume that the covariance operator
commutes with the generator of the semigroup: the first order term in the weak
error expansion cancels out thanks to an independence property. Second, we
remove the commuting assumption, and extend the previous result, thanks to the
analysis of a new error term depending on a commutator.

We investigate, by means of a field-theory analysis combined with the
density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method, a theoretical model for a
strongly correlated quantum system in one dimension realizing a
topologically-ordered Haldane phase ground state. The model consists of a
spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain coupled to a tight-binding chain via two competing
Kondo exchange couplings of different type: a "s-wave" Kondo coupling
($J^s_{K}$), and a less common "p-wave" ($J^p_{K}$) Kondo coupling. While the
first coupling is the standard Kondo interaction studied in many
condensed-matter systems, the latter has been recently introduced by Alexandrov
and Coleman [Phys. Rev. B 90, 115147 (2014)] as a possible mechanism leading to
a topological Kondo-insulating ground state in one dimension. As a result of
this competition, a topological quantum phase transition (TQPT) occurs in the
system for a critical value of the ratio $J^s_{K}/J^p_{K}$, separating a
(Haldane-type) topological phase from a topologically trivial ground state
where the system can be essentially described as a product of local singlets.
We study and characterize the TQPT by means for the magnetization profile, the
entanglement entropy and the full entanglement spectrum of the ground state.
Our results might be relevant to understand how topologically-ordered phases of
fermions emerge in strongly interacting quantum systems.

text: This study focuses on the detection of supernova neutrinos reaching the Earth's surface, particularly emphasizing the implications of large θ13 values. We explore the theoretical framework that predicts the flux and energy spectrum of these neutrinos, which are crucial for understanding core-collapse supernovae events. Our approach involves simulating supernova environments using astrophysical models and employing state-of-the-art computational techniques to estimate neutrino production rates. We then analyze the expected neutrino signals at the Earth's surface, focusing on how varying θ13 affects the detectability of these particles. The methodology includes Monte Carlo simulations to model neutrino interactions with Earth's matter and the use of statistical analysis to interpret experimental data. Results indicate that significant improvements in detection capabilities can be achieved with larger θ13 values, enhancing our ability to infer properties of distant supernova explosions. This research underscores the importance of ongoing experiments aimed at precisely measuring neutrino parameters, thereby advancing our knowledge of fundamental physics and astrophysics.

text: We investigated the initial stages of nitridation on InP(1 0 0) surfaces using a combination of Auger Electron Spectroscopy (AES), Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy (EELS), and Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (EPES). Our goal was to elucidate the surface chemistry and structural changes that occur during the nitridation process.  Upon exposure to nitrogen gas, the InP(1 0 0) surface underwent a series of surface transformations, resulting in the formation of nitride-rich layers. We observed a significant increase in the AES signal intensity at the surface, indicating the incorporation of nitrogen atoms into the surface lattice. EELS spectroscopy revealed a pronounced peak at the surface, corresponding to the formation of InN and InN2 species. EPES measurements provided evidence of the formation of nitrogen vacancies and the introduction of nitrogen atoms into the surface layer.  Our results indicate that the nitridation process on InP(1 0 0) surfaces is a complex, multi-step process involving the incorporation of nitrogen atoms, the formation of nitride-rich layers, and the creation of surface defects. We propose that the nitridation process is driven by the interaction between nitrogen gas and the InP surface, leading to the formation of a stable nitride-rich layer. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the surface chemistry and structural changes that occur during the nitridation of InP(1 0 0) surfaces.

The stability of Majorana fermions at the edges of a two-dimensional
topological supercondutor is studied, after quenches to either non-topological
phases or other topological phases. Both instantaneous and slow quenches are
considered. In general, the Majorana modes decay and, in the case of
instantaneous quenches, their revival times scale to infinity as the system
size grows. Considering fast quantum quenches within the same topological
phase, leads, in some cases, to robust edge modes. Quenches to a topological
$Z_2$ phase reveal some robustness of the Majorana fermions. Comparing strong
spin-orbit coupling with weak spin-orbit coupling, it is found that the
Majorana fermions are fairly robust, if the pairing is not aligned with the
spin-orbit Rashba coupling. It is also shown that the Chern number remains
invariant after the quench, until the propagation of the mode along the
transverse direction reaches the middle point, beyond which the Chern number
oscillates between increasing values. In some cases, the time average Chern
number seems to converge to the appropriate value, but often the decay is very
slow. The effect of varying the rate of change in slow quenches is also
analysed. It is found that the defect production is non-universal and does not
follow the Kibble-Zurek scaling with the quench rate, as obtained before for
other systems with topological edge states.

A $k$-uniform family of subsets of $[n]$ is intersecting if it does not
contain a disjoint pair of sets. The study of intersecting families is central
to extremal set theory, dating back to the seminal Erd\H{o}s-Ko-Rado theorem of
1961 that bounds the size of the largest such families. A recent trend has been
to investigate the structure of set families with few disjoint pairs. Friedgut
and Regev proved a general removal lemma, showing that when $\gamma n \le k \le
(\tfrac12 - \gamma)n$, a set family with few disjoint pairs can be made
intersecting by removing few sets.
  We provide a simple proof of a removal lemma for large families, showing that
families of size close to $\ell \binom{n-1}{k-1}$ with relatively few disjoint
pairs must be close to a union of $\ell$ stars. Our lemma holds for a wide
range of uniformities; in particular, when $\ell = 1$, the result holds for all
$2 \le k < \frac{n}{2}$ and provides sharp quantitative estimates.
  We use this removal lemma to settle a question of Bollob\'as, Narayanan and
Raigorodskii regarding the independence number of random subgraphs of the
Kneser graph $K(n,k)$. The Erd\H{o}s-Ko-Rado theorem shows $\alpha(K(n,k)) =
\binom{n-1}{k-1}$. For some constant $c > 0$ and $k \le cn$, we determine the
sharp threshold for when this equality holds for random subgraphs of $K(n,k)$,
and provide strong bounds on the critical probability for $k \le \tfrac12
(n-3)$.

text: We investigate the intricate interactions between coherence and entropy in a quantum setting through the lens of a quantum Maxwell demon. Our primary objective is to elucidate how quantum coherence can be harnessed to manipulate and reduce entropy in thermodynamic processes, thus challenging classical interpretations of the second law of thermodynamics. We model the demon's operation as a stochastic process, utilizing quantum measurement and feedback strategies to exchange coherence for entropy improvement in a thermal bath system.   Our results reveal that the presence of quantum coherence enables the demon to perform work efficiently by selecting specific configurations that minimize entropy. We quantify this relationship through the derivation of a trade-off inequality that connects the measures of coherence and entropy, confirming that maximizing quantum coherence does entail an inherent trade-off with system entropy.   Furthermore, we employ a combination of analytical and numerical methodologies, including Markovian dynamics and a coherent state formalism, to simulate the demon's operational mechanics. Our findings demonstrate that under optimal conditions, the quantum Maxwell demon can significantly enhance the work extraction efficiency, underscoring the role of quantum effects in thermodynamic processes. This work not only provides a novel theoretical framework for understanding the potential of quantum systems in energy management but also paves the way for future experimental implementations of quantum thermal machines. Thus, we contribute to the ongoing discourse on the implications of quantum coherence in thermodynamics, presenting compelling evidence for its utility in transforming energy landscapes.

text: Complex organic molecules are fundamental components of the building blocks of life, and their formation in extreme astrophysical environments, such as hot cores, has garnered significant attention in recent years. These regions, characterized by temperatures above 1000 K, are thought to be the sites of chemical reactions that lead to the synthesis of complex molecules, potentially seeding the origins of life. However, the precise mechanisms governing the formation and evolution of these molecules in hot cores remain poorly understood, and further research is necessary to elucidate the underlying chemistry.  This study aimed to investigate the formation and evolution of complex organic molecules in hot cores using high-resolution spectroscopic simulations. By employing advanced computational models, we investigated the chemical reactions that occur in hot cores, with a focus on the formation of complex molecules such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and fullerenes. Our results show that the presence of heavy metals, such as iron and nickel, plays a crucial role in the formation of these molecules, and that the chemical environment of the hot core influences the type and abundance of complex molecules produced.  Our findings suggest that hot cores may be more effective at producing complex organic molecules than previously thought, and that these molecules may be dispersed throughout the interstellar medium, providing a potential source of organic material for planetary formation. These results have significant implications for our understanding of the origins of life and the potential for the delivery of organic material to early Earth.

text: The T Tauri stars, renowned as pre-main sequence stellar systems, exhibit complex and variable ultraviolet (UV) emissions due to their young stellar age and presence of circumstellar disks. In this study, we present a comprehensive far-ultraviolet (FUV, 1150-1650 Angstroms, and NUV, 1650-3000 Angstroms) atlas of low-resolution Hubble Space Telescope (HST) spectra of 123 T Tauri stars, complementing existing optical and near-infrared studies. We utilize the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS) and the Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) to investigate the FUV and NUV spectral ranges, respectively. The spectral features observed include strong UV absorption lines from various atomic and molecular species, such as H I, C II, Si II, Fe II, and Mg II, as well as numerous emission lines. By comparing our atlas to previous studies, we find significant differences in line strengths and equivalent widths, highlighting the importance of FUV data for understanding the evolution of T Tauri stars and their environments. Furthermore, the identification of previously unreported emission lines in the FUV and NUV spectra provides valuable insights into the formation processes of these stars and the circumstellar disks. Our work underlines the significance of HST observations in studying the far-ultraviolet properties of T Tauri stars and contributes to a broader understanding of their physical and evolutionary characteristics.

In this paper, we present a new model of biped locomotion which is composed
of three linear pendulums (one per leg and one for the whole upper body) to
describe stance, swing and torso dynamics. In addition to double support, this
model has different actuation possibilities in the swing hip and stance ankle
which could be widely used to produce different walking gaits. Without the need
for numerical time-integration, closed-form solutions help finding periodic
gaits which could be simply scaled in certain dimensions to modulate the motion
online. Thanks to linearity properties, the proposed model can provide a
computationally fast platform for model predictive controllers to predict the
future and consider meaningful inequality constraints to ensure feasibility of
the motion. Such property is coming from describing dynamics with joint torques
directly and therefore, reflecting hardware limitations more precisely, even in
the very abstract high level template space. The proposed model produces
human-like torque and ground reaction force profiles and thus, compared to
point-mass models, it is more promising for precise control of humanoid robots.
Despite being linear and lacking many other features of human walking like CoM
excursion, knee flexion and ground clearance, we show that the proposed model
can predict one of the main optimality trends in human walking, i.e. nonlinear
speed-frequency relationship. In this paper, we mainly focus on describing the
model and its capabilities, comparing it with human data and calculating
optimal human gait variables. Setting up control problems and advanced
biomechanical analysis still remain for future works.

text: This study investigates the potential of autoencoding techniques to enhance the retrieval of relevant medical images from large databases. The background of medical image retrieval is characterized by the need for accurate and efficient image searching, particularly in high-stakes applications such as cancer diagnosis and treatment planning. Current state-of-the-art methods often rely on hand-crafted features and manual annotation, which can be time-consuming and prone to variability. Autoencoding techniques, inspired by deep learning architectures, offer a promising approach to learning compact representations of medical images that can capture subtle patterns and relationships.  The objective of this research is to develop an autoencoding-based framework for retrieving relevant medical images from large databases, with a focus on improving the accuracy and efficiency of image search. The proposed method utilizes a variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn a compact representation of medical images, which is then used to generate a set of retrieval candidates. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated on a large dataset of medical images, with results showing significant improvements in retrieval accuracy and efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods.  Key findings indicate that the proposed autoencoding-based framework can learn effective representations of medical images that capture subtle patterns and relationships, leading to improved retrieval accuracy and efficiency. The results also demonstrate that the proposed method can be fine-tuned for specific medical applications, such as cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, with improved performance compared to existing methods. Overall, the proposed method offers a promising approach to enhancing the retrieval of relevant medical images from large databases, with potential applications in clinical practice and research.

We explore the ramification of associating the energetics of extreme mag-
netic reconnection events with transient mass loss in a stellar analogy with
solar eruptive events. We establish energy partitions relative to the total
bolometric radiated flare energy for different observed components of stellar
flares, and show that there is rough agreement for these values with solar
flares. We apply an equipartition between the bolometric radiated flare energy
and kinetic energy in an accompanying mass ejection, seen in solar eruptive
events and expected from reconnection. This allows an integrated flare rate in
a particular waveband to be used to estimate the amount of associated transient
mass loss. This approach is supported by a good correspondence between
observational flare signatures on high flaring rate stars and the Sun, which
suggests a common physical origin. If the frequent and extreme flares that
young solar-like stars and low-mass stars experience are accompanied by
transient mass loss in the form of coronal mass ejections, then the cumulative
effect of this mass loss could be large. We find that for young solar-like
stars and active M dwarfs, the total mass lost due to transient magnetic
eruptions could have significant impacts on disk evolution, and thus planet
formation, and also exoplanet habitability.

text: Reed-Muller codes are a class of error-correcting codes that play a crucial role in both theoretical and practical applications within communication systems. Decoding such codes efficiently remains a significant challenge. This research explores syndrome decoding of Reed-Muller codes by leveraging tensor decomposition techniques over finite fields. The primary objective is to enhance the decoding process by employing mathematical tools that reduce computational complexity. The methodology involves representing the codes as multidimensional arrays and applying tensor decomposition to reveal underlying patterns that facilitate syndrome decoding. This approach fundamentally connects the algebraic structure of Reed-Muller codes with modern computational techniques, particularly those related to finite field algebra. Key findings suggest that using tensor decomposition can significantly reduce the time complexity involved in decoding processes while maintaining or enhancing decoding accuracy. This advancement stems from the novel application of tensor algebra in the analysis and manipulation of the code's structural properties, providing new insights into their symmetry and redundancy. The results indicate that using finite fields in conjunction with tensor methods creates a powerful framework that can be adapted for various types of Reed-Muller codes, potentially inspiring further research in the area of error correction. In conclusion, the study demonstrates that the integration of tensor decomposition techniques offers a promising pathway to more efficient decoding of Reed-Muller codes, thus contributing valuable strategies to the field of coding theory. This advancement could pave the way for improved data transmission efficiency in digital communication systems.

text: The region surrounding the galactic mini-starburst W43 is a quintessential site for studying the onset of high-mass star formation, a process pivotal to understanding stellar evolution and galaxy dynamics. Several massive protostars and dense cores with masses exceeding 100 solar masses were identified, marking initial stages of massive star nursery amidst ongoing accretion and collapse. This research underscores the importance of feedback mechanisms and the interplay between different phases of interstellar medium in catalyzing high-mass star formation.  The study concludes that the starburst nature of W43 plays a pivotal role in influencing the initial mass function and the subsequent evolution of high-mass stars. The High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.) is an array of five Imaging
Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes (IACTs) designed to detect cosmogenic
gamma-rays with very high energies. Originally consisting of just four
identical IACTs (CT1-4) with an effective mirror diameter of 12$\,$m each, it
was expanded with a fifth IACT (CT5) with a mirror diameter of 28$\,$m in 2012.
Being the largest IACT worldwide, CT5 allows to lower the energy threshold of
H.E.S.S., making the array sensitive at energies where space-based detectors
run out of statistics. Events can be analysed either monoscopically (i.e. using
only information of CT5) or stereoscopically (requiring at least two triggered
telescopes per event). To achieve a good performance, a sophisticated event
reconstruction and analysis framework is indispensable. This is particularly
important for H.E.S.S. since it is now the first IACT array that consists of
different telescope types. An advanced reconstruction method is based on a
semi-analytical model of electromagnetic particle showers in the atmosphere
(model analysis). The properties of the primary particle are reconstructed by
comparing the image recorded by each triggered telescope with the Cherenkov
emission from the shower model using a log-likelihood maximisation. Due to its
performance, this method has become one of the standard analysis techniques
applied to CT1-4 data. Now it has been modified for use with the five-telescope
array. We present the adapted model analysis and its performance in both
monoscopic and stereoscopic analysis mode.

text: We present a novel methodology for compressing parameters in Bayesian models, specifically applied to logistic sequence prediction models. In addressing the increasingly complex demands of data-driven applications, we aim to alleviate the computational burden associated with high-dimensional parameter spaces while maintaining prediction accuracy. Our approach leverages advanced regularization techniques to identify and eliminate redundant parameters, thereby facilitating a more efficient model that retains sufficient descriptive power. We employed a Bayesian framework that integrates variational inference with parameter sparsity constraints, allowing us to systematically assess the influence of each parameter on model performance.  In our experiments, we implemented this method on multiple datasets characterized by sequential logistic outcomes. We compared the compressed models against traditional Bayesian logistic regression and other state-of-the-art prediction techniques. The results demonstrated a significant reduction in computational time and memory usage, achieving up to a 70% decrease in parameter load without compromising the accuracy of predictions. Moreover, our method exhibited greater generalization capabilities across diverse datasets, highlighting its robustness.  We conclude that our proposed parameter compression technique not only optimally streamlines logistic sequence prediction models but also serves as a foundation for further research in Bayesian model efficiency. This work contributes to the ongoing discourse on the intersection of Bayesian statistics and machine learning, offering a practical solution to parameter overfitting and model complexity in contemporary computational frameworks.

Random walks on expander graphs were thoroughly studied, with the important
motivation that, under some natural conditions, these walks mix quickly and
provide an efficient method of sampling the vertices of a graph. Alon,
Benjamini, Lubetzky and Sodin studied non-backtracking random walks on regular
graphs, and showed that their mixing rate may be up to twice as fast as that of
the simple random walk. As an application, they showed that the maximal number
of visits to a vertex, made by a non-backtracking random walk of length $n$ on
a high-girth $n$-vertex regular expander, is typically $(1+o(1))\frac{\log
n}{\log\log n}$, as in the case of the balls and bins experiment. They further
asked whether one can establish the precise distribution of the visits such a
walk makes.
  In this work, we answer the above question by combining a generalized form of
Brun's sieve with some extensions of the ideas in Alon et al. Let $N_t$ denote
the number of vertices visited precisely $t$ times by a non-backtracking random
walk of length $n$ on a regular $n$-vertex expander of fixed degree and girth
$g$. We prove that if $g=\omega(1)$, then for any fixed $t$, $N_t/n$ is
typically $\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}t!}+o(1)$. Furthermore, if $g=\Omega(\log\log
n)$, then $N_t/n$ is typically $\frac{1+o(1)}{\mathrm{e}t!}$ uniformly on all
$t \leq (1-o(1))\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}$ and 0 for all $t \geq
(1+o(1))\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}$. In particular, we obtain the above result
on the typical maximal number of visits to a single vertex, with an improved
threshold window. The essence of the proof lies in showing that variables
counting the number of visits to a set of sufficiently distant vertices are
asymptotically independent Poisson variables.

Our main result is that the Steiner Point Removal (SPR) problem can always be
solved with polylogarithmic distortion, which answers in the affirmative a
question posed by Chan, Xia, Konjevod, and Richa (2006). Specifically, we prove
that for every edge-weighted graph $G = (V,E,w)$ and a subset of terminals $T
\subseteq V$, there is a graph $G'=(T,E',w')$ that is isomorphic to a minor of
$G$, such that for every two terminals $u,v\in T$, the shortest-path distances
between them in $G$ and in $G'$ satisfy $d_{G,w}(u,v) \le d_{G',w'}(u,v) \le
O(\log^5|T|) \cdot d_{G,w}(u,v)$. Our existence proof actually gives a
randomized polynomial-time algorithm. Our proof features a new variant of
metric decomposition. It is well-known that every $n$-point metric space
$(X,d)$ admits a $\beta$-separating decomposition for $\beta=O(\log n)$, which
roughly means for every desired diameter bound $\Delta>0$ there is a randomized
partitioning of $X$, which satisfies the following separation requirement: for
every $x,y \in X$, the probability they lie in different clusters of the
partition is at most $\beta\,d(x,y)/\Delta$. We introduce an additional
requirement, which is the following tail bound: for every shortest-path $P$ of
length $d(P) \leq \Delta/\beta$, the number of clusters of the partition that
meet the path $P$, denoted $Z_P$, satisfies $\Pr[Z_P > t] \le 2e^{-\Omega(t)}$
for all $t>0$.

text: In this study, we examine the locality of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence in isothermal accretion disks, focusing on the vertical structure and the radial evolution of the turbulent properties. We employ three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations to model the MHD turbulence in the disks, incorporating the effects of magnetic fields and gravitational forces. Our results reveal that the MHD turbulence in isothermal disks exhibits a complex vertical structure, with stronger turbulence occurring near the midplane due to the enhanced magnetic field and gas surface density. The radial profiles of the turbulent properties, including the turbulent dissipation rate and the magnetic energy density, also display notable variations. We find that the turbulent dissipation rate increases with radius, while the magnetic energy density decreases. These findings suggest that the locality of MHD turbulence in isothermal disks is dependent on both the vertical and radial distributions of magnetic fields and gas surface density. Our results contribute significantly to the understanding of MHD turbulence in the context of accretion disks and have implications for the transport of angular momentum and energy within these systems.

text: We present a study on the abrupt phase change of the core rotation in the 143 Sm nucleus. Our work aimed to investigate the sudden alteration in the core rotation behavior of this nucleus, which transitions from a regular to a chaotic state. By utilizing nuclear mean-field theory combined with shell model calculations, we determined the critical angular momentum where this abrupt phase change occurs. Our results reveal that the phase transition is triggered by the interplay between collective rotation and single-particle motion in the nucleus, leading to a drastic shift in the rotational properties of the system. Through detailed analysis of the energy spectra and electromagnetic transition rates, we provide insights into the underlying dynamics governing this phase change. The methodology involved in our research includes the use of nuclear models to understand the intricate behavior of the nuclear core and its response to changing angular momentum. Overall, our findings shed light on the unique phenomenon of abrupt phase changes in nuclear rotation, offering valuable contributions to the understanding of nuclear structure and dynamics in the 143 Sm nucleus.

text: This study explores the nucleon form factors using quenched lattice QCD with domain wall fermions, a numerical approach to simulate the behavior of quarks and gluons in quantum chromodynamics. The nucleon form factor, a measure of the distribution of quarks within the nucleon, is a fundamental quantity in understanding the structure of atomic nuclei. Background research in lattice QCD has shown that the form factor is an essential parameter in determining the properties of hadrons, such as the nucleon.  The objective of this research is to investigate the nucleon form factors using quenched lattice QCD with domain wall fermions, with a focus on improving the accuracy of previous results. The methodology employed involves generating high-quality lattice configurations using a combination of cooling and reweighting techniques to minimize systematic errors. The form factors are then extracted from the lattice data using a combination of numerical and analytical methods.  Key findings indicate significant improvements in the accuracy of the nucleon form factors compared to previous studies. The results show a more precise description of the nucleon structure, with a better agreement between the lattice data and experimental measurements. The study also explores the implications of the form factor results for our understanding of the nucleon's quark distribution and the properties of hadrons. The findings of this research provide valuable insights into the behavior of quarks and gluons in the nucleon, shedding light on the fundamental nature of the strong nuclear force.

We study coherent synchrotron radiation (CSR) in a perfectly conducting
vacuum chamber of rectangular cross section, in a formalism allowing an
arbitrary sequence of bends and straight sections. We apply the paraxial method
in the frequency domain, with a Fourier development in the vertical coordinate
but with no other mode expansions. A line charge source is handled numerically
by a new method that rids the equations of singularities through a change of
dependent variable. The resulting algorithm is fast compared to earlier
methods, works for short bunches with complicated structure, and yields all six
field components at any space-time point. As an example we compute the
tangential magnetic field at the walls. From that one can make a perturbative
treatment of the Poynting flux to estimate the energy deposited in resistive
walls. The calculation was motivated by a design issue for LCLS-II, the
question of how much wall heating from CSR occurs in the last bend of a bunch
compressor and the following straight section. Working with a realistic
longitudinal bunch form of r.m.s. length $10.4~\mu$m and a charge of 100 pC we
conclude that the radiated power is quite small (28 W at a 1 MHz repetition
rate), and all radiated energy is absorbed in the walls within 7 m along the
straight section.

text: Information theoretic caching has emerged as an effective solution for reducing network traffic and improving response times in data-intensive applications. In the context of multi-user systems, information theoretic caching offers further benefits by optimizing the delivery of popular content to a large and diverse user base. This abstract describes the background of information theoretic caching, the objective of extending this technique to multi-user systems, and the methodology used to achieve this goal. Firstly, we review the basics of information theoretic caching, including the cache eviction policy, which is based on minimizing the overall rate of information transfer in the system. We discuss the application of this technique in single-user systems and the resulting improvements in terms of reduced network traffic and improved response times. Secondly, we address the challenges posed by multi-user systems, where the objective is to optimize the delivery of popular content to multiple users. We propose a novel approach based on a multi-user cache replacement policy, which takes into account the popularity of content and the demand for it among different users. We provide a detailed analysis of the performance of this policy, showing that it significantly outperforms traditional cache replacement policies in terms of network traffic reduction and fairness. Finally, we conclude by discussing the potential applications of our approach in various domains, including content delivery networks, mobile networks, and cloud computing. We also highlight some areas for future research, including the integration of our approach with other caching techniques and the consideration of dynamic user behavior.  Information theoretic caching is an effective solution for reducing network traffic and improving response times in data-intensive applications.  This study aims to extend the information theoretic caching technique to multi-user systems and optimize the delivery of popular content to a large and diverse user base.  We propose a novel multi-user cache replacement policy based on minimizing the overall rate of information transfer in the system. Key findings Our approach significantly outperforms traditional cache replacement policies in terms of network traffic reduction and fairness.  The proposed approach has potential applications in various domains and highlights areas for future research.

text: This research paper investigates the diverse stellar haloes present in nearby Milky Way-mass disc galaxies. The objective of the study is to characterize and understand the composition and structure of these stellar haloes. The methodology employed involves analyzing deep imaging data collected from a sample of Milky Way-mass disc galaxies to study the properties of their stellar haloes, including metallicity, age, and spatial distribution. Our key findings reveal a wide variety of stellar halo properties among these galaxies, indicating diverse formation histories and environmental influences. The analysis shows that while some stellar haloes exhibit uniform characteristics consistent with a single accretion event, others display complex structures suggesting multiple accretion events or in-situ formation processes. In conclusion, the presence of diverse stellar haloes in nearby Milky Way-mass disc galaxies implies a rich history of interactions and mergers, highlighting the complex nature of galaxy evolution. Understanding the formation and evolution of these stellar haloes provides valuable insights into the assembly history of disc galaxies and the role of mergers in shaping their present-day structures.

We present the first results from an ongoing survey for multiplicity among
the bright stars using the Navy Precision Optical Interferometer (NPOI). We
first present a summary of NPOI observations of known multiple systems,
including the first detection of the companion of $\beta$ Scuti with precise
relative astrometry, to illustrate the instrument's detection sensitivity for
binaries at magnitude differences $\Delta$$m$ $\lessapprox$ 3 over the range of
angular separation 3 - 860 milliarcseconds (mas). A limiting $\Delta$$m_{700}$
$\sim$ 3.5 is likely for binaries where the component spectral types differ by
less than two. Model fits to these data show good agreement with published
orbits, and we additionally present a new orbit solution for one of these
stars, $\sigma$ Her. We then discuss early results of the survey of bright
stars at $\delta$ $\geq$ -20$\deg$. This survey, which complements previous
surveys of the bright stars by speckle interferometry, initially emphasizes
bright stars of spectral types F0 through K2. We report observations of 41
stars of apparent visual magnitude $m_V$ $\leq$ 4.30, all having been observed
on multiple nights. Analysis of these data produces fitted angular separations,
position angles, and component magnitude differences for six previously known
visual binaries. Three additional systems were examined as possible binaries,
but no conclusive detection could be made. No evidence of close stellar
companions within our detection limit of $\Delta$$m$ $\approx$ 3 was found for
the remaining 32 stars observed; however, uniform-disk angular diameters are
reported for 11 of the resolved stars in this last group.

We test the ability of large scale velocity fields inferred from geomagnetic
secular variation data to produce the global magnetic field of the Earth.Our
kinematic dynamo calculations use quasi-geostrophic (QG) flows inverted from
geomagnetic field models which, as such, incorporate flow structures that are
Earth-like and may be important for the geodynamo.Furthermore, the QG
hypothesis allows straightforward prolongation of the flow from the core
surface to the bulk.As expected from previous studies, we check that a simple
quasi-geostrophic flow is not able to sustain the magnetic field against ohmic
decay.Additional complexity is then introduced in the flow, inspired by the
action of the Lorentz force.Indeed, on centenial time-scales, the Lorentz force
can balance the Coriolis force and strict quasi-geostrophy may not be the best
ansatz.When the columnar flow is modified to account for the action of the
Lorentz force, magnetic field is generated for Elsasser numbers larger than
0.25 and magnetic Reynolds numbers larger than 100.This suggests that our large
scale flow captures the relevant features for the generation of the Earth's
magnetic field and that the invisible small scale flow may not be directly
involved in this process.Near the threshold, the resulting magnetic field is
dominated by an axial dipole, with some reversed flux patches.Time-dependence
is also considered, derived from principal component analysis applied to the
inverted flows.We find that time periods from 120 to 50 years do not affect the
mean growth rate of the kinematic dynamos.Finally we notice the footprint of
the inner-core in the magnetic field generated deep in the bulk of the shell,
although we did not include one in our computations.

Precision radial velocities from Keck/HIRES reveal a Saturn-mass planet
orbiting the nearby M4V star HIP 57050. The planet has a minimum mass of 0.3
Jupiter-mass, an orbital period of 41.4 days, and an orbital eccentricity of
0.31. V-band photometry reveals a clear stellar rotation signature of the host
star with a period of 98 days, well separated from the period of the radial
velocity variations and reinforcing a Keplerian origin for the observed
velocity variations. The orbital period of this planet corresponds to an orbit
in the habitable zone of HIP 57050, with an expected planetary temperature of
approximately 230 K. The star has a metallicity of [Fe/H] = 0.32+/-0.06 dex, of
order twice solar and among the highest metallicity stars in the immediate
solar neighborhood. This newly discovered planet provides further support that
the well-known planet-metallicity correlation for F, G, and K stars also
extends down into the M-dwarf regime. The a priori geometric probability for
transits of this planet is only about 1%. However, the expected eclipse depth
is ~7%, considerably larger than that yet observed for any transiting planet.
Though long on the odds, such a transit is worth pursuing as it would allow for
high quality studies of the atmosphere via transmission spectroscopy with HST.
At the expected planetary effective temperature, the atmosphere may contain
water clouds.

text: In the universe, galaxy interactions play a pivotal role in shaping the large-scale structure and evolution of the cosmos. Binary systems of interacting galaxies offer a unique laboratory to study the complex dynamics of gravitational interactions, leading to a plethora of astrophysical phenomena. This study focuses on the escape dynamics in a binary system of interacting galaxies, exploring the intricate relationships between the gravitational potential, galaxy properties, and the escape of gas and stars.  The objective of this research is to investigate the escape dynamics in a binary system of interacting galaxies, with a particular emphasis on the impact of galaxy interactions on the escape of gas and stars. To achieve this, a numerical simulation framework is employed to model the binary system, incorporating a self-consistent treatment of galaxy interactions, gas dynamics, and stellar evolution.  The numerical simulations reveal that the escape dynamics in a binary system of interacting galaxies is characterized by a complex interplay between the gravitational potential, galaxy properties, and the escape mechanisms. The results indicate that the galaxy interactions lead to the formation of a galactic fountain, where gas and stars are transported between the galaxies, resulting in the enrichment of the intergalactic medium. Furthermore, the simulations suggest that the escape of gas and stars from the galaxies is influenced by the galaxy properties, such as mass, spin, and orbital eccentricity.  The key findings of this study highlight the importance of considering the escape dynamics in binary systems of interacting galaxies, with significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution, gas cycling, and the formation of stars. The results of this research provide a new perspective on the complex interactions between galaxies, shedding light on the intricate mechanisms that govern the escape dynamics in these systems.

In this paper, we investigate predictions of the SO(10) Grand Unified Theory
(GUT), where an extra U(1)$^\prime$ gauge symmetry remains up to the
supersymmetry (SUSY) breaking scale. The minimal setup of SO(10) GUT unifies
quarks and leptons into a ${\bf 16}$-representational field in each
generations. The setup, however, suffers from the realization of the realistic
Yukawa couplings at the electroweak scale. In order to solve this problem, we
introduce ${\bf 10}$-representational matter fields, and then the two kinds of
matter fields mix with each other at the SUSY breaking scale, where the extra
U(1)$^\prime$ gauge symmetry breaks down radiatively. One crucial prediction is
that the Standard Model quarks and leptons are given by the linear combinations
of the fields with two different U(1)$^\prime$ charges. The mixing also depends
on the flavor. Consequently, the U(1)$^\prime$ interaction becomes flavor
violating, and the flavor physics is the smoking-gun signal of our GUT model.
The flavor violating $Z'$ couplings are related to the fermion masses and the
CKM matrix, so that we can derive some explicit predictions in flavor physics.
We especially discuss $K$-$\overline{K}$ mixing, $B_{(s)}$-$\overline{B_{(s)}}$
mixing, and the (semi)leptonic decays of $K$ and $B$ in our model. We also
study the flavor violating $\mu$ and $\tau$ decays and discuss the correlations
among the physical observables in this SO(10) GUT framework.

text: In our study, we investigate the band structure and optical absorption properties of multilayer armchair graphene nanoribbons using a Pariser-Parr-Pople (PPP) model. The problem we address is the need for a thorough understanding of the electronic and optical characteristics of these nanostructures to optimize their potential applications in electronics and photonics. Our results reveal the evolution of the band structure with the number of layers, showing a transition from quantum confinement effects to bulk-like behavior. Additionally, we analyze the optical absorption spectra to identify prominent absorption peaks and their dependence on the ribbon's width and the number of layers. The key ideas of our work involve elucidating the intricate interplay between the structural parameters of multilayer armchair graphene nanoribbons and their electronic and optical properties. To achieve this, we employ the PPP model, a robust theoretical framework widely utilized in studying conjugated polymers and carbon-based nanostructures. Our methodology involves solving the PPP Hamiltonian numerically to calculate the band structure and optical absorption spectra, providing insights into the fundamental physics governing the behavior of multilayer armchair graphene nanoribbons. Overall, our study offers valuable insights for the design and optimization of graphene-based nanoelectronic and optoelectronic devices.

text: We report on our efforts to develop a novel approach for catching the radio flare in the context of CTA 102 using Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) kinematic analysis. Our primary objective was to investigate the variability of the radio flare in CTA 102, a blazar located at a redshift of 0.092, and to determine its kinematic properties.   To achieve this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the VLBI data obtained from the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) project. We applied a combination of techniques, including time-domain and frequency-domain analyses, to extract the kinematic parameters of the radio flare. Our results indicate that the radio flare exhibits a highly variable and dynamic behavior, with a significant variation in its spectral index and polarization properties.  We also found that the kinematic parameters of the radio flare are closely related to the accretion disk properties of the black hole. Our analysis suggests that the radio flare is an intrinsic property of the black hole and is not a result of external factors. Furthermore, we identified a correlation between the kinematic parameters of the radio flare and the jet properties of the blazar.  Our study provides new insights into the kinematic properties of the radio flare in CTA 102 and sheds light on the complex relationships between the accretion disk, jet, and radio flare in blazars. The results of our analysis have significant implications for our understanding of the physics of blazars and the behavior of matter in extreme environments.

This thesis is aimed at clarifying one of the least studied phases of stellar
evolution: the asymptotic giant branch (AGB). Recent results obtained for
Galactic globular clusters (GCs) suggest that the AGB stage may contain crucial
information about the evolutionary history of exotic stars (Beccari et al.
2006) and multiple-populations (Campbell et al. 2013) in the parent cluster.
The thesis presents the analysis of a large sample of high-resolution spectra
of AGB stars in four Galactic GCs, acquired at the Very Large Telescope (ESO)
and the 2.2 meter telescope (MPG). The obtained results provide evidence of a
previously unknown physical mechanism affecting the neutral species of some
chemical elements in the atmosphere of most AGB stars: because of it, the
abundances derived from neutral lines are systematically underestimated, while
those measured from ionized lines remain unaffected. Such a behaviour exactly
corresponds to what expected in the case of non-local thermodynamic equilibrium
(NLTE) conditions in the star atmosphere. For this reason, in this work we
refer to it as "NLTE effect", with the caveat that this could be not the case.
In fact, the current NLTE models are unable to account for the observed effect,
thus demonstrating that either our comprehension of NLTE is not adequate
enough, or that some more complex physical phenomena are occurring in AGB
atmospheres. This effect has been found in all the investigated GCs. It affects
most (but not all) AGB stars and, in some cases, also some RGB stars. It is
particularly evident for iron and titanium lines (i.e., the elements providing
the largest number of both neutral and ionized lines). The deep understanding
of the detected phenomenon is of paramount importance since it has a huge
impact on the proper determination of GC chemistry and enrichment history (for
instance, it can mimic spurious iron spreads).

Using 347.5 fb-1 of data recorded by the BABAR detector at the PEP-II
electron-positron collider, 244*10^3 signal events for the D+ --> K- pi+ e+
nu_e decay channel are analyzed. This decay mode is dominated by the
\bar{K}^*(892)^0 contribution. We determine the \bar{K}^*(892)^0 parameters:
m_{K^*(892)^0}=(895.4 +- 0.2 +- 0.2) MeV/c^{2}, \Gamma^0_{K^*(892)^0}=(46.5 +-
0.3 +- 0.2) MeV/c^{2} and the Blatt-Weisskopf parameter $r_{BW}=2.1 +- 0.5 +-
0.5 (GeV/c)^{-1} where the first uncertainty comes from statistics and the
second from systematic uncertainties. We also measure the parameters defining
the corresponding hadronic form factors at q^{2}=0 (r_{V} = V(0) /
A_{1}(0)=1.463 +- 0.017 +- 0.031, r_{2} = A_{2}(0) / A_{1}(0) = 0.801 +- 0.020
+- 0.020) and the value of the axial-vector pole mass parameterizing the q^2
variation of A_{1} and A_{2}: m_{A}=(2.63 +- 0.10 +- 0.13) GeV/c^{2}. The

pi+ e+ nu_e) = (4.04 +- 0.03 +- 0.04 +- 0.09) \times 10^{-2} where the third

hadronic form factor A_1 at q^{2}=0: A_{1}(0) = 0.6226 +- 0.0056 +- 0.0065 +-
0.0074. Fixing the P-wave parameters we measure the phase of the S-wave for
several values of the Kpi mass. These results confirm those obtained with Kpi
production at small momentum transfer in fixed target experiments.

text: We investigate the challenge of managing Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) refresh overheads, which significantly impede system performance and energy efficiency. Our research focuses on the concept of refresh-access parallelism, where we explore methods to concurrently execute memory accesses while performing refresh operations. We propose a novel architecture that integrates a refresh scheduling algorithm with access requests, allowing for overlapping execution periods. By leveraging typical access patterns and the inherent structure of DRAM cells, we are able to minimize idle time during refresh intervals.  We conducted a series of experiments using a variety of memory-intensive workloads to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach. Our results indicate an average reduction of up to 40% in refresh-induced latency across different configurations, compared to traditional refresh methods. Additionally, we observed a significant decrease in energy consumption, resulting from the reduction in the number of required refresh cycles and the duration of individual refresh operations.  Through our methodology, we synthesized a detailed analysis of both architectural and workload characteristics that contribute to the efficacy of refresh-access parallelism. We demonstrate that optimizing the timing and execution of memory operations during refresh intervals not only addresses performance bottlenecks but also enhances the overall energy efficiency of the system. This work provides a foundational step towards advancing DRAM technology and improving memory system designs, while laying the groundwork for further research into adaptive refresh mechanisms.

text: In this study, we investigate the origins of the thin and thick disc structures observed in the ESO 243-49 galaxy using a monolithic collapse model. The analysis begins by simulating the formation of a single, initially spherical protogalaxy under the influence of gravity and random motions. Through detailed numerical simulations, we explore how angular momentum and mass redistribution lead to the formation of a disk-like structure over time. Our results indicate that the thin disc corresponds to the inner region formed early on, characterized by high velocity dispersion and tight kinematics, while the outer regions develop into the thick disc, marked by lower velocity dispersion and broader kinematic spread. Key insights include the role of initial conditions, such as the concentration of mass towards the center and the distribution of angular momentum, in determining the final structure of the galaxy. The methodology involves a combination of hydrodynamic simulations and analytical models to interpret the observational data from ESO 243-49. This approach not only provides a plausible explanation for the observed disc structure but also offers a framework for understanding similar phenomena in other galaxies.

text: Bivariate Gaussian Markov random fields (GMRF) are essential in various statistical applications, particularly in spatial modeling and image analysis. This study investigates the valid parameter space associated with a bivariate GMRF that utilizes a generalized block-Toeplitz precision matrix. The objective is to delineate the constraints governing the parameterization, ensuring the resulting Markov field maintains its probabilistic validity and adheres to the requirements of the generalized block-Toeplitz structure.   To achieve this, we employ a mathematical framework that characterizes the properties of the precision matrix, analyzing its eigenstructure and associated spatial autocorrelation structures. We derive criteria for the positive definiteness of the block-Toeplitz matrix and elucidate how these criteria translate into implications for the parameters of the bivariate GMRF. Key findings indicate that while the bivariate structure offers increased flexibility over standard univariate models, it also introduces complexity in the parameter relationships. Specifically, we identify a constrained geometric region in parameter space that guarantees the validity of the model while accommodating various correlation structures.  In conclusion, this study outlines the necessary conditions for establishing a valid parameter space for bivariate GMRFs with generalized block-Toeplitz precision matrices. These findings enhance the theoretical understanding of GMRFs and provide a robust framework for future research, facilitating the formulation of models that capture complex dependencies in multivariate contexts.

We explore the possibilities of enforcing and preventing consensus in
continuous opinion dynamics that result from modifications in the communication
rules. We refer to the model of Weisbuch and Deffuant, where $n$ agents adjust
their continuous opinions as a result of random pairwise encounters whenever
their opinions differ not more than a given bound of confidence $\eps$. A high
$\eps$ leads to consensus, while a lower $\eps$ leads to a fragmentation into
several opinion clusters. We drop the random encounter assumption and ask: How
small may $\eps$ be such that consensus is still possible with a certain
communication plan for the entire group? Mathematical analysis shows that
$\eps$ may be significantly smaller than in the random pairwise case. On the
other hand we ask: How large may $\eps$ be such that preventing consensus is
still possible? In answering this question we prove Fortunato's simulation
result that consensus cannot be prevented for $\eps>0.5$ for large groups. %
Next we consider opinion dynamics under different individual strategies and
examine their power to increase the chances of consensus. One result is that
balancing agents increase chances of consensus, especially if the agents are
cautious in adapting their opinions. However, curious agents increase chances
of consensus only if those agents are not cautious in adapting their opinions.

If \(A \) is a set of natural numbers containing \(0 \), then there is a
unique nonempty "reciprocal" set \(B \) of natural numbers (containing \(0 \))
such that every positive integer can be written in the form \(a + b \), where
\(a \in A \) and \(b \in B \), in an even number of ways. Furthermore, the
generating functions for \(A \) and \(B \) over \(\FF_2 \) are reciprocals in
\(\FF_2 [[q]] \). We consider the reciprocal set \(B \) for the set \(A \)
containing \(0 \) and all integers such that \(\sigma(n) \) is odd, where
\(\sigma(n) \) is the sum of all the positive divisors of \(n \). This problem
is motivated by Euler's "Pentagonal Number Theorem", a corollary of which is
that the set of natural numbers \(n \) so that the number \(p(n) \) of
partitions of an integer \(n \) is odd is the reciprocal of the set of
generalized pentagonal numbers (integers of the form \(k(3k\pm1)/2 \), where
\(k \) is a natural number). An old (1967) conjecture of Parkin and Shanks is
that the density of integers \(n \) so that \(p(n) \) is odd (equivalently,
even) is \(1/2 \). Euler also found that \(\sigma(n) \) satisfies an almost
identical recurrence as that given by the Pentagonal Number Theorem, so we hope
to shed light on the Parkin-Shanks conjecture by computing the density of the
reciprocal of the set containing the natural numbers with \(\sigma(n) \) odd
(\(\sigma(0)=1 \) by convention). We conjecture this particular density is
\(1/32 \) and prove that it lies between \(0 \) and \(1/16 \). We finish with a
few surprising connections between certain Beatty sequences and the sequence of
integers \(n \) for which \(\sigma(n) \) is odd.

Shortened abstract: Observations of the nearby Chamaeleon clouds in gamma
rays with the Fermi Large Area Telescope and in thermal dust emission with
Planck and IRAS have been used with the HI and CO radio data to (i) map the gas
column densities in the different phases and at the dark neutral medium (DNM)
transition between the HI-bright and CO-bright media; (ii) constrain the
CO-to-$H_2$ conversion factor, $X_{CO}$; (iii) probe the dust properties per
gas nucleon in each gas phase and spatially across the clouds. We have
separated clouds in velocity in HI and CO emission and modelled the 0.4-100 GeV
intensity, the dust optical depth at 353 GHz, the thermal radiance of the large
grains, and an estimate of the dust extinction empirically corrected for the
starlight intensity, $A_{VQ}$. The gamma-ray emissivity spectra confirm that
the GeV-TeV cosmic rays uniformly permeate all gas phases up to the CO cores.
The dust and cosmic rays reveal large amounts of DNM gas, with comparable
spatial distributions and twice as much mass as in the CO-bright clouds. We
give constraints on the HI-DNM-CO transitions and CO-dark $H_2$ fractions for
separate clouds. The corrected extinction provides the best fit to the total
gas traced by the gamma rays, but we find evidence for a rise in $A_{VQ}/N_H$
and a steep rise in opacity, with increasing $N_H$ and $H_2$ fraction, and with
decreasing dust temperature. We observe less variations for the specific power
of the grains, except for a decline by half in the CO cores. This combined
information suggests grain evolution. The gamma rays and dust radiance yield
consistent $X_{CO}$ estimates near $0.7\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-2}$ (K
km/s)$^{-1}$. The other dust tracers yield biased values because of the grain
opacity rise in the CO clouds. These results also confirm a factor of 2
difference between $X_{CO}$ estimates at pc and kpc scales.

text: In the digital era, the need for secure communication has intensified, leading to the exploration of advanced steganographic techniques. This research investigates the innovative approach of Convolutional Video Steganography (CVS) enhanced with Temporal Residual Modeling (TRM). The primary objective is to develop a robust steganographic framework that efficiently embeds secret messages within video files while minimizing perceptual distortion. To achieve this, we employed a convolutional neural network architecture that leverages TRM to capture temporal dependencies across video frames effectively.   A comprehensive dataset of videos was utilized to train and evaluate the proposed model, emphasizing the balance between data hiding capacity and visual quality. Key findings reveal that the integration of TRM significantly enhances the imperceptibility of hidden data, achieving a remarkable peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM) compared to existing CVS methods. Furthermore, the proposed technique demonstrates resilience against common video processing attacks, such as compression and resizing, thus maintaining data integrity.  In conclusion, the results indicate that the combination of convolutional networks and temporal modeling techniques presents a promising advancement in video steganography, offering an effective solution for secure communication. This research lays the groundwork for future explorations into more sophisticated steganographic applications incorporating deep learning methodologies, paving the way for enhanced security in digital multimedia content.

text: We investigated the asymptotic behavior of pion-pion total cross-sections using a combination of analytical and numerical approaches. Our analysis aimed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the high-energy scattering of pions, with a focus on the role of soft gluon exchange and the emergence of a saturation scale. We employed a chiral Lagrangian framework to model the pion-pion interaction, incorporating both the leading-order (LO) and next-to-leading-order (NLO) contributions to the cross-section.  Our results indicate that the pion-pion total cross-section exhibits a characteristic saturation behavior, characterized by a rapid increase at high energies followed by a plateau. This behavior is consistent with the expectation of a saturation scale, which arises from the interplay between the strong coupling and the soft gluon exchange. We observed that the saturation scale is significantly larger than the typical scale of the pion mass, implying that the saturation regime is accessible at high energies.  Our analysis revealed that the NLO corrections to the cross-section play a crucial role in determining the saturation scale and the overall behavior of the cross-section. We also found that the chiral Lagrangian framework provides a reliable description of the pion-pion interaction at high energies, allowing for a precise determination of the saturation scale. These findings have implications for our understanding of the high-energy behavior of hadronic interactions and the emergence of saturation in the strong coupling.

Herschel-HIFI observations of water in the low-mass star-forming object
L1448-MM, known for its prominent outflow, are presented, as obtained within
the `Water in star-forming regions with Herschel' (WISH) key programme. Six
H2-16O lines are targeted and detected (E_up/k_B ~ 50-250 K), as is CO J= 10-9
(E_up/k_B ~ 305 K), and tentatively H2-18O 110-101 at 548 GHz. All lines show
strong emission in the "bullets" at |v| > 50 km/s from the source velocity, in
addition to a broad, central component and narrow absorption. The bullets are
seen much more prominently in H$_2$O than in CO with respect to the central
component, and show little variation with excitation in H2O profile shape.
Excitation conditions in the bullets derived from CO lines imply a temperature
>150 K and density >10^5 cm^-3, similar to that of the broad component. The
H2O/CO abundance ratio is similar in the "bullets" and the broad component, ~
0.05-1.0, in spite of their different origins in the molecular jet and the
interaction between the outflow and the envelope. The high H2O abundance
indicates that the bullets are H2 rich. The H2O cooling in the "bullets" and
the broad component is similar and higher than the CO cooling in the same
components. These data illustrate the power of Herschel-HIFI to disentangle
different dynamical components in low-mass star-forming objects and determine
their excitation and chemical conditions.

A stellar occultation by a trans-Neptunian object (TNO) provides an
opportunity to probe its size and shape. Very few occultations by TNOs have
been sampled simultaneously from multiple locations, while a robust estimation
of shadow size has been possible for only two objects. We present the first
observation of an occultation by the TNO 2007 UK126 on 15 November 2014,
measured by three observers, one nearly on and two almost symmetrical to the
shadow's centerline. This is the first multi-chord dataset obtained for a
so-called detached object, a TNO subgroup with perihelion distances so large
that the giant planets have likely not perturbed their orbits. We revisit
Herschel/PACS far-infrared data, applying a new reduction method to improve the
accuracy of the measured fluxes. Combining both datasets allows us to
comprehensively characterize 2007 UK126. We use error-in-variable regression to
solve the non-linear problem of propagating timing errors into uncertainties of
the ellipse parameters. Based on the shadow's size and a previously reported
rotation period, we expect a shape of a Maclaurin spheroid and derive a
geometrically plausible size range. To refine our size estimate of 2007 UK126,
we model its thermal emission using a thermophysical model code. We conduct a
parametric study to predict far-infrared fluxes and compare them to the
Herschel/PACS measurements. The favorable geometry of our occultation chords,
combined with minimal dead-time imaging, and precise GPS time measurements,
allow for an accurate estimation of the shadow size (best-fitting ellipse with
axes 645.80 $\pm$ 5.68 km $\times$ 597.81 $\pm$ 12.74 km) and the visual
geometric albedo (15.0 $\pm$ 1.6 %). By combining our analyses of the
occultation and the far-infrared data, we can constrain the effective diameter
of 2007 UK126 to 599 - 629 km. We conclude that subsolar surface temperatures
are $\approx$ 50 - 55 K.

text: This study describes the development of a new radiation magnetohydrodynamics (RMHD) algorithm that solves the time-dependent transfer equation. The motivation for this work arises from the need for accurate simulations of radiation transport in plasma environments, particularly in the context of nuclear fusion and astrophysical applications. The traditional methods for solving RMHD equations, such as the flux-limited diffusion (FLD) and Monte Carlo techniques, face several challenges, including numerical instability, long computational times, and difficulty in handling complex geometries. Our proposed algorithm addresses these issues by employing a second-order implicit time integration scheme to ensure stability, and by discretizing the velocity and angular momenta using the finite volume method, which enables the straightforward handling of complex geometries.    The methodology begins by deriving the full time-dependent transfer equation, which includes the radiative and collisional processes, in the context of the MHD equations. Next, we implement the algorithm in the open-source plasma simulation code EPOCH, and conduct thorough validation tests against both analytical and numerical solutions. These tests confirm the accuracy and robustness of the new algorithm. Additionally, we demonstrate its applicability to astrophysical problems by simulating a supernova shock, revealing that the new algorithm offers a significant reduction in computational time compared to previous RMHD methods. The proposed algorithm offers a promising solution to the challenges of RMHD simulations, paving the way for more accurate and efficient studies in nuclear fusion and astrophysics.    In summary, we have developed a novel algorithm for RMHD simulations that solves the time-dependent transfer equation, enabling accurate and efficient simulations of radiation transport in plasma environments. The methodology addresses the challenges faced by traditional methods, ensuring stability, reducing computational time, and handling complex geometries. The new algorithm has been validated against analytical and numerical solutions and demonstrated its applicability to astrophysical problems, providing a significant advancement in the field of plasma simulations.

text: This study investigates the recurrent frequency-size distribution of characteristic events in complex systems. Using high-resolution data from various sources, including neurophysiological recordings and financial markets, we analyze the occurrence patterns of events with distinct sizes and frequencies. We find that the distribution of event sizes follows a power-law decay, while the frequency distribution exhibits a multi-peaked structure. These findings suggest that the underlying mechanisms generating these events have both stochastic and deterministic components, with critical points leading to large-scale events.  We employ a novel methodology based on wavelet analysis to characterize the temporal structure of these events. By decomposing the data into time-frequency domains, we extract information on the scaling properties and temporal clustering of the events. We demonstrate that the power-law decay of event sizes and multi-peaked frequency distribution can be explained by the presence of self-similarity and long-range temporal correlations.  Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics and mechanisms underlying the recurrence of characteristic events in complex systems. They provide a theoretical foundation for modeling and forecasting these events in various domains, from neuroscience to finance and beyond. The findings also have implications for risk assessment and disaster preparedness, as they indicate that the occurrence of large-scale events is influenced by a complex interplay of temporal and spatial factors.  In conclusion, we present a comprehensive analysis of the recurrent frequency-size distribution of characteristic events in complex systems. Our findings reveal the underlying mechanisms responsible for the distribution of event sizes and frequencies, and demonstrate the utility of wavelet analysis in characterizing the temporal structure of these events. Our work has implications for a wide range of fields and offers a valuable framework for understanding the recurrent dynamics of complex systems.

In recent years, the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) algorithm has been found
to work more efficiently compared to other popular Markov Chain Monte Carlo
(MCMC) methods (such as random walk Metropolis-Hastings) in generating samples
from a posterior distribution. A general framework for HMC based on the use of
graphical processing units (GPUs) is shown to greatly reduce the computing time
needed for Bayesian inference. The most expensive computational tasks in HMC
are the evaluation of the posterior kernel and computing its gradient with
respect to the parameters of interest. One of primary goals of this article to
show that by expressing each of these tasks in terms of simple matrix or
element-wise operations and maintaining persistent objects in GPU memory, the
computational time can be drastically reduced. By using GPU objects to perform
the entire HMC simulation, most of the latency penalties associated with
transferring data from main to GPU memory can be avoided. Thus, the proposed
computational framework is conceptually very simple, but also is general enough
to be applied to most problems that use HMC sampling. For clarity of
exposition, the effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated in the
high-dimensional setting on a standard statistical model - multinomial
regression. Using GPUs, analyses of data sets that were previously intractable
for fully Bayesian approaches due to the prohibitively high computational cost
are now feasible.
