text: We investigate the neutrino-induced one-pion production process, specifically focusing on the channel \(\nu_\mu n \to \mu^- n \pi^+\). Our primary aim is to refine the theoretical framework and computational techniques utilized in modeling this interaction, which has implications for both particle physics and astrophysical observations. We employ a combination of effective field theory and advanced simulation methods to analyze the transition dynamics and kinematic distributions associated with this reaction. Our results reveal significant contributions from both resonant and non-resonant mechanisms, with particular emphasis on the intermediate \(\Delta(1232)\) resonance.   Through a series of detailed calculations, we delineate the dependence of the differential cross-sections on neutrino energy and the angular distribution of the produced particles. We also compare our findings with existing experimental data from neutrino interactions on deuterium, highlighting discrepancies that may suggest the need for revisiting current models. Furthermore, we explore the impact of nuclear effects on the one-pion production rate, demonstrating that consideration of medium modifications leads to a more accurate representation of the data.   Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanics of neutrino interactions with nucleons, reinforcing the importance of one-pion production in neutrino oscillation experiments and cosmic neutrino studies. We posit that the insights garnered from our work can enhance the theoretical predictions, thereby supporting future experimental efforts to investigate neutrino characteristics and their role in the universe.

The quantum theory of measurement has been a matter of debate for over eighty
years. Most of the discussion has focused on theoretical issues with the
consequence that operational prescriptions, which are integral to experimental
physics, have been largely ignored. This has undoubtedly exacerbated attempts
to find a solution to the "measurement problem". In this paper, we fully
embrace the ensemble interpretation of quantum mechanics that obviates the need
to entertain reduction of the state vector, one of the primary dilemmas of the
measurement problem. The other major aspect of the measurement problem, the
necessity of describing measurements in terms of classical concepts, remains.
However, we argue that the ultimate interface with experiments is described by
operational prescriptions and not in terms of the concepts of classical theory.
The pedestrian approach presented here suggests that the measurement problem
is, in some sense, ill-posed and might never be resolved. This state of affairs
is, in part, the result of searching for a theoretical answer to what is
fundamentally an experimental question. This point of view is tenable so long
as one is willing to view physical theories as providing models of nature
rather than complete descriptions of reality. Among other things, these
considerations lead us to suggest that the Copenhagen interpretation's
insistence on the classicality of the measurement apparatus should be replaced
by the requirement that a measurement, which is specified operationally, should
simply be of sufficient precision.

text: The study explores the development and application of advanced multi-scale turbulence modeling techniques, grounded in the maximum information principle. The objective is to enhance the predictive accuracy of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations in complex turbulent flows. This research builds on previous foundational work by integrating the maximum information principle into multi-scale models, which allows for capturing a broader range of turbulent structures and their interactions across different scales. Methodologically, the research employs a combination of theoretical development, numerical simulations, and validation against experimental data. Key innovations include the formulation of new algorithms that better represent energy transfer dynamics within turbulent flows. The model's performance was assessed through a series of benchmark tests, including the simulation of canonical flows and industrial applications such as aerodynamics and hydrodynamics scenarios. Results indicate a significant improvement in the predictive capabilities of the models, showing both increased accuracy in flow predictions and better alignment with empirical observations. These findings suggest that leveraging the maximum information principle in turbulence modeling can bridge existing gaps between theoretical predictions and experimental outcomes, offering a new pathway for achieving higher fidelity in simulations without incurring excessive computational costs. In conclusion, this research contributes to the field by providing a robust framework for multi-scale turbulence analysis, with implications for future research and applications in engineering and environmental fluid dynamics.

text: This study presents an analysis of high-energy transient (HST) and optical data on the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) emitting white dwarf binary system SDSSJ0804+5103, also known as EZ Lyn, one year after its outburst. The outburst of EZ Lyn was a rare and intriguing event that triggered a significant increase in EUV emission from the system, making it an ideal target for studying the physics of dwarf novae.  The objective of this research is to investigate the long-term behavior of EZ Lyn's EUV emission and its relationship with the system's optical variability. We combined data from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the Catalina Sky Survey (CSS) to analyze the EUV and optical light curves of EZ Lyn over a period of one year.  Our results show that the EUV emission from EZ Lyn declined significantly over the first six months after the outburst, followed by a slow increase in EUV luminosity. The optical light curve of EZ Lyn also exhibited a complex pattern of variability, with multiple peaks and dips observed over the study period. We found a correlation between the EUV and optical variability, suggesting that the EUV emission is driven by the accretion of material onto the white dwarf.  The long-term behavior of EZ Lyn's EUV emission and optical variability has significant implications for our understanding of the physics of dwarf novae and the role of EUV emission in the accretion process. Our findings provide new insights into the complex interactions between the accretion disk and the white dwarf, and have important implications for the development of models of dwarf nova outbursts.

In this paper we will give an account of Dan's reduction method for reducing
the weight $ n $ multiple logarithm $ I_{1,1,\ldots,1}(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) $
to an explicit sum of lower depth multiple polylogarithms in $ \leq n - 2 $
variables.
  We provide a detailed explanation of the method Dan outlines, and we fill in
the missing proofs for Dan's claims. This establishes the validity of the
method itself, and allows us to produce a corrected version of Dan's reduction
of $ I_{1,1,1,1} $ to $ I_{3,1} $'s and $ I_4 $'s. We then use the symbol of
multiple polylogarithms to answer Dan's question about how this reduction
compares with his earlier reduction of $ I_{1,1,1,1} $, and his question about
the nature of the resulting functional equation of $ I_{3,1} $.
  Finally, we apply the method to $ I_{1,1,1,1,1} $ at weight 5 to first
produce a reduction to depth $ \leq 3 $ integrals. Using some functional
equations from our thesis, we further reduce this to $ I_{3,1,1} $, $ I_{3,2} $
and $ I_5 $, modulo products. We also see how to reduce $ I_{3,1,1} $ to $
I_{3,2} $, modulo $ \delta $ (modulo products and depth 1 terms), and indicate
how this allows us to reduce $ I_{1,1,1,1,1} $ to $ I_{3,2} $'s only, modulo $
\delta $.

In this paper, we demonstrate the use of physical models to evaluate the
production of $^{39}$Ar and $^{40}$Ar underground. Considering both cosmogenic
$^{39}$Ar production and radiogenic $^{40}$Ar production in situ and from
external sources, we can derive the ratio of $^{39}$Ar to $^{40}$Ar in
underground sources. We show for the first time that the $^{39}$Ar production
underground is dominated by stopping negative muon capture on $^{39}$K and
($\alpha,n)$ induced subsequent $^{39}$K(n,p)$^{39}$Ar reactions. The
production of $^{39}$Ar is shown as a function of depth. We demonstrate that
argon depleted in $^{39}$Ar can be obtained only if the depth of the
underground resources is greater than 500 m.w.e. below the surface. Stopping
negative muon capture on $^{39}$K dominates over radiogenic production at
depths of less than 2000 m.w.e., and that production by muon-induced neutrons
is subdominant at any depth. The depletion factor depends strongly on both
radioactivity level and potassium content in the rock. We measure the
radioactivity concentration and potassium concentration in the rock for a
potential site of an underground argon source in South Dakota. Depending on the
probability of $^{39}$Ar and $^{40}$Ar produced underground being dissolved in
the water, the upper limit of the concentration of $^{39}$Ar in the underground
water at this site is estimated to be in a range of a factor of 1.6 to 155 less
than the $^{39}$Ar concentration in the atmosphere.
  The calculation tools presented in this paper are also critical to the dating
method with $^{39}$Ar.

text: Recent advancements in data storage technologies have heightened the importance of dependability in cache-based RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) systems, particularly in commercial applications. This study aims to establish a hierarchical approach that systematically evaluates the dependability of a cache-based RAID storage architecture. We propose a multi-level assessment framework that integrates quantitative and qualitative metrics across three tiers component reliability, system resilience, and operational performance. Methodologically, we utilized both fault injection and simulation techniques to model various failure scenarios, allowing us to analyze the impact of individual component failures on overall system dependability. Key findings demonstrate that while traditional RAID configurations primarily focus on disk redundancy, incorporating cache considerations significantly enhances fault tolerance and recovery rates. Our results indicate that optimized cache management can reduce data loss risks by up to 30% during catastrophic failures when compared to conventional RAID setups. Conclusionally, this hierarchical approach not only provides a robust mechanism for assessing dependability but also serves as a foundational framework for designing more resilient cache-based storage systems. The proposed methodology offers practical implications for practitioners in the field, presenting a path forward for improving data integrity and availability in commercial environments reliant on advanced storage architectures. This study contributes to the growing body of knowledge in storage system design, urging further exploration into integrated approaches to dependability analysis.

text: We report the first multi-messenger observations of neutron-rich matter, providing a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between neutron star mergers and heavy element formation. Our analysis combines data from gravitational wave detections by LIGO and Virgo with electromagnetic observations from gamma-ray bursts and optical transients. By correlating these diverse signals, we identify a population of neutron-rich systems that exhibit characteristic spectral signatures and kinematic properties.  Through a systematic study of the observed neutron-rich matter, we demonstrate that the neutron star merger remnants exhibit a unique pattern of heavy element enrichment, which is distinct from that of the progenitor neutron stars. Our results indicate that the neutron star merger process is responsible for the formation of a significant fraction of the heavy elements observed in the universe.  Our findings are based on a combination of theoretical modeling and empirical analysis, utilizing advanced computational simulations of neutron star mergers and heavy element nucleosynthesis. By integrating these approaches, we are able to reconstruct the complex astrophysical processes that govern the formation of neutron-rich matter and its subsequent heavy element production. Our research provides a new perspective on the interplay between neutron star mergers and heavy element formation, shedding light on the fundamental mechanisms that shape the chemical composition of the universe.

text: In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of Gamma Ray Burst (GRB) afterglows through a unifying theoretical framework. Our research is primarily motivated by the need to reconcile diverse observational data and address inconsistencies in the understanding of GRB afterglow phenomena. To this end, we employ a robust model that integrates the synchrotron radiation theory with the evolving dynamics of relativistic jets. We conducted systematic simulations and applied our model to a significant dataset of afterglow light curves from various GRBs. Our findings indicate that the unifying model accurately reconstructs the observed afterglow profiles across multiple wavelengths, including radio, optical, and X-ray bands. These results underscore the capacity of the model to capture the essential features of GRB afterglows, such as the chromatic behavior of the light curves and the temporal decay indices. Furthermore, we identify a parameter space that effectively characterizes the energy distribution and collimation of the jet, providing insights into the intrinsic properties of GRB sources. Through rigorous statistical tests, we demonstrate the model's predictive power and its potential to resolve discrepancies associated with previously unexplained observational trends. The success of our approach highlights the feasibility of achieving a cohesive understanding of GRB afterglows, offering a paradigm for future observational campaigns and theoretical developments. Our study significantly contributes to the astrophysical community's efforts to demystify the complex nature of GRBs and their afterglows, advancing the frontier of high-energy astrophysics.

Regions of rapid variation in the internal structure of a star are often
referred to as acoustic glitches since they create a characteristic periodic
signature in the frequencies of p modes. Here we examine the localized
disturbance arising from the helium second ionization zone in red giant branch
and clump stars. More specifically, we determine how accurately and precisely
the parameters of the ionization zone can be obtained from the oscillation
frequencies of stellar models. We use models produced by three different
generation codes that not only cover a wide range of stages of evolution along
the red giant phase but also incorporate different initial helium abundances.
We discuss the conditions under which such fits robustly and accurately
determine the acoustic radius of the second ionization zone of helium. The
determined radii of the ionization zones as inferred from the mode frequencies
were found to be coincident with the local maximum in the first adiabatic
exponent described by the models, which is associated with the outer edge of
the second ionization zone of helium. Finally, we consider whether this method
can be used to distinguish stars with different helium abundances. Although a
definite trend in the amplitude of the signal is observed any distinction would
be difficult unless the stars come from populations with vastly different
helium abundances or the uncertainties associated with the fitted parameters
can be reduced. However, application of our methodology could be useful for
distinguishing between different populations of red giant stars in globular
clusters, where distinct populations with very different helium abundances have
been observed.

Poaching continues to be a significant threat to the conservation of wildlife
and the associated ecosystem. Estimating and predicting where the poachers have
committed or would commit crimes is essential to more effective allocation of
patrolling resources. The real-world data in this domain is often sparse, noisy
and incomplete, consisting of a small number of positive data (poaching signs),
a large number of negative data with label uncertainty, and an even larger
number of unlabeled data. Fortunately, domain experts such as rangers can
provide complementary information about poaching activity patterns. However,
this kind of human knowledge has rarely been used in previous approaches. In
this paper, we contribute new solutions to the predictive analysis of poaching
patterns by exploiting both very limited data and human knowledge. We propose
an approach to elicit quantitative information from domain experts through a
questionnaire built upon a clustering-based division of the conservation area.
In addition, we propose algorithms that exploit qualitative and quantitative
information provided by the domain experts to augment the dataset and improve
learning. In collaboration with World Wild Fund for Nature, we show that
incorporating human knowledge leads to better predictions in a conservation
area in Northeastern China where the charismatic species is Siberian Tiger. The
results show the importance of exploiting human knowledge when learning from
limited data.

Reconstruction error bounds in compressed sensing under Gaussian or uniform
bounded noise do not translate easily to the case of Poisson noise. Reasons for
this include the signal dependent nature of Poisson noise, and also the fact
that the negative log likelihood (NLL) in case of a Poisson distribution (which
is related to the generalized Kullback-Leibler divergence (GKLD)) is not a
metric and does not obey the triangle inequality. There exist prior theoretical
results in the form of provable error bounds for computationally tractable
estimators for compressed sensing problems under Poisson noise. However, these
results do not apply to realistic compressive systems, which must obey some
crucial constraints such as non-negativity and flux preservation. On the other
hand, there exist provable error bounds for such realistic systems in the
published literature, but they are for estimators that are computationally
intractable. In this paper, we develop error bounds for a computationally
tractable estimator which also applies to realistic compressive systems obeying
the required constraints. Our technique replaces the GKLD, with an information
theoretic metric - namely the square root of the Jensen-Shannon divergence
(JSD), which is related to an approximate, symmetrized version of the Poisson
NLL. We show that this allows for simple proofs of the error bounds. We propose
and prove interesting statistical properties of the square root of JSD and
exploit other known ones. Numerical experiments are performed showing the use
of the technique in signal and image reconstruction from compressed
measurements under Poisson noise. Our technique applies to sparse/ compressible
signals in any orthonormal basis, works with high probability for any randomly
generated non-negative and flux-preserving sensing matrix and is proposes an
estimator whose parameters are purely statistically motivated.

text: The Carina Project, an ongoing astrophysical investigation, focuses on understanding the structure and dynamics of the Carina Arm, a significant spiral arm in our Galaxy. This study specifically examines the radial velocity distribution within the Carina Arm using a sample of 162 red giant stars.  The objective of this research is to identify any deviations from the expected radial velocity distribution, which could indicate the presence of substructures or disturbances within the Carina Arm.  Observational data were obtained from the Hipparcos and Tycho-2 catalogs, providing precise parallax measurements and accurate radial velocities. The Gaia Radial Velocity Spectrometer (RVS) data were also used to cross-check and refine radial velocity measurements.  The results of this analysis revealed a radial velocity distribution that exhibits clear asymmetry towards the inner parts of the Carina Arm, with an apparent shift in mean radial velocity. This shift could be explained by the presence of the Scutum-Centaurus Arm and the Gould's Belt, known structures in the Galaxy that interact with the Carina Arm.  Additionally, this study identified several stars that exhibit significant radial velocity variations, which could be indicative of binary systems or other complex astrophysical phenomena. These findings provide new insights into the complex structure of the Carina Arm and contribute to our understanding of the dynamics of spiral arms in our Galaxy.  In conclusion, this research on the radial velocity distribution in the Carina Arm utilizing red giant stars reveals significant asymmetry and identifies potential substructures, providing valuable insights into the complex dynamics of the Carina Arm and contributing to our overall understanding of spiral arms in the Milky Way.

Proper design and manufacturing thermal bridges based on molecular junctions
at the contact between graphene platelets or other thermally conductive
nanoparticles would provide a fascinating way to produce efficient heat
transport networks for the exploitation in heat management applications. In
this work, using Non Equilibrium Molecular Dynamics, we calculated thermal
conductance of alkyl chains used as molecular junctions between two graphene
nanoribbons, both as covalently bound and Van der Waals interdigitated chains.
Effect of chain length, grafting density, temperature and chain interdigitation
were systematically studied. A clear reduction of conductivity was found with
increasing chain length and decreasing grafting density, while lower
conductivity was observed for Van der Waals interdigitated chains compared to
covalently bound ones. The importance of molecular junctions in enhancing
thermal conductance at graphene nanoribbons contacts was further evidenced by
calculating the conductance equivalence between a single chain and an
overlapping of un-functionalized graphene sheets. As an example, one single
pentyl covalently bound chain was found to have a conductance equivalent to the
overlapping of an area corresponding to about 152 carbon atoms. These results
contribute to the understanding of thermal phenomena occurring within networks
of thermally conductive nanoparticles, including graphene nanopapers and
graphene-based polymer nanocomposites, which are or high interest for the heat
management application in electronics and generally in low-temperature heat
exchange and recovery.

text:
The identification of the most influential spreaders in networks is important
to control and understand the spreading capabilities of the system as well as
to ensure an efficient information diffusion such as in rumor-like dynamics.
Recent works have suggested that the identification of influential spreaders is
not independent of the dynamics being studied. For instance, the key disease
spreaders might not necessarily be so when it comes to analyze social contagion
or rumor propagation. Additionally, it has been shown that different metrics
(degree, coreness, etc) might identify different influential nodes even for the
same dynamical processes with diverse degree of accuracy. In this paper, we
investigate how nine centrality measures correlate with the disease and rumor
spreading capabilities of the nodes that made up different synthetic and
real-world (both spatial and non-spatial) networks. We also propose a
generalization of the random walk accessibility as a new centrality measure and
derive analytical expressions for the latter measure for simple network
configurations. Our results show that for non-spatial networks, the $k$-core
and degree centralities are most correlated to epidemic spreading, whereas the
average neighborhood degree, the closeness centrality and accessibility are
most related to rumor dynamics. On the contrary, for spatial networks, the
accessibility measure outperforms the rest of centrality metrics in almost all
cases regardless of the kind of dynamics considered. Therefore, an important
consequence of our analysis is that previous studies performed in synthetic
random networks cannot be generalized to the case of spatial networks.

text: We investigate the spectral properties of Low-luminosity Active Galactic Nuclei (LAGNs) in Luminous Infrared Galaxies (LINERs) using advection-dominated accretion and jet models. Our analysis reveals that the spectral characteristics of LAGNs in LINERs can be explained by the interplay between advection-dominated accretion and jet emission. We find that the presence of a jet is a crucial factor in shaping the spectral energy distribution of LAGNs in LINERs, particularly in the infrared and radio regimes. Our results suggest that the jet is responsible for the observed increase in luminosity and the broadening of the spectral lines. We also identify a correlation between the accretion rate and the jet power, which is consistent with the predictions of advection-dominated accretion models. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the spectral properties of LAGNs in LINERs can be described by a combination of a Comptonization model and a jet model, which provides a more accurate representation of the observed spectral energy distribution. Our findings have important implications for our understanding of the role of jets in LAGNs and the interplay between accretion and jet emission in these objects.

text: The Gaia-ESO Survey, a large-scale spectroscopic survey, aims to investigate the intricate chemical and kinematic substructures within the Milky Way's disk. The primary objective is to leverage high-resolution spectroscopic data from the Gaia-ESO Survey to classify and characterize distinct stellar populations and their chemical signatures within the disk. Utilizing state-of-the-art clustering algorithms, including Gaussian Mixture Models and hierarchical clustering, the methodology involved analyzing elemental abundances and stellar parameters from the sample. Key findings reveal a distinct bimodal distribution in the [$\alpha$/Fe] vs. [Fe/H] plane, suggesting the presence of two dominant chemical substructures corresponding to the thin and thick disk components. Additionally, the study identifies a correlation between the dynamical properties of the identified clusters and their chemical composition, offering insights into the mechanisms shaping disk evolution. These results underscore the complexity of the Galactic disk and the importance of chemical tagging in distinguishing its components. Conclusively, this research advances our comprehension of the Milky Way's structure and provides a framework for future studies aimed at unraveling the Galaxy's formation history through chemical and dynamical investigations. The findings hold significant implications for constraining models of Galactic evolution and enrich our understanding of stellar population synthesis and migration within the disk.

In this paper, a general model for cyber-physical systems (CPSs), that
captures the diffusion of attacks from the cyber layer to the physical system,
is studied. In particular, a game-theoretic approach is proposed to analyze the
interactions between one defender and one attacker over a CPS. In this game,
the attacker launches cyber attacks on a number of cyber components of the CPS
to maximize the potential harm to the physical system while the system operator
chooses to defend a number of cyber nodes to thwart the attacks and minimize
potential damage to the physical side. The proposed game explicitly accounts
for the fact that both attacker and defender can have different computational
capabilities and disparate levels of knowledge of the system. To capture such
bounded rationality of attacker and defender, a novel approach inspired from
the behavioral framework of cognitive hierarchy theory is developed. In this
framework, the defender is assumed to be faced with an attacker that can have
different possible thinking levels reflecting its knowledge of the system and
computational capabilities. To solve the game, the optimal strategies of each
attacker type are characterized and the optimal response of the defender facing
these different types is computed. This general approach is applied to smart
grid security considering wide area protection with energy markets
implications. Numerical results show that a deviation from the Nash equilibrium
strategy is beneficial when the bounded rationality of the attacker is
considered. Moreover, the results show that the defender's incentive to deviate
from the Nash equilibrium decreases when faced with an attacker that has high
computational ability.

text: In this study, we investigate optimal probabilistic dense coding schemes aimed at maximizing information transmission efficiency between sender and receiver using quantum channels. Our work attempts to solve the challenge of determining the best strategies for encoding classical messages into quantum states, ensuring that the probability of successful decoding is maximized while minimizing errors. We explore various scenarios, including different types of noise models and varying capacities of the quantum channel. The key methodology involves employing linear programming techniques to derive the optimal encoding and decoding probabilities. Through rigorous simulations and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that our proposed schemes significantly outperform existing methods in terms of information transmission fidelity under realistic conditions. Our findings highlight the potential of these schemes in enhancing secure communication protocols and data transmission systems.

Anderson localization is studied for two flavors of massless Dirac fermions
in 2D space perturbed by static disorder that is invariant under a chiral
symmetry (chS) and a time-reversal symmetry (TRS) operation which, when
squared, is equal either to plus or minus the identity. The former TRS
(symmetry class BDI) can for example be realized when the Dirac fermions emerge
from spinless fermions hopping on a 2D lattice with a linear energy dispersion
such as the honeycomb lattice (graphene) or the square lattice with $\pi$-flux
per plaquette. The latter TRS is realized by the surface states of 3D
$\mathbb{Z}_{2}$-topological band insulators in symmetry class CII. In the
phase diagram parametrized by the disorder strengths, there is an infrared
stable line of critical points for both symmetry classes BDI and CII. Here we
discuss a "global phase diagram" in which disordered Dirac fermion systems in
all three chiral symmetry classes, AIII, CII, and BDI, occur in 4 quadrants,
sharing one corner which represents the clean Dirac fermion limit. This phase
diagram also includes symmetry classes AII [e.g., appearing at the surface of a
disordered 3D $\mathbb{Z}_2$-topological band insulator in the spin-orbit
(symplectic) symmetry class] and D (e.g., the random bond Ising model in two
dimensions) as boundaries separating regions of the phase diagram belonging to
the three chS classes AIII, BDI, and CII. Moreover, we argue that physics of
Anderson localization in the CII phase can be presented in terms of a
non-linear-sigma model (NLsM) with a $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$-topological term. We
thereby complete the derivation of topological or Wess-Zumino-Novikov-Witten
terms in the NLsM description of disordered fermionic models in all 10 symmetry
classes relevant to Anderson localization in two spatial dimensions.

When homogenizing elliptic partial differential equations, the so-called
corrector problem is pivotal to compute the macroscale effective coefficients
from the microscale information. To solve this corrector problem in the
periodic setting, Moulinec and Suquet introduced in the mid-nineties a
numerical strategy based on the reformulation of that problem as an integral
equation (known as the Lippmann--Schwinger equation), which is then suitably
discretized. This results in an iterative, matrix-free method, which is of
particular interest for complex microstructures. Since the seminal work of
Moulinec and Suquet, several variants of their scheme have been proposed.
  The aim of this contribution is twofold. First, we provide an overview of
these methods, recast in the language of the applied mathematics community.
These methods are presented as asymptotically consistent Galerkin
discretizations of the Lippmann--Schwinger equation. The bilinear form arising
in the weak form of this integral equation is indeed the sum of a local and a
non-local term. We show that most of the variants proposed in the literature
correspond to alternative approximations of this non-local term. Second, we
propose a mathematical analysis of the discretized problem. In particular, we
prove under mild hypotheses the convergence of these numerical schemes with
respect to the grid-size. We also provide a priori error estimates on the
solution.
  The article closes on a three-dimensional numerical application within the
framework of linear elasticity.

Gravitational microlensing is the only method capable of exploring the entire
population of free-floating planets down to Mars-mass objects, because the
microlensing signal does not depend on the brightness of the lensing object. A
characteristic timescale of microlensing events depends on the mass of the
lens: the less massive the lens, the shorter the microlensing event. A previous
analysis of 474 microlensing events found an excess of very short events (1-2
days) - more than known stellar populations would suggest - indicating the
existence of a large population of unbound or wide-orbit Jupiter-mass planets
(reported to be almost twice as common as main-sequence stars). These results,
however, do not match predictions of planet formation theories and are in
conflict with surveys of young clusters. Here we report the analysis of a six
times larger sample of microlensing events discovered during the years
2010-2015. Although our survey has very high sensitivity (detection efficiency)
to short-timescale (1--2 days) microlensing events, we found no excess of
events with timescales in this range, with a 95% upper limit on the frequency
of Jupiter-mass free-floating or wide-orbit planets of 0.25 planet per
main-sequence star. We detected a few possible ultrashort-timescale events
(with timescales of less than 0.5 day), which may indicate the existence of
Earth- and super-Earth-mass free-floating planets, as predicted by
planet-formation theories. [abridged]

text: The magnetic properties of biatomic Fe chains on Ir(001) have been extensively studied due to their potential applications in spintronics and magnetoelectronics. In this work, we investigate the structural origin of the magnetic state transition in these systems using density functional theory calculations and first-principles molecular dynamics simulations. We find that the magnetic transition is driven by the interaction between the Fe chains and the underlying Ir(001) substrate. Specifically, we identify the Ir atoms beneath the Fe atoms as the key players in mediating the magnetic coupling between adjacent Fe chains. Our simulations reveal that the magnetic transition occurs when the Ir-Fe-Ir bond angle reaches a critical value, leading to a change in the magnetic ground state from ferromagnetic to antiferromagnetic. The implications of these findings for the design and fabrication of magnetic nanostructures on Ir(001) are discussed. This study offers new insights into the interplay between structure and magnetism in biatomic Fe chains on Ir(001), which is essential for understanding the fundamental mechanisms underlying their magnetic behavior and for advancing the development of spintronic and magnetoelectronic devices.

text: This study investigates the long-term stability of Cu surface nanotips, a crucial aspect of their applications in various fields such as electronics, catalysis, and biomedicine. However, their long-term stability remains a significant challenge due to the inherent instability of the Cu surface.  The objective of this research is to explore the long-term stability of Cu surface nanotips under various environmental conditions, including temperature, humidity, and exposure to chemicals. A combination of experimental and theoretical approaches was employed to investigate the stability of Cu surface nanotips. The Cu surface nanotips were fabricated using a combination of mechanical and chemical methods, and their stability was evaluated using techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy.  The results show that the Cu surface nanotips exhibit significant stability under ambient conditions, with minimal changes in their structure and surface composition over a period of several weeks. However, exposure to high temperatures and chemicals leads to significant degradation of the Cu surface, resulting in the formation of surface oxide layers and the loss of nanotip morphology. Theoretical modeling suggests that the stability of Cu surface nanotips is influenced by the surface energy and the presence of surface defects. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the long-term stability of Cu surface nanotips and have implications for their applications in various fields.

Using the AdS/CFT duality, we study the expectation value of stress tensor in
$2+1$-dimensional quantum critical theories with a general dynamical scaling
$z$, and explore various constrains on negative energy density for strongly
coupled field theories. The holographic dual theory is the theory of gravity in
3+1-dimensional Lifshitz backgrounds. We adopt a consistent approach to obtain
the boundary stress tensor from bulk construction, which satisfies the trace
Ward identity associated with Lifshitz scaling symmetry. In particular, the
boundary stress tensor, constructed from the gravitational wave deformed
Lifshitz geometry, is found up to second order in gravitational wave
perturbations. {The result} is compared to its counterpart in free {scalar}
field theory at the same order in an expansion of small squeezing parameters.
This allows us to relate the boundary values of gravitational waves to the
squeezing parameters of squeezed vacuum states. We find that, in both cases
with $z=1$, the stress tensor satisfies the averaged null energy condition, and
is consistent with the quantum interest conjecture. Moreover, the negative
lower bound on null-contracted stress tensor, which is averaged over time-like
trajectories along nearly null directions, is obtained. We find a weaker
constraint on the magnitude and duration of negative null energy density in
strongly coupled field theory as compared with the constraint in free
relativistic field theory. The implications are discussed.

text: In this study, we investigate the role of dispersal in interconnected habitat patches influenced by an Allee effect, a phenomenon where population decline occurs below a critical density threshold. We aim to address the challenge of maintaining viable populations across fragmented landscapes, where local extinctions are likely under the Allee effect. Utilizing a mathematical model, we explore how varying dispersal rates can influence population dynamics and persistence across said habitat networks. Our methodology involves the formulation and analysis of coupled differential equations representing population densities within a two-patch system. Key findings indicate that intermediate dispersal rates can enhance population persistence by mitigating local extinctions, whereas low dispersal rates restrict the rescue effect, and excessively high rates lead to synchrony in population declines. This suggests a non-linear relationship between dispersal intensity and population survival. Additionally, we identify conditions under which dispersal-induced destabilization occurs, thereby contributing to population collapse. We further demonstrate that spatial heterogeneity in habitat quality can modulate the outcomes of dispersal, potentially offsetting some negative impacts of the Allee effect. Our results underscore the importance of optimizing dispersal strategies to foster connectivity and stability in ecosystems characterized by potentially destabilizing demographic processes. These findings provide a quantitative basis for ecological management practices aimed at conserving species vulnerable to joint pressures of habitat fragmentation and Allee dynamics, particularly in scenarios involving deliberate introduction or translocation efforts. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of ecological connectivity, with implications for biodiversity conservation strategies in the face of environmental change.

Modern theories of the hydrophobic effect highlight its dependence on length
scale, emphasizing in particular the importance of interfaces that emerge in
the vicinity of sizable hydrophobes. We recently showed that a faithful
treatment of such nanoscale interfaces requires careful attention to the
statistics of capillary waves, with significant quantitative implications for
the calculation of solvation thermodynamics. Here we show that a coarse-grained
lattice model in the spirit of those pioneered by Chandler and coworkers, when
informed by this understanding, can capture a broad range of hydrophobic
behaviors with striking accuracy. Specifically, we calculate probability
distributions for microscopic density fluctuations that agree very well with
results of atomistic simulations, even many standard deviations from the mean,
and even for probe volumes in highly heterogeneous environments. This accuracy
is achieved without adjustment of free parameters, as the model is fully
specified by well-known properties of liquid water. As illustrative examples of
its utility, we characterize the free energy profile for a solute crossing the
air-water interface, and compute the thermodynamic cost of evacuating the space
between extended nanoscale surfaces. Together, these calculations suggest that
a highly reduced model for aqueous solvation can serve as the basis for
efficient multiscale modeling of spatial organization driven by hydrophobic and
interfacial forces.

text:
Prequantum classical statistical field theory (PCSFT) is a model which
provides a possibility to represent averages of quantum observables, including
correlations of observables on subsystems of a composite system, as averages
with respect to fluctuations of classical random fields. PCSFT is a classical
model of the wave type. For example, "electron" is described by electronic
field. In contrast to QM, this field is a real physical field and not a field
of probabilities. An important point is that the prequantum field of e.g.
electron contains the irreducible contribution of the background field, vacuum
fluctuations. In principle, the traditional QM-formalism can be considered as a
special regularization procedure: subtraction of averages with respect to
vacuum fluctuations. In this paper we derive a classical analog of the
Heisenberg-Robertson inequality for dispersions of functionals of classical
(prequantum) fields. PCSFT Robertson-like inequality provides a restriction on
the product of classical dispersions. However, this restriction is not so rigid
as in QM. The quantum dispersion corresponds to the difference between e.g. the
electron field dispersion and the dispersion of vacuum fluctuations. Classical
Robertson-like inequality contains these differences. Hence, it does not imply
such a rigid estimate from below for dispersions as it was done in QM.

text: We propose a novel approach to one-shot learning through the implementation of Multi-level Semantic Feature Augmentation (MSFA). One-shot learning presents challenges, particularly in effectively generalizing from a single example, which limits model performance in diverse applications. Our work addresses this problem by enriching the representation of input data using hierarchical semantic features derived from a rich knowledge base.   We systematically augment the feature set at multiple semantic levels, enabling our models to leverage contextual information alongside inherent characteristics. We utilize convolutional neural networks to extract initial features, followed by a semantic feature extraction phase that incorporates taxonomical relationships and word embeddings to capture deeper contextual insights. By applying feature augmentation across different levels, we enhance the model's ability to understand and generalize from minimal input.  To evaluate our method, we conduct extensive experiments on standard one-shot learning benchmarks, including Omniglot and Mini-Imagenet datasets. Our results demonstrate that MSFA outperforms traditional one-shot learning approaches, achieving an improvement of X% in accuracy and Y% in F1-score. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of different semantic levels on performance, providing insights into optimal configurations for feature augmentation.  In conclusion, MSFA represents a significant advancement in one-shot learning, offering a robust methodology that incorporates semantic depth to improve model generalization. Our findings pave the way for future research into enhanced learning paradigms that exploit semantic information across various domains.

text: The enigmatic behavior of the black hole binary GRS 1915+105 has been a focal point of astrophysical studies due to its highly variable emission patterns. The inner mechanics of its accretion disk and associated outflows play a pivotal role in these observations, yet remain inadequately understood. This study aims to delve into the wind mechanisms emanating from the accretion disk surrounding GRS 1915+105. Utilizing high-resolution spectra obtained from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, we analyze the wind's properties, focusing on its velocity, ionization state, and composition. Through spectroscopic diagnostics, we address the correlation between wind characteristics and distinct spectral states of the system. Our findings indicate that the wind velocity is markedly higher during the softer spectral states, while its ionization level shifts in accordance with fluctuations in disk luminosity. A noteworthy discovery is the presence of highly ionized iron, suggesting that radiative processes significantly influence wind dynamics. Moreover, wind detections appear intimately linked to the emergence of jet ejections, implying a potential regulatory mechanism between the accretion disk wind and jet formation. These insights contribute to a refined understanding of the underlying processes governing energy and mass transfer in black hole systems. We conclude that accretion disk winds in GRS 1915+105 are crucial for interpreting its complex variability, highlighting the need for further multi-wavelength observations and theoretical modeling to elucidate the intricate interplay between accretion disks, winds, and jets in black hole X-ray binaries.

We propose a machine learning-based approach that utilizes these API call sequences as features for classification. The model achieved high accuracy rates when trained on our dataset, demonstrating the potential of system API information for improving Android ransomware detection. Future research will focus on refining the model's performance and exploring additional API features for enhanced detection capabilities.

text: We present the results of our study on the destruction of star clusters in spiral galaxies due to radial migration. Radial migration, a process by which stars are scattered from their original orbits to the outer regions of a galaxy, plays a significant role in shaping the structure and evolution of spiral galaxies. By employing state-of-the-art N-body simulations and analysis techniques, we investigate the effects of radial migration on star clusters in spiral galaxies.    We find that radial migration significantly reduces the number of star clusters in the inner regions of spiral galaxies. Our simulations reveal that this is due to a combination of factors, including the tidal disruption of star clusters as they pass through the dense central regions of the galaxy, and the subsequent escape of their members due to the galactic potential. Additionally, we observe that radial migration leads to the formation of new star clusters in the outer regions of the galaxy, as stars scattered from the inner regions settle into new orbits.    Our study highlights the importance of radial migration in shaping the star cluster populations of spiral galaxies. We argue that a better understanding of this process is crucial for unraveling the complex history of galactic evolution. Our findings provide a critical foundation for future research into the formation and evolution of star clusters in spiral galaxies, as well as their connection to other galaxy properties. We conclude that the interplay between radial migration and star cluster dynamics is a key area for continued exploration in the field of astrophysics.

Compared with the start-of-art energy integration detectors (EIDs),
photon-counting detectors (PCDs) with energy discrimination capabilities have
demonstrated great potentials in various applications of medical x-ray
radiography and computed tomography (CT). However, the advantages of PCDs may
be compromised by various hardware-related degradation factors. For example, at
high count rate, quasi-coincident photons may be piled up and result in not
only lost counts but also distorted spectrums, which is called the pulse pileup
effects. Considering the relative slow detection speed of current PCDs and high
x-ray flux for clinical imaging, it is vital to develop an effective approach
to compensate or correct for the pileup effect. The aim of this paper was to
develop a model-free, end-to-end, and data-driven approach in the neural
network framework. We first introduce the trigger threshold concept to
regularize the correction process. Then, we design a fully-connected cascade
artificial neural network and train it with measurements and true counts. After
training, the network is used to recover raw photon-counting data for higher
fidelity. To evaluate the proposed approach, Monte Carlo simulations are
conducted. We simulate four types of PCDs combining the unipolar or bipolar
pulse shape with the nonparalyzable or paralyzable detection mode. The
simulation results demonstrate that the trained neural network decreases the
relative error of count averages of raw data by an order of magnitude while
maintaining a reasonable variance over a wide range of attenuation paths.

We present the first results of an ALMA spectral survey of strong absorption
lines for common interstellar species in the z=0.89 molecular absorber toward
the lensed blazar PKS1830-211. The dataset brings essential information on the
structure and composition of the absorbing gas in the foreground galaxy. In
particular, we find absorption over large velocity intervals (gtrsim 100 km/s)
toward both lensed images of the blazar. This suggests either that the galaxy
inclination is intermediate and that we sample velocity gradients or streaming
motions in the disk plane, that the molecular gas has a large vertical
distribution or extraplanar components, or that the absorber is not a simple
spiral galaxy but might be a merger system. The number of detected species is
now reaching a total of 42 different species plus 14 different rare
isotopologues toward the SW image, and 14 species toward the NE line-of-sight.
The abundances of CH, H2O, HCO+, HCN, and NH3 relative to H2 are found to be
comparable to those in the Galactic diffuse medium. Of all the lines detected
so far toward PKS1830-211, the ground-state line of ortho-water has the deepest
absorption. We argue that ground-state lines of water have the best potential
for detecting diffuse molecular gas in absorption at high redshift.

In this article, we establish optimality of the Bramble-Pasciak-Xu (BPX) norm
equivalence and optimality of the wavelet modified (or stabilized) hierarchical
basis (WHB) preconditioner in the setting of local 3D mesh refinement. In the
analysis of WHB methods, a critical first step is to establish the optimality
of BPX norm equivalence for the refinement procedures under consideration.
While the available optimality results for the BPX norm have been constructed
primarily in the setting of uniformly refined meshes, a notable exception is
the local 2D red-green result due to Dahmen and Kunoth. The purpose of this
article is to extend this original 2D optimality result to the local 3D
red-green refinement procedure introduced by Bornemann-Erdmann-Kornhuber (BEK),
and then to use this result to extend the WHB optimality results from the
quasiuniform setting to local 2D and 3D red-green refinement scenarios. The BPX
extension is reduced to establishing that locally enriched finite element
subspaces allow for the construction of a scaled basis which is formally Riesz
stable. It is possible to show that the number of degrees of freedom used for
smoothing is bounded by a constant times the number of degrees of freedom
introduced at that level of refinement, indicating that a practical
implementable version of the resulting BPX preconditioner for the BEK
refinement setting has provably optimal (linear) computational complexity per
iteration. An interesting implication of the optimality of the WHB
preconditioner is the a priori H1-stability of the L2-projection. The
theoretical framework employed supports arbitrary spatial dimension d >= 1 and
requires no coefficient smoothness assumptions beyond those required for
well-posedness in H1.

text: We investigated the properties of very hard states in neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries, a phenomenon characterized by the emission of intense X-ray radiation from a compact object with a mass of approximately 1.4 solar masses. Through a comprehensive analysis of archival data from the Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) and the Neutron Star Interior Composition Experiment (NICER), we uncovered a population of binary systems exhibiting extremely hard X-ray spectra, with peak energies exceeding 20 keV. Our results suggest that these systems are driven by the accretion of material onto the neutron star surface, which leads to a significant increase in the X-ray luminosity and a corresponding decrease in the orbital period. We propose that the hardening of the X-ray spectrum is due to the presence of a strong magnetic field in the neutron star, which facilitates the acceleration of high-energy particles. Our findings indicate that the very hard states are a distinct population of binary systems, with distinct properties and behavior compared to other accreting neutron star populations. The observed characteristics of these systems provide valuable insights into the physics of neutron star accretion and the role of magnetic fields in regulating the X-ray emission.

text: We present the results of a comprehensive analysis of the intermediate mass core (IMC) population from a 50 square degree submillimeter survey in the Vela region of the sky (l = ~265). Utilizing a novel approach, we employed the Bolocello Line Spectral Analysis Tool (BLAST) to model the mass function, lifetimes, and properties of IMCs. Our survey area covers a significant portion of the Vela molecular cloud, allowing us to constrain the physical parameters of IMCs in a previously unexplored region.  Our analysis reveals a complex mass function for IMCs, with a significant fraction of cores exhibiting multiple peaks and a broad mass range. We also observe a strong correlation between core mass and lifetime, suggesting that IMCs are born with a broad range of masses and evolve over time through mergers and other dynamical processes. Furthermore, our results indicate that IMCs are characterized by a unique set of physical properties, including high core temperatures and densities, and a high proportion of cores with multiple outflows.  Through a combination of Bayesian modeling and Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the BLAST algorithm in accurately recovering the physical parameters of IMCs. Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of IMCs, and provide new insights into the role of these objects in the formation of stars and planetary systems.

One of the most tantalizing questions in astronomy and astrophysics, namely
the origin and the evolution of the cosmic accelerators that produce the
highest energy cosmic rays (UHECR), may be best addressed through the
observation of ultra high energy (UHE) cosmogenic neutrinos. Neutrinos travel
from their source undeflected by magnetic fields and unimpeded by interactions
with the cosmic microwave background. At high energies, neutrinos could be
detected in dense, radio frequency (RF) transparent media via the Askaryan
effect. The abundant cold ice covering the geographic South Pole, with its
exceptional RF clarity, has been host to several pioneering efforts to develop
this approach, including RICE and ANITA. Building on the expertise gained in
these efforts, and the infrastructure developed in the construction of the
IceCube optical Cherenkov observatory, a low-cost array of radio frequency
antenna stations could be deployed near the Pole to efficiently detect a
significant number of UHE neutrinos with degree scale angular resolution within
the next decade. Such an array, if installed in close proximity to IceCube,
could allow cross-calibration on a small but invaluable subset of neutrino
events detected by both the optical and radio methods. In addition to providing
critical information in the identification of the source of UHECRs, such an
observatory could also provide a unique probe of long baseline high energy
neutrino interactions unattainable in any man-made neutrino beam.

text: Our study explores the application of blinded and unblinded sample size re-estimation in crossover trials balanced for periods. The key issue addressed is the need for accurate sample size determination in crossover trials to ensure statistical power while accounting for period effects. We conducted simulations comparing the performance of blinded and unblinded sample size re-estimation methods in achieving the desired power levels under various scenarios. Our results indicate that both blinded and unblinded approaches can effectively re-estimate sample sizes to maintain the desired power, with subtle differences in their performances depending on factors such as the magnitude of period effects and variability within subjects. Notably, we found that the unblinded approach showed slightly better performance in certain scenarios, indicating its potential usefulness in this context. Our study provides valuable insights into the implications of blinded and unblinded sample size re-estimation methods in crossover trials balanced for periods, aiding researchers in making informed decisions regarding sample size adjustments while maintaining trial integrity.

text: We investigated the magnetic field topology and chemical spot distributions in the extreme Ap star HD 75049, employing a multi-wavelength approach combining ultraviolet and X-ray observations with spectroscopic analysis. Our analysis revealed a complex magnetic field configuration, characterized by a combination of open and closed field lines, with a dominant component oriented perpendicular to the stellar equator. This configuration is likely responsible for the observed high-energy particle acceleration and subsequent emission of X-ray and ultraviolet radiation.  Chemical spot distributions were also observed, which are indicative of localized magnetic reconnection events. These events are thought to be driven by the interaction between the magnetic field and the stellar wind, leading to the formation of compact magnetic reconnection regions. Spectroscopic analysis revealed a high degree of magnetic field orientation correlation with the chemical spot distributions, suggesting a causal relationship between the two phenomena.  Our results indicate that the extreme Ap star HD 75049 exhibits a highly dynamic and complex magnetic field configuration, with significant implications for our understanding of magnetic reconnection and particle acceleration processes in Ap stars. The observed chemical spot distributions provide a unique window into the underlying magnetic field topology, allowing us to test theoretical models of magnetic reconnection and particle acceleration.

In this era of large-scale stellar spectroscopic surveys, measurements of
stellar attributes ("labels," i.e. parameters and abundances) must be made
precise and consistent across surveys. Here, we demonstrate that this can be
achieved by a data-driven approach to spectral modeling. With The Cannon, we
transfer information from the APOGEE survey to determine precise Teff, log g,
[Fe/H], and [$\alpha$/M] from the spectra of 450,000 LAMOST giants. The Cannon
fits a predictive model for LAMOST spectra using 9952 stars observed in common
between the two surveys, taking five labels from APOGEE DR12 as ground truth:
Teff, log g, [Fe/H], [\alpha/M], and K-band extinction $A_k$. The model is then
used to infer Teff, log g, [Fe/H], and [$\alpha$/M] for 454,180 giants, 20% of
the LAMOST DR2 stellar sample. These are the first [$\alpha$/M] values for the
full set of LAMOST giants, and the largest catalog of [$\alpha$/M] for giant
stars to date. Furthermore, these labels are by construction on the APOGEE
label scale; for spectra with S/N > 50, cross-validation of the model yields
typical uncertainties of 70K in Teff, 0.1 in log g, 0.1 in [Fe/H], and 0.04 in
[$\alpha$/M], values comparable to the broadly stated, conservative APOGEE DR12
uncertainties. Thus, by using "label transfer" to tie low-resolution (LAMOST R
$\sim$ 1800) spectra to the label scale of a much higher-resolution (APOGEE R
$\sim$ 22,500) survey, we substantially reduce the inconsistencies between
labels measured by the individual survey pipelines. This demonstrates that
label transfer with The Cannon can successfully bring different surveys onto
the same physical scale.

text: We investigate the time-dependent mass of cosmological perturbations in the context of loop quantum cosmology (LQC) using both the hybrid and dressed metric approaches. Our primary objective is to resolve inconsistencies in the treatment of perturbations under quantum gravity effects, particularly within the framework of cosmological models. We employ a systematic methodology that integrates canonical quantization and effective dynamics to explore how perturbations evolve in an expanding universe characterized by a modified background geometry.  Through our analysis, we derive expressions for the mass of perturbations that account for the dynamical character of spacetime under LQC’s unique quantization scheme. We demonstrate that the hybrid approach provides a coherent framework for understanding the interplay between cosmic evolution and the quantization of gravitational degrees of freedom. In contrast, the dressed metric approach allows us to encapsulate the effects of discrete spacetime structure on cosmological perturbations.  Our results reveal that the effective mass of perturbations exhibits significant time-dependence influenced by the underlying quantum geometry, leading to implications for their growth and evolution during the inflationary phase. We show that our findings can reconcile previously conflicting results in the literature, offering a deeper understanding of how quantum spacetime modifies conventional cosmological scenarios. Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for future studies on the implications of loop quantum gravity on structure formation and the early universe, highlighting the necessity of considering quantum effects in cosmological analyses.

text: This study investigates the energy dependence of potential barriers and its impact on fusion cross-sections. In the context of nuclear fusion, potential barriers refer to the electrostatic and Coulombic interactions between fusion nuclei, which hinder the successful fusion reaction. The energy dependence of these barriers is a critical factor in understanding the behavior of fusion reactions.  The objective of this research is to analyze the relationship between potential barriers and fusion cross-sections using various fusion models, including the barrier penetrability model and the distorted wave Born approximation model. The study employs a comprehensive literature review to provide theoretical background and context for the analysis.  The methodology involves a comparative analysis of the predictions made by these models with respect to energy dependence and fusion cross-sections. The study also employs numerical simulations to provide visualizations of the potential barriers and their impact on fusion cross-sections.  Key findings reveal a strong correlation between potential barriers and fusion cross-sections, indicating that the energy dependence of potential barriers plays a significant role in determining the efficiency of fusion reactions. The analysis suggests that an understanding of this correlation could lead to the development of novel strategies for improving fusion energy production.  In conclusion, this research provides valuable insights into the energy dependence of potential barriers and its influence on fusion cross-sections. The findings highlight the importance of this correlation in the context of nuclear fusion research and have significant implications for the development of future fusion technologies.

text: We investigate the performance of lowered isothermal models in simulating the dynamics of multimass globular clusters using direct N-body simulations. Our approach involves modifying the standard isothermal model to accommodate multiple mass components, including a central, dominant mass and a smaller, satellite mass. We employ a direct N-body simulation framework to model the gravitational interactions between these mass components and other cluster members.   Our results indicate that the lowered isothermal model with a central mass component exhibits improved agreement with observed cluster properties, such as velocity dispersion and mass distribution, compared to the standard isothermal model. However, the model's performance is sensitive to the mass ratio between the central and satellite mass components. Furthermore, we find that the model's ability to reproduce the observed tidal tail morphology is limited, suggesting that a more complex mass distribution is required.   We also explore the impact of different mass component configurations on the model's performance, including the effects of varying the mass ratio, the number of mass components, and the inclusion of other dynamical effects such as stellar mergers. Our findings suggest that a more nuanced understanding of the mass distribution within globular clusters is necessary to accurately simulate their dynamics.

text: This research paper investigates the potential of aggregated edge networks to enhance crowdsourced live streaming. Existing solutions often rely on centralized cloud infrastructure, which can lead to scalability issues and increased latency.  The objective of this study is to explore the feasibility of utilizing aggregated edge networks to improve the quality and efficiency of crowdsourced live streaming. An edge network is a distributed system of devices that are geographically closer to the end-users, which can reduce latency and improve content delivery. Methodology involves designing and implementing an edge network architecture that aggregates the resources of multiple edge devices to deliver live video content to users.  Key findings indicate that the proposed edge network architecture can significantly reduce latency and improve content delivery efficiency compared to traditional cloud-based solutions. The aggregated edge network can also reduce bandwidth consumption by caching frequently accessed content at the edge devices. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of aggregated edge networks to enhance crowdsourced live streaming, and provide a foundation for future research into the optimization of edge network architectures for live streaming applications.

Cascaded or central-moment-based lattice Boltzmann method (CLBM) proposed in
[Geier \textit{et al.}, Phys. Rev. E \textbf{63}, 066705 (2006)] possesses very
good numerical stability. However, two constraints exist in three-dimensional
(3D) CLBM simulations. Firstly, the conventional implementation for 3D CLBM
involves cumbersome operations and requires much higher computational cost
compared to the single-relaxation-time (SRT) LBM. Secondly, it is a challenge
to accurately incorporate a general force field into the 3D CLBM. In this
paper, we present an improved method to implement CLBM in 3D. The main strategy
is to adopt a simplified central moment set, and carry out the
central-moment-based collision operator based on a general
multi-relaxation-time (GMRT) framework. Next, the recently proposed consistent
forcing scheme in CLBM [L. Fei and K. H. Luo, Phys. Rev. E \textbf{96}, 053307
(2017)] is extended to incorporate a general force field into 3D CLBM. Compared
with the recently developed non-orthogonal CLBM [A. D. Rosis, Phys. Rev. E
\textbf{95}, 013310 (2017)], our implementation is proved to reduce the
computational cost significantly. The inconsistency of adopting the discrete
equilibrium distribution functions (EDFs) in the non-orthogonal CLBM is
revealed and discussed. The 3D CLBM developed here in conjunction with the
consistent forcing scheme is verified through numerical simulations of several
canonical force-driven flows, highlighting very good properties in terms of
accuracy, convergence and consistency with the nonslip rule. Finally, the
techniques developed here for 3D CLBM can be applied to make the implementation
and execution of 3D MRT-LBM much more efficient.

We discuss the transient and steady state fluctuation relation for a
mechanical system in contact with two deterministic thermostats at different
temperatures. The system is a modified Lorentz gas in which the fixed
scatterers exchange energy with the gas of particles, and the thermostats are
modelled by two Nos\'e-Hoover thermostats applied at the boundaries of the
system. The transient fluctuation relation, which holds only for a precise
choice of the initial ensemble, is verified at all times, as expected. Times
longer than the mesoscopic scale, needed for local equilibrium to be settled,
are required if a different initial ensemble is considered. This shows how the
transient fluctuation relation asymptotically leads to the steady state
relation when, as explicitly checked in our systems, the condition found in
[D.J. Searles, {\em et al.}, J. Stat. Phys. 128, 1337 (2007)], for the validity
of the steady state fluctuation relation, is verified. For the steady state
fluctuations of the phase space contraction rate $\zL$ and of the dissipation
function $\zW$, a similar relaxation regime at shorter averaging times is
found. The quantity $\zW$ satisfies with good accuracy the fluctuation relation
for times larger than the mesoscopic time scale; the quantity $\zL$ appears to
begin a monotonic convergence after such times. This is consistent with the
fact that $\zW$ and $\zL$ differ by a total time derivative, and that the tails
of the probability distribution function of $\zL$ are Gaussian.

text: This study presents a novel approach to searching for dark matter signals in Fermi-LAT gamma rays, utilizing a multi-messenger strategy that combines machine learning techniques with traditional statistical methods. The background of the search is set against the backdrop of the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope's (FGST) decade-long mission to map the high-energy sky, revealing a wealth of gamma-ray data that can be leveraged to detect faint signals from dark matter annihilation or decay.  The objective of this research is to develop a hybrid search algorithm that integrates machine learning models with traditional statistical methods to identify potential dark matter signals in the Fermi-LAT data. The proposed algorithm, dubbed "DarkFinder," employs a combination of neural networks and Bayesian inference to identify patterns in the data that are indicative of dark matter activity. The DarkFinder algorithm is trained on a diverse set of simulated dark matter signals, allowing it to learn the characteristic signatures of dark matter annihilation and decay.  The methodology employed in this study involves the application of the DarkFinder algorithm to a large sample of Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data, including the latest 10 years of data from the FGST. The results of the analysis are presented in the form of a set of likelihood maps that highlight regions of the sky where dark matter signals may be most prominent. The key findings of this study reveal a significant enhancement in the detection of dark matter signals in regions of the sky where traditional statistical methods would have been inconclusive. The implications of these findings are discussed in terms of the potential for dark matter detection and the need for further investigation using next-generation telescopes.

The main purpose of the paper is the analysis of seismic site effects in
various alluvial basins. The analysis is performed considering a numerical
approach (Boundary Element Method). Two main cases are considered : a shallow
deposit in the centre of Nice (France) [1] and a deep irregular basin in
Caracas (Venezuela) [2]. The amplification of seismic motion is analysed in
terms of level, occuring frequency and location. For both sites, the
amplification factor is found to reach maximum values of 20 (weak motion). Site
effects nevertheless have very different features concerning the frequency
dependence and the location of maximum amplification. For the shallow deposit
in Nice, the amplification factor is very small for low frequencies and fastly
increases above 1.0 Hz. The irregular Caracas basin gives a much different
frequency dependence with many different peaks at various frequencies. The
model for Caracas deep alluvial basin also includes a part of the local
topography such as the nearest mountain. One can estimate seismic site effects
due to both velocity contrast (between the basin and the bedrock) and local
topography of the site. Furthermore, the maximum amplification is located on
the surface for Nice, whereas some strong amplification areas also appear
inside the basin itself in the case of Caracas. One investigates the influence
of this focusing effect on the motion vs depth dependence. This is of great
interest for the analysis of seismic response of underground structures. The
form and the depth of alluvial deposits are then found to have a great
influence on the location of maximum amplification on the surface but also
inside the deposit for deep irregular basins. It is essential for the analysis
of the seismic response of both surface and underground structures.

We present nebular emission associated with 198 strong Mg II absorbers at
0.35 $\le z \le$ 1.1 in the fibre spectra of quasars from the Sloan Digital Sky
Survey. Measured [O II] luminosities (L$_{[O II]}$) are typical of
sub-L$^{\star}$ galaxies with derived star formation rate (uncorrected for
fibre losses and dust reddening) in the range of 0.5-20 ${\rm M_\odot\
yr^{-1}}$. Typically less than $\sim$ 3% of the Mg II systems with rest
equivalent width, $W_{2796}$ $\ge$ 2 \AA, show L$_{[O II]} \ge 0.3$
L$^{\star}_{[O II]}$. The detection rate is found to increase with increasing
$W_{2796}$ and $z$. No significant correlation is found between $W_{2796}$ and
L$_{[O II]}$ even when we restrict the samples to narrow $z$-ranges. A strong
correlation is seen between L$_{[O II]}$ and $z$. While this is expected from
the luminosity evolution of galaxies, we show finite fibre size plays a very
crucial role in this correlation. The measured nebular line ratios (like [O
III]/[O II] and [O III]/H$\beta$) and their $z$ evolution are consistent with
those of galaxies detected in deep surveys. Based on the median stacked
spectra, we infer the average metallicity (log Z $\sim$8.3), ionization
parameter (log $q$ $\sim$7.5) and stellar mass (log (M/M$_\odot$)$\sim$9.3).
The Mg II systems with nebular emission typically have $W_{2796}$ $\ge 2$ \AA,
Mg II doublet ratio close to 1 and W(Fe II$\lambda$2600)/$W_{2796}$ $\sim 0.5$
as often seen in damped Ly$\alpha$ and 21-cm absorbers at these redshifts. This
is the biggest reported sample of [O II] emission from Mg II absorbers at low
impact parameters ideally suited for probing various feedback processes at play
in $z\le 1$ galaxies.

In this paper we describe a framework towards computing well-localized,
robust motion plans through the perception-aware motion planning problem,
whereby we seek a low-cost motion plan subject to a separate constraint on
perception localization quality. To solve this problem we introduce the
Multiobjective Perception-Aware Planning (MPAP) algorithm which explores the
state space via a multiobjective search, considering both cost and a perception
heuristic. This framework can accommodate a large range of heuristics, allowing
those that capture the history dependence of localization drift and represent
complex modern perception methods. We present two such heuristics, one derived
from a simplified model of robot perception and a second learned from
ground-truth sensor error, which we show to be capable of predicting the
performance of a state-of-the-art perception system. The solution trajectory
from this heuristic-based search is then certified via Monte Carlo methods to
be well-localized and robust. The additional computational burden of
perception-aware planning is offset by GPU massive parallelization. Through
numerical experiments the algorithm is shown to find well-localized, robust
solutions in about a second. Finally, we demonstrate MPAP on a quadrotor flying
perception-aware and perception-agnostic plans using Google Tango for
localization, finding the quadrotor safely executes the perception-aware plan
every time, while crashing in over 20% of the perception-agnostic runs due to
loss of localization.
