Electrostatic control of the metal-insulator transition (MIT) in an oxide
semiconductor could potentially impact the emerging field of oxide electronics.
Vanadium dioxide is of particular interest due to the fact that the MIT happens
in the vicinity of room temperature and it is considered to exhibit the Mott
transition. We present a detailed account of our experimental investigation
into three-terminal field effect transistor-like devices using thin film VO2 as
the channel layer. The gate is separated from the channel through an insulating
gate oxide layer, enabling true probing of the field effect with minimal or no
interference from large leakage currents flowing directly from the electrode.
The influence of the fabrication of multiple components of the device,
including the gate oxide deposition, on the VO2 film characteristics is
discussed. Further, we discuss the effect of the gate voltage on the device
response, point out some of the unusual characteristics including temporal
dependence. A reversible unipolar modulation of the channel resistance upon the
gate voltage is demonstrated for the first time in optimally engineered
devices. The results presented in this work are of relevance towards
interpreting gate voltage response in such oxides as well as addressing
challenges in advancing gate stack processing for oxide semiconductors.

text: In this study, we present a novel dynamic nonstationary spatio-temporal model for short-term precipitation prediction. Our approach employs a multivariate dynamic vector autoregressive (VAR) model with exogenous variables to account for the complex spatio-temporal dependencies of precipitation data. The model's flexibility enables it to adapt to nonstationarities and capture changing spatial and temporal patterns in the data.  To illustrate the model's effectiveness, we apply it to daily precipitation data from 187 stations across the conterminous United States for the period 1901–2017. We use a combination of traditional statistical methods, such as autocorrelation functions and spatial correlation matrices, and machine learning algorithms, including principal component analysis and random forest models, to identify potential exogenous variables. These variables include sea surface temperature anomalies, El Niño Southern Oscillation indices, and various climatological indices.  Our results demonstrate that the dynamic nonstationary spatio-temporal model significantly outperforms other commonly used models for short-term precipitation prediction. For example, the root mean squared errors (RMSEs) of the proposed model are up to 11.8% lower than those of the ARIMA model, and the mean absolute errors (MAEs) are up to 9.2% lower than those of the random forest model. Furthermore, our model effectively captures the evolution of spatio-temporal patterns during significant weather events, such as Hurricane Katrina and the California drought.  In conclusion, this study introduces an innovative dynamic nonstationary spatio-temporal model for short-term precipitation prediction. The proposed model's ability to adapt to nonstationarities and capture complex spatio-temporal dependencies makes it a valuable tool for improved precipitation forecasting, especially in the context of climate change and extreme weather events. Future work includes extending the model to longer-term precipitation forecasting and applying it to other environmental applications.

We present an analysis of long-term X-ray and optical observations of the
Wolf-Rayet binary WR 25. Using archival data from observations with the
XMM-Newton and the Swift observatories spanning over ~10 yr, we show that WR 25
is a periodic variable in X-rays with a period of $208 \pm 3$ days. X-ray light
curves in the 0.5-10.0 keV energy band show phase-locked variability, where the
flux increased by a factor of ~2 from minimum to maximum, being maximum near
periastron passage. The light curve in the soft energy band (0.5-2.0 keV) shows
two minima indicating the presence of two eclipses. However, the light curve in
the hard energy band (2.0-10.0 keV) shows only one minimum during the apastron
passage. The X-ray spectra of WR 25 were explained by a two-temperature plasma
model. Both the cool and the hot plasmas were constant at 0.628+/-0.008 and
2.75+/-0.06 keV throughout an orbital cycle, where the cooler plasma could be
due to the small scale shocks in a radiation-driven outflow and the high
temperature plasma could be due to the collision of winds. The column density
varied with the orbital phase and was found to be maximum after the periastron
passage, when the WN star is in front of the O star. The abundances of WR 25
were found to be non-solar. Optical V-band data of WR 25 also show the
phase-locked variability, being at maximum near periastron passage. The results
based on the present analysis indicate that WR 25 is a colliding wind binary
where the presence of soft X-rays is attributed to individual components;
however, hard X-rays are due to the collision of winds.

In the Solar System, interplanetary dust particles (IDPs) originating mainly
from asteroid collisions and cometary activities drift to the Earth orbit due
to the Poynting-Robertson drag. We analyzed the thermal emission from IDPs that
was observed by the first Japanese infrared astronomical satellite, AKARI. The
observed surface brightness in the trailing direction of the Earth orbit is
3.7% greater than that in the leading direction in the $9{\rm \mu m}$ band and
3.0% in the $18{\rm \mu m}$ band. In order to reveal dust properties causing
the leading-trailing surface brightness asymmetry, we numerically integrated
orbits of the Sun, the Earth, and a dust particle as a restricted three-body
problem including radiation from the Sun. The initial orbits of particles are
determined according to the orbits of main-belt asteroids or Jupiter-family
comets. The orbital trapping in mean motion resonances results in a significant
leading-trailing asymmetry so that intermediate sized dust (~10-100${\rm \mu
m}$) produces a greater asymmetry than the zodiacal light has. The
leading-trailing surface brightness difference integrated over the size
distribution of the asteroidal dust is obtained to be the values of 27.7% and
25.3% in the $9{\rm \mu m}$ and $18{\rm \mu m}$ bands, respectively. In
contrast, the brightness difference for cometary dust is calculated as the
values of 3.6% and 3.1% in the $9{\rm \mu m}$ and $18{\rm \mu m}$ bands,
respectively, if the maximum dust radius is set to be $s_{\rm max} = 3000{\rm
\mu m}$. Taking into account these values and their errors, we conclude that
the contribution of asteroidal dust to the zodiacal infrared emission is less
than ~10%, while cometary dust of the order of 1 mm mainly accounts for the
zodiacal light in infrared.

Variability at all observed wavelengths is a distinctive property of AGN.
Hard X-rays provide us with a view of the innermost regions of AGN, mostly
unbiased by absorption along the line of sight. Swift/BAT offers the unique
opportunity to follow, on time scales of days to years and with a regular
sampling, the 14-195 keV emission of the largest AGN sample available up to
date for this kind of investigation. We study the amplitude of the variations,
and their dependence on sub-class and on energy, for a sample of 110 radio
quiet and radio loud AGN selected from the BAT 58-month survey. About 80% of
the AGN in the sample are found to exhibit significant variability on months to
years time scales, radio loud sources being the most variable. The amplitude of
the variations and their energy dependence are incompatible with variability
being driven at hard X-rays by changes of the absorption column density. In
general, the variations in the 14-24 and 35-100 keV bands are well correlated,
suggesting a common origin of the variability across the BAT energy band.
However, radio quiet AGN display on average 10% larger variations at 14-24 keV
than at 35-100 keV and a softer-when-brighter behavior for most of the Seyfert
galaxies with detectable spectral variability on month time scale. In addition,
sources with harder spectra are found to be more variable than softer ones.
These properties are generally consistent with a variable power law continuum,
in flux and shape, pivoting at energies >~ 50 keV, to which a constant
reflection component is superposed. When the same time scales are considered,
the timing properties of AGN at hard X-rays are comparable to those at lower
energies, with at least some of the differences possibly ascribable to
components contributing differently in the two energy domains (e.g.,
reflection, absorption).

text: We present a novel computational framework combining the lattice Boltzmann method with an immersed boundary approach to predict the vascular transport of differently shaped particles. Our methodology enables the simulation of complex particle-particle and particle-wall interactions, allowing for a more accurate representation of the dynamic behavior of particles in blood flow.   We employed a multi-scale lattice Boltzmann approach to model the fluid dynamics, incorporating a dynamic viscosity model to account for the non-Newtonian properties of blood. The immersed boundary method was utilized to model the complex particle-wall interactions, enabling the simulation of particles with varying geometries, such as spheres, cylinders, and ellipsoids.   Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in predicting the transport behavior of differently shaped particles in a vascular network. The simulations show that the particle shape and size significantly impact the flow field and particle transport, with larger and more complex particles exhibiting greater resistance to flow and increased deposition.   Key findings include the identification of a correlation between particle diameter and deposition rate, as well as the impact of particle shape on the formation of recirculation zones in the flow field. Our results have important implications for the design and optimization of medical devices, such as stents and catheters, which must navigate complex vascular geometries and interact with particles suspended in blood. The proposed approach provides a powerful tool for predicting the vascular transport of differently shaped particles, enabling the development of more effective and targeted therapies.

text: In this study, we investigate the relationship between topology and field strength in spherical, anelastic dynamo simulations. Our work aims to address the unresolved question of how the topology of the system impacts the strength of the magnetic field generated within the dynamo. Through extensive simulations and analyses, we have discovered that certain topological configurations of the system lead to a significant increase in the strength of the magnetic field, while others result in a diminished field strength. We have identified key mechanisms that contribute to these variations, shedding light on the intricate interplay between the system's geometry and the resulting magnetic field properties. Our methodology involves solving the magnetohydrodynamic equations in a spherical, anelastic framework, allowing us to capture the complex dynamics of the system accurately. By systematically varying the topology and boundary conditions of the simulations, we have been able to discern patterns that illuminate the underlying factors influencing field strength. The implications of our findings extend to a better understanding of dynamo processes in natural systems, such as planetary cores and stellar interiors, where similar topological effects may play a crucial role in shaping magnetic fields.

We investigate the effective interactions between two nanoparticles (or
colloids) immersed in a solvent exhibiting two-phase separation. Using a
non-local density functional theory, we determine the dependence of the
effective potential on the separation of the nanoparticles when the solvent is
near bulk two-phase coexistence. If identical nanoparticles preferentially
adsorbing phase $\alpha$ are inserted into phase $\beta$, thick wetting layers
of the preferable phase $\alpha$ develop at their surfaces. At some particular
separation $h_b$ of the nanoparticles, the wetting layers connect to form a
single bridge, and the induced effective potential becomes strongly attractive
for all distances $h<h_b$. The bridging is a first order capillary condensation
like transition for all radii of the nanoparticles greater than the critical
radius $R_c$, the value of which was estimated to be approximately
$R_c\approx20\sigma$ for a temperature $T/T_c\approx0.9$, where $\sigma$ is the
size of the solvent (square-well) particles. For radii $R<R_c$ the process of
bridging is continuous. If the same particles are inserted into the preferable
phase $\alpha$, the only effective interaction between them is induced by the
short-ranged depletion potential. If the nanoparticles have opposite adsorption
preferences, only a single wetting layer forms around one of the nanoparticles
and the effective interaction is strongly repulsive in both phases. The
repulsion, induced by a disruption of the wetting film by the presence of the
second particle, is larger and slightly longer-ranged in a low density state.

This paper investigates the sum-rate gains brought by power allocation
strategies in multicell massive multipleinput multiple-output systems, assuming
time-division duplex transmission. For both uplink and downlink, we derive
tractable expressions for the achievable rate with zero-forcing receivers and
precoders respectively. To avoid high complexity joint optimization across the
network, we propose a scheduling mechanism for power allocation, where in a
single time slot, only cells that do not interfere with each other adjust their
transmit powers. Based on this, corresponding transmit power allocation
strategies are derived, aimed at maximizing the sum rate per-cell. These
schemes are shown to bring considerable gains over equal power allocation for
practical antenna configurations (e.g., up to a few hundred). However, with
fixed number of users (N), these gains diminish as M turns to infinity, and
equal power allocation becomes optimal. A different conclusion is drawn for the
case where both M and N grow large together, in which case: (i) improved rates
are achieved as M grows with fixed M/N ratio, and (ii) the relative gains over
the equal power allocation diminish as M/N grows. Moreover, we also provide
applicable values of M/N under an acceptable power allocation gain threshold,
which can be used as to determine when the proposed power allocation schemes
yield appreciable gains, and when they do not. From the network point of view,
the proposed scheduling approach can achieve almost the same performance as the
joint power allocation after one scheduling round, with much reduced
complexity.

text: Dark matter, an enigmatic substance accounting for approximately 27% of the total mass-energy content of the universe, has remained elusive due to its lack of electromagnetic interactions. The conventional understanding of dark matter models includes the existence of a hidden sector. However, recent theoretical developments propose the possibility of exciting dark matter directly via its interactions with the Standard Model particles. One such model, the "dark dipole" model, predicts the emission of a 3.55 keV line from WIMP (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) annihilation or decay. In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of the possible origin of this line using X-ray observations and astrophysical simulations. We examine the spectral features and spatial distributions of the line in various astrophysical environments, including the Galactic halo, the intracluster medium of galaxy clusters, and active galactic nuclei. Our findings suggest that the 3.55 keV line could originate from radiative decay of excited WIMPs, which do not require a hidden sector. We also discuss potential experimental tests of this model and its implications for the interpretation of observed astrophysical phenomena. This research provides new insights into the nature of dark matter and challenges the conventional assumptions of dark matter models.

text: This study presents a stability-reversibility map that integrates the behavior of elasticity, plasticity, yielding, and jamming observed in hard sphere glasses. Through a comprehensive analysis, we identified a common framework where these distinct phenomena can be unified under a single theoretical approach. The methodology involved extensive molecular dynamics simulations to track the mechanical responses of glassy systems under various stress conditions. Key insights were derived by systematically varying stress levels and observing the transitions between elastic, plastic, yield, and jammed states. Results revealed that at specific stress points, transitions between these states are reversible, providing evidence for their interrelated nature. This work not only elucidates the underlying mechanisms but also offers a novel perspective on how different material behaviors can coexist within the same system, thereby enriching our understanding of the complex mechanics of hard sphere glasses.

text: We investigate the phenomenon of helium enrichment and carbon-star production within metal-rich stellar populations, addressing the associated challenges of understanding these complex astrophysical processes. Through a comprehensive analysis, we demonstrate that increased metallicity significantly influences the stellar evolution pathways leading to helium enrichment and the formation of carbon stars. Utilizing advanced stellar evolution models, we simulate a range of initial parameters, including metallicity, mass, and rotational velocity, to explore their effects on nucleosynthesis and subsequent chemical enrichment in stellar atmospheres.  Our results indicate a clear correlation between higher metallicity and enhanced helium production, attributing this relationship to the increased efficiency of double helium shell flashes in advanced stages of stellar evolution. Furthermore, we elucidate the conditions under which a considerable fraction of stars evolve into carbon-rich entities, highlighting the roles of mass-loss mechanisms and the interaction between stellar wind and metallicity.   We also identify key threshold values of metallicity that trigger significant changes in helium content and carbon star prevalence. The implications of our findings extend to the broader understanding of chemical evolution in galaxies, particularly in environments rich in heavy elements. Our study contributes to the existing literature by providing a deeper insight into the interplay of metallicity and stellar evolution, paving the way for future investigations of the impact of these factors on star formation and galactic chemical enrichment. We advocate for further observational studies to validate our theoretical predictions and enhance our comprehension of these stellar phenomena.

text: We investigate the impact of transverse momentum resummation effects on W^+W^- measurements, a crucial process in the Standard Model of particle physics. Our analysis focuses on the resummation of transverse momentum corrections to the W boson pair production cross-section, which are essential for precise measurements at the LHC. Through a combination of theoretical models and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that transverse momentum resummation effects can significantly impact the accuracy of W^+W^- measurements, particularly at high energies and large transverse momenta.  We employ a state-of-the-art resummation framework, which incorporates next-to-leading logarithmic (NLL) and next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic (NNLL) corrections to the transverse momentum distribution of the W boson pair. Our results show that NNLL resummation effects can improve the accuracy of W^+W^- measurements by up to 20%, particularly at high energies and large transverse momenta. We also explore the impact of resummation effects on the extraction of key physics parameters, such as the W boson mass and the strong coupling constant.  Our analysis highlights the importance of transverse momentum resummation effects in W^+W^- measurements and demonstrates the need for a more precise theoretical treatment of these effects. The results of this study have significant implications for the interpretation of future W^+W^- measurements at the LHC and other colliders, and provide a foundation for future resummation improvements and experimental searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

text: We investigated the geophysical applicability of atomic clocks in direct continental geoid mapping, utilizing a novel approach that combines high-resolution gravity measurements with precise timekeeping. Our primary objective was to assess the feasibility of leveraging atomic clocks to improve the accuracy of continental geoid models.   Through a comprehensive analysis of existing data and theoretical models, we identified significant discrepancies between traditional geoid models and observed gravity anomalies, highlighting the need for enhanced resolution and accuracy. We then developed a novel methodology that integrates atomic clock data with high-resolution gravity measurements, allowing for the precise calculation of the geoid.   Our results indicate that atomic clock data can significantly improve the accuracy of continental geoid models, enabling the detection of subtle variations in the Earth's gravitational field. Notably, our approach demonstrated a reduction in error of up to 30% compared to traditional methods.   Key to our success was the adoption of a novel data fusion strategy, which effectively combined the strengths of atomic clock data and high-resolution gravity measurements. This approach enabled the generation of high-precision geoid models, with implications for a range of geophysical applications, including seismic hazard assessment, oceanography, and natural resource management.

We present the first images of the pulsar wind nebula (PWN) MSH 15-52 in the
hard X-ray band (>8 keV), as measured with the Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope
Array (NuSTAR). Overall, the morphology of the PWN as measured by NuSTAR in the
3-7 keV band is similar to that seen in Chandra high-resolution imaging.
However, the spatial extent decreases with energy, which we attribute to
synchrotron energy losses as the particles move away from the shock. The
hard-band maps show a relative deficit of counts in the northern region towards
the RCW 89 thermal remnant, with significant asymmetry. We find that the
integrated PWN spectra measured with NuSTAR and Chandra suggest that there is a
spectral break at 6 keV which may be explained by a break in the
synchrotron-emitting electron distribution at ~200 TeV and/or imperfect cross
calibration. We also measure spatially resolved spectra, showing that the
spectrum of the PWN softens away from the central pulsar B1509-58, and that
there exists a roughly sinusoidal variation of spectral hardness in the
azimuthal direction. We discuss the results using particle flow models. We find
non-monotonic structure in the variation with distance of spectral hardness
within 50" of the pulsar moving in the jet direction, which may imply particle
and magnetic-field compression by magnetic hoop stress as previously suggested
for this source. We also present 2-D maps of spectral parameters and find an
interesting shell-like structure in the NH map. We discuss possible origins of
the shell-like structure and their implications.

text: In high-energy particle collisions, such as those occurring in heavy-ion experiments, the measurement of charged jet suppression is crucial for understanding the underlying physics of the collision. The suppression of charged jets in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=2.76$ TeV is a key aspect of the study of the quark-gluon plasma. This phenomenon is thought to be related to the energy loss of partons as they interact with the hot and dense quark-gluon plasma created in these collisions.  The objective of this research is to measure the charged jet suppression in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=2.76$ TeV using a combination of data from the ALICE experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. The measurements were taken using the central exclusive $\rho$-meson decay channel, which allows for the separation of jets from the underlying event. The data were analyzed using a Bayesian approach to account for systematic uncertainties and to improve the precision of the measurements.  The key findings of this research show that the charged jet suppression is consistent with previous measurements and is in good agreement with theoretical models. The results indicate that the suppression is strongest for jets with higher transverse momenta, and that the suppression is more pronounced in the most central collisions. The measurements provide valuable insights into the properties of the quark-gluon plasma and the energy loss of partons in these collisions.  The conclusions of this research highlight the importance of measuring charged jet suppression in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=2.76$ TeV. The results demonstrate that the suppression is a robust feature of the quark-gluon plasma and provide a new tool for studying the properties of this state of matter. The measurements also provide a unique opportunity to test theoretical models of jet suppression and to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying physics of these collisions.

To study the evolution of protoplanetary dust aggregates, we performed
experiments with up to 2600 collisions between single, highly-porous dust
aggregates and a solid plate. The dust aggregates consisted of spherical
SiO$_2$ grains with 1.5$\mu$m diameter and had an initial volume filling factor
(the volume fraction of material) of $\phi_0=0.15$. The aggregates were put
onto a vibrating baseplate and, thus, performed multiple collisions with the
plate at a mean velocity of 0.2 m s$^{-1}$. The dust aggregates were observed
by a high-speed camera to measure their size which apparently decreased over
time as a measure for their compaction. After 1000 collisions the volume
filling factor was increased by a factor of two, while after $\sim2000$
collisions it converged to an equilibrium of $\phi\approx0.36$. In few
experiments the aggregate fragmented, although the collision velocity was well
below the canonical fragmentation threshold of $\sim1$ m s$^{-1}$. The
compaction of the aggregate has an influence on the surface-to-mass ratio and
thereby the dynamic behavior and relative velocities of dust aggregates in the
protoplanetary nebula. Moreover, macroscopic material parameters, namely the
tensile strength, shear strength, and compressive strength, are altered by the
compaction of the aggregates, which has an influence on their further
collisional behavior. The occurrence of fragmentation requires a reassessment
of the fragmentation threshold velocity.

text: In this study, we introduce KL-UCB-switch, an algorithm designed to optimize regret bounds for stochastic multi-armed bandit problems. Our approach addresses both distribution-dependent and distribution-free settings, ensuring robust performance across various scenarios. The algorithm leverages the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to dynamically switch between exploitation and exploration strategies based on the observed arm distributions. Through rigorous theoretical analysis, we establish upper bounds on the cumulative regret that are both distribution-dependent and distribution-free. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that KL-UCB-switch outperforms existing methods, particularly in scenarios where arm distributions are non-uniform or unknown. Key insights include the effectiveness of the KL divergence-based switching mechanism and the adaptability of our approach to different problem complexities. This work not only enhances our understanding of stochastic bandit theory but also provides practical tools for real-world applications involving decision-making under uncertainty.

text: In the domain of quantum information theory, the construction of orthogonal product bases that are locally indistinguishable plays a critical role in quantum state discrimination and teleportation schemes. This study aims to develop a systematic approach for constructing locally indistinguishable orthogonal product bases within the framework of an $m \otimes n$ quantum system, where $m$ and $n$ represent the dimensions of the respective subsystems. We employ a mathematical framework that leverages properties of finite-dimensional vector spaces and group representation theory to identify and construct these bases. A series of theoretical results are derived which confirm the presence of locally indistinguishable properties in the constructed bases—specifically, that measurements performed locally cannot distinguish between certain orthogonal states. The results demonstrate that for a given integer $k$, it is possible to construct a set of $k$ orthogonal product states in an $m \otimes n$ bipartite system, such that no local measurement can ascertain which state has been prepared. This finding has significant implications for quantum communication protocols, enhancing the robustness of information transfer against local eavesdropping. In conclusion, the proposed method not only enriches the existing literature on orthogonal product bases but also paves the way for practical applications in quantum computing and cryptography, where the security of information is paramount. The construction algorithm is outlined, and examples illustrate the effectiveness and applicability of the proposed bases in various scenarios.

text: We report the development of ultrahigh-gain phototransistors based on graphene-MoS2 heterostructures, which exhibit exceptional optoelectronic properties. Our work aimed to overcome the limitations of traditional phototransistors, such as low gain and limited sensitivity, by leveraging the unique properties of graphene and MoS2. We fabricated heterostructures by depositing graphene on top of MoS2, and then integrated these structures into phototransistor devices.  Through systematic optimization of the heterostructure parameters, we achieved a significant increase in the gain of the phototransistors, reaching up to 30 dB. Furthermore, we observed a substantial enhancement in the sensitivity of the devices, with a detection limit of 10^-7 A/cm^2. The high gain and sensitivity of our phototransistors are attributed to the excellent light-matter interactions between graphene and MoS2.  Our results demonstrate the potential of graphene-MoS2 heterostructures for the development of high-performance phototransistors. The key to our success lies in the optimized design of the heterostructure, which enables the efficient transfer of optical energy to the phototransistor. Our findings have important implications for the development of next-generation optoelectronic devices, such as high-sensitivity photodetectors and high-speed optoelectronic switches.

text: This study investigates the placement of an obstacle with dihedral symmetry centered at a designated point within a circular domain (disk) to maximize the fundamental Dirichlet eigenvalue. Through rigorous mathematical analysis and computational simulations, we explore various configurations that adhere to the symmetry constraint. The methodology involves solving the corresponding boundary value problem numerically and comparing the eigenvalues for different placements. Key findings indicate that placing the obstacle such that its axis of symmetry aligns with the diameter of the disk yields the highest eigenvalue. This result challenges previous assumptions about optimal configurations and provides insights into how symmetry influences spectral properties in domains with complex geometries. The study contributes to the understanding of eigenvalue optimization problems in confined spaces, offering potential applications in wave propagation studies.

text: We investigated the uniqueness of solutions to the periodic 3D Gross-Pitaevskii hierarchy, a fundamental model in Bose-Einstein condensation. Our work aimed to address the longstanding problem of whether multiple solutions exist for a given set of parameters. Through a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we derived a set of necessary conditions for the existence of multiple solutions, which we termed the "multiplicity criterion." This criterion revealed that the multiplicity of solutions is determined by the interplay between the nonlinearity of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation and the periodic boundary conditions.  Our numerical simulations and analytical calculations revealed that the multiplicity criterion can be satisfied under specific conditions, leading to the existence of multiple solutions. We found that the number of solutions is closely related to the topology of the phase space, and that the solutions are often connected by a network of periodic orbits. Furthermore, we discovered that the multiplicity of solutions can be used to predict the stability of the solutions, allowing us to identify the conditions under which multiple solutions coexist.  Our results demonstrate that the periodic 3D Gross-Pitaevskii hierarchy is a highly non-trivial system, and that the existence of multiple solutions is a generic phenomenon. The multiplicity criterion provides a powerful tool for understanding the behavior of solutions to the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, and has important implications for the study of Bose-Einstein condensation and other related systems.

text: Neutron stars, astrophysical objects composed predominantly of neutron-rich matter, present a unique laboratory for probing the properties of high-density nuclear physics. Nuclear constraints on the structure and composition of neutron star crusts have long been a subject of interest, as these constraints can shed light on the behavior of nuclear matter under extreme conditions. In this study, we investigate the impact of various isoscalar and isovector nuclear interactions on the structure and composition of neutron star crusts. Utilizing density functional theory and a self-consistent density functional approach, we calculate the equation of state (EOS) for neutron-rich nuclear matter and study the resulting crustal properties. Our results indicate that the crustal composition and structure are highly dependent on the choice of nuclear interactions, particularly the density-dependent terms in isovector channels. We find that the inclusion of density-dependent symmetry energy terms leads to significantly more complex crustal structure, with the presence of multiple layers and transitions between different nuclear phases. Our findings not only provide valuable insights into the neutron star crust properties but also highlight the importance of including density-dependent nuclear interactions in theoretical models. Furthermore, these results have significant implications for future experiments aiming to probe the neutron star interior using X-ray and neutrino observations.

Motivated by the latest improved measurements of B-meson decays, we make a
comprehensive analysis of the impact of a family non-universal $Z^{\prime}$
boson on $B_s-\bar{B}_s$ mixing and two-body hadronic B-meson decays, all being
characterized by the quark-level $b\to s$ transition. Explicitly 22 decay modes
and the related 52 observables are considered, and some interesting
correlations between them are also carefully examined. Firstly, the allowed
oases of $b-s-Z^{\prime}$ coupling parameters $|B^{L,R}_{sb}|$ and
$\phi^{L,R}_s$ are extracted from $B_s-\bar{B}_s$ mixing. Then, in the "SM
limit"~({\it i.e.,} no new types of $Z^{\prime}$-induced four-quark operators
arise compared to the SM case), we study the $Z^{\prime}$ effects on $B\to\pi
K$, $\pi K^{\ast}$ and $\rho K$ decays. It is found that a new weak phase
$\phi^{L}_s\sim -90^{\circ}$ is crucial for resolving the observed "$\pi K$ CP
puzzle" and the allowed oases of the other $Z^{\prime}$ coupling parameters are
also strongly restricted. Moreover, the $Z^{\prime}$ effects on $\bar{B}_s\to K
K$, $K K^{\ast}$ and $\pi^0 \phi$ decays, being induced by the same quark-level
$b\to s q\bar{q}~(q=u,d)$ transitions, are also investigated. Especially, it is
found that the decay $\bar{B}_s \to \pi^0 \phi$, once measured, would play a
key role in revealing the observed "$\pi K$ CP puzzle" and probing possible new
physics hints. Finally, to check the non-universality of $Z^{\prime}$ couplings
to light-quark pairs, we have studied the $B\to \phi K$ decays in detail and
found that the left-handed $s-s-Z^{\prime}$ coupling is different from the
$d-d-Z^{\prime}$ one, which is due to the large $A_{CP}^{dir}(B^-\to\phi K^-)$
reported by the BaBar collaboration.

text: We have investigated the effects of exact nonlinear inhomogeneities on the large-scale structure of the universe in the context of $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. Our analysis focused on the impact of these inhomogeneities on the matter power spectrum, which is a crucial parameter in the study of cosmic structure formation.   Through a combination of analytical and numerical simulations, we have demonstrated that exact nonlinear inhomogeneities can significantly alter the matter power spectrum, leading to a reduction in the amplitude of the large-scale fluctuations and a modification of the characteristic scale of the power spectrum.   Our results indicate that these inhomogeneities can be described by a non-trivial modification to the linear matter power spectrum, which we have termed the "inhomogeneous correction." We have shown that this correction can be incorporated into the standard $\Lambda$CDM model through a simple, non-local correction term, which can be evaluated using a Fourier transform.  Our analysis has also highlighted the importance of considering the interplay between inhomogeneities and the large-scale structure of the universe. We have found that the inhomogeneous correction can lead to a non-zero value of the curvature perturbation, which is a fundamental quantity in the study of cosmic structure formation. Our findings have implications for our understanding of the universe on large scales and suggest that exact nonlinear inhomogeneities may play a more significant role in the formation of structure than previously thought.

Consider an asynchronous network in a shared-memory environment consisting of
n nodes. Assume that up to f of the nodes might be Byzantine (n > 12f), where
the adversary is full-information and dynamic (sometimes called adaptive). In
addition, the non-Byzantine nodes may undergo transient failures. Nodes advance
in atomic steps, which consist of reading all registers, performing some
calculation and writing to all registers.
  This paper contains three main contributions. First, the clock-function
problem is defined, which is a generalization of the clock synchronization
problem. This generalization encapsulates previous clock synchronization
problem definitions while extending them to the current paper's model. Second,
a randomized asynchronous self-stabilizing Byzantine tolerant clock
synchronization algorithm is presented.
  In the construction of the clock synchronization algorithm, a building block
that ensures different nodes advance at similar rates is developed. This
feature is the third contribution of the paper. It is self-stabilizing and
Byzantine tolerant and can be used as a building block for different algorithms
that operate in an asynchronous self-stabilizing Byzantine model.
  The convergence time of the presented algorithm is exponential. Observe that
in the asynchronous setting the best known full-information dynamic Byzantine
agreement also has expected exponential convergence time, even though currently
there is no known reduction between the two.

We study the problem of counting the number of popular matchings in a given
instance. A popular matching instance consists of agents A and houses H, where
each agent ranks a subset of houses according to their preferences. A matching
is an assignment of agents to houses. A matching M is more popular than
matching M' if the number of agents that prefer M to M' is more than the number
of people that prefer M' to M. A matching M is called popular if there exists
no matching more popular than M. McDermid and Irving gave a poly-time algorithm
for counting the number of popular matchings when the preference lists are
strictly ordered.
  We first consider the case of ties in preference lists. Nasre proved that the
problem of counting the number of popular matching is #P-hard when there are
ties. We give an FPRAS for this problem.
  We then consider the popular matching problem where preference lists are
strictly ordered but each house has a capacity associated with it. We give a
switching graph characterization of popular matchings in this case. Such
characterizations were studied earlier for the case of strictly ordered
preference lists (McDermid and Irving) and for preference lists with ties
(Nasre). We use our characterization to prove that counting popular matchings
in capacitated case is #P-hard.

text: This study explores the structure of quasiparticles and their fusion algebra within fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states, aiming to uncover the underlying symmetries and topological properties that govern these exotic phases of matter. We investigate the nature of composite fermions as the primary building blocks of FQH states, focusing on their interactions and the formation of quasiparticles through the exchange processes. Utilizing numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we identify distinct types of quasiparticles, such as edge excitations and vortices, and analyze their behavior under various conditions.  The key innovation lies in our approach to defining the fusion algebra among these quasiparticles, which allows us to predict how they combine or merge to form new composite objects. This algebraic framework not only simplifies the description of complex FQH systems but also provides insights into the classification of different FQH phases based on the fusion rules. Our findings reveal that the fusion algebra is closely tied to the topological order of the system, suggesting a deeper connection between quasiparticle interactions and the global topology of FQH states.  Through rigorous testing of our model against existing experimental data and theoretical predictions, we validate the accuracy of our method and its applicability across a wide range of FQH systems. The results contribute significantly to our understanding of quasiparticle dynamics in FQH states and pave the way for future studies exploring applications in condensed matter physics and quantum computing.

text: This study investigates stellar halos in galaxies simulated within the Illustris project, focusing on Milky Way-mass systems. We analyze the spatial distribution, kinematics, and metallicity gradients of stars in these halos to understand their formation histories. Our methodology involves detailed spectral analysis and modeling of stellar populations using multi-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations. Results indicate that the stellar halos are predominantly dominated by low-metallicity stars, consistent with predictions from theoretical models. Additionally, we observe a correlation between the concentration of the stellar halo and the mass accretion history of the host galaxy, suggesting that tidal stripping plays a significant role in shaping these structures. The key findings highlight the importance of considering both internal and external processes in understanding the formation and evolution of Milky Way-like galaxies.

text:
Despite the intense theoretical and experimental effort, an understanding of
the superconducting pairing mechanism of the high-temperature superconductors
is still lacking. An additional puzzle is the unknown connection between the
superconducting gap and the so-called pseudogap which is a central property of
the most unusual normal state. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy
(ARPES) measurements have revealed a gap-like behavior on parts of the Fermi
surface, leaving a non-gapped segment known as Fermi arc around the diagonal of
the Brillouin zone. Starting from the $t$-$J$ model, in this paper we present a
microscopic approach to investigate physical properties of the pseudogap phase
in the framework of a novel renormalization scheme called PRM. This approach is
based on a stepwise elimination of high-energy transitions using unitary
transformations. We arrive at a renormalized 'free' Hamiltonian for correlated
electrons. The ARPES spectral function along the Fermi surface turns out to be
in good agreement with experiment: We find well-defined excitation peaks around
$\omega=0$ near the nodal direction, which become strongly suppressed around
the antinodal point. The origin of the pseudogap can be traced back to a
suppression of spectral weight from incoherent excitations in a small
$\omega$-range around the Fermi energy. In a subsequent paper, also the
supercunducting phase at moderate hole doping will be discussed within the PRM
approach.

text: This study investigates the impact of Quark Sector Minimal Flavor Violation (QSMFV) on neutrinoless double beta decay (0νββ). Previous works have shown that flavor violation at the quark level can influence nuclear matrix elements (NMEs), which are crucial for calculating the half-life of 0νββ processes. We employed a comprehensive theoretical framework incorporating QSMFV effects within the Standard Model extension. Our methodology involved detailed calculations of NMEs using effective field theory techniques, taking into account various contributions from charged-current and neutral-current interactions. The results indicate that QSMFV introduces additional terms proportional to the fermionic mass splittings, which significantly affect the 0νββ decay rate. Notably, we found that the inclusion of these QSMFV effects leads to a reduction in the half-life compared to predictions based solely on the Standard Model. This research underscores the importance of considering flavor violation beyond the Standard Model framework when assessing the feasibility of future 0νββ experiments.

[abridged] Three years of optical monitoring of the low-mass X-ray binary
(LMXB) 4U 1957+11 is presented. The source was observed in V, R and i-bands
using the Faulkes Telescopes North and South. The light curve is dominated by
long-term variations which are correlated (at the > 3 sigma level) with the
RXTE ASM soft X-ray flux. The variations span one magnitude in all three
filters. We find no evidence for periodicities in our light curves, contrary to
a previous short-timescale optical study in which the flux varied on a 9.3-hour
sinusoidal period by a smaller amplitude. The optical spectral energy
distribution is blue and typical of LMXBs in outburst, as is the power law
index of the correlation beta = 0.5, where F_{nu,OPT} propto F_X^beta. The
discrete cross-correlation function reveals a peak at an X-ray lag of 2 - 14
days, which could be the viscous timescale. However, adopting the least squares
method the strongest correlation is at a lag of 0 +/- 4 days, consistent with
X-ray reprocessing on the surface of the disc. We therefore constrain the
optical lag behind X-ray to be between -14 and +4 days. In addition, we use the
optical - X-ray luminosity diagram for LMXBs as a diagnostic tool to constrain
the nature of the compact object in 4U 1957+11, since black hole (BH) and
neutron star (NS) sources reside in different regions of this diagram. If the
system contains a BH (as is the currently favoured hypothesis), its distance
must exceed ~ 20 kpc for the optical and X-ray luminosities to be consistent
with other soft state BH systems. For distances < 20 kpc, the data lie in a
region of the diagram populated only by NS sources. 4U 1957+11 is unique: it is
either the only BH LMXB to exist in an apparent persistent soft state, or it is
a NS LMXB which behaves like a black hole.

Aims: We present a polarimetric and spectroscopic study of the persistent
ultra compact X-ray binary 4U 0614+091 aimed at searching for the emission of a
relativistic particle jet and at unveiling the orbital period of the system.
Methods: We obtained r-band polarimetric observations with the Telescopio
Nazionale Galileo (TNG) equipped with the PAOLO polarimeter and with the Nordic
Optical Telescope (NOT) equipped with the ALFOSC instrument, covering ~ 2 hours
and ~ 0.5 hours observations, respectively. We carried out low resolution
spectroscopy of the system using the ESO Very Large Telescope equipped with
FORS1 for ~ 1.5 hours (16 spectra covering the range 430-800 nm). Results: The
polarimetric analysis performed starting from the TNG dataset revealed a
polarisation degree in the r-band of 3 % +/- 1 %. From the NOT dataset, due to
the lower S/N ratio, we could obtain only a 3 sigma upper limit of 3.4 %. From
the joining of a spectroscopic and photometric analysis, through the study of
the equivalent width variations of the CII 724 nm line and the r-band light
curve, we could find a hint of a ~ 45 min periodicity. Conclusions: A
polarisation degree P of ~ 3 % in the r-band is consistent with the emission of
a relativistic particle jet, which is supposed to emit intrinsically linearly
polarised synchrotron radiation. Since no variations of P with time have been
detected, and the accretion disc of the system does not contain ionised
hydrogen, scattering by free electrons in the accretion disc has been rejected.
The period of ~ 45 min obtained through the analysis of the system light curve
and of the equivalent width variations of the selected spectral line is
probably linked to the presence of a hot spot or a superhump in the accretion
disc, and lead to an orbital period > 1 hour for the binary system.

text: The concept of holographic renormalization has been a subject of intense debate in theoretical physics, with various interpretations and applications across different frameworks. At its core, holographic renormalization is a method for resolving the ultraviolet divergences that arise in quantum field theories, which describe the behavior of fundamental particles and forces. By employing a canonical transformation, holographic renormalization offers a novel approach to addressing these divergences, providing a more unified and coherent understanding of the interplay between gravity and quantum mechanics.  This research paper aims to explore the relationship between holographic renormalization and canonical transformations, with a focus on their implications for our understanding of spacetime and the behavior of matter and energy within it. Through a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we investigate the conditions under which holographic renormalization can be viewed as a canonical transformation, and examine the resulting constraints on the theory.  Our key findings suggest that holographic renormalization can indeed be cast as a canonical transformation, with significant implications for the renormalization group flow and the holographic principle. We also demonstrate that this approach provides a more complete and consistent description of the theory, resolving long-standing issues related to the behavior of quantum systems in strong gravitational fields.  Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between gravity, quantum mechanics, and renormalization, with potential applications in a wide range of areas, from condensed matter physics to cosmology and theoretical particle physics.

text: The rapid growth of vehicles on roads has led to an increasing need for efficient and accurate automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) systems. Traditional ALPR methods often rely on static images and are vulnerable to various factors such as lighting conditions, weather, and occlusion. To address these limitations, this study proposes a robust real-time automatic license plate recognition system based on the You Only Look Once (YOLO) detector.   The YOLO detector is a state-of-the-art object detection algorithm that has shown impressive performance in various applications. However, its application in ALPR has not been extensively explored. This study aims to develop a robust and efficient ALPR system using the YOLO detector, which can effectively handle real-world scenarios with varying lighting conditions and occlusions.   The proposed system utilizes a pre-processing stage to enhance the quality of the input images, followed by the application of the YOLO detector to detect license plates. The detected plates are then processed using a custom-designed algorithm to extract the license plate number. The system is evaluated using a large-scale dataset and compared with existing ALPR systems.   The results show that the proposed system achieves a high accuracy of 95% in detecting license plates and a real-time processing speed of 30 frames per second. The system's robustness is demonstrated through its ability to handle various lighting conditions and occlusions. The proposed system has significant implications for real-time traffic monitoring, surveillance, and smart city applications.

Through the Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) formalism, quantum-scale
device simulation can be performed with the inclusion of electron-phonon
scattering. However, the simulation of realistically sized devices under the
NEGF formalism typically requires prohibitive amounts of memory and computation
time. Two of the most demanding computational problems for NEGF simulation
involve mathematical operations with structured matrices called semiseparable
matrices. In this work, we present parallel approaches for these computational
problems which allow for efficient distribution of both memory and computation
based upon the underlying device structure. This is critical when simulating
realistically sized devices due to the aforementioned computational burdens.
First, we consider determining a distributed compact representation for the
retarded Green's function matrix $G^{R}$. This compact representation is exact
and allows for any entry in the matrix to be generated through the inherent
semiseparable structure. The second parallel operation allows for the
computation of electron density and current characteristics for the device.
Specifically, matrix products between the distributed representation for the
semiseparable matrix $G^{R}$ and the self-energy scattering terms in
$\Sigma^{<}$ produce the less-than Green's function $G^{<}$. As an illustration
of the computational efficiency of our approach, we stably generate the
mobility for nanowires with cross-sectional sizes of up to 4.5nm, assuming an
atomistic model with scattering.

Critical properties of the two-dimensional $XY$ model involving solely
nematic-like biquadratic and bicubic terms are investigated by spin-wave
analysis and Monte Carlo simulation. It is found that, even though neither of
the nematic-like terms alone can induce magnetic ordering, their coexistence
and competition leads to an extended phase of magnetic quasi-long-range order
phase, wedged between the two nematic-like phases induced by the respective
couplings. Thus, except for the muticritical point, at which all the phases
meet, for any finite value of the coupling parameters ratio there are two phase
transition: one from the paramagnetic phase to one of the two nematic-like
phases followed by another one at lower temperatures to the magnetic phase. The
finite-size scaling analysis indicate that the phase transitions between the
magnetic and nematic-like phases belong to the Ising and three-state Potts
universality classes. Inside the competition-induced algebraic magnetic phase
the spin-pair correlation function is found to decay even much more slowly than
in the standard $XY$ model with purely magnetic interactions. Such a magnetic
phase is characterized by an extremely low vortex-antivortex pair density
attaining a minimum close to the point at which the biquadratic and bicubic
couplings are of about equal strengths and thus competition is the fiercest.

text: This study aims to quantify the hydrodynamical effects on the growth of protoplanetary dust grains, a crucial process in the formation of planets. Background research indicates that dust grains in protoplanetary disks are subject to various hydrodynamical forces, including turbulence, shear, and radiation pressure, which can significantly impact their growth and evolution. However, the magnitude of these effects remains poorly understood, particularly in the context of dust growth in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks.  The objective of this research is to investigate the hydrodynamical effects on protoplanetary dust growth using a combination of numerical simulations and theoretical models. We employ a 3D hydrodynamical code to simulate the dynamics of protoplanetary disks and dust grains, taking into account the effects of turbulence, shear, and radiation pressure. We also develop a theoretical framework to describe the growth of dust grains in response to these hydrodynamical forces.  Our results show that hydrodynamical effects can significantly impact the growth of protoplanetary dust grains, particularly in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. We find that turbulence and shear can lead to the formation of dust aggregates, while radiation pressure can cause dust grains to be accelerated and scattered. Our simulations also reveal that the growth of dust grains is highly dependent on the strength of hydrodynamical forces and the properties of the protoplanetary disk.  Overall, this study provides new insights into the hydrodynamical effects on protoplanetary dust growth, which is essential for understanding the formation of planets and the delivery of water and organic molecules to terrestrial planets. Our findings have significant implications for the development of planetary formation models and the search for life beyond Earth.

text: This study investigates the phenomena of charge expulsion, spin Meissner effect, and charge inhomogeneity within superconducting materials. Through a series of comprehensive experiments, we observed the expulsion of mobile charges from regions near surfaces or interfaces, which is a critical aspect of the spin Meissner effect. We also identified significant charge inhomogeneities that arise due to these effects, leading to spatial variations in magnetic fields and resistance. Employing advanced microscopy techniques and spectroscopic methods, we systematically analyzed these phenomena across various superconductors. Our key findings reveal that the interplay between charge expulsion and the spin Meissner effect significantly impacts the macroscopic properties of superconductors, including their critical temperature and coherence length. The methodologies employed include angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), and time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations. These results contribute to our understanding of superconductivity at the microscopic level and pave the way for novel applications in quantum computing and energy-efficient devices.

Quantum circuit synthesis is the process in which an arbitrary unitary
operation is decomposed into a sequence of gates from a universal set,
typically one which a quantum computer can implement both efficiently and
fault-tolerantly. As physical implementations of quantum computers improve, the
need is growing for tools which can effectively synthesize components of the
circuits and algorithms they will run. Existing algorithms for exact,
multi-qubit circuit synthesis scale exponentially in the number of qubits and
circuit depth, leaving synthesis intractable for circuits on more than a
handful of qubits. Even modest improvements in circuit synthesis procedures may
lead to significant advances, pushing forward the boundaries of not only the
size of solvable circuit synthesis problems, but also in what can be realized
physically as a result of having more efficient circuits.
  We present a method for quantum circuit synthesis using deterministic walks.
Also termed pseudorandom walks, these are walks in which once a starting point
is chosen, its path is completely determined. We apply our method to construct
a parallel framework for circuit synthesis, and implement one such version
performing optimal $T$-count synthesis over the Clifford+$T$ gate set. We use
our software to present examples where parallelization offers a significant
speedup on the runtime, as well as directly confirm that the 4-qubit 1-bit full
adder has optimal $T$-count 7 and $T$-depth 3.

We study the secular, hierarchical three-body problem to first-order in a
post-Newtonian expansion of General Relativity. We expand the first-order
post-Newtonian Hamiltonian to leading-order in the ratio of the semi-major axis
of the two orbits. In addition to the well-known terms that correspond to the
GR precession of the inner and outer orbits, we find a new secular
post-Newtonian interaction term that can affect the long-term evolution of the
triple. We explore the parameter space for highly inclined and eccentric
systems, where the Kozai-Lidov mechanism can produce large-amplitude
oscillations in the eccentricities. The standard lore, i.e., that General
Relativity effects suppress eccentricity, is only consistent with the parts of
phase space where the General Relativity timescales are several orders of
magnitude shorter than the secular Newtonian one. In other parts of phase
space, however, post-Newtonian corrections combined with the three body ones,
can excite eccentricities. In particular, for systems where the General
Relativity timescale is comparable to the secular Newtonian timescales, the
three-body interactions give rise to a resonant-like eccentricity excitation.
Furthermore, for triples with a comparable-mass inner binary, where the
eccentric Kozai-Lidov mechanism is suppressed, post-Newtonian corrections can
further increase the eccentricity and lead to orbital flips even when the
timescale of the former is much longer than the timescale of the secular
Kozai-Lidov quadrupole perturbations.

We introduce an innovative three-dimensional spectral approach (three band
parameter space with polyhedrons) that can be used for both qualitative and
quantitative analyses improving the characterization of surface heterogeneity
of (4) Vesta. It is an advanced and more robust methodology compared to the
standard two-dimensional spectral approach (two band parameter space). The Dawn
Framing Camera (FC) color data obtained during High Altitude Mapping Orbit
(resolution ~ 60 m/pixel) is used. The main focus is on the
howardite-eucrite-diogenite (HED) lithologies containing carbonaceous
chondritic material, olivine, and impact-melt. The archived spectra of HEDs and
their mixtures, from RELAB, HOSERLab and USGS databases as well as our
laboratory-measured spectra are used for this study. Three-dimensional convex
polyhedrons are defined using computed band parameter values of laboratory
spectra. Polyhedrons based on the parameters of Band Tilt
(R0.92{\mu}m/R0.96{\mu}m), Mid Ratio
((R0.75{\mu}m/R0.83{\mu}m)/(R0.83{\mu}m/R0.92{\mu}m)) and reflectance at 0.55
{\mu}m (R0.55{\mu}m) are chosen for the present analysis. An algorithm in IDL
programming language is employed to assign FC data points to the respective
polyhedrons. The Arruntia region in the northern hemisphere of Vesta is
selected for a case study because of its geological and mineralogical
importance. We observe that this region is eucrite-dominated howarditic in
composition. The extent of olivine-rich exposures within an area of 2.5 crater
radii is ~ 12% larger than the previous finding (Thangjam et al., 2014).
Lithologies of nearly pure CM2-chondrite, olivine, glass, and diogenite are not
found in this region. Our spectral approach can be extended to the entire
Vestan surface to study the heterogeneous surface composition and its geology.

text: We investigate spin-orbit interactions in inversion-asymmetric two-dimensional hole systems through a comprehensive variational analysis. Our primary objective is to elucidate the effects of these interactions on the spin dynamics and electronic properties of hole systems, which are critical for spintronic applications. By employing a variational approach, we systematically derive the ground state wavefunctions and energy spectra under varying magnetic fields and spin-orbit coupling strengths. Our results reveal a significant enhancement of spin splitting in comparison to their electron counterparts, attributable to the unique symmetry properties of hole systems.   We observe that the interplay between the Rashba and Dresselhaus spin-orbit terms leads to distinctive spin textures that can be manipulated by external fields. Additionally, we identify the role of confinement potential in modulating spin lifetimes, highlighting the potential for optimized spin coherence times in practical devices. Our findings indicate that these inversion-asymmetric systems possess a rich phase diagram, showcasing a variety of spin states that emerge due to the non-linear coupling between orbital and spin degrees of freedom.  Through this work, we address the challenges posed by the complex nature of spin-orbit interactions in hole-based platforms, providing a framework for future experimental investigations and the design of spintronic materials. Our variational analysis not only advances the theoretical understanding of spin dynamics in two-dimensional systems but also lays the groundwork for leveraging these effects in next-generation spintronic devices.

text: Solar flares, intense bursts of radiation originating from the sun, present significant interest due to their impact on space weather and terrestrial technologies. The objective of this study was to investigate the triggering mechanisms of solar flares, utilizing high-resolution observations from the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) aboard the Hinode satellite. By analyzing observations of solar active regions, this research sought to identify precursor phenomena and magnetic activity leading to flare onset. Methodologically, we employed imaging and spectroscopic techniques to evaluate changes in the photospheric and chromospheric magnetic fields, employing data sets from multiple flare events. Techniques included differential affine velocity estimator and nonlinear force-free field extrapolation to detect local magnetic complexities. Key findings reveal that prior to flare initiation, there is a marked increase in localized magnetic shear and rapid changes in line-of-sight magnetic flux, often accompanied by filament destabilization. The analysis also indicates a consistent pattern of emerging flux interacting with pre-existing magnetic structures, acting as a catalyst for the energy release process. These interactions often lead to reconnection events, substantiating that magnetic reconnection is a core component of the flare triggering process. The study concludes that integrating detailed magnetic field observations with dynamic plasma monitoring can significantly enhance the predictive capability for solar flares, offering insights relevant for advancing space weather forecasting. The synthesis of Hinode/SOT observations underscores the critical role of high-resolution solar monitoring, emphasizing the need for continued development in solar observation technologies to refine our understanding of solar phenomena.

We present Keck laser guide star adaptive optics imaging of the M8+M8 binary
2MASS J2206-2047AB. Together with archival HST, Gemini-North, and VLT data, our
observations span 8.3 years of the binary's 35 year orbital period, and we
determine a total dynamical mass of 0.15 (+0.05,-0.03) Msun, with the
uncertainty dominated by the parallax error. Using the measured total mass and
individual luminosities, the Tucson and Lyon evolutionary models both give an
age for the system of 0.4 (+9.6, -0.2) Gyr, which is consistent with its thin
disk space motion derived from the Besancon Galactic structure model. Our mass
measurement combined with the Tucson (Lyon) evolutionary models also yields
precise effective temperatures, giving 2660+-100 K and 2640+-100K (2550+-100 K
and 2530+-100 K) for components A and B, respectively. These temperatures are
in good agreement with estimates for other M8 dwarfs (from the infrared flux
method and the M8 mass benchmark LHS 2397aA), but atmospheric model fitting of
the NIR spectrum gives hotter temperatures of 2800+-100 K for both components.
This modest discrepancy can be explained by systematic errors in the
atmospheric models or by a slight underestimate of the distance (and thus mass
and age) of the system. We also find the observed near-infrared colors and
magnitudes do not agree with those predicted by the Lyon Dusty models, given
the known mass.

text: In this study, we explore the vertical atmospheric structure of a variable brown dwarf using simultaneous observations from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and Spitzer Space Telescope. By analyzing HST-vis and NIRCam-J and H bands and Spitzer-IRAC-[3.6], [4.5], [5.8], and [8.0] data, we identify clear phase shifts in the light curves of this brown dwarf. These phase shifts, which arise from pressure-dependent molecular condensation, provide insights into the vertical atmospheric composition and dynamics of the brown dwarf.  Our results reveal a complex and layered atmospheric structure, with distinct features in the visible and infrared spectra. We observe the emergence of a water vapor cloud deck in the visible, while the infrared data show evidence for the presence of other condensates, such as silicates and iron. The pressure-dependent phase shifts indicate that these condensates form at specific atmospheric levels, suggesting a vertical temperature gradient and potentially shedding light on the brown dwarf's climate and evolution.  We also compare our findings with theoretical models and previous studies of brown dwarf atmospheres to gain a better understanding of the physical processes driving the phase shifts. Our results contribute to the ongoing investigation of brown dwarf atmospheres and their role in the broader context of planetary and stellar science. Further analysis of these data and additional observations are necessary to fully elucidate the atmospheric dynamics of this brown dwarf and to inform theoretical models.

We report the generation of photo-induced electromotive force (EMF) on the
surface of c-axis oriented InN epitaxial films grown on sapphire substrates. It
has been found that under the illumination of above band gap light, EMFs of
different magnitudes and polarities are developed on different parts of the
surface of these layers. The effect is not the same as the surface photovoltaic
or Dember potential effects, both of which result in the development of EMF
across the layer thickness, not between different contacts on the surface.
These layers are also found to show negative photoconductivity effect.
Interplay between surface photo-EMF and negative photoconductivity result in a
unique scenario, where the magnitude as well as the sign of the photo-induced
change in conductivity become bias dependent. A theoretical model is developed,
where both the effects are attributed to the 2D electron gas (2DEG) channel
formed just below the film surface as a result of the transfer of electrons
from certain donor-like-surfacestates, which are likely to be resulting due to
the adsorption of certain groups/adatoms on the film surface. In the model, the
photo-EMF effect is explained in terms of a spatially inhomogeneous
distribution of these groups/adatoms over the surface resulting in a lateral
non-uniformity in the depth distribution of the potential profile confining the
2DEG. Existence of such an inhomogeneity in the distribution of surface
potential has indeed been experimentally found for these layers.

text: This paper examines the limitation of some fully observable multiple session resilient shoulder surfing defense mechanisms. Shoulder surfing attacks, a type of physical attack on computer users, have gained popularity due to their effectiveness and ease of implementation. Multiple session resilient mechanisms, such as session key regeneration and secure random number generators, have been proposed to counter these attacks. However, this study demonstrates that these defense mechanisms have their limitations.  Through an in-depth analysis of previous research, we identify that session key regeneration can be bypassed by employing various techniques, such as key-logging or man-in-the-middle attacks. Furthermore, the use of secure random number generators can be thwarted by sophisticated attackers, who can manipulate the generation process to predict future codes.  To assess the practicality of these defense mechanisms, we conducted experiments using a custom-built shoulder surfing setup. Our findings suggest that both session key regeneration and secure random number generators can be defeated within a relatively short time frame, leaving users vulnerable to attacks.  In conclusion, while multiple session resilient mechanisms offer some protection against shoulder surfing attacks, they should not be relied upon as the sole defense. Instead, a multi-layered approach that combines both technical and physical security measures is recommended to effectively counter these attacks. Future research should focus on developing more robust and effective defense mechanisms against shoulder surfing attacks.

text: This study explores the multi-wavelength variability properties of the Fermi blazar S5 0716+714, aiming to unravel the complex nature of the observed variability in this astrophysical object. By analyzing data from various telescopes spanning gamma-ray to radio wavelengths, we conducted a comprehensive investigation into the temporal behavior of this blazar. Our results reveal intricate patterns of variability across different wavelengths, providing insights into the underlying physical processes in the blazar's emission region. To address the challenges posed by the inherent complexities of blazar variability, we employed innovative statistical techniques to characterize the observed trends and fluctuations. Through our analysis, we identified correlations and potential causal relationships between the variability patterns at different wavelengths, shedding light on the mechanisms driving the observed phenomena. Furthermore, our findings contribute to the broader understanding of blazar physics and the nature of high-energy astrophysical sources. This research enhances our knowledge of the intricate interplay between various emission mechanisms and the dynamics of relativistic jets in blazars. Overall, our study offers valuable contributions to the field of multi-wavelength astrophysics and advances our comprehension of the variability properties of Fermi blazar S5 0716+714.

text: We present an application of Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition (DWD) for mechanism design problems. Mechanism design is a classic area in microeconomics that aims to create institutions to achieve desired social goals while incentivizing truthful reporting from agents. Our focus is on combinatorial mechanism design problems with discrete items, which can be modeled as integer linear programs (ILPs) with a large number of constraints. Solving such problems directly can be computationally intensive and not scalable, especially for large-scale instances.  To address the computational challenges, we apply DWD to this class of mechanism design problems. We reformulate the original ILP as a master program and its subproblems as pricing functions. The master program optimizes the social welfare by balancing the demand and the supply of items, while the pricing functions determine the prices for each agent based on their reported types. The key idea is that the optimal prices can be derived recursively using the subgradients of the objective function with respect to the constraints.  We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the performance of our approach on several benchmark datasets. Our results demonstrate that DWD significantly outperforms traditional approaches such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism and the Myerson mechanism in terms of both computational time and solution quality. Furthermore, our approach can handle large-scale instances, providing a promising avenue for addressing the challenges in mechanism design with discrete items. We also discuss the extensions and potential applications of our methodology in other areas of mechanism design and optimization, such as multi-item auctions, combinatorial pricing, and revenue management.

We investigate the evolution of differential emission measure distribution
(DEM[T]) in various phases of a B8.3 flare, which occurred on July 04, 2009. We
analyze the soft X-ray (SXR) emission in 1.6-8.0 keV range, recorded
collectively by Solar Photometer in X-rays (SphinX; Polish) and Solar X-ray
Spectrometer (SOXS; Indian) instruments. We make a comparative investigation of
the best-fit DEM[T] distributions derived by employing various inversion
schemes viz. single gaussian, power-law, functions and Withbroe-Sylwester (W-S)
maximum likelihood algorithm. In addition, SXR spectrum in three different
energy bands viz. 1.6-5.0 keV (low), 5.0-8.0 keV (high) and 1.6-8.0 keV
(combined) is analyzed to determine the dependence of the best-fit DEM[T]
distribution on the selection of energy interval. The evolution of DEM[T]
distribution, derived using W-S algorithm, reveals the plasma of multi-thermal
nature during the rise to the maximum phase of the flare, while of isothermal
nature in the post-maximum phase of the flare. Thermal energy content is
estimated considering the flare plasma to be of 1) iso-thermal and 2)
multi-thermal nature. We find that the energy content during the flare,
estimated from the multi-thermal approach, is in good agreement with that
derived using the iso-thermal assumption except during the maximum of the
flare. Further, (multi-) thermal energy estimated employing low-energy band of
the SXR spectrum result in higher values than that derived from the
combined-energy band. On the contrary, the analysis of high-energy band of SXR
spectrum lead to lower thermal energy than that estimated from the
combined-energy band.
