text:
Context. The gamma-ray binary LS 5039 and the isolated pulsar PSR J1825-1446
were proposed to have been formed in the supernova remnant (SNR) G016.8-01.1.
Aims. We aim to obtain the Galactic trajectory of LS 5039 and PSR J1825-1446 to
find their origin in the Galaxy, and in particular to check their association
with SNR G016.8-01.1 to restrict their age. Methods. By means of radio and
optical observations we obtained the proper motion and the space velocity of
the sources. Results. The proper motion of PSR J1825-1446 corresponds to a
transverse space velocity of 690 km/s at a distance of 5 kpc. Its Galactic
velocity at different distances is not compatible with the expected Galactic
rotation. The velocity and characteristic age of PSR J1825-1446 make it
incompatible with SNR G016.8-01.1. There are no clear OB associations or SNRs
crossing the past trajectory of PSR J1825-1446. We estimate the age of the
pulsar to be 80-245 kyr, which is compatible with its characteristic age. The
proper motion of LS 5039 is 7.09 and -8.82 mas/yr in right ascension and
declination, respectively. The association of LS 5039 with SNR G016.8-01.1 is
unlikely, although we cannot to discard it. The system would have had to be
formed in the association Ser OB2 (at 2.0 kpc) if the age of the system is
1.0-1.2 Myr, or in the association Sct OB3 (distance 1.5-2 kpc) for an age of
0.1-0.2 Myr. If the system were not formed close to Ser OB2, the
pseudo-synchronization of the orbit would be unlikely. Conclusions. PSR
J1825-1446 is a high-velocity isolated pulsar ejected from the Galaxy. The
distance to LS 5039, which needs to be constrained by future astrometric
missions such as Gaia, is a key parameter for restricting its origin and age.

text: In the study of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the renormalization of quark propagators is pivotal for understanding the behavior of quarks in a lattice framework, particularly under twisted-mass formulations. This paper investigates the renormalization properties of quark propagators in twisted-mass lattice QCD with two flavors of quarks (N_f=2). The objective is to derive and evaluate the renormalization constants essential for non-perturbative analyses and to assess the implications of twisted-mass formulations on quark masses and couplings.   Utilizing lattice simulations, we compute the quark propagators across different lattice volumes and configurations, employing a combination of the Wilson and twisted-mass formulations. Our methodology includes the application of various techniques for extracting renormalization constants through measures such as the momentum space and the ratio method, as well as conducting chiral extrapolations to the physical point.   Key findings indicate that the renormalization constants exhibit distinct behaviors when compared to standard mass terms, showing sensitivity to the twisted quark masses. Furthermore, the evaluation of the beta function suggests a significant reduction in systematic uncertainties associated with the renormalization procedure.   In conclusion, this work demonstrates the efficacy of twisted-mass lattice QCD in providing a robust framework for the renormalization of quark propagators, contributing valuable insights into the non-perturbative aspects of quark dynamics and enhancing our understanding of lattice QCD formulations. These results lay the groundwork for future studies in hadron physics and beyond.

text: The study of Quasi Periodic Oscillations (QPOs) in black hole accretion disks continues to be an area of great interest in astrophysics. In this work, we investigate the origin of QPOs through the analysis of axisymmetric and non-axisymmetric shock oscillations in a two-dimensional hydrodynamic model of a black hole accretion flow. Our simulations reveal the presence of both low-frequency QPOs (LFQPOs) and high-frequency QPOs (HFQPOs) in the power spectral density (PSD) of the accretion flow. We find that axisymmetric shocks generate LFQPOs, while non-axisymmetric shocks give rise to HFQPOs. To understand the underlying physical mechanisms, we explore the properties of the shock structures in detail. For axisymmetric shocks, we find that the QPO emission arises from the footpoints of the reconnection current sheets that form in the downstream regions. The emission is modulated by the Lorentz force acting on the plasma, resulting in a sinusoidal variation in the emission. In contrast, for non-axisymmetric shocks, the QPO emission originates from the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI) at the interface between the shock and the accretion flow. The KHI generates a vortex sheet that twists and wrinkles, leading to a modulation in the emission. Our findings suggest a possible explanation for the observed properties of QPOs in black hole accretion disks, providing new insights into the physical mechanisms responsible for these intriguing phenomena. Future work will focus on extending these simulations to three dimensions and incorporating magnetic fields to explore the effects on QPO emission.

text: In this study, we present a comprehensive simulation of the solar eruptive event observed on July 14, 2000, known as the "Bastille Day" eruption. Our simulation utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) framework to model the dynamics of the solar corona and solar wind emanating from the Sun's surface. The primary objective was to accurately reproduce the observed features such as the eruption's acceleration, the associated shock wave propagation, and the evolution of the coronal mass ejection (CME).  The simulation employs a state-of-the-art computational approach that incorporates realistic solar parameters and physical processes, including the effects of magnetic reconnection, plasma heating, and thermal conduction. By comparing our simulated output with observational data, we were able to validate the accuracy of our model. Key findings include the successful replication of the CME's expansion velocity and the formation of a shock front propagating into the interplanetary medium.  Through iterative refinement of the model parameters and the inclusion of detailed boundary conditions, we aimed to minimize discrepancies between the simulation and observations. This research not only enhances our understanding of solar eruptions but also provides valuable insights into predicting space weather events. The methodologies employed underscore the importance of integrating advanced numerical simulations with observational data to refine models of solar phenomena.

text: The universe is home to an abundance of high-energy cosmic rays, predominantly composed of protons and heavy ions, which bombard the Earth's atmosphere at incredible velocities. Among these particles, leptons, particularly electrons and muons, have garnered significant attention due to their unique properties and the potential to reveal insights into the most energetic astrophysical phenomena. The energy spectra of GeV/TeV cosmic ray leptons have been a subject of intense study, as they offer a window into the origins of these high-energy particles.  This research aims to investigate the energy spectra of GeV/TeV cosmic ray leptons, with a focus on the detection and analysis of these particles using cutting-edge experiments and simulations. Utilizing a combination of Monte Carlo simulations, data analysis techniques, and theoretical models, this study seeks to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the production and propagation of these high-energy leptons.  The results of this research indicate that the energy spectra of GeV/TeV cosmic ray leptons are characterized by a complex distribution, with multiple peaks and valleys that suggest the presence of multiple astrophysical sources. The findings also reveal a significant correlation between the energy spectra of leptons and the properties of their parent particles, providing valuable insights into the relationship between the sources of high-energy cosmic rays and the particles they produce. Overall, this research contributes to our understanding of the most energetic astrophysical phenomena, shedding light on the origins and properties of GeV/TeV cosmic ray leptons.

text:
In a graph, a community may be loosely defined as a group of nodes that are
more closely connected to one another than to the rest of the graph. While
there are a variety of metrics that can be used to specify the quality of a
given community, one common theme is that flows tend to stay within
communities. Hence, we expect cycles to play an important role in community
detection. For undirected graphs, the importance of triangles -- an undirected
3-cycle -- has been known for a long time and can be used to improve community
detection. In directed graphs, the situation is more nuanced. The smallest
cycle is simply two nodes with a reciprocal connection, and using information
about reciprocation has proven to improve community detection. Our new idea is
based on the four types of directed triangles that contain cycles. To identify
communities in directed networks, then, we propose an undirected edge-weighting
scheme based on the type of the directed triangles in which edges are involved.
We also propose a new metric on quality of the communities that is based on the
number of 3-cycles that are split across communities. To demonstrate the impact
of our new weighting, we use the standard METIS graph partitioning tool to
determine communities and show experimentally that the resulting communities
result in fewer 3-cycles being cut. The magnitude of the effect varies between
a 10 and 50% reduction, and we also find evidence that this weighting scheme
improves a task where plausible ground-truth communities are known.

text:
Studies of high-redshift gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) provide important
information about the early Universe such as the rates of stellar collapsars
and mergers, the metallicity content, constraints on the re-ionization period,
and probes of the Hubble expansion. Rapid selection of high-z candidates from
GRB samples reported in real time by dedicated space missions such as Swift is
the key to identifying the most distant bursts before the optical afterglow
becomes too dim to warrant a good spectrum. Here we introduce "machine-z", a
redshift prediction algorithm and a "high-z" classifier for Swift GRBs based on
machine learning. Our method relies exclusively on canonical data commonly
available within the first few hours after the GRB trigger. Using a sample of
284 bursts with measured redshifts, we trained a randomized ensemble of
decision trees (random forest) to perform both regression and classification.
Cross-validated performance studies show that the correlation coefficient
between machine-z predictions and the true redshift is nearly 0.6. At the same
time our high-z classifier can achieve 80% recall of true high-redshift bursts,
while incurring a false positive rate of 20%. With 40% false positive rate the
classifier can achieve ~100% recall. The most reliable selection of
high-redshift GRBs is obtained by combining predictions from both the high-z
classifier and the machine-z regressor.

text: We investigate the accretion disk structure of LMC X-3 utilizing high-resolution X-ray data from the Suzaku satellite. Our primary objective is to enhance the understanding of the physical processes occurring in the vicinity of a black hole as material is accreted from its companion star. By analyzing the spectral data obtained from the X-ray emissions, we identify emissions from iron Kα lines and other relevant features that provide insight into the geometry and dynamics of the accretion disk.  We employ a combination of analytical modeling and simulation techniques to interpret the data, focusing on the temperature distribution and density profiles of the accretion disk. Our results reveal a pronounced temperature gradient within the disk, and we establish a correlation between the luminosity variations and the inner radius of the accretion region. These findings suggest that the accretion disk in LMC X-3 operates under the influence of both relativistic effects and magnetic fields, indicating a complex interaction between the stellar wind and the disk material.  Our study not only tests theoretical predictions regarding accretion disk structure but also addresses inconsistencies observed in previous models. By providing new constraints on parameters like disk thickness and flow dynamics, we contribute valuable data to the evolving understanding of black hole systems. Ultimately, our findings reinforce the significance of Suzaku data in elucidating the intricate mechanisms governing accretion phenomena in high-energy astrophysical contexts.

text:
Measurement shows that 85% of TCP flows in the internet are short-lived flows
that stay most of their operation in the TCP startup phase. However, many
previous studies indicate that the traditional TCP Slow Start algorithm does
not perform well, especially in long fat networks. Two obvious problems are
known to impact the Slow Start performance, which are the blind initial setting
of the Slow Start threshold and the aggressive increase of the probing rate
during the startup phase regardless of the buffer sizes along the path. Current
efforts focusing on tuning the Slow Start threshold and/or probing rate during
the startup phase have not been considered very effective, which has prompted
an investigation with a different approach. In this paper, we present a novel
TCP startup method, called threshold-less slow start or SSthreshless Start,
which does not need the Slow Start threshold to operate. Instead, SSthreshless
Start uses the backlog status at bottleneck buffer to adaptively adjust probing
rate which allows better seizing of the available bandwidth. Comparing to the
traditional and other major modified startup methods, our simulation results
show that SSthreshless Start achieves significant performance improvement
during the startup phase. Moreover, SSthreshless Start scales well with a wide
range of buffer size, propagation delay and network bandwidth. Besides, it
shows excellent friendliness when operating simultaneously with the currently
popular TCP NewReno connections.

text:
THESEUS is a space mission concept aimed at exploiting Gamma-Ray Bursts for
investigating the early Universe and at providing a substantial advancement of
multi-messenger and time-domain astrophysics. These goals will be achieved
through a unique combination of instruments allowing GRB and X-ray transient
detection over a broad field of view (more than 1sr) with 0.5-1 arcmin
localization, an energy band extending from several MeV down to 0.3 keV and
high sensitivity to transient sources in the soft X-ray domain, as well as
on-board prompt (few minutes) follow-up with a 0.7 m class IR telescope with
both imaging and spectroscopic capabilities. THESEUS will be perfectly suited
for addressing the main open issues in cosmology such as, e.g., star formation
rate and metallicity evolution of the inter-stellar and intra-galactic medium
up to redshift $\sim$10, signatures of Pop III stars, sources and physics of
re-ionization, and the faint end of the galaxy luminosity function. In
addition, it will provide unprecedented capability to monitor the X-ray
variable sky, thus detecting, localizing, and identifying the electromagnetic
counterparts to sources of gravitational radiation, which may be routinely
detected in the late '20s / early '30s by next generation facilities like
aLIGO/ aVirgo, eLISA, KAGRA, and Einstein Telescope. THESEUS will also provide
powerful synergies with the next generation of multi-wavelength observatories
(e.g., LSST, ELT, SKA, CTA, ATHENA).

text: We investigate the characteristics of jump-type Hunt processes induced by lower bounded semi-Dirichlet forms, focusing on their potential applications and theoretical implications. Our research addresses the problem of understanding the probabilistic behavior and structural properties of such processes, which play a crucial role in non-symmetric Markov processes with jumps. We employ an analytical framework centered on the construction of these processes via semi-Dirichlet forms, exploring the conditions under which they exhibit desirable properties such as recurrence, transience, and heat kernel estimates. Our methodology involves the development of a comprehensive theory that integrates potential theory, Dirichlet form techniques, and the specific attributes of non-local operators. We derive a set of sufficient conditions under which these processes are well-defined and demonstrate their ability to model complex stochastic dynamics characterized by jumps. Our results include precise characterizations of the process's resolvent and Green functions, along with criteria for their approximate continuity and local properties. Moreover, we identify connections between the geometric features of the underlying state space and the probabilistic behavior of these processes, offering insights that contribute to a deeper understanding of their long-term behavior. Our findings not only enrich the landscape of non-symmetric Markov processes but also pave the way for new applications in fields where modeling jump phenomena is pertinent. This work sets the stage for further exploration into generalized Hunt processes, inviting future studies to extend our theoretical advancements and explore practical implementations.

text:
Deep neural networks (NN) are extensively used for machine learning tasks
such as image classification, perception and control of autonomous systems.
Increasingly, these deep NNs are also been deployed in high-assurance
applications. Thus, there is a pressing need for developing techniques to
verify neural networks to check whether certain user-expected properties are
satisfied. In this paper, we study a specific verification problem of computing
a guaranteed range for the output of a deep neural network given a set of
inputs represented as a convex polyhedron. Range estimation is a key primitive
for verifying deep NNs. We present an efficient range estimation algorithm that
uses a combination of local search and linear programming problems to
efficiently find the maximum and minimum values taken by the outputs of the NN
over the given input set. In contrast to recently proposed "monolithic"
optimization approaches, we use local gradient descent to repeatedly find and
eliminate local minima of the function. The final global optimum is certified
using a mixed integer programming instance. We implement our approach and
compare it with Reluplex, a recently proposed solver for deep neural networks.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for verification of
NNs used in automated control as well as those used in classification.

text:
We first review the spontaneous Lorentz symmetry breaking in the presence of
massless gauge fields and infraparticles. This result was obtained long time
ago in the context of rigorious quantum field theory by Frohlich et. al. and
reformulated by Balachandran and Vaidya using the notion of superselection
sectors and direction-dependent test functions at spatial infinity for the
non-local observables. Inspired by these developments and under the assumption
that the spectrum of the electric charge is quantized, (in units of a
fundamental charge e) we construct a family of vertex operators which create
winding number k, electrically charged Abelian vortices from the vacuum (zero
winding number sector) and/or shift the winding number by k units. In
particular, we find that for rotating vortices the vertex operator at level k
shifts the angular momentum of the vortex by k \frac{{\tilde q}}{q}, where
\tilde q is the electric charge of the quantum state of the vortex and q is the
charge of the vortex scalar field under the U(1) gauge field. We also show
that, for charged-particle-vortex composites angular momentum eigenvalues shift
by k \frac{{\tilde q}}{q}, {\tilde q} being the electric charge of the
charged-particle-vortex composite. This leads to the result that for
\frac{{\tilde q}}{q} half-odd integral and for odd k our vertex operators flip
the statistics of charged-particle-vortex composites from bosons to fermions
and vice versa. For fractional values of \frac{{\tilde q}}{q}, application of
vertex operator on charged-particle-vortex composite leads in general to
composites with anyonic statistics.

text: This research paper presents a novel approach to asynchronous code-division random access (CDRA) using convex optimization techniques. CDRA is a fundamental technique in digital communication systems, enabling efficient data transmission over multiple channels with varying propagation delays. However, existing CDRA schemes often suffer from suboptimal performance due to the complexity of the optimization problem.  The objective of this research is to develop a convex optimization-based framework for CDRA, which can efficiently handle the non-linear relationships between the transmitter and receiver signals. The proposed scheme utilizes a quadratic program (QP) to optimize the code-division mapping, ensuring that the resulting CDRA scheme achieves the maximum achievable rate while satisfying the constraints of the transmission system.  The proposed method is evaluated using numerical simulations, demonstrating its ability to outperform existing CDRA schemes in terms of spectral efficiency and bit error rate. The results show that the proposed scheme can achieve significant gains in CDRA performance, particularly in scenarios with high propagation delays and multiple interfering channels.  The key findings of this research highlight the potential of convex optimization techniques in optimizing CDRA schemes. The proposed method offers a promising solution for the design of efficient CDRA systems, which can be applied in various communication systems, including wireless networks, satellite communications, and optical communication systems. The results of this research demonstrate the feasibility of using convex optimization techniques in optimizing CDRA schemes, paving the way for the development of more efficient and reliable communication systems.

text: Our study investigates the Neutrino mixing matrix and masses within the framework of a generalized Friedberg-Lee model. In this work, we aim to address the longstanding issue of understanding the nature and properties of neutrinos, which play a crucial role in the Standard Model of particle physics. By extending the Friedberg-Lee model, we propose a novel approach to describe neutrino mixing and mass generation.   Through our analysis, we successfully derive the Neutrino mixing matrix and masses taking into account the modifications introduced by the generalized Friedberg-Lee model. Our results reveal interesting insights into the neutrino sector, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying neutrino oscillations and the origin of neutrino masses within this modified framework.   The key ideas in our research involve the incorporation of the generalized Friedberg-Lee model into the study of neutrinos, offering a new perspective on neutrino physics beyond the traditional approaches. The methodology employed in our investigation combines theoretical calculations with numerical simulations to elucidate the implications of the modified model on the Neutrino mixing matrix and mass spectrum. Our findings contribute to the ongoing efforts to deepen our understanding of neutrinos and their properties, potentially paving the way for new advancements in particle physics.

text: In this study, we present the first data release from the Herschel-wide Area Lensing Survey (Herschel-ATLAS), encompassing detailed maps, catalogues, and number counts of submillimeter sources across a significant extragalactic sky area. Our objective is to provide a comprehensive dataset that addresses the challenges of identifying and characterizing cold dust emissions in distant galaxies, which are crucial for understanding galaxy evolution and star formation rates in the early universe. We employed a methodology including robust data processing techniques utilizing the Herschel Space Observatory's capabilities, along with advanced algorithms for source extraction and photometric measurements across multiple wavelengths. Our results include high-resolution, multi-band maps detailing the spatial distribution of 500 µm emissions, accompanied by a catalog of over 100,000 sources extracted from these maps. We quantify the number counts of submillimeter sources and provide insights into their brightness distribution, thereby revealing the overall statistical properties of this population. We also evaluate the completeness and reliability of our catalog through extensive simulations and cross-matching with existing surveys. Our findings highlight the significance of the Herschel-ATLAS in bridging the gap between optical and submillimeter astronomy, contributing vital data that will enhance our understanding of the role of dust in galaxy formation and evolution. This data release serves as a foundational resource for future studies in the field of extragalactic astrophysics, paving the way for new inquiries into the cosmic processes shaping our universe.

text:
The crystal structures of Ni$X_2$(pyz)$_2$ ($X$ = Cl (\textbf{1}), Br
(\textbf{2}), I (\textbf{3}) and NCS (\textbf{4})) were determined at 298~K by
synchrotron X-ray powder diffraction. All four compounds consist of
two-dimensional (2D) square arrays self-assembled from octahedral NiN$_4$$X_2$
units that are bridged by pyz ligands. The 2D layered motifs displayed by
\textbf{1}-\textbf{4} are relevant to bifluoride-bridged
[Ni(HF$_2$)(pyz)$_2$]$Z$F$_6$ ($Z$ = P, Sb) which also possess the same 2D
layers. In contrast, terminal $X$ ligands occupy axial positions in
\textbf{1}-\textbf{4} and cause a staggering of adjacent layers. Long-range
antiferromagnetic order occurs below 1.5 (Cl), 1.9 (Br and NCS) and 2.5~K (I)
as determined by heat capacity and muon-spin relaxation. The single-ion
anisotropy and $g$ factor of \textbf{2}, \textbf{3} and \textbf{4} are measured
by electron spin resonance where no zero--field splitting was found. The
magnetism of \textbf{1}-\textbf{4} crosses a spectrum from
quasi-two-dimensional to three-dimensional antiferromagnetism. An excellent
agreement was found between the pulsed-field magnetization, magnetic
susceptibility and $T_\textrm{N}$ of \textbf{2} and \textbf{4}. Magnetization
curves for \textbf{2} and \textbf{4} calculated by quantum Monte Carlo
simulation also show excellent agreement with the pulsed-field data. \textbf{3}
is characterized as a three-dimensional antiferromagnet with the interlayer
interaction ($J_\perp$) slightly stronger than the interaction within the
two-dimensional [Ni(pyz)$_2$]$^{2+}$ square planes ($J_\textrm{pyz}$).

We review how the renormalized force correlator Delta(u), the function
computed in the functional RG field theory, can be measured directly in
numerics and experiments on the dynamics of elastic manifolds in presence of
pinning disorder. We show how this function can be computed analytically for a
particle dragged through a 1-dimensional random-force landscape. The limit of
small velocity allows to access the critical behavior at the depinning
transition. For uncorrelated forces one finds three universality classes,
corresponding to the three extreme value statistics, Gumbel, Weibull, and
Frechet. For each class we obtain analytically the universal function Delta(u),
the corrections to the critical force, and the joint probability distribution
of avalanche sizes s and waiting times w. We find P(s)=P(w) for all three
cases. All results are checked numerically. For a Brownian force landscape,
known as the ABBM model, avalanche distributions and Delta(u) can be computed
for any velocity. For 2-dimensional disorder, we perform large-scale numerical
simulations to calculate the renormalized force correlator tensor
Delta_{ij}(u), and to extract the anisotropic scaling exponents zeta_x >
zeta_y. We also show how the Middleton theorem is violated. Our results are
relevant for the record statistics of random sequences with linear trends, as
encountered e.g. in some models of global warming. We give the joint
distribution of the time s between two successive records and their difference
in value w.

text: This study investigates the application of point cloud compression techniques to efficiently encode and transmit light field data. We aim to address the challenge of compressing large datasets associated with complex scenes, particularly those captured by light field cameras, which are inherently high-dimensional and require significant storage resources. Our approach utilizes a point cloud codec, leveraging its ability to handle sparse and irregularly distributed data points. The methodology involves preprocessing the light field data into a set of point clouds, applying a lossy compression algorithm tailored to preserve critical visual information while reducing redundancy. We evaluate our method through simulations and real-world experiments, comparing it against existing state-of-the-art compression techniques. Results indicate that our method achieves substantial compression ratios without compromising essential visual fidelity, demonstrating its potential for efficient transmission and storage of light field data. Key insights include the importance of encoding strategies for light field points and the trade-offs between compression efficiency and visual quality.

Large-scale multiple testing with highly correlated test statistics arises
frequently in many scientific research. Incorporating correlation information
in estimating false discovery proportion has attracted increasing attention in
recent years. When the covariance matrix of test statistics is known, Fan, Han
& Gu (2012) provided a consistent estimate of False Discovery Proportion (FDP)
under arbitrary dependence structure. However, the covariance matrix is often
unknown in many applications and such dependence information has to be
estimated before estimating FDP (Efron, 2010). The estimation accuracy can
greatly affect the convergence result of FDP or even violate its consistency.
In the current paper, we provide methodological modification and theoretical
investigations for estimation of FDP with unknown covariance. First we develop
requirements for estimates of eigenvalues and eigenvectors such that we can
obtain a consistent estimate of FDP. Secondly we give conditions on the
dependence structures such that the estimate of FDP is consistent. Such
dependence structures include sparse covariance matrices, which have been
popularly considered in the contemporary random matrix theory. When data are
sampled from an approximate factor model, which encompasses most practical
situations, we provide a consistent estimate of FDP via exploiting this
specific dependence structure. The results are further demonstrated by
simulation studies and some real data applications.
label: human

text: In this study, we examine the interplay between user privacy and recommendation accuracy in the context of untrusted recommendation engines. The ubiquity of collaborative filtering algorithms for personalizing user experience often necessitates the collection and analysis of sensitive user data, potentially compromising privacy. We aim to quantify the trade-off between privacy protection measures and the resulting degradation of recommendation performance. Utilizing an approach that integrates differential privacy mechanisms within recommendation systems, we rigorously evaluate the impact on predictive accuracy and user satisfaction across various privacy parameter settings. We employ a synthetic dataset reflecting diverse recommendation scenarios to simulate and analyze the privacy-accuracy balance. Our results demonstrate a notable decline in recommendation accuracy proportional to the increase in privacy budget, quantifying the privacy cost in effective and interpretable metrics. Methodologically, we introduce a novel framework for deriving optimum privacy budgets that minimally affect system accuracy. Our findings indicate that while stringent privacy requirements can significantly impair recommendation quality, strategically designed privacy controls can ameliorate such effects, optimizing both user privacy and system utility. This work underscores the necessity for a holistic approach to privacy-preserving recommendation systems that prioritize both user confidentiality and service effectiveness. The presented methodologies offer a valuable contribution to the development of privacy-aware recommendation engines, charting pathways for further refinements in balancing privacy and usability in digital services. We recommend future exploration into adaptive privacy schemas that dynamically adjust to individual user preferences, providing tailored privacy solutions without compromising service quality.
label: machine

We study integrability of fishnet-type Feynman graphs arising in planar
four-dimensional bi-scalar chiral theory recently proposed in arXiv:1512.06704
as a special double scaling limit of gamma-deformed $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory.
We show that the transfer matrix "building" the fishnet graphs emerges from the
$R-$matrix of non-compact conformal $SU(2,2)$ Heisenberg spin chain with spins
belonging to principal series representations of the four-dimensional conformal
group. We demonstrate explicitly a relationship between this integrable spin
chain and the Quantum Spectral Curve (QSC) of $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM. Using QSC
and spin chain methods, we construct Baxter equation for $Q-$functions of the
conformal spin chain needed for computation of the anomalous dimensions of
operators of the type $\text{tr}(\phi_1^J)$ where $\phi_1$ is one of the two
scalars of the theory. For $J=3$ we derive from QSC a quantization condition
that fixes the relevant solution of Baxter equation. The scaling dimensions of
the operators only receive contributions from wheel-like graphs. We develop
integrability techniques to compute the divergent part of these graphs and use
it to present the weak coupling expansion of dimensions to very high orders.
Then we apply our exact equations to calculate the anomalous dimensions with
$J=3$ to practically unlimited precision at any coupling. These equations also
describe an infinite tower of local conformal operators all carrying the same
charge $J=3$. The method should be applicable for any $J$ and, in principle, to
any local operators of bi-scalar theory. We show that at strong coupling the
scaling dimensions can be derived from semiclassical quantization of finite gap
solutions describing an integrable system of noncompact $SU(2,2)$ spins. This
bears similarities with the classical strings arising in the strongly coupled
limit of $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM.

interacting with dark matter and another unknown component of dark energy of
the universe. We have assumed two interaction terms $Q$ and $Q'$ in order to
include the scenario in which the mutual interaction between the two principal
components (i.e., holographic dark energy and dark matter) of the universe
leads to some loss in other forms of cosmic constituents. Our model is valid
for any sign of $Q$ and $Q'$. If $Q<Q'$, then part of the dark energy density
decays into dark matter and the rest in the other unknown energy density
component. But if $Q>Q'$, then dark matter energy receives from dark energy and
from the unknown component of dark energy. Observation suggests that dark
energy decays into dark matter. Here we have presented a general prescription
of a cosmological model of dark energy which imposes mutual interaction between
holographic dark energy, dark matter and another fluid. We have obtained the
equation of state for the holographic dark energy density which is interacting
with dark matter and other unknown component of dark energy. Using first law of
thermodynamics, we have obtained the entropies for holographic dark energy,
dark matter and other component of dark energy, when holographic dark energy
interacting with two fluids (i.e., dark matter and other component of dark

text: We present a novel implementation of a high-order conservative semi-Lagrangian discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method for two-dimensional transport simulations. Our approach leverages the strengths of the semi-Lagrangian framework, which inherently preserves the accuracy of transport equations, and the discontinuous Galerkin method, which efficiently captures complex geometries and discontinuities. We develop a high-order conservative semi-Lagrangian DG scheme that incorporates a novel flux reconstruction technique, allowing for the accurate capture of shocks and discontinuities. This technique enables the scheme to maintain its high-order accuracy even in the presence of complex geometries and strong discontinuities.   Our numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in simulating various two-dimensional transport scenarios, including shock waves, rarefaction waves, and complex geometries. We observe that the method accurately captures the physical phenomena, including the formation and propagation of shocks, while maintaining a high level of accuracy. The numerical results are compared with existing methods, showcasing the superiority of the proposed approach. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of the method's parameters on the accuracy and stability, providing insights into the optimal choice of these parameters. The results demonstrate the potential of the high-order conservative semi-Lagrangian DG method for accurate and efficient two-dimensional transport simulations.
label: machine

text: We investigate the concept of k-tuple total domination in inflated graphs, a novel extension of total domination in graphs. Our work aims to address the scarcity of research on total domination in inflated graphs by introducing and studying k-tuple total domination as a new parameter for graph domination. We define k-tuple total domination as a set of vertices such that each vertex in the graph is adjacent to at least k vertices in the set.   Through our research, we establish key properties and bounds for k-tuple total domination in inflated graphs, shedding light on the behavior of this parameter in such structures. We also provide algorithms for efficiently computing k-tuple total domination in inflated graphs. Our methodology involves rigorous theoretical analysis of the properties of k-tuple total domination, as well as the development of strategic algorithms for practical implementation.   The results of our study demonstrate the significance of k-tuple total domination in inflated graphs and its potential applications in various domains such as network security and facility location. By introducing this new parameter and exploring its properties, our work contributes to the enrichment of the theory of domination in graphs and opens up avenues for further research in this area.
label: machine

text: We address the challenge of deriving higher-order scheme-independent series expansions for the anomalous dimension $\gamma_{\bar\psi\psi,IR}$ and the derivative of the beta function, $\beta'_{IR}$, evaluated at the infrared fixed point in conformal field theories. Our work focuses on enhancing the precision and applicability of these series expansions, which are crucial for understanding the scaling dimensions of operators and the running of coupling constants near the fixed point. By employing a refined methodology that incorporates advanced renormalization group techniques and leveraging both perturbative and non-perturbative insights, we present a framework that transcends specific renormalization schemes. We build upon the established $\varepsilon$-expansion and large $N_f$ expansion, extending them to capture higher-order corrections reliably. Through this approach, we recognize the feasibility of achieving scheme-independent results that offer enhanced predictive power in various theoretical contexts. Our expansions exhibit improved convergence properties, providing meaningful theoretical predictions closer to the fixed point. We benchmark our results against known exact and numerical calculations, demonstrating consistency and enhanced accuracy. This work not only refines existing methods for analyzing critical phenomena but also paves the way for future studies in exploring non-trivial fixed points in diverse theories. Our findings potentially impact the broader field of quantum field theory, where accurate characterization of the infrared behavior is essential for the development of new models and for gaining deeper insights into strongly coupled systems.
label: machine

Authentication is the act of confirming the truth of an attribute of a datum
or entity. This might involve confirming the identity of a person, tracing the
origins of an artefact, ensuring that a product is what it's packaging and
labelling claims to be, or assuring that a computer program is a trusted one.
The authentication of information can pose special problems (especially
man-in-the-middle attacks), and is often wrapped up with authenticating
identity. Literary can involve imitating the style of a famous author. If an
original manuscript, typewritten text, or recording is available, then the
medium itself (or its packaging - anything from a box to e-mail headers) can
help prove or disprove the authenticity of the document. The use of digital
images of handwritten historical documents has become more popular in recent
years. Volunteers around the world now read thousands of these images as part
of their indexing process. Handwritten text images of old documents are
sometimes difficult to read or noisy due to the preservation of the document
and quality of the image [1]. Handwritten text offers challenges that are
rarely encountered in machine-printed text. In addition, most problems faced in
reading machine- printed text (e.g., character recognition, word segmentation,
letter segmentation, etc.) are more severe, in handwritten text. In this paper
we Here in this paper we proposed a method for authenticating hand written text
images using back propagation algorithm..

Protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks are the backbone of all processes
in living cells. In this work we relate conservation, essentiality and
functional repertoire of a gene to the connectivity $k$ (i.e., the number of
interaction links) of the corresponding protein in the PPI network. On a set of
42 bacterial genomes of different sizes, and with reasonably separated
evolutionary trajectories, we investigate three issues: i) whether the
distribution of connectivities changes between PPI subnetworks of essential and
nonessential genes; ii) how gene conservation, measured both by the
evolutionary retention index (ERI) and by evolutionary pressures, is related to
the the connectivity of the corresponding protein; iii) how PPI connectivities
are modulated by evolutionary and functional relationships, as represented by
the Clusters of Orthologous Genes (COGs). We show that conservation,
essentiality and functional specialisation of genes constrain the connectivity
of the corresponding proteins in bacterial PPI networks. In particular, we
isolate a core of highly connected proteins (with connectivities $k\ge40$),
which is ubiquitous among the species considered here -- though mostly visible
in the degree distributions of bacteria with small genomes (less than 1000
genes). The genes that belong to this highly connected core are conserved,
essential and, in most cases, belong to the COG cluster J, related to ribosomal
functions and to the processing of genetic information.
label: human

text: This study employs resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to investigate the selective excitations within correlated materials, focusing on the resonant profile to reveal two-magnon scattering processes. The primary objective is to elucidate the dynamical structure factor associated with these two-magnon events. Initial attempts at data acquisition were hindered by background interference, which necessitated rigorous background subtraction techniques. Through advanced signal processing and spectral fitting algorithms, we successfully isolated the resonant signals indicative of two-magnon scattering. Key methodologies include the use of high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy combined with RIXS, along with detailed analysis of the scattering profiles to discern the characteristic features of two-magnon excitations. The results demonstrate that the resonant profile provides a robust method to observe and characterize two-magnon scattering, offering insights into the dynamic behavior of correlated electron systems. This approach opens avenues for further studies on the interplay between magnons and lattice vibrations in complex materials.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the issue of tail fitting for both truncated and non-truncated Pareto-type distributions. The importance of accurately modeling the tail behavior of distributions has been increasingly recognized, especially in applications related to risk analysis and extreme value statistics. In particular, for Pareto-type distributions, understanding the tail behavior is essential due to their heavy-tailed nature.  To address the challenge of accurately estimating the parameters of Pareto-type distributions from truncated or non-truncated data, we employ maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and the method of moments (MOM). We demonstrate that, under certain conditions, both methods can provide reliable estimates for the shape and scale parameters of Pareto-type distributions. However, we also illustrate that the choice between MLE and MOM depends on the data structure, i.e., truncated or non-truncated.  Moreover, we investigate the potential for overfitting when using truncated data and propose a methodology to avoid this issue. Specifically, we implement a procedure based on the Kupiec test to determine the appropriate truncation point that balances the trade-off between model accuracy and the potential for overfitting.  In our empirical analysis, we apply our methodology to synthetic datasets and real-world financial data to validate the theoretical findings. The results show that our proposed approach can effectively estimate the parameters of Pareto-type distributions and provide insights into the appropriate truncation point for accurate modeling of the tail behavior. Our study contributes to the growing body of research on tail estimation for Pareto-type distributions and offers practical implications for applications in finance, engineering, and other fields.
label: machine

We propose a novel statistical model to answer three challenges in direct
marketing: which channel to use, which offer to make, and when to offer. There
are several potential applications for the proposed model, for example,
developing personalized marketing strategies and monitoring members' needs.
Furthermore, the results from the model can complement and can be integrated
with other existing models.
  The proposed model, named Dynamic Propensity Model, is a latent variable time
series model that utilizes both marketing and purchase histories of a customer.
The latent variable in the model represents the customer's propensity to buy a
product. The propensity derives from purchases and other observable responses.
Marketing touches increase a member's propensity, and propensity score
attenuates and propagates over time as governed by data-driven parameters. To
estimate the parameters of the model, a new statistical methodology has been
developed. This methodology makes use of particle methods with a stochastic
gradient descent approach, resulting in fast estimation of the model
coefficients even from big datasets. The model is validated using six months'
marketing records from one of the largest insurance companies in the U.S.
Experimental results indicate that the effects of marketing touches vary
depending on both channels and products. We compare the predictive performance
of the proposed model with lagged variable logistic regression. Limitations and
extensions of the proposed algorithm are also discussed.

A study of possible superconducting phases of graphene has been constructed
in detail. A realistic tight binding model, fit to ab initio calculations,
accounts for the Li-decoration of graphene with broken lattice symmetry, and
includes $s$ and $d$ symmetry Bloch character that influences the gap
symmetries that can arise. The resulting seven hybridized Li-C orbitals that
support nine possible bond pairing amplitudes. The gap equation is solved for
all possible gap symmetries. One band is weakly dispersive near the Fermi
energy along $\Gamma\rightarrow M$ where its Bloch wave function has linear
combination of $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{xy}$ character, and is responsible for $
d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}$ and $d_{xy}$ pairing with lowest pairing energy in our model.
These symmetries almost preserve properties from a two band model of pristine
graphene. Another part of this band, along $K\rightarrow \Gamma$, is nearly
degenerate with upper $s$ band that favors extended $s$ wave pairing which is
not found in two band model. Upon electron doping to a critical chemical
potential $\mu_1=0.22 eV$ the pairing potential decreases, then increases until
a second critical value $\mu_2$=1.3 eV at which a phase transition to a new
phase which is not appear in two band model. This phase in the pristine
graphene converts to usual extended s-wave pairing.

text: In the realm of high-dimensional time series analysis, variable screening has become an essential technique to manage the complexity and dimensionality inherent in massive datasets. The objective of this study is to develop an efficient variable screening method tailored for high-dimensional time series data, which are commonplace in fields such as finance, genomics, and climate science. We propose a novel approach that integrates a penalized likelihood framework with temporal dependence structures, to identify the most informative variables while discarding redundant or irrelevant ones. Our methodology employs a two-step procedure an initial marginal screening based on an adaptive threshold, followed by a selection refinement through a regularization path constructed via systematic control of false discoveries. We test our method on synthetically generated datasets and real-world financial data to evaluate its effectiveness. Key findings indicate that the proposed approach successfully retains variables that capture true underlying temporal dynamics, significantly enhancing predictive performance while maintaining computational efficiency. Moreover, our method demonstrates robustness against noise and varying time series lengths, outperforming traditional techniques such as LASSO and SCAD in terms of both selection accuracy and computational speed. In conclusion, this study offers a powerful and practical screening technique that substantially reduces dimensionality without sacrificing critical information, paving the way for more accurate modeling and analysis of high-dimensional time series data. Future work may extend this framework to accommodate non-linear relationships and integrate machine learning algorithms for further refinement in variable selection processes.
label: machine

We compute the n-point two-loop form factors of the half-BPS operators
Tr(phi_{AB}^n) in N=4 super Yang-Mills for arbitrary n >2 using generalised
unitarity and symbols. These form factors are minimal in the sense that the
n^{th} power of the scalar field in the operator requires the presence of at
least n on-shell legs. Infrared divergences are shown to exponentiate as for
amplitudes, reproducing the known cusp and collinear anomalous dimensions at
two loops. We define appropriate infrared-finite remainder functions and
compute them analytically for all n. The results obtained by using the known
expressions of the integral functions involve complicated combinations of
Goncharov multiple polylogarithms, but we show that much simpler expressions
can in fact be derived using the symbol of transcendental functions. For n=3 we
find a very compact remainder function expressed in terms of classical
polylogarithms only. For arbitrary n>3 we are able to write all the remainder
functions in terms of a single compact building block, expressed as a sum of
classical polylogarithms augmented by two multiple polylogarithms. The
decomposition of the symbol into specific components is crucial in order to
single out a natural combination of multiple polylogarithms. Finally, we
analyse in detail the behaviour of these minimal form factors in collinear and
soft limits, which deviates from the usual behaviour of amplitudes and
non-minimal form factors.

The growing focus in research policy worldwide on top scientists makes it
increasingly important to define adequate supporting measures to help identify
excellent scientists. Highly cited publications have since long been associated
to research excellence. At the same time, the analysis of the high-end of
citation distributions still is a challenging topic in evaluative
bibliometrics. Evaluations typically require indicators that generate
sufficiently stable results when applied to recent publication records of
limited size. Highly cited publications have been identified using two
techniques in particular: pre-set percentiles, and the parameter free
Characteristic Scores and Scales (CSS) (Gl\"anzel & Schubert, 1988). The
stability required in assessments of relatively small publication records,
concerns size as well as content of groups of highly cited publications.
Influencing factors include domain delineation and citation window length.
Stability in size is evident for the pre-set percentiles, and has been
demonstrated for the CSS-methodology beyond an initial citation period of about
three years (Gl\"anzel, 2007). Stability in content is less straightforward,
considering for instance that more highly cited publications can have a later
citation peak, as observed by Abt (1981) for astronomical papers. This paper
investigates the stability in content of groups of highly cited publications,
i.e. the extent to which individual publications enter and leave the group as
the citation window is enlarged.
label: human

The Lie-group-based symmetry analysis, as first proposed in Avsarkisov et al.
(2014) and then later modified in Oberlack et al. (2015), to generate invariant
solutions in order to predict the scaling behavior of a channel flow with
uniform wall transpiration, is revisited. By focusing first on the results
obtained in Avsarkisov et al. (2014), we failed to reproduce two key results:
(i) For different transpiration rates at a constant Reynolds number, the mean
velocity profiles (in deficit form) do not universally collapse onto a single
curve as claimed. (ii) The universally proposed logarithmic scaling law in the
center of the channel does not match the direct numerical simulation (DNS) data
for the presented parameter values. In fact, no universal scaling behavior in
the center of the channel can be detected from their DNS data, as it is
misleadingly claimed in Avsarkisov et al. (2014). Moreover, we will demonstrate
that the assumption of a Reynolds-number independent symmetry analysis is not
justified for the flow conditions considered therein. Only when including also
the viscous terms, an overall consistent symmetry analysis can be provided.
This has been attempted in their subsequent study Oberlack et al. (2015). But,
also the (viscous) Lie-group-based scaling theory proposed therein is
inconsistent, apart from the additional fact that this study of Oberlack et al.
(2015) is also technically flawed. The reason for this permanent inconsistency
is that their symmetry analysis constantly involves several unphysical
statistical symmetries that are incompatible to the underlying deterministic
description of Navier-Stokes turbulence.

text: This study investigates the magnetic interaction and activity in late-type stars hosting close-in planets, focusing on the implications of such proximity on stellar magnetic fields and activity levels. Our research aims to address the problem of understanding how the presence of close-in planets influences the stellar magnetic field and activity, offering insights into the dynamics of star-planet interactions. We analyze data from various observational sources, such as photometric surveys and magnetic field measurements, to examine the effects of close-in planets on the stellar magnetic field strength and activity indicators. Key findings reveal that close-in planets can perturb the stellar magnetic field, leading to enhanced activity levels in late-type stars. Our methodology involves statistical analysis of observational data coupled with theoretical models to interpret the impact of star-planet magnetic interaction on stellar activity. Through this comprehensive approach, we provide new perspectives on the connection between close-in planets and the magnetic properties of late-type stars, contributing to the broader understanding of stellar evolution and planetary system dynamics. The results of this study offer valuable insights into the complex interplay between stars and their planetary companions, shedding light on the effects of close-in planets on stellar magnetic fields and activity.
label: machine

text: This research paper investigates the phenomenon of spinon fractionalization in a spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the Kagome lattice through analysis of the dynamic structure factor. The objective of the study is to explore the manifestation of spin liquids and emergent fractionalized excitations in the given system. The methodology involves utilizing numerical techniques, such as Lanczos exact diagonalization, to calculate the dynamic structure factor and identify signatures of spinon fractionalization. The key findings reveal distinct spectral features indicative of fractionalized excitations in the dynamic structure factor, supporting the existence of spin liquids and fractionalized particles in the Kagome lattice system. Through the analysis of the spinon excitations and their fractional nature, this research sheds light on the unique quantum phenomena that arise in frustrated magnetic systems on the Kagome lattice. In conclusion, the study provides valuable insights into the fractionalization behavior of spins in the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the Kagome lattice, contributing to the understanding of exotic quantum states and emergent phenomena in strongly correlated spin systems.
label: machine

text:
We discuss physical properties of `integer' topological phases of bosons in
D=3+1 dimensions, protected by internal symmetries like time reversal and/or
charge conservation. These phases invoke interactions in a fundamental way but
do not possess topological order and are bosonic analogs of free fermion
topological insulators and superconductors. While a formal cohomology based
classification of such states was recently discovered, their physical
properties remain mysterious. Here we develop a field theoretic description of
several of these states and show that they possess unusual surface states,
which if gapped, must either break the underlying symmetry, or develop
topological order. In the latter case, symmetries are implemented in a way that
is forbidden in a strictly two dimensional theory. While this is the usual fate
of the surface states, exotic gapless states can also be realized. For example,
tuning parameters can naturally lead to a deconfined quantum critical point or,
in other situations, a fully symmetric vortex metal phase. We discuss cases
where the topological phases are characterized by quantized magnetoelectric
response \theta, which, somewhat surprisingly, is an odd multiple of 2\pi. Two
different surface theories are shown to capture these phenomena - the first is
a nonlinear sigma model with a topological term. The second invokes vortices on
the surface that transform under a projective representation of the symmetry
group. A bulk field theory consistent with these properties is identified,
which is a multicomponent `BF' theory supplemented, crucially, with a
topological term. A possible topological phase characterized by the thermal
analog of the magnetoelectric effect is also discussed.
label: human

text: In highly congested urban environments, crowd counting is a crucial task for surveillance systems, emergency response, and urban planning. Traditional crowd counting methods often struggle with accurately counting large crowds, especially in scenes with complex backgrounds and varying densities. This study proposes a novel approach to crowd counting using fully convolutional neural networks (FCNs) on highly congested scenes.   The objective of this research is to develop a robust and accurate crowd counting system that can effectively handle complex scenes with dense crowds. Our approach leverages the capabilities of FCNs to learn spatial hierarchies and contextual relationships between objects, enabling the model to accurately count crowds in various scenarios.  The proposed methodology involves a two-stage architecture the first stage consists of a feature extraction network, which extracts contextual features from the input image; the second stage is a classification network, which predicts the number of people in the scene. We utilize a data augmentation strategy to increase the diversity of the training dataset, and employ a loss function that combines the mean squared error and the mean absolute error to balance the accuracy and precision of the crowd count.  Our key findings indicate that the proposed FCN-based approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and precision, especially in scenes with complex backgrounds and varying densities. The model achieves an average precision of 92.5% and an average recall of 91.2%, with an average F1-score of 91.85%. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in crowd counting on highly congested scenes, and provide a solid foundation for further research in this area.
label: machine

The lighter mass eigenstate ($\widetilde{t}_1$) of the two top squarks, the
scalar superpartners of the top quark, is extremely difficult to discover if it
is almost degenerate with the lightest neutralino ($\widetilde{\chi}_1^0$), the
lightest and stable supersymmetric particle in the R-parity conserving
supersymmetry. The current experimental bound on $\widetilde{t}_1$ mass in this
scenario stands only around 200 GeV. For such a light $\widetilde{t}_1$, the
heavier top squark ($\widetilde{t}_2$) can also be around the TeV scale.
Moreover, the high value of the higgs ($h$) mass prefers the left and right
handed top squarks to be highly mixed allowing the possibility of a
considerable branching ratio for $\widetilde{t}_2 \to \widetilde{t}_1 h$ and
$\widetilde{t}_2 \to \widetilde{t}_1 Z$. In this paper, we explore the above
possibility together with the pair production of $\widetilde{t}_2$
$\widetilde{t}_2^*$ giving rise to the spectacular di-boson + missing
transverse energy final state. For an approximately 1 TeV $\widetilde{t}_2$ and
a few hundred GeV $\widetilde{t}_1$ the final state particles can be moderately
boosted which encourages us to propose a novel search strategy employing the
jet substructure technique to tag the boosted $h$ and $Z$. The reconstruction
of the $h$ and $Z$ momenta also allows us to construct the stransverse mass
$M_{T2}$ providing an additional efficient handle to fight the backgrounds. We
show that a 4--5$\sigma$ signal can be observed at the 14 TeV LHC for $\sim$ 1
TeV $\widetilde{t}_2$ with 100 fb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity.
label: human

Voyager observations for over 3 years beyond the heliopause have started to
define features of the low energy, less than 100 MeV per nuc, cosmic ray
secondary nuclei that have a zero or negligibly small source component. As an
example, the abundance of B between about 7 and 15 MeV per nuc is unexpectedly
large, greater than the prediction of a LBM by 2 or 3 in the measurement and
cross section error. On the other hand, for several other heavier secondary
nuclei with a low source abundance such as F and Z equal 17 to 19 and 21 to 23
nuclei, in the corresponding energy channels between about 10-20 MeV/nuc, zero
nuclei have been observed. The same LBM calculations would predict about 6 to 7
events for the sum of these three groups of nuclei. The B observed intensities
could be more closely matched by considering a nested LBM with 0.3-1.0 g/cm2 of
matter near the cosmic ray sources, essentially a source component of B. This
nested LBM calculation, if extended to the production of the above groups of
secondaries, would however predict a total 8 to 12 events thus leading to an
even larger discrepancy with the zero events that are observed. The
measurements of heavier secondaries at low energies therefore make it very
problematical that a nested LBM with more than a few 0.1 g/cm2 or more of
matter near the sources could be the source of the large B abundance seen by
Voyager. The large abundance of B at the lowest energies is best understood, so
far, as the result of production mostly from a matter traversal of 10 g/cm2 in
the galaxy, possibly in combination with uncertainties in the data and cross
sections at these low energies.
label: human

text: This study explores the application of the homogeneous 5D projection technique to elucidate the masses of quarks and hadrons. Historically, the Standard Model has struggled to explain the observed mass hierarchy among quarks and hadronic particles. Building upon previous theoretical frameworks, this research aims to provide a novel approach by embedding the Standard Model into a five-dimensional spacetime, where the dynamics of the four-dimensional effective theory emerge naturally. The methodology involves constructing a model where the fifth dimension is compactified and then analyzing how the effective four-dimensional theory reproduces the masses and interactions of quarks and hadrons. Key findings include a successful prediction of quark masses within the theoretical framework, as well as an explanation for the observed pattern of mass ratios among different quarks. Additionally, the model provides insights into the structure of hadrons, suggesting new ways to understand their mass spectra. The results indicate that the homogeneous 5D projection can offer a promising avenue for addressing the challenges posed by the hierarchical nature of quark and hadron masses in particle physics.

Recently emerging large-area single-layer MoS2 grown by chemical vapor
deposition has triggered great interest due to its exciting potential for
applications in advanced electronic and optoelectronic devices. Unlike gapless
graphene, MoS2 has an intrinsic band gap in the visible which crosses over from
an indirect to a direct gap when reduced to a single atomic layer. In this
article, we report a comprehensive study of fundamental optical properties of
MoS2 revealed by optical spectroscopy of Raman, photoluminescence, and vacuum
ultraviolet spectroscopic ellipsometry. A band gap of 1.42 eV is determined by
the absorption threshold of bulk MoS2 that shifts to 1.83 eV in monolayer MoS2.
We extracted the high precision dielectric function up to 9.0 eV which leads to
the identification of many unique interband transitions at high symmetry points
in the MoS2 momentum space. The positions of the A and B excitons in single
layers are found to shift upwards in energy compared with those of the bulk
form and have smaller separation. A very strong optical critical point
predicted to correspond to a quasi-particle gap is observed at 2.86 eV, which
is attributed to optical transitions along the parallel bands between the M and
gama points in the reduced Brillouin zone. The absence of the bulk MoS2
spin-orbit interaction peak at ~ 3.0 eV in monolayer MoS2 is, as predicted, the
consequence of the coalescence of nearby excitons. A higher energy optical
transition at 3.98 eV, commonly occurred in bulk semiconductors, is associated
with a combination of several critical points.These optical transitions herein
reported enhance our understanding of monolayer MoS2 as well as of
two-dimensional systems in general, and thus provide informative guidelines for
MoS2 optical device designs and theoretical considerations.

text: This research addresses the long-term dynamics of a viscous Cahn-Hilliard system incorporating convection effects and dynamic boundary conditions. The study is motivated by the need to understand phase separation phenomena in complex physical models where fluid movement and surface interactions play a critical role. The primary objective is to analyze the evolution of solutions and establish the existence of global attractors for this system, which reflect the stable states of the dynamics. The methodology involves a combination of functional analysis and dynamical systems theory to rigorously prove the existence of solutions and characterize their asymptotic behavior. The inclusion of convection terms and dynamic boundaries introduces significant mathematical challenges, which are tackled by extending existing theoretical frameworks for classic Cahn-Hilliard systems. Our key findings reveal that under suitable conditions, the system admits a unique global attractor, indicating the stabilization of patterns over time. Notably, the interplay between convection and dynamic boundaries is shown to influence the rate of convergence to equilibrium, highlighting new dynamics not captured by traditional models. These results contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of phase separation in environments where external influences cannot be ignored. In conclusion, this study enhances the theoretical foundation for modeling complex interfaces and provides insights that could inform experimental and numerical approaches in related fields. Future research may explore the impact of varying parameter regimes and multidimensional effects to further elucidate the intricacies of coupled convection and boundary dynamics in phase transition phenomena.

MGRO J1908+06 is a bright, extended TeV gamma-ray source located near the
Galactic plane. The TeV emission has previously been attributed to the pulsar
wind nebula of the radio-faint gamma-ray pulsar PSR J1907+0602 discovered with
Fermi. However, studies of the TeV morphology with VERITAS have shown that MGRO
J1908+06 is somewhat larger than other pulsar wind nebulae of similar age and
that the TeV spectrum does not soften with distance from the pulsar as is
observed for other pulsar wind nebulae. Although MGRO J1908+06 is very bright
in gamma rays with a flux corresponding to ~80% of the Crab Nebula flux at 20
TeV, no extended emission at other energies has so far been detected. We report
on our analysis of X-ray data obtained with XMM-Newton of the region near MGRO
J1908+06. We searched the data for point-like sources and detected several
hard-spectrum X-ray sources that could be associated with the TeV emission,
including the gamma-ray pulsar PSR J1907+0602. We also performed an extended
source analysis to search for diffuse emission from MGRO J1908+06 but found no
evidence of diffuse X-ray emission coincident with the TeV source. We place an
upper limit of $8.7\times10^{33}\rm~erg~s^{-1}$ on the X-ray luminosity of MGRO
J1908+06 in the 1-10 keV energy range. The corresponding limit on the ratio of
gamma-ray to X-ray luminosity is consistent with the ratios found for other
pulsar wind nebulae of similar age.

A delayed-acceptance version of a Metropolis--Hastings algorithm can be
useful for Bayesian inference when it is computationally expensive to calculate
the true posterior, but a computationally cheap approximation is available; the
delayed-acceptance kernel targets the same posterior as its associated "parent"
Metropolis-Hastings kernel. Although the asymptotic variance of the ergodic
average of any functional of the chain cannot be less than that obtained using
its parent, the average computational time per iteration can be much smaller
and so for a given computational budget the delayed-acceptance kernel can be
more efficient.
  When the asymptotic variance of the ergodic averages of all $L^2$ functionals
of the chain is finite, the kernel is said to be variance bounding. It has
recently been noted that a delayed-acceptance kernel need not be variance
bounding even when its parent is. We provide sufficient conditions for
inheritance: for non-local algorithms, such as the independence sampler, the
discrepancy between the log density of the approximation and that of the truth
should be bounded; for local algorithms, two alternative sets of conditions are
provided.
  As a by-product of our initial, general result we also supply sufficient
conditions on any pair of proposals such that, for any shared target
distribution, if a Metropolis-Hastings kernel using one of the proposals is
variance bounding then so is the Metropolis-Hastings kernel using the other
proposal.

Quasi-Periodic Oscillations (QPOs) are very puzzling since they remain
totally unexplained by popular earlier models of accretion disks. The
significant rms value in power density spectrum implies that the oscillation
involves in the dynamical and non-linear variation of certain region of the
accretion disk itself. The nature of the energy dependence implies that the
region which produces Comptonized hard tail is also responsible for QPOs.
Similarly, the occurrences of the QPOs are strongly related to the jet
formation and the spectral states. These features are the natural consequences
of the advective disk paradigm that we are advocating. In the mid 90s, some of
the present authors first pointed out that the QPOs in all possible types of
black holes may be simply due to the oscillations of the CENBOL, the
CENtrifugal pressure supported BOundary Layer which is formed in the
sub-Keplerian flows around a black hole. This CENBOL could be axi-symmetric as
well as non-axisymteric in nature since its boundary, namely, the centrifugally
driven shocks could be axi-symmetric or non-axisymmetric. In addition, we
pointed out that the transition radius where the flow becomes Keplerian to
sub-Keplerian, as well as the location of the inner sonic point can also
oscillate and produce the QPOs. Since the shock locations are functions of the
specific angular momentum ($\lambda$) and specific energy (${\cal E}$) of the
flow, our model naturally predicts that the QPO frequency should vary with
mass, spin, $\lambda$ and ${\cal E}$. The QPO frequencies with specific ratios,
such as, 2:3 must be due to non-axisymmetric effects when the shock switches
between the two-armed and the three-armed spirals. We also discuss the possible
effects that the disk inclination might have with the line of sight.

text: This research paper explores the interplay between supernova explosions and the interstellar medium (ISM) by investigating space- and time-correlations. The background of the study involves understanding how supernovae impact the ISM, influencing its structure and composition. The primary objective is to analyze the spatial and temporal relationships between supernova events and ISM properties.  Methodology involves utilizing observational data of supernova remnants and ISM characteristics to map out their spatial distributions and evolution over time. Statistical analysis is employed to quantify the correlations between supernova occurrences and various ISM parameters, such as density, temperature, and magnetic fields.  Key findings reveal significant correlations between supernova locations and specific ISM features, indicating the localized effects of supernovae on the surrounding interstellar environment. These findings provide insights into the dynamic nature of the ISM and the role of supernovae in shaping its properties.  In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of considering both space and time factors when studying the impact of supernovae on the ISM. By elucidating these correlations, we enhance our understanding of the complex interactions between supernova explosions and the interstellar medium, contributing to further advancements in astrophysical research.

text: This study investigates perturbed Hankel determinants and their applications in the information theory domain of Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) wireless communications. The primary objective is to analyze how perturbations affect the performance metrics of MIMO systems, specifically focusing on channel capacity and diversity-multiplexing tradeoff (DMT). We employ advanced mathematical techniques to derive expressions for perturbed Hankel determinants, which are crucial in quantifying these performance metrics. Through rigorous simulations, we observe how variations in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and channel conditions influence the system's reliability and efficiency. Our findings reveal that perturbed Hankel determinants offer a precise method for evaluating the robustness of MIMO systems under different operating scenarios. The key methodologies include the application of matrix analysis, spectral theory, and probabilistic models to derive theoretical bounds and practical estimations of channel capacity. This work not only contributes to the theoretical understanding of MIMO systems but also provides valuable insights for optimizing communication protocols and enhancing network performance.

Capillary attraction between identical millimeter sized spheres floating at a
liquid-air interface and the resulting aggregation is investigated at low
Reynolds number. We show that the measured capillary forces between two spheres
as a function of distance can be described by expressions obtained using the
Nicolson approximation at low Bond numbers for far greater particle sizes than
previously assumed. We find that viscous hydrodynamics interactions between the
spheres needs to be included to describe the dynamics close to contact. We then
consider the aggregates formed when a third sphere is added after the initial
two spheres are already in contact. In this case, we find that linear
superposition of capillary forces describes the observed approach qualitatively
but not quantitatively. Further, we observe an angular dependence of the
structure due to a rapid decrease of capillary force with distance of
separation which has a tendency to align the particles before contact. When the
three particles come in contact, they may preserve their shape or rearrange to
form an equilateral triangle cluster - the lowest energy state - depending on
the competition between attraction between particles and friction. Using these
observations, we demonstrate that a linear particle chain can be built from
frictional particles with capillary attraction.
