Our results suggest that the B1 shock plays a pivotal role in shaping the surrounding environment, influencing star formation processes and the distribution of molecular gas. We quantify the shock's density enhancements and velocity structures, revealing a complex interplay between shock-driven turbulence and ambient medium properties.  Additionally, we employ numerical simulations to validate our observational findings, integrating radiative transfer models to interpret the emission features observed at various wavelengths. We illustrate that the B1 shock not only initiates local heating and compression but also triggers secondary shock formations along its path, further complicating the dynamics of the entire outflow system.  This study contributes to a deeper understanding of outflow-shock interactions in star-forming regions, thereby enhancing our comprehension of the star formation cycle and the role of such shocks in the evolution of molecular clouds. text: We investigate the detection and characterization of gravitationally lensed quasars using data from the Gaia mission, focusing on the resolution of small-separation lenses. Our strategic approach combines Gaia's high-precision astrometry with innovative machine learning algorithms to enhance the identification efficiency of small-separation quasar lenses. We develop a robust classification framework leveraging supervised learning techniques on simulated lensing datasets, tailored to capture subtle astrometric signatures indicative of small-separation lenses. This methodology enables the distinction between lensed and unlensed quasar images with remarkable accuracy. Our analysis yields a substantial catalog of candidate lensed quasars that satisfy criteria indicative of gravitational lensing at sub-arcsecond separations. The catalog significantly augments existing samples, opening avenues for a comprehensive investigation of the structural characteristics and cosmological implications of these systems. Additionally, we address observational biases inherent in Gaia's dataset and propose mitigation techniques to improve lens detection rates. Our results demonstrate that Gaia's astrometric capabilities, augmented by advanced algorithms, are instrumental in resolving small-separation lenses previously inaccessible through traditional techniques. This advancement not only enriches our understanding of cosmic lensing phenomena but also offers profound insights into the underlying mass distribution in the universe and the nature of distant quasars. We present a first-principles computational study of solid 4He at T=0K and
pressures up to 160GPa. Our computational strategy consists in using van der
Waals density functional theory (DFT-vdW) to describe the electronic degrees of
freedom in this material, and the diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) method to solve
the Schrodinger equation describing the behavior of the quantum nuclei. For
this, we construct an analytical interaction function based on the pairwise
Aziz potential that closely matches the volume variation of the cohesive energy
calculated with DFT-vdW in dense helium. Interestingly, we find that the
kinetic energy of solid 4He does not increase appreciably with compression for
P > 85GPa. Also, we show that the Lindemann ratio in dense solid 4He amounts to
0.10 almost independently of pressure. The reliability of customary
quasi-harmonic DFT (QH DFT) approaches in the description of quantum nuclear
effects in solids is also studied. We find that QH DFT simulations, although
provide a reasonable equation of state in agreement with experiments, are not
able to reproduce correctly these critical effects in compressed 4He. In
particular, we disclose huge discrepancies of at least ~50% in the calculated
4He kinetic energies using both the QH DFT and present DFT-DMC methods.

text: This study investigates the conditional stability of solutions to operator equations involving monotone operators within the framework of Hilbert spaces. The research aims to distinguish between stable and unstable conditions under which solutions to such equations remain meaningful despite potential ill-posedness. We employ variational methods and regularization techniques to analyze these equations, focusing on how the choice of regularization parameters influences the stability of solutions. The analysis reveals that while monotonicity provides a necessary condition for the existence of solutions, it does not guarantee stability; instead, it can lead to ill-posed problems where small perturbations in the data can cause large changes in the solution. Key methodologies include the application of Tikhonov regularization and the use of Bregman distances to quantify the stability of solutions. The findings underscore the importance of carefully selecting regularization strategies to ensure meaningful and stable solutions in the presence of monotone operators.

Condensate clouds strongly impact the spectra of brown dwarfs and exoplanets.
Recent discoveries of variable L/T transition dwarfs argued for patchy clouds
in at least some ultracool atmospheres. This study aims to measure the
frequency and level of spectral variability in brown dwarfs and to search for
correlations with spectral type. We used HST/WFC3 to obtain spectroscopic time
series for 22 brown dwarfs of spectral types ranging from L5 to T6 at 1.1-1.7
$\mu$m for $\approx$40 min per object. Using Bayesian analysis, we find 6 brown
dwarfs with confident $(p>95\%)$ variability in the relative flux in at least
one wavelength region at sub-percent precision, and 5 brown dwarfs with
tentative $(p>68\%)$ variability. We derive a minimum variability fraction
$f_{min}=27^{+11}_{-7}\%$ over all covered spectral types. The fraction of
variables is equal within errors for mid L, late L and mid T spectral types;
for early T dwarfs we do not find any confident variable but the sample is too
small to derive meaningful limits. For some objects, the variability occurs
primarily in the flux peak in the J or H band, others are variable throughout
the spectrum or only in specific absorption regions. Four sources may have
broad-band peak-to-peak amplitudes exceeding 1%. Our measurements are not
sensitive to very long periods, inclinations near pole-on and rotationally
symmetric heterogeneity. The detection statistics are consistent with most
brown dwarf photospheres being patchy. While multiple-percent near-infrared
variability may be rare and confined to the L/T transition, low-level
heterogeneities are a frequent characteristic of brown dwarf atmospheres.

The effects of the stellar rotation and the consequent azimuthal stellar wind
flow in Parker's [9] hydrodynamic stellar wind model are discussed. Of special
interest is the emergence of a whole new hydrodynamic physics via a new
critical point in the stellar wind flow, which supersedes the critical point in
Parker's [9] hydrodynamic model. The effect of the stellar rotation is shown to
cause the new critical point to occur lower in the corona, so the stellar wind
experiences a stronger afterburner (as in an aircraft jet engine) action in the
corona. For strong rotators, the new critical point is shown to occur at a
fixed location for a given star, determined only by the basic stellar
parameters like the mass M and the angular velocity, the variations in the
stellar wind environment notwithstanding. The stellar rotation leads to
stronger density fall-off and enhanced acceleration of the stellar wind at
large distances from the star - this effect materializes even close to the
star, for strong rotators. The stellar rotation causes the physical throat
section of the effective de Laval nozzle associated with the stellar wind flow
to become narrower, indicative of an enhanced flow acceleration. Thus, the
stellar rotation leads to tenuous and faster stellar wind flows without change
in the mass flux, and hence provides an efficient physical mechanism for
protostars and strong rotators to lose their angular momentum quickly.

text: In the study of the actinide nitrides, understanding their electronic structure and properties is crucial for potential applications in nuclear fuel technology. This research employs density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of a series of actinide nitrides, including UN, NpN, and PuN. The objective is to provide a detailed comparison of these compounds, enhancing comprehension of their behavior under various conditions. Using a generalized gradient approximation (GGA) for the exchange-correlation functional, we analyze the lattice constants, band structures, density of states, and magnetic moments of each nitride. Our computational approach includes spin-orbit coupling effects and Hubbard U correction to account for the strongly correlated f-electrons in actinides, providing more accurate simulations. The key findings reveal that the actinide nitrides exhibit unique magnetic characteristics, with substantial hybridization between the actinide 5f and nitrogen 2p orbitals influencing the electronic properties. Our results show that these materials possess metallic conductivity and complex magnetic behavior, which varies across the series due to the distinct balance of exchange interactions and crystal field effects. The study also confirms that the inclusion of spin-orbit coupling and Hubbard U is essential in capturing the subtle electronic interactions within these materials. In conclusion, the density functional study enhances the fundamental understanding of actinide nitrides, offering insights into their potential use in advanced nuclear systems. These findings have broader implications for the design of new materials with tailored electronic and magnetic properties.

[GKH94] 41 and IRAS 04191+1523B were previously identified to be proto-brown
dwarf candidates in Taurus. [GKH94] 41 was classified to be a class I object.
The dereddened spectral energy distribution of the source was later found to be
suggestive of a class II object. IRAS 04191+1523B is a class I object that is
the secondary component of a binary. We determine the evolutionary stage of
[GKH94] 41 and estimate the final masses of the two proto-brown dwarf
candidates. We used archive millimeter observations to produce continuum maps
and collected data from the literature to construct the spectral energy
distribution of the targets. Our continuum maps revealed that both [GKH94] 41
and IRAS 04191+1523B are surrounded by envelopes. This provides direct evidence
that [GKH94] 41 is a class I object, not class II, as previously classified.
For IRAS 04191+1523B, our continuum map spatially resolved the binary. Our
estimated final masses are below 49$^{+56}_{-27}$ $M_{\rm J}$ and
75$^{+40}_{-26}$ $M_{\rm J}$ for [GKH94] 41 and IRAS 04191+1523B, respectively.
This indicates that both sources will likely become brown dwarfs or very
low-mass stars. Therefore, [GKH94] 41 and IRAS 04191+1523B are two new
confirmed class I very low-mass objects. Their existence also supports the
scenario that brown dwarfs have the same formation stages as low-mass stars.

We consider the detection and estimation of a zero-mean Gaussian signal in a
wireless sensor network with a coherent multiple access channel, when the
fusion center (FC) is configured with a large number of antennas and the
wireless channels between the sensor nodes and FC experience Rayleigh fading.
For the detection problem, we study the Neyman-Pearson (NP) Detector and Energy
Detector (ED), and find optimal values for the sensor transmission gains. For
the NP detector which requires channel state information (CSI), we show that
detection performance remains asymptotically constant with the number of FC
antennas if the sensor transmit power decreases proportionally with the
increase in the number of antennas. Performance bounds show that the benefit of
multiple antennas at the FC disappears as the transmit power grows. The results
of the NP detector are also generalized to the linear minimum mean squared
error estimator. For the ED which does not require CSI, we derive optimal gains
that maximize the deflection coefficient of the detector, and we show that a
constant deflection can be asymptotically achieved if the sensor transmit power
scales as the inverse square root of the number of FC antennas. Unlike the NP
detector, for high sensor power the multi-antenna ED is observed to empirically
have significantly better performance than the single-antenna implementation. A
number of simulation results are included to validate the analysis.

The standard general relativistic model of a razor-thin accretion disk around
a black hole, developed by Novikov & Thorne (NT) in 1973, assumes the shear
stress vanishes at the radius of the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) and
that, outside the ISCO, the shear stress is produced by an effective turbulent
viscosity. However, astrophysical accretion disks are not razor-thin, it is
uncertain whether the shear stress necessarily vanishes at the ISCO, and the
magnetic field, which is thought to drive turbulence in disks, may contain
large-scale structures that do not behave like a simple local scalar viscosity.
We describe three-dimensional general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic
simulations of accretion disks around black holes with a range of spin
parameters, and we use the simulations to assess the validity of the NT model.
Our fiducial initial magnetic field consists of multiple (alternating polarity)
poloidal field loops whose shape is roughly isotropic in the disk in order to
match the isotropic turbulence expected in the poloidal plane. For a thin disk
with an aspect ratio |h/r| ~ 0.07 around a non-spinning black hole, we find a
decrease in the accreted specific angular momentum of 2.9% relative to the NT
model and an excess luminosity from inside the ISCO of 3.5%. The deviations in
the case of spinning black holes are of the same order. In addition, the
deviations decrease with decreasing |h/r|. We therefore conclude that
magnetized thin accretion disks in x-ray binaries in the thermal/high-soft
spectral state ought to be well-described by the NT model, especially at
luminosities below 30% of Eddington where we expect a very small disk thickness
|h/r| <~ 0.05. We also discuss how the stress and the luminosity inside the
ISCO depend on the assumed initial magnetic field geometry. (abridged)

text: This research paper presents a novel approach for mapping the local interstellar medium (ISM) in three dimensions using composite data. The objective of this study is to provide a comprehensive and detailed map of the ISM within our galactic neighborhood. To achieve this, we collate multiple sources of data, including spectroscopic observations, radio measurements, and stellar photometry. Our methodology involves integrating these diverse datasets through advanced computational techniques, such as data fusion algorithms and 3D visualization tools.   Key findings from this research include the identification of previously unknown structures and variations in the density and composition of the local ISM. The three-dimensional map generated through our approach reveals intricate details of the ISM environment surrounding the Sun and nearby stars, shedding light on the distribution of gas, dust, and magnetic fields in our region of the Milky Way.  In conclusion, the utilization of composite data and three-dimensional mapping techniques offers a valuable tool for studying the local ISM in unprecedented detail. This research contributes to a better understanding of the complex interstellar environment in which our solar system resides, with implications for fields such as astrophysics, heliophysics, and planetary science.

The black-hole binary V404 Cyg entered the outburst phase in June 2015 after
26 years of X-ray quiescence, and with its behaviour broke the outburst
evolution pattern typical of most black-hole binaries. We observed the entire
outburst with the Swift satellite and performed time-resolved spectroscopy of
its most active phase, obtaining over a thousand spectra with exposures from
tens to hundreds of seconds. All the spectra can be fitted with an absorbed
power law model, which most of the time required the presence of a partial
covering. A blue-shifted iron-Kalpha line appears in 10% of the spectra
together with the signature of high column densities, and about 20% of the
spectra seem to show signatures of reflection. None of the spectra showed the
unambiguous presence of soft disk-blackbody emission, while the observed
bolometric flux exceeded the Eddington value in 3% of the spectra. Our results
can be explained assuming that the inner part of the accretion flow is inflated
into a slim disk that both hides the innermost (and brightest) regions of the
flow, and produces a cold, clumpy, high-density outflow that introduces the
high-absorption and fast spectral variability observed. We argue that the black
hole in V404 Cyg might have been accreting erratically or even continuously at
Eddington/Super-Eddington rates - thus sustaining a surrounding slim disk -
while being partly or completely obscured by the inflated disk and its outflow.
Hence, the largest flares produced by the source might not be accretion-driven
events, but instead the effects of the unveiling of the extremely bright source
hidden within the system.

text: This research paper explores the concept of indicated coloring within various graph classes, aiming to extend the understanding of graph coloring techniques beyond traditional methods. Indicated coloring involves assigning colors to vertices such that adjacent vertices receive different colors, with the additional constraint that each vertex must be colored according to its designated color from a predefined set. The study focuses on several specific graph classes, including planar graphs, outerplanar graphs, and graphs with bounded treewidth.  The methodology employed includes theoretical analysis, computational experiments, and comparison with known coloring algorithms. Key findings include the identification of optimal coloring strategies for these graph classes, which often involve more efficient coloring processes compared to traditional methods. Additionally, the research reveals that indicated coloring can lead to significant reductions in the number of colors required for certain graph structures, particularly those with high levels of symmetry or specific connectivity patterns.  In conclusion, the findings suggest that indicated coloring offers a promising approach to enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of graph coloring algorithms, especially for complex graph classes. Future research could further investigate the application of indicated coloring in real-world scenarios, such as network design and scheduling problems, where the constraints imposed by the designated colors may provide unique advantages.

text: In this work, we investigate the role of mechanical AGN feedback in regulating the thermodynamical properties of elliptical galaxies. Our study aims to address the problem of excessive cooling flows in the centers of these galaxies, which theoretical models have struggled to accurately replicate. We propose that mechanical feedback from actively accreting supermassive black holes plays a crucial role in distributing energy throughout the interstellar medium, thereby preventing the runaway cooling that leads to the formation of subsequent generations of stars. Utilizing a suite of hydrodynamical simulations, we incorporate models of jet-driven outflows and their interactions with the ambient gas. Our simulations demonstrate that AGN jets can efficiently redistribute thermal energy and sustain a stable thermal equilibrium over cosmological timescales. We observe the suppression of star formation rates, maintaining a low level of active galactic nucleus activity, which aligns closely with observed properties of elliptical galaxies. Key ideas that underpin our methodology include the coupling of kinetic energy feedback with the large-scale galactic halo and accounting for non-linear effects of turbulence and heat conduction. The results reveal the critical thresholds for jet power and feedback efficiencies necessary to maintain observed galactic states. Our findings suggest that mechanical AGN feedback mechanisms are integral to the thermal regulation of elliptical galaxies, potentially offering a resolution to discrepancies noted in current galaxy formation models. This work enhances our understanding of galaxy evolution and emphasizes the importance of incorporating multi-phase feedback processes in cosmological simulations.

text: The elliptical galaxy NGC 4125, located in the Virgo Cluster, exhibits an unusual cold dust component in its central region, contrasting with the warm ionized gas. We explore this intriguing phenomenon using mid-infrared observations from the Spitzer Space Telescope and 21-cm hydrogen observations from the Very Large Array. The background reveals previous studies that suggest the presence of cold dust in elliptical galaxies and the importance of understanding the formation and evolution of such dust. The objective of this research is to provide new insights into the origin and properties of this cold dust component in NGC 4125. Our methodology involves analyzing Spitzer's Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) data, specifically the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) features, to determine the temperature and mass of the cold dust. We also compare our results with those of earlier studies on this topic. The key findings reveal a significant cold dust component, with a temperature of approximately 30 K, and a mass of 1.4 x 107 M☉. We suggest potential explanations for the presence of this cold dust, including the possible involvement of mergers, supernova explosions, or an ongoing star formation process. In conclusion, the discovery of a cold dust component in the unusual elliptical galaxy NGC 4125 challenges our current understanding of dust formation and evolution in these galaxies and underscores the importance of further investigations to unravel the underlying physical processes.

text: We investigate the dynamics near the soliton of the critical Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (cKdV) equation, a quintic nonlinear wave equation that exhibits a unique blow-up phenomenon. Through a series of numerical simulations, we demonstrate the emergence of a sharp, localized singularity, accompanied by a catastrophic loss of energy. Our analysis reveals that the blow-up is triggered by the interplay between the nonlinear term and the dispersive term, leading to an exponentially growing amplitude and a shrinking wavelength.   To gain insight into the underlying mechanisms, we employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods. We derive a reduced model that captures the essential dynamics near the soliton, and employ numerical simulations to validate our results. Our analysis reveals that the blow-up is preceded by a sequence of bifurcations, where the system transitions from a stable soliton to an unstable one. We also identify a critical value of the parameter that marks the onset of the blow-up.  Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of nonlinear wave dynamics and the behavior of the cKdV equation near the soliton. We provide a detailed comparison of our numerical results with existing analytical solutions, and discuss the limitations and potential extensions of our work. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the blow-up phenomenon for the cKdV equation, and offers a foundation for further research into the dynamics of nonlinear wave equations.

text: Quantum mechanics has led to a plethora of research in the field of quantum information processing, where the manipulation of quantum states plays a pivotal role. In this context, random sampling of quantum states has emerged as a crucial technique, enabling the generation of diverse and unbiased quantum states, which is essential for various quantum applications. However, the existing methods for random sampling of quantum states are often computationally intensive and lack standardization, hindering their widespread adoption.  This survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current methods for random sampling of quantum states, highlighting their strengths, limitations, and potential applications. The review encompasses a range of techniques, including the use of quantum random number generators, quantum circuits, and classical algorithms. A detailed analysis of the most prominent methods, such as the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), is presented, along with discussions on their respective advantages and disadvantages.  The survey also explores the role of post-processing techniques in enhancing the quality of the sampled states, such as quantum error correction and state purification. Furthermore, the impact of noise and interference on the random sampling process is examined, highlighting the need for robust and fault-tolerant methods. The findings of this survey provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop efficient and reliable methods for random sampling of quantum states, paving the way for the widespread adoption of quantum technologies.

text: In this study, we investigate the performance of cooperative multiple access channels (C-MAC) with delayed channel state information (CSI) at transmitters. Specifically, we consider a C-MAC system where multiple users cooperate to transmit data to a common receiver, with each user possessing CSI only from the previous time step. We propose two novel transmission schemes, namely Delayed Dirty Paper Coding (DDPC) and Delayed Max-Interference Alignment (DMIA), to tackle the challenges arising from delayed CSI.  DDPC scheme employs a dirty paper coding (DPC) structure, where each user's transmission is designed to cancel the interference caused by the other users' transmissions. However, due to the delay in CSI at transmitters, each user's transmission is based on outdated channel information. We derive the achievable rate region of the DDPC scheme and show that it is a proper subset of the scheme with instantaneous CSI. Simulation results demonstrate that the DDPC scheme outperforms the scheme with perfect CSI at moderate to high SNR regimes but has a worse performance at low SNRs.  DMIA scheme aligns the interfering signals in the spatial domain to achieve zero-forcing at the receiver. Like the DDPC scheme, DMIA also relies on delayed CSI at the transmitters. We prove that the DMIA scheme achieves the optimal rate region of the C-MAC system with delayed CSI at transmitters when the number of users is equal to the number of antennas at the receiver. We also provide numerical results to validate the performance of the DMIA scheme, demonstrating its significant improvement over the benchmark scheme with perfect CSI.  Overall, this study reveals the significant impact of delayed CSI on the performance of cooperative multiple access channels and introduces two novel transmission schemes, DDPC and DMIA, to mitigate the challenges arising from delayed CSI. Our findings contribute to the ongoing research in the field of cooperative communication systems and open new avenues for the exploration of delayed CSI schemes in various wireless communication applications.

text: In this study, we propose a novel method for implementing Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with GPU acceleration, significantly improving its sampling efficiency for large-scale statistical models. Our approach, termed Fast HMC (FHMC), employs dynamic batching and efficient parallelization strategies to process multiple particles in parallel on a GPU. We compare FHMC with standard HMC and other state-of-the-art GPU-accelerated sampling methods, including the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) and Langevin Dynamics.  Our experimental evaluation on various large-scale models, including Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) and Bayesian Nonparametric models, demonstrates substantial computational gains. For instance, on a BNN model with 10,000 hidden units, FHMC required 35 minutes to converge, whereas standard HMC took over 4 hours. On a large-scale Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Model (DPGMM), FHMC yielded a 12-fold increase in throughput compared to NUTS.  Key contributions of this work include (i) the development of FHMC, a highly parallelizable and efficient GPU implementation of HMC; (ii) the empirical validation of FHMC's superior performance on large-scale models; (iii) the identification of dynamic batching as a crucial strategy to balance computational resources and sampling performance in the GPU context. By bridging the gap between the sampling efficiency of HMC and the parallel processing capabilities of GPUs, FHMC provides a valuable tool for addressing the computational demands of increasingly complex statistical models.

text:
A discrete tensegrity framework can be thought of as a graph in Euclidean
n-space where each edge is of one of three types: an edge with a fixed length
(bar) or an edge with an upper (cable) or lower (strut) bound on its length.
Roth and Whiteley, in their 1981 paper "Tensegrity Frameworks", showed that in
certain cases, the struts and cables can be replaced with bars when analyzing
the framework for infinitesimal rigidity. In that case we call the tensegrity
"bar equivalent". In specific, they showed that if there exists a set of
positive weights, called a positive "stress", on the edges such that the
weighted sum of the edge vectors is zero at every vertex, then the tensegrity
is bar equivalent.
  In this paper we consider an extended version of the tensegrity framework in
which the vertex set is a (possibly infinite) set of points in Euclidean
n-space and the edgeset is a compact set of unordered pairs of vertices. These
are called "continuous tensegrities". We show that if a continuous tensegrity
has a strictly positive stress, it is bar equivalent and that it has a
semipositive stress if and only if it is partially bar equivalent. We also show
that if a tensegrity is minimally bar equivalent (it is bar equivalent but
removing any open set of edges makes it no longer so), then it has a strictly
positive stress.
  In particular, we examine the case where the vertices form a rectifiable
curve and the possible motions of the curve are limited to local isometries of
it. Our methods provide an attractive proof of the following result: There is
no locally arclength preserving motion of a circle that increases any antipodal
distance without decreasing some other one.

text: We investigate the concept of Parallel Search with no Coordination, focusing on the strategy where multiple agents independently search a solution space without communication or coordination. Our work aims to address the challenges and opportunities presented by this decentralized approach. By simulating scenarios where agents navigate a complex search space simultaneously, we examine their ability to collectively converge on optimal solutions without a centralized guiding mechanism.  Our results demonstrate that Parallel Search without Coordination can be a robust method for exploring solution spaces, especially in non-deterministic environments or when centralized coordination is infeasible. Despite the absence of explicit communication, the agents exhibit emergent behaviors that lead to the discovery of high-quality solutions. We also find that the effectiveness of this approach is influenced by factors such as the diversity of search strategies employed by the agents and the complexity of the problem space.  To delve into these findings, we utilize computational simulations and agent-based models to study the dynamics of Parallel Search with no Coordination. Through a series of experiments with varying problem complexities and agent characteristics, we analyze the effectiveness of decentralized search strategies. Our research sheds light on the mechanisms underlying collective intelligence in decentralized systems and provides insights into the potential applications of Parallel Search without Coordination in real-world problem-solving scenarios.

text:
Recognizing human activities in a sequence is a challenging area of research
in ubiquitous computing. Most approaches use a fixed size sliding window over
consecutive samples to extract features---either handcrafted or learned
features---and predict a single label for all samples in the window. Two key
problems emanate from this approach: i) the samples in one window may not
always share the same label. Consequently, using one label for all samples
within a window inevitably lead to loss of information; ii) the testing phase
is constrained by the window size selected during training while the best
window size is difficult to tune in practice. We propose an efficient algorithm
that can predict the label of each sample, which we call dense labeling, in a
sequence of human activities of arbitrary length using a fully convolutional
network. In particular, our approach overcomes the problems posed by the
sliding window step. Additionally, our algorithm learns both the features and
classifier automatically. We release a new daily activity dataset based on a
wearable sensor with hospitalized patients. We conduct extensive experiments
and demonstrate that our proposed approach is able to outperform the
state-of-the-arts in terms of classification and label misalignment measures on
three challenging datasets: Opportunity, Hand Gesture, and our new dataset.

text: Understanding the mechanisms governing star formation efficiency (SFE) is crucial for elucidating galaxy evolution and dynamics. This study investigates the phenomenon of feedback in star-forming regions, specifically focusing on the scaling and saturation effects that emerge as stellar populations evolve. The primary objective was to assess how various feedback processes, including radiation pressure, supernova explosions, and stellar winds, influence SFE in different environmental contexts. We employed a combination of observational data from deep-sky surveys and numerical simulations to analyze star-forming regions across galaxies of varying morphological types. Our findings reveal a non-linear relationship between SFE and factors such as gas density and metallicity, suggesting a saturation point beyond which feedback becomes increasingly ineffective. This saturation leads to a diminished ability of feedback processes to regulate star formation as stellar densities rise. Additionally, we observed that in low-density environments, feedback remains efficient, while in high-density environments, the feedback mechanisms often fail to counteract gravitational forces effectively. These insights provide a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between star formation and feedback in shaping galactic structures. Ultimately, our results indicate that the inefficacy of feedback in high-density regions could have significant implications for the overall star formation rates in galaxies, shedding light on the thresholds that govern the transition from star-forming to passive galaxy populations.

text: Our work presents a novel approach to causal discovery in high-dimensional datasets through the development of a fast PC algorithm optimized for multi-core processing units. Existing PC algorithms struggle to scale efficiently to these high-dimensional settings, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we propose a parallelized version of the PC algorithm that leverages the processing power of multi-core CPUs to accelerate causal discovery tasks.  Our experimental results demonstrate a significant improvement in computational efficiency with our proposed fast PC algorithm compared to traditional single-threaded approaches. By distributing the computational load across multiple CPU cores, we achieved faster causal inference in high-dimensional datasets without compromising accuracy. Our methodology involves parallelizing the key steps of the PC algorithm to enable simultaneous processing of different subsets of data, thus reducing the overall computational time required for causal discovery.  The outcomes of our study highlight the potential of utilizing multi-core PCs for enhancing causal discovery in high-dimensional data settings. The proposed fast PC algorithm offers a scalable and efficient solution for researchers and practitioners seeking to perform causal inference in complex datasets.

text: The increasing interest in space-time fractional parabolic equations arises from their applications in physics, finance, and various fields of engineering, necessitating the development of effective numerical methods for their approximation. We employ an adaptive finite difference scheme, combined with a fractional discretization technique, to enhance computational accuracy while maintaining efficiency. The proposed methodology is rigorously analyzed, focusing on stability and convergence properties. Numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of the method across diverse test cases, representing both linear and nonlinear scenarios. Key findings indicate that the adaptive scheme significantly outperforms conventional methods in terms of accuracy, with a reduction in computational complexity. The results also reveal that our approach can handle a wide range of fractional orders effectively, demonstrating its robustness. The findings suggest that the introduced numerical method is not only feasible but also superior for applications involving space-time fractional parabolic equations, paving the way for its use in real-world problems requiring precise modeling of fractional dynamics. In conclusion, this study contributes to the understanding of fractional calculus by providing a systematic numerical tool that broadens the scope for future research in fractional differential equations.

text: We present a comprehensive analysis of navigable maps depicting structural brain networks across multiple species. text: Chiral perturbation theory (ChPT) is a low-energy effective theory widely used to describe the dynamics of strongly interacting particles in the presence of light quarks. ChPT is based on power counting, which assumes that the chiral limit is attained when all quark masses are set to zero and the pion mass is the only low-energy scale. However, the validity of power counting is questioned when considering chiral extrapolations beyond the power-counting regime. In this paper, we examine the limitations and possible extensions of ChPT for chiral extrapolations beyond the power-counting regime. We start with a brief review of the fundamental concepts of ChPT and its power-counting rules. We then discuss the limitations of power counting in describing the pion-nucleon system, focusing on the role of large scattering angles and high energies. Subsequently, we explore several approaches for extending ChPT, including modified power counting, relativized ChPT, and dispersive ChPT. We compare the merits and limitations of these approaches and discuss their implications for chiral extrapolations beyond the power-counting regime. Our findings suggest that while none of these approaches can fully replace power counting, they offer valuable insights into the behavior of ChPT beyond its traditional regime, paving the way for future research in this area. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the challenges and potential solutions for chiral extrapolations beyond the power-counting regime in ChPT.

text: This study explores the hierarchy of orientational phases and axial anisotropies within the theoretical framework of generalized nematics. We systematically investigate the behavior of these phases under different conditions, identifying key transitions and their underlying mechanisms. Theoretical models are developed to describe the phase diagrams, focusing on the interplay between orientational order and axial anisotropy. Problematically, our initial attempts to model the transition between different phases often resulted in discrepancies due to oversimplification of the interaction potentials. To address this, we introduced a more refined potential function that better captures the energetic landscape of the system. Our key idea is the development of a hierarchical classification of orientational phases based on their stability and the extent of axial anisotropy they exhibit. This classification aids in understanding the emergent properties of the materials across various scales. Methodologically, we employ both analytical calculations and numerical simulations to validate our theoretical predictions. The results indicate that the hierarchy of phases is influenced significantly by the strength and nature of axial anisotropy, providing valuable insights into the complex behavior of generalized nematic systems.

In the classical Node-Disjoint Paths (NDP) problem, the input consists of an
undirected $n$-vertex graph $G$, and a collection
$\mathcal{M}=\{(s_1,t_1),\ldots,(s_k,t_k)\}$ of pairs of its vertices, called
source-destination, or demand, pairs. The goal is to route the largest possible
number of the demand pairs via node-disjoint paths. The best current
approximation for the problem is achieved by a simple greedy algorithm, whose
approximation factor is $O(\sqrt n)$, while the best current negative result is
an $\Omega(\log^{1/2-\delta}n)$-hardness of approximation for any constant
$\delta$, under standard complexity assumptions. Even seemingly simple special
cases of the problem are still poorly understood: when the input graph is a
grid, the best current algorithm achieves an $\tilde O(n^{1/4})$-approximation,
and when it is a general planar graph, the best current approximation ratio of
an efficient algorithm is $\tilde O(n^{9/19})$. The best currently known lower
bound on the approximability of both these versions of the problem is
APX-hardness.
  In this paper we prove that NDP is $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$-hard to
approximate, unless all problems in NP have algorithms with running time
$n^{O(\log n)}$. Our result holds even when the underlying graph is a planar
graph with maximum vertex degree $3$, and all source vertices lie on the
boundary of a single face (but the destination vertices may lie anywhere in the
graph). We extend this result to the closely related Edge-Disjoint Paths
problem, showing the same hardness of approximation ratio even for sub-cubic
planar graphs with all sources lying on the boundary of a single face.

We study the spin- and energy dynamics in one-dimensional spin-1/2 systems
induced by local quantum quenches at finite temperatures using a time-dependent
density matrix renormalization group method. System sizes are chosen large
enough to ensure that the time-dependent data for the accesible time scales
represents the behavior in the thermodynamic limit. As a main result, we
observe a ballistic spreading of perturbations of the energy density in the
integrable spin-1/2 XXZ chain for all temperatures and exchange anisotropies,
related to the divergent thermal conductivity in this model and the exact
conservation of the energy current. In contrast, the spin dynamics is ballistic
in the massless phase, but shows a diffusive behavior at high temperatures in
the easy-axis phase in the case of a vanishing background spin density. We
extract a quantitative estimate for the spin diffusion constant from the time
dependence of the spatial variance of the spin density, which agrees well with
values obtained from current-current correlation functions using an Einstein
relation. As an example for non-integrable models, we consider two-leg ladders,
for which we observe indications of diffusive energy and spin dynamics. The
relevance of our results for recent experiments with quantum magnets and bosons
in optical lattices is discussed.

text: This research investigates the challenges of sampling biased monotonic surfaces by employing exponential metrics. Monotonic surfaces, characterized by consistently increasing or decreasing values, often exhibit inherent biases that complicate the sampling process. Understanding and correcting for these biases is critical for effective data representation and subsequent analysis. The primary objective of this study is to develop a robust methodology that utilizes exponential metrics to enhance the accuracy and reliability of sampling such surfaces.   We begin by formulating a theoretical framework that integrates exponential metrics into the sampling process, allowing for a more nuanced capture of surface characteristics. The methodology is validated through a series of simulations and real-world applications, where we examine the efficiency of our approach in generating representative samples from various monotonic surface types. Key findings indicate that our proposed sampling technique significantly reduces bias while providing a more comprehensive representation of the underlying surface.   Additionally, we quantify improvements in sampling distribution and highlight the versatility of exponential metrics in adapting to different monotonic structures. Ultimately, this research contributes to the fields of computational geometry and data science by establishing a novel framework for bias mitigation in surface sampling. We conclude that the integration of exponential metrics not only improves the fidelity of sampled data but also opens avenues for advanced analytical techniques in assessing monotonic phenomena across diverse applications.

text: In this study, we present the validation and benchmarking of a practical method for calculating free magnetic energy and relative magnetic helicity budgets in solar magnetic structures. The key problem addressed is the accurate quantification of these crucial parameters in solar magnetic environments. By comparing our calculations with established theoretical models and observational data from solar events, we demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of our approach. The results indicate a high level of agreement between our calculated values and those derived from existing methods, thus validating our proposed technique. Our methodology involves combining numerical simulations with observational data to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the magnetic energy and helicity distribution within solar structures. We use advanced computational tools to analyze the complex magnetic fields in these regions and quantify the energy and helicity budgets accurately. The successful validation and benchmarking of our calculation method provide a robust framework for studying solar magnetic structures and their impact on space weather phenomena. Overall, this work contributes to the advancement of solar physics by offering a practical and reliable way to assess magnetic energy and helicity budgets in solar magnetic structures.

text: We present a study on enhancing the achromatization of phase mask coronagraphs through the implementation of colored apodization. Our work addresses the significant issue of chromaticity, which poses a challenge to the performance of coronagraphs by causing wavelength-dependent phase shifts, leading to reduced contrast ratios. Through systematic simulations using numerical optimization techniques, we demonstrate that by introducing tailored color-dependent apodization profiles, the achromatic behavior of a phase mask coronagraph can be significantly improved across a broad range of wavelengths. Our findings reveal that by carefully designing the spectral dependence of the apodization functions, we can effectively mitigate chromaticity-induced contrast degradation in the coronagraph system. The key idea behind our approach lies in the customization of apodization functions to compensate for wavelength-dependent phase errors, thereby achieving enhanced achromatization performance. Our methodology involves the optimization of colored apodization profiles to minimize chromaticity effects on coronagraph performance, leading to superior contrast ratios and improved exoplanet detection capabilities. This research contributes valuable insights into the advancement of coronagraph technologies for high-contrast imaging applications, laying the foundation for the development of next-generation space-based telescopes with enhanced capabilities for studying exoplanetary systems and characterizing faint astrophysical sources.

BepiColombo is a joint ESA/JAXA mission to Mercury with challenging
objectives regarding geophysics, geodesy and fundamental physics. The Mercury
Orbiter Radioscience Experiment (MORE) is one of the on-board experiments,
including three different but linked experiments: gravimetry, rotation and
relativity. The aim of the relativity experiment is the measurement of the
post-Newtonian parameters. Thanks to accurate tracking between Earth and
spacecraft, the results are expected to be very precise. However, the outcomes
of the experiment strictly depends on our "knowledge" about solar system:
ephemerides, number of bodies (planets, satellites and asteroids) and their
masses. In this paper we describe a semi-analytic model used to perform a
covariance analysis to quantify the effects, on the relativity experiment, due
to the uncertainties of solar system bodies parameters. In particular, our
attention is focused on the Nordtvedt parameter $\eta$ used to parametrize the
strong equivalence principle violation. After our analysis we estimated
$\sigma[\eta]\lessapprox 4.5\times 10^{-5}$ which is about 1~order of magnitude
larger than the "ideal" case where masses of planets and asteroids have no
errors. The current value, obtained from ground based experiments and lunar
laser ranging measurements, is $\sigma[\eta]\approx 4.4\times 10^{-4}$.
Therefore, we conclude that, even in presence of uncertainties on solar system
parameters, the measurement of $\eta$ by MORE can improve the current precision
of about 1~order of magnitude.

text: This research endeavors to constrain nonperturbative strong-field effects in scalar-tensor gravity by combining pulsar timing and laser-interferometer gravitational-wave detectors. Pulsars, incredibly stable celestial objects, offer a unique opportunity to test the predictions of general relativity and alternative theories of gravity, such as scalar-tensor theories. The precise timing of pulsar signals can be affected by gravitational waves, which are ripples in the fabric of spacetime produced by massive cosmic events.   The objective of this study is to investigate the potential of pulsar timing and gravitational-wave detectors to constrain scalar-tensor gravity models. A combination of numerical simulations and analytical calculations are employed to evaluate the impact of strong-field effects on pulsar timing and the detection of gravitational waves. By comparing the predicted effects with observational data from the North American Nanosecond Institute's (NANOGRAV) and LIGO's (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) third-generation detectors, this research aims to establish the viability of scalar-tensor gravity models in the strong-field regime.  The results of this study indicate that the combined use of pulsar timing and gravitational-wave detectors can provide stringent constraints on scalar-tensor gravity models. The findings suggest that the effects of strong-field scalar-tensor gravity on pulsar timing and gravitational waves can be detected with high precision, potentially ruling out certain models and shedding light on the underlying physics of gravity. These results have significant implications for our understanding of gravity in the strong-field regime and underscore the importance of multi-messenger astronomy in testing fundamental theories of gravity.

text: This study examines the nature of the soft Ultraluminous X-ray (ULX) source in NGC 247, focusing on the super-Eddington outflow and the transition between the supersoft and soft ULX regimes. NGC 247, a nearby spiral galaxy, harbors a bright soft ULX, which is characterized by a luminosity of approximately 10^40 erg/s. The object's emission is dominated by the soft X-ray band, with a peak energy of around 0.5-1.5 keV.   The objective of this research is to investigate the physical mechanisms driving the soft ULX emission in NGC 247, with particular emphasis on the role of super-Eddington outflows in regulating the object's luminosity. To achieve this, we have analyzed archival X-ray data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, supplemented by spectroscopic and photometric observations from the XMM-Newton and Spitzer Space Telescope.   Key findings indicate that the soft ULX in NGC 247 is powered by a super-Eddington outflow, with a mass-loss rate of approximately 10^-5 M. The outflow's interaction with the circumgalactic medium leads to a significant heating of the surrounding gas, resulting in the observed soft X-ray emission. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a transition between the supersoft and soft ULX regimes, with the latter being characterized by a more efficient energy transfer between the outflow and the accretion disk.   The study's conclusions suggest that the soft ULX in NGC 247 represents a unique regime in the ULX sequence, with implications for our understanding of the physical mechanisms driving the emission from these objects.

text: The study of isothermal voids and shocks within dynamic systems is crucial for understanding material behaviors under extreme conditions. This research paper aims to develop a comprehensive dynamic evolution model that accurately simulates the formation and propagation of isothermal voids and shocks. The primary objective is to bridge gaps in existing models by incorporating multifaceted interactions among thermal, mechanical, and material properties. The methodology employs a combination of finite element analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to achieve a high-fidelity simulation environment. These simulations are designed to observe the impact of varying thermal gradients and shock intensities on the density and distribution of voids within a given material. The model was validated against a set of experimental data collected from controlled laboratory tests on metallic samples. Key findings suggest that the formation of isothermal voids is significantly influenced by the rate of applied shock and the material's thermal conductivity. Moreover, the interaction between voids and shock waves leads to variations in shockwave speed and intensity, affecting material integrity. Notably, the model predicts that materials with low thermal conductivities exhibit a higher propensity for void formation, which can guide the selection of materials in engineering applications exposed to shock environments. In conclusion, the dynamic evolution model provides critical insights into the complex interplay between thermal and mechanical factors in shock-induced environments. This advancement in modeling can enhance predictive capabilities in various industrial applications, from aerospace engineering to materials science.

text: The study explores the stabilizing influence of spacetime expansion on relativistic fluids, a topic that has significant implications for understanding cosmic evolution and structural formation in the Universe. This research specifically investigates the impact of an expanding spacetime metric within the framework of general relativity on the behavior of fluids with a radiation equation of state. Utilizing mathematical tools from differential geometry and partial differential equations, the stability of solutions to the relativistic Euler equations in a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker spacetime is rigorously analyzed. Through detailed perturbation analysis, it is demonstrated that the expansion of the universe exerts a dissipative force on perturbations in the fluid, leading to a global stabilization effect. Key findings include the derivation of sharp estimates for the decay rates of perturbations, providing new insights into the long-term behavior of the solutions. These estimates are calculated for a range of parameters relevant to cosmological models, showcasing the conditions under which the stabilizing mechanism is most effective. The results not only reaffirm the role of cosmological expansion in maintaining hydrodynamical stability but also highlight the ability of the radiation equation of state to accommodate sharp perturbation damping. Conclusively, the research underscores the pivotal role of spacetime geometry in dictating fluid behavior at cosmological scales and provides a comprehensive framework that enhances the predictive power of relativistic fluid dynamics in an expanding universe. These findings hold potential applications in both theoretical physics and observational cosmology.

Most previous work related to tweet classification have focused on
identifying a given tweet as a spam, or to classify a Twitter user account as a
spammer or a bot. In most cases the tweet classification has taken place
offline, on a pre-collected dataset of tweets. In this paper we present an
\emph{on-the-fly} approach to classify each newly downloaded tweet as
\emph{autogenerated} or not. We define an autogenerated tweet (AGT) as a tweet
where all or parts of the natural language content is generated automatically
by a bot or other type of program.
  Our on-the-fly approach makes use of two classifiers. The first classifies a
tweet solely based on the twitter text and the tweet metadata that comes with
every tweet. It is used for tweets posted by unknown users with no available
tweet history. An unknown user also triggers a batch job to start downloading
the missing user timeline information. The second classifier is used for tweets
posted by a user where the user timeline is downloaded and available.
Initially, it will be the first classifier that handles most of the tweets.
This will gradually change and after an initialization phase where we download
historic data for the most active users, we reach a state where the second
classifier handles a vast majority of all the tweets.
  A simulation using our on-the-fly detection mechanism indicates that we can
handle Twitter streams with up to 68,000 unique users each day. The bottleneck
is the time required to download new user timelines. The AGT detection is very
accurate. In a set of 5,000 tweets we correctly classified about 98\% of all
AGTs using a subject-wise cross-validation.

text: In this study, we investigate the application of time-delayed feedback control (TDFC) on a flashing ratchet system to enhance its performance and stability. The flashing ratchet is a model system that exhibits directed motion of particles under periodic driving, coupled with stochastic switching between two states. Initially, we encounter challenges due to the inherent complexity and nonlinearity of the system, which can lead to instability and oscillations in particle dynamics.  To address these issues, we implement TDFC by introducing a delayed signal back into the system. This method involves monitoring the state of the system at a previous time point and adjusting the driving parameters accordingly. Our methodology includes both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations to evaluate the effectiveness of TDFC.  Results indicate that the application of time-delayed feedback significantly reduces the occurrence of oscillatory behavior, stabilizing the system and enhancing its overall performance. We observe a marked improvement in the mean particle velocity and a reduction in fluctuations, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach. Key insights suggest that the optimal delay period and feedback strength depend on the system parameters and can be tuned to achieve desired outcomes.  Through this research, we propose a robust strategy for controlling the flashing ratchet using TDFC, offering potential applications in various fields including nanotechnology, biophysics, and chemical engineering where precise control over particle dynamics is crucial.

text:
Human migration is a type of human mobility, where a trip involves a person
moving with the intention of changing their home location. Predicting human
migration as accurately as possible is important in city planning applications,
international trade, spread of infectious diseases, conservation planning, and
public policy development. Traditional human mobility models, such as gravity
models or the more recent radiation model, predict human mobility flows based
on population and distance features only. These models have been validated on
commuting flows, a different type of human mobility, and are mainly used in
modeling scenarios where large amounts of prior ground truth mobility data are
not available. One downside of these models is that they have a fixed form and
are therefore not able to capture more complicated migration dynamics. We
propose machine learning models that are able to incorporate any number of
exogenous features, to predict origin/destination human migration flows. Our
machine learning models outperform traditional human mobility models on a
variety of evaluation metrics, both in the task of predicting migrations
between US counties as well as international migrations. In general, predictive
machine learning models of human migration will provide a flexible base with
which to model human migration under different what-if conditions, such as
potential sea level rise or population growth scenarios.

text: We investigate the presence of binary supermassive black holes (SMBHs) through the analysis of variable broad emission line shifts in active galactic nuclei (AGNs). The presence of binary SMBHs is suggested to explain certain dynamical phenomena observed in galaxy mergers; however, detecting them has proven challenging. Our research aims to quantify the binary fraction by examining a sample of AGNs with prominent broad emission lines, focusing on their variability over time. Utilizing time-resolved spectroscopy, we measure the shifts in broad emission line profiles across multiple epochs to identify potential binary signatures. We implemented a robust data analysis framework that incorporates both statistical techniques and machine learning models to differentiate between intrinsic AGN variability and signatures of binary interactions.   Our findings suggest a significantly low binary fraction of supermassive black holes, estimated at approximately 1-2% within our sample. This low detection rate casts doubt on the prevalence of binary systems in SMBHs and raises questions about the mechanisms driving their formation and evolution. Additionally, we explore the implications of our results for theoretical models of galaxy evolution and merging events. We conclude that while our methodology provides valuable insights into AGN dynamics, the inherent complexities of supermassive black hole interactions necessitate further study. Future efforts should focus on larger samples and advanced observational techniques to enhance our understanding of binary SMBH populations and their impact on cosmic evolution.

High accuracy in cancer prediction is important to improve the quality of the

challenge exists in double. The use of effective sampling technique in
classification algorithms always yields good prediction accuracy. The SEER
public use cancer database provides various prominent class labels for
prognosis prediction. The main objective of this paper is to find the effect of
sampling techniques in classifying the prognosis variable and propose an ideal
sampling method based on the outcome of the experimentation. In the first phase
of this work the traditional random sampling and stratified sampling techniques
have been used. At the next level the balanced stratified sampling with

text: This study employs an atomically inspired $k \cdot p$ approach to investigate the valley Zeeman effect within transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) monolayers. Our primary objective is to elucidate the impact of external magnetic fields on the electronic structure of TMDCs, focusing specifically on the valley splitting phenomenon. Through theoretical calculations, we have identified key parameters that govern the valley Zeeman splitting in these materials. The methodology involves constructing tight-binding models based on density functional theory (DFT) calculations to accurately represent the electronic band structure of TMDC monolayers. We then apply the $k \cdot p$ approximation to derive effective Hamiltonians that capture the spin-orbit coupling and valley splitting effects. Results indicate significant valley splitting under applied magnetic fields, which varies with the type of TMDC and the orientation of the magnetic field relative to the crystallographic axes. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of valleytronics in two-dimensional materials and pave the way for future experimental studies aiming to manipulate valley states for information storage and processing applications.

The dilepton emission in heavy-ion reactions at low beam energies is examined
within a hadronic transport approach. In this article the production of
electron-positron pairs from a new approach named SMASH (Simulating Many
Accelerated Strongly-interacting Hadrons) is introduced. The dilepton emission
is consistently taken into account below the hadronic threshold. The
calculations are systematically confronted with HADES data in the kinetic
energy range of $1 - 3.5A$ GeV for elementary, proton-nucleus and
nucleus-nucleus reactions. The present approach employing a resonance treatment
based on vacuum properties is validated by an excellent agreement with
experimental data up to system sizes of carbon-carbon collisions. After
establishing this well-understood baseline in elementary and small systems, the
significance of medium effects is investigated with a coarse-graining approach
based on the same hadronic evolution. The effect of explicit in-medium
modifications to the vector meson spectral functions is important for dilepton
invariant mass spectra in ArKCl and larger systems, even though the transport
approach with vacuum properties reveals similar features due the coupling to
baryonic resonance and the intrinsically included collisional broadening. This
article provides a comprehensive comparison of our calculations with published
dielectron results from the HADES collaboration. In addition, the emission of
dileptons is predicted in gold-gold and pion-beam experiments for which results
are expected soon.

text:
The inclusion of the global effects of semiconductor doping poses a unique
challenge for first-principles simulations, because the typically low
concentration of dopants renders an explicit treatment intractable. In systems
which do not display long-range band bending, a satisfactory remedy is offered
by the use of "pseudoatoms", with a fractional nuclear charge matching the bulk
doping concentration. However, this alone is not always sufficient for charged
surfaces, where the width of the space-charge region (SCR) often exceeds
realistic supercell dimensions. One generalization of the pseudoatom approach
which overcomes this difficulty relies on the introduction of an artificially
high doping level within a slab calculation, in conjunction with a multi-scale
electrostatic energy correction. Here, we present an alternative technique that
naturally extends the pseudoatom approach while bypassing the need for
calculations with an unrealistically high doping level. It is based on the
introduction of excess charge, mimicking free charge carriers from the SCR,
along with a fixed sheet of counter-charge mimicking the SCR-related field.
Self-consistency is obtained by imposing charge conservation and Fermi level
equilibration between the bulk, treated semi-classically, and the electronic
states of the slab/surface, which are treated quantum-mechanically. The method,
which we call CREST - the Charge-Reservoir Electrostatic Sheet Technique - can
be used with standard electronic structure codes. We validate the approach
using a simple tight-binding model, which allows for comparison of its results
with calculations encompassing the full SCR explicitly. We then employ it with
density functional theory, where it is used to obtain insights into the
electronic structures of the "clean-cleaved" Si(111) surface and its buckled
(2x1) reconstruction, at various doping densities.

Using the ratios conjectures as introduced by Conrey, Farmer and Zirnbauer,
we obtain closed formulas for the one-level density for two families of
L-functions attached to elliptic curves. From those closed formulas, we can
determine the underlying symmetry types of the families. The one-level scaling
density for the first family corresponds to the orthogonal distribution as
predicted by the conjectures of Katz and Sarnak, and the one-level scaling
density for the second family is the sum of the Dirac distribution and the even
orthogonal distribution. This seems to be a new phenomenon, caused by the fact
that the curves of the second families have odd rank. Then, there is a trivial
zero at the central point which accounts for the Dirac distribution, and also
affects the remaining part of the scaling density which is then (maybe
surprisingly) the even orthogonal distribution. The one-level density for this
second family was studied in the past for test functions with Fourier
transforms of small support, but since the Fourier transforms of the even
orthogonal and odd orthogonal distributions are undistinguishable for small
support, it was not possible to identify the distribution with those
techniques. This can be done with the ratios conjectures, and it sheds more
light on "independent" and "non-independent" zeroes and the repulsion
phenomenon.

text:
Bulk toroidal rotation has proven capable of stabilising both dangerous MHD
modes and turbulence. In this thesis, we explore a method to drive rotation in
large tokamaks: up-down asymmetry in the magnetic equilibrium. We seek to
maximise this rotation by finding optimal up-down asymmetric flux surface
shapes.
  First, we use the ideal MHD model to show that low order external shaping
(e.g. elongation) is best for creating up-down asymmetric flux surfaces
throughout the device. Then, we calculate realistic up-down asymmetric
equilibria for input into nonlinear gyrokinetic turbulence analysis. Analytic
gyrokinetics shows that, in the limit of fast shaping effects, a poloidal tilt
of the flux surface shaping has little effect on turbulent transport. Since
up-down symmetric surfaces do not transport momentum, this invariance to tilt
implies that devices with mirror symmetry about any line in the poloidal plane
will drive minimal rotation. Accordingly, further analytic investigation
suggests that non-mirror symmetric flux surfaces with envelopes created by the
beating of fast shaping effects may create significantly stronger momentum
transport.
  Guided by these analytic results, we carry out local nonlinear gyrokinetic
simulations of non-mirror symmetric flux surfaces created with the lowest
possible shaping effects. First, we consider tilted elliptical flux surfaces
with a Shafranov shift and find little increase in the momentum transport when
the effect of the pressure profile on the equilibrium is included. We then
simulate flux surfaces with independently-tilted elongation and triangularity.
These two-mode configurations show a $60\%$ increase over configurations with
just elongation or triangularity. A rough analytic estimate indicates that the
optimal two-mode configuration can drive rotation with an on-axis Alfven Mach
number of $1.5 \%$ in an ITER-like machine.
label: human

text: We investigate the Abelian complexifications of Euclidean R^n spaces, shedding light on the fundamental structures underlying these mathematical objects. Our research focuses on the interplay between the geometric and algebraic properties of these spaces, with a particular emphasis on the role of the gauge group in shaping their topological and differential properties.  Through a combination of analytical and computational techniques, we have successfully constructed and analyzed various Abelian complexifications of Euclidean R^n spaces, including the complexified Euclidean space itself. Our results demonstrate the existence of non-trivial gauge transformations that can lead to the emergence of topological defects and singularities in these spaces.  We have also explored the implications of these findings for our understanding of the structure of spacetime in the context of quantum gravity theories. Our work suggests that the Abelian complexifications of Euclidean R^n spaces may play a crucial role in the development of a consistent and predictive theory of quantum gravity.  Furthermore, we have identified key connections between the Abelian complexifications of Euclidean R^n spaces and other areas of mathematics, including algebraic topology and differential geometry. These connections have far-reaching implications for our understanding of the fundamental laws of physics and the behavior of complex systems.  Our research has significant implications for the development of a unified theory of quantum gravity, and has the potential to shed new light on the nature of spacetime and the behavior of fundamental particles.
label: machine

text:
Flare ribbons are always dynamic, and sometimes sweep across sunspots.
Examining 588 (513 M-class and 75 X-class) flare events observed by Transition
Region and Coronal Explorer (TRACE) satellite and Hinode Solar Optical
Telescope (SOT) from 1998 May to 2009 May, we choose the event displaying that
one of the flare ribbons completely sweeps across the umbra of a main sunspot
of the corresponding active region, and finally obtain 20 (7 X-class and 13
M-class) events as our sample. In each event, we define the main sunspot
completely swept across by the flare ribbon as A-sunspot, and its nearby
opposite polarity sunspots, B-sunspot. Observations show that the A-sunspot is
a following polarity sunspot in 18 events, and displays flux emergence in 13
cases. All the B-sunspots are relatively simple, exhibiting either one main
sunspot or one main sunspot and several small neighboring sunspots (pores). In
two days prior to the flare occurrence, the A-sunspot rotates in all the cases,
while the B-sunspot, in 19 events. The total rotating angle of the A-sunspot
and B-sunspot is 193 degrees on average, and the rotating directions, are the
same in 12 events. In all cases, the A-sunspot and B-sunspot manifest shear
motions with an average shearing angle of 28.5 degrees, and in 14 cases, the
shearing direction is opposite to the rotating direction of the A-sunspot. We
suggest that the emergence, the rotation and the shear motions of the A-sunspot
and B-sunspot result in the phenomenon that flare ribbons sweep across sunspots
completely.
