Our methodology entails dynamically refining and coarsening the computational mesh based on local error estimations, thereby concentrating computational resources in critical areas that contain steep gradients or discontinuities. By integrating the compact WENO reconstruction into the AMR scheme, we achieve significant reductions in numerical dissipation and dispersion errors, which are commonly encountered in traditional AMR approaches.  Our results demonstrate that the proposed AMR scheme effectively captures shock waves and complex wave interactions with minimal numerical artifacts. Testing against established benchmark problems, including shock tube and Rayleigh-Taylor instability scenarios, indicates substantial improvements in solution accuracy and computational cost, compared to fixed-mesh and non-compact reconstruction methods. We further validate the robustness of our approach through multi-dimensional hyperbolic problems, showcasing its adaptability to varying problem scales and configurations. This research contributes to the field by advancing the fidelity of simulations in computational fluid dynamics, particularly in contexts where high accuracy and efficiency are paramount. Our findings suggest promising implications for future implementations of adaptive methods in hyperbolic systems and underscore the potential for enhanced solution strategies in broader scientific and engineering applications.

The proposed model is based on a Bayesian inference framework, which allows for the estimation of model parameters and the computation of predictive distributions. The results are evaluated using a range of metrics, including the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). A rigorous solution for the spectrum of quasioptical cylindrical cavity
resonator with a randomly rough side boundary has been obtained for the first
time. To accomplish this task, we have developed a novel method for variables
separation in wave equation, which enables one, in principle, to rigorously
examine any limiting case --- from negligibly weak to arbitrarily strong
disorder. It is shown that the effect of disorder-induced scattering can be
properly described in terms of two geometric potentials, specifically, the
"amplitude" and the "gradient" potentials, which appear in wave equation in the
course of conformal smoothing of the resonator boundaries. The scattering
resulting from the gradient potential appears to be dominant, and its impact on
the whole spectrum is governed by the unique sharpness parameter $\Xi$, the
mean tangent of the asperity slope. As opposed to the resonator with bulk
disorder, the distribution of nearest-neighbor spacings (NNS) in the
rough-resonator spectrum acquires Wigner-like features only when the wave
operator loses its unitarity, i.e., with the availability in the system of
either openness or dissipation channels. Our numeric experiments suggest that
in the absence of dissipation loss the random-rough resonator spectrum is
always regular, whatever the degree of roughness. Yet, the spectrum structure
is quite different in the domains of small and large values of the parameter
$\Xi$. For the dissipation-free resonator, the NNS distribution changes its
form with growing the asperity sharpness from Poissonian-like distribution in
the limit of $\Xi<<1$ to the bell-shaped distribution in the domain where
$\Xi>>1$.

text: This study focuses on analyzing the rank 1 real Wishart spiked model, addressing the challenge of identifying signal components amidst noise in high-dimensional data. We employ a methodological approach that involves deriving the asymptotic distribution of the sample covariance matrix under the assumption of a rank 1 perturbation in the population covariance matrix. Our methodology leverages techniques from random matrix theory to establish theoretical foundations for understanding the behavior of the sample covariance matrix under such conditions. The results obtained demonstrate how the presence of a single non-zero eigenvalue (spike) affects the distribution of the sample eigenvalues. Specifically, we find that the eigenvalues near the spike exhibit distinct behavior compared to those far from it, which is crucial for detecting the presence of the signal. This work contributes to the broader field by providing rigorous statistical insights into the identifiability and estimation of signals in high-dimensional settings, offering valuable tools for applications in signal processing, finance, and machine learning.

text: Scale-free networks, characterized by power-law degree distributions, are ubiquitous in various complex systems. Incorporating traps into these networks alters the dynamics of random walkers significantly. Previous studies have explored random walks in unweighted modular scale-free networks but neglect the impact of traps in weighted networks.   This research aims to investigate the effects of traps on the behavior of random walkers in unweighted and weighted modular scale-free networks.   To accomplish this objective, we generated unweighted and weighted modular scale-free networks using the Barabasi-Albert model with modularity constraints. We introduced perfect traps by randomly removing links within each module, keeping the degree distribution intact. Subsequently, we simulated random walks on both types of networks with and without traps, recorded their progression, and analyzed the results using mean first-passage time and average trapping probability.   Our simulations revealed that traps significantly affect the diffusion properties of random walkers. In unweighted networks, the presence of traps increases the mean first-passage time and average trapping probability. In contrast, weighted networks show minimal effect on the mean first-passage time but exhibit a substantial increase in the average trapping probability.   This study sheds light on the importance of considering traps in the context of random walks in modular scale-free networks, both unweighted and weighted. By exploring the implications of traps in these networks, we contribute to a better understanding of the complex dynamics governing the behavior of random walkers in scale-free systems.

Radio pulsar B1933+16 is brightest core-radiation dominated pulsar in the
Arecibo sky, and here we carry out a comprehensive high resolution polarimetric
study of its radiation at both 1.5 and 4.6 GHz. At 1.5 GHz, the polarization is
largely compatible with a rotating-vector model with $\alpha$ and $\beta$
values of 125 and --1.2$^{\circ}$, such that the core and conal regions can be
identified with the primary and secondary polarization modes and plausibly with
the extraordinary and ordinary propagation modes. Polarization modal
segregation of profiles shows that the core is comprised of two parts which we
associate with later X-mode and earlier O-mode emission. Analysis of the broad
microstructures under the core shows that they have similar timescales to those
of the largely conal radiation of other pulsars studied earlier.
Aberration/retardation analysis was here possible for both the conal and core
radiation and showed average physical emission heights of about 200 km for
each. Comparison with other core-cone pulsars suggests that the core and conal
emission arises from similar heights. Assuming the inner vacuum gap model, we
note that at these emission altitudes the frequency of the observed radiation
$\nu_{obs}$ is less than the plasma frequency $\nu_p$. We then conclude that
the radio emission properties are consistent with the theory of coherent
curvature radiation by charged solitons where the condition $\nu_{obs} <
\nu_{p}$ is satisfied. However, the differences that exist between core and
conal emission in their geometric locations within a pulse, polarization and
modulation properties are yet to be understood.

From a mathematical perspective, radiation hydrodynamics can be thought of as
a system of hyperbolic balance laws with dual multiscale behavior (multiscale
behavior associated with the hyperbolic wave speeds as well as multiscale
behavior associated with source term relaxation). With this outlook in mind,
this paper presents a hybrid Godunov method for one-dimensional radiation
hydrodynamics that is uniformly well behaved from the photon free streaming
(hyperbolic) limit through the weak equilibrium diffusion (parabolic) limit and
to the strong equilibrium diffusion (hyperbolic) limit. Moreover, one finds
that the technique preserves certain asymptotic limits. The method incorporates
a backward Euler upwinding scheme for the radiation energy density and flux as
well as a modified Godunov scheme for the material density, momentum density,
and energy density. The backward Euler upwinding scheme is first-order accurate
and uses an implicit HLLE flux function to temporally advance the radiation
components according to the material flow scale. The modified Godunov scheme is
second-order accurate and directly couples stiff source term effects to the
hyperbolic structure of the system of balance laws. This Godunov technique is
composed of a predictor step that is based on Duhamel's principle and a
corrector step that is based on Picard iteration. The Godunov scheme is
explicit on the material flow scale but is unsplit and fully couples matter and
radiation without invoking a diffusion-type approximation for radiation
hydrodynamics. This technique derives from earlier work by Miniati & Colella
2007. Numerical tests demonstrate that the method is stable, robust, and
accurate across various parameter regimes.

text: In the fourth installment of the Gould's Belt Distances Survey (GOBELINS), we present a comprehensive analysis of the Taurus star-forming region, detailing its distances, depth, and kinematic characteristics. We employ a multi-wavelength approach, integrating data from the Gaia DR2 astrometry, ALMA spectral line observations, and archival Hubble Space Telescope images. Our results indicate that the Taurus molecular cloud is approximately 130 parsecs away from the Sun, with significant spatial variations in distance within the region. We find that the Taurus star-forming region extends over a depth of about 20 parsecs, revealing a complex structure dominated by several sub-regions of star formation. In terms of kinematics, our study reveals a predominantly radial outflow motion, consistent with previous studies, but also identifies localized inflow motions indicative of ongoing star formation activity. Key methodologies include robust statistical techniques for astrometric parallax and proper motion measurements, as well as advanced computational algorithms for kinematic modeling. These findings contribute to our understanding of the dynamical processes shaping the Taurus star-forming region and provide valuable constraints for theoretical models of star formation.

We present the results of the observations of the (J,K)=(1,1) and the
(J,K)=(2,2) inversion transitions of the NH3 molecule toward a large sample of
40 regions with molecular or optical outflows, using the 37 m radio telescope
of the Haystack Observatory. We detected NH3 emission in 27 of the observed
regions, which we mapped in 25 of them. Additionally, we searched for the
6{16}-5{23} H2O maser line toward six regions, detecting H2O maser emission in
two of them, HH265 and AFGL 5173. We estimate the physical parameters of the
regions mapped in NH3 and analyze for each particular region the distribution
of high density gas and its relationship with the presence of young stellar
objects. From the global analysis of our data we find that in general the
highest values of the line width are obtained for the regions with the highest
values of mass and kinetic temperature. We also found a correlation between the
nonthermal line width and the bolometric luminosity of the sources, and between
the mass of the core and the bolometric luminosity. We confirm with a larger
sample of regions the conclusion of Anglada et al. (1997) that the NH3 line
emission is more intense toward molecular outflow sources than toward sources
with optical outflow, suggesting a possible evolutionary scheme in which young
stellar objects associated with molecular outflows progressively lose their
neighboring high-density gas, weakening both the NH3 emission and the molecular
outflow in the process, and making optical jets more easily detectable as the

A general family of peakon equations is introduced, involving two arbitrary
functions of the wave amplitude and the wave gradient. This family contains all
of the known breaking wave equations, including the integrable ones:
Camassa-Holm equation, Degasperis-Procesi equation, Novikov equation, and
FORQ/modified Camassa-Holm equation. One main result is to show that all of the
equations in the general family possess weak solutions given by multi-peakons
which are a linear superposition of peakons with time-dependent amplitudes and
positions. In particular, neither an integrability structure nor a Hamiltonian
structure is needed to derive $N$-peakon weak solutions for arbitrary $N>1$. As
a further result, single peakon travelling-wave solutions are shown to exist
under a simple condition on one of the two arbitrary functions in the general
family of equations, and when this condition fails, generalized single peakon
solutions that have a time-dependent amplitude and a time-dependent speed are
shown to exist. Wave breaking criteria are outlined for this general family of
peakon equations. An interesting generalization of the Camassa-Holm and
FORQ/modified Camassa-Holm equations is obtained by deriving the most general
subfamily of peakon equations that possess the Hamiltonian structure shared by
the Camassa-Holm and FORQ/modified Camassa-Holm equations. Peakon
travelling-wave solutions and their features, including a variational
formulation (minimizer problem), are derived for these generalized equations. A
final main result is that $2$-peakon weak solutions are investigated and shown
to exhibit several novel kinds of behaviour, including the formation of a bound
pair consisting of a peakon and an anti-peakon that have a maximum finite
separation.

text: We investigated the convergence of a family of discrete distributed mixed elliptic optimal control problems with a parameter, revealing a double convergence phenomenon. Our analysis focused on a class of mixed elliptic problems, where the control variable is subject to a quadratic constraint. We employed a finite element discretization approach, utilizing a semi-implicit time-stepping scheme to solve the resulting nonlinear algebraic equations.  We demonstrated that the numerical solution exhibits a double convergence behavior, where the convergence rate of the solution to the optimal control problem improves quadratically with respect to the spatial mesh size and linearly with respect to the time step size. This unexpected convergence behavior was attributed to the interplay between the quadratic constraint and the mixed elliptic formulation, which leads to a stabilizing effect on the numerical solution.  Our results were obtained through a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, including the derivation of a priori error estimates and the implementation of a numerical solver using the FEniCS framework. The obtained convergence rates were validated through a series of numerical experiments, which revealed a consistent improvement in the accuracy of the solution as the mesh size and time step size are reduced. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development of efficient numerical methods for solving large-scale mixed elliptic optimal control problems.

Learning the governing equations in dynamical systems from time-varying
measurements is of great interest across different scientific fields. This task
becomes prohibitive when such data is moreover highly corrupted, for example,
due to the recording mechanism failing over unknown intervals of time. When the
underlying system exhibits chaotic behavior, such as sensitivity to initial
conditions, it is crucial to recover the governing equations with high
precision. In this work, we consider continuous time dynamical systems $\dot{x}
= f(x)$ where each component of $f: \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ is
a multivariate polynomial of maximal degree $p$; we aim to identify $f$ exactly
from possibly highly corrupted measurements $x(t_1), x(t_2), \dots, x(t_m)$. As
our main theoretical result, we show that if the system is sufficiently ergodic
that this data satisfies a strong central limit theorem (as is known to hold
for chaotic Lorenz systems), then the governing equations $f$ can be exactly
recovered as the solution to an $\ell_1$ minimization problem -- even if a
large percentage of the data is corrupted by outliers. Numerically, we apply
the alternating minimization method to solve the corresponding constrained
optimization problem. Through several examples of 3D chaotic systems and higher
dimensional hyperchaotic systems, we illustrate the power, generality, and
efficiency of the algorithm for recovering governing equations from noisy and
highly corrupted measurement data.

text: This research presents a novel multi-beam radio transient detector designed to efficiently detect and analyze rapid radio bursts across a broad range of dispersion measures (DM). The primary objective was to develop a system capable of real-time de-dispersion processing to accurately identify and characterize transient signals within a wide DM range, which can be challenging due to the varying propagation delays associated with different DM values.  The methodology employed an array of multiple radio telescopes configured to observe in parallel beams, each optimized for specific DM ranges. The data collected from these beams were then processed using advanced algorithms that account for the effects of interstellar medium dispersion. Real-time de-dispersion techniques were implemented to compensate for the delay caused by the medium between the source and the observer, ensuring accurate timing and spectral analysis of detected transients.  Key findings revealed the system's capability to detect transient events with unprecedented precision, even over a large DM range. The algorithm successfully corrected for dispersion, allowing for the identification of true signals rather than artifacts introduced by the propagation effects. This approach not only enhanced the detection efficiency but also improved the accuracy of subsequent analyses.  Concluding, the developed multi-beam radio transient detector demonstrated significant advancements in the field of radio astronomy, particularly in handling the challenges posed by wide DM ranges. Its real-time de-dispersion capabilities represent a crucial step towards more comprehensive and reliable observations of transient phenomena in the radio spectrum.

text: We investigated the precessional instability of binary black holes with aligned spins, a phenomenon predicted by general relativity. Our numerical simulations revealed that the precessional instability arises due to the coupling between the orbital angular momentum and the spin of the black holes, leading to a destabilization of the binary system.   The precessional instability is characterized by a rapid increase in the eccentricity of the binary orbit, resulting in a chaotic evolution of the system. We found that the growth rate of the eccentricity is proportional to the product of the spins of the black holes, with a dependence on the mass ratio of the system.   Our results indicate that the precessional instability is a significant effect, even in systems with relatively small spin magnitudes. We also observed that the instability can lead to a merger of the binary system, resulting in the formation of a single, more massive black hole.   The key to our simulations was the implementation of a new numerical scheme, which allows for the accurate treatment of the coupled orbital and spin dynamics of the black holes. Our findings have important implications for the study of binary black hole mergers, which are expected to be observed by future gravitational wave detectors.

Let S be a closed oriented surface of genus at least two. Labourie and the
author have independently used the theory of hyperbolic affine spheres to find
a natural correspondence between convex RP^2 structures on S and pairs
(\Sigma,U) consisting of a conformal structure \Sigma on S and a holomorphic
cubic differential U over \Sigma. The pairs (\Sigma,U$, for \Sigma varying in
moduli space, allow us to define natural holomorphic coordinates on the moduli
space of convex RP^2 structures. We consider geometric limits of convex RP^2
structures on S in which the RP^2 structure degenerates only along a set of
simple, non-intersecting, non-homotopic loops c. We classify the resulting RP^2
structures on S-c and call them regular convex RP^2 structures. We put a
natural topology on the moduli space of all regular convex RP^2 structures on S
and show that this space is naturally homeomorphic to the total space of the
vector bundle over the Deligne-Mumford compactification of the moduli space of
curves each of whose fibers over a noded Riemann surface is the space of
regular cubic differentials. In other words, we can extend our holomorphic
coordinates to bordify the moduli space of convex RP^2 structures along all
neck pinches. The proof relies on previous techniques of the author,
Benoist-Hulin, and Dumas-Wolf, as well as some details due to Wolpert of the
geometry of hyperbolic metrics on conformal surfaces in the Deligne-Mumford
compactification.

text: Spectrahedral cones, arising from the intersection of the cone of positive semidefinite matrices with affine subspaces, are crucial in convex algebraic geometry and optimization. This study investigates the spectrahedral cones generated by rank 1 matrices to understand their structural and geometric properties. The primary objective is to characterize these cones and explore their representation and extremal structure, which are important for applications in semidefinite programming. Employing a combination of algebraic and geometric techniques, this work utilizes matrix theory to identify the conditions under which a spectrahedral cone is generated by rank 1 matrices. The methodology includes analyzing the linear spans of these matrices and examining their affine dimension, providing insights into the facial structure of the cones. Key findings reveal that the spectrahedral cones generated by rank 1 matrices exhibit unique properties not present in higher-rank representations, including a potentially simplified decomposition into elementary cones. Moreover, these cones are identified as having singularities corresponding to linear dependencies among rank 1 matrix generators, impacting their feasible regions in optimization problems. The study concludes that spectrahedral cones generated by rank 1 matrices offer a rich ground for advancing both theoretical understanding and practical applications, leading to the development of more efficient computational techniques in semidefinite programming. Future work could extend these insights to broader classes of cones and rank-specific phenomena, thus enriching the fields of convex geometry and optimization.

text: We investigated the application of sex-disaggregated systematics in the review process of the Canadian Time Allocation Committee (CTAC) telescope proposal reviews, with a focus on identifying biases and improving the fairness of the evaluation process. We also identified that the use of standardized evaluation criteria, such as the CTAC proposal evaluation form, did not adequately address sex-disaggregated biases. To address these issues, we proposed the development of sex-disaggregated evaluation criteria and training for CTAC reviewers to increase awareness of and mitigate sex-disaggregated biases in the evaluation process. Our findings highlight the need for sex-disaggregated systematics in the evaluation process of CTAC proposal reviews and underscore the importance of addressing biases to ensure fair and equitable treatment of all proposals.

The results have implications for our understanding of the role of banks in the Japanese economy, and highlight the need for further research into the dynamics of bank-firm credit networks. text: This study investigates the broad band optical properties of large area monolayer CVD molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) films. However, the synthesis of large area high-quality MoS2 films remains a significant challenge.   To explore the optical properties of large area monolayer CVD MoS2 films, focusing on their absorption, reflectance, and photoluminescence spectra.   Large area monolayer MoS2 films were grown using chemical vapor deposition (CVD) on silicon substrates. The optical properties of the films were characterized using ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy, photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy, and reflectance spectroscopy. The reflectance spectra reveal a high reflectivity in the visible range, indicating a high transparency of the films. The optical properties of the films are found to be highly dependent on the growth conditions, including substrate temperature and gas flow rates.   This study demonstrates the successful growth of large area high-quality monolayer CVD MoS2 films with exceptional optical properties. text: The $^3$He anomaly is a long-standing phenomenon in astrophysics, characterized by the presence of a narrow, unresolved absorption line in the spectra of subluminous B-type stars. This anomaly has been observed in various studies, but its underlying mechanism remains poorly understood. The objective of this research is to investigate the nature of the $^3$He anomaly using Non-LTE (NLTE) spectroscopic analysis.  In this study, we employed the NLTE code, NLTE3, to simulate the atmospheric conditions of subluminous B-type stars. We applied the code to a sample of 30 stars with known surface temperatures and chemical compositions. Our analysis revealed that the $^3$He anomaly is not a result of non-LTE effects, but rather a consequence of the star's internal dynamics. Specifically, we found that the anomaly is caused by the presence of a small, cool region in the star's interior, where $^3$He is abundant.  Our results indicate that the $^3$He anomaly is a common feature of subluminous B-type stars, and that it can be used as a diagnostic tool to infer the internal structure of these stars. The implications of this study are significant, as they provide new insights into the formation and evolution of these stars, and shed light on the complex processes that govern their atmospheric properties. Neutron rich matter is central to many fundamental questions in nuclear
physics and astrophysics. Moreover, this material is being studied with an
extraordinary variety of new tools such as the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams
(FRIB) and the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO). We
describe the Lead Radius Experiment (PREX) that uses parity violating electron
scattering to measure the neutron radius in $^{208}$Pb. This has important
implications for neutron stars and their crusts. We discuss X-ray observations
of neutron star radii. These also have important implications for neutron rich
matter. Gravitational waves (GW) open a new window on neutron rich matter. They
come from sources such as neutron star mergers, rotating neutron star
mountains, and collective r-mode oscillations. Using large scale molecular
dynamics simulations, we find neutron star crust to be very strong. It can
support mountains on rotating neutron stars large enough to generate detectable
gravitational waves. Finally, neutrinos from core collapse supernovae (SN)
provide another, qualitatively different probe of neutron rich matter.
Neutrinos escape from the surface of last scattering known as the
neutrino-sphere. This is a low density warm gas of neutron rich matter.
Observations of neutrinos can probe nucleosyntheses in SN. Simulations of SN
depend on the equation of state (EOS) of neutron rich matter. We discuss a new
EOS based on virial and relativistic mean field calculations. We believe that
combing astronomical observations using photos, GW, and neutrinos, with
laboratory experiments on nuclei, heavy ion collisions, and radioactive beams
will fundamentally advance our knowledge of compact objects in the heavens, the
dense phases of QCD, the origin of the elements, and of neutron rich matter.

$k$ Nearest Neighbors ($k$NN) is one of the most widely used supervised
learning algorithms to classify Gaussian distributed data, but it does not
achieve good results when it is applied to nonlinear manifold distributed data,
especially when a very limited amount of labeled samples are available. In this
paper, we propose a new graph-based $k$NN algorithm which can effectively
handle both Gaussian distributed data and nonlinear manifold distributed data.
To achieve this goal, we first propose a constrained Tired Random Walk (TRW) by
constructing an $R$-level nearest-neighbor strengthened tree over the graph,
and then compute a TRW matrix for similarity measurement purposes. After this,
the nearest neighbors are identified according to the TRW matrix and the class
label of a query point is determined by the sum of all the TRW weights of its
nearest neighbors. To deal with online situations, we also propose a new
algorithm to handle sequential samples based a local neighborhood
reconstruction. Comparison experiments are conducted on both synthetic data
sets and real-world data sets to demonstrate the validity of the proposed new
$k$NN algorithm and its improvements to other version of $k$NN algorithms.
Given the widespread appearance of manifold structures in real-world problems
and the popularity of the traditional $k$NN algorithm, the proposed manifold
version $k$NN shows promising potential for classifying manifold-distributed
data.

We present a density functional study of graphene adhesion on a realistic
SiO$_2$ surface taking into account van der Waals (vdW) interactions. The
SiO$_2$ substrate is modeled at the local scale by using two main types of
surface defects, typical for amorphous silica: the oxygen dangling bond and
three-coordinated silicon. The results show that the nature of adhesion between
graphene and its substrate is qualitatively dependent on the surface defect
type. In particular, the interaction between graphene and silicon-terminated
SiO$_2$ originates exclusively from the vdW interaction, whereas the
oxygen-terminated surface provides additional ionic contribution to the binding
arising from interfacial charge transfer ($p$-type doping of graphene). Strong
doping contrast for the different surface terminations provides a mechanism for
the charge inhomogeneity of graphene on amorphous SiO$_2$ observed in
experiments. We found that independent of the considered surface morphologies,
the typical electronic structure of graphene in the vicinity of the Dirac point
remains unaltered in contact with the SiO$_2$ substrate, which points to the
absence of the covalent interactions between graphene and amorphous silica. The
case of hydrogen-passivated SiO$_2$ surfaces is also examined. In this
situation, the binding with graphene is practically independent of the type of
surface defects and arises, as expected, from the vdW interactions. Finally,
the interface distances obtained are shown to be in good agreement with recent
experimental studies.

text: In the context of multi-agent systems, where agents must collaborate to achieve collective goals, the problem of strategyproof selection from selectors arises. This problem refers to the design of a mechanism to ensure that agents report their true preferences without being incentivized to misrepresent them. In this study, we propose the Sum of Us algorithm, a novel strategyproof selection mechanism that enables a group of agents to democratically elect representatives from a pool of candidate selectors. The mechanism is inspired by the concept of Quorum Dynamics, where agents are organized into quorums, each of which can make a decision on behalf of the group.  To ensure strategyproofness, Sum of Us introduces a novel concept called "selector influence function," which quantifies the degree of influence a selector has on the final outcome of the selection process. Agents report their preferences to their respective quorums, and the algorithm uses the influence functions of selectors to determine the winning selector. This mechanism guarantees that agents have no incentive to misrepresent their preferences, as the outcome is independent of their individual reports.  We evaluate the performance of the Sum of Us algorithm through simulations and analyze its efficiency, fairness, and robustness. Our results demonstrate that the proposed mechanism achieves high efficiency, with an average time complexity of O(n), and provides excellent fairness, as each selector has an equal probability of being elected. Furthermore, the mechanism is robust against various types of attacks, including Sybil and collusion attacks, thereby ensuring the integrity and trustworthiness of the selection process.  The Sum of Us algorithm offers a practical and effective solution to the problem of strategyproof selection from selectors in multi-agent systems. Its novel concepts and efficient implementation make it a valuable contribution to the field of cooperative game theory and multi-agent systems. Future work will explore the application of the Sum of Us algorithm in real-world multi-agent systems and examine its performance under various scenarios and conditions.

Inter-domain routing is a crucial part of the Internet designed for arbitrary
policies, economical models, and topologies. This versatility translates into a
substantially complex system that is hard to comprehend. Monitoring the
inter-domain routing infrastructure is however essential for understanding the
current state of the Internet and improving it. In this paper we design a
methodology to answer two simple questions: Which are the common transit
networks used to reach a certain AS? How much does this AS depends on these
transit networks? To answer these questions we digest AS paths advertised with
the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) into AS graphs and measure node centrality,
that is the likelihood of an AS to lie on paths between two other ASes. Our
proposal relies solely on the AS hegemony metric, a new way to quantify node
centrality while taking into account the bias towards the partial view offered
by BGP. Our analysis using 14 years of BGP data refines our knowledge on
Internet flattening but also exhibits the consolidated position of tier-1
networks in today's IPv4 and IPv6 Internet. We also study the connectivity to
two content providers (Google and Akamai) and investigate the AS dependency of
networks hosting DNS root servers. These case studies emphasize the benefits of
the proposed method to assist ISPs in planning and assessing infrastructure
deployment.

We present the results of the measurements of the detection efficiency for a
4.7 \r{A} neutron beam incident upon a detector incorporating a stack of up to
five MultiWire Proportional Counters (MWPC) with Boron-coated cathodes. The
cathodes were made of Aluminum and had a surface exhibiting millimeter-deep
V-shaped grooves of 45{\deg}, upon which the thin Boron film was deposited by
DC magnetron sputtering. The incident neutrons interacting with the converter
layer deposited on the sidewalls of the grooves have a higher capture
probability, owing to the larger effective absorption film thickness. This
leads to a higher overall detection efficiency for the grooved cathode when
compared to a cathode with a flat surface. Both the experimental results and
the predictions of the GEANT4 model suggests that a 5-counter detector stack
with coated grooved cathodes has the same efficiency as a 7-counter stack with
flat cathodes. The reduction in the number of counters in the stack without
altering the detection efficiency will prove highly beneficial for large-area
position-sensitive detectors for neutron scattering applications, for which the
cost-effective manufacturing of the detector and associated readout electronics
is an important objective. The proposed detector concept could be a
technological option for one of the new chopper spectrometers and other
instruments planned to be built at the future European Spallation Source in
Sweden. These results with macrostructured cathodes generally apply not just to
MWPCs but to other gaseous detectors as well.

Social media platforms have recently seen an increase in the occurrence of
hate speech discourse which has led to calls for improved detection methods.
Most of these rely on annotated data, keywords, and a classification technique.
While this approach provides good coverage, it can fall short when dealing with
new terms produced by online extremist communities which act as original
sources of words which have alternate hate speech meanings. These code words
(which can be both created and adopted words) are designed to evade automatic
detection and often have benign meanings in regular discourse. As an example,
"skypes", "googles", and "yahoos" are all instances of words which have an
alternate meaning that can be used for hate speech. This overlap introduces
additional challenges when relying on keywords for both the collection of data
that is specific to hate speech, and downstream classification. In this work,
we develop a community detection approach for finding extremist hate speech
communities and collecting data from their members. We also develop a word
embedding model that learns the alternate hate speech meaning of words and
demonstrate the candidacy of our code words with several annotation
experiments, designed to determine if it is possible to recognize a word as
being used for hate speech without knowing its alternate meaning. We report an
inter-annotator agreement rate of K=0.871, and K=0.676 for data drawn from our
extremist community and the keyword approach respectively, supporting our claim
that hate speech detection is a contextual task and does not depend on a fixed
list of keywords. Our goal is to advance the domain by providing a high quality
hate speech dataset in addition to learned code words that can be fed into
existing classification approaches, thus improving the accuracy of automated
detection.

In this thesis we study electron transport through magnetic nanocontacts and
nanowires with ab initio quantum transport calculations. The aim is to gain a
thorough understanding of the interplay between electrical conduction and
magnetism in atomic-size conductors and how it is affected by different aspects
as e.g. the atomic structure and the chemical composition of the conductor. To
this end our ab initio quantum transport program ALACANT which combines the
non-equilibrium Green's function formalism (NEGF) with density functional
theory (DFT) calculations has been extended to describe spin-polarized systems.
We present calculations on nanocontacts made of Ni as a prototypical magnetic
material. We find that atomic disorder in the contact region strongly reduces
the a priori high spin-polarization of the conductance leading to rather
moderate values of the so-called ballistic magnetoresistance (BMR). On the
other hand, we show that the adsorption of oxygen in the contact region could
strongly enhance the spin-polarization of the conduction electrons and thus BMR
by eliminating the spin-unpolarized s-channel. Finally, we show that short
atomic Pt chains suspended between the tips of a nanocontact are magnetic in
contrast to bulk Pt. However, this emergent nanoscale magnetism barely affects
the overall conductance of the nanocontact making it thus difficult to
demonstrate by simple conductance measurements. In conclusion, we find that
spin-transport through atomic-scale conductors is quite sensitive to the actual
atomic structure as well as to the chemical composition of the conductor. This
presents both, opportunities and challenges for the realization of future
nanoscale spintronics devices.

text: In recent years, the study of ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs) at redshifts around 2 has garnered significant attention due to their potential association with active galactic nuclei (AGN). This research aims to elucidate the AGN properties in Spitzer-IRS identified ULIRGs at z ~ 2 by employing X-ray observations to characterize the accretion processes and star formation activities within these galaxies. Utilizing data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, we conducted a systematic analysis of the X-ray emission of a sample of ULIRGs, cross-referencing their spectral signatures derived from Spitzer-IRS. We developed a comprehensive methodology combining spectral fitting and stacking techniques to estimate intrinsic X-ray luminosities and AGN fractions within the sample. Our key findings reveal that a substantial proportion of these ULIRGs harbor active AGN, with X-ray luminosities up to several orders of magnitude higher than previously reported. Furthermore, we observed a correlation between X-ray luminosity and infrared luminosity, suggesting that the mechanisms of star formation and AGN activity are intricately linked in these galaxies. The results indicate that many z ~ 2 ULIRGs are not merely star-forming systems but also host powerful AGN, challenging traditional paradigms of galaxy evolution. In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of X-ray diagnostics in understanding the coexistence of AGN and star formation in distant ULIRGs, thereby contributing to the broader discourse on galaxy formation and evolution in the early universe.

text: We investigate the solar cycle variation of topological structures within the global solar corona, focusing on the interplay between magnetic field evolution and coronal dynamics. Utilizing multi-wavelength observational data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory and advanced computational modeling techniques, we analyze the magnetic topology of the corona at different phases of the solar cycle, particularly during solar minimum and maximum conditions. Our results demonstrate significant variations in the distribution and configuration of coronal structures, including coronal holes, active regions, and prominence formations, in response to the solar magnetic field's cyclic behavior. We observe that during solar maximum, increased magnetic complexity leads to a higher density and spatial distribution of active regions, while solar minimum is characterized by more simplistic and streamlined topological forms. Furthermore, we employ magnetohydrodynamic simulations to elucidate the dynamics of plasma flows and magnetic reconnections associated with these topological variations. Our findings confirm that the solar cycle's periodic nature induces recurrent changes in the coronal magnetic field configuration, directly affecting coronal heating and solar wind characteristics. The implications of our study extend to understanding space weather phenomena, emphasizing the necessity for integrating topological analysis in forecasting solar activity and its impact on planetary environments. This work provides a comprehensive framework for interpreting the solar corona's structural evolution and sets the stage for future investigations into the underlying mechanisms driving solar magnetic variability and its global influence.

Multiple testing problems are a staple of modern statistical analysis. The
fundamental objective of multiple testing procedures is to reject as many false
null hypotheses as possible (that is, maximize some notion of power), subject
to controlling an overall measure of false discovery, like family-wise error
rate (FWER) or false discovery rate (FDR). In this paper we formulate multiple
testing of simple hypotheses as an infinite-dimensional optimization problem,
seeking the most powerful rejection policy which guarantees strong control of
the selected measure. In that sense, our approach is a generalization of the
optimal Neyman-Pearson test for a single hypothesis. We show that for
exchangeable hypotheses, for both FWER and FDR and relevant notions of power,
these problems can be formulated as infinite linear programs and can in
principle be solved for any number of hypotheses. We also characterize maximin
rules for complex alternatives, and demonstrate that such rules can be found in
practice, leading to improved practical procedures compared to existing
alternatives. We derive explicit optimal tests for FWER or FDR control for
three independent normal means. We find that the power gain over natural
competitors is substantial in all settings examined. Finally, we apply our
optimal maximin rule to subgroup analyses in systematic reviews from the
Cochrane library, leading to an increase in the number of findings while
guaranteeing strong FWER control against the one sided alternative.

We study feedback during massive star formation using semi-analytic methods,
considering the effects of disk winds, radiation pressure, photoevaporation and
stellar winds, while following protostellar evolution in collapsing massive gas
cores. We find that disk winds are the dominant feedback mechanism setting star
formation efficiencies (SFEs) from initial cores of ~0.3-0.5. However,
radiation pressure is also significant to widen the outflow cavity causing
reductions of SFE compared to the disk-wind only case, especially for >100Msun
star formation at clump mass surface densities Sigma<0.3g/cm2. Photoevaporation
is of relatively minor importance due to dust attenuation of ionizing photons.
Stellar winds have even smaller effects during the accretion stage. For core
masses Mc~10-1000Msun and Sigma~0.1-3g/cm2, we find the overall SFE to be
0.31(Rc/0.1pc)^{-0.39}, potentially a useful sub-grid star-formation model in
simulations that can resolve pre-stellar core radii,
Rc=0.057(Mc/60Msun)^{1/2}(Sigma/g/cm2)^{-1/2}pc. The decline of SFE with Mc is
gradual with no evidence for a maximum stellar-mass set by feedback processes
up to stellar masses of ~300Msun. We thus conclude that the observed truncation
of the high-mass end of the IMF is shaped mostly by the pre-stellar core mass
function or internal stellar processes. To form massive stars with the observed
maximum masses of ~150-300Msun, initial core masses need to be >500-1000Msun.
We also apply our feedback model to zero-metallicity primordial star formation,
showing that, in the absence of dust, photoevaporation staunches accretion at
~50Msun. Our model implies radiative feedback is most significant at
metallicities ~10^{-2}Zsun, since both radiation pressure and photoevaporation
are effective in this regime.

text: Our work investigates the theory of tunneling conductance in anomalous Rashba metal/superconductor junctions. The study aims to address the unique electronic properties arising at the interface between these materials. Through our research, we have obtained significant results which shed light on the behavior of tunneling conductance in such systems. Our analysis reveals intriguing phenomena such as the emergence of novel Andreev bound states and the manifestation of unconventional proximity effects due to the presence of a strong Rashba spin-orbit coupling.   The primary challenge our work attempts to overcome is the comprehensive understanding of the tunneling conductance characteristics specific to anomalous Rashba metal/superconductor junctions. By developing a theoretical framework grounded in the principles of quantum transport and superconductivity, we have formulated a sophisticated model that accurately captures the intricate interplay of spin-polarized phenomena and proximity-induced superconducting correlations at the interface.   Key ideas in our methodology involve the utilization of advanced mathematical techniques such as Bogoliubov-de Gennes formalism and Usadel equations to describe the physics of the system. By systematically analyzing the density of states and conductance spectra, we provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms governing the tunneling process in these unconventional junctions. Overall, our work contributes to the deeper comprehension of electron transport in anomalous Rashba metal/superconductor systems, paving the way for potential applications in spintronics and quantum computing.

With the energy scales opened up by RHIC and LHC the age of high-pT physics
is upon us. This has created new opportunities and novel mysteries, both of
which will be explored in this thesis. The possibility now exists
experimentally to exploit these high momentum particles to uniquely probe the
unprecedented state of matter produced in heavy ion collisions. At the same
time naive theoretical expectations have been dashed by data.
  The first puzzle we confront is that of the enormous intermediate-pT
azimuthal anisotropy, or v2, of jets observed at RHIC. The second puzzle is the
surprisingly similar suppression of light mesons and nonphotonic electrons,
which precludes perturbative predictions predicated on gluon bremsstrahlung
radiation as the dominant energy loss channel. Near qualitative agreement
results from including collisional energy loss and integrating over the
fluctuating jet pathlengths. Another conjecture for heavy quark energy loss
comes via explicit construction using the AdS/CFT correspondence; the momentum
loss of a hanging dragging string moving through the deconfined plasma leads to
qualitative agreement with heavy quark decay data. We propose a robust test to
experimentally differentiate these two competing ideas: the ratio of charm to
bottom suppression rapidly approaches 1 for pQCD but is independent of momentum
and well below 1 for AdS/CFT. Finally as a warmup problem to calculating the
photon bremsstrahlung associated with jet energy loss we quantify improvements
to the perturbative estimates of the Ter-Mikayelian effect.

text: This research paper focuses on the covariant and infrared-free graviton two-point function in de Sitter spacetime. The objective is to investigate the behavior of gravitons in a de Sitter background, crucial for cosmological applications. The methodology involves employing advanced quantum field theory techniques to analyze the two-point function of gravitons in de Sitter spacetime, ensuring covariance and freedom from infrared divergences.   Key findings indicate that by carefully implementing specific gauge-fixing conditions and employing a novel regularization scheme, the graviton two-point function in de Sitter spacetime remains finite and free from infrared singularities. Furthermore, the results demonstrate the importance of maintaining covariance and ensuring infrared finiteness in calculations involving gravitons in a de Sitter universe.  In conclusion, this study successfully establishes a covariant and infrared-free framework for analyzing the graviton two-point function in de Sitter spacetime, essential for accurately describing gravitational interactions in a cosmological context. The findings not only contribute to the theoretical understanding of gravitons in de Sitter backgrounds but also have implications for the broader field of quantum gravity and cosmology.

text: We investigated the peculiar radio-quiet quasar, Storm in a "Teacup", characterized by a multitude of ~10 kiloparsec radio-emitting bubbles and extreme gas kinematics. Through a combination of radio and optical observations, we aimed to unravel the physical mechanisms driving these extraordinary features. Our analysis revealed a complex interplay between relativistic jets, thermal gas, and magnetic fields, which collectively contribute to the quasar's unique morphology.  We discovered that the radio-emitting bubbles are not isolated entities, but rather, they are dynamically connected, with gas flowing between them. This gas motion is driven by a combination of jet-driven turbulence and magnetic reconnection, resulting in the observed extreme gas kinematics. Our data also indicate that the quasar's radio emission is not solely powered by the jets, but also by the thermal energy released from the interaction between the jets and the surrounding intergalactic medium.  The quasar's extreme gas kinematics and radio-emitting bubbles are best explained by a scenario where a powerful, relativistic jet interacts with a dense, magnetized intergalactic medium. This interaction triggers a complex series of events, including magnetic reconnection, turbulence, and gas acceleration, which collectively produce the observed radio and optical phenomena. Our findings provide new insights into the physics of radio-quiet quasars and highlight the importance of considering the complex interplay between jets, gas, and magnetic fields in these objects.

Our current understanding of split, Jupiter-family comets is reviewed. The
focus is on what recent studies of comets have told us about the nature of the
splitting phenomenon. The goal is to not repeat the information given in recent
reviews of split comets, but to build upon it. In particular, we discuss comets
that have suffered splitting or fragmentation events in the past few years.
These include comets (a) 57P/du Toit-Neujmin-Delporte, observed with a long
train of fragments in 2002; (b) 73P/Schwassmann-Wachmann 3, which split in 1995
and was extensively studied during its relatively close passage to Earth in
2006, during which dozens of fragments were discovered and studied; and (c)
174P/Echeclus, a Centaur and potentially future JFC, which split in late 2005
and was the first such Centaur observed to do so. We also discuss recent
observations by SOHO of split comets that are likely of short-period. The
Spitzer Space Telescope has observed many JFCs and provided us with
unprecedented detailed views of cometary debris trails, which may be thought of
as a middle ground between "normal" ejection of micron-sized dust grains and
the cleaving off of meter-to-kilometer sized fragments. We will also discuss
potential breakthroughs in studying splitting JFCs that may come from future
surveys.

text: Green power control is crucial in cognitive wireless networks to optimize energy consumption and reduce environmental impact. This research aims to investigate the effectiveness of incorporating green power control strategies in enhancing the overall performance of cognitive wireless networks. The methodology involves modeling the cognitive network environment, analyzing different power control algorithms, and simulating their impact on network performance metrics such as throughput, delay, and energy efficiency.   Key findings reveal that implementing green power control techniques significantly improves the energy efficiency of cognitive wireless networks while maintaining satisfactory levels of network performance. Specifically, dynamic power control schemes demonstrate better adaptability to varying network conditions compared to traditional fixed power control methods. Moreover, the research highlights the importance of balancing energy consumption with network performance to achieve sustainable and efficient operation in cognitive wireless networks.   In conclusion, integrating green power control mechanisms is essential for achieving environmentally friendly and energy-efficient cognitive wireless networks. By optimizing power usage based on dynamic network conditions, cognitive networks can achieve improved performance and reduced carbon footprint, contributing to a more sustainable and eco-friendly wireless communication infrastructure.

Analysis of the 2007-8 credit crisis has concentrated on issues of relaxed
lending standards, and the perception of irrational behaviour by speculative
investors in real estate and other assets. Asset backed securities have been
extensively criticised for creating a moral hazard in loan issuance and an
associated increase in default risk, by removing the immediate lender's
incentive to ensure that the underlying loans could be repaid. However
significant monetary issues can accompany any form of increased commercial bank
lending, and these appear to have been overlooked by this analysis. In this
paper we propose a general explanation for credit crises based on an
examination of the mechanics of the banking system, and in particular its
internal controls on the supply of credit. We suggest that the current credit
crisis is the result of multiple failures in the Basel regulatory framework,
including the removal of central bank reserve requirements from some classes of
deposit accounts within the banking system, allowing financial instruments
representing debt to be used as regulatory capital, and in particular the
introduction of securitized lending which effectively removed a previously
implicit control over the total quantity of lending originating from the
banking system. We further argue that the interaction of these problems has led
to a destabilising imbalance between total money and loan supply growth, in
that total lending sourced from the commercial bank sector increased at a
faster rate than accompanying growth in the money supply. This not only created
a multi-decade macro-economic debt spiral, but by increasing the ratio of debt
to money within the monetary system acted to increase the risk of loan
defaults, and consequentially reduce the overall stability of the banking
system.

text: Directional statistics play a critical role in understanding complex patterns and relationships in various fields, including image classification and retrieval. This research paper aims to explore the integration of directional statistics with deep metric learning to enhance image representation and retrieval accuracy. We develop a novel deep learning framework that leverages directional statistical measures to effectively model the angular relationships among image features. Our methodology involves designing a specialized loss function that incorporates angular distance metrics, allowing for more robust learning of image embeddings. We evaluated our approach on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10 and MS-COCO, comparing its performance against traditional metric learning and deep learning techniques. The results demonstrate significant improvements in both image classification accuracy and retrieval performance, achieving up to 15% higher retrieval precision compared to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the incorporation of directional statistics helps reduce the effects of noise and variations in image orientation, further enhancing model robustness. In conclusion, our findings suggest that integrating directional statistics with deep metric learning offers a powerful approach to improving image classification and retrieval tasks, providing a valuable framework for future research in the field of computer vision. This work opens new avenues for employing statistical methodologies in deep learning frameworks, highlighting the potential for more accurate and efficient image data processing.

text: We investigate the secular light curve of Comet 103P/Hartley 2, which was the focal target of NASA's EPOXI mission. Our study aims to advance the understanding of the comet’s photometric behavior over an extended observational arc. We have compiled and analyzed photometric data from both ground-based observatories and the EPOXI spacecraft to construct the comet's light curve. Our analysis addresses the periodic and long-term variations in brightness, which are critical for deciphering the activity and physical characteristics of the comet. We employ statistical techniques to isolate intrinsic variability from observational noise and to identify any significant trends over multiple perihelion passages. The results demonstrate a discernible periodic pattern in the light curve, suggestive of rotational modulation combined with a secular fading trend. We attribute these phenomena to jets of gas and dust, emanating from discrete regions on the cometary nucleus, in conjunction with an evolving surface activity. Furthermore, our findings corroborate the presence of anisotropic outgassing and its impact on the non-gravitational forces acting on the nucleus. The methodologies developed and insights obtained enhance the predictive modeling of cometary brightness for future missions. We conclude that accounting for the secular evolution in cometary light curves is pivotal for precise mission planning and interpretation of in-situ data. Our study underscores the interplay between cometary rotation, surface activity, and the resulting photometric signatures, contributing significantly to the field of cometary science.

text: In this study, we present advancements in next-generation radio astronomy receiver systems aimed at enhancing sensitivity, bandwidth, and versatility for astronomical observations. We address the critical challenges of detecting faint celestial signals amidst significant thermal noise and interference. Our methodology employs a hybrid approach that integrates superconductor technology with novel digital signal processing techniques. We design and prototype a receiver system featuring low-noise amplifiers (LNAs) based on superconducting materials, which demonstrate a considerable reduction in noise temperatures compared to conventional designs.   We implement a wideband sampling architecture that allows for a broader frequency range while maintaining signal fidelity. Our results indicate a sensitivity improvement of approximately 25% in signal reception and an effective increase in the dynamic range of our receiver. Additionally, we introduce a computational framework utilizing machine learning algorithms to efficiently analyze the large volumes of data generated, enabling real-time signal identification and classification.  The findings underscore the potential of hybrid receiver systems to revolutionize radio astronomy by enabling more precise measurements of cosmic phenomena, such as pulsars and distant galaxies. By overcoming existing limitations in receiver technology, we contribute significantly to the field, facilitating deeper exploration of the universe's complexities. Our work delineates a pathway for future development in radio receiver systems, emphasizing the integration of advanced materials and intelligent data processing techniques to push the boundaries of astronomical research.

text: We report the discovery of novel superconducting phases in lithium decorated graphene LiC6 through transport measurements and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). Our studies reveal the coexistence of two distinct superconducting phases at different temperatures, with transition temperatures Tc1=13.8K and Tc2=18.2K. The resistive transition of the first phase Tc1 is sharp and broad, while the second phase shows a narrow resistive transition with a well-defined onset. The superconducting transition temperatures Tc were found to depend strongly on the lithium intercalation depth. The highest Tc was obtained for the maximum intercalation, indicating the importance of lithium doping in the superconducting properties. STM imaging of the surface revealed the formation of uniform islands of lithium intercalated graphene, suggesting a possible connection between the superconducting phases and the nanostructure of the material. To gain insight into the superconducting mechanism, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations to study the electronic structure of LiC6. Our results reveal the presence of strong electron-phonon coupling, suggesting a phonon-mediated mechanism for superconductivity in this material. Moreover, the calculations predict that Li vacancies play a critical role in the superconducting properties, providing an explanation for the observed dependence of Tc on the intercalation depth. Our findings demonstrate the potential of lithium decorated graphene LiC6 as a novel platform for exploring unconventional superconductivity.

text:
The first 48-antenna stage of the Siberian Radioheliograph (SRH) started
single-frequency test observations early in 2016, and since August 2016 it
routinely observes the Sun at several frequencies in the 4-8 GHz range with an
angular resolution of 1-2 arc minutes and an imaging interval of about 12
seconds. With limited opportunities of the incomplete antenna configuration, a
high sensitivity of about 100 Jy allows the SRH to contribute to the studies of
eruptive phenomena along three lines. First, some eruptions are directly
visible in SRH images. Second, some small eruptions are detectable even without
a detailed imaging information from microwave depressions caused by screening
the background emission by cool erupted plasma. Third, SRH observations reveal
new aspects of some events to be studied with different instruments. We focus
on an eruptive C2.2 flare on 16 March 2016 around 06:40, one of the first
flares observed by the SRH. Proceeding from SRH observations, we analyze this
event using extreme-ultraviolet, hard X-ray, white-light, and metric radio
data. An eruptive prominence expanded, brightened, and twisted, which indicates
a time-extended process of the flux-rope formation together with the
development of a large coronal mass ejection (CME). The observations rule out a
passive role of the prominence in the CME formation. The abrupt prominence
eruption impulsively excited a blast-wave-like shock, which appeared during the
microwave burst and was manifested in an "EUV wave" and Type II radio burst.
The shock wave decayed and did not transform into a bow shock because of the
low speed of the CME. Nevertheless, this event produced a clear proton
enhancement near Earth. Comparison with our previous studies of several events
confirms that the impulsive-piston shock-excitation scenario is typical of
various events.

text: We investigated the complex interplay between gas and dust in the Taurus Molecular Cloud, a prominent star-forming region. Through a combination of observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Spitzer Space Telescope, we mapped the distribution of gas and dust in unprecedented detail. Our results reveal a hierarchical structure, with dense cores surrounded by lower-density gas and a diffuse dust disk extending far beyond the core. We found that the gas and dust are dynamically coupled, with gas flows and outflows playing a crucial role in regulating the growth of the cores. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the dust is the primary reservoir for the formation of small dust grains, which are then incorporated into the cores. We also observed a significant correlation between the gas and dust temperatures, indicating that the two phases are closely linked through thermal processes. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the complex processes that govern the formation of stars and planetary systems in the Taurus Molecular Cloud. Our results highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between gas and dust in these regions, and suggest that future studies should focus on the detailed dynamics of these systems.

A large volume of research has been conducted in the cognitive radio (CR)
area the last decade. However, the deployment of a commercial CR network is yet
to emerge. A large portion of the existing literature does not build on real
world scenarios, hence, neglecting various important interactions of the
research with commercial telecommunication networks. For instance, a lot of
attention has been paid to spectrum sensing as the front line functionality
that needs to be completed in an efficient and accurate manner to enable an
opportunistic CR network architecture. This is necessary to detect the
existence of spectrum holes without which no other procedure can be fulfilled.
However, simply sensing (cooperatively or not) the energy received from a
primary transmitter cannot enable correct dynamic spectrum access. For example,
the low strength of a primary transmitter's signal does not assure that there
will be no interference to a nearby primary receiver. In addition, the presence
of a primary transmitter's signal does not mean that CR network users cannot
access the spectrum since there might not be any primary receiver in the
vicinity. Despite the existing elegant and clever solutions to the DSA problem
no robust, implementable scheme has emerged. In this paper, we challenge the
basic premises of the proposed schemes. We further argue that addressing the
technical challenges we face in deploying robust CR networks can only be
achieved if we radically change the way we design their basic functionalities.
In support of our argument, we present a set of real-world scenarios, inspired
by realistic settings in commercial telecommunications networks, focusing on
spectrum sensing as a basic and critical functionality in the deployment of
CRs. We use these scenarios to show why existing DSA paradigms are not amenable
to realistic deployment in complex wireless environments.
