text: Cavitation, the formation of vapor cavities in a liquid, poses significant challenges to structural integrity in various engineering applications. Among the phenomena of interest is quiescent cavitation, where vapor bubbles are generated without turbulence, potentially leading to catastrophic material damage. This study aims to investigate the mechanisms by which quiescent cavitation contributes to cracking in solid materials, focusing on its impact on surface integrity and component lifespan. A series of controlled laboratory experiments were conducted using advanced high-speed imaging techniques and pressure sensors to observe bubble dynamics and their interactions with material surfaces. Computational simulations complemented these experiments to provide insight into the stress distribution and crack propagation initiated by cavitation events. Key findings reveal that in the absence of turbulent flow, quiescent cavitation can still induce significant pitting through rapid bubble collapse, leading to localized stress concentrations and subsequent crack formation. These observations challenge the traditional understanding that turbulent flow is a prerequisite for cavitation-induced damage. Additionally, materials with lower ductility were more susceptible to such damage, indicating a potential correlation between material properties and cavitation resilience. The findings emphasize the need for revised design considerations in engineering applications that encounter cavitation scenarios, particularly in sectors such as marine, hydraulic machinery, and aerospace, where failure can have catastrophic consequences. In conclusion, understanding the nuanced role of quiescent cavitation in catastrophic cracking necessitates a reassessment of current mitigation strategies, underscoring the imperative for innovative materials and protective mechanisms to enhance durability and reliability in affected systems.

text: The Palomar Transient Factory (PTF) is a time-domain imaging survey that utilizes the 48-inch Oschin Schmidt Telescope at Palomar Observatory to discover and study transient astronomical phenomena. This project employs a 512-megapixel camera, the Large Area Sky Survey Imager (LAS3), capable of capturing 120 square degrees of the sky in a single exposure. The PTF system architecture includes an image processing pipeline, a database management system, and an alerting system. Our first phase of operation, conducted from 2009 to 2012, yielded over 28 million source detections, 147,000 transient candidates, and the discovery of 434 supernovae. The second phase, currently ongoing, utilizes expanded observation strategies to discover various types of transients, including gravitational wave counterparts, fast radio bursts, and other exotic objects.  Our system development efforts focused on maximizing survey efficiency by implementing real-time image processing and automated source detection algorithms. These techniques enable rapid identification of transient events, with an average time from exposure to alert delivery being less than three minutes. The system architecture and hardware design were optimized for high-throughput data processing, with data redundancy and fault tolerance features to ensure reliability and data preservation.  This study represents the first comprehensive overview of the PTF system, its capabilities, and its initial results. We outline the design, implementation, and performance of the PTF data acquisition pipeline, the image processing pipeline, and the alerting system. We also discuss the system's successes in discovering and characterizing transient events, demonstrating the power and utility of a large-scale time-domain imaging survey.  Through ongoing improvements and advances in technology, the Palomar Transient Factory continues to push the boundaries of transient discovery and investigation. The wealth of data generated by this project will significantly expand our understanding of various astrophysical processes and phenomena.

In this paper, we study incentive mechanisms for retrieving information from
networked agents. Following the model in [Kleinberg and Raghavan 2005], the
agents are represented as nodes in an infinite tree, which is generated by a
random branching process. A query is issued by the root, and each node
possesses an answer with an independent probability $p=1/n$. Further, each node
in the tree acts strategically to maximize its own payoff. In order to
encourage the agents to participate in the information acquisition process, an
incentive mechanism is needed to reward agents who provide the information as
well as agents who help to facilitate such acquisition.
  We focus on designing efficient sybil-proof incentive mechanisms, i.e., which
are robust to fake identity attacks. %We consider incentive mechanisms which
are sybil-proof, i.e., robust to fake identity attacks. We propose a family of
mechanisms, called the direct referral (DR) mechanisms, which allocate most
reward to the information holder as well as its direct parent (or direct
referral). We show that, when designed properly, the direct referral mechanism
is sybil-proof and efficient. In particular, we show that we may achieve an
expected cost of $O(h^2)$ for propagating the query down $h$ levels for any
branching factor $b>1$. This result exponentially improves on previous work
when requiring to find an answer with high probability. When the underlying
network is a deterministic chain, our mechanism is optimal under some mild
assumptions. In addition, due to its simple reward structure, the DR mechanism
might have good chance to be adopted in practice.

text: Protoplanetary disks play a crucial role in the formation of planetary systems. One of the key processes in the evolution of these disks is the destruction of refractory carbon grains. Refractory carbon grains, including graphite and diamond, play a significant role in the thermal balance of protoplanetary disks by absorbing and re-radiating heat. However, their presence in the outer regions of the disk can impede the growth of planetesimals, which are the building blocks of planets. Thus, understanding the mechanisms that lead to the destruction of refractory carbon grains in protoplanetary disks is essential for unraveling the complex process of planetary system formation.  In this study, we investigate the role of photo-processing in the destruction of refractory carbon grains in protoplanetary disks. We employ a three-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamic simulation to model the disk structure and the photochemistry of carbon species. Our results show that the destruction of refractory carbon grains is facilitated by a combination of UV photodesorption and sputtering induced by energetic photons and cosmic rays. We find that the location and abundance of refractory carbon grains depend on the disk surface density, temperature, and the intensity of the stellar radiation field. Moreover, our simulations suggest that the destruction of refractory carbon grains can enhance the growth of planetesimals in the outer regions of the disk, providing a new perspective on the role of refractory carbon in planetary system formation.  In conclusion, the destruction of refractory carbon grains is an important process in the evolution of protoplanetary disks. This study provides new insights into the mechanisms that drive the destruction of refractory carbon grains through the combined effects of photo-processing and cosmic rays. Our findings highlight the complexity of the thermal and chemical processes that govern the formation of planetary systems and emphasize the need for further research in this area.

text: We investigate the measurement of Diffuse Interstellar Bands (DIBs) in the spectra of cool stars, striving to enhance our understanding of interstellar medium properties and the chemical processes involved in the formation of these spectral features. Our primary objective is to develop an improved line list for modeling the background stellar spectra, which is crucial for isolating and accurately measuring DIBs. We utilized high-resolution spectroscopy data from a diverse sample of cool stars, applying advanced statistical techniques to refine the line list.   Our methodology involved a comprehensive analysis of the stellar spectra, complemented by systematic comparisons with laboratory data and theoretical predictions. We employed a Bayesian approach to assess the significance and robustness of identified DIB features, which led to the discovery of several previously unrecognized bands. The enriched line list, now encompassing new transitions and improved parameters, enhances the accuracy of DIB measurements and allows for better correlation with physical conditions in the interstellar medium.  Our results reveal that the identified DIBs exhibit varied patterns of correlation with elemental abundances and specific environmental factors, suggesting that they serve as effective probes of interstellar conditions. This work not only deepens our understanding of atomic and molecular processes in the interstellar medium but also provides a critical tool for the astrophysical community, facilitating future studies that aim to unravel the complexities of interstellar chemistry. We conclude that our enhanced line list significantly contributes to the ongoing exploration of the origins and implications of DIBs in various cosmic environments.

text: Recent advancements in cosmology have spurred significant interest in modified gravity theories as alternatives to the standard ΛCDM model. This study aims to investigate the constraints imposed on the effective gravitational parameter, \(G_{\textrm{eff}}(z)\), by the growth rate of cosmic structures and Planck data. We employ a comprehensive analytical framework that integrates observations of large-scale structure growth with the cosmic microwave background (CMB) data provided by the Planck satellite. Our methodology involves a detailed statistical analysis, leveraging Bayesian inference to extract limits on various modified gravity cosmologies.  We find that the growth rate measurements, when combined with Planck's CMB data, yield stringent constraints on \(G_{\textrm{eff}}(z)\), revealing a tension between traditional matter-dominated frameworks and some modified gravity scenarios. Specifically, our results indicate that models proposing substantial deviations from General Relativity face significant difficulties in reconciling growth rate observations with the CMB power spectrum. Furthermore, we highlight that any viable modified gravity model must align closely with both the local gravitational dynamics and large-scale structure formation.  In conclusion, our analysis underscores the necessity for refined observational data and theoretical models, suggesting that future research should focus on reconciling these tensions. This work contributes to the broader discourse on modified gravity, providing a clearer understanding of the cosmic dynamics governed by gravitational interactions and setting the stage for future explorations in the field.

text: We present a novel approach to algorithmically verify single-pass list processing programs, a class of algorithms notoriously challenging to prove correct by traditional methods. Our work focuses on developing a framework that leverages the inherent structure of list processing algorithms to systematically identify and eliminate potential sources of error. We introduce a novel, modular verification framework that separates the verification of algorithmic correctness from the verification of data integrity. This modular approach enables us to efficiently verify a wide range of list processing algorithms, including insertion, deletion, and search operations. Our framework utilizes a combination of formal methods, including predicate logic and model checking, to systematically analyze the algorithm's behavior and detect potential errors. Through a series of rigorous case studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in verifying the correctness of several real-world list processing algorithms. We also explore the limitations of our approach and discuss potential avenues for future research. Our results show that algorithmic verification of single-pass list processing programs is indeed possible, and our framework provides a valuable tool for developers seeking to ensure the correctness of their list processing code.

text: In this work, we explore the properties of central-max-point tolerance graphs (CMPTGs) and their relationship to certain subclasses of interval catch digraphs. Our investigation begins by defining CMPTGs as graphs that can be represented by intervals on a line where each vertex corresponds to a point on the line, and edges connect points within a specified tolerance range around a central point. We then extend our study to include specific subclasses of interval catch digraphs, demonstrating how these structures can be embedded within the broader framework of CMPTGs.  Our methodology involves rigorous graph-theoretical analysis, including the examination of adjacency conditions, degree sequences, and the construction of examples. Through computational algorithms, we identify patterns and properties that distinguish CMPTGs from other graph types, particularly those that are interval catch digraphs. The results obtained show that CMPTGs offer a robust theoretical foundation for understanding complex network structures, while also providing insights into the behavior of interval catch digraphs.  The problem at hand is to classify and analyze the structural characteristics of these graphs, which has implications for various applications such as network design, data organization, and algorithm optimization. Key methodologies employed include graph theory, combinatorial mathematics, and computational methods to validate theoretical findings. This research not only contributes to the foundational knowledge of graph theory but also opens avenues for further exploration in interdisciplinary fields.

text: The interstellar medium (ISM) of irregular galaxies is known for its complex magnetic fields and dynamic environments, which are thought to be driven by cosmic rays (CRs). We present the results of simulations exploring the role of CRs in generating magnetic fields in the ISM of irregular galaxies. Our model incorporates a state-of-the-art CR-driven turbulence and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) solver. We find that CRs efficiently amplify magnetic fields in the ISM of irregular galaxies, generating dynamos that operate at low magnetic Reynolds numbers. These dynamos exhibit a clear signature of a cosmic-ray-driven turbulent dynamo, characterized by a strong correlation between CR pressure and turbulent magnetic fields.  The problem we address in this study is the lack of a clear understanding of the origin and maintenance of the complex magnetic fields observed in the ISM of irregular galaxies. Previous works have suggested that CRs may play a role, but the exact mechanism has remained unclear. Our approach is to simulate the ISM of an irregular galaxy using a state-of-the-art CR-driven turbulence and MHD solver.  The key ideas of our work are the identification of a cosmic-ray-driven dynamo in the ISM of irregular galaxies, and the exploration of its properties and implications. We find that CRs efficiently amplify magnetic fields in the ISM of irregular galaxies, generating a turbulent dynamo that operates at low magnetic Reynolds numbers. Our results suggest that CRs may play a crucial role in the dynamic evolution of the ISM in irregular galaxies, with important implications for the formation of stars and the intergalactic medium.  Further research is needed to validate and extend these findings, including observations of magnetic fields in irregular galaxies and theoretical studies of the microphysical processes involved. Overall, this study provides new insights into the role of CRs in the magnetization and dynamical evolution of the ISM in irregular galaxies, and highlights the importance of incorporating CRs into models of galaxy formation and evolution.

We discuss black hole spin measurements employing the relativistic iron line
profiles in the X-ray domain. We investigate the iron line band for two
representative sources -- MCG -6-30-15 (active galaxy) and GX 339-4 (X-ray
binary). We compare two models of the broad iron line, LAOR and KYRLINE. We
realise that the spin is currently determined entirely from the position of the
marginally stable orbit while the effect of the spin on the overall line shape
would be resolvable with higher resolution X-ray missions. We show that the
precision of the spin measurements depends on an unknown angular distribution
of the disc emission. We study how sensitive the spin determination is to the
assumptions about the intrinsic angular distribution of the emitted photons. We
find that the uncertainty of the directional emission distribution translates
to 20% uncertainty in the determination of the radius of marginally stable
orbit. We perform radiation transfer computations of an X-ray irradiated disc
atmosphere (NOAR code) to determine the directionality of outgoing X-rays in
the 2-10 keV energy band. Based on these computations, we find that from the
simple formulae for the directionality, the isotropic case reproduces the
simulated data with the best accuracy. The most frequently used limb-darkening
law favours higher values of spin and, in addition, a steeper radial emissivity
profile. Furthermore, we present a spectral analysis of an XMM-Newton
observation of a Seyfert 1.5 galaxy IRAS 05078+1626 being the first X-ray
spectroscopic study of this source. The lack of the significant relativistic
blurring of the reflection model component suggests the accretion disc to be
truncated at a farther radius.

text:
We investigate the mass-metallicity relations for the gaseous (MZRgas) and
stellar components (MZRstar) of local star-forming galaxies based on a
representative sample from SDSS DR12. The mass-weighted average stellar
metallicities are systematically lower than the gas metallicities. This
difference in metallicity increases toward galaxies with lower masses and
reaches 0.4-0.8 dex at 10^9 Msun (depending on the gas metallicity
calibration). As a result, the MZRstar is much steeper than the MZRgas. The
much lower metallicities in stars compared to the gas in low mass galaxies
implies dramatic metallicity evolution with suppressed metal enrichment at
early times. The aim of this paper is to explain the observed large difference
in gas and stellar metallicity and to infer the origin of the mass-metallicity
relations. To this end we develop a galactic chemical evolution model
accounting for star formation, gas inflow and outflow. By combining the
observed mass-metallicity relation for both gas and stellar components to
constrain the models, we find that only two scenarios are able to reproduce the
observations. Either strong metal outflow or a steep IMF slope at early epochs
of galaxy evolution is needed. Based on these two scenarios, for the first time
we successfully reproduce the observed MZRgas and MZRstar simultaneously,
together with other independent observational constraints in the local
universe. Our model also naturally reproduces the flattening of the MZRgas at
the high mass end leaving the MZRstar intact, as seen in observational data.

text: We propose a novel formula to characterize the scaffold structure of spiral galaxies, addressing the longstanding challenge of quantifying their complex formations. Our work stems from the need for a comprehensive mathematical framework that encompasses the diverse morphological features observed across various spiral galaxies. We employed a combination of observational data analysis and computational modeling, synthesizing data from multiple telescopes and existing astronomical catalogs.  Through systematic evaluation of over 500 spiral galaxies, we established a set of parameters essential for defining the scaffold structure, including the pitch angle, arm strength, and core density. Our new formula incorporates these parameters into a cohesive model that effectively predicts the spatial distribution of stars and interstellar matter within the galaxy. By analyzing the correlation between our model's predictions and actual observational data, we enhanced its accuracy, achieving a predictive capability that surpasses existing theoretical frameworks.  The results indicate that our formula can successfully replicate the observed features of spiral arms and their dynamics, thereby providing astrophysicists a valuable tool for understanding galaxy formation and evolution. Notably, we contribute insights into the influence of dark matter distribution on spiral galaxy structure, suggesting that our model may aid in future cosmological studies. Our work lays the groundwork for further exploration into the interactions between galactic components, ultimately fostering a deeper comprehension of the underlying physics governing spiral galaxy formation and stability.

text: The Hartshorne-Hirschowitz theorem is a fundamental result in algebraic geometry that addresses the conditions under which a finite set of points in projective space can be the base locus of a complete intersection of two hypersurfaces. This abstract will outline the historical context, the stated objectives, the methods employed, the key findings, and the concluding remarks regarding this theorem.  Starting with the historical background, the Hartshorne-Hirschowitz theorem was initially proposed by Robin Hartshorne and Leo Hirschowitz as a generalization of the classical Bertini's theorem to the case of higher-dimensional spaces. The theorem asserts that if \( n \) points in projective space \( \mathbb{P}^d \) (where \( d \geq n+1 \)) are in sufficiently general position, then they can be realized as the base locus of a complete intersection of two hypersurfaces of degrees \( d_1 \) and \( d_2 \), provided that \( d_1 + d_2 = d + 1 \).  The objective of the research was to explore and refine these conditions, focusing particularly on the constraints imposed by the number of points and their positions. To achieve this, the methodology involved a detailed analysis of the intersection theory in projective spaces, utilizing tools from commutative algebra and algebraic geometry.  Key findings include the identification of precise numerical conditions for the existence of such complete intersections. It was demonstrated that the theorem holds true under specific configurations of the points, where the sum of the degrees of the hypersurfaces equals the dimension of the projective space plus one. Additionally, the research explored scenarios where the points were not in general position but still allowed for the construction of complete intersections through modifications.  Concluding remarks highlight the importance of these results in understanding the structure of projective varieties and the interplay between algebraic geometry and commutative algebra. The findings contribute to a deeper comprehension of the Hartshorne-Hirschowitz theorem and open avenues for further investigation into the geometric properties of point configurations in projective spaces.

The $k$ nearest neighbor ($k$NN) query is a fundamental problem in databases.
Given a set of multidimensional data points and a query point, $k$NN returns
the $k$ nearest neighbors based on a scoring function such as weighted sum
given an attribute weight vector. However, the attribute weight vector can be
difficult to specify in practice. Skyline returns the points including all
possible nearest neighbors without requiring the exact attribute weight vector
or a scoring function but the number of returned points can be prohibitively
large for practical use.
  In this paper, we propose a novel \emph{eclipse} definition which provides a
more flexible and customizable definition than the classic $1$NN and skyline.
In eclipse, users can specify a range of attribute weights and control the
number of returned points. We show that both $1$NN and skyline are
instantiations of eclipse. To compute eclipse points, we propose a baseline
algorithm with time complexity of $O(n^22^{d-1})$, and an improved $O(n\log
^{d-1}n)$ time transformation-based algorithm by transforming the eclipse
problem to the skyline problem, where $n$ is the number of points and $d$ is
the number of dimensions. Furthermore, we propose a novel index-based algorithm
utilizing duality transform with much better efficiency. The experimental
results on the real NBA dataset and the synthetic datasets demonstrate the
effectiveness and efficiency of our eclipse algorithms.

In the paper the spectral temporal evolution of a steeply rising
submillimeter (THz) burst occurred on 2003 November 2 was investigated in
detail for the first time. Observations show that the flux density of the THz
spectrum increased steeply with frequency above 200 GHz. Their average rising
rates reached a value of 235 sfu/GHz (corresponding spectral index $\alpha$ of
4.8) during the burst. The flux densities reached about 4,000 and 70,000 sfu at
212 and 405 GHz at maximum phase, respectively. The emissions at 405 GHz
maintained continuous high level that they exceed largely the peak values of
the microwave (MW) spectra during the main phase. Our studies suggest that only
energetic electrons with a low-energy cutoff of $\sim$1 MeV and number density
of $\sim$$10^{6}$--$10^{8}$ cm$^{-3}$ can produce such strong and steeply
rising THz component via gyrosynchrotron (GS) radiation based on numerical
simulations of burst spectra in the nonuniform magnetic field case. The
electron number density $N$, derived from our numerical fits to the THz
temporal evolution spectra, increased substantially from $8\times10^{6}$ to
$4\times10^{8}$ cm$^{-3}$, i.e., $N$ value increased 50 times during the rise
phase. During the decay phase it decreased to $7\times10^{7}$ cm$^{-3}$, i.e.,
decreased about five times from the maximum phase. The total electron number
decreased an order of magnitude from the maximum phase to the decay phase.
Nevertheless the variation amplitude of $N$ is only about one time in the MW
emission source during this burst, and the total electron number did not
decrease but increased by about 20$\%$ during the decay phase. Interestingly,
we find that the THz source radius decreased by about 24$\%$ while the MW
source one, on the contrary, increased by 28$\%$ during the decay phase.

text: In this study, we examine the impact of indirect dependencies on the performance of a mutual information minimization (MIM) approach for separating nonlinear recurrent systems. Indirect dependencies, which occur when the separation of two systems results in the creation of dependencies between previously unconnected variables, pose a significant challenge for separation techniques. We employ a simulated biosystem model consisting of two interconnected nonlinear recurrent systems to investigate this effect. Our experimental results reveal that the presence of indirect dependencies can deteriorate the performance of the MIM approach. Specifically, we observe increased false positives, false negatives, and convergence time.  To address the detrimental effects of indirect dependencies, we propose an extension to the MIM approach that integrates a decoupling step. This step aims to eliminate the indirect dependencies before implementing the mutual information minimization algorithm. Our approach, termed mutual information minimization with decoupling (MIMD), is demonstrated to produce accurate separations in the presence of indirect dependencies.  In summary, this work highlights the importance of considering indirect dependencies when applying the mutual information minimization approach to nonlinear recurrent systems. We develop a novel MIMD methodology to tackle this issue and demonstrate its efficacy through rigorous experiments. Our results provide insights into the behavior of indirect dependencies and lay the foundation for further research on more advanced separation techniques for complex, interconnected systems.

text: We investigate the relationship between mass, kinematic morphology, and density in galaxy clusters using data from the SAMI Galaxy Survey. Through a detailed analysis of a sample of galaxy clusters, we employ a multi-faceted methodology that includes spectral data decomposition, stellar kinematics measurements, and the calculation of cluster mass profiles.   Our results indicate a significant correlation between the mass of a galaxy and its kinematic morphology—specifically, we observe that more massive galaxies tend to exhibit distinct kinematic characteristics that are influenced by their surrounding environment. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the kinematic morphology-density relation is predominantly driven by mass rather than purely environmental factors. We analyze the velocity dispersion profiles and the spatial distribution of galaxy subpopulations, revealing that within higher-density regions, more massive galaxies display a higher frequency of ordered rotational motion compared to their less massive counterparts.  This work contributes to our understanding of galaxy evolution in clusters, suggesting that mass plays a crucial role in shaping the kinematic properties and spatial distributions of galaxies. Our findings underscore the necessity of considering mass as a central parameter when exploring the dynamics of galaxy clusters, paving the way for future studies aimed at unraveling the complexities of galaxy formation and evolution in dense environments.

text: The increasing pressures on freshwater resources necessitate effective management strategies to optimize supply and meet varying demand in multi-connection water reservoir networks. Key findings reveal that prioritizing risk management alongside demand-supply optimization leads to a 15% improvement in the system's overall resilience and operational efficiency. Additionally, the results indicate that adopting flexible supply strategies can significantly mitigate supply shortages and enhance service reliability. The analysis demonstrates the importance of integrating risk management principles in water resource planning, as it allows for adaptive strategies that respond to uncertain environmental conditions. In conclusion, this study highlights the critical need for sophisticated optimization models that encompass risk management elements in the design and operation of water reservoir networks, ultimately contributing to sustainable water resource management practices. A stable oscillon was found in the (classical) analysis of the SU(2) gauged
Higgs model under a 2:1 ratio between the Higgs and W masses, both analytically
and numerically. We extend these results by constructing oscillons for all
values of the Higgs mass and examining their stability, finding them to be
stable when the Higgs mass is almost equal to twice the W mass. We also
investigate the dependence of the oscillon lifetime on the mass of the Higgs,
seeing different behavior for different regions of the Higgs mass. Close to the
2:1 mass ratio the interaction of the two fields leads to either a stable
oscillon or to its quick decay, based on its amplitude and the exact masses of
the fields. Moving further away from this ratio the fields seize to interact
and the oscillon disperses. Furthermore, we show that the oscillon lifetime
scales quadratically with the small amplitude parameter which is linked to the
small amplitude expansion that we use to construct the oscillon. Finally, we
list all families of oscillon solutions that can be formally constructed in
this model and discuss their properties. The results can be easily extended to
other composite oscillons in particle physics and beyond.

We present the results of hydrodynamic simulations of the interaction between
a 10 Jupiter mass planet and a red or asymptotic giant branch stars, both with
a zero-age main sequence mass of 3.5 $M_\odot$. Dynamic in-spiral timescales
are of the order of few years and a few decades for the red and asymptotic
giant branch stars, respectively. The planets will eventually be destroyed at a
separation from the core of the giants smaller than the resolution of our
simulations, either through evaporation or tidal disruption. As the planets
in-spiral, the giant stars' envelopes are somewhat puffed up. Based on
relatively long timescales and even considering the fact that further in-spiral
should take place before the planets are destroyed, we predict that the merger
would be difficult to observe, with only a relatively small, slow brightening.
Very little mass is unbound in the process. These conclusions may change if the
planet's orbit enhances the star's main pulsation modes. Based on the angular
momentum transfer, we also suspect that this star-planet interaction may be
unable to lead to large scale outflows via the rotation-mediated dynamo effect
of Nordhaus and Blackman. Detectable pollution from the destroyed planets would
only result for the lightest, lowest metallicity stars. We furthermore find
that in both simulations the planets move through the outer stellar envelopes
at Mach-3 to Mach-5, reaching Mach-1 towards the end of the simulations. The
gravitational drag force decreases and the in-spiral slows down at the sonic
transition, as predicted analytically.

Methodologically, we utilized state-of-the-art detector systems to capture the polarization signatures in collision events, focusing on distinguishing between Standard Model processes and those indicative of new physics. text: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of a multi-wavelength observation of a flux rope that failed during an M-class flare eruption from NOAA Active Region (AR) 11045. The M-class flare, observed on 2017 April 15, was characterized by a strong magnetic reconnection event, which led to the failure of a flux rope and the subsequent release of a massive amount of magnetic energy. The observation was conducted using a combination of multi-wavelength observations, including radio, X-ray, and ultraviolet spectroscopy, as well as high-cadence observations from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) and the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) on board the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO).  The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between the flux rope failure and the associated M-class flare, with a focus on the physical processes that govern the energy release during the event. Our analysis reveals that the flux rope failure was accompanied by a significant increase in coronal heating, which led to the development of a coronal mass ejection (CME) that was observed at the Earth's distance. The observations also indicate that the M-class flare was accompanied by a strong increase in the coronal magnetic field, which was driven by the reconnection process.  The key findings of this study show that the flux rope failure and the associated M-class flare were closely linked, with the failure of the flux rope triggering the reconnection process and the subsequent release of magnetic energy. Our results suggest that the energy release during the event was governed by a complex interplay between coronal heating, magnetic reconnection, and the coronal magnetic field. The findings of this study have important implications for our understanding of the physical processes that govern the behavior of magnetic reconnection in the solar corona, and for the development of models that can predict the occurrence of M-class flares and CMEs.

text: The near-infrared region of the electromagnetic spectrum, particularly the presence of hydroxyl (OH) night sky lines, poses significant challenges for astronomical observations, limiting the sensitivity and accuracy of spectral data. We designed a series of FBGs specifically tuned to target and mitigate OH emissions in the near-infrared range. The methodology involved fabricating FBGs with varying parameters and deploying them in a controlled observational environment. The performance of these gratings was evaluated through comparative spectral analysis, focusing on their efficacy in attenuating the intensity of the OH lines while maintaining the integrity of astronomical signals. Key findings indicate that the application of FBGs successfully reduced the intensity of prominent OH night sky lines by an average of 40%, leading to enhanced signal-to-noise ratios in the observed spectra. Furthermore, the results demonstrate potential for further optimization of FBG designs to achieve even greater suppression levels. In conclusion, this study provides promising preliminary evidence that fiber Bragg gratings can significantly improve the quality of near-infrared astronomical observations by effectively suppressing night sky interference. The implications of these findings suggest that FBGs could become a standard tool in astrophysical instrumentation, paving the way for advanced exploration of celestial phenomena.

text: In this study, we investigate the phenomenon of reduced jet-medium coupling in lead-lead (Pb+Pb) collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Our research aims to address the observed discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental outcomes regarding jet energy loss and medium-induced modifications. We employ state-of-the-art computational techniques, utilizing both hydrodynamic models and perturbative QCD calculations to simulate the jet-medium interactions under varying conditions of temperature and density found in the quark-gluon plasma. Our methodology entails a systematic comparison of jet quenching observables, including the nuclear modification factor and jet structure alterations, across different model implementations.  The results indicate a significant reduction in the effective coupling between jets and the medium at LHC energies, suggesting a possible oversimplification in current theoretical models. The introduction of dynamic temperature-dependent coupling constants within our framework provides a better fit to the experimental data, particularly in regions of low transverse momentum spectra where discrepancies were most pronounced. Furthermore, our findings highlight the importance of considering spatial anisotropy and in-medium scattering effects to accurately characterize the jet quenching phenomena. These insights have profound implications for the theoretical understanding of parton-medium interactions and suggest avenues for refining existing models to enhance their predictive capabilities. Our work contributes to a more comprehensive interpretation of heavy-ion collision data and underscores the necessity for further studies in this domain to elucidate the properties of the quark-gluon plasma.

The Greek aperitif Ouzo is not only famous for its specific anise-flavored
taste, but also for its ability to turn from a transparent miscible liquid to a
milky-white colored emulsion when water is added. Recently, it has been shown
that this so-called Ouzo effect, i.e. the spontaneous emulsification of oil
microdroplets, can also be triggered by the preferential evaporation of ethanol
in an evaporating sessile Ouzo drop, leading to an amazingly rich drying
process with multiple phase transitions [H. Tan et al., Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.
USA 113(31) (2016) 8642]. Due to the enhanced evaporation near the contact
line, the nucleation of oil droplets starts at the rim which results in an oil
ring encircling the drop. Furthermore, the oil droplets are advected through
the Ouzo drop by a fast solutal Marangoni flow. In this article, we investigate
the evaporation of mixture droplets in more detail, by successively increasing
the mixture complexity from pure water over a binary water-ethanol mixture to
the ternary Ouzo mixture (water, ethanol and anise oil). In particular,
axisymmetric and full three-dimensional finite element method simulations have
been performed on these droplets to discuss thermal effects and the complicated
flow in the droplet driven by an interplay of preferential evaporation,
evaporative cooling and solutal and thermal Marangoni flow. By using image
analysis techniques and micro-PIV measurements, we are able to compare the
numerically predicted volume evolutions and velocity fields with experimental
data. The Ouzo droplet is furthermore investigated by confocal microscopy. It
is shown that the oil ring predominantly emerges due to coalescence.

text: In this study, we explore the dynamical laws governing superenergetic phenomena within the framework of General Relativity. We attempt to address the challenges posed by the existence of superenergies, which challenge classical limits on energy density. By employing advanced tensor calculus and variational principles, we derive expressions for the stress-energy tensor that incorporate superenergetic components. These expressions are then used to analyze specific scenarios where superenergies play a significant role, such as near black hole event horizons or in regions of strong gravitational fields. The results obtained show that superenergetic fields significantly alter the dynamics of spacetime, leading to novel effects not observed in conventional General Relativity. Key methodologies include the use of Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations to handle the non-linear interactions between superenergetic fields and spacetime geometry. This research not only expands our understanding of extreme energy conditions but also provides a foundation for further theoretical investigations into the nature of spacetime under extreme energy densities.

The elementary 2-terminal network consisting of a resistively ($R-$) shunted
inductance ($L$) in series with a capacitatively ($C-$) shunted resistance
($R$) with $R = \sqrt{L/C}$, is known for its non-dispersive dissipative
response, $i.e.,$ with the input impedance $Z_0(\omega) = R$, independent of
the frequency ($\omega$). In this communication we examine the properties of a
novel equivalent network derived iteratively from this 2-terminal network by
replacing everywhere the elemental resistive part $R$ with the whole 2-terminal
network. This replacement suggests a recursion $Z_{n+1}(\omega) =
f(Z_n(\omega))$, with the recursive function $f(z) = (i\omega Lz/i\omega L + z)
+ (z/1+i\omega Cz)$. The recursive map has two fixed points -- an unstable
fixed point $Z_u^\star = 0$, and a stable fixed point $Z_s^\star = R$. Thus,
resistances at the boundary terminating the infinitely iterated network can now
be made arbitrarily small without changing the input impedance $Z_\infty (=
R)$. This, therefore, leads to realizing in the limit $n\to\infty$ an
effectively dissipative network comprising essentially non-dissipative reactive
elements ($L$ and $C$) only. Hence the oxymoron -- resistance without
resistors! This is best viewed as a classical anomaly akin to the one
encountered in turbulence. Possible application as a formal decoherence device
-- the {\it fake channel} -- is briefly discussed for its quantum analogue.

text: This research paper proposes a novel neural machine translation (NMT) model that leverages the strengths of both recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and self-attention mechanisms to achieve state-of-the-art performance. The proposed model, dubbed GRU-Gated Attention (GGA), integrates a gated recurrent unit (GRU) encoder with an attention-based decoder to enable more efficient and effective processing of sequential data.  The background of this research highlights the limitations of traditional NMT models, which often rely on fixed-length encoder-decoder architectures and suffer from issues such as vanishing gradients and limited contextual understanding. In contrast, the proposed GGA model addresses these limitations by incorporating a dynamic attention mechanism that selectively focuses on relevant source sequence elements during decoding, thereby improving the model's ability to capture nuanced semantic relationships and contextual dependencies.  The objective of this research is to investigate the effectiveness of the proposed GGA model in improving NMT performance, particularly in low-resource language pairs. To achieve this, we employ a range of experimental evaluation protocols, including automatic metrics (e.g., BLEU score) and human evaluation (e.g., fluency and coherence assessments).  The methodology employed in this research involves training and testing the proposed GGA model on a large-scale NMT dataset, comprising 100,000 pairs of source and target sentences in 10 language pairs. The results of this study indicate that the proposed GGA model achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art NMT baselines, with gains in BLEU score and fluency ratings of up to 10% and 20%, respectively. The key findings of this research highlight the potential of attention-based models to revolutionize the field of NMT, and the proposed GGA model is shown to be a viable and effective solution for improving NMT performance in low-resource language pairs. The conclusions drawn from this research emphasize the importance of incorporating dynamic attention mechanisms into NMT models, and the potential applications of this research in real-world translation tasks.

We want to determine the lithium abundances of solar twin stars as a function
of stellar age to provide constraints for stellar evolutions models and to
investigate whether there is a connection between low Li abundance and the
occurrence of planets. For a sample of 21 solar twins observed with the HARPS
spectrograph at high spectral resolution (R~115.000) and very high
signal-to-noise ratio (600 < S/N < 2400), precise lithium abundances were
obtained by spectral synthesis of the LiI 6707.8 A line and compared to stellar
ages, masses, and metallicities determined from a spectroscopic analysis of the
same set of HARPS spectra. We show that for the large majority of the solar
twins there is a strong correlation between lithium abundance and stellar age.
As the age increases from 1 to 9 Gyr, the Li abundance decreases by a factor of
~ 50. The relation agrees fairly well with predictions from non-standard
stellar evolution models of Li destruction at the bottom of the upper
convection zone. Two stars deviate from the relation by having Li abundances
enhanced by a factor of ~ 10, which may be due to planet engulfment. On the
other hand, we find no indication of a link between planet hosting stars and
enhanced lithium depletion.

text: This study investigates the interfacial interactions between local defects in amorphous SiO$_2$ and supported graphene, with a focus on the impact of these interactions on the electronic and optical properties of the graphene-SiO$_2$ interface. Amorphous SiO$_2$ is a widely used gate dielectric material in MOSFETs, but its high density of local defects can significantly degrade device performance. Graphene, on the other hand, has emerged as a promising material for next-generation electronics due to its exceptional electrical conductivity and optical properties. The interface between graphene and amorphous SiO$_2$ is critical in determining the overall performance of graphene-based devices.  To explore the interfacial interactions, we employed a combination of theoretical modeling and molecular dynamics simulations. Our results show that the local defects in amorphous SiO$_2$ can interact with graphene through both electrostatic and van der Waals forces, leading to the formation of defect-induced states in the graphene bandgap. These defect-induced states can significantly alter the electronic and optical properties of graphene, including its carrier mobility and absorption spectrum. Furthermore, our simulations suggest that the interface can be modified by introducing defects into the graphene lattice, which can lead to the formation of graphene-based devices with improved performance. Our findings provide valuable insights into the interfacial interactions between local defects in amorphous SiO$_2$ and supported graphene, and have significant implications for the development of graphene-based devices.

text: We present a novel one-step replica symmetry breaking solution for a highly asymmetric two-sublattice fermionic Ising spin glass model in a transverse field. Our work addresses the challenge of accurately describing the complex interplay of interactions in such systems, where traditional replica symmetry breaking methods face limitations due to the presence of strong asymmetry between the sublattices. Through our proposed solution, we successfully capture the intricate behavior of the system, providing insights into its unique properties.  Our key idea involves introducing a one-step breaking of replica symmetry, allowing us to account for the asymmetry between the sublattices while maintaining computational tractability. By utilizing advanced mathematical techniques alongside physical intuition, we derive analytical expressions for the order parameters, free energy, and magnetization, shedding light on the system's ground state properties. Our methodology combines elements of mean-field theory with rigorous mathematical analysis, offering a comprehensive framework for studying highly asymmetric fermionic Ising spin glass models in transverse fields.  The results of our study unveil the rich phase diagram of the system, revealing novel phases and critical points that were previously unexplored. Moreover, our findings provide a deeper understanding of the role of asymmetry in shaping the behavior of such complex quantum spin glass models, paving the way for further research in this intriguing field.

text: This study investigates the suppression of quantum-mechanical collapse in a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) through the application of repulsive interactions between atoms. Our approach involves manipulating the interatomic potential using Feshbach resonances to induce a repulsive interaction regime. We demonstrate that in such a regime, the collapse is significantly mitigated compared to the attractive interaction case, where collapse dynamics are more pronounced. Our methodology relies on experimental techniques to create and manipulate BECs, including laser cooling, optical trapping, and magnetic field tuning to control interatomic interactions. Through detailed measurements of correlation functions and density profiles, we confirm the reduction in collapse effects, which are quantified via the visibility of interference fringes in our interferometric setup. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of quantum dynamics under repulsive interactions and pave the way for exploring non-collapsing quantum states in various physical systems.

text: In recent years, the study of interacting open quantum systems has gained significant attention due to their potential applications in quantum technology and information processing. However, the characterization of such systems remains a challenging task due to the non-equilibrium nature of their dynamics. In this paper, we explore the use of gauge freedom in observables and Landsberg's nonadiabatic geometric phase to describe the dynamics of interacting open quantum systems through pumping spectroscopy. We begin by providing a brief background on the concepts of gauge freedom in observables and Landsberg's nonadiabatic geometric phase. Next, we outline the objective of our research, which is to develop a theoretical framework for understanding the relationship between these concepts and their role in the description of pumping spectroscopy in open quantum systems. We then describe the methodology used in our research, which involves a combination of analytical calculations and numerical simulations. Our key findings reveal that the use of gauge freedom in observables and Landsberg's nonadiabatic geometric phase provides a powerful tool for understanding the dynamics of interacting open quantum systems, enabling the identification of new physical phenomena and the development of novel spectroscopic techniques. We conclude by discussing the implications of our research for the field of quantum physics and the potential applications of our findings in the area of quantum technology and information processing.

We study the disordered topological Anderson insulator in a 2-D (square not
strip) geometry. We first report the phase diagram of finite systems and then
study the evolution of phase boundaries when the system size is increased to a
very large $1120 \times 1120$ area. We establish that conductance quantization
can occur without a bulk band gap, and that there are two distinct scaling
regions with quantized conductance: TAI-I with a bulk band gap, and TAI-II with
localized bulk states. We show that there is no intervening insulating phase
between the bulk conduction phase and the TAI-I and TAI-II scaling regions, and
that there is no metallic phase at the transition between the quantized and
insulating phases. Centered near the quantized-insulating transition there are
very broad peaks in the eigenstate size and fractal dimension $d_2$; in a large
portion of the conductance plateau eigenstates grow when the disorder strength
is increased. The fractal dimension at the peak maximum is $d_2 \approx 1.5$.
Effective medium theory (CPA, SCBA) predicts well the boundaries and interior
of the gapped TAI-I scaling region, but fails to predict all boundaries save
one of the ungapped TAI-II scaling region. We report conductance distributions
near several phase transitions and compare them with critical conductance
distributions for well-known models.

Let $k$ be \emph{any} algebraically closed field in any characteristic, let
$R$ be any regular local ring such that $R$ contains $k$ as a subring, the
residue field of $R$ is isomorphic to $k$ as $k$-algebras and $\dim R\geq 1$,
let $P$ be any parameter system of $R$ and let $z\in P$. We consider any
$\phi\in R$ with $\phi\neq 0$.
  In our main theorem we assume several conditions depending on $P$, $z$ and
Newton polyhedrons. By our assumptions the normal fan $\Sigma$ of the Newton
polyhedron $\Gamma_+(P,\phi)$ of $\phi$ over $P$ has simple structure and we
can make a special regular subdivision $\Sigma^*$ of $\Sigma$ called an upward
subdivision, starting from a regular cone with dimension equal to $\dim R$ and
repeating star subdivisions with center in a regular cone of dimension two. Let
$X$ and $\sigma:X\rightarrow\Spec(R)$ denote the toric variety over $\Spec(R)$
and the toric morphism associated with $\Sigma^*$. We consider any closed point
$a\in X$ such that $\sigma(a)$ is the unique closed point of $\Spec(R)$ and the
morphism $\sigma^*: R \rightarrow\mathcal{O}_{X,a}$ of local $k$-algebras
induced by $\sigma$. We show that our numerical invariant of $\sigma^*(\phi)\in
\mathcal{O}_{X,a}$ measuring the badness of the singularity is strictly less
than the same invariant of $\phi\in R$ and the singularity $\phi$ is strictly
improved by $\sigma$.
  We notice that this result opens a way toward the theory of resolution of
singularities in arbitrary characteristic. We add several submain theorems to
make bridges toward it and to show that our assumptions of the main theorem are
not strong.
  By these results we can show that in a mathematical game with two players A
and B related to the resolution of singularities of $\phi$, the player A can
always win the game after finite steps. It follows "the local uniformization
theorem in arbitrary characteristic and in arbitrary dimension".
label: human

text: We investigated the magnetoresistance in ambipolar topological insulator (TI) transistors with gate-tunable bulk and surface conduction, exploring the interplay between quantum and classical mechanisms. Our experiments revealed a significant enhancement of the magnetoresistance in TI transistors, which we attributed to the interplay between the gate-tunable bulk and surface conduction channels. We observed a pronounced increase in the magnetoresistance with increasing gate voltage, indicative of a gate-tunable bandgap in the bulk conduction channel.  Through a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental characterization, we demonstrated the importance of considering both quantum and classical contributions to the magnetoresistance in TI transistors. Our results showed that the classical contributions, mediated by the surface and bulk conduction channels, dominate the magnetoresistance at high gate voltages, while the quantum contributions, arising from the bulk bandgap, become increasingly significant at lower gate voltages. We proposed a new theoretical framework that accounts for the interplay between quantum and classical mechanisms in TI transistors, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the magnetoresistance in these devices.  Our findings have significant implications for the development of TI-based transistors, enabling the design of devices with tunable magnetoresistance and potentially leading to breakthroughs in spintronics and quantum computing applications. The gate-tunable bulk and surface conduction channels in TI transistors offer a promising platform for exploring the interplay between quantum and classical mechanisms, and our work provides a foundation for future research in this area.
label: machine

text:
The mid- and far-infrared view on high-mass star formation, in particular
with the results from the Herschel space observatory, has shed light on many
aspects of massive star formation. However, these continuum studies lack
kinematic information.
  We study the kinematics of the molecular gas in high-mass star-forming
regions.
  We complemented the PACS and SPIRE far-infrared data of 16 high-mass
star-forming regions from the Herschel key project EPoS with N2H+ molecular
line data from the MOPRA and Nobeyama 45m telescope. Using the full N2H+
hyperfine structure, we produced column density, velocity, and linewidth maps.
These were correlated with PACS 70micron images and PACS point sources. In
addition, we searched for velocity gradients.
  For several regions, the data suggest that the linewidth on the scale of
clumps is dominated by outflows or unresolved velocity gradients. IRDC18454 and
G11.11 show two velocity components along several lines of sight. We find that
all regions with a diameter larger than 1pc show either velocity gradients or
fragment into independent structures with distinct velocities. The velocity
profiles of three regions with a smooth gradient are consistent with gas flows
along the filament, suggesting accretion flows onto the densest regions.
  We show that the kinematics of several regions have a significant and complex
velocity structure. For three filaments, we suggest that gas flows toward the
more massive clumps are present.

text: The Local Group (LG), a collection of over 50 galaxies, is a unique laboratory for studying the large-scale structure of the universe and probing the nature of Dark Energy and Modified Gravity (MG). In this study, we investigate the dynamics of the LG using observational data, such as the distances, velocities, and mass distributions of its member galaxies. We find that the dynamics of the LG cannot be explained solely by the standard ΛCDM cosmology, suggesting the need for additional physical phenomena, such as MG. We present a comparative analysis of various MG models and their impact on the LG dynamics, considering both the inner and outer regions of the group. Our results show that certain MG models, such as the Milgromian MOND and the Modified Newtonian Dynamics, can provide a better fit to the observational data than the ΛCDM model. Moreover, we discuss the implications of our findings for the future of dark energy and MG research, highlighting the importance of continued observations and theoretical developments in this field. Overall, this study underscores the significance of the LG as a valuable probe of Dark Energy and MG, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the fundamental properties of the universe.

Situations where a group of agents come together to jointly buy a resource
that they individually cannot afford to buy are commonly observed in markets.
For example in the US market for radio spectrum, a recent proposal invited
small firms who would benefit from gaining additional access to spectrum to
jointly submit bids for blocks of spectrum with the idea that its utilization
could be shared. In such a scenario, the problem is to design a mechanism that
truthfully elicits and aggregates the privately held preferences of these
agents, and enables them to act as a single decision-making body in order to
participate in the market. In this paper, we design a class of mechanisms
called monotonic aggregation mechanisms that achieves this under a specific
setting. We assume that the resource is being sold in a sealed-bid second-price
auction that solicits bids for the entire resource. Our mechanism truthfully
elicits utility functions from the buyers, prescribes a joint bid, and
prescribes a division of the payment and the resource in the event that they
win the resource in the auction. This mechanism further satisfies a popular
notion of collusion-resistance known as coalition-strategyproofness. We give
two explicit examples of this generic class for the case where the utility
functions of the buyers are non-decreasing and concave.

text: In this study, we investigate the consequences of high effective Prandtl numbers on solar differential rotation and convective velocities, using a three-dimensional, compressible, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) solar convection model. Our primary focus is on the impact of enhanced effective Prandtl number on the tachocline region and its implications for the solar differential rotation.  Our numerical simulations reveal that the enhanced effective Prandtl number leads to a reduced tachocline thickness and a slower solar differential rotation compared to the conventional models. We attribute these findings to the stronger radiative damping, which inhibits the convective motions, and the stabilizing effect of magnetic fields on the tachocline region.  Moreover, we observe an increase in the convective velocities near the base of the convection zone due to the suppression of the turbulent convective flows in the tachocline. Our results also indicate that these effects can significantly alter the solar interior dynamics, leading to variations in the solar oscillation modes and potentially contributing to solar activity cycles.  In summary, this study sheds light on the role of effective Prandtl number in shaping the solar differential rotation and convective velocities. Our findings provide important insights into the solar convection dynamics and contribute to the ongoing efforts to understand the complex solar interior processes and their implications for solar and stellar astrophysics.  This abstract focuses on the exploration of the consequences of high effective Prandtl numbers on solar differential rotation and convective velocities using a three-dimensional, compressible, magnetohydrodynamic solar convection model. The results reveal a reduced tachocline thickness and slower solar differential rotation due to stronger radiative damping and the stabilizing effect of magnetic fields. The study also demonstrates an increase in convective velocities near the base of the convection zone due to the suppression of turbulent convective flows in the tachocline. The findings have significant implications for solar interior dynamics and solar and stellar astrophysics.

text: This research paper investigates the effects of time-dependent dissipation on the basins of attraction for the pendulum with an oscillating support. By analyzing the dynamical system of the pendulum under the influence of time-dependent dissipation, the objective is to explore how varying dissipation parameters impact the basins of attraction. The methodology involves numerical simulations of the pendulum's motion with different dissipation profiles to observe changes in the basins of attraction. Key findings suggest that time-dependent dissipation significantly alters the structure and boundaries of the basins of attraction, leading to potential shifts in stability regions. Moreover, varying dissipation parameters can either expand or contract the basins of attraction, affecting the pendulum's stability and behavior. In conclusion, this study highlights the intricate relationship between time-dependent dissipation and the basins of attraction in the dynamics of the pendulum with an oscillating support, emphasizing the importance of considering dissipation effects in the analysis of nonlinear dynamical systems.

text: Our study explores the phenomenon of neutrino emission from supernovae, aiming to shed light on the mechanisms underlying this crucial astrophysical process. By conducting detailed simulations using state-of-the-art numerical models, we have obtained results that offer valuable insights into the neutrino emission characteristics during various phases of a supernova event. Our research addresses the longstanding problem of understanding the complex interplay of nuclear reactions, gravitational collapse, and neutrino interactions that govern the emission of neutrinos from these cataclysmic stellar explosions.  The key ideas in our work revolve around the importance of neutrinos in the dynamics and energetics of supernovae, as well as their role in carrying away a substantial fraction of the gravitational binding energy released during the collapse of massive stars. Through sophisticated computational techniques and sophisticated physical models, we have uncovered the intricate relationship between the neutrino emission properties and the underlying astrophysical conditions in supernovae. Our methodology involves integrating fundamental principles of nuclear and particle physics with advanced computational tools to simulate the evolution of neutrino emission from supernovae accurately.  Overall, our findings significantly contribute to the comprehension of neutrino emission mechanisms in supernovae and pave the way for further advancements in understanding the physics of these cosmic phenomena.

text: In this study, we present our findings from Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations of the star-forming region N83C in the Small Magellanic Cloud. Our research aims to investigate the early stages of star formation processes in this region. Our results reveal the presence of dense molecular gas and dust concentrations, indicative of active star formation within N83C. Through high-resolution imaging, we identify several protostellar cores and potential sites of ongoing star formation. Additionally, our analysis of the gas kinematics provides insights into the dynamics of the region, shedding light on the processes driving the formation of young stars within N83C.   The key objective of this work is to understand the physical conditions and mechanisms involved in the initial phases of star formation in an external galaxy like the Small Magellanic Cloud. By employing ALMA's capabilities, we are able to resolve the structures at high spatial resolutions, allowing for a detailed analysis of the protostellar cores and the surrounding molecular gas. This study contributes to our broader understanding of star formation in different environments and highlights the importance of high-resolution observations in probing the earliest stages of star formation.

text: Fluctuation theorems have emerged as a cornerstone in the understanding of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, particularly regarding entropy production and heat dissipation. This study investigates the application of fluctuation theorems in the context of periodically driven Markov chains to elucidate the relationship between these thermodynamic quantities. The primary objective is to derive and validate fluctuation theorems that govern entropy production and heat dissipation for systems under periodic driving conditions. Employing a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we model a class of periodically driven Markov processes, focusing on how the periodicity influences the system's dynamical properties and thermodynamic behavior. Key findings reveal that the derived fluctuation theorems maintain their validity even in the presence of strong periodic driving, highlighting the robustness of these relations in describing the non-equilibrium dynamics of Markov chains. Additionally, we demonstrate that the rate of entropy production exhibits a distinct dependence on the driving frequency, which has implications for the efficiency of energy dissipation in such systems. Our results not only contribute to the theoretical framework of fluctuation theorems but also offer insights into practical applications, such as optimizing energy processes in small-scale systems. In conclusion, this research reinforces the significance of fluctuation theorems in bridging the gap between microscopic dynamics and macroscopic thermodynamic laws, particularly in periodically driven non-equilibrium systems.

We derive an online learning algorithm with improved regret guarantees for
`easy' loss sequences. We consider two types of `easiness': (a) stochastic loss
sequences and (b) adversarial loss sequences with small effective range of the
losses. While a number of algorithms have been proposed for exploiting small
effective range in the full information setting, Gerchinovitz and Lattimore
[2016] have shown the impossibility of regret scaling with the effective range
of the losses in the bandit setting. We show that just one additional
observation per round is sufficient to circumvent the impossibility result. The
proposed Second Order Difference Adjustments (SODA) algorithm requires no prior
knowledge of the effective range of the losses, $\varepsilon$, and achieves an
$O(\varepsilon \sqrt{KT \ln K}) + \tilde{O}(\varepsilon K \sqrt[4]{T})$
expected regret guarantee, where $T$ is the time horizon and $K$ is the number
of actions. The scaling with the effective loss range is achieved under
significantly weaker assumptions than those made by Cesa-Bianchi and Shamir
[2018] in an earlier attempt to circumvent the impossibility result. We also
provide a regret lower bound of $\Omega(\varepsilon\sqrt{T K})$, which almost
matches the upper bound. In addition, we show that in the stochastic setting
SODA achieves an $O\left(\sum_{a:\Delta_a>0} \frac{K^3
\varepsilon^2}{\Delta_a}\right)$ pseudo-regret bound that holds simultaneously
with the adversarial regret guarantee. In other words, SODA is safe against an
unrestricted oblivious adversary and provides improved regret guarantees for at
least two different types of `easiness' simultaneously.

text:
We present an Analytic Model of Intergalactic-medium and GAlaxy evolution
since the dark ages. AMIGA is in the spirit of the popular semi-analytic models
of galaxy formation, although it does not use halo merger trees but
interpolates halo properties in grids that are progressively built. This
strategy is less memory-demanding and allows one to start the modeling at
redshifts high enough and halo masses low enough to have trivial boundary
conditions. The number of free parameters is minimized by making the causal
connection between physical processes usually treated as independent from each
other, which leads to more reliable predictions. But the strongest points of
AMIGA are: i) the inclusion of molecular cooling and metal-poor, population III
(Pop III) stars, with the most dramatic feedback, and ii) the accurate
follow-up of the temperature and volume filling factor of neutral, singly, and
doubly ionized regions, taking into account the distinct halo mass functions in
those environments. We find the following general results. Massive Pop III
stars determine the IGM metallicity and temperature, and the growth of
spheroids and disks is self-regulated by that of massive black holes developed
from the remnants of those stars. Yet, the properties of normal galaxies and
active galactic nuclei appear to be quite insensitive to Pop III star
properties owing to the much higher yield of ordinary stars compared to Pop III
stars and the dramatic growth of MBHs when normal galaxies begin to develop,
which cause the memory loss of the initial conditions.
label: human

text:
We study the projected radial distribution of satellite galaxies around more
than 28,000 Luminous Red Galaxies (LRGs) at 0.28<z<0.40 and trace the
gravitational potential of LRG groups in the range 15<r/kpc<700. We show that
at large radii the satellite number density profile is well fitted by a
projected NFW profile with r_s~270 kpc and that at small radii this model
underestimates the number of satellite galaxies. Utilizing the previously
measured stellar light distribution of LRGs from deep imaging stacks we
demonstrate that this small scale excess is consistent with a non-negligible
baryonic mass contribution to the gravitational potential of massive groups and
clusters. The combined NFW+scaled stellar profile provides an excellent fit to
the satellite number density profile all the way from 15 kpc to 700 kpc. Dark
matter dominates the total mass profile of LRG halos at r>25 kpc whereas
baryons account for more than 50% of the mass at smaller radii. We calculate
the total dark-to-baryonic mass ratio and show that it is consistent with
measurements from weak lensing for environments dominated by massive early type
galaxies. Finally, we divide the satellite galaxies in our sample into three
luminosity bins and show that the satellite light profiles of all brightness
levels are consistent with each other outside of roughly 25 kpc. At smaller
radii we find evidence for a mild mass segregation with an increasing fraction
of bright satellites close to the central LRG.
label: human

text:
Using our sample of the most metal-rich damped Lyman $\alpha$ systems (DLAs)
at z$\sim2$, and two literature compilations of chemical abundances in 341 DLAs
and 2818 stars, we present an analysis of the chemical composition of DLAs in
the context of the Local Group. The metal-rich sample of DLAs at z$\sim2$
probes metallicities as high as the Galactic disc and the most metal-rich dwarf
spheroidals (dSphs), permitting an analysis of many elements typically observed
in DLAs (Fe, Zn, Cr, Mn, Si, and S) in comparison to stellar abundances
observed in the Galaxy and its satellites (in particular dSphs). Our main
conclusions are: (1) non-solar [Zn/Fe] abundances in metal-poor Galactic stars
and in dSphs over the full metallicity range probed by DLAs, suggest that Zn is
not a simple proxy for Fe in DLAs and therefore not a suitable indicator of
dust depletion. After correcting for dust depletion, the majority of DLAs have
subsolar [Zn/Fe] similar to dSphs; (2) at [Fe/H]$\sim-0.5$, a constant
[Mn/Fe]$\sim-0.5$ and near-solar [$\alpha$/Fe] (requiring an assumption about
dust depletion) are in better agreement with dwarf galaxies than Galactic disc
stars; (3) [$\alpha$/Zn] is usually solar or subsolar in DLAs. However,
although low ratios of [$\alpha$/Fe] are usually considered more `dwarf-like'
than `Milky Way-like', subsolar [Zn/Fe] in Local Group dwarfs leads to
supersolar [$\alpha$/Zn] in the dSphs, in contrast with the DLAs. Therefore,
whilst DLAs exhibit some similarities with the Local Group dwarf population,
there are also notable differences.
label: human

text: Elasto-capillary interactions play a pivotal role in the behavior of particles on the surfaces of ultra-soft gels, offering a unique platform for the study of self-assembly and soft lubrication phenomena. In this work, we investigate the behavior of hydrophilic polystyrene (PS) spheres of different sizes (5-40 μm) on the surfaces of hydrogel layers, prepared from a low-concentration solution of poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA). Using a combination of time-lapse microscopy, force spectroscopy, and finite element simulations, we examine the particle dynamics, interparticle forces, and lubrication properties of the PS spheres on the PEGDA hydrogel. Our results reveal the complex interplay between capillary forces, elastic deformation, and particle size, leading to novel self-assembly patterns and emergent soft lubrication behaviors. Specifically, we observe the formation of dynamic clusters and the emergence of size-dependent non-uniform frictional behavior, which is attributed to the interplay between the capillary forces, elastic deformation, and surface roughness. Our findings shed new light on the intricacies of elasto-capillary interactions in soft materials and demonstrate the potential of ultra-soft gels as a versatile tool for studying self-assembly and lubrication in complex systems. Future work will focus on the optimization of hydrogel properties and the exploration of other particle shapes and materials to further expand our understanding of these phenomena.
label: machine

text:
C58 fullerenes were adsorbed onto room temperature Au(111) surface by
low-energy (~6 eV) cluster ion beam deposition under ultrahigh vacuum
conditions. The topographic and electronic properties of the deposits were
monitored by means of scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM at 4.2 K).
Topographic images reveal that at low coverages fullerene cages are pinned by
point dislocation defects on the herringbone reconstructed gold terraces (as
well as by step edges). At intermediate coverages, pinned monomers, act as
nucleation centres for the formation of oligomeric C58 chains and 2D islands.
At the largest coverages studied, the surface becomes covered by 3D interlinked
C58 cages. STM topographic images of pinned single adsorbates are essentially
featureless. The corresponding local densities of states are consistent with
strong cage-substrate interactions. Topographic images of [C58]n oligomers show
a stripe-like intensity pattern oriented perpendicular to the axis connecting
the cage centers. This striped pattern becomes even more pronounced in maps of
the local density of states. As supported by density functional theory, DFT
calculations, and also by analogous STM images previously obtained for C60
polymers (M. Nakaya et al., J. Nanosci. Nanotechnol. 11, 2829 (2011)), we
conclude that these striped orbital patterns are a fingerprint of covalent
intercage bonds. For thick C58 films we have derived a band gap of 1.2 eV from
scanning tunnelling spectroscopy data, STS, confirming that the outermost C58
layer behaves as a wide band semiconductor.
