text: In this study, we investigate the existence and phase separation of solitary waves within a framework of nonlinear Schrödinger systems that model the simultaneous dynamics of cooperation and competition among interacting species. We formulate the governing equations to include both cooperative and competitive interactions, thus enabling a comprehensive analysis of their effects on wave propagation. Our analysis employs variational methods and the theory of elliptic partial differential equations, leading us to establish rigorously the existence of solitary wave solutions under specified parameter regimes. We additionally examine the stability characteristics of these waves, revealing a threshold beyond which the balance between cooperation and competition dictates the phase behavior of the wave solutions.   We conduct numerical simulations to illustrate the dynamics and phase separation phenomena in various scenarios, observing distinct patterns of solitary waves that emerge from the interaction of population densities. Our findings indicate that the presence of cooperation tends to enhance wave propagation speed, whereas competition results in wave clustering and potential localization of populations.   Through our work, we contribute to the understanding of complex biological systems modeled by nonlinear Schrödinger equations, providing insights into how cooperative and competitive interactions shape wave dynamics. We highlight the implications of our results for theoretical biology and the potential applications in ecological modeling, specifically in the context of species interactions. The insights gained from our exploration may lead to future investigations on enhancing biodiversity and managing ecosystems within competitive environments.

text: In this study, we explore the correlation functions of twist fields in the massive Dirac theory, leveraging Ward identities to achieve a comprehensive understanding of their behavior. We address the challenge of calculating these correlation functions, which are pivotal for understanding phase transitions and topological properties in quantum field theories involving fermions. Our primary aim is to derive explicit expressions for the correlation functions in the presence of a mass term, which traditionally complicates computation due to the breaking of conformal symmetry. By systematically employing Ward identities, we link the variations of twist fields with conserved currents, allowing us to ascertain integral constraints that simplify the computation of correlation functions. Our methodology involves constructing the massive Dirac theory's framework to consistently incorporate twist field operators, ensuring all symmetries and anomalies are accurately captured. The results obtained reveal robust expressions for the correlation functions, characterizing the interplay between mass, twist, and topological configurations within the Dirac field. Our findings demonstrate that even in the presence of a mass term, the correlation functions exhibit distinctive scaling behavior, offering insights into the massive Dirac theory's rich structure. These expressions enrich the theoretical toolbox available for analyzing models with similar symmetry-breaking phenomena. Additionally, while the focus is on massive theories, our findings significantly contribute to understanding the fundamental nature of twist fields in broad quantum field contexts. This study underscores the utility of Ward identities in unraveling complex field-theoretic interactions, paving the way for future research in topological aspects of quantum theories.

We exploit the high sensitivity and moderate spectral resolution of the
$HST$-Cosmic Origins Spectrograph to detect far-ultraviolet spectral features
of carbon monoxide (CO) present in the inner regions of protoplanetary disks
for the first time. We present spectra of the classical T Tauri stars HN Tau,
RECX-11, and V4046 Sgr, representative of a range of CO radiative processes. HN
Tau shows CO bands in absorption against the accretion continuum. We measure a
CO column density and rotational excitation temperature of N(CO) = 2 +/- 1
$\times$ 10$^{17}$ cm$^{-2}$ and T_rot(CO) 500 +/- 200 K for the absorbing gas.
We also detect CO A-X band emission in RECX-11 and V4046 Sgr, excited by
ultraviolet line photons, predominantly HI LyA. All three objects show emission
from CO bands at $\lambda$ $>$ 1560 \AA, which may be excited by a combination
of UV photons and collisions with non-thermal electrons. In previous
observations these emission processes were not accounted for due to blending
with emission from the accretion shock, collisionally excited H$_{2}$, and
photo-excited H2; all of which appeared as a "continuum" whose components could
not be separated. The CO emission spectrum is strongly dependent upon the shape
of the incident stellar LyA emission profile. We find CO parameters in the
range: N(CO) 10$^{18-19}$ cm$^{-2}$, T_{rot}(CO) > 300 K for the LyA-pumped
emission. We combine these results with recent work on photo- and
collisionally-excited H$_{2}$ emission, concluding that the observations of
ultraviolet-emitting CO and H2 are consistent with a common spatial origin. We
suggest that the CO/H2 ratio in the inner disk is ~1, a transition between the
much lower interstellar value and the higher value observed in solar system
comets today, a result that will require future observational and theoretical
study to confirm.

We have studied the magnetic and transport behavior of doped La0.65 A0.35
Mn0.95Fe0.05 O3 (A= Ca, Sr, Pb, Ba) compounds. All the compositions show
ferromagnetic/metal to paramagnetic/insulator transition except the Pb doped
sample which is insulating and ferromagnetic in the entire temperature range.
The simultaneous occurrence of ferromagnetism and insulating behavior in Pb
doped compound is most likely due to the presence of FM clusters separated by
Fe and Mn ions that are coupled AFM and hence prevent the current from crossing
the inter-domain region. The magnetization and Tc are decreased by decreasing
the Cation size on La site. We observed that (for a fixed Fe content of 5%) the
transition temperature and magnetic moment at 77 K is a maximum for Sr doped
sample and is decreasing if we increase or decrease the cation size from Sr
size. The maximum value of Tc and magnetic moment for Sr based sample is most
likely due to the closer ionic sizes of La and Sr as compared to the other
dopants (Ca, Pb, Ba). The decrease in the transition temperature and magnetic
moment is due to the deviation of Mn-O-Mn angle from 1800 caused by the size
mismatch of the A site cations. This deviation leads to weakening of the FM
double exchange (DE). We observed a spin freezing type effect in the Pb doped
sample below 120 K in resistivity, AC susceptibility and in magnetization. This
suggests that the AFM interactions introduced by the Fe are most effective in
the Pb doped composition leading to increased competition between the FM and
AFM interactions. This FM and AFM interaction generates some degree of
frustration leading to the appearance of spin glass like phase whose typical
magnetic behavior is studied for small ion when the metallic like behavior is
lost.

The next generation wireless networks (i.e. 5G and beyond), which would be
extremely dynamic and complex due to the ultra-dense deployment of
heterogeneous networks (HetNets), poses many critical challenges for network
planning, operation, management and troubleshooting. At the same time,
generation and consumption of wireless data are becoming increasingly
distributed with ongoing paradigm shift from people-centric to machine-oriented
communications, making the operation of future wireless networks even more
complex. In mitigating the complexity of future network operation, new
approaches of intelligently utilizing distributed computational resources with
improved context-awareness becomes extremely important. In this regard, the
emerging fog (edge) computing architecture aiming to distribute computing,
storage, control, communication, and networking functions closer to end users,
have a great potential for enabling efficient operation of future wireless
networks. These promising architectures make the adoption of artificial
intelligence (AI) principles which incorporate learning, reasoning and
decision-making mechanism, as natural choices for designing a tightly
integrated network. Towards this end, this article provides a comprehensive
survey on the utilization of AI integrating machine learning, data analytics
and natural language processing (NLP) techniques for enhancing the efficiency
of wireless network operation. In particular, we provide comprehensive
discussion on the utilization of these techniques for efficient data
acquisition, knowledge discovery, network planning, operation and management of
the next generation wireless networks. A brief case study utilizing the AI
techniques for this network has also been provided.

text: We investigated the propagation of plasmonic waves on a chain of metallic nanoparticles, with a focus on the impact of a liquid crystalline host and an applied magnetic field. Through a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental verification, we demonstrated that the introduction of a liquid crystalline host significantly enhances the propagation of plasmonic waves along the chain, resulting in a substantial increase in wave velocity and propagation length. This is attributed to the alignment of the nanoparticles within the host matrix, which facilitates the formation of a more uniform and efficient plasmonic waveguide.  In contrast, the application of a magnetic field to the chain of nanoparticles resulted in a complex interplay between magnetic and electric interactions, leading to a modulation of the plasmonic wave's propagation characteristics. Specifically, we observed a periodic variation in wave velocity and amplitude, which can be attributed to the magnetic field's influence on the nanoparticles' collective behavior. Our results suggest that the interplay between magnetic and electric interactions can be harnessed to control the propagation of plasmonic waves, potentially enabling novel applications in fields such as sensing, imaging, and energy harvesting.  Our findings highlight the importance of considering the interplay between electromagnetic and magnetic interactions in the design and optimization of plasmonic waveguides. By exploring the effects of liquid crystalline hosts and applied magnetic fields, we have gained valuable insights into the complex dynamics of plasmonic wave propagation, and have identified potential avenues for the development of novel plasmonic devices.

text: We investigate the magnetic field geometry and chemical abundance distribution of the He-strong star CPD -57 3509, a critical area of research in stellar astrophysics. Our primary objective is to elucidate the relationship between magnetic fields and elemental abundances, which significantly influence the observables of chemically peculiar stars. Utilizing high-resolution spectropolarimetry, we acquired spectroscopic data spanning multiple epochs to achieve a comprehensive understanding of the magnetic field structure. We employed the tomographic inversion technique to reconstruct the magnetic field configuration, revealing a pronounced dipolar nature aligned with the star’s rotation axis.   Simultaneously, we analyzed the elemental abundance profiles through sophisticated atmospheric models, incorporating radiative transfer calculations to interpret the observed spectral lines. Our findings indicate a distinct distribution of He and other heavy elements, with pronounced overabundance in specific equatorial regions, suggesting a correlation with the magnetic field lines. This anisotropic abundance distribution appears to enhance the star's observed spectral features, reinforcing the notion that magnetic fields play a pivotal role in the atmospheric dynamics of CPD -57 3509.  Ultimately, our work demonstrates that the interplay between magnetic geometry and chemical distribution significantly affects the physical characteristics of He-strong stars. We propose that further studies integrating both magnetic field modeling and abundance analysis are essential to advance our understanding of the mechanisms governing chemical peculiarity in stellar atmospheres, thereby contributing to the broader field of stellar evolution and magnetohydrodynamic interactions.

text: Feedforward artificial neural networks (FFANNs) have become fundamental tools in machine learning due to their ability to model complex patterns and non-linear relationships. Despite their widespread use, understanding the dynamics of FFANNs often remains obscure. This study aims to elucidate the functioning of FFANNs through the lens of network flow, providing a novel perspective on their operational mechanisms.   The research focuses on mapping the network flow within FFANNs, analyzing how information traverses from inputs to outputs. We employed a combination of theoretical analysis and experimental simulation to trace the flow across different layers of the network, emphasizing how network architecture influences data propagation. The methodology involves evaluating flow efficiency and identifying critical paths that dictate information processing.  Key findings include the observation that certain nodes and connections play pivotal roles in optimizing flow efficiency, equivalent to bottlenecks in traditional network flow theory. These nodes act as high-influence conduits, affecting the robustness and accuracy of the neural network. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that altering connectivity patterns can significantly impact the performance of FFANNs, offering strategies for network design and training optimization.  In conclusion, viewing FFANNs from a network flow perspective provides valuable insights into their internal workings, highlights critical structural elements, and suggests improvements for network architecture. This approach not only deepens our understanding but also enhances the development and application of feedforward networks in diverse machine learning tasks. Future work will explore the extension of this framework to other neural network architectures.

text: Extended Large Eddy Simulation (XLES) has emerged as a significant advancement in the field of computational fluid dynamics, offering enhanced modeling capabilities for turbulent flows. The objective of this research paper is to introduce the foundational principles and methodologies underlying XLES, elucidating its advantages over traditional Large Eddy Simulation (LES) approaches. This study employs a comprehensive review of existing literature coupled with a systematic comparison of XLES with conventional LES, direct numerical simulation (DNS), and other turbulence modeling techniques. Key findings indicate that XLES demonstrates improved accuracy in capturing complex flow phenomena, particularly in scenarios characterized by a wide range of scales and multifarious physical processes. Notably, the incorporation of additional filtering techniques and innovative subgrid-scale models in XLES facilitates better resolution of turbulence structures, thereby enhancing predictive capabilities. Moreover, the adaptability of XLES in various applications—from urban airflow modeling to industrial mixing processes—underscores its versatility and efficacy. In conclusion, this paper establishes XLES as a pivotal methodology in the simulation of turbulent flows, providing researchers and practitioners with a robust framework for addressing contemporary challenges in fluid dynamics. The insights gained from this introduction serve as a foundation for subsequent parts of the research, where more specialized aspects of XLES will be explored in depth.

The primary objective was to investigate the nature and stability of the magnetic ground states in EuRh4Si2 and EuIr4Si2 using neutron diffraction techniques.  Neutron diffraction experiments were conducted at various temperatures to map out the magnetic order parameters and to probe the anisotropy of the magnetic structure. Key findings indicate the emergence of an anisotropic "up-up-down" configuration, characterized by distinct magnetic moments aligned along specific crystallographic directions. This structural arrangement suggests a strong influence of crystal field effects and interatomic interactions on the magnetic ordering. Additionally, the data reveal a phase transition temperature consistent with theoretical predictions, confirming the stability of the observed magnetic structure.  In conclusion, the research provides insights into the complex magnetic behavior of EuTAl4Si2 compounds, emphasizing the role of electronic structure and crystal symmetry in determining the magnetic ground state. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of magnetic systems with potential applications in spintronics and quantum computing.

We present new methods for radiative transfer on hierarchial grids. We
develop a new method for calculating the scattered flux that employs the grid
structure to speed up the computation. We describe a novel subiteration
algorithm that can be used to accelerate calculations with strong dust
temperature self-coupling. We compute two test models, a molecular cloud and a
circumstellar disc, and compare the accuracy and speed of the new algorithms
against existing methods. An adaptive model of the molecular cloud with less
than 8 % of the cells in the uniform grid produced results in good agreement
with the full resolution model. The relative RMS error of the surface
brightness <4 % at all wavelengths, and in regions of high column density the
relative RMS error was only 10^{-4}. Computation with the adaptive model was
faster by a factor of ~5. The new method for calculating the scattered flux is
faster by a factor of ~4 in large models with a deep hierarchy structure, when
images of the scattered light are computed towards several observing
directions. The efficiency of the subiteration algorithm is highly dependent on
the details of the model. In the circumstellar disc test the speed-up was a
factor of two, but much larger gains are possible. The algorithm is expected to
be most beneficial in models where a large number of small, dense regions are
embedded in an environment with a lower mean density.

The paper deals with the mechanism of particle creation in the framework of
irreversible thermodynamics. The second order non-equilibrium thermodynamical
prescription of Israel and Stewart has been presented with particle creation
rate, treated as the dissipative effect. In the background of a flat FRW model,
we assume the non-equilibrium thermodynamical process to be isentropic so that
the entropy per particle does not change and consequently the dissipative
pressure can be expressed linearly in terms of the particle creation rate. Here
the dissipative pressure behaves as a dynamical variable having a non-linear
inhomogeneous evolution equation and the entropy flow vector satisfies the
second law of thermodynamics. Further, using the Friedmann equations and by
proper choice of the particle creation rate as a function of the Hubble
parameter, it is possible to show (separately) a transition from the
inflationary phase to the radiation era and also from matter dominated era to
late time acceleration. Also, in analogy to analytic continuation, it is
possible to show a continuous cosmic evolution from inflation to late time
acceleration by adjusting the parameters. It is found that in the de Sitter
phase, the comoving entropy increases exponentially with time, keeping entropy
per particle unchanged. Subsequently, the above cosmological scenarios has been
described from field theoretic point of view by introducing a scalar field
having self interacting potential. Finally, we make an attempt to show the
cosmological phenomenon of particle creation as Hawking radiation, particularly
during the inflationary era.

text: In the contemporary scientific landscape, nanomaterials and nanoparticles have garnered significant attention due to their unique properties and potential applications in various industrial sectors. However, the production and application of these novel materials pose potential risks to human health and the environment. In this study, we explored the sources of nanomaterials and nanoparticles, focusing on industrial processes, consumer products, and natural sources. We then examined the available scientific evidence on their toxicological effects.  Our research reveals that industrial processes, such as catalysis, energy production, and electronics manufacturing, are major contributors to the global release of nanomaterials and nanoparticles. Consumer products, including food packaging, cosmetics, and household cleaners, also contribute to the exposure of the general population to these materials. Moreover, natural sources, such as volcanic eruptions, wildfires, and dust storms, can release nanomaterials and nanoparticles into the environment.  Regarding toxicological effects, we found that nanomaterials and nanoparticles can cause harm by penetrating biological membranes, interacting with cells and biomolecules, inducing oxidative stress, and triggering inflammatory responses. Among the specific nanomaterials studied, silver nanoparticles, titanium dioxide nanoparticles, and carbon nanotubes were found to exhibit toxic effects at certain doses and exposure conditions. Additionally, we reviewed the existing regulatory frameworks and research efforts aimed at addressing the challenges posed by nanomaterials and nanoparticles.  Our study underscores the need for a comprehensive understanding of the sources and toxicity of nanomaterials and nanoparticles and calls for the development of effective strategies to mitigate their potential risks. Specifically, we recommend the implementation of rigorous safety protocols during the production and application of nanomaterials and nanoparticles and the establishment of regulatory standards for their use in consumer products. Furthermore, we advocate for continued research in the fields of nanotoxicology and nanoremediation to advance our knowledge of these materials and their environmental impact.

It is often argued that the minimal supersymmetric standard model has O(100)
free parameters and the generic parameter region is already excluded by the
null observation of the flavor and CP violating processes as well as the
constraints from the LHC experiments. This situation naturally leads us to
consider the case where all the dangerous soft supersymmetry breaking terms
such as the scalar masses and scalar couplings are absent, while only the
unified gaugino mass term and the mu term are non-vanishing at the grand
unification scale. We revisit this simple situation taking into account the
observed Higgs boson mass, 125 GeV. Since the gaugino mass and the mu term are
fixed in order to explain the Higgs boson and the Z boson masses, there is no
free parameter left in this scenario. We find that there are three independent
parameter sets exist including ones which have not been discussed in the
literature. We also find that the abundance of the dark matter can be explained
by relic gravitinos which are non-thermally produced as decay products of the
SUSY particles while satisfying constraints from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis. We
discuss the effects of the gravity mediation which generically give
contribution to the soft terms of the order of the gravitino mass. It turns out
that newly found parameter set is preferable to explain the Higgs boson mass as
well as the gravitino dark matter while satisfying the constraints from the
electric dipole moments of the electron and the nucleon.

Diphoton searches at high invariant mass are an integral part of the
experimental high energy frontier. Using the analyses of the 750\,GeV diphoton
resonance as a case study, we examine the methodology currently employed by the
experimental analyses in estimating the dominant standard model backgrounds. We
assess the dependence of the significance associated with the excess on the
background modeling. In particular, we show that close to the high energy tails
of the distributions, estimates of the jet faking backgrounds relying on
functional extrapolations or Monte Carlo estimates of the challenging
photon-jet contributions introduce a large uncertainty. Analyses with loose
photon cuts, low photon $p_T$ cuts and those susceptible to high photon
rapidity regions are especially affected. Given that diphoton-based searches
beyond 1\,TeV are highly motivated as discovery modes, these considerations are
relevant and applicable in the future.
  We first consider a physics-driven deformation of the shape of the diphoton
faking photon-jet spectrum by next-to-leading order effects combined with a
rapidity and transverse momentum dependent fake rate. We show that the
resulting local significance of the excess is reduced due to such a
deformation. Then using a simple, but more general, ansatz to modify the
contribution of the jet faking backgrounds at high invariant masses but keeping
the inclusive and differential sample purities within experimental uncertainty
estimates, we demonstrate that the originally reported local 750\,GeV excess
significances could have been overestimated by more than one standard
deviation. We furthermore cross-check our analysis by comparing fit results
based on the smaller 2015 and the larger 2016 LHC datasets. Finally we employ
our methodology on the complete 13\,TeV LHC dataset to asses the systematics
involved in the current diphoton searches beyond the TeV region.

Smart contracts are programs running on cryptocurrency (e.g., Ethereum)
blockchains, whose popularity stem from the possibility to perform financial
transactions, such as payments and auctions, in a distributed environment
without need for any trusted third party. Given their financial nature, bugs or
vulnerabilities in these programs may lead to catastrophic consequences, as
witnessed by recent attacks. Unfortunately, programming smart contracts is a
delicate task that requires strong expertise: Ethereum smart contracts are
written in Solidity, a dedicated language resembling JavaScript, and shipped
over the blockchain in the EVM bytecode format. In order to rigorously verify
the security of smart contracts, it is of paramount importance to formalize
their semantics as well as the security properties of interest, in particular
at the level of the bytecode being executed.
  In this paper, we present the first complete small-step semantics of EVM
bytecode, which we formalize in the F* proof assistant, obtaining executable
code that we successfully validate against the official Ethereum test suite.
Furthermore, we formally define for the first time a number of central security
properties for smart contracts, such as call integrity, atomicity, and
independence from miner controlled parameters. This formalization relies on a
combination of hyper- and safety properties. Along this work, we identified
various mistakes and imprecisions in existing semantics and verification tools
for Ethereum smart contracts, thereby demonstrating once more the importance of
rigorous semantic foundations for the design of security verification
techniques.

text: This research paper presents the findings from the Canada-France Ecliptic Plane Survey (CFEPS) Full Data Release, focusing on the orbital structure of the Kuiper Belt. Key findings reveal the presence of distinct dynamical substructures within the Kuiper Belt that provide insights into its formation and evolution processes. These findings enhance our understanding of the Kuiper Belt's origin and evolution and have implications for the migration of giant planets in the early solar system.  In conclusion, the study contributes significant insights into the orbital structure of the Kuiper Belt, shedding light on the dynamical complexities within this distant region of our solar system. The findings from this research have broader implications for planetary formation mechanisms and the dynamics of the outer solar system.

It is usually thought that a single equation of state (EoS) model "correctly"
represents cores of all compact stars. Here we emphasize that two families of
compact stars, viz., neutron stars and strange stars, can coexist in nature,
and that neutron stars can get converted to strange stars through the
nucleation process of quark matter in the stellar center. From our fully
general relativistic numerical computations of the structures of fast-spinning
compact stars, known as millisecond pulsars, we find that such a stellar
conversion causes a simultaneous spin-up and decrease in gravitational mass of
these stars. This is a new type of millisecond pulsar evolution through a new
mechanism, which gives rise to relatively lower mass compact stars with higher
spin rates. This could have implication for the observed mass and spin
distributions of millisecond pulsars. Such a stellar conversion can also rescue
some massive, spin-supported millisecond pulsars from collapsing into black
holes. Besides, we extend the concept of critical mass $M_{\rm cr}$ for the
neutron star sequence (Berezhiani et al. 2003; Bombaci et al. 2004) to the case
of fast-spinning neutron stars, and point out that neutron star EoS models
cannot be ruled out by the stellar mass measurement alone. Finally, we
emphasize the additional complexity for constraining EoS models, for example,
by stellar radius measurements using X-ray observations, if two families of
compact stars coexist.

text: We investigated the prediction of lethal and synthetically lethal knock-outs in regulatory networks, a critical aspect of understanding the dynamics of cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Through a systematic analysis of existing literature and computational modeling, we identified key regulatory networks involved in essential cellular processes, such as metabolism, cell cycle regulation, and apoptosis.  Our computational approach integrated machine learning algorithms with network topology and centrality measures to predict lethal and synthetically lethal knock-outs. We trained models on a large dataset of known knock-out experiments and validated their performance using independent datasets. The results showed that our approach was able to accurately predict lethal knock-outs in 85% of cases and synthetically lethal knock-outs in 70% of cases.  Our analysis revealed that the key factors influencing the prediction of lethal and synthetically lethal knock-outs include network topology, protein-protein interaction, and functional annotations. We also identified specific regulatory nodes and modules that are critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis and that are more likely to be involved in lethal knock-outs.  Our study provides a framework for predicting lethal and synthetically lethal knock-outs in regulatory networks, which can be used to identify potential therapeutic targets for diseases and to understand the underlying mechanisms of cellular responses to genetic perturbations.

text: We investigated the challenges of checking conformance of finite state machines (FSMs) to distributed observations, a common scenario in network protocols and distributed systems. Our research aimed to develop a framework for verifying FSM conformance in the presence of distributed observations, which are inherently asynchronous and may be subject to varying levels of noise and latency.  Our approach involves designing and implementing a novel distributed conformance checking algorithm that leverages a combination of centralized and decentralized techniques. We employed a hybrid model, where a central controller collects and aggregates observations from distributed sensors, while a distributed ensemble of FSM evaluators processes the aggregated observations and verifies the FSM's behavior.  Our results show that our framework can efficiently and accurately check FSM conformance in distributed scenarios, even in the presence of noisy and delayed observations. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach through extensive simulations and case studies, which involved modeling various network protocols and distributed systems. Our evaluation results indicate that our framework can achieve high conformance checking accuracy, while also ensuring scalability and fault tolerance.  The key ideas underlying our approach are the use of distributed evaluators to process aggregated observations, and the incorporation of noise-tolerant and latency-aware techniques to ensure accurate conformance checking. Our methodology involves designing and implementing a custom FSM evaluation framework, as well as developing a distributed system architecture to support the hybrid conformance checking algorithm.

text: This study investigates the activity-related variations of high-degree p-mode oscillations in solar active regions, focusing on their amplitude, width, and energy characteristics. The objective is to enhance the understanding of solar dynamics and improve solar activity forecasting. Utilizing spectral analysis of helioseismic data collected from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we examined high-degree p-modes in various active regions over a one-year period characterized by differing solar activity levels. Key findings reveal that both the amplitude and energy of high-degree p-modes exhibit a significant correlation with the intensity of solar activity. Specifically, in active regions, we observed an increase in amplitude by up to 30%, accompanied by a narrowing of the mode width, suggesting enhanced coherence. Additionally, the overall energy distribution in the identified p-modes displayed a dependence on the magnetic field strength within the regions, indicating a direct impact of magnetic activity on wave propagation. These results imply that solar activity modulates not only the occurrence of p-modes but also their intrinsic properties. The conclusions underscore the potential of high-degree p-modes as a diagnostic tool for probing solar active regions and their magnetic dynamics, contributing to improved models of solar behavior. This research provides a foundation for future investigations into the interplay between solar oscillations and magnetic fields, facilitating advancements in solar activity predictions.

text: In this study, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of molecular absorption lines toward PKS1830-211 using data acquired from an ALMA Early Science survey. We focus on evaluating absorption profiles of several molecular species, including CO, HCO+, and HCN, which serve as critical tracers of the physical conditions within the galaxy. Employing a high spectral resolution approach, we analyze the profiles to deduce the kinematic properties and distributions of these molecules.  Our methodology involves meticulous spectral line fitting and modeling to identify sub-velocity components and derive column densities. We apply a Bayesian inference framework to quantify uncertainties and improve the robustness of derived parameters. Results indicate the presence of multiple distinct velocity components in the absorption profiles, providing insights into the complex dynamics and possible interaction history of the absorber. Notably, the variations in relative abundances of molecular species suggest non-uniform chemical enrichment and differential depletion effects.  This work contributes to the broader field of galaxy evolution by showcasing the potential of ALMA Early Science surveys in unraveling the intricacies of high-redshift interstellar environments. Our findings emphasize the importance of molecular absorptions as diagnostic tools for probing the cold gas in the universe, advancing our understanding of the chemical and physical processes in cosmic structures during critical epochs.

We present extensive ultraviolet (UV) and optical photometry, as well as
dense optical spectroscopy for type II Plateau (IIP) supernova SN 2016X that
exploded in the nearby ($\sim$ 15 Mpc) spiral galaxy UGC 08041. The
observations span the period from 2 to 180 days after the explosion; in
particular, the Swift UV data probably captured the signature of shock breakout
associated with the explosion of SN 2016X. It shows very strong UV emission
during the first week after explosion, with contribution of $\sim$ 20 -- 30% to
the bolometric luminosity (versus $\lesssim$ 15% for normal SNe IIP). Moreover,
we found that this supernova has an unusually long rise time of about 12.6
$\pm$ 0.5 days in the $R$ band (versus $\sim$ 7.0 days for typical SNe IIP).
The optical light curves and spectral evolution are quite similar to the
fast-declining type IIP object SN 2013ej, except that SN 2016X has a relatively
brighter tail. Based on the evolution of photospheric temperature as inferred
from the $Swift$ data in the early phase, we derive that the progenitor of SN
2016X has a radius of about 930 $\pm$ 70 R$_{\odot}$. This large-size star is
expected to be a red supergiant star with an initial mass of $\gtrsim$ 19 -- 20
M$_{\odot}$ based on the mass $--$ radius relation of the Galactic red
supergiants, and it represents one of the most largest and massive progenitors
found for SNe IIP.

text: In this study, we investigate non-equilibrium steady states (NESS) in both ideal bosonic and fermionic quantum gases. Our work attempts to elucidate the unique characteristics of these states that arise from the fundamental differences between bosons and fermions, as well as the effects of external driving forces. We employ a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical simulations to explore the phase diagrams of these systems under various conditions. Key insights include the emergence of distinct nonequilibrium patterns such as density waves and vortices, which are influenced by the statistics of particles and the nature of interactions within the gas. The methodology involves solving Gross-Pitaevskii equations for bosonic systems and incorporating Fermi-Dirac statistics for fermionic systems, alongside detailed energy balance calculations. Our findings reveal how particle statistics play a crucial role in shaping the dynamics and stability of non-equilibrium states in quantum gases, providing valuable information for future experiments and applications in quantum technologies.

In this paper, we show how to study the evolution of a system, given
imprecise knowledge about the state of the system and the dynamics laws. Our
approach is based on Fuzzy Set Theory, and it will be shown that the
\emph{Fuzzy Dynamics} of a $n$-dimensional system is equivalent to Lagrangian
(or Hamiltonian) mechanics in a $n+1$-dimensional space. In some cases,
however, the corresponding Lagrangian is more general than the usual one and
could depend on the action. In this case, Lagrange's equations gain a non-zero
right side proportional to the derivative of the Lagrangian with respect to the
action. Examples of such systems are unstable systems, systems with dissipation
and systems which can remember their history. Moreover, in certain situations,
the Lagrangian could be a set-valued function. The corresponding equations of
motion then become differential inclusions instead of differential equations.
We will also show that the principal of least action is a consequence of the
causality principle and the local topology of the state space and not an
independent axiom of classical mechanics.
  We emphasize that our adaptation of Lagrangian mechanics does not use or
depend on specific properties of the physical system being modeled. Therefore,
this Lagrangian approach may be equally applied to \emph{non-physical} systems.
An example of such an application is presented as well.
label: human

text: Asynchronous polar pulsars, characterized by the alignment of their magnetic and rotation axes, exhibit complex and intriguing phenomena. In this study, we focus on the asynchronous polar pulsar V1500 Cygni, a well-known and interesting object in the field. We reexamine its orbital, spin, and beat period solutions using data collected from various observatories, including the Arecibo Observatory, the Green Bank Observatory, and the Parkes Observatory. Through the analysis of pulse profile evolution, timing residuals, and period derivative studies, we identify three possible sets of solutions (A) a 3.5-hour orbit with a 2.65-second spin period, a 14.9-second beat period, and a relatively stable period derivative; (B) a 3.6-hour orbit with a 2.63-second spin period, a 13.9-second beat period, and a rapidly decreasing period derivative; and (C) a 3.7-hour orbit with a 2.62-second spin period, a 14.3-second beat period, and an almost constant period derivative. Our results show that each solution corresponds to a distinct emission mechanism, either toroidal magnetic field emission, conal emission, or magnetic reconnection. These findings offer new insights into the complex emission mechanisms of asynchronous polar pulsars and serve as a foundation for further investigations into their underlying physical processes.
label: machine

text: This study presents almost-linear-time algorithms for analyzing Markov chains, significantly reducing the computational complexity compared to previous methods. The primary problem addressed is the efficient computation of hitting times, commute times, and mixing times, which are fundamental metrics in understanding the behavior of stochastic processes on graphs. To achieve this, we introduce novel spectral primitives specifically tailored for directed graphs, enhancing our ability to compute these metrics more accurately and efficiently.  The methodology involves developing new spectral decompositions and leveraging them within a divide-and-conquer framework that minimizes the number of operations required for large-scale problems. Our approach allows us to process graphs with millions of nodes and edges in linearithmic time relative to the number of nodes, making it feasible for real-world applications such as network analysis, recommendation systems, and biological pathway modeling.  The results demonstrate substantial improvements in both speed and scalability, outperforming existing techniques by orders of magnitude. These advancements not only accelerate traditional Markov chain computations but also open up possibilities for integrating these methods into broader algorithmic frameworks, thereby broadening their applicability across various fields.

In large-scale wireless acoustic sensor networks (WASNs), many of the sensors
will only have a marginal contribution to a certain estimation task. Involving
all sensors increases the energy budget unnecessarily and decreases the
lifetime of the WASN. Using microphone subset selection, also termed as sensor
selection, the most informative sensors can be chosen from a set of candidate
sensors to achieve a prescribed inference performance. In this paper, we
consider microphone subset selection for minimum variance distortionless
response (MVDR) beamformer based noise reduction. The best subset of sensors is
determined by minimizing the transmission cost while constraining the output
noise power (or signal-to-noise ratio). Assuming the statistical information on
correlation matrices of the sensor measurements is available, the sensor
selection problem for this model-driven scheme is first solved by utilizing
convex optimization techniques. In addition, to avoid estimating the statistics
related to all the candidate sensors beforehand, we also propose a data-driven
approach to select the best subset using a greedy strategy. The performance of
the greedy algorithm converges to that of the model-driven method, while it
displays advantages in dynamic scenarios as well as on computational
complexity. Compared to a sparse MVDR or radius-based beamformer, experiments
show that the proposed methods can guarantee the desired performance with
significantly less transmission costs.

text:
Quantitative measurement of functional and anatomical traits of 4D tongue
motion in the course of speech or other lingual behaviors remains a major
challenge in scientific research and clinical applications. Here, we introduce
a statistical multimodal atlas of 4D tongue motion using healthy subjects,
which enables a combined quantitative characterization of tongue motion in a
reference anatomical configuration. This atlas framework, termed Speech Map,
combines cine- and tagged-MRI in order to provide both the anatomic reference
and motion information during speech. Our approach involves a series of steps
including (1) construction of a common reference anatomical configuration from
cine-MRI, (2) motion estimation from tagged-MRI, (3) transformation of the
motion estimations to the reference anatomical configuration, and (4)
computation of motion quantities such as Lagrangian strain. Using this
framework, the anatomic configuration of the tongue appears motionless, while
the motion fields and associated strain measurements change over the time
course of speech. In addition, to form a succinct representation of the
high-dimensional and complex motion fields, principal component analysis is
carried out to characterize the central tendencies and variations of motion
fields of our speech tasks. Our proposed method provides a platform to
quantitatively and objectively explain the differences and variability of
tongue motion by illuminating internal motion and strain that have so far been
intractable. The findings are used to understand how tongue function for speech
is limited by abnormal internal motion and strain in glossectomy patients.
label: human

Rapidly-rotating neutron stars are the only candidates for persistent
high-frequency gravitational wave emission, for which a targeted search can be
performed based on the spin period measured from electromagnetic (e.g. radio
and X-ray) observations. The principal factor determining the sensitivity of
such searches is the measurement precision of the physical parameters of the
system. Neutron stars in X-ray binaries present additional computational
demands for searches due to the uncertainty in the binary parameters. We
present the results of a pilot study with the goal of improving the measurement
precision of binary orbital parameters for candidate gravitational wave
sources. We observed the optical counterpart of Sco X-1 in 2011 June with the
William Herschel Telescope, and also made use of Very Large Telescope
observations in 2011, to provide an additional epoch of radial-velocity
measurements to earlier measurements in 1999. From a circular orbit fit to the
combined dataset, we obtained an improvement of a factor of two in the orbital
period precision, and a factor of 2.5 in the epoch of inferior conjunction
$T_0$. While the new orbital period is consistent with the previous value of
Gottllieb et al. (1975), the new $T_0$ (and the amplitude of variation of the
Bowen line velocities) exhibited a significant shift, which we attribute to
variations in the emission geometry with epoch. We propagate the uncertainties
on these parameters through to the expected Advanced LIGO & VIRGO detector
network observation epochs, and quantify the improvement obtained with
additional optical observations.

text:
One of the most popular scenarios for the superconductivity in Fe-based
superconductors (FeBSC) posits that the bosons responsible for electronic
pairing are spin-fluctuations with a wave vector spanning the hole Fermi
surfaces (FSs) near $\Gamma$ and the electron FSs near M points. So far all
FeBSC for which neutron data are available do demonstrate such excitations, and
the band structure calculations so far were finding quasi-nested FSs in all
FeBSC, providing for a peak in the spin susceptibility at the desired wave
vectors. However, the newest addition to the family, Sr$_{2}$VO$_{3}$FeAs, has
been calculated to have a very complex FS with no visible quasi-nesting
features. It was argued therefore that this material does not fall under the
existing paradigm and calls for revisiting our current ideas about what is the
likely cause of superconductivity in FeBSC. In this paper, I show that the
visible complexity of the FS is entirely due to the V-derived electronic
states. Assuming that superconductivity in Sr$_{2}$VO$_{3}$FeAs, as in the
other FeBSC, originates in the FeAs layers, and the superconducting electrons
are sensitive to the susceptibility of the FeAs electronic subsystem, I
recalculate the bare susceptibility, weighting the electronic states with their
Fe character, and obtain a susceptibility that fully supports the existing
quasi-nesting model.

More than a third of all exoplanets can be classified as super-Earths based
on radius (1-2 $R_{\bigoplus}$) and mass (< 10 $M_{\bigoplus}$). Here we model
mass-radius relations based on silicate mantle and iron core equations of state
to infer to first order the structure and composition range of rocky
super-Earths assuming insignificant gas envelopes. We develop a new equation of
state of hexagonal close packed (hcp) iron for super-Earth conditions (SEOS)
based on density functional theory results for pressures up to 137~TPa. A
comparison of SEOS and extrapolated equations of state for iron from the
literature reveals differences in density of up to 4% at 1~TPa and up to 20% at
10~TPa. Such density differences change the derived mass by up to 10\% for
Earth-like super-Earths (core radius fraction of 0.5) and 20% for Mercury-like
super-Earths (core radius fraction of 0.8). We find that the effect of
temperature on mass (< 5%) is smaller than that resulting from the
extrapolation of the equations of state of iron and lower mantle temperatures
are too low to allow for rock and iron miscibility for R<1.75 $R_{\bigoplus}$.
We find that modeling uncertainties dominate over observational uncertainties
for many observed super-Earths. We illustrate these uncertainties explicitly
for Kepler-36b with well-constrained mass and radius. Assuming a core
composition of 0.8$\rho$ Fe (equivalent to 50 mol% S) instead of pure Fe leads
to an increase of the core radius fraction from 0.53 to 0.64. Using a mantle
composition of Mg$_{0.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$SiO$_3$ instead of MgSiO$_3$ leads to a
decrease of the core radius fraction to 0.33. Effects of thermal structure and
the choice of equation of state for the core material on the core radius of
Kepler-36b are small but non-negligible, reaching 2% and 5%, respectively.

text:
Blazars are among the most variable objects in the universe. They feature
energetic jets of plasma that launch from the cores of these active galactic
nuclei (AGN), triggering activity from radio up to gamma-ray energies. Spatial
localization of the region of their MeV/GeV emission is a key question in
understanding the blazar phenomenon.
  The flat spectrum radio quasar (FSRQ) PKS 1502+106 has exhibited extreme and
correlated, radio and high-energy activity that triggered intense monitoring by
the Fermi-GST AGN Multi-frequency Monitoring Alliance (F-GAMMA) program and the
Global Millimeter VLBI Array (GMVA) down to $\lambda$3 mm (or 86 GHz), enabling
the sharpest view to date towards this extreme object.
  Here, we report on preliminary results of our study of the gamma-ray loud
blazar PKS 1502+106, combining VLBI and single dish data. We deduce the
critical aspect angle towards the source to be $\theta_{\rm c} = 2.6^{\circ}$,
calculate the apparent and intrinsic opening angles and constrain the distance
of the 86 GHz core from the base of the conical jet, directly from mm-VLBI but
also through a single dish relative timing analysis.
  Finally, we conclude that gamma rays from PKS 1502+106 originate from a
region between ~1-16 pc away from the base of the hypothesized conical jet,
well beyond the bulk of broad-line region (BLR) material of the source.
label: human

text: The Massive and Nearby Galaxies in Andromeda and the Milky Way (MaNGA) survey, a component of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV, provides spatially resolved observations of star formation histories (SFHs) in galaxies with masses ranging from 10^9 to 10^11.5 M☉. In this study, we analyze the SFHs of a sample of 1863 MaNGA galaxies as a function of galaxy mass and type. The objective of our research is to investigate how SFHs vary with galaxy mass and morphology, and to explore the underlying physical processes driving these variations. We employ a Bayesian inference methodology, utilizing stellar population modeling and spectroscopic data, to extract SFHs for each galaxy. Our key findings reveal that early-type galaxies exhibit a clear bimodal SFH, consisting of a quenched component and a recent star formation episode. Conversely, late-type galaxies display continuous SFHs, characterized by ongoing star formation across their entire lives. Moreover, we find that the quenching timescale of early-type galaxies increases with galaxy mass. Our results further indicate that central galaxies in galaxy clusters exhibit distinct SFHs compared to field galaxies, implying a role for environment in the evolution of SFHs. In conclusion, this research provides insight into the relationship between galaxy mass, morphology, and star formation histories, expanding our understanding of galaxy evolution. The findings from this study can inform theoretical models and contribute to future observational efforts aimed at understanding the complexities of galaxy formation and evolution.

text:
Background: The global spread of the severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS)
epidemic has clearly shown the importance of considering the long-range
transportation networks in the understanding of emerging diseases outbreaks.
The introduction of extensive transportation data sets is therefore an
important step in order to develop epidemic models endowed with realism.
Methods: We develop a general stochastic meta-population model that
incorporates actual travel and census data among 3 100 urban areas in 220
countries. The model allows probabilistic predictions on the likelihood of
country outbreaks and their magnitude. The level of predictability offered by
the model can be quantitatively analyzed and related to the appearance of
robust epidemic pathways that represent the most probable routes for the spread
of the disease. Results: In order to assess the predictive power of the model,
the case study of the global spread of SARS is considered. The disease
parameter values and initial conditions used in the model are evaluated from
empirical data for Hong Kong. The outbreak likelihood for specific countries is
evaluated along with the emerging epidemic pathways. Simulation results are in
agreement with the empirical data of the SARS worldwide epidemic. Conclusions:
The presented computational approach shows that the integration of long-range
mobility and demographic data provides epidemic models with a predictive power
that can be consistently tested and theoretically motivated. This computational
strategy can be therefore considered as a general tool in the analysis and
forecast of the global spreading of emerging diseases and in the definition of
containment policies aimed at reducing the effects of potentially catastrophic
outbreaks.
label: human

text: This research explores the Dynamic Connectivity Game (DCG) approach applied to adversarial Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) systems to enhance network resilience and security against cyber-attacks. Building upon existing literature on connectivity games and their application to network security, the study introduces a dynamic framework that accounts for the strategic interactions between nodes in the IoBT system, particularly under adversarial conditions. The objective is to develop a model that can predict and mitigate potential vulnerabilities, ensuring robust communication among nodes while minimizing attack opportunities.  The methodology involves formulating a DCG based on game theory principles, where each node's strategy influences its connectivity with others. This model is then simulated using various scenarios to evaluate its effectiveness in maintaining network integrity. A set of adversarial strategies is employed to test the robustness of the proposed model against different types of attacks, including denial-of-service and malware propagation.  Key findings indicate that the DCG model significantly improves network stability by dynamically adjusting connections in response to threats, thereby reducing the impact of attacks. Additionally, it demonstrates superior performance in terms of minimizing attack vectors and preserving critical functionalities compared to static connectivity approaches. The analysis also highlights the importance of adaptive algorithms in enhancing security and resilience within IoBT networks.  In conclusion, the Dynamic Connectivity Game provides a promising framework for securing adversarial IoBT systems. By enabling proactive and reactive adjustments to network structures, the model offers a robust solution for mitigating cyber threats and maintaining effective communication in dynamic battlefield environments. Further research is recommended to refine the model and integrate it into real-world applications for enhanced cybersecurity.
label: machine

Using the Low Dispersion Survey Spectrograph 3 at the Magellan II Clay
Telescope, we target {candidate absorption host galaxies} detected in deep
optical imaging {(reaching limiting apparent magnitudes of 23.0-26.5 in $g, r,
i,$ and $z$ filters) in the fields of three QSOs, each of which shows the
presence of high metallicity, high $N_{\rm HI}$ absorption systems in their
spectra (Q0826-2230: $z_{abs}$=0.9110, Q1323-0021: $z_{abs}=0.7160$,
Q1436-0051: $z_{abs}=0.7377, 0.9281$). We confirm three host galaxies {at
redshifts 0.7387, 0.7401, and 0.9286} for two of the Lyman-$\alpha$ absorption
systems (one with two galaxies interacting). For these systems, we are able to
determine the star formation rates (SFRs); impact parameters (from previous
imaging detections); the velocity shift between the absorption and emission
redshifts; and, for one system, also the emission metallicity.} Based on
previous photometry, we find these galaxies have L$>$L$^{\ast}$. The [O II]
SFRs for these galaxies are in the range $11-25$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$
{(uncorrected for dust)}, while the impact parameters lie in the range $35-54$
kpc. {Despite the fact that we have confirmed galaxies at 50 kpc from the QSO,
no gradient in metallicity is indicated between the absorption metallicity
along the QSO line of sight and the emission line metallicity in the galaxies.}
We confirm the anti-correlation between impact parameter and $N_{\rm HI}$ from
the literature. We also report the emission redshift of five other galaxies:
three at $z_{em}>z_{QSO}$, and two (L$<$L$^{\ast}$) at $z_{em}<z_{QSO}$ not
corresponding to any known absorption systems.

We discuss two aspects of turbulent Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection (RBC) on
the basis of high-resolution direct numerical simulations in a unique setting;
a closed cylindrical cell of aspect ratio of one. First, we present a
comprehensive comparison of statistical quantities such as energy dissipation
rates and boundary layer thickness scales. Data are used from three simulation
run series at Prandtl numbers $Pr$ that cover two orders of magnitude. In
contrast to most previous studies in RBC the focus of the present work is on
convective turbulence at very low Prandtl numbers including $Pr=0.021$ for
liquid mercury or gallium and $Pr=0.005$ for liquid sodium. In this parameter
range of RBC, inertial effects cause a dominating turbulent momentum transport
that is in line with highly intermittent fluid turbulence both in the bulk and
in the boundary layers and thus should be able to trigger a transition to the
fully turbulent boundary layers of the ultimate regime of convection for higher
Rayleigh number. Secondly, we predict the ranges of Rayleigh numbers for which
the viscous boundary layer will transition to turbulence and the flow as a
whole will cross over into the ultimate regime. These transition ranges are
obtained by extrapolation from our simulation data. The extrapolation methods
are based on the large-scale properties of the velocity profile. Two of the
three methods predict similar ranges for the transition to ultimate convection
when their uncertainties are taken into account. All three extrapolation
methods indicate that the range of critical Rayleigh numbers $Ra_c$ is shifted
to smaller magnitudes as the Prandtl number becomes smaller.
label: human

text: We present the discovery of a low-mass new double neutron star system, pulsar J1411+2551, located in the constellation of Cassiopeia. Through a combination of high-energy observations with the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, we identified a binary system consisting of two neutron stars with masses of approximately 1.35 and 1.40 solar masses. The binary's orbital period of 8.87 hours and eccentricity of 0.32 suggest a complex evolution history, with the possibility of a common envelope interaction or a merger event. Spectroscopic analysis of the pulsar's emission reveals a unique characteristic of a "millisecond" pulsar, with a spin period of 1.97 milliseconds. Our findings suggest that the pulsar's spin-down rate is significantly higher than expected, indicating an interaction with a companion star. We propose that the companion star is a low-mass white dwarf, which has transferred material to the neutron star, leading to an increase in its magnetic field strength and spin-down rate. The discovery of pulsar J1411+2551 provides new insights into the formation and evolution of double neutron star systems, and highlights the importance of multi-messenger astronomy in understanding the complex astrophysical processes governing these systems.
label: machine

text: Gravitational lensing is a crucial phenomenon in astrophysics, providing insights into black hole properties and spacetime geometry. This study investigates the gravitational lensing effects of charged Ayon-Beato-Garcia (ABG) black holes, particularly emphasizing the influence of non-linear Maxwell fields. The primary objective is to enhance the understanding of lensing features induced by such black holes and the implications of their electric charge. Utilizing a theoretical framework based on general relativity and non-linear electrodynamics, we developed mathematical models to simulate light bending around ABG black holes under various charge configurations and background conditions.  Key findings reveal that the presence of charge significantly alters the bending angle of light rays, introducing distinctive brightness profiles and multiple images in the lensing pattern. Furthermore, non-linear effects of the Maxwell fields lead to more complex trajectories, resulting in additional lensing features not observable in classical scenarios. The implications of these results contribute to the broader understanding of black hole physics and may have observable consequences for future astronomical observations, particularly in probing the nature of dark matter and the fundamental forces governing celestial objects.   In conclusion, this research provides a detailed analysis of gravitational lensing in the context of charged ABG black holes and highlights the significant role of non-linear Maxwell fields, proposing a rich avenue for further exploration within theoretical and observational astrophysics.
label: machine

text: In this study, we explore the complex stellar evolution of red giants by analyzing their photometric and spectroscopic properties in the context of mixed modes. These mixed modes, representing the intersection of acoustic and gravitational waves, provide a unique insight into the interior structure and dynamics of these evolving stars. We employed a combination of photometric analysis from the Kepler spacecraft and spectroscopic data from the Hubble Space Telescope to identify and characterize mixed modes in three red giant stars.  Our findings reveal the evolutionary significance of mixed modes. We discovered that the mixed modes in our target stars exhibit a distinct frequency separation pattern, providing strong evidence for the coexistence of acoustic and gravitational modes. The measured frequency separations were in good agreement with the predictions from stellar evolution models, indicating the robustness of current theoretical frameworks. Furthermore, we found that the mixed modes' amplitudes and damping rates significantly varied between the stars, suggesting that individual star properties such as mass, age, and internal structure play a crucial role in their evolution.  Our analysis confirms the importance of mixed modes as a powerful tool for understanding the intricacies of stellar evolution in red giants. The insights gained from this research will contribute to refining existing stellar evolution models and ultimately advance our knowledge of the various phases of stellar life cycles. Moreover, the study of mixed modes in red giants opens up avenues for the exploration of similar phenomena in other stellar types, broadening our understanding of stellar physics.
label: machine

text:
We examine a broad range of mass flow diagnostics in a large sample of Herbig
Ae/Be stars (HAEBES) using high resolution optical spectra. The H-beta and He I
5876 angstrom lines show the highest incidence of P-Cygni (30%) and inverse
P-Cygni (14%) morphologies, respectively. The Fe II 4924 angstrom line also
shows a large incidence of P-Cygni profiles (11%). We find support for many of
the conclusions reached in a study based on the analysis of the He I 10830
angstrom line in a large sample of HAEBES. Namely, HAEBES exhibit smaller
fractions of both blue-shifted absorption (i.e. mass outflow) and red-shifted
absorption (i.e. mass infall or accretion) than their lower mass cousins, the
classical T Tauri stars (CTTSs). In particular, the optical data supports the
conclusion that HAEBES displaying red-shifted absorption, in general, show
maximum red-shifted absorption velocities that are smaller fractions of their
stellar escape velocities than is found for CTTSs. This suggests that HAEBE
accretion flows are originating deeper in the gravitational potentials of their
stars than in CTTS systems. In addition, we find a lack of inner disk wind
signatures in the blue-shifted absorption objects; only stellar wind signatures
are clearly observed. These findings, along with the lack of detected magnetic
fields around HAEBES, support the idea that large magnetospheres are not
prevalent around HAEBES and that accretion flows are instead mediated by
significantly smaller magnetospheres with relatively smaller truncation radii
(e.g. 1-2 stellar radii). Red-shifted absorption is much more common around
Herbig Ae stars than Be stars, suggesting that Herbig Be stars may accrete via
a boundary layer rather than along magnetic field lines.

The precision of the CP phases $2\beta$ and $2\beta_s$ determined from the
mixing-induced CP asymmetries in $B_d\to J/\psi K_S$ and $B_s\to J/\psi \phi$,
respectively, is limited by the unknown long-distance contribution of a penguin
diagram involving up quarks. The penguin contribution is expected to be
comparable in size to the precision of the LHCb and Belle II experiments and
therefore limits the sensitivity of the measured quantities to new physics. We
analyze the infrared QCD structure of this contribution and find that all soft
and collinear divergences either cancel between different diagrams or factorize
into matrix elements of local four-quark operators up to terms suppressed by
$\Lambda_{QCD}/m_{\psi}$, where $m_{\psi}$ denotes the $J/\psi$ mass. Our
results, which are based on an operator product expansion, allow us to
calculate the penguin-to-tree ratio $P/T$ in terms of the matrix elements of
these operators and to constrain the penguin contribution to the phase $2\beta$
as $|\Delta \phi_d|\leq {0.68}^\circ$. The penguin contribution to $2\beta_s$
is bounded as $|\Delta \phi_s^{0}|\leq {0.97}^\circ$, $|\Delta
\phi_s^{\parallel}|\leq {1.22}^\circ$, and $|\Delta \phi_s^{\perp}|\leq
{0.99}^\circ$ for the case of longitudinal, parallel, and perpendicular $\phi$
and $J/\psi$ polarizations, respectively. We further place bounds on $|\Delta
\phi_d|$ for $B_d\to \psi(2S) K_S$ and the polarization amplitudes in $B_d\to
J/\psi K^*$. In our approach it is further possible to constrain $P/T$ for
decays in which $P/T$ is Cabibbo-unsuppressed and we derive upper limits on the
penguin contribution to the mixing-induced CP asymmetries in $B_d\to J/\psi
\pi^0$, $B_d\to J/\psi \rho^0$, $B_s\to J/\psi K_S$, and $B_s\to J/\psi K^*$.
For all studied decay modes we also constrain the sizes of the direct CP
asymmetries.

text: The universe's early evolution is marked by the presence of active galactic nuclei (AGN) in the centers of galaxies. Protoclusters, the precursors to galaxy clusters, are of particular interest as they provide a unique window into the formation and evolution of these massive structures. The z=2.30 protocluster in HS 1700+64 is one such example, offering insights into the early AGN activity and the role of these objects in shaping the cluster's morphology.  Our research focuses on the excess AGN activity observed in the z=2.30 protocluster in HS 1700+64, with the objective of understanding the mechanisms driving this phenomenon. To achieve this, we employed a multi-wavelength approach, combining archival data from the Hubble Space Telescope, the Spitzer Space Telescope, and the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Our analysis revealed a complex picture of AGN activity, with multiple sources of excess emission detected across the 0.5-10 keV X-ray band.  Key findings indicate that the excess AGN activity is primarily driven by a population of compact radio sources, which are thought to be the precursors to quasars. These sources are observed to be located at the cluster's center, suggesting a close relationship between the AGN and the cluster's dynamical evolution. Our results have implications for our understanding of the early universe, highlighting the importance of AGN activity in shaping the morphology and evolution of protoclusters. Ultimately, our study provides new insights into the complex interplay between AGN and galaxy clusters in the early universe, and highlights the need for further research into the role of these objects in the formation and evolution of massive structures.

text: This study investigates the robustness of complex networks under attacks that are guided by the extent of damage they inflict, aiming to understand how different attack strategies affect network resilience. We employ a combination of theoretical models and simulations to analyze various types of damage-based attack scenarios on both synthetic and real-world networks. The results reveal that nodes with higher centrality, such as hubs and bridges, are disproportionately targeted by damage-guided attacks, leading to significant fragmentation and reduction in network connectivity. Key methodologies include node vulnerability assessment using centrality measures and propagation dynamics simulation to evaluate the impact of targeted attacks. The findings highlight the necessity of incorporating node vulnerability into attack planning and suggest that defensive strategies should focus on protecting critical infrastructure and high-degree nodes to enhance overall network stability.
label: machine

text: We investigated the cost optimisation of an instrument suite at an accelerator-driven spallation source, with a focus on reducing operational expenses without compromising scientific performance. Our analysis revealed that the suite's current configuration, with multiple, dedicated beamlines, resulted in significant energy losses and increased maintenance costs. To address this, we proposed a novel, multi-functional beamline design that integrates multiple scientific instruments into a single, shared beamline. This design enables more efficient energy transfer, reduces beamline losses, and minimises the need for dedicated beamline maintenance.  Our results demonstrate that the proposed design can reduce operational costs by up to 30% compared to the current configuration. Furthermore, we found that the multi-functional design allows for greater flexibility in instrument arrangement and can accommodate a wider range of scientific experiments. We also identified opportunities for energy recovery and reuse, which can further reduce costs. The key to the proposed design lies in the use of advanced beamline components, such as cryogenic lenses and high-precision beam steering systems, which enable efficient energy transfer and precise beam manipulation.  By adopting the proposed multi-functional beamline design, instrument suites at accelerator-driven spallation sources can achieve significant cost savings without compromising scientific performance. Our findings have important implications for the optimisation of instrument suites in various scientific fields, including materials science, chemistry, and physics.
label: machine

text: The embedded intermediate-mass T Tauri star DK Cha represents a unique case for studying young stellar objects due to its peculiar characteristics. This research aims to investigate the nature of DK Cha through a comprehensive observational analysis. Utilizing multi-wavelength data from telescopes, including X-ray, infrared, and optical observations, we aim to probe the physical properties and evolutionary stage of DK Cha. By conducting a detailed spectroscopic analysis, we aim to determine the stellar parameters, such as temperature, luminosity, and mass accretion rate of DK Cha. Additionally, we will investigate the circumstellar environment of DK Cha, including the presence of disks and outflows. Our key findings reveal the complex nature of DK Cha, including indications of disk evolution and accretion processes. The results shed light on the formation mechanisms of intermediate-mass stars and provide insights into the early stages of stellar evolution. In conclusion, our study contributes valuable insights into the understanding of embedded intermediate-mass T Tauri stars, highlighting the importance of DK Cha as a unique laboratory for investigating young stellar objects.

text:
The ISM, powered by SNe, is turbulent and permeated by a magnetic field (with
a mean and a turbulent component). It constitutes a frothy medium that is
mostly out of equilibrium and is ram pressure dominated on most of the
temperature ranges, except for T< 200 K and T> 1E6 K, where magnetic and
thermal pressures dominate, respectively. Such lack of equilibrium is also
imposed by the feedback of the radiative processes into the ISM flow. Many
models of the ISM or isolated phenomena, such as bubbles, superbubbles, clouds
evolution, etc., take for granted that the flow is in the so-called collisional
ionization equilibrium (CIE). However, recombination time scales of most of the
ions below 1E6 K are longer than the cooling time scale. This implies that the
recombination lags behind and the plasma is overionized while it cools. As a
consequence cooling deviates from CIE. This has severe implications on the
evolution of the ISM flow and its ionization structure. Here, besides reviewing
several models of the ISM, including bubbles and superbubbles, the validity of
the CIE approximation is discussed, and a presentation of recent developments
in modeling the ISM by taking into account the time-dependent ionization
structure of the flow in a full-blown numerical 3D high resolution simulation
is presented.

We have performed the most comprehensive resonance-model fit of
$\pi^-\pi^-\pi^+$ states using the results of our previously published
partial-wave analysis (PWA) of a large data set of diffractive-dissociation
events from the reaction $\pi^- + p \to \pi^-\pi^-\pi^+ + p_\text{recoil}$ with
a 190 GeV/$c$ pion beam. The PWA results, which were obtained in 100 bins of
three-pion mass, $0.5 < m_{3\pi} < 2.5$ GeV/$c^2$, and simultaneously in 11
bins of the reduced four-momentum transfer squared, $0.1 < t' < 1.0$
$($GeV$/c)^2$, are subjected to a resonance-model fit using Breit-Wigner
amplitudes to simultaneously describe a subset of 14 selected waves using 11
isovector light-meson states with $J^{PC} = 0^{-+}$, $1^{++}$, $2^{++}$,
$2^{-+}$, $4^{++}$, and spin-exotic $1^{-+}$ quantum numbers. The model
contains the well-known resonances $\pi(1800)$, $a_1(1260)$, $a_2(1320)$,
$\pi_2(1670)$, $\pi_2(1880)$, and $a_4(2040)$. In addition, it includes the
disputed $\pi_1(1600)$, the excited states $a_1(1640)$, $a_2(1700)$, and
$\pi_2(2005)$, as well as the resonancelike $a_1(1420)$. We measure the
resonance parameters mass and width of these objects by combining the
information from the PWA results obtained in the 11 $t'$ bins. We extract the
relative branching fractions of the $\rho(770) \pi$ and $f_2(1270) \pi$ decays
of $a_2(1320)$ and $a_4(2040)$, where the former one is measured for the first
time. In a novel approach, we extract the $t'$ dependence of the intensity of
the resonances and of their phases. The $t'$ dependence of the intensities of
most resonances differs distinctly from the $t'$ dependence of the nonresonant
components. For the first time, we determine the $t'$ dependence of the phases
of the production amplitudes and confirm that the production mechanism of the
Pomeron exchange is common to all resonances.

text: In the context of edge computing, dense small cell networks (DSCNs) present unique opportunities and challenges, primarily due to their ability to enhance data processing efficiency by bringing computational resources closer to end-users. However, the limited resources at each cell site necessitate innovative solutions to optimize service delivery. This research investigates collaborative service caching strategies within DSCNs to bolster edge computing efficiency. The objective is to develop caching mechanisms that minimize latency and improve bandwidth utilization by leveraging inter-cell collaboration. The methodology involves the creation of a decentralized caching framework that allows small cells to share cached services intelligently based on predicted demand patterns and network conditions. Simulation-based experiments were conducted using a model of a dense urban DSCN environment with varying service demand scenarios. Key findings indicate that collaborative caching significantly reduces service latency and network congestion compared to traditional independent caching approaches. Specifically, the proposed model demonstrates a reduction in average service response time by up to 30% and decreases bandwidth consumption by a substantial margin. Furthermore, our framework effectively balances the load across the network, enhancing overall system resilience and scalability. In conclusion, the collaborative service caching model presents a promising avenue for DSCN optimization, advancing edge computing capabilities by improving service delivery metrics. Future work will focus on refining the predictive analytics aspect of the model to better anticipate dynamic user demands and further enhance collaboration efficiency among small cells.
