Maps are an important source of information in archaeology and other
sciences. Users want to search for historical maps to determine recorded
history of the political geography of regions at different eras, to find out
where exactly archaeological artifacts were discovered, etc. Currently, they
have to use a generic search engine and add the term map along with other
keywords to search for maps. This crude method will generate a significant
number of false positives that the user will need to cull through to get the
desired results. To reduce their manual effort, we propose an automatic map
identification, indexing, and retrieval system that enables users to search and
retrieve maps appearing in a large corpus of digital documents using simple
keyword queries. We identify features that can help in distinguishing maps from
other figures in digital documents and show how a Support-Vector-Machine-based
classifier can be used to identify maps. We propose map-level-metadata e.g.,
captions, references to the maps in text, etc. and document-level metadata,
e.g., title, abstract, citations, how recent the publication is, etc. and show
how they can be automatically extracted and indexed. Our novel ranking
algorithm weights different metadata fields differently and also uses the
document-level metadata to help rank retrieved maps. Empirical evaluations show
which features should be selected and which metadata fields should be weighted
more. We also demonstrate improved retrieval results in comparison to
adaptations of existing methods for map retrieval. Our map search engine has
been deployed in an online map-search system that is part of the Blind-Review
digital library system.

text: We present a novel bottom-up approach for pancreas segmentation, leveraging a cascaded superpixel framework and deep image patch labeling. Our method initially employs a superpixel segmentation algorithm to divide the input medical image into non-overlapping regions, which are then further refined through a cascaded process of image patch labeling. The cascaded superpixels are generated by iteratively applying a superpixel segmentation algorithm to the previously labeled regions, resulting in a hierarchical representation of the pancreas. Each superpixel is then labeled with a corresponding region of interest, such as the pancreas, spleen, or background, using a deep convolutional neural network. The deep learning model is trained on a large dataset of annotated medical images, allowing it to learn spatial relationships and contextual dependencies between the superpixels and the corresponding labels. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art segmentation performance on the ISBI Challenge 2019 dataset, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness compared to existing methods. By combining the strengths of bottom-up superpixel segmentation and deep image patch labeling, our method provides a robust and efficient framework for pancreas segmentation, enabling accurate delineation of the pancreas and its surrounding structures in medical images.

Red-giant stars are an incredible source of information for testing models of
stellar evolution, as asteroseismology has opened up a window into their
interiors. Such insights are a direct result of the unprecedented data from
space missions Kepler and CoRoT as well as recent theoretical advances.
Eclipsing binaries are also fundamental astrophysical objects, and when coupled
with asteroseismology, binaries would provide two independent methods to obtain
masses and radii and exciting opportunities to develop highly constrained
stellar models. The possibility of discovering pulsating red giants in
eclipsing binary systems is therefore an important goal that could potentially
offer very robust characterization of these systems. Hitherto, only 1 case has
been discovered with Kepler. We cross-correlated the detected red-giant and
eclipsing-binary catalogs from Kepler data to find candidate systems.
Light-curve modeling and mean asteroseismic properties are combined to yield
measurements of periods, masses, radii, temperatures, eclipse timing
variations, core rotation rates, and red-giant evolutionary state. After
elimination of false positives, out of the 70 systems common to the red-giant
and eclipsing-binary catalogs we find 13 new strong candidates that are
pulsating red giants in eclipsing binaries, and 10 more that are pulsating red
giants in hierarchical triple systems. The systems span a range of orbital
eccentricities, periods, and spectral types for the red-giant companion. One
case even suggests a system composed of two red-giants. The discovery of
pulsating red giants in multiple systems provides exciting test beds for
precise astrophysical modeling, and follow-up spectroscopic observations of the
candidate systems are encouraged.

Digital learning environments generate a precise record of the actions
learners take as they interact with learning materials and complete exercises
towards comprehension. With this high quantity of sequential data comes the
potential to apply time series models to learn about underlying behavioral
patterns and trends that characterize successful learning based on the granular
record of student actions. There exist several methods for looking at
longitudinal, sequential data like those recorded from learning environments.
In the field of language modelling, traditional n-gram techniques and modern
recurrent neural network (RNN) approaches have been applied to algorithmically
find structure in language and predict the next word given the previous words
in the sentence or paragraph as input. In this paper, we draw an analogy to
this work by treating student sequences of resource views and interactions in a
MOOC as the inputs and predicting students' next interaction as outputs. In
this study, we train only on students who received a certificate of completion.
In doing so, the model could potentially be used for recommendation of
sequences eventually leading to success, as opposed to perpetuating
unproductive behavior. Given that the MOOC used in our study had over 3,500
unique resources, predicting the exact resource that a student will interact
with next might appear to be a difficult classification problem. We find that
simply following the syllabus (built-in structure of the course) gives on
average 23% accuracy in making this prediction, followed by the n-gram method
with 70.4%, and RNN based methods with 72.2%. This research lays the ground
work for recommendation in a MOOC and other digital learning environments where
high volumes of sequential data exist.

text: The rapid evolution of technology necessitates systems that can seamlessly adapt to external changes to maintain performance stability and user satisfaction. This paper investigates extrinsically adaptable systems, focusing on their ability to respond dynamically to varying environmental conditions and user demands. The objective is to explore the mechanisms that enable such systems to adjust their functionalities and optimize their operations based on external inputs. Methodologically, the study employs a mixed-methods approach. A series of controlled experiments were conducted to assess the adaptability of different system architectures, alongside a qualitative analysis of user feedback to evaluate systems’ real-world applicability. Key findings reveal that systems embedded with modular frameworks and machine learning capabilities exhibit superior adaptability, managing to recalibrate their operations efficiently when faced with new data or changing conditions. Particularly, systems that utilize feedback loops and predictive analytics outperform traditional static systems by up to 30% in terms of responsiveness and user satisfaction. Furthermore, the integration of user-centric adaptive interfaces enhances the overall experience, ensuring systems align closely with user expectations and requirements. The study concludes that adopting an extrinsically adaptable approach in system design is essential for future technological advancements, offering significant improvements in flexibility, efficiency, and user engagement. These findings suggest that further research into adaptive algorithms and user interface design will be crucial in facilitating the development of next-generation adaptable systems.

Early and correct diagnosis is a very important aspect of cancer treatment.
Detection of tumour in Computed Tomography scan is a tedious and tricky task
which requires expert knowledge and a lot of human working hours. As small
human error is present in any work he does, it is possible that a CT scan could
be misdiagnosed causing the patient to become terminal. This paper introduces a
novel fully automated framework which helps to detect and segment tumour, if
present in a lung CT scan series. It also provides useful analysis of the
detected tumour such as its approximate volume, centre location and more. The
framework provides a single click solution which analyses all CT images of a
single patient series in one go. It helps to reduce the work of manually going
through each CT slice and provides quicker and more accurate tumour diagnosis.
It makes use of customized image processing and image segmentation methods, to
detect and segment the prospective tumour region from the CT scan. It then uses
a trained ensemble classifier to correctly classify the segmented region as
being tumour or not. Tumour analysis further computed can then be used to
determine malignity of the tumour. With an accuracy of 98.14%, the implemented
framework can be used in various practical scenarios, capable of eliminating
need of any expert pathologist intervention.

A Physical layer Network Coding (PNC) scheme is proposed for the $K$-user
wireless Multiple Access Relay Channel (MARC), in which $K$ source nodes
transmit their messages to the destination node $D$ with the help of a relay
node $R.$ The proposed PNC scheme involves two transmission phases: (i) Phase 1
during which the source nodes transmit, the relay node and the destination node
receive and (ii) Phase 2 during which the source nodes and the relay node
transmit, and the destination node receives. At the end of Phase 1, the relay
node decodes the messages of the source nodes and during Phase 2 transmits a
many-to-one function of the decoded messages. Wireless networks in which the
relay node decodes, suffer from loss of diversity order if the decoder at the
destination is not chosen properly. A novel decoder is proposed for the PNC
scheme, which offers the maximum possible diversity order of $2,$ for a proper
choice of certain parameters and the network coding map. Specifically, the
network coding map used at the relay is chosen to be a $K$-dimensional Latin
Hypercube, in order to ensure the maximum diversity order of $2.$ Also, it is
shown that the proposed decoder can be implemented by a fast decoding
algorithm. Simulation results presented for the 3-user MARC show that the
proposed scheme offers a large gain over the existing scheme for the $K$-user
MARC.

We present a radiative transfer code to model the nebular phase spectra of
supernovae (SNe) in non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE). We apply it to
a systematic study of Type Ia SNe using parameterized 1D models and show how
nebular spectral features depend on key physical parameters, such as the time
since explosion, total ejecta mass, kinetic energy, radial density profile, and
the masses of 56Ni, intermediate mass elements (IMEs), and stable iron-group
elements (IGEs). We also quantify the impact of uncertainties in atomic data
inputs. Among the results of the study are: (1) The main features of SNe Ia
nebular spectra are relatively insensitive to most physical parameters.
Degeneracy among parameters precludes a unique determination of the ejecta
properties from spectral fitting. In particular, features can be equally well
fit with generic Chandrasekhar mass (M_ch), sub-M_Ch, and super-M_Ch models;
(2) A sizable (~0.1 Msun) central region of stable IGEs, often claimed as
evidence for M_Ch models, is not essential to fit the optical spectra and may
produce an unusual flat-top [CoIII] profile; (3) The strength of [SIII]
emission near 9500A can provide a useful diagnostic of explosion
nucleosynthesis; (4) Substantial amounts (~0.1 Msun) of unburned C/O mixed
throughout the ejecta produce [OIII] emission not seen in observations; (5)
Shifts in the wavelength of line peaks, sometimes used to infer ejecta
geometry, can also arise from line blending effects; (6) The steepness of the
ejecta density profile affects the line shapes, with flatter slopes providing
better fits to the observations of SN 2011fe, offering a constraint on
explosion models; (7) Uncertainties in atomic data affect spectral line ratios
by ~30%, a level similar to the effect of varying physical parameters.

text: We investigated the effectiveness of two advanced techniques, Lucky Imaging and Speckle Stabilization, for improving the resolution and signal-to-noise ratio of astronomical imaging. Our work aimed to address the limitations of traditional imaging methods, which are often plagued by atmospheric distortion and noise, thereby hindering the detection of faint celestial objects.   To overcome these challenges, we applied Lucky Imaging, a technique that utilizes a series of short exposures and adaptive optics to suppress the effects of atmospheric turbulence. In contrast, Speckle Stabilization exploits the natural correlation between successive frames to reduce the impact of noise and atmospheric distortion.   Our results demonstrate that both techniques are capable of producing high-quality images with improved resolution and signal-to-noise ratio. However, Lucky Imaging outperforms Speckle Stabilization in terms of resolution, particularly at shorter wavelengths. On the other hand, Speckle Stabilization exhibits better performance in reducing noise and improving the fidelity of faint objects.   The key findings of our study highlight the importance of selecting the most suitable technique for specific astronomical applications. We also identified the need for further optimization of the Lucky Imaging algorithm to further enhance its performance. By comparing the strengths and weaknesses of these two techniques, we contribute to the ongoing efforts to advance the field of astronomical imaging and enable the detection of faint celestial objects.

text: This research paper investigates second-order cosmological perturbations generated by scalar-scalar coupling in synchronous gauge. The background of the study lies in understanding the evolution of cosmological perturbations beyond linear order, providing valuable insights into the large-scale structure of the universe. The objective is to analyze the effects of scalar-scalar coupling on the emergence and evolution of these second-order perturbations.   The methodology employed in this research involves solving the set of second-order perturbation equations in synchronous gauge, considering the influence of scalar-scalar coupling terms. Numerical simulations are conducted to calculate the evolution of these perturbations over cosmological timescales, considering various cosmological parameters and initial conditions.   Key findings of this study reveal that scalar-scalar coupling significantly impacts the growth and evolution of second-order cosmological perturbations, leading to observable consequences in the cosmic microwave background radiation and large-scale structure formation. These results highlight the importance of considering second-order effects in cosmological perturbation theory to attain a more comprehensive understanding of the universe's dynamics.  In conclusion, this research provides new insights into the role of scalar-scalar coupling in generating second-order cosmological perturbations, shedding light on the intricate interplay between different components in the universe and enhancing our comprehension of its overall structure and evolution.

Aiming to distinguish two types of progenitors of core collapse supernovae,
i.e., one with a core composed mainly of oxygen and neon (abbreviated as ONe
core) and the other with an iron core (or Fe core), we calculated the
luminosities and spectra of neutrinos emitted from these cores prior to
gravitational collapse, taking neutrino oscillation into account. We found that
the total energies emitted as $\bar{\nu}_e$ from the ONe core are $\lesssim
10^{46}\ {\rm erg}$, which is much smaller than $\sim 10^{47}\ {\rm erg}$ for
Fe cores. The average energy, on the other hand, is twice as large for the ONe
core as those for the Fe cores. The neutrinos produced by the plasmon decays in
the ONe core are more numerous than those from the electron-positron
annihilation in both cores but they have much lower average energies $\lesssim
1\ {\rm MeV}$. Although it is difficult to detect the pre-supernova neutrinos
from the ONe core even if it is located within 200$\ $pc from the earth, we
expect $ \sim 9 - 43$ and $\sim 7 - 61$ events for Fe cores at KamLAND and
Super-Kamiokande, respectively, depending on the progenitor mass and
neutrino-mass hierarchy. These numbers might be increased by an order of
magnitude if we envisage next-generation detectors such as JUNO. We will hence
be able to distinguish the two types of progenitors by the detection or
non-detection of the pre-supernova neutrinos if they are close enough
($\lesssim1\ {\rm kpc}$).

text: We investigated the observational signatures of coronal loop heating and cooling driven by footpoint shuffling, a process by which the positions of the footpoints of coronal loops are periodically rearranged. Through a comprehensive analysis of high-cadence observations of the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) and the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), we identified distinct signatures of footpoint shuffling in the coronal loop dynamics. We found that footpoint shuffling leads to a temporary increase in loop brightness and temperature, followed by a rapid cooling phase, resulting in a characteristic 'loop brightening and cooling' (LBC) phenomenon. This LBC pattern is observed in the visible and ultraviolet spectral ranges, with the visible light observations revealing a characteristic 'loop brightening' phase, while the ultraviolet observations reveal a 'cooling' phase. Our analysis suggests that the LBC phenomenon is a direct consequence of the footpoint shuffling process, which drives the coronal loops into a state of increased instability and reconnection. By analyzing the spatial and temporal characteristics of the LBC phenomenon, we shed new light on the underlying mechanisms driving coronal loop heating and cooling, and provide insights into the complex processes governing coronal dynamics.

Large Galactic stellar surveys and new generations of stellar atmosphere
models and spectral line formation computations need to be subjected to careful
calibration and validation and to benchmark tests. We focus on cool stars and
aim at establishing a sample of 34 Gaia FGK Benchmark Stars with a range of
different metallicities. The goal was to determine the effective temperature
and the surface gravity independently from spectroscopy and atmospheric models
as far as possible. Fundamental determinations of Teff and logg were obtained
in a systematic way from a compilation of angular diameter measurements and
bolometric fluxes, and from a homogeneous mass determination based on stellar
evolution models. The derived parameters were compared to recent spectroscopic
and photometric determinations and to gravity estimates based on seismic data.
Most of the adopted diameter measurements have formal uncertainties around 1%,
which translate into uncertainties in effective temperature of 0.5%. The
measurements of bolometric flux seem to be accurate to 5% or better, which
contributes about 1% or less to the uncertainties in effective temperature. The
comparisons of parameter determinations with the literature show in general
good agreements with a few exceptions, most notably for the coolest stars and
for metal-poor stars. The sample consists of 29 FGK-type stars and 5 M giants.
Among the FGK stars, 21 have reliable parameters suitable for testing,
validation, or calibration purposes. For four stars, future adjustments of the
fundamental Teff are required, and for five stars the logg determination needs
to be improved. Future extensions of the sample of Gaia FGK Benchmark Stars are
required to fill gaps in parameter space, and we include a list of suggested
candidates.

text: This study explores the concept of gravitation as a pressure force within a scalar ether theoretical framework, aiming to redefine our understanding of gravitational interactions. Through a series of rigorous mathematical derivations and simulations, we have demonstrated that gravitation can be modeled as a manifestation of pressure exerted by a hypothetical medium known as the scalar ether. Our approach posits that mass is not inherently responsible for creating gravitational fields but rather that these fields emerge from the interaction between the scalar ether and matter. Key methodologies include the application of Newton's laws of motion and gravitational equations within this new theoretical context, which predict consistent behaviors when compared to existing empirical data. The research also identifies potential anomalies in current cosmological models that could be reconciled with the proposed model, suggesting novel avenues for further investigation into the nature of gravity. This study thus advances the scalar ether theory, offering a fresh perspective on gravitation that challenges conventional interpretations and opens up possibilities for unifying gravity with other fundamental forces.

text: Quantum measurements have been a pivotal aspect of quantum mechanics, enabling researchers to study the behavior of particles at the atomic and subatomic level. However, the existing apparatuses used for quantum measurements are often complex, cumbersome, and limited in their precision. The need for more accurate and efficient quantum measurement tools has led to the development of single apparatus quantum measurements. These advancements have opened up new avenues for quantum research, allowing scientists to explore the intricacies of quantum systems in unprecedented detail.  This paper provides an in-depth analysis of single apparatus quantum measurements, focusing on the theoretical frameworks, experimental methods, and practical applications of these measurements. The objective of this study is to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of single apparatus quantum measurements, highlighting their potential and limitations.  The methodology employed in this study involves a review of existing literature on quantum measurements, experimental techniques, and theoretical models. A comprehensive analysis of the key findings from various studies on single apparatus quantum measurements is also presented. The results of this analysis reveal that single apparatus quantum measurements have the potential to revolutionize our understanding of quantum systems, enabling more precise and efficient measurements of quantum properties.  The conclusions drawn from this study highlight the significance of single apparatus quantum measurements in advancing our knowledge of quantum mechanics. The findings of this research have important implications for future research in quantum computing, quantum information processing, and quantum metrology. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of single apparatus quantum measurements to transform our understanding of quantum systems, enabling more accurate and efficient measurements of quantum properties.

text: Brown dwarfs, though classed as failed stars, exhibit unique astrophysical phenomena due to their low mass and temperature. One such phenomenon is the presence of an accretion disk, a rotating, flattened structure surrounding the brown dwarf where gas and dust particles collide and coalesce. The study of metal depletion and the presence of molecular hydrogen (H2) in the accretion disk of the brown dwarf 2M1207 has gained significant interest due to its potential implications for planet formation. This paper presents an analysis of mid-infrared spectra data obtained from the Spitzer Space Telescope, focusing on the identification and quantification of various metal and hydrogen species in the accretion disk of 2M1207. The results suggest significant metal depletion in the inner regions of the disk, as evidenced by the lack of detectable silicon monoxide (SiO) and titanium oxide (TiO) gas features. However, a strong signature of warm H2 was detected at higher radial distances, suggesting the presence of a warm H2 layer in the outer regions of the disk. This finding sheds light on the complex gas dynamics within the accretion disk of 2M1207 and provides crucial insights into the ongoing process of planet formation in these objects. Future work will focus on modeling the temperature and density profiles of the accretion disk to better understand the spatial distribution of H2 and the mechanisms driving metal depletion.

text: This research investigates predictive density estimation within the framework of location families while addressing integrated $L_2$ and $L_1$ losses. Predictive density estimation serves as a crucial component in statistical modeling, enabling the capture of uncertainty in predictions. The primary objective of this study is to develop a robust methodology that seamlessly incorporates both $L_2$ and $L_1$ loss functions to enhance the accuracy and reliability of predictive models. We utilized a comprehensive theoretical approach, combining asymptotic analysis and computational techniques, to derive an optimal predictive density estimator that minimizes the integrated loss. The proposed estimator was evaluated through extensive simulations across various distributional scenarios, including Gaussian and heavy-tailed cases. Key findings indicate that the proposed method outperformed traditional single-loss estimators in terms of predictive accuracy, particularly in scenarios involving skewed or multimodal data distributions. Furthermore, the integration of $L_1$ loss proved to be beneficial in scenarios with significant outliers or heavy-tailed distributions, improving robustness without compromising overall performance. In conclusion, our results underscore the efficacy of utilizing integrated $L_2$ and $L_1$ losses in predictive density estimation for location families, offering a versatile framework suitable for a wide range of applications in statistical inference and machine learning. This advancement contributes significantly to the field, facilitating improved predictive performance in real-world scenarios characterized by complex data structures.

text: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are among the most luminous objects in the universe, characterized by the presence of broad emission lines, which are thought to originate from the accretion disk surrounding the supermassive black hole at the center of these galaxies. However, the exact origin of these broad emission lines remains a topic of debate, with various mechanisms proposed to explain their formation. This study aims to investigate the possibility that tidally disrupted dusty clumps are the origin of broad emission lines in AGN.  The objective of this research is to explore the role of tidally disrupted dusty clumps in the formation of broad emission lines in AGN. To achieve this, we employ a combination of numerical simulations and observational data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Hubble Space Telescope. Our simulations model the interaction between the accretion disk and tidally disrupted dusty clumps, and we find that these clumps can produce broad emission lines through the collision and fragmentation of gas and dust. We also observe that the presence of broad emission lines is correlated with the presence of tidally disrupted dusty clumps in our sample of AGN.  Our key findings suggest that tidally disrupted dusty clumps are a significant contributor to the formation of broad emission lines in AGN. We also find that the properties of the broad emission lines, such as their width and luminosity, are consistent with the predictions of our simulations. These results provide strong evidence for the role of tidally disrupted dusty clumps in the formation of broad emission lines in AGN, and have important implications for our understanding of the physics of AGN and the formation of heavy elements in the universe.

text: The abstract for the research paper on "A search for water maser emission from brown dwarfs and low-luminosity young stellar objects" begins with an overview of the context and importance of detecting water masers in these celestial bodies. In this work we study the dynamics of the Local Group (LG) within the context
of cosmological models beyond General Relativity (GR). Using observable
kinematic quantities to identify candidate pairs we build up samples of
simulated LG-like objects drawing from $f(R)$, symmetron, DGP and quintessence
N-body simulations together with their $\Lambda$CDM counterparts featuring the
same initial random phase realisations. The variables and intervals used to
define LG-like objects are referred to as Local Group model; different models
are used throughout this work and adapted to study their dynamical and
kinematic properties. The aim is to determine how well the observed LG-dynamics
can be reproduced within cosmological theories beyond GR, We compute kinematic
properties of samples drawn from alternative theories and $\Lambda$CDM and
compare them to actual observations of the LG mass, velocity and position. As a
consequence of the additional pull, pairwise tangential and radial velocities
are enhanced in modified gravity and coupled dark energy with respect to
$\Lambda$CDM, inducing significant changes to the total angular momentum and
energy of the LG. For example, in models such as $f(R)$ and the symmetron this
increase can be as large as $60\%$, peaking well outside of the $95\%$
confidence region allowed by the data. This shows how simple considerations
about the LG dynamics can lead to clear small-scale observational signatures
for alternative scenarios, without the need of expensive high-resolution
simulations.

text:
We report a set of measurements of particle production in inelastic pbar{p}
collisions collected with a minimum-bias trigger at the Tevatron Collider with
the CDF II experiment. The inclusive charged particle transverse momentum
differential cross section is measured, with improved precision, over a range
about ten times wider than in previous measurements. The former modeling of the
spectrum appears to be incompatible with the high particle momenta observed.
The dependence of the charged particle transverse momentum on the event
particle multiplicity is analyzed to study the various components of hadron
interactions. This is one of the observable variables most poorly reproduced by
the available Monte Carlo generators. A first measurement of the event
transverse energy sum differential cross section is also reported. A comparison
with a Pythia prediction at the hadron level is performed. The inclusive
charged particle differential production cross section is fairly well
reproduced only in the transverse momentum range available from previous
measurements. At higher momentum the agreement is poor. The transverse energy
sum is poorly reproduced over the whole spectrum. The dependence of the charged
particle transverse momentum on the particle multiplicity needs the
introduction of more sophisticated particle production mechanisms, such as
multiple parton interactions, in order to be better explained.

Let $G$ be a simple graph or hypergraph, and let $A(G),L(G),Q(G)$ be the
adjacency, Laplacian and signless Laplacian tensors of $G$ respectively. The
largest $H$-eigenvalues (resp., the spectral radii) of $L(G),Q(G)$ are denoted
respectively by $\lambda_{\max}^L(G), \lambda_{\max}^Q(G)$ (resp., $\rho^L(G),
\rho^Q(G)$). For a connected non-bipartite simple graph $G$,
$\lambda_{\max}^L(G)=\rho^L(G) < \rho^Q(G)$. But this does not hold for
non-odd-bipartite hypergraphs. We will investigate this problem by considering
a class of generalized power hypergraphs $G^{k,\frac{k}{2}}$, which are
constructed from simple connected graphs $G$ by blowing up each vertex of $G$
into a $\frac{k}{2}$-set and preserving the adjacency of vertices.
  Suppose that $G$ is non-bipartite, or equivalently $G^{k,\frac{k}{2}}$ is
non-odd-bipartite. We get the following spectral properties: (1)
$\rho^L(G^{k,{k \over 2}}) =\rho^Q(G^{k,{k \over 2}})$ if and only if $k$ is a
multiple of $4$; in this case
$\lambda_{\max}^L(G^{k,\frac{k}{2}})<\rho^L(G^{k,{k \over 2}})$. (2) If
$k\equiv 2 (\!\!\!\mod 4)$, then for sufficiently large $k$,
$\lambda_{\max}^L(G^{k,\frac{k}{2}})<\rho^L(G^{k,{k \over 2}})$. Motivated by
the study of hypergraphs $G^{k,\frac{k}{2}}$, for a connected non-odd-bipartite
hypergraph $G$, we give a characterization of $L(G)$ and $Q(G)$ having the same
spectra or the spectrum of $A(G)$ being symmetric with respect to the origin,
that is, $L(G)$ and $Q(G)$, or $A(G)$ and $-A(G)$ are similar via a complex
(necessarily non-real) diagonal matrix with modular-$1$ diagonal entries. So we
give an answer to a question raised by Shao et al., that is, for a
non-odd-bipartite hypergraph $G$, that $L(G)$ and $Q(G)$ have the same spectra
can not imply they have the same $H$-spectra.

text: The investigation of operator spreading in random unitary circuits is a rapidly evolving field that examines the dynamic properties of quantum systems. This study aims to deepen understanding of how local operators evolve into non-local ones, a fundamental aspect of quantum information scrambling and chaos. We employ random unitary circuits as our model due to their ability to encapsulate key features of quantum chaotic systems while allowing for analytical tractability. Utilizing a combination of analytic techniques and numerical simulations, we explore the spread of initially localized operators across a quantum system. Key findings illustrate that in the context of a random unitary circuit, operator spreading exhibits ballistic growth characterized by a well-defined light cone structure, reflecting the fastest speed at which information can be transmitted. Moreover, our results indicate that the nature of these circuits enables a detailed characterization of operator scrambling through the use of out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs), providing insight into the temporal and spatial scales at which scrambling occurs. Conclusively, our research contributes to the broader comprehension of the dynamics Governing information propagation in chaotic quantum systems and underscores the significance of random unitary models in elucidating the mechanisms of quantum chaos. This work lays a foundation for future explorations into more complex systems, potentially influencing quantum computation and the development of algorithms that leverage the chaotic properties of quantum systems for enhanced information processing capabilities.

We present first results from an unbiased 50 deg^2 submillimeter Galactic
survey at 250, 350, and 500 micron from the 2006 flight of the Balloon-borne
Large Aperture Submillimeter Telescope (BLAST). The map has resolution ranging
from 36 arcsec to 60 arcsec in the three submillimeter bands spanning the
thermal emission peak of cold starless cores. We determine the temperature,
luminosity, and mass of more than one thousand compact sources in a range of
evolutionary stages and an unbiased statistical characterization of the
population. From comparison with C^(18)O data, we find the dust opacity per gas
mass, kappa r = 0.16 cm^2 g^(-1) at 250 micron, for cold clumps. We find that
2% of the mass of the molecular gas over this diverse region is in cores colder
than 14 K, and that the mass function for these cold cores is consistent with a
power law with index alpha = -3.22 +/- 0.14 over the mass range 14 M_sun < M <
80 M_sun. Additionally, we infer a mass-dependent cold core lifetime of t_c(M)
= 4E6 (M/20 M_sun)^(-0.9) years - longer than what has been found in previous
surveys of either low or high mass cores, and significantly longer than free
fall or likely turbulent decay times. This implies some form of non-thermal
support for cold cores during this early stage of star formation.

text: This study investigates the role of angular momentum in the formation and evolution of isolated dwarf galaxies, a long-standing open question in galaxy evolution. The formation of isolated dwarf galaxies is a complex process, influenced by various factors including gas accretion, stellar feedback, and gravitational interactions with the intergalactic medium. While angular momentum is a crucial parameter in the formation of spiral galaxies, its impact on isolated dwarf galaxies remains unclear.   The objective of this research is to simulate the formation and evolution of isolated dwarf galaxies using a combination of numerical and semi-analytical methods, incorporating angular momentum as a second parameter. The simulations are performed using a modified version of the SPH code, GADGET-2, with a focus on the early stages of galaxy formation. The results show that angular momentum plays a significant role in shaping the morphology and kinematics of isolated dwarf galaxies, particularly in the early stages of their formation.   The key findings of this study reveal that the angular momentum of isolated dwarf galaxies can influence their star formation rates, gas content, and overall morphology. The simulations also suggest that the interplay between angular momentum, gas accretion, and stellar feedback is critical in determining the final properties of isolated dwarf galaxies.   In conclusion, this research highlights the importance of angular momentum in the formation and evolution of isolated dwarf galaxies, and demonstrates the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complex interplay between angular momentum, gas accretion, and stellar feedback in the early stages of galaxy formation.
label: machine

text: The increasing miniaturization of electronic and photonic devices has highlighted the critical necessity to understand size effects in thermal conduction by phonons. The objective of this study is to investigate how phonon transport is influenced by dimensional constraints, and to quantify the associated impact on thermal conductivity in nanoscale materials. Employing a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and the Boltzmann transport equation, we explore phonon behavior as the characteristic dimensions of materials are reduced to the nanoscale. Our analysis considers different boundary conditions and material types, focusing on silicon thin films and nanowires as representative case studies. Key findings reveal a substantial reduction in thermal conductivity as the dimensions approach the phonon mean free path, linking this attenuation to increased phonon-boundary scattering. Notably, this study identifies the crossover point where size effects drastically alter thermal transport, marking a deviation from bulk behavior. Moreover, we provide a comparative analysis of the phonon scattering mechanisms, illustrating that boundary scattering predominates over intrinsic lattice scattering in sub-100 nm structures. The findings offer deeper insights into heat management for nanoscale device engineering, underscoring the importance of integrating size-dependent thermal properties into the design phase. By enhancing the understanding of phonon confinement effects, this research contributes to the optimization of thermal management strategies in the development of next-generation nanotechnologies. In conclusion, acknowledging the size effects on phonon transport can significantly influence the thermal design of cutting-edge miniaturized devices, facilitating improved performance and reliability.
label: machine

text: We conducted a comprehensive review of observations aimed at elucidating the magnetic structure of the Milky Way galaxy. Our analysis encompassed a broad range of observational data, including radio and gamma-ray observations, stellar and interstellar medium (ISM) surveys, and space-based and ground-based telescopic surveys.   We found that the Milky Way's magnetic field is a complex, multi-scale phenomenon, exhibiting a hierarchical structure that extends from the galactic center to the outer reaches of the disk. The field's strength and orientation vary significantly across different regions, with the strongest fields detected in the galactic center and outer halo.   Our review revealed that the Milky Way's magnetic field is influenced by various astrophysical processes, including the motion of stars, gas, and cosmic rays, as well as the presence of magnetic reconnection events. The field's interaction with the ISM and its role in regulating the galaxy's star formation and evolution are also essential topics of investigation.   We also identified several key challenges in understanding the Milky Way's magnetic structure, including the difficulty in measuring the field's strength and orientation with high precision, as well as the need for further observational and theoretical work to account for the complex interplay between magnetic fields and other astrophysical processes.   Our review highlights the importance of continued observational efforts to map the Milky Way's magnetic structure in unprecedented detail, as well as the need for theoretical models that can accurately simulate the complex interactions between magnetic fields and the galaxy's various components.

text:
A function $f: \mathbb{F}_2^n \rightarrow \{0,1\}$ is triangle-free if there
are no $x_1,x_2,x_3 \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ satisfying $x_1+x_2+x_3=0$ and
$f(x_1)=f(x_2)=f(x_3)=1$. In testing triangle-freeness, the goal is to
distinguish with high probability triangle-free functions from those that are
$\varepsilon$-far from being triangle-free. It was shown by Green that the
query complexity of the canonical tester for the problem is upper bounded by a
function that depends only on $\varepsilon$ (GAFA, 2005), however the best
known upper bound is a tower type function of $1/\varepsilon$. The best known
lower bound on the query complexity of the canonical tester is
$1/\varepsilon^{13.239}$ (Fu and Kleinberg, RANDOM, 2014).
  In this work we introduce a new approach to proving lower bounds on the query
complexity of triangle-freeness. We relate the problem to combinatorial
questions on collections of vectors in $\mathbb{Z}_D^n$ and to sunflower
conjectures studied by Alon, Shpilka, and Umans (Comput. Complex., 2013). The
relations yield that a refutation of the Weak Sunflower Conjecture over
$\mathbb{Z}_4$ implies a super-polynomial lower bound on the query complexity
of the canonical tester for triangle-freeness. Our results are extended to
testing $k$-cycle-freeness of functions with domain $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ for every
$k \geq 3$ and a prime $p$. In addition, we generalize the lower bound of Fu
and Kleinberg to $k$-cycle-freeness for $k \geq 4$ by generalizing the
construction of uniquely solvable puzzles due to Coppersmith and Winograd (J.
Symbolic Comput., 1990).

text: Brown dwarfs, often described as failed stars, have been instrumental in enhancing our understanding of substellar atmospheres. This study investigates the photospheric properties of brown dwarfs by examining low-level variability in their near-infrared spectra. The objective was to determine the nature and extent of patchiness in the photospheres of these objects. Utilizing near-infrared spectroscopy data collected from the Hubble Space Telescope, we conducted a systematic survey that focused on multiple brown dwarfs over varying timescales. The methodology involved analyzing spectral features to assess variability and identifying the potential role of atmospheric inhomogeneities on the photospheric appearance. Key findings reveal that the majority of brown dwarfs exhibit substantial low-level variability, suggesting that their atmospheres are not only dynamic but also unevenly composed. This patchy nature challenges existing models of brown dwarf atmospheres, indicating that the presence of clouds, dust, and varying elemental abundances significantly influence their observable characteristics over time. Our conclusions emphasize the need for a revised theoretical framework to accommodate the observed variability, advocating for the integration of dynamic atmospheric models in future studies. These findings have broader implications for our understanding of exoplanet atmospheres and the classification of substellar objects, highlighting the complex interactions between atmospheric dynamics and observational signatures in the substellar regime.

The hypothesis of selective exposure assumes that people seek out information
that supports their views and eschew information that conflicts with their
beliefs, and that has negative consequences on our society. Few researchers
have recently found counter evidence of selective exposure in social media:
users are exposed to politically diverse articles. No work has looked at what
happens after exposure, particularly how individuals react to such exposure,
though. Users might well be exposed to diverse articles but share only the
partisan ones. To test this, we study partisan sharing on Facebook: the
tendency for users to predominantly share like-minded news articles and avoid
conflicting ones. We verified four main hypotheses. That is, whether partisan
sharing: 1) exists at all; 2) changes across individuals (e.g., depending on
their interest in politics); 3) changes over time (e.g., around elections); and
4) changes depending on perceived importance of topics. We indeed find strong
evidence for partisan sharing. To test whether it has any consequence in the
real world, we built a web application for BBC viewers of a popular political
program, resulting in a controlled experiment involving more than 70
individuals. Based on what they share and on survey data, we find that partisan
sharing has negative consequences: distorted perception of reality. However, we
do also find positive aspects of partisan sharing: it is associated with people
who are more knowledgeable about politics and engage more with it as they are
more likely to vote in the general elections.
label: human

In observations, it is important to deproject the two fundamental quantities
characterizing a bar, i.e., its length ($a$) and ellipticity ($e$), to face-on
values before any careful analyses. However, systematic estimation on the
uncertainties of the commonly used deprojection methods is still lacking.
Simulated galaxies are well suited in this study. We project two simulated
barred galaxies onto a 2D plane with different bar orientations and disk
inclination angles ($i$). Bar properties are measured and deprojected with the
popular deprojection methods in the literature. Generally speaking,
deprojection uncertainties increase with increasing $i$. All the deprojection
methods behave badly when $i$ is larger than $60^\circ$, due to vertical
thickness of the bar. Thus, future statistical studies of barred galaxies
should exclude galaxies more inclined than $60^\circ$. At moderate inclination
angles ($i\leq60^\circ$), 2D deprojection methods (analytical and image
stretching) and Fourier-based methods (Fourier decomposition and bar-interbar
contrast) perform reasonably well with uncertainties $\sim10\%$ in both the bar
length and ellipticity. Whereas the uncertainties of the 1D analytical
deprojection can be as high as $100\%$ in certain extreme case.
  We find that different bar measurement methods show systematic differences in
the deprojection uncertainties. We further discuss the deprojection uncertainty
factors with the emphasis on the most important one, i.e., the 3D structure of
the bar itself. We construct two triaxial toy bar models that can qualitatively
reproduce the results of the 1D and 2D analytical deprojections; they confirm
that the vertical thickness of the bar is the main source of uncertainties.
label: human

text: The study utilizes the Dwarf Galaxy Survey with Amateur Telescopes (DGSAT) to explore the relatively underexamined domain of isolated nearby edge-on disk galaxies. This research aims to expand the catalog of such systems and identify previously undetected low surface brightness (LSB) galaxies. By leveraging amateur telescopes in combination with advanced data processing techniques, the survey systematically captured high-resolution images of edge-on disk galaxies in isolated settings. The methodology involved rigorous selection criteria to differentiate true edge-on galaxies from other disc orientations, and advanced photometric analysis to detect LSB features that standard surveys may overlook. Our findings contribute a comprehensive catalogue outlining the physical properties and spatial distribution of these galaxies, revealing several new LSB systems that demonstrate an intriguing variation in luminosity and structural composition relative to more densely populated galactic environments. The research highlights the potential of coordinated amateur astronomy efforts to make significant contributions to the field, providing valuable insights into galaxy formation and evolution. The discovery of new LSB systems underlines the importance of edge-on perspectives in understanding mass distribution and the stellar population of disk galaxies, emphasizing gaps in existing models of galactic evolution that often focus on brighter, more eminent galaxy types. Ultimately, this survey sets a foundation for subsequent in-depth spectral analyses and potential large-scale follow-up studies using more sophisticated telescopic technology, with implications for improving the accuracy of cosmological models.

text: Our research introduces SegAN, an innovative adversarial network architecture that employs a multi-scale $L_1$ loss function for precise medical image segmentation. The primary issue we address is the challenge of accurately segmenting medical images with fine structures and complex backgrounds. Through our study, we achieved promising results in enhancing the segmentation accuracy compared to traditional methods. The key concept underlying SegAN is the integration of a multi-scale $L_1$ loss into the adversarial training process, promoting the generation of sharper and more refined segmentation maps. To confirm the effectiveness of our proposed model, we conducted experiments on various medical image datasets, demonstrating superior segmentation performance in terms of both quantitative metrics and visual quality. Our methodology involves training the SegAN framework using a combination of adversarial and supervision losses, facilitating the generation of detailed segmentation maps. Overall, the SegAN framework with the multi-scale $L_1$ loss presents a robust solution for high-fidelity medical image segmentation tasks, showcasing the potential for significant advancements in the field of medical image analysis and enhancing the accuracy of diagnostic procedures.
label: machine

text:
Accurate parameters of the host stars of exoplanets are important for the
interpretation of the new planet systems that continue to emerge. The CoRoT
satellite recently discovered a transiting rocky planet with a density similar
to the inner planets in our solar system, a so-called Super Earth. This planet
is orbiting a relatively faint G9V star called CoRoT-7, and we wish to refine
its physical properties, which are important for the interpretation of the
properties of the planet system. We used spectra from HARPS@ESO-3.6m and
UVES@VLT-8.2m. From the analysis of Fe-1 and Fe-2 lines we determine Teff, log
g and microturbulence. We use the Balmer lines to constrain Teff and pressure
sensitive Mg-1b and Ca lines to constrain log g. From the analysis we find
Teff=5250+-60K, log g = 4.47+-0.05, [M/H]=+0.12+-0.06, and vsini = 1.1 km/s. We
compared the L/M ratio with isochrones to constrain the evolutionary status.
Using the age estimate of 1.2-2.3 Gyr based on stellar activity, we determine
the mass and radius 0.91+-0.03 Msun and 0.82+-0.04 Rsun. With these updated
constraints we fitted the CoRoT transit light curve for CoRoT-7b. We revise the
planet radius to be slightly smaller, R = 1.58+-0.10 Rearth, and the density
becomes higher, rho = 7.2+-1.8 g/cm3. The host star CoRoT-7 is a slowly
rotating, metal rich, unevolved type G9V star. The star is relatively faint
(V=11.7) and its fundamental parameters can only be determined through indirect
methods. Our methods rely on detailed spectral analyses that depend on the
adopted model atmospheres. From the analysis of spectra of stars with
well-known parameters with similar parameters to CoRoT-7 (the Sun and alpha Cen
B) we demonstrate that our methods are robust within the claimed uncertainties.
Therefore our methods can be reliably used in subsequent analyses of similar
exoplanet host stars.
label: human

text: The Hajnal-Szemerédi theorem is a seminal result in extremal set theory, establishing the conditions under which a graph can be colored without creating large monochromatic complete subgraphs. This study explores a Ramsey-Turán variant of the Hajnal-Szemerédi theorem, investigating the interplay between colorings and edge density in graphs. The objective of this research is to extend the classical findings by examining how the Ramsey number and Turán-type parameters can be amalgamated to define new thresholds for monochromatic complete subgraphs in colored graphs. To achieve this, we employ a combination of probabilistic techniques and combinatorial constructions, focusing on the asymptotic behavior of graphs as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Our findings reveal that for sufficiently large graphs, the presence of a certain minimum edge density guarantees that at least one color class will contain a complete subgraph of a prescribed order, while still adhering to Turán's principle of avoiding large independent sets. The implications of these results significantly enhance the understanding of colorings in the realm of combinatorial graph theory, providing a deeper insight into the structural aspects of graphs and their chromatic properties. In conclusion, this variant not only reinforces the original Hajnal-Szemerédi theorem but also opens avenues for further research into more general coloring principles and their applications in theoretical computer science and discrete mathematics.
label: machine

text: In this work, we investigate the problem of approximating the distribution of non-backtracking random walks on finite graphs using Poisson approximations. Non-backtracking random walks, wherein the walker is forbidden from revisiting its immediate prior state in consecutive steps, have gained prominence due to their applications in network exploration and statistical mechanics. We aim to provide a comprehensive analysis of the asymptotic behavior of these walks to facilitate their approximation by a Poisson distribution under specific conditions. Our methodology leverages coupling techniques and moment calculations to establish bounds for the Poisson approximation in terms of the total variation distance. We extend classical results by addressing complex dependencies intrinsic to non-backtracking constraints. Through rigorous derivations, we demonstrate that for large graphs with sparsity characteristics akin to regular graphs, the distribution of visitations to vertices follows a Poisson-like behavior, thus validating our hypothesis. The results obtained have significant implications, notably in improving the efficiency of algorithms related to network dynamics and providing insights into epidemic spread modeling. Empirically, we validate our theoretical findings on various graph structures, observing a high degree of conformity between observed distributions and their Poisson counterparts. Our approach not only emphasizes the relevance of non-backtracking constraints in enhancing the fidelity of approximation but also opens new avenues for research into dynamic processes on complex networks. This work, by systematically analyzing the interplay between random walk dynamics and graph structure, contributes a substantive advancement in the theory of stochastic processes on graphs.
label: machine

text:
Supermassive black holes may be described by their mass and spin. When
supermassive black holes are active, the activity provides a probe of the state
of the black hole system. The spin of a hole can be estimated when the black
hole mass and beam power of the source are known for sources with powerful
outflows. Seventy-five sources for which both the black hole mass and beam
power could be obtained are identified and used to obtain estimates of black
hole spins. The 75 supermassive black holes studied include 52 FRII radio
galaxies and 23 FRII radio loud quasars with redshifts ranging from about zero
to two. The new values are combined with those obtained previously for 19 FRII
radio galaxies, 7 FRII radio loud quasars, and 29 radio sources associated with
CD galaxies to form samples of 71 FRII radio galaxies, 30 FRII quasars, and a
total sample of 130 spin values; all of the sources are associated with massive
elliptical galaxies. The new values obtained are similar to those obtained
earlier at similar redshift, and range from about 0.1 to 1 for FRII sources.
The overall results are consistent with those obtained previously: the spins
tend to decrease with decreasing redshift for the FRII sources studied. There
is a hint that the range of values of black hole spin at a given redshift is
larger for FRII quasars than for FRII radio galaxies. There is no indication of
a strong correlation between supermassive black hole mass and spin for the
supermassive black holes studied here. The relation between beam power and
black hole mass is obtained and used as a diagnostic of the outflows and the
dependence of the magnetic field strength on black hole mass.

text: The Cauchy problem for a tenth-order thin film equation is explored with a focus on oscillatory source-type and fundamental similarity solutions. This study aims to investigate the behavior of solutions under specific initial conditions and boundary values. Utilizing a combination of analytical techniques and numerical simulations, the research delves into the oscillatory nature of the solutions, examining how these solutions evolve over time. Key findings include the identification of distinct oscillatory patterns and the establishment of fundamental similarity solutions that provide insights into the long-term behavior of the system. The work contributes to the understanding of the complex dynamics inherent in such high-order partial differential equations, offering potential applications in fluid dynamics and pattern formation.

text: We investigated the impact of scattering on the temperature stratification in the photosphere of metal-poor stars through three-dimensional surface convection simulations. Our goal was to understand how scattering influences the thermal structure of these stars, which are of particular interest in the study of stellar evolution and the formation of heavy elements.   We employed a numerical model that incorporates the effects of scattering on the radiative transfer and the resulting temperature stratification in the photosphere. The simulations revealed that scattering significantly affects the temperature distribution, particularly in the upper layers of the photosphere. The degree of scattering dependence on the metallicity of the star was found to be crucial in determining the resulting temperature stratification.  Our results indicate that a higher level of scattering leads to a more pronounced temperature stratification, with a greater difference between the photospheric surface and the core. Conversely, a lower level of scattering results in a more uniform temperature distribution. These findings suggest that scattering plays a critical role in shaping the temperature structure of metal-poor stars, which in turn affects the overall stellar evolution and the formation of heavy elements.  The simulations also revealed that the temperature stratification is influenced by the frequency and strength of scattering events, as well as the composition of the stellar atmosphere. Our study provides new insights into the complex interplay between scattering, radiative transfer, and the resulting temperature stratification in metal-poor stars, highlighting the importance of considering the effects of scattering in stellar evolution models.
label: machine

Gravitational wave (GW) source counts have been recently shown to be able to
test how gravitational radiation propagates with the distance from the source.
Here, we extend this formalism to cosmological scales, i.e. the high redshift
regime, and we discuss the complications of applying this methodology to high
redshift sources. We also allow for models with compactified extra dimensions
like in the Kaluza-Klein model. Furthermore, we also consider the case of
intermediate redshifts, i.e. $0<z\lesssim1$, where we show it is possible to
find an analytical approximation for the source counts $\frac{dN}{d(S/N)}$.
This can be done in terms of cosmological parameters, such as the matter
density $\Omega_{m,0}$ of the cosmological constant model or the cosmographic
parameters for a general dark energy model. Our analysis is as general as
possible, but it depends on two important factors: a source model for the black
hole binary mergers and the GW source to galaxy bias. This methodology also
allows us to obtain the higher order corrections of the source counts in terms
of the signal-to-noise $S/N$. We then forecast the sensitivity of future
observations in constraining GW physics but also the underlying cosmology by
simulating sources distributed over a finite range of signal-to-noise with a
number of sources ranging from 10 to 500 sources as expected from future
detectors. We find that with 500 events it will be possible to provide
constraints on the matter density parameter at present $\Omega_{m,0}$ on the
order of a few percent and with the precision growing fast with the number of
events. In the case of extra dimensions we find that depending on the
degeneracies of the model, with 500 events it may be possible to provide
stringent limits on the existence of the extra dimensions if the aforementioned
degeneracies can be broken.
label: human

In this paper, I review to what extent we can understand the photometric
properties of star clusters, and of low-mass, unresolved galaxies, in terms of
population synthesis models designed to describe `simple stellar populations'
(SSPs), i.e., groups of stars born at the same time, in the same volume of
space, and from a gas cloud of homogeneous chemical composition. The
photometric properties predicted by these models do not readily match the
observations of most star clusters, unless we properly take into account the
expected variation in the number of stars occupying sparsely populated
evolutionary stages, due to stochastic fluctuations in the stellar initial mass
function. In this case, population synthesis models reproduce remarkably well
the full ranges of observed integrated colours and absolute magnitudes of star
clusters of various ages and metallicities. The disagreement between the model
predictions and observations of cluster colours and magnitudes may indicate
problems with or deficiencies in the modelling, and dioes not necessarily tell
us that star clusters do not behave like SSPs. Matching the photometric
properties of star clusters using SSP models is a necessary (but not
sufficient) condition for clusters to be considered simple stellar populations.
Composite models, characterized by complex star-formation histories, also match
the observed cluster colours.
label: human

text:
Dirac electrons in solids show characteristic physical properties due to
their linear dispersion relation and two-band nature. Although the transport
phenomena of Dirac electrons in a normal state have intensively been studied,
the transport phenomena in a superconducting state have not been fully
understood. In particular, it is not clear whether Dirac electrons in a
superconducting state show Meissner effect (ME), since a diamagnetic term of a
current operator is absent as a result of the linear dispersion. We investigate
the ME of three dimensional massive Dirac electrons in a superconducting state
on the basis of Kubo formula, and clarify that Meissner kernel becomes finite
by use of the inter-band contribution. This mechanism of the ME for Dirac
electrons is completely different from that for the electrons in usual metals.
Our result shows that the Meissner kernel remains finite even when the
superconducting gap vanishes. This is an unavoidable problem in the Dirac
electron system as reported in the previous works. Thus, we use a prescription
in which we subtract the normal state contribution. In order to justify this
prescription, we develop a specific model where the Meissner kernel is obtained
by the prescription. We also derive the result for the electron gas by taking
the non-relativistic limit of Dirac Hamiltonian, and clarify that the
diamagnetic term of the Meissner kernel can be regarded as the inter-band
contribution between electrons and positrons in terms of the Dirac model.
label: human

text:
One of the most promising proposals for engineering topological
superconductivity and Majorana fermions employs a spin-orbit coupled nanowire
subjected to a magnetic field and proximate to an s-wave superconductor. When
only part of the wire's length contacts to the superconductor, the remaining
conducting portion serves as a natural lead that can be used to probe these
Majorana modes via tunneling. The enhanced role of interactions in one
dimension dictates that this configuration should be viewed as a
superconductor-Luttinger liquid junction. We investigate such junctions between
both helical and spinful Luttinger liquids, and topological as well as
non-topological superconductors. We determine the phase diagram for each case
and show that universal low-energy transport in these systems is governed by
fixed points describing either perfect normal reflection or perfect Andreev
reflection. In addition to capturing (in some instances) the familiar
Majorana-mediated `zero-bias anomaly' in a new framework, we show that
interactions yield dramatic consequences in certain regimes. Indeed, we
establish that strong repulsion removes this conductance anomaly altogether
while strong attraction produces dynamically generated effective Majorana modes
even in a junction with a trivial superconductor. Interactions further lead to
striking signatures in the local density of states and the line-shape of the
conductance peak at finite voltage, and also are essential for establishing
smoking-gun transport signatures of Majorana fermions in spinful Luttinger
liquid junctions.
label: human

text: Photosynthetic systems are crucial for converting solar energy into chemical energy efficiently. Understanding the impact of the system-bath coupling on photosynthetic heat engines is essential for optimizing their performance. In this study, we employ a polaron master equation approach to investigate the effects of system-bath coupling on photosynthetic heat engines. The methodology involves modeling the photosynthetic system as a network of coupled chromophores interacting with a thermal environment. By solving the polaron master equation, we can capture the non-Markovian dynamics of exciton energy transfer and dissipation in the presence of system-bath coupling. Our key findings reveal that strong system-bath coupling can lead to enhanced quantum coherence and energy transfer efficiency within the photosynthetic system. However, excessive coupling may also result in energy dissipation and reduced overall efficiency of the heat engine. These results provide valuable insights into the intricate interplay between system-bath coupling and the performance of photosynthetic heat engines. Ultimately, this research contributes to advancing our understanding of how to optimize the design of artificial photosynthetic systems for sustainable energy applications.

text: The study of halo nuclei, characterized by their extended, loosely bound peripheral nucleons, has gained prominence in contemporary nuclear physics. This work investigates the applicability of effective field theory (EFT) as a comprehensive framework for describing halo nuclei, aiming to bridge gaps in understanding their unique structure and dynamics. The primary objective is to derive a systematic and model-independent approach to capture the essential low-energy characteristics of halo systems. The methodology employs an EFT framework that exploits the separation of scale inherent in halo nuclei, integrating inputs from few-body quantum mechanics and low-energy nuclear interactions. By using a renormalizable and expandable approach, we delineate the universal properties of halo nuclei, isolating the effects of their distinctive nuclear and Coulomb interactions. Key findings reveal that halo nuclei exhibit scale invariance at leading order, with higher-order corrections providing insights into the fine structural details and weakly bound nature of these systems. The EFT framework successfully reproduces experimental observables, such as binding energies and reaction cross-sections, with enhanced predictive power. In conclusion, the effective field theory description offers a robust and versatile model that unifies the theoretical treatment of halo nuclei, facilitating predictions beyond specific computational models. This approach not only deepens our understanding of halo nuclei but also paves the way for future exploration of exotic nuclei near the limits of nuclear stability.

text: In this study, we investigate the sign-imbalance of permutation tableaux, which are combinatorial structures intricately linked to the symmetric group and have applications in algebraic combinatorics and representation theory. Our objective is to address the conspicuous gap in literature concerning the distribution of sign-imbalance within these tableaux. By employing a blend of analytic and combinatorial techniques, we derive explicit formulas for computing the sign-imbalance of permutation tableaux based on their underlying parameters.   Our principal approach involves the utilization of generating functions, which provide a robust framework for encapsulating the enumerative properties of permutation tableaux. Through this methodology, we uncover significant insights into the symmetries and variabilities that characterize tableaux of different dimensions. Furthermore, we establish connections between permutation tableaux and alternating permutations, revealing underlying algebraic structures that influence their sign-imbalance.  The findings illustrate a nuanced interplay between the tableau entries and their configuration, leading to comprehensive results, including both upper and lower bounds for their sign-imbalance distribution. Additionally, our investigation extends to identifying the critical role of certain classes of tableaux, particularly those with prescribed restrictions, which exhibit distinctive balance properties.  This work not only provides a deeper understanding of permutation tableaux but also sets the stage for future explorations into their algebraic and geometric interpretations. Through these contributions, we aim to enhance the existing combinatorial literature and open prospects for further research in related mathematical domains.

text: This research paper presents a broad-band spectral analysis of magnetar sources utilizing data from the Suzaku X-ray observatory. The primary objective was to investigate the high-energy emission properties of magnetars across various energy bands, aiming to understand their unique physical processes and magnetic field structures. The study employed multi-wavelength data collected over multiple observations, covering the energy range from soft X-rays to hard X-rays. Methodologically, the analysis involved detailed spectral fitting techniques to extract parameters such as the photon index, absorption column density, and electron density. Key findings revealed that magnetars exhibit distinct spectral features, including a steepening of the power-law tail at higher energies, which correlates with the presence of strong magnetic fields. Additionally, the study observed a correlation between the absorption column density and the energy band, suggesting that the obscuring material varies in density across different wavelengths. The research concluded by proposing models that integrate these observations with theoretical predictions, providing insights into the magnetar's environment and potential mechanisms driving its high-energy emissions.

Ultrasound localization microscopy offers new radiation-free diagnostic tools
for vascular imaging deep within the tissue. Sequential localization of echoes
returned from inert microbubbles with low-concentration within the bloodstream
reveal the vasculature with capillary resolution. Despite its high spatial
resolution, low microbubble concentrations dictate the acquisition of tens of
thousands of images, over the course of several seconds to tens of seconds, to
produce a single super-resolved image. %since each echo is required to be well
separated from adjacent microbubbles. Such long acquisition times and stringent
constraints on microbubble concentration are undesirable in many clinical
scenarios. To address these restrictions, sparsity-based approaches have
recently been developed. These methods reduce the total acquisition time
dramatically, while maintaining good spatial resolution in settings with
considerable microbubble overlap. %Yet, non of the reported methods exploit the
fact that microbubbles actually flow within the bloodstream. % to improve
recovery. Here, we further improve sparsity-based super-resolution ultrasound
imaging by exploiting the inherent flow of microbubbles and utilize their
motion kinematics. While doing so, we also provide quantitative measurements of
microbubble velocities. Our method relies on simultaneous tracking and
super-localization of individual microbubbles in a frame-by-frame manner, and
as such, may be suitable for real-time implementation. We demonstrate the
effectiveness of the proposed approach on both simulations and {\it in-vivo}
contrast enhanced human prostate scans, acquired with a clinically approved
scanner.

text: The rapid advancement of deep learning techniques has spurred interest in optimizing neural network architectures for performance in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and memory usage. This study explores Hybrid Binary Networks (HBNs), which integrate both binary and non-binary representation schemes, aiming to enhance the robustness of neural networks while reducing resource consumption. The objective of this research is to develop a novel HBN framework that leverages the strengths of binary quantization for weight and activation functions, coupled with traditional floating-point approaches for specific layers that require higher precision.   To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model, we employed a systematic methodology involving comparative experiments on benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Our proposed HBN architecture was subjected to varying levels of quantization and memory constraints, and the resulting accuracy, efficiency, and memory metrics were meticulously analyzed.   The key findings demonstrate that the HBN framework significantly outperforms conventional binary networks in terms of classification accuracy, achieving improvements of up to 5% on CIFAR-10 while maintaining a 50% reduction in model size. Furthermore, the hybrid approach also exhibited enhanced computational efficiency, resulting in faster inference times on edge devices.   In conclusion, Hybrid Binary Networks present a promising solution for addressing the trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and memory utilization in deep learning applications. This research contributes to the ongoing discourse on neural network optimization, paving the way for more effective deployment of deep learning models in resource-constrained environments.

Two special calorimeters are foreseen for the instrumentation of the very
forward region of an ILC or CLIC detector; a luminometer (LumiCal) designed to
measure the rate of low angle Bhabha scattering events with a precision better
than 10$^{-3}$ at the ILC and 10$^{-2}$ at CLIC, and a low polar-angle
calorimeter (BeamCal). The latter will be hit by a large amount of
beamstrahlung remnants. The intensity and the spatial shape of these
depositions will provide a fast luminosity estimate, as well as determination
of beam parameters. The sensors of this calorimeter must be radiation-hard.
Both devices will improve the e.m. hermeticity of the detector in the search
for new particles. Finely segmented and very compact electromagnetic
calorimeters will match these requirements. Due to the high occupancy, fast
front-end electronics will be needed. Monte Carlo studies were performed to
investigate the impact of beam-beam interactions and physics background
processes on the luminosity measurement, and of beamstrahlung on the
performance of BeamCal, as well as to optimise the design of both calorimeters.
Dedicated sensors, front-end and ADC ASICs have been designed for the ILC and
prototypes are available. Prototypes of sensor planes fully assembled with
readout electronics have been studied in electron beams.
