text: We investigated the properties of projective varieties $n$-covered by curves of degree $\delta$, focusing on the relationship between the number of curves and the degree of the projective variety. Through a systematic analysis of the intersections of the curves with the projective variety, we derived a lower bound for the number of curves required to cover the variety, which we found to be $n\left(1+\frac{\delta}{n}\right)$. This bound is achieved by a specific configuration of curves, demonstrating the optimality of this arrangement. We also explored the implications of this result on the geometry of the projective variety, revealing that the number of curves covering the variety is closely tied to the degree of the curves. Furthermore, we investigated the relationship between the number of curves and the degree of the projective variety, finding that the degree of the variety is bounded above by $n\delta$. Our findings have significant implications for the study of projective varieties and their geometric properties, providing new insights into the structure of these objects. By establishing a precise relationship between the number of curves and the degree of the projective variety, we have advanced our understanding of the geometry of projective varieties.

We seek to characterize how the change of global rotation rate influences the
overall dynamics and large scale flows arising in the convective envelopes of
stars covering stellar spectral types from early G to late K. We do so through
numerical simulations with the ASH code, where we consider stellar convective
envelopes coupled to a radiative interior with various global properties. As
solar-like stars spin down over the course of their main sequence evolution,
such change must have a direct impact on their dynamics and rotation state. We
indeed find that three main states of rotation may exist for a given star:
anti-solar-like (fast poles, slow equator), solar-like (fast equator, slow
poles), or a cylindrical rotation profile. Under increasingly strict rotational
constraints, the latter profile can further evolve into a Jupiter-like profile,
with alternating prograde and retrograde zonal jets. We have further assessed
how far the convection and meridional flows overshoot into the radiative zone
and investigated the morphology of the established tachocline. Using simple
mixing length arguments, we are able to construct a scaling of the fluid Rossby
number $R_{of} = \tilde{\omega}/2\Omega_* \sim \tilde{v}/2\Omega_* R_*$, which
we calibrate based on our 3-D ASH simulations. We can use this scaling to map
the behavior of differential rotation versus the global parameters of stellar
mass and rotation rate. Finally, we isolate a region on this map ($R_{of}
\gtrsim 1.5-2$) where we posit that stars with an anti-solar differential
rotation may exist in order to encourage observers to hunt for such targets.

Diffuse interstellar bands are usually observed in spectra of hot stars,
where interstellar lines are rarely blended with stellar ones. The need for hot
stars is a strong limitation in the number of sightlines we can observe and the
distribution of sightlines in the Galaxy, as hot stars are rare and
concentrated in the Galactic plane. We are introducing a new method, where
interstellar lines can be observed in spectra of cool stars in large
spectroscopic surveys. The method is completely automated and does not require
prior knowledge of the stellar parameters. If known, the stellar parameters
only reduce the computational time and are not involved in the extraction of
the interstellar spectrum. The main step in extracting interstellar lines is a
construction of the stellar spectrum, which is in our method done by finding
other observed spectra that lack interstellar features and are otherwise very
similar to the spectrum in question. Such spectra are then combined into a
single stellar spectrum template, which matches the stellar component in an
observed spectrum. We demonstrate the performance of this new method on a
sample of 482,430 spectra observed in RAVE survey. However, many spectra have
to be combined (48 on average) in order to achieve a S/N ratio high enough to
measure the DIB's profile, hence limiting the spatial information about the
ISM. Only one strong interstellar line is included in the RAVE spectral range,
a diffuse interstellar band at 8620 \AA. We compare its equivalent width with
extinction maps and with Bayesian reddening, calculated for individual stars,
and provide a linear relation between the equivalent width and reddening.
Separately from the introduced method, we calculate equivalent widths of the
diffuse interstellar band in spectra of hot stars with known extinction and
compare all three linear relations with each other and with relations from the
literature.

text: We present a novel approach to understanding the dynamics of massive starless cores by developing and applying the Deuteration Clock, a novel method to constrain the formation timescales of these enigmatic objects. Through a combination of high-resolution radio and millimeter-wave observations of CO and HCN, we mapped the spatial distribution of deuterium in a sample of 15 massive starless cores. Our results reveal a characteristic signature of deuterium enhancement in the inner regions of these cores, indicating a complex interplay between chemical and dynamical processes. By analyzing the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio in the cores, we estimate the formation timescales of these objects to be on the order of 100,000 to 500,000 years, which is significantly longer than previously thought. These findings suggest that massive starless cores may have undergone a prolonged period of collapse, potentially triggered by the collapse of a giant molecular cloud. Our Deuteration Clock method provides a powerful tool for probing the formation histories of these cores, and we demonstrate its applicability to a range of astrophysical contexts, including the study of prestellar cores, protostellar disks, and the early stages of star formation.

Magellanic spiral galaxies are a class of one-armed systems that often
exhibit an offset stellar bar, and are rarely found around massive spiral
galaxies. Using a set of N-body and hydrodynamic simulations we consider a
dwarf-dwarf galaxy interaction as the driving mechanism for the formation of
this peculiar class of systems. We investigate here the relation between the
dynamical, stellar and gaseous disk center and the bar. In all our simulations
the bar center always coincides with the dynamical center, while the stellar
disk becomes highly asymmetric during the encounter causing the photometric
center of the Magellanic galaxy disk to become mismatched with both the bar and
the dynamical center. The disk asymmetries persist for almost 2 Gyrs, the time
that it takes for the disk to be re-centered with the bar, and well after the
companion has passed. This explains the nature of the offset bar found in many
Magellanic-type galaxies, including the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and NGC
3906. In particular, these results, once applied to the LMC, suggest that the
dynamical center should reside in the bar center instead of the HI center as
previously assumed, pointing to a variation in the current estimate of the
north component of the LMC proper motion.

text: This paper investigates the properties and structures of reducible families of height three level algebras, which play a significant role in the broader context of algebraic geometry and representation theory. The primary objective is to establish a comprehensive framework for understanding the conditions under which these algebras can be classified as reducible, focusing on their dimensional characteristics and the interrelations between their ideals.   A combination of theoretical constructs and computational methods is employed to analyze families of height three level algebras systematically. The study utilizes a mix of homological algebra techniques and geometric interpretation to elucidate the hierarchies within these algebras, particularly emphasizing their behavior under various operations such as extension and contraction.   Key findings reveal that reducible families often exhibit specific invariants, which can be utilized to predict their structure and interactions with other algebraic entities. Moreover, the presence of certain configurations of ideals within the algebras significantly influences their reducibility, leading to a set of criteria that can determine the reducibility status of any given algebra within this family.  In conclusion, this research not only contributes to the theoretical understanding of reducible families of height three level algebras but also opens avenues for further exploration into their applications in algebraic studies and potential connections with other mathematical domains. The insights gained may pave the way for future research focused on enhancing the classification systems for various algebraic structures.

This paper is to analyze the properties of evolving bipartite networks from
four aspects, the growth of networks, the degree distribution, the popularity
of objects and the diversity of user behaviours, leading a deep understanding
on the empirical data. By empirical studies of data from the online bookstore
Amazon and a question and answer site Stack Overflow, which are both rating
bipartite networks, we could reveal the rules for the evolution of bipartite
networks. These rules have significant meanings in practice for maintaining the
operation of real systems and preparing for their future development. We find
that the degree distribution of users follows a power law with an exponential
cutoff. Also, according to the evolution of popularity for objects, we find
that the large-degree objects tend to receive more new ratings than expected
depending on their current degrees while the small-degree objects receive less
ratings in terms of their degrees. Moreover, the user behaviours show such a
trend that the larger degree the users have, the stronger purposes are with
their behaviours except the initial periods when users choose a diversity of
products to learn about what they want. Finally, we conclude with a discussion
on how the bipartite network evolves, which provides guideline for meeting
challenges brought by the growth of network.

text: We investigate the variability of the broad absorption lines (BALs) in the CIV region as part of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Reverberation Mapping Project. Our primary aim is to elucidate the rapid changes in absorption line profiles, which can provide insights into the dynamics of outflows in quasars. We utilize a comprehensive dataset combining multi-epoch spectroscopy and photometry of a sample of quasars exhibiting strong CIV absorption features. Using cross-correlation analysis, we analyze the time lag between continuum fluctuations and corresponding changes in the BAL profile over multiple observations.  Our results reveal significant variability in the CIV BALs, with time lags ranging from days to weeks, demonstrating a consequential response of the absorption lines to continuum brightness alterations. We note that these rapid fluctuations in absorption strength and width are indicative of moving clouds in the outflow region. Additionally, the observed variability does not correlate uniformly across all quasars, hinting at differing outflow geometries and structures.  The findings emphasize the potential of CIV BAL variability as a crucial tool in understanding quasar outflows and their influence on the intergalactic medium. By comparing our results with theoretical models of outflow dynamics, we propose refinements to existing frameworks that account for rapid BAL variability. Thus, our work contributes to a deeper comprehension of the feedback mechanisms between quasars and their surrounding environments.

text:
When the upper layer of an accreting neutron star experiences a thermonuclear
runaway of helium and hydrogen, it exhibits an X-ray burst of a few keV with a
cool-down phase of typically 1~minute. When there is a surplus of hydrogen,
hydrogen fusion is expected to simmer during that same minute due to the rp
process, which consists of rapid proton captures and slow beta-decays of
proton-rich isotopes. We have analyzed the high-quality light curves of 1254
X-ray bursts, obtained with the Proportional Counter Array on the Rossi X-ray
Timing Explorer between 1996 and 2012, to systematically study the cooling and
rp process. This is a follow-up of a study on a selection of 37 bursts from
systems that lack hydrogen and show only cooling during the bursts. We find
that the bolometric light curves are well described by the combination of a
power law and a one-sided Gaussian. The power-law decay index is between 1.3
and 2.1 and similar to that for the 37-bursts sample. There are individual
bursters with a narrower range. The Gaussian is detected in half of all bursts,
with a typical standard deviation of 50~s and a fluence ranging up to 60% of
the total fluence. The Gaussian appears consistent with being due to the rp
process. The Gaussian fluence fraction suggests that the layer where the rp
process is active is underabundant in H by a factor of at least five with
respect to cosmic abundances. Ninety-four percent of all bursts from
ultracompact X-ray binaries lack the Gaussian component, and the remaining 6%
are marginal detections. This is consistent with a hydrogen deficiency in these
binaries. We find no clear correlation between the power law and Gaussian
light-curve components.

The HII complex N159 in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) is used to study
massive star formation in different environments, as it contains three giant
molecular clouds (GMCs) that have similar sizes and masses but exhibit
different intensities of star formation. We identify candidate massive young
stellar objects (YSOs) using infrared photometry, and model their SEDs to
constrain mass and evolutionary state. Good fits are obtained for less evolved
Type I, I/II, and II sources. Our analysis suggests that there are massive
embedded YSOs in N159B, a maser source, and several ultracompact HII regions.
Massive O-type YSOs are found in GMCs N159-E and N159-W, which are associated
with ionized gas, i.e., where massive stars formed a few Myr ago. The third
GMC, N159-S, has neither O-type YSOs nor evidence of previous massive star
formation. This correlation between current and antecedent formation of massive
stars suggests that energy feedback is relevant. We present evidence that
N159-W is forming YSOs spontaneously, while collapse in N159-E may be
triggered. Finally, we compare star formation rates determined from YSO counts
with those from integrated H-alpha and 24 micron luminosities and expected from
gas surface densities. Detailed dissection of extragalactic GMCs like the one
presented here is key to revealing the physics underlying commonly used star
formation scaling laws.

text: The Solar Twin Planet Search (STPS) is a significant endeavor to discover Earth-size exoplanets orbiting solar twin stars, aiming to explore potential habitability. This study investigates the age-chromospheric activity relation in solar twins, as chromospheric activity significantly affects planetary habitability. We analyzed high-resolution, high-S/N spectra of solar twin candidates obtained from the HARPS and ESPaDOnS spectrographs to calculate their chromospheric activity indicators. We utilized age determinations derived from lithium depletion and gyrochronology, to assess the correlation between age and chromospheric activity. Our results revealed a strong inverse correlation, suggesting that as solar twins age, their chromospheric activity decreases. This correlation has implications for potential habitability of planets in the habitable zones of solar twins. The decrease in chromospheric activity with age implies a reduction in extreme ultraviolet radiation and energetic particles, enhancing long-term planetary habitability. Our findings expand our understanding of solar twin stars and their planets' habitability prospects. Further investigation into the age-activity relation and its implications for planetary habitability is necessary, as it plays a crucial role in shaping the environment for potential life.

text:
Permutation tableaux were introduced by Steingr\'{\i}msson and Williams.
Corteel and Kim defined the sign of a permutation tableau in terms of the
number of unrestricted columns. The sign-imbalance of permutation tableaux of
length $n$ is the sum of signs over permutation tableaux of length $n$. They
have btained a formula for the sign-imbalance of permutation tableaux of length
$n$ by using generating functions and asked for a combinatorial proof.
Moreover, they raised the question of finding a sign-imbalance formula for type
$B$ permutation tableaux introduced by Lam and Williams. We define a statistic
$\nwnm$ over permutations and show that the number of unrestricted columns over
permutation tableaux of length $n$ is equally distributed with $\nwnm$ over
permutations of length $n$. This leads to a combinatorial interpretation of the
formula of Corteel and Kim. For type $B$ permutation tableaux, we define the
sign of a type $B$ permutation tableau in term of the number of certain rows
and columns. On the other hand, we construct a bijection between the type $B$
permutation tableaux of length $n$ and symmetric permutations of length $2n$
and we show that the statistic $\nwnm$ over symmetric permutations of length
$2n$ is equally distributed with the number of certain rows and columns over
type $B$ permutation tableaux of length $n$. Based on this correspondence and
an involution on symmetric permutation of length $2n$, we obtain a
sign-imbalance formula for type $B$ permutation tableaux.

text: We investigate the stabilization of Majorana modes in vortices within the superconducting phase of topological insulators through the introduction of topologically trivial bands. Our study aims to address the challenge of controlling and sustaining Majorana modes, which are promising candidates for robust quantum information processing due to their non-Abelian statistics. By incorporating topologically trivial bands into the superconducting system, we successfully enhance the stability of Majorana modes against perturbations. The results demonstrate that the presence of these additional bands can effectively shield the Majorana modes from decoherence and extend their lifetime, improving their suitability for practical applications. We employ a theoretical framework combining topological band theory and superconducting physics to analyze the behavior of Majorana modes in the presence of vortices and topologically trivial bands. Our findings highlight the potential of utilizing topologically trivial bands as a strategy for manipulating and preserving Majorana modes in topological insulators, paving the way for advancements in topological quantum computation and quantum information processing.

text: Neutrinos play a pivotal role in the evolution of protoneutron stars (PNS), cooling the core and regulating its contraction. However, the effects of neutrino viscosity and drag on the magnetorotational instability (MRI) in PNS remain unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the impact of neutrino viscosity and drag on the MRI by considering neutrinos as an additional fluid component, using a two-fluid model. We perform a set of MHD simulations to study the dynamics of the PNS during the early stages of evolution. Our results reveal that the inclusion of neutrinos significantly affects the MRI, with neutrino viscosity suppressing the growth rate of the instability. Moreover, neutrino drag increases the effective magnetic diffusivity, weakening the magnetic fields and contributing to a faster accretion disk formation. The findings from this study highlight the importance of properly modeling neutrino effects in understanding the magnetized dynamics of PNS and their role in producing observed gamma-ray bursts.

text: In this study, we present the results of spectroscopic abundance analyses conducted on the 3He-enriched stars HD 185330 and 3 Cen A. These unique stars, showing enhanced levels of the light isotope 3He, present an intriguing astrophysical puzzle due to the rarity of such abundance anomalies. Our work aims to shed light on the origin and evolution of these stars by investigating their chemical compositions. Using high-resolution spectra obtained from the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope, we determined the elemental abundances of key elements such as lithium, carbon, oxygen, and nitrogen in HD 185330 and 3 Cen A. Our results reveal significant deviations from the standard stellar abundance patterns, indicating non-standard nucleosynthetic processes at play in these 3He-enriched stars. Through comparisons with theoretical models and known nucleosynthetic pathways, we aim to decipher the mechanisms responsible for the anomalous abundances observed in these stars. Our approach involves sophisticated spectroscopic techniques and detailed abundance determinations, providing valuable insights into the peculiar chemical signatures of 3He stars. Ultimately, our study contributes to the broader understanding of stellar evolution and nucleosynthesis processes in the universe.

text:
We characterise the radial density, metallicity and flattening profile of the
Milky Way's stellar halo, based on the large sample of 1757 spectroscopically
confirmed giant stars from SDSS/SEGUE-2 after excising stars that were
algorithmically attributed to apparent halo substructure (including the
Sagittarius stream). Compared to BHB stars or RR Lyrae, giants are more readily
understood tracers of the overall halo star population, with less bias in age
or metallicity. The well-characterized selection function of the sample enables
forward modelling of those data, based on ellipsoidal stellar density models,
$\nu_* (R,z)$, with Einasto profiles and (broken) power laws for their radial
dependence, combined with a model for the metallicity gradient and the
flattening profile. Among models with constant flattening, these data are
reasonably well fit by an Einasto profile of $n=3.1\pm 0.5$ with an effective
radius $\rm r_{eff} = 15\pm2~$kpc and a flattening of $q=0.7\pm 0.02$; or
comparably well by an equally flattened broken power-law, with radial slopes of
$\alpha_{in}=2.1\pm 0.3$ and $\alpha_{out}=3.8\pm 0.1$, with a break-radius of
$r_{break}=18\pm1$~kpc; this is largely consistent with earlier work. We find a
modest, but significant metallicity gradient within the "outer" stellar halo,
$\rm [Fe/H]$ decreasing outward. If we allow for a variable flattening $q =
f(r_{GC} )$, we find the distribution of halo giants to be considerably more
flattened at small radii, $q({\rm 10~kpc})\sim 0.57$, compared to $q(>30{\rm
kpc})\sim 0.8$. Remarkably, the data are then very well fit by a single
power-law of index $\rm \sim 4.2\pm0.1$ of the variable
$r_q\equiv\sqrt{R^2+(z/q(r))^2}$. In this simple and better fitting model,
there is a break in flattening at $\sim 20$~kpc, instead of a break in the
radial density function.

text:
In experimental design and causal inference, it may happen that the treatment
is not defined on individual experimental units, but rather on pairs or, more
generally, on groups of units. For example, teachers may choose pairs of
students who do not know each other to teach a new curriculum; regulators might
allow or disallow merging of firms, and biologists may introduce or inhibit
interactions between genes or proteins. In this paper, we formalize this
experimental setting, and we refer to the individual treatments in such setting
as entangled treatments. We then consider the special case where individual
treatments depend on a common population quantity, and develop theory and
methodology to deal with this case. In our target applications, the common
population quantity is a network, and the individual treatments are defined as
functions of the change in the network between two specific time points. Our
focus is on estimating the causal effect of entangled treatments in
observational studies where entangled treatments are endogenous and cannot be
directly manipulated. When treatment cannot be manipulated, be it entangled or
not, it is necessary to account for the treatment assignment mechanism to avoid
selection bias, commonly through a propensity score methodology. In this paper,
we quantify the extent to which classical propensity score methodology ignores
treatment entanglement, and characterize the bias in the estimated causal
effects. To characterize such bias we introduce a novel similarity function
between propensity score models, and a practical approximation of it, which we
use to quantify model misspecification of propensity scores due to
entanglement. One solution to avoid the bias in the presence of entangled
treatments is to model the change in the network, directly, and calculate an
individual unit's propensity score by averaging treatment assignments over this
change.

text: The abstract focuses on measuring the vertical age structure of the Galactic disc through asteroseismology and the Spiral Ages Global Age (SAGA) method. Asteroseismology, a technique that exploits stellar oscillations to probe stellar interiors, provides valuable insights into stellar ages and chemical compositions. In this study, we employ asteroseismic data from the Kepler mission to analyze the vertical stratification within the Galactic disc. We also utilize the SAGA method, which relies on the kinematics of old disk stars to estimate their ages and locations. By combining these two approaches, we aim to understand the distribution of stellar populations with varying ages across different heights in the Galactic disc. Key findings include distinct age gradients and age segregation at various vertical levels, suggesting complex dynamical processes shaping the Milky Way's structure. The results contribute to our understanding of the Milky Way's history and evolution, offering new perspectives on its formation and ongoing processes.
label: machine

text: In our recent experiment, we successfully investigated the gravitomagnetic effects using a pair of high-precision ring lasers. The set-up consisted of two identical ring lasers suspended in ultra-high vacuum conditions, with their planes perpendicular to each other. A test mass was positioned at the intersection of the two beams, and a constant gravitational force was applied to the mass through a nearby fixed reference mass. By measuring the slight shifts in the resonance frequencies of the two lasers caused by the gravitational field, we were able to detect the gravitomagnetic effects. Our results showed a significant difference in the gravitational redshift between the inner and outer rings, in agreement with the theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we observed an apparent gravitational force acting on the test mass in the direction of the rotating reference mass, demonstrating the presence of the centrifugal gravitomagnetic effect. These findings provide crucial insights into the nature of gravitational fields and confirm the validity of Einstein's theory of general relativity in the strong-field regime. Our experimental methodology offers a new approach to the precise measurement of gravitomagnetic effects and has the potential to advance the field of gravitational physics.

text: The Robber Locating game is a classic strategy game that involves searching for a hidden opponent in a finite, grid-based environment. This game has been extensively studied in the field of artificial intelligence and game theory, with a focus on developing efficient algorithms for locating the opponent. The objective of this research is to develop a novel algorithm for locating the opponent in the Robber Locating game, and to evaluate its performance in a series of experiments.  The background of this research is rooted in the study of finite, grid-based games, where the opponent's location is unknown. In such games, the player must use a combination of exploration and exploitation strategies to locate the opponent. The Robber Locating game is particularly challenging due to the finite size of the grid, which limits the number of possible locations for the opponent. The existing algorithms for locating the opponent in the Robber Locating game are often based on exhaustive search or random search, which are computationally expensive and inefficient.  This research employs a novel algorithm that combines elements of breadth-first search and depth-first search to efficiently locate the opponent. The algorithm is based on the idea of exploring the grid in a systematic manner, using a combination of random and deterministic moves. The performance of the algorithm is evaluated using a series of experiments, where the opponent's location is randomly chosen and the algorithm is run multiple times to estimate the probability of locating the opponent.  The key findings of this research indicate that the proposed algorithm is significantly more efficient than existing algorithms for locating the opponent in the Robber Locating game. The algorithm is able to locate the opponent in approximately 50% of the cases, which is significantly better than the existing algorithms. The results also show that the algorithm is able to adapt to different grid sizes and opponent locations, making it a versatile solution for a wide range of applications.
label: machine

text: This study presents advancements in the theoretical framework for testing Dyck languages, focusing on enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of algorithms designed for their identification. Initially, we faced challenges in achieving optimal bounds for recognizing these languages, which are characterized by balanced pairs of symbols. By employing novel proof techniques rooted in automata theory and combinatorial methods, we derived tighter lower and upper bounds. These improvements were achieved through rigorous analysis of state complexity and the use of advanced graph-theoretic properties inherent to Dyck languages. The methodology involved constructing more sophisticated automata models and applying probabilistic arguments to establish the limits of possible recognition processes. We present a new method to standardize Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) luminosities
to ~<0.13 magnitudes using flux ratios from a single flux-calibrated spectrum
per SN. Using Nearby Supernova Factory spectrophotomery of 58 SNe Ia, we
performed an unbiased search for flux ratios which correlate with SN Ia
luminosity. After developing the method and selecting the best ratios from a
training sample, we verified the results on a separate validation sample and
with data from the literature. We identified multiple flux ratios whose
correlations with luminosity are stronger than those of light curve shape and
color, previously identified spectral feature ratios, or equivalent width
measurements. In particular, the flux ratio R(642/443) = F(642 nm) / F(443 nm)
has a correlation of 0.95 with SN Ia absolute magnitudes. Using this single
ratio as a correction factor produces a Hubble diagram with a residual scatter
standard deviation of 0.125 +- 0.011 mag, compared with 0.161 +- 0.015 mag when
fit with the SALT2 light curve shape and color parameters x1 and c. The ratio
R(642/443) is an effective correction factor for both extrinsic dust reddening
and instrinsic variations such as those of SN 1991T-like and SN 1999aa-like
SNe. When combined with broad-band color measurements, spectral flux ratios can
standardize SN Ia magnitudes to ~0.12 mag. These are the first spectral metrics
that improve over the standard normalization methods based upon light curve
shape and color and they provide among the lowest scatter Hubble diagrams ever
published.

Though QCD Factorization(QCDF) could produce sufficiently large $B\to K\pi$
branching ratios close to experiments, the predicted direct CP asymmetry in
${\bar B}^{0}\to K^{+}\pi^{-}$ decay is however still quite below experiment,
even with a large negative phase in the annihilation term, according to
existing calculations. This suggests the presence of an additional strong phase
in the decay amplitude which could come from the long-distance final state
interactions(FSI) like charming penguin. In this paper, we show that, by adding
to the $B\to K\pi$ decay QCDF amplitude, a real part and an absorptive part
with a strength 10% and 30% of the penguin amplitude, respectively, we could
bring the
  $B\to K\pi$ branching ratios and the ${\bar B}^{0}\to K^{-}\pi^{+}$ CP
asymmetry close to the measured values. We also find that the color-allowed
electroweak penguin is appreciable and that from the QCDF electroweak-strong
penguin interference terms and the measured $B^{-}\to {\bar K}^{0}\pi^{-}$ we
obtain $(9.0\pm 0.3)\times 10^{-6}$ for the ${\bar B}^{0}\to {\bar
K}^{0}\pi^{0}$ branching ratio, a bit lower than experiment. Similarly, the
predicted value for $B^{-}\to K^{-}\pi^{0}$ in terms of the ${\bar B}^{0}\to
K^{-}\pi^{+}$ branching ratio agrees well with experiment. This suggests that
the measured value for ${\bar B}^{0}\to {\bar K}^{0}\pi^{0}$ in fact should be
lower than the current measured value.

text: In this work, we present a detailed beyond-mean-field (BMF) investigation of the hyperon impurity effect on hypernuclei with shape coexistence. We adopt a relativistic mean-field (RMF) theory with the relativistic Hartree-Fock (RHF) approach and an effective chiral interaction to study the hyperon-nucleon ($YN$) interaction in the context of hypernuclear structure. We extend the RHF method to a quasiparticle random phase approximation (QRPA) approach, which accounts for both the collective and correlational effects of hyperon impurities.  Our results reveal a rich structure for the hypernuclei studied, with multiple solutions for both the ground and excited states. In particular, we find strong hyperon-nucleon coupling and shape coexistence in the hyperon-rich hypernuclei. The presence of hyperon impurities modifies the nuclear shape and leads to a significant change in the binding energy and mean-square radius of the hypernucleus.  Moreover, we calculate the electromagnetic moments and transition probabilities between the hypernuclear ground and excited states. We discuss the implications of our findings for ongoing and future experiments in hypernuclear physics, particularly in relation to the study of shape coexistence and the hyperon impurity effect.  To validate our results, we compare them with available experimental data and other theoretical calculations. Our study provides a solid foundation for the understanding of hypernuclear structure and opens new avenues for investigating the role of hyperons in nuclear systems.  This research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the National Key Research and Development Program of China. The computational resources were provided by the National Supercomputing Center in China.

For a pair of positive parameters $D,\chi$, a partition ${\cal P}$ of the
vertex set $V$ of an $n$-vertex graph $G = (V,E)$ into disjoint clusters of
diameter at most $D$ each is called a $(D,\chi)$ network decomposition, if the
supergraph ${\cal G}({\cal P})$, obtained by contracting each of the clusters
of ${\cal P}$, can be properly $\chi$-colored. The decomposition ${\cal P}$ is
said to be strong (resp., weak) if each of the clusters has strong (resp.,
weak) diameter at most $D$, i.e., if for every cluster $C \in {\cal P}$ and
every two vertices $u,v \in C$, the distance between them in the induced graph
$G(C)$ of $C$ (resp., in $G$) is at most $D$.
  Network decomposition is a powerful construct, very useful in distributed
computing and beyond. It was shown by Awerbuch \etal \cite{AGLP89} and
Panconesi and Srinivasan \cite{PS92}, that strong $(2^{O(\sqrt{\log
n})},2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})})$ network decompositions can be computed in
$2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ distributed time. Linial and Saks \cite{LS93} devised an
ingenious randomized algorithm that constructs {\em weak} $(O(\log n),O(\log
n))$ network decompositions in $O(\log^2 n)$ time. It was however open till now
if {\em strong} network decompositions with both parameters $2^{o(\sqrt{\log
n})}$ can be constructed in distributed $2^{o(\sqrt{\log n})}$ time.
  In this paper we answer this long-standing open question in the affirmative,
and show that strong $(O(\log n),O(\log n))$ network decompositions can be
computed in $O(\log^2 n)$ time. We also present a tradeoff between parameters
of our network decomposition. Our work is inspired by and relies on the
"shifted shortest path approach", due to Blelloch \etal \cite{BGKMPT11}, and
Miller \etal \cite{MPX13}. These authors developed this approach for PRAM
algorithms for padded partitions. We adapt their approach to network
decompositions in the distributed model of computation.

text: Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) are pivotal in numerous applications, including environmental monitoring and smart cities, due to their ability to autonomously collect data across vast areas. However, efficient node estimation and topology discovery in large-scale WSNs remain challenging due to dynamic network conditions and resource constraints. This research proposes a novel Robust Node Estimation and Topology Discovery Algorithm designed to enhance the accuracy of node localization and the efficiency of network topology mapping. The objective is to optimize network operations through improved positioning accuracy and adaptive topology adjustments. The methodology involves developing a hybrid model incorporating both probabilistic graphical models and machine learning techniques to predict node locations and capture network dynamics effectively. Extensive simulations were conducted under varying conditions of node density, mobility, and environmental disturbances to evaluate the algorithm's performance. Key findings demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods, offering up to a 25% improvement in localization accuracy and a 30% reduction in energy consumption. Additionally, the algorithm adapts well to network changes, maintaining performance by dynamically adjusting the network topology. These findings suggest that the algorithm could substantially enhance the resilience and operational efficiency of large-scale WSN deployments. In conclusion, the novel algorithm provides a robust framework for accurate node estimation and efficient topology discovery, addressing critical challenges in the management of large-scale WSNs. Future work will focus on testing the algorithm in real-world deployments across different WSN scenarios to validate and refine its applicability and performance.

In the continuum, close connections exist between mean curvature flow, the
Allen-Cahn (AC) partial differential equation, and the Merriman-Bence-Osher
(MBO) threshold dynamics scheme. Graph analogues of these processes have
recently seen a rise in popularity as relaxations of NP-complete combinatorial
problems, which demands deeper theoretical underpinnings of the graph
processes. The aim of this paper is to introduce these graph processes in the
light of their continuum counterparts, provide some background, prove the first
results connecting them, illustrate these processes with examples and identify
open questions for future study. We derive a graph curvature from the graph cut
function, the natural graph counterpart of total variation (perimeter). This
derivation and the resulting curvature definition differ from those in earlier
literature, where the continuum mean curvature is simply discretized, and bears
many similarities to the continuum nonlocal curvature or nonlocal means
formulation. This new graph curvature is not only relevant for graph MBO
dynamics, but also appears in the variational formulation of a discrete time
graph mean curvature flow. We prove estimates showing that the dynamics are
trivial for both MBO and AC evolutions if the parameters (the time-step and
diffuse interface scale, respectively) are sufficiently small (a phenomenon
known as "freezing" or "pinning") and also that the dynamics for MBO are
nontrivial if the time step is large enough. These bounds are in terms of graph
quantities such as the spectrum of the graph Laplacian and the graph curvature.
Adapting a Lyapunov functional for the continuum MBO scheme to graphs, we prove
that the graph MBO scheme converges to a stationary state in a finite number of
iterations. Variations on this scheme have recently become popular in the
literature as ways to minimize (continuum) nonlocal total variation.

Religious adherence can be considered as a degree of freedom, in a
statistical physics sense, for a human agent belonging to a population. The
distribution, performance and life time of religions can thus be studied having
in mind heterogeneous interacting agent modeling in mind. We present a
comprehensive analysis of 58 so called religion (to be better defined in the
main text) evolutions, as measured through their number of adherents between
1900 and 2000, - data taken from the World Christian Encyclopedia: 40 are
considered to be ''presently growing'' cases, including 11 turn overs in the XX
century; 18 are ''presently decaying'', among which 12 are found to have had a
recent maximum, in the XIX or the XX century. The Avrami-Kolmogorov
differential equation which usually describes solid state transformations, like
crystal growth, is used in each case in order to obtain the preferential
attachment parameter introduced previously. It is often found close to unity,
indicating a smooth evolution. However large values suggest the occurrence of
extreme cases which we conjecture are controlled by so called external fields.
A few cases indicate the likeliness of a detachment process. We discuss
different growing and decaying religions, and illustrate various fits. Some
cases seem to indicate the lack of reliability of the data. Others, departure
from Avrami law. We point out two difficulties in the analysis : (i) the
''precise'' original time of apparition of a religion, (ii) the time of its
maximum, both informations being necessary for integrating reliably any
evolution equation. Moreover the Avrami evolution equation might be surely
improved, in particular, and somewhat obviously, for the decaying religion
cases.

text: Symbiotic systems, a combination of a luminous asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star and a compact companion such as a white dwarf or neutron star, are believed to play a crucial role in the formation of Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia). The explosive nature of SNe Ia has long been a topic of interest, and recent studies have shed light on the importance of symbiotic systems in their progenitor.   The objective of this study is to investigate the X-ray, radio, and UV luminosity expected from symbiotic systems as the progenitor of SNe Ia. By employing a combination of theoretical models and simulations, this research aims to elucidate the key physical processes that govern the evolution of these systems.   The methodology employed in this study involves the use of 1D and 3D hydrodynamic simulations to model the evolution of symbiotic systems, taking into account the effects of mass loss, accretion, and thermal pulses. The simulations are performed using the MESA code, which allows for the modeling of complex stellar evolution processes.   The key findings of this study reveal that symbiotic systems can exhibit a range of luminosity characteristics, including X-ray, radio, and UV emission. The simulations indicate that the luminosity of these systems can increase significantly as the companion star evolves, leading to the formation of a massive helium shell.   The conclusion of this study highlights the importance of symbiotic systems in the formation of SNe Ia. The results suggest that these systems can provide a viable explanation for the observed properties of SNe Ia, and further research is needed to confirm this hypothesis.

We present the implementation of turbulence transport equations in addition
to the Reynolds-averaged MHD equations within the Cronos framework. The model
is validated by comparisons with earlier findings before it is extended to be
applicable to regions in the solar wind that are not highly super-Alfv\'enic.
We find that the respective additional terms result in absolute normalized
cross-helicity to decline more slowly, while a proper implementation of the
mixing terms can even lead to increased cross-helicities in the inner
heliosphere. The model extension allows to place the inner boundary of the
simulations closer to the Sun, where we choose its location at 0.1 AU for
future application to the Wang-Sheeley-Arge model. Here, we concentrate on
effects on the turbulence evolution for transient events by injecting a coronal
mass ejection (CME). We find that the steep gradients and shocks associated
with these structures result in enhanced turbulence levels and reduced
cross-helicity. Our results can now be used straightforwardly for studying the
transport of charged energetic particles, where the elements of the diffusion
tensor can now benefit from the self-consistently computed solar wind
turbulence. Furthermore, we find that there is no strong back-reaction of the
turbulence on the large-scale flow so that CME studies concentrating on the
latter need not be extended to include turbulence transport effects.

text: We present a self-consistent, absolute isochronal age scale for young moving groups within the solar neighborhood, addressing the challenge of establishing precise ages for these stellar associations, which are critical for understanding stellar evolution and the formation of the Milky Way. Our methodology involves the synthesis of recent high-precision astrometric data, spectroscopic observations, and theoretical isochrones derived from updated stellar evolutionary models. By employing Bayesian inference techniques, we simultaneously fit the age, metallicity, and distance of stars in selected moving groups, thereby enhancing the reliability of our age estimates.  The results of our analysis yield a refined age scale for these stellar groups, revealing notable discrepancies with previously established age determinations. We find that many moving groups are younger than currently accepted, suggesting a need to revise the timeline of star formation in the solar neighborhood. Notably, our age scale elucidates the spatial distribution of younger stellar populations, linking their ages to dynamical interactions and galactic processes.  Key outcomes of our work include a set of empirical age benchmarks for the young moving groups, which are critical for further studies in stellar astrophysics and the broader contexts of galactic formation. We also highlight the implications of our findings for understanding the age-metallicity relation and the birth and evolution of stars within the Milky Way. Our self-consistent isochronal age scale not only provides a valuable reference for future research but also fosters a deeper comprehension of the complexities inherent in stellar and galactic evolution.

Aims. I look for and characterise very wide binaries and multiple systems
with projected physical separations larger than s = 0.1 pc, which is generally
believed to be a sharp upper limit to the distribution of wide binay semimajor
axes. Methods. I investigated in detail 30 Washington Double Stars with angular
separations rho > 1000 arcsec. I discarded 23 of them as probably unbound
systems based on discordant astrometry, photometry, spectral types, and radial
velocities. The remaining seven systems were subject to a comprehensive data
compilation and derivation (multi-wavelength photometry, heliocentric distance,
multiplicity, age, mass, metallicity, membership in young kinematic group).
Results. Of the seven very wide systems, six have projected physical
separations larger than the hypothetical cutoff at s = 0.1 pc; four of them
have separations s > 0.2 pc. Although there are two systems in young kinematic
groups (namely HD 136654 and BD+32 2572 in the Hyades Supercluster, and AU Mic
and AT Mic AB in the beta Pictoris moving group), there is not a clear
prevalence of young systems (tau < 1 Ga) among these very wide binaries.
Finally, I compare the binding energies of the seven systems with those of
other weakly bound systems in the field.

Theories of gravity with a preferred foliation usually display arbitrarily
fast signal propagation, changing the black hole definition. A new inescapable
barrier, the universal horizon, has been defined and many static and
spherically symmetric examples have been studied in the literature. Here, we
translate the usual definition of the universal horizon in terms of an optical
scalar built with the preferred flow defined by the preferred spacetime
foliation. The new expression has the advantages of being of quasilocal nature
and independent of specific spacetime symmetries in order to be well defined.
Therefore, we propose it as a definition for general quasilocal universal
horizons. Using the new formalism we show that there are no universal analog of
cosmological horizons for FLRW models for any scale factor function, and we
also state that quasilocal universal horizons are restricted to trapped regions
of the spacetime. Using the evolution equation, we analyze the formation of
universal horizons under a truncated Horava-Lifshitz theory, in spherical
symmetry, showing the existence of regions in parameter space where the
universal horizon formation cannot be smooth from the center, under some
physically reasonable assumptions. We conclude with our view on the next steps
for the understanding of black holes in nonrelativistic gravity theories.

The objective of the present paper is to investigate the solution of fully
coupled mean-field forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs
in short) and to study the stochastic control problems of mean-field type as
well as the mean-field stochastic game problems both in which state processes
are described as FBSDEs. By combining classical FBSDEs methods introduced by Hu
and Peng [Y. Hu, S. Peng, Solution of forward-backward stochastic differential
equations, Probab. Theory Relat. Fields 103 (1995)] with specific arguments for
fully coupled mean-field FBSDEs, we prove the existence and uniqueness of the
solution to this kind of fully coupled mean-field FBSDEs under a certain
\textquotedblleft monotonicity" condition. Next, we are interested in optimal
control problems for (fully coupled respectively) FBSDEs of mean-field type
with a convex control domain. Note that the control problems are time
inconsistent in the sense that the Bellman optimality principle does not hold.
The stochastic maximum principle (SMP) in integral form for mean-field
controls, which is different from the classical one, is derived, specifying the
necessary conditions for optimality. Sufficient conditions for the optimality
of a control is also obtained under additional assumptions. Then we are
concerned the maximum principle for a new class of non-zero sum stochastic
differential games. This game system differs from the existing literature in
the sense that the game systems here are characterized by (fully coupled
respectively) FBSDEs in the mean-field framework. Our paper deduces necessary
conditions as well as sufficient conditions in the form of maximum principle
for open equilibrium point of this class of games respectively.

In recent years, there has been increasing interest in developing a Computer
Science curriculum for K-8 students. However, there have been significant
barriers to creating and deploying a Computer Science curriculum in many areas,
including teacher time and the prioritization of other 21st-century skills. At
McMaster University, we have developed both general computer literacy
activities and specific programming activities. Integration of these activities
is made easy as they each support existing curricular goals. In this paper, we
focus on programming in the functional language Elm and the graphics library
GraphicSVG. Elm is in the ML (Meta Language) family, with a lean syntax and
easy inclusion of Domain Specific Languages. This allows children to start
experimenting with GraphicSVG as a language for describing shape, and pick up
the core Elm language as they grow in sophistication. Teachers see children
making connections between computer graphics and mathematics within the first
hour. Graphics are defined declaratively, and support aggregation and
transformation, i.e., Algebra. Variables are not needed initially, but are
introduced as a time-saving feature, which is immediately accepted. Since
variables are declarative, they match students' expectations. Advanced students
are also exposed to State by making programs that react to user taps or clicks.
The syntax required to do so closely follows the theoretical concepts, making
it easy for them to grasp. For each of these concepts, we explain how they fit
into the presentations we make to students, like the 5200 children taught in
2016.
  Finally, we describe ongoing work on a touch-based Elm editor for iPad, which
features (1) type highlighting (as opposed to syntax highlighting), (2)
preservation of correct syntax and typing across transformations, (3) context
information (e.g. displaying parameter names for GraphicSVG functions), and (4)
immediate feedback (e.g. restarting animations after every program change).

The Ehrhart polynomial $L_P$ of an integral polytope $P$ counts the number of
integer points in integral dilates of $P$. Ehrhart polynomials of polytopes are
often described in terms of their Ehrhart $h^*$-vector (aka Ehrhart
$\delta$-vector), which is the vector of coefficients of $L_P$ with respect to
a certain binomial basis and which coincides with the $h$-vector of a regular
unimodular triangulation of $P$ (if one exists). One important result by
Stanley about $h^*$-vectors of polytopes is that their entries are always
non-negative. However, recent combinatorial applications of Ehrhart theory give
rise to polytopal complexes with $h^*$-vectors that have negative entries.
  In this article we introduce the Ehrhart $f^*$-vector of polytopes or, more
generally, of polytopal complexes $K$. These are again coefficient vectors of
$L_K$ with respect to a certain binomial basis of the space of polynomials and
they have the property that the $f^*$-vector of a unimodular simplicial complex
coincides with its $f$-vector. The main result of this article is a counting
interpretation for the $f^*$-coefficients which implies that $f^*$-coefficients
of integral polytopal complexes are always non-negative integers. This holds
even if the polytopal complex does not have a unimodular triangulation and if
its $h^*$-vector does have negative entries. Our main technical tool is a new
partition of the set of lattice points in a simplicial cone into discrete
cones. Further results include a complete characterization of Ehrhart
polynomials of integral partial polytopal complexes and a non-negativity
theorem for the $f^*$-vectors of rational polytopal complexes.

text: We present an observational study designed to investigate potential correlations between cosmic ray distributions and interstellar magnetic fields. The enigmatic nature of cosmic rays and their interactions with galactic magnetic fields poses significant challenges in astrophysics, and addressing these challenges is crucial for understanding cosmic ray propagation and their origin. Employing data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope, we analyze the anisotropy in cosmic ray trajectories in relation to the Planck satellite's foreground magnetic field data. Our methodology involves cross-correlating high-energy cosmic ray arrival directions with magnetic field vectors derived from polarized dust emission maps. We focus on small and large angular scale structures, employing advanced statistical techniques, including power spectrum analysis and two-point correlation functions, to quantify the extent of alignment or misalignment between cosmic ray paths and magnetic field orientations. Our results reveal a statistically significant alignment at medium angular scales, suggesting the influence of galactic magnetic fields in orienting cosmic ray trajectories. Conversely, at small scales, we observe a lack of correlation, indicative of turbulence effects, which may randomize cosmic ray paths. These findings provide novel insights into the degree to which magnetic fields shape cosmic ray propagation, highlighting the potential for cosmic rays to act as probes of the interstellar medium's magneto-dynamic environment. Future work will extend this analysis to multi-wavelength magnetic data to refine our understanding of cosmic ray anisotropy and its relationship with the complex morphology of galactic magnetic fields.

text: The study of scalar fields in the context of anisotropic universes offers significant insights into the dynamics of the early universe and the characteristics of cosmic evolution. This research aims to investigate the behavior of scalar fields in anisotropic cosmological models, specifically exploring their role in driving cosmic acceleration and structure formation. Utilizing a combination of analytical and numerical methodologies, various anisotropic models, such as Bianchi-type universes, are examined under the influence of a scalar field with potential energy. The study employs Einstein's field equations and explores the stability of these models through perturbation techniques. Key findings reveal that scalar fields significantly impact the anisotropic expansion rates, with specific potential forms leading to isotropization of the universe under certain conditions. Additionally, the presence of a scalar field can enhance the anisotropic stress-energy contribution, altering the overall geometry and expansion dynamics. The results indicate that the interplay between scalar fields and anisotropy may provide a better understanding of the universe's evolution, with implications for both the inflationary paradigm and late-time acceleration phenomena. In conclusion, this research highlights the importance of incorporating scalar fields into anisotropic cosmological models, paving the way for future investigations into the complex interplay of fields and geometry in a universe that deviates from perfect isotropy.

A revolution in elementary particle physics occurred during the period from
the ICHEP1968 to the ICHEP1982 with the advent of the parton model from
discoveries in Deeply Inelastic electron-proton Scattering at SLAC, neutrino
experiments, hard-scattering observed in p$+$p collisions at the CERN ISR, the
development of QCD, the discovery of the J/$\Psi$ at BNL and SLAC and the clear
observation of high transverse momentum jets at the CERN SPS $\bar{p}+p$
collider. These and other discoveries in this period led to the acceptance of
QCD as the theory of the strong interactions. The desire to understand nuclear
physics at high density such as in neutron stars led to the application of QCD
to this problem and to the prediction of a Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) in nuclei
at high energy density and temperatures. This eventually led to the
construction of the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at BNL to observe
superdense nuclear matter in the laboratory. This article discusses how
experimental methods and results which confirmed QCD at the first hadron
collider, the CERN ISR, played an important role in experiments at the first
heavy ion collider, RHIC, leading to the discovery of the QGP as a perfect
liquid as well as discoveries at RHIC and the LHC which continue to the present
day.

text: The quantum reverse Shannon theorem investigates the fundamental limits of data compression in quantum communication channels. Building on the classical Shannon theory, which establishes the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted reliably over a noisy channel, the quantum version explores the analogous scenario but with quantum states. This abstract outlines the theoretical background, objectives, methodologies employed, key findings, and concludes with implications.  In recent years, significant progress has been made in understanding quantum data compression through the lens of the quantum reverse Shannon theorem. The theorem aims to determine the minimum amount of quantum communication required to transmit a quantum state from one party to another, even when errors are present. This study seeks to extend our understanding by analyzing various quantum channels and different forms of quantum information processing.  To achieve these goals, we developed a comprehensive framework that includes both classical and quantum information measures. Our approach involved rigorous mathematical derivations and simulations using quantum computational models. Key findings include the identification of optimal strategies for achieving the minimum communication requirements, as well as insights into the trade-offs between error rates and communication efficiency under different conditions.  The results highlight the importance of considering quantum coherence and entanglement in designing effective quantum communication protocols. Moreover, they underscore the potential for quantum technology to surpass classical methods in terms of information transmission reliability and efficiency. In conclusion, this research contributes valuable knowledge to the field of quantum information science, providing a solid foundation for future advancements in quantum communication technologies.

text: We investigate the subtractive renormalization of chiral potentials in nucleon-nucleon (NN) interactions up to next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) in higher partial waves. Our effort addresses the persistent issue of non-perturbative divergences that arise in the calculations of chiral effective field theory (EFT) at higher energies and partial waves, which can hinder the predictive power of the theory. We employ a subtractive renormalization procedure, which maintains the chiral symmetry inherent in the EFT framework while effectively handling divergences without introducing arbitrary cutoff dependence. Our methodology involves constructing the on-shell scattering matrix from the chiral NN potential, followed by the systematic application of the subtractive renormalization scheme. We derive analytical expressions for the renormalized T-matrix up to NNLO and test its convergence properties in the context of higher partial waves, particularly those beyond the S-waves, for various NN channels. Our results demonstrate improved convergence and stability across the examined energy ranges and partial waves, compared to traditional renormalization techniques. Furthermore, our approach provides a systematic path to extend these calculations to higher orders in perturbation theory without compromising the consistency with low-energy QCD constraints. The findings suggest that the subtractive renormalization could serve as a robust tool for refining chiral potentials in NN interactions, potentially enhancing their applicability in nuclear structure and reaction calculations. This work paves the way for more accurate and reliable theoretical predictions in nuclear physics research.

text: We employed an alternating optimization approach to integrate genetic and environmental factors in a genome-wide association study (GWAS) framework, specifically targeting the interactions between genetic variants and environmental exposures. Our method, termed weighted genetic and environmental (WGE) modeling, leverages a weighted sum of genetic and environmental scores to predict phenotypic outcomes, thereby accounting for the complex interplay between genetic predispositions and environmental influences.   We applied this WGE modeling framework to the MAVAN (Multigenerational Assessment of Variability Among Natives) study, a comprehensive dataset of twins and family members with varying levels of environmental exposure. Our results indicate that the alternating optimization approach successfully integrated genetic and environmental factors, yielding more accurate predictions of phenotypic outcomes compared to traditional GWAS models.   Notably, the WGE model demonstrated a significant improvement in predictive power for complex traits, such as cognitive function and behavioral disorders, which are influenced by both genetic and environmental factors. The alternating optimization approach also enabled the identification of novel genetic variants and environmental exposures that contribute to these complex traits, providing new insights into the underlying mechanisms. Our findings have significant implications for the development of personalized medicine approaches, where genetic and environmental factors are integrated to inform treatment decisions.

text: This study investigates the limits of atomic entanglement induced by cavity-feedback in a two-level atom, transitioning from weak to strong coupling regimes. Background research highlights the importance of entanglement in quantum information processing and the role of cavity-feedback in enhancing entanglement dynamics. However, the interplay between cavity-feedback and entanglement remains poorly understood, particularly in the strong coupling regime.   The objective of this research is to explore the effects of cavity-feedback on entanglement dynamics, shedding light on the limits of entanglement in the weak and strong coupling regimes. To achieve this, a theoretical framework is developed, incorporating the effects of cavity-feedback on the atomic system, including dissipation and non-linear interactions. The framework is applied to a two-level atom, and the resulting entanglement dynamics are analyzed in both the weak and strong coupling regimes.  Key findings indicate that cavity-feedback significantly enhances entanglement dynamics, particularly in the strong coupling regime. However, the optimal entanglement generation is found to be limited by the presence of dissipation and non-linear interactions. The results also reveal a critical threshold beyond which the entanglement dynamics become unstable. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the cavity-feedback regime exhibits unique characteristics, such as entanglement squeezing and non-classical correlations, which are absent in the weak coupling regime.  In conclusion, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the limits of atomic entanglement induced by cavity-feedback, highlighting the importance of considering dissipation and non-linear interactions in the strong coupling regime. The findings have significant implications for the development of quantum information processing technologies, including quantum computing and quantum communication.

text: The discrepancy in the microlensing optical depth toward the Galactic Bulge has been an enduring challenge in astrophysical research, raising questions about the distribution and population of stellar objects in this region. This study aims to address this issue by reassessing stellar number counts, which are crucial for accurately determining microlensing parameters. Using advanced statistical methods and revised stellar census data from contemporary surveys, we analyze the density and distribution of stars in the Galactic Bulge. Our methodology involves comparing traditional models of stellar populations with new observational data, focusing on factors such as extinction and crowding effects that may have skewed previous counts. Key findings indicate that incorporating recent advancements in photometric techniques and accounting for variable stellar populations significantly alters the estimated optical depth values. Contrary to most machine learning models, modern deep artificial neural
networks typically include multiple components that contribute to
regularization. Despite the fact that some (explicit) regularization
techniques, such as weight decay and dropout, require costly fine-tuning of
sensitive hyperparameters, the interplay between them and other elements that
provide implicit regularization is not well understood yet. Shedding light upon
these interactions is key to efficiently using computational resources and may
contribute to solving the puzzle of generalization in deep learning. Here, we
first provide formal definitions of explicit and implicit regularization that
help understand essential differences between techniques. Second, we contrast
data augmentation with weight decay and dropout. Our results show that visual
object categorization models trained with data augmentation alone achieve the
same performance or higher than models trained also with weight decay and
dropout, as is common practice. We conclude that the contribution on
generalization of weight decay and dropout is not only superfluous when
sufficient implicit regularization is provided, but also such techniques can
dramatically deteriorate the performance if the hyperparameters are not
carefully tuned for the architecture and data set. In contrast, data
augmentation systematically provides large generalization gains and does not
require hyperparameter re-tuning. In view of our results, we suggest to
optimize neural networks without weight decay and dropout to save computational
resources, hence carbon emissions, and focus more on data augmentation and
other inductive biases to improve performance and robustness.

We present a new method of Stokes inversion of spectropolarimetric data and
evaluate it by taking the example of a SUNRISE/IMaX observation. An archive of
synthetic Stokes profiles is obtained by the spectral synthesis of
state-of-the-art magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations and a realistic
degradation to the level of the observed data. The definition of a merit
function allows the archive to be searched for the synthetic Stokes profiles
that match the observed profiles best. In contrast to traditional Stokes
inversion codes, which solve the Unno-Rachkovsky equations for the polarized
radiative transfer numerically and fit the Stokes profiles iteratively, the new
technique provides the full set of atmospheric parameters. This gives us the
ability to start an MHD simulation that takes the inversion result as initial
condition. After a relaxation process of half an hour solar time we obtain
physically consistent MHD data sets with a target similar to the observation.
The new MHD simulation is used to repeat the method in a second iteration,
which further improves the match between observation and simulation, resulting
in a factor of 2.2 lower mean $\chi^2$ value. One advantage of the new
technique is that it provides the physical parameters on a geometrical height
scale. It constitutes a first step towards inversions giving results consistent
with the MHD equations.

text: We investigated the radiative processes of two entangled atoms located outside a Schwarzschild black hole, exploring the intricate interplay between gravitational radiation and quantum entanglement. Through a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we modeled the behavior of the entangled atoms in the vicinity of the event horizon, where strong gravitational curvature and intense radiation dominate.  Our results indicate that the entangled atoms exhibit non-classical behavior, exhibiting correlations that are not bound by the principles of classical physics. We found that the presence of the black hole induces a significant modification of the atoms' energy levels, leading to a substantial increase in the entanglement entropy. Furthermore, our simulations reveal that the radiative processes of the atoms are strongly influenced by the black hole's gravitational radiation, which generates a complex network of quantum correlations.  We employed a modified version of the Riemann-symmetric quantum field theory, which accounts for the non-linear effects of gravitational radiation on the entangled atoms. Our numerical simulations utilized a combination of the Wigner function and the density matrix formalism, allowing us to accurately capture the non-classical behavior of the entangled atoms. By comparing our results with those obtained in the absence of the black hole, we demonstrate that the presence of the event horizon has a profound impact on the radiative processes of the entangled atoms, leading to the emergence of novel quantum phenomena.

text: In this study, we conduct fully resolved numerical simulations to dissect the intricacies of solidification, residual stresses, and nozzle dynamics in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM). Our objective is to elucidate the physical processes and interactions between deposition and thermal solidification, which influence the final structural properties of printed materials. The simulation framework integrates a coupled thermal-fluid-solid model to capture the multi-physics environment during FDM. By resolving the transient heat transfer and solidification phenomena, we provide insights into how cooling rates and thermal gradients contribute to residual stress formation and potential warping in printed layers. We further explore nozzle behavior and its influence on material deposition, examining aspects such as temperature distribution, flow uniformity, and shear effects on layer adhesion. Through parametric studies, we assess how variations in nozzle velocity, extrusion temperature, and ambient conditions affect solidification and mechanical integrity. Results demonstrate that optimized nozzle parameters can significantly mitigate adverse stress accumulation and enhance layer consistency. Comparisons with experimental observations validate our model's predictive capability, reinforcing the importance of precise control over deposition parameters for improved FDM outcomes. This comprehensive approach advances our understanding of the solidification dynamics in FDM, providing a foundation for developing improved fabrication strategies that minimize defects and enhance the mechanical performance of printed components. Our findings contribute to the strategic design of FDM processes, offering guidelines for achieving superior material quality and structural reliability in additive manufacturing applications.

This work focuses on the dynamics of a train of unconfined bubbles flowing in
microchan- nels. We investigate the transverse position of a train of bubbles,
its velocity and the associated pressure drop when flowing in a microchannel
depending on the internal forces due to viscosity, inertia and capillarity.
Despite the small scales of the system, inertia, referred to as inertial
migration force, play a crucial role in determining the transverse equilibrium
position of the bubbles. Beside inertia and viscosity, other effects may also
affect the transverse migration of bubbles such as the Marangoni surface
stresses and the surface deformability. We look at the influence of surfactants
in the limit of infinite Marangoni effect which yields rigid bubble interface.
The resulting migration force may balance external body forces if present such
as buoyancy, Dean or magnetic ones. This balance not only determines the
transverse position of the bubbles but, consequently, the surrounding flow
structure, which can be determinant for any mass/heat transfer process
involved. Finally, we look at the influence of the bubble deformation on the
equilibrium position and compare it to the inertial migration force at the
centred position, explaining the stable or unstable character of this position
accordingly. A systematic study of the influence of the parameters - such as
the bubble size, uniform body force, Reynolds and capillary numbers - has been
carried out using numerical simulations based on the Finite Element Method,
solving the full steady Navier-Stokes equations and its asymptotic counterpart
for the limits of small Reynolds and/or capillary numbers.

This document provides a writeup of all contributions to the workshop on
"High precision measurements of $\alpha_s$: From LHC to FCC-ee" held at CERN,
Oct. 12--13, 2015. The workshop explored in depth the latest developments on
the determination of the QCD coupling $\alpha_s$ from 15 methods where high
precision measurements are (or will be) available. Those include low-energy
observables: (i) lattice QCD, (ii) pion decay factor, (iii) quarkonia and (iv)
$\tau$ decays, (v) soft parton-to-hadron fragmentation functions, as well as
high-energy observables: (vi) global fits of parton distribution functions,
(vii) hard parton-to-hadron fragmentation functions, (viii) jets in $e^\pm$p
DIS and $\gamma$-p photoproduction, (ix) photon structure function in
$\gamma$-$\gamma$, (x) event shapes and (xi) jet cross sections in $e^+e^-$
collisions, (xii) W boson and (xiii) Z boson decays, and (xiv) jets and (xv)
top-quark cross sections in proton-(anti)proton collisions. The current status
of the theoretical and experimental uncertainties associated to each extraction
method, the improvements expected from LHC data in the coming years, and future
perspectives achievable in $e^+e^-$ collisions at the Future Circular Collider
(FCC-ee) with $\cal{O}$(1--100 ab$^{-1}$) integrated luminosities yielding
10$^{12}$ Z bosons and jets, and 10$^{8}$ W bosons and $\tau$ leptons, are
thoroughly reviewed. The current uncertainty of the (preliminary) 2015 strong
coupling world-average value, $\alpha_s(m_Z)$ = 0.1177 $\pm$ 0.0013, is about
1\%. Some participants believed this may be reduced by a factor of three in the
near future by including novel high-precision observables, although this
opinion was not universally shared. At the FCC-ee facility, a factor of ten
reduction in the $\alpha_s$ uncertainty should be possible, mostly thanks to
the huge Z and W data samples available.

text: We report on multi-frequency observations of the afterglow of the short-duration gamma-ray burst (GRB) 130427A, obtained from 1 GHz to 1016 GHz. Our observations span a period from 2 hours to 10 days post-burst. Initially, the radio emission was detected at 15 GHz with the Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) technique, and later at 1, 4.8, 8, 22, and 43 GHz using the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA). The initial radio emission was bright and peaked at 8 hours, consistent with synchrotron emission from shocked ejecta.  Further analysis of the early radio light curve revealed a spectral index evolution with time, indicating a changing emission mechanism. The early spectral index evolution could not be explained solely by synchrotron cooling or aging. Instead, we propose the presence of an additional component, likely synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) emission, contributing to the broadband emission. This component is expected to appear after the cooling synchrotron emission has decayed.  At later times, the radio emission became more diffuse, and the spectral index flattened. We suggest that this could be due to a transition from a relativistic shocked ejecta to a non-relativistic interstellar medium interaction. The late-time spectral flattening was also observed at higher energies, indicating a link between the radio and high-energy emission. Our results contribute to the ongoing investigation of the physical processes occurring in the afterglows of short GRBs. The detection and analysis of the SSC component provide valuable insights into the underlying physics and allow for improved models and predictions.
