text: Quasimorphisms are important tools in the study of group theory as they provide insights into the algebraic structure of groups. This paper explores a novel family of quasimorphisms constructed from various group-theoretic approaches. The objective is to develop a comprehensive framework that highlights the relationships and interplay between different types of quasimorphisms and their applications in pure and applied mathematics. We employ a combination of topological and combinatorial methods to construct these quasimorphisms, including the use of symmetries and invariants derived from group actions. Our key findings reveal new classes of quasimorphisms that yield greater flexibility in manipulation and application across diverse groups, including free groups, nilpotent groups, and certain classes of Lie groups. Additionally, we demonstrate that these constructions exhibit unique properties, such as bounded divergence and stability under various operations, which were not previously understood in conventional frameworks. The implications of this research extend to areas such as geometric topology and mathematical physics, where quasimorphisms play a crucial role in understanding the dynamics of systems. text: In this study, we present a novel approach to stable Gabor phase retrieval and spectral clustering. To achieve stability, we introduce a novel loss function, which employs a combination of L1 and L2 regularization terms and a unique Gabor phase constraint. This constraint ensures a consistent phase relationship between Gabor coefficients, ensuring the stability of the solution.  Subsequently, we apply spectral clustering to the extracted features to identify distinct clusters within the data. We use normalized cuts, as they provide an effective way to separate dense clusters from sparse background and preserve the cluster structure. The efficiency of our proposed approach is demonstrated via extensive experimental evaluation using various datasets, where we observe significant improvements in accuracy and stability compared to existing methods. Furthermore, our work reveals valuable insights into the benefits of utilizing both Gabor phase retrieval and spectral clustering techniques for analyzing complex data, paving the way for future research in related domains.

The High Efficiency and Resolution Multi Element Spectrograph, HERMES, is a
facility-class optical spectrograph for the Anglo-Australian Telescope (AAT).
It is designed primarily for Galactic Archaeology, the first major attempt to
create a detailed understanding of galaxy formation and evolution by studying
the history of our own galaxy, the Milky Way. The goal of the GALAH survey is
to reconstruct the mass assembly history of the Milky Way through a detailed
chemical abundance study of one million stars. The spectrograph is based at the
AAT and is fed by the existing 2dF robotic fiber positioning system. The
spectrograph uses volume phase holographic gratings to achieve a spectral
resolving power of 28,000 in standard mode and also provides a high-resolution
mode ranging between 40,000 and 50,000 using a slit mask. The GALAH survey
requires an SNR greater than 100 for a star brightness of V ?= 14 in an
exposure time of one hour. The total spectral coverage of the four channels is
about 100 nm between 370 and 1000 nm for up to 392 simultaneous targets within
the 2-degree field of view. HERMES has been commissioned over three runs,
during bright time in October, November, and December 2013, in parallel with
the beginning of the GALAH pilot survey, which started in November 2013. We
present the first-light results from the commissioning run and the beginning of
the GALAH survey, including performance results such as throughput and
resolution, as well as instrument reliability.

text: We present an adaptive mixed Generalized Multiscale Finite Element Method (GMsFEM) tailored for simulating fluid flows in heterogeneous media. Our work addresses the challenge posed by complex subsurface structures, which often exhibit significant variability that traditional numerical methods struggle to accommodate. By integrating adaptive refinement strategies, we enhance both the accuracy and computational efficiency of the GMsFEM framework for capturing flow dynamics across variable scales.  Utilizing a systematic approach, we derive multiscale basis functions that efficiently represent solutions in regions of high heterogeneity. We implement an adaptive algorithm that strategically refines the computational mesh based on a posteriori error estimates, focusing computational resources on areas necessitating greater resolution. The methodology incorporates mixed finite element formulations, facilitating accurate pressure and velocity field representation while ensuring mass conservation.  We validate our approach against established benchmarks in porous media flow and demonstrate that our adaptive mixed GMsFEM significantly outperforms conventional methods in terms of convergence rates and computational cost, especially in the presence of pronounced heterogeneities. Our numerical experiments reveal that the adaptive strategy not only reduces the overall computational time but also enhances the predictive capability of flow behavior in complex geological settings. Through this research, we establish a robust framework for simulating heterogeneous media flows, paving the way for improved modeling in fields such as hydrology, petroleum engineering, and environmental management.

We study spinless electrons in a single channel quantum wire interacting
through attractive interaction, and the quantum Hall states that may be
constructed by an array of such wires. For a single wire the electrons may form
two phases, the Luttinger liquid and the strongly paired phase. The Luttinger
liquid is gapless to one- and two-electron excitations, while the strongly
paired state is gapped to the former and gapless to the latter. In contrast to
the case in which the wire is proximity-coupled to an external superconductor,
for an isolated wire there is no separate phase of a topological, weakly
paired, superconductor. Rather, this phase is adiabatically connected to the
Luttinger liquid phase. The properties of the one dimensional topological
superconductor emerge when the number of channels in the wire becomes large.
The quantum Hall states that may be formed by an array of single-channel wires
depend on the Landau level filling factors. For odd-denominator fillings
$\nu=1/(2n+1)$, wires at the Luttinger phase form Laughlin states while wires
in the strongly paired phase form bosonic fractional quantum Hall state of
strongly-bound pairs at a filling of $1/(8n+4)$. The transition between the two
is of the universality class of Ising transitions in three dimensions. For
even-denominator fractions $\nu=1/2n$ the two single-wire phases translate into
four quantum Hall states. Two of those states are bosonic fractional quantum
Hall states of weakly- and strongly- bound pairs of electrons. The other two
are non-Abelian quantum Hall states, which originate from coupling wires close
to their critical point. One of these non-Abelian states is the Moore-Read
state. The transition between all these states are of the universality class of
Majorana transitions. We point out some of the properties that characterize the
different phases and the phase transitions.

We present simultaneous HST WFC3 + Spitzer IRAC variability monitoring for
the highly-variable young ($\sim$20 Myr) planetary-mass object PSO J318.5-22.
Our simultaneous HST + Spitzer observations covered $\sim$2 rotation periods
with Spitzer and most of a rotation period with HST. We derive a period of
8.6$\pm$0.1 hours from the Spitzer lightcurve. Combining this period with the
measured $v sin i$ for this object, we find an inclination of 56.2$\pm
8.1^{\circ}$. We measure peak-to-trough variability amplitudes of
3.4$\pm$0.1$\%$ for Spitzer Channel 2 and 4.4 - 5.8$\%$ (typical 68$\%$
confidence errors of $\sim$0.3$\%$) in the near-IR bands (1.07-1.67 $\mu$m)
covered by the WFC3 G141 prism -- the mid-IR variability amplitude for PSO
J318.5-22 one of the highest variability amplitudes measured in the mid-IR for
any brown dwarf or planetary mass object. Additionally, we detect phase offsets
ranging from 200--210$^{\circ}$ (typical error of $\sim$4$^{\circ}$) between
synthesized near-IR lightcurves and the Spitzer mid-IR lightcurve, likely
indicating depth-dependent longitudinal atmospheric structure in this
atmosphere. The detection of similar variability amplitudes in wide spectral
bands relative to absorption features suggests that the driver of the
variability may be inhomogeneous clouds (perhaps a patchy haze layer over thick
clouds), as opposed to hot spots or compositional inhomogeneities at the
top-of-atmosphere level.

text: In the context of Turkey's volatile energy market, accurately forecasting electricity tariff prices is crucial for stakeholders, including policymakers, energy providers, and consumers. This research examines various electricity tariff price forecasting techniques and explores the impact of different time series periods on prediction accuracy. We evaluated multiple forecasting models, including traditional statistical methods such as ARIMA, advanced machine learning techniques like support vector regression (SVR), and neural networks, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Historical electricity tariff price data from the Turkish energy market were analyzed over different time series periods to identify trends and fluctuations. Our evaluation criteria focused on model accuracy, computational efficiency, and adaptability to varying time frames. The key findings indicate that while all methods demonstrate some level of proficiency in forecasting, LSTM networks consistently outperformed other models in capturing complex patterns and providing more accurate projections. However, the performance varied significantly with different time series periods, with shorter periods resulting in higher accuracy across most models. This suggests that the choice of time series period is a critical factor influencing the effectiveness of forecasting models. The study concludes that while LSTM networks represent a promising approach for electricity tariff forecasting in Turkey, the integration of multiple models and optimization of time series periods could enhance prediction accuracy. These insights provide valuable guidance for energy stakeholders aiming to optimize forecasting practices, thereby contributing to more informed decision-making in the energy sector.

literature search with the word 'spondylolisthesis', and updated till September
18, 2016. We selected original research data involving surgical treatment of
degenerative spondylolisthesis, and in total there were n articles, including

China (n=5 series), and ROC (Taiwan, n=3 series), America (n=20 series), Europe
(n=23 series). The mean age of each study were extracted and used a single
entry. We tried our best to filter out double/multiple reported data. Our
results showed the median age of degenerative spondylolisthesis patients
underwent surgical treatment was 66 years in Japan, 60 years in South Korea, 59

Surveys of the binary populations in the solar neighbourhood have shown that
the periods of G- and M-type stars are log-normally distributed. However,
observations of young binary populations suggest a log-uniform distribution.
Clearly some process(es) change the period distribution over time. Most stars
form in star clusters, in which two important dynamical processes occur: i)
gas-induced orbital decay of embedded binary systems and ii) destruction of
soft binaries in three-body interactions. The emphasis here is on orbital decay
which has been largely neglected so far. Using a combination of Monte-Carlo and
dynamical nbody modelling it is demonstrated here that the cluster dynamics
destroys the number of wide binaries, but leaves short-period binaries
basically undisturbed even for a initially log-uniform distribution. By
contrast orbital decay significantly reduces the number and changes the
properties of short-period binaries, but leaves wide binaries largely
uneffected. Until now it was unclear whether the short period distribution of
the field is unaltered since its formation. It is shown here, that orbital
decay is a prime candidate for such a task. In combination the dynamics of
these two processes, convert an initial log-uniform distribution to a
log-normal period distribution. The probability is 94% that the evolved and
observed period distribution were sampled from the same parent distribution.
This means binaries can be formed with periods that are sampled from the
log-uniform distribution. As the cluster evolves, short-period binaries are
merged to single stars by the gas-induced orbital decay while the dynamical
evolution in the cluster destroys wide binaries. The combination of these two
equally important processes reshapes a initial log-uniform period distribution
to the log-normal period distribution, that is observed in the field
(abridged).

We study actions for massive bosonic particles of higher spins by
dimensionally reducing an action for massless particles. For the latter we take
a model with a SO(N) extended local supersymmetry on the worldline, that is
known to describe massless (conformal) particles of higher spins in flat
spacetimes of even dimensions. Dimensional reduction produces an action for
massive spinning particles in odd dimensions. The field equations that emerge
in a quantization a la Dirac are shown to be equivalent to the Fierz-Pauli
ones. The massless limit generates a multiplet of massless states with higher
spins, whose first quantized field equations have a geometric form with fields
belonging to various types of Young tableaux. These geometric equations can be
partially integrated to show their equivalence with the standard
Fronsdal-Labastida equations. We covariantize our model to check whether an
extension to curved spacetimes can be achieved. Restricting to (A)dS spaces, we
find that the worldline gauge algebra becomes nonlinear, but remains first
class. This guarantees consistency on such backgrounds. A light cone analysis
confirms the presence of the expected propagating degrees of freedom. A
covariant analysis is worked out explicitly for the massive case, which is seen
to give rise to the Fierz-Pauli equations extended to (A)dS spaces. It is worth
noting that in D=3 the massless limit of our model when N goes to infinity has
the same field content of the Vasiliev's theory that accommodates each spin
exactly once.

We develop a numerical code to compute gravitational waves induced by a
particle moving on eccentric inclined orbits around a Kerr black hole. For such
systems, the black hole perturbation method is applicable. The gravitational
waves can be evaluated by solving the Teukolsky equation with a point like
source term, which is computed from the stress-energy tensor of a test particle
moving on generic bound geodesic orbits. In our previous papers, we computed
the homogeneous solutions of the Teukolsky equation using a formalism developed
by Mano, Suzuki and Takasugi and showed that we could compute gravitational
waves efficiently and very accurately in the case of circular orbits on the
equatorial plane. Here, we apply this method to eccentric inclined orbits. The
geodesics around a Kerr black hole have three constants of motion: energy,
angular momentum and the Carter constant. We compute the rates of change of the
Carter constant as well as those of energy and angular momentum. This is the
first time that the rate of change of the Carter constant has been evaluated
accurately. We also treat the case of highly eccentric orbits with $e=0.9$. To
confirm the accuracy of our codes, several tests are performed. We find that
the accuracy is only limited by the truncation of $\ell$-, $k$- and $n$-modes,
where $\ell$ is the index of the spin-weighted spheroidal harmonics, and $n$
and $k$ are the harmonics of the radial and polar motion, respectively. When we
set the maximum of $\ell$ to 20, we obtain a relative accuracy of $10^{-5}$
even in the highly eccentric case of $e=0.9$. The accuracy is better for lower
eccentricity. Our numerical code is expected to be useful for computing
templates of the extreme mass ratio inspirals, which is one of the main targets
of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA).

text: In this study, we compare various indicators used to determine the orientation of quasars, aiming to enhance our understanding of their accretion disk structures and black hole spins. We evaluate the effectiveness of polarization measurements, spectral energy distribution (SED) analysis, and kinematical parameters derived from multi-wavelength imaging data. The problem we address is the inherent complexity in accurately measuring quasar orientations due to the obscured nature of these sources and the limitations of current observational techniques. Our methodology involves cross-calibrating these indicators across multiple quasars, employing statistical methods to identify correlations and discrepancies between them. Results indicate that while polarization measurements are highly reliable, they are often limited by the quality and coverage of polarimetric observations. SED analysis, on the other hand, offers robust insights into the physical conditions within the quasar, but its interpretation can be influenced by dust extinction. Kinematical parameters, derived from high-resolution spectroscopy, provide detailed information about the motion of gas in the quasar, which is crucial for estimating spin orientations. Combining these indicators, we propose a novel approach that integrates their strengths to achieve more comprehensive assessments of quasar orientations, thereby advancing our comprehension of quasar dynamics and black hole physics.

Background: The interacting boson model (IBM) has been used extensively to
calculate the matrix elements governing neutrinoless double-beta decay. Studies
within other models indicate that a good description of neutron-proton pairing
is essential for accurate calculations of those matrix elements. The usual
interacting boson model is based only on like-particle pairs, however, and the
extent to which it captures neutron-proton pairing is not clear.
  Purpose: To determine whether neutron-proton pairing should be explicitly
included as neutron-proton bosons in IBM calculations of neutrinoless
double-beta decay matrix elements.
  Method: An isospin-invariant version of the nucleon-pair shell model is
applied to carry out shell-model calculations in a large space and in a
collective subspace, and to define effective operators in the latter. A
democratic mapping is then used to define corresponding boson operators for the
IBM, with and without an isoscalar neutron-proton pair boson.
  Results: IBM calculations with and without the isoscalar boson are carried
out for nuclei near the beginning of the $pf$ shell, with a realistic
shell-model Hamiltonian and neutrinoless double-beta-decay operator as the
starting point. Energy spectra and double-beta matrix elements are compared to
those obtained in the underlying shell model.
  Conclusions: The isoscalar boson does not improve energy spectra but does
improve double-beta matrix elements. To be useful at the level of precision we
need, the mapping procedure must be further developed to better determine the
dependence of the boson Hamiltonian and decay operator on particle number and
isospin. But the benefits provided by the isoscalar boson suggest that through
an appropriate combination of mappings and fitting, it would make IBM matrix
elements more accurate for the heavier nuclei used in experiments.

text: In this study, we investigate the ion energy distributions (IEDs) of acetylene-argon plasmas interacting with a biased substrate electrode during the deposition of diamond-like carbon (DLC). We aim to elucidate the influence of bias voltage on the ionization dynamics and energy characteristics of the plasma, which are crucial for optimizing DLC film properties. We employed mass spectrometry and Langmuir probe diagnostics to meticulously measure the IEDs under varying bias conditions across a range of acetylene concentrations. Our results reveal significant variations in ion energy, with higher bias voltages promoting increased ionization and acceleration effects that contribute to a pronounced tail in the IEDs. This behavior correlates with the observed enhancement in film hardness and adhesion quality, which confirms the hypothesis that controlling ion energy is paramount in tailoring DLC characteristics. Additionally, our analysis highlights the role of argon as both a carrier gas and energy modulator, influencing ion species distribution and energy transfer mechanisms within the plasma. We further explored the relationship between substrate bias, ion energy, and film microstructure, employing Raman spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy to assess resultant film properties. This work provides a deeper understanding of how substrate bias influences ion dynamics in plasma systems, ultimately contributing to the fields of materials science and surface engineering, particularly in optimizing the deposition processes of DLC films for diverse technological applications.

Given existing empirical spectral patterns of excited hadrons it has been
suggested that chiral symmetry is approximately restored in excited hadrons at
zero temperature/density (effective symmetry restoration). If correct, this
implies that mass generation mechanisms and physics in excited hadrons is very
different as compared to the lowest states. One needs an alternative and
independent experimental information to confirm this conjecture. Using very
general chiral symmetry arguments it is shown that strict chiral restoration in
a given excited nucleon forbids its decay into the N \pi channel. Hence those
excited nucleons which are assumed from the spectroscopic patterns to be in
approximate chiral multiplets must only "weakly" decay into the N \pi channel,
(f_{N^*N\pi}/f_{NN\pi})^2 << 1. However, those baryons which have no chiral
partner must decay strongly with a decay constant comparable with f_{NN\pi}.
Decay constants can be extracted from the existing decay widths and branching
ratios. It turnes out that for all those well established excited nucleons
which can be classified into chiral doublets N_+(1440) - N_-(1535), N_+(1710) -
N_-(1650), N_+(1720) - N_-(1700), N_+(1680) - N_-(1675), N_+(2220) - N_-(2250),
N_+(?) - N_-(2190), N_+(?) - N_-(2600), the ratio is (f_{N^*N\pi}/f_{NN\pi})^2
~ 0.1 or much smaller for the high-spin states. In contrast, the only well
established excited nucleon for which the chiral partner cannot be identified
from the spectroscopic data, N(1520), has a decay constant into the N\pi
channel that is comparable with f_{NN\pi}. This gives an independent
experimental verification of the chiral symmetry restoration scenario.

text: A significant challenge in large-scale distributed systems is efficiently estimating the diameter of networks. Diameter is the longest shortest path between any two nodes in a network. We present a distributed algorithm, DS-Diameter, for estimating the diameter of a strongly connected distributed network. Our methodology is based on a novel network decomposition technique called Distributed Strong Diameter Decomposition (DSDD). The DS-Diameter algorithm constructs a tree structure rooted at a randomly selected node using a modified version of the classic breadth-first search algorithm. Simultaneously, we use the DSDD decomposition to partition the network into smaller components, and each partition is assigned to a distinct node. When a node receives a diameter estimate from all other partitions, it calculates a local estimate by combining the minimum and maximum estimates from the partitions and returns the result to the entire system. We evaluate the performance of DS-Diameter using simulations on synthetic datasets. Results demonstrate that DS-Diameter outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by achieving faster convergence and lower estimation error in large-scale strongly connected distributed networks. This research contributes significantly to the development of efficient distributed algorithms for network diameter estimation, which has important applications in various domains such as telecommunications, transportation systems, and social networks.

In this paper we prove the Kneser-Poulsen conjecture for the case of large
radii. Namely, if a finite number of points in Euclidean space $E^n$ is
rearranged so that the distance between each pair of points does not decrease,
then there exists a positive number $r_0$ that depends on the rearrangement of
the points, such that if we consider $n$-dimensional balls of radius $r>r_0$
with centers at these points, then the volume of the union (intersection) of
the balls before the rearrangement is not less (not greater) than the volume of
the union (intersection) after the rearrangement. Moreover, the inequality is
strict whenever the new point set is not congruent to the original one. Also
under the same conditions we prove a similar result about surface volumes
instead of volumes.
  In order to prove the above mentioned results we use ideas from tensegrity
theory to strengthen the theorem of Sudakov, R. Alexander and Capoyleas and
Pach, which says that the mean width of the convex hull of a finite number of
points does not decrease after an expansive rearrangement of those points. In
this paper we show that the mean width increases strictly, unless the expansive
rearrangement was a congruence.
  We also show that if the configuration of centers of the balls is fixed and
the volume of the intersection of the balls is considered as a function of the
radius $r$, then the second highest term in the asymptotic expansion of this
function is equal to $-M_n r^{n-1}$, where $M_n$ is the mean width of the
convex hall of the centers. This theorem was conjectured by Balazs Csikos in
2009.

text: In this study, we investigate the temporal aspect in identifying influential bloggers. Using a dataset of blog posts and engagement metrics from various bloggers, we aim to address the problem of determining the temporal influence of bloggers on specific topics. Our results indicate that the timing of blog posts significantly impacts their influence, with posts published at certain times garnering higher engagement rates. We introduce a novel methodology that incorporates time-based algorithms to analyze the temporal patterns of blog posts and their corresponding impact on audience engagement. By considering the time of publication as a crucial factor, we offer insights into optimizing the timing of blog posts to maximize influence. The findings emphasize the importance of not only the content but also the temporal dimension in the evaluation of influential bloggers. This research contributes to the understanding of temporal dynamics in social media influence and provides a framework for identifying influential bloggers based on when they publish their content. Our approach underscores the significance of time considerations for bloggers seeking to enhance their influence and reach a broader audience.

text: The interaction between quasiparticles in condensed matter systems, particularly exciton generation, is a topic of significant interest in the context of optoelectronic applications. This study focuses on the derivation of time-dependent transition probabilities for the transition from a one electron-hole pair ($1\mathrm{e}-1\mathrm{h}$) state to a two electron-hole pair ($2\mathrm{e}-2\mathrm{h}$) state under the influence of an external electromagnetic field. The objective is to understand the role of external perturbations in facilitating multiple exciton generation, a phenomenon essential for enhancing the efficiency of photovoltaic devices. Using time-dependent perturbation theory, the study develops an analytical framework to derive the transition probabilities, incorporating the effects of electromagnetic field strength and frequency. The methodology includes solving the Schrödinger equation with a time-dependent Hamiltonian representing the interaction of the electron-hole system with the electromagnetic field. Key findings indicate that the transition probability is highly sensitive to the field’s parameters, with resonance conditions leading to enhanced transition rates. Additionally, non-linear interactions facilitated by high-intensity fields significantly increase the likelihood of transitioning from $1\mathrm{e}-1\mathrm{h}$ to $2\mathrm{e}-2\mathrm{h}$ states. The results underscore the importance of electromagnetic field tuning in optimizing exciton generation processes. Conclusively, the study provides a theoretical foundation for experimental explorations aimed at improving material designs for photovoltaic and other optoelectronic devices through controlled multiple exciton generation.

Recently, the LIGO-Virgo collaboration reported their first detection of
gravitational wave (GW) signals from a low mass compact binary merger GW170817,
which is most likely due to a double neutron star (NS) merger. With the GW
signals only, the chirp mass of the binary is precisely constrained to
$1.188^{+0.004}_{-0.002}~\rm{M_{\odot}}$, but the mass ratio is loosely
constrained in the range $0.4-1$, so that a very rough estimation of the
individual NS masses ($0.86~{\rm M_{\odot}}<M_1<1.36~\rm{M_{\odot}}$ and
$1.36~{\rm M_{\odot}}<M_2<2.26~\rm{M_{\odot}}$) was obtained. Here we propose
that if one can constrain the dynamical ejecta mass through performing kilonova
modeling of the optical/IR data, by utilizing an empirical relation between the
dynamical ejecta mass and the mass ratio of NS binaries, one may place a more
stringent constraint on the mass ratio of the system. For instance, considering
that the red "kilonova" component is powered by the dynamical ejecta, we reach
a tight constraint on the mass ratio in the range of $0.46-0.59$.
Alternatively, if the blue "kilonova" component is powered by the dynamical
ejecta, the mass ratio would be constrained in the range of $0.53-0.67$.
Overall, such a multi-messenger approach could narrow down the mass ratio of
GW170817 system to the range of $0.46-0.67$, which gives a more precise
estimation of the individual NS mass than pure GW signal analysis, i.e.
$0.90~{\rm M_{\odot}}<M_1<1.16~{\rm M_{\odot}}$ and $1.61~{\rm
M_{\odot}}<M_2<2.11~{\rm M_{\odot}}$.

text: This study investigates the dynamics of off-equatorial orbits in strong gravitational fields near compact objects, with a focus on halo motion around magnetic compact stars and magnetized black holes. The background of this research is the understanding of the complex interactions between strong gravitational fields and the surrounding environment, particularly in the context of compact objects such as neutron stars and black holes. These objects are known to have strong magnetic fields and accretion disks that can significantly affect the motion of nearby objects.  The objective of this research is to explore the effects of magnetic fields on the motion of objects in off-equatorial orbits around compact stars and magnetized black holes. Using numerical simulations, we investigate the stability and evolution of these orbits, and how they interact with the surrounding environment, including the accretion disk and magnetic field.  Our results show that the presence of a strong magnetic field can significantly affect the motion of objects in off-equatorial orbits, leading to changes in their stability and evolution. We also find that the motion of these objects can be influenced by the accretion disk and the surrounding environment, leading to complex and chaotic dynamics. The implications of these findings are significant, as they provide new insights into the behavior of compact objects and their environments, and have important consequences for our understanding of the behavior of matter in extreme gravitational fields.

text: We investigate the Hilbert problem for a multiply connected circular domain, a fundamental problem in complex analysis, by employing a novel approach that combines numerical methods and topological insights. Our analysis reveals that the problem's solution is intimately linked to the topological properties of the domain, specifically its fundamental group. We demonstrate that the solution can be computed using a combination of numerical integration and topological invariants, providing a more efficient and accurate approach than existing methods.  In parallel, we examine the Hall effect in a plate, a phenomenon that arises from the interaction between a magnetic field and a current-carrying conductor. Our analysis reveals that the Hall effect can be understood as a consequence of the interaction between the magnetic field and the topological properties of the plate's surface. We develop a theoretical framework that incorporates the topological properties of the plate into the analysis of the Hall effect, providing a more comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon.  Our results demonstrate that the Hilbert problem for a multiply connected circular domain can be solved using a combination of numerical and topological methods, providing a more efficient and accurate approach than existing methods. Similarly, our analysis of the Hall effect reveals that the topological properties of the plate's surface play a crucial role in understanding this phenomenon. These findings have implications for a wide range of fields, including complex analysis, materials science, and electrical engineering.

In a communication network, point-to-point traffic volumes over time are
critical for designing protocols that route information efficiently and for
maintaining security, whether at the scale of an internet service provider or
within a corporation. While technically feasible, the direct measurement of
point-to-point traffic imposes a heavy burden on network performance and is
typically not implemented. Instead, indirect aggregate traffic volumes are
routinely collected. We consider the problem of estimating point-to-point
traffic volumes, x_t, from aggregate traffic volumes, y_t, given information
about the network routing protocol encoded in a matrix A. This estimation task
can be reformulated as finding the solutions to a sequence of ill-posed linear
inverse problems, y_t = A x_t, since the number of origin-destination routes of
interest is higher than the number of aggregate measurements available.
  Here, we introduce a novel multilevel state-space model of aggregate traffic
volumes with realistic features. We implement a naive strategy for estimating
unobserved point-to-point traffic volumes from indirect measurements of
aggregate traffic, based on particle filtering. We then develop a more
efficient two-stage inference strategy that relies on model-based
regularization: a simple model is used to calibrate regularization parameters
that lead to efficient and scalable inference in the multilevel state-space
model. We apply our methods to corporate and academic networks, where we show
that the proposed inference strategy outperforms existing approaches and scales
to larger networks. We also design a simulation study to explore the factors
that influence the performance. Our results suggest that model-based
regularization may be an efficient strategy for inference in other complex
multilevel models.

text: This research investigates the molecular cloud formation through the mechanism of thermal instability in finite resistive, viscous, radiating plasma, incorporating corrections for finite Larmor radius effects. The study begins by examining the theoretical framework that describes the thermal instability within such plasmas, considering both ideal and realistic conditions. Key objectives include elucidating how these corrections influence the onset and evolution of thermal instability, and thereby the formation of molecular clouds.  Methodologically, the research employs numerical simulations and analytical models to explore the dynamics of plasma under various parameters, including magnetic field strength, temperature gradients, and plasma resistivity. The simulations account for finite Larmor radius corrections, which are essential for accurately modeling plasmas with charged particles moving at relativistic speeds.  The results reveal that finite Larmor radius effects significantly alter the critical parameters required for thermal instability to occur, leading to a more robust and stable plasma environment. This finding has important implications for understanding the conditions under which molecular clouds can form in interstellar space. The study concludes that thermal instability remains a viable mechanism for molecular cloud formation, but its manifestation depends critically on plasma properties, particularly those related to finite Larmor radius effects.

We study the mass transfer rates and disk stability conditions of
ultracompact X-ray binaries (UCXBs) using empirical time-averaged X-ray
luminosities from Paper I (Cartwright et al. 2013) and compiled information
from the literature. The majority of UCXBs are consistent with evolutionary
tracks for white dwarf donors. Three UCXBs with orbital periods longer than 40
minutes have mass transfer rates above 10^{-10} Msun/year, inconsistent with
white dwarf donor tracks. We show that if helium star donors can retain their
initial high entropy, they can explain the observed mass transfer rates of
these UCXBs. Several UCXBs show persistent luminosities apparently below the
disk instability limit for irradiated He accretion disks. We point out that a
predominantly C and/or O disk (as observed in the optical spectra of several)
lowers the disk instability limit, explaining this disagreement. The orbital
period and low time-averaged mass transfer rate of 2S 0918-549 provide evidence
that the donor star is a low-entropy C/O white dwarf, consistent with optical
spectra. We combine existing information to constrain the masses of the donors
in 4U 1916-053 (0.064+-0.010 Msun) and 4U 1626-67 (<0.036 Msun for a 1.4 Msun
neutron star). We show that 4U 1626-67 is indeed persistent, and not undergoing
a transient outburst, leaving He star models as the best explanation for the
donor.

This paper describes a new method, HGV2C, for pattern analysis. The HGV2C
method involves the construction of a computer ego (CE) based on an individual
object that can be either a part of the system under analysis or a newly
created object based on a certain hypothesis. The CE provides a capability to
analyze data from a specific standpoint, e.g. from a viewpoint of a certain
object. The CE is constructed from two identical copies of a query object, and
its functioning mechanism involves: a hypothesis-parameter (HP) and
infothyristor (IT). HP is a parameter that is introduced into an existing set
of parameters. The HP value for one of the clones of a query object is set to
equal 1, whereas for another clone it is greater than 1. The IT is based on the
previously described algorithm of iterative averaging and performs three
functions: 1) computation of a similarity matrix for the group of three objects
including two clones of a query object and a target object; 2) division of the
group into two alternative subgroups; and 3) a successive increase of the HP
weight in the totality of all the parameters. Initially, both clones of the
query object appear together in one of the subgroups as all of their parameter
values, except the HP, are identical. At a certain point of the HP
multiplication, one of the clones moves to the group of the target object. A
respective number of the HP multiplications represents the dissimilarity (D)
between the query and target objects. The product of D multiplied by the
difference in HP values of the clones is strictly constant and linearly
increases as the difference in HP values of the clones decreases. This new
approach to knowledge representation is demonstrated on the example of
population pyramids of 220 countries.

text: This study investigates the slow quenching of star formation in cluster galaxies through the analysis of the LoCuSS (Local Universe Spectroscopic Survey) dataset. Cluster galaxies are known to exhibit reduced star formation rates compared to their field counterparts, and understanding the mechanisms driving this quenching is crucial for understanding galaxy evolution. The LoCuSS survey provides a unique opportunity to study the quenching process in a large sample of cluster galaxies, allowing for the identification of key factors influencing star formation.  The objective of this study is to examine the relationship between quenching and environmental factors, such as galaxy interaction, gas stripping, and cluster density. To achieve this, we applied a pre-processing pipeline to the LoCuSS dataset, correcting for observational biases and accounting for the effects of galaxy evolution. The resulting dataset was then analyzed using a combination of statistical and machine learning techniques to identify correlations between quenching and environmental factors.  Key findings indicate that galaxy interaction and gas stripping play a significant role in quenching star formation in cluster galaxies. However, the effect of cluster density is less pronounced, suggesting that the quenching process is more complex and influenced by multiple factors. The pre-processing pipeline was found to be essential in mitigating observational biases and improving the accuracy of quenching estimates. Overall, this study contributes to our understanding of the quenching process in cluster galaxies, highlighting the importance of pre-processing in galaxy evolution research.
label: machine

text: This study focuses on the 3-dimensional (3D) superconformal bootstrap, a framework that seeks to understand the behavior of conformal field theories in three spatial dimensions. The bootstrap is a mathematical framework that postulates that a conformal field theory can be understood by analyzing the correlation functions of its operators. The BPS (Bogomolnyi-Prasad-Shifman) operators play a crucial role in the 3D superconformal bootstrap, as they are associated with the protected operators that are expected to be conserved in the theory.  The objective of this research is to identify the exact correlators of BPS operators from the 3D superconformal bootstrap. To achieve this, we employed a combination of analytical and computational techniques. We utilized the conformal bootstrap equation, which relates the correlation functions of operators to the conformal dimension of the theory. We also employed a numerical method to solve the conformal bootstrap equation and obtain the exact correlators of BPS operators.  Our key findings indicate that the correlators of BPS operators can be expressed in terms of the conformal dimension of the theory and the conformal structure constants. We also found that the correlators of BPS operators exhibit a universal behavior, independent of the specific theory being considered. Furthermore, we discovered that the correlators of BPS operators can be used to constrain the conformal dimension of the theory, providing a new approach to testing the 3D superconformal bootstrap.  In conclusion, our study provides a new understanding of the exact correlators of BPS operators from the 3D superconformal bootstrap. Our results have important implications for our understanding of conformal field theories and the 3D superconformal bootstrap, and provide a new tool for testing the validity of the bootstrap.
label: machine

text: We investigated the effects of continuous use of ERP-based Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) with varying visual angles on patients with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). Our study aimed to explore the impact of visual angle on the performance and comfort of ALS patients using ERP-based BCIs.   Previous studies have shown that ERP-based BCIs can be an effective tool for ALS patients to communicate, but the limited understanding of the effects of visual angle on their performance and comfort is a significant gap. To address this, we conducted a mixed-methods study with 20 ALS patients who used ERP-based BCIs with different visual angles (30°, 60°, and 90°).   Our results showed that ALS patients performed significantly better in tasks requiring attention and focus when using the 60° visual angle, while the 90° visual angle led to higher levels of eye strain and discomfort. Conversely, the 30° visual angle resulted in reduced cognitive load and improved performance in tasks requiring mental effort.   Our findings highlight the importance of considering visual angle in the design of ERP-based BCIs for ALS patients. We propose that the optimal visual angle should be individualized to balance performance, comfort, and cognitive load. Our study contributes to the development of more effective and user-friendly ERP-based BCIs for ALS patients, ultimately improving their quality of life.
label: machine

text: We investigated the phenomenon of Coulomb drag in graphene by employing a perturbative approach to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing interlayer interactions. Our study addresses the challenge of understanding electron-electron correlations in two-dimensional materials, specifically in the context of graphene systems with varying carrier concentrations. By utilizing perturbation theory, we derived expressions for the drag resistivity and identified the contributions from various interaction channels.   We experimentally observed the distinct behavior of Coulomb drag as a function of temperature, charge density, and applied magnetic fields. Our results reveal that the drag resistivity scales nonlinearly with the carrier density and exhibits a pronounced dependence on temperature, confirming the theoretical predictions. Additionally, we explored the role of the thermal energy scale relative to the Fermi energy, which significantly alters the drag response.   We argue that the enhancement of Coulomb drag due to electron correlations highlights the unique characteristics of graphene as a medium for exploring quantum transport phenomena. Our methodology combined analytical calculations with numerical simulations, enabling us to rigorously test the perturbative framework against experimental data. The outcomes of our work not only demonstrate the viability of perturbation theory in capturing the essence of Coulomb drag in graphene but also pave the way for further studies into the interplay between electronic correlations and transport properties in low-dimensional systems. This research contributes to the broader understanding of quantum effects in graphene and establishes a foundational basis for future investigations of correlated electron systems.

text: This study investigates the diagnostic capabilities of line emission from EUV (Extreme Ultraviolet) and X-ray sources in low mass star systems, specifically focusing on illuminated disks and shocks. The primary objective was to explore how these emissions can provide insights into the physical conditions within these environments, such as temperature, density, and magnetic field strength. Utilizing numerical simulations and theoretical models, we examined the spectral signatures produced by ionized gas in both EUV and X-ray regimes under various conditions. Key findings indicate that specific line features in the EUV and X-ray spectra offer unique diagnostics, enabling the determination of plasma parameters with high precision. Additionally, the study highlighted the importance of shock heating in modifying the emission properties, leading to distinct spectral signatures compared to those observed in steady-state disk environments. The conclusion emphasizes the potential of EUV and X-ray diagnostics in probing the complex physical processes occurring in low mass star systems, particularly in regions where shocks and disks interact.

A set of new, sensitive, and spectrally resolved, sub-millimeter line
observations are used to probe the warm circumstellar gas around the S-type AGB
star chi Cyg. The observed lines involve high rotational quantum numbers,
which, combined with previously obtained lower-frequency data, make it possible
to study in detail the chemical and physical properties of, essentially, the
entire circumstellar envelope of chi Cyg. The data were obtained using the HIFI
instrument aboard Herschel, whose high spectral resolution provides valuable
information about the line profiles. Detailed, non-LTE, radiative transfer
modelling, including dust radiative transfer coupled with a dynamical model,
has been performed to derive the temperature, density, and velocity structure
of the circumstellar envelope. We report the first detection of circumstellar
H2O rotational emission lines in an S-star. Using the high-J CO lines to derive
the parameters for the circumstellar envelope, we modelled both the ortho- and
para-H2O lines. Our modelling results are consistent with the velocity
structure expected for a dust-driven wind. The derived total H2O abundance
(relative to H2) is (1.1 +/- 0.2)E-5, much lower than that in O-rich stars. The
derived ortho-to-para ratio of 2.1 +/- 0.6 is close to the high-temperature
equilibrium limit, consistent with H2O being formed in the photosphere.

text: We conducted a comprehensive review of spatial modelling with R-INLA, a Bayesian approach that integrates information from both spatial and non-spatial data. Our investigation aimed to assess the capabilities and limitations of R-INLA in addressing various spatial modelling challenges. We examined the strengths and weaknesses of R-INLA in handling different spatial data structures, including point, line, and area data, and evaluated its performance in terms of model estimation, prediction, and model selection.  Our analysis revealed that R-INLA offers an efficient and flexible framework for spatial modelling, allowing for the incorporation of prior knowledge and the estimation of model parameters. We found that R-INLA can effectively handle large datasets and complex spatial relationships, and that it is particularly well-suited for modelling spatially correlated data. However, we also identified some limitations, including the need for careful model specification and the potential for overfitting.  Our review highlighted the key ideas underlying R-INLA, including the use of Gaussian processes and Markov chain Monte Carlo methods to estimate model parameters. We also discussed the importance of model selection and the use of diagnostic tools to evaluate model performance. Our findings suggest that R-INLA is a powerful tool for spatial modelling, offering a flexible and efficient approach to addressing a wide range of spatial modelling challenges.

text: We present an extensive quantitative spectroscopic analysis of blue supergiant stars within the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 3109 to further our understanding of stellar evolution in low metallicity environments. Addressing the dearth of large, comprehensive stellar studies in such galaxies, our research aims to determine the physical parameters and chemical abundances of these massive stars and assess their implications on galaxy evolution and the chemical enrichment processes. Utilizing high-resolution spectroscopic data from the Very Large Telescope, we employ state-of-the-art non-LTE model atmosphere codes to determine key parameters, including effective temperature, surface gravity, and metal abundances. Our methodology incorporates precise spectral line modeling and fitting, allowing for robust abundance derivations. Our results indicate a significant underabundance of elements such as iron and calcium, consistent with an overall metallicity approximately one-tenth that of the Milky Way. Additionally, we find elevated helium and nitrogen abundances, suggesting a prior phase of substantial stellar nucleosynthesis and subsequent mixing. The comparison of our findings with theoretical stellar evolution models enhances constraints on mass-loss rates and rotational velocities in low-metallicity regimes. Through this research, we provide critical insights into the chemical evolution of NGC 3109 and refine models predicting the life cycles of massive stars in similar low-metallicity dwarf galaxies. These findings are instrumental in developing a more comprehensive framework for interpreting the role of such galaxies in the larger cosmic context and for informing future observational strategies in the study of early universe galaxy formation and evolution.

text: This study investigates the deuterium fractionation and H2D+ evolution in turbulent and magnetized cloud cores. The background section highlights the significance of understanding deuterium fractionation in astrochemistry, with a focus on cloud cores. The objective of this research is to model the deuterium fractionation and H2D+ evolution in a turbulent and magnetized environment using a chemical network and radiative transfer model. The methodology involves setting up a 3D radiative transfer and chemical network model, incorporating turbulent and magnetic effects to study deuterium fractionation and H2D+ evolution in a representative cloud core. Key findings reveal that deuterium fractionation increases towards the inner regions of the cloud core due to the denser environment and enhanced reaction rates. Additionally, H2D+ abundance is highest near the cloud core surface where turbulent heating dominates. The results suggest that both turbulence and magnetic fields play crucial roles in shaping the deuterium fractionation and H2D+ evolution in cloud cores, paving the way for further investigations into the deuterium chemistry in molecular clouds.

text:
When one splits spacetime into space plus time, the Weyl curvature tensor
(which equals the Riemann tensor in vacuum) splits into two spatial, symmetric,
traceless tensors: the tidal field $E$, which produces tidal forces, and the
frame-drag field $B$, which produces differential frame dragging. In recent
papers, we and colleagues have introduced ways to visualize these two fields:
tidal tendex lines (integral curves of the three eigenvector fields of $E$) and
their tendicities (eigenvalues of these eigenvector fields); and the
corresponding entities for the frame-drag field: frame-drag vortex lines and
their vorticities. These entities fully characterize the vacuum Riemann tensor.
In this paper, we compute and depict the tendex and vortex lines, and their
tendicities and vorticities, outside the horizons of stationary (Schwarzschild
and Kerr) black holes; and we introduce and depict the black holes' horizon
tendicity and vorticity (the normal-normal components of $E$ and $B$ on the
horizon). For Schwarzschild and Kerr black holes, the horizon tendicity is
proportional to the horizon's intrinsic scalar curvature, and the horizon
vorticity is proportional to an extrinsic scalar curvature. We show that, for
horizon-penetrating time slices, all these entities ($E$, $B$, the tendex lines
and vortex lines, the lines' tendicities and vorticities, and the horizon
tendicities and vorticities) are affected only weakly by changes of slicing and
changes of spatial coordinates, within those slicing and coordinate choices
that are commonly used for black holes. [Abstract is abbreviated.]

text: The detection of circumbinary planets is a challenging endeavor in the field of astrophysics, primarily due to the complex dynamics involved in binary star systems. This study investigates the viability of using eclipse timing variations (ETVs) as a method for detecting circumbinary planets. The objective is to assess the potential of ETVs as a reliable indicator by employing numerical simulations to model the interaction between circumbinary planets and their host binary systems. A series of simulations were conducted, where the timing of stellar eclipses was computed for binaries with and without the presence of a planet. Each simulation varied parameters such as the planet's mass, orbital radius, and inclination to evaluate their impact on ETV signatures. The analysis focused on identifying consistent patterns and distinguishing signals attributable to the gravitational influence of an orbiting planet. The key findings reveal that ETVs exhibit distinctive periodic fluctuations that correlate strongly with planetary characteristics, thus providing a viable method for detection when other methods fall short. The study concludes that ETV analysis, enhanced by precise timing measurements, offers a promising technique to identify and characterize circumbinary planets, even in scenarios with faint or distant binaries. text: In this study, we investigate the jet base of the blazar PKS1830-211 by analyzing the chromatic variability of its lensed images, leveraging serendipitous Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations coinciding with a strong gamma-ray flare. Our analysis reveals distinct redshifted and blueshifted components within the lensed images, indicating the presence of a relativistic jet emanating from the blazar's core region. We propose that these observed variations are indicative of the jet's dynamic behavior, with the redshifted component likely tracing material farther away from the central engine and the blueshifted component suggesting closer proximity to the jet base. Methodologically, we employ advanced image processing techniques to isolate and characterize the variable features in the lensed images, complemented by theoretical models of relativistic jets. The findings contribute to our understanding of blazar jets and their interaction with the surrounding environment, providing insights into the physical processes governing relativistic outflows in active galactic nuclei.

text: We investigate the fate of Majorana fermions and Chern numbers after a quantum quench in a driven-dissipative system. Our approach involves numerically solving the time-dependent Dirac equation for a two-dimensional system with a periodically driven potential, subject to a non-conservative dissipation term. We find that the Majorana fermions exhibit a non-trivial behavior, surviving the quench only if the dissipation is sufficiently weak. In this regime, we observe a non-zero Chern number, which is a topological invariant of the system. However, upon increasing the dissipation strength, the Chern number decays to zero, indicating the loss of topological protection. We also find that the Majorana fermions become entangled with the dissipative degrees of freedom, leading to a loss of their individuality. Our results suggest that the fate of Majorana fermions and Chern numbers after a quantum quench is determined by the interplay between the driving and dissipation terms. We propose a theoretical framework to understand this phenomenon, which involves the interplay between the Majorana fermion's topological properties and the dissipative environment. Our work provides insights into the interplay between quantum mechanics and dissipation, and has implications for the study of topological phases of matter in driven-dissipative systems.

text: This study investigates the correlation effects and collective excitations in bosonic bilayers, focusing on the pivotal roles of quantum statistics, superfluidity, and dimerization transition. The background of the research is rooted in the understanding of bosonic systems, where the interplay between quantum statistics and interactions gives rise to emergent phenomena. In the context of bilayers, the interplay between two layers of bosons leads to complex correlations and excitations.  The objective of this research is to elucidate the interplay between quantum statistics, superfluidity, and dimerization transition in bosonic bilayers. We employ a theoretical framework that incorporates the effects of quantum statistics, superfluidity, and dimerization transition on the correlation effects and collective excitations in bosonic bilayers.  Our results reveal that the interplay between quantum statistics and superfluidity gives rise to a novel type of collective excitation, characterized by a unique set of correlations and properties. Furthermore, we find that the dimerization transition plays a crucial role in modulating the correlation effects and collective excitations in bosonic bilayers.  The key findings of this research indicate that the interplay between quantum statistics, superfluidity, and dimerization transition is essential in understanding the behavior of bosonic bilayers. Our results provide new insights into the complex correlations and excitations in bosonic bilayers and have significant implications for the understanding of superfluidity and quantum statistics in condensed matter systems.

text: LaFeAsO is a member of the rare earth 1111-type iron pnictide superconductors, exhibiting unusual magnetic and structural behaviors, particularly under oxygen deficiency. To gain insights into the microscopic mechanisms behind these phenomena, we employed combined 57Fe Mossbauer spectroscopy and magnetic measurements on oxygen-deficient LaFeAsO single crystals grown by the self-flux method. The Mossbauer results revealed two distinct magnetic phases a high-temperature antiferromagnetic phase and a low-temperature superconducting phase. In the antiferromagnetic phase, the 57Fe isotropic quadrupole splitting (QS) is negative, and the magnetic ordering temperature TN is 117.4 K. In the superconducting phase, the QS becomes positive, indicating a reversal of the magnetization direction. Additionally, we observed a crossover in the T-dependent magnetic susceptibility, which is attributed to a static magnetic field arising from the vortex lattice. The magnetic measurements were performed using a SQUID magnetometer, and they confirmed the presence of the antiferromagnetic and superconducting phases, with Tc = 21.5 K. Moreover, the magnetization data showed a hysteresis loop, indicating the presence of a net magnetic moment in the superconducting state. Our findings provide crucial information regarding the interplay between magnetism and superconductivity in LaFeAsO under oxygen deficiency, which is essential for understanding the unconventional superconductivity mechanism in this material.

By training the neural network on simulated data sets generated from the CMSSM, we were able to accurately predict the model parameters with high precision. Our methodology involves training the neural network on a large dataset of CMSSM parameter points, optimizing the network architecture to achieve the best performance, and validating the model on independent test sets. We consider two eigenvalue problems for Laplacian on some specific doubly
connected domain. In particular, we study the following two eigenvalue
problems. Let $B_1$ be an open ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $B_0$ be a ball
contained in $B_1$. Let $\nu$ be the outward unit normal on $\partial B_1$.
Then the first eigenvalue of the problem \begin{align*} \begin{array}{rcll}
\Delta u &=& 0 \, &\mbox{ in } \, B_1 \setminus \bar{B}_0 , \\ u &=& 0 \,
&\mbox{ on } \, {\partial B_0}, \\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu} &=& \tau \,
u \, &\mbox{ on } \, {\partial B_1}, \end{array} \end{align*} attains maximum
if and only if $B_0$ and $B_1$ are concentric. Let $D$ be a domain in a
non-compact rank-$1$ symmetric space $(\mathbb{M}, ds^2)$, geodesically
symmetric with respect to the point $ p\in \mathbb{M}$. Let $B_0$ be a ball in
$\mathbb{M}$ centered at $p$ such that $\bar{{B}_0}\subset D$ and $\nu$ be the
outward unit normal on ${\partial (D \setminus \bar{B}_0)}$. Then the first
non-zero eigenvalue of \begin{align*} \begin{array}{rcll} \Delta u &=& \mu \ u
\, &\mbox{ in } \, D \setminus \bar{B}_0, \\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu}
&=& 0 \, &\mbox{ on } \, {\partial (D \setminus \bar{B}_0)}, \end{array}
\end{align*} attains maximum if and only if $D$ is a geodesic ball centered at
$p$.

text: This study investigates the detection of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) activity in a compact, hyper-starburst galaxy at a redshift of z = 5.7. The galaxy in question, SPT0346-52, is characterized by an exceptionally high rate of star formation, rivaling that of some of the most luminous galaxies in the universe. However, despite its intense starburst, SPT0346-52 is found to exhibit negligible AGN activity, challenging our understanding of the relationship between star formation and AGN activity.  The objective of this research is to determine the presence and characteristics of AGN activity in SPT0346-52, and to explore the implications of its absence for our understanding of galaxy evolution. To achieve this, we utilized a combination of multi-wavelength observations, including Hubble Space Telescope and Spitzer Space Telescope data, as well as radio and X-ray observations from the Chandra X-ray Observatory.  Our results indicate that SPT0346-52 is a compact, dust-enshrouded galaxy with a high rate of star formation, but no detectable AGN activity. This is consistent with the predictions of some theoretical models, which suggest that the growth of supermassive black holes is often decoupled from the growth of stars. Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution, particularly in the early universe, and highlight the need for further studies to determine the relationship between star formation and AGN activity in compact, hyper-starburst galaxies.

The quench dynamics of topological phases have received intensive
investigations in recent years. In this work, we prove exactly that the
topological invariants for both $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ indexes are
independent of time in symmetry preserving dynamics. We first reach this
conclusion by a direct relation between the time derivative of Berry connection
and the Hamiltonian energy based on the time dependent Hellman-Feynman theorem,
with which we show exactly that the topological indexes for systems without and
with time reversal symmetry are unchanged during evolution. In contrast, the
geometry phase without symmetry protection in a closed parameter space can
change dramtically with time, as revealed from the parameterized Landau-Zener
model. Then we interpret this result by showing that the time dependent wave
function is essentially the eigenvector of an auxiliary Hamiltonian, which has
exactly the same spectra and symmetries as the original Hamiltonian. For this
reason, the adiabatic evolution between the original and auxiliary Hamiltonian
will not lead to gap closing and reopening, thus the topological indexes are
independent of time. This result has generality and can be applied to models
with other symmetries and dimensions, and may even be applied to gapless
phases. Finally, possible ways to outreach this rigorous result are discussed.

We present a long-term programme for timing the eclipses of white dwarfs in
close binaries to measure apparent and/or real variations in their orbital
periods. Our programme includes 67 close binaries, both detached and
semi-detached and with M-dwarfs, K-dwarfs, brown dwarfs or white dwarfs
secondaries. In total, we have observed more than 650 white dwarf eclipses. We
use this sample to search for orbital period variations and aim to identify the
underlying cause of these variations. We find that the probability of observing
orbital period variations increases significantly with the observational
baseline. In particular, all binaries with baselines exceeding 10 yrs, with
secondaries of spectral type K2 -- M5.5, show variations in the eclipse arrival
times that in most cases amount to several minutes. In addition, among those
with baselines shorter than 10 yrs, binaries with late spectral type (>M6),
brown dwarf or white dwarf secondaries appear to show no orbital period
variations. This is in agreement with the so-called Applegate mechanism, which
proposes that magnetic cycles in the secondary stars can drive variability in
the binary orbits. We also present new eclipse times of NN Ser, which are still
compatible with the previously published circumbinary planetary system model,
although only with the addition of a quadratic term to the ephemeris. Finally,
we conclude that we are limited by the relatively short observational baseline
for many of the binaries in the eclipse timing programme, and therefore cannot
yet draw robust conclusions about the cause of orbital period variations in
evolved, white dwarf binaries.

We present the results of simultaneous Suzaku and NuSTAR observations of the
nearest Low-Luminosity Active Galactic Nucleus (LLAGN), M81*. The spectrum is
well described by a cut-off power law plus narrow emission lines from Fe
K$\alpha$, Fe XXV and Fe XXVI. There is no evidence of Compton reflection from
an optically thick disc, and we obtain the strongest constraint on the
reflection fraction in M81* to date, with a best-fit value of $R = 0.0$ with an
upper limit of $R < 0.1$. The Fe K$\alpha$ line may be produced in optically
thin, $N_H = 1 \times 10^{23}$ cm$^{-2}$, gas located in the equatorial plane
that could be the broad line region. The ionized iron lines may originate in
the hot, inner accretion flow. The X-ray continuum shows significant
variability on $\sim 40$ ks timescales suggesting that the primary X-ray source
is $\sim 100$s of gravitational radii in size. If this X-ray source illuminates
any putative optically thick disc, the weakness of reflection implies that such
a disc lies outside a few $\times 10^3$ gravitational radii. An optically thin
accretion flow inside a truncated optically thick disc appears to be a common
feature of LLAGN that are accreting at only a tiny fraction of the Eddington
limit.

text: This study presents a comprehensive high-resolution hindcast of wind and wave conditions across the North Sea, Norwegian Sea, and Barents Sea, addressing the need for improved understanding of marine environments under varying climatic conditions. The objective was to generate a spatiotemporally detailed dataset that serves as a valuable resource for various applications, including maritime navigation, coastal management, and climate impact assessments. Utilizing an advanced numerical modeling system, we integrated observational data with state-of-the-art forecasting techniques to create high-resolution hindcasts over a 30-year period (1990-2020). Our methodology involved calibrating the model with in-situ and satellite data, ensuring the accuracy of wind and wave predictions. Key findings indicate that significant wave heights show a marked increase in the Barents Sea, while the North Sea exhibits variable trends influenced by regional climatic events. The spatial distribution of severe wind events reveals distinct patterns relevant to understanding maritime hazards. Furthermore, the study highlights the influence of North Atlantic Oscillation on wave energy distribution across the regions. In conclusion, the high-resolution hindcast provides critical insights for stakeholders, enhances predictive capabilities for marine safety, and contributes to ongoing research in oceanography and climate variability. This dataset serves as a foundational tool for future studies focused on the interplay between wind, wave dynamics, and climate change in marine environments.

text: This research focuses on the formation process of a Milky Way-sized disk galaxy through a comparative analysis of different numerical methods. Various numerical simulations were conducted using different codes, including Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH), Moving Mesh (MM), and N-body/SPH hybrid methods. Key findings indicate that SPH simulations best capture the detailed dynamics of the interstellar medium, while MM simulations provide more accurate representations of the gravitational forces acting on the particles. The N-body/SPH hybrid method shows promise in balancing computational efficiency with physical accuracy. The analysis reveals that gas accretion rates, initial conditions, and the presence of massive black holes influence the formation and evolution of disk galaxies. text: This study explores the creation of micropatterned charge heterogeneities through vapor deposition of aminosilanes on silicon substrates. Initially, we aimed to understand how the deposition parameters such as temperature and time influence the uniformity and depth of these heterogeneities. Through systematic experimentation, we found that varying the deposition temperature significantly affects the formation of distinct surface features. Higher temperatures led to deeper penetration into the substrate, while lower temperatures resulted in shallower patterns. We also observed that prolonged deposition times increased the overall coverage and complexity of the micropatterns. To quantify these effects, we employed atomic force microscopy (AFM) and spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE). The AFM images revealed the spatial distribution of the aminosilane molecules across the substrate, indicating the formation of well-defined and reproducible patterns. Spectroscopic ellipsometry measurements provided insights into the thickness and refractive index variations induced by the deposition process. Our findings suggest that this method can be used to create controlled charge heterogeneities, which are crucial for applications in nanoelectronics and biosensors. Key methodologies include precise control over deposition conditions, characterization techniques, and computational modeling to predict the outcomes of different deposition scenarios. This research paves the way for further exploration into the electrical properties of micropatterned surfaces and their potential use in advanced device fabrication.

text: We present a comprehensive study of the Spitzer Space Telescope observations of the young massive star-forming region N159 in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), a prototypical HII complex. Our analysis aims to elucidate the physical and chemical properties of the region, shedding light on the early stages of massive star formation.  Through a combination of Spitzer's infrared and ultraviolet channels, we mapped the distribution of dust and gas within N159, revealing a complex network of filaments and dense cores. Spectroscopic analysis of the ionized gas and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) revealed a diverse range of chemical species, including H2, H2S, and C2, which are indicative of intense star formation activity. The Spitzer data also revealed a population of young, luminous stars, with effective temperatures ranging from 20,000 to 40,000 K, suggesting that N159 is a hotbed of star formation.  Our results suggest that N159 is a dynamic and evolving region, with a high rate of star formation and a complex interplay between gas and dust. We also found evidence of shock-induced chemistry, which plays a crucial role in the formation of complex molecules. The Spitzer observations provide a unique insight into the early stages of massive star formation, highlighting the importance of the LMC as a laboratory for studying the physical and chemical processes that govern the birth of massive stars.

The primary objective was to identify binary or multiple star systems within these stellar populations through detailed angular resolution measurements. Key findings revealed that 30% of the surveyed stars exhibited signs of multiplicity, with some showing evidence of close companions at separations below one arcsecond. The results provide valuable insights into the multiplicity rates and spatial distribution of binary systems across the F-K spectral types, contributing to our understanding of stellar formation and evolution. This study sets a foundation for further investigations into the nature and dynamics of binary star systems in the F-K spectral range.

text:
In hadronic collisions, interference between different production channels
affects momentum distributions of multi-particle final states. As this QCD
interference does not depend on the strong coupling constant, it is part of the
no-interaction baseline that needs to be controlled prior to searching for
other manifestations of collective dynamics. Here, we introduce a model that is
based on the QCD theory of multi-parton interactions and that allows one to
study interference effects in the production of $m$ particles in hadronic
collisions with $N$ parton-parton interactions ("sources"). In an expansion in
powers of $1/(N_c^2-1)$ and to leading order in the number of sources $N$, we
calculate interference effects in the $m$-particle spectra and we determine
from them the second and fourth order cumulant momentum anisotropies $v_n$.
Without invoking any azimuthal asymmetry and any density dependent non-linear
dynamics in the incoming state, and without invoking any interaction in the
final state, we find that QCD interference alone can give rise to values for
$v_n\lbrace 2\rbrace$ and $v_n\lbrace 4\rbrace$, $n$ even, that persist
unattenuated for increasing number of sources, that may increase with
increasing multiplicity and that agree with measurements in proton-proton (pp)
collisions in terms of the order of magnitude of the signal and the approximate
shape of the transverse momentum dependence. We further find that the
non-abelian features of QCD interference can give rise to odd harmonic
anisotropies. These findings indicate that the no-interaction baseline
including QCD interference effects can make a sizeable if not dominant
contribution to the measured $v_n$ coefficients in pp collisions. Prospects for
analyzing QCD interference contributions further and their possible relevance
for proton-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions are discussed shortly.

text:
High-energy gamma rays of interstellar origin are produced by the interaction
of cosmic-ray (CR) particles with the diffuse gas and radiation fields in the
Galaxy. The main features of this emission are well understood and are
reproduced by existing CR propagation models employing 2D Galactocentric
cylindrically symmetrical geometry. However, the high-quality data from
instruments like the Fermi Large Area Telescope reveal significant deviations
from the model predictions on few to tens of degree scales indicating the need
to include the details of the Galactic spiral structure and thus require 3D
spatial modelling. In this paper the high-energy interstellar emissions from
the Galaxy are calculated using the new release of the GALPROP code employing
3D spatial models for the CR source and interstellar radiation field (ISRF)
densities. Three models for the spatial distribution of CR sources are used
that are differentiated by their relative proportion of input luminosity
attributed to the smooth disc or spiral arms. Two ISRF models are developed
based on stellar and dust spatial density distributions taken from the
literature that reproduce local near- to far-infrared observations. The
interstellar emission models that include arms and bulges for the CR source and
ISRF densities provide plausible physical interpretations for features found in
the residual maps from high-energy gamma-ray data analysis. The 3D models for
CR and ISRF densities provide a more realistic basis that can be used for the
interpretation of the non-thermal interstellar emissions from the Galaxy.
