text: We investigate the geometrical clusterization behavior of SU(2) gluodynamics in the liquid-gas phase transition using lattice simulations. Our main goal is to unravel the interplay between topology and critical phenomena in the context of non-Abelian gauge theories. We employ the Wilson loop observable, which is an order parameter sensitive to the underlying topological structure of the gauge field configurations. We analyze the distribution of Wilson loops sizes in various volume sizes and temperature regimes, finding evidence for a phase transition characterized by a power-law behavior in the Wilson loop size distribution. This result indicates a continuous percolation transition with topological character. Furthermore, we perform a finite-size scaling analysis to determine the critical point and exponents for the geometrical clusterization. Our findings suggest a strong connection between geometrical clusterization and the liquid-gas phase transition in SU(2) gluodynamics, providing insights into the non-perturbative properties of this theory and their relation to critical phenomena. These results lay the groundwork for future investigations into the role of topological structures in other non-Abelian gauge theories and their critical transitions.

text: This study explores the potential of externally-polluted white dwarfs as a novel source of information on the compositions of extrasolar planetary systems. Background research has shown that white dwarfs, the remnants of low-mass stars, can accumulate material from planetary systems through stellar winds and planetary nebulae. This material, in turn, can be used to infer the presence and properties of planets. However, the current understanding of the planetary system compositions is limited due to the lack of direct observations.   The objective of this research is to investigate the relationship between the composition of material accumulated on white dwarfs and the properties of the planetary systems that generated it. By analyzing the spectroscopic and photometric data of white dwarfs, we aim to derive the chemical signatures of planetary systems and shed light on the diversity of planetary compositions in the galaxy.   To achieve this goal, we employed a multi-messenger approach combining spectroscopic and photometric observations of white dwarfs with computational modeling. Our results show that the chemical composition of material accumulated on white dwarfs is closely related to the metallicity and planetary system architecture of the host stars. We found that white dwarfs with high metallicity and multiple planets exhibit distinct chemical signatures, which can be used to infer the presence of planetary systems.   This study provides new insights into the relationship between planetary system compositions and the evolution of white dwarfs, and has implications for the search for life beyond our solar system. The findings of this research suggest that externally-polluted white dwarfs can serve as a valuable tool for the detection and characterization of planetary systems, and highlight the potential of this approach for future studies.
label: machine

text:
Despite numerous efforts to better understand binary star evolution, some
aspects of it remain poorly constrained. In particular, the evolution of
eccentric binaries has remained elusive mainly because the Roche lobe formalism
derived for circular binaries does not apply. Here, we report the results of
our Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics simulations of mass transfer in eccentric
binaries using an alternate method in which we model only the outermost layers
of the stars with appropriate boundary conditions. Using this technique, along
with properly relaxed model stars, we characterize the mass transfer episodes
of binaries with various orbital parameters. In particular, we show that these
episodes can be described by Gaussians with a FWMH of ~0.12 P_orb and that the
peak rates occur after periastron, at an orbital phase of ~0.58, independently
of the eccentricity and mass of the stars. The accreted material is observed to
form a rather sparse envelope around either or both stars. Although the fate of
this envelope is not modeled in our simulations, we show that a constant
fraction (~5%) of the material transferred is ejected from the systems. We
discuss this result in terms of the non-conservative mass transfer scenario. We
suggest our results could be incorporated in analytical and binary population
synthesis studies to help better understand the evolution of eccentric binaries
and the formation of exotic stellar populations.

text: We investigated the origin of the Aquarius Stream, a significant tributary of the White River in Michigan, USA. Our research aimed to reconstruct the stream's hydrological history, focusing on the Pleistocene era, when the region underwent significant glacial fluctuations. By analyzing a combination of geomorphological, sedimentological, and paleoclimatic data, we identified a series of glacial features, including drumlins and eskers, that suggest a complex glacial landscape during the last ice age.  Our analysis of glacial moraines and drumlin fields revealed a north-south trending orientation, indicative of a glacial advance from the north. We also detected a network of glacial tunnels and channels that likely played a crucial role in shaping the stream's morphology. By correlating these features with paleoclimatic data, we inferred that the Aquarius Stream originated in the northern part of its catchment area, where the glacial ice sheet was at its thickest.  Our results suggest that the stream's early course was influenced by the glacial landscape, with its flow being controlled by a series of glacial features, including drumlins, eskers, and moraines. The combination of these features likely created a complex network of channels and tunnels that eventually gave rise to the modern-day Aquarius Stream. Our findings provide new insights into the hydrological history of the region and highlight the importance of considering glacial processes in the reconstruction of past water courses.
label: machine

text: In this work, we investigate properties of affine fractals as boundaries and their implications for harmonic analysis. Affine fractals, being self-similar structures defined through affine transformations, present challenging yet rich frameworks for exploring boundary behaviors in mathematical and analytical contexts. Our study aims to bridge the gap between geometrical complexity and analytical tractability by examining how affine fractal boundaries impact harmonic measures and potential theory.   We employ a combination of techniques from fractal geometry, spectral theory, and functional analysis to address this problem. Specifically, we develop an analytical framework that leverages the self-similarity and scaling properties of affine fractals to construct boundary value problems that are solvable within these complex boundaries. This involves the derivation of harmonic measure estimates and the critical examination of the Laplacian and its spectrum on these non-trivial boundaries.   Our findings demonstrate that affine fractals can serve as effective models for understanding boundary effects in complex systems, potentially leading to novel insights into multi-scale phenomena. We provide evidence that the harmonic structure induced by affine fractal boundaries supports the existence of eigenfunctions with fractal-like properties, thereby enriching the existing literature on spectral dimension and eigenvalue distributions. Our methodology further suggests new approaches to harmonic analysis on irregular domains, and invites future research into potential applications of affine fractals in physics and engineering. Through this exploration, we contribute a foundational theoretical framework that enhances the understanding of the interplay between geometric novelty and analytical dynamics in affine fractal settings.
label: machine

text: The economic load dispatch problem is a critical issue in power systems, where the objective is to minimize the total economic load of generators while satisfying the power balance and other constraints. However, the valve-point effect, which represents the non-linear relationship between the valve opening and the valve-point voltage, significantly complicates the problem. This effect can lead to suboptimal dispatch decisions, resulting in increased fuel consumption and emissions.   To address this challenge, this research proposes the application of mixed integer programming (MIP) to globally minimize the economic load dispatch problem with the valve-point effect. The MIP formulation takes into account the valve-point effect by incorporating the valve-point voltage into the objective function and the power balance constraints. The proposed model also considers the valve-point characteristics of each generator, which are obtained through a detailed analysis of the valve-point curves.   The proposed MIP model is solved using a branch-and-bound algorithm, which is capable of handling large-scale power systems with complex valve-point effects. The results show that the proposed MIP model can significantly improve the economic load dispatch decisions, reducing the total economic load by up to 15% compared to the conventional dispatch method. The proposed approach also demonstrates robustness to uncertainty in valve-point effects and generator characteristics. The findings of this research contribute to the development of more accurate and efficient economic load dispatch models for power systems with valve-point effects.
label: machine

text:
We measure evolution of spectra, spatial correlation functions and
probability density functions (PDFs) of waves appearance for a set of
one-dimensional NLS-like equations of focusing type, namely for the classical
integrable Nonlinear Schrodinger equation (1), nonintegrable NLS equation
accounting for dumping (linear dissipation, two- and three-photon absorption)
and pumping terms (2) and generalized NLS equation accounting for six-wave
interactions, dumping and pumping terms (3). All additional terms beyond the
classical NLS equation are small. As initial conditions we choose seeded by
noise modulationally unstable solutions of the considered systems in the form
of (a) condensate for systems (1)-(3) and (b) cnoidal wave for the classical
NLS equation (1). We observe 'strange' results for the classical NLS equation
(1) with condensate initial condition including peak at zeroth harmonic in
averaged over ensemble spectra, non-decaying spacial correlation functions and
a 'breathing' region on the PDFs for medium waves amplitudes where frequency of
waves appearance oscillates with time, while the far-tails of the PDFs remain
Rayleigh ones. Addition of small dumping and pumping terms in model (2) breaks
integrability that results in absence of the peak at zeroth harmonic in
spectra, spacial correlation functions decaying to zero level and strictly
Rayleigh PDFs for waves amplitudes. For the classical NLS equation (1) with
cnoidal wave initial condition PDFs turn out to be significantly different from
Rayleigh ones with 'fat tails' in the region of large amplitudes where higher
waves appear more frequently, while for generalized NLS equation with six-wave
interactions, dumping and pumping terms (3) we demonstrate absence of
non-Rayleigh addition to the PDFs for zeroth six-wave interactions coefficient
and increase of non-Rayleigh addition with six-wave interactions term.

text: The study of spectral shift functions plays a crucial role in understanding the stability of spectra in perturbation theory, which is essential in mathematical physics and operator theory. This research investigates the application of double operator integral (DOI) methods to the continuity of spectral shift functions. The primary objective is to extend existing frameworks to accommodate broader classes of operators, thereby enhancing the robustness of spectral analysis. Utilizing a DOI framework, which effectively handles the interaction of two non-commuting operators, we focus on establishing the conditions under which spectral shift functions exhibit continuity. The methodology involves a detailed examination of trace class perturbations alongside Lipschitz functions in the functional calculus context to derive sufficient conditions for continuity. Key findings reveal that the DOI approach not only simplifies the computation related to spectral shift functions but also broadens the applicability of continuity results to new operator classes, especially those involving non-trivial commutators. This advancement demonstrates how DOI techniques can seamlessly integrate with other operator methods, providing deeper insights into spectral regularity. In conclusion, the study underscores the efficacy of double operator integral methods in spectral theory and offers a comprehensive framework that paves the way for future research into spectral properties of operators under complex perturbations.
label: machine

text: Cosmologically distant lens galaxies, a subset of gravitational lensing systems, offer a unique window into the formation and evolution of galaxies in the early universe. These systems, characterized by the bending of light around massive foreground galaxies, provide a means to study the interplay between gas, dust, and stellar populations in the distant universe. However, the properties of these systems remain poorly understood, particularly with regards to their metallicities, which are crucial in determining their chemical evolution and star formation histories.  This study aimed to investigate the dust, gas, and metallicities of cosmologically distant lens galaxies using a combination of spectroscopic and photometric data. We selected a sample of 20 lens systems, covering a range of redshifts from 0.3 to 2.5, and analyzed their optical spectra to derive gas and dust properties. We also employed a novel method to estimate the metallicities of these galaxies, utilizing the Balmer break and the H-alpha emission line. Our results reveal a diverse range of gas and dust properties, including significant variations in dust extinction and gas kinematics.  The metallicities of the lens galaxies range from [Fe/H] = -1.5 to +1.0, indicating a complex chemical evolution history. We find that the most metal-poor galaxies are more likely to be lensed by massive foreground galaxies, while the most metal-rich galaxies are associated with lower-mass foreground systems. These findings suggest that the chemical evolution of galaxies in the distant universe is influenced by the interactions with their environment. Our study provides new insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies in the early universe, highlighting the importance of considering the interplay between gas, dust, and stellar populations in the study of cosmologically distant lens galaxies.

text:
A basic feature of many field experiments is that investigators are only able
to randomize clusters of individuals--such as households, communities, firms,
medical practices, schools or classrooms--even when the individual is the unit
of interest. To recoup the resulting efficiency loss, some studies pair similar
clusters and randomize treatment within pairs. However, many other studies
avoid pairing, in part because of claims in the literature, echoed by clinical
trials standards organizations, that this matched-pair, cluster-randomization
design has serious problems. We argue that all such claims are unfounded. We
also prove that the estimator recommended for this design in the literature is
unbiased only in situations when matching is unnecessary; its standard error is
also invalid. To overcome this problem without modeling assumptions, we develop
a simple design-based estimator with much improved statistical properties. We
also propose a model-based approach that includes some of the benefits of our
design-based estimator as well as the estimator in the literature. Our methods
also address individual-level noncompliance, which is common in applications
but not allowed for in most existing methods. We show that from the perspective
of bias, efficiency, power, robustness or research costs, and in large or small
samples, pairing should be used in cluster-randomized experiments whenever
feasible; failing to do so is equivalent to discarding a considerable fraction
of one's data. We develop these techniques in the context of a randomized
evaluation we are conducting of the Mexican Universal Health Insurance Program.
label: human

text: This study investigates the Reverberation Mapping (RM) technique applied to the Broad Line Region (BLR) of AGN to infer properties of the underlying accretion disk. We employ a hydrodynamical model that simulates a line-driven disk wind, which is used as a framework to interpret RM data. The methodology involves modeling the BLR continuum variability in response to the accretion disk luminosity variations, capturing how these variations are observed in the light curves of AGN. We simulate RM maps by propagating light from the BLR back towards the observer, considering the complex geometry and kinematics of the BLR. Our simulations demonstrate that the observed RM patterns can be used to determine the mass accretion rate onto the central engine, the size and shape of the BLR, and the spatial distribution of ionized gas. The results show that the hydrodynamical model successfully reproduces key features of the observed RM maps, thereby validating the approach for extracting physical parameters of the BLR. This work highlights the potential of reverberation mapping to probe the dynamics and structure of the accretion disk in AGN.
label: machine

text:
Four of nine exoplanets found by microlensing were detected by the resonant
caustic, which represents the merging of the planetary and central caustics at
the position when the projected separation of a host star and a bounded planet
is s~1. One of the resonant caustic lensing events, OGLE-2005-BLG-169, was a
caustic-crossing high-magnification event with $A_{max} \sim$ 800 and the
source star was much smaller than the caustic, nevertheless the perturbation
was not obviously apparent on the light curve of the event. In this paper, we
investigate the perturbation pattern of the resonant caustic to understand why
the perturbations induced by the caustic do not leave strong traces on the
light curves of high-magnification events despite a small source/caustic size
ratio. From this study, we find that the regions with
small-magnification-excess around the center of the resonant caustic are rather
widely formed, and the event passing the small-excess region produces a
high-magnification event with a weak perturbation that is small relative to the
amplification caused by the star and thus does not noticeably appear on the
light curve of the event. We also find that the positive excess of the inside
edge of the resonant caustic and the negative excess inside the caustic become
stronger and wider as $q$ increases, and thus the resonant caustic-crossing
high-magnification events with the weak perturbation occur in the range of $q
\leqslant 10^{-4}$. We determine the probability of the occurrence of events
with the small excess $|\epsilon| \leqslant 3 %$ in high-magnification events
induced by a resonant caustic. As a result, we find that for the Earth-mass
planets with a separation of ~ 2.5 AU, the resonant caustic high-magnification
events with the weak perturbation can occur with a significant frequency.

We consider real world task-oriented dialog settings, where agents need to
generate both fluent natural language responses and correct external actions
like database queries and updates. We demonstrate that, when applied to
customer support chat transcripts, Sequence to Sequence (Seq2Seq) models often
generate short, incoherent and ungrammatical natural language responses that
are dominated by words that occur with high frequency in the training data.
These phenomena do not arise in synthetic datasets such as bAbI, where we show
Seq2Seq models are nearly perfect. We develop techniques to learn embeddings
that succinctly capture relevant information from the dialog history, and
demonstrate that nearest neighbor based approaches in this learned neural
embedding space generate more fluent responses. However, we see that these
methods are not able to accurately predict when to execute an external action.
We show how to combine nearest neighbor and Seq2Seq methods in a hybrid model,
where nearest neighbor is used to generate fluent responses and Seq2Seq type
models ensure dialog coherency and generate accurate external actions. We show
that this approach is well suited for customer support scenarios, where agents'
responses are typically script-driven, and correct external actions are
critically important. The hybrid model on the customer support data achieves a
78% relative improvement in fluency scores, and a 130% improvement in accuracy
of external calls.

The present communication reports the first direct measurement of the
conformation of a polymer corona grafted around silica nano-particles dispersed
inside a nanocomposite, a matrix of the same polymer. This measurement
constitutes an experimental breakthrough based on a refined combination of
chemical synthesis, which permits to match the contribution of the neutron
silica signal inside the composite, and the use of complementary scattering
methods SANS and SAXS to extract the grafted polymer layer form factor from the
inter-particles silica structure factor. The modelization of the signal of the
grafted polymer on nanoparticles inside the matrix and the direct comparison
with the form factor of the same particles in solution show a clear-cut change
of the polymer conformation from bulk to the nanocomposite: a transition from a
stretched and swollen form in solution to a Gaussian conformation in the matrix
followed with a compression of a factor two of the grafted corona. In the
probed range, increasing the interactions between the grafted particles (by
increasing the particle volume fraction) or between the grafted and the free
matrix chains (decreasing the grafted-free chain length ratio) does not
influence the amplitude of the grafted brush compression. This is the first
direct observation of the wet-to-dry conformational transition theoretically
expected to minimize the free energy of swelling of grafted chains in
interaction with free matrix chains, illustrating the competition between the
mixing entropy of grafted and free chains, and the elastic deformation of the
grafted chains. In addition to the experimental validation of the theoretical
prediction, this result constitutes a new insight for the nderstanding of the
general problem of dispersion of nanoparticles inside a polymer matrix for the
design of new nanocomposites materials.

text:
Full-duplex communication has the potential to substantially increase the
throughput in wireless networks. However, the benefits of full-duplex are still
not well understood. In this paper, we characterize the full-duplex rate gains
in both single-channel and multi-channel use cases. For the single-channel
case, we quantify the rate gain as a function of the remaining
self-interference and SNR values. We also provide a sufficient condition under
which the sum of uplink and downlink rates on a full-duplex channel is concave
in the transmission power levels. Building on these results, we consider the
multi-channel case. For that case, we introduce a new realistic model of a
small form-factor (e.g., smartphone) full-duplex receiver and demonstrate its
accuracy via measurements. We study the problem of jointly allocating power
levels to different channels and selecting the frequency of maximum
self-interference suppression, where the objective is maximizing the sum of the
rates over uplink and downlink OFDM channels. We develop a polynomial time
algorithm which is nearly optimal in practice under very mild restrictions. To
reduce the running time, we develop an efficient nearly-optimal algorithm under
the high SINR approximation. Finally, we demonstrate via numerical evaluations
the capacity gains in the different use cases and obtain insights into the
impact of the remaining self-interference and wireless channel states on the
performance.

text: This study investigates the evolution of the OH and CO-dark molecular gas fraction across a molecular cloud boundary in the Taurus region. Our research aims to address the longstanding problem of understanding the transition of molecular gas properties at cloud boundaries within the interstellar medium. Utilizing observational data from various telescopes, we analyze the distribution and characteristics of OH and CO-dark gas components, crucial for comprehending the complex nature of molecular clouds. The results demonstrate a clear spatial variation in the fractions of OH and CO-dark gas across the cloud boundary in Taurus, indicating a significant shift in the chemistry and physical conditions of the gas. We interpret these findings in the context of cloud dynamics, heating mechanisms, and the impact of external factors on molecular gas properties. Our approach combines observational constraints with theoretical models to explore the underlying processes driving the evolution of molecular gas fractions. This study contributes to advancing our knowledge of the interstellar medium's complex structure and provides insights into the mechanisms shaping the molecular gas distribution within molecular cloud boundaries.

text:
The Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) is the future large observatory in the
very high energy (VHE) domain. Operating from 20 GeV to 300 TeV, it will be
composed of tens of Imaging Air Cherenkov Telescopes (IACTs) displaced in a
large area of a few square kilometers in both the southern and northern
hemispheres. The CTA/DATA On-Site Analysis (OSA) is the system devoted to the
development of dedicated pipelines and algorithms to be used at the CTA site
for the reconstruction, data quality monitoring, science monitoring and
realtime science alerting during observations. The OSA integral sensitivity is
computed here for the most studied source at Gamma-rays, the Crab Nebula, for a
set of exposures ranging from 1000 seconds to 50 hours, using the full CTA
Southern array. The reason for the Crab Nebula selection as the first example
of OSA integral sensitivity is twofold: (i) this source is characterized by a
broad spectrum covering the entire CTA energy range; (ii) it represents, at the
time of writing, the standard candle in VHE and it is often used as unit for
the IACTs sensitivity. The effect of different Crab Nebula emission models on
the CTA integral sensitivity is evaluated, to emphasize the need for
representative spectra of the CTA science targets in the evaluation of the OSA
use cases. Using the most complete model as input to the OSA integral
sensitivity, we obtain a significant detection of the Crab nebula (about 10% of
flux) even for a 1000 second exposure, for an energy threshold less than 10
TeV.

text: This research paper explores the hierarchical floorplans of order k, where k represents the level of hierarchy in the floorplan design. The objective of this study is to analyze the impact of different levels of hierarchy on the performance and efficiency of floorplan designs in electronic systems. The methodology involves conducting a comparative analysis of floorplans with varying levels of hierarchy using simulation tools and performance metrics.  Key findings indicate that the hierarchical floorplans of order k offer a balance between complexity and performance in electronic system designs. Higher levels of hierarchy (larger k values) tend to improve design scalability and reduce the overall area and wirelength of the floorplan. However, excessive hierarchy levels may lead to increased design complexity and overhead costs.  In conclusion, this research highlights the significance of hierarchical floorplans in optimizing the design of electronic systems. It suggests that an optimal level of hierarchy should be chosen based on the specific requirements of the system to achieve an efficient and scalable floorplan design. This study contributes to the understanding of hierarchical floorplans and provides insights for practitioners and researchers in the field of electronic design automation.
label: machine

text:
A systematic study of charged hadron multiplicities ($n_{ch}$) at various
collision energies is very much important in understanding the basic production
mechanism of the hadrons in nucleus-nucleus collision experiments. Furthermore,
the variations of $n_{ch}$ in nucleus-nucleus collisions with respect to the
colliding energy and mass number can provide a potential probe for the
formation of quark gluon plasma (QGP) in the laboratory. In this paper, we
propose a phenomenological model based on the constituent quark-quark
interactions to calculate the average multiplicity ($n_{ch}$) and
pseudorapidity density at mid-rapidity ($(dn_{ch}/d\eta)_{\eta=0}$) of charged
hadrons at various center-of-mass energies $(\sqrt{s_{NN}})$ for
nucleus-nucleus ($A-A$) collisions. We first propose a new parametrization for
$n_{ch}^{pp}$ and $(dn_{ch}/d\eta)^{pp}_{\eta=0}$ in $p-p$ interactions based
on some initial inputs which fit the experimental data very well. We further
extend this parametrization by using simple phenomenological assumptions
regarding mean number of participating quarks and mean number of collisions to
obtain the $n_{ch}$ and $(dn_{ch}/d\eta)_{\eta=0}$ for $A-A$ collisions and
show their dependencies on the mass number of colliding nuclei as well as on
$\sqrt{s_{NN}}$. We also compare the results obtained from our model with the
results obtained from the modified Glauber model in order to demonstrate the
difference between the two formalisms. Finally, we compare the charged hadron
multiplicity and pseudorapidity density at mid-rapidity for $A-A$ collisions
obtained from our model with the available experimetal data from various
heavy-ion collision experiments and give our predictions for $A-A$ collisions
at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and at Compressed Baryonic Matter (CBM)
experiments.

text: Fractional lattice dynamics is a novel approach to modeling nonlocal constitutive behavior in materials, which has garnered significant attention in recent years. This phenomenon arises from the interplay between the material's microstructure and its macroscopic response, exhibiting characteristics that deviate from classical, local behavior. The underlying mechanism involves the interaction between the material's lattice structure and its environment, resulting in a nonlocal, power-law dependence of the material's response.  The objective of this research is to develop a theoretical framework for fractional lattice dynamics, focusing on the role of power-law matrix functions and their fractional continuum limit kernels. By analyzing the mathematical structure of these functions, we aim to establish a general framework for understanding the nonlocal behavior of materials. The proposed framework is based on the concept of fractional calculus, which provides a powerful tool for modeling nonlocal phenomena.  A comprehensive analytical and numerical approach was employed to investigate the behavior of power-law matrix functions and their fractional continuum limit kernels. The results demonstrate the existence of a nonlocal, power-law dependence of the material's response, which is consistent with experimental observations. The proposed framework was further validated through simulations of various material models, showcasing its ability to capture the nonlocal behavior of materials.  The key findings of this research indicate that fractional lattice dynamics provides a valuable tool for understanding the nonlocal behavior of materials, with significant implications for the development of new materials and structures. The proposed framework offers a general and flexible approach to modeling nonlocal phenomena, which can be applied to a wide range of materials and systems. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between materials and their environment, paving the way for the development of innovative materials and technologies.

A low complexity, essentially-ML decoding technique for the Golden code and
the 3 antenna Perfect code was introduced by Sirianunpiboon, Howard and
Calderbank. Though no theoretical analysis of the decoder was given, the
simulations showed that this decoding technique has almost maximum-likelihood
(ML) performance. Inspired by this technique, in this paper we introduce two
new low complexity decoders for Space-Time Block Codes (STBCs) - the Adaptive
Conditional Zero-Forcing (ACZF) decoder and the ACZF decoder with successive
interference cancellation (ACZF-SIC), which include as a special case the
decoding technique of Sirianunpiboon et al. We show that both ACZF and ACZF-SIC
decoders are capable of achieving full-diversity, and we give sufficient
conditions for an STBC to give full-diversity with these decoders. We then show
that the Golden code, the 3 and 4 antenna Perfect codes, the 3 antenna Threaded
Algebraic Space-Time code and the 4 antenna rate 2 code of Srinath and Rajan
are all full-diversity ACZF/ACZF-SIC decodable with complexity strictly less
than that of their ML decoders. Simulations show that the proposed decoding
method performs identical to ML decoding for all these five codes. These STBCs
along with the proposed decoding algorithm outperform all known codes in terms
of decoding complexity and error performance for 2,3 and 4 transmit antennas.
We further provide a lower bound on the complexity of full-diversity
ACZF/ACZF-SIC decoding. All the five codes listed above achieve this lower
bound and hence are optimal in terms of minimizing the ACZF/ACZF-SIC decoding
complexity. Both ACZF and ACZF-SIC decoders are amenable to sphere decoding
implementation.

We are presenting here a follow-up study of the molecular gas and dust in the
environs of the star forming region NGC 3503. This study aims at dealing with
the interaction of NGC 3503 with its parental molecular cloud, and also with
the star formation in the region. To analyze the molecular gas we use CO(2-1),
13CO(2-1), C18O(2-1), and HCN(3-2) line data obtained with the APEX telescope.
To study the distribution of the dust, we make use of images at 870 microns
from the ATLASGAL survey and IRAC-GLIMPSE archival images. We use public 2MASS
and WISE data to search for candidate YSOs in the region. The new APEX
observations allowed the substructure of the molecular gas in the velocity
range from -28 to -23 km/s to be imaged in detail. The morphology of the
molecular gas close to the nebula, the location of the PDR, and the shape of
radio continuum emission suggest that the ionized gas is expanding against its
parental cloud, and confirm the "champagne flow" scenario. We have identified
several molecular clumps and determined some of their physical and dynamical
properties. We have compared the physical properties of the clumps to
investigate how the molecular gas has been affected by the HII region. Clumps
adjacent to the ionization fronts of NGC 3503 and/or the bright rimmed cloud
SFO62 have been heated and compressed by the ionized gas, but their line width
is not different to those that are too distant to the ionization fronts. We
identified several candidate YSOs in the region. Their spatial distribution
suggests that stellar formation might have been boosted by the expansion of the
nebula. We discard the "collect and collapse" scenario and propose alternative
mechanisms such as radiatively driven implosion on pre-existing molecular
clumps or small-scale Jeans gravitational instabilities.

The origin of lithium (Li) and its production process have long been an
unsettled question in cosmology and astrophysics. Candidates environments of Li
production events or sites suggested by previous studies include big bang
nucleosynthesis, interactions of energetic cosmic rays with interstellar
matter, evolved low mass stars, novae, and supernova explosions. Chemical
evolution models and observed stellar Li abundances suggest that at least half
of the present Li abundance may have been produced in red giants, asymptotic
giant branch (AGB) stars, and novae. However, no direct evidence for the supply
of Li from stellar objects to the Galactic medium has yet been found. Here we
report on the detection of highly blue-shifted resonance lines of the singly
ionized radioactive isotope of beryllium, $^{7}$Be, in the near ultraviolet
(UV) spectra of the classical nova V339 Del (Nova Delphini 2013). Spectra were
obtained 38 to 48 days after the explosion. $^{7}$Be decays to form $^{7}$Li
within a short time (half-life 53.22 days). The spectroscopic detection of this
fragile isotope implies that it has been created during the nova explosion via
the reaction $^{3}\mbox{He}(\alpha,\gamma)^{7}\mbox{Be}$, and supports the
theoretical prediction that a significant amount of $^{7}$Li could be produced
in classical nova explosions. This finding opens a new way to explore $^{7}$Li
production in classical novae and provides a clue to the mystery of the
Galactic evolution of lithium.

text: In this study, we address the computational challenges associated with the Hitting Set and Directed Dominating Set problems by employing kernelization techniques tailored to their respective parameterized complexity. We introduce novel kernels for these problems under the framework of Below-Upper-Bound (BUB) parameterizations, focusing on minimizing the size of the reduced instances.  Our approach involves developing an algorithm that reduces the input instances to smaller, equivalent instances while adhering to the BUB constraints. We demonstrate that our kernelization process can significantly reduce the problem size, thereby enhancing the efficiency of exact algorithms and approximation schemes designed for these problems. The key methodologies include rigorous analysis of the structure of the input instances and the application of combinatorial techniques to identify and eliminate non-relevant elements.  Results show that our kernels achieve substantial reductions in instance sizes, with the reduction factor being polynomially bounded. This leads to more efficient solvers and faster computation times for large-scale instances of both the Hitting Set and Directed Dominating Set problems. Our findings contribute to the broader field of parameterized algorithms by providing practical tools for handling computationally intensive graph problems within feasible time frames.

Human brain structural networks contain sets of centrally embedded hub
regions that enable efficient information communication. However, it remains
largely unknown about categories of structural brain hubs and their
microstructural, functional and cognitive characteristics as well as
contributions to individual identification. Here, we employed three multi-modal
imaging data sets with structural MRI, diffusion MRI and resting-state
functional MRI to construct individual structural brain networks, identify
brain hubs based on eight commonly used graph-nodal metrics, and perform
comprehensive validation analysis. We found three categories of structural hubs
in the brain networks, namely, aggregated, distributed and connector hubs.
Spatially, these distinct categories of hubs were primarily located in the
default-mode system and additionally in the visual and limbic systems for
aggregated hubs, in the frontoparietal system for distributed hubs, and in the
sensorimotor and ventral attention systems for connector hubs. Importantly,
these three categories of hubs exhibited various distinct characteristics, with
the highest level of microstructural organization in the aggregated hubs, the
largest wiring cost and topological vulnerability in the distributed hubs, and
the highest functional associations and cognitive flexibility in the connector
hubs, although they behaved better regarding these characteristics compared to
non-hubs. Finally, all three categories of hub indices displayed high
across-session spatial similarities and acted as a structural fingerprint with
high predictive rates (100%, 100% and 84.2%) for individual identification.
Collectively, our findings highlighted three categories of brain hubs with
differential microstructural, functional and cognitive associations, which may
shed light on the topological mechanisms of the human connectome.

text: We investigate the precise asymptotics for the solution of the parabolic Anderson model (PAM) with a moving catalyst or trap, focusing on the long-time behavior. We derive an explicit formula for the asymptotic distribution of the PAM solution when the strength of the catalyst or trap jumps at a random rate λt, following a renewal process. The moving catalyst or trap is assumed to move with a deterministic velocity vt and has a Gaussian shape with a time-dependent variance. Our derivation is based on the theory of singular perturbations and the Fourier-Laplace transform method. The key idea is to separate the fast and slow processes and apply an averaging method to the fast process. We show that the limiting distribution of the PAM solution is a Gaussian process with a time-dependent covariance function, which depends on the moving catalyst or trap's parameters. The derived formula provides a theoretical justification for the empirical findings in finance and physics, where the PAM model with a moving catalyst or trap is commonly used. Our results have important implications for the pricing of options and the study of stochastic processes in various fields, including finance, physics, and engineering. In particular, the precise asymptotics for the PAM solution with a moving catalyst or trap help to understand the long-term behavior of systems with random catalysts or traps and provide a framework for analyzing more complex models with multiple moving catalysts or traps.

Mobility is valued greatly in the highly industrialized societies. The need
for radical change in propulsion technologies is obvious to all actors,
irrespective of whether they originate from industry, politics or the general
public. This paper analyses the tension between innovation pressure and pull of
convention in the automobile industries. This tension is currently giving rise
to a situation of stalemate in relation to alternative propulsion and fuel
technologies. We map the situation by means of a taxonomy of current and future
incremental and radical innovations. Based on in-depth field observation of
engineering and manufacturing in Germany, we present an innovation landscape in
the form of a two-dimensional matrix composed of propulsion innovations and
fuel innovations. We use mathematical models of hyperselection to develop a
rationale for escape strategies from the current lock-in into conventional
combustion-engine technology. Based on the heuristic guidance of these models,
we discuss several empirical cases in which buses act as pioneers in markets
for alternative propulsion vehicles. Neither the model nor the basic empirical
material used in this paper are new. Instead, we show that using mathematical
models as a kind of substratum on which empirical observations and theoretical
arguments can be ordered leads to new and partly unexpected insights into the
nature of socioeconomic innovations. We apply this approach to the case of new
driving technologies and argue that there is a 'third epistemic function' of
models in the continuum between data driven, exactly validated models at the
one extreme and a metaphoric use of models in thought experiments at the other.
This is what we call a holistic description.

text: We present a study investigating the impact of feedback on the fidelity of information transmission of time-varying signals. The primary goal of our work is to understand how feedback mechanisms influence the accuracy and reliability of signal transmission in dynamic systems. Through simulations and analytical methods, we demonstrate that feedback plays a crucial role in maintaining signal fidelity, particularly in the presence of noise and disturbances. Our results indicate that appropriate feedback mechanisms can enhance the robustness of signal transmission, leading to improved performance in dynamic environments. By systematically varying feedback parameters, we have identified optimal conditions that maximize information fidelity while minimizing distortions. Our findings contribute to the understanding of the fundamental principles governing information transmission in complex systems and have implications for various fields, including communication systems, control theory, and neuroscience. The methodology employed in this study involves mathematical modeling, simulation of time-varying signals, and analysis of feedback mechanisms. Our research provides valuable insights into the design and optimization of systems that deal with time-varying signals, shedding light on the role of feedback in ensuring reliable signal transmission in dynamic settings.
label: machine

text: The study of quantum open systems is pivotal for advancing the fields of quantum optics and optomechanics, where dissipative processes and thermal effects play crucial roles. This research explores the thermodynamics of quantum open systems, focusing on their interactions with external environments and the implications for quantum technologies. The primary objective is to investigate the thermodynamic behavior of such systems and identify applications that leverage their unique properties. Utilizing a combination of canonical and non-canonical statistical mechanics frameworks, our methodology involves the development of analytical models and numerical simulations to analyze energy flows, entropy production, and coherence dynamics. Key findings demonstrate that the intricate balance of dissipation and coherence can be harnessed to improve the stability and efficiency of quantum devices, exemplified by enhanced control over photon emissions in quantum optics and precision measurements in optomechanical systems. Additionally, we uncover novel mechanisms of heat exchange that can be optimized for energy-efficient quantum cooling and amplification. The research concludes that a deeper understanding of thermodynamic principles at the quantum level facilitates the development of more robust quantum technologies, offering insights into designing systems with reduced decoherence and energy loss. This work highlights the potential of employing thermodynamic strategies to transcend classical limitations in quantum device functionality, paving the way for advancements in quantum computing, information processing, and precision measurement technologies.
label: machine

Our aim is to study the thermal and dynamical evolution of protoplanetary
disks in global simulations, including the physics of radiation transfer and
magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence caused by the magneto-rotational
instability. We develop a radiative transfer method based on the flux-limited
diffusion approximation that includes frequency dependent irradiation by the
central star. This hybrid scheme is implemented in the PLUTO code. The focus of
our implementation is on the performance of the radiative transfer method.
Using an optimized Jacobi preconditioned BiCGSTAB solver, the radiative module
is three times faster than the MHD step for the disk setup we consider. We
obtain weak scaling efficiencies of 70% up to 1024 cores. We present the first
global 3D radiation MHD simulations of a stratified protoplanetary disk. The
disk model parameters are chosen to approximate those of the system AS 209 in
the star-forming region Ophiuchus. Starting the simulation from a disk in
radiative and hydrostatic equilibrium, the magnetorotational instability
quickly causes MHD turbulence and heating in the disk. For the disk parameters
we use, turbulent dissipation heats the disk midplane and raises the
temperature by about 15% compared to passive disk models. A roughly flat
vertical temperature profile establishes in the disk optically thick region
close to the midplane. We reproduce the vertical temperature profile with a
viscous disk models for which the stress tensor vertical profile is flat in the
bulk of the disk and vanishes in the disk corona. The present paper
demonstrates for the first time that global radiation MHD simulations of
turbulent protoplanetary disks are feasible with current computational
facilities. This opens up the windows to a wide range of studies of the
dynamics of protoplanetary disks inner parts, for which there are significant
observational constraints.
label: human

text:
Context: Clumping in the radiation-driven winds of hot, massive stars arises
naturally due to the strong, intrinsic instability of line-driving (the `LDI').
But LDI wind models have so far mostly been limited to 1D, mainly because of
severe computational challenges regarding calculation of the multi-dimensional
radiation force. Aims: To simulate and examine the dynamics and
multi-dimensional nature of wind structure resulting from the LDI. Methods: We
introduce a `pseudo-planar', `box-in-a-wind' method that allows us to
efficiently compute the line-force in the radial and lateral directions, and
then use this approach to carry out 2D radiation-hydrodynamical simulations of
the time-dependent wind. Results: Our 2D simulations show that the LDI first
manifests itself by mimicking the typical shell-structure seen in 1D models,
but how these shells then quickly break up into complex 2D density and velocity
structures, characterized by small-scale density `clumps' embedded in larger
regions of fast and rarefied gas. Key results of the simulations are that
density-variations in the well-developed wind statistically are quite isotropic
and that characteristic length-scales are small; a typical clump size is ~0.01R
at 2R, thus resulting also in rather low typical clump-masses ~10^17 g.
Overall, our results agree well with the theoretical expectation that the
characteristic scale for LDI-generated wind-structure is of order the Sobolev
length. We further confirm some earlier results that lateral `filling-in' of
radially compressed gas leads to somewhat lower clumping factors in 2D
simulations than in comparable 1D models. We conclude by discussing an
extension of our method toward rotating LDI wind models that exhibit an
intriguing combination of large- and small-scale structure extending down to
the wind base.
label: human

A clock synchronization thought experiment is modeled by a diffeomorphism
invariant "time delay" observable. In a sense, this observable probes the
causal structure of the ambient Lorentzian spacetime. Thus, upon quantization,
it is sensitive to the long expected smearing of the light cone by vacuum
fluctuations in quantum gravity. After perturbative linearization, its mean and
variance are computed in the Minkowski Fock vacuum of linearized gravity. The
na\"ive divergence of the variance is meaningfully regularized by a length
scale $\mu$, the physical detector resolution. This is the first time vacuum
fluctuations have been fully taken into account in a similar calculation.
Despite some drawbacks this calculation provides a useful template for the
study of a large class of similar observables in quantum gravity. Due to their
large volume, intermediate calculations were performed using computer algebra
software. The resulting variance scales like $(s \ell_p/\mu)^2$, where $\ell_p$
is the Planck length and $s$ is the distance scale separating the ("lab" and
"probe") clocks. Additionally, the variance depends on the relative velocity of
the lab and the probe, diverging for low velocities. This puzzling behavior may
be due to an oversimplified detector resolution model or a neglected second
order term in the time delay.
label: human

text:
The ULIRG Mrk 231 exhibits very strong water rotational lines between \lambda
= 200-670\mu m, comparable to the strength of the CO rotational lines. High
redshift quasars also show similar CO and H2O line properties, while starburst
galaxies, such as M82, lack these very strong H2O lines in the same wavelength
range, but do show strong CO lines. We explore the possibility of enhancing the
gas phase H2O abundance in X-ray exposed environments, using bare interstellar
carbonaceous dust grains as a catalyst. Cloud-cloud collisions cause C and J
shocks, and strip the grains of their ice layers. The internal UV field created
by X-rays from the accreting black hole does not allow to reform the ice. We
determine formation rates of both OH and H2O on dust grains, having temperature
T_dust=10-60 K, using both Monte Carlo as well as rate equation method
simulations. The acquired formation rates are added to our X-ray chemistry
code, that allows us to calculate the thermal and chemical structure of the
interstellar medium near an active galactic nucleus. We derive analytic
expressions for the formation of OH and H2O on bare dust grains as a catalyst.
Oxygen atoms arriving on the dust are released into the gas phase under the
form of OH and H2O. The efficiencies of this conversion due to the chemistry
occurring on dust are of order 30 percent for oxygen converted into OH and 60
percent for oxygen converted into H_2O between T_dust=15-40 K. At higher
temperatures, the efficiencies rapidly decline. When the gas is mostly atomic,
molecule formation on dust is dominant over the gas-phase route, which is then
quenched by the low H2 abundance. Here, it is possible to enhance the warm (T>
200 K) water abundance by an order of magnitude in X-ray exposed environments.
This helps to explain the observed bright water lines in nearby and
high-redshift ULIRGs and Quasars.
label: human

In the early 1980's, computers made it possible to observe that in complex
dynamics, one often sees dynamical behavior reflected in parameter space and
vice versa. This duality was first exploited by Douady, Hubbard and their
students in early work on rational maps. See \cite{DH,BH} for example. Here, we
continue to study these ideas in the realm of transcendental functions.
  In \cite{KK1}, it was shown that for the tangent family, $\lambda \tan z$,
the way the hyperbolic components meet at a point where the asymptotic value
eventually lands on infinity reflects the dynamic behavior of the functions at
infinity. In the first part of this paper we show that this duality extends to
a much more general class of transcendental meromorphic functions that we call
{\em generalized Nevanlinna functions} with the additional property that
infinity is not an asymptotic value. In particular, we show that in
"dynamically natural" one dimensional slices of parameter space, there are
"hyperbolic-like" components with a unique distinguished boundary point whose
dynamics reflect the behavior inside an asymptotic tract at infinity. Our main
result is that {\em every} parameter point in such a slice for which the
asymptotic value eventually lands on a pole is such a distinguished boundary
point.
  In the second part of the paper, we apply this result to the families
$\lambda \tan^p z^q$, $p,q \in \mathbb Z^+$, to prove that all hyperbolic
components of period greater than $1$ are bounded.

This paper discusses the ATLAS potential to study Supersymmetry for the
"Focus-Point" region of the parameter space of mSUGRA models. The potential to
discovery a deviation from Standard Model expectations with the first few
${fb}^{-1}$ of LHC data was studied using the parametrized simulation of the
ATLAS detector. Several signatures were considered, involving hard jets, large
missing energy, and either $b$-tagged jets, opposite-sign isolated electron or
muon pairs, or top quarks reconstructed exploiting their fully hadronic decays.
With only 1 ${fb}^{-1}$ of data each of these signatures may allow to observe
an excess of events over Standard Model expectation with a statistical
significance exceeding 5 standard deviations. An analytical expression was
derived for the shape of the distribution of the dilepton invariant mass
arising from the three-body leptonic decay of the neutralinos under the
hypothesis of heavy scalars, which is appropriate for the focus-point scenario.
The resulting function was used to fit the distribution of the dilepton
invariant mass obtained with simulated LHC data, and to extract the value of
two kinematic endpoints measuring the $\tilde \chi^0_2 - \tilde \chi^0_1$ and
the $\tilde \chi^0_3 - \tilde \chi^0_1$ mass differences. This information was
used to constrain the MSSM parameter space compatible with the data.

text: This abstract outlines the findings of an observational study estimating the short gamma-ray burst (GRB) cooling timescales using data from the PdBI Arcsecond Whirlpool Survey (PAWS). The background involves understanding the cooling processes of GRBs afterglows, which are crucial for constraining their cosmological parameters and progenitor models. The primary objective was to measure these cooling timescales by analyzing the spatially resolved spectra of distant GRBs detected by PAWS.  The methodology employed involved detailed spectral analysis of GRB afterglows observed with the Plateau de Bure Interferometer (PdBI), a millimeter-wave interferometer. This allowed for the detection of the cooling light curves at high angular resolution, enabling precise measurements of the cooling timescales. The dataset included GRBs with redshifts up to z=3.5, providing a broad range of distances and thus different cooling timescales.  Key findings revealed that the observed cooling timescales were significantly shorter than theoretical predictions, indicating either faster cooling mechanisms or a more compact structure of the GRB emission region. These results suggest that the environments in which GRBs form might be more conducive to rapid energy loss than previously thought.  In conclusion, the study provides robust observational constraints on GRB cooling timescales, highlighting the importance of high-resolution observations for advancing our understanding of GRB progenitors and their surrounding environments.
label: machine

text: The outer solar corona and inner heliosphere are dynamic environments characterized by the presence of evolving waves and turbulent plasma flows influenced by solar activity. This study aims to elucidate the mechanisms underlying wave propagation and turbulence in these regions, specifically focusing on the phenomenon of the accelerating expanding solar wind and its interaction with coronal mass ejections (CMEs). Utilizing a combination of numerical simulations and observational data from space missions such as Parker Solar Probe and Solar Orbiter, we assess the role of magnetic field configurations and plasma density variations in shaping the propagation of Alfvénic and magnetosonic waves.   Key findings reveal that wave structures are significantly modulated by turbulence originating from both solar wind interactions and transient events like CMEs, leading to enhanced energy dissipation and particle acceleration processes. Notably, the study demonstrates a correlation between wave activity and the expansion rate of the solar wind, suggesting that accelerating wave patterns can amplify turbulence in the heliospheric medium.   The results underscore the importance of understanding wave-turbulence interactions in the solar atmosphere and their implications for space weather phenomena. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of solar dynamics and offers insights into how these processes may impact the heliospheric environment, with potential implications for space weather forecasting and the safety of space-based technologies.
label: machine

text: We investigated patterns of positive selection in seven ant genomes, a group of highly diverse and ecologically successful insects. Through a combination of comparative genomics and phylogenetic analyses, we identified 1,433 nonsynonymous substitutions in protein-coding genes that were fixed in at least one of the seven genomes, with 44% of these substitutions occurring in genes involved in immune function. Notably, we found that the majority of these substitutions were located in the genes of the immune-related proteins, such as the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and the Toll pathway, which are critical for the ants' defense against pathogens. Our analysis also revealed significant correlations between the rate of positive selection and the evolutionary distance of the genes, suggesting that the immune system has been a key driver of evolutionary innovation in ants. Furthermore, we found evidence of adaptive evolution in genes involved in social behavior, such as the caste determination gene, which is thought to be a key factor in the evolution of complex social structures in ants. Our results highlight the importance of the immune system and social behavior in shaping the evolution of ant genomes and underscore the need for a more nuanced understanding of the selective forces that have driven the evolution of these highly successful organisms.
label: machine

text: The centaur objects, which are irregular bodies in the outer Solar System, have long been a subject of interest due to their dynamic behavior and potential for harboring simple organic molecules. Among these centaurs, those in retrograde co-orbit resonance with Saturn have drawn particular attention. In this study, we investigated the orbital dynamics of 13 known Saturnian retrograde centaurs, using numerical integrations of their orbital elements over 300 years. Our analysis revealed that five of these centaurs, namely Pholus, Chiron, Nessus, Tritia, and Ixion, exhibit a stable, long-term co-orbit resonance with Saturn. This resonance, denoted as the 123 mean motion resonance, is a triangular resonance in which the orbital periods of the centaur, the centaur's moon, and Saturn are in the ratio of 123. We also explored the implications of these findings for the origin and evolution of retrograde centaurs and their potential role as suppliers of simple organics to the outer Solar System. Our results provide a better understanding of the intricacies of the Saturnian system and contribute to the ongoing efforts to explain the observed distribution and dynamics of these intriguing objects.
label: machine

text:
(Abridged) We propose a new method to estimate the Bondi (hot gas) accretion
rates, \dot M_B, onto the supermassive black holes (SMBHs) at the centres of
elliptical galaxies. It can be applied even if the Bondi radius is not
well-resolved in X-ray observations. This method is based on two simple
assumptions: (1) hot gas outside the Bondi radius is in nearly a hydrostatic
equilibrium, and (2) the gas temperature near the galaxy centre is close to the
virial temperature. We apply this method to 28 bright elliptical galaxies in
nearby galaxy clusters (27 of them are the brightest cluster galaxies; BCGs).
We find a correlation between the Bondi accretion rates and the power of jets
associated with the SMBHs over four orders of magnitude in \dot M_B. For most
galaxies, the accretion rates are large enough to account for the jet powers.
Our results indicate that the feedback from the active galactic nuclei (AGN)
correlates with the properties of the hot gas surrounding the SMBHs. We also
find that more massive SMBHs in BCGs tend to have larger specific growth rates.
This may explain the hyper masses (~ 10^10 M_sun) of some of the SMBHs.
Comparison between the accretion rates and the X-ray luminosities of the AGN
suggests that the AGN in the BCGs are extremely radiatively inefficient
compared with X-ray binaries in the Milky Way, even when their Eddington
accretion ratio, \dot M_B/\dot M_Edd, exceeds 0.01. Lastly, we find a tight
correlation between the Bondi accretion rates and the X-ray luminosities of
cool cores. Their relation is linear and the power generated by the Bondi
accretion is large enough to compensate the radiative cooling of the cool
cores. Although the `classical' Bondi accretion model is a greatly

text: In our study, we examine the peculiar Type Ia supernova SN 2011hr, and compare its properties with those of the well-studied supernovae SN 1991T and SN 2007if, to understand its peculiarities and place it within the existing supernova classification framework. Utilizing observational data collected from photometric and spectroscopic analysis, we aim to identify the supernova's intrinsic characteristics, including peak luminosity, spectral features, and temporal evolution. Through comparative analysis, we observe that SN 2011hr exhibits an unusually high peak luminosity and strong spectral similarities to SN 1991T, characterized by weakened Si II absorption lines and strong iron-group element imprints. However, deviations, such as a broader light curve width, align more closely with the properties of super-luminous SN 2007if, suggesting potential commonality with super-Chandrasekhar mass progenitors. Methodologically, we apply spectral synthesis and template fitting techniques to accurately delineate SN 2011hr’s spectral features and light curve parameters, providing insights into its explosion mechanics and progenitor system. Our findings suggest that SN 2011hr represents a unique transitional archetype between "normal" Type Ia supernovae like SN 1991T and the super-luminous variety exemplified by SN 2007if. We propose that SN 2011hr might be indicative of an evolutionary link within the heterogeneous Type Ia supernova class, with implications for theoretical models concerning the progenitor mass and explosion mechanisms. Further, the outcomes of our study enhance the understanding of the diversity and complexity inherent in Type Ia supernovae, contributing to the broader discourse on cosmic distance scaling and dark energy studies.

Let $B=(X,Y,E)$ be a bipartite graph. A half-square of $B$ has one color
class of $B$ as vertex set, say $X$; two vertices are adjacent whenever they
have a common neighbor in $Y$. Every planar graph is a half-square of a planar
bipartite graph, namely of its subdivision. Until recently, only half-squares
of planar bipartite graphs, also known as map graphs (Chen, Grigni and
Papadimitriou [STOC 1998, J. ACM 2002]), have been investigated, and the most
discussed problem is whether it is possible to recognize these graphs faster
and simpler than Thorup's $O(n^{120})$-time algorithm (Thorup [FOCS 1998]).
  In this paper, we identify the first hardness case, namely that deciding if a
graph is a half-square of a balanced bisplit graph is NP-complete. (Balanced
bisplit graphs form a proper subclass of star convex bipartite graphs.) For
classical subclasses of tree convex bipartite graphs such as biconvex, convex,
and chordal bipartite graphs, we give good structural characterizations of
their half-squares that imply efficient recognition algorithms. As a
by-product, we obtain new characterizations of unit interval graphs, interval
graphs, and of strongly chordal graphs in terms of half-squares of biconvex
bipartite, convex bipartite, and of chordal bipartite graphs, respectively.
Good characterizations of half-squares of star convex and star biconvex
bipartite graphs are also given, giving linear-time recognition algorithms for
these half-squares.

text: In this study, we investigate the interplay between dark energy and the potential time variation of fundamental constants, seeking to address several unresolved questions in cosmological and theoretical physics. We hypothesize that the behavior of dark energy, traditionally modeled as a cosmological constant, may exhibit temporal fluctuations correlated with changes in fundamental constants. To test this hypothesis, we employ a multi-faceted methodology, integrating observational data from distant supernovae and cosmic microwave background measurements with theoretical frameworks from quantum field theory and general relativity.   Our analysis reveals a slight, yet statistically significant, variation in the fine-structure constant over cosmological timescales, suggesting that dark energy density may not be a constant but subject to gradual evolution. We utilize Bayesian inference techniques to evaluate the likelihood of different models attributing time dependence to both dark energy and fundamental constants, resulting in an improved fit to observational data compared to traditional models relying on constant parameters. Furthermore, we explore the implications of our findings for the structure of the universe and the fundamental laws of physics.   Our results compel us to reconsider established paradigms surrounding cosmic acceleration and the foundational nature of physical constants, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the universe's evolution. We propose future observational strategies aimed at further elucidating these relationships, potentially reshaping our understanding of fundamental physics and dark energy in the context of an expanding universe.

Glyph-based visualization is an effective tool for depicting multivariate
information. Since sorting is one of the most common analytical tasks performed
on individual attributes of a multi-dimensional data set, this motivates the
hypothesis that introducing glyph sorting would significantly enhance the
usability of glyph-based visualization. In this paper, we present a glyph-based
conceptual framework as part of a visualization process for interactive sorting
of multivariate data. We examine several technical aspects of glyph sorting and
provide design principles for developing effective, visually sortable glyphs.
Glyphs that are visually sortable provide two key benefits: 1) performing
comparative analysis of multiple attributes between glyphs and 2) to support
multi-dimensional visual search. We describe a system that incorporates focus
and context glyphs to control sorting in a visually intuitive manner and for
viewing sorted results in an Interactive, Multi-dimensional Glyph (IMG) plot
that enables users to perform high-dimensional sorting, analyse and examine
data trends in detail. To demonstrate the usability of glyph sorting, we
present a case study in rugby event analysis for comparing and analysing trends
within matches. This work is undertaken in conjunction with a national rugby
team. From using glyph sorting, analysts have reported the discovery of new
insight beyond traditional match analysis.

text: In this study, we investigate the mechanism design framework to address risk-averse behavior among participants in economic settings. Our primary objective is to understand how incentive mechanisms can be tailored to incentivize cooperative outcomes while accounting for risk aversion. We propose a novel mechanism that incorporates risk aversion into the utility function of participants. Through extensive simulations and empirical testing, we demonstrate that by incorporating risk aversion into the design of incentive schemes, it is possible to achieve higher levels of cooperation compared to models without such considerations. Key methodologies include game theory analysis, stochastic optimization, and behavioral economics principles. The results indicate that mechanisms that explicitly account for risk aversion lead to more stable and cooperative interactions, thereby enhancing overall efficiency and stability in economic systems.

We propose a new optimal Location-Based Beamforming (LBB) scheme for the
wiretap channel, where both the main channel and the eavesdropper's channel are
subject to Rician fading. In our LBB scheme the two key inputs are the location
of the legitimate receiver and the location of the potential eavesdropper.
Notably, our scheme does not require as direct inputs any channel state
information of the main channel or the eavesdropper's channel, making it easy
to deploy in a host of application settings in which the location inputs are
known. Our beamforming solution assumes a multiple-antenna transmitter, a
multiple-antenna eavesdropper, and a single-antenna receiver, and its aim is to
maximize the physical layer security of the channel. To obtain our solution we
first derive the secrecy outage probability of the LBB scheme in a closed-form
expression that is valid for arbitrary values of the Rician K-factors of the
main channel and the eavesdropper's channel. Using this expression we then
determine the location-based beamformer solution that minimizes the secrecy
outage probability. To assess the usefulness of our new scheme, and to quantify
the value of the location information to the beamformer, we compare our scheme
to other schemes, some of which do not utilize any location information. Our
new beamformer solution provides optimal physical layer security for a wide
range of location-based applications.

text: In today's rapidly evolving business landscape, managing complex rule sets has become a crucial challenge for organizations. Traditional rule management systems lack the agility and flexibility to adapt to changing business needs. To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach to business rule management a Wiki for Business Rules in Open Vocabulary, Executable English. Our solution integrates a Wiki platform with a Business Rule Engine, enabling users to author, edit, and collaborate on rules using natural language. Rules are stored in a repository using Open Vocabulary, making them easily discoverable and interoperable across systems. The system's Executable English capability ensures that rules are automatically translated into executable code, enabling real-time implementation and testing. We evaluated the proposed solution by implementing it in a large-scale finance organization, where business rules are a crucial aspect of operations. The results were promising. Users reported increased productivity and agility, as they were able to quickly collaborate on rule changes and make updates in real-time. The system's open vocabulary feature allowed for improved rule reuse and interoperability, reducing the need for custom integrations and ensuring consistent rule application across the organization. Our research contributes to the field of Business Rule Management Systems by proposing a new approach that leverages the flexibility and collaborative nature of Wiki technology. By integrating a Wiki platform with a Business Rule Engine, we enable users to author, edit, and collaborate on rules using natural language, while ensuring that rules are automatically translated into executable code for real-time implementation. Our solution offers significant benefits for organizations facing the challenge of managing complex rule sets in today's dynamic business environment.

A fundamental gap in the current understanding of galaxies concerns the
thermodynamical evolution of the ordinary, baryonic matter. On one hand,
radiative emission drastically decreases the thermal energy content of the
interstellar plasma (ISM), inducing a slow cooling flow toward the centre. On
the other hand, the active galactic nucleus (AGN) struggles to prevent the
runaway cooling catastrophe, injecting huge amount of energy in the ISM. The
present study intends to deeply investigate the role of mechanical AGN feedback
in (isolated or massive) elliptical galaxies, extending and completing the mass
range of tested cosmic environments. Our previously successful feedback models,
in galaxy clusters and groups, demonstrated that AGN outflows, self-regulated
by cold gas accretion, are able to properly quench the cooling flow, without
destroying the cool core. Via 3D hydrodynamic simulations (FLASH 3.3),
including also stellar evolution, we show that massive mechanical AGN outflows
can indeed solve the cooling flow problem for the entire life of the galaxy, at
the same time reproducing typical observational features and constraints, such
as buoyant underdense bubbles, elliptical shock cocoons, sonic ripples,
dredge-up of metals, subsonic turbulence, and extended filamentary or nuclear
cold gas. In order to avoid overheating and totally emptying the isolated
galaxy, the frequent mechanical AGN feedback should be less powerful and
efficient (~1.e-4), compared to the heating required for more massive and bound
ellipticals surrounded by the intragroup medium (efficiency ~1.e-3).

text: We investigated the development of a novel approach to automatically select context trees and retrieve linguistic rhythms from written texts. Our methodology involved the creation of a hybrid model that integrates deep learning and symbolic reasoning to analyze the rhythmic patterns in written language. By training the model on a large corpus of texts, we identified key features that distinguish rhythmic and non-rhythmic patterns, including phonetic and morphological characteristics.  Through extensive experimentation, we found that our model achieved significant accuracy in context tree selection, with an average F1-score of 0.83 and a precision of 0.85. Furthermore, the model successfully retrieved linguistic rhythms from written texts with an average accuracy of 0.92 and a recall of 0.88. Our results suggest that the hybrid model is capable of effectively capturing the complex rhythmic patterns in written language.  We also explored the application of our model to various genres of texts, including poetry, prose, and dialogues. Our findings indicate that the model is able to generalize well across different text types, with an average accuracy of 0.89. Notably, our model was able to distinguish between rhythmic and non-rhythmic patterns in texts with varying levels of linguistic complexity. The implications of our study are significant, as they suggest that context tree selection and linguistic rhythm retrieval can be automated using deep learning and symbolic reasoning techniques.
