text: This study explores the self-consistency requirements of the renormalization group (RG) framework in determining the appropriate renormalization scale. It begins by outlining the conventional understanding of RG, emphasizing its role in predicting physical properties at different energy scales. The objective is to investigate how these predictions can be made more accurate and reliable through the identification of consistent renormalization scales.  The methodology employed involves a theoretical analysis of various models, including quantum field theories, where the RG equations are solved to derive effective field theories at different scales. The analysis includes numerical simulations to validate the theoretical predictions and assess their consistency across different scales. Additionally, comparisons with experimental data from particle physics experiments are conducted to evaluate the practical implications of the chosen renormalization scales.  Key findings reveal that there exists a critical scale at which the predictions from RG theory align most accurately with both theoretical expectations and empirical observations. This scale acts as a self-consistent reference point within the RG framework. Furthermore, deviations from this scale indicate inconsistencies that could arise due to model assumptions or approximations used in the calculations.  In conclusion, this research underscores the importance of adhering to self-consistency principles when setting the renormalization scale in RG analyses. The findings suggest that a precise determination of this scale is crucial for enhancing the predictive power of RG methods, particularly in applications such as high-energy physics and condensed matter systems. Future work will focus on extending these insights to broader classes of models and experimental settings.

text: This work explores the Kibble-Zurek problem concerning the dynamics of phase transitions in various physical systems. We investigate the concept of universality and the scaling limit in the context of the Kibble-Zurek mechanism. By studying the behavior of systems near critical points during quenches, we aim to understand how universal features emerge across different systems irrespective of their microscopic details. Our results demonstrate the presence of critical scaling behavior characterized by power-law dependencies on the quench rate and system size. Through numerical simulations and theoretical analyses, we provide insights into the emergence of universal scaling laws and critical exponents in the Kibble-Zurek framework. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of nonequilibrium dynamics near critical points and sheds light on the fundamental aspects of phase transitions in diverse physical systems. The methodology involves numerical simulations of quantum and classical systems undergoing quenches across critical points, followed by a detailed analysis of the scaling behavior and universality present in the system's dynamics. By elucidating the connection between quench dynamics, critical scaling, and universal features, our findings offer valuable contributions to the broader understanding of phase transitions and critical phenomena in physics.

text: We present a comprehensive analysis of the bolometric light curve (BLC) of Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) 2017egm, utilizing circumstellar interaction (CSI) models to interpret its distinct features. Our primary goal is to understand the mechanisms driving the asymmetric energy deposition leading to observable deviations from the canonical light curve shape. We fit the early-time BLC data with the well-known Arnett model, which indicates the presence of significant CSI. Then, we explore CSI models, including the standard CSM density profile, the double-DDen profile, and the asymmetric CSM profile, to analyze the temporal evolution of SN 2017egm's bolometric light curve.  The standard CSM density profile model, assuming a constant ejecta mass, exhibits a poor fit to the BLC data. However, employing a more flexible approach by allowing a varying ejecta mass results in a marginally acceptable fit. Furthermore, the double-DDen model, representing a more complex CSM structure, exhibits superior fitting results, suggesting a multi-component CSM environment. The asymmetric CSM profile model, accounting for the observed asymmetry, also shows a satisfactory fit to the BLC data, providing further evidence for asymmetric CSI.  Our findings highlight the importance of detailed CSI models for interpreting the BLCs of SN Ia. This study contributes to the ongoing efforts to deepen our understanding of the physical conditions surrounding SN Ia progenitor stars and the consequences on their explosive properties. By examining various CSI models and comparing their fitting abilities, we can identify the most probable model and refine our understanding of the role of circumstellar environments in shaping the BLCs of SN Ia.

The reaction $NN \to NN \pi$ offers a good testing ground for chiral
effective field theory at intermediate energies. It challenges our
understanding of the first inelastic channel in nucleon-nucleon scattering and
of the charge-symmetry breaking pattern in hadronic reactions. In our previous
studies, we presented a complete calculation of the pion-production operator
for s-wave pions up-to-and-including next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) in
the formulation of chiral effective field theory, which includes pions,
nucleons and $\Delta(1232)$ degrees of freedom. In this paper we calculate the
near threshold cross section for the $pp \to d \pi^{+}$ reaction by performing
the convolution of the obtained operators with nuclear wave functions based on
modern phenomenological and chiral potentials. The available chiral $NN$ wave
functions are constructed with a cutoff comparable with the momentum transfer
scale inherent in pion production reactions. Hence, a significant portion of
the dynamical intermediate-range physics is thereby cut off by them. On the
other hand, the NNLO amplitudes evaluated with phenomenological wave functions
appear to be largely independent of the $NN$ model used and give corrections to
the dominant leading order contributions as expected from dimensional analysis.
The result gives support to the counting scheme used to classify the pion
production operators, which is a precondition for a reliable investigation of
the chirally suppressed neutral pion production. The explicit inclusion of the
$\Delta(1232)$ is found to be important but smaller than expected due to
cancellations.

text: This research paper explores the multidimensional chemical modeling of diatomic hydrides, focusing on their abundance and excitation states. The study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of these molecules by employing advanced computational methods that account for electronic structure and vibrational dynamics.  The methodology involves extensive use of density functional theory (DFT) combined with post-Hartree-Fock methods such as configuration interaction singles (CIS) and coupled-cluster techniques. These methods were utilized to accurately calculate the ground and excited states of diatomic hydrides, including hydrogen molecules (H₂), deuterium molecules (D₂), and their isotopologues.  Key findings reveal significant insights into the electronic configurations and vibrational modes of these systems. The analysis shows that certain diatomic hydrides exhibit higher excitation energies compared to previously reported values, which could be attributed to the inclusion of electron correlation effects. Additionally, the study identifies regions of high molecular stability, providing critical information for the development of more accurate quantum chemistry models.  The conclusions drawn from this work highlight the importance of considering both electronic structure and vibrational dynamics in the modeling of diatomic hydrides. This approach not only enhances our theoretical understanding but also has implications for practical applications in spectroscopy, chemical reactions, and astrophysics. Future research directions include the extension of these methods to more complex molecular systems and the incorporation of experimental data to validate theoretical predictions.

In recent years, gas has been observed in an increasing number of debris
discs, though its nature remains to be determined. Here, we analyse CO
molecular excitation in optically thin debris discs, and search ALMA Cycle-0
data for CO J=3-2 emission in the Fomalhaut ring. No significant line emission
is observed; we set a 3-$\sigma$ upper limit on the integrated line flux of
0.16 Jy km s$^{-1}$. We show a significant dependency of the CO excitation on
the density of collisional partners $n$, on the gas kinetic temperature $T_k$
and on the ambient radiation field $J$, suggesting that assumptions widely used
for protoplanetary discs (e.g. LTE) do not necessarily apply to their low
density debris counterparts. When applied to the Fomalhaut ring, we consider a
primordial origin scenario where H$_2$ dominates collisional excitation of CO,
and a secondary origin scenario dominated by e$^-$ and H$_2$O. In either
scenario, we obtain a strict upper limit on the CO mass of 4.9 $\times$
10$^{-4}$ M$_{\oplus}$. This arises in the non-LTE regime, where the excitation
of the molecule is determined solely by the well-known radiation field. In the
secondary scenario, assuming any CO present to be in steady state allows us to
set an upper limit of $\sim$55% on the CO/H$_2$O ice ratio in the parent
planetesimals. This could drop to $\sim$3% if LTE applies, covering the range
observed in Solar System comets (0.4-30%). Finally, in light of our analysis,
we present prospects for CO detection and characterisation in debris discs with
ALMA.

text: This study investigates the dynamics of both coherently and incoherently coupled multicomponent solitons and their interactions. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we elucidate how coherence affects the stability and propagation characteristics of these soliton pairs. In coherent coupling, solitons maintain phase relationships, leading to predictable collision outcomes and enhanced interaction strength. Conversely, incoherent coupling disrupts these phase relationships, resulting in less predictable and weaker collision events. Our findings reveal that incoherent coupling introduces complexity in the soliton dynamics but also opens avenues for novel control strategies. The methodologies employed include perturbation theory for analyzing small deviations from exact solutions and direct numerical integration for simulating large-scale scenarios. These approaches collectively provide insights into the fundamental physics governing multicomponent solitons under various coupling conditions, contributing to our understanding of nonlinear wave interactions in diverse physical systems.

We consider how dynamical friction acts on black holes that receive a
velocity kick while located at the center of a gravitational potential,
analogous to a star cluster, due to either a natal kick or the anisotropic
emission of gravitational waves during a black hole-black hole merger. Our
investigation specifically focuses on how well various Chandrasekhar-based
dynamical friction models can predict the orbital decay of kicked black holes
with $m_{bh} \lesssim 100 M_\odot$ due to an inhomogeneous background stellar
field. In general, the orbital evolution of a kicked black hole follows that of
a damped oscillator where two-body encounters and dynamical friction serve as
sources of damping. However, we find models for approximating the effects of
dynamical friction do not accurately predict the amount of energy lost by the
black hole if the initial kick velocity $v_{k}$ is greater than the stellar
velocity dispersion $\sigma$. For all kick velocities, we also find that
two-body encounters with nearby stars can cause the energy evolution of a
kicked BH to stray significantly from standard dynamical friction theory as
encounters can sometimes lead to an energy gain. For larger kick velocities, we
find the orbital decay of a black hole departs from classical theory completely
as the black hole's orbital amplitude decays linearly with time as opposed to
exponentially. Therefore, we have developed a linear decay formalism which
scales linearly with black hole mass and $\frac{v_{k}}{\sigma}$ in order to
account for the variations in the local gravitational potential.

text: We compare globular clusters (GCs) and field low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) within elliptical galaxies using deep Chandra and Hubble Space Telescope data. Our research addresses the ongoing challenge of understanding the formation and evolution of LMXBs in relation to their host environments. By analyzing the spatial distribution and luminosity functions of GCs in conjunction with the population of field LMXBs, we aim to discern the underlying physical processes influencing their formation mechanisms.   We conduct our study by applying advanced statistical techniques to the high-resolution data obtained from Chandra and Hubble. We investigate the correlation between GC density and LMXB incidence, focusing on the stellar density profiles of the elliptical galaxies in our sample. Our results reveal a significant association between the abundance of GCs and the distribution of LMXBs, suggesting that the formation of LMXBs is preferentially influenced by the density environments typically found in and around GCs.   Furthermore, we explore the potential differences in X-ray luminosities between GCs and field LMXBs, indicating a variation in the accretion processes or binary interactions depending on their environments. This work enhances our understanding of LMXB demographics and the role of GCs in the broader context of stellar evolution in elliptical galaxies, contributing valuable insights into the dynamics of stellar populations. Our findings have implications for the development of future models addressing the connection between environment and binary formation.

text: In the realm of multi-category support vector machines (SVMs), selecting the optimal set of variables is imperative for enhancing model interpretability and prediction accuracy. Traditional methods, however, often grapple with cumbersome variable-selection processes, especially when dealing with high-dimensional data. This research introduces a novel methodology for variable selection in multi-category SVMs using an adaptive sup-norm regularization technique. The primary objective of this approach is to efficiently identify and retain significant variables while discarding irrelevant ones, thereby streamlining the model complexity without compromising its predictive capabilities. The methodology employs an adaptive sup-norm, which dynamically adjusts the regularization parameters for each variable, facilitating a tailored selection process that is more robust against noise and irrelevant features in the dataset. We implement this method across various high-dimensional datasets to evaluate its performance against existing variable selection techniques. Our findings demonstrate a marked improvement in the accuracy and simplicity of the models developed via our proposed approach, with significant reductions in computational complexity observed during the variable selection phase. The adaptive nature of this technique not only enhances the selection process but also provides a more interpretable model through a reduced number of significant variables. In conclusion, the adaptive sup-norm regularization for variable selection proves to be a promising advancement for multi-category SVMs, offering substantial benefits in terms of both model efficiency and interpretability, making it a valuable tool for complex predictive modeling tasks in high-dimensional spaces.
label: machine

text: We investigate networks of reinforced stochastic processes and provide asymptotic results for the empirical means within these networks. Our work addresses the challenge of analyzing complex systems where stochastic processes are coupled and reinforced by network interactions. The key problem we aim to solve is understanding how the empirical means of these processes evolve over time, as influenced by the network structure and reinforcement mechanisms.   Our results reveal that in these networks, the empirical means converge to deterministic limits under certain conditions. We establish the convergence rate and characterize the limiting behavior of the empirical means. To achieve this, we develop a methodology that combines tools from probability theory, stochastic processes, and network analysis.   By studying the asymptotics of empirical means in networks of reinforced stochastic processes, we contribute to the understanding of dynamic systems with interdependencies. Our findings shed light on how network structures impact the evolution of empirical means and provide insights into the stability and convergence properties of these systems. This research has implications for various domains, including computer networks, social networks, and biological systems, where understanding the behavior of interconnected stochastic processes is crucial for predicting system dynamics and emergent properties.

text: Recent advancements in high-resolution imaging have enabled the study of spiral features in protoplanetary disks, providing crucial insights into planet formation processes. The objective of this study is to investigate the hypothesis that such spiral arms, observed in scattered light imaging, can be induced by the presence of embedded planets within the disk. Utilizing state-of-the-art hydrodynamical simulations, we model the interaction between a protoplanetary disk and embedded planets of varying masses and orbital properties. The simulations are followed by radiative transfer calculations to create synthetic images for direct comparison with observations. Our findings reveal that planets, particularly those with masses exceeding a few Jupiter masses, are capable of exciting prominent spiral density waves in the disk material, which are subsequently detectable in scattered light observations. These spiral arms exhibit distinct morphological and kinematic signatures that correlate with the properties of the inducing planet, such as mass and orbital separation. Notably, our results demonstrate that observed spiral patterns can serve as scalable diagnostics for inferring planetary characteristics in evolving disks. This study not only supports the scenario of planet-induced structures in disks but also enhances the interpretative framework for astrometric data, thus contributing to the broader understanding of early-stage planetary system evolution. Conclusively, the correlation between observed spiral arms and planet presence accentuates the role of direct imaging as a vital tool in uncovering formative processes within protoplanetary environments.

text: Entanglement is a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, characterized by the interconnectedness of particles across vast distances. Despite its importance, quantifying entanglement remains a significant challenge due to the inherent complexity of measuring and interpreting entanglement measures. This paper aims to address the issue by proposing a framework for establishing measurable bounds on entanglement measures, thereby providing a more precise understanding of entanglement in various systems.  Entanglement measures, such as concurrence and Bell entropy, have been widely used to quantify entanglement. However, these measures often exhibit non-linear relationships with the underlying physical parameters, making it difficult to establish a clear connection between entanglement and system properties. The objective of this research is to develop a theoretical framework that enables the derivation of measurable bounds on entanglement measures, thereby facilitating a more accurate characterization of entanglement in various systems.  The proposed framework relies on a combination of mathematical techniques, including convex optimization and machine learning algorithms. By applying these methods, we derive a set of bounds on entanglement measures that are both rigorous and computationally efficient. Our results demonstrate that these bounds can be used to distinguish between entangled and separable states, as well as to identify the optimal entanglement measures for specific systems. The proposed framework has far-reaching implications for the study of entanglement in quantum information processing, quantum computing, and quantum communication.

text: This study investigates the line profiles observed in tidal disruption events (TDEs), focusing on the mechanisms that define their distinctive characteristics. We explore various theoretical models, including accretion disk emission, relativistic beaming, and the effects of the central black hole's spin. Through detailed numerical simulations, we analyze how these factors influence the observed spectral features such as iron Kα lines and other absorption features. Our findings suggest that the line profiles are significantly influenced by the geometry of the accretion flow and the orientation of the jet relative to the observer. Additionally, we find that the presence of a significant amount of gas close to the event horizon can produce complex line profiles, which may contain multiple components indicative of different physical processes occurring simultaneously. The key methodologies employed include Monte Carlo radiative transfer calculations and relativistic radiative transfer codes, providing a comprehensive framework to interpret the observational data from TDEs. These insights help clarify the physical conditions within TDEs and contribute to our understanding of the dynamics and radiation mechanisms involved in these cataclysmic phenomena.

T Cha is a nearby (d = 100 pc) transition disk known to have an optically
thin gap separating optically thick inner and outer disk components. Huelamo et
al. (2011) recently reported the presence of a low-mass object candidate within
the gap of the T Cha disk, giving credence to the suspected planetary origin of
this gap. Here we present the Herschel photometry (70, 160, 250, 350, and 500
micron) of T Cha from the "Dust, Ice, and Gas in Time" (DIGIT) Key Program,
which bridges the wavelength range between existing Spitzer and millimeter data
and provide important constraints on the outer disk properties of this
extraordinary system. We model the entire optical to millimeter wavelength
spectral energy distribution (SED) of T Cha (19 data points between 0.36 and
3300 micron without any major gaps in wavelength coverage). T Cha shows a steep
spectral slope in the far-IR, which we find clearly favors models with outer
disks containing little or no dust beyond 40 AU. The full SED can be modeled
equally well with either an outer disk that is very compact (only a few AU
wide) or a much larger one that has a very steep surface density profile. That
is, T Cha's outer disk seems to be either very small or very tenuous. Both
scenarios suggest a highly unusual outer disk and have important but different
implications for the nature of T Cha. Spatially resolved images are needed to
distinguish between the two scenarios.

text: This research paper explores optimal and maximin procedures for handling multiple testing problems. The background of the study sets the context for the necessity of robust methods in multiple testing scenarios due to the increased likelihood of false positives. The objective is to compare and analyze optimal and maximin procedures to determine their effectiveness in controlling Type I errors and maximizing statistical power. The methodology involves a comprehensive review of existing literature on multiple testing procedures, focusing on optimal procedures that aim to maximize power and minimax procedures that prioritize error control.  Key findings indicate that optimal procedures often achieve higher power but come at the cost of increased Type I errors, while maximin procedures are more conservative, aiming to control errors but potentially sacrificing power. Through simulations and comparisons, this research sheds light on the strengths and limitations of each approach in various multiple testing settings. In conclusion, understanding the trade-offs between optimal and maximin procedures is crucial for researchers to make informed decisions based on their specific research objectives and constraints. This study provides valuable insights for researchers aiming to navigate the complexities of multiple testing problems effectively.

text: In this observational study focusing on dust nucleation in the atmosphere of the variable star Mira ($o$ Ceti), we investigate the impact of titanium oxides on the nucleation process at elevated temperatures. Our results reveal that titanium oxides exhibit a negligible effect on nucleation phenomena, particularly at high temperatures. The study aimed to address the uncertainties surrounding the role of titanium oxides in dust nucleation processes in stellar environments, specifically in the case of Mira ($o$ Ceti). By employing observational data and analytical techniques, we sought to elucidate the contributions of titanium oxides to nucleation and understand their significance in the context of high-temperature environments. The methodology involved the analysis of spectral data and atmospheric conditions in the vicinity of Mira ($o$ Ceti), allowing us to draw robust conclusions regarding the role of titanium oxides in nucleation processes. The findings presented in this study contribute to our understanding of dust formation mechanisms in stellar atmospheres, shedding light on the relative importance of titanium oxides in nucleation at elevated temperatures.

text:
We propose three private information retrieval (PIR) protocols for
distributed storage systems (DSSs) where data is stored using an arbitrary
linear code. The first two protocols, named Protocol 1 and Protocol 2, achieve
privacy for the scenario with noncolluding nodes. Protocol 1 requires a file
size that is exponential in the number of files in the system, while Protocol 2
requires a file size that is independent of the number of files and is hence
simpler. We prove that, for certain linear codes, Protocol 1 achieves the
maximum distance separable (MDS) PIR capacity, i.e., the maximum PIR rate (the
ratio of the amount of retrieved stored data per unit of downloaded data) for a
DSS that uses an MDS code to store any given (finite and infinite) number of
files, and Protocol 2 achieves the asymptotic MDS-PIR capacity (with infinitely
large number of files in the DSS). In particular, we provide a necessary and a
sufficient condition for a code to achieve the MDS-PIR capacity with Protocols
1 and 2 and prove that cyclic codes, Reed-Muller (RM) codes, and a class of
distance-optimal local reconstruction codes achieve both the finite MDS-PIR
capacity (i.e., with any given number of files) and the asymptotic MDS-PIR
capacity with Protocols 1 and 2, respectively. Furthermore, we present a third
protocol, Protocol 3, for the scenario with multiple colluding nodes, which can
be seen as an improvement of a protocol recently introduced by Freij-Hollanti
et al.. Similar to the noncolluding case, we provide a necessary and a
sufficient condition to achieve the maximum possible PIR rate of Protocol 3.
Moreover, we provide a particular class of codes that is suitable for this
protocol and show that RM codes achieve the maximum possible PIR rate for the
protocol. For all three protocols, we present an algorithm to optimize their
PIR rates.

In this paper, we identify the moduli space for germs of generic unfoldings
of nonresonant linear differential systems with an irregular singularity of
Poincar\'e rank $k$ at the origin, under analytic equivalence. The modulus of a
given family was determined in \cite{HLR}: it comprises a formal part depending
analytically on the parameters, and an analytic part given by unfoldings of the
Stokes matrices. These unfoldings are given on "Douady-Sentenac" (DS) domains
in the parameter space covering the generic values of the parameters
corresponding to Fuchsian singular points. Here we identify exactly which
moduli can be realized. A necessary condition on the analytic part, called
compatibility condition, is saying that the unfoldings define the same
monodromy group (up to conjugacy) for the different presentations of the
modulus on the intersections of DS domains. With the additional requirement
that the corresponding cocycle is trivial and good limit behavior at some
boundary points of the DS domains, this condition becomes sufficient. In
particular we show that any modulus can be realized by a $k$-parameter family
of systems of rational linear differential equations over $\mathbb C\mathbb
P^1$ with $k+1$, $k+2$ or $k+3$ singular points (with multiplicities). Under
the generic condition of irreducibility, there are precisely $k+2$ singular
points which are Fuchsian as soon as simple. This in turn implies that any
unfolding of an irregular singularity of Poincar\'e rank $k$ is analytically
equivalent to a rational system of the form $y'=\frac{A(x)}{p_\epsilon(x)}\cdot
y$, with $A(x)$ polynomial of degree at most $k$ and $p_\epsilon(x)$ is the
generic unfolding of the polynomial $x^{k+1}$.

text:
Background / Aims ClO2, the so-called "ideal biocide", could also be applied
as an antiseptic if it was understood why the solution's rapid killing of
microbes does not cause any harm to humans or to animals. Our aim was to study
both theoretically and experimentally its reaction-diffusion mechanism to find
the source of that selectivity. Methods ClO2 permeation measurements through
protein membranes were performed and the time delay of ClO2 transport due to
reaction and diffusion was determined. To calculate ClO2 penetration depths and
estimate bacterial killing times, approximate solutions of the
reaction-diffusion equation were derived. Additionally, as a preliminary test,
three patients with infected wounds were treated with a 300 ppm high purity
ClO2 solution and the healing process was documented. Results The rate law of
the reaction-diffusion model predicts that the killing time is proportional to
the square of the characteristic size (e.g. diameter) of a body, thus, small
ones will be killed extremely fast. For example, the killing time for a
bacterium is on the order of milliseconds in a 300 ppm ClO2 solution. Thus, the
few minutes of contact time (owing to the volatility of ClO2) is quite enough
to kill all bacteria, but short enough to keep ClO2 penetration into the living
tissues safely below 0.1 mm, minimizing cytotoxic effects. Pictures of
successful wound healings confirm these considerations. Various properties of
ClO2, advantageous for an antiseptic, are also discussed. Most importantly,
bacteria are not able to develop resistance against ClO2 as it reacts with
biological thiols which play a vital role in all living organisms. Conclusion
Selectivity of ClO2 between humans and bacteria is based not on their different
biochemistry, but on their different size. Preliminary clinical results
encourage further research with this promising local antiseptic.
label: human

text:
We present the statistics of the ratio, ${\cal R}$, between the prompt and
afterglow "plateau" fluxes of GRB. This we define as the ratio between the mean
prompt energy flux in {\em Swift} BAT and the {\em Swift} XRT one, immediately
following the steep transition between these two states and the beginning of
the afterglow stage referred to as the "plateau". Like the distribution of many
other GRB observables, the histogram of ${\cal R}$~ is log-normal with maximum
at a value ${\cal R}_m \simeq 2,000$, FWHM of about 2 decades and with the
entire distribution spanning about 5 decades in the value of ${\cal R}$. We
note that the peak of the distribution is close to the proton-to-electron mass
ratio $({\cal R}_m \simeq m_p/m_e = 1836)$, as proposed to be the case in an
earlier publication, on the basis of a specific model of the GRB dissipation
process. It therefore appears that, in addition to the values of the energy of
peak luminosity ${E_{\rm pk}\sim m_{e} c^2}$, GRB present us with one more
quantity with an apparent characteristic value. The fact that the values of
both these quantities (\Ep~and \R) are consistent with the same specific model
invoked to account for the efficient conversion of their relativistic proton
energies to electrons, argues favorably for its underlying assumptions.

Motivated by its role as a central pillar of current theories of dynamics of
spin ice in and out of equilibrium, we study the single-ion dynamics of the
magnetic rare earth ions in their local environments, subject to the effective
fields set up by the magnetic moments they interact with. This effective field
has a transverse component with respect to the local easy-axis of the crystal
electric field, which can induce quantum tunnelling. We go beyond the
projective spin-1/2 picture and use instead the full crystal-field Hamiltonian.
We find that the Kramers vs non-Kramers nature, as well as the symmetries of
the crystal-field Hamiltonian, result in different perturbative behaviour at
small fields ($\lesssim 1$ T), with transverse field effects being more
pronounced in Ho$_{2}$Ti$_{2}$O$_{7}$ than in Dy$_{2}$Ti$_{2}$O$_{7}$.
Remarkably, the energy splitting range we find is consistent with time scales
extracted from experiments. We also present a study of the static magnetic
response which highlights the anisotropy of the system in the form of an
off-diagonal $g$ tensor and we investigate the effects of thermal fluctuations
in the temperature regime of relevance to experiments. We show that there is a
narrow yet accessible window of experimental parameters where the anisotropic
response can be observed.

text:
We present a model that explains the observed deviation of the spectra of
some pulsars and magnetars from the power-law spectra which are seen in the
bulk of the pulsar population. Our model is based on the assumption that the
observed variety of pulsar spectra can be naturally explained by the thermal
free-free absorption that takes place in the surroundings of the pulsars. In
this context, the variety of the pulsar spectra can be explained according to
the shape, density and temperature of the absorbing media and the optical path
of the line-of-sight across that. We have put specific emphasis on the case of
the radio magnetar SGR J1745-2900 (also known as Sgr A* magnetar), modeling the
rapid variations of the pulsar spectrum after the outburst of Apr 2013 as due
to the free-free absorption of the radio emission in the electron material
ejected during the magnetar outburst. The ejecta expands with time and
consequently the absorption rate decreases and the shape of the spectrum
changes in such a way that the peak frequency shifts towards the lower radio
frequencies. In the hypothesis of an absorbing medium, we also discuss the
similarity between the spectral behaviour of the binary pulsar B1259-63 and the
spectral peculiarities of isolated pulsars.

text: The $\bar{K} + N \to K + \Xi$ reaction plays a significant role in understanding the strangeness production mechanisms in nuclear collisions. This reaction is dominated by the existence of $S=-1$ hyperon resonances, which have been a long-standing puzzle in nuclear physics. In this study, we investigate the role of these resonances in the $\bar{K} + N \to K + \Xi$ reaction using a chiral effective theory approach.  Firstly, we present a brief overview of the theoretical background of the reaction and the $S=-1$ hyperon resonances. We then outline the objective of our work, which is to provide a detailed analysis of the contributions of these resonances to the reaction cross section.  The methodology of our study involves calculating the reaction cross section using a chiral effective theory model, which includes the contributions of various $S=-1$ hyperon resonances. We perform a systematic analysis of the model parameters and investigate the sensitivity of the results to different resonance masses and widths.  Our key findings reveal that the $S=-1$ hyperon resonances, particularly the $\Lambda(1405)$ and $\Sigma(1385)$, significantly contribute to the $\bar{K} + N \to K + \Xi$ reaction cross section. We observe that the contributions of these resonances depend on the energy and momentum transfer in the reaction. Furthermore, we provide a comparison of our results with experimental data and previous theoretical studies.  In conclusion, our work provides a detailed analysis of the role of $S=-1$ hyperon resonances in the $\bar{K} + N \to K + \Xi$ reaction using a chiral effective theory approach. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of strangeness production mechanisms in nuclear collisions.

text: This study aims to enhance the performance of goal-oriented dialogue systems by developing advanced dialogue managers that can effectively navigate complex conversational paths towards user goals. The problem addressed is the limitation of current dialogue systems in handling intricate user intents and context transitions, leading to suboptimal interaction experiences. We propose a novel approach that integrates deep learning techniques with traditional rule-based methods to create a robust dialogue manager architecture. This includes employing neural networks for natural language understanding (NLU) to accurately interpret user inputs and extract intent, as well as using reinforcement learning algorithms to optimize dialogue management policies based on user feedback. Empirical evaluations conducted on a diverse set of dialogues demonstrate significant improvements in system performance, including higher accuracy in goal achievement and more fluent dialogue flow. Key methodologies involve training models on large annotated datasets and incorporating real-time adaptation mechanisms to learn from ongoing interactions. These advancements not only refine the dialogue manager's ability to understand and respond to user needs but also pave the way for more sophisticated and user-centric conversational interfaces.

text: Grain growth within dense interstellar clouds plays a crucial role in understanding the formation of complex organic molecules in space. This study aims to investigate the occurrence of grain growth towards the center of the prestellar core L1544, which represents a pristine environment conducive to such processes. The methodology involves analyzing infrared spectroscopic data obtained from the Spitzer Space Telescope to identify evidence of grain growth based on changes in the dust emission properties. Our key findings reveal a significant enhancement in the abundance of large grains towards the core's center, implying the presence of active grain growth mechanisms in this region. This suggests that L1544 serves as a promising site for studying the early stages of grain evolution in interstellar environments. In conclusion, the observed grain growth towards the core's center in L1544 provides valuable insights into the physical and chemical processes governing dust evolution in dense molecular clouds, shedding light on the mechanisms responsible for the formation of complex organic molecules in space.

text: This paper explores functions in the continuous function space C(X) over a compact Hausdorff space X, whose supports lie on ideals of closed sets. We begin by providing a brief overview of the concept of supports on ideals and their significance in functional analysis. The objective of this research is twofold to investigate existence and uniqueness conditions for such functions and to characterize their properties.  To achieve these objectives, we employ the Mittag-Leffler theorem, fixed point theory, and set-valued analysis. We show that under certain assumptions, functions with supports on ideals of closed sets form a non-empty compact set in C(X). Furthermore, we demonstrate that these functions can be characterized as solutions to certain variational inclusion problems and fixed point equations.  Our key findings reveal that functions with supports on ideals of closed sets share several desirable properties, including being continuous, bounded, and having closed graph. Additionally, we prove that these functions can be approximated by functions with supports on finite unions of closed sets. This approximation property provides practical significance, as it allows for the numerical computation of functions with supports on ideals of closed sets.  In conclusion, this research contributes to the understanding of functions in C(X) with supports on ideals of closed sets and their properties. The results obtained provide a theoretical foundation for further exploration in functional analysis and offer potential applications in optimization, control theory, and mathematical finance.

We report high precision charged-particle pair (2-D) correlation analyses in
the space of $\Delta \phi$ (azimuth) and $\Delta \eta$ (pseudorapidity), for
minimum bias Au + Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV as a function of
centrality (0-80%). The intermediate transverse momenta region chosen $0.8 <
p_t < 4.0$ GeV/c corresponds to an emission source size $\sim2$fm obtained from
HBT measurements and should resolve substructures at the scale of $\sim2$fm.
The difference and the sum of unlike-sign and like-sign charged pairs form
Charge Dependent (CD) correlations and Charge Independent (CI) correlations
respectively. The CD displays the initial correlation at hadronization of the
opposite sign pairs emitted from the same space-time region as modified by
further medium interactions before kinetic freeze-out. Our analysis of the CD
correlations shows approximately jet-like structure, independent of centrality
and is consistent with the initial correlation which is predicted by Pythia (or
HIJING) jets. The CI correlation displays the average structure of the
correlated emitting sources after kinetic freeze-out. For the most central
bins, the $\Delta \eta$ width of the CI correlation on the near side ($\Delta
\phi$ around $0^\circ$) is elongated by a factor $\sim$3 destroying the
jet-like symmetry. This elongation decreases continually with decreasing
centrality and essentially restores the jet-like symmetric structure in the
most peripheral bins. The Pythia and HIJING event generators together with a
QCD inspired Parton Bubble Model (PBM), which motivated this analysis, are used
to compare to our data. We discuss the arguments for substructure, surface
emission, and opacity in the central fireball region.

text: Our research delves into the intricate interplay between aging, jamming, and the limits of stability within amorphous solids. By exploring the behavior of these materials under varying conditions, we have uncovered compelling results that shed light on the fundamental principles governing their mechanical properties. The key problem we address is understanding how aging affects the jamming transition in amorphous systems and its ramifications on their stability limits.  Through extensive simulations and experimental observations, we reveal that aging plays a pivotal role in the mechanical response of amorphous solids, influencing their capacity to transition between jammed and unjammed states. Our study demonstrates that aging induces structural rearrangements within these materials, leading to alterations in their stability thresholds. This insight underscores the critical importance of temporal evolution in shaping the mechanical behavior of amorphous solids.  Our methodology incorporates a combination of computational modeling techniques and physical experiments to investigate the aging process and its implications on the jamming and stability limits of amorphous solids. By bridging theory and practice, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the complex dynamics at play in these systems, offering new perspectives on their mechanical behavior. Our findings not only contribute to the fundamental understanding of aging in amorphous materials but also have significant implications for diverse fields ranging from materials science to geophysics.

text: In this research, we investigate the phase control of entanglement and quantum steering in a three-mode optomechanical system. By using a coherent feedback scheme, we demonstrate the ability to manipulate the phase of the entangled states generated in the system. Our results show that by adjusting the phase, we can enhance or suppress the entanglement shared among the modes. Additionally, we explore the steering properties between different modes and observe that by controlling the phase, we can regulate the amount of steering present in the system. The key idea behind our work is to utilize phase control as a tool to influence the quantum correlations within the optomechanical system. We aim to provide insight into the role of phase manipulation in shaping the quantum features of the system. Our methodology involves theoretical analysis supported by numerical simulations to study the effects of varying phases on entanglement and steering. Overall, our findings contribute to the understanding of phase-dependent quantum phenomena in multi-mode optomechanical systems, offering possibilities for enhanced quantum information processing and communication protocols.

In proposals for quantum computers using arrays of trapped ultracold polar
molecules as qubits, a strong external field with appreciable gradient is
imposed in order to prevent quenching of the dipole moments by rotation and to
distinguish among the qubit sites. That field induces the molecular dipoles to
undergo pendular oscillations, which markedly affect the qubit states and the
dipole-dipole interaction. We evaluate entanglement of the pendular qubit
states for two linear dipoles, characterized by pairwise concurrence, as a
function of the molecular dipole moment and rotational constant, strengths of
the external field and the dipole-dipole coupling, and ambient temperature. We
also evaluate a key frequency shift, $\triangle\omega$, produced by the
dipole-dipole interaction. Under conditions envisioned for the proposed quantum
computers, both the concurrence and $\triangle\omega$ become very small for the
ground eigenstate. In principle, such weak entanglement can be sufficient for
operation of logic gates, provided the resolution is high enough to detect the
$\triangle\omega$ shift unambiguously. In practice, however, for many candidate
polar molecules it appears a challenging task to attain adequate resolution.
Simple approximate formulas fitted to our numerical results are provided from
which the concurrence and $\triangle\omega$ shift can be obtained in terms of
unitless reduced variables.

text:
We present a variational study of pseudo-spin $1/2$ Bose gases in a harmonic
trap with weak 3D spin-orbit coupling of $\bmsigma\cdot\mathbf{p}$ type. This
spin-orbit coupling mixes states with different parities, which inspires us to
approximate the single particle state with the eigenstates of the total angular
momentum, i.e. superposition of harmonic $s$-wave and $p$-wave states. As the
time reversal symmetry is protected by two-body interaction, we set the
variational order parameter as the combination of two mutually time reversal
symmetric eigenstates of the total angular momentum. The variational results
essentially reproduce the 3D skyrmion-like ground state recently identified by
Kawakami {\it et al.}. We show that these skyrmion-like ground states emerging
in this model are primarily caused by $p$ wave spatial mode involving in the
variational order parameter that drives two spin components spatially
separated. We find the ground state of this system falls into two phases with
different density distribution symmetries depending on the relative magnitude
of intraspecies and interspecies interaction: Phase I has parity symmetric and
axisymmetric density distributions, while Phase II is featured with special
joint symmetries of discrete rotational and time reversal symmetry. With the
increasing interaction strength the transition occurs between two phases with
distinct density distributions, while the topological 3D skyrmion-like spin
texture is symmetry protected.

text:
The correspondence principle offered a unique opportunity to test the
Horowitz and Maldacena mechanism at correspondence point "the centre of mass
energies around $(M_{s}/(g_{s})^{2})$". First by using Horowitz and Maldacena
proposal, the black hole final state for closed strings is studied and the
entropy of these states is calculated.Then, to consider the closed string
states, a copy of the original Hilbert space is constructed with a set of
operators of creation/anihilation that have the same commutation properties as
the original ones. The total Hilbert space is the tensor product of the two
spaces $H_{right}\otimes H_{left}$, where in this case $H_{left/right}$ denotes
the physical quantum states space of the closed string .It is shown that closed
string states can be represented by a maximally entangled two-mode squeezed
state of the left and right spaces of closed string. Also, the entropy for
these string states is calculated.It is found that black hole entropy matches
the closed string entropy at transition point.This means that our result is
consistent with correspondence principle and thus HM mechanism in string theory
works . Consequently the unitarity of the black hole in string theory can be
reconciled.However Gottesman and Preskill point out that, in this scenario,
departures from unitarity can arise due to interactions between the collapsing
body and the infalling Hawking radiation inside the event horizon and
information can be lost. By extending the Gottesman and Preskill method to
string theory, the amount of information transformation from the matter to the
state of outgoing Hagedorn radiation for closed strings is obtained.It is
observed that information is lost for closed strings.

text: This study investigates the gender differences in communication behaviors, spatial proximity patterns, and mobility habits among various social contexts. Understanding these differences is crucial for enhancing interpersonal interactions and optimizing social environments. The objective was to analyze how gender influences these facets of communication and mobility, thereby contributing to the broader field of gender studies and social psychology. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, the research involved quantitative surveys and qualitative observational studies across diverse demographic groups. Data were collected from over 300 participants, focusing on their communication styles, preferred spatial arrangements during interactions, and mobility patterns in different settings. The results reveal significant disparities; females demonstrated a higher tendency for expressive communication and closer spatial proximity, while males exhibited more assertive communication styles and preferred greater distances during interactions. Additionally, mobility habits indicated that females were more likely to gather in smaller, intimate groups, whereas males tended to engage in larger social structures. These findings underscore the necessity of considering gender when analyzing social behaviors in communication and space utilization. In conclusion, the study highlights that gender differences are not merely sociocultural constructs but integral elements that shape communication dynamics and mobility patterns, affecting both personal and professional interactions. The implications of these insights may inform future policies in organizational behavior, urban planning, and social services to foster inclusive environments accommodating diverse communication needs.

text: In this study, we investigate the intricate relationship between the optical mass-to-light (M/L) ratio and galaxy color, utilizing data from the ALHAMBRA survey, which encompasses a comprehensive sample of galaxies up to redshift z = 1.5. Our analysis reveals a pronounced dependence of the optical M/L ratio on the observed color of galaxies, indicating that bluer galaxies exhibit significantly lower M/L ratios compared to their redder counterparts. We employ a robust methodology that combines multi-band photometry and spectral energy distribution fitting to derive accurate stellar masses and assess galaxy colors across various redshift bins. Our findings illustrate that this color-dependent M/L ratio persists even at high redshifts, suggesting that fundamental processes linked to star formation and stellar evolution play a crucial role in shaping the baryonic content of galaxies over cosmic time. We address the implications of our results for galaxy formation models, highlighting the importance of incorporating color diversity when estimating mass from light in both observational studies and theoretical frameworks. Furthermore, we explore the potential significance of our findings in relation to dark matter halo interaction and the baryon cycle within the context of galaxy evolution. Overall, our work underscores the necessity of accounting for color when interpreting the optical M/L ratio, paving the way for more nuanced insights into the mass assembly and evolutionary pathways of galaxies throughout the universe's history.

We present calculated rate coefficients for ro-vibrational transitions of CO
in collisions with H atoms for a gas temperature range of 10 K $\leq T \leq$
3000 K, based on the recent three-dimensional ab initio H-CO interaction
potential of Song et al(2013). Rate coefficients for ro-vibrational $v=1,j=0-30
\rightarrow v'=0, j'$ transitions were obtained from scattering cross sections
previously computed with the close-coupling method by Song et al(2015).
Combining these with the rate coefficients for vibrational $v=1-5 \rightarrow
v' < v$ quenching obtained with the infinite-order sudden approximation, we
propose a new extrapolation scheme that yields the rate coefficients for
ro-vibrational $v=2-5,j=0-30 \rightarrow v',j'$ de-excitation. Cross sections
and rate coefficients for ro-vibrational $v=2, j=0-30 \rightarrow v'=1,j'$
transitions calculated with the close-coupling method confirm the effectiveness
of this extrapolation scheme. Our calculated and extrapolated rates are very
different from those that have been adopted in the modeling of many
astrophysical environments. The current work provides the most comprehensive
and accurate set of ro-vibrational de-excitation rate coefficients for the
astrophysical modeling of the H-CO collision system. Application of the
previously available and new data sets in astrophysical slab models shows that
the line fluxes typically change by 20-70% in high temperature environments
(800 K) with an H/H$_2$ ratio of 1; larger changes occur for lower
temperatures.

text: Our study investigates the mass-loss return from evolved stars to the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) through empirical relations concerning excess emission at 8 and 24 μm. The aim is to understand the mechanisms behind the mass loss from evolved stars and its contribution to the interstellar medium of the LMC. We utilize observational data from the Spitzer Space Telescope combined with multi-wavelength surveys to analyze the infrared excess emission from evolved stars in the LMC. The empirical relations derived from our analysis reveal a correlation between the mass-loss rates of evolved stars and the excess emission at 8 and 24 μm. This correlation sheds light on the mass-loss processes of evolved stars and their impact on the chemical enrichment of the LMC. Our findings provide valuable insights into the feedback loop between evolved stars and their host galaxy, emphasizing the intricate interplay between stellar evolution and galactic chemical evolution. By uncovering these empirical relations, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the role of evolved stars in shaping the interstellar medium of the LMC and possibly other galaxies in the universe.

text: We investigate the boundary between stellar kinematic groups and very wide binaries, focusing on the Washington Double Stars (WDS) with the widest angular separations. Our principal objective is to elucidate the nature and origin of these celestial pairings by examining their dynamical properties and potential common origin. We employ a comprehensive methodology that integrates high-precision astrometric data from Gaia DR3 with radial velocities and proper motions to identify bona fide binaries among these widely separated star pairs. By performing detailed orbit simulations, we discern gravitational binding and exclude chance alignments and statistical duplications. Our analysis reveals that a significant proportion of these wide pairs exhibit consistent kinematic signatures that align with known stellar kinematic groups, suggesting a shared evolutionary history. Additionally, we identify a subset of pairs that challenge current theoretical models due to their extreme separations and seemingly stable orbits, implying additional dynamics such as perturbations or past interactions with molecular clouds. These findings enhance our understanding of the transition zone between gravitationally bound binaries and unbound stellar associations. The implications of our study are multifaceted, contributing to the refinement of binary star formation theories and providing vital benchmarks for future astrometric missions. Our results underscore the importance of precise astrometric measurements in resolving fundamental questions about binary star evolution and the broader context of stellar dynamical systems.

text: This research explores the constraints imposed by Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) and Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) observations on scenarios involving brane-world theories and particle dark radiation. The study focuses on understanding how these models fit within the observed limits set by BBN, which provides stringent constraints on the abundances of light elements formed during the early universe. Additionally, the analysis utilizes CMB data, including measurements of the angular power spectrum and polarization, to further probe these theoretical possibilities. The research employs numerical simulations and analytical models to investigate the implications of varying parameters in brane-world theories and the presence of particle dark radiation on nucleosynthesis processes and CMB features. Key findings indicate that under certain conditions, brane-world models with particle dark radiation can be consistent with observational data, but these models must adhere strictly to the bounds derived from BBN and CMB analyses. The study concludes with a discussion of potential avenues for future research to refine these constraints and explore new theoretical frameworks that reconcile dark matter and dark energy with standard cosmological observations.

text:
AdaBoost is an important algorithm in machine learning and is being widely
used in object detection. AdaBoost works by iteratively selecting the best
amongst weak classifiers, and then combines several weak classifiers to obtain
a strong classifier. Even though AdaBoost has proven to be very effective, its
learning execution time can be quite large depending upon the application e.g.,
in face detection, the learning time can be several days. Due to its increasing
use in computer vision applications, the learning time needs to be drastically
reduced so that an adaptive near real time object detection system can be
incorporated. In this paper, we develop a hybrid parallel and distributed
AdaBoost algorithm that exploits the multiple cores in a CPU via light weight
threads, and also uses multiple machines via a web service software
architecture to achieve high scalability. We present a novel hierarchical web
services based distributed architecture and achieve nearly linear speedup up to
the number of processors available to us. In comparison with the previously
published work, which used a single level master-slave parallel and distributed
implementation [1] and only achieved a speedup of 2.66 on four nodes, we
achieve a speedup of 95.1 on 31 workstations each having a quad-core processor,
resulting in a learning time of only 4.8 seconds per feature.

text: This research examines the Hall instability within solar flux tubes, focusing on the mechanisms that lead to the formation of structures such as coronal loops and their associated magnetic fields. Utilizing numerical simulations and theoretical models, the study aims to understand the role of plasma pressure gradients and the Hall effect in driving the instability. Key findings indicate that the Hall term significantly enhances the instability growth rate compared to ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) theory, leading to the development of complex magnetic configurations. The analysis reveals that the stability of solar flux tubes is fundamentally altered by the inclusion of the Hall effect, which plays a crucial role in shaping the observed solar phenomena. The results contribute to our understanding of the dynamic processes occurring in the solar corona and provide insights into the mechanisms behind solar eruptive events.

text: The rapid growth of cloud computing has led to a burgeoning demand for efficient resource allocation strategies, particularly in the selection of optimal virtual machines (VMs) for diverse operational requirements. This paper introduces a novel approach termed Low-Level Augmented Bayesian Optimization (LLABO), designed specifically to enhance the selection process of cloud VMs by intelligently navigating the trade-offs between performance and cost. The primary objective of this research is to develop a systematic framework that reduces latency and improves workload management in cloud environments through optimized VM selection.  Employing LLABO, we integrated low-level system metrics and augmented Bayesian techniques to formulate an adaptive optimization algorithm. This methodology was tested across various cloud platforms, involving extensive simulations to evaluate performance across multiple real-world scenarios that simulate fluctuating workloads.  Key findings indicate that LLABO outperforms traditional optimization methods by achieving up to 30% improvement in resource utilization and reducing operational costs by an average of 20% without compromising service quality. Furthermore, the results demonstrate enhanced responsiveness to dynamic workload conditions, showcasing the adaptability of the model in real-time applications.  In conclusion, the LLABO framework presents a significant advancement in the field of cloud resource management, offering a robust and efficient solution for organizations seeking to optimize their cloud VM selections. This research contributes to the ongoing discourse on improving cloud service efficiency and lays the groundwork for future studies on advanced optimization techniques in cloud computing.

text:
The capacity region of the Finite-State Multiple Access Channel (FS-MAC) with
feedback that may be an arbitrary time-invariant function of the channel output
samples is considered. We characterize both an inner and an outer bound for
this region, using Masseys's directed information. These bounds are shown to
coincide, and hence yield the capacity region, of FS-MACs where the state
process is stationary and ergodic and not affected by the inputs.
  Though `multi-letter' in general, our results yield explicit conclusions when
applied to specific scenarios of interest. E.g., our results allow us to:
  - Identify a large class of FS-MACs, that includes the additive mod-2 noise
MAC where the noise may have memory, for which feedback does not enlarge the
capacity region.
  - Deduce that, for a general FS-MAC with states that are not affected by the
input, if the capacity (region) without feedback is zero, then so is the
capacity (region) with feedback.
  - Deduce that the capacity region of a MAC that can be decomposed into a
`multiplexer' concatenated by a point-to-point channel (with, without, or with
partial feedback), the capacity region is given by $\sum_{m} R_m \leq C$, where
C is the capacity of the point to point channel and m indexes the encoders.
Moreover, we show that for this family of channels source-channel coding
separation holds.

text: We designed and implemented a low-cost mobile ad-hoc network test bed in a laboratory environment, with the aim of emulating an actual multi-hop wireless ad-hoc network (MANET). The test bed consisted of a custom-built wireless communication system utilizing low-cost hardware components, including Wi-Fi enabled devices, Raspberry Pi-based nodes, and a network interface card. Our approach focused on replicating the complexities of real-world MANETs, including node mobility, varying channel conditions, and packet loss, by utilizing a combination of simulation software and real-world experimentation.   Through extensive experimentation, we observed that our test bed successfully replicated the characteristics of real-world MANETs, including node mobility-induced packet loss and channel fading effects. Our results also demonstrated the effectiveness of various network protocols and algorithms, such as AODV and DSDV, in handling node mobility and packet loss. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of varying network topologies and node densities on network performance, and found that our test bed provided a flexible and scalable platform for evaluating different network scenarios. Our findings have significant implications for the development of low-cost and efficient MANETs, and our test bed serves as a valuable resource for researchers and engineers seeking to evaluate and optimize MANET protocols and algorithms.

text: The magnetic canopy, the outermost region of the solar atmosphere, plays a crucial role in the transmission and conversion of magnetoacoustic waves. These waves, generated by the dynamic processes in the Sun's interior, can propagate through the canopy and interact with the coronal plasma, leading to significant effects on the solar atmosphere. In a quiet Sun region, the magnetic canopy is characterized by a complex network of magnetic field lines, which can amplify or dampen the propagation of magnetoacoustic waves.  This study aims to investigate the transmission and conversion of magnetoacoustic waves on the magnetic canopy in a quiet Sun region. Using a combination of numerical simulations and observational data, we have explored the effects of the magnetic field on the wave propagation and interaction with the coronal plasma. Our results show that the magnetic field lines can significantly affect the wave propagation, leading to the formation of waveguides and the enhancement of wave energy. Additionally, we have found that the coronal plasma can convert the magnetoacoustic waves into other types of waves, such as Alfvén waves, through a process known as wave-wave interactions.  Our study provides new insights into the dynamics of the magnetic canopy and the role of magnetoacoustic waves in the solar atmosphere. The findings of this research have important implications for our understanding of the Sun's internal dynamics and the behavior of solar flares and coronal mass ejections. By exploring the transmission and conversion of magnetoacoustic waves on the magnetic canopy, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex processes that govern the solar atmosphere.

A new algorithm is presented for computing a canonical rank-R tensor
approximation that has minimal distance to a given tensor in the Frobenius
norm, where the canonical rank-R tensor consists of the sum of R rank-one
components. Each iteration of the method consists of three steps. In the first
step, a tentative new iterate is generated by a stand-alone one-step process,
for which we use alternating least squares (ALS). In the second step, an
accelerated iterate is generated by a nonlinear generalized minimal residual
(GMRES) approach, recombining previous iterates in an optimal way, and
essentially using the stand-alone one-step process as a preconditioner. In
particular, the nonlinear extension of GMRES is used that was proposed by
Washio and Oosterlee in [ETNA Vol. 15 (2003), pp. 165-185] for nonlinear
partial differential equation problems. In the third step, a line search is
performed for globalization. The resulting nonlinear GMRES (N-GMRES)
optimization algorithm is applied to dense and sparse tensor decomposition test
problems. The numerical tests show that ALS accelerated by N-GMRES may
significantly outperform both stand-alone ALS and a standard nonlinear
conjugate gradient optimization method, especially when highly accurate
stationary points are desired for difficult problems. The proposed N-GMRES
optimization algorithm is based on general concepts and may be applied to other
nonlinear optimization problems.

text: In this study, we explore the structural ground states of spinel solid solutions ($A,A'$)Cr$_2$O$_4$ where $A$ = Mg, Zn and $A'$ = Co, Cu, focusing on the interplay between Spin-Jahn-Teller and Jahn-Teller effects. Utilizing first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we investigate the electronic, magnetic, and structural properties of these systems. Our primary objective is to delineate how Jahn-Teller active Co$^{2+}$ and Cu$^{2+}$ ions influence the ground state of these compounds, potentially leading to novel magnetic behaviors. We observe that the incorporation of Co and Cu results in a distortion of the crystal lattice, which can be attributed to the Jahn-Teller effect, prominently modifying the local environments and electronic structures. This distortion induces a cooperative coupling with the spin configurations, characteristic of the Spin-Jahn-Teller effect, subsequently impacting the magnetic interactions crucially. The results reveal a complex interplay between structural distortions and magnetic ordering, offering insights into the mechanisms driving the stabilization of unique ground states in these mixed spinel systems. Our findings advance the understanding of the role of Jahn-Teller and Spin-Jahn-Teller effects in the context of solid solutions' structural and magnetic properties, opening pathways for the design of materials with tailored functionalities. Furthermore, our analysis provides a foundational framework for future experimental and theoretical investigations into the cooperative phenomena manifesting in other spinel oxide systems.

text: In this study, we present a novel neural networks-based approach for photon-counting data correction that addresses the pulse pileup effect prevalent in high-throughput photon detection systems. Pulse pileup, a significant source of error, occurs when multiple photons are detected within a temporal frame too narrow for individual resolution, leading to an inaccurate count and spectral distortion. Our approach leverages deep learning architectures to model the complex relationships inherent in the data affected by pileup. We have developed and trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) using synthetically generated datasets that simulate various pileup scenarios. The CNN has been optimized to predict the true photon count and reconstruct the underlying intensity spectrum. Results demonstrate significant improvements over traditional correction methods, such as pulse-height analysis and statistical folding, in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Our methodology can effectively disentangle superimposed signals, achieving a reduction in error rates by approximately 40% compared to linear correction algorithms. Furthermore, our model exhibits scalability to different photon environments and maintains robust performance across varying pulse rates and amplitudes. The proposed neural network framework provides a promising tool for real-time compensation of the pulse pileup effect and enhances the fidelity of photon-counting data critical to quantitative analysis in fields such as medical imaging, materials science, and astroparticle physics. Our research suggests that integrating advanced neural network techniques can significantly improve the precision of photon detection systems, fostering developments in high-resolution imaging and spectroscopy.

We investigate the ground and low energy states of a one dimensional non
local free energy functional describing at a mean field level a spin system
with both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions. In particular, the
antiferromagnetic interaction is assumed to have a range much larger than the
ferromagnetic one. The competition between these two effects is expected to
lead to the spontaneous emergence of a regular alternation of long intervals on
which the spin profile is magnetized either up or down, with an oscillation
scale intermediate between the range of the ferromagnetic and that of the
antiferromagnetic interaction. In this sense, the optimal or quasi-optimal
profiles are "froth-like": if seen on the scale of the antiferromagnetic
potential they look neutral, but if seen at the microscope they actually
consist of big bubbles of two different phases alternating among each other. In
this paper we prove the validity of this picture, we compute the oscillation
scale of the quasi-optimal profiles and we quantify their distance in norm from
a reference periodic profile. The proof consists of two main steps: we first
coarse grain the system on a scale intermediate between the range of the
ferromagnetic potential and the expected optimal oscillation scale; in this way
we reduce the original functional to an effective "sharp interface" one. Next,
we study the latter by reflection positivity methods, which require as a key
ingredient the exact locality of the short range term. Our proof has the
conceptual interest of combining coarse graining with reflection positivity
methods, an idea that is presumably useful in much more general contexts than
the one studied here.

The Keck telescope's HIRES spectrograph has previously provided evidence for
a smaller fine-structure constant, alpha, compared to the current laboratory
value, in a sample of 143 quasar absorption systems:
da/a=(-0.57+/-0.11)x10^{-5}. This was based on a variety of metal-ion
transitions which, if alpha varies, experience different relative velocity
shifts. This result is yet to be robustly contradicted, or confirmed, by
measurements on other telescopes and spectrographs; it remains crucial to do
so. It is also important to consider new possible instrumental systematic
effects which may explain the Keck/HIRES results. Griest et al. (2009,
arXiv:0904.4725v1) recently identified distortions in the echelle order
wavelength scales of HIRES with typical amplitudes +/-250m/s. Here we
investigate the effect such distortions may have had on the Keck/HIRES varying
alpha results. We demonstrate that they cause a random effect on da/a from
absorber to absorber because the systems are at different redshifts, placing
the relevant absorption lines at different positions in different echelle
orders. The typical magnitude of the effect on da/a is ~0.4x10^{-5} per
absorber which, compared to the median error on da/a in the sample,
~1.9x10^{-5}, is relatively small. Consequently, the weighted mean value
changes by less than 0.05x10^{-5} if the corrections we calculate are applied.
Nevertheless, we urge caution, particularly for analyses aiming to achieve high
precision da/a measurements on individual systems or small samples, that a much
more detailed understanding of such intra-order distortions and their
dependence on observational parameters is important if they are to be avoided
or modelled reliably. [Abridged]

text: In this study, we present a submillimeter continuum survey targeting local dust-obscured galaxies (DOGs), focusing on their star formation activity and obscured nature. The survey employed the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) at its highest frequency bands, enabling us to probe into the far-infrared and submillimeter wavelengths where these galaxies are most luminous due to their dust-obscured regions. Our methodology involved selecting a sample of DOGs from existing catalogs based on their far-infrared colors indicative of obscured star formation, then conducting a targeted ALMA observation to map their submillimeter continuum emission.  The results indicate that our survey successfully identified a population of DOGs characterized by high submillimeter luminosities, suggesting significant ongoing star formation obscured by dust. We observed strong correlations between submillimeter flux densities and far-infrared luminosities, supporting the idea that these galaxies are indeed dusty and actively forming stars. Furthermore, detailed spectral energy distribution modeling revealed that the majority of these sources exhibit steep spectral slopes typical of starbursts, confirming their role as star-forming systems heavily veiled by dust.  Key methodologies included careful selection criteria for the target sample, rigorous data reduction techniques, and advanced spectral analysis methods to extract accurate flux densities and physical parameters. This work not only contributes to our understanding of obscured star formation but also provides a valuable dataset for further studies on the evolution and feedback mechanisms within these galaxies.

Antennas of transmitters and receivers have been manipulated to increase the
capacity of transmission and reception of signals. Using many elements in
antennas to shape beams and direct nulls in a particular point for optimum
signal transmission and reception has over decades, had tremendous positive
influence in received power and signal to noise ratio (SNR). However, since the
antenna elements manipulation can be done both at base station and device
terminal, it gives rise to an important method of using several antennas to put
and obtain signals to and from space with increased capacity. This principle is
termed Multiple-input and Multiple-output (MIMO). This paper discusses
application of MIMO in the state of the art and next generation of wireless
systems (5G). It also discusses four models of MIMO, SISO, SIMO, MISO and MIMO,
considering three method of combing the signals from multipath propagations,
Selection combining (SC), Equal gain combing (EGC) and maximum ratio combining
(MRC). Spatial diversity and spatial multiplexing are also discussed as form of
MIMO. Finally, Massive or Hyper MIMO which is a new method of increasing
transmission capacity by very large scale for fifth generation of wireless
system is discussed with its challenges and opportunities. Key terms-Diversity
combining techniques, spatial multiplexing, channel state information (CSI).
