[Abridged] We calculate the structural evolution and nucleosynthesis of a
grid of models covering the metallicity range: -6.5 < [Fe/H] < -3.0 (plus Z=0),
and mass range: 0.85 < M < 3.0 Msun, amounting to 20 stars in total. In this
paper, the first of a series describing and analysing this large data set, we
present the resulting stellar yields. Many of the models experience violent
nuclear burning episodes not seen at higher metallicities. We refer to these
events as `Dual Flashes'. These events have also been reported by previous
studies. Some of the material processed by the Dual Flashes is dredged up
causing significant surface pollution with a distinct chemical composition. We
also analyse the yields in terms of C and N, comparing them to the observed
CEMP abundances. At the lowest metallicities ([Fe/H] < -4.0) we find the yields
to contain ~1 to 2 dex too much carbon, in agreement with all previous studies.
At higher metallicities ([Fe/H] = -3.0), where the observed data set is much
larger, all our models produce yields with [C/Fe] values consistent with those
observed in the most C-rich CEMPs. However it is only the low-mass models that
undergo the Dual Shell Flash (which occurs at the start of the TPAGB) that can
best reproduce the C and N observations. Normal Third Dredge-Up can not
reproduce the observations because at these metallicities intermediate mass
models (M > 2 Msun) suffer HBB which converts the C to N thus lowering [C/N]
well below the observations, whilst if TDU were to occur in the low-mass (M < 1
Msun) models (we do not find it to occur in our models), the yields would be
expected to be C-rich only, which is at odds with the `dual pollution' of C and
N generally observed in the CEMPs.

As digital games continue to be explored as solutions to educational and
behavioural challenges, the need for evaluation methodologies which support
both the unique nature of the format and the need for comparison with other
approaches continues to increase. In this workshop paper, a range of challenges
are described related specifically to the case of cultural learning using
digital games, in terms of how it may best be assessed, understood, and
sustained through an iterative process supported by research. An evaluation
framework is proposed, identifying metrics for reach and impact and their
associated challenges, as well as presenting ethical considerations and the
means to utilize evaluation outcomes within an iterative cycle, and to provide
feedback to learners. Presenting as a case study a serious game from the Mobile
Assistance for Social Inclusion and Empowerment of Immigrants with Persuasive
Learning Technologies and Social Networks (MASELTOV) project, the use of the
framework in the context of an integrative project is discussed, with emphasis
on the need to view game-based learning as a blended component of the cultural
learning process, rather than a standalone solution. The particular case of
mobile gaming is also considered within this case study, providing a platform
by which to deliver and update content in response to evaluation outcomes.
Discussion reflects upon the general challenges related to the assessment of
cultural learning, and behavioural change in more general terms, suggesting
future work should address the need to provide sustainable, research-driven
platforms for game-based learning content.

text: In this survey, we explore the 3/4-Conjecture concerning fix-free codes, a pivotal concept in coding theory that aims to identify the upper bounds of the size of fix-free codes relative to their parameters. We systematically review the existing literature, highlighting recent advancements and theoretical frameworks that have emerged since the conjecture's proposal. Our analysis underscores that while significant progress has been made in establishing bounds for fix-free codes, a comprehensive proof of the 3/4-Conjecture remains elusive. We compile and present various methodologies employed by researchers, including combinatorial approaches, graph-theoretical perspectives, and algebraic techniques, which have provided insights into the characteristics of fix-free codes. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these findings in practical coding scenarios, such as error correction and data transmission. By synthesizing the key ideas and results from numerous studies, we elucidate the challenges posed by the conjecture and delineate potential pathways for future research. Ultimately, we assert that resolving the 3/4-Conjecture is not only essential for the theoretical understanding of fix-free codes but also for its applications in enhancing data integrity in communication systems. This comprehensive survey thus serves as a foundational reference for researchers aiming to delve deeper into the intricacies of fix-free codes and their pivotal role within coding theory.

text: This study investigates the strategic timing of arrivals in a linear slowdown processor sharing system, a mechanism pertinent in optimizing network performance and resource allocation. Processor sharing systems allocate resources among competing users, where the slowdown function dictates how waiting and service times are influenced by the system load. This research addresses the strategic decision-making processes of users regarding when to access such a system to minimize their expected wait and service times, thus enhancing overall efficiency. Our objective was to model the decision-making environment where each user's entry time is a strategic choice influenced by other users' times of arrival. We employed game-theory based modeling techniques to analyze the equilibrium behaviors of users in a shared processing environment. Through analytical modeling, we derived conditions under which users have incentives to delay their access to avoid congestion and characterized the Nash equilibrium in terms of these arrival strategies. We found that under certain conditions, users can reduce their expected processing times by strategically timing their arrivals, balancing load, and mitigating congestion. The results highlighted the shift from individual to collective optimization, providing insights into how centralized scheduling can be improved through decentralized user strategies. Conclusively, our findings suggest that better insights into user behavior and system dynamics can guide the design of more resilient and efficient processor sharing systems, ultimately leading to improved performance and user satisfaction in shared computing environments. This research contributes to the broader understanding of optimizing shared resource systems through strategic user interactions.

Many phone vendors use Android as their underlying OS, but often extend it to
add new functionality and to make it compatible with their specific phones.
When a new version of Android is released, phone vendors need to merge or
re-apply their customizations and changes to the new release. This is a
difficult and time-consuming process, which often leads to late adoption of new
versions. In this paper, we perform an empirical study to understand the nature
of changes that phone vendors make, versus changes made in the original
development of Android. By investigating the overlap of different changes, we
also determine the possibility of having automated support for merging them. We
develop a publicly available tool chain, based on a combination of existing
tools, to study such changes and their overlap. As a proxy case study, we
analyze the changes in the popular community-based variant of Android,
LineageOS, and its corresponding Android versions. We investigate and report
the common types of changes that occur in practice. Our findings show that 83%
of subsystems modified by LineageOS are also modified in the next release of
Android. By taking the nature of overlapping changes into account, we assess
the feasibility of having automated tool support to help phone vendors with the
Android update problem. Our results show that 56% of the changes in LineageOS
have the potential to be safely automated.

We investigate the correlation between infrared (JHKL) and optical (B) fluxes
of the variable nucleus of the Seyfert galaxy NGC 4151 using partially
published data for the last 6 years (2008-2013.). Here we are using the same
data as in Oknyansky et al. (2014), but include also optical (B) data from Guo
et al. We find that the lag of flux in all the infrared bands is the same, 40
+- 6 days, to within the measurement accuracy. Variability in the J and K bands
is not quite simultaneous, perhaps due to the differing contributions of the
accretion disk in these bands. The lag found for the K band compared with the B
band is not significantly different from earlier values obtained for the period
2000-2007. However, finding approximately the same lags in all IR bands for
2008-2013 differs from previous results at earlier epochs when the lag
increased with increasing wavelength. Examples of almost the same lag in
different IR bands are known for some other active nuclei. In the case of NGC
4151 it appears that the relative lags between the IR bands may be different in
different years. The available data, unfortunately, do not allow us to
investigate a possible change in the lags during the test interval. We discuss
our results in the framework of the standard model where the variable infrared
radiation is mainly due to thermal re-emission from the part of the dusty torus
closest to the central source. There is also a contribution of some IR emission
from the accretion disk, and this contribution increases with decreasing
wavelength. Some cosmological applications of obtained results are discussed.

Transport modeling of idealized, cone-guided fast ignition targets indicates
the severe challenge posed by fast-electron source divergence. The hybrid
particle-in-cell [PIC] code Zuma is run in tandem with the
radiation-hydrodynamics code Hydra to model fast-electron propagation, fuel
heating, and thermonuclear burn. The fast electron source is based on a 3D
explicit-PIC laser-plasma simulation with the PSC code. This shows a quasi
two-temperature energy spectrum, and a divergent angle spectrum (average
velocity-space polar angle of 52 degrees). Transport simulations with the
PIC-based divergence do not ignite for > 1 MJ of fast-electron energy, for a
modest 70 micron standoff distance from fast-electron injection to the dense
fuel. However, artificially collimating the source gives an ignition energy of
132 kJ. To mitigate the divergence, we consider imposed axial magnetic fields.
Uniform fields ~50 MG are sufficient to recover the artificially collimated
ignition energy. Experiments at the Omega laser facility have generated fields
of this magnitude by imploding a capsule in seed fields of 50-100 kG. Such
imploded fields are however more compressed in the transport region than in the
laser absorption region. When fast electrons encounter increasing field
strength, magnetic mirroring can reflect a substantial fraction of them and
reduce coupling to the fuel. A hollow magnetic pipe, which peaks at a finite
radius, is presented as one field configuration which circumvents mirroring.

Binary measurements arise naturally in a variety of statistical and
engineering applications. They may be inherent to the problem---e.g., in
determining the relationship between genetics and the presence or absence of a
disease---or they may be a result of extreme quantization. In one-bit
compressed sensing it has recently been shown that the number of one-bit
measurements required for signal estimation mirrors that of unquantized
compressed sensing. Indeed, $s$-sparse signals in $\mathbb{R}^n$ can be
estimated (up to normalization) from $\Omega(s \log (n/s))$ one-bit
measurements. Nevertheless, controlling the precise accuracy of the error
estimate remains an open challenge. In this paper, we focus on optimizing the
decay of the error as a function of the oversampling factor $\lambda := m/(s
\log(n/s))$, where $m$ is the number of measurements. It is known that the
error in reconstructing sparse signals from standard one-bit measurements is
bounded below by $\Omega(\lambda^{-1})$. Without adjusting the measurement
procedure, reducing this polynomial error decay rate is impossible. However, we
show that an adaptive choice of the thresholds used for quantization may lower
the error rate to $e^{-\Omega(\lambda)}$. This improves upon guarantees for
other methods of adaptive thresholding as proposed in Sigma-Delta quantization.
We develop a general recursive strategy to achieve this exponential decay and
two specific polynomial-time algorithms which fall into this framework, one
based on convex programming and one on hard thresholding. This work is inspired
by the one-bit compressed sensing model, in which the engineer controls the
measurement procedure. Nevertheless, the principle is extendable to signal
reconstruction problems in a variety of binary statistical models as well as
statistical estimation problems like logistic regression.

text: Transient uncoupling induced synchronization through modified dynamic coupling is a phenomenon where two or more oscillators, initially disconnected, synchronize with each other after a temporary disruption in their coupling. This phenomenon has been observed in various natural and artificial systems, including biological networks, electrical circuits, and mechanical systems. However, the underlying mechanisms driving this synchronization remain poorly understood.  The objective of this study is to investigate the role of modified dynamic coupling in inducing synchronization in transiently uncoupled oscillators. We developed a theoretical framework to analyze the effects of dynamic coupling on the synchronization dynamics of uncoupled oscillators. Our approach combines elements of nonlinear dynamics, network science, and control theory to model the complex interactions between oscillators.  Using numerical simulations, we demonstrated that modified dynamic coupling can indeed induce synchronization in transiently uncoupled oscillators. We found that the synchronization dynamics are influenced by the strength and form of the coupling, as well as the initial conditions of the oscillators. Furthermore, we identified a critical threshold beyond which synchronization is achieved, regardless of the initial conditions.  Our results have important implications for understanding the emergence of synchronization in complex systems. We suggest that modified dynamic coupling may play a key role in the synchronization of oscillators in various natural and artificial systems. This study provides a foundation for further research into the mechanisms driving synchronization in transiently uncoupled oscillators, with potential applications in fields such as control systems, network science, and biomedicine.

text: In this study, we address the critical challenge of understanding the intricate network of synaptic connections within the Drosophila antennal lobe through large-scale electron microscopy (EM) analysis. Our primary objective is to develop a comprehensive three-dimensional model of synaptic connectivity by employing advanced computational techniques to derive synapse point clouds automatically. We implement a robust methodology that integrates deep learning algorithms and automated image processing tools to accurately detect and reconstruct synaptic sites from high-resolution EM datasets. Our approach significantly improves both the speed and precision of synapse identification compared to traditional manual annotation methods.  We successfully generate detailed synapse point clouds, which enable us to construct a densely interconnected map of neural circuits within the antennal lobe. Our results reveal previously undetected synaptic patterns and connections, providing novel insights into the neuroanatomy of Drosophila. We demonstrate that our automated pipeline can handle vast volumes of data with high fidelity, facilitating scalability for broader application in complex neural systems. The synaptic maps produced in our study are validated through cross-referencing with known anatomical features and correlation with existing EM datasets.  This pioneering work lays the groundwork for further research into synaptic plasticity, circuitry functionality, and information processing within the Drosophila olfactory system. Our methodology highlights the potential of computational neuroscience to unravel neural complexities, offering a template for future studies aiming to decode the synaptic architectures of higher-order brain structures across different species.

We use high-angular-resolution images obtained with SPHERE/ZIMPOL to study
the photosphere, the warm molecular layer, and the inner wind of the close-by
oxygen-rich AGB star R Doradus. We present observations in filters V,
cntH$\alpha$, and cnt820 and investigate the surface brightness distribution of
the star and of the polarised light produced in the inner envelope. Thanks to
second-epoch observations in cntH$\alpha$, we are able to see variability on
the stellar photosphere. We find that in the first epoch the surface brightness
of R Dor is asymmetric in V and cntH$\alpha$, the filters where molecular
opacity is stronger, while in cnt820 the surface brightness is closer to being
axisymmetric. The second-epoch observations in cntH$\alpha$ show that the
morphology of R Dor changes completely in a timespan of 48 days to a more
axisymmetric and compact configuration. The polarised intensity is asymmetric
in all epochs and varies by between a factor of 2.3 and 3.7 with azimuth for
the different images. We fit the radial profile of the polarised intensity
using a spherically symmetric model and a parametric description of the dust
density profile, $\rho(r)=\rho_\circ r^{-n}$. On average, we find exponents of
$- 4.5 \pm 0.5$ that correspond to a much steeper density profile than that of
a wind expanding at constant velocity. The dust densities we derive imply an
upper limit for the dust-to-gas ratio of $\sim 2\times10^{-4}$ at 5.0
$R_\star$. Given the uncertainties in observations and models, this value is
consistent with the minimum values required by wind-driving models for the
onset of a wind, of $\sim 3.3\times10^{-4}$. However, if the steep density
profile we find extends to larger distances from the star, the dust-to-gas
ratio will quickly become too small for the wind of R Dor to be driven by the
grains that produce the scattered light.

text: NGC 4151 is an active Seyfert 1 galaxy located in the Virgo cluster. This study focuses on the X-ray morphology of the 3 kpc-diameter circum-nuclear region (CNR) of NGC 4151, utilizing Chandra Advanced CCD Imaging Spectrometer (ACIS) data. Previous studies have suggested the presence of a cold interstellar medium (CIM) in the CNR, which could significantly influence the X-ray emissivity and morphology. To investigate this further, we analyzed the Chandra data using image processing techniques and spectral analysis.  Our results reveal an intricate X-ray morphology in the CNR, characterized by a central bright X-ray source and several extended features. The central source is identified as the active galactic nucleus (AGN), which is surrounded by a complex structure consisting of multiple X-ray filaments, bubbles, and a large-scale outflow. The extended structures in the CNR exhibit strong spectral lines, indicating the presence of shocked gas and potential interactions with the CIM.  The spectra obtained from several points within the CNR show absorption features consistent with the previously suggested presence of the CIM. Our analysis suggests that the CIM plays a role in shaping the X-ray morphology and in the absorption of X-rays within the CNR. These findings contribute to our understanding of the complex interplay between the AGN, the CIM, and the interstellar medium in the CNR of NGC 4151.  In conclusion, this research presents new insights into the X-ray morphology and the role of the cold interstellar medium in the 3 kpc-diameter circum-nuclear region of NGC 4151. The Chandra ACIS data reveals a complex X-ray structure and the absorption features, providing evidence for the presence of the CIM and its influence on the X-ray properties of the AGN environment.

text: We present a novel approach to regression analysis using I-priors, which achieve regularization through the use of a fixed prior on the regression coefficients. Our work focuses on addressing the challenge of model specification in regression by employing I-priors to flexibly model the relationship between the response variable and covariates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of I-priors in handling complex data structures, high-dimensional covariates, and non-linear relationships by conducting extensive simulations and real data analyses. Our results show that the use of I-priors leads to improved predictive performance and robustness compared to traditional methods such as ridge regression and lasso.   The key idea behind our approach is to place a Gaussian prior on the coefficients, which allows for intuitive interpretation of the regularization parameter and enables us to incorporate prior knowledge into the model in a principled manner. We develop a computationally efficient algorithm for estimating the model parameters by maximizing a penalized likelihood function. This methodology ensures that the estimation process is scalable to large datasets and enables straightforward inference on the regression coefficients. Overall, our work contributes to the advancement of regression analysis by introducing a flexible and interpretable framework based on I-priors.

text: This study presents Speech Map, a statistical multimodal atlas that integrates 4D tongue motion data derived from both tagged and cine magnetic resonance (MR) images. The atlas aims to capture the dynamic nature of tongue movements during speech production, which is crucial for understanding speech disorders and developing personalized treatment strategies. We collected paired datasets from 20 subjects, acquiring tagged and cine MR images during spontaneous speech. Using advanced image registration techniques, we aligned these datasets to create a comprehensive 4D tongue motion dataset. Subsequently, we employed statistical methods to derive a probabilistic atlas of tongue motion, characterized by principal components analysis (PCA) to identify the dominant modes of tongue movement. The key findings indicate that our approach can accurately represent the variability in tongue motion across different speakers and speaking conditions. This work not only provides a robust statistical framework for analyzing 4D tongue motion but also opens avenues for future research on speech disorders and individualized speech therapy.

text: Charge transfer processes in DNA have been the subject of extensive study due to their potential implications in various biological processes and emerging nanotechnologies.   This research investigates the feasibility of superfast charge transfer in DNA, aiming to understand the underlying mechanisms that govern the speed of charge transfer in DNA molecules.   Through a combination of computational modeling and theoretical analysis, we explore the electronic structure of DNA and factors influencing the rate of charge transfer, such as sequence specificity, environmental conditions, and stacking interactions.   Our study reveals that certain DNA sequences exhibit the potential for superfast charge transfer, with transfer rates exceeding the conventional values observed in standard DNA systems. We identify specific sequence motifs and environmental conditions that enhance charge transfer efficiency.   The findings suggest that superfast charge transfer in DNA is a possibility under specific conditions, offering insights into the design of DNA-based electronic devices and potential applications in biosensing and nanotechnology. Further research in this area could lead to the development of novel strategies for manipulating charge transfer dynamics in DNA-based systems.

text: This study employs full three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations to investigate the accretion flow structures in magnetic cataclysmic variable stars, focusing on systems characterized by strong and intricate magnetic fields. The objective was to understand the dynamics and stability of accretion flows under such conditions, which can provide insights into the mass transfer processes in these binary systems. The methodology involved numerical simulations using computational fluid dynamics techniques, incorporating realistic magnetic field configurations derived from observational data. Key findings highlighted the formation of structured accretion discs with significant radial velocity shear layers, enhanced by the interaction between the stellar wind and the magnetic field. Additionally, the simulations revealed complex magnetic reconnection events that could significantly impact the accretion rate and structure. These results contribute to our understanding of the physical mechanisms governing the mass transfer in magnetic cataclysmic variables and offer new perspectives for interpreting observational data. The study concludes with recommendations for future work, emphasizing the need for more detailed modeling and observational comparisons to validate theoretical predictions.

Since future, precise theory of neutrino oscillations should include the
understanding of the neutrino mass generation and a precise, relativistic
description of hadrons, and observing that such a future theory may require
Dirac's FF of Hamiltonian dynamics, we provide a preliminary FF description of
neutrino oscillations using the Feynman--Gell-Mann-Levy version of an effective
theory in which leptons interact directly with whole nucleons and pions,
instead of with quarks via intermediate bosons. The interactions are treated in
the lowest-order perturbative expansion in the coupling constants in the
effective theory, including a perturbative solution of the coupled constraint
equations. Despite missing quarks and their binding mechanism, the effective
Hamiltonian description is sufficiently precise for showing that the standard
oscillation formula results from the interference of amplitudes with different
neutrinos in virtual intermediate states. This holds provided that the inherent
experimental uncertainties of preparing beams of incoming and measuring rates
of production of outgoing particles are large enough for all of the different
neutrino intermediate states to contribute as alternative virtual paths through
which the long-baseline scattering process can manifest itself. The result that
an approximate, effective FF theory reproduces the standard oscillation formula
at the level of transition rates for currently considered long-baseline
experiments--even though the space-time development of scattering is traced
differently and the relevant interaction Hamiltonians are constructed
differently than in the commonly used IF of dynamics--has two implications. It
shows that the common interpretation of experimental results is not the only
one, and it opens the possibility of considering more precise theories taking
advantage of the features of the FF that are not available in the IF.

We consider the stochastic dynamics of the pure and random ferromagnetic
Ising model on the hierarchical diamond lattice of branching ratio $K$ with
fractal dimension $d_f=(\ln (2K))/\ln 2$. We adapt the Real Space
Renormalization procedure introduced in our previous work [C. Monthus and T.
Garel, J. Stat. Mech. P02037 (2013)] to study the equilibrium time $t_{eq}(L)$
as a function of the system size $L$ near zero-temperature. For the pure Ising
model, we obtain the behavior $t_{eq}(L) \sim L^{\alpha} e^{\beta 2J L^{d_s}} $
where $d_s=d_f-1$ is the interface dimension, and we compute the prefactor
exponent $\alpha$. For the random ferromagnetic Ising model, we derive the
renormalization rules for dynamical barriers $B_{eq}(L) \equiv (\ln
t_{eq}/\beta)$ near zero temperature. For the fractal dimension $d_f=2$, we
obtain that the dynamical barrier scales as $ B_{eq}(L)= c L+L^{1/2} u$ where
$u$ is a Gaussian random variable of non-zero-mean. While the non-random term
scaling as $L$ corresponds to the energy-cost of the creation of a system-size
domain-wall, the fluctuation part scaling as $L^{1/2}$ characterizes the
barriers for the motion of the system-size domain-wall after its creation. This
scaling corresponds to the dynamical exponent $\psi=1/2$, in agreement with the
conjecture $\psi=d_s/2$ proposed in [C. Monthus and T. Garel, J. Phys. A 41,
115002 (2008)]. In particular, it is clearly different from the droplet
exponent $\theta \simeq 0.299$ involved in the statics of the random
ferromagnet on the same lattice.

We employed femtosecond time- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy
to analyze the response of the electronic structure of the 122 Fe-pnictide
parent compounds Ba/EuFe_2As_2 and optimally doped BaFe_{1.85}Co_{0.15}As_2
near the \Gamma point to femtosecond optical excitation. We identify pronounced
changes of the electron population within several 100 meV above and below the
Fermi level, which we explain as combination of (i) coherent lattice
vibrations, (ii) a hot electron and hole distribution, and (iii) transient
modifications of the chemical potential. The response of the three different
materials is very similar. In the Fourier transformation of the time-dependent
photoemission intensity we identify three modes at 5.6, 3.3, and 2.6 THz. While
the highest frequency mode is safely assigned to the A_{1g} mode, the other two
modes require a discussion in comparison to literature. The time-dependent
evolution of the hot electron distribution follows a simplified description of
a transient three temperature model which considers two heat baths of lattice
vibrations, which are more weakly and strongly coupled to transiently excited
electron population. Still the energy transfer from electrons to the strongly
coupled phonons results in a rather weak, momentum-averaged electron-phonon
coupling quantified by values for \lambda<\omega^2> between 30 and 70 meV^2.
The chemical potential is found to present a transient modulation induced by
the coherent phonons. This change in the chemical potential is particularly
strong in a two band system like in the 122 Fe-pnictide compounds investigated
here due to the pronounced variation of the electrons density of states close
to the equilibrium chemical potential.

text: We investigated the influence of dynamical fermions on the structure of the Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) vacuum, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms that govern the chiral condensate and the gluon condensate. Through a combination of lattice QCD simulations and analytical calculations, we demonstrated that the introduction of dynamical fermions significantly alters the vacuum structure, leading to a substantial decrease in the chiral condensate and a corresponding increase in the gluon condensate.  Our results indicate that the dynamical fermion mass, which plays a crucial role in determining the vacuum structure, exhibits a non-trivial dependence on the lattice spacing and the fermion mass parameter. We found that the chiral condensate exhibits a non-monotonic behavior with respect to the lattice spacing, whereas the gluon condensate shows a monotonic increase with decreasing lattice spacing. These findings suggest that the dynamical fermion mass plays a key role in regulating the chiral and gluon condensates, and that the interplay between the fermion and gluon sectors gives rise to a rich and complex vacuum structure.  Our analysis reveals that the dynamical fermion mass can be effectively described by a non-perturbative chiral effective action, which provides a novel framework for understanding the vacuum structure of QCD. The implications of our results for our understanding of the strong interaction and the behavior of hadrons at low energies are far-reaching, and we propose that a deeper understanding of the interplay between the fermion and gluon sectors is essential for a complete description of the QCD vacuum.

text: This study investigates the finite volume method (FVM) for simulating poroelastic-fluid wave propagation using mapped grids. The primary objective is to develop a robust numerical model that accurately captures the complex interactions between fluid flow and solid deformation within porous media. To achieve this, we implement a stabilized finite volume formulation specifically tailored for poroelasticity, which accounts for the coupled dynamics between the fluid pressure, solid displacement, and hydraulic conductivity changes. We employ mapped grids to enhance computational efficiency and accuracy by ensuring high resolution near boundaries and interfaces. The model's performance is validated against analytical solutions and compared with experimental data from literature. Key methodologies include the application of the generalized minimum residual (GMRES) method for solving the resulting large sparse linear systems and the use of adaptive mesh refinement techniques to focus computational resources where they are most needed. Results demonstrate the capability of the proposed approach to simulate realistic scenarios involving wave propagation in heterogeneous porous structures, providing valuable insights into the behavior of such systems under various conditions.

text: We develop and evaluate Lasso-type estimators for semiparametric nonlinear mixed-effects models, addressing the challenges of simultaneously estimating individual-level nonlinear relationships and model parameters in the presence of correlated data. Our approach employs a novel Lasso-based regularization scheme that jointly penalizes the estimation of individual-level nonlinear effects and model parameters, thereby promoting sparsity in both the model and the data.  Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our Lasso-type estimators in recovering true model parameters and individual-level nonlinear effects, even in the presence of high-dimensional data and strong correlations. Our results show that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of estimation accuracy, model parsimony, and computational efficiency.  We also investigate the impact of model misspecification and data quality on the performance of our Lasso-type estimators, finding that our approach is robust to minor model misspecifications and data quality issues. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive theoretical framework for the asymptotic properties of our Lasso-type estimators, establishing the consistency and asymptotic normality of our estimators under certain regularity conditions.  Our work contributes to the development of efficient and accurate estimation methods for semiparametric nonlinear mixed-effects models, with implications for a wide range of applications in fields such as medicine, ecology, and economics.

text: We investigated the feasibility of estimating or propagating gradients through stochastic neurons for conditional computation, a fundamental component of deep learning models. Our primary objective was to develop an efficient method for approximating the gradients of the loss function with respect to the model parameters, enabling the training of complex neural networks.  We attempted to tackle this problem by designing a novel stochastic neuron architecture that incorporates a stochastic gradient estimator. Our approach leverages the properties of stochastic neurons to approximate the gradients of the loss function, thereby alleviating the need for explicit gradient computation. By employing a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed architecture in estimating gradients with high accuracy.  Our key idea was to utilize the stochastic nature of the neurons to propagate gradients through the network, allowing for the efficient computation of gradients without requiring explicit gradient computation. We employed a Bayesian approach to regularize the stochastic gradient estimator, ensuring that the approximated gradients are consistent with the true gradients. Our results showed that our proposed architecture can effectively estimate gradients with a high degree of accuracy, outperforming existing methods in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy.  Through our work, we have made significant contributions to the field of deep learning, providing a novel approach to estimating gradients through stochastic neurons. Our results have far-reaching implications for the training of complex neural networks, enabling the development of more efficient and accurate models.

text: Tensor Regression Networks A Novel Approach for High-Dimensional Data Analysis   The increasing availability of high-dimensional data has led to a growing need for efficient and effective methods for data analysis and prediction. Traditional regression models often struggle to handle high-dimensional data due to the curse of dimensionality, leading to suboptimal performance and increased computational costs. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of Tensor Regression Networks (TRNs), which leverage the power of tensor operations to tackle high-dimensional data.   This study aims to investigate the efficacy of TRNs in predicting continuous outcomes from high-dimensional data. We seek to explore the strengths and limitations of TRNs in comparison to traditional regression models, and to identify the key factors that influence their performance.   This study employs a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation to examine the performance of TRNs on a range of high-dimensional datasets. We develop a novel TRN architecture that incorporates tensor-based operations, and evaluate its performance using various metrics, including mean squared error and R-squared. Additionally, we conduct a comparative analysis with traditional regression models, including linear regression and random forests.   Our results demonstrate that TRNs outperform traditional regression models in predicting continuous outcomes from high-dimensional data. The proposed TRN architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets, with significant improvements in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the performance of TRNs is highly sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, and that careful tuning of these parameters is essential for optimal performance.   This study contributes to the growing body of research on TRNs, and highlights their potential as a powerful tool for high-dimensional data analysis. Our findings have implications for a range of applications, including data science, machine learning, and scientific computing.

text: In recent years, the increasing use of robots in various domestic and industrial settings has necessitated the development of advanced object recognition systems capable of accurately identifying objects within confined spaces. The traditional approach to object recognition, relying on visual cues and external references, is often hindered by the limitations of line-of-sight and the absence of a clear visual environment. This study addresses these challenges by proposing a novel robot-object recognition system designed to operate effectively in closed environments, where robots are often confined to a single room.  The objective of this research is to develop an object recognition system that can accurately identify objects within a closed environment, despite the absence of external references and the presence of occlusions, reflections, and other visual distortions. To achieve this, we employ a multi-sensor approach, integrating computer vision, lidar, and tactile sensors to provide a comprehensive understanding of the environment.  Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed system in recognizing objects in various closed environments, including cluttered rooms and areas with occlusions. The results show that the system can accurately identify objects, even when they are partially occluded or reflected. The findings of this study contribute to the development of more robust and reliable object recognition systems for robots operating in confined spaces, with potential applications in industries such as logistics, healthcare, and manufacturing.

Airborne transient electromagnetic (TEM) is a cost-effective method to image
the distribution of electrical conductivity in the ground. We consider layered
earth inversion to interpret large data sets of hundreds of kilometre.
Different strategies can be used to solve this inverse problem. This consists
in managing the a priori information to avoid the mathematical instability and
provide the most plausible model of conductivity in depth. In order to obtain
fast and realistic inversion program, we tested three kinds of regularization:
two are based on standard Tikhonov procedure which consist in minimizing not
only the data misfit function but a balanced optimization function with
additional terms constraining the lateral and the vertical smoothness of the
conductivity; another kind of regularization is based on reducing the condition
number of the kernel by changing the layout of layers before minimizing the
data misfit function. Finally, in order to get a more realistic distribution of
conductivity, notably by removing negative conductivity values, we suggest an
additional recursive filter based upon the inversion of the logarithm of the
conductivity. All these methods are tested on synthetic and real data sets.
Synthetic data have been calculated by 2.5D modelling; they are used to
demonstrate that these methods provide equivalent quality in terms of data
misfit and accuracy of the resulting image; the limit essentially comes on
special targets with sharp 2D geometries. The real data case is from
Helicopter-borne TEM data acquired in the basin of Franceville (Gabon) where
borehole conductivity loggings are used to show the good accuracy of the
inverted models in most areas, and some biased depths in areas where strong
lateral changes may occur.

The effects of random magnetic fields are considered in an Ising spin-glass
model defined in the limit of infinite-range interactions. The probability
distribution for the random magnetic fields is a double Gaussian, which
consists of two Gaussian distributions centered respectively, at $+H_{0}$ and
$-H_{0}$, presenting the same width $\sigma$. It is argued that such a
distribution is more appropriate for a theoretical description of real systems
than its simpler particular two well-known limits, namely the single Gaussian
distribution ($\sigma \gg H_{0}$), and the bimodal one ($\sigma = 0$). The
model is investigated by means of the replica method, and phase diagrams are
obtained within the replica-symmetric solution. Critical frontiers exhibiting
tricritical points occur for different values of $\sigma$, with the possibility
of two tricritical points along the same critical frontier. To our knowledge,
it is the first time that such a behavior is verified for a spin-glass model in
the presence of a continuous-distribution random field, which represents a
typical situation of a real system. The stability of the replica-symmetric
solution is analyzed, and the usual Almeida-Thouless instability is verified
for low temperatures. It is verified that, the higher-temperature tricritical
point always appears in the region of stability of the replica-symmetric
solution; a condition involving the parameters $H_{0}$ and $\sigma$, for the
occurrence of this tricritical point only, is obtained analytically. Some of
our results are discussed in view of experimental measurements available in the
literature.

Direct numerical simulation (DNS), mostly used in fundamental turbulence
research, is limited to low turbulent intensities due the current and future
computer resources. Standard turbulence models, like RaNS (Reynolds averaged
Navier-Stokes) and LES (Large Eddy Simulation), are applied to flows in
engineering, but they miss small scale effects, which are frequently of
importance, see e.g. the whole area of reactive flows, flows with apparent
Prandtl or Schmidt number effects, or even wall bounded flows. A recent
alternative to these standard approaches is the one-dimensional turbulence
(ODT) model, which is limited to 1D sub-domains. In two papers we will provide
a generalized filter strategy, called XLES (extended LES), including a formal
theory (part I) and one special approach in the XLES family of models, called
ODTLES (in part II (see Glawe et al. (2015))). ODTLES uses an ODT sub-grid
model to describe all turbulent scales not represented by XLES, which leaves
the larger scales to be simulated in 3D. This allows a turbulence modeling
approach with a 3D resolution mainly independent of the turbulent intensity.
Thus ODTLES is able to compute highly turbulent flows in domains of moderate
complexity affordably and including the full range of turbulent and diffusive
scales. The convergence of XLES to DNS is shown and the unconventional XLES
advection approach is investigated in basic numerical tests. In part II, highly
turbulent channel and duct flow results are discussed and show the future
potential of XLES and ODTLES.

John Nash has proposed a new theory of gravity. We define a Nash-tensor equal
to the curvature tensor appearing in the Nash field equations for empty space,
and calculate its components for two cases. 1. A static, spherically symmetric
space, and 2. The expanding, homogeneous and isotropic space of the
Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) universe models. We find the
general, exact solution of the Nash field equations for empty space in the
static case. The line element turns out to represent the Schwarzschild-de
Sitter spacetime. Also we find the simplest non-trivial solution of the field
equations in the cosmological case, which gives the scale factor corresponding
to the de Sitter spacetime. Hence empty space in the Nash theory corresponds to
a space with Lorentz Invariant Vacuum Energy (LIVE) in the Einstein theory.
This suggests that dark energy may be superfluous according to the Nash theory.
We also consider a radiation filled universe model in an effort to find out how
energy and matter may be incorporated into the Nash theory. A tentative
interpretation of the Nash theory as a unified theory of gravity and
electromagnetism leads to a very simple form of the field equations in the
presence of matter. It should be noted, however, that the Nash theory is still
unfinished. A satifying way of including energy-momentum into the theory has
yet to be found.

Smart environments integrates various types of technologies, including cloud
computing, fog computing, and the IoT paradigm. In such environments, it is
essential to organize and manage efficiently the broad and complex set of
heterogeneous resources. For this reason, resources classification and
categorization becomes a vital issue in the control system. In this paper we
make an exhaustive literature survey about the various computing systems and
architectures which defines any type of ontology in the context of smart
environments, considering both, authors that explicitly propose resources
categorization and authors that implicitly propose some resources
classification as part of their system architecture. As part of this research
survey, we have built a table that summarizes all research works considered,
and which provides a compact and graphical snapshot of the current
classification trends. The goal and primary motivation of this literature
survey has been to understand the current state of the art and identify the
gaps between the different computing paradigms involved in smart environment
scenarios. As a result, we have found that it is essential to consider together
several computing paradigms and technologies, and that there is not, yet, any
research work that integrates a merged resources classification, taxonomy or
ontology required in such heterogeneous scenarios.

We cross-matched the 6-year Swift/Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) survey of
active galactic nuclei (AGN) with the AT20G radio survey of the southern sky,
which is one of the largest high-frequency radio surveys available. With these
data we investigated the possible correlation between the radio and the X-ray
emission at the highest radio and X-ray frequencies. We found 37 AGN with a
high probability of association (>80 per cent), among which 19 are local
Seyfert galaxies (with median redshift z = 0.03) and 18 blazars. We found that
\approx 20 per cent of the AGN detected in hard X-rays are also bright radio
sources at 20 GHz, but the apparent correlation between the radio and hard
X-ray luminosity is completely driven by the different median redshifts of the
two subgroups of AGN. When we consider only the local Seyfert sample we find no
evidence of a correlation between their 20 GHz and 15-55 keV power. Therefore
it appears that at high frequencies the radio-X connection, which had been
previously observed at lower frequencies, disappears. The disappearance of the
radio-X correlation at high radio and X-ray frequencies could be tested through
Very Long Baseline Interferometry and the use of the Nuclear Spectroscopic
Telescope Array (NuSTAR) satellite.

text: Chirality and multipolar orders are crucial phenomena in frustrated quantum systems, especially in the presence of external magnetic fields. This study aims to investigate the intricate interplay of vector chiral and multipolar orders in a spin-1/2 frustrated ferromagnetic chain under the influence of a magnetic field. Additionally, the study uncovers how these orders evolve with changing interactions and magnetic field strengths. In conclusion, the research sheds light on the nuanced connection between vector chiral and multipolar orders in the spin-1/2 frustrated ferromagnetic chain system, providing insights into the fundamental physics of quantum magnetic materials in challenging regimes.

The average stellar mass (Mstar) of high-mass galaxies (Mstar > 3e11 Msun) is
expected to grow by ~30% since z~1, largely through ongoing mergers that are
also invoked to explain the observed increase in galaxy sizes. Direct evidence
for the corresponding growth in stellar mass has been elusive, however, in part
because the volumes sampled by previous redshift surveys have been too small to
yield reliable statistics. In this work, we make use of the Stripe 82 Massive
Galaxy Catalog to build a mass-limited sample of 41,770 galaxies (Mstar >
1.6e11) with optical to near-IR photometry and a large fraction (>55%) of
spectroscopic redshifts. Our sample spans 139 square degrees, significantly
larger than most previous efforts. After accounting for a number of potential
systematic errors, including the effects of Mstar scatter, we measure galaxy
stellar mass functions over 0.3 < z < 0.65 and detect no growth in the typical
Mstar of massive galaxies with an uncertainty of 9%. This confidence level is
dominated by uncertainties in the star formation history assumed for Mstar
estimates, although our inability to characterize low surface-brightness
outskirts may be the most important limitation of our study. Even among these
high-mass galaxies, we find evidence for differential evolution when splitting
the sample by recent star formation (SF) activity. While low-SF systems appear
to become completely passive, we find a mostly sub-dominant population of
galaxies with residual, but low rates of star formation (~1 Msun/yr) number
density does not evolve. Interestingly, these galaxies become more prominent at
higher Mstar, representing ~10% of all galaxies at Mstar ~ 1e12 Msun and
perhaps dominating at even larger masses.

Nowadays, the message diffusion links among users or websites drive the
development of countless innovative applications. However, in reality, it is
easier for us to observe the timestamps when different nodes in the network
react on a message, while the connections empowering the diffusion of the
message remain hidden. This motivates recent extensive studies on the network
inference problem: unveiling the edges from the records of messages
disseminated through them. Existing solutions are computationally expensive,
which motivates us to develop an efficient two-step general framework,
Clustering Embedded Network Inference (CENI). CENI integrates clustering
strategies to improve the efficiency of network inference. By clustering nodes
directly on the timelines of messages, we propose two naive implementations of
CENI: Infection-centric CENI and Cascade-centric CENI. Additionally, we point
out the critical dimension problem of CENI: instead of one-dimensional
timelines, we need to first project the nodes to an Euclidean space of certain
dimension before clustering. A CENI adopting clustering method on the projected
space can better preserve the structure hidden in the cascades, and generate
more accurately inferred links. This insight sheds light on other related work
attempting to discover or utilize the latent cluster structure in the
disseminated messages. By addressing the critical dimension problem, we propose
the third implementation of the CENI framework: Projection-based CENI. Through
extensive experiments on two real datasets, we show that the three CENI models
only need around 20% $\sim$ 50% of the running time of state-of-the-art
methods. Moreover, the inferred edges of Projection-based CENI preserves or
even outperforms the effectiveness of state-of-the-art methods.

We show optimal Direct Sum result for the one-way entanglement-assisted
quantum communication complexity for any relation f subset of X x Y x Z. We
show: Q^{1,pub}(f^m) = Omega(m Q^{1,pub}(f)), where Q^{1,pub}(f), represents
the one-way entanglement-assisted quantum communication complexity of f with
error at most 1/3 and f^m represents m-copies of f. Similarly for the one-way
public-coin classical communication complexity we show: R^{1,pub}(f^m) =
Omega(m R^{1,pub}(f)), where R^{1,pub}(f), represents the one-way public-coin
classical communication complexity of f with error at most 1/3. We show similar
optimal Direct Sum results for the Simultaneous Message Passing quantum and
classical models. For two-way protocols we present optimal Privacy Trade-off
results leading to a Weak Direct Sum result for such protocols. We show our
Direct Sum and Privacy Trade-off results via message compression arguments
which also imply a new round elimination lemma in quantum communication. This
allows us to extend classical lower bounds on the cell probe complexity of some
data structure problems, e.g. Approximate Nearest Neighbor Searching on the
Hamming cube {0,1}^n and Predecessor Search to the quantum setting. In a
separate result we show that Newman's technique of reducing the number of
public-coins in a classical protocol cannot be lifted to the quantum setting.
We do this by defining a general notion of black-box reduction of prior
entanglement that subsumes Newman's technique. We prove that such a black-box
reduction is impossible for quantum protocols. In the final result in the theme
of message compression, we provide an upper bound on the problem of Exact
Remote State Preparation.

text: We investigate the existence and properties of cryptogauge symmetry and cryptoghosts for crypto-Hermitian Hamiltonians, a class of non-Hermitian operators with real eigenvalues and eigenvalues that are not necessarily orthogonal. Our analysis reveals that cryptogauge symmetry is a non-trivial symmetry that can be used to classify crypto-Hermitian Hamiltonians into different categories. We demonstrate that cryptogauge symmetry is closely related to the presence of cryptoghosts, which are non-trivial eigenvalue eigenstates that do not satisfy the standard eigenvalue equation. Our results show that cryptoghosts are a natural consequence of the presence of cryptogauge symmetry, and that they play a crucial role in the classification of crypto-Hermitian Hamiltonians. We develop a mathematical framework to study the properties of cryptogauge symmetry and cryptoghosts, including their relation to the spectral properties of the Hamiltonian. Our work provides a new perspective on the study of crypto-Hermitian Hamiltonians, and highlights the importance of considering non-trivial symmetries and eigenvalue eigenstates in the classification of these operators.

text: Vigorous convection in sunspot granular light bridges plays a crucial role in understanding solar magnetic activity and its atmospheric implications. This study aims to analyze the convective dynamics within a granular light bridge, focusing on their thermal and hydrodynamic characteristics. Utilizing high-resolution observational data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we employed advanced image processing techniques and computational fluid dynamics simulations to investigate the velocity fields, temperature gradients, and magnetic field interactions within the light bridge. Key findings indicate that the light bridge exhibits rapid convective motions, characterized by upward flows and downward plumes, contributing to localized heating effects. Moreover, we observed that the intensity of convective activity is modulated by the strength of the underlying magnetic field, which influences granule formation and lifetime. The results suggest that vigorous convection not only facilitates energy transport but also impacts the stability of the sunspot structure. This research deepens our understanding of the dynamic processes occurring in sunspots and their broader implications for solar physics, specifically in relation to solar eruptions and variability. Ultimately, this study highlights the significance of granular light bridges as vital components in the complex interplay of convection and magnetism on the sun's surface.

text: This study investigates the physical state of hot gas halos surrounding two nearby galaxies, NGC 4649 and NGC 5846, using multi-wavelength observations and hydrodynamical simulations. Additionally, we analyzed optical spectra to determine metallicity levels and kinematic properties indicative of the gas dynamics.  Our analysis reveals that both halos exhibit complex thermal histories characterized by multiple heating and cooling episodes. In NGC 4649, evidence suggests recent heating events that could be associated with mergers, while NGC 5846's halo shows signs of prolonged cooling since its formation. Simulations are used to model these observed properties, allowing us to infer the physical processes governing the gas behavior. Key findings include the identification of regions where gas may still be cooling outwards, suggesting ongoing star formation activity. This study thus provides constraints on the physical state of hot gas halos, offering a deeper understanding of galaxy evolution and the interplay between galaxies and their surrounding environments.

text: This research explores the possibility of inert doublet dark matter (IDDM) in the context of a minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) with an additional scalar singlet. The IDDM scenario posits that the dark matter particles are part of a doublet of scalar bosons, which are not in direct interaction with normal matter, thereby avoiding detection by current experimental searches. The introduction of a scalar singlet, a new particle that can interact with the Higgs boson, offers an opportunity to explain the observed 125 GeV Higgs boson mass and its implications for dark matter.  The MSSM is employed as a theoretical framework to examine the interplay between the IDDM and the Higgs boson. The scalar singlet is assumed to be a neutral scalar boson, denoted by S, which can couple to the Higgs boson through a dimensionless coupling constant. Theoretical calculations reveal that the S-SH coupling can lead to a significant impact on the Higgs boson's decay modes, providing a potential explanation for the observed 125 GeV mass.  The key findings of this research indicate that the IDDM scenario with an additional scalar singlet can effectively explain the observed Higgs boson mass while providing a viable dark matter candidate. The S-SH coupling is found to be crucial in modulating the Higgs boson's properties, and its value is constrained to be within a narrow range. The implications of this research are significant, as they suggest that the IDDM scenario with a scalar singlet may be a viable alternative to traditional dark matter models, offering a new perspective on the interplay between dark matter and the Higgs boson.  The MSSM is used to constrain the parameters of the IDDM scenario, and the results indicate that the dark matter candidate can be consistent with current experimental constraints. The research concludes that the IDDM scenario with an additional scalar singlet is a promising approach to explaining the observed 125 GeV Higgs boson mass and providing a viable dark matter candidate, warranting further investigation and experimental verification.

text: In this study, we investigate the complex dynamics of magnetic flux transport on the solar surface, focusing on its implications for solar magnetic activity and the solar cycle. We attempt to resolve the discrepancy in existing models that fail to accurately predict the migration and evolution patterns of magnetic flux elements. Utilizing high-resolution observational data from space-based solar observatories and advanced computational simulations, we examine the underlying mechanisms driving the advection and diffusion of magnetic flux. Our approach integrates a combination of magnetohydrodynamic simulations and sophisticated statistical techniques to trace the interaction between supergranular flows and flux emergence. Results demonstrate that surface flux transport is subject to significant modulation by meridional flows and differential rotation, with emerging evidence of previously unexplored feedback mechanisms influencing the polarity oscillation of magnetic elements. Notably, we observe that large-scale flow patterns substantially impact the decay and dispersal of active regions, contributing to the variability observed in solar cycle amplitudes. Our findings suggest that incorporating variable flow dynamics and feedback processes into solar surface transport models enhances predictive accuracy and provides deeper insights into the processes governing solar magnetic phenomena. These results have significant implications for advancing our understanding of solar magnetism, with potential applications in forecasting solar activity and its related space weather effects. Our work underscores the necessity for continuous observation and model refinement, advocating for the integration of multidimensional data to capture the intricacies of solar surface magnetic flux transport effectively.

In a recent article (J. Comput. Chem. 2013, 34, 132-140), convective
Replica-Exchange (convective-RE) has been presented as an alternative to the
standard even-odd transition scheme. Computations on systems of various
complexity have shown that convective-RE may increase the number of replica
round-trips in temperature space with respect to the standard exchange scheme,
leading to a more effective sampling of energy basins. Moreover, it has been
shown that the method may prevent the formation of bottlenecks in the diffusive
walk of replicas through the space of temperature states. By using an ideal
temperature-RE model and a classical harmonic-oscillator RE scheme, we study
the performances of convective-RE when ergodicity is not broken and convergence
of acceptance probabilities is attained. In this dynamic regime, the round-trip
ratio between convective and standard-RE is at maximum ~1.5, a value much
smaller than that observed in non-ergodic simulations. For large acceptance
probabilities, the standard-RE outperforms convective-RE. Our observations
suggest that convective-RE can safely be used in either ergodic or non ergodic
regimes; however, convective-RE is advantageous only when bottlenecks occur in
the state-space diffusion of replicas, or when acceptance probabilities are
globally low. We also show that decoupling of the state-space dynamics of the
stick replica from the dynamics of the remaining replicas improves the
efficiency of convective-RE at low acceptance probability regimes.

text: This study focuses on the optimal placement of reflex edge guards for the perimeter protection of 2-reflex orthogonal polyhedra. The problem aims to minimize the number of guards required while ensuring complete coverage of all reflex edges. Various configurations of reflex edges within the polyhedron were analyzed through computational methods, employing algorithms designed to efficiently determine the minimal guard set. Key methodologies included exhaustive search techniques and heuristic approaches to identify placements that maximize coverage without redundancy. Results indicate that reflex edge guards can significantly reduce the number of necessary guards compared to traditional vertex guards. The findings contribute to the understanding of geometric properties and efficient guarding strategies for complex polyhedral structures, offering practical applications in fields such as robotics and computer graphics.

text: We investigate the properties of Ly$\alpha$ emitters (LAEs) among star-forming galaxies at a redshift of z=2.5, with a focus on understanding the similarities and uniqueness of these emitters. Through a combination of spectroscopic and photometric observations, we have identified a sample of 150 LAEs and 500 control galaxies, covering a total of 5.4 square degrees of the Hubble Deep Field North. Our analysis reveals that LAEs at z=2.5 exhibit distinct characteristics, including a high luminosity function, a significant fraction of objects with luminosities above the Lyman continuum break, and a strong correlation between Ly$\alpha$ luminosity and galaxy stellar mass. In contrast, control galaxies show a more typical luminosity function, with a smaller fraction of objects above the Lyman continuum break. We also find that LAEs tend to be located in denser environments, with a higher fraction of objects residing in the central regions of their host galaxies. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the unique properties of LAEs at z=2.5 may be driven by the interaction between the interstellar medium and the intense radiation field, leading to the formation of compact, high-redshift galaxies. Our results provide new insights into the nature of Ly$\alpha$ emitters and the star-forming processes in the early universe.

DIBs are ubiquitous in stellar spectra. Traditionally, they have been studied
through their extraction from hot stars, because of their smooth continuum. In
an era where there are several going-on or planned massive Galactic surveys
using multi-object spectrographs, cool stars constitute an appealing set of
targets. From the technical point of view, the extraction of DIBs in their
spectra is more challenging due to the complexity of the continuum. In this
contribution we will provide the community with an improved set of stellar
lines in the spectral regions associated to the strong DIBs at l6196, l6269,
l6284, and l6379. These lines will allow for the creation of better stellar
synthetic spectra, reproducing the background emission and a more accurate
extraction of the magnitudes associated with a given DIB. The Sun and Arcturus
were used as representative examples of dwarf and giant stars, respectively. A
high quality spectrum for each of them was modeled using TURBOSPECTRUM and the
VALD stellar line list. The oscillator strength log(gf) and/or wavelength of
specific lines were modified to create synthetic spectra where the residuals in
both the Sun and Arcturus were minimized. The synthetic spectra based on the
improved line lists reproduce the observed spectra for the Sun and Arcturus in
the mentioned spectral ranges with greater accuracy. Residuals between the
synthetic and observed spectra are always <10%, much better than with
previously existing options. The new line list has been tested with some
characteristic spectra, from a variety of stars, including both giant and dwarf
stars, and under different degrees of extinction. As it happened with the Sun
and Arcturus residuals in the fits used to extract the DIB information are
smaller when using synthetic spectra made with the updated line lists. Tables
with the updated parameters are provided to the community.

text: The time-dependent Schrödinger equation (TDSE) is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics that describes the evolution of a quantum system over time. In atomic physics, solving the TDSE for large systems can be computationally demanding due to the high dimensionality of the problem. To address this challenge, we propose a combined approach that utilizes the R-matrix eigenstate basis set and finite-differences propagation method. In this approach, the R-matrix eigenstate basis set is used to expand the initial wavefunction, and the finite-differences propagation method is employed to solve the TDSE in this basis. The proposed method is applicable to the one-electron case and is shown to be efficient in capturing the dynamics of the system.  The background of the research begins with an explanation of the TDSE and the challenges associated with solving it for large systems. The objective of the study is to develop an efficient method for solving the TDSE using a combined approach of R-matrix eigenstate basis set and finite-differences propagation method. The methodology section describes how the R-matrix eigenstate basis set is used to expand the initial wavefunction and how the finite-differences propagation method is employed to solve the TDSE in this basis.  The key findings of the study are presented, demonstrating the efficiency and accuracy of the proposed method in capturing the dynamics of the one-electron system. The conclusion reaffirms the applicability of the approach to the one-electron case and suggests potential extensions to more complex systems.

text: The exploration of young massive star clusters (YMSCs) in external galaxies is a significant aspect of understanding stellar evolution and the formation of massive stars. To gain insight into the physical properties of YMSCs, precise photometry measurements are crucial. In this study, we present resolved photometry of six YMSCs located in nearby galaxies using the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) and the Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3). Our observations cover the ultraviolet (UV), visible, and near-infrared (NIR) bands, enabling a comprehensive analysis of their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and stellar populations. The star clusters were identified using various selection criteria such as their young ages, compact sizes, and high stellar densities. We employed aperture photometry and point spread function (PSF) fitting methods to extract the fluxes of individual stars and background contamination subtraction. The stellar populations were analyzed through spectral fitting with Padova isochrones, and the ages, masses, and extinction values were derived. Our results reveal that these YMSCs exhibit complex stellar populations, with multiple stellar populations identified in each cluster. The masses and ages of the clusters were found to range from 10$^4$ M$_{\odot}$ to 10$^6$ M$_{\odot}$, and their ages from 1 Myr to 10 Myr. The extinction values varied from A$_V$ = 0.5 to 7.8 magnitudes, indicating significant differences in the environments and formation histories of the clusters. Our study demonstrates the importance of precise photometry measurements for understanding the complex stellar populations and formation scenarios of YMSCs in external galaxies. The data presented in this work will contribute to ongoing research in the field of stellar astrophysics and provide a valuable database for future studies.

text: Star formation in low density HI gas around the elliptical galaxy NGC2865 has been a subject of interest for astrophysicists due to its unusual properties compared to spiral and irregular galaxies. The background of this study examines the observations of HI gas in elliptical galaxies, which differ significantly from spiral and irregular galaxies in terms of gas surface densities and star formation efficiencies. This study aims to explore the star formation processes in NGC2865, an elliptical galaxy with a considerable amount of HI gas, and to understand how low-density HI gas environments can foster star formation.  The objective of this research is to investigate the star formation efficiency and rate in the low-density HI gas surrounding NGC2865 using observational data from radio and optical wavelengths. We employ the methodology of analyzing the HI gas distribution, star formation rates, and stellar populations using data from the HI Nearby Galaxies Survey and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.  Our key findings suggest that the star formation efficiency in the low-density HI gas environment around NGC2865 is lower compared to that in spiral and irregular galaxies, but not completely absent. We detect ongoing star formation, and the youngest stellar populations appear to be associated with the HI gas clouds. The origin of these stars could be due to the infall of intergalactic medium, mergers, or the in situ evolution of gas clouds in low-density environments.  In conclusion, our research sheds light on the unusual star formation processes occurring in the low-density HI gas environment around the elliptical galaxy NGC2865. Despite the generally lower star formation efficiencies in such environments, we find evidence for ongoing star formation and the presence of young stellar populations. Further studies are required to understand the physical processes behind these phenomena and their implications for the evolution of elliptical galaxies.

text: This research investigates the phenomenon of Gibbs-non-Gibbs dynamical transitions in mean-field interacting Brownian motions, a fundamental concept in statistical physics. The Gibbs state represents an equilibrium state where the probability distribution of the system is maximal, whereas the non-Gibbs state is a metastable state that can be accessed through a dynamical process. In the context of mean-field interacting Brownian motions, the interplay between the individual Brownian motions and their interactions leads to complex phase transitions.  The objective of this study is to explore the emergence of Gibbs-non-Gibbs dynamical transitions in mean-field interacting Brownian motions, focusing on the interplay between the mean-field interaction and the individual Brownian motions. We employ a numerical approach, utilizing a Monte Carlo simulation to study the phase behavior of the system.  Our results show that the mean-field interaction plays a crucial role in the emergence of Gibbs-non-Gibbs dynamical transitions, leading to the formation of non-equilibrium phases that are stable under certain conditions. The simulations reveal a complex phase diagram, where the transition between the Gibbs and non-Gibbs states is accompanied by a significant change in the dynamics of the system. Furthermore, we observe the formation of novel phase structures, including non-Gibbs equilibrium phases, which exhibit unique properties. The findings of this study provide new insights into the dynamics of mean-field interacting Brownian motions and have implications for the understanding of complex phase transitions in statistical physics.

The frequency dependence of the longitudinal group speeds of trapped sausage
waves plays an important role in determining impulsively generated wave trains,
which have often been invoked to account for quasi-periodic signals in coronal
loops. We examine how the group speeds ($v_{\rm gr}$) depend on angular
frequency ($\omega$) for sausage modes in pressureless coronal tubes with
continuous transverse density distributions by solving the dispersion relation
pertinent to the case where the density inhomogeneity of arbitrary form takes
place in a transition layer of arbitrary thickness. We find that in addition to
the transverse lengthscale $l$ and density contrast $\rho_{\rm i}/\rho_{\rm
e}$, the group speed behavior depends also on the detailed form of the density
inhomogeneity. For parabolic profiles, $v_{\rm gr}$ always decreases with
$\omega$ first before increasing again, as happens for the much studied top-hat
profiles. For linear profiles, however, the behavior of the $\omega-v_{\rm gr}$
curves is more complex. When $\rho_{\rm i}/\rho_{\rm e} \lesssim 6$, the curves
become monotonical for large values of $l$. On the other hand, for higher
density contrasts, a local maximum $v_{\rm gr}^{\rm max}$ exists in addition to
a local minimum $v_{\rm gr}^{\rm min}$ when coronal tubes are diffuse. With
time-dependent computations, we show that the different behavior of group speed
curves, the characteristic speeds $v_{\rm gr}^{\rm min}$ and $v_{\rm gr}^{\rm
max}$ in particular, is reflected in the temporal evolution and Morlet spectra
of impulsively generated wave trains. We conclude that the observed
quasi-periodic wave trains not only can be employed to probe such key
parameters as density contrasts and profile steepness, but also have the
potential to discriminate between the unknown forms of the transverse density
distribution.

text: This research paper addresses the issue of power control for packet streaming with head-of-line deadlines. The objective of the study is to optimize power control strategies to meet strict deadlines in packet streaming applications, where delaying packets can lead to significant performance degradation. The methodology involves developing a dynamic power control algorithm that adjusts the transmission power based on the queue status and deadline requirements of packets. The key findings indicate that the proposed algorithm effectively balances the trade-off between meeting deadlines and minimizing power consumption, thereby enhancing overall system performance. Through simulations and analysis, we demonstrate that the dynamic power control algorithm outperforms traditional static power control methods in terms of meeting deadlines while conserving energy. In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of tailored power control mechanisms for packet streaming with head-of-line deadlines, showcasing the benefits of dynamic power adjustment in enhancing performance efficiency and meeting stringent packet transmission requirements.
