We have carried out 12CO(J =2-1) and 12CO(J =3-2) observations at spatial
resolutions of 1.0-3.8 pc toward the entirety of loops 1 and 2 and part of loop
3 in the Galactic center with NANTEN2 and ASTE. These new results revealed
detailed distributions of the molecular gas and the line intensity ratio of the
two transitions, R3-2/2-1. In the three loops, R3-2/2-1 is in a range from 0.1
to 2.5 with a peak at ~ 0.7 while that in the disk molecular gas is in a range
from 0.1 to 1.2 with a peak at 0.4. This supports that the loops are more
highly excited than the disk molecular gas. An LVG analysis of three
transitions, 12CO J =3-2 and 2-1 and 13CO J =2-1, toward six positions in loops
1 and 2 shows density and temperature are in a range 102.2 - 104.7 cm-3 and
15-100 K or higher, respectively. Three regions extended by 50-100 pc in the
loops tend to have higher excitation conditions as characterized by R3-2/2-1
greater than 1.2. The highest ratio of 2.5 is found in the most developed foot
points between loops 1 and 2. This is interpreted that the foot points indicate
strongly shocked conditions as inferred from their large linewidths of 50-100
km s-1, confirming the suggestion by Torii et al. (2010b). The other two
regions outside the foot points suggest that the molecular gas is heated up by
some additional heating mechanisms possibly including magnetic reconnection. A
detailed analysis of four foot points have shown a U shape, an L shape or a
mirrored-L shape in the b-v distribution. It is shown that a simple kinematical
model which incorporates global rotation and expansion of the loops is able to
explain these characteristic shapes.
label: human

text: This research paper examines the phenomenon of a low escape fraction of ionizing photons in Lyman break galaxies with luminosities greater than L* at redshift z = 3.3. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the factors contributing to the low escape fraction of ionizing photons in these high-luminosity galaxies and its implications for early galaxy formation and evolution. The methodology involves analyzing spectroscopic data obtained from ground-based observatories and conducting detailed modeling of the Lyman break galaxy population at z = 3.3. The key findings reveal a significant correlation between high luminosities and low escape fractions of ionizing photons, suggesting a possible connection between galaxy luminosity and the ability to produce ionizing radiation. This study underscores the importance of understanding the mechanisms that regulate the escape of ionizing photons in high-redshift galaxies and their role in driving reionization processes in the early universe. In conclusion, the results provide valuable insights into the complex interplay between galaxy properties and the escape of ionizing radiation, shedding light on the intricate nature of galaxy evolution at cosmic dawn.
label: machine

text:
Classical Supergiant X-ray Binaries host a neutron star orbiting a supergiant
OB star and display persistent X-ray luminosities of 10$^{35}$ to 10$^{37}$
erg/s. The stellar wind from the massive companion is believed to be the main
source of matter accreted by the compact object. With this first paper, we
introduce a ballistic model to characterize the structure of the wind at the
orbital scale as it accelerates, from the stellar surface to the vicinity of
the accretor. Thanks to the parametrization we retained and the numerical
pipeline we designed, we can investigate the supersonic flow and the subsequent
observables as a function of a reduced set of characteristic numbers and
scales. We show that the shape of the permanent flow is entirely determined by
the mass ratio, the filling factor, the Eddington factor and the $\alpha$-force
multiplier which drives the stellar wind acceleration. Provided scales such as
the orbital period are known, we can trace back the observables to evaluate the
mass accretion rates, the accretion mechanism, the shearing of the inflow and
the stellar parameters. We confront our model to three persistent Supergiant
X-ray Binaries (Vela X-1, IGR J18027-2016, XTE J1855-026) and discuss the
likelihood of wind-formed accretion discs around the accretors in each case,
further investigated in a following paper.
label: human

text:
A decentralized network of cognitive and non-cognitive transmitters where
each transmitter aims at maximizing his energy-efficiency is considered. The
cognitive transmitters are assumed to be able to sense the transmit power of
their non-cognitive counterparts and the former have a cost for sensing. The
Stackelberg equilibrium analysis of this $2-$level hierarchical game is
conducted, which allows us to better understand the effects of cognition on
energy-efficiency. In particular, it is proven that the network
energy-efficiency is maximized when only a given fraction of terminals are
cognitive. Then, we study a sensing game where all the transmitters are assumed
to take the decision whether to sense (namely to be cognitive) or not. This
game is shown to be a weighted potential game and its set of equilibria is
studied. Playing the sensing game in a first phase (e.g., of a time-slot) and
then playing the power control game is shown to be more efficient individually
for all transmitters than playing a game where a transmitter would jointly
optimize whether to sense and his power level, showing the existence of a kind
of Braess paradox. The derived results are illustrated by numerical results and
provide some insights on how to deploy cognitive radios in heterogeneous
networks in terms of sensing capabilities. Keywords: Power Control, Stackelberg
Equilibrium, Energy-Efficiency.
label: human

text: We present high angular resolution observations of C18O toward the Class 0 protostars IRAS 16293-2422 and IRAS 16234-2426, obtained with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. Our observations reveal clear evidence for accretion bursts in these protostars, revealed by the presence of enhanced C18O sublimation emission. Using a radiative transfer model, we demonstrate that the observed C18O sublimation emission arises from a disk inner radius that varies by a factor of two during these bursts. This result is consistent with the predictions of theoretical models for magnetically driven accretion bursts. Our findings suggest that C18O sublimation emission can serve as a powerful tracer of protostellar accretion activity, allowing for the study of accretion bursts in the early stages of star formation. Future observations with even higher spatial and spectral resolution will be necessary to further test this hypothesis and to investigate the physical conditions in the innermost regions of these disks. This work highlights the importance of high-resolution observations of molecular emission lines in the study of protostellar accretion.
label: machine

text:
We study the interaction of small hydrophobic particles on the surface of an
ultra-soft elastic gel, in which a small amount of elasticity of the medium
balances the weights of the particles. The excess energy of the surface of the
deformed gel causes them to attract as is the case with the generic capillary
interactions of particles on a liquid surface. The variation of the
gravitational potential energies of the particles resulting from their descents
in the gel coupled with the superposition principle of Nicolson allow a fair
estimation of the distance dependent attractive energy of the particles. This
energy follows a modified Bessel function of the second kind with a
characteristic elastocapillary decay length that decreases with the elasticity
of the medium. An interesting finding of this study is that the particles on
the gel move towards each other as if the system possesses a negative
diffusivity that is inversely proportional to friction. This study illustrates
how the capillary interaction of particles is modified by the elasticity of the
medium, which is expected to have important implications in the surface force
driven self-assembly of particles. In particular, this study points out that
the range and the strength of the capillary interaction can be tuned in by
appropriate choices of the elasticity of the support and the interfacial
tension of the surrounding medium. Manipulation of the particle interactions is
exemplified in such fascinating mimicry of the biological processes as the
tubulation, phagocytic engulfment and in the assembly of particles that can be
used to study nucleation and clustering phenomena in well controlled settings.
label: human

text:
The first-price auction is popular in practice for its simplicity and
transparency. Moreover, its potential virtues grow in complex settings where
incentive compatible auctions may generate little or no revenue. Unfortunately,
the first-price auction is poorly understood in theory because equilibrium is
not {\em a priori} a credible predictor of bidder behavior.
  We take a dynamic approach to studying first-price auctions: rather than
basing performance guarantees solely on static equilibria, we study the
repeated setting and show that robust performance guarantees may be derived
from simple axioms of bidder behavior. For example, as long as a loser raises
her bid quickly, a standard first-price auction will generate at least as much
revenue as a second-price auction. We generalize this dynamic technique to
complex pay-your-bid auction settings and show that progressively stronger
assumptions about bidder behavior imply progressively stronger guarantees about
the auction's performance.
  Along the way, we find that the auctioneer's choice of bidding language is
critical when generalizing beyond the single-item setting, and we propose a
specific construction called the {\em utility-target auction} that performs
well. The utility-target auction includes a bidder's final utility as an
additional parameter, identifying the single dimension along which she wishes
to compete. This auction is closely related to profit-target bidding in
first-price and ascending proxy package auctions and gives strong revenue
guarantees for a variety of complex auction environments. Of particular
interest, the guaranteed existence of a pure-strategy equilibrium in the
utility-target auction shows how Overture might have eliminated the cyclic
behavior in their generalized first-price sponsored search auction if bidders
could have placed more sophisticated bids.
label: human

text: The abstract for the research paper on "Divergence in Age-Patterns of Mortality Change Drives International Divergence in Lifespan Inequality" begins with an overview of the study's context, then outlines the objectives, methodologies employed, key findings, and concludes with the implications of these findings.  The world is witnessing significant variations in how mortality rates evolve across different populations and countries. This research aims to investigate the underlying causes of these divergences in age-patterns of mortality change, which in turn influence the disparities in lifespan inequality internationally. Utilizing a comparative analysis of life expectancy data from multiple regions over several decades, the study examines how demographic shifts, health improvements, and socioeconomic factors contribute to these patterns.  Methodologically, the research combines longitudinal statistical models with cross-sectional comparisons to assess trends and identify causal relationships. Key findings reveal that while some regions have seen substantial improvements in longevity, others have experienced stagnation or even declines in certain age groups. These variations in mortality change patterns are found to be more pronounced in regions with higher initial life expectancies, indicating that the pace and nature of mortality decline can significantly affect lifespan inequality.  Conclusively, the study underscores that divergences in age-patterns of mortality change are crucial drivers of international differences in lifespan inequality. Understanding these dynamics could inform targeted interventions aimed at enhancing public health strategies and improving overall population health outcomes globally.
label: machine

text:
We consider the problem of learning a structured multi-task regression, where
the output consists of multiple responses that are related by a graph and the
correlated response variables are dependent on the common inputs in a sparse
but synergistic manner. Previous methods such as l1/l2-regularized multi-task
regression assume that all of the output variables are equally related to the
inputs, although in many real-world problems, outputs are related in a complex
manner. In this paper, we propose graph-guided fused lasso (GFlasso) for
structured multi-task regression that exploits the graph structure over the
output variables. We introduce a novel penalty function based on fusion penalty
to encourage highly correlated outputs to share a common set of relevant
inputs. In addition, we propose a simple yet efficient proximal-gradient method
for optimizing GFlasso that can also be applied to any optimization problems
with a convex smooth loss and the general class of fusion penalty defined on
arbitrary graph structures. By exploiting the structure of the non-smooth
''fusion penalty'', our method achieves a faster convergence rate than the
standard first-order method, sub-gradient method, and is significantly more
scalable than the widely adopted second-order cone-programming and
quadratic-programming formulations. In addition, we provide an analysis of the
consistency property of the GFlasso model. Experimental results not only
demonstrate the superiority of GFlasso over the standard lasso but also show
the efficiency and scalability of our proximal-gradient method.
label: human

text:
We present an imaging and spectral analysis of the nuclear region of the
ULIRG merger Arp 220, using deep \textit{Chandra}-ACIS observations summing up
to \(\sim 300\mbox{ ks}\). Narrow-band imaging with sub-pixel resolution of the
innermost nuclear region reveals two distinct Fe-K emitting sources, coincident
with the infrared and radio nuclear clusters. These sources are separated by 1'
(\(\sim 380\) pc). The X-ray emission is extended and elongated in the eastern
nucleus, like the disk emission observed in millimeter radio images, suggesting
starburst dominance in this region. We estimate Fe-K equivalent width \(\gtrsim
1\) keV for both sources, and observed 2-10 keV luminosities \(\sim
2\times{10}^{40}\mbox{ erg}\mbox{ s}^{-1}\) (W) and \(\sim 3 \times
{10}^{40}\mbox{ erg}\mbox{ s}^{-1}\) (E). In the 6-7 keV band the emission from
these regions is dominated by the 6.7 keV Fe \textsc{xxv} line, suggesting
contribution from collisionally ionized gas. The thermal energy content of this
gas is consistent with kinetic energy injection in the interstellar medium by
Type II SNe. However, nuclear winds from hidden AGN (\(\varv\sim 2000 \mbox{
km}\mbox{ s}^{-1}\)) cannot be excluded. The \(3\sigma\) upper limits on the
neutral Fe-K\(\alpha\) flux of the nuclear regions correspond to intrinsic AGN
2-10 keV luminosities \(< 1\times {10}^{42}\mbox{ erg}\mbox{ s}^{-1}\) (W) and
\(< 0.4\times {10}^{42}\mbox{ erg}\mbox{ s}^{-1}\) (E). For typical AGN SEDs
the bolometric luminosities are \(< 3\times {10}^{43}\mbox{ erg}\mbox{
s}^{-1}\) (W) and \(< 8\times {10}^{43}\mbox{ erg}\mbox{ s}^{-1}\) (E), and
black hole masses \(<1\times{10}^5 M_{\astrosun}\) (W) and \(< 5\times{10}^5
M_{\astrosun}\) (E) for Eddington limited AGNs with a standard 10\% efficiency.
label: human

text:
A qualitative model describing the "anomalous" features of the conductivity
of polymer nanocomposites, in particular, switching to the conducting state in
relatively thick (tens of microns or more) of flexible PVC films is considered.
In previously published experimental results, change of conductivity by 10 or
more orders of magnitude occurred both in the absence of external influences
(spontaneously), and under the influence of an applied electric field, as well
as other initiating factors (such as uniaxial pressure) . In a model of hopping
conduction mechanism it is shown, that switching in the conduction states under
the action of external field significantly (by orders of magnitude) below
threshold can be associated with a high-resistance state instability that
results from the sequence of "shorting" (reversible soft breakdown) of narrow
insulating gaps between regions with relatively high conductivity. Increasing
the field strength in the remaining insulating gaps ultimately leads to the
formation of a conducting channel between the external electrodes and switching
conductivity of the composite film sample in a state of high conductivity. This
cascade model is essentially based on the transition from the usual description
of the charge tunneling through single independent insulating gap to take into
account correlations between adjacent gaps. In the frame of developed model
other "anomalies" such as exponential dependence of the resistance on the
sample thickness, pressure, and other influences can be qualitative explained.
An analogy of the model with a cascading breakdown of avalanche transistors is
also considered.
label: human

text: The transient X-ray binary A0538-66, a millisecond pulsar in a 4.09-hour orbit with a massive O-type companion, has been extensively studied in various wavelengths. However, its optical and near-infrared (NIR) photometric behavior remains poorly understood, particularly during its transient outbursts. This study aims to investigate the optical and NIR photometric monitoring of A0538-66 using data from the REM (Robotic Equatorial Multi-Spectral Telescope) telescope.  A total of 44 nights of observations were conducted, covering a 2.5-year period, using the REM's 0.4-m telescope and a custom-built CCD camera. The data were obtained in the R-band and NIR (J, H, and K) passbands, with a time sampling of 1-30 minutes, depending on the observing conditions. The photometric measurements were calibrated using standard stars and compared with the available X-ray data from the MAXI/GRO and Swift/XRT satellites.  The key findings of this study reveal a strong correlation between the optical and NIR light curves of A0538-66 during its transient outbursts. The NIR light curves show a significant lag of approximately 3-5 days with respect to the optical light curves, suggesting that the NIR emission is dominated by the companion star. The photometric measurements also reveal a high level of variability in the optical and NIR light curves, with amplitudes ranging from 0.5 to 3 magnitudes. The study demonstrates the potential of the REM telescope to monitor the optical and NIR photometric behavior of A0538-66 during its transient outbursts, providing valuable insights into the physics of this binary system.
label: machine

text:
Context. Understanding the role of fragmentation is one of the most important
current questions of star formation. To better understand the process of star
and cluster formation, we need to study in detail the physical structure and
properties of the parental molecular cloud. The Spokes cluster, or NGC 2264 D,
is a rich protostellar cluster where previous N2H+(1-0) observations of its
dense cores presented linewidths consistent with supersonic turbulence.
However, the fragmentation of the most massive of these cores appears to have a
scale length consistent with that of the thermal Jeans length, suggesting that
turbulence was not dominant. Aims. These two results probe different density
regimes. Our aim is to determine if there is subsonic or less-turbulent gas
(than previously reported) in the Spokes cluster at higher densities. Methods.
We present APEX N2H+(3-2) and N2D+(3-2) observations of the NGC2264-D region to
measure the linewidths and the deuteration fraction of the higher density gas.
The critical densities of the selected transitions are more than an order of
magnitude higher than that of N2H+(1-0). Results. We find that the N2H+(3-2)
and N2D+(3-2) emission present significantly narrower linewidths than the
emission from N2H+(1-0) for most cores. In two of the spectra, the nonthermal
component is close (within 1-sigma) to the sound speed. In addition, we find
that the three spatially segregated cores, for which no protostar had been
confirmed show the highest levels of deuteration. Conclusions. These results
show that the higher density gas, probed with N2H+ and N2D+(3-2), reveals more
quiescent gas in the Spokes cluster than previously reported. More high-angular
resolution interferometric observations using high-density tracers are needed
to truly assess the kinematics and substructure within NGC2264-D. (Abridged)
label: human

text:
It is shown that dynamical screening of the Coulomb interaction in LaCuO
leads to low-energy electronic collective excitations in a small region around
the c-axis, strongly mixing with interlayer phonons. The manifestation of such
a phonon-plasmon scenario based on a nonadiabatic charge response is
quantitatively supported by a realistic calculation of the frequency and
wavevector dependent irreducible polarization part of the density response
function. The latter is used within linear response theory to calculate the
coupled mode dispersion in the main symmetry directions of the Brillouin zone
and the charge density redistributions excited by certain strongly coupling
phonon-like and plasmon-like modes. Moreover, the corresponding mode induced
orbital averaged changes of the selfconsistent potential felt by the electrons
are assessed. Our analysis should be representative for the optimally to
overdoped state of the cuprates where experimental evidence of a coherent
three-dimensional Fermi surface and a coherent c-axis charge transport is
given. It is demonstrated that modes from the outside of a small region around
the c-axis can reliably be calculated within the adiabatic limit. Only a minor
nonadiabatic correction is found for these modes in form of stiffening of the
high-frequency oxygen-bond-stretching mode at the X-point which is attributed
to dynamical reduced nesting. On the other hand, modes inside the nonadiabatic
sector of the BZ have to be determined nonadiabatically owing to the poor
dynamical screening of the long-ranged Coulomb interaction around the c-axis by
the slow charge dynamics. In particular, the relevance of the strongly coupling
phonon-like apex oxygen $Z$-point breathing mode at about 40 meV is emphasized
whose mode energy decreases with less doping.
label: human

text:
3D printing of plastics, ceramics, and metals has existed for several decades
and has revolutionized many areas of manufacturing and science. Printing of
metals in particular has found a number of applications in fields as diverse as
customized medical implants, jet engine bearings, and rapid prototyping in the
automotive industry. Whilst many techniques can be used for 3D printing metals,
they commonly rely on computer controlled melting or sintering of a metal alloy
powder using a laser or electron beam. The mechanical properties of parts
produced in such a way have been well studied, but little attention has been
paid to their electrical properties. Here we show that a microwave cavity
(resonant frequencies 9.9 and 11.2 GHz) 3D printed using an Al-12Si alloy
exhibits superconductivity when cooled below the critical temperature of
aluminium (1.2 K), with a performance comparable to the common 6061 alloy of
aluminium. Superconducting cavities find application in numerous areas of
physics, from particle accelerators to cavity quantum electrodynamics
experiments. The result is achieved even with a very large concentration of
non-superconducting silicon in the alloy of 12.18%, compared to Al-6061, which
has between 0.4 to 0.8%. Our results may pave the way for the possibility of 3D
printing superconducting cavity configurations that are otherwise impossible to
machine.
label: human

text:
Aedes aegypti is the main vector of multiple diseases, such as Dengue, Zika,
and Chikungunya. Due to modifications in weather patterns, its geographical
range is continuously evolving. Temperature is a key factor for its expansion
into regions with cool winters, but rainfall can also have a strong impact on
the colonization of these regions, since larvae emerging after a rainfall are
likely to die at temperatures below $10^{\circ}$C. As climate change is
expected to affect rainfall regimes, with a higher frequency of heavy storms
and an increase in drought-affected areas, it is important to understand how
different rainfall scenarios may shape Ae. aegypti's range. We develop a model
for the population dynamics of Ae. aegypti, coupled with a rainfall model to
study the effect of the temporal distribution of rainfall on mosquito
abundance. Using a fracturing process, we then investigate the effect of a
higher variability in the daily rainfall. As an example, we show that rainfall
distribution is necessary to explain the geographic range of Ae. aegypti in
Taiwan, an island characterized by rainy winters in the north and dry winters
in the south. We also predict that a higher variability in the rainfall time
distribution will decrease the maximum abundance of Ae. aegypti during the
summer. An increase in daily rainfall variability will likewise enhance its
extinction probability. Finally, we obtain a nonlinear relationship between dry
season duration and extinction probability. These findings can have a
significant impact on our ability to predict disease outbreaks.
label: human

text: In the field of fluid dynamics, the optimization of flow structures in complex geometries is a challenging task. Topology optimization (TO), a powerful computational tool, is utilized to obtain optimal fluid structures based on given design objectives and constraints. This study focuses on employing CutFEM (Cutting Finite Element Method) for the topology optimization of three-dimensional (3D) incompressible laminar flow problems.  The objective of this research is to apply CutFEM for the topology optimization of 3D incompressible laminar flow around an obstacle. To achieve this, the governing equations of incompressible laminar flow, i.e., the Navier-Stokes equations, are discretized using CutFEM. A density-based methodology is employed for the topology optimization process with the objective of minimizing the drag force exerted on the obstacle. The Squire-Gordon vortex sheet instability constraint and the volumetric constraint are imposed as constraints during the optimization process.  The key findings of this study reveal that CutFEM-based TO successfully generates flow structures that minimize the drag force on the obstacle while satisfying the vortex sheet instability and volumetric constraints. The obtained results indicate that CutFEM-based TO is an effective technique for the design of optimal flow structures in 3D incompressible laminar flow problems. Additionally, the computational efficiency of CutFEM in handling complex geometries is advantageous for the practical application of topology optimization methods in fluid dynamics.  In conclusion, this research investigates the application of CutFEM for the topology optimization of 3D incompressible laminar flow problems. The results confirm that CutFEM-based TO is a viable solution for generating optimal flow structures while maintaining computational efficiency. The findings of this study contribute to the development of advanced design methods for fluid dynamics applications.
label: machine

text: This study investigates whether the Interstellar Boundary Explorer (IBEX) mission can identify variations in the galactic environment near the solar system by analyzing energetic neutral atoms (ENAs). The research method involves a detailed examination of IBEX data, focusing on ENA emissions that originate from the boundary region between the heliosphere and interstellar medium. The analysis aims to detect changes in the composition and flux of ENAs as they pass through different galactic environments. Problematically, previous studies have suggested that ENA measurements alone may not fully capture all aspects of the galactic environment due to their neutral nature. Our work addresses this limitation by employing statistical methods and comparing ENA data with other solar system parameters such as solar wind speed and interplanetary magnetic field direction. Key findings indicate that while ENAs do not reveal absolute environmental conditions, they can highlight significant changes indicative of varying galactic conditions. This study underscores the utility of IBEX in providing insights into the dynamic interactions between the solar system and the broader galactic environment, thus expanding our understanding of the Sun's cosmic context.
label: machine

text: In this work, we revisit the coordinate coherent states approach, aiming to bridge gaps in the existing theoretical framework and enhance its applicability in quantum mechanics. We systematically analyze the mathematical formulation of coherent states defined within specific coordinate systems, highlighting their significance in representing quantum states with classical-like properties. Our findings indicate that by employing a refined technique based on symplectic geometry, we can derive new criteria for the stability and completeness of these states.  We demonstrate that the coherent states constructed in this adjusted framework exhibit improved localization and reduced uncertainty, which we validate through both analytical methods and numerical simulations. Our methodology involves an extensive application of the Weyl quantization scheme, fostering a robust connection between position-momentum representations and coherent state formulations.   We further address challenges related to the non-uniformity in the distribution of state parameters, establishing a methodology to ensure a more uniform sampling of the parameter space. Our results culminate in clear guidelines for selecting coordinate systems that optimize the coherent states for specific quantum systems. We anticipate that this refined approach to coordinate coherent states will not only enhance theoretical understanding but also facilitate practical applications in fields such as quantum optics, quantum information, and condensed matter physics. By systematically revisiting and expanding upon the coordinate coherent states, we contribute valuable insights that may inspire further research and innovation in the quantum domain.
label: machine

text:
We report high-precision measurements of the Nusselt number $Nu$ as a
function of the Rayleigh number $Ra$ in water-filled rectangular
Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection cells. The horizontal length $L$ and width $W$
of the cells are 50.0 cm and 15.0 cm, respectively, and the heights $H=49.9$,
25.0, 12.5, 6.9, 3.5, and 2.4 cm, corresponding to the aspect ratios
$(\Gamma_x\equiv L/H,\Gamma_y\equiv W/H)=(1,0.3)$, $(2,0.6)$, $(4,1.2)$,
$(7.3,2.2)$, $(14.3,4.3)$, and $(20.8,6.3)$. The measurements were carried out
over the Rayleigh number range $6\times10^5\lesssim Ra\lesssim10^{11}$ and the
Prandtl number range $5.2\lesssim Pr\lesssim7$. Our results show that for
rectangular geometry turbulent heat transport is independent of the cells'
aspect ratios and hence is insensitive to the nature and structures of the
large-scale mean flows of the system. This is slightly different from the
observations in cylindrical cells where $Nu$ is found to be in general a
decreasing function of $\Gamma$, at least for $\Gamma=1$ and larger. Such a
difference is probably a manifestation of the finite plate conductivity effect.
Corrections for the influence of the finite conductivity of the top and bottom
plates are made to obtain the estimates of $Nu_{\infty}$ for plates with
perfect conductivity. The local scaling exponents $\beta_l$ of $Nu_{\infty}\sim
Ra^{\beta_l}$ are calculated and found to increase from 0.243 at
$Ra\simeq9\times10^5$ to 0.327 at $Ra\simeq4\times10^{10}$.
label: human

text:
The structure of ecological interactions is commonly understood through
analyses of interaction networks. However, these analyses may be sensitive to
sampling biases in both the interactors (the nodes of the network) and
interactions (the links between nodes). These issues may affect the accuracy of
empirically constructed ecological networks. We explore the properties of
sampled ecological networks by simulating large-scale ecological networks with
predetermined topologies, and sampling them with different mathematical
procedures. Several types of modular networks were generated, intended to
represent a wide variety of communities that vary in size and types of
ecological interactions. We sampled these networks with different sampling
designs that may be encountered in field experiments. The observed networks
generated by each sampling process were analyzed with respect to number and
size of components. We show that the sampling effort needed to estimate
underlying network properties depends both on the sampling design and on
network topology. Networks with random or scale-free modules require more
complete sampling compared to networks whose modules are nested or bipartite.
Overall, the structure of nested modules was the easiest to detect, regardless
of sampling design. Sampling according to species degree was consistently found
to be the most accurate strategy to estimate network structure. Conversely,
sampling according to module results in an accurate view of certain modules,
but fails to provide a global picture of the underlying network. We recommend
that these findings are incorporated into the design of projects aiming to
characterize large networks of species interactions in the field, to reduce
sampling biases. The software scripts developed to construct and sample
networks are provided for further explorations of network structure and
comparisons to real interaction data.
label: human

text: This study investigates the nucleosynthetic history of elements in the Galactic disk by examining [X/Fe]-age relations through high-precision spectroscopy. Our research aims to address the problem of understanding the evolution of elements in the Milky Way's disk and how their ratios vary with stellar age. By analyzing high-quality spectroscopic data of stars in the Galactic disk, we have obtained results that shed light on the enrichment processes and timescales involved in the formation of these elements.  The key findings of our work reveal distinct trends in [X/Fe] ratios as a function of stellar age, suggesting different nucleosynthetic pathways and timescales for the production of elements in the Galactic disk. Our methodology involves determining stellar ages using isochrone fitting and stellar parameters derived from spectroscopic observations.  We compare the abundance patterns of different elements such as alpha elements, iron-peak elements, and light neutron-capture elements to uncover the chemical evolution history of the Galactic disk. This research provides valuable insights into the nucleosynthetic processes that have shaped the elemental composition of our Galaxy and contributes to our broader understanding of stellar evolution and Galactic chemical evolution.
label: machine

text: This paper explores the relationship between student understanding of symmetry principles and Gauss' law in the context of electromagnetism. The main problem addressed is the common misconception among students that symmetry considerations are not crucial in applying Gauss' law. Our study employs a mixed-methods approach combining qualitative analysis of student responses to conceptual questions and quantitative evaluation of their performance on traditional problem-solving tasks.   The results indicate that students who demonstrate a deeper understanding of symmetry principles are more successful in applying Gauss' law accurately and efficiently. Specifically, those who can identify the symmetries present in a problem scenario are better equipped to simplify the integration process required by Gauss' law, leading to more robust solutions. Moreover, our analysis reveals specific misconceptions held by students regarding the role of symmetry, which can act as barriers to their effective application of Gauss' law.  In conclusion, our study underscores the importance of emphasizing symmetry principles in teaching Gauss' law to enhance student comprehension and problem-solving skills in electromagnetism. By pinpointing and addressing common misconceptions, educators can better support students in developing a more coherent understanding of these fundamental concepts in physics.
label: machine

text: Intrinsic noise, a fundamental aspect of stochastic systems, plays a significant role in the dynamics of chemical reactions, particularly in systems characterized by autocatalytic processes. This study investigates the effects of intrinsic noise on a cubic autocatalytic reaction-diffusion system, which is a prototypical model for understanding pattern formation and chemical instabilities. Our objective is to quantify how stochastic fluctuations impact system behavior compared to deterministic approaches. We employed a combination of analytical methods and stochastic simulations utilizing the Gillespie algorithm to model noise effects on the reaction rates and diffusion processes. Our key findings reveal that intrinsic noise can significantly alter the stability and dynamics of the system, leading to emergent behaviors that are not predicted by purely deterministic models. Notably, noise-induced phenomena include the stabilization of otherwise unstable states and the emergence of spatial patterns at parameter values where deterministic models fail to predict pattern formation. Furthermore, we observed that noise can induce transitions between different dynamical regimes, impacting the overall reaction kinetics and diffusion characteristics. These results underscore the critical interplay between stochasticity and non-linear dynamics in chemical systems. In conclusion, our research highlights the necessity of considering intrinsic noise in modeling reaction-diffusion systems, particularly in understanding complex biochemical and ecological processes where noise plays a pivotal role. Our findings contribute to a deeper comprehension of stochastic effects in autocatalytic reactions, potentially informing the design of more robust chemical and biotechnological systems.

text: In our study, we present evidence supporting the evolved nature of the B[e] star MWC 137, utilizing spectroscopic and photometric data. The star's high metallicity and strong Balmer line broadening further support this evolutionary stage. Our research also explores the potential influence of companion stars on the observed spectral characteristics, suggesting that interactions between MWC 137 and its environment could be significant. Key methodologies include multi-object spectroscopy, high-resolution imaging, and detailed statistical analysis of light curves. These findings contribute to our understanding of B[e] stars as indicators of advanced stellar evolution and their role in galactic environments.

We identify an object previously thought to be a star in the disk of M31,
J0045+41, as a background $z\approx0.215$ AGN seen through a low-absorption
region of M31. We present moderate resolution spectroscopy of J0045+41 obtained
using GMOS at Gemini-North. The spectrum contains features attributable to the
host galaxy. We model the spectrum to estimate the AGN contribution, from which
we estimate the luminosity and virial mass of the central engine. Residuals to
our fit reveal a blue-shifted component to the broad H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ at
a relative velocity of $\sim4800$ km s$^{-1}$. We also detect \ion{Na}{1}
absorption in the Milky Way restframe. We search for evidence of periodicity
using $g$-band photometry from the Palomar Transient Factory and find evidence
for multiple periodicities ranging from $\sim80-350$ days. Two of the detected
periods are in a 1:4 ratio, which is identical to the predictions of
hydrodynamical simulations of binary supermassive black hole systems. If these
signals arise due to such a system, J0045+41 is well within the gravitational
wave regime. We calculate the time until inspiral due to gravitational
radiation, assuming reasonable values of the mass ratio of the two black holes.
We discuss the implications of our findings and forthcoming work to identify
other such interlopers in the light of upcoming photometric surveys such as the
Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) or the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST)
projects.

text: This research paper explores the expressive power and decidability of first-order logic with the successor function over infinite words. The main objective is to investigate the limitations and capabilities of first-order logic extended with a successor relation when applied to infinite sequences. The methodology employed involves analyzing the ability of the logic to express properties and reason about relationships within infinite words using the successor function. Key findings reveal that despite the addition of the successor function, first-order logic remains limited in its ability to capture certain properties and relationships within infinite words. The study also highlights the decidability of various fragments of first-order logic with the successor function over infinite words. In conclusion, while first-order logic with the successor function enriches the expressiveness of logic when dealing with infinite sequences, it also demonstrates limitations in capturing certain properties, thus emphasizing the balance between expressive power and decidability in formal systems dealing with infinite structures.

We present the first polarimetric space VLBI imaging observations at 22 GHz.
BL Lacertae was observed in 2013 November 10 with the RadioAstron space VLBI
mission, including a ground array of 15 radio telescopes. The instrumental
polarization of the space radio telescope is found to be within 9%,
demonstrating the polarimetric imaging capabilities of RadioAstron at 22 GHz.
Ground-space fringes were obtained up to a projected baseline distance of 7.9
Earth's diameters in length, allowing us to image the jet in BL Lacertae with a
maximum angular resolution of 21 $\mu$as, the highest achieved to date. We find
evidence for emission upstream of the radio core, which may correspond to a
recollimation shock at about 40 $\mu$as from the jet apex, in a pattern that
includes other recollimation shocks at approximately 100 $\mu$as and 250
$\mu$as from the jet apex. Polarized emission is detected in two components
within the innermost 0.5 mas from the core, as well as in some knots 3 mas
downstream. Faraday rotation analysis, obtained from combining RadioAstron 22
GHz and ground-based 15 GHz and 43 GHz images, shows a gradient in rotation
measure and Faraday corrected polarization vector as a function of position
angle with respect to the core, suggesting that the jet in BL Lacertae is
threaded by a helical magnetic field. The intrinsic de-boosted brightness
temperature in the unresolved core exceeds $3\!\times\!10^{12}$ K, suggesting
at the very least departure from equipartition of energy between the magnetic
field and radiating particles.

The thesis deals with the first stage of planet formation, namely dust
coagulation from micron to millimeter sizes in circumstellar disks. For the
first time, we collect and compile the recent laboratory experiments on dust
aggregates into a collision model that can be implemented into dust coagulation
models. We put this model into a Monte Carlo code that uses representative
particles to simulate dust evolution. Simulations are performed using three
different disk models in a local box (0D) located at 1 AU distance from the
central star. We find that the dust evolution does not follow the previously
assumed growth-fragmentation cycle, but growth is halted by bouncing before the
fragmentation regime is reached. We call this the bouncing barrier which is an
additional obstacle during the already complex formation process of
planetesimals. The absence of the growth-fragmentation cycle and the halted
growth has two important consequences for planet formation. 1) It is observed
that disk atmospheres are dusty throughout their lifetime. Previous models
concluded that the small, continuously produced fragments can keep the disk
atmospheres dusty. We however show that small fragments are not produced
because bouncing prevents fragmentation. 2) As particles do not reach the
fragmentation barrier, their sizes are smaller compared to the sizes reached in
previous dust models. We decided to investigate point 1) in more detail. A
vertical column of a disk (1D) is modeled including the sedimentation of the
particles. We find that already intermediate levels of turbulence can prevent
particles settling to the midplane.

text: In this study, we investigate the connection between compact star-forming galaxies at redshift ~2 and their quiescent descendants by examining the role of low gas fractions in driving the evolutionary path of these galaxies. Our research reveals that compact star-forming galaxies with low gas fractions undergo a transformation over time, transitioning into quiescent galaxies. By utilizing a combination of observational data and simulations, we demonstrate that low gas fractions play a crucial role in triggering the cessation of star formation and subsequent quenching of these compact systems. Through in-depth analyses, we establish a clear evolutionary link between gas-poor compact galaxies at high redshifts and their quiescent descendants at later cosmic epochs. The methodology employed in this work involves detailed measurements of gas fractions, stellar properties, and morphological characteristics of galaxies across different redshifts, complemented by theoretical modeling to understand the underlying physical processes driving the observed evolution. Our findings provide valuable insights into the mechanisms governing the transformation of compact star-forming galaxies into quiescent systems, shedding light on the pivotal role of gas content in shaping the evolutionary pathways of galaxies from the high-redshift Universe to the present day.

We have conducted a near-infrared monitoring campaign at the UK InfraRed
Telescope, of the Local Group spiral galaxy M33. The main aim was to identify
stars in the very final stage of their evolution, and for which the luminosity
is more directly related to the birth mass than the more numerous less--evolved
giant stars that continue to increase in luminosity. In first instance, only
the central square kiloparsec were monitored and analysed, with the UIST
camera. Photometry was obtained for 18,398 stars; of these 812 stars were found
to be variable, most of which are asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars. We
constructed the birth mass function and hence derived the star formation
history. These stars are also important dust factories. We measure their dust
production rates from a combination of our data with Spitzer Space Telescope
mid-IR photometry. The mass loss rates are seen to increase with increasing
strength of pulsation and with increasing bolometric luminosity. We construct a
2D map of the mass return rate, showing a radial decline but also local
enhancements due to the concentration of red supergiants. We conclude that star
formation in the central region of M33 can only be sustained if gas is accreted
from further out in the disc or from circum--galactic regions. By using data of
wide-field camera (WFCAM), the campaign was expanded to cover two orders of
magnitude larger area, comprising the disc of M33 and its spiral arms.
Photometry was obtained for 403,734 stars; of these 4643 stars were found to be
variable. We here present the star formation history across the disc of M33.

We present an in-depth analysis of the spectral and temporal behavior of a
long almost uninterrupted INTEGRAL observation of Vela X-1 in Nov/Dec 2003. In
addition to an already high activity level, Vela X-1 exhibited several very
intense flares with a maximum intensity of more than 5 Crab in the 20-40 keV
band. Furthermore Vela X-1 exhibited several off states where the source became
undetectable with ISGRI. We interpret flares and off states as being due to the
strongly structured wind of the optical companion: when Vela X-1 encounters a
cavity in the wind with strongly reduced density, the flux drops, thus
potentially triggering the onset of the propeller effect which inhibits further
accretion, thus giving rise to the off states. The required drop in density to
trigger the propeller effect in Vela X-1 is of the same order as predicted by
theoretical papers for the densities in the OB star winds. The same structured
wind can give rise to the giant flares when Vela X-1 encounters a dense blob in
the wind. Further temporal analysis reveals that a short lived QPO with a
period of ~6800 sec is present. The part of the light curve during which the
QPO is present is very close to the off states and just following a high
intensity state, thus showing that all these phenomena are related.

text: The interstellar extinction in open star clusters plays a crucial role in understanding the physical conditions of the interstellar medium (ISM) and the evolution of stars within these environments. In this study, we present measurements of interstellar extinction in twenty open star clusters, using optical and near-infrared photometry of stars in each cluster. We determine the reddening values and extinction curves by fitting the observed colors and magnitudes of cluster stars to stellar photospheric models. The results reveal significant variations in the interstellar extinction across the clusters, ranging from low to high extinction values. Our findings suggest that these variations are primarily driven by the physical conditions of the surrounding ISM. We identify three distinct categories of star clusters based on their extinction properties low-extinction clusters, intermediate-extinction clusters, and high-extinction clusters. The low-extinction clusters, located in relatively quiescent regions of the ISM, exhibit a uniform extinction pattern consistent with the standard Galactic extinction curve. In contrast, the intermediate- and high-extinction clusters, located in denser ISM environments, display complex extinction patterns that deviate significantly from the standard curve. Our analysis reveals that the interstellar extinction in open star clusters is a useful probe of the ISM's physical conditions. The complex extinction patterns observed in some clusters suggest the presence of multiple dust components and the effects of radiation fields on the dust grain composition. Further studies are required to fully understand the interplay between the ISM and star formation in these environments. This work contributes to our understanding of the ISM's role in shaping the properties of stellar populations and the overall evolution of galaxies.

text: White dwarf binaries are compact stellar systems that emit gravitational waves as they inspiral towards each other. In this study, we investigate the phenomenon of tidal resonance in white dwarf binaries, where tidal forces from one white dwarf excite normal modes in the other, leading to a lock-in effect that impacts the inspiral dynamics.   The objective of this research is to understand how tidal resonance influences the evolution of inspiraling white dwarf binaries and to determine its implications for the emission of gravitational waves. To achieve this, we employ analytical methods and numerical simulations to model the tidal interactions between the white dwarfs and analyze their effects on the binary's orbital parameters.   Our key findings demonstrate that tidal resonance can significantly alter the inspiral timescale of white dwarf binaries, influencing the frequency and amplitude of the emitted gravitational waves. This resonance-induced locking mechanism can also affect the final coalescence of the binaries and contribute to the overall gravitational wave signal characteristics.  In conclusion, our research highlights the importance of tidal resonance effects in understanding the dynamics of inspiraling white dwarf binaries and their gravitational wave signatures. These findings provide valuable insights for future studies on compact binary systems and their contribution to gravitational wave astronomy.

text: The Casimir effect, a quantum mechanical force between two uncharged, perfectly conducting parallel plates, has been observed and studied extensively in macroscopic systems. In microelectromechanical systems (MEMS), the interaction between metallic surfaces exhibits unique properties due to their finite size and material characteristics. This study investigates the Casimir attractive-repulsive transition in MEMS devices, aiming to understand the underlying mechanisms that govern this phenomenon.  The methodology involved the fabrication of MEMS structures with varying geometries and materials, followed by the measurement of the forces acting between these structures using atomic force microscopy. Key parameters such as plate separation distance, plate area, and material type were systematically varied to observe the transition from repulsion to attraction and vice versa.  Key findings revealed that the Casimir force significantly deviates from the classical predictions at extremely short separations, primarily influenced by quantum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field. For small plate separations, the attractive nature of the Casimir force becomes dominant, which can be attributed to the increased quantum vacuum fluctuations near the surfaces. Additionally, the material properties of the MEMS structures play a crucial role in determining the strength and direction of the Casimir force.  The results highlight the importance of considering quantum effects in the design and operation of MEMS devices, particularly in applications involving nanoscale interactions. The study concludes that further investigation into the Casimir force in MEMS could lead to innovative designs for miniaturized sensors, actuators, and energy harvesting devices.

text: We present our research on characterising the modal definability of team-based logics utilizing the universal modality. Our study aims to address the problem of understanding the modal definability within team semantics, a key concept in multi-agent systems and artificial intelligence. Through our investigation, we obtained results that shed light on the expressive power of team-based logics, particularly focusing on the universal modality's role in defining modal operators in this context.  Our work delves into the complexities of team-based logics and the modal definability constraints they pose, offering valuable insights into the interactions between modalities and team semantics. We explore the relationship between modal operators and the universal modality, highlighting its significance in defining the modal properties of team-based logics.  We develop a systematic methodology to analyse the modal definability of team-based logics, establishing a framework for understanding the interplay between modal operators and the universal modality within this setting. By providing a detailed examination of these concepts, our research contributes to the advancement of knowledge in logic and formal methods for multi-agent systems.  Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of modal definability in team-based logics, offering new perspectives on the expressive capabilities of these logics and their applications in various computational domains.

The majority of magnetic materials possess some degree of magnetic
anisotropy, either at the level of a single ion, or in the exchange
interactions between different magnetic ions. Where these exchange interactions
are also frustrated, the competition between them and anisotropy can stabilize
a wide variety of new phases in applied magnetic field. Motivated by the
hexagonal delafossite 2H-AgNiO 2, we study the Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a
layered triangular lattice with competing first- and second-neighbour
interactions and single-ion easy-axis anisotropy. Using a combination of
classical Monte Carlo simulation, mean-field analysis, and Landau theory, we
establish the magnetic phase diagram of this model as a function of temperature
and magnetic field for a fixed ratio of exchange interactions, but with values
of easy-axis anisotropy D extending from the Heisenberg (D =0) to the Ising
(D=&#8734) limits. We uncover a rich variety of different magnetic phases.
These include several phases which are magnetic supersolids (in the sense of
Matsuda and Tstuneto or Liu and Fisher), one of which may already have been
observed in AgNiO 2. We explore how this particular supersolid arises through
the closing of a gap in the spin-wave spectrum, and how it competes with rival
collinear phases as the easy-axis anisotropy is increased. The finite
temperature properties of this phase are found to be different from those of
any previously studied magnetic supersolid.

text: We investigated the application of the lasso method to predict short-term wind speeds in space-time, with a focus on improving the accuracy of wind speed forecasts. Our analysis revealed that the lasso method, a technique used to optimize sparse regression models, can be effectively utilized to identify the most relevant features and parameters influencing wind speed variations. By incorporating this approach, we were able to reduce the dimensionality of the input data and enhance the generalizability of our models.   Our results indicate that the lasso method outperforms traditional machine learning techniques, such as linear regression and random forest, in predicting short-term wind speeds. The proposed model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.2 m/s, which is significantly lower than the MAE of the baseline models (4.5 m/s and 5.1 m/s, respectively). Moreover, the lasso method allowed us to identify the most critical wind speed features, including atmospheric pressure, temperature, and wind direction, which are essential for accurate wind speed predictions.   The key idea behind our approach is to incorporate the lasso method into a space-time framework, enabling the estimation of wind speed variations across different spatial and temporal scales. By leveraging this approach, we can provide more accurate and reliable wind speed forecasts, which are crucial for various applications, including wind energy production, aviation, and meteorology. Our findings have significant implications for the development of more sophisticated wind speed prediction models and highlight the potential of the lasso method in improving the accuracy of space-time predictions.

We analyse the Kormendy relations (KRs) of the two Frontier Fields clusters,
Abell S1063, at z = 0.348, and MACS J1149.5+2223, at z = 0.542, exploiting very
deep Hubble Space Telescope photometry and VLT/MUSE integral field
spectroscopy. With this novel dataset, we are able to investigate how the KR
parameters depend on the cluster galaxy sample selection and how this affects
studies of galaxy evolution based on the KR. We define and compare four
different galaxy samples according to: (a) S\'ersic indices: early-type
('ETG'), (b) visual inspection: 'ellipticals', (c) colours: 'red', (d) spectral
properties: 'passive'. The classification is performed for a complete sample of
galaxies with m$_{\textit{F814W}} \le$ 22.5 ABmag (M$_{*}$ $\gtrsim 10^{10.0}$
M$_{\odot}$). To derive robust galaxy structural parameters, we use two
methods: (1) an iterative estimate of structural parameters using images of
increasing size, in order to deal with closely separated galaxies and (2)
different background estimations, to deal with the Intracluster light
contamination. The comparison between the KRs obtained from the different
samples suggests that the sample selection could affect the estimate of the
best-fitting KR parameters. The KR built with ETGs is fully consistent with the
one obtained for ellipticals and passive. On the other hand, the KR slope built
on the red sample is only marginally consistent with those obtained with the
other samples. We also release the photometric catalogue with structural
parameters for the galaxies included in the present analysis.

text: This research paper presents an integrated full-field model that combines concurrent plastic deformation with microstructure evolution, focusing on the 3D simulation of dynamic recrystallization in polycrystalline copper. The objective of this study is to develop a comprehensive model that accounts for the complex interplay between plastic deformation and microstructure evolution during dynamic recrystallization processes.   To achieve this, a computational methodology based on crystal plasticity theory and phase-field modeling is utilized. The crystal plasticity framework captures the material's anisotropic mechanical behavior, while the phase-field method tracks microstructural changes such as grain boundary migration and nucleation.   Key findings from the simulations reveal the spatiotemporal evolution of grain structures, dislocation densities, and recrystallized fractions under dynamic loading conditions. The model successfully predicts the formation of new grains, grain growth, and strain localization during deformation.  In conclusion, this integrated model provides valuable insights into the complex mechanisms governing dynamic recrystallization in polycrystalline materials. The findings contribute to a better understanding of material behavior under extreme loading conditions, with implications for optimizing industrial processes and enhancing material performance.

The ALICE (A Large Ion Collider Experiment) Time Projection Chamber (TPC) at
CERN LHC is presently equipped with Multi Wire Proportional Chambers (MWPCs). A
gating grid prevents ions produced during the gas amplification from moving
into the drift volume. The maximum drift time of the electrons together with
the closure time of the gating grid allows a maximum readout rate of about 3
kHz. After the Long Shutdown 2 (from 2021 onwards), the LHC will provide
lead-lead collisions at an expected interaction rate of 50 kHz. To take data at
this rate the TPC will be upgraded with new readout chambers, allowing for
continuous read-out and preserving the energy and momentum resolution of the
current MWPCs.
  Chambers with a stack of four Gas Electron Multipliers (GEMs) fulfil all the
performance requirements, if the voltages applied to the GEMs are tuned
properly. In order to ensure that these chambers are stable while being
operated at the LHC, studies of the discharge behaviour were performed. We
report on studies done with small prototypes equipped with one or two GEMs.
Discharges were voluntarily induced by a combination of high-voltages across
the GEM(s) and highly ionising particles. During these studies, the phenomenon
of "secondary discharges" has been observed. These occur only after an initial
discharge when the electric field above or below the GEM is high enough. The
time between the initial and the secondary discharge ranges from several 10 us
to less than 1 us, decreasing with increasing field. Using decoupling resistors
in the high-voltage supply path of the bottom side of the GEM shifts the
occurrence of these discharges to higher electric fields.

text: We present a novel approach to efficient predecessor search with distance-sensitive query time, addressing the limitations of existing methods that either sacrifice query time or accuracy. Our solution utilizes a hybrid indexing structure that combines the strengths of R-trees and k-d trees, allowing for efficient nearest neighbor search and predecessor retrieval. By leveraging a distance-aware pruning strategy, we significantly reduce the number of nodes to be traversed during the search process, resulting in substantial query time improvements. Our method, dubbed "Distance-Sensitive Predecessor Search" (DSPS), demonstrates a striking trade-off between query time and accuracy, achieving state-of-the-art results in various benchmark datasets.   Through extensive experimentation, we evaluate DSPS on a range of scenarios, including 3D point clouds, geographic information systems, and social networks. Our results show that DSPS outperforms existing methods in terms of query time, while maintaining high accuracy rates. Notably, DSPS achieves a 3x reduction in query time for large-scale datasets, making it an attractive solution for applications requiring efficient predecessor search. By providing a flexible and efficient framework for distance-sensitive query time, DSPS has the potential to revolutionize various fields, including computer vision, geographic information systems, and social network analysis.

We analyzed observations of interstellar neutral helium (ISN~He) obtained
from the Interstellar Boundary Explorer (IBEX) satellite during its first six
years of operation. We used a refined version of the ISN~He simulation model,
presented in the companion paper by Sokol_et al. 2015, and a sophisticated data
correlation and uncertainty system and parameter fitting method, described in
the companion paper by Swaczyna et al 2015. We analyzed the entire data set
together and the yearly subsets, and found the temperature and velocity vector
of ISN~He in front of the heliosphere. As seen in the previous studies, the
allowable parameters are highly correlated and form a four-dimensional tube in
the parameter space. The inflow longitudes obtained from the yearly data
subsets show a spread of ~6 degree, with the other parameters varying
accordingly along the parameter tube, and the minimum chi-square value is
larger than expected. We found, however, that the Mach number of the ISN~He
flow shows very little scatter and is thus very tightly constrained. It is in
excellent agreement with the original analysis of ISN~He observations from IBEX
and recent reanalyses of observations from Ulysses. We identify a possible
inaccuracy in the Warm Breeze parameters as the likely cause of the scatter in
the ISN~He parameters obtained from the yearly subsets, and we suppose that
another component may exist in the signal, or a process that is not accounted
for in the current physical model of ISN~He in front of the heliosphere. From
our analysis, the inflow velocity vector, temperature, and Mach number of the
flow are equal to lambda_ISNHe = 255.8 +/- 0.5 degree, beta_ISNHe = 5.16 +/-
0.10 degree, T_ISNHe = 7440 +/- 260 K, v_ISNHe = 25.8 +/- 0.4$ km/s, and
M_ISNHe = 5.079 +/- 0.028, with uncertainties strongly correlated along the
parameter tube.

We examine the properties of a recently proposed observationally viable
alternative to homogeneous cosmology with smooth dark energy, the timescape
cosmology. In the timescape model cosmic acceleration is realized as an
apparent effect related to the calibration of clocks and rods of observers in
bound systems relative to volume-average observers in an inhomogeneous geometry
in ordinary general relativity. The model is based on an exact solution to a
Buchert average of the Einstein equations with backreaction. The present paper
examines a number of observational tests which will enable the timescape model
to be distinguished from homogeneous cosmologies with a cosmological constant
or other smooth dark energy, in current and future generations of dark energy
experiments. Predictions are presented for: comoving distance measures; H(z);
the equivalent of the dark energy equation of state, w(z); the Om(z) measure of
Sahni, Shafieloo and Starobinsky; the Alcock-Paczynski test; the baryon
acoustic oscillation measure, D_v; the inhomogeneity test of Clarkson, Bassett
and Lu; and the time drift of cosmological redshifts. Where possible, the
predictions are compared to recent independent studies of similar measures in
homogeneous cosmologies with dark energy. Three separate tests with indications
of results in possible tension with the Lambda CDM model are found to be
consistent with the expectations of the timescape cosmology.

text: Polycrystalline diamond (PCD) is a versatile material with unique electromagnetic (EM) properties, making it an attractive candidate for various applications, including high-frequency electronics and energy harvesting devices. This study investigates the EM properties of PCD from 35K to room temperature and microwave to terahertz frequencies.   PCD has drawn significant attention due to its excellent thermal conductivity, hardness, and exceptional electrical properties. Its EM behavior, however, is not yet fully understood, especially in the microwave to terahertz frequency range, which is crucial for many emerging applications.   The primary objective of this study is to characterize the EM properties of PCD in the specified temperature and frequency range through experiments and simulations.   The experiment employed three primary techniques electrical impedance spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, and terahertz time-domain spectroscopy. Complementary density functional theory simulations were carried out to validate and interpret the experimental results.   The experimental and simulation results reveal a complex EM behavior of PCD in the studied frequency and temperature range. PCD displays semiconducting properties at higher temperatures, whereas it exhibits insulating behavior at lower temperatures and microwave frequencies. Additionally, the study uncovers the presence of phonon polariton modes, which significantly contribute to the overall EM response of PCD.   This study contributes significantly to the understanding of PCD's EM properties and sheds light on the potential applications of PCD in various fields, including high-frequency electronics, sensing, and energy harvesting devices. The obtained results provide a foundation for further research in this area and pave the way for engineering PCD-based materials with tailored EM properties.

text: In this study, we present an enhanced two-stream radiative transfer (2SRT) model to treat aerosols in the context of exoplanetary atmospheres. Our approach is a key improvement over traditional 2SRT models, which typically neglect the effects of aerosols on the energy balance and transmission of an exoplanetary atmosphere. We developed a novel method to compute the phase function of aerosols using a precomputed set of Mie scattering solutions, allowing for a significant reduction in the computational cost of the 2SRT calculation. This approach also enables the handling of a wide range of aerosol properties and sizes without the need for extensive external databases.  We performed a series of test calculations to evaluate the performance of our new model. Our results show that including aerosols in 2SRT calculations can significantly affect the radiative equilibrium and transmission spectra of exoplanetary atmospheres. Moreover, the presence of aerosols can mimic the effects of clouds, leading to complex spectral features and variations in the apparent atmospheric temperature structure.  Our new two-stream radiative transfer model for exoplanetary atmospheres with improved aerosol handling will be an essential tool for the analysis and interpretation of future exoplanet data from space-borne observatories like the James Webb Space Telescope and the upcoming European Extremely Large Telescope. The availability of such a model will help researchers understand the role of aerosols in shaping the energy balance and spectral properties of exoplanetary atmospheres and improve our ability to characterize the compositions and environments of planets orbiting other stars.  Keywords Exoplanetary atmospheres, radiative transfer, aerosols, Mie scattering, two-stream model.
label: machine

text: The formation of planets in close binary star systems has long been a subject of intrigue due to their complex dynamical environments. This study aims to investigate the plausibility and factors influencing planet formation in close binary systems, where stellar companions are separated by tens of astronomical units or less. We employ a combination of theoretical models and numerical simulations to explore protoplanetary disk dynamics, accretion processes, and orbital stability within these binary configurations. Our analysis focuses on the impact of gravitational perturbations and disk viscosity on planetesimal formation and the conditions that may lead to the development of stable planetary orbits. Key findings suggest that while the presence of a companion star introduces significant gravitational challenges, it also enhances certain disk properties, such as spiral wave activity, which can promote dust aggregation and enhance accretion rates. Simulations reveal that planets are more likely to form in circumbinary disks with mass concentrations toward the center and stable resonance locations. Furthermore, the inclination angle and eccentricity of the binary orbit play crucial roles in dictating the efficiency of planetesimal formation and accretion. Our results indicate that, contrary to some previous beliefs, close binaries might not significantly impede planet formation, provided certain conditions are fulfilled. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of planetary system diversity and challenges established paradigms by highlighting potential pathways for planet formation in complex binary star environments. Conclusively, our findings pave the way for more nuanced criteria in the search for exoplanets within binary systems.

The Yuan-Tseh Lee Array for Microwave Background Anisotropy (AMiBA) is a
co-planar interferometer array operating at a wavelength of 3mm to measure the
Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect (SZE) of galaxy clusters. In the first phase of
operation -- with a compact 7-element array with 0.6m antennas (AMiBA-7) -- we
observed six clusters at angular scales from 5\arcmin to 23\arcmin. Here, we
describe the expansion of AMiBA to a 13-element array with 1.2m antennas
(AMiBA-13), its subsequent commissioning, and our cluster SZE observing
program. The most important changes compared to AMiBA-7 are (1) array
re-configuration with baselines ranging from 1.4m to 4.8m covering angular
scales from 2\arcmin to 11.5\arcmin, (2) thirteen new lightweight
carbon-fiber-reinforced plastic (CFRP) 1.2m reflectors, and (3) additional
correlators and six new receivers. From the AMiBA-13 SZE observing program, we
present here maps of a subset of twelve clusters. In highlights, we combine
AMiBA-7 and AMiBA-13 observations of Abell 1689 and perform a joint fitting
assuming a generalized NFW pressure profile. Our cylindrically integrated
Compton-y values for this cluster are consistent with the BIMA/OVRA, SZA, and
Planck results. We report the first targeted SZE detection towards the
optically selected galaxy cluster RCS J1447+0828, and we demonstrate the
ability of AMiBA SZE data to serve as a proxy for the total cluster mass.
Finally, we show that our AMiBA-SZE derived cluster masses are consistent with
recent lensing mass measurements in the literature.

text: Discrete-time linear multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly being used to model and analyze complex networks of interconnected agents, each with its own dynamics and objectives. In such systems, achieving consensus among agents is crucial for efficient coordination and decision-making. However, the inherent noise and uncertainty in the system can lead to non-consensus or even instability. To address this challenge, this research focuses on the design and analysis of observer-type protocols for discrete-time linear MAS.  The objective of this study is to develop a novel consensus protocol that utilizes observer-type dynamics to improve the robustness and stability of MAS. The proposed protocol is based on the idea of designing an observer that estimates the state of each agent and then uses this estimate to compute the control input. This approach allows for the incorporation of external disturbances and uncertainties into the system, leading to improved robustness and stability.  The proposed protocol is analyzed using Lyapunov theory and numerical simulations are conducted to evaluate its performance. The results show that the proposed protocol is able to achieve consensus among agents in the presence of noise and uncertainty, while also improving the overall stability of the system. The protocol is also compared with existing consensus protocols, demonstrating its superiority in terms of robustness and stability. Overall, this research contributes to the development of more robust and efficient consensus protocols for discrete-time linear MAS, with potential applications in areas such as distributed control and optimization.

text: This research paper proposes a novel approach to asset allocation by framing the minimization of systemic risk as a network optimization problem. Systemic risk, a measure of the interconnectedness and potential cascading effects of asset failures, has become a critical concern in the investment industry. Traditional methods for mitigating systemic risk often rely on simplistic and ad-hoc approaches, neglecting the complex dynamics of interconnected assets.  In this study, we model the asset network as a weighted graph, where nodes represent assets and edges represent trade relationships between them. Our objective is to minimize the systemic risk by optimizing the asset allocation, subject to constraints on the total portfolio value and the maximum allowed leverage. We employ a network optimization algorithm, specifically the Graph Convolutional Network (GCN), to learn the optimal asset allocation by propagating information through the graph.  Our results show that the proposed approach significantly outperforms traditional methods in terms of minimizing systemic risk, while maintaining a robust and efficient portfolio. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a series of empirical experiments using large-scale asset networks, including the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones indices. Our findings suggest that systemic risk-efficient asset allocation can be achieved through a network optimization framework, providing a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between assets. This research contributes to the development of more robust and resilient investment strategies, essential for navigating the increasingly interconnected financial landscape.

In arXiv:0707.2151 the authors introduced the theory of local representations
of the quantum Teichm\"uller space $\mathcal{T}^q_S$ ($q$ being a fixed
primitive $N$-th root of $(-1)^{N + 1}$) and they studied the behaviour of the
intertwining operators in this theory. One of the main results [Theorem 20,
arXiv:0707.2151] was the possibility to select one distinguished operator (up
to scalar multiplication) for every choice of a surface $S$, ideal
triangulations $\lambda, \lambda'$ and isomorphic local representations $\rho,

and Composition properties. By analyzing the constructions of arXiv:0707.2151,
we found a difficulty that we eventually fix by a slightly weaker (but actually
