text: We investigated the thermomagnetic instability in superconducting films with an adjacent metal layer, with a focus on the interplay between the superconducting and metal components. Our experimental approach involved fabricating superconducting films with varying thicknesses of the metal layer and characterizing their thermomagnetic properties using a combination of magnetization and resistivity measurements. The results showed that the presence of the metal layer leads to a significant enhancement of the thermomagnetic instability in the superconducting films, resulting in a reduced critical temperature and increased magnetic field hysteresis.  Our theoretical modeling employed a simplified phenomenological approach, incorporating the effects of the metal layer on the superconducting film's thermomagnetic properties. We found that the metal layer's thickness and composition play a crucial role in determining the thermomagnetic instability, with thicker metal layers and those with higher resistivity leading to a more pronounced instability. Furthermore, our simulations revealed that the metal layer can act as a thermal sink, reducing the thermal conductivity of the superconducting film and exacerbating the thermomagnetic instability.  The findings of this study have significant implications for the design and operation of superconducting devices, particularly those that incorporate metal layers to enhance their performance. Our results suggest that careful consideration must be given to the interplay between the superconducting and metal components in order to achieve optimal thermomagnetic stability and performance.

text: This study investigates the properties of Toeplitz operators within the context of the symmetrized bidisc, aiming to elucidate their spectral characteristics and functional calculus. Initially, we encountered challenges in defining appropriate symbols for these operators due to the non-commutative nature of the symmetrized bidisc. We overcame this by employing techniques from complex analysis and operator theory, particularly focusing on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces associated with the symmetrized bidisc. Our methodology involved constructing specific symbols that are holomorphic on the bidisc and then determining the Toeplitz operators generated by these symbols. The results obtained demonstrate that the spectrum of these Toeplitz operators is closely related to the boundary behavior of the symbols. Furthermore, we developed a functional calculus for these operators, which allows us to compute functionals of interest in terms of the symbols. This work not only contributes to the theoretical understanding of Toeplitz operators but also provides new insights into the spectral theory of operators defined on non-commutative domains.

We study the asymptotic behaviour of sharp front solutions arising from the
nonlinear diffusion equation \theta_t = (D(\theta)\theta_x)_x, where the
diffusivity is an exponential function D({\theta}) = D_o exp(\beta\theta). This
problem arises for example in the study of unsaturated flow in porous media
where {\theta} represents the liquid saturation. For physical parameters
corresponding to actual porous media, the diffusivity at the residual
saturation is D(0) = D_o << 1 so that the diffusion problem is nearly
degenerate. Such problems are characterised by wetting fronts that sharply
delineate regions of saturated and unsaturated flow, and that propagate with a
well-defined speed. Using matched asymptotic expansions in the limit of large
{\beta}, we derive an analytical description of the solution that is uniformly
valid throughout the wetting front. This is in contrast with most other related
analyses that instead truncate the solution at some specific wetting front
location, which is then calculated as part of the solution, and beyond that
location the solution is undefined. Our asymptotic analysis demonstrates that
the solution has a four-layer structure, and by matching through the adjacent
layers we obtain an estimate of the wetting front location in terms of the
material parameters describing the porous medium. Using numerical simulations
of the original nonlinear diffusion equation, we demonstrate that the first few
terms in our series solution provide approximations of physical quantities such
as wetting front location and speed of propagation that are more accurate (over
a wide range of admissible {\beta} values) than other asymptotic approximations
reported in the literature.

text: The investigation of low column density neutral hydrogen (HI) around the spiral galaxies NGC 2997 and NGC 6946 provides critical insights into galactic structure and evolution. The Green Bank Telescope (GBT) was employed to observe HI emissions at these sites, aiming to elucidate the nature and distribution of HI in low density environments. The study seeks to understand the role of low column density HI in galactic processes and its implications for the broader interstellar medium. Using a systematic observational strategy, GBT spectral-line data were collected, and sophisticated data processing techniques were applied to isolate the low column density HI signals from galactic backgrounds. The methodology included the calibration of wide-field maps to enhance sensitivity and resolution, thereby enabling the detection of faint HI emissions extended beyond the optical disks of the galaxies. Key findings indicate significant elongated HI structures extending several kiloparsecs beyond the conventional galactic boundaries in both NGC 2997 and NGC 6946. The detected low-density HI suggests ongoing gas accretion and potential interaction with surrounding environments, contributing to the enduring star formation processes. Furthermore, the extended HI structures imply the presence of tidal interactions or minor merger events affecting the stellar and gaseous components externally. Conclusively, these observations confirm that low column density HI is a vital component in understanding the gas dynamics and evolutionary pathways of spiral galaxies. Future studies incorporating multi-wavelength data could further unravel the complex interactions within and beyond these galactic systems.

text: The discovery of planetary mass objects (PMOs) has expanded the study of celestial bodies beyond the traditional stellar classification. The PMO PSO J318.5-22, located in the Lower Scorpius OB association, has been observed to display significant variability in multiple wavelength bands. In this study, we present the results of simultaneous multi-wavelength variability analysis using optical and infrared data from the All-Sky Automated Survey for SuperNovae (ASAS-SN) and the Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE). We utilized photometric data and machine learning techniques to identify and classify variability patterns.  Our analysis revealed that the optical and infrared variability of PSO J318.5-22 are linked, with a significant correlation in the power density spectra of the two datasets. The optical and infrared variations can be described by a dipping pattern, with deep dips occurring every 0.6 days. This period is consistent with previous determinations based on optical data alone. We also observed a long-term trend in the data, with the optical and infrared brightnesses increasing over the observational period.  The cause of the variability in PSO J318.5-22 is not well understood, but several possibilities have been suggested, including rotation, accretion, or magnetic activity. Our results are consistent with a model involving accretion from a circumplanetary disk, where the observed dips correspond to the passage of clumps of material across the line of sight. Further observations and theoretical modeling are required to fully understand the nature of this intriguing object.  In summary, we have conducted a simultaneous multi-wavelength variability analysis of the PMO PSO J318.5-22 using data from ASAS-SN and WISE. Our results reveal a correlation between the optical and infrared variations, with a dipping pattern and a long-term trend. The cause of the variability remains uncertain, but our findings are consistent with a model involving accretion from a circumplanetary disk. Further investigation is needed to fully understand the complex behavior of this fascinating object.

A non-parametric smoothing method is presented that reduces noise in
multi-wavelength imaging data sets. Using Principle Component Analysis
(hereafter PCA) to associate pixels according to their $ugriz$-band colors,
smoothing is done over pixels with a similar location in PCA space. This method
smoothes over pixels with similar color, which reduces the amount of mixing of
different colors within the smoothing region. The method is tested using a mock
galaxy with signal-to-noise levels and color characteristics of SDSS data. When
comparing this method to smoothing methods using a fixed radial profile or an
adaptive radial profile, the chi^2-like statistic for the method presented here
is smaller. The method shows a small dependence on input parameters. Running
this method on SDSS data and fitting theoretical stellar population models to
the smoothed data of the mock galaxy and SDSS data, shows that the method
reduces scatter in the best-fit stellar population analysis parameters, when
compared to cases where no smoothing is done. For an area centered on the star
forming region of the mock galaxy, the median and standard deviation of the
PCA-smoothed data is 7 Myr (+/- 3 Myr), as compared to 10 Myr (+/- 1 Myr) for a
simple radial average, where the noise-free true value is 7.5 Myr (+/- 3.7
Myr).

Recent works on zero-shot learning make use of side information such as
visual attributes or natural language semantics to define the relations between
output visual classes and then use these relationships to draw inference on new
unseen classes at test time. In a novel extension to this idea, we propose the
use of visual prototypical concepts as side information. For most real-world
visual object categories, it may be difficult to establish a unique prototype.
However, in cases such as traffic signs, brand logos, flags, and even natural
language characters, these prototypical templates are available and can be
leveraged for an improved recognition performance. The present work proposes a
way to incorporate this prototypical information in a deep learning framework.
Using prototypes as prior information, the deepnet pipeline learns the input
image projections into the prototypical embedding space subject to minimization
of the final classification loss. Based on our experiments with two different
datasets of traffic signs and brand logos, prototypical embeddings incorporated
in a conventional convolutional neural network improve the recognition
performance. Recognition accuracy on the Belga logo dataset is especially
noteworthy and establishes a new state-of-the-art. In zero-shot learning
scenarios, the same system can be directly deployed to draw inference on unseen
classes by simply adding the prototypical information for these new classes at
test time. Thus, unlike earlier approaches, testing on seen and unseen classes
is handled using the same pipeline, and the system can be tuned for a trade-off
of seen and unseen class performance as per task requirement. Comparison with
one of the latest works in the zero-shot learning domain yields top results on
the two datasets mentioned above.

text: This work presents the results of an investigation into the performance of Least Squares (LS) and Linear Minimum Mean Square Error (LMMSE) channel estimation techniques for Long Term Evolution (LTE) downlink systems. The analysis was conducted using Monte Carlo simulations and a comprehensive set of performance metrics including mean square error (MSE), symbol error rate (SER), and bit error rate (BER). The simulation results demonstrated that the LMMSE technique outperformed the LS method in terms of MSE, SER, and BER, revealing significant reductions in these error rates in the range of up to 6 dB, 1.5 dB, and 1.3 dB respectively.  In this work, we considered two different channel models, namely, the Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) channel and the Rayleigh Fading channel. We implemented the LS and LMMSE techniques using the standard equations provided in the literature for each channel model. Simulation scenarios were designed to investigate the impact of varying key system parameters such as channel length, sampling rate, and number of subcarriers.  Our study further revealed that, while the improvement obtained by employing LMMSE over LS was consistent across the considered channel models, the magnitude of the improvements was greater for the Rayleigh Fading channel model. This observation highlights the importance of the choice of channel model in the selection of channel estimation techniques and can lead to significant performance benefits in LTE downlink systems operating under fading conditions.  In conclusion, this research demonstrates that LMMSE provides superior channel estimation performance over the LS method in LTE downlink systems, leading to substantial reductions in error rates. The findings of this study can guide the design and optimization of channel estimation techniques for LTE and other wireless communication systems.

text: Our study delves into the "wet-to-dry" conformational transition exhibited by polymer layers grafted onto nanoparticles within nanocomposites. The investigation aims to elucidate the structural transformations of these grafted polymer layers as they transition from a wet to a dry environment. We address the challenge of understanding the dynamic behavior of these polymer layers and how it influences the overall properties of nanocomposites.  Through a combination of experimental techniques including atomic force microscopy, infrared spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, we observed distinct changes in the conformation and orientation of the grafted polymer chains as the hydration level varied. Our results reveal that the transition from a wet to a dry environment induces significant alterations in the interfacial interactions between the polymer chains and the nanoparticles, consequently affecting the mechanical, thermal, and barrier properties of the nanocomposites.  The key findings highlight the critical role played by the "wet-to-dry" transition in determining the overall performance of nanocomposite materials. Our study provides valuable insights into the design and optimization of nanocomposites through a comprehensive understanding of the conformational dynamics of grafted polymer layers.

text: We investigated the single-ion anisotropy and magnetic field response in two spin ice materials, Ho$_{2}$Ti$_{2}$O$_{7}$ and Dy$_{2}$Ti$_{2}$O$_{7}$. Single-ion anisotropy was probed through the temperature dependence of magnetic susceptibility and specific heat capacity, revealing a strong correlation between the spin ice ground state and the material's magnetic properties. Our results show that both Ho$_{2}$Ti$_{2}$O$_{7}$ and Dy$_{2}$Ti$_{2}$O$_{7}$ exhibit single-ion anisotropy, with Dy$_{2}$Ti$_{2}$O$_{7}$ displaying a more pronounced anisotropy. Magnetic field response was studied using magnetic hysteresis loops and temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility, demonstrating a complex interplay between the spin ice ground state and the material's response to external magnetic fields. We found that both materials exhibit a significant increase in magnetic susceptibility with increasing magnetic field, but Dy$_{2}$Ti$_{2}$O$_{7}$ shows a more pronounced hysteresis loop. Our findings provide insights into the single-ion anisotropy and magnetic field response in spin ice materials, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms that govern their magnetic properties.

This paper presents an inverse optimality method to solve the
Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation for a class of nonlinear problems for which
the cost is quadratic and the dynamics are affine in the input. The method is
inverse optimal because the running cost that renders the control input optimal
is also explicitly determined. One special feature of this work, as compared to
other methods in the literature, is the fact that the solution is obtained
directly for the control input. The value function can also be obtained after
one solves for the control input. Furthermore, a Lyapunov function that proves
at least local stability of the controller is also obtained. In this regard the
main contribution of this paper can be interpreted in two different ways:
offering an analytical expression for Lyapunov functions for a class of
nonlinear systems and obtaining an optimal controller for the same class of
systems using a specific optimization functional. We also believe that an
additional contribution of this paper is to identify explicit classes of
systems and optimization functionals for which optimal control problems can be
solved analytically. In particular, for second order systems three cases are
identified: i) control input only as a function of the second state variable,
ii) control input affine in the second state variable when the dynamics are
affine in that variable and iii) control input affine in the first state
variable when the dyamics are affine in that variable. The relevance of the
proposed methodology is illustrated in several examples, including the Van der
Pol oscillator, mass-spring systems and vehicle path following.

text: The search for exoplanets and their moons has become a vibrant area of research in the field of astrobiology, as the discovery of potentially habitable worlds beyond our solar system has garnered significant attention in recent years. Self-luminous giant exoplanets, characterized by their own internal light sources, pose a unique challenge in the detection of their surrounding moons due to their intense radiation and strong gravitational influences.   This study aimed to explore the feasibility of using polarization as a novel method for detecting exomoons around self-luminous giant exoplanets. By analyzing the polarization patterns of the exoplanet's light, astronomers can infer the presence of a moon, even if it is too small to be directly observed. The research employed a combination of theoretical modeling and simulations to investigate the effects of the exoplanet's radiation and gravity on the polarization of the light, as well as the potential for detection using advanced telescopes and polarimetric instruments.   Key findings revealed that the polarization patterns of the exoplanet's light can indeed be influenced by the presence of a moon, and that this effect can be used to detect exomoons with a high degree of accuracy. The study also identified the optimal wavelength range for polarization measurements and the required instrumental sensitivities for successful detection.   The study's results have significant implications for the search for life beyond our solar system, as they provide a novel and potentially powerful tool for detecting exomoons around self-luminous giant exoplanets. The findings also highlight the importance of considering the complex interactions between the exoplanet and its surrounding environment in the detection of exomoons.

Background and objective: Stacking is an ensemble machine learning method
that averages predictions from multiple other algorithms, such as generalized
linear models and regression trees. An implementation of stacking, called super
learning, has been developed as a general approach to supervised learning and
has seen frequent usage, in part due to the availability of an R package. We
develop super learning in the SAS software system using a new macro, and
demonstrate its performance relative to the R package.
  Methods: Following previous work using the R SuperLearner package we assess
the performance of super learning in a number of domains. We compare the R
package with the new SAS macro in a small set of simulations assessing curve
fitting in a predictive model as well in a set of 14 publicly available
datasets to assess cross-validated accuracy.
  Results: Across the simulated data and the publicly available data, the SAS
macro performed similarly to the R package, despite a different set of
potential algorithms available natively in R and SAS.
  Conclusions: Our super learner macro performs as well as the R package at a
number of tasks. Further, by extending the macro to include the use of R
packages, the macro can leverage both the robust, enterprise oriented
procedures in SAS and the nimble, cutting edge packages in R. In the spirit of
ensemble learning, this macro extends the potential library of algorithms
beyond a single software system and provides a simple avenue into machine
learning in SAS.

Competing geophysical/geochemical hypotheses for how Earth's surface became
oxygenated - organic carbon burial, hydrogen escape to space, and changes in
the redox state of volcanic gases - are examined and a more biologically-based
hypothesis is offered in response. It is argued that organic carbon burial is
of minor importance to the accumulation of oxygen in a mainly anoxic world
where aerobic respiration is not globally significant. Thus, for the Great
Oxidation Event (GOE) ~ 2.4 Gyr ago, an increasing flux of O2 due to its
production by an expanding population of cyanobacteria is parameterized as the
primary source of O2. Various factors would have constrained cyanobacterial
proliferation and O2 production during most of the Archean and therefore a long
delay between the appearance of cyanobacteria and oxygenation of the atmosphere
is to be expected. Destruction of O2 via CH4 oxidation in the atmosphere was a
major O2 sink during the Archean, and the GOE is explained to a significant
extent by a large decline in the methanogen population and corresponding CH4
flux which, in turn, was caused primarily by partial oxygenation of the surface
ocean. The partially oxygenated state of these waters also made it possible for
an aerobic methanotroph population to become established. This further
contributed to the large reduction in the CH4 flux to the atmosphere by
increasing the consumption of CH4 diffusing upwards from the deeper anoxic
depths of the water column as well as any CH4 still being produced in the upper
layer. The reduction in the CH4 flux lowered the CH4 oxidation sink for O2 at
about the same time the metamorphic and volcanic gas sinks for O2 also
declined. As the O2 source increased from an expanding population of
cyanobacteria - triggered by a burst of continent formation ~ 2.7-2.4 Gyr ago -
the atmosphere flipped and became permanently oxygenated.

We improve our filament automated detection method which was proposed in our
previous works. It is then applied to process the full disk H$\alpha$ data
mainly obtained by Big Bear Solar Observatory (BBSO) from 1988 to 2013,
spanning nearly 3 solar cycles. The butterfly diagrams of the filaments,
showing the information of the filament area, spine length, tilt angle, and the
barb number, are obtained. The variations of these features with the calendar
year and the latitude band are analyzed. The drift velocities of the filaments
in different latitude bands are calculated and studied. We also investigate the
north-south (N-S) asymmetries of the filament numbers in total and in each
subclass classified according to the filament area, spine length, and tilt
angle. The latitudinal distribution of the filament number is found to be
bimodal. About 80% of all the filaments have tilt angles within [0{\deg},
60{\deg}]. For the filaments within latitudes lower (higher) than 50{\deg} the
northeast (northwest) direction is dominant in the northern hemisphere and the
southeast (southwest) direction is dominant in the southern hemisphere. The
latitudinal migrations of the filaments experience three stages with declining
drift velocities in each of solar cycles 22 and 23, and it seems that the drift
velocity is faster in shorter solar cycles. Most filaments in latitudes lower
(higher) than 50{\deg} migrate toward the equator (polar region). The N-S
asymmetry indices indicate that the southern hemisphere is the dominant
hemisphere in solar cycle 22 and the northern hemisphere is the dominant one in
solar cycle 23.

[abridged] The black hole X-ray binary XTE J1550-564 was monitored
extensively at X-ray, optical and infrared wavelengths throughout its outburst
in 2000. We show that it is possible to separate the optical/near-infrared
(OIR) jet emission from the OIR disc emission. Focussing on the jet component,
we find that as the source fades in the X-ray hard state, the OIR jet emission
has a spectral index consistent with optically thin synchrotron emission (alpha
~ -0.6 to -0.7, where F_nu \propto nu^alpha). This jet emission is tightly and
linearly correlated with the X-ray flux; L_OIR,jet \propto L_X^(0.98 +- 0.08)
suggesting a common origin. This is supported by the OIR, X-ray and OIR to
X-ray spectral indices being consistent with a single power law (alpha =
-0.73). Ostensibly the compact, synchrotron jet could therefore account for ~
100 % of the X-ray flux at low luminosities in the hard state. At the same
time, (i) an excess is seen over the power law decay of the X-ray flux at the
point in which the jet would start to dominate, (ii) the X-ray spectrum
slightly softens, which seems to be due to a high energy cut-off or break
shifting to a lower energy, and (iii) the X-ray rms variability increases. This
may be the strongest evidence to date of synchrotron emission from the compact,
steady jet dominating the X-ray flux of an X-ray binary. For XTE J1550-564,
this is likely to occur within the luminosity range ~ (2 e-4 - 2 e-3) L_Edd on
the hard state decline of this outburst. However, on the hard state rise of the
outburst and initially on the hard state decline, the synchrotron jet can only
provide a small fraction (~ a few per cent) of the X-ray flux. Both thermal
Comptonization and the synchrotron jet can therefore produce the hard X-ray
power law in accreting black holes.

A new class of modified theories of gravity, consisting of the superposition
of the metric Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian with an $f(\cal R)$ term constructed
\`{a} la Palatini was proposed recently. The dynamically equivalent
scalar-tensor representation of the model was also formulated, and it was shown
that even if the scalar field is very light, the theory passes the Solar System
observational constraints. Therefore the model predicts the existence of a
long-range scalar field, modifying the cosmological and galactic dynamics. An
explicit model that passes the local tests and leads to cosmic acceleration was
also obtained. In the present work, it is shown that the theory can be also
formulated in terms of the quantity $X\equiv \kappa^2 T+R$, where T and R are
the traces of the stress-energy and Ricci tensors, respectively. The variable X
represents the deviation with respect to the field equation trace of general
relativity. The cosmological applications of this hybrid metric-Palatini
gravitational theory are also explored, and cosmological solutions coming from
the scalar-tensor representation of f(X)-gravity are presented. Criteria to
obtain cosmic acceleration are discussed and the field equations are analyzed
as a dynamical system. Several classes of dynamical cosmological solutions,
depending on the functional form of the effective scalar field potential,
describing both accelerating and decelerating Universes are explicitly
obtained. Furthermore, the cosmological perturbation equations are derived and
applied to uncover the nature of the propagating scalar degree of freedom and
the signatures these models predict in the large-scale structure.

Empirical studies show that real world networks often exhibit multiple scales
of topological descriptions. However, it is still an open problem how to
identify the intrinsic multiple scales of networks. In this article, we
consider detecting the multi-scale community structure of network from the
perspective of dimension reduction. According to this perspective, a covariance
matrix of network is defined to uncover the multi-scale community structure
through the translation and rotation transformations. It is proved that the
covariance matrix is the unbiased version of the well-known modularity matrix.
We then point out that the translation and rotation transformations fail to

society. To address this problem, a correlation matrix is proposed through
introducing the rescaling transformation into the covariance matrix. Extensive
tests on real world and artificial networks demonstrate that the correlation
matrix significantly outperforms the covariance matrix, identically the
modularity matrix, as regards identifying the multi-scale community structure
of network. This work provides a novel perspective to the identification of
community structure and thus various dimension reduction methods might be used
for the identification of community structure. Through introducing the
correlation matrix, we further conclude that the rescaling transformation is
crucial to identify the multi-scale community structure of network, as well as
the translation and rotation transformations.

Stochastic (Markovian) process algebra extend classical process algebra with
probabilistic exponentially distributed time durations denoted by rates (the
parameter of the exponential distribution). Defining a semantics for such an
algebra, so to derive Continuous Time Markov Chains from system specifications,
requires dealing with transitions labeled by rates. With respect to standard
process algebra semantics this poses a problem: we have to take into account
the multiplicity of several identical transitions (with the same rate). Several
techniques addressing this problem have been introduced in the literature, but
they can only be used for semantic definitions that do not exploit a structural
congruence relation on terms while inferring transitions. On the other hand,
using a structural congruence relation is a useful mechanism that is commonly
adopted, for instance, in order to define semantics in reduction style for
non-basic process algebras such as the pi-calculus or richer ones. In this
paper we show how to define semantics for Markovian process algebra when
structural congruence is used while inferring transitions and, as an
application example, we define the reduction semantics for a stochastic version
of the pi-calculus. Moreover we show such semantics to be correct with respect
to the standard one (defined in labeled operational semantics style).

The Earth and other rocky bodies in the inner solar system contain
significantly less carbon than the primordial materials that seeded their
formation. These carbon-poor objects include the parent bodies of primitive
meteorites, suggesting that at least one process responsible for solid-phase
carbon depletion was active prior to the early stages of planet formation.
Potential mechanisms include the erosion of carbonaceous materials by photons
or atomic oxygen in the surface layers of the protoplanetary disk. Under
photochemically generated favorable conditions, these reactions can deplete the
near-surface abundance of carbon grains and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons by
several orders of magnitude on short timescales relative to the lifetime of the
disk out to radii of ~20-100+ au from the central star depending on the form of
refractory carbon present. Due to the reliance of destruction mechanisms on a
high influx of photons, the extent of refractory carbon depletion is quite
sensitive to the disk's internal radiation field. Dust transport within the
disk is required to affect the composition of the midplane. In our current
model of a passive, constant-alpha disk, where alpha = 0.01, carbon grains can
be turbulently lofted into the destructive surface layers and depleted out to
radii of ~3-10 au for 0.1-1 um grains. Smaller grains can be cleared out of the
planet-forming region completely. Destruction may be more effective in an
actively accreting disk or when considering individual grain trajectories in
non-idealized disks.

We studied the pc-scale core shift effect using radio light curves for three
blazars, S5 0716+714, 3C 279 and BL Lacertae, which were monitored at five
frequencies ($\nu$) between 4.8 GHz and 36.8 GHz using the University of
Michigan Radio Astronomical Observatory (UMRAO), the Crimean Astrophysical
Observatory (CrAO), and Metsahovi Radio Observatory for over 40 years. Flares
were Gaussian fitted to derive time delays between observed frequencies for
each flare ($\Delta t$), peak amplitude ($A$), and their half width. Using $A
\propto \nu^{\alpha}$ we infer $\alpha$ in the range $-$16.67 to 2.41 and using
$\Delta t \propto \nu^{1/k_r}$, we infer $k_r \sim 1$, employed in the context
of equipartition between magnetic and kinetic energy density for parameter
estimation. From the estimated core position offset ($\Omega_{r \nu}$) and the
core radius ($r_{\rm core}$), we infer that opacity model may not be valid in
all cases. The mean magnetic field strength at 1 pc ($B_1$) and at the core
($B_{\rm core}$), are in agreement with previous estimates. We apply the
magnetically arrested disk model to estimate black hole spins in the range
$0.15-0.9$ for these blazars, indicating that the model is consistent with
expected accretion mode in such sources. The power law shaped power spectral
density has slopes $-$1.3 to $-$2.3 and is interpreted in terms of multiple
shocks or magnetic instabilities.

Introgressions from Neanderthals and Denisovans were detected in modern
humans. Introgressions from other archaic hominins were also implicated,
however, identification of which poses a great technical challenge. Here, we
introduced an approach in identifying introgressions from all possible archaic
hominins in Eurasian genomes, without referring to archaic hominin sequences.
We focused on mutations emerged in archaic hominins after their divergence from
modern humans (denoted as archaic-specific mutations), and identified
introgressive segments which showed significant enrichment of archaic-specific
mutations over the rest of the genome. Furthermore, boundaries of
introgressions were identified using a dynamic programming approach to
partition whole genome into segments which contained different levels of
archaic-specific mutations. We found that detected introgressions shared more
archaic-specific mutations with Altai Neanderthal than they shared with
Denisovan, and 60.3% of archaic hominin introgressions were from Neanderthals.
Furthermore, we detected more introgressions from two unknown archaic hominins
whom diverged with modern humans approximately 859 and 3,464 thousand years
ago. The latter unknown archaic hominin contributed to the genomes of the
common ancestors of modern humans and Neanderthals. In total, archaic hominin
introgressions comprised 2.4% of Eurasian genomes. Above results suggested a
complex admixture history among hominins. The proposed approach could also
facilitate admixture research across species.

text: The abstract discusses the dynamics involved in directing the edges of connectomes, focusing on the development of neural connections within the human brain. Connectomics, the study of neuronal connections in the brain, has advanced significantly with the advent of high-resolution imaging techniques like diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI). However, interpreting these connectomes remains challenging due to their complex nature and the need for understanding how these connections develop over time.  The objective of this research is to explore the mechanisms underlying the formation of neuronal connections and how these can be represented and analyzed using consensus connectomes. A consensus connectome is an average representation of connectivity patterns across multiple subjects, providing a standardized framework for comparative studies. This research aims to elucidate the temporal dynamics of these connections, identifying patterns that emerge during development and comparing them across different age groups.  To achieve this, we employed computational methods to analyze DSI data from a large cohort of healthy individuals spanning various developmental stages. We utilized graph theoretical approaches to quantify connectivity measures such as degree centrality, clustering coefficient, and modularity. Our methodology also included longitudinal analysis to track changes in connectivity patterns over time.  Key findings indicate that the human brain's connectome undergoes significant reorganization throughout development, particularly in early childhood. These findings suggest that the early establishment of strong connections in specific regions supports later specialization and functional integration. Moreover, our results highlight the importance of considering both static and dynamic aspects of connectomes when studying brain development.  In conclusion, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of how the edges of connectomes are dynamically shaped during brain development, offering valuable insights into the principles governing the organization and evolution of neural networks. Future work will focus on integrating additional data types and exploring the impact of environmental factors on these developmental trajectories.

High energy cosmic neutrino fluxes can be produced inside relativistic jets
under the envelopes of collapsing stars. In the energy range E ~ (0.3 - 1e5)
GeV, flavor conversion of these neutrinos is modified by various matter effects
inside the star and the Earth. We present a comprehensive (both analytic and
numerical) description of the flavor conversion of these neutrinos which
includes: (i) oscillations inside jets, (ii) flavor-to-mass state transitions
in an envelope, (iii) loss of coherence on the way to observer, and (iv)
oscillations of the mass states inside the Earth. We show that conversion has
several new features which are not realized in other objects, in particular
interference effects ("L- and H- wiggles") induced by the adiabaticity
violation. The neutrino-neutrino scattering inside jet and inelastic neutrino
interactions in the envelope may produce some additional features at E > 1e4
GeV. We study dependence of the probabilities and flavor ratios in the
matter-affected region on angles theta13 and theta23, on the CP-phase delta, as
well as on the initial flavor content and density profile of the star. We show
that measurements of the energy dependence of the flavor ratios will, in
principle, allow to determine independently the neutrino and astrophysical
parameters.

text: In this work, we present a novel pumping lemma tailored for non-cooperative self-assembly processes, aimed at elucidating the structural characteristics of complex assembly systems. Our primary objective is to address the limitations of traditional models, which primarily account for cooperative interactions, thereby providing a comprehensive framework applicable to non-cooperative scenarios. We employ combinatorial techniques and formal language theory to establish the lemma, facilitating a deeper understanding of the limitations and capabilities inherent in self-assembling systems.   The results reveal that non-cooperative self-assembly exhibits unique behavior, characterized by the existence of repetitive patterns that can be “pumped” or expanded indefinitely without violating the structural integrity of the assembly. We demonstrate that this lemma not only identifies constraints applicable to various self-assembly configurations but also highlights specific instances where complexity can lead to unpredictable outcomes. Through rigorous mathematical proofs and illustrative examples, we validate the applicability of our lemma in multiple contexts, such as DNA origami and colloidal assembly processes.   Our findings contribute significantly to the field of self-assembly, suggesting new avenues for research into non-cooperative interactions and their implications for material design. The insights gained from this study have far-reaching implications, paving the way for the development of more robust self-assembling systems that leverage non-cooperative dynamics. Ultimately, our work lays a critical foundation for further exploration into the complexities of self-assembly, encouraging a reevaluation of the principles underpinning these fascinating processes.

We present a large suite of simulations of the formation of low-mass star
clusters. Our simulations include an extensive set of physical processes --
magnetohydrodynamics, radiative transfer, and protostellar outflows -- and span
a wide range of virial parameters and magnetic field strengths. Comparing the
outcomes of our simulations to observations, we find that simulations remaining
close to virial balance throughout their history produce star formation
efficiencies and initial mass function (IMF) peaks that are stable in time and
in reasonable agreement with observations. Our results indicate that
small-scale dissipation effects near the protostellar surface provide a
feedback loop for stabilizing the star formation efficiency. This is true
regardless of whether the balance is maintained by input of energy from large
scale forcing or by strong magnetic fields that inhibit collapse. In contrast,
simulations that leave virial balance and undergo runaway collapse form stars
too efficiently and produce an IMF that becomes increasingly top-heavy with
time. In all cases we find that the competition between magnetic flux advection
toward the protostar and outward advection due to magnetic interchange
instabilities, and the competition between turbulent amplification and
reconnection close to newly-formed protostars renders the local magnetic field
structure insensitive to the strength of the large-scale field, ensuring that
radiation is always more important than magnetic support in setting the
fragmentation scale and thus the IMF peak mass. The statistics of multiple
stellar systems are similarly insensitive to variations in the initial
conditions and generally agree with observations within the range of
statistical uncertainty.

text: We investigated the sticky nature of the chaos/order boundary, a concept fundamental to understanding the interplay between complex systems and their respective states of organization. Through a combination of theoretical modeling and numerical simulations, we aimed to elucidate the dynamics governing the transition from ordered to chaotic behavior. Our results indicate that the chaos/order boundary is characterized by a non-trivial and highly sensitive dependence on initial conditions, rendering it remarkably sticky. This sensitivity is quantified by the Lyapunov exponent, which we found to be significantly elevated in the vicinity of the boundary, indicating an exponentially increasing divergence of nearby trajectories. Furthermore, our simulations revealed that the sticky nature of the boundary is not solely a result of the inherent nonlinearities of the system, but also influenced by the presence of noise and external perturbations. We propose that this sticky boundary arises from the interplay between the system's nonlinear dynamics and the environmental noise, leading to a complex interplay between stability and sensitivity. Our findings have implications for understanding the robustness of complex systems and the role of noise in shaping their behavior, and highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between order and chaos in complex systems.

text: The abstract for the research paper on "Image Reconstruction in Optical Interferometry Benchmarking the Regularization" outlines the study's background, objectives, methodology, key findings, and conclusions.  In optical interferometry, precise image reconstruction from noisy data is essential for resolving intricate astronomical structures. This study benchmarks various regularization techniques to enhance the clarity and accuracy of reconstructed images. The primary objective is to identify the most effective regularization method that minimizes artifacts and maximizes signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in interferometric data.   Methodologically, the research employs both synthetic and real interferometric data sets, applying a range of regularization methods including Tikhonov, Total Variation (TV), and Learned Regularization. These methods are compared based on their performance in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM), and visual quality assessment. The effectiveness of each technique is evaluated under varying levels of noise and different configurations of the interferometer setup.  Key findings indicate that while Tikhonov regularization provides a robust baseline, learned regularization, particularly when trained on specific types of astronomical data, shows superior performance, especially in capturing fine details and reducing noise. The study also highlights the importance of parameter tuning for achieving optimal results with each method.  Conclusively, this research underscores the critical role of regularization techniques in enhancing image quality in optical interferometry. The findings suggest that learned regularization offers promising potential for future applications, particularly in the context of high-resolution imaging of astrophysical sources. Future work will focus on integrating machine learning approaches directly into the image reconstruction process to further improve accuracy and efficiency.

Analytical calculations based on a Landau Level (LL) picture are reported for
a many-electron system moving in an interface (with a finite-width Quantum Well
(QW)) and in the presence of an external perpendicular magnetic field. They
lead to a sequence of previously unnoticed singular features in global
magnetization and magnetic susceptibility that give rise to nontrivial
corrections to the standard de Haas-van Alphen periods. Additional features due
to Zeeman splitting are also reported (such as new energy minima that originate
from the interplay of QW, Zeeman and LL Physics). A corresponding calculation
in a Composite Fermion picture leads to new predictions on magnetic response
properties of a fully-interacting electron liquid in a finite-width interface.
Exact solutions for the energetics of a fully three-dimensional system of many
noninteracting electrons in a magnetic field are also presented (a system
mostly discussed in astrophysical applications), with Hurwitz zeta functions
playing an important role on thermodynamic properties. Finally, exact solutions
for the energetics of an electron gas on a cylindrical surface (and in the
presence of an Aharonov-Bohm flux threading the cylinder) are presented, in two
cases: when the radius R of the cylinder is microscopically small and the
length of the cylinder is macrocopically large (an electron gas nanotube), and
vice versa. Inclusion in the above systems of a radial magnetic field and also
of Zeeman splitting gives rise to curvature-induced spin-orbit coupling, that
leads to interesting behaviors that can also be dealt with analytically. A
corresponding SU(2) formulation and a number of diagonalization results for the
energy of such curved systems have, in the limit of vanishing curvature, the
correct behaviors (namely, the standard spin-Physics in flat space, that is
decoupled from the standard orbital-Physics of Landau Levels).

By constructing scaling relations for galaxies in the massive cluster
MACSJ0717.5 at $z=0.545$ and comparing with those of Coma, we model the
luminosity evolution of the stellar populations and the structural evolution of
the galaxies. We calculate magnitudes, surface brightnesses and effective radii
using HST/ACS images and velocity dispersions using Gemini/GMOS spectra, and
present a catalogue of our measurements for 17 galaxies. We also generate
photometric catalogues for $\sim 3000$ galaxies from the HST imaging. With
these, we construct the colour-magnitude relation, the fundamental plane, the
mass-to-light versus mass relation, the mass-size relation and the
mass-velocity dispersion relation for both clusters. We present a new, coherent
way of modelling these scaling relations simultaneously using a simple physical
model in order to infer the evolution in luminosity, size and velocity
dispersion as a function of redshift, and show that the data can be fully
accounted for with this model. We find that (a) the evolution in size and
velocity dispersion undergone by these galaxies between $z \sim 0.5$ and $z
\sim 0$ is mild, with $R_e(z) \sim (1+z)^{-0.40\pm0.32}$ and $\sigma(z) \sim
(1+z)^{0.09 \pm 0.27}$, and (b) the stellar populations are old, $\sim 10$ Gyr,
with a $\sim 3$ Gyr dispersion in age, and are consistent with evolving purely
passively since $z \sim 0.5$ with $\Delta \log M/L_B = -0.55_{-0.07}^{+0.15}
z$. The implication is that these galaxies formed their stars early and
subsequently grew dissipationlessly so as to have their mass already in place
by $z \sim 0.5$, and suggests a dominant role for dry mergers, which may have
accelerated the growth in these high-density cluster environments.

text: The abstract presents a detailed exploration of the rotational modulation of X-ray emission observed in the close T Tauri binary system V4046 Sgr, which is characterized by accretion shocks. This study focuses on understanding the physical processes that give rise to the X-ray variability within this system.  V4046 Sgr is a binary star system consisting of a low-mass main-sequence star and a young, massive companion. The system exhibits periodic variations in its X-ray emission, which has been attributed to the rotationally modulated accretion shocks. Accretion onto the more massive companion generates shocks that produce X-rays, and these shocks are thought to rotate with the binary orbit.  The research employs high-resolution X-ray observations from various space-based telescopes to analyze the temporal and spectral characteristics of the X-ray emission. By analyzing the light curves and spectra, it was found that the X-ray flux varies periodically with a period corresponding to the binary's orbital period, suggesting a direct link between the binary's rotation and the X-ray variability.  Key findings indicate that the X-ray modulation is driven by the rotation of the accretion shocks, which are aligned with the binary's orbital plane. This alignment results in a periodic enhancement of the X-ray emission as the shocks cross the line of sight towards Earth. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the X-ray spectrum shows distinct features indicative of shock heating and electron acceleration, supporting the hypothesis that the shocks are responsible for the observed variability.  In conclusion, this study provides significant insights into the dynamics of close binary systems and the mechanisms underlying their X-ray emissions. The results underscore the importance of rotational modulation in shaping the X-ray signatures of accreting binaries, offering valuable data for refining theoretical models of stellar evolution and accretion processes.

text: In this study, we investigate whether black holes described by alternative theories, specifically Einstein-Dilaton-Gauss-Bonnet (EDGB) gravity, can be considered serious astrophysical candidates alongside their classical counterparts. Our analysis begins by outlining the EDGB theory's fundamental differences from general relativity, emphasizing its inclusion of a dilaton field and Gauss-Bonnet term, which modify the curvature of spacetime. We then systematically explore the properties of EDGB black holes, focusing on their event horizons, singularity structure, and thermodynamic behavior.  Through numerical simulations and analytical solutions, we demonstrate that EDGB black holes exhibit unique features not present in standard Schwarzschild or Kerr black holes. These include deviations in the event horizon radius, altered singularity structures, and distinct Hawking radiation spectra. Furthermore, we assess these black holes' stability under various perturbations and compare them with observational constraints derived from astrophysical phenomena such as compact objects and gravitational waves.  Our findings suggest that while EDGB black holes are not yet definitively confirmed by current observations, they offer intriguing possibilities that warrant further investigation. This work underscores the importance of testing alternative gravity theories against empirical data to refine our understanding of black hole physics and potentially discover new astrophysical phenomena.

text: In this work, we investigate the structure and properties of z-finite distributions on p-adic groups, which play a central role in the representation theory of p-adic groups and are essential for understanding automorphic forms and local zeta functions. The primary problem addressed is the characterization of these distributions and their applications in the broader context of algebraic and number theory. Our key contribution involves the development of a novel framework that exploits the strong symmetries and compact open subgroups characteristic of p-adic groups. By employing this framework, we have successfully delineated the conditions under which distributions are finitely supported, providing insight into their support and continuity properties. Methodologically, we employ harmonic analysis over locally compact groups, along with intricate algebraic techniques, to derive our main results. This approach allows us to explicitly compute examples of z-finite distributions and explicate their behavior under various group actions. Our findings offer new methods for classifying admissible representations and understanding their moduli, significantly impacting the understanding of p-adic representation theory. We also discuss the implications of our results for future work, particularly in the context of the Langlands program. This work not only broadens the mathematical understanding of p-adic distribution theory but also lays the groundwork for subsequent studies in number theory and arithmetic geometry, potentially extending the application of z-finite distributions to broader mathematical problems.

Spectroscopic analysis of these candidates revealed a range of X-ray emission mechanisms, including coronal heating, magnetically driven winds, and shock-heating. We present ALMA observations of the largest protoplanetary disk in the Orion
Nebula, 114-426. Detectable 345 GHz (856 micron) dust continuum is produced
only in the 350 AU central region of the ~1000 AU diameter silhouette seen
against the bright H-alpha background in HST images. Assuming optically thin
dust emission at 345 GHz, a gas-to-dust ratio of 100, and a grain temperature
of 20 K, the disk gas-mass is estimated to be 3.1 +/- 0.6 Jupiter masses. If
most solids and ices have have been incorporated into large grains, however,
this value is a lower limit. The disk is not detected in dense-gas tracers such

114-426 disk is evolved and depleted in some light organic compounds found in
molecular clouds. The CO J=3-2 line is seen in absorption against the bright 50
to 80 K background of the Orion A molecular cloud over the full spatial extent
and a little beyond the dust continuum emission. The CO absorption reaches a
depth of 27 K below the background CO emission at VLSR ~6.7 km/s about 0.52
arcseconds (210 AU) northeast and 12 K below the background CO emission at VLSR
~ 9.7 km/s about 0.34 arcseconds (140 AU) southwest of the suspected location
of the central star, implying that the embedded star has a mass less than 1
Solar mass .

text: In this study, we investigate the transformation of a set of distinct parts into a cohesive indivisible whole, focusing on operations conducted in an open comparative mode. Through a series of empirical experiments, we apply a systematic methodology that encompasses both qualitative and quantitative analysis. Our approach includes the establishment of comparative frameworks that facilitate the evaluation of the interrelationships and interactions among the parts.   We present significant findings that highlight the efficacy of collaborative operations in fostering integrative dynamics, enhancing overall functionality, and producing emergent properties not present in isolated parts. Our results demonstrate that engaging in open assessment modes allows for a broader perspective on potential synergies, leading to more innovative solutions and greater adaptability in the integration process.   Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for various fields, including systems theory, organizational behavior, and interdisciplinary research. We argue that our methodology not only addresses the challenges of assembling varied components but also offers insights into fostering environments conducive to collaboration and innovation. This work advances the discourse on integration processes by elucidating the critical role of comparative operations, which ultimately enable the transition from a fragmented ensemble to a unified structure. Our results contribute to theoretical frameworks and practical applications aimed at optimizing integration strategies in complex systems.

Lattice models are useful for understanding behaviors of interacting complex
many-body systems. The lattice dimer model has been proposed to study the
adsorption of diatomic molecules on a substrate. Here we analyze the partition
function of the dimer model on an $2 M \times 2 N$ checkerboard lattice wrapped
on a torus and derive the exact asymptotic expansion of the logarithm of the
partition function. We find that the internal energy at the critical point is
equal to zero. We also derive the exact finite-size corrections for the free
energy, the internal energy, and the specific heat. Using the exact partition
function and finite-size corrections for the dimer model on finite checkerboard
lattice we obtain finite-size scaling functions for the free energy, the
internal energy, and the specific heat of the dimer model. We investigate the
properties of the specific heat near the critical point and find that
specific-heat pseudocritical point coincides with the critical point of the
thermodynamic limit, which means that the specific-heat shift exponent
$\lambda$ is equal to $\infty$. We have also considered the limit $N \to
\infty$ for which we obtain the expansion of the free energy for the dimer
model on the infinitely long cylinder. From a finite-size analysis we have
found that two conformal field theories with the central charges $c = 1$ for
the height function description and $c = -2$ for the construction using a
mapping of spanning trees can be used to describe the dimer model on the
checkerboard lattice.

text: In this extensive numerical survey, we explore the intricate relationship between outflow dynamics and the magnetization of accretion disks. We employ a suite of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations to investigate how variations in magnetic field strength influence the structure and behavior of stellar winds and jets emanating from the vicinity of supermassive black holes. Our methodology involves varying parameters such as disk temperature, viscosity, and magnetic field intensity while maintaining consistent boundary conditions. The results indicate that higher levels of magnetization lead to more efficient conversion of rotational energy into kinetic energy, thereby enhancing the outflow's velocity and momentum. Additionally, we observe a transition from collimated jet-like structures to broader, more diffuse outflows as the disk magnetization increases. Key findings suggest that the observed outflow morphology is not solely determined by gravitational forces but also significantly influenced by the underlying magnetic field configuration. This work highlights the critical role of magnetization in shaping the energetics and dynamics of galactic nuclei.

text: In the context of distributed coded computing systems, the challenge of exploiting the stragglers, i.e., nodes that take significantly longer time to compute and transmit their shares, has been an open research question. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm for straggler mitigation, named Early Stopped Adaptive Regenerating Codes (ESARC), which combines adaptive coding with early stopping techniques to efficiently harness the contributions of stragglers. By leveraging the inherent redundancy in coded computing, ESARC progressively adapts to stragglers and enables early decoding of the computation results.  ESARC exploits the observation that the computation time of a node follows a heavy-tailed distribution. We design a coding scheme based on a novel variant of the Reed-Solomon codes, termed early stopping Reed-Solomon codes, which enable the early decoding of the computation results even when stragglers are present. The coding scheme is adaptive, enabling the encoding of new nodes as they join the computation and the removal of departing nodes. ESARC also includes a dynamic error correction mechanism to enable the robust decoding of computation results in the presence of stragglers.  We evaluate ESARC through extensive simulations and compare it with several state-of-the-art methods for straggler mitigation. The results demonstrate that ESARC outperforms these methods in terms of the completion time, achievable throughput, and error correction capabilities. Specifically, our experiments show that ESARC achieves a 61% reduction in completion time, an 87% increase in achievable throughput, and a 21% improvement in error correction capabilities compared to the best-performing method in our simulations. The proposed ESARC algorithm provides a significant step towards efficient exploitation of stragglers in distributed coded computing systems.

text: We investigate the phenomenon of hot-Jupiter inflation caused by deep energy deposition mechanisms within these exoplanets. Our work specifically addresses the persistent issue of reconciling the observed radii of hot Jupiters with current theoretical models, which often underpredict their sizes due to inadequate consideration of energy sources. We utilize a combination of numerical simulations and theoretical frameworks to model the effects of intense irradiation from their host stars, as well as the potential influence of deep internal heating processes, such as tidal interactions and core differentiation. Through our analysis, we identify a significant correlation between the depth of energy deposition and the resultant atmospheric expansion, providing a clearer understanding of the thermal dynamics at play. Our results reveal that when considering deep energy deposition, the inflated radii of hot Jupiters can be adequately explained, aligning theoretical predictions with observational data. Additionally, we explore the implications of these findings on the atmospheric composition and stability of hot Jupiters, suggesting that such inflated states may affect their capacity to retain volatile elements. Ultimately, this work enhances the understanding of the energy transfer mechanisms in gas giants and prompts a re-evaluation of current models regarding planetary formation and evolution. Our findings underscore the necessity of integrating deep energy deposition into future studies of hot Jupiters, offering new pathways for research into exoplanetary atmospheres and their climatic conditions.

A major open question in the study of synchronization of coupled oscillators
is to find necessary and sufficient condition for a system to synchronize on a
given family of graphs. This is a difficult question that requires to
understand exactly how the nonlienar interaction between local entities evolves
over the underlying graph. Another open question is to obtain bounds on the
time complexity of synchronization, which has important practical implications
in clock synchronization algorithms. We address these questions for
one-parameter family of discrete pulse-coupled inhibitory oscillatorscalled the
$\kappa$-color firefly cellular automata (FCA). Namely, we show that for
$\kappa\le 6$, recurrence of each oscillator is a necessary and sufficient
condition for synchronization on finite trees, while for $\kappa \ge 7$ this
condition is only necessary. As a corollary, we show that any non-synchronizing
dynamics for $\kappa\le 6$ on trees decompose into synchronized subtrees
partitioned by `dead' oscillators. Furthermore, on trees with diameter $d$ and
maximum degree at most $\kappa$, we show that the worst-case number of
iterations until synchronization is of order $O(\kappa d)$ for $\kappa\in
\{3,4,5\}$, $O(\kappa d^{2})$ for $\kappa=6$, and infinity for $\kappa \ge 7$.
Lastly, we report simulation results of FCA on lattices and conjecture that on
a finite square lattice, arbitrary initial configuration is synchronized under
$\kappa$-color FCA if and only if $\kappa=4$.

text: In recent years, sensitivity analysis has become an increasingly popular tool in various fields of research. However, the growing volume of published sensitivity analyses raises concerns about their accuracy and reliability. To address this issue, we conducted a systematic review of sensitivity analysis practices in peer-reviewed literature. Our sample consisted of 100 randomly selected studies published between 2010 and 2020 in diverse scientific disciplines. We identified several key problems in sensitivity analysis practices. First, inadequate justification of the choice of sensitivity analysis methods and assumptions was found in 60% of the studies. Second, inconsistency in the reporting of sensitivity analysis results, including unclear presentation of the data and lack of standardized methods, was a common issue in 70% of the studies. Third, a significant number of studies (40%) did not thoroughly investigate the uncertainty associated with their models, leading to potential inaccuracies and false conclusions. Our findings underscore the need for greater transparency and standardization in sensitivity analysis reporting. To improve the accuracy and reliability of sensitivity analyses, we recommend the following best practices clearly stating the rationale and assumptions behind the choice of sensitivity analysis methods, using standardized methods and reporting guidelines, and thoroughly investigating the uncertainty associated with models. Additionally, we encourage researchers to consult relevant literature and engage in interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the validity and applicability of sensitivity analysis methods. In conclusion, our systematic review highlights the importance of addressing the methodological and reporting issues in sensitivity analysis practices. By implementing best practices and promoting standardization, we can enhance the accuracy and reliability of sensitivity analyses and increase confidence in their results.

Due to rapid advances in multielectrode recording technology, the local field
potential (LFP) has again become a popular measure of neuronal activity in both
basic research and clinical applications. Proper understanding of the LFP
requires detailed mathematical modeling incorporating the anatomical and
electrophysiological features of neurons near the recording electrode, as well
as synaptic inputs from the entire network. Here we propose a hybrid modeling
scheme combining the efficiency of commonly used simplified point-neuron
network models with the biophysical principles underlying LFP generation by
real neurons. The scheme can be used with an arbitrary number of point-neuron
network populations. The LFP predictions rely on populations of
network-equivalent, anatomically reconstructed multicompartment neuron models
with layer-specific synaptic connectivity. The present scheme allows for a full
separation of the network dynamics simulation and LFP generation. For
illustration, we apply the scheme to a full-scale cortical network model for a
$\sim$1 mm$^2$ patch of primary visual cortex and predict laminar LFPs for
different network states, assess the relative LFP contribution from different
laminar populations, and investigate the role of synaptic input correlations
and neuron density on the LFP. The generic nature of the hybrid scheme and its
publicly available implementation in \texttt{hybridLFPy} form the basis for LFP
predictions from other point-neuron network models, as well as extensions of
the current application to larger circuitry and additional biological detail.

text: In this study, we investigate the resonant post-Newtonian excitation of eccentricities in hierarchical three-body systems, focusing on the effects of the third body on the motion of a central binary pair. We employ the Euler-Maclaurin formula to analytically calculate the third-body contribution to the resonant forces at leading order in the post-Newtonian expansion. Our findings reveal that the presence of the third body leads to the excitation of eccentricities in the central binary, even when the third body is relatively far from the binary. These results extend previous work on resonant eccentricity excitation in hierarchical three-body systems, which primarily focused on the case where the third body orbits in a mean-motion resonance with one of the binary components. We also examine the role of various parameters, including mass ratios, eccentricities, and initial relative orientations, in determining the strength and direction of resonant forces. Our analytical calculations are supported by numerical integrations of the gravitational N-body equations, providing confirmation of the predicted excitation effects. Our results contribute to a better understanding of the dynamics of hierarchical three-body systems and have implications for the study of systems in astrophysics, such as planetary systems and binary star systems.

Tor provides anonymity online by routing traffic through encrypted tunnels,
called circuits, over paths of anonymizing relays. To enable users to connect
to their selected destination servers without waiting for the circuit to be
build, the Tor client maintains a few circuits at all times. Nevertheless, Tor
is slower to use than directly connecting to the destination server. In this
paper, we propose to have the Tor client measure the performance of the
pre-built circuits and select the fastest circuits for users to send their
traffic over. To this end, we define and evaluate nine metrics for selecting
which pre-built circuit to use based on different combinations of circuit
length, Round Trip Time (RTT), and congestion. We also explore the effect on
performance of the number of pre-built circuits at the time of the selection.
Through whole-network experiments in Shadow, we show that using circuit RTT
with at least three pre-built circuits allows the Tor client to identify fast
circuits and improves median time to first byte (TTFB) by 22% over Tor and 15%
over congestion-aware routing, the state-of-the-art in Tor circuit selection.
We evaluate the security of the proposed circuit selection mechanism against
both a relay-level and a network-level adversary and find no loss of security
compared with Tor.

text: The Casimir force, a quantum force arising from fluctuations in vacuum electromagnetic fields, has recently attracted significant attention due to its potential applications in various fields, including precision measurements and nanotechnology. This study explores the concept of harnessing the Casimir force to drive an optical chopper for potential applications in optical interference and modulation systems.  The background section of the paper establishes the fundamental principles of the Casimir force and its experimental applications. The objective of this research is to investigate the feasibility of using the Casimir force to drive an optical chopper. To achieve this, we present a theoretical analysis of the Casimir force's interaction with a microfabricated cantilever oscillator, which serves as the optical chopper's base.  Our methodology consists of performing finite-element simulations to model the Casimir force's interaction with the cantilever oscillator under various environmental conditions. We analyze the resulting data to determine the chopper's resonant frequency shifts and its optimal operating conditions.  The key findings reveal that the Casimir force's interaction with the cantilever oscillator can generate significant frequency shifts, enabling precise control and modulation of the optical chopper's operation. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the proposed system can potentially achieve high resolution and low power consumption compared to conventional optical choppers.  In conclusion, this research showcases the potential application of the Casimir force in driving an optical chopper for optical interference and modulation systems. Our findings provide a theoretical foundation for future experimental work to validate and optimize this innovative approach to optical chopper technology.

Context. Generating a synthetic dataset of meteoroid orbits is a crucial step
in analysing the probabilities of random grouping of meteoroid orbits in
automated meteor shower surveys. Recent works have shown the importance of
choosing a low similarity threshold value of meteoroid orbits, some pointing
out that the recent meteor shower surveys produced false positives due to
similarity thresholds which were too high. On the other hand, the methods of
synthetic meteoroid orbit generation introduce additional biases into the data,
thus making the final decision on an appropriate threshold value uncertain.
  Aims. As a part of the ongoing effort to determine the nature of meteor
showers and improve automated methods, it was decided to tackle the problem of
synthetic meteoroid orbit generation, the main goal being to reproduce the
underlying structure and the statistics of the observed data in the synthetic
orbits.
  Methods. A new method of generating synthetic meteoroid orbits using the
Kernel Density Estimation method is presented. Several types of approaches are
recommended, depending on whether one strives to preserve the data structure,
the data statistics or to have a compromise between the two.
  Results. The improvements over the existing methods of synthetic orbit
generation are demonstrated. The comparison between the previous and newly
developed methods are given, as well as the visualization tools one can use to
estimate the influence of different input parameters on the final data.

We report observations of the high (R$\sim$18000) and medium (R$\sim$5900)
resolution, near-infrared spectra of Jupiter's polar regions with the GNIRS
instrument at the Gemini North telescope. The observations correspond to the
area of main auroral oval in the South and the main spot of the Io footprint in
the North. We detected and assigned 18 emission lines of the H$_{3}^{+}$,
2$\nu_{2}\rightarrow 0$ overtone band in the region from 4800 to 4980 cm$^{-1}$
and 5 additional lines in the extended low-resolution spectrum. We use our new
modelling scheme, ATMOF to remove telluric absorption bands of CO$_2$ that
feature strongly in the 2 $\mu$m region. The H${_2}$ 1-0 S(1), S(2) and S(3)
emission lines are also detected in the observed spectral region. We found the
rotational temperature and column density of H$_{3}^{+}$ emission at the peak
intensity for both northern and southern auroral regions to be the same within
the measurement errors (T$_{rot} \sim950$K and N(H$_{3}^{+}$) $\sim$
4.5$\times10^{16}$m$^{-2}$). The estimates of T$_{rot}$ from H$_{2}$ are
consistent within much higher uncertainties with temperatures derived from
H$_{3}^{+}$ emissions. We derived the profiles of the H$_{3}^{+}$ emissivity
and ion density for both auroral regions providing the first such measurement
for the emission associated with the main spot of the Io footprint. We also
found a number of weaker lines in the high-resolution spectra that could be
associated with emission from high excitation levels in neutral iron, which
could be deposited in Jupiter's atmosphere as a result of meteor ablation.

Multipartite nonlocality is of great fundamental interest and constitutes a
useful resource for many quantum information protocols. However, demonstrating
it in practice, by violating a Bell inequality, can be difficult. In
particular, standard experimental setups require the alignment of distant
parties' reference frames, which can be challenging or impossible in practice.
In this work we study the violation of certain Bell inequalities, namely the
Mermin, Mermin-Klyshko and Svetlichny inequalities, without shared reference
frames, when parties share a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state.
Furthermore, we analyse how these violations demonstrate genuine multipartite
features of entanglement and nonlocality. For 3, 4 and 5 parties, we show that
it is possible to violate these inequalities with high probability, when the
parties choose their measurements from the three Pauli operators, defined only
with respect to their local frames. Moreover, the probability of violation, and
the amount of violation, are increased when each party chooses their
measurements from the four operators describing the vertices of a tetrahedron.
We also consider how many randomly chosen measurement directions are needed to
violate the Bell inequalities with high probability. We see that the obtained
levels of violation are sufficient to also demonstrate genuine multipartite
entanglement and nonseparability. Finally, we show analytically that choosing
from two measurement settings per party is sufficient to demonstrate the
maximum degree of genuine multipartite entanglement and nonseparability with
certainty when the parties' reference frames are aligned in one direction so
that they differ only in rotations around one axis.
