We present a systematic study of the properties of TiN films by varying the
deposition conditions in an ultra-high-vacuum reactive magnetron sputtering
chamber. By increasing the deposition pressure from 2 to 9 mTorr while keeping
a nearly stoichiometric composition of Ti(1-x)N(x) (x=0.5), the film
resistivity increases, the dominant crystal orientation changes from (100) to
(111), grain boundaries become clearer, and the strong compressive strain
changes to weak tensile strain. The TiN films absorb a high concentration of
contaminants including hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen when they are exposed to
air after deposition. With the target-substrate distance set to 88 mm the
contaminant levels increase from ~0.1% to ~10% as the pressure is increased
from 2 to 9 mTorr. The contaminant concentrations also correlate with in-plane
distance from the center of the substrate and increase by roughly two orders of
magnitude as the target-substrate distance is increased from 88 mm to 266 mm.
These contaminants are found to strongly influence the properties of TiN films.
For instance, the resistivity of stoichiometric films increases by around a
factor of 5 as the oxygen content increases from 0.1% to 11%. These results
suggest that the sputtered TiN particle energy is critical in determining the
TiN film properties, and that it is important to control this energy to obtain
high-quality TiN films. Superconducting coplanar waveguide resonators made from
a series of nearly stoichiometric films grown at pressures from 2 mTorr to 7
mTorr show an increase in intrinsic quality factor from ~10^4 to ~10^6 as the
magnitude of the compressive strain decreases from nearly 3800 MPa to
approximately 150 MPa and the oxygen content increases from 0.1% to 8%. The
films with a higher oxygen content exhibit lower loss, but the nonuniformity of
the oxygen incorporation hinders the use of sputtered TiN in larger circuits.

text: In recent years, the demand for decentralized applications has surged, prompting the exploration of innovative protocols that enhance transparency and security. This paper introduces Gruut, a fully-decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) public ledger designed to address the limitations of traditional blockchain technologies. The objective of this study is to evaluate Gruut's architecture, emphasizing its novel consensus mechanism, scalability, and energy efficiency. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, we conducted a comprehensive analysis through simulation studies and real-world applications to assess network performance, transaction throughput, and security resilience. Key findings indicate that Gruut significantly improves on existing solutions by achieving a transaction processing speed three times faster than conventional blockchains while maintaining a low energy footprint. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that Gruut's decentralized structure mitigates the risk of centralization and fosters enhanced user participation, leading to a more robust ecosystem. The research concludes that Gruut not only presents a viable alternative to current ledger technologies but also contributes to the broader discourse on decentralized systems by providing a scalable and efficient framework that can support a wide range of applications. The implications of this work suggest potential pathways for future research and development in the field of decentralized finance and beyond, advocating for a transition to more sustainable digital infrastructures.

In a bi-directional relay channel, two nodes wish to exchange independent
messages over a shared wireless half-duplex channel with the help of relays.
Recent work has considered information theoretic limits of the bi-directional
relay channel with a single relay. In this work we consider bi-directional
relaying with multiple relays. We derive achievable rate regions and outer
bounds for half-duplex protocols with multiple decode and forward relays and
compare these to the same protocols with amplify and forward relays in an
additive white Gaussian noise channel. We consider three novel classes of
half-duplex protocols: the (m,2) 2 phase protocol with m relays, the (m,3) 3
phase protocol with m relays, and general (m, t) Multiple Hops and Multiple
Relays (MHMR) protocols, where m is the total number of relays and 3<t< m+3 is
the number of temporal phases in the protocol. The (m,2) and (m,3) protocols
extend previous bi-directional relaying protocols for a single m=1 relay, while
the new (m,t) protocol efficiently combines multi-hop routing with
message-level network coding. Finally, we provide a comprehensive treatment of
the MHMR protocols with decode and forward relaying and amplify and forward
relaying in the Gaussian noise, obtaining their respective achievable rate
regions, outer bounds and relative performance under different SNRs and relay
geometries, including an analytical comparison on the protocols at low and high
SNR.

text: The origins of de novo genes, which are genes that arise from mutations rather than being inherited from ancestral species, have long been a topic of debate in the scientific community. Recent studies have shed light on the evolutionary history of de novo genes in humans and chimpanzees, revealing intriguing insights into the mechanisms of gene creation and function.    De novo genes, which account for approximately 10-20% of the human genome, are thought to have emerged in response to various selective pressures, such as adaptation to new environments or the evolution of new traits. However, the exact origins and functions of these genes remain poorly understood.    This study aimed to investigate the origins of de novo genes in humans and chimpanzees using a combination of comparative genomics and phylogenetic analysis.    We analyzed the genomes of humans and chimpanzees using a novel approach that integrated de novo gene identification with phylogenetic tree reconstruction. Our results revealed a significant increase in de novo gene density in the human genome compared to chimpanzees, suggesting that de novo gene creation may have played a more significant role in human evolution.   Key findings Our study identified a group of de novo genes that are uniquely present in the human genome and are involved in various biological processes, including metabolism and immune response. We also found that these genes are more likely to be under positive selection, suggesting that they have been subject to adaptive evolution.    Our findings provide new insights into the origins of de novo genes in humans and chimpanzees, highlighting their potential role in shaping human evolution and biology. The identification of these genes also underscores the importance of considering de novo genes in the study of human disease and evolution.

text: This study investigates the efficiency of cache-aided interference management in partially connected linear networks. Partially connected linear networks are ubiquitous in wireless communication systems, where nodes are arranged in a linear fashion but some nodes are connected to each other. The objective of this research is to analyze the impact of cache-aided interference management on the performance of these networks, particularly in terms of interference reduction and network throughput.  A simulation-based approach is employed to model and analyze the performance of partially connected linear networks. A cache-aided interference management system is designed to store and manage interference information, enabling nodes to make informed decisions about transmission scheduling and power allocation. The simulation results show that the cache-aided interference management system can significantly reduce interference levels in partially connected linear networks, resulting in improved network throughput and reliability.  Key findings include a decrease in interference levels of up to 30% and a corresponding increase in network throughput of up to 25%. The results also indicate that the cache-aided interference management system can adapt to changing network conditions, such as node mobility and channel variations. The study demonstrates the potential of cache-aided interference management to improve the performance of partially connected linear networks in various wireless communication scenarios.  Overall, the findings of this research have important implications for the design and optimization of wireless communication systems, particularly in environments where interference is a significant challenge. The results suggest that cache-aided interference management can be an effective solution for improving network performance in partially connected linear networks.

text: Galaxy formation theories can be broadly classified into dissipational and dissipationless models. Dissipational models suggest galaxies form from a collapsing gas cloud through a dissipative process, leading to the formation of a rotating disk with a high baryonic matter content. Dissipationless models, on the other hand, propose the assembly of galaxies through the mergers of dark matter halos without significant baryonic matter infall.  This study investigates the implication of these two contrasting galaxy formation scenarios on the dark matter content of galaxies. Using numerical simulations, we compare the dark matter content of galaxies formed through dissipational processes versus those formed through dissipationless mergers. Our results suggest that galaxies formed via dissipational processes possess a higher central dark matter content compared to their dissipationless counterparts. This difference can be attributed to the efficient transfer of angular momentum during the dissipative collapse of gas, which limits the central dark matter concentration.  Conversely, dissipationless galaxies show a less concentrated dark matter distribution, with a larger fraction of their total dark matter content residing in their outer regions. These findings suggest that the observed diversity in dark matter content among galaxies might be explained by the differences between dissipational and dissipationless formation mechanisms.  In summary, this study reveals the significant role of dissipative processes in shaping the dark matter content of galaxies, with implications for the understanding of the fundamental nature of galaxies and their relation to the enigmatic dark matter component.

text:
The zodiacal cloud is a thick circumsolar disk of small debris particles
produced by asteroid collisions and comets. Here, we present a zodiacal cloud
model based on the orbital properties and lifetimes of comets and asteroids,
and on the dynamical evolution of dust after ejection. The model is
quantitatively constrained by IRAS observations of thermal emission, but also
qualitatively consistent with other zodiacal cloud observations. We find that
85-95% of the observed mid-infrared emission is produced by particles from the
Jupiter-family comets (JFCs) and $<$10% by dust from long period comets.
Asteroidal dust is found to be present at $<$10%. We suggest that spontaneous
disruptions of JFCs, rather than the usual cometary activity driven by
sublimating volatiles, is the main mechanism that librates cometary particles
into the zodiacal cloud. Our results imply that JFC particles represent
$\sim$85% of the total mass influx at Earth. Since their atmospheric entry
speeds are typically low ($\approx$14.5 km s$^{-1}$ mean for D=100-200 $\mu$m
with $\approx$12 km s$^{-1}$ being the most common case), many JFC grains
should survive frictional heating and land on the Earth's surface. This
explains why most micrometeorites collected in antarctic ice have primitive
carbonaceous composition. The present mass of the inner zodiacal cloud at $<$5
AU is estimated to be 1-$2\times10^{19}$ g, mainly in D=100-200 $\mu$m
particles. The inner zodiacal cloud should have been $>10^4$ times brighter
during the Late Heavy Bombardment (LHB) epoch $\approx$3.8 Gyr ago, when the
outer planets scattered numerous comets into the inner solar system. The bright
debris disks with a large 24-$\mu$m excess observed around mature stars may be
an indication of massive cometary populations existing in those systems.

text: In this study, we explore the thermal conductivity of boron nitride (BN) nanostructures, including hexagonal boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs) and boron nitride nanosheets (BNNSs). Boron nitride is a promising material for thermal management applications due to its high thermal conductivity, thermal stability, and electrical insulation properties. However, the thermal conductivity of BN nanostructures varies significantly depending on their morphology and size. To investigate the thermal conductivity of BNNTs and BNNSs, we employed the thermal diffusion method and the 3ω technique. The thermal diffusivity and specific heat capacity were measured for both nanostructures, and thermal conductivity was calculated using these values. The results revealed that the thermal conductivity of BNNTs was 80-110 Wm-1K-1, which is higher than that of graphite (50-60 Wm-1K-1), making them attractive for high-thermal conductivity applications. On the other hand, the thermal conductivity of BNNSs was found to be 10-35 Wm-1K-1, which is lower than that of BNNTs, but still superior to most commonly used insulating materials. Our findings demonstrate that BN nanostructures can be used as high-performance thermal conductors and insulators depending on their morphology and size. These results could be helpful in designing and optimizing thermal management systems for various applications, such as electronics, energy storage, and aerospace industries.

text: In this study, we investigate finite-size corrections and scaling properties for the dimer model on the checkerboard lattice. Our research addresses the challenge of accurately modeling the behavior of dimers on a lattice with specific constraints in systems of varying sizes. By employing Monte Carlo simulations and finite-size scaling analysis, we quantitatively characterize the finite-size effects on the dimer model and elucidate the scaling behavior. Our results reveal significant finite-size corrections to the thermodynamic limit predictions, shedding light on the system's behavior as the lattice size varies. Through rigorous numerical computations and statistical analysis, we establish the scaling relations governing the dimer model on the checkerboard lattice and provide insights into the system's critical properties. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the dimer model's behavior on complex lattices and offer valuable implications for diverse physical systems exhibiting similar characteristics. This study enhances our comprehension of finite-size effects in lattice models and provides a framework for analyzing scaling properties in systems governed by specific constraints.

text:
Many time-dependent deformation processes at elevated temperatures produce
significant concurrent microstructure changes that can alter the mechanical
properties in a profound manner. Such microstructure evolution is usually
absent in mesoscale deformation models and simulations. Here we present an
integrated full-field modeling scheme that couples the mechanical response with
the underlying microstructure evolution. As a first demonstration, we integrate
a fast Fourier transform-based elasto-viscoplastic (FFT-EVP) model with a
phase-field (PF) recrystallization model, and carry out three-dimensional (3D)
simulations of dynamic recrystallization (DRX) in polycrystalline copper. A
physics-based coupling between FFT-EVP and PF is achieved by (1) adopting a
dislocation-based constitutive model in FFT-EVP, which allows the predicted
dislocation density distribution to be converted to a stored energy
distribution and passed to PF, and (2) implementing a stochastic nucleation
model for DRX. Calibrated with the experimental DRX stress-strain curves, the
integrated model is able to deliver full-field mechanical and microstructural
information, from which quantitative description and analysis of DRX can be
achieved. It is suggested that the initiation of DRX occurs significantly
earlier than previous predictions, due to heterogeneous deformation. DRX grains
are revealed to form at both grain boundaries and junctions (e.g., quadruple
junctions) and tend to maintain a triple line with old grains during the
growth. The resulted stress redistribution is found to have a profound
influence on the subsequent dislocation evolution and the softening.

text: In this study, we investigate the symmetry-induced interference effects in metalloporphyrin wire systems, focusing on their potential in nanoelectronics applications. Our research delineates a quantitative analysis of electronic transmission through metalloporphyrin molecular wires, revealing the pivotal role of symmetry. Using a combination of density functional theory (DFT) and non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) techniques, we systematically explore the consequences of variations in the symmetry of the porphyrin core and peripheral substitutions on electronic transport properties. Our results highlight that the electronic transmission properties of these wires are markedly influenced by their symmetry characteristics, which can lead to constructive or destructive interference effects. We find that certain symmetry configurations can significantly enhance conductance by promoting constructive interference, while others suppress it through destructive interference patterns. This discovery underscores the importance of architectural symmetry in designing molecular electronic components. We further demonstrate that strategically altering the symmetry of metalloporphyrin wires allows the modulation of charge transport, suggesting an avenue for controlling conductance in molecular wires. These findings solve the critical challenge of achieving controllable electronic properties in molecular electronics through symmetry manipulation. Our methodology provides an essential framework for investigating symmetry-driven phenomena in molecular conductors, offering a robust toolset for exploring the electronic behavior of complex molecular systems. Consequently, this work advances the fundamental understanding of interference effects in molecular wires and opens new pathways for the design of high-performance nanoelectronic devices.
label: machine

text: In this work, we report the first measurement of the charged particle pseudorapidity density at mid-rapidity, $\rho_{ch}$, in proton-proton (pp) collisions at a center-of-mass energy, $\sqrt{s}$, of 900 GeV using the ALICE detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Our analysis focuses on the central region, $| \eta | < 0.8$, and utilizes data collected during 2010 running conditions. To measure the density, we implement a centrality selection based on the multiplicity difference, $\Delta V_0$, between two zero-degree calorimeters. Furthermore, we apply correction techniques to eliminate biases from non-collision background and detector inefficiencies.  Our results reveal an increasing charged particle pseudorapidity density as a function of energy, showing a significant enhancement compared to previous measurements at the Tevatron collider. At $\sqrt{s}$ = 900 GeV, we obtain a value of $\rho_{ch} = 4.32 \pm 0.15$ (stat.) $\pm 0.19$ (sys.) particles per unit rapidity. This measurement supports the QCD predictions for small systems and serves as an important benchmark for future studies involving more complex collisions.  In summary, this study represents the first observation of pp collisions at the LHC energy and marks a significant advancement in understanding the particle production properties at such energies. By providing precise measurements of the charged particle pseudorapidity density, we contribute valuable data to the understanding of the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) formation and help further the development of the LHC collider capabilities.
label: machine

text: This study explores the mechanisms behind attractive and driven interactions within quantum dot systems, focusing on geometric pumping effects. Quantum dots, confined semiconductor structures, exhibit unique electronic properties due to their size-dependent bandgap. The objective of this research was to investigate how geometric constraints influence the dynamics of carriers (electrons and holes) within these structures, particularly through geometric pumping. Geometric pumping involves the manipulation of carrier flow by external geometrical changes, which can be harnessed to drive energy transfer processes.  The methodology employed a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental techniques, including scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), photoluminescence spectroscopy, and quantum mechanical calculations. STM provided direct visualization of quantum dot morphology and carrier distributions, while photoluminescence spectroscopy and quantum mechanical calculations were used to analyze carrier dynamics under various geometrical conditions.  Key findings revealed that geometric modifications significantly affect the carrier transport pathways, leading to observable changes in photoluminescence spectra indicative of altered carrier interactions. Theoretical models elucidated the underlying mechanisms, such as the formation of quantized conductance states and the role of potential barriers in carrier confinement. These results highlight the importance of geometric parameters in controlling the interplay between attractive and driven interactions within quantum dots.  In conclusion, this research underscores the potential of geometrically driven interactions in quantum dots for applications ranging from optoelectronics to quantum information processing. Understanding these mechanisms could lead to more precise control over carrier dynamics, paving the way for innovative device designs.
label: machine

text:
Heterogeneities in environmental conditions often induce corresponding
heterogeneities in the distribution of species. In the extreme case of a
localized patch of increased growth rates, reproducing populations can become
strongly concentrated at the patch despite the entropic tendency for population
to distribute evenly. Several deterministic mathematical models have been used
to characterize the conditions under which localized states can form, and how
they break down due to convective driving forces. Here, we study the
delocalization of a finite population in the presence of number fluctuations.
We find that any finite population delocalizes on sufficiently long time
scales. Depending on parameters, however, populations may remain localized for
a very long time. The typical waiting time to delocalization increases
exponentially with both population size and distance to the critical wind speed
of the deterministic approximation. We augment these simulation results by a
mathematical analysis that treats the reproduction and migration of individuals
as branching random walks subject to global constraints. For a particular
constraint, different from a fixed population size constraint, this model
yields a solvable first moment equation. We find that this solvable model
approximates very well the fixed population size model for large populations,
but starts to deviate as population sizes are small. The analytical approach
allows us to map out a phase diagram of the order parameter as a function of
the two driving parameters, inverse population size and wind speed. Our results
may be used to extend the analysis of delocalization transitions to different
settings, such as the viral quasi-species scenario.
label: human

text: In this study, we investigate the cooling rates of relativistic electrons under Compton scattering in strong magnetic fields. Our primary objective is to understand how the presence of a strong magnetic field influences the cooling dynamics of these particles. We employ a combination of theoretical modeling and numerical simulations to explore various scenarios where the magnetic field strength varies. The results indicate that the cooling rate decreases significantly in the presence of strong magnetic fields due to the enhanced energy transfer mechanisms within the system. Key findings show that electron cooling rates are inversely proportional to the square of the magnetic field strength. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the electron's motion becomes more confined, leading to a reduction in the effective cross-sectional area available for Compton scattering. The methodology involved solving the Boltzmann equation for electron distribution functions, incorporating effects from the Lorentz force and magnetic confinement. These results contribute to our understanding of particle acceleration and cooling processes in astrophysical environments, particularly in magnetized plasmas.

text:
Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) images from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA)
on board the Solar Dynamic Observatory (SDO) are providing new insights into
the early phase of CME evolution. Observations now show the ejection of
magnetic flux ropes from the solar corona and how they evolve into CMEs. These
observations are difficult to interpret in terms of basic physical mechanisms
and quantities. To fully understand CMEs we need to compare equivalent
quantities derived from both observations and theoretical models. To this end
we aim to produce synthesised AIA observations from simluations of a flux rope
ejection. To carry this out we include the role of thermal conduction and
radiative losses, both of which are important for determining the temperature
distribution of the solar corona during a CME. We perform a simulation where a
flux rope is ejected from the solar corona. From the density and temperature of
the plasma in the simulation we synthesise AIA observations. The emission is
then integrated along the line of sight using the instrumental response
function of AIA. We sythesise observations of AIA in the channels at 304 A, 171
A, 335 A, and 94 A. The synthesised observations show a number of features
similar to actual observations and in particular reproduce the general
development of CMEs in the low corona as observed by AIA. In particular we
reproduce an erupting and expanding arcade in the 304 A and 171 A channels with
a high density core. The ejection of a flux rope reproduces many of the
features found in the AIA observations. This work is therefore a step forward
in bridging the gap between observations and models, and can lead to more
direct interpretations of EUV observations in terms of flux rope ejections. We
plan to improve the model in future studies in order to perform a more
quantitative comparison.
label: human

text:
We report the discovery of four Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) in the ongoing
SUrvey for Pulsars and Extragalactic Radio Bursts (SUPERB) at the Parkes Radio
Telescope: FRBs 150610, 151206, 151230 and 160102. Our real-time discoveries
have enabled us to conduct extensive, rapid multi-messenger follow-up at 12
major facilities sensitive to radio, optical, X-ray, gamma-ray photons and
neutrinos on time scales ranging from an hour to a few months post-burst. No
counterparts to the FRBs were found and we provide upper limits on afterglow
luminosities. None of the FRBs were seen to repeat. Formal fits to all FRBs
show hints of scattering while their intrinsic widths are unresolved in time.
FRB 151206 is at low Galactic latitude, FRB 151230 shows a sharp spectral
cutoff, and FRB 160102 has the highest dispersion measure (DM = $2596.1\pm0.3$
pc cm$^{-3}$) detected to date. Three of the FRBs have high dispersion measures
(DM >$1500$ pc cm$^{-3}$), favouring a scenario where the DM is dominated by
contributions from the Intergalactic Medium. The slope of the Parkes FRB source
counts distribution with fluences $>2$ Jyms is $\alpha=-2.2^{+0.6}_{-1.2}$ and
still consistent with a Euclidean distribution ($\alpha=-3/2$). We also find
that the all-sky rate is $1.7^{+1.5}_{-0.9}\times10^3$FRBs/($4\pi$ sr)/day
above $\sim2$ Jyms and there is currently no strong evidence for a
latitude-dependent FRB sky-rate.

text:
In close binary systems composed of a normal, donor star and an accreting
neutron star, the amount of material received by the accreting component is, so
far, a real intrigue. In the literature there are available models that link
the accretion disk surrounding the neutron star with the amount of material it
receives, but there is no model linking the amount of matter lost by the donor
star to that falling onto the neutron star.
  In this paper we explore the evolutionary response of these close binary
systems when we vary the amount of material accreted by the neutron star. We
consider a parameter \beta, which represents the fraction of material lost by
the normal star that can be accreted by the neutron star. \beta is considered
as constant throughout evolution. We have computed the evolution of a set of
models considering initial donor star masses (in solar units) between 0.5 and
3.50, initial orbital periods (in days) between 0.175 and 12, initial masses of
neutron stars (in solar units) of 0.80, 1.00, 1.20 and 1.40 and several values
of beta. We assumed solar abundances. These systems evolve to ultracompact or
to open binary systems, many of which form low mass helium white dwarfs. We
present a grid of calculations and analyze how these results are affected upon
changes in the value of \beta. We find a weak dependence of the final donor
star mass with respect to \beta. In most cases this is also true for the final
orbital period. The most sensitive quantity is the final mass of the accreting
neutron star.
  As we do not know the initial mass and rotation rate of the neutron star of
any system, we find that performing evolutionary studies is not helpful for
determining \beta.
label: human

text: We investigate the quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) observed in the black hole transient XTE J1817-330, a binary system consisting of a compact object and a low-mass companion star. Through a comprehensive analysis of archival X-ray data from the XTE-Newton and RXTE-PCA, we detect a QPO with a frequency of 18.5 Hz and a amplitude of 0.13. This frequency corresponds to a characteristic QPO frequency, which is a hallmark of black hole accretion disks. Our results indicate that the QPO is likely to be a relativistic effect, arising from the innermost stable orbit of the compact object. We employ a combination of theoretical models and numerical simulations to constrain the parameters of the black hole and the accretion disk. Our analysis reveals that the QPO frequency is consistent with a black hole mass of approximately 6.5 solar masses and a spin parameter of 0.75. These findings provide valuable insights into the physics of black hole accretion disks and the properties of compact objects in binary systems. Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of X-ray observations in constraining the parameters of compact objects and testing theoretical models of QPOs.
label: machine

text:
We consider a particular class of equations of motion, generalizing to n
degrees of freedom the "dissipative spin--orbit problem", commonly studied in
Celestial Mechanics. Those equations are formulated in a pseudo-Hamiltonian
framework with action-angle coordinates; they contain a quasi-integrable
conservative part and friction terms, assumed to be linear and isotropic with
respect to the action variables. In such a context, we transfer two methods
determining quasi-periodic solutions, which were originally designed to analyze
purely Hamiltonian quasi-integrable problems.
  First, we show how the frequency map analysis can be adapted to this kind of
dissipative models. Our approach is based on a key remark: the method can work
as usual, by studying the behavior of the angular velocities of the motions as
a function of the so called "external frequencies", instead of the actions.
Moreover, we explicitly implement the Kolmogorov's normalization algorithm for
the dissipative systems considered here. In a previous article, we proved a
theoretical result: such a constructing procedure is convergent under the
hypotheses usually assumed in KAM theory. In the present work, we show that it
can be translated to a code making algebraic manipulations on a computer, so to
calculate effectively quasi-periodic solutions on invariant tori. Both the
methods are carefully tested, by checking that their predictions are in
agreement, in the case of the so called "dissipative forced pendulum".
Furthermore, the results obtained by applying our adaptation of the frequency
analysis method to the dissipative standard map are compared with some existing
ones in the literature.

text: We present a comprehensive study of global simulations of the inner regions of protoplanetary disks, incorporating detailed disk microphysics. Our simulations employed a novel, adaptive, multi-resolution numerical framework, allowing for the seamless integration of sub-grid scale processes, such as grain growth, dust accretion, and magnetic reconnection. By resolving the complex interplay between these processes, we investigated the formation of planetesimals and the subsequent growth of planetary cores in the inner regions of protoplanetary disks.  Our results indicate that the incorporation of comprehensive disk microphysics significantly impacts the formation of planetesimals, with grain growth and dust accretion playing crucial roles in the initial stages of planetary core formation. The simulations also revealed the importance of magnetic reconnection in the inner disk, where it facilitates the efficient transport of angular momentum and influences the formation of planetesimals. Furthermore, our results suggest that the presence of a strong magnetic field in the inner disk can lead to the formation of planetesimals with distinct, magnetically-driven architectures.  The key findings of this study highlight the critical role of comprehensive disk microphysics in understanding the formation of planetary cores in the inner regions of protoplanetary disks. By providing a more detailed and realistic representation of the complex processes involved, our simulations offer new insights into the early stages of planetary formation and have significant implications for our understanding of the origins of our solar system and the formation of exoplanetary systems.
label: machine

text: In this study, we explore the dynamical interactions within galaxy clusters, examining the impact of anisotropic thermal conduction on cold fronts and gas sloshing phenomena. Utilizing high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations integrated with advanced models of anisotropic thermal conduction, we aim to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the thermal and kinetic behavior of intracluster gases. Our results reveal that anisotropic thermal conduction significantly alters the stability and morphology of cold fronts, promoting a more diffusive interface that modifies the thermal gradient. This, in turn, influences the persistence and amplitude of gas sloshing motions. We quantitatively demonstrate that neglecting anisotropic effects leads to deviations in predicted thermal equilibrium states and erroneous estimations of gas cooling timescales. Our methodology involved a comparative analysis between isotropic and anisotropic conduction frameworks, accompanied by a thorough assessment of their respective impacts on thermodynamic variables. In particular, we observed that anisotropic conduction suppresses the thermal insulation of cold fronts, accelerating heat exchange with surrounding hotter intra-cluster medium, which can either mitigate or exacerbate sloshing, depending on cluster-specific conditions such as magnetic field orientation and strength. Furthermore, our results indicate that incorporating anisotropic thermal conduction in simulations affords a more accurate representation of observed cluster phenomena, including surface brightness discontinuities and temperature distribution profiles. This work provides crucial insights into the complex thermal dynamics of galaxy clusters and underscores the necessity of incorporating directional thermal conduction to achieve realistic modeling outcomes. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy cluster evolution and the interpretation of observational data in extragalactic astronomy.
label: machine

text: Dark Matter (DM) is an unobserved substance that is believed to make up approximately 27% of the universe's total mass. One of the leading theories to explain the nature of Dark Matter is the presence of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs). DAMA/LIBRA is an experiment designed to detect WIMP dark matter through its elastic scattering off nuclei in a liquid xenon target.  The objective of this study is to analyze the DAMA/LIBRA data and determine if it provides evidence for the presence of leptonically interacting WIMP dark matter. The experiment's data, spanning over two decades, is analyzed using a Bayesian statistical approach. The results show an excess of events with an annual modulation signal, which is consistent with the signature of WIMP dark matter interacting with xenon nuclei. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that these WIMPs have a mass of around 8.6 GeV/c² and preferentially interact through the leptonic channel.  This finding is significant because it provides the first evidence for leptonically interacting WIMP dark matter. The standard WIMP model assumes that these particles primarily interact through the strong and electromagnetic forces. However, the DAMA/LIBRA results suggest that a sizeable leptonic interaction channel may exist. This discovery could lead to a more comprehensive understanding of the properties of Dark Matter and potentially unify various particle physics theories.  In conclusion, this study provides strong evidence for the presence of leptonically interacting WIMP dark matter based on the DAMA/LIBRA experiment's data analysis. The findings challenge the current understanding of the standard WIMP model and open up new avenues for further research in Dark Matter physics.
label: machine

text:
The dielectric behavior of the single crystals of the spin-chain system
Ca3Co2O6, undergoing geometrically frustrated antiferromagnetic ordering below
25 K, has been investigated as a function of temperature and magnetic field (H)
and compared with magnetization (M) behavior. The results provide evidence for
anisotropic magnetodielectric (MDE) coupling in this compound. Ac
susceptibility exhibits a strong frequency dependence for H parallel c with
changes of this feature with the application of external dc magnetic field. No
feature in ac susceptibility could be observed for H perpendicular c, thereby
providing evidence for strong anisotropic spin-glass behavior. Interestingly,
the strong frequency dependence in dielectric is present for both the
crystallographic directions (E parallel c and E perpendicular c where E is the
electric field) with a negligible influence of H, despite the existence of MDE
coupling. This result appears to suggest different dynamics of electric dipole
and spin-glass, although they are coupled with each other. In addition,
interestingly, there is also a step at one-third of high-(magnetic) field value
of MDE at some temperatures tracking a similar step in M(H). This work also
confirms following unusual features reported on polycrystals, when measured
along c-axis. The dielectric constant exhibits a broad peak around 50-130 K
when the electric field is applied along the spin-chain (crystallographic c
direction); however this feature is essentially absent for the perpendicular
orientation. This finding supports the role of incipient spin-chain ordering to
induce magnetodielectric coupling. There is a signature of magnetoelectric
phase coexistence when the magnetic field is applied along the spin-chain
irrespective of the direction of applied electric field.

text: In this work, we investigate the development and application of free and constrained symplectic integrators for numerical solutions in general relativity, addressing the critical need for preserving the Hamiltonian structure and inherent geometrical properties of spacetime. Traditional numerical methods frequently encounter difficulties in maintaining these properties over long simulations, leading to inaccurate predictions. Our approach leverages symplectic integrators, which are inherently designed to conserve the symplectic structure and integral invariants of Hamiltonian systems, thus offering a robust framework for numerical general relativity.  We present a novel formulation of both free and constrained symplectic integrators, carefully tailored to address the challenges posed by the Einstein field equations. These formulations are rigorously constructed to handle the Hamiltonian constraints intrinsic to general relativity. We apply these integrators to benchmark scenarios, including binary black hole mergers and cosmological models, and demonstrate their superior performance compared to conventional methods.  Our numerical experiments show that our symplectic integrators achieve higher accuracy in the conservation of energy and momentum, as well as the maintenance of constraint surfaces, over extended integration times. The results indicate a significant step forward in the stable, long-term simulation of complex spacetime dynamics, providing a powerful tool for researchers exploring gravitational phenomena. This study not only bridges a crucial gap in computational general relativity but also opens new avenues for future research in the precise modeling of relativistic systems.
label: machine

text:
We present results of new XMM-Newton observations of the ultraluminous X-ray
source (ULX) NGC 5408 X-1, one of the few ULXs to show quasi-periodic
oscillations (QPO). We detect QPOs in each of four new (~ 100 ks) pointings,
expanding the range of frequencies observed from 10 - 40 mHz. We compare our
results with the timing and spectral correlations seen in stellar-mass black
hole systems, and find that the qualitative nature of the timing and spectral
behavior of NGC 5408 X-1 is similar to systems in the steep power-law state
exhibiting Type-C QPOs. However, in order for this analogy to quantitatively
hold we must only be seeing the so-called saturated portion of the QPO
frequency - photon index (or disk flux) relation. Assuming this to be the case,
we place a lower limit on the mass of NGC 5408 X-1 of > 800 solar masses.
Alternatively, the QPO frequency is largely independent of the spectral
parameters, in which case a close analogy with the Type-C QPOs in stellar
systems is problematic. Measurement of the source's timing properties over a
wider range of energy spectral index is needed to definitively resolve this
ambiguity. We searched all the available data for both a broad Fe emission line
as well as high frequency QPO analogs (0.1 - 1 Hz), but detected neither. We
place upper limits on the equivalent width of any Fe emission feature in the 6
- 7 keV band, and of the amplitude (rms) of a high frequency QPO analog of
approximately 10 eV and approximately 4%, respectively.

text: This study investigates the efficacy of operator-like wavelets in representing sparse Autoregressive (AR(1)) processes. Background research indicates that sparse AR(1) models possess a significant advantage over traditional dense models, particularly in terms of data compression and computational efficiency. However, the choice of wavelet basis remains a crucial factor in achieving optimal sparse representation.   The objective of this research is to explore the optimality of operator-like wavelets for representing sparse AR(1) processes. We employ a theoretical framework that combines the properties of wavelet bases with the characteristics of AR(1) models. Our approach involves analyzing the wavelet coefficients of a given AR(1) process and deriving a set of operator-like wavelets that can effectively capture the sparse structure of the signal.  Methodologically, we develop a novel wavelet construction technique that incorporates the AR(1) model's autocorrelation structure into the wavelet basis. Our method, dubbed "AR- wavelet," is designed to selectively amplify the coefficients of the AR(1) process, resulting in a sparse representation that accurately captures the underlying signal.  Key findings indicate that the AR-wavelet exhibits superior sparse representation capabilities compared to traditional wavelets. Our results demonstrate that the AR-wavelet can effectively compress sparse AR(1) signals while preserving their essential characteristics. Moreover, we show that the AR-wavelet can outperform other wavelet-based methods in terms of sparse representation accuracy and computational efficiency.  In conclusion, our research demonstrates the optimality of operator-like wavelets for representing sparse AR(1) processes. The AR-wavelet offers a novel approach to sparse signal representation, which has significant implications for data compression, signal processing, and machine learning applications.
label: machine

text: We investigate the propagation and interaction characteristics of successive coronal mass ejections (CMEs) in the context of a complex Type II radio burst. Our primary aim is to elucidate the underlying mechanisms through which CMEs impact solar radio emissions and to comprehend the implications of such interactions for space weather phenomena. We analyzed a series of CMEs observed during a solar event, utilizing data from the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) and the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) alongside radio observations from the Wind spacecraft.  In our methodological approach, we employed a combination of remote sensing techniques and numerical simulations to trace the trajectory and velocity variations of the CMEs as they interacted with the ambient solar wind and each other. We identified distinct phases of propagation and interaction, characterized by heightened radio emissions corresponding to shocks produced during the CME collisions. Our results reveal a strong correlation between the dynamic behavior of the CMEs and the intensity and frequency characteristics of the Type II bursts, suggesting that multiple CME interactions can significantly amplify radio emissions.  Furthermore, we explore the implications of our findings for predicting space weather scenarios, particularly in assessing the risks associated with CME-induced disturbances in Earth's magnetosphere. Overall, our study provides critical insights into the complex dynamics of CME interactions and their resultant effects on solar radio emissions, advancing our understanding of solar-terrestrial relationships.
label: machine

text:
We investigate the dynamics of drop impacts on dry solid surfaces. By
synchronising high-speed photography with fast force sensing, we simultaneously
measure the temporal evolution of the shape and impact force of impacting drops
over a wide range of Reynolds numbers (Re). At high Re, when inertia dominates
the impact processes, we show that the early-time evolution of impact force
follows a square-root scaling, quantitatively agreeing with a recent
self-similar theory. This observation provides direct experimental evidence on
the existence of upward propagating self-similar pressure fields during the
initial impact of liquid drops at high Re. When viscous forces gradually set in
with decreasing Re, we analyse the early-time scaling of the impact force of
viscous drops using a perturbation method. The analysis quantitatively matches
our experiments and successfully predicts the trends of the maximum impact
force and the associated peak time with decreasing Re. Furthermore, we discuss
the influence of viscoelasticity on the temporal signature of impact forces.
Last but not least, we also investigate the spreading of liquid drops at high
Re following the initial impact. Particularly, we find an exact parameter-free
self-similar solution for the inertia-driven drop spreading, which
quantitatively predicts the height of spreading drops at high Re. The limit of
the self-similar approach for drop spreading is also discussed. As such, our
study provides a quantitative understanding of the temporal evolution of impact
forces across the inertial, viscous and viscoelastic regimes and sheds new
light on the self-similar dynamics of drop impact processes.
label: human

text:
Bornmann, Stefaner, de Moya Anegon, and Mutz (in press) have introduced a web
application (www.excellencemapping.net) which is linked to both academic
ranking lists published hitherto (e.g. the Academic Ranking of World
Universities) as well as spatial visualization approaches. The web application
visualizes institutional performance within specific subject areas as ranking
lists and on custom tile-based maps. The new, substantially enhanced version of
the web application and the multilevel logistic regression on which it is based
are described in this paper. Scopus data were used which have been collected
for the SCImago Institutions Ranking. Only those universities and
research-focused institutions are considered that have published at least 500
articles, reviews and conference papers in the period 2006 to 2010 in a certain
Scopus subject area. In the enhanced version, the effect of single covariates
(such as the per capita GDP of a country in which an institution is located) on
two performance metrics (best paper rate and best journal rate) is examined and
visualized. A covariate-adjusted ranking and mapping of the institutions is
produced in which the single covariates are held constant. The results on the
performance of institutions can then be interpreted as if the institutions all
had the same value (reference point) for the covariate in question. For
example, those institutions can be identified worldwide showing a very good
performance despite a bad financial situation in the corresponding country.

text: Recent studies have shown that outflows driven by quasars play a crucial role in the evolution of high-redshift galaxies. However, the specific mechanisms governing these processes, especially in relation to radiation hydrodynamics, remain unclear. This study aims to investigate the dynamics of these outflows in high-redshift galaxies using radiation hydrodynamics simulations.    We employ state-of-the-art numerical simulations that incorporate radiation hydrodynamics to model the interaction between quasar activity and the surrounding gas in galaxies. By varying parameters such as quasar luminosity and host galaxy properties, we analyze how these factors influence the outflow properties.   Our results demonstrate that radiation feedback significantly impacts the outflow properties, affecting their morphology, velocity, and mass outflow rates. We observe a strong correlation between quasar luminosity and the strength of the outflows, highlighting the intricate interplay between the central quasar and the host galaxy.   In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the role of quasar-driven outflows in shaping high-redshift galaxies, emphasizing the importance of considering radiation hydrodynamics in understanding these processes. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of galaxy evolution mechanisms and have implications for future studies on the impact of active galactic nuclei on their host environments.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the properties of massive and massless higher-spin particles in odd spacetime dimensions. We explore their dynamics within the framework of effective field theories, focusing on how these particles interact and propagate through various scenarios. The primary challenge addressed is the construction of consistent higher-spin theories that are compatible with the symmetries of odd-dimensional spacetimes. Key methodologies employed include the analysis of conserved currents associated with higher-spin charges and the examination of Ward identities to ensure gauge invariance. Results indicate that massless higher-spin fields exhibit unique behaviors compared to their massless counterparts in even dimensions, such as the presence of non-trivial dispersion relations and constraints on the coupling constants. For massive particles, we find that the spin-dependent interactions play a crucial role in determining their stability and propagation characteristics. This work not only advances our understanding of higher-spin physics but also provides insights into the structure of gravity in higher dimensions, particularly focusing on the implications for the theory of gravitons and other massless fields.
label: machine

text:
We present predictions for the galaxy-galaxy lensing profile from the EAGLE
hydrodynamical cosmological simulation at redshift z=0.18, in the spatial range
0.02 < R/(Mpc/h) < 2, and for five logarithmically equi-spaced stellar mass
bins in the range 10.3 < $\log_{10}$(Mstar/ $M_{\odot}$) < 11.8. We compare
these excess surface density profiles to the observed signal from background
galaxies imaged by the Kilo Degree Survey around spectroscopically confirmed
foreground galaxies from the GAMA survey. Exploiting the GAMA galaxy group
catalogue, the profiles of central and satellite galaxies are computed
separately for groups with at least five members to minimise contamination.
EAGLE predictions are in broad agreement with the observed profiles for both
central and satellite galaxies, although the signal is underestimated at
R$\approx$0.5-2 Mpc/h for the highest stellar mass bins. When central and
satellite galaxies are considered simultaneously, agreement is found only when
the selection function of lens galaxies is taken into account in detail.
Specifically, in the case of GAMA galaxies, it is crucial to account for the
variation of the fraction of satellite galaxies in bins of stellar mass induced
by the flux-limited nature of the survey. We report the inferred
stellar-to-halo mass relation and we find good agreement with recent published
results. We note how the precision of the galaxy-galaxy lensing profiles in the
simulation holds the potential to constrain fine-grained aspects of the
galaxy-dark matter connection.
label: human

text:
Background: Nuclear excited states within a wide range of excitation energies
are formally described by the linear response theory. Besides its conventional
formulation within the quasiparticle random phase approximation (QRPA)
representing excited states as two correlated quasiparticles (2q), there exist
extensions for 4q configurations. Such extended approaches are quite successful
in the description of gross properties of nuclear spectra, however, accounting
for many of their fine features requires further extension of the configuration
space. Purpose: This work aims at the development of an approach which is
capable of such an extension as well as of reproducing and predicting fine
spectral properties, which are of special interest at low energies. Method: The
method is based on the covariant density functional theory and time blocking
approximation, which is extended for couplings between quasiparticles and
multiphonon excitations. Results: The covariant multiphonon response theory is
developed and adopted for nuclear structure calculations in medium-mass and
heavy nuclei. The equations are formulated in both general and coupled forms in
the spherical basis. Conclusions: The developed covariant multiphonon response
theory represents a new generation of the approaches to nuclear response, which
aims at a unified description of both high-frequency collective states and
low-energy spectroscopy in medium-mass and heavy nuclei.
label: human

In most (weakly interacting) extensions of the Standard Model the relation
mapping the parameter values onto experimentally measurable quantities can be
computed (with some uncertainties), but the inverse relation is usually not
known. In this paper we demonstrate the ability of artificial neural networks
to find this unknown relation, by determining the unknown parameters of the
constrained minimal supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model (CMSSM) from
quantities that can be measured at the LHC. We expect that the method works
also for many other new physics models. We compare its performance with the
results of a straightforward \chi^2 minimization. We simulate LHC signals at a
center of mass energy of 14 TeV at the hadron level. In this proof-of-concept
study we do not explicitly simulate Standard Model backgrounds, but apply cuts
that have been shown to enhance the signal-to-background ratio. We analyze four
different benchmark points that lie just beyond current lower limits on
superparticle masses, each of which leads to around 1000 events after cuts for
an integrated luminosity of 10 fb^{-1}. We use up to 84 observables, most of
which are counting observables; we do not attempt to directly reconstruct
(differences of) masses from kinematic edges or kinks of distributions. We
nevertheless find that m_0 and m_{1/2} can be determined reliably, with errors
as small as 1% in some cases. With 500 fb^{-1} of data tan\beta as well as A_0
can also be determined quite accurately. For comparable computational effort
the \chi^2 minimization yielded much worse results.
label: human

For a real reductive group G, the center
$\mathfrak{z}(\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g}))$ of the universal enveloping algebra
of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ of G acts on the space of distributions on G.
This action proved to be very useful (see e.g. [HC63, HC65, Sha74, Bar03]).
  Over non-Archimedean local fields, one can replace this action by the action
of the Bernstein center z of G, i.e. the center of the category of smooth
representations. However, this action is not well studied. In this paper we
provide some tools to work with this action and prove the following results.
  1) The wave-front set of any z-finite distribution on G over any point $g\in
G$ lies inside the nilpotent cone of $T_g^*G \cong \mathfrak{g}$.
  2) Let $H_1,H_2 \subset G$ be symmetric subgroups. Consider the space J of
$H_1\times H_2$-invariant distributions on G. We prove that the z-finite
distributions in J form a dense subspace. In fact we prove this result in wider
generality, where the groups $H_i$ are spherical groups of certain type and the
invariance condition is replaced by equivariance. Further we apply those
results to density and regularity of spherical characters.
  The first result can be viewed as a version of Howe's expansion of
characters. The second result can be viewed as a spherical space analog of a
classical theorem on density of characters of admissible representations. It
can also be viewed as a spectral version of Bernstein's localization principle.
  In the Archimedean case, the first result is well-known and the second
remains open.
label: human

In this paper we investigate the performance of periodogram based estimators
of the spectral density matrix of possibly high-dimensional time series. We
suggest and study shrinkage as a remedy against numerical instabilities due to
deteriorating condition numbers of (kernel) smoothed periodogram matrices.
Moreover, shrinking the empirical eigenvalues in the frequency domain towards
one another also improves at the same time the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of
these widely used nonparametric spectral estimators. Compared to some existing
time domain approaches, restricted to i.i.d. data, in the frequency domain it
is necessary to take the size of the smoothing span as "effective or local
sample size" into account. While B\"{o}hm and von Sachs (2007) proposes a
multiple of the identity matrix as optimal shrinkage target in the absence of
knowledge about the multidimensional structure of the data, here we consider
"structural" shrinkage. We assume that the spectral structure of the data is
induced by underlying factors. However, in contrast to actual factor modelling
suffering from the need to choose the number of factors, we suggest a
model-free approach. Our final estimator is the asymptotically MSE-optimal
linear combination of the smoothed periodogram and the parametric estimator
based on an underfitting (and hence deliberately misspecified) factor model. We
complete our theoretical considerations by some extensive simulation studies.
In the situation of data generated from a higher-order factor model, we compare
all four types of involved estimators (including the one of B\"{o}hm and von
Sachs (2007)).
label: human

A classification of spinor fields according to the associated bilinear
covariants is constructed in arbitrary dimensions and metric signatures,
generalizing Lounesto's 4D spinor field classification. In such a generalized
classification a basic role is played by the geometric Fierz identities. In 4D
Minkowski spacetime the standard bilinear covariants can be either null or
non-null -- with the exception of the current density which is invariably
different from zero for physical reasons -- and sweep all types of spinor
fields, including Dirac, Weyl, Majorana and more generally flagpoles,
flag-dipoles and dipole spinor fields. To obtain an analogous classification in
higher dimensions we use the Fierz identities, which constrain the covariant
bilinears in the spinor fields and force some of them to vanish. A generalized
graded Fierz aggregate is moreover obtained in such a context simply from the
completeness relation. We analyze the particular and important case of
Riemannian 7-manifolds, where the Majorana spinor fields turn out to have a
quite special place. In particular, at variance with spinor fields in 4D
Minkowski spacetime that are classified in six disjoint classes, spinors in
Riemannian 7-manifolds are shown to be classified, according to the bilinear
covariants: (a) in just one class, in the real case of Majorana spinors; (b) in
four classes, in the most general case. Much like new classes of spinor fields
in 4D Minkowski spacetime have been evincing new possibilities in physics, we
think these new classes of spinor fields in seven dimensions are, in
particular, potential candidates for new solutions in the compactification of
supergravity on a seven-dimensional manifold and its exotic versions.
label: human

We consider the quasi-one dimensional system realized by an array of weakly
coupled parallel one-dimensional "tubes" in a two-dimensional lattice which
permits free motion of atoms in an axial direction in the presence of a Zeeman
field, Rashba type spin orbit coupling (SOC), and an s-wave attractive
interaction, while the radial motion is tightly confined. We solve the
zero-temperature (T=0) Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) equations for the quasi-1D
Fermi gas with the dispersion modified by tunneling between the tubes, and show
that the T=0 phase diagram hosts the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov (FFLO)
phase with non-zero center of mass momentum Cooper pairs for small values of
the SOC while for larger values of the SOC and high Zeeman fields the uniform
superfluid phase with zero center of mass momentum Cooper pairs has an
instability towards the topological uniform superfluid phase with Majorana
fermions at the tube ends. Also, we show that tuning the two-dimensional
optical lattice strength in this model allows one to explore the crossover
behaviors of the phases during the transition between the 3D and the 1D system
and in general the FFLO (for small SOC) and the topological uniform superfluid
phase (for large SOC) are favored as the system becomes more one-dimensional.
We also find evidence of the existence of a Zeeman tuned topological quantum
phase transition (TQPT) within the FFLO phase itself and for large values of
the Zeeman field and small SOC the TQPT gives rise to a topologically distinct
FFLO phase.
label: human

text:
Aim: The aim of this work is to search Seyfert 2 galaxy NGC 4945, a
well-known 22 GHz water megamaser galaxy, for water (mega)maser emission at 183
GHz. Method: We used APEX SEPIA Band 5 to perform the observations. Results: We
detected 183 GHz water maser emission towards NGC 4945 with a peak flux density
of ~3 Jy near the galactic systemic velocity. The emission spans a velocity
range of several hundred km/s. We estimate an isotropic luminosity of > 1000
Lsun, classifying the emission as a megamaser. A comparison of the 183 GHz
spectrum with that observed at 22 GHz suggests that 183 GHz emission also
arises from the active galactic nucleus (AGN) central engine. If the 183 GHz
emission originates from the circumnuclear disk, then we estimate that a
redshifted feature at 1084 km/s in the spectrum should arise from a distance of
0.022 pc from the supermassive black hole (1.6 x 10(5) Schwarzschild radii),
i.e. closer than the water maser emission previously detected at 22 GHz. This
is only the second time 183 GHz maser emission has been detected towards an AGN
central engine (the other galaxy being NGC 3079). It is also the strongest
extragalactic millimetre/submillimetre water maser detected to date.
Conclusions: Strong millimetre 183 GHz water maser emission has now been shown
to occur in an external galaxy. For NGC 4945, we believe that the maser
emission arises, or is dominated by, emission from the AGN central engine.
Emission at higher velocity, i.e. for a Keplerian disk closer to the black
hole, has been detected at 183 GHz compared with that for the 22 GHz megamaser.
This indicates that millimetre/submillimetre water masers can indeed be useful
probes for tracing out more of AGN central engine structures and dynamics than
previously probed. Future observations using ALMA Band 5 should unequivocally
determine the origin of the emission in this and other galaxies.
label: human

text:
Higgs triplet models are known to have difficulties obtaining agreement with
electroweak precision data and in particular constraints on the $\rho$
parameter. Either a global $SU(2)_L \otimes SU(2)_R$ symmetry has to be imposed
on the scalar potential at the electroweak scale, as done in the well-known
Georgi-Machacek (GM) model, or the triplet vacuum expectation values must be
very small. We construct a supersymmetric model that can satisfy constraints on
the $\rho$ parameter, even if these two conditions are not fulfilled. We
supersymmetrize the GM model by imposing the $SU(2)_L \otimes SU(2)_R$ symmetry
at a scale $\mathcal M$, which we argue should be at or above the messenger
scale, where supersymmetry breaking is transmitted to the observable sector. We
show that scales $\mathcal M$ well above 100 TeV and sizable contributions from
the triplets to electroweak symmetry breaking can be comfortably accommodated.
We discuss the main phenomenological properties of the model and demonstrate
that the departure from custodial symmetry at the electroweak scale, due to
radiative breaking, can show up at the LHC as a deviation in the `universal'
relation for the Higgs couplings to $WW$ and $ZZ$. As a by-product of
supersymmetry, we also show that one can easily obtain both large tree-level
\emph{and} one loop corrections to the Higgs mass. This allows for stops that
can be significantly lighter and with smaller mixing than those needed in the
MSSM.
label: human

text:
Among presolar materials recovered in meteorites, abundant SiC and
Al$_{2}$O$_{3}$ grains of AGB origins were found. They showed records of C, N,
O, $^{26}$Al and s-element isotopic ratios that proved invaluable in
constraining the nucleosynthesis models for AGB stars \cite{zin,gal}. In
particular, when these ratios are measured in SiC grains, they clearly reveal
their prevalent origin in cool AGB circumstellar envelopes and provide
information on both the local physics and the conditions at the nucleosynthesis
site (the H- and He-burning layers deep inside the structure). Among the
properties ascertained for the main part of the SiC data (the so-called {\it
mainstream} ones), we mention a large range of $^{14}$N/$^{15}$N ratios,
extending below the solar value \cite{mar}, and $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratios
$\gtrsim$ 30. Other classes of grains, instead, display low carbon isotopic
ratios ($\gtrsim 10$) and a huge dispersion for N isotopes, with cases of large
$^{15}$N excess. In the same grains, isotopes currently feeded by slow neutron
captures reveal the characteristic pattern expected from this process at an
efficiency slightly lower than necessary to explain the solar main s-process
component. Complementary constraints can be found in oxide grains, especially
Al$_{2}$O$_{3}$ crystals. Here, the oxygen isotopes and the content in
$^{26}$Al are of a special importance for clarifying the partial mixing
processes that are known to affect evolved low-mass stars. Successes in
modeling the data, as well as problems in explaining some of the mentioned
isotopic ratios through current nucleosynthesis models are briefly outlined.
label: human

text:
Given a graph $G$, the $G$-parking function ideal $M_G$ is an artinian
monomial ideal in the polynomial ring $S$ with the property that a linear basis
for $S/M_G$ is provided by the set of $G$-parking functions. It follows that
the dimension of $S/M_G$ is given by the number of spanning trees of $G$, which
by the Matrix Tree Theorem is equal to the determinant of the reduced Laplacian
of $G$. The ideals $M_G$ and related algebras were introduced by Postnikov and
Shapiro where they studied their Hilbert functions and homological properties.
The author and Sanyal showed that a minimal resolution of $M_G$ can be
constructed from the graphical hyperplane arrangement associated to $G$,
providing a combinatorial interpretation of the Betti numbers.
  Motivated by constructions in the theory of chip-firing on graphs, we study
certain `skeleton' ideals $M_G^{(k)} \subset M_G$ generated by subsets of
vertices of $G$ of size at most $k+1$. Here we focus our attention on the case
$k=1$, the $1$-skeleton of the $G$-parking functions ideals. We consider
standard monomials of $M_G^{(1)}$ and provide a combinatorial interpretation
for the dimension of $S/M_G^{(1)}$ in terms of the signless Laplacian for the
case $G = K_{n+1}$ is the complete graph. Our main study concerns homological
properties of these ideals. We study resolutions of $M_G^{(1)}$ and show that
for a certain class of graphs minimal resolution is supported on decompositions
of Euclidean space coming from the theory of tropical hyperplane arrangements.
This leads to combinatorial interpretations of the Betti numbers of these
ideals.
label: human

text: This paper investigates the properties and applications of Parseval frames constituted by exponentially decaying composite Wannier functions. Background exploration reveals that while conventional Wannier functions have provided invaluable insights into the electronic structure of materials, their extensions into composite forms remain underexplored in the context of frame theory. The objective of this study is to establish conditions under which these composite Wannier functions can form Parseval frames, facilitating energy localization and signal representation within quantum mechanics. Utilizing techniques from functional analysis, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of Parseval frames composed of exponentially decaying composite Wannier functions in various dimensional settings. The methodology encompasses the construction of specific composite functions and the application of frame theory to prove their Parseval quality. Key findings indicate that not only can exponentially decaying composite Wannier functions construct Parseval frames, but they also exhibit enhanced adaptability in representing localized functions in complex systems, leading to improved computational efficiency in numerical simulations. Furthermore, the paper identifies potential applications in areas such as condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry, where precise localization of electronic states is essential. In conclusion, our results significantly contribute to the understanding of frame constructions in quantum mechanics, suggesting that the use of composite Wannier functions may offer a powerful tool for future studies on wavefunction localization and material property characterization. This work lays the foundation for subsequent innovations in both theoretical frameworks and practical applications.
label: machine

text:
Spontaneous decays of small, hot silver cluster anions Ag$_{n}$, $n=4-7$ have
been studied using one of the rings of the Double ElectroStatic Ion Ring
ExpEriment (DESIREE). Observation of these decays over very long time scales is
possible due to the very low residual gas pressure ($\sim10^{-14}$) and
cryogenic (13 K) operation of DESIREE. The yield of neutral particles from
stored beams of Ag$_{6}$ and Ag$_{7}$ anions were measured for 100 milliseconds
and were found to follow single power law behaviour with millisecond time scale
exponential cut-offs. The Ag$_{4}$ and Ag$_{5}$ anions were stored for 60
seconds and the observed decays show two-component power law behaviors. We
present calculations of the rate constants for electron detachment from, and
fragmentation of Ag$_{4}$ and Ag$_{5}$. In these calculations, we assume that
the internal energy distribution of the clusters are flat and with this we
reproduce the early steep parts of the experimentally measured decay curves for
Ag$_{4}$ and Ag$_{5}$, which extends to tens and hundreds of milliseconds,
respectively. The fact that the calculations reproduce the early slopes of
Ag$_{4}$ and Ag$_{5}$, which differ for the two cases, suggests that it is the
changes in fragmentation rates with internal cluster energies of Ag$_{4}$ and
Ag$_{5}$ rather than conditions in the ion source that determines this
behavior. Comparisons with the measurements strongly suggest that the neutral
particles detected in these time domains originate from Ag$_{4} \rightarrow$
Ag$_{3}+$ Ag and Ag$_{5}\rightarrow$ Ag$_{3}+$ Ag$_{2}$ fragmentation
processes.
label: human

text: In this study, we present an interactive decomposition multi-objective optimization framework that leverages progressively learned value functions to address complex decision-making problems. The method employs an iterative process where the decision-maker iteratively refines their preferences through feedback loops. Initially, a generic value function is trained using historical data and decomposes the multi-objective problem into a series of single-objective sub-problems. Subsequently, the value function is refined based on user feedback, allowing for more accurate representation of the decision-maker's preferences. This iterative refinement process continues until the decision-maker is satisfied with the solution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through various synthetic and real-world applications, showcasing its capability to handle high-dimensional, non-linear, and conflicting objectives efficiently. The results indicate significant improvements in solution quality and user satisfaction compared to existing methods. Our key innovation lies in the integration of machine learning techniques within an interactive optimization paradigm, enabling continuous adaptation to evolving user preferences.
label: machine

text: This research explores the application of large deviation principles to improve the efficiency of irreversible Langevin samplers, aiming to reduce the variance of the sampling process. Starting from a background that highlights the limitations of traditional Langevin dynamics in achieving high statistical accuracy, the study introduces irreversible Langevin samplers as a novel approach to overcome these challenges. The objective is to demonstrate how the theoretical framework of large deviation theory can be utilized to enhance the performance of these samplers.  The methodology involves formulating a mathematical model based on large deviation principles to analyze the behavior of irreversible Langevin processes. This model is then applied to various sampling scenarios, including high-dimensional and multimodal distributions, to evaluate its effectiveness. Key findings reveal that by incorporating the large deviation approach, the variance of the sampling process can be significantly reduced, leading to more efficient and accurate simulations. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the rate of convergence to the target distribution improves under certain conditions, which are further explored and validated through numerical experiments.  In conclusion, this research underscores the potential of large deviation theory in enhancing the performance of irreversible Langevin samplers. The findings suggest that integrating these principles could lead to substantial improvements in computational efficiency and accuracy for complex sampling tasks, particularly in high-dimensional and challenging distribution landscapes.
label: machine

text:
With a uniform VLT SINFONI data set of nine targets, we have developed an
empirical grid of J,H,K spectra of the atmospheres of objects estimated to have
very low substellar masses of \sim5-20 MJup and young ages of \sim1-50 Myr.
Most of the targets are companions, objects which are especially valuable for
comparison with atmosphere and evolutionary models, as they present rare cases
in which the age is accurately known from the primary. Based on the sample
youth, all objects are expected to have low surface gravity, and this study
investigates the critical early phases of the evolution of substellar objects.
The spectra are compared with grids of five different theoretical atmosphere
models. This analysis represents the first systematic model comparison with
infrared spectra of young brown dwarfs. The fits to the full JHK spectra of
each object result in a range of best fit effective temperatures of +/-150-300K
whether or not the full model grid or a subset restricted to lower log(g)
values is used. This effective temperature range is significantly larger than
the uncertainty typically assigned when using a single model grid. Fits to a
single wavelength band can vary by up to 1000K using the different models.
Since the overall shape of these spectra is governed more by the temperature
than surface gravity, unconstrained model fits did not find matches with low
surface gravity or a trend in log(g) with age. This suggests that empirical
comparison with spectra of unambiguously young objects targets (such as these
SINFONI data) may be the most reliable method to search for indications of low
surface gravity and youth. For two targets, the SINFONI data are a second epoch
and the data show no variations in morphology over time. The analysis of two
other targets, AB Pic B and CT Cha B, suggests that these objects may have
lower temperatures, and consequently lower masses, than previously estimated.
label: human
