Electron cloud beam instabilities are an important consideration in virtually
all high-energy particle accelerators and could pose a formidable challenge to
forthcoming high-intensity accelerator upgrades. Dedicated tests have shown
beampipe coatings dramatically reduce the density of electron cloud in particle
accelerators. In this work, we evaluate the performance of titanium nitride,
amorphous carbon, and diamond-like carbon as beampipe coatings for the
mitigation of electron cloud in the Fermilab Main Injector. Altogether our
tests represent 2700 ampere-hours of proton operation spanning five years.
Three electron cloud detectors, retarding field analyzers, are installed in a
straight section and allow a direct comparison between the electron flux in the
coated and uncoated stainless steel beampipe. We characterize the electron flux
as a function of intensity up to a maximum of 50 trillion protons per cycle.
Each beampipe material conditions in response to electron bombardment from the
electron cloud and we track the changes in these materials as a function of
time and the number of absorbed electrons. Contamination from an unexpected
vacuum leak revealed a potential vulnerability in the amorphous carbon beampipe
coating. We measure the energy spectrum of electrons incident on the stainless
steel, titanium nitride and amorphous carbon beampipes. We find the electron
cloud signal is highly sensitive to stray magnetic fields and bunch-length over
the Main Injector ramp cycle. We conduct a complete survey of the stray
magnetic fields at the test station and compare the electron cloud signal to
that in a field-free region.
label: human

text: Proton therapy has emerged as a promising modality in cancer treatment due to its unique physical properties, particularly its ability to deliver targeted radiation while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissues. This study investigates the effects of collimator design on proton beam planning and its subsequent impact on dose distribution and treatment efficacy. The objective was to evaluate the influence of various collimator geometries and materials on the precision of dose delivery in clinical treatment scenarios. A Monte Carlo simulation approach was employed, combining sophisticated proton transport algorithms with patient-specific geometrical models derived from CT imaging. Key findings revealed that optimized collimator configurations significantly improve dose conformity to target volumes, while simultaneously reducing the dose to critical structures. Specifically, modifications in collimator angle and aperture sizes were found to enhance the dosimetric characteristics, achieving better dose gradients and sharper fall-off curves. Additionally, it was observed that materials with higher atomic numbers substantially reduced scattering effects, further refining dose accuracy. The results underscore the importance of meticulous collimator design in proton therapy planning, advocating for tailored approaches depending on tumor location and size. In conclusion, the findings of this study provide valuable insights for clinical applications, suggesting that innovative collimator designs can substantially enhance the therapeutic ratio in proton therapy, ultimately leading to improved patient outcomes. Further research is recommended to explore the implications of dynamic collimation techniques in real-time treatment adaptation.
label: machine

text: This study focuses on developing a comprehensive framework for modeling galactic density in the presence of dust extinction. Background research indicates that dust extinction significantly affects the observed brightness of celestial objects, leading to inaccurate density estimates. Current methods often rely on simplistic models, neglecting the complex interplay between dust and radiation. The objective of this research is to create a more accurate and robust model that incorporates dust extinction effects into galactic density calculations.  A novel approach is proposed, combining Bayesian inference and radiative transfer simulations to account for dust extinction. The model incorporates a detailed description of dust properties, including size distribution and optical depth, to simulate the complex interactions between radiation and dust. The Bayesian framework allows for the incorporation of prior knowledge and observational constraints, enabling the estimation of galactic density with improved accuracy.  The methodology involves a series of simulations, where the radiative transfer model is coupled with the Bayesian inference framework. The results are compared to existing density estimates, demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy. Key findings indicate that incorporating dust extinction into galactic density models leads to a better representation of the true density structure. The study also highlights the importance of considering dust extinction in density modeling, emphasizing the need for more accurate and comprehensive models. The research contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between dust and radiation in galaxies, with implications for various astrophysical applications, including star formation and galaxy evolution.

The bar pattern speed ($\Omega_{\rm b}$) is defined as the rotational
frequency of the bar, and it determines the bar dynamics. Several methods have
been proposed for measuring $\Omega_{\rm b}$. The non-parametric method
proposed by Tremaine \& Weinberg (1984; TW) and based on stellar kinematics is
the most accurate. This method has been applied so far to 17 galaxies, most of
them SB0 and SBa types. We have applied the TW method to a new sample of 15
strong and bright barred galaxies, spanning a wide range of morphological types
from SB0 to SBbc. Combining our analysis with previous studies, we investigate
32 barred galaxies with their pattern speed measured by the TW method. The
resulting total sample of barred galaxies allows us to study the dependence of
$\Omega_{\rm b}$ on galaxy properties, such as the Hubble type. We measured
$\Omega_{\rm b}$ using the TW method on the stellar velocity maps provided by
the integral-field spectroscopy data from the CALIFA survey. Integral-field
data solve the problems that long-slit data present when applying the TW
method, resulting in the determination of more accurate $\Omega_{\rm b}$. In
addition, we have also derived the ratio $\cal{R}$ of the corotation radius to
the bar length of the galaxies. According to this parameter, bars can be
classified as fast ($\cal{R}$ $< 1.4$) and slow ($\cal{R}$>1.4). For all the
galaxies, $\cal{R}$ is compatible within the errors with fast bars. We cannot
rule out (at 95$\%$ level) the fast bar solution for any galaxy. We have not
observed any significant trend between $\cal{R}$ and the galaxy morphological
type. Our results indicate that independent of the Hubble type, bars have been
formed and then evolve as fast rotators. This observational result will
constrain the scenarios of formation and evolution of bars proposed by
numerical simulations.

Electronic cloaking has been recently suggested to design invisible dopants
with electronic scattering cross sections smaller than 1% of the physical cross
section ( . Cloaking layers could be designed to coat nanoparticle dopants to
minimally scatter conduction electrons and to enhance the electronic mobility.
In some cases, such enhancements would result in larger thermoelectric power
factors. The main difficulty is the fact that the created potential upon
coating is not tunable and is determined by the band alignment of the chosen
materials for the core, the shell and the host as well as the charge
distribution in these layers. To find proper combinations of materials, one
needs to probe a large class of materials combinations and layer sizes. This
approach is time-consuming and impractical. Here we introduce a mapping method
to identify possible combinations by comparing the dimensionless parameters of
the chosen materials with the provided maps and without any transport
calculations. Using this approach, we have identified several combinations of
core, shell and host materials for which electronic cloaking is achievable. We
have optimized the size and doping level of some of these materials
combinations to maximize their thermoelectric power factor. Compared to
traditional impurity-doped samples, up to 14.50 times improvement in the
thermoelectric power factor was observed at T=77K.
label: human

text: This study investigates exclusive backward-angle omega meson electroproduction, focusing on the production of omega mesons at large scattering angles relative to the incident photon direction. Our primary objective is to explore the kinematic region where the omega meson emerges predominantly in a back-to-back configuration with respect to the initial photon beam, thereby providing insights into the underlying quark-gluon dynamics.  To achieve this, we employed a high-energy electron beam interacting with a liquid hydrogen target, utilizing the Jefferson Lab Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator Facility (CEBAF). The data collected were analyzed using state-of-the-art Monte Carlo simulations and experimental techniques to precisely determine cross-sections and angular distributions of omega meson production.  Our findings reveal distinct signatures of omega meson production in the forward and backward regions, with significant enhancements observed in the backward angle regime. This observation suggests that the quark content of the omega meson may be influenced by the strong interaction environment near the proton's surface. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the angular distribution of omega meson production is well described by theoretical models incorporating quantum chromodynamics effects, particularly those involving parton distribution functions and fragmentation functions.  The key methodologies involved include detailed kinematic fitting, event-by-event simulation, and comparison with theoretical predictions from lattice QCD calculations. These studies underscore the importance of understanding omega meson production in the forward-backward plane, which can provide crucial information about the structure of hadrons and the strong interaction at small momentum transfers.
label: machine

text:
We present the identification of 634 variable stars in the Milky Way dSph
satellite Sculptor based on archival ground-based optical observations spanning
$\sim$24 years and covering $\sim$ 2.5 deg$^2$. We employed the same
methodologies as the "Homogeneous Photometry" series published by Stetson. In
particular, we have identified and characterized one of the largest (536) RR
Lyrae samples so far in a Milky Way dSph satellite. We have also detected four
Anomalous Cepheids, 23 SX Phoenicis stars, five eclipsing binaries, three field
variable stars, three peculiar variable stars located above the horizontal
branch - near to the locus of BL Herculis - that we are unable to classify
properly. Additionally we identify 37 Long Period Variables plus 23 probable
variable stars, for which the current data do not allow us to determine the
period. We report positions and finding charts for all the variable stars, and
basic properties (period, amplitude, mean magnitude) and light curves for 574
of them. We discuss the properties of the RR Lyrae stars in the Bailey diagram,
which supports the coexistence of subpopulations with different chemical
compositions. We estimate the mean mass of Anomalous Cepheids
($\sim$1.5M$_{\odot}$) and SX Phoenicis stars ($\sim$1M$_{\odot}$). We discuss
in detail the nature of the former. The connections between the properties of
the different families of variable stars are discussed in the context of the
star formation history of the Sculptor dSph galaxy.

text: We present a novel machine learning approach aimed at inferring fundamental stellar parameters from photometric light curves. Our work addresses the challenge of extracting precise stellar characteristics, such as temperature, luminosity, and mass, from the often noisy and irregular data produced by modern astronomical surveys. By leveraging extensive datasets obtained from both ground-based and space observatories, we developed a supervised learning model that utilizes convolutional neural networks (CNNs) as well as gradient boosting techniques.   We systematically trained our models on a carefully curated dataset comprising light curves accompanied by known stellar parameters derived from spectroscopic observations. Through this process, we employed data augmentation strategies to enhance the robustness of our model against varied observational conditions and noise types. Our method demonstrated high predictive accuracy, yielding root mean square errors significantly lower than traditional techniques across all tested parameters.  The results indicate a reliable framework for deriving stellar parameters, showcasing the potential of machine learning in astronomical research. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for future studies, particularly in the realm of exoplanet detection and characterization. By facilitating a more efficient analysis of light curve data, our methodology contributes to the ongoing efforts to unravel the complexities of stellar astrophysics. Ultimately, we affirm that machine learning serves as a powerful tool for advancing our understanding of stellar properties and their evolution in the cosmos.
label: machine

Context. Based on their overwhelming dominance among associated Fermi gamma
ray catalogue sources, it is expected that a large fraction of the unidentified
Fermi objects are blazars. Through crossmatching between the positions of
unidentified gamma ray sources from the First Fermi Catalog of gamma ray
sources emitting above 10 GeV (1FHL) and the ROSAT and Swift XRT catalogues of
X ray objects and between pointed XRT observations, a sample of 36 potential
associations was found in previous works with less than 15 arcsec of positional
offset. One third of them have recently been classified; the remainder, though
believed to belong to the blazar class, still lack spectroscopic
classifications. Aims. We study the optical spectrum of the putative
counterparts of these unidentified gamma ray sources in order to find their
redshifts and to determine their nature and main spectral characteristics.
Methods. An observational campaign was carried out on the putative counterparts
of 13 1FHL sources using medium resolution optical spectroscopy from the
Osservatorio Astronomico di Bologna in Loiano, Italy; the Telescopio Nazionale
Galileo and the Nordic Optical Telescope, both in the Canary Islands, Spain;
and the Observatorio Astronomico Nacional San Pedro Martir in Baja California,
Mexico. Results. We were able to classify 14 new objects based on their
continuum shapes and spectral features. Conclusions. Twelve new blazars were
found, along with one new quasar and one new narrow line Seyfert 1 (NLS1) to be
potentially associated with the 1FHL sources of our sample. Redshifts or lower
limits were obtained when possible alongside central black hole mass and
luminosity estimates for the NLS1 and the quasar.

text:
A new definition of coarse-grained quantities describing the dust flow in
General Relativity is proposed. It assigns the coarse--grained expansion, shear
and vorticity to finite-size comoving domains of fluid in a covariant,
coordinate-independent manner. The coarse--grained quantities are all
quasi-local functionals, depending only on the geometry of the boundary of the
considered domain. They can be thought of as relativistic generalizations of
simple volume averages of local quantities in a flat space. The procedure is
based on the isometric embedding theorem for S^2 surfaces and thus requires the
boundary of the domain in question to have spherical topology and positive
scalar curvature. We prove that in the limit of infinitesimally small volume
the proposed quantities reproduce the local expansion, shear and vorticity. In
case of irrotational flow we derive the time evolution for the coarse-grained
quantities and show that its structure is very similar to the evolution
equation for their local counterparts. Additional terms appearing in it may
serve as a measure of the backreacton of small-scale inhomogeneities of the
flow on the large-scale motion of the fluid inside the domain and therefore the
result may be interesting in the context of the cosmological backreaction
problem. We also consider the application of the proposed coarse-graining
procedure to a number of known exact solutions of Einstein equations with dust
and show that it yields reasonable results.
label: human

In most of the previous studies related to collisional disruption of
planetesimals in the gravity regime, Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH)
simulations have been used. On the other hand, impact simulations using
grid-based hydrodynamic code have not been sufficiently performed. In the
present study, we execute impact simulations in the gravity regime using the
shock-physics code iSALE, which is a grid-based Eulerian hydrocode. We examine
the dependence of the critical specific impact energy Q_RD* on impact
conditions for a wide range of specific impact energy (Q_R) from disruptive
collisions to erosive collisions, and compare our results with previous
studies. We find collision outcomes of the iSALE simulation agree well with
those of the SPH simulation. Detailed analysis mainly gives three results. (1)
The value of Q_RD* depends on numerical resolution, and is close to convergence
with increasing numerical resolution. The difference in converged value of
Q_RD* between the iSALE code and the SPH code is within 30%. (2) Ejected mass
normalized by total mass (M_ej/M_tot) generally depends on various impact
conditions. However, when Q_R is normalized by Q_RD* that is calculated for
each impact simulation, M_ej/M_tot can be scaled by Q_R/Q_RD*, and is
independent of numerical resolution, impact velocity and target size. (3) This
similarity law for Q_R/Q_RD* is confirmed for a wide range of specific impact
energy. We also derive a semi-analytic formula for Q_RD* based on the
similarity law and the crater scaling law. We find that the semi-analytic
formula for the case with a non-porous object is consistent with numerical
results.
label: human

text:
We give a Las Vegas algorithm which computes the shifted Popov form of an $m
\times m$ nonsingular polynomial matrix of degree $d$ in expected
$\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(m^\omega d)$ field operations, where $\omega$ is the
exponent of matrix multiplication and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot)$
indicates that logarithmic factors are omitted. This is the first algorithm in
$\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(m^\omega d)$ for shifted row reduction with arbitrary
shifts.
  Using partial linearization, we reduce the problem to the case $d \le \lceil
\sigma/m \rceil$ where $\sigma$ is the generic determinant bound, with $\sigma
/ m$ bounded from above by both the average row degree and the average column
degree of the matrix. The cost above becomes $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(m^\omega
\lceil \sigma/m \rceil)$, improving upon the cost of the fastest previously
known algorithm for row reduction, which is deterministic.
  Our algorithm first builds a system of modular equations whose solution set
is the row space of the input matrix, and then finds the basis in shifted Popov
form of this set. We give a deterministic algorithm for this second step
supporting arbitrary moduli in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(m^{\omega-1} \sigma)$
field operations, where $m$ is the number of unknowns and $\sigma$ is the sum
of the degrees of the moduli. This extends previous results with the same cost
bound in the specific cases of order basis computation and M-Pad\'e
approximation, in which the moduli are products of known linear factors.
label: human

text: Recent advancements in composite materials with embedded microwires have catalyzed interest in tailoring electromagnetic properties for applications in telecommunications and sensing devices. Current-modulation annealing presents a promising technique to manipulate the microwave permittivity of such composites non-invasively. This study explores the effect of controlled current-modulation annealing on the microwave permittivity of polymer composites containing melt-extracted metallic microwires. The objective is to ascertain precise modulation parameters that alter permittivity without degrading the mechanical integrity of the composites. We employed a combination of alternating current annealing and permittivity measurement techniques, using a network analyzer to track changes in dielectric properties as the annealing current parameters were systematically varied. Our findings reveal a distinct correlation between annealing conditions—specifically current amplitude and frequency—and permittivity alterations. Particularly, composites subjected to periodic current modulations exhibited observable permittivity enhancements, attributable to the optimized redistribution of induced dipole moments within the microwires. Additionally, the method proved versatile in fine-tuning permittivity to specific application needs through targeted adjustments of the annealing protocol. Conclusively, current-modulation annealing emerges as an effective tool for dynamic control over the electromagnetic characteristics of microwire composites, facilitating the development of adaptive materials for advanced electromagnetic applications. The technique's scalability and precision highlight its potential for industry adoption, encouraging further exploration into its long-term stability and performance under varied environmental conditions.
label: machine

text: This study addresses the precision of global measurements of London penetration depth in Fe(Te$_{0.58}$Se$_{0.42}$) by employing a combination of experimental techniques. The London penetration depth, a measure of superconducting material's ability to expel magnetic fields, is crucial for understanding the behavior of high-temperature superconductors. Previous studies have reported varying results for Fe(Te$_{0.58}$Se$_{0.42}$), which may be attributed to the lack of precise measurements.   The objective of this research is to investigate the London penetration depth of Fe(Te$_{0.58}$Se$_{0.42}$) using a multi-technique approach, including inductively coupled plasma spectroscopy (ICPS), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). These techniques provide complementary information on the material's composition, crystal structure, and electronic properties.   Our results indicate that the London penetration depth of Fe(Te$_{0.58}$Se$_{0.42}$) is approximately 0.4 nm at 4.2 K. We also observe a significant correlation between the material's composition and its electronic properties, which is consistent with previous theoretical predictions.   This study contributes to a better understanding of the electronic properties of Fe(Te$_{0.58}$Se$_{0.42}$) and provides precise measurements of its London penetration depth. The findings have implications for the development of high-temperature superconducting materials and devices.
label: machine

text:
We performed a systematic analysis of the 4.67 $\mu$m CO ro-vibrational
absorption band toward nearby active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and analyzed the
absorption profiles of ten nearby galaxies collected from the AKARI and Spitzer
spectroscopic observations that show the CO absorption feature by fitting a
plane-parallel local thermal equilibrium gas model. We found that CO gas is
warm (200--500 K) and has a large column density
($N_\mathrm{H}\gtrsim10^{23}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$). The heating of the gas is not
explicable by either UV heating or shock heating because these processes cannot
represent the large column densities of the warm gas. Instead, X-ray photons
from the nuclei, which can produce large columns of warm gas with up to
$N_\mathrm{H}\sim10^{24}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$, are the most convincing power
source. The hydrogen column density estimated from the CO band is smaller than
that inferred from X-ray observations. These results indicate that the region
probed by the near-infrared CO absorption is in the vicinity of the nuclei and
is located outside the X-ray emitting region. Furthermore, the covering factors
close to unity required by the observed deep absorption profiles suggest that
the probed region is close to the continuum source, which can be designated as
the inner rim of the obscuring material around the AGN.
label: human

text: We investigate the application of Bayesian inference to model selection and likelihood estimation using fast rejection sampling, specifically focusing on the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson (CMP) distribution. Our primary objective is to address the computational challenges associated with traditional sampling methods in the Bayesian framework. Through our methodology, we propose an efficient rejection sampling algorithm that significantly reduces computation time while maintaining robust accuracy in parameter estimation. We derive the likelihood function for the CMP distribution and utilize it to inform our Bayesian models.   In our experiments, we assess the performance of our rejection sampling approach by comparing it to conventional Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, which are often computationally prohibitive for large datasets. We demonstrate that our rejection sampling technique effectively captures the posterior distributions of the CMP parameters and selects the optimal model amongst competing distributions. Our results reveal that the proposed method not only accelerates the entire inference process but also enhances the reliability of model selection through improved likelihood estimations. The methodology paves the way for practical applications in fields such as biostatistics and machine learning, where the CMP distribution can be employed to model count data exhibiting overdispersion and underdispersion. Overall, our findings contribute to the growing body of literature on Bayesian computational methods and underscore the viability of fast rejection sampling techniques in complex statistical modeling.
label: machine

text:
(Abridged) We report on a complete study of the single top-quark production
by direct supersymmetric flavor-changing neutral-current (FCNC) processes at
the LHC. The total cross section for pp(gg)->t\bar{c}+\bar{t}c is computed at
the 1-loop order within the unconstrained Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model
(MSSM). The present study extends the results of the supersymmetric strong
effects (SUSY-QCD), which were advanced by some of us in a previous work, and
includes the computation of the full supersymmetric electroweak corrections
(SUSY-EW). Our analysis of pp(gg)->t\bar{c}+\bar{t}c in the MSSM has been
performed in correspondence with the stringent low-energy constraints from b->s
gamma. In the most favorable scenarios, the SUSY-QCD contribution can give rise
to production rates of around 10^5 events per 100 fb^{-1} of integrated
luminosity. Furthermore, we show that there exist regions of the MSSM parameter
space where the SUSY-EW correction becomes sizeable. In the SUSY-EW favored
regions, one obtains lower, but still appreciable, event production rates that
can reach the 10^3 level for the same range of integrated luminosity. We study
also the possible reduction in the maximum event rate obtained from the full
MSSM contribution if we additionally include the constraints from
B^0_s-\bar{B}^0_s. In view of the fact that the FCNC production of heavy quark
pairs of different flavors is extremely suppressed in the SM, the detection of
a significant number of these events could lead to evidence of new physics --
of likely supersymmetric origin.
label: human

text: Saturn's inner mid-sized moons, such as Pan and Daphnis, are believed to have originated from a massive primordial ice ring that surrounded the planet during its early stages of formation. This ice ring, thought to be composed of water ice and rocky debris, is hypothesized to have been destroyed by Saturn's gravitational forces, resulting in the accretion of the moons. However, the exact mechanisms and processes involved in this process remain poorly understood, and the formation of these moons has been the subject of ongoing debate among planetary scientists.  This research aims to investigate the accretion of Saturn's inner mid-sized moons from the massive primordial ice ring, using a combination of numerical simulations and laboratory experiments. The simulations employed a 3D hydrodynamic code, which allowed for the modeling of the ice ring's collapse and the subsequent formation of the moons. The results of the simulations indicate that the ice ring's collapse led to the formation of a complex system of moonlets and ring particles, which eventually grew to form the observed moons.  The laboratory experiments, conducted using a high-pressure and high-temperature apparatus, aimed to simulate the conditions present in the early Saturnian system. The results of the experiments showed that the ice ring's collapse led to the formation of small, icy bodies that could have been the precursors to the moons. The findings of this research provide new insights into the formation of Saturn's inner mid-sized moons and shed light on the complex processes involved in the accretion of these moons from the massive primordial ice ring.
label: machine

text: We investigated the iron line emission from the inner black hole accretion disc using relativistic models, shedding light on the intricate dynamics of matter in extreme gravitational environments. Our analysis employed a combination of numerical simulations and theoretical frameworks to probe the effects of strong gravity on the accretion disc's iron line spectrum. By incorporating relativistic corrections to the traditional narrow-line width approximation, we successfully replicated the observed broadening of the iron line emission in X-ray binaries, thereby validating our approach.  Through our simulations, we demonstrated that the relativistic effects on the iron line emission are largely driven by the strong gravitational field of the black hole, leading to a significant broadening of the line. Furthermore, we found that the broadening is closely tied to the accretion rate and the spin of the black hole, providing valuable insights into the complex interplay between these parameters. Our results also highlighted the importance of considering the effects of frame-dragging and gravitational redshift on the iron line emission, which are crucial for accurately modeling the observed spectral features.  By providing a more accurate and nuanced understanding of the iron line emission from the inner black hole accretion disc, our work contributes to the ongoing efforts to constrain the properties of supermassive black holes and their role in regulating the growth of galaxies.
label: machine

text: This research explores the phenomenon of multiple resonances in fluid-loaded vibrating structures, focusing on their impact on structural integrity and performance. Previous studies have primarily examined single resonance effects, overlooking the complex interactions that occur when multiple resonant frequencies coexist. This study aims to investigate the conditions under which these multiple resonances arise and how they influence the behavior of structures subjected to fluid loads.  Methodologically, the research employs both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations to model various scenarios involving fluid loading. Experimental setups were designed to replicate real-world conditions, allowing for direct comparison between theoretical predictions and empirical data. Key findings indicate that the presence of multiple resonances can lead to significant amplification of vibrations, thereby increasing the risk of structural failure. Furthermore, the study identifies specific design parameters that mitigate the adverse effects of multiple resonances.  The conclusions drawn from this research highlight the importance of considering multiple resonances in the design and analysis of fluid-loaded structures. It underscores the need for enhanced predictive models and more rigorous testing protocols to ensure safety and reliability in practical applications. Future work will focus on developing adaptive control strategies to manage and minimize the detrimental effects of multiple resonances.
label: machine

text:
Photo-Acoustic Tomography (PAT) can reconstruct a distribution of optical
absorbers acting as instantaneous sound sources in subcutaneous
microvasculature of a human breast. Adjoint methods for PAT, typically
Time-Reversal (TR) and Back-Projection (BP), are ways to refocus time-reversed
acoustic signals on sources by wave propagation from the position of sensors.
TR and BP have different treatments for received signals, but they are
equivalent under continuously sampling on a closed circular sensor array in two
dimensions. Here, we analyze image quality with discrete under-sampled sensors
in the sense of the Shannon sampling theorem. We investigate resolution and
contrast of TR and BP, respectively in one source-sensor pair configuration and
the frequency domain. With Hankel's asymptotic expansion to the integrands of
imaging functions, our main contribution is to demonstrate that TR and BP have
better performance on contrast and resolution, respectively. We also show that
the integrand of TR includes additional side lobes which degrade axial
resolution whereas that of BP conversely has relatively small amplitudes.
Moreover, omnidirectional resolution is improved if more sensors are employed
to collect the received signals. Nevertheless, for the under-sampled sensors,
we propose the Truncated Back-Projection (TBP) method to enhance the contrast
of BP using removing higher frequency components in the received signals. We
conduct numerical experiments on the two-dimensional projected phantom model
extracted from OA-Breast Database. The experiments verify our theories and show
that the proposed TBP possesses better omnidirectional resolution as well as
contrast compared with TR and BP with under-sampled sensors.
label: human

text:
In this paper a new watermarking scheme is presented based on log-average
luminance. A colored-image is divided into blocks after converting the RGB
colored image to YCbCr color space. A monochrome image of 1024 bytes is used as
the watermark. To embed the watermark, 16 blocks of size 8X8 are selected and
used to embed the watermark image into the original image. The selected blocks
are chosen spirally (beginning form the center of the image) among the blocks
that have log-average luminance higher than or equal the log-average luminance
of the entire image. Each byte of the monochrome watermark is added by updating
a luminance value of a pixel of the image. If the byte of the watermark image
represented white color (255) a value <alpha> is added to the image pixel
luminance value, if it is black (0) the <alpha> is subtracted from the
luminance value. To extract the watermark, the selected blocks are chosen as
the above, if the difference between the luminance value of the watermarked
image pixel and the original image pixel is greater than 0, the watermark pixel
is supposed to be white, otherwise it supposed to be black. Experimental
results show that the proposed scheme is efficient against changing the
watermarked image to grayscale, image cropping, and JPEG compression.
label: human

text:
We present RFexpress! the first-ever network-edge based system to recognize
emotion from movement, gesture and pose via Device-Free Activity Recognition
(DFAR). With the proliferation of the IoT, also wireless access points are
deployed at increasingly dense scale. in particular, this includes vehicular
nodes (in-car WiFi or Bluetooth), office (Wlan APs, WiFi printer or projector)
and private indoor domains (home WiFi mesh, Wireless media access), as well as
public spaces (City/open WiFi, Cafes, shopping spaces). Processing
RF-fluctuation at such edge-devices, enables environmental perception. In this
paper, we focus on the distinction between neutral and agitated emotional
states of humans from RF-fluctuation at the wireless network edge in realistic
environments. In particular, the system is able to detect risky driving
behaviour in a vehicular setting as well as spotting angry conversations in an
indoor environment. We also study the effectiveness of edge-based DFAR emotion
and activity recognition systems in real environments such as cafes, malls,
outdoor and office spaces. We measure radio characteristics in these
environments at different days and times and analyse the impact of variations
in the Signal to Noise Ratio (SNR) on the accuracy of DFAR emotion and activity
recognition. In a case study with 5 subjects, we then exploit the limits of
edge-based DFAR by deriving critical SNR values under which activity and

The difference in restricted mean survival times between two groups is a
clinically relevant summary measure. With observational data, there may be
imbalances in confounding variables between the two groups. One approach to
account for such imbalances is to estimate a covariate-adjusted restricted mean
difference by modeling the covariate-adjusted survival distribution and then
marginalizing over the covariate distribution. We demonstrate that the
mean-squared error of the restricted mean difference is bounded by the
mean-squared error of the covariate-adjusted survival distribution estimators.
This implies that a better estimator of the covariate-adjusted survival
distributions is associated with a better estimator of the restricted mean
difference. Thus, this paper proposes estimating restricted mean differences
with stacked survival models. Stacked survival models estimate a weighted
average of several survival models by minimizing predicted error. By including
a range of parametric and semi-parametric models, stacked survival models can
effectively estimate a covariate-adjusted survival distribution and, therefore,
the restricted mean treatment effect in a wide range of scenarios. We
demonstrate through a simulation study that the new estimator can perform
nearly as well as Cox regression when the proportional hazards assumption is
satisfied and significantly better when proportional hazards is violated. The
proposed estimator is also illustrated with data from the United Network for
Organ Sharing to evaluate post-lung transplant survival between large and
small-volume centers.

Current understanding holds that financial contagion is driven mainly by the
system-wide interconnectedness of institutions. A distinction has been made
between systematic and idiosyncratic channels of contagion, with shocks
transmitted through the latter expected to be substantially more likely to lead
to systemic crisis than through the former. Idiosyncratic connectivity is
thought to be driven not simply by obviously shared characteristics among
institutions, but more by latent characteristics that lead to the holding of
related securities. We develop a graphical model for multivariate financial
time series with interest in uncovering the latent positions of nodes in a
network intended to capture idiosyncratic relationships. We propose a
hierarchical model consisting of a VAR, a covariance graphical model (CGM) and
a latent position model (LPM). The VAR enables us to extract useful information
on the idiosyncratic components, which are used by the CGM to model the network
and the LPM uncovers the spatial position of the nodes. We also develop a
Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that iterates between sampling parameters of
the CGM and the LPM, using samples from the latter to update prior information
for covariance graph selection. We show empirically that modeling the
idiosyncratic channel of contagion using our approach can relate latent
institutional features to systemic vulnerabilities prior to a crisis.

The subdiffusion equation with a Caputo fractional derivative of order
$\alpha\in(0,1)$ in time arises in a wide variety of practical applications,
and it is often adopted to model anomalous subdiffusion processes in
heterogeneous media. The L1 scheme is one of the most popular and successful
numerical methods for discretizing the Caputo fractional derivative in time.
The scheme was analyzed earlier independently by Lin and Xu (2007) and Sun and
Wu (2006), and an $O(\tau^{2-\alpha})$ convergence rate was established, under
the assumption that the solution is twice continuously differentiable in time.
However, in view of the smoothing property of the subdiffusion equation, this
regularity condition is restrictive, since it does not hold even for the
homogeneous problem with a smooth initial data. In this work, we revisit the
error analysis of the scheme, and establish an $O(\tau)$ convergence rate for
both smooth and nonsmooth initial data. The analysis is valid for more general
sectorial operators. In particular, the L1 scheme is applied to one-dimensional
space-time fractional diffusion equations, which involves also a
Riemann-Liouville derivative of order $\beta\in(3/2,2)$ in space, and error
estimates are provided for the fully discrete scheme. Numerical experiments are
provided to verify the sharpness of the error estimates, and robustness of the
scheme with respect to data regularity.

Moreover, these idempotents contribute significantly to reducing computational complexity by breaking down complex matrices into simpler, more manageable forms, thus facilitating practical applications in quantum mechanics and theoretical physics. The SOL width is a parameter of paramount importance in modern tokamaks as it
controls the power density deposited at the divertor plates, critical for
plasma-facing material survivability. An understanding of the parameters
controlling it has consequently long been sought (Connor et al. 1999 NF 39 2).
Prior to Chang et al.(2017 NF 57 11), studies of the tokamak edge have been
mostly confined to reduced fluid models and simplified geometries, leaving out
important pieces of physics. Here, we analyze the results of a DIII-D
simulation performed with the full-f gyrokinetic code XGC1 which includes both
turbulence and neoclassical effects in realistic divertor geometry. More
specifically, we calculate the particle and heat ExB fluxes along the
separatrix, discriminating between equilibrium and turbulent contributions. We
find that the density SOL width is impacted almost exclusively by the turbulent
electron flux. In this simulation, the level of edge turbulence is regulated by
a mechanism we are only beginning to understand: $\nabla B$-drifts and ion
X-point losses at the top and bottom of the machine, along with ion banana
orbits at the low field side (LFS), result in a complex poloidal potential
structure at the separatrix which is the cause of the ExB drift pattern that we
observe. Turbulence is being suppressed by the shear flows that this potential
generates. At the same time, turbulence, along with increased edge
collisionality and electron inertia, can influence the shape of the potential
structure by making the electrons non-adiabatic. Moreover, being the only means
through which the electrons can lose confinement, it needs to be in a balance
with the original direct ion orbit losses to maintain charge neutrality.

Our results have significant implications for our understanding of the galactic bulge, including the role of star formation and supernovae in shaping its morphology and the presence of a large, unseen dark matter halo. The Galactic Bulge Survey provides a unique window into the physics of the galactic bulge, and our findings have important implications for the study of galaxy evolution and the formation of structure in the universe.

text: Luminous Blue Variables (LBVs) are a rare and unstable class of massive stars that exhibit large amplitude eruptions, which can last from years to decades. These eruptions are characterized by the ejection of large amounts of mass, commonly referred to as eruptive mass ejections (EMEs). In this study, we aim to investigate the physical mechanisms that trigger the onset of EMEs in LBVs.  We analyzed multi-epoch spectroscopic observations of four well-studied LBVs - HD 168625, HD 198501, Hen 3-1357, and NGC 300 O6(f) - using time-series spectral analysis. Our analysis revealed a strong correlation between the appearance of prominent emission lines, such as He II λ4686 and Hα, and the onset of EMEs. Furthermore, we detected a significant increase in the line widths and luminosities of these lines prior to each EME.  We propose a mechanism where the onset of EMEs is triggered by a sudden increase in the mass accretion rate onto the surface of the LBVs due to the interaction between the stellar wind and the circumstellar medium. This interaction creates a dense accretion disk, which leads to the formation of a strong magnetic field. The magnetic field subsequently causes a large-scale, convective instability, which results in the ejection of a massive amount of material from the stellar surface.  Our results provide new insights into the physical processes that govern the eruptive behavior of LBVs and have important implications for the understanding of stellar evolution and the role that these stars play in shaping their environments. Further investigations are required to test the validity of our proposed mechanism and to clarify the underlying physical processes that trigger the onset of EMEs in LBVs.

Motivated by the increasing ability of experimentalists to perform detector
tomography, we consider how to incorporate the imperfections and restrictions
of available measurements directly into the quantification of entanglement.
Exploiting the idea that the recently introduced semiquantum nonlocal games as
the gauge of the amount of entanglement in a state, we define an effective
entanglement functional giving us effective entanglement when the measurement
operators one has at their disposal are restricted by either fundamental
considerations, such as superselection rules, or practical inability to conduct
precise measurements. We show that effective entanglement is always reduced by
restricting measurements. We define effective entanglement as the least amount
of entanglement necessary to play all semiquantum nonlocal games at least as
well with unrestricted measurements as with the more entangled original state
and restricted measurements. We show that simple linear relationship between
effective and conventional G-concurrence, generalization of concurrence, can be
obtained when completely positive maps are used to describe measurement
restrictions. We consider how typical measurement errors like photon loss and
phase damping degrade effective entanglement in quantum optical experiments, as
well as the impact of mass superselection rules on entanglement of massive
indistinguishable particles. The flexibility of the effective entanglement
formalism allows this single-particle entanglement to be calculated in the
presence of a local Bose Einstein condensate reference frame with varying phase
uncertainty, thereby interpolating between the complete breaking or strict
application of the super-selection rule.

text: Sparse Combinatorial Group Testing (SCGT) is a method used to identify a small number of defective items within a larger set by testing groups of items rather than each item individually. This approach is particularly useful when the number of defective items is significantly smaller than the total population, allowing for substantial reduction in testing costs and time. Traditional group testing methods often assume a dense model where the number of defective items is not negligible. However, in scenarios with sparse defect rates, existing techniques may become inefficient.  The objective of this research is to develop new SCGT algorithms that can effectively handle sparse conditions while maintaining high accuracy in identifying defective items. To achieve this, we propose an innovative algorithm that leverages probabilistic models to minimize false positives and negatives. The methodology involves simulations and theoretical analysis to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm under various sparse conditions. We also compare it with existing methods using benchmark datasets.  Key findings indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms traditional group testing methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency, especially in environments characterized by low defect rates. Notably, the algorithm demonstrates superior performance even when the number of defective items is an order of magnitude smaller than the total population size. These results suggest that the proposed SCGT method can be a valuable tool for applications such as bioinformatics, network security, and quality control, where efficient identification of rare events is crucial.  In conclusion, this research contributes to the advancement of SCGT methodologies by providing a robust framework for handling sparse defect rates. The findings highlight the potential of these techniques in enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of various practical applications.

Specifically, it utilizes techniques such as sheaf cohomology, covering spaces, and the study of asymptotic cones. The key findings reveal that non-cocompact group actions often lead to $\pi_1$-semistability at infinity under specific geometric configurations, which is a significant departure from previous studies on cocompact actions.  The research concludes by offering new insights into the structure of non-cocompact group actions and their implications for the topological and geometric properties of the underlying spaces. text: In our study, we investigated the mechanisms underlying the formation of binary black hole (BBH) systems with low effective spins, high masses, and O1/O2 rate ratios, as observed by LIGO/Virgo. We adopted a population synthesis approach, where we modeled the evolution of binary stellar systems, taking into account the mass transfer, common envelope, and merger processes. Our simulations demonstrated that the observed properties could be explained by a combination of factors, including the initial mass ratio, metallicity, and common envelope evolution. Specifically, we found that wide initial mass ratios, metal-rich environments, and inefficient common envelope ejections led to the formation of BBHs with low effective spins, high masses, and O1/O2 rate ratios. Conversely, more equal mass ratios, metal-poor environments, and efficient common envelope ejections resulted in BBHs with higher effective spins, lower masses, and O1/O2 rate ratios consistent with earlier detections. Our results provide new insights into the formation channels of BBHs and have implications for the ongoing effort to test general relativity and astrophysical theories with gravitational wave signals. Further studies are warranted to validate and extend these findings, including the investigation of the impact of magnetic fields and star formation environments on BBH properties.

Based on high-resolution spectroscopy performed with the NES echelle
spectrograph of the 6-m telescope, we have studied the peculiarities of the
spectrum and the velocity field in the atmosphere and envelope of the cool
supergiant V1027 Cyg, the optical counterpart of the infrared source IRAS
20004+2955. For the first time, a splitting of the cores of strong absorptions
of metals and their ions (SiII, NiI, TiI, TiII, ScII, CrI, FeI, FeII, BaII) has
been detected in the stellar spectrum. The broad profile of these lines
contains a stable weak emission in the core whose position may be considered as
the systematic velocity Vsys=5.5 km/s. Small radial velocity variations with an
amplitude of 5-6 km/s due to pulsations have been revealed by symmetric low-
and moderate-intensity absorptions. A long-wavelength shift of the H$\alpha$
profile due to line core distortion is observed in the stellar spectrum.
Numerous weak CN molecular lines and the KI 7696 \AA\ line with a P Cyg profile
have been identified in the red spectral region. The coincidence of the radial
velocities measured from symmetric metal absorptions and CN lines suggests that
the CN spectrum is formed in the stellar atmosphere. We have also identified
numerous diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) whose positions in the spectrum,
Vr(DIBs)=$-12.0$ km/s, correspond to the velocity of the interstellar medium in
the Local arm of the Galaxy.

Our results showed that the FRBs exhibited a characteristic "millisecond-duration" emission pattern, consistent with magnetar activity. Furthermore, we detected a significant increase in X-ray flux from the associated magnetars following the FRB events, indicating that the bursts may be linked to magnetar flares.  Our findings suggest that magnetars are capable of producing FRBs through the collapse of their magnetic fields, potentially triggering a massive release of energy. This interpretation is supported by simulations that model the interaction between a magnetar's magnetic field and the surrounding interstellar medium. Our results provide strong evidence for the magnetar hypothesis, highlighting the importance of considering magnetar activity as a potential origin for FRBs.

Determining the properties of the warm ionized medium (WIM) at the leading
edge of spiral arms is important for understanding its dynamics and cloud
formation. The inner edge of the Scutum arm tangency is a unique location in
which to disentangle the WIM from other components. We use high spectral
resolution [C II] 158 micron and [N II] 205 micron fine structure line
observations taken with the upGREAT and GREAT instruments on SOFIA, along with
auxiliary HI and 13CO observations. The observations were in and out of the
Galactic plane along 18 lines of sight between longitude 30deg and 32deg. We
detect strong [N II] emission throughout the Scutum tangency. At VLSR = 110 to
125 km/s, where there is little, if any, 13CO, we could disentangle the [N II]
and [C II] emission that arises from the WIM at the inner edge. We find an
average electron density, <n(e)> about 0.9 cm{-3} in the plane, and about 0.4
cm{-3} above the plane. For VLSR < 110 km/s there is [N II] emission tracing
highly ionized gas throughout the arm's molecular layer. This ionized gas has a
high density, n(e) ~ 30 cm{-3}, and a few percent filling factor. Thus, [N II]
and [C II] at the Scutum arm tangency reveal a highly ionized gas with <n(e)>
about 10 to 20 times those of the interarm WIM, which is best explained by a
model in which the interarm WIM is compressed as it falls into the potential
well of the arm. The widespread distribution of [N II] in the molecular layers
shows that high density ionized gas is distributed throughout the Scutum arm.
The n(e) derived from [N II] for these molecular cloud regions are about 30
cm{-3}, and probably arise in the ionized boundary layers of clouds. This [N
II] emission from the ionized boundary layers is probably the result of the
shock compression of the WIM as it impacts the arm's neutral gas, but some
could arise from extended HII regions.

The most general case of self-induced neutrino flavor evolution is described
by a set of kinetic equations for a dense neutrino gas evolving both in space
and time. Solutions of these equations have been typically worked out assuming
that either the time (in the core-collapse supernova environment) or space (in
the early universe) homogeneity in the initial conditions is preserved through
the evolution. In these cases one can gauge away the homogeneous variable and
reduce the dimensionality of the problem. In this paper we investigate if small
deviations from an initial postulated homogeneity can be amplified by the
interacting neutrino gas, leading to a new flavor instability. To this end, we
consider a simple two flavor isotropic neutrino gas evolving in time, and
initially composed by only $\nu_e$ and $\bar\nu_e$ with equal densities. In the
homogeneous case, this system shows a bimodal instability in the inverted mass
hierarchy scheme, leading to the well studied flavor pendulum behavior. This
would lead to periodic pair conversions $\nu_e \bar\nu_e \leftrightarrow \nu_x
\bar\nu_x$. To break space homogeneity, we introduce small amplitude
space-dependent perturbations in the matter potential. By Fourier transforming
the equations of motion with respect to the space coordinate, we then
numerically solve a set of coupled equations for the different Fourier modes.
We find that even for arbitrarily tiny inhomogeneities, the system evolution
runs away from the stable pendulum behavior: the different modes are excited
and the space-averaged ensemble evolves towards flavor equilibrium. We finally
comment on the role of a time decaying neutrino background density in weakening
these results.

There has lately been increased interest in describing complex systems not
merely as single networks but rather as collections of networks that are
coupled to one another. We introduce an analytically tractable model that
enables one to connect two layers in a multilayer network by controlling the
locality of coupling. In particular we introduce a tractable model for
embedding one network (A) into another (B), focusing on the case where network
A has many more nodes than network B. In our model, nodes in network A are
assigned, or embedded, to the nodes in network B using an assignment rule where
the extent of node localization is controlled by a single parameter. We start
by mapping an unassigned `source' node in network A to a randomly chosen
`target' node in network B. We then assign the neighbors of the source node to
the neighborhood of the target node using a random walk starting at the target
node and with a per-step stopping probability $q$. By varying the parameter
$q$, we are able to produce a range of embeddings from local ($q = 1$) to
global ($q \to 0$). The simplicity of the model allows us to calculate key
quantities, making it a useful starting point for more realistic models.

Ensemble model output statistics (EMOS) is a statistical tool for
post-processing forecast ensembles of weather variables obtained from multiple
runs of numerical weather prediction models in order to produce calibrated
predictive probability density functions (PDFs). The EMOS predictive PDF is
given by a parametric distribution with parameters depending on the ensemble
forecasts. We propose an EMOS model for calibrating wind speed forecasts based
on weighted mixtures of truncated normal (TN) and log-normal (LN) distributions
where model parameters and component weights are estimated by optimizing the
values of proper scoring rules over a rolling training period. The new model is
tested on wind speed forecasts of the 50 member European Centre for
Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble, the 11 member Aire Limit\'ee
Adaptation dynamique D\'eveloppement International-Hungary Ensemble Prediction
System ensemble of the Hungarian Meteorological Service and the eight-member
University of Washington mesoscale ensemble, and its predictive performance is
compared to that of various benchmark EMOS models based on single parametric
families and combinations thereof. The results indicate improved calibration of
probabilistic and accuracy of point forecasts in comparison with the raw
ensemble and climatological forecasts. The mixture EMOS model significantly
outperforms the TN and LN EMOS methods, moreover, it provides better calibrated
forecasts than the TN-LN combination model and offers an increased flexibility
while avoiding covariate selection problems.

The research addresses the challenge of optimizing resource allocation while combating the inherent interuser interference in MIMO-OFDM systems.   Our results indicate that by utilizing advanced prediction models to estimate the channel states, incorporating efficient feedback mechanisms, and implementing intelligent scheduling algorithms, significant improvements in system capacity and user throughput can be achieved. These enhancements are pivotal for meeting the increasing demands of high data rate applications in modern wireless communications.  Key methodologies employed in this research include developing prediction algorithms based on historical channel information, designing feedback mechanisms to relay channel state information accurately, and devising scheduling policies that exploit the predicted channel states to allocate resources effectively among users. The proposed strategies are evaluated through simulations, demonstrating notable enhancements in system performance metrics compared to traditional approaches. Overall, our findings underscore the significance of Channel State Prediction, Feedback, and Scheduling techniques in optimizing multiuser MIMO-OFDM downlink systems for future wireless communication networks.

The size and complexity of software and hardware systems have significantly
increased in the past years. As a result, it is harder to guarantee their
correct behavior. One of the most successful methods for automated verification
of finite-state systems is model checking. Most of the current model-checking
systems use binary decision diagrams (BDDs) for the representation of the
tested model and in the verification process of its properties. Generally, BDDs
allow a canonical compact representation of a boolean function (given an order
of its variables). The more compact the BDD is, the better performance one gets
from the verifier. However, finding an optimal order for a BDD is an
NP-complete problem. Therefore, several heuristic methods based on expert
knowledge have been developed for variable ordering. We propose an alternative
approach in which the variable ordering algorithm gains 'ordering experience'
from training models and uses the learned knowledge for finding good orders.
Our methodology is based on offline learning of pair precedence classifiers
from training models, that is, learning which variable pair permutation is more
likely to lead to a good order. For each training model, a number of training
sequences are evaluated. Every training model variable pair permutation is then
tagged based on its performance on the evaluated orders. The tagged
permutations are then passed through a feature extractor and are given as
examples to a classifier creation algorithm. Given a model for which an order
is requested, the ordering algorithm consults each precedence classifier and
constructs a pair precedence table which is used to create the order. Our
algorithm was integrated with SMV, which is one of the most widely used
verification systems. Preliminary empirical evaluation of our methodology,
using real benchmark models, shows performance that is better than random
ordering and is competitive with existing algorithms that use expert knowledge.
We believe that in sub-domains of models (alu, caches, etc.) our system will
prove even more valuable. This is because it features the ability to learn
sub-domain knowledge, something that no other ordering algorithm does.

text: The Gaia-ESO Survey aims to investigate the dynamical properties of globular clusters through precise measurements of their kinematics. This study focuses on dynamically flattened, rotating globular clusters. Employing multi-band photometry and spectroscopy from the Gaia-ESO Survey, we construct detailed kinematic models using the GALPY software package. Our models incorporate various parameters such as velocity dispersion, rotation, and tidal effects to accurately describe the observed stellar populations within these clusters. Key findings indicate that many of the studied globular clusters exhibit significant flattening along their major axes, which is consistent with predictions from theoretical models of cluster evolution under tidal forces. Additionally, our results suggest that these clusters rotate, with some showing evidence of prograde rotation while others exhibit retrograde motion. The data also reveal a correlation between flattening and rotation rate, providing insights into the balance between tidal stripping and internal dynamical processes. In conclusion, the comprehensive analysis of these clusters highlights the importance of tidal forces in shaping the dynamics and morphology of globular clusters, contributing to our understanding of stellar cluster evolution.

text: Key-value storage systems are foundational to modern data-intensive applications, necessitating efficient data placement strategies to optimize performance. This study investigates Gang-GC, a novel locality-aware parallel data placement optimization framework for key-value storages. The objective is to enhance the efficiency of data retrieval and storage operations by leveraging data locality and parallel processing techniques. To achieve this, we integrate a locality-aware grouping mechanism that clusters related keys spatially and temporally, alongside employing parallel garbage collection processes that maximize throughput and minimize latency. Our methodology includes the development of an algorithm that dynamically adapts to workload changes, ensuring optimal data placement alignment with evolving access patterns. Furthermore, we conducted extensive experiments using real-world benchmark datasets to evaluate the performance gains offered by Gang-GC compared to traditional data placement strategies. The key findings reveal that Gang-GC significantly improves read/write performance and reduces garbage collection overhead by up to 30%, highlighting its superiority in handling large-scale, distributed key-value storage systems. Additionally, the locality-aware design contributes to better cache utilization and lower network traffic, further amplifying system efficiency. In conclusion, Gang-GC presents a robust solution to the challenges of data placement in key-value storages, demonstrating enhanced scalability and adaptability that benefit a wide array of applications. Our research underscores the importance of locality-awareness in storage optimizations and offers insights into future developments in data-intensive system performance enhancements.

text: In this work, we investigate the moments of the Hilbert-Schmidt probability distributions as they pertain to the determinants of real two-qubit density matrices and their partial transposes. These moments are instrumental in exploring the geometric structure of quantum state spaces and offer insights into the separability problem that arises in quantum information theory. Utilizing advanced methods of integration over matrix manifolds, we formulate the explicit computation of these moments, both for the density matrices themselves and their partial transposes. Our approach builds upon the framework of statistical geometry, where the positive semidefinite constraint of density matrices is rigorously managed. We apply group-invariant measures to effectively handle the inherent isotropy and ensure the tractability of the integrations involved. The canonical parametrization of the real two-qubit space is employed to facilitate exact analytical evaluations. Our findings reveal distinctive behaviors in the distributions' higher moments, elucidating the nuanced relationship between entangled and separable states when exposed to partial transpositions. The results demonstrate that certain moment patterns serve as markers for the presence of entanglement, confirmed through comprehensive computational simulations. These insights advance the understanding of entanglement metric distribution in bipartite systems, contributing a pivotal analytic tool for future studies focused on larger systems or where density matrices display more intricate symmetries. This work underscores the utility of moment analysis as a powerful technique in probing the quantum mechanical properties of multi-qubit systems and denotes significant applications in quantum computing, particularly in tasks necessitating efficient entanglement detection and management.

In an effort to produce Giant Magnetocaloric effect (GMCE) near room
temperature, in a first ever such study, the austenite transformation
temperature (As) was fine tuned to ferromagnetic Curie temperature (TC) in
Ferromagnetic Shape Memory Alloys (FSMA) and a large GMCE of delta-SM = - 81.75
J/Kg-K was achieved in Ni50Mn18.5Cu6.5Ga25 alloy during reverse martensitic
transformation (heating cycle) for a magnetic field change of 9 T at 302.5 K.
Fine tuning of As with TC was achieved by Cu substitution in Ni50Mn25-xCuxGa25
(0< x < 7.0)-based FSMAs. Characterizations of these alloys were carried out
using Optical and Scanning Electron Microscopy, X-ray Diffraction (XRD),
Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and DC magnetization measurements.
Addition of Cu to stoichiometric Heusler type Ni2MnGa increases the martensitic
transformation temperatures and decreases TC. Concurrently, DSM increases with
Cu addition and peaks at 6.5 at. % Cu for which there is a virtual overlap
between TC and As. Maximum Refrigerant Capacity (RCP) of 327.01 J/Kg was also
achieved in the heating cycle for 9 T field change at 302.5 K. Corresponding
values for the cooling cycle measurements (measured during forward
transformation) were 30.4 J/Kg-K and 123.52 J/Kg respectively for the same 6.5

The launching mechanism of the jets of active galactic nuclei is
observationally poorly constrained, due to the large distances to these objects
and the very small scales (sub-parsec) involved. In order to better constrain
theoretical models, it is especially important to get information from the
region close to the physical base of the jet, where the plasma acceleration
takes place. In this paper, we report multi-epoch and multi-frequency continuum
observations of the z=2.5 blazar PKS1830-211 with ALMA, serendipitously
coincident with a strong $\gamma$-ray flare reported by Fermi-LAT. The blazar
is lensed by a foreground z=0.89 galaxy, with two bright images of the compact
core separated by 1". Our ALMA observations individually resolve these two
images (although not any of their substructures), and we study the change of
their relative flux ratio with time (four epochs spread over nearly three times
the time delay between the two lensed images) and frequency (between 350 and
1050 GHz, rest-frame of the blazar), during the $\gamma$-ray flare. In
particular, we detect a remarkable frequency-dependent behaviour of the flux
ratio, which implies the presence of a chromatic structure in the blazar (i.e.,
a core-shift effect). We rule out the possiblity of micro- and milli-lensing
effects and propose instead a simple model of plasmon ejection in the blazar's
jet to explain the time and frequency variability of the flux ratio. We suggest
that PKS1830-211 is likely one of the best sources to probe the activity at the
base of a blazar's jet at submillimeter wavelengths, thanks to the peculiar
geometry of the system. The implications of the core-shift in absorption
studies of the foreground z=0.89 galaxy (e.g., constraints on the cosmological
variations of fundamental constants) are discussed.

text: The search for sterile neutrino mixing is a critical area of investigation that seeks to resolve anomalies in neutrino oscillations, potentially indicating physics beyond the Standard Model. The MINOS (Main Injector Neutrino Oscillation Search) long-baseline experiment provides an ideal framework for this study due to its ability to measure neutrino oscillations over a distance of 735 km from Fermilab to the Soudan Underground Laboratory. The objective of this research is to investigate the presence of sterile neutrinos, which could mix with active neutrinos, leading to deviations from expected oscillation patterns. The methodology involves an analysis of the muon neutrino and antineutrino disappearance data collected by the MINOS experiment over several years, utilizing both charged-current and neutral-current interactions to enhance sensitivity to sterile neutrino mixing parameters.   Our key findings suggest that the data are generally consistent with a three-flavor neutrino model, showing no significant statistical evidence for the existence of sterile neutrinos in the parameter space probed. However, the measurement allows us to set new constraints on the sterile neutrino mixing angle θ_24 and the mass-squared difference Δm^2_41, thereby tightening the limits from prior experiments. In conclusion, while this investigation does not confirm the presence of sterile neutrinos, it provides essential constraints that guide future searches. The results reinforce the significance of continued exploration of neutrino properties, which is crucial for understanding fundamental particle physics and cosmology.

We develop and demonstrate a classification system constituted by several
Support Vector Machines (SVM) classifiers, which can be applied to select
quasar candidates from large sky survey projects, such as SDSS, UKIDSS, GALEX.
How to construct this SVM classification system is presented in detail. When
the SVM classification system works on the test set to predict quasar
candidates, it acquires the efficiency of 93.21% and the completeness of
97.49%. In order to further prove the reliability and feasibility of this
system, two chunks are randomly chosen to compare its performance with that of
the XDQSO method used for SDSS-III's BOSS. The experimental results show that
the high faction of overlap exists between the quasar candidates selected by
this system and those extracted by the XDQSO technique in the dereddened i-band
magnitude range between 17.75 and 22.45, especially in the interval of
dereddened i-band magnitude < 20.0. In the two test areas, 57.38% and 87.15% of
the quasar candidates predicted by the system are also targeted by the XDQSO
method. Similarly, the prediction of subcategories of quasars according to
redshift achieves a high level of overlap with these two approaches. Depending
on the effectiveness of this system, the SVM classification system can be used
to create the input catalog of quasars for the GuoShouJing Telescope (LAMOST)

We report the magnetic, heat-capacity, dielectric and magnetodielectric (MDE)
behaviour of a Haldane spin-chain compound containing light rare-earth ion,
Nd2BaNiO5, in detail, as a function of temperature (T) and magnetic field (H)
down to 2 K. In addition to the well-known long range antiferromagnetic order
setting in at (T_N=) 48 K as indicated in dc magnetization (M), we have
observed another magnetic transition near 10 K; this transition appears to be
of a glassy-type which vanishes with a marginal application of external
magnetic field (even H= 100 Oe). There are corresponding anomalies in
dielectric constant as well with variation of T. The isothermal M(H) curves at
2 and 5 K reveal the existence of a magnetic-field induced transition around 90
kOe; the isothermal H-dependent dielectric constant also tracks such a
metamagnetic transition. These results illustrate the MDE coupling in this
compound. Additionally, we observe a strong frequency dependence of a step in
T-dependent dielectric constant with this feature appearing around 25-30 K for
the lowest frequency of 1 kHz, far below T_N. This is attributed to interplay
between crystal-field effect and exchange interaction between Nd and Ni, which
establishes the sensitivity of dielectric measurements to detect such effects.
Interestingly enough, the observed dispersions of the T-dependent dielectric
constant curves is essentially H-independent in the entire T-range of
measurement, despite the existence of MDE coupling, which is in sharp contrast
with other heavy rare-earth members in this series.

text: In this study, we propose a novel approach for testing hypotheses in complex high-dimensional systems using a mixture estimation model. The methodology allows for the identification and estimation of latent subpopulations within the data, enabling the testing of hypotheses regarding their respective differences in model parameters. By formulating the hypothesis testing problem as a maximum likelihood estimation problem, we derive an iterative algorithm for estimating the mixing coefficients and subpopulation parameters.  We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through an application to a genomic dataset, where we test hypotheses regarding differential expression between two subpopulations of cells. The mixture estimation model successfully identifies the subpopulations and estimates their differential expression profiles, enabling accurate hypothesis testing with a controlled false discovery rate. Our methodology offers several advantages over traditional methods, including the ability to handle large datasets, the flexibility to model heterogeneous subpopulations, and the ability to simultaneously estimate subpopulation and model parameter differences.  Our results highlight the utility of mixture estimation models for hypothesis testing in complex systems, offering a powerful tool for data analysts and researchers in various domains, including genomics, imaging, and finance. The proposed iterative algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation of the mixture model provides a computationally efficient approach for testing hypotheses, providing researchers with valuable insights and confidence in their findings. Future work includes the extension of our methodology to more complex models, such as those with dependent observations or latent variables, as well as the development of more sophisticated techniques for hypothesis testing within the framework of mixture estimation models.

text: We investigate the fusion of light nuclei at near-barrier energies utilizing a quantum diffusion approach to enhance our understanding of the underlying mechanisms dictating fusion processes. Fusion at these energies is an intricate phenomenon, often hindered by potential barriers that must be overcome for reactions to occur. Our work aims to elucidate the dynamics of fusion by employing a quantum diffusion framework that incorporates the subtle interplay between nuclear interactions and quantum tunneling effects.   We conduct simulations that reveal how fluctuations in nuclear structure, coupled with dissipative processes, influence the fusion probability. Our results demonstrate that the effective diffusion coefficients are sensitive to the parameters of the nuclear potential, and we explore the dependence of fusion cross-sections on impact parameters and interaction timescales. We specifically observe that incorporating a temperature-dependent potential enhances the agreement between theoretical predictions and experimentally measured fusion rates at near-barrier energies.  Our findings contribute to the understanding of fusion processes in astrophysical environments, where low-energy collisions predominate, and they offer insights into the behavior of heavier nuclei where fusion barriers are significantly more pronounced. We propose that our quantum diffusion methodology serves as a robust tool for modeling nuclear reactions across various energy regimes, paving the way for future research that may explore more complex systems. The implications of our results extend to both theoretical frameworks and experimental approaches in nuclear physics, highlighting the critical balance between quantum mechanics and collective nuclear behavior in fusion processes.
