Several methods are available for the detection of covarying positions from a
multiple sequence alignment (MSA). If the MSA contains a large number of
sequences, information about the proximities between residues derived from
covariation maps can be sufficient to predict a protein fold. If the structure
is already known, information on the covarying positions can be valuable to
understand the protein mechanism.
  In this study we have sought to determine whether a multivariate extension of
traditional mutual information (MI) can be an additional tool to study
covariation. The performance of two multidimensional MI (mdMI) methods,
designed to remove the effect of ternary/quaternary interdependencies, was
tested with a set of 9 MSAs each containing <400 sequences, and was shown to be
comparable to that of methods based on maximum entropy/pseudolikelyhood
statistical models of protein sequences. However, while all the methods tested
detected a similar number of covarying pairs among the residues separated by <
8 {\AA} in the reference X-ray structures, there was on average less than 65%
overlap between the top scoring pairs detected by methods that are based on
different principles.
  We have also attempted to identify whether the difference in performance
among methods is due to different efficiency in removing covariation
originating from chains of structural contacts. We found that the reason why
methods that derive partial correlation between the columns of a MSA provide a
better recognition of close contacts is not because they remove chaining
effects, but because they filter out the correlation between distant residues
that originates from general fitness constraints. In contrast we found that
true chaining effects are expression of real physical perturbations that
propagate inside proteins, and therefore are not removed by the derivation of
partial correlation between variables.

The complex interactions involved in regulation of a cell's function are
captured by its interaction graph. More often than not, detailed knowledge
about enhancing or suppressive regulatory influences and cooperative effects is
lacking and merely the presence or absence of directed interactions is known.
Here we investigate to which extent such reduced information allows to forecast
the effect of a knock-out or a combination of knock-outs. Specifically we ask
in how far the lethality of eliminating nodes may be predicted by their network
centrality, such as degree and betweenness, without knowing the function of the
system. The function is taken as the ability to reproduce a fixed point under a
discrete Boolean dynamics. We investigate two types of stochastically generated
networks: fully random networks and structures grown with a mechanism of node
duplication and subsequent divergence of interactions. On all networks we find
that the out-degree is a good predictor of the lethality of a single node
knock-out. For knock-outs of node pairs, the fraction of successors shared
between the two knocked-out nodes (out-overlap) is a good predictor of
synthetic lethality. Out-degree and out-overlap are locally defined and
computationally simple centrality measures that provide a predictive power
close to the optimal predictor.

text: This study presents a comprehensive investigation of the multiwavelength variability of the blazar Mrk 421 using a Monte Carlo multi-zone code. Blazars, a class of active galactic nuclei, exhibit intense and rapid variability across the electromagnetic spectrum, which is a key characteristic of these objects. Mrk 421, a well-studied blazar, is particularly notable for its extreme variability, making it an ideal target for investigating the underlying physical processes.  The objective of this research is to simulate the time-dependent variability of Mrk 421 using a Monte Carlo multi-zone code, which allows for the treatment of complex physical processes and the incorporation of multiple wavelength regimes. The code is based on a semi-analytical model of the blazar's emission, which includes the effects of relativistic jet formation, synchrotron radiation, and Compton scattering.  The simulations are performed using a combination of physical parameters and emission models, which are randomly drawn from a predefined probability distribution. The results show that the Monte Carlo code is able to reproduce the observed variability patterns of Mrk 421, including the characteristic "humps" and "dips" in the light curves. The simulations also reveal the importance of relativistic effects, such as jet formation and acceleration, in shaping the variability patterns.  The key findings of this study highlight the potential of Monte Carlo simulations to model the complex variability of blazars, such as Mrk 421. The results also demonstrate the importance of considering relativistic effects in the modeling of blazar variability. Overall, this research contributes to our understanding of the physical processes that govern the variability of blazars and provides a framework for future studies of this phenomenon.

text: In this study, we explore the transient wave resistance encountered when a wave interacts with a real, three-dimensional, fluid shear current. Employing the methodology of potential flow theory, we modeled the wave-current interaction using a complex computational fluid dynamics model, the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations. The model simulated the interaction between a JONSWAP spectrum wave and a shear current with varying velocities and directions. Our results revealed significant fluctuations in wave resistance as a function of wave frequency and the orientation of the shear current.  These findings confirm the importance of accounting for the impact of real currents on wave resistance measurements, as shear currents are a common feature in many aquatic environments. By elucidating the dynamics of the wave-current interaction, our study provides valuable insight into the complex physical processes that govern the exchange of energy between waves and currents. Furthermore, the results obtained from this study can serve as a basis for the development of improved wave resistance prediction models, particularly in areas such as ocean engineering, coastal management, and offshore renewable energy.  This research represents a significant advancement in understanding the transient nature of wave resistance in the presence of real shear currents. By utilizing advanced computational modeling techniques, we were able to provide a more comprehensive representation of wave resistance behavior, providing essential information for accurately predicting wave energy exchange and assessing the effects of currents on wave propagation in natural and engineered systems.

text: Hilbert's Theorem 90 is a pivotal result in algebraic K-theory and Galois cohomology, traditionally applied within finite settings. This paper explores an analogue of Hilbert's Theorem 90 in the context of infinite symmetric groups, which are fundamental structures in algebra and have significant implications in combinatorial and representation theory. The primary objective of this study is to establish a cohomological framework that adapts Hilbert's insights into the realm of infinite permutations, focusing on the group’s action on infinitely many objects.  Employing tools from homological algebra and infinite group theory, we utilize a combination of spectral sequences and cohomological dimensions to analyze the properties and behaviors of infinite symmetric groups. We derive key results regarding the calculation of cohomological dimensions and provide a detailed investigation into the implications of our findings for the understanding of classifying spaces and their topological properties.  Our key findings reveal that, analogous to finite cases, the first cohomology group of the infinite symmetric group vanishes under certain conditions, thereby affirming a form of the classical theorem in an infinite setting. Furthermore, the results extend to characterize the relationships between various infinite symmetric groups and their subgroups.   In conclusion, this research not only provides a new perspective on Hilbert's Theorem 90 but also enriches the understanding of cohomological aspects in infinite group theory, opening avenues for further exploration in both theoretical and applied mathematical contexts.

text: This research explores the detailed spectral analysis of the emission line AM CVn systems GP Com and V396 Hya using UVES (Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph) and X-Shooter spectrographs. The primary objectives were to investigate the chemical abundances, stellar parameters, and kinematic properties of these systems. Observations were conducted at the Very Large Telescope (VLT) to capture high-resolution spectra that provide insights into the complex interactions between the compact white dwarf and the red giant component.  The methodology involved detailed spectral fitting of the observed emission lines to derive stellar parameters such as effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity. Additionally, kinematic studies were performed to assess the orbital velocities and spatial distribution of the material in the system. The UVES provided high-resolution data suitable for precise velocity measurements, while X-Shooter enabled broader wavelength coverage, facilitating comprehensive elemental analyses.  Key findings include the determination of enhanced carbon abundances in both systems, indicating significant accretion processes from the red giant onto the white dwarf. The spectroscopic analysis also revealed distinct variations in kinematics, suggesting differences in the mass transfer rates and the dynamics of material around each star. These results contribute to our understanding of the evolutionary stages of AM CVn systems and the mechanisms driving their variability.  In conclusion, the combined use of UVES and X-Shooter spectroscopy has significantly advanced our knowledge of AM CVn systems by providing unprecedented details about their structural and dynamical properties. Further studies with similar techniques will be crucial for unraveling the full complexity of these fascinating objects.

text: We present an adaptive conditional zero-forcing decoder that promises full-diversity, minimal computational complexity, and near maximum-likelihood performance when applied to space-time block codes (STBCs). This work aims to tackle the crucial problem of balancing performance and complexity in decoding mechanisms for STBCs, a fundamental challenge in wireless communications. To achieve this, our methodology incorporates conditional processing mechanisms that adaptively determine the necessity of zero-forcing operations, thereby optimizing computational resources without compromising error performance. We establish mathematical models to characterize this adaptive technique and demonstrate that the proposed decoder retains full-diversity performance. Our empirical analysis, conducted through extensive simulations across varying channel conditions and signal configurations, confirms that our decoder achieves essentially maximum-likelihood performance but at substantially reduced complexity compared to existing zero-forcing methods. Furthermore, we include comparative analysis illustrating the superiority of our methodology against traditional fixed-complexity zero-forcing and linear decoders. The results demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of our approach, emphasizing its practical applicability in real-world wireless systems. We conclude that our adaptive conditional zero-forcing decoder provides a promising solution for STBC decoding, capable of enhancing the reliability and efficiency of modern communication networks. This work paves the way for further innovations in the design of low-complexity, high-performance decoding algorithms that can meet the burgeoning demands of future wireless systems.

text: This study presents a systematic analysis of non-LTE abundances for F and G dwarfs with metallicities ranging from -2.6 to +0.2 solar units (dex) within the solar neighborhood. The primary objective was to investigate the abundance patterns of elements from lithium (Li) to europium (Eu). Utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy and advanced radiative transfer models, we aimed to refine our understanding of stellar atmospheres under conditions where the assumptions of local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) do not hold. Key findings include the detection and precise measurement of non-LTE effects on key elements such as iron group elements, rare earths, and light metals. These results highlight deviations from LTE predictions, particularly in regions where the temperature and density profiles deviate significantly from those assumed in LTE calculations. The analysis reveals that non-LTE effects can lead to substantial variations in elemental abundances, influencing our interpretation of stellar properties and chemical evolution studies. The comprehensive dataset provides a robust framework for future studies of stellar atmospheres and their impact on elemental abundances across different metallicity ranges.

text: This research explores the application of super learning techniques in the SAS (Statistical Analysis System) for data analysis and predictive modeling. Super learning, an ensemble learning method, combines several weak learners to create a strong model with improved accuracy and generalization capabilities. The SAS system offers various built-in functions and procedures to implement super learning algorithms, including SAS Enterprise Miner and SAS Proc MLCV.  The objective of this study is to evaluate the performance of super learning algorithms in the SAS system using a real-world dataset for churn prediction. The methodology consists of three main stages data preprocessing, model selection, and model evaluation. Data preprocessing involves cleaning, transforming, and encoding the data. Model selection includes comparing the performance of super learning algorithms such as Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Support Vector Machines using the given dataset. Model evaluation is carried out using performance metrics like accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.  The key findings reveal that the Gradient Boosting model outperforms other super learning algorithms in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Furthermore, this model's predictions are stable and reliable, even with complex interaction effects and non-linear relationships in the data. The implemented super learning techniques in the SAS system significantly improve the performance of predictive models, making them valuable for businesses to reduce churn rates and improve customer retention.  In conclusion, this study demonstrates the potential of super learning techniques in the SAS system for data analysis and predictive modeling. By combining multiple weak learners, the SAS system can generate strong and accurate models for various applications, including churn prediction. The superior performance of these models highlights the importance of integrating super learning techniques in data analytics and business intelligence solutions.

text: Transitional disks are crucial objects for understanding the processes of planet formation and disk evolution. This study investigates the physical characteristics of these disks, emphasizing the evidence for disk flattening or gas depletion. Our primary objective was to assess the structural changes in transitional disks using data from the Herschel Space Observatory. We conducted a detailed analysis of the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and gas line emissions from a sample of transitional disks. Utilizing Herschel's Photodetecting Array Camera and Spectrometer (PACS) and Spectral and Photometric Imaging Receiver (SPIRE), we obtained high-resolution far-infrared observations. These data allowed us to trace the dust and gas components of the disks with unprecedented clarity. The results reveal a significant diversity in the disk architectures, where some transitional disks exhibit evidence of flattening, as indicated by their SED profiles and reduced mid-infrared excess. Additionally, a comparative analysis of the gas-to-dust mass ratios suggests a substantial gas depletion in certain systems. These findings support the hypothesis that transitional disks undergo structural flattening or gas depletion, which is potentially linked to the formation of planetary bodies within the disk. Our research confirms that these transformations may be indicative of advanced evolutionary stages in disk lifecycles. This work advances the current understanding of transitional disks and their role in the protoplanetary evolution, providing insights that will inform future observational and theoretical studies in the field.

text: Our study presents the Planck collaboration's intermediate results on probing interstellar gas and dust within the Chamaeleon clouds using data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) and the Planck satellite. The Chamaeleon clouds, known for their proximity and richness in star-forming regions, offer a unique opportunity to investigate the interplay between interstellar gas, dust, and high-energy processes.   Our research aims to address the complex interactions between cosmic rays, interstellar gas, and dust in the Chamaeleon clouds by utilizing the Fermi LAT data to map the high-energy emission associated with cosmic rays, while Planck observations provide insight into the thermal emission from interstellar dust.   Our findings reveal a detailed distribution of interstellar gas traced by carbon monoxide emission and interstellar dust thermal emission across the Chamaeleon clouds. Additionally, we identify regions of enhanced cosmic-ray activity and investigate their impact on the surrounding interstellar medium. The combination of Fermi LAT and Planck data allows us to better understand the physical properties of the interstellar medium in the Chamaeleon clouds, shedding light on the dynamics of star formation and the influence of high-energy processes on the surrounding environment. Our methodology demonstrates the power of multi-wavelength observations in studying the complex astrophysical phenomena in our Galaxy.

text: This study examines the impact of network externality on the pricing strategy of mobile social services, shifting from separate pricing to bundled pricing models. The proliferation of mobile social services, such as messaging, social media, and online gaming, has led to an increase in user engagement and retention, resulting in network effects. However, the current pricing strategies of these services often fail to capture the full value of these network effects, leading to revenue shortfalls.  The objective of this research is to investigate the effectiveness of bundled pricing models in capturing the network externality of mobile social services, with a focus on user behavior, revenue maximization, and business sustainability. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis methods.  The results indicate that bundled pricing models can significantly increase revenue and user engagement, as they provide users with a more comprehensive and value-added service experience. The findings also suggest that separate pricing models can lead to user dissatisfaction and churn, highlighting the need for more integrated pricing strategies. Furthermore, the study identifies key factors influencing the adoption of bundled pricing models, including user demographics, service offerings, and market competition.  The study's conclusion highlights the importance of considering network externality in mobile social services pricing strategies, with a focus on developing more integrated and value-added service models. The findings contribute to the existing literature on pricing strategy and network effects, providing insights for mobile social services providers seeking to maximize revenue and user engagement.

text: The dynamic critical behavior of model A under zero-mode boundary conditions in film geometries is explored, focusing on an expansion near four dimensions. The study aims to understand the modifications in critical dynamics when spatial confinement alters the fluctuations near the critical point. Our objective is to elucidate the evolution of dynamic scaling laws when transitioning from bulk to confined geometries, which capture essential features of systems such as thin magnetic films. Utilizing a renormalization group framework, dynamic renormalization group techniques are employed to analyze the model's behavior. Calculations are performed in the epsilon expansion, where epsilon represents the deviation from the upper critical dimension, specifically examining the zero-mode boundary conditions which modify the system's dynamic scaling exponents. Key findings reveal that the critical exponents exhibit film-specific modifications, distinguishing them from bulk values and manifesting unique crossover behavior dependent on film thickness and the nature of the boundary conditions. The presence of zero modes, a consequence of the confinement, leads to significant departures from the expected bulk-critical behavior and highlights the necessity of incorporating these effects into critical dynamic studies of low-dimensional systems. The research contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of critical dynamics in confined geometries and offers valuable insights into the application of renormalization group theory in non-bulk systems. Conclusionally, this study enhances the theoretical framework necessary for interpreting experiments on spatially restricted critical systems, providing a stepping stone for further investigations into complex boundary-induced phenomena in critical dynamics.

Given that Campaign 16 of the K2 mission is one of just two K2 campaigns
observed so far in "forward-facing" mode, which enables immediate follow-up
observations from the ground, we present a catalog of interesting targets
identified through photometry alone. Our catalog includes 30 high-quality
planet candidates (showing no signs of being non-planetary in nature), 48 more
ambiguous events that may be either planets or false positives, 164 eclipsing
binaries, and 231 other regularly periodic variable sources. We have released
light curves for all targets in C16, and have also released system parameters
and transit vetting plots for all interesting candidates identified in this
paper. Of particular interest is a candidate planet orbiting the bright F dwarf
HD 73344 (V=6.9, K=5.6) with an orbital period of 15 days. If confirmed, this
object would correspond to a $2.56 \pm 0.18 \ R_\oplus$ planet and would likely
be a favorable target for radial velocity characterization. This paper is
intended as a rapid release of planet candidates, eclipsing binaries and other
interesting periodic variables to maximize the scientific yield of this
campaign, and as a test run for the upcoming TESS mission, whose frequent data
releases call for similarly rapid candidate identification and efficient
follow-up.

The resonant activation effect (RA) has been well studied in different ways
during the last two decades. It consists in the presence of a minimum in the
mean time spent by a Brownian particle to exit from a potential well in the
presence of a fluctuating external force, as a function of the mean frequency
(or the correlation time) of the latter. This work studies the role played by
the asymmetry of a piecewise linear potential in the RA effect, and, in
general, the behavior of the mean first passage time and the mean velocity of
the particle crossing through the potential barrier. A strong dependence on the
asymmetry of the potential has been found which can be put in relationship with
the current in the ratchet whose the potential here used is an elementary
module. In this case a current reversal as a function of the frequency of the
switching potential occurs. Comparison of the calculations with the
Doering-Gadua model have been performed, as well as comparison with smooth
symmetrical potentials, by checking for the robustness of the resonant
correlation time. The calculations have been done by solving numerically the
Langevin equation in the presence of an uncorrelated Gaussian noise. The
resonant mean first passage times show an unexpected behavior as a function of
the thermal noise intensity. The related curves present for the different
symmetries an unexpected inversion of their relative behavior beyond a certain
threshold value of the noise. This means that the current reversal can only
occur for weak noise intensities, lower than that threshold value.

text: This research investigates the fragmentation and dynamical collapse processes occurring within the starless high-mass star-forming region IRDC18310-4. The objective of this study is to understand the mechanisms leading to the formation of high-mass stars within fragmented regions like IRDC18310-4.   Methodology involved the application of a variety of analytical tools, such as dendrogram analysis, position-velocity diagrams, and spectral energy distribution fitting, to characterize the fragmentation and collapse processes in the region.   Key findings include the identification of multiple high-density substructures within IRDC18310-4, indicating ongoing fragmentation processes. The analysis also revealed velocity gradients and infall signatures, suggesting dynamical collapse occurring within the region. Additionally, the study found evidence of potential high-mass star formation activities within the identified substructures.  In conclusion, this research highlights the complex interplay between fragmentation and dynamical collapse processes in the high-mass star-forming region IRDC18310-4. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for elucidating the formation of high-mass stars and the evolution of star-forming regions.

Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) produce characteristic infrared
emission bands that have been observed in a wide range of astrophysical
environments, where carbonaceous material is subjected to ultraviolet (UV)
radiation. Although PAHs are expected to form in carbon-rich AGB stars, they
have up to now only been observed in binary systems where a hot companion
provides a hard radiation field. In this letter, we present low-resolution
infrared spectra of four S-type AGB stars, selected from a sample of 90 S-type
AGB stars observed with the infrared spectrograph aboard the Spitzer satellite.
The spectra of these four stars show the typical infrared features of PAH
molecules. We confirm the correlation between the temperature of the central
star and the centroid wavelength of the 7.9 {\mu}m feature, present in a wide
variety of stars spanning a temperature range from 3 000 to 12 000 K. Three of
four sources presented in this paper extend this relation towards lower
temperatures. We argue that the mixture of hydrocarbons we see in these S-stars
has a rich aliphatic component. The fourth star, BZ CMa, deviates from this
correlation. Based on the similarity with the evolved binary TU Tau, we predict
that BZ CMa has a hot companion as well.

We examine phase transitions between the easy, hard, and the unsolvable
phases when attempting to identify structure in large complex networks
(community detection) in the presence of disorder induced by network noise
(spurious links that obscure structure), heat bath temperature $T$, and system
size $N$. When present, transitions at low temperature or low noise correspond
to entropy driven (or "order by disorder") annealing effects wherein stability
may initially increase as temperature or noise is increased before becoming
unsolvable at sufficiently high temperature or noise. Additional transitions
between contending viable solutions (such as those at different natural scales)
are also possible. When analyzing community structure via a dynamical approach,
"chaotic-type" transitions were previously identified [Phil. Mag. {\bf 92} 406
(2012)]. The correspondence between the spin-glass-type complexity transitions
and transitions into chaos in dynamical analogs might extend to other hard
computational problems. In this work, we examine large networks that have a
large number of communities. We infer that large systems at a constant ratio of
$q$ to the number of nodes $N$ asymptotically tend toward insolvability in the
limit of large $N$ for any positive $T$. The asymptotic behavior of
temperatures below which structure identification might be possible, $T_\times
=O[1/\log q]$, decreases slowly, so for practical system sizes, there remains
an accessible, and generally easy, global solvable phase at low temperature. We
further employ multivariate Tutte polynomials to show that increasing $q$
emulates increasing $T$ for a general Potts model, leading to a similar
stability region at low $T$. Given the relation between Tutte and Jones
polynomials, our results further suggest a link between the above complexity
transitions and transitions associated with random knots.

text: This study explores the scalar Casimir effect within a linearly expanding universe, investigating how cosmic expansion influences the Casimir force between two uncharged conducting plates. Building upon existing theories that consider the Casimir effect in static spacetime, this research extends the analysis to include the dynamic effects of an expanding universe. The methodology involves employing quantum field theory in curved spacetime, with a particular focus on the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric to model the expanding universe. Key findings indicate that the Casimir force exhibits a complex behavior under cosmic expansion, characterized by variations in both magnitude and direction depending on the scale factor of the universe. Additionally, the results suggest that the Casimir force becomes more significant as the universe expands, potentially offering insights into the interplay between quantum mechanics and cosmology. The conclusion highlights the importance of accounting for cosmic expansion when studying the Casimir effect, emphasizing the need for further theoretical and experimental investigations to better understand these phenomena.

text: Cosmic rays, subatomic particles originating from outer space, have long been a fascinating subject in particle physics. Traditionally, observing and studying cosmic rays relied on stationary detectors situated on Earth. However, the advent of technology and the increasing interest in space exploration have opened new possibilities for observing these particles. In this research, we propose a novel approach to cosmic ray detection the Cosmic-Ray Extremely Distributed Observatory (CREDO).  The objective of CREDO is to leverage the vast computational power and vast sensor networks available to ordinary citizens to build a massive distributed observatory for cosmic ray detection. By harnessing the capabilities of smartphones, laptops, and other Internet of Things (IoT) devices, we aim to create a global network of sensors that can detect and record cosmic rays in real-time.  The methodology involves developing software that can detect cosmic ray signals using the sensors available on these devices and transmitting the data to a central server for analysis. The software is designed to be lightweight and easy to integrate into existing applications, ensuring minimal disruption to the user experience.  The key findings of this research include the feasibility of using CREDO to detect cosmic rays at a scale not previously possible and the potential for enhancing scientific research and education by engaging the public in the scientific process. Furthermore, we propose several potential applications of CREDO, such as real-time monitoring of the solar wind, tracking cosmic ray showers, and studying the effects of cosmic rays on electronic devices.  In conclusion, CREDO represents a novel and promising approach to cosmic ray detection that harnesses the power of distributed computing and the vast sensor networks available to ordinary citizens. This research outlines the potential benefits and applications of CREDO and provides a roadmap for its implementation.

text: We investigated the application of fixed point and Bregman iterative methods to matrix rank minimization problems, a class of non-convex optimization problems. Our goal was to develop efficient algorithms for solving these problems, which are of significant interest in various fields, including data analysis, machine learning, and signal processing.   We first reviewed the existing literature on matrix rank minimization and its connections to fixed point and Bregman iterative methods. We then proposed two novel iterative methods, one based on the fixed point iteration and the other on the Bregman iteration, to minimize the rank of a given matrix.   Our numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms in solving matrix rank minimization problems. We found that the fixed point iteration method is particularly well-suited for problems with a small number of non-zero singular values, while the Bregman iteration method performs better for problems with a large number of non-zero singular values.   The key idea behind our approach is to utilize the properties of the rank function and the fixed point and Bregman iterations to develop efficient algorithms for minimizing the rank of a matrix. We also employed a novel technique to measure the convergence of the iterative methods, which allows us to accurately assess the quality of the solutions obtained.   Overall, our results show that the proposed algorithms can be used to efficiently solve matrix rank minimization problems, and we believe that they have the potential to be applied in various fields where matrix rank minimization is a critical problem.

Optimizing amino-acid mutations has been a most challenging task in modern
bio- industrial enzyme designing. It is well known that many successful designs
often hinge on extensive correlations among mutations at different sites within
the enzyme, however, the underpinning mechanism for these correlations is far
from clear. Here, we present a topology-based model to quantitively
characterize correlation effects between mutations. The method is based on the
molecular dynamic simulations and the amino-acid network clique analysis that
simply examines if two single mutation sites belong to some 3-clique. We
analyzed 13 dual mutations of T4 phage lysozyme and found that the clique-based
model successfully distinguishes highly correlated or non-additive double-site
mutations from those with less correlation or additive mutations. We also
applied the model to the protein Eglin c whose topology is significantly
distinct from that of T4 phage lysozyme, and found that the model can, to some
extension, still identify non-additive mutations from additive ones. Our
calculations showed that mutation correlation effects may heavily depend on
topology relationship among mutation sites, which can be quantitatively
characterized using amino-acid network k-cliques. We also showed that
double-site mutation correlations can be significantly altered by exerting a
third mutation, indicating that more detailed physico-chemistry interactions
might be considered with the network model for better understanding of the
elusive mutation-correlation principle.

text: In the pursuit of understanding stellar magnetism, this study investigates dynamo cycles within global convection simulations of solar-like stars. The objective is to elucidate the mechanisms behind magnetic field generation and its variability over time, which have profound implications for stellar activity and the surrounding exoplanetary environments. We employed advanced numerical simulations that incorporate realistic treatment of stellar convection and rotation, thereby enabling the exploration of dynamo processes across different stellar masses and rotation rates. Key findings indicate that the dynamo cycles exhibit significant variability that correlates with both meridional circulation patterns and differential rotation. Specifically, we observe that faster rotating stars demonstrate a dominance of axisymmetric magnetic structures and shorter cycle periods, while slowly rotating stars exhibit more complex, non-axisymmetric field configurations with longer cycle durations. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a consistent relationship between the amplitude of the magnetic field and the energy transfer within the convective zones, suggesting a feedback mechanism that stabilizes or disrupts the dynamo action. Conclusively, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the magnetic dynamo processes in solar-like stars, proposing that magnetic field variability is a critical factor influencing stellar evolution and activity, potentially shaping habitability conditions for orbiting exoplanets. This research lays the groundwork for future investigations into the impacts of magnetic activity on stellar lifespan and planetary atmospheres.

text: We investigated the potential of the GLLB-SC (Gallium-Lithium-Bismuth-Selenium) compound for exhibiting solid-state properties, with a focus on its electronic and optical behavior. Our research aimed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the compound's structural and electronic transitions, with the ultimate goal of enhancing its performance in various applications.   Through a combination of experimental techniques, including X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, and photoluminescence measurements, we characterized the GLLB-SC compound's crystal structure, electronic bandgap, and optical properties. Our results revealed a complex interplay between the metal-ligand interactions and the semiconductor-like behavior of the selenium component, which significantly influences the compound's electronic and optical characteristics.   Notably, we observed a substantial increase in the compound's luminescence efficiency and a reduction in its bandgap energy following the incorporation of a ligand, which enabled the realization of a more efficient optoelectronic device. Furthermore, our computational simulations suggested that the introduction of a bismuth ion into the compound's structure could further enhance its luminescence properties and reduce its thermal conductivity. These findings provide valuable insights into the potential of the GLLB-SC compound for solid-state applications and highlight the importance of optimizing its structure and composition for improved performance.

The recursive least-squares (RLS) algorithm is one of the most well-known
algorithms used in adaptive filtering, system identification and adaptive
control. Its popularity is mainly due to its fast convergence speed, which is
considered to be optimal in practice. In this paper, RLS methods are used to
solve reinforcement learning problems, where two new reinforcement learning
algorithms using linear value function approximators are proposed and analyzed.
The two algorithms are called RLS-TD(lambda) and Fast-AHC (Fast Adaptive
Heuristic Critic), respectively. RLS-TD(lambda) can be viewed as the extension
of RLS-TD(0) from lambda=0 to general lambda within interval [0,1], so it is a
multi-step temporal-difference (TD) learning algorithm using RLS methods. The
convergence with probability one and the limit of convergence of RLS-TD(lambda)
are proved for ergodic Markov chains. Compared to the existing LS-TD(lambda)
algorithm, RLS-TD(lambda) has advantages in computation and is more suitable
for online learning. The effectiveness of RLS-TD(lambda) is analyzed and
verified by learning prediction experiments of Markov chains with a wide range
of parameter settings. The Fast-AHC algorithm is derived by applying the
proposed RLS-TD(lambda) algorithm in the critic network of the adaptive
heuristic critic method. Unlike conventional AHC algorithm, Fast-AHC makes use
of RLS methods to improve the learning-prediction efficiency in the critic.
Learning control experiments of the cart-pole balancing and the acrobot
swing-up problems are conducted to compare the data efficiency of Fast-AHC with
conventional AHC. From the experimental results, it is shown that the data
efficiency of learning control can also be improved by using RLS methods in the
learning-prediction process of the critic. The performance of Fast-AHC is also
compared with that of the AHC method using LS-TD(lambda). Furthermore, it is
demonstrated in the experiments that different initial values of the variance
matrix in RLS-TD(lambda) are required to get better performance not only in
learning prediction but also in learning control. The experimental results are
analyzed based on the existing theoretical work on the transient phase of
forgetting factor RLS methods.

text: Gyrokinetic theory has been widely used to study the collective behavior of magnetized plasmas in fusion devices. However, existing formulations are often restricted to specific geometries or equilibrium assumptions, limiting their applicability to general plasma systems.   This research aims to develop a generalized covariant framework for gyrokinetic dynamics in magnetoplasmas, allowing for the study of plasma instabilities and turbulence in a broader range of configurations. By incorporating the fundamental principles of general relativity, this work seeks to provide a more comprehensive understanding of plasma dynamics in curved spacetimes.   The research employs a covariant formalism to derive the gyrokinetic equations in a way that is independent of specific coordinate systems or magnetic field configurations. By utilizing tools from differential geometry and tensor calculus, the dynamics of magnetized plasmas can be described in a coordinate-free manner, facilitating a more robust analysis of instabilities and transport processes.   Our study demonstrates that the covariant gyrokinetic framework can accurately capture the behavior of magnetoplasmas in diverse geometries, including those with strong magnetic fields or curved spacetimes. The generalized approach reveals new insights into the interplay between plasma turbulence, magnetic geometry, and relativistic effects.   This research establishes a foundation for a unified description of gyrokinetic dynamics in magnetized plasmas, offering a versatile tool for modeling complex plasma behaviors in fusion devices and astrophysical environments. The development of a covariant formalism opens up new avenues for investigating the rich dynamics of magnetoplasmas beyond the limitations of traditional approaches.

text: We investigate the implications of dark radiation for neutrino and dark matter detection, aiming to elucidate its potential signatures in forthcoming experimental setups. Dark radiation, which involves the presence of additional relativistic degrees of freedom beyond the standard model, is hypothesized to influence both the thermalization processes in neutrino interactions and the scattering phenomena pertinent to dark matter detection. Our work employs a combination of theoretical analysis and simulation techniques to model the interactions between dark radiation and standard model particles. We specifically focus on the parameter space of light dark matter candidates coupled with dark radiation, analyzing their decay and interaction rates that could lead to observable signals in next-generation detectors.  Our results indicate that the inclusion of dark radiation alters the expected neutrino flux distributions, resulting in distinctive energy thresholds observable in neutrino detectors. Furthermore, we find enhanced signal rates in dark matter experiments, providing significant divergence from standard expectations due to additional scattering channels introduced by dark radiation mediators. These findings suggest that future experimental designs must account for interactions with dark radiation to improve our understanding of cosmic structure formation and the underlying nature of dark matter. We conclude that the detection of dark radiation signatures stands to refine models of particle physics and cosmology, potentially offering a critical avenue toward uncovering the fundamental properties of dark matter and its interactions with the visible universe.

text: We present an all-sky catalog of solar-type dwarf stars specifically tailored for exoplanetary transit surveys. Our work addresses the critical need for a comprehensive and accessible database to facilitate the identification of suitable host stars for detecting exoplanets via transit methods. Utilizing a combination of spectroscopic and photometric data from extensive surveys, we have systematically compiled a catalog that includes over 10,000 solar-type dwarfs, characterized by their effective temperatures, metallicities, and distances. We implemented a robust selection criterion based on stellar parameters to ensure the inclusion of solar-like stars, enhancing the catalog’s utility for transit surveys. The resulting database not only offers astronomers an efficient tool for targeting potential exoplanetary systems but also enables subsequent analyses of stellar and planetary properties.   Our methodology involved cross-referencing multiple astronomical databases, including Gaia, SDSS, and 2MASS, to achieve a high degree of accuracy in stellar classification and characterization. We performed data validation through various statistical checks, ensuring the reliability of the stellar parameters included. We further analyzed the spatial distribution of the cataloged stars, revealing their accessibility for ground-based and space-based survey initiatives. The integration of machine learning techniques in filtering and categorizing data significantly expedited the processing of large datasets. Our findings indicate a diverse population of solar-type dwarfs, providing a robust framework for future exoplanet discoveries. We conclude that our catalog serves as an invaluable resource for both current and forthcoming astronomical studies seeking to uncover new exoplanetary systems.

The Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope has greatly expanded the number and
energy window of observations of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). However, the coarse
localizations of tens to a hundred square degrees provided by the Fermi GRB
Monitor instrument have posed a formidable obstacle to locating the bursts'
host galaxies, measuring their redshifts, and tracking their panchromatic
afterglows. We have built a target-of-opportunity mode for the intermediate
Palomar Transient Factory in order to perform targeted searches for Fermi
afterglows. Here, we present the results of one year of this program: 8
afterglow discoveries out of 35 searches. Two of the bursts with detected
afterglows (GRBs 130702A and 140606B) were at low redshift (z=0.145 and 0.384
respectively) and had spectroscopically confirmed broad-line Type Ic
supernovae. We present our broadband follow-up including spectroscopy as well
as X-ray, UV, optical, millimeter, and radio observations. We study possible
selection effects in the context of the total Fermi and Swift GRB samples. We
identify one new outlier on the Amati relation. We find that two bursts are
consistent with a mildly relativistic shock breaking out from the progenitor
star, rather than the ultra-relativistic internal shock mechanism that powers
standard cosmological bursts. Finally, in the context of the Zwicky Transient
Facility, we discuss how we will continue to expand this effort to find optical
counterparts of binary neutron star mergers that may soon be detected by
Advanced LIGO and Virgo.

Recently, deviations in flavor observables of B -> D(*) tau nu have been
shown between the predictions in the Standard Model and the experimental
results reported by BaBar, Belle, and LHCb collaborations. One of the solutions
to this anomaly is obtained in a class of leptoquark model with a scalar
leptoquark boson S_1, which is a SU(3)_c triplet and SU(2)_L singlet particle
with -1/3 hypercharge interacting with a quark-lepton pair. With well-adjusted
couplings, this model can explain the anomaly and be compatible with all flavor
constraints. In such a case, the S_1 boson can be pair-produced at CERN's Large
Hadron Collider (LHC) and subsequently decay as S_1 -> t tau, b nu, c tau. This
paper explores the current 8 and 13 TeV constraints, as well as the detailed
prospects at 14 TeV, of this flavor-motivated S_1 model. From the current
available 8 and 13 TeV LHC searches, we obtain constraints on the S_1 boson
mass for M_{S_1} < 400 GeV - 640 GeV depending on values of the leptoquark
couplings to fermions. Then we study future prospects for this scenario at the
14 TeV LHC using detailed cut analyses and evaluate exclusion/discovery
potentials for the flavor-motivated S_1 leptoquark model from searches for the
(b nu) (b nu) and (c tau) (c tau) final states. In the latter case, we consider
several scenarios for the identification of charm jets. As a result, we find
that the S_1 leptoquark origin of the B -> D(*) tau nu anomaly can be probed
with mass less than around 600/800 GeV at the 14 TeV LHC with 300/3000 fb^-1 of
accumulated data.

The origin of the near-ultraviolet and optical continuum radiation in flares
is critical for understanding particle acceleration and impulsive heating in
stellar atmospheres. Radiative-hydrodynamic simulations in 1D have shown that
high energy deposition rates from electron beams produce two flaring layers at
T~10^4 K that develop in the chromosphere: a cooling condensation (downflowing
compression) and heated non-moving (stationary) flare layers just below the
condensation. These atmospheres reproduce several observed phenomena in flare
spectra, such as the red wing asymmetry of the emission lines in solar flares
and a small Balmer jump ratio in M dwarf flares. The high beam flux simulations
are computationally expensive in 1D, and the (human) timescales for completing
NLTE models with adaptive grids in 3D will likely be unwieldy for a time to
come. We have developed a prescription for predicting the approximate evolved
states, continuum optical depth, and the emergent continuum flux spectra of
radiative-hydrodynamic model flare atmospheres. These approximate prescriptions
are based on an important atmospheric parameter: the column mass (m_ref) at
which hydrogen becomes nearly completely ionized at the depths that are
approximately in steady state with the electron beam heating. Using this new
modeling approach, we find that high energy flux density (>F11) electron beams
are needed to reproduce the brightest observed continuum intensity in IRIS data
of the 2014-Mar-29 X1 solar flare and that variation in m_ref from 0.001 to
0.02 g/cm2 reproduces most of the observed range of the optical continuum flux
ratios at the peaks of M dwarf flares.

The HVAC systems in subway stations are energy consuming giants, each of
which may consume over 10, 000 Kilowatts per day for cooling and ventilation.
To save energy for the HVAC systems, it is critically important to firstly know
the "load signatures" of the HVAC system, i.e., the quantity of heat imported
from the outdoor environments and by the passengers respectively in different
periods of a day, which will significantly benefit the design of control
policies. In this paper, we present a novel sensing and learning approach to
identify the load signature of the HVAC system in the subway stations. In
particular, sensors and smart meters were deployed to monitor the indoor,
outdoor temperatures, and the energy consumptions of the HVAC system in
real-time. The number of passengers was counted by the ticket checking system.
At the same time, the cooling supply provided by the HVAC system was inferred
via the energy consumption logs of the HVAC system. Since the indoor
temperature variations are driven by the difference of the loads and the
cooling supply, linear regression model was proposed for the load signature,
whose coefficients are derived via a proposed algorithm . We collected real
sensing data and energy log data from HaiDianHuangZhuang Subway station, which
is in line 4 of Beijing from the duration of July 2012 to Sept. 2012. The data
was used to evaluate the coefficients of the regression model. The experiment
results show typical variation signatures of the loads from the passengers and
from the outdoor environments respectively, which provide important contexts
for smart control policies.

text: We investigated the feasibility of estimating latent processes on a network from indirect measurements, a problem that arises in various fields, including epidemiology, social network analysis, and systems biology. Our approach employed a multivariate regression-based method to infer the underlying dynamics of a network from noisy and indirect measurements of node-level variables.   By leveraging the structural properties of the network and the correlations between node-level variables, we developed a novel algorithm that can effectively recover the latent processes driving the network's behavior. Our results demonstrated the efficacy of this approach in estimating latent processes with high accuracy, even in the presence of significant measurement noise and uncertainty.  We applied our method to a range of synthetic and real-world networks, including a social network dataset and a protein-protein interaction network. The results showed that our algorithm was able to accurately recover the latent processes driving the network's behavior, even when the measurements were indirect and noisy.   Our findings have significant implications for understanding complex systems and networks, where indirect measurements are often the only available data. We also discussed the potential applications of our approach in various fields, including epidemiology, social network analysis, and systems biology.

text: This research examines the thick disks within the Hubble Space Telescope's Frontier Fields, a set of strongly lensed galaxy clusters. The primary objective was to investigate the structural properties and formation mechanisms of these thick disks, which are defined as galactic disks with significant thickness relative to their radii. Utilizing photometric data from the Frontier Fields program and spectroscopic observations, the study aimed to understand how gravitational lensing affects disk structure and whether thick disks are a common feature in the early universe.  The methodology involved analyzing light curves from multiply imaged galaxies to infer the properties of their host dark matter halos, thereby providing insights into the mass distribution and gravitational influence on the disks. Additionally, spectroscopic analyses were conducted to measure stellar kinematics and estimate the disk thickness through velocity dispersion measurements. Key findings indicated that the thick disks observed in the Frontier Fields exhibit distinct structural features compared to thin disks, suggesting unique formation processes influenced by the environment around massive galaxy clusters.  The results suggest that thick disks may be more prevalent than previously thought, potentially offering new clues about the assembly history and evolution of galaxies in the early universe. The conclusion underscores the importance of ongoing studies using advanced observational techniques to uncover the underlying physical mechanisms governing the formation and stability of galactic disks.

text: We present our findings from high-contrast imaging of the debris disk surrounding the young star TW Hydrae, employing the Spectro-Polarimetric High-contrast Exoplanet REsearch (SPHERE) instrument at the Very Large Telescope. Our analysis reveals the presence of three distinct radial gaps within the disk, indicative of potential planet-disk interactions. These gaps exhibit asymmetric brightness profiles, suggesting that they are likely shaped by the gravitational influence of one or more low-mass companions still hidden within the disk. By employing advanced image processing techniques, we successfully enhanced the visibility of these features, allowing us to characterize their sizes and positions relative to the central star. We estimate the widths and locations of these gaps, which correspond to orbital distances that are consistent with the theoretical models of planet formation and migration. Our findings address the ongoing debate regarding the mechanisms of gap formation and the evidence for planetary bodies within protoplanetary disks. We discuss the implications of our results for the evolution of planetary systems and the processes by which disks evolve over time. Through this work, we advance the understanding of the TW Hydrae system and contribute to the broader context of early planet formation in debris disks. These findings highlight the capability of SPHERE in resolving fine structural details in protoplanetary environments and pave the way for future studies aimed at uncovering the dynamics and composition of similar disks.

A fundamental challenge for wide-field imaging surveys is obtaining follow-up
spectroscopic observations: there are > $10^9$ photometrically cataloged
sources, yet modern spectroscopic surveys are limited to ~few x $10^6$ targets.
As we approach the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) era, new algorithmic
solutions are required to cope with the data deluge. Here we report the
development of a machine-learning framework capable of inferring fundamental
stellar parameters (Teff, log g, and [Fe/H]) using photometric-brightness
variations and color alone. A training set is constructed from a systematic
spectroscopic survey of variables with Hectospec/MMT. In sum, the training set
includes ~9000 spectra, for which stellar parameters are measured using the
SEGUE Stellar Parameters Pipeline (SSPP). We employed the random forest
algorithm to perform a non-parametric regression that predicts Teff, log g, and
[Fe/H] from photometric time-domain observations. Our final, optimized model
produces a cross-validated root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 165 K, 0.39 dex,
and 0.33 dex for Teff, log g, and [Fe/H], respectively. Examining the subset of
sources for which the SSPP measurements are most reliable, the RMSE reduces to
125 K, 0.37 dex, and 0.27 dex, respectively, comparable to what is achievable
via low-resolution spectroscopy. For variable stars this represents a ~12-20%
improvement in RMSE relative to models trained with single-epoch photometric
colors. As an application of our method, we estimate stellar parameters for
~54,000 known variables. We argue that this method may convert photometric
time-domain surveys into pseudo-spectrographic engines, enabling the
construction of extremely detailed maps of the Milky Way, its structure, and
history.

text: In this study, we address the challenge of multiuser detection (MUD) in a dynamic environment, specifically focusing on the initial stages of user identification and subsequent data detection. Our approach integrates advanced signal processing techniques to enhance the accuracy of user identification, particularly in environments where users frequently change their positions and the communication channel conditions are highly variable.  We begin by employing a combination of machine learning algorithms and pattern recognition methods to identify users based on their unique characteristics such as movement patterns and signal strength variations. These features are extracted from received signals and fed into classifiers to predict user identities.  For data detection, we utilize a novel approach that combines channel state information with iterative detection algorithms to improve performance under varying conditions. This method involves estimating the channel state at each iteration and incorporating these estimates into the detection process to refine the data recovery.  Our experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in both user identification accuracy and data detection efficiency compared to conventional methods. The methodology is validated through simulations and real-world testbeds, showcasing its robustness in handling dynamic environments. Key insights include the importance of adaptability in signal processing algorithms and the synergistic effect of integrating machine learning with traditional signal processing techniques for enhanced performance in MUD applications.

This paper addresses the problem of matching pedestrians across multiple
camera views, known as person re-identification. Variations in lighting
conditions, environment and pose changes across camera views make
re-identification a challenging problem. Previous methods address these
challenges by designing specific features or by learning a distance function.
We propose a hierarchical feature learning framework that learns invariant
representations from labeled image pairs. A mapping is learned such that the
extracted features are invariant for images belonging to same individual across
views. To learn robust representations and to achieve better generalization to
unseen data, the system has to be trained with a large amount of data.
Critically, most of the person re-identification datasets are small. Manually
augmenting the dataset by partial corruption of input data introduces
additional computational burden as it requires several training epochs to
converge. We propose a hierarchical network which incorporates a
marginalization technique that can reap the benefits of training on large
datasets without explicit augmentation. We compare our approach with several
baseline algorithms as well as popular linear and non-linear metric learning
algorithms and demonstrate improved performance on challenging publicly
available datasets, VIPeR, CUHK01, CAVIAR4REID and iLIDS. Our approach also
achieves the stateof-the-art results on these datasets.

text: Recent advancements in digital communication have underscored the significance of efficient receiver designs for Quadrature Phase Shift Keying (QPSK) modulation, particularly within monobit architectures. This study aims to explore the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of monobit digital receivers for QPSK signals, addressing the challenges posed by limited sampling capabilities while maintaining effective demodulation in noisy environments. We employed a simulation-based approach to assess the receiver's performance under various conditions, comparing its functionality with traditional multi-bit receivers. Our methodology involved the development of a specialized algorithm that leverages singular decision feedback and tailored filtering techniques, enabling effective recovery of the transmitted symbols from monobit samples. The key findings indicate that although the monobit receiver experiences a degradation in bit error rate (BER) performance compared to multi-bit systems, the design facilitates significant reductions in complexity and power consumption. Specifically, under moderate noise conditions, the monobit receiver achieved a BER within acceptable limits for practical applications, demonstrating promising trade-offs between performance and efficiency. Conclusion drawn from our analysis reveals that monobit digital receivers for QPSK can serve as a viable solution in scenarios where resource constraints demand lower-cost implementations without severely compromising communication integrity. Future work will focus on optimizing the receiver’s algorithmic components and exploring adaptive techniques to further enhance performance in dynamic channel conditions.

text: In this study, we investigate the optimal values of parameters for the interaction holographic dark energy (HDE) model with a Gauss-Bonnet term infrared (IR) cutoff within the framework of Brans-Dicke cosmology. The primary objective is to determine the parameter values that best describe the evolution of the universe in this specific cosmological setup. By utilizing observational data such as the cosmic microwave background radiation and type Ia supernovae data, we aim to constrain the parameter space and identify the values that yield the most consistent cosmological evolution. Our work addresses the challenge of reconciling the HDE and Gauss-Bonnet term with Brans-Dicke theory, and seeks to provide insights into the behavior of dark energy within this modified gravity framework. We utilize a systematic methodology involving numerical simulations and statistical analysis to explore the parameter space and identify the values that offer the best fit to observational data. The results obtained shed light on the viability of the interacting HDE model with Gauss-Bonnet IR cutoff in Brans-Dicke cosmology, providing valuable implications for understanding the dynamics of dark energy and the overall cosmic evolution within the framework of modified gravity theories.

text: We present the results of our study aiming to investigate the molecular-cloud-scale chemical composition through a spectral line survey towards the W3(OH) region in the 3 mm band. Our findings reveal the spatial distribution and abundance variations of different molecules within the W3(OH) region, shedding light on the underlying chemical processes at play. To achieve this, we employed state-of-the-art data analysis techniques, including line identification, spectral stacking, and mapping of emission regions.   By conducting a comprehensive spectral line survey in the 3 mm band towards W3(OH), we have deepened our understanding of the chemical composition in molecular clouds, providing valuable insights into the intricate network of reactions shaping the interstellar medium. The methodologies and findings presented in this study contribute significantly to the broader field of astrochemistry and deepen our knowledge of the molecular complexity in star-forming regions.

The shape of LOSVDs (line-of-sight velocity distributions) carries important
information about the internal dynamics of galaxies. The skewness of LOSVDs
represents their asymmetric deviation from a Gaussian profile. Correlations
between the skewness parameter ($h_3$) and the mean velocity (\vm) of a
Gauss-Hermite series reflect the underlying stellar orbital configurations of
different morphological components. Using two self-consistent $N$-body
simulations of disk galaxies with different bar strengths, we investigate \hv\
correlations at different inclination angles. Similar to previous studies, we
find anticorrelations in the disk area, and positive correlations in the bar
area when viewed edge-on. However, at intermediate inclinations, the outer
parts of bars exhibit anticorrelations, while the core areas dominated by the
boxy/peanut-shaped (B/PS) bulges still maintain weak positive correlations.
When viewed edge-on, particles in the foreground/background disk (the wing
region) in the bar area constitute the main velocity peak, whereas the
particles in the bar contribute to the high-velocity tail, generating the \hv\
correlation. If we remove the wing particles, the LOSVDs of the particles in
the outer part of the bar only exhibit a low-velocity tail, resulting in a
negative \hv\ correlation, whereas the core areas in the central region still
show weakly positive correlations. We discuss implications for IFU observations
on bars, and show that the variation of the \hv\ correlation in the disk galaxy
may be used as a kinematic indicator of the bar and the B/PS bulge.

The purpose of these lectures is to give a pedagogical introduction to
inflation and the production of primordial perturbations, as well as a review
of some of the latest developments in this domain. After a short introduction,
we review the main principles of the Hot Big Bang model, as well as its
limitations. This motivates the study of cosmological inflation induced by a
slow-rolling scalar field. We then turn to the analysis of cosmological
perturbations, and explain how the vacuum quantum fluctuations are amplified
during an inflationary phase. The next step consists in relating the
perturbations generated during inflation to the perturbations of the
cosmological fluid in the radiation dominated phase. The final part of these
lectures gives a review of more general models of inflation, involving multiple
fields or non standard kinetic terms. Although more complicated, these models
are usually motivated by high energy physics and they can lead to specific
signatures that are not expected in the simplest models of inflation. After
introducing a very general formalism to describe perturbations in multi-field
models with arbitrary kinetic terms, several interesting cases are presented.
We also stress the role of entropy perturbations in the context of multi-field
models. Finally, we discuss in detail the non-Gaussianities of the primordial
perturbations and some models that could produce a detectable level of
non-Gaussianities.
label: human

text: We investigate the multivalley spin relaxation mechanisms in n-type bulk gallium arsenide (GaAs) under the influence of high electric fields. This study addresses the critical challenge of understanding spin dynamics within semiconductor materials, particularly under conditions where multiple energy valleys contribute to electronic and spin transport. Utilizing a combination of spin-dependent kinetic models and Monte Carlo simulations, we examine the impact of strong electric fields on spin relaxation processes, considering intervalley scattering effects and spin-orbit interactions.  Our analysis reveals that the spin relaxation rates are significantly enhanced under high electric field conditions, diverging from behaviors observed in low-field scenarios. We attribute these findings to the increased probability of intervalley electron transfer, which couples distinct valley spin dynamics and intensifies the spin relaxation pathways. Results indicate a non-trivial dependency on the electric field strength, which modifies the predominant scattering mechanisms, thereby altering spin coherence times.  The key methodological advance in this work is the incorporation of detailed spin-valley coupling dynamics within our Monte Carlo simulations, which enables a robust quantification of the electric field-induced modifications to spin relaxation. Our findings contribute to the broader understanding of spin transport in semiconductor materials under non-equilibrium conditions, offering potential implications for the development of spintronic devices that leverage high-field regimes. Future research will extend to explore temperature dependence and material-specific parameters influencing multivalley spin relaxation, facilitating novel approaches to control spin dynamics in complex semiconductor systems.
label: machine

We performed a mid-infrared imaging survey of evolved stars in order to study
the dust distribution in circumstellar envelopes around these objects and to
better understand the mass-loss mechanism responsible for the formation of
these envelopes. During this survey, we resolved for the first time the
circumstellar environment of IRAS 17163-3907 (hereinafter IRAS17163), which is
one of the brightest objects in the mid-infrared sky, but is surprisingly not
well studied. Our aim is to determine the evolutionary status of IRAS 17163 and
study its circumstellar environment in order to understand its mass-loss
history. We obtained diffraction-limited images of IRAS 17163 in the
mid-infrared using VISIR on the VLT. Optical spectra of the object allowed us
to determine its spectral type and estimate its distance via the presence of
diffuse interstellar bands. We show that IRAS 17163 is a Post-Red Supergiant,
possibly belonging to the rare class of Yellow Hypergiants, and is very similar
to the well studied object IRC +10420. Our mid-infrared images of IRAS 17163
are the first direct images of this bright mid-infrared source. These images
clearly show the presence of a double dusty detached shell around the central
star, due to successive ejections of material with a timescale of the order of
400 years and a total circumstellar mass larger than 4 M$_{\odot}$. This
indicates that non quiescent mass-loss occurs during this phase of stellar
evolution.
label: human

text: In our ongoing quest to map the cold neutral hydrogen (HI) gas distribution around galaxies, we present here the results of an observational study using the HI4PI all-sky HI emission data catalog (Kerkwijk et al., 2013). Our goal was to probe for faint HI structures surrounding nearby galaxies, focusing on those with known extended HI (EHI) or high-velocity HI (HVHI) features. We employed a scraping algorithm to systematically search for local peaks in the HI emission, which we took to be potential HI structures. We then tested each candidate structure for its spatial overlap with nearby galaxies, and applied a velocity offset threshold to ensure that the HI structures were not merely part of the galaxy's HI disk.  Our analysis revealed numerous faint HI structures located within the virial radius of nearby galaxies, many of which were previously unknown. The smallest structures had HI masses of around 10^7 M☉, and extended up to several hundred pc in size. The most massive structures had HI masses of around 10^9 M☉, and were located at larger distances from their host galaxies. We also found that a significant fraction of the HI structures were associated with optical counterparts, suggesting that they may represent dwarf galaxies or gas-rich stellar complexes in the process of being assembled.  Our study demonstrates that the HI4PI catalog provides a valuable tool for identifying faint HI structures in the vicinity of nearby galaxies, even in regions where the HI surface brightness is very low. We believe that further investigation of these structures could shed light on the nature of the interstellar medium in the outskirts of galaxies, and provide new insights into the formation and evolution of dwarf galaxies and other low-mass systems. Ongoing and future surveys, such as the HI JIVE and WALLABY, will undoubtedly reveal even more faint HI structures, allowing us to push the boundaries of our understanding of the astrophysical universe.

We calculate in three-flavor lattice QCD the short-distance hadronic matrix
elements of all five $\Delta C=2$ four-fermion operators that contribute to
neutral $D$-meson mixing both in and beyond the Standard Model. We use the MILC
Collaboration's $N_f = 2+1$ lattice gauge-field configurations generated with
asqtad-improved staggered sea quarks. We also employ the asqtad action for the
valence light quarks and use the clover action with the Fermilab interpretation
for the charm quark. We analyze a large set of ensembles with pions as light as
$M_\pi \approx 180$ MeV and lattice spacings as fine as $a\approx 0.045$ fm,
thereby enabling good control over the extrapolation to the physical pion mass
and continuum limit. We obtain for the matrix elements in the
$\overline{\text{MS}}$-NDR scheme using the choice of evanescent operators
proposed by Beneke \emph{et al.}, evaluated at 3 GeV, $\langle
D^0|\mathcal{O}_i|\bar{D}^0 \rangle = \{0.0805(55)(16), -0.1561(70)(31),
0.0464(31)(9), 0.2747(129)(55), 0.1035(71)(21)\}~\text{GeV}^4$ ($i=1$--5). The
errors shown are from statistics and lattice systematics, and the omission of
charmed sea quarks, respectively. To illustrate the utility of our
matrix-element results, we place bounds on the scale of CP-violating new
physics in $D^0$~mixing, finding lower limits of about 10--50$\times 10^3$ TeV
for couplings of $\mathrm{O}(1)$. To enable our results to be employed in more
sophisticated or model-specific phenomenological studies, we provide the
correlations among our matrix-element results. For convenience, we also present
numerical results in the other commonly-used scheme of Buras, Misiak, and
Urban.
