We report the results of an analysis of all Spitzer/MIPS 24 micron
observations of HD 209458b, one of the touchstone objects in the study of
irradiated giant planet atmospheres. Altogether we analyze 2.5 transits, 3
eclipses, and a 58-hour near-continuous observation designed to detect the
planet's thermal phase curve. The results of our analysis are: (1) A mean
transit depth of 1.484% +/- 0.035%, consistent with previous measurements and
showing no evidence of variability in transit depth at the 3% level. (2) A mean
eclipse depth of 0.332% +/- 0.026%, somewhat higher than that previously
reported for this system; this new value brings observations into better
agreement with models. The dayside flux shows no evidence of variability at the
12% level. (3) Eclipses in the system occur 32 s +/- 129 s earlier than would
be expected from a circular orbit, which constrains the orbital quantity (e cos
omega) to be 0.00004 +/- 0.00033. This result is fully consistent with a
circular orbit and sets an upper limit of 140 m/s (3 sigma) on any
eccentricity-induced velocity offset during transit. The phase curve
observations (including one of the transits) exhibit an anomalous trend similar
to the detector ramp seen in previous Spitzer/IRAC observations; by modeling
this ramp we recover the system parameters. The photometry which follows the
ramp and transit exhibits a gradual, ~0.2% decrease in flux, similar to that
seen in pre-launch calibration data. The large uncertainties associated with
this poorly-understood, likely instrumental effect prevent us from usefully
constraining the planet's thermal phase curve. Our observations highlight the
need for a thorough understanding of detector-related instrumental effects on
long time scales when making the high-precision mid-infrared measurements
planned for future missions such as EChO, SPICA, and JWST. [abridged]

text: Blazars are a unique class of active galactic nuclei known for their exceptional brightness and variability. Understanding their properties is crucial for advancing our knowledge of high-energy astrophysical phenomena. This study aims to identify potential blazars within a sample of unidentified high-energy emitting sources detected by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. We employed a systematic approach, combining multi-wavelength observational data and statistical analysis to probe the characteristics of these Fermi sources. A sample of 200 unidentified sources was analyzed using various criteria, including spectral energy distribution, optical and infrared counterparts, and association with known blazar populations.  Our findings indicate that approximately 30% of the sources exhibit characteristics consistent with those of blazars, such as spectral variability and distinct emission patterns across multiple wavelengths. The identification of these potential blazars enhances the understanding of the high-energy universe and provides implications for the study of cosmic rays and the intergalactic medium. Additionally, the results may inform future observational strategies for detecting and categorizing high-energy sources in gamma-ray astronomy. Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader effort of mapping the Fermi source population and advancing astrophysical models that seek to explain the mechanisms driving high-energy emissions in galaxies. The identification of these blazars represents a significant step forward in the quest to decipher the nature of the high-energy universe.

text: This study investigates the high-energy emission from the gamma-ray burst (GRB) 130427A, focusing on the evidence supporting inverse Compton radiation as a significant component of its spectrum. Our analysis reveals that the observed spectral features are consistent with inverse Compton scattering of lower-energy photons by a relativistic electron population. We employed advanced modeling techniques to simulate the energy distribution and polarization characteristics expected from inverse Compton processes. The results indicate that the photon energy conversion mechanism can adequately explain the observed high-energy tail of the GRB spectrum. Furthermore, we found that the electron energy distribution required for these observations is compatible with predictions based on synchrotron self-Compton models. This research not only strengthens the case for inverse Compton radiation but also provides valuable insights into the physical conditions and acceleration mechanisms within GRB jets.

We have carried out a large grid of N-body simulations in order to
investigate if mass-loss as a result of primordial gas expulsion can be
responsible for the large fraction of second generation stars in globular
clusters (GCs) with multiple stellar populations (MSPs). Our clusters start
with two stellar populations in which $10\%$ of all stars are second generation
stars. We simulate clusters with different initial masses, different ratios of
the half-mass radius of first to second generation stars, different primordial
gas fractions and Galactic tidal fields with varying strength. We then let our
clusters undergo primordial gas-loss and obtain their final properties such as
mass, half-mass radius and the fraction of second generation stars. Using our
N-body grid we then perform a Monte Carlo analysis to constrain the initial
masses, radii and required gas expulsion time-scales of GCs with MSPs. Our
results can explain the present-day properties of GCs only if (1) a substantial
amount of gas was present in the clusters after the formation of second
generation stars and (2) gas expulsion time-scales were extremely short
($\lesssim 10^5$ yr). Such short gas expulsion time-scales are in agreement
with recent predictions that dark remnants have ejected the primordial gas from
globular clusters, and pose a potential problem for the AGB scenario. In
addition, our results predict a strong anti-correlation between the number
ratio of second-generation stars in GCs and the present-day mass of GCs. So
far, the observational data show only a significantly weaker anti-correlation,
if any at all.

text: We investigated the application of a Mixture Ensemble Model (MEM) to calibrate ensemble forecasts of wind speed, with a focus on improving the accuracy of wind speed predictions. Our approach involved developing a MEM model that can effectively handle the complex interplay between multiple ensemble models and their respective uncertainties. We employed a hybrid ensemble strategy, combining the strengths of multiple ensemble models, including the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) model, and the Canadian Environment and Climate Change Service (CANSIM) model.  Through a series of experiments, we evaluated the performance of the MEM model in calibrating ensemble forecasts of wind speed. Our results showed that the MEM model significantly improved the accuracy of wind speed predictions, particularly for short-term forecasts, by reducing the mean absolute error (MAE) by up to 30%. We also found that the MEM model was able to effectively handle the complex interplay between multiple ensemble models, reducing the impact of ensemble spread and improving the overall robustness of the forecasts.  Our study highlights the potential of the MEM model for calibrating ensemble forecasts of wind speed, and demonstrates the importance of considering multiple ensemble models in wind speed forecasting. The findings of this study have implications for wind energy production and other applications where accurate wind speed forecasts are critical.

Molecular cloud observations show that clouds have non-thermal velocity
dispersions that scale with the cloud size as $\sigma\propto R^{1/2}$ at
constant surface density, and for varying surface density scale with both the
cloud`s size and surface density, $\sigma^2 \propto R \Sigma$. The energy
source driving these chaotic motions remains poorly understood. We describe the
velocity dispersions observed in a cloud population formed in a
kiloparsec-scale numerical simulation of a magnetized, supernova-driven,
self-gravitating, interstellar medium, including diffuse heating and radiative
cooling. We compare the relationships between velocity dispersion, size, and
surface density measured in the simulated cloud population to those found in
observations of Galactic molecular clouds. We find that external supernova
explosions can not drive turbulent motions of the observed magnitudes within
dense clouds. On the other hand, self-gravity also induces non-thermal motions
as gravitationally bound clouds begin to collapse in our model, and by doing so
their internal velocity dispersions recover the observed relations. Energy
conservation suggests that the observed behavior is consistent with the kinetic
energy being proportional to the gravitational energy. However, the clouds in
our model show no sign of reaching a stable equilibrium state at any time, even
for strongly magnetized clouds. We conclude that gravitationally bound
molecular clouds are always in a state of gravitational collapse and their
properties are a natural result of this chaotic collapse. In order to agree
with observed star formation efficiencies, this process must be terminated by
the early destruction of the clouds, presumably from internal stellar feedback.

text: We present a comprehensive dusty photoionization model of the Herschel Planetary Nebula Survey (HerPlaNS) target, NGC6781, utilizing the latest observational data from the Herschel Space Observatory. Through a combination of radiative transfer simulations and detailed spectroscopic analysis, we investigate the physical and chemical properties of this planetary nebula. Our results indicate a complex and dynamic environment, characterized by a dense, dusty shell surrounding a hot, ionized core. The model suggests that the nebula's morphology and spectral features can be explained by the interaction between the stellar wind, the nebular gas, and the interstellar medium. Our analysis reveals a high level of dust destruction and condensation, leading to the formation of complex dust structures. The photoionization model successfully reproduces the observed spectral lines, including the forbidden emission lines and the dust continuum. We also identify a significant correlation between the nebular density and the dust-to-gas ratio, highlighting the importance of dust in regulating the nebular evolution. By integrating the latest observational data and computational models, we provide a detailed understanding of the physical and chemical processes governing the HerPlaNS target, NGC6781. Our findings have implications for our understanding of planetary nebulae and the role of dust in shaping their morphology and spectral features.

text: We present the results of our investigation into the application of panchromatic spectral energy distribution (SED) modelling to the study of spatially-resolved galaxies. Using a sample of 30 nearby galaxies with existing multi-wavelength photometry and Hubble Space Telescope (HST) structural data, we develop a new methodology that incorporates spatial information to accurately model the complex broadband emission from these systems. Our approach involves the creation of spatially-resolved stellar population maps, which are then combined with nebular emission templates to derive the best-fit SED models for each spaxel (spectro-photometric element) in the galaxies. We find that this method provides significant improvements in the fitting accuracy compared to traditional bulge-disc models, particularly for galaxies with complex morphologies.  Our analysis reveals a strong correlation between the star formation history (SFH) and the spatial distribution of star formation, with starbursts located predominantly in the central regions of galaxies and ongoing star formation occurring in the outer discs. The presence of significant amounts of ongoing star formation in the outer discs of galaxies challenges current understanding of galaxy evolution and suggests that the outer regions may play a more active role in shaping the galaxy than previously thought. Moreover, our methodology provides new insights into the role of dust in regulating star formation, demonstrating the importance of accounting for its effects in SED modelling. Overall, this study highlights the power of panchromatic SED modelling in unveiling the complex SFHs of spatially-resolved galaxies and sheds new light on the role of star formation in shaping the outer discs of these systems.

text: The abstract outlines a study focused on investigating higher-order corrections to XYZ-SU3 breaking phenomena using Laplace sum rules. The background highlights the importance of understanding SU3 symmetry breaking in quantum chromodynamics (QCD), particularly in the context of XYZ particles which exhibit unique properties not found in ordinary quarks. This research aims to extend previous studies by incorporating more sophisticated theoretical frameworks that account for non-perturbative effects.  Methodologically, the study employs advanced lattice QCD techniques combined with high-order perturbation theory to compute relevant correlation functions necessary for applying Laplace sum rules. These calculations are performed at different lattice spacings to ensure reliability and accuracy across various energy scales. Additionally, Bayesian inference methods are utilized to extract reliable estimates of the XYZ-SU3 breaking parameters from the data obtained through these simulations.  Key findings reveal significant deviations from SU3 symmetry, indicating that higher-order corrections play a crucial role in shaping the dynamics of XYZ particles. These results challenge traditional assumptions about the nature of these particles and provide new insights into their behavior. Furthermore, the study identifies specific patterns in the correlations between different observables that can be attributed to underlying SU3 symmetry breaking mechanisms.  Concluding the analysis, the research underscores the necessity of considering higher-order corrections when studying XYZ-SU3 breaking. It suggests that future work should focus on refining theoretical models to better capture the complexities involved in these phenomena. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental forces governing subatomic particles and pave the way for further experimental and theoretical investigations.

text: In recent years, the recovery of sparsity patterns in high-dimensional data has gained prominence due to its applications across various fields, including signal processing and machine learning. This research addresses the critical challenge of sparsity pattern recovery in the presence of noise, an often overlooked aspect that can significantly hinder the performance of traditional estimation techniques. The primary objective of this study is to develop an estimation theoretic framework that enhances the robustness and accuracy of sparsity pattern recovery under noisy conditions. We employ a combination of statistical models and optimization techniques to formulate the recovery problem, leveraging techniques such as compressed sensing and Bayesian inference. Our methodology involves the formulation of a likelihood-based estimation problem, followed by a systematic application of analytical methods to derive optimal recovery algorithms. Key findings demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly in terms of recovery accuracy and computational efficiency, even as noise levels increase. Additionally, we establish theoretical guarantees for the recovery performance, providing insight into the relationships between the noise characteristics and the underlying sparsity patterns. This study concludes by highlighting the practicality of our estimation theoretic approach, paving the way for more reliable sparse data analysis in various noisy environments, thus contributing vital knowledge to the field of statistical signal processing and its applications.

text: We investigate the role of magnetars as potential central engines powering short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs) with extended emission and X-ray plateaus in their afterglows. The traditional models of sGRB progenitors, primarily focused on neutron star mergers, often inadequately account for the prolonged emission phases observed in some sGRB light curves. We propose a magnetar-driven framework, positing that the creation and rapid spin-down of a newly formed millisecond magnetar could provide the continuous energy injection necessary for such phenomena. Our study employs a detailed magneto-hydrodynamic model incorporating the magnetic field and rotational properties of the magnetar. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the energy supplied by the magnetar's spin-down can sustain the X-ray light curve plateau seen in some bursts. Consistent with observations, our model predicts a correlation between the properties of magnetar decay and the duration and properties of the extended emission. We analyze a select sample of sGRBs with well-documented afterglows and show that fitting our magnetar model provides a compelling explanation for the observed features. Our results underscore the importance of considering magnetars in the broader context of sGRB progenitor systems. We conclude that the characteristic energy and time profiles generated by the magnetar hypothesis offer a viable alternative, or complement, to the traditional neutron star merger paradigm for sGRBs exhibiting extended emissions. Future observational efforts could verify our predictions by precisely measuring sGRB afterglow light curves, offering new insights into the fundamental nature of these cosmic phenomena.

Using the multipolar expansion of electrostatic and magnetostatic potential
energies, we characterize the long-range interactions between two weakly-bound
diatomic molecules, taking as an example the paramagnetic Er$_2$ Feshbach
molecules which were produced recently. Since inside each molecule, individual
atoms conserve their identity, the intermolecular potential energy can be
expanded as the sum of pairwise atomic potential energies. In the case of
Er$_2$ Feshbach molecules, we show that the interaction between atomic magnetic
dipoles gives rise to the usual $R^{-3}$ term of the multipolar expansion, with
$R$ the intermolecular distance, but also to additional terms scaling as
$R^{-5}$, $R^{-7}$, and so on. Those terms are due to the interaction between
effective molecular multipole moments, and are strongly anisotropic with
respect to the orientation of the molecules. Similarly the atomic pairwise van
der Waals interaction results in $R^{-6}$, $R^{-8}$, ... terms in the
intermolecular potential energy. By calculating the reduced electric-quadrupole
moment of erbium ground level $\langle J=6||\hat{Q}_2||J=6\rangle = -1.305$
a.u., we also demonstrate that the electric-quadrupole interaction energy is
negligible with respect to the magnetic-dipole and van der Waals interaction
energies. The general formalism presented in this article can be applied to
calculate the long-range potential energy between arbitrary charge
distributions composed of almost free subsystems.

Recent work has demonstrated that using a carefully designed dictionary
instead of a predefined one, can improve the sparsity in jointly representing a
class of signals. This has motivated the derivation of learning methods for
designing a dictionary which leads to the sparsest representation for a given
set of signals. In some applications, the signals of interest can have further
structure, so that they can be well approximated by a union of a small number
of subspaces (e.g., face recognition and motion segmentation). This implies the
existence of a dictionary which enables block-sparse representations of the
input signals once its atoms are properly sorted into blocks. In this paper, we
propose an algorithm for learning a block-sparsifying dictionary of a given set
of signals. We do not require prior knowledge on the association of signals
into groups (subspaces). Instead, we develop a method that automatically
detects the underlying block structure. This is achieved by iteratively
alternating between updating the block structure of the dictionary and updating
the dictionary atoms to better fit the data. Our experiments show that for
block-sparse data the proposed algorithm significantly improves the dictionary
recovery ability and lowers the representation error compared to dictionary
learning methods that do not employ block structure.

text: We present our findings on the near-infrared polarimetry of a normal spiral galaxy as observed through the obscuring medium of the Taurus Molecular Cloud Complex. This study aims to discern the influence of interstellar dust on the polarimetric signatures of background galaxies, thereby enhancing our understanding of galactic polarization mechanisms and intervening dust properties. Employing VISTA's near-infrared capabilities, we conducted polarimetric observations across multiple bands to determine polarization vectors and starlight scattering properties. The data reveal that the intervening molecular cloud significantly alters the polarization percentage and angle, indicative of foreground dust grain alignment along the magnetic field lines. By employing Stokes parameters and transforming these data through vectorial calculus, we corrected for the cloud’s impact, enabling us to extract the intrinsic polarization properties of the galaxy. Our results demonstrate a notable polarization variability between the unaffected and corrected galaxy regions, underscoring the cloud's impact on the observed polarization metrics. Our methodological approach combines an innovative calibration of polarimetric vectors with a robust statistical analysis of polarized intensity distributions, providing a comprehensive model for future studies in similar obscured astrophysical environments. The findings offer critical insights into both intrinsic galactic polarization and the nature of light-dust interaction through foreground interstellar media. This work promises to refine polarimetric techniques and enhance observational accuracy in scenarios where intervening media significantly influence the observed astrophysical phenomena.

The interior of cells is crowded thus making it important to assess the
effects of macromolecules on the folding of proteins. Using the Self-Organized
Polymer (SOP) model, which is a coarse-grained representation of polypeptide
chains, we probe the mechanical stability of Ubiquitin (Ub) monomers and
trimers ((Ub)$_3$) in the presence of monodisperse spherical crowding agents.
Crowding increases the volume fraction ($\Phi_c$)-dependent average force
($<f_u(\Phi_c)>$), relative to the value at $\Phi_c = 0$, needed to unfold Ub
and the polyprotein. For a given $\Phi_c$, the values of $<f_u(\Phi_c)>$
increase as the diameter ($\sigma_c$) of the crowding particles decreases. The
average unfolding force $<f_u(\Phi_c)>$ depends on the ratio $\frac{D}{R_g}$,
where $D \approx \sigma_c (\frac{\pi}{6 \Phi_c})^{{1/3}}$ with $R_g$ being the
radius of gyration of Ub (or (Ub)$_3$) in the unfolded state. Examination of
the unfolding pathways shows that, relative to $\Phi_c = 0$, crowding promotes
reassociation of ruptured secondary structural elements. Both the nature of the
unfolding pathways and $<f_u(\Phi_c)>$ for (Ub)$_3$ are altered in the presence
of crowding particles with the effect being most dramatic for the subunit that
unfolds last. We predict, based on SOP simulations and theoretical arguments,
that $<f_u(\Phi_c) > \sim \Phi_c^{\frac{1}{3\nu}}$, where $\nu$ is the Flory
exponent that describes the unfolded (random coil) state of the protein.

text: The evolution of cosmic star formation is a complex and multifaceted phenomenon that has been shaped by various factors, including gas dynamics, magnetic fields, and the interplay between star formation and galaxy evolution. The SCUBA-2 Cosmology Legacy Survey (SCLS) is a comprehensive study that aims to understand the evolution of star formation in the early universe, with a focus on the epoch of reionization (EoR). This period, spanning from z = 5.5 to z = 6.5, is characterized by the transition from a neutral to an ionized universe, and it is believed to be a critical period for the formation of the first stars and galaxies.  The objective of this study is to investigate the relationship between star formation and the large-scale structure of the universe, using a combination of observations and simulations. By analyzing the SCLS data, we aim to constrain the physical processes that govern star formation in the early universe, and to better understand the role of magnetic fields and gas dynamics in shaping the cosmic web. Our analysis reveals significant correlations between star formation rates and the large-scale structure of the universe, suggesting that the EoR was a period of intense star formation activity. We also identify the presence of magnetic fields that play a crucial role in regulating star formation, and that are essential for the formation of the first galaxies. Our results have significant implications for our understanding of the early universe and the evolution of cosmic star formation, and highlight the importance of continued observations and simulations to further explore this complex phenomenon.

We have designed a plenoptic sensor to retrieve phase and amplitude changes
resulting from a laser beam's propagation through atmospheric turbulence.
Compared with the commonly restricted domain of (-pi, pi) in phase
reconstruction by interferometers, the reconstructed phase obtained by the
plenoptic sensors can be continuous up to a multiple of 2pi. When compared with
conventional Shack-Hartmann sensors, ambiguities caused by interference or low
intensity, such as branch points and branch cuts, are less likely to happen and
can be adaptively avoided by our reconstruction algorithm. In the design of our
plenoptic sensor, we modified the fundamental structure of a light field camera
into a mini Keplerian telescope array by accurately cascading the back focal
plane of its object lens with a microlens array's front focal plane and
matching the numerical aperture of both components. Unlike light field cameras
designed for incoherent imaging purposes, our plenoptic sensor operates on the
complex amplitude of the incident beam and distributes it into a matrix of
images that are simpler and less subject to interference than a global image of
the beam. Then, with the proposed reconstruction algorithms, the plenoptic
sensor is able to reconstruct the wavefront and a phase screen at an
appropriate depth in the field that causes the equivalent distortion on the
beam. The reconstructed results can be used to guide adaptive optics systems in
directing beam propagation through atmospheric turbulence. In this paper we
will show the theoretical analysis and experimental results obtained with the
plenoptic sensor and its reconstruction algorithms.

Designing optimal structure favorable to diffusion and effectively
controlling the trapping process are crucial in the study of trapping
problem---random walks with a single trap. In this paper, we study the trapping
problem occurring on unweighted and weighted networks, respectively. The
networks under consideration display the striking scale-free, small-world, and
modular properties, as observed in diverse real-world systems. For binary
networks, we concentrate on three cases of trapping problems with the trap
located at a peripheral node, a neighbor of the root with the least
connectivity, and a farthest node, respectively. For weighted networks with
edge weights controlled by a parameter, we also study three trapping problems,
in which the trap is placed separately at the root, a neighbor of the root with
the least degree, and a farthest node. For all the trapping problems, we obtain
the analytical formulas for the average trapping time (ATT) measuring the
efficiency of the trapping process, as well as the leading scaling of ATT. We
show that for all the trapping problems in the binary networks with a trap
located at different nodes, the dominating scalings of ATT reach the possible
minimum scalings, implying that the networks have optimal structure that is
advantageous to efficient trapping. Furthermore, we show that for trapping in
the weighted networks, the ATT is controlled by the weight parameter, through
modifying which, the ATT can behave superlinealy, linearly, sublinearly, or
logarithmically with the system size. This work could help improving the design
of systems with efficient trapping process and offers new insight into control
of trapping in complex systems.

text: In this work, we investigate the properties and potential applications of two-dimensional (2D) wide-band-gap II-V semiconductors exhibiting a dilated graphene-like structure. Our principal aim is to address the limitations of conventional semiconductor materials in optoelectronic applications by exploring the unique electronic properties conferred by this novel structural arrangement. We employed first-principles computational methods, specifically density functional theory (DFT), to evaluate the structural stability, electronic band structure, and optical characteristics of a range of II-V compounds. Our results demonstrate that the dilated graphene-like structure leads to significant band gap widening, ranging from 2.0 eV to 3.5 eV, thus rendering these materials promising candidates for ultraviolet (UV) light-emitting diodes and photodetectors. Furthermore, we elucidate the interplay between structural parameters and electronic properties, revealing a correlation between inter-atomic distances and band gap values. The optical simulations indicate strong absorbance in the UV range, which further supports the suitability of these semiconductors in high-performance electronic devices. We also discuss the role of substrate interaction and potential methods for synthesizing these 2D materials, highlighting challenges associated with their fabrication. Our findings contribute to the understanding of wide-band-gap materials and open pathways for the development of advanced optoelectronic devices that leverage the advantageous characteristics of dilated graphene-like II-V semiconductors. This study represents a significant step towards addressing the demand for materials that combine high efficiency with enhanced performance in next-generation electronic applications.

Aim: We aim to study in detail the peculiar mineralogy and structure of the
circumstellar environment of two binary post-AGB stars, EPLyr and HD52961. Both
stars were selected from a larger sample of evolved disc sources observed with
Spitzer and show unique solid-state and gas features in their infrared spectra.
Moreover, they show a very small infrared excess in comparison with the other
sample stars. Methods: The different dust and gas species are identified on the
basis of high-resolution Spitzer-IRS spectra. We fit the full spectrum to
constrain grain sizes and temperature distributions in the discs. This,
combined with our broad-band spectral energy distribution and interferometric
measurements, allows us to study the physical structure of the disc, using a
self-consistent 2D radiative-transfer disc model. Results: We find that both
stars have strong emission features due to CO_2 gas, dominated by
^{12}C^{16}O_2, but with clear ^{13}C^{16}O_2 and even ^{16}O^{12}C^{18}O
isotopic signatures. Crystalline silicates are apparent in both sources but
proved very hard to model. EP Lyr also shows evidence of mixed chemistry, with
emission features of the rare class-C PAHs. Whether these PAHs reside in the
oxygen-rich disc or in a carbon-rich outflow is still unclear. With the
strongly processed silicates, the mixed chemistry and the low ^{12}C/^{13}C
ratio, EP Lyr resembles some silicate J-type stars, although the depleted
photosphere makes nucleosynthetic signatures difficult to probe. We find that
the disc environment of both sources is, to a first approximation, well
modelled with a passive disc, but additional physics such as grain settling,
radial dust distributions, and an outflow component must be included to explain
the details of the observed spectral energy distributions in both stars.

text: This study aims to identify R Coronae Borealis (RCB) stars using mid-infrared colors from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) catalogue. We begin by selecting stars within a specified area of the sky known to host RCB variables based on historical observations. The mid-infrared colors are then calculated and compared against a set of color-magnitude diagrams that have been compiled for RCB stars. By applying machine learning algorithms trained on these color-magnitude relationships, we are able to predict which of our selected stars are likely to be RCB variables. The results indicate a high accuracy rate, with over 90% of the predicted candidates matching known RCB stars in both classification and location. This approach not only provides a more efficient method for identifying RCB stars but also opens up possibilities for automated surveys in the future. The methodology leverages the wealth of data available from WISE, combined with robust statistical and machine learning techniques, to address the challenge of identifying faint, variable stars in the mid-infrared domain.

We model the intensity of emission lines from the CO molecule, based on
hydrodynamic simulations of spirals, mergers, and high-redshift galaxies with
very high resolutions (3pc and 10^3 Msun) and detailed models for the
phase-space structure of the interstellar gas including shock heating, stellar
feedback processes and galactic winds. The simulations are analyzed with a
Large Velocity Gradient (LVG) model to compute the local emission in various
molecular lines in each resolution element, radiation transfer and opacity
effects, and the intensity emerging from galaxies, to generate synthetic
spectra for various transitions of the CO molecule. This model reproduces the
known properties of CO spectra and CO-to-H2 conversion factors in nearby
spirals and starbursting major mergers. The high excitation of CO lines in
mergers is dominated by an excess of high-density gas, and the high turbulent
velocities and compression that create this dense gas excess result in broad
linewidths and low CO intensity-to-H2 mass ratios. When applied to
high-redshift gas-rich disks galaxies, the same model predicts that their
CO-to-H2 conversion factor is almost as high as in nearby spirals, and much
higher than in starbursting mergers. High-redshift disk galaxies contain giant
star-forming clumps that host a high-excitation component associated to gas
warmed by the spatially-concentrated stellar feedback sources, although CO(1-0)
to CO(3-2) emission is overall dominated by low-excitation gas around the
densest clumps. These results overall highlight a strong dependence of CO
excitation and the CO-to-H2 conversion factor on galaxy type, even at similar
star formation rates or densities. The underlying processes are driven by the
interstellar medium structure and turbulence and its response to stellar
feedback, which depend on global galaxy structure and in turn impact the CO
emission properties.

text: The increasing competition for publication in prestigious journals like those of the Nature group has sparked interest in understanding the factors influencing manuscript acceptance and impact. This study investigates the relationship between the review model, such as single-blind or double-blind review, and author characteristics, including experience and institutional affiliation, on the uptake and outcome of manuscripts in Nature journals.    A comprehensive data analysis was conducted on a sample of manuscripts submitted to Nature journals over a specific period. Various factors, including review model, author demographics, publication history, and institution type, were analyzed to determine their influence on manuscript acceptance rates and citation impact.   The study found that manuscripts submitted under different review models exhibited variations in acceptance rates and citation impact. Additionally, author characteristics, such as publication history and institutional affiliation, significantly influenced the likelihood of manuscript acceptance and subsequent impact in Nature journals.   Understanding how review models and author characteristics affect manuscript uptake and outcome in prestigious journals like those of the Nature group is crucial for authors seeking to enhance their publication success. These findings provide valuable insights for researchers aiming to optimize their publication strategies and increase the visibility and impact of their work in high-impact scientific journals.

text: This study explores the development and evaluation of cognitive and immersive systems within a controlled microworld environment, aiming to address challenges in human-computer interaction and cognitive task augmentation. We present a novel cognitive microworld designed to facilitate the exploration of how immersive technologies can enhance cognitive processes in complex task execution. Our methodology involves iterative experimentation with immersive interfaces, coupled with cognitive load assessment metrics, to gauge system efficacy. We implement a multi-modal approach, integrating virtual reality and artificial intelligence-driven computational models to simulate dynamic environments for the participants. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in task performance and cognitive processing speed when utilizing the cognitive microworld, compared to traditional systems. Specifically, users exhibited increased problem-solving efficiency and reduced cognitive load, validated through objective performance measures and subjective self-reports. Our experiments indicate that the synergy between cognitive computing elements and immersive interfaces fosters a more intuitive and effective user interaction paradigm. Furthermore, we identify key system design elements that enhance user engagement and cognitive function, providing a framework for future cognitive and immersive system applications. These findings contribute to the broader dialogue on optimizing interactive systems for complex problem-solving in both educational and professional domains. We conclude that integrating cognitive and immersive dynamics holds substantial promise for advancing intelligent system design, offering transformative potential for enhancing human cognitive capabilities in interactive environments. Future work will focus on refining adaptive algorithms that personalize user experiences and further exploring the scalability of these systems in real-world applications.

We present low-resolution (R~850) spectra for 67 asymptotic giant branch
(AGB), horizontal branch and red giant branch (RGB) stars in the
low-metallicity globular cluster NGC 5466, taken with the VIRUS-P
integral-field spectrograph at the 2.7-m Harlan J. Smith telescope at McDonald
Observatory. Sixty-six stars are confirmed, and one rejected, as cluster
members based on radial velocity, which we measure to an accuracy of 16 km s-1
via template-matching techniques. CN and CH band strengths have been measured
for 29 RGB and AGB stars in NGC 5466, and the band strength indices measured
from VIRUS-P data show close agreement with those measured from Keck/LRIS
spectra previously taken of five of our target stars. We also determine carbon
abundances from comparisons with synthetic spectra. The RGB stars in our data
set cover a range in absolute V magnitude from +2 to -3, which permits us to
study the rate of carbon depletion on the giant branch as well as the point of
its onset. The data show a clear decline in carbon abundance with rising
luminosity above the luminosity function "bump" on the giant branch, and also a
subdued range in CN band strength, suggesting ongoing internal mixing in
individual stars but minor or no primordial star-to-star variation in
light-element abundances.

Imaging spectroscopy in X-rays with RHESSI provide the possibility to
investigate the spatial evolution of the X-ray emitting electron distribution
and therefore to study the transport effects on energetic electrons during
solar flares. We study the energy dependence of the energetic electron
scattering mean free path in the solar corona. We use the imaging spectroscopy
technique with RHESSI to study the evolution of energetic electrons
distribution in different part of the magnetic loop during the 2004 May 21
flare. These observations are compared with the radio observations of the
gyrosynchrotron radiation of the same flare by Kuznetsov and Kontar (2015), and
with the predictions of the diffusive transport model described by Kontar et
al. (2014). The X-ray analysis shows a trapping of energetic electrons in the
corona and a spectral hardening of the energetic electron distribution between
the top of the loop and the footpoints. Coronal trapping of electrons is
stronger for the radio-emitting electrons than for the X-ray-emitting
electrons. These observations can be explained by the diffusive transport model
derived by Kontar et al. (2014). We show that the combination of X-ray and
radio diagnostics is a powerful tool to study electron transport in the solar
corona in different energy domains. We show that the diffusive transport model
can explain our observations; and in the range 25-500 keV, the electron
scattering mean free path decreases with electron energy. We can estimate for
the first time the scattering mean free path dependence on energy in the
corona.

text: This study investigates the multiscale filler structure within simplified industrial nanocomposites consisting of silica reinforced SBR (Styrene-butadiene rubber) systems using Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS) and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM). The primary objective was to elucidate the distribution and interaction of nanoscale silica particles at different length scales, from atomic to mesoscopic dimensions, to optimize reinforcement effectiveness. Using SAXS, we characterized the overall nanostructure and its spatial arrangement within the polymer matrix. Concurrently, TEM provided detailed morphological insights into the filler dispersion and agglomeration behavior. Key findings revealed that the filler structure significantly influenced the mechanical properties of the composite, with enhanced tensile strength and improved elasticity observed in composites with well-dispersed and uniformly sized silica nanoparticles. The multiscale analysis highlighted the importance of both microstructural organization and particle agglomeration in determining the composite's performance. This research underscores the significance of employing complementary techniques such as SAXS and TEM to understand complex filler structures in nanocomposites comprehensively.

Recent numerical results on advection dynamics have shown that particles
denser than the fluid can remain trapped indefinitely in a bounded region of an
open fluid flow. Here, we investigate this counterintuitive phenomenon both
numerically and analytically to establish the conditions under which the
underlying particle-trapping attractors can form. We focus on a two-dimensional
open flow composed of a pair of vortices and its specular image, which is a
system we represent as a vortex pair plus a wall along the symmetry line.
Considering particles that are much denser than the fluid, we show that two
point attractors form in the neighborhood of the vortex pair provided that the
particle Stokes number is smaller than a critical value of order unity. In the
absence of the wall, the boundaries of the basins of the attracting points are
smooth. When the wall is present, the point attractors describe
counter-rotating ellipses in this frame, with a period equal to half the period
of one isolated vortex pair. However, their boundaries are shown to become
fractal if the distance to the wall is smaller than a critical distance that
scales with the inverse square root of the Stokes number. This transformation
is related to the breakdown of a separatrix that gives rise to a heteroclinic
tangle close to the vortices, which we describe using a Melnikov function. For
an even smaller distance to the wall, we demonstrate that a second separatrix
breaks down and a new heteroclinic tangle forms farther away from the vortices.
Particles released in the open part of the flow can approach the attractors and
be trapped permanently provided that they cross the two separatrices.
Furthermore, the trapping of heavy particles from the open flow is shown to be
robust to the presence of gravity, viscosity, and noise.

Many applications require recovering a matrix of minimal rank within an
affine constraint set, with matrix completion a notable special case. Because
the problem is NP-hard in general, it is common to replace the matrix rank with
the nuclear norm, which acts as a convenient convex surrogate. While elegant
theoretical conditions elucidate when this replacement is likely to be
successful, they are highly restrictive and convex algorithms fail when the
ambient rank is too high or when the constraint set is poorly structured.
Non-convex alternatives fare somewhat better when carefully tuned; however,
convergence to locally optimal solutions remains a continuing source of
failure. Against this backdrop we derive a deceptively simple and
parameter-free probabilistic PCA-like algorithm that is capable, over a wide
battery of empirical tests, of successful recovery even at the theoretical
limit where the number of measurements equal the degrees of freedom in the
unknown low-rank matrix. Somewhat surprisingly, this is possible even when the
affine constraint set is highly ill-conditioned. While proving general recovery
guarantees remains evasive for non-convex algorithms, Bayesian-inspired or
otherwise, we nonetheless show conditions whereby the underlying cost function
has a unique stationary point located at the global optimum; no existing cost
function we are aware of satisfies this same property. We conclude with a
simple computer vision application involving image rectification and a standard
collaborative filtering benchmark.

text: In this study, we analyze galaxy pairs within the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS)-IX data set to investigate the merger-induced activity of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) using data from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE). Our analysis focuses on identifying candidate AGN in these pairs through their infrared signatures, distinguishing them from star-forming galaxies. We employ machine learning algorithms to classify objects based on their spectral energy distributions (SEDs), optimizing classification performance with cross-validation techniques. The results indicate that significant merger events are associated with enhanced AGN activity, as evidenced by increased infrared luminosity and broad emission lines. Key findings suggest that AGN activity is more pronounced in systems where one member of the pair is undergoing a merger event, highlighting the importance of mergers in driving AGN activity. Our study underscores the utility of multi-wavelength surveys like WISE in studying AGN evolution within merging systems.

text: We explore the development and analysis of incremental constraint projection methods tailored for addressing monotone stochastic variational inequalities (SVIs). Our work aims to resolve the challenges posed by the inherent complexity and computational intensiveness of solving SVIs in high-dimensional spaces with dynamic, uncertain environments. These challenges often result in inefficiencies and suboptimal solutions when using traditional techniques. We introduce an innovative framework that incrementally integrates constraint projections to refine approximate solutions iteratively. Our methodology leverages stochastic approximation techniques combined with projection mechanisms to ensure convergence towards the solution. Through theoretical analysis, we establish the convergence properties of our proposed methods under standard assumptions of monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity. We demonstrate that our framework achieves a significant reduction in computational overhead while maintaining robust convergence guarantees. Our approach offers superior scalability and efficiency, making it feasible for large-scale applications. Numerical experiments confirm the efficacy of our methods by achieving improved solution accuracy and reduced computation times compared to benchmark variational inequality solvers. These results substantiate the potential of incremental constraint projection methods in streamlining the resolution of monotone SVIs, thereby providing a powerful tool for optimization problems prevalent in various fields, such as economics, engineering, and machine learning. Further extensions could involve adapting our methods to accommodate more complex structures, including those with time-varying dynamics, to enhance versatility and broaden applicability. Thus, our study provides a solid foundation for future advancements in the optimization of monotone stochastic variational inequalities.

text: This study explores dynamic state estimation using Poisson spike trains as a foundational approach towards developing an optimal encoding theory. We begin by addressing the inherent variability and stochastic nature of spike trains, which are crucial for understanding neural coding. Our methodology involves constructing a mathematical framework that models the spiking activity of neurons under varying conditions, aiming to estimate the underlying dynamical states accurately.  We employ a Bayesian approach to infer these states from observed spike trains, leveraging the properties of Poisson processes to characterize the firing rates of neurons. The core contribution lies in deriving optimal encoding strategies that minimize the mean squared error between the estimated and true states. This is achieved through iterative refinement of our model parameters based on the likelihood of spike train observations.  Our findings reveal that optimal encoding can be significantly enhanced by incorporating temporal dependencies within spike trains, thereby improving the precision of state estimation. Additionally, we identify conditions under which certain types of noise can actually facilitate better encoding performance. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding but also have practical implications for designing more efficient neural prosthetics and decoding systems.  In summary, this research provides a robust theoretical foundation for optimal encoding using Poisson spike trains, paving the way for future advancements in neuroscience and artificial intelligence applications.

Work presented in this paper describes a general algorithm and its finite
element implementation for performing concurrent multiple sub-domain
simulations in linear structural dynamics. Using this approach one can solve
problems in which the domain under analysis can be selectively discretized
spatially and temporally, hence allowing the user to obtain a desired level of
accuracy in critical regions while improving computational efficiency globally.
The mathematical background for this approach is largely based upon the
fundamental principles of domain decomposition methods (DDM) and Lagrange
multipliers, used to obtain coupled equations of motion for distinct regions of
a continuous domain. These methods when combined together systematically yield
constraint forces that not only ensure conservation of energy but also enforce
continuity of velocities across sub-domain interfaces. Multiple grid (MG)
connections between non-conforming sub-domains are modeled using mortar
elements whereas coupled multiple time-scale (MT) equations are derived for the
classical Newmark integration algorithm (and its constituents). Fully
discretized equations of motion for component sub-domains, augmented with an
interface condition are then solved using block elimination method and Crout
factorization.
  A proof of stability is provided using Energy method and overall efficiency,
accuracy and stability of multiple sub-domain coupling is evaluated using a
series of numerical examples. Primary observations are made for the evolution
and distribution of kinematic quantities and structural wave propagation across
connecting sub-domain. Numerical stability is verified by ensuring energy
balance at global as well as component sub-domain level. Discussed examples
highlight the greatest advantage of MGMT method; which is high simulation
speedups (at the cost of reasonably small errors).

text: We investigate the robustness of structurally equivalent concurrent parity games, focusing specifically on the stability of optimal strategies against structural perturbations. These games are instrumental in model-checking and synthesis in computer science, where they provide a framework to model interactive systems with a high degree of concurrency. Our work attempts to address the critical problem of how small changes in the game's structure can impact the long-term optimal strategies, which has implications for the reliability and predictability of automated systems operating under dynamic conditions.  We employ a rigorous mathematical framework to analyze the resilience of equilibrium strategies when confronted with structural variations. By leveraging topological game theory and quantitative parity objectives, we develop a suite of metrics to quantify the robustness of strategy profiles within concurrent parity games. These metrics allow us to systematically assess the extent to which non-deterministic choices influence the stability of winning strategies.  Our results indicate that structurally equivalent concurrent parity games exhibit a notable degree of robustness, with only marginal variations in strategy performance even under moderate structural changes. Specifically, the optimal strategies retain their efficacy despite alterations, suggesting that such systems can maintain operational reliability. Through comprehensive simulations, we validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating that the proposed metrics effectively capture the robustness characteristics of the games under examination.  The insights derived from this work have the potential to significantly enhance the design and analysis of robust concurrent systems, making them better suited for deployment in environments where structural uncertainties are prevalent.

We present spectra of 14 A-type supergiants in the metal-rich spiral galaxy
M83. We derive stellar parameters and metallicities, and measure a
spectroscopic distance modulus m-M = 28.47 +\- 0.10 (4.9 +\- 0.2 Mpc), in
agreement with other methods. We use the stellar characteristic metallicity of
M83 and other systems to discuss a version of the galaxy mass-metallicity
relation that is independent of the analysis of nebular emission lines and the
associated systematic uncertainties. We reproduce the radial metallicity
gradient of M83, which flattens at large radii, with a chemical evolution
model, constraining gas inflow and outflow processes. We carry out a
comparative analysis of the metallicities we derive from the stellar spectra
and published HII region line fluxes, utilizing both the direct, Te-based
method and different strong-line abundance diagnostics. The direct abundances
are in relatively good agreement with the stellar metallicities, once we apply
a modest correction to the nebular oxygen abundance due to depletion onto dust.
Popular empirically calibrated strong-line diagnostics tend to provide nebular
abundances that underestimate the stellar metallicities above the solar value
by ~0.2 dex. This result could be related to difficulties in selecting
calibration samples at high metallicity. The O3N2 method calibrated by Pettini
and Pagel gives the best agreement with our stellar metallicities. We confirm
that metal recombination lines yield nebular abundances that agree with the
stellar abundances for high metallicity systems, but find evidence that in more
metal-poor environments they tend to underestimate the stellar metallicities by
a significant amount, opposite to the behavior of the direct method.

Characterizing the transcriptome architecture of the human brain is
fundamental in gaining an understanding of brain function and disease. A number
of recent studies have investigated patterns of brain gene expression obtained
from an extensive anatomical coverage across the entire human brain using
experimental data generated by the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) project. In
this paper, we propose a new representation of a gene's transcription activity
that explicitly captures the pattern of spatial co-expression across different
anatomical brain regions. For each gene, we define a Spatial Expression Network
(SEN), a network quantifying co-expression patterns amongst several anatomical
locations. Network similarity measures are then employed to quantify the
topological resemblance between pairs of SENs and identify naturally occurring
clusters. Using network-theoretical measures, three large clusters have been
detected featuring distinct topological properties. We then evaluate whether
topological diversity of the SENs reflects significant differences in
biological function through a gene ontology analysis. We report on evidence
suggesting that one of the three SEN clusters consists of genes specifically
involved in the nervous system, including genes related to brain disorders,
while the remaining two clusters are representative of immunity, transcription
and translation. These findings are consistent with previous studies showing
that brain gene clusters are generally associated with one of these three major
biological processes.

We consider the maximum matching problem in the semi-streaming model
formalized by Feigenbaum, Kannan, McGregor, Suri, and Zhang that is inspired by
giant graphs of today. As our main result, we give a two-pass $(1/2 +
1/16)$-approximation algorithm for triangle-free graphs and a two-pass $(1/2 +
1/32)$-approximation algorithm for general graphs; these improve the
approximation ratios of $1/2 + 1/52$ for bipartite graphs and $1/2 + 1/140$ for
general graphs by Konrad, Magniez, and Mathieu. In three passes, we achieve
approximation ratios of $1/2 + 1/10$ for triangle-free graphs and $1/2 +
1/19.753$ for general graphs. We also give a multi-pass algorithm where we
bound the number of passes precisely---we give a $(2/3
-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm that uses $2/(3\varepsilon)$ passes for
triangle-free graphs and $4/(3\varepsilon)$ passes for general graphs. Our
algorithms are simple and combinatorial, use $O(n \log n)$ space, and have
$O(1)$ update time per edge.
  For general graphs, our multi-pass algorithm improves the best known
deterministic algorithms in terms of the number of passes:
  --Ahn and Guha give a $(2/3 - \varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm that uses
$O(\log(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^2)$ passes, whereas our $(2/3 -
\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm uses $4/(3\varepsilon)$ passes;
  --they also give a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm that uses
$O(\log n \cdot \mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon))$ passes, where $n$ is the number
of vertices of the input graph; although our algorithm is $(2/3 -
\varepsilon)$-approximation, our number of passes do not depend on $n$.
  Earlier multi-pass algorithms either have a large constant inside big-$O$
notation for the number of passes or the constant cannot be determined due to
the involved analysis, so our multi-pass algorithm should use much fewer passes
for approximation ratios bounded slightly below $2/3$.

text: Recent advancements in materials science have highlighted the significance of understanding microstructural features for optimizing material properties. This study aims to explore the statistical reconstruction of microstructures through the application of entropic descriptors, which serve as quantifiable metrics of disorder within a given system. To achieve this objective, we developed a novel methodology that employs a combination of computational simulations and empirical data to derive entropic measures from microstructural images. The entropic descriptors were calculated to capture various aspects of microstructural complexity, facilitating the reconstruction process through a probabilistic framework.  Our findings reveal that the statistical reconstruction achieved through entropic descriptors significantly correlates with the observed physical properties of the materials modeled. The reconstructed microstructures exhibited a high degree of fidelity to the original structures, as confirmed through quantitative assessments using metrics such as spatial correlation and phase distribution. Furthermore, the ability to manipulate these descriptors allows for tailored microstructural features, leading to enhanced material attributes.  In conclusion, this research provides a robust framework for the statistical reconstruction of microstructures using entropic descriptors, offering a powerful tool for materials design and characterization. The implications of these findings extend beyond theoretical interest, paving the way for practical applications in areas such as nanotechnology and advanced manufacturing, where precise control over microstructural attributes is essential for achieving desired performance outcomes.

text: This research focuses on the intriguing genus 2 family, boasting an impressive number of 226 sections. The family, hitherto unstudied in depth, has piqued the interest of taxonomists and mathematicians alike due to its complex mathematical properties and intriguing biological characteristics. In the background section, we delve into the history and classification of the family, providing context for its unique position within the plant kingdom. The objective of this study is to explore the taxonomic relationships and morphological traits of this genus 2 family, with a particular focus on its sections. Using comprehensive literature review and molecular techniques, we examine the morphological features and molecular data of various species within the family. Our key findings reveal intriguing patterns of evolution and distinct morphological variations within the family. Furthermore, we identify the presence of novel compounds with potential medicinal value in some sections. The conclusion summarizes the significance of our findings, highlighting the importance of further research into this genus 2 family for both taxonomic and biomedical purposes.

The intrinsic column density (NH) distribution of quasars is poorly known. At
the high obscuration end of the quasar population and for redshifts z<1, the
X-ray spectra can only be reliably characterized using broad-band measurements
which extend to energies above 10 keV. Using the hard X-ray observatory NuSTAR,
along with archival Chandra and XMM-Newton data, we study the broad-band X-ray
spectra of nine optically selected (from the SDSS), candidate Compton-thick (NH
> 1.5e24 cm^-2) type 2 quasars (CTQSO2s); five new NuSTAR observations are
reported herein, and four have been previously published. The candidate CTQSO2s
lie at z<0.5, have observed [OIII] luminosities in the range 8.4 < log
(L_[OIII]/L_solar) < 9.6, and show evidence for extreme, Compton-thick
absorption when indirect absorption diagnostics are considered. Amongst the
nine candidate CTQSO2s, five are detected by NuSTAR in the high energy (8-24
keV) band: two are weakly detected at the ~ 3 sigma confidence level and three
are strongly detected with sufficient counts for spectral modeling (>~ 90 net
source counts at 8-24 keV). For these NuSTAR-detected sources direct (i.e.,
X-ray spectral) constraints on the intrinsic AGN properties are feasible, and
we measure column densities ~2.5-1600 times higher and intrinsic (unabsorbed)
X-ray luminosities ~10-70 times higher than pre-NuSTAR constraints from Chandra
and XMM-Newton. Assuming the NuSTAR-detected type 2 quasars are representative
of other Compton-thick candidates, we make a correction to the NH distribution
for optically selected type 2 quasars as measured by Chandra and XMM-Newton for
39 objects. With this approach, we predict a Compton-thick fraction of f_CT =
36^{+14}_{-12} %, although higher fractions (up to 76%) are possible if
indirect absorption diagnostics are assumed to be reliable.

Many high voltage applications are realized with series connected thyristors.
Voltage imbalance among series connected thyristors during steady state as well
as in transients is one of the major concerns. This voltage imbalance is
mitigated by using static and dynamic balancing network. Dynamic balancing
networks are typically designed based on reverse recovery charge of the
thyristor during turn-off, which suits many applications. But this is not the
case for a crowbar application, where turn-off of the thyristor is not a major
circuit constraint. This paper proposes the design method for dynamic balancing
network considering gate turn-on delay time and the balancing network component
tolerances. The paper derives two models for the dynamic balancing network
based on its charge-discharge cycle. The importance of charge-discharge cycle
in the design of dynamic balancing network during high di/dt operation is
emphasized. Influence of dynamic balancing resistance and crowbar current
limiting inductance on voltage imbalance, charging current and discharging
current is studied using the analytical model. The proposed design method also
offers flexibility to incorporate differences in propagation delays among the
thyristor drivers that are used to trigger individual thyristors. Such delays
cannot be directly incorporated in the conventional balancing network design
method based on reverse recovery. Further, it is also analytically shown that
designing the dynamic balancing network based on reverse recovery charge makes
the balancing network lossy and bulky for crowbar application. Simulation
studies and experimental results on a 12kV , 1kA crowbar consisting of six
series connected thyristors confirms the theoretical analysis and validates the
proposed approach for crowbar applications.

Inferring interior properties of the Sun from photospheric measurements of
the seismic wavefield constitutes the helioseismic inverse problem. Deviations
in seismic measurements (such as wave travel times) from their fiducial values
estimated for a given model of the solar interior imply that the model is
inaccurate. Contemporary inversions in local helioseismology assume that
properties of the solar interior are linearly related to measured travel-time
deviations. It is widely known, however, that this assumption is invalid for
sunspots and active regions, and likely for supergranular flows as well. Here,
we introduce nonlinear optimization, executed iteratively, as a means of
inverting for the sub-surface structure of large-amplitude perturbations.
Defining the penalty functional as the $L_2$ norm of wave travel-time
deviations, we compute the the total misfit gradient of this functional with
respect to the relevant model parameters %(only sound speed in this case) at
each iteration around the corresponding model. The model is successively
improved using either steepest descent, conjugate gradient, or quasi-Newton
limited-memory BFGS. Performing nonlinear iterations requires privileging
pixels (such as those in the near-field of the scatterer), a practice not
compliant with the standard assumption of translational invariance.
Measurements for these inversions, although similar in principle to those used
in time-distance helioseismology, require some retooling. For the sake of
simplicity in illustrating the method, we consider a 2-D inverse problem with
only a sound-speed perturbation.

text: This research paper explores approximation schemes for clustering problems that include outliers, focusing on developing efficient algorithms to handle datasets with a significant number of anomalies. The study aims to provide robust solutions that can effectively group data points into clusters while minimizing the impact of outliers. To achieve this, various existing methods are reviewed and analyzed, including those based on density-based techniques and hierarchical approaches. The methodology involves implementing these schemes on synthetic and real-world datasets to evaluate their performance in terms of computational efficiency and clustering quality. Key findings indicate that certain density-based algorithms, when combined with outlier detection mechanisms, outperform traditional clustering techniques by significantly reducing the influence of outliers. The proposed schemes demonstrate improved accuracy and scalability compared to baseline methods, making them suitable for large-scale applications where data quality may be compromised due to outliers. The conclusion emphasizes the importance of integrating outlier handling strategies within clustering algorithms to enhance overall data analysis capabilities.

text: We investigated the properties of an algebraic spin liquid on the kagome lattice, a paradigmatic model system for topological phases of matter. Through a combination of numerical and analytical methods, we obtained evidence for the existence of a topological spin liquid phase in the kagome lattice, characterized by a non-trivial topological invariant. This phase is supported by the presence of a gapless spinon spectrum and the emergence of a non-zero spinon condensate, which is a hallmark of topological spin liquids.  Our numerical simulations utilized the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) technique to study the low-energy excitations of the kagome lattice. We found that the system exhibits a non-trivial spinon spectrum, with a non-zero spinon mass and a non-trivial spinon scattering amplitude. These results are consistent with the predictions of topological spin liquid theory, which predicts the existence of a non-trivial topological invariant.  Furthermore, we developed a theoretical framework to describe the phase transition between the topological spin liquid phase and the conventional gapped phases of the kagome lattice. Our results suggest that the phase transition is driven by a non-trivial topological invariant, which is protected by the symmetry of the system. This work provides new insights into the properties of topological spin liquids and their potential realization in exotic materials.

text: In our recent study of the Wolf-Rayet (WR) star WR 110, we discovered the presence of corotating interaction regions (CIRs) in its wind. This is a significant finding in the field of stellar astrophysics, as CIRs are typically associated with binary star systems. The detection of CIRs in a single WR star challenges our current understanding of stellar wind interaction processes.  To investigate this phenomenon, we analyzed high-resolution ultraviolet spectra obtained from the Hubble Space Telescope. We identified several distinct spectral features that could be attributed to CIRs in the WR 110 wind. These features exhibited a clear periodicity in their line profiles, suggesting that they are indeed corotating with the star.  We also performed hydrodynamic simulations to model the wind interaction processes in WR 110. Our simulations revealed that the CIRs form as a result of instabilities in the wind shock caused by the interaction with a dense equatorial clump. The presence of this clump is likely due to an asymmetrical mass ejection history of the star.  These results not only provide new insights into the wind interaction processes in WR stars, but they also highlight the importance of considering asymmetrical mass loss histories in the interpretation of stellar wind observations. Future observations with next-generation telescopes and spectrographs will be essential to confirm and expand upon these findings, paving the way for a better understanding of the complex processes that govern stellar winds in general.

text: This research investigates the properties of galaxies within the faint end of the Hα luminosity function at redshift $z \sim 0.62$. Utilizing data from the Hubble Space Telescope, we aimed to characterize the star-forming activity and stellar mass distribution of these galaxies. Our methodology involved detailed spectroscopic observations to measure Hα emission line fluxes, combined with multi-wavelength photometry to infer stellar masses. Key findings include a significant proportion of galaxies showing signs of active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity, which correlates with higher stellar masses. Additionally, there is evidence of a transition from predominantly blue to redder color distributions as galaxy masses increase, suggesting a shift towards more evolved star formation histories. The results highlight the importance of AGN feedback in regulating star formation rates across different mass scales. The study concludes by proposing that understanding these faint galaxies is crucial for elucidating the evolution of cosmic star formation and galaxy assembly over cosmic time.

text: The phenomenon of baryogenesis, which describes the imbalance between baryons and antibaryons in the universe, has been a longstanding challenge in particle physics and cosmology. This research explores the potential of natural cold baryogenesis stemming from strongly interacting electroweak symmetry breaking (EWSB). The primary objective of this study is to investigate how non-perturbative dynamics during the EWSB phase can generate a baryon asymmetry at temperatures well below the electroweak scale. Utilizing a robust framework of effective field theory, this work employs computational techniques to analyze the interaction processes and resulting baryon number violation in scenarios with strong couplings. Key findings indicate that specific configurations of scalar fields and gauge bosons lead to observable asymmetries that align with current astrophysical observations. Additionally, we find that the dynamics associated with strong electroweak interactions can lead to novel baryogenesis mechanisms that do not require the introduction of exotic particles or fine-tuned parameters. Our results suggest that cold baryogenesis can occur naturally in a strongly interacting electroweak sector, providing a compelling explanation for the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry without the need for high-energy physics beyond the Standard Model. The implications of these findings extend to various areas of theoretical physics, including the understanding of inflationary scenarios and the evolution of the early universe. This study contributes to a deeper comprehension of baryogenesis and reinforces the significance of non-perturbative phenomena in high-energy physics.

text: We investigated the original ejection velocity fields of asteroid families to constrain their formation mechanisms. Through a comprehensive analysis of the orbital distributions and physical characteristics of 43 identified families, we identified a correlation between family size and the magnitude of the original ejection velocity. Our results indicate that the largest families exhibit velocity dispersions of up to 3 km/s, while the smallest families have dispersions of less than 1 km/s.  Our work suggests that the original ejection velocity fields of asteroid families are characterized by a bimodal distribution, with a majority of families exhibiting moderate velocities (1-2 km/s) and a smaller subset of families displaying more extreme velocities. We also found that the physical characteristics of family members, such as their shape, size, and albedo, are consistent with the predicted effects of the original ejection velocity.  Our methodology involved a detailed examination of the orbital distributions of family members, as well as a comparison with numerical simulations of asteroid family formation. We employed a combination of analytical and numerical techniques to constrain the possible ejection velocity fields, and we found that the majority of families can be explained by a scenario in which the original ejection velocity is moderate (1-2 km/s). Our results provide new insights into the formation mechanisms of asteroid families and have implications for our understanding of the early solar system.

Nonlinear registration of 2D histological sections with corresponding slices
of MRI data is a critical step of 3D histology reconstruction. This task is
difficult due to the large differences in image contrast and resolution, as
well as the complex nonrigid distortions produced when sectioning the sample
and mounting it on the glass slide. It has been shown in brain MRI registration
that better spatial alignment across modalities can be obtained by synthesizing
one modality from the other and then using intra-modality registration metrics,
rather than by using mutual information (MI) as metric. However, such an
approach typically requires a database of aligned images from the two
modalities, which is very difficult to obtain for histology/MRI.
  Here, we overcome this limitation with a probabilistic method that
simultaneously solves for registration and synthesis directly on the target
images, without any training data. In our model, the MRI slice is assumed to be
a contrast-warped, spatially deformed version of the histological section. We
use approximate Bayesian inference to iteratively refine the probabilistic
estimate of the synthesis and the registration, while accounting for each
other's uncertainty. Moreover, manually placed landmarks can be seamlessly
integrated in the framework for increased performance.
  Experiments on a synthetic dataset show that, compared with MI, the proposed
method makes it possible to use a much more flexible deformation model in the
registration to improve its accuracy, without compromising robustness.
Moreover, our framework also exploits information in manually placed landmarks
more efficiently than MI, since landmarks inform both synthesis and
registration - as opposed to registration alone. Finally, we show qualitative
results on the public Allen atlas, in which the proposed method provides a
clear improvement over MI based registration.
