text: The Minimum Manhattan Network (MMN) problem involves finding a minimum-cost network such that any pair of points can be connected by a path consisting of axis-aligned line segments in a plane. This study focuses on extending the MMN problem to normed planes where the cost of connections is measured using a different metric, specifically polygonal balls, which are defined by a set of convex polygons. Our objective is to develop a factor 2.5 approximation algorithm for the MMN problem in normed planes equipped with polygonal balls.  To achieve this, we adopt a methodology inspired by the classical MMN problem but adapted to handle the non-Euclidean geometry of normed planes. We start by formulating the problem within the framework of graph theory, where vertices represent points in the plane and edges represent potential connections. The challenge lies in optimizing the placement of these connections to minimize total cost while ensuring connectivity. Our approach leverages known techniques from approximation algorithms and geometric optimization.  Our key findings demonstrate that it is possible to construct an approximate solution that guarantees no more than a factor of 2.5 higher cost compared to the optimal solution. Specifically, our algorithm constructs a network that is at most 2.5 times the cost of the optimal network under the polygonal ball metric. This result is significant as it provides a practical and efficient way to solve the MMN problem in normed planes, even when using a non-Euclidean distance measure.  In conclusion, this research contributes to the field of computational geometry by offering a novel factor 2.5 approximation algorithm for the Minimum Manhattan Network problem in normed planes with polygonal balls. The findings not only advance theoretical knowledge but also have potential applications in various fields requiring efficient network design under non-standard distance metrics.

Real-time 3D navigation during minimally invasive procedures is an essential
yet challenging task, especially when considerable tissue motion is involved.
To balance image acquisition speed and resolution, only 2D images or
low-resolution 3D volumes can be used clinically. In this paper, a real-time
and registration-free framework for dynamic shape instantiation, generalizable
to multiple anatomical applications, is proposed to instantiate high-resolution
3D shapes of an organ from a single 2D image intra-operatively. Firstly, an
approximate optimal scan plane was determined by analyzing the pre-operative 3D
statistical shape model (SSM) of the anatomy with sparse principal component
analysis (SPCA) and considering practical constraints . Secondly, kernel
partial least squares regression (KPLSR) was used to learn the relationship
between the pre-operative 3D SSM and a synchronized 2D SSM constructed from 2D
images obtained at the approximate optimal scan plane. Finally, the derived
relationship was applied to the new intra-operative 2D image obtained at the
same scan plane to predict the high-resolution 3D shape intra-operatively. A
major feature of the proposed framework is that no extra registration between
the pre-operative 3D SSM and the synchronized 2D SSM is required. Detailed
validation was performed on studies including the liver and right ventricle
(RV) of the heart. The derived results (mean accuracy of 2.19mm on patients and
computation speed of 1ms) demonstrate its potential clinical value for
real-time, high-resolution, dynamic and 3D interventional guidance.

We report on a timing analysis performed on a 62-ks long XMM-Newton
observation of the accreting millisecond pulsar SAX J1808.4-3658 during the
latest X-ray outburst that started on September 21, 2008. By connecting the
time of arrivals of the pulses observed during the XMM observation, we derived
the best-fit orbital solution and a best-fit value of the spin period for the
2008 outburst. Comparing this new set of orbital parameters and, in particular,
the value of the time of ascending-node passage with the orbital parameters
derived for the previous four X-ray outbursts of SAX J1808.4-3658 observed by
the PCA on board RXTE, we find an updated value of the orbital period
derivative, which turns out to be $\dot P_{\rm orb} = (3.89 \pm 0.15) \times
10^{-12}$ s/s. This new value of the orbital period derivative agrees with the
previously reported value, demonstrating that the orbital period derivative in
this source has remained stable over the past ten years. Although this timespan
is not sufficient yet for confirming the secular evolution of the system, we
again propose an explanation of this behavior in terms of a highly
non-conservative mass transfer in this system, where the accreted mass (as
derived from the X-ray luminosity during outbursts) accounts for a mere 1% of
the mass lost by the companion.

The DustPedia project is capitalising on the legacy of the Herschel Space
Observatory, using cutting-edge modelling techniques to study dust in the 875
DustPedia galaxies - representing the vast majority of extended galaxies within
3000 km s$^{-1}$ that were observed by Herschel. This work requires a database
of multiwavelength imagery and photometry that greatly exceeds the scope (in
terms of wavelength coverage and number of galaxies) of any previous
local-Universe survey. We constructed a database containing our own custom
Herschel reductions, along with standardised archival observations from GALEX,
SDSS, DSS, 2MASS, WISE, Spitzer, and Planck. Using these data, we performed
consistent aperture-matched photometry, which we combined with external
supplementary photometry from IRAS and Planck. We present our multiwavelength
imagery and photometry across 42 UV-microwave bands for the 875 DustPedia
galaxies. Our aperture-matched photometry, combined with the external
supplementary photometry, represents a total of 21,857 photometric
measurements. A typical DustPedia galaxy has multiwavelength photometry
spanning 25 bands. We also present the Comprehensive & Adaptable Aperture
Photometry Routine (CAAPR), the pipeline we developed to carry out our
aperture-matched photometry. CAAPR is designed to produce consistent photometry
for the enormous range of galaxy and observation types in our data. In
particular, CAAPR is able to determine robust cross-compatible uncertainties,
thanks to a novel method for reliably extrapolating the aperture noise for
observations that cover a very limited amount of background. Our rich database
of imagery and photometry is being made available to the community

The analysis reveals that the presence of other individuals displaying secessionist flags significantly increases the likelihood of an individual adopting or maintaining such symbols. Key findings indicate that proximity and visibility play crucial roles in this process. Our methodology involved systematic observation and interviews, supplemented by statistical analyses to quantify the observed effects. The research underscores the importance of environmental factors in shaping individual political expressions, providing empirical support for the concept of social influence in political contexts.

We use Monte Carlo simulations to explore the statistical challenges of
constraining the characteristic mass ($m_c$) and width ($\sigma$) of a
lognormal sub-solar initial mass function (IMF) in Local Group dwarf galaxies
using direct star counts. For a typical Milky Way (MW) satellite ($M_{V} =
-8$), jointly constraining $m_c$ and $\sigma$ to a precision of $\lesssim 20\%$
requires that observations be complete to $\lesssim 0.2 M_{\odot}$, if the IMF
is similar to the MW IMF. A similar statistical precision can be obtained if
observations are only complete down to $0.4M_{\odot}$, but this requires
measurement of nearly 100$\times$ more stars, and thus, a significantly more
massive satellite ($M_{V} \sim -12$). In the absence of sufficiently deep data
to constrain the low-mass turnover, it is common practice to fit a
single-sloped power law to the low-mass IMF, or to fit $m_c$ for a lognormal
while holding $\sigma$ fixed. We show that the former approximation leads to
best-fit power law slopes that vary with the mass range observed and can
largely explain existing claims of low-mass IMF variations in MW satellites,
even if satellite galaxies have the same IMF as the MW. In addition, fixing
$\sigma$ during fitting leads to substantially underestimated uncertainties in
the recovered value of $m_c$ (by a factor of $\sim 4$ for typical
observations). If the IMFs of nearby dwarf galaxies are lognormal and do vary,
observations must reach down to $\sim m_c$ in order to robustly detect these
variations. The high-sensitivity, near-infrared capabilities of JWST and WFIRST
have the potential to dramatically improve constraints on the low-mass IMF. We
present an efficient observational strategy for using these facilities to
measure the IMFs of Local Group dwarf galaxies.

text: Our work delves into the intricacies of vesicle growth in high membrane tension environments driven by endocytic proteins. We investigate the phenomenon where the presence of these proteins leads to vesicle growth through inducing instability in the membrane. The key problem addressed in our research is understanding the specific mechanisms through which endocytic proteins facilitate vesicle growth under high membrane tension conditions. To tackle this issue, we employ a combination of experimental techniques and computational modeling.  Through our experiments, we have successfully demonstrated that endocytic proteins play a crucial role in promoting vesicle growth in high membrane tension environments by inducing membrane instability. Our findings shed light on the underlying processes that govern vesicle dynamics in such challenging conditions. Furthermore, our computational models provide valuable insights into the molecular interactions and forces at play during vesicle growth.  Overall, our research contributes to the advancement of the understanding of vesicle formation and dynamics in high membrane tension environments, with implications for various cell biological processes where endocytic proteins are involved. The novel insights gained from our study pave the way for future investigations into the role of endocytic proteins in vesicle formation under different cellular conditions.

text: Hard mixtures of experts (HME) have emerged as a promising approach for large-scale weakly supervised vision tasks, where labeling data is costly and time-consuming. In this work, we propose a new HME framework, called Adaptive Weighted HME, to address the challenges in large-scale weakly supervised vision tasks, including the lack of annotated training data, domain shift, and catastrophic forgetting.     Our framework consists of two main components an ensemble of experts and a gating network. The experts are pretrained on a large dataset using standard supervised learning, and the gating network is trained to adaptively adjust the weights of each expert based on input features and uncertainty estimates. We demonstrate that Adaptive Weighted HME outperforms traditional HME approaches and achieves comparable performance to supervised learning on several large-scale weakly supervised vision benchmarks, including ImageNet and Objects365.     To address the lack of annotated training data, we propose a novel approach for pretraining the gating network using unlabeled data and transfer learning from a pretrained supervised model. To handle domain shift, we use a feature adaptation technique to align the feature distributions between the source and target domains. To mitigate catastrophic forgetting, we propose a dynamic expert pruning method that gradually prunes the least relevant experts as new data is encountered.     In summary, we present a novel HME framework for large-scale weakly supervised vision tasks that addresses the challenges of lacking annotated data, domain shift, and catastrophic forgetting. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and its competitive performance compared to supervised learning approaches.

text: We investigated the intricate dynamics of quantum systems under extreme magnetic fields, with a focus on elucidating the underlying path mechanisms that govern their behavior. Our work aimed to bridge the gap between theoretical models and experimental observations, shedding light on the complex interplay between quantum coherence, decoherence, and lattice interactions.  Through a combination of theoretical modeling and numerical simulations, we explored the impact of high-field physics on quantum many-body systems, including superconducting and superfluids. Our calculations revealed the emergence of novel path dynamics, characterized by the interplay between quantum fluctuations and lattice vibrations, which in turn influence the system's thermodynamic and transport properties.  Notably, we demonstrated the importance of considering the quantum path as a distinct entity, rather than a mere byproduct of other physical processes. By doing so, we uncovered a range of previously unobserved path-dependent effects, including the modification of quantum coherence timescales and the emergence of non-equilibrium dynamics.  Our findings have significant implications for the development of new experimental techniques, such as quantum simulation and spectroscopy, which rely on the manipulation of quantum paths in high-field systems. Furthermore, our results provide a foundation for the development of novel theoretical frameworks, capable of capturing the intricate dynamics of quantum systems under extreme conditions.

text: The abstract outlines the perspective on detecting and measuring Supersymmetry (SUSY) within the focus point region of Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (mSUGRA) scenarios using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Key findings include the identification of distinctive patterns that could be characteristic of SUSY production, such as displaced vertices and specific decay channels. The conclusion highlights the importance of ongoing and future LHC runs to further refine these analyses and potentially uncover evidence for SUSY beyond the reach of current experimental limits.

text: We investigated the decay of a two-component Dark Atom Model, which comprises a dark matter component and a dark radiation component. Our results indicate that the decay of these constituents leads to the emission of high-energy positrons and gamma radiation, with a characteristic energy spectrum that deviates from the standard model of particle physics. Through a series of numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we demonstrated that the decay of the dark matter component results in the emission of a significant amount of positrons, while the decay of the dark radiation component leads to the emission of gamma radiation. Our findings suggest that the two-component Dark Atom Model provides a plausible explanation for the observed anomalies in the cosmic microwave background radiation and the high-energy gamma-ray signals detected by space-based observatories. The key to our approach lies in the application of relativistic quantum mechanics and quantum field theory to describe the decay of the dark constituents, allowing us to accurately predict the energy spectrum of the emitted particles. Our results have significant implications for our understanding of the early universe and the properties of dark matter and dark radiation.

Given CW complexes X and Y, let map(X,Y) denote the space of continuous
functions from X to Y with the compact open topology. The space map(X,Y) need
not have the homotopy type of a CW complex. Here the results of an extensive
investigation of various necessary and various sufficient conditions for
map(X,Y) to have the homotopy type of a CW complex are exhibited. The results
extend all previously known results on this topic. Moreover, appropriate
converses are given for the previously known sufficient conditions.
  It is shown that this difficult question is related to well known problems in
algebraic topology. For example, the geometric Moore conjecture (asserting that
a simply connected finite complex admits an eventual geometric exponent at any
prime if and only if it is elliptic) can be restated in terms of CW homotopy
type of certain function spaces.
  Spaces of maps between CW complexes are a particular case of inverse limits
of systems whose bonds are Hurewicz fibrations between spaces of CW homotopy
type. Related problems concerning CW homotopy type of the limit space of such a
system are also studied. In particular, an almost complete solution to a well
known problem concerning towers of fibrations is presented.

The Hubbard model on a square lattice is one of the most studied
condensed-matter quantum problems.Here we find evidence that for intermediate
$U/4t$ values and a hole-concentration range $x\in (x_c,x_*)$ the ground state
of the Hubbard model on the square lattice perturbed by weak three-dimensional
(3D) uniaxial anisotropy has long-range d-wave superconducting order. Here $t$
is the effective nearest-neighbor transfer integral and $U$ the effective
on-site repulsion. The lower critical concentration $x_c$ involves the Ginzburg
number Gi and is approximately given by $x_c\approx {\rm Gi}+x_0\approx 0.05$.
Here $x_0<{\rm Gi}$ is a small critical hole concentration that marks a sharp
quantum phase transition from a Mott-Hubbard insulator with long-range
antiferromagnetic order for $x<x_0$ to an Anderson insulator with short-range
incommensurate spiral spin order for $x\in (x_0,x_c)$. The value of the
critical hole concentration $x_*$ depends on $U/4t$ and is given by $x_*\approx
0.27$ for $U/4t\approx 1.525$. The long-range d-wave superconducting order
emerges below a critical temperature $T_c$ for a hole concentration range
centered at $x_{op}= (x_c+x_*)/2\approx 0.16$. It results from the effects of
the residual interactions of the charge $c$ and spin-neutral two-spinon $s1$
fermions of Ref. \cite{companion2}, as a by-product of the short-range spin
correlations. The spin subsystem provides through such interactions the energy
needed for the effective pairing coupling between the $c$ fermions of the
virtual-electron pair configurations.

Any injection of electromagnetically interacting particles during the cosmic
dark ages will lead to increased ionization, heating, production of Lyman-alpha
photons and distortions to the energy spectrum of the cosmic microwave
background, with potentially observable consequences. In this note we describe
numerical results for the low-energy electrons and photons produced by the
cooling of particles injected at energies from keV to multi-TeV scales, at
arbitrary injection redshifts (but focusing on the post-recombination epoch).
We use these data, combined with existing calculations modeling the cooling of
these low-energy particles, to estimate the resulting contributions to
ionization, excitation and heating of the gas, and production of low-energy
photons below the threshold for excitation and ionization. We compute corrected
deposition-efficiency curves for annihilating dark matter, and demonstrate how
to compute equivalent curves for arbitrary energy-injection histories. These
calculations provide the necessary inputs for the limits on dark matter
annihilation presented in the accompanying Paper I, but also have potential
applications in the context of dark matter decay or de-excitation, decay of
other metastable species, or similar energy injections from new physics. We
make our full results publicly available at
http://nebel.rc.fas.harvard.edu/epsilon, to facilitate further independent
studies. In particular, we provide the full low-energy electron and photon
spectra, to allow matching onto more detailed codes that describe the cooling
of such particles at low energies.

text: In this study, we delve into the intricacies of energy conservation in the context of first order 2+1 gravity. We begin by discussing the underlying theory and field equations that govern the dynamics of this system. Specifically, we focus on the ADM formalism and the Hamiltonian formulation, emphasizing the key differences between these approaches. Next, we present several attempts to solve the problem of energy conservation in first order 2+1 gravity. We consider both the canonical and path integral approaches, and we discuss the challenges encountered in each method. We further explore the concept of energy in the context of general covariance and the fact that energy is a function of the metric. Despite the difficulties, we manage to gain insights into the nature of energy conservation in first order 2+1 gravity. We find that the total energy in this system is not conserved in general, but it can be locally conserved in certain cases. We also demonstrate that the concept of energy in this context is closely related to the concept of momentum and the Hamiltonian. Our findings provide a better understanding of the subtleties of energy conservation in first order 2+1 gravity. They also have implications for the study of other gravity theories, such as loop quantum gravity and string theory. Moreover, they can be useful for the development of new approaches to quantum gravity and cosmology. In summary, we have explored the intricacies of energy conservation in first order 2+1 gravity, discussing the underlying theory, various attempts to solve the problem, and the insights gained from these efforts. We have found that energy conservation in this system is a complex issue that requires a nuanced understanding of the underlying theory and its implications for the concept of energy. Our results provide new insights and open up new avenues for future research in this area.

text: This study presents the results of a comprehensive analysis of stellar astrometry observations obtained using the SIM Lite instrument, a high-contrast imaging camera designed for the Keck Observatory. The primary objective of this research is to model the astrometric behavior of interacting binaries, a class of systems where two stars are gravitationally bound and orbiting each other. By analyzing the SIM Lite observations, we aim to improve our understanding of the complex dynamics of these systems, which are crucial for testing theoretical models of binary evolution and testing the predictions of general relativity.  The SIM Lite observations were obtained over a period of two nights, covering a range of wavelengths from 0.8 to 1.8 μm. The data were reduced using a custom-built pipeline, which included bias correction, flat fielding, and astrometric calibration. The resulting astrometric measurements were then analyzed using a Bayesian approach, which allowed us to model the complex dynamics of the interacting binaries. Our results show that the SIM Lite observations provide high-precision astrometric measurements, with an average error of 1.2 mas for the binary systems observed.  The key findings of this study indicate that the SIM Lite observations are capable of measuring the orbital eccentricity and inclination of interacting binaries with high accuracy. These results have important implications for our understanding of binary evolution and the testing of theoretical models. Our analysis also highlights the potential of the SIM Lite instrument for measuring the masses and radii of interacting binaries, which are essential for understanding the internal structure of these systems.

A total of over 300,000 galaxy images were analyzed by volunteers, leading to the identification and classification of numerous radio sources. Key findings included the discovery of previously unidentified radio structures within galaxies, the correlation between the radio morphology and the underlying physical processes driving the emission, and the identification of distinct radio source populations with varying morphological characteristics.  The analysis revealed that some radio sources exhibit extended and complex structures, while others show more compact and localized emissions. These findings contribute to our understanding of how radio galaxies form and evolve, as well as the mechanisms responsible for their powerful radio emissions. The study concludes by highlighting the potential of citizen science projects in addressing large-scale astronomical data analysis challenges and the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration between professional astronomers and the general public.

We present a sample of 75 extinction curves derived from FUSE far-ultraviolet
spectra supplemented by existing IUE spectra. The extinction curves were
created using the standard pair method based on a new set of dereddened
FUSE+IUE comparison stars. Molecular hydrogen absorption features were removed
using individualized H_2 models for each sightline. The general shape of the
FUSE extinction (8.4 micron^-1 < lambda^-1 < 11 micron^-1) was found to be
broadly consistent with extrapolations from the IUE extinction (3.3 micron-1 <
lambda^-1 < 8.6 micron^-1) curve. Significant differences were seen in the
strength of the far-UV rise and the width of the 2175 A bump. All the FUSE+IUE
extinction curves had positive far-UV slopes giving no indication that the
far-UV rise was turning over at the shortest wavelengths. The dependence of
A(lambda)/A(V) versus R(V)^-1 in the far-UV using the sightlines in our sample
was found to be stronger than tentatively indicated by previous work. We
present an updated R(V) dependent relationship for the full UV wavelength range
(3.3 micron^-1 <= lambda^-1 <= 11 micron^-1). Finally, we searched for discrete
absorption features in the far-ultraviolet. We found a 3 sigma upper limit of
~0.12 A(V) on features with a resolution of 250 (~4 A width) and 3 sigma upper
limits of ~0.15 A(V) for lambda^-1 < 9.6 micron^-1 and ~0.68 A(V) for lambda^-1
> 9.6 micron^-1 on features with a resolution of 10^4 (~0.1 A width).

Here we study the thermodynamic cost of computation and control using
'physically universal' cellular automata or Hamiltonians. The latter were
previously defined as systems that admit the implementation of any desired
transformation on a finite target region by first initializing the state of the
surrounding and then letting the system evolve according to its autonomous
dynamics. This way, one obtains a model of control where each region can play
both roles the controller or the system to be controlled. In physically
universal systems every degree of freedom is indirectly accessible by operating
on the remaining degrees of freedom.
  In a nutshell, the thermodynamic cost of an operation is then given by the
size of the region around the target region that needs to be initialized. In
the meantime, physically universal CAs have been constructed by Schaeffer (in
two dimensions) and Salo & T\"orm\"a (in one dimension). Here we show that in
Schaeffer's CA the cost for implementing $n$ operations grows linearly in $n$,
while operating in a thermodynamic cycle requires sublinear growth to ensure
zero cost *per operation* in the limit $n\to\infty$. Although this particular
result need not hold for general physically universal CAs, this strong notion
of universality does imply a certain kind of instability of information, which
could result in lower bounds on the cost of protecting information from its
noisy environment.
  The technical results of the paper are sparse and quite simple. The
contribution of the paper is mainly conceptual and consists in illustrating the
type of thermodynamic questions raised by models of control that rely on the
concept of physical universality.

Alzheimer's disease is a neurodegenerative condition that accelerates
cognitive decline relative to normal aging. It is of critical scientific
importance to gain a better understanding of early disease mechanisms in the
brain to facilitate effective, targeted therapies. The volume of the
hippocampus is often used in diagnosis and monitoring of the disease. Measuring
this volume via neuroimaging is difficult since each hippocampus must either be
manually identified or automatically delineated, a task referred to as
segmentation. Automatic hippocampal segmentation often involves mapping a
previously manually segmented image to a new brain image and propagating the
labels to obtain an estimate of where each hippocampus is located in the new
image. A more recent approach to this problem is to propagate labels from
multiple manually segmented atlases and combine the results using a process
known as label fusion. To date, most label fusion algorithms employ voting
procedures with voting weights assigned directly or estimated via optimization.
We propose using a fully Bayesian spatial regression model for label fusion
that facilitates direct incorporation of covariate information while making
accessible the entire posterior distribution. Our results suggest that
incorporating tissue classification (e.g, gray matter) into the label fusion
procedure can greatly improve segmentation when relatively homogeneous, healthy
brains are used as atlases for diseased brains. The fully Bayesian approach
also produces meaningful uncertainty measures about hippocampal volumes,
information which can be leveraged to detect significant, scientifically
meaningful differences between healthy and diseased populations, improving the
potential for early detection and tracking of the disease.

We consider nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws, posed on a differential
(n+1)-manifold with boundary referred to as a spacetime, and in which the
"flux" is defined as a flux field of n-forms depending on a parameter (the
unknown variable). We introduce a formulation of the initial and boundary value
problem which is geometric in nature and is more natural than the vector field
approach recently developed for Riemannian manifolds. Our main assumption on
the manifold and the flux field is a global hyperbolicity condition, which
provides a global time-orientation as is standard in Lorentzian geometry and
general relativity. Assuming that the manifold admits a foliation by compact
slices, we establish the existence of a semi-group of entropy solutions.
Moreover, given any two hypersurfaces with one lying in the future of the
other, we establish a "contraction" property which compares two entropy
solutions, in a (geometrically natural) distance equivalent to the L1 distance.
To carry out the proofs, we rely on a new version of the finite volume method,
which only requires the knowledge of the given n-volume form structure on the
(n+1)-manifold and involves the {\sl total flux} across faces of the elements
of the triangulations, only, rather than the product of a numerical flux times
the measure of that face.

The edit distance problem is a classical fundamental problem in computer
science in general, and in combinatorial pattern matching in particular. The
standard dynamic programming solution for this problem computes the
edit-distance between a pair of strings of total length O(N) in O(N^2) time. To
this date, this quadratic upper-bound has never been substantially improved for
general strings. However, there are known techniques for breaking this bound in
case the strings are known to compress well under a particular compression
scheme. The basic idea is to first compress the strings, and then to compute
the edit distance between the compressed strings. As it turns out, practically
all known o(N^2) edit-distance algorithms work, in some sense, under the same
paradigm described above. It is therefore natural to ask whether there is a
single edit-distance algorithm that works for strings which are compressed
under any compression scheme. A rephrasing of this question is to ask whether a
single algorithm can exploit the compressibility properties of strings under
any compression method, even if each string is compressed using a different
compression. In this paper we set out to answer this question by using straight
line programs. These provide a generic platform for representing many popular
compression schemes including the LZ-family, Run-Length Encoding, Byte-Pair
Encoding, and dictionary methods. For two strings of total length N having
straight-line program representations of total size n, we present an algorithm
running in O(nN log(N/n)) time for computing the edit-distance of these two
strings under any rational scoring function, and an O(n^{2/3}N^{4/3}) time
algorithm for arbitrary scoring functions. Our new result, while providing a
signi cant speed up for highly compressible strings, does not surpass the
quadratic time bound even in the worst case scenario.

A number of prominent spectral lines in the spectra of magnetic A and B main
sequence stars are produced by closely spaced doublets or triplets. Depending
on the strength and orientation of magnetic field, the PPB magnetic splitting
can result in the Stokes $I$ profiles of a spectral line that differ
significantly from those predicted by the theory of Zeeman effect. Such lines
should be treated using the theory of the partial Paschen-Back (PPB) effect. To
estimate the error introduced by the use of the Zeeman approximation, numerical
simulations have been performed for Si II and Si III lines assuming an oblique
rotator model. The analysis indicates that for high precision studies of some
spectral lines the PPB approach should be used if the field strength at the
magnetic poles is Bp> 6-10 kG and Vsin(i) < 15 km/s. In the case of the Si II
line 5041A the difference between the simulated PPB and Zeeman profiles is
caused by a significant contribution from a so called "ghost" line. The Stokes
I and V profiles of this particular line simulated in the PPB regime provide a
significantly better fit to the observed profiles in the spectrum of the
magnetic Ap star HD318107 than the profiles calculated assuming the Zeeman
effect.

text: Our work focuses on the separation of pulsar signals from noise using supervised machine learning algorithms. Pulsars are highly magnetized rotating neutron stars that emit electromagnetic radiation at regular intervals. Detecting these signals amidst noise poses a significant challenge in radio astronomy. We address this problem by employing supervised machine learning techniques to classify pulsar candidates based on their unique characteristics.  Our study presents promising results in effectively differentiating pulsar signals from background noise using a dataset containing both pulsar and non-pulsar examples. By training our model on this labeled dataset, we were able to achieve high accuracy in discriminating between true pulsar signals and interference. Our approach not only enhances the efficiency of pulsar detection but also reduces the likelihood of false positives, which is crucial in accurately characterizing pulsar properties.  The key ideas underpinning our methodology involve feature extraction, model training, and validation. We extract relevant features from the dataset, such as signal-to-noise ratios and pulse profiles, to capture the distinguishing traits of pulsar signals. Subsequently, we train supervised machine learning algorithms like Support Vector Machines or Random Forests to learn and classify pulsar candidates. Through rigorous validation and testing, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately segregating pulsar signals from noise, offering a valuable tool for future pulsar surveys and astronomical research.

Spontaneous symmetry breaking mechanism in quantum phase transitions
manifests the existence of degenerate groundstates in broken symmetry phases.
To detect such degenerate groundstates, we introduce a quantum fidelity as an
overlap measurement between system groundstates and an arbitrary reference
state. This quantum fidelity is shown a multiple bifurcation as an indicator of
quantum phase transitions, without knowing any detailed broken symmetry,
between a broken symmetry phase and symmetry phases as well as between a broken
symmetry phase and other broken symmetry phases, when a system parameter
crosses its critical value (i.e., multiple bifurcation point). Each order
parameter, characterizing a broken symmetry phase, from each of degenerate
groundstates is shown similar multiple bifurcation behavior. Furthermore, to
complete the description of an ordered phase, it is possible to specify how
each order parameter from each of degenerate groundstates transforms under a
symmetry group that is possessed by the Hamiltonian because each order
parameter is invariant under only a subgroup of the symmetry group although the
Hamiltonian remains invariant under the full symmetry group. Examples are given
in the quantum $q$-state Potts models with a transverse magnetic field by
employing the tensor network algorithms based on infinite-size lattices. For
any $q$, a general relation between the local order parameters is found to
clearly show the subgroup of the $Z_q$ symmetry group. In addition, we
systematically discuss the criticality in the $q$-state Potts model.

Two different aspects of formation control of multiple agents subjected to
linear transformation have been addressed in this paper. We consider a set of
complex single integrator systems so that the dimension of the system reduces
to half as opposed to the vector representation in Cartesian coordinate system.
We first design a stable formation controller in an attempt to solve the
formation control turned to stabilization problem and then find a collision
avoidance controller in the transformed domain, respectively. Different linear
transformations are used to facilitate the formation control task in a
different way. For example Jacobi transformation is used to separate the shape
control and trajectory control. The inverse of the transformation must have
nonzero eigenvalues with both positive and negative real parts which may lead
the system to instability. If the inverse of the transformation appears in
closed loop then a diagonal stabilizing matrix is required to reassign the
eigenvalues of the inverse of transformation in the right half of complex
plane. The algorithm to find such stabilizing matrix is provided. We then
define a matrix of potential in the actual domain which is the stepping stone
to find a matrix of potential in the transformed domain. Thus collision
avoidance controller can be designed directly in the transformed domain. The
mathematical proof is given that both the actual and transformed system behaves
identically. Simulation results are provided to support our claim.

text: The solar corona, a region of complex magnetic structures, plays a pivotal role in space weather phenomena impacting Earth's environment. This study investigates the efficacy of various coronal magnetic field extrapolation methods during Solar Cycle 24 using data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory. Our objective is to compare the performance of three prominent extrapolation techniques Potential Field Source Surface (PFSS), Linear Force-Free Field (LFFF) extrapolations, and Nonlinear Force-Free Field (NLFFF) models. Each method's capacity to reproduce coronal magnetic field configurations is evaluated by analyzing specific metrics such as magnetic energy, helicity, and field line connectivity against observational data including coronagraph images and Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) emissions. Methodologically, this research utilizes synoptic maps of the photospheric magnetic field to initialize each extrapolation technique, generating comprehensive coronal field reconstructions over the cycle's duration. Key findings highlight NLFFF models as providing the most realistic magnetic field configurations, capturing the complex, three-dimensional nature of the corona with higher fidelity. In contrast, PFSS and LFFF modes exhibit limitations in depicting dynamic and non-potential features. Assessment against observational data points to NLFFF’s superiority in potential application for predictive space weather modeling. The study concludes that, despite their computational intensity, advanced non-linear models are crucial for understanding the corona's intricacies and improving forecasts of geomagnetic disturbances. These insights recommend further investment in refining nonlinear extrapolation techniques to achieve more accurate representations of solar magnetic fields.

We define an appropriate problem for benchmarking dust emissivity
calculations in the context of radiative transfer (RT) simulations,
specifically including the emission from stochastically heated dust grains. Our
aim is to provide a self-contained guide for implementors of such
functionality, and to offer insights in the effects of the various
approximations and heuristics implemented by the participating codes to
accelerate the calculations. The benchmark problem definition includes the
optical and calorimetric material properties, and the grain size distributions,
for a typical astronomical dust mixture with silicate, graphite and PAH
components; a series of analytically defined radiation fields to which the dust
population is to be exposed; and instructions for the desired output. We
process this problem using six RT codes participating in this benchmark effort,
and compare the results to a reference solution computed with the publicly
available dust emission code DustEM. The participating codes implement
different heuristics to keep the calculation time at an acceptable level. We
study the effects of these mechanisms on the calculated solutions, and report
on the level of (dis)agreement between the participating codes. For all but the
most extreme input fields, we find agreement within 10% across the important
wavelength range from 3 to 1000 micron. We conclude that the relevant modules
in RT codes can and do produce fairly consistent results for the emissivity
spectra of stochastically heated dust grains.

Future dense small-cell networks are one key 5G candidates to offer outdoor
high access data rates, especially in millimeter wave (mmWave) frequency bands.
At those frequencies, the free space propagation loss and shadowing (from
buildings, vegetation or any kind of obstacles) are far stronger than in the
traditional radio cellular spectrum. Therefore, the cell range is expected to
be limited to 50 - 100 meters, and directive high gain antennas are required at
least for the base stations. This paper investigates the kind of topology that
is required to serve a suburban area with a small-cell network operating at 60
GHz and equipped with beam-steering antennas. A real environment is considered
to introduce practical deployment and propagation constraints. The analysis
relies on Monte-Carlo system simulations with non-full buffer, and ray-based
predictions. The ray-tracing techniques are today identified as a relevant
solution to capture the main channel properties impacting the beam-steering
performance (angular dispersion, inter-link correlation); and the one involved
in the present study was specifically enhanced to deal with detailed vegetation
modeling. In addition to the user outage, the paper evaluates the evolution of
the inter-cell interference along with the user density, and investigates the
network behavior in case of local strong obstructions.

text: The accurate determination of stellar parameters is crucial for understanding exoplanetary systems, particularly those hosted by stars such as CoRoT-7. This study aims to refine the stellar parameters of CoRoT-7, a solar-type star with a known exoplanetary system, using a combination of updated spectroscopic and photometric data. Utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy obtained from the HARPS instrument, alongside photometric data from the CoRoT mission, we recalibrate effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity. Our methodology involves the application of the Spectroscopy Made Easy (SME) and the Global Modeling of Stellar Interiors (GSMI) tool, ensuring a robust synthesis of data for precise parameter estimation. Key findings reveal that CoRoT-7 has an effective temperature of 5275 K, a surface gravity of log g = 4.47, and a metallicity of [Fe/H] = 0.02, slightly refining previous measurements. Additionally, improvements in stellar parameters have significant implications for the characterization of the orbiting exoplanets, allowing for more accurate determinations of their radii and masses. Enhanced parameters contribute to a better understanding of the planetary composition and potential habitability. The prudent application of advanced modeling and high-quality data gathering techniques underscores the potential for further refinement of stellar and exoplanetary parameters in similar systems. Our research not only aids in the precise characterization of CoRoT-7 but also sets a precedent for future studies focusing on parameter refinement in exoplanet-hosting stars, ultimately advancing the field of exoplanetary science.

text: In this study, we investigate the separation of electroweak and strong interactions within Drell-Yan processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) by analyzing the angular distributions of leptons produced in these events. text: In this study, we present the results of our numerical investigation into wind accretion in persistent Supergiant X-ray Binaries (SGXBs) with a focus on the structure of the flow at the orbital scale. The primary problem we aim to address is the understanding of how the complex interaction between the massive donor star's stellar wind and the compact object's gravitational field shapes the accretion flow in these systems. Our key idea is to utilize state-of-the-art hydrodynamical simulations to elucidate the detailed structure and dynamics of the accretion flow in SGXBs.   Our methodology involves solving the equations of hydrodynamics coupled with gravity in a 3D numerical simulation framework tailored to capture the intricacies of the flow around the compact object. By systematically varying the physical parameters such as the mass loss rate of the donor star, the orbital separation, and the wind velocity, we explore the parameter space to uncover the dependencies of the flow structure on these key factors. The results reveal the formation of complex shock structures, accretion streams, and the development of accretion disks in certain regimes.   Overall, our findings provide crucial insights into the mechanisms governing wind accretion in persistent SGXBs and offer a detailed characterization of the flow morphology at the orbital scale, laying the groundwork for a deeper understanding of these enigmatic binary systems.

We monitored the action of phospholipase A2 (PLA2) on L- and
D-dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) Langmuir monolayers by mounting a
Langmuir-trough on a wide-field fluorescence microscope with single molecule
sensitivity. This made it possible to directly visualize the activity and
diffusion behavior of single PLA2 molecules in a heterogeneous lipid
environment during active hydrolysis. The experiments showed that enzyme
molecules adsorbed and interacted almost exclusively with the fluid region of
the DPPC monolayers. Domains of gel state L-DPPC were degraded exclusively from
the gel-fluid interface where the build-up of negatively charged hydrolysis
products, fatty acid salts, led to changes in the mobility of PLA2. The
mobility of individual enzymes on the monolayers was characterized by single
particle tracking (SPT). Diffusion coefficients of enzymes adsorbed to the
fluid interface were between 3 mu m^2/s on the L-DPPC and 4.6 mu m^/s on the
D-DPPC monolayers. In regions enriched with hydrolysis products the diffusion
dropped to approx. 0.2 mu m^2/s. In addition, slower normal and anomalous
diffusion modes were seen at the L-DPPC gel domain boundaries where hydrolysis
took place. The average residence times of the enzyme in the fluid regions of
the monolayer and on the product domain were between approx. 30 and 220 ms. At
the gel domains it was below the experimental time resolution, i.e. enzymes
were simply reflected from the gel domains back into solution.

text: This study investigates the stability of solitons in time-modulated two-dimensional lattices, a system that has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its potential applications in various fields, including optics and quantum physics. The background of this research is rooted in the understanding that solitons, which are stable waves that maintain their shape over long distances, play a crucial role in the propagation of information in these systems.  The objective of this research is to analyze the stability of solitons in time-modulated two-dimensional lattices, with a focus on the impact of temporal modulation on the soliton's properties. To achieve this, we employ a numerical approach, utilizing a finite difference method to simulate the dynamics of the system. Our methodology involves solving the two-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation, which governs the behavior of solitons in these systems.  The key findings of this research indicate that the stability of solitons in time-modulated two-dimensional lattices is highly dependent on the temporal modulation parameters. Specifically, we observe that the soliton's stability is enhanced when the temporal modulation is synchronized with the lattice's spatial structure. Furthermore, our results suggest that the soliton's properties, such as its amplitude and width, are significantly affected by the temporal modulation. These findings have important implications for the design and control of solitons in time-modulated two-dimensional lattices, and may lead to the development of new applications in fields such as telecommunications and quantum information processing.  In conclusion, this research provides a comprehensive analysis of the stability of solitons in time-modulated two-dimensional lattices, highlighting the critical role of temporal modulation in determining the soliton's properties. Our results have significant implications for the development of new applications in fields such as optics and quantum physics, and demonstrate the importance of understanding the complex dynamics of these systems.

In this visualisation the instantaneous local velocity is expressed in terms
of four components to capture the development of and interactions between
coherent structures in turbulent flows. It is then possible to isolate the
terms linked with each major type of structure and identify the corresponding
subsets of the Navier-Stokes equations that are easier to solve than the full
version. Each of these subsets applies to a domain in the flow field not a flow
regime. The traditional statistics of turbulence are shown to be not specific
to turbulent flow. In particular the Reynolds stresses, the probability density
function, the dissipation, the production and the energy spectrum are obtained
from one subset associated with unsteady "laminar" flow. The evidence also
indicates that the Kolmogorov scale does not represent an eddy size and more
importantly that it does not require the assumption of local isotropy.
Applications of this visualisation include a proposal for a theoretical closure
of the Reynolds equations, the collapse of velocity and skin friction profiles

Space missions like CoRoT and Kepler have provided numerous new observations
of stellar oscillations in a multitude of stars by high precision photometry.
This work compares the observed rich oscillation spectrum of the rapidly
rotating B3 IV star HD 43317 with the first results obtained by a new method to
calculate unstable oscillation modes in rapidly rotating stars in order to see
whether some of the observed modes can be identified. The new numerical method
consists of two parts. We first search for modes resonant with a prescribed
forcing symmetry by moving through relevant regions of complex frequency space
and monitoring any increase of the stellar response to the applied forcing and
zooming in onto the resonance. These resonant non-adiabatic 2D-solutions are
then fed into a 2D relaxation code with the same equations but without forcing
terms. The complex oscillation frequency used in the forcing is now no longer
prescribed, but added as an extra unknown. The corresponding free oscillation
mode is usually obtained after a few ($<10$) iterations with only minor
adjustment of the complex oscillation frequency. To compare with the observed
light variations we calculate the `visibility' of the found unstable
oscillation modes, taking into account the cancellation of the various parts of
the radiating oscillating stellar surface as seen by the observer. The
frequencies of unstable axisymmetric g-modes, which have the highest
visibility, appear to nearly coincide with the observed largest amplitude
photometric variations of HD 43317, making an identification of the latter
oscillations as $m$=0 modes plausible. The identification of $m$=1 g-modes is
less straightforward, while many of the unstable even $m$=2 g-modes may
correspond to observed weaker photometric variations.

The methodology involved detailed characterization using magnetic force microscopy (MFM) for dislocation density mapping and X-ray diffraction (XRD) for film thickness and composition analysis. Key insights suggest that a balance between pinning and density is crucial for optimizing magnetic properties, highlighting the importance of both factors in material design.

We model polydomain liquid-crystal elastomers by extending the neo-classical
soft and semi-soft free energies used successfully to describe monodomain
samples. We show that there is a significant difference between polydomains
cross-linked in homogeneous high symmetry states then cooled to low symmetry
polydomain states and those cross-linked directly in the low symmetry
polydomain state. For example, elastomers cross-linked in the isotropic state
then cooled to a nematic polydomain will, in the ideal limit, be perfectly
soft, and with the introduction of non-ideality, will deform at very low stress
until they are macroscopically aligned. The director patterns observed in them
will be disordered, characteristic of combinations of random deformations, and
not disclination patterns. We expect these samples to exhibit elasticity
significantly softer than monodomain samples. Polydomains cross-linked in the
nematic polydomain state will be mechanically harder and contain characteristic
schlieren director patterns. The models we use for polydomain elastomers are
spatially heterogeneous, so rather than solving them exactly we elucidate this
behavior by bounding the energies using Taylor-like (compatible test strain
fields) and Sachs (constant stress) limits extended to non-linear elasticity.
Good agreement is found with experiments that reveal the supersoft response of
some polydomains. We also analyze smectic polydomain elastomers and propose
that polydomain SmC* elastomers cross-linked in the SmA monodomain state are
promising candidates for low field electrical actuation.

text: Single Spin Magnetic Resonance (SSMR) represents a significant advancement in nanoscale imaging and quantum information processing. Furthermore, we identified specific conditions under which decoherence effects are minimized, thereby improving signal-to-noise ratio and measurement accuracy. Our results suggest that SSMR can significantly augment sensitivity in nanoscale magnetic resonance imaging, providing insights into the atomic structure and dynamics of materials. Further research aimed at integrating SSMR with existing technologies could pave the way for revolutionary applications in ultrafast computing and personalized medicine. symmetric and asymmetric component of the ring current. Here, an attempt is
made to develop a prediction model for these indices using ANN. The ring
current state depends on its past conditions therefore, it is necessary to
consider its history for prediction. To account this effect Nonlinear
Autoregressive Network with eXogenous inputs (NARX) is implemented. This
network considers input history of 30 minutes and output feedback of 120

magnetic field are used as inputs. SYMH and ASYH indices during geomagnetic
storms of 1998-2013, having minimum SYMH <-85 nT are used as the target for
training two independent networks. We present the prediction of SYMH and ASYH
indices during 9 geomagnetic storms of solar cycle 24 including the recent
largest storm occurred on St. Patrick's day, 2015. The present prediction model
reproduces the entire time profile of SYMH and ASYH indices along with small
variations of ~ 10-30 minutes to good extent within noise level, indicating
significant contribution of interplanetary sources and past state of the
magnetosphere. Therefore, the developed networks can predict SYMH and ASYH
indices about an hour before, provided, real-time upstream solar wind data is
available. However, during the main phase of major storms, residuals

text: In the rapidly evolving field of nanophotonics, ultrafast tuning of resonant optical nanostructures plays a crucial role in achieving dynamic control over light-matter interactions. Phase change materials (PCMs) have emerged as promising candidates for ultrafast tuning due to their high refractive index modulation and fast response times. This paper presents a comprehensive study of the ultrafast broadband tuning of resonant optical nanostructures using PCMs. We begin by providing a background on PCMs and their unique properties, highlighting their potential for ultrafast tuning. The objective of this research is to experimentally demonstrate the ultrafast tuning of resonant optical nanostructures using PCMs. To achieve this, we employed a conjugated polymer-doped nanocrystal composite as a PCM and fabricated a grating structure using nanostructure lithography. The optical response of the grating was characterized using time-resolved spectroscopy, revealing an ultrafast tuning response of approximately 100 ps. We further explore the broadband tuning capabilities of the PCM by investigating the dependence of the tuning response on the grating pitch and the temperature. Our results show that the PCM grating can be tuned over a broad spectral range, extending from the visible to the near-infrared region, and can be reversibly switched at a rate of several hundred kHz. The significant implications of this research for the development of ultrafast tunable optical devices are discussed in the conclusion. The presented results demonstrate the feasibility of using PCMs for ultrafast broadband tuning of resonant optical nanostructures, paving the way for future research in this area.

Neutron and x-ray diffraction techniques have been used to study the
competing long and short-range polar order in the relaxor ferroelectric
Pb(Mg$_{1/3}$Nb$_{2/3}$)O$_{3}$ (PMN) under a [111] applied electric field.
Despite reports of a structural transition from a cubic phase to a rhombohedral
phase for fields E $>$ 1.7 kV/cm, we find that the bulk unit cell remains cubic
(within a sensitivity of 90$^{\circ}$-$\alpha$ =0.03$^{\circ}$)for fields up to
8 kV/cm. Furthermore, we observe a structural transition confined to the near
surface volume or `skin' of the crystal where the cubic cell is transformed to
a rhombohedral unit cell at T$_{c}$=210 K for E $>$ 4 kV/cm, for which
90$^{\circ}$-$\alpha$=0.08 $\pm$ 0.03$^{\circ}$ below 50 K. While the bulk unit
cell remains cubic, a suppression of the diffuse scattering and concomitant
enhancement of the Bragg peak intensity is observed below T$_{c}$=210 K,
indicating a more ordered structure with increasing electric field yet an
absence of a long-range ferroelectric ground state in the bulk. The electric
field strength has little effect on the diffuse scattering above T$_{c}$,
however below T$_{c}$ the diffuse scattering is reduced in intensity and adopts
an asymmetric lineshape in reciprocal space. The absence of hysteresis in our
neutron measurements (on the bulk) and the presence of two distinct temperature
scales suggests that the ground state of PMN is not a frozen glassy phase as
suggested by some theories but is better understood in terms of random fields
introduced through the presence of structural disorder. Based on these results,
we also suggest that PMN represents an extreme example of the two-length scale
problem, and that the presence of a distinct skin maybe necessary for a relaxor
ground state.

text: The study explores the dynamics of the solar corona, particularly focusing on the nonlinear force-free field (NLFFF) and potential field models during the Whole Heliospheric Interval (WHI), a period of minimal solar activity. Accurate modeling of active-region and global coronal magnetic fields is crucial for understanding solar phenomena and predicting space weather. This research aims to compare and contrast the NLFFF with potential field models to assess their effectiveness and limitations in representing coronal fields during a solar minimum. Utilizing data from Hinode, STEREO, and SOHO, the study employs advanced computational techniques for modeling, including optimization methods for extrapolating nonlinear force-free fields from observed photospheric magnetograms. Findings indicate that while both models effectively capture the broad characteristics of coronal fields, the NLFFF model offers a significantly more accurate representation of the complex magnetic structures within active regions. The potential field model, however, remains useful for global coronal field approximations due to its simplicity and computational efficiency. The identified discrepancies between models suggest potential avenues for refinement, particularly in enhancing NLFFF model resolution and computational speed. The study concludes that integrating both models, leveraging the detailed accuracy of the NLFFF on smaller scales and the computational efficiency of potential field models on a global scale, could offer a comprehensive approach to modeling coronal fields. These results have implications for improving solar event predictions, which are vital for mitigating the impact of space weather on Earth's technology-dependent infrastructure.

text: The kinetics of slow electronic rearrangement in YBa2Cu3Oy (Y123) superconductors have been the subject of extensive research due to their potential applications in high-temperature superconductors. One significant phenomenon related to this is O- aftershot quenching, which occurs after the application of an electrical pulse to the superconductor.  The objective of this study is to investigate the kinetics of O- aftershot quenching in Y123 superconductors using time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy (TR-XAS) and temperature-dependent measurements.  Experiments were conducted using a TR-XAS setup with a synchrotron source and a cryostat to maintain the sample at temperatures above the critical temperature Tc. The O K-edge spectra were measured at different time delays after the application of an electrical pulse, and the temperature dependence was studied by varying the sample temperature.  Our results reveal that the O- aftershot quenching process involves two distinct stages. The first stage is a rapid oxidation process that occurs within a few nanoseconds, leading to the formation of oxygen vacancies. The second stage is a much slower reduction process, which takes place over several microseconds and results in the recovery of the original superconducting properties. The temperature dependence of this process was found to be complex, with both activation energy and Arrhenius-type behavior observed.  In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the kinetics of O- aftershot quenching in Y123 superconductors, which is important for understanding the mechanism of this phenomenon and its potential applications in high-temperature superconductors. The findings from this research could help in the development of new materials and technologies for energy storage and transportation applications. text: We present our investigation into the nonthermal emission properties of the northwestern rim of the supernova remnant RX J0852-4622. This study aims to resolve the characteristics and mechanisms underlying the nonthermal radiation emanating from this region. Utilizing a multi-wavelength observational approach, we employed data obtained from X-ray and radio telescopes, including the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Parkes Radio Telescope, to perform a comprehensive analysis of the emission spectra. Our findings reveal a prominent synchrotron emission component indicative of high-energy electron acceleration processes at play within the remnant’s shock front. We observed a significant correlation between the intensity of the detected X-ray and radio emissions, suggesting the presence of highly relativistic particles. Additionally, we identified spectral variations across different regions of the northwestern rim, pointing towards spatial inhomogeneities in magnetic field strength and electron energy distribution. Our analysis indicates that the particle acceleration mechanism resembles the diffusive shock acceleration model, providing new insights into the dynamics and evolution of the supernova remnant. The results contribute a deeper understanding of cosmic ray origin and propagation, offering potential implications for broader astrophysical phenomena. Further investigations, particularly in the gamma-ray regime, are required to comprehensively elucidate the full spectrum of nonthermal emissions. This work underscores the necessity for high-resolution observational data and advanced modeling techniques to accurately characterize supernova remnants and the fundamental processes of particle acceleration within these extraordinary cosmic laboratories.

text: This research paper presents PRESY, a novel context-based query reformulation tool designed to improve information retrieval on the web. The web is characterized by its vast and dynamic nature, with users frequently accessing and interacting with web pages from diverse domains. Existing query reformulation techniques often rely on simplistic or static approaches, failing to account for the complex and dynamic context of web queries.  The objective of this research is to develop a context-based query reformulation tool that can effectively adapt to the nuances of web queries, enabling users to retrieve more accurate and relevant results. PRESY employs a multi-faceted approach, incorporating natural language processing, machine learning, and web analytics to analyze the context of user queries, identify semantic relationships, and reformulate queries accordingly.  The proposed tool is evaluated using a large-scale dataset of web queries and their corresponding results, demonstrating its ability to improve query effectiveness by up to 25% compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Key findings reveal that PRESY's context-based approach outperforms traditional query reformulation methods in handling complex queries, noisy user input, and diverse domain knowledge.  The research contributes to the development of more effective information retrieval systems, enabling users to access accurate and relevant information on the web. By providing a flexible and adaptive query reformulation tool, PRESY has the potential to revolutionize the way users interact with web-based information systems.

text: The Andromeda galaxy (M31), our closest spiral neighbor, is an excellent laboratory for studying the interstellar medium (ISM) of nearby spiral galaxies. Observations of the ISM in M31 have shown that a significant fraction of the total infrared (IR) emission originates from warm dust heated by young massive stars. However, the dust heating mechanism and the distribution of warm dust within M31 are still not well understood.   We aim to model the dust heating process in M31 using the radiative transfer code SKIRT and compare our results with observations. We utilize the Herschel Evolutionary Gallery of Local Apprentices (HELGA) VII dataset, which provides far-infrared imaging and spectroscopy for M31.   We employ the SKIRT code to simulate the dust heating process in M31 under various star formation scenarios. We consider star formation models with different stellar initial mass functions (IMFs) and star formation efficiencies. We also investigate the effects of dust properties, such as grain size distribution and composition, on the heating process.  Key findings Our results show that the choice of star formation efficiency significantly influences the dust heating efficiency. Higher star formation efficiencies lead to a higher fraction of warm dust mass. Furthermore, we find that the observed far-IR emission from M31 is better reproduced when assuming a top-heavy IMF. Additionally, we find that the observed far-IR spectral energy distribution can be well explained by a mixture of young massive stars and older evolved stars, with both populations contributing significantly to the warm dust heating.   Our study provides important insights into the dust heating process in M31 and highlights the importance of considering star formation efficiency and IMF when modeling the ISM in nearby spiral galaxies. The results of our investigation may contribute to a better understanding of the ISM in other spiral galaxies and lead to more accurate modeling of the IR emission from these galaxies.

text: In this study, we investigate point- and cluster-defects in radiation-damaged silicon to understand their impact on the material's properties. The results reveal a complex interplay between different types of defects, shedding light on the mechanisms governing their formation and migration. Furthermore, our findings provide insights into the effects of these defects on the electronic and optical properties of radiation-damaged silicon. By elucidating the behavior of point- and cluster-defects in silicon, this research contributes to the development of strategies for enhancing the radiation tolerance of semiconductor devices and optimizing their performance in harsh environments.

The Large Area Telescope (LAT) on board the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope
routinely detects the highly dust-absorbed, reddened, and MeV-peaked flat
spectrum radio quasar PKS 1830-211 (z=2.507). Its apparent isotropic gamma-ray
luminosity (E>100 MeV) averaged over $\sim$ 3 years of observations and peaking
on 2010 October 14/15 at 2.9 X 10^{50} erg s^{-1}, makes it among the brightest
high-redshift Fermi blazars. No published model with a single lens can account
for all of the observed characteristics of this complex system. Based on radio
observations, one expects time delayed variability to follow about 25 days
after a primary flare, with flux about a factor 1.5 less. Two large gamma-ray
flares of PKS 1830-211 have been detected by the LAT in the considered period
and no substantial evidence for such a delayed activity was found. This allows
us to place a lower limit of about 6 on the gamma rays flux ratio between the
two lensed images. Swift XRT observations from a dedicated Target of
Opportunity program indicate a hard spectrum and with no significant
correlation of X-ray flux with the gamma-ray variability. The spectral energy
distribution can be modeled with inverse Compton scattering of thermal photons
from the dusty torus. The implications of the LAT data in terms of variability,
the lack of evident delayed flare events, and different radio and gamma-ray
flux ratios are discussed. Microlensing effects, absorption, size and location
of the emitting regions, the complex mass distribution of the system, an
energy-dependent inner structure of the source, and flux suppression by the
lens galaxy for one image path may be considered as hypotheses for
understanding our results.

text: This research investigates the process by which Mercury became locked in a 3/2 spin-orbit resonance, focusing on the influence of core-mantle friction. Key findings indicate that core-mantle friction can significantly alter Mercury's rotational characteristics, potentially explaining the observed 3/2 spin-orbit resonance. The results suggest that this mechanism could be more effective at transferring angular momentum from the planet's rotation to its orbit than previously thought, offering a plausible explanation for Mercury's current state. The study underscores the importance of incorporating complex internal processes, such as core-mantle friction, in planetary dynamical models.

We have revisited the X-ray scaling relations of early type galaxies (ETG) by
investigating, for the first time, the LX,Gas - MTotal relation in a sample of
14 ETGs. In contrast to the large scatter (by a factor of 102-103) in the
LX,Total - LB relation, we found a tight correlation between these physically
motivated quantities with a rms deviation of a factor of 3 in LX,Gas = 1038 -
1043 erg s-1 or MTotal = a few x 1010 - a few x 1012 Mo. More striking, this
relation becomes even tighter with a rms deviation of a factor of 1.3 among the
gas-rich galaxies (with LX,Gas > 1040 erg s-1). In a simple power-law form, the
new relation is (LX,Gas / 1040 erg s-1) = (MTotal / 3.2 x 1011 Mo)3. This
relation is also consistent with the steep relation between the gas luminosity
and temperature, LX,Gas ~ TGas4.5, identified by Boroson, Kim & Fabbiano
(2011), if the gas is virialized. Our results indicate that the total mass of
an ETG is the primary factor in regulating the amount of hot gas. Among the
gas-poor galaxies (with LX,Gas < a few x 1039 erg s-1), the scatter in the
LX,Gas - MTotal (and LX,Gas - TGas) relation increases, suggesting that
secondary factors (e.g., rotation, flattening, star formation history, cold gas
etc.) may become important.

We present results from high-resolution, optical to near-IR imaging of host
stars of Kepler Objects of Interest (KOIs), identified in the original Kepler
field. Part of the data were obtained under the Kepler imaging follow-up
observation program over seven years (2009 - 2015). Almost 90% of stars that
are hosts to planet candidates or confirmed planets were observed. We combine
measurements of companions to KOI host stars from different bands to create a
comprehensive catalog of projected separations, position angles, and magnitude
differences for all detected companion stars (some of which may not be bound).
Our compilation includes 2297 companions around 1903 primary stars. From
high-resolution imaging, we find that ~10% (~30%) of the observed stars have at
least one companion detected within 1" (4"). The true fraction of systems with
close (< ~4") companions is larger than the observed one due to the limited
sensitivities of the imaging data. We derive correction factors for planet
radii caused by the dilution of the transit depth: assuming that planets orbit
the primary stars or the brightest companion stars, the average correction
factors are 1.06 and 3.09, respectively. The true effect of transit dilution
lies in between these two cases and varies with each system. Applying these
factors to planet radii decreases the number of KOI planets with radii smaller
than 2 R_Earth by ~2-23% and thus affects planet occurrence rates. This effect
will also be important for the yield of small planets from future transit
missions such as TESS.

text: We investigated the structural and dynamical properties of the edge of the young Galactic disc, a region of intense star formation and stellar feedback. Through a combination of observations with the Hubble Space Telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, we mapped the distribution of molecular gas, dust, and young stellar populations within a 2-kiloparsec radius of the Galactic centre. Our results reveal a complex interplay between the ongoing collapse of molecular clouds, the formation of massive stars, and the regulation of gas flow by stellar feedback.  We found that the edge of the young Galactic disc is characterized by a high density of molecular gas, which is being compressed and fragmented by the gravitational influence of nearby stars. This compression leads to the formation of dense cores, which in turn give rise to the birth of massive stars. Our observations also suggest that the edge of the young Galactic disc is subject to a significant amount of stellar feedback, which regulates the flow of gas and suppresses the formation of new stars.  Our analysis of the spatial and temporal correlations between molecular gas, dust, and young stellar populations reveals a dynamic and self-regulating system, in which the formation of new stars is balanced by the loss of gas through stellar feedback. This work provides new insights into the mechanisms that govern the formation of young stars and the regulation of gas flow in the early stages of galaxy evolution.

The substantial gender gap in the science, technology, engineering, and
mathematics (STEM) workforce can be traced back to the underrepresentation of
women at various milestones in the career pathway. Calculus is a necessary step
in this pathway and has been shown to often dissuade people from pursuing STEM
fields. We examine the characteristics of students who begin college interested
in STEM and either persist or switch out of the calculus sequence after taking
Calculus I, and hence either continue to pursue a STEM major or are dissuaded
from STEM disciplines. The data come from a unique, national survey focused on
mainstream college calculus. Our analyses show that, while controlling for
academic preparedness, career intentions, and instruction, the odds of a woman
being dissuaded from continuing in calculus is 1.5 times greater than that for
a man. Furthermore, women report they do not understand the course material
well enough to continue significantly more often than men. When comparing women
and men with above-average mathematical abilities and preparedness, we find
women start and end the term with significantly lower mathematical confidence
than men. This suggests a lack of mathematical confidence, rather than a lack
of mathematically ability, may be responsible for the high departure rate of
women. While it would be ideal to increase interest and participation of women
in STEM at all stages of their careers, our findings indicate that simply
increasing the retention of women starting in college calculus would almost
double the number of women entering the STEM workforce.
