Markowitz (1952, 1959) laid down the ground-breaking work on the
mean-variance analysis. Under his framework, the theoretical optimal allocation
vector can be very different from the estimated one for large portfolios due to
the intrinsic difficulty of estimating a vast covariance matrix and return
vector. This can result in adverse performance in portfolio selected based on
empirical data due to the accumulation of estimation errors. We address this
problem by introducing the gross-exposure constrained mean-variance portfolio
selection. We show that with gross-exposure constraint the theoretical optimal
portfolios have similar performance to the empirically selected ones based on
estimated covariance matrices and there is no error accumulation effect from
estimation of vast covariance matrices. This gives theoretical justification to
the empirical results in Jagannathan and Ma (2003). We also show that the
no-short-sale portfolio is not diversified enough and can be improved by
allowing some short positions. As the constraint on short sales relaxes, the
number of selected assets varies from a small number to the total number of
stocks, when tracking portfolios or selecting assets. This achieves the optimal
sparse portfolio selection, which has close performance to the theoretical
optimal one. Among 1000 stocks, for example, we are able to identify all
optimal subsets of portfolios of different sizes, their associated allocation
vectors, and their estimated risks. The utility of our new approach is
illustrated by simulation and empirical studies on the 100 Fama-French
industrial portfolios and the 400 stocks randomly selected from Russell 3000.

text: We investigated the quasi-periodic variations of solar photospheric fields, with a focus on their potential role as precursors to the deep solar minimum in solar cycle 23. Our analysis revealed a significant decrease in the amplitude of quasi-periodic variations in the late 1990s, approximately two years prior to the onset of the deep solar minimum. This decrease was observed in the photospheric magnetic field strength, as well as in the amplitude of the 11-month oscillations in the sunspot number.  Our study employed a combination of observations from the Michelson Doppler Imager and the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory, as well as simulations using the MHD code GONG. We found that the decrease in quasi-periodic variations was associated with a weakening of the solar dynamo, which is the process responsible for generating the solar magnetic field. This weakening was reflected in a decrease in the strength of the photospheric magnetic field, as well as in a reduction in the amplitude of the 11-month oscillations.  Our results suggest that the decrease in quasi-periodic variations may have played a key role in the development of the deep solar minimum in solar cycle 23. We propose that the weakening of the solar dynamo, and the resulting decrease in quasi-periodic variations, may have contributed to a prolonged period of low solar activity, characterized by a prolonged deep minimum. This hypothesis is supported by the observation that the deep solar minimum in cycle 23 was preceded by a prolonged period of low solar activity, lasting several years.

the formation of hot hydrostatic haloes and their dependence on feedback
mechanisms. We find that the appearance of a strong bimodality in the
probability density function (PDF) of the ratio of the radiative cooling and
dynamical times for halo gas provides a clear signature of the formation of a
hot corona. Haloes of total mass $10^{11.5}-10^{12}{\rm{M}}_{\odot}$ develop a
hot corona independent of redshift, at least in the interval $z=0-4$ where the
simulation has sufficiently good statistics. We analyse the build up of the hot
gas mass in the halo, $M_{\rm{hot}}$, as a function of halo mass and redshift
and find that while more energetic galactic winds powered by SNe increases
$M_{\rm{hot}}$, AGN feedback reduces it by ejecting gas from the halo. We also
study the thermal properties of gas accreting onto haloes and measure the
fraction of shock-heated gas as a function of redshift and halo mass. We
develop analytic and semianalytic approaches to estimate a `critical halo
mass', $M_{\rm{crit}}$, for hot halo formation. We find that the mass for which
the heating rate produced by accretion shocks equals the radiative cooling
rate, reproduces the mass above which haloes develop a significant hot
atmosphere. This yields a mass estimate of $M_{\rm{crit}} \approx
10^{11.7}{\rm{M}}_{\odot}$ at $z=0$, which agrees with the simulation results.
The value of $M_{\rm{crit}}$ depends more strongly on the cooling rate than on
any of the feedback parameters.

A northern subsample of 89 Spitzer GLIMPSE extended green objects (EGOs), the
candidate massive young stellar objects, are surveyed for molecular lines in
two 1-GHz ranges: 251.5- 252.5 and 260.188-261.188 GHz. A comprehensive catalog
of observed molecular line data and spectral plots are presented. Eight
molecular species are undoubtedly detected: H13CO+, SiO, SO, CH3OH, CH3OCH3,
CH3CH2CN, HCOOCH3, and HN13C. H13CO+ 3-2 line is detected in 70 EGOs among
which 37 ones also show SiO 6-5 line, demonstrating their association to dense
gas and supporting the outflow interpretation of the extended 4.5 um excess
emission. Our major dense gas and outflow tracers (H13CO+, SiO, SO and CH3OH)
are combined with our previous survey of 13CO, 12CO and C18O 1-0 toward the
same sample of EGOs for a multi-line multi- cloud analysis of line width and
luminosity correlations. Good log-linear correlations are found among all
considered line luminosities, which requires a universal similarity of density
and thermal structures and probably of shock properties among all EGO clouds to
explain. It also requires that the shocks should be produced within the natal
clouds of the EGOs. Diverse degrees of correlation are found among the line
widths. However, both the line width and luminosity correlations tend to
progressively worsen across larger cloud subcomponent size-scales, depicting
the increase of randomness across cloud subcomponent sizes. Moreover, the line
width correlations among the three isotopic CO 1-0 lines show data scatter as
linear functions of the line width itself, indicating that the velocity
randomness also increases with whole-cloud sizes and has some regularity
behind.

text: Multiple polylogarithms are significant in various fields of mathematics and theoretical physics, particularly in the evaluation of higher-order Feynman integrals and special functions. This paper presents a comprehensive review of Dan's reduction method, which offers an efficient approach to simplifying complex multiple polylogarithmic expressions. The primary objective is to elucidate the principles and applications of this reduction technique, assessing its effectiveness in reducing computational complexity in polylogarithm calculations.   The methodology involves an in-depth analysis of the mathematical framework underlying Dan’s reduction method, including the recursive relations and identities employed in the simplification process. By synthesizing existing literature and providing illustrative examples, we critically evaluate the versatility and limitations of the method across various scenarios involving multiple polylogarithms.  Key findings reveal that Dan's reduction method significantly streamlines computations, enabling the successful evaluation of previously intractable polylogarithmic integrals. Furthermore, this approach demonstrates improved convergence characteristics, providing researchers with a robust tool for mathematical manipulations in both algebraic and analytic forms.   In conclusion, this review will serve as an essential resource for mathematicians and physicists seeking to leverage Dan's reduction method in their work with multiple polylogarithms, promoting further exploration of this powerful technique within the broader context of computational mathematics and theoretical physics. The insights provided aim to enhance understanding and inspire future advancements in the study of polylogarithmic functions.

Improving the efficiency of malaria diagnosis is one of the main goals of
current malaria research. We have recently developed a magneto-optical (MO)
method which allows high-sensitivity detection of malaria pigment (hemozoin)
crystals via their magnetically induced rotation in blood. Here, we validate
this technique on laboratory derived blood samples infected with
\textit{Plasmodium falciparum}. Using two parasite cultures, the first
containing mostly ring stages and the second corresponding to the end of the
parasite life cycle, we demonstrate that our novel method can detect parasite
densities as low as $\sim$40 and $\sim$10\,parasites per microliter of blood
for ring and schizont stage parasites, respectively. This detection limit
exceeds the performance of rapid diagnostic tests and competes with the
threshold achievable by light microscopic observation of blood smears. Our
method can be performed with as little as 50\,microliter of capillary blood and
is sensitive to the presence of hemozoin micro-crystals down to ppm
concentrations. The device, designed to a portable format for clinical and
in-field tests, requires no special training of the operator or specific
reagents, except for an inexpensive lysis solution to release intracellular
hemozoin. Beyond diagnostics, this technique may offer an efficient tool to
study hemozoin formation, trace hemozoin kinetics in the body and test
susceptibility/resistance of parasites to new antimalarial drugs inhibiting
hemozoin formation.

text:
The dawn of the fourth industrial revolution, Industry 4.0 has created great
enthusiasm among companies and researchers by giving them an opportunity to
pave the path towards the vision of a connected smart factory ecosystem.
However, in context of automotive industry there is an evident gap between the
requirements supported by the current automotive manufacturing execution
systems (MES) and the requirements proposed by industrial standards from the
International Society of Automation (ISA) such as, ISA-95, ISA-88 over which
the Industry 4.0 is being built on. In this paper, we bridge this gap by
following a model-based requirements engineering approach along with a gap
analysis process. Our work is mainly divided into three phases, (i) automotive
MES tool selection phase, (ii) requirements modeling phase, (iii) and gap
analysis phase based on the modeled requirements. During the MES tool selection
phase, we used known reliable sources such as, MES product survey reports,
white papers that provide in-depth and comprehensive information about various
comparison criteria and tool vendors list for the current MES landscape. During
the requirement modeling phase, we specified requirements derived from the
needs of ISA-95 and ISA-88 industrial standards using the general purpose
Systems Modeling Language (SysML). During the gap analysis phase, we find the
misalignment between standard requirements and the compliance of the existing
software tools to those standards.

text: We investigate the ground-state selection and spin-liquid behavior within the classical Heisenberg model on the breathing pyrochlore lattice, which possesses varying interatomic distances. By employing a combination of analytical and numerical approaches, we explore the conditions leading to distinct ground states and delve into the emergence of spin-liquid phases. Our findings reveal a rich phase diagram characterized by a competition between magnetic order and frustration, driven by the lattice geometry and exchange interactions. We systematically vary the ratio of nearest-neighbor to next-nearest-neighbor interactions to observe transitions between classical spin configurations, including collinear and non-collinear states, and highlight the significance of local symmetry-breaking mechanisms.   Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations and linear spin-wave theory, we identify regions of parameter space where long-range order gives way to spin-liquid behavior, indicating the presence of extensive degeneracy in the ground state. Our results demonstrate that the breathing pyrochlore lattice supports a unique interplay between geometrical frustration and thermal fluctuations, fostering the stability of a spin-liquid state, particularly at higher temperatures. Moreover, we analyze the implications of our findings on potential experimental realizations and the relevance of these phenomena in materials exhibiting similar lattice structures. Overall, our work emphasizes the critical role of lattice breathe in shaping ground-state landscapes and enhancing our understanding of frustrated magnetism within complex materials systems.

text: In this study, we report the successful detection and characterization of protonated cyanogen (NCCNH+) in interstellar environments, addressing the longstanding challenge of probing nonpolar molecules in space. Nonpolar molecules, due to their weak dipole moments, elude observation through conventional radioastronomy techniques. Our work focuses on identifying such molecules through their protonated counterparts, which possess enhanced dipole moments allowing more straightforward detection. We employed high-resolution radioastronomy observations toward well-known molecular clouds and utilized spectral line analysis to identify specific rotational transitions indicative of NCCNH+. Quantum chemical calculations backed our observational efforts, providing theoretically predicted spectra for comparison and verification. Our findings demonstrate that NCCNH+, though detected in relatively low abundance, serves as a robust tracer for cyanogen, expanding our understanding of interstellar chemistry. Furthermore, the methodology developed in this work opens a new avenue for investigating nonpolar interstellar species through their ionized variants. This approach significantly enhances our ability to explore the molecular complexity of diffused interstellar mediums, contributing to our understanding of chemical evolution in the cosmos. The implications of these results are profound, not only providing insight into the molecular inventory of molecular clouds but also offering a tool to explore chemical processes and elemental cycles in space. Future studies will aim to apply our methodology to other nonpolar molecules, potentially unveiling new molecular species and providing a deeper comprehension of astrochemical phenomena.

text:
We describe a simple scheme to construct a low-energy effective Hamiltonian
H_eff for highly correlated systems containing non-metals like O, P or As (O in
what follows) and a transition-metal (M) as the active part in the electronic
structure, eliminating the O degrees of freedom from a starting Hamiltonian
that contains all M d orbitals and all non-metal p orbitals. We calculate all
interaction terms between d electrons originating from Coulomb repulsion, as a
function of three parameters (F_0, F_2 and F_4) and write them in a basis of
orbitals appropriate for cubic, tetragonal, tetrahedral or hexagonal symmetry
around M. The approach is based on solving exactly (numerically if necessary) a
MO_n cluster containing the transition-metal atom and its n nearest O atoms
(for example a CoO_6 cluster in the case of the cobaltates, or a CuO_n cluster
in the case of the cuprates, in which n depends on the number of apical O
atoms), and mapping them into many-body states of the same symmetry containing
d holes only. We illustrate the procedure for the case of Na_xCoO_2. The
resulting H_eff, including a trigonal distortion D, has been studied recently
and its electronic structure agrees well with angle-resolved photoemission
spectra [A. Bourgeois, A. A. Aligia, and M. J. Rozenberg, Phys. Rev. Lett. 102,
066402 (2009)]. Although H_eff contains only 3d t_2g holes, the highly
correlated states that they represent contain an important amount not only of O
2p holes but also of 3d e_g holes. When more holes are added, a significant
redistribution of charge takes place. As a consequence of these facts, the
resulting values of the effective interactions between t_2g states are smaller
than previously assumed, rendering more important the effect of D in obtaining
only one sheet around the center of the Brillouin zone for the Fermi surface
(without additional pockets).

text: Pulsars are highly magnetic, rapidly rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation, primarily X-rays. Four old pulsars, known as Vela, Geminga, Crab, and PSR B1055-52, have been the subject of numerous studies due to their unique properties. These pulsars have been observed to exhibit various X-ray emission phenomena, including thermal emission, non-thermal emission, and X-ray pulsations.   The objective of this study is to examine the X-ray properties of the aforementioned four old pulsars using Chandra X-ray Observatory data. The primary focus is to investigate the thermal and non-thermal X-ray emission mechanisms and to compare the results with previous observations.   Chandra X-ray Observatory data for each pulsar was analyzed using standard data reduction techniques and X-ray spectral analysis tools. The thermal and non-thermal emission components were separated using a two-component spectral model. The resulting spectra were fitted with different theoretical models to determine the physical conditions of the emission regions.   Vela and Geminga exhibited significant non-thermal X-ray emission, with power law indices consistent with previous observations. The Crab pulsar displayed a complex X-ray spectrum, with both thermal and non-thermal components. The thermal component was attributed to the emission from the neutron star surface, while the non-thermal component was suggested to originate from the magnetospheric interaction between the neutron star and the companion star. PSR B1055-52 exhibited predominantly thermal emission, with a blackbody temperature of approximately 1.1 keV.   The results of this study provide new insights into the X-ray properties of the four old pulsars and contribute to our understanding of the complex emission mechanisms associated with these astronomical objects. The Chandra X-ray Observatory data have allowed for a more detailed investigation of the thermal and non-thermal X-ray components, providing valuable information for further research in this area.
label: machine

text: This study investigates the near-surface convection in cool main-sequence stars through the use of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. Cool main-sequence stars, such as red dwarfs and M-dwarfs, are of great interest due to their proximity to Earth and the potential for hosting exoplanets. The near-surface convection in these stars plays a crucial role in determining their atmospheric properties, including the formation of planetary atmospheres.  The objective of this research is to simulate the near-surface convection in cool main-sequence stars and to examine the effects of magnetic fields on the convective transport of energy and heat. The simulations are performed using a high-resolution MHD code, which takes into account the complex interplay between magnetic fields, rotation, and convective motions.  The key findings of this study reveal that the presence of magnetic fields significantly affects the convective transport of energy and heat in cool main-sequence stars. The simulations indicate that the magnetic fields can either enhance or suppress the convective transport, depending on the strength and orientation of the fields. Furthermore, the study shows that the convective transport is highly dependent on the rotation rate and the surface gravity of the star.  The results of this study have significant implications for our understanding of the atmospheric properties of cool main-sequence stars and the potential for hosting exoplanets. The findings suggest that the presence of magnetic fields can play a crucial role in shaping the atmospheric properties of these stars, and that the rotation rate and surface gravity of the star can also have a significant impact on the convective transport.

MilkyWay@home is a volunteer computing project that allows people from every
country in the world to volunteer their otherwise idle processors to Milky Way
research. Currently, more than 25,000 people (150,000 since November 9, 2007)
contribute about half a PetaFLOPS of computing power to our project. We
currently run two types of applications: one application fits the spatial
density profile of tidal streams using statistical photometric parallax, and
the other application finds the N-body simulation parameters that produce tidal
streams that best match the measured density profile of known tidal streams.
The stream fitting application is well developed and is producing published
results. The Sagittarius dwarf leading tidal tail has been fit, and the
algorithm is currently running on the trailing tidal tail and bifurcated
pieces. We will soon have a self-consistent model for the density of the smooth
component of the stellar halo and the largest tidal streams. The $N$-body
application has been implemented for fitting dwarf galaxy progenitor properties
only, and is in the testing stages. We use an Earth-Mover Distance method to
measure goodness-of-fit for density of stars along the tidal stream. We will
add additional spatial dimensions as well as kinematic measures in a piecemeal
fashion, with the eventual goal of fitting the orbit and parameters of the
Milky Way potential (and thus the density distribution of dark matter) using
multiple tidal streams.

The evolutionary phase of B[e] stars is difficult to establish due to the
uncertainties in their fundamental parameters. For instance, possible
classifications for the Galactic B[e] star MWC 137 include pre-main-sequence
and post-main-sequence phases, with a large range in luminosity. Our goal is to
clarify the evolutionary stage of this peculiar object, and to study the CO
molecular component of its circumstellar medium. To this purpose, we modeled
the CO molecular bands using high-resolution K-band spectra. We find that MWC
137 is surrounded by a detached cool (T = 1900 +-100 K) and dense (N = (3 +- 1)
x 10^21 cm^(-2)) ring of CO gas orbiting the star with a rotational velocity,
projected to the line of sight, of 84 +- 2 km/s. We also find that the
molecular gas is enriched in the isotope 13C, excluding the classification of
the star as a Herbig Be. The observed isotopic abundance ratio (12C / 13C = 25
+- 2) derived from our modeling is compatible with a proto-PN, main-sequence or
supergiant evolutionary phase. However, based on some observable
characteristics of MWC 137, we propose that the supergiant scenario seems to be
the most plausible. Hence, we suggest that MWC 137 could be in an extremely
short-lived phase, evolving from a B[e] supergiant to a blue supergiant with a
bipolar ring nebula.

Complex structures on a material surface can significantly reduce total
secondary electron emission from that surface. A velvet is a surface that
consists of an array of vertically standing whiskers. The reduction occurs due
to the capture of low-energy, true secondary electrons emitted at the bottom of
the structure and on the sides of the velvet whiskers. We performed numerical
simulations and developed an approximate analytical model that calculates the
net secondary electron emission yield from a velvet surface as a function of
the velvet whisker length and packing density, and the angle of incidence of
primary electrons. We found that to suppress secondary electrons, the following
condition on dimensionless parameters must be met: {\pi}/2 DA tan {\theta} >> 1
where {\theta} is the angle of incidence of the primary electron from the
normal, D is the fraction of surface area taken up by the velvet whisker bases,
and A is the aspect ratio, A {\equiv} h/r, the ratio of height to radius of the
velvet whiskers. We find that velvets available today can reduce the secondary
electron yield by 90% from the value of a flat surface. The values of optimal
velvet whisker packing density that maximally suppresses secondary electron
emission yield are determined as a function of velvet aspect ratio and electron
angle of incidence.

text: In this study, we investigate the impact of limb darkening on the accurate determination of transit parameters of exoplanets. Our work focuses on testing stellar model atmospheres to identify potential biases introduced in the estimation of planet-to-star size ratios and transit durations. By comparing theoretical predictions with observational data from transiting exoplanets, we reveal discrepancies that highlight the importance of considering the effects of limb darkening in transit modeling. Through a comprehensive analysis of transit light curves, we quantify the deviations caused by the neglect of limb darkening, emphasizing the necessity of incorporating realistic stellar atmospheres in exoplanetary studies.  Our research aims to provide a more refined understanding of the complexities involved in determining exoplanet properties from transit observations. We adopt a methodology that involves simulating transit events using various limb darkening models and scrutinizing the resulting differences in inferred transit parameters. By systematically exploring the impact of limb darkening on transit analyses, we aim to improve the accuracy of exoplanet characterization and refine existing methodologies for parameter estimation. Overall, our study contributes to advancing the field of exoplanetary science by shedding light on the significance of limb darkening effects in transit studies.

text:
We present a thorough stability analysis of modified gravity theories in the
presence of matter fields. We use the Effective Field Theory framework for Dark
Energy and Modified Gravity to retain a general approach for the gravity sector
and a Sorkin-Schutz action for the matter one. Then, we work out the proper
viability conditions to guarantee in the scalar sector the absence of ghosts,
gradient and tachyonic instabilities. The absence of ghosts can be achieved by
demanding a positive kinetic matrix, while the lack of a gradient instability
is ensured by imposing a positive speed of propagation for all the scalar
modes. In case of tachyonic instability, the mass eigenvalues have been studied
and we work out the appropriate expressions. For the latter, an instability
occurs only when the negative mass eigenvalue is much larger, in absolute
value, than the Hubble parameter. We discuss the results for the minimally
coupled quintessence model showing for a particular set of parameters two
typical behaviours which in turn lead to a stable and an unstable
configuration. Moreover, we find that the speeds of propagation of the scalar
modes strongly depend on matter densities, for the beyond Horndeski theories.
Our findings can be directly employed when testing modified gravity theories as
they allow to identify the correct viability space.

text: In this study, we investigate the dynamical effects of highly inclined and eccentric massive planets on their protoplanetary discs. We model the system using N-body simulations, focusing on how these planetary parameters influence the disc structure, planet migration, and potential clearing of gaps. The results show that highly inclined planets significantly alter the orientation of gas flow within the disc, leading to more complex and elongated structures compared to systems without inclination. Eccentricity is found to enhance the disc's turbulence, causing enhanced transport of angular momentum and leading to more pronounced gap formation. These findings highlight the importance of inclinations and eccentricities in shaping the early stages of planetary system formation, providing insights into the mechanisms governing planet-disc interactions in young stellar systems.
label: machine

text: The study explores the impact of drainage system volume on the accuracy of measuring undrained thermo-poro-elastic parameters, which are pivotal in evaluating the mechanical and thermal response of porous materials under strain. Understanding these parameters is essential in fields such as geomechanics and reservoir engineering, where precise assessment of subsurface conditions is required. The research objective was to determine how variations in drainage system volume influence the derived values of these parameters. A series of controlled laboratory experiments were conducted on representative porous samples subjected to distinct drainage configurations and volumes. By integrating state-of-the-art thermal and mechanical sensors with advanced fluid flow measurement techniques, the experiments were designed to capture detailed responses of the material under controlled thermal-mechanical loading conditions. Key findings indicate that larger drainage volumes tend to skew the measurement of undrained parameters by altering the pore pressure response time, thus affecting the poro-elastic interactions. Conversely, smaller volumes improve the sensitivity and accuracy of these measurements, closely aligning with theoretical predictions. The results emphasize the necessity to optimize drainage system design to acquire reliable undrained response parameters. These findings contribute significantly to refining current methodologies used in engineering applications and can guide future development of more robust models that accurately predict the undrained behavior in various engineering contexts. In conclusion, effective management of drainage volume is crucial to obtaining precise measurements of thermo-poro-elastic parameters, thus enhancing the reliability of subsurface assessments and engineering applications.

text:
The nonnegativity of the determinant of the partial transpose of a two-qubit
(4 x 4) density matrix is both a necessary and sufficient condition for its
separability. While the determinant is restricted to the interval [0,1/256],
the determinant of the partial transpose can range over [-1/16,1/256], with
negative values corresponding to entangled states. We report here the exact
values of the first nine moments of the probability distribution of the partial
transpose over this interval, with respect to the Hilbert-Schmidt (metric
volume element) measure on the nine-dimensional convex set of real two-qubit
density matrices. Rational functions C_{2 j}(m), yielding the coefficients of
the 2j-th power of even polynomials occurring at intermediate steps in our
derivation of the m-th moment, emerge. These functions possess poles at finite
series of consecutive half-integers (m=-3/2,-1/2,...,(2j-1)/2), and certain
(trivial) roots at finite series of consecutive natural numbers (m=0, 1,...).
Additionally, the (nontrivial) dominant roots of C_{2 j}(m) approach the same
half-integer values (m = (2 j-1)/2, (2 j-3)/2,...), as j increases. The first
two moments (mean and variance) found--when employed in the one-sided Chebyshev
inequality--give an upper bound of 30397/34749 = 0.874759 on the separability
probability of real two-qubit density matrices. We are able to report general
formulas for the m-th moment of the Hilbert-Schmidt probability distribution of
the density matrix determinant over [0,1/256], in the real, complex and
quaternionic two-qubit cases.

text: In this work, we present an analysis of the $\pi^- p \to \pi^-\pi^-\pi^+ p$ reaction at a center-of-mass energy of 190 GeV/$c$, using data collected by the HADES experiment. The main objective of this study is to investigate the presence and properties of light isovector resonances in this reaction channel. To achieve this goal, we employ a partial wave analysis (PWA) approach, using the Bonn-Gatchina model as the foundation for our analysis.  Our results reveal the presence of several resonances with isovector quantum numbers, most notably the $\Delta(1700)P_{33}$, $\Delta(1950)S_{11}$, and $\Delta(1920)D_{13}$ resonances. The extracted mass and width values for these resonances agree well with previous experimental and theoretical studies, providing validation of our methodology and analysis. Additionally, we observe clear evidence of the $f_0(1710)$ scalar meson in the invariant mass distribution of the $\pi^-\pi^-$ system.  Furthermore, we perform a detailed study of the interference patterns between various resonances and background processes, which provides valuable insights into the decay dynamics of these resonances. These findings are crucial for the understanding of isospin symmetry in baryon resonances and the underlying physics of the production and decay mechanisms in the $\pi^- p \to \pi^-\pi^-\pi^+ p$ reaction.  In conclusion, our study provides a comprehensive investigation of the presence and properties of light isovector resonances in the $\pi^- p \to \pi^-\pi^-\pi^+ p$ reaction at a center-of-mass energy of 190 GeV/$c$. The extracted mass and width values, as well as the insights gained from the interference patterns, contribute significantly to our understanding of baryon resonances and the underlying physics in this reaction channel.

text:
In 1917, Marian von Smoluchowski presented a simple mathematical description
of diffusion-controlled reactions on the scale of individual molecules. His
model postulated that a reaction would occur when two reactants were
sufficiently close and, more specifically, presented a succinct relationship
between the relative proximity of two reactants at the moment of reaction and
the macroscopic reaction rate. Over the last century, Smoluchowski reaction
theory has been applied widely in the physical, chemical, environmental and,
more recently, the biological sciences. Despite the widespread utility of the
Smoluchowski theory, it only describes the rates of second order reactions and
is inadequate for the description of higher order reactions for which there is
no equivalent method for theoretical investigation. In this paper, we derive a
generalised Smoluchowski framework in which we define what should be meant by
proximity in this context when more than two reactants are involved. We derive
the relationship between the macroscopic reaction rate and the critical
proximity at which a reaction occurs for higher order reactions. Using this
theoretical framework and using numerical experiments we explore various
peculiar properties of multimolecular diffusion-controlled reactions which, due
to there being no other numerical method of this nature, have not been previous
reported.
label: human

We present an alternative scheme to the widely used method of representing
the basis of one-band Hubbard model through the relation
$I=I_{\uparrow}+2^{M}I_{\downarrow}$ given by H. Q. Lin and J. E. Gubernatis
[Comput. Phys. 7, 400 (1993)], where $I_{\uparrow}$, $I_{\downarrow}$ and $I$
are the integer equivalents of binary representations of occupation patterns of
spin up, spin down and both spin up and spin down electrons respectively, with
$M$ being the number of sites. We compute and store only $I_{\uparrow}$ or
$I_{\downarrow}$ at a time to generate the full Hamiltonian matrix. The
non-diagonal part of the Hamiltonian matrix given as
${\cal{I}}_{\downarrow}\otimes{\bf{H}_{\uparrow}} \oplus
{\bf{H}_{\downarrow}}\otimes{\cal{I}}_{\uparrow}$ is generated using a
bottom-up approach by computing the small matrices ${\bf{H}_{\uparrow}}$(spin
up hopping Hamiltonian) and ${\bf{H}_{\downarrow}}$(spin down hopping
Hamiltonian) and then forming the tensor product with respective identity
matrices ${\cal{I}}_{\downarrow}$ and ${\cal{I}}_{\uparrow}$, thereby saving
significant computation time and memory. We find that the total CPU time to
generate the non-diagonal part of the Hamiltonian matrix using the new one spin
configuration basis scheme is reduced by about an order of magnitude as
compared to the two spin configuration basis scheme. The present scheme is
shown to be inherently parallelizable. Its application to translationally
invariant systems, computation of Green's functions and in impurity solver part
of DMFT procedure is discussed and its extention to other models is also
pointed out.

text:
This work will incorporate a few related tools for addressing the conceptual
difficulties arising from sewing together classical and quantum mechanics:
deterministic operators, weak measurements and post-selection. Weak
Measurement, based on a very weak von Neumann coupling, is a unique kind of
quantum measurement with numerous theoretical and practical applications. In
contrast to other measurement techniques, it allows to gather a small amount of
information regarding the quantum system, with only a negligible probability of
collapsing it. A single weak measurement yields an almost random outcome, but
when performed repeatedly over a large ensemble, the averaged outcome becomes
increasingly robust and accurate. Importantly, a long sequence of weak
measurements can be thought of as a single projective measurement. I claim in
this work that classical variables appearing in the macro-world, such as centre
of mass, moment of inertia, pressure and average forces, result from a
multitude of quantum weak measurements performed in the micro-world. Here
again, the quantum outcomes are highly uncertain, but the law of large numbers
obliges their convergence to the definite quantities we know from our everyday
lives. By augmenting this description with a final boundary condition and
employing the notion of "classical robustness under time-reversal" I will draw
a quantitative borderline between the classical and quantum regimes. I will
conclude by analyzing the role of macroscopic systems in amplifying and
recording quantum outcomes.
label: human

text: In this study, we investigate the orbital modulation of X-ray emission lines from the binary system Cygnus X-3. Through detailed analysis of high-resolution spectroscopic data collected over multiple orbital periods, we observe systematic variations in the line profiles, which are attributed to changes in the accretion disk's geometry as the system rotates. Our findings confirm that the observed modulation is consistent with predictions from theoretical models that describe the interaction between the compact object's gravitational field and the surrounding accretion disk. Key methodologies employed include spectral fitting techniques to extract line parameters and time series analysis to quantify periodic variations. The results highlight the importance of orbital modulation in understanding the physical processes occurring within the accretion environment of Cygnus X-3, particularly regarding the mass transfer dynamics and the structure of the accretion flow. This research advances our understanding of relativistic phenomena in black hole binaries and provides valuable insights into the nature of these exotic objects.
label: machine

text:
Semiconducting 2D materials, such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs),
are emerging in nanomechanics, optoelectronics, and thermal transport. In each
of these fields, perfect control over 2D material properties including strain,
doping, and heating is necessary, especially on the nanoscale. Here, we study
clean devices consisting of membranes of single-layer MoS2 suspended on pillar
arrays. Using Raman and photoluminescence spectroscopy, we have been able to
extract, separate and simulate the different contributions on the nanoscale and
to correlate these to the pillar array design. This control has been used to
design a periodic MoS2 mechanical membrane with a high reproducibility and to
perform optomechanical measurements on arrays of similar resonators with a
high-quality factor of 600 at ambient temperature, hence opening the way to
multi-resonator applications with 2D materials. At the same time, this study
constitutes a reference for the future development of well-controlled optical
emissions within 2D materials on periodic arrays with reproducible behavior. We
measured a strong reduction of the MoS2 band-gap induced by the strain
generated from the pillars. A transition from direct to indirect band gap was
observed in isolated tent structures made of MoS2 and pinched by a pillar. In
fully suspended devices, simulations were performed allowing both the
extraction of the thermal conductance and doping of the layer. Using the
correlation between the influences of strain and doping on the MoS2 Raman
spectrum, we have developed a simple, elegant method to extract the local
strain in suspended and non-suspended parts of a membrane. This opens the way
to experimenting with tunable coupling between light emission and vibration.

AIMS Our aim is to characterize the size, mass, density and temperature
profiles of the protostellar envelope of HH~46 IRS 1 and its surrounding cloud
material as well as the effect the outflow has on its environment.METHODS The
CHAMP+ and LABOCA arrays on the APEX telescope, combined with lower frequency
line receivers, are used to obtain a large continuum map and smaller heterodyne
maps in various isotopologues of CO and HCO+. The high-J lines of CO (6--5 and
7--6) and its isotopologues together with [C I] 2--1, observed with CHAMP+, are
used to probe the warm molecular gas in the inner few hundred AU and in the
outflowing gas. The data are interpreted with continuum and line radiative
transfer models. RESULTS Broad outflow wings are seen in CO low- and high-J
lines at several positions, constraining the gas temperatures to a constant
value of ~100 K along the red outflow axis and to ~60 K for the blue outflow.
The derived outflow mass is of order 0.4--0.8 M_sol, significantly higher than
previously found. The bulk of the strong high-J CO line emission has a
surprisingly narrow width, however, even at outflow positions. These lines
cannot be fit by a passively heated model of the HH 46 IRS envelope. We propose
that it originates from photon heating of the outflow cavity walls by
ultraviolet photons originating in outflow shocks and the accretion disk
boundary layers. At the position of the bow shock itself, the UV photons are
energetic enough to dissociate CO. The envelope mass of ~5 M_sol is strongly
concentrated towards HH 46 IRS with a density power law of -1.8.

text: One-dimensional atomic superfluids have emerged as a paradigmatic model system for studying quantum thermodynamics, offering a unique blend of quantum mechanics and thermodynamic principles. The objective of this research is to investigate the thermodynamic behavior of one-dimensional atomic superfluids, with a focus on their thermodynamic properties, such as entropy, free energy, and heat capacity, in order to shed light on the fundamental principles of quantum thermodynamics.  The research employed a combination of theoretical and numerical methods, including density functional theory and Monte Carlo simulations, to study the thermodynamic behavior of one-dimensional atomic superfluids. The results show that these systems exhibit a rich thermodynamic landscape, with complex phase diagrams and unusual thermodynamic properties. Notably, the calculations reveal that one-dimensional atomic superfluids can exhibit non-equilibrium thermodynamics, where the system can exhibit non-thermal equilibrium behavior, and the concept of temperature becomes ill-defined. The findings of this research provide new insights into the thermodynamic behavior of one-dimensional atomic superfluids and have implications for our understanding of quantum thermodynamics.  The key findings of this research demonstrate that one-dimensional atomic superfluids offer a unique platform for studying the interplay between quantum mechanics and thermodynamics. The results also highlight the importance of considering non-equilibrium thermodynamics in the study of quantum systems. The study of one-dimensional atomic superfluids has far-reaching implications for our understanding of quantum thermodynamics and the development of new thermodynamic theories that can accurately describe the behavior of quantum systems.

The key ideas underlying our work include the use of the Mellin transform to transfer the analysis from the representation theory to the arithmetic geometry, and the exploitation of the properties of the zeta functions to derive explicit formulas and establish their validity. We study various representations for cyclic lambda-terms as higher-order or
as first-order term graphs. We focus on the relation between
'lambda-higher-order term graphs' (lambda-ho-term-graphs), which are
first-order term graphs endowed with a well-behaved scope function, and their
representations as 'lambda-term-graphs', which are plain first-order term
graphs with scope-delimiter vertices that meet certain scoping requirements.
Specifically we tackle the question: Which class of first-order term graphs
admits a faithful embedding of lambda-ho-term-graphs in the sense that (i) the
homomorphism-based sharing-order on lambda-ho-term-graphs is preserved and
reflected, and (ii) the image of the embedding corresponds closely to a natural
class (of lambda-term-graphs) that is closed under homomorphism?
  We systematically examine whether a number of classes of lambda-term-graphs
have this property, and we find a particular class of lambda-term-graphs that
satisfies this criterion. Term graphs of this class are built from application,
abstraction, variable, and scope-delimiter vertices, and have the
characteristic feature that the latter two kinds of vertices have back-links to
the corresponding abstraction.
  This result puts a handle on the concept of subterm sharing for higher-order
term graphs, both theoretically and algorithmically: We obtain an easily
implementable method for obtaining the maximally shared form of
lambda-ho-term-graphs. Furthermore, we open up the possibility to pull back
properties from first-order term graphs to lambda-ho-term-graphs, properties
such as the complete lattice structure of bisimulation equivalence classes with
respect to the sharing order.

These insights provide a detailed understanding of how physical and technical constraints affect imaging performance.  Our results reveal that strategic adjustments in system parameters can lead to significant improvements in information capacity without substantial loss of image fidelity. This research delineates the critical parameters affecting linear imaging systems and proposes methodologies for achieving optimal trade-offs. The derived framework serves as a pivotal guide for designing high-performance imaging systems in various applications, including medical imaging and remote sensing. The differential charged jet cross sections, jet fragmentation distributions,
and jet shapes are measured in minimum bias proton-proton collisions at
centre-of-mass energy $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV using the ALICE detector at the LHC.
Jets are reconstructed from charged particle momenta in the mid-rapidity region
using the sequential recombination $k_{\rm T}$ and anti-$k_{\rm T}$ as well as
the SISCone jet finding algorithms with several resolution parameters in the
range $R=0.2$ to $0.6$. Differential jet production cross sections measured
with the three jet finders are in agreement in the transverse momentum ($p_{\rm
T}$) interval $20<p_{\rm T}^{\rm jet,ch}<100$ GeV/$c$. They are also consistent
with prior measurements carried out at the LHC by the ATLAS collaboration. The
jet charged particle multiplicity rises monotonically with increasing jet
$p_{\rm T}$, in qualitative agreement with prior observations at lower
energies. The transverse profiles of leading jets are investigated using radial
momentum density distributions as well as distributions of the average radius
containing 80% ($\langle R_{\rm 80} \rangle$) of the reconstructed jet $p_{\rm
T}$. The fragmentation of leading jets with $R=0.4$ using scaled $p_{\rm T}$
spectra of the jet constituents is studied. The measurements are compared to
model calculations from event generators (PYTHIA, PHOJET, HERWIG). The measured
radial density distributions and $\langle R_{\rm 80} \rangle$ distributions are
well described by the PYTHIA model (tune Perugia-2011). The fragmentation
distributions are better described by HERWIG.

Non-ionising energy loss of radiation produces point defects and defect
clusters in silicon, which result in a signifcant degradation of sensor
performance. In this contribution results from TSC (Thermally Stimulated
Current) defect spectroscopy for silicon pad diodes irradiated by electrons to
fluences of a few $10^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$ and energies between 3.5 and 27 MeV for
isochronal annealing between 80 and 280{\deg}C, are presented. A method based
on SRH (Shockley-Read-Hall) statistics is introduced, which assumes that the
ionisation energy of the defects in a cluster depends on the fraction of
occupied traps. The dfference of ionisation energy of an isolated point defect
and a fully occupied cluster, $\Delta E_a$, is extracted from the TSC data.
  For the VOi (vacancy-oxygen interstitial) defect $\Delta E_a = 0$ is found,
which cofirms that it is a point defect, and validates the method for point
defects. For clusters made of deep acceptors the $\Delta E_a$ values for
different defects are determined after annealing at 80{\deg}C as a function of
electron energy, and for the irradiation with 15 MeV electrons as a function of
annealing temperature. For the irradiation with 3.5 MeV electrons the value
$\Delta E_a = 0$ is found, whereas for the electron energies of 6 to 27 MeV
$\Delta E_a > 0$. This agrees with the expected threshold of about 5 MeV for
cluster formation by electrons. The $\Delta E_a$ values determined as a
function of annealing temperature show that the annealing rate is different for
different defects. A naive diffusion model is used to estimate the temperature
dependencies of the diffusion of the defects in the clusters.

text: In the era of social media, public reactions to corporate earnings announcements have gained significant attention as valuable indicators of investors' sentiment towards companies. Our analysis reveals substantial fluctuations in the average sentiment scores preceding, during, and following EAEs. Specifically, we observed a decline in positive sentiment and an increase in negative sentiment during the day of the EAEs. Furthermore, we identified significant correlations between sentiment scores and stock price returns around EAEs. Additionally, we examined the effect of positive or negative Earnings Surprise (ES) announcements on sentiment. Our results demonstrate that positive ES announcements led to a noticeable surge in positive sentiment, while negative ES announcements resulted in a significant increase in negative sentiment. Our study contributes to the literature by highlighting the potential of Twitter sentiment analysis as a timely and valuable tool for investors in the rapidly evolving technology sector. We recommend future research to investigate the role of sentiment analysis in predicting longer-term stock price trends and identifying potential market anomalies.

The quantum thermal bath (QTB) has been presented as analternative to
path-integral-based methods to introduce nuclear quantumeffects in molecular
dynamics simulations. The method has proved to beefficient, yielding accurate
results for various systems. However, the QTBmethod is prone to zero-point
energy leakage (ZPEL) in highly anharmonicsystems. This is a well-known problem
in methods based on classicaltrajectories where part of the energy of the
high-frequency modes istransferred to the low-frequency modes leading to a
wrong energydistribution. In some cases, the ZPEL can have dramatic
consequences onthe properties of the system. Thus, we investigate the ZPEL by
testing theQTB method on selected systems with increasing complexity in order
to studythe conditions and the parameters that influence the leakage. We also
analyze the consequences of the ZPEL on the structuraland vibrational
properties of the system. We find that the leakage is particularly dependent on
the damping coefficient and thatincreasing its value can reduce and, in some
cases, completely remove the ZPEL. When using sufficiently high values for
thedamping coefficient, the expected energy distribution among the vibrational
modes is ensured. In this case, the QTB methodgives very encouraging results.
In particular, the structural properties are well-reproduced. The dynamical
properties should beregarded with caution although valuable information can
still be extracted from the vibrational spectrum, even for large values ofthe
damping term.

text: We investigate the thermodynamic and statistical-mechanical principles underlying neural synchronization, aiming to provide a coherent framework that elucidates the complex dynamics of this phenomenon. Our work addresses the gap in existing models that inadequately capture the interplay between temperature, entropy, and the emerging synchronized states of neural assemblies. By applying rigorous statistical mechanics, we derive a set of thermodynamic measures that quantify synchronization levels and transition states between orderly and chaotic behaviors. Through simulations and analytical approaches, we reveal how energy dissipation relates to synchronization efficiency, highlighting the critical role of external perturbations and intrinsic noise.   We successfully demonstrate the existence of a phase transition in neural networks, characterized by distinct synchronization regimes as functions of temperature and coupling strength. Our findings suggest that increasing temperature leads to enhanced disorder, yet also facilitates synchronization under certain conditions, indicating a non-trivial relationship between thermal fluctuations and collective neural dynamics. We propose a novel framework integrating these thermodynamic measures with traditional synchronization metrics, offering a comprehensive understanding of the stability and robustness of synchronized states in neural systems.   This study not only advances theoretical insights into neural synchronization but also provides practical implications for developing therapeutic strategies in neurological disorders characterized by synchronization anomalies. Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of how statistical mechanics can inform biological processes and the potential of thermodynamic approaches in neuroscience research.

The bulk of the rare earth elements are believed to be synthesized in the
rapid neutron capture process or $r$ process of nucleosynthesis. The solar
$r$-process residuals show a small peak in the rare earths around $A\sim 160$,
which is proposed to be formed dynamically during the end phase of the $r$
process by a pileup of material. This abundance feature is of particular
importance as it is sensitive to both the nuclear physics inputs and the
astrophysical conditions of the main $r$ process. We explore the formation of
the rare earth peak from the perspective of an inverse problem, using Monte
Carlo studies of nuclear masses to investigate the unknown nuclear properties
required to best match rare earth abundance sector of the solar isotopic
residuals. When nuclear masses are changed, we recalculate the relevant
$\beta$-decay properties and neutron capture rates in the rare earth region.
The feedback provided by this observational constraint allows for the reverse
engineering of nuclear properties far from stability where no experimental
information exists. We investigate a range of astrophysical conditions with
this method and show how these lead to different predictions in the nuclear
properties influential to the formation of the rare earth peak. We conclude
that targeted experimental campaigns in this region will help to resolve the
type of conditions responsible for the production of the rare earth nuclei, and
will provide new insights into the longstanding problem of the astrophysical
site(s) of the $r$ process.

text: We investigate the implications of the Large Hadron Collider's (LHC) missing-transverse-energy (MET) constraints on models with universal extra dimensions. Through a comprehensive analysis of the 8 TeV and 13 TeV LHC run 1 and 2 datasets, we find that the MET constraints significantly constrain the parameter space of the universal extra dimensions (UED) models, particularly those with five and six extra dimensions.   We perform a global fit to the LHC data using the MadGraph5 and Pythia8 Monte Carlo generators, and obtain constraints on the UED model parameters that are consistent with the LHC data. Our results show that the MET constraints from the 8 TeV LHC run 1 data are less stringent than those from the 13 TeV LHC run 2 data, due to the improved luminosity and precision of the latter.   We also find that the MET constraints from the LHC data are in tension with the predictions of the five-dimensional UED model, which predicts a significant MET signal. In contrast, the six-dimensional UED model predicts a MET signal that is consistent with the LHC data.   Our study highlights the importance of the MET constraints in testing the validity of UED models, and underscores the need for further experimental and theoretical work to resolve the tension between the LHC data and the UED predictions. We conclude that the LHC MET constraints provide a stringent test of UED models, and that future experiments will be necessary to determine the validity of these models.

0.4-2.4 micron range. We analyzed them together with previously published data

text: The study of surname distribution serves as an insightful proxy for understanding demographic patterns and evolutionary dynamics within human populations. The results reveal that surname distributions in the sample population exhibit a power-law behavior, with a small number of surnames being extremely common, while most remain rare. This finding aligns with predictions from neutral models of population genetics, indicating that random fluctuations and lineage extinctions contribute significantly to surname diversity. Additionally, the study uncovers correlations between migration patterns and fluctuations in surname distributions, underscoring the impact of historical population movements on genetic and cultural transmission. Conclusively, this research highlights the potential of surname analysis as a tool for deciphering complex demographic patterns. These findings underscore the universality of surname distribution characteristics and their value in tracing historical and evolutionary processes within human societies. Insights from this study not only enhance the understanding of surname dynamics but also have implications for broader sociocultural and population genetic research.

text: Top-gated single-layer molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) has emerged as a promising material for flexible electronics due to its outstanding electronic properties. In this study, we investigate the mobility enhancement and temperature dependence of top-gated MoS2 field-effect transistors (FETs). The device fabrication was performed by a standard dry transfer method. Our experimental results reveal that the gate dielectric thickness significantly affects the electrical properties of MoS2 FETs. Specifically, decreasing the gate dielectric thickness from 160 nm to 3 nm leads to a remarkable increase in the on-state mobility from 5.72 to 129.35 cm2/Vs at room temperature. Furthermore, we observe a strong negative temperature coefficient (Tc) of -3.21%/°C for the on-state mobility in the temperature range of -120°C to 80°C. This Tc value is higher than most of the reported MoS2 FETs in the literature, and we attribute this to the enhanced carrier scattering effect resulting from the thin gate dielectric. The gate dielectric engineering is also a key factor in designing high-performance MoS2 FETs for low-power applications. The findings in this work suggest that the MoS2 FETs with sub-nanometer gate dielectrics exhibit exceptional mobility enhancement and strong temperature dependence, making them ideal candidates for future flexible and wearable electronic devices.

text: In this study, we propose a distributed framework designed to address the growing challenge of executing scalable search operations on encrypted documents. To achieve this, we employ a combination of homomorphic encryption and secure index creation techniques, allowing for encrypted document sets to be queried without exposing their contents. The framework utilizes a distributed architecture, where each node independently executes search operations on a segmented share of the encrypted database, integrating results through a secure aggregation protocol. This allows for linear scalability with respect to data volume increments and facilitates parallel processing, significantly reducing search latencies compared to traditional centralized approaches.  Our experimental evaluation, conducted on diverse datasets simulating real-world conditions, demonstrates that our distributed framework not only maintains strong security guarantees, as evidenced by its resilience against inference attacks, but also delivers enhanced performance metrics. Notably, the framework exhibits scalable throughput and reduced computational overhead, with search times remaining consistently low even as data size increases. These results reveal the potential of our methodology to support enterprises that require both high data security and efficient information retrieval capabilities. Our work lays the foundation for future exploration into more robust, versatile, and secure data management solutions in distributed systems.

The size distribution in the cold classical Kuiper belt can be approximated
by two idealized power laws: one with steep slope for radii R>R* and one with
shallow slope for R<R*, where R*~25-50 km. Previous works suggested that the
SFD roll-over at R* can be the result of extensive collisional grinding in the
Kuiper belt that led to the catastrophic disruption of most bodies with R<R*.
Here we use a new code to test the effect of collisions in the Kuiper belt. We
find that the observed roll-over could indeed be explained by collisional
grinding provided that the initial mass in large bodies was much larger than
the one in the present Kuiper belt, and was dynamically depleted. In addition
to the size distribution changes, our code also tracks the effects of
collisions on binary systems. We find that it is generally easier to dissolve
wide binary systems, such as the ones existing in the cold Kuiper belt today,
than to catastrophically disrupt objects with R~R*. Thus, the binary survival
sets important limits on the extent of collisional grinding in the Kuiper belt.
We find that the extensive collisional grinding required to produce the SFD
roll-over at R* would imply a strong gradient of the binary fraction with R and
separation, because it is generally easier to dissolve binaries with small
components and/or those with wide orbits. The expected binary fraction for R<R*
is <0.1. The present observational data do not show such a gradient. Instead,
they suggest a large binary fraction of ~0.4 for R=30-40 km. This may indicate
that the roll-over was not produced by disruptive collisions, but is instead a
fossil remnant of the KBO formation process.

text: We present a detailed analysis of Chandra X-ray Observatory observations targeting the enigmatic neutron star candidate 1RXS J141256.0+792204, commonly known as Calvera. Our investigation aims to elucidate the nature of Calvera by probing its X-ray emission characteristics, which are pivotal for understanding its classification within isolated neutron stars. We employ spectroscopic and temporal analysis techniques on Chandra's high-resolution data, focusing on its energy distributions and temporal variability. We detect no significant spectral lines or prominent periodic signals above noise thresholds, which constrains pulsation amplitudes and suggests an absence of magnetospheric activity typically associated with radio pulsars.  By applying model fitting to the extracted spectra, we estimate key parameters such as effective temperature and potential gravitational redshift, which align with theoretical predictions for isolated neutron stars. These findings corroborate observations from other quiescent neutron stars and advance our understanding of their cooling processes.  The methodology employed involved utilizing advanced X-ray astronomy tools and comprehensive data analysis software designed for high-energy astrophysics. Our work makes a significant contribution to neutron star astrophysics by refining models of neutron star populations and shedding light on their evolutionary pathways. Through collaboration with broader observational campaigns, we aim to further decipher the diverse manifestations of isolated neutron stars in our galaxy.

Obtaining semantic labels on a large scale radiology image database (215,786
key images from 61,845 unique patients) is a prerequisite yet bottleneck to
train highly effective deep convolutional neural network (CNN) models for image
recognition. Nevertheless, conventional methods for collecting image labels
(e.g., Google search followed by crowd-sourcing) are not applicable due to the
formidable difficulties of medical annotation tasks for those who are not
clinically trained. This type of image labeling task remains non-trivial even
for radiologists due to uncertainty and possible drastic inter-observer
variation or inconsistency.
  In this paper, we present a looped deep pseudo-task optimization procedure
for automatic category discovery of visually coherent and clinically semantic
(concept) clusters. Our system can be initialized by domain-specific (CNN
trained on radiology images and text report derived labels) or generic
(ImageNet based) CNN models. Afterwards, a sequence of pseudo-tasks are
exploited by the looped deep image feature clustering (to refine image labels)
and deep CNN training/classification using new labels (to obtain more task
representative deep features). Our method is conceptually simple and based on
the hypothesized "convergence" of better labels leading to better trained CNN
models which in turn feed more effective deep image features to facilitate more
meaningful clustering/labels. We have empirically validated the convergence and
demonstrated promising quantitative and qualitative results. Category labels of
significantly higher quality than those in previous work are discovered. This
allows for further investigation of the hierarchical semantic nature of the
given large-scale radiology image database.

In recent years, the embedding approach for solving switched optimal control
problems has been developed in a series of papers. However, the embedding
approach, which advantageously converts the hybrid optimal control problem to a
classical nonlinear optimization, has not been extensively compared to
alternative solution approaches. The goal of this paper is thus to compare the
embedding approach to multi-parametric programming, mixed-integer programming
(e.g., CPLEX), and gradient-descent based methods in the context of five
recently published examples: a spring-mass system, moving-target tracking for a
mobile robot, two-tank filling, DC-DC boost converter, and skid-steered
vehicle. A sixth example, an autonomous switched 11-region linear system, is
used to compare a hybrid minimum principle method and traditional numerical
programming. For a given performance index for each case, cost and solution
times are presented. It is shown that there are numerical advantages of the
embedding approach: lower performance index cost (except in some instances when
autonomous switches are present), generally faster solution time, and
convergence to a solution when other methods may fail. In addition, the
embedding method requires no ad hoc assumptions (e.g., predetermined mode
sequences) or specialized control models. Theoretical advantages of the
embedding approach over the other methods are also described: guaranteed
existence of a solution under mild conditions, convexity of the embedded hybrid
optimization problem (under the customary conditions on the performance index),
solvability with traditional techniques (e.g., sequential quadratic
programming) avoiding the combinatorial complexity in the number of
modes/discrete variables of mixed-integer programming, applicability to affine
nonlinear systems, and no need to explicitly assign discrete/mode variables to
autonomous switches.

text: The study explores the statistical properties of rogue waves within the context of the one-dimensional Generalized Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation (GNLSE). This equation serves as a fundamental model for describing wave propagation in various nonlinear media, such as optical fibers and deep-water environments. The primary objective was to investigate how the parameters of the GNLSE influence the occurrence and characteristics of rogue waves, which are rare but significantly impactful extreme events.  Methodologically, the research employed both analytical and numerical techniques. Analytical solutions were derived for specific cases of the GNLSE to understand underlying patterns. Numerical simulations were conducted using finite difference methods to generate wave profiles over time and space, allowing for the identification of rogue wave occurrences.  Key findings indicate that the amplitude and frequency of rogue waves are highly sensitive to the nonlinearity and dispersion coefficients in the GNLSE. Additionally, the study revealed that under certain conditions, the probability distribution of rogue waves follows a power-law distribution, consistent with theoretical predictions based on the N-soliton solutions of the GNLSE. These findings contribute to our understanding of rogue wave generation mechanisms and their predictability.  In conclusion, this research provides valuable insights into the statistical behavior of rogue waves through the lens of the GNLSE, offering potential implications for the management of extreme sea conditions and the design of robust communication systems.

text: Sunspot rotation, a fundamental feature of solar activity, plays a significant role in the development and evolution of major solar eruptions. In this study, we investigate the relationship between sunspot rotation and eruptive events in NOAA Active Region 12158 using high-resolution solar observations and magnetic field measurements from the Helioviewer spacecraft. The objective of this research is to understand the underlying physics governing sunspot rotation and its role in shaping solar activity.  The background section sets the stage by discussing the observed association between sunspot rotation and solar eruptions. It also introduces the concept of magnetic shear and its importance in understanding the eruption process. The methodology section outlines the approach used in the analysis, including the data sources and processing techniques.  Our key findings reveal a clear correlation between the sunspot rotation rate and the occurrence of major eruptions. We found that rapid rotation rates significantly increased the likelihood of solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs), particularly in areas of strong magnetic shear. These results demonstrate that the dynamic interaction between sunspot rotation and magnetic fields drives solar eruptions in NOAA Active Region 12158, shedding light on the fundamental mechanisms at play in solar activity.  In the conclusion, we discuss the implications of these findings for the broader understanding of solar activity and the potential applications of our results for space weather forecasting and solar physics research. We emphasize the importance of continued investigation into the interplay between sunspot rotation, magnetic fields, and solar activity to improve our ability to predict and mitigate the impacts of solar eruptions on Earth.

We present a method for speckle holography that is optimised for crowded
fields. Its two key features are an iterativ improvement of the instantaneous
Point Spread Functions (PSFs) extracted from each speckle frame and the
(optional) simultaneous use of multiple reference stars. In this way, high
signal-to-noise and accuracy can be achieved on the PSF for each short
exposure, which results in sensitive, high-Strehl re- constructed images. We
have tested our method with different instruments, on a range of targets, and
from the N- to the I-band. In terms of PSF cosmetics, stability and Strehl
ratio, holographic imaging can be equal, and even superior, to the capabilities
of currently available Adaptive Optics (AO) systems, particularly at short
near-infrared to optical wavelengths. It outperforms lucky imaging because it
makes use of the entire PSF and reduces the need for frame selection, thus
leading to higher Strehl and improved sensitivity. Image reconstruction a
posteriori, the possibility to use multiple reference stars and the fact that
these reference stars can be rather faint means that holographic imaging offers
a simple way to image large, dense stellar fields near the diffraction limit of
large telescopes, similar to, but much less technologically demanding than, the
capabilities of a multi-conjugate adaptive optics system. The method can be
used with a large range of already existing imaging instruments and can also be
combined with AO imaging when the corrected PSF is unstable.

text: Requirements Engineering (RE) plays a crucial role in the success of software development projects, yet the quantification of challenges faced during requirements elicitation and management has been insufficiently addressed. Employing a mixed-methods approach, we first conducted qualitative interviews with RE professionals in Germany to gather insights on their experiences and challenges. Subsequently, we developed a structured survey instrument based on the qualitative findings, which was then distributed to a broader audience of RE practitioners in Germany. Key findings reveal a significant prevalence of communication-related issues, unclear stakeholder requirements, and inadequate tools that hinder effective requirements management. Preliminary analysis indicates that these challenges vary by industry and organizational size. The study concludes that a standardized global survey framework can provide valuable insights into the multifaceted nature of pain points in RE, fostering a more nuanced understanding of the field and facilitating targeted interventions. This research not only contributes to the empirical understanding of RE challenges in Germany but also lays the groundwork for a broader international discourse on improving requirements engineering practices.

GPGPU applications exploit on-chip scratchpad memory available in the
Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) to improve performance. The amount of thread
level parallelism present in the GPU is limited by the number of resident
threads, which in turn depends on the availability of scratchpad memory in its
streaming multiprocessor (SM). Since the scratchpad memory is allocated at
thread block granularity, part of the memory may remain unutilized. In this
paper, we propose architectural and compiler optimizations to improve the
scratchpad utilization. Our approach, Scratchpad Sharing, addresses scratchpad
under-utilization by launching additional thread blocks in each SM. These
thread blocks use unutilized scratchpad and also share scratchpad with other
resident blocks. To improve the performance of scratchpad sharing, we propose
Owner Warp First (OWF) scheduling that schedules warps from the additional
thread blocks effectively. The performance of this approach, however, is
limited by the availability of the shared part of scratchpad.
  We propose compiler optimizations to improve the availability of shared
scratchpad. We describe a scratchpad allocation scheme that helps in allocating
scratchpad variables such that shared scratchpad is accessed for short
duration. We introduce a new instruction, relssp, that when executed, releases
the shared scratchpad. Finally, we describe an analysis for optimal placement
of relssp instructions such that shared scratchpad is released as early as
possible.
  We implemented the hardware changes using the GPGPU-Sim simulator and
implemented the compiler optimizations in Ocelot framework. We evaluated the
effectiveness of our approach on 19 kernels from 3 benchmarks suites: CUDA-SDK,
GPGPU-Sim, and Rodinia. The kernels that underutilize scratchpad memory show an
average improvement of 19% and maximum improvement of 92.17% compared to the
baseline approach.

text: This study investigates the first-principles electronic structures and magnetism of substitutional $3d$ transition metal (TM) impurities within body-centered cubic (bcc) iron using density functional theory (DFT). The goal is to elucidate how the substitution of TM atoms affects the local magnetic properties and electronic configurations of the host lattice. Various TM elements including Cr, Mn, Co, and Ni were considered as representative substitutions. By employing the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional, we calculated the formation energies, electronic band structures, and total energies for each substitution. Analysis revealed that the magnetic moment and spin polarization of Fe are influenced by the substitutional TM elements, which alter the local electron density around the TM sites. Additionally, our calculations indicated that the exchange interactions between Fe and the TM atoms play a crucial role in determining the overall magnetic behavior. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between dopant-induced magnetic changes and the underlying electronic structure in metallic systems.

text: In this work, we address the Beachcombers' Problem, focusing on the task of effectively employing mobile robots for searching and exploring designated areas. We formulate and implement a novel algorithm designed to optimize the search patterns of autonomous robots, ensuring maximal coverage and minimizing redundant efforts. Our methodology integrates principles of swarm intelligence and reinforcement learning to enable collaborative behavior among multiple robots.   We conduct extensive simulations in various environmental scenarios, including different terrain types and obstacle placements, to evaluate the performance of our algorithm. The results indicate a significant improvement in search efficiency compared to traditional pathfinding techniques. Specifically, our algorithm reduced the average search time by up to 30%, while coordination among robots improved the overall area coverage by 25%.  Moreover, we tackle the inherent challenges of dynamic environments where unknown obstacles might obstruct a robot's path. We propose adaptive heuristics that allow the robots to recalibrate their strategies in real-time. The key contributions of this work lie in the empirical validation of our approach, revealing its robustness and flexibility, as well as its potential applicability in real-world scenarios such as disaster management and environmental monitoring.   Through our findings, we demonstrate that the Beachcombers' Problem can be efficiently solved with our proposed framework, ultimately paving the way for future advancements in mobile robotics and autonomous search operations.
