text: Our research delves into the constraints imposed on hydrodynamical subgrid models by scrutinizing quasar absorption line studies of the simulated circumgalactic medium. By evaluating these models against observational data from quasar absorption line studies, our work aims to address the challenges faced in accurately simulating the complex gas dynamics of the circumgalactic medium surrounding galaxies. The primary focus lies in enhancing the fidelity of simulations by refining the subgrid models used to represent the unresolved physical processes within the simulated gas environment. Through a systematic analysis of the discrepancies between the simulated outputs and observational measurements of quasar absorption lines, we aim to pinpoint the deficiencies in current subgrid models and propose improvements to achieve a more realistic representation of the circumgalactic medium.  Our methodology involves comparing the properties of simulated quasar absorption lines with observed data, identifying key discrepancies, and iteratively adjusting the subgrid models to better match the observational constraints. By iteratively refining these subgrid models, our study seeks to advance the understanding of the circumgalactic medium and pave the way for more accurate and reliable simulations of gas dynamics in galaxy environments.

In today global age, e-government services have become the main channel for
online communication between the government and its citizens. They aim to
provide citizens with more accessible, accurate, real-time and high quality
services. Therefore, the quality of government websites which provide
e-services is an essential factor in the successful adoption of e-government
services by the public. This paper discusses an investigation of the effect of
the Website Quality (WQ) factor on the acceptance of using e-government
services (G2C) in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA) by adopting the Unified
Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) Model. Survey Data collected
from 400 respondents were examined using the structural equation modelling
(SEM) technique and utilising AMOS tools. This study found that the factors
that significantly influenced the Use Behaviour of e-government services in KSA
(USE) include Performance Expectancy (PE), Effort expectancy (EE), Facilitating
Conditions (FC) and Website Quality (WQ), while the construct known Social
Influence (SI) did not. Moreover, the results confirm the importance of quality
government websites and support systems as one of the main significant and
influential factors of e-government services adoption. The results of this

We studied the formation of a pore in AR NOAA 11462. We analysed data
obtained with the IBIS at the DST on April 17, 2012, consisting of full Stokes
measurements of the Fe I 617.3 nm lines. Furthermore, we analysed SDO/HMI
observations in the continuum and vector magnetograms derived from the Fe I
617.3 nm line data taken from April 15 to 19, 2012. We estimated the magnetic
field strength and vector components and the LOS and horizontal motions in the
photospheric region hosting the pore formation. We discuss our results in light
of other observational studies and recent advances of numerical simulations.
The pore formation occurs in less than 1 hour in the leading region of the AR.
The evolution of the flux patch in the leading part of the AR is faster (< 12
hour) than the evolution (20-30 hour) of the more diffuse and smaller scale
flux patches in the trailing region. During the pore formation, the ratio
between magnetic and dark area decreases from 5 to 2. We observe strong
downflows at the forming pore boundary and diverging proper motions of plasma
in the vicinity of the evolving feature that are directed towards the forming
pore. The average values and trends of the various quantities estimated in the
AR are in agreement with results of former observational studies of steady
pores and with their modelled counterparts, as seen in recent numerical
simulations of a rising-tube process. The agreement with the outcomes of the
numerical studies holds for both the signatures of the flux emergence process
(e.g. appearance of small-scale mixed polarity patterns and elongated granules)
and the evolution of the region. The processes driving the formation of the
pore are identified with the emergence of a magnetic flux concentration and the
subsequent reorganization of the emerged flux, by the combined effect of
velocity and magnetic field, in and around the evolving structure.

We investigate the approach to the universal regime of the dilute unitary
Fermi gas as the density is reduced to zero in a lattice model. To this end we
study the chemical potential, superfluid order parameter and internal energy of
the attractive Hubbard model in three different lattices with densities of
states (DOS) which share the same low-energy behavior of fermions in
three-dimensional free space: a cubic lattice, a "Bethe lattice" with a
semicircular DOS, and a "lattice gas" with parabolic dispersion and a sharp
energy cut-off that ensures the normalization of the DOS. The model is solved
using Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, that treats directly the thermodynamic limit
and arbitrarily low densities, eliminating finite-size effects. At densities of
the order of one fermion per site the lattice and its specific form dominate
the results. The evolution to the low-density limit is smooth and it does not
allow to define an unambiguous low-density regime. Such finite-density effects
are significantly reduced using the lattice gas, and they are maximal for the
three-dimensional cubic lattice. Even though dynamical mean-field theory is
bound to reduce to the more standard static mean field in the limit of zero
density due to the local nature of the self-energy and of the vertex functions,
it compares well with accurate Monte Carlo simulations down to the lowest
densities accessible to the latter.

text: In this study, we explore the concept of emergent dark matter within the context of a late-time universe embedded in a holographic screen. Our approach involves utilizing the AdS/CFT correspondence to model the dynamics of dark matter particles in the boundary theory. We present a theoretical framework that suggests dark matter could emerge as a collective behavior of microscopic degrees of freedom localized on the holographic screen. The emergence is characterized by a phase transition that occurs at late times, leading to the formation of dark matter structures similar to those observed in the cosmos.  Our analysis demonstrates that under certain conditions, such as a high energy density regime, the emergent dark matter exhibits properties consistent with observed dark matter phenomena, including gravitational lensing and the formation of large-scale structures. To validate our model, we perform numerical simulations using the holographic renormalization technique to compute the effective action for the emergent dark matter fields. These simulations show agreement with observational data from cosmic microwave background radiation and galaxy surveys.  The key methodology involves bridging the gap between quantum gravity and cosmology through the holographic principle. By leveraging the correspondence between bulk spacetime geometry and boundary field theory, we infer the nature of dark matter from the holographic screen perspective. This approach not only provides a new perspective on dark matter but also offers insights into the fundamental nature of space and time in the context of late-time universes.

Inside individual cells, expression of genes is inherently stochastic and
manifests as cell-to-cell variability or noise in protein copy numbers. Since
proteins half-lives can be comparable to the cell-cycle length, randomness in
cell-division times generates additional intercellular variability in protein
levels. Moreover, as many mRNA/protein species are expressed at low-copy
numbers, errors incurred in partitioning of molecules between the mother and
daughter cells are significant. We derive analytical formulas for the total
noise in protein levels for a general class of cell-division time and
partitioning error distributions. Using a novel hybrid approach the total noise
is decomposed into components arising from i) stochastic expression; ii)
partitioning errors at the time of cell-division and iii) random cell-division
events. These formulas reveal that random cell-division times not only generate
additional extrinsic noise but also critically affect the mean protein copy
numbers and intrinsic noise components. Counter intuitively, in some parameter
regimes noise in protein levels can decrease as cell-division times become more
stochastic. Computations are extended to consider genome duplication, where the
gene dosage is increased by two-fold at a random point in the cell-cycle. We
systematically investigate how the timing of genome duplication influences
different protein noise components. Intriguingly, results show that noise
contribution from stochastic expression is minimized at an optimal genome
duplication time. Our theoretical results motivate new experimental methods for
decomposing protein noise levels from single-cell expression data.
Characterizing the contributions of individual noise mechanisms will lead to
precise estimates of gene expression parameters and techniques for altering
stochasticity to change phenotype of individual cells.

text: This research explores the final state interactions in the decay process $D^+ \to K^- \pi^+ \pi^+$, specifically investigating the interplay between the isospin channels $K\pi$ I=1/2 and I=3/2. The objective is to understand how these interactions influence the decay dynamics, especially in terms of isospin interference effects, which have implications for both decay amplitude analysis and CP violation studies. Utilizing a model-independent approach, the study analyzes data obtained from high-energy collider experiments involving charmed mesons. The methodology involves a partial wave analysis supplemented with isobar models to isolate contributions from each isospin channel. Additionally, advanced fitting techniques are employed to extract precise decay amplitudes and phase differences between the interacting channels. Key findings indicate that the contributions from the I=1/2 channel are significantly more dominant compared to I=3/2, impacting the overall decay amplitude structure. However, the presence of the I=3/2 channel cannot be neglected, as it introduces notable interference effects that are crucial for accurate amplitude modeling. The results also suggest subtle indications of CP violation within the system, warranting further investigation. In conclusion, this analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of final state interactions in $D^+ \to K^- \pi^+ \pi^+$ decays, emphasizing the need for considering both isospin channels in future spectral and CP violation studies. Such insights are valuable for refining theoretical models and enhancing our understanding of strong interaction effects in charm meson decays.

text: We investigated the impact of the Peclet number on the microstructure and transient cluster aggregation in sedimenting colloidal suspensions. The Peclet number, a dimensionless quantity representing the ratio of convective to diffusive transport, plays a crucial role in determining the dynamics of colloidal particles in suspension. Through a combination of numerical simulations and experimental measurements, we observed that the Peclet number significantly influences the formation and evolution of clusters in sedimenting colloidal suspensions. At low Peclet numbers, we found that clusters tend to form through a process of diffusion-limited aggregation, characterized by the gradual accumulation of particles at the interface between two regions of high particle concentration. In contrast, at high Peclet numbers, clusters exhibit a more rapid growth rate, driven by convective transport and the formation of dense, compact structures. Our results suggest that the Peclet number acts as a critical parameter in determining the microstructural characteristics of sedimenting colloidal suspensions, and that understanding its role is essential for controlling the behavior of these systems in various applications, including materials synthesis and biophysics. By elucidating the relationship between the Peclet number and cluster aggregation, we provide insights into the fundamental physics underlying the behavior of sedimenting colloidal suspensions, and highlight the potential for tailoring the microstructure of these systems through the manipulation of the Peclet number.

text:
Lens time delays are a powerful probe of cosmology, provided that the
gravitational potential of the main deflector can be modeled with sufficient
precision. Recent work has shown that this can be achieved by detailed modeling
of the host galaxies of lensed quasars, which appear as "Einstein Rings" in
high resolution images. We carry out a systematic exploration of the high
resolution imaging required to exploit the thousands of lensed quasars that
will be discovered by current and upcoming surveys with the next decade.
Specifically, we simulate realistic lens systems as imaged by the Hubble Space
Telescope (HST), James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), and ground based adaptive
optics images taken with Keck or the Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT). We compare
the performance of these pointed observations with that of images taken by the
Euclid (VIS), Wide-Field Infrared Survey Telescope (WFIRST) and Large Synoptic
Survey Telescope (LSST) surveys. We use as our metric the precision with which
the slope $\gamma'$ of the total mass density profile $\rho_{tot}\propto
r^{-\gamma'}$ for the main deflector can be measured. Ideally, we require that
the statistical error on $\gamma'$ be less than 0.02, such that it is
subdominant to other sources of random and systematic uncertainties. We find
that survey data will likely have sufficient depth and resolution to meet the
target only for the brighter gravitational lens systems, comparable to those
discovered by the SDSS survey. For fainter systems, that will be discovered by
current and future surveys, targeted follow-up will be required. However, the
exposure time required with upcoming facilitites such as JWST, the Keck Next
Generation Adaptive Optics System, and TMT, will only be of order a few minutes
per system, thus making the follow-up of hundreds of systems a practical and
efficient cosmological probe.

text: This research investigates the concept of Reverse Classification Accuracy (RCA), which aims to predict segmentation performance in medical imaging studies where ground truth data is unavailable. The primary objective is to establish RCA as a robust method for evaluating segmentation algorithms, thereby facilitating more efficient and cost-effective image analysis processes. These classifiers are then tested against different segmentation datasets to evaluate their predictive capabilities. Key findings indicate that certain feature combinations significantly enhance the accuracy of RCA predictions, particularly when dealing with complex and diverse image types. The study concludes by suggesting that RCA could serve as a valuable tool in the field of medical imaging, enabling researchers and clinicians to make informed decisions regarding the reliability of their segmentation outcomes without relying solely on time-consuming and resource-intensive ground truth acquisition.

All the state-of-the-art rowhammer attacks can break the MMU-enforced
inter-domain isolation because the physical memory owned by each domain is
adjacent to each other. To mitigate these attacks, physical domain isolation,
introduced by CATT, physically separates each domain by dividing the physical
memory into multiple partitions and keeping each partition occupied by only one
domain. CATT implemented physical kernel isolation as the first generic and
practical software-only defense to protect kernel from being rowhammered as
kernel is one of the most appealing targets.
  In this paper, we develop a novel exploit that could effectively defeat the
physical kernel isolation and gain both root and kernel privileges. Our exploit
can work without exhausting the page cache or the system memory, or relying on
the information of the virtual-to-physical address mapping. The exploit is
motivated by our key observation that the modern OSes have double-owned kernel
buffers (e.g., video buffers and SCSI Generic buffers) owned concurrently by
the kernel and user domains. The existence of such buffers invalidates the
physical kernel isolation and makes the rowhammer-based attack possible again.
Existing conspicuous rowhammer attacks achieving the root/kernel privilege
escalation exhaust the page cache or even the whole system memory. Instead, we
propose a new technique, named memory ambush. It is able to place the
hammerable double-owned kernel buffers physically adjacent to the target
objects (e.g., page tables) with only a small amount of memory. As a result,
our exploit is stealthier and has fewer memory footprints. We also replace the
inefficient rowhammer algorithm that blindly picks up addresses to hammer with
an efficient one. Our algorithm selects suitable addresses based on an existing
timing channel.

text: Research in parameterized complexity has increasingly focused on the efficient computation of graph and matrix problems within the context of low treewidth. This study investigates fully polynomial-time parameterized algorithms (FPT) for a variety of computational challenges in graphs and matrices that exhibit bounded treewidth. The objective is to harness the structural properties of low treewidth to develop algorithms that can solve problems in a time complexity that is polynomial in both the input size and the parameter. We employ a combination of dynamic programming, structural decomposition, and kernelization techniques to explore the computational landscape of well-known problems, including the Vertex Cover, Dominating Set, and Matrix Multiplication. Key findings reveal that our algorithms achieve significant improvements over traditional methods, demonstrating FPT results with explicit polynomial bounds on the parameter. Specifically, we present new theoretical insights into algorithmic design for handling instances where trees serve as the underlying structure, allowing for the handling of larger datasets more effectively. Our results not only affirm the viability of FPT approaches in low treewidth scenarios but also contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between graph properties and computational feasibility. In conclusion, this research validates the potential of low treewidth as a powerful framework for enhancing the efficiency of parameterized algorithms, offering new pathways for tackling complex computational problems in graphs and matrices.

text: The Praesepe open cluster, also known as M44 or the Beehive Cluster, is a rich and densely populated Galactic structure located in the constellation Cancer. With an age estimated to be around 680 million years, it hosts a vast population of late-type stars, providing an excellent opportunity for the study of stellar rotation. In this work, we present the results of our investigation into the rotation properties of late-type stars in Praesepe, using the K2 spectral classification as a reference.  We gathered photometric data from literature and new observations using the 1.07m Shanghai Observatory Reflector Telescope. Through the analysis of these data, we identified a sample of K2 stars with sufficient quality and quantity. Utilizing the K2 spectral type as a proxy for stellar age, we employed the rotational broadening technique to estimate the stellar rotational velocities. Our results indicate a significant spread in rotation periods, with values ranging from 0.4 to 34 days. This finding highlights the presence of both rapid and slow rotators in the Praesepe cluster.  Furthermore, our results suggest a possible correlation between stellar rotation and spectral type, revealing a potential relation between stellar mass, age, and rotation. Additionally, we discovered that the distribution of rotational velocities deviates significantly from a Gaussian distribution, exhibiting a distinct peak at low velocities and a long tail toward high velocities. This deviation may be indicative of complex processes, such as magnetic braking and mass loss, influencing the evolution of late-type stars in Praesepe.  In conclusion, our study contributes to the growing body of knowledge regarding the rotation of late-type stars in open clusters, providing new insights into the role of stellar mass, age, and complex processes in shaping their rotation properties. Future work will focus on expanding the sample size and extending the investigation to additional open clusters to further explore the underlying mechanisms.

text:
LARS is an Absolute Reference Spectrograph designed for ultra-precise solar
observations. The high-resolution echelle spectrograph of the Vacuum Tower
Telescope is supported by a state-of-the-art laser frequency comb to calibrate
the solar spectrum on an absolute wavelength scale. In this article, we
describe the scientific instrument and focus on the upgrades in the last two
years to turn the prototype into a turn-key system. The pursued goal was to
improve the short-term and long-term stability of the systems, and enable a
user-friendly and more versatile operation of the instrument. The first upgrade
involved the modernization of the frequency comb. The Fabry-Perot cavities were
adjusted to filter to a repetition frequency of 8GHz. A technologically matured
photonic crystal fiber was implemented for spectral broadening. The second,
quite recent upgrade was performed on the optics feeding the sunlight into a
single-mode fiber connected to the spectrograph. A motorized translation stage
was deployed to allow the automated selection of three different fields-of-view
with diameters of 1", 3", and 10" for the analysis of the solar spectrum. The
successful upgrades allow for long-term observations of up to several hours per
day with a stable spectral accuracy of 1 m/s limited by the spectrograph.
Stable, user-friendly operation of the instrument is supported. The selection
of the pre-aligned fiber to change the field of view can now be done within
seconds. LARS offers the possibility to observe absolute wavelength positions
of spectral lines and Doppler velocities in the solar atmosphere. First results
demonstrate the capabilities of the instrument for solar science. The accurate
measurement of the solar convection, p-modes, and atmospheric waves will
enhance our knowledge of the solar atmosphere and its physical conditions to
improve current atmospheric models.

We introduce a multispecies exclusion model where length-conserving
probabilistic fusion and fission of the hard rods are allowed. Although all
rods enter the system with the same initial length ${\ell}=1$, their length can
keep changing, because of fusion and fission, as they move in a step-by-step
manner towards the exit. Two neighboring hard rods of lengths ${\ell}_{1}$ and
${\ell}_{2}$ can fuse into a single rod of longer length
${\ell}={\ell}_{1}+{\ell}_{2}$ provided ${\ell} \leq N$. Similarly,
length-conserving fission of a rod of length ${\ell}' \leq N$ results in two
shorter daughter rods. Based on the extremum current hypothesis, we plot the
phase diagram of the model under open boundary conditions utilizing the results
derived for the same model under periodic boundary condition using mean-field
approximation. The density profile and the flux profile of rods are in
excellent agreement with computer simulations. Although the fusion and fission
of the rods are motivated by similar phenomena observed in Intraflagellar
Transport (IFT) in eukaryotic flagella, this exclusion model is too simple to
account for the quantitative experimental data for any specific organism.
Nevertheless, the concepts of `flux profile' and `transition zone' that emerge
from the interplay of fusion and fission in this model are likely to have
important implications for IFT and for other similar transport phenomena in
long cell protrusions.

We present line and continuum observations made with the Submillimeter Array
(SMA) of the young stellar object Barnard 5 - IRS1 located in the Perseus
molecular cloud. Our $^{12}$CO(2-1) line observations resolve the high-velocity
bipolar northeast-southwest outflow associated with this source. We find that
the outflowing gas shows different structures at three different velocity
regimes, in both lobes, resulting in a spider-like morphology. In addition to
the low-velocity, cone-like (wide-angle) lobes that have previously been
observed, we report the presence of intermediate-velocity parabolic shells
emerging very close to the Class I protostar, as well as high velocity
molecular bullets that appear to be associated to the optical/IR jet emanating
from this source. These compact high-velocity features reach radial velocities
of about 50 km s$^{-1}$ away from the cloud velocity. We interpret the peculiar
spider-like morphology is a result of the molecular material being entrained by
a wind with both a collimated jet-like component and a wide-angle component. We
suggest the outflow is in a transitional evolutionary phase between a mostly
jet-driven flow and an outflow in which the entrainment is dominated by the
wide-angle wind component. We also detect 1300 $\mu$m continuum emission at the
position of the protostar, which likely arises from the dusty envelope and disk
surrounding the protostar. Finally, we report the detection of $^{13}$CO(2-1)
and SO(6$_5$-5$_4$) emission arising from the outflow and the location of the
young stellar object.

HIP96515A is a double-lined spectroscopic binary with a visual companion
(HIP96515B) at 8.6 arcsec. It is included in the SACY catalog as a potential
young star and classified as an eclipsing binary in the ASAS Catalog. We have
analyzed spectroscopic and photometric observations of the triple system. The
high-resolution optical spectrum of HIP96515A has been used to derive a mass
ratio, M_2/M_1, close to 0.9, with the SB2 components showing spectral types of
M1 and M2. The ASAS and Hipparcos light-curves of HIP96515A show periodic
variations with P=2.3456 days, confirming that HIP96515A is an eclipsing binary
with preliminary parameters of i=89, M_Aa=0.59+-0.03 Msun and M_Ab=0.54+-0.03
Msun, for the primary and secondary, respectively, at an estimated distance of
42+-3 pc. This is a new eclipsing binary with component masses below 0.6 Msun.
Multi-epoch observations of HIP 96515 A&B show that the system is a common
proper motion pair. The optical spectrum of HIP 96515B is consistent with a
pure helium atmosphere (DB) white dwarf. We estimate a total age (main-sequence
lifetime plus cooling age) of 400 Myr for the white dwarf. If HIP 96515 A&B are
coeval, and assuming a common age of 400 Myr, the comparison of the masses of
the eclipsing binary members with evolutionary tracks shows that they are
underestimated by ~15% and ~10%, for the primary and secondary, respectively.

text: We investigate the rank deficiency of sparse random matrices over the finite field GF[2], aiming to elucidate the conditions under which such matrices exhibit full rank or suffer from significant rank deficiency. Our study addresses the challenging problem of understanding how sparsity impacts the linear independence of rows and columns, which is crucial for applications in coding theory and network theory. Utilizing probabilistic methods and tools from algebraic combinatorics, we derive rigorous bounds on the expected rank of these matrices based on their sparsity patterns and the total number of entries.  Through extensive simulations and mathematical proofs, we identify critical thresholds in the density of non-zero entries that determine the transition from full rank to rank deficiency. Specifically, we demonstrate that as the number of non-zero entries increases, the likelihood of achieving full rank approaches certainty, provided that a certain ratio of non-zeros to dimensions is maintained. Our results indicate that there exists a critical threshold density that delineates the boundary between high rank and rank deficiency in sparse random GF[2] matrices.   Moreover, we explore the implications of our findings for practical applications, such as error correction codes and secure communication systems, where the integrity of information transmission is paramount. Our work contributes valuable insights to the study of random matrices and their properties, establishing a foundational understanding that may guide future research in both theoretical and applied domains.

We present a new exploration of the cosmic star-formation history and dust
obscuration in massive galaxies at redshifts $0.5< z<6$. We utilize the deepest
450 and 850$\mu$m imaging from SCUBA-2 CLS, covering 230arcmin$^2$ in the
AEGIS, COSMOS and UDS fields, together with 100-250$\mu$m imaging from
Herschel. We demonstrate the capability of the T-PHOT deconfusion code to reach
below the confusion limit, using multi-wavelength prior catalogues from
CANDELS/3D-HST. By combining IR and UV data, we measure the relationship
between total star-formation rate (SFR) and stellar mass up to $z\sim5$,
indicating that UV-derived dust corrections underestimate the SFR in massive
galaxies. We investigate the relationship between obscuration and the UV slope
(the IRX-$\beta$ relation) in our sample, which is similar to that of
low-redshift starburst galaxies, although it deviates at high stellar masses.
Our data provide new measurements of the total SFR density (SFRD) in
$M_\ast>10^{10}M_\odot$ galaxies at $0.5<z<6$. This is dominated by obscured
star formation by a factor of $>10$. One third of this is accounted for by
450$\mu$m-detected sources, while one fifth is attributed to UV-luminous
sources (brighter than $L^\ast_{UV}$), although even these are largely
obscured. By extrapolating our results to include all stellar masses, we
estimate a total SFRD that is in good agreement with previous results from IR
and UV data at $z\lesssim3$, and from UV-only data at $z\sim5$. The cosmic
star-formation history undergoes a transition at $z\sim3-4$, as predominantly
unobscured growth in the early Universe is overtaken by obscured star
formation, driven by the build-up of the most massive galaxies during the peak
of cosmic assembly.

text:
At the solar equinox in August 2009, the Composite Infrared Spectrometer
(CIRS) onboard Cassini showed the lowest Saturn's ring temperatures ever
observed. Detailed radiative transfer models show that the observed equinox
temperatures of Saturn's A ring are much higher than model predictions as long
as only the flux from Saturn is taken into account. This indicates that the A
ring was not completely cooled down at the equinox. We develop a simple
seasonal model for ring temperatures and first assume that the internal density
and the thermal inertia of a ring particle are uniform with depth. The particle
size is estimated to be 1-2 m. The seasonal thermal inertia is found to be
30-50 Jm$^{-2}$K$^{-1}$s$^{-1/2}$ in the middle A ring whereas it is $\sim$ 10
Jm$^{-2}$K$^{-1}$s$^{-1/2}$ or as low as the diurnal thermal inertia in the
inner and outermost regions of the A ring. An additional internal structure
model, in which a particle has a high density core surrounded by a fluffy
regolith mantle, shows that the core radius relative to the particle radius is
about 0.9 for the middle A ring and is much less for the inner and outer
regions of the A ring. This means that the radial variation of the internal
density of ring particles exists across the A ring. Some mechanisms may be
confining dense particles in the middle A ring against viscous diffusion.
Alternatively, the (middle) A ring might have recently formed ($<$ 10$^{8}$ yr)
by destruction of an icy satellite, so that dense particles have not yet
diffused over the A ring and regolith mantles of particles have not grown
thick. Our model results also indicate that the composition of the core is
predominantly water ice, not rock.
label: human

text: Clean SNS (Superconductor-Insulator-Superconductor) graphene nanostructures have shown promising potential as versatile platforms for understanding the fundamental physics of superconductivity and its application in energy-efficient electronics. In this work, we report the systematic characterization of the energy landscapes, transition temperatures, and switching effects in a series of SNS graphene nanostructures using various micro and nanofabrication techniques. We fabricated SNS structures on both sides of the graphene sheet, and measured the superconducting critical current (Ic) and the insulating gap (Eg) by applying a magnetic field and a DC voltage bias, respectively. We found that the superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) exhibited strong dependence on the number and sizes of the insulating layers. Moreover, the switching effects, such as the resistance and resistance hysteresis, demonstrated clear relationships with the insulating layers' number and thickness. Furthermore, we observed notable thermal variation of the Tc and Ic values in the temperature range of interest. These results shed light on the complex energy landscapes and switching behaviors of SNS graphene nanostructures, which is essential for optimizing their design and functionality in the development of future electronic devices. Our findings also underline the need for further investigations into the role of interface engineering and nanostructure morphology in the electrical properties of SNS graphene nanostructures.
label: machine

text: Barium stars, a distinct group of evolved binary stars characterized by the presence of enhanced barium and other s-process elements, offer valuable insights into nucleosynthesis and stellar evolution. This study aims to investigate the chemical abundances and kinematic properties of barium stars to enhance our understanding of their formation and evolution. We conducted an extensive analysis of high-resolution spectra from a sample of twenty-five barium stars, focusing on their atmospheric chemical compositions, particularly the abundance ratios of barium, strontium, and other s-process elements. In parallel, we assessed the kinematic parameters of these stars by utilizing astrometric data from reputable databases to determine their galactic motions and orbits. Our findings reveal that barium stars show a significant chemical enhancement of s-process elements, indicating their interaction with a degenerate companion star, likely a white dwarf. The kinematic analysis suggests that barium stars are predominantly old and belong to the thick disk population of the Milky Way, with most displaying retrograde orbits. Furthermore, the derived abundance patterns align with nucleosynthesis models, supporting the hypothesis that the observed anomalies result from mass transfer in binary systems. This research highlights the complex interplay between chemical enrichment and stellar kinematics in barium stars, contributing to a broader understanding of their evolutionary processes and their role in the galactic chemical evolution of the Milky Way.
label: machine

text: We investigated the impact of an axion-like scalar field environment on the merger of binary black holes. Our simulations attempted to reconcile the observed gravitational wave signals with the theoretical predictions, taking into account the influence of axion-like scalar fields on the spacetime geometry. The results revealed a significant deviation from the standard general relativity predictions, indicating a possible signature of axion-like scalar field effects in the merger event.  Our approach involved numerically solving the Einstein field equations with the inclusion of an axion-like scalar field, which was modeled as a minimally coupled scalar field with a specific potential. The simulations were performed using a generalized relativistic waveform model, which allowed us to capture the effects of the axion-like scalar field on the binary black hole merger. The results showed that the axion-like scalar field environment can lead to a significant modification of the merger waveform, resulting in a characteristic "ringdown" feature that is distinct from the standard general relativity prediction.  The key findings of this study suggest that the detection of an axion-like scalar field environment effect on binary black hole merger could provide a novel probe of the early universe, offering insights into the fundamental laws of physics and the properties of scalar fields. The results also highlight the importance of considering the effects of scalar fields on the spacetime geometry in the study of gravitational wave astronomy, and demonstrate the potential of numerical simulations to provide new insights into the physics of binary black hole mergers.
label: machine

text:
We describe a mathematical models of grounded symbols in the brain. It also
serves as a computational foundations for Perceptual Symbol System (PSS). This
development requires new mathematical methods of dynamic logic (DL), which have
overcome limitations of classical artificial intelligence and connectionist
approaches. The paper discusses these past limitations, relates them to
combinatorial complexity (exponential explosion) of algorithms in the past, and
further to the static nature of classical logic. The new mathematical theory,
DL, is a process-logic. A salient property of this process is evolution of
vague representations into crisp. The paper first applies it to one aspect of
PSS: situation learning from object perceptions. Then we relate DL to the
essential PSS mechanisms of concepts, simulators, grounding, productivity,
binding, recursion, and to the mechanisms relating grounded and amodal symbols.
We discuss DL as a general theory describing the process of cognition on
multiple levels of abstraction. We also discuss the implications of this theory
for interactions between cognition and language, mechanisms of language
grounding, and possible role of language in grounding abstract cognition. The
developed theory makes experimental predictions, and will impact future
theoretical developments in cognitive science, including knowledge
representation, and perception-cognition interaction. Experimental neuroimaging
evidence for DL and PSS in brain imaging is discussed as well as future
research directions.
label: human

text: In the solar corona, long-period intensity pulsations (LPIPs) with periods between 5 and 30 minutes have been observed in coronal loops. The physical mechanisms underlying these pulsations are still not well understood. In this study, we propose a thermal non-equilibrium cycle model to explain the observed LPIPs. We first review previous observations and models of LPIPs, which suggest a possible relation to magnetic reconnection and thermal instabilities. Next, we develop a 1-D hydrodynamic model of a coronal loop undergoing repeated heating and cooling events. The model considers a non-uniform magnetic field, thermal conduction, and radiative losses. We find that the observed LPIPs can be explained by thermal non-equilibrium cycles, which result from a feedback mechanism between the heating rate and the cooling rate. The heating rate depends on the magnetic field strength and the thermal conduction efficiency, while the cooling rate depends on the loop length and the radiative losses. The model successfully reproduces the observed LPIP amplitudes and periods. Our findings suggest a new interpretation of LPIPs as thermal instabilities driven by magnetic energy release, which may have implications for solar flare prediction and understanding of coronal heating.
label: machine

text:
We study a gated quantum wire contacted to source and drain electrodes in the
Fabry-Perot regime. The wire is also coupled to a third terminal (tip), and we
allow for an asymmetry of the tip tunneling amplitudes of right and left moving
electrons. We analyze configurations where the tip acts as an electron injector
or as a voltage-probe, and show that the transport properties of this
three-terminal set-up exhibit very rich physical behavior. For a
non-interacting wire we find that a tip in the voltage-probe configuration
affects the source-drain transport in different ways, namely by suppressing the
conductance, by modulating the Fabry-Perot oscillations, and by reducing their
visibility. The combined effect of electron electron interaction and finite
length of the wire, accounted for by the inhomogeneous Luttinger liquid model,
leads to significantly modified predictions as compared to models based on
infinite wires. We show that when the tip injects electrons asymmetrically the
charge fractionalization induced by interaction cannot be inferred from the
asymmetry of the currents flowing in source and drain. Nevertheless interaction
effects are visible as oscillations in the non-linear tip-source and tip-drain
conductances. Important differences with respect to a two-terminal set-up
emerge, suggesting new strategies for the experimental investigation of
Luttinger liquid behavior.

text: Bernoulli Rank-$1$ bandits are a popular model for online learning systems, particularly in scenarios where the objective is to identify the best item among a set based on user feedback. In the context of click feedback, where user interactions are typically modeled as Bernoulli trials, this model has proven effective in optimizing ad delivery and improving user experience.  The objective of this study is to explore the applications of Bernoulli Rank-$1$ bandits in click feedback systems and to compare their performance with traditional methods such as Random Sampling and E-Greedy algorithms. Our methodology involves simulating user interactions and evaluating the performance of the algorithms under various conditions, including different user behavior models and feedback noise levels.  Our findings reveal that Bernoulli Rank-$1$ bandits significantly outperform Random Sampling and E-Greedy algorithms in terms of identification time and overall accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the performance of Bernoulli Rank-$1$ bandits is particularly robust to feedback noise and user behavior complexity. These results highlight the potential benefits of employing Bernoulli Rank-$1$ bandits in click feedback systems and suggest directions for future research, such as extending the model to Rank-$k$ scenarios and exploring its application in other domains.  In conclusion, this study provides evidence of the superiority of Bernoulli Rank-$1$ bandits over traditional methods in click feedback systems. The results have implications for online advertising, content recommendation, and other domains where identifying the best item from a set is crucial. The findings contribute to a growing body of literature on online learning systems and reinforce the value of model-based approaches in addressing complex problems in the digital age.
label: machine

text: We investigate the maximal density, deposition kinetics, and percolation threshold of loose-packed lattices to understand fundamental properties relevant to various fields such as material science and network theory. Our work addresses the challenge of determining how structural organization within loose-packed configurations influences their physical characteristics, particularly under varying deposition conditions. We employed a combination of experimental techniques and computational simulations to analyze the density of various lattice formations while tracking the kinetics of particle deposition across different lattice structures.   Our findings reveal that the maximal packing density achievable within these lattices correlates directly with the optimization of particle arrangement, showcasing a significant variance based on lattice geometry. We additionally observed that the percolation threshold, critical for assessing connectivity within these systems, demonstrates a distinct dependency on both the rate of deposition and the initial configuration of particles. Specifically, we demonstrate that slower deposition rates generally yield more extensive percolation clusters, highlighting the importance of deposition dynamics in determining structural integrity.  Through thorough statistical analysis and Monte Carlo simulations, we delineate the relationships between packing density and cluster formation, contributing to a deeper understanding of critical phenomena in disordered systems. This work provides crucial insights into optimizing material properties through controlled deposition strategies and lays a foundation for future research exploring similar phenomena in complex networks and soft matter systems.
label: machine

text: In primary care settings, accurate segmentation of skin regions from clinical photographs is essential for diagnosing dermatological conditions. This study addresses the challenge of segmenting both diseased and healthy skin using advanced image processing techniques. The objective is to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency, aiding clinicians in visual assessment through automated analysis. We developed a novel segmentation algorithm that integrates deep learning models and traditional image processing methods to differentiate between diseased and healthy skin areas marked in clinical images. The dataset comprises over 1,500 clinical photographs taken from primary care facilities, annotated by dermatological experts. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) were employed for feature extraction, supported by morphological operations to refine segmentation accuracy. Our methodology involves training the CNN with a balanced dataset to ensure robust performance across varying skin types and conditions. The results indicate a high mean intersection-over-union (IoU) score of 86% for diseased skin regions and 89% for healthy areas, demonstrating the model’s capability in handling diverse clinical scenarios. Further, the algorithm's execution time is optimized for real-time application, crucial for primary care environments. The study concludes that the proposed segmentation framework significantly improves over existing methods in accuracy and efficiency, rendering it a viable tool for assisting clinicians. Future work will focus on refining the algorithm for rare skin conditions and expanding the dataset to include a broader spectrum of demographic variables, ensuring generalizability and integration into clinical practice.

text:
Spectroscopic, polarimetric, and high spectral resolution interferometric
data covering the period 1995-2011 are analyzed to document the transition into
a new phase of circumstellar disk activity in the classical Be-shell star 48
Lib. The long-term disk evolution is described using the V/R ratio of the
violet and red emission components of H alpha and Br gamma, radial velocities
and profiles of He I and optical metal shell lines, multi-band BVRI
polarimetry, broad-band and high-resolution interferometric visibilities and
phases. Spectroscopic signatures of disk asymmetries in 48 Lib vanished in the
late nineties but recovered some time between 2004 and 2007. Variations in the
radial velocity and line profile of conventional shell lines correlate with the
V/R behavior. They are shared by narrow absorption cores superimposed on
otherwise seemingly photospheric He I lines, which may form in high-density gas
at the inner disk close to the photosphere. Large radial velocity variations
continued also during the V/R-quiet years. The broad H-band interferometry
gives a disk diameter of (1.72+-0.2) mas (equivalent to 15 stellar radii),
position angle of the disk (50+-9) deg and a relatively low disk flattening of
1.66+-0.3. Within the errors the same disk position angle is derived from
polarimetric observations and from photocenter shifts across Br gamma. The
high-resolution interferometric visibility and phase profiles show a double or
even multiple-component structure. A preliminary estimate based on the size of
the Br gamma emitting region indicates a large diameter for the disk (tens of
stellar radii).

text:
By pointing out an error in the previous derivation of the area spectrum
based on Ashtekar's variables, we suggest a new area spectrum; instead of the
norm of Ashtekar's gravitational electric field, we show that the norm of our
"new" gravitational electric field based on our "newer" variables, which we
construct in this paper for this purpose, gives the correct area spectrum. In
particular, our "newer" variables are mathematically consistent; the constraint
algebra is closed. Moreover, by using our new area spectrum, we "almost
correctly" predict the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy without having to adjust the
Immirzi parameter; we show that a numerical formula actually yielded
$0.997\cdots$, which is very close to 1, the expected value with the black hole
entropy given as $A/4$. We conjecture that the difference, 0.003, is due to the
extra dimensions that may modify the area spectrum. Then, we derive a formula
for the degeneracy for a single-partition black hole, i.e., a black hole made
of a single unit area, and explicitly show that our area spectrum correctly
reproduces the degeneracy. Furthermore, by using two totally different methods,
we obtain the proportionality constant "$C$" related to the degeneracy. The
first method based on fitting yields 172$\sim$173 while the second method
yields 172.87$\cdots$, which strongly suggest that our area spectrum is on the
right track. We also show that the area spectra based on Ashtekar variables
neither reproduce the degeneracy of single-partition black hole nor yield
agreement for $C$ obtained by using the two methods.

text: In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of 2+1D bosonic topological orders, aiming to establish a unifying theoretical framework for their classification and understanding. Our study addresses the fundamental problem of characterizing and discerning distinct topological orders in two spatial dimensions, crucial for unraveling the exotic quantum phenomena exhibited by such systems. Utilizing tools from topological quantum field theory, particularly Chern-Simons theory and the theory of anyons, we develop a formalism that encapsulates the key characteristics and properties of bosonic topological orders in 2+1D. Through a systematic exploration of various topological invariants and symmetry-enriched structures, we reveal a rich landscape of topologically distinct phases and demonstrate the interplay between topological order and symmetry in these systems. Our results offer valuable insights into the intricate nature of bosonic topological orders, shedding light on the underlying principles governing their emergence and classification. The methodology employed in this work combines theoretical analysis, numerical simulations, and mathematical rigor to provide a robust foundation for studying and categorizing 2+1D bosonic topological orders. This research contributes to the advancement of our understanding of topological phases of matter and paves the way for future investigations into exotic quantum states in low-dimensional systems.

text: In this study, we explore the problem of inverse scattering for the multidimensional Newton equation under the influence of an electromagnetic field at high energies. Our objectives include developing a methodology to retrieve essential scattering information from an incident wave interacting with complex electromagnetic potentials. The study addresses the challenge of reconstructing the potential functions from asymptotic measurements, which is pivotal in quantum mechanics and applied physics. By utilizing advanced mathematical techniques rooted in functional analysis and partial differential equations, we establish a framework that effectively decouples the wave functions and electromagnetic fields at elevated energy levels. Employing the Born approximation in a high-energy regime, we successfully derive asymptotic expansions that relate scattered waveforms to the underlying potential. Key results demonstrate the capability of the proposed approach to yield stable and accurate reconstructions, even for non-trivial field configurations. Furthermore, simulations validate the robustness of our framework against perturbations in the initial conditions and modeling errors. We highlight significant improvements in computational efficiency compared to traditional methods, marking a stride in the practical applicability of inverse scattering theory. By bridging the gap between theoretical constructs and empirical applicability, this research presents a potent tool for probing electromagnetic fields in multidimensional spaces. Our findings open avenues for further investigation into anisotropic and complex media, potentially informing the design of advanced sensors and imaging technologies. The methodology developed herein not only advances theoretical understanding but also sets a precedent for future explorations into high-energy scattering phenomena.
label: machine

text:
We explore the constraints on the parameter space of a Randall-Sundrum warped
geometry scenario, where a radion field arises out of the attempt to stabilise
the radius of the extra compact spacelike dimension, using the most recent data
from higgs searches at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the Tevatron. We
calculate contributions from both the scalar mass eigenstates arising from
radion-higgs kinetic mixing in all important search channels. The most
important channel to be affected is the decay via WW*, where no invariant mass
peak can discern the two distinct physical states. Improving upon the previous
studies, we perform a full analysis in the WW* channel, taking into account the
effect of various cuts and interference when the two scalar are closely spaced.
We examine both cases where the experimentally discovered scalar is either
'higgs-like' or 'radion-like'. The implications of a relatively massive scalar
decaying into a pair of 125 GeV scalars is also included. Based on a global
analysis of the current data, including not only a single 125 GeV scalar but
also another one with mass over the range 110 to 600 GeV, we obtain the
up-to-date exclusion contours in the parameter space. Side by side, regions
agreeing with the data within 68% and 95% confidence level based on a
\chi^2-minimisation procedure, are also presented.

text: We present the results of the Pan-STARRS1 survey targeting distant quasars with redshifts greater than 5.6, which has significantly expanded the known population of quasars within the first gigayear of the universe. In total, we identified more than 100 quasars, enhancing our understanding of early cosmic evolution and the formation of supermassive black holes. Our methodology involved leveraging the high-cadence imaging capabilities of the Pan-STARRS1 telescope, coupled with a rigorous selection algorithm that combined photometric and astrometric data to classify candidates accurately. We employed a multi-wavelength approach, incorporating data from optical, infrared, and ancillary observations to confirm quasar identities and assess their physical properties. Through spectral analysis, we determined black hole masses and accretion rates, revealing the presence of highly luminous objects at unprecedented distances. Our survey addresses the critical problem of understanding the growth of black holes in the early universe and the associated formation mechanisms of their host galaxies. The findings indicate that these quasars are not only significant in number but also exhibit a variety of properties, suggesting diverse evolutionary pathways. This work contributes to the ongoing exploration of the quasar population and provides essential context for future studies aimed at understanding the relationship between supermassive black holes and their environments in the evolving universe. We conclude that the Pan-STARRS1 survey has opened new avenues for investigation, providing a substantial dataset for probing the early epochs of cosmic history.

text:
Despite their important applications in metrology and in spite of numerous
experimental demonstrations, weak measurements are still confusing for part of
the community. This sometimes leads to unjustified criticism. Recent papers
have experimentally clarified the meaning and practical significance of weak
measurements, yet in [R.E. Kastner, Found. Phys. 47, 697-707 (2017)], Kastner
seems to take us many years backwards in the debate, casting doubt on the very
term "weak value" and the meaning of weak measurements. Kastner appears to
ignore both the basics and frontiers of weak measurements and misinterprets the
weak measurement process and its outcomes. In addition, she accuses the authors
of [Y. Aharonov et al., Ann. Phys. 355, 258-268 (2015)] in statements
completely opposite to the ones they have actually made. There are many points
of disagreement between Kastner and us, but in this short reply I will leave
aside the ontology (which is indeed interpretational and far more complex than
that described by Kastner) and focus mainly on the injustice in her criticism.
I shall add some general comments regarding the broader theory of weak
measurements and the Two-State-Vector Formalism (TSVF), as well as supporting
experimental results. Finally, I will point out some recent promising results,
which can be proven by (strong) projective measurements, without the need of
employing weak measurements.
label: human

text: The fluctuation relation is a cornerstone of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, providing insights into the behavior of systems driven away from thermal equilibrium. This study investigates the applicability of the fluctuation relation in Nose-Hoover boundary thermostated systems, characterized by their ability to maintain a fixed temperature while allowing for operational freedoms at the boundaries. The objective of this research is to derive and validate the fluctuation relation within the context of these thermostated systems. We employ a combination of analytical techniques and numerical simulations to explore the dynamics of these systems under various conditions, focusing on the impact of boundary temperature control on their statistical mechanics. Key findings reveal that the fluctuation relation holds true, even in the presence of thermostat-induced energy exchanges at the boundaries, provided that the system is sufficiently large and the boundary conditions are consistently applied. Furthermore, we observe that deviations from the ideal fluctuation relation arise under certain non-linear perturbations and non-equilibrium processes. These results underscore the robustness of the fluctuation relation in nonequilibrium systems, while simultaneously highlighting the complexities introduced by boundary thermoregulation. In conclusion, our findings extend the applicability of the fluctuation relation to Nose-Hoover boundary thermostated systems, offering a deeper understanding of their thermodynamic behavior and providing a framework for future studies on the interplay between boundary conditions and statistical mechanics.
label: machine

text: This study investigates the photo-centric variability observed in quasars, attributing it primarily to fluctuations in their inner structures. We aim to understand how these internal changes impact Gaia measurements, which are crucial for astrophysical research. Our approach involves detailed analysis of quasar light curves, focusing on identifying periodic and non-periodic variations. By employing advanced statistical methods and machine learning algorithms, we identify distinct patterns indicative of structural changes within quasars. The results indicate that significant variability in quasar brightness correlates with alterations in their accretion disks or central supermassive black holes. These findings suggest that unaccounted for intrinsic variability could introduce errors into Gaia's precise distance measurements. To mitigate this issue, we propose a refined data processing technique that incorporates variability models into the Gaia data reduction pipeline. This method aims to enhance the accuracy of Gaia's stellar parallax measurements, thereby improving our understanding of the universe's large-scale structure and evolution.

text: In this study, we explore the thermodynamic properties of squashed Kaluza-Klein black holes and black strings within the framework of modified gravity theories. Our primary objective is to investigate how different choices of reference backgrounds influence the thermodynamic stability and phase structure of these higher-dimensional compactified solutions. Employing a comparative analysis, we apply both the background subtraction method and the counterterm approach to different reference metrics, such as flat and conical backgrounds. We employ the Euclidean action formalism to derive expressions for thermodynamic quantities, including the mass, temperature, and entropy, in the context of these backgrounds.  Our results reveal that the choice of reference background substantially impacts the thermal properties and stability criteria of the solutions. Specifically, the thermodynamic analysis demonstrates that for black holes, conical reference backgrounds yield consistent entropy-area relations, whereas, for black strings, the flat background provides a more stable thermal equilibrium. Furthermore, phase transition scenarios emerge, delineating stability domains and indicating critical points depending on the dimensions and compactification scales of the extra spatial dimensions.  Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the thermodynamics in the context of compactified higher-dimensional spacetimes, highlighting the importance of reference background selection. This work offers new insights into the potential application of such solutions in the broader scope of string theory and quantum gravity, proposing guidelines for future research that seeks to unify gravitational theories by incorporating modifications at both classical and quantum levels.

The conclusion emphasizes the significance of the results, as they provide strong evidence for a continuous metallicity gradient in the solar neighborhood and contribute to our understanding of Galactic chemical evolution. We propose a new attack methodology, Graph Poisoning Attack (GPA), that generates adversarial graphs by manipulating the graph structure and node features. Our results demonstrate that, by introducing only a few malicious nodes and edges, we can degrade the performance of various GNN models up to 90%. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of these attacks on downstream tasks, such as node classification and graph clustering. Our findings shed light on the importance of developing robust GNN models and detection systems against adversarial inputs. We also provide empirical evidence that existing defense methods, such as adversarial training and input sanitization, are not sufficient to counteract the proposed attacks. Our work opens up new avenues for research in the field of GNN security and offers insights into the development of effective defense mechanisms against adversarial attacks.

Our findings indicate that the choice of mobility model significantly influences the performance of location management schemes. Specifically, the Gauss-Markov model, known for its realistic depiction of node movement, exhibits superior performance by minimizing location update overhead and enhancing packet delivery ratio in high-mobility environments.  The analysis concludes that selecting an appropriate mobility model is vital for optimizing location management in MANETs. Understanding the strengths and limitations of different models can guide the development of robust, efficient location management protocols in mobile ad hoc scenarios. modulation of the conduction channel width accompanying the adsorption and
desorption of ethanol gas, the catalytic activity of Co3O4 for the oxidation of
ethanol, the stronger oxygen adsorption of p-type Co3O4, and the formation of

We present observations of supernova (SN) 2008ge, which is spectroscopically
similar to the peculiar SN 2002cx, and its pre-explosion site that indicate
that its progenitor was probably a white dwarf. NGC 1527, the host galaxy of SN
2008ge, is an S0 galaxy with no evidence of star formation or massive stars.
Astrometrically matching late-time imaging of SN 2008ge to pre-explosion HST
imaging, we constrain the luminosity of the progenitor star. Since SN 2008ge
has no indication of hydrogen or helium in its spectrum, its progenitor must
have lost its outer layers before exploding, requiring that it be a white
dwarf, a Wolf-Rayet star, or a lower-mass star in a binary system. Observations
of the host galaxy show no signs of individual massive stars, star clusters, or
H II regions at the SN position or anywhere else, making a Wolf-Rayet
progenitor unlikely. Late-time spectroscopy of SN 2008ge show strong [Fe II]
lines with large velocity widths compared to other members of this class at
similar epochs. These previously unseen features indicate that a significant
amount of the SN ejecta is Fe (presumably the result of radioactive decay of
56Ni generated in the SN), further supporting a thermonuclear explosion.
Placing the observations of SN 2008ge in the context of observations of other
objects in the class of SN, we suggest that the progenitor was most likely a
white dwarf.

Chapter 16 in High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) : Preliminary
Design Report. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is one of the largest scientific
instruments ever built. Since opening up a new energy frontier for exploration
in 2010, it has gathered a global user community of about 7,000 scientists
working in fundamental particle physics and the physics of hadronic matter at
extreme temperature and density. To sustain and extend its discovery potential,
the LHC will need a major upgrade in the 2020s. This will increase its
luminosity (rate of collisions) by a factor of five beyond the original design
value and the integrated luminosity (total collisions created) by a factor ten.
The LHC is already a highly complex and exquisitely optimised machine so this
upgrade must be carefully conceived and will require about ten years to
implement. The new configuration, known as High Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), will
rely on a number of key innovations that push accelerator technology beyond its
present limits. Among these are cutting-edge 11-12 tesla superconducting
magnets, compact superconducting cavities for beam rotation with ultra-precise
phase control, new technology and physical processes for beam collimation and
300 metre-long high-power superconducting links with negligible energy
dissipation. The present document describes the technologies and components
that will be used to realise the project and is intended to serve as the basis
for the detailed engineering design of HL-LHC.

From the 27th to the 28th January 2009, the Cassini spacecraft remotely
acquired combined observations of Saturns southern aurorae at radio,
ultraviolet and infrared wavelengths, while monitoring ion injections in the
middle magnetosphere from energetic neutral atoms. Simultaneous measurements
included the sampling of a full planetary rotation, a relevant timescale to
investigate auroral emissions driven by processes internal to the
magnetosphere. In addition, this interval coincidently matched a powerful
substorm-like event in the magnetotail, which induced an overall dawnside
intensification of the magnetospheric and auroral activity. We comparatively
analyze this unique set of measurements to reach a comprehensive view of
kronian auroral processes over the investigated timescale. We identify three
source regions in atmospheric aurorae, including a main oval associated with
the bulk of Saturn Kilometric Radiation (SKR), together with polar and
equatorward emissions. These observations reveal the co-existence of
corotational and sub-corototational dynamics of emissions associated with the
main auroral oval. Precisely, we show that the atmospheric main oval hosts
short-lived sub-corotating isolated features together with a bright,
longitudinally extended, corotating region locked at the southern SKR phase. We
assign the susbtorm-like event to a regular, internally driven, nightside ion
injection possibly triggerred by a plasmoid ejection. We also investigate the
total auroral energy budget, from the power input to the atmosphere,
characterized by precipitating electrons up to 20 keV, to its dissipation
through the various radiating processes. Finally, through simulations, we
confirm the search-light nature of the SKR rotational modulation and we show
that SKR arcs relate to isolated auroral spots. The resulting findings are
discussed in the frame of pending questions.

The results showed that HNCO was detected in all environmental matrices, with the highest concentrations found in urban areas. The analysis of HNCO isotope ratios revealed significant correlations with nitrogen oxide emissions and industrial activities. The findings of this study suggest that HNCO can be used as a diagnostic marker of environmental pollution, particularly in urban areas. The results have implications for the development of environmental monitoring strategies and the assessment of pollution sources in different regions.

text: In this study, we present the results of the VLA Nascent Disk and Multiplicity Survey of Perseus Protostars (VANDAM) II, which aimed to investigate the multiplicity properties of protostars in the Perseus molecular cloud. We employed the VLA radio interferometer to conduct high-sensitivity observations of 140 Class 0 and I protostars in Perseus.  Our results reveal that approximately 50% of these protostars exhibit multiplicity, with a median separation of 320 au and a range up to 1200 au. The multiplicity fractions vary significantly among different evolutionary stages 76% of the Class 0 sources and 30% of the Class I sources are multiples. This trend may indicate that multiplicity is a characteristic feature of the early evolutionary stage.  We also discovered that binary separations and mass ratios of identified multiple systems are generally consistent with the hierarchical fragmentation model. In particular, the observed mass ratios follow a power law distribution, with a significant excess of lower-mass companions relative to the primary. This finding suggests a possible origin of low-mass stars and planets through the fragmentation of collapsing molecular clouds.  Furthermore, we found that the multiplicity properties of Perseus protostars are consistent with previous surveys, implying that the multiplicity phenomenon is a common feature of star formation across different environments. Our observations also yielded new detections of young stellar systems that were previously unknown, further expanding our understanding of the Perseus molecular cloud and the star formation process in general.  In conclusion, the VANDAM II survey provides crucial insights into the multiplicity properties of protostars in the Perseus molecular cloud. Our findings demonstrate that multiplicity is a prevalent phenomenon in the early stages of star formation and may play a significant role in shaping the mass spectrum of stars and planets. The data obtained from this survey serve as a valuable resource for future research and will contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the star formation process.

We present mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy of a Type II-plateau supernova, SN
2004dj, obtained with the Spitzer Space Telescope, spanning 106--1393 d after
explosion. MIR photometry plus optical/near-IR observations are also reported.
An early-time MIR excess is attributed to emission from non-silicate dust
formed within a cool dense shell (CDS). Most of the CDS dust condensed between
50 d and 165 d, reaching a mass of 0.3 x 10^{-5} Msun. Throughout the
observations much of the longer wavelength (>10 microns) part of the continuum
is explained as an IR echo from interstellar dust. The MIR excess strengthened
at later times. We show that this was due to thermal emission from warm,
non-silicate dust formed in the ejecta. Using optical/near-IR line-profiles and
the MIR continua, we show that the dust was distributed as a disk whose radius
appeared to be slowly shrinking. The disk radius may correspond to a grain
destruction zone caused by a reverse shock which also heated the dust. The
dust-disk lay nearly face-on, had high opacities in the optical/near-IR
regions, but remained optically thin in the MIR over much of the period
studied. Assuming a uniform dust density, the ejecta dust mass by 996 d was 0.5
+/- 0.1) x 10^{-4} Msun, and exceeded 10^{-4}Msun by 1393 d. For a dust density
rising toward the center the limit is higher. Nevertheless, this study suggests
that the amount of freshly-synthesized dust in the SN 2004dj ejecta is
consistent with that found from previous studies, and adds further weight to
the claim that such events could not have been major contributors to the cosmic
dust budget.

text: In this study, we present X-Shooter spectroscopic observations of a sample of young stellar objects (YSOs) located in the Lupus star-forming region. Our primary goals are to determine atmospheric parameters, membership status, and activity diagnostics for this population of YSOs. We employed an extensive wavelength coverage range of X-Shooter, from the near-ultraviolet to the near-infrared, which enabled us to study several emission lines in hydrogen, calcium, and helium, among others.  For the atmospheric parameter analysis, we utilized various spectral features, such as Hα and Hβ line profiles, Balmer jump, and spectral slope, to derive effective temperatures, surface gravities, and extinction values. We also considered the shape of the Ca II triplet line, which is particularly sensitive to the presence of accretion disks and their associated activity.  To ascertain membership status, we compared our spectra with template spectra for known Lupus members and non-members. We identified several key spectral features that helped us to distinguish members from non-members. This methodology proved valuable, as we were able to identify three new candidate members within our sample.  To diagnose the level of activity, we studied Hα and Ca II emission line strengths and their ratio, which served as indicators of accretion and chromospheric activity. Our findings suggest that the majority of the YSOs in our sample exhibit moderate to strong accretion signatures, which is consistent with previous studies of young stellar populations in Lupus.  In summary, this study contributes to our understanding of the atmospheric and activity properties of YSOs located in the Lupus star-forming region. Through X-Shooter spectroscopy, we were able to infer important atmospheric parameters, determine membership status, and diagnose the level of activity for a sample of Lupus YSOs, providing valuable insights for ongoing studies of this region.

Nantais et al. used the Hubble Space Telescope to localize probable globular
clusters (GCs) in M81, a spiral galaxy at a distance of 3.63 Mpc. Theory
predicts that GCs can host intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) with masses
M_BH \sim 100 - 100,000 M_sun. Finding IMBHs in GCs could validate a formation
channel for seed BHs in the early universe, bolster gravitational-wave
predictions for space missions, and test scaling relations between stellar
systems and the central BHs they host. We used the NRAO Karl G. Jansky Very
Large Array (VLA) to search for the radiative signatures of IMBH accretion from
206 probable GCs in a mosaic of M81. The observing wavelength was 5.5 cm and
the spatial resolution was 1.5 arcsec (26.4 pc). None of the individual GCs are
detected, nor are weighted-mean image stacks of the 206 GCs and the 49 massive
GCs with stellar masses M_star \gtrsim 200,000 M_sun. We apply a semi-empirical
model to predict the mass of an IMBH that, if undergoing accretion in the
long-lived hard X-ray state, is consistent with a given radio luminosity. The
3$\sigma$ radio-luminosity upper limits correspond to mean IMBH masses of
M_BH(all) < 42,000 M_sun for the all-cluster stack and M_BH(massive) < 51,000
M_sun for the massive-cluster stack. We also apply the empirical
fundamental-plane relation to two X-ray-detected clusters, finding that their
individual IMBH masses at 95% confidence are M_BH < 99,000 M_sun and M_BH <
15,000 M_sun. Finally, no analog of HLX-1, a strong IMBH candidate in an
extragalactic star cluster, occurs in any individual GC in M81. This
underscores the uniqueness or rarity of the HLX-1 phenomenon.

Incorporating relaying techniques into Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ)
mechanisms gives a general impression of diversity and throughput enhancements.
Allowing overhearing among multiple relays is also a known approach to increase
the number of participating relays in ARQs. However, when opportunistic
amplify-and-forward (AF) relaying is applied to cooperative ARQs, the system
design becomes nontrivial and even involved. Based on outage analysis, the
spatial and temporal diversities are first found sensitive to the received
signal qualities of relays, and a link quality control mechanism is then
developed to prescreen candidate relays in order to explore the diversity of
cooperative ARQs with a selective and opportunistic AF (SOAF) relaying method.
According to the analysis, the temporal and spatial diversities can be fully
exploited if proper thresholds are set for each hop along the relaying routes.
The SOAF relaying method is further examined from a packet delivery viewpoint.
By the principle of the maximum likelihood sequence detection (MLSD),
sufficient conditions on the link quality are established for the proposed
SOAF-relaying-based ARQ scheme to attain its potential diversity order in the
packet error rates (PERs) of MLSD. The conditions depend on the minimum
codeword distance and the average signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Furthermore,
from a heuristic viewpoint, we also develop a threshold searching algorithm for
the proposed SOAF relaying and link quality method to exploit both the
diversity and the SNR gains in PER. The effectiveness of the proposed
thresholding mechanism is verified via simulations with trellis codes.

We also proposed a novel optimization framework for determining the optimal node density, which balances the tradeoff between outage probability and network capacity.
