Increasing the sensitivity of a gravitational-wave (GW) detector improves our
ability to measure the characteristics of detected sources. It also increases
the number of weak signals that contribute to the data. Because GW detectors
have nearly all-sky sensitivity, they can be subject to a confusion limit: Many
sources which cannot be distinguished may be measured simultaneously, defining
a stochastic noise floor to the sensitivity. For GW detectors operating at
present and for their planned upgrades, the projected event rate is
sufficiently low that we are far from the confusion-limited regime. However,
some detectors currently under discussion may have large enough reach to binary
inspiral that they enter the confusion-limited regime. In this paper, we
examine the binary inspiral confusion limit for terrestrial detectors. We
consider a broad range of inspiral rates in the literature, several planned
advanced gravitational-wave detectors, and the highly advanced "Einstein
Telescope" design. Though most advanced detectors will not be impacted by this
limit, the Einstein Telescope with a very low frequency "seismic wall" may be
subject to confusion noise. At a minimum, careful data analysis will be require
to separate signals which will appear confused. This result should be borne in
mind when designing highly advanced future instruments.

In the present work, we provide a dielectric study on two differently
concentrated aqueous lysozyme solutions in the frequency range from 1 MHz to 40
GHz and for temperatures from 275 to 330 K. We analyze the three dispersion
regions, commonly found in protein solutions, usually termed beta-, gamma-, and
delta-relaxation. The beta-relaxation, occurring in the frequency range around
10 MHz and the gamma-relaxation around 20 GHz (at room temperature) can be
attributed to the rotation of the polar protein molecules in their aqueous
medium and the reorientational motion of the free water molecules,
respectively. The nature of the delta-relaxation, which often is ascribed to
the motion of bound water molecules, is not yet fully understood. Here we
provide data on the temperature dependence of the relaxation times and
relaxation strengths of all three detected processes and on the dc conductivity
arising from ionic charge transport. The temperature dependences of the beta-
and gamma-relaxations are closely correlated. We found a significant
temperature dependence of the dipole moment of the protein, indicating
conformational changes. Moreover we find a breakdown of the
Debye-Stokes-Einstein relation in this protein solution, i.e., the dc
conductivity is not completely governed by the mobility of the solvent
molecules. Instead it seems that the dc conductivity is closely connected to
the hydration shell dynamics.

In this paper, we theoretically study x-ray multiphoton ionization dynamics
of heavy atoms taking into account relativistic and resonance effects. When an
atom is exposed to an intense x-ray pulse generated by an x-ray free-electron
laser (XFEL), it is ionized to a highly charged ion via a sequence of
single-photon ionization and accompanying relaxation processes, and its final
charge state is limited by the last ionic state that can be ionized by a
single-photon ionization. If x-ray multiphoton ionization involves deep
inner-shell electrons in heavy atoms, energy shifts by relativistic effects
play an important role in ionization dynamics, as pointed out in [Phys.\ Rev.\
Lett.\ \textbf{110}, 173005 (2013)]. On the other hand, if the x-ray beam has a
broad energy bandwidth, the high-intensity x-ray pulse can drive resonant
photo-excitations for a broad range of ionic states and ionize even beyond the
direct one-photon ionization limit, as first proposed in [Nature\ Photon.\
\textbf{6}, 858 (2012)]. To investigate both relativistic and resonance
effects, we extend the \textsc{xatom} toolkit to incorporate relativistic
energy corrections and resonant excitations in x-ray multiphoton ionization
dynamics calculations. Charge-state distributions are calculated for Xe atoms
interacting with intense XFEL pulses at a photon energy of 1.5~keV and 5.5~keV,
respectively. For both photon energies, we demonstrate that the role of
resonant excitations in ionization dynamics is altered due to significant
shifts of orbital energy levels by relativistic effects. Therefore it is
necessary to take into account both effects to accurately simulate multiphoton
multiple ionization dynamics at high x-ray intensity.

\neq j \Rightarrow \neg(x_i \ E \ x_j))\}.$$

for every function $f : [X]^n_= \rightarrow X$, there exists some $Y \subseteq
X$ with $X$ and $Y$ in bijection so that $f[[Y]^n_=] \neq X$. A set $X$ has the
J\'onsson property if and only for every function $f : (\bigcup_{n \in
\omega}[X]^n_=) \rightarrow X$, there exists some $Y \subseteq X$ with $X$ and
$Y$ in bijection so that $f[\bigcup_{n \in \omega} [Y]^n_=] \neq X$.
  Let $n \in \omega$, $X$ be a Polish space, and $E$ be an equivalence relation
on $X$. $E$ has the $n$-Mycielski property if and only if for all comeager $C
\subseteq {}^nX$, there is some $\mathbf{\Delta_1^1}$ $A \subseteq X$ so that
$E \leq_{\mathbf{\Delta_1^1}} E \upharpoonright A$ and $[A]^n_E \subseteq C$.

${}^\omega2$ by $x \ E_0 \ y$ if and only if $(\exists n)(\forall k > n)(x(k) =
y(k))$. $E_1$ is defined on ${}^\omega({}^\omega2)$ by $x \ E_1 \ y$ if and
only if $(\exists n)(\forall k > n)(x(k) = y(k))$. $E_2$ is defined on

$E_3$ is defined on ${}^\omega({}^\omega2)$ by $x \ E_3 \ y$ if and only if

text: In this study, we critically assess the validity of the rotating wave approximation (RWA) when applied to coupled modes interacting with qubits. Our primary objective is to evaluate how deviations from the RWA affect the predictions of the system's dynamics, particularly focusing on the interaction strength and frequency detuning between the modes and the qubits.  We begin by constructing a theoretical model that incorporates both the RWA and non-RWA scenarios, including higher-order terms neglected in the RWA approximation. Through detailed numerical simulations, we explore various parameter regimes where the RWA fails, such as strong coupling and large detunings, which are crucial for practical applications involving qubit systems.  Our analysis reveals that the RWA significantly underestimates the energy exchange rates between the qubits and the coupled modes, especially at high detunings. This leads to discrepancies in the qubit population and coherences, which can have substantial implications for quantum information processing tasks. We also observe that the inclusion of higher-order terms, while computationally intensive, provides more accurate predictions, especially in regions where the RWA breaks down.  The key findings suggest that the RWA should be used cautiously, particularly in scenarios where strong coupling or large detunings are present. The inclusion of non-RWA corrections offers a more comprehensive understanding of the system dynamics, thereby enhancing the reliability of theoretical predictions and experimental designs.

text: We employ the spin cluster operator theory to investigate the magnetic properties of the Kagome lattice antiferromagnet, a two-dimensional system exhibiting rich spin frustration phenomena. Through a systematic analysis of the spin cluster operator expansion, we identify the dominant contributions to the magnetic susceptibility and specific heat, which are found to be significantly affected by the spin frustration arising from the Kagome lattice structure.  Our calculations reveal that the spin cluster operator theory successfully captures the low-temperature behavior of the system, including the formation of a non-trivial spin gap, which is a hallmark of the antiferromagnetic ground state. Furthermore, we find that the spin cluster operator theory provides a more accurate description of the system's magnetic properties compared to the mean-field approximation, which is commonly used in the literature.  Our results are based on a combination of analytical and numerical methods, including the use of cluster expansions and Monte Carlo simulations. We demonstrate that the spin cluster operator theory is a powerful tool for studying the complex magnetic behavior of the Kagome lattice antiferromagnet, and we provide new insights into the role of spin frustration in shaping the system's thermodynamic properties. By exploring the interplay between spin frustration and magnetic ordering, our work sheds light on the underlying physics of this fascinating system, which has been the subject of intense research in condensed matter physics.

text: We have investigated the phenomenon of disorder-induced half-integer thermal Hall conductance in two-dimensional systems, providing evidence for its existence and shedding light on its underlying mechanisms. Through a combination of theoretical modeling and numerical simulations, we have demonstrated that the presence of disorder can indeed give rise to half-integer thermal Hall conductance, which is a fundamental property of integer quantum Hall effect. Our calculations reveal that the disorder-induced half-integer thermal Hall conductance arises from the interplay between the disorder scattering and the electronic band structure, leading to a non-trivial relationship between the thermal conductivity and the magnetic field.  Our results show that the disorder-induced half-integer thermal Hall conductance is a robust feature of the system, insensitive to the strength of the disorder and the type of disorder scattering. Furthermore, we have found that the half-integer thermal Hall conductance exhibits a non-linear dependence on the temperature, which can be attributed to the interplay between the thermal excitations and the disorder-induced scattering. Our findings have significant implications for the understanding of thermal transport in disordered systems, and we propose that the disorder-induced half-integer thermal Hall conductance may be a key feature of the thermal Hall effect in disordered systems.  By developing a theoretical framework that incorporates disorder scattering and electronic band structure, we have provided a comprehensive understanding of the disorder-induced half-integer thermal Hall conductance. Our results open up new avenues for research on thermal transport in disordered systems, and we believe that this work will have a significant impact on the field of condensed matter physics.

We study the relaxation of the center-of-mass, or dipole oscillations in the
system of interacting fermions confined spatially. With the confinement
frequency $\omega_{\perp}$ fixed the particles were considered to freely move
along one (quasi-1D) or two (quasi-2D) spatial dimensions. We have focused on
the regime of rare collisions, such that the inelastic collision rate,
$1/\tau_{in} \ll \omega_{\perp}$. The dipole oscillations relaxation rate,
$1/\tau_{\perp}$ is obtained at three different levels: by direct perturbation
theory, solving the integral Bethe-Salpeter equation and applying the memory
function formalism. As long as anharmonicity is weak, $1/\tau_{\perp} \ll 1/
\tau_{in}$ the three methods are shown to give identical results. In quasi-2D
case $1/\tau_{\perp} \neq 0$ at zero temperature. In quasi-1D system
$1/\tau_{\perp} \propto T^3$ if the Fermi energy, $E_F$ lies below the critical
value, $E_F < 3 \omega_{\perp}/4$. Otherwise, unless the system is close to
integrability, the rate $1/\tau_{\perp}$ has the temperature dependence similar
to that in quasi-2D. In all cases the relaxation results from the excitation of
particle-hole pairs propagating along unconfined directions resulting in the
relationship $1/\tau_{\perp} \propto 1/\tau_{in}$, with the inelastic rate
$1/\tau_{in} \neq 0$ as the phase-space opens up at finite energy of
excitation, $\hbar \omega_{\perp}$. While $1/\tau_{\perp} \propto \tau_{in}$ in
the hydrodynamic regime, $\omega_{\perp} \ll 1/\tau_{in}$, in the regime of
rare collisions, $\omega_{\perp} \gg 1/\tau_{in}$, we obtain the opposite trend
$1/\tau_{\perp} \propto 1/\tau_{in}$.

text: The study investigates the adsorption behavior of indium (In) atoms on a wetting layer composed of indium arsenide (InAs) deposited on a gallium arsenide (GaAs) (001) substrate. This research aims to understand the interaction between indium and the InAs wetting layer, which plays a crucial role in the epitaxial growth of indium-based alloys. Using density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we explore the adsorption energies and geometries of indium atoms on the InAs wetting layer. Key findings indicate that indium atoms preferentially adsorb at specific sites on the InAs surface, leading to the formation of stable In-In and In-As bonds. These results provide insights into the potential applications of InAs as a wetting layer in the fabrication of indium-based devices, such as light-emitting diodes and lasers, by optimizing the initial growth stage of these materials. The findings contribute to the understanding of material interactions at the nanoscale and have implications for the development of new electronic and optoelectronic devices.

The crystal structure and magnetic properties of the RbMnPO4 zeolite-ABW type
material have been studied by temperature-dependent neutron powder diffraction,
low temperature magnetometry and heat capacity measurements. RbMnPO4 represents
a rare example of a weak ferromagnetic polar material, containing Mn2+ ions
with TN = 4.7 K. The neutron powder diffraction pattern recorded at T = 10 K
shows that the compound crystallizes in the chiral and polar monoclinic space
group P21 (No. 4) with the unit-cell parameters: a = 8.94635(9) {\AA}, b =
5.43415(5) {\AA}, c = 9.10250(8) {\AA} and beta = 90.4209(6){\deg}. A close
inspection of the crystal structure of RbMnPO4 shows that this material
presents two different types of zigzag chains running along the b axis. This is
a unique feature among the zeolite-ABW type materials exhibiting the P21
symmetry. At low temperature, RbMnPO4 exhibits a canted antiferromagnetic
structure characterized by the propagation vector k1 = 0 resulting in the
magnetic symmetry P21. The magnetic moments lie mostly along the b axis with
the ferromagnetic component being in the ac plane. Due to the geometrical
frustration present in this system, an intermediate phase appears within the
temperature range 4.7 - 5.1 K characterized by the propagation vector k2 = (kx,
0, kz) with kx/kz = 2. This ratio is reminiscent of the multiferroic phase of
the orthorhombic RMnO3 phases (R = rare earth). This suggests that RbMnPO4
could present some multiferroic properties at low temperature. Our density
functional calculations confirm the presence of magnetic frustration, which
explains this intermediate incommensurate phase. Taking into account the
strongest magnetic interactions, we are able to reproduce the magnetic
structure observed experimentally at low temperature.

Near-infrared medium-resolution spectra of seven bright brown dwarfs are
presented. The spectra were obtained with the Infrared Camera (IRC) on board
the infrared astronomical satellite AKARI, covering 2.5--5.0 um with a spectral
resolution of approximately 120. The spectral types of the objects range from
L5 to T8, and enable us to study the spectral evolution of brown dwarfs. The
observed spectra are in general consistent with the predictions from the
previous observations and photospheric models. We find that the CO fundamental
band around 4.6 um is clearly seen even in the T8 dwarf 2MASS J041519-0935,
confirming the presence of non-equilibrium chemical state in the atmosphere. We
also identify the CO_2 fundamental stretching-mode band at 4.2 um for the first
time in the spectra of late-L and T-type brown dwarfs.
  We analyze the observed spectra by comparing with the predicted ones based on
the Unified Cloudy Model (UCM). Although overall spectral energy distributions
(SEDs) can be reasonably fitted with the UCM, observed CO and CO_2 bands in
late-L and T-dwarfs are unexpectedly stronger than the model predictions
assuming local thermodynamical equilibrium (LTE). We examine the vertical
mixing model and find that this model explains the CO band at least partly in
the T-dwarfs 2MASS J041519-0935 and 2MASS J055919-1404. The CO fundamental band
also shows excess absorption against the predicted one in the L9 dwarf SDSS
J083008+4828. Since CO is already highly abundant in the upper photospheres of
late-L dwarfs, the extra CO by vertical mixing has little effect on the CO band
strengths, and the vertical mixing model cannot be applied to this L-dwarf. A
more serious problem is that the significant enhancement of the CO_2 4.2 um
band in both the late-L and T dwarfs cannot be explained at all by the vertical
mixing model. The enhancement of the CO_2 band remains puzzling.

The Reeb space of a generic map is the space of all connected components of
preimages of the map. Reeb spaces are fundamental and useful tools in the
theory of Morse functions and higher dimensional variants and their
applications to geometry. These spaces are polyhedra compatible with natural
simplicial structures of the manifolds in considerable cases. For example, for
Morse functions, fold maps, and proper stable maps, which are useful and
fundamental tools in these studies, they are polyhedra whose dimensions are
equal to those of the manifolds of the targets.
  In the 2010s, Hiratuka and Saeki found that the top-dimensional homology
group of the Reeb space does not vanish for smooth maps such as proper stable
maps having some preimages containing a component which is not (oriented)
null-cobordant and which has no singular points. Recently the author found some
extended versions of this fact formulating and using cobordism-like groups of
equivalence classes of smooth and closed manifolds.
  The present paper concerns cases where manifolds and preimages with no
singular points of maps may have additional algebraic topological or
differential topological structures other than differentiable structures and
orientations. We show a theorem for this case. We also give some explicit
applications of the result where the preimages have spin or spin^c structures
induced from the manifolds of the domains and structures of framed manifolds
for example. As important applications, we present new explicit construction of
spin cobordisms and spin^c cobordisms for example.

text: The abstract for the research paper focusing on pseudorandom generators (PRGs) and their relation to the computational complexity classes BQP (Bounded-error Quantum Polynomial time) and PH (Polynomial Hierarchy) is as follows  This study explores the role of pseudorandom generators in resolving the long-standing question of whether BQP (quantum computers) can solve problems that classical computers with access to an unbounded amount of random bits cannot. By constructing PRGs tailored to simulate quantum randomness, we investigate how efficiently these generators can mimic the behavior of quantum oracles within polynomial-time computations. Methodologically, we leverage quantum information theory and computational complexity analysis to derive upper bounds on the length of PRGs required to fool quantum circuits, thereby impacting our understanding of the power of quantum algorithms.  Key findings indicate that while current constructions of PRGs are insufficient to fully simulate quantum computations, they do provide evidence suggesting that quantum algorithms might not significantly outperform classical algorithms when restricted to polynomial-time resources. This aligns with the hypothesis that BQP is contained within PH, implying that any quantum advantage must be due to non-polynomial resources rather than the use of quantum randomness alone. The research thus contributes to the ongoing debate about the computational capabilities of quantum and classical computing models, emphasizing the critical role of PRGs in delineating computational boundaries between these two paradigms.

text: This research paper aims to investigate the stellar content of ultra diffuse galaxies (UDGs) using spectroscopic techniques. The background of this study lies in the growing interest in UDGs, which are low surface brightness galaxies with unexpectedly large sizes and low stellar densities. The objective is to better understand the nature and evolution of these enigmatic galaxies by analyzing their stellar populations through spectroscopic observations.  Methodology involves obtaining deep spectroscopic data of UDGs using telescopes equipped with spectrographs to study their stellar content, such as age, metallicity, and chemical composition. Key findings reveal diverse stellar populations within UDGs, including old and metal-poor stars, suggesting a complex formation history involving processes like mergers and tidal interactions.  The results shed light on the formation mechanisms and evolutionary paths of UDGs, offering insights into the broader context of galaxy formation and evolution. In conclusion, the spectroscopic characterisation of the stellar content of UDGs contributes to the understanding of these intriguing galaxies and their place in the diverse landscape of the universe.

text: This study investigates the equivalent width (EW) of the Fe Kα line observed in active galactic nuclei (AGN) when passing through a dusty medium. The primary objective is to understand how dust attenuation modifies the observed properties of this spectral feature. We employ detailed numerical simulations and analytical models to explore the impact of varying dust grain size, density, and distribution on the Fe Kα line's EW. Our results indicate that the presence of dust significantly broadens the line profile, leading to a decrease in its observed EW. Additionally, we find that the dust extinction coefficient plays a crucial role in determining the extent of this effect. Key methodologies include Monte Carlo radiative transfer calculations coupled with atomic physics models to accurately simulate the interaction between the Fe Kα photons and the dust grains. These findings contribute to our understanding of AGN spectral energy distributions and aid in the interpretation of observational data.

LHC experiments have placed strong bounds on the production of supersymmetric
colored particles (squarks and gluinos), under the assumption that all flavors
of squarks are nearly degenerate. However, the current experimental constraints
on stop squarks are much weaker, due to the smaller production cross section
and difficult backgrounds. While light stops are motivated by naturalness
arguments, it has been suggested that such particles become nearly impossible
to detect near the limit where their mass is degenerate with the sum of the
masses of their decay products. We show that this is not the case, and that
searches based on missing transverse energy (MET) have significant reach for
stop masses above 175 GeV, even in the degenerate limit. We consider direct
pair production of stops, decaying to invisible LSPs and tops with either
hadronic or semi-leptonic final states. Modest intrinsic differences in MET are
magnified by boosted kinematics and by shape analyses of MET or suitably-chosen
observables related to MET. For these observables we show that the
distributions of the relevant backgrounds and signals are well-described by
simple analytic functions, in the kinematic regime where signal is enhanced.
Shape analyses of MET-related distributions will allow the LHC experiments to
place significantly improved bounds on stop squarks, even in scenarios where
the stop-LSP mass difference is degenerate with the top mass. Assuming 20/fb of
luminosity at 8 TeV, we conservatively estimate that experiments can exclude or
discover degenerate stops with mass as large as ~ 360 GeV and 560 GeV for
massless LSPs.

text: This study explores the application of radio-frequency scanning tunnelling microscopy (rf-STM) to investigate the nuclear and electronic resonance spectroscopy of single molecules. Background information highlights the significance of understanding molecular properties at the atomic level, particularly in the context of quantum computing and molecular electronics. The objective of this research is to demonstrate the feasibility of using rf-STM to probe the nuclear and electronic resonance properties of individual molecules, thereby advancing our understanding of molecular behavior at the atomic scale.  The methodology employed in this study involves the use of rf-STM to scan individual molecules on a conductive surface, with the application of radio-frequency radiation to excite molecular vibrations. The resonance frequencies of the molecules are measured using the tunnelling current, which is modulated by the rf radiation. A custom-built rf-STM system is designed to generate and control the rf radiation, allowing for precise tuning of the excitation frequencies. The experiments are performed on a range of molecules, including alkynes, alkenes, and aromatic compounds.  The key findings of this study reveal that rf-STM can be used to detect and measure the nuclear and electronic resonance frequencies of individual molecules. The resonance frequencies are found to be in excellent agreement with theoretical predictions, demonstrating the accuracy of the rf-STM approach. The results also show that the rf-STM technique can be used to study the dynamics of molecular vibrations, providing insights into the molecular properties of individual molecules. The conclusions drawn from this study highlight the potential of rf-STM as a powerful tool for probing molecular behavior at the atomic scale.

text: The merger of a neutron star (NS) and a black hole (BH) on August 17, 2017 (GW170817), as inferred by the LIGO and Virgo Collaborations, produced a short gamma-ray burst (GRB) and a kilonova, an electromagnetic counterpart. The kilonova emission was composed of lanthanide-rich ejecta, with a total mass of ∼0.05 M⊙, consistent with the prediction of a binary neutron star merger. Using the spectral evolution of the kilonova, and assuming that the r-process nucleosynthesis occurred in a NS crust before the merger, we estimated the mass of the surviving NS to be ∼1.1 M⊙, with a 1σ uncertainty of 0.15 M⊙. This is smaller than the canonical maximum mass of an NS of 2.1 M⊙, which raises questions about the nature of neutron stars and the existence of a population of long-lived remnant neutron stars. Our analysis suggests that a fraction of NSs could in fact be heavier and longer lived than previously thought, providing a new perspective on the population of NSs and their evolution. Further studies of kilonova events associated with NS-NS mergers can help to clarify the mass distribution and properties of neutron stars.

text: In this work, we present an overview of gauge gravity, offering a forward-looking introduction to this emerging field. The traditional framework of General Relativity is extended by incorporating gauge symmetries from other fundamental interactions, such as Yang-Mills theory. Our results demonstrate how this novel approach facilitates a unified description of gravity and other gauge interactions, paving the way for a more comprehensive understanding of fundamental forces in the universe.  The primary problem this work addresses is the reconciliation of gravity with the other fundamental interactions in a consistent quantum framework. By exploring the concepts of local gauge invariance in the context of gravity, we aim to bridge the gap between General Relativity and the Standard Model of particle physics. Our methodology involves a comprehensive review of the foundational principles of gauge theories and gravity, followed by an exposition of the key ideas behind gauge gravity and its implications for theoretical physics.  Through elucidating the principles and potential applications of gauge gravity, our work contributes to laying the groundwork for future research in theoretical physics. By blending concepts from particle physics and gravitational theory, we offer a fresh perspective on the nature of gravity and its unification with other fundamental forces. This forward-looking introduction to gauge gravity sets the stage for further exploration and development in the pursuit of a unified theory of fundamental interactions.

text: We investigate the mass of the exoplanet Alpha Centauri B b, a terrestrial candidate orbiting the star Alpha Centauri B within the Alpha Centauri system. Our study addresses the overarching problem of determining the physical characteristics of exoplanets, which is crucial for understanding their potential habitability and composition. Utilizing a combination of radial velocity measurements and advanced computational models, we analyze data collected over several observation campaigns. By applying contemporary techniques, including Bayesian inference and Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations, we refine the existing mass estimates of Alpha Centauri B b. Our results indicate that the mass of Alpha Centauri B b is approximately 1.2 Earth masses, which suggests that the planet may be classified as a super-Earth. We also discuss the implications of our findings in the context of planetary formation theories, particularly in the vicinity of a binary star system. Additionally, we explore the limitations of our methodology and the need for further observational campaigns to enhance the precision of mass estimates for this intriguing exoplanet. Our study contributes to the broader understanding of planetary systems in close proximity to our own, thus fostering ongoing scientific inquiry into suitable targets for future astrobiological exploration. These insights also encourage the integration of interdisciplinary approaches in exoplanet research, emphasizing the collaboration between astrophysics and planetary science.

text: We investigated the formation of the cosmic web structure around the brightest galaxies during the epoch of reionization, a critical period in the early universe where the first stars and galaxies emerged. Through a combination of hydrodynamic simulations and radiative transfer modeling, we explored the impact of galaxy feedback on the surrounding intergalactic medium, shedding light on the complex interplay between galaxy evolution and the large-scale structure of the universe.  Our simulations revealed that the brightest galaxies played a pivotal role in shaping the cosmic web, with their powerful outflows and supernovae-driven winds sculpting the surrounding gas and triggering the formation of new galaxies. We found that the cosmic web's structure and properties were significantly influenced by the mass and luminosity of the brightest galaxies, with more massive galaxies producing more extensive and complex networks of filaments and voids.  Our results suggest that the epoch of reionization was a period of intense galaxy evolution and feedback, with the brightest galaxies serving as the seeds of the cosmic web. We propose that the cosmic web's structure and properties can be used to constrain models of galaxy evolution and the early universe, providing valuable insights into the complex interplay between galaxy formation and the large-scale structure of the universe.

Discrete polymatroids are the multi-set analogue of matroids. In this paper,
we explore the connections among linear network coding, linear index coding and
representable discrete polymatroids. We consider vector linear solutions of
networks over a field $\mathbb{F}_q,$ with possibly different message and edge
vector dimensions, which are referred to as linear fractional solutions. We
define a \textit{discrete polymatroidal} network and show that a linear
fractional solution over a field $\mathbb{F}_q,$ exists for a network if and
only if the network is discrete polymatroidal with respect to a discrete
polymatroid representable over $\mathbb{F}_q.$ An algorithm to construct
networks starting from certain class of discrete polymatroids is provided.
Every representation over $\mathbb{F}_q$ for the discrete polymatroid, results
in a linear fractional solution over $\mathbb{F}_q$ for the constructed
network. Next, we consider the index coding problem and show that a linear
solution to an index coding problem exists if and only if there exists a
representable discrete polymatroid satisfying certain conditions which are
determined by the index coding problem considered. El Rouayheb et. al. showed
that the problem of finding a multi-linear representation for a matroid can be
reduced to finding a \textit{perfect linear index coding solution} for an index
coding problem obtained from that matroid. We generalize the result of El
Rouayheb et. al. by showing that the problem of finding a representation for a
discrete polymatroid can be reduced to finding a perfect linear index coding
solution for an index coding problem obtained from that discrete polymatroid.

text:
Asteroseismic data can be used to determine surface gravities with precisions
of < 0.05 dex by using the global seismic quantities Deltanu and nu_max along
with Teff and [Fe/H]. Surface gravity is also one of the four stellar
properties to be derived by automatic analyses for 1 billion stars from Gaia
data (workpackage GSP_Phot). We explore seismic data from MS F, G, K stars
(solar-like stars) observed by Kepler as a potential calibration source for
methods that Gaia will use for object characterisation (log g). We calculate
log g for bright nearby stars for which radii and masses are known, and using
their global seismic quantities in a grid-based method, we determine an
asteroseismic log g to within 0.01 dex of the direct calculation, thus
validating the accuracy of our method. We find that errors in Teff and mainly
[Fe/H] can cause systematic errors of 0.02 dex. We then apply our method to a
list of 40 stars to deliver precise values of surface gravity, i.e. sigma <
0.02 dex, and we find agreement with recent literature values. Finally, we
explore the precision we expect in a sample of 400+ Kepler stars which have
their global seismic quantities measured. We find a mean uncertainty
(precision) on the order of <0.02 dex in log g over the full explored range 3.8
< log g < 4.6, with the mean value varying only with stellar magnitude (0.01 -
0.02 dex). We study sources of systematic errors in log g and find possible
biases on the order of 0.04 dex, independent of log g and magnitude, which
accounts for errors in the Teff and [Fe/H] measurements, as well as from using
a different grid-based method. We conclude that Kepler stars provide a wealth
of reliable information that can help to calibrate methods that Gaia will use,
in particular, for source characterisation with GSP_Phot where excellent
precision (small uncertainties) and accuracy in log g is obtained from seismic
data.

text: We investigated the profound effects of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) on their host galaxies, shedding light on the intricate interplay between these two celestial entities. Through a comprehensive analysis of archival data and simulations, we found that AGN activity significantly influences the host galaxy's morphological evolution, with prominent evidence of galaxy harassment, mergers, and starbursts. The luminous quasar-like activity of AGN fuels intense energy output, leading to the disruption of gas and dust distributions within the host galaxy, triggering the formation of new stars and the growth of supermassive black holes.  Our results indicate that the host galaxy's structural transformation is a complex, multi-generational process, influenced by the interplay between AGN activity, stellar feedback, and the galaxy's own internal dynamics. We observed a correlation between AGN luminosity and the host galaxy's star formation rate, suggesting that the energy released by AGN drives the galaxy's evolution. Furthermore, our simulations revealed that the host galaxy's response to AGN activity is highly dependent on its initial mass and the presence of dark matter.  Our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the AGN-host galaxy connection, highlighting the reciprocal influence of these two entities on each other's evolution. By elucidating the mechanisms governing this complex interplay, we provide new insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies, as well as the role of AGN in shaping the cosmic landscape.

In this study we attempt to assess the possibility of detection of variable
sources using the data of the 7.6-cm wavelength surveys carried out on the
RATAN-600 radio telescope in the period from 1980 through 1994. Objects
selected according to certain criteria from the RCR catalog are used to
construct the calibration curves and to estimate the accuracy of the resulting
calibration curves and determine the r.m.s. errors for the measured source flux
densities. To check the calibration sources for the presence of variable
objects, quantitative estimates are performed for a number of parameters that
characterize variability, in particular, for the long-term variability index V
and the chi-square probability p. The long-term variability index was found to
be positive for 14 out of approximately 80 calibration sources, possibly
indicating that these sources are variable. The most likely candidate variables
are the three sources with the chi-square probability p > 0.95. Five sources
have chi-square probabilities in the 0.85 < p < 0.95 interval, and the
remaining six in the 0.6 < p < 0.8 interval. Nine out of 14 objects are
possibly variable in the optical range. The light curves and spectra are
determined for possible variable sources and a number of "non-variable"
objects. We plan to use the results of this study in our future searches for
variable radio sources using the data of the "Cold" surveys.

The creep behaviour of a creep-resistant AE42 magnesium alloy reinforced with
Saffil short fibres and SiC particulates in various combinations has been
examined in the longitudinal direction, i.e., the plane containing random fibre
orientation was parallel to the loading direction, in the temperature range of
175-300 C at the stress levels ranging from 60 to 140 MPa using impression
creep test technique. At 175 C, normal creep behaviour, i.e., strain rate
decreasing with strain and then reaching a steady state, is observed at all the
stresses employed. At 240 C, normal creep behaviour is observed up to 80 MPa
and reverse creep behaviour, i.e., strain rate increasing with strain, then
reaching a steady state and again decreasing, is observed above that stress. At
300 C, reverse creep behaviour is observed at all the stresses employed. This
pattern remains the same for all the composites. The reverse creep behaviour is
found to be associated with the fibre breakage. The stress exponent is found to
be very high for all the composites. However, after taking the threshold stress
into account, the stress exponent varies from 3.9 to 7.0, which suggests
viscous glide and dislocation climb being the dominant creep mechanisms. The
apparent activation energy Qc was not calculated due to insufficient data at
any stress level either for normal or reverse creep behaviour. The creep
resistance of the hybrid composites is found to be comparable to that of the
composite reinforced with 20% Saffil short fibres at all the temperatures and
stress levels investigated.

text: As deep neural networks (DNNs) gain wider application, the need for efficient model training and deployment has become increasingly critical. The objective of this research is to explore group sparse regularization techniques to enhance the generalization capacity of DNNs while reducing model complexity. We implemented a group sparsity framework that encourages the learning of structured representations by penalizing the interconnected parameters of the network, thereby facilitating feature selection across groups of neurons. Our methodology involved the integration of a group lasso regularization term into the loss function of various DNN architectures, followed by extensive experiments across benchmark datasets. The evaluation metrics included accuracy, model size, and inference speed, allowing for a comprehensive assessment of the proposed method's effectiveness. Key findings indicate that models utilizing group sparse regularization achieved competitive performance levels compared to traditional DNNs, with significant reductions in the number of active parameters. Additionally, our approach demonstrated improved robustness to overfitting in high-dimensional settings. Ultimately, the results suggest that group sparse regularization not only streamlines model architecture but also enhances interpretability by identifying salient features. This work contributes to the growing field of model compression and interpretability in AI, underscoring the potential of sparsity-based methods for optimizing DNNs without sacrificing performance. Our findings pave the way for future research into adaptive regularization techniques that can further refine DNN training and deployment practices in resource-constrained environments.

The use of network Newton methods for the decentralized optimization of a sum
cost distributed through agents of a network is considered. Network Newton
methods reinterpret distributed gradient descent as a penalty method, observe
that the corresponding Hessian is sparse, and approximate the Newton step by
truncating a Taylor expansion of the inverse Hessian. Truncating the series at
$K$ terms yields the NN-$K$ that requires aggregating information from $K$ hops
away. Network Newton is introduced and shown to converge to the solution of the
penalized objective function at a rate that is at least linear in a companion
paper [3]. The contributions of this work are: (i) To complement the
convergence analysis by studying the methods' rate of convergence. (ii) To
introduce adaptive formulations that converge to the optimal argument of the
original objective. (iii) To perform numerical evaluations of NN-$K$ methods.
The convergence analysis relates the behavior of NN-$K$ with the behavior of
(regular) Newton's method and shows that the method goes through a quadratic
convergence phase in a specific interval. The length of this quadratic phase
grows with $K$ and can be made arbitrarily large. The numerical experiments
corroborate reductions in the number of iterations and the communication cost
that are necessary to achieve convergence relative to distributed gradient
descent.

Estimates of nuclear matrix elements for neutrinoless double beta decay
(0nu2beta) based on the quasiparticle random phase approximations (QRPA) are
affected by theoretical uncertainties, which can be substantially reduced by
fixing the unknown strength parameter g_pp of the residual particle-particle
interaction through one experimental constraint - most notably through the
two-neutrino double beta decay (2nu2beta) lifetime. However, it has been noted
that the g_pp adjustment via 2\nu2\beta data may bring QRPA models in
disagreement with independent data on electron capture (EC) and single beta
decay (beta^-) lifetimes. Actually, in two nuclei of interest for 0nu2beta
decay (Mo-100 and Cd-116), for which all such data are available, we show that
the disagreement vanishes, provided that the axial vector coupling g_A is
treated as a free parameter, with allowance for g_A<1 (``strong quenching'').
Three independent lifetime data (2nu2beta, EC, \beta^-) are then accurately
reproduced by means of two free parameters (g_pp, g_A), resulting in an
overconstrained parameter space. In addition, the sign of the 2nu2beta matrix
element M^2nu is unambiguously selected (M^2nu>0) by the combination of all
data. We discuss quantitatively, in each of the two nuclei, these
phenomenological constraints and their consequences for QRPA estimates of the
0nu2beta matrix elements and of their uncertainties.

text: We investigated the role of water content in protoplanetary discs on the migration and formation of planets, shedding light on the complex interplay between these two critical processes. Our simulations revealed that the presence of significant amounts of water in the disc significantly impacts the migration of planets, particularly those with masses below the Chandrasekhar limit. We found that water-rich discs facilitate the formation of planetary systems with multiple, densely packed planets, whereas dry discs tend to produce systems with fewer, more isolated planets.  Our results also indicate that the water content of the disc influences the type of planet migration mechanism employed. In water-rich discs, the disk's angular momentum is more efficiently transferred to the planets, leading to the formation of compact, Jupiter-like systems. Conversely, in dry discs, the transfer of angular momentum is more gradual, resulting in the formation of more distant, gas-giant-like systems.  Our study employed a combination of hydrodynamic simulations and N-body integrations to model the dynamics of protoplanetary discs and planetary systems. We employed a novel, water-dependent disc model, which accounts for the effects of water on the disc's viscosity and thermal evolution. Our findings suggest that the water content of protoplanetary discs plays a crucial role in shaping the architecture of planetary systems, and that the interplay between water and angular momentum is a key factor in determining the final configuration of planetary systems.

We have studied the electronic structure of Mo rich Mo$_{1-x}$Re$_x$ alloys
(0$\leq$ x $\leq$0.4) using valence band photoemission spectroscopy in the
photon energy range 23-70 eV and density of states calculations. Comparison of
the photoemission spectra with the density of states calculations suggests that
with respect to the Fermi level $E_F$, the $d$ states lie mostly in the range 0
to -6 eV binding energy whereas $s$ states lie in the range -4 to -10 eV
binding energy. We have observed two resonances in the photoemission spectra of
each sample, one at about 35 eV photon energy and other at about 45 eV photon
energy. Our analysis suggest that the resonance at 35 eV photon energy is
related to the Mo $4p$-$5s$ transition and the resonance at 45 eV photon energy
is related to the contribution from both the Mo $4p$-$4d$ transition
(threshold: 42 eV) and Re $5p$-$5d$ transition (threshold: 46 eV). In the CIS
plot, the resonance at 35 eV incident photon energy for binding energy features
in the range of $E_F$ (B.E. = 0) to -5 eV becomes progressively less prominent
with the increasing Re concentration $x$ and vanishes for $x>$ 0.2. The
difference plots obtained by subtracting the valence band photoemission
spectrum of Mo from that of Mo$_{1-x}$Re$_x$ alloys, measured at 47 eV photon
energy, reveal that the Re $d$ like states appear near $E_F$ when Re is alloyed
with Mo. These results indicate that interband $s$-$d$ interaction, which is
weak in Mo, increases with the increasing $x$ and influences the nature of
superconductivity in the alloys with higher $x$.

The top forward-backward asymmetry (tAFB) measured at the Tevatron remains
one of the most puzzling outstanding collider anomalies. After two years of LHC
running, however, few models for tAFB remain consistent with LHC data. In this
paper we take a detailed look at the most promising surviving class of models,
namely light (m_G' <~ 450 GeV), broad axigluons. We show which models
simultaneously satisfy constraints from Tevatron and LHC top measurements,
hadronic resonance searches, and LEP precision electroweak (PEW) observables.
We consider three flavor structures: flavor-universal; down-type nonuniversal,
designed to ease constraints from LHC charge asymmetry measurements; and
top-type nonuniversal, designed to ameliorate constraints from PEW. We compute
contributions to the PEW observables from states in the minimal UV completion
of the axigluon model and demonstrate that new heavy fermions make the
constraints universally more stringent, while related contributions from new
scalars are much smaller, but act to relax the constraints. Paired dijet
searches from ATLAS and CMS rule out all narrow axiglue models, while the LHC
charge asymmetry measurement is less constraining than expected due to the high
central value measured by ATLAS. Excepting the tension with the CMS charge
asymmetry measurement, a broad axigluon is consistent with all data over the
entire mass range we consider (50 GeV <~m_G' <~450 GeV) in the flavor-universal
and top-type nonuniversal models, while it is consistent for m_G' >~200 GeV in
the down-type non-universal model. The LHC charge asymmetry remains the best
avenue for excluding, or observing, these models.

We demonstrate that the chaotic nature of N-body systems can lead to
macroscopic variations in the evolution of collisionless simulations containing
rotationally supported discs. The unavoidable stochasticity that afflicts all
simulations generally causes mild differences between the evolution of similar
models but, in order to illustrate that this is not always true, we present a
case that shows extreme bimodal divergence. The divergent behaviour occurs in
two different types of code and is independent of all numerical parameters. We
identify and give explicit illustrations of several sources of stochasticity,
and also show that macroscopic variations in the evolution can originate from
differences at the round-off error level. We obtain somewhat more consistent
results from simulations in which the halo is set up with great care compared
with those started from more approximate equilibria, but we have been unable to
eliminate diverging behaviour entirely because the main sources of
stochasticity are intrinsic to the disc. We show that the divergence is only
temporary and that halo friction is merely delayed, for a substantial time in
some cases. We argue that the delays are unlikely to arise in real galaxies,
and that our results do not affect dynamical friction constraints on halo
density. Stochastic variations in the evolution are inevitable in all
simulations of disc-halo systems, irrespective of how they were created,
although their effect is generally far less extreme than we find here. The
possibility of divergent behaviour complicates comparison of results from
different workers.

text: The integration of joint imaging and RNA-seq data has emerged as a promising approach to studying complex diseases, particularly in the fields of orthopedics and rheumatology. This study explores various methods for joint imaging and RNA-seq data analysis, focusing on the identification of differentiating features between healthy and diseased states. The background section outlines the current understanding of joint diseases and the benefits of integrating imaging and transcriptomic data. The objective is to identify effective methods for analyzing these complex datasets and gaining insights into the underlying molecular mechanisms of joint diseases. The methodology section introduces several data analysis pipelines, including Image-RNA Fusion (IRF), Joint Analysis of Gene Expression and Radiology (JAGER), and the Integration of Transcriptome and Medical Imaging (ITMI) pipeline. Key findings highlight the advantages and limitations of each pipeline, with a focus on their ability to identify co-localized gene expression and imaging features. The conclusion emphasizes the importance of integrating joint imaging and RNA-seq data for a more comprehensive understanding of joint diseases and the potential for translating these insights into improved diagnosis and treatment strategies. Furthermore, the study discusses ongoing efforts to enhance these pipelines and overcome challenges related to data integration and preprocessing.

text: In this study, we explore the framework of multivariable $(\varphi,\Gamma)$-modules and their connection to locally analytic vectors, contributing to the broader understanding of $p$-adic Hodge theory and its applications in arithmetic geometry. These modules arise from the study of representations of the Galois group of a non-archimedean local field, and their properties have profound implications for the classification of such representations. The objective of this paper is to examine the structural properties of these multivariable modules and identify conditions under which locally analytic vectors exist and can be effectively characterized. Utilizing rigorous algebraic techniques, we construct these modules over certain Robba rings and develop criteria for the existence of locally analytic vectors through an exploration of their topological and algebraic structures. Our methodology includes an investigation of the trace map and the role of overconvergent series within this context.  Key findings reveal that these $(\varphi,\Gamma)$-modules, under appropriate conditions, admit a rich family of locally analytic vectors, shedding light on new dimensions of their representation theory implications. Additionally, we identify a set of stability properties for these vectors, particularly in relation to the action of the Frobenius and the Galois group. These results not only enhance the understanding of the local Langlands correspondence but also provide tools for further research in $p$-adic differential equations and their applications.  In conclusion, the interplay between multivariable $(\varphi,\Gamma)$-modules and locally analytic vectors offers substantial insights into $p$-adic representation theory, suggesting avenues for forthcoming investigations and potentially new classifications of local field representations.

text: In our study, we investigate the diversity of diffuse Ly$\alpha$ nebulae surrounding star-forming galaxies at high redshift, focusing on the intricate interplay between galactic-scale star formation and the intergalactic medium. We utilized a comprehensive set of deep spectroscopic observations obtained from the Keck Observatory, targeting a sample of high redshift galaxies in the redshift range of 2 < z < 4.5. Our results reveal a significant variation in the morphology and spatial extent of Ly$\alpha$ nebulae, highlighting a diverse population of diffuse gaseous structures extending up to several tens of kiloparsecs from the host galaxies. We identified a correlation between the luminosity and kinematics of the nebulae and the properties of their central galaxies, suggesting that the physical conditions of the nebulae are influenced by both intrinsic galactic processes and external environmental factors. We employed advanced radiative transfer modeling to discern the role of resonant scattering in shaping observable features of the nebulae. Our findings indicate that radiative transfer effects significantly contribute to the spectral and structural characteristics of Ly$\alpha$ emission, playing a crucial role in the observability of extended emissions. This study challenges previous assumptions regarding the homogeneity of circumgalactic environments and emphasizes the necessity of considering diverse environmental and evolutionary pathways in models of galaxy formation. Our work provides important constraints for theoretical models and encourages further exploration of the feedback mechanisms driving such nebulae, ultimately contributing to a more nuanced understanding of galaxy evolution in the early universe.

text: This study explores the application of full-Stokes polarimetry techniques using circularly polarized feeds to investigate sources exhibiting stable linear and circular polarization across the gigahertz frequency range. The primary objective is to enhance our understanding of polarization properties in these sources by employing advanced polarimetric methods that can independently measure all Stokes parameters. We present experimental setups designed to generate circular polarization through specific feed configurations, which are then used to collect data from selected astronomical sources. Results indicate significant improvements in the accuracy of polarization measurements compared to conventional linear polarization techniques, particularly in scenarios where linear polarization alone is insufficient to fully characterize the source's polarization state. Key methodologies include detailed calibration procedures to ensure precise measurement of both linear and circular components, as well as rigorous statistical analysis to validate the reliability of the derived polarization parameters. The findings underscore the potential of circular polarization in revealing new insights into the polarization dynamics of celestial objects at high frequencies.

text: We investigated the underlying mechanisms contributing to imperfect synchronization in Parkinsonian basal ganglia, a hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease. Our computational modeling approach employed a hybrid neural network framework to simulate the complex interactions between dopaminergic neurons, GABAergic interneurons, and motor neurons in the basal ganglia circuit. By systematically perturbing the parameters of the model, we identified several key factors that disrupt synchronization, including reduced dopaminergic neurotransmission, increased GABAergic inhibition, and altered neuronal connectivity.  Our results demonstrate that these factors can lead to the emergence of asynchronous activity patterns, characterized by distinct frequency bands and phase-locking values, which are distinct from the synchronized oscillations observed in healthy basal ganglia. Furthermore, we found that the impaired synchronization is not solely the result of individual neuronal dysfunction but rather a collective failure of the network to reach a stable state.  The key findings of this study highlight the complex interplay between different neural populations and neurotransmitter systems in the basal ganglia, and how their dysregulation can give rise to imperfect synchronization. These results have significant implications for our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying Parkinson's disease and suggest potential therapeutic targets for the development of novel treatments aimed at restoring basal ganglia function and promoting synchronized activity.

text: Nonlocality, a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, has long intrigued physicists due to its profound implications for our understanding of the natural world. In this work, we delve into the intricacies of nonlocality as it manifests in quantum field theory, quantum gravity, and cosmology.  In quantum field theory, nonlocality arises due to the interplay between quantum fields and interactions beyond the reach of classical signals. We examine the role of nonlocality in models such as quantum electrodynamics and the Higgs boson, demonstrating how it leads to phenomena like quantum entanglement, anomalous magnetic moments, and vacuum polarization.  Transitioning to quantum gravity, we explore the deep connections between nonlocality and the nature of space and time at the most fundamental level. Specifically, we examine the role of nonlocality in theories like loop quantum gravity, causal sets, and string theory, elucidating how these frameworks reconcile quantum mechanics with general relativity while retaining nonlocal features.  Lastly, we investigate the profound implications of nonlocality in cosmology, where it has been posited as a potential solution to the horizon problem and the flatness problem. We present a brief overview of approaches, such as the cyclic model and the multiverse hypothesis, that seek to address these challenges through nonlocal mechanisms.  Throughout this work, we employ a combination of analytical techniques and computational simulations to illuminate various facets of nonlocality in these diverse contexts. Our results shed light on the intriguing nature of nonlocality and its importance as a unifying concept in theoretical physics and cosmology.

text: In the ever-evolving field of wireless sensor networks (WSNs), three-dimensional (3D) configurations have gained significant attention due to their potential to enhance network coverage, increase data throughput, and reduce interference. However, optimal node placement in 3D WSNs remains a challenging problem. This study proposes an information estimation approach to optimize node placement in 3D WSNs. We begin by discussing the background of the problem, explaining the importance of node placement in WSNs and the unique challenges posed by 3D configurations. We then outline the objective of our research to develop a novel approach for estimating the required information at each node based on its spatial position and the communication range, resulting in an efficient node placement strategy for 3D WSNs.  Our methodology employs a graph-based modeling technique for representing the network in 3D space, followed by the application of optimization algorithms to determine the optimal node placement. We conduct extensive simulations to validate our approach, comparing the proposed method with existing solutions in terms of coverage, data throughput, and energy efficiency.  Our key findings reveal that the proposed information estimation approach significantly improves node placement efficiency in 3D WSNs, providing optimal coverage and data throughput while minimizing energy consumption. Furthermore, the simulation results indicate that our method performs better than existing methods, particularly in networks with large-scale deployments or complex geometries.  In conclusion, this study offers a valuable contribution to the ongoing research in the field of 3D WSNs by addressing the critical issue of node placement optimization through the development of an information estimation approach that provides efficient, optimal, and energy-efficient solutions. Our findings demonstrate the potential of this approach in enabling the deployment of advanced 3D WSN applications that require high coverage, data throughput, and energy efficiency.

text: We investigate the effective field theory (EFT) framework for weakly coupled inflationary models, aiming to clarify the connection between high-energy physics and observable cosmic phenomena. Our approach centers on identifying the relevant degrees of freedom and symmetries that characterize weakly coupled scenarios, ultimately leading to a systematic classification of potential inflationary models. Utilizing a combination of perturbative methods and renormalization group analysis, we derive the constraints that govern effective operators in the inflaton sector, focusing particularly on their implications for the spectral indices and non-Gaussianity of cosmic perturbations.  Our results demonstrate that the EFT descriptions yield particular predictions that can be tested against current observational data from the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure surveys. We find that, under certain conditions, the EFT framework allows for natural inflationary dynamics while suppressing unwanted higher-order corrections. Additionally, we explore the robustness of our findings against various forms of couplings and interactions, confirming that weakly coupled inflationary models can remain consistent with observable gravitational wave signals.  This work establishes a comprehensive toolset for researchers examining inflationary models within the broader context of quantum field theory and cosmology. By providing a coherent methodology to assess the viability and predictive power of weakly coupled inflationary scenarios, we pave the way for more refined analyses that can potentially resolve outstanding discrepancies in the observed cosmological parameters. Our findings elucidate the interplay between high-energy physics and cosmological observations, contributing to the ongoing discourse on the nature of inflation.

text: In this study, we investigate the dynamics near a tipping point in a system undergoing a delayed saddle node bifurcation under the influence of periodic forcing. Our work aims to address the challenge of predicting critical transitions in systems subject to external periodic perturbations. By employing theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we reveal that the system exhibits a complex interplay between the delayed saddle node bifurcation and the periodic forcing, leading to the emergence of tipping points. Our results demonstrate that the system's proximity to the delayed saddle node bifurcation significantly alters its response to the periodic forcing, ultimately driving the system towards abrupt qualitative changes. Through the identification of the tipping points and their associated basin boundaries, we provide insights into the mechanisms governing the system's behavior near critical transitions. Our findings highlight the importance of considering delayed bifurcations and external periodic forcing in the context of tipping point analysis. The methodology presented in this work offers a framework for understanding and predicting critical transitions in a broad range of dynamical systems experiencing delayed saddle node bifurcations and periodic forcing.

text:
Video streaming via TCP networks has become a popular and highly demanded
service, but its quality assessment in both objective and subjective terms has
not been properly addressed. In this paper, based on statistical analysis a
full analytic model of a no-reference objective metric, namely Pause Intensity,
for video quality assessment is presented. The model characterizes the video
playout buffer behavior in connection with the network performance (throughput)
and the video playout rate. This allows for instant quality measurement and
control without requiring a reference video. Pause intensity specifically
addresses the need for assessing the quality issue in terms of the continuity
in the playout of TCP streaming videos, which cannot be properly measured by
other objective metrics such as PSNR, SSIM and buffer underrun or pause
frequency. The performance of the analytical model is rigidly verified by
simulation results and subjective tests using a range of video clips. It is
demonstrated that pause intensity is closely correlated with viewer opinion
scores regardless of the vastly different composition of individual elements,
such as pause duration and pause frequency which jointly constitute this new
quality metric. It is also shown that the correlation performance of pause
intensity is consistent and content independent.

text:
Multivariate data occurs in a wide range of fields, with ever more flexible
model specifications being proposed, often within a multivariate generalised
linear mixed effects (MGLME) framework. In this article, we describe an
extended framework, encompassing multiple outcomes of any type, each of which
could be repeatedly measured (longitudinal), with any number of levels, and
with any number of random effects at each level. Many standard distributions
are described, as well as non-standard user-defined non-linear models. The
extension focuses on a complex linear predictor for each outcome model,
allowing sharing and linking between outcome models in an extremely flexible
way, either by linking random effects directly, or the expected value of one
outcome (or function of it) within the linear predictor of another. Non-linear
and time-dependent effects are also seamlessly incorporated to the linear
predictor through the use of splines or fractional polynomials. We further
propose level-specific random effect distributions and numerical integration
techniques to improve usability, relaxing the normally distributed random
effects assumption to allow multivariate $t$-distributed random effects. We
consider some special cases of the general framework, describing some new
models in the fields of clustered survival data, joint longitudinal-survival
models, and discuss various potential uses of the implementation. User
friendly, and easily extendable, software is provided.

text:
Mode-coupling theory provides a unified description of the rotational and
translational dynamics of polyatomic ions. These molecular ions are distinct
from usual models of ion diffusion, such as K+ , Cl- etc., and also different
from rotational dynamics of dipolar molecules often modeled in dielectric
continuum models as point dipoles. Both these approaches are untenable for
polyatomic ions. Here rotational and translational dynamics are so strongly
coupled that one obtains a more coherent description by treating them together.
We carry out theoretical and computational studies of a series of well-known
polyatomic ions, namely sulfate, nitrate and acetate ions. All the three ions
exhibit different rotational diffusivity, with that of nitrate ion being
considerably larger than the other two. They all defy the hydrodynamic laws of
size dependence. Study of the local structure around the ions provides valuable
insight into the origin of these differences. We carry out a detailed study of
the rotational diffusion of these ions by extensive computer simulation and
using the theoretical approaches of the dielectric friction developed by
Fatuzzo-Mason (FM) and Nee-Zwanzig (NZ), and subsequently generalized by Alavi
and Waldeck. We develop a self-consistent mode-coupling theory (SC-MCT)
formalism that helps elucidating the role of coupling between translational and
rotational motion of these ions. In fact, these two motions self-consistently
determine the value of each other. The RISM-based MCT suggests an interesting
relation between the torque-torque and the force-force time correlation
function with the proportionality constant being determined by the geometry and
the charge distribution of the polyatomic molecule.We point out several
parallelism between the theories of translational and rotation friction
calculations of ions in dipolar liquids.

text:
Measurements of the intracluster light (ICL) are still prone to
methodological ambiguities and there are multiple techniques in the literature
for that purpose, mostly based on the binding energy, the local density
distribution, or the surface brightness. A common issue with these methods is
the a priori assumption of a number of hypotheses on either the ICL morphology,
its surface brightness level or some properties of the brightest cluster galaxy
(BCG). The discrepancy on the results is high, and numerical simulations just
bound the ICL fraction in present-day galaxy clusters to the range 10-50%. We
developed a new algorithm based on the Chebyshev-Fourier functions (CHEFs) to
estimate the ICL fraction without relying on any a priori assumption on the
physical or geometrical characteristics of the ICL. We are able to not only
disentangle the ICL from the galatic luminosity but mark out the limits of the
BCG from the ICL in a natural way. We test our tecnique with the recently
released data of the cluster Abell 2744, observed by the Frontier Fields
program. The complexity of this multiple merging cluster system and the
formidable depth of these images make it a challenging test case to prove the
efficiency of our algorithm. We found a final ICL fraction of 19.17+-2.87%,
which is very consistent with numerical simulations.

text: Infalling low angular momentum gas towards the L1551 NE Keplerian circumbinary disk has been extensively studied using various observational techniques. We present new evidence from high-resolution Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations of the dense gas tracers, N2H+ and DCO+, toward this system. Our observations reveal strong velocity gradients along the disk midplane, which are suggestive of infalling gas motions towards the central binary system. The mean infall velocities for the north and south components are estimated to be 0.20 ± 0.03 km/s and 0.22 ± 0.02 km/s, respectively. These velocities are consistent with previous observations, indicating a constant infall rate onto the disk.  We also examine the large-scale gas dynamics of the L1551 NE system through a detailed modeling study. Our results suggest that the observed infalling motions are driven by the gravitational interaction between the two components of the binary system. We find that the infalling material forms a geometrically thin and dynamically cool inner disk, surrounded by a large, more massive, and dynamically hot outer disk. This structure is consistent with current theoretical models of circumbinary disk evolution.  The new ALMA data provide critical insights into the gas dynamics of the L1551 NE circumbinary disk and contribute to our understanding of the formation of binary stars in the early universe. These findings highlight the importance of high-resolution observations and theoretical modeling in unraveling the complexities of the star-formation process. Future work will focus on observing the outer regions of the disk and studying the effects of magnetic fields on the infalling gas.

text: This research paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the synergistic relationship between magnetism, chemical activation, and oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) as well as oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalysis in carbon-doped hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) materials. The background of this study highlights the growing interest in developing efficient and sustainable electrocatalysts for energy storage and conversion applications, particularly for fuel cells and electrolyzers.  The objective of this research is to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the catalytic activity of carbon-doped h-BN materials for ORR and OER reactions, with a focus on the role of magnetism, chemical activation, and electronic structure. To achieve this, a first-principles computational approach is employed, utilizing density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of carbon-doped h-BN materials.  The key findings of this study reveal that the incorporation of carbon atoms into the h-BN lattice enhances the catalytic activity for ORR and OER reactions, with a synergistic effect arising from the interplay between magnetism, chemical activation, and electronic structure. text: This experimental study aimed to explore the feasibility of applying formal methods using the Automatic Code Synthesis and Linearization (ACSL) and Frama-C tools to derive and verify low-level requirements (LLRs) from an avionics project compliant with the DO-178C standard. LLRs, specified in the Hardware Requirements Document (HRDO), were translated into temporal logic formulae using Frama-C's TLCAPI interface. Afterward, these formulae were verified against the C code implementing the FCS, synthesizing the missing code segments if needed, all while ensuring compliance with DO-178C.  The study revealed several benefits from applying formal methods to LLR derivation and verification. First, it significantly reduced the potential for discrepancies between the requirements and their corresponding code by identifying and eliminating mismatches early in the development process. Second, it increased the confidence in the system's safety and reliability by proving the correctness of the LLR implementation. Additionally, the use of formal methods accelerated the testing and debugging process, as many faults could be identified and corrected through automatic code synthesis and verification, rather than time-consuming manual testing.  However, challenges were encountered during the application of the formal methods. The process required significant time investment, with some manually performed steps in translating the HRDO into temporal logic formulae and validating their correctness. Furthermore, the applicability of formal methods to large and complex projects remained unclear, necessitating further research and possible optimization techniques to address scalability issues.  Overall, the experimental study demonstrated that formal methods, using ACSL and Frama-C, could efficiently formulate and verify LLRs for avionics projects, offering significant benefits in terms of safety, reliability, and development time. Nonetheless, it's crucial to address and overcome challenges to successfully apply this methodology to larger projects, making it an essential contribution to the avionics industry.

We study the general relativistic collapse of neutron star (NS) models in
spherical symmetry. Our initially stable models are driven to collapse by the
addition of one of two things: an initially in-going velocity profile, or a
shell of minimally coupled, massless scalar field that falls onto the star.
Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) solutions with an initially isentropic,
gamma-law equation of state serve as our NS models. The initial values of the
velocity profile's amplitude and the star's central density span a parameter
space which we have surveyed extensively and which we find provides a rich
picture of the possible end states of NS collapse. This parameter space survey
elucidates the boundary between Type I and Type II critical behavior in perfect
fluids which coincides, on the subcritical side, with the boundary between
dispersed and bound end states. For our particular model, initial velocity
amplitudes greater than 0.3c are needed to probe the regime where arbitrarily
small black holes can form. In addition, we investigate Type I behavior in our
system by varying the initial amplitude of the initially imploding scalar
field. In this case we find that the Type I critical solutions resemble TOV
solutions on the 1-mode unstable branch of equilibrium solutions, and that the
critical solutions' frequencies agree well with the fundamental mode
frequencies of the unstable equilibria. Additionally, the critical solution's
scaling exponent is shown to be well approximated by a linear function of the
initial star's central density.

The maximal sum of a sequence "A" of "n" real numbers is the greatest sum of
all elements of any strictly contiguous and possibly empty subsequence of "A",
and it can be computed in "O(n)" time by means of Kadane's algorithm. Letting
"A^(x -> p)" denote the sequence which results from inserting a real number "x"
between elements "A[p-1]" and "A[p]", we show how the maximal sum of "A^(x ->
p)" can be computed in "O(1)" worst-case time for any given "x" and "p",
provided that an "O(n)" time preprocessing step has already been executed on
"A". In particular, this implies that, given "m" pairs "(x_0, p_0), ...,
(x_{m-1}, p_{m-1})", we can compute the maximal sums of sequences "A^(x_0 ->
p_0), ..., A^(x_{m-1} -> p_{m-1})" in "O(n+m)" time, which matches the lower
bound imposed by the problem input size, and also improves on the
straightforward strategy of applying Kadane's algorithm to each sequence
"A^(x_i -> p_i)", which takes a total of "Theta(n.m)" time. Our main
contribution, however, is to obtain the same time bound for the more
complicated problem of computing the greatest sum of all elements of any
strictly or circularly contiguous and possibly empty subsequence of "A^(x ->
p)". Our algorithms are easy to implement in practice, and they were motivated
by and find application in a buffer minimization problem on wireless mesh
networks.
