The wide spread of location-based social networks brings about a huge volume
of user check-in data, which facilitates the recommendation of points of
interest (POIs). Recent advances on distributed representation shed light on
learning low dimensional dense vectors to alleviate the data sparsity problem.
Current studies on representation learning for POI recommendation embed both
users and POIs in a common latent space, and users' preference is inferred
based on the distance/similarity between a user and a POI. Such an approach is
not in accordance with the semantics of users and POIs as they are inherently
different objects. In this paper, we present a novel spatiotemporal aware (STA)
representation, which models the spatial and temporal information as \emph{a
relationship connecting users and POIs}. Our model generalizes the recent
advances in knowledge graph embedding. The basic idea is that the embedding of
a $<$time, location$>$ pair corresponds to a translation from embeddings of
users to POIs. Since the POI embedding should be close to the user embedding
plus the relationship vector, the recommendation can be performed by selecting
the top-\emph{k} POIs similar to the translated POI, which are all of the same
type of objects. We conduct extensive experiments on two real-world datasets.
The results demonstrate that our STA model achieves the state-of-the-art
performance in terms of high recommendation accuracy, robustness to data
sparsity and effectiveness in handling cold start problem.

text: The Gaussian cognitive interference channel (GCIC) represents a practical scenario where a secondary user (SU) aims to communicate with a primary user (PU) while simultaneously mitigating the impact of PU's signal that contains cognitive interference. This study investigates the achievable rate region for the GCIC under various conditions, focusing on the trade-offs between SU's transmission rates and the level of interference mitigation.  Methodologically, this research employs information-theoretic techniques and semi-definite programming (SDP) to derive outer bounds on the capacity region. The analysis considers different levels of knowledge about the PU's signal and varying degrees of interference suppression requirements. Additionally, numerical simulations are conducted to validate the derived theoretical results and provide insights into the performance limits under practical scenarios.  Key findings indicate that the achievable rate region significantly depends on the knowledge of PU's signal and the desired level of interference mitigation. Specifically, when the SU has perfect knowledge of the PU's signal, it can achieve higher rates than when it lacks such knowledge. Furthermore, stricter interference mitigation requirements generally result in lower achievable rates due to increased complexity in signal processing.  In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the capacity limits of the GCIC, offering valuable guidelines for designing effective communication strategies in cognitive radio networks.

The fluorescence of organic fluorophore molecules is enhanced when they are
placed in contact with certain metals (Al, Ag, Cu, Au, etc.) whose surface
plasmon waves couple into the radiative modes of the molecules and increase the
radiative efficiency. Here, we report a hitherto unknown size dependence of
this metal enhanced fluorescence (MEF) effect in the nanoscale. When the
molecules are deposited in nanoporous anodic alumina films with exposed
aluminum at the bottom of the pores, they form organic nanowires standing on
aluminum nanoparticles whose plasmon waves have much larger amplitudes. This
increases the MEF strongly, resulting in several orders of magnitude increase
in the fluorescence intensity of the organic fluorophores. The increase in
intensity shows an inverse super-linear dependence on nanowire diameter because
the nanowires also act as plasmonic 'waveguides' that concentrate the plasmons
and increase the coupling of the plasmons with the radiative modes of the
molecules. Furthermore, if the nanoporous template housing the nanowires has
built-in electric fields due to space charges, a strong molecule-specific red-
or blue-shift is induced in the fluorescence peak owing to a renormalization of
the dipole moment of the molecule. This can be exploited to detect minute
amounts of target molecules in a mixture using their optical signature
(fluorescence) despite the presence of confounding background signals. It can
result in a unique new technology for bio- and chemical-sensing.

text: This study addresses the challenge of geographical power allocation within cellular networks by integrating green technology principles. The primary objective is to enhance network efficiency while significantly reducing energy consumption and carbon footprint. We propose a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts transmitter power based on geographic data and user density, aiming to minimize interference and optimize signal coverage. Our approach leverages machine learning techniques to predict optimal power settings that align with environmental sustainability goals. Results demonstrate a 30% reduction in overall energy consumption compared to conventional methods, alongside a 15% improvement in network performance metrics. Key methodologies include the integration of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for real-time analysis of terrain features and user distribution, along with advanced optimization algorithms to fine-tune power distribution. The findings highlight the feasibility and effectiveness of greening power allocation strategies in cellular networks, paving the way for more sustainable telecommunications infrastructure.

Whilst in galaxy-size simulations, supermassive black holes (SMBH) are
entirely handled by sub-grid algorithms, computational power now allows the
accretion radius of such objects to be resolved in smaller scale simulations.
In this paper, we investigate the impact of resolution on two commonly used
SMBH sub-grid algorithms; the Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton (BHL) formula for accretion
onto a point mass, and the related estimate of the drag force exerted onto a
point mass by a gaseous medium. We find that when the accretion region around
the black hole scales with resolution, and the BHL formula is evaluated using
local mass-averaged quantities, the accretion algorithm smoothly transitions
from the analytic BHL formula (at low resolution) to a supply limited accretion
(SLA) scheme (at high resolution). However, when a similar procedure is
employed to estimate the drag force it can lead to significant errors in its
magnitude, and/or apply this force in the wrong direction in highly resolved
simulations. At high Mach numbers and for small accretors, we also find
evidence of the advective-acoustic instability operating in the adiabatic case,
and of an instability developing around the wake's stagnation point in the
quasi-isothermal case. Moreover, at very high resolution, and Mach numbers
above $\mathcal{M}_\infty \geq 3$, the flow behind the accretion bow shock
becomes entirely dominated by these instabilities. As a result, accretion rates
onto the black hole drop by about an order of magnitude in the adiabatic case,
compared to the analytic BHL formula.

Gaussian Process (GP) regression models typically assume that residuals are
Gaussian and have the same variance for all observations. However, applications
with input-dependent noise (heteroscedastic residuals) frequently arise in
practice, as do applications in which the residuals do not have a Gaussian
distribution. In this paper, we propose a GP Regression model with a latent
variable that serves as an additional unobserved covariate for the regression.
This model (which we call GPLC) allows for heteroscedasticity since it allows
the function to have a changing partial derivative with respect to this
unobserved covariate. With a suitable covariance function, our GPLC model can
handle (a) Gaussian residuals with input-dependent variance, or (b)
non-Gaussian residuals with input-dependent variance, or (c) Gaussian residuals
with constant variance. We compare our model, using synthetic datasets, with a
model proposed by Goldberg, Williams and Bishop (1998), which we refer to as
GPLV, which only deals with case (a), as well as a standard GP model which can
handle only case (c). Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods are developed for both
modelsl. Experiments show that when the data is heteroscedastic, both GPLC and
GPLV give better results (smaller mean squared error and negative
log-probability density) than standard GP regression. In addition, when the
residual are Gaussian, our GPLC model is generally nearly as good as GPLV,
while when the residuals are non-Gaussian, our GPLC model is better than GPLV.

text: We report the discovery of a young asteroid cluster associated with the dynamically new asteroid P/2012 F5 (Gibbs), using a combination of observational data and computational modeling. Our investigation addresses the need to understand the formation and evolution of such asteroid families, which may provide vital insights into the early solar system. We utilized high-resolution imaging from ground-based telescopes and analyzed the photometric data to identify a distinct clustering of objects within a coherent dynamical framework.   We applied clustering algorithms and statistical methods to establish the association of over 30 asteroids with P/2012 F5, revealing a characteristic age of approximately 25,000 years, suggesting a recent collisional origin. Our results highlight the presence of a pronounced dynamical resonance and indicate that the newly identified cluster exhibits unique orbital characteristics distinct from older asteroid families.   Through spectroscopic analysis, we classified the spectral types of the cluster members, further supporting the hypothesis of a shared compositional history derived from the parent body of P/2012 F5. The findings underscore the significance of P/2012 F5 as a source of young asteroids, contributing to our understanding of collisional processes and the evolution of asteroid belts.   This work provides a foundational basis for further exploration of young asteroid clusters, emphasizing their potential role in deciphering the processes that shaped our solar system’s development. Our ongoing research will seek to explore the implications of these findings in the context of planetary formation and the dynamic history of small bodies in the solar system.

text: The search for an ideal, broadly effective viral agent for oncolytic virotherapy is ongoing due to the potential of virotherapy as a promising cancer treatment modality. Various viruses have been studied for their oncolytic capabilities, with the aim of finding a universal agent that can target a wide range of cancer types.   This research aims to identify an optimal viral agent for oncolytic virotherapy that demonstrates potent anti-cancer effects across diverse types of cancer. The objective is to assess the efficacy and safety of different viruses to determine their suitability for oncolytic therapy.   A comprehensive review of literature was conducted to evaluate the oncolytic potential of different viruses currently being studied for cancer treatment. In vitro and in vivo studies on the efficacy, selectivity, and safety profiles of these viral agents were analyzed to determine their potential as a universal oncolytic therapy.   The research highlights key findings from studies investigating the oncolytic properties of various viruses, including their ability to selectively infect and destroy cancer cells while sparing normal cells. Additionally, the study identifies potential challenges and limitations associated with different viral agents for oncolytic virotherapy.   In conclusion, this research underscores the importance of finding an optimal viral agent for oncolytic virotherapy that can effectively target a broad spectrum of cancer types. The findings contribute to the ongoing efforts to develop more efficacious and safe virotherapies for cancer treatment.

Multidimensional coherent optical spectroscopy is one of the most powerful
tools for investigating complex quantum mechanical systems. While it was
conceived decades ago in magnetic resonance spectroscopy using micro- and
radio-waves, it has recently been extended into the visible and UV spectral
range. However, resolving MHz energy splittings with ultrashort laser pulses
has still remained a challenge. Here, we analyze two-dimensional Fourier
spectra for resonant optical excitation of resident electrons to localized
trions or donor-bound excitons in semiconductor nanostructures subject to a
transverse magnetic field. Particular attention is devoted to Raman coherence
spectra which allow one to accurately evaluate tiny splittings of the electron
ground state and to determine the relaxation times in the electron spin
ensemble. A stimulated step-like Raman process induced by a sequence of two
laser pulses creates a coherent superposition of the ground state doublet which
can be retrieved only optically due to selective excitation of the same
sub-ensemble with a third pulse. This provides the unique opportunity to
distinguish between different complexes that are closely spaced in energy in an
ensemble. The related experimental demonstration is based on photon echo
measurements in an n-type CdTe/(Cd,Mg)Te quantum well structure detected by a
heterodyne technique. The difference in the sub-$\mu$eV range between the
Zeeman splittings of donor-bound electrons and electrons localized at potential
fluctuations can be resolved even though the homogeneous linewidth of the
optical transitions is larger by two orders of magnitude.

The third catalog of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) detected by the Fermi-LAT
(3LAC) is presented. It is based on the third Fermi-LAT catalog (3FGL) of
sources detected between 100 MeV and 300 GeV with a Test Statistic (TS) greater
than 25, between 2008 August 4 and 2012 July 31. The 3LAC includes 1591 AGNs
located at high Galactic latitudes (|b|>10{\deg}), a 71% increase over the
second catalog based on 2 years of data. There are 28 duplicate associations,
thus 1563 of the 2192 high-latitude gamma-ray sources of the 3FGL catalog are
AGNs. Most of them (98%) are blazars. About half of the newly detected blazars
are of unknown type, i.e., they lack spectroscopic information of sufficient
quality to determine the strength of their emission lines. Based on their
gamma-ray spectral properties, these sources are evenly split between
flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs) and BL~Lacs. The most abundant detected
BL~Lacs are of the high-synchrotron-peaked (HSP) type. About 50% of the BL~Lacs
have no measured redshifts. A few new rare outliers (HSP-FSRQs and
high-luminosity HSP BL~Lacs) are reported. The general properties of the 3LAC
sample confirm previous findings from earlier catalogs. The fraction of 3LAC
blazars in the total population of blazars listed in BZCAT remains
non-negligible even at the faint ends of the BZCAT-blazar radio, optical and
X-ray flux distributions, which is a clue that even the faintest known blazars
could eventually shine in gamma rays at LAT-detection levels. The energy-flux
distributions of the different blazar populations are in good agreement with
extrapolation from earlier catalogs.

text: We investigate the phenomenon of cutoff latitude variation during solar proton events (SPEs), exploring both its causal mechanisms and its implications for geomagnetic and atmospheric conditions. Our study addresses the significant problem of predicting latitude shifts where charged solar particles are attenuated by Earth's magnetic field. Employing a comprehensive suite of satellite data, ground-based observations, and numerical simulations, we examine the correlation between solar wind parameters, geomagnetic activity, and cutoff latitude dynamics. Key results reveal that increased solar wind velocity and interplanetary magnetic field strength during SPEs correlate with equatorward shifts of the cutoff latitude. We also observe that these shifts are more pronounced in the Northern Hemisphere, attributed to its asymmetric magnetic field configuration.  Methodologically, we apply a combination of magnetohydrodynamic simulations and empirical modeling to deduce the spatial-temporal variations in cutoff latitudes. Our analysis concurrently assesses how changes in cutoff latitudes impact atmospheric ionization rates, which have downstream effects on space weather forecasting models, crucial for satellite operations and communication systems. The predictive model developed demonstrates a marked improvement in cutoff latitude estimation accuracy compared to existing models, reducing uncertainties by approximately 15%.  Our findings elucidate the dynamic interplay between solar-terrestrial interactions and geomagnetic configurations, offering deeper insights into the mitigation of SPE-related risks. This research provides a significant step forward in understanding the broader implications of space weather phenomena, paving the way for enhanced protective measures against geomagnetic perturbations.

In order to study a molecular-cloud-scale chemical composition, we have
conducted a mapping spectral line survey toward the Galactic molecular cloud
W3(OH), which is one of the most active star forming regions in the Perseus
arm, with the NRO 45 m telescope. We have observed the area of 16' $\times$
16', which corresponds to 9.0 pc $\times$ 9.0 pc. The observed frequency ranges
are 87--91, 96--103, and 108--112 GHz. We have prepared the spectrum averaged
over the observed area, in which 8 molecular species CCH, HCN, HCO$^+$, HNC,
CS, SO, C$^{18}$O, and $^{13}$CO are identified. On the other hand, the
spectrum of the W3(OH) hot core observed at a 0.17 pc resolution shows the
lines of various molecules such as OCS, H$_2$CS CH$_3$CCH, and CH$_3$CN, in
addition to the above species. In the spatially averaged spectrum, emission of
the species concentrated just around the star-forming core such as CH$_3$OH and
HC$_3$N is fainter than in the hot core spectrum, whereas emission of the
species widely extended over the cloud such as CCH is relatively brighter. We
have classified the observed area into 5 subregions according to the integrated
intensity of $^{13}$CO, and have evaluated the contribution to the averaged
spectrum from each subregion. The CCH, HCN, HCO$^+$, and CS lines can be seen
even in the spectrum of the subregion with the lowest $^{13}$CO integrated
intensity range ($< 10$ K km s$^{-1}$). Thus, the contributions of the
spatially extended emission is confirmed to be dominant in the spatially
averaged spectrum.

Ellerman bombs (EBs) are a kind of solar activities that is suggested to
occur in the lower atmosphere. Recent observations using the Interface Region
Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) show connections of EBs and IRIS bombs (IBs),
implying that EBs might be heated to a much higher temperature ($8\times10^{4}$
K) than previous results. Here we perform a spectral analysis of the EBs
simultaneously observed by the Fast Imaging Solar Spectrograph (FISS) and IRIS.
The observational results show clear evidence of heating in the lower
atmosphere, indicated by the wing enhancement in H$\alpha$, Ca II 8542 \r{A}
and Mg II triplet lines, and also by brightenings in the images of 1700 \r{A}
and 2832 \r{A} ultraviolet continuum channels. Additionally, the Mg II triplet
line intensity is correlated with that of H$\alpha$ when the EB occurs,
indicating the possibility to use the triplet as an alternative way to identify
EBs. However, we do not find any signal in IRIS hotter lines (C II and Si IV).
For further analysis, we employ a two-cloud model to fit the two chromospheric
lines (H$\alpha$ and Ca II 8542 \r{A}) simultaneously, and obtain a temperature
enhancement of 2300 K for a strong EB. This temperature is among the highest of
previous modeling results while still insufficient to produce IB signatures at
ultraviolet wavelengths.

In this work, the problem of signal parameter estimation from measurements
acquired by a low-complexity analog-to-digital converter (ADC) with $1$-bit
output resolution and an unknown quantization threshold is considered.
Single-comparator ADCs are energy-efficient and can be operated at ultra-high
sampling rates. For analysis of such systems, a fixed and known quantization
threshold is usually assumed. In the symmetric case, i.e., zero hard-limiting
offset, it is known that in the low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regime the
signal processing performance degrades moderately by ${2}/{\pi}$ ($-1.96$ dB)
when comparing to an ideal $\infty$-bit converter. Due to hardware
imperfections, low-complexity $1$-bit ADCs will in practice exhibit an unknown
threshold different from zero. Therefore, we study the accuracy which can be
obtained with receive data processed by a hard-limiter with unknown
quantization level by using asymptotically optimal channel estimation
algorithms. To characterize the estimation performance of these nonlinear
algorithms, we employ analytic error expressions for different setups while
modeling the offset as a nuisance parameter. In the low SNR regime, we
establish the necessary condition for a vanishing loss due to missing offset
knowledge at the receiver. As an application, we consider the estimation of
single-input single-output wireless channels with inter-symbol interference and
validate our analysis by comparing the analytic and experimental performance of
the studied estimation algorithms. Finally, we comment on the extension to
multiple-input multiple-output channel models.

text: In addressing the complexities of reverse supply chain networks operating under asymmetric information and carbon emission constraints, we propose a novel reward-penalty mechanism. This work investigates the dual challenges of limited visibility across supply chain nodes and the imperative to minimize carbon footprints in accordance with environmental regulations. We employ a theoretical framework built upon principal-agent theory to model the interactions between various stakeholders, such as manufacturers, collectors, and recyclers, characterized by disparate information and objectives. Our methodology integrates game-theoretic approaches to develop incentive schemes that bridge informational asymmetries, encouraging stakeholders to adhere to sustainable practices.  The proposed mechanism introduces targeted incentives for participants that enhance cooperation and operational efficiency while penalizing non-compliance and suboptimal behaviors. We conduct simulations to evaluate the mechanism's effectiveness in reducing carbon emissions and improving information transparency across the reverse logistics network. Results indicate a significant reduction in carbon emissions and improved information sharing, leading to enhanced decision-making and cost efficiencies. The reward-penalty mechanism also fosters greater alignment of individual objectives with collective sustainability goals, thereby promoting a more responsible and responsive reverse supply chain.  Our study contributes to the growing body of literature on sustainable supply chain management by providing actionable insights and a robust mechanism to manage environmental compliance and information asymmetry. Future research could extend our model to dynamic, large-scale networks and examine the long-term impact of such mechanisms on supply chain resilience and sustainability outcomes. This work presents a viable pathway toward harmonized supply chain practices that prioritize both environmental and operational objectives.

We study the vacuum stability and unitarity conditions for a 125 GeV Standard
Model (SM)-like Higgs boson mass in the type-II seesaw model. We find that, as
long as the seesaw scale is introduced below the SM vacuum instability bound,
there exists a large parameter space predicting a 125 GeV Higgs mass,
irrespective of the exact value of the seesaw scale, satisfying both stability
and unitarity conditions up to the Planck scale. We also study the model
predictions for the Higgs partial decay widths in the diphoton and Z+photon
channels with respect to their SM expectations and find that the decay rates
for these two processes are correlated. We further show that for any given
enhancement in the Higgs-to-diphoton rate over its SM expectation, there exists
an upper bound on the type-II seesaw scale, and hence, on the masses of the
associated doubly- and singly-charged Higgs bosons in the allowed parameter
space. For instance, if more than 10% enhancement persists in the
Higgs-to-diphoton channel, the upper limit on the type-II seesaw scale is about
450 GeV which is completely within the reach of the 14 TeV LHC. We believe this
to be an encouraging result for the experimental searches of the singly- and
doubly-charged Higgs bosons which, in combination with improved sensitivity in
the Higgs-to-diphoton and Higgs-to-Z+photon signal strengths, could probe the
entire allowed parameter space of the minimal type-II seesaw model, and
establish/eliminate it as a single viable extension of the SM.

We present the results of our search for a dynamical family around the active
asteroid P/2012F5 (Gibbs). By applying the hierarchical clustering method, we
discover an extremely compact 9-body cluster associated with P/2012F5. The
statistical significance of this newly discovered Gibbs cluster is estimated to
be >99.9%, strongly suggesting that its members share a common origin. The
cluster is located in a dynamically cold region of the outer main-belt at a
proper semi-major axis of about 3.005 AU, and all members are found to be
dynamically stable over very long time-scales. Backward numerical orbital
integrations show that the age of the cluster is only 1.5 $\pm$ 0.1 Myr.
Taxonomic classifications are unavailable for most of the cluster members, but
SDSS spectrophotometry available for two cluster members indicate that both
appear to be $Q$-type objects. We also estimate a lower limit of the size of
the parent body to be about 10 km, and find that the impact event which
produced the Gibbs cluster is intermediate between a cratering and a
catastrophic collision. In addition, we search for new main-belt comets in the
region of the Gibbs cluster by observing seven asteroids either belonging to
the cluster, or being very close in the space of orbital proper elements.
However, we do not detect any convincing evidence of the presence of a tail or
coma in any our targets. Finally, we obtain optical images of P/2012F5, and
find absolute R-band and V-band magnitudes of $H_R$ = 17.0 $\pm$ 0.1 mag and
$H_V$ = 17.4 $\pm$ 0.1 mag, respectively, corresponding to an upper limit on
the diameter of the P/2012F5 nucleus of about 2 km.

text: Understanding the oscillation frequencies of solar-type dwarfs is crucial for interpreting stellar evolution and improving asteroseismic techniques. This study aims to derive theoretical oscillation frequencies for solar-type dwarf stars using advanced stellar models that incorporate three-dimensional averaged atmospheres (⟨3D⟩-atmospheres). We employed a comprehensive approach by integrating a grid of stellar evolution models with detailed pulsation calculations. The models were constructed using current opacities and nuclear reaction rates, and the atmosphere's treatment was based on 3D hydrodynamical simulations that account for convective motions and their effect on pulsation modes.  Key findings reveal that the inclusion of ⟨3D⟩ atmospheric models significantly impacts the computed oscillation frequencies. Specifically, the frequencies of the lowest-order pressure modes exhibit systematic shifts compared to models using traditional one-dimensional (1D) atmospheres. Additionally, we find that the effects on the frequencies are more pronounced for stars at the hotter end of the solar-type spectrum, which suggests that the interplay between convection and oscillation is a vital process affecting pulsation characteristics.   In conclusion, this research enhances the precision of theoretical oscillation frequencies for solar-type dwarfs by incorporating realistic atmospheric conditions, paving the way for more accurate interpretations of asteroseismic data and improving our understanding of stellar structure and evolution. Future work will involve validating these models against observational data to refine our predictions further and improve stellar parameter estimations.

text: In this study, we investigate the linear rate convergence properties of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) when applied to convex composite quadratic and semi-definite programming problems. ADMM is widely used for solving large-scale optimization problems due to its decomposability and efficiency. However, theoretical guarantees on its convergence rate, particularly for non-ideal conditions, remain a significant research gap. We address this gap by proposing a novel analytical framework that extends existing convergence theories to encompass composite quadratic and semi-definite cases. Our approach leverages properties of convexity and Lipschitz continuity to establish explicit bounds on the convergence rate. Through rigorous mathematical derivation, we demonstrate that ADMM achieves a linear rate of convergence under mild assumptions on primal and dual regularities. The methodology involves the construction of error decay inequalities that are rooted in operator theory and spectral analysis. Experimental validations reveal that the derived theoretical rate bounds are not only achievable but also indicative of the practical performance of ADMM in computational scenarios. Moreover, comparative analyses with alternative optimization algorithms show that our enhanced ADMM formulation consistently outperforms in terms of convergence speed and solution accuracy for both synthetic and real-world problem instances. Our findings significantly contribute to the optimization literature, providing a robust theoretical underpinning for ADMM's applicability to complex convex problems. This work underscores the potential for applying similar analytical techniques to further explore ADMM's capabilities across diverse optimization scenarios.

Context: Methanol is thought to be mainly formed during the prestellar phase
and its deuterated form keeps memory of the conditions at that epoch. Thanks to
the unique combination of high angular resolution and sensitivity provided by
ALMA, we wish to measure methanol deuteration in the planet formation region
around a Class 0 protostar and to understand its origin. Aims: We mapped both
the $^{13}$CH$_3$OH and CH$_2$DOH distribution in the inner regions ($\sim$100
au) of the HH212 system in Orion B. To this end, we used ALMA Cycle 1 and Cycle
4 observations in Band 7 with angular resolution down to $\sim$0.15$"$.
Results: We detected 6 lines of $^{13}$CH$_3$OH and 13 lines of CH$_2$DOH with
upper level energies up to 438 K in temperature units. We derived a rotational
temperature of (171 $\pm$ 52) K and column densities of 7$\times$10$^{16}$
cm$^{-2}$ ($^{13}$CH$_3$OH) and 1$\times$10$^{17}$ cm$^{-2}$ (CH$_2$DOH),
respectively. Consequently, the D/H ratio is (2.4 $\pm$ 0.4)$\times$10$^{-2}$,
a value lower by an order of magnitude with respect to what was previously
measured using single dish telescopes toward protostars located in Perseus. Our
findings are consistent with the higher dust temperatures in Orion B with
respect to that derived for the Perseus cloud. The emission is tracing a
rotating structure extending up to 45 au from the jet axis and elongated by 90
au along the jet axis. So far, the origin of the observed emission appears to
be related with the accretion disk. Only higher spatial resolution measurements
however, will be able to disentangle between different possible scenarios: disk
wind, disk atmosphere, or accretion shocks.

It has been shown that geometrical, structural properties vary along the
length of the aortic arch. There is a scarcity of studies focus on the
variation in the vessel wall thickness of aortic arch. The central premise of
this study is that considering the variation in the vessel wall thickness along
the circumference of the aortic arch to be governed by the uniform stress
distribution across the vessel wall, meeting the principle of optimal
mechanical operation of which the distribution of stress across the vessel wall
is assumed to be uniform so as to create a favorable mechanical environment for
the mechanosensitive resident vascular cells. Aortic arch was created with
image-derived three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction technique. A
structure-motivated constitutive model was utilized in the numerical modeling
and direct boundary value problem was solved. Stress distribution across the
vessel wall under physiological loading condition was predicted in
circumferential direction to test the role of the wall thickness. The results
showed the variation of the vessel wall thickness in the circumferential
direction and uniform distribution of the circumferential stress in the aortic
wall which implies a favorable mechanical environment for the resident
mechano-sensitive vascular smooth muscle cells. Correlation of geometrical and
simulation data support the proposed principle of optimal mechanical operation
for the aortic arch.

We analyze the well observed flare-CME event from October 1, 2011
(SOL2011-10-01T09:18) covering the complete chain of action - from Sun to Earth
- for a better understanding of the dynamic evolution of the CME and its
embedded magnetic field. We study the solar surface and atmosphere associated
with the flare-CME from SDO and ground-based instruments, and also track the
CME signature off-limb from combined EUV and white-light data with STEREO. By
applying 3D reconstruction techniques (GCS, total mass) to stereoscopic
STEREO-SoHO coronagraph data, we track the temporal and spatial evolution of
the CME in interplanetary space and derive its geometry and 3D-mass. We combine
the GCS and Lundquist model results to derive the axial flux and helicity of
the MC from in-situ measurements (Wind). This is compared to nonlinear
force-free (NLFF) model results as well as to the reconnected magnetic flux
derived from the flare ribbons (flare reconnection flux) and the magnetic flux
encompassed by the associated dimming (dimming flux). We find that magnetic
reconnection processes were already ongoing before the start of the impulsive
flare phase, adding magnetic flux to the flux rope before its final eruption.
The dimming flux increases by more than 25% after the end of the flare,
indicating that magnetic flux is still added to the flux rope after eruption.
Hence, the derived flare reconnection flux is most probably a lower limit for
estimating the magnetic flux within the flux rope. We find that the magnetic
helicity and axial magnetic flux are reduced in interplanetary space by ~50%
and 75%, respectively, possibly indicating to an erosion process. A mass
increase of 10% for the CME is observed over the distance range from ~4-20 Rs.
The temporal evolution of the CME associated core dimming regions supports the
scenario that fast outflows might supply additional mass to the rear part of
the CME.

The launch of Google Scholar (GS) marked the beginning of a revolution in the
scientific information market. This search engine, unlike traditional
databases, automatically indexes information from the academic web. Its ease of
use, together with its wide coverage and fast indexing speed, have made it the
first tool most scientists currently turn to when they need to carry out a
literature search. Additionally, the fact that its search results were
accompanied from the beginning by citation counts, as well as the later
development of secondary products which leverage this citation data (such as
Google Scholar Metrics and Google Scholar Citations), made many scientists
wonder about its potential as a source of data for bibliometric analyses. The
goal of this chapter is to lay the foundations for the use of GS as a
supplementary source (and in some disciplines, arguably the best alternative)
for scientific evaluation. First, we present a general overview of how GS
works. Second, we present empirical evidences about its main characteristics
(size, coverage, and growth rate). Third, we carry out a systematic analysis of
the main limitations this search engine presents as a tool for the evaluation
of scientific performance. Lastly, we discuss the main differences between GS
and other more traditional bibliographic databases in light of the correlations
found between their citation data. We conclude that Google Scholar presents a
broader view of the academic world because it has brought to light a great
amount of sources that were not previously visible.

text: Output range analysis is a critical aspect of deep neural network (DNN) modeling and training. Understanding the output range of a DNN model is essential for various applications such as image recognition, speech recognition, and natural language processing. This analysis provides insights into the network's behavior and helps ensure model accuracy and reliability.  In this study, we propose an output range analysis methodology for deep neural networks based on quantile regression. We first review the related work on output range analysis in the context of DNNs. We then introduce quantile regression as a robust and flexible statistical technique for analyzing output ranges. Our methodology involves calculating output quantiles for individual neurons and layers, providing a more nuanced understanding of the network's output distribution.  Our experimental results demonstrate that our proposed methodology outperforms existing methods in terms of both computational efficiency and accuracy. We apply our methodology to several benchmark datasets and show that it effectively identifies neurons and layers with extreme output ranges, providing valuable insights into model behavior. Furthermore, we explore the implications of output range analysis for model optimization and propose potential directions for future research.  In conclusion, output range analysis is a vital component of deep neural network modeling and training. Our proposed methodology based on quantile regression offers a more accurate and efficient approach to output range analysis, providing valuable insights into model behavior and helping ensure model accuracy and reliability.

text: The quest for efficient quantum simulators has intensified interest in leveraging semiconductor quantum dot arrays to model complex quantum systems. The Fermi-Hubbard model, a fundamental paradigm for understanding strongly correlated electron systems, offers insights into high-temperature superconductivity and magnetic phenomena. This research focuses on utilizing a semiconductor quantum dot array to simulate the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model. Our objective is to explore the potential of quantum dots in accurately representing the model's intricate physics, thereby contributing to the broader field of quantum simulation.  We employed a layered approach to build an array of quantum dots, each closely mimicking the behavior of atoms on a lattice. Through fine-tuned electrostatic gates and precise control over tunneling rates, our system allows for adjustable on-site interactions and hopping parameters, emulating various electron-electron interactions within the Fermi-Hubbard framework. Quantum state preparation and manipulation were accomplished using state-of-the-art techniques, including spin-resolved imaging and charge sensing.  The key findings reveal that semiconductor quantum dots offer a high degree of tunability and coherence, crucial for accurately modeling the Fermi-Hubbard scenario. Our results demonstrate effective reproduction of expected quantum phases, including Mott insulating and antiferromagnetic states, corroborated through experimental measurements of spin correlations and electronic excitations.  In conclusion, our study confirms the feasibility of semiconductor quantum dot arrays as powerful simulators for the Fermi-Hubbard model, paving the way for advanced explorations into quantum materials and offering a scalable platform for future quantum computational endeavors.

The asymptotic giant branch (AGB) of the globular cluster NGC 4372 appears to
extend to unexpectedly high luminosities. We show, on the basis of proper
motions and spatial distribution, that the extended AGB is indeed a likely part
of the cluster. We also present the first spectra of the very cool (2600 K),
very luminous (8000 Lsun), very dusty, oxygen-rich, purported long-period
variable stars V1 and V2 that define the AGB tip. In particular, on the basis
of their radial velocities, we conclude that V1 and V2 are probably members. We
find that V1 and V2 are likely undergoing the superwind phase that terminates
their nuclear-burning evolution. We hypothesise that the mass-loss processes
that terminate the AGB are inhibited in NGC 4372 due to a lack of atmospheric
pulsation and the high gas-to-dust ratio in the ejecta, leading to a delay in
the associated enhanced mass loss and dust production. Previously predicted,
but never observed, this explains the high mass of the white dwarf in Pease 1
in M15 without the need to invoke a stellar merger. If commonplace, this
phenomenon has implications for the mass return from stars, the production of
carbon stars and supernovae through the Universe's history, and the AGB
contribution to light from unresolved metal-poor populations.

We investigate entanglement transmission over an unknown channel in the
presence of a third party (called the adversary), which is enabled to choose
the channel from a given set of memoryless but non-stationary channels without
informing the legitimate sender and receiver about the particular choice that
he made. This channel model is called arbitrarily varying quantum channel
(AVQC). We derive a quantum version of Ahlswede's dichotomy for classical
arbitrarily varying channels. This includes a regularized formula for the
common randomness-assisted capacity for entanglement transmission of an AVQC.
Quite surprisingly and in contrast to the classical analog of the problem
involving the maximal and average error probability, we find that the capacity
for entanglement transmission of an AVQC always equals its strong subspace
transmission capacity. These results are accompanied by different notions of
symmetrizability (zero-capacity conditions) as well as by conditions for an
AVQC to have a capacity described by a single-letter formula. In he final part
of the paper the capacity of the erasure-AVQC is computed and some light shed
on the connection between AVQCs and zero-error capacities. Additionally, we
show by entirely elementary and operational arguments motivated by the theory
of AVQCs that the quantum, classical, and entanglement-assisted zero-error
capacities of quantum channels are generically zero and are discontinuous at
every positivity point.

Thanks to the outstanding capabilites of the HST, our current knowledge about
the M31 globular clusters (GCs) is similar to our knowledge of the Milky Way
GCs in the 1960s-1970s, which set the basis for studying the halo and galaxy
formation using these objects as tracers, and established their importance in
defining the cosmic distance scale. We intend to derive a new calibration of
the M_V(HB)-[Fe/H] relation by exploiting the large photometric database of old
GCs in M31 in the HST archive. We collected the BVI data for 48 old GCs in M31
and analysed them by applying the same methods and procedures to all objects.
We obtained a set of homogeneous colour-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) that were
best-fitted with the fiducial CMD ridge lines of selected Milky Way template
GCs. Reddening, metallicity, Horizontal Branch (HB) luminosity and distance
were determined self-consistently for each cluster. There are three main
results of this study: i) the relation
M_V(HB)=(0.25+/-0.02)[Fe/H]+(0.89+/-0.03), which is obtained from the above
parameters and is calibrated on the distances of the template Galactic GCs; ii)
the distance modulus to M31 of (m-M)_0=24.42+/-0.06 mag, obtained by
normalising this relation at the reference value of [Fe/H]=-1.5 to a similar
relation using V_0(HB). This is the first determination of the distance to M31
based on the characteristics of its GC system which is calibrated on Galactic
GCs; iii) the distance to the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), which is estimated
to be 18.54+/-0.07 mag as a consequence of the previous results. These values
agree excellently with the most recent estimate based on HST parallaxes of
Galactic Cepheid and RR Lyrae stars, as well as with recent methods.

We aim at characterizing the accretion properties of several hundred members
of the star-forming cluster NGC 2264 (3 Myr). We performed a deep u,g,r,i
mapping and a simultaneous u+r monitoring of the region with CFHT/MegaCam in
order to directly probe the accretion process from UV excess measurements.
Photometric properties and stellar parameters are determined homogeneously for
about 750 monitored young objects, spanning the mass range 0.1-2 Mo. About 40%
are classical (accreting) T Tauri stars, based on various diagnostics (H_alpha,
UV and IR excesses). The remaining non-accreting members define the
(photospheric+chromospheric) reference UV emission level over which flux excess
is detected and measured. We revise the membership status of cluster members
based on UV accretion signatures and report a new population of 50 CTTS
candidates. A large range of UV excess is measured for the CTTS population,
varying from a few 0.1 to 3 mag. We convert these values to accretion
luminosities and obtain mass accretion rates ranging from 1e-10 to 1e-7 Mo/yr.
Taking into account a mass-dependent detection threshold for weakly accreting
objects, we find a >6sigma correlation between mass accretion rate and stellar
mass. A power-law fit, properly accounting for upper limits, yields M_acc
$\propto$ M^{1.4+/-0.3}. At any given stellar mass, we find a large spread of
accretion rates, extending over about 2 orders of magnitude. The monitoring of
the UV excess on a timescale of a couple of weeks indicates that its
variability typically amounts to 0.5 dex, much smaller than the observed
spread. We suggest that a non-negligible age spread across the cluster may
effectively contribute to the observed spread in accretion rates at a given
mass. In addition, different accretion mechanisms (like, e.g., short-lived
accretion bursts vs. more stable funnel-flow accretion) may be associated to
different M_acc regimes.

text: AirScript, an open-source JavaScript library, enables the creation and manipulation of Adobe Air applications, allowing for the generation of various document types. This paper explores the implementation of AirScript for document generation within Adobe Air applications.  The background section discusses Adobe Air's potential for creating dynamic and interactive applications, but its limitations in document creation. To address this gap, the emergence of AirScript as an effective solution is introduced.  The objective of this study is to explore the functionality and benefits of AirScript for document generation in Adobe Air applications. Through a case study, we demonstrate the capabilities of AirScript in creating Microsoft Word, Excel, and PDF documents directly within Air applications.  To accomplish the aforementioned objective, the methodology section outlines the installation of AirScript and the creation of a sample Air application that generates Word, Excel, and PDF documents using the library. The results are presented as key findings and discussed in the context of potential applications and their benefits.  Key findings reveal that AirScript offers a streamlined solution for document generation within Adobe Air applications, saving time and resources. It also provides advanced formatting capabilities, making it suitable for creating professional-looking documents. Furthermore, it is highly customizable, allowing for the development of documents tailored to specific user needs.  In conclusion, this study highlights AirScript as a powerful tool for document generation within Adobe Air applications. By eliminating the need for external document editors and integrating the document creation process, developers can create more efficient and user-friendly applications. Future work includes investigating the integration of other document types, such as PowerPoint, as well as exploring the possibilities of collaborative document creation.

text: This study investigates the concept of "thin" bridges within the context of Autonomous System (AS) connectivity, focusing on measuring dependency through AS hegemony. Building upon existing literature that highlights the role of ASes in network architecture and their interdependencies, this research aims to explore how the dominance and influence of certain ASes (hegemonic ASes) affect the stability and efficiency of global internet infrastructure. Through a combination of statistical analysis and case studies, the study identifies key hegemonic ASes and quantifies their impact on the connectivity patterns among ASes. The methodology involves analyzing historical AS routing data to determine the extent to which these hegemonic ASes mediate traffic flows between non-hegemonic ASes. Key findings reveal that hegemonic ASes significantly influence the dependency relationships within the AS-level internet topology, often acting as critical nodes that either facilitate or impede efficient data transmission. The research concludes by proposing strategies for mitigating potential negative impacts arising from such dependency structures, emphasizing the importance of fostering a more balanced AS ecosystem to enhance overall network resilience and performance.

The low energy neutrino factory has been proposed as a very sensitive setup
for future searches for CP violation and matter effects. Here we study how its
performance is affected when the experimental specifications of the setup are
varied. Most notably, we have considered the addition of the 'platinum' nu_{mu}
-> nu_{e} channel. We find that, whilst theoretically the extra channel
provides very useful complementary information and helps to lift degeneracies,
its practical usefulness is lost when considering realistic background levels.
Conversely, an increase in statistics in the 'golden' nu_{e} -> nu_{mu} channel
and, to some extent, an improvement in the energy resolution, lead to an
important increase in the performance of the facility, given the rich energy
dependence of the 'golden' channel at these energies. We show that a low energy
neutrino factory with a baseline of 1300 km, muon energy of 4.5 GeV, and either
a 20 kton totally active scintillating detector or 100 kton liquid argon
detector, can have outstanding sensitivity to the neutrino oscillation
parameters theta13, delta and the mass hierarchy. For our estimated exposure of
2.8 x 10^{23} kton x decays per muon polarity, the low energy neutrino factory
has sensitivity to theta13 and delta for sin^{2}(2theta13) > 10^{-4} and to the
mass hierarchy for sin^{2}(2theta13) > 10^{-3}.

text: This study presents the development and application of idealized synthetic signatures of dust polarization and Zeeman splitting in filamentary structures within star-forming regions. Building on existing knowledge about magnetic fields' influence on star formation, the objective was to create a comprehensive model that could simulate these phenomena under controlled conditions. Utilizing numerical simulations and theoretical frameworks, we aimed to elucidate the potential observational signatures of magnetic fields in interstellar dust grains within filamentary structures.  The methodology involved creating synthetic datasets representing various orientations and strengths of magnetic fields within simulated filaments. These datasets were designed to mimic real-world conditions found in star-forming environments, allowing us to explore how dust polarization and Zeeman splitting patterns might vary with different magnetic field configurations.  Key findings indicate that the synthetic datasets exhibit distinct polarization and Zeeman splitting patterns depending on the orientation and strength of the magnetic field. These patterns provide valuable insights into the detection of magnetic fields in star-forming regions through polarimetry and Zeeman spectroscopy techniques. The results highlight the importance of considering magnetic fields in the context of star formation, as they can significantly affect the alignment and dynamics of molecular clouds and protostellar disks.  In conclusion, this study offers a robust framework for understanding and predicting the observable signatures of magnetic fields in star-forming systems. By providing a detailed analysis of synthetic data, our work contributes to the broader goal of mapping out magnetic field structures in these critical regions of cosmic evolution. Future research should focus on validating these synthetic models using real astronomical data to further refine our comprehension of magnetic fields in star-forming environments.

text: This study investigates thermodynamic and transport anomalies occurring near the isotropic-nematic phase transition in liquid crystals. Through extensive Monte Carlo simulations, we observe significant deviations from the expected behavior of the order parameter and thermal conductivity as temperature approaches the critical point. We identify a distinct region where the specific heat exhibits a divergent behavior, indicative of the onset of long-range orientational correlations. Our analysis reveals that these anomalies are closely linked to the fluctuation-dissipation theorem violations at the critical point. The methodology involves detailed simulations at various temperatures and pressures, complemented by theoretical calculations based on the Landau theory of phase transitions. Key insights include the identification of a critical exponent for the order parameter fluctuations and the correlation length divergence near the transition, which aligns with theoretical predictions. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between thermodynamics and nematic order in liquid crystals.
label: machine

text: We investigated the anomalous increase in the correlation length of structural relaxation in amorphous glasses, a phenomenon that has garnered significant attention in the field of glass physics. Our experiments employed a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and experimental measurements of the glass transition temperature, allowing us to probe the behavior of glasses over a wide range of temperatures and densities.  Our results indicate a pronounced increase in the correlation length of structural relaxation with decreasing temperature, in stark contrast to the predictions of the conventional dynamic-structure-factor formalism. This finding suggests that the traditional understanding of glassy dynamics is inadequate, and that alternative mechanisms, such as topological frustration and disorder-induced entanglement, may be responsible for the observed behavior.  We found that the correlation length grows exponentially with temperature, with a characteristic length scale that is inversely proportional to the temperature. This scaling behavior is consistent with the idea that the glassy system is undergoing a transition from a disordered to a more ordered state, with the correlation length serving as a measure of the system's degree of order.  Our work highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of glassy dynamics, one that takes into account the complex interplay between topological order and disorder. We propose that the observed correlation length growth can be explained by the formation of a topological network, in which the glassy system is characterized by a non-trivial topological structure that is stabilized by the interplay between disorder and order.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the role of topological indexes in the context of symmetry-preserving dynamics, aiming to bridge the gap between topological considerations and dynamic system behavior. Our work focuses on characterizing how topological invariants can serve as essential indicators in systems where symmetry constraints play a critical role. We employ an analytical approach supplemented by computational simulations to examine systems with various symmetry groups, exploring the persistence of topological indexes under dynamic evolutions that respect these symmetries. Our results demonstrate that topological indexes, such as the Chern number and topological entropy, remain invariant in many scenarios, thereby offering a robust framework for predicting system behavior under symmetry adherence. Furthermore, we discover novel conditions under which these indexes can change, providing insights into symmetry breaking dynamics. By leveraging homotopy theory and group representation techniques, we provide a comprehensive methodology to analyze and classify topological phases within our studied systems. This research offers significant advancements in the understanding of the interplay between topological properties and symmetry in dynamic systems. Our findings lay the groundwork for future explorations into the application of topological indexes in broader physical systems, potentially influencing areas such as quantum computing and condensed matter physics. This work not only deepens theoretical understanding but also suggests practical implementations where symmetry-preserving dynamics can be harnessed for technological innovation.
label: machine

text:
Bidirectional typechecking, in which terms either synthesize a type or are
checked against a known type, has become popular for its applicability to a
variety of type systems, its error reporting, and its ease of implementation.
Following principles from proof theory, bidirectional typing can be applied to
many type constructs. The principles underlying a bidirectional approach to
indexed types (generalized algebraic datatypes) are less clear. Building on
proof-theoretic treatments of equality, we give a declarative specification of
typing based on focalization. This approach permits declarative rules for
coverage of pattern matching, as well as support for first-class existential
types using a focalized subtyping judgment. We use refinement types to avoid
explicitly passing equality proofs in our term syntax, making our calculus
similar to languages such as Haskell and OCaml. We also extend the declarative
specification with an explicit rules for deducing when a type is principal,
permitting us to give a complete declarative specification for a rich type
system with significant type inference. We also give a set of algorithmic
typing rules, and prove that it is sound and complete with respect to the
declarative system. The proof requires a number of technical innovations,
including proving soundness and completeness in a mutually recursive fashion.

In this second of a series of papers on spatially resolved star formation, we
investigate the impact of the density-morphology relation of galaxies on the
spatial variation of star formation (SF) and its dependence on environment. We
find that while a density-morphology relation is present for the sample, it
cannot solely explain the observed suppression of SF in galaxies in
high-density environments. We also find that early-type and late-type galaxies
exhibit distinct radial star formation rate (SFR) distributions, with
early-types having a SFR distribution that extends further relative to the
galaxy scale length, compared to late-types at all densities. We find that a
suppression of SF in the highest density environments is found in the highest
star forming galaxies for both galaxy types. This suppression occurs in the
innermost regions in late-types (r <= 0.125 Petrosian radii), and further out
in radius in early-types (0.125< r <= 0.25 Petrosian radii). When the full
sample is considered no clear suppression of SF is detected, indicating that
the environmental trends are driven only by the highest SF galaxies. We
demonstrate that the density-morphology relation alone cannot account for the
suppression of SF in the highest density environments. This points to an
environmentally-governed evolutionary mechanism that affects the SF in the
innermost regions in both early and late-type galaxies. We suggest that this is
a natural consequence of the "downsizing" of SF in galaxies.

text: Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) is the fundamental theory describing the strong interaction between quarks and gluons, the constituents of protons and neutrons. Recent developments in theoretical physics have led to the exploration of alternative quark models, including the sextet quark model, which proposes that the six known quarks are not the fundamental building blocks of matter, but rather a subset of a larger set of quarks. This study aims to investigate the implications of the sextet quark model on our understanding of QCD.  The objective of this research is to examine the effects of incorporating sextet quarks into QCD, with a focus on the impact on quark masses, coupling constants, and the strong nuclear force. A combination of analytical and numerical methods were employed to simulate the behavior of sextet quarks in QCD, using a modified version of the lattice gauge theory (LGT) framework. The results of this study indicate significant deviations from the conventional quark model, particularly in the prediction of quark masses and the strong coupling constant.  The key findings of this research reveal that the incorporation of sextet quarks into QCD leads to a more unified and consistent description of the strong interaction, with potential implications for our understanding of the fundamental forces of nature. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the potential of the sextet quark model to resolve long-standing issues in QCD, such as the hierarchy problem and the discrepancy between theoretical and experimental values of the strong coupling constant. The results of this research provide a new perspective on the nature of quarks and the strong interaction, and highlight the need for further investigation into the properties and behavior of sextet quarks in QCD.

text: The rise of Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4) laboratories in urban environments has significant implications for public health and urban planning. This paper examines the spatial dynamics behind the proliferation of BSL-4 facilities within cities, aiming to understand the factors driving their location choices and the potential consequences for urban communities. The research employs a mixed-methods approach that combines spatial data analysis with qualitative interviews of laboratory operators, city planners, and health officials in key metropolitan areas. The findings reveal that the increasing threat of infectious diseases, alongside enhanced funding for biotechnological research, has prompted cities to become hubs for advanced biosafety research. However, the study also highlights tensions regarding community acceptance, infrastructural demands, and regulatory challenges associated with these installations. Crucially, the analysis identifies that while BSL-4 laboratories contribute to global health security, their placement often raises concerns related to biosecurity and proper emergency preparedness measures. This research underscores the need for transparent communication and collaborative planning between laboratory operators and urban stakeholders to mitigate risks and foster communal trust. Ultimately, this paper contributes to the discourse on urban biosafety by providing insights into the intersection of public health infrastructure and urban development, advocating for policies that balance innovation with community welfare and safety.

We simulate the multi-phase interstellar medium randomly heated and stirred
by supernovae, with gravity, differential rotation and other parameters of the
solar neighbourhood. Here we describe in detail both numerical and physical
aspects of the model, including injection of thermal and kinetic energy by SN
explosions, radiative cooling, photoelectric heating and various transport
processes. With 3D domain extending 1 kpc^2 horizontally and 2 kpc vertically,
the model routinely spans gas number densities 10^-5 - 10^2 cm^-3, temperatures
10-10^8 K, local velocities up to 10^3 km s^-1 (with Mach number up to 25).
  The thermal structure of the modelled ISM is classified by inspection of the
joint probability density of the gas number density and temperature. We confirm
that most of the complexity can be captured in terms of just three phases,
separated by temperature borderlines at about 10^3 K and 5x10^5 K. The
probability distribution of gas density within each phase is approximately
lognormal. We clarify the connection between the fractional volume of a phase
and its various proxies, and derive an exact relation between the fractional
volume and the filling factors defined in terms of the volume and probabilistic
averages. These results are discussed in both observational and computational
contexts. The correlation scale of the random flows is calculated from the
velocity autocorrelation function; it is of order 100 pc and tends to grow with
distance from the mid-plane. We use two distinct parameterizations of radiative
cooling to show that the multi-phase structure of the gas is robust, as it does
not depend significantly on this choice.

We investigate the unicast problem for ad-hoc networks in the plane using
MIMO techniques. In particular, we use the multi-node beamforming gain and
present a self-synchronizing algorithm for the necessary carrier phase
synchronization. First, we consider $n$ nodes in a grid where the transmission
power per node is restricted to reach the neighboring node. We extend the idea
of multi-hop routing and relay the message by multiple nodes attaining joint
beamforming gain with higher reception range. In each round, the message is
repeated by relay nodes at dedicated positions after a fixed waiting period.
Such simple algorithms can send a message from any node to any other node in
time $\mathcal{O}(\log \log n - \log \lambda)$ and with asymptotical energy
$\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})$, the same energy an optimal multi-hop routing strategy
needs using short hops between source and target. Here, $\lambda$ denotes the
wavelength of the carrier. For $\lambda \in \Theta(1)$ we prove a tight lower
time bound of $\Omega(\log \log n)$. Then, we consider $n$ randomly distributed
nodes in a square of area $n$ and we show for a transmission range of
$\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$ and for a wavelength of $\lambda =
\Omega(\log^{-1/2}n)$ that the unicast problem can be solved in
$\mathcal{O}(\log \log n)$ rounds as well. The corresponding transmission
energy increases to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n} \log n)$. Finally, we present
simulation results visualizing the nature of our algorithms.

text: This study explores the application of nonnegative concolutive transfer function (NCTF) and spectro-temporal modeling for speech dereverberation. The primary objective is to enhance speech intelligibility in reverberant environments by effectively removing the reverberant effects that distort speech signals. To achieve this, we employ NCTF, which decomposes the reverberant signal into its source and room impulse response components, allowing for more accurate dereverberation. We also utilize spectro-temporal modeling to capture the time-varying characteristics of speech, ensuring that the dereverberated speech remains natural and coherent. Our approach involves training a model on a dataset of clean and reverberant speech pairs, where the model learns the mapping from reverberant to clean speech through NCTF. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in speech clarity and intelligibility, particularly in noisy conditions. These findings indicate that our method offers a robust solution for speech dereverberation, providing a valuable tool for applications such as hearing aids, teleconferencing systems, and speech recognition systems operating in challenging acoustic environments.

text: We present an analytical framework for deriving capture probabilities associated with the corotation eccentric mean motion resonances (CEMMRs) in planetary dynamics. Our work addresses the limitations of existing methodologies that primarily focus on either mean motion or eccentricity resonances in isolation, thereby neglecting the interplay between these dynamical regimes. We employ a multi-scale perturbation approach to systematically derive the conditions under which an object may be captured into resonance, using a combination of numerical simulations and analytic perturbation theory.   Our results indicate that the probability of capture is significantly influenced by initial eccentricity and inclination, with a nuanced resonance overlap effect being identified that enhances capture likelihood for specific configurations. We quantify these probabilities through detailed statistical analyses of trajectory evolution, employing both phase space analysis and resonance width calculations. By delineating the boundaries of stability associated with CEMMRs, we provide a comprehensive understanding of the resonant dynamics governing minor planetary bodies and their interactions with larger celestial objects.  The implications of our findings extend beyond theoretical considerations, as they offer valuable insights into the migration processes of exoplanets and the dynamical architecture of planetary systems. Furthermore, we highlight the applicability of our results in informing future observational studies aimed at identifying resonant capture among trans-Neptunian objects and their evolutionary pathways. Our methodology offers a robust framework for further exploration of resonant phenomena in various astrophysical contexts, laying the groundwork for subsequent investigations into the dynamics of celestial mechanics.

text: This research investigates the properties of convective motions within facular regions, focusing on their role in solar surface dynamics. Faculae are bright features observed on the Sun's photosphere that are associated with increased magnetic activity and convective flow. The objectives include elucidating the mechanisms governing convective motion, identifying distinct patterns of convection, and assessing how these patterns vary with solar cycle phases. Key findings indicate that facular regions exhibit strong convective upflows, often accompanied by turbulent mixing. These motions contribute significantly to the dynamic nature of the photosphere and play a crucial role in heat transport and energy distribution across the solar surface. The research concludes by proposing models that integrate observational data with theoretical predictions, offering insights into the complex interplay between magnetic fields and convective processes in solar faculae.

Key findings include the successful identification and mitigation of sensor defects through adaptive learning strategies, resulting in improved overall system performance and reduced false alarms. In this paper, we will report our achievements in developing large area
patterning of multilayered ceramic green composites using roller embossing. The
aim of our research is to pattern large area ceramic green composites using a
modified roller laminating apparatus, which is compatible with screen printing
machines, for integration of embossing and screen printing. The instrumentation
of our roller embossing apparatus, as shown in Figure1, consists of roller 1
and rollers 2. Roller 1 is heated up to the desired embossing temperature ;
roller 2 is, however, kept at room temperature. The mould is a nickel template
manufactured by plating nickel-based micro patterns (height : 50 $\mu$m) on a
nickel film (thickness : 70 $\mu$m) ; the substrate for the roller embossing is
a multilayered Heraeus Heralock HL 2000 ceramic green composite. Comparing with
the conventional simultaneous embossing, the advantages of roller embossing
include : (1) low embossing force ; (2) easiness of demoulding ; (3) localized
area in contact with heater ; and etc. We have demonstrated the capability of
large area roller embossing with a panel size of 150mmx 150mm on the mentioned
substrate. We have explored and confirmed the impact of parameters (feed speed,
temperature of roller and applied pressure) to the pattern quality of roller
embossing. Furthermore, under the optimized process parameters, we
characterized the variations of pattern dimension over the panel area, and
calculated a scaling factor in order to make the panel compatible with other
processes. Figure 2 shows the embossed patterns on a 150mmx 150mm green ceramic
panel.

text: This study focuses on the development of an automated method to extract and classify diving clips from continuous video footage of underwater environments. To achieve this goal, we propose a combination of computer vision and machine learning techniques. The preprocessing stage includes color correction, image denoising, and edge detection, which enhances the quality of the input data. Subsequently, we apply object detection algorithms, such as Haar cascades and deep learning models, to locate diving instances in the video frames. To classify diving types, we implement a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on a labeled dataset to recognize and distinguish between different types of dives. Our methodology further incorporates an adaptive thresholding technique to optimize the CNN's performance in dealing with underwater video's inherent challenges, such as low visibility and varying lighting conditions.   Our proposed method achieved an average extraction rate of 97.5% and a classification accuracy of 95.1%, demonstrating its efficiency and accuracy in handling underwater video data. The presented technique can be further applied in various fields, such as sports analysis, wildlife monitoring, and environmental studies. Additionally, the extracted diving clips can serve as input data for other analyses, such as athlete performance assessment or environmental impact assessment, further enhancing the potential of our proposed method.   In conclusion, this study presents an effective automated method for extracting and classifying diving clips from continuous underwater video footage using a combination of computer vision and machine learning techniques. Our methodology demonstrates high efficiency and accuracy, providing a foundation for various applications in different fields.

text: This research introduces SRPGAN (Perceptual Generative Adversarial Network) for enhancing single image super-resolution. Leveraging the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework, SRPGAN aims to improve the visual quality of low-resolution images by synthesizing high-resolution counterparts. The study explores the application of perceptual loss, which focuses on preserving semantic content across different resolutions, to ensure that the enhanced images retain meaningful details while improving resolution. The methodology involves training SRPGAN using a dataset of paired low and high-resolution images. Key findings indicate that SRPGAN outperforms baseline methods in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM), and perceptual quality scores. The results demonstrate that SRPGAN effectively enhances image resolution while maintaining or even improving visual quality. This work contributes to the field by proposing a novel approach to single image super-resolution, providing a robust solution for enhancing the clarity and detail of low-resolution images.

The finger-like branching pattern that occurs when a less viscous fluid
displaces a more viscous one confined between two parallel plates has been
widely studied as a classical example of a mathematically-tractable
hydrodynamic instability since the time of Saffman and Taylor. Fingering in
such Hele-Shaw geometries have been generated not only with Newtonian fluids
but also with various non-Newtonian fluids including fine granular material
displaced by gas, liquid, or large grains. Here we study a granular Hele-Shaw
system to explore whether the absence of cohesive forces in dry granular
material can produce an ideal venue for studying the hitherto-unrealizable
singular hydrodynamics predicted in the zero-surface-tension limit. We
demonstrate that the grain-gas interface does indeed exhibit fractal structure
and sharp cusps associated with finite-time singularities. Above the yield
stress, the scaling for the finger width is distinct from that for ordinary
fluids, reflecting unique granular properties such as friction-induced
dissipation as opposed to viscous damping. Despite such differences, the
dimension of the global fractal structure and the shape of the singular cusps
on the interface agree with the theories based on simple Laplacian growth of
conventional fluid fingering in the zero-surface-tension limit. Our study
provides new insights not only on the dynamics of two-phase dense granular
flows and granular pattern formation, but also on the fluid dynamics in the
zero-surface-tension limit.

text:
Smale's 7-th problem concerns N-point configurations on the 2-dim sphere
which minimize the logarithmic pair-energy V_0(r) = -ln r averaged over the
pairs in a configuration; here, r is the chordal distance between the points
forming a pair. More generally, V_0(r) may be replaced by the standardized
Riesz pair-energy V_s(r)= (r^{-s} -1)/s, which becomes - ln r in the limit s to
0, and the sphere may be replaced by other compact manifolds. This paper
inquires into the concavity of the map from the integers N>1 into the minimal
average standardized Riesz pair-energies v_s(N) of the N-point configurations
on the 2-sphere for various real s. It is known that v_s(N) is strictly
increasing for each real s, and for s<2 also bounded above, hence "overall
concave." It is (easily) proved that v_{-2}(N) is even locally strictly
concave, and that so is v_s(2n) for s<-2. By analyzing computer-experimental
data of putatively minimal average Riesz pair-energies v_s^x(N) for s in
{-1,0,1,2,3} and N in {2,...,200}, it is found that {v}_{-1}^x(N) is locally
strictly concave, while v_s^x(N) is not always locally strictly concave for s
in {0,1,2,3}: concavity defects occur whenever N in C^{x}_+(s) (an s-specific
empirical set of integers). It is found that the empirical map C^{x}_+(s), with
s in {-2,-1,0,1,2,3}, is set-theoretically increasing; moreover, the percentage
of odd numbers in C^{x}_+(s), s in {0,1,2,3}, is found to increase with s. The
integers in C^{x}_+(0) are few and far between, forming a curious sequence of
numbers, reminiscent of the "magic numbers" in nuclear physics. It is
conjectured that the "magic numbers" in Smale's 7-th problem are associated
with optimally symmetric optimal-energy configurations.
