text: We present a novel approach to the approximate computation of the canonical polyadic (CP) decomposition of 3-D noise-corrupted low-rank tensors, leveraging the SECSI framework as a first-order perturbation analysis tool. Our method involves a systematic exploration of the CP decomposition's sensitivity to noise, enabling the identification of critical components and their associated uncertainties. By applying the SECSI framework, we develop a rigorous framework for quantifying the effects of noise on the CP decomposition's accuracy and identifying potential sources of error.  Through a series of numerical experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in approximating the CP decomposition of 3-D noise-corrupted low-rank tensors. Our results show that the proposed method can effectively reduce the impact of noise on the decomposition, leading to improved accuracy and robustness. We also investigate the trade-offs between computation time and accuracy, revealing that our approach can balance these competing demands.  Our key findings suggest that the SECSI framework provides a valuable tool for analyzing the sensitivity of the CP decomposition to noise. By leveraging this framework, we can develop more accurate and reliable methods for approximating the CP decomposition of 3-D noise-corrupted low-rank tensors, with applications in various fields such as image and signal processing, machine learning, and data analysis.
label: machine

text: We investigate the rheological behavior of aqueous suspensions of Laponite, focusing on the mechanisms underlying the aging phenomena observed during their preparation and storage. Our study systematically evaluates the time-dependent viscosity changes as a function of concentration, temperature, and aging time. We employ a combination of dynamic and static rheological techniques to characterize the flow and structural properties of these suspensions, enabling us to discern how microstructural evolution correlates with macroscopic rheological behavior.   Our results reveal that the viscosity of Laponite suspensions exhibits a pronounced increase with aging, attributed to the formation and strengthening of a layered network within the dispersion. We identify distinct regimes of behavior associated with different aging times, demonstrating a transition from a Newtonian fluid behavior at short aging times to a yield stress fluid at longer aging periods. Notably, we observe that the onset of yielding is contingent upon both the concentration of Laponite and the specific interactions among particles as they age.   We propose a unified model that incorporates the effects of network connectivity and particle interactions to explain these observations. This model not only provides new insights into the aging behavior of Laponite suspensions but also has potential implications for understanding the rheological properties of other colloidal systems. Our findings contribute to the fundamental understanding of complex fluid behavior and highlight the importance of aging in regulating the properties of Laponite dispersions, paving the way for practical applications in various industries, including cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and food technology.
label: machine

When applying the support vector machine (SVM) to high-dimensional
classification problems, we often impose a sparse structure in the SVM to
eliminate the influences of the irrelevant predictors. The lasso and other
variable selection techniques have been successfully used in the SVM to perform
automatic variable selection. In some problems, there is a natural hierarchical
structure among the variables. Thus, in order to have an interpretable SVM
classifier, it is important to respect the heredity principle when enforcing
the sparsity in the SVM. Many variable selection methods, however, do not
respect the heredity principle. In this paper we enforce both sparsity and the
heredity principle in the SVM by using the so-called structured variable
selection (SVS) framework originally proposed in Yuan, Joseph and Zou (2007).
We minimize the empirical hinge loss under a set of linear inequality
constraints and a lasso-type penalty. The solution always obeys the desired
heredity principle and enjoys sparsity. The new SVM classifier can be
efficiently fitted, because the optimization problem is a linear program.
Another contribution of this work is to present a nonparametric extension of
the SVS framework, and we propose nonparametric heredity SVMs. Simulated and
real data are used to illustrate the merits of the proposed method.
label: human

text: This research builds upon the Network Newton algorithm introduced previously and investigates its convergence rate and practical implementation aspects. Our study focuses on enhancing the algorithm's efficiency by analyzing the convergence speed under various network topologies and sizes. By considering the impact of different network structures on the algorithm's performance, we aim to provide insights into optimizing its convergence rate. Furthermore, we present a detailed implementation framework for applying the Network Newton algorithm in real-world network settings. Our methodology involves theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence properties followed by extensive simulations to validate the results. Through experiments in diverse network scenarios, we demonstrate the algorithm's ability to achieve rapid convergence, thereby showcasing its effectiveness in practical applications. The key contribution of this work lies in offering a comprehensive understanding of the convergence behavior of the Network Newton algorithm, along with guidelines for its successful implementation in network optimization tasks. By elucidating the convergence rate and practical deployment aspects, this study paves the way for leveraging the algorithm's capabilities in various network optimization problems.

We have carried out an extensive search for the SiC Bucky-diamond structure
to confirm not only that a pair of Si and C atoms can form sp2- as well as
sp3-type bonds but also that these two types of bonds can co-exist in the same
SiC-based structure. The successful and surprising discovery of the SinCm
Bucky-diamond structure at the specific composition of n=68 and m=79 is the
result of the relaxation of the truncated bulk 3C-SiC network to yield a SinCm
cluster with m +n=147. It highlights the important role played by the
composition in determining the structure and hence other properties of
SiC-based nano-structures. We have also shed light on the mechanism behind the
formation of the Bucky-diamond structure. The formation process is initiated by
the induced bonds between pairs of surface carbon atoms of the initial
configuration of the Si68C79 cluster obtained by truncating bulk 3C-SiC
network. This action then continuously incorporates atoms in the six outer
shells of the Si68C79 clusters to form the 112-atom Fullerene shell through
nearest neighbor Si-C interactions. Because the 35-atom inner core with five
completely filled shells only interacts weakly with the Fullerene shell through
the six atoms on its "surface", the diamond-like inner core is barely perturbed
and is suspended inside the Fullerene shell. We have also suggested a likely
route of synthesizing the SiC Bucky-diamond structure based on the result of
our simulation.

text: This research explores the highly structured nature of wind patterns observed in Vela X-1, a binary pulsar system consisting of a neutron star and a white dwarf. The objective of this study was to investigate the detailed structure and behavior of the stellar wind emanating from the companion star, focusing on its velocity profiles, density distribution, and interaction with the neutron star's magnetic field.  Methodologically, the research utilized high-resolution spectroscopic observations and numerical simulations to analyze the data collected over several years. The spectral analysis provided insights into the variability of the wind parameters, while the simulations helped to model the interaction between the stellar wind and the strong magnetic field of the neutron star. Key findings revealed distinct velocity gradients and density enhancements in the wind, suggesting a multi-layered structure influenced by the pulsar's intense fields. Additionally, the study identified periodic variations in wind parameters that correlated with the pulsar's spin cycles, indicating a dynamic interplay between the two stars.  The results highlight the intricate nature of the stellar wind in Vela X-1 and its potential role in shaping the environment around the binary system. The conclusion underscores the importance of continued observational and theoretical efforts to understand these complex phenomena, which could provide valuable insights into the evolution of such systems and the fundamental physics governing stellar winds.

text: The study of solar flares is vital for understanding solar energetic events and their impact on the heliosphere. This research focuses on analyzing the thermal characteristics and differential emission measure (DEM) distribution of a B8.3 solar flare observed on July 04, 2009. Utilizing high-resolution spectroscopic data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory and complementary X-ray data from the RHESSI satellite, the study aims to unravel the temperature structure and emission properties of this moderate flare. By employing advanced inversion techniques, we derived the DEM, which provides a comprehensive temperature distribution of the emitting plasma. Key findings reveal a multimodal temperature distribution during the peak phase, indicative of complex plasma dynamics and energy dissipation mechanisms. We observed that the flare's DEM aligns with both a high-temperature component around 10 MK and a substantial cooler component, suggesting a stratified structure of the emitting regions. Additionally, the flare exhibits a rapid temperature increase followed by a gradual cooling trend, characteristic of thermal conduction-dominated processes. These findings significantly contribute to the understanding of energy partitioning and thermal evolution in solar flares. Further implications of this research underscore the importance of accurate DEM reconstruction in enhancing predictive models of solar flare behavior. Thus, this investigation not only elucidates the thermal dynamics during the specific B8.3 flare event but also proposes methodologies for broader applicability in solar physics research.

text: The magnetic properties and exchange integrals of the frustrated chain cuprate PbCuSO$_4$(OH)$_2$, commonly known as linarite, have been revisited through a combined experimental and theoretical study. We performed magnetization measurements on single crystals of linarite using a SQUID magnetometer and applied perturbative theory to calculate the exchange interactions. Our experimental results reveal a complex magnetic ground state, with evidence for a field-induced transition to a spin-gapped phase above 4 T. The temperature dependence of the magnetic susceptibility below T$_N$ = 3.4 K is well-described by a power law, indicating the presence of a quantum singlet ground state.  Our theoretical analysis focuses on the Heisenberg model with frustrated exchange integrals, which is a suitable description for linarite. Using perturbative theory, we calculated the exchange integrals and found that the dominating interactions are of first and third neighbor type, with alternating signs along the chain. The Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and next-nearest neighbor couplings were also considered and shown to have a minor effect on the overall magnetic behavior.  Our findings contribute to the understanding of the intricate magnetic properties of linarite and provide valuable insights into the physics of frustrated chain systems. The methods used in this study can be applied to the investigation of other related frustrated systems, potentially leading to a deeper understanding of their magnetic behavior and the underlying exchange interactions.

text:
A coupled cell network describes interacting (coupled) individual systems
(cells). As in networks from real applications, coupled cell networks can
represent inhomogeneous networks where different types of cells interact with
each other in different ways, which can be represented graphically by different
symbols, or abstractly by equivalence relations.
  Various synchronous behaviors, from full synchrony to partial synchrony, can
be observed for a given network. Patterns of synchrony, which do not depend on
specific dynamics of the network, but only on the network structure, are
associated with a special type of partition of cells, termed balanced
equivalence relations. Algorithms in Aldis (2008) and Belykh and Hasler (2011)
find the unique pattern of synchrony with the least clusters. In this paper, we
compute the set of all possible patterns of synchrony and show their hierarchy
structure as a complete lattice.
  We represent the network structure of a given coupled cell network by a
symbolic adjacency matrix encoding the different coupling types. We show that
balanced equivalence relations can be determined by a matrix computation on the
adjacency matrix which forms a block structure for each balanced equivalence
relation. This leads to a computer algorithm to search for all possible
balanced equivalence relations. Our computer program outputs the balanced
equivalence relations, quotient matrices, and a complete lattice for user
specified coupled cell networks. Finding the balanced equivalence relations of
any network of up to 15 nodes is tractable, but for larger networks this
depends on the pattern of synchrony with least clusters.
label: human

text:
We show that the expansion of ejecta in Tycho's supernova remnant (SNR) is
consistent with a spherically symmetric shell, based on Suzaku measurements of
the Doppler broadened X-ray emission lines. All the strong K_alpha line
emission show broader widths at the center than at the rim, while the centroid
energies are constant across the remnant (except for Ca). This is the pattern
expected for Doppler broadening due to expansion of the SNR ejecta in a
spherical shell. To determine the expansion velocities of the ejecta, we
applied a model for each emission line feature having two Gaussian components
separately representing red- and blue-shifted gas, and inferred the Doppler
velocity difference between these two components directly from the fitted
centroid energy difference. Taking into account the effect of projecting a
three-dimensional shell to the plane of the detector, we derived average
spherical expansion velocities independently for the K_alpha emission of Si, S,
Ar, and Fe, and K_beta of Si. We found that the expansion velocities of Si, S,
and Ar ejecta of 4700+/-100 km/s are distinctly higher than that obtained from
Fe K_alpha emission, 4000+/-300 km/s, which is consistent with segregation of
the Fe in the inner ejecta. Combining the observed ejecta velocities with the
ejecta proper-motion measurements by Chandra, we derived a distance to the
Tycho's SNR of 4+/-1 kpc.

text: Mo$_{1-x}$Re$_x$ alloys, a system of transition metal alloys with potential applications in catalysis, electrocatalysis, and magnetic storage materials, have been extensively studied due to their unique electronic structures. In this work, we investigate the electronic structure of Mo$_{1-x}$Re$_x$ alloys using resonant photoemission spectroscopy (RPES). We focus on the 4d core level spectra and the 4s-4p shake-up features, which provide valuable information about the local electronic environment around Mo and Re atoms.  The background section outlines the importance of Mo$_{1-x}$Re$_x$ alloys and their unique electronic structures. The objective of the study is to understand the changes in the electronic structure as a function of Re content (x) using RPES. We describe the methodology, including sample preparation, spectroscopic measurements, and data analysis techniques in this section.  Our key findings reveal distinct shifts in the Mo 4d core level spectra and Re 4d core level spectra as the Re content varies. We observe the appearance of additional features in the shake-up spectra that can be assigned to Re 4d states. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our results in terms of the potential applications of Mo$_{1-x}$Re$_x$ alloys and the role of RPES in understanding the electronic structure of alloy systems.  In conclusion, the Mo$_{1-x}$Re$_x$ alloy system is a vital area of research due to its potential applications in various industries. This study contributes to the understanding of the electronic structure of Mo$_{1-x}$Re$_x$ alloys using RPES, providing valuable insights into the role of Re atoms in modifying the Mo electronic structure. These findings have implications for the development of novel catalytic materials and magnetic storage systems.

text: This study explores the potential of solid core dipoles as a more cost-effective alternative to traditional light sources, particularly in switching power supply applications. We then propose the use of solid core dipoles, which offer significant advantages in terms of both energy efficiency and reduced material costs. Our methodology involves detailed simulations and experimental testing of solid core dipole configurations under various switching power supply conditions. Results demonstrate that solid core dipoles can achieve comparable performance to traditional light sources but with substantial reductions in operational costs and energy consumption. Key findings indicate that the switch from conventional to solid core dipole technology could lead to a reduction in overall system cost by up to 30%, while also contributing to environmental sustainability through decreased energy waste. This research not only challenges existing paradigms in lighting technology but also presents a viable solution for enhancing the economic viability of switching power supplies across diverse applications.

text: The study of star streams in the context of triaxial isochrone potentials with sub-halos has garnered significant attention in recent years, as it provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex dynamics of galaxy evolution. The triaxial isochrone potential is a theoretical model that describes the gravitational potential of a galaxy, taking into account its three-dimensional structure and the distribution of stars within it. However, the inclusion of sub-halos, which are smaller, satellite galaxies that orbit the main galaxy, adds an additional layer of complexity to this model.  This research paper aims to investigate the formation and evolution of star streams in triaxial isochrone potentials with sub-halos. To achieve this, we employed a combination of numerical simulations and analytical techniques, utilizing a state-of-the-art galaxy simulation code to model the dynamics of stars and sub-halos within a triaxial isochrone potential. Our results show that the presence of sub-halos can significantly impact the formation of star streams, leading to the creation of complex, multi-component streams that reflect the intricate dynamics of the galaxy.  The key findings of this study reveal that the interactions between stars and sub-halos can lead to the formation of star streams that are characterized by a high degree of complexity and diversity. We also demonstrate that the triaxial isochrone potential provides a robust framework for understanding the evolution of star streams, allowing for the prediction of their formation and evolution over a wide range of galaxy types and sub-halo masses. Overall, our results provide new insights into the formation and evolution of star streams in triaxial isochrone potentials with sub-halos, and have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution and the formation of galaxy-scale structures.

text: In our study, we investigate the emergence of resonant phenomena within the context of Brownian motion, focusing on the role of hydrodynamic memory in the generation of thermal noise. These resonances are attributed to the hydrodynamic interactions between particles that persist over time, creating a non-Markovian effect. Our methodology involves modeling particle dynamics using Langevin equations and incorporating analytical techniques to extract spectral properties. Key findings indicate that these resonances significantly influence the statistical characteristics of thermal noise, particularly at specific frequencies corresponding to the characteristic timescales of hydrodynamic interactions. This research not only enriches our understanding of the interplay between hydrodynamics and thermal effects but also provides insights into the broader mechanisms governing collective behavior in complex systems.

There has been growing observational evidence for the presence of condensates
in the atmospheres and/or comet-like tails of extrasolar planets. As a result,
systematic and homogeneous tables of dust properties are useful in order to
facilitate further observational and theoretical studies. In this paper we
present calculations and analysis of non-isotropic phase functions, asymmetry
parameter (mean cosine of the scattering angle), absorption and scattering
opacities, single scattering albedos, equilibrium temperatures, and radiative
accelerations of dust grains relevant for extrasolar planets. Our assumptions
include spherical grain shape, Deirmendjian particle size distribution, and Mie
theory. We consider several species: corundum/alumina, perovskite, olivines
with 0\% and 50\% iron content, pyroxenes with 0\%, 20\% and 60\% iron content,
pure iron, carbon at two different temperatures, water ice, liquid water, and
ammonia. The presented tables cover the wavelength range of 0.2 to 500 micron
and modal particle radii from 0.01 micron to 100 micron. Equilibrium
temperatures and radiative accelerations assume irradiation by a non-black-body
source of light with temperatures from 7000K to 700K seen at solid angles from
2$\pi$ to $10^{-6}$ sr. The tables are provided to the community together with
a simple code which allows for an optional, finite, angular dimension of the
source of light (star) in the phase function.

text: We present a novel class of stellar populations, dubbed "dark star clusters," characterized by an unprecedentedly high density of stars and an exceptionally low level of visible light emission. Through a combination of multi-wavelength observations and advanced data analysis techniques, we have identified and characterized a sample of these enigmatic clusters, revealing a complex interplay between stellar evolution, dust formation, and the interstellar medium.  Our initial attempts to explain the observed properties of dark star clusters were met with a mix of theoretical and observational challenges. We found that traditional models of stellar evolution and dust formation were unable to account for the extreme density and low luminosity of these clusters. However, by incorporating the effects of gravitational collapse and the role of dark matter, we were able to develop a comprehensive framework that successfully reproduces the observed properties of dark star clusters.  Our key findings indicate that dark star clusters are formed through the merger of smaller, denser stellar systems, which then undergo a rapid collapse under the influence of dark matter. This process leads to the formation of a dense, globular-like cluster with a high concentration of stars and a low level of visible light emission. We propose that dark star clusters provide a unique window into the early stages of galaxy formation and the role of dark matter in shaping the evolution of stellar populations.

We examine the prospects of using two alternative and complementary ways to
explore the regions that are favored by global constraints in two simple
unified supersymmetric models: the CMSSM and the NUHM. First, we consider
BR(Bs->\mu\mu), which has recently been for the first time measured by LHCb. In
the CMSSM we show that ultimate, but realistic, improvement in the
determination of the observable to about 5-10% around the Standard Model value
would strongly disfavor the A-funnel region, while not affecting much the other
favored regions. Second, we show that all the favored regions of the CMSSM will
be, for the most part, sensitive to direct dark matter searches in future
one-tonne detectors. A signal at low WIMP mass (<=450 GeV) and low
spin-independent cross section would then strongly favor the stau
coannihilation region while a signal at higher WIMP mass (~800 GeV to ~1.2 TeV)
would clearly point to the region where the neutralino is higgsino-like with
mass ~1 TeV. A nearly complete experimental testing of the CMSSM over multi-TeV
ranges of superpartner masses, far beyond the reach of direct SUSY searches at
the LHC, can therefore be achievable. In the NUHM, in contrast, similar favored
regions exist but a sample study reveals that even a precise determination of
BR(Bs->\mu\mu) would have a much less constraining power on the model,
including the A-funnel region. On the other hand, this could allow one to, by
detecting in one-tonne detectors a signal for 500 GeV<m_{\chi}<800 GeV,
strongly disfavor the CMSSM.

We calculate very long low- and high-temperature series for the
susceptibility $\chi$ of the square lattice Ising model as well as very long
series for the five-particle contribution $\chi^{(5)}$ and six-particle
contribution $\chi^{(6)}$. These calculations have been made possible by the
use of highly optimized polynomial time modular algorithms and a total of more
than 150000 CPU hours on computer clusters. For $\chi^{(5)}$ 10000 terms of the
series are calculated {\it modulo} a single prime, and have been used to find
the linear ODE satisfied by $\chi^{(5)}$ {\it modulo} a prime.
  A diff-Pad\'e analysis of 2000 terms series for $\chi^{(5)}$ and $\chi^{(6)}$
confirms to a very high degree of confidence previous conjectures about the
location and strength of the singularities of the $n$-particle components of
the susceptibility, up to a small set of ``additional'' singularities. We find
the presence of singularities at $w=1/2$ for the linear ODE of $\chi^{(5)}$,
and $w^2= 1/8$ for the ODE of $\chi^{(6)}$, which are {\it not} singularities
of the ``physical'' $\chi^{(5)}$ and $\chi^{(6)},$ that is to say the
series-solutions of the ODE's which are analytic at $w =0$.
  Furthermore, analysis of the long series for $\chi^{(5)}$ (and $\chi^{(6)}$)
combined with the corresponding long series for the full susceptibility $\chi$
yields previously conjectured singularities in some $\chi^{(n)}$, $n \ge 7$.
  We also present a mechanism of resummation of the logarithmic singularities
of the $\chi^{(n)}$ leading to the known power-law critical behaviour occurring
in the full $\chi$, and perform a power spectrum analysis giving strong
arguments in favor of the existence of a natural boundary for the full
susceptibility $\chi$.

text: We investigate the hierarchical star formation processes in the grand design spiral galaxy NGC 1566, revealing a complex interplay between gas inflow, star formation, and galaxy evolution. Through a combination of spectroscopic and photometric observations, we mapped the distribution of gas and dust across the galaxy, identifying regions of intense star formation and detecting the signatures of molecular gas inflow. Our results indicate that the galaxy's central bulge is a major site of star formation, with a high density of young, blue stars and a significant population of massive stars. In contrast, the outer spiral arms exhibit lower star formation rates, with a preponderance of older, red stars.  Our analysis of the galaxy's stellar population reveals a hierarchical structure, with a dominant population of young, massive stars in the central bulge and a secondary population of older, lower-mass stars in the outer spiral arms. We also identify a population of intermediate-mass stars, which are thought to be the result of galaxy-scale mergers and interactions. Our observations suggest that the hierarchical star formation processes in NGC 1566 are driven by a combination of gas inflow and galaxy-scale mergers, which have triggered the formation of a diverse range of stellar populations. By studying the hierarchical star formation processes in NGC 1566, we gain insights into the complex interplay between gas, stars, and galaxy evolution, and shed light on the formation and evolution of spiral galaxies.

text: This study addresses the challenge of noise reduction in audio signals by focusing on the optimization of microphone subset selection for Maximum Variance Dirichlet Beamforming (MVDR) beamformers. The objective is to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) while maintaining spatial resolution. We attempt to solve this problem through systematic evaluations of different microphone configurations, considering their impact on noise suppression efficiency and system performance.  The methodology involves conducting extensive simulations using synthetic and real-world audio datasets. These simulations are designed to test various subsets of microphones under varying noise conditions, including white noise, pink noise, and reverberant environments. Key metrics such as SNR improvement, signal fidelity, and computational complexity are used to assess the effectiveness of each configuration.  Results indicate that selecting a subset of microphones optimized for noise attenuation can significantly improve the SNR compared to using all available microphones. Additionally, certain configurations demonstrate better robustness to changes in environmental noise characteristics. Notably, the proposed approach achieves up to 15% improvement in SNR across simulated scenarios without compromising spatial resolution.  The findings suggest that careful selection of microphone subsets based on their inherent properties and the specific application requirements can lead to more effective noise reduction systems. This work contributes to the development of advanced beamforming techniques tailored for real-world acoustic environments, offering potential applications in hearing aids, medical imaging, and telecommunications.

text: Face alignment is a critical task in computer vision, enabling applications such as facial recognition, expression analysis, and augmented reality. This research paper addresses the current state of progress in solving the 2D and 3D face alignment problems, focusing on the integration of a newly developed dataset containing 230,000 3D facial landmarks. The objective of this study is to evaluate existing algorithms in terms of their accuracy and robustness, while also identifying gaps in current methodologies. We conducted a comparative analysis of leading algorithms, employing the aforementioned dataset to benchmark their performance under varying conditions of occlusion, lighting, and orientation. Our findings reveal that while 2D face alignment has achieved significant advancements, particularly with the application of deep learning techniques, challenges remain in 3D face alignment, especially in real-time applications and under diverse scenarios. Notably, state-of-the-art models demonstrated a mean error rate of approximately 3.2 mm, indicating considerable room for improvement. Additionally, we highlight the importance of dataset diversity and the incorporation of synthetic data to enhance model generalization. In conclusion, although there has been substantial progress, our study suggests that the field is still several years away from achieving comprehensive solutions for both 2D and 3D face alignment, necessitating further research into more robust algorithms and the utility of larger, more diverse datasets.

text: In this study, we explore potential new physics scenarios through an in-depth analysis of charm meson leptonic and semileptonic decays. Charm mesons, with their unique position in the quark model hierarchy, offer a fertile ground for uncovering deviations from the Standard Model predictions. We specifically target the decay modes \( D^+ \rightarrow \ell^+\nu \) and \( D^0 \rightarrow \pi^- \ell^+ \nu \), where \(\ell\) denotes a charged lepton. By employing a comprehensive methodology that integrates both experimental data and theoretical models, we aim to discern new physics contributions potentially arising from leptoquarks or flavor-changing neutral currents. Our analysis utilizes data collected from high-luminosity experiments such as those conducted at the LHCb and Belle II collaborations. We apply a refined statistical approach to test the compatibility of experimental results with the Standard Model predictions. We incorporate lattice QCD calculations to precisely handle the nonperturbative effects in hadronic transitions, thus enhancing the reliability of our theoretical inputs. The results indicate marginal yet intriguing deviations in the decay branching ratios and angular distributions when contrasted with the expected Standard Model values. These anomalies, though statistically inconclusive at current precision levels, could suggest the influence of new physics at higher energy scales. Our findings motivate further experimental efforts with enhanced sensitivity and open avenues for a deeper theoretical exploration of flavor physics beyond the current paradigm. Through this investigation, we underscore the critical role that charm meson decays can play in probing the foundational limits of the Standard Model and the existence of new physics phenomena.

Comparison of observations of radio recombination lines in the interstellar
medium with theoretical models can be used to constrain electron temperature
and density of the gas. An important component of the models is spontaneous
transition rates between bound levels. Calculating these rates relies on
accurate bound-bound oscillator strengths, which can be cast in terms of the
Gaunt factor. The Gaunt factor contains terminating hypergeometric functions
that cannot be calculated with sufficient accuracy for high quantum levels ($n
\gtrsim 50$) by standard machine-precision methods. Methods to overcome the
accuracy problem have been developed, which include asymptotic expansions and
recursion relations. These methods, used in astrophysical models to calculate
oscillator strengths, can introduce errors, sometimes up to as much as $\sim 8$
per cent. Detections of radio recombination lines with the new Low Frequency
Array (LOFAR) has prompted an examination of theoretical models of the
interstellar medium. We revisit the calculation of the Gaunt factor, employing
modern arbitrary-precision computational methods to tabulate the Gaunt factor
for transitions up to quantum level $n=2000$, sufficient to model low frequency
Carbon radio recombination lines. The calculations provide a relative error of
$\sim3\times 10^{-4}$ when compared to more detailed calculations including
relativistic corrections. Our values for the Gaunt factor are provided for
download in a tabular format to be used for a wide range of applications.

We study the energy spectrum of symmetric double quantum dots in narrow-gap
carbon nanotubes with one and two electrostatically confined electrons in the
presence of spin-orbit and Coulomb interactions. Compared to GaAs quantum dots,
the spectrum exhibits a much richer structure because of the spin-orbit
interaction that couples the electron's isospin to its real spin through two
independent coupling constants. In a single dot, both constants combine to
split the spectrum into two Kramers doublets, while the antisymmetric constant
solely controls the difference in the tunneling rates of the Kramers doublets
between the dots. For the two-electron regime, the detailed structure of the
spin-orbit split energy spectrum is investigated as a function of detuning
between the quantum dots in a 22-dimensional Hilbert space within the framework
of a single-longitudinal-mode model. We find a competing effect of the
tunneling and Coulomb interaction. The former favors a left-right symmetric
two-particle ground state, while in the regime where the Coulomb interaction
dominates over tunneling, a left-right antisymmetric ground state is found. As
a result, ground states on both sides of the $(11)$-$(02)$ degeneracy point may
possess opposite left-right symmetry, and the electron dynamics when tuning the
system from one side of the $(11)$-$(02)$ degeneracy point to the other is
controlled by three selection rules (in spin, isospin, and left-right
symmetry). We discuss implications for the spin-dephasing and Pauli blockade
experiments.

We demonstrate that the steep decay and long plateau in the early phases of
gamma ray burst (GRB) X-ray afterglows are naturally produced in the collapsar
model, by a means ultimately related to the dynamics of relativistic jet
propagation through a massive star. We present two-dimensional axisymmetric
hydrodynamical simulations which start from a collapsar engine and evolve all
the way through the late afterglow phase. The resultant outflow includes a jet
core which is highly relativistic after breaking out of the star, but becomes
baryon-loaded after colliding with a massive outer shell, corresponding to mass
from the stellar atmosphere of the progenitor star which became trapped in
front of the jet core at breakout. The prompt emission produced before or
during this collision would then have the signature of a high Lorentz factor
jet, but the afterglow is produced by the amalgamated post-collision ejecta
which has more inertia than the original highly relativistic jet core and thus
has a delayed deceleration. This naturally explains the early light curve
behavior discovered by Swift, including a steep decay and a long plateau,
without invoking late-time energy injection from the central engine. The
numerical simulation is performed continuously from engine to afterglow,
covering a dynamic range of over ten orders of magnitude in radius. Light
curves calculated from the numerical output demonstrate that this mechanism
reproduces basic features seen in early afterglow data. Initial steep decays
are produced by internal shocks, and the plateau corresponds to the coasting
phase of the outflow.

text: In this study, we address the problem of designing systematic distributed storage codes that achieve optimal storage efficiency and allow for fast encoding, which is paramount in modern distributed computing systems with large-scale data. Our work focuses on the development of novel encoding schemes that minimize overhead while maintaining data reliability, crucial for systems necessitating high throughput and rapid data accessibility. We propose a class of systematic distributed storage codes, termed Fast-Encode Systematic Codes (FESC), that leverages algebraic properties to streamline the encoding process without compromising the fault tolerance. By employing a matrix decomposition approach, we achieve a significant reduction in encoding complexity, thereby facilitating real-time data processing. Our methodology involves the strategic organization of data blocks and parity blocks to maximize fault redundancy and optimize retrieval processes in failure scenarios. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our codes attain optimal trade-offs between storage overhead and repair bandwidth. Extensive experimental evaluations on both synthetic datasets and real-world workloads validate that FESC achieves encoding speeds up to 50% faster than conventional erasure codes, with a marginal increase in storage space. Furthermore, resilience tests under simulated network conditions confirm that FESC sustains data integrity under various fault models, including node failures and data corruption. In conclusion, FESC offers an efficient and robust solution for systematic distributed storage, balancing performance and reliability—imperative for data-intensive applications in cloud and edge computing environments. Future work will explore the adaptability of our framework to dynamic network conditions and varying scalability requirements.

text: This study investigates the autoignition behavior of n-butanol at low to intermediate temperatures and elevated pressures. The background section discusses the significance of understanding the autoignition properties of alcohol fuels, especially in the context of their increasing use in engines due to environmental concerns. The objective of this research is to expand the knowledge on the autoignition characteristics of n-butanol by conducting systematic experiments under controlled conditions.  To achieve this objective, the methodology employed includes the use of an isobaric, constant-volume, bomb-type apparatus for conducting the autoignition tests. The experiments were carried out at six different temperatures (300°C, 350°C, 400°C, 450°C, 500°C, and 550°C) and four different pressures (10, 20, 30, and 40 bar). The ignition delay time and pressure were recorded for each test condition.  Key findings of this study reveal that the autoignition temperature and pressure of n-butanol decrease as the pressure increases. The results show that at 30 bar, the autoignition temperature is about 60°C lower than the minimum autoignition temperature at atmospheric pressure. Additionally, the ignition delay time decreases significantly with increasing pressure, indicating a greater reactivity of n-butanol under elevated conditions.  In conclusion, the current study provides valuable insights into the autoignition properties of n-butanol at low to intermediate temperatures and elevated pressures. These findings expand our understanding of the behavior of this alcohol fuel under engine conditions and contribute to the development of more efficient and cleaner engines. Further studies are encouraged to investigate the autoignition behavior of other alcohol fuels under similar conditions.

text: The presence of Supermassive Black Hole (SMBH) seeds, which are thought to be the precursors to the formation of large SMBHs, is a topic of significant interest in the field of astrophysics. The evolution of SMBH masses is closely linked to the growth of galaxies, and understanding this relationship is crucial for unraveling the mysteries of galaxy evolution. However, the existence of SMBH seeds is still a topic of debate, with various models attempting to explain their origin and growth.  This research aims to investigate the possibility of SMBH seeds being formed through the collapse of high-energy emission-based model, by exploring the evolution of scaling relations between SMBH masses and their host galaxy properties. By utilizing a combination of theoretical models and observational data, we seek to shed light on the conditions under which SMBH seeds can form and grow.  Our study employs a numerical simulation framework to model the evolution of SMBH masses and their host galaxy properties over a range of cosmological scenarios. We find that the growth of SMBH seeds is influenced by the interplay between high-energy emission, gas accretion, and galaxy evolution. Furthermore, our results suggest that the evolution of scaling relations between SMBH masses and their host galaxy properties can be used to distinguish between different models of SMBH seed formation.  Our findings have important implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution and the formation of SMBHs. By providing a more nuanced understanding of the role of high-energy emission in SMBH seed formation, this research contributes to the ongoing debate on the existence and properties of SMBH seeds.

text: This study explores the modelling of CO emission from hydrodynamic simulations of nearby spiral galaxies, starbursting mergers, and high-redshift galaxies. The objective of this research is to develop an accurate and efficient method for modelling CO emission based on hydrodynamic simulations. The methodology is tested on a set of nearby spiral galaxies and starbursting mergers, demonstrating excellent agreement with observed CO emission data. Furthermore, we apply this method to high-redshift galaxies, revealing CO emission features that are crucial for studying their star formation environment and evolution. Our findings provide valuable insights into the origin of CO emission and its relationship with star formation, enabling us to better understand the complex physics of galaxy evolution.

Parker instability arises from the presence of magnetic fields in a plasma in
a gravitational field such as the interstellar medium (ISM), wherein the
magnetic buoyant pressure expels the gas and causes the gas to move along the
field lines. The process of mixing of this instability in the ISM near the
Galactic plane is investigated. The initial ISM is assumed to consist of two
fluids: plasma gas and cosmic-ray particles, in hydrostatic equilibrium,
coupled with a uniform, azimuthally-aligned magnetic field. The evolution of
the instability is explored in two models: an isothermal exponential-declining
density model and a two-layered, hyperbolic tangent temperature model. After a
small perturbation, the unstable gas aggregates at the bottom of the magnetic
loops and forms dense blobs. The growth rate of the instability decreases as
the coupling between the cosmic rays and the plasma becomes stronger (meaning a
smaller CR diffusion coefficient). The mixing is enhanced by the cosmic-ray
diffusion, while the shape of the condensed gas depends sensitively on the
initial equilibrium conditions. The hyperbolic tangent temperature model
produces a more concentrated and round shape of clumps at the foot points of
rising magnetic arches, like the observed giant molecular cloud, whereas the
exponential density model gives rise to a filamentary morphology of the clumpy
structure. When considering a minimum perpendicular or cross field diffusion of
cosmic rays, which is often substantially smaller than the parallel coefficient
$\kappa_{\|}$, around $2%-4%$ of $\kappa_{\|}$, the flow speed is significantly
increased such that the magnetic loops extend to a greater altitude. We
speculate that the galactic wind flow perpendicular to the galactic disk may be
facilitated by Parker instabilities through the cross field diffusion of cosmic
rays.

Factor modeling is an essential tool for exploring intrinsic dependence
structures among high-dimensional random variables. Much progress has been made
for estimating the covariance matrix from a high-dimensional factor model.
However, the blessing of dimensionality has not yet been fully embraced in the
literature: much of the available data is often ignored in constructing
covariance matrix estimates. If our goal is to accurately estimate a covariance
matrix of a set of targeted variables, shall we employ additional data, which
are beyond the variables of interest, in the estimation? In this paper, we
provide sufficient conditions for an affirmative answer, and further quantify
its gain in terms of Fisher information and convergence rate. In fact, even an
oracle-like result (as if all the factors were known) can be achieved when a
sufficiently large number of variables is used. The idea of utilizing data as
much as possible brings computational challenges. A divide-and-conquer
algorithm is thus proposed to alleviate the computational burden, and also
shown not to sacrifice any statistical accuracy in comparison with a pooled
analysis. Simulation studies further confirm our advocacy for the use of full
data, and demonstrate the effectiveness of the above algorithm. Our proposal is
applied to a microarray data example that shows empirical benefits of using
more data.

text: This study focuses on the spatial resolution of spin-split edge states within chiral graphene nanoribbons (GNRs). Utilizing advanced scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) techniques, we systematically investigate the electronic structure of GNRs of varying widths and chiralities. Our results reveal distinct spin-split edge states that are sensitive to the ribbon's geometry, with a pronounced dependence on both the width and chirality. The spatial resolution achieved through STM enables us to map these edge states across the sample surface, providing a detailed understanding of their distribution and behavior. This research not only contributes to the fundamental knowledge of topological insulators but also offers insights into the design principles for future spintronic devices based on edge states. Key methodologies include precise fabrication techniques for GNRs, high-resolution STM imaging, and sophisticated data analysis to extract meaningful information from the experimental data.

text:
The G -->0 limit of Euclidean gravity introduced by Smolin is described by a
generally covariant U(1)xU(1)xU(1) gauge theory. The Poisson bracket algebra of
its Hamiltonian and diffeomorphism constraints is isomorphic to that of
gravity. Motivated by recent results in Parameterized Field Theory and by the
search for an anomaly-free quantum dynamics for Loop Quantum Gravity (LQG), the
quantum Hamiltonian constraint of density weight 4/3 for this U(1)xU(1)xU(1)
theory is constructed so as to produce a non-trivial LQG-type representation of
its Poisson brackets through the following steps. First, the constraint at
finite triangulation, as well as the commutator between a pair of such
constraints, are constructed as operators on the `charge' network basis. Next,
the continuum limit of the commutator is evaluated with respect to an operator
topology defined by a certain space of `vertex smooth' distributions. Finally,
the operator corresponding to the Poisson bracket between a pair of Hamiltonian
constraints is constructed at finite triangulation in such a way as to generate
a `generalised' diffeomorphism and its continuum limit is shown to agree with
that of the commutator between a pair of finite triangulation Hamiltonian
constraints. Our results in conjunction with the recent work of Henderson,
Laddha and Tomlin in a 2+1-dimensional context, constitute the necessary first
steps toward a satisfactory treatment of the quantum dynamics of this model.

text:
Near a critical point, the equilibrium relaxation time of a system diverges
and any change of control/thermodynamic parameters leads to non-equilibrium
behavior. The Kibble-Zurek problem is to determine the dynamical evolution of
the system parametrically close to its critical point when the change is
parametrically slow. The non-equilibrium behavior in this limit is controlled
entirely by the critical point and the details of the trajectory of the system
in parameter space (the protocol) close to the critical point. Together, they
define a universality class consisting of critical exponents-discussed in the
seminal work by Kibble and Zurek-and scaling functions for physical quantities,
which have not been discussed hitherto. In this article, we give an extended
and pedagogical discussion of the universal content in the Kibble-Zurek
problem. We formally define a scaling limit for physical quantities near
classical and quantum transitions for different sets of protocols. We report
computations of a few scaling functions in model Gaussian and large-N problems
and prove their universality with respect to protocol choice. We also introduce
a new protocol in which the critical point is approached asymptotically at late
times with the system marginally out of equilibrium, wherein logarithmic
violations to scaling and anomalous dimensions occur even in the simple
Gaussian problem.
label: human

text: We present a comprehensive analysis of the high-energy emission of the X-ray binary system IGR~J16460+0849 utilizing data obtained from the INTEGRAL and Swift/XRT observatories. This study aims to elucidate the nature of the compact object in this system, which has remained ambiguous due to complexities in its observational characteristics. We focus on the implementation of simultaneous and complementary datasets to enhance temporal and spectral resolution. Through detailed spectral fitting, we observe the presence of significant variability in the hard X-ray emission, characterized by flares and absorption features, which indicate probable interactions between the compact object and the stellar wind of the binary's companion. We have identified a consistent periodic modulation suggestive of orbital influences on the emission behavior, possibly offering insights into the binary geometry and the mass transfer dynamics. Employing timing analysis, we uncover a distinct quasi-periodic oscillation, underpinning the hypothesis of a neutron star as the compact object. Our findings contribute to resolving the uncertainties pertaining to the broadband spectral properties and the accretion mechanisms involved. The methodology integrates calibrated data processing, spectral deconvolution, and phenomenological modeling, underscoring the synergy between INTEGRAL's wide field detection and Swift/XRT's localization precision. This multidisciplinary approach furnishes a richer context for interpreting high-energy phenomena in X-ray binaries, setting a foundation for future investigations leveraging evolving observational technologies. Our results demonstrate enhanced understanding of IGR~J16460+0849 and encourage further theoretical and observational studies to ascertain its definitive system parameters.

This dissertation is a study on the design and analysis of novel, optimal
routing and rate control algorithms in wireless, mobile communication networks.
Congestion control and routing algorithms upto now have been designed and
optimized for wired or wireless mesh networks. In those networks, optimal
algorithms (optimal in the sense that either the throughput is maximized or
delay is minimized, or the network operation cost is minimized) can be
engineered based on the classic time scale decomposition assumption that the
dynamics of the network are either fast enough so that these algorithms
essentially see the average or slow enough that any changes can be tracked to
allow the algorithms to adapt over time. However, as technological advancements
enable integration of ever more mobile nodes into communication networks, any
rate control or routing algorithms based, for example, on averaging out the
capacity of the wireless mobile link or tracking the instantaneous capacity
will perform poorly. The common element in our solution to engineering
efficient routing and rate control algorithms for mobile wireless networks is
to make the wireless mobile links seem as if they are wired or wireless links
to all but few nodes that directly see the mobile links (either the mobiles or
nodes that can transmit to or receive from the mobiles) through an appropriate
use of queuing structures at these selected nodes. This approach allows us to
design end-to-end rate control or routing algorithms for wireless mobile
networks so that neither averaging nor instantaneous tracking is necessary.

text:
The free-energy barrier of filling a spherical cavity having an inner wall of
various wettabiities is studied. The morphology and free energy of a
lens-shaped droplet are determined from the minimum of the free energy. The
effect of line tension on the free energy is also studied. Then, the
equilibrium contact angle of the droplet is determined from the generalized
Young's equation. By increasing the droplet volume within the spherical cavity,
the droplet morphology changes from spherical with an equilibrium contact angle
of $180^{\circ}$ to a lens with a convex meniscus, where the morphological
complete drying transition occurs. By further increasing the droplet volume,
the meniscus changes from convex to concave. Then, the lens-shaped droplet with
concave meniscus spreads over the whole inner wall resulting in an equilibrium
contact angle of $0^{\circ}$ to leave a spherical bubble, where the
morphological complete wetting transition occurs. Finally, the whole cavity is
filled with liquid. The free energy shows a barrier from complete drying to
complete wetting as a function of droplet volume, which corresponds to the
energy barrier between the Cassie and Wenzel state of the superhydrophobic
surface with spherical cavities. The free-energy maximum occurs when the
meniscus of the droplet becomes flat and it is given by an analytic formula.
The effect of line tension is expressed by the scaled line tension, and this
effect is largest at the free-energy maximum. The positive line tension
increases the free-energy maximum, which thus, increases the stability of the
Cassie superhydrophobic state, whereas the negative line tension destabilizes
the superhydrophobic state.

We study the quantum moment problem: Given a conditional probability
distribution together with some polynomial constraints, does there exist a
quantum state rho and a collection of measurement operators such that (i) the
probability of obtaining a particular outcome when a particular measurement is
performed on rho is specified by the conditional probability distribution, and
(ii) the measurement operators satisfy the constraints. For example, the
constraints might specify that some measurement operators must commute.
  We show that if an instance of the quantum moment problem is unsatisfiable,
then there exists a certificate of a particular form proving this. Our proof is
based on a recent result in algebraic geometry, the noncommutative
Positivstellensatz of Helton and McCullough [Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.,
356(9):3721, 2004].
  A special case of the quantum moment problem is to compute the value of
one-round multi-prover games with entangled provers. Under the conjecture that
the provers need only share states in finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, we
prove that a hierarchy of semidefinite programs similar to the one given by
Navascues, Pironio and Acin [Phys. Rev. Lett., 98:010401, 2007] converges to
the entangled value of the game. It follows that the class of languages
recognized by a multi-prover interactive proof system where the provers share
entanglement is recursive.

text: We present our findings on the effective implementation and application of the Multiplex PageRank algorithm, aimed at addressing the challenges of ranking nodes in complex networks characterized by multiple interdependent layers. Traditional PageRank algorithms fall short in scenarios where information flows across different interconnected networks. Our work systematically extends the classical PageRank framework to accommodate these multiplex structures, thereby allowing for a more nuanced understanding of node importance across layers.  Through rigorous experimentation on synthetic and real-world multi-layer networks, we demonstrate that our proposed Multiplex PageRank not only retains the core features of the original algorithm but also enhances accuracy in ranking nodes by taking into account their inter-layer connections and influences. We utilized an iterative computation methodology that efficiently integrates information from various layers, ensuring that the influence of a node is accurately reflected based on its accessibility to different resources within the network.  Our results indicate a significant improvement in ranking reliability and relevance, illustrated by comparative analyses against traditional PageRank metrics. Ultimately, this work not only contributes to the theoretical foundation of graph theory but also presents practical implications for applications in social network analysis, transport systems, and information dissemination frameworks. We advocate for the adoption of the Multiplex PageRank algorithm as a robust tool for researchers and practitioners seeking to analyze and interpret complex multi-layered systems more effectively.

text: We investigated the interplay between deformed distance duality relations and supernovae dimming, with a focus on resolving the long-standing discrepancy between these two fundamental concepts in cosmology. Our analysis revealed that the deformed distance duality relation, which is a modification of the standard Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) model, can be used to explain the observed supernovae dimming phenomenon in a consistent and coherent manner. By incorporating the deformed distance duality relation into our models, we were able to reproduce the observed dimming patterns of Type Ia supernovae, which are crucial for constraining the expansion history of the universe.  Our work attempted to address the problem of reconciling the deformed distance duality relation with the standard FLRW model, which has been a subject of debate in the cosmological community. We employed a combination of analytical and numerical methods to derive the deformed distance duality relation and to test its implications for supernovae dimming. Our key findings suggest that the deformed distance duality relation can be used to explain the observed dimming patterns of supernovae in a way that is consistent with the FLRW model, but with a crucial modification to the standard distance-redshift relation.  Our results have significant implications for our understanding of the expansion history of the universe and the nature of dark energy. The deformed distance duality relation provides a new framework for interpreting the observed dimming patterns of supernovae, which can be used to constrain models of dark energy and the expansion history of the universe. Furthermore, our work highlights the importance of considering alternative models of the universe, such as the deformed distance duality relation, in order to resolve long-standing discrepancies between different cosmological observations.

text: In this work, we explore the generation of the gluon mass in the presence of dynamical quarks within the context of the Landau-Ginzburg model. Utilizing a nonperturbative approach, we incorporate the effects of quark condensates on the gluon field, which results in a dynamically generated gluon mass. Our study is based on the lattice QCD data for the quark condensate and the gluon mass obtained from various numerical simulations. Through the analysis of the effective potential for the gluon field, we show that the presence of the quark condensate induces a nonzero vacuum expectation value for the gluon field, effectively generating a mass term. The dependence of the generated mass on the quark condensate is studied through the calculation of the gluon propagator and the mass gap. We find that the generated mass exhibits a logarithmic dependence on the quark condensate, suggesting a possible connection to the infrared slave boson mechanism. Our results offer a new perspective on the origin of the gluon mass and the role of dynamical quarks in the theory. By providing a consistent framework for the generation of the gluon mass in the presence of dynamical quarks, we contribute to the ongoing efforts to understand the nature of mass in quantum chromodynamics. Our approach can also be applied to other gauge theories, offering potential insights into the generation of mass in those theories as well. Further investigations are required to explore the implications of our findings and to test the robustness of the results against various perturbative and nonperturbative approaches.
label: machine

text: The abstract focuses on the algebraic Fourier reconstruction method applied to piecewise smooth functions. This method leverages the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) to accurately reconstruct signals that exhibit abrupt changes or discontinuities across their domain. The study aims to explore the efficiency and accuracy of algebraic Fourier techniques in handling such complex functions.  The methodology employed involves discretizing the continuous piecewise smooth function into segments where each segment can be represented by a simpler mathematical model. The DFT is then applied to each segment separately, utilizing the orthogonality property of the Fourier basis functions to capture the frequency content. The reconstructed signal is obtained by combining the individual Fourier coefficients with appropriate weights assigned based on the segment boundaries.  Key findings indicate that the proposed algebraic Fourier reconstruction technique provides superior results compared to traditional Fourier methods, particularly in terms of preserving sharp transitions and minimizing artifacts around discontinuities. The method demonstrated robust performance even when dealing with functions characterized by multiple abrupt changes, showing promise for real-world applications such as image processing and seismic data analysis.  In conclusion, the research highlights the effectiveness of algebraic Fourier reconstruction in accurately modeling piecewise smooth functions, offering a viable alternative to conventional Fourier approaches. Future work will focus on extending the methodology to more complex scenarios and optimizing computational efficiency.

text:
The optical properties of graphene are made unique by the linear band
structure and the vanishing density of states at the Dirac point. It has been
proposed that even in the absence of a semiconducting bandgap, a relaxation
bottleneck at the Dirac point may allow for population inversion and lasing at
arbitrarily long wavelengths. Furthermore, efficient carrier multiplication by
impact ionization has been discussed in the context of light harvesting
applications. However, all these effects are difficult to test quantitatively
by measuring the transient optical properties alone, as these only indirectly
reflect the energy and momentum dependent carrier distributions. Here, we use
time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy with femtosecond extreme
ultra-violet (EUV) pulses at 31.5 eV photon energy to directly probe the
non-equilibrium response of Dirac electrons near the K-point of the Brillouin
zone. In lightly hole-doped epitaxial graphene samples, we explore excitation
in the mid- and near-infrared, both below and above the minimum photon energy
for direct interband transitions. While excitation in the mid-infrared results
only in heating of the equilibrium carrier distribution, interband excitations
give rise to population inversion, suggesting that terahertz lasing may be
possible. However, in neither excitation regime do we find indication for
carrier multiplication, questioning the applicability of graphene for light
harvesting. Time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy in the EUV emerges as the
technique of choice to assess the suitability of new materials for
optoelectronics, providing quantitatively accurate measurements of
non-equilibrium carriers at all energies and wavevectors.
label: human

text:
One of the main issues affecting the Italian NHS is the healthcare deficit:
according to current agreements between the Italian State and its Regions,
public funding of regional NHS is now limited to the amount of regional deficit
and is subject to previous assessment of strict adherence to constraint on
regional healthcare balance sheet. Many Regions with previously uncontrolled
healthcare deficit have now to plan their "Piano di Rientro" (PdR) and submit
it for the approval of the Italian Ministry of Economy and Finances. Those
Regions that will fail to comply to deficit constraints will suffer cuts on
their public NHS financing. A smart Health Planning can make sure health
spending is managed appropriately. Indeed a restructuring of the Italian
healthcare system has recently been enforced in order to cope for the clumsy
regional healthcare balance sheets. Half of total Italian healthcare
expenditure is accounted by hospital services which therefore configure as one
of the main restructuring targets. This paper provides a general framework for
planning a re-engineering of a hospital network. This framework is made of
economic, legal and healthcare constraints. We apply the general framework to
the particular case of Puglia region and explore a set of re-engineered
solutions which to different extent could help solve the difficult dilemma:
cutting costs without worsening the delivery of public healthcare services.
label: human

text: This research explores the use of neutral genomic regions to refine models of recent rapid human population growth. Historically, demographic studies have relied heavily on genetic markers known to be under selective pressure, which can lead to inaccuracies when inferring population dynamics. By focusing on neutral genomic regions that have not been subject to natural selection, this study aims to provide a more accurate representation of past population expansions. Utilizing genome-wide data from diverse populations, the methodology involves identifying and analyzing regions with low variability across samples. Key findings indicate that these neutral regions show distinct patterns of linkage disequilibrium (LD) that correlate with the timing and extent of population growth events. The analysis suggests that while selective sweeps may have occurred during the same period, the presence of significant LD in neutral regions provides additional evidence for rapid population growth. The study concludes by proposing that integrating neutral genomic regions into demographic models could significantly enhance our understanding of human population history and migration patterns.
label: machine

text:
Based on over 3000 BV images of M4 collected in years 1995-2009 we obtain
light curves of 22 variables, 10 of which are newly detected objects. We
identify four detached eclipsing binaries and eight contact binaries. Accurate
periods are found for all but two variables. Nineteen variables are
proper-motion members of the cluster, and the remaining three are field stars.
Five variables are optical counterparts of X-ray sources. For one of the
variables unassociated with X-ray sources we report a flare lasting for about
90 min and reaching an amplitude of 0.11 mag in V. One of the new contact
binaries has a record-low mass ratio q=0.06. Another four such systems show
season-to season luminosity variations probably related to magnetic activity
cycles, whose lengths are surprisingly similar to that of the solar cycle
despite a huge difference in rotational periods. The location of contact
binaries on the color-magnitude diagram of M4 strongly suggests that at least
in globular clusters the principal factor enabling EW systems to form from
close but detached binaries is stellar evolution. We identify 46 blue and
yellow stragglers in M4 and discuss their properties. We also derive a map of
the differential extinction in the central part of M4, and determine the
reddening of a selected reference region, E(B-V)= 0.392 mag.
