text: The study of exoplanet formation and evolution is crucial in understanding the diversity of planetary systems. Hot Jupiters, a class of massive, close-in gas giants, exhibit significant stellar obliquity trends, which refer to the tilt of the planet's orbital axis relative to the host star's rotational axis. These trends are thought to be influenced by tidal interactions between the planet and the star, leading to a reconfiguration of the planet's orbit and the star's rotation. However, the exact mechanisms driving these tidal-driven obliquity trends are still not well understood.  This study aims to investigate the tidal origin of hot Jupiter stellar obliquity trends, focusing on the interplay between planetary tidal heating, stellar rotation, and the resulting orbital evolution. We employed a combination of numerical simulations and semi-analytical models to explore the effects of tidal interactions on the orbital evolution of hot Jupiters. Our results indicate that tidal heating can lead to a significant increase in the planet's orbital eccentricity, which in turn drives the star's rotation and the planet's orbital inclination. We also find that the tidal-driven obliquity trends are more pronounced in systems with high stellar masses and radii, suggesting a correlation between tidal interactions and the planet's orbital properties.  Our findings suggest that tidal heating plays a crucial role in shaping the stellar obliquity trends of hot Jupiters, and that these interactions can have a significant impact on the long-term evolution of planetary systems. The results of this study provide new insights into the complex interplay between planetary and stellar evolution, and highlight the importance of considering tidal interactions in the study of exoplanet formation and evolution.

Several years back Angliker et al [Chem. Phys. Lett. 1982, 87, 208] predicted
nonacene to be the first linear acene with the triplet state $1^{3}B_{2u}$ as
the ground state, instead of the singlet $1^{1}A_{g}$ state. However, contrary
to that prediction, in a recent experimental work T\"onshoff and Bettinger [
Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2010, 49, 4125] demonstrated that nonacene has a singlet
ground state. Motivated by this experimental finding, we decided to perform a
systematic theoretical investigation of the nature of the ground, and the
low-lying excited states of long acenes, with an emphasis on the
singlet-triplet gap, starting from naphthalene, all the way up to decacene.
Methodology adopted in our work is based upon Pariser-Parr-Pople model (PPP)
Hamiltonian, along with large-scale multi-reference singles-doubles
configuration interaction (MRSDCI) approach. Our results predict that even
though the singlet-triplet gap decreases with the increasing conjugation
length, nevertheless, it remains finite till decacene, thus providing no
evidence of the predicted singlet-triplet crossover. We also analyze the nature
of many-particle wavefunction of the correlated singlet ground state and find
that the longer acenes exhibit tendency towards a open-shell singlet ground
state. Moreover, when we compare the experimental absorption spectra of
octacene and nonacene with their calculated singlet and triplet absorption
spectra, we observe excellent agreement for the singlet case. Hence, the
optical absorption results also confirm the singlet nature of the ground state
for longer acenes.

text: We present our measurements of the decay B(Ds+ → e+ ν) and the decay constant fDs utilizing 600 pb⁻¹ of e⁺e⁻ annihilation data collected near the 4170 MeV energy region. This study aims to address the challenging determination of the D_s decay constant, which plays a crucial role in understanding heavy meson physics and the framework of the Standard Model. We employ a robust analysis methodology that includes event selection based on particle identification criteria and kinematic fits to enhance signal-to-background ratios. We utilize advanced fitting techniques to extract signal yields from the data while minimizing systematic uncertainties associated with background contributions.  Our results yield a branching fraction B(Ds+ → e+ ν) = (5.78 ± 0.23(stat) ± 0.38(syst)) × 10⁻², which is consistent with theoretical predictions and previous experimental measurements. Furthermore, we extract the decay constant fDs = 250 ± 11 MeV, offering a significant advancement in our understanding of heavy quark physics. The methodologies we developed, including the optimization of event reconstruction algorithms and statistical fitting frameworks, contribute to our field's capabilities in analyzing complex decay processes. This work not only reinforces existing theoretical models but also enhances the precision in the measurements of decay constants that are pivotal in future flavor physics studies. Our findings pave the way for deeper investigations into the dynamics of charm mesons and their implications for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

Precision tests of the Standard Model in the Strong and Electroweak sectors
play an important role, among the physics goals of LHC experiments. Because of
the nature of proton-proton processes, observables based on the measurement of
the direction and energy of leptons provide the most precise signatures.
  In the present paper, we concentrate on the angular distribution of leptons
from W to l nu decays in the lepton-pair rest-frame. The vector nature of the
intermediate state imposes that distributions are to a good precision described
by spherical polynomials of at most second order. We argue, that contrary to
general belief often expressed in the literature, the full set of angular
coefficients can be measured experimentally, despite the presence in the final
state of neutrino escaping detection. There is thus no principle difference
with respect to the phenomenology of the Z/gamma to l^+ l^- Drell-Yan process.
  We show also, that with the proper choice of the coordinate frames, only one
coefficient in this polynomial decomposition remains sizable, even in the
presence of one or more high p_T jets. The necessary stochastic choice of the
frames relies on probabilities independent from any coupling constants. In this
way, electroweak effects (dominated by the V-A nature of W couplings to
fermions) can be better separated from the ones of strong interactions. The
separation is convenient for the measurements interpretation.

Microtubules, major elements of the cell skeleton are, most of the time, well
organized in vivo, but they can also show self-organizing behaviors in time
and/or space in purified solutions in vitro. Theoretical studies and models
based on the concepts of collective dynamics in complex systems,
reaction-diffusion processes and emergent phenomena were proposed to explain
some of these behaviors. In the particular case of microtubule spatial
self-organization, it has been advanced that microtubules could behave like
ants, self-organizing by 'talking to each other' by way of hypothetic (because
never observed) concentrated chemical trails of tubulin that are expected to be
released by their disassembling ends. Deterministic models based on this idea
yielded indeed like-looking spatio-temporal self-organizing behaviors.
Nevertheless the question remains of whether microscopic tubulin trails
produced by individual or bundles of several microtubules are intense enough to
allow microtubule self-organization at a macroscopic level. In the present
work, by simulating the diffusion of tubulin in microtubule solutions at the
microscopic scale, we measure the shape and intensity of tubulin trails and
discuss about the assumption of microtubule self-organization due to the
production of chemical trails by disassembling microtubules. We show that the
tubulin trails produced by individual microtubules or small microtubule arrays
are very weak and not elongated even at very high reactive rates. Although the
variations of concentration due to such trails are not significant compared to
natural fluctuations of the concentration of tubuline in the chemical
environment, the study shows that heterogeneities of biochemical composition
can form due to microtubule disassembly. They could become significant when
produced by numerous microtubule ends located in the same place. Their possible
formation could play a role in certain conditions of reaction. In particular,
it gives a mesoscopic basis to explain the collective dynamics observed in
excitable microtubule solutions showing the propagation of concentration waves
of microtubules at the millimeter scale, although we doubt that individual
microtubules or bundles can behave like molecular ants.

text: In this study, we revisit the framework of Lorentz violation within the context of Hořava gravity, aiming to clarify its theoretical implications and potential physical consequences. Hořava gravity, as a non-relativistic formulation of quantum gravity, inherently breaks Lorentz symmetry to achieve power-counting renormalizability. Our investigation examines the consistency of such symmetry breaking with current experimental bounds and cosmological observations. We utilize a modified action that incorporates higher derivative terms and anisotropic scaling, focusing on the UV completion of gravity. Through detailed analysis, we explore the theoretical landscape to determine constraints on Lorentz-violating parameters within the model. The methodology involves a perturbative approach, investigating metric perturbations and their dispersion relations in various gravitational regimes. Our results demonstrate that despite the inherent Lorentz violation, the theory can be consistent with low-energy effective field theory approaches, provided the Lorentz-violating parameters fall within an acceptable range. Specifically, we find that significant deviations from Lorentz invariance occur predominantly at high energy scales, suggesting negligible effects at observable scales, thus aligning the model with existing experimental data. Furthermore, our study provides insights into potential phenomenological signatures that may distinguish Hořava gravity from other quantum gravity candidates. We conclude that revisiting Lorentz violations in this framework not only enhances our understanding of the quantum gravity landscape but also aids in refining theoretical models in alignment with empirical evidence.

text: We present the initial findings of the VORTEX project, a multidisciplinary research initiative focused on the investigation of vortex dynamics in various environmental and engineering contexts. Through a series of experiments conducted in a controlled laboratory setting, we successfully generated and characterized vortices of varying intensities and scales, providing valuable insights into the fundamental physical mechanisms governing their formation and evolution. Furthermore, our numerical simulations enabled us to investigate the impact of vortex-geometry interactions on flow dynamics, revealing novel insights into the complex interplay between vortex dynamics and surface topography.   The results obtained through the VORTEX project demonstrate the critical role of vortex dynamics in various engineering applications, including fluid-structure interaction, aerodynamics, and heat transfer. Our findings have significant implications for the design and optimization of complex systems, such as wind turbines, aircraft, and biomedical devices, where vortex dynamics play a crucial role in determining performance and efficiency. As the VORTEX project continues to unfold, we anticipate that our research will contribute substantially to the development of more sophisticated models and predictive tools for vortex dynamics, ultimately informing the design of innovative and efficient systems in a wide range of fields.

Once the fractional quantum Hall (FQH) state for a finite size system is put
on the surface of a cylinder, the distance between the two ends with open
boundary conditions can be tuned as varying the aspect ratio $\gamma$. It
scales linearly as increasing the system size and therefore has a larger
adjustable range than that on disk. The previous study of the quasi-hole
tunneling amplitude on disk in Ref.~\cite{Zk2011} indicates that the tunneling
amplitudes have a scaling behavior as a function of the tunneling distance and
the scaling exponents are related to the scaling dimension and the charge of
the transported quasiparticles. However, the scaling behaviors poorly due to
the narrow range of the tunneling distance on disk. Here we systematically
study the quasiparticle tunneling amplitudes of the Laughlin state in the
cylinder geometry which shows a much better scaling behavior. Especially, there
are some corssover behaviors at two length scales when the two open edges are
close to each other. These lengths are also reflected in the bipartite
entanglement and the electron Green's function as either a singularity or a
crossover. These two critical length scales of the edge-edge distance,
$L_x^{c_1}$ and $L_x^{c_2}$, are found to be related to the dimension reduction
and back scattering point respectively.

The first stars and quasars are known sources of hard ionizing radiation in
the first billion years of the Universe. We examine the joint effects of X-rays
and hard UV radiation from such first-light sources on the hydrogen and helium
reionization of the intergalactic medium (IGM) at early times, and the
associated heating. We study the growth and evolution of individual HII, HeII
and HeIII regions around early galaxies with first stars and/or QSO
populations. We find that in the presence of helium-ionizing radiation, X-rays
may not dominate the ionization and thermal history of the IGM at redshifts, z,
of 10-20, contributing relatively modest increases to IGM ionization, and
heating up to about 10^3--10^5 K in IGM temperatures. We also calculate the 21
cm signal expected from a number of scenarios with metal-free starbursts and
quasars at these redshifts. The peak values for the spin temperature reach
about 10^4 to 10^5 K in such cases. The maximum values for the 21 cm brightness
temperature are around 30-40 mK in emission, while the net values of the 21 cm
absorption signal range from about a few to 60 mK on scales of 0.01-1 Mpc. We
find that the 21 cm signature of X-ray versus UV ionization could be distinct,
with the emission signal expected from X-rays alone occurring at smaller scales
than that from UV radiation, resulting from the inherently different spatial
scales at which X-ray and UV ionization/heating manifest. This difference is
time-dependent, and becomes harder to distinguish with an increasing X-ray
contribution to the total ionizing photon production. Such differing
scale-dependent contributions from X-ray and UV photons may therefore "blur"
the 21 cm signature of the percolation of ionized bubbles around early halos
(depending on whether a cosmic X-ray or UV background built up first), and
affect the interpretation of 21 cm data constraints on reionization.

text: Scratch iridescence is a phenomenon observed on surfaces with diffractive structures, characterized by colorful patterns resulting from light interference. This study aims to explore the wave-optical rendering of such surfaces to understand the intricacies of scratch iridescence. The methodology involves numerical simulations and modeling of light interactions with diffractive surface structures to analyze the behavior of diffracted light waves. Key findings reveal the role of surface topology in generating specific iridescent patterns and the influence of incident light angles on the visibility of scratch iridescence. Additionally, the study investigates the impact of surface parameters, such as groove depth and spacing, on the iridescent coloration produced. The results highlight the complex interplay between surface structure and light properties in scratch iridescence generation. In conclusion, this research advances our knowledge of how diffractive surface structures lead to scratch iridescence, offering valuable insights for designing surfaces with controllable optical effects in various applications.

text: Our work presents an all-optical three-dimensional spatio-temporal correlator utilizing a multiphoton atomic system for automatic event recognition. By exploiting the unique properties of the multiphoton atomic system, we have successfully demonstrated the capability to correlate complex spatio-temporal patterns in three dimensions using only optical means. Our correlator design aims to address the challenge of automatic event recognition in real-time by efficiently processing vast amounts of spatio-temporal data without the need for electronic conversion.  The results of our study show that the proposed correlator achieves high accuracy in event recognition tasks while maintaining fast processing speeds, making it suitable for real-time applications. Key to our methodology is the use of multiphoton interactions in the atomic system to encode and process spatio-temporal information, enabling the correlator to identify and differentiate between various events based on their unique spatio-temporal signatures. By leveraging the advantages of an all-optical approach, we offer a promising solution for rapid event recognition tasks in diverse fields such as image processing, surveillance, and pattern recognition. This research contributes to the advancement of optical information processing techniques by harnessing the capabilities of multiphoton atomic systems for complex spatio-temporal correlational tasks.

When using Wannier functions to study the electronic structure of
multi-parameter Hamiltonians $H^{(\boldsymbol k,\bf \lambda)}$ carrying a
dependence on crystal momentum $\boldsymbol k$ and an additional periodic
parameter $\bf\lambda$, one usually constructs several sets of Wannier
functions for a set of values of $\bf\lambda$. We present the concept of higher
dimensional Wannier functions (HDWFs), which provide a minimal and accurate
description of the electronic structure of multi-parameter Hamiltonians based
on a single set of HDWFs. The obstacle of non-orthogonality of Bloch functions
at different $\bf\lambda$ is overcome by introducing an auxiliary real space,
which is reciprocal to the parameter $\bf\lambda$. We derive a generalized
interpolation scheme and emphasize the essential conceptual and computational
simplifications in using the formalism, for instance, in the evaluation of
linear response coefficients. We further implement the necessary machinery to
construct HDWFs from ab initio within the full-potential linearized augmented
plane-wave method (FLAPW). We apply our implementation to accurately
interpolate the Hamiltonian of a one-dimensional magnetic chain of Mn atoms in
two important cases of $\bf\lambda$: (i) the spin-spiral vector $\boldsymbol
q$, and (ii) the direction of the ferromagnetic magnetization $\hat{\boldsymbol
m}$. Using the generalized interpolation of the energy, we extract the
corresponding values of magneto-crystalline anisotropy energy, Heisenberg
exchange constants, and spin stiffness, which compare very well with the values
obtained from direct first principles calculations. For toy models we
demonstrate that the method of HDWFs can also be used in applications such as
the virtual crystal approximation, ferroelectric polarization and spin torques.

text: Core collapse supernovae are crucial astronomical events that produce gravitational wave signals with unique features. Understanding the influence of model parameters on predicting these signals is paramount for accurate astrophysical interpretations. This research aims to investigate how varying model parameters, such as stellar mass, metallicity, and equation of state, impact the predicted gravitational wave signals from stellar core collapse events.   To achieve this, a series of numerical simulations using state-of-the-art astrophysical models will be conducted. These simulations will explore a range of parameter values to assess their individual and collective effects on the resulting gravitational wave signatures. By analyzing the simulated data, specific relationships between model parameters and predicted waveforms will be identified.  Key findings indicate that variations in model parameters significantly alter the characteristics of gravitational wave signals, such as peak frequency and amplitude. Interestingly, certain parameter combinations lead to distinct waveform patterns, suggesting a complex interplay between stellar properties and gravitational wave emissions during core collapse events.  In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of considering model parameters when predicting gravitational wave signals from stellar core collapse. By elucidating these interdependencies, our findings contribute to refining astrophysical models and enhancing the interpretative power of gravitational wave observations in studying stellar evolution.

Many scientific and engineering fields involve analyzing network data. For
document networks, relational topic models (RTMs) provide a probabilistic
generative process to describe both the link structure and document contents,
and they have shown promise on predicting network structures and discovering
latent topic representations. However, existing RTMs have limitations in both
the restricted model expressiveness and incapability of dealing with imbalanced
network data. To expand the scope and improve the inference accuracy of RTMs,
this paper presents three extensions: 1) unlike the common link likelihood with
a diagonal weight matrix that allows the-same-topic interactions only, we
generalize it to use a full weight matrix that captures all pairwise topic
interactions and is applicable to asymmetric networks; 2) instead of doing
standard Bayesian inference, we perform regularized Bayesian inference
(RegBayes) with a regularization parameter to deal with the imbalanced link
structure issue in common real networks and improve the discriminative ability
of learned latent representations; and 3) instead of doing variational
approximation with strict mean-field assumptions, we present collapsed Gibbs
sampling algorithms for the generalized relational topic models by exploring
data augmentation without making restricting assumptions. Under the generic
RegBayes framework, we carefully investigate two popular discriminative loss
functions, namely, the logistic log-loss and the max-margin hinge loss.
Experimental results on several real network datasets demonstrate the
significance of these extensions on improving the prediction performance, and
the time efficiency can be dramatically improved with a simple fast
approximation method.

text: Signed graphs are graph structures where edges carry a positive or negative sign. Edge-coloured graphs, on the other hand, have edges coloured with distinct hues. Homomorphisms between these graph structures play a crucial role in revealing similarities and differences. In this study, we explore the intricacy of homomorphisms between signed graphs and edge-coloured graphs.  To begin with, we provide a comprehensive background on signed graphs, edge-coloured graphs, and the concept of homomorphisms. We then discuss existing research on homomorphisms between these structures, highlighting the complexities and challenges involved.  Our objective is to investigate signed graph and edge-coloured graph homomorphisms through theoretical analysis and computational experiments. Specifically, we focus on developing efficient algorithms to determine the existence of homomorphisms between these graph structures.  The methodology of our study involves using a combination of theoretical analysis and computational simulations. We first present a theoretical framework for the analysis of signed graph and edge-coloured graph homomorphisms, followed by the development of an algorithmic approach based on this framework. We extensively test our algorithms using real-world datasets to evaluate their efficiency and effectiveness.  Our key findings reveal that the problem of determining the existence of homomorphisms between signed graphs and edge-coloured graphs is NP-complete. We propose an approximation algorithm, which, while not guaranteed to find the optimal solution, significantly reduces the computational time compared to exhaustive search techniques.  We conclude by summarising our findings and outlining potential avenues for future research in the field, including investigating the application of signed graph and edge-coloured graph homomorphisms in various domains such as social networks and bioinformatics. Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of the intricacies of graph homomorphisms and their applications in real-world scenarios.  In this abstract, we discuss the research on homomorphisms between signed graphs and edge-coloured graphs, focusing on the background, objective, methodology, key findings, and conclusion. The study aims to investigate the complexities of homomorphisms between these graph structures through theoretical analysis and computational experiments. The findings reveal that determining the existence of homomorphisms between signed graphs and edge-coloured graphs is NP-complete, and an approximation algorithm is proposed to address this challenge. The conclusion outlines potential future research directions in this field.

We consider a composite Higgs model embedded into a Grand Unified Theory(GUT)
based on the E_6 gauge group. The phenomenological viability of this E_6
inspired composite Higgs model (E6CHM) implies that standard model (SM)
elementary fermions with different baryon or lepton number should stem from
different 27 representations of E_6. We present a six-dimensional orbifold GUT
model in which the E_6 gauge symmetry is broken to the SM gauge group so that
the appropriate splitting of the bulk 27-plets takes place. In this model the
strongly coupled sector is localised on one of the branes and possesses an
SU(6) global symmetry that contains the SU(3)_C\times SU(2)_W\times U(1)_Y
subgroup. In this case the approximate gauge coupling unification can be
attained if the right-handed top quark is a composite state and the elementary
sector involves extra exotic matter beyond the SM which ensures anomaly
cancellation. The breakdown of the approximate SU(6) symmetry at low energies
in this model results in a set of the pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone states which
include a Higgs doublet and scalar colour triplet. We discuss the generation of
the masses of the SM fermions in the E6CHM. The presence of the TeV scale
vector-like exotic quarks and scalar colour triplet may provide spectacular new
physics signals that can be observed at the LHC.

text: In this study, we explore the evolving geometries of spacetime in the framework of General Relativity (GR). Specifically, we focus on the dynamics of spatial and temporal curvature in a simple, but non-trivial, model system. Our approach is based on the formalism of Riemannian geometry and its application to the evolution of spatial metrics. We consider an isotropic and homogeneous Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) spacetime filled with a perfect fluid, and analyze its evolution from an initially flat, homogeneous, and isotropic state. By employing a set of conformally related metrics, we derive a set of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that govern the time evolution of the spatial curvature scalar. Our main results reveal a transition from a de Sitter-like expanding phase to a matter dominated contracting phase, and vice versa, depending on the initial values of the matter density and spatial curvature. We argue that this behavior is a consequence of the interplay between the dynamics of matter fields and the geometric evolution of the spacetime. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the evolution of spatial curvature can be described in terms of a bouncing scenario, where the expansion and contraction phases are connected by a phase of zero spatial curvature. Our findings provide new insights into the nature of the expanding universe and suggest that the interplay between matter fields and the geometry of spacetime may play a crucial role in shaping its dynamical evolution. This study builds upon previous works on the dynamics of spatially homogeneous and isotropic models in GR, and extends them by incorporating the evolution of spatial curvature using the formalism of Riemannian geometry. Our analysis highlights the importance of geometric considerations in understanding the dynamics of spatially homogeneous models and the role of matter fields in shaping the evolution of the universe.

We report initial results from a quasi-simultaneous X-ray/optical observing
campaign targeting V4046 Sgr, a close, synchronous-rotating classical T Tauri
star (CTTS) binary in which both components are actively accreting. V4046 Sgr
is a strong X-ray source, with the X-rays mainly arising from high-density (n_e
~ 10^(11-12) cm^(-3)) plasma at temperatures of 3-4 MK. Our multiwavelength
campaign aims to simultaneously constrain the properties of this X-ray emitting
plasma, the large scale magnetic field, and the accretion geometry. In this
paper, we present key results obtained via time-resolved X-ray grating spectra,
gathered in a 360 ks XMM-Newton observation that covered 2.2 system rotations.
We find that the emission lines produced by this high-density plasma display
periodic flux variations with a measured period, 1.22+/-0.01 d, that is
precisely half that of the binary star system (2.42 d). The observed rotational
modulation can be explained assuming that the high-density plasma occupies
small portions of the stellar surfaces, corotating with the stars, and that the
high-density plasma is not azimuthally symmetrically distributed with respect
to the rotational axis of each star. These results strongly support models in
which high-density, X-ray-emitting CTTS plasma is material heated in accretion
shocks, located at the base of accretion flows tied to the system by magnetic
field lines.

We consider a nearest-neighbor random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ whose probability
$\omega_x(j)$ to jump to the right from site $x$ depends not only on $x$ but
also on the number of prior visits $j$ to $x$. The collection
$(\omega_x(j))_{x\in\mathbb{Z},n\ge 0}$ is sometimes called the "cookie
environment" due to the following informal interpretation. Upon each visit to a
site the walker eats a cookie from the cookie stack at that site and chooses
the transition probabilities according to the "strength" of the cookie eaten.
We assume that the cookie stacks are i.i.d. and that the cookie "strengths"
within the stack $(\omega_x(j))_{j\ge 0}$ at site $x$ follow a finite state
Markov chain. Thus, the environment at each site is dynamic, but it evolves
according to the local time of the walk at each site rather than the original
random walk time.
  The model admits two different regimes, critical or non-critical, depending
on whether the expected probability to jump to the right (or left) under the
invariant measure for the Markov chain is equal to $1/2$ or not. We show that
in the non-critical regime the walk is always transient, has non-zero linear
speed, and satisfies the classical central limit theorem. The critical regime
allows for a much more diverse behavior. We give necessary and sufficient
conditions for recurrence/transience and ballisticity of the walk in the
critical regime as well as a complete characterization of limit laws under the
averaged measure in the transient case.
  The setting considered in this paper generalizes the previously studied model
with periodic cookie stacks. Our results on ballisticity and limit theorems are
new even for the periodic model.

text: We investigate the phenomenon of phase synchronization in instrumental music signals, aiming to elucidate the underlying mechanisms that govern rhythmic coherence among musicians. Our study addresses the problem of quantifying synchronization levels within complex musical ensembles, which pose significant challenges due to the variability in timing and dynamics inherent in live performances. We employ a combination of time-frequency analysis and phase coherence metrics, utilizing techniques such as Hilbert transform and the mutual information approach to measure phase relationships among overlapping musical signals.   Through extensive experimental analysis of various instrumental compositions, we reveal that the degree of synchronization not only enhances musical richness but also significantly contributes to perceived aesthetic qualities. Our results indicate that musicians tend to intuitively align their playing through both explicit cues and implicit temporal structures. We observe a clear correlation between phase locking and the participants' musical training, suggesting that experienced musicians exhibit superior synchronization capabilities. Furthermore, we introduce a novel metric, the Synchronization Index (SI), which quantifies the synchronization levels across different musical styles.   The implications of our findings extend to the fields of music theory, psychology, and performance practice, offering new insights into how musicians collaboratively create cohesive musical experiences. By bridging the gap between quantitative analysis and artistic interpretation, we enhance the understanding of musical interactions, thereby enriching the dialogue surrounding the intricate dynamics of ensemble performances.

An Equation of State (\textit{EoS}) closes the set of fluid equations.
Although an ideal EoS with a constant \textit{adiabatic index} $\Gamma$ is the
preferred choice due to its simplistic implementation, many astrophysical fluid
simulations may benefit from a more sophisticated treatment that can account
for diverse chemical processes. Here, we first review the basic thermodynamic
principles of a gas mixture in terms of its thermal and caloric EoS by
including effects like ionization, dissociation as well as temperature
dependent degrees of freedom such as molecular vibrations and rotations. The
formulation is revisited in the context of plasmas that are either in
equilibrium conditions (local thermodynamic- or collisional excitation-
equilibria) or described by non-equilibrium chemistry coupled to optically thin
radiative cooling. We then present a numerical implementation of thermally
ideal gases obeying a more general caloric EoS with non-constant adiabatic
index in Godunov-type numerical schemes.We discuss the necessary modifications
to the Riemann solver and to the conversion between total energy and pressure
(or vice-versa) routinely invoked in Godunov-type schemes. We then present two
different approaches for computing the EoS.The first one employs root-finder
methods and it is best suited for EoS in analytical form. The second one leans
on lookup table and interpolation and results in a more computationally
efficient approach although care must be taken to ensure thermodynamic
consistency. A number of selected benchmarks demonstrate that the employment of
a non-ideal EoS can lead to important differences in the solution when the
temperature range is $500-10^4$ K where dissociation and ionization occur. The
implementation of selected EoS introduces additional computational costs
although using lookup table methods can significantly reduce the overhead by a
factor $3\sim 4$.

text: Endothelial cells play a crucial role in regulating vascular function, particularly through nitric oxide (NO) production, which is essential for maintaining vascular homeostasis. Shear stress, a mechanical force exerted by blood flow, has been shown to stimulate NO production in endothelial cells. This research aims to investigate the mechanisms underlying shear-induced NO production by endothelial cells.   Through a series of in vitro experiments using endothelial cell culture models exposed to controlled shear stress levels, NO production levels were measured and compared under varying conditions. Additionally, the involvement of specific signaling pathways and mechanotransduction mechanisms in shear-induced NO production was explored using pharmacological inhibitors and genetic manipulations.  Key findings demonstrate that shear stress significantly enhances NO production in endothelial cells in a dose-dependent manner. Furthermore, specific pathways such as the PI3K/Akt and eNOS signaling pathways were found to be crucial for mediating shear-induced NO production. These results provide valuable insights into the mechanobiology of endothelial cells and may have implications for understanding vascular diseases such as atherosclerosis and hypertension.  In conclusion, this study elucidates the importance of shear stress in regulating NO production by endothelial cells and highlights the signaling pathways involved in this mechanotransduction process. Further research in this area could lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies targeting endothelial dysfunction in cardiovascular diseases.

text: We investigate the intricate topology and features of quantum control landscapes, aiming to enhance the efficiency of optimization processes in quantum systems. Our work addresses the significant challenge of navigating complex, high-dimensional parameter spaces, which often impede the realization of optimal control strategies in quantum operations. We employ advanced computational techniques to analyze and visualize the geometric properties of these landscapes, revealing critical insights into the nature of local minima and saddle points that characterize typical quantum control problems. Through rigorous numerical simulations, we identify specific topological features that correlate with optimization performance, establishing a framework for enhancing control fidelity. Furthermore, we explore the scaling behavior of optimization algorithms in relation to key landscape attributes, which informs the development of more efficient strategies for quantum state manipulation and gate implementation. Our findings not only elucidate the fundamental structure of quantum control landscapes but also provide practical guidelines for optimizing quantum operations, thereby contributing to the broader field of quantum computing and information processing. The integration of topology with optimization methodologies fosters a deeper understanding of quantum dynamics and offers a pathway toward realizing robust quantum technologies. We anticipate that our results will inspire further research in quantum control theory, leading to improved algorithms and enhanced capabilities in the manipulation of quantum systems.

Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko was selected in 2003 as the new target of the
Rosetta mission. It has since been the subject of a detailed campaign of
observations to characterise its nucleus and activity. Here we present
previously unpublished data taken around the start of activity of the comet in
2007/8, before its last perihelion passage. We constrain the time of the start
of activity, and combine this with other data taken throughout the comet's
orbit to make predictions for its likely behaviour during 2014/5 while Rosetta
is operating. A considerable difficulty in observing 67P during the past years
has been its position against crowded fields towards the Galactic centre for
much of the time. The 2007/8 data presented here were particularly difficult,
and the comet will once again be badly placed for Earth-based observations in
2014/5. We make use of the difference image analysis (DIA) technique, which is
commonly used in variable star and exoplanet research, to remove background
sources and extract images of the comet. In addition, we reprocess a large
quantity of archival images of 67P covering its full orbit, to produce a
heliocentric lightcurve. By using consistent reduction, measurement and
calibration techniques we generate a remarkably clean lightcurve, which can be
used to measure a brightness-distance relationship and to predict the future
brightness of the comet. We determine that the comet was active around November
2007, at a pre-perihelion distance from the Sun of 4.3 AU. The comet will reach
this distance, and probably become active again, in March 2014. We find that
the dust brightness can be well described by Af\rho \propto r^-3.2
pre-perihelion and r^-3.4 post-perihelion, and that the comet has a higher
dust-to-gas ratio than average. A model fit to the photometric data suggests
that only a small fraction (1.4%) of the surface is active.

text: The merger of neutron stars with black holes is a complex astrophysical event that can generate a variety of observable phenomena, contributing significantly to our understanding of the universe. The study of such mergers requires sophisticated simulations to model the dynamics accurately.   This research aims to simulate the merger of polytropic neutron stars with black holes using the Paczynski-Wiita potential, a widely recognized gravitational potential describing the geometry around black holes. By employing this potential in the simulations, we seek to investigate the gravitational interactions and the subsequent outcomes of such mergers.   The simulations are conducted using numerical techniques to solve the equations of general relativity governing the dynamics of polytropic neutron star-black hole systems. By incorporating the Paczynski-Wiita potential into the simulations, we can accurately model the gravitational effects and track the evolution of the systems during the merger process.   Our results reveal important insights into the gravitational interactions and the impact of the Paczynski-Wiita potential on the merger dynamics of polytropic neutron star-black hole systems. We observe the formation of accretion disks, gravitational wave emissions, and potential electromagnetic signatures during the merger process.   The study provides valuable information on the merger dynamics of polytropic neutron stars with black holes when using the Paczynski-Wiita potential in simulations. These findings contribute to the broader understanding of astrophysical phenomena and have implications for future observational studies of neutron star-black hole mergers in the universe.

text: We report the discovery of a new population of planetary nebulae (PNe) in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), based on the analysis of the latest and deepest observations with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the Very Large Telescope (VLT). This new population, hereafter referred to as the LMC Population II PNe, exhibits distinct properties, including lower excitation levels, smaller sizes, and higher surface brightnesses compared to the previously known LMC Population I PNe. To investigate the characteristics of the newly discovered population, we derived their luminosity function, which describes the number of PNe as a function of their luminosity. By comparing the LMC Population II PNe luminosity function to those of other nearby galaxies, we found that it follows a different power-law slope compared to the LMC Population I PNe and other nearby galaxies. This finding suggests that the formation mechanisms and evolutionary paths of the LMC Population II PNe differ from those of the LMC Population I PNe and other galaxies. We also investigated the possible impact of environmental factors on the properties of the LMC Population II PNe by analyzing the spatial distribution and chemical abundances of this new population. Our results reveal that the LMC Population II PNe are more centrally located in the LMC and have lower metallicities compared to the LMC Population I PNe. These findings indicate that the LMC Population II PNe likely formed in denser environments with lower metallicities and provide new insights into the formation and evolution of low-metallicity PNe in the Local Group. In conclusion, this study reveals the existence of a new population of planetary nebulae in the LMC, which exhibits distinct properties and follows a different luminosity function compared to the previously known LMC Population I PNe and other nearby galaxies. Our results provide new insights into the formation and evolution of low-metallicity planetary nebulae and highlight the importance of continuous observations and analysis of nearby galaxies for advancing our understanding of the universe.

text: This study aims to explore and implement the most accurate methods for phase measurement across various applications. We conducted extensive experiments to evaluate different techniques including Fourier Transform, Fast Fourier Transform, and Wavelet Transform, comparing their performance under varying conditions. The results indicate that the Wavelet Transform offers superior accuracy, especially when dealing with non-stationary signals. Key methodologies employed include optimal wavelet selection based on signal characteristics, application of time-frequency analysis, and iterative refinement algorithms. Through rigorous testing, we identified parameters influencing measurement precision and developed guidelines for selecting the most suitable method based on signal complexity and specific requirements. These findings contribute to enhancing the reliability and precision of phase measurements in fields such as telecommunications, radar systems, and biomedical engineering.

Then detection and identification of extreme weather events in large-scale
climate simulations is an important problem for risk management, informing
governmental policy decisions and advancing our basic understanding of the
climate system. Recent work has shown that fully supervised convolutional
neural networks (CNNs) can yield acceptable accuracy for classifying well-known
types of extreme weather events when large amounts of labeled data are
available. However, many different types of spatially localized climate
patterns are of interest including hurricanes, extra-tropical cyclones, weather
fronts, and blocking events among others. Existing labeled data for these
patterns can be incomplete in various ways, such as covering only certain years
or geographic areas and having false negatives. This type of climate data
therefore poses a number of interesting machine learning challenges. We present
a multichannel spatiotemporal CNN architecture for semi-supervised bounding box
prediction and exploratory data analysis. We demonstrate that our approach is
able to leverage temporal information and unlabeled data to improve the
localization of extreme weather events. Further, we explore the representations
learned by our model in order to better understand this important data. We
present a dataset, ExtremeWeather, to encourage machine learning research in
this area and to help facilitate further work in understanding and mitigating
the effects of climate change. The dataset is available at
extremeweatherdataset.github.io and the code is available at
https://github.com/eracah/hur-detect.

text: In this work, we address the challenge of efficiently computing the shifted Popov forms of polynomial matrices, a task that has significant implications in control theory and numerical linear algebra. description of tritium production cross sections over the entire energy range

literature, either based on other calculations or from measurements. The
obtained tritium production rates, ranging from a few tens to a few hundreds of
nuclei per kg and per day at sea level, point to a significant contribution to
the background in dark matter experiments, requiring the application of
specific protocols for target material purification, material storing
underground and limiting the time the detector is on surface during the

The interference of two Bose-Einstein condensates, initially in Fock states,
can be described in terms of their relative phase, treated as a random unknown
variable. This phase can be understood, either as emerging from the
measurements, or preexisting to them; in the latter case, the originating
states could be phase states with unknown phases, so that an average over all
their possible values is taken. Both points of view lead to a description of
probabilities of results of experiments in terms of a phase angle, which plays
the role of a classical variable. Nevertheless, in some situations, this
description is not sufficient: another variable, which we call the "quantum
angle", emerges from the theory. This article studies various manifestations of
the quantum angle. We first introduce the quantum angle by expressing two Fock
states crossing a beam splitter in terms of phase states, and relate the
quantum angle to off-diagonal matrix elements in the phase representation. Then
we consider an experiment with two beam splitters, where two experimenters make
dichotomic measurements with two interferometers and detectors that are far
apart; the results lead to violations of the Bell-Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt
inequality (valid for local-realistic theories, including classical
descriptions of the phase). Finally, we discuss an experiment where particles
from each of two sources are either deviated via a beam splitter to a side
collector or proceed to the point of interference. For a given interference
result, we find "population oscillations" in the distributions of the deviated
particles, which are entirely controlled by the quantum angle. Various versions
of population oscillation experiments are discussed, with two or three
independent condensates.

Furthermore, under specific conditions, we demonstrate that secure transmission can be maintained even in the presence of a strong eavesdropper. In conclusion, this research provides new insights into the capacity limits of relay channels with confidential messages, suggesting that optimizing relay cooperation is crucial for enhancing secure communications in practical applications. These results lay the groundwork for further exploration into more complex network configurations and potential real-world implementations in secure communication systems.
label: machine

text: In combinatorial set theory, the study of containment relations within families of sets has significant implications for understanding structural properties of such families, particularly when certain substructures are forbidden. This paper investigates $P$-free families, a class of families of sets in which no subfamily forms a pattern of containment isomorphic to a poset $P$. Our primary objective is to analyze the maximum possible number of containment relations that can exist within a $P$-free family of subsets of an $n$-element set. Utilizing a combinatorial optimization approach, we employ extremal set theory tools and poset theory techniques to establish upper and lower bounds on the number of possible containments. Our methodology involves constructing specific examples of $P$-free families that achieve these bounds by leveraging the properties of specific forbidden subposets, augmented by inductive expansion techniques. Key findings reveal that these bounds are closely related to the structural characteristics of the poset $P$, such as width and height, demonstrating intricate interdependencies between these parameters and containment structures. Furthermore, our exploration identifies novel families of sets that serve as extremal examples, expanding the current understanding of containment limits in $P$-free constraints. In conclusion, our results advance the characterization of containment dynamics in poset-free set families, paving the way for future inquiries into more complex or higher-dimensional poset structures, while simultaneously refining the methodologies applicable to related combinatorial optimization problems.

We develop an analytical model for the accretion and gravitational drag on a
point mass that moves hypersonically in the midplane of a gaseous disk with a
Gaussian vertical density stratification. Such a model is of interest for
studying the interaction between a planet and a protoplanetary disk, as well as
the dynamical decay of massive black holes in galactic nuclei. The model
considers that the flow is ballistic, and gives fully analytical expressions
for both the accretion rate onto the point mass, and the gravitational drag it
suffers. The expressions are further simplified by taking the limits of a
thick, and of a thin disk. The results for the thick disk reduce correctly to
those for a uniform density environment (Cant\'o et al. 2011). We find that for
a thin disk (small vertical scaleheight compared to the gravitational radius)
the accretion rate is proportional to the mass of the moving object and to the
surface density of the disk, while the drag force is independent of the
velocity of the object. The gravitational deceleration of the hypersonic
perturber in a thin disk was found to be independent of its parameters (i.e.
mass or velocity) and depends only on the surface mass density of the disk. The
predictions of the model are compared to the results of three-dimensional
hydrodynamical simulations, with a reasonable agreement.

text:
Many theoretical and experimental studies suggest that range expansions can
have severe consequences for the gene pool of the expanding population. Due to
strongly enhanced genetic drift at the advancing frontier, neutral and weakly
deleterious mutations can reach large frequencies in the newly colonized
regions, as if they were surfing the front of the range expansion. These
findings raise the question of how frequently beneficial mutations successfully
surf at shifting range margins, thereby promoting adaptation towards a
range-expansion phenotype. Here, we use individual-based simulations to study
the surfing statistics of recurrent beneficial mutations on wave-like range
expansions in linear habitats. We show that the rate of surfing depends on two
strongly antagonistic factors, the probability of surfing given the spatial
location of a novel mutation and the rate of occurrence of mutations at that
location. The surfing probability strongly increases towards the tip of the
wave. Novel mutations are unlikely to surf unless they enjoy a spatial head
start compared to the bulk of the population. The needed head start is shown to
be proportional to the inverse fitness of the mutant type, and only weakly
dependent on the carrying capacity. The second factor is the mutation
occurrence which strongly decreases towards the tip of the wave. Thus, most
successful mutations arise at an intermediate position in the front of the
wave. We present an analytic theory for the tradeoff between these factors that
allows to predict how frequently substitutions by beneficial mutations occur at
invasion fronts. We find that small amounts of genetic drift increase the
fixation rate of beneficial mutations at the advancing front, and thus could be
important for adaptation during species invasions.

text:
The overtone and multi-mode RR Lyrae stars in the globular cluster M3 are
studied using a 200-d long, $B,V$ and $I_{\mathrm C}$ time-series photometry
obtained in 2012. 70\% of the 52 overtone variables observed show some kind of
multi-periodicity (additional frequency at ${f_{0.61}}={f_{\mathrm {1O}}}/0.61$
frequency ratio, Blazhko effect, double/multi-mode pulsation, period doubling).
A signal at 0.587 frequency ratio to the fundamental-mode frequency is detected
in the double-mode star, V13, which may be identified as the second radial
overtone mode. If this mode-identification is correct, than V13 is the first RR
Lyrae star showing triple-mode pulsation of the first three radial modes.
Either the Blazhko effect or the ${f_{0.61}}$ frequency (or both of these
phenomena) appear in 7 double-mode stars. The $P_{\mathrm{1O}}/P_{\mathrm{F}}$
period ratio of RRd stars showing the Blazhko effect are anomalous. A
displacement of the main frequency component at the fundamental-mode with the
value of modulation frequency (or its half) is detected in three Blazhko RRd
stars parallel with the appearance of the overtone-mode pulsation. The
${f_{0.61}}$ frequency appears in RRc stars that lie at the blue side of the
double-mode region and in RRd stars, raising the suspicion that its occurrence
may be connected to double-mode pulsation. The changes of the Blazhko and
double-mode properties of the stars are also reviewed using the recent and
archive photometric data.

text: We present a study on resource allocation and rate gains in practical full-duplex systems. Our research aims to address the challenge of maximizing throughput in full-duplex communication while considering the inherent self-interference. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that an optimized resource allocation strategy can significantly enhance the overall system throughput. By carefully allocating transmit power and scheduling transmissions, we show that the achievable rates in full-duplex systems can surpass those of traditional half-duplex systems under certain conditions. Additionally, we investigate the impact of varying system parameters such as self-interference cancellation capabilities and traffic load on the rate gains of full-duplex systems. Our results highlight the importance of adaptive resource allocation techniques to exploit the benefits of full-duplex communication effectively. Leveraging a combination of mathematical analysis and simulations, we propose a novel resource allocation algorithm that dynamically adjusts transmission parameters to maximize throughput while mitigating self-interference. This work contributes to the understanding of resource allocation strategies in practical full-duplex systems and provides insights for optimizing the performance of future communication networks.

text: In this study, we investigate the presence and characteristics of circumstellar disks in Class 0 protostars, which represent the earliest observable stage of star formation. Disentangling the disk's properties from its protostellar envelope at this nascent phase remains a formidable challenge due to substantial observational limitations. We employ high-resolution millimeter and submillimeter wavelength observations, combining data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and Very Large Array (VLA), to probe the immediate vicinities of a sample of Class 0 sources. Utilizing sophisticated imaging and modeling techniques, we analyze the spatial distribution of dust emission, seeking signatures indicative of rotationally-supported disk structures. Our results reveal evidence for compact, flattened, and rotationally-dominated structures consistent with early disk formation in a majority of observed Class 0 protostars. We derive disk properties such as mass, size, and inclination, emphasizing their variability even among objects of similar evolutionary status. Our findings suggest that disk formation is a prevalent and perhaps inevitable process that occurs concomitantly with or shortly after the collapse of the natal molecular cloud core. Additionally, our analysis highlights the intricate interplay between infall, outflow, and magnetic fields in shaping disk morphology and accretion processes. These discoveries advance our understanding of disk evolution at the onset of star and planet formation, providing crucial constraints on theoretical models of early stellar evolution. Our study underscores the necessity of high-resolution observations to further unravel the complexities of Class 0 disks and their role in the stellar birth environment.

text: In this study, we explore the evolution of parton energy loss mechanisms with transverse momentum in relative collision environments, specifically at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This research aims to resolve the intricate dynamics of parton interactions within the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) formed during high-energy heavy-nuclei collisions. Our primary focus lies in quantifying the dependence of energy loss mechanisms on transverse momentum, an area that remains inadequately understood. Utilizing state-of-the-art perturbative quantum chromodynamics calculations alongside data-driven simulations, we systematically analyze parton energy dissipation in both colliders' environments.  Our results indicate a significant momentum-dependent evolution in the energy loss mechanisms, characterized by a transition from radiative to collisional processes as transverse momentum increases. Notably, at RHIC energies, we observe the prominence of elastic scattering contributions, whereas at LHC energies, parton energy loss predominantly occurs through gluon radiation. By integrating the Hybrid Modell with hydrodynamic simulations of the QGP, we accurately quantify the energy loss parameter, shedding light on how the dense medium modifies parton propagation.  This investigation into the nuanced mechanism of parton energy loss fosters a deeper understanding of QGP characteristics and illuminates the stark contrast between RHIC and LHC environments. Our findings contribute to refining theoretical models, thereby enhancing predictive capabilities concerning partonic interactions in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. These contributions are vital for future experimental probing and the broader understanding of QGP properties, essential for the expanding body of high-energy nuclear physics research.

The influence of intrinsic Fe defects in FeO (either single cation vacancies
or prototypical 4:1 vacancy clusters) on the electronic and dielectric
properties is studied within the density functional theory. The importance of
local Coulomb interactions at Fe atoms is highlighted and shown to be
responsible for the observed insulating Mott gap in FeO which is reduced by the
presence of defects. We investigate nonstoichiometric configurations of Fe1-xO
with x ranging from 3 to 9 % and find the aliovalent Fe cations in both the
regular and interstitial lattice sites of the considered configurations.
Furthermore, we show that the trivalent Fe ions are induced by both isolated
and clustered Fe-vacancies and introduce the empty band states inside the
insulating gap, which decreases monotonically with increasing cation vacancy
concentration. The Fe1-xO systems with high defect content become metallic for
small values of the Coulomb interaction U, yielding the increase in the
dielectric functions and optical reflectivity at low energies in agreement with
the experimental data. Due to the crystal defects, the infrared-active
transverse optic phonons split and distribute over a wide range of frequencies
clarifying the origin of the exceptionally large spectral linewidths of the
dielectric loss functions observed for wustite in recent experiments.

text:
We present precise radial velocity observations of WASP-47, a star known to
host a hot Jupiter, a distant Jovian companion, and, uniquely, two additional
transiting planets in short-period orbits: a super-Earth in a ~19 hour orbit,
and a Neptune in a ~9 day orbit. We analyze our observations from the HARPS-N
spectrograph along with previously published data to measure the most precise
planet masses yet for this system. When combined with new stellar parameters
and reanalyzed transit photometry, our mass measurements place strong
constraints on the compositions of the two small planets. We find unlike most
other ultra-short-period planets, the inner planet, WASP-47 e, has a mass (6.83
+/- 0.66 Me) and radius (1.810 +/- 0.027 Re) inconsistent with an Earth-like
composition. Instead, WASP-47 e likely has a volatile-rich envelope surrounding
an Earth-like core and mantle. We also perform a dynamical analysis to
constrain the orbital inclination of WASP-47 c, the outer Jovian planet. This
planet likely orbits close to the plane of the inner three planets, suggesting
a quiet dynamical history for the system. Our dynamical constraints also imply
that WASP-47 c is much more likely to transit than a geometric calculation
would suggest. We calculate a transit probability for WASP-47 c of about 10%,
more than an order of magnitude larger than the geometric transit probability
of 0.6%.

text: This study explores the properties of M33 X-8, the nearest ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX), through a comprehensive analysis of its X-ray spectral data using Suzaku. With a luminosity of 1.4 × 1043 erg/s, M33 X-8 is an intriguing astrophysical phenomenon and has been a subject of extensive research due to its high luminosity exceeding that of any known stellar-mass black hole. Our investigation aimed to address the origin of M33 X-8's extreme X-ray luminosity, among other open questions.  Employing the unprecedented sensitivity and spectral resolution of Suzaku, we extracted high-quality X-ray spectra from the archival data of M33 X-8. Fitting the data with a multicomponent continuum model, we discovered an unusual combination of an absorbed power-law component and a complex iron Kα fluorescence line. The power-law component, attributed to the accretion disk corona, displayed a high photon index, Γ ≈ 2.7, while the iron line emission was found to be narrow and strongly self-absorbed. We interpret these findings as evidence of a variable, highly-obscured, and likely, inhomogeneous accretion disk.  Our results propose an alternate explanation for the extreme luminosity of M33 X-8. Unlike the traditional paradigm of a massive black hole as the power source, our findings suggest that a stellar-mass black hole with a highly-obscured, variable accretion disk could account for the observed luminosity. By re-evaluating the estimates of black hole masses, based on the observed X-ray luminosities, we broaden the scope of our understanding of ultraluminous X-ray sources.  In conclusion, our Suzaku investigation into M33 X-8 has yielded significant advancements in understanding the nature of the nearest ULX source. Our findings emphasize the importance of further exploration of the enigmatic ULXs with high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy to unravel their underlying astrophysical phenomena.

text:
We present a new variational method for investigating the ground state and
out of equilibrium dynamics of quantum many-body bosonic and fermionic systems.
Our approach is based on constructing variational wavefunctions which extend
Gaussian states by including generalized canonical transformations between the
fields. The key advantage of such states compared to simple Gaussian states is
presence of non-factorizable correlations and the possibility of describing
states with strong entanglement between particles. In contrast to the commonly
used canonical transformations, such as the polaron or Lang-Firsov
transformations, we allow parameters of the transformations to be time
dependent, which extends their regions of applicability. We derive equations of
motion for the parameters characterizing the states both in real and imaginary
time using the differential structure of the variational manifold. The ground
state can be found by following the imaginary time evolution until it converges
to a steady state. Collective excitations in the system can be obtained by
linearizing the real-time equations of motion in the vicinity of the imaginary
time steady-state solution. Our formalism allows us not only to determine the
energy spectrum of quasiparticles and their lifetime, but to obtain the
complete spectral functions and to explore far out of equilibrium dynamics such
as coherent evolution following a quantum quench. We illustrate and benchmark
this framework with several examples: a single polaron in the Holstein and
Su-Schrieer-Heeger models, non-equilibrium dynamics in the spin-boson and Kondo
models, the superconducting to charge density wave phase transitions in the
Holstein model.
label: human

text: This research explores the complex four-body long-range interactions between ultracold weakly-bound diatomic molecules. The study aims to elucidate the nature of these interactions, which are crucial for understanding molecular dynamics at very low temperatures. Utilizing state-of-the-art quantum chemistry calculations and theoretical models, the work focuses on identifying the dominant forces governing these interactions. Key findings include the identification of specific interaction patterns that deviate from simple two-body potentials, highlighting the significant role of three-body and four-body effects. The research also investigates how these interactions influence the stability and structural properties of molecular complexes. Ultimately, the study provides insights into the development of new methods for manipulating and controlling molecular systems, with potential applications in quantum technologies and chemical physics.
