text:
Classical novae are caused by mass transfer episodes from a main sequence
star onto a white dwarf via Roche lobe overflow. This material forms an
accretion disk around the white dwarf. Ultimately, a fraction of this material
spirals in and piles up on the white dwarf surface under electron-degenerate
conditions. The subsequently occurring thermonuclear runaway reaches hundreds
of megakelvin and explosively ejects matter into the interstellar medium. The
exact peak temperature strongly depends on the underlying white dwarf mass, the
accreted mass and metallicity, and the initial white dwarf luminosity.
Observations of elemental abundance enrichments in these classical nova events
imply that the ejected matter consists not only of processed solar material
from the main sequence partner but also of material from the outer layers of
the underlying white dwarf. This indicates that white dwarf and accreted matter
mix prior to the thermonuclear runaway. The processes by which this mixing
occurs require further investigation to be understood. In this work, we analyze
elemental abundances ejected from hydrodynamic nova models in search of
elemental abundance ratios that are useful indicators of the total amount of
mixing. We identify the abundance ratios $\Sigma$CNO/H, Ne/H, Mg/H, Al/H, and
Si/H as useful mixing meters in ONe novae. The impact of thermonuclear reaction
rate uncertainties on the mixing meters is investigated using Monte Carlo
post-processing network calculations with temperature-density evolutions of all
mass zones computed by the hydrodynamic models. We find that the current
uncertainties in the $^{30}$P($p$,$\gamma$)$^{31}$S rate influence the Si/H
abundance ratio, but overall the mixing meters found here are robust against
nuclear physics uncertainties. A comparison of our results with observations of
ONe novae provides strong constraints for classical nova models.
label: human

text: This paper investigates the motion behavior of a tired random walker in continua using a Brownian motion model and statistical analysis techniques. The tired random walker model assumes that a particle undergoes Brownian motion, but its mobility decreases exponentially over time due to fatigue. This is an extension of the traditional random walker model in which the particle's mobility remains constant. We develop a mathematical model to describe the motion of a tired random walker and derive the statistical properties of its trajectory. We then perform a Monte Carlo simulation to examine the effect of fatigue on the particle's motion. Our results demonstrate that the tired random walker exhibits sub-diffusive motion, with a time dependence of the mean-squared displacement different from the Brownian motion. Furthermore, the probability density function of the displacement and the autocorrelation function show clear deviations from those of the classical Brownian motion. The findings provide a better understanding of the motion behavior of particles in various biological and physical systems where fatigue plays a crucial role. This study may lead to improvements in modeling and simulating the motion of such systems, particularly in the field of biophysics and soft matter physics.
label: machine

text:
High Tc superconductivity in FeAs-based multilayers (pnictides), evading
temperature decoherence effects in a quantum condensate, is assigned to a
Feshbach resonance (called also shape resonance) in the exchange-like interband
pairing. The resonance is switched on by tuning the chemical potential at an
electronic topological transition (ETT) near a band edge, where the Fermi
surface topology of one of the subbands changes from 1D to 2D topology. We show
that the tuning is realized by changing i) the misfit strain between the
superconducting planes and the spacers ii) the charge density and iii) the
disorder. The system is at the verge of a catastrophe i.e. near a structural
and magnetic phase transition associated with the stripes (analogous to the 1/8
stripe phase in cuprates) order to disorder phase transition. Fine tuning of
both the chemical potential and the disorder pushes the critical temperature Ts
of this phase transition to zero giving a quantum critical point. Here the
quantum lattice and magnetic fluctuations promote the Feshbach resonance of the
exchange-like anisotropic pairing. This superconducting phase that resists to
the attacks of temperature is shown to be controlled by the interplay of the
hopping energy between stripes and the quantum fluctuations. The
superconducting gaps in the multiple Fermi surface spots reported by the recent
ARPES experiment of D. V. Evtushinsky et al. arXiv:0809.4455 are shown to
support the Feshbach scenario.
label: human

text: In this study, we investigate the dissolution process of star clusters within circular orbits around the Galactic Centre using numerical simulations. Our primary goal is to understand the mechanisms that lead to the fragmentation and eventual disappearance of these stellar systems. We employ state-of-the-art N-body simulations, incorporating realistic initial conditions and stellar evolution models to accurately represent the complex dynamics at play. The results indicate that star clusters initially orbiting in circular paths can fragment into smaller sub-clusters due to gravitational interactions with other stars and dark matter halos. These sub-clusters then undergo further fragmentation, eventually leading to the dissolution of the original cluster. Key findings include the critical role of tidal forces from the Galactic bulge and the importance of dynamical friction in destabilizing the orbits of individual stars. The methodology involves detailed analysis of cluster evolution over time, tracking the positions and velocities of stars within the clusters. This research provides valuable insights into the structural evolution of star clusters and their ultimate fate in galactic environments.
label: machine

text:
The scan statistic is by far the most popular method for anomaly detection,
being popular in syndromic surveillance, signal and image processing, and
target detection based on sensor networks, among other applications. The use of
the scan statistics in such settings yields a hypothesis testing procedure,
where the null hypothesis corresponds to the absence of anomalous behavior. If
the null distribution is known, then calibration of a scan-based test is
relatively easy, as it can be done by Monte Carlo simulation. When the null
distribution is unknown, it is less straightforward. We investigate two
procedures. The first one is a calibration by permutation and the other is a
rank-based scan test, which is distribution-free and less sensitive to
outliers. Furthermore, the rank scan test requires only a one-time calibration
for a given data size making it computationally much more appealing. In both
cases, we quantify the performance loss with respect to an oracle scan test
that knows the null distribution. We show that using one of these calibration
procedures results in only a very small loss of power in the context of a
natural exponential family. This includes the classical normal location model,
popular in signal processing, and the Poisson model, popular in syndromic
surveillance. We perform numerical experiments on simulated data further
supporting our theory and also on a real dataset from genomics.
label: human

text:
Deep neural networks is a branch in machine learning that has seen a meteoric
rise in popularity due to its powerful abilities to represent and model
high-level abstractions in highly complex data. One area in deep neural
networks that is ripe for exploration is neural connectivity formation. A
pivotal study on the brain tissue of rats found that synaptic formation for
specific functional connectivity in neocortical neural microcircuits can be
surprisingly well modeled and predicted as a random formation. Motivated by
this intriguing finding, we introduce the concept of StochasticNet, where deep
neural networks are formed via stochastic connectivity between neurons. As a
result, any type of deep neural networks can be formed as a StochasticNet by
allowing the neuron connectivity to be stochastic. Stochastic synaptic
formations, in a deep neural network architecture, can allow for efficient
utilization of neurons for performing specific tasks. To evaluate the
feasibility of such a deep neural network architecture, we train a
StochasticNet using four different image datasets (CIFAR-10, MNIST, SVHN, and
STL-10). Experimental results show that a StochasticNet, using less than half
the number of neural connections as a conventional deep neural network,
achieves comparable accuracy and reduces overfitting on the CIFAR-10, MNIST and
SVHN dataset. Interestingly, StochasticNet with less than half the number of
neural connections, achieved a higher accuracy (relative improvement in test
error rate of ~6% compared to ConvNet) on the STL-10 dataset than a
conventional deep neural network. Finally, StochasticNets have faster
operational speeds while achieving better or similar accuracy performances.
label: human

text: We investigated the dynamic evolution of galaxy protoclusters, a transitional phase between the formation of the first stars and the assembly of galaxy clusters. Through a combination of hydrodynamic simulations and observational studies, we sought to elucidate the role of gas accretion and mergers in shaping the morphology and properties of these systems.   Our simulations revealed that galaxy protoclusters undergo significant transformations as they accrete gas and merge with neighboring protoclusters, leading to the formation of a hierarchical structure. We found that the gas accretion rate and merger frequency play crucial roles in determining the final morphology and mass distribution of the protocluster. Furthermore, our simulations indicate that the formation of galaxy clusters is facilitated by the collapse of gas-rich regions within the protocluster.  Observational studies of galaxy protoclusters in the early universe revealed a high level of diversity in their morphological and kinematic properties. We identified a correlation between the gas content and the protocluster's ability to fragment into smaller sub-clusters, suggesting that gas accretion plays a key role in regulating the formation of galaxy clusters. Our results highlight the importance of considering the complex interplay between gas accretion, mergers, and gravitational collapse in understanding the evolution of galaxy clusters.
label: machine

text:
Dense coding with non-maximally entangled states has been investigated in
many different scenarios. We revisit this problem for protocols adopting the
standard encoding scheme. In this case, the set of possible classical messages
cannot be perfectly distinguished due to the non-orthogonality of the quantum
states carrying them. So far, the decoding process has been approached in two
ways: (i) The message is always inferred, but with an associated (minimum)
error; (ii) the message is inferred without error, but only sometimes; in case
of failure, nothing else is done. Here, we generalize on these approaches and
propose novel optimal probabilistic decoding schemes. The first uses
quantum-state separation to increase the distinguishability of the messages
with an optimal success probability. This scheme is shown to include (i) and
(ii) as special cases and continuously interpolate between them, which enables
the decoder to trade-off between the level of confidence desired to identify
the received messages and the success probability for doing so. The second
scheme, called multistage decoding, applies only for qudits ($d$-level quantum
systems with $d>2$) and consists of further attempts in the state
identification process in case of failure in the first one. We show that this
scheme is advantageous over (ii) as it increases the mutual information between
the sender and receiver.
label: human

text:
This paper studies the inviscid limit of the two-dimensional incompressible
viscoelasticity, which is a system coupling a Navier-Stokes equation with a
transport equation for the deformation tensor. The existence of global smooth
solutions near the equilibrium with a fixed positive viscosity was known since
the work of F. H. Lin, C. Liu, and P. Zhang in "On hydrodynamics of
viscoelastic fluids". The inviscid case was solved recently by the second
author Z. Lei. in "Global well-posedness of incompressible elastodynamics in
two dimensions". While the latter was solely based on the techniques from the
studies of hyperbolic equations, and hence the 2D problem is in general more
challenge than that in higher dimensions, the former was relied crucially upon
a dissipative mechanism. Indeed, after a symmetrization and a linearization
around the equilibrium, the system of the incompressible viscoelasticity
reduces to an incompressible system of damped wave equations for both the fluid
velocity and the deformation tensor. These two approaches are not compatible.
In this paper, we prove global existence of solutions, uniformly in both time
$t \in [0, \infty)$ and viscosity $\mu \geq 0$. This allows us to justify in
particular the vanishing viscosity limit for all time. In order to overcome
difficulties coming from the incompatibility between the purely hyperbolic
limiting system and the systems with additional parabolic viscous
perturbations, we introduce in this paper a rather robust method which may
apply to a wide class of physical systems of similar nature. Roughly speaking,
the method works in two dimensional case whenever the hyperbolic system
satisfies intrinsically a "Strong Null Condition". For dimensions not less than
three, the usual null condition is sufficient for this method to work.
label: human

text: This work explores the optimization of Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) placement in the context of Smart Grid observability and state estimation. The main problem addressed is to strategically position PMUs within the power system network to enhance observability and improve the accuracy of state estimation. Through analytical modeling and algorithm development, we investigate the optimal PMU placement strategy to ensure sufficient observability for effective grid monitoring and control. Our results demonstrate that the strategic placement of PMUs leads to improved grid observability, enabling the timely detection and mitigation of anomalies and enhancing the overall resilience of the Smart Grid. We formulate the PMU placement optimization as a mathematical problem, utilizing advanced techniques such as convex optimization and heuristic algorithms to achieve efficient solutions. By enhancing the observability and state estimation accuracy of the Smart Grid through optimized PMU placement, this research contributes to the advancement of grid monitoring and control systems. The findings highlight the significance of strategic PMU deployment in enhancing grid observability, enabling efficient fault detection, and facilitating timely decision-making for ensuring grid stability and reliability in Smart Grid environments.
label: machine

text:
A zigzag graphene nanodisk can be interpreted as a quantum dot with an
internal degree of freedom. It is well described by the infinite-range
Heisenberg model. We have investigated its thermodynamical properties. There
exists a quasi-phase transition between the quasi-ferromagnet and
quasi-paramagnet states, as signaled by a sharp peak in the specific heat and
in the susceptability. We have also analyzed how thermodynamical properties are
affected when two leads are attached to the nanodisk. It is shown that lead
effects are described by the many-spin Kondo Hamiltonian. There appears a new
peak in the specific heat, and the multiplicity of the ground state becomes
just one half of the system without leads. Another lead effect is to enhance
the ferromagnetic order. Being a ferromagnet, a nanodisk can be used as a spin
filter. Furthermore, since the relaxation time is finite, it is possible to
control the spin of the nanodisk by an external spin current. We then propose a
rich variety of spintronic devices made of nanodisks and leads, such as spin
memory, spin amplifier, spin valve, spin-field-effect transistor, spin diode
and spin logic gates such as spin-XNOR gate and spin-XOR gate. Graphene
nanodisks could well be basic components of future nanoelectronic and
spintronic devices.
label: human

text:
The evolution equations of the vorticities of the electrons, ions and photons
in a pre-decoupling plasma are derived, in a fully inhomogeneous geometry, by
combining the general relativistic gradient expansion and the drift
approximation within the Adler-Misner-Deser decomposition. The vorticity
transfer between the different species is discussed in this novel framework and
a set of general conservation laws, connecting the vorticities of the
three-component plasma with the magnetic field intensity, is derived. After
demonstrating that a source of large-scale vorticity resides in the spatial
gradients of the geometry and of the electromagnetic sources, the total
vorticity is estimated to lowest order in the spatial gradients and by
enforcing the validity of the momentum constraint. By acknowledging the current
bounds on the tensor to scalar ratio in the (minimal) tensor extension of the
$\Lambda$CDM paradigm the maximal comoving magnetic field induced by the total
vorticity turns out to be, at most, of the order of $10^{-37}$ G over the
typical comoving scales ranging between 1 and 10 Mpc. While the obtained
results seem to be irrelevant for seeding a reasonable galactic dynamo action,
they demonstrate how the proposed fully inhomogeneous treatment can be used for
the systematic scrutiny of pre-decoupling plasmas beyond the conventional
perturbative expansions.
label: human

text:
There is a commonality among contagious diseases, tweets, urban crimes,
nuclear reactions, and neuronal firings that past events facilitate the future
occurrence of events. The spread of events has been extensively studied such
that the systems exhibit catastrophic chain reactions if the interaction
represented by the ratio of reproduction exceeds unity; however, their
subthreshold states for the case of the weaker interaction are not fully
understood. Here, we report that these systems are possessed by nonstationary
cascades of event-occurrences already in the subthreshold regime. Event
cascades can be harmful in some contexts, when the peak-demand causes vaccine
shortages, heavy traffic on communication lines, frequent crimes, or large
fluctuations in nuclear reactions, but may be beneficial in other contexts,
such that spontaneous activity in neural networks may be used to generate
motion or store memory. Thus it is important to comprehend the mechanism by
which such cascades appear, and consider controlling a system to tame or
facilitate fluctuations in the event-occurrences. The critical interaction for
the emergence of cascades depends greatly on the network structure in which
individuals are connected. We demonstrate that we can predict whether cascades
may emerge in a network, given information about the interactions between
individuals. Furthermore, we develop a method of reallocating connections among
individuals so that event cascades may be either impeded or impelled in a
network.

Broadband spectral energy distributions (SEDs) are complied from literature
for 24 TeV BL Lac objects. Two SEDs, which are identified as low and high
states with their flux densities at $1\ {\rm TeV}$ ($F_{1 TeV}$), are available
for each of 11 objects. We fit the SEDs with the single-zone synchrotron +
synchrotron-self-Compton (SSC) model and determine the physical parameters of
the jets. The model well represents the SEDs, and the observed relation between
two peak frequencies $\nu_{\rm s}$ and $\nu_{\rm c}$ also favors the model. It
is found that the break of the electron spectrum ($\gamma_{\rm b}$) is
different among sources, but magnetic field strength distributes narrowly in
$0.1-0.6 $ G, indicating that the shocks in the jets are significantly
different among sources and the magnetic field may be independent of the
shocks. The ratio of $F_{1 TeV}$ is correlated with the ratio of the
$\gamma_{\rm b}$ in the low and high states, indicating that the relativistic
shocks in the jets may be responsible for the observed flux variations and the
spectral shift. The ratio of the two peak luminosities $L_{\rm c}/L_{\rm s}$ is
anti-correlated with $\nu_{\rm s}$ in the co-moving frame, which is possibly
due to the Klein-Nishina effect. No excess in the GeV band due to the
interaction between the TeV photons and the extragalactic background light is
observed, implying that the strength of the intergalactic magnetic field would
be much larger than $ 10^{-16}$ G. An anti-correlation between jet power and
the mass of the central black hole is observed, i.e., $P_{\rm jet}\propto
M^{-1}_{\rm BH}$, disfavoring the scenario of a pure accretion-driven jet. We
suggest that the spin energy extraction may be significant for powering jets in
these sources, implying that the black holes with smaller mass may spin more
rapidly.

The ATLAS and CMS experiments observed a particle at the LHC with a mass
$\approx 126$ GeV, which is compatible with the Higgs boson of the Standard
Model. A crucial question is, if for such a Higgs mass value, one could
extrapolate the model up to high scales while keeping the minimum of the scalar
potential that breaks the electroweak symmetry stable. Vacuum stability
requires indeed the Higgs boson mass to be $M_H \gsim 129 \pm 1$ GeV, but the
precise value depends critically on the input top quark pole mass which is
usually taken to be the one measured at the Tevatron, $m_t^{\rm exp}=173.2 \pm
0.9$ GeV. However, for an unambiguous and theoretically well-defined
determination of the top quark mass one should rather use the total cross
section for top quark pair production at hadron colliders. Confronting the
latest predictions of the inclusive $p \bar p \to t\bar t +X$ cross section up
to next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD to the experimental measurement at the
Tevatron, we determine the running mass in the $\bar{\rm MS}$-scheme to be
$m_t^{\bar{\rm MS}}(m_t) = 163.3 \pm 2.7$ GeV which gives a top quark pole mass
of $m_t^{\rm pole}= 173.3 \pm 2.8$ GeV. This leads to the vacuum stability
constraint $M_H \geq 129.8 \pm 5.6$ GeV to which a $\approx 126$ GeV Higgs
boson complies as the uncertainty is large. A very precise assessment of the
stability of the electroweak vacuum can only be made at a future high-energy
electron-positron collider, where the top quark pole mass could be determined
with a few hundred MeV accuracy.
label: human

The surface orientation can have profound effects on the atomic-scale
processes of crystal growth, and is essential to such technologies as GaN-based
light-emitting diodes and high-power electronics. We investigate the dependence
of homoepitaxial growth mechanisms on the surface orientation of a hexagonal
crystal using kinetic Monte Carlo simulations. To model GaN metal-organic vapor
phase epitaxy, in which N species are supplied in excess, only Ga atoms on a
hexagonal close-packed (HCP) lattice are considered. The results are thus
potentially applicable to any HCP material. Growth behaviors on c-plane ${(0 0
0 1)}$ and m-plane ${(0 1 \overline{1} 0)}$ surfaces are compared. We present a
reciprocal space analysis of the surface morphology, which allows extraction of
growth mode boundaries and direct comparison with surface X-ray diffraction
experiments. For each orientation we map the boundaries between 3-dimensional,
layer-by-layer, and step flow growth modes as a function of temperature and
growth rate. Two models for surface diffusion are used, which produce different
effective Ehrlich-Schwoebel step-edge barriers, and different adatom diffusion
anisotropies on m-plane surfaces. Simulation results in agreement with observed
GaN island morphologies and growth mode boundaries are obtained. These indicate
that anisotropy of step edge energy, rather than adatom diffusion, is
responsible for the elongated islands observed on m-plane surfaces. Island
nucleation spacing obeys a power-law dependence on growth rate, with exponents
of -0.24 and -0.29 for m- and c-plane, respectively.

In this study, we analyze nine CMEs from the Sun to Earth as observed in both
the remote sensing and in situ data sets. To date, this is the largest study of
Earth impacting CMEs using the multi-view point remote sensing and in situ
data. However, the remote sensing and in situ data of the same CME cannot be
directly compared. Thus, we use several models to parameterize the two data
sets. With the model results, we are able to compare the arrival time, Earth
impact speed, internal magnetic field, size and orientation as derived from the
remote sensing and in situ methods. From the derived kinematics, we compare the
predicted arrival times and impact velocities with the in situ data. We find
that even with nearly continuous observations and the best available model of
the CME structure, there is still a significant error in the predicted values.
We estimate the various forces acting on the CME as predicted by three
theoretical models of CME propagation and expansion and compare these results
with the observational results. We find that the flux rope model of Chen (1989)
provides the best agreement with the observations. With the flux rope model, we
are able to predict the internal magnetic field of the CME near Earth from the
remote sensing data to an order of magnitude. Finally, we compare the size and
orientation of the CMEs as predicted from the remote sensing and in situ data.
We find very little agreement between the values derived from the two data
sets.

text: In this study, we investigate the hydrogenation process of vanadium dioxide (VO2) by introducing protons in an acidic solution, aiming to modulate its electronic and structural properties. VO2 is noted for its thermally-induced metal-insulator transition near room temperature, a feature that positions it as a promising candidate for various applications, including smart windows and sensors. However, the transition's reliance on external thermal stimuli poses limitations. Our work seeks to address this challenge by exploring chemical hydrogenation, which offers a controllable method to adjust the transition properties without thermal inputs. We systematically conducted protonation experiments on VO2 samples in acidic environments, subsequently performing structural and electronic analyses using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and electrical conductivity measurements. Our results indicate successful proton intercalation, evidenced by significant changes in both lattice parameters and electronic conductivity. Specifically, the protonated VO2 displays an altered phase transition characterized by reduced thermal activation energy and a widened thermal hysteresis loop. This shift demonstrates the modulation of VO2’s transition properties via hydrogenation, potentially enabling room-temperature applications with enhanced efficiency and reduced energy requirements. Our findings suggest a viable pathway for the tunable control of metal-insulator transition materials through chemical means, presenting implications for developing energy-efficient smart materials. Future work will focus on optimizing protonation conditions to attain desired electronic attributes while exploring the long-term stability and scalability of hydrogenated VO2 for industrial applications.

text: The study focuses on the discovery and detailed monitoring of a new black hole candidate, XTE J1752-223, utilizing data from the Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) satellite. The primary goal was to investigate the spectral properties of this source, specifically analyzing the rise time modulation (RMS) spectrum, to infer information about the compact object's mass and the source's distance.  Using RXTE's high temporal resolution, the RMS spectra were analyzed over a period of several years, revealing characteristic features indicative of a neutron star or black hole. The evolution of these spectra provided insights into the accretion process around the compact object, which is crucial for understanding the nature of XTE J1752-223. By fitting the observed spectra with theoretical models, estimates were made regarding the mass of the central object. Additionally, the variability patterns in the RMS spectra were used to deduce the distance to the source, providing a critical piece of information for further astrophysical studies.  Key findings indicate that XTE J1752-223 exhibits spectral characteristics consistent with those expected from a stellar-mass black hole. The estimated mass falls within the range of 4 to 6 solar masses, suggesting the presence of a black hole. Furthermore, the distance determination places the source at a redshift z = 0.015, placing it within our local group of galaxies, approximately 2.5 million light-years away.  In conclusion, the analysis of XTE J1752-223 using RXTE's RMS spectra provides valuable constraints on the properties of this intriguing black hole candidate, including its mass and distance. These results contribute significantly to our understanding of low-mass black holes and their role in galactic dynamics.

We present VLT/X-Shooter and MUSE spectroscopy of an faint F814W=28.60+/-0.33
(Muv=-17.0), low mass (~<10^7 Msun) and compact (Reff=62pc) freshly
star-forming galaxy at z=3.1169 magnified (16x) by the Hubble Frontier Fields
galaxy cluster Abell S1063. Gravitational lensing allows for a significant jump
toward low-luminosity regimes, in moderately high resolution spectroscopy
(R=lambda/dlambda ~ 3000-7400). We measured CIV1548,1550, HeII1640,
OIII]1661,1666, CIII]1907,1909, Hbeta, [OIII]4959,5007, emission lines with
FWHM< 50 km/s and (de-lensed) fluxes spanning the interval 1.0x10^-19 -
2.0x10^-18 erg/s/cm2 at S/N=4-30. The double peaked Lya emission with
Delta_v(red-blue) = 280(+/-7)km/s and de-lensed fluxes
2.4_(blue)|8.5_(red)x10^-18 erg/s/cm2 (S/N=38_(blue)|110_(red)) indicate a low
column density of neutral hydrogen gas consistent with a highly ionized
interstellar medium as also inferred from the large [OIII]5007/[OII]3727>10
ratio. We detect CIV1548,1550 resonant doublet in emission, each component with
FWHM ~< 45 km/s, and redshifted by +51(+/-10)km/s relative to the systemic
redshift. We interpret this as nebular emission tracing an expanding
optically-thin interstellar medium. Both CIV1548,1550 and HeII1640 suggest the
presence of hot and massive stars (with a possible faint AGN). The ultraviolet
slope is remarkably blue, beta =-2.95 +/- 0.20 (F_lambda=lambda^beta),
consistent with a dust-free and young ~<20 Myr galaxy. Line ratios suggest an
oxygen abundance 12+log(O/H)<7.8. We are witnessing an early episode of
star-formation in which a relatively low NHI and negligible dust attenuation
might favor a leakage of ionizing radiation. This galaxy currently represents a
unique low-luminosity reference object for future studies of the reionization
epoch with JWST.

Surface recombination affects both light-to-electricity and
electricity-to-light conversion in solar cells (SCs). Therefore, quantitative
analysis and reduction of surface recombination is an important direction in SC
research. In this work, electroluminescence (EL) intensity and photoconversion
efficiency of a set of 93 large-area (239\,cm$^2$) a-Si:H/c-Si heterojunction
SCs (HJSCs) are measured under AM1.5 conditions at 298 K. The HJSC samples
differed only in surface recombination velocity, $S$, but otherwise were
identical. Variation in $S$ was due to the variation of the chemical conditions
under which the samples were treated. It is established that EL quantum
efficiency, is affected by $S$ much more strongly than photoconversion
efficiency, $\eta$: namely, the reduction of the latter from 20.5\% to 18\% due
to an increase of $S$ is accompanied by a decrease of the former by more than
an order of magnitude. In HJSCs with well passivated surfaces, i.e. low $S$, EL
efficiency reached 2.1\%, which is notably higher than the known values in
silicon homojunction diodes. For temperature-dependent measurements of EL and
dark I-V curves, one of the samples was cut into small-area (1 cm$^2$) pieces.
It was found that EL intensity as a function of temperature develops a maximum
at $T$ = 223 K. At low temperatures, the current at weak bias is shown to be
due to tunneling mechanism. A theoretical model is developed that explains all
these findings quantitatively.

text: This study investigates the impact of spatial inhomogeneities on high-precision cosmological distance measurements. Through simulations and theoretical analysis, we identify how density fluctuations affect the accuracy of standard candles like Type Ia supernovae used to measure cosmic distances. We employ Bayesian inference techniques to quantify the uncertainty introduced by these inhomogeneities, demonstrating that they can introduce significant errors beyond the cosmological constant. Our findings highlight the need for sophisticated data processing methods and detailed models of the universe's large-scale structure to mitigate these effects and achieve more precise cosmological distances. Key methodologies include advanced numerical algorithms for simulating the distribution of matter in the universe and rigorous statistical treatments to assess measurement uncertainties.

text: This research presents a comprehensive framework designed to estimate long-term driver behavior patterns with precision. The study aims to address the variability and complexity inherent in understanding how drivers behave over extended periods, which is crucial for developing effective transportation policies and safety measures. Utilizing a combination of longitudinal data from multiple sources including vehicle telematics, traffic camera systems, and self-reported surveys, the methodology involves statistical modeling techniques such as machine learning algorithms and time-series analysis. Key findings indicate that driver behavior is influenced by both intrinsic factors like personality traits and extrinsic factors such as road conditions and traffic volume. The framework successfully captures these dynamics, enabling more accurate predictions of future driving behaviors. Ultimately, this framework can contribute to enhancing public safety, improving resource allocation for transportation infrastructure, and promoting sustainable mobility practices.

text: This study delves into the intricate details of the Milky Way's formation, focusing on Cold Halo Substructure (ECHOS) and their elemental abundances. Our research presents the results obtained from analyzing the chemical compositions of ECHOS, shedding light on their role in enriching the Milky Way's elemental makeup. We aimed to solve the puzzle of how these ancient structures contribute to the overall elemental abundance patterns observed in our galaxy.  Through a meticulous analysis of stellar spectroscopic data, we identified characteristic elemental signatures within the ECHOS, unraveling clues about their origins and evolution. The key findings showcase distinct elemental abundance patterns in ECHOS compared to other Milky Way structures, highlighting their unique contribution to the galactic chemical enrichment history. Our methodology involved high-resolution spectroscopy coupled with advanced data analysis techniques to accurately measure the elemental abundances of a diverse sample of ECHOS.  Overall, our research provides critical insights into the formation and evolution of the Milky Way, emphasizing the significant role of Cold Halo Substructure in shaping the galactic elemental composition. By unraveling the elemental abundances of ECHOS, we contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex processes underlying the formation of our galaxy.

text:
We study the necking of a filament of complex fluid or soft solid subject to
uniaxial tensile stretching, under conditions of constant imposed stress and
force, by means of linear stability analysis and nonlinear simulations. We
demonstrate necking to be a flow instability that is an unavoidable consequence
of the constitutive behaviour of essentially any viscoelastic material. We
derive criteria for the onset of necking that can be reported in terms of
characteristic signatures in the shapes of the experimentally measured material
functions, and that should therefore apply universally to all materials. To
confirm their generality, we show them to hold numerically in six constitutive
models. Under conditions of constant stress, we find two distinct dynamical
regimes as a function of time. In the first regime the strain rate quickly
attains a value prescribed by the fluid's underlying homogeneous constitutive
curve, at the given stress. In this first regime, no appreciable necking
arises. A second regime then ensues in which the homogeneous flow destabilises
to form a neck. This necking instability can occur via two distinct modes. The
first mode is relatively gentle and arises in any regime where the slope of the
constitutive curve is positive. It has a rate of necking per accumulated strain
unit set by the inverse of the slope of the constitutive curve. The second mode
sets in when a carefully defined `elastic derivative' of the tensile force
first slopes down as a function of the time. We discuss the way in which these
modes of instability manifest themselves in entangled polymeric fluids,
demonstrating four distinct regimes of necking behaviour as a function of
stress. Under conditions of constant imposed force, typically the flow sweeps
up the underlying constitutive curve of the fluid in question, with instability
to necking in any regime where that curve is positively sloping.
label: human

We present a quantitative study on the properties at death of fast-rotating
massive stars evolved at low-metallicity, objects that are proposed as likely
progenitors of long-duration gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs). We perform 1D+rotation
stellar-collapse simulations on the progenitor models of Woosley & Heger (2006)
and critically assess their potential for the formation of a black hole and a
Keplerian disk (namely a collapsar) or a proto-magnetar. We note that
theoretical uncertainties in the treatment of magnetic fields and the
approximate handling of rotation compromises the accuracy of stellar-evolution
models. We find that only the fastest rotating progenitors achieve sufficient
compactness for black-hole formation while the bulk of models possess a core
density structure typical of garden-variety core-collapse supernova (SN)
progenitors evolved without rotation and at solar metallicity. Of the models
that do have sufficient compactness for black-hole formation, most of them also
retain a large amount of angular momentum in the core, making them prone to a
magneto-rotational explosion, therefore preferentially leaving behind a
proto-magnetar. A large progenitor angular-momentum budget is often the sole
criterion invoked in the community today to assess the suitability for
producing a collapsar. This simplification ignores equally important
considerations such as the core compactness, which conditions black-hole
formation, the core angular momentum, which may foster a magneto-rotational
explosion preventing black-hole formation, or the metallicity and the residual
envelope mass which must be compatible with inferences from observed LGRB/SNe.
Our study suggests that black-hole formation is non trivial, that there is room
for accommodating both collapsars and proto-magnetars as LGRB progenitors,
although proto-magnetars seem much more easily produced by current
stellar-evolutionary models.
label: human

We study the total mass-density profile for a sample of 14 fast-rotator
early-type galaxies (stellar masses $10.2<\log M_\ast/M_\odot<11.7$). We
combine observations from the SLUGGS and Atlas3D surveys to map out the stellar
kinematics in two-dimensions, out to a median radius for the sample of four
half-light radii $R_e$ (or 10 kpc), and a maximum radius of 2.0-6.2 $R_e$ (or
4-21 kpc). We use axisymmetric dynamical models based on the Jeans equations,
which allow for a spatially varying anisotropy, and employ quite general
profiles for the dark halos, and in particular do not place any restriction on
the profile slope. This is made possible by the availability of spatially
extended two-dimensional kinematics. We find that our relatively simple models
provide a remarkably good description of the observed kinematics. The resulting
total density profiles are well described by a nearly-isothermal power law
$\rho_{\rm tot}(r)\propto r^{-\gamma}$ from $R_e$/10 to at least 4$R_e$, the
largest average deviation being 11%. The average logarithmic slope is
$\langle\gamma\rangle=2.19\pm0.03$ with observed rms scatter of just
$\sigma_\gamma=0.11$. This scatter out to large radii, where dark matter
dominates, is as small as previously reported by lensing studies around
$r\approx R_e/2$, where the stars dominate. Our bulge-halo conspiracy places
much tighter constraints on galaxy formation models. It illustrates the power
of two-dimensional stellar kinematics observations at large radii. It would now
be important to test the generality of our results for different galaxy types
and larger samples.
label: human

text: This study introduces a novel approach to enhance the reliability of data transmission in Ad Hoc wireless networks by implementing a driven backup routing table. The primary objective is to identify alternative disjoint paths that can be utilized in case the primary path fails, ensuring continuous network operation. Problematically, traditional routing algorithms often fail to guarantee disjoint paths due to the dynamic nature and limited connectivity of Ad Hoc networks.   Our methodology involves developing a mechanism that periodically updates the backup routing table based on the current network topology and resource availability. This table stores multiple paths from source to destination, which are continuously evaluated for feasibility and redundancy. When the primary path experiences failure, the algorithm selects the most suitable backup path from the updated table.  The results demonstrate a significant improvement in network resilience and robustness. Network simulations show that our method reduces the average end-to-end delay by 30% and increases the probability of successful data delivery by 45% compared to conventional backup routing strategies. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is further validated through real-world experiments conducted in various Ad Hoc network scenarios, confirming its practical applicability and scalability.

text: We have developed a novel tracer driver, which enables easy and efficient dynamic analyses of constraint logic programs. Our approach is based on the design of a modular and flexible framework that allows for seamless integration with existing constraint logic programming systems. The tracer driver is capable of tracing the execution of constraint logic programs, providing detailed information on the program's behavior, including the propagation of constraints, variable assignments, and the detection of potential inconsistencies.  Through extensive experimentation, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our tracer driver in identifying and analyzing various types of errors and inconsistencies in constraint logic programs. Our results show that the tracer driver is able to detect errors that may have gone undetected by existing static analysis tools, and that it can provide valuable insights into the program's behavior that can be used to improve its performance and reliability.  The key to our approach lies in the use of a combination of static and dynamic analysis techniques, which allows us to provide a comprehensive understanding of the program's behavior. We have also implemented a range of features that enable the tracer driver to be easily integrated with existing constraint logic programming systems, making it a versatile and useful tool for developers and researchers.  Our implementation has been thoroughly tested and validated, and the results have been consistently positive. The tracer driver has been shown to be highly efficient, even for large and complex constraint logic programs, and it has been demonstrated to be effective in a wide range of scenarios, including those involving multiple variables, constraints, and rules.

We present a comprehensive study of two of the most experimentally relevant
extensions of Kitaev's spinless model of a 1D p-wave superconductor: those
involving (i) longer range hopping and superconductivity and (ii) inhomogeneous
potentials. We commence with a pedagogical review of the spinless model and, as
a means of characterizing topological phases exhibited by the systems studied
here, we introduce bulk topological invariants as well as those derived from an
explicit consideration of boundary modes. In time-reversal invariant systems,
we find that the longer range hopping leads to topological phases characterized
by multiple Majorana modes. In particular, we investigate a spin model, which
respects a duality and maps to a fermionic model with multiple Majorana modes;
we highlight the connection between these topological phases and the broken
symmetry phases in the original spin model. In the presence of time-reversal
symmetry breaking terms, we show that the topological phase diagram is
characterized by an extended gapless regime. For the case of inhomogeneous
potentials, we explore phase diagrams of periodic, quasiperiodic, and
disordered systems. We present a detailed mapping between normal state
localization properties of such systems and the topological phases of the
corresponding superconducting systems. This powerful tool allows us to leverage
the analyses of Hofstadter's butterfly and the vast literature on Anderson
localization to the question of Majorana modes in superconducting quasiperiodic
and disordered systems, respectively. We briefly touch upon the synergistic
effects that can be expected in cases where long-range hopping and disorder are
both present.

text: The Hermes spectrograph, installed at the Anglo-Australian Telescope (AAT), has provided exciting first light results. The objective of this research paper is to present and analyze these initial findings. Methodology involves the collection of spectral data using Hermes across various astronomical targets. Key findings include the successful commissioning of the spectrograph, with high-quality spectra obtained for a range of objects including stars, galaxies, and nebulae. The data reveal detailed information about the composition, temperature, and motion of these celestial bodies. Additionally, the performance of the spectrograph in terms of resolution, sensitivity, and accuracy is evaluated. The analysis of these results leads to a deeper understanding of the capabilities and potential scientific impact of Hermes and sets the stage for future astronomical observations. In conclusion, the first light results from the Hermes spectrograph demonstrate its effectiveness in producing high-quality data and its potential for making significant contributions to various areas of astrophysical research.

text: The scarcity of X-ray bright Type IIP supernovae is a compelling anomaly in the study of stellar explosions, challenging established paradigms of X-ray emissions in supernova remnants. Type IIP supernovae, commonly the result of massive star collapses featuring plateaus in their light curves, theoretically should exhibit significant X-ray emissions due to interaction with circumstellar material (CSM). This research investigates the factors contributing to the observed paucity of such X-ray emissions. Utilizing data from space-based telescopes including Chandra and XMM-Newton, we performed a systematic analysis of a large sample of Type IIP supernovae. Parameters studied include the density and structure of the progenitor's CSM, explosion energy, and shock velocities. Our findings suggest a predominance of low-density CSM in most cases, which results in weaker interactions and consequently, less X-ray emission. Additionally, we correlate a possible variation in shock velocity with the star's metallicity, influencing the progenitor's mass-loss rates. These findings underscore the complexity of mass-loss histories in massive stars and suggest that many Type IIP supernovae may indeed have X-ray signatures too faint to be detected with current instruments. This study concludes that a deeper understanding of progenitor evolution, alongside advancements in X-ray detection technology, is vital to resolve the underwhelming X-ray luminosity of Type IIP supernovae. These insights not only challenge our comprehension of supernova mechanisms but also provide pivotal directions for future observational strategies and theoretical models.
label: machine

text: In this study, we explore the application of treelet covariance smoothing to refine genetically inferred relationships between species based on DNA sequence data. Treelet covariance, a recently proposed method for multivariate time series analysis, allows for the estimation of correlations between time series at different time scales, which is crucial for accurately modeling the evolutionary processes underlying genetic divergence.  To evaluate the effectiveness of treelet covariance smoothing in refining genetically inferred relationships, we applied this method to a well-established dataset consisting of DNA sequences from 125 primate species. Our analyses revealed significant improvements in the estimation of evolutionary relationships, as evidenced by an increase in the number of monophyletic groups and the reduction of long-branch attraction (LBA) artifacts.  In particular, we demonstrate that treelet covariance smoothing effectively mitigates LBA artifacts, which are common in traditional phylogenetic methods. LBA artifacts occur when distantly related species are incorrectly grouped together, leading to incorrect inferences about evolutionary relationships. By smoothing the covariance across multiple scales, treelet covariance was able to account for the presence of both short- and long-term correlations between species, providing a more accurate representation of true relationships.  Additionally, we show that treelet covariance smoothing can help identify previously unresolved relationships, leading to a better understanding of the evolutionary history of primates. Overall, our findings demonstrate the promise of treelet covariance smoothing in refining genetically inferred relationships and provide a valuable tool for researchers in the field of molecular evolution.  In conclusion, this study provides evidence for the utility of treelet covariance smoothing in refining genetically inferred relationships by demonstrating its ability to mitigate LBA artifacts and identify previously unresolved relationships in a well-established primate dataset. This method offers a promising avenue for improving the accuracy of evolutionary analyses based on DNA sequence data.
label: machine

text:
The spin susceptibility of a two-dimensional electron system is calculated by
determining the spin-polarization dependence of the ground-state energy within
the self-consistent mean-field theory of Singwi et al. (STLS). Results are
presented for three different devices, viz. the Si (100) inversion layer, the
AlAs quantum well, and the GaAs heterojunction-insulated gate field-effect
transistor. We find a fairly good agreement with experiments for the Si (100)
system, on most of the experimental density range, whereas the agreement for
the AlAs and GaAs systems is less satisfactory; in all cases, however, it is
vital to include the characteristic device parameters like the valley
degeneracy, the finite transverse thickness, etc. Further, the STLS theory
predicts an abrupt spin-polarization transition at a sufficiently low electron
density irrespective of the valley degeneracy and/or the finite thickness, with
the partially spin-polarized states remaining unstable. Moreover, in the Si
(100) inversion layer, the spin-polarization transition is preceded by the
simultaneous valley- and spin- polarization; for its zero thickness model,
these transitions however grossly disagree with the recent quantum Monte Carlo
simulations. This drawback of the STLS theory is traced to its inaccuracy in
treating electron correlations, which in turn become more and more important as
the number of independent components (spin and valley) increases.
label: human

text: In this study, we investigated the morphological evolution of rainwater channelization in sandy soils under controlled laboratory conditions. Using a series of model sandboxes, we systematically varied the sand properties, including texture, grain size distribution, and structure, to study their impact on channel formation and evolution. Our results revealed significant variations in channel morphology with changes in soil properties. In coarser sands, channels formed wider and shallower, while in finer sands, channels exhibited a more pronounced U-shape profile. The influence of soil structure was also evident, with channels developing more complex morphologies in structured soils compared to unstructured ones. Our findings were in agreement with existing theories on rainwater channelization in sandy soils. However, we also identified some new phenomena, such as the development of multiple channels and the formation of lateral pit-and-mound structures, which have not been reported previously. To understand the underlying physical processes governing channel evolution, we employed a combination of observation, photography, and 3D modeling techniques. We found that gravity and sheet flow dominated the initial stages of channel development, while sediment transport and deposition controlled the later stages. These insights could have important implications for engineering applications, such as drainage design and soil erosion control in sandy areas. In conclusion, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the morphological evolution of rainwater channelization in sandy soils. By systematically varying soil properties and employing advanced measurement techniques, we have identified key morphological features and physical processes that govern channel evolution. Our findings could inform the design of drainage systems and erosion control measures for sandy soils.
label: machine

In this paper a spectrum sensing policy employing recency-based exploration
is proposed for cognitive radio networks. We formulate the problem of finding a
spectrum sensing policy for multi-band dynamic spectrum access as a stochastic
restless multi-armed bandit problem with stationary unknown reward
distributions. In cognitive radio networks the multi-armed bandit problem
arises when deciding where in the radio spectrum to look for idle frequencies
that could be efficiently exploited for data transmission. We consider two
models for the dynamics of the frequency bands: 1) the independent model where
the state of the band evolves randomly independently from the past and 2) the
Gilbert-Elliot model, where the states evolve according to a 2-state Markov
chain. It is shown that in these conditions the proposed sensing policy attains
asymptotically logarithmic weak regret. The policy proposed in this paper is an
index policy, in which the index of a frequency band is comprised of a sample
mean term and a recency-based exploration bonus term. The sample mean promotes
spectrum exploitation whereas the exploration bonus encourages for further
exploration for idle bands providing high data rates. The proposed recency
based approach readily allows constructing the exploration bonus such that it
will grow the time interval between consecutive sensing time instants of a
suboptimal band exponentially, which then leads to logarithmically increasing
weak regret. Simulation results confirming logarithmic weak regret are
presented and it is found that the proposed policy provides often improved
performance at low complexity over other state-of-the-art policies in the
literature.

text: Biaxial stress plays a crucial role in the manipulation of material properties, particularly in high-temperature ferromagnetic semiconductors, where tetragonal symmetry is a key factor influencing their functional characteristics. This study investigates the tetragonal symmetry breaking induced by biaxial stress in CrO2, a prototypical half-metallic ferromagnet. The objective of this research is to elucidate the mechanisms by which applied stress can alter the electronic and magnetic properties of CrO2, potentially paving the way for novel spintronic applications.   Utilizing a combination of density functional theory (DFT) calculations and experimental techniques, we systematically analyze the effects of varying levels of biaxial stress on the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of CrO2. Our results reveal that the application of biaxial stress results in significant changes in the band structure and magnetic ordering, leading to a pronounced tetragonal symmetry breaking. The critical stress threshold required for this transition is identified, along with its corresponding impact on the magnetic moment and half-metallic character of the material.   In conclusion, the findings highlight the potential of biaxial stress engineering as a versatile technique to tailor the properties of high-temperature ferromagnetic semiconductors. This investigation not only enhances the understanding of the relationship between mechanical strain and electronic behavior in CrO2 but also opens avenues for the development of future spintronic devices that exploit these tunable properties.

We investigate the origin of the FIR continuum of SDSS J1148+5251, using it
as a prototype for the more general class of high-luminosity high-redshift
QSOs. We run the radiative transfer code TRADING to follow the transfer of
radiation from the central source and from stellar sources through the dusty
environment of the host galaxy. The model is based on the output of the
semi-analytical merger tree code, GAMETE/QSOdust, which enables to predict the
evolution of the host galaxy and of its nuclear black hole, following the star
formation history and chemical evolution -- including dust -- in all the
progenitor galaxies of SDSS J1148+5251. We find that the radiation emitted by
the central source can also provide an important source of heating for the dust
distributed in the host galaxy, powering at least 30% and up to 70% of the
observed far infrared emission at rest-frame wavelengths [20 - 1000]micron. The
remaining fraction is contributed by stellar sources and can only be achieved
if the host galaxy is able to sustain a star formation rate of ~ 900 Msun/yr at
z=6.4. This points to a co-evolution scenario where, during their hierarchical
assembly, the first SMBHs and their host galaxies first grow at the same pace
until the black hole reaches a mass of ~ 2 10^8 Msun and starts growing faster
than its host, reaching the bright quasar phase when the black hole and stellar
mass fall within the scatter of the scaling relation observed in local
galaxies. This same evolutionary scenario has been recently shown to explain
the properties of a larger sample of 5 < z <6.4 QSOs, and imply that current
dynamical mass measurements may have missed an important fraction of the host
galaxy stellar mass. We conclude that the FIR luminosity of high-z quasars is a
sensitive tracer of the rapidly changing physical conditions in the host
galaxy.

text: We investigated the optimization of the greenfield Beta-beam, a type of particle accelerator, with the goal of improving its efficiency and reducing operational costs. Our analysis revealed that the existing design of the Beta-beam was inefficient due to inadequate beam focusing and cooling systems, resulting in significant energy losses and reduced beam intensity.  To address this issue, we employed a multi-disciplinary approach, combining theoretical modeling, numerical simulations, and experimental validation. We developed a novel optimization framework that integrated machine learning algorithms with traditional optimization techniques to minimize the energy losses and maximize the beam intensity. The results of our simulations and experiments showed that the optimized design of the Beta-beam achieved a 30% reduction in energy losses and a 25% increase in beam intensity compared to the original design.  Our key findings also highlighted the importance of considering the interactions between the beam focusing and cooling systems in the optimization process. We demonstrated that a more efficient cooling system can significantly improve the beam quality, while also reducing the overall energy consumption. Furthermore, we identified several opportunities for further optimization, including the use of advanced materials and novel beam manipulation techniques.  The optimized design of the greenfield Beta-beam has significant implications for the field of particle physics, enabling researchers to conduct more efficient and effective experiments. Our work provides a proof-of-concept for the application of machine learning and optimization techniques in the design and operation of complex particle accelerators, and we believe that our results will have a lasting impact on the field.

text: We present an examination of the gamma-ray flaring activity from the gravitationally lensed blazar PKS 1830-211 as observed by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi LAT). This study focuses on understanding the characteristics and temporal evolution of the identified gamma-ray flares, which could elucidate the emission mechanisms and intrinsic properties of the lensed blazar. We detected multiple high-energy flare events over the observational period, characterized by varying intensities and durations. Our analysis employed light curve inspection, spectral fitting, and temporal variability evaluation, facilitated by the Fermi Science Tools. We observed that the flares exhibit rapid variability on the order of hours, suggesting a compact emission region near the central engine. The spectral energy distributions during flaring states exhibited significant deviations from quiescent states, indicating potential changes in the underlying particle acceleration processes. Additionally, we explored the effects of gravitational lensing on the observed flaring activity, which may magnify and temporally extend intrinsic emission features. We derived constraints on the blazar’s intrinsic luminosity and employed lensing models to refine our interpretations. Our findings support the hypothesis that gamma-ray production involves complex interactions, potentially including both external Comptonization and magnetically-driven mechanisms. Ultimately, this work enhances our understanding of lensed blazar phenomena and contributes to the broader field of high-energy astrophysics by providing insights into the dynamics of active galactic nuclei under the influence of gravitational lensing effects. Further multi-wavelength observations and theoretical modeling are necessary to fully uncover the intricacies of these fascinating systems.

We present the Voigt profile analysis of 132 intervening CIV+CIII components
associated with optically-thin HI absorbers at 2.1 < z < 3.4 in the 19
high-quality UVES/VLT and HIRES/Keck QSO spectra. For log N(CIV) = [11.7,
14.1], N(CIII) is proportional to N(CIV) with an exponent (1.42 +- 0.11) and <
N(CIII)/N(CIV) > = 1.0 +- 0.3 with a negligible redshift evolution. For 54 CIV
components tied (aligned) with HI at log N(HI) = [12.2, 16.0] and log N(CIV) =
[11.8, 13.8], the gas temperature T_b estimated from absorption line widths is
well-approximated to a Gaussian peaking at log T_b ~ 4.4 +- 0.3 for log T_b =
[3.5, 5.5], with a negligible non-thermal contribution. For 32 of 54 tied
HI+CIV pairs, also tied with CIII at log N(CIII) = [11.7, 13.8], we ran both
photoionisation equilibrium (PIE) and non-PIE (using a fixed temperature T_b)
Cloudy models for the Haardt-Madau QSO+galaxy 2012 UV background. We find
evidence of bimodality in observed and derived physical properties.
High-metallicity branch absorbers have a carbon abundance [C/H]_temp > -1.0, a
line-of-sight length L_temp < 20 kpc, and a total (neutral and ionised)
hydrogen volume density log n(H, temp) = [-4.5, -3.3] and and log T_b = [3.9,
4.5]. Low-metallicity branch absorbers have [C/H]_temp < -1.0, L_temp = [20,
480] kpc and log n(H, temp) = [-5.2, -4.3] and log T_b ~ 4.5. High-metallicity
branch absorbers seem to be originated from extended disks, inner halos or
outflowing gas of intervening galaxies, while low-metallicity absorbers are
produced by galactic halos or the surrounding IGM filament.

BaV3O8 contains both magnetic V4+(S=1/2) ions and non-magnetic V5+(S=0) ions.
The V4+ ions are arranged in a coupled Majumdar-Ghosh chain like network. Our
magnetic susceptibility chi(T) data fit well with the Curie-Weiss formula in
the temperature range of 80-300K and it yields a Curie constant
C=0.39cm3K/mole-V4+ and an antiferromagnetic Weiss temperature theta=-26K. The
chi(T) curve shows a broad maximum at T~25K indicative of short-range order
(SRO) and an anomaly corresponding to long-range order (LRO) at TN~6K. The
value of the frustration index (f=mod[theta/TN]~5) suggests that the system is
moderately frustrated. Above the LRO temperature the experimental magnetic
susceptibility data match well with the coupled Majumdar-Ghosh chain model with
the ratio of the nnn (next-nearest neighbor) to nn (nearest neighbor) magnetic
coupling alpha=2 and Jnnn/kB=40K. In a mean-field approach when considering the
inter-chain interactions, we obtain the total inter-chain coupling to be about
16K. The LRO anomaly at TN is also observe in the specific heat Cp(T) data and
is not sensitive to an applied magnetic field up to 90kOe. A 51V NMR signal
corresponding to the non-magnetic vanadium was observed. Anomalies at 6K were
observed in the variation with temperature of the 51V NMR linewidth and in the
spin-lattice relaxation rate 1/T1, indicating that they are sensitive to the
LRO onset and fluctuations at the magnetic V sites. The existence of two
components (one short and another long) is observed in the spin-spin relaxation
rate 1/T2 data in the vicinity of TN. The shorter component seems to be
intimately connected with the magnetically ordered state. We suggest that both
magnetically ordered and non-long range ordered (non-LRO) regions coexist in
this compound below the long range ordering temperature.

text: In this study, we explore a novel mechanism for baryogenesis via Hawking-like radiation within the context of the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) space-time. The baryon asymmetry of the universe is a fundamental problem in cosmology, as the standard model of particle physics predicts a nearly equal abundance of matter and antimatter, contrary to observations. We propose that the dynamic expansion of the universe can give rise to asymmetric particle production, facilitated by a Hawking-like radiation process, which preferentially generates baryons over antibaryons. Our methodology integrates quantum field theory in curved space-time to model particle creation in an expanding universe, leveraging the analogy between cosmological horizons and black hole event horizons to derive expressions for the rates of particle emission.  Our results demonstrate that the baryon-to-photon ratio produced through this mechanism is sensitive to the expansion rate and evolution of the FRW universe. We establish that under certain conditions, the asymmetry generated aligns with empirical observations without violating existing constraints on cosmological parameters. This work addresses the inadequacies of traditional baryogenesis models that rely heavily on speculative physics beyond the standard model. By employing only well-established principles of quantum mechanics and general relativity, our approach provides a compelling alternative pathway to understanding the origin of the cosmic baryon asymmetry. Future research will focus on refining the parameters and exploring the implications of this mechanism across varying cosmological models, ultimately contributing to a potentially unifying framework for early universe cosmology and particle physics.

text: The study explores the temporal morphology of white-light flares observed on the star GJ 1243 using high-resolution photometric data from the Kepler space telescope. Previous observations have highlighted the variability of GJ 1243, particularly its frequent flaring activity, which has significant implications for our understanding of stellar evolution and the magnetic activity of low-mass stars. This research aims to provide a detailed analysis of the timing, duration, and intensity of these flares, as well as their spatial distribution across the stellar surface.  Methodologically, the study employs Fourier analysis to decompose the light curves into various harmonic components, allowing for a quantitative assessment of the flaring events. Additionally, machine learning techniques were applied to identify patterns that may indicate the underlying physical processes driving the flaring behavior. The analysis covers a period spanning several years, capturing both short-term and long-term variability.  Key findings include the identification of multiple flare episodes with durations ranging from minutes to hours, and an observation that the frequency and magnitude of flares exhibit a certain degree of periodicity, suggesting potential internal mechanisms such as differential rotation or magnetic activity cycles. Furthermore, spatial mapping reveals that flares often occur preferentially at specific latitudinal regions, indicating localized heating and cooling phenomena.  Conclusively, the research underscores the importance of continuous monitoring of GJ 1243 to better understand the complex interplay between stellar structure, magnetic fields, and energy release mechanisms. The results contribute to the broader field of exoplanetary science by offering insights into the conditions under which planets orbiting such stars might experience extreme irradiation events.

text: In this study, we focus on developing approximate solutions for fractional subdiffusion equations by employing the Heat-Balance Integral Method (HBIM). Fractional subdiffusion equations, which are integral in modeling anomalous diffusion processes found in complex systems, present significant analytical and computational challenges due to their non-local nature and intrinsic memory effects. We address these challenges by formulating an approach that leverages the simplified computational framework of HBIM, offering a feasible alternative to exact analytical solutions which are often intractable.  Our primary contribution is the adaptation of the HBIM to fractional time derivatives, incorporating Mittag-Leffler functions to encapsulate the memory kernels characteristic of fractional calculus. By constructing integral approximations, we derive generalized expressions that maintain computational efficiency and provide robust validation against known exact solutions and numerical benchmarks. These derived expressions bridge the gap between the precision of detailed numerical algorithms and the expediency of analytical approximations.  We apply our methodology to prototypical fractional subdiffusion scenarios and observe excellent agreement in sub-diffusive transport properties, notably capturing the sub-linear mean squared displacement and time-exponent scaling behaviors typical of subdiffusive processes. The results demonstrate that our approach effectively captures essential dynamics while significantly reducing computational effort. Our framework is extensible to higher-dimensional and more complex boundary conditions, suggesting broad applicability in fields such as material science, biology, and geophysics, where fractional diffusion processes are prevalent. This work advances the utility of HBIM in fractional calculus, offering a practical tool for theorists and applied scientists engaged in the modeling of anomalous diffusion phenomena.
label: machine

text: We investigated the phenomenon of Android update adoption and its impact on user experience, revealing a complex interplay of factors that hinder the widespread adoption of timely updates among Android users. Our study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining surveys, interviews, and log analysis to gather data from a sample of 1,000 Android users. The results indicate that users are often unaware of the importance of timely updates, and the update process is frequently marred by technical issues, such as slow download speeds and device boot times.  We identified three primary barriers to update adoption (1) perceived security risks, (2) lack of awareness about the benefits of updates, and (3) difficulties in updating multiple devices simultaneously. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that users tend to prioritize device functionality over update frequency, often leading to a "patchwork" approach to update adoption. We also found that users' update behaviors are influenced by their device ownership patterns, with those owning multiple devices exhibiting more frequent update adoption.  Our findings highlight the need for a more user-centric approach to update management, one that takes into account the complex interplay of technical, social, and psychological factors that influence update adoption. We propose a framework for addressing these challenges, which involves providing users with clear and concise information about the benefits of updates, simplifying the update process, and developing more intuitive update management tools. By adopting this framework, device manufacturers and mobile network operators can improve user experience and increase update adoption rates, ultimately enhancing the security and functionality of the Android ecosystem.
label: machine

text: We investigate the intricate relationship between matroid polytopes, combinatorial optimization, and their diverse applications across various computational problems. Our work addresses the challenge of efficiently exploring the geometric structure of matroid polytopes, which plays a crucial role in the understanding of matroid theory and its applications in optimization and computational geometry. Utilizing an innovative combination of geometric and combinatorial techniques, we develop polynomial-time algorithms for generating facets of matroid polytopes, thus enhancing existing algorithms for matroid optimization. We apply duality principles to derive results that contribute to both the theoretical foundation of matroid polytopes and their practical applications in fields such as network design, scheduling, and resource allocation. Furthermore, we extend previous results by establishing new connections between matroid polytopes and linear programming, highlighting their role in enabling efficient problem-solving strategies. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithms in improving computational performance for various graph-theoretic and optimization problems. Consequently, we present data that validates our theoretical findings, offering insights into the geometric properties of these polytopes. This work not only enriches the mathematical understanding of matroid polytopes but also provides practical methodologies for algorithm development in combinatorial optimization, setting the stage for future research in this vibrant area. We conclude by discussing potential future directions, emphasizing the significance of exploring the broader applications of matroid polytopes in emerging fields such as machine learning and network theory.

text:
Growing concern for individual privacy, driven by an increased public
awareness of the degree to which many of our electronic activities are tracked
by interested third parties (e.g. Google knows what I am thinking before I
finish entering my search query), is driving the development anonymizing
technologies (e.g. Tor). The coming mass migration to IPv6 as the primary
transport of Internet traffic promises to make one such technology, end-to-end
host based encryption, more readily available to the average user. In a world
where end-to-end encryption is ubiquitous, what can replace the existing models
for network intrusion detection? How can network administrators and operators,
responsible for securing networks against hostile activity, protect a network
they cannot see? In an encrypted world, signature based event detection is
unlikely to prove useful. In order to secure a network in such an environment,
without trampling the privacy afforded to users by end-to-end encryption, our
threat detection model needs to evolve from signature based detection to a
heuristic model that flags deviations from normal network-wide behavior for
further investigation. In this paper we present such a heuristic model and test
its effectiveness for detecting intrusions in an entirely encrypted network
environment. Our results demonstrate the network intrusion detection system's
ability to monitor a network carrying only host-to-host encrypted traffic. This
work indicates that a broad perspective change is required. Network security
models need to evolve from endeavoring to define attack signatures to
describing what the network looks like under normal conditions and searching
for deviations from the norm.
label: human

text:
Deep directed generative models have attracted much attention recently due to
their generative modeling nature and powerful data representation ability. In
this paper, we review different structures of deep directed generative models
and the learning and inference algorithms associated with the structures. We
focus on a specific structure that consists of layers of Bayesian Networks due
to the property of capturing inherent and rich dependencies among latent
variables. The major difficulty of learning and inference with deep directed
models with many latent variables is the intractable inference due to the
dependencies among the latent variables and the exponential number of latent
variable configurations. Current solutions use variational methods often
through an auxiliary network to approximate the posterior probability
inference. In contrast, inference can also be performed directly without using
any auxiliary network to maximally preserve the dependencies among the latent
variables. Specifically, by exploiting the sparse representation with the
latent space, max-max instead of max-sum operation can be used to overcome the
exponential number of latent configurations. Furthermore, the max-max operation
and augmented coordinate ascent are applied to both supervised and unsupervised
learning as well as to various inference. Quantitative evaluations on benchmark
datasets of different models are given for both data representation and feature
learning tasks.
