During the past decade there have been several attempts to detect cosmogenic
ultra high energy (UHE) neutrinos by searching for radio Cerenkov bursts
resulting from charged impact showers in terrestrial ice or the lunar regolith.
So far these radio searches have yielded no detections, but the inferred flux
upper limits have started to constrain physical models for UHE neutrino
generation. For searches which use the Moon as a target, we summarize the
physics of the interaction, properties of the resulting Cerenkov radio pulse,
detection statistics, effective aperture scaling laws, and derivation of upper
limits for isotropic and point source models. We report on initial results from
the RESUN search, which uses the Expanded Very Large Array configured in
multiple sub-arrays of four antennas at 1.45 GHz pointing along the lunar limb.
We detected no pulses of lunar origin during 45 observing hours. This implies
upper limits to the differential neutrino flux E^2 dN/dE < 0.003 EeV km^{-2}
s^{-1} sr^{-1} and < 0.0003 EeV km$^{-2} s^{-1} at 90% confidence level for
isotropic and sampled point sources respectively, in the neutrino energy range
10^{21.6} < E(eV) < 10^{22.6}. The isotropic flux limit is comparable to the
lowest published upper limits for lunar searches. The full RESUN search, with
an additional 200 hours observing time and an improved data acquisition scheme,
will be be an order of magnitude more sensitive in the energy range 10^{21} <
E(eV) < 10^{22} than previous lunar-target searches, and will test Z burst
models of neutrino generation.

text:
The black hole candidate, XTE J1752-223, was discovered in 2009 October when
it entered an outburst. We obtained radio data from the Australia Telescope
Compact Array for the duration of the ~9 month event. The lightcurves show that
the radio emission from the compact jet persisted for the duration of an
extended hard state and through the transition to the intermediate state. The
flux then rose rapidly by a factor of 10 and the radio source entered a series
of at least 7 maxima, the first of which was likely to be emission associated
with the compact jet. The subsequent 6 flares were accompanied by variable
behaviour in terms of radio spectrum, degree of linear polarisation, morphology
and associated X-ray behaviour. They were, however, remarkably similar in terms
of the estimated minimum power required to launch such an ejection event. We
compare the timing of radio peaks with the location of the ejecta, imaged by
contemporaneous VLBI experiments. We then discuss the mechanism behind the
events, in terms of whether discrete ejections is the most likely description
of the behaviour. One ejection, at least, appears to be travelling with
apparent superluminal motion. The range of properties, however, suggests that
mutiple mechanisms may be relevant and that at least some of the emission is
coming from shocked interactions amongst the ejecta and between the ejecta and
the interstellar medium. We also compare the radio flux density with the X-ray
source during the hard state and conclude that XTE J1752-223 is a
radio-weak/X-ray-bright outlier on the universal correlation for black hole
transient sources.

text: This research paper explores the second law of thermodynamics from the perspective of symmetry and unitarity. By examining the foundational principles of symmetry and unitarity in the context of thermodynamics, our objective is to provide a novel insight into the underlying mechanisms governing entropy production and irreversibility in physical systems.    We utilize theoretical and mathematical frameworks rooted in symmetry principles and unitarity conditions to analyze the behavior of thermodynamic processes. This includes employing group theory, statistical mechanics, and quantum field theory to derive relationships and constraints that govern entropy changes in diverse systems.   Our investigation reveals that the second law of thermodynamics can be elegantly understood and generalized through the principles of symmetry and unitarity. By elucidating the connections between these fundamental concepts and thermodynamic entropy, we present a unifying perspective that sheds light on the irreversibility of natural processes.   In conclusion, this study emphasizes the significance of symmetry and unitarity in elucidating the origins of the second law of thermodynamics. Our findings not only provide a deeper theoretical understanding of entropy production but also offer implications for diverse fields such as statistical physics, quantum mechanics, and cosmology.

A detailed microscopic and quantitative description of the electronic and
magnetic properties of Gd$^{3+}$-doped YCo$_{2}$Zn$_{20}$ single crystals
(Y$_{1-x}$Gd$_{x}$Co$_{2}$Zn$_{20}$: (0.002 $\lesssim x \leq $ 1.00) is
reported through a combination of temperature-dependent electron spin resonance
(ESR), heat capacity and $dc$ magnetic susceptibility experiments, plus
first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The ESR results
indicate that this system features an \emph{exchange bottleneck} scenario
wherein various channels for the spin-lattice relaxation mechanism of the
Gd$^{3+}$ ions can be identified via exchange interactions with different types
of conduction electrons at the Fermi level. Quantitative support from the other
techniques allow to extract the exchange interaction parameters between the
localized magnetic moments of the Gd$^{3+}$ ions and the different types of
conduction electrons present at the Fermi level ($J_{fs}$, $J_{fp}$ and
$J_{fd}$). Despite the complexity of the crystal structure, our combination of
experimental and electronic structure data establish GdCo$_{2}$Zn$_{20}$ as a
model RKKY system by predicting a Curie-Weiss temperature $\theta_{C} =
-1.2(2)$~K directly from microscopic parameters, in very good agreement with
the bulk value from magnetization data. The successful microscopic
understanding of the electronic structure and behavior for the two end
compounds YCo$_{2}$Zn$_{20}$ and GdCo$_{2}$Zn$_{20}$ means they can be used as
references to help describe the more complex electronic properties of related
materials.

We define a class of "optimal" coordinate systems by requiring that the
deviation from an exact Robertson-Walker metric is "as small as possible"
within a given four dimensional volume. The optimization is performed by
minimizing several volume integrals which would vanish for an exact
Robertson-Walker metric. Covariance is automatic. Foliation of space-time is
part of the optimization procedure. Only the metric is involved in the
procedure, no assumptions about the origin of the energy-momentum tensor are
needed. A scale factor does not show up during the optimization process, the
optimal scale factor is determined at the end. The general formulation is non
perturbative. An explicit perturbative treatment is possible. The shifts which
lead to the optimal coordinates obey Euler-Lagrange equations which are
formulated and solved in first order of the perturbation. The extension to
second order is sketched, but turns out to be unnecessary. The only freedom in
the choice of coordinates which finally remains are the rigid transformations
which keep the form of the Robertson-Walker metric intact, i.e. translations in
space and time, spatial rotations, and spatial scaling. Spatial averaging
becomes trivial. In first order of the perturbation there is no backreaction. A
simplified second order treatment results in a very small effect, excluding the
possibility to mimic dark energy from backreaction. This confirms (as well as
contradicts) statements in the literature.

text:
Protein structure prediction is one of the most important problems in
computational biology. The most successful computational approach, also called
template-based modeling, identifies templates with solved crystal structures
for the query proteins and constructs three dimensional models based on
sequence/structure alignments. Although substantial effort has been made to
improve protein sequence alignment, the accuracy of alignments between
distantly related proteins is still unsatisfactory. In this thesis, I will
introduce a number of statistical machine learning methods to build accurate
alignments between a protein sequence and its template structures, especially
for proteins having only distantly related templates. For a protein with only
one good template, we develop a regression-tree based Conditional Random Fields
(CRF) model for pairwise protein sequence/structure alignment. By learning a
nonlinear threading scoring function, we are able to leverage the correlation
among different sequence and structural features. We also introduce an
information-theoretic measure to guide the learning algorithm to better exploit
the structural features for low-homology proteins with little evolutionary
information in their sequence profile. For a protein with multiple good
templates, we design a probabilistic consistency approach to thread the protein
to all templates simultaneously. By minimizing the discordance between the
pairwise alignments of the protein and templates, we are able to construct a
multiple sequence/structure alignment, which leads to better structure
predictions than any single-template based prediction.

text: The role of non-scientific staff in scientific research is a vital but often overlooked aspect of the scientific process. This study aims to shed light on the invaluable contributions made by non-scientific staff in research settings. Through a qualitative research methodology involving interviews and observations, the study explores the diverse roles and responsibilities of non-scientific staff within scientific research teams. Key findings reveal that non-scientific staff play crucial roles in facilitating the smooth operation of research projects, providing logistical support, managing data, and enabling scientists to focus on their core research activities. Additionally, non-scientific staff often bring unique perspectives and skills that enhance the overall research outcomes. The study underscores the importance of recognizing and appreciating the contributions of non-scientific staff in scientific research endeavors. In conclusion, a more inclusive acknowledgement of the "village" of individuals involved in scientific research can lead to more effective and collaborative research environments, ultimately benefiting the scientific community as a whole.
label: machine

text: We present the results of a 3.3 cm JVLA observations campaign aimed at detecting centimeter-sized pebbles in transitional disks. Our study focused on a sample of 15 young stars with protoplanetary disks, selected based on their known disk properties and potential for hosting small planetesimals. Through a combination of imaging and spectroscopic observations, we searched for centimeter-scale pebbles, which are thought to play a crucial role in the formation and evolution of planetary systems.  Our survey revealed a significant number of disk candidates exhibiting centimeter-scale pebbles, with a detection rate of approximately 60%. These pebbles were found to be distributed throughout the disk, with a median size of 1.4 cm and a median mass of 1.3 g. Notably, we observed a strong correlation between the presence of centimeter-scale pebbles and the disk's gas-to-dust ratio, suggesting a link between pebble formation and disk evolution.  Our findings have important implications for our understanding of the role of small planetesimals in the formation of planetary systems. We propose a model in which centimeter-scale pebbles are formed through the accretion of dust grains and ice particles in the disk's outer regions. This model is consistent with observations of pebble distributions and can explain the observed correlation between pebble presence and disk gas-to-dust ratio. Our results highlight the importance of centimeter-scale pebbles in the formation of planetary systems and underscore the need for further studies to explore their role in shaping the architecture of protoplanetary disks.

text: The interaction between hydrogen (H) and helium (He) in 3C-β SiC is crucial for the development of advanced materials in semiconductor applications. This study investigates the site preference and diffusion behaviors of H influenced by He implantation in 3C-β SiC. The main objective was to elucidate the mechanisms that govern H localization and mobility in the presence of He, offering insights that could optimize material performance.   Using first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we evaluated various configurations of H and He incorporation into the SiC lattice. We systematically analyzed the preferred lattice sites for H in conjunction with different concentrations of He, while also employing migration energy calculations to assess H diffusion pathways. Key findings reveal that the presence of He significantly alters the site preference of H, promoting its localization at defect sites in the crystal structure. Moreover, He impedes H diffusion, resulting in higher activation energies compared to H in a He-free environment.   Further, temperature-dependent simulations suggest that the presence of He enhances the stability of H at certain lattice positions, potentially leading to enhanced retention of hydrogen in SiC under operational conditions. In conclusion, these findings provide a comprehensive understanding of H and He interactions in 3C-β SiC, with implications for controlling hydrogen behavior in semiconductor devices, thereby enabling more efficient performance in future applications.
label: machine

text: In this study, we explore the Stochastic Maximum Principle within the framework of mean-field controls and non-zero-sum mean-field game problems, particularly focusing on forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs). We identify the theoretical gaps in existing literature regarding the application of stochastic control principles to non-zero-sum games in mean-field settings. Our methodology integrates advanced techniques in stochastic calculus and variational inequalities to derive necessary conditions for optimal control strategies in FBSDEs under mean-field interactions.  Through rigorous mathematical analysis, we establish a Stochastic Maximum Principle that accommodates the complexities introduced by mean-field dynamics and non-zero-sum scenarios. The results demonstrate that solutions to the optimal control problems involve a dynamic program that balances the individual objectives of players while accounting for the collective influence of the mean-field term. We exemplify our theoretical insights through various numerical simulations that depict the equilibrium dynamics and optimal control strategies in illustrative mean-field game contexts.  Our findings provide a foundational framework for further research on advanced control problems featuring intricate interactions within large populations, highlighting the practical significance of optimizing decision-making processes in economics, finance, and social systems. By extending the applicability of the Stochastic Maximum Principle, we contribute to a deeper understanding of strategic behaviors and optimal planning in collective decision-making environments characterized by uncertainty and interdependencies among agents.

In this paper, we propose a device to device (D2D) communication scenario
underlaying a cellular network where both D2D and cellular users (CUs) are
discrete power-rate systems with limited feedback from the receivers. It is
assumed that there exists an adversary which wants to eavesdrop on the
information transmission from the base station (BS) to CUs. Since D2D
communication shares the same spectrum with cellular network, cross
interference must be considered. However, when secrecy capacity is considered,
the interference caused by D2D communication can help to improve the secrecy
communications by confusing the eavesdroppers. Since both systems share the
same spectrum, cross interference must be considered. We formulate the proposed
resource allocation into an optimization problem whose objective is to maximize
the average transmission rate of D2D pair in the presence of the cellular
communications under average transmission power constraint. For the cellular
network, we require a minimum average achievable secrecy rate in the absence of
D2D communication as well as a maximum secrecy outage probability in the
presence of D2D communication which should be satisfied. Due to high complexity
convex optimization methods, to solve the proposed optimization problem, we
apply Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) which is an evolutionary approach.
Moreover, we model and study the error in the feedback channel and the
imperfectness of channel distribution information (CDI) using parametric and
nonparametric methods. Finally, the impact of different system parameters on
the performance of the proposed scheme is investigated through simulations. The
performance of the proposed scheme is evaluated using numerical results for
different scenarios.

text: This study investigates the percentage depth dose (PDD) distributions in inhomogeneous phantoms with lung and bone equivalent media for small fields of the CyberKnife, a type of stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) system. Background radiation therapy has become increasingly common, and understanding the dosimetric characteristics of small fields is crucial for optimizing treatment outcomes. Inhomogeneous phantoms with lung and bone equivalent media are used to simulate the complex anatomy of the human body, which can affect radiation dose distribution.  The objective of this study is to measure and analyze the PDD distributions in small fields of the CyberKnife for inhomogeneous phantoms with lung and bone equivalent media. A total of 30 small fields (10x10mm, 10x20mm, 20x20mm) were measured using a Farmer's chamber and a ionization chamber. The PDD distributions were calculated using the dose rate and dose conversion factors.  The results show that the PDD distributions in small fields of the CyberKnife for inhomogeneous phantoms with lung and bone equivalent media are significantly affected by the media composition. The PDD values for lung equivalent media were lower than those for bone equivalent media, indicating a reduced radiation dose to the target volume. The results also indicate that the PDD distributions are highly dependent on the field size, with smaller fields exhibiting larger dose gradients. These findings are essential for optimizing the treatment planning of CyberKnife patients, particularly those with complex anatomy.  In conclusion, this study provides valuable insights into the dosimetric characteristics of small fields of the CyberKnife for inhomogeneous phantoms with lung and bone equivalent media. The results highlight the importance of considering the media composition and field size in treatment planning, and the findings can be used to improve the accuracy and efficacy of CyberKnife treatment.

text:
The identification of orientation relationships (ORs) plays a crucial r\^ole
in the understanding of solid phase transformations. In steels, the most common
models of ORs are the ones by Nishiyama-Wassermann (NW) and Kurdjumov-Sachs
(KS). The defining feature of these and other OR models is the matching of
directions and planes in the parent face-centred cubic $\gamma$-phase to ones
in the product body-centred cubic/tetragonal $\alpha/\alpha'$-phase.
  In this paper a novel method that identifies transformation strains with ORs
is introduced and used to develop a new strain-based approach to phase
transformation models in steels. Using this approach, it is shown that the
transformation strains that leave a close packed plane in the $\gamma$-phase
and a close packed direction within that plane unrotated are precisely those
giving rise to the NW and KS ORs when a cubic product phase is considered.
Further, it is outlined how, by choosing different pairs of unrotated planes
and directions, other common ORs such as the ones by Pitsch (PT) and
Greninger-Troiano (GT) can be derived.
  One of the advantages of our approach is that it leads to a natural
generalisation of the NW, KS and other ORs for different ratios of
tetragonality $r$ of the product bct $\alpha'$-phase. These generalised ORs
predict a sharpening of the transformation textures with increasing
tetragonality and are thus in qualitative agreement with experiments on steels
with varying alloy concentration.
label: human

text: In the SU(2) Gauged Higgs Model, a non-topological soliton solution, known as an oscillon, has been discovered. Oscillons are spherical field configurations that can exist as localized, stable, and dynamic solutions in the early universe. The existence of oscillons provides an alternative explanation for the observed baryon asymmetry in the universe. This study aims to analyze the properties and dynamics of oscillons in the SU(2) Gauged Higgs Model.  We begin by reviewing the theoretical background of the SU(2) Gauged Higgs Model and the derivation of the oscillon solution. The oscillon solution is found by solving the field equations of the model with spherical symmetry and appropriate boundary conditions. The stability and dynamic behavior of oscillons are investigated using the bounce solution and the tunneling method.  Our key findings reveal that the oscillon solution is stable against spherically symmetric perturbations and exhibits oscillatory behavior. The mass and lifetimes of oscillons depend on the choice of potential parameters in the model. The mass spectrum of oscillons is also analyzed, revealing a tower of excitations.  The study of oscillons in the SU(2) Gauged Higgs Model provides insights into the physics of non-topological solitons and their potential role in the early universe. The findings of this study can be extended to other models and may shed light on the origin of baryon asymmetry.  In conclusion, this study presents a thorough analysis of oscillons in the SU(2) Gauged Higgs Model, including their stability, dynamics, and mass spectrum. The results provide a better understanding of the role of non-topological solitons in the early universe and offer new perspectives for explaining the observed baryon asymmetry.
label: machine

text: The study investigates the application of label transfer techniques to derive precise stellar parameters for giant stars observed by the LAMOST survey, leveraging the rich dataset of the APOGEE survey. Recent advancements in stellar spectroscopy have enabled the extraction of detailed stellar parameters, yet challenges persist in achieving consistency across different survey instruments. This research aims to harmonize data between APOGEE, which provides high-resolution infrared spectra, and LAMOST, known for its extensive optical survey of the Milky Way. The methodology involves the utilization of machine learning algorithms to transfer labels—effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity—from the APOGEE dataset to approximately 450,000 LAMOST giants. The model is trained on stars common to both surveys, ensuring robust calibration between the two systems. Key findings demonstrate significant improvements in the precision of LAMOST stellar parameters, with reduced systematic uncertainties, allowing for a more detailed characterization of the Galactic structure and evolution. The enhanced parameter estimation not only improves our understanding of the chemical and kinematic properties of giant stars but also contributes to refining models of stellar populations within the Milky Way. The success of this label transfer approach underscores the potential of combining large-scale astronomical datasets to overcome limitations inherent in individual surveys. Conclusively, this research provides a framework for future cross-survey analyses, enhancing the scientific returns from ongoing and forthcoming spectroscopic efforts.

text: Solar jets are important dynamic phenomena in the solar atmosphere, particularly in polar coronal holes. These jets are believed to play a crucial role in the mass and energy transport within the Sun's outer corona. In this study, we investigate the magnetic untwisting process associated with solar jets emanating from polar coronal holes.   Our objective is to understand the relationship between magnetic field topology and the untwisting motions of these jets. We aim to uncover the mechanisms driving the untwisting process and its implications for the overall magnetic structure of the solar corona.  To achieve this, we analyze high-resolution observational data obtained from space-based telescopes and ground-based instruments. We apply advanced image processing techniques and magnetic field extrapolation methods to track the evolution of magnetic fields and plasma dynamics during the jet untwisting events.  Key findings reveal a clear correlation between the magnetic field topology and the untwisting behavior of solar jets in polar coronal holes. We observe rapid changes in the magnetic helicity during the untwisting process, indicating the release of stored magnetic energy.  In conclusion, our study provides valuable insights into the dynamics of solar jets in polar coronal holes, shedding light on the magnetic mechanisms driving these phenomena and their significance for the Sun-Earth system.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the potential role of stimulated radiative molecular association (SRMA) in the formation of planetesimals and small bodies in the early solar system. SRMA is a gas-phase reaction occurring under certain conditions that leads to the formation of loosely bound van der Waals complexes between two neutral molecules. By using state-of-the-art molecular simulation techniques, we modeled the interactions between H2 and He under conditions representative of the early solar nebula. Our results show that SRMA significantly enhances the rate of molecular association in comparison to collision-induced dissociative recombination (CIDR) and three-body association (3BA) under the considered conditions. This increased efficiency of molecular association can potentially explain the high abundance of certain planetesimal and satellite compositions observed in the solar system. Additionally, we demonstrate that SRMA may play a crucial role in the formation of large bodies in the presence of strong UV radiation fields. The proposed mechanism provides a plausible explanation for the observed chemical abundances in the early solar system, and our findings shed new light on the complex interplay between gas-phase reactions and solid-state processes in planetary formation. Further investigations are required to fully understand the implications of SRMA in the context of planetary accretion, and to assess its potential influence on the composition and distribution of other planetary systems.
label: machine

text:
We introduce version two of the fast star cluster evolution code Evolve Me A
Cluster of StarS (EMACSS). The first version (Alexander & Gieles) assumed that
cluster evolution is balanced for the majority of the life-cycle, meaning that
the rate of energy generation in the core of the cluster equals the diffusion
rate of energy by two-body relaxation, which makes the code suitable for
modelling clusters in weak tidal fields. In this new version we extend the
model to include an unbalanced phase of evolution to describe the pre-collapse
evolution and the accompanying escape rate such that clusters in strong tidal
fields can also be modelled. We also add a prescription for the evolution of
the core radius and density and a related cluster concentration parameter. The
model simultaneously solves a series of first-order ordinary differential
equations for the rate of change of the core radius, half-mass radius and the
number of member stars N. About two thousand integration steps in time are
required to solve for the entire evolution of a star cluster and this number is
approximately independent of N. We compare the model to the variation of these
parameters following from a series of direct N-body calculations of single-mass
clusters and find good agreement in the evolution of all parameters. Relevant
time-scales, such as the total lifetimes and core collapse times, are
reproduced with an accuracy of about 10% for clusters with various initial
half-mass radii (relative to their Jacobi radii) and a range of different
initial N up to N = 65536. We intend to extend this framework to include more
realistic initial conditions, such as a stellar mass spectrum and mass loss
from stars. The EMACSS code can be used in star cluster population studies and
in models that consider the co-evolution of (globular) star clusters and large
scale structures.
label: human

text: We report the results of a long-term observational study of four elusive binary systems within the globular cluster 47 Tucanae, a rich source of pulsars. Utilizing a combination of radio and optical surveys conducted over a period of nearly two decades, we identified and characterized four previously unconfirmed binary systems, namely PSR J0331-6605, PSR J0332-6603, PSR J0333-6604, and PSR J0334-6606. Through a systematic analysis of the observed light curves and pulse profiles, we demonstrate that these systems are indeed pulsars in binary motion, with periods ranging from 1.47 to 2.51 seconds. Our findings indicate that these pulsars are experiencing significant orbital evolution, with the most recent observations suggesting that the binary systems are dynamically decaying. We also observe significant variability in the pulsar's magnetic field and its impact on the surrounding interstellar medium. Our results provide new insights into the complex dynamics of pulsar binaries within globular clusters, highlighting the importance of long-term monitoring in understanding the evolution of these enigmatic objects. By combining archival data with new observations, we have shed light on the elusive nature of these binary systems, revealing a complex interplay between pulsar magnetic fields, orbital evolution, and the surrounding environment.
label: machine

text: The Integer Domination Problem (IDP) is a combinatorial optimization problem with significant applications in various fields. Vizing conjectured that the minimum number of integers needed to cover all the other integers in a given set is equal to the maximum degree plus one. This conjecture holds true for many sets, but not for all. To explore this phenomenon further, we focus on a Vizing-type conjecture for IDP in this paper.  Our objective is to study the validity of a Vizing-type conjecture related to IDP. Specifically, we consider the minimum number of integers required to dominate all the other integers in a given set, subject to the constraint that each integer is dominated by at least k other integers. We denote this problem as the k-Vizing Integer Domination Problem (k-VIDP).  Our methodology includes theoretical analysis, computational experiments, and comparisons with existing results. We derive bounds on the minimum number of integers required to solve k-VIDP based on the maximum degree and the value of k. Additionally, we investigate the performance of these bounds through computational experiments, comparing their accuracy with well-established results.  Our key findings indicate that the derived bounds are not always tight, but they provide useful insights into the behavior of k-VIDP. We observe that the problem exhibits a non-monotone relationship with the value of k, which can result in unexpected outcomes. We also observe that the performance of the bounds significantly depends on the underlying structure of the set.  In conclusion, our study sheds light on the intricacies of Vizing-type conjectures for IDP, providing new insights and understanding into the k-Vizing Integer Domination Problem. Our findings offer opportunities for further research, particularly in characterizing the sets for which these bounds hold true and developing more accurate bounds.
label: machine

text:
Hidden photons, gauge bosons of a U(1) symmetry of a hidden sector, can
constitute the dark matter of the universe and a smoking gun for large volume
compactifications of string theory. In the sub-eV mass range, a possible
discovery experiment consists on searching the copious flux of these particles
emitted from the Sun in a helioscope setup \`a la Sikivie. In this paper, we
compute the flux of transversely polarised HPs from the Sun, a necessary
ingredient for interpreting such experiments. We provide a detailed exposition
of photon-HP oscillations in inhomogenous media, with special focus on
resonance oscillations, which play a leading role in many cases. The region of
the Sun emitting HPs resonantly is a thin spherical shell for which we justify
an averaged-emission formula and which implies a distinctive morphology of the
angular distribution of HPs on Earth in many cases. Low mass HPs with energies
in the visible and IR have resonances very close to the photosphere where the
solar plasma is not fully ionised and requires building a detailed model of
solar refraction and absorption. We present results for a broad range of HP
masses (from 0-1 keV) and energies (from the IR to the X-ray range), the most
complete atlas of solar HP emission to date.
label: human

text:
Reconstructing who infected whom is a central challenge in analysing
epidemiological data. Recently, advances in sequencing technology have led to
increasing interest in Bayesian approaches to inferring who infected whom using
genetic data from pathogens. The logic behind such approaches is that isolates
that are nearly genetically identical are more likely to have been recently
transmitted than those that are very different. A number of methods have been
developed to perform this inference. However, testing their convergence,
examining posterior sets of transmission trees and comparing methods'
performance are challenged by the fact that the object of inference - the
transmission tree - is a complicated discrete structure. We introduce a metric
on transmission trees to quantify distances between them. The metric can
accommodate trees with unsampled individuals, and highlights differences in the
source case and in the number of infections per infector. We illustrate its
performance on simple simulated scenarios and on posterior transmission trees
from a TB outbreak. We find that the metric reveals where the posterior is
sensitive to the priors, and where collections of trees are composed of
distinct clusters. We use the metric to define median trees summarising these
clusters. Quantitative tools to compare transmission trees to each other will
be required for assessing MCMC convergence, exploring posterior trees and
benchmarking diverse methods as this field continues to mature.
label: human

text: We present the findings of our study on Holmberg II, utilizing data from the Suprime-Cam instrument to investigate evidence of ram pressure stripping in this galaxy. Ram pressure stripping is a phenomenon where the intergalactic medium strips gas and dust from a galaxy as it moves through a denser environment. Our work aims to contribute to the understanding of the effects of the intergalactic medium on the gas content and star formation in Holmberg II.   The key results reveal distinct asymmetries in the gas distribution and star formation regions within the galaxy, suggesting the presence of ram pressure effects. We observe an elongated structure of ionized gas, likely caused by the interaction of the interstellar medium with the surrounding environment. Additionally, our wide-field study provides insights into the spatial distribution of dust and star-forming regions, highlighting regions that have been heavily impacted by ram pressure stripping.   Our methodology involved deep observational analysis of Holmberg II using the Suprime-Cam instrument on the Subaru Telescope. By combining imaging and spectroscopic data, we were able to map the gas and dust distribution across the galaxy, providing essential insights into the physical processes at play. Our study contributes to the broader understanding of galaxy evolution and the impact of environmental influences on the properties of galaxies.
label: machine

text: Ambipolar high mobility hexagonal transistors on hydrogen-terminated silicon (111) surfaces have garnered significant interest due to their potential in next-generation electronic devices. This study aims to investigate the characteristics of these transistors and their performance on hydrogen-terminated silicon surfaces. The methodology involved fabricating hexagonal transistors using a combination of deposition techniques and material analysis on silicon (111) surfaces terminated with hydrogen. Key findings reveal that these transistors exhibit ambipolar behavior with high carrier mobilities, demonstrating their potential for use in high-speed and low-power electronic applications. The research highlights the importance of surface termination in achieving high device performance and provides insights into the design and optimization of hexagonal transistors on silicon substrates. Overall, this study contributes to the understanding of ambipolar transistors on hydrogen-terminated silicon surfaces and paves the way for their utilization in future electronic devices.

text:
We present a generator for the production of a Higgs boson H in association
with a vector boson V=W or Z (including subsequent V decay) plus zero and one
jet, that can be used in conjunction with general-purpose shower Monte Carlo
generators, according to the POWHEG method, as implemented within the POWHEG
BOX framework. We have computed the virtual corrections using GoSam, a program
for the automatic construction of virtual amplitudes. In order to do so, we
have built a general interface of the POWHEG BOX to the GoSam package. With
this addition, the construction of a POWHEG generator within the POWHEG BOX is
now fully automatized, except for the construction of the Born phase space. Our
HV + 1 jet generators can be run with the recently proposed MiNLO method for
the choice of scales and the inclusion of Sudakov form factors. Since the HV
production is very similar to V production, we were able to apply an improved
MiNLO procedure, that was recently used in H and V production, also in the
present case. This procedure is such that the resulting generator achieves NLO
accuracy not only for inclusive distributions in HV + 1 jet production but also
in HV production, i.e. when the associated jet is not resolved, yielding a
further example of matched calculation with no matching scale.

text:
Recent observations show that supergiant fast X-ray transients (SFXTs) spend
most of their lifetime at an intermediate level luminosity $\sim
10^{33}-10^{34}$ ergs$^{-1}$, and, when a blackbody model for the spectra is
adopted, the resulting radii of the emission region are always only a few
hundred meters, supporting the idea that during the intermediate state SFXTs
are accreting matter from the companion star. From these observational
phenomena we derive possible constraints on the magnetic field strengths of the
neutron stars in four SFXTs with known spin periods. While IGR J11215$-$5952,
IGR J16465$-$4507, and IGR J18483$-$0311 may have magnetic fields (up to a few
$10^{11}-10^{12}$ G) similar to those of normal X-ray pulsars, the magnetic
field of AX J1841.0$-$0536 is considerably low ($\la 10^{10}$ G). The high-mass
companion stars in SFXTs implies that the neutron stars are relatively young
objects, with age less than $\sim 10^7$ yr. Analysis of the spin evolution
shows that neutron stars like AX J1841.0$-$0536 should be born with relatively
long spin periods ($\la 1$ s). Considering the fact that among the four SFXTs
only AX J1841.0$-$0536 is a "proper" one, and the other three are either
"intermediate" SFXTs or have peculiar characteristics, we suggest that the
neutron stars in some of SFXTs may have similar characteristics as several
young central compact objects in supernova remnants called "anti-magnetars".
These features, combining with accretion from clumpy winds, could make them
distinct from standard supergiant X-ray binaries -- the low fields and
relatively long spin periods guarantee accretion at very low level, resulting
in a large dynamic range ($10^4-10^5$) of X-ray luminosity.
label: human

text:
Context. The analysis of stellar oscillations is one of the most reliable
ways to probe stellar interiors. Recent space missions such as Kepler have
provided us with an opportunity to study these oscillations with unprecedented
detail. For many multi-periodic pulsators such as {\gamma} Doradus stars, this
led to the detection of dozens to hundreds of oscillation frequencies that
could not be found from ground-based observations. Aims. We aim to detect
non-uniform period spacings in the Fourier spectra of a sample of {\gamma}
Doradus stars observed by Kepler. Such detection is complicated by both the
large number of significant frequencies in the space photometry and by
overlapping non-equidistant rotationally split multiplets. Methods. Guided by
theoretical properties of gravity-mode oscillation of {\gamma} Doradus stars,
we developed a period-spacing detection method and applied it to Kepler
observations of a few stars, after having tested the performance from
simulations. Results. The application of the technique resulted in the clear
detection of non-uniform period spacing series for three out of the five
treated Kepler targets. Disadvantages of the technique are also discussed, and
include the disability to distinguish between different values of the spherical
degree and azimuthal order of the oscillation modes without additional
theoretical modelling. Conclusions. Despite the shortcomings, the method is
shown to allow solid detections of period spacings for {\gamma} Doradus stars,
which will allow future asteroseismic analyses of these stars.
label: human

text:
This paper is an introduction to relationships between quantum topology and
quantum computing. We take a foundational approach, showing how knots are
related not just to braiding and quantum operators, but to quantum set
theoretical foundations and algebras of fermions. We show how the operation of
negation in logic, seen as both a value and an operator, can generate the
fusion algebra for a Majorana fermion, a particle that is its own anti-particle
and interacts with itself either to annihilate itself or to produce itself. We
call negation in this mode the mark, as it operates on itself to change from
marked to unmarked states. The mark viewed recursively as a simplest discrete
dynamical system naturally generates the fermion algebra, the quaternions and
the braid group representations related to Majorana fermions. The paper begins
with these fundmentals. They provide a conceptual key to many of the models
that appear later in the paper. In particular, the Fibonacci model for
topological quantum computing is seen to be based on the fusion rules for a
Majorana fermion and these in turn are the interaction rules for the mark seen
as a logical particle. It requires a shift in viewpoint to see that the
operator of negation can also be seen as a logical value. The quaternions
emerge naturally from the reentering mark. All these models have their roots in
unitary representations of the Artin braid group to the quaternions.
label: human

text:
We present polarimetric observations in the UBVRI bands of 72 stars located
in the direction of the medium age open cluster NGC 5617. Our intention is to
use polarimetry as a tool membership identification, by building on previous
investigations intended mainly to determine the cluster's general
characteristics rather than provide membership suitable for studies such as
stellar content and metallicity, as well as study the characteristics of the
dust lying between the Sun and the cluster. The obsevations were carried out
using the five-channel photopolarimeter of the Torino Astronomical Observatory
attached to the 2.15m telescope at the Complejo Astron\'omico El Leoncito
(CASLEO; Argentina. We are able to add 32 stars to the list of members of NGC
5617, and review the situation for others listed in the literature. In
particular, we find that five blue straggler stars in the region of the cluster
are located behind the same dust as the member stars are and we confirm the
membership of two red giants. The proposed polarimetric memberships are
compared with those derived by photometric and kinematical methods, with
excellent results. Among the observed stars, we identify 10 with intrinsic
polarization in their light. NGC 5617 can be polarimetrically characterized
with $P_{max}= 4.40%$ and $ \theta_{v}= 73^\circ.1$. The spread in polarization
values for the stars observed in the direction of the cluster seems to be
caused by the uneven distribution of dust in front of the cluster's face.
Finally, we find that in the direction of the cluster, the interstellar medium
is apparently free of dust, from the Sun's position up to the
Carina-Sagittarius arm, where NGC 5617 seems to be located at its farthest
border.
label: human

text: We investigate the Casimir self-entropy of an electromagnetic thin sheet, a long-standing problem in theoretical physics that has garnered significant attention in recent years. Our work aims to provide a rigorous and accurate treatment of this phenomenon, which arises from the interplay between the vacuum fluctuations and the electromagnetic fields in the presence of a conducting sheet.  Our approach involves a combination of analytical and numerical methods, utilizing the principles of quantum field theory and the Green's function formalism. We derive an expression for the Casimir self-entropy, which is a measure of the entropy generated by the fluctuations in the electromagnetic fields, and analyze its behavior in different regimes, including the zero-temperature and zero-frequency limits.  Our results indicate that the Casimir self-entropy of an electromagnetic thin sheet exhibits a non-trivial dependence on the sheet's thickness, surface charge density, and the frequency of the incident radiation. We find that the self-entropy can be significant even in the presence of a conducting sheet, and that it can be enhanced by the presence of surface plasmons. Our findings have important implications for the understanding of various physical phenomena, including the behavior of electromagnetic fields in nanostructures and the thermodynamics of quantum systems.
label: machine

text: In this study, we present a class of novel Space-Time Adaptive Processing (STAP) algorithms that leverage sparse recovery techniques to enhance target detection in complex environments. We address the problem of improving the performance of STAP in the presence of clutter and interference, which has traditionally hindered radar system efficacy. Our proposed algorithms utilize a sparse representation of the radar return signals, enabling effective separation between signal and noise.   We employ an innovative approach that integrates compressed sensing principles into the STAP framework, allowing for the reconstruction of high-dimensional data from a reduced set of measurements. This methodology not only reduces computational burden but also enhances accuracy in target detection.   We conducted extensive simulations to evaluate the performance of our algorithms under various conditions, including multiple clutter types and varying signal-to-noise ratios. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in detection probability and reduction in false alarm rates compared to conventional STAP algorithms. Furthermore, we illustrate how our approach maintains robustness against different environmental challenges, showcasing its applicability in real-world scenarios.  Through these findings, we contribute to the existing body of knowledge on sparse recovery methods in radar signal processing, providing a pathway for future research and practical implementations aimed at improving automated target detection systems. We believe that our results substantiate the potential of integrating sparse recovery techniques in STAP, fostering advancements in radar technology and its applications in defense and surveillance domains.
label: machine

text: This study explores the vacuum potentials associated with the two fundamental charged particles, the proton and the electron, employing the principles outlined in Appendix D of the Quantum Electrodynamics (QEM) theory. The analysis focuses on elucidating the unique interactions these particles have within the vacuum state, which is a theoretical concept central to quantum field theory.  The research method involves the application of advanced mathematical models derived from the QEM theory to calculate and visualize the vacuum potentials around both protons and electrons. By doing so, we aim to understand the nature of their interactions at the most fundamental level. Problematically, previous studies often overlook the specific contributions of individual particles to the overall vacuum potential landscape, leading to an incomplete understanding of particle behavior.  Key ideas include the identification of Interaction Vacuum Energy Bosons (IVBs) as mediators of particle interactions, and their connection to the Higgs mechanism, which provides mass to particles through its interaction with the Higgs field. This connection allows us to derive expressions for the vacuum potentials that account for both the electromagnetic and mass-related contributions.  Our findings reveal distinct patterns in the vacuum potentials around the proton and electron, highlighting differences that cannot be explained by classical electromagnetism alone. These insights contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of particle physics, particularly in the context of how particles interact within the vacuum and how their properties are influenced by the underlying vacuum structure.
label: machine

text: In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of ultraviolet-line diagnostics to characterize the ionized and neutral interstellar medium in star-forming galaxies. Our work focuses on developing a model that accurately captures the complex interactions between stars and the surrounding interstellar medium. Through detailed simulations and analyses, we aim to address the challenges associated with interpreting ultraviolet line emissions from different components within galaxies.  The key results of our research include the successful development of a novel model that incorporates the effects of stellar radiation on both the ionized and neutral phases of the interstellar medium. By applying this model to observational data, we have been able to disentangle the contributions from various sources and provide a clearer understanding of the physical processes at play in star-forming regions.  Our methodology involves utilizing sophisticated computational simulations combined with observational data to test and validate our model. By comparing the model predictions with empirical data, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach in accurately interpreting ultraviolet-line diagnostics in star-forming galaxies.  Overall, our study contributes to advancing the field of galactic astrophysics by offering a robust framework for interpreting ultraviolet-line emissions and shedding light on the intricate interplay between stars and the interstellar medium in star-forming galaxies.
label: machine

text: The abstract focuses on the development of efficient algorithms for designing multiple unimodular waveforms with favorable correlation properties. In many applications such as radar, cryptography, and communication systems, unimodular waveforms are utilized due to their desirable mathematical properties. This research aims to address the computational challenge of generating these waveforms, particularly in scenarios requiring multiple such waveforms simultaneously.  To achieve this, novel algorithms are proposed that leverage optimization techniques to efficiently generate multiple unimodular waveforms with good correlation characteristics. These methods aim to minimize the cross-correlation between different waveforms while ensuring they maintain a high level of auto-correlation within each waveform. The methodologies employed include iterative refinement and parallel processing strategies to enhance both the speed and accuracy of the waveform generation process.  Key findings indicate significant improvements in computational efficiency compared to existing approaches, demonstrating substantial reductions in the time required for waveform design. Furthermore, simulations show that the generated waveforms meet stringent correlation requirements, confirming their suitability for practical applications. The proposed algorithms pave the way for more efficient and effective use of unimodular waveforms in various fields, thereby enhancing system performance and security.  In conclusion, this study contributes valuable insights into the realm of fast algorithm design for multiple unimodular waveforms, offering practical solutions for enhancing the reliability and performance of correlated waveforms across diverse technological domains.
label: machine

text: In addressing the A{FB}^b anomaly within natural composite models, we have undertaken a comprehensive investigation aimed at reconciling discrepancies observed in astrophysical observations of baryonic matter. Our work employs a systematic approach that integrates detailed simulations of galactic environments, focusing on the interplay between dark matter and baryonic components. The primary objective is to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the observed anomalies in the distribution and abundance of baryons relative to their expected density.  Our methodology involves the development and application of advanced numerical codes designed to model complex composite structures formed by the interaction of dark matter halos with baryonic filaments. These codes are calibrated using observational data and theoretical predictions from cosmological models. By iteratively refining our models based on the latest empirical evidence, we have identified several key factors contributing to the anomaly, including substructure formation, feedback processes, and hierarchical clustering dynamics.  Results obtained through these simulations suggest that significant deviations from standard expectations arise due to localized regions of enhanced baryon accretion, often associated with transient gravitational interactions within the larger dark matter framework. We propose that these phenomena can be effectively modeled by incorporating stochastic perturbations into the initial conditions of our simulations, thereby capturing the stochastic nature of baryon assembly in the early universe.  The proposed solutions not only address the A{FB}^b anomaly but also offer insights into broader issues concerning the formation and evolution of galaxies and large-scale cosmic structures. Future research will focus on validating these findings through further experimental and observational data, as well as exploring potential extensions of our models to other cosmological scales.
label: machine

text:
To improve signal-to-interference ratio (SIR) and make better use of file
diversity provided by random caching, we consider two types of linear
receivers, i.e., maximal ratio combining (MRC) receiver and partial zero
forcing (PZF) receiver, at users in a large-scale cache-enabled single-input
multi-output (SIMO) network. First, for each receiver, by utilizing tools from
stochastic geometry, we derive a tractable expression and a tight upper bound
for the successful transmission probability (STP). In the case of the MRC
receiver, we also derive a closed-form expression for the asymptotic outage
probability in the low SIR threshold regime. Then, for each receiver, we
maximize the STP. In the case of the MRC receiver, we consider the maximization
of the tight upper bound on the STP by optimizing the caching distribution,
which is a non-convex problem. We obtain a stationary point, by solving an
equivalent difference of convex (DC) programming problem using concave-convex
procedure (CCCP). We also obtain a closed-form asymptotically optimal solution
in the low SIR threshold regime. In the case of the PZF receiver, we consider
the maximization of the tight upper bound on the STP by optimizing the caching
distribution and the degrees of freedom (DoF) allocation (for boosting the
signal power), which is a mixed discrete-continuous problem. Based on
structural properties, we obtain a low-complexity near optimal solution by
using an alternating optimization approach. The analysis and optimization
results reveal the impact of antenna resource at users on random caching.
Finally, by numerical results, we show that the random caching design with the
PZF receiver achieves significant performance gains over the random caching
design with the MRC receiver and some baseline caching designs.
label: human

text:
We report on the discovery and monitoring observations of a new galactic
black hole candidate XTE J1752-223 by Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE). The
new source appeared on the X-ray sky on October 21 2009 and was active for
almost 8 months. Phenomenologically, the source exhibited the
low-hard/high-soft spectral state bi-modality and the variability evolution
during the state transition that matches standard behavior expected from a
stellar mass black hole binary. We model the energy spectrum throughout the
outburst using a generic Comptonization model assuming that part of the input
soft radiation in the form of a black body spectrum gets reprocessed in the
Comptonizing medium. We follow the evolution of fractional root-mean-square
(RMS) variability in the RXTE/PCA energy band with the source spectral state
and conclude that broad band variability is strongly correlated with the source
hardness (or Comptonized fraction). We follow changes in the energy
distribution of rms variability during the low-hard state and the state
transition and find further evidence that variable emission is strongly
concentrated in the power-law spectral component. We discuss the implication of
our results to the Comptonization regimes during different spectral states.
Correlations of spectral and variability properties provide measurements of the
BH mass and distance to the source. The spectral-timing correlation scaling
technique applied to the RXTE observation during the hard-to-soft state
transition indicates a mass of the BH in XTE J1752-223 between 8 and 11 solar
masses and a distance to the source about 3.5 kiloparsec.
label: human

text:
Compressed sensing deals with the reconstruction of sparse signals using a
small number of linear measurements. One of the main challenges in compressed
sensing is to find the support of a sparse signal. In the literature, several
bounds on the scaling law of the number of measurements for successful support
recovery have been derived where the main focus is on random Gaussian
measurement matrices. In this paper, we investigate the noisy support recovery
problem from an estimation theoretic point of view, where no specific
assumption is made on the underlying measurement matrix. The linear
measurements are perturbed by additive white Gaussian noise. We define the
output of a support estimator to be a set of position values in increasing
order. We set the error between the true and estimated supports as the
$\ell_2$-norm of their difference. On the one hand, this choice allows us to
use the machinery behind the $\ell_2$-norm error metric and on the other hand,
converts the support recovery into a more intuitive and geometrical problem.
First, by using the Hammersley-Chapman-Robbins (HCR) bound, we derive a
fundamental lower bound on the performance of any \emph{unbiased} estimator of
the support set. This lower bound provides us with necessary conditions on the
number of measurements for reliable $\ell_2$-norm support recovery, which we
specifically evaluate for uniform Gaussian measurement matrices. Then, we
analyze the maximum likelihood estimator and derive conditions under which the
HCR bound is achievable. This leads us to the number of measurements for the
optimum decoder which is sufficient for reliable $\ell_2$-norm support
recovery. Using this framework, we specifically evaluate sufficient conditions
for uniform Gaussian measurement matrices.
label: human

text: The abstract focuses on the study of Majorana fermions within superconducting wires, exploring their behavior under various conditions including long-range hopping, broken time-reversal symmetry, and the influence of potential landscapes. Long-range hopping introduces complex interactions between electrons, affecting the density of states and the formation of Majorana zero modes (MZMs). The broken time-reversal symmetry, induced by external magnetic fields or proximity to magnetic impurities, significantly modifies the electronic structure and the topological properties of MZMs. Potential landscapes, such as those created by quantum dots or interfaces, can further modulate these properties, leading to distinct topological phases and MZM distributions. This research aims to elucidate how these factors interplay to shape the electronic and topological characteristics of Majorana fermions in superconducting environments, providing insights into novel quantum technologies and fundamental physics. Key findings include the identification of robust MZMs under specific conditions and the prediction of new topological phase transitions. The conclusion emphasizes the importance of understanding these phenomena for advancing applications in quantum computing and metrology.
label: machine

text:
In this paper, we study the properties of solar granulation in a facular
region from the photosphere up to the lower chromosphere. Our aim is to
investigate the dependence of granular structure on magnetic field strength. We
use observations obtained at the German Vacuum Tower Telescope (Observatorio
del Teide, Tenerife) using two different instruments: Triple Etalon SOlar
Spectrometer (TESOS), in the BaII 4554 A line to measure velocity and intensity
variations along the photosphere; and, simultaneously, Tenerife Infrared
Polarimeter (TIP-II), in the FeI 1.56 $\mu$m lines to the measure Stokes
parameters and the magnetic field strength at the lower photosphere. We obtain
that the convective velocities of granules in the facular area decrease with
magnetic field while the convective velocities of intergranular lanes increase
with the field strength. Similar to the quiet areas, there is a contrast and
velocity sign reversal taking place in the middle photosphere. The reversal
heights depend on the magnetic field strength and are, on average, about 100 km
higher than in the quiet regions. The correlation between convective velocity
and intensity decreases with magnetic field at the bottom photosphere, but
increases in the upper photosphere. The contrast of intergranular lanes
observed close to the disc center is almost independent of the magnetic field
strength. The strong magnetic field of facular area seems to stabilize the
convection and to promote more effective energy transfer in the upper layers of
the solar atmosphere, since the convective elements reach larger heights.
label: human

text: We investigated the cosmic metal evolution in the low-redshift intergalactic medium, shedding light on the complex interplay between gas, dust, and metal enrichment in the early universe. Through a combination of hydrodynamical simulations and observational data analysis, we probed the formation and dispersal of metals in the intergalactic medium, focusing on the impact of galaxy interactions and mergers on metal enrichment.  Our simulations revealed that the early universe was characterized by a complex network of galaxy filaments, with galaxies frequently interacting and merging to create a diverse range of metal-enriched environments. We found that these interactions led to the efficient dispersal of metals into the intergalactic medium, where they were subsequently incorporated into the formation of new stars and planets.  Observational data analysis of low-redshift quasar absorption lines and galaxy surveys provided further evidence for the importance of galaxy interactions in shaping the cosmic metal evolution. We detected a correlation between the metal content of galaxies and the presence of metal-rich filaments in the intergalactic medium, suggesting that these filaments played a crucial role in the distribution of metals throughout the universe.  Our results highlight the critical role of galaxy interactions in shaping the cosmic metal evolution, and demonstrate the importance of considering the interplay between gas, dust, and metal enrichment in understanding the early universe. By integrating simulations and observational data, we have provided a comprehensive picture of the complex processes that govern the evolution of metals in the intergalactic medium.
label: machine

text:
Functional brain networks are well described and estimated from data with
Gaussian Graphical Models (GGMs), e.g. using sparse inverse covariance
estimators. Comparing functional connectivity of subjects in two populations
calls for comparing these estimated GGMs. Our goal is to identify differences
in GGMs known to have similar structure. We characterize the uncertainty of
differences with confidence intervals obtained using a parametric distribution
on parameters of a sparse estimator. Sparse penalties enable statistical
guarantees and interpretable models even in high-dimensional and low-sample
settings. Characterizing the distributions of sparse models is inherently
challenging as the penalties produce a biased estimator. Recent work invokes
the sparsity assumptions to effectively remove the bias from a sparse estimator
such as the lasso. These distributions can be used to give confidence intervals
on edges in GGMs, and by extension their differences. However, in the case of
comparing GGMs, these estimators do not make use of any assumed joint structure
among the GGMs. Inspired by priors from brain functional connectivity we derive
the distribution of parameter differences under a joint penalty when parameters
are known to be sparse in the difference. This leads us to introduce the
debiased multi-task fused lasso, whose distribution can be characterized in an
efficient manner. We then show how the debiased lasso and multi-task fused
lasso can be used to obtain confidence intervals on edge differences in GGMs.
We validate the techniques proposed on a set of synthetic examples as well as
neuro-imaging dataset created for the study of autism.
label: human

text:
We investigated four major solar flare events that occurred in active regions
NOAA 10930 (December 13 and 14, 2006) and NOAA 11158 (February 13 and 15, 2011)
by using data observed by the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) onboard the Hinode
satellite. To reveal the trigger mechanism of solar flares, we analyzed the
spatio-temporal correlation between the detailed magnetic field structure and
the emission image of the Ca H line at the central part of flaring regions for
several hours prior to the onset of flares. We observed in all the flare events
that the magnetic shear angle in the flaring regions exceeded 70 degrees, as
well as that characteristic magnetic disturbances developed at the centers of
flaring regions in the pre-flare phase. These magnetic disturbances can be
classified into two groups depending on the structure of their magnetic
polarity inversion lines; the so-called "Opposite-Polarity" and
"Reversed-Shear" magnetic field recently proposed by our group, although the
magnetic disturbance in one event of the four samples is too subtle to clearly
recognize the detailed structure. The result suggests that some major solar
flares are triggered by rather small magnetic disturbances. We also show that
the critical size of the flare-trigger field varies among flare events and
briefly discuss how the flare-trigger process depends on the evolution of
active regions.
label: human

text:
The recently constructed Hubble diagram using a combined sample of SNLS and
SDSS-II Type Ia SNe, and an application of the Alcock-Paczynski (AP) test using
model-independent Baryon Acoustic Oscillation data, have suggested that the
principal constraint underlying the cosmic expansion is the total
equation-of-state of the cosmic fluid, rather than that of its dark energy.
These studies have focused on the critical redshift range (0 < z < 2) within
which the transition from decelerated to accelerated expansion is thought to
have occurred, and they suggest that the cosmic fluid has zero active mass,
consistent with a constant expansion rate. The evident impact of this
conclusion on cosmological theory calls for an independent confirmation. In
this paper, we carry out this crucial one-on-one comparison between the R_h=ct
Universe (an FRW cosmology with zero active mass) and wCDM/LCDM, using the
latest high-z measurements of H(z). Whereas the Type Ia SNe yield the
integrated luminosity distance, while the AP diagnostic tests the geometry of
the Universe, the Hubble parameter directly samples the expansion rate itself.
We find that the model-independent cosmic chronometer data prefer R_h}=ct over
wCDM/LCDM with a BIC likelihood of ~95% versus only ~5%, in strong support of
the earlier SNeIa and AP results. This contrasts with a recent analysis of H(z)
data based solely on BAO measurements which, however, strongly depend on the
assumed cosmology. We discuss why the latter approach is inappropriate for
model comparisons, and emphasize again the need for truly model-independent
observations to be used in cosmological tests.
label: human

text: Synchro-curvature losses, also known as synchro-focusing losses, occur when charged particles follow curved trajectories in a magnetic field, leading to energy losses and radiation. These losses are a significant concern in high-energy particle accelerators and storage rings, as they can cause beam instability and reduce the overall efficiency of the system. Despite the importance of this phenomenon, the compact formulae for calculating synchro-curvature losses are still limited, and a comprehensive understanding of their dynamics and radiation effects is lacking.   This research aims to develop compact formulae for calculating synchro-curvature losses, investigate their dynamics, and explore the radiation effects of charged particles under these losses. By providing a theoretical framework for understanding synchro-curvature losses, this study seeks to improve the design and operation of high-energy particle accelerators and storage rings.   This study employs a combination of analytical and numerical methods to derive compact formulae for synchro-curvature losses. The analytical approach involves a detailed examination of the particle's motion and the magnetic field, while the numerical approach utilizes simulations to validate the derived formulae. The radiation effects of charged particles under synchro-curvature losses are investigated using a Monte Carlo simulation.   The study presents a set of compact formulae for calculating synchro-curvature losses, which are validated through numerical simulations. The results show that the losses are influenced by the particle's energy, charge, and the curvature of the trajectory. The Monte Carlo simulation reveals significant radiation effects, including the emission of bremsstrahlung radiation and synchrotron radiation.   This research provides a comprehensive understanding of synchro-curvature losses and their dynamics, as well as the radiation effects of charged particles under these losses. The derived compact formulae can be used to optimize the design of high-energy particle accelerators and storage rings, leading to improved beam stability and efficiency. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development of new technologies and applications in fields such as medicine, materials science, and astrophysics.

text: We investigated the relativistic electron behavior in the M87 jet, focusing on its interaction with a magnetic field on a scale of approximately ten Schwarzschild radii. Utilizing a combination of numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we aimed to elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms governing the electron dynamics within this extreme environment. Our simulations employed a relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) model, which enabled us to capture the complex interactions between the relativistic electrons and the magnetic field.  The results obtained indicate that the relativistic electrons in the M87 jet exhibit a significant degree of acceleration, with velocities exceeding 10% of the speed of light. This acceleration is primarily driven by the magnetic reconnection process, which generates intense magnetic fields and accelerates the electrons through a series of relativistic shocks. Our calculations further reveal that the magnetic field strength in the jet is substantial, with values comparable to those found in high-energy astrophysical environments.  The key findings of this study suggest that the relativistic electron behavior in the M87 jet is deeply connected to the magnetic field configuration, with the magnetic reconnection process playing a crucial role in shaping the electron dynamics. Our results have important implications for our understanding of the M87 jet's formation and evolution, as well as the broader context of relativistic astrophysical phenomena. The findings of this study provide new insights into the complex interactions between relativistic electrons and magnetic fields in extreme environments.

Magnetic field diagnostics of the transition region from the chromosphere to
the corona faces us with the problem that one has to apply extreme UV
spectro-polarimetry. While for coronal diagnostic techniques already exist
through infrared coronagraphy above the limb and radio observations on the
disk, for the transition region one has to investigate extreme UV observations.
However, so far the success of such observations has been limited, but there
are various projects to get spectro-polarimetric data in the extreme UV in the
near future. Therefore it is timely to study the polarimetric signals we can
expect for such observations through realistic forward modeling.
  We employ a 3D MHD forward model of the solar corona and synthesize the
Stokes I and Stokes V profiles of C IV 1548 A. A signal well above 0.001 in
Stokes V can be expected, even when integrating for several minutes in order to
reach the required signal-to-noise ratio, despite the fact that the intensity
in the model is rapidly changing (just as in observations). Often this
variability of the intensity is used as an argument against transition region
magnetic diagnostics which requires exposure times of minutes. However, the
magnetic field is evolving much slower than the intensity, and thus when
integrating in time the degree of (circular) polarization remains rather
constant. Our study shows the feasibility to measure the transition region
magnetic field, if a polarimetric accuracy on the order of 0.001 can be
reached, which we can expect from planned instrumentation.

One strategy for winning a coevolutionary struggle is to evolve rapidly. Most
of the literature on host-pathogen coevolution focuses on this phenomenon, and
looks for consequent evidence of coevolutionary arms races. An alternative
strategy, less often considered in the literature, is to deter rapid
evolutionary change by the opponent. To study how this can be done, we
construct an evolutionary game between a controller that must process
information, and an adversary that can tamper with this information processing.
In this game, a species can foil its antagonist by processing information in a
way that is hard for the antagonist to manipulate. We show that the structure
of the information processing system induces a fitness landscape on which the
adversary population evolves. Complex processing logic can carve long, deep
fitness valleys that slow adaptive evolution in the adversary population. We
suggest that this type of defensive complexity on the part of the vertebrate
adaptive immune system may be an important element of coevolutionary dynamics
between pathogens and their vertebrate hosts. Furthermore, we cite evidence
that the immune control logic is phylogenetically conserved in mammalian
lineages. Thus our model of defensive complexity suggests a new hypothesis for
the lower rates of evolution for immune control logic compared to other immune
structures.

text: We investigate the phenomenon of resonant clumping and substructure in galactic discs, aiming to elucidate the underlying mechanisms that contribute to the formation of non-axisymmetric features such as spirals and bars. Utilizing both analytical models and high-resolution N-body simulations, we analyze the dynamics of stellar and gaseous components under the influence of gravitational perturbations. Our results demonstrate that resonant interactions between different components of the disc facilitate the emergence of clumps that manifest as coherent structures over time. We observe that the formation of these clumps is significantly influenced by the presence of a central supermassive black hole, which exerts tidal forces that can enhance stellar density variations. Moreover, we find that varying the disc's mass distribution and angular momentum plays a critical role in determining the stability and longevity of substructures. Through a series of controlled experiments, we assess the effects of varying formation scenarios and external influences, such as interactions with satellite galaxies. Our findings reveal that clumpy structures not only influence star formation rates but also impact the overall dynamical evolution of the galactic environment. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of how resonant dynamics shape the morphology and evolution of galaxies and underscores the importance of considering substructure when modeling galactic evolution in cosmological frameworks. The implications of our work extend to the study of galaxy formation in the early universe, offering new insights into the processes governing galactic structure and stability.
