text: In this work, we address the intricate problem of heterotic string compactifications on algebraic stacks and gerbes, identifying critical aspects that influence the geometric and physical properties of low-energy effective theories. We methodically explore the frameworks of moduli spaces, as well as the role of geometric data encoded within stacks and gerbes in the context of the heterotic string theory. By employing advanced techniques from algebraic geometry, we construct a coherent perturbative framework that outlines conditions for consistent compactifications. Our results reveal how different choices of geometric structures, particularly those involving non-trivial gerbes, yield diverse vacuum solutions with unique characteristics such as gauge symmetry breaking and the emergence of chiral matter. We develop a systematic methodology for analyzing stability conditions in this enriched setting, combining deformation theory with categorical insights from derived algebraic geometry. Our findings illustrate that the wealth of topological and geometric information intrinsic to stacks significantly enhances the flexibility of obtaining viable compactifications, offering pathways to model building beyond conventional approaches. Consequently, this work not only elucidates the mathematical foundations of heterotic string theory compactifications but also establishes a framework for future explorations in string phenomenology. We conclude by highlighting potential applications of our results in deriving effective field theories that exhibit desirable physical features, thus contributing to a deeper understanding of the landscape of string theory vacua.

In this paper, the capacity and energy efficiency of training-based
communication schemes employed for transmission over a-priori unknown Rayleigh
block fading channels are studied. In these schemes, periodically transmitted
training symbols are used at the receiver to obtain the minimum
mean-square-error (MMSE) estimate of the channel fading coefficients.
Initially, the case in which the product of the estimate error and transmitted
signal is assumed to be Gaussian noise is considered. In this case, it is shown
that bit energy requirements grow without bound as the signal-to-noise ratio
(SNR) goes to zero, and the minimum bit energy is achieved at a nonzero SNR
value below which one should not operate. The effect of the block length on
both the minimum bit energy and the SNR value at which the minimum is achieved
is investigated. Flash training and transmission schemes are analyzed and shown
to improve the energy efficiency in the low-SNR regime.
  In the second part of the paper, the capacity and energy efficiency of
training-based schemes are investigated when the channel input is subject to
peak power constraints. The capacity-achieving input structure is characterized
and the magnitude distribution of the optimal input is shown to be discrete
with a finite number of mass points. The capacity, bit energy requirements, and
optimal resource allocation strategies are obtained through numerical analysis.
The bit energy is again shown to grow without bound as SNR decreases to zero
due to the presence of peakedness constraints. The improvements in energy
efficiency when on-off keying with fixed peak power and vanishing duty cycle is
employed are studied. Comparisons of the performances of training-based and
noncoherent transmission schemes are provided.

text: Ordered k-flaw preferences (OkFP) sets emerged as a promising approach to deal with the lack of strict transitivity in human preferences. This study investigates the structure and properties of OkFP sets and sheds light on their applications in multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) problems.  The background section outlines the concept of OkFP sets and the problems associated with traditional transitive preference relations. The objective of this research is twofold first, to provide a deeper understanding of the structure of OkFP sets; and second, to demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of applying OkFP sets to MCDM problems compared to transitive preferences.  To achieve the research objectives, a comprehensive literature review is conducted on OkFP sets and their applications in MCDM. The methodology includes theoretical analysis and the implementation of several test scenarios using various real-life datasets.  Key findings of this study reveal that OkFP sets provide more flexibility in modeling complex human preferences that often exhibit non-transitivity. Moreover, these sets can be processed efficiently using existing MCDM techniques and provide more satisfactory results, particularly for preferences with many alternatives and criteria.  In conclusion, this research adds to the existing body of knowledge on OkFP sets and their applications in MCDM. The study provides valuable insights into the structure of OkFP sets and their potential advantages over traditional transitive preference relations. The results of this study contribute to the development of more effective MCDM methods capable of handling complex preference patterns.

text: We investigated the discrepancies in the frequency values of the 16CygA&B system obtained by various fitting methods, highlighting the challenges in deriving precise orbital parameters from Kepler space telescope data. Our analysis focused on the differences in frequency values calculated by distinct fitters, including the Kepler Object of Interest (KOI) fitters and the Open Exoplanet Catalogue (OEC) fitters, as well as the non-linear Bayesian fitter. We found that the KOI fitters yielded significantly higher frequency values compared to the OEC fitters, with the non-linear Bayesian fitter producing values that fell between the two. These discrepancies stem from differences in the models employed to account for stellar activity, instrumental effects, and other systematics. Our results underscore the need for careful consideration of the fitting methodology and its impact on the derived frequency values. Furthermore, we demonstrate the importance of cross-validation and validation of the frequency values against independent observations, such as those from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). Our study contributes to the ongoing efforts to refine the Kepler Legacy values and highlights the challenges in achieving precise orbital parameters for exoplanet systems. By exploring the differences in frequency values, we aim to provide a more nuanced understanding of the 16CygA&B system and its orbital characteristics.

text: We present a comprehensive catalog and diagnostic analysis of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon (PAH) emissions identified in Spitzer Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) maps. Our study aims to address the challenges associated with the cataloging and interpretation of PAH emissions in various astrophysical environments, including star-forming regions and planetary nebulae. We systematically analyzed IRS spectral data to extract and quantify PAH features, thereby providing a detailed inventory of PAH compounds present in these celestial bodies.  Utilizing advanced spectral fitting techniques, we meticulously mapped the distribution of PAH emissions, shedding light on their spatial variations and abundance. Our methodology incorporated both qualitative and quantitative assessments, enabling us to gauge the environmental conditions that influence PAH formation and excitation mechanisms. We highlight key observational trends and correlations between PAH emission intensities and star formation activity, offering valuable insights into the role of PAHs in the interstellar medium.  The results reveal the significant presence of various PAH species, demonstrating their potential as tracers of molecular and dust chemistry. We argue that our findings not only enhance the existing database of PAH emissions but also provide essential diagnostics for understanding the physical processes at play in diverse astronomical contexts. This work lays the groundwork for further studies on the origins, evolution, and destructive pathways of PAHs, contributing to our broader comprehension of cosmic chemistry and the lifecycle of carbonaceous molecules in the universe.

Loss of equilibrium of magnetic flux ropes is a leading candidate for the
origin of solar coronal mass ejections (CMEs). The aim of this paper is to
explore to what extent this mechanism can account for the initiation of CMEs in
the global context. A simplified MHD model for the global coronal magnetic
field evolution in response to flux emergence and shearing by large-scale
surface motions is described and motivated. Using automated algorithms for
detecting flux ropes and ejections in the global magnetic model, the effects of
key simulation parameters on the formation of flux ropes and the number of
ejections are considered, over a 177-day period in 1999. These key parameters
include the magnitude and sign of magnetic helicity emerging in active regions,
and coronal diffusion. The number of flux ropes found in the simulation at any
one time fluctuates between about 28 and 48, sustained by the emergence of new
bipolar regions, but with no systematic dependence on the helicity of these
regions. However, the emerging helicity does affect the rate of flux rope
ejections, which doubles from 0.67 per day if the bipoles emerge untwisted to
1.28 per day in the run with greatest emerging twist. The number of ejections
in the simulation is also increased by 20%-30% by choosing the majority sign of
emerging bipole helicity in each hemisphere, or by halving the turbulent
diffusivity in the corona. For reasonable parameter choices, the model produces
approximately 50% of the observed CME rate. This indicates that the formation
and loss of equilibrium of flux ropes may be a key element in explaining a
significant fraction of observed CMEs.

The chapter is situated in the fields of fiber materials sciences and

text: In this study, we propose a novel method for band-limited imaging using undersampled detectors. The problem at hand involves the challenge of acquiring high-quality images while reducing the number of samples taken, thereby decreasing the data acquisition time and resources needed. Our research aims to address this issue by introducing a new approach that optimally utilizes the limited detector samples while maintaining image fidelity.  Our method leverages mathematical techniques such as compressed sensing and iterative image reconstruction algorithms to efficiently reconstruct band-limited images from undersampled measurements. By exploiting the inherent sparsity in the image domain, we are able to achieve high-resolution reconstructions with a significantly reduced number of detector readings. Additionally, we incorporate constraints on the band-limited nature of the images to further improve the reconstruction accuracy.  Through extensive simulation studies and experimental validations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in accurately reconstructing band-limited images from undersampled detector data. Our results show that the new approach outperforms existing techniques in terms of both reconstruction quality and computational efficiency. This research offers a promising solution for imaging applications where undersampling is essential, enabling enhanced imaging capabilities with reduced resource requirements.

text: In this study, we investigate the dual impacts of dispersal limitation and interface roughening on ecological dynamics, aiming to address the complexities these factors introduce to habitat connectivity and species distribution patterns. We utilize a multidisciplinary approach, combining spatial modeling and field simulations, to elucidate the mechanisms by which dispersal restrictions and topographical irregularities at ecological boundaries influence species movement and community structure. Our results demonstrate that dispersal limitation significantly constrains species exchange across heterogeneous landscapes, intensifying the roughening of ecological interfaces. This roughening, in turn, fosters increased habitat fragmentation and localized species diversification. By employing advanced computational models, we quantify the interplay between dispersal rates and interface roughening, revealing a nonlinear relationship where minor variations in dispersal capability can profoundly impact ecosystem resilience and adaptability. We further explore how these processes contribute to the emergence of new niche opportunities and competitive interactions at the microhabitat scale. The findings underscore the necessity of integrating dispersal and interface considerations in ecological management strategies to preserve biodiversity and ecosystem function. We conclude that consideration of these factors is essential for predicting the resilience of ecosystems to environmental changes and for designing effective conservation interventions. This research not only enhances our theoretical understanding of ecological boundaries but also provides empirical evidence supporting the critical role of dispersal dynamics in shaping landscape-level biodiversity patterns.

text: The heating of the intracluster medium (ICM) by active galactic nucleus (AGN) jets is a crucial process in understanding the evolution of galaxy clusters. The ICM, a hot, ionized gas that fills the space between galaxies, plays a key role in regulating the growth and structure of galaxy clusters. AGN jets, powerful outflows of energy and matter, are thought to be responsible for heating the ICM, but the mechanisms underlying this process are still not well understood.  This study aims to investigate the role of AGN jets in heating the ICM using hydrodynamic simulations. We employ a state-of-the-art numerical code to simulate the interaction between AGN jets and the surrounding ICM. Our simulations reveal that AGN jets can heat the ICM through a combination of adiabatic compression and radiative cooling. The heating process is found to be highly dependent on the jet's energy, velocity, and the ICM's temperature and density.  Our results indicate that AGN jets can heat the ICM by up to 10% in a timescale of 10 million years, which is consistent with observations of galaxy clusters. We also find that the heating process is more efficient when the ICM is cooler and denser, suggesting that AGN jets may play a key role in regulating the ICM's temperature and density. These findings provide new insights into the role of AGN jets in shaping the evolution of galaxy clusters, and highlight the importance of considering the complex interactions between AGN jets and the ICM in models of cluster evolution.

Let R be a polynomial ring and M a finitely generated graded R-module of
maximal grade (which means that the ideal I_t(\cA) generated by the maximal
minors of a homogeneous presentation matrix, \cA, of M has maximal codimension
in R). Suppose X:=Proj(R/I_t(\cA)) is smooth in a sufficiently large open
subset and dim X > 0. Then we prove that the local graded deformation functor
of M is isomorphic to the local Hilbert (scheme) functor at X \subset Proj(R)
under a week assumption which holds if dim X > 1. Under this assumptions we get
that the Hilbert scheme is smooth at (X), and we give an explicit formula for
the dimension of its local ring. As a corollary we prove a conjecture of R. M.
Mir\'o-Roig and the author that the closure of the locus of standard
determinantal schemes with fixed degrees of the entries in a presentation
matrix is a generically smooth component V of the Hilbert scheme. Also their
conjecture on the dimension of V is proved for dim X > 0. The cohomology
H^i_{*}({\cN}_X) of the normal sheaf of X in Proj(R) is shown to vanish for 0 <
i < dim X-1. Finally the mentioned results, slightly adapted, remain true
replacing R by any Cohen-Macaulay quotient of a polynomial ring.

The correct identification of topological magnetic objects in experiments is
an important issue. In the present work we report on the characterization of
metastable skyrmionic spin structures with various topological charges
($Q=-3,-2,-1,0,+1,+2$) in the (Pt$_{1-x}$Ir$_{x}$)Fe/Pd(111) ultrathin magnetic
film by performing spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy (SP-STM)
calculations. We find that an out-of-plane magnetized tip already results in
distinguished SP-STM contrasts for the different skyrmionic structures
corresponding to their symmetries. Our work also establishes an understanding
of the relationship between in-plane SP-STM contrasts and skyrmionic topologies
through an investigation of the variation of the in-plane angle between the
spins along the perimeter of the structures, which can be characterized by the
local vorticity or linear density of the winding number. For spin structures
exhibiting a uniform sign of the local vorticity throughout the whole
skyrmionic area, we demonstrate that (i) $|Q|$ can be determined from a single
SP-STM image taken by any in-plane magnetized tip, and (ii) an in-plane tip
magnetization rotation provides the sign of $Q$ independently of the sign of
the effective spin polarization in the tunnel junction. We also discuss cases
where the local vorticity is changing sign. Finally, by increasing the Ir
content of the PtIr overlayer, we find an appearing secondary outer ring
in-plane SP-STM contrast that is indicative of attractive skyrmions or
antiskyrmions.

text: In the vast expanse of the Milky Way galaxy, open star clusters provide crucial insights into the formation, evolution, and dynamics of stellar systems. Open clusters are young, loosely bound stellar systems that form from a common molecular cloud. Their lifetimes are limited due to their lack of a stable potential well, making them ideal laboratories for studying stellar evolution in various environments. The solar circle, a region of the Milky Way encompassing the Sun's orbit, contains many open clusters that have important implications for understanding the solar neighborhood and its history.   The objective of this study is to investigate the structural, kinematic, and age properties of Teutsch 145 and Teutsch 146, two open clusters within the solar circle, and to discuss their implications for open cluster survival and evolution.   High-precision astrometry and photometry data were obtained from the Gaia Early Data Release 3 catalog and other publicly available sources. Structural parameters such as radius, core radius, and surface density were calculated using the King model. Age and distance estimates were derived using isochrone fitting techniques. Kinematic properties were analyzed through proper motions and radial velocities.  Key findings Teutsch 145 and Teutsch 146 are found to be structurally similar, with ages of approximately 100 Myr and 150 Myr, respectively. However, Teutsch 145 exhibits a larger core radius and lower surface density, suggesting differences in their formation environments and stellar populations. Their kinematics reveal that both clusters are moving away from the Galactic center, which may indicate a common origin or the influence of the Oort Cloud's tidal forces. text: In this study, we explore the dynamic role of X-ray embedded stars as the primary drivers of outflow-induced turbulence within the Orion Molecular Cloud 1 South (OMC1-S) region. By implementing advanced statistical analyses, including principal component analysis (PCA) and cross-correlation techniques, we observe that the presence of X-ray embedded stars coincides significantly with zones of enhanced turbulence, as evidenced by increased line widths and complex velocity structures. Our results suggest that X-ray emissions may play a crucial role in heating and ionizing the surrounding gas, thereby augmenting the intensity and spatial reach of stellar outflows. This work provides a deeper understanding of the feedback mechanisms at play between massive stars and their natal environments, specifically focusing on how X-ray emissions can influence star-forming activities by modifying local turbulence. We conclude that further investigation into the interaction between X-ray radiation and molecular gas is essential for refining current theoretical models of star formation within high-mass molecular clouds. This study underscores the importance of multi-wavelength observations in elucidating the complex interplay of processes involved in shaping interstellar medium dynamics.

High-mass stars are expected to form from dense prestellar cores. Their
precise formation conditions are widely discussed, including their virial
condition, which results in slow collapse for super-virial cores with strong
support by turbulence or magnetic fields, or fast collapse for sub-virial
sources. To disentangle their formation processes, measurements of the
deuterium fractions are frequently employed to approximately estimate the ages
of these cores and to obtain constraints on their dynamical evolution. We here
present 3D magneto-hydrodynamical simulations including for the first time an
accurate non-equilibrium chemical network with 21 gas-phase species plus dust
grains and 213 reactions. With this network we model the deuteration process in
fully depleted prestellar cores in great detail and determine its response to
variations in the initial conditions. We explore the dependence on the initial
gas column density, the turbulent Mach number, the mass-to-magnetic flux ratio
and the distribution of the magnetic field, as well as the initial
ortho-to-para ratio of H2. We find excellent agreement with recent observations
of deuterium fractions in quiescent sources. Our results show that deuteration
is rather efficient, even when assuming a conservative ortho-to-para ratio of 3
and highly sub-virial initial conditions, leading to large deuterium fractions
already within roughly a free-fall time. We discuss the implications of our
results and give an outlook to relevant future investigations.

text: The inner Fomalhaut ring system presents a unique opportunity to investigate dust emission in a relatively pristine debris disc. Recent observations of the CO gas distribution in the inner ring with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) have set new constraints on the gas mass surface density in the ring, challenging the prevailing models of ring formation and evolution. However, these observations assumed Local Thermodynamic Equilibrium (LTE) conditions for the CO gas emission, neglecting the importance of Non-LTE (NLTE) excitation in this complex astrophysical environment.  To address this limitation, we carried out radiative transfer modeling of CO emission in the inner Fomalhaut ring using both LTE and NLTE approaches. Our NLTE calculations considered the influence of strong UV radiation from the central star on CO excitation, as well as the effects of dust heating and collisional interactions. Our results demonstrate that NLTE excitation significantly alters the predicted CO emission, increasing the inferred gas mass surface density by a factor of three in the inner ring and up to five in the outer ring.  Furthermore, we explored the prospects of obtaining more accurate CO mass measurements using the improved NLTE modeling with future ALMA observations. Specifically, we propose observations of the CO rotational ladder in emission and absorption, which would enable precise measurements of gas surface densities, temperatures, and chemical abundances. Our findings highlight the crucial role of NLTE modeling in understanding the structure and composition of debris discs and have important implications for the interpretation of ongoing and future ALMA observations of exoplanetary systems.

text: Recent advancements in exoplanet research have highlighted the significance of rocky super-Earths in the search for potentially habitable worlds. The primary objective is to analyze the planet's atmospheric composition, thermal profile, and potential for hosting liquid water. Using high-precision transit photometry from space-based telescopes and ground-based observations, we developed a comprehensive model to estimate the planet's size, mass, and orbital parameters.  Our findings reveal that 55 Cancri e exhibits a mass approximately 8 times that of Earth and a radius about 2.5 times greater, indicating its rocky nature. The analysis of transit timing allows us to infer a surface temperature conducive to liquid water presence under certain atmospheric conditions. Furthermore, we explored various atmospheric scenarios using simulation models, suggesting the possibility of a stable atmosphere capable of supporting life.  In conclusion, our research underscores the potential habitability of rocky super-Earths like 55 Cancri e. By identifying such planets in close proximity to their host stars, we lay the groundwork for future observational campaigns aimed at studying their atmospheres and investigating the conditions necessary for life. This study not only contributes to our understanding of super-Earths but also emphasizes the importance of continued exploration of nearby exoplanetary systems.

text: We present a comprehensive analysis of Fermi Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) data, focusing on the spectral components and their potential physical origins. Our investigation utilizes the Large Area Telescope (LAT) and Gamma-Ray Burst Monitor (GBM) onboard the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope. By examining the high-energy spectral characteristics of 150 LAT/GBM GRBs, we identify distinct spectral components, including a hard power-law, a thermal component, and a possible recombination emission.  Our analysis reveals that the hard power-law component is a common feature among GRBs, suggesting a possible association with the central engine or the explosion mechanism. In contrast, the thermal component is observed in approximately 40% of the sample, which may indicate the presence of a neutron star or a black hole in the binary system. The recombination emission component is detected in only 10% of the sample, but its presence is thought to be indicative of a strong magnetic field in the binary system.  We employ a Bayesian inference approach to constrain the physical parameters of the spectral components, including the blackbody temperature and the magnetic field strength. Our results indicate that the thermal component is more likely to be associated with a neutron star merger, while the hard power-law component is more consistent with a black hole merger. These findings provide new insights into the physical origins of LAT/GBM GRBs and have implications for our understanding of the most powerful astrophysical events in the universe.

A distorted black hole radiates gravitational waves in order to settle down
in a smoother geometry. During that relaxation phase, a characteristic damped
ringing is generated. It can be theoretically constructed from both the black
hole quasinormal frequencies (which govern its oscillating behavior and its
decay) and the associated excitation factors (which determine intrinsically its
amplitude) by carefully taking into account the source of the distortion. In
the framework of massive gravity, the excitation factors of the Schwarzschild
black hole have an unexpected strong resonant behavior which, theoretically,
could lead to giant and slowly decaying ringings. If massive gravity is
relevant to physics, one can hope to observe these extraordinary ringings by
using the next generations of gravitational wave detectors. Indeed, they could
be generated by supermassive black holes if the graviton mass is not too small.
In fact, by focusing on the odd-parity $\ell=1$ mode of the Fierz-Pauli field,
we shall show here that such ringings are neutralized in waveforms due to (i)
the excitation of the quasibound states of the black hole and (ii) the
evanescent nature of the particular partial modes which could excite the
concerned quasinormal modes. Despite this, with observational consequences in
mind, it is interesting to note that the waveform amplitude is nevertheless
rather pronounced and slowly decaying (this effect is now due to the long-lived
quasibound states). It is worth noting also that, for very low values of the
graviton mass (corresponding to the weak instability regime for the black
hole), the waveform is now very clean and dominated by an ordinary ringing
which could be used as a signature of massive gravity.

We explore discovery signatures of techni-dilaton (TD) at LHC. The TD was
predicted long ago as a composite pseudo Nambu-Goldstone boson (pNGB)
associated with the spontaneous breaking of the approximate scale symmetry in
the walking technicolor (WTC). Being pNGB, whose mass arises from the explicit
scale-symmetry breaking due to the dynamical mass generation, the TD should
have a mass MTD lighter than other techni-hadrons, say MTD \simeq 600GeV for
the typical WTC model, which is well in the discovery range of the ongoing LHC
experiment. We develop a spurion method of nonlinear realization to calculate
the TD couplings to the standard model (SM) particles and explicitly evaluate
the TD LHC production cross sections at sqrt{s}=7TeV times the branching ratios
in terms of MTD as an input parameter for 200GeV<MTD<1TeV in the typical WTC
models: one-doublet model (1DM) and one-family model (1FM). It turns out that
the TD signatures are quite different from those of the SM Higgs. We compare
the TD->WW/ZZ signature with the recent ATLAS and CMS bounds and find that in
the case of 1DM the signature is consistent over the whole mass range due to
the large suppression of TD couplings, and by the same token the signal is too
tiny for the TD to be visible through this channel at LHC. As for the 1FM, on
the other hand, a severe constraint is given on MTD to exclude the TD with
MTD<600GeV, which, however, would imply an emergence of somewhat dramatic
excess as the TD signature at MTD>600GeV in the near future. We further find a
characteristic signature coming from the gamma gamma mode in the 1FM. In sharp
contrast to the SM Higgs case, it provides highly enhanced cross
section~0.10--1.0fb at around MTD \simeq 600GeV, which is large enough to be
discovered during the first few year's run at LHC.

text: In this work, we investigate the Arbitrarily Varying Wiretap Channel (AVWC) with a focus on secret randomness, stability, and super-activation. The AVWC poses a significant challenge in secure communication due to its dynamic and unpredictable nature. Our study aims to address the problem of secure transmission over this channel by introducing secret randomness into the communication process, enhancing stability, and exploring the concept of super-activation to improve the secrecy capacity beyond what is theoretically achievable.   Through our analysis, we have obtained results demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating secret randomness in enhancing the security of communication over the AVWC. Additionally, we have developed strategies to improve the stability of transmission by leveraging the dynamic nature of the channel. Furthermore, our investigation into super-activation has shown promising advancements in boosting the secrecy capacity, enabling secure communication beyond conventional limits.  Our methodology involves a combination of theoretical analysis, simulation studies, and mathematical modeling to derive insights into the behavior of the AVWC with secret randomness, stability enhancements, and super-activation. By delving into these aspects, we aim to contribute towards the development of more robust and secure communication systems in the presence of arbitrarily varying eavesdroppers.

text: We present our findings on high-precision measurements of carbon monoxide isotopologues (C17O, C18O, and C16O) in young stellar objects (YSOs), which serve as analogues for understanding CO self-shielding processes in the early solar system. Our study addresses the critical gap in knowledge regarding the isotopic composition of CO in these environments and its implications for the physical and chemical conditions prevalent during solar system formation. We utilized high-resolution spectroscopic techniques to obtain accurate isotopic ratios, analyzing a sample of YSOs located in various star-forming regions.   Our results demonstrate a distinct variation in the CO isotopic ratios across different objects, suggesting a complex interplay of factors influencing isotopic fractionation during the collapse of molecular clouds. We employed a multi-faceted approach that combined observational data with theoretical models of gas dynamics and thermochemistry, allowing us to derive self-shielding factors that significantly affect the isotopic distribution of CO. These findings indicate that self-shielding mechanisms likely played a pivotal role in the chemical evolution of the early solar system, contributing to the isotopic heterogeneity observed in primordial materials.  By elucidating the processes governing CO isotopic ratios in YSOs, we provide crucial insights into the conditions that prevailed during the formation of the solar system. Our work paves the way for further investigations into the isotopic signatures of other volatile compounds and their implications for planetary system development across different astrophysical contexts.

A Jupiter-family comet, 17P/Holmes, underwent outbursts in 1892 and 2007. In
particular, the 2007 outburst is known as the greatest outburst over the past
century. However, little is known about the activity before the outburst
because it was unpredicted. In addition, the time evolution of the nuclear
physical status has not been systematically studied. Here we study the activity
of 17P/Holmes before and after the 2007 outburst through optical and
mid-infrared observations. We found that the nucleus highly depleted its
near-surface icy component before but became activated after the 2007 outburst.
Assuming a conventional 1-um-sized grain model, we derived a surface fractional
active area of 0.58% +- 0.14% before the outburst whereas it was enlarged by a
factor of ~50 after the 2007 outburst. We also found that large (>=1 mm)
particles could be dominant in the dust tail observed around aphelion. Based on
the size of the particles, the dust production rate was >=170 kg/s at the
heliocentric distance rh = 4.1 AU, suggesting that the nucleus still held
active status around the aphelion passage. The nucleus color was similar to
that of the dust particles and average for a Jupiter-family comet but different
from most Kuiper Belt objects, implying that the color may be inherent to icy
bodies in the solar system. On the basis of these results, we concluded that
more than 76 m surface materials were blown off by the 2007 outburst.

Action recognition is a fundamental problem in computer vision with a lot of
potential applications such as video surveillance, human computer interaction,
and robot learning. Given pre-segmented videos, the task is to recognize
actions happening within videos. Historically, hand crafted video features were
used to address the task of action recognition. With the success of Deep
ConvNets as an image analysis method, a lot of extensions of standard ConvNets
were purposed to process variable length video data. In this work, we propose a
novel recurrent ConvNet architecture called recurrent residual networks to
address the task of action recognition. The approach extends ResNet, a state of
the art model for image classification. While the original formulation of
ResNet aims at learning spatial residuals in its layers, we extend the approach
by introducing recurrent connections that allow to learn a spatio-temporal
residual. In contrast to fully recurrent networks, our temporal connections
only allow a limited range of preceding frames to contribute to the output for
the current frame, enabling efficient training and inference as well as
limiting the temporal context to a reasonable local range around each frame. On
a large-scale action recognition dataset, we show that our model improves over
both, the standard ResNet architecture and a ResNet extended by a fully
recurrent layer.

A great deal of interest has recently focused on conducting inference on the
parameters in a high-dimensional linear model.
  In this paper, we consider a simple and very na\"{i}ve two-step procedure for
this task, in which we (i) fit a lasso model in order to obtain a subset of the
variables, and (ii) fit a least squares model on the lasso-selected set.
Conventional statistical wisdom tells us that we cannot make use of the
standard statistical inference tools for the resulting least squares model
(such as confidence intervals and $p$-values), since we peeked at the data
twice: once in running the lasso, and again in fitting the least squares model.
However, in this paper, we show that under a certain set of assumptions, with
high probability, the set of variables selected by the lasso is identical to
the one selected by the noiseless lasso and is hence deterministic.
Consequently, the na\"{i}ve two-step approach can yield asymptotically valid
inference. We utilize this finding to develop the \emph{na\"ive confidence
interval}, which can be used to draw inference on the regression coefficients
of the model selected by the lasso, as well as the \emph{na\"ive score test},
which can be used to test the hypotheses regarding the full-model regression
coefficients.

text: The discovery of exoplanets has revolutionized our understanding of planetary systems, particularly those orbiting small stars, or M-dwarfs. This study aims to investigate the occurrence rate of small planets, defined as those with radii less than 1.5 Earth radii, around small stars. We employed a comprehensive analysis of data obtained from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) and ground-based follow-up observations. The dataset includes light curves and stellar parameters for a sample of 1,200 M-dwarfs, from which we identified candidates for small planets based on their transit signatures. Our analysis involved the application of statistical methods to determine the occurrence rate while accounting for completeness and reliability in detection. Key findings indicate that approximately 45% of small stars host at least one small planet, with a significant fraction of these planets found in the temperate zone conducive to potential habitability. Furthermore, we observed trends suggesting that smaller stars exhibit a higher prevalence of small planets compared to their larger counterparts. This study concludes that the occurrence rate of small planets around small stars is notably high, highlighting the importance of M-dwarfs in the search for potentially habitable worlds. This research not only contributes to the current understanding of exoplanet demographics but also underscores the necessity for future observational missions targeting these abundant stellar types in the quest for life beyond our solar system.

We applied the currently most comprehensive version of the
statistical-parallax technique to derive kinematical parameters of the maser
sample with 136 sources. Our kinematic model comprises the overall rotation of
the Galactic disk and the spiral density-wave effects. We take into account the
variation of radial velocity dispersion with Galactocentric distance. The best
description of the velocity field is provided by the model with constant radial
and vertical velocity dispersions, $(\sigma U0, \sigma W0) \approx (9.4 \pm
0.9~, 5.9 \pm 0.8)~ km/s$. We compute flat Galactic rotation curve over the
Galactocentric distance interval from 3 to 15 kpc and find the local circular

\approx (-10.4 \pm 0.3)^\circ$ and the phase of the Sun $\chi_0 \approx (125
\pm 10) ^\circ$). The radial and tangential spiral perturbations are about $f_R
\approx (-6.9 \pm 1.4)$~km/s, $f_\Theta \approx (+2.8 \pm 1.0$) ~km/s. The
kinematic data yield a solar Galactocentric distance of $R_0 \approx (8.24 \pm
0.12)~kpc$. Based on rotation curve parameters and the asymmetric drift we
Infer the exponential disk scale $H_D \approx (2.7 \pm 0.2)$ ~kpc under

text: This research paper explores the relationship between refined black hole ensembles and topological strings. The background of this study lies in the intricate connections between black hole physics and string theory, where black holes serve as ideal laboratories to test the duality between gravity and quantum field theory. The objective of this paper is to investigate how refined ensembles of black holes, characterized by additional parameters beyond mass and charge, relate to the topological invariants computed in string theory.  Methodology involves analyzing black hole partition functions in the context of refined topological string theories, utilizing tools from both mathematical physics and string theory. By studying the interplay between refined black hole ensembles and topological strings, key findings reveal a deeper understanding of the underlying structures of both theories. Specifically, the research uncovers new insights into the correspondence between black hole microstates and string theory invariants, shedding light on the holographic nature of the black hole entropy.  In conclusion, this study contributes to the ongoing dialogue between black hole physics and string theory, offering a fresh perspective on the connection between these two fundamental pillars of modern theoretical physics. The findings not only deepen our grasp of black hole thermodynamics and quantum gravity but also enrich our comprehension of the profound links between different branches of theoretical physics.

Feedback from massive stars is thought to play an important role in the
evolution of molecular clouds. In this work we analyse the effects of stellar
winds and supernovae (SNe) in the evolution of two massive ($\sim
10^6\,M_\odot$) giant molecular clouds (GMCs): one gravitationally bound
collapsing cloud and one unbound cloud undergoing disruption by galactic shear.
These two clouds have been extracted from a large scale galaxy model and are
re-simulated at a spatial resolution of $\sim 0.01$ pc, including feedback from
winds, SNe, and the combined effect of both. We find that stellar winds stop
accretion of gas onto sink particles, and can also trigger star formation in
the shells formed by the winds, although the overall effect is to reduce the
global star formation rate of both clouds. Furthermore, we observe that winds
tend to escape through the corridors of diffuse gas. The effect of SNe is not
so prominent and the star formation rate is similar to models neglecting
stellar feedback. We find that most of the energy injected by the SNe is
radiated away, but overdense areas are created by multiple and concurrent SN
events especially in the most virialised cloud. Our results suggest that the
impact of stellar feedback is sensitive to the morphology of star forming
clouds, which is set by large scale galactic flows, being of greater importance
in clouds undergoing gravitational collapse.

text: The concept of market efficiency has long been a central topic in financial theory, influencing investment strategies and policy formulations. This study aims to critically evaluate the prevailing theories of market efficiency, particularly the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH), in light of recent empirical evidence and behavioral finance insights. Using a quantitative methodology, we analyze a range of financial markets, assessing their efficiency based on price behavior, information dissemination, and investor rationality. Data collected from stock exchanges and comparison with historical market anomalies reveal significant discrepancies that challenge the traditional EMH categorizations. Our findings indicate that while some markets exhibit strong forms of efficiency, others demonstrate persistent inefficiencies attributable to behavioral biases and asymmetric information. Specifically, anomalies such as the January effect and momentum trading patterns suggest that psychological factors frequently drive market outcomes contrary to classical efficiency assumptions. These results imply that a nuanced understanding of market dynamics is essential for both investors and policymakers. This study contributes to the ongoing debate by proposing a modified theory of market efficiency that incorporates behavioral aspects and recognizes the complexity of market operations. Ultimately, our work underscores the importance of considering both rational and irrational elements in financial markets, offering a comprehensive perspective that enhances the theoretical framework surrounding market efficiency.

text: Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars that emit electromagnetic radiation, commonly observed across the electromagnetic spectrum. This pulsar exhibits characteristics typical of young and energetic pulsars, further supporting its role in generating the observed gamma-ray emission.   The identification of this pulsar as the powerhouse of the gamma-ray source IGR J18490-0000/HESS J1849-0000 sheds light on the connection between pulsars and high-energy gamma-ray emission. This discovery contributes to our understanding of pulsar physics and the mechanisms behind high-energy radiation in the universe.

Stochastic simulation algorithms such as likelihood weighting often give
fast, accurate approximations to posterior probabilities in probabilistic
networks, and are the methods of choice for very large networks. Unfortunately,
the special characteristics of dynamic probabilistic networks (DPNs), which are
used to represent stochastic temporal processes, mean that standard simulation
algorithms perform very poorly. In essence, the simulation trials diverge
further and further from reality as the process is observed over time. In this
paper, we present simulation algorithms that use the evidence observed at each
time step to push the set of trials back towards reality. The first algorithm,
"evidence reversal" (ER) restructures each time slice of the DPN so that the
evidence nodes for the slice become ancestors of the state variables. The
second algorithm, called "survival of the fittest" sampling (SOF),
"repopulates" the set of trials at each time step using a stochastic
reproduction rate weighted by the likelihood of the evidence according to each
trial. We compare the performance of each algorithm with likelihood weighting
on the original network, and also investigate the benefits of combining the ER
and SOF methods. The ER/SOF combination appears to maintain bounded error
independent of the number of time steps in the simulation.

We propose a data-aided transmit beamforming scheme for the multi-user
multiple-input-single-output (MISO) downlink channel. While conventional
beamforming schemes aim at the minimization of the transmit power subject to
suppressing interference to guarantee quality of service (QoS) constraints,
here we use the knowledge of both data and channel state information (CSI) at
the transmitter to exploit, rather than suppress, constructive interference.
More specifically, we design a new precoding scheme for the MISO downlink that
minimizes the transmit power for generic phase shift keying (PSK) modulated
signals. The proposed precoder reduces the transmit power compared to
conventional schemes, by adapting the QoS constraints to accommodate
constructive interference as a source of useful signal power. By exploiting the
power of constructively interfering symbols, the proposed scheme achieves the
required QoS at lower transmit power. We extend this concept to the signal to
interference plus noise ratio (SINR) balancing problem, where higher SINR
values compared to the conventional SINR balancing optimization are achieved
for given transmit power budgets. In addition, we derive equivalent virtual
multicast formulations for both optimizations, both of which provide insights
of the optimal solution and facilitate the design of a more efficient solver.
Finally, we propose a robust beamforming technique to deal with imperfect CSI,
that also reduces the transmit power over conventional techniques, while
guaranteeing the required QoS. Our simulation and analysis show significant
power savings for small scale MISO downlink channels with the proposed
data-aided optimization compared to conventional beamforming optimization.

Recommender systems often use latent features to explain the behaviors of
users and capture the properties of items. As users interact with different
items over time, user and item features can influence each other, evolve and
co-evolve over time. The compatibility of user and item's feature further
influence the future interaction between users and items. Recently, point
process based models have been proposed in the literature aiming to capture the
temporally evolving nature of these latent features. However, these models
often make strong parametric assumptions about the evolution process of the
user and item latent features, which may not reflect the reality, and has
limited power in expressing the complex and nonlinear dynamics underlying these
processes. To address these limitations, we propose a novel deep coevolutionary
network model (DeepCoevolve), for learning user and item features based on
their interaction graph. DeepCoevolve use recurrent neural network (RNN) over
evolving networks to define the intensity function in point processes, which
allows the model to capture complex mutual influence between users and items,
and the feature evolution over time. We also develop an efficient procedure for
training the model parameters, and show that the learned models lead to
significant improvements in recommendation and activity prediction compared to
previous state-of-the-arts parametric models.

text:
The cost of communication is a substantial factor affecting the scalability
of many distributed applications. Every message sent can incur a cost in
storage, computation, energy and bandwidth. Consequently, reducing the
communication costs of distributed applications is highly desirable. The best
way to reduce message costs is by communicating without sending any messages
whatsoever. This paper initiates a rigorous investigation into the use of
silence in synchronous settings, in which processes can fail. We formalize
sufficient conditions for information transfer using silence, as well as
necessary conditions for particular cases of interest. This allows us to
identify message patterns that enable communication through silence. In
particular, a pattern called a {\em silent choir} is identified, and shown to
be central to information transfer via silence in failure-prone systems. The
power of the new framework is demonstrated on the {\em atomic commitment}
problem (AC). A complete characterization of the tradeoff between message
complexity and round complexity in the synchronous model with crash failures is
provided, in terms of lower bounds and matching protocols. In particular, a new
message-optimal AC protocol is designed using silence, in which processes
decide in~3 rounds in the common case. This significantly improves on the best
previously known message-optimal AC protocol, in which decisions were performed
in $\Theta(n)$ rounds.
label: human

text: Comet C/2013 A1 (Siding Spring) presents a unique opportunity to study the seasonal evolution of a cometary nucleus due to its close flyby of Mars and prolonged observational campaigns. This research aims to analyze the physical and chemical changes on the nucleus surface as it progresses through different seasonal phases. Utilizing a combination of ground-based telescopes and space-based instruments, high-resolution imaging and spectroscopic data were collected over two years, capturing the comet's transition from perihelion to aphelion. The methodology included photometric analysis to assess the comet's brightness variations and spectrometric assessments to identify volatile outgassing patterns. Thermal modeling was conducted to understand the subsurface temperatures and their impact on surface activity. Key findings reveal that the nucleus exhibits significant seasonal expansion and contraction of frost-covered regions, with distinct disparities in volatile expulsions correlating to varying solar insolation. Enhanced activity was observed as the nucleus approached perihelion, marked by increased sublimation of water ice and emergence of previously dormant jets. Conversely, post-perihelion phases displayed a reduction in outgassing, underscored by the reformation of a stable refractory crust. The study concludes that the nucleus of Comet C/2013 A1 undergoes complex seasonal transformations influenced by solar distance, significantly affecting its surface geology and activity. These findings augment our understanding of cometary behavior, offering insight into the temporal dynamics of cometary nuclei and informing future missions targeting similar celestial objects. This research emphasizes the necessity for continuous multi-seasonal observations to comprehensively comprehend the life cycle of cometary nuclei.
label: machine

text: This study investigates the theory of quasi-spherical accretion in X-ray pulsars. The research aims to address the mechanisms governing the accretion process in these pulsating X-ray sources. By utilizing analytical models and numerical simulations, we have obtained results that shed light on the dynamics of quasi-spherical accretion onto neutron stars in X-ray pulsar systems. Our findings reveal the impact of magnetic fields, the emission of X-ray photons, and the formation of accretion columns in the pulsar environment. Additionally, we explore the influence of viscosity, radiation pressure, and magnetic field geometry on the accretion flow onto the neutron star surface. Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of the accretion phenomena in X-ray pulsars and provides insights into the pulsating behavior observed in these systems. The methodology employed in this research involves solving the hydrodynamic equations of accretion flows in the presence of strong magnetic fields and incorporating the effects of X-ray radiation. Overall, this study enhances the current theoretical framework for quasi-spherical accretion in X-ray pulsars and opens avenues for further investigations into the complex physical processes occurring in these astrophysical systems.

text:
The New Vacuum Solar Telescope (NVST) is a 1-m solar telescope that aims to
observe the fine structures in both the photosphere and the chromosphere of the
Sun. The observational data acquired simultaneously from one channel for the
chromosphere and two channels for the photosphere bring great challenges to the
data storage of NVST. The multi-channel instruments of NVST, including
scientific cameras and multi-band spectrometers, generate at least 3 terabytes
data per day and require high access performance while storing massive
short-exposure images. It is worth studying and implementing a storage system
for NVST which would balance the data availability, access performance and the
cost of development. In this paper, we build a distributed data storage system
(DDSS) for NVST and then deeply evaluate the availability of real-time data
storage on a distributed computing environment. The experimental results show
that two factors, i.e., the number of concurrent read/write and the file size,
are critically important for improving the performance of data access on a
distributed environment. Referring to these two factors, three strategies for
storing FITS files are presented and implemented to ensure the access
performance of the DDSS under conditions of multi-host write and read
simultaneously. The real applications of the DDSS proves that the system is
capable of meeting the requirements of NVST real-time high performance
observational data storage. Our study on the DDSS is the first attempt for
modern astronomical telescope systems to store real-time observational data on
a low-cost distributed system. The research results and corresponding
techniques of the DDSS provide a new option for designing real-time massive
astronomical data storage system and will be a reference for future
astronomical data storage.

text:
We consider the prospects for detecting solar-like oscillations in the
"super-Nyquist" regime of long-cadence (LC) Kepler photometry, i.e., above the
associated Nyquist frequency of approximately 283 {\mu}Hz. Targets of interest
are cool, evolved subgiants and stars lying at the base of the red-giant
branch. These stars would ordinarily be studied using the short-cadence (SC)
data, since the associated SC Nyquist frequency lies well above the frequencies
of the detectable oscillations. However, the number of available SC target
slots is quite limited. This imposes a severe restriction on the size of the
ensemble available for SC asteroseismic study.We find that archival Kepler LC
data from the nominal Mission may be utilized for asteroseismic studies of
targets whose dominant oscillation frequencies lie as high as approximately 500
{\mu}Hz, i.e., about 1.75- times the LC Nyquist frequency. The frequency
detection threshold for the shorter-duration science campaigns of the
re-purposed Kepler Mission, K2, is lower. The maximum threshold will probably
lie somewhere between approximately 400 and 450 {\mu}Hz. The potential to
exploit the archival Kepler and K2 LC data in this manner opens the door to
increasing significantly the number of subgiant and low-luminosity red-giant
targets amenable to asteroseismic analysis, overcoming target limitations
imposed by the small number of SC slots.We estimate that around 400 such
targets are now available for study in the Kepler LC archive. That number could
potentially be a lot higher for K2, since there will be a new target list for
each of its campaigns.

text:
The ALICE Muon Trigger is currently yielded by a detector currently composed
of 72 Bakelite single-gap Resistive Plate Chambers operated in maxi-avalanche
mode, arranged in four 5.5x6.5 m2 detection planes. In order to meet the
requirements posed by the forthcoming LHC high luminosity runs starting from
2021 onwards, in which ALICE will be read out in continuous mode, the Muon
Trigger will become a Muon Identifier and will undergo a major upgrade. In the
current setup, signals from about 21k strips are discriminated by 2400
non-amplified Front End (FEE) cards, whose thresholds are provided by external
analog voltages (one for each chamber side). All these cards will be replaced
with discriminators equipped with a pre-amplification stage which will allow a
reduction in the operating high voltage of the detectors, thus prolonging their
lifetime. Furthermore, their reference thresholds will be passed via wireless
(and I2C chained per chamber side) allowing the tuning of the values at the
single card level. Moreover, the 24 most exposed chambers will be replaced with
new ones, equipped with high-quality (i.e. smoother surface) Bakelite
laminates. The tests performed on the new FEE cards, used both in a test bench
and on detectors, and on the new RPC chambers (with cosmic rays) are reported.

text: This study examines consistency tests for the extraction of the Boer-Mulders (BM) and Sivers functions from deep-inelastic scattering data. These functions characterize spin-dependent parton distributions and are crucial for understanding the spin structure of hadrons. The objective was to develop robust methods for validating theoretical predictions against experimental data, ensuring the reliability of extracted BM and Sivers functions. The methodology involved analyzing cross-sections for various kinematic configurations and comparing them with theoretical expectations derived from perturbative QCD. Key findings included identifying systematic errors that could affect the accuracy of function extraction and proposing corrections to improve consistency. The study concluded with a refined approach to extract the BM and Sivers functions with enhanced consistency, providing a solid foundation for future theoretical and experimental work in this field.

text:
Nonabelian anyons offer the prospect of storing quantum information in a
topological qubit protected from decoherence, with the degree of protection
determined by the energy gap separating the topological vacuum from its low
lying excitations. Originally proposed to occur in quantum wells in high
magnetic fields, experimental systems thought to harbor nonabelian anyons range
from p-wave superfluids to superconducting systems with strong spin orbit
coupling. However, all of these systems are characterized by small energy gaps,
and despite several decades of experimental work, definitive evidence for
nonabelian anyons remains elusive. Here, we report the observation of arobust,
incompressible even-denominator fractional quantum Hall phase in a new
generation of dual-gated, hexagonal boron nitride encapsulated bilayer graphene
samples. Numerical simulations suggest that this state is in the Pfaffian phase
and hosts nonabelian anyons, and the measured energy gaps are several times
larger than those observed in other systems. Moreover, the unique electronic
structure of bilayer graphene endows the electron system with two new control
parameters. Magnetic field continuously tunes the effective electron
interactions, changing the even-denominator gap non-monotonically and
consistent with predictions that a transition between the Pfaffian phase and
the composite Fermi liquid (CFL) occurs just beyond the experimentally explored
magnetic field range. Electric field, meanwhile, tunes crossings between levels
from different valleys. By directly measuring the valley polarization, we
observe a continuous transition from an incompressible to a compressible phase
at half-filling mediated by an unexpected incompressible, yet polarizable,
intermediate phase. Valley conservation implies this phase is an electrical
insulator with gapless neutral excitations.

text:
Recent studies exposed many remarkable properties of layered cobaltates
NaxCoO2. Surprisingly, many-body effects have been found to increase at
sodium-rich compositions of NaxCoO2 where one expects a simple, nearly free
motion of the dilute S=1/2 holes doped into a band insulator NaCoO2. Here we
discuss the origin of enigmatic correlations that turn a doped NaCoO2 into a
strongly correlated electronic system. A minimal model including orbital
degeneracy is proposed and its predictions are discussed. The model is based on
a key property of cobalt oxides - the spin-state quasidegeneracy of CoO6
octahedral complex - which has been known, e.g., in the context of an unusual
physics of LaCoO3 compound. Another important ingredient of the model is the
90-degree Co-O-Co bonding in NaxCoO2 which allows nearest-neighbor $t_{2g}-e_g$
hopping. This hopping introduces a dynamical mixture of electronic
configurations $t_{2g}^6, S=0$ and $t_{2g}^5e_g^1, S=1$ of neighboring cobalt
ions. We show that scattering of charge carriers on spin-state fluctuations
suppresses their coherent motion and leads to the spin-polaron physics at
$x\sim 1$. At larger doping when coherent fermionic bands are formed, the model
predicts singlet superconductivity of extended s-wave symmetry. The presence of
low-lying spin states of Co$^{3+}$ is essential for the pairing mechanism.
Implications of the model for magnetic orderings are also discussed.
label: human

text: In this study, we investigate the effects of zero-point energy (ZPE) on the thermal dynamics of small molecules immersed in quantum thermal baths using molecular dynamics simulations. Specifically, we focus on the hydrogen molecule, modeled as a pair of point charges with a harmonic spring connecting them. The bath is modeled as a collection of oscillators interacting with the molecule through harmonic forces. We employ a quantum-classical hybrid approach, in which the molecular degrees of freedom are treated quantum mechanically while the bath oscillators are treated classically, to perform the simulations.   Our results reveal that ZPE leakage, i.e., the transfer of energy from the ZPE to the bath, plays a significant role in the thermal relaxation of the molecular system. The rate of ZPE leakage depends on the bath temperature and the molecular vibrational frequencies. We find that at high bath temperatures and low vibrational frequencies, the ZPE leakage rate is largest, leading to a more rapid thermalization of the molecular system. Conversely, at low bath temperatures and high vibrational frequencies, the ZPE leakage rate is smallest, resulting in slower thermalization.   Our study provides insights into the role of ZPE in the thermal dynamics of molecular systems in quantum thermal baths and highlights the importance of accounting for ZPE in simulations of molecular thermodynamics in nonequilibrium conditions. Our findings can be applied to a variety of systems, including biological systems, where ZPE plays a crucial role in maintaining their stability and functionality. Future work will focus on extending our approach to larger molecular systems and exploring the effects of temperature gradients on ZPE leakage.

text: This research paper investigates the potential to generate neutrino masses through the decay of neutral top partners, which are hypothetical particles predicted by some models of supersymmetry. In these models, the top quark is paired with a neutral top partner, a scalar particle with a similar mass, to form a doublet. The decay of the top partner to a top quark and a neutrino can produce a neutrino mass, which is a significant prediction of these models.   The objective of this research is to explore the possibility of generating neutrino masses through this decay and to determine the constraints on the parameters of the model that govern this process. The authors employ a combination of theoretical calculations and numerical simulations to investigate the decay rates and the resulting neutrino masses.   The authors find that the decay rate of the top partner to a neutrino can be significant, depending on the mass of the top partner and the parameters of the model. The resulting neutrino masses are also found to be significant, with some models predicting neutrino masses that are comparable to those predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics.   The main findings of this research suggest that neutral top partners could be a viable source of neutrino masses, providing a new window into the physics beyond the Standard Model. The results also highlight the importance of further experimental searches for neutral top partners and their decays to neutrinos.   Overall, this research contributes to our understanding of the interplay between supersymmetry and the Standard Model of particle physics, and highlights the potential for new physics beyond the Standard Model to be revealed through the search for neutrino masses.

text: The characteristic approach, a relativistic methodology, provides an efficient and robust manner for performing large-scale simulations of various physical systems. In this paper, we present a framework that facilitates the application of this methodology to complex problems. The background section discusses the challenges of implementing large-scale simulations using the characteristic approach and the benefits it offers. The objective of this study is to develop a computational framework that enables the handling of large-scale problems while preserving the accuracy and efficiency of the characteristic method. In the methodology section, we outline the key steps of our framework, including the numerical scheme, the computational architecture, and the parallelization strategies. We then present several numerical tests and validation results, demonstrating the effectiveness of our framework in handling large-scale problems. Finally, the conclusion summarizes the achievements of our work and outlines potential future directions. The proposed framework lays the foundation for advancing the frontiers of large-scale relativistic simulations, paving the way for a more comprehensive understanding of complex physical phenomena.

text:
The structural properties of strongly coupled ions in dense plasmas with
moderately to strongly degenerate electrons are investigated in the framework
of the one-component plasma model of ions interacting through a screened pair
interaction potential. Special focus is put on the description of the
electronic screening in the Singwi-Tosi-Land-Sjoelander (STLS) approximation.
Different crosschecks and analyses using ion potentials obtained from
ground-state quantum Monte Carlo data, the random phase approximation (RPA),
and existing analytical models are presented for the computation of the
structural properties, such as the pair distribution and the static structure
factor, of strongly coupled ions. The results are highly sensitive to the
features of the screened pair interaction potential. This effect is
particularly visible in the static structure factor. The applicability range of
the screened potential computed from STLS is identified in terms of density and
temperature of the electrons. It is demonstrated that at r_s > 1, where rs is
the ratio of the mean inter-electronic distance to the Bohr radius, electronic
correlations beyond RPA have a non-negligible effect on the structural
properties. Additionally, the applicability of the hypernetted chain
approximation for the calculation of the structural properties using the
screened pair interaction potential is analyzed employing the effective
coupling parameter approach.
label: human

text: The atmospheric circulation and observable properties of non-synchronously rotating hot Jupiters have been the subject of intense research due to their unique features and complex dynamics. In the background, we discuss the general characteristics of hot Jupiters and the consequences of their misaligned rotation axes, leading to non-synchronous rotation. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the atmospheric dynamics and observable manifestations of non-synchronous rotation in hot Jupiters, using recent observations and numerical simulations. Our methodology includes a review of current observations, with a focus on transmission spectroscopy and differential emission maps, as well as simulations of the atmospheric circulation using 3D hydrodynamic models. We present key findings, such as enhanced meridional circulation, a warmer equator, and asymmetric temperature and wind patterns, induced by non-synchronous rotation. Additionally, we discuss potential mechanisms for the generation and maintenance of non-synchronous rotation, including tidal interactions and magnetohydrodynamic processes. In the conclusion, we summarize the implications of our findings for our understanding of planetary atmospheres and the importance of continuing research in this area.

text:
In this paper we study the tradeoff between parallelism and communication
cost in a map-reduce computation. For any problem that is not "embarrassingly
parallel," the finer we partition the work of the reducers so that more
parallelism can be extracted, the greater will be the total communication
between mappers and reducers. We introduce a model of problems that can be
solved in a single round of map-reduce computation. This model enables a
generic recipe for discovering lower bounds on communication cost as a function
of the maximum number of inputs that can be assigned to one reducer. We use the
model to analyze the tradeoff for three problems: finding pairs of strings at
Hamming distance $d$, finding triangles and other patterns in a larger graph,
and matrix multiplication. For finding strings of Hamming distance 1, we have
upper and lower bounds that match exactly. For triangles and many other graphs,
we have upper and lower bounds that are the same to within a constant factor.
For the problem of matrix multiplication, we have matching upper and lower
bounds for one-round map-reduce algorithms. We are also able to explore
two-round map-reduce algorithms for matrix multiplication and show that these
never have more communication, for a given reducer size, than the best
one-round algorithm, and often have significantly less.
label: human

text:
Relational joins are at the core of relational algebra, which in turn is the
core of the standard database query language SQL. As their evaluation is
expensive and very often dominated by the output size, it is an important task
for database query optimisers to compute estimates on the size of joins and to
find good execution plans for sequences of joins. We study these problems from
a theoretical perspective, both in the worst-case model, and in an average-case
model where the database is chosen according to a known probability
distribution. In the former case, our first key observation is that the
worst-case size of a query is characterised by the fractional edge cover number
of its underlying hypergraph, a combinatorial parameter previously known to
provide an upper bound. We complete the picture by proving a matching lower
bound, and by showing that there exist queries for which the join-project plan
suggested by the fractional edge cover approach may be substantially better
than any join plan that does not use intermediate projections. On the other
hand, we show that in the average-case model, every join-project plan can be
turned into a plan containing no projections in such a way that the expected
time to evaluate the plan increases only by a constant factor independent of
the size of the database. Not surprisingly, the key combinatorial parameter in
this context is the maximum density of the underlying hypergraph. We show how
to make effective use of this parameter to eliminate the projections.
label: human

text: This study delves into the intriguing dynamics of liquid nanoclusters interacting within the disordered confinement of a random porous medium, characterized by anomalously slow, power-law relaxation processes. The objective was to elucidate the mechanisms underpinning this unconventional relaxation behavior, which deviates from standard exponential relaxation. Using advanced time-resolved spectroscopy and small-angle scattering techniques, the investigation captured the intricate interplay between the liquid nanoclusters and the porous matrix. Our methodology involved synthesizing and characterizing liquid nanoclusters within controlled pore environments, followed by systematic observation of their relaxation dynamics over an extended time scale. The key findings reveal that these nanoclusters exhibit a remarkable power-law relaxation, a phenomenon attributed to the complex spatial heterogeneity and fractal-like topology of the porous medium. This behavior suggests significant deviations from classical theories of confined liquids, highlighting the crucial role of mesoscale interactions and pore structure irregularities. Furthermore, the observed power-law exponent was found to depend intricately on the pore size distribution and the degree of disorder, implying a strong coupling between the porous architecture and the relaxation mechanisms. In conclusion, this work provides novel insights into the relaxation dynamics of confined liquid systems, challenging existing theoretical models and paving the way for new approaches in designing materials with tailored dynamic properties. Understanding these mechanisms holds substantial promise for applications in filtration technologies, enhanced oil recovery, and the development of innovative nanomaterials with bespoke functional properties.

text: This research paper aims to analyze the relationship between speeds, directions, and arrival times of 22 coronal mass ejections (CMEs) from the Sun to 1 astronomical unit (AU). The study uses data collected from various space-based observatories to track these CMEs and determine their characteristics throughout their journey. Methodology involves a comprehensive analysis of the collected data, including speed measurements, trajectory calculations, and arrival time predictions at 1 AU.  Key findings reveal significant variations in the speeds and directions of the CMEs studied, with some exhibiting faster speeds and more geoeffective paths compared to others. Additionally, the arrival times at 1 AU differ among the observed CMEs, demonstrating the complex nature of solar ejecta propagation in interplanetary space.  In conclusion, this research provides valuable insights into the dynamics of CMEs and their impact on near-Earth space weather conditions. The findings underscore the importance of understanding the behavior of CMEs during their transit from the Sun to 1 AU, aiding in the development of more accurate space weather forecasting models and enhancing our ability to mitigate potential adverse effects on technological systems in space and on Earth.

text:
This artcile presents an optimisation of performance and cost of neutron
scattering instrumentation at the European Spallation Source. This is done by
trading detailed cost functions against beam transmission functions in a
multi-dimensional, yet simple, parameter space. On the one hand, the neutron
guide cost increases as a power of the desired beam divergence, and inversely
with the minimum wavelength, due to the supermirror coating needed. On the
other hand, the more neutrons are transported to the instrument the greater are
the shielding costs to deal with the gamma rays that result from the eventual
absorption of the neutrons. There are additional factors in that many of the
parameters defining the neutron guide geometry are continuous variables, and
the straightness of the guide increases the transmission of high energy
spallation products, which affect the specifications of particularly heavy
hardware, such as heavy shutters and additional shielding, beam stops etc. Over
the suite of 16 instruments, a maximum potential cost saving is identified in
the vicinity of 20 M\euro \,, with negligible penalties on instrument
performance and bandwidth, by trading minimum neutron wavelength $\lambda$
against total optical costs and shielding costs. Finally, these cost
calculations are shown to be consistent with those at real world, existing
spallation source facilities.

text: In this study, we investigate the use of OH as an alternative tracer for molecular gas excitation temperatures by analyzing the 18-cm main lines in the Galactic molecular cloud W5. Our approach involves detailed spectroscopic modeling of the observed OH emission to derive temperature-dependent line profiles. We collected high-resolution data from the Effelsberg 100-m telescope, which allowed us to resolve the complex rotational structure of the 18-cm transitions. The analysis reveals that the intensity ratios of the different rotational lines provide robust constraints on the excitation temperature. Our results indicate that OH emission can indeed serve as a reliable indicator of the temperature within molecular clouds, complementing existing tracers such as CO. Key methodologies include advanced spectral fitting techniques and state-of-the-art radiative transfer models. The findings contribute to our understanding of the thermal conditions in dense interstellar environments and offer new insights into the dynamics and chemistry of molecular clouds.
