text: Electroencephalographic (EEG) slowing is a common phenomenon in neurological processes that may pose significant challenges in the automated detection of seizures. The objective of this study is to assess the impact of EEG slowing on the accuracy of automatic seizure detection systems. We utilized a dataset comprising EEG recordings of patients with known seizure activity, annotating instances of both seizures and non-seizure slowing patterns. State-of-the-art machine learning algorithms were deployed to analyze the ability of current automated systems to differentiate between these two phenomena. Our methodology involved training the systems on an EEG dataset that included a balanced representation of seizures and non-seizure slowing episodes, followed by validation on an independent testing set to gauge performance. The key findings reveal that EEG slowing significantly contributes to false-positive rates in seizure detection, thereby reducing the overall accuracy of automated systems. In particular, we found that algorithms often misclassify periods of non-seizure-related slowing as epileptic seizures, leading to a substantial number of false alarms. Implementing advanced preprocessing techniques and refining feature extraction methods were shown to mitigate some of these errors. Moreover, integrating domain-specific knowledge into algorithm development substantially improved differentiation between slowing and seizure episodes. The conclusion of this research underscores the need for enhanced detection algorithms that can reliably distinguish between EEG slowing and seizure activity. Our findings highlight the importance of continued refinement in automatic seizure detection technologies to improve diagnostic reliability and patient outcomes in clinical settings.

Key findings indicated that OSCAR significantly improved bandwidth utilization by up to 30% compared to existing systems, with a notable reduction in congestion and latency. Additionally, the system demonstrated robustness in handling varying user loads and network disruptions, maintaining high levels of service availability and quality.  In conclusion, OSCAR represents a promising advancement in collaborative bandwidth management, offering enhanced flexibility, scalability, and efficiency in network resource sharing. Future work will focus on integrating OSCAR with existing infrastructure and expanding its application to broader geographic areas and diverse user types.

Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) are rapidly emerging as an important new area
in wireless and mobile computing research. Applications of WSNs are numerous
and growing, and range from indoor deployment scenarios in the home and office
to outdoor deployment scenarios in adversary's territory in a tactical
battleground (Akyildiz et al., 2002). For military environment, dispersal of
WSNs into an adversary's territory enables the detection and tracking of enemy
soldiers and vehicles. For home/office environments, indoor sensor networks
offer the ability to monitor the health of the elderly and to detect intruders
via a wireless home security system. In each of these scenarios, lives and
livelihoods may depend on the timeliness and correctness of the sensor data
obtained from dispersed sensor nodes. As a result, such WSNs must be secured to
prevent an intruder from obstructing the delivery of correct sensor data and
from forging sensor data. To address the latter problem, end-to-end data
integrity checksums and post-processing of senor data can be used to identify
forged sensor data (Estrin et al., 1999; Hu et al., 2003a; Ye et al., 2004).
The focus of this chapter is on routing security in WSNs. Most of the currently
existing routing protocols for WSNs make an optimization on the limited
capabilities of the nodes and the application-specific nature of the network,
but do not any the security aspects of the protocols. Although these protocols
have not been designed with security as a goal, it is extremely important to
analyze their security properties. When the defender has the liabilities of
insecure wireless communication, limited node capabilities, and possible
insider threats, and the adversaries can use powerful laptops with high energy
and long range communication to attack the network, designing a secure routing
protocol for WSNs is obviously a non-trivial task.

text: Surveys are an essential tool in various fields to collect data and gain insights. Traditional survey methods, however, face challenges such as response rates and accuracy. In response to these challenges, this study introduces a novel approach, Synthetic UniveRses For Surveys (SURFS), which utilizes synthetic data generation to enhance survey research.  The background section explains the limitations of traditional survey methods and the emergence of synthetic data as a potential solution. In the objective section, we outline the primary goal of this study to develop and evaluate a new survey methodology based on synthetic data generation.  The methodology section describes the design and implementation of SURFS, including data collection, preprocessing, and synthesis using generative models. We also discuss the validation techniques employed to ensure the synthetic data's authenticity and reliability.  Our key findings indicate that SURFS significantly improves survey research by addressing the challenges of low response rates and cost-effectiveness. Furthermore, SURFS delivers high data quality and is more flexible than traditional methods, enabling complex analysis and advanced sampling strategies.  In conclusion, this study introduces SURFS as a promising solution to overcome the limitations of traditional survey methods. The proposed approach not only enhances data collection and analysis but also paves the way for future advancements in survey research using synthetic data.

text: This study investigates the multicolour evolution of Red Sequence galaxy populations, focusing on the interplay between hydrodynamical simulations and semi-analytical models. The Red Sequence, a diagnostic tool for galaxy evolution, is characterized by a distinct colour-magnitude relation, where galaxies with lower luminosity and higher redshifts occupy the Red Sequence. However, the physical mechanisms driving this evolution are not yet fully understood.  The objective of this research is to elucidate the multicolour evolution of Red Sequence galaxy populations using a combination of hydrodynamical simulations and semi-analytical models. The simulations, performed using the IllustrisTNG suite, simulate the evolution of galaxies in a cosmological framework, accounting for gas physics, stellar feedback, and galaxy mergers. The semi-analytical models, based on the semi-analytical model of Bower et al. (2006), describe the stellar mass function and the evolution of galaxy colours in a simplified yet physically consistent manner.  Key findings reveal that hydrodynamical simulations reproduce the observed multicolour evolution of Red Sequence galaxies, with a strong dependence on gas accretion and stellar feedback. The semi-analytical models, in turn, provide a framework for interpreting the simulated results, highlighting the importance of stellar mass function and galaxy mergers in shaping the Red Sequence. By integrating both approaches, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the multicolour evolution of Red Sequence galaxy populations, shedding light on the complex interplay between physical processes and galaxy evolution. The results have implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution, the formation of galaxy clusters, and the cosmological properties of the universe.

text: This study explores the environments of high- and low-excitation radio galaxies within the Galaxy And Mass Assembly (GAMA) survey. Utilizing multi-wavelength data from GAMA, we investigate the spatial distributions and physical properties of these galaxies relative to their surroundings. High-excitation radio galaxies are characterized by their powerful jets that emit radio waves, while low-excitation radio galaxies exhibit weaker emissions. Through detailed analysis, we find that high-excitation radio galaxies predominantly inhabit regions with higher density of stars and gas, indicative of environments conducive to their energetic processes. Conversely, low-excitation radio galaxies are more evenly distributed across different environmental conditions, suggesting they may operate under less restrictive conditions. Our findings contribute to our understanding of how the interstellar medium and the presence of massive structures influence the evolution and energetics of these powerful galactic phenomena. Key methodologies employed include photometric redshift estimates, spectroscopic follow-up observations, and analysis of multi-wavelength imaging data.

In this review, we address the use of Monte Carlo methods for approximating
definite integrals of the form $Z = \int L(x) d P(x)$, where $L$ is a target
function (often a likelihood) and $P$ a finite measure. We present
vertical-likelihood Monte Carlo, which is an approach for designing the
importance function $g(x)$ used in importance sampling. Our approach exploits a
duality between two random variables: the random draw $X \sim g$, and the
corresponding random likelihood ordinate $Y\equiv L(X)$ of the draw. It is
natural to specify $g(x)$ and ask: what is the the implied distribution of $Y$?
In this paper, we take up the opposite question: what should the distribution
of $Y$ be so that the implied importance function $g(x)$ is good for
approximating $Z$? Our answer turns out to unite seven seemingly disparate
classes of algorithms under the vertical-likelihood perspective: importance
sampling, slice sampling, simulated annealing/tempering, the harmonic-mean
estimator, the vertical-density sampler, nested sampling, and energy-level
sampling (a suite of related methods from statistical physics). In particular,
we give an alterate presentation of nested sampling, paying special attention
to the connection between this method and the vertical-likelihood perspective
articulated here. As an alternative to nested sampling, we describe an MCMC
method based on re-weighted slice sampling. This method's convergence
properties are studied, and two examples demonstrate the promise of the overall
approach.

text: Coronagraphy is a crucial technique for observing astronomical objects obscured by bright sources, such as stars. The objective of this research is to explore the principle and application of a Coronagraphic Low Order Wavefront Sensor (CLOWFS) in enhancing the performance of a phase-induced amplitude coronagraph. We conducted a comprehensive investigation combining both theoretical analysis and simulated experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of CLOWFS in compensating for low-order wavefront errors in a coronagraphic setup. The methodology involved the design of a CLOWFS integrated with a phase-induced amplitude coronagraph to precisely measure wavefront distortions and adjust the optical components accordingly. Our key findings demonstrate that the CLOWFS significantly improves contrast levels by effectively reducing light from the primary star while retaining the fidelity of the detected exoplanets. The results illustrate a notable enhancement in the coronagraph's ability to discern dim objects near bright sources, achieving a contrast ratio improvement of up to three orders of magnitude. Additionally, the application of CLOWFS was found to be particularly beneficial in mitigating the effects of atmospheric turbulence and optical aberrations. In conclusion, the integration of the Coronagraphic Low Order Wavefront Sensor with phase-induced amplitude coronagraphy not only advances our understanding of exoplanet detection but also provides a robust tool for future astronomical observations, paving the way for more precise imaging of distant celestial bodies.

text: This study investigates the properties of spherical null geodesics emanating from the event horizon of a rotating Kerr black hole. The Kerr metric, a solution to the Einstein field equations, provides a fundamental framework for understanding the spacetime geometry around rotating black holes. Spherical null geodesics, which represent the paths of light emitted from the vicinity of the event horizon, play a crucial role in understanding the behavior of matter and radiation near these extreme objects.  The objective of this research is to derive and analyze the equations of motion for spherical null geodesics in the Kerr metric, with a focus on the effects of rotation on their behavior. By solving these equations, we aim to gain insights into the physical properties of the geodesics, such as their trajectories, energies, and angular momenta.  Using a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we solve the geodesic equations for a range of rotation parameters and spacetime coordinates. Our results reveal complex and dynamic behavior of the geodesics, including the formation of closed orbits and the emergence of a "frame-dragging" effect, where the rotation of the black hole causes a precession of the geodesics around the axis of rotation.  Our findings have implications for our understanding of the behavior of matter and radiation near rotating black holes, and provide a foundation for further studies on the properties of these extreme objects. By exploring the properties of spherical null geodesics, we shed light on the intricate relationships between gravity, rotation, and the behavior of light in the vicinity of black holes.

Presently there are several classes of detected gamma-ray extragalatic
sources. They are mostly associated to active galactic nuclei (AGN) and (at
soft gamma rays) to gamma-ray bursts (GRB), but not only. Active galactic
nuclei consist of accreting supermassive black holes hosted by a galaxy that
present in some cases powerful relativistic jet activity. These sources, which
have been studied in gamma rays for several decades, are probably the most
energetic astrophysical objects, and their appearance depends much on whether
their jets point to us. Gamma-ray bursts, thought to be associated to
collapsing or merging stellar-mass objects at cosmological distances, are also
accreting highly relativistic jet sources that shine strongly at high energies.
These are very short-duration events, but they are also the most luminous.
Recently, star formation galaxies have turned out to be also gamma-ray
emitters. On the other hand, clusters of galaxies have not been detected beyond
X-rays yet. These are the largest known structures in the Universe; in their
formation through accretion and merging, shocks and turbulence are generated,
which may lead to gamma-ray production. In this work, the gamma-ray physics of
AGNs is briefly presented, as well as that of starburst galaxies, GRBs and
clusters of galaxies. Afterwards, we consider some particular cases of
gamma-ray production in non-blazar AGN jets interacting with their medium at
different scales.

text: In the complex and dynamic world of cancer research, identifying complementary functional alterations in large-scale genomic data sets has become an increasingly important research question. The ability to uncover such alterations can lead to a deeper understanding of the underlying molecular mechanisms of cancer development and progression, potentially paving the way for novel therapeutic strategies. In this study, we propose and develop efficient algorithms to discover complementary functional associations in cancer genomic data.  First, we address the problem of identifying pairs of genes with complementary functional effects. We develop a novel scoring system, based on the hypergeometric distribution, to identify genes with significant overrepresentation of opposite functional effects in tumor samples compared to normal samples. We also propose a filtering method to eliminate redundant pairs and ensure the discovered associations are biologically meaningful.  Next, we investigate the use of multi-omics data, including genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic data, to identify complementary functional associations. We develop an algorithm that integrates multiple data types to construct a weighted network of functional associations, and uses network topology analysis to discover significantly enriched complementary associations.  Finally, we evaluate the performance of our algorithms using a large-scale, multi-cohort, multi-omics cancer dataset. We demonstrate that our algorithms are effective in identifying complementary functional associations with high accuracy and low false positive rates, and outperform existing methods in terms of sensitivity and specificity. Our results provide new insights into the complex molecular interplay of complementary functional alterations in cancer, and have important implications for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy development.  In conclusion, in this study, we propose and develop efficient algorithms to discover complementary functional associations in cancer genomic data. Our results demonstrate that our methods are effective in identifying meaningful associations with high accuracy and low false positive rates, and have important implications for cancer research and therapy development.

text: The Orion Bar, a prominent active galactic nucleus (AGN) located in the Orion constellation, has been extensively studied in the mid-infrared regime due to its complex dust morphology and significant star formation activity. In this study, we employ the Herschel Space Observatory and its Photodetector Array Camera and Spectrometer (PACS) to investigate the spatial variation of cooling lines within the Orion Bar. We specifically focus on the [Ne II] 12.81 µm, [Ne III] 15.56 µm, [S III] 33.48 µm, and [Si II] 34.81 µm lines in the central AGN region and the northeastern bar, where the star formation activity is most prominent.  Our results reveal significant spatial variations for the cooling lines. In the central AGN region, all lines show strong emission and broad line profiles, indicative of high gas surface densities and excitation temperatures. In contrast, the northeastern bar displays weaker [Ne II] and stronger [Ne III] emission, along with narrower line profiles. These discrepancies are attributed to differences in the physical conditions and radiation fields between the AGN and star formation regions.  We also compare our findings to existing studies of the Orion Bar in the optical and near-infrared regimes and to photoionization models. Our results suggest that the AGN ionizes the central region, while the northeastern bar is predominantly influenced by the young massive stars in the Orion Nebula. The spatial variation of the cooling lines not only offers insight into the complex interplay between AGN activity and star formation in the Orion Bar but also demonstrates the capabilities of Herschel/PACS for investigating the multi-wavelength evolution of AGNs.  In conclusion, the findings from our study reveal intriguing spatial variations in cooling lines within the Orion Bar, providing new insight into the complex interplay between AGN activity and star formation, and highlighting the versatility of Herschel/PACS in characterizing the multi-wavelength evolution of AGNs.

text: We investigate the existence and properties of sequences of compatible periodic hybrid orbits in prefractal Koch snowflake billiards. Through extensive numerical simulations and analytical derivations, we demonstrate the feasibility of generating stable and efficient trajectories in this complex system. By exploiting the inherent fractal structure of the Koch snowflake, we uncover a set of periodic hybrid orbits that exhibit a high degree of symmetry and stability. Our results reveal that these hybrid orbits can be iteratively combined to generate longer sequences of periodic orbits, thereby expanding the available phase space of the system. Furthermore, we identify a set of "resonant" hybrid orbits that exhibit enhanced stability and efficiency, enabling the system to achieve optimal energy transfer and trajectory control. Our methodology involves the use of high-precision numerical integration and advanced analytical techniques, such as the Fourier series expansion and the study of the system's invariant measures. By combining these approaches, we are able to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of prefractal Koch snowflake billiards and provide a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between the system's geometry, dynamics, and statistical properties. Our findings have significant implications for the development of novel control strategies and optimization techniques in complex systems.

Echo State Network (ESN) presents a distinguished kind of recurrent neural
networks. It is built upon a sparse, random and large hidden infrastructure
called reservoir. ESNs have succeeded in dealing with several non-linear
problems such as prediction, classification, etc. Thanks to its rich dynamics,
ESN is used as an Autoencoder (AE) to extract features from original data
representations. ESN is not only used with its basic single layer form but also
with the recently proposed Multi-Layer (ML) architecture. The well setting of
ESN (basic and ML) architectures and training parameters is a crucial and hard
labor task. Generally, a number of parameters (hidden neurons, sparsity rates,
input scaling) is manually altered to achieve minimum learning error. However,
this randomly hand crafted task, on one hand, may not guarantee best training
results and on the other hand, it can raise the network's complexity. In this
paper, a hierarchical bi-level evolutionary optimization is proposed to deal
with these issues. The first level includes a multi-objective architecture
optimization providing maximum learning accuracy while sustaining the
complexity at a reduced standard. Multi-objective Particle Swarm Optimization
(MOPSO) is used to optimize ESN structure in a way to provide a trade-off
between the network complexity decreasing and the accuracy increasing. A
pareto-front of optimal solutions is generated by the end of the MOPSO process.
These solutions present the set of candidates that succeeded in providing a
compromise between different objectives (learning error and network
complexity). At the second level, each of the solutions already found undergo a
mono-objective weights optimization to enhance the obtained pareto-front.
Empirical results ensure the effectiveness of the evolved ESN recurrent AEs
(basic and ML) for noisy and noise free data.

Many Type IIb supernovae (SNe) show a prominent additional early peak in
their light curves, which is generally thought to be due to the shock cooling
of extended hydrogen-rich material surrounding the helium core of the exploding
star. The recent SN 2016gkg was a nearby Type IIb SN discovered shortly after
explosion, which makes it an excellent candidate for studying this first peak.
We numerically explode a large grid of extended envelope models and compare
these to SN 2016gkg to investigate what constraints can be derived from its
light curve. This includes exploring density profiles for both a convective
envelope and an optically thick steady-state wind, the latter of which has not
typically been considered for Type IIb SNe models. We find that roughly
$\sim0.02\,M_\odot$ of extended material with a radius of
$\approx180-260\,R_\odot$ reproduces the photometric light curve data,
consistent with pre-explosion imaging. These values are independent of the
assumed density profile of this material, although a convective profile
provides a somewhat better fit. We infer from our modeling that the explosion
must have occurred within $\approx2-3\,{\rm hrs}$ of the first observed data
point, demonstrating that this event was caught very close to the moment of
explosion. Nevertheless, our best-fitting one-dimensional models overpredict
the earliest velocity measurements, which suggests that the hydrogen-rich
material is not distributed in a spherically symmetric manner. We compare this
to the asymmetries seen in the SN IIb remnant Cas A, and we discuss the
implications of this for Type IIb SN progenitors and explosion models.

text: This research presents a multi-dimensional modeling approach for X-ray spectra emitted by accretion-disk outflows in active galactic nuclei (AGN). Our study aims to understand the complex dynamics and emission characteristics of these outflows. By incorporating various physical parameters and considering the effects of ionization, density, and velocity distributions within the outflows, we have obtained comprehensive insights into the X-ray spectra. The primary goal of this work is to address the challenges associated with interpreting the observed X-ray emission from AGN accretion-disk outflows.  Our results reveal that the multi-dimensional modeling approach provides a more detailed understanding of the emission processes compared to traditional one-dimensional models. We found that the inclusion of varying physical parameters in our models significantly affects the resulting X-ray spectra, leading to a better representation of the observed data. By simulating different scenarios and comparing our model outputs with observational data, we demonstrate the importance of considering multi-dimensional effects in understanding the nature of AGN accretion-disk outflows.  The methodology employed in this study involves implementing state-of-the-art radiative transfer calculations coupled with hydrodynamic simulations to capture the intricate interplay of physical processes governing the X-ray emission from accretion-disk outflows in AGN. Overall, our research contributes to advancing the field of astrophysics by providing a more comprehensive framework for interpreting X-ray spectra from complex accretion-disk outflows.

text: We conducted a comprehensive mid-infrared study of RR Lyrae stars using the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) all-sky data release. Our primary objective was to investigate the variability patterns and infrared properties of these stars, which are crucial for understanding their fundamental parameters and evolutionary stages. To achieve this, we employed a combination of data reduction techniques and photometric analysis methods to extract reliable mid-infrared fluxes from the WISE catalog.  Our analysis revealed significant variability in the mid-infrared fluxes of RR Lyrae stars, with some exhibiting periodic or quasi-periodic behavior. We also discovered a correlation between the amplitude of the variability and the intrinsic brightness of the stars, suggesting a link between the infrared properties and the pulsation characteristics. Furthermore, our results indicate that the WISE data can be used to estimate the effective temperature and luminosity of RR Lyrae stars with a reasonable degree of accuracy.  The key findings of this study have important implications for our understanding of the RR Lyrae stars' properties and their role in the universe. Our results also highlight the potential of the WISE data for asteroseismology and the study of stellar populations. The methodology employed in this study can be applied to other mid-infrared surveys and datasets, expanding the possibilities for the analysis of RR Lyrae stars and other pulsating variables.

text: We investigated the intricate relationship between spin density wave (SDW) and superconductivity in underdoped NaFe1-xCoxAs, a class of cuprate superconductors, using a combination of experimental and theoretical techniques. Our experimental approach involved measuring the electrical resistivity and magnetic susceptibility of NaFe1-xCoxAs single crystals as a function of temperature and doping level. These measurements revealed a complex interplay between SDW and superconductivity, with the SDW state appearing to be a precursor to superconductivity in underdoped samples. Theoretical modeling, utilizing density functional theory, was employed to elucidate the electronic structure and phase diagram of NaFe1-xCoxAs. Our calculations showed that the SDW state is mediated by a strong electron-electron interaction, which is crucial for the emergence of superconductivity. We found that the SDW state is not a simple phase transition, but rather a complex, non-equilibrium state that is stabilized by the interplay between the SDW and superconducting order parameters. These results highlight the intricate interplay between SDW and superconductivity in underdoped NaFe1-xCoxAs, and provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying the emergence of superconductivity in these materials.

text: This study investigates the high-field phase diagram of iron arsenide superconductors by employing a combination of magnetic susceptibility measurements and transport properties under varying magnetic fields. The objective is to elucidate the influence of magnetic fields on the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and the critical current density (Jc). Through these measurements, we observe significant enhancements in Tc and Jc at certain magnetic field strengths, indicating a complex interplay between magnetic interactions and superconductivity. Key methodologies include precise control over magnetic fields using a superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID), which allows for the detailed examination of phase transitions without external perturbations. The analysis reveals that the presence of magnetic fields can lead to enhanced superconductivity, suggesting potential applications in magnetic field-cooled superconducting devices. This research contributes to our understanding of the magnetic-field-induced phase transformations in iron-based superconductors, offering insights into optimizing their performance under applied magnetic fields.

We investigate the origin of ubiquitous low energy kinks found in Angle
Resolved Photoemission (ARPES) experiments in a variety of correlated matter.
Such kinks are unexpected from weakly interacting electrons and hence
identifying their origin should lead to fundamental insights in strongly
correlated matter. We devise a protocol for extracting the kink momentum and
energy from the experimental data which relies solely on the two asymptotic
tangents of each dispersion curve, away from the feature itself. It is thereby
insensitive to the different shapes of the kinks as seen in experiments. The
body of available data is then analyzed using this method. We proceed to
discuss two alternate theoretical explanations of the origin of the kinks. Some
theoretical proposals invoke local Bosonic excitations (Einstein phonons or
other modes with spin or charge character), located exactly at the energy of
observed kinks, leading to a momentum independent self energy of the electrons.
A recent alternate is the theory of extremely correlated Fermi liquids (ECFL).
This theory predicts kinks in the dispersion arising from a momentum dependent
self energy of correlated electrons. We present the essential results from both
classes of theories, and identify experimental features that can help
distinguish between the two mechanisms. The ECFL theory is found to be
consistent with currently available data on kinks in the nodal direction of
cuprate superconductors, but conclusive tests require higher resolution energy
distribution curve data.

The study concluded with a refined understanding of LBV behavior, highlighting the importance of detailed categorization in astrophysical studies. Let $\mathbf d=(d_j)_{j\in\mathbb I_m}\in\mathbb N^m$ be a finite sequence
(of dimensions) and $\alpha=(\alpha_i)_{i\in\mathbb I_n}$ be a sequence of
positive numbers (of weights), where $\mathbb I_k=\{1,\ldots,k\}$ for
$k\in\mathbb N$. We introduce the $(\alpha\, , \,\mathbf d)$-designs i.e.,
$m$-tuples $\Phi=(\mathcal F_j)_{j\in\mathbb I_m}$ such that $\mathcal
F_j=\{f_{ij}\}_{i\in\mathbb I_n}$ is a finite sequence in $\mathbb C^{d_j}$,
$j\in\mathbb I_m$, and such that the sequence of non-negative numbers
$(\|f_{ij}\|^2)_{j\in\mathbb I_m}$ forms a partition of $\alpha_i$,
$i\in\mathbb I_n$. We characterize the existence of $(\alpha\, , \, \mathbf
d)$-designs with prescribed properties in terms of majorization relations. We
show, by means of a finite-step algorithm, that there exist $(\alpha\, , \,
\mathbf d)$-designs $\Phi^{\rm op}=(\mathcal F_j^{\rm op})_{j\in\mathbb I_m}$
that are universally optimal; that is, for every convex function
$\varphi:[0,\infty)\rightarrow [0,\infty)$ then $\Phi^{\rm op}$ minimizes the
joint convex potential induced by $\varphi$ among $(\alpha\, , \, \mathbf
d)$-designs, namely $$ \sum_{j\in\mathbb I_m}\text{P}_\varphi(\mathcal F_j^{\rm
op})\leq \sum_{j\in \mathbb I_m}\text{P}_\varphi(\mathcal F_j) $$ for every
$(\alpha\, , \, \mathbf d)$-design $\Phi=(\mathcal F_j)_{j\in\mathbb I_m}$,
where $\text{P}_\varphi(\mathcal F)=tr(\varphi(S_{\mathcal F}))$; in
particular, $\Phi^{\rm op}$ minimizes both the joint frame potential and the
joint mean square error among $(\alpha\, , \, \mathbf d)$-designs. We show that
in this case $\mathcal F_j^{\rm op}$ is a frame for $\mathbb C^{d_j}$, for
$j\in\mathbb I_m$. This corresponds to the existence of optimal
encoding-decoding schemes for multitasking devices with energy restrictions.

Analyses of multi-epoch, high-resolution (R ~ 50.000) optical spectra of the
O-type star HD 152246 (O9 IV according to the most recent classification),
complemented by a limited number of earlier published radial velocities, led to
the finding that the object is a hierarchical triple system, where a close
inner pair (Ba-Bb) with a slightly eccentric orbit (e = 0.11) and a period of
6.0049 days revolves in a 470-day highly eccentric orbit (e = 0.865) with
another massive and brighter component A. The mass ratio of the inner system
must be low since we were unable to find any traces of the secondary spectrum.
The mass ratio A/(Ba+Bb) is 0.89. The outer system has recently been resolved
using long-baseline interferometry on three occasions. The interferometry
confirms the spectroscopic results and specifies elements of the system. Our
orbital solutions, including the combined radial-velocity and interferometric
solution indicate an orbital inclination of the outer orbit of 112{\deg} and
stellar masses of 20.4 and 22.8 solar masses. We also disentangled the spectra
of components A and Ba and compare them to synthetic spectra from two
independent programmes, TLUSTY and FASTWIND. In either case, the fit was not
satisfactory and we postpone a better determination of the system properties
for a future study, after obtaining observations during the periastron passage
of the outer orbit (the nearest chance being March 2015). For the moment, we
can only conclude that component A is an O9 IV star with v*sin(i) = 210 +\- 10
km/s and effective temperature of 33000 +\- 500 K, while component Ba is an O9
V object with v*sin(i) = 65 +/- 3 km/s and T_eff = 33600 +\- 600 K.

text: This study investigates atomically flat carbon monolayers as a unique quasi-two-dimensional (2D) mesoscopic quantum system, focusing on their extreme instability and quantum properties. Our approach involved the synthesis of high-quality monolayers using chemical vapor deposition techniques, followed by detailed structural characterization through scanning tunneling microscopy and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. The results demonstrate that these systems exhibit pronounced quantum confinement effects due to their reduced dimensionality, leading to electronic band structures that are significantly different from bulk graphite. We observed pronounced quantum oscillations in the conductance spectra, indicative of quantized energy levels. Additionally, our experiments reveal a highly sensitive response to external perturbations, such as substrate interaction and thermal fluctuations, which further destabilize the atomic structure. This research not only highlights the intrinsic quantum behavior of these systems but also underscores the critical need for precise control over fabrication parameters to achieve stable and reproducible samples for future applications in quantum technology.

text: Grb 090227B, a short gamma-ray burst (GRB) event detected on February 27, 2009, presents a unique opportunity to study the connection between short and long GRBs (sGRBs and lGRBs, respectively). With a duration of approximately 2 seconds and a peak energy output of 1.1 x 1051 erg/s, this event lies at the interface between the two categories. Our analysis of the early afterglow data, obtained with the Swift and Hubble Space Telescopes, reveals that Grb 090227B exhibits both the rapid, non-thermal evolution typical of sGRBs and the slower, thermal evolution characteristic of lGRBs. This behavior suggests a unified model for GRBs, in which short and long events represent different stages of the same physical process.  We model the early afterglow emission using a relativistic shock in a dense medium, and find that a magnetar scenario with a magnetic field strength of B ~ 10^14-10^15 G is consistent with the observed data. The resulting shock dynamics and afterglow light curve predictions agree well with the Swift and Hubble observations. The presence of both non-thermal and thermal components in the afterglow emission also allows us to estimate the electron distribution and the total energy released in the burst. Our findings indicate that sGRBs and lGRBs may not represent distinct populations but rather different phases of the same GRB phenomenon, with the duration distinction serving as a useful empirical criterion.  Further study of the connection between sGRBs and lGRBs through the examination of additional events and the exploration of various theoretical models will contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the physical mechanisms behind these powerful astrophysical phenomena.

We study effects of inhomogeneities on distance measures in an exact
relativistic Swiss-cheese model of the universe, focusing on the distance
modulus. The model has LCDM background dynamics, and the `holes' are
non-symmetric structures described by the Szekeres metric. The Szekeres exact
solution of Einstein's equations, which is inhomogeneous and anisotropic,
allows us to capture potentially relevant effects on light propagation due to
nontrivial evolution of structures in an exact framework. Light beams
traversing a single Szekeres structure in different ways can experience either
magnification or demagnification, depending on the particular path, and we
explore a small additional effect due time evolution of the structures. We
study the probability distributions of $\Delta\mu=\mu_{LCDM}-\mu_{SC}$ for
sources at different redshifts in various Swiss-cheese constructions, where the

discuss the possibility that the escaping particle current may excite a
non-resonant instability that in turn leads to the formation of resonant modes
confining particles close to the shock and increasing the maximum energy. This
mechanism works throughout the expansion of the SN explosion, from the ejecta

not find any parameter combination that could explain all data sets. Indeed the

measurements suggest that the knee in the light component is at 650 TeV,

infinite-$N_c$ limits. For the cases analyzed in that study, the scalings of

$N_c^{-1}$ in the large-$t$ and large-$N_c$ asymptotics. Moreover, it was shown

Receiver noise is quickly approaching fundamental limits at most radio
wavelengths, so significant gains in sensitivity can only be made by increasing
collecting area. Jointly, these requirements suggest using large arrays of
smaller antennas, or many moderate-size antennas equipped with multi-beam
arrays. The challenge is to develop receivers and wide bandwidth data transport
systems which are lower cost, more compact, more reliable, lower weight, and
more reproducible than the best current systems, with no compromise to
performance. This can be achieved with a greater degree of component
integration, extensive use of digital signal processing and transport, and
replacement of functions currently performed in bulky waveguide and coaxial
cable components with digital arithmetic and thin optical fibers. In this white
paper, we outline the complete redesign and re-optimization of receiver
architecture to take advantage of the latest advancements in commercial
technology. This involves the seamless integration of the conversions from RF

text: In this study, we propose a novel methodology for the a priori estimation of time steps in the numerical solution of parabolic partial differential equations. Addressing the challenge of selecting an optimal time step size, which is crucial for both the stability and accuracy of numerical simulations, our approach integrates analytical techniques to preemptively mitigate potential computational inaccuracies. We employ a combination of stability analysis and error estimation to develop a comprehensive heuristic that predicts a suitable time step prior to numerical integration. Applying our method to a series of benchmark parabolic problems, including heat conduction equations and diffusion-reaction models, we demonstrate its efficacy in maintaining stability while optimizing computational resources.  Results indicate that our a priori estimation significantly reduces the number of iterations required for convergence compared to traditional methods that rely on fixed or adaptive time stepping post-computation. Furthermore, our methodology shows robust performance across varying initial conditions and parameter spaces, highlighting its generalizability. The potential of this estimation strategy not only lies in its practical application for computational simulations but also as a theoretical contribution to the numerical analysis of parabolic PDEs. Our findings underscore the importance of integrating analytical insights with numerical practices to enhance the efficiency and reliability of simulations. Future work will extend the applicability of our approach to more complex, higher-dimensional parabolic problems and explore its integration with adaptive mesh refinement techniques to further optimize computational strategies.

text: We employed a mixed-methods approach to investigate illicit drug use behaviors by leveraging social media data. We applied natural language processing (NLP) techniques to analyze the linguistic characteristics of posts, including sentiment analysis, keyword extraction, and topic modeling. Additionally, we employed network analysis to examine the structural properties of social connections, such as centrality and clustering coefficients. Our results indicate that individuals involved in illicit drug use behaviors exhibit distinct linguistic patterns, including the use of euphemisms and coded language, which can be detected through NLP analysis. Furthermore, we found that these individuals tend to form dense social networks with similar peers, often located in urban areas with high rates of substance abuse. We also identified geographic clusters of substance use, which can inform targeted public health interventions. Our findings suggest that social media can serve as a valuable tool for monitoring and understanding illicit drug use behaviors, and highlight the potential for NLP and network analysis to inform evidence-based policies and interventions.

An experimental study of the in-plane azimuthal behaviour and frequency
dependence of the ferromagnetic resonance field and the resonance linewidth as
a function of BiFeO$_3$ thickness is carried out in a polycrystalline
exchange-biased BiFeO$_3$/Ni$_{81}$Fe$_{19}$ system. The magnetization decrease
of the Pt/BiFeO$_3$/Ni$_{81}$Fe$_{19}$/Pt heterostructures with BiFeO$_3$
thickness deduced from static measurements has been confirmed by dynamic
investigations. Ferromagnetic resonance measurements have shown lower
gyromagnetic ratio in a perpendicular geometry compared with that of a parallel
geometry. The monotonous decrease of gyromagnetic ratio in a perpendicular
geometry as a function of the BiFeO$_3$ film thickness seems to be related to
the spin-orbit interactions due to the neighbouring Pt film at its interface
with Ni$_{81}$Fe$_{19}$ film. The in-plane azimuthal shape of the total
linewidth of the uniform mode shows isotropic behaviour that increases with
BiFeO$_3$ thickness. The study of the frequency dependence of the resonance
linewidth in a broad band of 3 to 35 GHz has allowed the determination of
intrinsic and extrinsic contributions to the relaxation as function of
BiFeO$_3$ thickness in perpendicular geometries. In our system the magnetic
relaxation is dominated by the spin-pumping mechanism due to the presence of

text: We present a comprehensive analysis of the early evolution of an energetic coronal mass ejection (CME) and its intricate relationship with extreme ultraviolet (EUV) waves. Our study aims to resolve the underlying dynamics and causal mechanisms influencing CME initiation and propagation in the solar corona, thereby improving our predictive capabilities for space weather phenomena. Utilizing high-resolution observational data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), coupled with advanced numerical simulations, we identified pivotal phases in the CME's evolution, emphasizing its acceleration and lateral expansion. Our results reveal a significant correlation between the rapid acceleration of the CME and the generation of EUV waves, suggesting that these waves act both as by-products and possibly as facilitators in CME dynamics. By examining the temporal and spatial characteristics of EUV waves, we found a propagation pattern consistent with fast-mode MHD waves, confirming their utility in deciphering the energy distribution and magnetic restructuring in the early stages of a CME. Furthermore, our analysis provides insight into the magnetic reconnection processes, highlighting their role in the initial energy release and subsequent CME evolution. This work suggests that the coupling between CMEs and EUV waves significantly influences the magnetohydrodynamic environment, potentially affecting interplanetary space weather conditions. The methodologies employed in this study, including advanced image processing and numerical modeling, exhibit substantial promise in enhancing our understanding of solar eruptive events. This research contributes to the broader goal of establishing a predictive framework for solar activity and its impact on space weather.

to the water surface has focused primarily on mapping the forces on the hull
and much less to the formation of the spray. The latter is the topic of the
present work, where the spray generated by the impact of a flat plate on a
quiescent water surface is studied by experiments and simulations at different
impact Froude numbers. Overall two types of sprays are formed: Type I, which is
a cloud of droplets and ligaments generated at the impact of the plate's
leading edge with the water surface, and Type II, which is formed after the
trailing edge of the plate enters the local water surface. Detailed analysis of
the experimental data for the Type II spray revealed that the spray envelopes
and root point trajectories are independent of Froude number close to the
trailing edge, while further away reach higher vertical positions for larger
Froude numbers. The numerical simulation captures the general behavior of the
Type II spray and agrees favorably with the experimental results. A series of
computations with a flexible plate is also reported, where it is shown that
increased flexibility reduces the height of the spray and suppresses the
formation of droplets.

text: This study addresses the problem of determining whether a given point belongs to an approximate polytope with a specified accuracy. An approximate polytope is a set of points that is a good approximation of a polytope, but may contain some error. The objective of this research is to develop an efficient algorithm for determining whether a given point belongs to an approximate polytope with a specified accuracy.  The problem is motivated by its applications in various fields, including computer-aided design, machine learning, and data analysis. In these fields, approximate polytopes are often used to represent complex shapes and relationships. However, the membership of a point in an approximate polytope is not always straightforward, and existing methods may be computationally expensive or inaccurate.  To address this problem, we develop a new algorithm that uses a combination of geometric and linear programming techniques. The algorithm first computes the closest point in the polytope to the given point, and then checks whether the distance between the given point and the closest point is within the specified accuracy. We also develop a method to handle the case where the accuracy is not specified, and instead, we use a trade-off between accuracy and computational cost.  Our experimental results show that the algorithm is efficient and accurate, and can handle large-scale approximate polytopes. The algorithm has been tested on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in determining membership in approximate polytopes. The study concludes that the proposed algorithm provides a reliable and efficient solution to the problem of optimal approximate polytope membership, and can be used in various applications where approximate polytopes are used to represent complex shapes and relationships.

text: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the Higgs boson production and decay rates, as well as constraints on its couplings, using a combined dataset from the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The analysis is based on the LHC $pp$ collision data collected at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s}=$ 7 and 8 TeV.  The objective of this analysis is to investigate the Higgs boson's properties, specifically its production and decay rates, and the strength of its couplings to fundamental particles. The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics, and its discovery at the LHC has confirmed the existence of this field. Understanding the Higgs boson's properties is crucial for making precise predictions about the behavior of matter and energy in the universe.  The analysis employed a combined dataset of approximately 5.3 fb$^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments. The production and decay rates of the Higgs boson were measured using a multivariate analysis technique, which identified the signal of the Higgs boson in the data. The results were then compared to theoretical predictions to constrain the strength of the Higgs boson's couplings to fundamental particles.  The key findings of this analysis include the measurement of the Higgs boson production and decay rates, as well as the constraints on its couplings to the $b$-quark and photon. The results of this analysis are consistent with the Standard Model predictions, and provide further evidence for the validity of the Higgs boson's existence.

We consider a networked control system (NCS) consisting of two plants, a
global plant and a local plant, and two controllers, a global controller and a
local controller. The global (resp. local) plant follows discrete-time
stochastically switched linear dynamics with a continuous global (resp. local)
state and a discrete global (resp. local) mode. We assume that the state and
mode of the global plant are observed by both controllers while the state and
mode of the local plant are only observed by the local controller. The local
controller can inform the global controller of the local plant's state and mode
through an unreliable TCP-like communication channel where successful
transmissions are acknowledged. The objective of the controllers is to
cooperatively minimize a modes-dependent quadratic cost over a finite time
horizon. Following the method developed in [1] and [2], we construct a dynamic
program based on common information and a decomposition of strategies, and use
it to obtain explicit optimal strategies for the controllers. In the optimal
strategies, both controllers compute a common estimate of the local plant's
state. The global controller's action is linear in the state of the global
plant and the common estimated state, and the local controller's action is
linear in the actual states of both plants and the common estimated state.
Furthermore, the gain matrices for the global controller depend on the global
mode and its observation about the local mode, while the gain matrices for the
local controller depend on the actual modes of both plants and the global
controller's observation about the local mode.

text: Graph cuts and network reliability are fundamental concepts in computer science and engineering, with applications in various fields such as computer vision, signal processing, and telecommunications. The problem of finding the minimum cut in a graph, which represents the minimum number of edges that need to be removed to disconnect the graph, is a well-studied problem in graph theory. However, existing algorithms for solving this problem are often computationally expensive, leading to suboptimal solutions for large-scale networks.  This paper presents improved bounds and algorithms for graph cuts and network reliability, with a focus on developing more efficient and scalable solutions. We begin by reviewing the current state of the art in graph cut algorithms, including the popular Floyd-Warshall and Bellman-Ford methods. We then present a new algorithm, called "GraphCut++", which utilizes a combination of dynamic programming and approximation techniques to achieve significant improvements in computational efficiency. Our experimental results show that GraphCut++ outperforms existing algorithms in terms of running time and solution quality.  In addition to the graph cut problem, we also investigate the problem of network reliability, which is the probability that a network remains connected in the presence of failures or disruptions. We present a new algorithm, called "ReliableNetwork", which uses a combination of graph cut and network flow techniques to compute the reliability of a network. Our results show that ReliableNetwork is more accurate and efficient than existing methods, and can be used to compute the reliability of complex networks with a large number of nodes and edges.  Overall, our paper presents significant advances in the field of graph cuts and network reliability, with improved bounds and algorithms that can be used to solve complex problems in a variety of applications.

Digital forensic evidence acquisition speed is traditionally limited by two
main factors: the read speed of the storage device being investigated, i.e.,
the read speed of the disk, memory, remote storage, mobile device, etc.), and
the write speed of the system used for storing the acquired data. Digital
forensic investigators can somewhat mitigate the latter issue through the use
of high-speed storage options, such as networked RAID storage, in the
controlled environment of the forensic laboratory. However, traditionally,
little can be done to improve the acquisition speed past its physical read
speed from the target device itself. The protracted time taken for data
acquisition wastes digital forensic experts' time, contributes to digital
forensic investigation backlogs worldwide, and delays pertinent information
from potentially influencing the direction of an investigation. In a remote
acquisition scenario, a third contributing factor can also become a detriment
to the overall acquisition time - typically the Internet upload speed of the
acquisition system. This paper explores an alternative to the traditional
evidence acquisition model through the leveraging of a forensic data
deduplication system. The advantages that a deduplicated approach can provide
over the current digital forensic evidence acquisition process are outlined and
some preliminary results of a prototype implementation are discussed.

Aims. We study whether rotational excitation makes a difference to the
abundances of the $\rm H_3^+$ isotopologs, including spin states, in physical
conditions corresponding to starless cores and protostellar envelopes.
  Methods. We developed a new rate coefficient set for the $\rm H_3^+$
isotopologs, allowing for rotational excitation, using the state-to-state rate
coefficients from Hugo et al. These new so-called species-to-species rate
coefficients are compared with previously-used ground state-to-species rate
coefficients.
  Results. The species-to-species and ground state-to-species model results
differ at high density and toward increasing temperatures ($T > 10$ K). The
species-to-species model predicts a lower $\rm H_3^+$ deuteration degree at
high density owing to an increase of the rate coefficients of endothermic
reactions that decrease deuteration. At 20 K the ground state-to-species model
overestimates the abundance of $\rm H_2D^+$ by a factor of about two while the
abundance of $\rm D_3^+$ can differ by an order of magnitude between the
models. Spin-state abundance ratios are also affected, and the new model better
reproduces recent observations of ortho and para $\rm H_2D^+$ and $\rm D_2H^+$.
The applicability regime of the new rate coefficients depends on the critical
densities of the various rotational transitions.
  Conclusions. The difference in the abundances of the $\rm H_3^+$ isotopologs
predicted by the two models is negligible at 10 K but excited states are very
important in studies of deuteration at higher temperatures, for example in
protostellar envelopes. The species-to-species rate coefficients provide a more
realistic approach to the chemistry of the $\rm H_3^+$ isotopologs than the
ground state-to-species rate coefficients do, and so the former should be
adopted in chemical models describing the chemistry of the $\rm H_3^+ + H_2$
reacting system.

text: The increasing complexity of microstructural materials presents a challenge for traditional design methodologies, necessitating innovative approaches to optimize material properties. This study investigates the application of deep adversarial learning techniques for microstructural materials design, intending to enhance material performance through tailored microstructures. The objective is to develop a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework that not only captures the intricate relationships between microstructure features and their resulting mechanical properties but also facilitates the exploration of novel microstructural designs.   Methodologically, we employ a two-tier adversarial learning architecture the generator synthesizes diverse microstructural patterns, while the discriminator evaluates their viability based on pre-defined mechanical performance metrics. Extensive datasets from existing literature and simulated microstructures are utilized for training, ensuring robustness and generalizability of the model.   Key findings indicate that the proposed GAN approach successfully generates microstructures that surpass conventional designs in strength, ductility, and other performance characteristics. Notably, the optimization process reveals latent design principles that can guide future material synthesis.   In conclusion, this research demonstrates the potential of deep adversarial learning as a transformative tool in microstructural materials design, enabling the discovery of innovative microstructures with enhanced performance attributes. The integration of machine learning into material design not only expedites the development process but also opens avenues for the intelligent design of next-generation materials.

text: This research explores the role of wind-driving dust species in the context of cool luminous giants, specifically focusing on models for M-type asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars. The primary objective is to investigate how these dust species influence the dynamic and photometric properties of stellar winds emanating from these evolved stars.   The study employs detailed stellar atmosphere models coupled with radiative transfer simulations to predict the behavior of stellar winds under various conditions. Key findings include the identification of specific dust species that significantly affect the mass loss rates and velocity profiles of stellar winds. These results highlight the importance of dust in regulating the mass transfer processes and energy transport mechanisms in AGB stars.  Furthermore, the research examines how variations in stellar parameters such as effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity impact the dynamics and photometric signatures of the stellar winds. The analysis reveals that these factors can lead to distinct spectral features observable in the light curves of AGB stars, which can be used to distinguish between different evolutionary stages.  In conclusion, this work provides valuable insights into the complex interplay between stellar atmospheres, dust formation, and the resulting stellar wind properties. The findings contribute to our understanding of the late-stage evolution of low-mass stars and have implications for studies of galactic chemical enrichment and stellar nucleosynthesis.

While quantum theory cannot be described by a local hidden variable model, it
is nevertheless possible to construct such models that exhibit features
commonly associated with quantum mechanics. These models are also used to
explore the question of {\psi}-ontic versus {\psi}-epistemic theories for
quantum mechanics. Spekkens' toy theory is one such model. It arises from
classical probabilistic mechanics via a limit on the knowledge an observer may
have about the state of a system. The toy theory for the simplest possible
underlying system closely resembles stabilizer quantum mechanics, a fragment of
quantum theory which is efficiently classically simulable but also non-local.
Further analysis of the similarities and differences between those two theories
can thus yield new insights into what distinguishes quantum theory from
classical theories, and {\psi}-ontic from {\psi}-epistemic theories.
  In this paper, we develop a graphical language for Spekkens' toy theory.
Graphical languages offer intuitive and rigorous formalisms for the analysis of
quantum mechanics and similar theories. To compare quantum mechanics and a toy
model, it is useful to have similar formalisms for both. We show that our
language fully describes Spekkens' toy theory and in particular, that it is
complete: meaning any equality that can be derived using other formalisms can
also be derived entirely graphically. Our language is inspired by a similar
graphical language for quantum mechanics called the ZX-calculus. Thus Spekkens'
toy bit theory and stabilizer quantum mechanics can be analysed and compared
using analogous graphical formalisms.

Recent analyses suggest that distance residuals measured from Type Ia
supernovae (SNe Ia) are correlated with local host galaxy properties within a
few kpc of the SN explosion. However, the well-established correlation with
global host galaxy properties is nearly as significant, with a shift of 0.06
mag across a low to high mass boundary (the mass step). Here, with 273 SNe Ia
at $z<0.1$, we investigate whether stellar masses and rest-frame $u-g$ colors
of regions within 1.5 kpc of the SN Ia explosion site are significantly better
correlated with SN distance measurements than global properties or properties
measured at random locations in SN hosts. At $\lesssim2\sigma$ significance,
local properties tend to correlate with distance residuals better than
properties at random locations, though despite using the largest low-$z$ sample
to date we cannot definitively prove that a local correlation is more
significant than a random correlation. Our data hint that SNe observed by
surveys that do not target a pre-selected set of galaxies may have a larger
local mass step than SNe from surveys that do, an increase of $0.071\pm0.036$
mag (2.0$\sigma$). We find a $3\sigma$ local mass step after global mass
correction, evidence that SNe Ia should be corrected for their local mass, but
we note that this effect is insignificant in the targeted low-$z$ sample. Only
the local mass step remains significant at $>2\sigma$ after global mass
correction, and we conservatively estimate a systematic shift in H$_0$
measurements of -0.14 $\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}\textrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ with an
additional uncertainty of 0.14 $\textrm{km}\,\textrm{s}^{-1}\textrm{Mpc}^{-1}$,
$\sim$10\% of the present uncertainty.

In this paper, we show that the Thomason model structure restricts to a
Quillen equivalent cofibrantly generated model structure on the category of
acyclic categories, whose generating cofibrations are the same as those
generating the Thomason model structure. To understand the Thomason model
structure, we need to have a closer look at the (barycentric) subdivision
endofunctor on the category of simplicial sets. This functor has a well known
right adjoint, called Kan's Ex functor. Taking the subdivision twice and then
the fundamental category yields a left adjoint of an adjunction between the
category of simplicial sets and the category of small categories, whose right
adjoint is given by applying the Ex functor twice on the nerve of a category.
This adjunction lifts the cofibrantly generated Quillen model structure on
simplicial sets to a cofibrantly generated model structure on the category of
small categories, the Thomason model structure. The generating sets are given
by the image of the generating sets of the Quillen model structure on
simplicial sets under the aforementioned adjunction. We furthermore show that
the category of acyclic categories is proper and combinatorial with respect to
said model structure. That is weak equivalences behave nicely with respect to
pushouts along fibrations and cofibrations, and cofibrations satisfy certain
smallness conditions which allow us to work with sets instead of proper
classes.

Grad's method of moments is employed to develop higher-order Grad's moment
equations---up to first 26-moments---for granular gases within the framework of
the (inelastic) Boltzmann equation. The homogeneous cooling state of a freely
cooling granular gas is investigated with the Grad's 26-moment equations in a
semi-linearized setting and it is shown that the granular temperature in the
homogeneous cooling state still decays according to Haff's law while the other
higher-order moments decay on a faster time scale. The constitutive relations
for stress and heat flux (the Navier--Stokes and Fourier relations) are
obtained by performing a Chapman--Enskog-like expansion on the Grad's 26-moment
equations and compared with those existing in the literature. The linear
stability of the homogeneous cooling state is analyzed through the Grad's
26-moment system and various sub-systems by decomposing them into longitudinal
and transverse systems. It is found that one eigenmode in both longitudinal and
transverse systems in case of inelastic gases is unstable. By comparing the
eigenmodes from various theories, it is established that the 13-moment
eigenmode theory predicts that the unstable eigenmode remains unstable for all
wavenumbers below a certain coefficient of restitution while any other
higher-order moment theory shows that this mode becomes stable above some
critical wavenumber for all values of coefficient of restitution. In
particular, the Grad's 26-moment theory leads to a smooth profile for the
critical wavenumber in contrast to the other considered theories. Furthermore,
the critical system size obtained through the Grad 26-moment and existing
theories are also in excellent agreement.

We present the largest sample of flares ever compiled for a single M dwarf,
the active M4 star GJ 1243. Over 6100 individual flare events, with energies
ranging from $10^{29}$ to $10^{33}$ erg, are found in 11 months of 1-minute
cadence data from Kepler. This sample is unique for its completeness and
dynamic range. We have developed automated tools for finding flares in
short-cadence Kepler light curves, and performed extensive validation and
classification of the sample by eye. From this pristine sample of flares we
generate a median flare template. This template shows that two exponential
cooling phases are present during the white-light flare decay, providing
fundamental constraints for models of flare physics. The template is also used
as a basis function to decompose complex multi-peaked flares, allowing us to
study the energy distribution of these events. Only a small number of flare
events are not well fit by our template. We find that complex, multi-peaked
flares occur in over 80% of flares with a duration of 50 minutes or greater.
The underlying distribution of flare durations for events 10 minutes and longer
appears to follow a broken power law. Our results support the idea that
sympathetic flaring may be responsible for some complex flare events.

text: We address the problem of accurately modeling the distribution and dynamics of early-type galaxies by examining small scatter and nearly-isothermal mass profiles extending to four half-light radii. Our work employs two-dimensional stellar dynamics to achieve precise measurements of mass distributions and kinematic properties in these galaxies. Utilizing high-resolution data and state-of-the-art dynamical modeling techniques, we derive mass profiles that reveal essential insights into the gravitational landscape and stellar distribution. Our methodology integrates orbit-based models with observational constraints, enabling us to evaluate the mass density profiles with unprecedented accuracy. The key results demonstrate that the mass profiles across our sample exhibit minimal scatter, suggesting a remarkable uniformity in their underlying gravitational potentials. Additionally, the profiles are found to be nearly isothermal, aligning closely with theoretical expectations for dynamically relaxed systems. These findings challenge existing paradigms and imply a more narrow range of formative processes and evolutionary pathways for early-type galaxies than previously assumed. Furthermore, our analysis underscores the reliability of two-dimensional stellar dynamical methods in retrieving intrinsic galaxy properties, offering significant implications for future studies on galactic structure and evolution. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of galactic mass distributions and provides a robust framework for interpreting observational data in terms of physical galaxy models, thereby advancing the field of galactic astrophysics.

We present multi-frequency (1-8 GHz) VLA data, combined with VIMOS IFU data
and HST imaging, of a z=0.085 radio-quiet type 2 quasar (with L(1.4GHz)~5e23
W/Hz and L(AGN)~2e45 erg/s). Due to the morphology of its emission-line region,
the target (J1430+1339) has been referred to as the Teacup AGN in the
literature. We identify "bubbles" of radio emission that are extended ~10-12
kpc to both the east and west of the nucleus. The edge of the brighter eastern
bubble is co-spatial with an arc of luminous ionized gas. We also show that the
Teacup AGN hosts a compact radio structure, located ~0.8 kpc from the core
position, at the base of the eastern bubble. This radio structure is co-spatial
with an ionized outflow with an observed velocity of v=-740 km/s. This is
likely to correspond to a jet, or possibly a quasar wind, interacting with the
interstellar medium at this position. The large-scale radio bubbles appear to
be inflated by the central AGN, which indicates that the AGN can also interact
with the gas on >~10 kpc scales. Our study highlights that even when a quasar
is formally "radio-quiet" the radio emission can be extremely effective for
observing the effects of AGN feedback.

In this paper, we study the scheduling problem for downlink transmission in a
multi-channel (e.g., OFDM-based) wireless network. We focus on a single cell,
with the aim of developing a unifying framework for designing low-complexity
scheduling policies that can provide optimal performance in terms of both
throughput and delay. We develop new easy-to-verify sufficient conditions for
rate-function delay optimality (in the many-channel many-user asymptotic
regime) and throughput optimality (in general non-asymptotic setting),
respectively. The sufficient conditions allow us to prove rate-function delay
optimality for a class of Oldest Packets First (OPF) policies and throughput
optimality for a large class of Maximum Weight in the Fluid limit (MWF)
policies, respectively. By exploiting the special features of our carefully
chosen sufficient conditions and intelligently combining policies from the
classes of OPF and MWF policies, we design hybrid policies that are both
rate-function delay-optimal and throughput-optimal with a complexity of
$O(n^{2.5} \log n)$, where $n$ is the number of channels or users. Our
sufficient condition is also used to show that a previously proposed policy
called Delay Weighted Matching (DWM) is rate-function delay-optimal. However,
DWM incurs a high complexity of $O(n^5)$. Thus, our approach yields
significantly lower complexity than the only previously designed delay and
throughput optimal scheduling policy. We also conduct numerical experiments to
validate our theoretical results.

text: We present a novel approach to full waveform inversion (FWI) that incorporates nonlocal similarity and model-derivative domain adaptive sparsity-promoting regularization. The proposed method, dubbed NS-DASPR, leverages the nonlocal similarity of seismic data to enhance the stability and efficiency of FWI. By incorporating nonlocal similarity constraints, NS-DIASPR reduces the impact of noise and artifacts, resulting in more accurate and reliable inversion results. Additionally, the model-derivative domain adaptive sparsity-promoting regularization term selectively promotes sparsity in the model parameters, allowing for more efficient and accurate imaging of complex geological structures. The NS-DASPR algorithm is designed to adaptively adjust the regularization strength based on the model-derivative, ensuring optimal trade-off between stability and accuracy. Through a series of numerical experiments, we demonstrate the superiority of NS-DASPR over existing FWI methods in terms of inversion accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency. Specifically, we show that NS-DASPR outperforms the standard FWI method by 25% in terms of inversion accuracy and 50% in terms of computational efficiency. Our results also indicate that the nonlocal similarity constraints and model-derivative adaptive regularization term work synergistically to improve the overall performance of the NS-DASPR algorithm.

text: Fractional powers of elliptic operators are important mathematical objects with applications in various fields such as quantum mechanics, material science, and image processing. However, due to their non-local and non-self-adjoint nature, numerical approximation of these operators presents challenges.   This research aims to develop efficient numerical methods for approximating fractional powers of elliptic operators. The focus is on overcoming the difficulties arising from the non-local and non-self-adjoint nature of these operators, while ensuring accuracy and stability in the computations.   The research proposes a novel approach based on spectral methods and domain decomposition techniques tailored for handling fractional powers of elliptic operators. By leveraging the properties of fractional calculus and the structure of elliptic operators, the developed numerical algorithms aim to provide reliable approximations that can be efficiently implemented.   The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed numerical methods in accurately computing fractional powers of elliptic operators. A positive linear operator $T$ between two unital $f$-algebras, with point
separating order duals, $A$ and $B$ is called a Markov operator for which $%
T\left( e_{1}\right) =e_{2}$ where $e_{1},e_{2}$ are the identities of $A$ and
$B$ respectively. Let $A$ and $B$ be semiprime $f$-algebras with point
separating order duals such that their second order duals $A^{\sim \sim }$ and
$B^{\sim \sim }$ are unital $f$-algebras. In this case, we will call a positive
linear operator $T:A\rightarrow B$ \ to be a Pre-Markov operator, if the second
adjoint operator of $T$ is a Markov operator. A positive linear operator $T$
between two semiprime $f$-algebras, with point separating order duals, $A$ and
$B$ is said to be contractive if $Ta\in B\cap \left[ 0,I_{B}\right] $ whenever
$a\in A\cap \left[ 0,I_{A}\right] $, where $I_{A}$ and $I_{B}$ are the identity
operators on $A$ and $B$ respectively. In this paper we characterize pre-Markov
algebra homomorphisms. In this regard, we show that a pre-Markov operator is an
algebra homomorphism if and only if its second adjoint operator is an extreme
point in the collection of all Markov operators from $A^{\sim \sim }$ to
$B^{\sim \sim }$. Moreover we characterize extreme points of contractive
mappings from $A$ to $B$. In addition, we give a condition that makes an order
bounded algebra homomorphism is a lattice homomorphism.

text: Quasars and active galactic nuclei have long been the focus of ultraviolet (UV) spectral studies, revealing complex emission lines and continuum spectra. However, understanding the UV properties of quiescent black holes (BHs) and neutron stars (NSs) is crucial for elucidating their accretion mechanisms and the evolution of compact stellar objects. In this study, we analyze UV spectral data from the Hubble Space Telescope archive for a sample of BH candidates in quiescent X-ray states and NSs with detected UV emission.  Our results reveal distinct UV spectral signatures for BHs and NSs. Quiescent BHs exhibit a soft UV spectrum with a power law continuum and weak emission lines, with the 1354 Å Fe II emission line being a notable exception. This finding is consistent with a reprocessing model, where the UV emission is produced through Compton scattering of X-rays from the accretion disk. NSs, on the other hand, display a hard UV spectrum dominated by strong hydrogen and helium emission lines, characteristic of a hot photoionized disk.  This investigation highlights the importance of UV spectroscopy for identifying and characterizing the properties of quiescent BHs and NSs. Furthermore, our findings provide insights into the accretion mechanisms of these objects, suggesting that reprocessing and photoionization play significant roles in shaping their UV spectra. The continuum slope, ionization state, and line ratios of the UV emission lines can serve as valuable diagnostics for distinguishing between BHs and NSs, contributing to the ongoing debate in the astrophysical community regarding the identification of these enigmatic objects.  Future observations with next-generation UV space missions, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, will enable more comprehensive studies of the UV emission from BHs and NSs, providing new insights into the physical processes that govern the behavior of these compact stellar objects.
