text: This study investigates the application of black-box compression algorithms in phase retrieval, aiming to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of signal reconstruction from intensity-only measurements. The research explores the use of variational autoencoders (VAEs) as a black-box compression technique, where the model is trained to minimize the difference between the input data and its reconstructed version. Our work attempts to solve the challenge of computational complexity and the high demand for computational resources in phase retrieval problems, particularly in applications such as X-ray crystallography and optical imaging.  Key methodologies involve training VAEs on simulated and real-world datasets to learn effective compression strategies. We evaluate the performance of these models through quantitative metrics such as mean squared error (MSE), structural similarity index (SSIM), and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR). The results demonstrate that black-box compression algorithms can significantly reduce the computational burden while maintaining acceptable levels of reconstruction quality. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the choice of hyperparameters and the architecture of the VAE directly influence the effectiveness of the compression process, highlighting the importance of fine-tuning these parameters for optimal performance.

text: We investigated the slow winds originating from T Tauri stars by analyzing low velocity forbidden line emission, aiming to understand the dynamics and characteristics of these winds, which are crucial for star and planet formation processes. T Tauri stars, being young and often surrounded by circumstellar disks, produce complex wind structures that significantly influence disk evolution and magnetic field dynamics. Employing high-resolution spectroscopic data, we traced low velocity forbidden line emissions, specifically examining features such as [O I] λ6300 and [S II] λ6731. By modeling these emissions, we identified key characteristics of the outflows, including their velocity distribution, density range, and mass-loss rates. Our analysis revealed a predominant presence of slow wind components with velocities under 20 km/s, suggesting that these low-velocity outflows are a widespread phenomenon among T Tauri stars. We found that the mass-loss rates associated with these slow winds are substantial enough to impact disk evolution significantly. Using radiative transfer models, we demonstrated that the origin of these emissions is consistent with solar-like magnetic activity coupled with disk-driven wind mechanisms. The results provide insights into the interaction between stellar winds and circumstellar environments, offering a plausible explanation for observed variability in emission line profiles. Our study emphasizes the importance of forbidden line diagnostics in characterizing the nature of stellar winds in young stellar objects, contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of early stellar evolution and its implications for planet-forming environments.

text: Cholera, a diarrheal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae, is a significant public health concern in many parts of the world. The transmission and loss of immunity to cholera are complex processes influenced by various factors, including environmental, social, and individual characteristics. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for developing effective control strategies and improving public health outcomes. However, the intricate relationships between cholera transmission and loss of immunity are not yet fully elucidated, particularly in the context of mechanisms that distinguish between susceptible and immune individuals.  This study aimed to investigate the relationships between cholera transmission, loss of immunity, and individual characteristics, with a focus on the distinguishability of mechanisms underlying these processes. A combination of mathematical modeling and statistical analysis was employed to analyze data from a large cohort study. The results showed that cholera transmission is influenced by a range of factors, including environmental contamination, sanitation, and individual immunity status. Notably, the study found that the mechanisms underlying cholera transmission and loss of immunity are distinguishable, with distinct patterns of transmission and loss of immunity observed in susceptible and immune individuals.  The key findings of this study have important implications for understanding the dynamics of cholera transmission and loss of immunity. The results suggest that targeted interventions aimed at distinguishing between susceptible and immune individuals could improve public health outcomes and reduce the risk of cholera transmission. text: In this study, we propose a novel algorithm, termed Influence-Receptivity learning (IRL), to learn the influence-receptivity network structure from observed data. The influence-receptivity network is a crucial modeling assumption in many complex systems, such as social networks, biological networks, and information propagation systems. However, estimating the network structure from limited observations is challenging due to the presence of errors, noise, and the intrinsic complexity of the networks. To address these issues, we introduce a novel constraint-based learning method to recover the influence-receptivity network structure. Recent solar flare observations in the sub-THz range have provided evidence
of a new spectral component with fluxes increasing for larger frequencies,
separated from the well-known microwave emission that maximizes in the GHz
range. Suggested interpretations explain the THz spectral component, but do not
account for the simultaneous microwave component. We present a mechanism for
producing the observed double-spectra. Based on coherent enhancement of
synchrotron emission at long wavelengths in laboratory accelerators, we
consider how similar processes may occur within a solar flare. The instability
known as microbunching arises from perturbations that produce electron beam
density modulations, giving rise to broadband coherent synchrotron emission at
wavelengths comparable to the characteristic size of the microbunch structure.
The spectral intensity of this coherent synchrotron radiation (CSR) can far
exceed that of the incoherent synchrotron radiation (ISR), which peaks at
higher frequency, thus producing a double-peaked spectrum. Successful CSR
simulations are shown to fit actual burst spectral observations, using typical
flaring physical parameters and power-law energy distributions for the
accelerated electrons. The simulations consider an energy threshold below which
microbunching is not possible because of Coulomb repulsion. Only a small
fraction of the radiating charges accelerated to energies above the threshold
is required to produce the microwave component observed for several events. The
ISR-CSR mechanism can occur together with other emission processes producing
the microwave component. It may bring an important contribution at microwaves
at least for certain events where physical conditions for the occurrence of the
ISR-CSR microbunching mechanism are possible.

The embedded hidden Markov model (EHMM) sampling method is a Markov chain
Monte Carlo (MCMC) technique for state inference in non-linear non-Gaussian
state-space models which was proposed in Neal (2003); Neal et al. (2004) and
extended in Shestopaloff and Neal (2016). An extension to Bayesian parameter
inference was presented in Shestopaloff and Neal (2013). An alternative class
of MCMC schemes addressing similar inference problems is provided by particle
MCMC (PMCMC) methods (Andrieu et al. 2009; 2010). All these methods rely on the
introduction of artificial extended target distributions for multiple state
sequences which, by construction, are such that one randomly indexed sequence
is distributed according to the posterior of interest. By adapting the
Metropolis-Hastings algorithms developed in the framework of PMCMC methods to
the EHMM framework, we obtain novel particle filter (PF)-type algorithms for
state inference and novel MCMC schemes for parameter and state inference. In
addition, we show that most of these algorithms can be viewed as particular
cases of a general PF and PMCMC framework. We compare the empirical performance
of the various algorithms on low- to high-dimensional state-space models. We
demonstrate that a properly tuned conditional PF with "local" MCMC moves
proposed in Shestopaloff and Neal (2016) can outperform the standard
conditional PF significantly when applied to high-dimensional state-space
models while the novel PF-type algorithm could prove to be an interesting
alternative to standard PFs for likelihood estimation in some lower-dimensional
scenarios.

To address undefinedness, we introduce a novel typing system with three possible types defined, undefined, and error. The defined type encompasses all values that are computable, while undefined and error types represent values that are uncomputable or erroneous, respectively. Our system provides a clear way to handle undefinedness and ensures that type errors are propagated appropriately.  Quotation is another extension we consider, enabling the representation of arbitrary computations as data. This feature facilitates a wide range of applications, such as metaprogramming and reflection. Our proposed solution is based on a system of explicit quotation and evaluation contexts.  Finally, we discuss the methodology of evaluating expressions in our system, emphasizing the importance of a systematic approach to ensure type safety. Our key findings indicate that the proposed extensions enhance the expressiveness and flexibility of the type theory, while preserving its fundamental guarantees.  In conclusion, this paper presents a simple type theory extension with undefinedness, quotation, and evaluation, providing a more robust foundation for type systems. By introducing a novel typing system, enabling the representation of arbitrary computations as data, and ensuring a systematic approach to evaluation, we demonstrate the potential benefits of these extensions. We report the observation of an X-class long-duration flare which is clearly
confined. It appears as a compact-loop flare in the traditional EUV passbands
(171 and 195 {\AA}), but in the passbands sensitive to flare plasmas (94 and
131 {\AA}), it exhibits a cusp-shaped structure above an arcade of loops like
other long-duration events. Inspecting images in a running difference approach,
we find that the seemingly diffuse, quasi-static cusp-shaped structure consists
of multiple nested loops that repeatedly rise upward and disappear approaching
the cusp edge. Over the gradual phase, we detect numerous episodes of loop
rising, each lasting minutes. A differential emission measure analysis reveals
that the temperature is highest at the top of the arcade and becomes cooler at
higher altitudes within the cusp-shaped structure, contrary to typical
long-duration flares. With a nonlinear force-free model, our analysis shows
that the event mainly involves two adjacent sheared arcades separated by a
T-type hyperbolic flux tube (HFT). One of the arcades harbors a magnetic flux
rope, which is identified with a filament that survives the flare owing to the
strong confining field. We conclude that a new emergence of magnetic flux in
the other arcade triggers the flare, while the preexisting HFT and flux rope
dictate the structure and dynamics of the flare loops and ribbons during the
long-lasting decay phase, and that a quasi-separatrix layer high above the HFT
could account for the cusp-shaped structure.

Genetic oscillators, such as circadian clocks, are constantly perturbed by
molecular noise arising from the small number of molecules involved in gene
regulation. One of the strongest sources of stochasticity is the binary noise
that arises from the binding of a regulatory protein to a promoter in the
chromosomal DNA. In this study, we focus on two minimal oscillators based on
activator titration and repressor titration to understand the key parameters
that are important for oscillations and for overcoming binary noise. We show
that the rate of unbinding from the DNA, despite traditionally being considered
a fast parameter, needs to be slow to broaden the space of oscillatory
solutions. The addition of multiple, independent DNA binding sites further
expands the oscillatory parameter space for the repressor-titration oscillator
and lengthens the period of both oscillators. This effect is a combination of
increased effective delay of the unbinding kinetics due to multiple binding
sites and increased promoter ultrasensitivity that is specific for repression.
We then use stochastic simulation to show that multiple binding sites increase
the coherence of the oscillations by mitigating the binary noise. Slow values
of DNA unbinding rate are also effective in alleviating molecular noise due to
the increased distance from the bifurcation point. Our work demonstrates how
DNA binding sites and slow unbinding kinetics, which are often omitted in
biophysical models of gene circuits, can have a significant impact on the
temporal and stochastic dynamics of genetic oscillators.

text: We investigate the period-eccentricity distribution of subdwarf-B + main-sequence binaries, a class of systems where the subdwarf-B component is a compact, degenerate star, and the main-sequence component is a normal, hydrogen-fused star. Specifically, we observe a pronounced peak at intermediate periods (P ≈ 1-3 days) and a tail extending towards shorter periods, which we attribute to the presence of subdwarf-B components. Furthermore, we note that the eccentricity distribution is skewed towards higher eccentricities, particularly in systems with shorter periods. This is likely due to the strong tidal interactions between the subdwarf-B and main-sequence components, which can lead to significant orbital distortions. Our results are consistent with predictions from stellar evolution models and suggest that subdwarf-B + main-sequence binaries are a significant population of close, eccentric binaries. The observed period-eccentricity distribution also implies that subdwarf-B + main-sequence binaries are more common than previously thought, with a potential impact on our understanding of the formation and evolution of compact binaries.

The D/H enrichment observed in Saturn's satellite Enceladus is remarkably
similar to the values observed in the nearly-isotropic comets. Given the
predicted strong variation of D/H with heliocentric distance in the solar
nebula, this observation links the primordial source region of the
nearly-isotropic comets with the formation location of Enceladus. That is,
comets from the nearly-isotropic class were most likely fed into their current
reservoir, the Oort cloud, from a source region near the formation location of
Enceladus. Dynamical simulations of the formation of the Oort cloud indicate
that Uranus and Neptune are, primarily, responsible for the delivery of
material into the Oort cloud. In addition, Enceladus formed from material that
condensed from the solar nebula near the location at which Saturn captured its
gas envelope, most likely at or near Saturn's current location in the solar
system. The coupling of these lines of evidence appears to require that Uranus
and Neptune were, during the epoch of the formation of the Oort cloud, much
closer to the current location of Saturn than they are currently. Such a
configuration is consistent with the Nice model of the evolution of the outer
solar system. Further measurements of the D/H enrichment in comets,
particularly in ecliptic comets, will provide an excellent discriminator among
various models of the formation of the outer solar system.

The thermodynamics of hydration changes gradually from entropic for small
solutes to enthalpic for large ones. The small-to-large crossover lengthscale
of hydrophobic hydration depends on the thermodynamic conditions of the solvent
such as temperature, pressure, presence of additives, etc... We attempt to shed
some light on the temperature dependence of the crossover lengthscale by using
a probabilistic approach to water hydrogen bonding that allows one to obtain an
analytic expression for the number of bonds per water molecule as a function of
both its distance to a solute and solute radius. Incorporating that approach
into the density functional theory, one can examine the solute size effects on
its hydration over the entire small-to-large lengthscale range at different
temperatures. Knowing the dependence of the hydration free energy on
temperature and solute size, one can obtain its enthalpic and entropic
contributions as functions of temperature and solute size. These function can
provide interesting insight into the temperature dependence of the crossover
lengthscale of hydrophobic hydration. The model was applied to the hydration of
spherical particles of various radii in water in the temperature range from
T=293.15 K to T=333.15 K. The model predictions for the temperature dependence
of the hydration free energy of small hydrophobes are consistent with the
experimental and simulational data. Three alternative definitions for the
small-to-large crossover length-scale of hydrophobic hydration are proposed,
and their temperature dependence is obtained. Depending on the definition and
temperature, the small-to-large crossover in the hydration mechanism is
predicted to occur for hydrophobes of radii from one to several nanometers.

We consider vertex partitions of the binomial random graph $G_{n,p}$. For
$np\to\infty$, we observe the following phenomenon: in any partition into
asymptotically fewer than $\chi(G_{n,p})$ parts, i.e. $o(np/\log np)$ parts,
one part must induce a connected component of order at least roughly the
average part size.
  Stated another way, we consider the $t$-component chromatic number, the
smallest number of colours needed in a colouring of the vertices for which no
monochromatic component has more than $t$ vertices. As long as $np \to \infty$,
there is a threshold for $t$ around $\Theta(p^{-1}\log np)$: if $t$ is smaller
then the $t$-component chromatic number is nearly as large as the chromatic
number, while if $t$ is greater then it is around $n/t$.
  For $0 < p <1$ fixed, we obtain more precise information. We find something
more subtle happens at the threshold $t = \Theta(\log n)$, and we determine
that the asymptotic first-order behaviour is characterised by a non-smooth
function. Moreover, we consider the $t$-component stability number, the maximum
order of a vertex subset that induces a subgraph with maximum component order
at most $t$, and show that it is concentrated in a constant length interval
about an explicitly given formula, so long as $t = O(\log \log n)$.
  We also consider a related Ramsey-type parameter and use bounds on the
component stability number of $G_{n,1/2}$ to describe its basic asymptotic
growth.

text: This research paper explores the intersection of cosmological horizons and the reconstruction of quantum field theories, shedding light on the fundamental nature of spacetime and the behavior of fundamental particles. However, the current understanding of quantum field theories, which describe the behavior of fundamental particles, is incomplete and often contradictory.  The objective of this study is to develop a novel approach to reconstructing quantum field theories, incorporating cosmological horizons as a fundamental constraint. By leveraging the principles of general relativity and the tools of quantum field theory, this research aims to derive a new framework for understanding the behavior of fundamental particles in the presence of cosmological horizons. Ultimately, this research provides a new perspective on the relationship between cosmological horizons and quantum field theories, offering a framework for understanding the fundamental nature of the universe and the behavior of fundamental particles. text: Prestellar cores, the dense and collapsing regions within molecular clouds, are believed to be the birthplaces of new stars. The mass distribution of these cores significantly influences the subsequent stellar mass function. This study investigates the relationship between the mass distributions of prestellar cores and the structure of their parental clouds. We analyzed a sample of 34 prestellar cores from both low- and high-mass star-forming regions in Perseus and Orion. We utilized the moment-of-inertia method to determine the mass enclosed within the cores' outlined surfaces. Additionally, we evaluated the cloud surface density and temperature distributions surrounding each core.  The results revealed that cores within lower-density clouds displayed a broader mass distribution compared to those within denser environments. Specifically, the median mass for low-density cores was found to be significantly lower than for high-density cores. Furthermore, we observed that cores within the lowest density quartile had a greater scatter in their mass distributions compared to those within the highest density quartile.  Our findings suggest that the structure of the parental cloud plays a crucial role in determining the mass distribution of prestellar cores. The lower mass cores may represent a transitional phase, where they are still assembling and have not yet reached the high densities required for efficient accretion. The higher mass cores, on the other hand, could be more evolved, as they have likely exceeded the density threshold necessary for core growth and stellar ignition.  In conclusion, this study provides insight into the dependence of prestellar core mass distributions on the structure of their parental clouds, contributing to a better understanding of stellar mass formation mechanisms. Further investigations are needed to explore the implications of these results on the resulting stellar mass function and star formation efficiency.

By modeling the rotational spectra of complex cyanides, we demonstrate that their abundances and isomeric ratios serve as reliable tracers for the physical conditions of hot cores. Our findings have important implications for understanding the chemical evolution of protostars and the formation of complex molecules in the interstellar medium. Further studies are required to extend this work to other molecular species and to investigate the role of complex cyanides in more diverse environments. Overall, this research highlights the importance of complex cyanides as key players in the molecular clocks of hot cores, paving the way for new discoveries and advancements in our understanding of stellar astrophysics.

Many studies have sought to determine if there is an association between air
quality and acute deaths. Many consider it plausible that current levels of air
quality cause acute deaths. However, several factors call causation and even
association into question. Observational data sets are large and complex.
Multiple testing and multiple modeling can lead to false positive findings.
Publication, confirmation and other biases are also possible problems.
  Moreover, the fact that most data sets used in studies evaluating the
relationships among air quality and public health outcomes are not publicly
available makes reproducing the claims nearly impossible. Here we have built
and made publicly available a dataset containing daily air quality levels,
PM2.5 and ozone, daily temperature levels, minimum and maximum and daily
relative humidity levels for the eight most populous California air basins. We
analyzed the dataset using a moving median analysis, a standard time series
analysis, and a prediction analysis within the following analysis strategy. We
examine the eight air basins separately to see if estimates replicate across
locations. We use leave one year out cross validation analysis to evaluate
predictions. Both the moving medians analysis and the standard time series
analysis found little evidence for association between air quality and acute
deaths. The prediction analysis process was a run as a large factorial design
using different models and holding out one year at a time. Among the variables
used to predict acute death, most of the daily death variability was explained
by time of year or weather variables. In summary, the empirical evidence is
that current levels of air quality, ozone and PM2.5, are not causally related
to acute deaths for California. An empirical and logical case can be made air
quality is not causally related to acute deaths for the rest of the United
States.

text: Graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) exhibit unique electronic properties due to their confined dimensions and spin-orbit coupling. In the quantum spin Hall (QSH) and quantum anomalous Hall (QAH) regimes, GNRs support topologically protected edge states, which facilitate spin-polarized quantum transport without the presence of external magnetic fields.  In this study, we explore the role of spin-polarized edge states in quantum transport through GNRs in the QSH and QAH regimes using first-principles calculations and nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) method. Our results reveal that the edge states exhibit unique conductance properties, with a conductance quantization of 2e^2/h in the QSH regime and chiral edge conductance in the QAH regime. The spin-polarized nature of these edge states is demonstrated by calculating the spin-resolved transmission probability.  Furthermore, we investigate the effect of edge roughness on the transport properties of edge states. Our findings show that small amounts of edge roughness can lead to a significant reduction in the edge conductance due to the scattering of edge states. We propose that engineering strategies such as gating or substrate manipulation can be employed to mitigate the effect of edge roughness and enhance the edge conductance.  In conclusion, our work sheds light on the fundamental electronic properties of spin-polarized edge states in GNRs in the QSH and QAH regimes, providing insights into potential applications in spintronics and topological quantum computing.

text: We investigate the role of neutron-proton pairing in the context of double-beta decay using the Interacting Boson Model (IBM). Our study addresses the challenge of accurately describing the interplay between nuclear structure and decay processes, particularly focusing on how neutron-proton correlations influence the transition rates and matrix elements involved in double-beta decay. We implement a refined version of the IBM that incorporates bosonic representations of nucleon pairs, thereby allowing us to model neutron-proton pairing interactions explicitly.   Through systematic calculations, we analyze the spectral properties of nuclei relevant to double-beta decay, paying particular attention to the lowest energy states and their associated pairing correlations. Our results indicate substantial enhancement in the transition probabilities due to the inclusion of neutron-proton pairing, demonstrating its critical impact on the decay processes. By comparing our findings with empirical data, we establish a correlation between the theoretical predictions and observed half-lives of various isotopes undergoing double-beta decay.  Furthermore, we explore the implications of our results for the understanding of neutrino physics and the potential for detecting neutrinoless double-beta decay. The enhanced model provides a robust framework for analyzing other nuclear phenomena linked to pairing effects, thereby expanding the applicability of the IBM in nuclear physics. Overall, our work highlights the significance of neutron-proton pairing in shaping the properties of nuclei and its consequential effects on double-beta decay, advancing both theoretical predictions and experimental understandings in this domain.

text: Underdispersion in experimental data presents significant challenges in statistical analysis, particularly when default models assume equidispersion. This paper investigates the application of the Gamma-count distribution as a robust alternative for analyzing underdispersed count data arising from various experimental designs. The primary objective is to evaluate the effectiveness of this distribution in accurately modeling and interpreting underdispersed datasets compared to conventional count models such as Poisson regression.  The methodology encompasses simulations and real-world data applications to assess the performance of the Gamma-count distribution in different scenarios of underdispersion. We implemented goodness-of-fit tests and examined key statistical properties, including the mean-variance relationship and predictive accuracy, across multiple datasets.   Key findings indicate that the Gamma-count distribution provides superior fit and interpretative clarity for underdispersed data, exhibiting reduced bias and improved efficiency in parameter estimation when juxtaposed with Poisson and negative binomial distributions. Furthermore, the findings underscore how the flexibility of the Gamma-count distribution facilitates enhanced modeling of intricate data structures common in experimental settings.  In conclusion, the Gamma-count distribution emerges as a potent tool for researchers encountering underdispersed count data, offering both theoretical and practical advantages. Our results advocate for its broader adoption in statistical methodologies, encouraging future research to further explore its applicability across various domains where underdispersion is a prevalent concern.

Amphiphilic phospholipids and nanoparticles functionalized with hydrophobic
capping ligands have previously been extensively investigated for their
capacity to self-assemble into Langmuir monolayers at the air/water interface.
However, understanding of composite films consisting of both nanoparticles and
phospholipids, and by extension, the complex interactions arising between
nanomaterials and biological membranes, remains limited. In this work,
dodecanethiol-capped gold nanoparticles (Au-NPs) with an average core diameter
of 6 nm were incorporated into 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine
(DPPC) monolayers in area ratios ranging from 0.1 to 20% area coverage at a
surface pressure of 30 mN/m. High resolution liquid surface X-ray scattering
studies revealed a phase separation of the DPPC and Au-NP components of the
composite film, as confirmed with atomic force microscopy after the film was
transferred to a substrate. At low Au-NP content, the structural organization
of the phase-separated film is best described as a DPPC film containing
isolated islands of Au-NPs. However, increasing the Au-NP content beyond 5%
area coverage transforms the structural organization of the composite film to a
long-range interconnected network of Au-NP strands surrounding small seas of
DPPC, where the density of the Au-NP network increases with increasing Au-NP
content. The observed phase separation and structural organization of the
phospholipid and nanoparticle components in these Langmuir monolayers are
useful for understanding interactions of nanoparticles with biological
membranes.

In this work, I explore an empirically motivated model for investigating the
relationship between galaxy stellar masses, star formation rates and their halo
masses and mass accretion histories. The core statistical quantity in this
model is the stellar mass assembly distribution, $P(dM_{*}/dt|\mathbf{X},a)$,
which specifies the probability density distribution of stellar mass assembly
rates given a set of halo properties $\mathbf{X}$ and epoch $a$. Predictions
from this model are obtained by integrating the stellar mass assembly
distribution (SMAD) over halo merger trees, easily obtained from modern,
high-resolution $N$-body simulations. Further properties of the galaxies hosted
by the halos can be obtained by post-processing the stellar mass assembly
histories with stellar population synthesis models. In my particular example
implementation of this model, I use the \citet{behroozi13a} constraint on the
median stellar mass assembly rates of halos as a function of their mass and
redshift to construct an example parameterization of
$P(dM_{*}/dt|\mathbf{X},a)$. This SMAD is then integrated over individual halo
mass accretion histories from $N$-body merger trees starting at z = 4, using
simple rules to account for merging halos. I find that this a simple model can
reproduce qualitatively the bimodal features of the low-redshift galaxy
population, including the qualitative split in the two-point clustering as a
function of specific star formation rate. These results indicate that models
which directly couple halo and galaxy growth through simple efficiency
functions can naturally predict the star formation rate bimodality in
higher-order statistics of the galaxy field, such as its two-point correlations
or galactic conformity signals.

In this paper, we report the detections of stellar variabilities from the
first 2-year observations of sky area of about 1300 square degrees from the
Tsinghua University-NAOC Transient Survey (TNTS). A total of 1237 variable
stars (including 299 new ones) were detected with brightness < 18.0 mag and
magnitude variation >= 0.1 mag on a timescale from a few hours to few hundred
days. Among such detections, we tentatively identified 661 RR Lyrae stars, 431
binaries, 72 Semiregular pulsators, 29 Mira stars, 11 slow irregular variables,
11 RS Canum Venaticorum stars, 7 Gamma Doradus stars, 5 long period variables,
3 W Virginis stars, 3 Delta Scuti stars, 2 Anomalous Cepheids, 1 Cepheid, and 1
nove-like star based on their time-series variability index Js and their phased
diagrams. Moreover, we found that 14 RR Lyrae stars show the Blazhko effect and
67 contact eclipsing binaries exhibit the O'Connell effect. Since the period
and amplitude of light variations of RR Lyrae variables depend on their
chemical compositions, their photometric observations can be used to
investigate distribution of metallicity along the direction perpendicular to
the Galactic disk. We find that the metallicity of RR Lyrae stars shows large
scatter at regions closer to the Galactic plane (e.g., -3.0 < [Fe/H] < 0) but
tends to converge at [Fe/H]~ -1.7 at larger Galactic latitudes. This variation
may be related to that the RRAB Lyrae stars in the Galactic halo come from
globular clusters with different metallicity and vertical distances, i.e. OoI
and OoII populations, favoring for the dual-halo model.

Many areas of physics rely upon adiabatic state transfer protocols, allowing
a quantum state to be moved between different physical systems for storage and
retrieval or state manipulation. However, these state-transfer protocols suffer
from dephasing and dissipation. In this thesis we go beyond the standard
open-systems treatment of quantum dissipation allowing us to consider
non-Markovian environments. We use adiabatic perturbation theory in order to
give analytic descriptions for various quantum state-transfer protocols. The
leading-order corrections will give rise to additional terms adding to the
geometric phase preventing us from achieving a perfect fidelity. We obtain
analytical descriptions for the effects of the geometric phase in non-Markovian
regimes. The Markovian regime is usually treated by solving a standard
Bloch-Redfield master equation, while in the non-Markovian regime, we perform a
secular approximation allowing us to obtain a solution to the density matrix
without solving master equations. This solution contains all the relevant phase
information for our state-transfer protocol. After developing the general
theoretical tools, we apply our methods to adiabatic state transfer between a
four-level atom in a driven cavity. We explicitly consider dephasing effects
due to unavoidable photon shot noise and give a protocol for performing a phase
gate. These results will be useful to ongoing experiments in circuit quantum
electrodynamics (QED) systems.

text: We investigated the phenomenon of hyper-domains in exchange bias micro-stripe patterns, a complex system exhibiting anisotropic magnetic properties. Through a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental measurements, we aimed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms driving the emergence of hyper-domains. Our results indicate that the exchange bias effect, which typically arises from the asymmetry in the magnetic anisotropy of adjacent ferromagnetic layers, gives rise to the formation of hyper-domains in the micro-stripe pattern. We found that the exchange bias-induced anisotropy in the ferromagnetic layers leads to a preferred alignment of the magnetic moments, resulting in the formation of hyper-domains with distinct magnetic properties. Our simulations suggest that the hyper-domains are stabilized by the exchange bias-induced anisotropy, which in turn affects the magnetic exchange interactions between the ferromagnetic layers. Furthermore, our measurements reveal that the hyper-domains exhibit a non-trivial relationship with the exchange bias-induced anisotropy, indicating a complex interplay between the magnetic properties of the ferromagnetic layers and the exchange bias effect. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex magnetic behavior in exchange-biased systems, with potential implications for the development of novel magnetic devices and materials.

text: We present the first comprehensive study of the blazar Mrk 501, utilizing a multi-messenger approach combining data from the Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR), the Very Energetic Radiation Imaging Telescope Array System (VERITAS), and the LIDAR-corrected optical observations from the High Energy Stereoscopic System (HESS) MAGIC telescope.   Our analysis reveals a complex and dynamic spectral energy distribution of Mrk 501, characterized by a hard power-law continuum, a broad Fe Kα emission line, and a strong and variable high-energy gamma-ray emission. NuSTAR's high-resolution spectroscopy provides a detailed insight into the accretion disk and coronal regions, while VERITAS' imaging capabilities reveal the variability of the blazar's gamma-ray emission on timescales of hours.   In contrast, the LIDAR-corrected optical observations from MAGIC reveal a unique and intriguing spectral signature, which we attribute to the presence of a dusty torus. This torus is thought to be a key component in the blazar's overall energy budget, influencing the spectral energy distribution and variability of Mrk 501. Our findings demonstrate the power of a multi-messenger approach in unveiling the complex physics underlying blazar activity, and highlight the importance of combining high-energy and optical observations to gain a deeper understanding of these enigmatic objects.

We consider the multidimensional (nonrelativistic) Newton equation in a
static electromagnetic field $$\ddot x = F(x,\dot x), F(x,\dot x)=-\nabla
V(x)+B(x)\dot x, \dot x={dx\over dt}, x\in C^2(\R,\R^n),\eqno{(*)}$$ where $V
\in C^2(\R^n,\R),$ $B(x)$ is the $n\times n$ real antisymmetric matrix with
elements $B_{i,k}(x)$, $B_{i,k}\in C^1(\R^n,\R)$ (and $B$ satisfies the closure
condition), and $|\pa^{j_1}_xV(x)| +|\pa^{j_2}_xB_{i,k}(x)| \le \beta_{|j_1|}
(1+|x|)^{-(\alpha+|j_1|)}$ for $x\in \R^n,$ $1\le|j_1|\le 2,$ $0\le|j_2|\le 1$,
$|j_2|=|j_1|-1$, $i,k=1... n$ and some $\alpha > 1$. We give estimates and
asymptotics for scattering solutions and scattering data for the equation $(*)$
for the case of small angle scattering. We show that at high energies the
velocity valued component of the scattering operator uniquely determines the
X-ray transforms $P\nabla V$ and $PB_{i,k}$ (on sufficiently rich sets of
straight lines). Applying results on inversion of the X-ray transform $P$ we
obtain that for $n\ge 2$ the velocity valued component of the scattering
operator at high energies uniquely determines $(\nabla V,B)$. We also consider
the problem of recovering $(\nabla V,B)$ from our high energies asymptotics
found for the configuration valued component of the scattering operator.
Results of the present work were obtained by developing the inverse scattering
approach of [R. Novikov, 1999] for $(*)$ with $B\equiv 0$ and of [Jollivet,
2005] for the relativistic version of $(*)$. We emphasize that there is an
interesting difference in asymptotics for scattering solutions and scattering
data for $(*)$ on the one hand and for its relativistic version on the other.

text: Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) have emerged as a crucial technology for enhancing security in computation by establishing protected enclaves. However, their widespread adoption is hindered by the potential for side-channel attacks that exploit microarchitectural features. The objective of this study is to explore the feasibility of inferring fine-grained control flow inside SGX enclaves through a technique known as branch shadowing. Leveraging side-channel vulnerabilities, branch shadowing involves monitoring branch predictions and their subsequent effects on CPU caches to deduce the execution paths and control flows of enclave-protected code. Utilizing a combination of reverse engineering of the branch prediction mechanism and profiling of cache access patterns, our methodology enables a non-intrusive and remote inference of the control flow within these secure environments. Our key findings indicate that branch shadowing can successfully reveal intricate control flow details, including conditional branches and indirect jumps, under experimental conditions. These results demonstrate the potential for significant security implications, such as breaching sensitive information within enclaves. Conclusively, this research underscores the necessity for enhanced countermeasures in the design of SGX and similar enclaving technologies to address such vulnerabilities. Further work is recommended to establish more robust defenses and to evaluate the long-term effectiveness of potential counterstrategies.

Given a task $\mathcal{T}$, a set of experts $V$ with multiple skills and a
social network $G(V, W)$ reflecting the compatibility among the experts, team
formation is the problem of identifying a team $C \subseteq V$ that is both
competent in performing the task $\mathcal{T}$ and compatible in working
together. Existing methods for this problem make too restrictive assumptions
and thus cannot model practical scenarios. The goal of this paper is to
consider the team formation problem in a realistic setting and present a novel
formulation based on densest subgraphs. Our formulation allows modeling of many
natural requirements such as (i) inclusion of a designated team leader and/or a
group of given experts, (ii) restriction of the size or more generally cost of
the team (iii) enforcing locality of the team, e.g., in a geographical sense or
social sense, etc.
  The proposed formulation leads to a generalized version of the classical
densest subgraph problem with cardinality constraints (DSP), which is an NP
hard problem and has many applications in social network analysis. In this
paper, we present a new method for (approximately) solving the generalized DSP
(GDSP). Our method, FORTE, is based on solving an equivalent continuous
relaxation of GDSP. The solution found by our method has a quality guarantee
and always satisfies the constraints of GDSP. Experiments show that the
proposed formulation (GDSP) is useful in modeling a broader range of team
formation problems and that our method produces more coherent and compact teams
of high quality. We also show, with the help of an LP relaxation of GDSP, that
our method gives close to optimal solutions to GDSP.

text: The Grassmann ontological model (GOM) is a mathematical framework for modeling physical systems based on the geometry of Grassmann spaces (G-spaces) [1]. In this work, we investigate the ontic states of a specific subset of physical systems modeled in the GOM, namely those described by non-disjoint basis vectors. Our findings show that these systems exhibit transformation contextuality, meaning that their ontic states cannot be fully determined from local contexts alone [2].     To illustrate this, we consider a simple example of a qubit subjected to a non-commuting unitary transformation [3]. We show that the ontic states of the qubit in this scenario cannot be determined without considering the entire transformation history. Specifically, we demonstrate that the ontic states of the qubit are contextually dependent on both the initial and final states of the transformation, violating the principle of local causality [4].     Building upon these results, we explore the implications of transformation contextuality for the single qubit stabilizer subtheory (SQS) [5], a key subtheory in quantum information theory. Our analysis reveals that the SQS must be extended to account for contextual effects, leading to a more nuanced understanding of this fundamental quantum concept.     In conclusion, this work sheds new light on the non-disjoint ontic states of physical systems modeled in the Grassmann ontological model and their transformation contextuality. Our findings challenge the assumption of local causality and provide valuable insights into the nature of quantum systems. Future research directions include investigating the implications of these results for other quantum systems and exploring the potential applications in quantum technology. References 1. Hestenes, M. For the past 400 years, astronomers have sought to observe and interpret the
Universe by building more powerful telescopes. These incredible instruments
extend the capabilities of one of our most important senses, sight, towards new
limits such as increased sensitivity and resolution, new dimensions such as
exploration of wavelengths across the full electromagnetic spectrum, new
information content such as analysis through spectroscopy, and new cadences
such as rapid time-series views of the variable sky. The results from these
investments, from small to large telescopes on the ground and in space, have
completely transformed our understanding of the Universe; including the
discovery that Earth is not the center of the Universe, that the Milky Way is
one among many galaxies in the Universe, that relic cosmic background radiation
fills all space in the early Universe, that that the expansion rate of the
Universe is accelerating, that exoplanets are common around stars, that
gravitational waves exist, and much more. For modern astronomical research, the
next wave of breakthroughs in fields ranging over planetary, stellar, galactic,
and extragalactic science motivate a general-purpose observatory that is
optimized at near- and mid-infrared wavelengths, and that has much greater
sensitivity, resolution, and spectroscopic multiplexing than all previous
telescopes. This scientific vision, from measuring the composition of rocky
worlds in the nearby Milky Way galaxy to finding the first sources of light in
the Universe to other topics at the forefront of modern astrophysics, motivates
the state-of-the-art James Webb Space Telescope (Webb). In this review paper, I
summarize the design and technical capabilities of Webb and the scientific
opportunities that it enables.

text: Comet 49P/Arend-Rigaux exhibits significant variability in its rotation period and other dynamic properties. Our study investigates the comet's rotational behavior from 1984 to 2012 using observational data from various astronomical surveys. We identified and analyzed 312 rotation periods using lightcurve analysis, revealing a complex rotational behavior. The comet's rotation period varied from 2.5 to 8.3 days, with an average of 4.9 days. This variability can be attributed to the comet's irregular shape and non-spherical nucleus.  Additionally, we analyzed the comet's jet behavior during its 2010 approach and observed two jets with different activity levels and spatial distributions. The primary jet, located near the nucleus, exhibited high activity, while the secondary jet, located further away, displayed weaker activity. Our findings suggest a heterogeneous nucleus, with different composition and structure zones.  To explain the observed rotation and jet behavior, we applied three-dimensional modeling using shape and spin axis variations. We found that the best-fitting model had an ellipsoidal shape with semi-major, semi-minor, and minor axes of approximately 2.35, 2.14, and 1.62 km, respectively. The model also suggested a highly elliptical orbit with an eccentricity of 0.66 and an inclination of 23.1 degrees.  In summary, our study reveals the complex rotational and jet behavior of Comet 49P/Arend-Rigaux, highlighting its heterogeneous nucleus and unique dynamic properties. Further research on this comet could provide valuable insights into cometary nuclei and their evolution.

text: This research paper investigates finite-density corrections to the unitary Fermi gas by employing a lattice perspective within the framework of Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT). The study aims to explore how particle number density affects the properties of a strongly interacting fermionic system, focusing on the behavior of the unitary Fermi gas at high densities.  The methodology involves constructing a DMFT model that incorporates the effects of finite density on the self-energy of the system. This is achieved through the use of a lattice approximation, which allows for a detailed analysis of local and non-local interactions. By solving the DMFT equations numerically, the authors aim to understand the impact of increasing particle number density on the spectral functions, quasiparticle weights, and other relevant thermodynamic quantities.  Key findings reveal significant deviations from the predictions of the ideal Fermi gas, particularly in the vicinity of the unitarity limit. The results indicate that finite-density effects lead to substantial modifications in the spectral functions, with pronounced changes in the quasiparticle weight near the chemical potential. These findings provide valuable insights into the nature of strongly correlated electron systems under finite density conditions.  In conclusion, this work highlights the importance of considering finite-density corrections when studying unitary Fermi gases, especially at high densities. The lattice-based approach and DMFT provide a robust theoretical framework for understanding these corrections, offering new perspectives on the behavior of strongly interacting fermions in condensed matter systems.

text: The accumulation of magnetic energy in the photosphere plays a crucial role in solar activities, including sunspots and solar flares. Understanding the underlying mechanisms requires efficient classification of various photospheric proxies that reflect magnetic energy build-up. This study aims to develop an automated classification approach to rank these proxies based on their effectiveness in predicting magnetic energy accumulation. We employed a machine learning framework utilizing support vector machines, random forests, and deep learning models, tested on a dataset comprising high-resolution solar images and associated magnetic field measurements from space missions. Data preprocessing involved normalization and feature extraction to enhance model performance. The results indicate that deep learning models outperformed traditional machine learning methods, achieving an accuracy of 92% in classification tasks. Specifically, proxies related to photospheric magnetic field gradients demonstrated the highest correlation with energy build-up metrics. Our findings reveal that not all proxies are equally effective, with some providing redundant information while others significantly enhance predictive power. This work emphasizes the potential of automated classification techniques in solar physics and provides a framework for future research aimed at understanding solar dynamics. The implications of our findings extend to improving space weather forecasting and enhancing the understanding of solar magnetic phenomena, ultimately contributing to the predictive modeling of solar activity and its impact on space weather.

text: We investigated the complex dynamics of two massive clumps, IRDC G030.88+00.13, utilizing a multi-wavelength approach that integrated observations from radio, millimeter, and infrared wavelengths. Our analysis revealed a rich interplay between the two clumps, with distinct differences in their physical properties and evolutionary stages. The northern clump exhibited a more compact and dense structure, with a higher column density and stronger magnetic field, whereas the southern clump displayed a more extended and less dense configuration, with a weaker magnetic field.  Our results indicate that the northern clump is undergoing a more rapid collapse, driven by the presence of a dense core surrounded by a cavity, whereas the southern clump is in a more quiescent state, with a lower density and a more diffuse envelope. We also detected significant variations in the temperature and dust extinction profiles across the two clumps, suggesting distinct differences in their thermal and chemical evolution. The observed differences in the clumps' properties are consistent with a scenario in which the two clumps have formed through the merger of separate molecular cloud cores, resulting in a complex and dynamic system with multiple evolutionary stages. Our study provides new insights into the formation and evolution of massive clumps, highlighting the importance of considering the interactions between multiple components in the context of star formation.

text: In this study, we critically examine the nature of monochromatic plane-fronted waves within the framework of conformal gravity, proposing that they are, in fact, pure gauge solutions. Our work addresses the longstanding debate over the physical relevance of such wave solutions by exploring their intrinsic geometrical properties and analyzing their implications in a conformally invariant gravitational context. Employing a rigorous mathematical approach, we conducted a comprehensive examination of the field equations derived from the Weyl tensor, tailored to accommodate the monochromatic plane-fronted ansatz. Utilizing advanced techniques in differential geometry and gauge theory, our investigation delineates the conditions under which these waveforms manifest as gauge artifacts.  Our results indicate that for any monochromatic plane-fronted wave solution to be characterized as a substantive physical entity in conformal gravity, it must deviate from the pure gauge classification. However, our analysis decisively shows that within the chosen theoretical construct, such solutions inevitably resolve into gauge-dependent expressions, devoid of tangible geometric distortion or gravitational interaction.  The primary contribution of this work lies in the clarification and formal proof of the gauge nature of these waves, which offers substantial insight into the theoretical underpinnings of gravity theories that extend beyond the conventional Einsteinian framework. Our findings substantiate the hypothesis that conformally invariant gravitational models permit, but do not necessarily necessitate, observable plane-fronted gravitational wave phenomena. This study, thus, provides a foundational reference point for future research aimed at exploring the potential limitations and peculiarities of alternative gravity theories.

Deep learning models for graphs have achieved strong performance for the task
of node classification. Despite their proliferation, currently there is no
study of their robustness to adversarial attacks. Yet, in domains where they
are likely to be used, e.g. the web, adversaries are common. Can deep learning
models for graphs be easily fooled? In this work, we introduce the first study
of adversarial attacks on attributed graphs, specifically focusing on models
exploiting ideas of graph convolutions. In addition to attacks at test time, we
tackle the more challenging class of poisoning/causative attacks, which focus
on the training phase of a machine learning model. We generate adversarial
perturbations targeting the node's features and the graph structure, thus,
taking the dependencies between instances in account. Moreover, we ensure that
the perturbations remain unnoticeable by preserving important data
characteristics. To cope with the underlying discrete domain we propose an
efficient algorithm Nettack exploiting incremental computations. Our
experimental study shows that accuracy of node classification significantly
drops even when performing only few perturbations. Even more, our attacks are
transferable: the learned attacks generalize to other state-of-the-art node
classification models and unsupervised approaches, and likewise are successful
even when only limited knowledge about the graph is given.

text: We present a novel consensus-based transfer linear support vector machines (L-SVM) framework for decentralized multi-task multi-agent learning. In this framework, multiple agents collaboratively learn to perform different tasks by exchanging information and updating their models through consensus-based algorithms. The L-SVM models are adopted to represent the agents' local expertise, and a transfer learning mechanism is employed to allow agents to adapt to new tasks with minimal label data. The proposed approach leverages the strengths of both consensus algorithms and transfer learning to achieve effective and efficient learning in a decentralized and multi-agent setting. The experiments were conducted on a set of benchmark multi-robot localization datasets to evaluate the proposed method. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art decentralized multi-task learning methods in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed framework also showcases improved robustness to label noise and agent heterogeneity. The methodology involved implementing the L-SVM models using the SVC algorithm, and consensus-based updates were performed using average consensus and adaptive consensus algorithms. The transfer learning mechanism was implemented using a kernel-based method. The results of this study extend the state-of-the-art in decentralized multi-task learning by introducing a novel consensus-based transfer learning framework that effectively leverages the strengths of both consensus algorithms and transfer learning. The proposed approach holds promising applications in various decentralized multi-agent systems, including multi-robot systems, decentralized healthcare systems, and decentralized energy systems. Future research directions include exploring the applicability of the proposed approach to non-linear problems and investigating the scalability of the proposed framework in large-scale multi-agent systems.

Seismic observations have shown that a number of evolved stars exhibit
low-amplitude dipole modes, which are referred to as depressed modes. Recently,
these low amplitudes have been attributed to the presence of a strong magnetic
field in the stellar core of those stars.
  We intend to study the properties of depressed modes in evolved stars, which
is a necessary condition before concluding on the physical nature of the
mechanism responsible for the reduction of the dipole mode amplitudes.
  We perform a thorough characterization of the global seismic parameters of
depressed dipole modes and show that these modes have a mixed character. The
observation of stars showing dipole mixed modes that are depressed is
especially useful for deriving model-independent conclusions on the dipole mode
damping.
  Observations prove that depressed dipole modes in red giants are not pure
pressure modes but mixed modes. This result invalidates the hypothesis that the
depressed dipole modes result from the suppression of the oscillation in the
radiative core of the stars. Observations also show that, except for the
visibility, the seismic properties of the stars with depressed modes are
equivalent to those of normal stars.
  The mixed nature of the depressed modes in red giants and their unperturbed
global seismic parameters carry strong constraints on the physical mechanism
responsible for the damping of the oscillation in the core. This mechanism is
able to damp the oscillation in the core but cannot fully suppress it.
Moreover, it cannot modify the radiative cavity probed by the gravity component
of the mixed modes. The recent mechanism involving high magnetic field proposed
for explaining depressed modes is not compliant with the observations and
cannot be used to infer the strength and the prevalence of high magnetic fields
in red giants.

Our findings indicate that the column densities of H2 correlate positively with the observed intensities of C I(1-0) and C I(CO)(1-0), suggesting a strong link between the abundance of atomic carbon and the density of neutral hydrogen. This correlation provides valuable insights into the chemistry and physical evolution of molecular clouds, offering a method to trace H2 column density without relying on direct H2 emission lines, which are often weak or absent in many regions. text: In the context of quantum computing, trust-free verification of steering is an essential problem that ensures the security of quantum communication protocols. Steering is a quantum phenomenon in which the measurement outcomes of two parties are instantaneously connected, defying classical physics. It can lead to security loopholes if not properly controlled. In this paper, we propose a trust-free method to verify steering based on quantum state tomography and Bell's inequalities. Our method does not require any prior trust between the parties involved. First, each party performs quantum state tomography on their respective subsystems and shares the results with the other. Next, they compare the tomography data using Bell's inequalities to check for steering. This process ensures that any potential cheating by one party can be detected. We provide a theoretical analysis of our method and demonstrate its experimental feasibility using simulated data and proof-of-concept experiments. Our results show that the proposed method can effectively verify steering in a trust-free manner, providing a significant contribution to the security of quantum communication protocols. The proposed method has broad implications for quantum network security, as it allows for the verification of steering in the absence of trust, enhancing the overall security and reliability of quantum communication systems.

M giants are among the longest-period pulsating stars which is why their
studies were traditionally restricted to analyses of low-precision visual
observations, and more recently, accurate ground-based data. Here we present an
overview of M giant variability on a wide range of time-scales (hours to
years), based on analysis of thirteen quarters of Kepler long-cadence
observations (one point per every 29.4 minutes), with a total time-span of over
1000 days. About two-thirds of the sample stars have been selected from the
ASAS-North survey of the Kepler field, with the rest supplemented from a
randomly chosen M giant control sample.
  We first describe the correction of the light curves from different quarters,
which was found to be essential. We use Fourier analysis to calculate multiple
frequencies for all stars in the sample. Over 50 stars show a relatively strong
signal with a period equal to the Kepler-year and a characteristic phase
dependence across the whole field-of-view. We interpret this as a so far
unidentified systematic effect in the Kepler data. We discuss the presence of
regular patterns in the distribution of multiple periodicities and amplitudes.
In the period-amplitude plane we find that it is possible to distinguish
between solar-like oscillations and larger amplitude pulsations which are
characteristic for Mira/SR stars. This may indicate the region of the
transition between two types of oscillations as we move upward along the giant
branch.

text: This study presents the development of a Linear Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE)-optimal turbo equalizer utilizing Context Trees (CTW) for efficient implementation. The background discusses the challenges of equalizing non-linear and time-varying channels, while the objective outlines the necessity of utilizing advanced equalization techniques such as MMSE-optimal turbo equalization with Context Trees for improving signal quality in communication systems.  The methodology entails the description of CTW-based MMSE-optimal turbo equalization architecture, which consists of two iterative equalization components a soft-output equalizer and a context tree based decision feedback equalizer. The soft-output equalizer performs maximum likelihood sequence estimation utilizing a priori information, whereas the context tree based decision feedback equalizer exploits the temporal correlation of channel impairments by implementing decision feedback.  Key findings reveal an improvement of up to 3dB in Bit Error Rate (BER) performance as compared to state-of-the-art methods, attributed to the utilization of both MMSE-optimal equalization and Context Trees in the turbo equalizer design. Furthermore, a significant reduction in computational complexity is achieved through the implementation of Context Trees.  In conclusion, the proposed Linear MMSE-optimal turbo equalizer design combining CTW enables superior signal quality enhancement in communication systems, outperforming state-of-the-art methods with respect to BER performance while maintaining computational efficiency.

text: In this study, we investigate the capability of coded aperture photography to simultaneously retrieve image and depth information from a single defocused image. Traditional depth sensing techniques often require multiple images or specialized hardware, which can be resource-intensive and impractical for real-time applications. We aim to address this limitation by utilizing a coded aperture to control the light entering the camera, allowing us to mathematically reconstruct sharp images and depth maps from a single defocused capture.   We employ a novel computational approach that integrates principles of inverse optics and blind deconvolution. By analyzing the spatial patterns encoded within the aperture, we develop an algorithm capable of estimating both the latent sharp image and the scene depth map from its defocused counterpart. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in both the quality of reconstructed images and the accuracy of depth estimation compared to baseline methods. We validate our approach through extensive testing on synthetic and real-world datasets, achieving superior performance in terms of depth accuracy and visual fidelity.   The insights gained from our research contribute to the fields of computer vision and computational photography, highlighting the potential of coded aperture systems for efficient imaging solutions. We conclude that our methodology presents a promising alternative for depth extraction in scenarios where obtaining multiple focus images is unfeasible, opening avenues for advancements in various applications such as robotics, augmented reality, and autonomous vehicles.

An integrated mechanical model for fiber-laden membranes is presented and
representative predictions of relevance to cellulose ordering and orientation
in the plant cell wall are presented. The model describes nematic liquid
crystalline self-assembly of rigid fibers on an arbitrarily curved fluid
membrane. The mechanics of the fluid membrane is described by the Helfrich
bending-torsion model, the fiber self-assembly is described by the 2D Landau-de
Gennes quadrupolar Q-tensor order parameter model, and the fiber-membrane
interactions (inspired by an extension of the 2D Maier-Saupe model to curved
surfaces) include competing curvo-philic (curvature-seeking) and curvo-phobic
(curvature-avoiding) effects. Analysis of the free energy reveals three fiber
orientation regimes: (a) along the major curvature, (b) along the minor
curvature, (c) away from the principal curvatures, according to the competing
curvo-philic and curvo-phobic interactions. The derived shape equation (normal
stress balance) now includes curvature-nematic ordering contributions, with
both bending and torsion renormalizations. Integration of the shape and nematic
order equations gives a complete model whose solution describes the coupled
membrane shape/fiber order state. Applications to cylindrical membranes,
relevant to the plant cell wall, shows how growth decreases the fiber order
parameter and moves the fiber's director from the axial direction towards the
azimuthal orientation, eventually leading to a state of stress predicted by
pure membranes. The ubiquitous 54.7o cellulose fibril orientation in a
cylindrical plant cell wall is shown to be predicted by the preset model when
the ratio of curvo-phobic and curvo-philic interactions is in the range of the
cylinder radius.

In multiple testing problems, where a large number of hypotheses are tested
simultaneously, false discovery rate (FDR) control can be achieved with the
well-known Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, which adapts to the amount of signal
present in the data. Many modifications of this procedure have been proposed to
improve power in scenarios where the hypotheses are organized into groups or
into a hierarchy, as well as other structured settings. Here we introduce
SABHA, the "structure-adaptive Benjamini-Hochberg algorithm", as a
generalization of these adaptive testing methods. SABHA incorporates prior
information about any pre-determined type of structure in the pattern of
locations of the signals and nulls within the list of hypotheses, to reweight
the p-values in a data-adaptive way. This raises the power by making more
discoveries in regions where signals appear to be more common. Our main
theoretical result proves that SABHA controls FDR at a level that is at most
slightly higher than the target FDR level, as long as the adaptive weights are
constrained sufficiently so as not to overfit too much to the
data-interestingly, the excess FDR can be related to the Rademacher complexity
or Gaussian width of the class from which we choose our data-adaptive weights.
We apply this general framework to various structured settings, including
ordered, grouped, and low total variation structures, and get the bounds on FDR
for each specific setting. We also examine the empirical performance of SABHA
on fMRI activity data and on gene/drug response data, as well as on simulated
data.

text: The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has provided ample opportunities to explore the properties of top quarks, the heaviest elementary particle in the Standard Model of particle physics. In this study, we report our analysis of high p_T top quarks produced in proton-proton collisions at sqrt{s} = 13 TeV, using data recorded by the ATLAS detector. To enhance the sensitivity to high p_T top quarks, we employ a kinematic selection strategy, utilizing the reconstructed transverse momentum and rapidity of the top quarks. We observe an excess of events in the high p_T top quark region, which is not fully explained by the expected background contributions. A fit to the observed data with a signal plus background model yields a post-trial p-value of 0.019, indicative of a potential new physics signal. We explore the implications of this excess by performing a series of hypothesis tests and exclusion limits. Our analysis suggests that the excess may be consistent with a new heavy resonance decaying to a top quark and a W boson, with a mass between 1 and 3 TeV. However, more data and further investigations are required to confirm the validity of this interpretation. In conclusion, we present a preliminary analysis of high p_T top quarks at the Large Hadron Collider, which uncovers an intriguing excess of events and opens up new avenues for exploring new physics beyond the Standard Model. The one-step replica symmetry breaking (RSB) is used to study a
two-sublattice fermionic infinite-range Ising spin glass (SG) model in a
transverse field $\Gamma$. The problem is formulated in a Grassmann path
integral formalism within the static approximation. In this model, a parallel
magnetic field $H$ breaks the symmetry of the sublattices. It destroys the
antiferromagnetic (AF) order, but it can favor the nonergodic mixed phase
(SG+AF) characterizing an asymmetric RSB region. In this region,
intra-sublattice disordered interactions $V$ increase the difference between
the RSB solutions of each sublattice. The freezing temperature shows a higher
increase with $H$ when $V$ enhances. A discontinue phase transition from the
replica symmetry (RS) solution to the RSB solution can appear with the presence
of an intra-sublattice ferromagnetic average coupling. The $\Gamma$ field
introduces a quantum spin flip mechanism that suppresses the magnetic orders
leading them to quantum critical points. Results suggest that the quantum
effects are not able to restore the RS solution. However, in the asymmetric RSB
region, $\Gamma$ can produce a stable RS solution at any finite temperature for
a particular sublattice while the other sublattice still presents RSB solution
for the special case in which only the intra-sublattice spins couple with
disordered interactions.

Fluorescent and luminescent gene reporters allow us to dynamically quantify
changes in molecular species concentration over time on the single cell level.
The mathematical modeling of their interaction through multivariate dynamical
models requires the development of effective statistical methods to calibrate
such models against available data. Given the prevalence of stochasticity and
noise in biochemical systems inference for stochastic models is of special
interest. In this paper we present a simple and computationally efficient
algorithm for the estimation of biochemical kinetic parameters from gene
reporter data. We use the linear noise approximation to model biochemical
reactions through a stochastic dynamic model which essentially approximates a
diffusion model by an ordinary differential equation model with an
appropriately defined noise process. An explicit formula for the likelihood
function can be derived allowing for computationally efficient parameter
estimation. The proposed algorithm is embedded in a Bayesian framework and
inference is performed using Markov chain Monte Carlo. The major advantage of
the method is that in contrast to the more established diffusion approximation
based methods the computationally costly methods of data augmentation are not
necessary. Our approach also allows for unobserved variables and measurement
error. The application of the method to both simulated and experimental data
shows that the proposed methodology provides a useful alternative to diffusion
approximation based methods.

We present a local sample (z<0.15) of 280 Star-Forming Compact Groups (SFCGs)
of galaxies identified in the ultraviolet Galaxy Evolution EXplorer (GALEX)
All-sky Imaging Survey (AIS). So far, just one prototypical example of SFCG,
the Blue Infalling Group, has been studied in detail in the Local Universe. The
sample of SFCGs is mainly the result of applying a Friends-of-Friends group
finder in the space of celestial coordinates with a maximum linking-length of
1.5 arcmin and choosing groups with a minimum number of four members of bright
UV-emitting 17<FUV<20.5 sources (mostly galaxies) from the GALEX/AIS catalogue.
The result from the search are 280 galaxy groups composed by 226, 39, 11 and 4
groups of four, five, six and seven bright ultraviolet (UV) members,
respectively. Only 59 of these 280 newly identified SFCGs have a previous
catalogued group counterpart. Group redshifts are available for at least one
member in 75% of the SFCGs, and over 40% of the SFCGs have redshifts measured
for two or more galaxies. Twenty-six of the SFCGs appear to be located in the
infalling regions of clusters with known redshift. The SFCG sample presents a
combination of properties different from the group samples studied up to now,
such as low velocity dispersions of $\sigma_{\rm{}l-o-s}$$\sim$120 km/s, small
crossing-times ($H_{0}$$t_{c}$$\sim$0.05) and high star-formation content (95%
of star-forming galaxies). This points to the SFCGs being in an evolutionary
stage distinct from those groups selected in the optical and near-infrared
ranges (see Fig. 6).

Very massive stars, 100 times heavier than the sun, are rare. It is not yet
known whether such stars can form in isolation or only in star clusters. The
answer to this question is of fundamental importance. The central region of our
Galaxy is ideal for investigating very massive stars and clusters located in
the same environment. We used archival infrared images to investigate the
surroundings of apparently isolated massive stars presently known in the
Galactic Center. We find that two such isolated massive stars display apparent
bow shocks and hence may be "runaways" from their birthplace. Thus, some
isolated massive stars in the Galactic Center region might have been born in
star clusters known in this region. However, no bow shock is detected around
the isolated star WR102ka (Peony nebula star), which is one of the most massive
and luminous stars in the Galaxy. This star is located at the center of an
associated dusty circumstellar nebula. To study whether a star cluster may be
"hidden" in the surroundings of WR102ka, to obtain new and better spectra of
this star, and to measure its radial velocity, we obtained observations with
the integral-field spectrograph SINFONI at the ESO's Very Large Telescope
(VLT). Our observations confirm that WR102ka is one of the most massive stars
in the Galaxy and reveal that this star is not associated with a star cluster.
We suggest that WR102ka has been born in relative isolation, outside of any
massive star cluster.

We calculate the dynamic structure factor S(q,omega) of a one-dimensional
(1D) interacting Bose gas confined in a harmonic trap. The effective
interaction depends on the strength of the confinement enforcing the 1D motion
of atoms; interaction may be further enhanced by superimposing an optical
lattice on the trap potential. In the compressible state, we find that the
smooth variation of the gas density around the trap center leads to softening
of the singular behavior of S(q,omega) at Lieb-1 mode compared to the behavior
predicted for homogeneous 1D systems. Nevertheless, the density-averaged
response remains a non-analytic function of q and omega at Lieb-1 mode in the
limit of weak trap confinement. The exponent of the power-law non-analyticity
is modified due to the inhomogeneity in a universal way, and thus, bears
unambiguously the information about the (homogeneous) Lieb-Liniger model. A
strong optical lattice causes formation of Mott phases. Deep in the Mott
regime, we predict a semi-circular peak in S(q,\omega) centered at the on-site
repulsion energy, omega=U. Similar peaks of smaller amplitudes exist at
multiples of U as well. We explain the suppression of the dynamic response with
entering into the Mott regime, observed recently by D. Clement et al., Phys.
Rev. Lett. v. 102, p. 155301 (2009), based on an f-sum rule for the
Bose-Hubbard model.
