We investigate thermodynamics constructed on different background reference
spacetimes for squashed Kaluza-Klein (SqKK) black hole and electrically charged
black string in five-dimensional Einstein-Maxwell system. Two spacetimes are
possible to be reference spacetimes giving finite gravitational classical
actions: one is four-dimensional Minkowski times a circle and the other is the
KK monopole. The boundary of the SqKK black hole can not be matched perfectly
to that of the former reference spacetime because of the difference in
topology. However, the resultant classical action coincides with that
calculated by the counterterm subtraction scheme. The boundary of the KK
monopole has the same topology with that of the SqKK black hole and can be
matched to the boundary of the black hole perfectly. The resultant action takes
different value from the result given by using the former reference spacetime.
After a brief review of thermodynamic quantities of the black hole solutions,
we calculate thermodynamic potentials relevant for several thermodynamic
environments. The most stable state is different for each environment: For
example, the KK monopole is the most stable state in isothermal environment
with fixed gravitational tension. On the other hand, when the size of the
extra-dimension is fixed, the Minkowski times a circle is the most stable. It
is shown that these two spacetimes can be reference spacetimes of the
five-dimensional black string.

text: We present an analytical and numerical investigation on the stability and instability of nonlinear defect states in the context of coupled mode equations. Our work aims to address the problem of understanding the dynamic behavior of nonlinear defect states in coupled mode systems. Through our study, we have obtained results that shed light on the conditions under which these states exhibit stability or instability. By employing a combination of analytical techniques and numerical simulations, we demonstrate how the nonlinear interactions within the coupled mode equations can lead to the emergence of stable or unstable defect states. The key ideas in our research revolve around the characterization of the bifurcation points that delineate the transition between stable and unstable behavior in the system. Our methodology involves analyzing the linear stability of the defect states and then verifying these findings through numerical simulations. The results highlight the intricate interplay between nonlinear effects and coupling in determining the stability properties of defect states in coupled mode systems. This study contributes to the understanding of the complex dynamics of nonlinear waves in coupled systems and provides valuable insights for the design and control of such systems in various engineering and physical applications.

The class of Double Period Variables (DPVs) consists of close interacting
binaries, with a characteristic long period that is an order of magnitude
longer than the corresponding orbital period, many of them with a
characteristic ratio of about 3.5x10^1. We consider here the possibility that
the accretion flow is modulated as a result of a magnetic dynamo cycle. Due to
the short binary separations, we expect the rotation of the donor star to be
synchronized with the rotation of the binary due to tidal locking. We here
present a model to estimate the dynamo number and the resulting relation
between the activity cycle length and the orbital period, as well as an
estimate for the modulation of the mass transfer rate. The latter is based on
Applegate's scenario, implying cyclic changes in the radius of the donor star
and thus in the mass transfer rate as a result of magnetic activity. Our model
is applied to a sample of 17 systems with known physical parameters, 10 also
with known orbital periods. In spite of the uncertainties of our simplified
framework, the results show a reasonable agreement, indicating that a dynamo
interpretation is potentially feasible. At the same time, we note that the
orbital period variations resulting from Applegate's model are sufficiently
small to be consistent with the data. We conclude that both larger samples with
known physical parameters as well as potential direct probes of the magnetism
of the donor star, including cold spots as well as polarization, will be
valuable to further constrain the nature of these systems.

We consider deterministic distributed communication in wireless ad hoc
networks of identical weak devices under the SINR model without predefined
infrastructure. Most algorithmic results in this model rely on various
additional features or capabilities, e.g., randomization, access to geographic
coordinates, power control, carrier sensing with various precision of
measurements, and/or interference cancellation. We study a pure scenario, when
no such properties are available. As a general tool, we develop a deterministic
distributed clustering algorithm. Our solution relies on a new type of
combinatorial structures (selectors), which might be of independent interest.
Using the clustering, we develop a deterministic distributed local broadcast
algorithm accomplishing this task in $O(\Delta \log^*N \log N)$ rounds, where
$\Delta$ is the density of the network. To the best of our knowledge, this is
the first solution in pure scenario which is only polylog$(n)$ away from the
universal lower bound $\Omega(\Delta)$, valid also for scenarios with
randomization and other features. Therefore, none of these features
substantially helps in performing the local broadcast task. Using clustering,
we also build a deterministic global broadcast algorithm that terminates within
$O(D(\Delta + \log^* N) \log N)$ rounds, where $D$ is the diameter of the
network. This result is complemented by a lower bound $\Omega(D
\Delta^{1-1/\alpha})$, where $\alpha > 2$ is the path-loss parameter of the
environment. This lower bound shows that randomization or knowledge of own
location substantially help (by a factor polynomial in $\Delta$) in the global
broadcast. Therefore, unlike in the case of local broadcast, some additional
model features may help in global broadcast.

The dramatic hard-soft spectral transition in Black Hole Binaries is
important as it is associated with the collapse of the jet and with the
strongest low frequency QPOs. These transition spectra (intermediate and very
high state: VHS) are complex, with soft but distinctly non-thermal
Comptonisation which merges smoothly into the disc emission. Here we develop a
physical model for the accretion flow which can accommodate all these features,
with an outer standard disc, which can make a transition to an energetically
coupled disc-corona region, and make a further transition to a hot inner flow
which can be radiatively inefficient if required. The code explicitly uses
fully relativistic emissivity (Novikov-Thorne), and all Comptonisation is
calculated with a hybrid (thermal and non-thermal) electron distribution. We
fit this to a VHS spectrum from GX 339-4. We show that the complex continuum
curvature produced by a hybrid electron distribution is enough to remove the
strong constraint on black hole spin derived from reflection using simpler
Comptonisation models. More fundamentally, we show that the VHS cannot be fit
with the same Novikov-Thorne emissivity which can fit the disc dominated
spectrum but instead requires that the inner flow is somewhat radiatively
inefficient. This is consistent with an accretion powered jet, but simultaneous
radio data show that the jet has already collapsed at the time of our data.
Instead, it could point to truncation of the inner flow at radii larger than
the innermost stable circular orbit, as predicted by the Lense-Thirring QPO
models.

text: The pursuit of a comprehensive understanding of particle physics has reignited interest in beyond the Standard Model scenarios, particularly Twin Higgs models. These models, rooted in the framework of naturalness, aim to provide solutions to the hierarchy problem while predicting new physical phenomena. This research paper investigates precision tests and fine-tuning measures within Twin Higgs models to evaluate their viability as a candidate for new physics. The objective is to dissect the implications of current experimental data and theoretical constructs on the parameters of these models, particularly focusing on their impact on Higgs properties and production channels. A systematic methodology is employed, integrating computational simulations and analytical calculations to assess deviations in observables compared to the Standard Model, with a specific emphasis on precision measurements of Higgs boson interactions and decay processes. Key findings reveal that certain regions of the model parameter space remain compatible with existing experimental results, while others face constraints from measurements such as those from the Large Hadron Collider. Furthermore, the investigation highlights the delicate balance required for fine-tuning these models to align with empirical data while preserving naturalness. In conclusion, this study underscores the importance of precision tests in constraining Twin Higgs models and demonstrates that while some scenarios retain compatibility with current theories, further experimental scrutiny is essential to confirm their validity in the context of a profound new physics landscape.

text: Distributed data mining (DDM) in peer-to-peer (P2P) networks represents a rapidly evolving field that addresses the challenges of effectively analyzing large-scale, decentralized datasets. This survey aims to consolidate current advancements and identify emerging trends in the domain of DDM within P2P architectures. The motivation behind this study stems from the increasing reliance on P2P networks for distributed storage and computation, necessitating innovative data mining strategies that bypass traditional centralized approaches. Through an extensive literature review, this research categorizes contemporary DDM techniques based on their architectural models, data partitioning methods, and mining algorithms employed. Key methodologies explored include collaborative filtering, collective model learning, and federated averaging, with a focus on their scalability, efficiency, and fault tolerance in dynamic P2P environments. The analysis reveals that while recent methods enhance data privacy and computational load distribution, they face challenges concerning resource heterogeneity and coordination overhead. Notably, the integration of machine learning techniques and blockchain technology has shown promising potential in enhancing data integrity and security. This survey concludes by outlining prospective directions for future research, emphasizing the need for robust frameworks capable of adaptive learning, peer incentivization, and overcoming network latencies. By providing a comprehensive overview of DDM practices in P2P networks, this work serves as a foundation for further investigation into sophisticated, decentralized data analysis solutions.

We present the second installment of GOSSS, a massive spectroscopic survey of
Galactic O stars, based on new homogeneous, high signal-to-noise ratio, R ~
2500 digital observations from both hemispheres selected from the Galactic
O-Star Catalog (GOSC). In this paper we include bright stars and other objects
drawn mostly from the first version of GOSC, all of them south of delta = -20
degrees, for a total number of 258 O stars. We also revise the northern sample
of paper I to provide the full list of spectroscopically classified Galactic O
stars complete to B = 8, bringing the total number of published GOSSS stars to
448. Extensive sequences of exceptional objects are given, including the early
Of/WN, O Iafpe, Ofc, ON/OC, Onfp, Of?p, and Oe types, as well as
double/triple-lined spectroscopic binaries. The new spectral subtype O9.2 is
also discussed. The magnitude and spatial distributions of the observed sample
are analyzed. We also present new results from OWN, a multi-epoch
high-resolution spectroscopic survey coordinated with GOSSS that is assembling
the largest sample of Galactic spectroscopic massive binaries ever attained.
The OWN data combined with additional information on spectroscopic and visual
binaries from the literature indicate that only a very small fraction (if any)
of the stars with masses above 15-20 M_Sol are born as single systems. In the
future we will publish the rest of the GOSSS survey, which is expected to
include over 1000 Galactic O stars.

We analyze the effective actions of anomalous models in which a
four-dimensional version of the Green-Schwarz mechanism is invoked for the
cancellation of the anomalies, and we compare it with those models in which
gauge invariance is restored by the presence of a Wess-Zumino term. Some issues
concerning an apparent violation of unitarity of the mechanism, which requires
Dolgov-Zakharov poles, are carefully examined, using a class of amplitudes
studied in the past by Bouchiat-Iliopoulos-Meyer (BIM), and elaborating on
previous studies. In the Wess-Zumino case we determine explicitly the unitarity
bound using a realistic model of intersecting branes (the Madrid model) by
studying the corresponding BIM amplitudes. This is shown to depend
significantly on the St\"uckelberg mass and on the coupling of the extra
anomalous gauge bosons and allows one to identify Standard-Model-like regions
(which are anomaly-free) from regions where the growth of certain amplitudes is
dominated by the anomaly, separated by an inflection point which could be
studied at the LHC. The bound can even be around 5-10 TeV's for a $Z'$ mass
around 1 TeV and varies sensitively with the anomalous coupling. The results
for the WZ case are quite general and apply to all the models in which an
axion-like interaction is introduced as a generalization of the Peccei-Quinn
mechanism, with a gauged axion.

text: The Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Host Galaxy Legacy Survey (SGRGLS-I) represents a systematic study aimed at identifying and characterizing the host galaxies of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). This survey focuses on selecting and analyzing a representative sample of GRB host galaxies, with the primary objective of understanding their properties, such as stellar populations and star formation histories, in relation to the environments they inhabit.  To achieve this, the selection process involved targeting GRBs detected by the Swift satellite within a specific time frame, ensuring that the sample was diverse across different redshifts and energy bands. The methodology included detailed optical and near-infrared observations, spectroscopic data, and photometric measurements from various telescopes to accurately determine the redshifts and physical properties of the host galaxies.  Key findings from the study include the identification of a significant number of distant GRB host galaxies at redshifts up to z ≈ 6, revealing a variety of galaxy types including star-forming systems and quiescent galaxies. The redshift distribution shows a bimodal pattern, with peaks corresponding to both early and late cosmic epochs, indicating the presence of a wide range of host galaxy environments and evolutionary stages.  Conclusively, SGRGLS-I provides valuable insights into the connection between GRBs and their host galaxies, contributing to our understanding of cosmic star formation and evolution over cosmic time.

Our approach includes optimizing communication protocols, employing lightweight encryption algorithms, and utilizing energy-efficient RFID tags. The results demonstrate a notable reduction in both hardware and operational expenses, making these schemes viable for a broad range of applications such as supply chain management, access control, and asset tracking. text: This study focuses on investigating the relationship between the ages of young stars and their lithium abundances, shedding light on the early stages of stellar evolution. In the context of the search for associations containing young stars, understanding the lithium content of these stars is crucial for determining their ages and understanding their place in the stellar population.  Previous research has shown that lithium abundance is a key indicator of stellar age, with younger stars exhibiting higher lithium content. However, the precise relationship between lithium abundance and age remains unclear, particularly for young stars with ages below 100 million years. To address this knowledge gap, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of lithium abundances in a sample of young stars from various associations.  Our sample consists of 150 young stars with ages ranging from 10 to 500 million years, obtained from the literature and observed with high-resolution spectroscopy. We have applied a combination of spectroscopic and photometric methods to determine the lithium abundance of these stars, utilizing the Li I 670.8 nm and Li I 1025.3 nm spectral lines.  The key findings of this study reveal a significant correlation between lithium abundance and age, with younger stars exhibiting higher lithium content. However, our results also indicate that the relationship between lithium abundance and age is more complex than previously thought, with a non-linear trend observed for ages below 100 million years. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the early stages of stellar evolution and the formation of young star associations.

text: Indonesia is highly susceptible to natural disasters, particularly earthquakes, due to its geographical position within the Pacific Ring of Fire. Understanding how to improve decision-making systems for earthquake disaster management is crucial for minimizing human loss and infrastructural damage. This study aims to evaluate existing decision-making frameworks and propose a comprehensive system tailored for Indonesia's unique contexts. Methodologically, we employed a mixed-method approach involving qualitative interviews with disaster management officials and quantitative analysis of previous earthquake responses across various provinces. We assessed the efficacy of current protocols, stakeholder cooperation, and community preparedness. Key findings reveal significant gaps in the existing frameworks, particularly in real-time communication and coordination among agencies. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of integrating local knowledge and technology in the decision-making process, which can enhance responsiveness and situational awareness during seismic events. The proposed decision-making system incorporates a multi-tiered approach, combining technological tools such as GIS and AI with grassroots involvement to ensure swift and effective disaster responses. In conclusion, the research underscores the necessity for a tailored decision-making system that not only leverages technology but also fosters collaboration among governmental and non-governmental entities. Implementing these recommendations could significantly enhance Indonesia's resilience to earthquake-related disasters, ultimately saving lives and reducing the economic impact on affected communities.

text: In this work, we explore the limits of context utilization in enhancing object detection methodologies. Our primary objective is to investigate how contextual information—such as spatial relationships, object co-occurrences, and scene semantics—can be integrated into contemporary detection frameworks to improve accuracy and robustness. We conduct a series of experiments utilizing state-of-the-art deep learning models, systematically varying the contextual inputs to assess their impact on detection performance across diverse datasets.   Our results demonstrate a significant enhancement in detection accuracy when contextual cues are employed, particularly in challenging scenarios involving occluded or partially visible objects. We quantify the improvement across different object classes and present an analysis of the diminishing returns when excessive context is introduced. Additionally, we showcase how specific contextual features can lead to a reduction in false positives, emphasizing the importance of relevance in context selection.   We implement a hybrid model that combines traditional object detection algorithms with contextual embeddings, utilizing frameworks such as Faster R-CNN and YOLO, and observe improved performance metrics compared to baseline models. Through comprehensive ablation studies, we identify key contextual elements that contribute most effectively to detection accuracy. Our findings suggest a paradigm shift in object detection research, advocating for the integration of contextual reasoning as a fundamental component rather than a supplementary aspect. Ultimately, we provide insights and guidelines for future research directions that prioritize context-driven approaches in object detection systems.

The Dulmage--Mendelsohn decomposition (or the DM-decomposition) gives a
unique partition of the vertex set of a bipartite graph reflecting the
structure of all the maximum matchings therein. A bipartite graph is said to be
DM-irreducible if its DM-decomposition consists of a single component.
  In this paper, we focus on the problem of making a given bipartite graph
DM-irreducible by adding edges. When the input bipartite graph is balanced
(i.e., both sides have the same number of vertices) and has a perfect matching,
this problem is equivalent to making a directed graph strongly connected by
adding edges, for which the minimum number of additional edges was
characterized by Eswaran and Tarjan (1976).
  We give a general solution to this problem, which is divided into three
parts. We first show that our problem can be formulated as a special case of a
general framework of covering supermodular functions, which was introduced by
Frank and Jord\'an (1995) to investigate the directed connectivity augmentation
problem. Secondly, when the input graph is not balanced, the problem is solved
via matroid intersection. This result can be extended to the minimum cost
version in which the addition of an edge gives rise to an individual cost.
Thirdly, for balanced input graphs, we devise a combinatorial algorithm that
finds a minimum number of additional edges to attain the DM-irreducibility,
while the minimum cost version of this problem is NP-hard. These results also
lead to min-max characterizations of the minimum number, which generalize the
result of Eswaran and Tarjan.

text: X-ray bright elliptical galaxies are among the most luminous objects in the universe, yet their environments remain poorly understood. Recent observations have revealed that these galaxies exhibit steepening mass profiles, which challenge the traditional hierarchical model of galaxy formation. The dark matter halo, a crucial component of these galaxies, is also poorly constrained. This study aims to investigate the relationship between the mass profile of X-ray bright elliptical galaxies and their environment, with a particular focus on the role of dark matter.  Our research employs a combination of hydrodynamical simulations and observational data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory to investigate the mass profile of X-ray bright elliptical galaxies. We find that these galaxies exhibit a steepening mass profile, with a concentration factor of approximately 10, which is significantly higher than that predicted by the traditional hierarchical model. Furthermore, our simulations reveal that the dark matter halo plays a crucial role in shaping the mass profile of these galaxies, with the halo's mass distribution influencing the galaxy's gravitational potential.  Our key findings suggest that X-ray bright elliptical galaxies are surrounded by a complex network of dark matter filaments, which provide the necessary gravitational scaffolding for galaxy formation. We also find that the environment of these galaxies is characterized by a high density of dark matter, which influences the galaxy's mass profile. Our results have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution and the role of dark matter in shaping the mass profiles of X-ray bright elliptical galaxies.

Science, especially large-scale basic research, is a collaborative endeavor,
often drawing on the skills of people from a wide variety of disciplines. These
people include not just scientists, but also administrators, engineers, and
many others. Fermilab, a Department of Energy National Laboratory and the
United States' premier particle physics laboratory, exemplifies this kind of
research; many of its high-energy physics experiments involve hundreds of
collaborators from all over the world. The Fermilab Archives seeks to document
the history of the lab and the unique scientific research its staff and
visitors perform. Adequately documenting the lab's work often requires us to go
far beyond things like the writings and correspondence of scientists to also
capture the administrative and social histories of the experiments and the
context in which they were performed. At Fermilab, we have sought to capture
these elements of the lab's activities through an oral history program that
focuses on support staff as well as physicists and collection development
choices that recognize the importance of records documenting the cultural life
of the lab. These materials are not merely supplementary, but rather essential
documentation of the many types of labor that go into the planning and
execution of an experiment or the construction of an accelerator and the
context in which this work is performed.

text: Injective sets play a crucial role in various branches of mathematics, including topology, algebra, and logic. An injective set is a set of points in a vector space such that every distinct pair of points has distinct images under a linear mapping. The study of injective sets was initiated by P.S. Alexandroff in 1931, who asked whether there exist infinite-dimensional vector spaces that contain only finitely many injective sets. This question, known as the Alexandroff problem, has been an open research problem for nearly a century.  The objective of this paper is to explore the Alexandroff problem and provide new insights into the existence and nonexistence of injective sets in infinite-dimensional vector spaces. We use different methods and techniques, such as topological, geometric, and combinatorial, to analyze various classes of vector spaces, including normed spaces, Hilbert spaces, and Banach spaces.  Our methodology includes a thorough literature review and the development of new results based on existing techniques and results. We introduce several classes of injective sets, including finite-dimensional injective sets, co-injective sets, and injective sets related to certain topological properties, and present conditions for their existence or nonexistence in different types of vector spaces.  Our key findings provide both positive and negative answers to the Alexandroff problem. We construct examples of infinite-dimensional vector spaces with uncountably many injective sets, as well as examples of vector spaces with no injective sets at all. Our results highlight the complexities and subtleties of the injective set problem, and suggest directions for future research.  In conclusion, this paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the Alexandroff problem, exploring the existence and nonexistence of injective sets in infinite-dimensional vector spaces using various methods and techniques. Our findings shed new light on this long-standing problem and open up new avenues for further research.

We investigate the valley depolarization dynamics and valley Hall effect of
exciton due to the electron-hole exchange interaction in mono- and bilayer
MoS$_2$ by solving the kinetic spin Bloch equations. The effect of the exciton
energy spectra by the electron-hole exchange interaction is explicitly
considered. For the valley depolarization dynamics, in the monolayer MoS$_2$,
it is found that in the strong scattering regime, the conventional motional
narrowing picture is no longer valid, and a novel valley depolarization channel
is opened. For the valley Hall effect of exciton, in both the mono- and bilayer
MoS$_2$, with the exciton equally pumped in the K and K' valleys, the system
can evolve into the equilibrium state where the valley polarization is parallel
to the effective magnetic field due to the exchange interaction. With the drift
of this equilibrium state by applied uniaxial strain, the exchange interaction
can induce the {\it momentum-dependent} valley/photoluminesence polarization,
which leads to the valley/photoluminesence Hall current. Specifically, the
disorder strength dependence of the valley Hall conductivity is revealed. In
the strong scattering regime, the valley Hall conductivity decreases with the
increase of the disorder strength; whereas in the weak scattering regime, it
saturates to a constant, which can be much larger than the one in Fermi system
due to the absence of the Pauli blocking.

The Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) - one of
the Sloan Digital Sky Survey III programs -- is using near-infrared spectra of
$\sim 100,000$ red giant branch star candidates to study the structure of the
Milky Way. In the course of the survey, APOGEE also acquires spectra of hot
field stars to serve as telluric calibrators for the primary science targets.
We report the serendipitous discovery of two rare, fast-rotating B stars of the
$\sigma$ Ori E type among those blue field stars observed during the first year
of APOGEE operations. Both of the discovered stars display the spectroscopic
signatures of the rigidly rotating magnetospheres (RRM) common to this class of
highly-magnetized ($B \sim 10$ kiloGauss) stars, increasing the number of known
RRM stars by $\sim 10 \%$. One (HD 345439) is a main-sequence B star with
unusually strong He absorption (similar to $\sigma$ Ori E), while the other (HD
23478) fits a "He-normal" B3IV classification. We combine the APOGEE discovery
spectra with other optical and near-infrared spectra of these two stars, and of
$\sigma$ Ori E itself, to show how near-infrared spectroscopy can be a uniquely
powerful tool for discovering more of these rare objects, which may show
little/no RRM signatures in their optical spectra. We discuss the potential for
further discovery of $\sigma$ Ori E type stars, as well as the implications of
our discoveries for the population of these objects and insights into their
origin and evolution.

This paper addresses the problem of single image super-resolution (SR), which
consists of recovering a high resolution image from its blurred, decimated and
noisy version. The existing algorithms for single image SR use different
strategies to handle the decimation and blurring operators. In addition to the
traditional first-order gradient methods, recent techniques investigate
splitting-based methods dividing the SR problem into up-sampling and
deconvolution steps that can be easily solved. Instead of following this
splitting strategy, we propose to deal with the decimation and blurring
operators simultaneously by taking advantage of their particular properties in
the frequency domain, leading to a new fast SR approach. Specifically, an
analytical solution can be obtained and implemented efficiently for the
Gaussian prior or any other regularization that can be formulated into an
$\ell_2$-regularized quadratic model, i.e., an $\ell_2$-$\ell_2$ optimization
problem. Furthermore, the flexibility of the proposed SR scheme is shown
through the use of various priors/regularizations, ranging from generic image
priors to learning-based approaches. In the case of non-Gaussian priors, we
show how the analytical solution derived from the Gaussian case can be embedded
intotraditional splitting frameworks, allowing the computation cost of existing
algorithms to be decreased significantly. Simulation results conducted on
several images with different priors illustrate the effectiveness of our fast
SR approach compared with the existing techniques.

Though switched dynamical systems have shown great utility in modeling a
variety of physical phenomena, the construction of an optimal control of such
systems has proven difficult since it demands some type of optimal mode
scheduling. In this paper, we devise an algorithm for the computation of an
optimal control of constrained nonlinear switched dynamical systems. The
control parameter for such systems include a continuous-valued input and
discrete-valued input, where the latter corresponds to the mode of the switched
system that is active at a particular instance in time. Our approach, which we
prove converges to local minimizers of the constrained optimal control problem,
first relaxes the discrete-valued input, then performs traditional optimal
control, and then projects the constructed relaxed discrete-valued input back
to a pure discrete-valued input by employing an extension to the classical
Chattering Lemma that we prove. We extend this algorithm by formulating a
computationally implementable algorithm which works by discretizing the time
interval over which the switched dynamical system is defined. Importantly, we
prove that this implementable algorithm constructs a sequence of points by
recursive application that converge to the local minimizers of the original
constrained optimal control problem. Four simulation experiments are included
to validate the theoretical developments.

text: The study of heavy sterile neutrinos, which are hypothesized extensions to the Standard Model, has significant implications for both particle physics and cosmology, particularly in understanding the origins of neutrino masses and the asymmetry between matter and antimatter in the universe. This research investigates the production of heavy sterile neutrinos from vector boson decay at electroweak temperatures, a process that can potentially occur in the early universe. Utilizing theoretical models combining elements of quantum field theory and particle cosmology, we analyze the decay rates and branching ratios of vector bosons, specifically W and Z bosons, in environments characterized by electroweak-scale temperatures. Our methodology involves the application of thermal field theoretical techniques to calculate the expected production rates of these neutrinos within a primordial plasma.    Key findings indicate that under the conditions present at electroweak transition temperatures, sterile neutrino production is significantly enhanced due to thermal effects, which alter the kinematic thresholds and decay widths of the vector bosons. These findings suggest that the sterile neutrinos may attain observable abundances, offering a viable production mechanism accessible within cosmological observables. Moreover, our results provide a window into potential detection strategies through indirect measurements, such as observing deviations in expected neutrino fluxes or in cosmic microwave background anisotropies that align with sterile neutrino scenarios. Overall, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of how new physics beyond the Standard Model, mediated by heavy sterile neutrinos, could manifest and influence early-universe dynamics, offering critical insights into future experimental investigation and theoretical explorations.

text: This study presents the results of a blind single pulse search conducted on the millisecond radio sky, aimed at detecting transient phenomena. Results indicate the detection of several transient events, which were characterized by their rapid rise and decay times, typical of single pulses. These findings contribute to our understanding of transient phenomena in the interstellar medium and expand the known population of radio transients. Key methodologies include signal processing techniques to isolate candidate single pulses from background noise and statistical methods to assess the significance of detected events.

text: In this study, we investigate the natural realization of the Higgs boson mass hierarchy in supersymmetric models and the resulting signatures of R-hadrons at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We begin by considering the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) and propose a solution based on a renormalization group approach to naturally generate the required mass splitting between the lightest Higgs boson (h) and the other supersymmetric particles. Subsequently, we explore the implications of this mass hierarchy on the production and decay of R-hadrons in the context of the MSSM. Our analysis reveals that the high mass R-hadron spectrum can lead to striking signatures at the LHC, such as charged R-hadron tracks with long lifetimes and high transverse momenta, along with missing energy and jets. Furthermore, we examine how the measurement of these signatures can be used to probe various aspects of supersymmetry, including the presence of new physics beyond the MSSM and the nature of the R-parity violation. Overall, our work provides a compelling framework for understanding the interplay between the Higgs boson mass hierarchy and the search for new physics at the LHC through R-hadron signatures.

text: The Higgs boson discovery at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) marked a significant milestone in our understanding of the Standard Model of particle physics. However, the Higgs boson's properties and interactions remain poorly understood, and its discovery at the Future Circular Collider (FCC) could revolutionize our comprehension of the fundamental forces of nature. The FCC, currently under construction, promises to deliver unprecedented luminosity and energy, enabling researchers to probe the Higgs sector in unprecedented detail.  The objective of this research is to investigate the potential of the FCC to uncover new physics beyond the Standard Model, focusing on the Higgs boson's interactions with other particles and its role in the early universe. To achieve this, we employ a combination of theoretical models, numerical simulations, and Monte Carlo studies to explore the FCC's potential for discovering new Higgs boson decay modes, studying the Higgs boson's spin and parity, and probing the Higgs sector's sensitivity to new physics.  Our results indicate that the FCC's advanced detectors and luminosity capabilities will allow for the discovery of new Higgs boson decay modes, including those involving heavy quarks and supersymmetric particles. We also find that the FCC's energy and luminosity will enable the study of the Higgs boson's spin and parity, providing insights into the fundamental forces of nature. Furthermore, our simulations reveal that the FCC's sensitivity to new physics in the Higgs sector will be significantly enhanced, enabling researchers to test key predictions of beyond-Standard-Model theories. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the FCC's potential to revolutionize our understanding of the Higgs boson and the fundamental forces of nature.

text: The study of supernova progenitors is crucial for understanding stellar evolution and the life cycles of massive stars. This paper focuses on SN 2011ja, exploring the characteristics of its progenitor through the analysis of circumstellar interaction. The objective is to investigate the structure and composition of the material ejected by the progenitor star before the explosion as well as its effects on the supernova event. Utilizing multi-wavelength observations, including radio and X-ray data, we examined the interaction between the supernova materials and pre-existing circumstellar matter. Through spectral analysis, we identified evidence for dense circumstellar material, indicating significant mass loss from the progenitor star in its late evolutionary stages. Our results reveal emission signatures consistent with a red supergiant progenitor, shedding light on its mass-loss history and reinforcing theoretical models of stellar evolution that predict extensive mass ejections. Key findings suggest that SN 2011ja's progenitor likely underwent episodic mass-loss events that are often not accounted for in traditional evolutionary pathways. Additionally, the circumstellar material's composition points to complex chemical processing prior to the explosion. In conclusion, our findings underscore the importance of circumstellar interaction studies for constraining parameters of progenitor stars and emphasize the need for continued observations to refine models of supernova progenitor evolution. Detailed understanding of such interactions can provide broader insights into the end-of-life phenomena of massive stars, ultimately enhancing our comprehension of stellar death and rebirth cycles in the cosmos.

text: The study investigates the impact of a powerful stellar flare on the atmospheric composition of an Earth-like planet situated in the habitable zone of an M dwarf star. This research emerges from the increasing interest in the habitability of exoplanets orbiting M dwarfs, known for their frequent and intense stellar flares. The objective is to assess the extent to which such flares might alter atmospheric chemistry, potentially influencing planetary habitability. Using a state-of-the-art three-dimensional atmospheric model, we simulated the effects of a strong stellar flare on an Earth-analog with a nitrogen-oxygen-rich atmosphere. The model incorporated photochemistry and ion chemistry processes to simulate the flare event's influence over different time scales. Key findings reveal that the flare significantly increases atmospheric production of nitrogen oxides (NOx), which in turn promotes the depletion of ozone (O3), a critical protective layer against harmful ultraviolet radiation. The results indicate a transient but substantial vulnerability to ultraviolet radiation following a flare, with ozone reduction levels reaching up to 40% in certain zones. This depletion could lead to increased surface UV exposure, potentially affecting biological viability. Additionally, the study observed enhanced production of hydrogen compounds that may alter surface conditions. The conclusion underscores the importance of considering stellar activity when evaluating the habitability of planets orbiting M dwarfs. Continuous monitoring of such stellar systems and further research into their effects on atmospheric stability are vital to understanding the broader implications for life sustainability in these planetary environments.

GPUs exploit a high degree of thread-level parallelism to hide long-latency
stalls. Due to the heterogeneous compute requirements of different
applications, there is a growing need to share the GPU across multiple
applications in large-scale computing environments. However, while CPUs offer
relatively seamless multi-application concurrency, and are an excellent fit for
multitasking and for virtualized environments, GPUs currently offer only
primitive support for multi-application concurrency. Much of the problem in a
contemporary GPU lies within the memory system, where multi-application
execution requires virtual memory support to manage the address spaces of each
application and to provide memory protection. In this work, we perform a
detailed analysis of the major problems in state-of-the-art GPU virtual memory
management that hinders multi-application execution. Existing GPUs are designed
to share memory between the CPU and GPU, but do not handle multi-application
support within the GPU well. We find that when multiple applications spatially
share the GPU, there is a significant amount of inter-core thrashing on the
shared TLB within the GPU. The TLB contention is high enough to prevent the GPU
from successfully hiding stall latencies, thus becoming a first-order
performance concern. We introduce MASK, a memory hierarchy design that provides
low-overhead virtual memory support for the concurrent execution of multiple
applications. MASK extends the GPU memory hierarchy to efficiently support
address translation through the use of multi-level TLBs, and uses
translation-aware memory and cache management to maximize throughput in the
presence of inter-application contention.

Whether in the thermodynamic limit, vanishing magnetic field $h\rightarrow
0$, and nonzero temperature the spin stiffness of the spin-$1/2$ $XXX$
Heisenberg chain is finite or vanishes within the grand-canonical ensemble
remains an unsolved and controversial issue, as different approaches yield
contradictory results. Here we provide an upper bound on the stiffness and show
that within that ensemble it vanishes for $h\rightarrow 0$ in the thermodynamic
limit of chain length $L\to\infty$, at high temperatures $T\rightarrow\infty$.
Our approach uses a representation in terms of the $L$ physical spins $1/2$.
For all configurations that generate the exact spin-$S$ energy and momentum
eigenstates such a configuration involves a number $2S$ of unpaired spins $1/2$
in multiplet configurations and $L-2S$ spins $1/2$ that are paired within
$M_{\rm sp}=L/2-S$ spin-singlet pairs. The Bethe-ansatz strings of length $n=1$
and $n>1$ describe a single unbound spin-singlet pair and a configuration
within which $n$ pairs are bound, respectively. In the case of $n>1$ pairs this
holds both for ideal and deformed strings associated with $n$ complex
rapidities with the same real part. The use of such a spin $1/2$ representation
provides useful physical information on the problem under investigation in
contrast to often less controllable numerical studies. Our results provide
strong evidence for the absence of ballistic transport in the spin-$1/2$ $XXX$
Heisenberg chain in the thermodynamic limit, for high temperatures
$T\to\infty$, vanishing magnetic field $h\rightarrow 0$ and within the
grand-canonical ensemble.

The development of high throughput single-cell sequencing technologies now
allows the investigation of the population level diversity of cellular
transcriptomes. This diversity has shown two faces. First, the expression
dynamics (gene to gene variability) can be quantified more accurately, thanks
to the measurement of lowly-expressed genes. Second, the cell-to-cell
variability is high, with a low proportion of cells expressing the same gene at
the same time/level. Those emerging patterns appear to be very challenging from
the statistical point of view, especially to represent and to provide a
summarized view of single-cell expression data. PCA is one of the most powerful
framework to provide a suitable representation of high dimensional datasets, by
searching for latent directions catching the most variability in the data.
Unfortunately, classical PCA is based on Euclidean distances and projections
that work poorly in presence of over-dispersed counts that show drop-out events
(zero-inflation) like single-cell expression data We propose a probabilistic
Count Matrix Factorization (pCMF) approach for single-cell expression data
analysis, that relies on a sparse Gamma-Poisson factor model. This hierarchical
model is inferred using a variational EM algorithm. It is able to jointly build
a low dimensional representation of cells and genes. We show how this
probabilistic framework induces a geometry that is suitable for single-cell
data visualization, and produces a compression of the data that is very
powerful for clustering purposes. Our method is competed against other standard
representation methods like t-SNE, and we illustrate its performance for the
representation of single-cell data. We especially focus on publicly available
single-cell RNA-seq datasets.

This paper investigates the compress-and-forward scheme for an uplink cloud
radio access network (C-RAN) model, where multi-antenna base-stations (BSs) are
connected to a cloud-computing based central processor (CP) via
capacity-limited fronthaul links. The BSs compress the received signals with
Wyner-Ziv coding and send the representation bits to the CP; the CP performs
the decoding of all the users' messages. Under this setup, this paper makes
progress toward the optimal structure of the fronthaul compression and CP
decoding strategies for the compress-and-forward scheme in C-RAN. On the CP
decoding strategy design, this paper shows that under a sum fronthaul capacity
constraint, a generalized successive decoding strategy of the quantization and
user message codewords that allows arbitrary interleaved order at the CP
achieves the same rate region as the optimal joint decoding. Further, it is
shown that a practical strategy of successively decoding the quantization
codewords first, then the user messages, achieves the same maximum sum rate as
joint decoding under individual fronthaul constraints. On the joint
optimization of user transmission and BS quantization strategies, this paper
shows that if the input distributions are assumed to be Gaussian, then under
joint decoding, the optimal quantization scheme for maximizing the achievable
rate region is Gaussian. Moreover, Gaussian input and Gaussian quantization
with joint decoding achieve to within a constant gap of the capacity region of
the Gaussian multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) uplink C-RAN model. Finally,
this paper addresses the computational aspect of optimizing uplink MIMO C-RAN
by showing that under fixed Gaussian input, the sum rate maximization problem
over the Gaussian quantization noise covariance matrices can be formulated as
convex optimization problems, thereby facilitating its efficient solution.

text: In this study, we propose a novel Jackknife Empirical Likelihood (JEL) method for estimating Gini correlations and testing for their equality. Gini correlation, a measure of the association between two variables, plays a crucial role in various fields such as economics, sociology, and epidemiology. The problem we address lies in the limited existing methods for estimating and testing equality of Gini correlations. Our approach aims to provide more robust estimates and reliable statistical inference for Gini correlations.  By implementing the JEL method, we are able to tackle the challenges associated with small sample sizes and non-normality of data, common issues in real-world applications. The results of our simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed JEL method outperforms traditional methods in terms of bias reduction and confidence interval coverage. Additionally, our method offers improved power for testing the equality of Gini correlations between two independent groups.  The key idea behind our methodology is the incorporation of empirical likelihood techniques and the jackknife resampling procedure to construct confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for Gini correlations. By leveraging these techniques, we are able to provide more accurate and robust statistical inference compared to existing methods. Overall, our study contributes to the advancement of statistical methods for Gini correlation estimation and equality testing.

text: In the search for planetary mass companions orbiting brown dwarfs, Hubble Space Telescope's Near Infrared Camera and Multi-Object Spectrometer (HST/NICMOS) has played a significant role. Brown dwarfs, being the boundary objects between stars and planets, present a unique challenge due to their faint luminosity and short-lived emission. This study aims to analyze the data obtained from HST/NICMOS observations of three brown dwarfs 2MASS 1207, 2MASS 1507, and TWA 5B. By performing adaptive optical imaging and near-infrared coronagraphic imaging, the presence and properties of planetary mass companions were sought. The data analysis involved the use of techniques such as image subtraction and radial velocity measurements.  The results showed no definitive evidence of planetary mass companions orbiting the three brown dwarfs studied. However, upper limits on the planetary masses and semi-major axes were determined for each system. These limits provide valuable constraints for future observations and theoretical models. Additionally, this research highlights the importance of sensitivity and angular resolution in the search for planetary mass companions to brown dwarfs. Despite the lack of discovery, the data and techniques used in this study contribute significantly to our understanding of the complex astrophysical processes surrounding brown dwarfs.

text: We investigate the influence of environmental factors on the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak by analyzing a comprehensive dataset derived from large-scale galaxy surveys. Our primary aim is to address the discrepancies observed in the BAO measurements across different cosmic environments, specifically focusing on variations induced by local density and large-scale structure. We employ a combination of three-dimensional spatial analysis and statistical modeling to quantify the relationship between the environmental parameters and the observed shifts in the BAO peak. Our results provide compelling evidence of a significant environment-dependent shift in the BAO peak position, suggesting a modulation of the acoustic scale based on local cosmic density. We find that regions of higher density exhibit a systematic shift in the BAO feature, exacerbated by non-linear structure formation patterns. This shift becomes particularly pronounced when contrasting low-density regions with dense clusters. We validate our findings by cross-referencing with simulations that incorporate environmental variables, which align with our observational data and enhance the robustness of our conclusions. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our results for cosmological models and the interpretation of dark energy dynamics. Our work emphasizes the necessity of considering environmental influences when interpreting BAO data, thereby refining the tools available for elucidating the large-scale structure of the universe and enhancing our understanding of fundamental cosmological parameters.

In recent work, Renaud, Venaille, and Bouchet (RVB) revisit the equilibrium
statistical mechanics theory of the shallow water equations, within a
microcanonical approach, focusing on a more careful treatment of the energy
partition between inertial gravity wave and eddy motions in the equilibrium
state, and deriving joint probability distributions for the corresponding
dynamical degrees of freedom. The authors derive a Liouville theorem that
determines the underlying phase space statistical measure, but then, through
some physical arguments, actually compute the equilibrium statistics using a
measure that \emph{violates} this theorem. Here, using a more convenient, but
essentially equivalent, grand canonical approach, the full statistical theory
consistent with the Liouville theorem is derived. The results reveal several
significant differences from the previous results: (1) The microscale wave
motions lead to a strongly fluctuating thermodynamics, including long-ranged
correlations, in contrast to the mean-field-like behavior found by RVB. The
final effective model is equivalent to that of an elastic membrane with a
nonlinear wave-renormalized surface tension. (2) Even when a mean field
approximation is made, a rather more complex joint probability distribution is
revealed. Alternative physical arguments fully support the consistency of the
results. Of course, the true fluid final steady state relies on dissipative
processes not included in the shallow water equations, such as wave breaking
and viscous effects, but it is argued that the current theory provides a more
mathematically consistent starting point for future work aimed at assessing
their impacts.

For an odd integer $k$, let $\mathcal{C}_k = \{C_3,C_5,...,C_k\}$ denote the
family of all odd cycles of length at most $k$ and let $\mathcal{C}$ denote the
family of all odd cycles. Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits \cite{ESi1} conjectured that
for every family $\mathcal{F}$ of bipartite graphs, there exists $k$ such that
$\ex{n}{\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{C}_k} \sim \ex{n}{\mathcal{F} \cup
\mathcal{C}}$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. This conjecture was proved by
Erd\H{o}s and Simonovits when $\mathcal{F} = \{C_4\}$, and for certain families
of even cycles in \cite{KSV}. In this paper, we give a general approach to the
conjecture using Scott's sparse regularity lemma. Our approach proves the
conjecture for complete bipartite graphs $K_{2,t}$ and $K_{3,3}$: we obtain
more strongly that for any odd $k \geq 5$, \[ \ex{n}{\mathcal{F} \cup \{C_k\}}
\sim \ex{n}{\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{C}}\] and we show further that the
extremal graphs can be made bipartite by deleting very few edges. In contrast,
this formula does not extend to triangles -- the case $k = 3$ -- and we give an
algebraic construction for odd $t \geq 3$ of $K_{2,t}$-free $C_3$-free graphs
with substantially more edges than an extremal $K_{2,t}$-free bipartite graph
on $n$ vertices. Our general approach to the Erd\H{o}s-Simonovits conjecture is
effective based on some reasonable assumptions on the maximum number of edges
in an $m$ by $n$ bipartite $\mathcal{F}$-free graph.

The primary concerns of this paper are twofold: to understand the economic
value of storage in the presence of ramp constraints and exogenous electricity
prices, and to understand the implications of the associated optimal storage
management policy on qualitative and quantitative characteristics of storage
response to real-time prices. We present an analytic characterization of the
optimal policy, along with the associated finite-horizon time-averaged value of
storage. We also derive an analytical upperbound on the infinite-horizon
time-averaged value of storage. This bound is valid for any achievable
realization of prices when the support of the distribution is fixed, and
highlights the dependence of the value of storage on ramp constraints and
storage capacity. While the value of storage is a non-decreasing function of
price volatility, due to the finite ramp rate, the value of storage saturates
quickly as the capacity increases, regardless of volatility. To study the
implications of the optimal policy, we first present computational experiments
that suggest that optimal utilization of storage can, in expectation, induce a
considerable amount of price elasticity near the average price, but little or
no elasticity far from it. We then present a computational framework for
understanding the behavior of storage as a function of price and the amount of
stored energy, and for characterization of the buy/sell phase transition region
in the price-state plane. Finally, we study the impact of market-based
operation of storage on the required reserves, and show that the reserves may
need to be expanded to accommodate market-based storage.

A fast trigger system is being designed as a potential upgrade to VERITAS, or
as the basis for a future array of imaging atmospheric-Cherenkov telescopes
such as AGIS. The scientific goal is a reduction of the energy threshold by a
factor of 2 over the current threshold of VERITAS of around 130 GeV. The
trigger is being designed to suppress both accidentals from the night-sky
background and cosmic rays. The trigger uses field-programmable gate arrays
(FPGAs) so that it is adaptable to different observing modes and special
physics triggers, e.g. pulsars. The trigger consists of three levels: The level
1 (L1.5) trigger operating on each telescope camera samples the discriminated
pixels at a rate of 400 MHz and searches for nearest-neighbor coincidences. In
L1.5, the received discriminated signals are delay-compensated with an accuracy
of 0.078 ns, facilitating a short coincidence time-window between any nearest
neighbor of 5 ns. The hit pixels are then sent to a second trigger level (L2)
that parameterizes the image shape and transmits this information along with a
GPS time stamp to the array-level trigger (L3) at a rate of 10 MHz via a fiber
optic link. The FPGA-based event analysis on L3 searches for coincident
time-stamps from multiple telescopes and carries out a comparison of the image
parameters against a look-up table at a rate of 10 kHz. A test of the
single-telescope trigger was carried out in spring 2009 on one VERITAS
telescope.

text: The study of topological phase transitions and the accompanying boundary-bulk duality has gained significant attention in modern condensed matter physics. A fundamental requirement for these phenomena is the satisfaction of a simplicity condition, which ensures the existence of gapless boundary modes. In this paper, we explore the role of the simplicity condition in the context of boundary-bulk duality for various topological phases.  First, we provide a brief overview of the topological phases, focusing on their bulk properties. We then discuss the boundary conditions required for these phases to exhibit boundary-bulk duality. We show that the simplicity condition is a necessary requirement for the existence of topological boundary modes and their dual bulk counterparts.  To illustrate this concept, we consider several examples of topological phases, including the integer quantum Hall effect and the topological insulator. For each example, we discuss the bulk and boundary properties and the conditions under which boundary-bulk duality emerges. We also explore the implications of the simplicity condition on the bulk and boundary excitations.  In conclusion, we demonstrate that the simplicity condition plays a crucial role in the emergence of boundary-bulk duality in topological phases. By examining various examples, we gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between the topological boundary modes and their bulk counterparts and the importance of satisfying the simplicity condition. This work lays the foundation for further investigations into the interplay between topological phases, boundary conditions, and simplicity conditions.
label: machine

text: The dissociation of heavy quarkonia in an anisotropic hot Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) medium holds significant implications for understanding quark-gluon plasma behavior. This study aims to elucidate the impact of medium anisotropy on quarkonium states using a quasi-particle model, which effectively incorporates the anisotropic pressures of the QCD medium. Utilizing an effective potential approach, we analyze the binding energies of heavy quarkonia, such as charmonium and bottomonium, and their dissociation temperatures under anisotropic conditions. The quasi-particle model enables the description of the medium's thermodynamic properties by attributing an effective mass to quarks and gluons, enhancing the realism of the simulation. Our findings demonstrate a reduction in quarkonium binding energies in anisotropic environments, leading to dissociation at lower temperatures compared to isotropic conditions. This suggests that medium anisotropy plays a critical role in modifying the screening effects experienced by quarkonia, thereby affecting their stability. The results underline the importance of considering anisotropic factors in QCD medium characterizations, especially relevant in non-central heavy-ion collisions where anisotropic expansion occurs. By providing a comparative analysis of isotropic versus anisotropic medium effects, the study advances the theoretical understanding of quarkonia behavior in extreme conditions of temperature and pressure. The conclusions drawn could offer deeper insights into experimental observations from heavy-ion collision experiments, shedding light on the properties of the early universe. Future investigations could extend these findings by exploring the impact of varying degrees of anisotropy and their correlation with experimental data.
label: machine

Synchronized brain rhythms, associated with diverse cognitive functions, have
been observed in electrical recordings of brain activity. Neural
synchronization may be well described by using the population-averaged global
potential $V_G$ in computational neuroscience. The time-averaged fluctuation of
$V_G$ plays the role of a "thermodynamic" order parameter $\cal {O}$ used for
describing the synchrony-asynchrony transition in neural systems. Population
spike synchronization may be well visualized in the raster plot of neural
spikes. The degree of neural synchronization seen in the raster plot is well
measured in terms of a "statistical-mechanical" spike-based measure $M_s$
introduced by considering the occupation and the pacing patterns of spikes. The
global potential $V_G$ is also used to give a reference global cycle for the
calculation of $M_s$. Hence, $V_G$ becomes an important collective quantity
because it is associated with calculation of both $\cal {O}$ and $M_s$.
However, it is practically difficult to directly get $V_G$ in real experiments.
To overcome this difficulty, instead of $V_G$, we employ the instantaneous
population spike rate (IPSR) which can be obtained in experiments, and develop
realistic thermodynamic and statistical-mechanical measures, based on IPSR, to
make practical characterization of the neural synchronization in both
computational and experimental neuroscience. Particularly, more accurate
characterization of weak sparse spike synchronization can be achieved in terms
of realistic statistical-mechanical IPSR-based measure, in comparison with the
conventional measure based on $V_G$.

The breakdown of the Stokes-Einstein (SE) relation between diffusivity and
viscosity at low temperatures is considered to be one of the hallmarks of
glassy dynamics in liquids. Theoretical analyses relate this breakdown with the
presence of heterogeneous dynamics, and by extension, with the fragility of
glass formers. We perform an investigation of the breakdown of the SE relation
in 2, 3 and 4 dimensions, in order to understand these interrelations. Results
from simulations of model glass formers show that the degree of the breakdown
of the SE relation decreases with increasing spatial dimensionality. The
breakdown itself can be rationalized via the difference between the activation
free energies for diffusivity and viscosity (or relaxation times) in the
Adam-Gibbs relation in three and four dimensions. The behavior in two
dimensions also can be understood in terms of a generalized Adam-Gibbs relation
that is observed in previous work. We calculate various measures of
heterogeneity of dynamics and find that the degree of the SE breakdown and
measures of heterogeneity of dynamics are generally well correlated but with
some exceptions. The two dimensional systems we study show deviations from the
pattern of behavior of the three and four dimensional systems both at high and
low temperatures. The fragility of the studied liquids is found to increase
with spatial dimensionality, contrary to the expectation based on the
association of fragility with heterogeneous dynamics.

text: We investigate the evolutionary influences on the acoustic oscillation spectra of red giants, utilizing 600 days of uninterrupted photometric observations from the Kepler spacecraft. Our analysis aims to elucidate the underlying astrophysical processes that shape the oscillation characteristics exhibited by these evolved stars. By employing time-series analysis techniques on the stellar light curves, we extract oscillation parameters including frequency separations, mode identifications, and amplitude variations. Our findings reveal that as red giants ascend the giant branch, evolutionary modifications distinctly impact their oscillation spectra. Specifically, we observe systematic shifts in the large frequency separations, indicative of changes in the stellar internal structure. Our methodology incorporates a grid-based approach to modeling these oscillations, where we calibrate theoretical models to our observational data. This allows us to infer stellar properties such as mass and age with improved precision. Furthermore, we identify correlations between oscillation amplitudes and evolutionary states, providing insight into the dynamic processes occurring within the stellar interiors. Through this comprehensive study, we contribute to a deeper understanding of the physical mechanisms driving oscillation pattern evolution in red giants. This research underscores the critical role of asteroseismology in complementing traditional stellar evolution models, providing a robust framework for future studies on stellar interiors across different phases of stellar evolution. Our results establish a refined perspective on stellar structure and dynamics that enhances predictive models of stellar behavior.
label: machine

text: In the rapidly evolving landscape of network management, the integration of Software Defined Networking (SDN) at the edge has emerged as a promising solution to enhance performance and resource utilization. This research aims to investigate offloading strategies within SDN architectures by leveraging information asymmetry through a contract theoretical framework. The primary objective is to develop a robust model that facilitates efficient decision-making in resource allocation, ensuring optimal network performance while addressing the disparities in information availability among network agents.   To achieve this, we employed a mixed-methods approach, combining theoretical analysis with simulations to evaluate resource offloading mechanisms in various edge scenarios. By modeling the interaction between service providers and users under conditions of asymmetric information, we derived key contracts that maximize utility for both parties.   Our findings reveal that strategically designed contracts can lead to significant improvements in offload efficiency, with a marked reduction in latency and enhanced QoS metrics, even in environments with limited shared information. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of aligning incentives to encourage cooperation among network nodes, thereby optimizing overall system performance.   In conclusion, this research contributes to the burgeoning field of edge computing by demonstrating the viability of contract theory in addressing the challenges posed by information asymmetry in SDN environments. The proposed offloading mechanisms not only enhance operational efficiencies but also pave the way for future innovations in network design and resource management.
label: machine

text: This study investigates the behavior of a one-channel conductor coupled to a quantum of resistance, focusing on the exact ac conductance and finite-frequency noise characteristics. Background research reveals that the interaction between a conductor and a quantum of resistance can lead to unique transport phenomena, including quantized resistance and non-equilibrium effects. However, the underlying mechanisms governing these phenomena remain poorly understood.  The objective of this research is to explore the exact ac conductance and finite-frequency noise properties of a one-channel conductor coupled to a quantum of resistance, with a focus on the interplay between the conductor and the quantum of resistance. To achieve this, we employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods, utilizing the Landauer-Büttiker formalism and the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) approach.  Key findings reveal that the ac conductance of the one-channel conductor exhibits quantized plateaus at specific frequencies, which are correlated with the quantum of resistance. Furthermore, the finite-frequency noise characteristics exhibit a unique power-law dependence on the frequency, which is attributed to the interplay between the conductor and the quantum of resistance. The results also suggest that the noise properties can be used to probe the underlying transport mechanisms, providing a new tool for the study of quantum transport phenomena.  The study provides a comprehensive understanding of the exact ac conductance and finite-frequency noise properties of a one-channel conductor coupled to a quantum of resistance, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms governing these phenomena. The findings have significant implications for the development of new quantum devices and the understanding of quantum transport phenomena, and may also have applications in fields such as quantum computing and quantum information processing.
label: machine

text: The Test Cover Problem (TCP) is a well-known problem in combinatorial optimization, where the objective is to select a subset of test sets from a given set of test sets such that the number of test sets that need to be performed is minimized, subject to certain constraints. Polynomial kernels have been widely used to solve the TCP, but recent studies have raised concerns about their existence and efficiency. This research investigates the non-existence of polynomial kernels for the TCP.    Polynomial kernels have been extensively used to solve the TCP due to their ability to reduce the complexity of the problem. However, the existence of polynomial kernels implies that the problem can be solved in polynomial time, which is not guaranteed for the TCP.    This research aims to show that there is no polynomial kernel for the TCP.    The research uses a reduction from the NP-complete problem of the Set Cover Problem to the TCP. It also employs a combination of approximation algorithms and hardness results to prove the non-existence of polynomial kernels.    The research demonstrates that there is no polynomial kernel for the TCP. The reduction from the Set Cover Problem to the TCP is used to show that any polynomial-time algorithm for the TCP must also solve the Set Cover Problem, which is NP-complete.    The non-existence of polynomial kernels for the TCP has significant implications for the design of efficient algorithms for the problem. The results of this research provide evidence that the TCP is NP-hard and that the development of efficient algorithms for the problem may require the use of approximation algorithms or other techniques.
label: machine

The {\em shortest common superstring} and the {\em shortest common
supersequence} are two well studied problems having a wide range of
applications. In this paper we consider both problems with resource
constraints, denoted as the Restricted Common Superstring (shortly
\textit{RCSstr}) problem and the Restricted Common Supersequence (shortly
\textit{RCSseq}). In the \textit{RCSstr} (\textit{RCSseq}) problem we are given
a set $S$ of $n$ strings, $s_1$, $s_2$, $\ldots$, $s_n$, and a multiset $t =
\{t_1, t_2, \dots, t_m\}$, and the goal is to find a permutation $\pi : \{1,
\dots, m\} \to \{1, \dots, m\}$ to maximize the number of strings in $S$ that
are substrings (subsequences) of $\pi(t) = t_{\pi(1)}t_{\pi(2)}...t_{\pi(m)}$
(we call this ordering of the multiset, $\pi(t)$, a permutation of $t$). We
first show that in its most general setting the \textit{RCSstr} problem is {\em
NP-complete} and hard to approximate within a factor of $n^{1-\epsilon}$, for
any $\epsilon > 0$, unless P = NP. Afterwards, we present two separate
reductions to show that the \textit{RCSstr} problem remains NP-Hard even in the
case where the elements of $t$ are drawn from a binary alphabet or for the case
where all input strings are of length two. We then present some approximation
results for several variants of the \textit{RCSstr} problem. In the second part
of this paper, we turn to the \textit{RCSseq} problem, where we present some
hardness results, tight lower bounds and approximation algorithms.

text: The abstract focuses on the study of periodic $p$-adic Gibbs measures for the $q$-state Potts model on a Cayley tree. The methodology involves analyzing the thermodynamic formalism and the properties of the Cayley tree structure. Key findings include the identification of multiple ergodic measures that coexist due to the chaotic dynamics, each representing different stable states of the system. The conclusion emphasizes the profound implications of chaos theory on the multiplicity of $p$-adic Gibbs measures, highlighting the intricate relationship between chaos and the variety of possible equilibrium states in such models.

text: This paper explores the search for natural and split supersymmetry in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, focusing on final states with jets and missing transverse momentum. The analysis is based on data collected by the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. In the context of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), the study sets limits on the masses of supersymmetric particles using various search strategies, including the use of multijet final states, and the optimization of event selection criteria. The study also employs a split supersymmetry scenario, where the supersymmetric partners of the electroweak gauginos and the scalar top quarks have significantly different masses. In this scenario, the study sets strong limits on the masses of the heavier partners, improving previous results. The investigation also includes the assessment of the implications of the results on the overall MSSM parameter space and potential future directions for supersymmetry searches at the LHC.

Distributionally robust stochastic optimization (DRSO) is an approach to
optimization under uncertainty in which, instead of assuming that there is a
known true underlying probability distribution, one hedges against a chosen set
of distributions. In this paper we first point out that the set of
distributions should be chosen to be appropriate for the application at hand,
and that some of the choices that have been popular until recently are, for
many applications, not good choices. We next consider sets of distributions
that are within a chosen Wasserstein distance from a nominal distribution. Such
a choice of sets has two advantages: (1) The resulting distributions hedged
against are more reasonable than those resulting from other popular choices of
sets. (2) The problem of determining the worst-case expectation over the
resulting set of distributions has desirable tractability properties. We derive
a strong duality reformulation of the corresponding DRSO problem and construct
approximate worst-case distributions explicitly via the first-order optimality
conditions of the dual problem.
  Our contributions are four-fold. (i) We identify necessary and sufficient
conditions for the existence of a worst-case distribution, which are naturally
related to the growth rate of the objective function. (ii) We show that the
worst-case distributions resulting from an appropriate Wasserstein distance
have a concise structure and a clear interpretation. (iii) Using this
structure, we show that data-driven DRSO problems can be approximated to any
accuracy by robust optimization problems, and thereby many DRSO problems become
tractable by using tools from robust optimization. (iv) Our strong duality
result holds in a very general setting. As examples, we show that it can be
applied to infinite-dimensional process control and intensity estimation for
point processes.
