We introduce a quantum Monte Carlo method at finite temperature for
interacting fermionic models in the canonical ensemble, where the conservation
of the particle number is enforced. Although general thermodynamic arguments
ensure the equivalence of the canonical and the grand-canonical ensembles in
the thermodynamic limit, their approach to the infinite-volume limit is
distinctively different. Observables computed in the canonical ensemble
generically display a finite-size correction proportional to the inverse
volume, whereas in the grand-canonical ensemble the approach is exponential in
the ratio of the linear size over the correlation length. We verify these
predictions by quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the Hubbard model in one and
two dimensions in the grand-canonical and the canonical ensemble. We prove an
exact formula for the finite-size part of the free energy density, energy
density and other observables in the canonical ensemble and relate this
correction to a susceptibility computed in the corresponding grand-canonical
ensemble. This result is confirmed by an exact computation of the
one-dimensional classical Ising model in the canonical ensemble, which for
classical models corresponds to the so-called fixed-magnetization ensemble. Our
method is useful for simulating finite systems which are not coupled to a
particle bath, such as in nuclear or cold atom physics.

(abridged for arXiv) The BEER algorithm searches stellar light curves for the
BEaming, Ellipsoidal, and Reflection photometric modulations that are caused by
a short-period companion. Applying the search to the first five long-run center
CoRoT fields, we identified $481$ non-eclipsing candidates with periodic flux
amplitudes of $0.5-87$ mmag. Optimizing the Anglo-Australian-Telescope pointing
coordinates and the AAOmega fiber-allocations with dedicated softwares, we
acquired six spectra for $231$ candidates and seven spectra for another $50$
candidates in a seven-night campaign. Analysis of the red-arm AAOmega spectra,
which covered the range of $8342-8842\AA{}$, yielded a radial-velocity
precision of $\sim1$ km/s. Spectra containing lines of more than one star were
analyzed with the two-dimensional correlation algorithm TODCOR. The measured
radial velocities confirmed the binarity of seventy of the BEER candidates$-45$
single-line binaries, $18$ double-line binaries, and $7$ diluted binaries. We
show that red giants introduce a major source of false candidates and
demonstrate a way to improve BEER's performance in extracting higher fidelity
samples from future searches of CoRoT light curves. The periods of the
confirmed binaries span a range of $0.3-10$ days and show a rise in the number
of binaries per $\Delta$log$P$ toward longer periods. The estimated mass ratios
of the double-line binaries and the mass ratios assigned to the single-line
binaries, assuming an isotropic inclination distribution, span a range of
$0.03-1$. On the low-mass end, we have detected two brown-dwarf candidates on a
$\sim1$ day period orbit. This is the first time non-eclipsing beaming binaries
are detected in CoRoT data, and we estimate that $\sim300$ such binaries can be
detected in the CoRoT long-run light curves.

text: In our study, we analyze the stellar evolution of NSV 11749, an evolved star that exhibits characteristics similar to born again stars, such as V605 Aql and V4334 Sgr. Our analysis focuses on understanding the mechanisms behind the sudden revival of nuclear fusion in these stars, which occurs after they have exhausted their hydrogen fuel. We employ high-resolution spectroscopy and detailed modeling of the star's spectral features to determine its current state and past evolutionary history. Key findings include the detection of strong neon lines indicative of deep convection zones, suggesting the presence of a significant amount of mixing between different layers of the star. This mixing is crucial for sustaining the nuclear reactions and explains the observed revival of nuclear burning. Our study also highlights the importance of progenitor mass and metallicity in determining the likelihood of a born again event. The methodology involves comprehensive spectral analysis, asteroseismology, and theoretical models to infer the internal structure and dynamics of NSV 11749. These insights contribute to our broader understanding of stellar evolution and the complex processes that govern the life cycles of massive stars.

We present a detailed study of a X -ray selected sample of 5 submillimeter
bright QSOs at $z\sim2$, where the highest rates of star formation (SF) and
further growth of black holes (BH) occur. Therefore, this sample is a great
laboratory to investigate the co-evolution of star formation and AGN. We
present here the analysis of the spectral energy distributions (SED) of the 5
QSOS, including new data from Herschel PACS and SPIRE. Both AGN components
(direct and reprocessed) and like Star Formation (SF) are needed to model its
SED. From the SED and their UV-optical spectra we have estimated the mass of
the black hole ($M_{BH} = 10^9 - 10^{10} M_{SUN}$) and bolometric luminosities
of AGN ($L_{BOL} = (0.8-20) \times 10^{13} L_{SUN}$). These objects show very
high luminosities in the far infrared range (at the H/ULIRG levels) and very
high rates of SF (SFR = 400-1400 $M_{SUN}$/y). Known their current SFR and
their BH masses, we deduce that their host galaxies must be already very
massive, or would not have time to get to the local relation between BH mass
and bulge. Finally, we found evidence of a possible correlation between the
column density of ionized gas detected in X-rays ($NH_{ion}$) and SFR, which
would provide a link between AGN and SF processes.

Loop Quantum Cosmology adapts the techniques of Loop Quantum Gravity in the
quantization of homogeneous cosmological models obtained from General
Relativity by symmetry reduction. As a necessary step towards the extraction of
realistic results from Loop Quantum Cosmology, we should consider the inclusion
of inhomogeneities, which play a central role in current cosmology. The main
goal of this thesis is to progress in this direction. With this aim we have
studied a natural test bed to incorporate inhomogeneities in Loop Quantum
Cosmology: the linearly polarized Gowdy T3 model. This model can be regarded as
a homogeneous Bianchi I background filled with inhomogeneities propagating in
one direction. We have completed its quantization by means of a hybrid
approach, that combines the loop quantization of the homogeneous sector, within
the so-called improved dynamics scheme, with a Fock quantization for the
inhomogeneities. In order to perform this quantization as thorough as possible,
we have also reviewed the (improved dynamics) loop quantization of flat FRW
cosmologies, paradigmatic model in LQC, as well as that of the Bianchi I model.
We have proposed a new prescription for the Hamiltonian constraint operator of
these models, that displays nicer features than those of previous proposals. In
particular, we get simpler superselection sectors with a global and
well-understood Wheeler-DeWitt limit in the large volume regime, which serve to
improve our understanding of the physical Hilbert space of these models.

text: This study identifies H₂C=CH−CH=CH₂ (H₂CCC) as a potential carrier of diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs). Through spectroscopic analysis, we have observed significant absorption features at wavelengths characteristic of H₂CCC within the DIB region. The investigation employed high-resolution Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy to detect the presence of H₂CCC in interstellar clouds. By comparing our experimental data with theoretical models of DIB spectra, we propose that H₂CCC could be responsible for several prominent DIBs observed across the electromagnetic spectrum. Key methodologies involved the use of state-of-the-art laboratory instrumentation to simulate interstellar conditions and the application of computational tools to interpret the observed spectra. Our findings suggest that H₂CCC may play a crucial role in the formation and detection of DIBs, offering new insights into the chemical processes occurring in the interstellar medium. Further research is needed to confirm this hypothesis through additional observational and laboratory studies.

The numerical evolution of Einstein's field equations in a generic background
has the potential to answer a variety of important questions in physics: from
applications to the gauge-gravity duality, to modelling black hole production
in TeV gravity scenarios, analysis of the stability of exact solutions and
tests of Cosmic Censorship. In order to investigate these questions, we extend
numerical relativity to more general space-times than those investigated
hitherto, by developing a framework to study the numerical evolution of D
dimensional vacuum space-times with an SO(D-2) isometry group for D\ge 5, or
SO(D-3) for D\ge 6.
  Performing a dimensional reduction on a (D-4)-sphere, the D dimensional
vacuum Einstein equations are rewritten as a 3+1 dimensional system with source
terms, and presented in the Baumgarte, Shapiro, Shibata and Nakamura (BSSN)
formulation. This allows the use of existing 3+1 dimensional numerical codes
with small adaptations. Brill-Lindquist initial data are constructed in D
dimensions and a procedure to match them to our 3+1 dimensional evolution
equations is given. We have implemented our framework by adapting the LEAN code
and perform a variety of simulations of non-spinning black hole space-times.
Specifically, we present a modified moving puncture gauge which facilitates
long term stable simulations in D=5. We further demonstrate the internal
consistency of the code by studying convergence and comparing numerical versus
analytic results in the case of geodesic slicing for D=5,6.

text: Our work focuses on embedding deep metric learning techniques for enhancing person re-identification performance against large variations in factors like illumination, pose, and occlusion. The primary objective of this study is to address the challenges faced in accurately identifying individuals across non-overlapping camera views in complex real-world scenarios. Leveraging the power of deep neural networks, we propose a novel approach to learn discriminative embeddings that can effectively capture the underlying similarities and differences between images of the same person while emphasizing variations across different individuals.  Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the superiority of our deep metric learning framework in achieving state-of-the-art results in person re-identification tasks. Our methodology involves training deep neural networks with large-scale labeled data to optimize embedding spaces that facilitate enhanced matching of person instances under diverse environmental conditions. The results indicate significant improvements in re-identification accuracy, especially when dealing with challenging scenarios characterized by substantial intra-class variance and inter-class similarity.  By integrating advanced deep metric learning techniques, our study makes notable contributions towards overcoming the limitations associated with conventional person re-identification systems when handling large variations. Overall, our findings highlight the efficacy of embedding deep metric learning approaches in significantly enhancing the robustness and performance of person re-identification systems in the presence of complex environmental variations.

text: The Kuiper Belt, a region located beyond Neptune's orbit in our solar system, is a reservoir of icy bodies and dwarf planets. Recent advances in observational technology have enabled the detection of Kuiper-like belts around nearby stars. This abstract provides an overview of the characteristics, formation mechanisms, and implications of these discovered belts.   The discovery of the Kuiper Belt in our solar system expanded our understanding of the planetary system's structure. Its distinct composition differs significantly from the inner planets. Similar structures, known as Kuiper Belts, have since been detected around nearby stars.   The primary objective of this study is to examine the current state of research on Kuiper-like belts around nearby stars, discuss their formation mechanisms, and explore their implications for exoplanetary systems and potential habitable worlds.   A comprehensive review of relevant literature was conducted, focusing on observational studies, theoretical models, and simulations related to Kuiper-like belts around nearby stars. The analysis included data from various telescopes, such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array and the Hubble Space Telescope.  Key findings Multiple Kuiper-like belts have been identified around nearby stars. These belts exhibit a wide range of sizes, orbital architectures, and compositions. Their formation mechanisms are still debated, with some theories suggesting that they may form through planet-planet scattering or through gas giant migration. The presence of Kuiper-like belts around nearby stars provides important insights into the formation and evolution of exoplanetary systems.   The detection and study of Kuiper-like belts around nearby stars have broadened our knowledge of planetary systems beyond our own. By exploring their characteristics and formation mechanisms, we can further understand the diversity of exoplanetary systems and potentially identify habitable worlds. Continued research in this area will likely lead to new discoveries and insights that challenge our current models of planetary systems.

The use of orthogonal signaling schemes such as time-, frequency-, or
code-division multiplexing (T-, F-, CDM) in multi-user systems allows for
power-efficient simple receivers. It is shown in this paper that by using
orthogonal signaling on frequency selective fading channels, the cooperative
Nash bargaining (NB)-based precoding games for multi-user systems, which aim at
maximizing the information rates of all users, are simplified to the
corresponding cooperative resource allocation games. The latter provides
additional practically desired simplifications to transmitter design and
significantly reduces the overhead during user cooperation. The complexity of
the corresponding precoding/resource allocation games, however, depends on the
constraints imposed on the users. If only spectral mask constraints are
present, the corresponding cooperative NB problem can be formulated as a convex
optimization problem and solved efficiently in a distributed manner using dual
decomposition based algorithm. However, the NB problem is non-convex if total
power constraints are also imposed on the users. In this case, the complexity
associate with finding the NB solution is unacceptably high. Therefore, the
multi-user systems are categorized into bandwidth- and power-dominant based on
a bottleneck resource, and different manners of cooperation are developed for
each type of systems for the case of two-users. Such classification guarantees
that the solution obtained in each case is Pareto-optimal and actually can be
identical to the optimal solution, while the complexity is significantly
reduced. Simulation results demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed
cooperative precoding/resource allocation strategies and the reduced complexity
of the proposed algorithms.

text: In this research, we investigate the concept of near optimality in covering and packing games by leveraging global information. Our study addresses the fundamental problem of achieving efficient solutions in scenarios where players have access to varying degrees of information. By exposing global information, we aim to enhance the performance of players in covering and packing games, ultimately leading to near-optimal outcomes.  Through our methodology, we analyze the impact of global information on the strategies employed by players in these games. We demonstrate that by strategically revealing pertinent information to players, we can significantly improve their decision-making processes, thereby approaching optimal solutions. Our results indicate that the judicious use of global information can lead to more efficient and effective outcomes in covering and packing games, bringing us closer to achieving near optimality.  Key ideas explored in this study include the importance of information dissemination in strategic decision-making, the dynamics of covering and packing games, and the concept of near optimality in game theory. By integrating these concepts and employing a rigorous analytical approach, we provide insights into the potential benefits of exposing global information in enhancing the performance of players in game scenarios.

text: This study examines the impact of ex-post interest rate (IR) notifications via bank accounts on the optimal dynamic mechanisms for managing debt. Background research indicates that traditional debt management strategies often rely on ex-ante interest rate forecasting, which can be unreliable. In contrast, ex-post IR notifications provide real-time information on interest rates, allowing for more accurate debt management decisions. Objective of this research is to investigate the effectiveness of dynamic mechanisms that incorporate ex-post IR notifications via bank accounts in managing debt, with a focus on minimizing debt servicing costs and maximizing debt repayment efficiency.  Methodology employed in this study involves a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative data. A survey of 500 individuals with outstanding debts was conducted to gather data on their current debt management practices and perceptions of ex-post IR notifications. Additionally, a computational model was developed to simulate the impact of ex-post IR notifications on debt management decisions. Key findings indicate that dynamic mechanisms incorporating ex-post IR notifications via bank accounts can lead to significant reductions in debt servicing costs and improved debt repayment efficiency. The study also reveals that individuals who receive ex-post IR notifications via bank accounts exhibit greater awareness and understanding of their debt obligations, leading to more informed debt management decisions.  Conclusion of this research highlights the potential benefits of integrating ex-post IR notifications via bank accounts into dynamic debt management mechanisms. The findings suggest that this approach can lead to more efficient debt repayment, reduced debt servicing costs, and improved financial well-being. The study's results have implications for policymakers and financial institutions seeking to develop more effective debt management strategies that incorporate real-time interest rate information.

text: In this study, we investigate the implications of low-mass right-handed sneutrino dark matter in the context of the Galactic Centre gamma-ray excess. By considering the SuperCDMS and LUX experimental constraints, we constrain the parameter space of the sneutrino dark matter model. Our analysis reveals that the low-mass regime of right-handed sneutrino dark matter is consistent with the observed Galactic Centre gamma-ray excess while satisfying the stringent direct detection limits imposed by SuperCDMS and LUX. We find that the key to reconciling these constraints lies in the interplay between sneutrino properties and the dark matter mass spectrum. Our methodology involves a comprehensive scan of the parameter space followed by a detailed statistical analysis to determine the regions that are compatible with both experimental constraints and the Galactic Centre gamma-ray excess. The results highlight the viability of low-mass right-handed sneutrino dark matter as a candidate for explaining the Galactic Centre gamma-ray excess while evading detection in direct experiments. This work contributes to the ongoing efforts to understand the nature of dark matter and its potential connections to astrophysical observations, providing valuable insights for future experimental and theoretical investigations in the field.

We analyzed broad-band X-ray and radio data of the magnetar SGR J1935+2154
taken in the aftermath of its 2014, 2015, and 2016 outbursts. The source soft
X-ray spectrum <10 keV is well described with a BB+PL or 2BB model during all
three outbursts. NuSTAR observations revealed a hard X-ray tail, $\Gamma=0.9$,
extending up to 79 keV, with flux larger than the one detected <10 keV. Imaging
analysis of Chandra data did not reveal small-scale extended emission around
the source. Following the outbursts, the total 0.5-10 keV flux from SGR
J1935+2154 increased in concordance to its bursting activity, with the flux at
activation onset increasing by a factor of $\sim7$ following its strongest June
2016 outburst. A Swift/XRT observation taken 1.5 days prior to the onset of
this outburst showed a flux level consistent with quiescence. We show that the
flux increase is due to the PL or hot BB component, which increased by a factor
of $25$ compared to quiescence, while the cold BB component $kT=0.47$ keV
remained more or less constant. The 2014 and 2015 outbursts decayed
quasi-exponentially with time-scales of $\sim40$ days, while the stronger May
and June 2016 outbursts showed a quick short-term decay with time-scales of
$\sim4$ days. Our Arecibo radio observations set the deepest limits on the
radio emission from a magnetar, with a maximum flux density limit of 14 $\mu$Jy
for the 4.6 GHz observations and 7 $\mu$Jy for the 1.4 GHz observations. We
discuss these results in the framework of the current magnetar theoretical
models.

A large fraction of the baryonic matter in the Universe is located in
filaments in the intergalactic medium. However, the low surface brightness of
these filaments has not yet allowed their direct detection except in very
special regions in the circum-galactic medium (CGM). Here we simulate the
intensity and spatial fluctuations in Lyman Alpha ${\rm (Ly\alpha)}$ emission
from filaments in the intergalactic medium (IGM) and discuss the prospects for
the next generation of space based instruments to detect the low surface
brightness universe at UV wavelengths. Starting with a high resolution N-body
simulation we obtain the dark matter density fluctuations and associate baryons
with the dark matter particles assuming that they follow the same spatial
distribution. The IGM thermal and ionization state is set by a model of the UV
background and by the relevant cooling processes for a hydrogen and helium gas.
The ${\rm Ly\alpha}$ emissivity is then estimated, taking into account
recombination and collisional excitation processes. We find that the detection
of these filaments through their ${\rm Ly\alpha}$ emission is well in the reach
of the next generation of UV space based instruments and so it should be
achieved in the next decade. The density field is populated with halos and
galaxies and their ${\rm Ly\alpha}$ emission is estimated. Galaxies are treated
as foregrounds and so we discuss methods to reduce their contamination from
observational maps. Finally, we estimate the UV continuum background as a
function of the redshift of the ${\rm Ly\alpha}$ emission line and discuss how
this continuum can affect observations.

text: Quark-Novae in Low-mass X-ray Binaries II Application to G87-7 and to GRB 110328A  Quark-Novae, a type of transient event in binary systems, have garnered significant attention due to their potential to reveal the properties of compact objects. These events are characterized by an explosion of material from a companion star, resulting in a bright X-ray emission. In this context, we investigate the applicability of Quark-Novae to low-mass X-ray binaries, specifically focusing on the binary system G87-7 and the Gamma-Ray Burst 110328A.  Our analysis reveals that G87-7, a binary system consisting of a low-mass companion star and a neutron star, exhibits characteristics consistent with a Quark-Novae event. The observed X-ray flux and light curve of G87-7 are consistent with a thermalized ejecta, suggesting that the event was triggered by a thermonuclear explosion on the companion star. Furthermore, the properties of the neutron star, such as its mass and radius, are consistent with the predictions of Quark-Novae theory.  In contrast, the analysis of GRB 110328A, a long-duration Gamma-Ray Burst, reveals that it is unlikely to be a Quark-Novae event. The burst's properties, such as its energy release and spectral characteristics, are more consistent with a collapsar or neutron star merger event. However, our results suggest that the possibility of a Quark-Novae event cannot be ruled out, and further observations are required to confirm or refute this hypothesis.  Our study highlights the importance of considering Quark-Novae as a potential explanation for transient events in low-mass X-ray binaries. By applying the theoretical framework of Quark-Novae to observed binary systems, we can gain insights into the properties of compact objects and the mechanisms driving these events.

Maximum output powers of vibration-driven inertial power harvesters reported
in literature exhibit sizable variations, even when normalized by the device
weight or their maximum linear size. To help establish a common benchmark, we
present a power-spectral-density based approach for estimating the maximum
power that can be obtained using a resonant inertial power harvester from a
random (aperiodic) vibration source with a given power spectral density. In the
simplest case of unlimited harvester size, the maximum obtainable power is
simply proportional to the maximum value of the power spectral density of
vibration acceleration. We describe in detail the underlying theory and the
practical method for evaluating these limits. We also present a simple
analytical formula to estimate the minimum harvester size required for
obtaining the maximum possible power. Specific power limits are derived as
function of harvester size for three practical examples of vibration sources:
(a) pneumatic power tool, (b) the body of an idling Mazda RX7 sports car, and
(c) human walking motion. Characteristic power spectra and optimum design
parameters (quality factor and resonant frequency) are presented for both
translational and rotational harvesters. Translational harvesters generally
outperform rotational ones for realistic harvester sizes, with the power tool
vibrations yielding a practical power limit of ~300 mW per gram of inertial
mass, followed by walking at ~1mW/g, while the vibrations of a car body yield
~0.1 mW/g or less.

text: We investigated the feasibility of predicting exoplanet observability in various astrophysical contexts, including time, contrast, separation, and polarization in scattered light. Our approach combined machine learning techniques with spectroscopic and imaging data to develop a predictive model that can forecast the likelihood of exoplanet detection. We trained the model on a large dataset of simulated observations, which allowed us to explore the effects of different atmospheric and stellar parameters on the detectability of exoplanets.  Our results indicate that the observability of exoplanets in scattered light is significantly affected by the time, contrast, and separation of the target and background objects. We found that the model can accurately predict the detectability of exoplanets in scenarios where the background object is relatively bright and the exoplanet is separated from it by a sufficient angular distance. However, the model's performance is limited in cases where the background object is faint or the exoplanet is closely aligned with it.  Our analysis also revealed that the polarization properties of the scattered light can provide valuable information about the exoplanet's atmosphere and its potential for hosting life. We demonstrated that the model can account for the effects of polarization on the detectability of exoplanets and provide predictions based on the polarization properties of the target and background objects. Overall, our study provides a framework for predicting exoplanet observability in complex astrophysical contexts and highlights the potential of machine learning techniques for improving exoplanet detection.

In 1904, while experimenting with high-speed photography, Lucien Bull
recorded a pellet passing through a soap bubble. We investigate the dynamics
that allow for a rigid body to pass through a hemispherical soap film without
rupturing it. In this fluid dynamics video spheres were dropped from rest above
a hemispherical soap film. At impact, the soap film stretches into a cavity
around the sphere. As the sphere continues to descend, the film cavity pinches
off and the film returns to its initial hemispherical shape. Upon closer
observation of the film-sphere-air interface, the stability of the soap film
appears to arise through a balance between the forces of the sphere inertia and
the film tension. Therefore the relevant experimental parameter is the Weber
number: We=rho*2*g*h*R*sigma, where R is the sphere radius and h is the height
that the sphere is dropped from. We vary the sphere radius and velocity to
provide a range of Weber numbers in order to investigate the dependence of film
stability. Three subtly distinct regimes arise across the observed experimental
range of Weber numbers. The first regime is demonstrated (We<3200) by a cavity
shape that resembles a catenoid which pinches off both near the sphere and the
hemispherical surface. The second regime is demonstrated (3200<We<6100) by a
uniformly narrowing cavity resembling an inverted cone that pinches off near
the sphere. The third regime initially appears similar to the second but the
greater sphere inertia (6100<We) elongates the cavity shape and causes
pinch-off and cavity collapse to be non-uniform in nature.

text: This study investigates the impact of seasonal light variations on cyanobacterial competition, aiming to determine which season offers the most advantageous conditions for different cyanobacterial species. Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic organisms that play a crucial role in aquatic ecosystems, affected significantly by changes in light availability across seasons. The research focuses on three representative species Microcystis aeruginosa, Anabaena flos-aquae, and Planktothrix agardhii. Using a controlled experimental setup, these species were cultured under simulated seasonal light conditions reflective of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Growth rates, chlorophyll-a concentrations, and photosynthetic efficiency were measured to assess competitive dominance and adaptability. Findings reveal that seasonal light variations notably influence cyanobacterial growth dynamics, with each species responding differently to changes in day length and light intensity. In contrast, Anabaena flos-aquae showed optimal performance in spring, while Planktothrix agardhii demonstrated resilience and competitive advantage in autumn and winter. These differences highlight the adaptive strategies employed by cyanobacteria to exploit seasonal niches, impacting their distribution and ecological roles in freshwater ecosystems. The conclusion emphasizes the importance of understanding seasonal light effects on cyanobacterial competition to predict bloom occurrences and inform management practices in response to climate change. This research contributes valuable insights into the ecological dynamics of cyanobacteria, supporting strategies to mitigate their adverse impacts on water quality and biodiversity.

Saturn's rings are rock-poor, containing 90%-95% ice by mass. As a group,
Saturn's moons interior to and including Tethys are also about 90% ice. Tethys
itself contains <6% rock by mass, in contrast to its similar-mass outer
neighbor Dione, which contains >40% rock. Here we simulate the evolution of a
massive primordial ice-rich ring and the production of satellites as ring
material spreads beyond the Roche limit. We describe the Roche-interior ring
with an analytic model, and use an N-body code to describe material beyond the
Roche limit. We track the accretion and interactions of spawned satellites,
including tidal interaction with the planet, assuming a tidal dissipation
factor for Saturn of $Q~10^4$. We find that ring torques and capture of moons
into mutual resonances produce a system of ice-rich inner moons that extends
outward to approximately Tethys's orbit in $10^9$ years, even with relatively
slow orbital expansion due to tides. The resulting mass and semimajor axis
distribution of spawned moons resembles that of Mimas, Enceladus, and Tethys.
We estimate the mass of rock delivered to the moons by external cometary
impactors during a late heavy bombardment. We find that the inner moons receive
a mass in rock comparable to their current total rock content, while Dione and
Rhea receive an order-of-magnitude less rock than their current rock content.
This suggests that external ontamination may have been the primary source of
rock in the inner moons, and that Dione and Rhea formed from much more
rock-rich source material. Reproducing the distribution of rock among the
current inner moons is challenging, and appears to require large impactors
stochasticity and/or the presence of some rock in the initial ring.

Furthermore, the results underscore the potential of composite materials in achieving desirable electromagnetic characteristics, paving the way for future innovations in microwave engineering. problem (IBVP) relative to a large class of quasilinear hyperbolic systems, in

for the generic linear transport equation on $S_{t_1 } = (0,t_1 ) \times G$
with uniformly locally Lipschitz data and associated vector field in $L_{x_d
}^{-} (S_{t_1 } \times \mathbb{R}^p )$ (this cone of $L_t^\infty (0,t_1
;L_{(x,y_{loc} )}^\infty (G \times \mathbb{R}^p ))^d $ is not cointained in

text: This study presents an advanced method for simulating particle transport through complex geometries using Vertical-Likelihood Monte Carlo (VLMC). The method aims to improve accuracy and efficiency in simulations by incorporating likelihood weighting techniques. Problematically, traditional Monte Carlo methods can suffer from statistical fluctuations when dealing with regions of low density, leading to biased results. Our approach addresses this issue by dynamically adjusting weights based on the likelihood of particles reaching their current position, thereby enhancing the convergence rate towards the true solution. Results demonstrate that VLMC significantly reduces computational time and improves accuracy compared to standard Monte Carlo simulations, particularly in scenarios involving heterogeneous media. Key methodologies include the implementation of a novel likelihood estimator and the development of adaptive sampling strategies tailored to the geometry and physics of the problem at hand. These innovations enable more reliable predictions in radiation transport applications, such as those found in nuclear engineering and medical imaging.

text: The stability of stagnation in accretion shock waves plays a crucial role in understanding astrophysical phenomena such as stellar formation, supernovae, and the growth of massive stars. This research investigates the dynamics of an expanding accretion shock wave manifest when inflowing material from an accretion disk collides with the surface of a compact object or dense stellar region. The objective is to determine the stability conditions of stagnation zones formed in such scenarios. Utilizing a combination of analytic modeling and computational simulations, this study explores the influence of variable parameters such as accretion rate, shock wave velocity, and thermal properties of the inflowing material. The methodology involves the application of hydrodynamic equations to model shock dynamics and linear stability analysis to assess perturbations in the shock structure. Key findings reveal that the stability of stagnation is strongly dependent on the accretion rate; higher rates tend to destabilize the stagnation region, leading to oscillatory behavior and potential fragmentation. Conversely, slower accretion stabilizes the shock front, promoting consistent energy dissipation and thermal equilibrium. The impact of initial conditions appears to significantly influence the resultant stability, with a parameter space delineating stable from unstable configurations. Conclusively, the research provides critical insights into the conditions required for maintaining shock-induced stability in accretion processes, thereby contributing to the broader understanding of shock wave behavior in astrophysical settings. These findings have implications for modeling the formation and evolution of compact astronomical objects under varying environmental conditions.

We employ a combination of theoretical models and numerical simulations to explore potential energy transfers, including magnetic reconnection in the magnetosphere and changes in the accretion flow dynamics. Our results indicate that magnetic reconnection plays a significant role in transferring angular momentum, driven by the strong differential rotation near the neutron star surface. We also find evidence supporting a connection between the accretion flow and the glitch mechanism, suggesting that variations in the accretion rate can influence the rotational state of the pulsar. Key methodologies include detailed modeling of the magnetospheric environment, coupled fluid dynamical simulations, and statistical analysis of glitch data. These findings contribute to our understanding of the physical processes governing pulsar glitches and provide insights into the complex interplay between the star's magnetic field and its accretion environment.

We present a comprehensive spectral analysis of the high mass X-ray binary
(HMXB) pulsar Centaurus X-3 with the Suzaku observatory covering nearly one
orbital period. The light curve shows the presence of extended dips which are
rarely seen in HMXBs. These dips are seen up to as high as ~40 keV. The pulsar
spectra during the eclipse, out-of-eclipse, and dips are found to be well
described by a partial covering power-law model with high energy cut-off and
three Gaussian functions for 6.4 keV, 6.7 keV, and 6.97 keV iron emission
lines. The dips in the light curve can be explained by the presence of an
additional absorption component with high column density and covering fraction,
the values of which are not significant during the rest of the orbital phases.
The iron line parameters during the dips and eclipse are significantly
different compared to those during the rest of the observation. During the
dips, the iron line intensities are found to be lesser by a factor of 2--3 with
significant increase in the line equivalent widths. However, the continuum flux
at the corresponding orbital phase is estimated to be lesser by more than an
order of magnitude. Similarities in the changes in the iron line flux and
equivalent widths during the dips and eclipse segments suggests the dipping
activity in Cen X-3 is caused by obscuration of the neutron star by dense
matter, probably structures in the outer region of the accretion disk, as in
case of dipping low mass X-ray binaries.

text: We investigated the challenges of achieving predictable real-time performance on multi-core platforms, where the inherent variability in task scheduling and thread execution poses significant obstacles to reliable and efficient system operation. Our research focused on developing a novel scheduling framework that incorporates a combination of static and dynamic scheduling techniques to mitigate the effects of thread scheduling overhead and improve system predictability.  Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrated the efficacy of our framework in reducing the variability in task execution times on multi-core systems, resulting in a significant improvement in overall system predictability. Our approach, which leverages a novel feedback control mechanism to adapt to changes in the system's workload and scheduling patterns, has been shown to maintain a consistent level of performance across a wide range of scenarios.  Key findings from our study reveal that the proposed framework can effectively reduce the variability in task execution times by up to 50% compared to traditional scheduling approaches. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the framework can maintain a predictable level of performance even in the presence of high levels of variability and uncertainty in the system's workload and scheduling patterns.  Our research contributes to the development of more reliable and efficient multi-core systems, which are critical for a wide range of applications, including real-time systems, embedded systems, and high-performance computing. By providing a framework for predictable real-time performance on multi-core platforms, our work has the potential to enable the widespread adoption of these systems in a variety of industries and applications.

In transiting planetary systems, the angle between the orbital angular
momentum and the stellar spin is usually constrained through the
Rossiter-McLaughlin effect observed in radial velocity and can be subject to
large uncertainties, especially for hot stars (T_eff > 6250 K). It is thus
interesting to have an alternative method to constrain the value of the
obliquity and to detect companions that might have disturbed the orbit of the
planet. We show how the long-term variations in the transit duration (TDV) can
be used to constrain the obliquity of the stellar rotation axis. We introduce a
simple theory to express the secular variations in the orbital elements and
their effects on the TDVs with a general formulation valid for both oblique and
eccentric systems. Parameters or orbital elements that cannot be directly
measured, such as the longitude of the ascending node of the orbit, are avoided
thus allowing us a straightforward application. We compute the expected TDVs
for the presently known transiting systems, adopting their parameters found in
the literature. Considering the capabilities of the present or next generation
space-borne telescopes, we point out the systems that could be readily observed
and discuss the constraints derivable on their fundamental parameters. TDVs can
be used to constrain the obliquity of the stars (and possibly of the planets in
systems younger than 10 -- 100 Myr), giving information about the formation
scenarios, the strength of the tidal coupling, and the internal structure of
both the stars and the planets. Moreover, they can provide an indirect
indication of the presence of other bodies, even with a mass comparable with
that of the Earth, because they give rise to additional contributions to the
nodal precession.

On general grounds, one may argue that a black hole stops radiation at the
Planck mass, where the radiated energy is comparable to the black hole's mass.
And also, it has been argued that there would be a "wormhole-like" structure,
known as "space-time foam", due to large fluctuations below the Planck length.
In this paper, as an explicit example, we consider an exact classical solution
which represents nicely those two properties in a recently proposed quantum
gravity model based on different scaling dimensions between space and time
coordinates. The solution, called "Black Wormhole", consists of two different
states, depending on its mass M and an IR parameter omega: For the black hole
state, a non-traversable wormhole occupies the interior region of the black
hole around the singularity at the origin, whereas for the wormhole state, the
interior wormhole is exposed to an outside observer as the black hole horizon
is disappeared from evaporation. The black hole state becomes thermodynamically
stable as it approaches to the merge point where the interior wormhole throat
and the black hole horizon merges, and the Hawking temperature vanishes at the
exact merge point. This solution suggests the "Generalized Cosmic Censorship"
by the existence of a wormhole-like structure which protects the naked
singularity even after the black hole evaporation. One could understand the
would-be wormholes inside the black hole horizon as the results of microscopic
wormholes created by "negative" energy quanta which have entered the black hole
horizon in Hawking radiation processes: The quantum black hole could be a
wormhole factory. It is found that this speculative picture may be consistent
with the recent "ER=EPR" proposal for resolving the recent black hole
entanglement debates.

text: We investigated the triangular flow of thermal photons in heavy-ion collisions, utilizing an event-by-event hydrodynamic model for 2.76A TeV Pb+Pb collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Through a detailed analysis of the model's output, we observed a significant enhancement of the triangular flow of thermal photons, which is a measure of the system's collective behavior. This phenomenon is attributed to the hydrodynamic flow of the QCD plasma, which gives rise to a non-trivial angular dependence of the photon emission.  Our results indicate that the triangular flow of thermal photons is strongly correlated with the eccentricity of the event-by-event hydrodynamic flow, suggesting a direct link between the collective behavior of the system and the thermal photon emission. We also found that the triangular flow of thermal photons is enhanced in the most central and peripheral regions of the collision, where the hydrodynamic flow is most pronounced.  The key to our findings lies in the interplay between the hydrodynamic flow and the thermal photon emission, which is mediated by the interactions between the QCD plasma and the thermal photons. By incorporating these interactions into the hydrodynamic model, we are able to reproduce the observed enhancement of the triangular flow of thermal photons, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics underlying heavy-ion collisions.

text: The potential of three remote sites, Ali in Tibet, Dome A in Antarctica, and Summit Camp in Greenland, has been evaluated for millimeter-wave (mm-wave) astronomical observations using NASA's MERRA-2 reanalysis data. As the atmospheric conditions at the observation site are crucial for mm-wave astronomy, where the measurements are sensitive to atmospheric moisture and temperature, this study aims to compare the climatological suitability of these sites for long-term mm-wave observatories. The MERRA-2 reanalysis data from 1980 to 2020 was analyzed to assess the precipitable water vapor (PWV) and surface temperature, the primary indicators for mm-wave observation quality. Our analysis revealed that Dome A offers the lowest average PWV levels, making it the most favorable site among the three for mm-wave observations. Ali and Summit Camp showed slightly higher PWV levels but remained competitive for certain mm-wave applications. Surface temperature analysis indicated that while Dome A's extreme cold may pose challenges for instrumentation, it contributes to reduced thermal noise in observations. The diurnal and seasonal variations at Ali and Summit Camp offer logistical advantages but come with increased atmospheric instability compared to Dome A's stability. Our findings suggest that while Dome A is the optimal site regarding atmospheric conditions, logistical and operational ease remain critical considerations in site selection. The study provides a comprehensive climatic assessment to inform decision-making for future mm-wave observational facilities and underscores the benefits of using reanalysis data for site evaluation in the absence of long-term, direct observational datasets.

text: This study investigates the reduced effective secondary electron emission yield from a velvet surface, focusing on its potential applications in various fields, including electron microscopy and vacuum technology. Previous research suggests that the roughness and microstructure of velvet surfaces can significantly influence secondary electron emission (SEE) characteristics. However, a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms behind this phenomenon remains elusive. To shed light on this, we employed a combined experimental and theoretical approach. Using a scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an in-situ secondary electron yield detector, we obtained experimental data by measuring the SEE yield from a velvet sample. Simultaneously, we employed density functional theory (DFT) calculations to explore the atomic-scale structure of velvet fibers and their electronic properties. Our findings reveal that the nanostructure of velvet fibers contributes to a reduced effective SEE yield through the presence of a unique nanoscale morphology. Specifically, the microscopic structure of velvet fibers comprises a large number of closely spaced, highly curved surfaces, which result in the scattering and trapping of secondary electrons. Moreover, DFT calculations suggest that the material properties of velvet, such as its work function and electron affinity, contribute to the observed reduction in effective SEE yield. Our results not only advance the fundamental understanding of SEE behavior from complex surfaces but also provide insights for the design of future materials and technologies tailored to optimize SEE yield in specific applications.

text: This research explores the application of continuous measurement in quantum tomography, focusing on the full hyperfine manifold of atomic spins. The hyperfine structure of atomic spins is a complex and sensitive phenomenon, where subtle changes in magnetic fields can significantly affect the spin states. Traditional quantum tomography methods often rely on discrete measurements, which may not be sufficient to fully characterize the hyperfine manifold.   The objective of this study is to develop a novel approach to quantum tomography that leverages continuous measurement on an ensemble of atoms. By analyzing the correlations between the atomic spins, we can reconstruct the full hyperfine manifold with unprecedented precision. This approach allows for the simultaneous measurement of multiple hyperfine transitions, enabling the accurate determination of the hyperfine structure.  The methodology employed in this research involves the use of a custom-built experimental setup, where a large ensemble of atoms is subjected to a continuous magnetic field. The atomic spins are measured using a combination of magnetic resonance and optical spectroscopy techniques. The correlations between the spins are then analyzed using advanced signal processing algorithms, which reconstruct the full hyperfine manifold.   Key findings of this study include the successful reconstruction of the hyperfine manifold with high accuracy, as well as the demonstration of improved sensitivity and resolution compared to traditional discrete measurement methods.   In conclusion, this research demonstrates the potential of continuous measurement in quantum tomography for the full hyperfine manifold of atomic spins. The results have significant implications for the study of atomic physics, quantum information processing, and the development of new quantum technologies.

Generalized parton distribution (GPD) contains rich information of partons in
a hadron, including transverse profile, and is also non-perturbative
information necessary in describing a variety of hard processes, such as meson
leptoproduction and double deeply virtual Compton scattering (DDVCS). In order
to unveil non-perturbative aspects of GPD, we study DDVCS at small $x$ in
gravitational dual description. Using the complex spin $j$-plane representation
of DDVCS amplitude, we show that GPD is well-defined and can be extracted from
the amplitude even in the strong coupling regime. It also turns out that the
saddle point value in the $j$-plane representation plays an important role;
there are two phases in the imaginary part of the amplitude of DDVCS and GPD,
depending on relative position of the saddle point and the leading pole in the
$j$-plane, and crossover between them is induced by the change of the
kinematical variables. The saddle point value also directly controls
kinematical variable dependence of many observables in one of the two phases,
and indeed the dependence is qualitatively in nice agreement with HERA
measurements. Such observation that the gravity dual shares basic properties of
the real world QCD suggests that information from BFKL theory might be used to
reduce error in the gravity dual predictions of the form factor and of GPD.
This article also serves as a brief summery of a preprint arXiv:1105.2999.

Context. The Galactic chemical evolution of sulphur is still under debate. At
low metallicities some studies find no correlation between [S/Fe] and [Fe/H],
others find [S/Fe] increasing towards lower metallicities, and still others
find a combination of the two. Each scenario has different implications for the
Galactic chemical evolution of sulphur.
  Aims. To contribute to the discussion on the Galactic chemical evolution of
sulphur by deriving sulphur abundances from non-LTE insensitive spectral
diagnostics in Disk and Halo stars with homogeneously determined stellar
parameters.
  Methods. We derive Teff from photometric colours, logg from stellar
isochrones and Bayesian estimation, and [Fe/H] and [S/Fe] from spectrum
synthesis. We derive [S/Fe] from the [S i] 1082 nm line in 39 mostly cool and
metal-poor giants, using 1D LTE MARCS model atmospheres to model our
high-resolution NIR spectra obtained with the VLT, NOT and Gemini South
telescopes.
  Results. We derive homogeneous stellar parameters for 29 stars. Our results
argue for a chemical evolution of sulphur that is typical for alpha-elements,
contrary to some previous studies. Our abundances are systematically higher by
about 0.1 dex in comparison to other studies that arrived at similar
conclusions using other sulphur diagnostics.
  Conclusions. We find the [S i] line to be a valuable diagnostic of sulphur
abundances in cool giants down to [Fe/H] ~ -2.3. We argue that a homogeneous
determination of stellar parameters is necessary, since the derived abundances
are sensitive to them. Our results ([S/Fe]) show reasonable agreement with
predictions of contemporary models of Galactic chemical evolution. In these
models sulphur is predominantly created in massive stars by oxygen burning, and
ejected in the ISM during Type II SNe explosions. Systematic differences with
previous studies likely fall within modelling uncertainties.

text: The Interstellar Medium (ISM) is a vast, gaseous and dusty environment that pervades the Galactic disk. Its complex structure, consisting of a multitude of gas and dust components, poses significant challenges to our understanding of the ISM's physical and chemical properties. In particular, the intricate relationship between the distribution, composition, and abundance of dust and gas in the Diffuse Interstellar Medium (DIM) remains an open research question. Our study investigates the spatial variations of dust and gas in the DIM towards two different sightlines the Taurus Molecular Cloud complex (TMC) and the Rho Ophiuchi Molecular Cloud (ROMC). We used a multi-technique approach, combining the near-infrared spectroscopy observations of the Spitzer Space Telescope with the optical extinction measurements from the 2MASS survey. By comparing the extinction curve shapes and gas-to-dust ratios, we found significant differences between the TMC and ROMC sightlines. Specifically, we detected a flatter extinction curve in the TMC and a steeper one in the ROMC, which we attribute to different levels of dust settling and gas depletion. Additionally, we derived gas-to-dust ratios that vary by a factor of two between the two sightlines. These results suggest that the dust and gas distribution and abundance in the DIM can be significantly influenced by the specific conditions of the surrounding molecular cloud complexes. Our findings contribute to the ongoing research on the ISM's structure and composition, shedding light on the intricate interplay between dust and gas in the DIM. The results of this study can also aid in the interpretation of observations from future missions, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, providing valuable insights into the physical and chemical properties of the ISM.

text: In this study, we investigate the evolving dynamics of Stops and MET (Metaphoric Engagement Theory) within contemporary contexts, aiming to elucidate their synergistic relationship and implications for effective communication. Our results indicate a significant enhancement in cognitive retention and emotional connection when employing carefully timed Stops in conjunction with metaphoric language. We utilized structured interviews and focus groups to gather qualitative insights, supported by quantitative measures such as comprehension tests and engagement metrics. The findings demonstrate that the intentional integration of Stops facilitates deeper processing of metaphors, resulting in a more impactful communication experience.  We address the pressing problem of ineffective communication in various fields, particularly in educational and corporate settings, where the potential for deeper understanding and engagement often remains unexploited. By highlighting the necessity of pauses in leveraging metaphoric discourse, we propose a model for practitioners seeking to refine their communicative strategies.  Our exploration contributes to the broader understanding of cognitive linguistics and communication theory, suggesting that the interplay between form (Stops) and content (MET) shapes future practices. Ultimately, our research underscores the transformative potential of combining these elements to foster more meaningful interactions across diverse audiences.

Red Supergiants (RSGs) are cool (~4000K), highly luminous stars (L - 10^5
Lsun), and are among the brightest near-infrared (NIR) sources in star-forming
galaxies. This makes them powerful probes of the properties of their host
galaxies, such as kinematics and chemical abundances. We have developed a
technique whereby metallicities of RSGs may be extracted from a narrow spectral
window around 1{\mu}m from only moderate resolution data. The method is
therefore extremely efficient, allowing stars at large distances to be studied,
and so has tremendous potential for extragalactic abundance work. Here, we
present an abundance study of the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and
SMC respectively) using samples of 9-10 RSGs in each. We find average
abundances for the two galaxies of [Z]LMC = -0.37 +/- 0.14 and [Z]SMC = -0.53
+/- 0.16 (with respect to a Solar metallicity of Zsun=0.012). These values are
consistent with other studies of young stars in these galaxies, and though our
result for the SMC may appear high it is consistent with recent studies of hot
stars which find 0.5-0.8dex below Solar. Our best-fit temperatures are on the
whole consistent with those from fits to the optical-infrared spectral energy
distributions, which is remarkable considering the narrow spectral range being
studied. Combined with our recent study of RSGs in the Galactic cluster Per
OB1, these results indicate that this technique performs well over a range of
metallicities, paving the way for forthcoming studies of more distant galaxies
beyond the Local Group.

text: In our study, we investigated the impact of antipsychotic medications on brain networks in schizophrenia patients compared to healthy controls. We recruited a cohort of individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia and an age-matched control group and employed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess resting-state brain connectivity before and after a 12-week treatment period with second-generation antipsychotics. Our analysis focused on the default mode network (DMN), salience network (SN), and central executive network (CEN), which are pivotal in cognitive and emotional processing.  Results demonstrated significant alterations in connectivity patterns within these networks attributable to antipsychotic treatment. Specifically, we observed enhanced connectivity in the DMN among treated patients, indicative of improved self-referential processing, alongside a reduction in connectivity within the SN, suggesting a dampening of emotional reactivity. Notably, CEN connectivity remained relatively stable, implying a preserved capacity for cognitive control. Furthermore, we identified a correlation between changes in network connectivity and clinical symptom improvement as measured by the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS).  Our findings underscore the therapeutic potential of antipsychotic medications in modulating dysfunctional brain networks associated with schizophrenia. We propose that these alterations may reflect underlying neurobiological mechanisms by which antipsychotic drugs facilitate symptom alleviation. This work contributes to our understanding of the neural underpinnings of schizophrenia and opens avenues for future research into personalized treatment strategies based on neuroimaging biomarkers.

We report measurements of the diffusion of atomic hydrogen in single
crystalline VO2 micro/nanobeams by direct exposure to atomic hydrogen, without
catalyst. The atomic hydrogen is generated by a hot filament, and the doping
process takes place at moderate temperature (373 K). Undoped VO2 has a
metal-to-insulator phase transition at ~340 K between a high-temperature,
rutile, metallic phase and a low-temperature, monoclinic, insulating phase with
a resistance exhibiting a semiconductor-like temperature dependence. Atomic
hydrogenation results in stabilization of the metallic phase of VO2
micro/nanobeams down to 2 K, the lowest point we could reach in our measurement
setup. Based on observing the movement of the hydrogen diffusion front in
single crystalline VO2 beams, we estimate the diffusion constant for hydrogen
along the c-axis of the rutile phase to be 6.7 x 10^{-10} cm^2/s at
approximately 373 K, exceeding the value in isostructural TiO2 by ~ 38x.
Moreover, we find that the diffusion constant along the c-axis of the rutile
phase exceeds that along the equivalent a-axis of the monoclinic phase by at
least three orders of magnitude. This remarkable change in kinetics must
originate from the distortion of the "channels" when the unit cell doubles
along this direction upon cooling into the monoclinic structure. Ab initio
calculation results are in good agreement with the experimental trends in the
relative kinetics of the two phases. This raises the possibility of a
switchable membrane for hydrogen transport.

text: In this study, we investigate Relaxed Highest Weight Modules arising from $\mathcal{D}$-Modules on the Kashiwara Flag Scheme. The problem this work addresses is the construction and analysis of these modules within the framework of algebraic geometry and representation theory. Our results demonstrate the existence of a correspondence between certain $\mathcal{D}$-Modules on the Kashiwara Flag Scheme and Relaxed Highest Weight Modules, providing insights into their structures and properties.  The key idea underlying this research is to utilize the theory of $\mathcal{D}$-Modules to study representation theory through the lens of algebraic geometry. We employ a combination of techniques from commutative algebra, algebraic geometry, and representation theory to establish the relationship between $\mathcal{D}$-Modules on the Kashiwara Flag Scheme and Relaxed Highest Weight Modules. Additionally, we leverage concepts from category theory to draw connections between these two seemingly disparate areas of mathematics.  Our methodology involves a rigorous examination of the functorial properties of $\mathcal{D}$-Modules and their relationships with representation theory, particularly in the context of highest weight modules. By establishing this connection, we are able to shed light on the intricate interplay between $\mathcal{D}$-Modules and Relaxed Highest Weight Modules, offering a new perspective on the structures underlying these mathematical objects.

We investigate galaxy formation in models with dark matter (DM) constituted
by sterile neutrinos. Given their large parameter space, defined by the
combinations of sterile neutrino mass $m_{\nu}$ and mixing parameter
$\sin^2(2\theta)$ with active neutrinos, we focus on models with $m_{\nu}=7$
keV, consistent with the tentative 3.5 keV line detected in several X-ray
spectra of clusters and galaxies. We consider i) two resonant production models
with $\sin^2(2\theta)=5\,10^{-11}$ and $\sin^2(2\theta)=2\,10^{-10}$, to cover
the range of mixing parameter consistent with the 3.5 keV line; ii) two
scalar-decay models, representative of the two possible cases characterizing
such a scenario: a freeze-in and a freeze-out case. We also consider thermal
Warm Dark Matter with particle mass $m_X=3$ keV. Using a semi-analytic model,
we compare the predictions for the different DM scenarios with a wide set of
observables. We find that comparing the predicted evolution of the stellar mass
function, the abundance of satellites of Milky Way-like galaxies, and the
global star formation history of galaxies with observations does not allow to
disentangle the effects of the baryonic physics from those related to the
different DM models. On the other hand, the distribution of the stellar-to-halo
mass ratios, the abundance of faint galaxies in the UV luminosity function at
$z\gtrsim 6$, and the specific star formation and age distribution of local,
low-mass galaxies constitute potential probes for the considered DM scenarios.
We discuss how next observations with upcoming facilities will enable to rule
out or to strongly support DM models based on sterile neutrinos.

We explore the impact of star formation and thermal stellar feedback on the
giant molecular cloud (GMC) population forming in a M83-type barred spiral
galaxy. We compare three high-resolution simulations (1.5 pc cell size) with
different star formation/feedback models: one with no star formation, one with
star formation but no feedback, and one with star formation and thermal energy
injection. We analyze the resulting population of clouds, finding that we can
identify the same population of massive, virialized clouds and transient,
low-surface density clouds found in our previous work (that did not include
star formation or feedback). Star formation and feedback can affect the mix of
clouds we identify. In particular, star formation alone simply converts dense
cloud gas into stars with only a small change to the cloud populations,
principally resulting in a slight decrease in the transient population.
Feedback, however, has a stronger impact: while it is not generally sufficient
to entirely destroy the clouds, it does eject gas out of them, increasing the
gas density in the inter-cloud region. This decreases the number of massive
clouds, but substantially increases the transient cloud population. We also
find that feedback tends to drive a net radial inflow of massive clouds,
leading to an increase in the star formation rate in the bar region. We examine
a number of possible reasons for this and conclude that it is possible that the
drag force from the enhanced intercloud density could be responsible.

text: In the realm of high-energy particle physics, the polarization of top quarks produced in decays of the W and Z bosons has been a subject of intense research. Top quarks, the heaviest elementary particle in the standard model, play a crucial role in understanding the electroweak sector and the mechanism of mass generation. This study focuses on the polarization of top quarks produced in arbitrary frames, which is essential for extracting valuable information from experimental data.  The objective of this paper is to analyze the polarization of top quarks in particle decays by calculating the decay amplitudes in various reference frames. Using the standard model, we employ the helicity amplitude formalism to compute the decay amplitudes for the processes W+- → tb and Z0 → tb, considering both the left- and right-handed top quark couplings to the W and Z bosons.  We derive expressions for the decay amplitudes in various frames including the W- and Z-boson rest frames, the top quark rest frame, and the helicity frame. These results can be applied to various experimental analyses and phenomenological studies to understand the production and decay mechanisms of top quarks.  Our key findings reveal that the polarization of top quarks depends on the reference frame and the specific decay channels. For instance, in the W-boson rest frame, the top quark is predominantly left-handed, while in the helicity frame, it exhibits a more complex polarization pattern with contributions from both left- and right-handed components.  In conclusion, this work provides a comprehensive analysis of the polarization of top quarks produced in particle decays in various frames, shedding light on the fundamental properties of top quarks and their role in the electroweak sector. The findings of this study can be employed in ongoing and future experimental efforts aimed at improving our understanding of the top quark system.

text: In this work, we investigate the concept of Loop Quasi-Invariant Chunk Motion, specifically through the lens of peeling with statement composition. Our primary objective is to address the challenges associated with maintaining loop invariants while ensuring the efficient execution of dynamic systems. We develop a methodological framework that incorporates peeling techniques to decompose complex statements into manageable chunks, facilitating a robust representation of loop structures.   Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly enhances the stability of quasi-invariant properties during runtime modifications of loop parameters. By applying our framework to a series of benchmark algorithms, we observe a marked improvement in both computational efficiency and the preservation of desired properties in loop execution. We employ rigorous formal analysis combined with empirical testing to validate our claims, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of the underlying dynamics at play.  Key contributions of this study include a systematic algorithm for peeling statements, which we integrate with a modular design paradigm to enhance code maintainability. Furthermore, we explore the implications of our findings on existing programming languages and frameworks, emphasizing the potential for broader application in diverse computational contexts. Overall, our research not only elucidates the mechanics behind loop quasi-invariance but also provides practical methodologies for programmers and researchers seeking to optimize dynamic system behaviors while retaining essential invariant characteristics.

Space-time adaptive processing (STAP) is an effective tool for detecting a
moving target in the airborne radar system. Due to the fast-changing clutter
scenario and/or non side-looking configuration, the stationarity of the
training data is destroyed such that the statistical-based methods suffer
performance degradation. Direct data domain (D3) methods avoid non-stationary
training data and can effectively suppress the clutter within the test cell.
However, this benefit comes at the cost of a reduced system degree of freedom
(DOF), which results in performance loss. In this paper, by exploiting the
intrinsic sparsity of the spectral distribution, a new direct data domain
approach using sparse representation (D3SR) is proposed, which seeks to
estimate the high-resolution space-time spectrum with only the test cell. The
simulation of both side-looking and non side-looking cases has illustrated the
effectiveness of the D3SR spectrum estimation using focal underdetermined
system solution (FOCUSS) and norm minimization. Then the clutter covariance
matrix (CCM) and the corresponding adaptive filter can be effectively obtained.
Since D3SR maintains the full system DOF, it can achieve better performance of
output signal-clutter-ratio (SCR) and minimum detectable velocity (MDV) than
current D3 methods, e.g., direct data domain least squares (D3LS). Thus D3SR is
more effective against the range-dependent clutter and interference in the
non-stationary clutter scenario.

Let ${\rm ind}(G)$ be the number of independent sets in a graph $G$. We show
that if $G$ has maximum degree at most $5$ then $$ {\rm ind}(G) \leq 2^{{\rm
iso}(G)} \prod_{uv \in E(G)} {\rm ind}(K_{d(u),d(v)})^{\frac{1}{d(u)d(v)}} $$
(where $d(\cdot)$ is vertex degree, ${\rm iso}(G)$ is the number of isolated
vertices in $G$ and $K_{a,b}$ is the complete bipartite graph with $a$ vertices
in one partition class and $b$ in the other), with equality if and only if each
connected component of $G$ is either a complete bipartite graph or a single
vertex. This bound (for all $G$) was conjectured by Kahn.
  A corollary of our result is that if $G$ is $d$-regular with $1 \leq d \leq
5$ then $$ {\rm ind}(G) \leq \left(2^{d+1}-1\right)^\frac{|V(G)|}{2d}, $$ with
equality if and only if $G$ is a disjoint union of $V(G)/2d$ copies of
$K_{d,d}$. This bound (for all $d$) was conjectured by Alon and Kahn and
recently proved for all $d$ by the second author, without the characterization
of the extreme cases.
  Our proof involves a reduction to a finite search. For graphs with maximum
degree at most $3$ the search could be done by hand, but for the case of
maximum degree $4$ or $5$, a computer is needed.

text: The abstract focuses on the application of infinite-dimensional compressed sensing techniques for function interpolation in settings where data dimensions are unbounded. This study explores how traditional compressed sensing principles can be extended to handle functions defined over infinite domains, such as in signal processing or machine learning applications involving high-dimensional data. The primary objective is to develop methods capable of efficiently reconstructing functions from a limited number of measurements, thereby reducing computational complexity and storage requirements.  The methodology employed involves theoretical analysis combined with numerical experiments. Theoretical foundations include leveraging properties of Banach spaces and frames to establish conditions under which function recovery is possible. Numerical experiments utilize both synthetic datasets and real-world applications to validate the proposed approaches. The key findings highlight the effectiveness of the developed methods in accurately interpolating functions across various infinite-dimensional settings, demonstrating improvements in reconstruction quality and computational efficiency compared to existing finite-dimensional techniques.  In conclusion, this research advances the field by providing robust theoretical guarantees and practical algorithms for infinite-dimensional compressed sensing, paving the way for novel applications in areas requiring the analysis of high-dimensional data.

text: We present the culmination of a comprehensive upgrade process for the LARS (Laser Absolute Reference Spectrograph) system, a cutting-edge instrument designed for precise solar observations. The LARS system has undergone significant enhancements, transforming it from a prototype to a turn-key, fully operational system. Our efforts focused on addressing the limitations of the initial design, which hindered its scalability and reliability.  Through extensive testing and refinement, we successfully integrated advanced technologies, including high-fidelity laser sources, precision optics, and sophisticated spectrography algorithms. This upgrade enabled the LARS system to achieve unprecedented levels of accuracy, precision, and spectral resolution, rendering it an invaluable asset for solar research.  Key innovations in the upgraded LARS system include the incorporation of advanced wavelength calibration techniques, optimized spectrography settings, and enhanced data processing capabilities. These advancements have significantly improved the system's ability to detect subtle changes in solar spectral lines, enabling researchers to gain deeper insights into solar activity and its impact on the Earth's atmosphere.  The upgraded LARS system has been rigorously tested and validated through a series of rigorous experiments, demonstrating its exceptional performance and reliability. Our results demonstrate the system's potential to revolutionize the field of solar spectroscopy, enabling scientists to make more accurate predictions and better understand the complex dynamics of the solar atmosphere.

In order to find Nash-equilibria for two-player zero-sum games where each
player plays combinatorial objects like spanning trees, matchings etc, we
consider two online learning algorithms: the online mirror descent (OMD)
algorithm and the multiplicative weights update (MWU) algorithm. The OMD
algorithm requires the computation of a certain Bregman projection, that has
closed form solutions for simple convex sets like the Euclidean ball or the
simplex. However, for general polyhedra one often needs to exploit the general
machinery of convex optimization. We give a novel primal-style algorithm for
computing Bregman projections on the base polytopes of polymatroids. Next, in
the case of the MWU algorithm, although it scales logarithmically in the number
of pure strategies or experts $N$ in terms of regret, the algorithm takes time
polynomial in $N$; this especially becomes a problem when learning
combinatorial objects. We give a general recipe to simulate the multiplicative
weights update algorithm in time polynomial in their natural dimension. This is
useful whenever there exists a polynomial time generalized counting oracle
(even if approximate) over these objects. Finally, using the combinatorial
structure of symmetric Nash-equilibria (SNE) when both players play bases of
matroids, we show that these can be found with a single projection or convex
minimization (without using online learning).

text: This research delves into the realm of statistical inference, examining the certainty provided by two distinct approaches. Through rigorous analysis and comparison, we aim to elucidate the strengths and limitations of frequentist and Bayesian methodologies in providing quantifiable levels of confidence in statistical conclusions. Utilizing simulated data sets and theoretical frameworks, we have assessed the accuracy and robustness of inferences drawn from both paradigms. Our results demonstrate that while frequentist methods offer valuable tools for hypothesis testing and parameter estimation, Bayesian approaches excel in incorporating prior knowledge and updating beliefs based on new evidence. By highlighting the nuances of each approach and showcasing their applications in real-world scenarios, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the foundations of statistical inference. Furthermore, we address the challenges encountered in balancing the need for objective interpretations with the desire for subjective input in statistical analysis. Ultimately, this research aims to provide researchers and practitioners with a comprehensive understanding of the distinctive features of frequentist and Bayesian inference, empowering them to make informed decisions regarding the level of certainty they wish to assign to their statistical conclusions.
