text: This study investigates the dielectric anomalies and magnetodielectric coupling behavior of single crystalline Ca3Co2O6, a geometrically frustrated magnetic spin-chain system. Ca3Co2O6 exhibits a complex magnetic phase diagram, with multiple magnetic transitions and a rich magnetodielectric response, making it an attractive candidate for understanding the interplay between magnetic and electric properties in correlated materials. Theoretical models predict that Ca3Co2O6 should exhibit strong magnetodielectric coupling, given its geometric frustration and spin-chain geometry.  To investigate the dielectric anomalies and magnetodielectric coupling behavior of Ca3Co2O6, a combination of experimental techniques, including dielectric spectroscopy, magnetization measurements, and single-crystal X-ray diffraction, were employed. The results show that Ca3Co2O6 exhibits a broad dielectric peak at low temperatures, indicative of strong magnetodielectric coupling, and a pronounced dielectric anomaly at the magnetic transition temperature. The magnetization data reveal a complex magnetic phase diagram, with multiple magnetic transitions and a non-linear magnetic response. The single-crystal X-ray diffraction data confirm the spin-chain geometry and provide insights into the magnetic interactions.  The key findings of this study indicate that Ca3Co2O6 exhibits strong magnetodielectric coupling, with a significant dielectric response at the magnetic transition temperature. The results also suggest that the geometric frustration and spin-chain geometry of Ca3Co2O6 play a crucial role in determining its magnetodielectric behavior. The findings of this study have important implications for understanding the behavior of correlated materials and the development of new materials with tailored magnetic and dielectric properties.

text: We investigate the effects of fluctuating energy input on small-scale turbulence, aiming to enhance our understanding of energy transfer mechanisms in turbulent flows. Our study utilizes a combination of direct numerical simulations and theoretical analyses to explore how varying energy input influences turbulence characteristics at small scales. We systematically alter energy injection rates and examine the resulting alterations in turbulent structures, such as energy dissipation rates and enstrophy production.   Our results reveal that fluctuating energy input significantly modulates the energy cascade process, with pronounced effects on small-scale dynamic behavior. Notably, we identify that irregular energy injections lead to enhanced intermittency in turbulence statistics, resulting in more pronounced bursts of energy dissipation. Through our methodological approach, we establish a correlation between the frequency of energy fluctuations and the resultant change in small-scale vorticity structures.   Furthermore, we delineate the role of these fluctuations in altering the spectral distribution of turbulent energy, emphasizing the shift towards higher wavenumbers. We also propose a new scaling law that captures the relationship between the amplitude of energy fluctuations and turbulence intensification at small scales. Our findings elucidate important implications for various fields, including atmospheric science, oceanography, and engineering applications, where understanding turbulence dynamics under non-constant energy conditions is critical. This work contributes to the broader discourse on turbulence modeling and informs future research directions aimed at effective control of turbulent flows in practical scenarios.

text:
The presence or absence of ice in protoplanetary disks is of great importance
for the formation of planets. By enhancing the solid surface density and
increasing the sticking efficiency, ice catalyzes the rapid formation of
planetesimals and decreases the time scale for giant planet core accretion.
Aims: In this paper we analyse the composition of the outer disk around the
Herbig star HD~142527. We focus on the composition of the water ice, but also
analyse the abundances of previously proposed minerals. Methods: We present new
Herschel far infrared spectra and a re-reduction of archival data from the
Infrared Space Observatory (ISO). We model the disk using full 3D radiative
transfer to obtain the disk structure. Also, we use an optically thin analysis
of the outer disk spectrum to obtain firm constraints on the composition of the
dust component. Results: The water ice in the disk around HD~142527 contains a
large reservoir of crystalline water ice. We determine the local abundance of
water ice in the outer disk (i.e. beyond 130\,AU). The re-reduced ISO spectrum
differs significantly from that previously published, but matches the new
Herschel spectrum at their common wavelength range. In particular, we do not
detect any significant contribution from carbonates or hydrous silicates, in
contrast to earlier claims. Conclusions: The amount of water ice detected in
the outer disk requires $\sim80\,$\% of the oxygen atoms. This is comparable to
the water ice abundance in the outer solar system, in comets and in dense
interstellar clouds. The water ice is highly crystalline while the temperatures
where we detect it are too low to crystallize the water on relevant time
scales. We discuss the implications of this finding.

Many studies have been conducted on seeking the efficient solution for
subgraph similarity search over certain (deterministic) graphs due to its wide
application in many fields, including bioinformatics, social network analysis,
and Resource Description Framework (RDF) data management. All these works
assume that the underlying data are certain. However, in reality, graphs are
often noisy and uncertain due to various factors, such as errors in data
extraction, inconsistencies in data integration, and privacy preserving
purposes. Therefore, in this paper, we study subgraph similarity search on
large probabilistic graph databases. Different from previous works assuming
that edges in an uncertain graph are independent of each other, we study the
uncertain graphs where edges' occurrences are correlated. We formally prove
that subgraph similarity search over probabilistic graphs is #P-complete, thus,
we employ a filter-and-verify framework to speed up the search. In the
filtering phase,we develop tight lower and upper bounds of subgraph similarity
probability based on a probabilistic matrix index, PMI. PMI is composed of
discriminative subgraph features associated with tight lower and upper bounds
of subgraph isomorphism probability. Based on PMI, we can sort out a large
number of probabilistic graphs and maximize the pruning capability. During the
verification phase, we develop an efficient sampling algorithm to validate the
remaining candidates. The efficiency of our proposed solutions has been
verified through extensive experiments.
label: human

Let $\phi: M\to M$ be a diffeomorphism of a $C^\infty$ compact connected
manifold, and $X$ its mapping torus. There is a natural fibration $p:X\to S^1$,
denote by $\xi\in H^1(X, \mathbb{Z})$ the corresponding cohomology class. Let
$\lambda\in \mathbb{Z}^*$. Consider the endomorphism $\phi_k^*$ induced by
$\phi$ in the cohomology of $M$ of degree $k$, and denote by $J_k(\lambda)$ the
maximal size of its Jordan block of eigenvalue $\lambda$. Define a
representation $\rho_\lambda : \pi_1(X)\to\mathbb{C}^*$ by $\rho_\lambda (g) =
\lambda^{p_*(g)}.$ Let $H^*(X,\rho_\lambda)$ be the corresponding twisted
cohomology of $X$. We prove that $J_k(\lambda)$ is equal to the maximal length
of a non-zero Massey product of the form $\langle \xi, \ldots , \xi, a\rangle$
where $a\in H^k(X,\rho_\lambda)$ (here the length means the number of entries
of $\xi$). In particular, if $X$ is a strongly formal space (e.g. a K\"ahler
manifold) then all the Jordan blocks of $\phi_k^*$ are of size 1. If $X$ is a
formal space, then all the Jordan blocks of eigenvalue 1 are of size 1. This
leads to a simple construction of formal but not strongly formal mapping tori.
The proof of the main theorem is based on the fact that the Massey products of
the above form can be identified with differentials in a Massey spectral
sequence, which in turn can be explicitly computed in terms of the Jordan
normal form of $\phi^*$.

The quantization of the electromagnetic field in lossy and dispersive
dielectric media has been widely studied during the last few decades. However,
several aspects of energy transfer and its relation to consistently defining
position-dependent ladder operators for the electromagnetic field in
nonequilibrium conditions have partly escaped the attention. In this work we
define the position-dependent ladder operators and an effective local
photon-number operator that are consistent with the canonical commutation
relations and use these concepts to describe the energy transfer and thermal
balance in layered geometries. This approach results in a position-dependent
photon-number concept that is simple and consistent with classical energy
conservation arguments. The operators are formed by first calculating the
vector potential operator using Green's function formalism and Langevin noise
source operators related to the medium and its temperature, and then defining
the corresponding position-dependent annihilation operator that is required to
satisfy the canonical commutation relations in arbitrary geometry. Our results
suggest that the effective photon number associated with the electric field is
generally position dependent and enables a straightforward method to calculate
the energy transfer rate between the field and the local medium. In particular,
our results predict that the effective photon number in a vacuum cavity formed
between two lossy material layers can oscillate as a function of the position
suggesting that also the local field temperature oscillates. These oscillations
are expected to be directly observable using relatively straightforward
experimental setups in which the field-matter interaction is dominated by the
coupling to the electric field.

In this work, we propose a new randomized algorithm for computing a low-rank
approximation to a given matrix. Taking an approach different from existing
literature, our method first involves a specific biased sampling, with an
element being chosen based on the leverage scores of its row and column, and
then involves weighted alternating minimization over the factored form of the
intended low-rank matrix, to minimize error only on these samples. Our method
can leverage input sparsity, yet produce approximations in {\em spectral} (as
opposed to the weaker Frobenius) norm; this combines the best aspects of
otherwise disparate current results, but with a dependence on the condition
number $\kappa = \sigma_1/\sigma_r$. In particular we require $O(nnz(M) +
\frac{n\kappa^2 r^5}{\epsilon^2})$ computations to generate a rank-$r$
approximation to $M$ in spectral norm. In contrast, the best existing method
requires $O(nnz(M)+ \frac{nr^2}{\epsilon^4})$ time to compute an approximation
in Frobenius norm. Besides the tightness in spectral norm, we have a better
dependence on the error $\epsilon$. Our method is naturally and highly
parallelizable.
  Our new approach enables two extensions that are interesting on their own.
The first is a new method to directly compute a low-rank approximation (in
efficient factored form) to the product of two given matrices; it computes a
small random set of entries of the product, and then executes weighted
alternating minimization (as before) on these. The sampling strategy is
different because now we cannot access leverage scores of the product matrix
(but instead have to work with input matrices). The second extension is an
improved algorithm with smaller communication complexity for the distributed
PCA setting (where each server has small set of rows of the matrix, and want to
compute low rank approximation with small amount of communication with other
servers).

text: In recent years, the exploration of positron bunch radiation in tightly-packed nanotube systems has gained significant attention due to its potential applications in advanced materials science and nanotechnology. This study aims to investigate the interaction dynamics of positron bunches within arrays of carbon nanotubes, focusing on their emission characteristics and the influence of structural parameters on radiation profiles. Utilizing a combination of numerical simulations and analytical modeling, we examine the behavior of positronium formation, annihilation processes, and the resulting radiation patterns as a function of nanotube density and orientation. Key findings illustrate that the confinement effects in tightly-packed nanotubes significantly enhance the radiative output of positrons, with variations in the emission spectrum linked to the geometric arrangement of the nanotubes. Specifically, we find that higher densities lead to increased positronium survival rates, subsequently resulting in pronounced peaks in the X-ray emission spectrum. These results suggest that manipulating the arrangement of carbon nanotubes can be harnessed to optimize positron bunch radiation for practical applications, such as in radiation therapy and advanced imaging techniques. In conclusion, our findings not only broaden the understanding of particle interactions at the nanoscale but also pave the way for innovative uses of nanotube systems in harnessing positron bunch radiation for technological advancements. Further research is warranted to explore the quantum mechanical underpinnings of these interactions and to evaluate the practical implications in various fields.

text: This study explores the interaction between the radio jets of the powerful radio galaxy 3C293 and the interstellar medium (ISM) through multi-wavelength observations. We present X-ray, optical, infrared, and molecular data obtained from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, Hubble Space Telescope, Spitzer Space Telescope, and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), respectively. Our results reveal the presence of extended X-ray emission along the radio jets, indicating jet-driven shocks that heat the ISM, producing X-ray emission.  The X-ray emission is accompanied by H2 molecular emission, providing evidence for the interaction of jets with dense molecular clouds in the ISM. The optical and infrared observations show that the radio galaxy is surrounded by a complex environment of cold and warm gas, which is excited by the jets. The presence of molecular hydrogen emission implies that the radio galaxy is capable of sustaining ongoing star formation due to the energy and mass input from the jets.  Our analysis of the X-ray and molecular data suggests that the jets are interacting with the ISM over large scales, leading to the formation of multiple shock fronts. These shock fronts are believed to compress and heat the ISM, resulting in the production of X-ray and molecular H2 emission. We propose that the interaction between the radio jets and the ISM in 3C293 plays a crucial role in the evolution of the radio galaxy and the surrounding galaxy.  This research advances our understanding of the role that radio jets play in interacting with the ISM and the production of X-ray and molecular emission in radio galaxies. Our findings contribute to the growing body of evidence that suggests that the interactions between jets and the ISM can have significant effects on the large-scale environments of active galactic nuclei and their host galaxies. Future work should focus on modeling the interaction between the jets and the ISM in more detail, and studying the dependence of the X-ray and molecular emission on jet power, jet composition, and ISM density.

text:
Strongly-magnetized, rapidly-rotating neutron stars are contenders for the
central engines of both long-duration gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) and
hydrogen-poor super-luminous supernovae (SLSNe-I). Models for typical (~minute
long) LGRBs invoke magnetars with high dipole magnetic fields (Bd > 1e15 G) and
short spin-down times, while models for SLSNe-I invoke neutron stars with
weaker fields and longer spin-down times of weeks. Here we identify a
transition region in the space of Bd and birth period for which a magnetar can
power both a long GRB and a luminous SN. In particular, we show that a 2 ms
period magnetar with a spin-down time of ~1e4 s can explain the observations of
both the ultra-long GRB 111209 and its associated luminous SN2011kl. For
magnetars with longer spin down times, we predict even longer duration (~1e6 s)
GRBs and brighter supernovae, a correlation that extends to Swift J2058+05
(commonly interpreted as a tidal disruption event). We further show that
previous estimates of the maximum rotational energy of a proto-magnetar were
too conservative and energies up to Emax ~1-2e53 erg are possible. The magnetar
model can therefore comfortably accommodate the extreme energy requirements
recently posed by the most luminous supernova ASASSN-15lh. The high ionization
flux from a pulsar wind nebula powering ASASSN-15lh may lead to an "ionization
break-out" X-ray burst over the coming months, which would be accompanied by an
abrupt change in the optical spectrum. We conclude by briefly contrasting
millisecond magnetar and black hole models for SLSNe and ultra-long GRBs.

text: The abstract for the research paper titled "An Asymptotic Analysis of the MIMO Broadcast Channel under Linear Filtering" is as follows  This research focuses on the asymptotic analysis of the Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) Broadcast Channel (BC) in the presence of linear filtering at the receiver. The study aims to derive theoretical insights into the system's performance as the number of transmit antennas and receive antennas grows large. Utilizing information-theoretic techniques, the paper establishes fundamental limits on the achievable rate regions for both discrete memoryless and Gaussian MIMO BCs under linear filtering constraints. Through detailed asymptotic derivations, it explores how the structure of the channel matrix and the properties of the filter affect these limits. Key findings include expressions for the asymptotic capacity region, which reveal the impact of spatial correlation between transmit antennas and the filter design on the overall communication efficiency. The analysis provides a robust foundation for understanding the practical implications of employing linear filtering schemes in MIMO broadcast scenarios, facilitating the design of more efficient and reliable communication systems.

text: This research explores the theoretical framework of hyperdense coding within the context of hypersphere theories, focusing on the manifestation of superadditivity in classical capacities. Building on foundational concepts from quantum information theory, the study delves into how entanglement can be utilized to transmit more than one bit of classical information per qubit, a phenomenon known as hyperdense coding. The objective is to investigate whether similar principles apply in classical communication settings when using hypersphere theories, which generalize the Bloch sphere representation of qubits.  The methodology involves constructing a mathematical model that incorporates the geometry of hyperspheres to represent states and operations in a quantum-like system. This model is then used to analyze the classical capacities of these systems, specifically examining scenarios where the capacity exceeds the sum of individual capacities, indicative of superadditivity.  Key findings reveal that under certain conditions, the classical capacities indeed exhibit superadditivity, mirroring the quantum scenario observed through hyperdense coding. This finding suggests that the principles governing quantum systems can have analogs in classical settings, particularly when considering complex geometrical representations such as those found in hypersphere theories.  Conclusively, this research underscores the potential for extending quantum-inspired techniques beyond their quantum domain, providing insights into the fundamental limits of classical communication and the role of entanglement in enhancing information transmission. The implications of these results could influence the design of future communication protocols and the development of new technologies leveraging entanglement effects in classical systems.
label: machine

text:
Visual robot navigation within large-scale, semi-structured environments
deals with various challenges such as computation intensive path planning
algorithms or insufficient knowledge about traversable spaces. Moreover, many
state-of-the-art navigation approaches only operate locally instead of gaining
a more conceptual understanding of the planning objective. This limits the
complexity of tasks a robot can accomplish and makes it harder to deal with
uncertainties that are present in the context of real-time robotics
applications. In this work, we present Topomap, a framework which simplifies
the navigation task by providing a map to the robot which is tailored for path
planning use. This novel approach transforms a sparse feature-based map from a
visual Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM) system into a
three-dimensional topological map. This is done in two steps. First, we extract
occupancy information directly from the noisy sparse point cloud. Then, we
create a set of convex free-space clusters, which are the vertices of the
topological map. We show that this representation improves the efficiency of
global planning, and we provide a complete derivation of our algorithm.
Planning experiments on real world datasets demonstrate that we achieve similar
performance as RRT* with significantly lower computation times and storage
requirements. Finally, we test our algorithm on a mobile robotic platform to
prove its advantages.

text: In this study, we present the analysis of high-contrast imaging data obtained for the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star R Doradus using the Spectro-Polarimetric High-contrast Exoplanet REsearch (SPHERE) instrument and the Zurich Imaging Polarimeter (ZIMPOL). Our objective was to investigate the inner dust envelope and stellar photosphere of R Doradus, a red M-type AGB star located in the Large Magellanic Cloud.  The observations were carried out in H-band polarimetry mode using SPHERE/ZIMPOL, which enabled us to study the dust environment and polarized light emitted by the stellar photosphere. The data were processed using standard reduction procedures and analyzed with the IDL reduction package and the DAOPHOT photometric analysis tool.  Our key findings reveal a complex dust envelope with a range of sizes, extending up to 2.2 arcsec (240 astronomical units) from the stellar surface. We detected several dust rings, with the innermost ring located at a separation of 0.1 arcsec (13 astronomical units) from the photosphere. The polarimetric measurements also revealed the presence of polarized emission from the stellar photosphere, confirming the presence of magnetic fields in the stellar atmosphere.  In conclusion, our study provides valuable insights into the dust environment and stellar photosphere of R Doradus, an important AGB star in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The observed complex dust envelope and polarized emission from the stellar photosphere have important implications for the understanding of AGB stars and the role they play in the interstellar medium.

text:
We address the NP-hard problem of finding a non-overlapping dense packing
pattern for n Unequal Circle items in a two-dimensional Square Container
(PUC-SC) such that the size of the container is minimized. Based on our
previous work on an Action Space based Global Optimization (ASGO) that
approximates each circle item as a square item to efficiently find the large
unoccupied spaces, we propose an optimization algorithm based on the
Partitioned Action Space and Partitioned Circle Items (PAS-PCI). The PAS is to
partition the narrow action space on the long side to find two equal action
spaces to fully utilize the unoccupied spaces. The PCI is to partition the
circle items into four groups based on size for the basin hopping strategy.
Experiments on two sets of benchmark instances show the effectiveness of the
proposed method. In comparison with our previous algorithm ASGO on the 68
tested instances that ASGO published, PAS-PCI not only gains smaller containers
in 64 instances and matches the other 4 but also runs faster in most instances.
In comparison with the best record of the Packomania website on a total of 98
instances, PAS-PCI finds smaller containers on 82 and matches the other 16.
Note that we updated 19 records for (47-48, 51-54, 57, 61-72) that had been
kept unchanged since 2013.

text: We present our findings from the very-high-energy gamma-ray observations of the Type Ia supernova SN 2014J conducted using the Major Atmospheric Gamma Imaging Cherenkov (MAGIC) telescopes. Our primary objective was to investigate the underlying mechanisms of gamma-ray emission in Type Ia supernovae and their potential as cosmic gamma-ray sources. We aimed to address existing uncertainties regarding the nucleosynthesis processes and the contribution of gamma-ray emissions to the overall energetics of these events. Our observations revealed a significant gamma-ray flux that aligns with the theoretical predictions of radioactive decay of \(^{56}\)Co, leading to a better understanding of the supernova's explosion dynamics. Additionally, we identified evidence for high-energy emission above 100 GeV, suggesting contributions from interactions between the supernova ejecta and the surrounding circumstellar medium. We employed advanced analysis techniques, including both model-fitting and time-dependent light curve assessments, to extract gamma-ray spectra and temporal behavior. Our results not only confirm the presence of very-high-energy gamma rays associated with SN 2014J but also provide crucial insights into the supernova's explosion mechanisms, thereby contributing to the broader knowledge of cosmic ray origins and the chemical evolution of galaxies. Ultimately, our work underscores the significance of using ground-based gamma-ray observatories, like MAGIC, to advance our comprehension of Type Ia supernovae and their role in the universe.

Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices and let $k$ be a fixed positive integer.
We denote by $\mathcal G_{\text{$k$-out}}(G)$ the probability space consisting
of subgraphs of $G$ where each vertex $v\in V(G)$ randomly picks $k$ neighbors
from $G$, independently from all other vertices. We show that if
$\delta(G)=\omega(\log n)$ and $k\geq 2$, then the following holds for every
$p=\omega(\log n/\delta(G))$. Let $H$ be a random graph obtained by keeping
each $e\in E(G)$ with probability $p$ independently at random and then coloring
its edges independently and uniformly at random with elements from the set
$[kn]$. Then, w.h.p. $H$ contains $t:=(1-o(1))\delta(G)p/(2k)$ edge-disjoint
graphs $H_1,...,H_t$ such that each of the $H_i$ is \emph{rainbow} (that is,
all the edges are colored with distinct colors), and such that for every
monotone increasing property of graphs $\mathcal P$ and for every $1\leq i\leq
t$ we have $\Pr[\mathcal G_{\text{$k$-out}}(G)\models \mathcal P]\leq
\Pr[H_i\models \mathcal P]+n^{-\omega(1)}$. Note that since (in this case) a
typical member of $\mathcal G_{\text{$k$-out}}(G)$ has average degree roughly
$2k$, this result is asymptotically best possible. We present several
applications of this; for example, we use this result to prove that for
$p=\omega(\log n/n)$ and $c=23n$, a graph $H\sim \mathcal G_{c}(K_n,p)$ w.h.p.
contains $(1-o(1))np/46$ edge-disjoint rainbow Hamilton cycles. More generally,
using a recent result of Frieze and Johansson, the same method allows us to
prove that if $G$ has minimum degree $\delta(G)\geq (1+\varepsilon)n/2$, then
there exist functions $c=O(n)$ and $t=\Theta(np)$ (depending on $\varepsilon$)
such that the random subgraph $H\sim \mathcal G_{c}(G,p)$ w.h.p. contains $t$
edge-disjoint rainbow Hamilton cycles.

Recently some papers, such as Aban, Meerschaert and Panorska (2006), Nuyts
(2010) and Clark (2013), have drawn attention to possible truncation in Pareto
tail modelling. Sometimes natural upper bounds exist that truncate the
probability tail, such as the Maximum Possible Loss in insurance treaties. At
other instances ultimately at the largest data, deviations from a Pareto tail
behaviour become apparent. This matter is especially important when
extrapolation outside the sample is required. Given that in practice one does
not always know whether the distribution is truncated or not, we consider
estimators for extreme quantiles both under truncated and non-truncated
Pareto-type distributions. Hereby we make use of the estimator of the tail
index for the truncated Pareto distribution first proposed in Aban {\it et al.}
(2006). We also propose a truncated Pareto QQ-plot and a formal test for
truncation in order to help deciding between a truncated and a non-truncated
case. In this way we enlarge the possibilities of extreme value modelling using
Pareto tails, offering an alternative scenario by adding a truncation point $T$
that is large with respect to the available data. In the mathematical modelling
we hence let $T \to \infty$ at different speeds compared to the limiting
fraction ($k/n \to 0$) of data used in the extreme value estimation. This work
is motivated using practical examples from different fields of applications,
simulation results, and some asymptotic results.

text: Photon reconstruction in ground-based gamma-ray astronomy is crucial for accurately determining the energy and direction of incoming photons. This research paper presents a study focused on photon reconstruction for the High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.) using a semi-analytical shower model. The objective of this study is to improve the accuracy and efficiency of photon reconstruction by developing a semi-analytical model that can simulate the shower development of gamma rays in the atmosphere.   The methodology involves implementing the semi-analytical shower model in the photon reconstruction process of the H.E.S.S. experiment and comparing the results with the traditional methods currently in use. Key findings indicate that the semi-analytical model yields more precise reconstructions of photon properties, such as energy and arrival direction, leading to enhanced sensitivity in gamma-ray observations.  In conclusion, the semi-analytical shower model shows promising results in improving the photon reconstruction process for H.E.S.S. The enhanced accuracy and efficiency achieved through this model can significantly benefit gamma-ray astronomy experiments by providing more reliable measurements of high-energy photons. This research contributes to advancing the field of ground-based gamma-ray astronomy and opens up new possibilities for studying the high-energy universe.

text: Our research investigates the strain rate effects in the mechanical behavior of polymer anchored carbon nanotube (CNT) foams. The study aims to address the limited understanding of how strain rates impact the mechanical response of these novel materials. Through experimental testing and computational modeling, we have uncovered significant insights. Our results reveal that at higher strain rates, the polymer anchored CNT foams exhibit enhanced mechanical properties such as increased strength and stiffness compared to traditional foams. We have identified a complex interplay between the viscoelasticity of the polymer matrix and the unique mechanical properties of CNTs under varying strain rates. Additionally, our findings demonstrate the importance of considering strain rate effects when designing polymer anchored CNT foams for applications requiring specific mechanical properties. The key methodology employed involves fabricating the foams, conducting mechanical tests at different strain rates, and developing computational models to simulate the mechanical behavior. Overall, our study contributes to advancing the understanding of strain rate effects on the mechanical response of polymer anchored CNT foams, offering valuable insights for the development of high-performance materials in various engineering applications.

text: Distributionally robust stochastic optimization (DRSO) provides a robust framework for decision-making under uncertainty, utilizing ambiguity sets to model uncertainty in the probability distribution of random variables. This study explores the application of Wasserstein distance in forming these ambiguity sets, aiming to address the limitations of traditional DRSO approaches that may rely on overly conservative estimates. Our objective is to develop a robust optimization strategy that leverages the Wasserstein distance to balance robustness and performance effectively. Employing a theoretical framework, we integrate the Wasserstein metric into a distributionally robust stochastic optimization model. We then implement this model using a numerical case study to assess its practical applicability and efficiency. Key findings demonstrate that the proposed Wasserstein-based DRSO framework exhibits enhanced performance and robustness over traditional methods, particularly in scenarios where distributional deviations occur. The results indicate that by using Wasserstein distance, the model captures more realistic distributional variations, reducing conservatism while maintaining a high level of protection against distributional uncertainty. Furthermore, our analysis exhibits that the computational complexity remains manageable, supporting the framework's feasibility for large-scale applications. In conclusion, this research contributes to the field of stochastic optimization by presenting a method that more accurately reflects real-world uncertainties, offering improved decision-making strategies under ambiguous conditions. Our findings suggest promising avenues for future research in expanding the applicability of Wasserstein-based approaches in diverse sectors, including finance, supply chain, and energy management.

It is commonly assumed that zero and non-zero photon mass would lead to
qualitatively different physics. For example, massless photon has two
polarization degrees of freedom, while massive photon at least three. This
feature seems counter-intuitive. In this paper we will show that if we change
propagator by setting $i \epsilon$ (needed to avoid poles) to a finite value,
and also introduce it in a way that breaks Lawrentz symmetry, then we would
obtain the continuous transition we desire once the speed of the photons is
"large enough" with respect to "preferred" frame. The two transverse
polarization degrees of freedom will be long lived, while longitudinal will be
short lived. Their lifetime will be near-zero if $m \ll \sqrt{\epsilon}$, which
is where the properties of two circular polarizations arize. The $i \epsilon$
corresponds to the intensity of Mensky's "continuous measurement" and the short
lifetime of the longitudinal photons can be understood as the "conversion" of
quantum degrees of freedom (photons) into "classical" ones by the measurement
device (thus getting rid of the former). While the "classical" trajectory of
the longitudinal photons does arize, it plays no physical role due to quantum
Zeno effect: intuitively, it is similar to an electron being kept at a ground
state due to continuous measurement.

text: In this study, we investigate the influence of both isolated and clustered defects on the electronic and dielectric properties of wustite (FeO). Our approach involves the use of density functional theory calculations to model the structures and analyze the electronic band structures. We find that isolated defects introduce significant local distortions and charge transfer effects, which lead to changes in the Fermi level and thereby affect the electronic conductivity. In contrast, clustered defects create larger regions of structural disorder, leading to broader and more complex bands, impacting the overall dielectric behavior. The key insight is that while isolated defects can be detrimental by disrupting the crystal lattice, clustered defects may offer opportunities for engineering materials with tailored electrical and dielectric characteristics through precise defect distribution. This research highlights the importance of understanding defect distributions in optimizing the performance of oxide-based materials.

Design of a Fabry-Perot (double point contact) interferometer to measure
fractional quantum Hall effect quasiparticle charge properties, and in
particular the 5/2 excitations, poses an important trade-off: the device size
should be minimized to allow two path interference, since the coherence length
of the quasiparticles in the correlated states are expected be limited, yet a
small device promotes the dominance of Coulomb charging effects which would
overwhelm the Aharonov-Bohm interference effect. In this study a series of
small but different size interferometers from the same high density
heterostructure wafer are examined for the presence of Coulomb effects versus
Aharonov-Bohm (A-B) interference effect when operated in gate configurations
that support the 5/2, 7/3, and 8/3 fractional quantum Hall effects. The device
sizes vary by more than a factor of three, and over this range explicitly show
specific properties of A-B interference, but not Coulomb dominated effects.
Given these A-B interference results, the coherence length of the charge e/4
interference is extracted. The coherence length of non-Abelian e/4
quasiparticles is an important parameter for design and development of complex
interference devices used to study and apply this exotic excitation. As in
prior observations of e/4 excitations, A-B e/4 and e/2 oscillations in
alternation are observed in these multiple devices. The amplitudes of the e/4
oscillations are observed to be dramatically reduced for larger area
interferometers. Path-length limits are derived from interferometer areas
determined directly by A-B measurements, and the attenuation lengths of the e/4
oscillations are shown to be micron to sub-micron scale. This coherence length
is consistent with that of the 7/3 excitations measured here, and consistent
with theoretical models.

text: This study focuses on inferring a dyadic measure and its simplicial geometry directly from binary feature data. The primary objective is to develop methods that can effectively extract meaningful structural information from high-dimensional binary datasets, which are common in various applications such as bioinformatics, social network analysis, and computer vision. To achieve this, we employ a combination of graph theory and algebraic topology techniques.  The methodology involves constructing a graph where nodes represent entities and edges indicate the presence or absence of certain features between them. We then use persistent homology—a tool from algebraic topology—to analyze the topological features of these graphs. This allows us to identify and quantify the simplicial complexes within the data, providing insights into the underlying geometric structure.  Key findings include the successful identification of significant simplicial complexes and the ability to accurately infer dyadic measures from binary feature data. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in uncovering complex relationships within the data, even when the data dimensions are high.  In conclusion, the proposed method offers a robust framework for understanding the dyadic structure and simplicial geometry embedded in binary feature data. It provides valuable tools for assessing data quality and has potential applications in enhancing data analysis across multiple domains.

text: Anisotropic magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) have been extensively studied for their potential applications in biomedicine due to their unique magnetic properties. In this study, we present the synthesis of anisotropic MNPs and their utilization in bridging frequency-separated AC-fields for controlled actuation. The MNPs were synthesized through a modified co-precipitation method, resulting in hexagonal shape with an average size of 25 nm and a saturation magnetization of 67 emu/g. Two distinct AC-fields were employed, with frequencies separated by a factor of three. The MNPs were suspended in a silicone oil medium and placed between two parallel plates, with each plate being driven by a separate AC-field. Magnetic field strengths of up to 200 Oe were applied to both fields, resulting in synchronized actuation of the MNPs. The actuation behavior was studied using a high-speed camera and verified through a time-series analysis of the resulting videos. The findings demonstrate the potential of using anisotropic MNPs as a platform for developing advanced biomedical devices, including drug delivery systems, tissue engineering scaffolds, and magnetic actuators, where precise control over nanoscale magnetic domains is required. The research also provides insights into optimizing the synthesis conditions and controlling the anisotropy of MNPs for various applications. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing efforts to develop innovative nanomaterials for biomedical applications and expands the understanding of the underlying mechanisms of anisotropic MNPs in AC-fields.

A quantum spin Hall insulator is a two-dimensional state of matter consisting
of an insulating bulk and one-dimensional helical edge states. While these edge
states are topologically protected against elastic backscattering in the
presence of disorder, interaction-induced inelastic terms may yield a finite
conductivity. By using a kinetic equation approach, we find the backscattering
rate $\tau^{-1}$ and the semiclassical conductivity in the regimes of high
($\omega \gg \tau^{-1}$) and low ($\omega \ll \tau^{-1}$) frequency. By
comparing the two limits, we find that the parametric dependence of
conductivity is described by the Drude formula for the case of a disordered
edge. On the other hand, in the clean case where the resistance originates from
umklapp interactions, the conductivity takes a non-Drude form with a parametric
suppression of scattering in the dc limit as compared to the ac case. This
behavior is due to the peculiarity of umklapp scattering processes involving
necessarily the state at the "Dirac point". In order to take into account
Luttinger liquid effects, we complement the kinetic equation analysis by
treating interactions exactly in bosonization and calculating conductivity
using the Kubo formula. In this way, we obtain the frequency and temperature
dependence of conductivity over a wide range of parameters. We find the
temperature and frequency dependence of the transport scattering time in a
disordered system as $\tau \sim [\max{(\omega,T)}]^{-2K-2}$, for $K>2/3$ and
$\tau \sim [\max{(\omega,T)}]^{-8K+2}$ for $K <2/3$.

An ordered pair $\hat{S}=(S,S^+)$ of subsets of $V$ is called a {\em biset}
if $S \subseteq S^+$; $(V-S^+,V-S)$ is the co-biset of $\hat{S}$. Two bisets
$\hat{X},\hat{Y}$ intersect if $X \cap Y \neq \emptyset$ and cross if both $X
\cap Y \neq \emptyset$ and $X^+ \cup Y^+ \neq V$. The intersection and the
union of two bisets $\hat{X},\hat{Y}$ is defined by $\hat{X} \cap \hat{Y} = (X
\cap Y, X^+ \cap Y^+)$ and $\hat{X} \cup \hat{Y} = (X \cup Y,X^+ \cup Y^+)$. A
biset-family ${\cal F}$ is crossing (intersecting) if $\hat{X} \cap \hat{Y},
\hat{X} \cup \hat{Y} \in {\cal F}$ for any $\hat{X},\hat{Y} \in {\cal F}$ that
cross (intersect). A directed edge covers a biset $\hat{S}$ if it goes from $S$
to $V-S^+$. We consider the problem of covering a crossing biset-family ${\cal
F}$ by a minimum-cost set of directed edges. While for intersecting ${\cal F}$,
a standard primal-dual algorithm computes an optimal solution, the
approximability of the case of crossing ${\cal F}$ is not yet understood, as it
includes several NP-hard problems, for which a poly-logarithmic approximation
was discovered only recently. Let us say that a biset-family ${\cal F}$ is
$k$-regular if $\hat{X} \cap \hat{Y}, \hat{X} \cup \hat{Y} \in {\cal F}$ for
any $\hat{X},\hat{Y} \in {\cal F}$ with $|V-(X \cup Y)| \geq k+1$ that
intersect. In this paper we obtain an $O(\log |V|)$-approximation algorithm for
arbitrary crossing ${\cal F}$; if in addition both ${\cal F}$ and the family of
co-bisets of ${\cal F}$ are $k$-regular, our ratios are: $O(\log
\frac{|V|}{|V|-k})$ if $|S^+ \setminus S|=k$ for all $\hat{S} \in {\cal F}$,
and $O(\frac{|V|}{|V|-k} \log \frac{|V|}{|V|-k})$ if $|S^+ \setminus S| \leq k$
for all $\hat{S} \in {\cal F}$. Using these generic algorithms, we derive
approximation algorithms for some network design problems.

text: In this work, we present a comprehensive study on the development and characterization of tunable subnanometer gap plasmonic metasurfaces. Our primary objective is to bridge the challenge of dynamically controlling plasmonic responses at subwavelength scales, which is a critical bottleneck in advancing applications such as sensing, photonic circuits, and nonlinear optics. We achieve tunability through precise engineering of gap distances in metallic nanostructures, reaching subnanometer separations. This is accomplished by employing a combination of advanced lithographic techniques and atomic layer deposition, which allows us to finely manipulate the dielectric environment and thus the optical properties of the metasurfaces.   Our methodology involves systematically varying the gap dimensions and utilizing broadband optical spectroscopy to probe the plasmonic behavior. We observe that the nanoscale gap modification leads to significant shifts in resonance frequencies and enhancement in field confinement, corroborated by finite-difference time-domain simulations. This tunability is further demonstrated through integration with liquid crystal materials, offering dynamic modulation of the plasmonic features in response to external stimuli.   The results indicate that our approach successfully enables exceedingly precise control over the electromagnetic interactions at the nanoscale, thus opening new pathways for actively tunable plasmonic devices. Our findings not only enhance the fundamental understanding of nanogap plasmonics but also provide a viable platform for the development of next-generation optical components with applications in various technologically relevant fields.

text: We present a comprehensive study of the ultra-dense broad-line region (BLR) scale outflow in the highly reddened quasar SDSS J145057.28+530007.6, employing a multi-wavelength approach that combines optical, ultraviolet, and X-ray observations. Our analysis reveals a complex outflow morphology, characterized by a dense, compact outflow with a velocity dispersion of approximately 1500 km/s. Utilizing a novel method to account for the reddening effects on the outflow's velocity distribution, we derive a corrected velocity dispersion of 2000 km/s, indicating a significant enhancement of the outflow's velocity.  Our observations and modeling efforts demonstrate that the outflow is powered by a combination of radiation pressure and stellar wind-driven acceleration, with a dominant role played by the quasar's central black hole. The outflow's high density and velocity suggest a strong interaction with the surrounding intergalactic medium, potentially leading to the quasar's reddening. Our results provide insights into the physics of quasar outflows and the role of radiation pressure in shaping their morphology. Furthermore, the observed outflow's properties are consistent with a scenario in which the quasar's accretion disk is embedded within a dense, circumgalactic medium, which is being stripped by the outflow. Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of quasar evolution and the role of outflows in regulating the growth of supermassive black holes.

text: The antiferromagnetic (AFM) states of Na0.5CoO2, a prominent candidate material for high-temperature superconductivity, have long been of great interest to the materials science community due to their intricate interplay between charge, orbital, and magnetic orders. In this study, we investigate the ground state properties of the two-dimensional triangular lattice d-p model for Na0.5CoO2, a minimal model capturing the essential physics of the system. Using large-scale density functional theory calculations, we show that the model exhibits both charge and orbital orders, which coexist and interact strongly with the AFM order. We find that the charge order occurs due to the interplay between the repulsive on-site Coulomb interactions and the Co 3d orbital interactions, leading to an ordering wavevector of Q = (π/2, π/2). The orbital order, on the other hand, arises from the competitive interactions between the intra-orbital and inter-orbital Hund's rule coupling. Our calculations reveal that the orbital order is predominantly of zigzag type, where the Co 3d orbitals align in rows in alternating directions along the triangular lattice. The magneto-electric effect, a hallmark property of multiferroics, is also examined in our study. We find that the coexistence of charge and orbital orders gives rise to a significant magneto-electric effect, suggesting that Na0.5CoO2 could exhibit multiferroic behavior. Our results provide new insights into the complex AFM states of Na0.5CoO2 and demonstrate the importance of considering the interplay between charge, orbital, and magnetic orders in understanding the physics of this intriguing material. text: This study undertakes a comparative analysis of two numerical methods, polynomial dealiasing and split form discontinuous Galerkin schemes, for simulating under-resolved turbulence in fluid dynamics. The background of this research is rooted in the limitations of existing numerical methods, which often struggle to accurately capture the complex dynamics of turbulent flows at low resolution. Polynomial dealiasing and discontinuous Galerkin schemes are two popular approaches employed to mitigate this issue, but their performance and efficiency in under-resolved turbulence computations remain unclear.  The objective of this research is to investigate the strengths and weaknesses of these two methods, with a focus on their ability to accurately capture turbulent fluctuations and minimize numerical artifacts. To achieve this, a comprehensive numerical study is conducted, employing a range of test cases with varying levels of under-resolution. The results of this study reveal that both methods exhibit improved performance in under-resolved turbulence computations, but with distinct differences in their treatment of high-frequency modes.  The key findings of this research indicate that polynomial dealiasing is effective in reducing aliasing errors, but at the cost of increased computational complexity. In contrast, the split form discontinuous Galerkin scheme demonstrates improved stability and accuracy, particularly at high frequencies. The comparison of these two methods highlights the importance of carefully selecting the numerical approach for under-resolved turbulence computations, with implications for the design of efficient and accurate numerical models. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the challenges and opportunities in simulating turbulent flows at low resolution, and provides guidance for the development of more effective numerical methods.

We present an optimization study of the spin sensitivity of nanoSQUIDs based
on resistively shunted grain boundary Josephson junctions. In addition the dc
SQUIDs contain a narrow constriction onto which a small magnetic particle can
be placed (with its magnetic moment in the plane of the SQUID loop and
perpendicular to the grain boundary) for efficient coupling of its stray
magnetic field to the SQUID loop. The separation of the location of optimum
coupling from the junctions allows for an independent optimization of the
coupling factor $\phi_\mu$ and junction properties. We present different
methods for calculating $\phi_\mu$ (for a magnetic nanoparticle placed 10\,nm
above the constriction) as a function of device geometry and show that those
yield consistent results. Furthermore, by numerical simulations we obtain a
general expression for the dependence of the SQUID inductance on geometrical
parameters of our devices, which allows to estimate their impact on the
spectral density of flux noise $S_\Phi$ of the SQUIDs in the thermal white
noise regime. Our analysis of the dependence of $S_\Phi$ and $\phi_\mu$ on the
geometric parameters of the SQUID layout yields a spin sensitivity
$S_\mu^{1/2}=S_\Phi^{1/2}/\phi_\mu$ of a few $\mu_{\rm{B}}/\rm{Hz^{1/2}}$
($\mu_B$ is the Bohr magneton) for optimized parameters, respecting
technological constraints. However, by comparison with experimentally realized
devices we find significantly larger values for the measured white flux noise,
as compared to our theoretical predictions. Still, a spin sensitivity on the
order of $10\,\mu_{\rm B}/\rm{Hz^{1/2}}$ for optimized devices seems to be
realistic.

text: This study explores the concept of energy equipartition within globular clusters, focusing on the distribution of kinetic energy among stellar populations. Through extensive numerical simulations, we have identified that while classical equipartition theory suggests equal energy sharing among stars, there are significant deviations observed. These deviations are attributed to various factors including mass segregation, binary interactions, and dissipative processes such as stellar winds and collisions. Our methodology involved modeling the dynamics of stellar systems using N-body simulations, incorporating realistic parameters derived from observational data. The results indicate that although equipartition is not strictly maintained, it still plays a crucial role in determining the overall stability and structure of these clusters. Key insights suggest that understanding these deviations can lead to more accurate models of star formation and evolution in globular clusters, thereby enhancing our comprehension of stellar dynamics in dense stellar environments.

text: The ATLAS3D project investigates the role of dynamical processes in regulating star formation within early-type galaxies. This study aims to elucidate how dynamic phenomena contribute to the suppression of star formation in such galaxies, which are typically composed of older stellar populations. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset from the ATLAS3D survey, which includes integrated field spectroscopy and photometric data, we analyze the kinematic and dynamic properties of 260 early-type galaxies. Employing advanced statistical techniques, we examine the relationship between galaxy dynamics, including rotation and velocity dispersions, and star formation activity indicators derived from multi-wavelength observations. Our findings reveal a significant correlation between high velocity dispersion environments and reduced star formation rates, suggesting that internal dynamical heating processes may inhibit molecular cloud collapse, thus quenching star formation. Additionally, evidence points to feedback mechanisms, such as AGN activity and stellar feedback, being augmented by these dynamical conditions, further suppressing star formation. Importantly, our analysis indicates that dynamically-driven quenching is more prevalent in high-mass galaxies, highlighting a mass-dependent influence on star formation activity. The results emphasize the role of internal galaxy dynamics as key drivers in the evolutionary pathways of early-type galaxies, contributing to their transition into quiescence. This research provides valuable insights into the complex interplay between galaxy dynamics and star formation, advancing our understanding of galaxy evolution mechanisms. Further investigation is required to explore the relative contributions of external environmental factors in concert with internal dynamics in shaping star formation histories.

We consider the fundamental problem of charged particles moving along and
around a curved magnetic field line, revising the synchro-curvature radiation
formulae introduced by Cheng and Zhang (1996). We provide more compact
expressions to evaluate the spectrum emitted by a single particle, identifying
the key parameter that controls the transition between the curvature-dominated
and the synchrotron-dominated regime. This parameter depends on the local
radius of curvature of the magnetic field line, the gyration radius, and the
pitch angle. We numerically solve the equations of motion for the emitting
particle by considering self-consistently the radiative losses, and provide the
radiated spectrum produced by a particle when an electric acceleration is
balanced by its radiative losses, as it is assumed to happen in the outer gaps
of pulsar's magnetospheres. We compute the average spectrum radiated throughout
the particle trajectory finding that the slope of the spectrum before the peak
depends on the location and size of the emission region. We show how this
effect could then lead to a variety of synchro-curvature spectra. Our results
reinforce the idea that the purely synchrotron or curvature losses are, in
general, inadequate to describe the radiative reaction on the particle motion,
and the spectrum of emitted photons. Finally, we discuss the applicability of
these calculations to different astrophysical scenarios.

We present a hierarchical simulation approach for the dependability analysis
and evaluation of a highly available commercial cache-based RAID storage
system. The archi-tecture is complex and includes several layers of
overlap-ping error detection and recovery mechanisms. Three ab-straction levels
have been developed to model the cache architecture, cache operations, and
error detection and recovery mechanism. The impact of faults and errors
oc-curring in the cache and in the disks is analyzed at each level of the
hierarchy. A simulation submodel is associated with each abstraction level. The
models have been devel-oped using DEPEND, a simulation-based environment for
system-level dependability analysis, which provides facili-ties to inject
faults into a functional behavior model, to simulate error detection and
recovery mechanisms, and to evaluate quantitative measures. Several fault
models are defined for each submodel to simulate cache component failures, disk
failures, transmission errors, and data errors in the cache memory and in the
disks. Some of the parame-ters characterizing fault injection in a given
submodel cor-respond to probabilities evaluated from the simulation of the
lower-level submodel. Based on the proposed method-ology, we evaluate and
analyze 1) the system behavior un-der a real workload and high error rate
(focusing on error bursts), 2) the coverage of the error detection mechanisms
implemented in the system and the error latency distribu-tions, and 3) the
accumulation of errors in the cache and in the disks.

text: This study examines the ultraviolet (UV) emission from main-sequence companions of asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, shedding light on the complex interactions between these binary systems. AGB stars, characterized by intense mass loss, are often accompanied by main-sequence companions, which can significantly influence the UV radiation of their host stars. The objective of this research is to investigate the impact of these main-sequence companions on the UV emission of AGB stars, with a focus on the roles of stellar rotation, mass ratio, and orbital eccentricity.  Using a comprehensive sample of AGB stars with main-sequence companions, we employed a combination of spectroscopic and photometric observations to quantify the UV radiation of these systems. Our analysis revealed a significant correlation between the UV emission of AGB stars and the properties of their main-sequence companions, including stellar rotation and mass ratio. Furthermore, we found that orbital eccentricity plays a crucial role in modulating the UV radiation of AGB stars, with systems exhibiting high eccentricity displaying increased UV emission.  Our key findings indicate that the main-sequence companions of AGB stars can significantly influence their UV radiation, with implications for our understanding of the complex interactions within these binary systems. The results of this study have important implications for the study of AGB stars, binary evolution, and the formation of planetary systems. Overall, this research provides new insights into the dynamics of AGB stars and their main-sequence companions, highlighting the need for further investigation into the complex interactions within these binary systems.

text: This study aims to minimize micromotion artifacts in ion trajectory analysis by employing advanced signal processing techniques and optimizing experimental conditions. The primary goal is to enhance the sensitivity and accuracy of force measurements at microscale levels. We have conducted systematic experiments to identify critical parameters affecting trajectory stability, including chamber pressure, ion source voltage, and sample placement. Through rigorous testing, we determined that reducing chamber pressure to below atmospheric levels significantly mitigates micromotion, thereby improving the fidelity of force measurements. Additionally, we implemented a novel algorithm for real-time correction of ion trajectories based on machine learning principles, which further enhances the precision of force detection. Our findings indicate that these methodologies can achieve force resolutions down to the femtonewton range, demonstrating the feasibility of detecting and quantifying extremely weak interactions. This work not only contributes to the development of more precise ion trajectory analysis techniques but also paves the way for applications in biochemistry, nanotechnology, and materials science where sensitive force measurements are crucial.

We present a novel generalization of the two-stream method of radiative
transfer, which allows for the accurate treatment of radiative transfer in the
presence of strong infrared scattering by aerosols. We prove that this
generalization involves only a simple modification of the coupling coefficients
and transmission functions in the hemispheric two-stream method. This
modification originates from allowing the ratio of the first Eddington
coefficients to depart from unity. At the heart of the method is the fact that
this ratio may be computed once and for all over the entire range of values of
the single-scattering albedo and scattering asymmetry factor. We benchmark our
improved two-stream method by calculating the fraction of flux reflected by a
single atmospheric layer (the reflectivity) and comparing these calculations to
those performed using a 32-stream discrete-ordinates method. We further compare
our improved two-stream method to the two-stream source function (16 streams)
and delta-Eddington methods, demonstrating that it is often more accurate at
the order-of-magnitude level. Finally, we illustrate its accuracy using a toy
model of the early Martian atmosphere hosting a cloud layer composed of
carbon-dioxide ice particles. The simplicity of implementation and accuracy of
our improved two-stream method renders it suitable for implementation in
three-dimensional general circulation models. In other words, our improved
two-stream method has the ease of implementation of a standard two-stream
method, but the accuracy of a 32-stream method.

text: In this work, we develop a semi-analytic dynamical friction model aimed at replicating the phenomenon of core stalling in astrophysical bodies. Core stalling, a critical aspect of stellar evolution, poses significant challenges in understanding the mechanisms governing angular momentum transfer and core-envelope interactions. Our approach combines rigorous analytical techniques with numerical simulations to characterize the transition states of stellar cores under varying conditions.   We model the frictional forces influencing the core's momentum and establish a set of governing equations that yield solutions representing core dynamics in response to gravitational interactions. Through systematic parameter variation, we examine the effects of core mass, rotation rate, and envelope density on the stalling behavior. Our results indicate that the efficiency of angular momentum transport is highly dependent on these parameters, leading to distinct regions of core behavior.   We validate our model against observational data from existing stellar populations and find a strong correlation between our predictions and empirical stalling instances across diverse star types. Moreover, our findings suggest a threshold dependency of core dynamics on the surrounding envelope's characteristics, proposing new insights into stellar evolution pathways. This semi-analytic framework not only provides a robust tool for forecasting core stalling but also enhances our understanding of the underlying physics governing stellar lifecycle processes. We conclude that our model serves as a foundation for further research in stellar dynamics, potentially guiding future astrophysical simulations and observations.

We speed up thermal simulations of quantum many-body systems in both one-
(1D) and two-dimensional (2D) models in an exponential way by iteratively
projecting the thermal density matrix $\hat\rho=e^{-\beta \hat{H}}$ onto
itself. We refer to this scheme of doubling $\beta$ in each step of the
imaginary time evolution as the exponential tensor renormalization group
(XTRG). This approach is in stark contrast to conventional Trotter-Suzuki-type
methods which evolve $\hat\rho$ on a linear quasi-continuous grid in inverse
temperature $\beta \equiv 1/T$. In general, XTRG can reach low temperatures
exponentially fast, and thus not only saves computational time but also merits
better accuracy due to significantly fewer truncation steps. We work in an
(effective) 1D setting exploiting matrix product operators (MPOs) which allows
us to fully and uniquely implement non-Abelian and Abelian symmetries to
greatly enhance numerical performance. We use our XTRG machinery to explore the
thermal properties of Heisenberg models on 1D chains and 2D square and
triangular lattices down to low temperatures approaching ground state
properties. The entanglement properties, as well as the renormalization group
flow of entanglement spectra in MPOs, are discussed, where logarithmic
entropies (approximately $\ln\beta$) are shown in both spin chains and square
lattice models with gapless towers of states. We also reveal that XTRG can be
employed to accurately simulate the Heisenberg XXZ model on the square lattice
which undergoes a thermal phase transition. We determine its critical
temperature based on thermal physical observables, as well as entanglement
measures. Overall, we demonstrate that XTRG provides an elegant, versatile, and
highly competitive approach to explore thermal properties in both 1D and 2D
quantum lattice models.

text: The pursuit of a precise response function for the magnetic component of Gravitational Waves in Scalar-Tensor Gravity stands as a crucial endeavor in contemporary gravitational wave research. This study aims to investigate and determine a definitive response function that accurately represents the behavior of the magnetic component of gravitational waves within the framework of Scalar-Tensor Gravity. Addressing this key problem is essential for enhancing our understanding of how gravitational waves manifest in alternative gravity theories beyond General Relativity.   Our work presents the results of comprehensive analytical calculations and numerical simulations that have led to the derivation of a novel response function specifically tailored for the magnetic component of gravitational waves in Scalar-Tensor Gravity. By employing sophisticated mathematical formalisms and computational techniques, we have successfully elucidated the intricate nature of this response function, offering a more nuanced perspective on the interactions between gravitational waves and scalar fields in alternative gravity theories.  The methodology employed in this research involved intricate mathematical modeling, theoretical analysis, and numerical computations to capture the nuanced behavior of the magnetic component of gravitational waves in Scalar-Tensor Gravity. Through our rigorous approach, we have not only addressed the key problem at hand but also made significant strides towards a more comprehensive understanding of gravitational wave phenomena in the context of alternative gravity theories.

Spintronic devices, such as non-volatile magnetic random access memories and
logic devices, have attracted considerable attention as potential candidates
for future high efficient data storage and computing technology. In a heavy
metal or other emerging material with strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC), the
charge currents induce spin currents or spin accumulations via SOC. The
generated spin currents can exert spin-orbit torques (SOTs) on an adjacent
ferromagnet, which opens up a new way to realize magnetization dynamics and
switching of the ferromagnetic layer for spintronic devices. In the SOT scheme,
the charge-to-spin interconversion efficiency (SOT efficiency) is an important
figure of merit for applications. For the effective characterization of this
efficiency, the ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) based methods, such as the spin
transfer torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) and the spin pumping, are
common utilized in addition to low frequency harmonic or dc measurements. In
this review, we focus on the ST-FMR measurements for the evaluation of the SOT
efficiency. We provide a brief summary of the different ST-FMR setups and data
analysis methods. We then discuss ST-FMR and SOT studies in various materials,
including heavy metals and alloys, topological insulators, two dimensional (2D)
materials, interfaces with strong Rashba effect, antiferromagnetic materials,
two dimensional electron gas (2DEG) in oxide materials and oxidized nonmagnetic
materials.

The primary science goal of the NASA-sponsored ANITA project is measurement
of ultra-high energy neutrinos and cosmic rays, observed via radio-frequency
signals resulting from a neutrino- or cosmic ray- interaction with terrestrial
matter (atmospheric or ice molecules, e.g.). Accurate inference of the energies
of these cosmic rays requires understanding the transmission/reflection of
radio wave signals across the ice-air boundary. Satellite-based measurements of
Antarctic surface reflectivity, using a co-located transmitter and receiver,
have been performed more-or-less continuously for the last few decades.
Satellite-based reflectivity surveys, at frequencies ranging from 2--45 GHz and
at near-normal incidence, yield generally consistent reflectivity maps across
Antarctica. Using the Sun as an RF source, and the ANITA-3 balloon borne
radio-frequency antenna array as the RF receiver, we have also measured the
surface reflectivity over the interval 200-1000 MHz, at elevation angles of
12-30 degrees, finding agreement with the Fresnel equations within systematic
errors. To probe low incidence angles, inaccessible to the Antarctic Solar
technique and not probed by previous satellite surveys, a novel experimental
approach ("HiCal-1") was devised. Unlike previous measurements, HiCal-ANITA
constitute a bi-static transmitter-receiver pair separated by hundreds of
kilometers. Data taken with HiCal, between 200--600 MHz shows a significant
departure from the Fresnel equations, constant with frequency over that band,
with the deficit increasing with obliquity of incidence, which we attribute to
the combined effects of possible surface roughness, surface grain effects,
radar clutter and/or shadowing of the reflection zone due to Earth curvature
effects.

text: The Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) is a high-resolution microwave telescope designed to study the cosmic microwave background (CMB), providing detailed insights into the early universe. This research focuses on the data characterization and map-making techniques employed by ACT to achieve these objectives. The study begins with an overview of the telescope's design and capabilities, emphasizing its sensitivity and angular resolution. Key methodologies involve advanced signal processing techniques to mitigate atmospheric noise and foreground contamination, ensuring robust cosmological parameter estimation.  Data analysis techniques include the application of Kalman filtering algorithms to track changes in the pointing accuracy over time and ensure consistent measurements across observations. A critical aspect of the research involves developing new methods for foreground removal, particularly targeting dust emission and synchrotron radiation, which can significantly impact CMB measurements. The effectiveness of these techniques is evaluated through simulations and real-world data sets from ACT.  The primary objective of this research is to enhance the quality and reliability of CMB maps produced by ACT, thereby improving our understanding of the large-scale structure of the universe and testing fundamental theories of cosmology. The key findings demonstrate significant improvements in the accuracy and precision of CMB maps compared to previous studies. These advancements not only validate the technological capabilities of ACT but also underscore the importance of ongoing data analysis and map-making processes in cosmology.  In conclusion, this research underscores the crucial role of sophisticated data analysis techniques in maximizing the scientific potential of high-end telescopes like ACT. The outcomes highlight the potential for future CMB surveys to yield even more precise cosmological information, driving advancements in both observational astronomy and theoretical physics.

text: We examine the intricate relationship between halo histories and galaxy properties at redshift z=0, focusing on the mechanisms underlying the quenching of star formation. In our analysis, we utilize a comprehensive dataset that integrates observational data from surveys and simulation results, thereby enabling us to investigate the influence of halo mass, assembly history, and environmental factors on galaxy evolution. Our results reveal a clear correlation between quenching mechanisms and the mass assembly of dark matter halos, suggesting that galaxies residing within massive, rapidly assembled halos exhibit a more pronounced suppression of star formation relative to those in lower mass, slowly evolving environments.  We identify key processes that contribute to quenching, including effective feedback from active galactic nuclei and stellar winds, which become increasingly significant in the context of high-mass halos. Furthermore, we employ a novel methodology that combines machine learning techniques with traditional astrophysical modeling to enhance the precision of our predictions regarding star formation rates across various galaxy types. Our findings provide critical insights into the evolutionary pathways of galaxies, elucidating how halo histories shape the observable properties of galaxies at z=0. Overall, this work not only addresses a vital problem in contemporary astrophysics but also lays the groundwork for future investigations into galaxy formation and evolution, emphasizing the necessity of a holistic approach that considers both halo dynamics and internal galaxy processes.

Signal analysis is one of the finest scientific techniques in communication
theory. Some quantitative and qualitative measures describe the pattern of a
music signal, vary from one to another. Same musical recital, when played by
different instrumentalists, generates different types of music patterns. The
reason behind various patterns is the psychoacoustic measures - Dynamics,
Timber, Tonality and Rhythm, varies in each time. However, the psycho-acoustic
study of the music signals does not reveal any idea about the similarity
between the signals. For such cases, study of synchronization of long-term
nonlinear dynamics may provide effective results. In this context, phase
synchronization (PS) is one of the measures to show synchronization between two
non-identical signals. In fact, it is very critical to investigate any other
kind of synchronization for experimental condition, because those are
completely non identical signals. Also, there exists equivalence between the
phases and the distances of the diagonal line in Recurrence plot (RP) of the
signals, which is quantifiable by the recurrence quantification measure
tau-recurrence rate. This paper considers two nonlinear music signals based on
same raga played by two eminent sitar instrumentalists as two non-identical
sources. The psycho-acoustic study shows how the Dynamics, Timber, Tonality and
Rhythm vary for the two music signals. Then, long term analysis in the form of
phase space reconstruction is performed, which reveals the chaotic phase spaces
for both the signals. From the RP of both the phase spaces, tau-recurrence rate
is calculated. Finally by the correlation of normalized tau-recurrence rate of
their 3D phase spaces and the PS of the two music signals has been established.
The numerical results well support the analysis.

We report on our progress in studying exotic, heavy tetraquark states,
$qq\prime \bar Q\bar Q\prime$. Using publicly available dynamical $n_f =2+1$
Wilson-Clover gauge configurations, generated by the PACS-CS collaboration,
with pion masses $\simeq$164, 299 and 415 MeV, we extend our previous analysis
to heavy quark components containing heavier than physical bottom quarks $\bar
Q\bar Q\prime=\bar b\prime\bar b\prime$ or $\bar Q\bar Q\prime=\bar b\bar
b\prime$, charm and bottom quarks $\bar c\bar b$ and also only charm quarks
$\bar c\bar c$. Throughout we employ NRQCD and relativistic heavy quarks for
the heavier than bottom, bottom and charm quarks. Using our previously
established diquark-antidiquark and meson-meson operator basis we comment in
particular on the dependence of the binding energy on the mass of the heavy
quark component $\bar Q\bar Q$, with heavy quarks ranging from $m_Q=0.85\ldots
6.3\cdot m_b$. In the heavy flavor non-degenerate case, $\bar Q\bar Q\prime$,
and especially for the tetraquark channel $ud\bar c\bar b$, we extend our work
to utilize a $3\times 3$ GEVP to study the ground and threshold states thereby
enabling a clear identification of possible binding. Finally, we present
initial work on the $\bar Q\bar Q\prime=\bar c\bar c$ system where a much
larger operator basis is available in comparison to flavor combinations with
NRQCD quarks.
