text: This research aims to determine the timing of tidal disruption events (TDEs) of globular clusters by utilizing Gaia astrometric data, focusing on the observable stellar streams that result from these disruptions. Previous studies have shown that TDEs can significantly affect the structure of globular clusters, leading to the formation of extended stellar debris known as tidal tails or streams. By analyzing the Gaia data, we aim to identify these streams and infer the ages of the disrupted globular clusters through their kinematic properties.  The methodology involves first identifying candidate globular clusters in the Gaia DR3 catalog based on their spatial distribution and velocity dispersion. Subsequently, we apply advanced computational techniques to detect and characterize stellar streams within these clusters. We then estimate the age of each stream using models that incorporate the observed velocities and spatial distributions of stars. This approach allows us to establish a chronological sequence of TDE events for different globular clusters.  Key findings indicate that the majority of identified stellar streams exhibit velocities consistent with being remnants of recent TDEs. The derived ages range from a few million years to tens of millions of years, with some streams showing evidence of ongoing disruption processes. These results provide valuable insights into the frequency and timescales of TDEs in globular cluster systems, contributing to our understanding of galactic evolution and dynamics.  In conclusion, this study successfully demonstrates the potential of Gaia data to probe the history of tidal disruption events in globular clusters, offering a new perspective on the lifecycle of these dense stellar populations. Future work will focus on refining the age estimates and expanding the sample size to better constrain the overall population of TDEs in galactic environments.

text: The Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) is an interatomic potential derived from first principles quantum mechanics calculations, which approximates the potential energy surface by expanding the electronic wave function in a basis set of Gaussian functions (1). This method, based on the density functional theory (DFT), provides a computationally efficient alternative to the more expensive ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, without sacrificing accuracy (2).  We applied the GAP methodology to model the solid-liquid phase transition in copper using large-scale molecular dynamics simulations (3). Our calculations showed that the liquid phase of copper, known to exhibit considerable structural disorder, is accurately described by the GAP potential. The potential energy surface of the GAP liquid displayed the characteristic oscillatory behavior of the Lennard-Jones liquid, with a correlation time consistent with the experimental results (4). Moreover, we observed an excellent agreement between the computed and experimental structural and dynamical properties, such as the pressure, density, and mean-square displacement of the atoms, as well as the sound velocity and self-diffusivity (5).  Our study demonstrates the ability of the GAP method to provide accurate results at a significantly reduced computational cost, making it a valuable tool for investigating complex systems, such as alloys and materials under extreme conditions, for which traditional ab initio simulations are too time-consuming. The methodology also has applications in fields like chemistry, materials science, and condensed matter physics, where computational efficiency and accuracy are essential.  In conclusion, we present the application of the Gaussian Approximation Potential method to model the solid-liquid phase transition in copper. Our results reveal the capability of the GAP potential to accurately capture the essential features of the system and provide a computationally efficient alternative to traditional ab initio simulations. Indoor localization has recently witnessed an increase in interest, due to
the potential wide range of services it can provide by leveraging Internet of
Things (IoT), and ubiquitous connectivity. Different techniques, wireless
technologies and mechanisms have been proposed in the literature to provide
indoor localization services in order to improve the services provided to the
users. However, there is a lack of an up-to-date survey paper that incorporates
some of the recently proposed accurate and reliable localization systems. In
this paper, we aim to provide a detailed survey of different indoor
localization techniques such as Angle of Arrival (AoA), Time of Flight (ToF),
Return Time of Flight (RTOF), Received Signal Strength (RSS); based on
technologies such as WiFi, Radio Frequency Identification Device (RFID), Ultra
Wideband (UWB), Bluetooth and systems that have been proposed in the
literature. The paper primarily discusses localization and positioning of human
users and their devices. We highlight the strengths of the existing systems
proposed in the literature. In contrast with the existing surveys, we also
evaluate different systems from the perspective of energy efficiency,
availability, cost, reception range, latency, scalability and tracking
accuracy. Rather than comparing the technologies or techniques, we compare the
localization systems and summarize their working principle. We also discuss
remaining challenges to accurate indoor localization.

text: This research paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the L1 Scheme applied to the subdiffusion equation characterized by nonsmooth data. The subdiffusion equation serves as a mathematical model for phenomena that exhibit anomalous diffusion behaviors, prevalent in various fields including physics and finance. The objective of this study is to develop an efficient numerical scheme for solving the subdiffusion equation that maintains accuracy and stability when faced with nonsmooth initial and boundary conditions. Employing a discrete L1 scheme, we formulate the problem and establish theoretical foundations by proving convergence and stability under certain regularity conditions. The methodology encompasses a detailed numerical analysis that examines the impact of nonsmooth data on the solution's behavior and convergence rates. Through various numerical experiments, our results illustrate the performance of the L1 Scheme in accurately capturing the dynamics of the subdiffusion process, even in the presence of discontinuities and irregularities in the data. Key findings reveal that the proposed L1 Scheme not only adheres to the expected convergence rates but also outperforms traditional methods in terms of computational efficiency and robustness against nonsmooth features. In conclusion, the findings of this study substantiate the viability of the L1 Scheme as an effective computational tool for addressing the challenges posed by nonsmooth initial data in subdiffusion equations, paving the way for its application in more complex systems and real-world scenarios.
