We discuss the central role played by the X-ray study of hot baryons within
galaxy clusters to reconstruct the assembly of cosmic structures and to trace
the past history of star formation and accretion onto supermassive Black Holes
(BHs). We shortly review the progress in this field contributed by the current
generation of X-ray telescopes. Then, we focus on the outstanding scientific
questions that have been opened by observations carried out in the last years
and that represent the legacy of Chandra and XMM: (a) When and how is entropy
injected into the inter-galactic medium (IGM)? (b) What is the history of metal
enrichment of the IGM? (c) What physical mechanisms determine the presence of
cool cores in galaxy clusters? (d) How is the appearance of proto-clusters at
z~2 related to the peak of star formation activity and BH accretion? We show
that a highly efficient observational strategy to address these questions is to
carry out a large-area X-ray survey, reaching a sensitivity comparable to that
of deep Chandra and XMM pointings, but extending over several thousands of
square degrees. A similar survey can only be carried out with a Wide-Field
X-ray Telescope (WFXT), which combines a high survey speed with a sharp PSF
across the entire FoV. We emphasize the important synergies that WFXT will have
with a number of future ground-based and space telescopes, covering from the
radio to the X-ray bands. Finally, we discuss the immense legacy value that
such a mission will have for extragalactic astronomy at large.

text: The Hubbard Model, a fundamental model in condensed matter physics, poses a significant computational challenge due to its high dimensionality and strong correlation effects. In this study, we propose a new methodology for the exact diagonalization (ED) of the Hubbard Model by optimally organizing its Hilbert space. Specifically, we apply a recently developed method, Flexible Localized Orbital Transformation (FLOT), to construct a minimal basis set, reducing the computational cost while maintaining ED accuracy.  We begin by introducing the essential aspects of the Hubbard Model, including the Hamiltonian, the Pauli principle, and the Hilbert space structure. We describe how the Hubbard Model's complexity arises from its large number of orbitals and strong correlation effects. To overcome these challenges, we apply the FLOT method, which consists of three main steps (1) a unitary transformation of the orbitals, (2) a localization procedure, and (3) a truncation of the resulting basis set.  Next, we present our results and discuss the advantages of our methodology. By optimally organizing the Hilbert space using FLOT, we can significantly reduce the computational cost for ED calculations of the Hubbard Model while preserving the accuracy of the results. Our results demonstrate that the proposed methodology can handle larger systems and more complex correlation effects than previous approaches. Additionally, we provide a comparative analysis with other methods in the literature to validate our findings.  In conclusion, this study proposes a new methodology for the exact diagonalization of the Hubbard Model by optimally organizing its Hilbert space using the FLOT method. By reducing the computational cost while maintaining accuracy, our methodology allows for larger systems and more complex correlation effects to be investigated, advancing the field of condensed matter physics.

text: We investigate the general boundary conditions applicable to quasiclassical theory of superconductivity in the diffusive limit, focusing specifically on their application to strongly spin-polarized systems. Our work addresses the challenge of accurately modeling the interface effects that arise in superconducting materials with significant spin polarization, which are critical for the development of spintronic devices. We derive a set of boundary conditions that incorporate both spin and charge transport phenomena, allowing for a comprehensive description of the superconducting state under varied conditions of magnetization. Employing the quasiclassical Green's function formalism, we systematically analyze the interplay between superconductivity and spin polarization in diffusive systems, guiding our approach through numerical simulations that validate our theoretical predictions. Our results reveal that the generalized boundary conditions enable us to capture the intricate effects of spin accumulation at the interfaces, leading to observable modifications in the superconducting gap and critical temperature. We find that the degree of spin polarization significantly influences the proximity effect and the overall stability of the superconducting state. Furthermore, we provide a detailed numerical example demonstrating these boundary conditions in practice, highlighting their applicability in designing novel superconducting devices that exploit spin-dependent phenomena. Our findings contribute to the fundamental understanding of superconductivity in the context of spintronics, establishing a framework for future research aimed at integrating superconductivity with robust spin transport properties.

The combination of gas-rich conditions and the observed radio morphology suggests that NGC 3998 represents a unique case of AGN-driven outflows in a heterogeneous environment. We conclude that NGC 3998 is an illustrative example of how low surface-brightness radio structures can provide essential clues to the processes governing the evolution of early-type galaxies and their role in the larger cosmic landscape.

The discovery of decay products of a short-lived radioisotope (SLRI) in the
Allende meteorite led to the hypothesis that a supernova shock wave transported
freshly synthesized SLRI to the presolar dense cloud core, triggered its
self-gravitational collapse, and injected the SLRI into the core. Previous
multidimensional numerical calculations of the shock-cloud collision process
showed that this hypothesis is plausible when the shock wave and dense cloud
core are assumed to remain isothermal at ~10 K, but not when compressional
heating to ~1000 K is assumed. Our two-dimensional models (Boss et al. 2008)
with the FLASH2.5 adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) hydrodynamics code have shown
that a 20 km/sec shock front can simultaneously trigger collapse of a 1 solar
mass core and inject shock wave material, provided that cooling by molecular
species such as H2O, CO, and H2 is included. Here we present the results for
similar calculations with shock speeds ranging from 1 km/sec to 100 km/sec. We
find that shock speeds in the range from 5 km/sec to 70 km/sec are able to
trigger the collapse of a 2.2 solar mass cloud while simultaneously injecting
shock wave material: lower speed shocks do not achieve injection, while higher
speed shocks do not trigger sustained collapse. The calculations continue to
support the shock-wave trigger hypothesis for the formation of the solar
system, though the injection efficiencies in the present models are lower than
desired.

text: The increasing adoption of renewable energy sources and power electronics in industrial applications has necessitated the development of more robust voltage transformation techniques. Traditional crowbar circuits, despite their simplicity, suffer from significant voltage fluctuations during load switching, leading to voltage surges and power system instability.  To mitigate these voltage fluctuations, this work proposes the design and simulation of a TVEN for a crowbar application. The network consists of a set of passive R-C filters and thyristors configured in a specific switching sequence. The R-C filters compensate for the input voltage ripple, while the thyristors enable controlled voltage equalization. The design process involved thorough simulation using PSpice, followed by laboratory testing to evaluate the network's performance under various load conditions.  The simulation results demonstrated an improvement in voltage regulation, with a reduction in peak-to-peak voltage fluctuations by over 40%. The experimental data confirmed these results, validating the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed TVEN design. The methodology employed in this study highlights the importance of designing voltage equalizing networks to maintain stable voltage levels during rapid load switching and enhance the overall system's reliability and robustness.  In conclusion, the proposed TVEN design effectively addresses the issue of voltage fluctuations in traditional crowbar applications, contributing to more stable voltage transformations and improved system performance. These findings are significant for the ongoing research and development in the areas of renewable energy sources, power electronics, and industrial power systems.

text: We investigate the interaction between dipolar and quadrupolar magnetic field geometries on thermally driven winds, a phenomenon crucial in understanding the atmospheric dynamics of exoplanets and the Earth's own climate. Through a series of numerical simulations, we explore the impact of combined magnetic field configurations on wind patterns, focusing on the interaction between the two types of fields. Our results show that the coexistence of dipolar and quadrupolar fields leads to a complex and nonlinear interaction, resulting in the formation of vortices and enhanced wind speeds in certain regions.  We find that the dipolar field plays a dominant role in shaping the large-scale wind patterns, while the quadrupolar field has a significant impact on the local wind structures. The interaction between the two fields leads to the formation of a unique wind regime, characterized by a mix of rotational and meridional flows. Our simulations also reveal that the strength and orientation of the magnetic fields have a significant impact on the wind patterns, with stronger and more aligned fields leading to more pronounced effects.  Our study demonstrates the importance of considering the combined effects of dipolar and quadrupolar magnetic fields in understanding thermally driven winds. The findings of this research have implications for the study of exoplanetary atmospheres and the Earth's own climate, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between magnetic fields, wind patterns, and atmospheric dynamics.

text: Horndeski gravity, a popular extension of the General Relativity (GR) theory, allows for a more diverse range of fields with non-minimal interactions. The critical point, where the expansion rate of the universe becomes zero, is an important cosmic epoch in studying the dynamics of the universe. In this paper, we derive an a-theorem for Horndeski gravity at the critical point, extending the results obtained for GR. The background of this study starts with an overview of Horndeski gravity, its differences with GR, and the significance of the critical point in cosmology. The objective of our research is to establish a relation between the a-coefficient, which measures the deviation from GR, and the dynamical properties at the critical point. We employ a perturbative approach in the linear regime, focusing on scalar perturbations around a spatially flat Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) background. By analyzing the second-order field equations and the conservation equations, we derive a general expression for the a-coefficient at the critical point. Our key findings indicate that the a-coefficient depends on the interaction term between the scalar field and the metric, as well as the equation of state parameter of the dominant energy component. These findings provide insights into the behavior of Horndeski gravity at the critical point and could potentially lead to new observational tests. In conclusion, we have derived an a-theorem for Horndeski gravity at the critical point, offering a valuable extension to the results obtained for GR. Our findings emphasize the significance of the interaction term and the equation of state parameter in shaping the dynamics of the universe at this crucial cosmic epoch. Further studies are warranted to explore the implications of our results on observational data and future experiments.

text: Cladocera, a major zooplankton group, is known for its diverse adaptation to various environmental conditions. In this study, we focus on two Cladoceran species, Bosmina longirostris and Daphnia galeata, living in contrasting ultraviolet (UV) environments eutrophic and oligotrophic lakes, respectively. Our objective was to explore population strategies of these species in response to different UV regimes.  To achieve this, we collected samples during late spring from various depths of five eutrophic and five oligotrophic lakes located in the same region. We measured UV transmittance and absorptance of the water, as well as the UV production by algal communities. Population density, body size, and reproductive activity of both species were quantified.  Our results revealed that Bosmina longirostris displayed a higher population density and smaller body size in eutrophic lakes with higher UV transmission and algal biomass. In contrast, Daphnia galeata exhibited larger body size and lower reproductive activity in oligotrophic lakes with lower UV transmission and scarce algal populations. Moreover, Bosmina longirostris showed a positive correlation between population density and UV transmission, whereas Daphnia galeata showed no significant correlation.  These findings suggest that Bosmina longirostris evolved to exploit higher algal production in eutrophic lakes under stronger UV conditions. In contrast, Daphnia galeata appears to have evolved to cope with lower UV intensity in oligotrophic lakes and may rely on other food sources, such as bacteria and organic matter.  In conclusion, this study disentangled population strategies of Bosmina longirostris and Daphnia galeata in response to different UV regimes, providing new insights into the adaptive mechanisms of these species in diverse aquatic environments.

We study compressed sensing (CS) signal reconstruction problems where an
input signal is measured via matrix multiplication under additive white
Gaussian noise. Our signals are assumed to be stationary and ergodic, but the
input statistics are unknown; the goal is to provide reconstruction algorithms
that are universal to the input statistics. We present a novel algorithmic
framework that combines: (i) the approximate message passing (AMP) CS
reconstruction framework, which solves the matrix channel recovery problem by
iterative scalar channel denoising; (ii) a universal denoising scheme based on
context quantization, which partitions the stationary ergodic signal denoising
into independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) subsequence denoising;
and (iii) a density estimation approach that approximates the probability
distribution of an i.i.d. sequence by fitting a Gaussian mixture (GM) model. In
addition to the algorithmic framework, we provide three contributions: (i)
numerical results showing that state evolution holds for non-separable Bayesian
sliding-window denoisers; (ii) an i.i.d. denoiser based on a modified GM
learning algorithm; and (iii) a universal denoiser that does not need
information about the range where the input takes values from or require the
input signal to be bounded. We provide two implementations of our universal CS
recovery algorithm with one being faster and the other being more accurate. The
two implementations compare favorably with existing universal reconstruction
algorithms in terms of both reconstruction quality and runtime.

In this work, a relay channel is studied in which a source encoder
communicates with a destination decoder through a number of out-of-band relays
that are connected to the decoder through capacity-constrained digital backhaul
links. This model is motivated by the uplink of cloud radio access networks. In
this scenario, a novel transmission and relaying strategies are proposed in
which multi-layer transmission is used, on the one hand, to adaptively leverage
the different decoding capabilities of the relays and, on the other hand, to
enable hybrid decode-and-forward (DF) and compress-and-forward (CF) relaying.
The hybrid relaying strategy allows each relay to forward part of the decoded
messages and a compressed version of the received signal to the decoder. The
problem of optimizing the power allocation across the layers and the
compression test channels is formulated. Albeit non-convex, the derived problem
is found to belong to the class of so called complementary geometric programs
(CGPs). Using this observation, an iterative algorithm based on the homotopy
method is proposed that achieves a stationary point of the original problem by
solving a sequence of geometric programming (GP), and thus convex, problems.
Numerical results are provided that show the effectiveness of the proposed
multi-layer hybrid scheme in achieving performance close to a theoretical
(cutset) upper bound.

text: In this study, we present a novel model to elucidate the origin of high density observed in loop-top X-ray sources associated with solar flares. Our research seeks to address the longstanding enigma of how such elevated densities occur at the apex of magnetic loops in the solar corona, which has implications for understanding coronal heating and energy release during solar flare events. We propose a mechanism combining magnetic reconnection and thermal conduction processes, supported by numerical simulations, to explain the observed density enhancements. Using magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations, we modeled the evolution of plasma density and temperature profiles in post-flare loops. Our results demonstrate that magnetic reconnection events lead to localized compressions, effectively increasing plasma density. Further, we identified a significant role of suppressed thermal conduction due to the geometry of magnetic field lines, which contributes to the retention of high densities in loop-top regions. By varying parameters such as magnetic field strength and loop length, our simulations reproduced observational features consistent with high-resolution X-ray imagery. These findings suggest a coherent picture where both magnetic and thermal dynamics are critical to high loop-top densities, advancing the theoretical framework of flare-associated coronal phenomena. Our work not only provides insights into the physical processes shaping loop-top X-ray sources but also lays the foundation for future explorations to predict solar flare behavior and their space weather implications.

text: We investigate the construction and properties of non-simplicial nerves for two-dimensional categorical structures, thereby providing a novel framework for understanding and analyzing these abstract objects. Our approach is based on the notion of a nerve as a topological space that encodes the structure of a category, and we adapt this concept to the context of two-dimensional categories. We develop a systematic method for constructing non-simplicial nerves, leveraging the properties of simplicial nerves and the relationships between categories and their nerves. Our results reveal that non-simplicial nerves can be used to encode complex categorical structures, including those with non-trivial 2-morphisms.  Through our analysis, we demonstrate that non-simplicial nerves can be used to distinguish between equivalent categories in certain cases, thereby providing a tool for categorical identification. Furthermore, we show that non-simplicial nerves can be used to study the properties of 2-morphisms, such as their relationships and interactions. Our work has implications for the study of higher category theory, as it provides a new perspective on the relationships between categories and their nerves. We also provide examples of non-simplicial nerves for various two-dimensional categorical structures, including those arising in homotopy type theory and higher category theory.

We investigate video classification via a two-stream convolutional neural
network (CNN) design that directly ingests information extracted from
compressed video bitstreams. Our approach begins with the observation that all
modern video codecs divide the input frames into macroblocks (MBs). We
demonstrate that selective access to MB motion vector (MV) information within
compressed video bitstreams can also provide for selective, motion-adaptive, MB
pixel decoding (a.k.a., MB texture decoding). This in turn allows for the
derivation of spatio-temporal video activity regions at extremely high speed in
comparison to conventional full-frame decoding followed by optical flow
estimation. In order to evaluate the accuracy of a video classification
framework based on such activity data, we independently train two CNN
architectures on MB texture and MV correspondences and then fuse their scores
to derive the final classification of each test video. Evaluation on two
standard datasets shows that the proposed approach is competitive to the best
two-stream video classification approaches found in the literature. At the same
time: (i) a CPU-based realization of our MV extraction is over 977 times faster
than GPU-based optical flow methods; (ii) selective decoding is up to 12 times
faster than full-frame decoding; (iii) our proposed spatial and temporal CNNs
perform inference at 5 to 49 times lower cloud computing cost than the fastest
methods from the literature.

text: In this study, we explore the dispersionless Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (dKP) equation with arbitrary nonlinearity and dimensionality to analyze exact solutions, the longtime asymptotics of the Cauchy problem, and the formation of wave breaks and discontinuous shocks. We aim to generalize the existing theoretical framework of the dKP equation to encompass more complex scenarios dictated by variable nonlinearity and dimensional parameters. phase space, leading to a large resonant increase in the current flow at
critical values of the applied voltage. This phase-space patterning provides a
sensitive mechanism for controlling electrical resistance. In this paper, we

commensurate, complex multistability phenomena occur in the system. In

In this paper, a few novel data hiding techniques are proposed. These
techniques are improvements over the classical LSB data hiding technique and
the Fibonacci LSB data-hiding technique proposed by Battisti et al. \cite{r1}.
The classical LSB technique is the simplest, but using this technique it is
possible to embed only in first few bit-planes, since image quality becomes
drastically distorted when embedding in higher bit-planes. Battisti et al.
\cite{r1} proposed an improvement over this by using Fibonacci decomposition
technique and generating a different set of virtual bit-planes all together,
thereby increasing the number of bit-planes. In this paper, first we
mathematically model and generalize this particular approach of virtual
bit-plane generation. Then we propose two novel embedding techniques, both of
which are special-cases of our generalized model. The first embedding scheme is
based on decomposition of a number (pixel-value) in sum of prime numbers, while
the second one is based on decomposition in sum of natural numbers. Each of
these particular representations generates a different set of (virtual)
bit-planes altogether, suitable for embedding purposes. They not only allow one
to embed secret message in higher bit-planes but also do it without much
distortion, with a much better stego-image quality, in a reliable and secured
manner, guaranteeing efficient retrieval of secret message. A comparative
performance study between the classical Least Significant Bit (LSB) method, the
data hiding technique using Fibonacci -p-Sequence decomposition and our
proposed schemes has been done. Theoretical analysis indicates that image
quality of the stego-image hidden by the technique using Fibonacci
decomposition improves against simple LSB substitution method, while the same
using the prime decomposition method improves drastically against that using
Fibonacci decomposition technique, and finally the natural number decomposition
method is a further improvement against that using prime decomposition
technique. Also, optimality for the last technique is proved. For both of our
data-hiding techniques, the experimental results show that, the stego-image is
visually indistinguishable from the original cover image.

text: This study develops a dynamic axiomatic approach to first-price auctions, providing a comprehensive framework for analyzing and understanding the strategic behavior of bidders in these auctions. In first-price auctions, bidders submit a sealed bid, and the highest bidder wins the item at the price they bid. The static model of first-price auctions has been widely used, but it fails to capture the dynamic nature of these auctions, where bidders may observe other bidders' actions and adjust their strategies accordingly.  The proposed dynamic axiomatic approach extends the traditional model by incorporating time-varying bidder types, information asymmetry, and strategic complementarity. We introduce a set of axioms that capture the key features of first-price auctions, including the existence of equilibrium, bidder rationality, and the absence of arbitrage opportunities. These axioms are used to derive a dynamic equilibrium concept, which describes the optimal bidding strategy for bidders in the presence of uncertainty and strategic complementarity.  Our analysis reveals that the dynamic axiomatic approach can capture the complexity of first-price auctions, including the emergence of bidder heterogeneity and the impact of information asymmetry on bidding behavior. We also demonstrate that the proposed framework can be used to analyze a wide range of first-price auction settings, including sealed-bid, open-outcry, and online auctions. The study provides a foundation for further research on dynamic auction theory and has implications for the design and analysis of first-price auctions in various economic and social contexts.

text: This study investigates the application of Kronecker algebra in the verification of concurrent systems that utilize shared memory. Traditional methods, such as model checking, suffer from state explosion and are often ineffective for large SMCS. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel method utilizing Kronecker algebra to verify SMCS.  First, we present a formal framework for modeling shared memory systems using Kronecker algebra. We define the system components, including the shared memory matrix, and the processes as linear transformations acting on the memory state. We then derive a set of necessary and sufficient conditions for the reachability of a given state in the system.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through an application to a well-known example in the literature the producer-consumer problem. Our method is able to efficiently verify the safety property of the system by exploiting the algebraic structure of the shared memory matrix.  Finally, we discuss the benefits and limitations of our approach, including its scalability and applicability to other concurrent systems with shared memory. Our results show that Kronecker algebra offers a promising alternative to traditional methods in the verification of SMCS, particularly for large and complex systems.  The application of Kronecker algebra to the verification of concurrent systems with shared memory provides a powerful and efficient solution to the challenges presented by this complex system design. Our results demonstrate that the approach is effective in verifying safety properties of the producer-consumer problem and offers a promising alternative to traditional methods, such as model checking, for larger and more complex systems. The use of Kronecker algebra allows for the explicit representation and manipulation of the shared memory matrix, enabling efficient reasoning about the state of the system and the behavior of its processes.

match that of the Local Group of Galaxies (LG). We find, in agreement with the
"timing argument" and earlier work, that the separation and approach velocity
of the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31) galaxies favour a total mass for the
pair of $\sim 5\times 10^{12} \,M_{\odot}$. A mass this large, however, is
difficult to reconcile with the small relative tangential velocity of the pair,
as well as with the small deceleration from the Hubble flow observed for the
most distant LG members. Halo pairs that match these three criteria have
average masses a factor of $\sim 2$ times smaller than suggested by the timing
argument, but with large dispersion. Guided by these results, we have selected

10^{12}\,M_{\odot}$ for the APOSTLE project (A Project Of Simulating The Local
Environment), a suite of hydrodynamical resimulations at various numerical
resolution levels (reaching up to $\sim10^{4}\,M_{\odot}$ per gas particle)
that use the subgrid physics developed for the EAGLE project. These simulations
reproduce, by construction, the main kinematics of the MW-M31 pair, and produce
satellite populations whose overall number, luminosities, and kinematics are in
good agreement with observations of the MW and M31 companions. The APOSTLE
candidate systems thus provide an excellent testbed to confront directly many

red-filter BRITE satellites over more than 10 revolutions of the binary, with

fading events take place typically 3 to 5 times per binary orbit. The
amplitudes of the disturbances (relative to the mean light curve, in units of

distribution with $\sigma=0.0130\pm0.0004$ f.u. Most of the disturbances appear

sometimes changing from brightening to fading or the reverse. Phases just
preceding the center of the deeper eclipse showed the most scatter while phases
around secondary eclipse were the quietest. This implies that the invisible
companion is the most likely source of the instabilities. Wavelet transform
analysis showed domination of the variability scales at phase intervals
$0.05-0.3$ (0.65--4 d), with the shorter (longer) scales dominating in numbers
(variability power) in this range. The series can be well described as a
stochastic Gaussian process with the signal at short timescales showing a
slightly stronger correlation than red noise. The signal de-correlation
timescale $\tau=(0.068\pm0.018)$ in phase or $(0.88\pm0.23)$~d appears to

determine the intrinsic mode and linear mode coupling in solar microwave

text: The development of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) has been significantly advanced by findings from hadron collider experiments, providing pivotal insights from hard-scattering processes to the properties of quark-gluon plasma, often described as a "perfect liquid." Our methodology involved a comprehensive review of experimental results from multiple collider collaborations, with a focus on phenomena such as jet production, heavy ion collisions, and parton distribution functions. Key findings reveal the successes in validating QCD predictions in perturbative regimes through hard-scattering experiments. Meanwhile, data from heavy ion collisions have unveiled the existence of quark-gluon plasma, a state of matter characterized by strong interactions and negligible viscosity, indicative of a nearly perfect fluid. These discoveries not only confirm theoretical predictions but also challenge existing paradigms by offering new parameters for QCD-based model refinements. In conclusion, hadron collider experiments have not only substantiated fundamental aspects of QCD but have also opened new avenues of research into the behavior of matter under extreme conditions, thereby shaping future investigations into particle physics. The diversified approach and advanced detection techniques continue to enhance our grasp of the subatomic world, implicating wider applications across theoretical physics.

In the Manhattan Sequence Consensus problem (MSC problem) we are given $k$
integer sequences, each of length $l$, and we are to find an integer sequence
$x$ of length $l$ (called a consensus sequence), such that the maximum
Manhattan distance of $x$ from each of the input sequences is minimized. For
binary sequences Manhattan distance coincides with Hamming distance, hence in
this case the string consensus problem (also called string center problem or
closest string problem) is a special case of MSC. Our main result is a
practically efficient $O(l)$-time algorithm solving MSC for $k\le 5$ sequences.
Practicality of our algorithms has been verified experimentally. It improves
upon the quadratic algorithm by Amir et al.\ (SPIRE 2012) for string consensus
problem for $k=5$ binary strings. Similarly as in Amir's algorithm we use a
column-based framework. We replace the implied general integer linear
programming by its easy special cases, due to combinatorial properties of the
MSC for $k\le 5$. We also show that for a general parameter $k$ any instance
can be reduced in linear time to a kernel of size $k!$, so the problem is
fixed-parameter tractable. Nevertheless, for $k\ge 4$ this is still too large
for any naive solution to be feasible in practice.

text: In this study, we present an in-depth analysis of the warm absorber in the Seyfert 1 galaxy Mrk 509, based on an extensive 600 ks observation with the Reflection Grating Spectrometer (RGS) on board XMM-Newton. This work, part of a broader multiwavelength campaign, aims to untangle the complex dynamical and ionization structure within the innermost regions of the active galactic nucleus (AGN). By employing sophisticated spectroscopic techniques and photoionization modeling, we have identified multiple distinct ionization components within the warm absorber. Our methodology utilizes Bayesian inference to robustly quantify the absorber's physical characteristics, such as ionization parameters, column densities, and outflow velocities. The results demonstrate a stratified ionization structure, with velocities reaching several thousand km/s, indicative of the AGN's significant impact on its immediate environment. Furthermore, correlations between different spectral features suggest a possible connection between the absorber dynamics and accretion processes. This comprehensive analysis of the RGS spectrum enhances our understanding of AGN feedback mechanisms and provides critical insights into the interaction between the central engine and its host galaxy. Our findings contribute to a more nuanced view of AGN unification models, highlighting the necessity for accounting for complex ionized winds in comprehensive theoretical frameworks. This work underscores the importance of high-resolution spectroscopy in disentangling the multifaceted nature of AGNs and sets a benchmark for future observational campaigns targeting similar cosmic phenomena.

text: In this study, we investigate the pressure characteristics of an exactly solvable model of active fluid, addressing a fundamental problem in understanding nonequilibrium statistical mechanics. Active fluids, composed of self-propelled particles, exhibit intricate behaviors significantly departing from equilibrium systems, posing challenges in defining pressure. We developed an analytically tractable model that allows us to compute pressure explicitly under varied conditions. Employing techniques from the realm of stochastic thermodynamics and statistical physics, we systematically analyzed the interaction forces, external potentials, and the intrinsic activity of particles to evaluate their effects on the system's pressure. Our results reveal that the pressure in active fluids cannot be solely attributed to particle density and kinetic terms, unlike passive fluids. A novel contribution of our work is the identification of a generalized pressure equation that incorporates activity-induced stresses, capturing the essence of non-conservative forces inherent in active systems. Comparisons with simulations demonstrate the robustness and predictive power of our model across different regimes of particle motility and interaction strengths. This research advances the theoretical understanding of how active forces affect macroscopic observables and informs the design of synthetic active materials. Furthermore, our findings provide valuable insights into experimental setups, facilitating the interpretation of pressure measurements in real-world active fluid systems. The methodology established here lays groundwork for future exploration into more complex active matter systems, bolstering the bridge between theoretical predictions and experimental observations in the field of active matter physics.

LISA Pathfinder is the technological demonstrator space mission for the
future gravitational waves observatory in space eLISA, with the aim of measure
the differential acceleration between free-falling test masses orbiting in the
same apparatus at a level of 30 fm/s-2Hz-1/2 at 1 mHz. Because the satellite
can't follow the two masses at the same time, the second mass must be forced to
follow either the other one or the spacecraft. The actuation force applied to
compensate this effect introduces a dominant source of force noise in the
mission noise budget at frequency near and below the mHz. The free-fall mode
actuation control scheme has been designed to suppress this noise source and
avoid actuation instabilities: actuation is limited to brief periodic impulses,
with test masses in free fall in between two kicks. This actuation-free motion
is then analyzed for the remaining sources of acceleration ultra noise. A
free-fall mode parallel testing has been successfully implemented on torsion
pendulum facility at the University of Trento and the results of the
measurement campaign are ready to be shown and discussed. The implementation of
the data analysis algorithms to estimate the spectrum of the acceleration of
the controlled test mass, and the estimation of system parameters such as the
force gradients, stiffness terms, are also part of this work. The free-fall
mode has been tested at the level of 2 fNm/Hz-1/2, at the frequencies of 1 mHz,
corresponding to an acceleration of about 100 fm /s-2 Hz-1/2. The ground tests
have nevertheless allowed to develop and test quantitatively this innovative
method of noise reduction due to actuation noise, contributing to its
development for the LISA Pathfinder mission.

Android apps could expose their components for cooperating with other apps.
This convenience, however, makes apps susceptible to the exposed component
vulnerability (ECV), in which a dangerous API (commonly known as sink) inside
its component can be triggered by other (malicious) apps. In the prior works,
detecting these ECVs use a set of sinks pertaining to the ECVs under detection.
In this paper, we argue that a more comprehensive and effective approach should
start by a systematic selection and classification of vulnerability-specific
sinks (VSinks). The set of VSinks is much larger than those used in the
previous works. Based on these VSinks, our sink-driven approach can detect
different kinds of ECVs in an app in two steps. First, VSinks and their
categories are identified through a typical forward reachability analysis.
Second, based on each VSink's category, a corresponding detection method is
used to identify the ECV via a customized backward dataflow analysis. We also
design a semi-auto guided analysis and validation capability for system-only
broadcast checking to remove some false positives. We implement our sink-driven
approach in a tool called ECVDetector and evaluate it with the top 1K Android
apps. Using ECVDetector we successfully identify a total of 49 vulnerable apps
across all four ECV categories we have defined. To our knowledge, most of them
are previously undisclosed, such as the very popular Go SMS Pro and Clean
Master. Moreover, the performance of ECVDetector is high, requiring only 9.257
seconds on average to process each component.

The objective is to develop a robust framework for solving the CTP using advanced algorithmic strategies, coupled with empirical assessments to validate the effectiveness of these methods. Experimental results were generated using diverse data sets representing different travel scenarios, encompassing both urban and rural landscapes affected by dynamic obstacles. Notably, the adaptive nature of these algorithms allows them to respond effectively to the unpredictability inherent in CTP scenarios. Furthermore, this research provides insights into the scalability of the proposed methods, suggesting their applicability to real-world navigation systems.  In conclusion, this study advances the understanding of the Canadian Traveler Problem by integrating theoretical frameworks with practical experimentation, offering valuable contributions to the fields of operations research and algorithm development. text: We investigate the AC conductivity of one-dimensional spin-1/2 chains, exploring the interplay between anomalous and regular transport phenomena. Our primary goal is to elucidate the transport mechanisms that dominate under various external conditions, focusing on the effects of interactions and external fields on conductivity profiles. Through extensive numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we analyze the AC response of the system across different frequency regimes. Our results reveal distinct transport regimes characterized by differing behaviors in conductivity, attributable to quantum interference effects and the presence of localized states due to disorder. We find that while regular transport manifests prominently in non-interacting chains, anomalous transport emerges in systems with strong interactions, leading to a pronounced frequency-dependent scaling of conductivity. Additionally, we highlight the emergence of critical points where the transition between these transport characteristics occurs, providing insights into the underlying physical processes governing spin dynamics. We employ techniques such as the Kubo formula and finite-size scaling to derive our results, ensuring that our findings offer robust and generalizable insights into the behavior of spin chains under AC driving forces. Our study contributes to the broader understanding of quantum transport phenomena in low-dimensional systems, with potential implications for the development of quantum materials and spintronic applications. Hence, we provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing complex transport dynamics in spin-1/2 chains, paving the way for future investigations into related quantum systems.

methods, the available energies of strain-induced interaction of
interstitial-interstitial, interstitial-substitutional and
substitutional-substitutional impurity atomic pairs are collected and analysed
for f.c.c.-(Ni,Fe)-C solutions allowing for discrete atomic structure of the
host-crystal lattice. The lattice spacings, elasticity moduli and/or
quasi-elastic force parameters of the host-crystal lattice, and concentration
coefficients of the dilatation of solid-solution lattice due to the respective
solutes are selected as the input numerical experimental data used. The
above-mentioned interaction energies prove to have non-monotonically decreasing
and anisotropic dependences on discrete interatomic radius-vector, and
themselves are strong and long-range. In all f.c.c.-(Ni,Fe)-base solutions,
there is strain-induced attraction in many coordination shells. In general, the
strain-induced interaction between impurity atoms in gamma-Fe is weaker than in
alpha-Ni. The verification of applicability of the approximation of
strain-induced interaction of impurities for f.c.c.-(Ni,Fe)-C alloys showed
that it must be supplemented with additional short-range (electrochemical)
repulsion in the first coordination shell. Nevertheless, in any case, the
strain-induced interaction of impurity atoms must be taken into account for
analysis of structure and properties of f.c.c.-(Ni,Fe)-base solutions. The
Monte Carlo simulation procedures applied for constitution of a nanoscale
Fe-C-austenite crystallite and based on analysis of the dependences of numbers
of the different atomic configurations on C-C interatomic-interaction energies

We present the results from a VLT/SINFONI and Keck/NIRSPEC near-infrared
spectroscopic survey of 16 Lyman-alpha emitters (LAEs) at $z$ = 2.1 - 2.5 in
the COSMOS and GOODS-N fields discovered from the HETDEX Pilot Survey. We
detect rest-frame optical nebular lines (H$\alpha$ and/or [OIII]$\lambda$5007)
for 10 of the LAEs and measure physical properties, including the star
formation rate (SFR), gas-phase metallicity, gas-mass fraction, and Ly$\alpha$
velocity offset. We find that LAEs may lie below the mass-metallicity relation
for continuum-selected star-forming galaxies at the same redshift. The LAEs all
show velocity shifts of Ly$\alpha$ relative to the systemic redshift ranging
between +85 and +296 km s$^{-1}$ with a mean of +180 km s$^{-1}$. This value is
smaller than measured for continuum-selected star-forming galaxies at similar
redshifts. The Ly$\alpha$ velocity offsets show a moderate correlation with the
measured star formation rate (2.5$\sigma$), but no significant correlations are
seen with the SFR surface density, specific SFR, stellar mass, or dynamical
mass ($\lesssim$ 1.5$\sigma$). Exploring the role of dust, kinematics of the
interstellar medium (ISM), and geometry on the escape of Ly$\alpha$ photons, we
find no signature of selective quenching of resonantly scattered Ly$\alpha$
photons. However, we also find no evidence that a clumpy ISM is enhancing the
Ly$\alpha$ equivalent width. Our results suggest that the low metallicity in
LAEs may be responsible for yielding an environment with a low neutral hydrogen
column density as well as less dust, easing the escape of Ly$\alpha$ photons
over that in continuum-selected star-forming galaxies.

We demonstrate and explain a simple and efficient way to remove gas bubbles
from liquid-filled microchannels, by integrating a hydrophobic porous membrane
on top of the microchannel. A prototype chip is manufactured in hard,
transparent polymer with the ability to completely filter gas plugs out of a
segmented flow at rates up to 7.4 microliter/s per mm2 of membrane area. The
device involves a bubble generation section and a gas removal section. In the
bubble generation section, a T-junction is used to generate a train of gas
plugs into a water stream. These gas plugs are then transported towards the gas
removal section, where they slide along a hydrophobic membrane until complete
removal. The system has been successfully modeled and four necessary operating
criteria have been determined to achieve a complete separation of the gas from
the liquid. The first criterion is that the bubble length needs to be larger
than the channel diameter. The second criterion is that the gas plug should
stay on the membrane for a time sufficient to transport all the gas through the
membrane. The third criterion is that the gas plug travel speed should be lower
than a critical value: otherwise a stable liquid film between the bubble and
the membrane prevents mass transfer. The fourth criterion is that the pressure
difference across the membrane should not be larger than the Laplace pressure
to prevent water from leaking through the membrane.

text: In this study, we investigate the influence of albedo on the spatial properties of hard X-ray flare sources, specifically their size, by analyzing observations collected from recent solar flare events. The solar albedo effect, caused by the reflection of X-rays from the solar photosphere, can significantly affect the apparent characteristics of flare emissions, potentially leading to misinterpretations of source size and energetics. We employ a sophisticated modeling approach that incorporates Monte Carlo simulations to account for the scattering and re-emission of X-rays, thereby enhancing the accuracy of source size measurements. By comparing flare source sizes observed directly with those corrected for albedo effects, we aim to quantify the degree to which albedo impacts these observations. Our results indicate a consistent overestimate in source size when albedo is neglected, with discrepancies up to 30% for certain flare orientations and energies. This finding underscores the importance of including albedo corrections in X-ray solar flare analysis. Methodologically, our work extends current models by integrating detailed angular distribution functions that better capture the anisotropic nature of flare emissions. This allows for enhanced precision in determining the morphological characteristics of X-ray sources. Our comprehensive approach provides novel insights into the real dimensions and energetics of flare events, offering critical data for the development of predictive flare models and contributing to the broader understanding of solar energetic phenomena. Our findings highlight the necessity for future observational strategies to incorporate albedo considerations for accurate characterization of solar flare dynamics.

In this paper, we study a general optimization model, which covers a large
class of existing models for many applications in imaging sciences. To solve
the resulting possibly nonconvex, nonsmooth and non-Lipschitz optimization
problem, we adapt the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) with a
general dual step-size to solve a reformulation that contains three blocks of
variables, and analyze its convergence. We show that for any dual step-size
less than the golden ratio, there exists a computable threshold such that if
the penalty parameter is chosen above such a threshold and the sequence thus
generated by our ADMM is bounded, then the cluster point of the sequence gives
a stationary point of the nonconvex optimization problem. We achieve this via a
potential function specifically constructed for our ADMM. Moreover, we
establish the global convergence of the whole sequence if, in addition, this
special potential function is a Kurdyka-{\L}ojasiewicz function. Furthermore,
we present a simple strategy for initializing the algorithm to guarantee
boundedness of the sequence. Finally, we perform numerical experiments
comparing our ADMM with the proximal alternating linearized minimization (PALM)
proposed in [5] on the background/foreground extraction problem with real data.
The numerical results show that our ADMM with a nontrivial dual step-size is
efficient.

text: The present study investigates the properties of the turbulent/non-turbulent (TNT) interface in boundary layers using large eddy simulation (LES) and experimental techniques. The LES results reveal that the TNT interface exhibits a complex structure, characterized by the presence of coherent vortical structures that penetrate the non-turbulent region. This finding is consistent with recent experimental observations and provides valuable insights into the physics of the TNT interface.  Moreover, the LES data shows that the location of the TNT interface is influenced by the streamwise pressure gradient. In regions of favorable pressure gradient, the TNT interface moves upstream, while in regions of adverse pressure gradient, it moves downstream. This behavior can be explained by the balance of shear stress and pressure forces acting on the interface.  To further validate these findings, we performed a series of experimental measurements of the TNT interface location in a flat-plate boundary layer at Re = 18,000. The results show good agreement with the LES data, confirming the importance of pressure gradients in controlling the location of the TNT interface.  Furthermore, we investigate the effect of surface roughness on the TNT interface using LES simulations. The results demonstrate that surface roughness leads to a thickening of the TNT interface and a decrease in the turbulence intensity in the non-turbulent region. This effect is attributed to the increased production of streamwise velocity fluctuations near the rough surface.  In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive investigation of the properties of the TNT interface in boundary layers using LES and experimental techniques. The results demonstrate the importance of pressure gradients in controlling the location of the TNT interface and shed new light on the role of surface roughness in modifying its structure. These findings have implications for the design of turbomachinery and the prediction of heat transfer and drag in boundary layers.

In this paper we explicitly demonstrate separability of the Maxwell equations
in a wide class of higher-dimensional metrics which include the Kerr-NUT-(A)dS
solution as a special case. Namely, we prove such separability for the most
general metric admitting the principal tensor (a non-degenerate closed
conformal Killing-Yano 2-form). To this purpose we use a special ansatz for the
electromagnetic potential, which we represent as a product of a (rank 2)
polarization tensor with the gradient of a potential function, generalizing the
ansatz recently proposed by Lunin. We show that for a special choice of the
polarization tensor written in terms of the principal tensor, both the Lorenz
gauge condition and the Maxwell equations reduce to a composition of mutually
commuting operators acting on the potential function. A solution to both these
equations can be written in terms of an eigenfunction of these commuting
operators. When incorporating a multiplicative separability ansatz, it turns
out that the eigenvalue equations reduce to a set of separated ordinary
differential equations with the eigenvalues playing a role of separability
constants. The remaining ambiguity in the separated equations is related to an
identification of D-2 polarizations of the electromagnetic field. We thus
obtained a sufficiently rich set of solutions for the Maxwell equations in
these spacetimes.

text: We investigate the Diversity-Multiplexing Tradeoff (DMT) of the Dynamic Decode-and-Forward (DDF) protocol in the context of a Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) half-duplex relay channel. Our objective is to characterize the optimal performance of the DDF protocol under varying degrees of source-relay and relay-destination channel conditions. To achieve this, we employ a systematic analytical approach, utilizing information theory principles and stochastic wireless channel modeling. We derive closed-form expressions for the DMT, demonstrating how the tradeoff between diversity gain and multiplexing gain is influenced by the relay's processing capability and the spatial diversity available at the relay. Our results indicate that the DDF protocol can significantly enhance the DMT outcomes when adequately exploiting the spatial dimensions at both the source and destination, particularly under high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions. Furthermore, we identify the critical threshold of relay power allocation that maximizes the DMT, guiding the design of practical relay systems. We also compare our findings with existing strategies, highlighting the superior performance of the DDF protocol in scenarios of limited relay cooperation. Overall, our study provides valuable insights into optimizing relay-assisted communication systems and contributes to the broader understanding of diversity-multiplexing interactions in advanced wireless networks, paving the way for future research in relay protocols and their applications in complex channel environments.

The study of galaxy protoclusters is beginning to fill in unknown details of
the important phase of the assembly of clusters and cluster galaxies. This
review describes the current status of this field and highlights promising
recent findings related to galaxy formation in the densest regions of the early
universe. We discuss the main search techniques and the characteristic
properties of protoclusters in observations and simulations, and show that
protoclusters will have present-day masses similar to galaxy clusters when
fully collapsed. We discuss the physical properties of galaxies in
protoclusters, including (proto-)brightest cluster galaxies, and the forming
red sequence. We highlight the fact that the most massive halos at high
redshift are found in protoclusters, making these objects uniquely suited for
testing important recent models of galaxy formation. We show that galaxies in
protoclusters should be among the first galaxies at high redshift making the
transition from a gas cooling regime dominated by cold streams to a regime
dominated by hot intracluster gas, which could be tested observationally. We
also discuss the possible connections between protoclusters and radio galaxies,
quasars, and Ly-alpha blobs. Because of their early formation, large spatial
sizes and high total star formation rates, protoclusters have also likely
played a crucial role during the epoch of reionization, which can be tested
with future experiments that will map the neutral and ionized cosmic web. Last,
we review a number of promising observational projects that are expected to
make significant impact in this growing, exciting field.

Numerical simulations and analytical derivations are utilized to determine the conditions under which a state becomes locally maximally entangled, considering local operations and classical communication constraints. Additionally, the research reveals how the presence of noise or imperfect local operations affects the preservation and generation of LMES, highlighting the importance of error correction techniques in practical applications.  Conclusively, the findings underscore the potential of LMES in enhancing quantum communication capabilities and suggest directions for further investigation into more complex scenarios involving larger quantum systems. Gravitational waves are considered as metric perturbations about a curved
background metric, rather than the flat Minkowski metric since several
situations of physical interest can be discussed by this generalization. In
this case, when the de Donder gauge is imposed, its preservation under
infinitesimal spacetime diffeomorphisms is guaranteed if and only if the
associated covector is ruled by a second-order hyperbolic operator which is the
classical counterpart of the ghost operator in quantum gravity. In such a wave
equation, the Ricci term has opposite sign with respect to the wave equation
for Maxwell theory in the Lorenz gauge. We are, nevertheless, able to relate
the solutions of the two problems, and the algorithm is applied to the case
when the curved background geometry is the de Sitter spacetime. Such vector
wave equations are studied in two different ways: i) an integral
representation, ii) through a solution by factorization of the hyperbolic
equation. The latter method is extended to the wave equation of metric
perturbations in the de Sitter spacetime. This approach is a step towards a
general discussion of gravitational waves in the de Sitter spacetime and might
assume relevance in cosmology in order to study the stochastic background
emerging from inflation.

text: In this research paper, we explore the intricacies of regulating the infrared sector in an expanding universe with constant deceleration, utilizing mode matching techniques for a massless scalar field. The backdrop involves the Cosmological Principle, which assumes that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic, allowing the analysis of the dynamics of perturbations in the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric. The objective is to apply mode matching to the FLRW metric to find a set of solutions for the evolution of the massless scalar field's perturbations. Our methodology employs the Green's function approach and the WKB approximation for the analysis of the perturbations.  Our key findings reveal the importance of the deceleration parameter in regulating the infrared sector. The results show that the scalar field mode functions exhibit an asymptotic behavior for late times, with the infrared modes dominating and displaying a sub-horizon behavior. Additionally, we demonstrate that the scalar field modes' behavior is influenced by the deceleration parameter, with the transition from an early decelerating universe to a late accelerating universe leading to a change in the mode function behavior.  In conclusion, our study provides insights into the role of the deceleration parameter in the dynamics of the massless scalar field in an expanding universe with constant deceleration. The findings contribute to the understanding of the behavior of the infrared sector and its impact on the cosmological evolution.

characteristic $p > 0$ with $[K:K^p] < \infty$. Let $R$ be the hypersurface
$S/fS$ where $f$ is a nonzero nonunit element of $S$. If $e$ is a positive
integer, $F_*^e(R)$ denotes the $R$-algebra structure induced on $R$ via the
$e$-times iterated Frobenius map ( $r\rightarrow r^{p^e}$ ). We show an
existence of a matrix factorization of $f$ whose cokernel is isomorphic to
$F_*^e(R)$ as $R$-module. The presentation of $F_*^e(R)$ as the cokernel of a
matrix factorization of $f$ enables us to find a characterization from which we
can decide when the ring $S[[u,v]]/(f+uv)$ has Finite F-representation type
(FFRT) where $S=K[[x_1,...,x_n]]$. This allows us to create a class of rings
that have Finite F-representation type but it does not have finite CM type. For
$S=K[[x_1,...,x_n]]$, we use this presentation to show that the ring
$S[[y]]/(y^{p^d} +f)$ has finite F-representation type for any $f$ in $S$.
Furthermore, we proved that $S/I$ has Finite F-representation type when $I$ is
a monomial ideal in either $S=K[x_1,...,x_n]$ or $S=K[[x_1,...,x_n]]$. Finally,
this presentation enables us to compute the F-signature of the rings
$S[[u,v]]/(f+uv)$ and $S[[z]]/(f+z^2)$ where $S=K[[x_1,...,x_n]]$ and $f$ is a
monomial in the ring $S$.

In this work, the simulation of optical photons is carried out in an
antineutrino detector module consisting of a plastic scintillator connected to
light guides and photomultipliers on both ends, which is considered to be used
for remote reactor monitoring in the field of nuclear safety. Using Monte Carlo
(MC) based GEANT4 simulation, numerous parameters influencing the light
collection and thereby the energy resolution of the antineutrino detector
module are studied: e.g., degrees of scintillator surface roughness, reflector
type, and its ap- plying method onto scintillator and light guide surface, the
reflectivity of the reflector, light guide geometries and diameter of the
photocathode. The impact of each parameter is inves- tigated by looking at the
detected spectrum, i.e. the number photoelectrons per depositing energy. In
addition, the average light collection efficiency of the detector module and
its spatial variation are calculated for each simulation setup. According to
the simulation re- sults, it is found that photocathode size, light guide
shape, reflectivity of reflecting material and wrapping method show a
significant impact on the light collection efficiency while scin- tillator
surface polishing level and the choose of reflector type show relatively less
impact. This study demonstrates that these parameters are very important in the
design of plastic scintillator included antineutrino detectors to improve the
energy resolution efficiency.

We use SDSS photometry of 73 million stars to simultaneously obtain best-fit
main-sequence stellar energy distribution (SED) and amount of dust extinction
along the line of sight towards each star. Using a subsample of 23 million
stars with 2MASS photometry, whose addition enables more robust results, we
show that SDSS photometry alone is sufficient to break degeneracies between
intrinsic stellar color and dust amount when the shape of extinction curve is
fixed. When using both SDSS and 2MASS photometry, the ratio of the total to
selective absorption, $R_V$, can be determined with an uncertainty of about 0.1
for most stars in high-extinction regions. These fits enable detailed studies
of the dust properties and its spatial distribution, and of the stellar spatial
distribution at low Galactic latitudes. Our results are in good agreement with
the extinction normalization given by the Schlegel et al. (1998, SFD) dust maps
at high northern Galactic latitudes, but indicate that the SFD extinction map
appears to be consistently overestimated by about 20% in the southern sky, in
agreement with Schlafly et al. (2010). The constraints on the shape of the dust
extinction curve across the SDSS and 2MASS bandpasses support the models by
Fitzpatrick (1999) and Cardelli et al. (1989). For the latter, we find an
$R_V=3.0\pm0.1$(random) $\pm0.1$(systematic) over most of the high-latitude
sky. At low Galactic latitudes (|b|<5), we demonstrate that the SFD map cannot
be reliably used to correct for extinction as most stars are embedded in dust,
rather than behind it. We introduce a method for efficient selection of
candidate red giant stars in the disk, dubbed "dusty parallax relation", which
utilizes a correlation between distance and the extinction along the line of
sight. We make these best-fit parameters, as well as all the input SDSS and
2MASS data, publicly available in a user-friendly format.

In this paper, we examine the hash functions expressed as scalar products,
i.e., $f(x)=<v,x>$, for some bounded random vector $v$. Such hash functions
have numerous applications, but often there is a need to optimize the choice of
the distribution of $v$. In the present work, we focus on so-called
anti-concentration bounds, i.e. the upper bounds of $\mathbb{P}\left[|<v,x>| <
\alpha \right]$. In many applications, $v$ is a vector of independent random
variables with standard normal distribution. In such case, the distribution of
$<v,x>$ is also normal and it is easy to approximate $\mathbb{P}\left[|<v,x>| <
\alpha \right]$. Here, we consider two bounded distributions in the context of
the anti-concentration bounds. Particularly, we analyze $v$ being a random
vector from the unit ball in $l_{\infty}$ and $v$ being a random vector from
the unit sphere in $l_{2}$. We show optimal up to a constant anti-concentration
measures for functions $f(x)=<v,x>$.
  As a consequence of our research, we obtain new best results for \newline
\textit{$c$-approximate nearest neighbors without false negatives} for $l_p$ in
high dimensional space for all $p\in[1,\infty]$, for
$c=\Omega(\max\{\sqrt{d},d^{1/p}\})$. These results improve over those
presented in [16]. Finally, our paper reports progress on answering the open
problem by Pagh~[17], who considered the nearest neighbor search without false
negatives for the Hamming distance.

text: The pursuit of optimizing low-energy neutrino factories has garnered substantial interest, leveraging their potential for unpacking the intricacies of neutrino masses and oscillations, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of fundamental particle physics. This research aims to evaluate and enhance the operational efficiency and output fidelity of low-energy neutrino factories by integrating advanced beam optics and innovative detector technology. We employed a comprehensive analysis combining computational simulations and empirical trials to examine the impact of modified beamline configurations on neutrino production rates and energy spectra. Key innovations include leveraging magnetically focused beamlines to increase neutrino flux and implementing high-resolution detector arrays to minimize observational discrepancies. Our findings reveal a significant enhancement in precision and neutrino yield, with optimized configurations achieving a 20% increase in effective neutrino flux compared to traditional setups. In addition, the integration of cutting-edge detection systems reduced systematic uncertainties by nearly 15%, establishing a new benchmark for experimental accuracy. These improvements not only bolster the detection sensitivity for CP-violation studies but also enhance the capacity for probing new physics beyond the Standard Model. In conclusion, our research presents a transformative approach to low-energy neutrino factory design, offering a substantial leap forward in neutrino science capabilities. This advancement holds promise for future experiments, paving the way for more nuanced investigations into the fundamental forces and particles shaping the universe.

We present a new method for replacing the outermost layers of stellar models
with interpolated atmospheres based on results from 3D simulations, in order to
correct for structural inadequacies of these layers. This replacement is known
as patching. Tests, based on 3D atmospheres from three different codes and
interior models with different input physics, are performed. Using solar
models, we investigate how different patching criteria affect the
eigenfrequencies. These criteria include the depth, at which the replacement is
performed, the quantity, on which the replacement is based, and the mismatch in
$T_\mathrm{eff}$ and $\log g$ between the un-patched model and patched 3D
atmosphere. We find the eigenfrequencies to be unaltered by the patching depth
deep within the adiabatic region, while changing the patching quantity or the
employed atmosphere grid leads to frequency shifts that may exceed
$1\,\mu\mathrm{Hz}$. Likewise, the eigenfrequencies are sensitive to mismatches
in $T_\mathrm{eff}$ or $\log g$. A thorough investigation of the accuracy of a
new scheme, for interpolating mean 3D stratifications within the atmosphere
grids, is furthermore performed. Throughout large parts of the atmosphere
grids, our interpolation scheme yields sufficiently accurate results for the
purpose of asteroseismology. We apply our procedure in asteroseismic analyses
of four \textit{Kepler} stars and draw the same conclusions as in the solar
case: Correcting for structural deficiencies lowers the eigenfrequencies, this
correction is slightly sensitive to the patching criteria, and the remaining
frequency discrepancy between models and observations is less
frequency-dependent. Our work shows the applicability and relevance of patching
in asteroseismology.

We study the reconstruction of visual stimuli from spike trains, recording
simultaneously from the two H1 neurons located in the lobula plate of the fly
Chrysomya megacephala. The fly views two types of stimuli, corresponding to
rotational and translational displacements. If the reconstructed stimulus is to
be represented by a Volterra series and correlations between spikes are to be
taken into account, first order expansions are insufficient and we have to go
to second order, at least. In this case higher order correlation functions have
to be manipulated, whose size may become prohibitively large. We therefore
develop a Gaussian-like representation for fourth order correlation functions,
which works exceedingly well in the case of the fly. The reconstructions using
this Gaussian-like representation are very similar to the reconstructions using
the experimental correlation functions. The overall contribution to rotational
stimulus reconstruction of the second order kernels - measured by a chi-squared
averaged over the whole experiment - is only about 8% of the first order
contribution. Yet if we introduce an instant-dependent chi-square to measure
the contribution of second order kernels at special events, we observe an up to
100% improvement. As may be expected, for translational stimuli the
reconstructions are rather poor. The Gaussian-like representation could be a
valuable aid in population coding with large number of neurons.

We uncover the H2 flows in the Corona Australis molecular cloud and in
particular identify the flows from the Coronet cluster. Near-infrared H2 v=1--0
S(1), 2.12micron-line, narrow-band imaging survey of the R CrA cloud core was
carried out. We identify the best candidate-driving source for each outflow by
comparing the flow properties, available proper motions, and the
known/estimated properties of the driving sources. We also adopted the
thumbrule of outflow power as proportional to source luminosity and inversely
proportional to the source age to reach a consensus.
  Results: Continuum-subtracted, narrow-band images reveal several new
Molecular Hydrogen emission-line Objects (MHOs). Together with previously known
MHOs and Herbig-Haro objects we catalog at least 14 individual flow components
of which 11 appear to be driven by the RCrA aggregate members. The flows
originating in the Coronet cluster have lengths of ~0.1-0.2 pc. Eight out of
nine submillimeter cores mapped in the Coronet cluster region display embedded
stars driving an outflow component. Roughly 80% of the youngest objects in the
Coronet are associated with outflows. The MHO flows to the west of the Coronet
display lobes moving to the west and vice-versa, resulting in nondetections of
the counter lobe in our deep imaging. We speculate that these counterflows may
be experiencing a stunting effect in penetrating the dense central core.
  Conclusions:Although this work has reduced the ambiguities for many flows in
the Coronet region, one of the brightest H2 feature (MHO2014) and a few fainter
features in the region remain unassociated with a clear driving source. The
flows from Coronet, therefore, continue to be interesting targets for future
studies.

This paper introduces the notion of second minimal $n$-periodic orbit of the
continuous map on the interval according as if $n$ is a successor of the
minimal period of the map in Sharkovski ordering. We pursue classification of
second minimal $7$-orbits in terms of cyclic permutations and digraphs. It is
proved that there are 9 types of second minimal orbits with accuracy up to
inverses. The result is applied to the problem on the distribution of periodic
windows within the chaotic regime of the bifurcation diagram of the
one-parameter family of unimodal maps. It is revealed that by fixing the
maximum number of appearances of the periodic windows there is a universal
pattern of distribution. In particular, the first appearance of all the orbits
is always a minimal orbit, while the second appearance is a second minimal
orbit. It is observed that the second appearance of 7-orbit is a second minimal
7-orbit with Type 1 digraph. The reason for the relevance of the Type 1 second
minimal orbit is the fact that the topological structure of the unimodal map
with single maximum is equivalent to the structure of the Type 1 piecewise
monotonic endomorphism associated with the second minimal 7-orbit. Yet another
important report of this paper is the revelation of the universal pattern
dynamics with respect to increased number of appearances.

Key findings include the determination of precise absolute dimensions for BK Pegasi and the F-type binaries under investigation, shedding light on their physical characteristics and evolutionary status. Through the analysis of convective core overshoot in these binaries, the study provides insights into the calibration of this phenomenon and its implications for stellar evolution models. text: Our work presents a model-based approach to climate reconstruction through the analysis of tree-ring data. Tree-ring records serve as natural archives of past climate conditions, offering valuable insights into environmental dynamics over time. The primary objective of our study is to develop a robust model that can accurately reconstruct historical climate patterns based on tree-ring data. By utilizing statistical techniques and machine learning algorithms, we aim to enhance the accuracy and precision of climate reconstructions, thereby improving our understanding of past climate variability.  Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in capturing complex climate signals embedded within tree-ring records. Through rigorous validation and comparison with existing reconstructions, we show that our approach yields more reliable and detailed climate reconstructions. The key innovation of our methodology lies in the integration of multiple tree-ring parameters, geographic information, and climate data into a comprehensive statistical framework. By incorporating diverse sources of information, our model can account for various factors influencing tree growth and enhance the accuracy of climate reconstructions.  Overall, our research contributes to the advancement of climate reconstruction methods by providing a systematic and data-driven approach that leverages the potential of tree-ring data. By improving the accuracy and reliability of historical climate reconstructions, our model-based approach offers valuable insights for understanding past climate dynamics and informing future climate projections.

text: In this study, we investigate the He$_2^+$ molecular ion and the He$^-$ atomic ion under the influence of strong magnetic fields, focusing on their spectroscopic properties and dynamics. Our approach involves detailed theoretical calculations combined with numerical simulations to explore how the magnetic field modifies the energy levels and transition probabilities of these ions. We aim to address the challenge of accurately predicting the effects of strong magnetic fields on these ions, which are crucial for understanding fundamental quantum mechanics and have implications for precision measurements and quantum computing. Key ideas include the application of relativistic many-body perturbation theory and variational methods to calculate the energy levels, as well as the use of effective Hamiltonian techniques to model the interactions within the ions. Through these methodologies, we seek to identify distinct spectral features and transitions that can be used to probe the strength and directionality of the magnetic field. Our findings contribute to the broader field by providing a deeper understanding of the behavior of these ions in extreme conditions, thereby enhancing our knowledge of atomic and molecular physics.

The CMS GEM collaboration is considering Gas Electron Multipliers (GEMs) for
upgrading the CMS forward muon system in the 1.5<|eta|<2.4 endcap region. GEM
detectors can provide precision tracking and fast trigger information. They
would improve the CMS muon trigger and muon momentum resolution and provide
missing redundancy in the high-eta region. Employing a new faster construction
and assembly technique, we built four full-scale Triple-GEM muon detectors for
the inner ring of the first muon endcap station. We plan to install these or
further improved versions in CMS during the first long LHC shutdown in 2013/14
for continued testing. These detectors are designed for the stringent rate and
resolution requirements in the increasingly hostile environments expected at
CMS after the second long LHC shutdown in 2018/19. The new prototypes were
studied in muon/pion beams at the CERN SPS. We discuss our experience with
constructing the new full-scale production prototypes and present preliminary
performance results from the beam test. We also tested smaller Triple-GEM
prototypes with zigzag readout strips with 2 mm pitch in these beams and
measured a spatial resolution of 73 microns. This readout offers a potential
reduction of channel count and consequently electronics cost for this system
while maintaining high spatial resolution.
