text: In this study, we employ a comprehensive multi-instrument approach to analyze solar eruptive events, specifically focusing on observations obtained from the Siberian Radioheliograph (SRH). Our investigation targets the detection and characterization of solar phenomena ranging from small-scale jets to large-scale manifestations, such as shock waves and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). Through a synthesis of data from SRH, supplemented by additional measurements from ultraviolet and X-ray instruments, we provide a detailed temporal and spatial assessment of these events. We achieve a higher resolution understanding of the physical processes underlying solar eruptions by integrating radio frequency imaging with data from space-based observatories.   Our findings reveal the nuanced interactions between small-scale jets and their propensity to evolve into more substantial phenomena, including CME initiation. We demonstrate the utility of the SRH in capturing these initial activations and trace their development with high precision. By employing advanced signal processing and image reconstruction techniques, we improve the detection sensitivity and temporal resolution of solar radio bursts associated with these events. This methodology enables us to not only detect early-stage eruptive processes but also to delineate their progression and identify associated shock fronts and the onset of CMEs.   The results provide significant insights into the pre-acceleration phase and trigger mechanisms of CMEs, contributing to more accurate space weather forecasting models. Our work underscores the importance of coordinated multi-wavelength and multi-instrument observations in advancing our understanding of solar eruptive dynamics.

text: In this work, we explore the intricate interplay between quantum estimation, quantum cloning, and finite quantum de Finetti theorems, aiming to address fundamental challenges in quantum information theory. By leveraging quantum estimation techniques, we enhance the execution of quantum cloning processes that inherently demand optimal precision. Our analysis elucidates how estimations can be refined within the framework of limited resource availability, a predicament central to real-world quantum systems. We propose a novel approach, incorporating finite quantum de Finetti theorems, to better understand and predict the behavior of large quantum systems based on their finite subsets. By integrating these theorems, we effectively circumvent the traditional limitations imposed by infinite symmetric extensions, thus providing a more applicable model for quantum state analysis. Our findings underscore the significant interdependence between accurate quantum estimation and the success of cloning protocols, driven by finite representation models. Through rigorous mathematical formulations and simulations, we demonstrate that incorporating finite quantum de Finetti theorems indeed enhances the fidelity and stability of quantum operations. These simulations validate our theoretical constructs, offering substantial improvements in predictions of large-scale quantum system behaviors. This study not only bridges theoretical gaps but also advances practical applications in quantum computing and quantum cryptography, providing a more nuanced understanding of information processing limits in quantum mechanics. Ultimately, our research offers a pivotal stride towards precise quantum state manipulation, supporting the development of robust, high-fidelity quantum technologies.

text: This study investigates the implications of declining rotation curves observed in galaxies on current gravitational theories. By analyzing data from numerous spiral galaxies, we find that the rotational velocities of stars and gas within galaxies decrease beyond a certain radius, challenging the predictions of Newtonian gravity. To address this discrepancy, we propose modifications to Einstein's general relativity, specifically focusing on deviations in the curvature of spacetime at galactic scales. Our approach involves a detailed examination of galaxy simulations under various modified gravity models, comparing these with empirical observations. Key methodologies include fitting theoretical rotation curves to observed data using least squares minimization techniques and assessing the goodness of fit through statistical tests. The results indicate that while traditional Newtonian gravity fails to account for the observed rotation curves, some modified gravity theories show promise in reconciling the discrepancies. This research highlights the need for a more comprehensive understanding of gravity at cosmic scales and suggests avenues for further investigation into the nature of dark matter and energy.

text: This study aims to develop a unified model that accurately describes neutrino-nucleus interactions, crucial for enhancing precision in neutrino oscillation experiments. Our approach integrates theoretical frameworks from weak interaction physics and nuclear dynamics, focusing on the underlying mechanisms governing neutrino scattering and absorption processes within atomic nuclei. We employ advanced computational methods to simulate various types of neutrino-nucleus reactions, including elastic scattering, quasi-elastic scattering, charged current interactions, and neutral current interactions. The model is validated against experimental data and Monte Carlo simulations, demonstrating improved consistency and predictive power compared to existing models. Key methodologies include Bayesian inference techniques for parameter estimation and machine learning algorithms for pattern recognition in complex reaction data sets. The results indicate significant enhancements in the accuracy of neutrino flux predictions and cross-section calculations, thereby contributing to more robust interpretations of neutrino oscillation data.

text: Our work presents a novel spatial domain watermarking scheme tailored for colored images, leveraging the log-average luminance property to embed imperceptible watermarks efficiently. The scheme addresses the challenge of maintaining both visual quality and robustness of the watermark amidst color variations and luminance discrepancies. Through experimental evaluation, we demonstrate that our proposed method achieves a delicate balance between watermark invisibility and robustness against common image processing attacks.  Our approach involves a multilayer embedding strategy, where the watermark bits are dispersed across several color channels based on the intensity of the log-average luminance in each region. By adaptively adjusting the embedding strength in different color planes, we enhance the watermark's resilience to color alterations while preserving visual integrity. Moreover, we employ a perceptual model to ensure that the imperceptibility of the watermark is optimized, rendering it invisible to the human eye.  The effectiveness of our methodology is validated through extensive simulations on a diverse set of colored images, showcasing superior performance compared to existing techniques. Our results indicate that the proposed scheme achieves robustness against various attacks, including noise addition, filtering, and compression, while maintaining high visual quality. Overall, our work contributes a promising solution for secure and imperceptible watermarking in colored images, paving the way for applications in multimedia content protection and authentication.

text:
Several trends have been identified in the prompt gamma-ray burst (GRB)
emission: e.g. hard-to-soft evolution, pulse width evolution with energy, time
lags, hardness-intensity/-fluence correlations. Recently Fermi has
significantly extended the spectral coverage of GRB observations and improved
the characterization of this spectral evolution. We study how internal shocks
can reproduce these observations. In this model the emission comes from the
synchrotron radiation of shock accelerated electrons, and the spectral
evolution is governed by the evolution of the physical conditions in the
shocked regions. We present a comprehensive set of simulations of a single
pulse and investigate the impact of the model parameters, related to the shock
microphysics and to the initial conditions in the ejecta.
  We find a general qualitative agreement between the model and the various
observations used for the comparison. All these properties or relations are
governed by the evolution of the peak energy and photon indices of the
spectrum. In addition, we identify the conditions for a quantitative agreement.
We find that the best agreement is obtained for (i) steep electron slopes
(p>~2.7), (ii) microphysics parameters varying with shock conditions so that
more electrons are accelerated in stronger shocks, (iii) steep variations of
the initial Lorentz factor in the ejecta. When simulating short GRBs by
contracting all timescales, all other parameters being unchanged, we show that
the hardness-duration correlation is reproduced, as well as the evolution with
duration of the pulse properties. Finally, we investigate the signature at high
energy of these different scenarios and find distinct properties - delayed
onset, longer emission, and flat spectrum in some cases - suggesting that
internal shocks could have a significant contribution to the prompt LAT
emission. [abridged]

A large polar-crown prominence composed of different segments spanning nearly
the entire solar disk erupted on 2010 December 6. Prior to the eruption, the
filament in the active region part splits into two layers: a lower layer and an
elevated layer. The eruption occurs in several episodes. Around 14:12 UT, the
lower layer of the active region filament breaks apart, one part ejects towards
the west, while the other part ejects towards the east, which leads to the
explosive eruption of the eastern quiescent filament. During the early rise
phase, part of the quiescent filament sheet displays strong rolling motion
(observed by STEREO$\_$B) in the clockwise direction (views from east to west)
around the filament axis. This rolling motion appears to start from the border
of the active region, then propagates towards the east. AIA observes another
type of rotating motion: in some other parts of the erupting quiescent
prominence the vertical threads turn horizontal, then turn upside down. The
elevated active region filament does not erupt until 18:00 UT, when the
erupting quiescent filament already reaches a very large height. We develop two
simplified three-dimensional models which qualitatively reproduce the observed
rolling and rotating motions. The prominence in the models is assumed to
consist of a collection of discrete blobs that are tied to particular field
lines of a helical flux rope. The observed rolling motion is reproduced by
continuous twist injection into the flux rope in Model 1 from the active region
side. Asymmetric reconnection induced by the asymmetric distribution of the
magnetic fields on the two sides of the filament may cause the observed rolling
motion. The rotating motion of the prominence threads observed by AIA is
consistent with the removal of the field line dips in Model 2 from the top down
during the eruption.

Domain walls in U(N) gauge theories, coupled to Higgs scalar fields with
degenerate masses, are shown to possess normalizable non-Abelian
Nambu-Goldstone(NG) modes, which we call non-Abelian clouds. We construct the
moduli space metric and its Kahler potential of the effective field theory on
the domain walls, by focusing on two models: a U(1) gauge theory with several
charged Higgs fields, and a U(N) gauge theory with 2N Higgs fields in the
fundamental representation. We find that non-Abelian clouds spread between two
domain walls and that their rotation induces long-range repulsive force, in
contrast to a U(1) mode in models with fully non-degenerate masses which gives
short-range force. We also construct a bound state of dyonic domain walls by
introducing the imaginary part of the Higgs masses. In the latter model we find
that when all walls coincide SU(N)_L x SU(N)_R x U(1) symmetry is broken down
to SU(N)_V, and U(N)_A NG modes and the same number of quasi-NG modes are
localized on the wall. When n walls separate, off diagonal elements of U(n) NG
modes have wave functions spreading between two separated walls (non-Abelian
clouds), whereas some quasi-NG modes turn to NG bosons as a result of further
symmetry breaking U(n)_V --> U(1)_V^n. In the case of 4+1 dimensional bulk, we
can dualize the effective theory to the supersymmetric Freedman-Townsend model
of non-Abelian 2-form fields.

A sparse precision matrix can be directly translated into a sparse Gaussian
graphical model under the assumption that the data follow a joint normal
distribution. This neat property makes high-dimensional precision matrix
estimation very appealing in many applications. However, in practice we often
face nonnormal data, and variable transformation is often used to achieve
normality. In this paper we consider the nonparanormal model that assumes that
the variables follow a joint normal distribution after a set of unknown
monotone transformations. The nonparanormal model is much more flexible than
the normal model while retaining the good interpretability of the latter in
that each zero entry in the sparse precision matrix of the nonparanormal model
corresponds to a pair of conditionally independent variables. In this paper we
show that the nonparanormal graphical model can be efficiently estimated by
using a rank-based estimation scheme which does not require estimating these
unknown transformation functions. In particular, we study the rank-based
graphical lasso, the rank-based neighborhood Dantzig selector and the
rank-based CLIME. We establish their theoretical properties in the setting
where the dimension is nearly exponentially large relative to the sample size.
It is shown that the proposed rank-based estimators work as well as their
oracle counterparts defined with the oracle data. Furthermore, the theory
motivates us to consider the adaptive version of the rank-based neighborhood
Dantzig selector and the rank-based CLIME that are shown to enjoy graphical
model selection consistency without assuming the irrepresentable condition for
the oracle and rank-based graphical lasso. Simulated and real data are used to
demonstrate the finite performance of the rank-based estimators.
label: human

text: The abstract for the research paper focusing on the properties of galaxies within the central surface brightness gap is as follows  This study investigates the characteristics of galaxies located within the central surface brightness gap (CSBG), which is a region characterized by a sharp drop in stellar density between the bulge and the disk of spiral galaxies. Utilizing a sample of galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), the research employs photometric data to analyze the surface brightness profiles of these galaxies. The primary objective is to explore the relationship between the CSBG and various galaxy properties such as morphology, star formation rate (SFR), and stellar mass.  Methodologically, the study involves fitting photometric models to the observed surface brightness profiles using Bayesian inference techniques. This approach allows for robust estimation of the galaxy's structural parameters, including the Sérsic index, which characterizes the light distribution. Additionally, the SFR is estimated through the Balmer decrement method, while stellar masses are inferred from the Sérsic profile parameters.  Key findings indicate that galaxies with significant CSBGs tend to have lower stellar masses compared to those without, suggesting a possible link between the presence of the CSBG and the cessation of star formation. Furthermore, there is a trend showing that galaxies with more extended CSBGs exhibit higher SFRs, indicating regions of ongoing star formation within the disk despite the overall decrease in surface brightness.  The results highlight the importance of the CSBG as a marker for understanding the complex processes involved in galaxy evolution, particularly the interplay between stellar mass assembly and star formation activity. The findings contribute to our comprehension of how galaxies transition from star-forming to quiescent phases, thereby advancing our knowledge of galaxy formation and evolution.

text: Coherent synchrotron radiation (CSR) plays a significant role in the dynamics of charged particle beams, particularly in the context of resistive wall heating in rectangular chambers. This paper aims to present an efficient computational method for modeling CSR within these confined geometries, addressing the challenges posed by the complex interactions between the beam and the chamber walls. We employed a hybrid numerical approach that combines analytical techniques and numerical simulations to enhance the accuracy and speed of CSR calculations. Specifically, we developed a novel algorithm that efficiently resolves the electromagnetic fields generated by the charged particles, taking into account the specific boundary conditions of rectangular chambers. Our results demonstrate a marked improvement in computational efficiency over traditional methods, enabling rapid assessment of CSR impacts on resistive wall heating. Key findings indicate that the intensity of CSR significantly increases with beam density and is influenced by the geometric parameters of the chamber. Moreover, the implications of these findings suggest a potential revision of design criteria for particle accelerators to mitigate resistive wall heating effects. In conclusion, our method not only streamlines the computation of CSR in rectangular chambers but also contributes valuable insights into the electromagnetic phenomena affecting high-energy particle beams, thereby advancing the understanding and optimization of particle accelerator design.

We give a new characterization of the class ${\bf N}^0_{\mathfrak M}[-1,1]$
of the operator-valued in the Hilbert space ${\mathfrak M}$ Nevanlinna
functions that admit representations as compressed resolvents ($m$-functions)
of selfadjoint contractions. We consider the automorphism ${\bf \Gamma}:$
$M(\lambda){\mapsto}M_{{\bf
\Gamma}}(\lambda):=\left((\lambda^2-1)M(\lambda)\right)^{-1}$ of the class
${\bf N}^0_{\mathfrak M}[-1,1]$ and construct a realization of $M_{{\bf
\Gamma}}(\lambda)$ as a compressed resolvent. The unique fixed point of
${\bf\Gamma}$ is the $m$-function of the block-operator Jacobi matrix related
to the Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind. We study a transformation
${\bf\widehat \Gamma}:$ ${\mathcal M}(\lambda)\mapsto {\mathcal
M}_{{\bf\widehat \Gamma}}(\lambda) :=-({\mathcal M}(\lambda)+\lambda
I_{\mathfrak M})^{-1}$ that maps the set of all Nevanlinna operator-valued
functions into its subset. The unique fixed point $\mathcal M_0$ of
${\bf\widehat\Gamma}$ admits a realization as the compressed resolvent of the
"free" discrete Schr\"{o}dinger operator ${\bf\widehat J}_0$ in the Hilbert
space ${\bf H}_0=\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)\bigotimes{\mathfrak M}$. We prove that
${\mathcal M}_0$ is the uniform limit on compact sets of the open upper/lower
half-plane in the operator norm topology of the iterations $\{{\mathcal
M}_{n+1}(\lambda)=-({\mathcal M}_n(\lambda)+\lambda I_\mathfrak M)^{-1}\}$ of
${\bf\widehat\Gamma}$. We show that the pair $\{{\bf H}_0,{\bf \widehat J}_0\}$
is the inductive limit of the sequence of realizations $\{\widehat{\mathfrak
H}_n,\widehat A_n\}$ of $\{{\mathcal M}_n\}$. In the scalar case $({\mathfrak
M}={\mathbb C})$, applying the algorithm of I.S.~Kac, a realization of iterates
$\{{\mathcal M}_n\}$ as $m$-functions of canonical (Hamiltonian) systems is
constructed.

text: In this study, we present iWinRNFL, a novel and intuitive model designed to estimate in-game win probabilities for National Football League (NFL) games. Our primary objective is to provide analysts and enthusiasts with a tool that not only produces accurate predictions but also offers interpretability and calibration throughout the game. We formulated the model using a comprehensive dataset that includes various game-related metrics, team performance statistics, and situational variables.   We implemented a logistic regression framework enriched by feature engineering, allowing for the identification of key indicators that influence the likelihood of a team's success at any given moment during the game. To enhance the model's calibration, we employed isotonic regression, ensuring that the predicted probabilities align closely with actual event outcomes.   Our results demonstrate that iWinRNFL significantly outperforms existing models in terms of predictive accuracy, evidenced by its higher area under the curve (AUC) in receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Additionally, the model's interpretability provides stakeholders with insights into how specific game situations impact win probabilities.   By integrating our findings into user-friendly visualizations, we facilitate the application of the model in real-time game analysis. Overall, iWinRNFL addresses the gap in accessible, reliable win probability modeling in NFL, offering a recalibrated approach that enhances strategic decision-making for teams and engagement for fans alike.
label: machine

Simplified silica (Zeosil 1165 MP) and SBR (140k carrying silanol end-groups)
nanocomposites have been formulated by mixing of a reduced number of
ingredients with respect to industrial applications. The thermo-mechanical
history of the samples during the mixing process was monitored and adjusted to
identical final temperatures. The filler structure on large scales up to
micrometers was studied by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and very
small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS). A complete quantitative model extending
from the primary silica nanoparticle (of radius \approx 10 nm), to
nanoparticles aggregates, up to micrometer-sized branches with typical lateral
dimension of 150 nm is proposed. Image analysis of the TEM-pictures yields the
fraction of zones of pure polymer, which extend between the branches of a
large-scale filler network. This network is compatible with a fractal of
average dimension 2.4 as measured by scattering. On smaller length scales,
inside the branches, small silica aggregates are present. Their average radius
has been deduced from a Kratky analysis, and it ranges between 35 and 40 nm for
all silica fractions investigated here (\phi_si = 8-21% vol.). A central piece
of our analysis is the description of the interaggregate interaction by a
simulated structure factor for polydisperse spheres representing aggregates. A
polydispersity of 30% in aggregate size is assumed, and interactions between
these aggregates are described with a hard core repulsive potential. The same
distribution in size is used to evaluate the polydisperse form factor.
Comparison with the experimental intensity leads to the determination of the
average aggregate compacity (assumed identical for all aggregates in the
distribution, between 31% and 38% depending on \phi_si), and thus aggregation
number (ca. 45, with a large spread). Because of the effect of aggregate
compacity and of pure polymer zones, the volume fraction of aggregates is
higher in the branches than \phi_si. The repulsion between aggregates has a
strong effect on the apparent isothermal compressibility: it leads to a
characteristic low-q depression, which cannot be interpreted as aggregate mass
decrease in our data. In addition, the reinforcement effect of these silica
structures in the SBR-matrix is characterized with oscillatory shear and
described with a model based on the same aggregate compacity. Finally, our
results show that it is possible to analyze the complex structure of
interacting aggregates in nanocomposites of industrial origin in a
self-consistent and quantitative manner.

text: We present our findings from the first high-resolution radio study of the Supernova Remnant (SNR) G338.3-0.0 associated with the gamma-ray source HESS J1640-465. Our work aims to investigate the morphology and spectral characteristics of this SNR to better understand its nature and origin. By utilizing high-resolution radio observations from the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) at 2.1 GHz, we were able to discern detailed structures within the SNR, revealing intricate features such as shell-like structures and possible interactions with the surrounding medium. Our analysis of the radio spectral index distribution provides insights into the physical processes, such as synchrotron radiation, occurring within the SNR. Additionally, by comparing our radio data with existing multi-wavelength observations, including X-ray and gamma-ray data, we aim to gain a comprehensive understanding of the overall properties and emission mechanisms of this intriguing astrophysical object. Our study employs advanced radio imaging techniques and spectral analysis methods to elucidate the complex morphology and emission properties of SNR G338.3-0.0, offering valuable insights into the connection between supernova remnants and associated gamma-ray sources.

The Kepler light curves used to detect thousands of planetary candidates are
susceptible to dilution due to blending with previously unknown nearby stars.
With the automated laser adaptive optics instrument, Robo-AO, we have observed
620 nearby stars around 3857 planetary candidates host stars. Many of the
nearby stars, however, are not bound to the KOI. In this paper, we quantify the
association probability between each KOI and detected nearby stars through
several methods. Galactic stellar models and the observed stellar density are
used to estimate the number and properties of unbound stars. We estimate the
spectral type and distance to 145 KOIs with nearby stars using multi-band
observations from Robo-AO and Keck-AO. We find most nearby stars within 1" of a
Kepler planetary candidate are likely bound, in agreement with past studies. We
use likely bound stars as well as the precise stellar parameters from the
California Kepler Survey to search for correlations between stellar binarity
and planetary properties. No significant difference between the binarity
fraction of single and multiple planet systems is found, and planet hosting
stars follow similar binarity trends as field stars, many of which likely host
their own non-aligned planets. We find that hot Jupiters are ~4x more likely
than other planets to reside in a binary star system. We correct the radius
estimates of the planet candidates in characterized systems and find that for
likely bound systems, the estimated planetary candidate radii will increase on
average by a factor of 1.77, if either star is equally likely to host the
planet. We find that the planetary radius gap is robust to the impact of
dilution, and find an intriguing 95%-confidence discrepancy between the radius
distribution of small planets in single and binary systems.

We present ground-based optical and near infrared photometric observations
and Hubble Space Telescope COS spectroscopic observations of the old nova V842
Cen (Nova Cen 1986). Analysis of the optical light curves reveals a peak at
56.5 +/- 0.3s with an amplitude of 8.9 +/- 4.2 mma, which is consistent with
the rotation of a magnetic white dwarf primary in V842 Cen that was detected
earlier by Woudt et al., and led to its classification as an intermediate
polar.However, our UV lightcurve created from the COS time-tag spectra does not
show this periodicity. Our synthetic spectral analysis of an HST COS spectrum
rules out a hot white dwarf photosphere as the source of the FUV flux. The
best-fitting model to the COS spectrum is a full optically thick accretion disk
with no magnetic truncation, a low disk inclination angle, low accretion rate
and a distance less than half the published distance that was determined on the
basis of interstellar sodium D line strengths.Truncated accretion disks with
truncation radii of 3Rwd and 5Rwd yielded unsatisfactory agreement with the COS
data. The accretion rate is unexpectedly low for a classical nova only 24 years
after the explosion when the accretion rate is expected to be high and the
white dwarf should still be very hot, especially if irradiation of the donor
star took place. Our low accretion rate is consistent with low accretion rates
derived from X-ray and ground-based optical data.

Planets are thought to form in the gas and dust disks around young stars. In
particular, it has been proposed that giant planets can form through the
gravitational instability of massive extended disks around intermediate-mass
stars. However, we still lack direct observations to constrain this mechanism.
We have spatially resolved the 8.6 and 11.2 $\mu$m emission of a massive
protoplanetary disk seen edge on around an A star, Gomez's Hamburger (GoHam),
using VISIR at the Very Large Telescope. A compact region situated at a
projected distance of $350\pm50$ AU south of the central star is found to have
a reduced emission.This asymmetry is fully consistent with the presence of a
cold density structure, or clump, identified in earlier CO observations, and we
derive physical characteristics consistent with those observations: a mass of
0.8-11.4 Jupiter masses (for a dust-to-gas mass ratio of 0.01), a radius of
about 10$^2$ astronomical units, and a local density of about $10^{7}$
cm$^{-3}$. Based on this evidence, we argue that this clump, which we call
GoHam b, is a promising candidate for a young protoplanet formed by
gravitational instability that might be representative of the precursors of
massive planets observed around A stars, such as HR 8799 or Beta pictoris. More
detailed studies at high angular resolution are needed to better constrain the
physical properties of this object to confirm this proposal.

text: The Smooth-Lasso and other $\ell_1+\ell_2$-penalized methods have garnered significant attention in recent years for their ability to efficiently handle high-dimensional data and provide sparse solutions. This class of methods combines the strengths of the Lasso and Ridge regression by adding an $\ell_2$ penalty term to the $\ell_1$ penalty term used in the Lasso, resulting in a single optimization problem that balances the two competing objectives. The Smooth-Lasso method, in particular, has been shown to outperform traditional Lasso methods in certain scenarios by incorporating a smoothness penalty term, which encourages the estimator to be smooth and continuous.  The objective of this research is to investigate the performance of the Smooth-Lasso method and other $\ell_1+\ell_2$-penalized methods in the context of high-dimensional data analysis. A comprehensive review of existing literature on $\ell_1+\ell_2$-penalized methods reveals that these methods have been successfully applied in various fields, including machine learning, signal processing, and image analysis. However, the choice of regularization parameters and the selection of optimal features remain open problems.  This study employs a simulation-based approach to evaluate the performance of the Smooth-Lasso method and other $\ell_1+\ell_2$-penalized methods on high-dimensional datasets. The results show that these methods can effectively handle high-dimensional data and provide sparse solutions, but the choice of regularization parameters can significantly impact the performance. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of feature selection in improving the accuracy of $\ell_1+\ell_2$-penalized methods. The findings of this research contribute to the existing literature on $\ell_1+\ell_2$-penalized methods and provide insights into the optimal choice of regularization parameters and feature selection strategies for these methods.

text: This study delves into the intricate radiation mechanisms and physical properties of GeV-TeV BL Lac objects. Through a comprehensive examination of high-energy astrophysical phenomena, we aim to unravel the enigmatic nature of these objects. We present an analysis of observational data obtained from various telescopes and satellites, shedding light on the emission processes taking place within these extreme environments.  Our research focuses on understanding the mechanisms responsible for the production of gamma-ray radiation in GeV-TeV BL Lac objects. By integrating theoretical models with observational data, we have identified key physical properties influencing the emission characteristics of these objects. Through detailed spectral analysis and modeling techniques, we have elucidated the role of magnetic fields, particle acceleration mechanisms, and relativistic beaming effects in shaping the observed high-energy spectra.  The significance of this study lies in advancing our knowledge of the fundamental astrophysical processes governing the behavior of GeV-TeV BL Lac objects. The insights gained from this research provide valuable contributions to the field of high-energy astrophysics and aid in elucidating the complex relationships between the physical properties and radiation mechanisms of these enigmatic objects.

The magnetic structure in the Galactic disk, the Galactic center and the
Galactic halo can be delineated more clearly than ever before. In the Galactic
disk, the magnetic structure has been revealed by starlight polarization within
2 or 3 kpc of the Solar vicinity, by the distribution of the Zeeman splitting
of OH masers in two or three nearby spiral arms, and by pulsar dispersion
measures and rotation measures in nearly half of the disk. The polarized
thermal dust emission of clouds at infrared, mm and submm wavelengths and the
diffuse synchrotron emission are also related to the large-scale magnetic field
in the disk. The rotation measures of extragalactic radio sources at low
Galactic latitudes can be modeled by electron distributions and large-scale
magnetic fields. The statistical properties of the magnetized interstellar
medium at various scales have been studied using rotation measure data and
polarization data. In the Galactic center, the non-thermal filaments indicate
poloidal fields. There is no consensus on the field strength, maybe mG, maybe
tens of uG. The polarized dust emission and much enhanced rotation measures of
background radio sources are probably related to toroidal fields. In the
Galactic halo, the antisymmetric RM sky reveals large-scale toroidal fields
with reversed directions above and below the Galactic plane. Magnetic fields
from all parts of our Galaxy are connected to form a global field structure.
More observations are needed to explore the untouched regions and delineate how
fields in different parts are connected.

The decoherence of a two-state tunneling molecule, such as a chiral molecule
or ammonia, due to collisions with a buffer gas is analyzed in terms of a
succession of quantum states of the molecule satisfying the conditions for a
consistent family of histories. With $\hbar \omega$ the separation in energy of
the levels in the isolated molecule and $\gamma$ a decoherence rate
proportional to the rate of collisions, we find for $\gamma \gg \omega$ (strong
decoherence) a consistent family in which the molecule flips randomly back and
forth between the left- and right-handed chiral states in a stationary Markov
process. For $\gamma < \omega$ there is a family in which the molecule
oscillates continuously between the different chiral states, but with
occasional random changes of phase, at a frequency that goes to zero at a phase
transition $\gamma = \omega$. This transition is similar to the behavior of the
inversion frequency of ammonia with increasing pressure, but will be difficult
to observe in chiral molecules such as D$_2$S$_2$. There are additional
consistent families both for $\gamma > \omega$ and for $\gamma < \omega$. In
addition we relate the speed with which chiral information is transferred to
the environment to the rate of decrease of complementary types of information
(e.g., parity information) remaining in the molecule itself.

Distributed adaptive signal processing has attracted much attention in the
recent decade owing to its effectiveness in many decentralized real-time
applications in networked systems. Because many natural signals are highly
sparse with most entries equal to zero, several decentralized sparse adaptive
algorithms have been proposed recently. Most of them is focused on the single
task estimation problems, in which all nodes receive data associated with the
same unknown vector and collaborate to estimate it. However, many applications
are inherently multitask oriented and each node has its own unknown vector
different from others'. The related multitask estimation problem benefits from
collaborations among the nodes as neighbor nodes usually share analogous
properties and thus similar unknown vectors. In this work, we study the
distributed sparse multitask recursive least squares (RLS) problem over
networks. We first propose a decentralized online alternating direction method
of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm for the formulated RLS problem. The algorithm
is simplified for easy implementation with closed-form computations in each
iteration and low storage requirements. Moreover, to further reduce the
complexity, we present a decentralized online subgradient method with low
computational overhead. We theoretically analyze the convergence behavior of
the proposed subgradient method and derive an error bound related to the
network topology and algorithm parameters. The effectiveness of the proposed
algorithms is corroborated by numerical simulations and an accuracy-complexity
tradeoff between the proposed two algorithms is highlighted.
label: human

text: We investigated the origins and evolution of fundamental molecules of life, specifically pigments, that have adapted to dissipate the solar spectrum. Through a comprehensive analysis of fossil records, biochemical pathways, and spectroscopic studies, we identified a critical transition in the history of life on Earth. Our research revealed that the emergence of photosynthetic pigments, such as chlorophyll and carotenoids, was a pivotal event in the evolution of life, enabling organisms to harness solar energy and sustain metabolic processes.   We found that the development of these pigments was a gradual process, with early organisms exhibiting simple, non-specific chromophores that gradually evolved into more complex, light-harvesting molecules. Our biochemical analysis of fossilized pigments and modern organisms revealed a common ancestor of photosynthetic pigments, highlighting the shared evolutionary history of these molecules.   We also discovered that the evolution of pigments was closely tied to the development of photosynthetic pathways, with the emergence of chlorophyll a being a key innovation that enabled the efficient capture of solar energy. Our spectroscopic studies confirmed that the unique absorption spectra of these pigments are responsible for their ability to dissipate the solar spectrum, allowing organisms to thrive in diverse environments. By elucidating the origins and evolution of fundamental molecules of life, we have shed new light on the complex interplay between light, energy, and life on Earth.
label: machine

text: In the study of binary star systems, wind accretion plays a crucial role in the formation and evolution of circumstellar discs. Traditional models often underestimate the size of these discs by neglecting the influence of the wind-driving force. This research investigates how incorporating the wind-driving force affects the estimation of disc sizes in binary systems. Utilizing hydrodynamic simulations, we modeled various scenarios of wind accretion, comparing configurations with and without the influence of the wind-driving force. Our simulations revealed that when the wind-driving force is accounted for, the resultant accretion discs are significantly larger, with sizes increasing by 15% to 30% compared to models that overlook this force. We systematically varied parameters such as wind velocity, binary separation, and mass transfer rates to determine their impact on the accretion process. These comprehensive simulations highlight the critical need to include the wind-driving force in models to better approximate disc dimensions. Our findings suggest that the omission of wind-driving dynamics leads to substantial underestimation of disc size, which can have profound implications for understanding the angular momentum distribution and subsequent evolutionary processes in binary systems. This research underscores the importance of refining current theoretical models to incorporate the physics of wind-driving forces, offering a more accurate depiction of disc formation mechanisms. Consequently, this refinement enhances predictions regarding the dynamics of mass transfer and the lifecycle of binary systems, providing insights that are essential for advancing our comprehension of stellar evolution.
label: machine

text: M81, a nearby spiral galaxy, is known for its large nuclear bar and central star cluster. However, an intriguing feature of M81 is the absence of a thin disc, unlike its massive companion M31 and other spiral galaxies. Previous studies suggested the presence of a thick disc in M81, but recent observations with the Hubble Space Telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array challenge this notion. This study aims to investigate the structure and composition of the M81 disc using data from multi-wavelength observations. The data includes optical and near-infrared images, ultraviolet emission, and far-infrared dust emission.  The analysis of the multi-wavelength data reveals that M81 exhibits a truncated thin disc and an extended thick disc. The truncated thin disc, which can be explained by tidal interactions with M32 and NGC 3077, has a radius of about 3.6 kpc and a scale height of 160 pc. The extended thick disc extends up to 12 kpc and has a scale height of 370 pc. The thin disc's truncation also affects the distribution of star formation activity in M81, resulting in a 'donut-like' structure of star formation.  These findings have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution. The absence of a thick disc in M81 challenges the common assumption that thick discs are ubiquitous in spiral galaxies. This study emphasizes the importance of considering galaxy interactions in shaping the structural and dynamical properties of disc galaxies. Further investigations are required to explore the origin and evolution of the thin and thick discs in M81 and their implications for galaxy evolution in general.
label: machine

text: We investigated the interplay between leanness and flexibility in distributed software development, a phenomenon largely understudied in the field. Our study sought to address the pressing problem of maintaining agility and adaptability in distributed teams, where communication and collaboration across geographical distances are hindered.   We conducted a mixed-methods analysis, combining both qualitative and quantitative data from a survey of 120 distributed software development teams and in-depth interviews with 30 team leaders and developers. Our results revealed a significant positive correlation between leanness (measured by codebase size, complexity, and maintainability) and flexibility (measured by adaptability, responsiveness, and innovation capacity).   We identified three key factors that contributed to this correlation (1) reduced technical debt, (2) improved communication and collaboration, and (3) increased trust and shared understanding among team members. Our findings also highlighted the importance of continuous learning and upskilling in distributed teams, as well as the need for flexible and adaptable project management practices.   Our study contributes to the existing literature on software development by providing empirical evidence for the benefits of leanness and flexibility in distributed teams. We propose a framework for implementing these principles in practice, which includes strategies for reducing technical debt, fostering communication and collaboration, and cultivating a culture of continuous learning and innovation.
label: machine

text: We investigated the large-scale structure within the Chamaeleon dark clouds, a region of intense star formation in the southern hemisphere, using archival data from the Herschel Space Observatory. Our primary objective was to assess the potential for Herschel's observations to reveal the underlying large-scale structure of this region. Through a systematic analysis of the cloud's morphology and the distribution of Herschel's key spectral lines, we identified a complex network of filaments and voids that underpin the cloud's structure. Notably, we detected a pronounced asymmetry in the cloud's morphology, with the southern region exhibiting a more pronounced concentration of molecular gas. This asymmetry is thought to be driven by the interaction between the cloud and the surrounding interstellar medium. Our results suggest that Herschel's observations are capable of capturing the large-scale structure of the Chamaeleon dark clouds, providing valuable insights into the cloud's evolution and the processes that govern its dynamics. By integrating Herschel data with other observational and theoretical frameworks, we aim to better understand the complex interplay between the cloud's internal dynamics and its large-scale environment, shedding new light on the formation and evolution of molecular clouds in the early universe.

Thin, magnetically aligned striations of relatively moderate contrast with
the background are commonly observed in both atomic and molecular clouds. They
are also prominent in MHD simulations with turbulent converging shocks. The
simulated striations develop within a dense, stagnated sheet in the mid plane
of the post-shock region where magnetically-induced converging flows collide.
We show analytically that the secondary flows are an inevitable consequence of
the jump conditions of oblique MHD shocks. They produce the stagnated,
sheet-like sub-layer through a secondary shock when, roughly speaking, the
Alfv\'enic speed in the primary converging flows is supersonic, a condition
that is relatively easy to satisfy in interstellar clouds. The dense sub-layer
is naturally threaded by a strong magnetic field that lies close to the plane
of the sub-layer. The substantial magnetic field makes the sheet highly
anisotropic, which is the key to the striation formation. Specifically,
perturbations of the primary inflow that vary spatially perpendicular to the
magnetic field can easily roll up the sheet around the field lines without
bending them, creating corrugations that appear as magnetically-aligned
striations in column density maps. On the other hand, perturbations that vary
spatially along the field lines curve the sub-layer and alter its orientation
relative to the magnetic field locally, seeding special locations that become
slanted overdense filaments and prestellar cores through enhanced mass
accumulation along field lines. In our scenario, the dense sub-layer unique to
magnetized oblique shocks is the birthplace for both magnetically-aligned
diffuse striations and massive star-forming structures.
label: human

text: In this study, we investigate the efficacy of utilizing data augmentation techniques as a substitute for explicit regularization methods in machine learning tasks. Our research aims to address the challenge of enhancing model generalization and robustness without relying on traditional regularization approaches such as L1 or L2 penalties. Through extensive experimentation on diverse datasets, we demonstrate that data augmentation can serve as a powerful tool to improve model performance by artificially expanding the training set and injecting noise into the learning process. Our results indicate that data augmentation not only aids in preventing overfitting but also encourages the model to learn invariant representations from augmented data, consequently boosting its ability to generalize well on unseen samples. We showcase the superiority of data augmentation over typical regularization methods in various tasks, including image classification and natural language processing, underscoring its versatility and effectiveness across different domains. By leveraging augmentation strategies like random cropping, flipping, and adding noise, we showcase a paradigm shift towards a regularization-free approach that can lead to significant performance gains in machine learning models. Our findings offer insights into the potential of data augmentation as a primary means for enhancing model generalization in the absence of explicit regularization, paving the way for more efficient and robust learning techniques in the field of machine learning.
label: machine

text: In this study, we investigate the dynamics of an Epidemic Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered (SIR) model on a face-to-face interaction network with the introduction of new mobility-induced phase transitions. Our research aims to address the limitations of traditional SIR models by incorporating a network structure that reflects realistic human interactions. Through extensive simulations and analytical calculations, we identify novel phase transitions induced by mobility patterns within the population. Our results reveal that varying mobility parameters can significantly impact the spread of infectious diseases, leading to transitions between different epidemic regimes. By integrating mobility data into the SIR model, we contribute to a better understanding of epidemic dynamics in real-world scenarios. We introduce a methodology that combines network theory, epidemiology, and statistical physics to analyze the effects of mobility on disease transmission. The insights gained from this research have implications for public health policies and strategies for controlling the spread of infectious diseases. Our work provides a foundation for further studies on complex contagion processes in networked populations, emphasizing the importance of considering mobility patterns in epidemic modeling.
label: machine

We have studied the distribution patterns of lateral density, arrival time
and angular position of Cherenkov photons generated in Extensive Air Showers
(EASs) initiated by $\gamma$-ray, proton and iron primaries incident with
various energies and at various zenith angles. This study is the extension of
our earlier work \cite{Hazarika} to cover a wide energy range of ground based
$\gamma$-ray astronomy with a wide range of zenith angles ($\le 40^\circ$) of
primary particles, as well as the extension to study the angular distribution
patterns of Cherenkov photons in EASs. This type of study is important for
distinguishing the $\gamma$-ray initiated showers from the hadronic showers in
the ground based $\gamma$-ray astronomy, where Atmospheric Cherenkov Technique
(ACT) is being used. Importantly, such study gives an insight on the nature of
$\gamma$-ray and hadronic showers in general. In this work, the CORSIKA 6.990
simulation code is used for generation of EASs. Similarly to the case of
Ref.\cite{Hazarika}, this study also revealed that, the lateral density and
arrival time distributions of Cherenkov photons vary almost in accordance with
the functions: $\rho_{ch}(r) = \rho_{0}\;e^{-\beta r}$ and $t_{ch}(r) =
t_{0}e^{\Gamma/r^{\lambda}}$ respectively by taking different values of the
parameters of functions for the type, energy and zenith angle of the primary
particle. The distribution of Cherenkov photon's angular positions with respect
to shower axis shows distinctive features depending on the primary type, its
energy and the zenith angle.

text: In this study, we address the measurement problem in quantum mechanics by adopting a pedestrian approach that emphasizes intuitive understanding over complex mathematical frameworks. Our primary objective is to elucidate the conceptual underpinnings of quantum measurement while critically analyzing the implications of different interpretations. We systematically explore key ideas such as the role of the observer, the collapse of the wave function, and the classical-quantum boundary, utilizing both qualitative and quantitative methodologies. Through a series of thought experiments, we illustrate the paradoxes associated with traditional interpretations, including epistemic and ontological perspectives.  Our results reveal that adopting a straightforward conceptual framework allows for a clearer comprehension of the measurement process, which, we assert, is often obscured by technical jargon and formalism. By emphasizing a dialogue between classical intuitions and quantum phenomena, we facilitate a more accessible discourse among scholars and the broader educational community. We propose that a reevaluation of the measurement problem—which has been a longstanding contention in the field—can lead to novel insights and prompt new research avenues. Our findings indicate that fostering an intuitive grasp of quantum concepts may not only serve pedagogical purposes but may also contribute to advancements in theoretical approaches to quantum measurement. We conclude that a pedestrian methodology can effectively bridge gaps in understanding and incite renewed interest in the foundational questions that continue to challenge physicists today.
label: machine

Max-point-tolerance graphs (MPTG) were studied by Catanzaro et al. in 2017
and the same class of graphs were introduced in the name of p-BOX(1) graphs by
Soto and Caro in 2015. In our paper we consider central-max-point tolerance
graphs (central MPTG) by taking the points of MPTG as center points of their
corresponding intervals. In course of study on this class of graphs we show
that the class of central MPTG is same as the class of unit max-tolerance
graphs. We prove the class of unit central max-point tolerance graphs is same
as that of proper central max-point tolerance graphs and both of them are
equivalent to the class of proper interval graphs. Next we introduce 50%
max-tolerance graphs and separate this class from unit max-tolerance graph
whereas for min-tolerance graphs 50% and unit denote the same graph class.
  Interval catch digraphs (ICD) was introduced by Maehera in 1984. In his
introducing paper Maehera proposed a conjecture for the characterization of
central interval catch digraph (central ICD) in terms of forbidden subdigraphs.
In this paper, we disprove the conjecture by showing counter examples. We find
close relation between a central MPTG and a central ICD. Also we characterize
this digraph by defining a suitable mapping from the vertex set to the real
line. Next we study oriented interval catch digraphs (oriented ICD). We
characterize augmented adjacency matrix of an oriented ICD when it is a
tournament. Also we characterize an oriented ICD whose underlying graph is a
tree. Further we obtain characterization of the adjacency matrix of a proper
interval catch digraph. Another important result is to provide forbidden
subdigraph characterization of those proper oriented interval catch digraphs
whose underlying undirected graph is chordal. In last section we discuss
relationships between these classes of graphs and digraphs.
label: human

text: We investigate the frontiers of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) to advance our understanding of strong interactions among quarks and gluons, the fundamental constituents of matter. Our primary objective is to elucidate the complexities underlying the confinement phenomenon and the emergence of mass in hadronic systems. We employ a multifaceted methodology that integrates lattice QCD simulations, perturbative techniques, and experimental data from high-energy collisions at particle accelerators. Through our comprehensive analysis, we derive new insights into the scaling behavior of parton distribution functions, facilitating a deeper comprehension of thebehavior of quarks under extreme conditions. Our results reveal significant deviations from classical expectations, particularly concerning the role of gluon dynamics in the non-perturbative regime. Furthermore, we explore the implications of color charge interactions in generating effective mass through dynamical symmetry breaking, highlighting the intricate relationship between confinement and mass generation. We also address the challenges posed by the computational intensity of lattice calculations, proposing innovative algorithmic enhancements that leverage recent advancements in quantum computing. This work not only contributes to a more profound theoretical framework but also sets the stage for future experimental validations, potentially guiding the search for novel states of matter in high-energy physics. The origin of the similary-sized binary asteroid (90) Antiope remains an
unsolved puzzle. To constrain the origin of this unique double system, we
recorded individual spectra of the components using SPIFFI, a near-infrared
integral field spectrograph fed by SINFONI, an adaptive optics module available
on VLT-UT4. Using our previously published orbital model, we requested
telescope time when the separation of the components of (90) Antiope was larger
than 0.087", to minimize the contamination between components, during the
February 2009 opposition. Several multi-spectral data-cubes in J band (SNR=40)
and H+K band (SNR=100) were recorded in three epochs and revealed the two
components of (90) Antiope. After developing a specific photometric extraction
method and running an error analysis by Monte-Carlo simulations, we
successfully extracted reliable spectra of both components from 1.1 to 2.4 um
taken on the night of February 21, 2009. These spectra do not display any
significant absorption features due to mafic mineral, ices, or organics, and
their slopes are in agreement with both components being C- or Cb- type
asteroids. Their constant flux ratio indicates that both components' surface
reflectances are quite similar, with a 1-sigma variation of 7%. By comparison
with 2MASS J, H, K color distribution of observed Themis family members, we
conclude that both bodies were most likely formed at the same time and from the
same material. The similarly-sized system could indeed be the result of the
breakup of a rubble-pile proto-Antiope into two equal-sized bodies, but other
scenarios of formation implying a common origin should also be considered.

The X-ray source 4U1820-30 in the globular cluster NGC 6624 is known as the
most compact binary among the identified X-ray binaries. Having an orbital
period of 685.0 s, the source consists of a neutron star primary and likely
0.06--0.08 Msun white dwarf secondary. Here we report on far-ultraviolet (FUV)
observations of this X-ray binary, made with the Space Telescope Imaging
Spectrograph on board the Hubble Space Telescope. From our Fourier spectral
analysis of the FUV timing data, we obtain a period of 693.5+/-1.3 s, which is
significantly different from the orbital period. The light curve folded at this
period can be described by a sinusoid, with a fractional semiamplitude of 6.3%
and the phase zero (maximum of the sinusoid) at MJD 50886.015384+/-0.000043
(TDB). While the discovered FUV period may be consistent with a hierarchical
triple system model that was previously considered for 4U 1820-30, we suggest
that it could instead be the indication of superhump modulation, which arises
from an eccentric accretion disk in the binary. The X-ray and FUV periods would
be the orbital and superhump periods, respectively, indicating a 1% superhump
excess and a white-dwarf/neutron-star mass ratio around 0.06. Considering 4U
1820-30 as a superhump source, we discuss the implications.
